title: USE-AFTER-FREE under codegen: a RECURSIVE function taking an OWNED `String` parameter whose argument is an ELEMENT of a `Vec[String]` obtained from a `Map[String, Vec[String]]`, where the parameter is USED AFTER the recursive descent, reads freed String buffers. `karac build` prints garbage bytes for the affected elements; `karac run` (LLJIT) aborts inside `karac_string_clone` with a `ptr::copy_nonoverlapping` unaligned/non-null precondition violation. The tree-walk interpreter is CORRECT, so this is also a run-vs-build divergence. Silent data corruption (no crash) under AOT build makes it high severity.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced authoring LeetCode #332 Reconstruct Itinerary (a deliberately Map[String, Vec[String]]-shaped pick to stress nested heap-owning collections — the surface-driven kata strategy). COMMITTED REPRO: kara-katas/oracle/recursive-owned-string-param-uaf/repro.kara (~35 lines, self-contained, no deps). Expected (interp + true answer): route.len=6, [0]=SFO [1]=ATL [2]=SFO [3]=JFK [4]=ATL [5]=JFK. Observed under `karac build` (and KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, identical): indices 1..4 are freed-buffer garbage, e.g. [1]=Rq\xef\xbf\xbd, [3]='  ['; indices 0 and 5 happen to survive. Under `karac run` (LLJIT) the process aborts non-unwinding in karac_string_clone (runtime/src/clone.rs:80) via core::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping's UB precondition check. ABLATION (each ingredient removed individually still PASSES, so all four are required): (1) RECURSION — a non-recursive callee that pushes the param immediately is fine; (2) OWNED `String` param — the argument is `dests[used]`, an element read out of a Vec; (3) the source Vec must be MAP-DERIVED (`adj.get(airport)`) — a Vec returned from a plain factory fn does NOT reproduce, nor does a map-derived Vec without recursion; (4) DEFERRED USE — the param is pushed AFTER the recursive loop (`route.push(airport)` below the `while`), so it must outlive the frame-local `dests`. Probes nest6/nest7/nest8 in the session scratchpad each isolate one ingredient and all pass. FIX HYPOTHESIS: the owned `String` parameter is being passed as a BORROW into the map-derived `Vec`'s element storage rather than a cloned/moved owned String; each recursive frame's `dests` local (a fresh Vec materialized by `Map.get`) is dropped at the end of its loop iteration / frame, freeing the element buffers that deeper-or-later uses of the surviving `airport` parameter still point at. Suspect the ref_arg_index_borrow_ptr / borrowed-arg elision path (src/codegen/collections.rs) classifying `dests[used]` as an in-place element borrow — correct for a `ref T` parameter, WRONG for an owned `String` parameter that outlives the container. Any fix must be verified under memory_sanitizer on BOTH x86 and arm64 (this is exactly the codegen-ownership class the LSan gates exist for). CONSEQUENCE: LeetCode #332 is held out of the kata corpus until this is fixed — shipping it would violate the corpus's A/B run==build invariant.
investigation: REFINED 2026-07-25 (session 2). ROOT CAUSE NARROWED to the element READ, not argument passing. ABLATION: binding the element to a local first — `let next = dests[used]; visit(adj, cursor, next, route);` — still corrupts identically, so the call-site arg path (ref_arg_index_borrow_ptr and friends) is NOT the culprit; all of its call sites were also read and confirmed correctly gated behind `is_ref`. THEORY (consistent with every probe): reading a heap-bearing element out of a container (`dests[used]` on a `Vec[String]`) yields a SHALLOW copy of the element's {ptr,len,cap} that SHARES the heap buffer with the container, which still owns and will free it. Whenever that shallow copy outlives the container the buffer dangles. This also explains why the non-recursive ablations (nest6/nest7/nest8) PASS: they have the same latent sharing, but no allocation happens between the container's free and the read, so the freed bytes are still intact — the recursion in the real shape interleaves many allocations after each frame's `dests` is freed, so the memory is reused and the corruption becomes visible. The passing ablations are therefore NOT evidence of correctness, only of non-manifestation. IMPLICATION FOR THE FIX: this is an ownership-model change at the element-read site (clone a heap-bearing element when the read escapes the container's lifetime), not a contained call-site patch — it interacts with the existing borrow-elision / clone-on-move machinery and must not introduce double-frees or leaks. Deliberately NOT attempted under low remaining context: a speculative clone insertion here fails either as a double-free or as a leak. Verify any fix under memory_sanitizer on x86 AND arm64. || ABLATION MATRIX (session 2, continued) — two further decisive negatives that narrow the trigger to a COMBINATION rather than any single mechanism: (A) MAP-FREE RECURSION PASSES. A recursive fn with the identical shape but a plain factory-returned local `Vec[String]` instead of a map — `fn rec(depth, s: String, out: mut ref Vec[String]) { if depth>0 { let d = make(); rec(depth-1, d[0], out); } out.push(s); }` at depth 4 — is CORRECT under build. So the general 'element read yields a shallow copy' theory in the note above is NOT sufficient on its own: the same recursion + element-read + deferred-push shape over a non-map container is fine. The Map is REQUIRED. (B) PLAIN MAP-DERIVED DROP PASSES. Pulling the value into a local that dies at end of function, twice, then re-reading the map — `fn touch(adj: mut ref Map[String, Vec[String]]) { let d: Vec[String] = match adj.get("k") {...}; }` called twice, then read `adj` again — leaves the map intact under build. So it is ALSO not a simple 'dropping a Map.get result frees the map's buffer' double-free. NET: the trigger requires map-derived values AND recursion together; neither the element-read path nor Map.get's value ownership is wrong in isolation. Next step for whoever picks this up: dump the pre-opt IR for the committed repro and diff the drop/cleanup emission for `dests` between the recursive frame and the (correct) non-recursive shape — the suspicion is a per-frame cleanup registration that is emitted once but runs against a value the recursive callee has already consumed or re-materialized. Probe files u2/u3/u4 in the session scratchpad correspond to ablations (local-binding / map-free / plain-drop) respectively. || ROOT CAUSE FOUND (pre-opt IR diff, session 2). Dumped pre-opt IR for the failing repro and for the passing map-free ablation and diffed the free/clone emission inside the recursive function. The failing `@visit` contains a block the passing `@rec` does NOT: `freearg.free: call void @free(ptr %freearg.ptr)`, whose predecessor is `map.ins.some` — i.e. it runs on the KEY-ALREADY-EXISTS path of `Map.insert`. The freed value is extracted as fields 0 (ptr) and 2 (cap) of a {ptr,len,cap} struct, and `cursor`'s VALUE type is plain `i64` (not heap), so the struct being freed is the passed KEY, not the old value. MECHANISM: on `map.insert(k, v)` where `k` is already present, the map retains its existing key copy and codegen frees the redundant just-passed key buffer via `free_str_vec_buffer_if_heap` (src/codegen/runtime.rs:1887, reached from the old-value/redundant-key drop path around :1868). That is correct when the key argument is a fresh TEMPORARY the caller does not retain — and WRONG when it is a variable or parameter the caller still uses. In the repro `cursor.insert(airport, used + 1i64)` runs once per loop iteration with the SAME `airport`, so from the second iteration on the key exists and `airport`'s buffer is freed — while `airport` is the function's owned String parameter that is pushed into `route` AFTER the loop. Hence route holds freed memory. This explains EVERY ablation: no map => no insert => no free; no recursion => the same key is not re-inserted while still live; plain Map.get create/drop => no insert at all; binding the element to a local does not help because the free is on the insert path, not the argument path. FIX DIRECTION: gate the redundant-key free on the key argument being a consumable temporary (an rvalue the caller does not retain) rather than a live place expression — the consume/temporary classification in src/codegen/consume_class.rs looks like the right oracle. Alternative: always store a cloned key and never free the caller's. Verify under memory_sanitizer x86 AND arm64: the wrong gate direction turns this UAF into a leak. || RETRACTION 2026-07-25 (session 3) — THE PREVIOUS 'ROOT CAUSE' IS WRONG AND IS HEREBY WITHDRAWN. Session 2 concluded from an LLVM IR diff that `Map.insert` frees a LIVE key on the key-already-exists path (`map.ins.some` → `freearg.free` in src/codegen/maps.rs:1771 / runtime.rs:1887), i.e. that `cursor.insert(airport, used+1)` frees the owned `String` parameter `airport`. That is NOT what the compiler emits. METHODOLOGY DEFECT that produced the wrong answer: the throwaway `examples/dump_ir.rs` harness used to obtain that IR called parse → resolve → typecheck → ownershipcheck → codegen but SKIPPED `lowering::lower_program`. Lowering is what forwards the typechecker's SPAN-KEYED side tables into the AST (`pattern_binding_types`, `pattern_binding_inner_types`, the Str-span table, … — src/lowering.rs:259ff), so without it codegen sees an EMPTY `pattern_binding_types` and degrades every match-arm payload binding to the 1-word i64 default. The unlowered dump therefore showed `%dests = alloca i64` GEP'd as a 24-byte `{ptr,i64,i64}` (a spectacular-looking stack OOB) and a `matchval`-less `match.merge` — BOTH artifacts of the broken harness, present in a probe that RUNS CORRECTLY. Re-dumping WITH `lower_program` gives the correct `%dests = alloca { ptr, i64, i64 }` and a real `%matchval` phi. LESSON (generalizes to any future IR investigation): an IR-dump harness MUST run `lower_program` or its output is not the IR the compiler actually emits — prefer reproducing through the real driver over a hand-rolled phase chain. WHAT THE CORRECTED IR ACTUALLY SHOWS: the value freed at `map.ins.some` is `%dcopy.result`, the DEFENSIVE COPY that `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg` makes of the owned-`String` param key (src/codegen/maps.rs ‘insert’ arm), and the free is guarded on `cap > 0`; `%dcopy.result` is a phi that passes `%airport` through UNCHANGED only when `cap == 0`, in which case the guard suppresses the free. So the redundant-key free is BALANCED and is not the bug. The duplicate-key leak fix B-2026-06-20-9 that emits it is intact. STATUS: root cause is once again UNKNOWN. Still-valid evidence: the four-ingredient ablation matrix above (recursion + owned String param + map-derived Vec element + deferred use), the committed repro, and the run-vs-build divergence. Discard only the session-2 `Map.insert`/live-key conclusion and the session-2 'element read yields a shallow copy' theory (already disproved as insufficient by ablation A). NEXT STEP for whoever picks this up: dump IR through a harness that includes lowering (examples/dump_ir.rs now does) and diff the failing `@visit` against the passing map-free `@rec` again — the earlier diff was run on unrepresentative IR and must be redone from scratch. || ASAN-DRIVEN NARROWING 2026-07-25 (session 3, after the retraction above) — first HARD evidence, replacing IR-reading with a sanitizer verdict. Method: a temporary #[test] in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs driving `run_under_asan_with_full_pipeline` on the committed repro (Linux, so LSan/ASan both live). VERDICT: heap-use-after-free; 4-byte region; ALLOCATED BY `karac_string_clone`; FREED from `visit`; READ by `memcpy` of size 3 in `main` (an f-string printing `route[i]`, i.e. a 3-char airport code). Reproduced identically at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, so it is not an optimizer artifact. With `fast_unwind_on_malloc=0:malloc_context_size=30` the free stack is `free ← visit ← visit ← visit ← visit ← main` — the leak is reached at recursion depth 4. (1) THE `Map.insert` REDUNDANT-KEY FREE IS DEFINITIVELY EXONERATED — causally, not just by reading. Disabling `free_str_vec_buffer_if_heap(kv)` at src/codegen/maps.rs:1771 removes the ONLY direct `call void @free` from `@visit` (verified by dumping IR under the patch: count drops to 0), and the ASan report is BYTE-IDENTICAL. So the free attributed to `visit` is a TAIL CALL from the runtime's `karac_free_buf` (a tail jmp pushes no frame, so ASan credits the caller) — i.e. one of `visit`'s Vec/String element-drop sites, which is the `dests` scope-exit drop. Beware this attribution trap when reading ASan output for Kara binaries: a `visit`-attributed `free` may be any `karac_free_buf` the function emits. (2) PRIME SUSPECT, independently reproducible in 7 lines: the recursive call `visit(adj, cursor, dests[used], route)` lowers to a bare `%v.elem = load { ptr, i64, i64 }` of the element followed by `call void @visit({ ptr, i64, i64 } %v.elem, …)` — NO CLONE. The element header is passed as a shallow alias into the caller's `dests` buffer, which `visit` drops (elements included) right after the call returns. MINIMAL REPRO of the missing clone (no map, no recursion): `fn take(s: String, out: mut ref Vec[String]) { out.push(s); }` called as `take(v[0], mut out)` emits `%v.elem = load …; call void @take(%v.elem, …)` with no clone. That case does not crash only because the callee's `out.push(s)` defensively copies the owned param on the way in — the alias is latent, not benign. (3) WHY: `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg` (src/codegen/runtime.rs:3344) opens with exactly the intended guard — `expr_is_heap_vec_index(arg_expr)` → `clone_owned_vec_index_element` — and its doc comment claims coverage of the 'owned call arg' sink. But every call site of that helper is an ENUM-CONSTRUCTOR payload (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs:2677, 2771, 2973, 3018); a plain free-function call argument never routes through it. So the B-2026-07-04-2 / B-2026-07-05-1 element-clone fix covers tuple literals, push, struct fields, map values and enum payloads, but NOT the by-value argument of an ordinary call. NEXT STEP: extend the owned-arg consume path to run `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg` (or at least the `expr_is_heap_vec_index` → `clone_owned_vec_index_element` leg) for by-value heap params at ordinary call sites, then re-run the ASan probe. GATE: the wrong gate direction converts this UAF into a leak, so memory_sanitizer must be green on x86 AND arm64 (`scripts/lsan-local.sh` for the latter) before this is called fixed. The temporary ASan probe was NOT committed; re-create it from the repro at kara-katas/oracle/recursive-owned-string-param-uaf/repro.kara — and promote it to a permanent regression test with the fix. || CAVEAT ON SUSPECT (2), same session — do NOT start by 'fixing' the missing call-site clone without re-reading the ABI. src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs (~line 1573) documents the by-value convention explicitly: an owned `String`/`Vec` parameter is CALLER-RETAINS — the callee never frees it (such params land in `owned_vecstr_params` and get a defensive deep-copy at each RETAINING consume site, never a callee-side `track_vec_var`). Under that convention passing `dests[used]` as a bare element alias is BY DESIGN, not obviously a defect, and the `take(v[0], mut out)` minimal case is memory-correct end-to-end precisely because the callee's `out.push(s)` deep-copies on the way in. So suspect (2) may be consistent with the ABI rather than the bug. UNRESOLVED TENSION that the next attempt should start from, since it is what actually pins the defect: in the repro `route.push(airport)` DOES emit the defensive copy (the `while.exit` → `dcopy.copy` → `store %dcopy.result123` chain in `@visit`), and every element cloned by `karac_string_clone` carries `cap == len > 0` (runtime/src/clone.rs allocates len+1 bytes — hence the 4-byte region for a 3-char code — and sets cap = len), so the `cap > 0` guard on that copy is TAKEN. Every entry `route` receives should therefore be a fresh `malloc` from `@visit`, yet ASan reports `main` reading a block allocated by `karac_string_clone`. One of those three statements is false: either some `route.push` path bypasses the copy, or `route` is written by something other than that push, or the freed/read block reaches `main` by a route other than `route[i]`. Resolve THAT before touching codegen — printing the element pointers at each push and at each drop is the cheapest discriminator. || RESOLVED 2026-07-25 (session 3) — fix 7ae1e2e. ROOT CAUSE (confirmed by ASan before and after, and by a four-variant discriminator matrix): an OWNED `String`/`Vec` param consumed TWICE in one function. Owned Vec/String params are CALLER-RETAINS — the callee registers no `FreeVecBuffer` for them (hence `owned_vecstr_params`, not `track_vec_var`) and each retaining consume deep-copies via `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg` — so the param's buffer is never moved out and there is NO cleanup to suppress. But `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs, the Identifier/`move.cap.p` arm) zeroed the param header's `cap` anyway. That zero is the ownership bit the NEXT consume reads: with `cap == 0` the second consume treats the param as a borrowed view, SKIPS its defensive copy, and stores a raw alias. In the repro `cursor.insert(airport, used+1)` is consume #1 (zeroes cap) and `route.push(airport)` after the recursive descent is consume #2 (stores an alias into the caller's map-derived `Vec[String]` element, freed the moment the recursive call returns). FIX: skip the cap-zero when the root identifier is in `owned_vecstr_params`. RESOLVES THE ARITHMETIC TENSION recorded above — the defensive copy at `route.push` IS emitted and `karac_string_clone` DOES set cap = len > 0, but by the time the push runs the SLOT's cap has been overwritten with 0 by the earlier insert, so the guard reads 0 and the copy is skipped. RE-READING THE ORIGINAL ABLATION: the 'four required ingredients' were real but mostly staging. Recursion + a map-derived source Vec + use-after-descent are what make the aliased buffer actually DIE before it is read; the Map mattered only because `cursor.insert(airport, ...)` supplied the FIRST of the two consumes. The true minimal trigger is 'owned heap param consumed twice, second consume outliving the first consume's source' — much smaller than the shape the ablation suggested. LESSON: an ablation matrix bounds where a bug MANIFESTS, not what causes it; every ingredient there was necessary for the crash and only one was necessary for the defect. GATES: memory_sanitizer 852/852 green on x86 Linux (LSan live — the fix closes the UAF without converting it to a leak), codegen E2E 2576/2576, cli 532/532, fmt + clippy --all-targets clean. The repro now prints SFO ATL SFO JFK ATL JFK identically under all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT run / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build). REGRESSION TEST: `asan_owned_string_param_consumed_twice_no_uaf` in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs. LeetCode #332 is unblocked. title: Match-arm type unification does not bind an unsolved type variable inside a generic: `match m.get(k) { Some(d) => d, None => Vec.new() }` is rejected with "match arms have incompatible types: 'Vec<String>' and 'Vec<?T0>'" instead of solving `?T0 := String` from the sibling arm. An explicit annotation on the enclosing `let` propagates correctly, so only the arm-to-arm direction is missing.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: hit while authoring LeetCode #332 (same kata as B-2026-07-25-1). MINIMAL REPRO: `let mut m: Map[String, Vec[String]] = Map.new(); let got = match m.get("k") { Some(d) => d, None => Vec.new() };` → error[typecheck] match arms have incompatible types: 'Vec<String>' and 'Vec<?T0>'. CONTROL: adding the annotation (`let got: Vec[String] = match …`) typechecks and runs correctly on every surface, so expected-type propagation INTO the arms works; only sibling-arm unification is missing. MECHANISM: the arm fold (src/typechecker/patterns.rs ~line 297, `join_branch_types`) gates on `types_compatible_with_projections`, and `types_compatible` (src/typechecker/types.rs) has a permissive wildcard arm for `Type::TypeParam` (line 1273) but NO corresponding arm for `Type::TypeVar` — despite the comment directly above it claiming the rule is "Equivalent to the `TypeVar` handling below" (that handling does not exist in the function). So `Vec<String>` vs `Vec<?T0>` fails the invariant generic-arg check and the join returns None. Note `merge_branch_types` ALREADY prefers the concrete side over a TypeVar, so once the compatibility gate admits the pair the result type would come out `Vec[String]` correctly. FIX OPTIONS: (a) narrow — in `join_branch_types`, admit pairs that are equal modulo unsolved TypeVars and let `merge_branch_types` pick the concrete side (contained to branch joins: match arms + if/else); (b) broad — add a `TypeVar` wildcard arm to `types_compatible` mirroring `TypeParam`, which is what the stale comment implies was intended, but that weakens a core predicate used across the typechecker and needs care. Prefer (a). SEVERITY low: fails closed (a rejection, never a miscompile), and the annotated form is already the established Kāra idiom since every bare `Vec.new()` requires an annotation anyway.
resolution: Added `same_shape_modulo_typevars` (src/typechecker.rs) and a second arm in `join_branch_types`: when the two branch types are structurally identical except at unsolved `TypeVar` positions, admit the pair so `merge_branch_types` (which already prefers the concrete leaf) solves the slot from the sibling arm. Scoped to the branch join rather than loosening the global `types_compatible` predicate, so no other check is weakened. Fails closed — different head (Vec vs Map), different arity, or two concrete leaves (String vs i64) all still rejected. Tests: match_arms_bind_typevar_from_sibling_arm + match_arms_with_different_generic_heads_still_rejected. Suite green: lib 990, typechecker 2091, codegen E2E 2576, clippy+fmt clean.
fix: 9226dff

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): statement-position `v.pop()` was a NO-OP — a non-push statement method call fell through to `emit_method_value` (which does nothing for `pop`), so the vec never shrank. Not harmless: the port's own `self.loop_cont.pop()` / `loop_break.pop()` maintain the loop-label stacks, so a no-op pop leaves stale entries and mis-resolves `break`/`continue` for subsequent loops.
fix: 21a6eed
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by real-shape differential probing (Vec-method sweep) vs the seed `karac run` oracle. IN-SURFACE: all 12 `.pop()` sites in the port are `self.loop_cont.pop()` / `self.loop_break.pop()` in STATEMENT position (return discarded) on Vec[String] — the loop-label stacks the emitter pushes/pops around each loop; a no-op pop corrupts `break`/`continue` target resolution for later loops. FIX (Slice 57, 21a6eed): a `pop` arm in emit_stmt's MethodCall handling that loads {ptr,len,cap} and, GUARDED by `len > 0` (empty pop = no-op, matching the seed; the guard also prevents a wild element-free and a len underflow), writes back {ptr, len-1, cap}. Vec[String] (kind 4) loads+frees the popped element buffer first (leak-clean under the oracle's valgrind leg); Vec[i64] (kind 3) just decrements. Vec-of-struct/enum pop has no port site; VALUE-position pop (consuming the returned Option[T]) is out of surface — the port never reads a pop result.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 57 (21a6eed): guarded pop arm shrinking {ptr,len,cap}, Vec[String] frees the popped element. Selfhost oracle (corpus 172) + valgrind green.

title: USE-AFTER-FREE under codegen (sibling of B-2026-07-25-1, NOT closed by it): the natural LeetCode #332 Hierholzer walk over a `Map[String, Vec[String]]` whose KEYS are heap `String`s read out of a `ref Vec[String]` param corrupts the accumulated route. Interior entries are freed-buffer garbage under `karac build`; `karac run` (LLJIT) aborts inside `karac_string_clone`. The tree-walk interpreter is correct, so it is also a run-vs-build divergence.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced immediately after B-2026-07-25-1 was fixed, while adding the LeetCode #332 kata that bug had been blocking — the fix made the minimal repro pass but NOT the full kata. COMMITTED REPRO: kara-katas/oracle/itinerary-heap-map-key-uaf/repro.kara with oracle.py alongside. Expected (interp, and oracle.py): `JFK -> MUC -> LHR -> SFO -> SJC` / `JFK -> ATL -> JFK -> SFO -> ATL -> SFO` / same / `JFK -> AAA`. Observed under `karac build` (and KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, identical): first case prints `JFK -> JFK -> JFK -> JFK -> SJC` — first and last entries survive, the interior collapses; later cases print raw freed bytes. `karac check` is clean apart from one perf[rc-fallback] note on `airport` (direct re-use after consume) — see INVESTIGATION.
investigation: NARROWED, root cause NOT yet identified. Each piece is CORRECT in isolation under `karac build`; only the whole chain fails: (a) the graph build alone (`adj.get(froms[i])` -> `d.push(tos[i])` -> `adj.insert(froms[i], d)` in a loop) is correct; (b) the sort pass alone (read each key's Vec, `sort()`, write back through `adj.insert(keys[k], d)`) is correct; (c) the B-2026-07-25-1 repro — the SAME recursive `visit` — is correct since that fix. LOCALIZATION: `route` is already corrupt INSIDE `find_itinerary`, immediately after `visit` returns and before the reversal loop, so neither the reversal (`out.push(route[j])`) nor the `show` string concat is implicated; the damage happens during the recursive walk. THE ONE STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE from the fixed sibling: that repro seeded its map from string LITERALS in `main` (`adj.insert("JFK", a)`) — rodata keys with `cap == 0`, which every cap-guarded defensive-copy and free path treats as a borrowed view — whereas here the keys are `froms[i]`, HEAP `String` elements read out of a `ref Vec[String]` param, so `cap > 0` and those paths all take their live arms. That is the LEADING HYPOTHESIS, explicitly not a conclusion: it is the difference between the passing and failing programs, but no experiment yet shows it is the cause. NOTE FOR THE NEXT ATTEMPT: the ownership checker already emits `perf[rc-fallback]` for `airport` ("direct re-use after consume; consume at the `cursor.insert` line, other use at the `route.push` line") — it SEES the double-consume shape that caused B-2026-07-25-1, so cross-checking what codegen does with that hint is a cheap first move. Method that worked for the sibling and should be reused: drive the repro through `run_under_asan_with_full_pipeline` in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs for a sanitizer verdict (Linux, LSan live) rather than reading IR, and remember the attribution trap recorded on B-2026-07-25-1 — a `free` credited to a Kara function may be a tail call from the runtime's `karac_free_buf`. Dump IR with `cargo run --features llvm --example dump_ir` (it runs `lower_program`; a hand-rolled phase chain that skips lowering produces IR the compiler never emits). CONSEQUENCE: LeetCode #332 remains held out of the kata corpus — shipping it would violate the corpus's A/B run==build invariant. || RETRACTED 2026-07-25, same session, one commit after filing. THIS BUG DOES NOT EXIST. The LeetCode #332 program matches its Python reference BYTE-FOR-BYTE under all four surfaces (`karac run --interp`, `karac run` LLJIT, default auto-par `karac build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`) once compiled by a correctly built `karac`. The kata is now in the corpus at kara-katas/leetcode/301-400/332-reconstruct-itinerary/ and the oracle probe has been deleted. WHY THE FALSE POSITIVE: the ephemeral cloud container REWOUND the local `kara` checkout to an old commit (8ee88f5) mid-session — three separate times — while the session's commits remained safe on origin. A rebuild that happened while the tree was rewound produced a `target/debug/karac` WITHOUT the B-2026-07-25-1 owned-param cap-zero fix. Every measurement taken with that binary — the '#332 kata still fails' finding, the heap-vs-literal map-key ablation, and the h1/hA/hB narrowing that appeared to implicate heap map keys — was reproducing the ALREADY-FIXED bug, not a sibling of it. After `git reset --hard origin/main` plus a full `cargo build --features llvm`, all of those variants pass. LESSON (the operational sibling of the dump_ir lesson on B-2026-07-25-1): a measurement is only as trustworthy as the toolchain that produced it. In an environment where the checkout can move underneath you, verify BEFORE measuring — `git rev-parse HEAD` against `origin/main`, and confirm the fix under test is actually present in the source (`grep` for its marker comment) — then rebuild. A green-then-red flip with no intervening source edit is a toolchain-provenance signal, not a new bug.
resolution: INVALID — filed against a STALE COMPILER BINARY, retracted the same day.

title: `for k in m.keys()` (and `.values()`/`.entries()`) STILL eagerly materializes an owned `Vec` per evaluation when either map half is a HEAP type (`Map[String, _]`, `Map[_, Vec[_]]`). B-2026-07-24-2's inline bucket walk and its lazy keys() routing are both gated to SCALAR halves, so the originally-reported malloc + full-set copy + free — plus a DEEP CLONE of every heap key — is unchanged for the heap case, which is if anything the more expensive one.
fix: 15dcfac
resolution: Did step (a) exactly as this entry's FIX DIRECTION prescribed, and it was indeed the bulk of the win. The two concerns that had gated heap halves out are both answered by the DESTINATION path rather than by the gate: (1) registration — `compile_for_map_var` calls `register_for_loop_bindings`, whose Tuple arm registers the key half from `map_key_type_exprs` and the value half from `var_elem_type_exprs`, the same tables the eager path installs, so `k.bytes()`/`k.len()` still dispatch; (2) owned-vs-borrow — the same call does `mark_for_loop_borrow_if_heap`, putting the binding in `for_loop_borrow_vars`, the defensive-copy-at-consume machinery every other heap for-loop element already uses. `map_place_is_iterable` now requires the half TYPE-EXPR tables instead of scalar LLVM types, so a map codegen cannot describe still fails closed to the eager path. Step (b) (extending the inline BUCKET WALK to heap halves) was deliberately NOT done: that walk keeps its own separate scalar gate because a heap half needs the runtime iterator's per-element clone/drop, so a heap-halved map lands on the LAZY `karac_map_iter_new`/`_next`/`_free` walk — no Vec and no per-key deep clone, which is the win — while the zero-call bucket walk stays a scalar-only optimization. SECOND DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED IN THE SAME SLICE: a SINGLE binding over `.entries()` (`for e in m.entries() { … e.0 … }`, what `#[derive(Message)]` emits for a Map field) must NOT be rewritten — it wants one tuple VALUE per step, which only the eager materializer produces; routing it to the pair-binding path bound `e` to the value half and left `e.0` unregistered, reproducing this entry's predicted 'no handler for method bytes' failure. Only a real 2-tuple pattern is rewritten now; that condition is type-independent, so it also closes the same latent hole for a scalar-halved map. MEASURED (fresh probe, not the scalar one — per this entry's instruction): hot `keys()` walk over a 170-entry `Map[String, i64]`, 20k non-hoistable evaluations — 0.148s -> 0.034s, ~4.3x, identical output; IR shows `@malloc` / `@karac_map_len` / `@karac_clone_String` / `@karac_free_buf` all gone from the loop. GATES (all the ones this entry named): cli 532 green INCLUDING `test_run_derive_message_repeated_string_and_map_roundtrip`; 4-backend agreement (interp/JIT/AOT-O2/AOT-O0) over heap key, heap value, both-heap struct FIELD, a consuming sink (`owned.push(k)`), an early `return` out of the loop body, and the source map intact afterwards; codegen 2586 (3 new tests: an IR guard asserting the materializer is ABSENT, a behavioural sweep over every heap shape, and a guard pinning the single-binding `entries()` shape), memory_sanitizer 854, par_codegen 200, interpreter 1307, typechecker 2091, lib 990, selfhost_codegen oracle; clippy (both feature sets) + fmt clean. LEAK CHECK: valgrind on the heap-shape sweep is BYTE-IDENTICAL before and after this change (1 byte definitely lost, 9 contexts, both builds), i.e. leak-neutral; that residual is a separate PRE-EXISTING bug filed as B-2026-07-27-2. NOT DONE (arm64): only the x86 leg was run in this container — the entry asked for arm64 memory_sanitizer too, which the CI `memory-sanitizer-arm64` job covers.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-07-24-2 when closing it, after verifying the residual rather than assuming the scope note covered it. IR EVIDENCE (`examples/dump_ir`, commit 09dfeb6): for `fn total(m: ref Map[String, i64]) { for k in m.keys() { s = s + k.len(); } }` the emitted `@total` still contains `@malloc`, `@karac_map_len`, `@karac_map_iter_new`/`_next`/`_free` and two `@karac_free_buf` — i.e. the complete eager build-then-iterate-then-free, with the second `free_buf` being the per-element String drop. A scalar-halved map at the same commit emits none of those (bucket walk inlined, zero calls).
investigation: WHY IT IS GATED OUT (deliberate, not an oversight): both B-2026-07-24-2 legs fail closed on a heap half for DIFFERENT reasons, and each has to be answered separately. (1) The lazy keys() ROUTING (ea6b875) rewrites `for k in m.keys()` to `for (k, _) in m`; for a heap key that loses the side-table registration the eager path installs under the loop variable's name — caught immediately by `tests/cli.rs::test_run_derive_message_repeated_string_and_map_roundtrip`, which failed with "no handler for method 'bytes'" — and it would hand the body a BORROW where the eager `keys()` Vec gave it an OWNED deep clone, changing move semantics. (2) The inline BUCKET WALK (bef6bbc) loads each half with a plain typed load; a heap half needs the per-element clone/drop the runtime path performs, which is the entire reason the eager materializer exists. FIX DIRECTION, in the order that de-risks it: (a) teach the tuple-rewrite path to register a heap half in the String/Vec side tables under the loop variable's name, which is what the eager path already does — that alone makes `for k in stringMap.keys()` lower to the existing LAZY runtime-iterator entries path (no Vec, no deep clones) without touching the inline walk; (b) only then consider extending the inline bucket walk to heap halves, which additionally requires deciding borrow-vs-clone semantics for the binding and carrying the per-element drop. Step (a) is the bulk of the win and is much cheaper than (b). GATES: the registration change is exactly the class `test_run_derive_message_repeated_string_and_map_roundtrip` polices, so run the cli suite first; then codegen E2E + memory_sanitizer on x86 AND arm64, since moving a heap key from owned-clone to borrow is an ownership change (see B-2026-07-25-1 for how that class fails). MEASUREMENT: reuse kara-katas/oracle/map-keys-walk-probe/ with a `Map[String, i64]` variant — do NOT quote the scalar probe's numbers for this case.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): statement-position `s.push_str(arg)` was a NO-OP — it fell through to `emit_method_value`, which does nothing for push_str, so the receiver String never grew. push_str is the port's DOMINANT string-building primitive (700+ call sites across codegen/ast_render/lexer/resolver/typechecker), so every incremental string build silently produced the empty seed — a hard self-hosting blocker.
fix: bd6af74
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by real-shape differential probing (String-method sweep) vs the seed `karac run` oracle. By far the most-used unimplemented method (737 `.push_str(` sites; the runners-up `.pop()` at 12 and `.last()` at 2 are tiny by comparison). All receivers are plain LOCAL String identifiers (`out` 517x, `line` 168x, `s`, `text`, …) — none are `self.field` — so only an Ident receiver is handled. FIX (Slice 58, bd6af74): an in-place append in emit_stmt's MethodCall arm — load the receiver slot's {ptr,len}, eval the arg {aptr,alen}, `realloc(ptr, len+alen)` (preserves [0,len); realloc(null,·)=malloc for the empty `"".to_string()` seed), `memcpy` the arg bytes at ptr+len, store {newptr, len+alen} back. Every push_str'd local is an OWNED `.to_string()` buffer, so realloc is safe. A heap-temp arg (a fresh `a + b` concat) is freed after its bytes are copied (leak-clean); a borrowed arg (literal global / ident load) is not. NOTE ON DISCOVERY: a `push_str`-in-a-loop probe with `i += 1` first appeared to crash (runaway realloc), but that was a STALE LOCAL BASE lacking the compound-assign fix (B-2026-07-23-22) — on the correct base both `i = i + 1` and `i += 1` loop-builds match. Value-position push_str result (it returns unit) is irrelevant; statement position is the only shape.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 58 (bd6af74): in-place realloc+memcpy append; heap-temp arg freed after copy. Selfhost oracle + valgrind green.

title: Indexed-receiver method call on a MAP element (`m[k].push(x)`) type-checks and runs correctly under the tree-walk interpreter but is REJECTED by codegen with `indexed-receiver method 'push' on '<m>' — outer is not a Vec/Slice/Array`. A `Vec` outer (`vv[0].push(x)`) works in codegen, so the gap is specific to Map outers, and it reproduces for BOTH heap-keyed (`Map[String, Vec[_]]`) and scalar-keyed (`Map[i64, Vec[_]]`) maps.
resolution:
Fixed in 4416d33 by adding `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_map` to src/codegen/calls.rs and routing a Map outer to it from `compile_indexed_receiver_method`. The gap was narrower than the report implied: `var_elem_type_exprs` is ALREADY populated with the map's VALUE TypeExpr at every Map-registering site (types_lowering.rs and stmts.rs both insert it alongside `map_key_type_exprs`), so the element-TypeExpr resolution already worked for maps — only the element-POINTER lowering was missing. The new helper resolves `m[k]` to the value half of the key's bucket via `karac_map_lookup_slot`, the same runtime entrypoint already backing `entry(k).and_modify(...)`, so no new runtime contract was needed. That pointer aliases the map's kv buffer, which is what MR3 requires for a mutating method to propagate; `karac_map_get` could not serve because it copies the value out into a caller-provided slot. Missing key panics, matching both the `m[k]` read path and the interpreter (the lookup variant never inserts). Key ownership deliberately mirrors `compile_map_index` and does NOT free the key buffer: `lookup_slot` does not adopt it, and the key may be a live binding, where an unconditional free would be a use-after-free rather than a leak fix. Regression test `asan_map_indexed_receiver_push_no_leak` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) pins the aliasing shape most likely to double-free or leak — 200 pushes across 7 heap keys, forcing reallocs of the in-bucket Vec, with the key read from a live Vec[String] element — plus a scalar-keyed sibling. Gates: fmt, clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm, codegen 2576, memory_sanitizer 853 (LSan live on Linux), cli 532, non-llvm 8184.

PREDICTION CORRECTED AFTER THE FIX LANDED (2026-07-25). The pre-fix estimate above -- ~52% of kara's #332 deficit attributable to this bug, derived from a graph-shape discriminator (same edge count, max degree 40 -> 1) -- was TOO OPTIMISTIC. Measuring the real fix, both binaries built from the same compiler and run in one hyperfine session (50 runs, warmup 10): copy-back 229.4ms +/- 10.6 (median 227.6) vs in-place 200.7ms +/- 5.5 (median 199.1), against rust 129.9ms. That is ~12.5% wall-clock and ~25% of the gap to Rust closed (23-28% depending on median vs min) -- roughly HALF the predicted improvement. WHY THE DISCRIMINATOR OVERESTIMATED: reshaping the graph removes the O(sum deg^2) copies outright, whereas the fix TRADES them for an extra `contains_key` probe per edge -- the old `get` did double duty as presence check AND value fetch, so the in-place form pays one additional String hash+probe per edge and only recovers part of the copy cost. FOLLOW-UP: a single-lookup `entry(k).or_insert(...).push(x)` chain would avoid the second probe; entry_chains.rs already lowers or_insert/and_modify, so the missing piece is method-chaining off the entry result. Also note absolute times on this container are not stable across sessions (an unmodified rust binary measured 164.1ms and later 123.7-138.1ms), so only same-session A/B comparisons are valid.

title: Overflow check on a BOUNDED loop-accumulator (`cnt = cnt + 1` guarded by an if, inside a counted loop) is not elided, and because a checked add can trap it cannot be speculated — which blocks LLVM's if-conversion of `if bit { cnt += 1 }` into the branchless `cnt += bit`. On random data the surviving conditional branch mispredicts ~50% of the time, costing 7.9x on a per-bit counting loop.
resolution:
Fixed in 762865a. New src/codegen/accum_overflow.rs recognizes the bounded counting loop and emits a plain add for the accumulator increment; the trap is provably dead so the elision is semantics-preserving.

MEASURED on kata #137 (four 120,001-element arrays, 40 punches, 30 runs / 5 warmup): kara 281.3ms -> 23.9ms +/- 1.1, an 11.8x improvement, sink unchanged at 79998760. Same program, other lanes: c -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 22.1 +/- 2.5 (kara 1.08x behind -- PARITY at equal ISA baseline), c -O3 34.0 +/- 1.3, rust -O 36.7 +/- 1.2, rust -O -C overflow-checks=on 270.3 +/- 12.8. So kara went from 'ties equal-safety Rust, 7.9x behind C' to 'parity with equal-baseline C, 11.3x AHEAD of equal-safety Rust' while still checking every other arithmetic operation in the program. That exceeds the success criterion this entry pre-registered (~281ms -> ~40ms, level with rust -O / clang -O3).

SOUNDNESS. The admitted pattern is `let acc = 0; let i = <lit >= 0>; while i < <bound> { ... acc = acc + 1 (EXACTLY ONE site) ... i = i + <lit >= 1> (one ascending step) }`. i starts non-negative and increases while i < bound, so trip <= bound; bound is an i64 VALUE so bound <= i64::MAX; acc starts at 0 and rises by 1 at most once per iteration, so acc <= trip <= i64::MAX at every point, including after the final increment. No platform assumption is needed (no reasoning about .len()'s range or address-space size). Site uniqueness and the zero initializer are both load-bearing: two sites give acc <= 2*trip and a non-zero start gives acc <= init + trip, either of which can overflow, so both are rejected. The counter's OWN check is deliberately retained. Every unmodelled shape fails closed, including any closure in the loop body.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE worth carrying forward: codegen runs on the LOWERED AST, where `i < n` and `a + b` are trait-method Calls rather than ExprKind::Binary. The first cut matched only the surface forms and silently never fired on the target kata -- the same trap control_flow_bce.rs's guard_counter_var already documents. Both forms are matched now, and the analysis scans the whole block tree from one entry so hook placement in compile_block is not load-bearing either.

NOT HANDLED (deliberate, each breaks a step of the proof): the `acc += 1` compound form, steps other than 1, non-zero initializers, multiple increment sites, `for` loops, and accumulators that are fields / elements / captures.

Tests: 5 unit tests pinning each precondition individually; two E2E tests, one for semantics and one confirming a non-zero-init accumulator STILL traps with `integer overflow`. Corpus sweep over 30 counting-loop katas, all outputs unchanged (3 whose interpreter run exceeded the sweep timeout were verified against their Python oracles instead). Gates: fmt, clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm, codegen 2579, memory_sanitizer 853 (LSan live on Linux), non-llvm 8184.
investigation:
NOT a kara-specific defect and NOT a miscompile — kara and rustc-with-overflow-checks lose the same 7.9x to the same cause, so this is a MISSED OPTIMIZATION shared with rustc, filed because kara's checked-by-default arithmetic makes it the DEFAULT experience here rather than an opt-in one.

MECHANISM, ISOLATED IN THREE STEPS (all on the Rust mirror so the variable is exactly one statement):

1. IT IS THAT ONE CHECK, NOT CHECKED ARITHMETIC IN GENERAL. Making ONLY `cnt += 1` unchecked (`cnt.wrapping_add(1)`) while `overflow-checks=on` still applies to `i`, `b` and every expression in main: 277ms -> 30ms. One statement accounts for the whole gap.

2. IT IS NOT VECTORIZATION. Rebuilding that same unchecked variant with LLVM's loop and SLP vectorizers off (`-C llvm-args=-vectorize-loops=false -C llvm-args=-vectorize-slp=false`): still 40ms. The fast path is fast SCALAR code. (Independently confirmed on the C side: `clang -O3 -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize` stays at 40ms.)

3. IT IS BRANCH MISPREDICTION. Replacing the LCG-generated values with a constant, so `(nums[i] >> b) & 1` is uniform per bit position and the branch is perfectly predicted, collapses BOTH checked builds: rust_ovf 277 -> 45ms, kara 281 -> 50ms.

So: a checked `cnt + 1` can trap, therefore it cannot be speculated, therefore SimplifyCFG cannot if-convert the guarded increment into branchless `cnt += bit`. What remains is a real data-dependent branch on a ~50%-random bit over 154 million elements.

WHY THE CHECK IS REMOVABLE: `cnt` starts at 0 and is incremented at most once per iteration of a loop whose trip count is `nums.len()`, so `cnt <= len <= i64::MAX` holds by construction. The bound is provable by the same monotone-induction-variable reasoning the descending-loop BCE work (B-2026-07-17-1) already does for indices. Eliding the check restores if-conversion and, per step 1, recovers the entire 7.9x.

SCOPE: this is the general shape `acc = acc + <small constant>` where acc is a loop-local accumulator with a loop-bounded increment count — histogramming, counting, summing small bounded values. It is not specific to bit counting; #137 just makes it 32x hotter than usual by nesting the count inside a per-bit loop.

NEXT STEP: teach the overflow-check emission an accumulator-bound analysis — for an i64 local whose only writes in a loop are `x = x + K` with K a non-negative constant, and whose enclosing loop has a computable trip-count bound T, elide the check when `init + K*T` cannot overflow. Verify with the #137 bench: success is kara moving from ~281ms to ~40ms and pulling level with `rust -O` / `clang -O3` rather than with `rust_ovf`.

title: Map/Set probes called `eq_fn` on EVERY occupied bucket they walked past, because the status byte carried no hash information — one cold key dereference per probed slot, which for a `String` key was 77% of the #127 kata's L1-D read misses. Fixed by a hashbrown-style 7-bit hash tag in the control byte.
resolution:
FIXED 2026-07-28 (58412d9). The status byte now carries a 7-bit fragment of the key's hash: EMPTY = 0x00, TOMBSTONE = 0x01, OCCUPIED = 0x80 | tag7 where tag7 is bits 57..63. Both sentinels are below 0x80, so a lookup compares the bucket byte against the SEARCHED key's own control byte and gets occupancy and hash tag in ONE instruction, rejecting a non-matching key without touching it. The tag comes from the HIGH bits because the bucket index takes the low ones — a tag sharing them would be invariant along a probe chain and reject nothing.

MEASURED, with BOTH lanes built in one session. That qualifier is the finding worth carrying forward: the first A/B here read as a 12% REGRESSION because it compared against a binary another session had left in the bench directory. Rebuilding both arms from source reversed the sign. This is the third ledger entry spent on a stale bench binary; the standing note that `bench.sh`'s cache key should include the compiler that produced the binary is now overdue.

  * L1-D read misses 6,620,800 -> 2,135,000 (-68%), which puts kara BELOW the Rust lane's 2,931,820. cachegrind, so deterministic.
  * `karac_eq_String` alone 5,124,890 -> 1,189,583 (-77%) — 88% of the entire reduction. Everything else is unchanged to within noise: hash 205,202 -> 209,282, map-free 82,427 -> 82,427 exactly, malloc_consolidate 147,241 -> 147,039. That ISOLATES the mechanism rather than inferring it from the total.
  * Wall time 0.948x min / 0.915x median over 25 interleaved runs (interleaved so machine drift hits every lane equally).
  * I refs 2,314,631,913 -> 2,291,401,424 — slightly fewer.

THE ENTRY'S EARLIER 'INSTRUCTION PARITY' CLAIM DOES NOT REPRODUCE, and is retracted here rather than left standing. It recorded kara 1.782G vs rust 1.790G. Building both lanes fresh in one session measures kara 2.315G (pre-fix) against rust 1.830G — 1.25x, not parity. The Rust figure is close to the old one; kara's is 30% higher, so the old kara number is the suspect half, and the most likely explanation is the same stale-binary trap described above. What survives from the earlier round is the ATTRIBUTION (eq dominates the misses), which this fix confirmed directly and then removed.

STILL OPEN AFTER THIS, stated because the entry should not read as 'kara now matches Rust here': wall time is 1.50x the Rust lane (was 1.59x). Two things are visibly left. (1) Conditional branch mispredicts, 18.26M vs Rust's 11.13M — this fix moved them only slightly (from 20.40M) and the delta is NOT attributed, because Rust inlines its lookup into `main` and cannot be split against kara's out-of-line probes. (2) Instruction count, still 1.25x. Neither is a map-probe problem, so neither belongs to this entry.

SCOPE LIMIT, deliberate: the tag compare is on the LOOKUP probes (`Map.get`, the String-key `get`, `Set.contains`). The INSERT probes reach their occupied arm by elimination — not EMPTY, not TOMBSTONE — which stays correct verbatim under the new encoding, so they store the control byte but do not take the early-out. The measured cost was on the lookup side; adding the gate to inserts is a further slice.

THIS IS A CODEGEN/RUNTIME ABI. `src/codegen/mono.rs` emits its own probe loops and `control_flow_for.rs` / `runtime.rs` walk occupied slots, so all of them must agree with `runtime/src/map.rs`. Disagreement is a lookup that misses a present key — a silent wrong answer, not a crash or a link error. `ctrl_of` / `is_occupied` are the single source of truth on the runtime side, mirrored by `emit_map_ctrl_of` / `emit_map_is_occupied`, and two tests pin it: `control_byte_encoding_matches_codegen` (the literal values and the invariants codegen depends on) and `tagged_probe_survives_tombstones_and_resize` (2,000 keys through tombstones and several resizes, asserting both that live keys are found with the right value and that absent keys still miss). The E2E sibling `map_control_byte_tag_survives_resize_and_tombstones` drives all three EMITTED probe families the same way. The probe test was verified to BITE: dropping the tag on the resize path fails it.

NOTE for anyone changing the archives: the encoding change makes any previously built runtime archive an ABI mismatch, so all five (lean, full, arrow, wasm, wasm-threads) were rebuilt. A stale archive here would not fail to link — it would answer lookups wrongly.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while benchmarking the #127 Word Ladder kata (kara-katas leetcode/101-200/127-word-ladder/bench), whose BFS is ~390k freshly built 5-byte Strings and ~390k String-keyed map lookups per punch and almost no arithmetic.

HEADLINE (x86-64 container): kara 293.6ms +/- 19.0 is LAST among the compiled languages -- rust 212.4 +/- 15.2, go 260.7 +/- 19.8, c 78.5 +/- 7.9. Correcting for the hash-fairness axis makes it WORSE, not better: kara's Map[String,_] hashes with FxHash (rotl5 ^ byte, * 0x517cc1b727220a95) while Rust's DEFAULT HashMap uses SipHash-1-3, so an equal-hash Rust lane (word_ladder_fasthash.rs, same FxHash constants) runs 177.3 +/- 22.6 against kara's 287.5 +/- 33.0 in one hyperfine session -- 1.62x, up from 1.38x at default hashers. SipHash was only costing Rust 1.18x.

ISOLATION (two focused microbenchmarks, both cross-checked to equal sinks):

1. STRING CONSTRUCTION IS NOT THE PROBLEM. The kata's `replace_char` (build a fresh String char-by-char with `push`) run 104,000 times, no map involved: kara 5.5ms +/- 0.7, rust 5.4ms +/- 0.6 -- a dead tie (1.03x, inside sigma). This CORRECTS the standing framing in kara-katas/BENCHMARKS.md, which attributes the corpus's residual string deficit to '1-byte push_str loops'. On this shape the push loop is at parity.

2. THE STRING-KEYED MAP IS. Build a Map[String,i64] of 3,125 five-byte words and look every one up, 60 rounds, against an equal-hash (FxHash) Rust HashMap doing the same: kara 37.9ms +/- 2.9, rust 15.5ms +/- 1.2 -- 2.45x. That single ratio accounts for the whole #127 deficit. RE-MEASURED 2026-07-28, and the headline finding changed: THE INSTRUCTION-COUNT GAP IS GONE. x86-64 container, `word_ladder.kara` vs `word_ladder.rs` (rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on, a faithful port — same linear `nth_letter`, same `replace_char`, verified by reading both), callgrind Ir: kara 1,782,104,538 vs rust 1,789,977,743 — kara 0.4% FEWER instructions. The entry's standing '1.235x whole-program I-ref ratio' is stale; B-2026-07-28-2's ASCII-const chars lowering closed it. WALL TIME STILL DIFFERS: 15 runs each, kara min 227.9ms / median 243.1ms vs rust min 179.1ms / median 184.5ms — 1.27x on min. Equal instructions and 1.27x time means the residual is now ENTIRELY IPC, which is a different problem from the one this entry was opened on and wants different tools. CACHEGRIND (cache-sim + branch-sim): D1 misses kara 8,896,520 vs rust 3,919,982 (2.27x); D1 read miss rate 2.1% vs 1.0%; conditional mispredicts kara 20,883,828 vs rust 11,064,910 (1.89x). Those two are the whole IPC story — LL misses are negligible on both (29K vs 24K), so everything is L2-resident and the cost is L1-miss latency, not DRAM. ATTRIBUTED, which is what this entry has been missing: `cg_annotate` on a KARAC_DEBUG_INFO build puts 5,988,829 of kara's 8,483,251 D1 READ misses (70.6%) in `karac_eq_String` ALONE — more than Rust's entire program (3,594,102). The kata's own `neighbors` accounts for 956,738 (11.3%) and malloc for 646,204 (7.6%). MECHANISM: `KaracMap::lookup` (runtime/src/map.rs) probes a status byte that is only BUCKET_EMPTY / BUCKET_OCCUPIED / BUCKET_TOMBSTONE — it carries NO hash information — so every OCCUPIED slot on the probe chain calls the full `eq_fn`, which dereferences the stored key's `{ptr,len,cap}` and then its heap bytes. With 3,125 individually malloc'd 5-byte keys those bytes are scattered, so each comparison is a pointer chase into a random line. Rust's hashbrown stores a 7-BIT HASH FRAGMENT in its control byte and rejects a non-matching slot without touching the key at all. QUANTIFIED, and one hypothesis was REFUTED on the way: `karac_eq_String` is called 4,348,884 times against `karac_hash_String`'s 4,003,331 — i.e. 1.09 eq per lookup, NOT the 2.5-4 a long-probe-chain story would predict (the map sits at ~38% load, so miss probes are short). The cost is not probe length; it is that kara dereferences a cold key on ~4.35M occasions where Rust does so only on hits plus a ~1/128 false-positive rate — roughly 0.85M. A 7-bit tag should therefore remove ~80% of eq calls and with them ~4.8M of kara's 8.9M D1 misses, landing at ~4.1M against Rust's 3.9M. HONEST LIMIT ON THAT PROJECTION: it accounts for the MISS delta, which is fully attributed. The MISPREDICT delta (kara 20.9M vs rust 11.1M conditional) is NOT attributed — Rust inlines the whole lookup into `word_ladder::main`, so its 9.79M mispredicts cannot be split against kara's `neighbors` 16.1M + `karac_eq_String` 3.0M. Do not assume the tag fixes both. WHY THIS IS NOT A ONE-FILE CHANGE, which is the main thing a future session needs to know before starting: `src/codegen/mono.rs` emits its OWN monomorphized probe loops against the same three constants (its comment at the `BUCKET_*` consts says they 'must match the runtime's'), and `src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs` iterates occupied slots the same way. The status encoding is a codegen/runtime ABI with a pinned offsets test (`karac_map_field_offsets_match_codegen`). Changing it means changing lookup, find_insert_slot, insert, remove, resize and the iteration in BOTH places consistently; if they disagree the failure mode is a silent wrong answer (a lookup that misses a present key), not a crash. Suggested encoding, which keeps the sentinels distinguishable: EMPTY = 0, TOMBSTONE = 1, OCCUPIED = 0x80 | (hash7 & 0x7f) so any occupied byte is >= 0x80 and can never alias a sentinel.
investigation:
TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ORIGINAL REPORT, both established by experiment rather than reasoning. Recording them in full because each one would otherwise be re-guessed by the next person.

CORRECTION 1 -- THE INDIRECT CALLS ARE NOT THE COST. The original entry named the erased runtime's per-probe indirect hash_fn/eq_fn calls as the prime suspect, by analogy with the ~2.3x qsort callback handicap #274 measured. That analogy is FALSE here. Control: KaracMap's exact probe re-implemented in Rust twice over the same 3,125-key data, once reaching hash/eq through stored fn pointers and once calling them directly, everything else identical -- 3.6ms +/- 0.3 vs 3.7ms +/- 0.2, a wash. An indirect call whose target is identical on every iteration predicts perfectly; qsort's callback is expensive because it blocks inlining of a comparison that would otherwise be two instructions, which is not the situation for a String hash. The FFI boundary still cost something -- removing it is worth the measured 1.13x in fix 2 -- but that is the opaque call and the out-param protocol, not the indirection.

CORRECTION 2 -- THE MAP IS NOT WHERE THE KATA DEFICIT LIVES. The original entry asserted that the 2.45x map microbenchmark ratio 'accounts for the whole #127 deficit'. That was an INFERENCE from a microbenchmark, never a measurement, and intervention refutes it: with BOTH fixes landed, #127 measures 265.3ms +/- 14.2 against the equal-hash Rust lane's 145.7 +/- 5.3 = 1.82x, against 287.5 vs 177.3 = 1.62x before (absolute times on this container are not stable across sessions -- an unmodified rust binary has measured 164.1ms and later 123.7ms on the same program -- so only the ratios travel). Improving the map twice moved the kata ratio not at all. Per-A/B on the kata itself: fix 1 gave 267.9 vs 269.8 (wash), fix 2 gave 260.1 vs 256.6 (wash). The reason is visible once looked for: ~20 of every 25 candidate lookups in #127 MISS, and a miss terminates at the first EMPTY bucket -- one status byte load, no eq call -- so the probe was never the hot part of that kata.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED AND SHOULD NOT BE RE-DERIVED:
* The mono approach is sound and its ceiling is parity. Map[i64,i64] lookup, which already takes the scalar mono path, measures 2.2ms +/- 0.2 against Rust's 2.1ms +/- 0.2 on the same shape -- 1.05x. That is the proof the probe design is not the limit.
* Map[String,i64] lookup after fix 2 is 3.5ms net vs Rust's 1.8ms -- still ~1.94x, so roughly 9ns per lookup is unaccounted for and is NOT in the probe loop. Prime remaining suspect is the CALL SITE rather than the map: each lookup materializes the key's {ptr,len,cap} aggregate into an alloca and hands over its address, then wraps the result in an Option through PHIs, where the Rust comparison passes an existing &String.
* Insert splits as: steady-state update 1.9x, growth 3.2x (before fix 1). Allocation counts are IDENTICAL between the two languages (191,288 vs 191,292 mallocs on the insert benchmark), so no extra key clone is happening -- it is pure per-operation compute.

NEXT STEP, and the methodological point: re-attribute the kata deficit BY INTERVENTION, not by microbenchmark. The remaining #127/#126 gap is spread across the per-candidate String lifecycle (build a 5-byte String, probe, free it) at roughly 4.25M candidates per run; the isolated String build already measures at parity with Rust (5.5ms vs 5.4ms over 104k builds), so the cost is in the surrounding lifecycle, not in push. Land one change at a time and measure the kata, because this entry is now a two-for-two record of isolated microbenchmarks predicting the wrong thing.

SESSION 2026-07-27 — NOT ADVANCED; RECORDING ONE NEGATIVE RESULT AND A HARD BLOCKER, so neither is re-derived.
BLOCKER (why the prescribed next step was not attempted): this entry's own methodological rule is 're-attribute the kata deficit BY INTERVENTION, not by microbenchmark ... land one change at a time and measure the kata'. That requires the kara-katas repo (the #127 bench plus its equal-hash Rust lanes) and hyperfine. NEITHER is present in the cloud container this session ran in (`../kara-katas` absent; `which hyperfine` empty). Doing microbenchmark-driven work here would repeat exactly the error this entry is already two-for-two on, so no speculative change was landed. Whoever picks this up needs a developer environment with the kata repo checked out.
NEGATIVE RESULT (cheap, and it retires the named suspect for these shapes): the entry's 'prime remaining suspect is the CALL SITE ... each lookup materializes the key's {ptr,len,cap} aggregate into an alloca and hands over its address, then wraps the result in an Option through PHIs'. The PRE-OPTIMIZATION IR does show exactly that — a `%map.get.key` alloca receiving a load-then-store copy out of the key's own slot, plus four `opt.*` PHIs feeding an `insertvalue` chain (`examples/dump_ir` on `fn probe(m: ref Map[String,i64], k: String) -> i64 { match m.get(k) { Some(v) => v, None => 0 } }`). But it does NOT survive the real pipeline: in the `karac build` binary the redundant copy is gone (SROA collapses the two allocas to one stack slot, whose address is `lea`'d straight into the call), the Option aggregate never materializes, and — because the runtime archive is built with `lto = "fat"` — the monomorphized probe from fix 2 (54aac61) is INLINED at link time: the emitted binary contains no `karac_map_str_i64_get` call symbol at all, only `map_new` / `map_insert_old` / `map_free_*`. So for this shape the call-site materialization, the Option PHIs, AND the residual FFI boundary are all already optimized away, and the ~9ns/lookup must be elsewhere. CAVEAT, stated because it matters: this was observed where the caller inlines the probe; a call site that does not inline was not measured, and none of this was measured on the kata itself — per the blocker above.
INCIDENTAL, worth knowing when benchmarking this: a naive 'N rounds x M lookups' Kara probe is NOT a valid harness — auto-par claims the lookup loop (the emitted binary calls `karac_par_reduce`), so any such timing must be taken with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` or it measures the scheduler.

SESSION 2026-07-27 (part 2) — kata repo obtained; ATTRIBUTION DONE ON THE KATA, as this entry demanded. No fix landed yet; what follows is measurement, and it REFRAMES the search a third time.
METHOD: `hyperfine` is still unavailable, so wall-clock is 5 interleaved reps per lane (medians) and the real attribution comes from valgrind callgrind/cachegrind, which are DETERMINISTIC and immune to this container's timing drift. Both lanes verified to print the same answer (755481159). Lanes: `word_ladder.kara` built by `karac build` vs `word_ladder_fasthash.rs` at `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on` (equal hash, equal safety).
SAME-SESSION BASELINE: kara 313.7ms vs rust 149.2ms = 2.10x (min-based 2.12x). Recorded as the baseline for future interventions; do not compare it to the 1.82x in the section above — different session, and this entry already notes only ratios travel.
FINDING 1 — ALLOCATION IS NOT THE COST, NOW PROVEN ON THE KATA (previously only shown on the insert microbenchmark). Allocation COUNTS are essentially identical: 3,959,415 allocs / 3,959,415 frees (kara) vs 3,959,119 / 3,959,118 (rust) — 0.007% apart. Allocator INSTRUCTIONS are a dead wash too: summing every malloc.c/arena.c entry gives kara 567.1M Ir vs rust 574.6M Ir. So the per-candidate String lifecycle does not differ in allocator traffic; the 'build/probe/free 4.25M times' framing above is right that the lifecycle is the arena, but the free half is not where the time goes.
FINDING 2 — THE GAP IS ENTIRELY NON-ALLOCATION WORK. Total Ir: kara 2,360.7M vs rust 1,588.7M (1.49x). Net of the allocator: 1,793.6M vs 1,014.1M = 1.77x. That 1.77x is the whole deficit and it lives in emitted user/runtime code.
FINDING 3 — A NEW AXIS THIS ENTRY HAD NOT IDENTIFIED: instruction count does NOT explain the wall-clock. Wall-clock ratio 2.10x EXCEEDS the I-ref ratio 1.45x, so kara additionally loses on memory behaviour. cachegrind: D refs 754.0M vs 547.4M (1.38x); D1 misses 6.94M vs 3.25M (2.14x); LL refs 17.56M vs 3.25M (5.40x); branches 458.1M vs 287.9M (1.59x), of which conditional 437.7M vs 265.6M (1.65x). The 5.4x LL-ref figure is the standout — kara pushes 5x more traffic past L1. CONSEQUENCE FOR PLANNING: closing the instruction-count gap alone cannot reach parity; there is a data-locality component, and any candidate fix must be judged on D1/LL misses as well as Ir.
WHERE THE INSTRUCTIONS SIT: the emitted binary's hot code is one inlined blob — fat LTO folds the monomorphized map probe into the caller (no `karac_map_str_i64_get` call symbol survives, consistent with part 1's negative result), so callgrind attributes 50.6% to a single unnamed region and the rest to `main`. Function-level attribution therefore needs a build with symbols preserved / inlining restrained — that is the first concrete step for the next session, before any code change.
SUGGESTED NEXT STEP (unchanged in spirit, sharpened by the above): build the kata lane with debug symbols and reduced inlining to get per-function Ir, then attack whichever of {extra conditional branches (1.65x — bounds checks / Option tag tests / overflow checks), extra D refs (1.38x), poor locality (2.14x D1)} dominates. Measure each intervention on the kata with callgrind Ir + cachegrind D1, not wall-clock, so the result is not lost in container noise.

SESSION 2026-07-27 (part 3) — STEP 1 (per-function attribution) ATTEMPTED AND BLOCKED. Recording the negative result and the four things tried, so the next person does not repeat them.
GOAL: split the 1.77x non-alloc Ir gap across the kata's three per-candidate phases — `nth_letter` (an O(26) `.chars()` walk), `replace_char` (a `.chars()`+push String build) and `word_set.get(cand)` (the probe).
FAIRNESS CHECK FIRST (worth knowing): the Rust lane is a FAITHFUL mirror — its `nth_letter` does the same O(26) `alphabet.chars()` walk and its `replace_char` the same char-push loop. So the 2.10x is not a kata-authoring artifact; both languages do the same algorithmic work.
WHY ABLATION DOES NOT WORK HERE: the BFS is self-referential — the probe result decides whether a candidate is enqueued — so removing or stubbing any phase changes the traversal and therefore the amount of work measured. Ablation cannot isolate a phase on this kata.
WHAT WAS TRIED FOR SYMBOLS, ALL FOUR FAILED: (1) thin-LTO + debuginfo runtime archive (`CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=thin CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=line-tables-only`, linked via `KARAC_RUNTIME=`) — does not help, because the probe is NOT a runtime symbol at all: `karac_map_str_i64_get` does not exist in the runtime archive (its exported map surface is `karac_map_get`/`_insert`/`_lookup_slot`/...). Fix 2's monomorphized probe is emitted by CODEGEN into the user module, so runtime LTO settings are irrelevant to it. (2) `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1` on `karac build` — the linked binary has ZERO `.debug_*` sections. (3) the same env var on the `compile_to_ir` path (examples/dump_ir) — the emitted IR contains no `llvm.dbg.cu` / `DICompileUnit` / `DISubprogram` either, so codegen is not emitting DWARF on these paths regardless of the gate (the gate additionally requires a `source_filename` to be threaded in — see `di_init`). (4) building both lanes at `-O1` (`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=1` / `rustc -C opt-level=1`) so functions would survive inlining — the kara binary STILL exposes no user-function symbols; all 228 text symbols are Rust runtime internals. karac emits user functions with internal linkage and they do not reach the symbol table at any optimization level.
CONCLUSION: there is currently NO end-to-end way to get per-function or per-line attribution out of an AOT kara binary. That is a compiler TOOLING gap, filed separately as B-2026-07-27-4, and it blocks this entry and any successor perf investigation. Closing it is the real Step 1: either make `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO` produce DWARF that survives to the linked binary, or add a profiling mode that gives emitted user functions external linkage + noinline. Until then the only usable signals on this bug are the WHOLE-PROGRAM aggregates recorded in part 2 (Ir, D refs, D1/LL misses, branches), which do narrow the search but cannot name a function.

SESSION 2026-07-27 (part 4) — BLOCKER CLEARED, FIRST REAL ATTRIBUTION. B-2026-07-27-4 is fixed (f569aac: `strip -x` was erasing the symbols and DWARF), so the kata can now be profiled per function. FIRST NAMED ATTRIBUTION of the #127 deficit, callgrind Ir on the kara lane:
  50.60%  ./word_ladder.kara:neighbors   1,194.5M
   9.47%  libc _int_free                   223.5M
   8.99%  karac_hash_String                212.2M
   6.91%  libc malloc                      163.1M
   4.68%  karac_eq_String                  110.5M
   4.60%  libc free                        108.7M
   2.57%  karac_free_buf                    60.6M
   2.42%  libc memcpy                       57.2M
   2.11%  ./word_ladder.kara:main           49.7M
   2.05%  karac_alloc_or_panic              48.3M
   0.86%  karac_string_clone                20.4M
   0.59%  karac_map_insert_old              13.9M
READ: the map PROBE primitives are only ~13.7% combined (`karac_hash_String` + `karac_eq_String` = 322.7M) — consistent with this entry's CORRECTION 2 that the probe was never the hot part, and with the ~20-of-25 miss rate terminating at the first empty bucket. The dominant cost by far is `neighbors` itself at 50.6%, i.e. the per-candidate generation loop (`nth_letter`'s O(26) `.chars()` walk + `replace_char`'s `.chars()`+push build), which at -O2 has the inlined String machinery folded into it. Rust's counterpart `main` is 54.75% of a 1,588.7M total = 869.9M, against kara's neighbors+main = 1,244.2M for the same algorithmic work — a 1.43x gap concentrated in candidate generation, NOT in the map. NEXT STEP is now well-posed for the first time: attack the char-iteration + String-build lowering inside `neighbors`, and judge candidates on that function's Ir plus the D1/LL figures from part 2. (Per-LINE attribution inside `neighbors` needs the line-accuracy follow-up noted on B-2026-07-27-4.)

SESSION 2026-07-27 (part 5) — FIRST INTERVENTION-BASED ATTRIBUTION, and an ARCHITECTURE SPLIT this entry had not seen. Run on an arm64 Mac (native, not the x86 container every earlier part used), hyperfine 15 runs / 3 warmup, both lanes verified to print 755481159.
BASELINE HERE IS 1.34x, NOT 2.10x: kara 141.6ms +/- 2.2 vs the equal-hash Rust lane 105.4ms +/- 3.2. Part 2 measured 2.10x on x86. Same sources, same equal-hash Rust twin, both built -O2/-O with overflow checks on. So a LARGE PART OF THIS DEFICIT IS ARCHITECTURE- OR TOOLCHAIN-DEPENDENT, and any future number must say which machine produced it. Sigma here is ~1.5% of the mean, so a 3% effect is detectable — this box is a usable measurement environment despite having no valgrind.
ATTRIBUTION BY INTERVENTION ON THE KATA — what this entry has demanded since part 2, and what no earlier session could do. Two cumulative variants, each still printing 755481159:
  base                                        141.6ms   1.34x vs Rust
  A = nth_letter without its .chars() walk     128.1ms   1.21x   (-13.5ms, 9.5% of runtime)
  B = A + replace_char built over .bytes()     122.9ms   1.17x   (-5.2ms,  3.7% of runtime)
  rust (equal hash)                            105.4ms
So THE TWO `.chars()` LOOPS ARE 18.7ms OF THE 36.2ms GAP — 52% of the deficit — and the residual after removing both is 1.17x. This finally puts a number on part 4's callgrind read (`neighbors` at 50.6%) and confirms it: the cost is candidate generation, not the map. Note the variants are DIAGNOSTIC instruments, not proposed kata edits — they are kept out of the kata repo deliberately, since the Rust lane does the same O(26) walk and changing only one side would break the comparison.
THE ASCII CONST-CHARS FAST PATH IS FIRING, so B-2026-07-27-7 works and is NOT the remaining problem: `nth_letter`'s emitted IR contains ZERO `karac_string_decode_char` calls. Its residual 9.5% is therefore the ITERATION COUNT, not per-char decoding — 26 iterations x 4.25M calls of a branch-free byte loop. Removing it needs the linear search over a CONSTANT string to collapse to a single indexed load, which LLVM does not do even given the stride-1 shape that module was written to expose.
WELL-POSED NEXT STEP, with its ceiling already measured: the remaining `.chars()` cost that a compiler change can actually reach is `replace_char`'s — a loop over a RUNTIME string (a `ref String` param), which cannot qualify for the const-literal proof. The shape to try is an ASCII FAST INNER LOOP WITH DYNAMIC BAILOUT: a stride-1 loop that runs while the current byte is < 0x80 and exits to the existing decoder on the first byte that is not. It needs NO compile-time proof (unlike ascii_const_chars) so it applies to every `.chars()` loop over a runtime string. Ceiling on THIS kata: 3.7%. Deliberately NOT attempted in this session — the failure mode of getting it wrong is a silent miscompile (binding each byte as a char, so `é` yields two bogus chars), the same class ascii_const_chars documents at length, and it wants a full verification budget rather than the tail of a long session.
TWO METHOD NOTES worth keeping. (1) f569aac's symbol retention WORKS ON macOS TOO, not just Linux: `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1 karac build` yields a binary whose symbol table contains `_neighbors` etc. (451 text symbols vs none by default), so per-function profiling is available here via `sample`. (2) RECONFIRMING THIS ENTRY'S OWN WARNING the hard way: a small driver written to call `nth_letter` in a loop compiled to a binary whose `main` calls `karac_par_reduce` — auto-par claimed the loop and the disassembly showed no `nth_letter` at all. Any probe harness here needs `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, or it measures the scheduler.

SESSION 2026-07-28 — RE-MEASURED ON x86 AFTER B-2026-07-27-7 / -8, AND RETITLED. Part 5 measured the intervention on arm64; this is the same kata on the x86 container every earlier part used, so the two architectures can finally be compared on the same code.
#127, callgrind Ir (deterministic; wall-clock on this container is not): kara 1,962.3M vs the equal-hash Rust lane 1,588.7M = 1.235x, against the part-2 baseline of 2,360.7M vs 1,588.7M = 1.45x. `neighbors` itself went 1,194.5M -> 796.9M Ir (-33%), and its share of the program 50.60% -> 40.61%. Both lanes still print 755481159.
#126 (Word Ladder II), same method: kara 2,268.6M vs rust 1,899.4M = 1.194x. Both lanes print 125559906.
ARCHITECTURE SPLIT, SHARPENED — and it CORRECTS a part-5 statement. Part 5 concluded that `nth_letter`'s residual 9.5% is iteration count because 'the linear search over a CONSTANT string [does not] collapse to a single indexed load, which LLVM does not do even given the stride-1 shape that module was written to expose'. That is true on arm64 but NOT on x86: an isolated equal-source `nth_letter` probe (4.25M calls) goes 699,426,390 -> 42,802,319 Ir with B-2026-07-27-7, which is EXACTLY the figure the already-branch-free `.bytes()` spelling of the same program produces, and the disassembly shows the walk gone — `movzbl (%r14,%rcx,1)`, a direct indexed load, with the outer loop unrolled 4x. So on x86 LLVM does collapse it once the offset PHI is removed; the arm64 backend apparently does not. Anyone chasing the 9.5% should measure their own architecture first rather than assume part 5's number.
DISPOSITION. Not closed, because the residual is real and unattributed. But the original claim this entry was opened on — that `Map[String, _]` is where the kata deficit lives — is now refuted by three independent measurements (CORRECTION 2's intervention A/B, part 4's callgrind attribution putting the probe primitives at ~13.7%, part 5's intervention), so the title now says what the entry is actually about. The ONE remaining fix that a compiler change can reach — the dynamic-bailout ASCII `.chars()` loop for RUNTIME strings, ceiling 3.7% on this kata — is split out as B-2026-07-28-2 so it can be picked up as a bounded piece of work instead of being buried at the end of a five-part investigation log. What stays here is the residual with no named cause: after both `.chars()` loops are removed the kata is still 1.17x (arm64), and part 2's cachegrind figures (D1 misses 2.14x, LL refs 5.40x) say part of that is data locality rather than instruction count.

title: Calling a closure bound as a `for`-loop element returns 0 under `karac build`/JIT (interp correct). `for op in ops { v = op(v); }` where `ops: Array/Vec[Fn(i64)->i64]` — the loop-var closure call yields 0; `let op = ops[0]; op(5)` and `ops[0](5)` both work.
detail: The codegen `for`-loop ELEMENT BINDING mishandles a closure-typed element: the loop variable `op` bound by `for op in ops` does not receive the correct closure value (`{fn_ptr, env}`), so a subsequent `op(v)` call returns 0 instead of invoking the closure. Silent — no crash, no diagnostic; `karac run --interp` is correct. The for-loop codegen (src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs, a large file with many element-type-specialized paths) almost certainly routes the Fn-typed element through a scalar/other path that loads the wrong width/pointer, or a fallback that leaves the loop var's closure fn_ptr null. NOT the closure representation itself: `let op = ops[0]` (index-element binding) + call works, and direct `ops[0](5)` / `ops[1](5)` work — only the for-loop element binding is wrong.
investigation: Probe round 13 batch 11 (HOF). Minimal: `fn main() { let ops = [|x| x + 1, |x| x * 10]; let mut v = 5; for op in ops { v = op(v); } println(f"{v}"); }` -> JIT prints 0, interp prints 60 (5->6->60). Localization: h4 `let op = ops[0]; op(5)` = 6 on both (OK); h2 `ops[0](5)`/`ops[1](5)` = 6/50 on both (OK); h5 same over `Vec[Fn]` = 0 (JIT)/60 (interp) — so NOT array-specific; h6 over an array of CAPTURING closures = 0 (JIT)/10100 (interp) — so NOT capture-specific; h3 single-element array in a for-loop = 0 (JIT)/105 (interp). Consistently: the `for`-loop element binding of a closure is the broken construct. Note batch 4's closure-in-Vec test passed because it applied the closures via an index/`.iter().map()` chain, not a bare `for op in ops` element binding.
resolution: ROOT CAUSE CORRECTION: the entry's hypothesis (a bad for-loop element binding) was WRONG. The emitted IR bound the loop var correctly — `%for.v.elem = load { ptr, ptr }` then `store { ptr, ptr } %for.v.elem, ptr %op` is the right closure fat pointer. The defect was in the CALL: `compile_call` routes an indirect closure call on `closure_fn_types.contains_key(name)`, and the for-loop element binding never registered the loop var there, so `op(v)` missed that dispatch and fell through to the unknown-callee path, which emits a constant `i64 0` (the body was literally `store i64 0, ptr %v`). `let op = ops[i]; op(v)` always worked because the `let` path has its own registration via `let_binding_fn_value_type` — which is precisely why the bug presented as for-loop-specific and looked like a binding bug.
