title: A PLAIN type alias whose base is not `i64`-shaped, used as a parameter or return type, lowers to the `i64` unknown-name fall-through in codegen: `type Plain = Vec[i64]; fn total(xs: Plain)` passes `karac check` and `karac run --interp` but fails LLVM module verification under `karac build` / `karac run` (JIT). A REFINEMENT alias over the same base works.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO (three files; `check` accepts all of them):

  // (a) generic plain alias — BUILD FAILS
  type Plain[T] = Vec[T];
  fn total(xs: Plain[i64]) -> i64 { let mut t = 0; for x in xs { t = t + x; } t }
  fn main() { let v = vec![1, 2, 3]; println(total(v)); }
  // error: codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Call parameter type
  //   does not match function signature!  %v1 = load { ptr, i64, i64 } ...
  //   i64  %call = call i64 @total({ ptr, i64, i64 } %v1)"

  // (b) NON-generic plain alias — SAME FAILURE, so this is not about generics
  type Plain = Vec[i64];
  fn total(xs: Plain) -> i64 { ... }

  // (c) plain alias over String — same class, hits the return position too
  type Name = String;
  fn shout(n: Name) -> String { n }
  // error: "Function return type does not match operand type of return inst!"

CONTROLS THAT PASS, which localize it precisely:
  * `type Count = i64; fn bump(n: Count) -> i64 { n + 1 }` BUILDS and runs —
    the alias base is already `i64`-shaped, so the fall-through happens to be
    the right layout. That is why this has stayed invisible: the aliases people
    write in tests are mostly newtype-ish integer aliases.
  * `type NonEmpty[T] = Vec[T] where self.len() > 0;` — the REFINEMENT sibling
    of (a) — builds and runs correctly. Codegen resolves refinement aliases
    through its `refinement_base` / `refinement_generic_params` maps
    (`src/codegen.rs` ~1164-1193, and `tests/codegen.rs::test_ir_refinement_
    over_string_matches_base_layout` pins exactly the non-`i64`-base layout arm
    that this bug is missing). Plain aliases have NO equivalent map, so the
    paradox is that adding a `where` clause FIXES the program.
  * `karac run --interp` prints the right answer for every case above.

So the failure axis is (plain alias) x (non-`i64` base) x (param/return
position), and the likely fix is the plain-alias twin of the existing
refinement-base map: populate an alias->base layout map before
`build_struct_types` / signature lowering, the same ordering fix the
refinement arm already needed.

SEVERITY high on divergence, not on blast radius of a wrong ANSWER: it is a
loud LLVM verification failure, never a silent miscompile. But `karac check`
reporting 'All checks passed' on a program `karac build` cannot compile is the
run-vs-build class this repo treats as high, and `type Name = String` is an
entirely ordinary thing to write.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced as the CONTROL in B-2026-07-29-26's own repro — the
`where`-free `type Plain[T] = Vec[T]` arm that was supposed to demonstrate
correct behavior type-checked but would not build. Pre-existing and untouched
by that fix (no `Type::Refinement` is involved); confirmed against 5445e85.

FIXED (b528fa2). Root cause exactly as filed: codegen kept a base map for the
REFINEMENT arm of `Item::TypeAlias` and none for the plain arm, so a plain
alias name fell through to `llvm_type_for_name`'s unknown-name `i64` default.
The fix is the plain-alias twin of that map, populated from the same
`populate_type_alias_bases` pass — which already runs before
`register_struct_metadata` / `build_struct_types`, so the ordering the
refinement arm once needed was in place.

  1. `plain_alias_bases` / `plain_alias_generic_params` (`src/codegen.rs`) —
     the `where`-free siblings of `refinement_bases` /
     `refinement_generic_params`, filled from the same loop's `else` arm.
     TAIT aliases (`type X = impl Trait;`) are excluded: the RHS has no
     layout to project and is still `E_TAIT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED_YET` at
     witness-required use sites, so peeling to it would only obscure that
     diagnostic.
  2. All four sites that peeled a refinement now peel a plain alias too, and
     were renamed to say so: `llvm_type_for_type_expr`, `llvm_type_for_name`,
     `refinement_base_name` -> `type_alias_base_name`, and
     `resolve_refinement_alias_te` -> `resolve_type_alias_te`. The
     `TypeExpr`-level arm additionally SUBSTITUTES the use-site generic args
     into the base (`Plain[i64]` -> `Vec[i64]`) rather than lowering the
     uninstantiated base — a strict improvement the refinement arm inherits.
  3. `register_struct_metadata` (`src/codegen/declarations.rs`) peels the
     alias before writing `struct_field_type_names` /
     `struct_field_type_exprs`. Found while widening the repro: the reported
     param/return failure is only half the surface — a FIELD declared through
     an alias recorded the ALIAS name, so `h.pt.x` (field `pt: Pt`,
     `type Pt = Point;`) died in `field_index_for` with "cannot resolve field
     'x' on this receiver", and an alias-typed `String`/`Vec` field was
     invisible to drop synthesis. A struct's own generic params shadow a
     same-named global alias here (`type T = String;` next to
     `struct S[T] { v: T }`), matching the `type_subst`-first precedence
     `llvm_type_for_name` already applied.
  4. `prune_cyclic_type_aliases` — a guard the peel newly requires, not part
     of the reported defect. Nothing upstream rejects `type A = A;`,
     `type A = B; type B = A;`, or `type Vec = Vec[i64];`, and peeling those
     recurses forever. Entries on a base-name cycle are dropped at population
     time, so such a program falls back to the bounded (wrong) unknown-name
     layout instead of overflowing the compiler's stack. Covers refinements
     too, where the same hazard was already latent.

VERIFIED: all three filed arms (generic alias, non-generic alias, `String`
alias reaching the return position) build and run, AOT output byte-identical
to `--interp`. Widened checks agree across both lanes for aliases over
struct / tuple / Map, alias CHAINS, enum-variant payloads, `shared struct`
fields, `Vec[Alias]` iteration, method dispatch on an alias-typed receiver,
and the generic-param shadowing case.

PINNED: `tests/codegen.rs` — `test_ir_plain_alias_over_string_matches_base_
layout` and `test_ir_plain_alias_over_vec_matches_base_layout` (IR-level, the
plain twins of `test_ir_refinement_over_string_matches_base_layout`),
`test_e2e_plain_alias_param_and_return` (the filed repro),
`test_e2e_plain_alias_struct_field_and_nested_access` (the field leg), and
`test_e2e_plain_alias_chain_and_cycle_are_bounded` (chain peel + cycle
guard). `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_plain_alias_struct_fields_no_leak`
covers the leak / double-free pair on either side of the struct-field peel.

title: Auto-par's early-exit gate declines a reduction for a `break`/`continue` that targets a NESTED loop and therefore cannot exit the reduction body at all -- the idiomatic `loop { match cur { Some(n) => ..., None => break } }` list walk never fans out
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while building the probe for B-2026-07-30-1. The first probe used the
idiomatic list-walk shape and did not fan out even after that bug's analyzer fix; rewriting
the walk as `while cur.is_some() { let n = cur.unwrap(); ... }` -- semantically identical, no
`break` -- made it fire. The analyzer had already recognized the reduction in both versions;
the decline is in CODEGEN.

MECHANISM. `try_emit_reduction_lowering` bails on `block_has_early_exit(&shape.body)`
(src/codegen/reduce.rs). The rationale is sound as stated: "early exits in the (post-stripped)
body would cross the worker-fn boundary and generate `ret <T>` inside a void worker fn ->
invalid IR." But `expr_has_early_exit` returns true for `Return | Break | Continue` at its
FIRST arm, and separately RECURSES into nested `While` / `For` / `Loop` bodies. So a `break`
that belongs to a loop nested inside the reduction body -- one that provably cannot transfer
control out of the body -- is counted as an early exit of the body.

REPRO (both bodies compute the same thing over the same `shared` list; only the walk differs):
  loop { match cur { Some(n) => { acc = acc + n.val; cur = n.next } None => break } }   0 karac_par_* DECLINES
  while cur.is_some() { let n = cur.unwrap(); acc = acc + n.val; cur = n.next }         1 karac_par_* FIRES
Measured on the second form: 400000 iterations x 12-node list, 0.10 s -> 0.04 s wall, 100% ->
~330% CPU. The first form gets none of that.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS ONE SHAPE: `loop { ... break }` is how you write a walk over an
`Option`-linked structure in Kara today (`while cur.is_some()` costs an extra `unwrap`), and
the whole point of B-2026-07-30-1 was to unblock exactly the per-iteration-list-build-and-fold
family. The two gates compose to leave the most idiomatic member of that family sequential.

LIKELY FIX: make the classification control-flow aware rather than shape-blind. An unlabeled
`break` / `continue` is an early exit of the BODY only if it is not enclosed by a nested loop
within the body; a LABELED one is an early exit iff its label is bound outside the body.
`Return` stays unconditional. The nesting depth is already available at the recursion site --
`expr_has_early_exit`'s `While` / `For` / `Loop` arms are where a nested-loop flag would be
set. Strictly a precision improvement; keep the current behaviour as the fallback for anything
the label analysis cannot resolve, since the failure mode it guards is invalid IR.

Related: B-2026-07-30-1 (the analyzer-side gate that had to be fixed before this one became
observable), B-2026-07-16-6 (the soundness gate that started the family).

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (3993c2e) ──
As the entry's LIKELY FIX predicted: made the classification control-flow-aware rather than shape-blind. `block_has_early_exit`/`expr_has_early_exit` (src/codegen/reduce.rs) now thread `(depth, labels)` — `depth` counts loops nested WITHIN the reduction body, `labels` the labels those nested loops bind. A `break`/`continue` is a BODY escape iff it targets the reduction loop: unlabeled at `depth == 0`, or labeled with a label NOT bound by a nested loop (so `break 'reduction` from inside a nested loop still escapes). `Return` stays unconditional; loop headers (`while` condition / `for` iterable) check at the current depth since a break there targets the enclosing loop. The idiomatic `loop { match cur { … None => break } }` walk now fans out. Verified: the nested-loop-break reduction emits `karac_par_reduce` and prints byte-identical to sequential (interp / auto-par ON / OFF all agree), valgrind identical to a pre-existing firing reduction (thread-pool baseline, definitely-lost 0); a break DIRECTLY in the body still declines. par_codegen 202 / codegen 2632 / memory_sanitizer 867 green; fmt + clippy clean. Tests `test_ir_reduction_fires_with_break_in_nested_loop` + `test_ir_reduction_declined_for_direct_break_in_body`. NOTE: kept as the deliberate fallback — a labeled break/continue whose label the walk cannot resolve to a nested loop still counts as an escape, since the failure it guards (a body escape emitting `ret` in a void worker fn → invalid IR) is loud.

fix: 36a7fa5
title:
`println` is not line-atomic across tasks: it emits TWO separate `write_console` calls (payload, then the newline), so two spawned tasks printing concurrently interleave into `12

` instead of `1
2
` -- makes tests/spawn_e2e.rs::test_spawn_fan_out_five_tasks_all_join flaky (~1 in 3 on a 4-core container)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by a full `cargo test --features llvm` run while working B-2026-07-30-1.
Unrelated to that change -- the failing program has no `shared` type and no reduction loop.

OBSERVED. `tests/spawn_e2e.rs::test_spawn_fan_out_five_tasks_all_join` spawns five tasks, each
`println(n)` for n in 1..=5, and asserts the printed set is {1,2,3,4,5}. Failing run printed:

  12
  <blank>
  3
  5
  4

parsed as {12, 3, 4, 5}. Re-ran the test three times in isolation: pass / FAIL / pass.

MECHANISM, CONFIRMED IN CODEGEN (not inferred from the output). `emit_nul_safe_write`
(src/codegen/control_flow.rs) writes the payload with one `write_console` call and then, when
`nl` is non-empty, emits a SECOND `write_console` call for the newline global. Each call locks
stdout on its own (`std::io::stdout().lock()` per call in the runtime), so the lock is
released between the two. Two tasks racing there produce payload-A, payload-B, newline-A,
newline-B -- exactly `12\n\n`. A single `println` is therefore atomic only for its payload,
never for the line.

WHY IT IS LOW AND NOT MEDIUM: it garbles interleaved output, it does not corrupt memory or
change computed results, and the auto-par paths that matter most already avoid it -- the
parallel-branch arm of `write_console` CAPTURES bytes for ordered replay at the join rather
than writing inline (the "auto-par never changes what your program prints" invariant). It is
the EXPLICIT-concurrency surface (`spawn` / `TaskGroup`) that writes straight through.

LIKELY FIX: make the line one write. Either append the newline into the payload buffer before
the single `write_console` (cheap for the f-string/Display arms, which already render into an
owned accumulator -- the literal-backed `cap == 0` case would need a copy), or give
`write_console` a `trailing_newline: bool` parameter so the runtime emits both under ONE
stdout lock. The second is smaller and covers every arm uniformly, at the cost of a runtime
signature change (all five archives rebuild).

NOTE the test would still be correct under the fix -- it asserts a SET, deliberately not an
order, since spawn order is not output order. The flake is purely the mid-line interleave.

── ATTEMPTED 2026-07-30, REVERTED — fix WORKS but exposes a latent leak that turns a green ASAN test red ──

MECHANISM CORRECTION. This entry says each call takes `std::io::stdout().lock()`. It does NOT. `karac_runtime_write_console` (runtime/src/lib.rs) calls raw `fwrite` on a `FILE*`; the lock is glibc's internal per-`FILE` lock, held for the duration of ONE `fwrite` and released between calls. Same race, different primitive — and it rules out the entry's suggested runtime-signature fix in favour of making the line ONE write.

SECOND CORRECTION, and the one that decides the design: a runtime-side fix would not even be REACHED by the flaking program. `finalize_write_console_wrapper` (src/codegen.rs) emits `__karac_write_console` as an inline `fwrite` whenever the program uses no `par` — the runtime chokepoint is only called when auto-par capture is needed. `spawn`/`TaskGroup` does not trip that, so the spawn test takes the inline path. The fix has to be in CODEGEN.

WHAT WAS BUILT, AND IT WORKS. A `__karac_write_console_line(data, len, nl, nl_len, stream)` internal wrapper: stage payload+newline into one function-scoped uninitialised 4 KiB alloca (two `memcpy`s, no allocation), then ONE `__karac_write_console` call — which feeds both the inline-`fwrite` path and the capture path unchanged. Lines over the buffer fall back to the original two writes. `emit_nul_safe_write` routes there only when `nl` is non-empty, so `print` keeps its single plain call. MEASURED: the five-spawned-task probe went from 14 garbled runs in 60 to 0 in 60. Oversized (4500-byte) lines, `print` vs `println`, and interp/AOT parity all verified; valgrind clean. Suites: codegen 2634, spawn_e2e 3, par_codegen 202, cli 507, interpreter 1327 — all green. Two IR regression tests written.

WHY IT WAS REVERTED. It makes `memory_sanitizer::asan_fnret_drop_temp_arg_passthrough_and_discard_single_fire` fail with a 47-byte leak. Investigated to root cause, and the leak is NOT in the println path — see the new entry B-2026-07-30-12. In short: before the change that test's program performs ONE heap allocation in total (the 4 KiB stdio buffer); the `Guard.name` strings are never allocated, because LLVM elides the whole malloc/free set. Staging adds a `memcpy` that reads the payload, which blocks that elision for this shape, so the allocations materialise — 3 × 47 bytes for 2 Guards, one of them never freed. The test has therefore been passing VACUOUSLY for this allocation class.

STATUS: the fix is ready to re-land as-is the moment B-2026-07-30-12 is fixed. Nothing about the println design needs to change; it was reverted only because landing it would turn a green test red, and a red suite on main is worse than a known cosmetic flake.

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (36a7fa5). Re-landed unchanged the moment its blocker cleared. ──

The reverted design needed no revision. B-2026-07-30-12 was fixed in 3ee768a and
`memory_sanitizer` went green (868/868) with this change applied, exactly as the
revert note predicted. Re-measured after re-landing rather than trusted: the
five-task fan-out probe went 10 garbled runs in 60 -> 0 in 60 (the earlier
attempt measured 14/60; same order, the rate is container- and load-dependent).

SHIPPED SHAPE. `__karac_write_console_line(data, len, nl, nl_len, stream)`,
internal linkage: two `memcpy`s into one function-scoped 4 KiB uninitialised
alloca, then a SINGLE `__karac_write_console`. `emit_nul_safe_write` routes there
only when the newline is non-empty, so `print` keeps its single plain call.
Over-buffer lines fall back to the original two writes -- correct, not atomic.
Emitted by `finalize_write_console_line_wrapper`, which MUST run after
`finalize_write_console_wrapper` (it calls that wrapper, whose body first has to
decide inline-`fwrite` vs capture from whether `par` is used anywhere).

THE LOAD-BEARING DESIGN POINT, restated because it is the one a re-reader will
want to undo: this belongs in CODEGEN, not the runtime. A `trailing_newline`
parameter on `karac_runtime_write_console` is smaller and DOES NOT WORK --
`finalize_write_console_wrapper` inlines `fwrite` directly whenever the program
uses no `par`, so the runtime chokepoint is never reached on precisely the
spawn-only programs that flake. Staging in front of that wrapper covers the
inline arm and the auto-par capture arm both, and needs no runtime-ABI change,
so none of the five archives rebuild.

A fixed alloca rather than a malloc because this is on every `println`; a
heap allocation per line would be a real cost on print-heavy paths.

VERIFIED BEYOND THE PROBE: a 4502-byte line takes the fallback and round-trips
byte-identically; interp and AOT output are md5-identical across print, println,
empty-line and oversized cases; valgrind clean. Suites: codegen 2636,
memory_sanitizer 868, spawn_e2e 3, cli 545, par_codegen 202, interpreter 1329,
concurrency 134, coro_e2e 34, wasm_codegen 3, typechecker 2105, ownership 381,
drop_differential 13, selfhost_codegen.

TESTS: `test_ir_println_fuses_payload_and_newline_into_one_write` and
`test_ir_print_without_newline_keeps_plain_write`, asserted on the emitted CALL
SHAPE rather than by running the program -- deliberately. The bug is a race: a
passing run proves nothing, and the pre-fix program passes most of the time
(50 of 60). The call shape is the invariant; the flake was only ever a symptom.

The entry's original "LIKELY FIX" text is left above for provenance but is
superseded on both counts -- the `stdout().lock()` mechanism was wrong (it is
glibc's per-`FILE` lock inside `fwrite`) and the runtime-signature option it
preferred is the one that cannot work.

title: `Result[T, E].clone()` is still rejected at typecheck (`no method 'clone' on type 'Result'`) after B-2026-07-29-31 gave `Option[T]` a callable one — codegen has no in-place deep-copy helper for Result's inline payload, so admitting it would emit a SHALLOW copy that aliases the source buffer.
detail:
Held back DELIBERATELY while closing B-2026-07-29-31, not overlooked.

REPRO:
  fn main() {
      let r: Result[String, i64] = Result.Ok("x");
      let c = r.clone();          // no method 'clone' on type 'Result'
  }
`Option[String]` in the same position now works.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST AN ALLOWLIST ENTRY. `Result` shares `Option`'s `{tag, w0, w1, w2}` inline-payload overlay, and `type_supports_clone` already answers TRUE for it — so the typechecker half is a one-line change. The backend half is not there: `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`'s `Option` arm routes to `emit_option_value_clone_fn`, which is `Option`-specific (it reads the `Option` layout and its `Some` tag, and calls `deep_copy_option_inline_payload_in_place`). `Result` falls to the generic enum arm, whose `emit_enum_clone_fn` returns None on the TYPE-ERASED layout — `field_drop_kinds` records no heap for the erased payload — and the dispatcher then takes `emit_primitive_clone_fn`, a plain load+store. For `Result[String, _]` that aliases the source's `{ptr,len,cap}`: both drops free it. The `Option` arm's own comment already records this ('`Result` has the same shape but no in-place deep-copy helper yet — it stays on the shallow path').

FIX SHAPE: a `emit_result_value_clone_fn` twin of `emit_option_value_clone_fn` (tag-guarded deep copy of whichever half is live, reusing `deep_copy_result_inline_heap_halves_in_place`, which already exists for the param entry-copy), then add `Result` back to `clone_receiver_self_type`'s allowlist and to the codegen aggregate arm in `try_compile_clone`. Interpreter needs nothing — `deep_clone_value` already covers `Value::EnumVariant`, so `Result.clone()` would work under `--interp` the moment typecheck admits it, which is exactly why the typecheck gate must stay until codegen catches up.

SEVERITY low: the workaround is a fresh `let` binding or a `match` + rebuild, and nothing miscompiles today — the gate is a clean rejection on every surface.

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (4b5f811) ──
Codegen half: `emit_result_value_clone_fn` (clone_drop.rs), the Result twin of `emit_option_value_clone_fn` — shallow-copy the whole `{tag,w0,w1,w2}` value, then rewrite the live half in place via the existing `deep_copy_result_inline_heap_halves_in_place`. Self-gates on `result_field_direct_vecstr_halves_ok`: returns None for a heap-free or uncovered-half Result so the shallow path (exact only when heap-free) is taken. Wired into `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr` and `aggregate_clone_fn_for_receiver` beside the Option arms. Typecheck half: `clone_receiver_self_type` admits Result for the direct String/Vec/scalar class via `result_halves_clone_codegen_safe`, a STRICT SUBSET of the codegen predicate (also accepts the all-scalar heap-free case) — so every admitted shape is one codegen provably clones correctly and no silent-alias miscompile can reach codegen. SCOPE / KNOWN GAP: struct-heap, shared, nested Option/Result, and Map halves stay REJECTED (the in-place overlay helper covers only the `{ptr,len,cap}` String/Vec class). That is a clean typecheck rejection on every surface, not a miscompile; Option still covers more (boxed struct/enum payloads) because its helper does. Extending the Result helper to those arms would lift the gate — deferred, not needed for the repro. Verified: check/interp/JIT/AOT parity + valgrind-clean across Result[String,i64]/[i64,String]/[i64,i64]/[String,String]/[Vec[i64],i64]/[Vec[String],i64]/[Vec[Vec[String]],i64]; uncovered shapes reject cleanly. Suites typechecker 2105 / interpreter 1327 / codegen 2632 / memory_sanitizer 867 green; fmt + clippy clean. Tests: codegen `e2e_result_clone_deep_copies_live_half`; typechecker `test_result_clone_admitted_for_direct_vecstr_scalar_halves` + two rejection tests.

fix: 8de98fe
tracker: src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs (field_bodies_fn_for_owned_temp, track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg, try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp), src/interpreter/eval_call.rs (run_fresh_temp_arg_drops), src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs (drop_user_drop_fields_of_value), src/codegen/synth_drop.rs (emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn)
title: A user `impl Drop` body ran only for a value reachable from a direct binding through STRUCT FIELDS. Fixed so far: owned aggregate temps (d794aad), Vec/VecDeque elements (b55743b, which also taught the NLL channel to carry container bindings), tuple elements at the let-site (9edc231), value-enum payloads at the let-site, Option/Result payloads at the let-site (with the ctor-arg + consuming-combinator + wrapper-name-collision fixes). Still silent: non-let positions only (tuple match/param/temp sites, the match arm binding that receives a moved payload, displaced/overwritten values).
detail:
Scoped out of B-2026-07-29-39 deliberately; both backends agree on both shapes, so run/build parity holds and only the leak remains.

SHAPE 1 — enum payload:
  struct Res { id: i64 }
  impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(99); } }
  enum Slot { Empty, Held(Res) }
  fn main() { let s = Slot.Held(Res { id: 1 }); }
  actual (interp AND compiled): nothing    expected: 99
The struct-field walk keys on `Value::Struct` / `struct_field_type_names`; an enum's payload is reached by neither. The codegen side needs the walk hung off `emit_enum_drop_switch`'s per-variant arms (which already tag-dispatch and know each payload's word offsets); the interpreter side needs an `EnumData::Tuple` / `EnumData::Struct` arm in `drop_user_drop_fields_of_value`.

SHAPE 2 — by-value aggregate param of a type with no Drop of its own:
  struct Holder { r: Res }
  fn consume(h: Holder) { }
  fn main() { consume(Holder { r: Res { id: 1 } }); }
The caller's owned-temp hook is gated on `drop_method_keys.contains_key(<type>)` on BOTH backends (codegen `call_dispatch`'s `__owned_agg_tmp` registration, interpreter `eval_call`'s fresh-temp hook), and `Holder` is not in it. The callee's `make_aggregate_param_callee_owned` registers only the memory drop. So neither side runs the field body. The same call with `Holder` given its own `impl Drop` DOES work (the wrapper carries the field-bodies call), which is the clean bisect.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE WITH -39: -39's blast radius was already the whole drop-glue surface, and both of these need a second mechanism rather than an extension of the first (a variant-tag-guarded walk; a widened temp-ownership gate). Splitting keeps each landable against the ASAN + parity gates -39 installed.

VALIDATION BAR when it is taken: the same pair -39 used — a `karac run --interp` vs `karac build` output parity test plus an LSan loop — extended to each shape.

── ATTEMPTED 2026-07-30, REVERTED — one blocker found that this entry does not record ──

Both shapes reproduce exactly as written, on both backends (`drop1`: enum payload;
`drop2`: by-value aggregate param). Interpreter half of SHAPE 1 was implemented and
WORKS, then reverted, because landing it alone would turn a leak into a RUN-VS-BUILD
PARITY BREAK — strictly worse than the bug. This entry's own note that "both backends
agree on both shapes, so run/build parity holds and only the leak remains" is the reason
the halves must land together.

INTERPRETER HALF (works, ~60 lines, reverted). A `Value::EnumVariant` arm at the head of
`drop_user_drop_fields_of_value` (eval_stmt.rs:744): resolve the `EnumDef`, take the
variant's declared payload types from `VariantKind::Tuple(Vec<TypeExpr>)` /
`VariantKind::Struct(Vec<StructField>)`, zip them against `EnumData::Tuple(Vec<Value>)` /
`EnumData::Struct(HashMap<..>)` in declaration order, and walk in reverse applying the
SAME declared-head gate the struct path uses (so an erased generic payload is skipped on
both backends, per -39's scoping decision). Needs `EnumData` added to the
`use super::value::{..}` import. Verified: `Slot.Held(Res)` printed `99`.

DROP-ORDER NOTE for whoever writes the test. This entry (and -39's) state the expectation
as drop firing at SCOPE EXIT, e.g. `7 1 99`. The shipped behaviour is NLL-immediate:
the reference struct shape prints `7 99 1` on BOTH backends, because the binding's last
use is the earlier statement. Write the oracle against `7 99 1`, not the entry text.

CODEGEN HALF — THE ACTUAL BLOCKER, not mentioned above. This entry says the walk should
hang off `emit_enum_drop_switch`'s per-variant arms "which already tag-dispatch and know
each payload's word offsets". For THIS shape those arms DO NOT EXIST.
`emit_enum_drop_switch` (synth_drop.rs:59) returns `None` early on:

    let any_heap = layout.field_drop_kinds.values()
        .any(|kinds| kinds.iter().any(|k| *k != EnumDropKind::None));
    if !any_heap { return None; }

`Res { id: i64 }` carries a user `impl Drop` but NO HEAP FIELD, so every kind is
`EnumDropKind::None`, the whole switch is skipped, and there is nothing to hang the walk
on. So the codegen half is not "add a call inside the existing arms" — it is at minimum:
(1) widen the `any_heap` gate to also fire when any variant payload satisfies
`type_runs_user_drop`; (2) emit the per-variant payload `<T>.drop` body call plus a
recursive `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn` for nested aggregates; and (3) confirm the
scope-exit cleanup actually REGISTERS `__karac_drop_<Enum>` for an enum that has no heap
kind at all — if that registration is gated the same way, widening the emitter alone
still runs nothing. Step 3 is unverified and is the thing to check FIRST, because it
determines whether this is an emitter change or a registration change too.

Cost this closer to -39 than to a patch. SHAPE 2 (by-value aggregate param) was not
attempted; its two gates are already named precisely in the text above and look
independent of this blocker.

STATE: fully reverted, parity re-verified (`drop1` prints `0` on both backends).

── STEP-3 CHECK RESOLVED 2026-07-30 (registration is NOT separately gated) ──
The entry's step 3 — "confirm the scope-exit cleanup actually REGISTERS `__karac_drop_<Enum>` for an enum that has no heap kind at all" — is answered: it is NOT a separate gate. `track_enum_var` (runtime.rs:4069, the let-binding-time registration) and the while-let miss-drop path (control_flow_match.rs:6723) BOTH express their decision as `match self.emit_enum_drop_switch(enum_name) { Some(f) => …, None => return }`. So registration is downstream of the emitter's return value: widen `emit_enum_drop_switch` to return Some for a user-Drop-bearing-but-heap-free enum and `track_enum_var` lights up automatically — this is an EMITTER-ONLY change on the codegen side, not emitter + registration. Good news that de-risks the slice; the emitter widening itself (new payload classification + per-variant user-drop dispatch that calls `karac_drop_<PayloadT>` rather than the heap-only `__karac_drop_struct_<S>`) plus SHAPE 2's separate temp-ownership gate is still ~-39-sized and must land with the interpreter half + full ASAN/LSan/parity.

── SECOND ATTEMPT 2026-07-30, REVERTED — the work is LAYERED, and layer 3 is the blocker (supersedes the step-3 note above) ──
The step-3 finding was right that scope-exit REGISTRATION cascades off `emit_enum_drop_switch`'s return value. It was WRONG to conclude from that that the codegen side is a single emitter change. Building it revealed three independent layers, each of which had to be discovered by running a new shape:

LAYER 1 — BODY EMISSION. Works, verified. Interpreter: a `Value::EnumVariant` arm at the head of `drop_user_drop_fields_of_value` resolving the `EnumDef`, zipping declared `VariantKind::Tuple`/`Struct` payload types against `EnumData`, walking in reverse under the declared-head gate (~70 lines). Codegen: `__karac_dropbodies_enum_<E>`, a tag switch calling `<T>.drop` + `__karac_dropbodies_<T>` per Drop-bearing payload. CRITICAL: emit the BODY only, never `__karac_drop_struct_<T>` — a heap-bearing payload already gets buffer cleanup from `emit_enum_drop_switch`'s `NestedStruct` arm, and adding it here double-frees. Verified with a `HeapRes { name: String }` payload: body ran AND the String was freed exactly once, valgrind clean.

LAYER 2 — DROP PLACEMENT. Not anticipated. Putting the body inside `emit_enum_drop_switch` compiles and runs, but that switch is the SCOPE-EXIT channel (`CleanupAction::EnumDrop`), while design.md § Drop ordering requires the NLL live-range end — which is what the interpreter does. Result: interp printed `99 0`, codegen `0 99`. A run-vs-build PARITY BREAK, strictly worse than the leak. Fix: a SEPARATE fn on the `UserDrop` channel via `track_user_drop_var_with_fn`, registered at the enum let-binding site (stmts.rs, next to `track_enum_var`, where `var_name` + `alloca` are both in hand), plus an arm in `fire_due_user_drops`'s NLL filter. That filter must key on the `__karac_dropbodies_enum_` SYMBOL PREFIX, not on `type_name` being an enum: enum-typed `UserDrop` entries ALREADY exist on that channel (`__owned_agg_tmp` at call_dispatch.rs:2055, `__freshtemp_enum_scrut` at control_flow_match.rs:6059) carrying `karac_drop_<T>` wrappers which intentionally drain at scope exit — a `type_name`-based widening retimes them. With this, interp/AOT/JIT all printed `99 0`; a 5-variant stress (2-payload reverse order, heap payload, struct variant, unit variant) was byte-identical on both backends and valgrind-clean.

LAYER 3 — MOVE-OUT SUPPRESSION. THE BLOCKER, and the reason this was reverted. A payload moved out by a match arm must DISARM the enum's registered body action, exactly as `disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field` does for struct fields. Without it:
    let a = Slot.Held(Res { id: 11 });
    match a { Slot.Held(r) => println(100), Slot.Empty => println(0) }
  interp `100 11 1` vs codegen `100 0 1` — codegen runs the body on the ZEROED, moved-from payload (`self.id` reads 0), i.e. a resource is dropped on a moved-out value. Note the failure mode: it printed a WRONG VALUE, silently. No crash, no verifier error, no sanitizer hit. That is the same silent profile that made B-2026-07-30-5 unlandable, and the audit surface is the same shape — every path that moves an enum value: match/if-let move-out (hook exists: `suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup` + `pattern_consumes_field`, but it takes `&self` and would need `&mut self` to call `suppress_user_drop_for_var`), `let b = a;`, by-value fn param, return, reassignment, Vec/Map element, nested enum. Each needs its own suppression, and under-suppression double-drops a resource while over-suppression only leaks.

COST, now measured rather than estimated: layers 1+2 are ~200 lines and DONE-and-working in the reverted tree; layer 3 is an audit of the enum move surface with a silent failure mode, which is a dedicated slice on a quiet main verified per-shape with valgrind/LSan — NOT the test suite (2632 codegen + 867 asan stayed green through the layer-3 parity break). Whoever takes it should start at layer 3 and treat layers 1+2 as a solved design, recorded above.

── SHAPE 2 FIXED 2026-07-30 (d794aad). SHAPE 1 remains open; this entry stays
   OPEN for it. ──

Scope was UNDERSTATED by this entry: SHAPE 2 is not one gate but THREE, one per
position an owned aggregate temp can occupy, each with its own registrar on each
backend. All three leaked; the entry named only the first.

  A  consume(H { a: A { .. } })   inline struct-literal arg
  C  consume(mk())                fn-call arg
  D  mk();                        discarded fn result
  B  let h = H { .. }; consume(h) ALREADY WORKED (-39's let-path)
  E  let h2 = mk();               ALREADY WORKED (same)

Both backends produced the same wrong output on A/C/D, so run/build parity held
and it was a pure leak — as the entry said. The two new tests fail on unmodified
src with the IDENTICAL string, which is the proof of that claim rather than an
assertion of it.

THE FIX. Widen the gate from `drop_method_keys.contains_key(T)` (has its own
Drop) to `type_runs_user_drop(T)` / `value_runs_user_drop(v)` (runs a user Drop,
possibly through a field), and register `__karac_dropbodies_<T>` on the UserDrop
channel — the same substitution -39 made for the let-path, since a type with no
`Drop` has no `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper to hang a body off. Bodies only; the walk
never frees, so it is additive and cannot double-free.
  codegen: `field_bodies_fn_for_owned_temp` (new), called from
           `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`'s StructLiteral and Call arms and
           from `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp`.
  interp:  `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` (A + C) and the `StmtKind::Expr` discard

TWO TRAPS, both found by RUNNING the code, not reading it. Either one alone

THE LSan-CLEAN BASELINE WILL NOT SURVIVE THE FIX. The note above reads "memory is NOT
leaked in any of these: ASan+LSan exit 0 while 49 of 50 Drop bodies are skipped" as a
property of the shapes. It is not — it is a property of the bug. With no drop body
reading the displaced value, nothing reads it at all, so LLVM elides the whole
initializer, allocation included; there is no leak because there is no allocation.
Measured on `let mut r = mk(1); r = mk(2);` with a heap-carrying field:

    baseline                    2 allocs / 2 frees   valgrind clean
    with a body call added      3 allocs / 2 frees   11 bytes definitely lost

The 11 bytes are the displaced value's buffer, and the alloc count is the tell. Two
earlier probes here looked clean for the same wrong reason and nearly shipped a leak
inside a leak fix: an f-string field (`f"res-{i}"`) FOLDED to a constant, so a 200-
iteration reassignment loop showed `1 allocs`. Whoever takes this must re-baseline
allocation COUNTS, not just leak summaries, and must not treat a green pre-fix LSan run
as the post-fix bar. There is no displaced-value memory reclamation for a struct
binding anywhere in the Assign arm — the eager-frees there are gated on container-ness
(`lhs_is_tracked_vec` / Map / tensor) and never reach a plain struct. So the displaced
leg is body AND memory together, not the additive bodies-only shape every prior leg had.

A DISPLACED DROP NEEDS AN ALIAS GATE, AND THE OBVIOUS ONE IS TOO WEAK. Three RHS shapes
build the new value out of the old, where dropping is a use-after-free rather than a
leak — and only the third is a call:

    r = Res { name: r.name }    the new value OWNS the old buffer
    r = r.inner                 same, through a field
    r = pass(r)                 leaves through the arg, returns through the result

A `fn_returns_param` passthrough analysis (the tool the owned-temp leg used) sees only
the third. What is needed is "does the RHS mention this binding at all", exhaustive over
`ExprKind` with NO wildcard arm — every existing `expr_mentions_*` helper in the tree
ends in one and would answer "no" for a shape it forgot. Two traps found by running it:
`self` is `Function::self_param`, NOT `params[0]`, so `fn_returns_param(f, 0)` silently
answers about the first ordinary parameter instead of the receiver; and `self` parses as
`ExprKind::SelfValue`, not `Identifier("self")`, so an identifier test never matches it.
Both made a receiver-passthrough gate a silent no-op on first cut.

fix: 3ee768a
tracker: src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs (__owned_agg_tmp registration), src/codegen/param_own.rs (passthrough defensive copy), tests/memory_sanitizer.rs (asan_fnret_drop_temp_arg_passthrough_and_discard_single_fire)
title: A by-value owned-struct arg that the callee RETURNS mishandled its caller temp TWO ways: a fn-call arg (`pass(mk())`) leaked the orphaned buffer, and a struct-literal arg (`pass(G { .. })`) ran the user Drop body TWICE under AOT/JIT vs once under the interpreter -- a run/build parity break live since B-2026-07-08-6.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-07-30-9. That fix stages a `println` line through a buffer, and the extra `memcpy` blocks an LLVM elision that had been hiding this leak. The println change is NOT the cause — it is the instrument that made the allocation real.

REPRO (the `asan_fnret_drop_temp_arg_passthrough_and_discard_single_fire` program, minimised to three statements):
  struct Guard { name: String, id: i64 }
  impl Drop for Guard { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(self.id); } }
  fn make(n: i64) -> Guard { Guard { name: f"guard payload padded beyond thirty-six bytes {n}", id: n } }
  fn pass(g: Guard) -> Guard { g }
  fn main() {
      make(60);                      // discarded fn-returned Drop temp
      let x = pass(make(50));        // passthrough
      println(x.name.len());
  }

EVIDENCE (valgrind `total heap usage`, same source both columns):
  main today                : 1 allocs, 1 frees, 4,096 bytes   <- only the stdio buffer
  with -9's staging applied : 4 allocs, 3 frees, 4,237 bytes   <- 4096 + 3 x 47, one unfreed
Output is byte-identical and correct in both (`60 47 50`); only the accounting differs.

TWO Guards, THREE 47-byte allocations. The extra one is most likely the passthrough's defensive param copy; it is the unowned one. Isolation results, all with the staging applied:
  1 Guard direct        -> 1 alloc, 1 free    (clean)
  1 Guard via pass      -> 1 alloc, 1 free    (clean)
  discarded temp alone  -> clean
  DISCARDED + PASS      -> 4 allocs, 3 frees, 47 bytes lost
So it is specifically the COMBINATION, which points at the `__owned_agg_tmp` registration for the discarded temp interacting with the passthrough's arg-temp suppression — the very interaction the test's own comment describes ('the passthrough guard skips the arg-temp registration'). B-2026-07-01-7 is the ancestor.

WHY IT IS INVISIBLE TODAY. Nothing observable depends on the string BYTES — only `x.name.len()`, which LLVM computes without the buffer — so the optimiser deletes every malloc/free in the set. ASAN then has nothing to report and the test passes. That is a vacuous pass, not a clean one, and it is the reason this survived a suite with 867 ASAN cases. NOTE the general hazard: an ASAN/LSan test whose allocations are optimisable proves nothing about the ownership balance of the code it is meant to cover.

COULD NOT BE REPRODUCED ON UNMODIFIED main, and that is a real caveat rather than a claim of absence: routing the size through an opaque `Env.args().len()` did NOT defeat the elision (the byte content still has no observable use), so no clean-main repro exists yet. The imbalance is therefore inferred from the materialised counts under -9's staging plus the isolation table above — strong, but not yet proven independent of that change. FIRST STEP for whoever takes this: build a program in which the Guard name's BYTES are genuinely observed (print the name itself, or compare it) so the allocation cannot be elided, then re-measure on unmodified main. That either confirms a pre-existing imbalance or narrows it to an interaction with staging.

BLOCKS: B-2026-07-30-9, whose fix is complete and verified but cannot land while this makes the ASAN test red.

── ROOT-CAUSED 2026-07-30. Caveat RESOLVED, scope CORRECTED, and the obvious one-line fix is a TRAP ──

1. CLEAN-MAIN REPRO FOUND, so this is confirmed pre-existing and independent of B-2026-07-30-9. The elision is defeated by making the drop body print the NAME (the string BYTES are then observed, so LLVM cannot delete the buffer):
     impl Drop for Guard { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(self.name); } }
   On UNMODIFIED main that program reports 4 allocs / 3 frees and `definitely lost: 47 bytes`. My earlier note that no clean-main repro existed is withdrawn — routing the SIZE through `Env.args()` was the wrong lever; the BYTES have to be observed.

2. SCOPE CORRECTION. This entry's title blamed the COMBINATION of a discarded temp with a passthrough. Wrong — the PASSTHROUGH ALONE leaks, and it scales linearly:
     let x = pass(make(50));                 -> 3 allocs, 2 frees, 47 lost
     two passthroughs                        -> 5 allocs, 3 frees, 94 lost
     direct binding / discarded temp alone   -> clean

3. MECHANISM, read off the IR. `fn pass(g: Guard) -> Guard { g }` emits a defensive ENTRY COPY (`dcopy.*`: malloc + memcpy of the name), points `%g` at the COPY, zeroes the original's cap so the struct drop skips it, and returns the copy. The caller passed a fresh temp expecting callee-ownership, so it registered no cleanup. Neither side frees the CALLER'S original buffer.

4. THE GAP IS ONE PREDICATE. B-2026-07-08-6 already fixed exactly this leak — but only for a struct-LITERAL argument. `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` (call_dispatch.rs) opens with `let ExprKind::StructLiteral { .. } = &arg.kind else { return false }`, so a fn-CALL arg (`pass(make(50))`) misses, the return-passthrough guard skips the caller-side registration, and it leaks. Confirmed by A/B: `pass(Guard { .. })` clean, `pass(make(50))` leaks. The registration helper `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` ALREADY handles call args (its B-2026-07-01-7 arm) — it is simply never reached.

5. WHY THE ONE-LINE FIX WAS NOT LANDED. Extending the predicate to the `Call` shape (~20 lines, built and measured) DOES fix the leak — every isolation case goes to allocs == frees, valgrind clean. But it buys that by making the caller free its original, which means the user `Drop` BODY now runs TWICE: once for the caller's temp, once for the callee's entry copy. For a resource type that is a double close. Per this repo's own stated bar (B-2026-07-29-39: 'an under-suppressed field drop double-frees; an over-suppressed one leaks' — leak is the safe side), that is a move in the WRONG direction, so it stays out.

6. AND THE DOUBLE-DROP IS ALREADY SHIPPING on the sibling path. On unmodified main:
     let x = pass(Guard { name: f"...", id: 50 });
     interp -> 47 | <name>            (one drop)
     AOT    -> 47 | <name> | <name>   (TWO drops)
   So B-2026-07-08-6 traded this leak for a run-vs-build parity break, and that break has been live since. BOTH halves of the predicate are wrong today: struct-literal arg double-drops, fn-call arg leaks. Neither is caught, for the same two reasons — the covering ASAN test's allocations are elidable (vacuous pass, see below) and nothing compares interp-vs-AOT drop COUNTS for this shape.

7. THE REAL FIX is to remove the spurious entry copy for a MOVED-IN owned temp, not to add a second free. Then there is one value, one drop, no leak — which is exactly what the interpreter does. The obstacle is that the entry copy lives in the callee (`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned`), which is compiled once and cannot see whether a given caller retained the argument; resolving that needs a caller-side ownership-transfer signal in the ABI, or a per-call-site specialisation. That is a design slice, not a patch.

8. TEST-INFRA RESIDUAL, worth fixing on its own: `asan_fnret_drop_temp_arg_passthrough_and_discard_single_fire` passes VACUOUSLY. Its program's only heap allocation at runtime is the 4 KiB stdio buffer — the `Guard.name` strings are never allocated, because nothing observes their bytes. Changing its Drop body to print `self.name` instead of `self.id` would make it cover what it claims to. The general hazard: an ASAN/LSan test whose allocations are optimisable proves nothing about the ownership balance it is meant to pin.

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (3ee768a). The previous revision called the one-line
   predicate extension a trap. It was — ALONE. Here is the missing half. ──

The trap diagnosis stands and is what made the fix findable: extending
`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` to fn-call args clears the leak but converts
it into a double user-`Drop` firing, and that double firing was ALREADY SHIPPING
on the struct-literal path. What the previous revision then concluded — that the
real fix needs a caller-side ownership-transfer signal in the ABI, i.e. a design
slice — was WRONG. No ABI change was needed. The missing piece was a distinction,
not a mechanism:

    MEMORY FOLLOWS THE BUFFER. BODIES FOLLOW THE VALUE.

On the passthrough path the caller's original buffer really IS orphaned (the
callee entry-copies and returns an independent copy), so freeing it here is
correct — that was B-2026-07-08-6's insight and it was right. But -08-6
registered the FULL `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper to do it, and the wrapper also runs
the user body, which belongs to the consumer of the RESULT. Register
`track_struct_var` — the memory half alone — and the leak closes with no second
body. Then the predicate extension becomes safe, and the fn-call arm gets the
same split.

That distinction came out of B-2026-07-30-11 SHAPE 2 (d794aad), which had to
thread `arg_flows_into_return` into `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` for a
different reason. Once that flag existed this fix was ~15 lines. Recording the
dependency because the ordering was not obvious in advance: -12 looked like the
blocker for -9 and turned out to be unblocked by -11.

SO -12 WAS TWO DEFECTS, NOT ONE, AND ONLY ONE WAS IN THIS ENTRY'S TITLE:
  * LEAK, fn-call arg — `pass(mk())` never reached the -08-6 override, because
    the predicate matched `ExprKind::StructLiteral` only. This entry's subject.
  * DOUBLE DROP BODY, struct-literal arg — `let p = pass(Guard { .. })` ran the
    body once under the interpreter and twice under AOT/JIT. A run/build PARITY
    BREAK live since -08-6, found while investigating the leak, and strictly the
    more serious of the two: for a resource type it is a double close.

MEASURED, canonical repro, baseline vs fixed under the same binary discipline:
    output       6 lines -> 5 lines, byte-identical to the interpreter
    valgrind     11 allocs / 9 frees, 37 bytes lost in 2 blocks
              -> 11 allocs / 10 frees,  5 bytes lost in 1 block
The 5-byte residual is an f-string intermediate present in both arms.

TEST-INFRA RESIDUAL, ALSO CLOSED — and it is the reason this bug survived so
long. `asan_fnret_drop_temp_arg_passthrough_and_discard_single_fire` covers
exactly this shape and passed VACUOUSLY: its Drop body printed `self.id`, so the
`Guard.name` buffers were never observed, LLVM deleted every malloc/free pair,
and the program's entire runtime heap was the 4 KiB stdio buffer — measured, 1
alloc / 1 free. `x.name.len()` does not rescue it; a length is a field read, not
a read of the bytes. The body now prints `self.name`: 7 allocs / 7 frees, five
real Guard buffers through the drop path, and on unmodified src it reports
47 bytes leaked. Landing it required fixing -12 first, because the leak it
exposes is real.

REGRESSION GATE. New codegen/interpreter twins,
`{e2e_,test_}fnret_passthrough_arg_drop_fires_once`, on identical source and
expected string. NOTE FOR ANYONE EDITING THEM: the struct MUST carry a heap
field. `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` requires one, so a scalar-only version
never reaches the override, is already correct on the unfixed compiler, and pins
nothing — the first draft of this test did exactly that and passed on baseline.
Verified: the codegen twin fails on unmodified src with precisely the extra
trailing drop; the interpreter twin passes there, because the interpreter was
always right and is the oracle.

UNBLOCKS B-2026-07-30-9 — the verified println line-atomic staging fix was
reverted only because it made this shape's latent leak visible to ASAN. That
blocker is gone; the -9 design needs no change.

fix: 3981fef
title: An arithmetic mismatch whose wrong operand is an Option/Result was reported as an integer/floating-point mix, naming a float type that appears nowhere in the program -- so the near-universal forgotten `.unwrap()` on `q.pop_front()` pointed the reader at a numeric cast that cannot help.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing a reproduction probe for B-2026-07-30-5. `pop_front()`
returns `Option[T]`, so this is the FIRST error anyone draining a VecDeque hits, and it
points away from the cause.

OBSERVED.
    let mut q: VecDeque[i64] = VecDeque.new();
    let s = 0i64 + q.pop_front();
  error[typecheck]: cannot mix integer and floating-point operands ('i64' and 'Option<i64>')
                    in arithmetic -- there is no implicit promotion; cast explicitly with
                    `as` (e.g. `i64 as Option<i64>`)
There is no floating-point type in that program. The suggested cast is not merely
unhelpful, it is not expressible: `i64 as Option<i64>` is not a cast.

MECHANISM. The cross-domain arm in `infer_binary` was keyed on
`left_is_int != right_is_int`. That does NOT mean "one int, one float": the enclosing
block is entered on `is_numeric(&left_ty)` alone, so the RIGHT operand can be any type in
the language. Every non-integer right operand of a numeric left operand therefore fell
into the int/float arm and was described as floating-point. `1i64 + "x"` had the same
defect.

FIX (3981fef). Require the other operand to actually be `Type::Float`. Everything else
falls through to the mismatch arm, which now reads `expected 'i64', found 'Option<i64>'`
and, when the wrapper's payload IS the compatible type, appends what to do:
"`Option` wraps the 'i64'; unwrap it first (`.unwrap()`, `.unwrap_or(<default>)`, or a
`match`)".

The hint is GATED ON PAYLOAD COMPATIBILITY, deliberately: it appears only where
unwrapping is actually the fix. `1i64 + Option[String]` stays a plain mismatch, because a
hint there would send the reader down a dead end. That gate is the discriminating test
case, not a nicety.

TESTS: `test_arith_with_option_operand_is_not_reported_as_float_mix`,
`test_arith_wrapper_hint_absent_when_payload_still_mismatches`, and

fix: af9a99a9
title: A MAP LITERAL typed as `HashMap<K, V>` — a name Kāra source cannot write — so it matched no annotation: `let m: Map[String, i64] = Map["x": 1];` failed with `expected 'Map<String, i64>', found 'HashMap<String, i64>'`. A map literal was usable only where nothing was expected of it.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO (every line fails; the `Map.new()` control passes):

  struct Holder { row: Map[String, i64] }
  fn main() {
      let a: Map[String, i64] = Map["x": 1];        // expected 'Map', found 'HashMap'
      let h = Holder { row: Map["y": 2] };            // same
      let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new();        // OK — the control
      m.insert("z".to_string(), 3);
  }

ROOT CAUSE: `infer_expr`'s `ExprKind::MapLiteral` arm returned
`Type::Named { name: "HashMap", .. }` while every other route to a map —
`Map.new()`, a `Map[K, V]` annotation, a parameter, a return type — uses `Map`.

`HashMap` is the RUST representation, not a Kāra type. design.md's type-mapping
table renders `Map[K, V]` as `HashMap<K, V>` to describe the runtime
representation, and the resolver rejects the name outright: `let m: HashMap[K,
V]` gives `undefined type 'HashMap'`. So the literal produced a type the user
could neither write nor annotate around — there was no spelling that accepted a
map literal in a typed position.

WHY IT SURVIVED: a map literal in an UNTYPED `let` works fine (nothing to unify
against), which is how most tests and examples use it. It only fails where a
type is expected, and `Map[]` (the EMPTY literal) was already special-cased —
`exprs.rs`'s empty-collection-literal path matches `("Map", ..) => name ==
"Map" || name == "HashMap"`, accepting both. That shim covered the empty case
and hid the non-empty one.

FIX (2026-07-30): the arm returns `Map`. Safe by inspection — every downstream
consumer already matches both spellings (`"Map" | "HashMap"` appears throughout
`codegen/synth_drop.rs`, `call_dispatch.rs`, `closures.rs`, and
`patterns.rs`), so nothing keyed on the old name. Verified against the full
suite plus codegen and memory_sanitizer under `--features llvm`, since map
literals flow into drop synthesis.

SOURCE NOTE: found in `examples/db_pipeline`, where three `Query.Insert { row:
Map["id": Value.Int(1), ...] }` seed rows could not be written at all. That
package is down from 18 errors to 15.

title: `Json` has no integer variant — every i64 serializes through f64, so whole numbers emit `1.0` (which Go's encoding/json REFUSES into an int field) and any value past 2^53 is silently corrupted. Both defects survive a `Json.parse` round-trip, so a service cannot echo an integer field unchanged.
detail:
SURFACE NOTE: `Json` is a compiler-known enum with exactly six variants -- Null | Bool | Number | String | Array | Object (src/codegen/json.rs:101, src/codegen/declarations.rs:3654, src/interpreter/helpers.rs:1000). `Number` carries an f64 and there is no integer variant, so an i64 must round-trip through f64 to become JSON.

SOURCE NOTE: found while assessing whether the corpus could carry a larger backend-service kata (kara-katas PLAN.md axis-1, marked v1-required with a Go comparator). The existing `backend/todo-api` already ships the symptom: `GET /todos` returns `{"id":1.0,...}` for an i64 id.

TWO DEFECTS, one root cause.

(1) WHOLE NUMBERS EMIT A TRAILING `.0`, WHICH GO REJECTS. `Json.Number(1 as f64).stringify()` gives `1.0`, not `1`. This is well-formed JSON but it is NOT interchangeable: Go's encoding/json refuses it into an integer field. Measured with the local Go toolchain:
  json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"id":1.0}`), &struct{ Id int `json:"id"` }{})
  -> json: cannot unmarshal number 1.0 into Go struct field Todo.id of type int
So any Kara service that returns an integer id cannot be consumed by an ordinary Go client struct. That matters directly for the PLAN.md backend kata, whose bench gate builds every language's mirror and CHECKS THEY ALL PRINT THE SAME RESULT -- a Kara/Go mirror pair cannot agree while ids serialize as `1.0` vs `1`.

(2) SILENT PRECISION LOSS ABOVE 2^53. Any i64 magnitude beyond f64's exact-integer range is corrupted with no diagnostic:
  Json.Number(9007199254740993 as f64).stringify()  ->  9007199254740992.0

PARSE ROUND-TRIP IS ALSO LOSSY -- both defects reproduce through `Json.parse`, so this is not confined to construction:
  input:  {"id":7,"n":9007199254740993,"ok":true}
  output: {"id":7.0,"n":9007199254740992.0,"ok":true}
An integer that was exact in the input text comes back changed. A service that reads a request body and echoes a field cannot preserve it.

FAILS SILENTLY in both directions -- no error, no warning, just a differently-shaped document. `frac` (1.5) is unaffected; only integers are.

DIRECTION (not prescriptive): the shapes worth considering are an `Int(i64)` variant alongside `Number(f64)`, or a stringify that emits whole f64 values without the `.0`. The first fixes both defects; the second fixes only (1) and leaves the 2^53 corruption. Note the parse side needs to choose a variant by the input token's syntax (no decimal point / no exponent -> integer) for round-trip fidelity, which is what serde_json and Go's json.Number both do.

REPRO (no service needed):
  fn main() {
      let o: Json = Json.Object(Vec[("id", Json.Number(1 as f64))]);
      println(o.stringify());                 // {"id":1.0}   want {"id":1}
      match Json.parse("{\"n\":9007199254740993}") {
          Ok(j) => println(j.stringify()),    // {"n":9007199254740992.0}
          Err(e) => println("parse error"),
      }
  }
Verified on main @96cafb7 under `karac run`.

── FIXED 2026-07-31: `Json.Int(i64)` LANDED AS THE SEVENTH VARIANT (tag 6) ──

Took the ledger's first suggested direction (the one that fixes both defects).
The variant is chosen by the input token's SYNTAX, exactly as the entry
prescribed: `7` parses as `Int`, `7.0` as `Number` — the discrimination comes
free from serde_json (`Number::as_i64()` is Some only for integer-syntax tokens
in i64 range), which both the interpreter bridge and the runtime FFI already
link. A u64 past i64::MAX has no `Int` home and falls to the f64 arm (documented
lossy; the payload is i64).

SURFACES TOUCHED (all seven, in dependency order):
  * runtime/stdlib/json.kara — `Int(i64)` appended LAST so the six original
    seeded tags stay stable; header note (i) revised in place with the bug id.
  * runtime/src/lib.rs — `KaracJsonTag::Int = 6`; `int_val: i64` appended at the
    END of `KaracJsonValue` so every pre-existing byte offset codegen hardcodes
    stays valid (offset 72, struct 72 → 80 bytes, layout-pin test extended);
    parse/stringify arms; `karac_runtime_json_make_int` + keep-list entry
    (the B-2026-07-12-22 class); `free_value` needs no arm — Int owns no heap
    and the `_ => {}` default covers it.
  * src/codegen/declarations.rs — layout seed: tag 6, 1 payload word,
    EnumDropKind::None.
  * src/codegen/json.rs — JSON_TAG_INT, KARAC_JSON_VALUE_INT_OFFSET=72, both
    variant-name lists, a make_int arm in the kara→FFI walker and an offset-72
    read arm in the FFI→kara lift walker.
  * src/codegen.rs — `make_int` extern declaration.
  * src/interpreter/helpers.rs — serde bridge both directions.

BOTH REPRO DEFECTS CLOSED, verified byte-identical across interp/JIT/AOT:
  {"id":1}  (was {"id":1.0});  {"n":9007199254740993}  (was ...992.0);  the
  entry's echo case {"id":7,"n":9007199254740993,"ok":true} round-trips
  unchanged. Float syntax is NOT collapsed: [7, 2.5, 1.0] round-trips as
  [7,2.5,1.0] — `1.0` keeps its fractional form because the choice is
  syntax-driven, so `Json.Number(1.0).stringify()` still prints `1.0` and every
  construct-side test that used float literals is untouched. `match` sees the
  seventh variant on all three backends (`Json.Int(i)` destructures; parse "41"
  lands in Int, "4.5" in Number).

EXPECTATION CHANGES, enumerated: 3 asserts in tests/json.rs, 3 parse-side
asserts in tests/codegen.rs, 1 runtime unit — every one a PARSE-side
integer-syntax token losing its wrong `.0`. Construct-side (`Json.Number(1.0)`)
asserts unchanged by design. `examples/json.kara` defines its own Json enum
(Str/Num/Arr/Obj) and is unaffected.

BREAKING-CHANGE NOTE, stated plainly: an existing user `match` over Json with
all six variants and no wildcard now fails exhaustiveness (a 7th variant
exists), and parse output for integer tokens changes shape. Both are the point
of the fix; no repo-internal code needed the former (no exhaustive stdlib-Json
matches existed outside the new tests).

VALGRIND: the Int construct/stringify/parse paths add no leak. A PRE-EXISTING
parse-path leak was observed while checking (Json.parse of any object leaks its
lifted tree — reproduces with a pure-float payload on the pre-change code path,
so it is not this fix's); not filed as this entry's concern.

Suites: codegen 2645 (24 json), memory_sanitizer 872, interpreter 1338,
typechecker 2118, cli 545, par_codegen 211, http_server 27, selfhost_codegen,
runtime units 359 (+2 new json), json 8, wasm clippy both arms, fmt + clippy
±llvm. Archives rebuilt lean-then-full (new runtime symbol).

title: `File.sync_all()` / `sync_data()` — the durability API design.md:9150 mandates — TYPECHECKS CLEAN but is unimplemented in codegen AND the interpreter, so `karac check` goes green on a program neither backend can run. No fsync path exists in the runtime at all (`file_flush` is Rust's no-op `Write::flush`), so a Kāra program cannot make any write durable.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while answering "where does a hosted service persist its data" for the PLAN.md axis-1 backend-service kata. The answer depends on whether Kara can make a write durable; it cannot, and the way it fails is worse than a plain gap.

THE SPEC MANDATES THE API. docs/design.md:9150, in the cancellation-safety table:
  | `File` before fsync | Drop closes the descriptor, but writes may sit in the page cache and not yet be durable. Cancellation could lose data the program "wrote" but did not flush. The user is responsible for issuing the documented sync call (`sync_data()` / `sync_all()`) before any yield point if durability is required. |
So the design names `sync_data()` / `sync_all()` as THE durability contract and explicitly assigns the caller responsibility for calling it.

NEITHER IS IMPLEMENTED, AND `karac check` PASSES ANYWAY. Measured on main @05c2921 with the probe below:
  karac check s.kara        -> All checks passed.
  karac build s.kara        -> error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method 'sync_all' on variable 'fh'
  karac run s.kara          -> same codegen error (JIT lane)
  karac run --interp s.kara -> wrote
                               runtime error: method 'sync_all' not found on type 'unknown' (no interpreter dispatch arm)
`sync_data()` behaves identically (typechecks clean).

THE FALSE GREEN IS THE SHARP EDGE. This is not merely an unimplemented method — the TYPECHECKER ACCEPTS IT. A project whose CI gate is `karac check` goes green on a program that cannot be built or run. That inverts the usual contract, where check is the conservative phase. Everything else in this probe is ordinary File surface that works (`File.create`, `.write(Slice[u8])` — the data does reach the file on the interpreter lane before the method blows up).

NO OTHER DURABILITY PATH EXISTS. The runtime exports karac_runtime_file_{open,create,read,read_to_string,write,append,seek,flush,close,roundtrip} and karac_runtime_fs_{read_lines,write} — there is no *_sync / *_fsync / *_sync_all symbol anywhere in runtime/src. And `karac_runtime_file_flush` is NOT a substitute: it calls Rust's `Write::flush` on the guarded handle (runtime/src/file.rs:493-511), which for `std::fs::File` is a documented no-op — it pushes userspace buffers, never the page cache. So today a Kara program has NO WAY to force a write to stable storage.

CONSEQUENCE FOR ANY HOSTED SERVICE. Writes survive a process crash (the page cache outlives the process) but NOT a power loss, kernel panic, or container host failure. There is also no file-locking primitive in the runtime (no flock / LOCK_EX), so two instances over one data file corrupt each other with no diagnostic. Both together mean a file-backed store is a demo artifact, not a durable one.

SCOPE / WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: not investigated whether the typechecker arm was added deliberately ahead of the backends (a staged slice) or by accident via a permissive File-method rule; the shallow clone gave no blame history. Also not checked: whether other File methods share the accepted-but-unimplemented shape — worth a sweep of the File method table against both dispatchers, since the same false green would hide there too.

REPRO:
  fn main() with panics {
      match File.create("/tmp/durability_probe.txt") {
          Ok(f) => {
              let mut fh = f;
              match fh.write("critical data".bytes()) {
                  Ok(n) => { println("wrote"); }
                  Err(e) => { println("write err"); }
              }
              match fh.sync_all() {
                  Ok(u) => println("sync_all OK"),
                  Err(e) => println("sync_all Err"),
              }
          }
          Err(e) => println("create failed"),
      }
  }
  karac check  -> All checks passed
  karac build  -> codegen: no handler for method 'sync_all'

FIXED (38808e0). Both calls now exist end to end — runtime entry points over the
Mutex-guarded std::fs::File, keep-list entries so the JIT runner resolves them,
`impl File` declarations, codegen extern decls + `compile_file_sync` + dispatcher
arm, interpreter dispatch arms, and `writes(FileSystem)` in the effect checker.
Verified at the SYSCALL level rather than by return value: strace shows
`fsync(3) = 0` for sync_all and `fdatasync(3) = 0` for sync_data, and ZERO of
either for a flush-only control — which also confirms this entry's claim that
flush never was a durability primitive. check / build / JIT / interpreter all
agree.

One thing the fix had to carry: `#[cancel_unsafe_until]` took a single clearing
method, so `write(); sync_all(); <yield>` was rejected with "call `f.flush`" —
telling the user to WEAKEN a stronger guarantee, since sync_all flushes and
fsyncs. The attribute now takes a comma-separated list and `File.write` names
"flush,sync_all,sync_data"; the diagnostic still suggests the first entry.

CORRECTION TO THIS ENTRY'S DIAGNOSIS. It said the typechecker "accepts" the
method and left open whether the arm was added deliberately or by accident.
Neither: there is no `sync_all` arm and never was. `File` has NO method-name
checking at all — `f.totally_bogus_method_xyz()` also typechecks clean, while
the same call on `String` / `Vec` / `Map` is correctly rejected. So the false
green was never specific to sync_all; implementing the two methods removes the
symptom for them and leaves the hole. Split out as B-2026-07-31-1, which
measures the blast radius (11 of 11 resolvable baked-stdlib handle types).

title: Map LOOKUP (`get` / `get_or` / `contains_key` / `remove`) rejected a borrowed key: `m.get(key)` where `key: ref String` failed with `expected 'String', found 'ref String'`, forcing a clone to look anything up from a borrow — even though these methods already borrow at runtime.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO:

  fn lookup(m: ref Map[String, i64], key: ref String) -> i64 {
      if m.contains_key(key) { ... }   // expected 'String', found 'ref String'
      m.get(key)                        // same
  }

NOT AN API CHANGE — the check disagreed with the semantics that already held.
Passing an OWNED key to `m.get(k)` leaves `k` LIVE afterwards today (verified:
`let k = "a".to_string(); let v = m.get(k); println(f"{k}")` compiles and
runs), so lookup already borrows. Only `check_map_slot_arg`'s
`check_assignable(K, ref K)` demanded ownership, and the clone it forced bought
nothing.

FIX (2026-07-30): an `allow_borrowed` flag on the shared slot helper, peeling
one `ref`/`mut ref` level before unification, routed to the four LOOKUP
methods only. With the flag `false` the path is byte-identical, so every VALUE
slot is untouched. The borrowed case must also skip the concrete-slot
`check_expr` — that call is precisely what rejects `ref String` against
`String` — falling back to the plain-infer path unresolved slots already used.

SCOPE, and the guard on it: `insert` and `entry` STORE the key and still
require ownership. `map_insert_still_requires_an_owned_key` asserts that,
because widening the relaxation to every key slot would let a map hold a
borrow.

IMPACT: `examples/db_pipeline` 15 errors -> 3. All five `Map.get` sites were
this, each `fn f(table: ref String)` then `self.tables.get(table)` — the
natural spelling for a provider method, unwritable before.

ADJACENT, NOT FIXED: `leetcode/course_schedule.kara` is pinned on `no method
'get_mut' on type 'Map'`, which is a MISSING method rather than this
borrow-vs-own mismatch. Same ergonomic neighbourhood, different gap.

fix: 103fbe4
title: NO METHOD-NAME CHECKING on baked-stdlib handle types — `f.totally_bogus_method_xyz()` on a `File`, `TcpStream`, `Mutex`, `Regex`, `Pool`, … typechecks clean, while the same call on `String`/`Vec`/`Map` is correctly rejected. 11 of 11 resolvable types affected, so every typo on those surfaces escapes `karac check` and fails later at codegen or runtime.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-07-30-16 while implementing `File.sync_all`. That entry read the false green as "the typechecker accepts sync_all"; the truth is broader and worse -- `File` accepts ANY method name, so the missing durability API was one visible instance of a general hole.

MEASURED BLAST RADIUS. Probe is a bogus method through a typed fn parameter, `fn t(f: ref <T>) { f.bogus_xyz(); }`, run under `karac check`:

  ACCEPTS BOGUS (hole):  File, BufReader, BufWriter, TcpStream, TcpListener,
                         Mutex, Regex, Arena, Pool, Interner, Semaphore
  rejects (correct):     String, Vec[i64], Map[i64,i64]
  not resolvable here:   Instant, Duration, Secret (undefined type -- not part
                         of the finding, just outside the probe's reach)

So it is 11 of 11 resolvable baked-stdlib handle types, and the correctly-behaving three are the non-baked builtins. That split is the shape of the bug: the types declared in `runtime/stdlib/*.kara` and registered via `register_baked_stdlib` never get their method tables consulted at call sites, while the compiler-native collection types do.

NOT AN INFERENCE HOLE. Ruled out by probe: an explicit annotation does not restore checking. `let fh: File = f; fh.bogus_xyz();` typechecks, and so does the bogus call on a bare `ref File` parameter -- so the receiver's type is known and the method lookup is simply permissive, rather than the type being lost to `unknown`. (The interpreter's runtime error does say "on type 'unknown'", but that is the interpreter's own value-level naming, not the typechecker's view.)

WHY IT MATTERS. `karac check` is the AI-first surface -- the Mend loop, `--output=json`, and any CI gate all run it. On these types it cannot catch a misspelled method, a method that was renamed, or a method the author assumed existed (exactly how B-2026-07-30-16 stayed invisible: design.md documented `sync_all`, the typechecker waved it through, and only build/run disagreed). Every such mistake is deferred to codegen's "no handler for method" or the interpreter's "no dispatch arm", both of which are late and phrased as internal-compiler errors rather than user errors.

SCOPE / WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: not investigated whether the permissiveness is a deliberate escape hatch for partially-implemented stdlib surfaces (plausible -- it would let a type ship constructors before all its methods land) or an oversight in how baked impls register. That distinction decides the fix: if deliberate, the right move is probably to check names against the baked `impl` block and let genuinely-unimplemented methods fail with a real "not yet implemented" diagnostic rather than silence. Also not measured: whether a wrong ARITY or wrong ARGUMENT TYPE is caught on these types, only that the NAME is not -- worth probing before sizing the fix.

REPRO:
  fn t(f: ref File) { f.bogus_xyz(); }
  fn main() {}
    karac check -> All checks passed.

  fn t(f: ref String) { f.bogus_xyz(); }
  fn main() {}
    karac check -> error[typecheck]: no method 'bogus_xyz' on type 'String'
Verified on main @1d0b6e2.

── FIXED 2026-07-31 (two prongs, both in the typechecker) ──

Two distinct dispatch paths were letting an unknown method through on a baked
stdlib handle type, so the fix is in two places:

PRONG 1 — the IMPL-TABLE path (10 of 11 types: File, TcpStream, TcpListener,
Mutex, Pool, Interner, Semaphore, Arena, BufReader, BufWriter). These resolve
their methods through `find_methods_with_args` and hit the method-not-found
`None` arm in `infer_method_call` when the name is absent. That arm only emits
`NoMethodFound` for `is_user_defined || is_exhaustive_prelude ||
method_on_other_specialization`, and `is_user_defined` explicitly excludes every
`PRELUDE_TYPES` name — so all baked handle types fell through silently to
`Type::Error`. Added `is_baked_stdlib_type` to that gate, computed by a new
`prelude::is_baked_stdlib_nominal_type(name)` that scans `STDLIB_PROGRAMS` for a
struct/enum/distinct declaration of the name.

  WHY NOT the `defining_stdlib_origin` flag: measured, it reads `false` for
  `File` — `STDLIB_PROGRAMS` items carry `stdlib_origin = false` at parse time
  (only the resolver-stub splice sets it), so a baked `File` is indistinguishable
  from a user struct by that flag. Scanning the baked programs by name is the
  authoritative signal.

  WHY IT DOESN'T OVER-FIRE on the compiler-native prelude collections that are
  ALSO declared in the baked sources (Vec/Map/Set/Option/Result/…): they are
  already covered — Vec/VecDeque/Option/Result/Tensor/DataFrame by
  `is_exhaustive_prelude`, Map/Set/SortedMap/… by their own dedicated arms that
  reject before this point. Any method that reaches this arm on a baked type is
  one no dedicated arm and no impl matched — genuinely absent.

PRONG 2 — the HARDCODED-ARM path (Regex, the 11th type). `Regex` dispatches
through `infer_regex_method`, not the impl table, and its `_` arm used
`handle_unknown_method`, which is SILENT unless the typo is edit-distance close.
Switched it to `require_known_method` (always emits, with a `did you mean` when
close). Safe because the four enumerated arms — find / find_all / is_match /
replace_all — are the complete Regex surface at interpreter + codegen parity
(B-2026-07-14-19).

TWO TESTS ENCODED THE OLD SILENCE and were updated, not deleted:
  * `user_trait_default_method_over_container_resolves` used `typecheck_ok`
    (which does NOT run `desugar_program`), so a user trait's default method
    spliced onto `Column` — a baked type — was never actually resolved; the test
    passed only via this silent fall-through. It runs correctly on both backends
    (verified `15 30`) because the real pipeline DOES desugar. Switched to
    `typecheck_desugared_ok`, which mirrors `karac check`/`run`/`build` and
    resolves the spliced method for real.
  * `test_method_resolution_stdlib_phase11_arms_silent_for_runtime_only` was
    renamed in spirit: `Regex` now asserts NoMethodFound; the HTTP arms are
    asserted still-silent (see NOT-DONE).

NOT DONE — the HTTP hardcoded arms (Client / Response / HttpError /
RequestBuilder in stdlib_io.rs) share prong 2's exact silent-`handle_unknown_method`
hole. They are NOT in this bug's measured blast radius (not among the 11 probed
resolvable types) and switching them to `require_known_method` needs a per-arm
audit that each enumerated method list is at interpreter/codegen parity — an
incomplete list would turn a valid runtime-only method into a false-positive
rejection. Left as a scoped follow-on; a test pins that they stay silent for now.

VERIFIED: the 11-type sweep all reject; valid methods (`Interner.intern`,
`Regex.is_match`, the Column default-method program) still check. Suites green —
typecheck 2118, interpreter 1335, resolver 335, ownership 381, effectchecker 409,
codegen 2644, cli 545, and the selfhost_codegen oracle (the real stress test that
a stricter typechecker still compiles the self-hosted compiler).

fix: dcdc9e1
title: `Ok(x)` / `Err(x)` / `Some(x)` did not push the expected PAYLOAD type inward, so a type-inferred constructor in the payload never resolved: `fn f() -> Result[Vec[i64], String] { Ok(Vec.new()) }` failed with `expected 'Result<Vec<i64>, String>', found 'Result<Vec<?T2>, E>'`.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO — a plain function tail, no `?` and no match:

  fn f() -> Result[Vec[i64], String] { Ok(Vec.new()) }        // FAILS
  fn g() -> Result[Vec[i64], Vec[String]] { Err(Vec.new()) }  // FAILS (Err slot)
  fn h() -> Option[Vec[i64]] { Some(Vec.new()) }              // FAILS

CONTROLS that always passed, and explain why this survived — each has a payload
whose type is already known, so synthesis mode suffices:

  Ok(0)  ·  Ok(Vec[1, 2])  ·  Ok(v) on an annotated binding  ·  Ok(None)

The defect needs a payload that is itself inference-driven (`Vec.new()`,
`Map.new()`): the argument was inferred in synthesis mode, minting a fresh
`Vec[?T]`, and the enclosing `Result[Vec[?T], E]` could not unify against the
declared type.

MISDIAGNOSED FIRST: pinned in `tests/example_corpus.rs` as "the error type of a
`?`-chained Result is not inferred through a trait method", because the two
instances in examples/db_pipeline sit in match arms after a `?`. Neither the
`?` nor the match is required; the label was wrong and the repro above is the
real shape.

FIX (2026-07-31): a check-mode short-circuit in the same style as the
neighbouring ones in `exprs.rs` — match `Ok`/`Err`/`Some` against an expected
`Result[T, E]` / `Option[T]`, push the corresponding payload slot via
`check_expr`, adopt the expected type. Note `Err` takes the SECOND type
argument.

SCOPE LIMIT, and why it is not optional: restricted to a payload that is a
zero-arg `X.new()` constructor. The unrestricted version REGRESSED integer
handling — `return Some(i)` with an `i64` loop index from an `Option[u64]`
function then check-mode-coerces and trips the i64 -> u64 narrowing diagnostic,
where synthesis mode had accepted it. Caught by `book_snippets_compile` on
ch08's `find[T]`. Both the fix and the scope limit have tests
(`enum_payload_receives_the_expected_type`,
