title: let-else with a moved Drop-bearing enum payload: the interpreter runs the payload's Drop body TWICE (once BEFORE the binding is even used) while AOT runs it once with the wrong owner — a live cross-backend divergence, not a silent-in-parity residual.
detail: PROBE (scratchpad b3011_letelse.kara): `struct Res { id } impl Drop; enum Box2 { Full(Res), Empty }; let w = Box2.Full(Res { id: 52 }); let Full(r2) = w else { println("nope"); return }; println(f"bound {r2.id}"); println("end")`. Interp prints a / drop 52 / bound 52 / drop 52 / end (body twice, the first BEFORE the binding use); AOT prints a / drop 52 / bound 52 / end (once, but fired by w's enum-payload walk at w's NLL while r2 — the payload's new owner — is still live; r2's own slot never fires). Baseline-verified with the overnight session's src/ changes stashed: PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by the B-2026-07-30-11 legs. Both backends are wrong differently: the let-else destructure-move should retract w's payload walk (the disarm the match/if-let sites run) and give r2 a real Drop slot firing at r2's NLL end — after `bound 52`. Correct output: a / bound 52 / drop 52 / end. WHERE: codegen compile_let_else (src/codegen/control_flow.rs ~513) lacks both the disarm and the current_variant_payload_bindings hook the match/if-let sites have; interp's let-else path apparently runs the source walk AND some binding-side fire without retraction (hence the double) — trace which two channels fire when taking this. The bindings ESCAPE into the enclosing scope (no arm frame), so the adoption mechanism differs from match/if-let: the binding must join the ENCLOSING block's cleanup slots. SOURCE NOTE: found while probing the if-let leg, 2026-08-01 overnight session; b3011_letelse.kara + b3011_wletelse.kara in the session scratchpad. FIXED 2a8f4a7: interp LetElse arm gains the disarm_moved_out_enum_payload_one call (retracts the source's walk; the escaped binding's existing slot is the single, correctly-placed fire); codegen compile_let_else gains the owned-variable suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup arm (match-edge only) + the current_variant_payload_bindings hook around bind_pattern_values. Both backends now print a / bound 52 / drop 52 / end; miss edges verified; tests e2e/test_let_else_moved_payload_single_drop (proven failing pre-fix). RESIDUAL NOTED on B-2026-07-30-11's list, not here: an enum-CTOR call argument's Drop payload (check(E2.B(Res { id: 55 })) whose callee drops the enum whole on the divergent edge) stays silent in parity — the arg-position sibling shape.

title: Chained get/first().unwrap() then len() on a fresh-temp Vec[Vec[scalar]] receiver double-frees the borrowed row: let n = mk_rows().first().unwrap().len(); aborts (free(): double free detected) under AOT while the interpreter prints the length.
detail: mk_rows() -> Vec[Vec[i64]] (two pushed rows); let n = mk_rows().first().unwrap().len(); AOT aborts with glibc 'free(): double free detected in tcache 2' (exit 134); interp prints 3. PRE-EXISTING: reproduced on ff3c218 with the B-2026-07-31-43 fix stashed, and the -43 fix neither worsens nor masks it (scalar row-elements are deliberately not recorded in temp_recv_len_elem_types, so the new path never fires here). MECHANISM (two independent trackers free the same row buffer): (1) the typechecker records the fresh-temp receiver's element type (Vec[i64], pod-vec) for first() in temp_recv_elem_types, so codegen's try_compile_freshtemp_vec_read_method materializes mk_rows() and drop-tracks it with the per-element vec-struct recursion — outer buffer plus EACH ROW buffer freed at frame exit; (2) .unwrap() reconstructs the borrowed row as a {ptr,len,cap} value (cap>0, aliasing the tracked storage), the len intercept's expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp admits the chain (MethodCall, not a borrow-returning Call — is_borrow_returning_call_expr only knows free fns), owned_temp_drops has no entry (span-collided chain), and materialize_owned_temp's degrade path track_vec_var(slot, None) frees the SAME row buffer again. Candidate fixes: teach the len-family intercept (and materialize_owned_temp callers generally) to refuse a receiver whose chain already routed through the freshtemp-read materialization (e.g. a span-keyed 'receiver already tracked' set), or classify unwrap-of-borrow chains as borrow-returning in expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp. NOTE the sibling shape Vec[Vec[String]] fails closed instead (first() on the non-recorded element type loud-bails 'no handler for method first on non-identifier receiver') — documented deferral, no UB. SOURCE NOTE: found probing hazard shapes for the B-2026-07-31-43 fix, 2026-08-01 overnight session; probe scratchpad/b43_chain1.kara. FIXED 54ac148: narrow structural gate at the len-family intercept — new expr_is_unwrap_of_borrow_accessor(expr) (MethodCall unwrap|expect whose object satisfies the existing scrutinee_is_borrow_call classification: get/first/last, non-Client) short-circuits the drop-track branch, so the unwrapped borrow is never materialized as an owned temp; the get-family materialization's per-element walk remains the single owner of the row storage (valgrind: 0 errors, 0 leaks — the walk frees outer + both rows exactly once). Sibling positions were probed and are ALREADY clean, confirming the intercept was the only borrow-blind consumer: let-binding of the unwrapped row (prints 3, valgrind clean), wildcard discard (clean), and the arg position is REJECTED by the typechecker (expected Vec[i64], found ref Vec[i64] — the checker knows the unwrap result is a borrow, which is also why the codegen-side structural gate is faithful to the type system rather than a heuristic). unwrap_or* variants deliberately excluded from the gate (miss arm substitutes an owned default — branch-dependent ownership, no proven double-free shape). Tests: e2e_len_of_unwrapped_borrow_row_single_free (first/last/get legs, proven ABORTING pre-fix with src/ stashed), asan_len_of_unwrapped_borrow_row_freed_once (200-iteration loop, proven failing pre-fix). Full B-43 probe battery re-verified valgrind-clean post-fix (no interaction with the -43 element-walk tracking).

title: wildcard-let user-enum discard fires the Drop payload body under karac run but not karac build (+ own-Drop-enum and erased-generic sibling divergences)
detail: Probe after the -30-11 user-method leg: `fn mk_enum(n: i64) -> Box2 { return Box2.Full(Res { id: n }); }` (Res has a user impl Drop) with `let _ = mk_enum(21);` — karac run prints 'drop 21', karac build prints NOTHING (bare `mk_enum(22);` was silent in both, an in-parity gap). Root cause: codegen's try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp resolved the enum return type and then returned at the deliberate 'SHAPE 1 stays out of scope' exclusion (the struct field-body walk GEPs parent fields and cannot reach an enum payload), while the interpreter's run_discarded_value_user_drops walked EnumVariant payloads VALUE-driven. The same pre-fix probe matrix surfaced two sibling wildcard-let divergences from that value-driven walk: an own-impl-Drop enum discard fired own body + payload bodies under interp vs own body only under AOT, and an erased-generic payload (enum MyBox[T] { Wrap(T) } instantiated at a Drop struct) fired under interp while codegen structurally cannot see through the erasure. FIXED 6915b47: codegen now registers __karac_dropelems_enum_<E> (declared-type-driven, BODIES ONLY) on the one-shot discard frame for a user-enum return — free fns AND user impl methods (the method arm's struct-only return filter widened to enum_layouts, closing the residual the -30-11 user-method leg recorded); the enum drop switch (track_enum_var) is pushed BEFORE the UserDrop body so the LIFO drain runs the body before the payload's heap is freed — the reverse order was caught IN-SLICE printing garbage ('drop 41 dro' instead of 'drop 41 h41') with valgrind Invalid reads on a String-carrying payload, the same ordering rule the ctor arm documents ('pushed AFTER the battery so the LIFO drain runs them before the battery's frees'). Interp: run_discarded_value_user_drops' EnumVariant arm split three ways — Option/Result keep the value-driven recursion (codegen twin: track_discarded_optres_payload_bodies, instantiation-driven), own-impl-Drop enums run their OWN body only (matching codegen's karac_drop_<E> wrapper and the enum-assign leg's exclusion), all other user enums take the extracted declared-type-driven run_enum_payload_user_drops_value walk — and the bare-statement StmtKind::Expr arms (Call + MethodCall) gained the enum leg. Post-fix all four quadrants (wildcard-let x bare, run x build) match the struct behavior: concrete payloads fire everywhere, erased generics are silent everywhere (their heap is still freed — valgrind 'all heap blocks freed' via the mono enum drop switch), own-Drop enums are own-body-only everywhere. user_method_returns_owned_struct renamed user_method_returns_owned_type (admits enum returns). Tests: e2e_enum_return_discard_runs_payload_body + test_enum_return_discard_runs_payload_body twins (identical source and expected string covering all shapes incl. the String payload that pins the LIFO ordering; both proven failing with src/ stashed); six-probe three-way parity sweep (interp/AOT/JIT identical) with valgrind zero-error on every AOT binary. title: enum reassign never frees the displaced payload's interior heap — Full(Res{name: String}) leaks the old String on every assignment (DCE-masked until the payload bodies walk made the value live)

title: fresh method-RECEIVER Drop temps: interp never fires their bodies, karac build fires them at scope exit — and owned-self passthrough chains DOUBLE-fire with stale slots
detail: Probes b156_recvtemp/b156_chain (2026-08-01 session; full design notes in the session state file). `let x = mk(1).ident();` (ref-self method on a fresh Drop-bearing receiver): the interpreter fires NO receiver-temp body ever (run_fresh_temp_arg_drops has no method-receiver sibling), while karac build's __urecv_tmp materialization (method_call.rs try_compile_user_method_on_fresh_temp region, track_user_drop_var registered unconditionally for fresh owned receivers) fires it at SCOPE EXIT — after 'end'. Worse, owned-self methods whose result flows onward multiply: `mk(3).me().ident()` where `fn me(self) -> Res { return self; }` printed 'drop 3 r3' TWICE at exit (receiver temp + result temp both tracked over the same conceptual value), `let y = mk(2).me();` printed r2's body at y's death AND again at exit, and `mk(1).plus(10)` (rebuild) printed a STALE-slot body ('drop 1 r1' after the value had become id 11). Memory is valgrind-clean throughout — the divergence is body observability. HAZARDS for the implementer, probed this session: (a) the karac_drop_<T> wrapper is body+MEMORY for structs, so any statement-end drain of __urecv_tmp must exclude borrow-RETURNING methods (user_ref_method_names) — freeing the receiver at statement end dangles a returned borrow that today survives to scope exit; (b) the owned-self registration needs a returns-self/passthrough guard (the fn_returns_param analog for receivers) or must be dropped entirely — the interpreter's silent-for-owned-self behavior is the current parity direction; (c) any interp receiver hook must admit exactly the codegen-registrable shapes (declared-type rule). Suggested target semantics (struct twin + design.md): ref-self fresh receivers fire at statement end on both backends; owned-self receiver temps stay silent on both (the callee consumed the value); passthrough results covered by the result consumer only. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b156 family), found while probing the -30-11 receiver-temp residual. FIXED 79f99b0 (struct receivers): the target semantics landed exactly as designed above. Codegen: the __urecv_tmp tracking is now self-mode-gated via impl_method_self_and_borrow_return (program-snapshot scan, impl target head + method name -> (SelfParam, returns-borrow)) — only a ref self / mut ref self method that does not return a borrow registers the user-Drop body, under the drain-eligible __urecv_drop_tmp name (fires at statement end via drain_statement_temp_user_drops); owned-self and borrow-returning methods are memory-only (track_struct_var), which removes ALL three chain pathologies (double fire, re-fire after the binding's own death, stale-slot fire). Interp: new run_fresh_recv_temp_drop hook in try_eval_impl_method's success path — fresh receiver shapes (Call to user fn / ctor, struct literal), ref-self only, borrow-return excluded (new method_returns_borrow helper), STRUCT values only. title: reassigning a struct/enum binding from a call that mentions it (`e = pass(e)`, `s = mk(s.id + 1)`) orphans the old value's heap under karac build — the mentions-guard assumed a move the caller-retains convention never makes
detail: Probe family b163 (chasing B-2026-08-01-3's recorded pass-roundtrip residual, which turned out to be one corner of a wider class): for `x = f(...x...)` over a heap-carrying non-shared STRUCT or value ENUM, the Assign arm's displacement legs skip the old value's eager free whenever the RHS mentions the target (expr_mentions_name_deep — 'moved into the callee, uncertain => silent'). But the old value never moves: an owned arg is deep-copied at CALLEE ENTRY (the caller-retains convention — IR shows the p14e dcopy region cloning the payload and the callee freeing its copy), a ref arg only borrows, and a scalar field read consumes nothing. The store then overwrites the only pointer to the original buffers — a hard leak, one block per reassign, on EVERY mention shape probed: owned-arg roundtrip `e = pass(e)` (enum, 2 bytes/run — the recorded -3 residual), struct `s = pass_res(s)` (with AND without impl Drop), ref-param mention `s = peekmk(s)`, scalar-field mention `s = mk(s.id + 1)`. DCE-masked in probes whose old payload is never read (constant f-strings lower to cap==0 statics — probe hygiene note: interpolate to force real heap). Vec/Map/Set/tensor LHS shapes are NOT affected (their reassign legs free the old handle without a mentions gate — probed clean). Output was already in three-way parity (the NLL channel fires the bodies once at the binding's last-use statement on both backends); only memory diverged. FIXED 6d95ba7: the struct and enum displacement legs admit the mentions case when the RHS is a free-fn Call to a top-level USER function returning an owned value (assign_rhs_is_owned_user_call — declines borrow-returning callees, whose result could alias the old heap, and names shadowed by locals), and fire MEMORY ONLY: emit_struct_drop_synthesis for structs (never the body+memory wrapper — the NLL fire already covers the body) and the cap-guarded __karac_drop_<E> switch for enums (bodies section skipped). Cap-guards make the eager free robust against RHS-internal moves: a legitimately moved heap field was cap-zeroed by the move machinery, so the free no-ops on exactly what left. Post-fix: three-way parity (interp/AOT/JIT) with output unchanged on all 9 b163 probes + valgrind 'all heap blocks freed / 0 errors' on every one; b154-b162 probe corpus re-swept (2 pre-existing flags recorded separately — bare user-enum ctor discard divergence and bare struct-call discard leak, see the b164 follow-up). RESIDUALS, recorded: MethodCall RHS (`s = other.build(s)`) and non-call mention shapes (if/match tails) keep the conservative silence — leak-side. Tests: asan_roundtrip_reassign_frees_displaced_original (LSan gate, proven failing with src/ stashed — LeakSanitizer detected the orphaned buffers) + e2e/test_roundtrip_reassign_single_nll_fire (output pins on both backends). title: `&&` / `||` diagnostics are emitted 2-3x per occurrence and carry NO `replacement`, so `karac fix` cannot apply a one-token substitution the message itself spells out. 11 real mistakes rendered as 24 JSON diagnostics, none machine-applicable.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found on the FIRST `karac check` of examples/sigv4.kara — writing `&&`/`||` out of Rust habit is exactly the mistake a fresh LLM author makes, which is what makes this a wedge issue rather than a cosmetic one.

MEASURED (examples/sigv4.kara, first pass):
  total diagnostics : 24
  distinct sites    : 11
  multiplicity      : every site >= 2x; three sites 3x
  with `replacement`: 0

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS, same two lines of source.

(1) DUPLICATE EMISSION, scaling with expression nesting. Both arms live in the Pratt parser's infix loop, keyed off `self.peek_token()`:
      Token::PipePipe => { self.error("the `||` operator is not used…"); (BinOp::Or, 6, 7) }
      Token::AmpAmp   => { self.error("the `&&` operator is not used…"); (BinOp::And, 8, 9) }
PEEK does not consume, so a given operator token is re-examined once per precedence level the climb unwinds through, and each visit re-emits. The multiplicity therefore tracks chain length: a lone `a && b` doubles, while the 4-operand `||` chain at line 301 of the source that found this emitted THREE copies of each of its four operators. The fix is to emit once per token position — a seen-set keyed on the operator's span, or emitting at the consume site rather than the peek site.

(2) NO MACHINE-APPLICABLE FIX, for the most mechanical substitution in the language. The message already names the replacement verbatim ("use `and` instead"); it is a single-token, context-free rewrite with no ownership or type consequences. But the site calls the plain `self.error(msg)` helper, so the JSON carries no `replacement` key and `karac fix` is a no-op — confirmed by running it: `fix` reprints the errors and changes nothing. The parser HAS the channel (src/parser.rs:157 documents edits hung there; src/parser/exprs.rs:487 is a sibling site that populates `replacement`), so this is an unconverted call site, not missing infrastructure.
This is the B-2026-07-31-31 class — 'mechanical diagnostics that name their own replacement carry no `karac fix`' — which was fixed for the diagnostics that leg enumerated. These two were not in that set. Worth an audit pass over the remaining `self.error(` call sites for others that name a literal replacement in prose.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE WEDGE: the Mend loop feeds structured diagnostics to an LLM and counts what the compiler fixes FOR it. Here the compiler hands back 24 items for 11 mistakes, tells the author the exact answer in prose, and then declines to apply any of it — so a trivially mechanical class lands in the 'fixed-by-llm' bucket instead of 'fixed-by-karac', understating the machine-fix rate while inflating the diagnostic volume the model has to read. Both halves push the measurement the wrong way.

REPRO: any file with a `&&` or `||`. `fn f(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool { a && b }` → two identical diagnostics, neither fixable.

FIXED 28438e8. Both defects, both at the parser's Pratt infix match (src/parser/exprs.rs). (1) DUPLICATE EMISSION: exactly as the row diagnosed — the `Token::PipePipe`/`Token::AmpAmp` arms emitted inside the PEEK-driven operator match, which re-examines the same token once per precedence level the climb unwinds through. The emission now lives at the CONSUME site (after the `l_bp < min_bp` break, immediately before `self.advance()`), which runs exactly once per source token — one diagnostic per occurrence, no seen-set needed. (2) MACHINE-APPLICABLE FIX: the same consume-site block registers a `fix_edits` TextEdit keyed on the operator token's span (the same span `error()` stamps on the diagnostic, so `collect_diagnostics`' span-join attaches it as `replacement`): `&&` -> `and`, `||` -> `or`, with the word-operator spacing rule from the `!` -> `not` sibling generalized to BOTH sides — a side that abuts its neighbor token gains one space (`a == 1&&b` fixes to `a == 1 and b`), a side with existing whitespace reuses it. Verified end-to-end on a 5-site probe (spaced `&&`, 4-operand `||` chain, abutting `&&`): `check --output=json` emits exactly 5 diagnostics (was 2-3x each), every one carrying `replacement`; one `karac fix` pass applies all 5; re-check clean; the fixed program runs correctly. Tests (both stash-proven failing pre-fix): tests/parser.rs test_amp_amp_pipe_pipe_diagnose_once_per_token_with_fix_edit (counts one error per token + the 4 replacement texts),  tests/cli.rs fix_applies_and_or_word_operator_edits (end-to-end through the real binary incl. the abutting-spacing rule and a clean re-check). Full suite green.
resolution: fixed in 28438e8 — moved the &&/|| emission from the Pratt peek site to the consume site (once per token) and registered span-keyed and/or fix edits with two-sided spacing.

PROBES (2026-08-01, b184_deepchain / b184_compidx):
  deep chain: struct Res{id,name:String} + Drop; Outer{h: Holder{r: Res}}; `o.h.r = Res{5,y5}` — expected `drop 9 z9` before the store per the displacement rule; BOTH backends print nothing for the displaced value (a/held 5/drop 5 y5/end); valgrind clean, so the memory half is handled by the field-store path — this leg is drop-observability only.
  computed index: `v[base - 1] = Res{5,y5}` with base=1 — BOTH backends silent on `drop 9 z9`, and AOT leaks the displaced element's name buffer (2 bytes / 1 block, exit-99 valgrind); the same store with a literal `v[0]` fires the body and frees (the b174 fix).

MECHANISM: both displacement emitters gate on simple place shapes — emit_displaced_field_bodies requires the target's object to be a bare Identifier (one-level field), and emit_displaced_index_elem_drop requires an Integer/Identifier index (effect-free re-evaluation rule). A deep chain or computed index declines both the bodies and (for the index leg) the cap-guarded field-buffer free. The interp's Assign-arm siblings share the gates, so the bodies half is IN PARITY (silent) — the codegen-only defect is the index-leg leak. FIX SHAPE: the deep-chain leg can resolve the chain base with lower_field_access_ptr recursion (the same trick the field-rooted index arm b175 used); the computed-index leg needs the index evaluated ONCE into a temp and reused by both the displacement walk and the store (lifting the effect-free re-evaluation restriction by construction).

SOURCE NOTE: probe family, b173/b174 recorded-residual follow-through, 2026-08-01 overnight window.

FIXED e23c570. Three legs. (1) DEEP-CHAIN bodies: emit_displaced_field_bodies (stmts.rs) flattens the target's object into (root, middles), runs every base gate against the ROOT (whose armed FULL UserDrop action covers the whole aggregate), and GEPs down plain non-shared non-generic middle structs to the parent; the interp Assign FieldAccess-target branch walks the chain identically. (2) DEEP-CHAIN memory: the nested plain-parent store in compile_field_store (expr_ops.rs) was a BARE overwrite — the displaced old value's heap was NEVER freed at any depth >= 2. The probe's pre-fix 'valgrind clean' was an artifact: LLVM DCE'd the never-read old allocation outright, so the leak was invisible for write-only old values and REAL for any read one (a print before the reassign exposed it: 2 bytes definitely lost). The store now runs the same in-place old-value drop the depth-1 fall-through uses (drop_old_plain_struct_field); shared parents and Option[shared] fields keep pre-existing behavior. (3) COMPUTED-INDEX gate: the typechecker desugars primitive-int operators into intrinsic calls (`base - 1` -> `i64.sub(base, 1)`) BEFORE either backend sees the AST — widening the gates' ExprKind::Binary arm was a no-op because Binary never reaches them. Both purity gates (index_expr_is_pure_scalar / assign_index_is_pure_scalar) now accept exactly the registered primitive arithmetic/bit intrinsics (add/sub/mul/div/rem/neg/bitand/bitor/bitxor/shl/shr/not on i8..i64/u8..u64/usize/isize) over pure operands, so `v[base - 1] = <new>` fires the displaced element's bodies and frees its field buffers on both backends. Verified: b184_deepchain / b184_compidx / b184_readleak / b184_refroot / b184_vecfld all parity + valgrind 0. Tests (stash-proven failing pre-fix): e2e/test_deep_chain_field_assign_displaced_bodies, e2e/test_computed_index_assign_displaced_elem_bodies, asan_nested_field_store_displaced_old_freed. Full suite 12782/0. Fixing leg (2) unmasked the deep-chain field MOVE-OUT double-free — split to B-2026-08-01-31 (fixed same commit).
resolution: fixed in e23c570 — chain-flattened displaced-bodies emitters (both backends), old-value drop on the nested plain-parent store, and desugared-intrinsic purity gates for computed indices.

tracker: src/codegen/param_own.rs suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal (Identifier/`self` object only — a deep-chain source `o.h.r` declines) and its enum deeper-place sibling suppress_place_field_enum_move_source (enum fields only, whose own doc records 'Vec/String/struct fields through a [deeper place] are a separate follow-on, not yet observed'); src/codegen/stmts.rs Let-arm disarm site (disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field, Identifier object only); src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs suppress_moved_out_drop_field (Identifier object only)
title: Deep-chain field move-out (`let x = o.h.r` / `let s = o.h.name`) never cap-zeroes the source: the moved-out binding AND the root's StructDrop both free the same buffer — a `karac check`-clean double-free abort under karac build (interp fine, run-vs-build divergence). Depth-1 (`let x = h.r`) is handled; every deeper place was not.
detail:
PROBE (2026-08-01, b184_movechainonly): struct R6{id,name:String}; H6{r:R6}; O6{h:H6}; `let x = o.h.r; println(x.name)` — AOT aborts `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (valgrind: Invalid free, 3 allocs/4 frees); `karac check` passes CLEAN (the move is legal, o is never reused). Interp is value-semantic and fine — a run-vs-build divergence on an accepted program. The depth-1 sibling `let x = h.r` balances (4/4): the Let arm cap-zeroes the source field via suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal, whose object match is Identifier/`self` ONLY, so any deeper chain silently skips the zeroing while the destination still registers its own cleanup.

INTERACTION that surfaced it (b184 slice): the B-2026-08-01-30 memory leg adds the displaced old-value drop to the nested chain-store path; on a move-then-reassign (`let x = o.h.r; o.h.r = Res{..}`) that drop freed the buffer x still owns — same missing-zeroing root cause, second symptom.

Drop-BODIES half: the Let-arm disarm (disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field, B-2026-07-29-39) and the interp's moved_out_drop_field_bindings record are also Identifier-object gated, so a deep-chain move of a Drop-carrying field left the root's bodies walk armed — double body on the moved value at the root's death.

SOURCE NOTE: probe family, found while fixing B-2026-08-01-30's move-then-reassign edge, 2026-08-01 overnight window.

FIXED e23c570 (same commit as B-2026-08-01-30 — found fixing its move-then-reassign edge). Memory: a new deeper-place suppressor `suppress_place_field_struct_move_source` (param_own.rs, next to the enum sibling whose doc predicted exactly this follow-on) resolves the parent via place_chain_type_name / field_chain_place_ptr and cap-zeroes the moved field in place — named non-shared non-generic struct fields route through zero_struct_move_caps, direct Vec/String fields cap-zero (generic-monomorph fields decline, keeping today's behavior — the B-2026-07-15-24 base-layout-GEP class). Called from both Let-arm depth-1 sites (vec/string-dest and struct-dest), self-gated to deeper-place objects and non-owned-param roots. Bodies: the Let-arm disarm (disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field) and the interp's suppress_moved_out_drop_field both flatten deep chains and disarm/record the ROOT — root-coarse, the depth-1 B-2026-07-29-39 trade, keeping both backends on identical single-fire sequencing (x fires the moved value at ITS death; the root walk and the displaced-fire stay silent). Verified: b184_movechainonly (was double-free abort, now parity + valgrind 0), b184_movereassign (was Invalid free 4a/5f, now 4/4), b184_movedropchain (Drop bodies, 3-way parity + vg 0). Tests (stash-proven failing pre-fix): asan_deep_chain_field_move_out_no_double_free (struct + String field legs), e2e/test_deep_chain_field_move_then_reassign (UAM-warned deliberate move-then-reinit, pinned in OWNERSHIP_GATE_GRANDFATHERED). Full suite 12782/0. RESIDUALS, recorded: owned-param-rooted deep chains (`fn f(o: O) { let x = o.h.r; }` under caller-retains) keep pre-existing behavior — the suppressor declines owned_struct_params roots exactly like the depth-1 sites, and the depth-1 deep-copy lane (deep_copy_owned_struct_param_field_move) is Identifier-object gated too; generic-monomorph deep-chain moved fields decline the zeroing (same as pre-fix); Map/Set-typed fields at deep places keep their existing handle paths (unprobed).
resolution: fixed in e23c570 — deeper-place struct/Vec-String move-out suppressor + root-coarse bodies disarm (codegen) and root-coarse move record (interp).

title: Vec.filled's calloc fast path only recognises a SCALAR constant zero, so Vec.filled(n, Vec.new()) store-loops an all-zero aggregate instead of calloc'ing it — measured ~100x (117.6 ms vs 1.2 ms on a 1e6-element fill)
detail:
`Vec.filled(n, v)` has a calloc fast path (B-2026-07-08-7) that turns a
statically all-zero fill into ONE lazily-zeroed allocation instead of a
per-element store loop. It fires only for a SCALAR constant zero, so the very
common `Vec.filled(n, <empty collection>)` misses it and writes every element
by hand.

MEASURED (during the B-2026-07-30-4 sub-localization, karac 79757f5d70a6):

    Vec.filled(cap + 1, Vec.new())   kara 117.6 ms
    calloc(cap + 1, sizeof(IntVec))  C       1.2 ms

for the same 1e6-element fill -- a ~100x gap. calloc gets lazily-zeroed pages
from the kernel; kara touches all 24 MB. (In that kata it was only 1.9% of
total runtime, which is why it was set aside rather than chased -- it is a
real gap, not the cause of that bug.)

WHY IT MISSES -- TWO guards in `build_vec_filled`
(src/codegen/collections.rs:1401-1422), and BOTH reject this case, so relaxing
either one alone is not a fix:

  1. `val_is_zero_bits` matches only `IntValue` / `FloatValue` constants:

         let val_is_zero_bits = match val {
             BasicValueEnum::IntValue(iv)   => iv.get_zero_extended_constant() == Some(0),
             BasicValueEnum::FloatValue(fv) => fv.get_constant().is_some_and(|(v,_)| v.to_bits()==0),
             _ => false,          // every struct/aggregate lands here
         };

     `Vec.new()` lowers to the aggregate `{ptr: null, len: 0, cap: 0}` -- all
     zero BYTES, but not an int/float constant, so it falls to `_ => false`.

  2. `needs_clone = !is_trivially_copyable_te(elem_te)` is TRUE for a `Vec`
     element (it owns a heap buffer), and the fast path requires `!needs_clone`.

SUGGESTED FIX (untested). Recognise a statically all-zero-bits AGGREGATE, and
note that the `needs_clone` guard is over-strict for exactly that value: the
per-element "clone" of an all-zero collection handle is the identity -- cloning
an empty Vec/String/Map/Set allocates nothing and copies `{null,0,0}` to
`{null,0,0}` -- so calloc is sound even when the element type is not trivially
copyable, PROVIDED the fill value is statically all-zero.

Guard the relaxation on that provability rather than on the element type: it
holds for empty collections and for `Option::None`, and should NOT be extended
to a bare `shared` handle (all-zero would be a null RC pointer, and a retain on
null is not the identity) -- though no surface syntax constructs that value
today.

SCOPE. Any `Vec.filled(n, <empty collection>)`, which is the natural way to
build an adjacency list / bucket table / grid of rows -- `Vec[Vec[T]]`,
`Vec[String]`, `Vec[Map[K,V]]`. The larger `n`, the larger the gap.

NOT MEASURED SINCE the karac that produced the numbers above; the figures are
from a loaded shared container and are indicative of the ratio, not precise.
A clean re-measure is the first step for whoever takes this. FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in 0872d65. Re-measure first (per the row): the gap had already narrowed from the filed 117ms to ~20ms vs Rust ~6ms for 1e6 Vec.filled(n, Vec.new()) -- the store loop improved in the interim -- but the per-slot clone loop was still the bottleneck. Fix in build_vec_filled (src/codegen/collections.rs): val_is_zero_bits gains a StructValue arm (ConstantAggregateZero detection via as_value_ref() == const_zero() ref-compare -- runtime-built values never match the uniqued constant, so the arm only fires for statically-all-zero aggregates like Vec.new()/String.new()/Map.new() literals in fill position), and the calloc gate relaxes from `!needs_clone && val_is_zero_bits` to `val_is_zero_bits && !elem_is_shared` -- an all-zero aggregate needs no per-slot clone even when the elem type is heap-bearing, since every slot starts as the same all-zero control block. shared elements stay excluded (RC headers must be per-slot). After: ~6ms, at parity with the Rust baseline. Slot independence + drop pairing pinned by test_e2e_vec_filled_empty_vec_elements_independent + asan_vec_filled_empty_aggregate_fill_and_drop; the calloc lowering itself pinned by test_ir_vec_filled_empty_aggregate_uses_calloc (stash-proven FAILED pre-fix). SPLIT: Vec.filled(n, Map.new()) segfaults under AOT -- stash-verified PRE-EXISTING (crashes identically without this change; interp fine) -- filed separately as B-2026-08-02-12.

fix: e061ab29. `frozen` adopted into the authoritative spec as design.md § Feature 4 Part 5c ('Frozen Handles'), which is the remainder this row's own last section named. The feature itself shipped across earlier commits (surface, escape check E0511, freeze-site check E0512, RC suppression via the borrow lowering, `par` + auto-par admission, projection stickiness, per-instance freeze, frozen-element containers) and the motivating kata is published with a measured par lane. Every rule in the new section was re-measured on the current compiler before being written, which corrected two of this row's own claims: the freeze site requires a unique source only for a `mut`-bearing type, and the frozen-element container is an ordinary `Vec[S]` local with no `frozen` in its spelling. The spec's normative example is pinned end to end by `design_md_part_5c_frozen_example_compiles_and_runs` with a keyword-stripped control that must still be refused by the capture gate.
title: `shared struct` was excluded from parallelism on BOTH surfaces — explicit `par {}` hard-errored (E_CONCURRENT_SHARED_STRUCT) and auto-par declined via the concurrency.rs B-2026-07-16-6 gate (reported, NOT silent — see the correction in detail); `frozen` now admits both
detail:
SHAPE. `kara-katas leetcode/101-200/133-clone-graph/bench/clone_bfs_par.kara`
builds a graph of `shared struct Node` once, sequentially, then reads it from
18 `par {}` branches. No branch mutates it. `karac build` refuses:

    error[ownership]: shared struct `Node` cannot be accessed from multiple
    concurrent tasks (binding `root` reachable from two par-block branches)

THE REJECTION IS CORRECT AND INTENDED, per design.md § Rc vs Arc — Two-Phase
Algorithm, quoted in `src/ownership/concurrent_shared.rs`: `live_range(v) ∩
parallel_region ≠ ∅` AND reachable from > 1 concurrent branch → compile error.
Rc→Arc promotion covers a sole-ownership move into exactly ONE branch. The
reason is refcount traffic, not payload mutation: `emit_rc_inc` is a plain
load/add/store, so even pure READS race on the refcount (this is what B-2026-
07-28-13's SIGSEGV was, from a stale pre-gate binary).

THE GAP. There is no way to express "share this immutable structure across
tasks, read-only, without locks". The two available answers both overshoot:

  * `par struct` + `Mutex[T]` on every `mut` field — the migration the
    diagnostic prescribes. Correct and safe, but it buys mutual exclusion for a
    structure nobody mutates, and every read pays a lock.
  * restructure so each branch owns its own copy — sound, but it means building
    N copies of a read-only structure purely to satisfy the checker.

For the benchmark corpus this has a concrete cost: the C mirror shares the same
read-only graph across pthreads with NO locking, because C has no refcount to
race. So there is no Kāra formulation of this kata that is both legal and
algorithm-matched to its own C mirror — the parity rule and the language rule
cannot both be satisfied. The kata's par lane is withdrawn rather than
published with a lock Kāra conceptually does not need (see the kata README).

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT (all unexplored, listed so nobody re-derives them):

  * An immutable/frozen `shared` handle whose reads emit no RC traffic, hence
    nothing to race. Needs a freeze point in the type system.
  * Admitting the read-only case in `concurrent_shared.rs` when every branch use
    is provably a read AND the retain/release for those uses is elided. NOTE:
    the existing `src/rc_elide.rs` machinery does NOT already do this — it is a
    per-FUNCTION param analysis (`nonescaping_param_names`, fail-closed), not a
    par-capture analysis. It is cited here as precedent for "read-only + non-
    escaping ⇒ RC traffic is skippable", not as an implementation that covers
    this case.
  * An arena / index-pool representation (`Vec[Vec[i64]]` adjacency, indices
    instead of handles) sidesteps RC entirely and is trivially shareable. This
    is the corpus's existing idiom for the same problem (#222 index-pool tree,
    #234 index-pool list) and is the recommended user-level answer TODAY — but
    it is a different program, not a fix to the restriction.

SEVERITY. Low as a correctness matter (the gate is sound and the diagnostic is
good, carrying a machine-applicable fix_diff). It is filed because it is a real
expressiveness hole that costs a benchmark lane and has no non-overshooting
workaround.

── SUBSTANTIALLY CORRECTED (2026-08-02). THE HEADLINE CLAIM WAS WRONG. ──

This entry asserted there is "no way to express 'share this immutable structure
across tasks, read-only, without locks'". THAT IS FALSE. `par struct` with
IMMUTABLE fields is exactly that mechanism, it is lock-free, and the compiler
says so in the diagnostic for a `mut` field:

    error[typecheck]: `mut` field `x` of `par struct Pt` must be `Atomic[T]` or
    `Mutex[T]`: a `par struct`'s concurrent-safety guarantee is structural, so
    plain mutable fields are not permitted. Wrap the field type in `Atomic[...]`
    for lock-free access or `Mutex[...]` for locked compound mutation, or drop
    `mut` to make the field immutable (IMMUTABLE FIELDS ARE FREELY READABLE
    ACROSS TASKS)

VERIFIED (scratchpad parimmut.kara): a `par struct Pt { x: i64, y: i64 }` read
by FOUR concurrent `par` branches — no Mutex, no Atomic, no annotation at the
use site — checks clean and produces identical correct output on interp and
AOT. So the "both available answers overshoot" framing was wrong: only the
`mut`-field case needs a lock, and `Atomic[T]` covers the lock-free scalar case
even then.

WHY THE `shared struct` GATE IS RIGHT, which this entry also under-explained.
RC atomicity is a property of the TYPE, not of a binding: codegen picks
`emit_rc_inc` (plain load/add/store) vs `emit_arc_inc` (atomic) from the type.
`ownership/par_capture_classify.rs`'s `SharedRc` mode already emits one ATOMIC
inc per branch with a balancing atomic dec, so the captured ROOT handle could be
made safe by relaxing the gate — but that is not sufficient. A branch traversing
the structure retains/releases the NESTED handles it walks, and those are
ordinary `shared struct` values whose inc/dec are non-atomic. Two branches
walking one graph therefore race on the interior nodes' refcounts regardless of
how the root was captured. That is precisely B-2026-07-28-13's SIGSEGV. Making
this safe requires the whole reachable graph to be atomically refcounted, which
IS what `par struct` means. Relaxing the gate alone would reintroduce the race.

WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS — a much narrower gap: there is NO FREEZE POINT. A type
that needs post-construction mutation to be BUILT (a cyclic graph must link its
nodes after they exist, so `mut neighbors: Vec[Node]`) cannot afterwards be
declared immutable. It must carry `Mutex[Vec[Node]]` for its whole lifetime,
including a purely read-only phase, and `Atomic[T]` does not help because the
field is compound. A `freeze`/`finalize` operation transitioning a value from
mutable-construction to immutable-shared is the missing piece — and only for
COMPOUND fields, since scalar mut fields already have the lock-free `Atomic[T]`
answer.

CONSEQUENCE FOR #133, unchanged in outcome but for a corrected reason: its par
lane stays withdrawn not because "Kāra cannot share read-only" (it can) but
because THIS type needs construction-time mutation of a compound field, so the
only legal form carries a Mutex its lock-free C mirror does not. The
recommended user-level answer is still an index-pool representation, which
sidesteps the whole question by not making the graph a `shared struct` at all.

SEVERITY: stays low, and is now better justified — this is a missing
convenience for one shape (compound-mut-then-frozen), not a hole in cross-task
sharing.

PROCESS NOTE: this entry was filed by the same session that later corrected it.
It was written from a failed `karac build` plus a reading of the gate, without
testing whether the sanctioned alternative actually required a lock. One probe
would have caught it. File what you measured, not what the failure implied.

── REFRAMED AGAIN (2026-08-02), and SEVERITY RAISED low → high. ──

The correction above narrowed this to "no freeze point". That is still too
narrow, and it mis-assigns the work. A freeze point is one possible MECHANISM;
filing it as THE gap bakes in the assumption that the USER should be the one to
resolve refcount atomicity. They should not. Which refcount flavour a type gets
is a codegen decision the compiler has all the information to make.

THE GAP, restated: a `shared struct` cannot participate in parallelism AT ALL,
and the choice is forced at TYPE-DECLARATION time — before the author knows
whether the value will ever cross a parallel region. Both parallel surfaces are
closed:

  * EXPLICIT `par {}` — E_CONCURRENT_SHARED_STRUCT, this entry's original
    subject. Hard compile error.
  * AUTO-PAR, the DEFAULT build path and the language's flagship feature —
    SILENTLY DECLINES. `concurrency.rs::classify_disjoint_write_loop`'s first
    soundness gate (B-2026-07-16-6) rejects any loop body touching a plain
    (non-`par`) `shared` value for exactly the same reason: "Disjoint element
    writes do not make the refcount traffic disjoint." No diagnostic at the
    decline site — the loop simply runs sequentially.

So the user-visible contract today is: pick `shared struct` and forfeit
parallelism, automatic and explicit both; pick `par struct` and pay atomic RC
everywhere plus `Mutex[T]`/`Atomic[T]` on every `mut` field, including in
programs that never go parallel. That is precisely the Rc-vs-Arc choice Kara
exists to remove, relocated from the allocation site to the type declaration.

WHAT SHOULD CLOSE IT, in cost order (all still unexplored):

  1. PAR-CAPTURE RC ELISION — cheapest, and closes the read-only case that
     motivated this entry. If every use of a value inside the parallel region is
     provably a read and its retain/release are elided, there is no refcount
     traffic left to race, so no atomics are needed at all. `src/rc_elide.rs`
     already proves the analogous "read-only + non-escaping ⇒ RC traffic is
     skippable" for function params; this needs the par-capture sibling. Would
     unblock BOTH surfaces for read-only sharing.
  2. WHOLE-PROGRAM ATOMICITY PROMOTION — general; covers RC-header mutation,
     not payload mutation. If a type is reachable from more than one concurrent
     branch ANYWHERE in the program, compile that type with `emit_arc_inc` /
     `emit_arc_dec` everywhere. Coarse — one shared use makes the type atomic on
     its sequential paths too — but exactly the kind of tradeoff a compiler
     should take silently rather than surface as an error. This must be a
     TYPE-level promotion: codegen picks atomic vs plain FROM THE TYPE, so
     per-binding promotion is not expressible without monomorphising by
     atomicity.
  3. FREEZE POINT — the previous framing, now demoted to a third option. Still
     independently useful (it is what lets a compound `mut` field that was built
     cyclically shed its `Mutex[T]` for its read-only phase), but it does NOT
     subsume 1 or 2 and it puts the annotation burden back on the user.

SEVERITY low → high. The earlier "low" rested on read-only sharing being fine
and this being one awkward shape. It is not one shape: it is the whole RC
ownership tier excluded from the language's headline feature, with the auto-par
half failing SILENTLY. The only workaround is a data-representation rewrite
(index pool), which is a different program, not a fix.

STILL TRUE from the correction above, and NOT walked back: `par struct` with
immutable fields shares lock-free across tasks with no annotation (verified),
and the existing gate is SOUND — relaxing it without 1 or 2 would reintroduce
B-2026-07-28-13's SIGSEGV on interior-node refcounts. Nothing here proposes
loosening the check; it proposes removing the NEED for it.

VERIFIED (2026-08-02) by single-keyword A/B, so the auto-par half of this is
measured rather than read off the source. Two programs differing ONLY in the
`shared` keyword on the struct declaration, bodies byte-identical:

    struct P { v: i64 }            // control
    shared struct P { v: i64 }     // subject
    ...
    for j in 0..n { let q = ps[j]; out[j] = q.v * 2; }

`karac build --concurrency-report` on the control reports
`disjoint_writes { loop_var: j, targets: out[1 per iteration], line: 12 }`.
On the subject that line is ABSENT — no decline entry, no reason, no
diagnostic. The decline is invisible even in `--concurrency-report`, which is
the one tool a user would reach for to ask this exact question; the
`DisjointDecline::NotCrossTaskSafe` reason string exists in
`classify_disjoint_write_loop` but does not reach the report here. That
reporting gap is worth closing on its own, independent of the atomicity work.

LOOSE END, not chased: a WEAKER body — `out[j] = j * p.v + 7` reading one i64
field off an outer `shared` handle — did NOT decline (the control and subject
both reported `disjoint_writes`). Either the span sweep records no `expr_types`
entry typed `P` for the bare receiver (the module doc concedes "a body
expression with no `expr_types` entry contributes nothing"), or the shape never
lowers to workers so nothing races. Neither build emitted `__par_branch` /
`par_reduce` / `par_run` symbols, so no race was demonstrated and none is
claimed here. Flagged for someone to settle; if the sweep does miss bare shared
receivers, that is a separate soundness item, not this entry.

LOOSE END SETTLED (2026-08-02) — AND IT NARROWS THE AUTO-PAR CLAIM ABOVE.

The note above said auto-par "silently declines any loop body touching a plain
`shared` value". MEASURED, THAT IS TOO STRONG. The gate keys on the span sweep
over `expr_types`, so it fires only when a body expression is itself TYPED as a
cross-task-unsafe type. Probed, all with a heavy inner loop so the `par_cost`
fan-out verdict clears (a trivial body is declined by the cost model, not the
safety gate — do not confuse the two):

  DECLINES (shared-typed expression present):
    let q = ps[j]; out[j] = q.v * 2      binding a Vec[shared] element
    acc = acc + take(p)                  shared handle as a function argument
    acc = acc + p.get()                  shared handle as a method receiver

  PARALLELIZES (no shared-typed expression; projection result is i64):
    out[j] = j * p.v + 7                 field read off an outer shared handle
    acc = acc + ps[j].v                  field read off a Vec[shared] element
    acc = acc + h.p.v                    field read through a plain struct
                                         holding a shared handle

AND THAT IS SOUND, not a hole. Disassembled `__karac_disjoint_worker_0` for the
`ps[j].v` case and diffed it against the byte-identical program with a PLAIN

    shared:  mov (%r11,%rsi,8),%rax   ; load the handle out of the Vec

    plain:   mov (%r11,%rsi,8),%r15   ; value is inline, one load

shared handle emits a plain deref, there is no refcount traffic in the worker,
and there is nothing for concurrent workers to race on. Every shape that WOULD
materialize a handle (and hence emit RC traffic) is exactly the set the sweep
catches. The miss and the safety line up.

Whole-program atomicity promotion, the entry's option 2, is now implemented
behind `KARAC_PAR_ATOMIC_PROMOTION=1`. DEFAULT OFF, and the reason it is off is
the finding, not a hedge — see "WHY IT IS NOT ON" below.

WHAT IT DOES. When a binding captured by 2+ branches of one `par {}` has a
transitively-reachable `shared` type set that is entirely free of `mut` fields,
the pass PROMOTES every type in that set to atomic refcounting and admits the
capture instead of erroring. Both halves are load-bearing: the promotion kills
the RC-HEADER race, the immutability means there is no PAYLOAD race for atomics
to fail to fix.

WHY IT REACHES THE INTERIOR NODES, which is what defeated the earlier leg. The
promotion is keyed on the HEAP TYPE, via a new `heap_type_uses_atomic_rc` that
all four refcount dispatchers in `codegen/runtime.rs` already funnel through —
not on `is_arc_binding`, which is per-binding-name per-function and therefore
blind to the handles a traversal retains inside a callee. MEASURED on a probe
whose 4 branches each traverse an immutable 3-node graph:

    __par_branch_0_0..0_3   atomic=4  PLAIN=0
    __par_branch_0_4        atomic=4  PLAIN=0   <- builds a FRESH LOCAL Node

Every refcount op on the promoted type is atomic, including in the branch that
constructs a local instance, which is the proof the promotion is type-level and
not capture-level. (Census by ADDRESS bounds; the last branch symbol otherwise
swallows trailing code — the method note recorded earlier in this entry.)
Three backends agree, 20 repeat AOT runs give one distinct output, valgrind
reports 0 definitely/indirectly lost.

NEGATIVES HOLD, including the one the transitive closure exists for: a `mut`
field on the captured type rejects, and a `mut` field on a type reachable only
THROUGH a field also rejects. Stopping the walk at the named type would have
silently admitted the second.

WHY IT IS NOT ON BY DEFAULT — the substantive finding.

Turning it on failed SIX existing tests, and inspecting them is what settled
the question. They are not stale: they encode design.md's rule (§ Rc vs Arc —
Two-Phase Algorithm) that a `shared struct` reachable from more than one
concurrent branch is a compile error. Their example types have no `mut` fields,
so promotion admits every one of them. That is not a precision fix to an
over-approximating gate — it is a change to a documented language rule, and it
would delete the diagnostic for essentially every immutable `shared` type.

A soundness argument does not settle that. Whether Kāra should silently promote
types to atomic RC is a language decision with user-visible cost (a promoted
type pays atomic refcounting on its SEQUENTIAL paths too), and it belongs to
the owner. So the capability ships the way `KARAC_RC_ELIDE_REF_PARAMS` and
`KARAC_PAR_ITER_LOCAL_SHARED` shipped before their defaults moved: inert,
tested, available to evaluate.

AND IT STILL WOULD NOT CLOSE #133. Read the real kata: its 18 branches each
call `sum_clones(root, 28)`, which BUILDS a fresh graph, writing `mut
neighbors` on branch-local clones. Those writes are to fresh instances, not to
the shared root — but they are to the same TYPE, and a type-level check cannot
tell those apart. Distinguishing them needs instance-level escape analysis,
which is mechanism 1. So mechanism 2's reach is exactly "deeply immutable
shared values", and #133's `mut neighbors` puts it outside, pending a freeze
point (mechanism 3) or mechanism 1.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE ENTRY'S SHAPE. The earlier note called mechanism 2
"the cheaper route to a genuine close". That was too optimistic and is
corrected here: mechanism 2 is cheap to IMPLEMENT (it lands in one funnel) but
it does not close the headline, because the headline case mutates. The three
mechanisms are not alternatives of equal reach — 1 is the only one that admits
a mutating traversal, and 2 and 3 both stop at immutability.

-- MECHANISM 3 DESIGN CALL MADE: docs/spikes/freeze-point-design.md (nothing built) --

THE CONSTRAINT THAT DECIDES THE DESIGN, and it is not the one this row's
"WHAT SHOULD CLOSE IT" list assumed: #133's traversal is IN A CALLEE
(`sum_clones(root, 28)` -> `clone_graph(root)`). So any freeze that is not
expressed IN THE TYPE must infer, across function boundaries, that the callee
never writes through the handle and that the handles it materializes are safe --
which IS mechanism 1, and inherits mechanism 1's failure mode. A freeze point
spelled as a local annotation or a statement-scoped fact is therefore not a
cheaper third option at all; it is mechanism 1 wearing a hat. This is why the
call is a TYPE-LEVEL MODE.

THE CALL: `frozen T` as a mode beside `ref T` / `mut ref T` -- a non-owning,
NON-COUNTING handle to a deeply-immutable `shared` value whose lifetime spans
the region. Four properties, each load-bearing: non-counting (removes the raced
header rather than making it atomic -- the same argument `rc_elide.rs` already
ships default-ON for read-only non-escaping `ref` params, B-2026-07-15-21);
DEEP/sticky through projection (without it the interior handles a traversal
materializes are ordinary `shared` values and the race returns -- the same
reason mechanism 2 had to close over the whole reachable type set); NON-ESCAPING
(the fail-closed condition that pays for non-counting; a non-counting handle
outliving its owner is a use-after-free); and CROSSES SIGNATURES (the property
that makes #133 reachable). Created by an explicit `let g = freeze graph;` --
declared, never inferred.

STAGED so it can land incrementally: (1) `frozen` as a parameter mode + par-branch
admission + escape checking, no stickiness -- this is the stage that shakes out
the escape checker, which is where the unsafety lives; (2) stickiness through
field access / indexing, the bulk of the typechecker work and what #133 needs;
(3) the deep-immutability check that lets a `mut`-bearing type freeze at all
(#133 needs this too -- `Node.neighbors` is `mut` -- but it is small and
separable).

WHY ONE SLICE, and this is the spike's own instruction rather than a
convenience: § "Deliberately NOT implemented now" says the alias condition
"could be enforced today, on its own. It should not be ... it would reject
programs that currently work and buy nothing until the relaxation it guards
actually lands." The Ordering list immediately below it says to do the alias
condition FIRST. Both are right and they are about different things -- BUILD
order versus LAND order. Step 1 alone, shipped, is a pure regression: every
program that freezes an immutable type with a live alias starts failing and
nothing gains. So the check was built first and landed with the relaxation.

THE PRECONDITION FAILS IN TWO DIRECTIONS, and closing one proves nothing.
Measured before the change, both accepted:

    let a = t;  let g = freeze t;    an alias made FROM the source
    let t = a;  let g = freeze t;    the source made FROM an alias

A THIRD case the spike did not record is worse than either: `let n = take(t);
let g = freeze t;` -- the source CONSUMED by a call and then frozen -- also
checked clean. All three now refuse for a `mut`-bearing type.

The implementation is two sets on the existing escape walk (`used_names`,
`place_bound`), read at the freeze site before the operand is walked. It is
deliberately COARSE: any earlier use of the root disqualifies, including a
scalar read that could not possibly produce a handle. A false NEGATIVE is a
refused freeze the author fixes by moving a line; a false POSITIVE is a data
race on a non-atomic refcount, which this repo has already had go arch-specific
and run green on x86 CI (B-2026-07-12-29).

WHAT THE RELAXATION TOUCHES, and what it does not. The proof relaxes exactly
one arm -- `MutableState`. `NotShared` and `AlreadyPar` are about the
REPRESENTATION (no refcount header to skip, or an atomic one that needs no
skipping) and no fact about aliasing can change either. A `frozen` PARAMETER
never receives the proof: its instance belongs to the caller, whose other live
handles this pass cannot see, and establishing it there would be the
interprocedural analysis mechanism 3 exists to avoid.

SOUNDNESS RESTS ON THREE GUARDS, each probed rather than argued:
  * uniqueness -- no other name existed to write through;
  * the escape walk freezes the SOURCE root for the rest of the scope, so the
    owner cannot be moved, reassigned, returned or captured while the frozen
    handle lives;
  * the projection walk still refuses every `mut` field, in READ and WRITE
    position alike (step 3, deliberately untouched).
Removing any one re-opens the race. The third is directly visible: after a
SUCCESSFUL freeze of `shared struct M { mut n: i64 }`, both `m.n = 99` and
`g.n` are still refused. The relaxation admits the FREEZE, not the mutation.

MEASURED -- the increment is real and bounded. `shared struct Node { val: i64,
mut neighbors: Vec[i64] }` shared across two `par` branches: REFUSED at the
freeze site before, and now compiles and runs. interp / `karac run` (JIT) / AOT
all agree; 20 repeat AOT runs give one distinct output; valgrind reports 0
definitely lost and 0 indirectly lost (the residual "possibly lost" is the
pthread TLS block the par scheduler allocates, present on every par program).

-- STAGE 3b STEP 2 LANDED (5f655fff): a `frozen` PARAMETER of a `mut`-bearing
   type, and the design's stated justification for it is WRONG --

THE SPIKE SAYS a `frozen T` parameter "can then inherit the guarantee from its
caller's already-frozen argument, which is how the mode composes today". That
last clause is false, and it was measured rather than reasoned about: a `frozen`
slot ACCEPTS AN ORDINARY BINDING. `fn frz(n: frozen Imm); let t = Imm{..};
frz(t)` checks clean. There is no inheritance to relax into.

BUILDING the inheritance would have meant demanding a frozen argument at every
call site, and TWO call forms resolve no signature today — both confirmed
accepting before any change: a free function taken as a VALUE (`let f = frz;
f(t)`), and a `frozen` parameter on a method whose RECEIVER is not frozen (the
`walk_call_args_with_sig` path passes `None` unless the receiver is frozen). An
enforcement built on that would have carried the silent hole this family keeps
producing.

IT IS NOT NEEDED. The parameter is not where the guarantee is established — the
PAR CAPTURE is. Probed with the parameter arm relaxed, every route for an
unfrozen `mut`-bearing handle to reach a `frozen` parameter concurrently was
refused AT THE CAPTURE: direct call, function-as-value, and method all give
"shared struct `Node` cannot be accessed from multiple concurrent tasks". A
FROZEN place passed to an unresolvable slot is refused as a non-`frozen` slot —
the unresolvable case fails CLOSED. The `mut` field stays unreadable and
unwritable through the parameter, the `frozen self` receiver and the frozen
source alike. A non-counting handle still cannot escape (E0511). A TEMPORARY
into a frozen slot is accepted, but that is pre-existing and identical for an
immutable type, so it is not something this step introduced.

WHAT IT BUYS: a RECURSIVE traversal IN A CALLEE over a `mut`-bearing graph,
shared across two `par` branches — #133's structure. interp / JIT / AOT agree,
20 repeat AOT runs give one distinct output, valgrind 0 definitely lost / 0
indirectly lost. #133 itself additionally READS its `mut` field, so it still
needs step 3.

-- THE REAL KATA WAS RUN, AND IT DOES NOT ADOPT. THE STEP-3 NOTE ABOVE
   OVERSTATED THE RESULT (2026-08-07, same session) --

The note above says "#133's shape runs" and hedges that the kata itself had not
been run because kara-katas was not attached. It was attached; it has now been
run; the answer is NO, and the hedge was the right instinct.

`bench/clone_bfs_par.kara` -- the file the kata repo keeps in-tree precisely
BECAUSE it does not compile -- still does not compile after stages 3b 1-3, and
the minimal `freeze` adoption (annotate `sum_clones` / `clone_graph` params
`frozen`, insert `let g = freeze root;`, pass `g`) produces TWO INDEPENDENT
refusals. Each was then reproduced in isolation:

  (1) UNIQUENESS FAILS AT THE FREEZE SITE. The kata builds an adjacency list and
      takes `let root = nodes[0];`. That is a PLACE-bound binding, so step 1's
      check refuses it -- and refuses it CORRECTLY: `nodes` stays live and holds
      every node including the root, so there genuinely are other live handles.
      This is not a conservatism to tune away; it is the check working on a
      program that really is aliased.

  (2) THE TRAVERSAL MATERIALIZES THE HANDLE, and this is the one that matters.
      `clone_graph` is a BFS: it pushes nodes into a local `VecDeque[Node]`
      worklist and inserts clones into a `Map[i64, Node]`. A `frozen` handle
      may not be stored in a non-`frozen` container -- property 3, the
      non-escaping condition that PAYS for non-counting -- so
      `queue.push_back(root)` is refused. Isolated repro:

          fn bfs(root: frozen Node) -> i64 {
              let mut queue: VecDeque[Node] = VecDeque.new();
              queue.push_back(root);        // refused
              return queue.len();
          }

WHY THE RECONSTRUCTION PASSED AND THE KATA DOES NOT. The fixture landed with
step 3 (`asan_kata133_clone_graph_frozen_across_par_branches_no_leak`) walks the
graph by RECURSION over `n.neighbors`, so no handle is ever stored. The real
kata is ITERATIVE and its worklist is the whole algorithm. Recursion-vs-worklist
is exactly the axis `frozen` currently discriminates on, and the reconstruction
happened to sit on the permitted side of it. The fixture is still worth keeping
-- it pins a real capability that did not exist before -- but it is NOT the
kata, and the step-3 note should not have implied the gap was closed.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE AFTER STAGE 3b: a `shared struct` with `mut` fields can be
shared read-only across `par` branches, traversed RECURSIVELY through a callee,
with its `mut` fields readable and unwritable. That is real and it is new. What
it does not reach is any traversal that materializes handles into a local
worklist -- which is most iterative graph algorithms, and both of this kata's
variants (`bfs.kara` and `dfs.kara` both carry a `visited: Map[i64, Node]`).

FILED as B-2026-08-07-23: a local worklist of frozen handles has no spelling.
The design's property 2 sketches `g.neighbors: frozen Vec[frozen Node]` for
PROJECTIONS, but there is no way to DECLARE a local `VecDeque[frozen Node]`, so
the handle has nowhere legal to go. That is the next thing #133 needs, and it is
a language-surface addition rather than a checker relaxation.

THIS SESSION'S TWO FINDINGS, both from re-running the real file afterwards.

(1) A LIVE SOUNDNESS HOLE THAT 200fa8d6 EXPOSED, filed as B-2026-08-07-26.
`try_admit_container_method` had no `in_closure` gate, so a container declared
INSIDE a closure was admitted while the frozen root pushed into it came from
the enclosing frame. Measured on `main` AFTER that commit, not inferred:

    fn leak(n: frozen Node) -> OnceFn() -> i64 {
        return || { let mut v: Vec[Node] = Vec.new(); v.push(n); v.len() };
    }

checks CLEAN. It did not before, and not because anything guarded it -- the
push was a type error for a parameter, and for a `freeze` local the ordinary
borrow-escape analysis catches the returned closure. Two unrelated masks, one
of them now removed. Fixed in the same slice.

(2) `.iter()` IS THE SPELLING THE CORPUS USES, AND IT WAS REFUSED. Stage 2.6
admits `for k in n.kids` only; the kata writes `for nb in curr.neighbors.iter()`.
COUNTED across kara-katas' leetcode corpus: `.iter()` 22 times, the bare-place
form over a field ZERO. So "the kata adopts" would have meant "the kata was
rewritten into a form nobody writes", which kara-katas CLAUDE.md forbids
outright -- and the first draft of this work had silently done exactly that
without noticing. Widened, on exactly the terms `len` / `is_empty` already had,
and it is the same lowering rather than a similar one: codegen's own for-loop
compiler peels the identical call, and the IR test now asserts both spellings at
(0, 0).

THE FREEZE SITE, which this row's last section listed as blocker (1), needs no
compiler change. It refuses `let root = nodes[0]` correctly -- `nodes` really
does hold every node -- and the answer is to build the graph in a helper that
returns the root, so `nodes` dies with it and the freeze source is untouched.

THE `VecDeque` HALF IS A PARITY IMPROVEMENT, NOT A WORKAROUND. Stage 3c is
`Vec`-only because `pop_front` returns a VALUE and not a place. The kata's own C
mirror does not pop: it is `Node **queue` with `q_head` / `q_tail` and
`while (q_head < q_tail)`. An index-cursor `Vec` in Kara is therefore CLOSER to
the mirror than the `VecDeque` the Kara file happens to use.

The par lane is back in the corpus with real numbers: kara 35.9 +/- 2.1 ms
against rayon 36.9 +/- 2.4 (a TIE, stated as one), C 10.1 (3.56x ahead) and Go

fix:
FIXED 0584af0. The open question in the filing — how to disambiguate script mode from a module binding — resolves cleanly against design.md § Script mode, which makes script mode and an explicit `fn main()` MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (a file with both is already an error). So in a file with explicit main, a top-level `let` cannot be a script statement; it can only be an incorrectly-named module binding. src/parser.rs now reclassifies those into Item::ModuleBinding BEFORE the ambiguity check, so the resolver's existing E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING fires — exactly the 'widen the recognizer and let the good diagnostic do its job' shape the filing proposed.

END-TO-END RESULT (verified, not inferred): `let mut my_count: i64 = 0;` + two use sites now reports E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING suggesting `MY_COUNT`, and `karac fix` rewrites the declaration AND both use sites, after which the file re-checks clean. The misdirecting ambiguity error is gone for this shape.

SCOPED DELIBERATELY: only plain-name `let` statements reclassify, and only in a root source file that has an explicit `main`. Expression statements, assignments and tuple destructures are not module-binding shaped, so they stay script statements and keep the ambiguity error — which is the correct diagnostic for them, and is regression-tested in both directions. A file with no explicit `main` is untouched, so script mode still parses `let x = 1;` as a genuine script statement.

Tests: 5 in tests/parser.rs (recognition of a lowercase binding, single-letter `c` on the far side of the old boundary, script mode untouched, expression-statement and tuple-destructure shapes still reporting ambiguity) + 1 in tests/resolver.rs asserting the naming diagnostic fires with the rename and the misdirecting error is absent.

title: A module-level `let` whose name starts with a LOWERCASE letter is not recognized as a module binding at all — it falls through to a top-level statement and the author is told to "move the statements into `main`, or remove the explicit `main`", two suggestions that both destroy the intent. `E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING` never fires.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found building canned LLM responses for the Mend corpus — the iteration-0 attempt for `link_registry` deliberately used lowercase module bindings, which is the mistake its notes.md predicts. Instead of the naming diagnostic, it produced one misdirecting parse error.

THE BOUNDARY IS THE FIRST LETTER'S CASE. Same three-line program each time, only the binding's name changes:

  let mut <NAME>: i64 = 0;
  fn bump() { <NAME> = <NAME> + 1; }
  fn main() { bump(); println(<NAME>.to_string()); }

  COUNT      -> All checks passed          (recognized as a module binding)
  MY_COUNT   -> All checks passed          (recognized)
  Count      -> E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING    (recognized; correct, actionable, machine-fixable)
  C          -> E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING    (recognized; correct)
  myCount    -> "file contains both top-level statements and an explicit `fn main()`"
  my_count   -> same
  c          -> same

An uppercase FIRST letter is what makes the parser treat the `let` as a module binding. Anything starting lowercase is parsed as a top-level (script-mode) statement, collides with the explicit `fn main()`, and produces an error about a completely different subject.

WHY THE DIAGNOSTIC IS WORSE THAN MERELY WRONG. It is confidently actionable and both of its actions are destructive:
  "move the statements into `main`"  — impossible by construction; the binding exists precisely
                                       because SEVERAL functions share it. Moving it into main
                                       breaks every reader.
  "remove the explicit `main`"       — deletes the program's entry point to silence a naming
                                       problem.
Neither mentions capitalisation. An author who follows either suggestion ends up further from a working program than when they started, and the actual one-token fix (rename to SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE) is never surfaced.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TYPICAL DIAGNOSTIC GAP:
 * Lowercase is the DEFAULT habit for a variable name in every mainstream language. This is not
   an exotic mistake; it is the first thing a new author types.
 * Module-level mutable state is how a service holds state — `examples/shortener/` needed exactly
   this shape (LINKS / HITS / SEQ), so it is on the main path, not a corner.
 * It lands squarely on the AI-first wedge. A fresh LLM author gets a diagnostic that is
   confidently wrong about the subject, with no `replacement`, and whose prose actively steers
   toward a worse program. That is the failure mode `karac fix` exists to prevent.

THE GOOD DIAGNOSTIC ALREADY EXISTS. `E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING` handles the uppercase-initial cases correctly today — it names the rule, and since B-2026-07-31-31/-32/-33 it carries a machine-applicable rename that also rewrites use sites. So the fix is to widen the RECOGNIZER so a lowercase-initial module-level `let` is still parsed as a module binding, and let the existing naming diagnostic do its job. That converts this from a misdirecting parse error into an auto-fixable rename.

OPEN QUESTION for whoever takes it: script mode is the reason the recognizer is case-keyed at all — a bare `let x = 1;` at top level is a legitimate script-mode statement. Disambiguating will need a rule (perhaps: a top-level `let` in a file that ALSO defines `fn main()` is a module binding, since script mode and explicit main are already mutually exclusive). Worth confirming that reading against design.md § Module-Level Bindings before implementing.

fix:
FIXED dd65d4f. Took the filing's suggested shape (phase-aware rather than code-set) and found TWO phase-blind predicates, not one — the filing flagged `fix_introduced_new_error` and suspected `fixes_resolved`; the suspicion was right and the second is worse. `fixes_resolved` was `max(0, len(before) - len(after))`, so the reported case scored ZERO resolved (1 diagnostic before, 2 after): the correct fix was counted AGAINST fix_precision_pct, not merely omitted from it.

New rules: a code is charged as a regression only when it appears at or BEFORE the phase that was blocking the build (so a parse fix yielding typecheck errors is progress, while a parse fix yielding a DIFFERENT parse error is still caught); resolved is a per-code multiset difference, since newly-unmasked codes only ADD to the after set and cannot mask a code that really went away. Unknown phase names sort LAST, so a phase the harness has not learned yet reads as newly-unmasked rather than as a regression — the conservative direction for a metric whose failure mode is over-reporting.

MEASURED, old -> new:
  batch_20260801T235833 (layered): 6 resolved / 75.0% / 1 'broke the build'
                                -> 7 resolved / 87.5% / 0
  batch_20260731T212520 (single-mistake): 5 / 100.0% / 0 — BYTE-IDENTICAL under both.
That second line is the filing's claim restated as a measurement: the bias fires only on multi-phase programs, so the metric looked fine until the fixtures got good.

Tests: examples/mend/harness/test_mend_score.py (new — the harness had none). Most of it guards the OPPOSITE direction from this bug, since the danger in relaxing a metric is making it always-pass: a different parse error at the same phase, a new earlier-phase error, and a same-phase newcomer alongside legitimately-unmasked ones are all still charged. Verified non-vacuous by stubbing the detector to always return 'no regression' — exactly those three fail. Wired into the CI lint job (pure python, no build).

title: The Mend scorer counts a CORRECT `karac fix` as having "broken the build" whenever it unmasks errors a earlier-phase failure was hiding. Because the compiler is phased, any fix to a parse error that reveals a typecheck error is scored as a regression — systematically understating fix precision on exactly the multi-layer programs that are most realistic.
detail:
SURFACE NOTE: the defect is in the measurement harness, not a compiler phase, so `surface` is `other`.

SOURCE NOTE: found running the first full 9-task dry-run batch after backfilling the missing canned_responses.json files. The new `canonical_request` fixture is deliberately LAYERED — a parse error hiding a type error hiding an ownership error — which is what exposed this.

MEASURED (batch_20260801T235833, canonical_request/iter_000):
  BEFORE fix : E0001  parse      the `&&` operator is not used in Kāra; use `and` instead
  AFTER  fix : E0210  typecheck  E_INT_AS_CHAR: cannot cast `i64` to `char` directly
               E0500  ownership  value 'h' moved here, used again here

The fix was CORRECT — `&&` → `and` is exactly right, and the run went on to converge cleanly. The two "new" codes were always present in the source; the parse failure simply meant the compiler never reached typecheck or ownership to report them. Fixing the parse error is what let it get further.

THE DEFECT. `fix_introduced_new_error` is computed as set-difference on diagnostic CODES across the fix boundary: any code present after and absent before counts as the fix introducing an error. In a PHASED compiler that is the normal, desirable outcome of any early-phase fix. The predicate conflates two opposite things:
  (a) the fix genuinely broke the program — a real regression, the thing worth catching;
  (b) the fix removed a blocker and later phases finally ran — progress.

CONSEQUENCES, both on headline numbers:
  * "fixes that broke the build : 1 run(s)" — reported for a run in which nothing broke.
  * fix precision 75.0% (6 resolved / 8 applied) — understated, since the unresolved count
    includes a fix that did its job.
The bias is not random: it fires precisely on programs with mistakes in more than one phase, which are the realistic ones. A corpus of single-mistake fixtures would never show it, so the metric looks fine right up until the fixtures get good.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (unverified): make the comparison phase-aware rather than code-set-based. The diagnostics already carry a `phase` field. A fix should only be charged with a regression when a NEW diagnostic appears at or BEFORE the phase of the diagnostic it fixed — a parse fix that yields typecheck errors is progress, while a parse fix that yields a DIFFERENT parse error is suspect. An alternative, cheaper rule: charge a regression only when the after-set contains a code from a phase that had already run clean before the fix. Either way, keep a real regression detectable — the metric is worth having, it is just measuring the wrong difference.

WORTH CHECKING WHILE IN THERE: whether `fixes_resolved` has the same phase-blindness, since it feeds `fix_precision_pct` from the same comparison.
