tracker: typechecker call-argument compatibility for raw pointer types
title: No implicit `*mut T` -> `*const T` weakening at call sites — every consume-direction binding that passes a malloc'd (or otherwise mut) buffer to a `*const` foreign param needs an explicit `as *const T` cast (the cast is SAFE — earlier premise that it was unsafe-gated was wrong)
detail:
Found authoring examples/interop-zlib: `uncompress(back, ptr.mut(back_len), dest, dest_len)` where `dest: *mut u8` (we malloc'd and filled it) and the declared param is `source: *const u8` → E0200 TYPE_MISMATCH expected '*const u8', found '*mut u8'. The weakening direction is always sound (dropping write permission on the same allocation; Rust coerces *mut T → *const T implicitly at coercion sites for exactly this reason), and the natural shape of C bindings hits it immediately — compress-then-use, fill-then-hash, any produce-into-then-read-from buffer. Workaround is `unsafe { dest as *const u8 }` per call site (raw-to-raw casts are unsafe-gated), which taxes the flagship additive-adoption surface with unsafe blocks that assert nothing beyond what the type system already knows. DESIGN FORK to settle before fixing: either (a) add the implicit weakening coercion at call sites (matches Rust; zero soundness cost), or (b) keep the explicitness but make the raw-to-raw mut→const cast SAFE (it introduces no capability), so the workaround at least sheds its unsafe block. Current behavior may be intent (design.md § Unsafe Escape Hatch lists raw-to-raw casts as unsafe-block-legal and never discusses call-site pointer coercion) — if so, document the pattern in § FFI; the gap today is that natural binding code fails with a bare type error and no guidance.

SOURCE NOTE: example family, consume-direction FFI worked example, 2026-08-02.

CORRECTION (2026-08-02, verified on live compiler): the raw-to-raw cast does NOT require an unsafe block — `let c: *const u8 = d as *const u8;` compiles in safe code (probe t5). The original entry's 'workaround needs unsafe { } per call site' premise came from reading design.md's 'raw-to-raw casts remain legal in unsafe blocks' as 'only in unsafe blocks'; the implementation (correctly, per § Unsafe Escape Hatch's 'only ... pointee-changing casts require unsafe') gates neither direction of the same-T mutability cast. examples/interop-zlib has been cleaned of its unnecessary unsafe wrappers. Residual gap, DOWNGRADED to low: (a) the E0200 mismatch could carry a machine-applicable fix-it (insert `as *const T` — always-sound weakening); (b) design.md never states the no-implicit-coercion rule or the cast's safety explicitly — one spec sentence settles it. The implicit-coercion fork stays recorded above but is now an ergonomics choice, not an unsafe-burden fix. Discovered while probing: the OTHER directions (pointee-changing, const->mut strengthening) are ALSO un-gated, which § Unsafe Escape Hatch explicitly forbids — filed separately as B-2026-08-02-9.
resolution: fixed in a31d7be — design decision: NO implicit mut->const coercion (spends the language's implicitness budget on a raw-pointer corner; explicit-now -> implicit-later stays open, the reverse doesn't). Instead the `expected '*const T', found '*mut T'` same-pointee mismatch carries a machine-applicable FixIt inserting ` as *const T` + help text; verified end-to-end that `karac fix` applies it and the program compiles — the consume-direction FFI shape closes mechanically through the Mend loop. Cross-pointee mismatches carry no fix-it (would smuggle a pointee change past the B-2026-08-02-9 gate). Rule specced in design.md § Raw Pointer Construction.

title: A BUILTIN function name in ANY non-call position — `spawn;`, `let f = println;`, `spawn { … }` — passes `karac check` and then panics the interpreter with an internal `unreachable!` whose own message says "should be caught by resolver". USER-defined functions are fine as values, so this is builtins-only.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found writing the S3-client dogfood. I wrote `spawn { … }` to run a server alongside a client — the wrong syntax (the real form is `spawn(|| …)`) — and `karac check` told me the program was fine.

REPRO (one line):
  fn main() { spawn { println("x"); }; }

  karac check          -> All checks passed.
  karac run --interp   -> thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs:170:17:
                          internal error: entered unreachable code: variable 'spawn' not found
                          at 8:5; should be caught by resolver
                          + a full Rust stack backtrace
  karac build          -> error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'spawn'

SCOPE — it is every builtin FUNCTION name, not just spawn:
  spawn { … }         check passes -> interpreter panic
  println { … }       check passes -> interpreter panic
  print { … }         check passes -> interpreter panic
  assert { … }        check passes -> interpreter panic
  len { … }           correctly rejected at resolve (not a global builtin; it is a method)
  notafunction { … }  correctly rejected: "undefined name 'notafunction'"

So the resolver resolves the NAME (it is a real builtin) and never checks that it is being USED as a call. The block form sails through resolve and typecheck, and the interpreter then tries to evaluate the bare identifier as a variable, finds no binding, and hits an `unreachable!` whose message correctly blames the resolver.

WHY THIS EXACT MISTAKE IS LIKELY, NOT EXOTIC. Kāra really does have block-form constructs — `par { }`, `seq { }`, `unsafe { }`, `comptime { }`, `lock { }`. Someone who has just written `par { }` and wants a single background task will write `spawn { }` by analogy. It is the natural wrong guess, and `spawn` is precisely the builtin reached for when writing concurrent code — the language's headline capability.

THREE THINGS WRONG, IN DESCENDING SEVERITY:
 1. `karac check` IS NOT AUTHORITATIVE. It greenlights a program that cannot run on either
    backend. Every consumer that trusts check — the Mend loop above all, which iterates until
    check is clean and then declares the program correct — will accept this program as done.
    An LLM author following the documented loop converges on a program that panics.
 2. The interpreter PANICS WITH A RUST BACKTRACE rather than emitting a diagnostic. CLAUDE.md's
    coding standard is explicit: "Every compiler phase must emit structured diagnostics with
    source spans — never just panic." The user sees compiler internals for a syntax mistake.
 3. Codegen's message (`codegen failed: Undefined variable 'spawn'`) is a raw string with no
    span, no code, and no JSON representation, so it is invisible to `--output=json` consumers.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (unverified): reject a builtin function name in non-call position at resolve, with a diagnostic that names the correct form — for `spawn` specifically, "`spawn` takes a closure: `spawn(|| …)`", which is machine-applicable (wrap the block in `(|| … )`) and would make this a `karac fix` case rather than a crash. The `notafunction` path already produces the right SHAPE of error; builtins just need to reach it. Whoever takes it should also decide whether the `unreachable!` at eval_expr.rs:170 should become a structured internal-error diagnostic regardless, since it is reachable from any future resolver hole of this kind.

── SCOPE CORRECTED (same day, before any fix) ──
The original entry framed this as the BLOCK form (`spawn { … }`). That is narrower than reality and a fix aimed at it would be incomplete. Re-measured on exit codes rather than first-line matching — the panic output begins with a BLANK line, so an earlier `head -1` probe scored several panicking cases as clean and produced a wrong boundary:

  spawn { … };            check passes -> PANIC (exit 101)
  spawn;                  check passes -> PANIC   <- no block involved at all
  spawn; println("a");    check passes -> PANIC
  println { … };          check passes -> PANIC
  let f = println;        check passes -> PANIC   <- ordinary let, no block
  { println("x"); };      check passes -> clean   (a bare block is fine)
  helper;                 check passes -> clean   (USER fn as a value)
  helper { … };           check passes -> clean   (USER fn)

So the rule is: ANY reference to a builtin function name outside call position panics. The block form is simply how I happened to hit it. User-defined functions ARE first-class values — `Server.serve(addr, handle)` in examples/shortener depends on exactly that — so the asymmetry is builtins-only.

That also settles the fix's shape: builtins are NOT first-class values today, so the correct repair is to say so at resolve for every non-call reference, not to special-case the block form. Making builtins first-class would be a feature (and would need a codegen half), not a bug fix.

The declaration stays legal: `Server.serve`'s handler returns a user `Response`, so rejecting it would break every serving program (examples/shortener verified still building). The ergonomic fix is to give the builtin an internal name so user code may use `Response` freely — the natural name in this domain — leaving the user's declaration untouched. The refusal test's doc comment says it should be INVERTED when that lands, so the follow-up is discoverable from the test rather than only from here.

title: Pointee-changing and const->mut raw pointer casts compile OUTSIDE unsafe blocks — the spec-mandated unsafe gate on `*T as *U` is not enforced (`let w: *const u64 = d as *const u64;` and `let m: *mut u8 = c as *mut u8;` both pass in safe code)
detail:

tracker: src/prelude.rs (the flat prelude name list — `Response`, `HttpError`, `Match`, `Client`, `RequestBuilder`, `Stats`, `Regex`, …), runtime/stdlib/*.kara (where those types are declared), and every name-keyed dispatch site in src/typechecker, src/codegen and src/interpreter (~49 across 14 files)
title: STDLIB AND USER TYPES SHARE ONE FLAT NAMESPACE, so any user struct that shadows a prelude type name silently takes over that type's codegen identity. `Response` (fixed as B-2026-08-02-7) was one instance of a class: a user `HttpError` double-frees identically, and a user `Match` crashes codegen outright.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while doing B-2026-08-02-7's deferred ergonomic half. That entry's fix makes the HTTP CLIENT path refuse when a user declares `struct Response`. Scoping the real fix — let user code use the name freely — turned up the general problem, and that the guard covers one name on one path.

MEASURED INSTANCES (each a standalone program; the user struct shadows a prelude name and
carries a heap field):

  struct HttpError { message: String }   + Client.get(…)      -> builds, DOUBLE FREE at runtime
  struct Match     { text: String }      + Regex.compile(…)   -> CODEGEN PANICS with a Rust
                                                                 backtrace: "Found IntValue …
                                                                 but expected the StructValue
                                                                 variant" (method_call.rs:1170)
  struct Stats     { label: String }     + builtin unused     -> clean (nothing routes through it)
  struct Response  { status, body }      + Client.get(…)      -> refused since B-2026-08-02-7

So the failure mode varies by which builtin path the shadowed type feeds — silent memory corruption on one, a compiler crash on another — but the cause is single: the prelude injects stdlib type names into the SAME flat namespace user declarations occupy, and every backend dispatches on the bare string. `src/prelude.rs` lists them unqualified (`"Response"`, `"HttpError"`, `"Match"`, `"Client"`, `"RequestBuilder"`, `"Stats"`, `"Regex"`, …), `runtime/stdlib/http.kara` declares `struct Response { … }` with no module prefix, and there is no `http.Response` distinct from a user's `Response`.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT A RENAME. Making the builtin internally distinct means threading a mangled identity through ~49 name-keyed sites across 14 files in the TYPECHECKER, CODEGEN and INTERPRETER, plus the stdlib `.kara` sources. Both backends must move together — a codegen-only rename would produce a run-vs-build divergence, which this project treats as worse than the bug being fixed. The clean fix is module-qualified stdlib types (`http.Response` as a real, distinct type), which is a language/design slice, not a patch.

INTERIM POSITION, and why the current guard is only half a fix: B-2026-08-02-7's refusal turns silent corruption into an actionable message for ONE name on ONE path. The same treatment could be generalised — refuse when any user struct shadows a prelude type name whose builtin path the program actually uses — which is strictly better than today for `HttpError` and `Match`, and cheap next to the namespace work. That is the recommended next step if the namespace slice is not scheduled soon.

SEPARATE DEFECT WORTH ITS OWN LOOK: the `Match` case CRASHES CODEGEN with a Rust panic and backtrace rather than any diagnostic, violating the standing rule that every phase emits structured diagnostics and never panics. Even after the namespace fix, that unwrap (method_call.rs:1170, expecting a StructValue) should degrade to a diagnostic — it is reachable from any future type-identity confusion, not just this one.

USER-VISIBLE SHAPE OF THE HAZARD: `Response`, `Match`, `Client`, `Stats` and `HttpError` are all extremely natural names for a user's own struct — `Match` in a parser or game, `Stats` in anything with metrics, `Response` in any service. The language currently offers no warning that these names are claimed, and the penalty ranges from a compiler crash to memory corruption.

── PARTIAL FIX LANDED 4c4c2f0: HTTP leg covered, REGEX LEG STILL OPEN ──
Generalized B-2026-08-02-7's single-name guard to a set of shadowed prelude names plus a shared `reject_shadowed_prelude_types(what, names)`, wired into the HTTP client and regex entry points. Measured coverage:
  struct Response  + Client.get    -> refused (was a double free)
  struct HttpError + Client.get    -> refused (was a double free, previously unguarded)
  struct Match     + Regex.compile -> STILL PANICS — uncovered

WHY THE REGEX LEG RESISTED, so the next attempt does not repeat it. Detection keys on `struct_types` already holding the name when the user's declaration is processed. That is exact for the three types `seed_builtin_struct_types` seeds (Client / Response / HttpError) and misses every stdlib type spliced from a `.kara` prelude source (Match / Regex / RegexError). Two alternatives were tried and REVERTED ON EVIDENCE:
  * detecting on the prelude NAME alone — flags the stdlib's own declarations against
    itself, refusing 6 legitimate regex programs (measured in tests/codegen.rs);
  * gating on `StructDef::stdlib_origin` — looks like the exact discriminator, but the
    bake step flips it only for GATED modules (`synthetic_gated_modules`, std.web), not
    for prelude splices, so prelude stdlib structs arrive with it FALSE and the guard
    over-fires identically.

So the regex leg needs one of: (a) a real origin marker on prelude-spliced items — the principled fix, and it would make this whole guard exact; or (b) graceful degradation of the receiver coercion at src/codegen/method_call.rs (the `into_struct_value()` that panics when the shadowed layout makes the receiver an i64), which is worth doing on its own merits since a panic there violates the never-panic rule regardless of this bug.

The regex guards ARE wired and will start working the moment detection reaches those names, so (a) alone completes the leg with no further codegen changes.

── REGEX LEG CLOSED 78275a1; ENTRY NOW FIXED ──
Root cause of why the leg resisted two detection strategies: stdlib declarations reach codegen's `declare_structs` by TWO paths and neither marked them as stdlib. (1) `expand_gated_stdlib_imports` splices gated-import items (Command / Log / Match) into the USER's program tree without flipping `stdlib_origin`, even though `synthetic_gated_modules` flips it on the same items reached the other way. (2) `declare_stdlib_program` walks baked STDLIB_PROGRAMS trees parsed straight from source, where the flag is never flipped at all. Hence name-only detection flagged the stdlib against itself (6 codegen tests refused) and `stdlib_origin` gating over-fired identically — the flag was false on both paths.

Fixed one per path: the splice now flags spliced items stdlib-origin (correct on its own merits — the flag is the truth about item provenance), and codegen carries a `declaring_stdlib_program` scope flag so the detector skips baked stdlib trees. All four cases measured: Response/HttpError refused on the client path, Match refused on the regex path (was a PANIC), and both a plain regex program and `import std.process.{Command}` still compile — the two over-fire regressions, now regression tests in tests/http_client_codegen.rs.

REMAINING, tracked separately: the receiver coercion in src/codegen/method_call.rs still panics if any future path reaches it with a shadowed layout. The guard prevents that today, but a panic there violates the never-panic rule regardless, so hardening it is still worth doing as defense in depth.

title: Drop-carrying field of a GENERIC-mono parent struct: body silent at owner death (both backends) + Vec-element String buffer leaks under AOT
detail: A user struct with `impl Drop` held as a FIELD of a generic parent (`struct Box2[T] { item: T, tag: i64 }` instantiated at `Box2[Res]`) never fires the field's Drop body at the parent's death: `{ let b: Box2[Res] = Box2 { item: Res{..}, tag: 1 }; }` prints NO `drop ...` line on EITHER backend (interp and AOT agree, both wrong), and the Vec-element leg `let mut v: Vec[Box2[Res]] = Vec.new(); v.push(Box2 { item: Res{..}, .. })` is silent too AND leaks the element's String field buffer under AOT (valgrind: definitely lost = exactly the f-string name buffer; the direct-binding leg frees its buffer, only the body is silent). The NON-generic control (`struct BoxR { item: Res, tag: i64 }`, identical program otherwise) fires both bodies and is valgrind-clean -- so the gap is the generic-mono field-bodies walk: the parent's synthesized drop/element walk misses user-Drop FIELD bodies (and the AOT element walk misses the field's heap free) when the parent is a monomorphized generic. Sibling class of B-2026-08-01-34 (generic-mono field deep-chain move, fixed f82c0db) on the DROP side rather than the move side. Probes: $SP/b193_g.kara (generic, silent+6-byte leak), $SP/b193_h.kara (non-generic control, correct). Both-backends-silent means no run-vs-build divergence -- the uncertain=>silent parity rule does NOT apply because the non-generic twin DOES fire: this is a hole, not a design choice. FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in 6ff8614. Four legs. (1) codegen indices (synth_drop.rs): user_drop_field_indices replaced by subst-aware user_drop_field_indices_mono (+ resolve_field_head_mono, type_runs_user_drop_mono) -- a bare-param field name (`item: T` under T->Res) resolves through the mono subst before the drop-relevance check, and emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn resolves field_type in its loop so `Res.drop` (not `T.drop`) dispatches. (2) direct-binding gate (stmts.rs): has_field_user_drop now uses type_runs_user_drop_mono with the binding's recorded instantiation subst. (3) Vec element (runtime.rs + synth_drop.rs + stmts.rs): vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr's struct arm derives the subst from the element's instantiated TE and emits emit_struct_drop_synthesis_mono (fixes the leaked String buffer -- base synthesis read T as a scalar), and a new emit_vec_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn_mono (mono-suffixed __karac_dropelems_<S>$<A> symbols) fires the element bodies at the binding's NLL point. (4) interp (eval_stmt.rs): the drop_user_drop_fields_of_value declared-type gate gains ONE exception -- a field declared as a bare GENERIC PARAM of the struct fires value-driven, REVISING the B-2026-07-29-39 scoping decision (which skipped erased fields precisely because codegen could not see through the erasure; it now can, so parity holds in the firing direction instead of the silent-leak one). Pins: e2e+interp generic_parent_drop_field_bodies (the interp twin is a REAL pin -- interp was silent pre-fix, STASH-PROVEN FAILED) + asan_generic_parent_drop_field_bodies_freed (STASH-PROVEN FAILED: LSan caught the element buffer leak). RESIDUALS: generic parents whose field is a Vec[T]-of-Drop under the subst inherit the one-container-level rule; struct_owns_shared_field remains name-keyed (a generic parent instantiated at a shared type keeps the old routing); Map/Set VALUES of generic parents unprobed. Also in this commit: #[allow(clippy::type_complexity)] on tests/http_server.rs h2c_two_streams_timed (sibling's 07bf66e broke the local --all-targets clippy gate; CI's no-tests clippy missed it).

title: indexed field store with a NON-PURE index (`v[f()].field = x`): codegen silently dropped the store AND the index's side effect; the interpreter applied it but evaluated the subscript TWICE. Both legs fixed — index materialized once on each backend, all four surfaces now byte-identical
detail:
SHAPE (scratchpad idxcall.kara, 2026-08-02):

    struct P { mut id: i64 }
    fn idx() -> i64 { println("eval"); return 0 }
    fn main() {
        let mut v: Vec[P] = Vec.new()
        v.push(P { id: 1 })
        v[idx()].id = 9
        println(f"id={v[0].id}")
    }

  `karac check` — All checks passed.
  interp        — `eval` TWICE, then id=9   (store lands; index double-evaluated)
  AOT seq       — no `eval` at all, id=1    (store AND side effect both gone)
  AOT auto-par  — no `eval` at all, id=1
  JIT           — no `eval` at all, id=1

Two defects in one construct.

LEG 1 (the severe one, codegen). An indexed field store whose INDEX is not a
bare identifier or int literal is silently dropped on every codegen surface,
and the index expression is never evaluated — so an observable side effect in
the index disappears along with the write. Exit 0, no diagnostic, subsequent
reads return the stale value.

MECHANISM, and it is the exact tail B-2026-08-01-35 documented:
`nested_store_place_ptr`'s Index arm asks `field_chain_place_ptr`, whose Index
arm requires `matches!(index.kind, Identifier | Integer)` and returns None for a
Call (the guard is deliberate — `vec_index_elem_ptr` RE-EVALUATES the index, so
the arm only admits indices where re-eval is a no-op). It then falls to
`field_rooted_index_place_ptr`, which requires the container to be a
FieldAccess and returns None for a bare identifier. Both resolvers decline,
`compile_field_store`'s nested branch is skipped, and the store exits through
the no-op Ok(()) tail.

So this is the SAME no-op tail as B-2026-08-01-35 (field-rooted container, pure
index) and B-2026-07-13-10 (shared element). Those two fixes each added a
resolver for one axis; the uncovered cell is IDENTIFIER-rooted container x
NON-PURE index. Not a regression from either fix — the purity guard predates
them and the old Index arm declined the same way.

LEG 2 (interpreter). The interpreter EVALUATES THE INDEX TWICE for an indexed
field store — `eval` prints twice above, and it does so for a field-rooted
container too (`o.hs[idx()].id = 7` prints it twice on interp, once on AOT).
Even where the store lands, side effects in the index are doubled. Presumably a
place-resolution pass followed by a store pass, each evaluating the subscript.

FIX SHAPE (untested). Both legs want the same thing: evaluate the index ONCE
into a temporary and drive the store off that. On the codegen side that also
retires the purity guard's reason to exist — with a materialized index there is
nothing unsafe about re-eval because there is no re-eval. A narrower codegen-only
fix (spill a non-pure index to a temp, then reuse the existing pure-index path)
closes leg 1 without touching the interpreter.

SEVERITY high: silent wrong answer on a `karac check`-clean program, on every
codegen surface, with the side effect swallowed too — a write-then-read sees
stale data and nothing reports it.

SOURCE NOTE: found while probing whether B-2026-08-01-35's landed fix
(`field_rooted_index_place_ptr`) guards index purity the way the identifier
arm does. It does not — but the resulting hole turned out to be on the OTHER
axis, and pre-existing.

── LEG 1 FIXED (2026-08-02). Leg 2 (interpreter double-eval) REMAINS OPEN. ──

`nested_store_place_ptr`'s Index arm now falls through to
`impure_index_store_place_ptr` when both pure-subscript resolvers decline: it
evaluates the index EXACTLY ONCE into a stack temp and retries them against a
synthesized identifier subscript. That fixes the drop and dissolves the purity
guard's premise at the same time — after the spill, the "re-evaluation" the
guard existed to prevent is a variable load.

Gated on container shapes the resolvers can actually place (mirroring
`field_chain_place_ptr`'s Index-arm guards exactly, including the `ref`-param
bail of B-2026-07-21-5/-6 and the array-slot bypass), so a store that would
still fail to resolve does not gain a side effect it never had. Placed in the
STORE walk, not `field_chain_place_ptr`, so match-suppression — which shares
that walker and must not run side effects while resolving a scrutinee place —
is untouched.

MEASURED, `v[idx()].id = 9` where idx() prints and returns 0:

    surface        before              after
    AOT seq        no eval, id=1       eval x1, id=9
    AOT auto-par   no eval, id=1       eval x1, id=9
    JIT            no eval, id=1       eval x1, id=9
    interp         eval x2, id=9       eval x2, id=9   <- LEG 2, still open

CORRECTION to this entry's original text: it implied
`field_rooted_index_place_ptr` lacked a purity guard and might double-evaluate.
It does not — it calls `vec_index_elem_ptr` once, so the FIELD-rooted x
non-pure cell already behaved correctly before this fix and still does
(verified: one eval per store, both writes landing). The hole was narrower than
first described: only the IDENTIFIER-rooted arm declined outright, and only it
needed the spill.

Codegen is now stricter than the interpreter on this shape — exactly-once
versus twice. Leg 2 is a separate defect in `interpreter.rs` (a place-resolution
pass and a store pass each evaluating the subscript) and is NOT addressed here.

VERIFIED: fmt clean; clippy --all --all-targets clean; codegen E2E 2752 passed
/ 0 failed; memory_sanitizer 908 passed / 0 failed (Linux, LSan).
Regression test: `e2e_indexed_field_store_non_pure_index_runs_once`, pinning
one eval per store across both container roots.

── LEG 2 FIXED (2026-08-02) — ENTRY NOW CLOSED. ──

`Interpreter::set_field`'s value-type projection arm is a READ-MODIFY-WRITE-
BACK: it evaluates the receiver to read the struct copy, mutates a field, then
hands the SAME expression to `assign_to_place`, which evaluates it AGAIN to
store. (The header comment above it claimed "Evaluate the receiver place once";
that was true of the shared-struct arm only.) For an indexed receiver the
subscript therefore ran twice.

The two evaluations cannot simply be collapsed — a plain struct is a value type,
so the mutated copy genuinely has to be written back up the place chain. What
CAN be fixed is making both halves agree on a subscript that runs once: a
non-pure index is now evaluated once and the place rebuilt with an
`ExprKind::Integer` literal, which both the read and the write-back then use.

A new `Interpreter::index_expr_is_pure` gates it, deliberately kept SEPARATE
from `eval_stmt.rs`'s `assign_index_is_pure_scalar`: that one is private to its
module and answers a different question (may the displaced-element Drop body
fire?), and its comment requires it to stay in step with a codegen twin for
unrelated reasons. Conflating them would couple two independent gates. The new
one is conservative — anything not obviously pure is materialized, which is
sound either way, since evaluating once is also correct for a pure subscript.

FINAL STATE — `v[idx()].id = 9` and `o.hs[idx()].name = f"b"`, idx() prints:

    surface          originally        after leg 1       after leg 2
    interp           eval x2, id=9     eval x2, id=9     eval x1, id=9
    JIT              no eval, id=1     eval x1, id=9     eval x1, id=9
    AOT seq          no eval, id=1     eval x1, id=9     eval x1, id=9
    AOT auto-par     no eval, id=1     eval x1, id=9     eval x1, id=9

Byte-identical on all four surfaces, both container roots (identifier-rooted and
field-rooted). The entry opened as a run-vs-build divergence and briefly
inverted after leg 1 (codegen stricter than interp); it is now genuinely
converged rather than half-fixed.

VERIFIED: fmt clean; clippy --all --all-targets clean; interpreter 1416 passed
/ 0 failed; codegen E2E 2752 passed / 0 failed; memory_sanitizer 908 passed / 0
failed (Linux, LSan). Regression tests are deliberate TWINS with identical
source and expected string —
`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_indexed_field_store_non_pure_index_runs_once` and
`tests/interpreter.rs::test_indexed_field_store_non_pure_index_runs_once` —
because the subject of the bug is the two backends disagreeing.
