MECHANISM. That lint's checks and its fix-it rewrite both reproduce the author's own spelling by span, so it genuinely needs the source text. It got it by adding `let source = read_source(&self.filename);` to the TAIL of `Pipeline::typecheck` -- which is why the read site is "deeper than `cmd_build_project`'s prologue" as the row predicted: it is not in `cmd_build_project` at all, it is in the shared Pipeline that `run_multi_file_codegen` drives. That function hand-constructs its Pipeline with `filename: mf.name.clone()` over a super-program stitched from every module, so `filename` is the package NAME by design. `read_source` hard-exits on any IO error, hence the single `openat(AT_FDCWD, "solo")` the row's strace caught and the immediate death.

THE FIX. The text was already in hand and being discarded -- `Pipeline::new(filename, source)` receives it. It is now kept on the struct as `source: Option<String>` and the lint reads that instead of touching the filesystem: correct, and one fewer full-file read per typecheck. Project mode passes `None` and the lint sits out; slicing spans against a stand-in string would have been worse than not running.

KNOWN GAP, deliberate and noted at the field: `map_value_clone_reinsert` does not run in project mode. It never has -- before d166203 the lint did not exist, and after it the build died -- so this is a coverage follow-up, not a regression. Running it project-wide needs the per-module source texts threaded to the super-program pipeline.

The gap was that `tests/cli.rs` went unrun between d166203 and here -- a session doing contained codegen work runs codegen / memory_sanitizer / interpreter, and `cli` is not in that set. Both sessions that hit this found it the same way: a full suite run for an unrelated reason. A green targeted run is evidence about its targets, not about the tree.

title: Bounds-check elimination fails for the CONVERGING two-pointer loop `while lo <= hi { v[base+lo] ... v[base+hi] }` when the index carries a base offset — the flat-2D / row-major scan shape. Isolated on kata #246 (strobogrammatic two-pointer over a flat Vec[u8] corpus of N*LEN bytes): kara keeps 2 per-iteration checks that clang -O3 does not, costing 1.28x on the kata and 1.93x on a work-identical minimal probe. Neither ingredient alone breaks BCE — base+ascending, base+descending, converging-without-base, and even both-ends-from-ONE-ascending-IV all elide cleanly; only the combination of a base offset with a converging two-IV guard defeats it.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: LeetCode #246 Strobogrammatic Number, bench lane; found while root-causing the kata's residual 1.30x vs C. Filed after the hypothesis recorded in the #246 README (kara-katas 4645548) was CONFIRMED by disassembly + a controlled experiment.

EVIDENCE 1 - the two loops are isomorphic except for bounds checks. Both binaries fully inline is_strobogrammatic into main (x86 container, karac AOT KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 vs clang -O3 -march=x86-64-v3). kara's punch loop is 21 instructions, C's is 15. The 6-instruction excess is EXACTLY 2 x (lea; cmp $0x9c400; jae <panic>) - i.e. 100% bounds checking; every other instruction matches one-for-one, including the 5-way rotate map, which LLVM table-izes identically in both (movzbl digit; add $0xd0; cmp $0x9; ja; bt <mask 0x343>; jae; table load). So this is NOT a rotate-map, string-layout, or codegen-quality gap - the earlier suspects (5-way if-chain not table-ized; scattered String corpus) were both ruled out.

EVIDENCE 2 - controlled experiment pins the cost. Added Kara-equivalent bounds checks to the C mirror (absolute index base+lo / base+hi, unsigned compare against total length, branch to abort). clang compiles that to a loop instruction-for-instruction ISOMORPHIC to kara's (21 insns, same order; only register allocation and the rotate table's element width differ). hyperfine 80 runs, min: C 65.1ms, C+bounds-checks 83.2ms (1.28x), kara 83.0ms (1.28x). kara is statistically INDISTINGUISHABLE from equal-safety C - so on this kata karac's codegen is at clang -O3 parity once safety is equalized, and the whole residual gap is the missing BCE.

EVIDENCE 3 - minimal probes isolate the exact trigger. Five variants, identical corpus (Vec.filled(20000*32), LCG-filled, loop-carried acc*131 sink so nothing hoists), differing ONLY in the scan loop; count of `cmp $0x9c400` (the length constant) in main:
  A  base+ASCENDING      `while lo < len { v[base+lo] }`                                -> 0 checks  (BCE fires)
  B  base+CONVERGING     `while lo <= hi { v[base+lo]; v[base+hi] }`                    -> 2 checks  (BCE FAILS)
  C  CONVERGING, no base `while lo <= hi { v[lo]; v[hi] }`                              -> 0 checks  (BCE fires)
  D  base+DESCENDING     `while hi >= 0 { v[base+hi] }`                                 -> 0 checks  (BCE fires)
  E  base, both ends from ONE ascending IV `while lo+lo < len { v[base+lo]; v[base+len-1-lo] }` -> 0 checks (BCE fires)
E is the decisive one: it performs the SAME memory accesses as B, at the same base offset, with the same trip count, and returns the SAME value (-607711579) - it differs only in deriving both indices from a single ascending induction variable instead of two converging ones. E: 28.1ms, B: 54.2ms => the missing BCE alone costs 1.93x on a work-identical program. (#246 shows only 1.28x because its loop body does more per iteration, diluting the check.)

WHY THE EXISTING MACHINERY MISSES IT. B-2026-06-16-1 covers binary-search `mid`; the canonical forward `j < v.len()` is covered (probe A, and #246's own fill loop, both elide); B-2026-07-17-1 (6474a73) added bce_length_pin.rs `compute_descending_skips` for the descending in-place rolling-DP shape (probe D elides). The uncovered case is the CONVERGING guard: two independent monotone IVs whose relation to the length is established only jointly (lo <= hi <= len-1, base = i*STRIDE, i < N, v.len() == N*STRIDE). The descending skip proves `k <= k_init < B_pin <= len` for a SINGLE index whose init is linear in an enclosing loop var; here `hi`'s bound is the co-moving `lo`, and the indexed expression is the SUM `base + hi` rather than a bare loop var, so neither the UpperBound guard path nor the monotone-assume tier produces a usable fact. NOTE the sum matters independently: probe C (converging, bare index) DOES elide, so a converging guard alone is fine - it is `base + {lo,hi}` under a converging guard that fails. FIX DIRECTION: extend the length-pin skip to the row-major shape - when v's length is pinned to N*STRIDE (Vec.filled / a counted fill), the offset is `i*STRIDE` with the enclosing loop bounding `i < N`, and an inner index j satisfies `0 <= j <= STRIDE-1` (from a converging or counted guard), then `base + j <= (N-1)*STRIDE + STRIDE-1 = N*STRIDE-1 < len` by the same linear-normal-form cancellation compute_descending_skips already uses. Push UpperBound facts for BOTH indices through the existing asserted_index_bounds channel. Soundness-critical (a wrong skip is an OOB): needs the full codegen-E2E + memory_sanitizer x86 AND arm64 gates.

BREADTH: this is the flat/row-major 2D array traversal shape (matrix scans, fixed-stride record buffers, per-row palindrome and two-pointer checks), so it recurs well beyond #246 - #246's own CONSTRUCTION loop (`corpus[base+lo] = ...; corpus[base+hi] = ...`) is the same shape and also keeps its checks (5 total `cmp $0x9c400` sites in main: 3 in construction, 2 in the punch loop). NOT a correctness issue - the checks are sound, just not elided. NOT worked around in the kata: #246 stays written as the natural converging two-pointer; probe E is diagnostic evidence only and must NOT be taken as a kata rewrite.

── FINDING 484c2c9 (row stays OPEN; the entry's FIX DIRECTION needs one correction) ──

REPRODUCED EXACTLY AS FILED, on this x86 container: probe B keeps 2
`cmp $0x9c400` sites in the punch loop, probe E keeps 0, and both print the
same value on the same corpus — so the two are work-identical and the checks
are the whole difference, as the entry says.

THE CORRECTION IS ABOUT WHERE THE FIX CAN GO. The entry's FIX DIRECTION is to
extend `compute_descending_skips`'s length-pin reasoning to the row-major
shape, pushing UpperBound facts through `asserted_index_bounds`. That works for
a scan written INLINE — and #246's own CONSTRUCTION loop is exactly that, so 2
of its 5 checks are reachable this way (the inner converging pair; the third
construction check is `corpus[base + pos]` with `pos = (state/65536) % len`,
which needs modulo-range reasoning, not this). It cannot reach the punch loop,
which is the 1.28x the entry is actually about:

    fn is_strobogrammatic(corpus: ref Vec[u8], base: i64, len: i64) -> bool {
        let mut lo = 0i64;
        let mut hi = len - 1i64;
        while lo <= hi { ... corpus[base + lo] ... corpus[base + hi] ... }
    }

`corpus`, `base` and `len` are all PARAMETERS. There is no fill loop, no
enclosing counter, and no length pin in this function — and `base + lo <
corpus.len()` is not intra-procedurally TRUE. It holds only because every
caller passes `base = k*len` with `k < n` and `corpus.len() == n*len`. Every
analysis in `bce_length_pin.rs` runs per-function over `func.body`, so no
amount of extending it reaches this. Closing the punch loop needs an
inter-procedural fact (a callee precondition `base + len <= corpus.len()`
discharged at call sites), which is a different and much larger piece of work
than the entry scopes.

AND LLVM WILL NOT DO IT EITHER — the entry's own EVIDENCE 2 already proves
this, though it does not draw the conclusion. Adding Kara-equivalent bounds
checks to the C mirror produced a loop ISOMORPHIC to kara's, 21 instructions,
checks intact. That is clang -O3 with full visibility after inlining, declining
to eliminate them. So the "help LLVM see it" route is closed by the entry's own
measurement, and probes A/C/D/E elide because LLVM handles THOSE shapes (no
pin/skip of ours fires on any of them — `Vec.filled` produces no length pin,
and `lo <= hi` is not a guard `control_flow_bce.rs` reads a fact from), not
because it would handle this one given a nudge.

Stated precisely, because it is easy to overclaim from: a further C probe here
showed `__builtin_assume` on the two induction variables (`lo >= 0`,
`hi <= len-1`, `lo <= len-1`) does NOT recover the elision. That result is
weaker than it looks and is not itself evidence about the inlined case — the
probe function was `noinline`, so `base` was unconstrained and the checks were
genuinely necessary there. It rules out "IV-level assumes alone are enough",
nothing more. EVIDENCE 2 remains the load-bearing measurement.

ONE PREREQUISITE THE ENTRY DOES NOT MENTION: neither the kata nor the probes
would be reachable by the row-major skip as the machinery stands, because both
allocate with `Vec.filled(n * len, ..)` and `vec_length_lower_bounds` only
recognises `Vec.new()` / `Vec.with_capacity(..)` plus a counted PUSH fill. A
`Vec.filled(N, x)` length lower bound is a small, independently sound addition
and is a precondition for any of this firing on the shapes that motivated the
entry.

ALSO NOTE the affine limit: `base = i * stride` and `B_pin = n * stride` are
products of two identifiers, which `bound_to_linear` refuses (it is affine, not
polynomial). The cancellation the entry describes only closes if `stride` folds
to a literal first — true in #246 (`let len = 32i64`) and in the probes, but it
means constant-folding let-bound scalars is part of the work, not an
optimisation of it.

SCOPE RESTATED, then: the reachable win here is the INLINE row-major scan
(#246's construction loop, matrix/record-buffer scans written in one function),
not the kata's headline 1.28x. Worth doing, and worth filing under its real
scope rather than the entry's current framing.

METHOD NOTE, since it cost real time: timing this shape is corpus-size
dependent in a way that inverts the result. At n=400000 (12.8 MB, memory-bound)
probe B with 2 checks measured FASTER than probe E with none — the checks are
free when the loop is waiting on DRAM. The entry's 1.93x is a cache-resident
measurement (640 KB), and only that regime is informative about BCE.

PARTIAL FIX LANDED (e94e6bd9) — the intra-function shape now elides BOTH halves; the
reported kata does NOT yet benefit, and this entry stays OPEN for that reason.

WHAT NOW ELIDES. `bce_length_pin.rs::compute_converging_skips` recognises the
row-major converging shape {`Vec.filled(E, _)` or counted fill pinning
`v.len() >= B_pin`} + {enclosing `while i < N` / `for i in 0..N` bounding
`i <= u_max`} + {`let base = E_base(i)` linear and unwritten in the inner body}
+ {inner `while lo <= hi` / `lo < hi` with `hi` monotone non-increasing and
`lo`'s only writes trailing clean increments}, and proves
`B_pin - (E_base + hi_init)[i := u_max] >= 1` by the same linear-normal-form
cancellation `compute_descending_skips` uses. It pushes a NEW
`AssertedIndexBound::SumIndexBound { base_var, idx_var, vec_var, lower_proven }`
through the existing `asserted_index_bounds` channel — new because the index is
a SUM of two variables and so never decomposes into the bare-index /
constant-offset shape `UpperBound` is keyed on. `index_bounds_already_proven`
matches it in either operand order, covering reads and index-assign targets
through the one choke point.

TWO GATES ARE LOAD-BEARING AND BOTH ARE NEW HERE. (1) `lo`'s increments must
come AFTER every mention of `lo` in the body: unlike the descending case
(`k <= k_init` holds regardless of ordering), an ascending index stepped BEFORE
its use can exceed the bound the `lo <= hi` guard established, so skipping the
check there would be an OOB. (2) The LOWER half additionally needs the mirrored
gate on `hi` (a lower bound on a shrinking value is only valid before it
shrinks) plus a non-negative row origin, proven by evaluating `E_base + lo_init`
at the counter's MINIMUM. Both halves are gated independently: a body that steps
`hi` early still gets the upper skip and keeps the sign check.

CONST FOLDING WAS REQUIRED, not an optimisation. The row extent is typically
`let n = ..; let len = ..` literals, and `n * len` is NOT affine in `{n, len}`,
so `bound_to_linear` fails closed on the identity. `int_const_bindings`
substitutes integer-literal `let`s that are bound exactly once, never assigned,
and never mut-used, which makes the products affine. Note `stmt_writes_bound`
reports a `let x = ..` binding as a write to `x` — correct for its
"unwritten AFTER this point" use, but it rejects every candidate here, so the
scan uses a statement-VALUE-only variant (`mut_used_anywhere`).

MEASURED. A work-identical probe (single function, `Vec.filled(20000*32)`,
loop-carried sink): punch loop 17 -> 14 instructions, both bounds checks gone
(the surviving `jo`s are Kāra's overflow checks, which are equal-safety and
stay); 47.4ms -> 39.4ms = 1.20x, hyperfine 60 runs. Upper-only was 15
instructions / 1.12x, so the lower half is worth roughly half the win here.
`KARAC_BCE_CONV_SKIP=0` restores the checks exactly (A/B lever + escape hatch,
mirroring `KARAC_BCE_DESC_SKIP`).

WHY #246 ITSELF IS UNCHANGED (measured, not assumed — still 5 `cmp $len` sites
in `main`, output unchanged at 325454619). Two independent blockers:

  (a) The PUNCH loop lives in the callee `is_strobogrammatic(corpus, base, len)`.
      Inside it there is genuinely no local fact relating `base` to
      `corpus.len()`, so no intraprocedural analysis can prove the bound — this
      needs either interprocedural facts or loop predication (hoisting one
      widened check to the preheader, which changes WHERE a panicking program
      panics and so needs the IRCE-style safe-prefix split to stay
      semantics-preserving). karac's BCE analyses are per-function by
      construction, and the shape still fails post-inline: the hand-inlined
      probe reproduced the gap before this fix, which is why the fix exists at
      all.

  (b) The CONSTRUCTION loop IS the intra-function shape and would qualify, but
      the length pin refuses it: `vec_readonly_after` disqualifies any Vec that
      appears as a function ARGUMENT, and #246 passes `corpus` to
      `is_strobogrammatic`. Verified by isolation — adding a single read-only
      `fn peek(c: ref Vec[u8]) -> i64` call to the otherwise-firing probe puts
      both checks back. Relaxing that gate looks tractable (an argument NOT
      `mut`-marked cannot be a `mut ref` param per design.md Feature 4 Part 1.5,
      so it cannot resize; an owned-param move would make any later index site
      a use-after-move the ownership checker already rejects) but it is a
      SHARED gate the ascending and descending pins also rely on, and the
      construction loop runs once against the punch loop's 100 passes, so it
      would not move the kata's number. Deliberately not taken here.

So the honest scope of this fix: it closes the shape for programs that keep the
buffer local to the function that walks it, and leaves #246's own measurement
where it was. Kata README updated to say exactly that.

TESTS. 13 analysis unit tests (3 positive incl. index-assign targets, 10
negatives covering each gate one at a time — reordered step, non-monotone `hi`,
written `base`, row wider than the pin, counter rewritten before the inner loop,
unpinned/resized Vec, mutated bound identifier, plain single-index loop); 3
lower-half tests pinning the two halves as independently gated; 2 IR wiring
tests (skip fires -> NO `vidx.` block at all; reordered variant -> combined
check survives); 1 ASAN E2E with ODD-width rows and an exact-size corpus so
`base + hi_init` must land on the final element, reading AND writing every cell.
Every negative goes through a `mutate` helper that asserts its anchor matched —
a silently-missed `.replace()` had made one negative a vacuous pass during
development, which is the failure mode these tests exist to prevent.

2026-08-05 SECOND SLICE — blocker (b) CLEARED, blocker (a) REFUTED AS A PIPELINE FIX.

(b) FIXED: the length pin now tolerates the Vec being passed to a function. `vec_len_stable_after` used to route through `vec_readonly_after`, which disqualifies ANY occurrence of `v` that is not an index base or a `.len()`/`.is_empty()` receiver — so a single `is_strobogrammatic(corpus, base, len)` anywhere in the function killed the pin for every index site in it. It now routes through a relaxed twin (`expr_vec_len_stable`) that additionally accepts `v` as an UNMARKED argument to a FREE-FUNCTION call. Soundness rests on design.md Feature 4 Part 1.5: a free-function call writes the `mut` marker on any argument whose place-expression root is a fresh owned binding when the callee's parameter is `mut ref T` / `mut Slice[T]`, and every pinned `v` is exactly such a binding (introduced by `let v = Vec.new() / with_capacity() / filled()` in the same function — never a `mut ref` binding being forwarded, which is the one case the spec lets through unmarked). So a `mut ref` callee is impossible without the marker (and marked args are refused), a `ref` callee cannot resize, and an owned callee MOVES `v`, making any later index a use-after-move the ownership checker already rejects. METHOD-call arguments are deliberately NOT relaxed: method calls never write the marker (same design.md section), so an unmarked method argument proves nothing about the parameter's mode — pinned by a negative test. The ascending pin path (`compute_vec_length_pins`) still uses the STRICT `vec_readonly_after` and is byte-identical.

Effect on kata #246: bounds-check sites in `main` 5 -> 3 (the construction loop's `corpus[base+lo] = ..` / `corpus[base+hi] = ..` pair now elides; the third construction site is the corruption step OUTSIDE the converging loop and keeps its check). Output unchanged at 325454619. Wall clock 42.8ms -> 42.0ms = 1.02x, INSIDE NOISE and expected: construction runs once against the punch loop's 100 passes. So the kata's headline 1.28x is STILL unchanged — the value of this slice is unblocking the pin for the general 'hand the buffer to a helper' shape, not this measurement.

(a) STILL OPEN, and one candidate cheap fix is now RULED OUT. LLVM ships IRCE (inductive range-check elimination) and it is NOT in the `default<O2>` pipeline karac runs, so enabling it looked like a one-line win for the callee-side loop. Tested directly on #246's pre-opt IR with opt-18: `default<O2>` versus `default<O2>,function(loop-simplify,lcssa,irce),default<O2>` produce BYTE-IDENTICAL assembly (same md5, same 8 `$640000` compares). IRCE does not match this shape — the index is a SUM `base + j` and `j`'s range is fixed jointly by two co-moving IVs, not by one affine IV against a loop-invariant bound. So the remaining callee-side gap needs interprocedural facts or IRCE-style loop VERSIONING (a checked and an unchecked copy chosen by one preheader test — semantics-preserving, unlike naive predication which would move where a panicking program panics). Recorded so the pipeline-flag idea is not re-derived.

Tests added this slice: 3 analysis unit tests (fires through an unmarked free-function call; refuses a `mut`-marked argument; refuses a method argument). Both converging test helpers now assert the mutated source PARSES — a mutation that fails to parse yields no skips and would make every negative a vacuous pass, the same failure mode the `mutate` anchor assert exists for. Full `--features llvm` suite green: 101 binaries, 12,980 passed, 0 failed, 0 skips (codegen 2785, memory_sanitizer 929, par_codegen 229); clippy and fmt clean.

CLOSED 2026-08-05 (e94e6bd9 + 55f3d4a3). The shape this entry NAMES is done: a
converging two-pointer over a base-offset index, `while lo <= hi { v[base+lo];
v[base+hi] }`, now elides BOTH halves, including when the buffer is handed to a
helper function. Probe B — the entry's own repro — goes from 2 checks to 0, its
punch loop from 17 instructions to 14, and runs 1.20x faster. Kata #246's
CONSTRUCTION loop, the second shape the entry called out, goes from 3 check
sites to 1; the survivor is `corpus[base + pos]` with `pos = (state/65536) %
len`, which needs modulo-range reasoning and is a different problem.

WHAT IS NOT CLOSED, STATED RATHER THAN IMPLIED. Kata #246's headline 1.28x vs
equal-safety C is UNCHANGED by both slices, and this row is closed with that on
the record. The kata's PUNCH loop lives in the callee
`is_strobogrammatic(corpus, base, len)`, where `corpus`, `base` and `len` are
all PARAMETERS and `base + lo < corpus.len()` is not an intra-procedural truth —
it holds only because every caller passes `base = k*len` with `k < n` and
`corpus.len() == n*len`. Every analysis in `bce_length_pin.rs` runs per-function
over `func.body`, so the remainder is not a deeper version of this fix; it needs
interprocedural preconditions or IRCE-style loop versioning, a different feature
at a different scale. SPLIT TO B-2026-08-05-6 rather than left as a
permanently-open tail on a row whose named shape is finished — the same
treatment B-2026-08-04-13 got when it came off this entry.

── CORRECTION 2026-08-05 (see B-2026-08-05-21) ──

THIS ENTRY'S HEADLINE ATTRIBUTION IS WRONG, and the row's own EVIDENCE 2 is the
reason it looked right. EVIDENCE 2 added Kara-equivalent BOUNDS checks to the C
mirror, measured 1.28x, and concluded "the whole residual gap is the missing
BCE". That is affirming the consequent: it shows bounds checks are SUFFICIENT to
cost ~1.28x in C, not that they are what costs Kara 1.28x.

The direct experiment, now possible because B-2026-08-05-6 (c87f488) eliminated
the callee-side checks, refutes it. With both punch-loop bounds checks provably
gone (disassembly: 21 -> 18 instructions, 2 -> 0 `cmp $0x9c400`), kata #246 moved
only 45.12ms -> 43.71ms (min of 80) -- about 3%, 1.29x -> 1.25x. The elision is
real and it is nearly worthless here.

WHAT ACTUALLY COSTS THE 1.23x is Kara's INTEGER OVERFLOW check on the index add
`base + lo`, which sits on the loop-carried critical path. C's mirror never
computes that add -- it passes `corpus + i*LEN`, folding the base into the
pointer -- so it was never an equal-safety comparison in the axis this entry
assumed. Isolated by control: C rewritten to the `base+idx` form UNCHECKED is
35.15ms (parity), and the same C plus `__builtin_add_overflow` is 43.04ms,
landing on Kara's 43.71ms. Full table in B-2026-08-05-21.

The BCE work this entry motivated remains correct and worth keeping -- the shape
recurs, and the elision is sound. Only the claim that it was #246's gap is
withdrawn.

title: `?` on an Option/Result whose payload is heap-BOXED unwraps the BOX POINTER as if it were the payload's first word -- the value comes out empty or garbage under AOT while `karac run` is correct, and the box leaks
detail:
REPRO (probe b231/i4, three lines, no destructure involved): `struct Full { name: String, buf: Vec[i64] }` (6 words), `fn res(i: i64) -> Result[Full, String] { return Result.Ok(mk(i)); }`, then inside a `Result`-returning fn: `let r = res(i)?; println(f"{r.name}");`. AOT prints an EMPTY string; `karac run --interp` prints the real one. Valgrind: 60 bytes definitely lost in 2 blocks. `karac check` is clean and nothing warns.  A full destructure makes the corruption visible rather than merely empty -- b231/i3 (`let Full { name, buf } = res(i)?;`) prints `i3::94197037118224`, i.e. `buf.len()` reading a pointer-shaped value.  WIDTH IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, not Option-vs-Result -- the same lesson as B-2026-08-02-25, and the 4-corner matrix was run to establish it rather than assumed:    b231/j1, j4: a 4-word payload (`{String, i64}`) through `Result` (5-word area) -- INLINE -- correct, vg=0.    b231/j3: the SAME 4-word payload through `Option` (3-word area) -- BOXED -- empty output, 28 bytes lost.    b231/j2, i1-i4: a 6-word payload through either carrier -- BOXED -- empty/garbage output, 60 bytes lost.  So one struct behaves correctly or not depending only on which carrier it rides, which is the signature of a missing debox.  IT IS `?`, NOT THE DESTRUCTURE OR THE CALL. Same payload, same fn: `let Full { name, buf: _ } = mk(i);` (b231/i5, no `?`) is clean, and `let Full { name, buf: _ } = res(i).unwrap();` (b231/i6, `.unwrap()` instead of `?`) is clean. Only the `?` spelling breaks. Every `?` shape tested breaks the same way: bare binding (i4), partial destructure (i2), full destructure (i3), and `let` destructure directly on the `?` (i1).  MECHANISM, read from the code and consistent with every measurement: `reconstruct_question_ok_payload` (src/codegen/exprs.rs) rebuilds the unwrapped payload by pulling words STRAIGHT OUT of the Result/Option aggregate -- `build_extract_value(sv, 1)`, `(sv, 2)`, `(sv, 3)` -> `rebuild_value_from_payload_words(ok_llvm, w0, w1, w2)` (and, for an all-i64 payload, a flat word-by-word copy just above it). Both branches assume the payload words ARE the payload. For a boxed payload w0 is the box POINTER and w1/w2 are undef, so a `{ptr,len,cap}` String rebuilds as `{box_ptr, undef, undef}` -- prints empty, and the real buffer plus the box itself are never freed (2 blocks: the box and the String buffer).  THE FIX SHAPE ALREADY EXISTS one module over. `reconstruct_payload_value` (control_flow_match.rs) has the debox: predicate `want > field_words.len()`, then inttoptr word 0, load the payload type through it, re-split via `coerce_to_payload_words`. `reconstruct_question_ok_payload` needs the same guard before either rebuild branch -- compare `llvm_type_word_count(ok_llvm)` against the carrier's payload area (3 for `Option`, 5 for `Result`, or just `n_fields - 1` off the aggregate it already has) and debox when it exceeds it.  OWNERSHIP IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is the part to get right rather than fast. `?` CONSUMES its operand, so after the debox the unwrapped value owns the interior and the BOX allocation itself must be freed -- that is one of the two leaked blocks and it stays leaked even if the debox alone lands. `suppress_question_source_inline_payload` is the existing disarm for this position and its doc is explicit that it only understands the INLINE overlay (it zeroes the slot's `cap` at field 3, which for a boxed payload is not a cap at all). It needs a boxed sibling.  PRE-EXISTING: not attributable to any of today's fixes. The `?` path was not touched by B-2026-08-04-5 or -6 (name resolution and box-drop field ownership respectively), and `.unwrap()` -- which shares the payload reconstruction machinery but not `compile_question` -- is clean.  HOW IT SURFACED: a post-fix sweep over the boxed-payload family after B-2026-08-04-6, deliberately probing axes the corpus under-covers. Nine other shapes in the same sweep were clean (borrow scrutinee partial and repeated-read, nested struct destructure both spellings, guard arm, escaping bound field, early return out of the arm, mutating Drop body, loop with `continue`, `Option`-typed payload field), so this is a narrow hole, not a broad one.  ORACLE NOTE: visible to ALL THREE oracles at once, which is unusual for this family and makes it cheap to pin -- parity diffing (AOT empty vs interp correct), direct output assertion, and valgrind/LSan (60 bytes). Prefer a parity + output pin; the leak count will change once the box free lands.  FIXED (2026-08-04, 60087fc), and the row's diagnosis held on the boxed half exactly as written -- the debox went in with the predicate, the three steps, and the ownership answer the row spelled out. `?` consumes its operand, so the loaded value owns the interior and the box is dead the moment it is read; freeing it AT the debox turned out to need no counterpart in `suppress_question_source_inline_payload`, which is a simpler answer than the row expected.  A SECOND, INDEPENDENT DEFECT in the same function, found while building the fixture for the first and NOT predicted by this row: a payload that is WIDE BUT INLINE. `Mid { name: String, pad: i64 }` is 4 words and FITS `Result`'s 5-word area, so it never boxes and never reaches the debox -- and it was still wrong, because `rebuild_value_from_payload_words` carries exactly w0/w1/w2 and silently dropped every word past the third. The String came back correct and `pad` came back 1 where the program stored 3 (probe b231/t1 line `b`; stash-proven identical at base, so pre-existing and unrelated to the debox). The flat-copy branch just above only rescues an ALL-i64 payload, which a String-bearing struct is not. Fixed by reading the full payload span and rebuilding through `reconstruct_struct_from_words` -- the same helper the match-arm path uses -- gated on `want > 3` so narrower payloads keep the original path byte-for-byte.  This is why the row's title understates the bug: `?` was wrong for BOTH over-area and over-three-words payloads, and only the first is a boxing question. `Mid` now appears under both carriers in the pins -- inline through `Result`, boxed through `Option` -- so one type exercises both defects.  VERIFIED: 24 probes (b231/a1..k4 and t1) all parity-EQUAL, valgrind 0 except the residual below. Suites: codegen 2778, memory_sanitizer 926, interpreter 1441, drop_differential 13, par_codegen 226 = 5384 passed, 0 failed. Both pins stash-proven RED -- the E2E against the exact garbage output (`a::94685901742848
b:mid-3:1
c:
...`), the ASAN pin at 12,800 bytes under LeakSanitizer.  RESIDUAL, filed as B-2026-08-04-10: `let <StructPattern> = <expr>?` -- destructuring DIRECTLY on the `?` rather than through a binding -- still leaks 60 bytes. Deliberately excluded from the ASAN pin.
fix: 60087fc (src/codegen/exprs.rs, src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs for the helper's visibility; pins codegen.rs::e2e_question_reconstructs_wide_and_boxed_ok_payloads, its interpreter oracle interpreter.rs::test_question_reconstructs_wide_and_boxed_ok_payloads, and memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box -- the first two stash-proven RED on the exact garbage output, the third at 12,800 bytes under LeakSanitizer)

title: `let <StructPattern> = <expr>?;` -- a struct destructure written DIRECTLY on a `?` whose payload is heap-boxed -- leaks the payload's heap fields; routing through an intermediate binding first is clean
detail: REPRO (probe b231/k4, 60 bytes definitely lost in 2 blocks under valgrind, parity-EQUAL so no run-vs-build split and the printed values are correct): `struct Full { name: String, buf: Vec[i64] }` (6 words, BOXED at either payload area), `fn res(i: i64) -> Result[Full, String] { return Result.Ok(mk(i)); }`, then inside a `Result`-returning fn: `let Full { name, buf } = res(i)?; println(f"{name}:{buf.len()}");`. The two lost blocks are the String buffer and the Vec buffer -- BOTH fields are bound, and neither binding owns its buffer.  THREE CLEAN CONTROLS, which localize it to one syntactic form:    b231/k3 -- `let t = res(i)?; let Full { name, buf } = t;` (the SAME destructure, one binding earlier) is vg=0.    b231/k2 -- `let Full { name, buf } = res(i).unwrap();` is vg=0.    b231/k1 -- `let Full { name, buf } = mk(i);` (no carrier at all) is vg=0.  So it is not the destructure, not the boxing, and not `?` on its own (a plain `let r = res(i)?;` binding is vg=0 -- probe b231/i4). It is the two together with no binding in between. The partial spelling (`buf: _`, b231/i1) leaks identically, so it is not about which fields are bound either.  LIKELY MECHANISM, unverified: the let-destructure path registers its leaf bindings' cleanup off the RHS being a recognized owned source, and the `?` expression is not in that roster -- `.unwrap()` and a direct call both are. The intermediate binding in k3 works because the binding itself registers, and the destructure then disarms it per field. Start by comparing what the `let`-with-struct-pattern path does for a `Call` RHS versus a `Question` RHS; do not start in `compile_question`, which B-2026-08-04-9 just fixed and which hands back a correct, owned value in every other spelling.  PRE-EXISTING but only now MEASURABLE: before 60087fc this shape produced garbage values as well as leaking, so the leak could not be attributed cleanly. The values are correct now and the leak is what is left.  ORACLE NOTE: valgrind/LSan only -- both backends print the same correct output. Deliberately kept OUT of `memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box` (which routes through a binding, the clean spelling) so LSan does not attribute this row's leak to that pin.  SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while verifying B-2026-08-04-9's fix, in the same b231 sweep.  FIXED (2026-08-04, a82b4ff). The row's LIKELY MECHANISM was right, and the roster it guessed at is a single predicate: `finish_owned_struct_destructure` asks `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` whether the RHS is a fresh owned temp, and that fn is literally `matches!(expr.kind, Call | MethodCall) && !is_borrow_returning_call_expr`. A `?` is neither variant, so `fresh` was false, the destructure took its place-source path, and the leaf bindings registered nothing. That also explains all three controls exactly: `.unwrap()` is a MethodCall, `mk(i)` is a Call, and the intermediate binding in k3 works because the BINDING registers and the destructure then disarms it per field.  SHIPPED: look THROUGH the `?` at its operand at this one site. `?` moves its Ok payload out and the operand's own cleanup is disarmed at the `?` site, so a fresh owned operand yields a fresh owned unwrapped value.  SCOPED ON PURPOSE, and this is the part worth keeping: the change is at the destructure, NOT inside `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`. That predicate's other callers are the fresh-temp scrutinee trackers, whose ownership contracts a `?` operand has not been measured against -- widening it there would silently change box tracking, inline-payload registration and shared Option release all at once. Recursing on the OPERAND rather than returning a flat `true` also leaves `let S { .. } = r?` (a named binding operand) at today's behavior, so only the shape the probes prove broken moves.  VERIFIED: all 15 `?` probes (b231/i1..k4 and t1) parity-EQUAL and vg=0, including the three that leaked -- i1 (partial destructure on `?`), i3 (full), k4 (the minimal form). Suites: codegen 2778, memory_sanitizer 926, interpreter 1441, drop_differential 13, par_codegen 226 = 5384 passed, 0 failed.  PIN: rather than a new test, `asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box` gained the direct-destructure spelling and lost its "deliberately not covered" note -- the two spellings belong in one fixture now that both are covered. Stash-proven RED against THIS commit's `stmts.rs` change alone (the B-2026-08-04-9 half left in place) at 6,400 bytes under LeakSanitizer, which is what attributes the leak to this row rather than to that one.

title: `?` PROPAGATING an Err whose payload is a struct wider than THREE words silently drops every word past the third -- the Err mirror of B-2026-08-04-9's second defect, in the error-staging path rather than the Ok-reconstruction one
detail: REPRO (probe b232/e3): `struct Err4 { msg: String, code: i64 }` (4 words, which FITS `Result`'s 5-word payload area, so it is INLINE and never boxed), `fn fail4(i: i64) -> Result[i64, Err4] { return Result.Err(mk4(i)); }`, and a propagating wrapper `fn prop4(i: i64) -> Result[i64, Err4] { let v = fail4(i)?; return Result.Ok(v); }`. Matching `prop4(4i64)`'s Err and printing `{e.msg}:{e.code}` gives `mid-err-4:0` under AOT and `mid-err-4:4` under `karac run`. The `String` survives; `code` -- word 3 -- does not. Probe b232/e1 shows the same value as 32 in a different program, i.e. it is whatever happens to be in that slot, not a consistent zero.  CONTROL: b232/e4 matches the SAME `Result` WITHOUT the `?` wrapper and is correct on both backends, so it is the propagation, not the construction or the match. b232/e2 (a 6-word Err, BOXED) is also correct -- the boxed path stores a pointer in w0 and does not depend on the word cap.  MECHANISM: `compile_question`'s error-staging path calls `rebuild_value_from_payload_words(e_ty, w0_i, w1_i, w2_i)` -- exactly three words, extracted as fields 1..3 of the Result aggregate. Any `E` wider than three words loses the rest. This is the SAME helper and the SAME three-word cap that B-2026-08-04-9's second defect hit on the Ok side, where `Mid { name: String, pad: i64 }` came back with a garbage `pad`; that one was fixed by reading the full payload span and rebuilding through `reconstruct_struct_from_words`. The Err side was not touched.  WHY IT WAS LEFT: the Ok-side fix sat in one function with one caller. The Err staging has at least TWO sites -- the fn-level return path and the `with_provider` return-retarget path just below it -- and both are interleaved with error-trace recording and errdefer draining. That is a bigger surgery than a same-shape patch, and a half-verified change to error propagation is worse than a filed row. Whoever takes it should port the Ok-side shape to BOTH sites and check the errdefer/error-trace interaction explicitly.  PRE-EXISTING and independent of everything landed today: the `?` Ok-side fix (60087fc) does not touch the Err staging, and the shape reproduces with the same values before it.  ORACLE NOTE: parity diffing only -- no leak, no crash, correct-looking output with one wrong field. This is the quiet corner of the family and the reason a wide MIXED payload deserves a fixture axis of its own: a 3-word `E` is immune, and 3 words is what most hand-written error structs happen to be.  SOURCE NOTE: surfaced in the b232 sweep of the `?` ERROR side, run after B-2026-08-04-9 fixed the Ok side.  FIXED (2026-08-04, e6a2eca), and it turned out SMALLER than this row estimated. The row deferred it on the grounds that the Err staging has two sites -- the fn-level return path and the `with_provider` retarget path -- both interleaved with error-trace recording and errdefer draining. That is true of the SITES but not of the DEFECT: both consumers build their Err aggregate from a single `ret_words` vector, and its non-converting branch was the literal `vec![w0_i, w1_i, w2_i]`. Widening that one expression covers both paths and touches neither the trace nor the errdefer drain.  The words are now taken as `min(inner_word_count, outer_word_count).max(1)` -- bounded on BOTH ends so the extract loop cannot index past the source aggregate when an outer `E` is wider than the inner one, which the conversion branch beside it can produce.  VERIFIED: probes b232/e1..e5 all correct, parity-EQUAL, vg=0. Suites: codegen 2780, memory_sanitizer 926, interpreter 1441, drop_differential 13, par_codegen 226 = 5386 passed, 0 failed. The pin is stash-proven RED on the exact wrong value (`b:mid-err-4:32`), which is worth more than a generic assertion here: the failure is one wrong integer field in otherwise correct output.  LESSON FOR THE FIXTURE CORPUS, restated because it is the transferable part: a 3-word error struct is IMMUNE to this whole class, and 3 words -- a lone `String`, or two scalars and a tag -- is what most hand-written error types happen to be. Payload WIDTH deserves an explicit axis (3 / 4-5 / >5) rather than one representative error type, on both the Ok and Err sides. Three separate defects this session (B-2026-08-04-9's two and this one) were all invisible at 3 words.

title: The descending-loop bounds-check skip (B-2026-07-17-1) reads the facts it rests on with `stmt_writes_ident`, which sees only TOP-LEVEL assignment targets. A write one block deep (`if c { i = 50 }`) therefore left every fact reading 'unchanged' while the program changed it, and the skip elided a load-bearing check. Three independent levers reach it: the enclosing counter, the index's init, and the fill counter (which makes the length pin overstate the buffer). Default-ON since 6474a73. Observed as an out-of-range Vec STORE — silent exit 0, `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer`, and a glibc malloc assertion, depending on the case.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while reading `bce_length_pin.rs` to scope the row-major extension B-2026-08-04-8 asks for. Not hypothesised from the code and then assumed — each of the three levers below was reproduced as a running binary before anything was changed, and the A/B was `KARAC_BCE_DESC_SKIP=0` on the SAME source (the flag exists as the escape hatch for exactly this class).

THE MECHANISM. The skip proves `k <= k_init < B_pin <= v.len()` for an inner descending loop. Each conjunct is read off a region scan, and five of those scans route through one helper, `stmt_writes_ident`. That helper descends into nested blocks via `expr_writes_ident`, which sees each nested statement's VALUE but never its assignment TARGET — so `if c { k = 100 }` answered 'does not write k'. The module already knew this shape of gap: its `region_bindings` collector exists specifically to close it, its section comment names it ('blind to ... assignment targets buried in an inner block'), and `only_monotone_decrement` was converted to use it. The five callers that read the OTHER facts never were.

THREE LEVERS, THREE REPRODUCTIONS. All on a Vec filled to 10, indexed by a descending `k`:
  (1) ENCLOSING COUNTER  `if flag == 1 { i = 50 }` before the inner loop. `i <= u_max` is
      then false where the proof substitutes it, so `k = i + 9` starts at 59. Ran to
      completion printing `len=10` — 60 out-of-range stores, exit 0.
  (2) INDEX INIT         `if flag == 1 { k = 50 }` after `let mut k`. `sole_scalar_init`
      reports a value `k` no longer holds. Aborted with `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer`.
  (3) FILL COUNTER       `if flag == 1 { j = 5 }` before the counted fill. Here the skip's
      arithmetic is right and its PREMISE is not: the fill runs 5 iterations, so the length
      pin claims a buffer twice the real one. Aborted inside glibc's malloc assertion.
Each panics correctly with `KARAC_BCE_DESC_SKIP=0`, and each panics correctly now.

THIS IS THE SECOND OCCURRENCE OF THE SAME CLASS, and the first one's fix is what should have prevented it. B-2026-07-04-13 (6ca6fe44) found exactly this — 'a GENERIC walker that only inspects statement VALUES ... blind to `let` patterns and assignment TARGETS buried in an inner block' — with two confirmed exploits, one of them a SILENT WRONG ANSWER. Its fix BUILT `region_bindings` for the purpose. But it wired the collector into the call sites it had in hand, the after-fill invariance scans (`vec_readonly_after` / `var_unwritten_after`), rather than into the blind helper itself. `compute_descending_skips` (B-2026-07-17-1, 6474a73) then landed AFTER that fix and added five fresh scans through the still-blind `stmt_writes_ident`. The guard existed and the new code simply did not reach for it.

THE FIX IS ONE PRE-CHECK AT THE SHARED HELPER, not five patched call sites. All five callers want the same predicate ('is this name written anywhere in this statement'), they were all wrong in the same way, and a per-caller fix would leave the next caller to rediscover it. `stmt_writes_ident` now consults `region_bindings`' assignment-target roots first and answers the question its own doc comment always claimed to answer. Only `assigned` is consulted, not `rebound`: a nested `let` shadows an inner name without writing the outer one, and treating that as a write would reject sound programs for nothing.

WHY THE EXISTING TESTS MISSED IT, which is the reusable part. There WAS a negative test for lever (1) — `desc_no_fire_when_counter_rewritten` — and it passed, because it spells the rewrite at the TOP level, which the blind helper does catch. The suite tested the fact, not the fact's reachability: every negative was written in the one syntactic position the analysis handles. So the new tests are built from a SHARED BASE with three empty slots, and the control asserts that base FIRES; each negative differs from a firing program only by the nested write, which is what makes it a test of the nesting rather than of some unrelated gate a longer program tripped. Verified both directions: with the pre-check reverted, all five new tests fail; the two controls pass either way.

THE E2E ASSERTS THE PANIC, NOT THE IR, and deliberately. The failure is a STORE past the end of a buffer, so what it looks like is allocator-dependent — the three cases produced three different symptoms above, one of them a clean exit 0. A clean panic is the only stable oracle; every corruption mode fails it.

THE GENERALISABLE LESSON, given it took two rounds: when a shared helper answers a question WRONG, fixing the callers that happen to be in front of you leaves the helper's doc comment still lying to the next caller — and here the next caller arrived five weeks later and wrote five new scans against it. The durable repair is at the helper, so that reaching for the obvious function is safe by default. Anything in this module still needing the raw structural match can call the inner one deliberately; nothing currently does.

NOT A REASON TO DISTRUST THE SKIP'S ARITHMETIC. The linear-normal-form proof (`init_below_bound`) was right throughout; what failed was the reading of its inputs. The Pascal-row and exclusive-bounds wins are unchanged, and `test_ir_descending_loop_bce_skip_wiring` still asserts the elision.

COMPILE-TIME COST, MEASURED (the pre-check adds a `region_bindings` walk per
statement, inside helpers that are themselves called in nested loops, so this
was an open question rather than an obvious no-op). Interleaved A/B on the same
container, `karac build` of bench/compile_speed/synthetic.kara (10,858 lines),
min of 6 runs each, binaries differing only in this file:

    pre-fix   9.66 s
    with fix  9.80 s      +133 ms, 1.014x

Accepted. The asymptotics are unchanged — `expr_writes_ident` already walked the
same subtree, so the added work is a HashMap/HashSet allocation per statement,
not a new traversal order. 1.4% on a debug-profile compiler is the right trade
for closing a heap-corrupting elision, and if this ever matters the collector
can be memoised per statement rather than the check reverted.

fix: a4ca760
title: The interpreter silently DROPPED an out-of-range index-assign: `v[100] = 7` on a 2-element Vec produced no error, no growth, and no store — while AOT and the JIT both panic with `vec index out of bounds`. The READ path was checked all along; only the store guarded itself with a bare `if i < len` and fell off the end. Compound assign (`v[100] += 7`) was also correct, because it reads first.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while reproducing B-2026-08-04-13. The probe that proved the codegen miscompile was run under `--interp` as a control, expecting the interpreter to name the out-of-range store the AOT binary was performing. It printed the same successful output the MISCOMPILED binary did.

THAT IS WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SEVERITY SUGGESTS. The interpreter is the reference oracle — the thing consulted to decide what a program is supposed to do. Here it agreed with a codegen bug, for an unrelated reason, and its agreement is what a reasonable investigator would have read as 'the AOT output is correct'. A silent oracle does not just miss its own bug; it launders someone else's.

THE SHAPE. `Interpreter::set_index` ended in two arms that each wrapped the store in `if i < len` with no else, so an out-of-range index fell off the end of the function. Characterised before fixing:
  v[100] = 7   (far past end)   -> silently dropped
  v[2]   = 7   (one past end)   -> silently dropped
  v[-1]  = 7   (negative)       -> silently dropped
  v[100] += 7  (compound)       -> correct error   <- reads first, and the READ is checked
  let x = v[100]                -> correct error
AOT and JIT panic on all of them. The compound-assign and read rows are what localise it: the gap is the store path specifically, not index bounds in the interpreter generally.

The fix reports through `record_runtime_error` with the READ path's exact message and the index's span, so the two directions are indistinguishable in output. Negative indices arrive already wrapped by `i as usize` and so are reported the way the read path has always reported them (`index 18446744073709551615 out of bounds`) — odd-looking, but pre-existing, shared, and deliberately not changed here; making the store nicer than the read would just be a new divergence.

STILL SILENT, and left that way on purpose: `set_index`'s `_ => {}` arm (a store through a receiver that is not an Array/Slice/Map/Tensor) and its `let Value::Int(i) = idx_val else { return }` guard (a non-integer index). Both are unreachable for type-checked programs, and this same `_ => return` has twice been found swallowing a REAL shape (kata-133-audit's field-rooted store; B-2026-07-20-3's tuple-rooted store) — so the arm deserves its own audit rather than a catch-all error bolted on next to an unrelated fix.

fix: 567d5aa
title: AUTO-PAR SILENTLY DROPS STORES through a tuple-element receiver: `t.0.push(x)` recorded NO write in the dependency walk, so two pushes to the same Vec (and the read after them) were grouped as 'no data or effect dependencies' and the stores vanished — `t.0.len()` returns 0 after two pushes under `karac build`, 2 under the interpreter, then an out-of-bounds abort on the read. `collect_assign_target_defines` walked FieldAccess/Index/Deref/MethodCall to the place root but let TupleIndex fall through its `_ => {}`, so the MethodCall arm recursed onto `t.0` and recorded nothing. Contained to the tuple spelling: identifier and struct-field receivers were always correct
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while auditing `set_index`'s `_ => {}` arm, the follow-up B-2026-08-04-14 deliberately left open. The audit probed every receiver spelling against the interpreter as oracle; the tuple row diverged, and the trail led out of the interpreter entirely.

REPRO, and it is small:
    let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
    let mut t: (Vec[i64], i64) = (v, 3);
    t.0.push(10); t.0.push(20);
    println(f"len {t.0.len()} v0 {t.0[0]} v1 {t.0[1]}");
  interp      -> len 2 v0 10 v1 20
  karac build -> panic: vec index out of bounds   (len was 0)
  karac run   -> same panic (JIT shares the pipeline)
A loop-free seven-line program. `KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1` makes it correct, which is the A/B that localises it to auto-par rather than to tuple-element codegen.

THE SMOKING GUN was `karac query concurrency`, which reported the decision outright:
    parallel_groups: [{statements: [2,3,4,5], reason: 'no data or effect dependencies'}]
Statements 2 and 3 are the two pushes; 4 and 5 are the printlns that READ the vec. The analysis had correctly found 1->2 and 1->3 (RAW on `t`), so it saw the pushes READ `t` — it just never recorded that they WRITE it.

BLAST RADIUS, measured on all three receiver spellings of the identical program:
    v.push(10); v.push(20)              -> serialized correctly (no group)
    h.items.push(10); h.items.push(20)  -> serialized correctly (no group)
    t.0.push(10); t.0.push(20)          -> WRONGLY grouped -> stores lost
The `FieldAccess` sibling arm being present is exactly why only the tuple spelling broke.

THE ARM'S OWN HISTORY IS THE FINDING. `collect_assign_target_defines` accumulated its cases one bug at a time: `SelfValue` for self-hosting #8 ('a `mut ref self` method call recorded no write'), `Unary{Deref}` for B-2026-06-20-16 ('the auto-par dependency check saw a histogram body as not writing the map, then parallelized the loop against a later `m.keys()` read'), `MethodCall` for method-chain places. Three prior single-variant additions, each after a miscompile with the same signature, none of which asked what ELSE the walk was missing. TupleIndex was the fourth. Fixed by folding FieldAccess/Index/TupleIndex into one place-projection arm with an explicit completeness requirement naming `place_root` (same file) as the canonical list of forms — `place_root` had TupleIndex right all along, which is what makes the omission a gap rather than an unknown.

The sibling `collect_assign_target_reads` had the identical hole and is fixed with it: a target spelled `t.0[i] = v` stopped at the TupleIndex and never reached the `Index` arm that contributes the read of `i`. No repro is filed for that half — it is the same walk and the same one-line omission, and leaving it for a future bug report would be choosing to be surprised twice.

WHY THE SUITE WAS GREEN, and this is the part worth carrying: `tests/codegen.rs`'s `run_program` passes `None` for the concurrency analysis, so NOTHING it runs is auto-parallel. `tests/par_codegen.rs`'s harness threads `Some(&analysis)` the way the CLI does. B-2026-08-02-10 had already written `e2e_tuple_elem_method_receivers` over this EXACT source — and it passed, throughout, while `karac build` on a byte-identical file aborted. The test was not weak; it was in the harness that cannot see auto-par. Any bug that only manifests under auto-par is invisible to the whole ~2780-test codegen suite, and the obvious home for a codegen test is precisely the harness that cannot catch it. Regression accordingly went into `par_codegen`: one E2E plus one analysis-level assertion that the group is not formed.

A TEST-SHAPE MISTAKE, recorded because it nearly shipped. The first E2E draft appended a struct-field control to the SAME `main` — and it PASSED against the unfixed compiler. The extra statements changed the grouping enough to hide the miscompile. A regression test that does not fail on the bug is worse than none, so the control moved to its own program and the regression source stays minimal. Both were then verified in BOTH directions: with the TupleIndex arm reverted the E2E and the analysis test fail, the control passes either way. This is the second time today that an unrelated statement in a test program moved the analysis off the shape under test (cf. B-2026-08-04-13's negatives, which had to be built from a shared base whose control asserts the base FIRES).

fix: e986284 (src/codegen/stmts.rs tuple-assign arm; src/codegen/expr_ops.rs tuple_index_elem_type_expr). Pins codegen.rs::e2e_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed, memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed (floored at 500 allocations against ~1.8k), interpreter.rs::test_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed. Both codegen tests are stash-proven RED against the unfixed compiler (the E2E aborts to empty output, the ASAN case reports a memory error); the interpreter twin passes both ways, as the oracle should. Verified across 16 probe shapes -- both element positions, Vec / String / Vec[String] elements, both-Vec tuples, fresh-temp vs named sources, and the struct-field control -- all clean on both backends with matching alloc/free counts. cargo test --features llvm: 12974 passed, 0 failed.
title: Moving a Vec OUT of a tuple element, mutating it, and moving it BACK (`let mut e = t.0; e.push(x); t.0 = e;`) aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` under both AOT and the JIT; the interpreter runs it. The struct-field analogue (`let mut e = h.items; ...; h.items = e;`) is correct, so this is again the TUPLE spelling of a walk that handles the field spelling. Independent of auto-par (`KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1` reproduces it) and independent of B-2026-08-04-15, which is fixed
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced in the same receiver-spelling audit that produced B-2026-08-04-15, and kept as its own row because the mechanism is different — that one was a missing WRITE in the auto-par dependency walk, this one is a double FREE with auto-par disabled.

REPRO:
    let mut t: (Vec[i64], i64) = (Vec.new(), 3i64);
    let mut e = t.0;      // move the Vec out of the tuple element
    e.push(10i64);
    t.0 = e;              // move it back
    println(f"{t.0.len()}");
  interp                 -> 1
  karac build            -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2
  KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1     -> same abort (so: not auto-par)
CONTROL, the same program through a struct field rather than a tuple element:
    let mut e = h.items; e.push(10i64); h.items = e;  -> 1, correct
The move-out presumably does not disarm the tuple element's cleanup, so the buffer is freed once for the element and once for `e` (or for the re-assigned element) — but that is a reading of the symptom, NOT a diagnosis: no IR was disassembled and no drop-tracking code was read. Treat it as unlocated.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ONE MORE TUPLE ROW: this is one of the two workarounds B-2026-08-02-10's diagnostic actively recommends. That diagnostic tells an author to 'annotate the tuple binding with its full element types ... or bind the element to a local first'. As of today the FIRST path is correct (it was broken by B-2026-08-04-15 until that fix landed) and the SECOND path is this double-free. The advice should not be shipped pointing at a heap corruption; either this is fixed or that suggestion drops the second clause. Both legs were verified against the current build, so the diagnostic's status is known rather than assumed.

NEXT STEP when picked up: check whether the tuple-element move-out marks the source place as moved-from in the same way the field move-out does (B-2026-08-01-31 covers a deep-chain field MOVE-OUT followed by a reassign, which is the working analogue and the natural place to start), then confirm under ASAN rather than glibc's tcache message, which names the symptom and not the site.  RESOLVED, and the characterization above needed correcting first. The row framed this as a move-out/move-BACK round trip; it is neither round-trip- nor move-out-dependent. A plain `t.0 = <named source>` with NO move-out anywhere aborts identically, and the move-out on its own (`let mut e = t.0; e.push(x);` with no store back) is clean. What matters is only that the RHS is a NAMED heap-owning binding: a fresh-temp RHS (`t.0 = mkvec(n)`) was always correct, because there is no source binding to disarm.  CAUSE: `compile_tuple_index_store` drops the old element and then MOVES the RHS header into the slot, but the tuple-assign arm (added by B-2026-08-02-5) never got the sibling of B-2026-07-15-25's field-assign move-suppression. The source binding was left owning nothing with its scope-exit cleanup still armed, so it and the tuple's element drop freed one buffer. The struct-FIELD spelling has carried that suppression since B-2026-07-15-25, which is exactly the asymmetry the row observed and the thing that located the missing arm.  ELEMENT KINDS: general, not Vec-specific. `String` and `Vec[String]` elements abort too -- `Vec[String]` is a TRIPLE free (11 allocations, 13 frees: the element buffer plus the Strings inside it). An earlier reading of this probe recorded String as clean; that was a dead-allocation artifact of the kind B-2026-08-04-17 describes (7 allocations, the payload never materialized), and it inverted once the fixture read the buffer's bytes.  FIX: the element-type resolution is factored out of `compile_tuple_index_store` into `tuple_index_elem_type_expr` and shared with the assign arm's new suppression, so the displaced-value drop and the source disarm cannot resolve the element differently -- that drift is what this bug was.  SPIN-OFF: the report's own `let mut e = t.0; …; t.0 = e;` spelling draws an ownership warning (`value 't' moved here, used again here`), so it could not go in the regression tests without tripping the harness's ownership gate. It fires on the struct-field spelling equally, so it is not another tuple asymmetry -- filed as B-2026-08-04-18.  DIAGNOSTIC FOLLOW-UP the row asked for: B-2026-08-02-10's suggestion ("bind the element to a local first") no longer produces heap corruption, so the advice can stand on the memory-safety ground it was failing on. It does still produce B-2026-08-04-18's warning, which is worth settling before considering that suggestion fully clean.

title: memory-fixture authoring hazard: a payload whose content is compile-time constant, or that is read only through `.len()`, is a DEAD allocation LLVM deletes at -O2 -- so an E2E/ASAN fixture for an ownership bug can pass against a compiler that aborts on the same shape
detail:
PROVEN TWICE, both in landed tests rather than hypothetically. (1) B-2026-08-04-11 leg (a)'s fixture (codegen.rs::e2e_fstring_interpolation_of_a_payload_heap_field_is_a_move) carries an arm `Result.Err(e) => { println("d:unused"); }` whose payload is built `Wrap { msg: f"err-payload-{i}" }` and called as `g(4i64)`. That is EXACTLY the shape leg (b) aborts on, and the test passed throughout leg (b) being open: with a literal argument the f-string const-folds, the payload is never allocated, and the double free has nothing to hit. (2) The first draft of leg (b)'s own fixture used a `String.new()`+`push_str` payload (so the content was NOT foldable) and read it back through `.len()` only -- it also passed against the unfixed compiler, because a buffer whose bytes are never read is a provably dead allocation and LLVM deletes the malloc outright.  MEASURED, same program shape, valgrind `total heap usage` over ~1200 intended payload allocations: constant-seeded loop + `.len()`-only = 1 alloc (the whole loop folds to its final total); opaque seed + `.len()`-only = 6 allocs (loop survives, mallocs are DCE'd); opaque seed + a `contains` byte read = 3,206 allocs. Only the third exercises anything, and only the third aborts against the unfixed compiler.  SCOPE -- this is a SHAPE hazard, not a corpus-wide defect, and the difference was checked rather than assumed. memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box has the same constant-seeded-loop structure and is NOT affected: 601 allocs as written vs 606 with an opaque seed and runtime-varying payload content, so its coverage is real. No claim is made here that other existing fixtures are vacuous; what is claimed is that nothing currently stops the next one from being so, and that two have already been.  RULE for any new memory fixture: (a) seed from something the optimizer cannot see through -- `env.args().len()` is 1 under both the codegen E2E harness and assert_clean_asan_run, since both exec the binary with no extra argv; (b) read the payload's BYTES, not just its length -- `contains` against a runtime-derived needle works and stays borrow-only, which matters when the bug shape requires a NON-consuming arm (printing the field would consume it and change the shape under test); (c) confirm `total heap usage` shows the buffers were actually allocated before trusting a clean run. An interpreter ORACLE twin should keep a literal seed instead: there is no optimizer to defeat, and `env.args()` inside an in-process interpreter test reports the TEST binary's argv (program_args is None, so resource_method.rs falls back to std::env::args), which varies with the filter.  WORTH DOING, not done here: a cheap harness-side guard. assert_clean_asan_run could assert a minimum allocation count, or the E2E harness could fail a fixture whose binary performs fewer allocations than a declared floor -- either turns this from a reviewer-discipline problem into a mechanical one.  RESOLVED as far as a mechanical guard can take it. `assert_clean_asan_run_min_allocs` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) runs the program with `print_stats=1:atexit=1`, parses the malloc count off ASAN's exit stats, and fails with a VACUOUS FIXTURE message naming both likely causes when the count falls under a caller-supplied floor. The ASAN option was verified to mask nothing: a leaky program still exits 23 with `ERROR: LeakSanitizer` and a double free still exits 23 with `ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free`. It is off unless a floor is requested, so the other 928 cases keep their quiet stderr. The assertion is proven LIVE rather than inert -- temporarily raising the floor fails with the real measured count (3208), which is what distinguishes a working parse from one that silently returns None and skips the check. When the runtime prints no stats line at all the check is skipped with a note, since that is "cannot measure", not "measured zero".  WHAT IS NOT COVERED, deliberately: (1) the plain codegen E2E harness (`run_program`) has no equivalent floor -- it does not link ASAN, so there is no allocation counter to read, and adding one would mean running every fixture under valgrind. The E2E half of this hazard is still reviewer discipline, and the leg (b) E2E fixture documents the two rules in its own doc comment. (2) No existing fixture was retrofitted. The one that was spot-checked (asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box) is NOT vacuous -- 601 allocs as written vs 606 with an opaque seed -- so a blanket retrofit is not obviously worth its churn; the floor is there for new fixtures and for any old one that a future measurement implicates.  MEASUREMENT CORRECTION worth recording, since the opposite was assumed for part of this session: `push_str("<literal>")` onto a `String.new()` DOES allocate -- measured 106 allocs over 100 iterations, i.e. one buffer per call. It is not a cap-0 static. The two things that actually make a payload disappear are the two named above (foldable content, and a buffer whose bytes are never read), not the literal-ness of the pushed argument.  SCOPE CORRECTION (same day, after the guard landed) -- the paragraph above saying this is a shape hazard rather than a corpus-wide defect is WRONG, and the reasoning behind it was bad: it generalized from ONE spot-check (asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box) that happens to be Vec-heavy and therefore unaffected. Sweeping the whole corpus with the counter that 49e126a made available says otherwise. Across all 864 counted `assert_clean_asan_run` fixtures: 102 allocate NOTHING, and 296 sit at or below a 7-alloc baseline. "Nothing" is exact, not inferred -- an allocation-free run reports 3 (the ASAN runtime's own startup allocations) and `asan_baseline_no_allocations` pins that value, so 3 means the program did no heap work of its own.  PROVEN INSTANCE, not an inference from the count: `asan_vec_with_capacity_push_past_n_grows_once`. Its own comment says it exists so that "both the original `with_capacity` malloc'd buffer AND the grown buffer need to be tracked correctly" and to catch "a double-free if the grow path doesn't free the original before swapping the data pointer". At -O2 it performed exactly ONE allocation -- the println buffer. The literal loop bound let the entire loop fold to the constant 16, and reading the result back through `v.len()` alone left the buffer a dead allocation LLVM deletes. A test for the Vec GROW path that never grew a Vec. At -O0 the same source allocates 3, which is the behaviour the comment describes. Fixed in dee8b8a (opaque bound + two ELEMENT reads + a floor of 6; 10 allocations now).  REMAINING WORK, which is why this row is open again: the other 101 zero-allocation fixtures are un-audited. Each needs the same three-way judgement rather than a blanket rewrite -- (a) genuinely heapless by design, so the count is correct and nothing is owed; (b) intends heap work that folds away, like the Vec-grow case, and needs an opaque seed plus a byte/element read; (c) allocates but only through a path the fixture does not assert on. Sweep with `KARAC_ASAN_ALLOC_AUDIT=1 cargo test --features llvm --test memory_sanitizer -- --nocapture`, which prints one `ALLOCAUDIT\t<n>\t<label>` line per fixture. Start with the ones whose NAMES promise heap work (grep the 3-alloc list for vec_ / string_ / map_ / drop / leak / double_free) -- that is how the Vec-grow case surfaced. Adopt `assert_clean_asan_run_min_allocs` as each is fixed, so it cannot drift back.  PROGRESS + A REFINEMENT THAT CHANGES THE REMAINING WORK'S SHAPE. Nine fixtures de-vacuumed so far (dee8b8a, 2467458): the Vec-grow case plus vec_growth_multiple_reallocs, vec_with_capacity_push_exact_n_no_grow, vec_with_capacity_unused_buffer_freed, struct_with_vec_field_freed_on_scope_exit, struct_with_string_field_freed_on_scope_exit, struct_with_multiple_vec_fields_freed_on_scope_exit, method_chain_intermediate_vec_freed and string_new_push_str -- each 0 program allocations before, 9-17 after, all now floored. Zero-allocation population 102 -> 93. None of the nine surfaced a codegen bug once they really ran, which is its own (weak but real) signal.  THE REFINEMENT: the standard recipe -- opaque seed plus a byte/element read -- provably does NOT apply to the DISCARD-shaped family (`make_vec();` as a bare statement, `let x = mk(n);` with x unused, `option_string_discarded_freed`, `result_{ok,err}_string_undestructured_freed`, `discarded_*`). Measured with a runtime-opaque seed and no other change: baseline for `env.args()` + a literal println is 6 allocations, and all three discard shapes tested come in at exactly 6 -- zero program allocations. That is not a fixture defect that better seeding fixes. A discarded value is by construction never read, so a CORRECTLY freed one is a dead malloc/free pair the optimizer is entitled to delete; the same program with the value RETAINED (pushed into a live Vec) allocates 8, which confirms the elision is about deadness rather than folding.  WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THEIR COVERAGE, stated at the confidence the evidence supports: the DOUBLE-FREE direction is still caught, and that is directly observed rather than argued -- B-2026-08-04-11 leg (b)'s probe allocated 9 while buggy and 8 once fixed, i.e. the second free is what kept the allocation alive. The LEAK direction is UNTESTED here and should not be assumed either way: LLVM can delete an unpaired malloc whose result is unused, so a fixture named for the freed/no-leak direction (option_string_discarded_freed and the two undestructured ones are named exactly that way) may be dark in the direction it advertises. Someone should settle it before rewriting that family.  SUGGESTED HANDLING for discard-shaped fixtures once that is settled: do not contort them into reading a value they exist to discard. Pair each with a RETAINED control in the same program -- build the same value, keep one alive and assert on it, discard the other -- so the fixture allocates for a reason adjacent to what it pins, and the floor has something real to measure.  THE LEAK-DIRECTION QUESTION IS NOW SETTLED, and the answer is the pessimistic one. LLVM at -O2 deletes an allocation whose result is never read REGARDLESS of whether it is freed. Measured directly at the C level, same host toolchain, `malloc(64 * argc)` with the pointer never read: freed -> 0 allocations, NEVER freed -> also 0 allocations. So a discard-shaped fixture is dark in BOTH directions for a fully dead buffer -- it would not catch a leak either, not just the ambiguity noted above. The only reason the double-free direction survives is that the SECOND free makes the pattern non-removable, which is exactly what B-2026-08-04-11 leg (b) showed (9 allocations while buggy, 8 once fixed). CAVEAT on transferring this: the C measurement is about LLVM's policy for a known allocator. Kara allocates through `karac_malloc_or_panic`, a runtime function, so the removal depends on LLVM seeing through it -- which it evidently does, since the paired Kara discard shapes measured 0 program allocations. The unpaired Kara case was not measured directly (producing a genuine leak needs a compiler bug or an RC cycle), so treat it as strongly indicated rather than proven.  CONSEQUENCE for the remaining work: the RETAINED-CONTROL suggestion above is not a stylistic preference, it is the only thing that can work for this family. Seeding cannot help, and neither failure direction is currently covered.

THE DISCARD-FAMILY QUESTION IS SOLVED, and the answer is NOT the retained-
control rewrite suggested above -- that suggestion should be considered
withdrawn. A retained control makes the FIXTURE allocate, but it does not
make the DISCARDED value non-dead, so the floor would measure the control
while the shape under test stayed elided: coverage-shaped, not coverage.

The lever that does work was already in the tree and was not considered:
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`. It skips the pass pipeline entirely, so nothing folds
and nothing is DCE'd, and the allocations these fixtures intend are real.
The `OnceLock` in `read_opt_level_env` prevents per-FIXTURE control, but the
knob does not need to vary per fixture -- one extra whole-suite run covers
the entire family at once, with no fixture rewritten and no production code
touched. Measured, baseline calibrated at 3 for BOTH levels so the counts are
directly comparable (`asan_baseline_no_allocations` reports 3 at -O0 too):

  fixture                                   -O2   -O0
  discarded_vec_temp_freed_no_double_free     3    11
  discarded_nested_vec_string_temp_freed      3    11
  discarded_rc_temp_freed                     3    11
  discarded_block_tail_temp_freed             3    11
  option_string_discarded_freed               3     4
  option_string_let_unused_freed              3     4
  result_ok_string_undestructured_freed       3     4
  result_err_string_undestructured_freed      3     4

iterations to survive unrolling. The iteration-count leg was not in the
original statement of this row and should be read as part of it.

AND THE CHECKBOX BUYS LESS THAN THIS ROW ASSUMED, which is the correction. A
required status check gates a MERGE. This repo commits straight to `main` from

direct push cannot be gated by a check that the push itself triggers -- there

then merged or pushed to a matching branch AFTER checks have passed.

So the promotion was deliberately made with "Do not allow bypassing the above
