  `karac run --interp` -> runtime error: shared struct field 'H.v' is not declared mut
  `karac build`  -> the same module-verification failure as (b)

TWO LEGS, one shape.

(b) CODEGEN GAP, the visible one: a `shared struct`'s Vec field cannot be coerced to `Slice[T]` at all. B-2026-08-05-40 (0949f9f) taught `coerce_to_slice` to rebuild a 2-word slice header from a PLACE argument, which is exactly this shape — but refused a `shared`/`par` receiver explicitly, on the correct reasoning that its slot holds a HANDLE rather than the aggregate. The refusal returns `None`, and the caller then forwards the raw 3-word `{ptr,len,cap}` against the 2-word formal, so LLVM verification hard-fails. Same structure as B-2026-08-05-41's codegen half: a fail-closed bail in a resolver whose caller treats `None` as "carry on with the old path" is not fail-closed. Here the outcome is at least LOUD (the program does not compile) rather than a silent miscompile.

(a) GATE BYPASS: the `SharedFieldNotMut` gate does not reach a `mut Slice[T]` formal. B-2026-08-05-41 closed the `mut ref T` spelling by keying on `borrow_context`, which `borrow_context_for_param` sets from `Type::Ref` / `Type::MutRef` only; a `mut Slice[T]` formal is a `Type::Slice` and carries no borrow context at all, so it never reaches the check. Confirmed adjacent and NOT bypassed: `zap(s: mut ref Vec[i64])` on the same immutable field IS refused, so this is specific to the Slice coercion, not a hole in the new gate.

The interpreter catches (a) at RUNTIME via `write_shared_struct_field` — defense in depth, the same guard B-2026-06-30-3 promoted to a compile error for the assignment spelling. So the surviving divergence is `karac check` reporting clean on a program the interpreter refuses.

NOT REACHABLE AS A SILENT MISCOMPILE TODAY, which is what keeps this at medium: leg (b) makes every program of this shape fail to BUILD, so the unsound write in (a) never reaches a binary. The exposure is `karac check` — and any tool built on it, including Mend — certifying a program that will not compile and that the interpreter rejects.

WHAT A FIX NEEDS:
  * `coerce_to_slice`'s place arm extended to a shared receiver, deriving the Vec header's address through the RC payload via `shared_gep_layout` — the same recipe B-2026-08-05-41's codegen half uses, so leg (b) compiles;
  * a mutability signal that survives to a `Type::Slice` formal, so leg (a) is refused at typecheck with the message the assignment spelling gets. `borrow_context` is the wrong channel for it, which is why B-2026-08-05-41 deliberately left this alone rather than papering it over.

Both legs must land together: fixing (b) alone would turn a loud compile failure into a silently-accepted unsound write, which is strictly worse than the status quo.

FIXED 2026-08-06 (28ceec6b). Both legs, in one commit, as this row required.

LEG (b), CODEGEN. `coerce_to_slice`'s place arm now resolves a `shared`/`par`
receiver through `shared_gep_layout` -- the funnel every other shared field
site uses -- and rebuilds the slice header exactly as the owned arm does. The
field-is-a-Vec test runs BEFORE any IR is emitted, so a declined field costs
nothing; the receiver re-compile is safe for the same reason B-2026-08-05-41's
is, `is_pure_field_chain` (an identifier or `self` root with FieldAccess hops,
no Index, so re-evaluating has no side effect).

A BONUS FELL OUT that this row under-stated: the READ-ONLY spelling was equally
broken. `fn total(s: Slice[i64])` given the same shared Vec field failed module
verification identically -- the gap was never limited to the mutating form, only
the soundness QUESTION was. Both build now.

LEG (a), TYPECHECK. The signal is a new `mut_through_param_arg`, set from
`param_mutates_through(param_ty)` -- `Type::MutRef(_) | Type::Slice { mutable:
true }` -- at the three call-argument sites that already set `borrow_context`,
and taken alongside it in `infer_field_access` so a nested read inside the same
argument does not inherit the write context.

WHY NOT `borrow_context`, confirming this row's own reading: that field's
contract is which UNION diagnostic applies (`E_UNION_BORROW_REQUIRES_UNSAFE` vs
the read-flavored one), and its doc records that `mut Slice[T]` deliberately
does NOT count there because the slice-assignment contract is write-only. Adding
the slice spelling to it would have changed union diagnostics to close a
shared-struct hole. The two questions are different and now have different
channels.

WHAT THE FIX IS REALLY ABOUT, and it is the same lesson a third time.
B-2026-06-30-3 gated the ASSIGNMENT spelling. B-2026-08-05-41 added the `mut
ref` spelling and its own comment named the flaw -- "the rule was enforced
against the spelling rather than against the operation" -- then keyed the fix on
`borrow_kind == Some("mut ref")`, which is a spelling. `mut Slice[T]` was the
next spelling. `param_mutates_through` asks the operation question once, and is
SHARED with `check_call_site_marker`'s `mut`-marker rule (which had computed the
identical predicate independently all along), so a fourth spelling would have to
be added to both rules at the same definition or to neither.

MEASURED, all three backends agreeing where they should:
  (b) legal   `shared struct H { mut v: Vec[i64] }` / `zap(s: mut Slice[i64])`
              check clean, interp 99, BUILD ok, AOT 99   (was: hard build fail)
  (a) unsound the same with `v` NOT declared mut
              refused at typecheck: "shared struct field 'H.v' is not declared
              mut" -- the identical message the assignment spelling gets
              (was: `karac check` reported All checks passed)

PROBES, each one variable away, all correct:
  * field at index 2 behind a SCALAR and another Vec -- AOT prints `7 1 99 98
    30`, byte-identical to the interpreter, so the header-shifted GEP is
    offset-correct where a plain-struct offset would have read a neighbour
  * a niche `Option[shared]` field PRECEDING the Vec -- also offset-correct
  * `self.v` inside a shared method
  * `par struct` with a read-only slice (a `par` struct cannot have a plain
    `mut` Vec field at all -- an unrelated pre-existing rule refuses it)
  * `mut ref Vec[i64]` on a non-mut shared field -- STILL gated, B-2026-08-05-41
    parity preserved
  * `ref Vec[i64]` read of a non-mut shared field -- NOT gated
  * bare `Slice[i64]` read of a non-mut shared field -- NOT gated, and now builds
  * a SCALAR field to `mut Slice[T]` -- clean type error, not a crash
  * a plain (non-shared) struct -- unchanged, B-2026-08-05-40 control
  * valgrind clean at -O2 AND -O0, output matching the interpreter

TESTS, six, and the split is the point. THREE WITNESSES proven RED against the
unfixed compiler: `shared_struct_non_mut_field_mut_slice_argument_rejected`
(leg a), `e2e_shared_struct_vec_field_coerces_to_slice` (leg b),
`asan_shared_struct_vec_field_slice_coercion_no_leak` (leg b memory, floored at
100 allocations). THREE CONTROLS green either way, which is what a control
should do: the legal program still typechecks, the read-only spelling still does
not gate, and the interpreter parity leg was correct all along -- that last one
is pinned precisely because the interpreter being right while codegen could not
build is what localized this row.

THE ASAN LEG GUARDS SOMETHING NEW, not a re-run of the value test: the slice
header points INTO the Vec buffer inside the shared node's RC box, so it must be
a pure BORROW -- neither making the callee an owner (freeing the box's buffer at
callee scope exit, leaving the reads after the call dangling) nor disarming the
node's own reclaim (one leaked buffer per iteration). Neither failure was
possible on the rvalue-copy path this replaces, and no earlier test can cover it
because no program of this shape could be built at all.

GATES: -O2 13,117 passed / 0 failed / 102 suites; -O0 `memory_sanitizer` failure
SET unchanged (generic_struct_heap_field_move_out,
nested_option_pattern_boxed_payload_lifecycle,
shared_payload_view_optres_field_call_arg_copy, tensor_lifecycle); fmt and
clippy --all-targets --features llvm clean.

title: A cast TO `char` inside an f-string hole is DROPPED by both compiled backends -- `println(f"{b as char}")` prints the integer codepoint (98) where the interpreter prints the glyph (b). Silent wrong answer on code the typechecker accepts; binding the cast to a `let` first is correct, so the bug is invisible in the obvious spelling. Every OTHER cast in the same position is honoured (300 as u8 -> 44, -1 as u8 -> 255, 2.9 as i64 -> 2), which localises it to codegen's `expr_is_char` -- a predicate with one arm per char-yielding form, where `Cast` had no arm.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: LeetCode #249 Group Shifted Strings, found by the kata's own
differential harness rather than by either solver. Both solvers were clean on
all four surfaces from the start; only `differential.kara` builds strings from
computed bytes, which is the shape that trips this.

HOW IT SURFACED, and why the harness is part of the bug-finding surface rather
than scaffolding: the generator emits random words one byte at a time --

    w.push_str(f"{(ch as u8) as char}");

-- so under the compiled backends every generated word became a run of DIGITS
instead of letters. The corpus was still self-consistent, so the differential's
own cross-check ("groupings disagree on 0 of 4000") stayed green; what gave it
away was the four-surface md5 check, and then the group COUNT: 6,135 groups
under `--interp` vs 13,217 under AOT over an identical 14,053 words.

REDUCTION, three lines, and the cast is dropped ONLY in interpolation:

    let n = 97i64; let b = n as u8;
    println(f"A:{b as char}");           // interp a  | JIT+AOT 98
    println(f"B:{(n as u8) as char}");   // interp a  | JIT+AOT 97
    let c = b as char; println(f"C:{c}");// interp a  | JIT+AOT a   <- correct

So the LET-BOUND spelling is right and the inline one is wrong, which is what
makes this dangerous: the author sees a working example next to a broken one and
has no reason to suspect the difference.

SCOPE, established by control rather than assumed -- every other cast in the
same position is honoured under AOT:

    f"{big as u8}"   300 -> 44    OK
    f"{neg as u8}"    -1 -> 255   OK
    f"{f as i64}"    2.9 -> 2     OK
    f"{b as char}"    98 -> 98    WRONG

That rules out "f-string lowering ignores casts" and points at char rendering
specifically.

ROOT CAUSE: `expr_is_char` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) decides whether an
f-string / println part renders as a glyph or as an integer. It matches one arm
per syntactic form that can YIELD a char -- CharLit, Identifier (via
var_type_names), Index (via the element TypeExpr), MethodCall (`clone`, the
ascii case-folds, `unwrap`/`expect` via recorded inner types) -- and had NO arm
for `ExprKind::Cast`. A cast is the most direct char-yielding form there is.

FOURTH INSTANCE OF ONE GAP, which is the part worth keeping. The function's own
comments already record this exact symptom twice for method-call results:
"without this last arm `println(b.get())` for `fn get(self) -> char` formats the
i32 scalar as its integer codepoint (77 instead of 'M')", and again for
`unwrap` ("90 instead of 'Z'"). Each was fixed by adding the one arm in front of
whoever hit it. B-2026-07-24-3 then made `u8 as char` LEGAL at typecheck without
teaching the renderer about it, which is what created this instance. The
durable repair is not another arm -- it is that this predicate is a
denylist-shaped allowlist, and every new char-producing form silently defaults
to the integer rendering. Filed as such; the arm is the fix that ships.

FIX: one `ExprKind::Cast { ty, .. }` arm matching a `char` target path.

TEST: `e2e_cast_to_char_in_fstring_renders_the_glyph` (tests/codegen.rs) asserts
the glyph for both the single and double-cast inline spellings, the let-bound
control, AND the three non-char casts. The non-char casts are controls, not
padding: a regression that re-broke every cast in interpolation would look
identical if only the char line were asserted. Stash-proven RED with the fix
reverted.

NOT A NEW SURFACE FOR run-vs-build: `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` (AOT)
agree with EACH OTHER and both differ from `--interp`, so this is a codegen
miscompile detected by the interpreter oracle, not a JIT/AOT split.

fix: 26b2176 (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs — the Map/Set arm in `zero_struct_field_move_cap`, plus the Sorted variants in `zero_struct_move_caps_mono`'s existing arm). Pins e2e_map_field_move_out_neutralizes_the_source, test_map_field_move_out_transfers_the_handle, asan_map_field_move_out_neutralizes_the_source.
title: a `Map`/`Set` field moved out INDIVIDUALLY left the source handle live, so the owner's struct drop freed storage the destination still owned — `fn take(h: MapH) -> Map[i64, String] { return h.m; }` SEGFAULTS on a use-after-free under AOT while the interpreter is correct; the WHOLE-struct move has nulled the handle since B-2026-07-15-23
detail:
SHAPE, concrete and non-generic — nothing about it is exotic:

    struct MapH { m: Map[i64, String] }
    fn take(h: MapH) -> Map[i64, String] { return h.m; }
    fn main() { … let h = MapH { m: mk(i) }; let m2 = take(h); println(m2.len()); … }

    AOT: Segmentation fault (exit 139). Interpreter: correct.
    valgrind: `Invalid read of size 8` in `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec`,
              address 16 bytes inside a 72-byte block already free'd by main.

MECHANISM, and the asymmetry IS the bug. `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` — the WHOLE-struct move neutralizer — has carried a Map/Set null-store since B-2026-07-15-23, with a comment spelling out exactly this hazard ('a whole-struct move or a struct-field move-out that leaves the SOURCE handle live double-frees the map storage'). The PER-FIELD neutralizer `zero_struct_field_move_cap` never got the same arm: it handles Vec/String (cap-zero), Option (tag), Result (payload area), enums and nested structs, and a Map field falls through its final `else` where both the `enum_layouts` and `struct_types` lookups miss. So the field stays live and `FieldDrop::MapOrSet` frees it.

THE FIX IS A PURE CODEGEN NULL-STORE, because the convention is already the runtime's: `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` early-returns on `map.is_null()`, and both half-walks (`emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk`, `emit_map_shared_half_rc_dec_walk`) null-guard internally. Exactly parallel to the Vec cap-zero beside it.

THREE MOVE-OUT SPELLINGS, all fixed and all tested, because they reach the neutralizer by different routes: returned out of a by-value param, bound to a local (`let m2 = h.m`), and passed to a consuming callee (`eat(h.m)`). TWO CONTROLS that were always correct and must stay so — a field only READ, and a whole-struct move (which retracts the source's entire StructDrop rather than neutralizing one field) — so an over-nulling fix turns them red.

`SortedMap` / `SortedSet` ADDED TO BOTH ARMS FOR SYMMETRY WITH THE DROP CLASSIFIER, which B-2026-08-02-21 taught to free them; leaving the free-list and the neutralize-list asymmetric is the shape of this bug. STATED HONESTLY: that pair is NOT independently reproducible today — a SortedMap field moved out measures clean both before and after (166 allocs / 166 frees, 0 valgrind errors), so it is defensive symmetry rather than a measured fix. Adding a type to a NEUTRALIZER list is safe by construction: it nulls a handle the drop would otherwise free. (Separately noted while probing it: `m2.len()` / `m2.get(k)` on a moved-out SortedMap LOCAL bails with 'no handler for method … (method dispatch fell through)', which is why the probe had to route through a consuming callee. Unrelated pre-existing dispatch gap, not filed here.)

PROVENANCE, and it is the useful part. Found while establishing the precondition B-2026-08-06-1 explicitly says to answer BEFORE classifying a bare-`T` Map field: 'whether a bare-`T` Map field moved out INDIVIDUALLY has the same protection is the thing to establish before adding the arm — if it does not, the arm trades this leak for a double free.' The cheapest decisive experiment was not on the generic shape at all but on the CONCRETE one, which already classifies `MapOrSet`: if `take(h: MapH) -> Map` is clean, the interaction is handled; if it crashes, it is not. It crashed. So the precondition's answer is NO, and it was a live high-severity UAF in its own right rather than a hypothetical.

TESTS: `e2e_map_field_move_out_neutralizes_the_source` (tests/codegen.rs), `test_map_field_move_out_transfers_the_handle` (tests/interpreter.rs, the oracle — passes either way by design), `asan_map_field_move_out_neutralizes_the_source` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs). Both codegen tests are STASH-PROVEN RED: the E2E with `left: ""` (the crash produces no output), the ASAN twin with `SEGV … in karac_map_free_with_drop_vec`, naming the function. The ASAN twin also catches the OPPOSITE mistake — over-nulling leaks instead. Expected total DERIVED rather than read off a run: 12 per round x 40 = 480.

SUITES: non-llvm 8648 pass, codegen E2E 2814, memory_sanitizer 945 pass / 0 fail / 10 ignored; clippy and fmt clean.

fix: ee551b8 (shift legs) + <this commit> (negation leg)
title: shift by >= the bit width is UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR in AOT output — one `let` variable prints two different values in the same run and different values across runs (LLVM shl poison), the JIT disagrees again, and the interpreter raises a raw Rust panic; design.md's `"shift amount out of range"` trap is unimplemented at every width, and narrow `<<` additionally computes at i64 so an `i32` binding can hold 1048576000000
detail:
SHAPE, minimal, and the symptom is NOT a wrong constant — it is POISON:

    fn main() {
        let a: i64 = 1i64;
        let s: i64 = 64i64;
        let r: i64 = a << s;
        println(r);
        println(r);          // SAME variable, printed twice
        let t: i64 = a << s; // SAME expression again
        println(t);
    }

  AOT run 1:  94721897766304 / 0 / 0
  AOT run 2:  94357552725408 / 0 / 0      <- differs BETWEEN RUNS (ASLR-shaped)
  JIT:        0 / -9223372036854775808 / 1
  interp:     thread panicked at src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs:513:
              'attempt to shift left with overflow'

One `let`-bound variable prints two different values in consecutive `println`s
of the same run; the value changes between runs; the three backends disagree;
and the interpreter raises a raw Rust panic instead of a Kāra diagnostic. That
is LLVM `shl`/`ashr` poison (shift >= bit width is UB in LLVM IR, and codegen
emits the raw instruction) leaking into shipped binaries, plus an ICE on the
interpreter — which also violates the repo's own standard that every phase
emits a structured diagnostic and never just panics.

THE RULE IS SPECIFIED AND SIMPLY UNIMPLEMENTED. design.md line 2142: "Shift by
the bit width or more traps. `(x: i32) << 32` panics (`\"shift amount out of
range\"`); `(x: i32) << 31` is legal regardless of whether it flips the sign
bit. Same rule for `>>`." The string "shift amount out of range" does not
appear anywhere in src/ — grep returns nothing. There is no shift-amount check
on any surface at any width.

SECOND, SEPARATE DEFECT ON THE SAME OPERATOR — the narrow width is not
respected, so a narrow-typed binding can hold a value far outside its declared
range with no trap:

    let a: i32 = 1000000i32;
    let s: i32 = a << 20i32;
    println(s);                    // 1048576000000  -- an i32 binding
    println(s > 2147483647i32);    // true           -- typed i32, exceeds i32::MAX
    let u: u8 = 200u8; println(u << 4u8);   // 3200  -- a u8 holding 3200

All three surfaces agree with EACH OTHER here (no run/build divergence) and all
three disagree with the spec. design.md says `<<` is a bit shift at the
declared width — `(1i32) << 31` must be -2147483648 — and codegen instead
computes at i64 and hands back a value the declared type cannot represent.
Measured: `1i32 << 31` yields 2147483648 on interp, JIT and AOT alike.

CAUSE. `compile_narrow_int_binop` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) widens both
operands to i64, computes there, and range-checks ONLY the arithmetic set
`+ - * / %`. Its comment states the exclusion's premise outright -- "Bitwise /
shift results always fit the width (the operands do)" -- which is true for
`& | ^` and FALSE for `<<`. The interpreter mirrors the same split:
eval_ops.rs:513-514 are bare Rust `a << b` / `a >> b` on the i64 carrier, with
neither an amount check nor a `narrow_oob` call, while every arithmetic arm
beside them is `checked_*` + `narrow_oob`.

A THIRD, SMALLER SIBLING found by the same sweep: unary negation of a narrow
minimum does not trap. `let a: i32 = -2147483648i32; println(-a)` prints
2147483648 -- again an out-of-range i32 -- where the i64 equivalent DOES trap
`integer overflow` correctly. Same root: the narrow width is enforced on the
arithmetic binop set and nowhere else.

SEVERITY IS HIGH FOR THE FIRST DEFECT, on the UB alone. It is not merely a
wrong answer: the value is unstable within a single run and across runs, so any
program that shifts by a runtime amount which can reach the width has
nondeterministic behaviour that no test can pin. The narrow-width leg is the
milder half -- deterministic and consistent across backends, just wrong.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, and why it matters beyond correctness: while measuring
B-2026-08-05-38's remaining WIDENING half. That row proposes computing narrow
ops at the declared width instead of widening to i64, which is sound only if a
narrow-typed value always fits its declared width. It does not, and `<<` is why
-- so this row is a hard PREREQUISITE for B-2026-08-05-38's larger half, not
just a correctness item that happens to sit nearby.

INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENT of that half, taken while finding this (x86_64,
callgrind instruction slope over 20k vs 40k iters of kata #9's bench, sinks
verified identical across all three builds):

    i32, current lowering (checked)     1,210,924
    i32, all narrow checks elided       1,178,191   <- the 2.7% ceiling, reproduced exactly
    i64 working variables, same data    1,019,892   <- 1.187x FASTER than i32

The i64 build is equal-safety (its `+`/`*` still trap through the
`llvm.*.with.overflow.i64` intrinsics), takes identical inputs, and prints an
identical sink -- so the 191,032-instruction gap is the narrow lowering itself.
Only 32,733 of it (17%) is the range check; 83% is the widening. That
independently confirms B-2026-08-05-38's 79% figure from a different direction.

WHAT A FIX NEEDS:
  * a shift-amount check on BOTH surfaces at the operand's DECLARED width --
    trap `shift amount out of range` when the amount is negative or >= width,
    for `<<` and `>>` alike, at every width including i64/u64 (the poison leg);
  * narrow `<<` computed at the declared width so the result is representable,
    making `1i32 << 31 == -2147483648` per the spec;
  * narrow unary negation range-checked like the arithmetic binops;
  * the interpreter's raw `a << b` / `a >> b` replaced with the checked form,
    so a shift never raises a Rust panic in place of a Kāra diagnostic.

Once all three hold, "a narrow-typed value always fits its declared width"
becomes a real invariant, and B-2026-08-05-38's widening half can compute at
native width via `llvm.{s,u}{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow.iN`.

── FIXED, the two shift legs, at ee551b8 ─────────────────────────────

BOTH SHIFT LEGS ARE CLOSED and the row stays OPEN for the negation leg alone.

The amount check is ONE unsigned compare: a negative amount reinterpreted as
unsigned is enormous, so `icmp uge amount, bits` catches `< 0` and `>= bits`
together. `bits` is the DECLARED width — 32 for an i32, 64 for an i64 — which
is why narrow shifts are intercepted in `compile_narrow_int_binop` before the
generic dispatch, which would have compared against the i64 carrier's 64 and
let every narrow over-shift through.

Narrow `<<` is re-narrowed after the shift (mask, then sign-extend for a
signed type), which is what makes the result representable in the declared
type. `>>` needed only the amount check: its operand reaches the carrier
already sign- or zero-extended from the declared width, so an i64 shift
smears the correct bit and the re-narrowing is a no-op.

COST IS ZERO for a constant amount, verified by DISASSEMBLY rather than
assumed — a six-shift mix function compiles to bare `sar $0x21` / `sar $0x1d`
/ `sar $0x20`, with no guard in the loop and no trap block anywhere in the
binary; LLVM folds every constant-amount check. Kata #9's callgrind slope is
unchanged to the instruction (1,210,924 before and after). Only a runtime
amount pays a compare, and those are exactly the cases that were undefined.

WHAT IS LEFT — the narrow unary-negation leg, and why it was NOT fixed here.
`-(-2147483648i32)` still yields 2147483648, an out-of-range i32, where the
i64 equivalent traps `integer overflow` correctly. Both surfaces agree with
each other today. The interpreter side is a one-line `narrow_oob` call in
`eval_unary`'s Neg arm, but codegen's `compile_unaryop` receives only a value
— it has no declared width to check against, and the span-keyed maps at its
call site (`tensor_typed_exprs` / `column_typed_exprs`) do not carry integer
widths. Fixing only the cheap side would CREATE a run/build divergence where
none currently exists, which is strictly worse than a consistent wrong answer.
So the leg needs the width plumbed to `compile_unaryop` first, and both sides
must land together.

CONSEQUENCE FOR B-2026-08-05-38: the invariant "a narrow-typed value always
fits its declared width" now holds for every operator EXCEPT narrow negation.
That row's widening half is unblocked for the arithmetic and shift surface and
still needs the negation leg (or an explicit carve-out) to be sound in full.

── FIXED, the negation leg — the row's last open item ─────────────────

ALL THREE LEGS ARE NOW CLOSED. The shift legs went at ee551b8; this closes
narrow unary negation, so the invariant the row set out to establish — "a
narrow-typed value always fits its declared width" — holds for EVERY operator
with no carve-out. B-2026-08-05-38's widening half is unblocked in full.

THE PLUMBING THIS ROW SAID WAS NEEDED TURNED OUT NOT TO BE. The previous pass
recorded "codegen's `compile_unaryop` receives only a value — it has no
declared width to check against", and deferred on that basis. That framing was
looking at the wrong site. `-a` is already lowered by `rewrite_unary`
(src/lowering.rs) into `iN.neg(a)`, exactly as `a + b` becomes `iN.add(a, b)`,
so the assoc-call arm in src/codegen/assoc_call.rs ALREADY has the declared
width in hand as `type_name`. The check goes there. `compile_unaryop` never
needed to learn the width, and nothing was threaded through it.

Worth recording as a method note: the deferral was reasoned from the callee's
signature rather than from the lowered AST, and the lowering had already solved
the problem. Checking what the operator actually lowers to would have found
that immediately.

SHAPE: `emit_narrow_range_check(rv, bits, is_unsigned)` extracted verbatim out
of `compile_narrow_int_binop` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) and called from both
sites, so the negate and the binops emit the IDENTICAL trap rather than two
copies that can drift. Signed-only by construction — `rewrite_unary` gates
`Neg` to `Type::Int`, so a narrow UNSIGNED negate never reaches the arm.

INTERPRETER: one `narrow_oob` call added to `eval_unary`'s Neg arm
(src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs), matching the arithmetic arms directly beside it.
Both surfaces landed together, per this row's own requirement — fixing only the
interpreter would have created a run/build divergence where none existed.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par / AOT
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), trap and legal-boundary alike:

    let a: i32 = -2147483648i32; -a    ->  integer overflow   (was 2147483648)
    let a: i32 = -2147483647i32; -a    ->  2147483647         (unchanged)

    i64 minimum                        ->  integer overflow   (already correct)

COST IS ONE NEVER-TAKEN BRANCH, established by DISASSEMBLY rather than
assumed. A negate loop over an i32 compiles to `neg %r8d` / `jo` — LLVM folds
the i64-domain range check into the native 32-bit negate's own overflow flag,
so there is no compare-and-branch pair, just the `jo`. Same shape as the
checked arithmetic already emitted beside it.

the fourth pins the legal boundary, which was already correct, and guards
against OVER-trapping):

  * e2e_narrow_negation_traps_at_declared_width (tests/codegen.rs)

The E2E trap fixture seeds its operand from `env.args().len()` rather than

FOUND WHILE WRITING THE i64 CONTROL, filed separately as B-2026-08-06-13:
`i64::MIN` cannot be written as a literal in ANY spelling (all four probed),
because a negative literal is `Neg(Integer(n))` and 9223372036854775808 does

tracker: src/codegen/synth_drop.rs::emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl -- the subst-driven bare-generic-param reclassification loop, which now promotes String/Vec/VecDeque and Map/Set heads but not a `shared` one
title: a generic wrapper's bare `T` field bound to a SHARED struct leaks 2,560 B / 80 blocks at -O0 (clean at -O2): `Box[T]` at `T = Node` where `Node` is a `shared struct` -- the third head the bare-param rescue loop does not recognise, after String/Vec (fixed B-2026-07-15-11) and Map/Set (fixed B-2026-08-06-1)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found as a WIDENING CONTROL while fixing B-2026-08-06-1, not as a
regression from it. Measured byte-identical before and after that change, which
is what makes it a separate row rather than a loose end of that one.

REPRO, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 karac build`, under valgrind:

    shared struct Node { s: String }
    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    fn sink(b: Box[Node]) -> i64 { let n = b.v; return n.s.len(); }
    fn main() {
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 40 {
            let b = Box { v: Node { s: f"shrv-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer" } };
            let c = b;
            acc = acc + sink(c);
            let b2 = Box { v: Node { s: f"shrv-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer" } };
            let n2 = b2.v;
            acc = acc + n2.s.len();
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> prints 3660 (correct, and matching the interpreter), 2,560 bytes direct
       in 80 blocks + 3,660 indirect in 80 blocks definitely lost, 2 valgrind
       errors. CLEAN at the default -O2 — the usual -O0-only signature for this
       family: at -O2 the rc box is provably dead and LLVM deletes the
       allocation along with the evidence. The leak is in the emitted code
       either way.

MECHANISM, by analogy rather than by instrumentation — stated as the hypothesis
it is. The bare-generic-param rescue loop in `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`
resolves the declared `T` through the struct subst and promotes the result to a
`FieldDrop`. It knows String/Vec/VecDeque (B-2026-07-15-11) and, since
B-2026-08-06-1, Map/Set. A `shared` head matches neither, so the field is
classified no-heap and its rc handle is never dec'd — exactly the shape of the
two rows before it. The 80 blocks over 40 rounds (two per round: the rc box and
its String) fit the two shared handles the fixture creates per iteration.

WHY LOW AND NOT MEDIUM, unlike its two predecessors: it is -O0-only, so a
default `karac build` is unaffected today. That is a statement about the
optimizer, not about the emitted code — any change that makes the handle
observable at -O2 promotes this to the severity the Map row carried.

THE FIX IS NOT SIMPLY ONE MORE ARM, which is why this is filed rather than
folded into B-2026-08-06-1. Adding a `shared` promotion to the rescue loop
without the matching neutralizer arms is exactly the trade that row proved turns
a leak into a double free. `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` DOES already have a
`shared_types` arm (B-2026-07-28-9), and B-2026-08-06-1's head resolution now
makes it reachable for a bare param, so the whole-struct-move side may already
be covered — but `zero_struct_field_move_cap`'s corresponding path and the
rc-inc side of the entry copy both need checking first. Establish the
neutralizer coverage BEFORE adding the promotion, in that order, the way
B-2026-08-06-1 eventually had to.

FIXED 2026-08-06 (0928227). The row's instruction — establish the neutralizer
coverage BEFORE adding the promotion — was the right order, and following it
changed the diagnosis: the defect is NOT one more arm in the drop classifier's
rescue loop, which is where this row pointed.

The gate is `track_struct_var_inst`, which decides whether a struct local gets
the COMBINED drop (value drop + shared-field rc-dec walker) or the value drop
alone. It asked the NAME-ONLY `struct_owns_shared_field`, which reads DECLARED
field types, so `Box[T] { v: T }` at `T = Node` answered `false` and nothing
ever rc-dec'd the box. Confirmed by instrumenting the gate rather than reasoning
about it (the B-2026-08-06-1 lesson, applied first this time): the concrete
`Holder` printed `owns_shared=true`, the generic `Box` printed `owns_shared=false`.

Three sites had to learn the instantiation together, since a drop that dec's a
field the walker cannot see is just a differently-shaped bug:
  (1) `struct_owns_shared_field_subst` — the gate;
  (2) `emit_nested_struct_shared_rc_decs_ex_mono` — the walker, whose every arm
      (direct `shared`, `Option[shared]`, `Vec[shared]`, nested-struct
      recursion) keyed off the erased `T`;
  (3) `emit_vec_elem_struct_with_shared_drop_fn_mono` — the combined drop, whose
      symbol needed mono-suffixing (`Box[Node]` and `Box[Other]` are different
      drops on one cached name) and whose VALUE half would otherwise revert to
      the name-keyed drop and lose B-2026-08-06-1's field frees.

THE PREDICTED TRADE HAPPENED TWICE, and both were fixed by neutralizing the
SOURCE rather than inc'ing the copy — which is what the rc-dec walker's existing
`build_is_null` guard was already built to expect:
  * `zero_struct_field_move_cap` gained a `shared` arm, the peer of the Map/Set
    null-store. Chosen over inc'ing the returned alias because an inc has to be
    threaded onto BOTH the explicit-return and tail paths — they diverge,
    `compile_tail_final_expr` is only reached from `return` when the fn returns
    `Option[shared]` — and an over-inc is a silent leak. Attempted the inc route
    first and abandoned it: instrumentation showed the helper was never reached
    for either spelling.
  * `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` gained a FieldAccess arm. It neutralized an
    Identifier tail and fell through on a FIELD tail, while its function-body
    sibling `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` hands any shape to the same
    suppressor.

THAT SECOND ARM FIXES A PRE-EXISTING BUG WITH NO GENERICS IN IT:
`let x = { let h = Holder { .. }; h.v }` printed 0 instead of 38 on a DEFAULT
-O2 build with 160 valgrind errors. It was latent for the buffer types (a
moved-out Vec/String tail escapes through its own value copy — the same shape
spelled with a String field is clean at HEAD) and became observable only once an
rc handle, which has no such copy, could reach that path. Found because the fix
routed the generic spelling onto it and turned a correct-but-leaking program
into a wrong answer — i.e. the regression check found someone else's bug.

MEASURED over 24 probe programs at -O2 AND -O0, each cross-checked against the
interpreter. Fixed: move-out from a by-value param, from a plain local, a
whole-struct move, a `ref`-param read, the MID field of a multi-field wrapper,
the field returned out of a by-value param, a consuming callee, the never-moved
control, and the block-tail escape in BOTH spellings. Unchanged controls:
String / Vec[shared] / Option[shared] / Map instantiations of the same wrapper,
and every concrete-spelling shape.

TWO RESIDUALS, measured byte-identical before and after and filed rather than
folded in — neither is generic-specific and neither regressed:
  * B-2026-08-06-14 — a shared field RETURNED out of a by-value param is a
    use-after-free in the CONCRETE path at -O2 (still open; the generic
    spelling is clean because the null-store arm reaches its move site).
  * B-2026-08-06-15 — a shared handle escaping a value-position block is never
    dec'd by its consumer binding: 64 B / 2 blocks at -O0, BOTH spellings.
    This row's block-tail arm fixed the use-after-free half of that shape and
    left the leak half.

TESTS: asan_bare_generic_param_shared_field_is_rc_dec_and_neutralized
(memory_sanitizer), e2e_shared_field_moved_out_of_a_value_block_survives_the_frame_drain
(codegen), test_bare_generic_param_shared_field_transfers_the_handle
(interpreter, the oracle). Both codegen tests are STASH-PROVEN RED against the
half each can observe: the ASAN twin fails at HEAD with `LeakSanitizer: 15870
byte(s) leaked in 398 allocation(s)`, the E2E with `left: "114", right: "152"` —
a WRONG ANSWER, which is why an E2E earns its place beside a leak fixture.

TEST-INFRA NOTE worth carrying forward: the ASAN fixture first tripped the
B-2026-08-04-17 vacuity floor at 48 allocations, because its reads were
`.len()`-only and LLVM folded the payloads away at the default -O2. Adding
byte-level `contains` reads took it to 526. A shared-box fixture needs its
PAYLOAD read, not its length — the box surviving is not the same as the box
being observable.

SUITES: non-llvm 8653; codegen E2E 2824; memory_sanitizer 954/0/10 at -O2 and
the -O0 leg matching the quarantine list exactly; cli 574; par_codegen 236;
selfhost_codegen, coro_e2e, disjoint_differential, drop_differential,
shared_ownership_matrix, rc_fallback, ownership 406, example_corpus, spawn_e2e.

fix: 9370f723 (leg B: fresh-temp enum arg registrar asks `enum_drop_switch_does_work`); de8881f8 (leg A: the callee owns a boxed non-struct Option payload)
title: TWO shapes where a heap-BOXED enum payload loses its owner AT A CALL BOUNDARY: (A) [FIXED] a NAMED `Option` binding passed by value has its let-site box drop disarmed by the call site's move-zeroing while the callee's param takes nothing over; (B) [FIXED] a fresh-temp user ENUM passed by value never registered `track_enum_var` at all, because the registrar's gate asked `enum_has_heap_payload` rather than whether the drop switch does any work. 320 B / 10 each
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: both were caught as CONTROLS in the new fixtures written for
B-2026-08-05-7's boxed-payload slice, and both measure IDENTICALLY before and
after that change (320 B / 10 blocks at HEAD and at the fix) -- which is what
makes them a separate row rather than a regression from it. The controls are
kept in those fixtures' doc comments as deliberately-not-covered rather than
deleted, so the gap stays visible where the next reader will be.

LEG A -- a NAMED `Option` binding passed BY VALUE. Reduction, 10 iterations,
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0:

    fn classify(v: Option[Option[i64]]) -> i64 {
        match v {
            Option.Some(Option.Some(x)) => x,
            Option.Some(Option.None) => -1,
            Option.None => -2,
        }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut i: i64 = 0; let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        while i < 10 {
            let bound: Option[Option[i64]] = Option.Some(Option.Some(1));
            acc = acc + classify(bound);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> definitely lost 320 bytes in 10 objects (one 32-byte box per call).

The inner `Option[i64]` is 4 LLVM words against `Option`'s seeded 3-word
payload area, so `coerce_to_payload_words` boxes it and `bound`'s let site
queues a `BoxedEnumDrop`. Passing `bound` by value then runs
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move`, which ZEROES the whole source
slot -- correct for the INLINE payload it was written for (the callee's param
consumption frees that), but for a BOXED payload it disarms the box drop's
`tag == Some` guard while the callee registers nothing (function params do not
register `track_enum_var` -- see its doc). Neither side owns the box.

CONTROLS, both CLEAN, so the shape needs the call: the same binding never
passed (`match bound { … }` in place) is clean, and the FRESH-TEMP form
`classify(Option.Some(Option.Some(42)))` is clean as of B-2026-08-05-7's fix
(the caller registers a box-only drop for it).

LEG B -- a fresh-temp user ENUM passed BY VALUE. Reduction, same 10 iterations:

    enum Wrap { W(Option[String]), N(Option[i64]), Empty }
    fn take(w: Wrap) -> i64 { match w { … Wrap.N(Option.Some(n)) => n, … } }
    fn main() {
        … while i < 10 { acc = acc + take(Wrap.N(Option.Some(2))); … }
    }

    -> definitely lost 320 bytes in 10 objects.

`Wrap` now HAS a drop fn (B-2026-08-05-7 added `EnumDropKind::BoxedOptRes`),
but a fresh temp has no binding, so nothing calls `track_enum_var` for it and
the drop never runs. The NAMED form (`let w = Wrap.N(…); take(w)`) is clean,
which localizes it to the temp rather than to the callee.

WHY THE TWO LEGS ARE ONE ROW: both are "the value crossed a by-value call
boundary and its box drop went with it or was never created". A fix for either
has to answer the same question -- after a by-value move into a param, WHICH
frame owns the box.

THE PRECEDENT ALREADY IN THE TREE ANSWERS "THE CALLEE", and it is the strongest
lead here. `compile_function` already registers a box-only `BoxedEnumDrop` for
an OWNED param of a GENERIC user enum whose monomorph boxes its payload
(`functions.rs`, via `user_enum_boxed_payload_variants` -- filed under this same
B-2026-08-05-7 family). Leg B is that helper's own stated premise being false:
it bails on a non-generic path with "only a generic instantiation can outgrow
its own area", and a NON-generic `Wrap { W(Option[String]) }` outgrows it too,
because the enum-in-enum carve-out sizes the payload at ONE word regardless of
its real width. Relaxing that gate to admit a non-generic enum whose variant
payload is `Option`/`Result` is self-limiting -- for every other payload the
area equals the real width, so the `> area` test cannot fire -- and it would
close leg B on the callee side, symmetric with the generic case rather than a
second convention.

Leg A is the same move one level out: an owned `Option[T]`/`Result[T, E]` PARAM
whose payload is boxed gets no callee-side box drop either (the helper returns
empty for the seeded pair by construction). A callee-side registration would
close leg A AND is likely the same fix the last quarantined fixture needs
(`asan_shared_payload_view_optres_field_call_arg_copy`: `hname(nd.hp)` over
`Option[H]`, H four words against Option's three-word area -- the field
sibling).

CAUTIONS for whoever takes it, both learned the hard way on this family:

  1. A callee-side registration for the SEEDED pair COLLIDES with the
     caller-side fresh-temp arm B-2026-08-05-7 just landed
     (`is_owned_boxed_option_param` in `call_dispatch.rs`, which registers a
     box-only drop for `classify(Some(Some(42)))`). Doing both double-frees.
     Whoever moves ownership to the callee must retract that caller-side arm in
     the same change, and re-run `asan_freshtemp_boxed_option_arg_no_leak`.

  2. A callee-side registration is exposed on the PASSTHROUGH shape
     (`fn id(o: Option[Wide]) -> Option[Wide] { o }`), where the caller keeps
     its own drop because `call_arg_flows_into_return` suppresses the move
     zeroing. The generic-enum precedent carries the same exposure; it should
     be measured rather than assumed benign.

  3. Leg A's caller-side suppressor is SHARED with the INLINE
     `Option[String]`/`Option[Vec]` payload shape (B-2026-07-10-4), where
     zeroing IS required -- there the callee's param consumption frees the
     payload and leaving the source armed double-frees. Any caller-side fix
     must discriminate boxed from inline at that site rather than weaken the
     suppressor wholesale.

LEG B FIXED (see the fix SHA). Row STAYS OPEN for leg A.

The site was the fresh-enum-temp ARGUMENT registrar in
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` -- which already existed and already
called `track_enum_var` for exactly this shape. It just asked the wrong
question: `enum_has_heap_payload`, which is keyed on `is_heap_bearing()` and
therefore answers FALSE for `EnumDropKind::BoxedOptRes`. That kind is not
heap-BEARING by design (the by-value entry-copy must not duplicate its box) yet
its drop switch does free a box, so the two questions had come apart the moment
the kind was introduced.

FIX: a separate predicate, `enum_drop_switch_does_work`, keyed on `!= None` --
the same gate `emit_enum_drop_switch` itself uses, so the two cannot drift --
consulted at that one registrar. Deliberately NOT a widening of
`enum_has_heap_payload`: that predicate ALSO selects `compile_enum_eq`'s
variant-aware comparison path, and changing which enums take it would change
`==` semantics for types that only needed an owner. Five other
`track_enum_var` gates still read the old predicate and were left alone --
none is a measured leak, and each is its own ownership argument.

MEASURED: the reduction goes 320 B / 10 -> 0. The other direction is checked
too, since a second owner here would double-free rather than leak: the NAMED
form (`let w = Wrap.N(…); take(w)`), the whole-value move, the passthrough
callee, a `Vec[Wrap]`, and a `.clone()` are all still clean. -O0 leg 950 passed
/ 1 known failure, matching the quarantine list exactly.

LEG A IS UNCHANGED and is now the whole of this row: a NAMED `Option` binding
passed by value still leaks its box (`let bound = Some(Some(1));
classify(bound);`, 320 B / 10). Its caution above still stands -- the
suppressor it needs is shared with the INLINE payload shape, where zeroing is
required.

── LEG A: THE CALLER-SIDE ROUTE IS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT (2026-08-06) ──

Implemented, measured, and REVERTED. The refutation is the deliverable: it
removes the cheapest-looking option and names the counterexample class.

WHAT WAS TRIED, and it is the fix caution 3 points at: at the by-value
user-fn ARG site only (`call_dispatch.rs`, the `!borrow_skip &&
!call_arg_flows_into_return` arm), SKIP the move-zeroing when the binding is
boxed-only. Fail-closed on two further conditions — not also inline (the
callee consumes an inline payload, so that shape must keep zeroing), and only
the SEEDED `Option`/`Result` pair (a generic user enum's owned param does get
a callee-side box drop, caution 1).

IT FIXES THE REDUCTION AND PASSES EVERY FIXTURE:
  * leg A goes 320 B / 10 -> 0 at `-O0`, output unchanged;
  * memory_sanitizer 956 pass / 0 fail at the DEFAULT opt level AND at
    `-O0` — the whole quarantine list stays empty;
  * a 7-shape control matrix at both opt levels (never-passed, fresh temp,
    passthrough, inline `Option[String]`, boxed+inline `Option[Option[String]]`,
    user enum, struct-field move) shows no new leak and no new invalid free.

AND IT IS STILL WRONG. `tests/selfhost_parser_items.rs::selfhost_parser_matches_rust_parser_items`
SIGSEGVs with it applied — A/B'd against the stashed tree, which passes. The
self-hosted item parser is the only thing in the suite that exercises the
counterexample:

  THE PREMISE "no param takes the box over" IS TRUE, AND INSUFFICIENT. The box
  can still escape through the callee's RETURN VALUE inside an aggregate:

      fn wrap(o: Option[Block]) -> Node { Node { body: o } }

  The param registers no drop — but the returned `Node` now owns the box, and
  its consumer frees it. `call_arg_flows_into_return` does NOT see this: it
  detects only a DIRECT passthrough (`fn id(o) -> o`), not a move into a
  returned aggregate. So the caller's retained drop is a second owner.

  The zeroing was doing DOUBLE DUTY that this row's leg-A analysis missed —
  it covers both "the callee consumes an inline payload" (the documented
  reason) and "the param escapes into the callee's result" (undocumented, and
  the one that bites).

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX DIRECTION: any caller-side answer needs escape
analysis of the callee's param, which is strictly more than
`call_arg_flows_into_return` provides. The CALLEE-side registration this row
already recommends does not need it — the callee knows whether it moved the
param out, and the existing move-suppression machinery disarms its own drop
when it does. So caution 1's route (register callee-side, retract the
caller-side fresh-temp arm in the same change) is now the ONLY route standing,
not merely the preferred one.

REUSABLE, and it is the reason this was caught: `selfhost_parser_items` is the
suite's sharpest ownership oracle. The 7-shape hand-written matrix and BOTH
memory_sanitizer legs were green on an unsound change; only the self-hosted
parser — a real program with real aggregate returns — found it. Run it before
trusting any ownership-convention change, and A/B any failure against a
stashed tree rather than assuming a flake.

TWO PRE-EXISTING DEFECTS FOUND BY THE CONTROL MATRIX, both A/B-confirmed
identical before and after the reverted change, so NEITHER is caused by it:

  1. PASSTHROUGH DOUBLE FREE at `-O0`, and this is caution 2's own shape
     measured rather than assumed:

         fn id(o: Option[Option[i64]]) -> Option[Option[i64]] { o }
         let bound = Option.Some(Option.Some(3)); let back = id(bound); …

     aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (valgrind:
     `Invalid free()`), 10 iterations, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`. CLEAN at the
     default `-O2`. Caution 2 warned a callee-side registration would be
     "exposed on the PASSTHROUGH shape" and said it "should be measured rather
     than assumed benign" — measured, and the shape is ALREADY broken with no
     callee-side registration anywhere. Whoever takes caution 1's route must
     fix this first or they will inherit it and think they caused it. Filed
     separately.

  2. STRUCT-FIELD MOVE LEAK at `-O0`: a boxed `Option` binding moved into a
     struct-literal field (`let bound = Some(Some(5)); Holder { o: bound }`)
     loses 320 B / 10. Clean at `-O2`. Different site from leg A — that
     suppressor (`exprs.rs`) was not touched — and the destination there DOES
     become an owner, so this one is a missing transfer rather than a missing
     retraction.

── AND THE CALLEE-SIDE ROUTE IS REFUTED TOO (2026-08-06, same session) ──

With the blocker (B-2026-08-06-21, the passthrough double free) fixed by
fe7fea77, caution 1's route — "register callee-side, retract the caller-side
fresh-temp arm in the same change" — became implementable. It was implemented,
measured, and REVERTED.

WHAT WAS BUILT, and it is a two-line change plus a retraction:
  * `functions.rs`, beside the generic-user-enum arm: also iterate
    `boxed_enum_payload_variants` (the SEEDED-pair sibling that knows Option's
    3-word and Result's 5-word areas) and register the same BOX-ONLY
    `BoxedEnumDrop` on the owned param. This sits INSIDE the existing
    `result_shared_nonescaping_param_names` guard.
  * `call_dispatch.rs`: delete B-2026-08-05-7's caller-side fresh-temp arm and
    its now-dead `is_owned_boxed_option_param` helper.

THE ESCAPE GUARD IS THE POINT, and it delivered. It is exactly the analysis the
caller lacks, so the shapes that refuted the caller-side attempt all pass here:

    leg A reduction        320 B / 10 at -O0  ->  CLEAN at -O0 AND -O2
    fresh temp             CLEAN  (callee now covers what the retraction removed)

64 B / 2), re-attributed here after reduction. That row guessed twice about it

caller-retains law (it did not move when that row closed), then that it was the
FIELD sibling of B-2026-08-06-9 leg A (the field form is clean). Both guesses

THE ISOLATION, 10 iterations each at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, four probes over the
same two structs:

    struct H { label: String, k: i64 }
    struct Node { hp: Option[H], k: i64 }
    // `H` is four LLVM words against Option's seeded three-word payload area,
    // so `coerce_to_payload_words` heap-boxes it: 32 bytes per Some.

  f1  callee returns `x.k`,     label a LITERAL       -> CLEAN
  f7  callee returns `x.k`,     label `.to_string()`  -> CLEAN
  f8  callee returns `x.label`, label a LITERAL       -> LEAKS 288 B / 9
  f5  callee returns `x.label`, label `.to_string()`  -> LEAKS 288 B / 9

The caller is byte-identical across all four (`let nd = Node { hp: Some(H { … }),
k: 7 }; hname(nd.hp)`). Only the CALLEE's arm changes. So:

  * it is NOT the heap-ness of the payload (f1 vs f7 clean, f8 vs f5 leak),
  * it is NOT the field-argument form (f1/f7 pass `nd.hp` and are clean),
  * it is NOT the shared enum -- the original fixture wraps `Node` in
    `shared enum E { V(Node) }`, and dropping that wrapper reproduces the leak
    unchanged (288 B / 9 either way).

WHAT IS LEFT: the callee's arm MOVES A FIELD OUT of the deboxed payload
(`Some(x) => x.label`). Returning a scalar read from the same payload
(`Some(x) => x.k`) is clean.

WHY THAT SHOULD NOT MATTER, and where to look. `Node`'s struct drop owns the
box: the `OptionInline` classification in `emit_struct_drop_synthesis` admits an
`Option[<user struct>]` field (`option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok`), and

runs the inner drop, then frees the box. f1/f7 prove that path fires. The callee
receives a shallow copy of the four-word Option struct, SHARING the caller's box
pointer, and its arm's move-out suppression then disarms something the CALLER
still needs. The candidate sites are the payload move-out suppressors in
`control_flow_match.rs` (`suppress_inline_option_agg_payload_cleanup` and the
boxed-view family), which were written for a payload whose source slot the
callee owns -- not for one reached through a box the caller owns.

MEASURE BEFORE FIXING, specifically: does the callee write through the BOX
POINTER (wiping a cap/tag the caller's `karac_drop_Option_H` later reads), or
does it retract an action? The first is a shared-storage bug and the fix is to
scope the write to the callee's own copy; the second is a registration bug. The
two have opposite fixes, and this family has already spent three diagnoses on
guesses.

DISTINCT FROM B-2026-08-06-9 leg A, which is the same family one step over and
should NOT be folded in: there a NAMED `Option[H]` local passed by value leaks
(320 B / 10) with a callee that returns only a SCALAR -- so it survives the
variable that drives this row. Its control (the same binding matched in place
rather than passed) is clean. Fixing either does not obviously fix the other.

MECHANISM ESTABLISHED, from IR that matches the built binary. The row's own
"measure before fixing" question -- does the callee write THROUGH the box
pointer, or is an action retracted -- is answered: NEITHER side writes through
the box, and the disarm is on the CALLER.

  f7 (clean): the caller's `nd.hp` tag stays 1, so `__karac_drop_struct_Node`
      -> `karac_drop_Option_H` deboxes, runs `__karac_drop_struct_H` and frees
      the box. That path is correct and fires.
  f8 (leaks): the caller emits `%opt.move.tag = getelementptr … ; store i64 0`
      into `nd.hp` BEFORE the call. `karac_drop_Option_H`'s `tag == 1` guard
      then fails and the box -- and every buffer inside it -- is orphaned.

The suppressor is doing what it was written for: the callee CONSUMES the
payload, so the source must not free it. That is right for an INLINE payload,
where the callee's own cleanup frees what it consumed. For a BOXED payload the
callee frees nothing -- it deboxes into a LOCAL alloca and moves the field out
of THAT copy.

THE NAIVE FIX TURNS THE LEAK INTO A DOUBLE FREE, and this is the part worth
carrying forward. Simply not zeroing the tag leaves the caller's drop running
`__karac_drop_struct_H(box_ptr)` over the box's ORIGINAL `{ptr, len, cap}` --
whose cap is still live, because the callee zeroed the cap in its local `%x`
and never through `%enumbox.p`. The caller would then free the buffer the
RETURNED String now owns. Confirmed in the emitted IR: the callee's only
move-out store is `getelementptr … ptr %x` -> `store i64 0, ptr
%sfld.move.cap`, and there is no `free` anywhere in the callee.

SO THE FIX HAS TO MAKE THE CONSUMPTION VISIBLE IN THE BOX -- the callee's
move-out zeroing the cap THROUGH the box pointer (shared storage the caller
still reads) rather than in its private copy, after which the caller's drop can
stay armed: it frees the box and skips the moved buffer. Equivalently, hand the
box to the callee. What must NOT happen is the caller silently dropping its
registration, which is the current behaviour.

leak into a different bug, which is why the row's own "measure before fixing"

      consumer registers its own free -- is true for the INLINE classes and
      false here: no parameter registers a box drop (caller-retains), and the

      bind sites) lets both move-out neutralizers in
      `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` repeat their zero into the box:

registration is gated on `pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`, i.e. only

title: an owned boxed-payload enum param that ESCAPES -- returned, or forwarded to another by-value param -- is freed by the callee anyway: `fn id(o: Opt[String]) -> Opt[String] { o }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` at the DEFAULT -O2, and the forwarding form SIGSEGVs at -O0
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-05-7 rather than reopening it: that row was closed
(70c15e83 + b359f437) after its last quarantine entry cleared, and this is a
distinct defect in one of the mechanisms it added, still live at de6dfe49.

    enum Opt[T] { Yes(T), No }
    fn get(o: Opt[String], d: i64) -> i64 { match o { Opt.Yes(s) => s.len(), Opt.No => d } }
    fn ident(o: Opt[String]) -> Opt[String] { o }          // returns the box
    fn fwd(o: Opt[String]) -> i64 { get(o, -1) }           // forwards the box

  ident  -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2, at -O2 AND -O0
  fwd    -> freed by both callees, then SIGSEGV (exit 139) at -O0
  get    -> correct, and must stay so: this is the shape the drop is FOR

`Opt[String]` packs a 3-word payload into the erased 1-word area, so
`coerce_to_payload_words` heap-boxes it and the owned-param registration
(compile_function + compile_mono_function) queues a scope-exit `BoxedEnumDrop`.
It queued one for EVERY owned param, including the two above that hand the box
on to someone else.

NOT MASKED AT -O2, unlike most of B-2026-08-05-7's population. The box is live
memory whichever way the pass pipeline goes, so there is no dead allocation for
LLVM to delete and no second free of something that never happened -- the
ordinary `karac build` aborts. That also makes it cheap to gate: a plain
codegen E2E catches it, no ASAN needed
(`e2e_boxed_enum_param_escape_no_double_free`, asserted strictly so an abort
cannot pass as a skip).

FIX: gate the registration on `crate::result_escape::nonescaping_param_names`
-- the escape walk the `Result[shared]` param arm has run since B-2026-07-12-24,
type-agnostic despite its Result-shaped name (a param qualifies when every use
is a match/if-let scrutinee, or it is unused). A forwarded or returned param
falls out and stays unregistered, so the terminal consumer's free remains the
only one and the chain self-balances with no call-site suppression -- exactly
the argument that arm already makes for its own case. The mono site computes
the set locally rather than reading the shared field: a mono body is compiled
INLINE inside its caller's, so that field still holds the CALLER's set there.

is the same trap from the other side. A non-generic enum whose payload is

tracker: ROOT CAUSE IS DEEPER THAN THE SPAN CLOBBER — see the ATTEMPTED FIX section. `impl[T] Box[T]` methods are declared ONCE at the erased layout (`@Box.take({ i64 }) -> i64`), so they are not monomorphized per instantiation the way `fn take[T]` free functions are. The span-clobbered literal layout (src/codegen/types_lowering.rs::struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr) is only the first of two mismatches.
title: a GENERIC struct LITERAL used directly as a METHOD RECEIVER cannot be built: `Box { v: <String> }.take()` passes `karac check`, runs correctly under the interpreter, and then fails `karac build` with an LLVM verifier error -- the literal lowers at the ERASED base layout `{ i64 }` because the outer method call's span CLOBBERS the literal's instantiation record
detail:
SHAPE, minimal and complete:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    impl[T] Box[T] { fn take(self) -> T { self.v } }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        println(Box { v: "payload-past-inline-width-here".repeat(n) }.take().len());
    }

    karac check          -> All checks passed.
    karac run --interp   -> 30            (correct)
    karac build          -> error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
                            "Invalid InsertValueInst operands!
                               %field = insertvalue { i64 } undef,
                                        { ptr, i64, i64 } %rep.load, 0"

So it is a LOUD failure, not a miscompile, and the workaround is one line
(bind the literal to a local first). That is why this is medium and not high.

ISOLATION -- six variants, each one condition away from the failing one:

    named receiver   `let b = Box { .. }; b.take()`        check ok  interp 30  AOT 30
    LITERAL receiver `Box { .. }.take()`                   check ok  interp 30  AOT FAIL
    literal receiver, field is i64                         check ok  interp 1   AOT 1
    literal receiver, NON-generic struct                   check ok  interp 30  AOT 30
    literal receiver, `ref self`, body ignores the field   check ok  interp 7   AOT FAIL
    same literal as a FREE-FN ARGUMENT `take(Box { .. })`  check ok  interp 30  AOT 30

It needs exactly two conditions -- a GENERIC struct, and a literal in RECEIVER
position with a WIDE instantiated field. It does NOT depend on the self mode
(`self` and `ref self` both fail) nor on the method body touching the field at
all (the `ref self` variant returns a constant 7 and still fails).

MECHANISM, MEASURED rather than inferred. Instrumenting
`struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr`'s span lookup on the two literals that differ
only in position:

    free-fn arg (BUILDS)     span=(122,53)   rec=Some("Box[1 args]")
    method receiver (FAILS)  span=(131,53)   rec=None

Same literal, same length. In the receiver case the record is not WRONG, it is
ABSENT. The chain:

  1. the parser gives a `MethodCall` its RECEIVER's span (the same defect
     B-2026-08-05-28 hit from another direction), so the literal and the call
     share one `expr_types` key;
  2. the method call's type wins that key -- here `i64`, from `.len()`;
  3. lowering.rs builds `enum_inst_type_exprs` by filtering `tc.expr_types` for
     `Named { args } if !args.is_empty()`. A primitive `i64` is not `Named`, so
     the entry is DROPPED ENTIRELY rather than overwritten with something
     wrong;
  4. `struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr` finds nothing, `mono_struct_type_from_
     active_subst` also returns None (there is no active monomorph subst -- we
     are in `main`), so `compile_struct_init` falls back to the pre-built
     all-i64 base layout `{ i64 }`;
  5. inserting a `{ptr,i64,i64}` String into `{ i64 }` fails LLVM verification.

EVERY VARIANT FOLLOWS FROM THAT, which is what makes the mechanism credible:
  * named receiver -- the literal is a `let` RHS with its own uncontested span,
    so the record survives;
  * i64 field -- the erased base layout is COINCIDENTALLY correct at `T = i64`,
    so the missing record costs nothing;
  * non-generic struct -- no instantiation is needed at all;
  * free-fn argument -- the `Call` node has its own span, so no clobber.

AND A THIRD, PREDICTED-THEN-CONFIRMED CASE. If the method returns a type that
IS `Named`-with-args, step 3 no longer drops the entry -- it overwrites it with
the RETURN type. Probed with `fn one(self) -> Vec[T]`: the record then holds
`Vec[String]`, `mono_struct_type("Vec", ..)` returns None because `Vec` is not
a user struct, and the build fails the same way. So the failure survives both
branches of the filter; a surviving entry just fails one step later.

RELATED, SEEN WHILE PROBING, NOT PART OF THIS ROW:
  * `impl[T] Box[T] { fn id(self) -> Box[T] { self } }` -- returning `self`
    from a generic impl is rejected at TYPECHECK with
    "expected 'Box<T>', found 'Box'" (note the `<T>` spelling in a language
    whose generics are `[T]`). Separate surface, not filed yet.
  * the same chained-receiver shape with the literal returning `Box[T]` fails
    AOT differently -- "codegen: cannot resolve field 'v' on this receiver
    (its type was not ...)" -- consistent with the same span clobber losing the
    chain's type, but not separately isolated.

FIX DIRECTION, in increasing order of blast radius:
  1. give the struct-literal path a span-INDEPENDENT way to recover its
     instantiation. The field-init expressions are sub-expressions with their
     OWN uncontested spans, and their types bind the struct's type params
     directly -- this is the same move that closed B-2026-08-05-28 (add a
     span-free signal rather than fight the clobber);
  2. record struct-literal instantiations in a table written ONLY from
     `StructLiteral` nodes, so a method call cannot clobber it (mirrors the
     existing `concrete_named_type_exprs` complement);
  3. give `MethodCall` its own span in the parser. That is the real defect, and
     it has now produced two rows; but many span-keyed tables are calibrated to
     today's behaviour, so it is not a contained change.

METHOD NOTE. The first detector tried here counted `movslq` in the disassembly
as a proxy for a different question and was WRONG -- those were jump tables in
inlined `println` machinery. Caught before it reached a claim, unlike the two
false controls on B-2026-08-06-2. The instrumented span dump above is the
evidence this row rests on; nothing here is read off a proxy.

── ATTEMPTED FIX, REVERTED — AND IT RESIZED THE ROW (same session) ──

Fix direction 1 was implemented and MEASURED, then reverted unlanded. What it
found is worth more than the patch was.

WHAT WAS BUILT: a span-free fallback in `struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr` that
recovers a generic struct literal's instantiation from its OWN FIELD
EXPRESSIONS (which are sub-expressions with uncontested spans) when the
span-keyed record is missing or unusable. Fail-closed at every step: struct
literals only, no spread, only a field whose DECLARED type is exactly a bare
generic param, every param must bind to a non-empty name.

FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG, and the reason generalizes: it used
`infer_arg_elem_te` alone, which resolves an identifier or a literal but yields
an EMPTY name for a METHOD CALL. `Box { v: "…".repeat(n) }` — a fresh heap
value built inline — is precisely the shape the fallback exists for, so the
helper returned None on every case it was written to fix. Instrumented output:
`DBG slmt struct=Box param=T inferred=""`. A chain
(`enum_inst_type_exprs` -> `concrete_named_type_exprs` -> `string_typed_exprs`
-> `infer_arg_elem_te`) resolves it.

WITH THAT IN PLACE THE LITERAL LOWERS CORRECTLY — and the build STILL fails,
one step later:

    Call parameter type does not match function signature!
      %__urecv_tmp_1 = load { { ptr, i64, i64 } }, ptr %__urecv_tmp
      %call = call i64 @Box.take({ { ptr, i64, i64 } } %__urecv_tmp_1)
                        ^ callee declared { i64 } -> i64

So the receiver aggregate is now right and the CALLEE is wrong: `@Box.take` is
emitted ONCE, at the ERASED base layout, for every instantiation. An
`impl[T] Box[T]` method is NOT monomorphized the way a `fn take[T]` free
function is — which is also why the free-function form (v6) was clean all
along, and why the row's isolation table shows every failing variant going
through an impl-block method.

CONSEQUENCE — SEVERITY medium -> high. The row was filed as a span-keyed
lookup gap with a one-line workaround. It is actually a MISSING
MONOMORPHIZATION for generic impl-block methods, of which the span clobber is
a downstream symptom. The workaround (bind the literal to a local) works only
because that path happens to keep both sides consistently erased; it is not
evidence the layout is right.

WHY IT WAS REVERTED RATHER THAN LANDED: the patch makes NO currently-failing
program build correctly. It fixes exactly one probe variant — a `ref self`
method whose body ignores the field and returns a constant — which proves
nothing about layout correctness, and converts the other three shapes from one
LLVM verifier error into a different one. Landing that would add code and
change an error message without moving any program from broken to working.

WHAT THE NEXT ATTEMPT SHOULD START FROM, so the measurement is not redone:
  * the literal-side fallback is a REAL and separable piece and is known to
    work (the receiver aggregate is correctly shaped with it in place); it is
    just not sufficient alone. It is worth re-landing TOGETHER with the callee
    side, not before it.
  * the callee side is the actual work: `impl[T] S[T]` methods need
    per-instantiation monomorphs, keyed and mangled like `compile_generic_call`
    does for free functions.
  * verify with the six-variant table in this row, and treat the `ref self`
    variant as a NON-oracle — its body must be changed to read the field
    before it proves anything.

── FIXED bbb6a9bf — AND THE ROW'S RECORDED DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG ──

The re-classification above ("a MISSING MONOMORPHIZATION for generic impl-block
methods") does not survive measurement. `impl[T] S[T]` methods ARE
monomorphized: a program using `Box[String]` and `Box[i64]` through NAMED
receivers emits `Box.take$i64` AND `Box.take$struct` and runs correctly, and two
instantiations coexist with no mangle collision. The single erased emission the
previous attempt saw was a SYMPTOM of the lost span record, not a separate gap
— with the record restored the failing case emits
`Box.take$struct$T_ct_String` and calls it.

WHY THE PREVIOUS ATTEMPT STALLED, which the note above got right in substance:
TWO consumers read the one missing record, and it only fixed the first.

  1. the literal's own layout, via `struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr`, which fell
     back to the pre-built erased base layout `{ i64 }`;
  2. the CALLEE selection. `materialize_user_method_receiver` spills a
     non-identifier receiver into a synth local and re-enters dispatch with an
     Identifier; the generic-method mono arm then reads `enum_inst_var_types`
     to pick the monomorph. Only `var_type_names` was seeded, so it saw a bare
     `Box`. `let b = Box { .. }; b.take()` works purely because the let-site
     seeds that same record (stmts.rs).

Fix either alone and the verifier error just moves — a correctly shaped
`{ { ptr, i64, i64 } }` receiver handed to a callee still declared `{ i64 }`,
which is exactly the second error the previous attempt hit and read as a
missing monomorph. Both sites now recover from the literal's own FIELD
INITIALIZERS, which are sub-expressions with uncontested spans.

Fail-closed, because a WRONG instantiation silently lowers a struct at another
type's layout and is worse than none: struct literals only, no spread, the
struct must be generic, EVERY param must be pinned by a field whose DECLARED
type is exactly that bare param, and every recovered argument must carry a
non-empty type name. A param reachable only through a container field
(`xs: Vec[T]`) is left to the annotation path (B-2026-07-11-31).

Verified against this row's six-variant table plus the `Pair`/second-field and
`ref self` shapes: all build and match the interpreter.
`e2e_generic_struct_literal_as_method_receiver` carries the table and is red
against the pre-fix compiler.

TWO SHAPES FOUND WHILE ISOLATING, SPLIT OUT RATHER THAN FOLDED IN — this row

  * B-2026-08-06-19 — a chained field access on a generic method's RETURN
    (`w.take().f`) fails where `let x = w.take(); x.f` builds. Same span

  * B-2026-08-06-20 — two instantiations of one generic struct reached through a

fix: <this commit>
title: `i64::MIN` cannot be WRITTEN as a literal in any spelling -- `-9223372036854775808i64` is a parse error (`Invalid integer literal`), because a negative literal parses as `Neg(Integer(n))` and the POSITIVE half must fit i64, which i64::MIN's does not. The value is reachable only by arithmetic (`-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64`). Same argument applies to every width's minimum, but only i64 is actually unreachable: a narrow minimum's positive half still fits the i64 carrier.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the i64 CONTROL case for B-2026-08-06-7's
narrow-negation regression test -- the test wanted `-9223372036854775808i64`
as the operand that already trapped correctly, and it would not parse.

MEASURED, all four spellings, `karac run --interp`:

    let a: i64 = -9223372036854775808i64;     parse error at the literal
    let a: i64 = -9223372036854775808;        parse error
    let a = -9223372036854775808i64;          parse error
    let a: i64 = (-9223372036854775808i64);   parse error

Every one reports `Expected expression, found Error("Invalid integer literal")`
with the column on the literal, so this is the LEXER rejecting the digits
before the parser ever sees the unary minus.

MECHANISM, and it is the same design note codegen already documents. A negative
literal is `Neg(Integer(n))` with `n` POSITIVE -- src/codegen/exprs.rs says so
explicitly ("Negative integer literals parse as `Neg(Integer(n))` and the
typechecker range-validates them as a UNIT"). That constant-folds correctly for
every value whose positive half is representable. i64::MIN is the one value
where it is not: 9223372036854775808 > i64::MAX, so the lexer rejects it as an
invalid i64 literal and the fold never happens.

WHY ONLY i64. A narrow minimum survives because the positive half is checked
against the i64 CARRIER, not the declared width -- `-2147483648i32` parses
fine (2147483648 fits i64) and the typechecker validates the negated unit
against i32. Only at the carrier's own width does the positive half run out of
room. u64::MAX is unaffected (no sign, fits the unsigned range).

SEVERITY LOW, deliberately. It is a write-ability gap, not a wrong answer:
nothing miscompiles, and the value is reachable as `-9223372036854775807i64 -
1i64` (which does NOT trap -- the result is representable). The cost is that
the most natural spelling of a common constant is a parse error, and the
message ("Invalid integer literal") does not hint at the workaround.

SHAPE OF A FIX, not attempted here: either lex the digit string into a u64 and
let the parser fold `Neg` before range-validating (so the UNIT is checked, as
the typechecker already claims to do), or special-case the exact i64::MIN
magnitude when it is immediately preceded by unary minus. The first is the
principled one and matches how Rust resolves the same problem.

WORKAROUND for anyone hitting it today: `-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64`.
B-2026-08-06-7's interpreter regression test uses exactly that and says why.

── CORRECTION, before the fix notes: THIS ROW OVERSTATED THE IMPACT ───

The title says the value "is reachable only by arithmetic
(`-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64`)". THAT IS WRONG, and it was wrong when
filed. `i64.MIN` is an existing primitive const and has been all along —
`tests/interpreter.rs::test_interp_primitive_const_i64_min` pins it, and it
was verified again here on interp and JIT (`let x = i64.MIN` prints
-9223372036854775808 on both). `u64.MAX` works the same way.

Found while writing this row's own regression test, by noticing the
neighbouring pre-existing test. The error came from probing four LITERAL
spellings, concluding "unwritable", and generalising that to "unreachable"
without checking the const surface at all.

What survives the correction: writing the literal — the spelling every other
language accepts and the one a reader reaches for first — was a parse error,
which is a real gap worth closing. What does NOT survive: any suggestion the
value was inaccessible. Severity stays LOW; the justification for LOW is now
"a workaround existed and was idiomatic", not "you had to compute it".

── FIXED ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MECHANISM. The lexer parsed the digit string straight into i64 and rejected
anything that did not fit, so the magnitude never reached a place that could
decide what to do with it. It now hands an out-of-i64-range magnitude up as
`Token::IntegerOutOfRange(u64, suffix)` (all four radix paths — decimal, hex,
binary, octal), and the PARSER decides.

WHY THE PARSER AND NOT THE LEXER, which is the whole design point: the lexer
cannot tell a unary minus from a binary one. `x - 9223372036854775808i64` and
`-9223372036854775808i64` differ only in context, and folding the sign in the
lexer would silently turn the first into `x + 2^63`. The parser knows, because
it is holding the `Token::Minus` prefix arm when it peeks. Exactly
`9223372036854775808` under a unary minus folds to a single, already-negative
`ExprKind::Integer(i64::MIN)`; every other path through
`Token::IntegerOutOfRange` is an error.

THE FOLD, not just the value, is what makes it work downstream. A surviving
`Unary { Neg, Integer(..) }` would re-negate i64::MIN and overflow again at
whichever backend folded it. Emitting one already-negative literal node means
the typechecker's range validation, codegen's constant fold, and the
interpreter's Neg arm all see a plain in-range literal and need no special
case. Zero downstream changes.

VERIFIED, all five spellings on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par
/ AOT KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), identical output:

    -9223372036854775808i64        -9223372036854775808
    -9223372036854775808           -9223372036854775808
    -9223372036854775808  (inferred)
    (-9223372036854775808i64)      -9223372036854775808
    -0x8000000000000000i64         -9223372036854775808   <- hex too

plus `a == -9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64` -> true, which is the check that
the fold produced the RIGHT value rather than merely a parseable one.

STILL REJECTED, deliberately, and tested as such — these are the cases a
sign-folding lexer would have broken:
    9223372036854775808i64            bare, no minus
    -9223372036854775809i64           one past the negative bound
    y - 9223372036854775808i64        BINARY minus, differs only by context
    99999999999999999999999999i64     past u64 as well; keeps the lexer error

DIAGNOSTIC. The old message was the lexer's bare "Invalid integer literal".
It now names the magnitude, the i64 maximum, and the one legal negative
spelling.

SCOPE HELD, and the discarded attempt is worth recording. The same mechanism
looked like it would make the upper half of u64 writable too (`u64.MAX` as a
literal), and it was implemented — but every integer rides an i64 carrier
downstream, so the literal arrives as a wrapped NEGATIVE value and the
typechecker rejects it: "negative integer literal -1 cannot initialize
unsigned type 'u64'". Making that work is a TYPECHECKER change, not a parser
one. Reverted rather than half-built, and filed as B-2026-08-06-16. The parser
error message is explicit that a `u64` suffix does not help, so nobody is
sent down that path by the diagnostic.

TESTS:
  * test_i64_min_literal_folds_to_a_single_integer_node (tests/parser.rs) —
    asserts the NODE SHAPE, not just that it parses, across all five spellings
  * test_magnitude_above_i64_max_without_unary_minus_is_an_error (parser.rs)
  * test_i64_min_literal_evaluates_to_i64_min (tests/interpreter.rs)
