title: the envelope chain is owned only at the LET site: passing a boxed-chain enum by value to an owned param leaks 320 B/10, and moving it into a struct literal or pushing it into a `Vec` leaks BOTH envelopes (320 + 320)
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-07-6, which gave `CleanupAction::BoxedEnumDrop` a `deeper_tags` chain at the LET site only. These three sites were measured IDENTICAL before and after that fix -- they are the deliberate residue, not a regression from it. SHAPES, all `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, 10 iterations, all clean at `-O2` where the envelopes fold away: (a) OWNED PARAM -- 320 B / 10 definitely lost, 0 indirectly. fn take(b: Option[Option[Option[i64]]]) -> i64 { match b { Option.Some(Option.Some(Option.Some(x))) => x, _ => 0 } } ... let b: Option[Option[Option[i64]]] = Option.Some(Option.Some(Option.Some(n + i))); acc = acc + take(b); One envelope leaks, not two, which localizes it: the caller's let-site registration is correctly disarmed by the by-value move, and the callee's param registration goes through `functions.rs` rather than the let site, so it carries an EMPTY chain. (b) MOVE INTO A STRUCT LITERAL -- 320 B definitely + 320 B indirectly. struct Holder { b: Option[Option[Option[i64]]] } ... let h: Holder = Holder { b: b }; (c) PUSH INTO A `Vec` -- 320 B definitely + 320 B indirectly. let mut v: Vec[Option[Option[Option[i64]]]] = Vec.new(); v.push(b); (b) and (c) lose BOTH envelopes rather than one, which is a different failure from (a): the destination becomes the owner and registers a single-box free, so the outer envelope is freed once and the chain below it is never walked at all. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN ROW RATHER THAN A WIDENING OF -6. The let site is the only one that has the declared `TypeExpr` the chain is derived from AND a measurement behind it. (a) needs the param's declared type at `compile_function`; (b) and (c) need the DESTINATION's element type, which is a different question again -- the struct field's / Vec's -- and neither destination currently knows it is taking over a chain. Doing all three from one derivation is how this family has produced double frees before (see B-2026-08-06-9's two refuted routes, where a registration that looked symmetric turned out to be a second owner). SEVERITY LOW for the same reason -6 was: `-O2` is unaffected, so no ordinary `karac build` leaks. It is `-O0`-only, and the `-O0` leg (B-2026-08-04-17) is where it shows. START HERE: (a) is the cheapest and the most contained -- `functions.rs` already resolves the param's monomorphized `TypeExpr` for the owned-param `BoxedEnumDrop` registration, so it is the same two-line shape -6 used, with `nested_box_deeper_tag_chain` called on the payload. Do NOT batch it with (b) and (c); their owner question is genuinely different and answering it wrongly double-frees rather than leaks. CONTROL that must stay clean through any fix here, and it is in `asan_direct_boxed_enum_chain_frees_every_envelope` already: a heap `String` interior under a two-envelope chain. The walk frees envelopes; the interior has its own owner. Widening past that boundary is what B-2026-08-06-32 did, and it aborted with a glibc double free at both opt levels. ── LEG (a) FIXED d5cfa3c8; THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS OF (b) AND (c) WAS WRONG ── LEG (a), the owned param, is closed and was exactly as cheap as this row predicted. `functions.rs`'s seeded-pair arm now derives `nested_box_deeper_tag_chain` from the param's monomorphized payload and passes it to `track_boxed_enum_var_with_chain`. 320 B / 10 -> clean at `-O0`, and the fixture is `asan_owned_param_boxed_enum_chain_frees_every_envelope`. WHY THAT ARM WAS SAFE TO WIDEN, and it is the pre-fix MEASUREMENT that says so rather than the argument: the callee is already the owner of the outermost envelope there, and the deeper ones live inside it, so nothing else can reach them once it frees the box they hang off. The caller cannot compete, because its let-site registration is disarmed at the by-value move by `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` -- which is why the failure was a LEAK of one envelope and not a double free of it. Had the caller still been armed, the same widening would have produced the opposite bug. THE TWO ESCAPE CONTROLS ARE IN THE FIXTURE for a reason this arm's own comment records: written without an escape guard, the owned-param registration double-freed at both opt levels and then SIGSEGV'd at `-O0` on a RETURNED param and a FORWARDED one. A chain makes each such mistake free one more box than it should, so `idc` (returns its param) and `fwd` (hands it to a second by-value param) are re-asserted rather than assumed still covered by `result_shared_nonescaping_param_names`. ── AND THE CORRECTION, which changes what legs (b) and (c) ARE ── This row states that for the struct-literal move and the `Vec` push "the destination becomes the owner and registers a single-box free, so the outer envelope is freed once and the chain below it is never walked at all". That is WRONG, and it was an inference from the 320-definitely + 320-indirectly signature rather than a measurement. MEASURED, the control this row should have run before claiming a mechanism: a SINGLE-box `Option[Option[i64]]` -- no chain anywhere, one envelope total -- leaks 320 B / 10 through BOTH shapes. struct Holder { b: Option[Option[i64]] } let h = Holder { b: b }; 320 B let mut v: Vec[Option[Option[i64]]] ... v.push(b); 320 B So the destination registers NOTHING, and (b)/(c) are not chain gaps at all. They are a destination-ownership defect: the source's registration is disarmed at the move (`boxed_enum_payload_vars` exists precisely so a destination can take the box over) and no destination ever does. The chain only changes the SIZE of the loss -- 320 + 320 instead of 320 + 0 -- which is what made the signature look chain-shaped and produced the wrong reading. CONSEQUENCE FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: do not start from `nested_box_deeper_tag_chain`. The question is which construct becomes the owner when a boxed-payload enum is moved into a struct literal or a container, and it has to be answered for the SINGLE-box case first -- the chain then follows for free, exactly as it did on leg (a). Fixing the chain without the owner would free envelopes that still have no first owner. DIRECTLY RELATED, and it should be read before either is attempted: B-2026-08-07-12 leg 2 is this same envelope-ownership question reached through a by-value struct ARGUMENT (`struct V { o: Option[Option[i64]] }` as a fresh temp, leaking its 32-byte envelope at `-O0`). That row deliberately did NOT apply the obvious patch, for the standing caution this family has earned: it hands the caller a claim on an envelope whose only other potential owner is machinery other open rows are actively changing, and a second owner here is a double free rather than a leak. The same caution governs (b) and (c). ROW STAYS OPEN for (b) and (c), now correctly characterized. Severity stays low: `-O2` is unaffected in every one of these shapes, so no ordinary `karac build` leaks, and the `-O0` leg is where they show. ── LEG (b) FIXED 49a12153, AND IT ONLY BECAME FIXABLE WHEN A SIBLING MOVED IT ── The correction above said (b) was a destination-ownership defect rather than a chain gap, because a SINGLE-box `Option[Option[i64]]` leaked through a struct-literal move too. 31768650 (B-2026-08-07-2 shape 3, landed independently) then fixed exactly that: a field whose type is a boxed-payload `Option` now carries a `FieldDrop::OptionInline`, on the argument that the ENVELOPE is heap even when what it holds is not. RE-MEASURED AFTER IT, which is what changed the leg: struct H2 { b: Option[Option[i64]] } 320 + 0 -> CLEAN struct H3 { b: Option[Option[Option[i64]]] } 320 + 320 -> 320 + 0 So the single-box case is closed and the chain case became a PURE chain gap -- the outer envelope freed, everything below it still owned by nobody. Both readings of this leg were right about different halves, and only the second measurement separates them. Worth recording as a fleet-coordination note as much as a technical one: the row's own diagnosis was correct when written, wrong an hour later, and correct again in a different sense, because another session changed the ground underneath it. THE FIX is in `emit_option_drop_fn`, one level of recursion it never had. Its boxed branch asked `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr` for the payload's drop, and that resolver bottoms out in the primitive no-op for a heapless-but-boxed `Option` -- every predicate on the path asks whether the payload owns HEAP, and a boxed scalar does not. When the payload is itself an `Option` whose own payload is boxed, it now recurses into `emit_option_drop_fn` instead. `emit_option_drop_fn(P)` drops an `Option[P]`, so the call takes the INNER payload, and termination is the same `> 3` word test that created the box: each level is strictly the next type down and the walk stops at the first payload that fits its area, which is a value rather than an envelope. MEASURED, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, 40 iterations, A/B against a stashed tree: struct field, triple nest 1,280 B -> clean struct field, quadruple nest 1,280 + 1,280 B -> clean struct field, built NEVER READ 1,280 B -> clean struct field, single box clean -> clean (31768650's) The never-read arm is the one that proves the owner is the FIELD rather than the match: the struct is built and its field never destructured, and it still balances. Fixture `asan_struct_field_boxed_enum_chain_frees_every_envelope`, deliberately UNFLOORED. At `-O2` the program performs 6 allocations -- the ASAN baseline plus `println` -- because every arm is a scalar-payload chain whose envelopes are frame-local and LLVM deletes the malloc/free pairs. A floor there would assert something the run does not do, which is B-2026-08-04-17's own coverage-shaped-versus-coverage failure. The `-O0` leg carries it, where the same program allocates 326. ── A NEW RESIDUAL, MEASURED RATHER THAN INFERRED ── `struct Hs { b: Option[Option[Option[String]]] }` still leaks 1,280 B / 40 at `-O0`, and it is NOT fixed by the above -- measured identical before and after, which is why it is out of the fixture rather than in it. It takes the OTHER branch of the same classifier. `payload_droppable` is true for it (the payload is a droppable `Option`), so it routes to `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` and never reaches the `boxed_envelope_only` path that 31768650 added or the recursion added here. So the struct-field classifier now has two routes to a boxed `Option` payload and only one of them walks a chain. Whoever takes it: the fix is probably to give the `payload_droppable` route the same recursion, but it must be measured rather than assumed symmetric -- that route reaches shapes with real heap interiors, where a second owner is a double free rather than a leak, and this family has produced exactly that mistake three times (B-2026-08-06-9's two refuted routes and B-2026-08-06-32's widened free). ── LEG (c) IS THE ONLY ONE LEFT, AND IT IS NOT A CHAIN GAP ── Pushing into a `Vec` still leaks, and the single-box control says why: let mut v: Vec[Option[Option[i64]]] ... v.push(b); 320 + 0 (SINGLE box) let mut v: Vec[Option[Option[Option[i64]]]] ... 320 + 320 (chain) The single-box case leaking is the whole diagnosis: the `Vec` element drop registers no owner for the envelope at all, exactly as the struct field did before 31768650. So leg (c) wants the `Vec`-element peer of that fix FIRST, and the chain then follows for free -- which is precisely the order legs (a) and (b) turned out to need. Do not start from the chain. ROW STAYS OPEN for leg (c) and for the `Hs` residual above. ── LEG (c) FIXED f5df577f, AND IT IS NOT `-O0`-ONLY — SEVERITY RAISED TO MEDIUM ── THE SEVERITY CORRECTION FIRST, because this row has asserted the opposite twice. Both earlier passes recorded "severity stays low: `-O2` is unaffected in every one of these shapes, so no ordinary `karac build` leaks". That is FALSE for leg (c), and it was never measured — it was carried forward from legs (a) and (b), where it is true. Measured at the DEFAULT opt level, 40 iterations: pre-fix, -O2: 5,120 B definitely lost + 3,840 B indirectly pre-fix, -O0: 6,400 B definitely lost + 5,120 B indirectly post-fix: clean at BOTH A `Vec` keeps its buffer live past the point LLVM can fold a frame-local envelope away, so the allocation survives to be leaked. An ordinary `karac build` leaks here. Severity low -> medium. That also makes this the one fixture in the family with real `-O2` coverage: it carries a FLOOR (766 allocations at `-O2`, against the baseline 6 its two siblings sit at) and is stash-proven red at the default level, not only on the `-O0` leg. THE FIX is the `Vec`-element peer of 31768650, in `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr`'s `Option` arm. That arm asked three questions of the PAYLOAD — inline `{ptr,len,cap}` overlay, shared handle, droppable struct/enum — and a boxed scalar answers no to all three, so the element got no per-element drop at all. It now also admits `option_payload_boxed_envelope_only`, the same predicate the struct-field arm uses, whose restriction to a non-shared struct-or-seeded-enum head is the soundness condition rather than a convenience: it is the set the element COPY descends into, and copy and drop have to name the same set. THE SINGLE-BOX ARM IS THE DIAGNOSIS, not a control. `Vec[Option[Option[i64]]]` -- one envelope, no chain -- leaked, which is what identified this as a missing OWNER rather than a missing chain walk. This row predicted that ordering ("wants the `Vec`-element peer of that fix FIRST, and the chain then follows for free") and it held exactly: admitting the envelope fixed the single-box, chain and two-deep-chain arms in one change, because leg (b)'s recursion inside `emit_option_drop_fn` was already there to walk them. MEASURED, every shape this family has accumulated, all clean after and none regressed: single box, triple nest, quadruple nest, `Vec[Option[String]]` (the pre-existing inline-overlay route, which must not gain a second owner), `Vec[Option[i64]]` (heapless, no box), a pushed element never read back, and the `Some(None)` / `None` guard elements. No invalid free at either level. ── WHAT IS LEFT: ONE RESIDUAL, AND IT IS NOT WHAT ITS SIZE SUGGESTED ── `struct Hs { b: Option[Option[Option[String]]] }` still leaks 1,280 B / 40 at `-O0`, unchanged by any of the three legs. CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the leaked blocks are 32 bytes each, and the test payload string was exactly 32 characters, so the obvious reading was that the String buffer leaks. It does not. Re-running with a much longer payload leaves the loss at 1,280 B in 40 blocks of 32 — so it is a genuine 32-byte ENVELOPE, and the string coincidence was a trap worth one command to disarm. So one envelope of a three-level chain in a struct field is still unowned, while the String interior and the other two envelopes are freed. The field takes the classifier's `payload_droppable` route (`vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` on the whole field type) rather than the `boxed_envelope_only` route, and that route reaches a different level of the chain than the two fixed here. Whoever takes it: read which of the three boxes survives before changing anything -- count `@free` calls against `@malloc` in the emitted module, the technique that settled B-2026-08-06-21 and -26. Two owners on this route is a double free rather than a leak, because the interior is real heap. ROW STAYS OPEN for that residual alone. All three filed legs are closed. ── THE RESIDUAL IS FIXED %s; ROW CLOSED ── `struct Hs { b: Option[Option[Option[String]]] }` was neither of the two things this row guessed. The site is `own_boxed_option_field_envelope_at` (control_flow_match.rs, added by B-2026-08-07-7), and it is a MATCH-ARM registration, not a field-classifier one — which is why neither leg (b)'s recursion nor leg (c)'s admission reached it. WHY IT EXISTS AT ALL, because that is what makes the fix safe. Zeroing an `Option` field's tag is a single guard away from two different frees: `karac_drop_Option_

` tests `tag == Some` ONCE and behind that one test does BOTH the deep drop of the interior and the `free` of the box. An arm that binds the interior out needs the first suppressed and the second kept, so it parks the box pointer in a private slot and registers a box-only `BoxedEnumDrop` against it. That registration carried `deeper_tags: Vec::new()`, so it owned exactly ONE envelope and a field whose payload boxes again left the rest owned by nobody. A FIRST OWNER, NOT A SECOND — measured, not argued. Pre-fix the shape LEAKED. The field's own drop is disarmed by the tag zero and the arm's binding owns the INTERIOR only; had anything else claimed these envelopes the result would have been a double free. 224c945f deferred them to this row on the opposite assumption while -6 and -11's legs were in flight; all of those have since landed and none of them reaches this path, which the measurement confirms rather than the reasoning. HOW THE SURVIVOR WAS FINALLY IDENTIFIED, and it is the step this row prescribed after guessing wrong twice: 1. The leak's ALLOCATION BACKTRACE put the block in `main`, not inside any drop fn — so it is an envelope minted at the construction site, which ruled out the drop-synthesis theories. 2. Varying ONLY the nesting depth: depth 2 clean, depth 3 loses one box, depth 4 loses two. Exactly one envelope freed at every depth. That is a missing WALK, not a missing owner — the opposite of legs (b) and (c). 3. The emitted module then showed every `karac_drop_Option_...` level freeing its own box and delegating correctly, so the drop functions were never wrong. `main` was reaching the value through a single-box PARKED action instead. That is the "count frees against mallocs" step, and it is what separated the two candidates. A COINCIDENCE WORTH RECORDING, because it nearly ended the investigation early: the leaked blocks are 32 bytes each and the test payload string was exactly 32 characters, which made "the String buffer leaks" look obvious. Re-running with a much longer payload left the loss at 1,280 B in 40 blocks of 32 — a genuine envelope. One command to disarm a wrong premise that would have sent the fix to the wrong site entirely. MEASURED, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, 40 iterations: 2,560 B definitely lost plus 1,280 B indirectly -> clean, and clean at `-O2` before and after (this shape, unlike leg (c), keeps its envelopes frame-local). Every shape this row accumulated re-measured clean with no regression: depths 1-4, the scalar sibling from leg (b), the `Vec` arms from leg (c), the owned param from leg (a), the bare-let chains from B-2026-08-07-6, and a non-binding arm over the same field. Fixture `asan_match_arm_parked_envelope_frees_every_level`. ── WHAT THIS ROW COST, AND THE ONE RULE WORTH KEEPING ── Four fix sites, three of which this row's own text predicted incorrectly at least once: (a) the owned param, (b) the struct-field drop recursion, (c) the `Vec` element admission, and this parked-arm registration. Two severity or mechanism claims were carried forward rather than measured and were false when finally checked — the `-O2`-is-unaffected claim (wrong for leg (c), which leaks an ordinary build) and the destination-registers-a-single-box-free claim (wrong for (b) and (c), which registered nothing). THE RULE: in this family, "which construct owns this box" is not answerable by reading the code that looks responsible. Every correct answer here came from a DIFFERENTIAL — vary one condition (depth, payload type, container, binding versus not) and read which measurement moves. The three wrong answers all came from reasoning about which classifier branch looked applicable.

fix: 00660c3,e0d88f2, and leg 1 5ab6e8e8 (synth_drop.rs promotion gate + payload_droppable; control_flow_match.rs both legs of place_optres_field_move_info_ex; runtime.rs option_payload_map_or_set_drop_ok). The Result twin is B-2026-08-07-19, not this row.
title: a fresh-temp struct literal passed BY VALUE leaked the heap inside an `Option`/`Result` field at BOTH opt levels, and the callee's entry copy of a BOXED payload shared its interior -- BOTH ROOTS FIXED (00660c3), and LEG 2 (an all-scalar boxed envelope) FIXED TOO (e0d88f2), which emptied the -O0 quarantine list. LEG 1 re-scoped: its corruption is not about `Option` at all and moved to B-2026-08-07-15; what stays here is an `Option[Map]` field that no drop arm covers
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-07-7's envelope residue, as the explanation for why that row's quarantine line survives its own fix. Not caused by it -- reproduces with c25c949 stashed, and with a callee that never touches the field. SHAPE. Pass a struct BY VALUE whose `Option` field has a heap-BOXED payload. No match, no pattern, no consumption -- the callee's body is a literal: struct W { o: Option[Option[String]] } fn ignore(w: W) -> i64 { 1 } let w: W = W { o: Option.Some(Option.Some(f"p{n + i}")); ignore(w) -> DOUBLE FREE, both opt levels (10 invalid frees over 10 iterations) ignore(W { o: Option.Some(Option.Some(f"p{n + i}")) }) -> 320 B / 10 blocks LEAK at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, clean at -O2 same value, no call at all, matched in the same frame -> CLEAN Any `Option[Option[T]]` boxes: an `Option` is 4 LLVM words and `Option`'s own payload area is 3, so the inner one never fits inline. `Option[Vec[..]]`, `Option[Result[..]]` and an `Option`-of-wide-struct field are the same shape. MECHANISM, one function. `deep_copy_option_struct_enum_payload_in_place` (`src/codegen/param_own.rs`) runs at fn entry to give a by-value aggregate param heap independent of the caller's. Its BOXED branch mallocs a fresh box, `load`/`store`s the old box's VALUE into it, and then calls deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_in_place(payload_name, new_box, layout) to duplicate what the copied value points AT. For `payload_te = Option[String]` the `payload_name` is `Option`, so `layout` is the ERASED generic `Option` layout -- and its `field_drop_kinds["Some"]` is not heap-bearing, so that helper's `has_heap` test is false, the variant's case block is never emitted, and the String buffer is not copied. Two boxes, one String. That single fact is both faces: * NAMED BINDING -- the caller keeps its own struct drop, which deep-frees the shared String the callee's copy already freed. Both opt levels, because a real free runs twice on a live pointer. * FRESH TEMP -- the caller has no drop, so its ORIGINAL box is unreferenced the instant word 1 is overwritten with the new one. -O0 only; at -O2 the allocation folds away with the evidence. It is the same ERASURE as B-2026-06-10-6 ("the erased-`Option` drop switch can't classify an inline `String`/`Vec` payload"), one function over. That row answered it at the SUPPRESSION site with a dedicated `suppress_inline_option_payload_cleanup` channel; the COPY site never got the equivalent. NOT B-2026-08-07-11, though they are neighbours and the distinction took a measurement to settle. That row is a bare `Option[Option[Option[i64]]]` passed to an owned param, leaking ONE envelope because the callee's param registration carries an empty `deeper_tags` chain -- a link of the chain never freed. This row has a single level of boxing, and what leaks is the caller's ORIGINAL box, replaced in the slot by the callee's copy. Different site, different mechanism, and only this one has a corrupting face. Fixing either does not fix the other. CAUTION FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: the two faces have to move together. Deepening the copy alone makes the fresh-temp case WORSE -- the callee would get its own String, after which the caller's original String joins its original box with no owner at all, turning a 32 B leak into 32 B plus the buffer. So the copy must deepen AND the caller's fresh temp must own its original, in one change. VERIFICATION this family demands (see B-2026-08-07-7's history for why): measure at BOTH opt levels, run the whole `memory_sanitizer` suite on x86 Linux where LeakSanitizer is live, and check the undestructured / borrow-only fixtures (`asan_b27_option_enum_undestructured_drop_no_leak`, `asan_b31_option_agg_payload_borrow_only_no_leak`, `asan_b04_7_option_heap_enum_struct_field_drop_no_leak`) -- a previous attempt in this area traded one corrupting shape for five leaking ones. WHERE IT IS ALREADY VISIBLE: `tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt` quarantines `asan_struct_field_boxed_payload_interior_match_out_no_double_free` for THIS row. Its remaining -O0 failure is 5,120 B over 160 blocks -- four by-value calls per iteration x 40 -- all of it the fresh-temp face. ── FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS TOO NARROW; TWO INDEPENDENT ROOTS, MEASURED (2026-08-07, second pass) ── The row above blamed ONE mechanism (the entry copy sharing the interior) for both faces. That is right for the corruption and WRONG for the leak, and the difference matters because it changes what a fix has to touch. A wider matrix, all `fn ig(x: S) -> i64 { 1 }` -- a callee that never reads the field -- 10 iterations, valgrind, at BOTH opt levels: struct S { s: String } fresh temp -> clean struct S { v: Vec[String] } fresh temp -> clean struct S { s: Option[String] } fresh temp -> LEAK 40 B / 10 struct S { s: Result[String, i64] } fresh temp -> LEAK 40 B / 10 struct S { s: Option[Map[String, i64]] } fresh temp -> LEAK 720 B / 10 struct S { s: Option[Vec[String]] } fresh temp -> LEAK 960 B / 10 struct S { s: Option[String] } NAMED -> clean struct S { s: Option[String] } no call -> clean struct S { s: Option[String] } `ref` param-> clean struct S { a: String, s: Option[String] } fresh temp -> CLEAN THE LAST LINE IS THE LOCALIZER. Adding an unrelated plain `String` field next to the `Option` one makes the leak disappear, so nothing is wrong with the drop -- once the struct qualifies for a caller-scope drop at all, its `Option` field is freed correctly. The defect is the GATE that decides whether to register one. None of this is -O0-only. `Option[String]` / `Result[String,_]` / `Option[Map]` / `Option[Vec]` fields all leak at the DEFAULT -O2, which makes this ordinary `karac build` output rather than a debug-build curiosity, and is why the severity stays high on the leak alone. ROOT A -- THE GATE, and it is a one-disjunct near-miss with its own sibling. `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst`'s STRUCT-LITERAL arm (`src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs`, the `needs_memory_drop` computation) tests two signals, both blind to `Option`/`Result`: * `aggregate_has_heap_field` (`runtime.rs`) is purely LLVM-structural -- it matches a field whose LLVM type IS the `{ptr,len,cap}` Vec shape. An `Option[String]` field lowers to erased i64 payload words, so it never matches. * `type_expr_has_drop_heap` (`synth_drop.rs`) hardcodes `"Option" | "Result" => false`. The FN-CALL arm of the SAME function, ~270 lines above, already ORs in `option_field_te_has_drop_heap` -- the companion written for exactly this ("for the one caller that must NOT inherit its `Option`/`Result` carve-out... A fresh-temp call ARGUMENT has no binding", B-2026-08-05-22). The struct-literal arm never got it. `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` has the identical blind spot in its own field test, so the passthrough path is a third site. ROOT B -- THE ENTRY COPY, which is what corrupts. `deep_copy_option_struct_enum_payload_in_place`'s BOXED branch mallocs a fresh box and copies the old box's VALUE into it, then calls `deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_in_place(payload_name, new_box, layout)` to duplicate what that value points at. For `payload_te = Option[String]` the `payload_name` is `Option`, so `layout` is the ERASED generic one, its `field_drop_kinds["Some"]` is not heap-bearing, `has_heap` is false, the variant's case block is never emitted -- two boxes, one String. For a `Map`/`Set` payload the copy does not run at all (the payload name is in neither `struct_types` nor `enum_layouts`). THE TWO ROOTS MUST MOVE TOGETHER, and this is now MEASURED rather than reasoned. Forcing the gate ON by adding a sibling `String` field -- the exact effect a root-A fix would have -- is a precise predictor: struct S { a: String, s: Option[String] } -> clean SAFE struct S { a: String, s: Result[String, i64] } -> clean SAFE struct S { a: String, s: Option[Vec[String]] } -> clean SAFE struct S { a: String, s: Option[H] } (H owns heap) -> clean SAFE struct S { a: String, o: Option[Option[String]] } -> DOUBLE FREE, both levels struct S { a: String, s: Option[Map[String, i64]] } -> DOUBLE FREE, both levels So a root-A fix alone converts two of these six from a leak into corruption. The split is not boxed-vs-inline: `Option[Vec[String]]` and `Option[H]` are BOXED and safe. It is whether the CALLEE's struct drop also claims the field -- true for a boxed `Option`-in-`Option` (routed to the deep `karac_drop_Option_

`, B-2026-08-07-7's subject) and for a `Map`/`Set` handle, false for everything else. ALREADY CORRUPTING ON MAIN, UNRECORDED UNTIL NOW. Because the FN-CALL arm already has the disjunct the struct-literal arm lacks, the boxed shape reached through a call temp is a live double free today: fn mk(k: i64) -> W { W { o: Option.Some(Option.Some(f"p{k}")) } } ig(mk(n + i)) -> 10 valgrind errors, invalid free, at -O0 That is root B with no root-A fix needed to expose it, and it is the strongest argument for fixing B FIRST: doing so removes an existing corruption instead of merely permitting a leak fix. RECOMMENDED ORDER, therefore, and it is the opposite of the obvious one: 1. ROOT B first, alone. Make the boxed entry copy actually deep for an erased `Option`/`Result` payload (recurse on the concrete payload `TypeExpr` rather than the erased layout) and for a `Map`/`Set` payload. This is strictly corruption-REMOVING: it fixes `ig(mk(..))` above, the named-binding double free, and the two DOUBLE FREE rows in the predictor table, while changing no leak into a free. 2. ROOT A second, once the predictor table is all-SAFE: add `|| self.option_field_te_has_drop_heap(f)` to the struct-literal arm's `needs_memory_drop`, and the same to `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct`. Re-run the predictor table before and after; every row must be clean. VERIFICATION for either step: both opt levels, the whole `memory_sanitizer` suite on x86 Linux where LeakSanitizer is live, the -O0 leg, and the undestructured / borrow-only fixtures this family has broken before (`asan_b27_option_enum_undestructured_drop_no_leak`, `asan_b31_option_agg_payload_borrow_only_no_leak`, `asan_b04_7_option_heap_enum_struct_field_drop_no_leak`). ── BOTH ROOTS FIXED (00660c3); TWO LEGS REMAIN, ROW STAYS OPEN ── Landed together, because the pass above established that either alone makes the other worse. ROOT A: the struct-LITERAL arm of `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` now ORs `option_field_te_has_drop_heap` into its `needs_memory_drop`, matching the fn-call arm ~270 lines above, and `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` gets the same disjunct in its own field test. Three sites, one predicate, kept in lockstep. ROOT B: the boxed branch of `deep_copy_option_struct_enum_payload_in_place` routes an `Option`/`Result` payload by its CONCRETE `TypeExpr` back through `deep_copy_option_inline_payload_in_place` instead of asking the erased generic layout. That is the return leg of a hand-off the two functions already document — the forward leg is the struct/enum arm of the inline copier, which calls into this one for exactly the shapes the buffer path cannot handle. The recursion terminates because each hop strips one `Option`/`Result` level. MEASURED CLEAN AFTER, every row at BOTH opt levels, 10 iterations, valgrind, each with its pre-fix figure: { s: Option[String] } fresh temp 40 B / 10 -> clean { s: Result[String, i64] } fresh temp 40 B / 10 -> clean { s: Option[Vec[String]] } fresh temp 960 B / 10 -> clean { a: String, s: Option[String] } fresh temp clean -> clean { o: Option[Option[String]] } NAMED double free -> clean { o: Option[Option[String]] } via mk() double free -> clean { a: String, o: Option[Option..]} fresh+named double free -> clean { s: Option[H] } (H owns heap) fresh temp clean -> clean `ref` param control clean -> clean The quarantined fixture `asan_struct_field_boxed_payload_interior_match_out_no_ double_free` went 5,120 B / 160 blocks to 1,280 B / 40 at -O0. Pinned by `asan_by_value_struct_option_field_owned_no_leak_no_double_free`, which carries all nine rows including both controls, and is red pre-fix with an explicit ASAN DOUBLE FREE at both opt levels (not merely a leak — the fixture's boxed rows corrupt without root B). ── TWO LEGS STILL OPEN; THE ROW STAYS OPEN FOR THEM ── LEG 1 -- a `Map`/`Set` PAYLOAD. `struct S { s: Option[Map[String, i64]] }` still leaks 720 B / 10 as a fresh temp, and DOUBLE-FREES at both opt levels once a sibling heap field turns the gate on. Root B does not reach it: the payload name is in neither `struct_types` nor `enum_layouts`, so `deep_copy_option_struct_enum_payload_in_place` returns before the routing added here, and the handle is shared rather than cloned. The fix is the `MapOrSet` peer of what landed -- `deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_in_place` already has a `MapOrSet` arm that deep-clones a handle in place (`emit_map_clone_fn`), so the shape of the answer exists; it needs reaching from the `Option`-payload path. Unchanged by this pass, measured before and after. LEG 2 -- an ALL-SCALAR boxed payload. `struct V { o: Option[Option[i64]] }` passed as a fresh temp leaks its 32-byte envelope at -O0. The gate declines it CORRECTLY by its own standard -- there is no heap inside the `Option`, so `option_field_te_has_drop_heap` is false -- but the envelope is itself heap and nothing owns it. This is the envelope-ownership question B-2026-08-07-6 / -11 own, reached through a by-value struct argument, and it is what the -O0 quarantine line now waits on (its THIRD distinct cause, which the entry records). The obvious patch for leg 2 -- also gate on `option_payload_is_boxed` -- was NOT applied, and the reason is this family's standing caution rather than doubt about the mechanism: it hands the caller a claim on an envelope whose only other potential owner is the chain machinery two other open rows are actively changing, and a second owner here is a double free rather than a leak. It wants measuring against those rows, not alongside them. ── LEG 2 FIXED (e0d88f2); LEG 1 RE-SCOPED AND HANDED OFF ── LEG 2 (an ALL-SCALAR boxed payload) is closed, and it closed as a consequence rather than by force. `option_field_te_has_drop_heap` exists to answer "will a drop free something in this field, so a fresh temp needs an owner", and while nothing freed that envelope the honest answer was NO. B-2026-08-07-2 shape 3 gave the struct's field drop the envelope, so the answer became yes and the predicate had not been told. One disjunct (`option_payload_boxed_envelope_only`), shared by all three callers. It cannot double-free, and the reason is structural rather than tested: the same predicate that admits the drop admits the entry COPY, so the callee's struct holds a box of its own. The NAMED-binding spelling had already gone clean under shape 3 for that reason; only the fresh temp, with no binding to hang an owner on, was left. Measured clean at both opt levels; the -12 fixture carries two new arms and was red at 1,280 B / 40. THE -O0 QUARANTINE LIST IS EMPTY AGAIN as a result, and the ratchet found it in its "a listed fixture that starts PASSING fails the leg too" direction. That one line had outlived THREE causes -- this row's two roots and then leg 2 -- and `tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt` records all three at its removal, because twice a fix was predicted to empty it and twice the arithmetic disagreed. LEG 1 (a `Map`/`Set` payload) IS NOT WHAT THIS ROW SAID IT WAS, and is being handed to B-2026-08-07-15 rather than kept here. This row described it as the copy failing to duplicate a handle. Reading the actual stacks says otherwise: both frames run `__karac_drop_struct_S`, and what they double-free is the SIBLING `String` field, not the map at all. The map is a separate, plain leak (no `FieldDrop` arm covers an `Option[Map]` field). And the corruption half is not about `Option`, or `Map`-inside-`Option`, or this row's subject in any form -- `struct S { a: String, m: Map[String, i64] }` as a fresh temp is 480 valgrind errors with 175 invalid frees at -O2. Filed as B-2026-08-07-15 at HIGH; what remains here is the ordinary leak of an `Option[Map]` field that no drop arm covers. ── LEG 1 MEASURED, NOT JUST RE-SCOPED: THE COPY IS IRRELEVANT AND THE BLAST RADIUS IS WIDER THAN "an `Option[Map]` field" ── The hand-off above is right that the copy was never the mechanism. Here is the measurement that settles it, and a second one that resizes the leak. IT REPRODUCES WITH NO CALL AT ALL. Ten iterations, valgrind, both opt levels: let s: S = S { s: Option.Some(m) }; // S { s: Option[Map[String,i64]] } -> 720 B direct + 5,320 B indirect over 10 blocks, -O2 AND -O0 No function, no by-value argument, no entry copy in the program. So no fix on the copy side can close this, and `deep_copy_option_struct_enum_payload_in_place` — the function both earlier passes named — is not on the path. THE ROOT IS THE `OptionInline` PROMOTION'S GATE, AND IT IS ALL-OR-NOTHING PER STRUCT. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis` promotes an `Option`/`Result` field to `FieldDrop::OptionInline` only when `struct_callee_owned` — i.e. `aggregate_param_copy_supported_struct` — holds for the WHOLE struct. `field_copy_supported` refuses an `Option[Map]` payload (not a String, not a Vec, not a struct/enum, not a boxed envelope), so the predicate is false and the promotion loop is skipped for EVERY `Option` field of that struct, not only the Map one. `struct S { p: Option[String], m: Option[Map[..]] }` therefore leaks the `String` payload too — a shape that is clean the moment the Map field is deleted. CONTROL MATRIX, ten iterations, both opt levels, each measured rather than reasoned: let o: Option[Map[..]] bare local, no struct clean struct S { s: Option[Map[..]] } plain let, no call LEAK 720 B / 10 struct S { s: Option[Set[i64]] } plain let, no call LEAK 720 B / 10 struct S { s: Result[Map[..], i64] } plain let, no call LEAK 720 B / 10 struct S { s: Option[Map[..]] } matched out clean struct S { s: Option[Vec[String]] } plain let, no call clean struct S { m: Map[..] } bare Map FIELD clean The last two are the localizers. A bare `Map` FIELD is freed correctly by `FieldDrop::MapOrSet`, which is NOT gated on copy-support; an `Option[Vec]` field is freed correctly because its payload keeps the promotion's gate open. The defect is exactly the intersection: a struct field, an `Option`/`Result` wrapper, and a payload that closes the gate. WHAT THE FIX LOOKS LIKE NOW, and B-2026-08-07-15 changed it. The gate's stated safety argument is that a copy-supported struct is entry-copied by the callee, so the two frames own independent heap and freeing the field here cannot double-free. B-2026-08-05-33 added a second way to have exactly one owner — own-by-transfer, where the callee takes the buffers and the caller does not register — and -15 made that second way actually hold for a fresh temp, which is the half that was broken. So the gate can widen from `copy-supported` to `copy-supported OR owned-by-transfer` (`struct_param_owned_by_transfer`), with `payload_droppable` admitting a `Map`/`Set` payload; `emit_option_drop_fn` already routes a Map payload to `emit_map_drop_fn` through `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`, and its param is a pointer to the handle SLOT, which is what the payload area hands it. The drop side needs no new emitter. AND NO CLONE IS NEEDED, which retires this leg's original premise entirely. The `MapOrSet` peer of `emit_map_clone_fn` was proposed because the callee's copy would otherwise share the handle. An own-by-transfer struct has NO entry copy — that is the definition — so there is nothing to keep symmetric. Copy == drop holds trivially at zero copies. NOT ATTEMPTED HERE. The widened gate gives an `Option` drop to every non-copy-supported struct in the program, not just Map-bearing ones, so it is a broad behavioural change that wants the whole `memory_sanitizer` suite at both opt levels plus the -O0 leg — the same verification -12's own roots demanded, for the same reason. ── LEG 1 FIXED. THE GATE WAS THE WHOLE STORY, AND THE PAIRING RULE COST THREE SITES RATHER THAN ONE ── The plan above was right about the mechanism and short by one site. Landed as predicted for the DROP; what it did not anticipate is that widening the drop OBLIGES the move sites to widen with it, and one of the two move legs is governed by a deliberately NARROWER class that no reading of this row would have flagged. WHAT LANDED, three sites and one predicate: * `synth_drop.rs` — the promotion gate widens exactly as prescribed, `aggregate_param_copy_supported_struct(s) || struct_param_owned_by_transfer(s)`, and `payload_droppable` gains a `Map`/`Set` disjunct. A Map payload is routed straight to `emit_option_drop_fn` rather than through `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr`: that helper is shared with the VEC-ELEMENT path, whose ownership story is not gated on this struct gate, so teaching it would hand `Vec[Option[Map]]` a drop nothing here measures. * `control_flow_match.rs` — BOTH legs of `place_optres_field_move_info_ex`. * `runtime.rs` — `option_payload_map_or_set_drop_ok`, the new predicate all three consult. Its head set is exactly what `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr` routes to `emit_map_drop_fn` (`Map`/`SortedMap`/`Set`/`SortedSet`), and that identity is load-bearing rather than tidy: the predicate promises a REAL drop, so admitting a head the emitter bottoms out on as the primitive no-op would arm the move-site zero against a free that never runs — the "too wide" half of the pairing rule, i.e. a leak. `HashMap`/`HashSet` are excluded for exactly that reason: they appear in the classifier's head lists but the drop emitter has no arm for them. THE PATTERN LEG IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING, because only measurement found it. `place_optres_field_move_info_ex` states the pairing rule in its own comment — the source zero must fire precisely when the struct drop would free the field — and its WHOLE-MOVE leg is written as a mirror of the classifier, so that one follows from reading. The PARTIAL/pattern leg is not a mirror: it uses a narrower class on purpose, because zeroing there is only right when the arm BINDING takes over the free, and the file records an earlier attempt where widening it wholesale turned an owner's single free into a leak. Whether a `Map` handle behaves like the inline class or the struct/enum class is not derivable from that comment. It was settled by MEASUREMENT: with the classifier widened and the pattern leg left alone, `match s.m { Some(inner) => .. }` went from clean to 470 valgrind errors with invalid frees at BOTH opt levels. Two frees means the binding demonstrably does own it, so the source must be neutralized — the Map handle joins the narrow class. Three shapes were affected (a bare match-out, a match-out reached inside a callee, and the `let taken = s.m` sibling, which the whole-move leg already covered). MEASURED, 10 iterations, valgrind, at the DEFAULT -O2 AND at -O0, each with its pre-fix figure: struct S { s: Option[Map[i64, String]] } no call 720 B / 10 -> clean struct S { s: Option[Set[i64]] } no call 720 B / 10 -> clean same, fresh temp by value 720 B / 10 -> clean same, NAMED binding by value 720 B / 10 -> clean struct S { p: Option[String], m: Option[Map] } 1,051 B / 20 -> clean match s.m { Some(inner) => .. } clean (would double-free) -> clean consume(s.m) (whole-move) clean (would double-free) -> clean let taken = s.m clean (would double-free) -> clean eat(S { .. }) matching x.m inside the callee clean (would double-free) -> clean CONTROLS clean before and after: a bare `Option[Map]` LOCAL with no struct, a bare `Map` FIELD (already covered by `FieldDrop::MapOrSet`, which is not gated on copy-support), `Option[Vec[String]]` and `Option[String]` fields (the promotion's gate was already open for those). THE SIBLING-FIELD ROW IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS THE DIAGNOSIS, and it is why the regression fixture carries a `Sib` struct rather than only the Map shapes. The gate holds for the WHOLE struct, so `struct S { p: Option[String], m: Option[Map] }` leaked the STRING too — 1,051 B / 20 blocks against 720 B / 10 for the Map alone, and clean the moment the Map field is deleted. Its 331 B half is invisible at -O2 (the String folds away) and only shows at -O0, which is one more instance of this family's standing rule about opt levels. REGRESSION: `asan_option_map_set_field_owned_by_transfer_no_leak_no_double_free` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), floored at 100 allocations, carrying all nine rows above plus the four controls. STASH-PROVEN RED at HEAD: 14,400 B / 200 blocks at -O2 and 15,751 B / 240 at -O0. Oracle: `test_option_map_set_field_transfers_and_frees_the_handle` (tests/interpreter.rs). NO codegen.rs E2E PEER, deliberately, and the reason generalizes: the stdout is 20440 before AND after the fix, so an output-only E2E cannot observe this defect at all and would be exactly the vacuous fixture B-2026-08-04-17 warns about. The sanitizer twin is the whole test. (Contrast B-2026-08-06-1, where the E2E WAS worth having because that fix had a double-free half an E2E can abort on.) THE `Result` TWIN IS NOT FIXED AND IS NOT A ONE-LINE EXTENSION — filed as B-2026-08-07-19. `struct S { s: Result[Map[i64, String], i64] }` still leaks 720 B / 10 at both opt levels, measured before and after this pass. The Option fix does not reach it: the `Result` arm of the promotion loop has its own gates (`result_field_direct_vecstr_halves_ok` / `result_field_struct_enum_payload_ok`) and neither admits a Map half. The reason it stays out of this commit is the surface, not doubt about the mechanism. The obvious widening point, `result_payload_inline_recursive_drop_ok`, has FIVE consumers including `types_lowering.rs`'s layout decisions, and `result_field_direct_vecstr_halves_ok` is consulted by `field_copy_supported` itself — so admitting a Map half there would make the struct COPY-SUPPORTED, promising an entry copy that `deep_copy_result_inline_heap_halves_in_place` cannot perform on a handle. That is precisely the over-broad widening this family has reverted three times, and it would trade a leak for a double free. Doing it safely needs a scoped predicate threaded through four or five further coupled sites (the promotion Result arm, both Result move legs, and the destructure-leaf registrations in `stmts.rs`), each carrying the same double-free risk the pattern leg just demonstrated. It wants its own measurement pass. COMPOSED WITH B-2026-08-07-17, which landed on `main` while this slice was in flight and changed the very predicate this gate now consults. `struct_param_owned_by_transfer` had excluded EVERY generic struct; -17 removed that exclusion for the concrete-param case and moved the decision to the callee's own `callee_entry_copies_mono` flag. So this gate is now open for generic structs too, a composition neither row measured on its own. The `memory_sanitizer` figures quoted above are from the REBASED tree, with -17 already in, and the probe matrix was re-run there — not from the pre-rebase tree this fix was developed on. The rebase was a SEMANTIC conflict git merged cleanly and the compiler did not: -17 gave the predicate a `callee_entry_copies_mono` parameter, so the merged tree failed to BUILD (E0061) rather than failing a test — worth noting because the re-run reported it as exit 101 with ZERO test results, the same shape a disk-exhaustion link failure produces in this repo. This gate passes `false` AND excludes generic structs at its own call site: -17 documents the `false` convention for CALL sites, which ask about one callee, and this is a per-TYPE drop synthesis that needs one answer for every death of the type. A generic struct has no such answer (concrete param transfers, monomorph param is entry-copied) and B-2026-08-07-18 is open on a monomorph shape here that miscompiles today, so inheriting -17s widening through a shared predicate would have been an unmeasured change riding on merge order. GATES: `memory_sanitizer` 984 passed / 0 failed at -O2 and 984 / 0 at -O0 (the new fixture is the +1 over the 983 baseline), the -O0 quarantine list still EMPTY. clippy (`--all --all-targets --features llvm -D warnings`) and fmt clean.

title: docs/bug-ledger.jsonl has no pinned JSON encoding, so writers flip it between raw UTF-8 and \uXXXX escapes and each flip rewrites all ~1000 rows
detail:
SHAPE. The ledger is hand-maintained through ad-hoc scripts, and
`json.dumps` escapes non-ASCII by DEFAULT (`ensure_ascii=True`) while
`ensure_ascii=False` leaves it raw. Both produce valid JSONL and both parse
identically, so nothing catches the difference — but a writer using the
opposite convention from the file's current state rewrites EVERY row.

OBSERVED over three consecutive slices on 2026-08-07, in this order:

    main raw UTF-8   -> a writer (mine) escaped it     -> 837 rows rewritten
    main escaped     -> a writer restored raw          -> ~840 rows rewritten
    main raw again   -> ...

Each flip buries a one-line semantic change in an ~840-line diff, makes the
file useless to `git blame`, and guarantees a conflict for any concurrent
lane touching the ledger — which on this repo is most of them.

COST SO FAR is churn and review noise, not data loss: the round-trip is
lossless in both directions and `scripts/bug-lint.sh` passes on both.

THE FIX is a convention plus enforcement, and the enforcement is the part
that matters — a convention nobody can check is what produced the flip.
`scripts/bug-lint.sh` already walks every row; a check that the file
round-trips byte-identically under the chosen `json.dumps` setting is a few
lines there, and it fails loudly on the next writer who picks the other one.

NOT DONE HERE, deliberately: settling it means reformatting all ~1000 rows
once, and doing that inside an unrelated feature slice is exactly the kind of
diff this row is complaining about. It wants its own commit.

WHICH CONVENTION is a genuine (small) choice and not obviously mine to make.
Raw UTF-8 is what the file has held most of the time and what makes it
readable with `grep`; ASCII escapes are what `json.dumps` gives by default,
which is why they keep coming back. Whichever is picked, the lint check is
what makes it stick.

CLOSED. `scripts/bug-ledger-normalize.py` defines the canonical form —
`json.dumps(row, ensure_ascii=False)`, one row per line — and
`scripts/bug-lint.sh` check 6 runs it in `--check` mode, so the convention is
ENFORCED rather than hoped-for. That is the whole fix: a convention nobody can
check is what produced the flip.

RAW UTF-8 was chosen over the `json.dumps` default for one reason that is
about this file specifically: CLAUDE.md's instruction for it is to GREP it
("open bugs are `grep '"status": "open"'`", "grep it by id"), and it is read
by people and by models. Escaped output turns every em-dash in the prose into
`\u2014`, and a grep for a phrase containing one fails outright.

THE FLIP HAPPENED AGAIN WHILE THIS WAS BEING FIXED, which is the best evidence
the row could have asked for. Measured immediately before the change, the file
was fully canonical — 1000 rows, zero differences — so the gate would have
cost no churn at all. One `git merge --ff-only origin/main`, seven commits,
thirty seconds later: 850 of 1000 rows non-canonical. So the normalization
this fix carries is 850 rows, and it is the last one.

The check runs LAST in bug-lint.sh and `set -e` aborts before it on any
content failure — encoding is the least interesting thing to be told about
when a row is actually malformed.

WIRED INTO CI, which the first cut of this fix was not. `bug-lint.sh` was
referenced only by the PR template ("run `./scripts/bug-lint.sh`") and by
CLAUDE.md — an instruction, not a gate, which is exactly the shape of
enforcement that let the encoding drift four times in a day. It now runs as a
step in the `lint` job, beside the Mend scorer self-test: pure python, seconds,
no build. The cross-repo kata link check needs kara-katas, which CI does not
have, so it degrades to a warning there and this gate covers the same-repo
rules only (B-ID uniqueness, the controlled enums, canonical encoding).
Verified with the kata repo absent and `KARA_KATAS_DIR` unset — the invocation
CI makes — exit 0.

fix: No karac change, and none is available -- this row closes by measurement and decision, not by a commit. All four directions are now closed. (1) A cheaper instruction sequence: karac emits the SAME `llvm.s{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow` intrinsic rustc does, so there is nothing to diff at the IR level. (2) Trap-block placement: already outlined `cold` + `noinline` + `noreturn`, ending in `unreachable`. (3) Range analysis: BUILT AND REJECTED 2026-07-03 (`docs/spikes/overflow-check-elision.md`), with the rejection promoted into design.md § Arithmetic Overflow as a standing decision. (4) The vectorizable checked reduction this row proposed: ILLEGAL -- checked add is non-associative, so partitioning a reduction into lanes deletes traps the language promises. Counterexample runs at HEAD: over [2^62, 2^62, -2^62, -2^62] the sequential form panics with integer overflow (exit 1) and the 2-lane form prints 0 (exit 0). Branchless reformulations do not rescue a reduction either (0 ymm for all three under clang 18 -O3 -mavx2, against a wrapping control at 8), because the overflow flag still depends on the sequential prefix. design.md already prices the residual as "the gap IS the guarantee, not a defect" and names `wrapping_*` plus the deferred scoped `#[wrapping]` region as the sanctioned levers. The elementwise sibling shape, which IS legal and DOES vectorize, is filed separately as B-2026-08-07-21.
tracker: Attributed by matched-pair ladder under B-2026-08-05-34 (arm64 M5 Pro, 2026-08-07). Mechanism commit e4047440 (2026-06-07, AOT integer arithmetic faults), parent ad240cad. NOT a revert candidate and NOT a correctness defect -- at equal safety kāra TIES rustc on this kata (191.4 vs 191.4 ms). The gap is that kāra's i64 overflow check costs 1.309x of its own unchecked baseline where rustc's costs 1.131x of its own, which spends a 1.16x lead kāra otherwise has. Corpus-wide equal-safety data ALREADY EXISTS (Kara/ovf_equal_safety_triage.tsv, 56 rows, kara/ovf median 0.999) and corroborates the tie from a different instrument; what it lacks is a kara-unchecked column, which is what this row's claim rests on. Next step: an IR/asm diff of the smulh+cmp-asr#63 sequence against what rustc emits for the same checked multiply, on the 25-of-56 subset where rustc actually pays for its check.
title: RESOLVED, NOT A DEFECT: the i64 OVERFLOW CHECK's real cost is LOST AUTO-VECTORIZATION -- the trap branch is a second loop exit, so kara drops from AVX2 16-wide to scalar on a `Vec[i64]` reduction (8.24x its own unchecked; rustc 3.74x) while costing exactly 2 instructions (rustc 3) on a non-vectorizable loop -- and the fix this row proposed, a VECTORIZABLE CHECKED REDUCTION, is ILLEGAL: checked add is non-associative, so lane-partitioning deletes traps the language promises (counterexample runs -- sequential panics, 2-lane prints 0). Removing the branch does not help a reduction either; the flag depends on the sequential prefix. Range analysis was already built and rejected; leads (1)/(2) discharged. Equal-safety TIE (#11) / kara ahead (reduction), reproduced on x86_64. Elementwise sibling split out as B-2026-08-07-21
detail:
SURFACED BY the B-2026-08-05-34 base-commit correction. That row's corpus regression, once measured from the CORRECT per-kata base, is substantially one commit -- e4047440 (2026-06-07), "feat(codegen): AOT integer arithmetic faults -- overflow/div-zero/MIN-div traps" -- costing 1.306x on kata #11, 1.204x on #8, 1.151x on #9. See that row for the full ladder and for why the earlier audit missed it entirely (it bisected from a base four hours AFTER the commit).

THE EQUAL-SAFETY REFRAME COMES FIRST, because it decides what this row is and is not. BENCHMARKS.md already requires comparing against `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on`, since kāra checks integer overflow by default and stock `rustc -O` silently wraps. Applying that rule to #11 on the same host, same session, all four binaries sink-verified at 4897500000, hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 30, BOTH ORDERS:

  kara @ad240cad (unchecked)         146.3 ms   sd 0.4-0.5
  rustc -O       (unchecked)         169.3      sd 1.0-2.1
  kara @main     (CHECKED)           191.4      sd 0.9-1.4
  rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on     191.4      sd 0.5-0.6

SO AT EQUAL SAFETY THIS IS A DEAD TIE -- 191.4 vs 191.4, order-independent. There is NO product-level regression here and nothing to revert: e4047440 bought a guarantee the mirrors still do not have. That is the honest headline and it should be the one quoted.

WHAT THIS ROW IS. The two languages do not pay the same PRICE for the same guarantee:

  kāra   146.3 -> 191.4   its check costs 1.309x of its own baseline
  rustc  169.3 -> 191.4   its check costs 1.131x of its own baseline

kāra's unchecked code is 1.16x FASTER than rustc's unchecked code (146.3 vs 169.3) and the dearer check spends exactly that lead. If kāra's check cost what rustc's costs, #11 would land near 165 ms and kāra would be ~1.16x AHEAD of equal-safety Rust rather than tied. That is the headroom this row is about, and it is a commercial number, not a cosmetic one: "ties Rust at equal safety" and "beats Rust by 16% at equal safety" are different sentences to a buyer.

WHAT SPECIFICALLY SURVIVES ON MAIN, from the disassembly rather than inferred. `max_area_off` is inlined into `_main`; counting the checked-arithmetic patterns in that function across the three builds:

  build             _main instrs   smulh   adds/subs   b.vs   cmp-asr#63
  ad240cad (pre)         89          0         0         0        0
  e4047440 (post)       138          1         1         1        1
  727f7c6d (main)       105          1         1         1        1

Later elision work (B-2026-06-16-1, B-2026-07-26-1, B-2026-08-05-21, B-2026-07-17-1) removed 33 static instructions from this function but left the checked-multiply sequence intact -- and left the wall time UNCHANGED to three figures (190.85 ms at e4047440, 190.85 at main). So the residual is specifically the i64 MULTIPLY check on `let area: i64 = h * (r - l)` in the two-pointer inner loop: `smulh` for the high word, a `cmp` against `asr #63` of the low word, and a branch to the trap block.

WHY IT IS NOT TRIVIALLY ELIDABLE, stated so the next person does not start with the wrong plan. The values genuinely are small -- the kata's own comment notes heights are LCG-mod-50 so the worst-case area is w*49 = 784 -- but proving that needs value-range facts flowing out of a `Vec[i64]` fill loop and through an index read, which is interprocedural range analysis kāra does not have. The existing elision rows all discharge a LOCAL fact (a bounds check already proven, a loop counter bounded by its own guard). This one is not that shape.

SO THE LIKELIER WIN IS LOWERING, NOT ELISION: emit the same guarantee more cheaply. Unmeasured, and in rough order of cost: (1) diff the emitted sequence against what rustc emits for a checked i64 multiply on arm64 -- the 1.131x-vs-1.309x split says rustc is doing something cheaper for the SAME check, and that difference is readable rather than theoretical; (2) check whether the trap block's placement forces a taken-branch or defeats the predictor, which on this host is worth real time (see B-2026-08-07-10, where placement alone was 1.09x on an unrelated kata); (3) only then consider range analysis.

THE CORPUS-WIDE EQUAL-SAFETY SWEEP ALREADY EXISTS AND INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATES THE TIE. `Kara/ovf_equal_safety_triage.tsv` (56 rows, instruction counts, from the SWEEP_TRACKER_v2 triage behind B-2026-07-18-8) compares kara against `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on` across the corpus. Its kara/ovf median is 0.999 -- a corpus-wide DEAD TIE -- with 22 katas ahead, 11 tied and 23 behind. #11's row there is kara/ovf = 0.999, matching the 191.4-vs-191.4 wall-time tie measured here from a DIFFERENT instrument (instructions vs wall clock) in a different session. So "kara ties equal-safety Rust" is not a one-kata result and should be stated as the corpus position.

WHAT THAT SWEEP CANNOT SETTLE, which is precisely this row. It has no kara-UNCHECKED column -- only kara, rustc -O, and rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on. The 1.309x-vs-1.131x split is a comparison of each language against ITS OWN unchecked build, so nothing in the tsv speaks to it. That measurement exists here only because the B-2026-08-05-34 ladder happened to build a pre-e4047440 kara. GENERALIZING THE LOWERING GAP THEREFORE STILL NEEDS WORK: re-run the triage with a fourth column from a kara built at ad240cad (or behind a check-suppressing lever, which does not currently exist), and the question is answered corpus-wide.

TWO THINGS IN THAT TSV WORTH FOLLOWING, both cross-linked rather than chased here. (1) Its single WORST equal-safety row is #1665 greedy at kara/ovf 3.100 -- and the B-2026-08-05-34 ladder attributes #1665's regression to 2406bab8's lean panic-free sort (3.41 -> 19.77 ms, partly recovered to 4.56 on main), so that outlier is a SORT cost, not an overflow cost, and belongs to lean-sort follow-up rather than here. (2) rustc's own check is free (ovf/O <= 1.005) on 31 of 56 rows, median 1.004, so LLVM elides most of them outright; #11 is one of the rows where rustc actually pays (1.068 on instructions). The interesting comparison for lowering work is that subset, not the corpus median.

CAVEAT ON THIS ROW'S OWN MEASUREMENT, because one kata is one kata. The 1.309x-vs-1.131x split is measured on #11's inner loop, which is unusually arithmetic-dense (a multiply, two compares and two increments per step, no allocation, no calls). #8 (1.204x) and #9 (1.151x) move the same direction against the same pre-trap base; #71 is flat.

── x86_64 COUNTERPART MEASURED (2026-08-07); THE RATIO INVERTS, AND TWO OF THE
   THREE PROPOSED LEADS ARE ALREADY DISCHARGED ──

NO FIX. What this adds is the fourth column this row says is missing, a lever it
says does not exist, and a bound on how far its headline generalizes.

THE LEVER EXISTS AFTER ALL, in the source rather than the compiler. This row
asks for "a kara built at ad240cad (or behind a check-suppressing lever, which
does not currently exist)". `wrapping_add` / `wrapping_sub` / `wrapping_mul` are
already lowered to bare `add`/`sub`/`mul` with no intrinsic and no trap branch
(`method_call.rs`), so rewriting a kernel's hot arithmetic in them IS a
check-suppressing lever for that kernel. Not equivalent to a pre-trap COMPILER
-- checks elsewhere in the program remain -- but exact for the measured loop,
which is what the ratio needs. That makes the fourth column reproducible on any
host without building an old compiler.

INSTRUMENT AND CAVEATS, stated before the numbers. Deterministic INSTRUCTION
COUNTS (`valgrind --tool=callgrind`), not wall clock, on x86_64 in a 4-core
container where wall clock would not be trustworthy. This row's own numbers are
arm64 wall clock. Instruction counts are the same instrument
`Kara/ovf_equal_safety_triage.tsv` uses, so they are comparable to that, not to
the hyperfine ladder above.

CONTROL A -- PURE ARITHMETIC, no indexing, structurally identical loops in both
languages (`acc = (acc + (i % 97) * (seed + 3)) % 1000003`, 20,000,000
iterations). This is the clean measurement because the only difference between
the four binaries is the check:

    kara  unchecked (all-wrapping)      450,306,993
    kara  CHECKED                       490,307,973    1.0888x of its own base
    rustc -O                            460,373,556
    rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on      520,373,628    1.1303x of its own base

    Per iteration the deltas are exact: kara's check adds 2.000 instructions,
    rustc's adds 3.000.

    Equal safety: 490.3M vs 520.4M -- kara/ovf = 0.942, i.e. kara ~6% AHEAD.

SO ON x86_64 THE RATIO INVERTS. This row's headline is that kara's check costs
1.309x of its own baseline against rustc's 1.131x -- kara's ~2.4x dearer,
relatively. On x86_64, measured the same way, it is 1.089x against 1.130x and
kara's check is the CHEAPER one. The headline is therefore an ARM64 finding, and
the row should say so; nothing here contradicts the arm64 measurement, it bounds
its scope.

CONTROL B -- THE #11 SHAPE (two-pointer over an LCG-mod-50 `Vec[i64]`, `hh * (r
- l)`, 1,999,800 inner iterations, all four binaries sink-verified at 97804000):

    kara  unchecked (all-wrapping)       36,555,074
    kara  CHECKED                        40,516,145    1.1084x
    rustc -O                             24,628,880
    rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on       40,637,332    1.6500x

    Equal safety: 40.52M vs 40.64M -- kara/ovf = 0.997, a DEAD TIE. That
    independently reproduces this row's arm64 wall-clock tie (191.4 vs 191.4)
    and the tsv's 0.999 median, on a third instrument and a different ISA.

    kara's check again adds 1.98 instructions per inner iteration -- the same
    ~2 as Control A, so the check's cost is stable across both shapes.

    DO NOT read rustc's 1.65x here as "rustc's check costs 8 instructions per
    iteration". Its unchecked build is 24.6M against kara's 36.6M, so the two
    baselines are not the same loop; turning checks on evidently also costs
    rustc some optimisation it had in the unchecked build. The honest statement
    is that the DELTA is not purely the check on rustc's side in this shape,
    which is exactly why Control A exists.

THE REAL x86_64 HEADROOM IN THE #11 SHAPE IS THE BASELINE LOOP, NOT THE CHECK,
and Control A is what proves it: with arithmetic alone kara's unchecked build is
2% AHEAD of rustc's (450.3M vs 460.4M), but in the #11 shape it is 1.48x BEHIND
(36.6M vs 24.6M). The difference between the two controls is `Vec` indexing and
loop structure, so that is where the x86_64 gap lives. Overflow is not the
subject on this ISA.

LEADS (1) AND (2) FROM THIS ROW ARE ALREADY DISCHARGED -- recorded so the next
person does not spend a day rediscovering it:

  * (1) "diff the emitted sequence against what rustc emits for a checked i64
    multiply". There is nothing to diff at the IR level: `emit_checked_int_arith`
    (`expr_ops.rs`) emits `llvm.smul.with.overflow.i64` -- the SAME intrinsic
    rustc emits -- and lets LLVM lower it per target. Any arm64 sequence
    difference is therefore downstream of identical IR, which makes it a
    surrounding-context question (what facts LLVM has) rather than a lowering
    choice kara makes.
  * (2) "check whether the trap block's placement forces a taken-branch". The
    panic landing pad is ALREADY outlined: `emit_panic` (`runtime.rs`) emits a
    per-site zero-arg `internal` function marked `cold` + `noinline` +
    `noreturn`, with every operand baked inside the outlined body specifically
    to keep the inline cost minimal, and the trap block ends in `unreachable`
    -- which LLVM's own branch-probability heuristic already treats as
    near-never-taken. There is no obvious placement win left to take.

WHAT REMAINS, then, is narrower than the row implied: on arm64 the question is
why identical IR lowers dearer relative to baseline there, and the answer is
likely about what LLVM can prove around the multiply rather than about the
multiply itself -- i.e. lead (3), range facts, which the row already flags as
the expensive one. On x86_64 the check is a non-issue and the `Vec`-indexing
baseline gap is the thing worth measuring next.

REPRODUCTION for whoever picks this up: the four kernels and the exact commands
are trivial to rebuild -- two `.kara` files (plain vs all-`wrapping_*`) and one
`.rs` built twice, each run under `valgrind --tool=callgrind`. No corpus, no
hyperfine, no arm64 host required.

── THE MECHANISM, FOUND (2026-08-07): THE CHECK BLOCKS AUTO-VECTORIZATION ──

Still no fix. But the cost is now explained rather than described, and the
explanation retires this row's proposed fix directions.

THE CHECK'S COST IS BIMODAL, which is why one ratio never fitted everything:

  * On a loop that CANNOT vectorize, it is ~2 instructions. Measured exactly:
    the pure-arithmetic control above adds 2.000 instructions per iteration for
    kara and 3.000 for rustc. Cheap, and kara's is the cheaper one.
  * On a loop that CAN vectorize, it costs the entire vector speedup, because
    the trap branch is a SECOND EXIT from the loop body and LLVM will not
    vectorize a multi-exit loop.

THE SECOND CASE, measured on a hoist-proof reduction (`s = s + (h[i] ^ t)` over
a `Vec[i64]`, 20,000,000 element-ops, callgrind Ir, x86_64):

    kara  wrapping (no check)        12,998,697    0.65 instr/elem
    kara  CHECKED                   107,130,636    5.36            8.24x
    rustc -O                         45,650,056    2.28
    rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on  170,572,108    8.53            3.74x

READ OFF THE DISASSEMBLY, not inferred. kara's wrapping build is AVX2 with four
accumulators, 16 elements per iteration:

    vpxor  -0xe0(%r14,%rdx,8),%ymm0,%ymm5
    vpaddq %ymm1,%ymm5,%ymm1            (x8, unrolled)

kara's CHECKED build of the same source is scalar, 3x unrolled, with the trap
branch after every add:

    mov  -0x10(%r14,%rsi,8),%rdi
    xor  %rdx,%rdi
    add  %r8,%rdi
    jo   8fdc                            <-- the second exit
    ...

AND THE BOUNDS CHECK IS ALREADY GONE in both -- there is no compare against the
length anywhere in either loop. kara's bounds-check elimination is doing its job
here; the only thing standing between this loop and AVX2 is the overflow trap.

THIS REFRAMES THE ROW'S HEADLINE RATHER THAN CONTRADICTING IT. The 1.309x vs
1.131x split is real, and the 8.24x vs 3.74x here is the same phenomenon at
larger amplitude: a language's relative check cost scales with HOW MUCH
VECTORIZATION IT HAD TO GIVE UP. kara's is dearer relatively because kara's
unchecked code vectorizes better -- it has more to lose. This row already
observed the fact ("kara's unchecked code is 1.16x FASTER ... and the dearer
check spends exactly that lead") without naming the cause; the cause is the
vectorizer, and "kara's check is 2.4x dearer per unit of guarantee" is therefore
the wrong way to say it. Nothing is being lowered badly.

EQUAL SAFETY ON THIS KERNEL STILL FAVOURS kara: 5.36 instr/elem against rustc's
8.53 (default target) or 7.78 (`-C target-cpu=native`), so ~1.45-1.59x ahead --
robust to the target-cpu confound, which was checked precisely because kara
emitted AVX2 while rustc defaults to the SSE2 baseline.

DO NOT QUOTE AN UNCHECKED CROSS-LANGUAGE RATIO FROM THIS KERNEL. `rustc -O -C
target-cpu=native` collapses it to 0.03 instr/elem -- it hoists the reduction
out entirely -- and two earlier attempts at this kernel were silently hoisted
the same way (`t + sum(h)` is decomposable, so seeding the accumulator with `t`
does not defeat it; the body itself has to depend on `t`). Only the
SELF-RELATIVE ratios and the equal-safety comparison survive that.

LEADS (1) AND (2) CANNOT RECOVER ANY OF THIS, on top of already being
discharged: a cheaper instruction sequence and a better-placed trap block both
leave the loop multi-exit, so the vectorizer still refuses. Lead (3), range
analysis, WOULD work where it applies -- proving no overflow deletes the branch
and restores vectorization -- which raises its value above what this row
estimated, though not its cost.

THE DIRECT FIX IS A VECTORIZABLE CHECKED REDUCTION: recognise the
`s = s + <elem>` accumulate-over-container shape and emit a vector add with the
overflow test done ONCE PER CHUNK (or in a widened accumulator) instead of once
per element, keeping the guarantee and the single loop exit. That is a real
piece of work, but it is the only one of the four directions that addresses the
measured mechanism, and it would apply to every reduction in the corpus rather
than to one multiply in kata #11.

── RESOLVED 2026-08-07: ALL FOUR DIRECTIONS CLOSED; THE PROPOSED FIX IS ILLEGAL ──

No compiler change. This row closes because its own last open direction -- the
"vectorizable checked reduction" the previous section recommended -- turns out
not to be a missing optimization but an ILLEGAL one, and the other three were
already discharged or already rejected on the record.

(4) A VECTORIZABLE CHECKED REDUCTION IS UNSOUND, PROVEN BY COUNTEREXAMPLE.
Checked addition is NOT ASSOCIATIVE: `(a+b)+c` can trap where `a+(b+c)` does
not. Vectorizing a reduction reassociates it into per-lane partial sums, so it
changes WHICH PROGRAMS TRAP. It is a semantics change wearing an optimization's
clothes. Two kara programs over the same four-element input (A = 2^62, giving
[A, A, -A, -A]), run at HEAD:

    reassoc.kara        s = s + v[i]              (sequential prefix)
      -> panic at reassoc.kara:14:19 in main: integer overflow    exit 1

    reassoc_lanes.kara  l0 += v[i]; l1 += v[i+1]  (two interleaved lanes)
      -> 0                                                        exit 0

Same input, same mathematical sum (zero). The sequential form overflows at step
2 (2^62 + 2^62 = 2^63 > i64::MAX); every 2-lane or 4-lane partition of that
input keeps all partials in range. So the transform would silently delete a
trap the language promises -- precisely the "we promised it traps on overflow
and it didn't" hole that the overflow-elision spike rejected the prover for.

AND FOR A REDUCTION THE BRANCH IS NOT THE BLOCKER -- THE DEPENDENCE IS. Measured
with clang 18 -O3 -mavx2 over five formulations of the same loop, counting ymm
references in the emitted function (a plain wrapping reduction control
vectorizes at 8, so the harness is known good):

    reduction,   per-element trap branch    (what karac emits)       0
    reduction,   OR-accumulated flag        (branchless, intrinsic)  0
    reduction,   OR-accumulated sign-trick  (branchless, pure int)   0
    ELEMENTWISE, OR-accumulated flag        (branchless, intrinsic)  0
    ELEMENTWISE, OR-accumulated sign-trick  (branchless, pure int)  36

Removing the branch does NOT restore vectorization for a reduction. The
overflow flag still depends on the sequential prefix `s`, which is the
non-associativity above reappearing in the dependence graph. There is no
reformulation left to reach for: the branch, the intrinsic and the flag are all
downstream of a dependence that vectorizing must break.

(3) RANGE ANALYSIS WAS ALREADY BUILT AND REJECTED, on 2026-07-03, in
`docs/spikes/overflow-check-elision.md` -- two prototype layers on branch
`feat-overflow-elision`. Layer 1 is redundant with LLVM's own
correlated-value-propagation (identical machine code, 1.00x); layer 2 works and
is also 1.00x; the residual is `bounded counter x unbounded heap element`,
needing array-content plus trip-count analysis. The rejection is not just a
spike note -- it is promoted into design.md § Arithmetic Overflow as a standing
decision ("do not grow the prover"). The previous section rated lead (3)'s
value UP on the strength of the vectorization finding; that re-rating is
withdrawn, because it was premised on (4) being the cheaper sibling of the same
idea, and (4) does not exist.

(1) AND (2) were discharged in the previous section: karac emits the same
`llvm.s{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow` intrinsic rustc does, and the trap block is
already outlined `cold` + `noinline` + `noreturn` and ends in `unreachable`.

THE SPEC ALREADY PRICES THIS AND CALLS IT CORRECT. design.md § Arithmetic
Overflow independently states the same ~1.2-1.3x on arithmetic-heavy kernels,
states that against `rustc -C overflow-checks=on` kara is level, and concludes
that "the gap IS the guarantee, not a defect" -- with the sanctioned levers
being the existing LOCAL `wrapping_*` family and the deferred scoped
`#[wrapping]` region (deferred.md), never a project-wide switch. Everything
this row measured corroborates that position on a third instrument and a second
ISA. Nothing here is a defect, and nothing actionable is left.

WHAT DOES SURVIVE IS SPLIT OUT AS B-2026-08-07-21: the ELEMENTWISE shape
(`out[i] = a[i] + t`, no loop-carried arithmetic dependence) loses
vectorization for the same reason but is LEGAL to fix, because per-element
overflow conditions are order-independent -- and the table above shows that
form does vectorize. Different legality conditions, different fix, so it does
not belong on this row.
