The callee owns by transfer (B-2026-08-05-33) whose comment calls the caller's retraction "the whole safety argument", but that retraction keys on a MOVED NAMED BINDING and a fresh temp is not one. The named spelling is clean. No `Option`, no pattern, callee body `1`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while controlling for B-2026-08-07-12 leg 1, which turned
out to be a symptom of this. Verified pre-existing by measuring with that row's
fix stashed -- identical error counts.

SHAPE, and there is nothing exotic in it:

    struct S { a: String, m: Map[String, i64] }
    fn ig(x: S) -> i64 { 1 }

    let mut mm: Map[String, i64] = Map.new(); mm.insert(k, v);
    ig(S { a: f"a{n}", m: mm })          -> 480 valgrind errors, 175 invalid
                                            frees at -O2 (19 at -O0)

    ... let s: S = S { a: .., m: mm }; ig(s)     -> CLEAN

A FRESH TEMP corrupts and the NAMED BINDING does not. That asymmetry is the
whole bug.

MECHANISM, read off the stacks rather than inferred. `__karac_drop_struct_S`
runs in BOTH frames over the same allocation -- once from `main` and once from
`ig` -- and what it double-frees is the `String` field `a`.

  * THE CALLEE owns by transfer. `param_own`'s non-copy-supported struct arm
    (B-2026-08-05-33) registers a drop WITHOUT an entry copy for a struct
    `field_copy_supported` refuses, which a `Map` field guarantees ("Heap the
    outer-buffer copy can't duplicate -> bail"). Its comment states the
    invariant: "Held in LOCKSTEP with the caller's retraction, which is the
    whole safety argument."
  * THE CALLER does not retract. That retraction is
    `move_declined_copy_struct_arg`, which keys on a MOVED NAMED BINDING -- the
    thing a fresh temp is not. Meanwhile the caller's own registrar fires on
    `aggregate_has_heap_field`, which the `String` field satisfies. So the temp
    gets an owner on one side and is transferred on the other.

The lockstep holds for the named spelling, which is why that arm is clean, and
that is also why this survived: the shape it breaks on is the one with no
binding to name.

WHY HIGH. `struct { String, Map }` is ordinary Kāra, the corruption is at the
DEFAULT -O2, and it needs no pattern, no match, and no `Option` -- a callee
whose body is `1` reproduces it. The error count (480) reflects the heap being
walked after a free, not one stray pointer.

WHERE TO START: the two halves must agree on one predicate, the same way
B-2026-08-07-12's copy and drop were made to. Either the caller's registrar
learns the callee-owns-by-transfer case (do not register), or the callee's arm
learns that a fresh temp was not "moved in" by the channel it relies on. The
first looks right -- ownership DID transfer, so the caller has nothing to own --
but the retraction and the registration live in different files and currently
answer different questions.

CAUTION: getting this backwards turns corruption into a leak of the whole
struct, which is the safe direction but not the fix. Measure both spellings
(fresh temp AND named binding) at BOTH opt levels, and include a struct with a
`Vec`/`String`-only field set as the control -- those ARE copy-supported, take
the other branch entirely, and must stay byte-identical.

── FIXED (db16f10); the row's own first option was the right one ──

"Either the caller's registrar learns the callee-owns-by-transfer case (do not
register), or the callee's arm learns that a fresh temp was not 'moved in' by
the channel it relies on. The first looks right." It was. Ownership DID
transfer, so the caller has nothing to own, and the caller is also the side that
can be asked cheaply — the callee's arm would have had to learn the shape of the
argument expression, which it never sees.

WHAT LANDED. One predicate, `struct_param_owned_by_transfer`
(`src/codegen/param_own.rs`), is the B-2026-08-05-33 arm's conditions read from
the caller's side, and `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst`'s struct arm
consults it before registering. Both halves now answer from ONE predicate,
which is the same resolution B-2026-08-07-12 used for its copy and its drop.

The head of that struct arm carried the stale claim and is corrected in place:
"whenever its drop frees a buffer the callee either entry-copies (independent)
or caller-retains (shares, never frees)". Exhaustive when written; -08-05-33
added the third case underneath it without revisiting it.

STRICTLY NARROWER THAN THE RETRACTION ALREADY SHIPPING, which is the safety
argument worth keeping. `move_declined_copy_struct_arg` — the identifier half of
the lockstep, live since B-2026-07-28-4 — excludes shared-owning structs only.

  * SELF-REFERENTIAL structs. The callee's arm declines them (B-2026-07-28-3:
    it may store the alias into an owning container), so ownership does NOT
    transfer and the caller must keep its drop. The identifier retraction does
    not exclude them, and that asymmetry is a KNOWN leak the callee arm's
    comment records ("That leak stays, unchanged") — not widened here.
  * GENERIC structs. The callee's arm tries
    `try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned` FIRST, and that rescue reads

    struct with no type params can never take the rescue, so excluding them
    makes the two agree by construction instead of by luck. It also keeps the
    monomorph path's `mono_inst` (only ever `Some` for a generic struct, and

MEASURED, 10 iterations, valgrind, BOTH opt levels. The before-column was

    { a: String, m: Map[String,i64] }  fresh temp   480 errs  -> clean
    { a: Vec[i64], m: Map[..] }        fresh temp   480 errs  -> clean
    { a: String, s: Set[i64] }         fresh temp    90 errs  -> clean
    same, via a METHOD                 fresh temp   480 errs  -> clean
    same, via a GENERIC fn             fresh temp   480 errs  -> clean
    { m: Map[..] } (no sibling heap)   fresh temp   clean     -> clean
    { a: String, m: Map[..] }          NAMED        clean     -> clean
    { a: String, m: Map[..] }          `ref` param  clean     -> clean
    { a: String, m: Map[..] }          ref LITERAL  clean     -> clean

title: the x86 hash-tag probe spills 2 of the caller's registers per key-probe (4 memory ops) because `ctrl` puts the loop one value over x86-64's 15 GPRs — diagnosed exactly; the obvious fix (free a register by bounding the probe on `mask` instead of `cap`) WINS 3.8% on kata:170 and LOSES 10.7% on kata:217, so it is reverted and the spill stands — RESOLVED AS PRICED, NOT FIXED: the two remaining levers (drop the bound test; walk the slot directly) were built and measured too. `SlotWalk` REMOVES the spill outright (kata:170's `main` goes from 5 stack stores + 3 reloads to 1 + 0) and is worth only 2.8%, while both forms lose on kata:217 again — the removed bound test was a perfectly-predicted branch (502 M of them, ~0 mispredicts saved) and freeing its register spilled the OUTER loop's counter instead (+181 M L1 loads). The probe loop is memory-bound, so its instruction budget is not the cost
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the loose thread left by B-2026-08-06-33, which measured the spill but did not chase it.

THE SPILL, now pinned exactly. On kata:170 the tag-on binary performs 2.00 stores per key-probe (403.2 M against tag-off's 42.8 K total). Disassembly of `main` (with `find` inlined) shows them on the COMMON path of the probe: `mov %bl,0x7(%rsp)` + `mov %rcx,0x8(%rsp)` ahead of the probe loop, reloaded at both exits — 2 stores + 2 reloads per key. The tag-off build's same region has ZERO stores; `found` stays in `%bpl` throughout. So it is a genuine register spill, not an artifact of the measurement.

CAUSE. The tag holds `ctrl` live across the probe loop, on top of the 6 values the loop already carries (probe accumulator, trip counter, mask, status ptr, kv ptr, key). That is one over what x86-64's 15 GPRs can hold together with the caller's live values, so the allocator evicts two of the CALLER's. This is an x86-64 phenomenon: arm64 has 31 GPRs and does not spill here.

RULED OUT: the optimizer. `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=3` leaves the spill in place and is wall-clock identical to -O2 (3865.8 vs 3869.2 ms min, interleaved). LLVM will not fix this on its own.

THE FIX THAT WAS BUILT AND REJECTED. The probe's bound test `i >= cap` keeps `cap` live across the loop ALONGSIDE `mask` (which the slot computation needs every iteration) — two long-lived registers for one quantity, since `mask == cap - 1`. Rewriting it as `i > mask` kills `cap` at the point `mask` is computed, giving the allocator back exactly the register the tag took. It is safe: `KaracMap::new` allocates `INITIAL_CAPACITY = 16` and `next_capacity` only doubles, so the `cap == 0` case that separates the two forms (mask underflows to u64::MAX and `i > mask` never fires) cannot arise, and the probe already stakes correctness on that same power-of-two invariant by masking instead of taking a remainder. It also deletes a `cap == 0` guard LLVM was emitting ahead of every probe that could never be taken.

It works as designed and is still not worth shipping. Clean control — SAME compiler tree, only this change toggled, `karac build` default (tag on), `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, strictly interleaved, min/median, sinks verified:
  kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` full-scan lookups   0.962 / 0.962  (3.8% FASTER)
  kata:128 `Set[i64]` scaled                  0.982 / 0.987  (1.8% faster)
  kata:217 `Set[i64]` fresh set per window    1.107 / 1.089  (10.7% SLOWER)
A 10.7% regression on a real kata against a 3.8% gain is a net loss, so it is REVERTED. The rejected patch is a one-line predicate change at the three LOOKUP probe sites (`IntPredicate::UGE, i_val, cap` -> `UGT, i_val, mask`); anyone re-deriving it should read this row first. It was verified green on the full suite before being rejected on perf alone (13,217 tests, 0 failures, including 2835 codegen E2E and 974 memory_sanitizer under LSan) — the revert is not a correctness story.

TWO THINGS THE ATTEMPT ESTABLISHED, both worth keeping:
 (1) Freeing the register does NOT remove the spill. The tag-on build still spills two values per probe after the change — LLVM simply spends the freed register elsewhere. kata:170's 3.8% came from the cheaper loop, not from the spill going away. So "give the allocator one more register" is not a route to killing this spill.
 (2) The sign is WORKLOAD-dependent, not site-dependent. The first cut of the fix suspected the two INSERT probes (kata:217 is insert-heavy, 191 M inserts) and excluded them; kata:217 still lost 10.7%, so the loss is in the LOOKUP probe that kata:170 gains from. Two Set/Map lookup workloads, opposite signs, same code change.

METHOD NOTE, and it cost a false result on the way: the first old-vs-new comparison used binaries from a compiler that ALSO predated 11 unrelated upstream commits, which conflates this change with theirs. The numbers above are from a baseline rebuilt at the same HEAD with only this change stashed. Any re-run must do the same.

STILL OPEN, because the spill is real and unfixed. The untried lever with the best odds: a LOOKUP probe provably cannot run out of buckets — the insert path grows whenever `(len + tombstones + 1) * 4 > capacity * 3` (`runtime/src/map.rs`), so at least 1/4 of buckets are EMPTY at all times and the probe always terminates on one. That makes the lookup bound test DEAD CODE, and removing it would free the trip counter as well as delete two instructions per iteration — strictly more than the `mask` trick recovered. It was not attempted here because it trades a robustness property (a corrupt or externally-built table would spin forever instead of terminating) and deserves its own measurement across the same kata set, kata:217 INCLUDED — this row's whole lesson is that kata:170 alone does not decide a probe-loop change.

── THE MEASUREMENT LANE EXISTS NOW (2026-08-07), THE FIX DOES NOT ──

This row's blocker was never the diagnosis — it was that deciding a probe-loop
change needs kata:170 AND 128 AND 217, and no session had the corpus. That is
resolved and recorded here so nobody rebuilds it:

  * `karalang/kara-katas` attaches cleanly to a Claude Code session via
    `add_repo` (read access is served anonymously; push needs access:"push").
  * All three katas build and run with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`. Native
    wall time on a 4-core x86 container: 170 = 4179 ms (sink 762965, matching
    this row's recorded sink), 128 = 167 ms (sink 2364), 217 = 5081 ms
    (sink 27979).
  * `bench/bench.sh` is NOT usable here — it requires hyperfine, rustc, clang
    and go, and this container has none of them. Neither `hyperfine` nor `perf`
    is installed. `valgrind` IS, so the instrument is
    `valgrind --tool=cachegrind --cache-sim=no --branch-sim=no`, which is the
    right one anyway: instruction counts are immune to the container noise that
    makes this host unable to settle a wall-clock ratio (B-2026-08-05-5
    measured 4.5% apparent effect in an A/A control at a 257 ms workload, and
    kata 128 is a 167 ms workload).
  * COST WARNING, learned by having a run killed: cachegrind is ~50x, so 170
    and 217 are 3-5 MINUTES each per build. Six runs for one A/B. Run them
    detached with a generous timeout; a backgrounded script died mid-run here.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE DECISION CRITERION. The rejected `mask` patch was
judged on WALL CLOCK (0.962 / 0.982 / 1.107). This lane cannot reproduce that
instrument. A re-decision on instruction counts is a DIFFERENT measurement and
must be reported as one — B-2026-08-05-5 is the precedent: on that row the two
instruments disagreed in SIGN, and the disagreement turned out to be the real
story. Do not quote an instruction-count verdict as if it settled the
wall-clock question.

THE UNTRIED LEVER, now located in code. The lookup probes are in
`src/codegen/mono.rs` — the `// ── probe.cond: PHI for i; bound-check vs cap`
blocks (three of them; the two carrying extra `first_tomb` state are the INSERT
probes and must keep their bound). Each emits
`IntPredicate::UGE, i_val, cap -> not_found_bb`. Deleting that conditional in
favour of an unconditional branch to `probe_body_bb` is the minimal form.

A BIGGER VARIANT WORTH PRICING AT THE SAME TIME, not attempted: the loop
carries `i` only to compute `slot = (start + i) & mask`. Walking the slot
directly (`slot = (slot + 1) & mask`) retires `i`, `start` AND `cap` — three
long-lived values against the one the rejected `mask` trick recovered. Since
finding (1) above says freeing ONE register did not remove the spill, a
three-register change is the first variant with a plausible mechanism for
actually removing it.

STILL OPEN. Nothing was changed in the compiler for this row.

── BOTH REMAINING LEVERS BUILT, MEASURED AND REJECTED 1d0fe05d; ROW CLOSED ──

WHAT SHIPPED IS NOT A SPEEDUP. `KARAC_MAP_PROBE` (an A/B lever) plus the three
LOOKUP probe sites folded into one `emit_lookup_probe_cursor` helper, so the
probe form is one edit rather than three kept in sync by hand. The default
`Bounded` form emits BYTE-IDENTICAL binaries to the pre-refactor compiler on
all three katas (`cmp`-verified), which is what lets every number below isolate
the form change alone — the control this row's first measurement lacked when it
compared across 11 unrelated commits.

THE TWO FORMS. `Unbounded` deletes the `i >= cap` test (this row's "minimal
form"). `SlotWalk` additionally walks the bucket index itself, retiring `i`,
`start` AND `cap` (this row's "bigger variant worth pricing"). Both rest on the
runtime's growth guard leaving at least 1/4 of buckets EMPTY, so a linear probe
always terminates on one.

THE HEADLINE, and it inverts this row's premise. Cachegrind Ir ratios against
the byte-identical baseline, and wall clock min/med over 9 strictly interleaved
reps:

    kata   Ir unbnd  Ir slotwlk | A/A control  wall unbnd    wall slotwlk
    170    0.749     0.683      | 1.006/0.996  0.972/0.958   0.983/0.972
    128    0.945     0.945      | --           0.987/0.981   0.993/0.987
    217    0.968     0.960      | 1.002/1.014  1.108/1.113   1.019/1.028

Removing up to 32% of the probe loop's instructions buys 3-4% of wall clock on
the kata built to showcase the spill, and LOSES on kata:217 — the same kata,
same sign, that killed the `mask` trick. The A/A control is a byte-identical
binary run under a different path name inside the same interleave: at
1.006/0.996 and 1.002/1.014 it puts this host's floor near +-1.5%, so 217's
regression is far outside noise and 170's gain is only just outside it.

── THE FINDING: THE SPILL IS REMOVABLE, AND REMOVING IT IS WORTH ~2% ──

`SlotWalk` eliminates the exact instruction pair B-2026-08-06-33 named. In
kata:170's `main` the baseline spills `mov %bl,0x7(%rsp)` + `mov %rcx,0x8(%rsp)`
and reloads at both probe exits — 5 stack stores / 3 reloads across `main`.
Under `SlotWalk` that is 1 store / 0 reloads: the probe's stack traffic is GONE,
not relocated. The kata gets 2.8% faster.

So the "4 memory ops per key-probe" this row was opened to remove are worth
about two percent. The loop is bound on the status-byte load, not on its
instruction budget — which is why a 32% instruction cut shows up as a 3% clock
cut. There is no headroom left in the register story.

── WHY kata:217 GETS SLOWER, MEASURED THREE WAYS ──

Fewer instructions costing 11% needs an explanation, and this is the receipt
for this row's own finding (1) — "LLVM simply spends the freed register
elsewhere" — with the address it spent it at.

 1. WHERE. Every function in the 217 binary is instruction-count-identical
    between base and `Unbounded` except `main` (159 -> 159: same count,
    different content). Diffing it, the baseline keeps the OUTER loop's counter
    in `%r14` and tests it with `cmp $0x31f,%r14`; `Unbounded` spills it
    (`mov %rcx,0x28(%rsp)`) and reloads it every outer iteration. Freeing
    registers inside the probe pushed the pressure OUT into the enclosing loop,
    which in a fresh-set-per-window kata runs far more often than the probe
    body does.
 2. THE COST OF THAT, cachegrind with full cache sim: BOTH variants add
    +181 M data reads (+1.40%) while cutting 1.5-1.9 G instructions. Writes are
    identical to the byte and the D1 miss rate moves +0.03%, so these are
    L1-resident loads on a loop-carried dependency chain, not a locality
    regression.
 3. WHAT WAS REMOVED WAS FREE. Branch sim: the bound test is 502 M conditional
    branches (7,654,862,110 -> 7,152,630,689) and removing all of them changes
    mispredicts by ~0 (492,562,519 -> 492,443,416, and 493,813,272 for
    `SlotWalk` — a slight LOSS). The loop's 489 M conditional mispredicts are
    the key compare, and they do not move. So the bound test was a
    perfectly-predicted branch costing ~nothing, traded for a spill costing
    real cycles.

NOT FULLY EXPLAINED, and flagged rather than papered over: `Unbounded` and
`SlotWalk` add the SAME +181 M reads and the same branch counts on 217, yet sit
8 points apart on the clock (1.113 vs 1.028 median). Whatever separates them is
not visible in Ir, D-refs, D1 or branch prediction. Do not read the mechanism
above as a complete account of the 11%; it accounts for the sign, not the size.

── THE RULE THIS ESTABLISHES ──

THE TWO INSTRUMENTS DISAGREE IN SIGN on kata:217 (Ir 0.968, wall 1.108). Second
time in this family — B-2026-08-05-5 was the first, and this row predicted it
would happen again before the measurement was taken. So: FOR A PROBE-LOOP
CHANGE, INSTRUCTION COUNT IS NOT A PROXY FOR TIME. Both times the loop was
memory-bound and the instrument that counts work-not-done said the opposite of
the clock. Cachegrind's value here was diagnostic, not decisive: it is what
showed the loop shedding a third of its instructions, which is exactly how we
know the remaining cost is not instructions.

CORRECTNESS OF THE REJECTED FORMS, verified so the lever is not a trap for
whoever flips it: codegen E2E is green under BOTH (2835 passed / 0 failed,
each), and at the default codegen (2835), memory_sanitizer (984 under LSan) and
par_codegen (245) are green alongside the rest of the suite.
`runtime/src/map.rs`'s `(len + tombstones + 1) * 4 > capacity * 3` guard now
carries a comment naming this dependency, because weakening that fraction
toward 1 would turn a lookup MISS into an infinite loop in those forms. CI does
not exercise them.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY MOVE THIS, for anyone who returns: not the probe's
instruction budget and not its register pressure — all three tricks
(`mask`-bound, unbounded, slot-walk) are now priced and all three lose on
kata:217. The loop waits on the status byte and mispredicts the key compare.
That points at SIMD group probing (16 control bytes per iteration, the
swisstable move) or a layout change putting more control bytes per cache line.
Different bug.

ALSO WORTH RE-RUNNING ELSEWHERE: the lever makes this a one-env-var comparison
now, and the spill is x86-only (arm64 has 31 GPRs and does not spill here), so
`SlotWalk` has never been priced on the architecture where it costs nothing to
free registers. This container has no `perf` and no `hyperfine`; a host with
either would also settle the 8-point gap left open above.

STATUS: closed as PRICED, not as fixed. The spill remains in shipped code BY
CHOICE — `Bounded` stays the default because the two forms that beat it on
instructions lose on the clock and additionally trade away termination on a
corrupt or externally-built table.

title: B-2026-08-07-15's own-by-transfer gate exempted EVERY generic struct, and a generic struct at a CONCRETE param (`fn take(x: Mix[String])` over `Mix[T] { v: T, s: String }`) is the same double-free -- 10 invalid frees per 10 iterations at BOTH opt levels after that row landed. The exclusion guards the MONOMORPH rescue, which a concrete param never takes; erasure is just another way to close `field_copy_supported`. Replaced with the callee's own `mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param` answer, threaded down as a flag -- NOT `mono_inst.is_some()`, which conflates it with a span-map lookup
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by probing B-2026-08-07-15's fix for the shapes its
predicate declines. Not a regression from that fix -- the shape corrupted before
it too; the fix simply did not reach it, by an exclusion the row states openly.

B-2026-08-07-15 gave the caller's registrar the callee's own-by-transfer
condition, and excluded every GENERIC struct from it. The reason was sound:
above the transfer arm sits `try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned`, whose
rescue reads the CALLEE's active substitution, and a caller-side predicate
cannot see that -- the trap B-2026-08-06-2 defect (B) documents. So the
exclusion buys agreement by construction.

IT BUYS IT TOO DEARLY, because the rescue only exists on the MONOMORPH path and
a generic struct reaches more than one kind of param:

    struct Mix[T] { v: T, s: String }

    fn take(x: Mix[String]) -> i64 { 1 }   CONCRETE param -- no monomorph, no
                                           subst, no rescue. The callee takes
                                           the transfer arm like any non-generic
                                           struct, the caller keeps registering,
                                           and both frames free the same heap:
                                           10 invalid frees per 10 iterations at
                                           BOTH opt levels, AFTER -15 landed.

    fn take[T](x: Mix[T]) -> i64 { 1 }     MONOMORPH -- the rescue fires, the
                                           callee entry-copies, and the caller's
                                           drop is RIGHT. Clean before and after.

Erasure is simply another way to close `field_copy_supported`: the bare `T`
lands on its conservative `_ => false` arm, the same door -15's own `Map` field
and `Array[i64, 4]` field already go through. Same predicate, same two owners,
same corruption -- this is that row's class, not a neighbour of it.

THE FIX REPLACES THE EXCLUSION WITH THE CALLEE'S ANSWER rather than a
caller-side reconstruction of it. `compile_generic_call` already evaluates
`mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param` with the callee's substitution installed --
it has done so since defect (B), to look up the instantiation -- so it now also
threads that predicate's raw boolean down as `callee_entry_copies_mono`. Every
other call path passes `false`, which is correct rather than merely
conservative: the rescue needs an active subst and there is none.

NOT `mono_inst.is_some()`, which is the shape that fits and the one to distrust.
`mono_inst` is the predicate's answer AND a successful span-map lookup, so it
reads `None` in two different situations -- the callee took the buffer, or the
callee entry-copies but the span carries no annotation. Only the first may
suppress the caller's drop. Reading the second off it would trade -15's
corruption for a leak, so the flag now rides ALONGSIDE the instantiation instead
of being recovered from it; the two callers want opposite defaults on that gap.

MEASURED, 10 iterations, valgrind, both opt levels, each against a tree with -15
already landed:

    fn take(x: Mix[String])     CONCRETE param   10 errs -> clean   (-O2)
                                                 10 errs -> clean   (-O0)
    fn take[T](x: Mix[T])       monomorph        clean   -> clean
    fn take(x: Box[String])     single bare T    clean   -> clean

The monomorph row is the control that had to stay clean, and it is why the flag
is the callee's: suppressing there re-opens defect (B), measured at 140 B in 4
blocks when the first cut of this change did exactly that.

Pinned by the two new arms of
`asan_fresh_temp_struct_arg_owned_by_transfer_no_double_free`, which is red
pre-fix with an explicit ASAN double free at both opt levels.

STILL BROKEN AND FILED SEPARATELY as B-2026-08-07-18: `fn take[U](x: Mix[U])`,
the monomorph whose fn-level type param is named differently from the struct's.
That is a different function's defect (`mono_struct_type_from_active_subst`) and
predates both rows.

fix: 592216a0. title: naming a generic fn's type param differently from the struct's silently miscompiles: `fn f[U](x: Mix[U])` is 30 valgrind errors / 10 invalid frees / 88 B lost at the DEFAULT -O2 where the character-for-character identical `fn f[T](x: Mix[T])` is clean. `mono_struct_type_from_active_subst` looks the STRUCT's declared param names up in the FN's substitution, so the match is a coincidence and the documented "falls back to the base layout" is a drop reading field 1 at the ERASED offset 8 (a length word) instead of the mono offset 24. NARROWED: a LEAK for all-bare-`T` structs, CORRUPTION once a concrete heap sibling exists. One fix approach tried and reverted -- see detail — FIXED IN TWO HALVES: the mono param loop now threads the param's concrete instantiation (which it already computed, eleven lines later) into the own-by-transfer drop, AND `compile_generic_call` retracts the caller's drop for an identifier argument the way `compile_call` always has. The second half is mandatory: correcting the drop's layout makes it real, which turns a lockstep that was never honoured on the generic path into a fresh double free in four shapes that had been clean
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-07-17, as the one arm of that
probe matrix which neither -15's fix nor -17's moved. Independent of both:
measured with each stashed, identical counts.

RENAMING A TYPE PARAMETER IS THE ENTIRE TRIGGER. These two functions differ in
one identifier and nothing else:

    struct Mix[T] { v: T, s: String }

    fn same[T](x: Mix[T]) -> i64 { 1 }      CLEAN
    fn diverge[U](x: Mix[U]) -> i64 { 1 }   30 valgrind errors, 10 invalid
                                            frees, 88 bytes lost at -O2

MEASURED, 10 iterations, valgrind, both opt levels:

    diverge[U](Mix[U])   fresh temp      30 errs / 10 invfree / 88 B  (-O2)
                                         14 errs /  1 invfree / 88 B  (-O0)
    diverge[U](Mix[U])   NAMED binding   10 errs / 10 invfree          (-O2)
                                         10 errs /  1 invfree          (-O0)
    same[T](Mix[T])      fresh temp      clean, both levels
    pair_diverge[U](Pair[U])  fresh      20 errs / 88 B lost           (-O2)
      (`Pair[T] { a: T, b: T }` -- all-bare-`T` fields: leaks and errors
       but does not invalid-free, because there is no concrete sibling
       field for a mis-GEP'd drop to reach)
    pair_same[T](Pair[T])     fresh      clean, both levels

NOTE THIS HITS THE NAMED BINDING TOO, unlike B-2026-08-07-15, whose whole
signature was that the fresh temp corrupted and the named spelling did not. So
the two are not the same bug wearing different clothes, and a fix for one is not
a fix for the other.

MECHANISM, and it is already written down in the code as a known fallback whose
cost was never measured. `mono_struct_type_from_active_subst` resolves the
STRUCT's declared field `TypeExpr`s through the ACTIVE MONOMORPH subst, which is
keyed by the enclosing FN's type-param names. Its own doc says:

    "The substitution keys on the active monomorph's param names -- which match
    the struct's own param names in the overwhelmingly common `struct Pair[T]` +
    `fn f[T](Pair[T])` shape; a struct whose param name diverges from the
    enclosing fn's falls back to the base layout (unchanged from before this
    fix)."

The fallback is not benign. With `U -> String` installed and `Mix`'s field typed
`T`, the lookup misses, `T` stays erased, `mono_struct_type_from_active_subst`
returns `None`, and `try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned` declines. The
param then drops to own-by-transfer with a drop synthesized against the ERASED
layout -- which mis-GEPs the concrete `String` sibling and leaks the bare-`T`
field. `active_subst_struct_inst` and `aggregate_param_copy_supported_struct_-
mono` key the same way and inherit the same miss.

WHERE TO START. The name match is a coincidence the code should not depend on.
The struct's params must be bound POSITIONALLY from the param's DECLARED type --
`Mix[U]` against `Mix`'s declared `[T]` gives `T -> subst(U) -> String` -- not
by hoping `T` appears in the fn's substitution. The declared instantiation is
already in hand at the site: `make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst` takes it
as `inst` (seeded from `enum_inst_var_types` in `functions.rs`, and threaded
there for B-2026-08-05-33 predicate (a), which needed it for the same reason).

The tidiest shape is probably a SCOPED subst install around the whole
non-copy-supported block -- save `type_subst_names` / `type_subst_type_exprs`,
overlay the struct's own param bindings, restore after -- because all four
consumers (`mono_struct_type_from_active_subst`, `aggregate_param_copy_-
supported_struct_mono`, `deep_copy_struct_heap_fields_in_place_mono`,
`active_subst_struct_inst`) go through `subst_monomorph_type_params` and would
all be corrected at once. Overlay rather than extend: where a fn param and a
struct param share a NAME but mean different types (`fn f[T](x: Mix[i64])`), the
struct's binding must win inside that scope.

CAUTION: the failure is currently a DECLINE, so getting the binding wrong turns
a leak into a double free rather than the reverse. Measure `same[T]` as the
control -- it already takes the rescue and its IR must not move -- and measure
BOTH the fresh-temp and NAMED spellings, since unlike -15 this bug breaks both.

WHY HIGH: the trigger is a cosmetic choice with no semantic content. `fn
apply[U](w: Wrapper[U])` is ordinary, idiomatic generic code -- nothing warns,
nothing differs at the source level, and the corruption is at the DEFAULT -O2.

── NARROWED, AND ONE APPROACH TRIED AND REJECTED (2026-08-07, no fix landed) ──

THE TRIGGER IS NARROWER THAN "a diverging type-param name". It additionally
needs the struct to mix a BARE-`T` field with a CONCRETE HEAP one. Measured, 10
iterations, valgrind, both opt levels, all under `fn t[U](x: S[U])`:

    struct A[T] { v: T, s: String }    10 invalid frees   (-O2 and -O0)
    struct B[T] { s: String, v: T }    10 invalid frees   -- field ORDER is
                                       irrelevant, which rules out an
                                       off-by-one in a field loop
    struct C[T] { v: T, n: i64 }       CLEAN -- a SCALAR sibling is fine
    struct D[T] { v: T }               CLEAN -- a lone bare `T` is fine

    struct Pair[T] { a: T, b: T }      20 errs, 88 B lost, NO invalid free
                                       -- all-bare-`T`: leaks only, because
                                       there is no concrete field for a
                                       mis-GEP'd drop to reach

So the row splits into a LEAK half (any all-bare-`T` generic struct under a
diverging name) and a CORRUPTION half (that plus a concrete heap sibling).

THE BAD POINTER IS `0x4`, AND IT NAMES THE MECHANISM EXACTLY. Valgrind reports
"Address 0x4 is not stack'd, malloc'd or (recently) free'd" -- 4 is the LENGTH
word of the first string (`"av-1"`), not a pointer at all. Field 1 sits at byte
offset 8 in the ERASED base layout `{ i64, {ptr,len,cap} }` and at byte offset
24 in the MONO layout `{ {ptr,len,cap}, {ptr,len,cap} }`. A drop walking the
mono-laid-out slot with base offsets reads offset 8 -- field 0's `len` -- and
frees it. That is a base-layout drop over a mono-layout value, stated precisely,
and it is one extra free per call (28 allocs against 38 frees on the 10-iteration
probe).

── APPROACH TRIED AND REJECTED: the scoped subst overlay ──

Recorded because it is the obvious fix, it is half-right, and the half that is
wrong produces a NEW double free in already-passing code.

WHAT WAS BUILT. `push_struct_param_subst_overlay(struct_name, declared)` binds
the struct's own params positionally from the declared param type (`Mix[U]`
against `Mix[T]` gives `T -> subst(U)`), installed into `type_subst_type_exprs`
(which wins inside `subst_monomorph_type_params`) around the non-copy-supported
arm, and restored after. Both sides were overlaid -- the callee in
`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst`, the caller in `compile_generic_call`
before `mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param` -- and, on the second attempt, from
the SAME source expression (the declared `param.ty`) so they could not disagree
about the mapping.

IT WORKS FOR THE LEAK HALF, MEASURED:

    Pair[U]  all-bare-`T`, fresh temp   20 errs / 88 B lost   -> CLEAN
    Trip[Q]  three bare fields          leaked                -> CLEAN
    Mix[U]   bare `T` + `String`        30 errs / 88 B        -> 10 errs, no
                                                                 leak (the
                                                                 corruption half
                                                                 survives)
    Mix[T]   matching name (control)    clean                 -> clean

A dedicated fixture over the all-bare-`T` shapes was red pre-change at 14,800
bytes in 200 blocks at BOTH opt levels and green after.

WHY IT WAS REVERTED ANYWAY. The overlay does not merely improve resolution -- it
flips which OWNERSHIP ARM the param takes, from own-by-transfer to the monomorph
entry-copy, for every generic struct whose param name diverges. The caller has
more than one predicate keyed to that decision, and they do not move together:
`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` and the `call_arg_flows_into_return` gate in
`compile_generic_call`'s registration loop both still answer from the
un-overlaid view. `asan_generic_struct_literal_arg_entry_copy_no_leak` -- the
B-2026-08-06-2 defect (B) pin, whose `takeu[U](b: Box[U]) -> U { b.v }` arm is
exactly this shape AND returns the moved-out field -- goes from green to an
explicit `AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free`. Full suite: 13,226 passed,
that one failed.

Making the two sides read one source fixed the mapping and did NOT fix this: the
disagreement is not about what `T` is, it is about which arm was taken, and the
flows-into-return path never asks.

WHAT THE NEXT ATTEMPT NEEDS. Every caller-side predicate gated on the entry-copy
decision has to move in lockstep with the overlay, not just
`mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param` -- at minimum
`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` and the flows-into-return branch, and those
should be audited for others rather than assumed to be the complete set. That is
a wider change than a fix slice, and the safe direction is not obvious: getting
it partly right converts today's leak into a fresh double free in code that
currently passes, which is what happened here.

An alternative worth weighing first: leave the ownership arm alone and fix only
the DROP's layout, so the base-vs-mono offset mismatch is corrected without
re-deciding who owns the param. That addresses the corruption half directly and
touches nothing the caller reasons about.

── FIXED 592216a0, IN TWO HALVES; THE SECOND IS WHY THE FIRST ATTEMPT FAILED ──

THIS ROW'S OWN CLOSING SUGGESTION WAS RIGHT, and smaller than it looked. "Leave
the ownership arm alone and fix only the DROP's layout" is what landed. No arm
moves, so the caller-side predicates the rejected overlay disturbed
(`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct`, the flows-into-return gate) are never
consulted differently and `asan_generic_struct_literal_arg_entry_copy_no_leak`
— the fixture that killed the overlay — stays green untouched.

HALF 1, THE CALLEE, AND THE VALUE IT NEEDED WAS ALREADY IN HAND ELEVEN LINES
LATER. `compile_mono_function` called the NON-`inst` spelling
`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned`, so a monomorph's own-by-transfer drop was
always keyed by bare name and synthesized against the ERASED layout. The same
loop then computed `concrete_generic_struct_inst(param.ty)` — which resolves
`Mix[U]` through `type_subst_names` to `Mix[String]`, exactly the positional
binding this row asked for — but AFTER the ownership call, and only to seed
`enum_inst_var_types` for nested method dispatch. Hoisting that computation
above the ownership call and threading it through
`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst` is the entire callee-side change.

Why it cannot move an arm: `inst` reaches ONLY `track_struct_var_inst`, which
binds the STRUCT's params positionally from it. Every arm-selection predicate
in `make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst` is name-keyed and cannot observe it.

The diagnosis that got there was one `eprintln` at the own-by-transfer arm, not
reading: it printed `inst=None subst_names={"U": "String"}` for the diverging
spelling and printed NOTHING for the matching one — which simultaneously
confirmed the missing binding and confirmed that the control never reaches this
arm at all. The seeding trace then showed the mono path's param loop running
BEFORE `compile_function`'s recording site ever fires, i.e. a different loop
entirely.

── HALF 2: THIS ROW'S "LEAK BECOMES A DOUBLE FREE" WARNING, COMING TRUE ──

spelling REGRESSED. Measured, `fn t[U](x: S[U])`, 10 iterations, valgrind:

  A[T] { v: T, s: String }      10 errs / 1 invfree  20 errs / 2 invfree
  B[T] { s: String, v: T }      10 / 1               20 / 2
  C[T] { v: T, n: i64 }         CLEAN                10 / 1
  D[T] { v: T }                 CLEAN                10 / 1
  Pair[T] { a: T, b: T }        CLEAN                20 / 2
  Trip[T] { a: T, b: T, c: T }  CLEAN                30 / 3, and 20 invalid
                                                     frees at -O2

Four shapes that had been clean started double-freeing. Caught by running the
matrix's PRE-FIX baseline rather than by trusting that the post-fix table looked
plausible — the post-fix numbers alone read as "some residual", not as "I broke
this".

THE CAUSE IS NOT THE FIX. IT IS AN INVARIANT THAT WAS NEVER TRUE ON THIS PATH.
The own-by-transfer arm's whole safety argument is a lockstep, stated in
`param_own.rs`: "the caller already retracts its drop for exactly this shape
(`move_declined_copy_struct_arg`)". `compile_call` honours it.
`compile_generic_call` NEVER DID — every ownership decision it makes is written
against `ExprKind::StructLiteral` args, so `t(b)` for a let-bound `b` left the
binding and the callee both owning the same buffers.

That was invisible for as long as the callee's drop was not real. Keyed by bare
name in a monomorph it froze a length word (this row's corruption) or, for an
all-bare-`T` struct with no concrete heap sibling, was never emitted at all
(this row's leak). Correcting the layout is what converted a silently-absent
owner into a second real one. So the two halves are one bug, not a fix plus its
fallout.

HALF 2 IS THE MISSING RETRACTION, and it needed no new predicate:
`compile_generic_call` now asks, per IDENTIFIER argument and under the CALLEE's
substitution, `struct_param_owned_by_transfer(sname,
mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param(sname))` — the pair that already existed for
the struct-literal path (B-2026-08-07-15) — then retracts through the same
`move_declined_copy_struct_arg` the concrete path uses. Decision under the
callee's subst; retraction with the caller's restored, since it edits
caller-scope cleanup frames.

All 32 cells clean: 8 shapes (A, B, C, D, Pair, Trip plus the two matching-name
controls) x fresh-temp and NAMED spellings x `-O2` and `-O0`. The matching-name

so if the fix ever moves them it moved an arm.

detail:
SOURCE NOTE: measured while closing B-2026-08-07-12 leg 1, as one row of that
row's own control matrix. Left out of the leg-1 commit deliberately; the reason
is the fix SURFACE, not any doubt about the mechanism.

REPRO, default -O2 `karac build`, under valgrind, 10 iterations:

    struct S { s: Result[Map[i64, String], i64] }
    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        while i < 10 {
            let mut m: Map[i64, String] = Map.new();
            m.insert(n + i, f"mapv-{n + i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer");
            let s: S = S { s: Result.Ok(m) };
            acc = acc + 1;

    }

    -> prints 10 (correct), 720 bytes in 10 blocks definitely lost. IDENTICAL
       at -O0, so not an optimizer-masking artifact. No call anywhere in the
       program -- like its Option sibling, this is the struct's own field drop,
       not anything about parameter passing.

MEASURED BEFORE AND AFTER the leg-1 commit: unchanged at 720 B / 10 on both
sides, i.e. that fix provably does not reach this shape.

MECHANISM, the same missing drop arm one wrapper over. A `Map`/`Set` handle is
a single word: not the inline `{ptr,len,cap}` overlay, not wide enough to be
boxed, and its head is in neither `struct_types` nor `enum_layouts`. Leg 1 added
`option_payload_map_or_set_drop_ok` for exactly that gap and wired it into the
`Option` arm of the promotion loop plus both move legs. The `Result` arm sits a
few lines above with its OWN gates -- `result_field_direct_vecstr_halves_ok` and
`result_field_struct_enum_payload_ok` -- and neither admits a Map half, so the
field is never promoted to `FieldDrop::OptionInline` and nothing frees it.

The DROP side is ready and needs no new emitter, exactly as on the Option side:
`emit_result_drop_fn` dispatches each half through `te_owns_heap_below_buffer`
-> `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`, which already routes `Map`/`SortedMap` to
`emit_map_drop_fn` and `Set`/`SortedSet` to the same fn as `Map[T, ()]`.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE EXTENSION, and this is the whole reason for a separate
row. There are two ways to widen and the obvious one is a trap:

  * `result_payload_inline_recursive_drop_ok` is the natural-looking point and
    has FIVE consumers, including `types_lowering.rs`'s LAYOUT decisions.
    Widening it changes lowering for every `Result` in the program.
  * `result_field_direct_vecstr_halves_ok` is consulted by
    `field_copy_supported` ITSELF (src/codegen/param_own.rs) and by the
    typechecker's `.clone()` derivation. Admitting a Map half there would make
    the struct COPY-SUPPORTED -- promising an entry copy that
    `deep_copy_result_inline_heap_halves_in_place` cannot perform on a handle,
    so the caller's original and the callee's copy would share it. That trades
    this leak for a DOUBLE FREE, and it is precisely the over-broad widening
    this family has reverted three times.

So the fix is a SCOPED predicate (the `Result` peer of
`option_payload_map_or_set_drop_ok`) threaded through the sites that pair with
it, and there are four or five rather than leg 1's three: the promotion loop's
Result arm, BOTH legs of `place_optres_field_move_info_ex`'s Result branch, and
the destructure-leaf registrations in `stmts.rs` (two call sites).

THE PAIRING RULE IS THE RISK, and leg 1 demonstrated it costs a measurement
rather than a reading. There, widening the drop alone converted the leak into
470 valgrind errors with invalid frees at both opt levels, and the leg that
broke was the PATTERN one -- whose class is deliberately narrower than the
classifier it otherwise mirrors, so no amount of reading the pairing comment
predicts it. Expect the same here, and note the Result neutralizer is different
machinery (`zero_result_payload_area` + `invalidate_result_tag_at`, not a tag
zero), so the Option answer does not transfer by analogy.

VERIFICATION this needs, same as leg 1: the whole `memory_sanitizer` suite at
BOTH opt levels (the -O2 suite alone provably cannot see a double free in this
family -- B-2026-08-05-33's method note), a probe matrix carrying every move leg
(pattern / whole-move / let-move / move inside a callee), and the sibling-field
row that detects the per-STRUCT blast radius (`struct S { p: Option[String],
s: Result[Map, i64] }` -- if the gate fails for the whole struct here too, the
String leaks with it).

── FIXED 31755b38, EXACTLY AS THIS ROW SCOPED IT ──

title: a SHARED-owning struct never frees its `Option[Map]`/`Option[Set]` field -- 720 B / 10 iterations at BOTH opt levels for a plain `let`, no call in the program. Not the `Option[Map]` gap (B-2026-08-07-12 leg 1 fixed that; the same struct WITHOUT the shared field is clean) and not a shared-struct gap (its `Option[String]` / `Option[Vec]` siblings are freed) -- it is the intersection, where the promotion gate's copy-supported arm is closed by the `Map` field and its own-by-transfer arm by the `shared` one. Both exclusions are individually correct -- one approach (the third disjunct) built and REVERTED: it fixes every measured shape but double-frees the self-hosted-parser destructure fixture, because struct destructure is a SECOND move-out gate; the three sites it must widen with are named in the detail
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found in the control matrix while independently working
B-2026-08-07-12 leg 1, and it is the row of that matrix leg 1 does NOT reach.
Distinct from B-2026-08-07-19, which is the same gap one WRAPPER over (`Result`);
this one is the same gap one FIELD over.

REPRO, default -O2 `karac build`, valgrind, 10 iterations, no call anywhere in
the program:

    shared struct Node { v: i64 }
    struct A { n: Option[Node], m: Option[Map[String, i64]] }

    let a: A = A { n: Option.Some(Node { v: i }), m: Option.Some(mk(i)) };

    -> 720 bytes in 10 blocks definitely lost. IDENTICAL at -O0.

The DIRECT-shared spelling behaves the same:

    struct D { n: Node, m: Option[Map[String, i64]] }        720 B / 10

THE FOUR-WAY COMPARISON IS THE WHOLE DIAGNOSIS, all measured on the same tree
AFTER leg 1 landed:

    A { Option[Node],  Option[Map]    }   720 B / 10   LEAKS
    D { Node,          Option[Map]    }   720 B / 10   LEAKS
    B { Option[Node],  Option[String] }   clean        -- shared sibling is NOT
                                                          the whole story
    C { Option[Node],  Option[Vec]    }   clean
    E {                Option[Map]    }   clean        -- leg 1 fixed this one

So it is neither "a shared-owning struct never frees its `Option` fields" (B and
C are freed) nor "an `Option[Map]` field is never freed" (E is freed). It is
exactly the INTERSECTION, and the reason is that the promotion gate has two arms
and this shape closes BOTH — each for its own unrelated reason:

  * `aggregate_param_copy_supported_struct` refuses because of the `Map` field
    ("heap the outer-buffer copy can't duplicate -> bail"). That is why E is
    not admitted by this arm either.
  * `struct_param_owned_by_transfer` -- the arm leg 1 added -- refuses because
    the struct owns a `shared` field. That exclusion is deliberate and load-
    bearing: B-2026-08-05-32 makes the CALLER keep its drop for shared-owning
    structs, so they are still caller-retains and freeing here would rc-dec
    twice.

B and C pass through the FIRST arm (a `String`/`Vec` payload is copy-supported,
so the struct is), which is why a shared sibling does not block them. E passes
through the SECOND. A and D can use neither.

PRE-EXISTING, verified rather than assumed: measured at leg 1's parent commit,
where A, D and E all leaked 720 B / 10. Leg 1 moved E to clean and left A and D
untouched.

WHY MEDIUM: it needs a `shared` field AND a `Map`/`Set` field in one struct,
which is narrower than either sibling row, and it is a plain leak with no
corruption at either opt level. But it is silent, needs no call, and an
RC-graph-plus-index struct (`{ parent: Option[Node], index: Map[String, i64] }`)
is an ordinary shape rather than a contrived one.

WHERE TO START, and the two obvious moves are both wrong:

  * DROPPING the shared exclusion from `struct_param_owned_by_transfer` is not
    it. That exclusion is about the STRUCT's ownership at a call boundary and
    B-2026-08-05-32 measured what removing it costs (a stranded RC box).
  * WIDENING the copy-support arm is not it either -- the `Map` field genuinely
    cannot be duplicated by the outer-buffer copy, which is the fact that
    predicate exists to report.

The promising direction is that neither arm is really answering the question
this gate asks. The gate wants "does anything else own this struct's field
heap", and for a `let`-bound local that never crosses a call boundary the answer
is no regardless of which parameter-passing convention the type WOULD take. Both
arms are proxies for that via the call-boundary story, and this shape is where
both proxies fail while the underlying answer stays no. A third disjunct keyed
on the OWNER SITE rather than the type may be the honest fix -- but note that
the drop fn is synthesized once per struct TYPE and used at every death of that
type (the reasoning B-2026-08-07-12 leg 1 records for why it passes `false` for
the mono flag), so a site-keyed condition does not fit the current shape of the
synthesis and that mismatch is the real work.

CAUTION, from the sibling rows: widening the drop obliges the MOVE SITES to
widen with it (`place_optres_field_move_info_ex`'s pairing rule). Leg 1 measured
that omitting the pattern leg turns `match s.m { Some(inner) => .. }` from clean
into 470 valgrind errors with invalid frees at both opt levels. Any fix here
must carry the same pairing and be measured on the match-arm shape, not only on
the `let`.

detail:
SURFACED BY B-2026-08-07-14's closing measurement. That row established that kara's
i64 overflow check costs the entire vector speedup on loops LLVM would otherwise
vectorize, because the trap branch is a second loop exit. It then proved the
reduction case unfixable: checked addition is non-associative, so partitioning
`s = s + h[i]` into lanes changes which programs trap. This row is the other
half -- the ELEMENTWISE shape, where that soundness argument does not apply.

THE SHAPE. A loop whose checked arithmetic has NO loop-carried dependence:

    while i < n {
        out[i] = a[i] + t;      // t loop-invariant, a and out distinct
        i = i + 1;
    }

Each element's overflow condition depends only on that element, not on any
prefix. Reordering, partitioning or vectorizing the loop therefore leaves the
SET of overflowing programs exactly unchanged -- which is precisely what fails
for a reduction.

MEASURED IN KARA (x86_64, callgrind Ir, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, 1M-element `Vec[i64]`
x 20 passes = 20M element-ops; both binaries sink-verified identical at
43,500,000):

    kara  wrapping (a[i].wrapping_add(t))      23,623,735    1.18 instr/elem
    kara  CHECKED  (a[i] + t)                  99,743,368    4.99          4.22x

READ OFF THE DISASSEMBLY, not inferred. The checked build's hot loop is scalar,
3x unrolled, with the trap branch after every add:

    mov  -0x20(%rbx,%rcx,8),%rdx
    inc  %rdx
    jo   98ad <main+0xd5d>          <-- the second exit
    mov  %rdx,-0x20(%rax,%rcx,8)

The wrapping build of the same source is AVX2, 16 elements per iteration:

    vpbroadcastq 0x361ea(%rip),%ymm0
    vpaddq -0xe0(%rbx,%rdx,8),%ymm0,%ymm1
    vpaddq -0xc0(%rbx,%rdx,8),%ymm0,%ymm2
    ...
    vmovdqu %ymm1,-0xe0(%rax,%rdx,8)

Whole-binary counts agree: ymm 56 / `jo` 107 for the checked build against ymm
379 / `jo` 12 for the wrapping one.

THE FORM THAT WOULD WORK, and evidence that it does. Replace the per-element
trap branch with a branchless overflow accumulator and one test after the loop.
The signed-overflow predicate is pure integer arithmetic -- for `r = x + y`,
overflow occurred iff `((x ^ r) & (y ^ r)) < 0` -- so the loop body becomes
straight-line vectorizable code and the flag folds as an `or`-reduction:

    acc |= (x ^ r) & (y ^ r);       ...then after the loop:  if acc < 0 { trap }

Measured under clang 18 -O3 -mavx2, ymm references in the emitted function
(plain wrapping control = 8, so the harness is known good):

    ELEMENTWISE, per-element trap branch                       0
    ELEMENTWISE, OR-accumulated `llvm.sadd.with.overflow` flag  0
    ELEMENTWISE, OR-accumulated sign-trick (pure integer)      36

Note the middle row: keeping the intrinsic but removing the BRANCH is not
enough -- `sadd.with.overflow` is not trivially vectorizable, so the sign-trick
formulation is load-bearing, not a stylistic choice.

WHY THIS IS NOT ALREADY A PATCH -- the blocker is diagnostics, not soundness.
Deferring the trap to the loop exit preserves WHICH programs panic but changes
WHEN, and kara's panic contract is specific enough that this is observable in
four ways, in rough order of how hard they are to dismiss:

  1. SITE ATTRIBUTION. design.md § Crash Report Format has built-in operator
     panics point at the operator's own source location. One coalesced flag
     cannot say which of several checked ops in the body overflowed, so either
     the reported location degrades or the transform needs a per-site flag
     (which costs back some of the win). Diagnostic precision is load-bearing
     for the Mend loop in this project, so this is the condition most likely to
     kill the idea rather than merely narrow it.
  2. OTHER TRAPS IN THE BODY. An index-out-of-bounds or divide-by-zero at a
     LATER element would, after the transform, fire BEFORE the earlier
     overflow, changing the panic's identity and message. Requires the loop's
     only trapping operation to be the arithmetic.
  3. SIDE EFFECTS. Any I/O or call in the body would execute for elements after
     the logical trap point. Requires a call-free, effect-free body.
  4. DROP OBSERVABILITY. Destructors run during panic unwind (design.md § Drop
     bodies must not panic), so a user `Drop` impl could in principle observe
     the extra stores written past the overflow point. Narrow, but it means
     "the buffer is dead anyway" is not automatically true.

Conditions 2-4 are ordinary gating predicates of the kind codegen already
computes elsewhere. Condition 1 is a design question and should be answered
first.

WHAT IS NOT MEASURED, and should be before anyone builds this: how often the
shape actually occurs. The 4.22x above is from a kernel written to isolate it.
Nothing here surveys the kata corpus for elementwise checked loops that are
otherwise vectorizable, and that number -- not this one -- decides whether the
work is worth its legality analysis. A cheap first pass would be to count loops
in the corpus whose bodies are call-free, trap-free apart from arithmetic, and
free of loop-carried arithmetic dependence.

    not the trapping `+`/`-`/`*` class, and `d`/`nr` come from
    `zip_with(..).sum()` calls in the loop body.
  * `examples/slice_basics.kara` — `xs[i] = xs[i] * 2`. The ONLY structurally
    qualifying instance in the corpus, and its loop is `while i < 5`: a
    five-iteration teaching example where vectorization is meaningless.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN BLOCKER (1), recorded because it is the opposite of
what the row claims and would otherwise mislead. The row calls site attribution
"the condition most likely to kill the idea". It is not: it dissolves under a
single-checked-op restriction. `emit_panic("integer overflow")` takes a STATIC
string and the location comes from the panic site, so a loop body containing
exactly one checked op has exactly one candidate site — the deferred trap
reports a byte-identical message and location to the immediate one. And the
single-op body is precisely the shape that vectorizes anyway, so the
restriction costs nothing. Blockers (2)-(4) remain ordinary gating predicates.
So the idea was MORE buildable than the row said; it just has nothing to be
built for.

THE PRECEDENT THAT SETTLES THE PRIORITY, which the row did not know about:
`src/codegen/accum_overflow.rs` (B-2026-07-26-1) is the repo's one successful
attack on "an overflow check blocks an LLVM transform" — and it took ELISION,
not deferral. It recognises a narrow guarded-counter shape
(`acc = acc + 1` from a literal zero, exactly one increment site, ascending
counter) and PROVES the trap dead from the trip count, so it deletes the check
outright. That pays NONE of this row's four observability blockers, because an
elided trap has no timing to preserve. Measured win: 7.9x on kata #137.

That route is unavailable here, and unavailable for a reason already on the
record: this row's shape adds an UNBOUNDED HEAP VALUE (`a[i]`), so no
trip-count argument bounds the result — exactly the
"bounded counter x unbounded heap element" residual that
`docs/spikes/overflow-check-elision.md` rejected building a prover for. So the
elementwise case can only be reached by deferral, which is strictly the worse
of the two routes: it pays four observability conditions the precedent pays
none of, for a shape that does not occur.

CAVEAT ON THE POPULATION, stated because it is the one thing that could reopen
this. The kata corpus is NOT part of a cloud clone (`../kara-katas` absent), and
katas skew more array-numeric than stdlib/selfhost, so the true rate there is
probably above zero. But the nine `examples/leetcode` files present here are
kata-shaped and produced one hit, itself disqualified by a real dependence; and
the qualifying conditions are restrictive enough (single checked op, no calls,
no other surviving trap, no loop-carried dependence, non-drop-observable
destination, trip count worth vectorizing) that a handful of extra numeric
katas is unlikely to flip the decision. REOPEN CRITERION, so this is falsifiable
rather than a judgement call: run the same scan over `kara-katas` and reopen if
more than a couple of loops survive hand-verification. The scan is a dozen
lines of regex plus manual inspection of the hits.

fix: b64a8b47 — `eval_par_block` now pushes a scope in each branch interpreter after seeding the environment snapshot, so the join merges only the bindings the branch INTRODUCED instead of the whole flattened enclosing environment. The merged snapshot was shadowing every outer variable in the parent's current scope, which swallowed any assignment made after the par block inside a nested block.
tracker: FIXED 2026-08-07 (b64a8b47). THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS SHOULD BE READ AS SUPERSEDED IN TWO WAYS, both of which make it worse rather than smaller. (1) IT IS NOT A HANG, IT IS AN INFINITE LOOP. A `println` on either side of the par block inside the loop body shows the body executing forever, so `i = i + 1` never sticks. The row's three named candidates -- scheduler deadlock, livelock, unbounded work per iteration -- are all wrong; nothing is deadlocked and the scheduler is fine. (2) THE HANG IS THE LOUD SYMPTOM OF A SILENT WRONG-ANSWER DEFECT, and the silent form is the bigger problem. `let mut n = 0; if 1 < 2 { par { let a = 1; let b = 2; } n = n + 5; } println(n)` prints 0 under --interp and 5 under AOT. No loop, no hang, no diagnostic -- just a wrong number out of the backend that serves as the Mend ORACLE.  ROOT CAUSE. `eval_par_block` seeds each branch interpreter with `env.snapshot()`, which FLATTENS every scope into a single map, and `define()` writes all of it into the branch's one scope. The join then merged `scopes.last()` back into the parent -- i.e. the entire enclosing environment, re-`define`d into the parent's CURRENT scope. At function top level that is invisible, because it rewrites bindings in the scope they already occupy; every existing par test puts the block at the top level of `main`, which is exactly why this survived. One block deeper the current scope is the block's, so each outer variable gained a SHADOW there and the next assignment updated the shadow, which died when the block scope popped.  THE TRIGGER IS NOT WHAT THE REPRO SUGGESTS. It is not tuples, not destructuring, not re-entry, and not `while` specifically: it is a par block with TWO OR MORE STATEMENTS, anywhere below function top level. At one statement or fewer `eval_par_block` returns early and never reaches the join, which is why `par { let a = 1; }` in a loop was fine and `par { let a = 1; let b = 2; }` in an `if` was not. ONE iteration is enough; the row's two-iteration framing implied re-entry mattered, and it does not. Narrowing that settled it: par-tuple in `if` -> wrong; par-tuple in `for` -> wrong; 2-stmt par with no tuple in `if` -> wrong; 1-stmt par in `if` -> correct; par at top level -> correct.  FIX: push a scope in the branch after seeding and `register_items()`, so `scopes.last()` holds only what the branch actually introduced. One line, plus the comment explaining why the seeded snapshot must not be merged back.  TESTS, both confirmed RED against the unfixed compiler: `test_par_block_join_does_not_shadow_enclosing_bindings` (the silent half -- fails fast, and is the one worth guarding hardest) and `test_par_block_inside_while_loop_terminates` (the loud half). The second runs on a worker with a 60-second deadline, because a regression there does not fail, it spins -- an un-timed assertion would hang the suite rather than report it.  GREEN: interpreter 1470, par_codegen 246, concurrency 139, spawn_e2e 16, cross_task_safe 4, concurrency_report 3, par_atomic_promotion 2, parallax 6, parallax_lite 5; fmt and clippy clean.
title: a `par {}` block inside a `while` loop HANGS under `--interp` (the DEFAULT for `karac check`-adjacent workflows and the Mend oracle) while the identical program builds and runs correctly AOT -- no shared type, no `frozen`, no captures needed to reproduce
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while building a fixture for B-2026-08-01-33 stage 3b, and
proven INDEPENDENT of that work before being filed -- reproduced with the
stage-3b change stashed and the compiler rebuilt, identical hang.

REPRO, and it is as small as the shape gets. No `shared` type, no `frozen`, no
captured heap -- just a `par` block whose branches read the loop counter:

    fn main() {
        let mut total: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 2 {
            let (a, b) = par {
                let a = i + 1;
                let b = i + 2;
                (a, b)
            };
            total = total + a + b;
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(total);
    }

    karac run --interp   -> HANGS (killed at 45 s, and at 60 s on a 2-iteration
                            variant; no output, no diagnostic, no progress)
    karac build + run    -> correct, immediate
    karac check          -> "All checks passed"

TWO ITERATIONS IS ENOUGH, which is what makes this a hang rather than slowness:
the AOT twin of the same program completes instantly, and a single `par` block
NOT inside a loop is fine under `--interp` (every existing par interpreter test
is that shape, which is presumably why this has gone unnoticed).

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A BACKEND CURIOSITY: `--interp` is the ORACLE half of
the Mend loop and of this repo's own differential testing -- the tree-walk
result is what a codegen result is checked against. A shape that hangs there
cannot be cross-checked at all, so any `par`-in-a-loop program is currently
un-oracled rather than merely slow to verify. It is also the backend `karac
run` falls back to for the opt-in runtime archives (regex, Arrow, gpu), so a
program combining one of those with a `par` loop has no working run path.

NOT MEASURED YET, and deliberately not guessed at: whether the hang is a
deadlock in the interpreter's par scheduler (a join that never completes when
the block is re-entered), a livelock, or unbounded work per iteration. The
distinguishing observation is cheap and is the obvious first step -- attach to
the hung process, or add a per-iteration trace -- but it was not done here
because this was found while landing an unrelated slice and filing it beat
folding it in.

CONTROLS ESTABLISHED:
  * `par` OUTSIDE a loop, same branches            -> fine under --interp
  * the same loop with the `par` block removed     -> fine
  * AOT build of the hanging program               -> correct output
  * with B-2026-08-01-33 stage 3b stashed          -> still hangs (so the hang
    predates that slice and is not caused by it)
