title: a `frozen` handle has no legal place to be STORED, so no iterative traversal can use one: a local `VecDeque[Node]` worklist refuses `queue.push_back(root)`, and there is no way to declare `VecDeque[frozen Node]`. This is what actually blocks kata #133 after B-2026-08-01-33 stage 3b -- recursion works, worklists do not, and both of that kata's variants carry a `visited: Map[i64, Node]`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by running the real kata after B-2026-08-01-33 stage 3b
landed, which is also what corrected that row's "#133's shape runs" claim -- the
fixture that passes walks the graph by RECURSION, the kata is ITERATIVE, and
that is the axis `frozen` discriminates on.

REPRO, minimal, both errors at the same site:

    shared struct Node { val: i64, mut neighbors: Vec[Node] }
    fn bfs(root: frozen Node) -> i64 {
        let mut queue: VecDeque[Node] = VecDeque.new();
        queue.push_back(root);
        return queue.len();
    }

    error[typecheck]: expected 'Node', found 'ref Node'
    error[ownership]: `frozen` parameter `root` is passed to a non-`frozen` slot

WHY IT IS REFUSED, and the refusal is correct as the rules stand: a `frozen`
value is non-counting, and property 3 (non-escaping) is what pays for that -- a
non-counting handle stored in a container that outlives the region is a
use-after-free. The checker cannot see that THIS worklist is local and dies with
the call, so it refuses the store.

WHY IT IS STILL A GAP: the container is not the problem, the absence of a
SPELLING is. The design's property 2 makes projection sticky (`g.neighbors`
yields frozen elements) but says nothing about DECLARING storage, so there is no
`VecDeque[frozen Node]` to push into. Every iterative graph algorithm -- BFS
with a queue, DFS with an explicit stack, anything with a `visited` map holding
handles -- is outside the mechanism. Both variants of kata 133 carry
`visited: Map[i64, Node]`.

SIZING, not a plan: this is language surface (a type-level `frozen` inside a
container type), so it is the owner's call in the same way the `frozen` mode
itself was. The cheaper-looking alternative -- inferring that a local container
never escapes -- is mechanism 1 wearing a hat again, and inherits its failure
mode, so it should not be reached for without that being said out loud.

NOT A REGRESSION. This shape never worked; before stage 3b the same program was
refused earlier, at the freeze site. What changed is that the refusal moved to
the point that names the real obstacle.

-- SCOPED (2026-08-07): the pop-free traversal QUESTION IS SETTLED YES, and two
   constraints found while scoping change what a first slice can be --

DECISION TAKEN: the BINDING-LEVEL route, not the type-level one this row
originally proposed. `src/parser/types.rs` records that the type-level path was
ATTEMPTED AND BACKED OUT -- `TypeKind::Frozen` exists and is handled at 25 sites
across 12+ files but is never CONSTRUCTED, because "every phase that unwraps
`Ref | MutRef` must learn a third form", and the attempt "turned up four rounds
of such sites in codegen alone ... with no reason to believe the fourth was the
last". The parser refuses `VecDeque[frozen Node]` with an explicit message
listing every position the mode is not accepted in. So this row's original
framing ("a language-surface addition") UNDERSTATED the cost, and the estimate
should not be trusted as written.

FINDING 1 -- A POP-FREE WORKLIST IS A REAL TRAVERSAL, so the slice is worth
building rather than motion. An INDEX-CURSOR BFS needs no `pop` at all:

    fn walk(root: frozen Node) -> i64 {
        let mut work: Vec[Node] = Vec.new();
        work.push(root);
        let mut i: i64 = 0; let mut total: i64 = 0;
        while i < work.len() {
            let n = work[i as u64];
            total = total + n.val;
            for k in n.kids { work.push(k); }
            i = i + 1;
        }
        return total;
    }

MEASURED: the identical function with an ORDINARY (unfrozen) `root` checks clean
and runs. With `frozen root` it produces exactly TWO errors, both at the SAME
site -- `work.push(root)` -- and nothing else in the traversal is refused. So
the whole gap for this shape is the container STORE. Note also `work[i]` is an
`Index`, which `frozen_place_root` already handles, so indexed read-back needs
no new abstraction; only `pop_front()`-style retrieval does, because a method
RETURN is a value and not a place.

FINDING 2 -- THE CHECKER AND CODEGEN HALVES CANNOT BE SPLIT, and this is the
constraint that shapes the slice. It is tempting to land the ownership
admission first and the refcount elision after, since admitting the store while
codegen still emits the ordinary retain-on-push / release-on-drop is BALANCED
and perfectly memory-safe in sequential code. It is not safe in the only context
this feature exists for: inside a `par` branch that retain is a write to the
SHARED refcount header, which is precisely the race `frozen` was introduced to
remove (`emit_rc_inc` is a plain load/add/store -- B-2026-07-28-13's SIGSEGV).
A checker-only slice would therefore compile a program that races, with no
diagnostic. Both halves land together or neither does.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE CODEGEN HALF: `frozen_alias_bindings` is a
`HashSet<SpanKey>` keyed on a single `let` initializer -- "skip the clone, the
inc, the dec" for ONE binding. There is no channel for container ELEMENTS, so
this needs a new plain-data hint (codegen-containment forbids the mode itself
crossing into codegen). That is the half where being wrong costs a leak or a
use-after-free, so it wants the `memory_sanitizer` suite at BOTH opt levels
before it is believed.

STILL TRUE, and worth repeating so the slice is not mis-sold: Vec/VecDeque
alone does NOT unblock kata 133. Both of that kata's variants carry
`visited: Map[i64, Node]`, so `Map[K, frozen V]` is a second slice.

-- (1) PROTOTYPED AND REVERTED; THREE FINDINGS THAT MAKE THE REMAINDER SMALL --

~142 lines in `frozen_escape.rs`, built and probed, then reverted because the
coupling above forbids landing the checker without the codegen half. Recorded
so the next attempt starts from the answers rather than rediscovering them.

WHAT WORKED: `<local Vec>.push(<frozen place>)` admits, the container joins the
frozen set, and the ownership error MOVES OFF the push site. On the index-cursor
BFS the diagnostic went from "passed to a non-`frozen` slot" at `work.push(root)`
to a single remaining error at the element read -- so the store half of the
design is right.

FINDING A -- IT NEEDS A FIXPOINT, and the naive fixpoint has a TIME-TRAVEL BUG
that a probe caught immediately. One ordered pass cannot work: `work[i]` is
walked before the `work.push(k)` below it in a loop body, while at runtime the
container already holds frozen handles from the previous iteration. So a pass
must DISCOVER and the next pass SEED. But carrying `cx.frozen` across passes is
wrong in the other direction -- a name frozen LATE in pass 1 (a `freeze`
statement's source root) is still frozen at the TOP of pass 2, so statements
ABOVE the freeze are judged against a guarantee that does not exist yet, and
`root.kids.push(..)` written before `let g = freeze root` was refused. Each pass
must rebuild `frozen` from the INITIAL set (params + `frozen self`) plus the
seeds.

FINDING B -- THE TYPECHECK BLOCKER IS CONFINED TO THE PARAMETER SPELLING, which
splits the work in a way this row did not have. A `frozen` PARAMETER is stored
as `Ref(T)` (see the parser's note), so `work.push(root)` fails typecheck with
"expected 'Node', found 'ref Node'" before ownership is consulted. A `freeze`
STATEMENT's local keeps type `Node` and pushes CLEANLY -- verified. So the
local-freeze spelling needs no typechecker change at all, and only the frozen-
param spelling does. A first slice can therefore be checker+codegen only, and
should be scoped to the statement form.

FINDING C -- THE CONTAINER'S TYPE MUST COME FROM ITS `let`, NOT ITS PUSH SITE.
The prototype seeded the element type from `tc.expr_types` at the method-call
RECEIVER span; instrumented, that returns `Unit`, not `Vec[Node]`, so
`element_type` failed and `try_admit_frozen_alias` declined the element read --
the one error left on the probe. The fix is to record local `Vec`/`VecDeque`
binding types at the `let` and look them up by name at the push. Small, and it
is the last known blocker for the checker half.

NOT REVERTED BECAUSE IT WAS WRONG -- reverted because a checker that admits the
store while codegen still retains would compile a racing program, per FINDING 2
above. The three findings hold regardless of when the codegen half is built.

-- FIXED (2026-08-08), stage 3c: BINDING-LEVEL FROZEN CONTAINERS, `Vec` only --

WHAT LANDS. `let mut work: Vec[S] = …` is now recognised as a FROZEN-ELEMENT
CONTAINER when the walk can prove three things about it, and the measured
index-cursor BFS of FINDING 1 checks clean and runs:

  * CONTAINMENT -- every use of the name is one of `push`/`push_back` (one
    unlabelled, non-`mut` argument), `len`/`is_empty`, or `c[i]`. Reaching
    `walk_expr`'s `Identifier` arm with the name means it was used BARE
    (returned, passed, captured, iterated, aliased) and disqualifies it. Same
    inverted whitelist as the rest of the module: a container refused is a
    frozen push reported, never an element that can leave the frame.
  * UNIFORMITY -- every push argument is a frozen place. One ordinary push and
    the container is refused outright, because the scope-exit element drop is
    ALL-OR-NOTHING: skipping it would leak the counted element, running it
    would over-release the frozen ones, and neither is available.
  * LIFETIME -- the owner whose refcount each element skips must OUTLIVE the
    container. Tracked as block PATHS, so "outlives" is prefix containment. A
    `frozen` parameter's owner is the caller, hence the empty path, hence it
    encloses everything -- which is why the parameter-rooted shape needs no
    analysis and the `freeze`-STATEMENT shape does.

CODEGEN, THE OTHER HALF, per FINDING 2 -- both suppressions land in the same
commit and each was PROVEN necessary by neutering it and running LSan:

  * push retain skipped (`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex(.., false)`
    plus the `share_shared_struct_ref_for_arg` aliasing-read sibling);
  * scope-exit per-element `__karac_vec_elem_rc_dec_*` drain skipped
    (`track_vec_var` instead of `track_vec_of_aggs_var`). The BUFFER is still
    freed -- that is the one thing the container does own.

MEASURED, on the identical traversal with an unfrozen root as the baseline:
rc_inc 4 -> 1, rc_dec 2 -> 1, element-drain loops 1 -> 0. The surviving pair is
the owned `src` parameter's own receive-inc and drop, outside the frozen region
and deliberately untouched.

HALF-ONLY RUNS, since "both halves or neither" was an argument before it was a
measurement -- each half disabled, the OTHER kept, on the ASAN fixture:
  * retain skipped / drain kept -> `AddressSanitizer: SEGV ... in
    __par_branch_0_0` (the over-release use-after-free);
  * drain skipped / retain kept -> `LeakSanitizer: 1928 byte(s) leaked in 62
    allocation(s)` -- one stranded ref per node of the 63-node graph.
So the pairing is not a precaution; either half alone is a memory bug, and the
two failure modes are the two the row predicted.

THE `par` REGION TEST IS POSITIONAL, NOT A FLAG, and that distinction carries
the feature rather than refining it. A worklist declared INSIDE a branch is
branch-local and is exactly what `frozen` exists to admit; one declared outside
and pushed to from two branches is two threads writing one `{ptr,len,cap}`. The
first draft used a bare "inside a par" flag, which refused both and left the
mechanism with nothing to do. Same positional rule for closures and `defer`.

THE FIXPOINT RUNS DOWNWARD (FINDING A, resolved). Upward from the empty set
never converges anywhere useful -- `work` is a container only if `work[i]` is
frozen and vice versa, so the LEAST fixpoint is empty and the shape stays
refused. It starts from "every candidate is a container" and removes what the
walk disproves. Sound despite being coinductive: a container starts EMPTY, so
the first push into it can never be self-sourced, and by induction every
element traces to a genuine seed. A purely self-referential container stays
empty forever. Round 0 is DISCOVERY ONLY -- its rejections are discarded,
because with nothing assumed frozen every element read looks like an ordinary
use. Each round rebuilds `frozen` from the initial set, which is the
time-travel fix.

FINDING C, resolved as recorded: the element type comes from the `let`
ANNOTATION (`container_candidate_type`), never from `tc.expr_types` at the
method-call receiver, which returns `Unit`.

SCOPE, stated so it is not mis-sold. `Vec` only -- `VecDeque` additionally
wants `pop_front`, whose result is a VALUE and not a place, so it needs a
second mechanism rather than a wider list. The `freeze`-STATEMENT spelling
only: a `frozen` PARAMETER is stored as `Ref(T)`, so `work.push(root)` still
fails typecheck with "expected 'Node', found 'ref Node'" before ownership is
consulted (FINDING B, re-measured and unchanged). And kata 133 is STILL NOT
unblocked: both its variants carry `visited: Map[i64, Node]`, so `Map[K, frozen
V]` remains a separate slice. What this buys is the class of iterative
traversal -- BFS with an index cursor, DFS with an explicit stack -- which had
no expression at all before.

GATES: memory_sanitizer 990/990 at -O2 AND at -O0 (LSan, Linux -- the
authoritative leg); ownership 415/0; par_codegen 246/0; concurrency 139/0;
codegen 2835/0; typechecker 2155/0; interpreter 1468/0; effectchecker 417/0;
clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm and fmt clean. Each of the four
checker guards was neutered individually and fails exactly its own reject row.
(`tests/cli.rs::test_build_text_pad_lever_moves_main_without_changing_behaviour`
fails on the unmodified tree too -- pre-existing, unrelated, not from this.)

-- CORRECTION (2026-08-08): the "kata 133 is STILL NOT unblocked ... both its
variants carry `visited: Map[i64, Node]`, so `Map[K, frozen V]` remains a
separate slice" claim above IS WRONG. That map holds the CLONES, which are
mutated throughout and can never be frozen; it needs nothing from the
mechanism. The claim was derived from the kata's type signatures rather than
from what it does with them. See B-2026-08-08-2 for the measurement and for the
gap that was actually left (the `frozen` PARAMETER spelling), which is now
fixed -- the kata adopts.

fix: DECLINED, PRICED, no code change -- and closed rather than parked, because all three shipping paths are settled noes rather than deferrals. (a) Carrying an LLVM patch for the Apple subtargets' `PrefLoopLogAlignment` is disqualified by DISTRIBUTION, not effort: karac builds against whatever LLVM the user has, so a fork breaks `cargo install karac --features llvm`, which is a launch gate traded for one kata. (b) Upstreaming needs multi-host, multi-workload data and would reach users only at LLVM 21+; the measurement here is a decent seed for it and nothing more. (c) Shipping the blanket flag as a documented opt-in is WORSE than doing nothing: `-align-all-nofallthru-blocks` is an internal cl::opt in MachineBlockPlacement.cpp with no stability guarantee, and `KARAC_LLVM_ARGS` silently ignores an unknown flag (verified), so an LLVM upgrade that drops it would revert the optimization with zero signal -- acceptable for a measurement lever, a trap for a user-facing recipe. REOPEN CONDITION, and it is a real one: if a Kara workload that actually ships -- not a kata -- is found placement-pathological the way kata:170 is, the 10% becomes worth an LLVM dependency and (b) gets its justification. `KARAC_TEXT_PAD` makes that detectable on any program in minutes, so the condition is testable rather than aspirational.
tracker: MEASURED AND RE-SCOPED 2026-08-07, same day as filing. The row's own numbers were taken single-point-per-kata and are corrected in `detail`: the method was invalid where the placement lottery is wide, two of eight readings (kata:8, kata:405) were noise, and the kata:170 win is 10.0% rather than 8.6%. The row's requested work -- narrow the trigger to loops -- is now ANSWERED but BLOCKED: the trigger exists in LLVM as the AArch64 subtarget's `PrefLoopLogAlignment`, every Apple CPU model sets it to zero, and no karac-side interface reaches it (checked against LLVM 18's full cl::opt alignment family and all 344 AArch64 subtarget features). So this is no longer a codegen design question; it is a decision about whether to carry or upstream an LLVM change, or to ship the blanket flag opt-in at a priced 0.18% median. Staying open on that decision, not on missing information. CLOSED 2026-08-07, same day, after being asked what it was staying open FOR. The answer was nothing: the row had no trigger, only three options already reasoned down to no. One nuance worth keeping, because it nearly went the other way: the 10% on kata:170 is NOT luck-harvesting -- aligned's median (0.9003) beats the BEST unaligned placement (0.9590), so alignment gives that kata something no placement can. It is a real win that simply does not generalise by workload class: kata:146 is also map-heavy and gains nothing (1.0021). The durable half of this row is a REPORTING risk, not a compiler one, and is now B-2026-08-07-25 rather than a paragraph buried here.

The NARROW trigger this row wanted is real, is worth most of the win at a twelfth of the padding, and is ONE LLVM AArch64 SUBTARGET CONSTANT (`PrefLoopLogAlignment`, which every Apple CPU model sets to ZERO and neoverse-v2/n2, cortex-x3, ampere1b and a64fx set non-zero) -- reachable through NO karac-side interface, so the row is blocked on LLVM rather than on a design
detail:
Apple M5 Pro / arm64, karac at HEAD with matched lean/full archives; metric CYCLES via scripts/pmc.c; arms interleaved in rotated order within one session; every binary sink-checked before timing. Reached with `KARAC_LLVM_ARGS` and `KARAC_TEXT_PAD`, the levers B-2026-08-07-10 shipped (c538a878).

METHOD CORRECTION FIRST, BECAUSE IT CHANGES THE NUMBERS THIS ROW WAS FILED WITH. The original filing compared ONE unaligned build against ONE aligned build per kata. That is not a measurement of alignment: for a kata whose placement lottery is 31% wide it is one draw against another draw -- the same hole that sank the parent row's 1.09x. Redone as DISTRIBUTION vs DISTRIBUTION: 8 placements (`KARAC_TEXT_PAD` 4..60 step 8) of BOTH configs, all 16 timed in one interleaved session, comparing medians across placements.

THE CORRECTED TABLE (aligned/unaligned, median across 8 placements):
  kata:170  0.9003   <- 10.0% faster, not the 8.6% filed
  kata:8    0.9821   <- 1.8% FASTER; the +2.0% filed at 16B was noise
  kata:11   0.9999   <- exactly neutral, and not placement-sensitive at all
  kata:405  ~1.002   <- neutral within its own noise; the +1.4% filed was noise
  kata:146  1.0021
  kata:9    1.0026   <- systematic, 7 of 8 placements slower
  kata:71   1.0112   <- systematic, 6 of 8; re-run at 27 rounds; the worst case
  MEDIAN 1.0018 (filed: 1.0034)
kata:1665 was dropped, not omitted: at 4 ms its own spread exceeds the effect.

So the SHAPE of the filing survives -- one large win, a small median tax -- but two of its eight readings were noise and the win is larger than stated. kata:170's result is the strong form: spread collapses 1.2987 -> 1.0144 and the WORST aligned placement (0.8959 of the unaligned median) beats the BEST unaligned one (0.9590). Alignment does not move that kata to a luckier spot; it removes the lottery.

THE NARROW TRIGGER IS NOT REACHABLE FROM karac, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. LLVM 18's whole alignment cl::opt family is `align-all-blocks`, `align-all-nofallthru-blocks`, `align-all-functions` and `max-bytes-for-alignment`; every loop-specific one is target-specific (x86's `x86-experimental-pref-{,innermost-}loop-alignment`, PPC's `disable-ppc-innermost-loop-align32`, AMDGPU, Hexagon, Mips) and there is NONE for AArch64. Nor is it a subtarget feature: none of the 344 features AArch64 lists is loop alignment.

`max-bytes-for-alignment` IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE. At 8 and 16 bytes it aligns nothing at all (0 nops in `main`); at 32 it emits 20 nops against the unbounded 118 but makes the fix placement-DEPENDENT again -- 0.9856 / 0.9887 / 0.8876 at three placements, against a flat ~0.877 unbounded. A budget is not a trigger: it skips whichever blocks are expensive to align, which is uncorrelated with which blocks matter.

BUT THE TRIGGER EXISTS IN LLVM, AND IT IS CPU-MODEL-DRIVEN. `MachineBlockPlacement` already aligns loop headers to `TargetLowering::getPrefLoopAlignment()`, which AArch64 takes from the subtarget's `PrefLoopLogAlignment`. Building kata:170 across CPU models and counting nops in `main` shows exactly who sets it: neoverse-v2 / neoverse-n2 / cortex-x3 emit 10, ampere1b 87, a64fx 4 -- and apple-m1, apple-m2, apple-m3, apple-latest, apple-a17 and generic emit ZERO. karac targets `apple-m1` on darwin-arm64 (driver.rs `default_cpu_and_features`), so no Kāra binary on Apple silicon has ever had a single loop aligned.

AND IT CARRIES MOST OF THE WIN AT A TWELFTH OF THE PADDING. On kata:170, neoverse-v2 runs 0.9221 of apple-m1 WHILE EXECUTING 1.7% MORE INSTRUCTIONS (12.207B vs 12.005B), and ampere1b 0.9381 with 3.4% more, against blanket block alignment's 0.9144 at an IDENTICAL instruction count. ~10 nops of loop-header alignment buys most of what 118 nops of blanket alignment buys. This is directional rather than isolated -- `--target-cpu` also swaps the scheduling model and instruction selection -- but the direction survives an instruction-count handicap, which is the strong form of the evidence.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS, and it is a decision, not a discovery. (a) Carry a one-line LLVM patch giving the Apple AArch64 subtargets a non-zero `PrefLoopLogAlignment`, and re-run this table; that is the version that takes the 10% without the 1.1% worst case, and it is the only version that gets the narrow trigger. (b) Upstream the same change, which needs the measurement on more than one host. (c) Ship blanket `-align-all-nofallthru-blocks=6` on Apple arm64 as an opt-in build flag and accept the priced trade: +10% on map-probe code, -1.1% worst case, +0.18% median. Doing NOTHING is also defensible at a 0.18% median, and is the current state.

NOT MEASURED: x86 (where the parent row found FUNCTION alignment neutral-to-worse), the par lane, and any kata outside these eight. One host, one ISA, one lane.

title: A BENCHED KATA'S HEADLINE NUMBER CAN CARRY A 1.31x PLACEMENT RANGE BEHIND IT AND THE CORPUS HAS NEVER BEEN CHECKED FOR IT: kata:170's recorded figure is one draw from a distribution spanning 0.970..1.269, so a reader who rebuilds it on their own machine can legitimately get a number ~30% off ours and we have no explanation on file -- the exposure is confined to katas whose headline is a CLOSE CALL against a comparator, which is a small and enumerable subset
detail:
NOT A COMPILER DEFECT -- a reporting risk, filed against the bench lane. It is the durable half of B-2026-08-07-24, which closed having declined the optimization.

THE FACT. On arm64, a kata's runtime can be a function of its code's address mod 64 (see B-2026-08-07-10 for the mechanism and the levers). kata:170 spans 0.970..1.269 across placements -- a 1.31x range -- and the single number in its README and in bench-results.json is one draw from that. Nothing about the compiler, the source, or the comparator changed; the same karac rebuilt after any commit that shifts emitted code size ahead of `main` re-draws it.

WHY IT MATTERS AT LAUNCH RATHER THAN IN GENERAL. Every published kata number is an invitation to reproduce it. A reader who rebuilds kata:170 and lands on a different placement gets a figure up to 30% off ours, and today we have no answer for them -- not "here is the range", not "here is why". That is a credibility problem out of proportion to the 10% of compiler performance behind it, and it is cheap to retire.

THE EXPOSURE IS ASYMMETRIC, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS BOUNDED. Where a kata is ahead 2x, a 5% placement swing changes no claim. Where a kata claims PARITY or a narrow win against rust/C/Go, a wide placement spread means the claim itself may not reproduce. So only close-call katas need checking, and only the SPREAD needs measuring -- no aligned arm, no second config, half the work of the B-2026-08-07-24 sweep.

THE PRIOR, from the seven katas already swept 8 placements deep (2026-08-07): most are flat -- kata:11 1.0010, kata:9 1.0045, kata:146 1.0091 -- with kata:71 at 1.0632 and kata:170 at 1.2987 the outliers. So the expected outcome is that a handful of katas need annotating and the rest are confirmed tight. That is a result worth having either way: "measured, and the corpus is tight" is itself a claim we cannot currently make.

METHOD. `KARAC_TEXT_PAD` 4..60 step 8, one interleaved timing session per kata, cycles via scripts/pmc.c, sink-checked; report median and max/min across placements. Roughly one session per kata, and the katas are done one at a time per the bench lane's own rule.

CLOSES WHEN every kata whose README quotes a within-~15% comparison against a comparator has had its placement spread measured, and each is either confirmed under a stated threshold or annotated with its range in the README and results.json. Not before, and there is nothing else it is waiting on.

title: the `par` capture gate is keyed on binding NAMES, so two branches that each declare their own local `let n = <shared>` read as ONE binding reachable from both and are refused — renaming one is the entire fix, which is the proof it is a false positive
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while writing the stage 3c tests (B-2026-08-07-23). Two
branches running the same iterative traversal is the natural way to write that
test, and the natural way to write it uses the same variable names in both.

REPRO, and the diff between the two files is one identifier:

    shared struct Node { val: i64, mut kids: Vec[Node] }
    fn build() -> Node { return Node { val: 3, kids: Vec.new() }; }
    fn main() {
        let root = build();
        let g = freeze root;
        let (a, b) = par {
            let a = { ... let n = wa[ia as u64]; for k in n.kids { ... } ... };
            let b = { ... let n = wb[ib as u64]; for k in n.kids { ... } ... };
            (a, b)
        };
        println(a + b);
    }

    error[ownership]: shared struct `Node` cannot be accessed from multiple
    concurrent tasks (binding `n` reachable from two par-block branches:
    first use at line 15:26, conflicting use here)

Rename the SECOND branch's `n` to `m` -- nothing else -- and the program checks
clean. The two `n`s are distinct bindings in distinct block scopes that never
alias; the gate conflates them because it tracks names rather than binding
identities.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW. The diagnostic prescribes a STRUCTURAL migration --
"convert `Node` to `par struct` and wrap mut fields in `Mutex[T]`", with a
machine-applicable fix_diff -- for a program that has no sharing problem at
all. A reader who trusts it converts a type to atomic refcounting and locks
every field to satisfy a name collision. That is a far worse outcome than an
ordinary false positive, and `karac fix` will offer it.

It also lands exactly where `frozen` is supposed to help: fan-out over one
shared read-only structure is the shape the mode exists for, and N branches
running the SAME traversal is its most obvious form.

NOT A SOUNDNESS BUG. The direction is refusal, and the workaround (rename) is
trivial once you know. It is filed as medium because the diagnostic actively
misleads about the cause, not because the refusal is dangerous.

NOT MEASURED: whether the conflation is in the collection of capture roots or
in the comparison, and whether for-loop variables are affected too -- in the
repro `k` is ALSO shared between the branches and is not reported, so either
the gate stops at the first conflict or loop variables take a different path.
Worth establishing before fixing, since it decides whether the fix is scoping
the walk or keying it on a binding id.

-- FIXED (2026-08-08), 8c26ad4a --

ROOT CAUSE, and the row's "NOT MEASURED" question is now answered: it is the
COLLECTION, not the comparison. `collect_tracked_bindings` builds a single flat
`HashMap<String, TrackedBinding>` per FUNCTION and walks into every nested
block, so two branch-local `let n` write the same entry and the comparison --
which was never wrong -- then sees one binding used from two branches.

The second half of the question is answered too: for-loop variables were NOT
unaffected, the detector simply stops at the first reported name. `for k in
n.kids` in both branches conflates `k` exactly as it conflates `n`.

FIX. A use is dropped when it falls inside a region over which the name refers
to a binding introduced INSIDE the par body. Regions are byte-offset intervals
carried on the use SINK (`BranchUses`) rather than threaded as a parameter --
the sink already reaches every recording site in the ~400-line collector, so
no call site changed. That placement was chosen for a second reason: the
collector is NOT exhaustive (it ends in `_ => {}`), so a filter hooked into
the walk would inherit that hole, while one on the sink filters whatever the
walk produces.

Computed ONCE over the whole par body, not per branch: each region carries its
own bounds, so a `let` in branch A yields an interval that cannot reach branch
B.

FAIL-CLOSED BY CONSTRUCTION, because the two directions are not symmetric. A
region MISSED leaves the use looking like a capture -- the over-reporting that
predates this fix, and safe. A region too WIDE hides a real cross-branch
capture, which is a race on a non-atomic refcount. So a `let`'s region runs
from the END of its own statement to the end of its block, never from the
block's start; a pattern-scoped binding (`for`, `if let`, `while let`, match
arm) covers only its body or arm, never the scrutinee or iterable; and the
`_ => {}` arm in the region walk contributes NO shadows rather than a
conservative wide one.

PINNED AGAINST THE THREE WAYS THE INTERVAL COULD COME OUT TOO WIDE
(tests/ownership.rs
`the_par_capture_gate_resolves_a_name_to_its_binding_not_its_spelling`), each
verified to still report:
  * a use of the outer binding EARLIER in the same block than the shadowing
    `let`;
  * a use of the outer binding AFTER a nested shadowing block has closed --
    this is the row that establishes `Block.span` actually ends where the
    block ends, which the whole interval scheme rests on, and it was the one
    genuinely uncertain assumption going in;
  * `for n in n.kids`, where the ITERABLE names the outer binding.
The accept rows use a MATERIAL capture (projecting the `mut` container, not an
immutable scalar field) -- otherwise the B-2026-08-01-33 scalar-projection
suppression drops the binding before the conflict is considered and every row
passes vacuously.

Accept rows stash-proven red against the unmodified source.

concurrency_report 4/0, cross_task_safe 16/0, disjoint_differential 7/0,
memory_sanitizer 990/0, codegen 2835/0, interpreter 1468/0, typechecker
2155/0, effectchecker 417/0, elision 71/0; clippy --all --all-targets
--features llvm and fmt clean. No existing test depended on the conflation.

title: this row's PREMISE WAS WRONG -- kata #133 was never blocked on `Map[K, frozen V]` (its `visited` map holds the CLONES, which are mutated and can never be frozen); the real remaining gap was the `frozen` PARAMETER spelling, `ref T` vs `T`, at a container store
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the remaining half of B-2026-08-07-23, split out so the kata's
blocker stays tracked now that its original row is closed. That row admitted
the CONTAINER STORE for `Vec` and said this was a separate slice; this is that
slice, stated as its own item rather than as a sentence inside a fixed row.

WHAT WORKS NOW (63caea3e): a local `Vec[S]` worklist holds non-counting
handles, so an index-cursor BFS / explicit-stack DFS over a frozen graph
compiles and runs with zero refcount traffic across `par` branches.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING: the same admission for `Map[K, S]` / `Set[S]`. Every
graph algorithm that needs to answer "have I seen this node" carries one, and
both variants of LeetCode #133 do (`visited: Map[i64, Node]`).

WHY IT IS NOT JUST A WIDER LIST. The `Vec` slice leans on three properties
that need re-establishing, not re-using, for a Map:

  * ELEMENT DROP. The `Vec` half works by swapping `track_vec_of_aggs_var` for
    `track_vec_var` — buffer freed, elements not. A Map handle's drop is
    `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` with a K/V drop classification
    (`vec_elem_map_drop_for_type_expr`), so the equivalent is "free the
    buckets, run neither half's value drop" and that is a different switch.
  * READ-BACK IS NOT A PLACE. `c[i]` on a Vec is an `Index`, which
    `frozen_place_root` already models. A Map read is `m.get(k)` returning
    `Option[V]` — a VALUE, so a non-counting handle coming back through it has
    nothing the escape walk can track. This is the same obstacle `pop` has and
    it is why `VecDeque` was also left out. Either the walk learns a
    place-shaped Map read, or the mechanism stops at containers with one.
  * THE KEY IS A SECOND VALUE. `Map[i64, Node]` is fine, but the general form
    has a key that may itself be heap-bearing, and the uniformity condition
    ("every stored value is a frozen place") has to be stated over values only
    while the key stays ordinarily owned.

SIZING, honestly: the checker side is close to the `Vec` shape (containment,
uniformity, the block-path lifetime test all carry over unchanged). The
codegen side and the read-back question are the real work, and the read-back
question is a DESIGN decision — a value-returning accessor cannot yield a
non-counting handle under the current rules — so it should be settled before
anything is built.

-- CORRECTED AND FIXED (2026-08-08), d174d04c --

THE ROW'S PREMISE WAS WRONG, and so was the same claim in B-2026-08-07-23 and
in the messages that filed it. It was derived from the kata's TYPE SIGNATURES
(`visited: Map[i64, Node]` -- a Map of shared structs, therefore surely needing
`Map[K, frozen V]`) instead of from what the kata DOES with it. Reading the
body:

    let curr_clone = visited.get(curr.val).unwrap();
    curr_clone.neighbors.push(nb_clone);          // <- WRITTEN THROUGH

`visited` holds the CLONES. They are freshly constructed, owned, and mutated
for the whole algorithm; they are the OUTPUT. Freezing them is not merely
unnecessary, it is the opposite of what they are. The map needs nothing at all
from the mechanism, and `Map[K, frozen V]` would not have unblocked a single
line of this kata.

The frozen structure is the SOURCE graph, and the only container holding it is
the worklist -- `queue`, which B-2026-08-07-23 already handled for `Vec`.

MEASURED, per variant, before this commit:
  * DFS variant -- ALREADY WORKED. Recursive, `frozen Node` parameter, map of
    clones, two `par` branches: checks clean, builds, runs, output correct. It
    needed nothing.
  * BFS variant, index-cursor form, freeze STATEMENT, called once -- ALREADY
    CHECKED CLEAN (0 errors), and its clone checksums EQUAL to the source on a
    4-node cyclic graph.
  * BFS variant across `par` branches -- blocked, by ONE thing: the frozen
    PARAMETER spelling.

THE REAL GAP. `frozen T` lowers to `ref T` in the parser (deliberately -- that
spelling is what gives codegen the borrow convention, measured 0/0 and still
0/0 with the rc-elide pass off). So `queue.push(g)` with `g: frozen Node`
reported `expected 'Node', found 'ref Node'` -- against a type the author never
wrote, at a site whose OWNERSHIP side already admitted the store. Probed
position by position: the `Vec` push had a typecheck error and NO ownership
error, while `Map.insert` and `VecDeque.push_back` had both. So exactly one
surface was left.

FIX. `TypeChecker::current_fn_frozen_params` (saved/restored per function on
the same pattern as `current_fn_is_gpu`) plus `deref_frozen_param_arg`, which
strips one `Ref` when the argument is a bare identifier naming a `frozen`
parameter and the inner type matches the slot.

DELIBERATELY NOT A GENERAL COERCION, and the negative test is the load-bearing
one: relaxing `ref T` -> `T` for an ordinary borrow is the double-free
`types_compatible`'s `Ref` rule exists to stop (B-2026-07-18-31, masked at -O2
and live under -O0). `tests/typechecker.rs
a_frozen_param_is_storable_as_a_vec_element_but_a_ref_param_is_not` runs the
identical body under both modes and requires the `ref` one to still fail.

ADMITTING THE TYPE IS NOT ADMITTING THE STORE. Map inserts and VecDeque pushes
of a frozen handle still fail the escape walk; they simply stop failing twice,
with one of the two messages naming a type nobody wrote.

RESULT: kata #133's BFS clones a shared frozen graph from two `par` branches,
each branch's clone checksumming equal to the source. The kata ADOPTS.

STILL OPEN, and neither is what this row claimed:
  * `VecDeque` as a frozen-element container, which additionally needs
    `pop_front` -- a method RETURN is a value, not a place, so a non-counting
    handle coming back through one has nothing the escape walk can track. That
    is a design question about where frozen handles may come from, not an
    implementation gap. The kata's own BFS is written with `pop_front`; the
    index-cursor rewrite is what adopts today.
  * `Map[K, frozen V]` remains unbuilt -- but nothing in kata #133 wants it,

title: a `par` branch whose body is a BLOCK EXPRESSION containing a `Map` fails codegen with `Undefined variable '<outer destructured name>'`, while `karac check` passes — a clean run-vs-build divergence
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while measuring kata #133 for B-2026-08-08-2. Nothing to do
with `frozen`; reproduces on the pre-slice compiler.

REPRO, minimal:

    fn main() {
        let (x, y) = par {
            let x = { let mut va: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new(); let _ = va.insert(1, 2); va.len() };
            let y = 5;
            (x, y)
        };
        println(x + y);
    }

    error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'x'

`karac check` reports nothing. Removing the Map -- `let x = { let a: i64 = 1; a
+ 1 };` -- builds and runs, so the trigger is the Map inside a branch whose
body is a BLOCK EXPRESSION rather than a plain expression. Hoisting the block
into a helper function called from the branch also works, which is the
workaround.

WHY IT MATTERS: the reported name is the OUTER destructured binding (`x`), not
anything the block declares, so the message points away from the cause. And a
per-branch scratch Map is the natural shape for exactly the fan-out this
release is opening up -- every branch cloning or memoising into its own map.

CONFIRMED PRE-EXISTING: fails identically with `src/` checked out at 7a1d29f2,
before both B-2026-08-07-23 and B-2026-08-08-1.

NOT MEASURED: whether other handle-typed locals (Set, File, Tensor) in the same
position do it too, or whether it is specific to the Map slot-ownership
transfer at the branch boundary. The `Undefined variable` phrasing suggests the
branch outliner drops the destructured name's slot registration when the branch
body opens a scope that registers a transferable cleanup.

── FIXED da9ae409 ──

THREE OF THIS ROW'S OWN CLAIMS WERE WRONG, and each one pointed away from the
cause.

1. NOT MAP-SPECIFIC. `Vec`, `String` and `Set` reproduce it identically, so the
   row's "specific to the Map slot-ownership transfer at the branch boundary"
   hypothesis (and the `tracker` field naming the let-stmt Map arm) is off.
   Nothing about ownership is involved.

2. THE REPORTED NAME IS THE BRANCH BINDING, not the outer destructured one.
   The row says "the reported name is the OUTER destructured binding (`x`), not
   anything the block declares, so the message points away from the cause". It
   points AT the branch binding — the repro just spells both the same. Renaming
   them apart settles it:

       let (p, q) = par { let a = { .. }; let b = 5; (a, b) };
       -> Undefined variable 'a'

3. THE BLOCK EXPRESSION IS NOT THE TRIGGER, and neither is a heap local inside
   it. Both of these BUILD:

       let a = { let z: i64 = 1; z + 1 };                        (no heap)
       let a = { let mut va: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); va.push(2); 7 };  (heap, unused by the tail)

   The trigger is a TAIL whose type depends on a heap local — `va.len()`.

── THE MECHANISM, which the row's own last paragraph half-guessed ──

`infer_let_binding_llvm_type` sizes every branch's return slot BEFORE any branch
body is emitted (the return struct's layout has to be known up front), and its
documented contract is to drop the slot on any shape it cannot type. The drop is
silent, and the join expression's read of that binding then falls out of
`load_variable` as the generic `Undefined variable` — a diagnostic that names
the binding rather than the un-inferrable RHS. So an INFERENCE gap presents as a
scoping error, which is why the message points nowhere useful.

Two independent holes let this shape through, and both had to close:

  * `infer_block_tail_llvm_type` consulted only each inner `let`'s RHS and never
    its type ANNOTATION — while its own caller, one frame up, checks the
    annotation first. So `let mut va: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new()` dropped `va`
    from the local scope (nothing infers `Map.new()`), and the tail could not
    resolve its receiver. Proven separately: annotating the INTERMEDIATE
    (`let n: i64 = va.len(); n`) still failed pre-fix.

  * the `MethodCall` arm had no way to type a builtin `len()`. There is no
    `Map.len` LLVM function whose return type it could read, and `len` makes no
    `-> Self` claim, so it fell to `None`. Now resolved from
    `method_callee_types` — the TYPECHECKER's own record of what the receiver
    is, keyed by the call's span — rather than a second inference that could
    disagree with it. The admitted set is only methods with one possible return
    type across every receiver, because a slot sized WRONG is silent corruption
    where a slot left unsized is merely a bad diagnostic.

── MEASURED ──

18 variants, each built and run AOT against the interpreter, all agreeing: the
row's repro, its Vec / String / Set twins, `len()` through an unannotated
intermediate, the map-in-first-branch and both-branches-map shapes, a
three-branch middle-branch case, and the five controls that already built.
Valgrind clean at `-O0` and `-O2` (the one remaining `possibly lost` record is
`_dl_allocate_tls` from the pool threads, identical on a par program that built
before this change).

Fixtures `par_branch_block_body_ending_in_container_len` and
`par_branch_block_body_binding_distinct_from_destructured_name`
(`tests/par_codegen.rs`), both stash-proven red — the second exists because the
misreading in (2) above cost this row a wrong diagnosis, and pinning the two
names apart is what prevents it recurring.

── STILL TRUE, AND WORTH A ROW OF ITS OWN EVENTUALLY ──

The underlying fragility is unchanged: `infer_expr_llvm_type` is a hand-rolled
re-inference of types the typechecker already computed, and every shape it
cannot classify becomes a build failure on a program that checks and interprets
cleanly. This commit closes two holes in it; it does not remove the class.
Threading `TypeCheckResult.expr_types` through to codegen the way the narrower
span-keyed side-tables already are would, and `method_callee_types` is the proof
that the plumbing pattern exists.

Not fixed either, and separate: `let a = { .. va }` — a branch that returns the
CONTAINER rather than its length — still fails, with a different diagnostic
(`no handler for method 'len' on variable 'a'`). That is a method-dispatch gap
on the joined binding, not this one.

tracker: runtime refcounting — no cycle collector; src/codegen/runtime.rs rc drop walk
title: a CONTAINER-mediated strong cycle in a `shared struct` (`mut ns: Vec[N]`, `mut next: Option[N]`) is accepted and leaks the whole graph -- design.md said the compiler should REJECT it, and design.md was WRONG: the rejection would refuse every tree and AST, and its only escape hatch (`Vec[weak N]`) kills the children. Doc corrected; the genuinely unconstructible TUPLE case now rejected
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while building the kata-#133 sanitizer fixture for
B-2026-08-08-2. The kata's real inputs are cyclic graphs -- that is the point
of LeetCode #133 -- so this is squarely in the way of gating that kata under
LSan.

REPRO, and it contains nothing exotic:

    shared struct Node { val: i64, mut neighbors: Vec[Node] }
    fn build(seed: i64) -> Node {
        let a = Node { val: seed, neighbors: Vec.new() };
        let b = ...; let c = ...; let d = ...;
        a.neighbors.push(b); a.neighbors.push(d);
        b.neighbors.push(a); b.neighbors.push(c);
        c.neighbors.push(b); c.neighbors.push(d);
        d.neighbors.push(a); d.neighbors.push(c);
        return a;
    }
    fn main() { let r = build(env.args().len()); println(checksum(r)); }

    SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 288 byte(s) leaked in 8 allocation(s).

8 allocations for 4 nodes = one box plus one neighbours buffer each, i.e. the
whole graph.

WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A ROW RATHER THAN A SHRUG. The obvious reading is
"reference counting cannot collect cycles, working as intended". That reading
is WRONG as stated, because a TWO-node cycle (`a.neighbors.push(b);
b.neighbors.push(a);`) is measured CLEAN. So something already breaks the
simple case and does not scale to the four-node one, and which it is decides
whether this is a design limit to document or a bug to fix. Not established
either way.

ALSO MEASURED: cloning the cyclic graph into a second cyclic graph leaks the
SAME 288 bytes / 8 allocations, not double. So exactly one of the two graphs is
being collected. That asymmetry is a strong hint and should be the first thing
the next investigation pulls on -- the surviving one is reachable from a `Map`
that is dropped, the leaking one from a plain local.

CONSEQUENCE TODAY: the kata-#133 sanitizer fixture
(`asan_kata133_clone_graph_bfs_across_par_branches_no_leak`) is deliberately
ACYCLIC, so it gates the `frozen` mechanism rather than this. That is a real
coverage gap in the fixture and it is noted there, not hidden.

NOT CAUSED BY THE FROZEN WORK: reproduces with no `frozen`, no `freeze`, no
`par`, and its size is unchanged by them.

-- CORRECTED (2026-08-08). THE 'A 2-NODE CYCLE IS CLEAN' CLAIM ABOVE IS WRONG,
   AND HOW IT WAS WRONG MATTERS MORE THAN THAT IT WAS --

It was an LSan FALSE NEGATIVE, not a property of the program. Measured under
valgrind, EVERY cycle size leaks, and the total is exactly 72 bytes per node:

    self-cycle (1 node)   72 bytes  (40 direct + 32 indirect)
    2-node               144 bytes  (40 direct + 104 indirect)
    3-node               216 bytes
    4-node               288 bytes

Perfectly linear, so the whole graph leaks at every size and there is no
shape-dependence to explain.

WHY LSAN SAID OTHERWISE, established by construction rather than guessed: the
handles were still sitting in a DEAD STACK FRAME that nothing had overwritten,
and LSan scans the stack region conservatively, so it treated them as
reachable. Adding a deep recursion AFTER the graph dies -- purely to overwrite
that frame, changing nothing else -- makes LSan report exactly the valgrind
number:

    SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 144 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocation(s).

CAVEAT ON THE WHOLE `memory_sanitizer` CORPUS, which is why this belongs in the
ledger rather than in a comment. CLAUDE.md calls the Linux LSan job the
authoritative leak gate for the codegen-ownership class. It is still the best
instrument available, but it can UNDER-REPORT: a fixture that builds a
structure and drops it in `main` with no further stack activity may pass while
leaking, because the last pointers survive in the dead frame. The two cheap
mitigations are to do the allocating work in a HELPER and then churn the stack
before returning, or to cross-check with valgrind, which reports these
independently of stack residue. This is a different failure mode from the
already-documented vacuous-pass traps (`min_allocs`, missing archives) and is
not covered by them.

-- IT IS NOT 'RC CANNOT COLLECT CYCLES, WORKING AS INTENDED' --

design.md § Cycles is explicit: "The compiler analyzes the type graph at
compile time and REJECTS types that form ownership cycles. The `weak`
annotation breaks back-edges ... No runtime cycle collector." The summary table
reads "| Cycles | Compile-time rejected | `weak` required on back-edges |", and
§ 8305 gives this exact graph shape with `Vec[weak GraphNode]`.

Both mechanisms EXIST. `check_cycles` (src/ownership.rs) is real, and `weak` is
implemented end-to-end (B-2026-07-19-8: two-count control block, downgrade
store coercion, `Option[T]` read typing, LSan-gated). So this is not a missing
feature; it is two narrow holes in shipped ones.

-- GAP A: THE CYCLE CHECKER DOES NOT LOOK THROUGH CONTAINERS --

    shared struct N { v: i64, mut next: N }          -> REJECTED (correct)
      "shared-type cycle detected: N -> N"
    shared struct N { v: i64, mut next: Option[N] }  -> ACCEPTED, leaks
    shared struct N { v: i64, mut ns: Vec[N] }       -> ACCEPTED, leaks

So the walk follows a field's own type but not its generic ARGUMENTS. The
container-mediated form is the one every real graph uses, so the check is
missing exactly the case it exists for.

-- GAP B: `weak` CANNOT BE STORED INTO A CONTAINER, so gap A has no fix --

    shared struct C { v: i64, mut parent: weak P }
    c.parent = p;                       -> ACCEPTED, and measured LEAK-FREE

    shared struct N { v: i64, mut ns: Vec[weak N] }
    a.ns.push(b);                       -> error[typecheck]: expected 'weak N', found 'N'

The downgrade store coercion reaches a direct FIELD store and not a
container-ELEMENT store. design.md's own worked example (§ 8310,
`b.neighbors.push(a); // bidirectional, no cycle leak`) therefore does not
compile.

-- THE TWO ARE COUPLED, AND THE ORDER IS FORCED --

Landing gap A alone would reject every graph program in the corpus (kata #133's
`Node`, the `frozen` fixtures, anything with `Vec[Self]`) while gap B leaves
`Vec[weak N]` unusable -- a rejection with no compilable alternative. So:

  1. GAP B FIRST. Non-breaking on its own: it only widens what typechecks, and
     it is what makes the migration writable. Note the typecheck half alone is
     NOT enough -- codegen must emit the downgrade at the container store or
     the program compiles and stores a strong ref, which is the silent-wrong
     outcome this ledger is full of. Both halves, same commit, LSan-gated.
  2. GAP A SECOND, and it is a BREAKING language change for every graph
     program, so whether it lands as an error (what design.md says) or first as
     a lint is the owner's call, not an implementation detail.

NOT CAUSED BY THE FROZEN WORK: reproduces with no `frozen`, no `freeze`, no
`par`, and unchanged by them.

-- GAP B IS COMPLETE (f869989f). GAP A IS THE ONLY THING LEFT, AND IT IS THE
   OWNER'S CALL --

The read-back half landed, so `Vec[weak T]` is no longer store-only:
`match v[i] { Some(x) => .. }` reads `Some` while the target lives and `None`
once it dies, valgrind-clean at both opt levels. design.md's worked example
(§ 8310) now compiles AND runs. Four changes, three of them found by following
the first one's failures:

  1. TYPECHECK — a `weak T` ELEMENT read upgrades to `Option[T]`, the twin of
     the field read. A store LHS keeps the raw place type so B-2026-08-08-5's
     downgrade still applies.
  2. CODEGEN, THE READ — `compile_vec_index` emits the upgrade and materializes
     the niche Option, reusing the field path's own helpers. It also SKIPS the
     deep-clone that guards against aliasing a container slot: the upgraded
     value aliases nothing, and cloning it at the DECLARED element type (`weak
     N`, one word) over a 4-word Option made the match read a mangled tag and
     take `None` with the target plainly alive.
  3. CODEGEN, THE BOX LAYOUT — see B-2026-08-08-13. A silent corruption, and
     the most important thing this slice found.
  4. CODEGEN, THE BALANCE — `expr_is_weak_field_read` gates the acquire that
     balances an `Option[shared]` binding's scope-exit dec, and matched only
     `ExprKind::FieldAccess`. The element read took the dec without the inc:
     valgrind `Invalid read of size 8` on an already-freed 24-byte box, and
     `karac run` printing the right answer then dying in `malloc(): unaligned
     tcache chunk detected`. Exactly B-2026-07-21-21's failure, through a
     container instead of a field.

A NOTE ON THE INDEX ARM, because it bit and the reason is not obvious:
`assigning_lhs` is captured there WITHOUT being cleared. Clearing it made
`orig[1].random = x` upgrade its weak FIELD slot to `Option[Node]` and reject
the strong RHS — because `infer_field_access` infers its OBJECT before
capturing its own `is_lhs`, so the inner index arm runs first and a clear there
is a clear for the enclosing field access. Two existing ASAN fixtures caught it.

STILL OPEN in this row, and now the whole of it:

  * GAP A — the cycle checker does not look through containers. UNCHANGED and
    deliberately so: it is a BREAKING language change for every graph program
    in the corpus, and whether it lands as an error (what design.md says) or
    first as a lint is the owner's call. The precondition the row set for it is
    now met — `Vec[weak N]` is fully usable, so a rejection would have a
    compilable alternative to point at.
  * A `Vec[weak N]` held as a struct FIELD still leaks (2,264 bytes on the
    probe). PRE-EXISTING — measured identically on a stashed tree — and
    untouched by this slice, which fixes the bare-variable and param shapes.
  * The INTERPRETER does not implement the weak-element read: `karac run
    --interp` reports "non-exhaustive match ... the typechecker should have
    rejected this", which is both wrong and the misleading-message class
    B-2026-08-06-24 covers. `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` are correct.
    Filed as B-2026-08-08-14.
  * `Map[K, weak V]` / `Set` / array / tuple element reads — untouched, same
    as their stores.

-- GAP A RESOLVED (2026-08-08), BY OVERTURNING IT RATHER THAN IMPLEMENTING IT.
   THE ROW'S PREMISE -- "design.md specifies REJECTION, so this is a hole" --
   IS WRONG, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES IT IS THE ESCAPE HATCH ITSELF --

The row framed gap A as a shipped mechanism with a hole in it, and left the
error-vs-lint choice to the owner as though those were the only two options.
Both readings were wrong. Measured, with the fix for gap B already in:

    shared struct Node { mut v: i64, mut kids: Vec[Node] }   -- acyclic tree
      valgrind: "All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible"

    shared struct Cell { mut v: i64, mut next: Option[Cell] } -- acyclic list
      correct, no leak

    THE SAME TREE WRITTEN Vec[weak Node] -- the alternative a rejection would
    have to point at -- compiles, runs, and prints -1: the children are ALREADY
    DEAD when `build` returns.

That last row is the whole argument. `weak` breaks BACK-EDGES; it is not a
substitute for DOWNWARD OWNERSHIP. A `Vec[weak Node]` child list holds nothing
alive, so rejecting `Vec[Node]` would refuse every tree and AST in the language
and hand the author a workaround that silently produces a WRONG PROGRAM. A
rejection with no correct alternative is worse than the leak it prevents --
which is why it does not ship as an error, and why it does not ship as a lint
either: a warning that fires on every correct tree is noise, and it cannot
distinguish the leaking instance from the fine one, because the difference is
in the VALUES, not the types.

IT ALSO CONTRADICTED THE CHECKER'S OWN PRINCIPLE, which the row did not notice.
`cycle_has_base_escape` (src/ownership.rs) already accepts a cycle that can
TERMINATE -- that is why `shared enum Expr { Num(i64), Add(Expr, Expr) }`
compiles. `None` and the empty container ARE base escapes. So `Option[N]` /
`Vec[N]` were not slipping through an incomplete walk; they were accepted by
exactly the rule that makes recursive enums work. "Plugging gap A" would have
applied that rule to enums and denied it to containers.

WHAT ACTUALLY SHIPPED, because probing gap A did turn up a real hole -- a
NARROWER one, in the opposite direction:

    shared struct N { mut v: i64, mut kid: (N, i64) }          -- ACCEPTED (!)
    shared struct A { mut b: (B, i64) } / B { mut a: (A, i64) } -- ACCEPTED (!)

A TUPLE has no empty inhabitant. Every position must be filled, so every `N`
needs a complete `N` inside it: the type is UNINHABITABLE, the same class as the
bare `mut kid: N` this checker has always rejected, one level down. Accepted
silently before this; the only symptom was a confusing innermost typecheck error
at the first attempt to build one (`expected '(N, i64)', found '(i64, i64)'`),
which names the wrong problem entirely.

So the walk now descends into TUPLE generic positions and only tuples, with the
asymmetry documented at `owned_edge_targets` rather than left to be rediscovered
as "container blindness" a fourth time. It rejects no constructible program --
the three accept-side regression tests are green both with and against the
change, which is exactly their job.

THE DIAGNOSTIC IS SEPARATE ON PURPOSE. A tuple cycle gets its own message
("recursing through a tuple ... no value of this type can ever be constructed")
and its own suggestion (wrap the recursive position in something that can
terminate). Reporting it as the existing "will leak" + "add 'weak'" would be
wrong twice: nothing leaks because nothing can be built, and there is no `weak`
coercion at a tuple position, so the advice would not compile. An edge that is
realized BOTH directly and through a tuple keeps the direct `weak` diagnostic --
the direct back-edge is the real one.

design.md IS CORRECTED, not worked around. "rejects types that form ownership
cycles" overstated what a type-graph walk can soundly do; it now reads "rejects
types that CANNOT BE CONSTRUCTED ACYCLICALLY", and the summary table's "Cycles |
Compile-time rejected" now says container-mediated cycles are accepted and leak
without a `weak` back-edge. The leak in this row's original repro is therefore a
DOCUMENTED LIMIT OF REFERENCE COUNTING and the programmer's obligation to place
`weak` at the back-edge -- which gap B made possible and which is measured
leak-free.

ROW CLOSED. Every part now has a disposition:
  * gap B (weak at container element, store + read-back) -- fixed, f869989f /
    1bb5328a.
  * gap A -- overturned as specified, tuple sliver landed, design.md corrected.
  * the `Vec[weak N]`-as-struct-FIELD remainder -- fixed by B-2026-08-08-28
    (02f8a0c8), where probing it showed the leak was the mildest of three
    symptoms of one missing gate.
  * the interpreter leg -- B-2026-08-08-14, fixed (f0c47394).
  * `Map[K, weak V]` / `Set` / tuple weak ELEMENTS -- handed to B-2026-08-08-29,
    and NOT the dull completeness item this row assumed. Measuring them before
    filing showed `Set[weak T]` and `(weak N, i64)` are honestly REFUSED at
    typecheck, while `Map[K, weak V]` is ACCEPTED and lowers a strong ref, so
    adding `weak` to a Map value LEAKS where the strong twin is clean. The
    long-unanswered question from B-2026-08-08-5 -- one coercion site or several
    -- is answered: several, in inconsistent states.

GATES: ownership 422/0, typechecker 2166/0, codegen 2841/0, memory_sanitizer
1001/0, par_codegen 254/0, interpreter 1471/0, concurrency 140/0, effectchecker
417/0, parser 796/0, resolver 352/0; fmt and clippy --all --all-targets
--features llvm clean.

title: a `Vec[weak N]` push SILENTLY CORRUPTED the target's first field — `w.push(a)` changed `a.v` from 41 to 42, because the weak-target scan never saw through the container and `N` was laid out without its weak-count word
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while implementing B-2026-08-08-4 gap B's read-back; the
read is what made it visible, but the bug is entirely in the STORE half
B-2026-08-08-5 shipped. Reproduced on a stashed tree.

    shared struct N { mut v: i64 }
    fn main() {
        let a: N = N { v: 41i64 };
        println(a.v);              // 41
        let mut w: Vec[weak N] = Vec.new();
        w.push(a);
        println(a.v);              // 42   <-- nothing in the program wrote this
    }

No diagnostic, no sanitizer report, no crash. The push returns and an unrelated
field of an unrelated binding has changed value.

MECHANISM. A shared type that is the target of a `weak` ref is force-headed
with a two-word `{ strong, weak, fields… }` control box; every other shared
type gets `{ strong, fields… }`. The whole-program set driving that decision
(`weak_targeted_types`) was collected by `weak_target_name`, which matches a
field whose type is DIRECTLY `TypeKind::Weak(_)`. A field of type `Vec[weak N]`
is `Path(Vec)` with `Weak(N)` in its GENERIC ARGUMENTS, so `N` was never added
and kept the one-word layout. `karac_weak_downgrade` then incremented the word
it takes to be the weak count -- word 1 -- which in that layout is the struct's
FIRST FIELD.

THE THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE ROOT CAUSE. B-2026-08-08-4 gap A is `check_cycles`
following a field's own type but not its generic arguments; gap B was the
downgrade coercion reaching a field store but not a container-element store;
this is the box-layout scan doing the same thing. Same blindness, three
independent places, and this one is the only one that corrupts memory rather
than leaking or rejecting.

FIX: the collection recurses through generic args, tuples, arrays, refs and
pointers, so `Map[K, weak V]`, `Vec[Vec[weak N]]` and tuple positions are
reached too. It also now walks FUNCTION SIGNATURES and local `let` type
annotations, because the shape that surfaced this has no struct in it at all --
`let mut w: Vec[weak N] = Vec.new();` in a plain function body. Annotations
only; an unannotated `let` whose weak-ness comes from inference is not
reachable at declaration time.

WHY HIGH RATHER THAN MEDIUM: it is a silent wrong answer in already-shipped
code, reachable from a two-line program, and the corrupted word is a live
user-visible field. It leaves no trace for either sanitizer -- the write is
in-bounds for the allocation, just aimed at the wrong word.

tracker: probe: `let mut w: Vec[weak N] = Vec.new(); w.push(a); match w[0] { Some(x) => .. }` under `karac run --interp`
title: the interpreter has no weak CONTAINER element, so a `Vec[weak T]` read-back reports `non-exhaustive match ... the typechecker should have rejected this` where `karac build` and `karac run` are both correct
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the interpreter leg B-2026-08-08-4 gap B's read-back left behind.
Codegen (AOT) and `karac run` (the default JIT, which goes through codegen)
both produce the correct `Some(x)` / `None`; only the explicit `--interp`
backend diverges.

    runtime error: internal error: non-exhaustive match at 7:5 -- no arm matched
    the scrutinee value (the typechecker should have rejected this)

TWO PROBLEMS, and the second is the worse one:

  1. The interpreter models `weak` PER FIELD -- dedicated `weak_immutable_fields`
     / `weak_mut_fields` maps on `SharedStructInner`, upgraded at the field-read
     site. There is no weak VALUE, so a `Vec[weak N]` element is stored as an
     ordinary strong `Value::SharedStruct` and the element read yields a bare
     struct where the typechecker now promises `Option[N]`. Hence no arm matches.
  2. The message BLAMES THE TYPECHECKER for a gap in the interpreter. That is
     the B-2026-08-06-24 class exactly: an internal-error string that sends the
     next reader to the wrong phase. Worth fixing even if (1) is deferred.

WHAT (1) NEEDS: a weak representation at VALUE level rather than at field level
(a `std::sync::Weak` carried in a `Value` variant), so a container element can
hold one and the existing `upgrade_weak_to_option` can run at the element read.
That is a contained change but it touches every exhaustive `match` over
`Value`, which is why it is filed rather than folded into the codegen slice.

NOT A REGRESSION: before f869989f this program failed on BOTH backends
(codegen: `Undefined variable 'x'`). The codegen half is now correct and the
interpreter half is not, which is what makes it a run-vs-build row.

RESOLUTION (f0c47394). Both halves, and the row's own size estimate was wrong
in the helpful direction.

  1. `Value::WeakRef(std::sync::Weak<SharedStructInner>)` is the missing home.
     The row warned this "touches every exhaustive `match` over `Value`, which
     is why it is filed rather than folded into the codegen slice". Measured:
     TWO arms, `Display` and `variant_name`. The worry did not survive contact
     with the compiler, and the change is small enough that filing it
     separately was the more expensive choice.
  2. The misleading message is gone because the condition that produced it is
     gone -- the match now receives the `Option[T]` it was promised. Nothing
     was special-cased in the diagnostic itself.

THE UPGRADE IS ONE POST-STEP IN `eval_expr_inner`, not an arm inside the
`Index` evaluation, and that is the design point worth keeping: `WeakRef` has
exactly ONE producer -- the downgrade at a `Vec[weak T]` push -- so any
expression that yields one is a read of that element and owes the upgrade. The
push's own downgrade runs AFTER `eval_expr_inner` returns, on the
already-evaluated argument, so it is not undone by its own rule. `Display`
renders through the upgrade too (a live target prints as its struct, a dead one
as `None`), so the handle never reaches user-visible output.

THE SITE SETS COME FROM THE TYPECHECKER because the interpreter has no static
element type to consult -- a plain-data span-keyed side channel
(`weak_elem_store_sites` / `weak_elem_read_sites`). Codegen needs neither; it
reads the element `TypeExpr` directly. So these exist purely to keep the two
backends agreeing, which is the opposite of the usual reason for a side table.
The store set is keyed by the ARGUMENT's span rather than the call's: a method
call shares its receiver's span here, so the call span is not unique to the push.

Run now matches build on every probe from the gap-B slice, including the one
that makes this a weak ref rather than an awkward strong one -- `None` once the
target's frame dies.

because it is independently landable and NON-BREAKING, while its sibling (the

MEASURED, and the contrast is the whole report:

    shared struct P { v: i64, mut kid: Option[C] }
    shared struct C { v: i64, mut parent: weak P }
    c.parent = p;                       // ACCEPTED, and measured LEAK-FREE

    shared struct N { v: i64, mut ns: Vec[weak N] }
    a.ns.push(b);                       // error[typecheck]:
                                        //   expected 'weak N', found 'N'

So `weak` itself is fine -- B-2026-07-19-8 shipped it end-to-end (two-count
control block, downgrade coercion, `Option[T]` read typing) and the field path
reclaims a cycle with no leak. What is missing is the coercion at a CONTAINER
element store.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: design.md § Cycles gives the graph shape as
`mut neighbors: Vec[weak GraphNode]` and writes `b.neighbors.push(a); //
bidirectional, no cycle leak`. That line does not compile. Every real graph
holds its back-edges in a container, so the container store is the ONLY form
that matters for the mechanism's actual purpose, and it is the one form absent.

BOTH HALVES OR NEITHER. The typecheck relaxation alone is worse than the
current error: it would compile a program that stores a STRONG reference into a
slot the author declared `weak`, so the cycle would still leak while the source
says it does not. Codegen must emit the downgrade at the store (and the
matching weak-drop in the container's element drain) in the same commit, gated
on LSan at both opt levels -- the same pairing rule B-2026-08-07-23 established
for frozen containers, and for the same reason.

NOT MEASURED: whether `Map[K, weak V]` / `Set[weak T]` / array and tuple
element stores share one coercion site or several, and whether the container's
per-element drop already routes weak elements to the weak-drop primitive or
would need its own arm. Both decide whether this is one narrow edit or a family
of them, and both should be established before the shape of the fix is
chosen.

-- FIXED (2026-08-08), 1bb5328a. `Vec[weak T]` NOW RECLAIMS A CYCLE --

design.md § Cycles' worked example compiles and is measured leak-free: a
bidirectional 2-node graph and a 4-node / 8-edge one both report "All heap
blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible" under valgrind, where the
strong-`Vec[N]` twin leaks 72 bytes per node (B-2026-08-08-4).

THREE PIECES, not the two this row predicted:
  * typecheck accepts a bare strong handle at a `weak` element;
  * the push emits `karac_weak_downgrade` (`emit_weak_field_init` -- the fresh
    slot sibling, since a push writes `data[len]` with no prior occupant);
  * the push takes NO STRONG COUNT, and the container's scope-exit drain
    weak-drops each element (`__karac_vec_elem_weak_drop`, a new element-drop
    arm in `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` checked BEFORE the name-keyed
    dispatch, which would otherwise hand back the referent's strong `rc_dec`).

THE STRONG-COUNT PIECE WAS NOT IN THE PLAN and is the one worth recording.
With only the store and the drop, the measurement came back "payloads freed,
every control block still leaked" -- the ordinary transfer inc was still
firing, so the strong count never reached zero and the box could not be
released even once weak hit zero. The row's "both halves or neither" framing
was right in spirit and short by one.

NARROWER THAN THE FIELD RULE, DELIBERATELY. A `weak` FIELD also accepts
`Option[T]` and `None`; routing the container store through the same
`check_expr` coercion admitted them and compiled a program that SEGFAULTED at
runtime. The gate is therefore hand-written: a bare strong handle only, with a
diagnostic that names the limitation. The typechecker must admit exactly what
codegen lowers, and the reject row in tests/typechecker.rs is what keeps them
in step. Widening to `Option[T]` is a codegen change first.

-- A VACUOUS-PASS HOLE IN THE ASAN HARNESS, FOUND BY STASH-PROVING THIS --

The new LSan fixture PASSED against a compiler with the fix reverted. Cause:
`run_under_asan_opts` asserted the OWNERSHIP result (`assert_ownership_clean`)
but never the TYPECHECK one, so a fixture whose program fails typecheck was
still handed to codegen and ran. A test written for a not-yet-supported shape
could therefore report `ok` for a program `karac build` REFUSES.

The harness now panics on typecheck errors, the same discrimination the
codegen-failure panic already applies. That exposed SIX existing fixtures in
exactly that state (tensor `ref Tensor[f32,[?]]` vs `Tensor[f64,[N]]`, a
`Vec[u32]`/`Vec[i64]` mismatch, an uninferrable `E`); they are marked
`#[ignore]` with their errors and filed as B-2026-08-08-6, per the harness's own
rule that a gap be visibly deferred rather than silently green.

-- WHAT GATES WHAT, since the answer is not the obvious one --

The LSan fixture gates the TYPECHECK half only. Reverting EITHER codegen half
leaves a program that leaks its entire graph -- 288 bytes, valgrind -- while
LeakSanitizer still reports it clean, even with the stack-churn technique
B-2026-08-08-4 documents. So the codegen halves are gated by an IR assertion
(`tests/codegen.rs
vec_of_weak_push_downgrades_and_takes_no_strong_count`): the downgrade call,
the element weak-drop, and fewer retains than the identical strong-element
build, with a strong-`Vec[N]` control row so the comparison means something.
Each half was proven red with its own change reverted.

STILL OPEN, and both were measured rather than assumed:
  * READ-BACK. `match v[i] { Some(x) => .. }` over a `Vec[weak N]` fails with
    `codegen failed: Undefined variable 'x'` -- the same signature as
    B-2026-08-08-3. The weak FIELD read-back works and is leak-free, so this is
    the container twin of the upgrade, not a missing mechanism. A `Vec[weak T]`
    is therefore STORE-ONLY today, which is enough for cycle-breaking
    back-edges (they exist to not be traversed) and not enough for a
    parent-pointer walk.
  * `Option[T]` / `None` elements, per the narrowing above.
  * `Map[K, weak V]` / `Set` / array / tuple element stores -- untouched, and
    the row's open question about whether they share one coercion site is still
    unanswered.

GATES: typechecker 2157/0, codegen 2836/0, memory_sanitizer 986/0 at -O2 AND
-O0, ownership 416/0, par_codegen 246/0, interpreter 1470/0, concurrency 139/0,
effectchecker 417/0; clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm and fmt clean.

title: a frozen-element container declared INSIDE a closure was still admitted -- `try_admit_container_method` had no `in_closure` gate, so an escaping closure could carry a non-counting handle past its owner; latent until 200fa8d6 removed the typecheck mask, live on main after it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by the negative sweep while re-running kata #133
against `main` after 200fa8d6 (B-2026-08-08-2). Not found by reading the code.
It is the class of hole this family keeps producing -- an admission arm that
never asks whether it is inside a closure -- and it is the fourth one on
B-2026-08-01-33.

SHAPE. Stage 3c (B-2026-08-07-23) admits a local `Vec[S]` as a FROZEN-ELEMENT
container: its elements are non-counting, so the push takes no retain and scope
exit runs no per-element drain. `try_admit_container_method` guards that with
`container_visible_here`, which disqualifies a container declared OUTSIDE the
closure / `defer` / `par` body the push sits in. A container declared INSIDE the
closure passes that test -- while the frozen root pushed into it still comes
from the ENCLOSING frame, and a closure's environment can outlive the call. So
the container carries a non-counting handle past the value whose refcount it
skips, which is exactly the use-after-free property 3 exists to prevent.

    shared struct Node { val: i64, mut kids: Vec[Node] }
    fn leak(n: frozen Node) -> OnceFn() -> i64 {
        return || { let mut v: Vec[Node] = Vec.new(); v.push(n); v.len() };
    }

MEASURED ON `main`, not inferred: that checks CLEAN as of 200fa8d6.

Every other admission in `frozen_escape.rs` is suppressed by `in_closure` --
stage 1's first draft accepted a scalar read inside a closure body and was
closed for this reason at the time. The container arm, added later in 3c, never
got the same gate.

WHY IT ONLY BECAME REACHABLE NOW, which is worth stating because it means
nothing unsound had shipped before: the shape was covered by two unrelated
masks. For a `frozen` PARAMETER the push was a TYPE error first (`expected
'Node', found 'ref Node'`), and for a `freeze`-statement LOCAL the ordinary
borrow-escape analysis catches the returned closure ("closure with `ref` capture
of `g` escapes its scope by being returned"). 200fa8d6 removed the first, and
the second never covered the parameter case. A mask is not a guard.

FIX. `try_admit_container_method` rejects the container outright when
`cx.in_closure`. Rejecting rather than merely declining is deliberate: it takes
the container out of the candidate set, so `c[i]` inside the closure stops being
a frozen place too, and the push falls through to the ordinary walk that reports
it as the capture it is. A container declared inside a `par` branch is
unaffected -- branches join before return, and admitting that sharing is the
point of the feature.

TESTS: tests/ownership.rs `a_frozen_container_store_is_refused_inside_a_closure`
-- three reject rows (an escaping closure holding a `frozen` parameter, a local
closure holding one, and a `freeze`-statement local), each asserting a frozen
diagnostic, plus the control that keeps the gate from being "refuse every
container": the identical push OUTSIDE a closure is still admitted.
Stash-proved red.

detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the kata-side half of B-2026-08-01-33, split out so the
task stays tracked now that the compiler half is done.

WHAT IS DONE: kata #133's par lane compiles and runs. Measured on the real file
