title: a `File` MOVED out of its binding (into a `Vec`, a struct, or a return) is still closed by the origin binding at scope exit, so the new owner holds freed memory and the next method call blocks forever on a Mutex inside it -- the interpreter runs the same program correctly
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while designing streaming integration for the Cumulus
dogfooding app (kara-katas apps/cumulus). Streaming needs N subs open at once
so each output strip can be gathered from every frame without holding whole
frames in memory, and `Vec[File]` is the natural way to carry the handles.
This bug BLOCKS that design -- there is no workaround that keeps the I/O
sequential, because the alternative is reopening every file per strip.

REPRO (hangs forever under AOT, correct under `--interp`):

    fn main() with reads(FileSystem) writes(FileSystem) {
        let mut hs: Vec[File] = Vec.new();
        match File.open("a.txt") {
            Ok(f) => { hs.push(f); }
            Err(e) => { println("open failed"); }
        }
        let mut buf: Array[u8, 4] = [0u8; 4];
        println("about to read via hs[0]");
        match hs[0].read(mut buf) {
            Ok(n) => { println(f"read {n}: {buf[0]}"); }
            Err(e) => { println("read failed"); }
        }
        println("done");
    }

    $ karac run --interp v3.kara
    about to read via hs[0]
    read 4: 65
    done

    $ karac build v3.kara -o v3 && ./v3
    about to read via hs[0]
    <hangs>

`karac check` passes. Run unbuffered (`stdbuf -o0`) to see the last println --
stdout is block-buffered when redirected, so a naive capture shows NO output
at all and reads like a hang before `main` starts, which is misleading.

SCOPE, measured by bisection:

  - `Vec[File]` push + `len()`, no method call            OK
  - repeated `f.read()` on a handle NOT in a container    OK (position advances)
  - `File` in a STRUCT FIELD, then `h.f.read(buf)`        OK
  - `hs[0].read(buf)` where `hs: Vec[File]`               HANGS
  - `hs.pop()` then `f.read(buf)` on the moved-out value  HANGS
  - `hs[0].flush()`                                       HANGS

Two things narrow it. First, moving the handle back OUT with `pop()` does not
help, so this is not about an index expression as a method receiver -- the
handle is already damaged by having been stored. Second, a struct field holding
the same handle works, so it is not `File` in aggregates generally; it is the
Vec element path specifically. Every File method hangs, not just `read`, so it
is the receiver rather than the operation.

LIKELY MECHANISM (hypothesis, not verified in the IR). Codegen represents a
`File` as a pointer to a runtime `KaracFile` (`self_val.into_pointer_value()`
in `compile_file_read`), and `KaracFile` wraps `Mutex<std::fs::File>` with
every entry point doing `file.inner.lock()`. A `std::sync::Mutex` blocks
rather than faulting, so if the pointer read back out of the Vec is not the
pointer that went in, the runtime locks whatever the bytes at that address
happen to be and waits forever. That is consistent with every observation
here: a hang rather than a crash, every method affected, and the struct case
-- which stores the pointer in a field of known type -- being unaffected.
It predicts the Vec element type for an opaque handle is being mapped to
something that does not preserve a pointer.

WHY HIGH: it is a run-vs-build divergence that HANGS rather than producing a
wrong answer, with no diagnostic from any phase, in a pattern (a collection of
open handles) that any program doing multi-file I/O will reach. The
interpreter running it correctly is what makes it expensive -- the natural
debugging move is `--interp`, which says the program is fine.

RELATED: `File` has no `seek` (`src/interpreter/method_call_file.rs`: "Seek /
metadata are deferred to a follow-on slice"). Seek would not fix this, but
the two together are what make streaming file access hard to express today: no
seek forces sequential access, and sequential access across many files forces
many concurrently-open handles, which is exactly the shape that trips this.

RESOLUTION (fdc874b), AND A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS.

The scope recorded above is WRONG. This row claimed the defect was
Vec-element-specific because a `File` in a struct FIELD appeared to work -- but
that probe read the handle while the origin binding was still in scope, so the
close had not fired yet. Re-probed with the read moved past the origin's scope:

    Vec[File], read after the arm closes              HANGS
    Vec[Holder] where Holder { f: File }              HANGS
    struct returned from a fn, no Vec, no match arm   HANGS   <- no container
    control: Vec[i64] in a struct, same shape         OK      <- not File

Containers were never the discriminator. OUTLIVING THE ORIGIN BINDING is. The
hypothesis about a Vec element type failing to round-trip a pointer was wrong
too; the pointer round-trips fine. What actually happens is that the origin
binding's queued `FreeFileHandle` fires at its own scope exit even though the
handle was moved, `karac_runtime_file_close` reconstructs the Box and drops it,
and the new owner is left holding freed memory. The Mutex prediction was right
for the wrong reason: the lock sits inside a freed allocation, not at a garbage
address.

`FreeFileHandle` is queue-driven exactly like `FreeMapHandle`, which has carried
move-out suppression since B-2026-07-15-25 and simply had no File arm. The fix
adds it to the shared suppressor, retracting the action for the moved binding's
slot from EVERY live frame -- the same rationale the Map arm documents, since a
move site can fire with a transient arg/method-eval frame above the frame that
owns the action. One arm covers all ~20 existing move sites instead of
duplicating them.

Both shapes are pinned as regression tests, and both were confirmed to FAIL
without the fix by taking the full 15s watchdog timeout -- they reproduce the
hang and are killed, rather than merely asserting. The Vec test reads TWICE and
requires the second read to continue where the first stopped: a reopened handle
or a struct copy would restart at byte 0 and still look healthy, so the
advancing file position is what distinguishes the same LIVE handle from merely a
non-crashing one.

NOT FIXED HERE: nothing closes the handle once moved -- see B-2026-08-09-20.

title: Interpreter ICEs (`internal error: entered unreachable code`) on a METHOD CALL whose RECEIVER faulted, instead of reporting the receiver's runtime error. `let n = v[3].len();` on an empty `Vec[Vec[i64]]` panics with `len() receiver at L:C was Value::Unit; either an interpreter codepath produced the wrong receiver variant or the typechecker accepted .len() on a type without one` -- the assertion's own two hypotheses are both wrong: the typechecker is right and no codepath produced a wrong variant. The out-of-bounds index set pending_cf and yielded the Unit POISON value, and the method-call receiver path dispatches on it without first checking pending_cf. The bare index `v[3]` with no method call reports correctly (`runtime error: index 3 out of bounds (len 0)`), so it is purely the receiver position. RUN-VS-BUILD: interp ICEs; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` both report cleanly (`panic ...: vec index out of bounds`), so this is an interpreter-only diagnostics divergence, not a miscompile. FIX DIRECTION: check pending_cf before method dispatch in method_call_seq.rs and propagate the pending fault, mirroring the Binary/Unary/Match arms; then the assertion at :74 becomes genuinely unreachable and its misleading message can stay. detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while authoring kata #251 (Flatten 2D Vector) -- specifically while PROVING that the `and` in `while v.row < v.data.len() and v.col >= v.data[v.row].len()` is a load-bearing bounds guard. Swapping the operands so the guard no longer runs first was expected to produce a clean out-of-bounds runtime error; it produced the ICE instead. The kata itself is unaffected (the correct operand order never faults) -- this was surfaced by a deliberate negative probe, which is the same way B-2026-06-19-13's sibling ICE was found. -- SURFACE NOTE: interpreter runtime-error propagation, method-call receiver position.

-- FIXED by bb46a68d (2026-08-09), the fix direction as filed --

ONE guard at the single receiver-eval site in `eval_method_call`
(method_call.rs, right after `let obj = self.eval_expr_inner(object)`):
`pending_cf` set means the receiver already failed, so return the poison and
let the caller propagate.

WHY THERE and not in the arm the ICE named, which is the part worth keeping:
the receiver assertions are PER-METHOD. `len` (:74) and `chars` (:101) each
carry their own `unreachable!`; `is_empty` instead falls through to a tolerant
default and reported the fault correctly all along. So which arm the program
happens to land in decides whether you get an ICE or the truth -- and that is
not a property of the program. Checking once covers every method on every
builtin receiver, and leaves the arms' assertions meaning what they say: a
NON-faulted receiver of the wrong variant really is a compiler bug. The row's
closing note ("then the assertion at :74 becomes genuinely unreachable and its
misleading message can stay") holds, and now holds for every sibling assertion
too, not just that one.

WIDER THAN THE ROW RECORDED, both axes measured under `karac run --interp`:

    receiver expression                     BEFORE            AFTER
    `v[3].len()`, empty Vec[Vec[i64]]       ICE (:74)         index 3 out of bounds
    `o.unwrap().len()`, o = None            ICE (:74)         called unwrap() on None
    `v[2].chars()`, empty Vec[String]       ICE (:101)        index 2 out of bounds
    `v[0].len()`, empty Vec[Map[..]]        ICE (:74)         index 0 out of bounds
    `v[1].is_empty()`                       already clean     unchanged
    `v[0].get()`, user-struct method        already clean     unchanged
    `w.push(v[5])` -- faulted ARG, not rcvr already clean     unchanged

So the trigger is not the index operation the repro used: ANY fault in the
receiver position does it (`unwrap` of `None` is the second one measured).
Arg position was never affected.

Exit code is 1 after the fix, matching `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build`,
which reported cleanly throughout. Their message text still differs from the
interpreter's (`panic ...: vec index out of bounds` vs `runtime error: index 3
out of bounds (len 0)`), but that wording gap is interpreter-wide and
pre-existing -- visible on the `is_empty` shape that never ICEd -- so it is NOT
part of this row.

PINNED: `test_faulted_method_receiver_reports_the_fault_not_an_ice`
(tests/interpreter.rs) -- two faults across two asserting arms, plus the
tolerant `is_empty` arm as the converse control, each case asserting both the
receiver's own error AND the absence of compiler-bug framing. Stash-proven RED:
without the fix it dies on the real `unreachable!` rather than failing an
assert. `test_method_call_on_a_healthy_receiver_still_dispatches` pins the
over-fire direction, which is the fix's own risk surface -- the guard keys on
interpreter state, not on the expression, so a healthy call must be untouched.

VERIFIED: interpreter 1474, cli 577, lowering 137, example_packages 28, plus
comptime / comptime_ast / comptime_derive / comptime_reflection, json, closures,
repl, walker, book_snippets, example_corpus and the four selfhost suites -- all
green. NOT run: codegen and memory_sanitizer, and the full `--features llvm`
suite in a single pass -- this container's disk allowance cannot hold every
test binary at once, so the interpreter-exercising targets were batched
instead. The change is confined to the tree-walk interpreter's method dispatch
and cli.rs exercises `karac run` on both backends, so the codegen surface is
covered by construction rather than by omission.

title: SIBLING OF B-2026-08-09-18, NOT CLOSED BY bb46a68d: a faulted operand still ICEs the interpreter in THREE more positions, all with the same shape (`unreachable!` whose message proposes two causes and both are wrong -- the typechecker is right and no codepath produced a bad variant; the operand faulted, set pending_cf, and yielded the `Unit` poison, which is then asserted against). bb46a68d guarded the METHOD-CALL RECEIVER only. Still ICEing: (1) `if v[3] > 0i64 and true {}` -> eval_ops.rs:140 `short-circuit `And` LHS ... was Value::Unit not Bool`; (2) same with `or` -> same site, ``Or` LHS`; (3) `if true and v[3] > 0i64 {}` -> interpreter.rs:1966 `condition was Value::Unit not Bool` (the RHS fault escapes the short-circuit evaluator and poisons the enclosing `if` condition instead). So the guard is missing on the short-circuit operator's LHS, its RHS, and the if-condition consumer. NOTE the earlier row's fix note asserted `Binary, Unary and Match all short-circuit on pending_cf` -- that holds for the NON-short-circuit Binary path; `eval_short_circuit` is a separate evaluator with its own operand assertions and was never given the guard. RUN-VS-BUILD: interpreter-only in all three; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` report `vec index out of bounds` cleanly at the right span. FIX DIRECTION: same one-line-per-site treatment as bb46a68d -- check pending_cf after evaluating each operand in `eval_short_circuit` and before the enclosing condition test -- or, better, hoist the check to the single place a `Value` is consumed as a Bool, since this is now the third distinct site found for one root cause.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by re-running the SAME negative probe that produced B-2026-08-09-18 after that row was closed -- the 4-line minimal repro (`v[3].len()`) is fixed, but the real kata-shaped case that originally surfaced it (`while v.col >= v.data[v.row].len() and v.row < v.data.len()`, kata #251's skip-empty guard with its operands deliberately swapped) still ICEs, now at eval_ops.rs:140 instead of method_call_seq.rs:74. Worth noting as process: verifying a closed row against the ORIGINAL finding case, not only against the minimised repro that was filed, is what exposed the incompleteness. -- SURFACE NOTE: interpreter runtime-error propagation, short-circuit operator operands and if-condition.

FIXED at 512f59a, with the hoist the row asked for rather than one guard per
reported site — and that choice closed a FOURTH position the row does not list.

TWO guards, not three:

  - `eval_short_circuit`, right after the LHS eval: propagate the poison
    instead of asserting it is a Bool. This covers sites (1) and (2), which
    were always one site with two operators. Returning early also preserves
    the short-circuit's own guarantee: a faulted LHS must not evaluate the RHS.

  - `is_truthy`, the single place a `Value` is consumed as a Bool: answer
    `false` when `pending_cf` is set. This covers site (3), where the RHS fault
    escapes the short-circuit evaluator and poisons the enclosing condition.
    `false` is safe for every caller — the fault is already pending, so the
    enclosing block unwinds and reports the operand's real error at its own
    span before the not-taken branch can be observed.

THE FOURTH SITE. `is_truthy` has exactly three callers: the `if` condition, the
`while` condition, and a MATCH GUARD. The guard consumes its Bool through the
same helper and ICEd identically on

    match n { x if v[3] > 0i64 => { … } _ => { … } }

which nobody had reported. Hoisting to `is_truthy` fixed it for free; guarding
the two condition sites named in the row would have left it, and this defect
has now been found three times by exactly that pattern of fixing the reported
spelling. Worth stating as the general lesson: the assertion sites are where
the ICE surfaces, but the CONSUMERS of a poisoned value are where the guard
belongs.

WHY THE EARLIER NOTE'S CLAIM WAS RIGHT BUT IRRELEVANT. B-2026-08-09-18's fix
note said "Binary, Unary and Match all short-circuit on pending_cf". True — of
the NON-short-circuit `Binary` evaluator (B-2026-07-15-7). `and`/`or` are
routed away from it precisely so the RHS stays unevaluated, so `eval_short_
circuit` never saw that guard and needed its own.

VERIFIED. All five shapes report the operand's own fault at the right span,
with `--interp`, `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` agreeing — including the
row's source case, kata #251's `while it.col >= it.data[it.row].len() and
it.row < it.data.len()`, which still ICEd after -18 closed. Full `--features
llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy `--all-targets`, fmt.

TESTS. `test_faulted_short_circuit_operand_reports_the_fault_not_an_ice` pins
all three reported sites plus the match guard plus the kata shape; reaching its
assertions at all is the no-ICE half, since the old failure was a Rust
`unreachable!` that aborts before the errors can be inspected.
`test_short_circuit_still_skips_its_rhs_and_evaluates_healthy_operands` is the
converse control for the two things these guards could plausibly break: a
false `and` and a true `or` must still leave a FAULTING RHS unevaluated (the
program completing is the assertion), and conditions reached with no pending
fault must still decide normally.

PROCESS NOTE, seconding the row's own. It was found by re-running the ORIGINAL
finding case against the closed row rather than the minimised repro that was
filed. The minimisation dropped the short-circuit that turned out to be the
whole point.

tracker: src/codegen/synth_drop.rs (`vec_element_drain_fn`) and the struct drop glue -- neither emits `karac_runtime_file_close` for a `File` element/field
fix: FIXED by cc48dcca -- two arms, one per container kind: a `File` element arm in `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` (new `emit_file_slot_close_fn`, threaded as `elem_agg_drop` so every `track_vec_of_aggs_var` site picks it up) and a `FieldDrop::FileHandleClose` in the struct drop glue; `te_recursive_drop_fully_supported` admits `File` so `Vec[Vec[File]]` leaves the one-level fast path. Both null the slot after closing, because `karac_runtime_file_close` is not idempotent, and both defer to a user type that shadows the name `File`. Also fixes two shapes the row did not record -- a handle read back out of a container into a fresh binding (`let g = hs[0]` / `let g = h.f`) leaked identically. Pinned by four ASAN fixtures including an over-fire control. The row's unverified `DropChannelEnd` sibling risk was probed and does NOT reproduce.
title: a `File` moved into a `Vec` or a struct is never closed -- the container has no element/field drop for the handle, so the fd leaks until process exit (253 of 400 opens succeed under `ulimit -n 256`)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the other half of B-2026-08-09-17, split out because the two have
different severities and different fixes.

B-2026-08-09-17 stopped a moved-out `File` being closed by its ORIGIN binding,
which is what made the handle usable at all. Nothing took over the closing. A
`Vec[File]`, or a struct holding a `File`, has no element/field drop that emits
`karac_runtime_file_close`, so the fd (and the `Box<KaracFile>` behind it) lives
until process exit.

MEASURED, under `ulimit -n 256`:

    handle opened and dropped, never moved        3000 of 3000   closes fine
    Vec[File] built and dropped per iteration       253 of 400    LEAKS
    struct holding a File, dropped per iteration    253 of 400    LEAKS

253 is the limit minus the standard streams. The failure is SILENT: the program
does not crash, `File.open` simply starts returning `Err`, and a caller that
ignores the error arm just stops making progress.

This is a strictly better failure mode than the use-after-free hang it replaced,
and for the streaming design that motivated the work it is immaterial -- those
handles are held for the program's lifetime by construction. But a long-running
program that opens files in a loop and parks them in a container will exhaust
its descriptors.

FIX SHAPE: teach the container drop paths about `File`, the way `FreeMapHandle`
already carries `val_drop_fn` / `key_drop_fn` for per-entry drops.
`vec_element_drain_fn` is the Vec-side hook; struct fields need the equivalent
in the struct drop glue.

SIBLING RISK, unverified: `CleanupAction::DropChannelEnd` (`track_channel_var`)
is registered the same queue-driven way and has no suppression arm either, so a
`Sender`/`Receiver` moved into a container is likely to reproduce the ORIGINAL
B-2026-08-09-17 shape rather than this one. `FreeGpuBuffer` is explicitly safe:
its comment records that `karac_runtime_gpu_free_soa` is idempotent, which is
exactly the property `karac_runtime_file_close` lacks. Not probed -- noted so the
next person starts from the pattern rather than from a single symptom.

-- FIXED by cc48dcca (2026-08-10), the fix shape as filed --

TWO arms, one per container kind, because they are two code paths that merely
shared a symptom -- the same trap B-2026-08-09-17's first diagnosis fell into
when it read "struct field works, Vec element fails" as a statement about
containers:

  (a) `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` gains a `File` element arm returning a
      new `emit_file_slot_close_fn` (`__karac_file_slot_close`). It is threaded
      as `elem_agg_drop`, so EVERY `track_vec_of_aggs_var` registration site --
      let-binding, for-loop iterable, pattern binding, par block, method result
      -- picks it up at once rather than one site at a time.

  (b) The struct drop glue gains `FieldDrop::FileHandleClose`, classified by
      declared field type name in a post-pass beside the HTTP handle-field
      override, which is the same shape of gap: an opaque runtime-owned handle
      no layout-driven classifier can see.

  (c) `te_recursive_drop_fully_supported` admits `File`, which is what keeps a
      `Vec[Vec[File]]` off the one-level buffer-only fast path. Without it (a)
      alone would not have reached the nested shape.

MEASURED under `ulimit -n 256`, before -> after:

    Vec[File] built and dropped per iteration       253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    struct holding a File, per iteration            253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    Vec[Vec[File]], per iteration                   253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    handle read out of a Vec by index               253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    handle read out of a struct field               253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    handle opened and dropped, never moved         3000 of 3000 -> unchanged
    element popped out (`Some(g)` binding owns it)  400 of 400  -> unchanged

Rows 4-5 were NOT in the row as filed: reading a handle back out of a container
into a fresh binding (`let g = hs[0]` / `let g = h.f`) gave that binding no
cleanup either, so those shapes leaked for the same reason and are fixed by the
same owner. Rows 6-7 are the controls -- `pop` already had an owner, and the
drain walks `0..len`, so a popped element is outside the walk.

NEITHER arm guards on null: `karac_runtime_file_close` returns early on null, so
a branch would only restate the runtime's own check in IR. Both NULL the slot
after closing, and that IS load-bearing -- close reconstructs the `Box` and
drops it, so it is not idempotent (precisely the property the row noted
`karac_runtime_gpu_free_soa` has and this lacks), and the null is what makes a
second drop of the same storage inert. Both are also guarded against a user type
named `File` shadowing the builtin: the element arm sits AFTER the
struct/enum/shared checks so a shadowing type is claimed by those, and the field
arm additionally requires the LLVM field to be the `ptr` the handle lowers to.

PINNED: four fixtures in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs --
`asan_file_moved_into_a_vec_is_closed_by_the_vec`,
`asan_file_moved_into_a_struct_field_is_closed_by_the_struct`,
`asan_file_inside_a_nested_vec_is_closed_at_every_level`, and
`asan_file_handed_to_a_second_owner_is_closed_exactly_once` (the over-fire
direction: three shapes that hand the handle to a second candidate owner).
All four stash-proven RED, leaking 468 B/39, 480 B/40, 480 B/40 and 960 B/80
respectively. The fourth's count is itself evidence rather than decoration: 80
of its 120 opens leaked, and the 40 that did not are exactly the popped ones --
the measurement that shows `pop` was already covered.

LSan is the right gate here even though the user-visible symptom is descriptor
exhaustion: fd counts are awkward to assert portably, and the leaked
`Box<KaracFile>` behind each fd is the same defect one level down.

SIBLING RISK -- PROBED, DOES NOT REPRODUCE. The row flagged
`CleanupAction::DropChannelEnd` as likely to reproduce the ORIGINAL
B-2026-08-09-17 UAF shape. It does not, in either direction: a `Sender[i64]`
moved into a `Vec[Sender[i64]]` and a `Sender` moved into a struct field both
run correctly AND come back clean under ASAN/LSan, including the variant where
the origin binding dies in an inner scope while the container outlives it (the
shape that actually distinguished B-2026-08-09-17). The probes were exploratory
and are not kept as tests; the negative result is recorded here instead.
`FreeGpuBuffer` remains safe for the reason its own comment gives.

VERIFIED: codegen 2869 (including B-2026-08-09-17's two File pins, which are the
behavioural controls that the handle is still live and readable while its
container is), memory_sanitizer 1027, clippy --all --all-targets and cargo fmt
--check clean. Re-verified after rebasing onto 52eee01b.

fix: FIXED by 4f3d6921, BOTH halves. READ: `compile_nested_index_read` gained a struct-FIELD arm -- `nested_index_field_base_elem` resolves the element `TypeExpr` from the field's DECLARED type and the container pointer via `lower_field_access_ptr`, then rejoins the existing synth-identifier tail (factored out as `finish_nested_index_read`). The name-keyed lowering was split into a by-POINTER core, `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_vec_at`, so the field base reuses the identical bounds check and GEP. WRITE: `compile_index_store` gained a matching arm that normalises the field to a synth identifier and recurses, so the existing named-outer nested store handles it unchanged. Pin: e2e `test_e2e_nested_index_rooted_at_struct_field` (7 cases), stash-proven red.
title: A NESTED index whose base is a STRUCT FIELD (`h.data[i][j]`) is rejected by codegen -- `codegen: nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable in v1 (got non-identifier inner expression)` -- while the interpreter runs it. RUN-VS-BUILD: `karac run --interp` prints the right value; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` both fail. LOUD, not a miscompile, and the JIT failure carries an actionable `--interp` hint. BOUNDARY (probed): `d[i][j]` on a named local BUILDS; `h.data[i][j]` FAILS; `let row = h.data[i]; row[j]` BUILDS; `h.data[i].len()` (single index on a field, then a method) BUILDS; the nested WRITE `h.data[i][j] = v` FAILS the same way. So it is specifically the DOUBLE index rooted at a field access, read and write alike -- single-index-on-field and double-index-on-local are both fine. CAUSE: `compile_nested_index_read` requires `inner_object` to be `ExprKind::Identifier` because it recovers the element TypeExpr from `var_elem_type_exprs[outer_name]` and registers a synthetic identifier for the element slot; a field access has no entry in that map. FIX DIRECTION: resolve the element TypeExpr from the FIELD's declared type (struct field type -> Vec/Slice/Array element) rather than from the variable map, and compile the base to a pointer via the existing place-expression path, so the synthetic-element machinery can stay as-is. Sibling deferral in the same function: chained `a[i][j][k]` is rejected by an explicit MR5 guard, so any fix should decide whether it generalises to arbitrary place expressions or only to field bases. REPRO (9 lines): `struct H { data: Vec[Vec[i64]] } fn main() { let mut i: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); i.push(1i64); let mut d: Vec[Vec[i64]] = Vec.new(); d.push(i); let h = H { data: d }; println(f"{h.data[0][0]}"); }`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while authoring kata #251 (Flatten 2D Vector). An iterator over a 2D vector naturally stores the data as a struct field and reads `v.data[v.row][v.col]` -- that is the canonical spelling of the whole problem, so 3 of the kata's 4 programs (the lazy two-cursor solver, the prefix-offset solver, and the differential) cannot AOT-build. The eager-flatten solver builds because it copies through a named local. Per the kata policy the natural spelling is KEPT rather than rewritten around the gap: the kata's README records that its `karac build` leg is blocked on this row. -- SURFACE NOTE: codegen nested-index lowering, field-access base.

=== FIXED (4f3d6921). Two halves, two different gates, and one gate choice that
decided whether the fix was worth anything. ===

THE WRITE HALF WAS A SEPARATE DEFECT with its own error string. The row records
`h.data[i][j] = v` as failing "the same way"; it does not -- the read dies on
`nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable`, the
write on `Index assignment target must be a variable`, from
`compile_index_store` in collections.rs, a different function the row's tracker
never points at. Same user-visible gap, two edits.

  The write half needed no new lowering at all. `compile_index_store` already
  has a nested arm (named outer) and a field arm (single index); this shape fell
  between them. Resolving the field to a synth identifier and recursing hands it
  to the existing nested arm unchanged, so the store logic keeps one
  implementation.

THE GATE CHOICE THAT MATTERED, and the row's suggested one would have missed
the case the row itself cares about. The obvious base-pointer helper is
`field_chain_place_ptr` -- and it DELIBERATELY returns `None` for a `ref`-param
root, because the slot holds a pointer rather than the aggregate. Built that
way first and measured: `h.data[i][j]` worked for an owned local, and still
failed for `fn read(h: ref H)` and for every `ref self` / `mut ref self`
method. That is the shape the motivating kata actually writes -- a 2D cursor
keeps its grid in a field and reads `self.data[self.row][self.col]` from a
method -- so the fix would have left the reported use case broken while looking
green on the filed reproduction. `lower_field_access_ptr` is the right helper:
it derefs a `ref` param, loads the handle for a shared struct, and normalises
`SelfValue`. Both halves use it.

  GENERAL LESSON, not specific to this row: when a repro is a `main`-level
  program but the reported SOURCE is a method on a struct, verify the borrowed
  spelling before believing the fix. The two differ by exactly one deref, and
  only one of them is in the reproduction.

MEASURED BOUNDARY on the fixed tree, `--interp` vs `karac build`, all matching:
owned local field base (read + write), `ref self` / `mut ref self` methods,
`ref` / `mut ref` params, `shared struct` receiver, `Vec[Vec[String]]` heap
elements, computed indices in nested loops, and OOB on the outer index still
panicking through the same checked helper.

STILL DEFERRED, deliberately: the TRIPLE index `a[i][j][k]` remains refused by
the separate MR5 guard, loudly. The row asked whether a fix should generalise
to arbitrary place expressions -- it does not, and the pin's case 5 holds that
line so a later widening is a decision rather than a side effect.

FOUND BESIDE IT, NOT INTRODUCED BY IT: a nested indexed STORE that overwrites a
heap element leaks the old value. Filed as B-2026-08-10-1. Measured identical
on the pre-change tree via the already-supported local spelling
(`d[i][j] = f"zz"`), so this fix inherits it by routing field bases into the
same store, rather than creating it.

fix: 1b6ed41
tracker: probe: `let mut d: Vec[Vec[String]] = …; d[0][0] = f"zz";` -- the overwritten String is never freed (valgrind --leak-check=full at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0: 1 definitely-lost block)
title: a NESTED indexed store that overwrites a heap element (`d[i][j] = <String>`) leaks the old value -- the single-index store frees it, the nested one does not
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-09-21 (nested index rooted at a struct field). NOT
introduced by it: measured identical on the pre-change tree using the local
spelling, which has always compiled.

    let mut r: Vec[String] = Vec.new();
    r.push(f"aa"); r.push(f"bb");
    let mut d: Vec[Vec[String]] = Vec.new();
    d.push(r);
    d[0][0] = f"zz";        -> "aa" is never freed

NARROWED, each line measured at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 with `--leak-check=full`:

    r[0] = f"zz"            single index, local        clean
    h.data[0] = f"zz"       single index, field        clean
    d[0][0] = f"zz"         NESTED, local              1 leak
    h.data[0][0] = f"zz"    NESTED, field              1 leak

So the single-index store already frees the displaced element and the NESTED
one does not -- the gap is the nested store path
(`compile_nested_vec_vec_index_store`), independent of whether the base is a
name or a field. The field-base half only reaches it because B-2026-08-09-21
now routes there, which is why this is filed rather than treated as that row's
regression.

WHY IT IS ONLY VISIBLE AT -O0: at the default level the overwritten element is
frequently a dead allocation LLVM deletes outright, so a default-level valgrind
run reports clean. Same trap as B-2026-08-09-13 and B-2026-08-09-4. Any
measurement on this path must be taken at -O0.

FIX DIRECTION: the single-index store's displaced-value free is the model --
whatever it does before overwriting a heap element, the nested store should do
at the same point. Worth checking whether the nested path can simply delegate
to it once the inner element pointer is known, rather than growing its own
copy of the release logic; the two would then not drift again.

NOT PINNED as a test yet -- filed at the point of discovery with the narrowing
above. Note that an ASAN fixture for it needs `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (the -O0 leg)
to witness anything.

FIXED at __SHA__, by DELEGATION rather than a second copy — the row's own
preferred shape ("worth checking whether the nested path can simply delegate to
it once the inner element pointer is known").

The displaced-release-then-store logic is now
`emit_elem_store_releasing_displaced(elem_ptr, elem_ty, elem_te, val,
rhs_is_fresh)`, taking an ALREADY-COMPUTED element slot so it is indifferent to
how the caller got there. `compile_vec_index_store` calls it after its single
GEP; `compile_nested_vec_vec_index_store` calls it after its leaf GEP, passing
the inner element `TypeExpr` it already had to derive in order to GEP at all.
The four shape rules — vec-struct buffer free, tensor block free, `shared` /
`Option[shared]` refcount release, scalar width coercion — now live in one
place. The nested path also threads `rhs_is_fresh`, so the refcount shapes get
the same retain-new → store → release-old ordering that keeps a self-alias
safe.

Worth stating why the diff is small but not trivial: two of the four shapes
(tensor, shared) do the STORE themselves and return early, so the extraction
had to take the store with it rather than leaving it at the call sites.

VERIFIED at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 with `--leak-check=full`, since per the note
above a default-level run cannot see this class:

    d[0][0] = f"zz"           the row's repro          clean (was 1 block)
    h.data[0][0] = f"zz"      struct-FIELD base        clean (was 1 block)
    d[0][0] = 9i64            scalar leaf, control     clean, value correct
    d[0][0] = d[0][0]         SELF-alias               clean, no invalid free
    d[0][0] = d[0][1]         sibling alias            clean, value correct
    o[j][0] = f"n{j}" in a loop                        clean (was 4 blocks)

title: `File` has no `seek` on the Kāra surface even though the runtime entry point `karac_runtime_file_seek` is already implemented and exported — so any random-access file workload has to be restructured around sequential reads
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: this is what forced the whole shape of Cumulus's streaming
integrator (kara-katas apps/cumulus). It is a GAP, not a defect — the deferral
is deliberate and documented — but dogfooding has now produced a concrete
consumer and a measured cost, which the original deferral could not have.

The runtime half is already done. `runtime/src/file.rs` defines and exports

    pub unsafe extern "C" fn karac_runtime_file_seek(...)

with a comment stating that v1 does not expose seek through the Kāra surface,
and that shipping the runtime entry point early "avoids a runtime-rebuild
requirement when seek ships". The interpreter's file-method module says the same
from the other side: "Seek / metadata are deferred to a follow-on slice." So
what is missing is the surface — typechecker signature, interpreter arm, codegen
lowering — not the plumbing.

WHAT IT COST, concretely. Cumulus streams subs off disk so peak memory stops
scaling with frame height. Without seek, access must be strictly sequential,
which forces:

  - a sliding row window that RETAINS the halo across strip boundaries instead
    of simply re-reading those rows, and
  - N concurrently-open handles (one per sub) rather than one handle revisited,
    because each file must be walked forward exactly once.

Both are sound designs and the result is correct — but they are shaped by the
missing primitive, not by the problem. It also means a `.cstack` (one file
holding every frame back to back) CANNOT be streamed at all, because the same
strip of consecutive frames is a whole frame apart in the byte stream. That is
a real capability lost, not an inconvenience.

The concurrently-open-handles requirement is also what surfaced
B-2026-08-09-17 (a `File` in a `Vec` deadlocked under AOT). One missing
primitive pushed the design onto a path that then hit a genuine codegen bug.

FIX SHAPE: expose the existing runtime call. A `SeekFrom`-shaped enum
(Start/Current/End) matching the runtime's whence parameter, `File.seek` in the
typechecker's file-method table, the interpreter arm over
`Arc<Mutex<std::fs::File>>` (std's `Seek` is right there), and the codegen
lowering next to `compile_file_read` / `compile_file_write`, which already have
the exact call shape to copy.

=== FIXED (9f1e3c6f). The early-export bet paid off; the surface hid one trap. ===

WHAT IT TOOK, and it was as small as the row predicted on the runtime side.
`karac_runtime_file_seek` was already implemented, exported, AND on the
`__preserve_no_mangle_symbols` keep-list, so the JIT resolved it with no
runtime rebuild -- the deferral comment's stated reason for shipping the symbol
early turned out to be exactly right. Everything added was surface: stdlib
stub, prelude type entry, interpreter arm, codegen lowering.

API SHAPE, and the trade taken. `seek(whence: SeekFrom, offset: i64)` with a
PAYLOAD-FREE `SeekFrom`, rather than Rust's payload-carrying
`SeekFrom::Start(n)`. The row's own phrasing ("matching the runtime's whence
parameter") describes this shape, and it keeps the enum exactly equal to the
ABI byte, so the lowering is a tag truncation with nothing to unpack. The cost
is that a call reads `f.seek(SeekFrom.Start, 1024)` rather than
`f.seek(SeekFrom.Start(1024))`. If the payload form is later preferred, the
enum gains payloads and only `compile_file_seek` changes -- the runtime call is
identical either way.

  Returns the NEW absolute position, so `f.seek(SeekFrom.Current, 0)` is the
  "where am I" query and no separate `tell` is needed.

  `reads(FileSystem)`, not `writes`: seek moves the cursor and never touches
  contents, which is the same reason `read` is `reads` despite also advancing
  the cursor. The effect describes the resource's data, not the handle.

THE TRAP, worth more than the feature. A PRELUDE enum reaches the typechecker
through `STDLIB_PROGRAMS` but never codegen's `declare_enums`, which walks only
the user's `program.items`. Every such enum needs an explicit layout seed in
`declarations.rs` -- `Ordering`, `VarError` and `IoError` each carry one -- and
without it every variant construction falls through to the `i64 0` placeholder.

  The failure is SILENT AND DIRECTIONAL, which is what makes it dangerous:
  `Start` is tag 0, so seeking from the start kept working while `Current` and
  `End` both silently became `Start`. Measured before the seed:
  `f.seek(SeekFrom.End, -1)` returned `Err` (the runtime rejects a negative
  ABSOLUTE position) and `f.seek(SeekFrom.Current, 0)` reported position 0. A
  half-working seek, not a broken one.

  It is also invisible to `--interp`, which reads the variant by NAME. So the
  bug existed only in the two compiled backends, and only a codegen test could
  see it. Pinned as `test_e2e_seek_from_prelude_enum_discriminates`, deliberately
  SEPARATE from the seek tests: it pins the cause, so it catches the same
  omission for any future prelude enum rather than only for this one.

  Variant order in io.kara IS the ABI encoding (Start=0, Current=1, End=2 is
  the runtime's `whence`). Reordering the variants silently changes the mapping;
  both sites say so.

NEGATIVE `Start` IS AN ERROR, not a wrap-around. The runtime takes `u64` there,
so an unguarded cast would turn -5 into ~1.8e19 and seek far past EOF instead
of failing. The interpreter rejects it before the cast; the runtime rejects it
at the syscall. Both report `Err`, and the pins cover it.

VERIFIED three-way (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac build` AOT) producing
identical output, on: seek-then-READ (the byte at position 2 of "ABCD" must be
'C' -- a position check alone passes even if the cursor never moved), End with
a negative offset, Current-as-tell, and the negative-Start rejection.

NOT DONE: `metadata`, still deferred, and design.md is unchanged -- it carries
no `File` method table to update (only usage examples and the cancellation-
safety note about `sync_all`/`sync_data`), so the stdlib stub remains the
declaration of record. The Cumulus consumer that motivated this row was not
re-worked to use seek; that is app-side work in kara-katas, and the container
here has no checkout of it.

title: `split_at_mut` is fully specified in design.md but implemented nowhere, so there is NO way to obtain a mutable sub-view of a buffer — `buf[n..]` yields `Slice[u8]`, not `mut Slice[u8]`, and a partly-filled buffer cannot be topped up in place
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found writing Cumulus's streaming FITS reader. Filed as the
narrow, checked claim rather than the one I first assumed — my initial reading
was "Kāra has no mutable sub-slice at all", which is wrong in an important way:
the READ-ONLY half shipped and the mutable half did not.

    $ grep '"split_at"'     src/  ->  typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs, interpreter/method_call_seq.rs
    $ grep '"split_at_mut"' src/  ->  (nothing)

design.md specifies it in full, under "`split_at_mut` — disjoint mutable
partition", including the signature, the panic condition, and the aliasing
argument for why both halves may be live at once:

    fn split_at_mut(mut ref self, mid: i64) -> (mut Slice[T], mut Slice[T]) with panics

Neither receiver the spec names accepts it:

    error[typecheck]: no method 'split_at_mut' on type 'Array'
    error[typecheck]: no method 'split_at_mut' on type 'Vec'

WHY IT BITES. `File.read(buf: mut Slice[u8])` fills from the START of its
buffer and may return short. With no way to name "the tail of this buffer" as a
mutable view, a short read cannot be topped up in place, so reading exactly N
bytes is impossible to express directly. Cumulus works around it with a
per-frame CARRY QUEUE: read whole fixed 4096-byte chunks into a `Vec[u8]`, hand
the caller what it asked for, keep the remainder for next time. That is ~40
lines and a per-byte copy on every refill, and all of it exists solely because
the tail of an array cannot be borrowed mutably.

Range syntax does not substitute: `buf[2..]` typechecks as `Slice[u8]`, so
passing it where `mut Slice[u8]` is wanted gives

    error[typecheck]: expected 'mut Slice[u8]', found 'Slice[u8]'

which is a correct diagnostic and leaves no alternative spelling.

FIX SHAPE: `split_at` already exists on both surfaces and returns two
`Slice[T]`; the mut variant is the same index arithmetic over a `mut ref`
receiver, returning two `mut Slice[T]`. The aliasing argument the spec makes —
disjointness is structural, so both halves may be simultaneously live — is what
the ownership checker needs to be told; everything else mirrors the existing
method. Worth pairing with B-2026-08-10-3, since together they are what make
streaming file access awkward to express, and neither is hard on its own.

IMPLEMENTED at __SHA__ on all three surfaces.

RECEIVERS. `Vec[T]` and `mut Slice[T]`, exactly as design.md names them.
`Array` is NOT wired, and the row's `no method 'split_at_mut' on type 'Array'`
should not be read as a remaining gap: `split_at` has no Array arm either
(`a.split_at(2)` reports the same "no method"), so the family is consistently
Vec-and-Slice and an Array reaches it through `as_slice_mut()`.

WHERE THE ROW'S FIX SHAPE HELD, AND WHERE IT DID NOT. "The same index
arithmetic over a `mut ref` receiver" is right for typecheck and codegen. It is
WRONG for the interpreter, and following it would have shipped a silently
useless method: the existing `split_at` arm returns `Value::array_of(v[..i]
.to_vec())` -- two COPIES. Fine for a read-only view, fatal for a mutable one,
since a write through either half would land in a detached buffer and the
caller's collection would never see it. The mut arm instead builds two
`Value::Slice` windows over the receiver's own `Arc<RwLock<...>>`, the same
aliasing construction `as_slice_mut` uses.

THE INTERPRETER TRAP WORTH RECORDING. There is a Slice->Array NORMALIZATION
that snapshots a `Value::Slice` receiver into a fresh Array before the seq
method surface sees it -- correct for the read-only methods it was built for,
and it silently defeats this one. `split_at_mut` is now exempted alongside
`as_slice`/`as_slice_mut`. Before the exemption the bug was INVISIBLE: returned
lengths correct, reads through the halves correct, every write silently lost --
and it discriminated by receiver, so a `Vec` receiver propagated while a `mut
Slice` receiver did not on otherwise identical programs. Only a
write-then-read-back through the ORIGINAL collection distinguishes them, which
is why the tests are written that way and cover both receivers.

PANICS rather than clamping, per the spec. `split_at` saturates with
`.min(v.len())`; a mutable partition must not, because a clamped split hands
back an EMPTY second half where the caller expected a writable tail and the
write then goes nowhere -- the same invisible-loss failure as above, reached
from the other side. `mid == 0` and `mid == len` are legal boundaries; only
`mid > len` (and negative) faults.

NO OWNERSHIP-CHECKER WORK WAS NEEDED. The row anticipated having to teach the
checker that disjointness is structural. In practice nothing rejected the two
simultaneously-live halves -- they are ordinary values of a tuple, and the
existing rules already permit it -- so the spec's "without additional
annotation" is satisfied by construction rather than by a new rule. Recorded
because the row predicted otherwise.

READ-ONLY `split_at` IS STILL CODEGEN-LESS and deliberately untouched:
`karac build` on `v.split_at(2)` still reports "Vec/String method 'split_at' is
not yet supported in codegen", so it remains interpreter-only. The row's
premise that it "already exists on both surfaces" is true of typecheck+interp,
not codegen. Giving it an arm means deciding whether ITS halves may alias the
source, which is that method's question, not this one's.

ONE SPELLING DOES NOT BUILD, filed as B-2026-08-10-5. Writing through a half by

`--interp` accepts it, so it is a build-time refusal rather than a miscompile.
The workaround -- pass each half to a function taking `mut Slice[T]` -- builds
and runs correctly on both backends and is what the tests use.

`karac build` and agree; boundary mids; the out-of-range panic on both

detail:
FOUND while implementing B-2026-08-10-4 (`split_at_mut`), and measured
PRE-EXISTING and INDEPENDENTLY REACHABLE rather than caused by it:

    let mut v: Vec[i64] = [1i64, 2i64, 3i64, 4i64];
    let mut t: (mut Slice[i64], i64) = (v.as_slice_mut(), 5i64);
    t.0[0] = 9i64;

    --interp    -> 9
    karac build -> error: codegen failed: Index assignment target must be a variable

No `split_at_mut` involved. It is filed separately for that reason, but it is
what stops that row's most natural spelling from building:

    let mut p: (mut Slice[u8], mut Slice[u8]) = buf.split_at_mut(2i64);
    p.0[0] = 7u8;          // same error

NARROWED, each line measured:

    t.0[0] = x   where t.0 is a Vec        -> BUILDS, correct
    t.0[0] = x   where t.0 is a mut Slice  -> codegen error
    s[0]   = x   where s is a mut Slice    -> BUILDS, correct
    a[0][0] = x  nested Vec[Vec[T]]        -> BUILDS (B-2026-08-10-1)

Vec-typed field of the same tuple works, and a Slice held in a plain binding
works; only the combination fails. That pairing suggests the index-assign
target dispatch recognises a tuple field by the field's container kind and has
a Vec arm but no Slice arm, rather than rejecting tuple fields generally --
the error text ("must be a variable") is the generic fall-through, so it reads
like a missing arm rather than a deliberate refusal.

obtain a tuple of mutable slices, so this shape was rare. `split_at_mut`

`Type::Slice`, a different Type variant, so it missed the gate and codegen
never got the element type it needs. The fall-through error text is what made
it look like a codegen-side refusal.

So the fix is in two places rather than one:

  - typechecker: record the element type for a `Type::Slice` receiver too.
  - codegen, BOTH tuple-index arms: stop assuming the container is a Vec. They
    built the synth binding with `vec_type_expr_from_element` unconditionally;
    a slice slot is 16 bytes `{ptr,len}` against a Vec's 24 `{ptr,len,cap}`, so
    a slice registered as a Vec would read a `cap` word that is not there. They
    now choose between that and a new `slice_type_expr_from_element` by
    comparing the tuple's own LLVM field type against `slice_struct_type()` —
    structural, so no new side-table and nothing threaded down from the
    surface type.

The synth binding is registered as `MutSlice` regardless of the field's surface
mutability: both spellings lower to the same slot, and this binding exists only
to give the identifier-keyed dispatch the right LAYOUT. Whether the write was
permitted is a typechecker question, already settled before codegen runs.

CLOSES THE GAP B-2026-08-10-4 SHIPPED WITH. That row's tests route each half
through a function taking `mut Slice[T]` precisely because `p.0[0] = 7u8` did
not build; it now does, and is pinned.

VERIFIED: read and write through a slice-typed tuple field, the `split_at_mut`
halves, and a Vec-typed field control that must keep working (the direction a
wrong container choice breaks). All three agree with `--interp` and are
valgrind-clean at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`. Full `--features llvm` suite green
(102/102), clippy `--all-targets`, fmt.

title: `Vec.sort_by`'s mono path was a NON-ADAPTIVE fixed-32-run bottom-up merge sort: it did ceil(log2(n/32)) = 13 full passes over 2.4 MB for 150k elements REGARDLESS of input order, where Rust's driftsort detects the existing run and does one scan. FIXED in 50a50e8 by replacing phases 1+2 of `emit_sort_by_mono` with a natural-run merge sort: phase 1 splits the array into maximal already-sorted runs (probe the first pair, extend ascending while `cmp<=0` or STRICTLY descending while `cmp>0`, reversing the latter in place, then pad anything shorter than RUN=32 by insertion sort, recording run ends in a scratch i64 list); phase 2 merges adjacent runs pairwise, ping-ponging both the element buffers and the run lists, until one run remains. Strictness in the descending test is what keeps the reversal stable -- a strictly descending run has no two elements that compare equal, so reversing it cannot reorder equals. MEASURED karac pure sort (clone subtracted), before -> after: random 14.91 -> 14.60 ms (UNCHANGED), sorted 4.91 -> 0.14 (35x), reverse 6.65 -> 0.19 (35x), sawtooth 4.99 -> 3.15 (1.58x), few-unique 6.43 -> 6.11. Exactly the predicted shape: shuffled input has ~2-element natural runs so the RUN padding reproduces the old 32-element runs and the old pass count, while ordered input collapses to one scan. Sorted/reverse now sit within 1.1-1.6x of driftsort instead of 39-54x behind, and sawtooth is now FASTER than driftsort. THE ORIGINAL 2.1x ON SHUFFLED-UNIFORM IS NOT CLOSED and is refiled as B-2026-08-10-19 -- it needs driftsort's other half, a stable quicksort. WHAT THIS ROW ALSO SETTLED, and the reason its original `codegen` framing was misleading: hand-writing karac's exact algorithm AND its exact comparator lowering (Ordering tag, minus 1, test `<=0`) in Rust put karac at 14.91 ms vs rustc's 15.6-16.2 on random -- karac is 5-8% FASTER than rustc compiling the same algorithm, so this was never a lowering-quality gap. And no contained merge-kernel tweak is a win: branchless merge is a TRADE (1.28x on random, 1.8-2.0x SLOWER on few-unique/sawtooth/nearly-sorted), the ordered-run bulk-copy fast path only reaches ~2x on sorted because the 13 passes still happen as memcpys, cached merge heads shrink from 18% in isolation to 3-5% in a full sweep, and RUN tuning 8/16/32/64 is flat within 3%. Full matrix in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while benching kata #253 (Meeting Rooms II), sort-dominated, cross-checked against #252. Measured and fixed 2026-08-10 on an x86_64 Xeon @2.80GHz 4-vCPU SHARED CLOUD CONTAINER -- still NOT the canonical Apple-silicon bench host, so the single-host caveat stands; the branch-prediction-sensitive REJECTED options (branchless especially) are the most likely to move on another microarch, though the landed change is a pass-count win and is not microarch-sensitive in the same way. -- METHOD NOTE: karac timings are pure sort -- 1-round/25-round slope (removes startup and input build) minus a clone-only build (removes the per-round base.clone(), 1.13-1.23 ms and flat across patterns). The 35x on sorted input is itself the proof the new path is live. -- VERIFICATION: full --features llvm suite 102 targets / 13381 passed / 0 failed, including codegen 2882/0 and memory_sanitizer 1028/0 (LSan on Linux, the authoritative gate for the two extra allocations); valgrind --leak-check=full at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 over a program hitting all three new paths (ordinary merge, the nr==1 skip, the descending reversal) = 20 allocs / 20 frees, 0 errors; sortedness + stability + permutation over 98 (pattern, size) pairs AOT against --interp as oracle. Two regression tests pinned in tests/codegen.rs, both with teeth: under a NON-STRICT (`>=`) descending extension natural_run_sort_keeps_descending_runs_stable prints 33 before 32 and 40 before 39, because a reversed run containing equal keys inverts them. -- INVARIANT NOTE: the codegen sort and the runtime's sort_fixed_width now run DIFFERENT algorithms but still agree element-for-element, because any two stable sorts produce the same permutation -- so the 'IR mirrors the runtime' comment is satisfied by stability alone and the runtime did NOT have to change in lockstep. Panic-freedom preserved: the two extra allocations are null-checked and unwind through paired bail blocks, so the ~262 KiB DWARF symbolizer stays dead-strippable.

tracker: compile_method_call (dispatch fall-through); sort_by closure param typing
title: Inside a `sort_by` COMPARATOR CLOSURE, a closure parameter supports only TUPLE-FIELD access; any METHOD CALL or INDEX on it falls through codegen's method dispatch. `v.sort_by(|x, y| x.len().cmp(y.len()))` on a `Vec[Vec[i64]]` or `Vec[String]` fails with `codegen: no handler for method 'len' on variable 'x' (method dispatch fell through; this is a codegen bug -- add a dispatcher arm in compile_method_call ...)`; the interpreter runs it correctly. The diagnostic SELF-IDENTIFIES as a codegen bug, so this is a known-shaped fall-through rather than a deliberate deferral. BOUNDARY (probed): inside the closure, `x.len()` on Vec[Vec[i64]] FAILS; `x.len()` on Vec[String] FAILS; `x[0]` index FAILS; tuple field `x.0` BUILDS. Outside any closure, `v[0].len()` BUILDS. So the closure parameter is reaching codegen without an element type attached -- field access works because it needs no type lookup, while method dispatch and index lowering both do. IMPACT: this is a whole family, not an edge case -- sorting a `Vec[Vec[T]]` or `Vec[String]` by ANY content-derived key (length, first element, lexicographic) cannot be built. `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by(|a,b| a.0.cmp(b.0))` works, which is why #56/#252/#253 never hit it: every earlier sort_by in the corpus compares tuple fields. FIX DIRECTION: register the comparator parameters' element TypeExpr when lowering the sort_by closure (the same registration `var_elem_type_exprs` gets for an ordinary binding), so method dispatch and index lowering can resolve them. REPRO (8 lines): `fn main() { let mut v: Vec[Vec[i64]] = Vec.new(); let mut a: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); a.push(1i64); v.push(a); v.sort_by(|x, y| x.len().cmp(y.len())); println(f"{v.len()}"); }`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while authoring kata #254 (Factor Combinations). The kata's three solvers each generate combinations in a different order, so their shared `render` sorts the `Vec[Vec[i64]]` lexicographically before printing -- comparing lengths and elements, which is the natural and arguably only way to canonicalise a list of lists. All three solvers therefore fail to build while the differential (which compares by an order-independent summed hash and never sorts) builds and runs on all four surfaces. Per kata policy the natural spelling is KEPT and the kata's README records the blocked leg. -- SURFACE NOTE: codegen, sort_by comparator closure parameter typing.

FIXED at __SHA__, by the registration the row proposed — and the row's boundary
probe turns out to explain itself exactly.

The comparator params were registered with `record_var_type_name` ONLY. That
serves `compile_field_access`, which needs nothing but a struct name, and it
does not serve method dispatch or index lowering, both of which resolve the
receiver through `vec_elem_types` / `slice_elem_types` / `var_elem_type_exprs`.
So the params arrived typed enough to read a field and not typed enough to call
a method — which is precisely the observed split (`x.0` builds, `x.len()` and
`x[0]` do not), rather than "reaching codegen without an element type" in
general.

The fix registers from the element's full `TypeExpr` through
`register_var_from_type_expr`, the same registrar an ordinary `let` binding
uses, so Vec / String / Slice / nested elements are covered by one arm instead
of a method-by-method allowlist. Registrations are torn down when the thunk
returns, recomputed from `params` rather than tracked in a side list so the
teardown cannot drift from the binding loop; without it a comparator param
named `x` would shadow an enclosing `x` of a different shape for the rest of
the function.

WHY THE CORPUS MISSED IT, confirmed mechanically rather than by inspection.
`Vec[(i64,i64)]` does not merely happen to use tuple fields — it takes a
DIFFERENT CODE PATH. `should_use_mono_vec_sort_by_for` admits an element only
when every LLVM field is an int, so `(i64,i64)` routes to the mono sort while a
`Vec[T]`/`String` element (`{ptr,i64,i64}` — the pointer fails the gate) falls
to the thunk this fix touches. That is why #56/#252/#253 were clean, and it is
why the tuple case is kept as the control: it exercises the path the fix does
NOT modify.

`sort_by_key` HAD THE SAME GAP and is fixed alongside. `v.sort_by_key(|x|
x.len())` over a `Vec[String]` failed identically. Found by probing the sibling
immediately after the reported method worked, rather than leaving it for the
next kata to rediscover as a separate row.

Only the thunk emitters needed changing. `emit_sort_by_inline_compare` (factored
out of `emit_sort_by_mono`) sits behind the all-int gate, so the registration
would be dead code there; that is recorded at the call site so it is not added
later "for symmetry".

VERIFIED: length and index comparators over `Vec[Vec[i64]]` and `Vec[String]`,
both `sort_by` and `sort_by_key`, plus the tuple control — six shapes, all
matching `--interp` and valgrind-clean at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`. Full
`--features llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy `--all-targets`, fmt.

NOT ADDRESSED: kata #254 itself. This unblocks the spelling the row reports, so
the kata's three solvers should now build, but re-running the kata and clearing
its README's blocked-leg note is a separate step and was not done here.
