tracker: sort_by comparator lowering; closure return-value unwrapping
title: An explicit `return` inside a `sort_by` COMPARATOR CLOSURE emits an LLVM module-verification failure: `Module verification failed: "Function return type does not match operand type of return inst! ret { i64 } %ord / i64"`. The comparator is declared to return `i64` but an explicit `return <Ordering>` yields the `{ i64 }` struct unwrapped only on the implicit-tail path. Interpreter runs it. BOUNDARY (probed, all on Vec[(i64,i64)] so the element-type axis is held fixed): single-expression `|x,y| x.0.cmp(y.0)` BUILDS; block with IMPLICIT tail `|x,y| { let d = x.0; d.cmp(y.0) }` BUILDS; if-EXPRESSION tail `|x,y| if .. { .. } else { .. }` BUILDS; block with EXPLICIT `return` `|x,y| { return x.0.cmp(y.0) }` FAILS. So it is the `return` KEYWORD in comparator position, independent of element type -- it fails identically on Vec[Vec[i64]] and on the tuple-field path that #56/#252/#253 use. NOT A REGRESSION FROM B-2026-08-10-13 (b90027e): that commit's diff touches no return-type or fn_type logic (only element-type registration), its tests are all single-expression comparators, and #254 is the ONLY program in the whole kata corpus with a block-bodied comparator -- so nothing else could have exercised this path before or after. It is a SECOND, PRE-EXISTING gap that the first one was masking: before b90027e the same kata failed earlier, at method dispatch on `x.len()`, and never reached module verification. Not bisected against a pre-fix build; the evidence above is circumstantial but consistent. FIX DIRECTION: apply the same Ordering unwrap on the explicit-return path that the implicit-tail path already performs. REPRO (3 lines): `fn main(){ let mut v: Vec[(i64,i64)] = Vec.new(); v.push((1i64,2i64)); v.sort_by(|x,y| { return x.0.cmp(y.0) }); println(f"{v.len()}"); }`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: exposed while re-verifying B-2026-08-10-13's fix against the ORIGINAL finding case (kata #254's render comparator) rather than against the 8-line repro that was filed -- the repro is genuinely fixed, the kata is not. Same pattern as B-2026-08-09-18 -> -19 one day earlier, where a fix closed the minimised case and the kata-shaped case kept failing at a different site. #254's comparator needs an EARLY return from inside a while loop (compare element-by-element, exit at the first difference), which cannot be written as an implicit tail without restructuring into a sentinel-and-flag shape, so per kata policy the natural spelling is kept and the kata's three solvers stay interpreter-only. -- SURFACE NOTE: codegen, sort_by comparator closure return lowering.

FIXED at __SHA__.

THE VERIFIER SAID MORE THAN THE ROW QUOTES, and the extra half changes the fix.
The full message carries TWO distinct failures:

    Found return instr that returns non-void in Function of void return type!
      ret { i64 } %ord
    Instruction does not dominate all uses!
      %v = alloca { ptr, i64, i64 }      <- the CALLER's vec, GEP'd for cleanup

Note "void return type", not the `i64`/`{i64}` mismatch the row records: on the
mono path the body is inlined straight into the VOID sort function, so the
`return` was not merely returning the wrong type, it was trying to return from
the wrong function. And the fn-level return path also drained the WHOLE cleanup
stack — including the caller's frames — which is what put the caller's alloca
inside the emitted sort function.

So the row's fix direction ("apply the same Ordering unwrap on the explicit-
return path") would not have been sufficient. Unwrapping fixes the type of a
`ret` that should not be emitted at all.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY NEEDED, and it already existed: the `ReturnRetarget`
machinery `with_provider` uses for the identical problem (B-2026-07-31-16, a
`return` inside an inline-lowered closure body). A retargeted return stores its
value into a slot, drains ONLY the frames pushed since the retarget, and
branches to a merge block; the joined value is then an ordinary value, so the
caller's existing Ordering unwrap covers the `return` path and the implicit-tail
path identically. That asymmetry — only the tail path unwrapping — was the
row's correct observation; the mechanism is just further back than it looked.

Applied at ALL FOUR body compiles: the `sort_by` thunk, the mono compare
(`emit_sort_by_inline_compare`), and both of `sort_by_key`'s. The mono and
thunk emitters fail differently, so one does not cover the other, and the tests
pin one of each.

REGRESSION DIRECTION PINNED. Every comparator body now routes through the
retarget, including ones that never return early, so the implicit-tail and
if-expression-tail shapes are in the test as controls: a mishandled join would
break those while the `return` cases passed.

DOES NOT UNBLOCK KATA #254 — verified, not assumed. Re-running the kata's own
comparator (not the filed repro) shows it now fails one phase EARLIER: a
`return` nested inside an `if`/loop within a closure is typechecked against
`()` rather than the closure's return type. Filed as B-2026-08-10-17. The
boundary is sharp and worth recording here too:

    |x, y| { return x.0.cmp(y.0) }                        All checks passed.
    |x, y| { if c { return Ordering.Less; } return .. }   expected '()', found 'Ordering'

Same closure, same return type; only the NESTING differs. So #254's three
solvers stay interpreter-only and its README's blocked-leg note stands, now
pointing at -17 rather than this row.

THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE PATTERN, worth stating as process rather than as three
coincidences: B-2026-08-09-18 -> -19, B-2026-08-10-13 -> -16, and now -16 ->
-17. Each time a fix closed the minimised repro and the ORIGINAL kata-shaped
case kept failing at the next site along. Re-verifying against the finding case
rather than the filed minimisation is what caught all three.

Full `--features llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy `--all-targets`, fmt.

title: a `return` NESTED inside a closure body (in an `if` / loop) is typechecked against `()` instead of the closure's return type, so an early return from a comparator is rejected -- a TOP-LEVEL `return` in the same closure body is accepted
tracker: closure body return-type checking; probe: `v.sort_by(|x, y| { if x.0 < y.0 { return Ordering.Less; } return Ordering.Greater; })`
detail:
FOUND while verifying B-2026-08-10-16's codegen fix against kata #254's own
comparator rather than against the filed repro. The repro is genuinely fixed;
the kata is still blocked, one phase EARLIER.

    v.sort_by(|x, y| { return x.0.cmp(y.0) });                       All checks passed.
    v.sort_by(|x, y| { if x.0 < y.0 { return Ordering.Less; }
                       return Ordering.Greater; });
        -> error[typecheck]: expected '()', found 'Ordering'

Both returns are in the SAME closure with the SAME return type. The only
difference is nesting: the accepted one is the block's top-level statement, the
rejected one is inside an `if`. So the closure's return type is threaded into
the immediate body but not into nested blocks, where `return` falls back to
checking against `()`.

NOT specific to `Ordering` or to `sort_by`. The same shape reports
`expected '()', found 'i64'` for a `sort_by_key` key closure
(`v.sort_by_key(|x| { return x.len() })` -- note this one is rejected even at
the TOP level, so the key-closure surface may be a slightly different case
worth checking separately).

WHY IT MATTERS: an early return from inside a loop is the natural way to write
a lexicographic comparator -- compare element-by-element, exit at the first
difference -- and it cannot be expressed without it except by restructuring
into a sentinel-and-flag shape. Kata #254's three solvers need exactly this,
which is why they remain interpreter-only even with B-2026-08-10-16 fixed.

INTERPRETER PARITY: this is a typecheck REJECTION, so `--interp` refuses it
too. Not a run-vs-build divergence -- the program is simply unwritable, which
is why it presents as a missing capability rather than a miscompile.

RELATED: B-2026-08-10-16 is the codegen half of the same user-visible
complaint. That one is fixed; this is what is left. Same pattern as
B-2026-08-09-18 -> -19 and -13 -> -16: a fix closes the minimised repro while
the original kata-shaped case keeps failing at the next site along. Worth
noting as a third instance -- re-verifying against the ORIGINAL finding case,
not the filed minimisation, is what keeps catching these.

FIXED at __SHA__ — and BOTH of my framings in the row above are wrong. Recorded
because each one would have sent the next person to the wrong place.

1. NOT NESTING-DEPENDENT. I wrote that a top-level `return` in a closure body
   is accepted and a nested one is not. That is what the `sort_by` probe
   showed, but it is not the rule. In an annotated `let`:

       let g: Fn(i64) -> i64 = |n| { if n > 0i64 { return 1i64; } return 0i64; };

   BOTH returns are rejected — the nested one and the top-level one. Nesting
   was incidental to the probe I happened to write.

2. NOT SORT-SPECIFIC. A plain `Fn(i64) -> i64` argument to an ordinary function
   reproduces it identically, with no comparator anywhere.

WHAT ACTUALLY DECIDES IT is which closure arm typed the body. B-2026-07-31-18
added the closure-scoped `return` collector to the INFER-direction arm only.
A closure whose type is known from context — annotated `let`, an argument to a
fn with a declared `Fn` param, a comparator — goes through the CHECK-direction
arm (`exprs.rs`, `check_expr(body, expected_ret)`), which pushed no frame, so
the Return arm fell through to `current_return_type`: the ENCLOSING FN's.

THE DIAGNOSTIC ITSELF WAS THE CLUE, in hindsight. "expected '()'" is not a
plausible closure return type for any of these programs — it is `main`'s. And
the error DISAPPEARS when the enclosing fn's return type coincides with the
closure's (an i64-returning fn wrapping an `Fn(..) -> i64` closure typechecks
clean), which is the signature of checking against the wrong scope rather than
of a missing feature.

THE FIX pushes the collector on the check path too. Because the expected return
type is already known there, the collected returns are CHECKED against it
rather than unified with the tail the way the infer arm has to. The negative
direction is pinned: a genuinely wrong return is still rejected, now against
the CLOSURE's type. `ClosureReturnFrame` grew a per-return span for that — the
check runs after the body, so without one every mismatch reported at the
closure body's span instead of at the offending `return`.

KATA #254 IS UNBLOCKED, verified rather than inferred. Its lexicographic
comparator — early `return` from inside a while loop, the shape that cannot be
written any other way without a sentinel-and-flag rewrite — now typechecks,
builds, and sorts correctly on both backends, and is pinned as an E2E test
(`test_e2e_lexicographic_comparator_with_early_returns`). -16 and -17 are only
JOINTLY sufficient: -17 makes it typecheck, -16 makes it codegen.

That terminates the chain. B-2026-08-09-18 -> -19, then -13 -> -16 -> -17: four
rows over two days where a fix closed the filed minimisation while the original
kata-shaped case kept failing one site further along. The kata case is now the
test, which is what should have been pinned at the start of the chain.

Full `--features llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy `--all-targets`, fmt.

STILL OPEN, noticed here and not chased: `v.sort_by_key(|x| { return x.len() })`
is rejected even with a TOP-LEVEL return, where the `sort_by` equivalent is
accepted. The key-closure surface may take yet another typing path. Not filed
as its own row without a proper probe, but recorded so it is not lost.

CORRECTION to the "STILL OPEN" note above: it is WRONG, and was stale when
written. `v.sort_by_key(|x| { return x.len() })` is NOT rejected — that
observation was made from a probe run BEFORE this row's own fix landed, when
only B-2026-08-10-16's codegen change was in the tree. Re-measured after the
fix, the whole `sort_by_key` family typechecks, builds, and runs correctly on
both backends, with a top-level return AND with one nested in an `if`. There is
no separate key-closure typing path; it went through the same CHECK-direction
arm this row fixed.

Probing that note DID turn up something real, filed as B-2026-08-10-18: the
same explicit-return spelling in an ITERATOR ADAPTOR closure (`map` / `filter`
/ `any` / `all` / `retain`) now typechecks and then fails codegen, and `fold`
silently miscompiles. That is a pre-existing codegen gap this row UNMASKED, not
one it caused — verified by rebuilding with this row's typechecker change
reverted, where all six shapes are rejected at typecheck and never reach
codegen at all.

title: an explicit `return` inside an ITERATOR ADAPTOR closure (`map`/`filter`/`any`/`all`/`retain`) fails codegen with `Terminator found in the middle of a basic block!`, and `fold` SILENTLY MISCOMPILES to no output -- the sort-comparator twin of this was B-2026-08-10-16
tracker: iterator-adaptor closure body lowering; the `fold` arm is the silent one. Probe: `v.iter().map(|n| { return n * 2i64; }).collect()`
detail:
FOUND by probing an observation left on B-2026-08-10-17. Same root as
B-2026-08-10-16 (an explicit `return` inside an INLINED closure body emits a
real `ret` in the middle of the host function) but at the iterator-adaptor
sites rather than the sort comparators, which -16 fixed.

MEASURED, on `let v: Vec[i64] = [1i64, 2i64, 3i64, 4i64];`:

    v.iter().map(|n| { return n * 2i64; }).collect()      codegen fail
    v.iter().filter(|n| { return n > 2i64; }).collect()   codegen fail
    v.iter().any(|n| { return n > 3i64; })                codegen fail
    v.iter().all(|n| { return n > 0i64; })                codegen fail
    w.retain(|n| { return n > 2i64; })                    codegen fail
    v.iter().fold(0i64, |acc, n| { return acc + n; })     BUILDS, WRONG

    error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
      "Terminator found in the middle of a basic block!\nlabel %cleanup.skip8\n"

`--interp` runs all six correctly. The implicit-tail spelling of each builds
and runs correctly on both backends, so this is the `return` KEYWORD in adaptor
position, exactly as -16 was in comparator position.

WHY SEVERITY high RATHER THAN medium LIKE -16: the `fold` arm does not fail the
build. It compiles, exits 0, and produces NO OUTPUT where the interpreter
prints `10` -- the `println` after it vanishes. A loud verifier failure is
survivable; a silent wrong answer in a fold is the shape that reaches
production. The other five are loud.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-10-17, verified rather than assumed. Rebuilding with
that row's typechecker change reverted, all six shapes are rejected at
TYPECHECK ("expected '()', found ...") and never reach codegen. So the codegen
gap predates it and was masked by a typechecker false-positive; -17 removed the
mask. This is the same unmasking pattern as B-2026-08-10-13 -> -16.

FIX DIRECTION: -16's, applied at the adaptor closure body compiles --
`compile_sort_body_retargeting_return` (added by that row) is the shape,
reusing the `ReturnRetarget` machinery so the `return` stores its value, drains
only the frames pushed since the retarget, and branches to a merge block
instead of emitting `ret`. Worth checking whether the adaptor emitters can
share that helper directly rather than each growing a copy. The `fold` arm
should be looked at FIRST and separately: it fails differently (silently), so
it may not be the same emit path as the other five and could need its own
treatment.

INVESTIGATED, NOT FIXED. Three things established that change the row's shape;
recording them so the next attempt does not re-derive them.

1. `fold` DOES NOT "produce no output" — IT RETURNS FROM THE ENCLOSING
   FUNCTION. Measured:

       fn main() {
           println(f"before");
           let v: Vec[i64] = [1i64, 2i64, 3i64];
           let s: i64 = v.iter().fold(0i64, |acc, n| { return acc + n; });
           println(f"after {s}");
       }

       --interp    -> before / after 6
       karac build -> before          (exit 0)

   The `return` fires on the FIRST element and exits `main`. So this is not a
   wrong value, it is silent early termination of the program with a success
   exit code — strictly worse than the row's "silently miscompiles to no
   output" and the reason the severity is high.

   The cause is visible in the source: `try_compile_iter_chain_fold` splices
   the closure body as the RHS of `acc = <body>` inside a SYNTHESIZED for-loop
   (method_call.rs, the `value: fold_body.clone()` line), which is then
   compiled by the ordinary expression compiler in the ENCLOSING function. A
   `return` in it is therefore a genuine function return. The other five
   adaptors splice the same way; they fail the verifier instead of running
   because their spliced position leaves the `ret` mid-block.

2. THE LABELED-BLOCK REWRITE ROUTE IS CLOSED. The obvious contained fix —
   rewrite the closure body to `'k: { … break 'k E; … }` at splice time and
   reuse existing lowering — does not work: a labeled block is not an
   expression that can carry a break value at the surface.

       let x: i64 = 'k: { if true { break 'k 7i64; } 0i64 };
       error[parse]: Expected expression, found ...

3. THE `ReturnRetarget` ROUTE (B-2026-08-10-16's fix, and the row's own
   suggested direction) DOES NOT TRANSFER AS-IS, for a structural reason. That
   fix works because the sort comparator body is compiled by a call the
   emitter OWNS (`compile_sort_body_retargeting_return` wraps one
   `compile_expr(body)`), so the retarget's merge block lands exactly at the
   body's continuation. The adaptor emitters own no such call: they splice the
   body into a synthesized loop AST and compile the whole loop in one go.
   Wrapping that whole compile puts the merge AFTER the loop, which is the
   wrong semantics — `return` inside a `map`/`fold` closure must produce THAT
   ELEMENT's value and let the loop continue, not exit it.

   So a correct fix needs the retarget scoped to the body sub-expression,
   which means restructuring the splice sites to compile the body themselves
   rather than handing it to the loop compiler embedded in a larger AST. That
   is the actual work, across at least `try_compile_iter_chain_fold`,
   `try_compile_iter_chain_any_all`, the `IterAdaptor::Map`/`Filter` pipeline
   in `try_compile_iter_adaptor_collect_to_vec`, and `retain`.

INTERIM WORTH CONSIDERING, not implemented: reject `return` inside an
adaptor/terminal closure body at TYPECHECK with an explicit "not yet supported
here" diagnostic. That trades a silent early exit for a clear error, which is
the right direction while the restructuring is pending. It is a deliberate
narrow re-rejection of a shape B-2026-08-10-17 made typecheck, so it needs an
owner decision rather than being slipped in.

GUARDED at __SHA__ — the row STAYS OPEN. The silent miscompile is gone; the
capability is still missing.

All six shapes now fail the build with the limitation named and the interpreter
pointed to as the workaround, instead of `fold` silently exiting `main` and the
other five dying in LLVM verification with "Terminator found in the middle of a
basic block". Severity is really two bugs in one row: the silent-truncation
half is closed, the missing-capability half is not.

TWO ROUTES TRIED AND REJECTED ON EVIDENCE, so they are not re-attempted:

  * DECLINING the fast path does not help. There is no general fallback — the
    fused emitters ARE the implementation of these terminals. Gating them to
    return `Ok(None)` produces "no handler for method 'fold' on non-identifier
    receiver (method dispatch fell through; this is a codegen bug …)", which is
    worse than the guard: it is loud but points at entirely the wrong thing.

  * `ReturnRetarget` (B-2026-08-10-16's fix, and this row's own suggested
    direction) does not transfer. That fix works because the comparator emitter
    OWNS the body's `compile_expr` call, so the retarget's merge block lands at
    the body's continuation. These emitters own no such call: they splice the
    body into a synthesized loop AST and compile the whole loop in one go.
    Wrapping that compile puts the merge AFTER the loop, which is the wrong
    semantics — a `return` in a `map`/`fold` closure must produce THAT
    element's value and let the loop continue, not exit it.

So the real fix is restructuring the emitters to compile the body themselves:
`try_compile_iter_chain_fold`, `try_compile_iter_chain_any_all`, the
`Map`/`Filter` peel inside `try_compile_iter_adaptor_collect_to_vec`, and
`retain` in vec_method.rs. That is the remaining work.

ONE TRAP THE GUARD ITSELF HIT, worth recording because the fix will face it
too. The first version walked the whole body for `ExprKind::Return` and
rejected

    xs.iter().map(|n| apply(|m| { if m > 1i64 { return m * 10i64; } return m; }, n))

which BUILDS AND RUNS CORRECTLY: that `return` belongs to the NESTED closure,
which is lowered as a real closure body. The walker now treats a nested closure
as opaque, and both directions are pinned — the rejection cases and the
nested-closure case, alongside the no-`return` pipelines that must stay on the
fused path.

`--interp` is unaffected throughout and runs all six correctly.

FIXED at __SHA__, superseding the guard. The shapes COMPILE and run correctly
now; the guard's rejection is gone.

MY OWN "REAL FIX NEEDS RESTRUCTURING" CONCLUSION ABOVE WAS WRONG, and the way
it was wrong is the useful part. I had it that `ReturnRetarget` could not be
used because it must be scoped to the body's `compile_expr` call and these
emitters never own one — they splice the body into a synthesized loop and hand
the loop to the compiler. Both halves are true. The inference is not: the
emitter does not have to own the call, because the body keeps its SPAN through
the splice, and `compile_expr` is the single place that sees it as a distinct
sub-expression. Registering the span there scopes the retarget exactly, no
matter where the splice put the body.

So the fix is a span-keyed hook plus four one-line registrations
(`try_compile_iter_chain_fold`, `try_compile_iter_chain_any_all`, the
`map`/`filter`/`take_while`/`skip_while` peel in
`try_compile_iter_adaptor_collect_to_vec`, and `retain`), not the emitter
rewrite the guard note predicted. The general lesson: "the emitter must own the
compile call" was really "something must identify the body at compile time",
and a span does that as well as ownership does.

THE CORRECTNESS QUESTION is where the merge block lands, and it is easy to get
wrong invisibly. Merging AFTER the loop compiles fine and looks plausible, but
it makes `return` EXIT the iteration — a `map` would yield one element. The
retarget merging at the body's continuation is what makes it mean "this
element's value, continue". Pinned by returning early on exactly ONE element of
four and asserting the rest are still mapped (`1 99 3 4`), and by a `fold` that
skips one element and still sums the others (`7`). A single-element test cannot
tell the two apart, which is why neither is one.

REGISTRATION IS GATED on the body actually containing a `return`, so the
overwhelmingly common fused pipeline keeps its existing lowering untouched.

THE NESTED-CLOSURE TRAP the guard note flagged is real and the fix faces it:
the walker treats a nested closure as OPAQUE, because a `return` inside one
belongs to that closure and is lowered as a real closure body where it already
worked. An earlier iteration descended and broke
`xs.iter().map(|n| apply(|m| { … return m; }, n))`, a program that built
correctly; that case is pinned alongside the no-`return` pipelines.

VERIFIED: all six shapes agree with `--interp` and are valgrind-clean at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, including `fold`, whose spliced `return` used to exit
`main` on the first element with status 0 — its test asserts the LATER println
runs at all. Full `--features llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy
`--all-targets`, fmt.

title: `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by` on SHUFFLED-UNIFORM input is ~1.66x Rust's `sort_by` (karac 14.82 ms vs driftsort 8.93 ms, 150k pairs, this host, both programs generating input IDENTICALLY -- the parent row's 7.0 ms driftsort figure came from a Rust bench whose generator differed, so the true starting ratio was 1.66x, not 2.1x). Residual of B-2026-08-10-9. FIXED in 31485cd down to ~1.28-1.33x. THE ROW WAS FILED WITH THE WRONG DIAGNOSIS and the fix is not what it predicted: `cachegrind --branch-sim` over one 150k sort (differenced against a clone-only twin) shows karac executing FEWER instructions than driftsort (52.79M vs 48.56M is 1.09x), FEWER data references (18.82M vs 30.59M = 0.62x), FEWER conditional branches (0.79x) and an indistinguishable cache profile (D1 0.91x, LL 1.02x) -- and losing on ONE counter, branch mispredicts, 1.061M vs 0.233M = 4.56x. The 0.83M excess at ~20 cycles is 5.9 ms and the measured gap was 14.82-8.93 = 5.9 ms, i.e. the ENTIRE gap is mispredicts. Cross-pattern proof: random and few-unique run essentially the same instruction count (52.79M vs 50.79M) and differ 2.3x in wall clock (14.82 vs 6.51 ms), with mispredict rates 12.96% vs 2.75%. THE FIX: phase 2 now emits TWO merge kernels with identical output -- the existing branchy one and a branchless one that selects the value and advances both cursors by `zext` of the same `cmp <= 0` predicate -- and picks one PER PASS. Unconditional branchlessness remains the bad trade the parent row measured (1.8-2.0x SLOWER on ordered-ish shapes, where it swaps working speculation for a serial load->compare->cursor->next-load chain), so the choice is made by SIMULATING a branch predictor over the pass's first PROBE=256 outputs: a 16-entry 1-bit table indexed by 4 bits of global take history, six integer ops, committing to branchless above a 40% simulated miss rate. Inputs shorter than 4*PROBE skip the measurement and stay branchy, so a small sort runs exactly the code it ran before. MEASURED (interleaved A/B, both binaries in one process so host drift cancels; karac pure sort, clone subtracted): random 14.22 -> 11.05 ms (1.29x; three sweeps read 1.28x/1.32x/1.29x), few-unique 6.13 -> 5.96, sawtooth 3.38 -> 3.04, sorted/reverse untouched. Full matrix in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md. The remaining ~1.3x is refiled as B-2026-08-10-20.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-10-9 (fixed in 50a50e8). -- TWO DESIGN POINTS THAT ARE LOAD-BEARING, both found by measurement, do not 'simplify' either away. (1) A SWITCH-RATE COUNTER IS THE WRONG SIGNAL. It reads 1.0 on perfect alternation, which is exactly what merging two identical runs produces on sawtooth -- where the hardware mispredicts 1.86% -- so it routes the BEST-predicted case to the branchless kernel. The question being asked is predictability, not switch frequency, which is why the code simulates a predictor instead of counting switches. (2) THE HISTORY WIDTH IS NOT A ROUND NUMBER. A sawtooth merge at pass k has period 2^k (alternation, then AABB, then AAAABBBB), and an n-bit history predicts a period-p sequence perfectly exactly when p <= 2^n. The first version used 2 bits and a 1-in-3 threshold, read 25% on AAAABBBB, and misrouted: MEASURED 8% and 6% REGRESSIONS on few-unique and sawtooth. 4 bits covers periods to 8 and degrades to one miss per period beyond (6% at period 16). The 40% threshold is likewise asymmetric on purpose -- a wrong branchless choice costs up to 2x, a wrong branchy choice ~1.3x. (3) THE PROBE NEEDS A LENGTH GATE. A pass emits ~len outputs, so on a 64-element sort the 256-output budget covers ALL of phase 2 and the simulation stops being amortised -- an estimated ~5% tax on exactly the small-Vec sorts that are the common case. Below 4*PROBE the budget is zero, which the STRICT threshold resolves to branchy, so short sorts execute precisely the pre-change code. -- ROUTING IS VERIFIED BY COUNTERS, NOT INFERRED FROM TIMINGS: with the shipped 4-bit predictor, few-unique and sawtooth report mispredict counts IDENTICAL TO BASELINE (0.221M and 0.073M, to the digit), proving every one of their passes stayed branchy, while random collapses 1.061M -> 0.192M. The branchless kernel costs 1.40x the instructions on random (52.79M -> 74.07M) and wins anyway -- the same point from the other direction. -- MEASUREMENT NOTE, worth reusing: sorted and reverse-sorted are a single natural run, so phase 2 is skipped and the kernel choice never happens, but their TIMINGS sit at the harness noise floor (clone dominates and the subtraction amplifies it -- successive sweeps read 4.30x and 0.84x on the SAME pair of binaries). They were settled by INSTRUCTION COUNT instead, which is deterministic: +-1 instruction out of 3.2M and 4.0M. When a timing difference is smaller than the harness noise, count instructions. -- VERIFICATION: full --features llvm suite green including codegen and memory_sanitizer (LSan on Linux, the authoritative leak gate); valgrind --leak-check=full at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 over a program hitting the probe kernel, the branchless kernel, the branchy kernel, the nr==1 skip and the descending reversal = 28 allocs / 28 frees, 0 bytes in use at exit, 0 errors; sortedness + stability + permutation over 98 (pattern,size) combinations AOT against --interp. ELEMENT-TYPE COVERAGE mattered here specifically because the branchless kernel `select`s a WHOLE ELEMENT rather than a key, so it was checked on bare i64, a mixed-width (i64,i32,i64) tuple and an all-int-field named struct at 4096 shuffled elements each, agreeing across AOT, LLJIT and interp. This change adds NO allocation -- the six pieces of probe state are allocas -- so the panic-freedom and dead-strippable-symbolizer properties are unchanged. -- TEST NOTE: the two kernels produce identical output BY CONSTRUCTION, so no behavioural test can observe which one ran. Confirmed empirically: with the branchless tie-break weakened to `cmp < 0`, ALL 79 pre-existing sort tests in tests/codegen.rs still pass. Hence two new tests -- a behavioural one (4096 elements over a 64-key alphabet, large enough to outrun the probe and tie-heavy enough that an inverted tie-break shows up; it DOES fail under that break) and a structural one pinning the probe, both kernels and the dispatch in the IR so the 1.3x cannot be silently deleted.

tracker: the method-existence check in src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs -- enforced for String / i64 / f64 / u8, absent for `char` and `bool`
fix:
FIXED by c2be671. `char` and `bool` receivers now route through the
SCALAR-PRIMITIVE arm in `src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs` -- the same arm
`i64`/`u32`/`f64`/`u8` have used since B-2026-07-03-5. One `matches!` gains
`Type::Bool | Type::Char`, which buys both halves at once: a method with no impl
candidate is rejected `no method 'X' on type 'char'` (`NoMethodFound`) instead of
poisoning to `Type::Error`, and a method that HAS one dispatches through the impl
table and gets a real return type. `char` numeric-conversion typos (`to_i64` /
`as_i64` / `to_int` / `to_u32` / `as_u32` / `code_point` / `ord`) and `is_digit`
carry a hint naming the spelling that exists. Pins: five tests in
`tests/typechecker.rs` -- the bogus-name matrix, the four-annotation unification
case, the full real char/bool surface, user impls on both (dispatch AND return
type), and the hint.
title: `char` and `bool` receivers skip method-existence checking entirely, so ANY method name passes `karac check` and unifies with ANY return type -- the program then dies at run time under `--interp` or, under `build`, with a message that blames codegen for what is user error
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found dogfooding the same evaluator as B-2026-08-11-1. I guessed
`c.to_i64()` for a digit's numeric value. `karac check` said "All checks
passed"; the program then failed at run time. (The correct spelling is the cast
`c as i64`, so my code was wrong -- the bug is that nothing told me so.)

MEASURED. `v.completely_bogus_method()` on each primitive receiver:

    char     All checks passed.        <-- accepts anything
    bool     All checks passed.        <-- accepts anything
    i64      error: no method 'completely_bogus_method' on type 'i64'
    f64      error: no method 'completely_bogus_method' on type 'f64'
    u8       error: no method 'completely_bogus_method' on type 'u8'
    String   error: no method 'completely_bogus_method' on type 'String'

The hole is exactly `char` and `bool`.

THE RETURN TYPE IS UNCONSTRAINED TOO, which is the part that makes it more than
a missing lookup. The same bogus call typechecks as `i64`, as `String`, AND as
`Vec[i64]` depending only on the annotation at the use site:

    let n: i64      = c.completely_bogus_method();   // passes
    let s: String   = c.completely_bogus_method();   // passes
    let v: Vec[i64] = c.another_bogus_one();         // passes

So it is not "unknown method, unknown type" -- it unifies with whatever is
asked, which means downstream type errors are suppressed as well.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS A FALSE COMPILER-BUG REPORT, which is the same defect class
as B-2026-08-06-24 (extern call under `--interp` reporting a false compiler
bug):

    karac check   All checks passed.
    --interp      runtime error: method 'completely_bogus_method' not found on
                  type 'char' (no interpreter dispatch arm)
    build         error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method
                  'completely_bogus_method' on variable 'v' (method dispatch
                  fell through; this is a codegen bug -- add a dispatcher arm in
                  `compile_method_call` or mark the test `#[ignore]` if the
                  method is genuinely deferred)

A typo on a char method tells the author they have found a compiler bug and
invites them to edit `compile_method_call`. That is worse than a plain "no such
method", and it is squarely in the Mend loop's path: an LLM writing
character-level text processing gets "All checks passed" followed by an
instruction to patch the compiler.

FOR REFERENCE, the actual `char` surface is nearly empty -- `to_string()` works;
`is_digit`, `is_alpha`, `to_i64`, `as_i64`, `to_int`, `code_point`, `ord` all do
not exist. The numeric route is the cast `c as i64` (verified: `'7' as i64` ->
55), and `String.bytes()` gives the same. That is a workable surface, so this row
is about the MISSING CHECK, not about the missing methods; the methods are a
separate question nobody has to answer to fix this.

FIX SHAPE: route `char` and `bool` receivers through the same method-existence
check the other primitives already use, so an unknown method is rejected at
typecheck with the same "no method 'X' on type 'char'" wording. That also stops
the return type unifying freely, since the call no longer typechecks at all.

CORRECTED ON INVESTIGATION. The row's own measurements all reproduce verbatim at
HEAD -- the matrix, the free unification, both downstream messages. Three things
it did not have.

1. IT WAS NOT ONLY BOGUS NAMES THAT ESCAPED CHECKING. Every `char`/`bool` method
   call returned poison, CORRECT ones included, because the fall-through was
   unconditional. A genuine user impl:

       impl char { fn shout(self) -> String { return f"{self}!" } }
       let n: i64 = c.shout();     // typechecked clean, pre-fix

   So the receiver was not merely missing a lookup -- it had no return type at
   all, and every downstream check on the result was suppressed. That is why the
   fix is a ROUTING change rather than an added error: moving `char`/`bool` onto
   the numeric arm rejects the typo AND types the real call, and the second half
   was invisible from the row's probes (all of which used names that do not
   exist, so all of which were supposed to fail).

2. THE `char` SURFACE IS NOT NEARLY EMPTY. The row lists `to_string()` as the
   only thing that works. Probed exhaustively against `--interp`, it is:

       clone, to_string, is_alphabetic, is_numeric, is_alphanumeric,
       is_whitespace, is_uppercase, is_lowercase, is_ascii,
       to_ascii_uppercase, to_ascii_lowercase, to_digit(radix),
       eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, cmp

   and for `bool`: clone, to_string, eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, cmp.

   BOTH names the dogfood probed were near-misses, not absences: `is_alpha` is
   spelled `is_alphabetic`, and `is_digit` is spelled `is_numeric()` (Unicode
   predicate) or `to_digit(radix)`. `to_digit(10)` is precisely the "digit's
   numeric value" the dogfood set out to find -- it existed the whole time, on
   BOTH backends. The row's advice (`c as i64`) is correct but is the wrong
   answer to the question that was actually being asked: `'7' as i64` is 55, the
   codepoint; `'7'.to_digit(10)` is `Some(7)`, the value. Hence the hint wording
   -- the cast for the codepoint spellings, `to_digit(radix)` for `is_digit`.

   (While confirming that, a stale comment on `to_digit` in the same file --
   "codegen emits an honest 'not yet supported under `karac build`' error" --
   was corrected: codegen has lowered it inline via
   `build_checked_to_int_option` for some time. The comment outlived the
   lowering, and it sits directly on the surface this row's diagnostic now
   points authors at.)

3. ONE RESIDUAL, DELIBERATELY LEFT, AND IT IS NOT CHAR/BOOL-SPECIFIC. `cast`
   stays on the `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` exemption, so `v.cast()` is still
   check-green/run-red. Measured on all four receivers -- `i64`, `f64`, `char`,
   `bool` -- it is identical: `All checks passed`, then `method 'cast' not
   found`. So `char`/`bool` are now EXACTLY as tight as the numeric primitives,
   no tighter and no looser, which is the invariant this row was asking for.
   Closing `cast` is a separate cross-primitive change and is filed as
   B-2026-08-11-4; grepping `src/` and `runtime/src/` finds the string in that
   exemption list and NOWHERE else (the other hits are the `as` operator's
   internals -- `cast_value`, `build_signed_int_to_float` -- not a `.cast()`
   method), so the guard entry protects nothing.

VERIFICATION. Full non-llvm suite green (100 binaries, 0 failures), including
the 2183-test `tests/typechecker.rs` with the five new pins. Codegen E2E green
under `--features llvm`. The real char/bool surface above was re-probed
post-fix, name by name, and all 28 still typecheck and run.
investigation: 2026-08-11: found dogfooding a recursive-descent evaluator. Probed all primitive receivers with a deliberately nonsensical method name; only `char` and `bool` accept it. Confirmed the return type unifies with i64 / String / Vec[i64] at the same call. Confirmed the downstream messages for both receivers under `--interp` and `build`. Separately confirmed `c as i64` works, so the missing char methods are not a blocker and are deliberately NOT part of this row.

fix:
FIXED by 3dd2e4b, in `src/codegen/mono.rs`.

`compile_generic_call` now materializes a fresh heap Vec/String temp into the
caller's scope when the callee's param at that index is written as a bare type
param AND the callee's declared return type does not mention that type param
(the new `generic_param_is_bare_type_param` + `type_expr_mentions`). That is
the third of the three legs B-2026-07-11-35's comment names — the deep-copy
registration and per-monomorph struct-drop synthesis shipped; caller-side
fresh-owned-temp cleanup never did.

The return-type guard is load-bearing, not defensive. Without it the fix aborts
`e2e_return_owned_generic_param_no_double_free` and
`test_e2e_generic_forward_owned_string_param_no_double_free` with a real
`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`: `fn echo[T](x: T) -> T { x }` is
also a bare type param, and the caller's binding for the RESULT already owns
the buffer. The test is syntactic rather than a body walk because
`fn_returns_param` answers false for a forwarding tail — `pick[T](a: T, b: T)
-> T { id(a) }` and `nest[T](x: T) -> T { id(id(x)) }` both slip past it and
both were measured aborting. An unrecognized return shape answers "mentions
it", so the conservative direction is a leak, never a double free.

Regression test: `asan_generic_struct_method_bare_type_param_temp_arg_no_leak`
(`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`), 50 iterations so LSan sees accumulation, pushing
a temporary and a named binding side by side — the named one is the
double-free control. Verified to FAIL pre-fix. Full `--features llvm` suite
green (102 targets, 13399 passed, 0 failed).
title: a generic struct's method whose parameter is the TYPE PARAMETER leaks a fresh TEMPORARY argument's buffer -- `s.push([1i64,2i64])` on a `Stack[T]` leaks while the same call with a NAMED binding is clean. The row's original framing (a `Vec[T]` field's element resolution at drop, char/element-type specific) is REFUTED by measurement: the drop synthesis already resolves the monomorph correctly, and `Vec[String]` leaks too
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found dogfooding a generic container + trait-dispatch program
(`Stack[T]` instantiated at `i64`, `String`, and `Vec[i64]`, plus a
`describe_all[T: Describe]`). Output matched the oracle on all three backends;
LSan caught 16 bytes in 1 allocation that no oracle could see.

MINIMAL REPRODUCER -- 11 lines, leaks on `karac build`:

    struct Stack[T] { items: Vec[T] }
    impl[T] Stack[T] {
        fn new() -> Stack[T] { Stack { items: Vec.new() } }
        fn push(mut ref self, v: T) { self.items.push(v); }
        fn len(ref self) -> i64 { self.items.len() }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut s: Stack[Vec[i64]] = Stack.new();
        s.push([1i64, 2i64]);
        println(f"{s.len()}");
    }

    LeakSanitizer: 16 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s)

THE GENERIC IS REQUIRED, which is the discriminator worth having: the
non-generic twin with the SAME concrete field type is clean.

    struct Stack[T] { items: Vec[T] }   at T = Vec[i64]   LEAKS
    struct Holder { items: Vec[Vec[i64]] }                clean

WHICH MONOMORPHS LEAK, measured:

    Stack[i64]        clean      (scalar element owns no buffer)
    Stack[String]     clean      (the String monomorph IS resolved)
    Stack[Vec[i64]]   LEAKS      (the nested-Vec monomorph is not)

So this is not "generic struct drops are broken" -- the `String` monomorph works,
which is exactly what B-2026-07-15-11 and B-2026-07-15-24 fixed. The gap is the
NESTED container element: `Vec[T]` where `T` itself resolves to a `Vec`.

PER-ELEMENT PATTERN -- the whole buffer of every unconsumed element goes:

    push([3i64])                     clean   (1-element payload does not heap-allocate)
    push([1i64, 2i64])               16 B in 1 alloc
    push([1i64, 2i64, 3i64, 4i64])   32 B in 1 alloc
    push([1,2]) + push([3])          16 B in 1 alloc   (the [3] has no allocation to leak)

The 1-element case being clean is an allocation artifact, not a partial fix --
there is simply nothing on the heap for that element. Read the rule as "every
heap-allocated element buffer leaks".

CONSUMED ELEMENTS ARE FINE. Popping every element out before the container dies
is clean, because the popped `Some(v)` binding owns and frees the buffer:

    push([1,2]); push([3]); pop(); pop();   clean
    push([1,2]); push([3]); pop();          LEAKS (the un-popped one)

So the defect is squarely the container's DROP path, not `push` and not the
monomorph's construction.

UNBOUNDED IN A LOOP, and invisible without a sanitizer: the program is correct on
all three backends and prints the right answers. A long-running program that
builds a generic container of collections leaks one buffer per element per
iteration.

FIX SHAPE: `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_mono` already threads the concrete
`param -> arg` substitution so a `Vec[T]` field resolves its element before
picking a per-element drop -- that is what makes the `String` monomorph correct.
Extend that resolution to a `T` that is itself a container, so the element drop
becomes the recursive `emit_vec_drop_fn` rather than the buffer-only fast path.
Worth checking `Stack[Map[..]]`, `Stack[Set[..]]` and `Stack[VecDeque[..]]` in
the same pass rather than one dogfooding session at a time; `Vec` and `String`

=== RE-DIAGNOSED 2026-08-11 (not yet fixed) ===

The headline reproducer still reproduces EXACTLY as filed (16 bytes, 1 allocation, and 32 bytes at four elements). Everything this row concluded ABOUT it is wrong, and the FIX SHAPE it proposes would have been a no-op. Re-measured on a tree ~100 commits later; each row below is valgrind on `karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

REFUTED (1) -- "the nested-Vec monomorph is not resolved". It is. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`'s `FieldDrop::VecOrString` arm was instrumented to print the resolved element and whether a per-element drain fn was selected. Both monomorphs resolve and both select one:

    Stack[Vec[i64]]    PROBE struct=Stack field=0 elem="Vec_i64"  drain=true
    Stack[String]      PROBE struct=Stack field=0 elem="String"   drain=true

So the container's drop path is correct for the leaking case, and extending "that resolution to a `T` that is itself a container" — the row's FIX SHAPE — would have changed nothing.

REFUTED (2) -- "which monomorphs leak". The `String`-vs-`Vec` split was an artifact of how the two probes were WRITTEN, not of the element type. Holding the element type fixed and varying only the ARGUMENT FORM:

    Stack[Vec[i64]]    s.push([1i64, 2i64])            LEAKS 16 B
    Stack[Vec[i64]]    let v = ...; s.push(v)          clean
    Stack[Vec[String]] s.push(["a long string ..."])   LEAKS 24 B
    Stack[Vec[String]] let v = ...; s.push(v)          clean

`Vec[String]` leaks just as readily; the original `Stack[String]`-clean row used a string LITERAL, whose buffer is static.

REFUTED (3) -- "consumed elements are fine / pop-all is clean". It is not, and popping makes it WORSE: with two pushes, no pop leaks 16 B in 1 block, one pop leaks 24 B in 2, and popping BOTH leaks 40 B in 3. (Measured with a `pop` method added to the row's own `Stack`.) So the drop path is not where this lives, which is consistent with (1).

THE ACTUAL DISCRIMINATOR, isolated by holding the argument a fresh temporary and varying only the callee:

    generic struct's method, param is bare `T`   s.push([1i64,2i64])       LEAKS
    non-generic struct's method, param Vec[i64]  h.push_one([1i64,2i64])   clean
    free fn, param Vec[i64]                      take([1i64,2i64])         clean
    GENERIC free fn, param bare `T`              take([1i64,2i64])         clean
    builtin Vec.push                             items.push([1i64,2i64])   clean
    non-generic struct, same field type          h.items.push([...])       clean

So it needs ALL THREE: a generic STRUCT, a METHOD on it (a generic free function is clean), and a parameter typed as the bare type PARAMETER, called with a temporary. A named binding is clean because the move is tracked; the temporary's buffer is what goes.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE NEXT ATTEMPT. Look at the caller-side cleanup for the argument temporary of a mono'd generic method, not at drop synthesis. The container ends up owning a live buffer (the program prints correct answers and the element is readable), so the temp is either deep-copied with the original never freed, or moved with the caller's cleanup still armed on a slot it no longer owns — the pop numbers going UP rather than down suggests the former. Note the sibling family already in flight: B-2026-08-10-21 (the `UseAfterMove` defensive copy) and B-2026-08-07-12 (a heapless boxed envelope counting as heap for the caller-temp gate) are both about caller temporaries, and this may be a third facet of the same gate rather than its own mechanism.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE, deliberately: the sibling containers the row asks about (`Stack[Map[..]]`, `Stack[Set[..]]`, `Stack[VecDeque[..]]`) were measured CLEAN, but every one of those probes used a named binding, which is now known to be the clean arm — so they prove nothing and must be re-run with temporaries before anyone concludes the shape is Vec-specific.

=== FIXED 2026-08-11 ===

The re-diagnosis above was right about WHERE and wrong only in not going one step
further. Root cause, confirmed in the emitted IR:

A parameter written as the BARE TYPE PARAMETER (`fn push(mut ref self, v: T)`)
is resolved to its concrete type by the mono prologue
(`subst_monomorph_type_params`), which enters it in `owned_vecstr_params` —
B-2026-07-11-35's "push leg". That registration makes every RETAINING CONSUME
SITE in the mono body deep-copy the argument: `self.items.push(v)` emits a
`dcopy` malloc + memcpy and stores the COPY into the container. That is the
caller-retains convention, so the callee never frees the caller's buffer. A
fresh TEMPORARY argument had no owner in any frame and leaked; a NAMED binding
was clean only because its own let-drop still owned the original.

That is why every earlier conclusion pointed the wrong way. The container's
per-element drain is correct AND fires — it frees the callee's independent copy,
which is exactly why instrumenting it showed `drain=true` and changing it would
have been a no-op. Confirmed by allocation accounting: the leaking and clean
programs make the SAME number of allocations and differ by exactly one free.

B-2026-07-11-35's own comment names three legs — "paired with per-monomorph
struct-drop synthesis (so the now-deep-copied element buffers are freed at the
container's drop) and caller-side fresh-owned-temp cleanup". The first two
shipped; the third never did. This is the third leg.

FIX: `compile_generic_call` (mono.rs) materializes a fresh heap Vec temp into
the caller's scope when the callee's param at that index is written as a bare
type param, via the new `generic_param_is_bare_type_param`. Deliberately
narrower than `compile_call`'s #20 arm, which materializes EVERY fresh heap Vec
temp. Borrow forms (`ref T` / `mut ref T` / `mut Slice[T]`) are excluded — they
never enter `owned_vecstr_params`. Collection literals are admitted explicitly
because `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` is Call/MethodCall-only and the headline
reproducer passes a literal.

THE PASSTHROUGH GUARD, and the near-miss that produced it. The first version of
this fix gated only on "param is a bare type param" and was WRONG — it aborted
`e2e_return_owned_generic_param_no_double_free` and
`test_e2e_generic_forward_owned_string_param_no_double_free` with a real
`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. B-2026-07-14-12's note ("a `Vec[T]`
param temp MOVES/aliases into the callee's sink, so materializing it would add a
spurious second free") was RIGHT, and the reasoning that a bare-`T` gate could
not disturb it was wrong: `fn echo[T](x: T) -> T { x }` IS a bare type param,
and it hands the argument straight back out, so the caller's binding for the
RESULT already owns that buffer.

So the gate additionally requires that the callee's declared RETURN TYPE not
mention the same type param anywhere (`-> T`, `-> Vec[T]`, `-> Option[T]` all
reject). The test is deliberately syntactic rather than a body walk, because
`fn_returns_param` is NOT sufficient here: it recognizes a param reaching a
return site bare or inside an aggregate literal, so it answers false for a
FORWARDING tail — `fn pick[T](a: T, b: T) -> T { id(a) }` and
`fn nest[T](x: T) -> T { id(id(x)) }` both slip past it, and both were measured
aborting. An unrecognized return-type shape answers "mentions it", so the
conservative direction is a leak, never a double free. The leak this fix targets
lives on a `push`-shaped sink whose return type is unit, which the rule admits.

Worth stating plainly for the next person: `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` admits
`String` as well as `Vec` (both lower to `{ptr,len,cap}`), and
`string_typed_exprs` does NOT cover every String-valued expression — a String
temp produced by a nested generic call inside a mono is absent from it. So an
arm that means "Vec" cannot be spelled as "vec-struct shaped and not in
`string_typed_exprs`"; the return-type guard is what makes it safe, not the
String exclusion.

title: `v.cast()` on ANY primitive receiver passes `karac check` and then fails at run time -- `cast` sits on the PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS exemption but is not implemented on any backend, so the exemption guards nothing and only holds the hole open
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while closing B-2026-08-11-2, which routed `char`/`bool`
onto the same scalar-primitive arm the numeric receivers use. This is the one
hole that arm still has, and it predates that change on every receiver.

MEASURED, all four receivers, identical:

    i64    All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'i64'
    f64    All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'f64'
    char   All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'char'
    bool   All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'bool'

WHY IT SURVIVES. `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` exists for a real reason: the baked
stdlib `Ord`/`Eq` impls on primitives carry a `(self, other)`-shaped signature
that impl-table dispatch mis-counts (`a.cmp(b)` -> "expects 2 args, found 1"), so
those names are held off the dispatch path AND off the `NoMethodFound` error.
`cmp`/`eq`/`ne`/`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` all genuinely dispatch and need the
exemption. `cast` does not: grepping `src/` and `runtime/src/` finds the method
name in that list and nowhere else. The other `cast` hits are the `as` operator's
internals (`cast_value` in the interpreter, `build_signed_int_to_float` in
codegen, `cast_ctor` in the WGSL backend) -- none of them a `.cast()` method
dispatch arm. No test, example or `.kara` source calls `.cast()` either.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, both small:
  - the typo `v.cast()` is check-green/run-red, the class this family keeps
    closing;
  - a USER impl named `cast` on a primitive (`impl i64 { fn cast(self) -> f64 }`)
    is unreachable, because the exemption short-circuits before the impl lookup.

FIX SHAPE: drop `"cast"` from `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS`. It then takes the normal

that row is scoped to `char`/`bool`, and this changes behavior for every numeric
receiver too, so it wants its own commit and its own suite run.

title: EVERY parse-phase diagnostic raised inside an f-string interpolation hole is DISCARDED. Two consequences: (a) a hard syntax error degrades SILENTLY to literal text -- `println(f"typo={n.}")` passes `karac check` and prints `typo={n.}` on all three backends; (b) recoverable errors go unenforced -- `f"{takes(ref xs)}"` compiles clean while the identical call outside an f-string is a hard parse error.
tracker: src/parser/exprs.rs:771 -- `let result = crate::parse(&wrapper);` consumes only `result.program.items`; `result.errors` and `result.fix_edits` are dropped on the floor.
detail:
ROOT CAUSE (single site, both legs). An f-string interpolation hole is not parsed inline: `parse_primary`'s InterpolatedStringLit arm re-parses the hole's source by wrapping it in a synthetic function -- `format!("fn __interp__() {{ {}; }}", expr_src)` -- and calling `crate::parse(&wrapper)` recursively (exprs.rs:770-771). The returned `ParseResult` has three fields (`program`, `errors`, `fix_edits`); the arm reads ONLY `program.items`, pattern-matching out the single `StmtKind::Expr`. `errors` and `fix_edits` are never touched, so every diagnostic the nested parse raised is destroyed at the call site.

LEG A -- HARD parse error becomes SILENT literal text (the severe leg). When the hole does not parse, the `find_map` yields `None` and the `else` branch (exprs.rs:792) pushes `ParsedInterpolationPart::Text(format!("{{{}}}", raw))` -- i.e. the malformed source is re-emitted as the literal characters it was written as, braces included. `karac check` reports `All checks passed.` and `karac check --output=json` reports `"diagnostics":[]`. All three backends then agree on the wrong output:

    fn main() {
        let n = 3;
        println(f"good={n}");
        println(f"typo={n.}");
        println(f"trunc={n * }");
    }

  interp / JIT / AOT all print:
    good=3
    typo={n.}
    trunc={n * }

Because all three backends agree, the 3-backend differential oracle CANNOT see this class -- it is unanimous silent-wrong-output, found only by reading program output against an intended result.

LEG B -- RECOVERABLE parse errors go unenforced. When the nested parser recovers, a well-formed expression IS produced, so the program compiles and behaves correctly, but the diagnostic that should have rejected it is gone. The cleanest instance is the call-site borrow-marker rule (design.md Feature 4 Part 1.5, `ref` is never legal at call sites): `println(f"{takes(ref xs)}")` and the `mut ref` twin both pass `karac check` and run, while `let s = takes(ref xs);` is a hard parse error with a machine-applicable fix-it. So a documented language rule is enforced in statement position and unenforced one character inside an f-string.

BOUNDARY -- the loss is exactly the PARSE phase, no wider. Post-parse phases walk the real AST (whose spans `shift_expr_spans` has already rebased to absolute coordinates), so they are unaffected: an undefined name in a hole IS reported (`f"{nope()}"` -> `error[resolve]: undefined name 'nope', did you mean 'name'?`, correct line:column into the hole), and so is a typecheck error (`f"{if x { 1 }}"` -> `condition must be 'bool', found 'i64'`). Measured 6-shape in-hole vs outside-hole table, `karac check` first line each:

    expression        in-hole                       outside
    Vec<i64>.new()    All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected expression, found Dot
    x as              All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected type, found Semicolon
    [1,2              All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected RightBracket, found Semicolon
    x.0.              All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected field name or tuple index after '.'
    foo(,)            All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected expression, found Comma
    if x { 1 }        error[typecheck]: ...         error[typecheck]: ...        <- parses fine, so survives

5/6 swallowed; the only survivor is the one that is not a parse error.

MEND-LOOP CONSEQUENCE. `karac check --output=json` emits `"diagnostics":[]` for Leg A, so the Mend loop has nothing to feed back and `karac fix` has nothing to apply -- a typo inside an interpolation hole is unrepairable by the AI-first path, not merely unreported. Leg B compounds it: the nested `fix_edits` map is discarded alongside `errors`, so even after B-2026-08-10-2 taught the marker diagnostics to emit a deletion edit, that edit cannot reach `cmd_fix` from inside a hole.

FIX SHAPE. The rebasing machinery this needs already exists and is already applied to the expression on the success path. `span_visitor::shift_expr_spans(&mut e, offset, line, column)` computes `offset_delta = hole_offset - PREFIX_LEN` and `col_delta = hole_column - (PREFIX_LEN + 1)` where `PREFIX_LEN = "fn __interp__() { ".len()` = 18, then maps line 1 of the wrapper onto `hole_line`. The same two deltas rebase a `ParseError`'s span and a `fix_edits` `SpanKey`/`TextEdit`. So: (1) rebase `result.errors` with those deltas and append them to the enclosing parser's error list; (2) rebase and merge `result.fix_edits` into the enclosing `ParseResult`'s map; (3) on the `None` arm, stop falling back to `Text` -- an unparseable hole must be an error, since with (1) in place the nested parse has already produced the precise diagnostic and the `Text` fallback would only re-hide it. Guard against double-reporting: the wrapper's own trailing `;` and closing brace must not manufacture spurious errors for a hole that parsed cleanly.

NOT a duplicate of the prior f-string entries: B-2026-06-09-1 was the LEXER's hole EXTRACTOR miscounting braces/quotes (which hole text is extracted); this is the PARSER discarding the result of re-parsing an already-correctly-extracted hole. B-2026-07-15-12 / -07-12-5 / -06-14-15 are codegen/auto-par behaviour on holes that parsed fine.

CONFIRMED AS FILED and fixed with the prescribed shape. The row's diagnosis was
exact -- single site, both legs, correct fix in three parts -- so this is a
confirmation rather than a correction. Two things worth adding.

1. THE `fix_edits` HALF HAS A TRAP THE ROW DID NOT NAME, and the first attempt
   at this fix fell into it. The map is keyed by the DIAGNOSTIC's span, not by
   the edit's own range: `record_call_site_mode_deletion` deletes the `ref`
   token while keying the entry on the error's span. Rebasing the edit and then
   deriving a fresh key from it therefore compiles, merges, and silently loses
   the association -- the diagnostic comes back with `replacement: null` while
   the identical construct outside a hole carries its edit. Key and edit must be
   rebased SEPARATELY. Caught by diffing `--output=json` for the same program in
   and out of a hole, which is the check worth repeating for any future
   edit-plumbing change.

   End to end in-hole after the fix: diagnostic -> `{'offset': 121, 'length': 4,
   'text': ''}` -> `karac fix` applies it -> `println(f"{takes(xs)}")` ->
   `All checks passed`.

2. NO TEST DEPENDED ON THE SILENT FALLBACK. The concern with removing it was
   that some test or example leaned on a malformed hole degrading to literal

title: A bare TYPE NAME in call position -- `i64(42)`, `F64(1.5)`, `bool(1)`, `String("hi")`, `Vec(1)`, or a named-field user struct `P(1)` -- is accepted by EVERY checking phase, then breaks downstream: the interpreter panics on an `unreachable!` (or raises its own 'This is a compiler bug' internal error) while the compiled backends silently evaluate it to `0`.
tracker: src/interpreter/eval_call.rs:2101 (the `unreachable!` whose message already says 'the typechecker accepted a non-callable callee'); the missing rejection belongs in the typechecker's call-callee resolution.
detail:
`karac check` reports `All checks passed.` for a bare type name applied to arguments. Nothing downstream can honour it, and the three backends fail three different ways -- none of them a diagnostic.

    fn main() {
        let a = i64(42);
        println(f"val={a}");
    }

    karac check       All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  runtime error: internal: name 'i64' resolved but has no binding at run time.
                        This is a compiler bug (the resolver should have rejected or bound it)
                        -- please report it with the source.   at u.kara:3:13
    karac run (JIT)   val=0
    karac build (AOT) val=0

Measured matrix (`karac check` was `All checks passed.` for every row):

    expression       interpreter                          JIT / AOT
    i64(42)          runtime error: internal (compiler bug)  prints val=0
    bool(1)          runtime error: internal (compiler bug)  prints val=0
    String("hi")     runtime error: internal (compiler bug)  codegen refuses (struct-Display msg)
    F64(1.5)         PANIC, unreachable! eval_call.rs:2101   prints val=0
    F32(1.5)         PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    F16(1.5)         PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    Bf16(1.5)        PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    Vec(1)           PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    P(1)  (struct P { x: i64 } -- NAMED fields, not a tuple struct)
                     PANIC, unreachable!                     -

The panic text is self-diagnosing: "call target at 2:28 was Value::TypeVal (not Function, not an enum-variant constructor); either an interpreter codepath produced the wrong variant or the typechecker accepted a non-callable callee". It is the second disjunct. The typechecker resolves the callee to a type and then types the call without ever asking whether that type has a callable (tuple-struct / enum-variant) constructor form.

THE SILENT LEG IS THE WORSE ONE. On JIT and AOT the argument is simply discarded and the binding takes `0`; there is no diagnostic at any stage. `let a = i64(42); println(f"val={a}")` prints `val=0` on both compiled backends. A user who writes a C/Java-style conversion cast gets a zero, not an error.

REACHABILITY -- this is not an exotic typo. It is the shape a user lands on by following the compiler's own advice. `max(1.5, 2.5)` is correctly rejected with a diagnostic that says "use the total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`)"; `F64.from` does not exist (B-2026-08-11-8), and `F64(1.5)` is the next thing anyone tries -- and it is the row that PANICS the interpreter.

STRUCTURAL PRECEDENT: B-2026-08-02-5 (tuple-element assignment targets accepted by every checking phase, unimplemented downstream) is the same shape -- a construct that no phase rejects and no backend implements. Same fix discipline applies: reject at the typechecker, since neither backend can be made to mean anything sensible here.

CONFIRMED AS FILED -- the matrix reproduces exactly -- with the ROOT CAUSE
CORRECTED and one leg added.

1. THE CAUSE IS NOT WHERE THE TRACKER POINTS. Not the interpreter's
   `unreachable!`, and not "the typechecker's call-callee resolution": it is
   `resolve_identifier_type`'s closing fallback, whose comment reads "likely a
   name the resolver already handled -- return Error silently (resolver already
   reported it)". True for a typo; FALSE for a type name, which resolves
   perfectly well and simply is not a value. `infer_call` then took its silent
   `Type::Error` arm rather than the `NotCallable` arm immediately below it --
   the rejection the row wanted was already there, unreachable.

2. A LEG THE ROW DID NOT HAVE: the same fallback made `let x = i64;` pass, with
   no call involved. Any fix confined to call position would have left it.

3. THE LEGAL SET IS SMALLER THAN THE ROW ASSUMES. It refers to the
   "(tuple-struct / enum-variant) constructor form", but KARA HAS NO TUPLE
   STRUCTS -- `struct T(i64)` is a parse error. Enum variants and distinct
   types are the whole list, which is what makes a blanket rejection safe.

4. THE REMEDY HAD TO BE PER-FAMILY, and the ordering is load-bearing. The baked
   types are registered in `env.structs` too, so keying on that first told
   authors to write `F64 { … }` and `Vec { … }`, neither of which exists.
   `F64`/`F32` -> `.from(x)` (which now exists, B-2026-08-11-8, and is exactly
   the remedy this row's REACHABILITY paragraph said was missing); numeric
   primitives -> the cast; `String` -> `String.from` / `to_string`; prelude
   containers -> `.new(…)`; a user struct -> a literal naming a real field.

TWO COLLATERAL PATHS, both found by the suite rather than by inspection, and
both now pinned because they are where a future refactor reintroduces this:

  - `resolve_path_type` falls back to `resolve_identifier_type` on a path's
    FIRST segment before later machinery runs -- resource dispatch resolves
    that way, so erroring there rejected `RandomSource.next()` outright (two
    repl tests). The silent `Error` is load-bearing for that caller.
  - a field-access base must keep its silent `Type::Error` (`i64.NONEXISTENT`),
    which `test_primitive_const_unknown_silent_fall_through` already pins as
    deliberate; "is a type, not a function" is also the wrong wording there.

title: `Vec[f64].sort()` bypasses the `Ord` gate that design.md § Float semantics REQUIRES -- the spec's own verbatim counter-example compiles. With a NaN present, `sort()` silently leaves the Vec UNSORTED (all three backends agree), so a percentile/statistics program yields wrong answers with no diagnostic. `.sorted()`, `.max()`, `.min()` and `.contains()` on `Vec[f64]` are ungated the same way, while `Map[f64,_]`, `Set[f64]`, `SortedSet[f64]` and free `max(f64,f64)` all gate correctly.
tracker: src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs:1436 -- the Vec `"sort" | "reverse"` arm calls `expect_no_args` and returns `Type::Unit` with NO element-type Ord check; the Slice twin at :1164 checks mutability only. Working gate to copy: stdlib_map.rs:516/633 (SortedSet/SortedMap element+key Ord).
detail:
design.md § Float semantics (around line 2263) is explicit and gives this exact example:

    let scores: Vec[f64] = [1.0, f64.NAN, 2.0];
    scores.sort()                 # compile error: f64 does not implement Ord
    scores.map(F64.from).sort()   # OK

The first line compiles. The spec's stated rule -- `f32`/`f64` implement `PartialEq`/`PartialOrd` but NOT `Eq`/`Ord`/`Hash`, so "`f64` cannot be used ... in any context requiring `Ord`" -- is enforced in some contexts and not others.

GATED CORRECTLY (measured, `karac check` first line):
    Map[f64, String]   error[typecheck]: key type does not implement `Hash + Eq`
    Set[f64]           error[typecheck]: element type does not implement `Hash + Eq`
    SortedSet[f64]     error[typecheck]: element type does not implement `Ord`
    max(1.5, 2.5)      error[typecheck]: trait bound `T: Ord` is not satisfied ...
                       (with the good note pointing at the F64 wrapper)

NOT GATED (all report `All checks passed.`):
    Vec[f64].sort()      <- design.md's verbatim counter-example
    Vec[f64].sorted()
    Vec[f64].max()       <- note the asymmetry: free `max(a,b)` IS rejected
    Vec[f64].min()
    Vec[f64].contains(x) <- an Eq context; f64 has PartialEq only

So the machinery exists and is wired up for the Sorted* containers and for the generic trait-bound solver; the Vec method arms just never consult it. The `max`/`v.max()` split is the sharpest instance -- the same ordering question is rejected as a free call and accepted as a method.

THE HARM IS A SILENT WRONG ANSWER, not just a missing message. Because `value_compare` is not a total order over NaN, `sort_by` is free to leave elements where they are, and it does -- observed identical on interp, JIT and AOT:

    let nan = 0.0 / 0.0;
    let mut b: Vec[f64] = [3.0, nan, 1.0, 2.0];
    b.sort();
    // prints: 3 NaN 1 2      <- COMPLETELY unsorted; even 3/1/2 are untouched

    let e: Vec[f64] = [5.0, nan, 4.0, 6.0];
    let f = e.sorted();
    // prints: 5 NaN 4 6

    let c: Vec[f64] = [3.0, nan, 1.0];
    c.max() -> Some(3)   c.min() -> Some(1)     <- NaN silently skipped

No panic, no diagnostic, no divergence between backends -- so the 3-backend differential oracle cannot see this either. The realistic failure is exactly the program this was found in: a latency-percentile reporter that sorts its samples and reads p50/p90/p99 off the sorted Vec. One NaN in the input (a division by a zero count, a failed parse defaulted to `0.0/0.0`) and every percentile is read from unsorted data, silently.

FIX SHAPE. Add the element-type Ord check to the Vec/Slice `sort`/`sorted` arms and the Ord/Eq checks to `max`/`min`/`contains`, reusing the SortedSet/SortedMap diagnostic text (which already names the `F64` fix). Note the ordering dependency: the diagnostic and design.md both direct users to `F64.from(x)`, which does not exist -- B-2026-08-11-8 must land first or the gate will send users into a dead end, and the obvious next thing they type (`F64(1.5)`) panics the interpreter (B-2026-08-11-6).

JUDGEMENT CALL worth recording: `contains` is the one leg where rejection is arguable, since `contains` needs only `PartialEq`, which f64 does have. The spec's blanket wording ("not `Eq`") says reject; a narrower reading says allow. Whoever fixes this should decide deliberately rather than inherit it -- `sort`/`sorted`/`max`/`min` are not ambiguous. -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in e51d3e7, PARTIALLY AND ON PURPOSE; the residual is B-2026-08-11-15. -- PREMISE RE-VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY rather than inherited, and it is worse than filed: `[3.0, NaN, 1.0, 2.0].sort()` does not merely fail to place the NaN, it returns the sequence COMPLETELY UNTOUCHED (`3 NaN 1 2`) — the 3/1/2 do not move either — identically on interpreter and compiled backends. NaN-free float data sorts correctly, which is why this survived: the failure needs a NaN to appear. (Probed through a generic `fn gsort[T](v: mut ref Vec[T])`, which incidentally documents a HOLE IN THE GATE: the element type at a generic call site is a TypeParam, so `Ord` passes and monomorphization does not re-check. A `Vec[f64]` laundered through a generic sorts unchecked. Narrow, but real, and it is the shape a stdlib helper would have.) -- WHAT WAS GATED AND WHAT WAS NOT, since this departs from the filed fix shape. Gated: `sort`, `sorted`, `binary_search` (the last NOT named in the row — found ungated while fixing its siblings; binary search over unordered data is meaningless). Not gated: `reverse` (compares nothing; it shared a match arm with `sort`, which is part of why the check was never added), `contains`, and `max`/`min`. -- THE `contains` JUDGEMENT CALL, which the row explicitly asked the fixer to make deliberately: ALLOW. It needs only `PartialEq`, which design.md says `f64` does implement, and measured behaviour is IEEE-correct and identical across backends — it finds elements positioned after a NaN, `contains(NaN)` is correctly `false` (NaN != NaN), and `-0.0` finds `0.0`. There is no silent wrong answer to prevent, so gating it would break correct code for no soundness gain. The spec's blanket 'not Eq' wording is about Eq/Ord/Hash CONTEXTS; a linear scan is not one. -- WHY `max`/`min` WERE DEFERRED rather than gated: they ARE broken (NaN first makes BOTH answer NaN; NaN in the middle is silently skipped), but every remedy measured worse than the disease, and shipping a gate whose advice dead-ends is exactly what B-2026-08-11-8 was filed for. `Vec[F64].max()` typechecks only if the iterator arm's numeric-or-String test is widened, and then FAILS IN CODEGEN ('no handler for method max'), trading a wrong answer for a run-vs-build gap; `Stats.max(v)` is itself wrong and BACKEND-DIVERGENT on the same input. Both measurements are in B-2026-08-11-15. -- THE GATE KEYS ON FLOATS, NOT ON `!type_supports_ord`, and that distinction is load-bearing: `type_supports_ord` is STRICTER than what the sort comparators actually implement, because `Vec` is a baked stdlib struct with no `#[derive(Ord)]`, so it answers false for `Vec[Vec[String]]` — whose sort is supported and tested (B-2026-06-30-15's recursive lexicographic comparator). The first version gated on it and broke that ASAN fixture. Scoping to 'element type reaches an IEEE float' (recursing through tuples, arrays, slices, Vec/Option, refs) cannot reject a sort that works today. Anyone widening this gate to other non-Ord element types must first check what the comparators support, not what the predicate says. -- ORDERING DEPENDENCY HONOURED: the diagnostic prescribes `F64.from(x)` and a copy-pasteable `xs.iter().map(F64.from).collect()`, both verified end-to-end on all three backends. That remedy only became real in B-2026-08-11-8 (d8ddc56), landed first for exactly this reason.

Checked design.md, which specifies the sort call as a compile error verbatim. Built the 9-row gated/ungated matrix above, then measured NaN behaviour on all three backends (identical) to establish the harm is silent wrong output rather than a missing diagnostic.
