fix:
FIXED by 3d0064f, in three parts, in the order the row prescribed:
codegen first, then the typecheck widening, then the gate.

1. `src/codegen/method_call.rs` — the total-order wrappers are admitted to the
   iterator `max`/`min` arm's element test and to `try_compile_iter_chain_reduce`.
   The reduce gate keys on `is_trivially_copyable_te`, a PRIMITIVE-name list
   shared by 36 call sites, so it was NOT widened: a new
   `is_total_float_wrapper_te` (`src/codegen/assoc_call.rs`) is OR'd in at the
   one site that needs it. A `{ float }` wrapper is trivially copyable in the
   sense that gate cares about (no heap payload to double-free in the synthetic
   `Some(acc) => Some(f(acc, x))` match), but that is not the question the other
   35 callers ask, and answering it for them would have been a silent change to
   every one of those sites.

2. `src/typechecker/stdlib_iter.rs` — the numeric-or-String element test admits
   `F32`/`F64`/`F16`/`Bf16`.

3. The gate itself, plus a per-method harm clause in `require_ord_element`
   (`src/typechecker/derives.rs`): quoting `sort()`'s "leaves the sequence
   completely unsorted" under `max`/`min` would describe a symptom those methods
   do not have.

WHY IT IS LANDABLE NOW AND WAS NOT IN -7. -7 withdrew this gate because the
remedy dead-ended; the missing precondition was not only codegen but
B-2026-08-11-13. The wrapper's total order is IEEE totalOrder, which is
SIGN-SENSITIVE, and nothing at source level chooses a NaN's sign — measured
before -13 landed, `Vec[F64].sorted()` on `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` gave `NaN,1,3` under
the interpreter and `1,3,NaN` under both compiled backends, because interp
produced 0xFFF8... and compiled produced 0x7FF8... (confirmed via `to_bits()`).
Gating on top of that would have swapped a silent wrong answer for a NEW
run-vs-build gap. -13's construction-side canonicalization removed it, and
`max`/`min` inherit the fix.

MEASURED, interp / JIT / AOT, all three identical: `[3.0, 1.0, 2.0]` as
`Vec[F64]` gives max 3 / min 1; `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` AND `[3.0, NaN, 1.0]` both
give max NaN / min 1 — position-independent, which is the property the wrapper
buys and the raw `f64` path could not provide. On raw `f64` the same three
inputs gave 3 / NaN / 3, i.e. the answer moved with the NaN.

ONE CLAIM IN THIS ROW WAS WRONG, and one thing I first recorded as a
correction to it was itself wrong -- both settled by measurement:

  * The row's predicted codegen failure ("no handler for method 'max' on
    non-identifier receiver") never occurs. Admitting the wrapper at typecheck
    produces a LOUD, correct deferral from `Iterator.reduce()` instead, because
    the reduce lowering gates on trivially-copyable elements. That is the gate
    this fix opens, and it is a different site from the one the row names.

  * The row's `Vec[f64].max()` spelling is CORRECT and I briefly recorded that
    it was not. Mid-investigation I concluded "`Vec.max()` does not exist on
    either backend" from a single probe that failed on both. It does exist:
    `let fs: Vec[f64] = [1.5, 2.5, 0.5]; println(fs.max().unwrap())` answers
    2.5 on interpreter, JIT and AOT alike (verified with the gate temporarily
    disabled), and a shipped ASAN fixture has been compiling that exact form
    all along. What my probe actually hit is a SEPARATE gap, filed as its own
    row: the direct-Vec terminal desugar is POSITION-SENSITIVE, so
    `println("max=" + fs.max().unwrap().to_string())` fails on both backends
    with an error that blames `max` itself. Generalizing from one expression
    shape's misleading message is what produced the wrong correction; the fix
    was to vary the shape rather than trust the diagnostic's noun.

The `Stats.max(v)` divergence the row folded in is NOT fixed here and is not the
remedy the diagnostic names. Re-measured on all three backends it is also
sharper than recorded: interp 3, JIT NaN, AOT 3 — the JIT is the outlier, not
"interpreter vs compiled". The row speculated the fix might be shared with
max/min ("one total-order float reduce that both surfaces call"); it is not —
this fix routes through the iterator reduce path and does not touch `Stats` —
so per the row's own instruction it is split out rather than closed here.

Tests: `test_float_iter_max_min_are_gated_and_wrapper_is_accepted`
(tests/typechecker.rs) asserts gate AND remedy together, since a gate whose
remedy stops compiling is a regression a rejection-only test reports green on;
`test_e2e_iter_max_min_over_total_order_wrapper` (tests/codegen.rs) pins the
NaN-first / NaN-middle agreement.

KNOWN REMAINDER, deliberately not worked around: chained
`.max().unwrap().value` still fails in codegen ("cannot resolve field 'value'
on this receiver"). It is PRE-EXISTING and unrelated — it reproduces with a
plain `struct P { x: i64 }` and an `Option[P]`, no iterator or wrapper involved
— so it is filed separately rather than papered over. The remedy is fully
usable via a `let` binding or a `match`, both verified on all three backends,
and the E2E test spells it the `let` way for exactly this reason.
tracker: `max`/`min` on a float sequence: the numeric-or-String element test and the (withdrawn) Ord gate in typechecker/stdlib_iter.rs `"max" | "min"`; the missing codegen dispatcher arm for max/min over a wrapper struct; and Stats.max/min in the interpreter vs try_compile_stats_call
title: `Vec[f64].max()` / `.min()` return an ORDER-DEPENDENT element instead of erroring, and there is currently no working remedy to point users at -- which is why B-2026-08-11-7 gated `sort`/`sorted`/`binary_search` but deliberately left these alone. Measured: `[3.0, NaN, 1.0].max()` silently skips the NaN and answers 3, while `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` makes BOTH `max()` and `min()` answer NaN -- the result depends on where the NaN sits. The two obvious remedies are both broken: (a) `Vec[F64].max()`, the wrapper -7's own sort gate prescribes, is rejected at typecheck by the iterator arm's numeric-or-String element test, and when that test is widened to admit the wrapper it then FAILS IN CODEGEN with 'no handler for method max on non-identifier receiver' -- i.e. it would trade a wrong answer for a run-vs-build gap; (b) `Stats.max(v)`, the f64-shaped alternative, is itself wrong AND BACKEND-DIVERGENT -- on `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` the interpreter answers 3 and the JIT answers NaN. Fixing (a) is the real task: add the codegen max/min-over-wrapper arm, then widen the element test, then gate. That makes `F64` a COMPLETE answer instead of a partial one.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-11-7 (fixed in e51d3e7) when the gate for these two was written and then WITHDRAWN. Recorded in full because the withdrawal was a judgement call with measurements behind it, not an oversight, and because re-deriving those measurements is the expensive part. -- WHY NOT JUST GATE THEM. The gate is one line and the bug is real, but a diagnostic is only worth shipping if the fix it names exists and works -- that is the entire lesson of B-2026-08-11-8, where design.md and the compiler both prescribed `F64.from(x)` for two months while it did not exist, and the natural next guess (`F64(1.5)`) panicked the interpreter. Gating max/min today would recreate that one row later: the user follows the advice to `F64`, and either typecheck rejects it or codegen does. Meanwhile the status quo is at least CONSISTENT across backends and correct on NaN-free data, which is the overwhelmingly common case -- so gating without a remedy would break far more working code than it protects. -- THE STATS DIVERGENCE IS ITS OWN BUG and is arguably worse than the max/min one, since a run-vs-build split cannot be reasoned about from the source at all. It is recorded here rather than filed separately only because the fix is likely shared (one total-order float reduce that both surfaces call); split it out if that turns out not to be true. -- RELATED: B-2026-08-11-13 (the wrapper's own NaN ordering depends on the NaN's sign bit, which no source construct controls) should probably land FIRST, since it decides what 'correct' even means for a NaN-bearing max/min over `F64`. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 shared cloud container; the NaN-sign behaviour that drives the Stats split is architecture-specific, though the order-dependence of max/min is not.

fix: d8ddc56 (three parts: an ordinary Kāra `impl <W> { fn from }` in each of runtime/stdlib/{f32,f64,f16,bf16}.kara makes the call typecheck; a codegen intercept in assoc_call.rs BUILDS the wrapper struct, because codegen does not route path-calls to baked stdlib impls and the call was otherwise reaching the unknown-callee tail as a const i64 0; and type_name_of_expr in expr_ops.rs types the call-result temp so a direct `F64.from(x).value` chain resolves its field. Display is a fourth part: one seam in build_struct_display_parts covering both println and f-strings.)
title: `F64.from(x)` / `F32.from(x)` -- the total-order wrapper constructor that design.md AND the compiler's own `T: Ord` diagnostic both name as THE fix for `f64` in an Ord/Eq/Hash context -- is unimplemented: `no associated function 'from' on type 'F64'`. Every spelling a user would try next fails, and one of them (`F64(1.5)`) panics the interpreter.
tracker: the `F64`/`F32` stdlib surface; the diagnostic that prescribes it is the `T: Ord` bound message (it renders "use the total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`)"), and design.md § Float semantics line ~2264 writes `scores.map(F64.from).sort()  # OK`.
detail:
design.md § Float semantics introduces `F32`/`F64` as the sanctioned total-order wrappers -- "Implement `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash` -- usable as `Map`/`Set` keys, in `TreeMap`, and anywhere `T: Ord` is required" -- and shows construction as `F64.from`:

    scores.map(F64.from).sort()  # OK

The compiler agrees in prose. `max(1.5, 2.5)` is rejected with a genuinely good note: "`f64` is not totally ordered (IEEE-754 NaN), so it does not implement `Ord` -- use the total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`) in `Ord`/`Eq`/`Hash` contexts, or drop the `Ord` bound if you only need arithmetic".

Then the prescribed call does not exist. Measured, every construction spelling:

    F64.from(1.5)   error[typecheck]: no associated function 'from' on type 'F64'
    F64.new(1.5)    error[typecheck]: no associated function 'new' on type 'F64'
    F64.of(1.5)     error[typecheck]: no associated function 'of' on type 'F64'
    1.5 as F64      error[typecheck]: cannot cast 'f64' to 'F64'
    F64(1.5)        All checks passed  -- then PANICS the interpreter (B-2026-08-11-6)
                                       and evaluates to 0 on JIT/AOT

So there is NO working way to construct an `F64` from an `f64`. The type is reachable enough to annotate (`let mut v: Vec[F64] = ...`, `Map[F64, String]` both typecheck) but not to populate.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE MISSING METHOD. It makes a correct diagnostic actively harmful: the user hits the (correctly-firing) `Ord` gate, follows the advice verbatim, hits a second error, and the most natural next guess is the one shape that crashes the compiler. For the Mend loop this is worse than silence -- `karac fix` and any LLM reading the diagnostic are steered toward an API that is not there, so the repair attempt cannot converge.

Second-order Display gap noticed while probing and worth folding into the same slice: with `F64` values obtained any way at all, `f"{v[0]}"` on a `Vec[F64]` element reports "type 'F64' does not implement Display; cannot interpolate in f-string". If `F64` is to be the recommended wrapper it needs Display too, or the recommendation costs users their `println`s.

FIX SHAPE: implement `F64.from(f64) -> F64` and `F32.from(f32) -> F32` (plus the inverse accessor to get the bits back out as `f64`/`f32`), give both `Display`, and keep the bit-level total order design.md specifies (`-Inf < ... < -0.0 == 0.0 < ... < +Inf < NaN`, `NaN == NaN` true). Sequencing: this should land BEFORE B-2026-08-11-7's Ord gate, or that gate will start rejecting `Vec[f64].sort()` and point users at an API that still does not exist. -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in d8ddc56. WHAT IT ACTUALLY TOOK, vs what the row predicted. The row's fix shape asked for `from`, the inverse accessor, and Display. The inverse accessor ALREADY existed and needed nothing — unwrap is the plain field read `x.value`, verified on all three backends — so the round trip is `F64.from(v).value`. The wrapper itself was also already built (B-2026-07-22-11 shipped total-order compare, Map/Set keys, sort and `.value` across all three backends), which made this a much smaller slice than the row reads: the type was reachable enough to annotate and to construct via the `F64 { value: x }` STRUCT LITERAL, just not via the constructor the docs and diagnostics name. -- THE INTERPRETER ALREADY IMPLEMENTED `F64.from`: eval_call.rs has carried a hardcoded `"F32.from"`/`"F64.from"`/`"F16.from"`/`"Bf16.from"` arm for a long time, and tests/interpreter.rs has carried PASSING tests for it (test_f64_from_constructor et al). They passed because that harness's `run()` bypasses the typechecker, which is exactly what hid the bug: the feature worked and was tested, but no CHECKED program could reach it. A test that skips a gate cannot see a gate-shaped bug. -- DISPLAY RENDERING WAS A REAL CHOICE, recorded because it is not recoverable from the code. Both `println(x)` and `f"{x}"` rejected every wrapper, so the type the compiler RECOMMENDS for Ord contexts was unprintable, and no rendering was reachable — meaning the `F64(3.14)` form in the interpreter's `Display for Value` had never been observable from checked Kāra. It now renders as the bare inner float (`3.14`), on the reasoning that the wrapper is an ORDERING CONTRACT, not a distinct textual form: a percentile report that wraps its samples to sort them should print numbers, and `Vec[F64]` should print `[1, 2, 3]`. Java's `Double` makes the same choice. Three interpreter tests asserted the old form and were updated; because the form was unreachable, this changes no reachable behaviour. -- KNOWN ADJACENT LIMITATION, pre-existing and NOT wrapper-specific: Display of a struct in a non-place position (`println(v[0])`, `f"{F64.from(x)}"`) is a standing codegen restriction for ALL user structs — 'bind a struct literal or call result to a `let` first'. Wrappers inherit it. -- FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, filed separately: B-2026-08-11-13 (the wrapper's NaN ordering diverges across backends and optimization levels — directly relevant to B-2026-08-11-7, which steers users to `F64` for exactly the NaN case) and B-2026-08-11-14 (design.md says `-0.0 == 0.0`, every backend implements `-0.0 < 0.0`). Also noticed: design.md's example writes `scores.map(F64.from)`, but the compiler requires an explicit `.iter()` and says so in a good diagnostic; the spec line is stale.
investigation: 2026-08-11 (hunt, domain 6 -- numeric/f64 dogfood). Found by following B-2026-08-11-7's own remedy: after establishing that `Vec[f64].sort()` should be rejected per spec, I wrote the spec-blessed alternative `scores.map(F64.from).sort()` to confirm it works, and it does not compile. Probed five construction spellings and the Display path. Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix:
FIXED by 284d44a4, by canonicalizing NaN at CONSTRUCTION in all three backends --
the row's own preferred shape ("doing it at construction is the stronger
invariant"), chosen over normalizing in the comparison key.

1. Codegen: `canonicalize_wrapper_nan` (src/codegen/assoc_call.rs) emits
   `select(fcmp uno x, x, <canonical quiet NaN>, x)` and runs inside
   `compile_total_order_wrapper_from`.
2. Codegen: `F64 { value: x }` previously fell through the GENERIC struct-init
   path and stored raw bits. It is now intercepted at the top of
   `compile_struct_init` and routed through that same
   `compile_total_order_wrapper_from`, so the literal and `.from` are ONE
   lowering rather than two that can drift apart.
3. Interpreter: `canonical_wrapper_f64` / `_f32` (src/interpreter/helpers.rs)
   applied at both producers -- the four `X.from` arms in eval_call.rs and the
   struct-literal arm in interpreter.rs.

The canonical value is spelled as an explicit bit pattern on both sides
(0x7FF8000000000000 / 0x7FC00000, plus the 16-bit siblings) rather than
`f64::NAN`, so the interpreter and the compiled backends are provably the same
bits instead of the same by convention.

WHY CONSTRUCTION AND NOT THE COMPARISON KEY. The key-side fix is narrower per
site but has MORE sites -- cmp, eq, the two sort-key paths in vec_method.rs, and
the Map/Set hash -- and a site that forgot would fail SILENTLY: `eq` calls two
keys equal while `hash` sends them to different buckets. Construction gives one
invariant ("no wrapper ever holds a non-canonical NaN") that every consumer
inherits, at two sites per backend. The producer set is closed and small, which
is what makes that tractable: there is no `F64.NAN` constant (it does not
exist -- see B-2026-08-11-14) and the wrapper has no arithmetic, so `X.from` and
the struct literal are the ONLY ways to make one.

`-0.0` is deliberately NOT normalized. Unlike a NaN's sign it is a distinct,
well-defined point of the total order that all three backends already agreed on,
with a pin (`test_e2e_total_order_float_wrappers`) asserting it.

WHAT THE ROW UNDER-STATED. It reported a 3-way split; measured here it is 4-way,
and the extra leg is the sharpest evidence: the default `-O2` AOT build and
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` disagree on the SAME source, because -O2 inlines the call and
constant-folds the division while -O0 leaves a real one. Two further findings the
row did not have, both worse than a split:
  - `Vec[F64].sort()` under the JIT returned NaN at BOTH ENDS (`NaN -1 1 NaN`).
    That IS correctly sorted under raw totalOrder -- -NaN precedes -Infinity,
    +NaN follows +Infinity -- and completely unreadable, since both print `NaN`.
  - A two-NaN `Map[F64, i64]` had a different LEN per backend (interp 1, JIT 2,
    AOT -O2 1, AOT -O0 2), so a collection silently gained or lost an entry
    depending on how the program was run.

MEASUREMENT TRAP WORTH RECORDING. The first codegen pin PASSED pre-fix. At -O2
LLVM folds both the constant NaN and the nominally-runtime one to the same
positive NaN, so AOT agreed with the correct answer by luck, and the bug is only
visible where a NaN genuinely survives to run time. The pin now sources its zero
from `env.args().len()`, which the optimizer cannot see through; that made it red
at every opt level. A codegen E2E test that exercises constant-foldable
arithmetic is testing the folder, not the backend.

Pins: twin tests asserting the SAME string in tests/interpreter.rs
(`test_total_order_wrapper_nan_canonicalized_interp_parity`) and tests/codegen.rs
(`test_e2e_total_order_wrapper_nan_canonicalized`) -- the pairing IS the
contract, run == build. Both stash-proven red.
tracker: the total-order float wrappers: total_order_key / compile_total_order_wrapper_cmp in src/codegen/assoc_call.rs, and the `TotalFloat*` arms of value_compare in src/interpreter/helpers.rs (both correct in isolation — see detail)
title: `F64`/`F32` ordering and equality depend on the SIGN BIT of a NaN, which is not stable across backends or optimization levels -- so `Vec[F64].sort()` on NaN-bearing data puts NaN FIRST under the interpreter and LAST under both compiled backends, and `F64 { value: nan } < F64 { value: 1.0 }` is `true` interp / `false` compiled. Measured three ways on one program: a NaN from a constant `0.0 / 0.0` gives interp true / JIT false / AOT false, while a NaN computed at runtime (`z / z` behind a fn call) gives interp true / JIT true / AOT FALSE -- i.e. the same source expression flips answer with optimization level, because AOT inlines the call and constant-folds the division. NOT a comparator bug: both backends implement the same documented IEEE-754 totalOrder key and agree on every non-NaN value. The divergence is in WHICH NaN gets produced -- x86 runtime division yields a NEGATIVE NaN (sign bit set) while LLVM's constant folder yields a POSITIVE one, and totalOrder sorts -NaN before -Infinity but +NaN after +Infinity.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-11-8 (fixed in d8ddc56) against design.md's own `scores.iter().map(F64.from).collect()` example, which sorts a NaN-bearing Vec and printed `NaN 1 2` on interp vs `1 2 NaN` compiled. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING and independent of that fix by reproducing with only constructs that already worked (`F64 { value: nan }` struct literals and a `.value` read, no `F64.from`, no wrapper Display). -- WHY IT IS A SPEC VIOLATION AND NOT JUST A SPLIT. design.md § Float semantics states the wrapper contract as `NaN == NaN` is TRUE and the ordering `-Infinity < ... < +Infinity < NaN` -- i.e. NaN is ONE value that sorts last. Bit-level totalOrder does not give that: it distinguishes NaNs by sign (and by payload), so -NaN sorts FIRST, and two NaNs with different payloads compare UNEQUAL, contradicting the stated `NaN == NaN`. `a == a` only holds today because both sides are the same bits. So the compiled backends are not 'right' either -- they happen to match the spec's ordering only for positive NaN. -- FIX SHAPE: CANONICALIZE NaN in the wrapper rather than picking a winner between the backends. At construction (`F64.from`, the struct literal, and any other producer) or in the comparison key, map every NaN bit pattern to one canonical quiet NaN. That makes `NaN == NaN` true as specified, makes NaN sort last regardless of sign or payload, and makes the order independent of whether a NaN was folded at compile time or produced at run time -- which is the property that actually matters, since otherwise the same program changes answer between `karac run` and `karac build`. Doing it in the comparison key alone is cheaper but leaves the raw bits observable through `.value`; doing it at construction is the stronger invariant. -- COUPLING, and the reason this is worth doing before or with B-2026-08-11-7: that row adds the `Ord` gate that REJECTS `Vec[f64].sort()` and directs users to `F64` precisely so their NaN-bearing data sorts predictably. Landing it while the wrapper's own NaN order is backend-dependent would move the silent wrong answer rather than remove it -- the user follows the diagnostic, wraps, and gets a different sort order from `karac run` than from `karac build`. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 shared cloud container. The NaN-sign behaviour of hardware division is architecture-specific, so the exact interp/JIT/AOT pattern above may differ on arm64 -- but the CLASS of bug (order depends on a bit no source-level construct controls) is architecture-independent.

FIX VERIFICATION (2026-08-11). One program, four execution paths, before and
after (`c` = constant-folded NaN, `r` = NaN from an optimizer-opaque runtime
division via `env.args().len()`):

                    c==r    c<one   r<one   sort              map len
    BEFORE
      interp        true    true    true    NaN NaN -1 1      1
      JIT           false   false   true    NaN -1 1 NaN      2
      AOT -O2       true    false   false   -1 1 NaN NaN      1
      AOT -O0       false   false   true    NaN -1 1 NaN      2
    AFTER
      all four      true    false   false   -1 1 NaN NaN      1

Verified identical across interp / JIT / AOT -O2 / AOT -O0 for all four wrapper
types (F64, F32, F16, Bf16). `-0.0 < 0.0` and `-0.0 != 0.0` unchanged in every
leg, as intended.

Full `--features llvm` suite green (102 binaries, 13418 tests, 0 failures);
clippy `--all --all-targets` and `cargo fmt --check` clean; `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`
exit 0 with the quarantine list matching exactly.

fix:
FIXED by 284d44a4, in the same commit as B-2026-08-11-13 and for the reason this row
gave: once NaN is canonicalized, the bullet can be stated CORRECTLY as a whole
instead of patched in place. Doing this row alone was not actually possible
honestly -- writing today's raw-totalOrder NaN behaviour into the spec would have
documented a run-vs-build divergence as intended semantics.

The `F32`/`F64` bullet list in docs/design.md § Float semantics now reads:
  - Ordering `-Infinity < ... < -0.0 < 0.0 < ... < +Infinity < NaN`, with `-0.0`
    and `0.0` called out as DISTINCT adjacent values and `-0.0 == 0.0` stated
    explicitly as `false`, contrasted against the `f64` primitive where it is
    `true`. That is the correction this row asked for.
  - Equality is bit-equality, with the reason attached: it is what makes `Hash`
    sound, since equal keys have identical bits and cannot hash apart.
  - NaN is ONE value, canonicalized at construction -- now true of the code as
    well as the spec.
Plus a paragraph on why canonicalizing is not cosmetic, since a reader who
assumes raw totalOrder would reasonably expect the sign to matter.

THE CODE BLOCK WAS ALSO WRONG, in three ways this row did not list, each found by
RUNNING it rather than reading it:
  - It used `#` for comments. Kāra's comment is `//`; `#` begins an attribute, so
    every commented line was a parse error. This was the ONLY `#`-commented kara
    block in design.md, against 600 `//` comments elsewhere.
  - `F64.NAN` does not exist -- no associated constants are implemented on the
    wrapper (`no associated function 'NAN' on type 'F64'`). Rewritten as
    `F64.from(f64.NAN)`.
  - `scores.map(F64.from)` is rejected: iterator adaptors require an explicit
    `.iter()`. Rewritten as `scores.iter().map(F64.from).collect()` -- which is
    also verbatim what B-2026-08-11-7's new `Ord`-gate diagnostic tells users to
    write, so the spec and the compiler's own advice now agree.

Every line of the replacement block was executed on interp, JIT and AOT before
being written down, including the two claims stated as compile errors
(`Map[f64, String]` and `Vec[f64].sort()`).
tracker: docs/design.md § Float semantics, the `F32`/`F64` total-order bullet list
title: design.md § Float semantics specifies the `F32`/`F64` total order as `-Infinity < ... < -0.0 == 0.0 < ... < +Infinity < NaN`, but ALL THREE backends implement `-0.0 < 0.0` (and `-0.0 != 0.0`) -- the IEEE-754 totalOrder / Rust `total_cmp` behaviour, verified interp/JIT/AOT agreeing. The implementation is the more standard reading and is already shipped with tests (test_e2e_total_order_float_wrappers asserts `-0<+0` true and `-0==+0` false), so the SPEC LINE is what should change, not the code.
detail: SURFACE NOTE: filed under `other` because the defect is in docs/design.md, not a compiler phase; the ledger's surface vocabulary has no `docs` value. SOURCE NOTE: noticed while implementing B-2026-08-11-8 (fixed in d8ddc56) -- had to know which order was authoritative before writing the constructor. Recorded rather than silently picking a side. -- WHY THE CODE IS RIGHT: bit-level totalOrder makes the wrapper's equality exactly bit-equality, which is what makes it sound as a `Map`/`Set` key and a `Hash` impl (equal keys must hash equal; `-0.0 == 0.0` with distinct bits would need explicit normalization in the hash to stay consistent). It also matches Rust's `f64::total_cmp`, which is the reference every reader will have in mind. -- SCOPE: this is a one-line doc correction, EXCEPT that it interacts with B-2026-08-11-13: if that row's fix canonicalizes NaN at construction, the spec bullet should be rewritten as a whole to state the real contract (bit-equality for finite values and -0/+0 distinct, all NaNs canonicalized to one value that sorts last) rather than patched in place. Prefer doing both together.

carries the baked impl instead of on the method name alone: one
`let exempt_comparison_ops = !matches!(&receiver_for_lookup, Type::Float(_));`
guarding both `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS.contains(&method)` sites in
`src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs`. Floats have no baked candidate, so no new
code is needed -- `find_methods_with_args` comes back empty and the existing

Pins: four tests in `tests/typechecker.rs` -- all seven names on f32 and f64
rejected, the operators and the real float methods left working, a user

title: the seven comparison-op names are exempted from method-existence checking by NAME rather than by whether the receiver carries the baked impl, so `f.cmp(g)` / `f.eq(g)` / `f.lt(g)` on a FLOAT receiver pass `karac check` and then fail at run time -- floats are deliberately excluded from the Eq/Ord registration
tracker: the PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS list in src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs, against eq_ord_targets in src/typechecker/env_build.rs
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found closing B-2026-08-11-4 (which removed the dead `cast`
entry from the same list), while writing the regression guard that the REMAINING
entries still dispatch. They do -- except on floats.

MEASURED, every exempted name against every primitive receiver, `karac check`
then `karac run --interp`:

    recv      cmp    eq     ne     lt     le     gt     ge
    i8..i64   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    u8..u64   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    char      runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    bool      runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    f32       RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED
    f64       RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED

RUNRED = `All checks passed.` then `runtime error: method 'cmp' not found on
type 'f64' (no interpreter dispatch arm)`. A clean dead ROW; `cast` (fixed in
B-2026-08-11-4) was the dead COLUMN of the same table.

THE FLOAT EXCLUSION ITSELF IS CORRECT AND IS NOT THE BUG. `env_build.rs`'s
`eq_ord_targets` registers the baked `Eq`/`Ord` impls for the integers, `bool`,
`char`, `String` and the F32/F64 WRAPPER types, and carries the comment "Floats
(f32/f64) deliberately excluded -- IEEE NaN breaks Eq/Ord". That matches Rust
(`f64: PartialOrd` but not `Ord`) and should stay. The operators `==` / `<` /
`>` work on floats and are unaffected -- this is only about the METHOD
spellings.

THE DEFECT IS THE KEYING. `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` holds a name off BOTH the
impl-table dispatch and the `NoMethodFound` error. It is keyed on the name
alone, so it shields the float receivers just as strongly as the integer ones
that actually have the impl. The exemption exists for a real reason -- the baked
impls' `(self, other)` signature mis-counts under impl-table dispatch (`a.cmp(b)`
-> "expects 2 args, found 1") -- but that reason only applies where the impl
exists.

FIX SHAPE: gate the exemption on the receiver carrying the baked impl rather
than on the name. Practically, do not exempt `Type::Float(_)`. Since floats have
NO baked candidate, `find_methods_with_args` comes back empty and the existing
error branch produces exactly the right message with no new code: `no method
'cmp' on type 'f64'`. Verified there is no mis-count risk on that path -- the
mis-count only arises when a baked `(self, other)` impl IS found, which is
precisely the case floats do not have.

SEE ALSO B-2026-08-11-7 (`Vec[f64].sort()` bypasses the `Ord` gate) and -8
(`F64.from` unimplemented) -- the same `f64`-Ord-gating family, found the same
day from an unrelated dogfood. Those two are about the COLLECTION surface and
the wrapper constructor; this row is about the direct method spelling, and the
three fix sites are disjoint.

A `total_cmp` / `partial_cmp` surface for floats is a SEPARATE question and is
deliberately not part of this row; rejecting the name that does not work is
correct whether or not a working one is ever added.

CONFIRMED AS FILED and fixed with the proposed shape. Four things the row did
not have.

1. THE ROW MEASURED ONLY `--interp`. All three paths are broken, and the AOT one
   is worse than run-red -- it is the FALSE COMPILER-BUG REPORT that motivated
   B-2026-08-11-2, verbatim:

       karac check   All checks passed.
       --interp      runtime error: method 'cmp' not found on type 'f64'
                     (no interpreter dispatch arm)
       build         error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method 'cmp'
                     on variable 'a' (method dispatch fell through; this is a
                     codegen bug - add a dispatcher arm in `compile_method_call`
                     or mark the test `#[ignore]` if the method is genuinely
                     deferred)

   So this row belonged to that same class and not merely to the run-vs-build
   one: `f.cmp(g)` told the author to go patch the compiler. Checked the codegen
   side too -- its `cmp` arm is guarded `if let (IntValue(l), IntValue(r))`, so a
   float operand falls straight through to the "no handler" panic. Nothing was
   ever going to dispatch.

2. THE BOUND SURFACE WAS ALREADY CORRECT, which is what makes this a leak rather
   than a missing feature. A `T: Ord` instantiation at `f64` has always been
   rejected, with a diagnostic that is genuinely good:

       trait bound `T: Ord` is not satisfied; `f64` does not implement `Ord`;
       trait `Ord` is implemented by: Bf16, F16, F32, F64, String, bool, char,
       i16, i32, i64, i8, u16, u32, u64, u8, usize; note: `f64` is not totally
       ordered (IEEE-754 NaN), so it does not implement `Ord` - use the
       total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`) in `Ord`/`Eq`/`Hash` contexts

   So `pick(1.0, 2.0)` under `T: Ord` was a hard error while a bare `a.cmp(b)`
   on the same `f64` typechecked clean. The two surfaces disagreed; this aligns
   them. Pinned as `test_generic_ord_bound_still_gates_floats_the_same_way`.

3. THE SECOND-ORDER WIN REPEATS. Exactly as with `cast` (B-2026-08-11-4), the
   exemption short-circuits AHEAD of the impl lookup, so while it applied to
   floats these seven names were undefinable on a float receiver. A user
   `impl f64 { fn cmp(self, other: f64) -> i64 }` now dispatches (verified: -1)
   and its return type is enforced. That pattern -- an exemption meant to protect
   a builtin also blocking every user impl of the same name -- has now shown up
   twice in this one list.

4. ONE THING NOT VERIFIED END-TO-END, stated rather than implied. The F32/F64
   WRAPPER types keep their baked `Eq`/`Ord` impls and are untouched, but I could
   not exercise them, because an `F64` value cannot currently be constructed at
   all -- `F64.new` and `F64.from` are both unimplemented (that is
   B-2026-08-11-8, filed independently the same day). The wrapper is nonetheless
   unaffected BY CONSTRUCTION: `F64` is a `Type::Named`, so it resolves on the
   named-receiver arm and never reaches the scalar-primitive fall-through this
   change lives in.

SCOPE, unchanged from the filing: the comparison OPERATORS `==` / `!=` / `<` /
`<=` / `>` / `>=` on floats are a separate lowering and keep working -- that is
the point, `a < b` is how floats are compared -- as do `abs` / `to_string` /
`clone`, which are handled by the early scalar intercept and never reach here.
A `partial_cmp` / `total_cmp` surface for floats remains a separate question;
rejecting the spelling that does not work is right either way.

title: ACCEPTED COST, not a pending fix: `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by` on SHUFFLED-UNIFORM input is ~1.30x Rust's `sort_by` (karac ~11.1 ms vs driftsort 8.2-8.9, 150k pairs, this host). Residual of B-2026-08-10-19. FIVE DIRECTIONS WERE MEASURED AGAINST IT AND NONE CLOSES IT -- merge-kernel tweaks, RUN tuning, the bounds-check hoist, a 3-way quicksort run-builder and a 2-way one; do not reopen any of them without new information. The last and most promising, a stable 2-way branchless quicksort run-builder, was BUILT IN FULL, verified correct (98/98 pattern x size, element-type coverage across AOT/LLJIT/interp) and measured: random 11.11 -> 11.73 ms (0.95x, i.e. SLOWER) with instructions 74.05M -> 82.18M (+11%); sawtooth 2.82 -> 3.22 (0.87x). A sweep of the configuration space (span 512/2048/8192/16384/65536, base 16/32/64) found NO setting that beats main on random -- the best, span 16384 base 64, reaches 11.17 vs main's 11.11, i.e. parity. Not merged; the implementation was reverted. This is the cost of the algorithm karac has. The one direction that DID pay, few-unique, is split out as its own open row B-2026-08-11-10. Full write-up in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-10-19 (fixed in 31485cd). Reshaped five times on 2026-08-11 as measurements landed; this is the terminal state. -- WHY THE BUDGET CHECK POINTED THE WRONG WAY, the methodological lesson and the most reusable thing here. The probe measured 14.38 instructions per element per partition level against the merge's 26.93 and that number was correct, but it was measured the wrong way round: the probe partitioned the FULL 150k array at every level, so every loop had a huge trip count, unrolled well, and amortised its per-range setup to nothing. It captured the kernel's ASYMPTOTIC cost. A real quicksort spends most of its work on SMALL ranges -- recursing from 16384 to a base of 16 makes roughly 2*span/base ranges, most near base size, each paying a fixed cost (pivot xorshift plus a 64-bit urem, stack push/pop, block dispatch, two helper calls) over very few elements with loops too short to unroll. The merge has no such problem: every pass is one long loop per run pair, so it already sits at its asymptotic cost. GENERAL RULE: when costing a kernel for a RECURSIVE algorithm, measure it at the range sizes the recursion actually produces (a geometric mix from span down to base), never on one range of n. -- WHAT WAS BUILT, if anyone revisits for the few-unique win: `__vec_<m>_qs_<id>(data, scratch, lo, hi)`, a stable 2-way count-then-scatter partition into alternating buffers that borrows PHASE 2's OWN SCRATCH at matching indices and so needs no allocation at all (the 3-way attempt needed a fourth malloc). Progress without a 3-way equal block comes from making the split predicate `cmp(x,pivot) < t` with `t` loop-invariant and re-running with t=1 when nlt==0: the retry cannot return 0 because the pivot is <= pivot, so the left half is then the block of elements equal to the pivot, already sorted and stable and needing no recursion, and two passes restore buffer parity so nothing downstream knows a retry happened -- ONE kernel, not two. Phase 1 accumulates only CONSECUTIVE short runs, so a long run ends the accumulation and is recorded untouched, which is what keeps nearly-sorted input from being destroyed. -- ALL FIVE DIRECTIONS, with the data that closed them: (1) contained merge-kernel tweaks -- unconditional branchless merge is 2x worse on ordered-ish shapes, cached merge heads 3-5%, ordered-run bulk copy helps only already-sorted; (2) RUN tuning -- flat within ~3% across 4/8/16/32/64 under BOTH the branchy and branchless kernels; (3) bounds-check hoist -- net-neutral, -9.1% instructions bought only +3-4% wall clock, proving the merge is latency-bound not throughput-bound; (4) 3-way quicksort run-builder -- ~47 instructions/element/level, MORE than the merge pass it replaced; (5) 2-way quicksort run-builder -- this row, parity at best on random across the whole configuration sweep. -- ALSO STILL TRUE: not a codegen-quality gap (karac is 5-8% faster than rustc compiling the identical algorithm); karac now runs 1.53x driftsort's instructions and 0.82x its mispredicts, i.e. it mispredicts LESS OFTEN than driftsort. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 Xeon @2.80GHz 4-vCPU shared cloud container, NOT the canonical Apple-silicon bench host. Instruction counts are host-independent; the wall-clock figures and anything resting on cache or unrolling behaviour are not. -- SEVERITY LOW and should stay there: ~1.30x on one input shape, where karac is 7x FASTER than driftsort on sorted and reverse-sorted input, 1.85x faster on sawtooth, and the parent rows were 54x and 1.66x. -- DISPOSITION 2026-08-11: moved from `open` to `wontfix`. `open` is the work queue (bug-curve.py renders open rows in full precisely because you are expected to act on them), and this row has no action left, so leaving it open would have parked a permanent no-op in the queue. It is NOT `invalid` -- the 1.30x is real and reproduces on demand; `invalid` in this ledger means the premise was refuted (see B-2026-07-17-14, B-2026-07-29-8) and claiming that here would be false. The `wontfix` status was added to the lint enum and to the rollup for exactly this case. The live remainder of the investigation moved to B-2026-08-11-10.

Before/after on the same container, baseline reproducing this row's own
recorded checksum (48.8M / 22.5M) exactly:

    pattern         instructions           driftsort   was            now
    few-unique      48.8M -> 13.2M  3.70x     14.2M    3.44x behind   1.08x AHEAD
    sawtooth        22.5M -> 23.4M  0.96x     31.6M    1.40x ahead    1.35x ahead
    random          72.3M -> 72.1M  1.00x     48.2M    1.50x behind   unchanged
    nearly-sorted   31.5M -> 32.9M  0.96x
    sorted           1.0M ->  1.0M  1.00x
    reverse          1.8M ->  1.8M  1.00x

Wall clock on the target, same session and slope method: 4.760 -> 1.742 ms
(2.73x), against driftsort's 1.514 ms best / 1.764 ms bulk average. Wall clock
on the other five rows is noise -- it swings several percent in BOTH directions
against IDENTICAL instruction counts, and sorted/reverse sit at 0.03-0.4 ms,
under the slope method's floor. Argue from the instruction column.

THE 4% ON SAWTOOTH AND NEARLY-SORTED IS REAL AND IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE, and
three candidate explanations were each measured and killed. Not the probe:
sorted and reverse call it on every sort and did not move off 1.0M / 1.8M, which
bounds it under 0.05M. Not the partition running: neither pattern passes the
gate. Not the call-graph change: the obvious suspect was that `qpart` calling
back into the merge gives the merge a second caller, but DELETING that call (a
deliberately incorrect build, valid to measure because neither pattern ever
reaches `qpart`) made both WORSE, 24.4M and 34.4M. What is left is codegen
jitter -- perturbing the module around a 60-block function moves these two
patterns a few percent either way, and the shipped arrangement is the better end
of the measured range. Also measured and rejected: hoisting the probe into its
own function changed nothing (13.2/23.4/72.1/32.9 identical), so it is kept out
of line on structure, not on evidence of a win.

THE DESIGN, and the two things that made it work where six earlier directions
did not. (1) It occupies the OTHER END OF THE RECURSION from the bounded
run-builder that was built and reverted for B-2026-08-10-20: partition from n
DOWN to a span and merge below, rather than merge above a span and partition
below. So it removes the TOP passes, and every partition runs on a large range
rather than paying a fixed per-range cost near its base size. (2) It STOPS
EARLY, which no merge can -- a range whose every element ties with the pivot is
sorted and stable and is finished. Instrumented on few-unique: 8 all-equal exits
for 8 distinct keys, and NOT ONE merge pass over the array.

GATE PLACEMENT WAS MOST OF THE WORK, because ungated this is 11-13x WORSE on
sorted and reverse. Both full-pass placements lose: a counting pass BEFORE phase
1 costs ~1.3M, which is 42% of sorted's entire budget; AFTER phase 1 it is free
for sorted/reverse but costs few-unique 19.4M -> 33.9M, because phase 1's RUN=32
insertion padding spends ~14.5M on an input whose natural runs are ~2 long and
the partition then discards it -- no better than the 34.25M run-builder this row
already rejected. So the entry gate is O(1): 512 samples estimating BOTH
cardinality (ties with a random pivot) and existing orderedness (ordered
adjacent pairs). Both are needed -- cardinality alone would partition an input
that is ALREADY SORTED over few keys. The in-recursion gate is exact and free:
`neq = nle - nlt` is already computed by the partition's own counting pass, so
each range re-decides for nothing and a mixed input partitions the part that
pays and merges the part that does not.

FOUR KERNEL DETAILS, NONE OPTIONAL. (a) The pivot must be RANDOMISED; a
fixed-position median-of-3 is degenerate on periodic input -- on the sawtooth
lo/lo+len/2/hi-1 hold 0, 0, 999, the median is 0, and 0 is the range MINIMUM, so
each level peels only the copies of the minimum: measured 2328.7M instructions,
~100x the merge. (b) ONE counting pass tallies both `< pivot` and `<= pivot`,
which picks the split predicate without a second pass and folds the old t=1
retry into it. (c) Count-then-scatter, two cursors over one in-order walk --
the whole stability argument. (d) `allow_part` on the merge sort's signature:
without it an abandoned range is re-probed, accepted by the sampling estimate
that the exact tie count just rejected, and handed straight back -- same range,
same pivot, forever. A depth limit of 64 keeps the worst case O(n log n) after
introducing a randomised pivot.

GATE THRESHOLD VALIDATED AGAINST A MEASURED CROSSOVER, not tuned to the
benchmark. With the partition forced on, so the crossover is a property of the
algorithms: distinct keys 2/8/32/64/128/256/512 -> partition 7.6/22.4/30.7/36.8/
60.6/64.8/67.0M against merge 38.7/49.7/53.0/52.0/51.0/50.5/50.5M, i.e. the
crossover is between 64 and 128. The arithmetic predicts d < 68 (a partition
level costs two passes against the merge's one, so it wins while 2*log2(d) <
log2(n/RUN) = 12.2). GATE = 64 sits just on the winning side of both.

VERIFICATION. A 756-case sweep -- 6 patterns x 14 sizes x 9 cardinalities,
sizes straddling the probe floor (4095/4096/4097) and cardinalities straddling
the gate (63/64/65/129) -- asserting sorted AND stable, with the ORACLE ITSELF
VALIDATED by poisoning it (two deliberately unsorted cases produce 27,500 FAIL
lines, so a silent pass means something). Element types i64, all-int struct and
heap String. Full `cargo test --features llvm` green; ASAN clean at the default
level and on the `-O0` leg (1032 passed, quarantine list matched exactly).
`should_use_mono_vec_sort_by_for` admits only i64 and all-int structs, so no
heap-owning element ever reaches this path -- the memory-safety class here is
bounds, not ownership. Pins: `test_e2e_vec_sort_by_partition_path_low_cardinality`
(tests/codegen.rs, strict assert_eq so a stale archive fails loudly) and
`asan_vec_sort_by_partition_path_in_bounds` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), both
checking sortedness, stability, and the all-equal early exit -- that branch
returns a range declaring it sorted WITHOUT writing it, so only stability can
catch it having moved anything.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLOSE: B-2026-08-10-20, the shuffled-uniform 1.50x, which
remains `wontfix`. Random is untouched here (72.3M -> 72.1M) by design -- the
gate rejects it after one 512-sample probe.
title: `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by` on FEW-UNIQUE input (150k pairs over 8 distinct keys) is 5.93 ms / 48.8M instructions vs driftsort's 1.81 ms / 14.2M on this host -- a 3.3x gap, NOT the 1.3-1.5x originally filed. The stable 2-way quicksort run-builder built for B-2026-08-10-20 is a real 1.43x (to 34.25M / 4.15 ms) but is NOT a route to parity as this row first claimed: it still leaves 2.4x on instructions and 2.3x on wall clock. Both previously proposed options (pay down the sawtooth regression; gate on a cardinality signal) only bank that 1.43x, and the sawtooth one defends the pattern karac ALREADY WINS (22.5M vs 31.6M). Any future attempt should be budgeted against driftsort's 14.2M -- ~95 instructions per element against karac's ~325 -- before a line is written.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-10-20 on 2026-08-11 when that row was closed as `wontfix`. The parent is about SHUFFLED-UNIFORM input and is finished; this row exists because the same experiment produced one genuine unexploited win on a DIFFERENT input shape, and burying an actionable finding inside a closed row is how it gets lost. -- WHY IT IS SEPARATE AND NOT A REOPENING: the parent's five dead ends were all attempts on random input, where the run-builder reaches parity at best. Few-unique is the one shape where it is decisively ahead, and it is ahead for a legible reason -- 8 distinct keys means the partition resolves the array in ~3 levels while the merge still pays all 12 passes, and the comparisons become almost perfectly predictable (the 10x mispredict drop). -- WHAT EXISTS ALREADY: the full emitter was written and verified (98/98 pattern x size combinations, element-type coverage on i64, a mixed-width (i64,i32,i64) tuple and a named struct, agreeing across AOT, LLJIT and the interpreter) and then REVERTED, so there is no code on main. Recover it from the B-2026-08-10-20 investigation rather than rewriting: `__vec_<m>_qs_<id>(data, scratch, lo, hi)`, a stable 2-way count-then-scatter partition into alternating buffers that borrows phase 2's own scratch at matching indices and so needs no allocation; progress without a 3-way equal block comes from a loop-invariant threshold t in `cmp(x,pivot) < t` with a t=1 retry when nlt==0. Design notes and the configuration sweep are in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md. -- MEASURE OPTION (a) FIRST: it is the cheaper experiment and it is the one that would let the win land unconditionally, whereas (b) adds a cardinality probe to every sort and has to earn its own keep. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 Xeon @2.80GHz 4-vCPU shared cloud container, NOT the canonical Apple-silicon bench host. Instruction and mispredict counts are host-independent; the wall-clock figures are not, and branch-prediction-sensitive results are the most likely to move on a different microarchitecture. -- SEVERITY LOW: it is one input shape, karac is already 7x faster than driftsort on sorted and reverse-sorted input and 1.85x faster on sawtooth, and nothing here is a correctness or codegen-quality defect.

PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-11 -- THE ROUTE IS NOT TO PARITY, AND THE GAP IS
BIGGER THAN FILED. Re-measured with a rebuilt harness, now checked into
docs/spikes/sortbench/ (the original was lost with its session scratchpad,
which is why this row had to be re-measured from scratch at all).

THE HARNESS WAS VALIDATED BEFORE IT WAS BELIEVED, on host-independent numbers
this row's own spike already recorded: karac few-unique 48.8M instructions
(recorded 48.85M), karac sawtooth 22.5M (recorded 22.53M), clone-only slope
1.13-1.24 ms (recorded 1.13-1.23). Three significant figures from an
independently written harness, so what follows is not a harness artifact.

WHAT CHANGED IS THE DRIFTSORT SIDE:

    pattern      karac              filed driftsort   RE-MEASURED driftsort
    random       10.92 ms / 72.3M   8.2-8.9 ms        8.65 ms / 48.2M
    few-unique    5.93 ms / 48.8M   3.6-4.1 ms        1.81 ms / 14.2M
    sawtooth      3.58 ms / 22.5M   6.0-6.5 ms        4.50 ms / 31.6M

Random lands inside the filed range -- that is the control, and it says the two
measurements are of the same thing. Few-unique does not: driftsort is 1.81 ms,
not 3.6-4.1, and its 14.2M instruction count corroborates that on a metric that
does not move between hosts. The filed figure appears never to have been
cross-checked against instructions.

(Method note, because it nearly produced a wrong correction: without `black_box`
on the Rust timing loop, random measures 6.77 ms instead of 8.65 and flatters
driftsort by 28%. The mismatch against the spike's own recorded 8.2-8.9 is what
caught it. The Rust input generator is now mirrored line-for-line from the Kara
one, per the spike's own caveat 3.)

CONSEQUENCES FOR THIS ROW, both halves of the title:

  1. THE GAP IS 3.3x WALL / 3.4x INSTRUCTIONS, not 1.3-1.5x. The row is worth
     MORE than filed, not less.
  2. THE MEASURED ROUTE DOES NOT REACH PARITY. The run-builder's 34.25M /
     4.15 ms against driftsort's 14.2M / 1.81 ms is still 2.4x on instructions
     and 2.3x on wall clock -- the two ratios agree, which is what you want
     before believing either. A genuine 1.43x, and not parity.

So BOTH proposed options are worth less than they looked, because both are ways
to keep a 1.43x that leaves 2.4x on the table. Option (a) is the weaker of the
two on this evidence: it spends its effort protecting sawtooth, which is THE
PATTERN KARAC ALREADY WINS (22.5M vs driftsort's 31.6M; 3.58 ms vs 4.50).
Regressing the best pattern 10-18% to bank a fraction of the worst is a worse
trade than the row assumed.

THE TARGET FOR ANY FUTURE ATTEMPT IS 14.2M INSTRUCTIONS -- ~95 per element
against karac's ~325. At 8 distinct keys driftsort is not running a merge sort
with a better constant; it is resolving the array in a couple of passes. A
design that cannot plausibly reach the low 20s of millions is not worth
building. That is the budget-check lesson from B-2026-08-10-20 applied BEFORE
the code instead of after.

NOT ATTEMPTED, DELIBERATELY: the run-builder was not rebuilt. It was reverted
and is not in git history (`git log -S'_qs_'` finds nothing), so option (a)
requires writing ~500 lines of emitter before it can be measured at all --
to chase a target this measurement says it cannot hit.

STATUS STAYS OPEN: the gap is real, reproducible, and larger than filed. What
is retired is the FIX SHAPE, not the row.
DIRECTION 6 MEASURED AND REFUTED 2026-08-11 -- THE GALLOPING MERGE, plus the
arithmetic that retires every merge-side direction at once. No code change; the
measurement is the deliverable. Written up in full at
docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md § "Direction 6", harness in
docs/spikes/sortbench/mirror.rs.

WHY THIS ONE HAD TO BE MEASURED. Galloping is THE textbook answer to few-unique
stable sorting -- timsort's, therefore Java's and CPython's -- and karac's merge
does not have it. Anyone picking this row up tries it first. It is also the one
lever that attacks the property this document already identified as the real
bottleneck: the bounds-check hoist showed the merge is LATENCY-bound on its
loop-carried chain (-9.1% instructions bought +3.5% wall clock), and a bulk
memcpy has no such chain at all.

THE MIRROR, VALIDATED BEFORE IT WAS BELIEVED. A faithful Rust reimplementation
of `emit_sort_by_mono`'s algorithm, plain vs galloping, run on the real input so
every pass sees the real run-size distribution -- explicitly not the mistake of
the earlier budget check, which measured a kernel over the full array at every
level and so priced its asymptotic cost. Against a LIVE re-run of the harness
checksum (few-unique 48.8M, sawtooth 22.5M, random 72.3M -- reproduced exactly):
mirror plain is 50.5M / 24.0M, i.e. +3.5% / +6.7%. It did NOT start there: the
first draft indexed slices normally and read 68.2M, 40% high, purely on Rust
bounds checks that karac's raw-GEP merge does not emit. A mirror that pays them
is measuring a different loop.

    pattern         instructions          wall clock
                    plain -> gallop       plain -> gallop
    few-unique      50.5 -> 40.1M  1.26x  5.472 -> 5.908 ms  0.93x
    sawtooth        24.0 -> 20.4M  1.18x  3.877 -> 3.563 ms  1.09x
    random          50.8 -> 61.4M  0.83x  13.222 -> 14.044   0.94x
    nearly-sorted   32.0 -> 23.6M  1.35x  4.264 -> 4.077 ms  1.05x

ON THE TARGET PATTERN IT IS A WALL-CLOCK REGRESSION WHILE REMOVING 26% OF THE
INSTRUCTIONS -- the bounds-check-hoist signature again, and for the same reason:
a gallop's binary search has a WORSE dependency chain than the streaming merge
it replaces, since each probe address depends on the previous comparison.

NOT A DUD IMPLEMENTATION, AND NOT A TUNING MISS. Instrumented: few-unique
bulk-copies 1,619,133 of ~1.76M merge outputs (92%) across 35,145 copies, and
random correctly self-disables (693 galloped of 1.9M). A MIN_GALLOP sweep is
flat -- 40.3/40.3/40.3/40.1/40.1/41.1M at thresholds 1/2/3/4/7/12 -- while
threshold 1 costs random 27%.

THE ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Every phase-2 pass writes all n
elements, so with RUN=32 and n=150k the sort does ceil(log2(150000/32)) = 13
passes ~= 1.8M merge outputs, AND THAT VOLUME IS INDEPENDENT OF KEY CARDINALITY.
Galloping makes an output cheaper; it cannot make one fewer of them. It also
only reaches the TOP passes -- with 8 keys a run of length L holds ~8 blocks of
L/8, so a gallop pays only once L/8 clears the threshold, while the bottom
passes contribute exactly as many outputs and are untouched (measured average
bulk copy: 46 elements, not hundreds).

Against that, driftsort's 14.2M is ~95 instructions per ELEMENT. Spread over 13
passes that is 7.9 instructions per merge output -- less than one
compare-and-move. Driftsort is not running a cheaper merge; it is running about
THREE PASSES. And the pass count cannot be bought by raising the insertion base,
because phase 1 is O(n*RUN) -- measured RUN 32/64/128/256/1024 -> 13/12/11/10/8
passes -> 50.5/58.2/76.8/116.0/362.4M. RUN=32 is already optimal.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS ROW'S FIX SHAPE. Four of the six measured directions --
merge-kernel tweaks, RUN tuning, the bounds-check hoist, and now galloping --
optimize COST PER MERGE OUTPUT, and n*log2(n/RUN) outputs is fixed, so that
whole family provably cannot reach 14.2M at any per-output cost. The other two
(the 3-way and 2-way quicksort run-builders) were pass-count reducers but
bounded the partition to a `span` and merged above it, removing only
log2(span/RUN) passes -- which is why the better of them landed at 34.25M.

So the requirement on any future attempt is now specific: IT MUST REDUCE THE
NUMBER OF FULL PASSES OVER THE ARRAY, AND BOUNDING THE PARTITION TO A SPAN
FORFEITS MOST OF THAT. A full-array stable partition is the only shape left that
qualifies.

NOT ATTEMPTED, DELIBERATELY: that full-array partition. It is a ~500-line
emitter whose bounded cousin has already been built and reverted once; this row
is severity `low`; and karac remains 7x faster than driftsort on sorted and
reverse-sorted input and 1.85x on sawtooth. Building it is a separate decision,
now with better information than it had.

STATUS STAYS OPEN: the 3.3x gap is unchanged and reproducible. What this
entry retires is a family of fix shapes, not the row.

DIRECTION 7 MEASURED AND CONFIRMED 2026-08-11 -- THE FULL-ARRAY STABLE
PARTITION WORKS, and it is the first of seven directions that improves the
target pattern without charging any other pattern for it. Budget-checked in the
mirror before any emitter, as this row requires. Written up in full at
docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md § "Direction 7"; harness mode
`docs/spikes/sortbench/mirror.rs part`.

    pattern         instructions              wall clock
                    merge  -> partition       merge  -> partition
    few-unique      49.7M  -> 19.8M   2.5x    6.377  -> 3.640 ms   1.75x
    sawtooth        23.8M  -> 23.8M   1.00x   4.015  -> 4.398 ms
    random          50.0M  -> 50.0M   1.00x   13.804 -> 12.273 ms
    nearly-sorted   31.5M  -> 31.6M   1.00x   5.048  -> 5.203 ms
    sorted           3.1M  ->  3.1M   1.00x   2.157  -> 2.218 ms
    reverse          3.7M  ->  3.7M   1.00x   2.225  -> 1.974 ms

The five non-target patterns are unchanged TO THREE SIGNIFICANT FIGURES because
on those inputs the algorithm IS today's algorithm -- the gates divert to it.
Their wall-clock column is noise and nothing else: it swings +-11% (random
13.804 -> 12.273) against an IDENTICAL instruction count, which is this shared
4-vCPU container's floor. On few-unique the two metrics AGREE IN DIRECTION,
which is exactly what galloping failed to do. Across eight pivot seeds
few-unique reads 18.4/18.9/18.9/19.6/19.8/19.9/21.1/22.4M, so the honest figure
is 2.2x-2.7x and the table quotes the median. Residual gap to driftsort's 14.2M
falls from 3.4x to ~1.4x.

WHY IT REDUCES PASSES WHERE THE BOUNDED RUN-BUILDER COULD NOT. Same kernel as
the reverted B-2026-08-10-20 attempt -- stable 2-way count-then-scatter into
alternating buffers, borrowing phase 2's own scratch, still no extra allocation.
The inversion is which end of the recursion it occupies: the bounded one merged
ABOVE a span and partitioned BELOW (removing log2(span/RUN) passes off the
bottom, and paying a partition's fixed per-range cost on ranges near its base
size); this one partitions from n DOWN to a span and merges below, so it removes
the TOP passes and every partition it performs is on a large range. And it can
STOP EARLY, which no merge can: a range whose every element ties with the pivot
is sorted and stable and is finished. Instrumented on few-unique:
partitions=12, all_equal_exits=8, merged=0 -- eight all-equal exits for eight
distinct keys, and not one merge pass over the array.

TWO KERNEL DETAILS, NEITHER OPTIONAL. (1) The pivot must be RANDOMISED, not a
fixed-position median-of-3: sampling lo, lo+len/2, hi-1 is degenerate on
periodic input -- on the sawtooth those hold 0, 0, 999, the median is 0, and 0
is the range MINIMUM, so each level peels only the 150 copies of it. Measured
2328.7M instructions, ~100x the merge. (2) ONE counting pass tallies both
`< pivot` and `<= pivot`, which chooses the split predicate without a second
pass and folds the old t=1 retry into it: nlt == 0 means the left block is
exactly the elements equal to the pivot, already sorted and stable, no recursion.

THE TWO GATES, AND WHY PLACEMENT WAS MOST OF THE WORK. Ungated, this is
UNSHIPPABLE: 11-13x worse on sorted and reverse (3.1M -> 40.2M, 3.7M -> 39.7M)
and 1.3-2.7x worse on random, sawtooth and nearly-sorted. Two plausible
placements both lose. A full counting pass BEFORE phase 1 costs ~1.3M, which is
42% of sorted's entire 3.1M (sorted -> 4.4M, reverse -> 5.0M) -- and those are
the patterns karac beats driftsort 7x on. AFTER phase 1 it is free for
sorted/reverse but few-unique goes 19.4M -> 33.9M, because phase 1's RUN=32
insertion padding costs ~14.5M on an input whose natural runs are ~2 long and
the partition then discards that work -- no better than the 34.25M run-builder
already rejected. So the entry decision must PRECEDE phase 1 and be O(1) in n.
256 random samples settle both halves: distinct keys among the sample estimate
cardinality (8 true keys reads 8, 1000 reads 231, all-distinct reads 256), and
the fraction of sampled ADJACENT PAIRS already in order estimates what phase 1
would find (sorted 100%, nearly-sorted 99%, shuffled 57-61%). Both are needed --
cardinality alone would partition an input that is ALREADY SORTED over few keys.
Inside the recursion the gate is exact and genuinely free: part_once's counting
pass has already computed neq = nle - nlt, so len/neq is an unbiased cardinality
estimate available BEFORE a single element is written; a range that fails it
abandons having moved no data and is merged as today. The decision is therefore
per-range, not a global mode.

WHERE THE THRESHOLD BELONGS, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Sweeping cardinality
with the partition forced on, so the crossover is a property of the algorithms
and not of the gate:

    distinct keys      2     8    32    64   128   256   512
    merge          38.7M 49.7M 53.0M 52.0M 51.0M 50.5M 50.5M
    partition       7.6M 22.4M 30.7M 36.8M 60.6M 64.8M 67.0M
    ratio           5.1x  2.2x  1.7x  1.4x  0.84x 0.78x 0.75x

Crossover is between 64 and 128 distinct keys. The analytic prediction is that
partitioning wins while 2*log2(d) < log2(n/RUN) = 12.2 -- two passes per level
against the merge's one -- i.e. d < 68. Measurement and arithmetic agree, which
is the corroboration worth having before trusting either. GATE = 64 therefore
sits just on the winning side of a crossover it was not tuned to.

STATUS STAYS OPEN, but for the opposite reason to Direction 6: the budget check
this row demanded is POSITIVE. It reaches 18.4-22.4M against the row's own
stated bar of "the low 20s of millions", holds every other pattern at parity,

title: the `UseAfterMove` defensive copy that `cli.rs` promises DOES NOT EXIST for any heap type on the binding-to-binding move path -- `karac check` exits 0 by design, `karac build` exits 0, and the reuse reads freed memory: garbage for String/Vec/struct, a hard SEGFAULT for Map and Set. Filed as a container-source gap; measured, the container read is the one case that IS defended and the 'working' rows were static-literal and `.len()` artifacts
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found dogfooding a ~100-line log aggregator (parse a
whitespace-delimited log, group by service through a `Map[String, i64]` index
into a `Vec[Stat]`, report sorted by total). The interpreter matched the
hand-computed oracle exactly; AOT printed the right NUMBERS with a garbage
service NAME on every row, and the JIT aborted. The numbers surviving while
only the String was corrupt is what pointed at a buffer rather than at logic.

THE INVARIANT THAT IS BROKEN is stated in the compiler itself, at
`src/cli.rs:1477` (`is_fatal_ownership_kind`):

    `UseAfterMove` -- codegen defensive-copies the reuse, so the binary is
    memory-safe; the diagnostic carries a machine-applicable `.clone()` fix
    precisely because the program compiles and runs. Keeping it non-fatal for
    `build` is deliberate ...

B-2026-07-19-3 reached the same conclusion explicitly ("build's leniency is
intended, NOT a soundness hole") and that is the conclusion this row narrows:
the defensive copy is real for the sources those investigations looked at, and
does not exist for a container element read. For that subset the leniency IS a
soundness hole -- `karac check` exits 0 with "All checks passed", `karac build`
exits 0, and the emitted program reads freed memory.

MEASURED. Identical 10-line shape each time -- first owner dies in an inner
block, second copy read after it -- varying ONLY where the doubly-moved String
came from:

    source of the doubly-moved String        interp     AOT
    plain local binding (`let s: String`)    alpha      alpha      copy emitted
    struct field (`h.name`)                  alpha      alpha      copy emitted
    Map value (`m.get(k)` payload)           alpha      GARBAGE    no copy
    Vec element (`names[0]`)                 alpha      GARBAGE    no copy

The minimal reproducer is 10 lines with no function boundary at all:

    fn main() {
        let names: Vec[String] = ["alpha"];
        let mut out: String = f"";
        {
            let n = names[0];
            let _keep: String = n;
            out = n;
        }
        println(out);
    }

    interp: alpha        AOT: JofY (garbage)

THE INNER BLOCK IS THE INSTRUMENT, not incidental. Without it the same program
prints correctly -- but only because the read happens BEFORE the first owner's
scope exit frees the shared buffer. That is why this looked at first like an
escape-analysis bug (it reproduces through a returned `Vec[Stat]`, through a
returned bare `String`, and across a by-value or `ref` Vec parameter, and NOT
when the value is consumed in the same scope). All of those are the same defect
seen through different lifetimes: the two owners always alias, and whether you
observe it depends only on whether the first one has died yet. Any "working"
case here is timing, not a copy.

THREE BACKENDS, THREE BEHAVIOURS, which is the sharpest symptom:
  - `--interp`  correct
  - `run` (JIT) ABORTS: "unsafe precondition(s) violated:
    ptr::copy_nonoverlapping requires that both pointer arguments are aligned
    and non-null" at `karac_string_clone` (runtime/src/clone.rs:80)
  - `build` (AOT) silently prints garbage bytes

`.clone()` at the move site -- what the diagnostic prescribes -- does fix it, so
the escape hatch works. That is the mitigation, not the fix: the whole reason
the diagnostic is a warning rather than an error is the promise that you do not
have to take it.

WHY THE CORPUS NEVER HIT IT, and this is the actionable part beyond the fix
itself: `tests/common/mod.rs`'s ownership gate (`assert_ownership_clean`)
REFUSES any fixture whose program has ownership errors, `UseAfterMove`
included, on the stated grounds that "`karac check` would reject it, so codegen
is being fed input it never sees in production". That premise is false for this
one kind -- `karac check` exits 0 on it BY DESIGN (`is_fatal_ownership_kind`
excludes `UseAfterMove` and `RcFallbackNote`). So the ~1000-fixture
memory_sanitizer suite, the codebase's primary memory gate, structurally cannot
contain a single test of the defensive-copy mechanism, which is exactly the
mechanism whose correctness `UseAfterMove`'s non-fatal status depends on. Any
fix here needs the gate widened (or a grandfathered lane) or it will not be
regression-testable under ASAN.

FIX SHAPE: find where the `UseAfterMove` defensive copy is emitted for a
binding / struct-field source and extend it to a container element read. Both
`Vec` index and `Map` get reproduce, so the right level is likely wherever the
reuse site is classified, not a per-container arm. Worth checking `Set` /
`VecDeque` / tuple-element / enum-payload sources at the same time rather than
one dogfooding session at a time -- Vec and Map both failing suggests "every
container read" rather than two independent gaps.

=== RE-MEASURED. THE ROW'S OWN TABLE IS WRONG, AND THE GAP IS MUCH WIDER. ===

This row concluded the defensive copy "is real for a plain binding and a struct
field, ABSENT for a Vec element and a Map value". Every one of those four
readings is a measurement artifact. The copy is absent for ALL of them.

WHAT THE ORIGINAL TABLE ACTUALLY MEASURED, artifact by artifact:

  * "plain local binding works" -- the probe used `let s: String = "alpha"`. A
    string LITERAL is STATIC: no heap buffer, so nothing is ever freed and no
    use-after-free is possible regardless of copying. Re-run with `f"alpha"`
    (or `"al" + "pha"`) and the same program prints garbage.

  * "struct field works" -- same artifact: the field was initialised from a
    literal. With `H { name: f"alpha" }` it fails.

  * "Vec element / Map value fail" -- these fail, but not for the filed reason.
    The doubly-moved value in those programs is the STRING the container yields,
    not the container. The container read itself is the one step that IS
    defended (`clone_owned_vec_index_element` via
    `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg`). So the row indicted the only working
    part of the chain.

THE CONTROLLING VARIABLE IS LIFETIME, NOT SOURCE. Move the value into a binding
whose scope ENDS, then read the source AFTER it:

    let s: String = f"alpha";
    { let keep: String = s; }
    println(s);            // karac check: "All checks passed"

    interp  alpha        build  garbage        run (JIT)  garbage

Measured that way, at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, EVERY heap type fails:

    String            garbage
    Vec[i64]          garbage (prints 8475182884243973504)
    Vec[String]       empty
    struct H{String}  empty
    Map[String,i64]   SEGFAULT
    Set[i64]          SEGFAULT

Map and Set are hard segfaults, which the original row did not record at all.

A THIRD ARTIFACT, and the reason `Vec` looked defended for longer than the
rest: read the moved-from Vec with `.len()` and it always "works", because
`.len()` loads the length word and never dereferences the buffer. That is
exactly what the existing pin `e2e_let_move_source_frozen` does (`w.push(1);
let mut v = w; v.push(2); println(w.len())`), so that test does NOT demonstrate
a defensive copy and never did -- change it to `w[1]` and it fails. Same trap
as B-2026-08-09-13 and B-2026-08-09-4; any probe here must read a real element
at -O0.

SO THE INVARIANT AT `src/cli.rs`'s `is_fatal_ownership_kind` was never
implemented, rather than implemented-with-a-hole. Codegen contains no mechanism
keyed on `UseAfterMove` at all -- two incidental comment mentions, no pass. The
leniency is a soundness hole for the whole kind, not a subset of it.

FIX DESIGN, validated against the code rather than guessed:

  1. The ownership checker ALREADY has both spans. `OwnershipError` carries
     `span` (the later use) and `consume_span` (the move). No new analysis is
     needed -- only a plain-data hint on `OwnershipCheckResult` (the
     `elidable_ref_params` channel is the precedent for shipping a hint to
     codegen without breaking codegen-containment).

  2. The disarm has ONE funnel. All 87 `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`
     call sites route through `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex`
     (call_dispatch.rs). Making that a no-op when the arg expr's span is a
     flagged consume site keeps the SOURCE's cleanup armed, in one edit, for
     every consume shape.

  3. The copy needs a type-directed clone at the consume site.
     `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr` is exactly that and already handles String,
     Vec (element-deep since B-2026-08-09-9), Map, Set, and user structs.

  Both halves are required together and in that order of care: a copy without
  the disarm-skip leaks the source; a disarm-skip without the copy converts the
  use-after-free into a DOUBLE free. Neither half is independently landable.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE, deliberately. This is implementing a documented invariant
that was never built, across the move subsystem, and the row itself establishes
that the primary memory gate structurally cannot test it today
(`assert_ownership_clean` refuses `UseAfterMove` programs on a premise that is
false for this one kind). Landing a half-verified fix on a memory path is worse
than landing none -- the same reasoning that kept B-2026-08-09-9's element depth
opt-in. Handed back with the measurements and the design above rather than
half-applied.

PINNED as `#[ignore]`d `test_e2e_use_after_move_defensive_copy_still_missing`
(5 cases: String, Map, Set, `Vec[i64]`, struct-with-heap-field), so the shapes

=== FIXED for String/Vec (bb663f1d). The gate first, then the pair. ===

WIDENING THE GATE WAS THE PREREQUISITE, not housekeeping. `assert_ownership_clean`
failed on any ownership error, justified by "`karac check` would reject it, so
codegen is being fed input it never sees in production". For the two ADVISORY
kinds that is backwards: `cli.rs`'s `is_fatal_ownership_kind` excludes
`UseAfterMove` and `RcFallbackNote` deliberately, so `karac check` exits 0 and
`karac build` compiles them. The gate now mirrors that function. Until it did,
the ~1000-fixture memory suite could not hold a single test of the
defensive-copy mechanism -- which is exactly how the copy could be ENTIRELY
ABSENT without one fixture noticing.

  The first ASAN fixture of the mechanism now exists
  (`asan_use_after_move_defensive_copy_frees_each_buffer_once`), and it fails
  pre-fix with a heap-use-after-free.

THE TWO HALVES, and the measured reason they are welded together. The copy
alone leaks the source; the disarm-skip alone turns the use-after-free into a
DOUBLE free. That is not a hypothetical -- the first build keyed the disarm skip
on the FLAGGED SPAN, and because the copy covers only the `{ptr,len,cap}`
family, a struct-typed move got a skipped disarm with no copy and went from
"prints an empty field" to `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. Keying
the skip on `uam_copied_sites` -- did a copy actually get emitted here --
makes the pair inseparable by construction, so widening the copy to further
types can never get out of step with the disarm.

  That is also what makes PARTIAL coverage legitimate here.
  `emit_vecstr_defensive_copy` self-gates on the value's LLVM shape, and the
  skip keys on a real copy, so an uncovered type keeps BOTH its old copy
  behaviour and its old disarm: it is untouched, not half-converted. The fix
  removes use-after-frees without inventing a double-free anywhere.

MEASURED after the fix, at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, `--interp` vs `karac build`, on
the "move into a dying binding, then read the source" shape:

    String            alpha   ==  interp    0 leaks, 0 invalid
    Vec[i64]          22      ==  interp    0 leaks, 0 invalid
    Vec[String]       alpha   ==  interp    0 leaks, 0 invalid   (element-deep)
    the filed repro   alpha   ==  interp    0 leaks, 0 invalid

AND THE PIN THAT NEVER TESTED WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE IT TESTED. `e2e_let_move_

=== TYPE AXIS CLOSED (aafb6b69). THE ROW IS FULLY FIXED. ===

The last three families now get a defensive copy at the same hook, each with
the duplicator its own layout needs:

  * `Map` / `Set` -- the value is a HANDLE to a `KaracMap`, so a bit-copy left
    two owners of one table and the reuse SEGFAULTED, the most severe symptom
    this bug had. `emit_map_clone_fn` deep-clones entries and writes the new
    handle back (src == dst), the same call the enum payload duplicator's

    the type-directed clone dispatcher already uses.
  * USER STRUCT -- its own words are bit-copied already; what aliases is the
    heap its FIELDS point at, so the fix recurses into them in place.

`shared struct` is deliberately NOT covered: it is RC-managed, so a move is an
aliasing acquire rather than a transfer and there is no second free to prevent.
