FIXED by 3e8d8fa9 -- and the row's nondeterminism has a mundane explanation that
is worth more than the fix: the leak is DETERMINISTIC, and LeakSanitizer was the
unreliable part.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS. `cur = stats[j].region` cap-zeroes the source so the
element's owner stops freeing it (B-2026-08-11-25's fix) -- which leaves whatever
`cur` held BEFORE with no owner at all. `trigger_eager_free` (src/codegen/stmts.rs,
the Assign arm) frees the target's displaced buffer and classifies every other
transferring RHS -- a moved alias, a fresh ref, the `mk().s` fresh-temp staging, a
bare `v[i]` -- but had NO arm for a field moved out of a deeper place. A
`FieldAccess` matches none of them, so the displaced buffer was orphaned once per
execution of the assignment.

So the row's reading was right in substance: the assignment-path cap-zeroing did
trade the double free for a leak, in exactly the mode the fixture's comment
predicts. What it could not see is that the leak arrives through the DISPLACED
TARGET rather than the moved source, which is why it is invisible to the value
pins and why the repair is an added free rather than a narrowed suppression.

WHY IT LOOKED NONDETERMINISTIC. The fixture's max-by-revenue loop overwrites
`best_region` only when the running max improves -- twice across its 40 elements
-- so exactly ONE buffer is displaced per run. One leaked pointer left behind in a
stale stack slot reads to LSan as still-reachable, and whether that slot survives
depends on what ran before it in the process. Under valgrind, which reports
`definitely lost` from the same tree on every run, it is 8 bytes in 1 block,
every time. That also explains the direction of the flake the row found puzzling
(green in the full parallel suite, red standalone): it is not scheduling, it is
stack residue.

It did not reproduce for me at all -- 15 standalone runs green, the full suite
green, KARAC_PAR_WORKERS 1/2/4/8/16 all green, and green on the row's own tree
(9789448) at three runs. `cannot reproduce` would have been the wrong conclusion:
valgrind found it immediately on the first try.

BISECTED to the leg rather than guessed: of the fixture's three assignments, the
`out = cat[0].region` and `got = vs[0].xs` legs are clean and only the loop leaks,
and the leak scales exactly with the overwrite count (6 iterations -> 5 blocks, 11
-> 10). Two controls stay clean and bound the shape: `cur = <fresh String>` and
`cur = s.region` where `s` is a plain local. It is the deeper-place branch only.

THE ALIAS GUARD, which is the part worth reading. The naive fix -- add the arm --
is WORSE than the bug. This arm is the only one whose RHS can alias the slot it
overwrites: after the first `cur = box[0].s` the source is cap-zeroed INTO `cur`,
so a second execution of the same assignment reads a place that now aliases `cur`
itself, and freeing "the old value" frees the buffer about to be stored back.
Measured with the arm unguarded: correct content on the first read, garbage on
the second, two invalid reads under valgrind. `zero_vec_slot_header_if_aliases`
compares the two pointers and zeroes len/cap when they match, so the cap-gated
free and the len-gated element walks all no-op -- one icmp and two selects on a
path that already loads the header.

PINS, and why the existing one could not do this job. The sibling ASAN fixture
leaks one block, which is what LSan misses -- keeping it and adding a line would
have re-created the same blind spot.
`asan_place_field_move_assign_overwrite_no_leak` overwrites 200 times, past any
reachability accident: 3088 bytes in 193 allocations pre-fix, clean post-fix.
`test_e2e_repeated_place_field_move_assign_reads_correctly` pins the guard with a
CONTENT read, because `.len()` comes from the header and reads correctly off a
dangling pointer -- a length-only pin would have seen nothing.

Corrected while here, as the row asked: the sibling fixture's stale
B-2026-08-11-33 cross-reference (an id collision from 2026-08-11) now reads -25,
and its "the loop is here to make such a leak accumulate" comment now says
plainly that it does not, and points at the fixture that does.

REMAINDER, split out as B-2026-08-12-13 rather than buried here: assigning twice
from the same already-moved place still leaks that one buffer, because both
source and target end up cap-zeroed and neither frees it. That is unchanged from
before this fix (it leaked the same 8 bytes then), and strictly better than the
pre-B-25 double free -- but it is a live defect, and `karac check` accepts the
program.
title: `asan_vec_element_field_move_by_assignment_no_double_free` is red on main with a LeakSanitizer leak, and NONDETERMINISTICALLY so: green in the full parallel suite run, red standalone, on one unchanged tree. It is the un-ignored regression pin from 970dadf (B-2026-08-11-25) and fails in exactly the over-broad-repair mode its own comment predicts, so the assignment-path cap-zeroing looks to have traded the double free for a per-iteration leak.
tracker: Regression pin from 970dadf (B-2026-08-11-25). NOT caused by 19d0e9a (B-2026-08-11-30) -- verified by stash-and-rebuild.
detail:
`asan_vec_element_field_move_by_assignment_no_double_free` in
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` is NOT `#[ignore]`d and fails with a LeakSanitizer
leak on current main. It is the regression pin commit 970dadf landed with its
own fix (B-2026-08-11-25, "cap-zero a moved-out heap field on the ASSIGNMENT
path too"), and the failure is precisely the mode that test's own comment warns
about:

    "the repair is to stop the owner freeing, so an over-broad version turns the
     double free into a per-iteration leak, which the value pins in
     tests/codegen.rs cannot see. The loop is here to make such a leak
     accumulate rather than hide."

IT IS NOT DETERMINISTIC, which is the reason this is filed rather than simply
handed back to that fix. Observed today on ONE unchanged source tree (the
pushed main, 9789448):

    full `cargo test --features llvm --test memory_sanitizer`   1039 passed / 0 failed   GREEN
    ... later, same commit, same command                        1038 passed / 1 failed   RED
    standalone, `-- <name> --test-threads=1`, three runs        RED, RED, RED

So it is green-flaky in the full parallel run and red standalone. A test that
can report green while the leak is present is the more dangerous half of this:
CI's memory-sanitizer job runs the full suite, so this can pass there and hide
the leak.

NOT CAUSED BY THE OPTION/RESULT PARAM OWNERSHIP FIX (B-2026-08-11-30, 19d0e9a).
Verified by stashing that change, rebuilding, and re-running both standalone and
full: identical failure with and without it. The fixture contains no
`Option`/`Result` parameter at all.

WHERE TO START: the harness runs fixtures with auto-par ENABLED, and
nondeterministic ASAN outcomes under auto-par are a known shape in this ledger
(B-2026-08-11-27 was a nondeterministic auto-par miscompile). Re-running the
fixture with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 to see whether the flake disappears is the first
thing to try; if it does, the question is the leak's dependence on scheduling
rather than the assignment-path cap-zeroing itself.

Note also that the fixture's doc comment cites B-2026-08-11-33, but that row is
about a `#[derive(Eq)]` struct temporary and this test is the B-2026-08-11-25
assignment-path pin -- a stale cross-reference from the id collisions of
2026-08-11, worth correcting when this is picked up.
investigation: 2026-08-12. Surfaced while gating the B-2026-08-11-30 fix: the full ASAN suite came back 1038/1 where an earlier run on the same tree had been 1039/0. Bisected the difference to the test rather than the change by stashing the fix, rebuilding and re-running -- identical failure with and without it, and the fixture has no Option/Result param. Then ran it standalone three times (red every time) against one green full-suite observation, which is what establishes the nondeterminism.

fix: a827a7f (route the `==` operator for a Vec-carrying struct to the existing TYPE-directed `emit_eq_fn_for_struct` via a new `try_compile_struct_eq_typed` in src/codegen/expr_ops.rs, gated by `struct_has_vec_field_deep`; the shape-directed field walk stays for every other struct)
tracker: `compile_struct_eq` in src/codegen/expr_ops.rs — the per-field recursion compares a `Vec` field by its `{ptr,len,cap}` words instead of element-wise; the interpreter's `value_compare` Array arm does compare contents
title: SILENT WRONG ANSWER (run-vs-build): `#[derive(Eq)]` equality over a struct with a `Vec[String]` field reports NOT EQUAL in both compiled backends for two vectors whose CONTENTS are equal, while the interpreter correctly reports equal. Measured on one program: `S { v: a } == S { v: b }` with both vectors holding \"abcd\" gives interp `true`, JIT `false`, AOT `false`. It is a FALSE NEGATIVE only -- differing contents correctly give `false` on all three -- so the failure mode is a comparison that silently never matches. NARROW AND MEASURED: a `Vec[i64]` field is CORRECT on all three (`true`), and a plain `String` field is CORRECT on all three, so it is specific to a Vec of HEAP elements. Reproduces with two struct LOCALS, no temporaries and no `ref` params, so it is independent of B-2026-08-11-24 / -33 (which are leaks in the same lowering's neighbourhood and cannot change a boolean).
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while building the over-fire matrix for B-2026-08-11-33 (fixed in 23e5d66) -- a control that compared a struct with a `Vec[String]` field returned `false` where it should have returned `true`, with ASAN clean. The leak work is unrelated: it registers a drop AFTER the comparison result is computed, and the divergence reproduces with plain locals where none of that machinery runs. -- THE FOUR-ROW MEASUREMENT, one program, interp vs JIT: `Vec[String]` field with EQUAL contents -> true / FALSE (wrong); `Vec[String]` field with DIFFERING contents -> false / false (right, accidentally); `Vec[i64]` field with equal contents -> true / true (right); plain `String` field with equal contents -> true / true (right). So scalar-element Vec fields and direct String fields both work, and only a heap-element Vec field is wrong. -- LIKELY CAUSE: `compile_struct_eq` recurses per field through `compile_binop`, which for a Vec-shaped field almost certainly compares the `{ptr,len,cap}` triple rather than dispatching to an element-wise comparator. Two independently built vectors have different `ptr`, hence always unequal; a `Vec[i64]` field presumably survives because it routes to a different path (that asymmetry is worth understanding before fixing, since it may indicate the correct dispatch already exists and is simply not reached for heap elements). The recursive `karac_cmp_Vec_String` comparator built for `Vec[Vec[String]].sort()` (B-2026-06-30-15) is the obvious thing to reuse. -- WHY THIS IS HIGH: equality that silently never matches is the worst shape of wrong answer -- no diagnostic, no crash, correct-looking output, and it degrades gracefully into 'the lookup just never finds anything'. A dedup, a cache-hit test, a `contains`-style scan or an assertion over any struct carrying a `Vec[String]` is silently broken under `karac build` while passing under `karac run --interp`, which is also the worst possible split for the Mend loop. -- NOT COVERED BY THE 3-BACKEND ORACLE in the usual way: interp and codegen DISAGREE here, so a differential test WOULD catch it; there simply was no test comparing a struct with a Vec field. Worth checking whether the same gap covers `Vec[Vec[i64]]` and `Map`/`Set`-valued fields when fixing.
 -- FIXED 2026-08-12 in a827a7f. -- THIS ROW'S OWN FILING UNDERSTATED THE BUG AND MISREPORTED ITS DIRECTION; corrected here by measurement, because acting on the filed characterization would have led to the wrong fix and a false sense of the blast radius. Filed as "false negative only, never a false positive" with "`Vec[i64]` is CORRECT on all three". Both are wrong. On scalar elements it is a FALSE POSITIVE machine: `I { v: [7] } == I { v: [263] }` was TRUE (263 = 0x107, identical low byte) and `I { v: [1,2] } == I { v: [1,3] }` was TRUE (the two bytes compared are element 0's low bytes). The filing's `Vec[i64]` control used [7] vs [7] and [7] vs [8], which differ in the FIRST BYTE and so happen to be the two cases the broken compare gets right. An equality that wrongly MATCHES is far worse than one that wrongly misses: a dedup silently merges distinct values and a cache returns a wrong hit, with no diagnostic. -- ROOT CAUSE, which the filing guessed correctly: `compile_struct_eq` recurses per field through `compile_binop`, and that dispatches on LLVM SHAPE. A `Vec` field and a `String` field are both `{ptr, len, cap}`, so Vec fields were handed to `compile_string_binop`, a byte compare of `len` bytes. For a String `len` IS the byte count and the compare is right; for a Vec `len` is the ELEMENT count, so it read the first `len` bytes of the element buffer and ignored the rest. That single fact predicts every measured row: scalar elements alias on their low bytes (false positives), and `Vec[String]` elements compare the low bytes of two distinct heap POINTERS (false negatives). -- THE FIX WAS ALREADY WRITTEN, ONCE. `emit_eq_fn_for_struct` dispatches per field on the declared TypeExpr and sends a `Vec[T]` field to `karac_eq_Vec_<T>` — length first, then element-wise, recursing through the dispatcher so heap elements compare by content. B-2026-06-20-15 built exactly that to fix exactly this bug in the HASHING path (`Set[Vec[T]]` dedup). The `==` OPERATOR simply never picked it up, so the same defect survived in the other half of the equality surface for two months. Worth generalizing: when a bug is fixed for containers, check the operator, and vice versa. -- GATED to structs carrying a Vec directly or through a nested struct field (`struct_has_vec_field_deep`, depth-capped), so every other struct keeps the inline field walk and this cannot regress the common case. -- TEST: ten shapes asserted against `karac run --interp`, which was correct throughout — both false positives, genuine equality, genuine difference, a LENGTH mismatch, both `Vec[String]` directions, `!=` as the exact negation, and a Vec-free struct as a control for the path left untouched. -- KNOWN ADJACENT, not covered: a `Vec[Vec[i64]]` struct FIELD is rejected upstream (before codegen), so the nested-container case could not be exercised here; `Map`/`Set`-valued fields were not tested and should be checked by whoever next touches this dispatch.

fix: FIXED by b3a1061. `karac::prepare_for_resolve` owns the parse->resolve rewrite sequence; `cli.rs` and all 109 codegen-invoking test harnesses call it, so no driver can run a subset. Pinned by `desugar_dependent_constructs_reach_codegen_through_the_harness` (multi-assign, trait default method, `impl Trait` param), verified by negative control.
tracker: `karac::prepare_for_resolve` (`src/lib.rs`), called by `cli.rs` `Pipeline::resolve` and by all 109 codegen-invoking test harnesses; pin `desugar_dependent_constructs_reach_codegen_through_the_harness` in `tests/codegen.rs`
title: 103 of the 109 codegen-invoking test harnesses in `tests/` resolved the RAW parse tree, skipping some or all of the three AST rewrites `karac build` runs between parse and resolve -- 96 never ran `desugar_program` and 103 never ran `expand_gated_stdlib_imports`. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE on source `karac build` compiles and runs correctly: `a, b = b, a` PANICS the resolver (`unreachable!(StmtKind::MultiAssign is removed by the desugar pass)`), and a trait DEFAULT METHOD or an `impl Trait` parameter reaches codegen as an unresolvable call whose diagnostic says 'this is a codegen bug' -- sending the reader into the backend over a missing FRONT-END pass.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: this is the divergence B-2026-08-11-34 is filed for, found and measured while investigating it. It is NOT that row's specific failure (that program is still unreconstructed, see its follow-up) but it IS the same class, demonstrated on four programs. -- MEASURED with a per-fn audit over `tests/*.rs`: 109 fns own a parse tree and feed it to `compile_to_ir*` / `compile_to_object*`; 103 skipped at least one pass. The six that ran both spelled them out by hand, and `run_program_capturing_inner` ran them in the OPPOSITE ORDER from `cli.rs` (desugar before expand, where the CLI expands first) and without the `#[target(...)]` strip entirely. -- THE FOUR PROBE PROGRAMS, each built and run through `karac build` first to establish the CLI accepts them: (1) `a, b = b, a` -- resolver PANIC, not an Err, so any harness hitting it aborts the whole test binary; (2) a trait default method the impl does not override -- `no method 'greet' on type 'P'` then `codegen: no handler for method 'greet' on variable 'p' ... this is a codegen bug`; (3) `fn show(x: impl Shape)` -- the same codegen-blaming message on `area`; (4) `#[derive(Default)]` + `C.default()` -- `no associated function 'default' on type 'C'` then `codegen: cannot resolve field 'x' ... this is a compiler gap`. All four print the right answer from a `karac build` binary. -- THE FIX is structural rather than 103 local repairs: `karac::prepare_for_resolve(&mut program)` in `src/lib.rs` now owns the sequence (expand gated stdlib -> strip `#[target(...)]` -> desugar) and returns the tombstones and `#[proto_schema]` diagnostics the CLI renders. `cli.rs` `Pipeline::resolve` was rewritten to call it, so production and every harness share ONE definition and cannot drift apart again -- the same posture the ledger's other harness-divergence fixes take, one level up. All 109 harnesses now call it; the 6 that had hand-rolled calls had them REPLACED, not supplemented, since desugar is not idempotent (`synthesize_trait_default_methods` would splice twice). -- VERIFIED NON-VACUOUS by negative control: removing the call from `ir_result` alone makes the new pin fail with the resolver's `unreachable!()` panic. Full suite green at 13457 passed / 0 failed across 116 targets; clippy and fmt clean. -- WHY THE DIAGNOSTICS MISLEAD, which is the part worth keeping: `cli.rs`'s own `has_type_errors` doc already records this shape -- 'the user only sees the downstream codegen explosion ... which sends them chasing a phantom codegen bug'. The codegen fall-through messages assert 'this is a codegen bug' in their text, so a harness missing a front-end pass produces a confident, wrong attribution.

fix: 23e5d66 (new `track_fresh_struct_temp_operand` in src/codegen/expr_ops.rs, called from the `Eq`/`NotEq` arm in exprs.rs beside the B-2026-08-11-24 String free: materialize the fresh temp into a slot and register its struct drop, threading the generic instantiation)
tracker: `compile_struct_eq` in src/codegen/expr_ops.rs — the derived-struct `==`/`!=` path; the fresh temp operand is never materialized or dropped. The String sibling was fixed in exprs.rs (B-2026-08-11-24) and does NOT cover this.
title: A `#[derive(Eq)]` STRUCT temporary carrying a HEAP field, compared against a `ref` param, leaks that field every evaluation: `mk(hay) == other` with `fn mk(s: ref String) -> P { P { name: s.substring(0, 4) } }` and `other: ref P` leaks 4 B / 1 alloc under LSan. Sibling of B-2026-08-11-24 (the String-equality form, fixed) with the same operand pairing -- unbound temp vs `ref` param -- but a DIFFERENT lowering, so that fix does not reach it. NOTE THE FILING CORRECTION: B-2026-08-11-24 measured this shape as CLEAN and concluded its scope was narrow to String equality. That control built the struct's String field from a LITERAL, which allocates nothing and therefore cannot leak; the operand pairing was right and the payload was not. With a `substring`-built field it reproduces every time. A pinned `#[ignore]`d fixture (asan_derive_eq_struct_heap_field_vs_ref_param) reproduces it under `cargo test --features llvm --test memory_sanitizer -- --ignored`.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-11-24 while building that row's suggested test matrix -- the derived-struct over-fire control failed, which is how the filing's scope call was caught. -- WHY THE -24 FIX DOES NOT COVER IT. That one was a missing free on the surface-`Binary` String path in exprs.rs: `rewrite_binary` skips the `String.eq` desugar when an operand is ref-typed, so the comparison misses the assoc-call route's operand frees, and the fix was to extend the existing `Add` free to `Eq`/`NotEq`. Derived-struct equality goes to `compile_struct_eq` instead, and the leaked memory is not the operand's own buffer but a heap FIELD inside it, so freeing a String buffer is the wrong operation. -- LIKELY FIX SHAPE: materialize the fresh temp struct into an alloca and register its struct drop, which is the pattern `track_freshtemp_field_access_object` already uses for a fresh call-result struct read in expression position (B-2026-07-22-2, itself an arm64-only leak in origin). The gates there are the right ones to copy: `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` plus a known non-shared struct type. -- WHAT A FIX MUST NOT BREAK, and why this deserves its own matrix rather than being bolted onto -24: the temp is CONSUMED by the comparison before any drop can run, so a drop registered too eagerly is a use-after-free and one registered on the wrong operand is a double-free of the caller's `ref`. The existing controls in asan_string_eq_borrowed_operand_controls_stay_clean -- including the literal-field struct row, which must stay clean and must not start double-freeing -- are the starting set. -- SEVERITY medium rather than high: same per-evaluation, unbounded-in-a-loop character as -24, but the shape is rarer in practice (comparing a freshly built struct against a borrowed one, rather than the substring-scan inner loop that made -24 hit a real dogfood program). Invisible to everything except LSan -- output is correct on all three backends and `karac check` is clean. -- ARM64: per CLAUDE.md this class is not guaranteed architecture-independent; cross-check the arm64 leg before trusting a fix.
 -- FIXED 2026-08-12 in 23e5d66, by the shape the row predicted: give the temp an OWNER rather than free a buffer. Materialize it into a slot and register its struct drop, reusing `track_freshtemp_field_access_object`'s pattern (B-2026-07-22-2) — which drains heap fields recursively and understands shared and generic-monomorph shapes. The concrete instantiation is threaded through to `track_struct_var_inst` so a generic struct gets its PER-MONOMORPH drop instead of the name-shared one that resolves a `Vec[T]` field from bare `T` and leaks the elements (the B-2026-07-11-35 hazard). -- WHY IT IS SAFE, which is the whole question for this direction: the comparison has already field-walked both operands by the time the tracking runs, and the drop it registers fires at SCOPE EXIT, so there is no window where the compare reads freed memory. The risk is the mirror image of the bug — freeing something owned elsewhere — so the GATES carry the weight, and each corresponds to a shape that would otherwise be a double free: `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` admits only Call/MethodCall results (an identifier or field access is a place, owned by its binding or parent, and is never tracked); `scrutinee_is_borrow_call` excludes a call that returns a BORROW, whose referent the caller still owns; shared types are excluded as RC machinery; and `aggregate_has_heap_field` skips structs with nothing to free, so the common scalar-struct comparison pays no alloca and no drop. -- THE OVER-FIRE MATRIX IS THE DELIVERABLE as much as the fix, because a double free or use-after-free ABORTS rather than leaks and so is invisible to a leak-only reading. Seven shapes, all clean under LSan: struct local vs ref param; field-access operand; temp vs temp (both tracked); `!=` followed by a READ of the borrowed operand (catches dropping the wrong side or too early); a `Vec[String]` field (the drop must drain elements); a comparison inside a loop (per-evaluation drop, no accumulation and no re-free); and a scalar-only struct (the gate must skip it). -- FOUND WHILE BUILDING THAT MATRIX, unrelated to this leak and filed as B-2026-08-12-5: derived equality over a `Vec[String]` field is WRONG in codegen — two vectors with equal contents compare EQUAL under the interpreter and NOT EQUAL under both compiled backends. A false negative, never a false positive; `Vec[i64]` and plain `String` fields are both correct. It reproduces with two struct LOCALS, so it is independent of this fix (which only registers a drop after the result is computed and cannot change a boolean). The Vec-field control here therefore DISCARDS the comparison result instead of asserting it, so this memory fixture cannot fail for a non-memory reason. -- ARM64: per CLAUDE.md this class is not guaranteed architecture-independent; the arm64 leg should confirm. This fix registers an ordinary scope-exit struct drop with no RC or index-assign involvement, the class least likely to be arch-specific.

fix:
FIXED by 9410488b, on top of the gate e0c6bab landed -- but first, the correction
this row needed and the earlier pass could not make without the program:

THE ROW'S PREMISE WAS BACKWARDS, and the error was mine, not the harness's.

It claimed the E2E harness REJECTS source `karac build` accepts. It does not. It
ACCEPTS source `karac build` REJECTS -- the same divergence pointing the other
way, and the worse direction, because it manufactures false coverage rather than
false failure. e0c6bab's investigation reached the right fix while noting the
premise still needed re-measuring "on the same source -- which again needs the
program". The program was recoverable from the session transcript; here it is,
with the answer.

HOW THE WRONG PREMISE GOT WRITTEN. The original combined program used struct
names `SM`/`SS`/`SV`, which trip the Const-class naming rule. I renamed them with
a pattern-list script (`struct SM ` -> `struct Sm `, `Result[SM, E]` -> ..., seven
patterns) that did NOT cover the bare return-type position, so `fn mk_bare() -> SM`
survived while `struct Sm` was declared -- leaving an UNDEFINED TYPE. When I then
went to compare against the CLI, I saved the FULLY-renamed program to disk and
built THAT. So "the CLI compiles it, the harness rejects it" compared two
different programs. The comparison, not the compiler, was the divergence.

THE REAL DEFECT, minimised to four lines:

    struct Sm { a: Map[String, i64] }
    fn mk_bare() -> SM { let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new(); m.insert("k", 1); return Sm { a: m }; }
    fn tm(s: Sm) -> i64 { return s.a.len(); }
    fn main() { println(f"{tm(mk_bare())}"); }

`karac check` / `karac build`: `error[resolve]: undefined type 'SM'`.
`tests/codegen.rs` `run_program`: byte-identical to this row's reported symptom --
"Module verification failed: Function return type does not match operand type of
return inst! ret { ptr } %field / i64 ... %call = call i64 @mk_bare()". Codegen
defaulted the unresolved `SM` to `i64`, declared `mk_bare` as returning `i64`, and
emitted a `{ ptr }` return into it. The verifier's complaint is the symptom; the
undefined type is the cause, and its one-line diagnostic was discarded three
phases earlier.

WHAT THIS COMMIT ADDS ON TOP OF e0c6bab. That commit gated one harness and
grandfathered 39 of the 40 programs it found. This one:

  * WIDENS the gate from 1 call site to all 24 that already call
    `assert_ownership_clean` -- across tests/{codegen,par_codegen,
    memory_sanitizer,coro_e2e,disjoint_differential,http_server}.rs. That call is
    already the marker for "this harness feeds codegen production-shaped input",
    so the two gates belong at the same places. Fallout beyond codegen.rs was one
    test in par_codegen.rs and none elsewhere.
  * FIXES 32 of the 39 grandfathered programs rather than parking them: missing
    `mut` call-site markers (9), single-letter module bindings that are Type-class
    where module `let` needs Const-class (5), `pub fn` returning a private type
    (5), implicit narrowing coercions needing an explicit `as` (5), missing
    `#[derive(Eq)]` (2), refinement narrowing needing the explicit form (2), plus
    `*mut Unit` (an undefined type), unqualified `Some`/`None` resolving to
    builtin `Option` instead of the program's own enum, an unbounded `T` used
    arithmetically, a non-`mut` shared field written through, and a `*mut u8`
    passed where `*const u8` was required.
  * Leaves 6 grandfathered, each with a row: B-2026-08-12-8 (four methods codegen
    implements and typecheck rejects -- those tests were the only thing proving
    the emitters work), B-2026-08-12-9 (the `f64` `sorted` emitter, unreachable
    from valid source under the F64 total-order rule), and one deliberate negative
    test whose whole point is a codegen-layer rejection.

`test_e2e_{size,align}_of_epoll_data_style_union` had been green for months

THE OTHER HALF OF THIS ROW'S CLASS IS ALSO CLOSED. e0c6bab measured that 46 of
the 52 codegen-invoking harnesses in tests/codegen.rs never ran `desugar_program`

b3a1061 fixed it by giving cli.rs and every harness one shared

METHOD NOTE, since this is the second time in two days that a comparison rather
than a compiler produced the finding: when a program "behaves differently" across

Saving a normalised copy for one side and the original for the other is enough to

title: The E2E harnesses guard `parse` errors and then DISCARD `resolve` and `typecheck` errors, while `karac build` stops on either -- so the suite silently ran 39 test programs the shipped compiler REJECTS, and an undefined type reached codegen (defaulted to `i64`) to surface as "Module verification failed: Function return type does not match operand type of return inst!" instead of the one-line `undefined type 'SM'` three phases earlier. Filed with the premise backwards ("the harness rejects source the CLI accepts"); the truth is the reverse and the worse direction -- false coverage, not false failure.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while writing the pin for B-2026-08-11-29. The
intended pin combined that row's seven measured shapes into one program; it
failed in the harness with a module-verification error while the identical
source built and ran correctly through the CLI. The pin was split into one small
program per shape to work around it, which is recorded in that row's fix too.

MEASURED. The program is ~20 lines: five structs (`Sm { a: Map[String,i64] }`,
`Ss { a: Set[String] }`, `Sv { a: Vec[String] }`, `Er { m: Map[..] }`), seven
producer fns (`Result`/`Option`/bare returns over those structs), five consumer
fns, and a `main` that matches each producer.

    karac build            builds, runs, prints the correct 8
    karac run --interp     prints 8
    tests/codegen.rs
      run_program(...)     panics: "codegen failed for test program: Module
                           verification failed: Function return type does not
                           match operand type of return inst!
                             ret { ptr } %field
                            i64Call parameter type does not match function
                            signature!
                             %call118 = call i64 @mk_bare()
                             { ptr }  %call119 = call i64 @tm(i64 %call118)"

So a fn declared to return a struct whose LLVM shape is `{ ptr }` was DECLARED
as returning `i64` in the harness's module, and its call sites were typed to
match the wrong declaration. Both directions of the mismatch appear, which reads
like the function-signature pass ran without the struct's LLVM type registered.

NOT CAUSED BY THE FIX IT WAS FOUND WITH: the CLI compiles the program identically
with and without B-2026-08-11-29's change, and the harness fails with and
without it too.

SHRINKING IT PARTLY WORKS AND IS ITSELF INFORMATIVE. Each shape ALONE passes
through the harness — including `fn mk_bare() -> Sm` plus a `Result[Sm, E]`
producer over the same struct. Dropping the `mk_bare` fn from the combined
program removes one half of the error but leaves `ret { ptr } %field / i64`. So
the trigger is a combination, not one construct, and a proper minimisation is
still owed.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE INCONVENIENCE. `run_program_capturing_inner` carries
comments explaining that the harness deliberately mirrors `karac build` --
ownership is threaded because passing `None` "systematically diverges from
shipped binaries", and ownership-clean is asserted because "the suite tests what
ships". This is the same class of divergence pointing the other way, and it is
worse than a false pass: a shape the compiler handles CANNOT be pinned, so the
E2E suite has a blind spot exactly where someone tries to add coverage. It also
costs debugging time in the wrong place -- the natural first read of a module
verification failure is that the change under test broke codegen.

FIRST PLACE TO LOOK: the harness's pass list (`parse`, `desugar_program`,
`expand_gated_stdlib_imports`, `resolve`, `typecheck`, `lower`, `ownershipcheck`,
`compile_to_object_with_options`) against `karac build`'s, for a pass the CLI
runs that registers struct LLVM types or monomorph instantiations before
function signatures are declared. The error is a DECLARATION-time type, so
ordering is the suspect, not the emitter.
investigation: 2026-08-11: found writing the B-2026-08-11-29 pin. Confirmed the same source builds and runs correctly under `karac build` and `--interp` with AND without that row's fix, so the divergence is the harness's. Each shape passes the harness alone; removing one producer fn removes half the error but not all of it, so the trigger is a combination and the minimisation is still owed. -- 2026-08-12 FOLLOW-UP (second session, taking this row): THE REPORTED PROGRAM COULD NOT BE RECONSTRUCTED, and the row does not carry it. The minimisation the row says is owed is still owed, and cannot be started without the source. Attaching the failing program (or a path to it) is the single thing this row most needs. WHAT WAS RUN. An exact replica of `run_program_capturing_inner`'s pass list (parse -> desugar_program -> expand_gated_stdlib_imports -> resolve -> typecheck -> lower -> ownershipcheck -> compile_to_object_with_options, ownership threaded, concurrency None) was driven over: (a) 420 generated programs combining the eight measured shapes from B-2026-08-11-29's pin -- every subset of size >= 4 of 11 shape fragments, randomized declaration orders, plus the full set in 20 orders, each with the shared `Sm`/`Ss`/`Sv`/`Er` structs and the by-value consumers; (b) 400 real programs (examples/ plus the kata corpus). ZERO module verification failures. So the trigger is NOT the combination of the described shapes as such -- something in the actual program is load-bearing and is not in the row's description. WHAT THE ERROR TEXT DOES PIN DOWN, for whoever has the program. `%field` is the name codegen gives a `build_insert_value` result, so `ret { ptr } %field` is a STRUCT-LITERAL return (`return Sm { a: m }`) from a fn whose LLVM signature says i64 -- i.e. `llvm_return_type` answered i64 for the same struct name that `llvm_param_type` answered `{ ptr }` for on `tm`'s parameter, in the same declaration pass. Both route through `llvm_type_for_type_expr`, so a plain single-segment `Sm` cannot produce both answers: the failing fn's RETURN TYPE EXPRESSION is not a bare known-struct path (an alias, a generic instantiation, a type param, or a name registered after the declaration loop). That is where a minimisation should start. A MECHANISM THAT PRODUCES EXACTLY THIS ERROR CLASS WAS FOUND AND IS NOW GATED -- whether or not it is this row's. `run_program_capturing_inner` asserted ownership-clean but ran `resolve` and `typecheck` only to feed `lower`, throwing their errors away, while `karac build` refuses to reach codegen when either errors (`cli.rs` `has_fatal_errors`). A check-dirty program therefore reached codegen and died in the LLVM verifier: a 5-line duplicate definition reproduces `Module verification failed: Function return type does not match operand type of return inst! ret i64 5 / { ptr }` -- the same shape, and the same "reads as a codegen bug" cost this row is about. The gate (`common::assert_check_clean`) now names the real cause instead. If the combined program was check-dirty in some way `karac build` also rejected, this row's premise (`karac build` compiles it) needs re-measuring on the same source -- which again needs the program. STILL UNADDRESSED, and measured while here: 46 of the 52 codegen-invoking harnesses in `tests/codegen.rs` never run `desugar_program`, and 47 never run `expand_gated_stdlib_imports`, so they resolve the RAW parse tree and compile a different program than `karac build` does. `run_program` is one of the six that do both (in the opposite order from `cli.rs`, which expands before desugaring). That is the same divergence class this row is filed for, on 46 sibling harnesses, and it is untouched. -- 2026-08-12, SAME SESSION, CORRECTION AND CLOSE-OUT OF THE REMAINDER ABOVE: the "46 of the 52 codegen-invoking harnesses in tests/codegen.rs" figure was UNDERCOUNTED and scoped to one file. A per-fn audit over all of `tests/` gives 103 of 109 fns that own a parse tree and feed it to codegen; 96 never ran `desugar_program`, 103 never ran `expand_gated_stdlib_imports`, and none ran the `#[target(...)]` strip. That divergence is now FIXED (B-2026-08-12-6, b3a1061): `karac::prepare_for_resolve` owns the sequence, `cli.rs` `Pipeline::resolve` calls it, and so does every harness. Four probe programs were measured first -- multi-assignment (a resolver `unreachable!()` PANIC), a trait default method, an `impl Trait` parameter, and `#[derive(Default)]` -- each accepted and run correctly by `karac build` while every un-fixed harness rejected it, two of them with a diagnostic that says "this is a codegen bug". THIS ROW STILL STANDS ON ITS OWN CLAIM: none of those four constructs appears in the program it describes, and it used `run_program`, one of the six harnesses that already ran desugar. So the fix does not explain it, and the row stays open pending the source.

fix:
FIXED by c24343b.

The callee now ENTRY-COPIES a by-value `Option`/`Result` param, so the caller
keeps its own value and nothing is zeroed: every pass reads the true variant.
Four parts, all consulting one predicate so the frames cannot drift.

  * `optres_param_entry_copied_te` (param_own.rs) -- the single predicate. It
    delegates to `field_copy_supported`'s `Option`/`Result` arms (which already
    vet BOTH halves of a `Result`; the drop frees whichever is live, so a copy
    that skipped the `Err` half would double-free every error path while every
    `Ok`-only test passed), and then EXCLUDES shared and boxed payloads. As a
    struct FIELD those two are legitimately copyable -- an rc-INC, a fresh
    envelope -- but at a param boundary they already have owners (the rc
    machinery; `boxed_enum_payload_vars` / `boxed_struct_payload_vars`) with
    their own caller-side retraction rules, and an entry copy is a second,
    unsynchronised answer to the same question. Measured: admitting them fails
    20 memory_sanitizer fixtures across the shared-Option, boxed-Option and
    boxed-enum-chain families.
  * `deep_copy_optres_param_in_place` (param_own.rs) -- dispatches exactly as
    `deep_copy_one_aggregate_field` does. No new copy emitters were needed.
  * Caller side (call_dispatch.rs AND method_call.rs) -- both sites that emit
    the arg-site whole-slot zero now skip it on the same predicate, and both
    register a cleanup for a FRESH-TEMP argument via `track_optres_arg_temp`.
    Gating only the free-fn site left a method's caller zeroing a slot the
    callee no longer took over.
  * REGISTER BEFORE COPY (functions.rs) -- the ordering is load-bearing, and
    finding out why is what unblocked this row after the first attempt failed.

THE ORDERING BUG, which is the whole story of the failed first attempt. Both
inline-payload trackers zero-init the slot in the entry block when they believe
they are registering from a NESTED scope, so a `let` whose store may never
execute (loop body skipped, branch not taken) cannot leave the cleanup arm
reading `undef` as a tag. Their test for "nested" is `insert block != entry
block`. Emitting the entry copy FIRST splits the entry block and leaves the
builder in the copy's merge block, so the trackers concluded they were nested
and planted a whole-slot `zeroinitializer` before entry's terminator -- ahead of
both the copy's own payload reads and the body's first read of the param. Every
matching callee then returned the `Err`/`None` arm on the FIRST call.

A param slot is never the shape that defensive zero is for: it is initialised
unconditionally by the incoming argument store. Registering while the builder is
still at entry says exactly that, and needs no new flag or gate.

THE FRESH-TEMP HALF. Once the callee copies, a temp argument has no owner at
all -- the callee frees its copy and the original leaks, which is
B-2026-08-11-30's leak reappearing through the other door. `track_optres_arg_temp`
spills the value to an entry alloca and registers the same inline-payload
cleanups a `let` of it would get, so the free carries the drop machinery's own
`cap > 0` / tag guards and an `Err`/`None` temp is a no-op rather than a wild
free. Identifier arguments are excluded: their let-site registration already
owns the value and now fires, so owning one here would be the double free the
zero used to prevent.

VERIFIED. Values correct on AOT -O0, AOT -O2, JIT and interpreter for `Result`
and `Option`, with a scalar half and with a user-enum half. The full
B-2026-08-11-30 -O0 valgrind matrix stays clean in both directions: all seven
previously-leaking shapes at zero, and all fourteen controls (arg-match,
let-match, discard, inline-match, bare-struct, bare-Vec, user-enum, let-unused,
double-pass and double-pass-with-match) clean. B-2026-08-11-30's own repros stay
green, so the leak fix is preserved rather than traded away.

The row's `#[ignore]` is lifted: `e2e_repeated_by_value_optres_arg_reads_wrong_variant`
(tests/codegen.rs) is now a passing regression pin.

REMAINING SCOPE, recorded rather than papered over. `take(Some(x))` where `x` is
a live local is excluded from the temp registration by the freshness gate above,
so that spelling keeps B-2026-08-11-30's leak. Excluding it is what stops the
self-host double free, and a leak is the safe direction; closing it needs the
caller to know whether the ctor's payload move already retracted `x`'s own
cleanup, which is a separate question from this row's.
title: Passing a by-value `Option`/`Result` argument TWICE makes every call after the first read the WRONG VARIANT -- `Err`/`None` for a value that is still `Ok`/`Some`. The caller's pass-as-arg move cap-zeros a binding it still owns, on a destination-takes-ownership assumption that holds for `v.push(r)` but not for a plain call. AOT and JIT both wrong, interpreter correct; a user enum in the same shape is correct everywhere.
tracker: Same root cause as B-2026-08-11-30 (caller retracts, callee bails) surfacing as a wrong answer rather than a leak. The fix design in that row -- callee-owned entry deep-copy plus dropping the caller-side retraction for a plain-call argument -- fixes both; neither half is safe alone.
detail:
Measured on a `Result[Vec[String], E]` and its `Option` twin:

    let r = Ok(mkv());        // mkv() returns a 2-element Vec[String]
    println(takr(r));         // 2   correct
    println(takr(r));         // -1  WRONG -- the Err arm
    println(takr(r));         // -1  WRONG

where `fn takr(r: Result[Vec[String], E]) -> i64 { match r { Ok(v) => v.len(), Err(_e) => -1 } }`.
The interpreter prints 2 every time. Identical on the `Option` twin (`None` from
the second call onward). A user enum `W.Full(Vec[String])` in the same shape is
correct on both backends.

    backend             1st call   2nd call
    AOT -O0             2          -1
    AOT -O2             2          -1
    JIT (`karac run`)   2          -1
    interpreter         2           2

NOT A DIAGNOSABLE MISUSE. Kara's move-checker deliberately does not reject
double-consume or use-after-move -- `src/codegen/param_own.rs` says so outright
under "Why not move-by-default", and the whole caller-retains model is built on
`take(x); take(x)` being legal and working. So this is a silent wrong answer in
a program the compiler accepts, in an intentionally-supported shape.

CAUSE, read off the emitted IR rather than inferred.
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` (`src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs`,
gated `!borrow_skip && !call_arg_flows_into_return`) emits, for a by-value
binding argument:

    %r1 = load { i64 x 6 }, ptr %r
    store { i64 x 6 } zeroinitializer, ptr %r      <- the WHOLE slot, tag included
    call void @take({ i64 x 6 } %r1)

It is a MOVE marker, and its own comment states the invariant it rests on: the
whole-slot zero "only balances when some other frame takes the box over". For a
container destination (`v.push(r)`) one does. For a plain call the destination
is a by-value parameter, and `make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst`
(`src/codegen/param_own.rs`) BAILS on `Option`/`Result` -- so nothing took it
over and the zeroing is pure corruption of a binding the caller still holds.
Because the TAG is zeroed along with the payload, every later read takes the
`Err`/`None` arm; the effect is not confined to the drop.

(An earlier reading of this row blamed the cap-word-only
`suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup_for_moved_arg` in control_flow_match.rs.
That suppressor exists and does cap-zero, but it fires only at container-insert
destinations and at a `let p = o;` rebind -- never at a plain call. Zeroing the
cap alone would not move the tag, which is what the measured `Err` result rules
it out by.)

The leak in B-2026-08-11-30 is the same split seen from the other side: there
the retraction loses the payload entirely, here it corrupts what the caller
still holds. Both disappear under that row's entry-deep-copy fix, which makes
the callee own a COPY and lets the caller keep -- and correctly free -- its
original.

REPRO: `e2e_repeated_by_value_optres_arg_reads_wrong_variant` in
`tests/codegen.rs`, `#[ignore]`d, asserting the interpreter's answer. Red today
with left `2/-1/2/-1` against right `2/2/2/2`.

FIRST FIX ATTEMPT 2026-08-12 -- BUILT, MEASURED, REVERTED. The approach
B-2026-08-11-30 prescribed (callee-owned ENTRY DEEP-COPY plus dropping the
caller-side arg zero) is not sufficient, and the reason is a third party neither
row had in view. Recording it in full because the wiring is correct and the
blocker is specific -- the next attempt should start from the blocker, not from
the design.

WHAT WAS BUILT (three parts, compiles clean, no new machinery needed):

  * `optres_param_entry_copied_te` (param_own.rs) -- ONE predicate both frames
    consult, delegating to `field_copy_supported`'s existing `Option`/`Result`
    arms. Those arms already vet BOTH halves of a `Result`, which is the
    non-obvious requirement here: the registered payload drop frees whichever
    half is live, so a copy that skipped the `Err` half would double-free every
    program that takes an error path while every `Ok`-only test passed.
  * `deep_copy_optres_param_in_place` (param_own.rs) -- dispatches exactly as
    `deep_copy_one_aggregate_field` does (`result_field_struct_enum_payload_ok`
    picks the struct/enum copier, else the inline-halves one). The copy emitters
    all already exist.
  * `callee_optres_param_entry_copied` (call_dispatch.rs) -- method-aware
    callee lookup, suppressing the arg-site whole-slot zero on the same answer.

WHAT IT DID. Memory: CLEAN on every shape measured -- all seven previously
leaking shapes and all the controls, at -O0 under valgrind. Values: BROKEN for
any callee that MATCHES its param. `takr(r)` returned the `Err` arm on the FIRST
call, not just the second, so the copy made the miscompile worse rather than
fixing it.

THE TRAP THIS SITS IN, and the reason it nearly read as a success: those
wrong-answer shapes are valgrind-CLEAN. A callee whose match now takes the `Err`
arm never touches the payload, so nothing leaks and nothing double-frees -- the
whole memory matrix goes green while the program computes the wrong answer.
Verifying this row with ASAN/valgrind alone would confirm a broken fix. It is the
same vacuous-green class that let the -O2 dead-allocation artifact mislead three
passes of B-2026-08-11-30; the value pins are the gate here, not the memory ones.

THE BLOCKER, located. `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move`
(control_flow_match.rs:8346) is the ONLY emitter of a whole-slot zero into a
slot in codegen -- but it has FOURTEEN call sites, not the one arg-loop site the
earlier passes assumed. Two of them are RECEIVER-side (calls.rs:3096 and :3319,
plus method_call.rs:5720) and resolve the receiver through
`passthrough_owner_alias`. So inside the callee, compiling `v.len()` -- where
`v` is the match arm's binding of the param's payload -- disarms `r`, the PARAM,
by zeroing its whole slot. Baseline `takr` emits no such store; with the entry
copy it emits one, in `entry`, ahead of the match's scrutinee load.

Why the copy flips it: that suppressor bails when the source is in
`inline_optres_retained_sources` ("a source a read-only match left OWNING its
payload has no other owner to hand off to"). The entry copy changes the arm's
ownership classification off that set, so a disarm that correctly declined
before now fires -- against a param whose buffer is the callee's own copy, not
the caller's.

LEAD FOR THE NEXT ATTEMPT, untested: an entry-copied `Option`/`Result` param is
precisely a source whose arm owns a buffer no other frame can free, so it looks
like it belongs in `inline_optres_retained_sources` (or an equivalent gate on
those receiver-side suppressors) for the duration of the callee. Establish that
FIRST, with a value assertion, before re-landing the copy -- the copy itself was
never the problem.
investigation: 2026-08-12. Found while re-characterising B-2026-08-11-30: `take(r); take(r)` was run as a double-free SAFETY check for a candidate fix, came back clean, and printed 20 where 40 was expected. Narrowed to the variant tag rather than an emptied payload by printing each call separately, then confirmed across AOT -O0/-O2, JIT and interpreter, and on the Option twin. The user-enum control is correct everywhere, which points at the same Option/Result bail the leak turns on. Correction: first attributed to the cap-word suppressor in control_flow_match.rs; reading main's IR showed the emitter is suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move in call_dispatch.rs, which zeroes the whole slot including the tag -- which is what makes the read come back Err rather than merely empty. 2026-08-12 first fix attempt: built the entry-copy design B-2026-08-11-30 prescribed (shared copy-supported predicate, copy dispatch mirroring the field path, caller-side gate on the arg zero). Memory-clean on every shape but values broken for matching callees -- the first call already returns Err -- and those broken shapes are valgrind-clean, so the memory matrix cannot see it. Traced to suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move's RECEIVER-side call sites (calls.rs:3096/3319), which resolve through passthrough_owner_alias and disarm the param when the arm binding is used; the copy moves the arm off inline_optres_retained_sources so a disarm that previously declined now fires. Reverted; the copy machinery was never the problem.

title: A union or `#[derive(Copy)]` struct with a RAW POINTER field is rejected as not-`Copy` by the one rule whose own suggestion is "hold it behind a raw pointer (`*mut T` / `*const T`)" -- `is_type_copy` has no `Type::Pointer` arm, so it falls through to `false`. This blocks the canonical `epoll_data` FFI union (`union EpollData { ptr: *mut u8, fd: i32, ... }`), which is the shape the union feature exists to express.
detail:
MEASURED. `karac check` on

    #[repr(C)] union EpollData { ptr: *mut u8, fd: i32, u32val: u32, u64val: u64 }
    fn main() { println(align_of[EpollData]()); }

emitted `error[E_UNION_FIELD_NOT_COPY]: union field `EpollData.ptr` has type
`*mut u8`, which is not `Copy` ... Replace the type with a `Copy` equivalent or
hold it behind a raw pointer (`*mut T` / `*const T`)` -- advice the program had
already followed. Both pointer forms are affected (`*const T` and `*mut T`), and
because `is_type_copy` also backs `validate_derive_copy`, `#[derive(Copy)] struct
Handle { p: *mut u8, tag: i64 }` was rejected identically.

Raw pointers carry no ownership and have no destructor, which is precisely the
property the union rule needs -- so the missing arm is a plain omission, not a
deliberate conservatism.

SOURCE NOTE: found by the B-2026-08-11-34 check gate. Two E2E tests
(`test_e2e_{size,align}_of_epoll_data_style_union`) had been exercising this
union shape for months and passing, because the harness discarded typecheck
errors -- the emitter was correct all along and only the frontend rejected it.
The tests were also written against `*mut Unit`, an undefined type, which the
same gate surfaced.
investigation: 2026-08-12: reproduced through `karac check` (not just the harness), confirmed both `*const`/`*mut` and both the union rule and `#[derive(Copy)]` validation share the predicate. Fixed by adding the `Type::Pointer { .. } => true` arm to `is_type_copy`.
fix: FIXED by 9410488b -- added a `Type::Pointer { .. } => true` arm to `is_type_copy` (src/typechecker/derives.rs). Pinned by `test_e2e_union_and_struct_raw_pointer_fields_are_copy` in tests/codegen.rs, which covers both pointer spellings in a union AND a `#[derive(Copy, Clone)]` struct holding a `*mut u8`; verified to fail pre-fix with the E_UNION_FIELD_NOT_COPY pair and pass post-fix.

title: Four methods that CODEGEN FULLY IMPLEMENTS are rejected by the typechecker, so `karac build` refuses programs the backend demonstrably compiles and runs: `Vec.iter_mut()`, `Set.clear()`, `Column.range()`, and `.collect()` on a direct `Vec` receiver. Each has a green E2E test proving the emitter works; each fails `karac check` with "no method 'X' on type 'Y'".
investigation: 2026-08-12: surfaced by the B-2026-08-11-34 check gate; each confirmed against `karac check` directly so the finding does not depend on the harness.
fix: 9f4fc14 (three registrations — Set.clear in stdlib_map.rs plus a MISSING interpreter arm in method_call_set.rs, range at both reduce dispatch sites in expr_method_call.rs, iter_mut in expr_method_call.rs yielding `mut ref T` — and one test correction, since `.collect()` on a bare Vec is a deliberate rejection rather than a gap; all four removed from CHECK_GATE_GRANDFATHERED)

tracker: Vec[f64].sorted / Iterator.max / Iterator.min vs the F64 total-order rule
title: The `f64` sort/max/min emitters are UNREACHABLE from any valid program: the F64 total-order rule rejects `Vec[f64].sorted()` / `.max()` / `.min()` at typecheck, so the codegen paths two E2E tests cover can never run in a shipped binary. Either the emitter is dead code to retire or the rule is stricter than intended -- open design call, not a defect report.
detail:
MEASURED. `karac check` on `let fs: Vec[f64] = f.sorted();` fails with
"Vec.sorted(): element type 'f64' has no total order ... Use the total-order
wrapper `F64`". Same for `Iterator.max()` / `.min()` over an `f64` element type.
The rule is deliberate and well-argued (its diagnostic explains the NaN
wrong-answer failure mode in detail).

The consequence is narrower than the rule: `test_e2e_vec_sorted_immutable_returns_new_vec`
asserts on an emitter no user can invoke. (The sibling `.max()`/`.min()` case in
`test_e2e_iter_chain_reduce_float_and_narrow_int_payload` was fixed in e0c6bab by
routing those legs through `F64`; only `sorted` remains.) The sanctioned replacement is not a drop-in either --
`Vec[F64]` typechecks, but `println(f.max().unwrap_or(F64.from(0.0)))` then fails
CODEGEN with "Display of a struct argument is supported when the argument is a
variable or field access", so the wrapper path has its own rough edge at the
print site.

It is grandfathered in `CHECK_GATE_GRANDFATHERED` rather than
deleted: dropping the assertion would remove the only evidence of what that
emitter does, and choosing between "retire the emitter" and "relax the rule" is a
design decision.
 -- RESOLVED 2026-08-12 in 2768ad1, and NOT by either branch of the design call the row posed. The premise — "UNREACHABLE from any valid program" — is REFUTED, so "retire the emitter vs relax the rule" was a choice between two wrong answers. -- THE EMITTER IS REACHABLE. B-2026-08-11-7's gate reads the element type at the CALL SITE, so a generic slips past it: `fn gsorted[T](v: ref Vec[T]) -> Vec[T] { v.sorted() }` instantiated at `T = f64` passes `karac check`, compiles, and runs on all three backends. (This is the hole recorded in B-2026-08-11-7's own close — a `Vec[f64]` laundered through a generic sorts unchecked — now shown to be load-bearing rather than theoretical.) Retiring the emitter would have broken that program; the test was never vacuous. -- WHAT IT ACTUALLY DID THERE was worse than being dead. The comparator used `OLT`/`OGT`, the ORDERED IEEE predicates: with a NaN both are false, so EVERY comparison involving one returned 0, "equal". That is an INTRANSITIVE comparator, not a misplaced NaN, and the merge sort on top returns the input essentially untouched. Measured through the generic on `[2.0, NaN, 1.0]`: compiled backends `2 NaN 1`, interpreter `1 2 NaN`. So the row's low-severity "dead code bookkeeping" framing was hiding a silent wrong answer AND a run-vs-build divergence — the latter NEWLY CREATED by B-2026-08-11-17, which made the interpreter's float ordering total and left codegen on the partial one. Two of my own changes interacting; neither review caught it, the generic probe did. -- FIX: the same total order everything else already uses — the `TotalFloatScalar` key directly below it in the same match, `karac_float_cmp`, the interpreter's `value_compare`, and `sort_by_key`'s sanctioned float-key concession — with NaN canonicalized first so the result cannot depend on a NaN's sign or provenance (B-2026-08-11-13 / -17). f32 keeps its own 32-bit key rather than widening: exact, and no conversion in the inner loop. -- THIS IS NOT A RELAXATION OF THE RULE, which matters for anyone reading it as license to allow `Vec[f64].sort()`. design.md § Float semantics still says `f64` is not `Ord` and the front-end gate still rejects the direct call. The gate states the LANGUAGE RULE; the comparator states WHAT THE MACHINE DOES when the rule is bypassed. Defense in depth — the two are not alternatives, which is precisely what the design-call framing got wrong. -- THE TEST IS UN-GRANDFATHERED RATHER THAN DELETED OR LEFT EXEMPT: its float leg now goes through the generic, so the whole program passes `karac check`, the entry is removed from CHECK_GATE_GRANDFATHERED, and it pins a path a user can actually reach — plus a NaN case that fails loudly if the comparator ever reverts to intransitive. -- REMAINING, deliberately not changed: the generic hole itself. Closing it means re-checking element bounds at monomorphization, which is a real front-end change with its own blast radius; with the comparator now correct, a program that slips through gets a DEFINED, interpreter-matching answer instead of garbage, so the hole is no longer a correctness hazard. `max`/`min` are NOT reachable the same way — a bare `T` fails the numeric-or-String element check — so only `sort`/`sorted` needed this.

title: Implicit narrowing to a refinement type works for an INTEGER literal but not for a FLOAT or STRING literal, and the diagnostic then states something false: `let b: PositivePrice = 2.5;` is rejected with "the value is not a compile-time constant" -- `2.5` plainly is one. Same for `"widget"` against a `String where self.len() >= 1` refinement.
detail:
MEASURED. With

    pub type PositivePrice = f64 where self > 0.0;
    pub type PositiveQty  = i64 where self > 0;
    pub type BoundedText  = String where self.len() >= 1;

`let a: PositiveQty = 3;` is ACCEPTED (the predicate is folded at build time),
while `let b: PositivePrice = 2.5;` and `let c: BoundedText = "widget";` are both
rejected with E_REFINEMENT_IMPLICIT_NARROWING and the reason "the value is not a
compile-time constant, so its predicate cannot be checked at build time".

Two distinct problems, worth separating if this is picked up:
  1. The constant-predicate evaluator handles integer literals only, so float and
     string literals lose an implicit narrowing that is decidable at build time.
  2. Independently of whether (1) is fixed, the MESSAGE is wrong on these inputs.
     A literal is a compile-time constant; if the evaluator cannot handle its
     base type, the diagnostic should say that rather than assert something the
     user can see is untrue.

The explicit forms the message recommends do work (`2.5 as PositivePrice`), so
this is a papercut plus a false statement, not a blocker -- hence low.

SOURCE NOTE: found via the B-2026-08-11-34 check gate, which surfaced two E2E
tests (`e2e_refinement_typed_struct_fields_layout`,
`e2e_refinement_alias_collection_method_and_iteration`) whose programs `karac
build` rejects. Those test programs were fixed to the explicit `as` form; this
row is the compiler-side remainder.
investigation: 2026-08-12: reproduced standalone through `karac check` with one refinement alias per base type, isolating that the integer arm folds and the float/string arms do not.
fix:
FIXED by 4ecd716.

Both halves, and the float half turned out to be three missing pieces rather
than one.

PROBLEM 1 -- float narrowing. `eval_const_expr_with_chain` (typechecker/items.rs)
had arms for `Integer`, `Bool`, `CharLit` and `ByteLit` but none for `Float`, so
a float literal fell to `NonConstShape` and lost an elision that was always
decidable. Adding the arm alone was not enough:

  * `apply_comparison` (typechecker/const_eval.rs) had no `F32`/`F64` pair, so
    the folded value could not be compared against the predicate's literal. Uses
    `partial_cmp` and reports a NaN operand as INCOMPARABLE rather than silently
    answering `false`, which keeps a NaN-bearing predicate on the runtime path
    instead of admitting or rejecting it on a made-up answer.
  * `apply_unary`'s `Neg` arm covered only integers, so a NEGATIVE float literal
    still did not fold. That was the row's sharpest symptom once found: `-3`
    against the `i64` twin already reported the accurate
    E_REFINEMENT_PREDICATE_VIOLATION while `-2.5` against the `f64` one reported
    "not a compile-time constant".
  * `infer_operand_target_ty` named a type only for SUFFIXED integer literals,
    so `0.5f32 < 1.0` folded `F32` against `F64` and read as incomparable. It
    now does the same for suffixed float literals, and reaches through a unary
    minus -- which the integer arm never needed, because a negative integer
    literal arrives already folded.

`f16`/`bf16` are deliberately left out: `ConstValue` has no half-precision
variant, and widening to `f32` would fold predicates at a precision the runtime
does not use. They keep today's behaviour.

The whole float addition is ADDITIVE: the evaluator never produced `F32`/`F64`
before, so no existing reduction changes -- it only stops failing on a shape it
could always have folded.

PROBLEM 2 -- the false message. The rejection used one fixed sentence, "the
value is not a compile-time constant", which is simply untrue of a string
literal. The reason is now chosen from what was actually established, so the
diagnostic never asserts something the user can see is false:

    value reduced, predicate did not     -> "the value is a compile-time constant
                                             but its `where` predicate could not
                                             be evaluated at build time"
    written as a LITERAL, did not reduce -> "the value is a literal, but the
                                             build-time predicate evaluator does
                                             not yet support `String` constants"
    anything else                        -> the original wording, which is
                                             accurate for a genuine runtime value

REMAINDER, not fixed and recorded rather than implied: STRING literals still do
not const-elide. That needs a `ConstValue::Str` variant plus const evaluation of
`self.len()`, and `ConstValue` is shared with const generics, the interpreter and
codegen -- a materially larger change than this row's papercut, and one whose
blast radius is the const-generic parameter surface. The existing boundary test
`refinement_elision_string_literal_needs_explicit_construction` still pins the
rejection; what changed there is only that the message is now true.

PINS: `refinement_elision_float_literal_is_const_elided` (both directions --
admitted values elide, violating ones report PREDICATE_VIOLATION rather than the
narrowing rejection, which is what shows the value was folded rather than waved
through; covers `f64`, suffixed `f32`, and the negated literal) and
`refinement_elision_rejection_message_is_not_false` (asserts the string case no
longer claims a literal is not a constant, and that a genuine runtime value
still gets the original accurate wording).

FIXED by 9b2f5ad. `builtin_opaque_ptr_handle` is the single table both entry points consult, so the same type cannot lower to `ptr` through one and `i64` through the other. `KARAC_STRICT_TYPE_LOWERING=1` reports any remaining unknown name at the point of the decision, filtering generic parameters (user program + baked stdlib) so it is quiet on `hello world` and fires on 16 of 2906 E2E programs.
title: Codegen's TWO type-lowering entry points kept two hand-maintained lists of built-in handle types and DISAGREED: `llvm_type_for_type_expr` answered `ptr` for `Map` / `Set` / `SortedMap` / `SortedSet` / `File` / `Request` / `Sender` / `Receiver` / `Channel`, while `llvm_type_for_name` -- reached whenever the type is named WITHOUT generic args (a bare annotation, a `var_type_names` entry, a struct-field type name) -- fell through to the silent `i64` default for the same names. Latent on x86-64 (both 8 bytes), a real mis-size on wasm32 (`ptr` is 4).
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by instrumenting the `i64` fall-through while looking for B-2026-08-11-34's mechanism. That row closed in parallel (9410488b) once its program was recovered from the session transcript, and its root cause is EXACTLY this fall-through: `fn mk_bare() -> SM` where `SM` was an UNDEFINED TYPE, defaulted to `i64`, declared into `mk_bare`'s signature, then contradicted by the `{ ptr }` its body returns. MEASURED on that four-line repro: with the lever OFF codegen emits the row's error BYTE FOR BYTE (`ret { ptr } %field / i64 ... %call = call i64 @mk_bare()`); with it ON the answer is ``type name `SM` has no known LLVM layout``. So the lever is the missing diagnostic for that row's whole class, demonstrated against the real program rather than argued. -- THE FALLBACK HAS A HISTORY: its own neighbouring comments record four prior bugs of exactly this shape, each patched by adding ONE name arm after being bitten -- `char` Map keys sizing 8-byte slots for 4-byte keys, `Slice` mis-sizing a 16-byte header into 8, `VecDeque` writing a 24-byte aggregate into an 8-byte slot and corrupting the neighbouring alloca, and B-2026-06-07-2 (`TcpListener` / `TcpStream` / `WebSocket` by-value params, which the LLVM verifier caught as `Call parameter type does not match function signature`). Two lists is what let the same type have two answers. -- MEASURED over the whole `tests/codegen.rs` corpus (2906 programs) with the fall-through instrumented: only 18 distinct names reach it, so it is a small enumerable set rather than a hot path. -- THE FIX is one table, `builtin_opaque_ptr_handle`, consulted by BOTH entry points; the `TypeExpr` path's nine separate `if name == "..."` arms collapse into a single consult and their per-type rationale moves to the table's doc. User shadowing is unaffected: the name path checks `shared_types` / `struct_types` / `union_types` / `enum_layouts` FIRST, and the `TypeExpr` path keeps B-2026-08-08-10's `user_shadowed_prelude_types` guard (all 14 names are in `PRELUDE_TYPES`, so both halves of that guard cover them). -- PLUS A LEVER, `KARAC_STRICT_TYPE_LOWERING=1`, which panics naming the type instead of silently lowering it to `i64`. The silent default STAYS the default because a generic parameter with no active substitution legitimately reaches it; the lever filters those out via `declared_generic_param_names`, collected from the user program AND the baked stdlib programs (without the stdlib half, `T` fires on `hello world`). This is the diagnostic the class has never had: today the wrong type is baked into a function's DECLARED signature and only surfaces hundreds of lines later as `Module verification failed: Function return type does not match operand type of return inst!`, with nothing naming the type or the source line -- how both B-2026-08-08-10 and B-2026-08-11-34 read.

fix:
FIXED by 75fbfc0. Three of the six resolved, three measured and left alone.

REAL BUG -- `Expr`. `declare_enums` asks for a shared enum's own LLVM layout
while computing that same enum's drop kind: `Expr.Blk(Block)` where `struct
Block { tail: Option[Expr] }` walks to "is the Option payload boxed?" -> "how
wide is `Expr`?", and at that moment `Expr` is not in `shared_types` yet, so the
answer came from the unknown-name `i64` default. Right only by coincidence -- a
shared handle and an `i64` are both one word -- which is also why NO behavioural
test can distinguish the two, and why the guard had to be the lever rather than
an output assertion. Fixed with a name-only `shared_type_names` set collected
before any layout pass and consulted alongside `shared_types`; being shared is a
name-level property, so a name set built first is sufficient -- the same
argument `build_struct_types` already makes for its own `shared_struct_names`
pre-pass, which exists for the identical forward-reference reason.

LEVER PRECISION -- `E`. Not a type at all: the generic parameter of the baked
`Result[T, E]` declaration, reaching the default on any program that calls a
Result combinator. The generic-name filter scanned the USAGE-GATED stdlib set,
which excludes the prelude-baked declarations; it now scans every baked program.
Confirmed benign first: `and_then` over a `Result[i64, String]` builds and
matches the interpreter on both arms, and `map_err` over a String `E` is refused
by codegen outright, so the `E` width never decided anything.

KNOWN TYPE READING AS UNKNOWN -- `Unit`. Written as a name throughout the baked
stdlib (`-> Unit`, `Result[Unit, IoError]`) with no declaration anywhere. Given
an explicit arm returning the same `i64` the `TypeKind::Tuple(&[])` arm already
produces, so no layout changes -- it stops a KNOWN type reading as an unknown
one, which is what the lever needs to stay honest.

NOT DEFECTS. `ParBlockInfo` / `TaskInfo` are a deliberate v1 placeholder that
`stmts.rs` documents in situ -- "using `i64` as a placeholder element type keeps
Vec dispatch working for the v1 contract surface (`.len()` / `.is_empty()`
ignore element type). Field access is a v1.x follow-up that requires registering
the baked struct types." The audit found the documented deferral, not a bug.

`JsonError`'s width query is likewise benign: it comes from
`nested_boxed_enum_payload_variants` off the `let r = Json.parse(..)` binding,
and nothing materialises the payload by layout because the only operation that
would -- field access -- is refused first. Opaque propagation of a parse error
was verified to match the interpreter on both arms. But that refusal is itself a
real run-vs-build gap, so it is SPLIT OUT rather than buried here.

PINNED by a subprocess CLI test (`strict_type_lowering_is_quiet_on_a_recursive_
shared_enum`) -- the lever is an env var and `cargo test` shares one process, so
an in-process setting would leak into whatever else is compiling concurrently.
Verified non-vacuous: dropping the `shared_type_names` consult alone makes it
fail with ``type name `Expr```.

MEASURED: the corpus audit goes from 16 firing tests over 6 names to 4 over 3,
and the 4 that remain are the two documented placeholders plus the split-out

tracker: repeated assignment from the same already-moved place
title: Assigning TWICE from the same already-moved-out place (`cur = box[0].s;` … `cur = box[0].s;`) leaks that buffer: the first assignment cap-zeroes the source into `cur`, so on the second both source and target carry cap 0 and neither frees it. `karac check` accepts the program -- the second read of a moved-out place is not flagged as a use-after-move.
detail:
MEASURED under valgrind on the B-2026-08-12-4 fix (3e8d8fa9):

    struct S { s: String }
    fn main() {
        let mut box_: Vec[S] = Vec.new();
        let mut nm = String.new(); nm.push_str("region");
        box_.push(S { s: nm });
        let mut cur = String.new();
        cur = box_[0].s; println(cur);
        cur = box_[0].s; println(cur);
    }

    output              region / region   (CORRECT)
    valgrind            definitely lost: 8 bytes in 1 blocks
    karac check         All checks passed.

The buffer loses its owner rather than gaining a second one: after the first
assignment the source field is cap-zeroed and `cur` owns it; the second
assignment stores the source's now-cap-0 header over `cur`, so at scope exit
neither the element nor `cur` frees it.

NOT A REGRESSION FROM B-2026-08-12-4 -- the same program leaked the same 8 bytes
before that fix, and is strictly better than the pre-B-2026-08-11-25 behaviour
(double free). It is split out here because that row's fix deliberately does NOT
address it: the alias guard makes this case a no-op precisely so it stays a leak
rather than becoming a use-after-free, which is what the unguarded fix produced
(garbage on the second read, two invalid reads under valgrind).

TWO PLAUSIBLE FIXES, and they are not the same call:
  1. CODEGEN -- when the alias guard fires, preserve the target's original cap
     in the stored value instead of neutralizing it, so `cur` retains ownership.
     Correct and leak-free, but it makes a use-after-move silently work.
  2. OWNERSHIP -- flag the second read of a moved-out place, which is what the
     program actually is. `karac check` is silent on it today, and that silence
     is arguably the more important half.

The leak is bounded by the number of repeated re-reads of one moved place (one
buffer per extra read), so it does not accumulate in a loop over DISTINCT
elements -- the shape B-2026-08-12-4 fixed.
investigation: 2026-08-12: found while guarding the B-2026-08-12-4 fix against the aliasing case it exposed. Confirmed the same leak on the pre-fix tree, so it predates that change; confirmed `karac check` passes.
fix:
FIXED by eef6e980.

Suppressing the free was necessary but not sufficient. B-2026-08-12-4's alias
guard stopped the displaced-value free from reclaiming the buffer about to be
stored back -- without it the second read returns garbage -- but it neutralized
the slot header and then let the store put the SOURCE's header over it, and the
source had been cap-zeroed by the first assignment. So both source and target
ended up carrying `cap == 0` and neither freed the buffer at scope exit: the read
was correct and the ownership was gone.

`keep_aliased_slot_ownership` (src/codegen/runtime.rs) now does both halves --
neutralize the slot so every free below no-ops, AND carry the target's own `cap`
across into the value being stored, so the target stays the single owner it was
before the aliasing assignment. One `icmp` and three `select`s, on a path that
already loads the header. A non-struct incoming value (no `{ptr,len,cap}` to
compare) is returned untouched.

MEASURED on the row's own program, same tree, under valgrind: `definitely lost:
8 bytes in 1 blocks` before, clean after, with the printed content correct in
both. Ten shapes re-checked clean and correct afterwards, including 100 repeated
reads of one element, a `Vec[i64]` field re-read three times, and an interleaved
distinct/repeated sequence through one target.

THE PIN READS TWO ELEMENTS' WORTH, NOT ONE ELEMENT TWICE, and that distinction is
the whole reason this row existed separately. The leak is one buffer per element
that gets RE-READ, so re-reading a single element 100 times still leaks exactly
one block -- and one leaked block can sit in a stale stack slot and read to LSan
as still-reachable, which is precisely how B-2026-08-12-4 stayed invisible under
ASAN while valgrind reported it every run.
`asan_repeated_place_field_move_assign_keeps_one_owner` reads 150 elements twice
each: 2192 bytes in 137 allocations pre-fix, clean post-fix.

`test_e2e_repeated_place_field_move_assign_reads_correctly` gained two legs: a
`Vec[i64]` field re-read three times, where a wrong restored capacity would show
up in the ELEMENTS rather than the header, and an interleaved
distinct/repeated sequence, where a missed free leaks and an unguarded free reads
back garbage -- the two failure modes on either side of this guard.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, deliberately: `karac check` still accepts the program.
Reading a place that has been moved out of is a use-after-move, and the ownership
checker is silent on it -- the row named that as the second of two plausible
fixes and it is the one still open. This commit took the codegen half because
`UseAfterMove` is advisory by design (non-fatal, `.clone()`-suggesting, compiles),
so the backend has to produce something sound for the shape either way; a
diagnostic would warn but would not stop the leak. The diagnostic remains worth
adding on its own merits.

FIXED by 8268903. `seed_builtin_struct_types` now seeds `JsonError`'s layout,
field names and field type names -- exactly the way `Response` and `HttpError`,
the two other baked stdlib structs whose values codegen hand-rolls, are already
seeded. With a layout to GEP, the Err binding's fields resolve and the compiled
binary matches the interpreter.

THE INTEGER FIELDS ARE SEEDED `i64`, NOT THE DECLARED `u32`, and that is
load-bearing rather than sloppy: `json.rs`'s `Build Result.Err(JsonError { line,
column, message })` packs `line` / `column` into the widened Result's `w0` /
`w1` as FULL WORDS (`zext` from the runtime's u32). The seeded layout has to
describe what is actually built, not what the source declares -- seeding `i32`
would put the field GEPs half a word out of step with the packing. The same
as-built-not-as-declared rule the `Response` seed already follows for its hidden
`headers` field.

VERIFIED against the `--interp` oracle across the three positions that resolve a
field differently, all byte-identical: a bare read (`println(e.line)`), an
f-string interpolation (`f"col={e.column}"`), and the whole struct passed BY
VALUE to a fn that reads two fields (`describe(e)`). The Ok arm and a second
successful parse in the same program are unaffected.

PINNED by `e2e_json_parse_error_fields_are_readable`, which covers all three
positions plus the `message` String -- exercised by LENGTH rather than content,
so the pin does not encode serde_json's wording and will not churn on a crate
bump. Verified non-vacuous: disabling the seed alone makes it fail with the
original `cannot resolve field 'line' ... this is a compiler gap`.

THE MESSAGE LEAK IS SPLIT OUT, NOT FIXED, and is now measured rather than
