A `Map`/`Set`/`Tensor` value IS a pointer and the closure ABI passes it directly, so registering the param as a borrow adds a second load and hands the runtime the control block's first WORD as a pointer.
tracker: the closure param registration in src/codegen/closures.rs: `ref_params` / `signature_ref_params` make `load_variable` deref, which is correct for every other `ref` param and wrong for a `builtin_opaque_ptr_handle`.
detail:
FOUND AND FIXED WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-15-25, and filed as its own row because it
is a DIFFERENT defect with a worse failure mode: -25 was a loud build error, this
one was a SILENT WRONG NUMBER that had been live the whole time.

REPRO on the parent of B-2026-08-15-25's fix — nothing to do with predicates,
closures over captures, or once-callability:

    fn msize() -> Fn(ref Map[String, i64]) -> i64 { |m| m.len() }
    fn main() {
        let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new();
        let _ = m.insert("k", 1);
        println(f"{msize()(m)}");
    }

    karac check         clean
    karac run --interp  1        (correct)
    karac build         529      WRONG, silently, and the value varies

CAUSE, from the emitted IR rather than inference. A `Map`/`Set`/`Tensor`/… value
is an opaque POINTER, and the closure ABI passes it directly — the caller emits
`%m = load ptr, ptr %m.slot` then `call %closure_fn(ptr %env, ptr %m)`, so the
argument IS the handle. But the closure param registration treated a `ref`-declared
param as a borrow (`ref_params`), which makes `load_variable` deref it, so the body
emitted:

    store ptr %1, ptr %m            ; %1 IS the handle
    %m.ref.ptr = load ptr, ptr %m   ; -> the handle
    %map.handle = load ptr, ptr %m.ref.ptr   ; <- one load too many
    call i64 @karac_map_len(ptr %map.handle)

The runtime is then handed the map control block's first word as a pointer. `len`
read it as a count (529); `contains_key` / `contains` dereferenced it and
segfaulted.

The borrow registration is correct and load-bearing for every OTHER `ref` closure
param — `ref Vec[u8]`, `ref String`, a user struct, `ref Vec[String]` all need the
deref (B-2026-08-05-15 leg 2 added it for exactly that). Handles are the exception
because the handle already IS the reference.

FIXED alongside B-2026-08-15-25 by skipping the borrow registration when the
borrowed-of type is a `builtin_opaque_ptr_handle`. It had to be fixed there rather
than later: correcting -25's return type turned these programs from a loud build
failure into a segfault, and shipping that trade alone would have been strictly
worse than leaving -25 open.

WHY IT SURVIVED: the `contains` spellings crashed loudly but could not be reached,
because -25 stopped them at module verification first. The one spelling that DID
compile — `|m| m.len()` — returned a plausible-looking integer, and no fixture
asked what that integer was.

fix:
FIXED in 55ae608. `param_types_for_function` now recovers a FUNCTION-TYPED
param's declared modes from its ANNOTATION when the span lookup answers nothing.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT BUT UNDERSTATED THE SCOPE. It says "a
function-typed param appears to have none [no `expr_types` entry]". Measured: NO
param of ANY type has one. Instrumented `param_types_for_function` on
`fn run(f: Fn(ref String) -> bool, tag: String, n: i64)` and every one of the
three answered `None`, at both the param span and the pattern span. So that map
arrives holding only `self`, for every function in the program. Harmless for an
ordinary param — `classify_identifier` falls through to a span-keyed lookup and a
plain identifier use has its own span, so the answer is right — which is why this
has never been visible before something needed the map for modes rather than for
Copy-ness.

WRONG CALL SITE FIRST, worth recording so the next person skips it. The obvious
patch is at `ownership.rs`'s `classify_function_body_with` call, where a RELIABLE
`param_types` (built from `lower_type_for_ownership(&param.ty)`) is already in
scope and goes only to the legacy state machine. Seeding the classifier map there
changed nothing: the UAM warning is emitted from `populate_predicate_outputs` →
`run_predicate_for_function_with`, which runs EARLIER (ownership.rs:2107 vs 2153)
and builds its own map via the same shared helper. Debug output made it obvious —
two `None` lookups from the predicate path, then one `Some` from the patched
path, with the warning already emitted. Fixing the shared builder covers all
three callers (`ownership.rs` and two in `rc_predicate.rs`).

A SECOND DEAD END, also recorded: `lower_type_for_ownership` has no `FnType` arm
either, so a `Fn(...)` param lowers to `Named { name: "unknown" }` there. Adding
one makes the legacy state machine treat function-typed params as Copy rather
than non-Copy — a real behaviour change that this bug does not need, so it was
reverted rather than shipped. Anyone touching that lowering should know the arm
is missing and why it was left alone.

FUNCTION TYPES ONLY, which is what makes the change safe. The row's own concern —
"populating that table changes what `classify_identifier` answers for
closure-typed identifiers generally" — resolves cleanly: `is_copy_type` already
answers TRUE for `Type::Function` (a capture-free code pointer, B-2026-07-02-24),
which is the same Read the span fallback produces today, so no identifier's
classification moves. Filling in EVERY param would not be safe: it would flip
`mut ref` params from Read to Consume, since `MutRef` is deliberately non-Copy.
Only the modes are recovered — each parameter lowers to a bare `Ref` / `MutRef` /
`Error` marker, the same mode-only idiom the function already uses for `ref self`
— because that is all the mode lookup reads and inventing pointees would suggest
a fidelity the value does not have.

A CLAIM I WROTE AND THEN RETRACTED, since the ledger should carry the correction
rather than the first draft. The first version of this change asserted in a code
comment that mapping `is_once` faithfully "keeps `f(); f();` on a once-callable
closure reported as a reuse". Measured, that is false as stated: the report comes
from `once_callable_closures`, populated at `let` bindings, and is identical
before and after (1 warning both ways — now pinned by a control test). The
`is_once` mapping matters only in that it keeps the two types from being
conflated. The comment was corrected before commit.

SCOPE MEASURED. Warned before, clean after: `fn run(f: Fn(ref String) -> bool)`
and the borrowed position of a `Fn(ref String, String)` parameter. Still warns,
correctly: `Fn(String)` as a parameter, the owned position of the mixed
parameter, and every local form B-2026-08-15-27 already covered. Run/build/auto-par
output identical on the fixed shapes.

REMAINDER, filed as its own row: an `OnceFn()` PARAMETER called twice
(`fn run(g: OnceFn()) { g(); g(); }`) is reported by NEITHER mechanism, before
this change or after. The local twin IS reported. Deliberately not asserted in
either direction by the control test here, since it is neither this fix's doing
nor its business.

TESTS (`tests/ownership.rs`): two accept cases and two controls, the controls
again load-bearing — both accept tests would pass against a checker that had
stopped classifying closure arguments entirely. Verified RED at baseline for the
two accepts and GREEN at both for the two controls.

Gates: full `--features llvm` sweep of all 98 targets, 12563 tests, 0 failures;
clippy `--all --all-targets` and fmt clean.
title: The B-2026-08-15-27 false positive SURVIVES when the closure arrives as a PARAMETER rather than a local — `fn run(f: Fn(ref String) -> bool)` calling `f(q)` twice still warns 'value q moved here, used again here'. 8242fae fixed the local and returned-closure forms; a function-typed PARAMETER has no entry in `param_types`, so its declared modes reach neither name-keyed table.
tracker: `param_types_for_function` (src/use_classifier.rs) records a param only when `tc.expr_types` has an entry at the param's span; a function-typed param appears to have none, so `fn_typed_callee_modes` finds nothing and the `Call` arm's consume default stands.
detail:
REPRO — the parameter twin of B-2026-08-15-27's local:

    fn run(f: Fn(ref String) -> bool) -> bool {
        let q = "alpha";
        let a = f(q);
        let b = f(q);
        return a;
    }
    fn main() { println(run(|s| s.len() > 2)); }

    warning[ownership]: value 'q' moved here, used again here

The LOCAL form of the same thing is clean after 8242fae:

    let p: Fn(ref String) -> bool = |s| s.len() > 2;   // clean
    fn longer(n: i64) -> Fn(ref String) -> bool { .. }  // clean

MEASURED CAUSE. `fn_typed_callee_modes` consults `param_types` then
`local_types`. For the local form `local_types` holds
`Function { params: [Ref(Str)], return_type: Bool }` and the fix applies. For the
parameter form BOTH tables miss — instrumented output:
`name=f ty=Bool in_param_types=false in_local_types=false`. `param_types_for_function`
builds its map from `tc.expr_types.get(param.span)`, so a function-typed parameter
is simply absent.

WHY 8242fae DID NOT JUST WIDEN THE LOOKUP, recorded so the next person does not
re-derive it: adding function-typed params to `param_types` also changes what
`classify_identifier` answers for those identifiers. Today `f` misses every
name-keyed table and falls through to the span-keyed `expr_types`, which returns
the CALL's type (`Bool`, Copy) and so classifies `f` itself as a Read. Give it a
real `Function` entry and the answer becomes whatever `is_copy_type` says for a
function type — if that is false, `f(q); f(q);` starts reporting a move of `f`
ITSELF, a new false positive strictly worse than the one being fixed. So the
change needs `is_copy_type`'s answer for `Type::Function` established first, and a
sweep of the other `param_types` consumers, which is why it was split out rather
than bundled.

SEVERITY LOW, same as its parent: a warning only, no error, no wrong answer, and
the program runs correctly on every backend. Filed because the parameter form is
if anything the MORE idiomatic half of the pattern B-2026-08-15-22 exists to
enable — a predicate accepted by a function and applied to several values — so
the surviving half will be met at least as often as the fixed one.
investigation: 2026-08-15. Split out while fixing B-2026-08-15-27: the parameter form was probed alongside the local one, stayed red after the fix, and was instrumented to the missing `param_types` entry. Not bundled because the fix for it changes a shared table's contract.

fix: FIXED by 93ea7a86. Routed high-cardinality shuffled input to the stable quicksort that was already in the emitter, by widening BOTH of its cardinality gates into an orderedness band around ord ~ 0.5. Isolated pure-sort cycles, `(i64,i64)`, n=150k x 25, same-commit control: random 545M -> 350M (0.64x), gap to Rust's driftsort 2.80x -> 1.80x, every other pattern unchanged (sorted 1.01x, reverse 1.01x, few-unique 1.00x, sawtooth 1.01x, nearly-sorted 1.02x). Whole-kata, the two katas that filed this row: #252 679M -> 465M (0.68x), gap to Rust 2.63x -> 1.80x; #253 892M -> 705M (0.79x), 1.61x -> 1.27x. The residual ~1.80x is tracked in its own row.
tracker: mono sort_by lowering (natural-run merge sort, 50a50e8) -- shuffled-uniform residual, on arm64
title: The shuffled-uniform `sort_by` residual closed as `wontfix` in B-2026-08-11-28 at ~1.6x Rust is MATERIALLY LARGER on the canonical Apple-silicon host: 3.70x on kata #252 and 2.04x on kata #253, measured on M5 Pro with 50a50e8 IN the compiler. The disposition was reached entirely on a shared x86 cloud container, and `wontfix` was argued from a residual roughly half this size. Not a regression of 50a50e8 -- that fix is present and the ordered-input win it bought is not in question -- but the remaining gap is bigger than the number the wontfix was decided against, so the disposition deserves re-deciding on this host rather than inheriting.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while adding the missing M5 lane to the 244-275 kata block (kara-katas 5e50806). Both #252 and #253 SHUFFLE their input once and sort a fresh copy per round, so both land squarely on the shuffled-uniform path B-2026-08-11-28 measured and dispositioned -- they are not exercising the ordered-input case 50a50e8 fixed.

MEASUREMENTS (Apple M5 Pro 6P+12E, karac 0.1.0-dev.6106+g50267795a, hyperfine 30 runs, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, every lane 99% CPU):
  #252 meeting-rooms   kara 217.3 +/- 3.8 ms   rust -O 58.8 +/- 1.4   rust_ovf 59.1 +/- 1.4  -> 3.70x
  #253 meeting-rooms-ii kara 244.7 +/- 0.9 ms  rust -O 121.3 +/- 1.1  rust_ovf 119.7 +/- 0.6 -> 2.04x
sigma is 0.4-2.4% of mean on every row, so neither ratio is noise; #253 is the cleanest measurement in the whole 27-kata block.

PRIOR x86 NUMBERS for the same two katas (container, results.container-x86.json): #252 kara 469.0 vs rust 247.9 = 1.89x; #253 kara 598.6 vs rust 370.5 = 1.62x. So the gap WIDENS on arm64 in both, by 1.96x and 1.26x respectively.

WHY THIS IS NOT A 50a50e8 REGRESSION: `git merge-base --is-ancestor 50a50e8 50267795` is true, so the natural-run merge sort is in the measured binary. B-2026-08-11-28 explicitly predicted the shuffled case would not move (`random 14.91 -> 14.60 ms (UNCHANGED)`, ~2-element natural runs reproduce the old pass count). This row is about the SIZE of that predicted-unchanged residual on a host it was never measured on.

ISOLATED KERNEL MEASURED ON THE M5, 2026-08-15 -- the step this row asked for, and its prediction was right. 150k (i64,i64) pairs x 25 rounds, `clone + sort_by` only, with an identical no-sort run subtracted, six input patterns, kara and rust agreeing on the sink in all six. PURE SORT, kara/rust:
    random        instrs 1.37x   CYCLES 3.95x   (kara IPC 1.44 vs rust 4.18)
    sorted        instrs 1.16x   cycles 1.07x
    reverse       instrs 1.37x   cycles 1.05x
    few-unique    instrs 1.29x   cycles 1.01x
    sawtooth      instrs 1.06x   cycles 0.23x   (kara 4.4x FASTER)
    nearly-sorted instrs 0.51x   cycles 0.34x   (kara 2.9x FASTER)
  So the isolated arm64 residual is 3.95x, LARGER than the 3.70x whole-kata figure exactly as predicted, and against the ~1.6x this row's parent measured on x86.
  THE SHAPE OF IT IS THE FINDING, and it is not what the parent row assumed. This is NOT an instruction-count problem -- kara runs only 1.37x the instructions on random. It is an IPC collapse: 1.44 against rust's 4.18. And it is confined to ONE pattern: kara is at parity or far ahead on all five predictable-merge patterns, and beats driftsort outright on sawtooth (4.4x) and nearly-sorted (2.9x). Any future work should target the unpredictable-merge case only; there is nothing to win on the other five.
  THE BRANCH-PREDICTION QUESTION THIS ROW LEFT OPEN IS ANSWERED, in the opposite direction to the obvious guess. B-2026-08-10-9 flagged the REJECTED branchless option as most likely to rank differently on another microarch. It does -- it is WORSE here. Forced-kernel A/B (branchless/branchy, cycles): random 1.28x, sorted 1.07x, reverse 1.01x, few-unique 0.98x, sawtooth 7.98x, nearly-sorted 5.44x. Branchless loses on five of six and is catastrophic on two. The probe still routes random toward branchless, which costs 1.21x there.
  PINNING BRANCHY IS STILL NOT A CORPUS WIN, so the default is unchanged. Against a same-commit control over every kata that sorts, binary-hash gated: #252 0.815x, #253 0.865x, #1665 0.976x, #40 0.996x, #47 0.996x, #18 1.010x, #15 1.031x, #16 1.037x, #56 1.042x -- two large wins, four real regressions, median flat. #56 sorts (i64,i64) exactly as #252 does and moves the other way, so element type is not the discriminator either. `KARAC_SORT_FORCE` (kara 8d302dfb) ships as the A/B lever so the next attempt starts from measurement.
  ELEMENT WIDTH IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, and the fix landed (kara 10a07058). The corpus A/B above left one thing unexplained -- forcing branchy won #252/#253 but LOST #15/#16/#18. Those three sort scalar `i64`; the winners sort 16-byte tuples. Isolated kernel, both element types, branchless/branchy cycles on the random pattern (the only one where the probe's answer is in doubt):
      i64        8 B   0.81x   branchless wins by 1.24x
      (i64,i64) 16 B   1.27x   branchy     wins by 1.27x
  The ranking INVERTS with width: a branchless merge selects the whole element, so at 16 bytes it is two selects and a wider copy on the loop-carried cursor chain, while at 8 bytes it is one and cheap enough to beat the ~50% misprediction a random merge pays. karac now consults the probe for narrow elements and forces branchy for wide ones, aarch64 only; the x86 calibration is untouched.
  MEASURED against a same-commit control over every kata that sorts: #252 0.816x, #253 0.857x, #18 0.990x, #1665 1.010x, #56 unstable around 1.0, and every other sorting kata byte-identical. Net -348M cycles. That is 1.23x and 1.17x on the two katas this row is about, with no stable regression -- strictly better than the blanket arch gate, which bought those same wins for four regressions.
  TWO TRAPS, both of which produced a wrong answer before being caught. (1) `BasicTypeEnum::size_of()` is unusable for this: on a struct it yields a `getelementptr` constant EXPRESSION, so `get_zero_extended_constant()` returns None and every tuple reads as NARROW -- exactly backwards, and it made the first version of the gate a silent no-op that still appeared to move three katas. `ensure_target_data().get_store_size()` is the correct query. (2) karac codegen is NONDETERMINISTIC (filed as B-2026-08-15-33): three builds of #253 from one karac gave two distinct binaries, so hash equality proves 'unaffected' but hash inequality proves nothing, and #56's apparent 2.6% regression reads 0.963x / 1.055x / 1.068x across three independent build rounds -- the sign flips. Any codegen perf claim under ~5% needs repeated BUILDS, not just repeated runs.
  WHAT REMAINS ON THIS ROW: the residual itself. Even with the right kernel, kara is 3.30x behind driftsort on random (650M vs 197M cycles isolated), and that is an IPC problem (1.54 vs 4.18), not an instruction-count one. The kernel choice was worth 1.21x of it; the rest is the algorithm.

  METHOD, because two false signals nearly shipped as conclusions: (1) comparing against a baseline built from an OLDER karac attributed main's drift to the change -- six of nine apparent regressions vanished against a same-commit control; (2) retired instruction counts are NOT always deterministic -- kata #249 spans 4.3% run-to-run on ONE binary (hash-seeded probing), manufacturing three more regressions on katas whose two binaries are byte-identical. Hash the binaries first and rank only what differs.

CROSS-CHECK that isolates it to the sort: kata #254 (factor-combinations) is deep recursion plus millions of small allocations and NO sort, and kara is level with rust on BOTH hosts (M5: kara 317.0 vs rust 330.0 = 0.96x). Two sort-dominated lanes diverging while an allocation-dominated one stays pinned is stronger evidence than either host produced alone.

THE BRANCHLESS KERNEL WAS THE PROBLEM, NOT THE ELEMENT WIDTH -- fixed in 85513d55, and the width gate from 8e370297 removed with it.
  Reading the emitted merge loop showed why branchless lost on wide elements: it selected the VALUE, which forces both elements live at the select, and for an element wider than a register LLVM materialises each in a SIMD register and extracts every field back to GP so the `csel` pair can run -- `ldr q0; mov.d; fmov` per operand, 17 instrs/element, with the SIMD->GP moves on the loop-carried critical path. That is the IPC ~1.4.
  Selecting the source ADDRESS instead leaves one `csel` on a GP register and one element copy from the winner, and the comparator's loads narrow to the key it actually reads. Isolated kernel, pure-sort cycles, `(i64,i64)`: random 834M -> 564M (0.68x), sawtooth 438M -> 275M, nearly-sorted 363M -> 240M; sorted/reverse/few-unique unchanged; scalar `i64` unchanged at 1.00x throughout, since a register-width element never needed the round-trip.
  CONSEQUENCE: branchless is now AHEAD of branchy on random `(i64,i64)` (0.86x), so the width gate -- which existed only because branchless lost there -- became a pessimisation and was removed. The split was never width-shaped anyway: at the SAME 16-byte width, branchy still wins 5.0x on sawtooth and 3.6x on nearly-sorted. Only the probe can express that, and with the kernel fixed its premise holds on arm64 as it does on x86.
  Corpus, same-commit control, binary-hash gated: #252 0.865x, #253 0.929x, #16 0.945x, #56 0.983x, #15 1.009x, #1665 1.011x, all others byte-identical; net -198M cycles. #252/#253 run MORE instructions (1.089x) for FEWER cycles, which is the branchless trade working as intended.

WHAT REMAINS, and it is now clearly ALGORITHMIC rather than codegen. Even with the fixed kernel, kara is ~2.87x driftsort on random `(i64,i64)` (564M vs 197M cycles isolated). Rust's binary carries `core::slice::sort::stable::quicksort` and `driftsort_main`: on low-structure input driftsort does NOT merge, it runs a stable QUICKSORT. kara always bottom-up merges -- ~12 passes over 2.4 MB of ping-pong buffers. That is a different algorithm, not a slower kernel, which is consistent with the x86-era note on B-2026-08-10-19 measuring kara at 0.62x driftsort's DATA REFERENCES while losing on mispredicts. Closing the rest means a stable quicksort for the low-structure case; note B-2026-08-10-20 already tried a quicksort RUN-BUILDER feeding the merge (reverted at parity), which is a different thing from replacing the sort.
THE ALGORITHMIC HALF IS CLOSED, AND THE STABLE QUICKSORT DID NOT NEED BUILDING — IT WAS ALREADY IN THE EMITTER. WHAT WAS WRONG WAS THE ROUTING.

The note above ended "closing the rest means a stable quicksort for the low-structure case". That reading was wrong in a way worth recording, because the search it implies is expensive and unnecessary. The stable quicksort has shipped since B-2026-08-11-10 § Direction 7 (`emit_sort_partition_body`: median-of-3 randomised pivot, one counting pass tallying both `< pivot` and `<= pivot`, count-then-scatter with two advancing cursors, ping-ponging through phase 2's scratch). What was missing was that BOTH of its gates keyed on cardinality, so high-cardinality shuffled input — precisely this residual — could never reach it.

WHY THE GATES WERE SET THAT WAY, AND WHAT IS WRONG WITH THE REASONING. The gate's own comment states the model: "partitioning costs two passes per level against the merge's one, so it wins while 2*log2(d) < log2(n/RUN)". That prices a level in PASS COUNT, which assumes a partition pass and a merge pass cost the same per element. On M5 they differ by 4.7x. Isolated single-level measurement, 3.75M elements of `(i64,i64)`:

  merge pass (post-a50d42fd kernel)   22.67 instr/elem   11.75 cyc/elem   IPC 1.93
  partition scatter, branchless       17.27 instr/elem    2.49 cyc/elem   IPC 6.93
  partition scatter, branchy          12.30 instr/elem   12.16 cyc/elem   IPC 1.01

The mechanism is the READ cursor. A merge cannot know which side to load next until it has compared, so every element sits on a serial load -> cmp -> cursor -> load chain and the kernel runs at IPC 1.93 however few instructions it retires. A partition reads SEQUENTIALLY and only the WRITE destination is data-dependent, so the loads pipeline: it retires MORE instructions in a fifth of the cycles. Same arm64 theme as this row's kernel half and as #259/#275 — on Apple silicon the instruction count is not the cost, the dependency chain is. (The branchy row is why this only works branchless, and is also why the earlier three-way-scatter attempt at B-2026-08-10-19 could not pay: three stores per element.)

THE TRAP THAT MAKES THIS DIRECTION LOOK DEAD. Forcing only the ENTRY probe open measures 550M against the merge's 545M on random — a wash, which reads as "the partition does not help". It does not: there is a SECOND per-range gate inside `qpart` keyed on the same tie estimate (`neq * 64 < len`), and on random `neq ~ len/32768`, so every range counted a pass and fell straight back to the merge. The partition never ran. Anyone re-testing this must open BOTH gates or they will measure the counting pass alone and conclude the opposite of the truth.

WHAT THE ROUTING RULE IS, MEASURED NOT ARGUED. With both gates open the partition wins on shuffled input and loses badly on structured input, so the fix is a routing rule and the crossover was measured. Input is runs of length R with random starts, which sweeps orderedness continuously; `ord` is the fraction of ordered adjacent pairs, exactly the statistic the entry probe already samples. Ratio is quicksort/merge, lower is better:

  ord    0.004  0.016  0.063  0.125  0.250  0.500  0.750  0.875  0.938  0.984  0.996
  ratio   3.34   2.48   1.35   1.05   0.77   0.64   0.78   1.04   1.31   2.51   3.36

The curve is a V. The partition exploits no structure at all — its cost is flat across the entire sweep (256M-351M) — while the merge's cost peaks exactly at shuffled. So admission is a BAND around 0.5, not a threshold, and that distinction is load-bearing: reverse-sorted input samples at ord ~ 0, and the pre-existing `ord < 95%` test would have admitted it and lost 13x. Band set to [25%, 80%], one measured step inside the crossover at both edges (0.25 and 0.75 are wins at 0.77x / 0.78x; 0.125 and 0.875 are already ties or losses). At 512 samples the standard error on ord is ~0.022, so both edges sit >3 sigma from a true 0.5.

WHAT SHIPPED (93ea7a86). The probe answers with the ARM rather than a bool — 0 reject, 1 admitted on low cardinality, 2 admitted on being unstructured — and `qpart` takes a seventh `gate` param carrying it, because the arms want opposite per-range behaviour: arm 1 keeps the tie test so a mixed input partitions only the part that pays, arm 2 disables it since a tie count is near zero there by construction. Arm 1 wins the tie when both match, so low-cardinality behaviour is unchanged (few-unique measures 1.00x). Leaf handoff SPAN also drops 4096 -> 64: it was sized for arm 1, which bottoms out in a few levels and never reaches a deep leaf (across 32..4096 on few-unique it moves nothing, 1.00-1.01x), but on arm 2 every element descends the full log2(n/SPAN) and a 4096 leaf leaves 6 merge passes under every partition. Sweep on random: SPAN 32 0.66x, 64 0.65x, 128 0.66x, 256 0.70x, 512 0.74x, 1024 0.81x, 4096 0.80x — flat from 32 to 128, so 64 sits mid-plateau.

RESULT. Same-commit control throughout: both binaries built from the same base, differing only by the patch. Isolated pure-sort cycles, `(i64,i64)`, n=150k x 25 rounds — random 545M -> 350M (0.64x), taking the gap to Rust's driftsort from 2.80x to 1.80x; sorted 1.01x, reverse 1.01x, few-unique 1.00x, sawtooth 1.01x, nearly-sorted 1.02x. Across the full orderedness sweep the band routed all eleven inputs correctly: the three inside it win 0.77x / 0.64x / 0.78x, the eight outside sit at 1.00-1.02x, no regression anywhere. Whole-kata, the two katas that filed this row: #252 679M -> 465M (0.68x), gap to Rust 2.63x -> 1.80x; #253 892M -> 705M (0.79x), 1.61x -> 1.27x. Both run MORE instructions for FEWER cycles, the same trade visible at whole-program scale. NOTE the kata baselines here are 2.63x / 1.61x, not the 3.70x / 2.04x this row was filed with — those predate the merge-kernel fix a50d42fd, and these were re-measured on the shipping base rather than re-quoted.

VERIFICATION. 462-case sweep (11 sizes x 7 cardinalities x 6 orderedness shapes) asserting sorted AND stable, sizes straddling both the probe floor (4096) and the new leaf span (64), cardinalities straddling the tie gate in both directions, and one shape that is half sorted and half shuffled so ranges cross the gate mid-recursion — 0 violations. The oracle was poisoned first and detects both failure modes it claims to (an unsorted pair, and an equal-key pair whose original indices invert). Full `--features llvm` suite: 119 binaries, 13784 passed, 0 failed. Note `should_use_mono_vec_sort_by_for` admits only `i64` and all-int structs, so no heap-owning element reaches this path.

`KARAC_SORT_PART=always|never` pins the routing and `KARAC_SORT_PART_SPAN` overrides the leaf; both are how the above was measured and are retained as A/B levers.

WHAT REMAINS: kara is still ~1.80x driftsort on shuffled `(i64,i64)`, down from 2.80x. Tracked separately rather than left implicit here — see the follow-up row for the one concrete lead (the shipped scatter is count-then-scatter over a single buffer; a two-buffer variant measured 2.49 cyc/elem in isolation, and whether the shipped kernel sits near that or well above it was NOT isolated, because the probe's counting pass was branchy while the emitter's is not).

fix:
WONTFIX -- real, reproduced, and measured to a standstill across THREE unroll
strategies, none of which pays. No code change; the deliverable is the
measurement and the disposition, recorded in c878d001 (hint + gate widening) and
71056795 (the canonicalisation), both comments-only reverts.

  (a) HINT the converging guard -- LLVM refuses it outright, answering `loop not
      unrolled: the optimizer was unable to perform the requested
      transformation` twice per #246 build where shipped karac warns not at all.
      Not an inlining artifact: refused identically with lo=0/hi=31 as literal
      constants in `main`.
  (b) CANONICALISE + FULL UNROLL -- works exactly as designed (#246 527.8M ->
      401.0M retired instructions, 1.42x behind clang -O3 becomes 1.08x) and is
      unbounded: the canonicalised gap is the REAL trip count, so #189's
      `reverse_range` over a million-element array took `karac build` from 0.6 s
      to killed at 300 s.
  (c) CANONICALISE + BOUNDED PARTIAL UNROLL (factor 4) -- fixes the blowup and
      still improves #246 to 482.3M, but is a corpus NET REGRESSION: 10 rows
      improved >1%, ELEVEN regressed, median 1.362 -> 1.363, rows where kara
      leads clang -O3 fell 22 -> 21, and the regressions land on the very shape
      targeted (#31 +15.1%, #60 +13.3%, #189 +7.7%).

WHAT WOULD REOPEN THIS: a way to BOUND THE GAP at compile time, so a converging
loop's unroll can be capped the way `UNROLL_FULL_MAX_BOUND` caps the literal
path. That single missing fact -- `hi = len - 1` is opaque until inlining -- is
what defeats all three strategies above, and it is the only thing worth
attacking. Another unroll strategy is not: hint, full and partial-4 are measured.

SCOPE, so the closure is not read as bigger than it is: this is ONE row of the 27
pure-unroll rows the corpus screen found (kara-katas unroll-screen.json). Closing
it does not retire the class -- it records that the class's most-studied member
has no route in with today's information. The corpus-level finding stands
separately: there is NO systemic bias (median kara/C moves only 1.36 -> 1.32 with
C's unroller off), so nothing here calls the published benchmark ratios into
question.
tracker: converging two-pointer full-unroll -- the trip count has no COMPILE-TIME BOUND, which is what blocks every unroll strategy (control_flow_bce.rs `while_loop_wants_full_unroll` + the canonicalisation that was built and reverted)
title: MECHANISM PINNED (was: not pinned). Kata #246's 1.57x deficit to `clang -O3` on arm64 is ENTIRELY LOOP UNROLLING, and karac is at `clang -O2` PARITY. Dynamic counts: kara 527.4M instrs / 66.2M cycles, clang -O3 370.7M / 42.0M, clang -O2 500.5M / 74.4M, clang -O3 -fno-unroll-loops 500.6M / 63.7M. So kara vs equal-treatment C is 1.05x on instructions and 1.06x on wall time, and kara is 11% AHEAD of clang -O2 on cycles. karac's own full-unroll hint machinery is live and working but declines this loop, and THREE ways of making it fire were then built and measured -- hint the converging guard (LLVM refuses and warns), canonicalise to a counted loop + full unroll (works, #246 -> 1.08x of clang -O3, but unbounded: kata #189's million-iteration reverse took `karac build` from 0.6s to killed at 300s), and canonicalise + bounded partial unroll (safe, but a corpus NET REGRESSION -- 10 rows better, 11 worse). WONTFIX: the blocker is that a converging loop's trip count has NO COMPILE-TIME BOUND, and until that changes every unroll strategy either misfires or over-applies.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: filed 2026-08-15 with no mechanism; pinned the same day. This row REPLACES the original diagnosis, which was wrong in a way worth recording: it reasoned from `main` being 213 instructions in kara against 432 in C and concluded kara 'emits less code and runs slower, which rules out the extra-per-iteration-check mechanism'. That conflated STATIC code size with DYNAMIC instruction count -- C's larger `main` IS the unrolled loop, and unrolling LOWERS the dynamic count. Measuring retired instructions (scripts/pmc.c) inverted the conclusion.

THE PER-PAIR SEQUENCES ARE INSTRUCTION-FOR-INSTRUCTION IDENTICAL. Both lower `rotate_byte` to the same range-check + bitmask + table-load: `ldrb/ldurb; sub #0x30; cmp #9; b.hi; lsr; tbz; and; ldr(b); ldr(s)b; cmp; b.ne` = 11 instructions of real work. kara then adds 5 of loop bookkeeping (`sub hi,#1; add lo,#1; cmp; mov; b.lt`) that clang's unroll amortizes to zero. 16/11 = 1.45x, matching the measured 1.42x dynamic ratio. One of kara's 5 is a redundant `mov x1,x3` where `add x1,x1,#1` would do -- a register-allocation artifact of comparing the pre-increment `lo`, worth ~6% of the loop and a separate, smaller question.

PROOF IT IS THE UNROLL, not a codegen-quality difference: `clang -O3 -fno-unroll-loops` lands on kara (500.6M vs 527.4M instrs, 13.28 vs 14.14 ms min -- 1.06x), and `clang -O2` does not unroll either (121-instruction `main`, 15-instruction tight loop, the same shape kara emits).

KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=3 DOES NOT FIX IT (527.4M at both O2 and O3, byte-identical loop) -- so this is not a pipeline-string difference. Note clang -O2 also declines it unhinted while clang -O2 + `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` reaches -O3 (372.3M vs 370.3M): both compilers' COST MODELS decline this loop, and both take it when hinted. That is the same situation kata:37 (B-2026-06-17-7) created the hint machinery for.

WHY THE EXISTING HINT DECLINES THIS LOOP -- three independent gates, each deliberate and each calibrated on prior measurements:
  1. `guard_upper_bounded_counter` requires a LITERAL (or const-local, B-2026-08-13-10) upper bound. #246 is `while lo <= hi` -- a CONVERGING two-pointer whose bound is itself a decrementing induction variable. No literal, so the gate returns None immediately.
  2. `expr_is_unroll_cheap_free` rejects any user `Call`; the body calls `rotate_byte(...)`. That gate is measured, not cautious: relaxing it regressed #134 by 40% (484 -> 677 ms).
  3. `body_is_unroll_cheap_free` maps `StmtKind::Return` to false; the body's early `return false` is the loop's exit and is intrinsic to a search.

WHAT IS ALREADY RULED OUT AS A BLOCKER: the machinery itself works in this build (a literal-bound, call-free, return-free scalar probe fully unrolls -- 135-instruction body), and TWO-ENDED indexing is fine (`v[base+lo]` and `v[base+31-lo]` in one body also fully unrolls, 186-instruction body). So the blockers are exactly the three AST gates, not the access pattern and not the hint plumbing.

FIX ATTEMPTED AND ABANDONED 2026-08-15 (kara c878d001, comments only -- the gate is UNCHANGED). All three gates were relaxed and measured; none of it is shippable.
  CONVERGING BOUND -- the one #246 needs. THREE strategies tried, ALL measured, NONE pays.
    (a) HINT IT: LLVM refuses -- takes the metadata and answers `loop not unrolled: the optimizer was unable to perform the requested transformation`, twice per #246 build, where shipped karac warns not at all. Not an inlining artifact: a converging loop written straight into `main` with lo=0 and hi=31 as literal constants is refused identically, so LLVM cannot establish a trip count for the two-induction-variable exit as karac emits it.
    (b) CANONICALISE + FULL UNROLL (kara f0419a58 documents it; built and reverted): emit a synthetic gap counter `d = hi - lo` in the preheader, step it by -(c1+c2) on the back edge, branch on `d >= 0`. Works exactly as designed -- loop becomes countable, warnings stop, #246 goes 527.8M -> 401.0M retired instructions, i.e. 1.42x behind clang -O3 becomes 1.08x. BUT the canonicalised gap is the REAL trip count, so kata #189's `reverse_range` over a million-element array unrolls a million times and `karac build` went 0.6s -> killed at 300s. The literal path is immune only because UNROLL_FULL_MAX_BOUND caps it at 32; a converging loop has no AST-visible bound to cap (`hi = len - 1` is opaque until inlining -- the same fact that made the hint necessary).
    (c) CANONICALISE + BOUNDED PARTIAL UNROLL (factor 4): fixes the blowup (#189 back to 0.6s) and #246 still improves to 482.3M, but it is a NET REGRESSION over the corpus -- 10 rows improved >1%, ELEVEN regressed, median 1.362 -> 1.363, and rows where kara leads clang -O3 fell 22 -> 21. The regressions land on the very shape targeted: #31 next_permutation +15.1%, #60 +13.3%, #189 +7.7%, because 4x-ing a reverse loop buys a remainder loop and code growth and nothing else.
    WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY BE NEEDED: a way to BOUND THE GAP at compile time, so the unroll can be capped the way the literal path is. Not another unroll strategy -- all three are measured.
  FREE-FUNCTION CALLS + EARLY RETURN -- a wash that buys regressions. Screened over all 278 corpus program-rows on retired instructions: 11 improved >1%, SEVEN regressed >1% (#165 +5.4%, #22 +3.5%), corpus median UNMOVED at 1.362, rows where kara leads clang -O3 unchanged at 22. The `return` arm alone: one win (#17 2.3%), two regressions (#22 +1.5%, #85 +1.7%).
  ONE CORRECTION THE DATA DOES SUPPORT: the call gate's stated rationale is misattributed. It cites #134's 40% loss, but #134's cost is its `push` -- a METHOD call on a heap container, a different ExprKind that fails the check regardless -- and #134 never moved under the widening (4.378B -> 4.384B instructions). The gate still earns its place on the corpus evidence above, for a different reason than the one written next to it.
  Gates verified green after the revert: 1207 lib tests, the 3 full-unroll IR tests, fmt and clippy clean.

CORPUS SCREEN DONE 2026-08-15 -- kara-katas `scripts/unroll-screen.py` + `unroll-screen.json`, 278 program-rows, 0 skipped, every sink matched across all three builds.
  NO SYSTEMIC BIAS: corpus median kara/C moves only 1.36 -> 1.32 when C loses its unroller, so the default<O2>-vs-clang -O3 comparison is not quietly unfair at the aggregate level.
  BUT THE TAIL IS REAL: 51 rows have >=5% of their deficit explained by the unroller, and TEN read as 'kara behind clang -O3' while landing at parity (<=1.10x) against equal-treatment C: #139 2.62->1.09, #80 1.45->0.97, #246 1.42->1.05, #63 1.34->1.05, #153 1.26->0.89, #136 1.25->0.50, #221 1.24->1.05, #265 1.21->0.95, #31 1.20->0.86, #214 1.17->1.09.
  THE 51 SPLIT TWO WAYS, because `-fno-unroll-loops` also removes the interleaving the vectoriser needs on some loops: counting NEON ops in both C builds gives 27 PURE-UNROLL (this row's family -- #190, #139, #80, #36, #31, #174, #246, #157, #63, #265, #77, #49, #158, #234 lead it) and 24 VECTORIZATION, which is the separate checked-arithmetic-forfeits-vectorisation question BENCHMARKS.md already covers. Reading all 51 as unrolling would be wrong.
  DO NOT READ A LARGE `c_unroll_effect` AS A KARA WIN: #190 goes 59.5M -> 1.62B instructions without the unroll, but kara is already within 1.14x of clang -O3 there -- C depended on the unroll, kara was not rescued by removing it.
  So the fix scoped above is worth roughly 27 program-rows, not one, which strengthens the case for doing it properly (gate-by-gate, with the #134/#259/#265/#291 calibration katas re-measured) rather than locally.

fix:
FIXED in eec3aa5. `once_callable_closures` is now seeded from `param_types` for
every parameter whose declared type is `Type::OnceFunction`, alongside the
existing `let`-binding inference.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS HELD. "The two halves of once-callability (inferred for
locals, declared for params) have only the first wired up" is exactly it, and the
fix is the second half. `Type::Function` is deliberately NOT seeded: a repeatable
closure may be called any number of times, which is the whole distinction between
the two annotations, and a control pins it.

SEEDING BROKE AN INVARIANT, and this is the part worth carrying forward. The
`let` arm only ever INSERTED into the set, which was sound while `let` was the
only source — a name could not be marked before its own `let`. Parameters are
marked at function entry, so a `let` shadowing one left the parameter's mark in
place, and `fn run(g: OnceFn()) { let g = || …; g(); g(); }` reported a move of
the LOCAL, a repeatable closure that may be called freely. Found in the shape
sweep, not by a failing test — nothing in the suite covered shadowing here. The
arm now clears on rebind as well as sets.

The clear is NOT gated on the RHS being a closure: `let g = 5;` shadowing an
`OnceFn` parameter must clear the mark too, and it produces no capture consume to
distinguish it from a closure that does.

A PRE-EXISTING FALSE POSITIVE FELL OUT of that clear, with no parameter involved:

    let g = || apply(cfg);        // once-callable
    let g = || println("y");      // repeatable, shadows it
    g(); g();                     // reported at the parent commit; clean now

Measured red at b0abfae and green after. The insert-only arm kept the FIRST
binding's mark alive across the rebind. So the bug this row is about had a twin
in the mechanism it was extending, and closing one closed both.

ALSO NEWLY REPORTED: two distinct `OnceFn` parameters where only the second is
reused (`fn run(a: OnceFn(), b: OnceFn()) { a(); b(); b(); }`) — marks are per
name, not per signature. Silent at the parent commit.

MEASURED AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED — an `OnceFn` called inside a LOOP
(`while i < 3 { g(); }`) is still not reported. Checked the LOCAL twin at the
parent commit: it misses identically, so this belongs to the dominance analysis
(a single call site that executes repeatedly is not two dominance-comparable use
sites), not to once-callability or to parameters. Filing it would be a separate
row about the CFG predicate; noting it here so the next person does not assume
this fix covered it. An `OnceFn` called once per branch of an `if` IS correctly
accepted — exclusive paths, one call executes.

TESTS (`tests/ownership.rs`): seven. Three red at baseline — the parameter
report, the two-parameter case, and the pre-existing shadowing false positive.
Four green at baseline, and two of those are green BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by
luck: the shadowing controls guard this change's own failure mode, which could
not exist before it. Recorded plainly rather than counted as baseline-verified
coverage.

Gates: full `--features llvm` sweep of all 98 targets, 12570 tests, 0 failures;
clippy `--all --all-targets` and fmt clean; run/build/auto-par output identical
on every fixture (these are warnings, so all four programs compile and run).
title: An `OnceFn()` PARAMETER called twice is NOT reported — `fn run(g: OnceFn()) { g(); g(); }` passes clean, while the identical local (`let g = || apply(cfg); g(); g();`) correctly reports a use-after-move. A once-callable closure invoked twice is exactly what `OnceFn` exists to forbid, so this is a missing report rather than a spurious one — the mirror image of the -27/-29 family.
tracker: `once_callable_closures` (src/use_classifier.rs / OwnershipChecker) is populated from `let` bindings whose initializer is a closure whose body consumes a capture; a PARAMETER declared `OnceFn(...)` never enters it, and nothing else consults the declared once-ness at a call site.
detail:
MEASURED BOTH WAYS while fixing B-2026-08-15-29, at that row's parent AND after
its fix — identical, so this is neither caused nor fixed by it:

    // NOT reported (should be):
    struct Cfg { name: i64 }
    fn apply(c: Cfg) { }
    fn run(g: OnceFn()) { g(); g(); }
    fn main() { let cfg = Cfg { name: 7 }; run(|| apply(cfg)); }
        karac check   All checks passed.

    // Correctly reported (the local twin):
    fn main() { let cfg = Cfg { name: 7 }; let g = || apply(cfg); g(); g(); }
        warning[ownership]: value 'g' moved here, used again here

THE INTERESTING DIRECTION. B-2026-08-15-27 and -29 were both FALSE POSITIVES —
the checker reporting a move that could not happen. This is the opposite: a
reuse the type system explicitly forbids, going unreported. `OnceFn(...)` means
"callable once"; calling it twice is the single thing the annotation exists to
prevent, and the callee is where the annotation is most load-bearing, since the
caller cannot see the body.

WHY THE LOCAL WORKS AND THE PARAMETER DOES NOT. The local report comes from
`once_callable_closures`, a name-keyed set populated when a `let` initializer is
a closure whose body consumes a captured outer binding — an INFERRED property of
a body the checker can see. A parameter has no body here; its once-ness is
DECLARED, in the annotation, and nothing consults it at the call site. So the
two halves of once-callability (inferred for locals, declared for params) have
only the first wired up.

NOT A REGRESSION and not adjacent to the -29 fix beyond sharing a file: -29
seeds `Type::OnceFunction` into the classifier's param map, which is why the
shape was noticed, but nothing reads once-ness from there. A fix presumably
means consulting the declared type at the call site the way
`fn_typed_callee_modes` now consults declared parameter modes.

SEVERITY LOW despite being a MISSED error rather than a spurious one, and the
reasoning is worth stating rather than assuming: the consequence is a
diagnostic that does not fire, not a miscompile. Calling a once-callable closure
twice is defensive-copied by codegen (the same reason the whole UAM family is
advisory rather than fatal — see the auto-fix note on the diagnostic), so the
program still runs correctly; what is lost is the compile-time signal. Raise it
if a shape is found where the second call observes freed or stale state.

DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED in `local_once_callable_closure_reuse_is_still_reported`
(tests/ownership.rs), the control added with -29 — that test pins the LOCAL
report and says in its comment that the parameter case is unasserted in either
direction, so closing this row will not fight an existing test.
investigation: 2026-08-15. Found while checking a claim written into the B-2026-08-15-29 change — that mapping `is_once` faithfully preserves the once-callable reuse report. Probing that claim showed the report comes from `once_callable_closures` (locals only) and that the parameter form is unreported at every commit tested. The claim was corrected in the code comment; this row records the gap it exposed.

fix:
WONTFIX -- real, reproduced, and measured to a standstill IN THIS REPO, because
the defect is not in this repo. No code change; the deliverable is the diagnosis
and the reproducer, recorded in 8294eab9 and 4fbd6096.

  IT IS LLVM, NOT KARAC. Stock `opt` 18.1.8 reproduces it on a FIXED .ll file:
  six runs of `opt -passes='default<O2>' preopt.ll -S` yield two distinct
  outputs, same at O1. karac is not in the loop -- same input, same binary, same
  flags. karac's own IR construction is deterministic (pre-opt module
  byte-identical across processes; `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` byte-reproducible).

  THE VARYING THING IS THE PASS MANAGER'S FUNCTION VISIT ORDER, not any one
  pass. `-opt-bisect-limit` bisects to slot 513, which READS as
  `InstCombinePass on __karac_panic_site_18` -- a trap, because repeating the
  same limit shows slot 513 naming a different function per run. Order first
  diverges at slot 494 among the `__karac_panic_site_*` leaves; the two orders
  then do 1811 vs 2036 passes, which is where the ~376-byte, less-inlined
  variant comes from.

  NO KARAC-SIDE FIX THAT IS NOT A PESSIMISATION. The trigger is 66 identical
  3-instruction cold leaves (`printf`; `exit`; `unreachable`) differing only in
  constants -- a tie-heavy call-graph leaf set. Collapsing them into one
  parameterised `__karac_panic` would remove the tie set and the nondeterminism
  with it, but a no-argument cold function per site exists precisely so the HOT
  path spends one argument-free `call`; merging moves six argument setups to
  every panic site. Trading hot-path code for build reproducibility is the wrong
  side of that trade, so it is rejected rather than deferred.

  IMPACT IS BOUNDED AND THE OUTPUT IS CORRECT. Both variants produce identical
  sinks -- they are equivalent programs, one optimised slightly less. Prevalence
  is rare: 22 katas sampled at 4 builds each, one varied (#18) plus the known
  #253; 4 builds under-detect a coin flip ~12% of the time, so treat 5-10% as a
  floor rather than a ceiling.

  WHAT SURVIVES THIS CLOSURE, and is the reason it was worth chasing: the
  measurement discipline it forced. Binary-hash EQUALITY is a sound proof that a
  codegen change did not affect a given program; hash INEQUALITY proves nothing.
  Any codegen perf claim under ~5% needs repeated BUILDS, not just repeated runs
  of one binary -- kata #56 read 0.963x / 1.055x / 1.068x across three build
  rounds of the same two compilers, sign included. That guidance is what stops
  this from silently corrupting future benchmarking, and it applies whether or
  not LLVM ever changes.

  IF REOPENED, it belongs at llvm/llvm-project, not here. Reproducer: any
  affected module's pre-opt .ll plus `-passes='default<O2>'`, six runs, two
  outputs. Regenerate the .ll by dumping the module inside
  `apply_optimization_passes` -- NOT via the `compile_to_ir` test helper, which
  takes a different path and shows nothing. `opt` lives in the llvm@18 keg
  (/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm@18/bin/opt) even though the plain llvm keg's bin dir
  is empty. Note also that the ASLR / pointer-keyed-container attribution is
  INFERRED from the shape of the evidence and was never proven; a maintainer
  would want that narrowed first.
