title: `karac build` IS NOT REPRODUCIBLE: the SAME karac binary, on the SAME source, emits DIFFERENT executables across runs. Three consecutive builds of kata #253's min_meeting_rooms.kara gave two distinct sha256s (c909a866 / 76932c29 / c909a866); #252, #16 and #18 were stable across the same test, so it is program-dependent rather than universal. Sinks are unaffected -- the binaries are equivalent, not wrong -- so this is a build-reproducibility defect, not a miscompile. UPSTREAM: reproduces in stock `opt` 18.1.8 on a fixed .ll, so karac is not in the loop; the varying thing is the pass manager's FUNCTION VISIT ORDER (slot 513 names a different function per run), first diverging among the 66 identical `__karac_panic_site_*` cold leaves.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while A/B-ing the sort merge kernel for B-2026-08-15-30. That A/B used binary-hash equality to decide which katas a codegen change could possibly have affected, which is what exposed this: katas the change provably could not touch were nonetheless producing different binaries.

REPRO: build one .kara file three times with one karac and hash the output.
    for i in 1 2 3; do KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build min_meeting_rooms.kara; shasum -a 256 min_meeting_rooms; done
  -> c909a866c3eb150ca34012beb5f7286a / 76932c29b35675450547fdbe3b807974 / c909a866c3eb150ca34012beb5f7286a
Same karac, same source, same env, same flags. #252 meeting_rooms, #16 three_sum_closest and #18 four_sum each produced 3/3 identical hashes in the same test, so whatever varies is reachable from some programs and not others.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. It silently corrupts perf methodology, which is how it was found. Retired-instruction and cycle counts are the corpus's precision tool precisely because they are deterministic; if the BINARY varies run to run then so do they, and a 1-3% A/B delta can be entirely build variance. Concretely: kata #56 measured 0.963x / 1.055x / 1.068x across three independent build+measure rounds of the SAME two compilers -- the sign flips. Any codegen perf claim under ~5% needs repeated BUILDS, not just repeated runs, until this is fixed. It also means binary-hash equality is a sound test for 'this change did not affect kata X' while hash INequality proves nothing.

MECHANISM PINNED TO THE LLVM PASS PIPELINE, 2026-08-15 -- and the hypothesis this row was filed with is REFUTED. It guessed hash-ordered iteration in karac's own codegen (the `closure_counter` mono-symbol numbering). Two measurements kill that:
  (1) THE PRE-OPT MODULE IS BYTE-IDENTICAL across runs. Dumped from the REAL build path (`apply_optimization_passes`, not the `compile_to_ir` test helper -- an earlier dump via that helper was measuring a different path) over 6 separate processes: preopt.ll hashed the same every time while the final binary varied. karac's IR CONSTRUCTION is deterministic.
  (2) `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` IS BYTE-REPRODUCIBLE. 6 builds, one hash. O1, O2 and O3 each give TWO hashes over the same 6 builds. O0 is the level that skips the pass run, so the divergence is entirely inside LLVM's `default<O...>` pipeline: identical input IR, same pipeline string, different output IR (postopt.ll varies, and the binary tracks postopt exactly).

WHAT ACTUALLY DIFFERS: one variant is LESS OPTIMISED. On kata #253 the two binaries differ by ~376 bytes of __text (0x271c vs 0x2894) with matching __unwind_info/__eh_frame growth, +94 instructions, +12 `bl`, +4 `brk`, +8 `unreachable`, same 6 function symbols -- the signature of inlining decisions going differently, not of different source being compiled. Sinks are identical, so both are correct.

NOT ISOLATED TO A SINGLE PASS. Running individual passes via a pipeline override -- `cgscc(inline)`, `function(sroa)`, `function(instcombine)`, `function(simplifycfg)`, `function(gvn)`, and small combinations -- each produced ONE post-pass module hash over 6 runs. Only the full `default<O1>` pipeline varied. So it emerges from the pipeline as a whole rather than from any pass sampled here. This is the classic pointer-keyed-container / ASLR nondeterminism class in LLVM, but that attribution is INFERRED from the shape of the evidence, not proven.

PREVALENCE: rare. 22 katas sampled across the corpus, 4 builds each -- ONE varied (#18 four_sum), 21 were stable; #253 was already known. Note 4 builds under-detects: a 50/50 program looks stable ~12% of the time, so ~5-10% is a floor, not a ceiling.

NEXT STEP, and why it stopped here: pinning the exact pass needs `opt -print-pipeline-passes` to expand `default<O2>` into its component list so the halves can be bisected. No standalone `opt` is installed on this host (the Homebrew llvm bin dir is empty), and karac's pipeline-string override is not a substitute -- partial pipelines leave IR the backend aborts on. With that expansion the bisect is mechanical, and the result belongs upstream rather than in karac: nothing on the karac side chooses this.

PRACTICAL GUIDANCE MEANWHILE, which is the part that actually costs time: binary-hash EQUALITY is a sound proof that a codegen change did not affect a given program; hash INEQUALITY proves nothing. Any codegen perf claim under ~5% needs repeated BUILDS, not just repeated runs of one binary -- kata #56 read 0.963x / 1.055x / 1.068x across three build rounds of the same two compilers, sign included.

UPSTREAM, AND FULLY PINNED (same day, after `opt` was located at /opt/homebrew/opt/llvm@18/bin/opt -- the earlier 'blocked on tooling' note was wrong, the Homebrew llvm@18 keg has it even though the llvm keg's bin dir is empty).

  IT IS NOT KARAC. Stock `opt` 18.1.8 reproduces it on a FIXED .ll file: `opt -passes='default<O2>' preopt.ll -S` run six times yields TWO distinct outputs, and the same at `default<O1>`. karac is not in the loop at all -- same input file, same binary, same flags.

  IT IS NOT A SPECIFIC PASS EITHER -- IT IS THE VISIT ORDER. `-opt-bisect-limit` binary search puts the first divergence at limit 513 (stable at 512), which reads as `InstCombinePass on __karac_panic_site_18`. That reading is a trap: repeating the same limit shows slot 513 naming a DIFFERENT FUNCTION between runs -- `__karac_panic_site_18` on some, `karac_clone_tuple_i64_i64` on others. So no pass is misbehaving; the ORDER in which the pass manager visits functions varies, and a fixed bisect limit therefore cuts the pipeline at a different place.

  WHERE THE ORDER DIVERGES: slot 494, inside the run of `__karac_panic_site_*` leaves. One order visits them numerically (…10, 11, 12…), the other jumps (…10, 16, 18…). Downstream the two orders do materially different amounts of work -- full traces are 1811 vs 2036 passes, a 225-pass difference -- which is why one binary ends up ~376 bytes larger with less inlining.

  WHY THIS MODULE AND NOT MOST: it emits 66 `__karac_panic_site_N` functions, every one an identical 3-instruction cold leaf (`printf`; `exit`; `unreachable`) differing only in the constants passed. That is a large set of structurally identical leaf functions in the call graph -- exactly the tie-heavy shape where an order that is unspecified becomes an order that is observable. It also fits the measured prevalence (rare: 1 of 22 sampled katas plus #253).

  THE OBVIOUS KARAC-SIDE MITIGATION IS A PESSIMISATION, so it is not proposed: collapsing the 66 wrappers into one `__karac_panic(file, line, col, fn, prefix, msg)` would remove the tie-heavy leaf set, but the whole point of a no-argument cold function per site is that the HOT path spends one argument-free `call` -- merging moves six argument setups to every panic site. Trading hot-path code for build reproducibility is the wrong side of that trade.

  SO THE REMAINING ACTION IS UPSTREAM, not in this repo: file against LLVM with the reproducer (any affected module's pre-opt .ll plus `-passes='default<O2>'`, six runs, two outputs). Regenerate one by dumping the module in `apply_optimization_passes` -- NOT via the `compile_to_ir` test helper, which takes a different path and shows nothing.

fix:
ROOT CAUSE: `refs_in_expr` (src/codegen/closures.rs) — the walker that decides
which names are read OUTSIDE an auto-par group, and therefore which bindings
need a return slot across the join — had an arm for `ExprKind::ArrayLiteral`
but NONE for `ExprKind::PrefixCollectionLiteral`, and ended in a `_ => {}`
wildcard that swallowed it silently.

A bare `[a, b]` checked against a `Vec`-typed annotation is NORMALIZED to
`PrefixCollectionLiteral{type_name:"Vec"}` before codegen runs. So the ordinary
`let c: Vec[Vec[i64]] = [a, b]` never matched the ArrayLiteral arm: `a` and `b`
never entered the outside-reads set, `compute_return_slots_checked` produced
ZERO slots (`defined ∩ refs` was empty), the bindings stayed branch-local
allocas, and the parent body had nothing to load — "Undefined variable 'a'".

Instrumented proof, failing vs. working program, same group [0,1]:
    [a, b]              DBG group_indices=[0,1] refs=["c","println"]      slots=[]
    a.len() + b.len()   DBG group_indices=[0,1] refs=["a","b","println"]  slots=["a","b"]

THE REPORT'S BOUNDING EXPERIMENTS WERE RIGHT ABOUT THE SYMPTOM AND WRONG ABOUT
THE MECHANISM, which matters because they point a fix at the wrong place. The
row reads as "it takes all three: fork + heap element + collection literal",
with scalars and tuples as controls that isolate the heap element. They do not:
`--concurrency-report` shows the scalar and tuple programs form NO parallel
group at all, so they never reach the walker. Heap-ness was never a condition —
it is only what earns the `allocates(Heap)` effect that makes two calls worth
forking. The single real condition is the third one: consumption by a
collection literal. The honest control is `a.len() + b.len()`, which forks
identically and works because a Binary/MethodCall chain was always covered.

FIX (two parts):
1. Added the missing arms — `PrefixCollectionLiteral` (the bug), plus
   `RepeatLiteral` and `MapLiteral`, which were missing the same way, plus
   `StructLiteral`'s `spread` (unreachable today: the parser accepts spread,
   the typechecker rejects it, design.md does not spec it — kept correct ahead
   of the language per the arm-group's own stated policy).
2. Replaced the `_ => {}` wildcard with an EXPLICIT leaf list, making the match
   exhaustive. This walker fails OPEN: a missed name gets no slot and becomes a
   build failure, while an EXTRA name is free (slots are `defined ∩ refs`, so a
   name no group statement binds is simply filtered out). With the asymmetry
   entirely one-directional, a wildcard is the wrong default — a new ExprKind
   must break the build rather than silently read as "mentions nothing". This
   is the fail-closed discipline `bce_length_pin::block_all` already documents.
   It paid immediately: making the match exhaustive surfaced two more variants
   (`PipePlaceholder`, `Error`) the audit had missed.

A SECOND COPY OF THE WALKER HAD THE SAME GAP.
`src/ownership/par_capture_classify.rs` carries a free-function twin of this
walker, and its module doc states the contract outright: the capture set it
produces "MUST match the codegen path's free-variable collection ... any
divergence between the two is a bug." It was missing the same three literal
arms, so a `shared` binding captured ONLY inside a collection literal in a
`par {}` block was invisible to the classifier, defaulted to `Copy`, and its
branch got no rc_inc — the exact latent miscompile that module exists to close.
Auditing the pair turned up nine further recursing arms the copy had drifted
without (`Question`, `Pipe`, `NilCoalesce`, `OptionalChain`, `Lock`, `WhileLet`,
`LabeledBlock`, `Comptime`, `Providers`), each the same defect for its own form.
Both walkers are now exhaustive and handle an identical 55-variant set, so the
contract is enforced by the compiler instead of by a comment.

VERIFIED on the 6-line repro and on kata 277's 5-element shape: `karac build`
(default auto-par), `karac run` (JIT), `karac run --interp`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` now all agree. Regression test
`test_e2e_autopar_joined_binding_in_collection_literal` (tests/par_codegen.rs)
covers the bare literal, the explicit `Vec[a, b]` prefix form, the Map and
repeat literals, the 5-element nested shape, and the `a.len() + b.len()`
control; confirmed FAILING on the parent commit and passing with the fix.
title: AUTO-PAR FORKS TWO INDEPENDENT `let`s AND THEN CODEGEN CANNOT SEE THEIR BINDINGS: two locals initialized from calls returning a heap collection, gathered into a collection literal `[a, b]`, fail the DEFAULT build with `codegen failed: Undefined variable 'a'`. The same program compiles and runs under `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` and under `--interp`.
tracker: The auto-par fork lowering's handling of a parallel group's `let` bindings in the CONTINUATION. The group is formed correctly (`--concurrency-report` shows both statements grouped, `reason: no data or effect dependencies`); what breaks is that a later collection literal referencing the forked bindings cannot resolve them. Only the collection-literal consumer is affected — `.len()` arithmetic, `push(a)`, and tuples all resolve fine.
detail:
FOUND BY kata 277, whose three solvers build a table of test matrices with a
`row(...)` helper and collect them: `let cases: Vec[Vec[Vec[bool]]] = [m1, m2,
m3, m4, m5];`. All three fail `karac build` and `karac run` (JIT) while passing
`--interp` and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`.

MINIMAL REPRO — six lines, no nesting required:

    fn mk(x: i64) -> Vec[i64] { let mut r: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); r.push(x); return r; }
    fn main() {
        let a: Vec[i64] = mk(1i64);
        let b: Vec[i64] = mk(2i64);
        let c: Vec[Vec[i64]] = [a, b];
        println(f"{c.len()}");
    }

    karac build            error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'a'
    karac run (JIT)        same
    karac run --interp     2
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build 2

AND THE COMPILER SAYS WHY, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART. `--concurrency-report` on
the failing program:

    function main (line 2):
      parallel_group {
        [3] mk(...)  // allocates(Heap)
        [4] mk(...)  // allocates(Heap)
        reason: no data or effect dependencies
      }
    error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'a'

The grouping is CORRECT — the two calls really are independent. The defect is
downstream: the bindings the group produces are not visible to the continuation
that consumes them.

WHY ONE CALL IS FINE. A parallel group needs >= 2 statements to be a real fork
(`fork_threshold_queries.rs` says so explicitly). One `let x = mk(1)` is a group
of one, is never forked, and compiles. So the bug needs exactly what a normal
program does: two or more independent helper calls in a row.

BOUNDED BY EXPERIMENT — the shape is narrower than "forked bindings are lost",
and the boundary is worth recording because it is where the fix has to look:

    FAILS   let a = mk(..); let b = mk(..); let c: Vec[Vec[i64]] = [a, b];
    FAILS   ... three of them collected into a literal
    OK      ... consumed as `a.len() + b.len()`
    OK      ... `c.push(a); c.push(b);` instead of the literal
    OK      ... `let c = (a, b);` (tuple)
    OK      ... `mk` returning i64 instead of Vec — SCALARS ARE FINE
    OK      ... only one of the two used afterwards
    OK      ... two locals from Vec.new()+push instead of from calls
    OK      ... two locals from Vec LITERALS

So it takes all three: (1) two or more bindings from CALLS, so a fork group
forms, (2) the calls returning a HEAP COLLECTION, and (3) the bindings consumed
as ELEMENTS OF A COLLECTION LITERAL. Scalars passing is the sharpest clue — the
same fork, the same two bindings, the same literal, and it compiles.

SEVERITY HIGH because it is on the DEFAULT path for an ordinary construct: build
a few things with a helper, put them in a list. Nothing about it is exotic and
nothing warns you — auto-par is on by default, so the natural program simply does
not build, and the two workarounds (turn auto-par off, or push instead of
collecting) both require already knowing this row exists. It is at least LOUD: a
build error, not a miscompile, and the interpreter disagreeing with the compiled
backends is a run-vs-build divergence in what COMPILES rather than in output.

THE KATA IS LEFT IN ITS NATURAL FORM AND CURRENTLY FAILS TWO OF ITS FOUR
SURFACES. Per the kata rules the fix is to the compiler, not to the kata —
rewriting `[m1, ..., m5]` as five `push` calls would hide this and is exactly the
contortion the corpus forbids. kata 277's README records the blocked surfaces and
points here. Its `differential.kara` builds `Vec[Vec[bool]]` from a bitmask
instead of a literal table and passes all four surfaces, so the kata's actual
verification is unaffected.

fix: FIXED by e953aae0. Guarded `LSAN_OPTIONS` on macOS the way `ASAN_OPTIONS` already was, and made the frontier ratchet Linux-only — both are needed, since the first change alone makes every cell read `Clean` and the assert then fails on every expected-`Leak` cell. Safety and value-correctness assertions still run everywhere and the grid still reports `0 skipped` on macOS, so use-after-free / double-free coverage is unchanged there.
title: `shared_ownership_matrix` CANNOT PASS ON macOS: 84529948 added an LSAN_OPTIONS env without the macOS guard ASAN_OPTIONS already had, so every cell aborts and reads `Leak`
detail:
`cargo test --features llvm` — the local pre-commit gate CLAUDE.md names — has been unconditionally red on macOS since 84529948, failing at the frontier assert with all 33 cells reporting `Leak` against a table that is almost entirely `Clean`. Nothing was leaking. The detector could not run.

MECHANISM. `classify` builds each case once and runs it twice, classifying by exit status: clean with leaks OFF but failing with leaks ON is read as `Leak`. It already guarded `ASAN_OPTIONS` on macOS, from the test's original commit dabcf943. 84529948 then added an `LSAN_OPTIONS` env WITHOUT that guard — and it added it precisely BECAUSE `LSAN_OPTIONS` takes precedence for leak detection, so the unsupported request stayed live through the variable that wins. Apple-clang ASAN ships no LSan, and asking for it does not degrade gracefully: it aborts before `main`. Reproduced outside the harness on a C program that mallocs and never frees:

    ASAN_OPTIONS=abort_on_error=0:exitcode=23 LSAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 ./lk  -> exit 0
    ASAN_OPTIONS=abort_on_error=0:exitcode=23 LSAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 ./lk  -> exit 23,
        "AddressSanitizer: detect_leaks is not supported on this platform."

So every cell's leaks-on run failed for a reason unrelated to the program under test, giving `off_ok && !on_ok` — the exact signature of `Leak` — for all 33 at once.

WHY IT SURVIVED REVIEW. The file already knows the platform story: its header says the Leak/Clean split "is meaningful on the CI `memory-sanitizer` job", and B-2026-08-06-34 added a `leak_detection_works()` canary for exactly this failure mode. But that canary is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` — it guards the platform that does not need it and is compiled out on the one that does, while the three assertions below it still run everywhere. The one check that would have caught an inert detector was absent precisely where the detector was inert.

CONSEQUENCE beyond the red itself: with cargo's default fail-fast this binary aborting also stops every test target ordered after it, so a genuine regression elsewhere never gets to run. A permanently-failing gate also trains the reader to skip its output.

FIX (e953aae0) is two changes, because either alone is wrong. Guarding `LSAN_OPTIONS` makes both runs identical off Linux, after which every cell reads `Clean` and the same assert fails the other way on every expected-`Leak` cell; so the frontier ratchet is also made Linux-only. The safety and value-correctness assertions still run everywhere and lose nothing by it — both read the leaks-OFF run, which needs no LSan — and the grid still reports `0 skipped` on macOS, so every case is built and executed and use-after-free / double-free / value-corruption coverage is unchanged there.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: relaxing `FLOWS.expected` to match the observed grid. That writes a dead detector's output into the ratchet as if it were the frontier — the exact failure B-2026-08-06-34 added the control to prevent — and would have deleted real leaks from the gate. If this row's symptom ever recurs, the fix is to the detector or its guards, never to the expected table.

SOURCE NOTE. Surfaced while verifying B-2026-08-15-30 against the full suite, and established as pre-existing and unrelated by re-running the same test with that change stashed, on the same commit, where it failed identically.

fix: FIXED by 012645a5. The row's own re-aimed lead, acted on: the partition's short leaves now go to a dedicated stable insertion sort instead of back to the natural-run merge. Isolated shuffled sort 352.3M -> 313.2M cycles (0.889x), gap to driftsort 1.81x -> 1.61x; katas #252 0.882x and #253 0.930x with byte-identical output. Structured patterns flat (reverse 0.989x, few-unique 0.996x, sawtooth 0.996x, nearly-sorted 1.005x; `sorted` reads 1.018x but never takes the partition path, so that is placement on a 3.9M baseline). Both element widths win too — scalar i64 0.858x, 32-byte 4-tuple 0.925x — which mattered because width has flipped the sign on this path before. Every figure is same-commit, both arms from one karac via the new `KARAC_SORT_LEAF=merge|insertion` lever, with checksum agreement asserted on every pair. Stability holds by the strictly-greater shift, same argument as phase 1's insertion padding; 462-case sweep 0 violations with its poison control still failing, plus a new E2E driving the unstructured arm. SPAN re-swept and deliberately left at 64: the merge leaf's tight U is gone and an insertion leaf is flat 8..64. What this row got RIGHT and what it got WRONG is worth keeping: the kernel lead it was filed on was wrong (measured dead, step 2), and the leaf lead it was re-aimed at was right and worth 0.89x. The remainder is B-2026-08-16-9.
title: Shuffled `sort_by` is still ~1.80x driftsort after B-2026-08-15-30 routed it to the partition; the one measured lead is the scatter kernel's shape
detail:
After B-2026-08-15-30 (93ea7a86) routed shuffled input to the stable quicksort, kara sits at ~1.80x Rust's driftsort on shuffled `(i64,i64)`, down from 2.80x. Isolated pure-sort cycles, n=150k x 25: kara 350M, driftsort 194M. Whole-kata the same shape — #252 1.80x, #253 1.27x. Filed separately rather than left implicit in the closed row, because the remainder is real and there is exactly one measured lead.

THE LEAD: the scatter kernel's shape. The shipped partition is count-then-scatter over a SINGLE destination buffer — one counting pass, then one placement pass whose two cursors write into one buffer, which is what makes the two halves land contiguous without a third allocation. An alternative writes to TWO buffers with no counting pass: one sequential load, an unconditional store to BOTH buffers, and only the winning cursor advances, so the losing store is overwritten next iteration. Measured in isolation over 3.75M elements of `(i64,i64)`:

  two-buffer, no count pass     17.27 instr/elem    2.49 cyc/elem   IPC 6.93
  merge pass it would replace   22.67 instr/elem   11.75 cyc/elem   IPC 1.93

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN, and this is the honest state: the SHIPPED count-then-scatter kernel was never isolated. A Kara-level approximation of it measured 23.31 instr/elem and 12.91 cyc/elem at IPC 1.81 — no cheaper than the merge pass — but that approximation's counting pass was written BRANCHY, and the branchy row of the same experiment shows a branchy partition collapsing to IPC 1.01, so the figure is not attributable to the count-then-scatter design. The emitter's own count is branchless ("two tallies from one comparison", `build_int_add` of a zext'd bool), so the shipped kernel plausibly sits far below 12.91. Until it is isolated, the gap between 2.49 and whatever the shipped kernel actually costs is unquantified, and the size of the available win with it.

NEXT MEASUREMENT, in order: (1) isolate the shipped `qpart` scatter's per-element cost directly — instrument the emitted function rather than approximate it in Kara, since the approximation is what went wrong above; (2) only if it is materially above ~4 cyc/elem, evaluate the two-buffer variant, whose cost is a third n-sized buffer plus reconciling the two halves into contiguity, neither of which the single-buffer form pays.

DO NOT re-open this by re-testing the ROUTING. That is settled and measured: both gates must be opened together, the admission band is [25%, 80%] of ordered adjacent pairs, and the closed row carries the full crossover curve. This row is about the kernel inside the partition, not about which input reaches it.

STEP (1) DONE — THE SHIPPED KERNEL IS NOW ISOLATED, on x86-64 (Intel Xeon @
2.80GHz, cloud container), NOT on the M5 the rest of this row is measured on.
Read the ISA caveat at the bottom before comparing numbers.

METHOD, and it is the direct instrumentation the row asked for rather than
another Kara-level approximation: `qpart` is emitted `Linkage::Internal`, so it
carries no symbol and no profiler can name it. Building with that one linkage
flipped to External (measurement-only, not committed) makes it addressable;
callgrind then attributes instruction counts to it directly, and `objdump` over
the same binary gives the emitted loop bodies.

PER-ELEMENT COST OF THE TWO PASSES, from the emitted x86:

  count pass    51 instrs / 16 elements =  3.2 instr/elem   AVX2, 16-wide
  scatter pass  39 instrs /  2 elements = 19.5 instr/elem   scalar, 2x unrolled
  ------------------------------------------------------------------
  pair                                   ~22.7 instr/elem

BOTH PASSES ARE BRANCHLESS, as the row supposed — `setl`/`setle`/`cmove` in the
scatter, `vpcmpgtq`/`vpsubq` tallies in the count, and the only branch in either
body is the loop back-edge.

THE COUNT PASS IS NOT THE PROBLEM, which is the substantive correction to this
row's framing. It vectorizes 16 elements wide because it is a pure branchless
reduction, and at 3.2 instr/elem it is ~14% of the pair. The row treats
"count-then-scatter (two passes)" versus "two-buffer (one pass)" as a contest
about the extra pass; the extra pass costs almost nothing. Whatever the
two-buffer form wins, it does not win by deleting the count.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE CASE FOR THE TWO-BUFFER VARIANT: weakens it on
instruction count, leaves it entirely open on ILP. Against the row's own table,
the shipped pair at ~22.7 instr/elem is 1.31x the two-buffer's 17.27 and level
with the 22.67 merge pass it replaces — so on instructions there is ~13% in it
for the scatter, not the 2x a two-passes-versus-one reading implies. The M5 case
for the rewrite was never really instruction count: it was 2.49 cyc/elem at IPC
6.93 against the merge's 11.75 at IPC 1.93. The shipped scatter is scalar and
only 2x unrolled BECAUSE its store address is data-dependent (`cmove` between
the two cursors, then one store), which is exactly the dependency an
unconditional-store-to-both-buffers form removes. So the ILP lead the row
identified is real in kind and still unquantified.

STILL NOT MEASURED, and it needs the M5: cyc/elem and IPC for the shipped
kernel. This container has no `perf` and no cycle counter — callgrind counts
instructions only. The row's own gate ("only if it is materially above ~4
cyc/elem") is therefore still unmet, and no rewrite should be attempted on the
strength of instruction counts alone.

x86 CONTEXT FOR THE 1.80x, since it is not the same number here: on this host
the residual is 1.42x, not 1.80x. Min-of-9 wall clock, n=150k x 25 reps of
shuffled `(i64,i64)`, sort time isolated by subtracting a build-only control
binary, kara and Rust driving identical LCG input and agreeing on the checksum:
kara 194 ms, Rust 137 ms. The B-2026-08-15-30 routing is confirmed firing here —
`KARAC_SORT_PART=always` reproduces the default exactly (193 ms vs 194 ms) and
`=never` costs 277 ms, so the partition is worth 0.70x on x86 against 0.64x
reported on M5. Same direction, smaller magnitude, consistent with the arm64
divergence B-2026-08-15-30 and -31 both document.

ISA CAVEAT: x86 and arm64 instruction counts are not comparable unit-for-unit,
so the ~22.7 figure should not be read straight against the 17.27/22.67 arm64
rows. What does transfer is structural and ISA-independent: which pass
vectorizes, which is scalar, that both are branchless, and that the count pass
is a small fraction of the pair.

STEP (2) RESOLVED — DO NOT DO THE REWRITE. The shipped kernel is now measured in
CYCLES on the M5, the gate step (1) could not meet, and it comes in BELOW that
gate. 2026-08-16, M5 Pro, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0.

METHOD. Same principle as step (1) — instrument the emitted code, do not
approximate it in Kara — but cycles need per-function attribution that macOS
cannot give (no callgrind, and `scripts/pmc` counts whole processes). So instead
of profiling one function, TRUNCATE it at codegen and difference whole-process
counters. Three binaries differing only in how far into `qpart` the emitted code
runs:

  entry   returns before the count pass    baseline
  count   returns after the count pass     count   = count - entry
  pair    returns after the scatter pass   scatter = pair  - count

n = 1,000,000 x 20 rounds = 20M element-passes through ONE partition level,
min-of-9. A truncated `qpart` writes only into scratch, so the input survives
each call and the same vector is re-sorted every round — no clone sitting in the
baseline to dilute the signal. Each mode sinks its own result into `data`,
because everything a truncated qpart writes is otherwise provably dead and LLVM
deletes the LOOP rather than the branch; the three binaries print three
different sinks, which is what proves both truncations actually ran.

  stage              instr/elem   cyc/elem    IPC
  count pass               3.26       0.79   4.15
  scatter pass            16.43       2.52   6.53
  count + scatter         19.69       3.30   5.96

THE ANSWER: the shipped scatter is 2.52 cyc/elem at IPC 6.53. The two-buffer
variant this row was held open for is 2.49 cyc/elem at IPC 6.93. They are the
same kernel speed. The data-dependent store address — the dependency the whole
lead rested on — costs essentially nothing: the two cursors are independent
accumulator chains and the store is fire-and-forget, so the M5 resolves the
`csel` destination without stalling. This row's gate ("only if it is materially
above ~4 cyc/elem") is not met by the scatter (2.52) and not met by the whole
level either (3.30). STEP (2) DOES NOT FIRE. The two-buffer form would pay a
third n-sized buffer and a contiguity reconciliation for nothing.

THE KARA APPROXIMATION WAS WRONG BY 5.1x, which retires the caveat this row was
written around: it said 12.91 cyc/elem at IPC 1.81 where the real kernel is 2.52
at 6.53. The row was right to refuse to act on it.

STRUCTURAL CONFIRMATION from the emitted arm64, agreeing with the differential
to under 3%. Both loops are identified without guessing — the pair build has
exactly one loop the count build does not, found by matching every loop across
the two disassemblies:

  count    26 instrs / 8 elements = 3.25/elem   NEON: 4x `ld2.2d` deinterleaving
           load, `cmgt.2d`/`cmge.2d` compares, `sub.2d` tallies
  scatter  16 instrs / 1 element  = 16.0/elem   scalar, branchless — `cset`,
           `cset`, two `csel`, one `str` to a computed index, both cursors
           advanced by `add` of a bool; the only branch is the back-edge

Cross-ISA agreement with step (1) is close on the count pass (3.26 here vs 3.2
on x86) and on the pair (19.69 vs ~22.7), so the two hosts corroborate.

WHERE THE 1.80x ACTUALLY IS — THE RE-AIMED LEAD. Same rig, a fourth mode
`noleaf` runs the whole partition tree but never sorts a leaf. The tree is
unaffected by that: every recursion decision comes from pivots and counts taken
before any leaf runs, and leaves are terminal. On sortk.kara's own n=150000 x 25
pattern 0, default routing, sort-minus-clone inside each binary:

  partition tree   188.2M cyc   50.2 cyc/elem   53.6%
  leaf merges      162.9M cyc   43.4 cyc/elem   46.4%
  total            351.1M cyc   93.6 cyc/elem   — reproduces this row's 350M
  rust driftsort   194.0M cyc   51.7 cyc/elem

The leaf merges ALONE cost 84% of driftsort's entire budget, and the partition
tree alone is already about equal to it. The residual is not in the partition.

AND SPAN IS ALREADY AT ITS OPTIMUM, so this is a lead about the leaf ALGORITHM
and not a tuning knob. Sweeping SPAN with the tree/leaf split at every point
(separate run, min-of-7; its 64 column reproduces the split above to 0.7%):

  SPAN       8       16       32       64      128      256
  total  385.8M   377.7M   359.1M   349.9M   356.1M   381.6M
  tree   288.2M   249.4M   214.8M   188.2M   166.7M   149.2M
  leaf    97.6M   128.3M   144.3M   161.7M   189.3M   232.4M
  ratio    1.99x    1.95x    1.85x    1.80x    1.84x    1.97x

A genuine U with the shipped 64 at its minimum and tight on both sides (64->32
costs +9.2M net, 64->128 costs +6.2M). This also explains why the sweep recorded
in the SPAN doc-comment read as a flat plateau over 32..128 and stopped at 32:
in that band a partition level and a leaf merge pass trade almost evenly, and
below 64 the marginal level exceeds the marginal leaf saving.

NEXT MEASUREMENT: the leaf sorter at n <= 64 is the natural-run MERGE sort. On
random input its natural runs are ~2 long, so each 64-element block is padded
and then makes ~log2(64/RUN) passes, and every leaf re-enters `sort_by` with its
own setup. 43.4 cyc/elem is NOT anomalous for a merge sort at that size — the
whole-array merge measures 145 cyc/elem over ~16 passes, which pro-rates to ~54
at 6 — so the leaf is not broken, it is the wrong algorithm at that size. Before
building anything, measure an insertion sort at the leaf against it: one pass
with a short shift distance, no allocation, no run detection.

fix: FIXED by ea042102. One shared recursion counter (`Parser::recursion_depth`, ceiling `MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH = 128`) claimed at the three mutually-recursive descent entries — `parse_expr_bp_with_ctx`, `parse_type`, `parse_pattern` — via enter/exit wrappers; at the ceiling the parser emits a single spanned E0001 ("nesting too deep") and unwinds instead of overflowing. title: Parser had NO recursion-depth limit: ~210 nested `(` crashed `karac check` with a stack-overflow abort (exit 134) instead of a diagnostic
detail:
`karac check` on `let x = ((((…1…))))` with ~210+ nesting levels died with `fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting` in a debug build — an unconditional process abort on arbitrary (adversarial or machine-generated) input, violating the repo's 'structured diagnostics, never panic' rule. The fat-stack mitigation (`run_on_interp_thread`, src/lib.rs) covered only the interpreter; parse/resolve/typecheck all ran on the caller's stack. All three descent surfaces reproduced (expressions, types via `fn f(x: (((i64))))`, patterns via `let (((a))) = 1`).

SIZING NOTE. The ceiling is sized for the stack the product parses on — the CLI / JIT-runner MAIN thread (8 MiB): one expression-descent level costs ~38 KiB in a debug build, so 128 levels ≈ 4.9 MiB with headroom. It is NOT sized for Rust's default 2 MiB spawned threads — debug frames overflow those at ~24 levels, below any useful ceiling — so an embedder driving `karac::parse` from its own small thread must size that thread's stack; the regression tests parse on a 32 MiB thread for exactly this reason. A future hardening option is `stacker::maybe_grow` at the guarded entries, which would decouple acceptance from frame-size drift entirely.

title: `env_set`/`env_var` fed the canonical empty Kāra String's null pointer to `slice::from_raw_parts` — library UB (benign today, a Miri/hardening trap)
detail:
The canonical empty Kāra String is `{null, 0, 0}` (documented at the lib.rs string helpers), so `env.var("")` / `env.set("", …)` passed a null pointer to `slice::from_raw_parts`, which requires a non-null, aligned pointer even for len 0. No misbehavior is observable today (the resulting `&[u8]` is never dereferenced at len 0), but it is undefined behavior by the `from_raw_parts` contract — the kind Miri or a hardened allocator turns into a real failure.

WHY IT EXISTED: the crate has two documented null-handling conventions — defensive (`is_null() || len == 0` guards: json/string fns, channel handles, alloc) and trust-codegen (map.rs module contract: access fns deref unconditionally, exclusivity proven by the effect system). Both are declared per-module, but there is no crate-level rule, and `env_set`/`env_var` sat in the crack: written in the trust-codegen style while the codegen contract (`a Kāra String's {ptr,len}`) actually INCLUDES the null-empty form. The fix moves them to the defensive side, matching every other string-taking entry in lib.rs.

FIXED by 7320d68. `check_function` only reconciled the declared return type
when the body had a final expression; a tail-less body went through
`infer_block` and the declared type was never consulted. The fix keys on what
`infer_block` already computes: `Never` (every path diverged) is fine under any
declared type; `Unit` (control can fall off the end) is an error against any

todo/unreachable/panic as one diverging family, but the typechecker's intercept
covered only todo/unreachable, so a `panic` call fell to the lenient

title: A function whose body produces NO VALUE passes `karac check` despite a declared non-Unit return type: `fn f() -> String { }` is accepted, the interpreter hands back `()` (so `f"[{f()}]"` prints `[()]` for a String-typed call), and the AOT binary prints nothing. Holds for `String`, `i64`, a user struct, a `ref`-parameter signature, and a body with a statement but no tail expression.
tracker: the function-body return check -- a declared return type is never reconciled against the body's tail type when the body yields Unit.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO -- 2 lines:

    fn f() -> String { }
    fn main() { println(f"[{f()}]"); }

    karac check          All checks passed.
    karac run --interp   [()]           <- a `String`-typed call rendering the UNIT value
    karac build (AOT)    (prints nothing)

EVERY SHAPE TRIED IS ACCEPTED (each a separate fixture, `karac check` first line):

    fn f() -> String { }                          All checks passed.
    fn f() -> i64 { }                             All checks passed.
    fn f() -> S { }        (user struct)          All checks passed.
    fn f(d: ref Doc) -> String { }                All checks passed.
    fn f() -> i64 { let x = 1; }   (stmt, no tail) All checks passed.

So it is not an empty-block special case -- a body that runs statements and simply never produces a value is accepted the same way. The declared type is not checked against the body at all on this path.

WHY HIGH. A return type is the most basic contract in a signature, and this is the front-end silently issuing `()` in its place. The interpreter's `[()]` is at least visible; the compiled backends produce nothing at all, so a function that forgot its tail expression yields an empty String / a zero / an unfilled struct rather than any error. It also weakens the whole checking story downstream -- anything that reasons about a callee's return value is reasoning about a type the body never had to produce.

SECOND-ORDER CONSEQUENCE, WHICH IS HOW IT WAS FOUND: this hole makes AUTOMATED REDUCTION unreliable. A delta debugger reducing an unrelated run-vs-build divergence, with a predicate that required `karac check` clean AND `karac run --interp` to succeed, reduced straight into a program containing `fn render(d: ref Doc) -> String { }` -- because check accepts it and the interpreter happily runs it returning `()`. That is the SECOND time a mechanical reduction in this session escaped through a `check` hole rather than shrinking the bug it was pointed at (the first was B-2026-08-15-11). Any reducer used on this codebase needs a predicate strong enough to reject degenerate programs -- comparing interpreter output against an expected value, not merely requiring it to run.

SUGGESTED FIXTURES: the five-shape table, all currently accepted; plus a guard that the correct forms still compile (a tail expression, an explicit `return`, and a genuine `-> Unit`/no-return function).
investigation: 2026-08-16 (hunt, regression sweep after the codegen cluster refactor). Isolated to two lines and widened across five signature shapes. Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix:
FIXED in c049126. The defensive-copy planner covered ONE move per binding; the
program has two.

MECHANISM, walked end to end. `UseAfterMove` diagnostics dedup to one witness
per binding — `direct_uam_candidates` returns `HashMap<String, UamWitness>` and
`first_uam_witness` stops at the first (C, U) pair — which is the right UX for
warnings. B-2026-08-10-21 then derived the defensive-copy site set FROM the
diagnostics ("so the set and the warning can never disagree"), inheriting the
dedup. With `e.doc` moved twice and reused after each move:

    let cur = e.doc;            // consume #1 — IN the set: deep-copied
    … apply(mut e.doc, ..);     // reuse #1 — reads the intact source, fine
    let after = e.doc;          // consume #2 — NOT in the set: the move's
                                //   source-zeroing suppression runs UNCOPIED,
                                //   zeroing e.doc.lines' len AND cap
    render(e.doc)               // reuse #2 — reads a zero-length Vec

The IR confirms it: one `uam.fld.struct` deep copy (at `cur`), then `smv.f0.len`
/ `smv.f0.cap` stored 0 at `after` with nothing copied. `render` sees len=0 —
so "[ ] lines=1": the length in the output comes from `after`'s moved copy, the
emptiness from the zeroed source. ONE CORRECTION to the row's reading: the
element does not "read back empty" — the source Vec reads as length ZERO at the
render site; the intact length the program prints is the copy's. Same
observable, different mechanism, and it matters for anyone probing the family.

THE FIX keeps the diagnostic exactly as it was and widens only the copy set.
`first_uam_witness`'s body moved into `uam_witnesses_for_binding(.., first_only)`;
a new `direct_uam_all_consume_sites` collects EVERY (C, U) witness's consume
span (one per consume site C, breaking on its first U). One shared function, so
the diagnostic and the planner can never again drift on the filter set — the
drift IS this bug. `OwnershipChecker::all_uam_consume_sites` accumulates across
functions and is unioned into `use_after_move_consume_sites` at harvest. The
documented invariant survives in the direction that matters: if the user was
told, codegen copies. This only ADDS sites, and only for moves of a binding the
user was already warned about.

THE ROW'S REDUCTION FLOOR IS EXPLAINED, and there is a smaller red member than
its 31 lines once you know the mechanism. Its failed reductions all removed one
of {second move, reuse-after-second-move} and so left the family. Knowing the
cause, this is red at the parent commit with no `mut ref` call and no enum:

    struct Doc { lines: Vec[String] }
    struct Ed { doc: Doc }
    fn text(d: ref Doc) -> String { return d.lines[0]; }
    fn main() {
        …
        let cur = e.doc;
        let after = e.doc;
        println(f"… {text(e.doc)} …");   // PANICS: vec index out of bounds
    }

— a louder symptom too (len zeroed under a live element ⇒ OOB, not silent
emptiness). Both the row's repro and this minimal are now E2E tests.

ALSO MEASURED, recorded because it prunes the search space: a chain of
consuming CALLS on a plain binding — `eat(a); eat(a); eat(a); println(a)` — is
NOT in this family. Green at the parent commit, heap-backed or not, so by-value
call args reach a different copy path; field MOVES are the shape the dedup
starved.

WHETHER THE CLUSTER REFACTOR INTRODUCED IT — the row left this open. Neither:
the defect is B-2026-08-10-21's harvest design (2026-08-10), predating the
BorrowVars/ModBindings extraction. The refactor merely reshuffled which dogfood
run tripped it.

MEMORY IS THE RISK OF THIS FIX, not the values: after two copied moves there
are THREE live owners of one heap shape (source + two deep copies), and a copy
that aliased double-frees at the three scope exits while an over-suppressed
source leaks. Gated: an ASAN fixture carrying the row's repro, the panicking
minimal, and a 10-iteration loop of a reused-move pair so a per-iteration
imbalance accumulates; the full memory_sanitizer suite (1110 green); and the
LSan corpus at both KARAC_AUTO_PAR settings.

TESTS: E2E (row's repro, red at baseline with "[] lines=1"), E2E minimal (red
at baseline with the OOB panic), ASAN fixture (red at baseline), interpreter
oracle (green throughout, as an oracle should be).

Gates: full `--features llvm` sweep of all 100 targets, 12591 tests, 0
failures; clippy `--all --all-targets` and fmt clean.

fix: Not fixed — measured to a standstill at 1.252x, closed so the open queue stops advertising work that has none. Two changes shipped over this row's life took shuffled `sort_by` from 1.52x to 1.252x against driftsort: the scatter unswitch (15 -> 9 instructions per element, by emitting the loop once per split predicate so the comparison stays in flags) and the fused single pass (count-then-scatter collapsed to one pass, trading a serial dependency for a reversal; +2.2% instructions, -3.2% cycles, IPC 3.95 -> 4.10). Every remaining block is measured and closed: the tree runs 1.15-1.81 instructions per element per level above the cost of its own passes; effective levels are 1.224x ideal against textbook median-of-3's ~1.19x; SPAN sits on a 24-64 plateau and moving it trades a documented few-unique strength for less than the noise band; the leaf has lost three shapes (binary insertion 1.603x, linear scan + memmove 1.149x, instruction removal at 0.043 cyc/instr) because it is bound by a mispredicted branch rather than work; the reversal is already three instructions per element moved with paired ldp/stp and the vectorize hint is inert on it; and the addressing premium is removable but removal is free of benefit (13.7 instructions per element saved, 1.001x cycles, because the identity that removes it also serialises the two cursors). Three independent demonstrations now say the remaining gap will not be found by removing instructions from this design.
title: Shuffled `sort_by` is ~1.26x driftsort after the fused single pass — the win is IPC, not work; tree at its two-pass floor and levels at the median-of-3 limit
detail:
After B-2026-08-16-3 (012645a5) replaced the partition's leaf merge with an insertion sort, shuffled `(i64,i64)` sits at ~1.61x Rust's driftsort on the M5, down from 1.81x (and from 2.80x before B-2026-08-15-30 routed it to the partition at all). Isolated pure sort, n=150000 x 25, min-of-7, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0: kāra 313.2M cycles against driftsort's 194.0M.

WHAT IS ALREADY RULED OUT, so this is not re-opened from the top:

1. THE ROUTING. Settled and measured in B-2026-08-15-30 — both gates must open together, the admission band is [25%, 80%] of ordered adjacent pairs, and that row carries the full crossover curve. Do not re-test which input reaches the partition.

2. THE PARTITION KERNEL. Measured dead in B-2026-08-16-3 step (2). The shipped count-then-scatter is 2.52 cyc/elem at IPC 6.53 against the two-buffer alternative's 2.49 at 6.93 — same speed, because the data-dependent store address costs nothing when the two cursors are independent accumulator chains. The count pass is 3.26 instr/elem, NEON 8-wide, ~16% of the level. Do not rebuild this kernel.

3. SPAN. Re-swept for the NEW leaf and left at 64 deliberately: with an insertion leaf the total is flat from 8 to 64 (311-316M, a 1.6% spread inside run-to-run noise) and degrades only at 96. There is no tuning left on this axis; the old tight U belonged to the merge leaf.

WHERE THE REMAINDER IS, and the honest state of the evidence. Splitting the pre-fix 351.1M with a codegen-truncated `noleaf` build gave partition tree 188.2M / leaf merges 162.9M. The tree figure carries over unchanged — the leaf is terminal and does not affect any partitioning decision — so the post-fix leaf is 313.2 - 188.2 = ~125M. That number is DERIVED, not measured; the truncation rig was reverted with the measurement patch and has not been re-run against the insertion leaf.

On that derivation the split is now roughly 60% tree / 40% leaf, and the tree is the larger half for the first time. Two candidate leads, neither measured:

  (a) THE TREE, at 188.2M / 50.2 cyc/elem for ~11 levels. Per level that is 3.30 cyc/elem measured directly, so ~37 cyc/elem is accounted for by the kernel and the remaining ~13 is per-call overhead — pivot selection (three splitmix64 draws, three loads, two compares), prologue, and the recursion itself, across ~2300 calls per round at the leaf end. Cheap to test: the per-call cost should fall out of a call-count sweep against SPAN, and the pivot draw is the obvious first suspect.

  (b) THE LEAF AGAIN, at ~125M / ~33 cyc/elem for 64-element blocks. An insertion sort at 64 does ~1024 shift iterations per block (n^2/4) with a data-dependent inner-loop trip count, so it is branch-mispredict bound. Standard answers are a smaller SPAN with a cheaper leaf, or a branchless/binary-search insertion. Note SPAN 8 measured 311.2M against 64's 312.8M — inside noise, but it is the direction a cheaper leaf would reward, so re-sweep SPAN if the leaf algorithm changes again.

FIRST MEASUREMENT: re-run the `noleaf` split against the insertion leaf to replace the derived ~125M with a measured one, before choosing between (a) and (b). The method is in B-2026-08-16-3 — truncate at codegen behind an env var and difference whole-process counters; every mode needs a sink or LLVM deletes the loop rather than the branch.

HOST NOTE: this is an M5 number. The same residual measured 1.42x on an x86 container before the leaf fix, and B-2026-08-11-28 was once closed `wontfix` at ~1.6x on x86 when the M5 read 3.70x. Any disposition of this row needs the arm64 measurement, not a container one.

FIRST MEASUREMENT DONE 2026-08-16, and it closes BOTH candidate leads. M5 Pro,
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, sortk.kara pattern 0, n=150000 x 25, min-of-9.

THE SPLIT, now measured instead of derived. A `noleaf` build (codegen-truncated
to run the whole partition tree but sort no leaf — BOTH leaf sorters skipped, not
just the insertion one) against the normal build:

  partition tree   188.0M cyc   50.1 cyc/elem   60.3%
  leaf sorts       123.9M cyc   33.0 cyc/elem   39.7%
  total            311.9M cyc                   1.61x driftsort

The derived figure this row was filed with was right: predicted ~125M, measured
123.9M. The tree also carried over from the pre-fix split unchanged (188.0M vs
188.2M), which is the assumption the derivation rested on, so it is now checked
rather than assumed.

LEAD (a), PER-CALL OVERHEAD — CLOSED, it is 2.6% of the tree. Measured two ways:

  1. The pivot's three runtime `s % len` reductions, the row's named first
     suspect, are a `udiv` + `msub` each on a divider that is not pipelined.
     Replacing them with Lemire's `(s * len) >> 64` (one `umulh`) is worth
     0.990x on random and 0.980x on few-unique, flat on the other four, with
     instruction counts corroborating (-1.2%, -3.4%). Shipped as 93ed7a16
     because it is free and strictly better, but it is a 1% change, not a lead.

  2. The per-call floor directly. In `noleaf` mode there is no leaf, so tree
     instructions as a function of SPAN isolate depth; the intercept of that
     line is everything that is NOT per-level work. Five points, SPAN 32..512:

       SPAN         32      64     128     256     512
       tree     1181.4M 1076.5M  981.2M  887.4M  797.0M   instructions

     Slope 95.8M instr per level (25.55 instr/elem/level), intercept 8.1M —
     2.6% of the tree at SPAN 64. There is nothing else to win per call.

LEAD (a'), PIVOT QUALITY — CLOSED BEFORE BUILDING, the tree is already balanced.
Total/slope gives 11.24 EFFECTIVE levels against a balanced log2(150000/64) =
11.19, an imbalance of 1.00x. The linearity across five points is itself the
evidence: an imbalanced tree contributes less work per level as it deepens, so
the line would bend, and it does not. Median-of-3 is delivering a balanced tree,
so a ninther (which would take a median-of-3 quicksort's ~1.19x work constant
toward ~1.09) has nothing to collect here. DO NOT BUILD IT.

A FALSE START WORTH RECORDING, because it nearly sent this row at the ninther: a
first pass estimated levels by dividing tree instructions by the 19.69 instr/elem
that B-2026-08-16-3 measured for one count+scatter pair, giving 14.82 levels and
an imbalance of 1.32x — which would have made pivot quality worth ~10% of the
whole sort. That constant came from a TRUNCATED build (no recursion, leaf edges
cut) whose register allocation and per-call terms need not match the shipped
recursive qpart, and in situ the real figure is 25.55, 30% higher. Measuring the
constant in the same build it is applied to is what turned 1.32x into 1.00x. The
general form of this trap is in B-2026-08-16-3: a figure measured on a truncated
build is valid for the truncated build.

THE ONE QUANTITY LEFT, and the row's new lead. The two passes measure 19.69
instr/elem in isolation; a level costs 25.55 in situ. So ~24% of per-level cost
— roughly 6 instr/elem, ~5.9 instr/elem x 11.24 levels x 3.75M elements, call it
250M instructions or a sixth of the whole sort's 1447M — is spent OUTSIDE the
count and scatter loops. Candidates, none yet measured: the ping-pong parity
memcpys (`alleq_cp`, `l_eq_cp`, `r_eq_cp`, `leaf_cp`), per-level loop setup, and
the pivot's three loads plus two comparator inlinings. Note the isolation figure
carries the caveat above, so step one is to re-measure the two passes' cost IN
the recursive build (a `pair`-style truncation that keeps the recursion) before
attributing the difference to anything.

WHAT IS NOW RULED OUT ON THIS SORT, cumulatively: the routing (B-2026-08-15-30),
the partition kernel's shape (B-2026-08-16-3 step 2), SPAN (re-swept twice, flat
8..64 with the insertion leaf), per-call overhead (2.6%), and pivot quality
(imbalance 1.00x). Both halves of the sort are at their local optima; what
remains is a work-count difference against driftsort, not a tuning gap.

CORPUS IMPACT, measured 2026-08-16 (kara-katas 9a94975). Nine benchmarked katas
call `sort_by`; TWO moved, and the other seven were measured rather than assumed:

  #252  kara 217.3 -> 91.7 ms (0.42x)   vs equal-safety Rust  3.67x -> 1.57x
  #253  kara 244.7 -> 145.4 ms (0.59x)  vs equal-safety Rust  2.04x -> 1.20x

Comparators held still across the same runs (#252: Rust 58.8 -> 58.7, C 265.0 ->
255.6, Go 467.0 -> 464.2 ms), so these are compiler results and not machine
drift. They also corroborate this row's isolated 1.61x from a different
direction, and #253 staying relatively better than #252 (1.20x vs 1.57x, as it

That test needed its own noise floor first, which is the transferable part:
INSTRUCTION COUNTS ARE NOT DETERMINISTIC for these katas — #15 spans 1.459% on a
SINGLE binary, #18 0.441%, #1665 0.165%, #252 0.112%. A first pass using "any
instruction difference" flagged all nine. Against each binary's own measured

LEAF VARIANTS TRIED AND REJECTED 2026-08-16 — both LOSE, nothing shipped. The
leaf is 39.7% of the sort and its inner loop pays one comparison per shift step
(~16 per element at a 64-element leaf, ~1024 per leaf), so the two textbook
answers were worth measuring. Both arms of each A/B came from one karac via
`KARAC_SORT_ISORT`, checksums asserted equal, 462-case stability sweep clean on
both — these are performance rejections, not correctness ones.

1. BINARY INSERTION (binary-search the landing slot, then `memmove`):
   **1.603x SLOWER on random** — 310.6M -> 498.0M cycles. Instructions were
   FLAT at 1.016x, so this is pure IPC: **4.66 -> 2.95**. Trading ~16
   independent, sequential, prefetchable comparisons for ~5 SERIALLY DEPENDENT
   ones is a bad trade on this core — each `mid` depends on the previous
   compare and each load depends on that `mid`, which is a load->compare->
   select->load chain. This is the same shape as the merge's data-dependent
   READ cursor (IPC 1.93) that B-2026-08-15-30 routed away from in the first
   place. Comparison COUNT is not the leaf's cost; the dependency chain is.

2. LINEAR SCAN + `memmove` (keep the sequential scan, block-move the shift):
   **1.149x slower on random** — 311.3M -> 357.7M — and this one costs
   INSTRUCTIONS, 1446.9M -> 1571.5M (+8.6%), with IPC roughly unchanged
   (4.65 -> 4.39). The reason is structural and it is the useful finding: the
   shipped scan-and-shift FUSES the search and the shift into ONE backward pass,
   comparing and storing per step. Any form that separates them reads the range
   twice, and at an average shift distance of ~16 elements the second pass costs
   more than the vectorised block move saves. Structured patterns were flat
   (few-unique 0.986x, nearly-sorted 1.003x), so the loss is entirely on the
   path that actually uses the leaf.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE ROW: the shipped leaf beats both textbook alternatives,
and the reason it does is that it is a single fused sequential pass. That is a
strong constraint on any future leaf proposal — it must stay one pass and stay
sequential, which rules out the whole search-then-move family. Combined with
SPAN already being at its optimum, the leaf half now looks as closed as the tree
half. The remaining lead is unchanged: the ~24% of per-level tree cost sitting
outside the count and scatter loops, and its first step is still to re-measure
the two passes IN the recursive build.

STEP ONE DONE 2026-08-16 — the two passes measured IN the recursive build, by
disassembling the shipped binary rather than by another truncation. The gap is
explained and it is NOT the loops' compilation.

  pass       truncated build      shipped (in situ)
  count      3.25 instr/elem      5.00 instr/elem   10 instrs / 2 elements
             NEON 8-wide          2x-unrolled SCALAR
  scatter   16.43 instr/elem     15.00 instr/elem   15 instrs / 1 element
  pair      19.69                20.00

The SCATTER is the same loop in both — 15 instrs against 16, marginally BETTER
in situ — so register pressure from the recursion was not the story. The COUNT
is 54% worse, and the reason is concrete: the shipped binary contains ZERO NEON
(`ld2.2d` = 0, `cmgt.2d` = 0 across the whole text), while the truncated build
vectorised the identical reduction 8-wide. That is a real, quantified
codegen-quality gap: 3.25 instr/elem is demonstrably achievable for this loop and
the shipped one gets 5.00.

BUT IT DOES NOT ACCOUNT FOR THE 24%, which is the useful finding. Even with the
in-situ numbers the two loop bodies come to 20.00 instr/elem against a per-level
cost of 25.55 — a 5.55 gap, essentially the same 5.86 the truncated figures gave.
Substituting better loop measurements barely moved it, so the gap is not in the
loops at all. What is left per level is PER-RANGE FIXED COST: two loop
setups/prologues, the pivot draw, the call itself, and the parity memcpys, none
of which scale with range length. At the deepest levels ranges are 64-128
elements, so ~100 instructions of fixed cost per range is ~1 instr/elem there and
grows as ranges shrink.

THAT TIES THE TWO HALVES TOGETHER AND EXPLAINS THE SPAN OPTIMUM. Per-range fixed
cost is reduced only by having fewer, larger ranges — a bigger SPAN — and the
SPAN sweep already showed that loses more in the O(n^2) leaf than it recovers in
the tree. The two halves are coupled through exactly this term, which is why 64
sits at a minimum rather than on a plateau edge.

restore vectorisation — still zero NEON — but it does change the loop from

So the instruction win is unambiguous and the cycle win is not demonstrated.
Sub-1% on random for ~150 lines of emitter and a new function is not worth it;

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY BE WORTH BUILDING, if this row is picked up again: get the

THE COUNT PASS NOW VECTORISES — FIXED IN 3afcee6e, and it is the first win in
this row. The gap recorded above (3.25 instr/elem achievable, 5.00 shipped) was
NOT a legality problem and not a consequence of the recursion: it was the
vectoriser's COST MODEL declining a loop it was perfectly able to vectorise.

HOW IT WAS ISOLATED, since karac exposes no per-loop remark attribution:
`-pass-remarks-analysis=loop-vectorize` forwarded through `KARAC_LLVM_ARGS`
gives an unattributed stream (karac does not wire `-pass-remarks-output`, so
there is no YAML with function names, and `<unknown>:0:0` is all the text
carries). Attribute by DIFFERENCE instead — `KARAC_SORT_PART=never` leaves
`qpart` uncalled, an Internal uncalled function is dead-stripped before the
vectoriser runs, so whatever remarks disappear between the two builds belong to
the partition. That leaves exactly:

  +2  value that could not be identified as reduction is used outside the loop
  +1  could not determine number of loop iterations
  +1  cannot identify array bounds
  +1  the cost-model indicates that vectorization is not beneficial

The +2 reduction remarks are the SCATTER's two cursors — they are used as store
ADDRESSES inside the loop, so they are not reductions and that loop is
unvectorisable by construction. That leaves the cost-model remark for the count
pass, the only loop in the partition that can vectorise at all.

THE FIX is therefore an override, not a reshape: `llvm.loop.vectorize.enable` on
the count loop's back-edge, built with the same self-referential loop-id recipe
`attach_unroll_full_metadata` already uses. `cmgt.2d`/`cmge.2d` appear where the
binary previously had zero NEON.

  pattern      cycles   instructions
  random        0.954x   0.970x
  few-unique    0.916x   0.953x
  other four    flat     1.000x

Against each binary's OWN floor over 21 interleaved reps: random -3.05% instr at
160x floor and -4.42% cycles at 4.2x, both clear; few-unique -4.71% instr at 75x
floor, with its -10.6% cycle delta INSIDE its own 11.6% floor so only the
instruction result is claimed. Shuffled sort vs driftsort 1.60x -> 1.52x.

NOTE WHAT THIS SAYS ABOUT THE COST MODEL. The hint overrides pricing only, so
the win is direct evidence the model was WRONG here, not merely conservative: a
strided read of `.0` out of a 16-byte element is exactly the access pattern it
prices badly, and it mispriced it by enough to cost 4%.

WHICH RE-AIMS THIS ROW. Everything before this was structural — routing, kernel
shape, SPAN, per-call overhead, pivot quality, two leaf variants — and every
answer was "already at its optimum". This one was codegen QUALITY, a different
category, and it was found by asking the backend rather than by reasoning about
the algorithm. The remaining ~1.52x should be searched the same way before any
more algorithm work: the scatter is unvectorisable and the leaf is a fused
sequential pass by necessity, but nothing has yet checked whether the merge
sort's own passes, phase 1's run detection, or the leaf's inner loop are being
declined the same way. `KARAC_SORT_PART=never` plus the remark diff is the tool,
and it took about ten minutes.

FOLLOW-ON, filed as its own question rather than buried here: if one hot loop in
this emitter was being silently declined by the cost model, others may be. A
corpus-wide sweep for `the cost-model indicates that vectorization is not
beneficial` across the kata corpus would say whether this is a one-off or a

FOLLOW-ON ANSWERED: THE MISPRICING IS NOT SYSTEMATIC. Swept all 294 kata bench
sources (build-only, `-pass-remarks-analysis=loop-vectorize`, karac d8399be6):
37 cost-model declines total across 35 katas, almost all exactly one each. A
trivial program declines ZERO, so there is no runtime baseline inflating that
and every decline is real code — but 37 across 294 programs, none of them shown
to be hot, is a background rate and not a pattern.

The counting pass was special for a reason worth writing down, because it is
what makes the negative result make sense. It accumulates a CONDITIONAL
INCREMENT — the emitted loop is `cmp` / `cinc` / `cinc`, with no overflow check,
because a counter bounded by the range length cannot overflow. That is why it
was merely DECLINED on cost and therefore rescuable with a hint. An ordinary
integer reduction in user code is not declined at all; it is BLOCKED, and by
something else entirely — see B-2026-08-16-11, filed from this sweep.

THE SCATTER WAS PAYING SIX INSTRUCTIONS PER ELEMENT FOR A LOOP-INVARIANT SELECT
— FIXED IN 3faf1f2e. Second win from asking what the backend emitted rather than
reasoning about the algorithm, and four times the size of the first. Shuffled
sort vs driftsort 1.52x -> 1.30x.

WHAT WAS THERE. The scatter picks a side with `select(no_lt, sc <= 0, sc < 0)`,
where `sc` is the comparator's three-way result and `no_lt` is fixed for the
whole range. A select needs its operands as VALUES, so both predicates were
materialised and the invariant was re-tested every iteration:

  ldr  q0, [x9], #0x10
  fmov x16, d0
  cmp  x16, x10
  cset w16, lt              <- materialise `sc < 0`
  cset w17, le              <- materialise `sc <= 0`
  cmp  x12, #0x0            <- LOOP-INVARIANT, re-executed per element
  csel w16, w17, w16, eq
  cmp  w16, #0x0            <- re-test what the flags already held
  csel x17, x15, x14, ne
  str  q0, [x8, x17, lsl #4]
  eor  w17, w16, #0x1
  add  x15, x15, x16
  add  x14, x14, x17
  subs x13, x13, #0x1
  b.ne

THE CONTROL WAS TWO BLOCKS UP IN THE SAME FUNCTION. The counting pass uses the
SAME comparator and the SAME two predicates, but consumes them as condition
codes rather than through a select, and compiles to six instructions:
`ldr / cmp / cinc lt / cinc le / subs / b.ne`. That comparison is what turned
"15 instr/elem is presumably what a scatter costs" into a measurable defect —
the emitter already contained proof that this comparator folds into flags when
nothing forces it into a register.

THE FIX is a loop unswitch done in the emitter: emit the loop once per predicate
and branch to the right one before entering. Both arms compile to exactly nine
instructions — `ldr / fmov / cmp / csel / cinc / str / cinc / subs / b.ne`.

WHY LLVM DOES NOT DO IT. SimpleLoopUnswitch unswitches invariant BRANCHES; this
is a select, and no pass turns an invariant select into a branch to unswitch.
Nor is there a cheaper spelling: folding the two predicates into one comparison
against a precomputed threshold (`sc < thr`, `thr = no_lt ? 1 : 0`, valid since
`sc` is three-valued) would force `sc` itself into a register, which is the cost
being removed. Duplicating the loop is what keeps the compare in flags.

same signature — two `cset`s off one `cmp`, a three-way compare forced into

`ldr ldr cmp csel cset cset ldp stp add add cmp ccmp b.ne`, where the
`cset/cset/add/add` tail should be `cinc/cinc`. That loop does not run on random
input so it cannot move this row's headline — it is the sorted / nearly-sorted /

The insertion leaf is the better lead for the random path now that the tree has
shrunk under it. Its inner loop is nine instructions per shift step:

  ldur x13, [x12, #-0x10]     key of data[j-1]
  cmp  x13, x11
  b.le exit
  sub  x10, x10, #0x1
  ldur x14, [x12, #-0x8]      the OTHER half of the same 16 bytes
  stp  x13, x14, [x12], #-0x10
  add  x13, x10, #0x1         re-derives the old j
  cmp  x13, #0x1              ...to test `jm1 > 0` the long way
  b.gt

Two of the nine look removable. The emitter loads the whole element in the
compare block but only `.0` is used there, so the backend SINKS the `.1` load
into the shift block, splitting one `ldp` into two `ldur`s — a trade that saves
a load on the single iteration that exits and costs one on each of the ~11 that
do not. And `add x13, x10, #1 / cmp x13, #1` is `cmp x10, #0` the long way. The
leaf is now the largest single term at ~34% of remaining instructions, so 2-of-9
there is worth roughly what the scatter fix was.

THE LEAF LEAD, BOTH HALVES MEASURED. The row named two removable-looking
instructions in the insertion leaf's nine-instruction inner loop. One was an
illusion, the other is real on instructions and worth nothing in cycles — and
that second result closes the direction.

HALF ONE, THE DOUBLED LOAD — NOT A DEFECT, NOTHING TO FIX. The emitter loaded
`data[j-1]` in the compare block and again in the shift block, and the binary
showed the pair split into two `ldur`s where one `ldp` would do. The obvious
reading was that the redundant IR load caused it. It does not: rewriting the
shift to reuse the value the compare block already loaded produces a
BYTE-IDENTICAL binary (51,447 disassembly lines, the only difference the symbol
name). LLVM's GVN had already CSE'd it, and the split is a downstream SINKING
decision the backend makes on a single load — `.0` is needed before the branch,
`.1` only after it, so it sinks `.1`. Not addressable by changing the IR shape.
The patch was reverted rather than shipped as a no-op.

HALF TWO, THE LOOP TEST — SHIPPED IN 6235491f, and it is bigger than the row
guessed. `j` starts at `i >= 1` and is decremented only under the guard being
tested, so `j != 0` and `j > 0` are the same test; but the signed form costs
TWO instructions per shift step, not one. LLVM rewrites the induction variable
to `j-1` and then re-derives the old `j` purely to compare it:

  ldur x13, [x12, #-0x10]        ldur x13, [x12, #-0x10]
  cmp  x13, x11                  cmp  x13, x11
  b.le exit                      b.le exit
  sub  x10, x10, #0x1            ldur x14, [x12, #-0x8]
  ldur x14, [x12, #-0x8]         stp  x13, x14, [x12], #-0x10
  stp  x13, x14, [x12], #-0x10   sub  x10, x10, #0x1
  add  x13, x10, #0x1            cbnz x10, loop
  cmp  x13, #0x1
  b.gt loop                      (9 instructions -> 7)

Worth -7.31% of the WHOLE shuffled sort's instructions, at 44x its own floor
over 21 interleaved reps on the wide-key harness.

AND WORTH NO CYCLES AT ALL — established by amplification, not by a floor
comparison. Raising SPAN makes the leaf a larger share of the sort, so a real
cycle effect has to scale with it. The instruction win does, by exactly the
amount removing 2 of 9 instructions predicts; the cycle response does not move:

  SPAN      instructions    cycles
    64          0.927        0.993
   128          0.884        1.005
   256          0.843        1.004

Instructions fall by up to 15.7% across a 2x change in leaf share while cycles
sit flat. THE LEAF'S INNER LOOP IS BOUND BY ITS MISPREDICTED EXIT BRANCH AND THE
LOAD->COMPARE LATENCY, NOT BY INSTRUCTION COUNT. That is a much stronger
statement than "the cycle win is not shown against the floor", and it closes
this direction: no further instruction-removal in that loop can pay.

It was shipped anyway — one predicate, no cycle regression at the shipped SPAN,
and two instructions per shift step may well matter on a narrower core than the
M5, where this row has already been burned once by an x86/arm64 disagreement.
`KARAC_SORT_ISORT_NE=0` restores `> 0`.

WHAT THIS LEAVES. The leaf resists instruction-level work (this), a cheaper
search (binary insertion, 1.603x slower), and a block move (linear scan +
memmove, 1.149x slower) — three independent attempts, three losses, and the
reason is the same each time: its cost is a data-dependent branch and a
serial dependency chain, not work. The tree's per-range fixed cost is coupled to
SPAN, and SPAN is at its measured optimum on honestly-uniform data. So the
remaining ~1.29x is not obviously reachable from either half, and any further
attempt should start by finding a cheaper SHAPE for the leaf — one that keeps
the single fused sequential pass but breaks the per-element branch dependency —
rather than by trimming what is already there.

TWO RESULTS: THE RESIDUAL IS NOT LAYOUT, AND IT IS NOT THE LEAF.

relative ORDER — and that a relative-order change alone moved kata 236 by 15.5%
with byte-identical hot code. So this row's placement clearances covered less
than they appeared to, and the residual had never been tested against the effect
that actually bites.
