entirely. Rust's own layout spread being twice kāra's (3.51% vs 1.75%) is also
worth knowing — driftsort is the more placement-sensitive of the two.

SECOND — WHERE THE WORK IS. Still a work gap at IPC parity, confirmed on today's
build: kāra 273.1 instr/elem at IPC 3.99, driftsort 222.0 at IPC 4.19;
instruction ratio 1.230x, cycle ratio 1.291x. So ~78% of the residual is doing
more work and ~22% is slightly worse ILP.

The two halves scale in OPPOSITE directions with SPAN — leaf ~ n*SPAN, tree ~
n*log2(n/SPAN) — so a SPAN sweep separates them with no per-function profiling
at all:

  SPAN   instr/elem   cyc/elem    IPC
    16        260.2       72.7   3.58
    32        254.9       68.8   3.70
    64        273.2       68.8   3.97
   128        333.4       77.5   4.30
   256        471.9       99.7   4.73

  fit: instr/elem = 1.280*SPAN + 23.57*log2(n/SPAN) - 72.2   (|err| <= 0.5%)

A two-term model fitting five points to within half a percent is itself evidence
the shape is right. The marginals are the finding:

  A PARTITION LEVEL COSTS 23.57 INSTRUCTIONS PER ELEMENT.
  A leaf element costs 1.28 instructions per unit of SPAN.

At the shipped SPAN 64 that is ~11.2 levels x 23.57 = ~264 instr/elem of tree
against ~82 of leaf. Driftsort spends 222 in TOTAL over ~17.2 merge passes,
about 12.9 per pass. So kāra does FEWER levels than driftsort and each one costs
1.8x a merge pass. THE TREE IS THE ENTIRE RESIDUAL; the leaf is not where the
gap lives, which retires the direction this row last recommended.

WHAT 23.57 SHOULD BE. A level is a count pass plus a scatter pass over the same
elements. The scatter is 9 instructions per element since the unswitch, and a
count pass is 4-6, so the two passes floor at ~15 and the per-range costs
(median-of-3 pivot, entry probe, tie gate) amortise over >= SPAN elements at
roughly 3. That accounts for ~18 of 23.57, leaving ~5-6 instructions per element
per level unexplained — and THAT is the next thing to find, not another leaf
shape.

SPAN STAYS AT 64. The sweep also re-confirms it: 32 and 64 are identical on
cycles (68.8 both) despite 32 using 18.3 fewer instructions per element, because
IPC falls from 3.97 to 3.70 and cancels it exactly. Both beat 16 (72.7) and 128
(77.5). The optimum is a plateau, not a point, and moving along it trades
instructions for ILP at par.

CORRECTION TO THE ABOVE: THE TREE IS AT ITS FLOOR. THERE ARE NO 5-6
INSTRUCTIONS TO FIND.

The previous append derived "a partition level costs 23.57 instr/elem" from the
SPAN fit and concluded ~5-6 of them were unaccounted for. That was an artifact
of the arithmetic, not a property of the sort: dividing TOTAL instructions by
the level count charges the LEAF's work to the tree, and the leaf is the half
that scales with SPAN.

MEASURED INSTEAD OF FITTED, using two levers whose per-iteration instruction
delta is exactly known, so loop iteration counts can be COUNTED rather than
modelled:

    KARAC_SORT_SCATTER_SPLIT=0  reverts the unswitch, +6 per scatter iteration
    KARAC_SORT_ISORT_NE=0       restores `> 0`,      +2 per leaf shift iteration

The scatter runs once per element per level, so its iteration count divided by
elements IS the effective level count — with no assumption that the tree
achieves log2, which it does not.

  SPAN  total  levels   leaf    tree  per-lvl  floor  excess  cyc/el
    16  260.2   16.06   18.3   241.9    15.06  13.25    1.81    74.0
    32  254.9   14.88   37.3   217.6    14.63  13.25    1.38    68.6
    64  273.2   13.69   75.5   197.7    14.44  13.25    1.19    68.8
   128  333.4   12.49  153.5   179.9    14.40  13.25    1.15    77.4

  floor = 9 (scatter, post-unswitch) + 4.25 (count, 8-wide NEON)

THE TREE RUNS 1.15 TO 1.81 INSTRUCTIONS PER ELEMENT PER LEVEL ABOVE THE COST OF
ITS OWN TWO PASSES. That is loop bookkeeping and the amortised per-range pivot /
probe / tie-gate, and it is not a defect with 5-6 instructions hiding in it.
The direction proposed in the previous append is closed.

TWO INDEPENDENT VALIDATIONS THAT THE DECOMPOSITION IS RIGHT:
  * Leaf cost is almost exactly linear in SPAN — 18.3, 37.3, 75.5, 153.5 for
    SPAN 16/32/64/128, ratios 2.04, 2.02, 2.03 — which is what an insertion sort
    over a span of that size must do, and is not something the measurement was
    constructed to produce.
  * Effective levels come out 1.224x the ideal log2(n/SPAN) at SPAN 64. Textbook
    median-of-3 quicksort is ~1.19x ideal. The pivot is doing as well as the
    algorithm allows, so there is no level-count win available either.

WHERE THE 1.30x ACTUALLY SITS. At SPAN 32 — kāra's instruction optimum — the
TREE ALONE costs 217.6 instr/elem over 14.88 levels, against driftsort's 222.0
for its ENTIRE sort over ~17.2 merge passes. kāra's level is ~13% dearer than a
merge pass and it runs ~13% fewer of them, and those cancel: kāra's partition
tree ties driftsort's whole instruction budget. What kāra spends ON TOP is its
leaf.

But the leaf does not convert to cycles, which is the same wall this row hit
three times before. SPAN 32 uses 18.3 fewer instructions per element than SPAN
64 and costs the same 68.6 vs 68.8 cycles, because IPC falls 3.97 -> 3.72 and
cancels it exactly. Instruction removal in the leaf is free of charge and free
of benefit.

SO THE RESIDUAL IS NOT AN INSTRUCTION PROBLEM ANYWHERE. The tree is at its
two-pass floor, the level count is at the median-of-3 limit, and the leaf's
instructions are not what its cycles are made of. At SPAN 64 kāra is 68.8
cyc/elem against driftsort's 53.0 — 1.298x — with an instruction ratio of only
1.230x and an IPC of 3.99 against 4.19. What is left is a microarchitectural
gap: the partition's two dependent passes over the same elements, and the leaf's
data-dependent branch, both of which retire fewer instructions per cycle than
driftsort's merge does.

That is a different kind of problem from any this row has attacked, and it is
NOT reachable by removing work. Any further attempt has to raise IPC — more
independent work in flight per element — which for the partition means breaking
the count->scatter dependency (a fused single-pass or a speculative scatter),
not trimming either pass.

THE FUSED SINGLE PASS — SHIPPED IN ff1e03cb, 1.297x -> 1.256x.

The previous append closed instruction removal as a direction and named the one
remaining lever: raise IPC by breaking the count->scatter dependency. This does
that.

WHY IT CAN BE ONE PASS. The count exists to place the right cursor, which cannot
be known before the range has been read. Writing the `>=` side BACKWARD from
`hi` needs no such base — the two cursors meet exactly at `lo + nlt` — so the
pass can start writing immediately. The right half comes out reversed, and a
reversal pass restores stability. That trades a full read of the range whose
result the scatter must WAIT for, against a dependency-free pair swap.

MEASURED BEFORE BUILDING, which is what justified building it. The count pass
had never been shown to convert to cycles, and this row had already found three
times that the leaf's instructions do not. KARAC_SORT_COUNT_VEC=0 swaps the
8-wide NEON count for the scalar one, a change confined to the count pass:

  vector  273.14 instr/elem   68.32 cyc/elem   IPC 4.00
  scalar  284.61 instr/elem   72.41 cyc/elem   IPC 3.93
  => 0.356 cycles per count-pass instruction

Count work converts at 0.356 cyc/instr where leaf work converts at ~0. That is
the go signal, and it is the reason this direction was worth spending on when
three previous ones were not.

RESULT, and it is NOT what the instruction analysis predicted:

  instructions  273.2 -> 279.1   (+2.2%, WORSE)
  cycles         68.75 -> 66.58  (-3.2%)
  IPC             3.95 ->  4.10  (+3.8%)

The reversal costs more instructions than the count saved — it is a two-ended
swap, which LLVM's vectoriser will not widen (the hint is attached and is
inert). The win is entirely ILP: the same work, with the serial dependency
removed, retires 3.8% faster. A row that had spent three attempts removing
instructions ends up taking its win by ADDING 6 of them per element.

VALIDATED AGAINST LAYOUT, not as a point estimate — the same day a 15.5% swing
on kata 236 turned out to be emission order alone. Five emission orders per arm:

  count  68.37 .. 68.88 cyc/elem   spread 0.74%
  fused  66.45 .. 66.71 cyc/elem   spread 0.39%

The distributions DO NOT OVERLAP: the worst layout for fused (66.71) still beats
the best for count (68.37). Worst-case ratio 0.976x, median 0.968x.

SCOPE: THE UNSTRUCTURED ARM ONLY. `gate == 0` marks a range admitted for being
unstructured, and that is exactly where the gate test is skipped — so the count
feeds nothing but cursor placement and can be deleted. On the low-cardinality
arm the same count answers the tie gate, which is worth far more than the pass,
so that arm is untouched. Measured: instruction ratios are 1.000 on sorted,
reverse, few-unique, sawtooth and near-sorted; only shuffled moves.

CORRECTNESS. Stability is no longer preserved by construction the way an
in-order append is — it depends on the reversal being exactly right — so it was
checked rather than argued:
  * 462-case stability + sortedness sweep, 0 violations, identical to the count
    path. Its second field is the original index, so an inversion at equal keys
    IS an instability.
  * All six patterns, sink-identical.
  * `KARAC_SORT_FUSED=0` produces code byte-identical to the pre-change
    compiler, so the opt-out is a true opt-out.

AND THE RETRY, WHICH WOULD OTHERWISE HAVE SHIPPED UNTESTED. Both halves must be
non-empty or the recursion does not terminate; `nlt == 0` (the pivot is the range
minimum) is the one case a `<` split cannot satisfy, and the count path handles
it by splitting on `<=`, a choice that needs the count. The fused pass re-runs
the count path for that range — safe because it writes only to the dead buffer
and never touches its source. On the arm it serves, a median-of-3 pivot is the
range minimum with probability ~3/m², so normal runs barely reach it. Hence
`KARAC_SORT_FUSED=2`: a test mode that forces every range through the fused
pass, gate or not, so the low-cardinality cases — where the pivot IS frequently
the minimum — drive the retry hard. Under it the 462-case sweep still reports 0
violations and all six patterns still match.

SPAN RE-SWEPT AFTER FUSION, AND IT STAYS AT 64. The fused pass removed a whole
pass from every level, so the price of a level fell and the leaf/tree balance
should shift toward more levels and a smaller span. It does — but not by enough
to move the constant.

  SPAN   instr    cyc    IPC     (pre-fusion, same harness and machine)
    16   263.8  70.79   3.73      260.2  74.0
    24   259.4  67.38   3.85          —     —
    32   260.2  65.62   3.97      254.9  68.6
    48   267.9  65.71   4.08          —     —
    64   279.1  66.43   4.20      273.2  68.8
    96   307.8  70.89   4.34          —     —
   128   339.4  75.74   4.48      333.4  77.4

On one layout that reads as 32 beating the incumbent by 1.23%. It does not
survive being measured properly. Five emission orders per span:

  span64  66.32 .. 66.69   median 66.53   spread 0.55%
  span32  65.45 .. 66.31   median 66.01   spread 1.31%

  median ratio 0.992x, but WORST CASE FOR 32 IS 1.000x — its unluckiest layout
  exactly ties span 64's luckiest, and it is more than twice as layout-sensitive.

AND SPAN IS NOT A SHUFFLED-ARM KNOB. It is the leaf handoff for every pattern,
so a win there has to be paid for somewhere. Measured at both spans:

  shuffled 0.998   sorted 0.980   reverse 0.995
  few-uniq 1.011   sawtooth 0.986  near-sort 1.005

Few-unique REGRESSES 1.1% and near-sorted 0.5%, against ~0.2-0.8% on the arm
this row cares about. Trading a documented strength for less than the noise band
on the target is not a trade worth making, so the constant stands.

WHAT DID CHANGE is the shape of the curve, and that is the part worth keeping:
the optimum was a two-point tie at 32/64 and is now a PLATEAU from 24 to 64,
inside about 1.5%. Fusion made the tree cheap enough that the span barely
matters across a 2.7x range of it. A future change that alters the leaf — not
the tree — is the one that would move this constant; this one did not.

POST-FUSION BUDGET, ALL COUNTED — AND IT RETIRES THE NEXT IDEA BEFORE IT WAS
BUILT. The plan after fusion was to vectorise the reversal, on the reasoning
that it costs "+6 instr/elem" and that instructions convert again now that IPC
is at parity. Both halves of that turn out to be wrong, and the second one
matters more.

The pre-fusion decomposition could not be reused: its levers (SCATTER_SPLIT,
ISORT_NE) reach loops the fused path does not use, and it was measured against a
two-pass tree that no longer exists. So a measurement-only pad was added —
`KARAC_SORT_FU_PAD=N` / `KARAC_SORT_REV_PAD=N` emit N volatile stores into the
fused body and the reversal body. A volatile store is one `str` LLVM may not
eliminate, so the instruction delta between PAD=0 and PAD=N is N x that loop's
iteration count. Run at N=2 and N=4 as a self-calibration; they agree to 0.04%
(fused) and 0.18% (reversal), so the delta is exactly linear and the counts are
counts, not fits.

  levels                        13.685   (13.69 pre-fusion — unchanged, as the
                                          tree's SHAPE did not change)
  reversal iterations / element  3.608

An independent check on that second number: each iteration swaps two elements,
so the reversal touches 2 x 3.608 / 13.685 = 52.7% of the elements at every
level. That is the `>=` side, and a median-of-3 split predicts ~50%. Nothing in
the measurement was constructed to produce that.

BUDGET at SPAN 64, 279.1 instr/elem total:

  fused pass     123.2    9 instr/elem x 13.685 levels
  leaf shift      75.4    10.77 iterations x 7 instr
  reversal        21.6    3.608 iterations x 6 instr
  remainder       58.9    leaf outer loop, per-range pivot/probe/tie-gate, calls

THE REVERSAL IS 21.6, NOT 6-PER-ELEMENT, AND IT IS ALREADY TIGHT. Its loop is
`ldp ldp stp stp subs b.ne` — six instructions swapping two 16-byte elements
using PAIRED loads and stores, so three instructions per element moved. LLVM
already widened it; what it would not do is form the reversing shuffle a
vectorised version needs. Going wider could save perhaps one instruction per
element against a 279.1 total. The "+6 instr/elem" the fused-pass commit quotes
is the NET of (reversal - count), not the reversal, and reading it as the
reversal's cost is what made this look like the obvious next move.

AND THE LEAF STILL DOES NOT CONVERT, post-fusion. The SPAN sweep is the
amplification test for free: 64 -> 32 removes 18.9 instr/elem, most of it leaf,
and buys 0.81 cyc/elem. That is 0.043 cycles per instruction, against the count
pass's 0.356 — the ratio that justified building the fused pass in the first
place. Leaf instructions were worth ~nothing before fusion and are worth ~nothing
after it; IPC reaching parity did not change that, because the leaf's cost was
never its instruction count.

SO THE LARGEST TERM IS THE ONE THAT CANNOT BE SPENT. The leaf is 75.4 instr/elem
plus its outer loop — comfortably the biggest identified item, roughly 3.5x the
reversal — and it converts at 0.043 cyc/instr. The reversal converts unknown but
is only 21.6 to begin with. Neither is a lever worth pulling, which leaves the
58.9 remainder (per-range pivot, probe, tie gate, call overhead) as the only
unexamined block, and at 13.685 levels that is ~4.3 instr/elem/level amortised
over ranges of >= 64 elements.

THE BUDGET CLOSES, AND IT NAMES A LEAD BIGGER THAN THE REVERSAL.

The previous append's split did not close: attributing the 58.9 remainder to
per-range work implied 1266 instructions per range, which no median-of-3 plus
two calls can cost. Two more pads found why, and the answer was a wrong constant
rather than a missing term.

  KARAC_SORT_LEAFOUT_PAD  counts leaf OUTER iterations: 0.970 per element
                          (every element reaches the leaf once — expect 1.0)
  KARAC_SORT_RANGE_PAD    counts partition CALLS: 0.0465 per element,
                          one per 21.5, against the ~117k tree nodes SPAN 64
                          implies. Its calibration is poor (17% between N=2 and
                          N=4) because the delta is under 0.1 instr/elem against
                          a billion — it fixes an order of magnitude, not a
                          digit.

THE WRONG CONSTANT: THE FUSED PASS IS 11 INSTRUCTIONS PER ITERATION, NOT 9.
Identified by building with PAD=4 and finding the loop whose signature grew by
exactly four, rather than by matching a shape:

  scatter (pre-fusion)  ldr fmov cmp csel cinc str cinc subs b.ne         =  9
  fused                 ldr fmov cmp csel cset str cinc sub sub cmp b.ne  = 11

The 9 was carried over from the scatter's disassembly and assumed to hold. It
does not: the old scatter advanced BOTH cursors with `cinc`, and the fused pass
needs a DESCENDING right cursor, which costs a `cset` to materialise the
predicate plus a `sub`, where an ascending one costs one `cinc`.

  fused pass   150.5   11 x 13.685 levels
  leaf shift    75.4   10.77 x 7
  reversal      21.6   3.608 x 6
  leaf outer    11.6   0.970 x 12
  accounted    259.2
  remainder     19.9   = 427 instr per range — pivot, probe, gate, two calls,
                       prologue. Plausible where 1266 was not.

INTERNALLY CONSISTENT, which is the check that the whole account is right:
fusion removed the count pass and added both the addressing premium and the
reversal, so 273.2 - C + 27.4 + 21.6 = 279.1 gives C = 43.1 instr/elem for the
count pass, i.e. 3.15 per level — the right size for an 8-wide NEON count with a
scalar tail. Net +5.9, which is exactly the measured 279.1 - 273.2.

THE LEAD. Fusion's cost is 49.0 instr/elem: 27.4 for the addressing premium and
21.6 for the reversal. THE PREMIUM IS THE LARGER OF THE TWO and it is the larger
of every remaining reducible item — the reversal is already three instructions
per element moved with paired `ldp`/`stp`, and the leaf does not convert. If the
fused loop could be brought back to the scatter's 9, the sort would be 251.7
instr/elem, or 1.134x driftsort on instructions.

Whether it CAN is not established. The premium buys the property that makes
fusion work — a right cursor needing no counted base — and the obvious
reformulations do not shed it: deriving `hi-1-i+l` costs `cinc` plus `sub`,
carrying a descending pointer costs a conditional 16-byte decrement, and both
land back at two instructions. Anything that fixes it has to find a
single-instruction conditional descent, or a placement for the `>=` side that
needs no descent at all — and there is no third buffer to put it in. That is the
next thing to look at, and it is a genuine open question rather than a plan.

THE ADDRESSING PREMIUM IS RULED OUT — BUILT, MEASURED, REJECTED (277809cf).

The previous append named it as the largest remaining reducible item and called
whether it could be removed an open question. It can be removed. Removing it
buys nothing, and the reason it buys nothing is the reason it exists.

THE ALTERNATIVE. Every element goes exactly one way, so `l + k == i - lo` holds
at every step and the right destination `hi-1-k` is exactly `(hi-1) - i + lcur`
— the ASCENDING left cursor plus an affine function of the loop counter. No
descending cursor, so no `cset` to materialise a predicate for a `sub`; both
cursors advance with `cinc` straight out of the flags. The loop goes from 11
instructions to 9, precisely as predicted.

IT IS CORRECT: six patterns sink-identical, 462-case stability sweep 0
violations. (First attempt was not: the `lo` terms cancel in the derivation and
adding one anyway is an off-by-lo. It crashed rather than mis-sorting, which was
luck — the same slip at a different offset would have silently corrupted a
range, which is why the sweep runs before the stopwatch.)

AND IT IS WORTH NOTHING, layout-validated across five emission orders:

              instr/elem   cyc/elem    IPC
  descending      279.1      66.89    4.17
  affine          265.4      66.96    3.96
                  -13.7      +0.1%

13.7 instructions per element removed — 4.9% — for 1.001x on cycles. IPC falls
4.17 -> 3.96 and eats exactly the saving.

WHY, AND THIS IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Deriving the right index FROM `lcur`
makes both cursors ONE loop-carried dependency chain: the store address cannot
be computed until the previous iteration's `cinc` has retired. The descending
`rcur` is an INDEPENDENT chain that advances in parallel with the ascending one.
The two extra instructions are not overhead — they buy cursor independence, and
they are worth precisely what they cost.

That also corrects this row's own reading two appends ago, that with IPC at
parity "instruction removal is live once more". It is not. Both attempts since —
the leaf (0.043 cyc/instr) and this one (0.000) — removed real instructions and
converted none of them. Every remaining instruction in this sort is either on a
dependency chain that already has slack, or is paying for slack elsewhere.

CLOSING wontfix. Real, reproducible, and measured to a standstill:

  tree        at its two-pass floor (1.15-1.81 instr/elem/level above the cost
              of its own passes)
  levels      1.224x ideal against textbook median-of-3's ~1.19x
  SPAN        at a plateau; 24-64 within 1.5%, and moving it trades a
              documented few-unique strength for less than the noise band
  leaf        three shapes tried (binary insertion 1.603x, memmove 1.149x,
              instruction removal 0.043 cyc/instr) — bound by a mispredicted
              branch, not by work
  reversal    3 instructions per element moved with paired ldp/stp; the
              vectorize hint is inert because a two-ended swap needs a
              reversing shuffle LLVM will not form
  addressing  this — removable, and removal is free of benefit

Shuffled `sort_by` went 1.52x -> 1.252x over this row's life, in two shipped
changes: the scatter unswitch (15 -> 9 instructions per element) and the fused
single pass (a serial dependency traded for a reversal). What is left is 1.252x
with no identified lever, and the row is closed rather than parked so the open
queue stops advertising work that has been measured to have none.

The remaining gap is real and someone may yet find a way at it — but it will not
be found by removing instructions from this design, and that is now three
independent demonstrations deep.

title: CI never built the regex/arrow opt-in archives, so the 8 Regex / Arrow-IPC codegen E2E tests (and memory_sanitizer's regex fixtures) green-skipped in CI and never ran there
detail:
Found the moment KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1 (220070be, review item 4) ran against a full codegen E2E suite: the Regex and Arrow-IPC programs hard-require the opt-in `libkarac_runtime_regex.a` / `libkarac_runtime_arrow.a`, and no CI job built either — the jobs built only lean → full. The link failure soft-skipped, so `regex_compile_is_match_runs`, `test_e2e_from_arrow_ipc_round_trips`, and 6 siblings reported ok in every CI run without ever executing a binary; local dev machines that had built the archives were the only place they ran. Same failure shape as the dark-llvm-tests class (B-2026-07-31-44 / B-2026-08-08-26): green is exactly why it stayed invisible, and the require-gate is what made it loud.

SOURCE NOTE. Surfaced by the project-review item-4 verification run in a cloud container, where the gate turned the skip into 8 explicit failures naming the missing archives.

fix:
CLOSED WONTFIX after the second measurement pass: every lever on the row's fix
menu is either already shipped, already rejected with a spike, or blocked on an
owner design decision. Nothing is left that a session can act on, and the
numbers that close each branch are recorded here and in the detail.

OPTION (3) EXISTS AND DELIVERS IN FULL — the row's claim that it is "the escape
hatch Rust has and Kāra does not" is REFUTED. The `wrapping_*` families are v1
core (design.md § Arithmetic Overflow), codegen lowers them to plain adds, and
LLVM vectorises the result: `s.wrapping_add(v[j])` on the row's own probe
measures 6ms contiguous-L1 against unchecked-AVX2 Rust's 6ms — EXACT parity —
and 10ms against 9.5ms on the strided shape (checked Kāra: 23ms on both). The
per-element trap, not anything structural, was the entire gap, and the
opt-out that removes it is already in the language.

OPTION (1)'s STATIC FORM WAS BUILT AND REJECTED thirteen months of ledger ago:
docs/spikes/overflow-check-elision.md (resolved 2026-07-03, two prototype
layers on a dropped branch). LLVM's correlated-value-propagation already
elides every check a sound source-level pass can prove (measured 1.00x, twice);
the residual sits on unbounded-heap-value shapes needing array-content +
trip-count analysis, where "every bug is a 'we promised a trap and didn't'
hole". The spike's own recommendation was the wrapping_* lever above. The row
proposed rebuilding this without citing the spike.

OPTION (2) IS NOT SEMANTICS-PRESERVING (first append): lane reassociation
changes the trap set bidirectionally, so a widened/deferred-check AOT diverges
from the sequential-checked interpreter on which programs trap — the
run-vs-build class the corpus holds to byte identity. Adopting it is a design
decision about trap semantics, not emitter work.

THE ONE UNEXPLORED SEMANTICS-PRESERVING LEVER — the runtime-guard twin loop
(vectorised saturating |v| pre-pass gating an unchecked vectorised sum, scalar
checked fallback) — is costed by composition at ~1.9x of the 3.8x ceiling,
LOSES outright in the bandwidth-bound regime, and requires reduction-loop
recognition plus twin-loop emission that the AST-walking emitter has no
framework for. Prize-per-engineering is far below the sort work that spawned
this row.

WHAT SURVIVES FOR THE OWNER, and the reason to read this row before reopening:
the settled record priced the trap default at 1.19-1.34x behind unchecked
peers (elision spike, multiply kernels) and 1.25x (noalias spike, NEON add
kernel). The reduction ladder here measures the same default at up to 3.8x on
cache-resident integer reductions — the documented cost of the design decision
is understated for this class. If that reprices anything, it is the promotion
gate on deferred.md § Scoped `#[wrapping]` / `#[checked]` Arithmetic Regions
(P2), which is exactly the mechanism design.md reserves for this: safe by
default, fast on request, named at the site. Reopening should start there, not
at the emitter.
title: The default integer overflow check is emitted inside the loop, blocking auto-vectorisation of EVERY integer reduction
detail:
Kāra checks integer overflow by default, and the check is emitted INSIDE the loop, which blocks LLVM from auto-vectorising any integer reduction. Found while sweeping for cost-model declines under B-2026-08-16-9; it is a different and larger problem than that row, so it is filed separately.

THE EVIDENCE. A plain reduction over a Vec — `while j < n { s = s + v[j].0; j = j + 1 }` on `Vec[(i64,i64)]`, n = 1,000,000 — emits, on arm64:

  ldr   x12, [x11], #0x10     load v[j].0, stride 16
  adds  x8, x8, x12           s += ..., SETTING FLAGS
  b.vs  <panic>               branch on oVerflow
  subs  x10, x10, #0x1
  b.ne  <loop>

The `b.vs` is the whole problem. `-pass-remarks-analysis=loop-vectorize` reports "control flow cannot be substituted for a select" and "value that could not be identified as reduction is used outside the loop" — the accumulator's update is conditional on not trapping, so it is not a recognisable reduction. `-force-vector-width=2` does not override it, which confirms this is a LEGALITY block and not a pricing decision (contrast B-2026-08-16-9, where the same flag family did rescue a declined loop).

NOT a bounds check: karac's BCE elided that correctly, and there is no bounds compare in the loop body. The only control flow left is the overflow trap.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. Integer reduction over a vector is the single most vectorisable shape there is, and it is everywhere in real code. This means Kāra forfeits SIMD on the entire class, on every element type, not just the strided-field case the probe used. It also means the published equal-safety comparison is measuring something subtler than it appears: `rustc -C overflow-checks=on` is the right comparator for SAFETY, but rustc's overflow check has the same vectorisation-blocking effect, so the equal-safety row flatters both languages relative to their unchecked builds. The gap that matters commercially is checked-Kāra against UNCHECKED-Rust, which is what most Rust in production actually is.

WHAT A FIX WOULD LOOK LIKE, none of which is attempted here:
(1) HOIST THE CHECK. For a sum of n values of width w, the result cannot exceed n * max|v|, so a compile-time bound on n (or a runtime pre-check) can prove the whole reduction cannot overflow and drop the per-iteration test entirely. This is the strongest option and it is exactly the range analysis the BCE pass already does for indices.
(2) WIDEN AND CHECK ONCE. Accumulate i64 lanes into i128, or accumulate in vector lanes and detect overflow per lane with a saturating add compared against the wrapping one, then branch ONCE at loop exit. LLVM will not do this for you; the emitter would.
(3) LET THE USER SAY SO. A wrapping/unchecked reduction form, which is the escape hatch Rust has and Kāra does not.

MEASURE FIRST: none of the above is costed yet. The probe in the session scratchpad (`probe.kara`, reduction over 1M elements x 60 rounds with a build-only control) is the harness, and the first number wanted is simply how much a hand-vectorised version of that loop beats the emitted one — that bounds the whole prize before any design work.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the corpus sweep filed under B-2026-08-16-9, whose own question (is cost-model mispricing systematic?) came back NO — 37 declines across 294 bench programs, mostly one each. This was the more interesting thing the sweep found.

MEASURE-FIRST DONE — THE PRIZE IS NOW BOUNDED, on x86-64 (Intel Xeon @ 2.80GHz,
cloud container; the row's own numbers are arm64/M5, ISA caveat at the end).
First: the block reproduces on x86 exactly as filed — the emitted loop is
scalar `add` + `jo <panic>` per element, 5x unrolled, zero SIMD, no bounds
compare (BCE held). Same legality story, different ISA.

THE LADDER. Same LCG data, same reduction, checksums identical across every
binary. rust_checked is `checked_add` per element (the equal-safety
comparator); rust_unchecked is default `+` at `-C target-feature=+avx2`;
manual_v2 is the row's option (2) written by hand — AVX2 wrapping lane adds,
per-lane overflow poison OR-accumulated ((acc^r)&(a^r) sign bit), tested ONCE
at exit, strided loads done with two pair-loads + one unpack. min-of-9 wall
clock, total adds held at ~61M for every n:

  shape                 set     kara  rust_chk  rust_unchk  manual_v2
  (i64,i64).0 strided   16KB    23ms    23ms      9.5ms      14ms
  (i64,i64).0 strided   128KB   23ms    24ms     13ms        16ms
  (i64,i64).0 strided   2MB     35ms    35ms     33ms        35ms
  (i64,i64).0 strided   16MB    ~55ms   ~55ms    ~48ms       ~53ms
  Vec[i64] contiguous   8KB     23ms    24ms      6ms         —

FOUR CONCLUSIONS THE ROW CAN NOW STAND ON:

1. THE PRIZE IS 3.8x AT ITS LARGEST (contiguous i64 sum, L1-resident) and it
is a CACHE-RESIDENCY STORY: 2.4x strided-L1, 1.8x L2, and ~1.05-1.15x once the
working set passes ~2MB, where the loop is bandwidth-bound and SIMD has
nothing to add. The commercial "checked Kara vs unchecked Rust" gap this row
worries about is real and large in cache and near zero out of it.

2. EQUAL-SAFETY PARITY IS EXACT, everywhere on the ladder: kara and
rust-checked are within 1ms at every point. Confirms the row's reading that
the published comparison flatters both languages by the same amount — rustc's
checked build forfeits the identical prize.

3. OPTION (2) IS COSTED: the deferred-lane-check kernel captures ~60% of the
prize where there is one (14ms against the 9.5ms floor and the 23ms status
quo). Its overhead over pure unchecked is the poison bookkeeping (2 xor + and
+ or per lane-add, one movemask at exit). A first implementation attempt used
scalar gathers for the strided field and captured NOTHING (22ms) — the load
strategy is where the option-2 win lives or dies; interleaved loads + unpack
are mandatory on this shape.

4. OPTION (2) IS NOT SEMANTICS-PRESERVING, which the row does not yet say and
which is bigger than any of its numbers: reassociating the sum changes WHICH
PROGRAMS TRAP, in both directions. [i64::MAX, 1, -5] summed sequentially traps
at the second element; split across 4 lanes it completes cleanly. Conversely a
lane's partial series can overflow where the sequential interleaving never
does. Kara's interpreter is the sequential-checked semantics, so a
lane-reassociated AOT diverges from `--interp` on the trap set — precisely the
run-vs-build class the corpus holds to byte identity. Option (2) therefore
requires either an interpreter twin or an explicit decision to accept
divergence; it is not just emitter work.

BONUS COSTING for option (1)'s runtime-guard form, the one variant that is
both semantics-preserving and needs no static value bound: a vectorised
saturating |v| pre-pass (overflow-free, so it vectorises freely) proving
sum|v_i| < 2^63, gating a fully unchecked vectorised sum, falling back to
today's scalar checked loop when the guard fails. Estimated BY COMPOSITION of
measured pieces (guard pass ~ one unchecked sum): contiguous-L1 ~12ms vs 23
today (~1.9x, against the 3.8x ceiling), and a net LOSS in the bandwidth-bound
regime where the extra pass doubles traffic. Not measured as a single binary.

ISA CAVEAT: all numbers Xeon/AVX2. The M5's wider scalar issue and 128-bit
NEON will shrink the scalar-to-vector ratio, so the arm64 prize is plausibly
SMALLER than these — the 3.8x should not be quoted for the M5 without
re-running the ladder there. The structural findings (legality block, exact
equal-safety parity, option-2 trap-set divergence) are ISA-independent.

fix: FIXED by 3d466756. A method_name_index (bare method name -> the method_bodies keys ending in .name), built once at the end of collect_function_info, replaces the per-call-site scan; the same commit moves the effectchecker's internal String-keyed working tables to FxHashMap/FxHashSet (public result structs and signatures stay std HashMap). title: collect_calls_in_expr name-only method fallback scans all method_bodies keys per call site, allocating a format! probe per key — O(call sites x impl methods) allocations, the single largest front-end cost on call-graph-heavy programs
detail: Found by the name-interning spike's baseline profile (docs/spikes/name-interning.md): callgrind put ~32% of ALL front-end instructions inside format! calls issued by collect_calls_in_expr, and the phase benchmark showed effectcheck at 136.6 ms of a 240.8 ms front end (57%) with 2.44M heap allocations on the 10.9k-line synthetic corpus (34 traits x 100 impls). The fallback `for key in self.method_bodies.keys() { if key.ends_with(&format!(".{}", method)) ... }` ran for EVERY MethodCall expression — even when the precise typechecker-resolved callee key had already matched — and was re-paid by every pass that re-walks bodies (target gate, GPU gate, bounds). On real-shaped code (kara-katas cumulus, 2k lines) the phase was only ~10% of the front end: the blowup needed the many-impls stress shape, which is why it survived unnoticed. SOURCE NOTE: spike measurement harness examples/bench_frontend.rs, landed in the fix commit.

title: The `chained_field_receiver` lint that closed B-2026-08-13-12 only walks SOME expression positions: it catches `let n = e.doc.lines.len();` and an `if` condition, and MISSES the same expression inside an f-string hole, behind an `as` cast, in a `for` range bound, and as an INDEX chain. All of them are still refused by `karac build`, so the check-vs-build gap that row was filed to close is only half closed.
tracker: src/chained_receiver_lint.rs -- the AST traversal that looks for `is_chained_field_receiver`. Two unvisited positions are named below; the pattern is that the walk covers statement-level and condition positions and not general sub-expressions.
detail:
B-2026-08-13-12 was closed by 30ea825 with a check-phase lint at Deny, so that `karac check` stops accepting programs `karac build` refuses. The lint works -- for the positions it visits. Measured, same expression (`e.doc.lines.len()` on `struct Ed { doc: Doc }` / `struct Doc { lines: Vec[String] }`) in eleven positions; `build` REFUSES every single one:

    position                                              lint
    `let n = e.doc.lines.len();`                          caught
    `if e.doc.lines.len() > 0 { .. }`                     caught
    `let n = e.doc.lines.len() + 1;`                      caught
    `take(e.doc.lines.len())`      (call arg, no cast)    caught
    `fn c(..) -> usize { e.doc.lines.len() }` (tail)      caught
    `match e.doc.lines.len() { .. }`                      caught
    `println(f"{e.doc.lines.len()}")`   (f-string hole)   MISSED
    `let n = e.doc.lines.len() as i64;` (behind a cast)   MISSED
    `take(e.doc.lines.len() as i64)`    (cast in an arg)  MISSED
    `fn c(..) -> i64 { e.doc.lines.len() as i64 }`        MISSED
    `for i in 0..e.doc.lines.len() { .. }`  (range bound) MISSED
    `println(f"{e.doc.lines[0]}")`     (INDEX chain)      MISSED

TWO CLEAN DISCRIMINATORS come out of that table, each with a caught control one character away:

  1. THE `as` CAST. `let n = e.doc.lines.len();` is caught and `let n = e.doc.lines.len() as i64;` is not -- identical otherwise. The three other cast rows (call arg, tail, and a cast nested inside a parenthesised sum) confirm it: the walk does not descend into a `Cast`'s operand. That also explains two rows that first looked like separate position bugs.

  2. THE F-STRING HOLE. `println(f"{e.doc.lines.len()}")` has no cast and is still missed, while the same call as a `let` initialiser is caught. This is the same blind spot CLASS as B-2026-08-11-5 (parse errors raised inside an interpolation hole were discarded) -- a different pass with the same hole, since a hole's expression is not reached by the ordinary walk.

The INDEX row is worth separating: B-2026-08-13-12's own close note records that the shape is wider than that row's table because `e.doc.lines[0]` is refused by the same `lower_field_access_ptr` helper, and says one predicate covers both. The predicate does; the traversal does not reach this one either.

CONSEQUENCE: unchanged from the original row. `karac check` reports `All checks passed.`, `--output=json` carries no diagnostic, `karac fix` has nothing to apply, `--targets=native` passes -- and `karac build` refuses. For the Mend loop that is still a program that checks clean and cannot be built, just in fewer places than before. The f-string position is the one that matters most in practice: interpolating a length or an element is exactly where this expression is written.

FIX SHAPE: the predicate is already right; only the traversal needs widening. Visit `Cast` operands and f-string interpolation-hole expressions (and index bases) with the same visitor. `span_visitor::visit_expr_spans_mut` already enumerates every expression kind including `InterpolatedStringLit` parts, so a complete walk exists in-tree to mirror.

SUGGESTED FIXTURES: the eleven-row table above -- six currently-caught positions as over-fire controls, five currently-missed as pins.
investigation: 2026-08-16 (hunt, regression sweep after the method_call.rs split). Thirteen of fourteen earlier dogfood programs agreed across backends. While confirming an unrelated deferral was invisible to `check`, I wrote a chained-receiver control expecting the B-2026-08-13-12 lint to fire, and it did not -- because I happened to write it inside an f-string. Widened to the eleven-position table, which isolated the cast and the hole as the two mechanisms. Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix: Fixed by the extraction the re-aimed tracker prescribed, in one commit consumed from both sides. (1) THE MODULE: the entire escape analysis -- both validators (`reject_escaping_capturing_closure`, `reject_heap_env_misuse`), all four producer-set fixpoints, and their helper walks (~2,200 lines) -- moved VERBATIM from src/codegen/closures.rs into `crate::closure_escape`, a plain-AST crate-level module with zero inkwell dependence. Codegen holds an `EscapeAnalysis` in `closure_state.escape`: `compile()` builds the five producer sets once, `compile_function()` runs `check_function()` per function (validators + that function's owner tables), emission reads the same tables for FreeClosureEnv wiring. Behavior-identical: the codegen suite including every E_ESCAPING_CLOSURE_NOT_YET message pin is unchanged-green. The shared walkers (refs_in_expr/refs_in_block), the Vec recognizers, vec_inner_type_expr, and the impl-method synthesis (make_impl_method_function + rewrite_self_in_type_expr) moved too; codegen keeps one-line delegates. (2) THE LINT: `escaping_closure` (registry Deny, `-A` opt-out, `codegen_bound` gate so `run --interp` is exempt) runs THE SAME compute+check_function over the same function set -- free fns mirroring the compile loop's gates, impl methods through the same synthesis. Zero predicate drift by construction, and feature-independent: a non-llvm `karac check` runs the full gate. PLACEMENT FINDING: the lint runs at the END of Pipeline::lower(), not beside the chained-receiver lint in typecheck() -- the escape analysis is NOT lowering-invariant. Measured: bare `[min_len(2)]` is an ArrayLiteral pre-lower (array-owner sanctioned, clean) but lowers to a Vec PrefixCollectionLiteral whose element store the guard rejects -- pre-lower placement under-fired vs build; post-lower restores parity, pinned by tests/closure_escape.rs::refused_bare_vec_literal_with_heap_env_element. CONFORMANCE: tests/closure_escape.rs (ungated) is the row's measured boundary table as executable fixtures -- 11 building shapes clean, 13 refused shapes flagged -- and EVERY fixture was cross-validated against the real `karac build -A escaping_closure` oracle: 24/24 agree. The table had ALREADY drifted once since the row measured it: `takes(r)` with a call-only callee now BUILDS (the epic's by-value borrows-only arg sanction landed after 0431984/cdd9bd8), so a mirrored lint pinned to the row's table would have shipped a Deny-level false positive on day one -- the row's drift argument, demonstrated inside its own conformance suite; the still-refused half (callee RETURNS its param) is pinned separately. CLI four-surface test mirrors the chained precedent: text check fails and names the boundary, JSON names the lint for the Mend loop, -A passes, run --interp executes. RESIDUALS RECORDED: (a) validator 2's misuse walk is boolean, so its violations carry the whole function's span; site-precise spans need the walk to thread the offending expr out. (b) generic fns/impls are validated by build only per instantiation, so the lint skips them -- under-fire, the safe direction. (c) trait default methods are not enumerated (under-fire). Future epic slices edit closure_escape once and move a conformance fixture between tables in the same commit.
title: The ESCAPING-CLOSURE deferral (`E_ESCAPING_CLOSURE_NOT_YET`, epic B-2026-06-22-2) is invisible to `karac check` -- storing a returned capturing closure in a struct field held in a `Vec` passes check, `--targets=native`, and `--output=json` with no diagnostic, runs correctly under `--interp`, and is then refused by `karac build`. Same check-time gap B-2026-08-13-12 was filed and fixed for, one deferral over.
tracker: extract the escape analysis (closures.rs validators + 4 fixpoints) into a plain-AST module consumed by BOTH codegen and check — NOT a hand-mirrored lint; see 2026-08-17 append
detail:
REPRO -- the ordinary rule-list shape:

    struct Rule { name: String, check: Fn(ref String) -> bool }
    fn min_len(n: i64) -> Fn(ref String) -> bool { |s| (s.len() as i64) >= n }
    ...
    rules.push(Rule { name: "min8", check: min_len(8) });

    karac check                    All checks passed.
    karac check --targets=native   All checks passed under target 'native'.
    karac check --output=json      "diagnostics": []
    karac run --interp             runs correctly (all four inputs, output hand-checked)
    karac build                    error: codegen failed: error[E_ESCAPING_CLOSURE_NOT_YET]: ...
                                   Storing it (struct / collection / index / field) ... is not
                                   yet supported ... (heap-closure-environment epic B-2026-06-22-2)

THE DEFERRAL ITSELF IS FINE and its message is one of the better ones in the compiler -- it enumerates exactly what IS supported (call where bound, copy to another binding, bare tail return), what is not, why (the RC closure environment would outlive or be double-freed by its owner set), and a workaround. This row is NOT a request to implement escaping closures.

IT IS ABOUT WHERE THE MESSAGE ARRIVES. B-2026-08-13-12 established the project's answer for exactly this situation: a deliberate codegen deferral that `karac check` cannot see is a run-vs-build gap worth closing, and it was closed with a check-phase lint at Deny plus an `-A` opt-out and an `--interp` exemption. That precedent applies here unchanged, and this deferral is arguably the more valuable one to surface -- storing a closure in a struct is a design decision made early, so the author writes the whole program before `build` tells them it cannot compile. Mine ran correctly under `--interp` for every input before I discovered it does not build.

MEND-LOOP CONSEQUENCE, same as the sibling: no JSON diagnostic, so `karac fix` has nothing to apply and an LLM author gets a clean check on a program that cannot be built.

NOTE ON SCOPE: unlike the chained-receiver case there is NO mechanical rewrite to offer as a fix-it here -- the workaround is a design change (store the closure's DATA and write a plain fn, which is what I did). So the ask is the gate and the diagnostic at check time, not an autofix.

RE-VERIFIED LIVE ON HEAD (749f305) and then INVESTIGATED THE PRESCRIBED FIX
RATHER THAN BUILDING IT. The minimal shape (a `Rule { check: min_len(8) }`
pushed into a `Vec[Rule]`, the field copied out and called) still shows the
full gap: check clean, `--interp` correct, build refused with
E_ESCAPING_CLOSURE_NOT_YET. But the row's fix shape — "copy
chained_receiver_lint.rs" — does not survive contact with the codegen gate it
would have to mirror, and the next session should not start there.

WHY THE B-2026-08-13-12 PRECEDENT DOES NOT TRANSFER. The chained-receiver
predicate is TWO LINES and frozen: a FieldAccess whose object is a
FieldAccess, unchanged since FR4 was deferred. The escaping-closure gate is a
LIVE STATE MACHINE: two validators (`reject_escaping_capturing_closure`,
`reject_heap_env_misuse`, src/codegen/closures.rs) fed by FOUR fixpoint passes
(`compute_fns_returning_heap_env{,_aggregate,_tuple_array,_vec}`) plus
sanctioned-shape carve-outs (reassignment, bare-tail, owner relays) — ~1500
lines whose supported set the epic B-2026-06-22-2 has widened FOUR times
already (bare-tail slice, aggregate slice, tuple/array slice, vec-owner
slice). A hand-mirrored check lint is a standing two-copy sync obligation, and
it drifts in the WORSE direction: each landed slice makes the mirror OVER-FIRE
at Deny — `karac check` rejecting programs `karac build` accepts — which for
the Mend loop is a strictly worse failure than the current silence, because it
hands the author a diagnostic that no edit can satisfy. The codegen E2E
harness calls codegen directly, so nothing in CI would catch the stale mirror.

THE DURABLE FIX, now cheaper than when this row was filed: EXTRACT the escape
analysis into a plain-AST module (no inkwell — the validators and fixpoints
read only ASTs and name-sets; the LLVM-typed fields of ClosureState are
emission machinery the analysis never touches) that RETURNS (a) the four
owner/producer name-sets and (b) per-function verdicts. Codegen consumes the
sets for FreeClosureEnv drop wiring exactly as today; check consumes the
verdicts as diagnostics with the -A / --interp story the row asks for. One
predicate, zero drift, feature-independent (works in a non-llvm karac, which a
lint behind the codegen feature could never be), and codegen-containment
holds. The just-completed extract-clusters spike (e344a56 pulled ClosureState
out of Codegen; f92421d closed the spike) is the natural substrate — this was
a much bigger refactor before that landed.

WHY NOT DONE IN THIS SESSION: the extraction is a >1500-line surgery through
an area with seven closure-adjacent commits in the past three days, including
the epic's own active slices — a mid-flight collision with the next slice
would cost more than the row's LOW severity buys. It should land either as
the epic's next slice or immediately after one, by whoever holds the epic's
context.

INTERIM OPTION, decided AGAINST, recorded so it is not re-proposed: a
Warn-level partial lint (under-fire only) closes some of the JSON gap without
the broken-build risk, but every shape it pins is a bet against the epic's
next slice, and a stale warning on a shape that now builds still poisons the
Mend loop's diagnostics feed. The gap's cost is bounded (the author finds out
at build; the message is one of the compiler's best); a wrong diagnostic's
cost is not.

--- 2026-08-17 SESSION APPEND (16e7b06): the message half is fixed; the lint
was BUILT, VALIDATED, AND DISCARDED — recording both so neither is redone ---

THE RE-AIM ARRIVED MID-SESSION. This session took the row before cdd9bd8
landed, followed the then-current tracker ("copy chained_receiver_lint.rs"),
and had the full lint working when the re-aim appeared on a pre-push fetch:
`escaping_closure` at Deny with `-A` and the `codegen_bound` exemption, arms
scoped to a 20-program measured boundary, 8/8 refused shapes flagged, and a
394-file sweep across examples/ + kara-katas with ZERO false positives. It was
then discarded unpushed, because the re-aim's drift argument survives contact
with exactly that work: every arm was calibrated to the CURRENT gate, the epic
has widened the gate four times, and each future slice turns some arm into a
Deny-level false positive on a program that builds — with nothing in CI to
catch it. The 394-clean sweep validates today's boundary, not tomorrow's,
which is precisely the trap. The extraction tracker stands.

TWO FINDINGS FROM THE DISCARDED WORK THAT TRANSFER:

1. THE GATE'S OWN MESSAGE HAD GONE STALE — fixed in 16e7b06, the durable half
   of this row's original ask. The refusal list named "passing it as a call
   argument" and "capturing it in a nested closure"; both BUILD (measured on
   HEAD), and the first sat in the same sentence as a workaround recommending
   exactly that hand-off. The real distinction is BINDING vs UNBOUND CALL:
   `use_it(f)` builds, `use_it(min_len(3))` is refused. Both lists are
   rewritten to the measured boundary, a site comment tells each future slice
   to move its phrase between lists, and a test per side pins the distinction
   — the refused side also pins the ABSENCE of the old self-contradicting
   claim. Whoever does the extraction inherits accurate prose to surface.

2. THE MEASURED BOUNDARY, as extraction-acceptance input (all on HEAD at
   0431984/cdd9bd8; `min_len` returns a capturing closure):

   builds:  let f = min_len(8) · let g = f · use_it(f) [Fn param] ·
            v.push(min_len(2)) [Vec[Fn]] · let r = Rule{check: min_len(8)} ·
            let t = (min_len(2), 5) · [min_len(2)] array let ·
            (r.check)(s) · (v[0])(s) · nested-closure capture of f ·
            capture-free returned closures stored anywhere ·
            inline capturing closures stored anywhere
   refused: rules.push(Rule{check: min_len(8)}) · takes(Rule{..}) ·
            return Rule{..} · takes(r)/rules.push(r) [r an owner] ·
            let f = r.check / t.0 [copy out of an owner] ·
            min_len(2); · min_len(2)(s) · use_it(min_len(3)) ·
            if b { return min_len(2); }

   A conformance suite for the extracted module is one mechanical pass over
   this table.

ONE WALKER PITFALL, for the extraction author: the dogfood's own misuse sat
inside an f-string interpolation (`println(f"{takes(r)}")`), and the first
walker was blind to it — `InterpolatedStringLit` holes are expressions and two
of eight refused shapes hid there until the walker learned it. The codegen

title: A 31-bit LCG shifted by 16 gives 15-bit keys, so `% 1000000` never fires — 'shuffled-uniform' benchmark data has 32768 distinct keys
detail:
sortk.kara's pattern 0, the "random / shuffled-uniform" workload this row and B-2026-08-15-30 and B-2026-08-16-3 were all measured on, draws far narrower keys than it reads as. It cost a wrong tuning decision before it was caught, which is why it is filed rather than just fixed in place.

THE DEFECT. The generator is a 31-bit LCG:

  fn lcg(state: i64) -> i64 { (state * 1103515245 + 12345) & 2147483647 }
  ...
  state = lcg(state);
  k = (state / 65536i64) % 1000000i64;

`state` is 31 bits, so `state / 65536` is 15 bits and lands in [0, 32768). The `% 1000000` therefore NEVER FIRES. The pattern documented as uniform over a million values actually has 32768 distinct keys — at n = 150000 that is ~4.6 duplicates per key, not the ~1% collision rate a million-wide draw would give.

WHAT IT COST. Under B-2026-08-16-9 the partition's leaf span SPAN was re-swept after the scatter unswitch made the tree ~23% cheaper per level. On this harness the optimum moved decisively to SPAN 8 — 238.8M cycles against 64's 256.6M, a proper interior minimum at 4.4x the noise floor. On the two real katas that exercise the same sort, SPAN 8 is 1.20x SLOWER (#252) and 1.08x slower (#253). Rebuilding the harness key from two draws instead of one makes it agree with the katas exactly (SPAN 8 becomes 18% worse, optimum returns to 32/64). Had the sweep been trusted, a global constant would have been moved the wrong way on the strength of a mislabelled distribution.

WHAT IT DOES NOT COST. The Rust, C and Go mirrors carry the SAME generator, so every cross-language comparison ever taken on this harness is apples-to-apples on identical data, and no published ratio is wrong. Re-measured on a genuinely wide key the headline moves only slightly and in kāra's favour: 1.463x -> 1.289x against the narrow key's 1.512x -> 1.302x. The narrow keys flattered kāra a little in BOTH arms.

SCOPE, counted rather than assumed. Scanning every kata source that combines a 31-bit LCG with a `/65536` shift and a modulus wider than 32768 finds THREE, of which one is a benchmarked kata:

  201-300/270-closest-binary-search-tree-value/bench/bst_close.kara      (moduli 1000000, 1100000)
  201-300/270-closest-binary-search-tree-value/bench/bst_close_seq.kara  (moduli 1000000, 1100000)
  201-300/248-strobogrammatic-number-iii/differential.kara               (modulus 100000)

The other 67 kata sources that mention 65536 use a modulus at or below 32768, where the shift is harmless. So this is contained, not systemic.

WHAT TO DO. #270's published numbers are internally consistent (all languages get the same keys) but its data is 30x narrower than its source claims, which matters for a BST-search kata where key cardinality drives tree shape and hit rate. Widening the key there is a data change that invalidates its recorded numbers, so it needs a re-bench and a README note in the same pass — not a silent edit. The two-draw form used to check this is:

  state = lcg(state);
  let hi = state / 65536i64;
  state = lcg(state);
  k = (hi * 32768i64 + state / 65536i64) % 1000000i64;

The transferable lesson, and the reason this is a row rather than a footnote: a modulus that never fires is invisible in review and invisible in the output — the data still looks shuffled and the checksums still agree across languages. It only surfaced because a tuning sweep on the harness disagreed with the same sweep on a real workload, and the disagreement was chased instead of averaged.

SCOPE CORRECTION — THE SCAN ABOVE IS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Re-run with a
predicate that can actually tell the broken form from the fixed one, it names a
different set: the one benchmarked kata it listed is FINE, and three benchmarked
katas it never looked at are NOT.

WHY THE FIRST SCAN FAILED. It matched "31-bit LCG + a /65536 shift + a modulus
above 32768". That predicate cannot separate

    v = (state / 65536) % 1000000                  <- broken, 15 bits
    v = (hi * 32768 + state / 65536) % 1000000     <- correct, 30 bits

because the CORRECT form still contains a /65536 and still carries a wide
modulus. And it recognised a 31-bit LCG only as `& 2147483647`, while the corpus
also spells it `% 2147483648`. So it false-positived on the fixed spelling and
false-negatived on the other mask spelling — and it ran over .kara only, when
the mirrors are where the question actually lives.

#270 WAS NEVER AFFECTED. `bench/bst_close.kara` and `bst_close_seq.kara` have
used the two-draw form since their first commit (2aa64d32), and carry a source
comment saying so in as many words: "The first version of this lane used one,
which silently confined every value — and every target — to a 32K window". The
two-draw form quoted as the fix in this row was LIFTED FROM THAT FILE. Listing
as broken the file the recommendation was copied out of should have been the
tell; it was not noticed because the scan output was trusted over the source.
No re-bench, no README note, nothing to do for #270.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY AFFECTED — four katas, counted with the corrected predicate
over every language mirror:

  137-single-number-ii          ALL FIVE mirrors narrow  (mod 100000)
  235-lowest-common-ancestor    ALL FIVE mirrors narrow  (mod 1000000)
  260-single-number-iii         ALL FIVE mirrors narrow  (mod 100000)
  248-strobogrammatic-number-iii  differential.kara + .py only (mod 100000);
                                  its five BENCH mirrors are clean

Every affected kata is internally consistent — kāra, Rust, C, Go and Python all
draw the same narrow keys — so once again NO PUBLISHED RATIO IS WRONG. What is
wrong is what the workload IS, and for two of these that is not cosmetic:

  * 235 builds a 200,000-node BST and its generated workload text claims
    "randomly shaped, depth ~35". At 32,768 distinct values over 200,000
    inserts that claim is unsupported — the tree is mostly duplicate keys and
    its shape is decided by duplicate handling, not by the LCG. This is the
    same failure #270 documents having already fixed, in the neighbouring kata.
  * 137 and 260 count set bits per plane across 32 planes. Confining values to
    [0, 32768) makes bits 15..31 ALWAYS ZERO, so seventeen of the thirty-two
    planes are trivially predictable and contribute a branch the predictor
    never misses. The bit-counting loop is being measured on a distribution far
    easier than the one it is documented to use.
  * 248 is a correctness differential, not a benchmark: the narrow key costs
    input-space COVERAGE (a third of the intended range is never generated),
    not a number. Cheapest of the four to fix and verify.

WHAT A FIX COSTS, since the placement question turns on it. `bench.sh`
cross-validates a single sink across kara/rust/c/go/python, so a kata's five
mirrors must be widened in ONE atomic change and the published sink moves with
them. That invalidates BOTH recorded lanes — canonical M5 `results.json` and
`results.container-x86.json` — for each of the three benchmarked katas, plus the
generated workload prose. The source edit itself is machine-independent; the two
re-bench lanes are not, and must be measured from the same post-fix revision.

Severity raised low -> medium: three benchmarked katas with published numbers on
both lanes, and one documented workload property (235's tree depth) that the
data does not support.

SECOND SCOPE CORRECTION — THE SHUFFLE BOUND. Both previous scans classified only
LITERAL moduli. That hid the shape that does the most damage, a Fisher-Yates
bound, which is symbolic by construction:

    k = n-1 .. 1:  swap = (state / 65536) % (k + 1);  swap a[k], a[swap]

`state / 65536` is 15 bits, so for every k >= 32768 the modulus CANNOT FIRE and
the draw is uniform over [0, 32768) instead of [0, k]. The array stops being
shuffled above index 32768 while still looking thoroughly shuffled below it.
At kata 252's n = 120,000 that is 87,232 of 119,999 steps — 72.7% of the
shuffle. At 253's n = 150,000 it is 117,232 of 149,999 — 78.2%.

252-meeting-rooms AND 253-meeting-rooms-ii ARE AFFECTED. Those are the two
katas that carry B-2026-08-16-9's published sort numbers, so the obvious
question is whether that row's conclusions rest on a workload that is not what
it claims.

THEY DO NOT — MEASURED, NOT ARGUED. Built kāra and Rust twins of 252 from one
karac and one rustc, differing only in the shuffle draw, and counted:

  arm                 instructions   spread        cycles   spread   IPC
  narrow kara        1,346,137,980    0.07%   345,680,523    0.46%  3.89
  narrow rust        1,101,602,010    0.23%   266,189,244    5.86%  4.14
  wide   kara        1,368,887,208    0.01%   346,118,271    0.64%  3.95
  wide   rust        1,092,150,693    0.04%   265,426,391    1.72%  4.11

  kāra/rust on cycles:        1.299x -> 1.304x   (+0.4%)
  kāra/rust on instructions:  1.222x -> 1.253x   (+2.6%)

The CYCLE ratio — what the kata publishes — moves 0.4%, inside the cycle
spread and two orders below the 19% that B-2026-08-16-9's scatter fix delivered.
So the sort residual is independent of this defect and needs no re-measurement.
The INSTRUCTION ratio moves a real +2.6% (against a 0.23% spread), which matters
only because instruction count is the metric that row tunes on — and its own
harness (sortk_wide.kara) was already widened, so that is already handled.

WHY THE DISTORTION IS SO MILD, given 73% of the steps are wrong. Ascending-run
count is what a run-adaptive sort like driftsort actually consumes, and it is
essentially unchanged: 60,224 narrow vs 60,052 wide at n = 120,000 (0.3%), and
75,067 vs 75,085 at n = 150,000 (0.02%) — both sitting at the (n+1)/2 a uniform
permutation gives. A truncated Fisher-Yates still touches every position, so it
destroys presortedness just as thoroughly; what it biases is the distribution
OVER permutations, which no comparison sort can feel. Mean displacement does
move (44,345 -> 50,099 on 253, 11.5%), which is why displacement is the wrong
proxy to have reasoned from.

THE SINK CANNOT CATCH THIS. 252's narrow and wide binaries emit the IDENTICAL
sink (537953186), because the fold is over `ok` and `s[n-1].1 - s[0].0` — the
span of the sorted array, invariant under permutation. So bench.sh's
cross-language sink check, which is the corpus's only automatic correctness net
here, is structurally blind to a shuffle-quality change. Anything that fixes
these generators must be verified by re-measuring, not by the sink agreeing.

SCOPE, THIRD COUNT. Confirmed narrow, bound resolved from source:

  137-single-number-ii            mod 100000, all 5 mirrors
  235-lowest-common-ancestor-bst  mod 1000000 and % n (n = 200000), all 5
  236-lowest-common-ancestor-bt   % n (n = 100000)
  248-strobogrammatic-number-iii  mod 100000, differential only
  252-meeting-rooms               % (k+1) (n = 120000), all 5 + differential
  253-meeting-rooms-ii            % (k+1) (n = 150000), all 5 + differential
  260-single-number-iii           mod 100000, all 5 mirrors
  261-graph-valid-tree            % i and % (sh+1) (n = 100000)
  287-find-the-duplicate-number   % (k+1) (n = 200000), all 5 mirrors

Confirmed CLEAN, bound resolved and below 32768: 243/244/245 (vocab_n = 256),
246 (len = 32), 250 (alphabet = 3), 269 (alpha = 8, m <= 6), 270 (two-draw
form). Still UNRESOLVED and needing a look: 132 (% alpha), 134 and 135 (% cap),
240 (% (maxv+2)), 257 (% open.len).

That this row has now been re-scoped twice is itself the finding. Each pass
used a predicate that was correct for the examples in front of it and silently
wrong elsewhere — literal-only, mask-spelling-only, .kara-only. A scan is a
claim about a corpus, and it deserves the same falsification effort as a
performance claim; three of the four scan predicates here would have looked
fine in review.

--- 2026-08-17 FIX APPEND (kara-katas bb43ae5): source widened everywhere,
container lane re-benched; the M5 lane is all that remains open ---

ALL FOUR KATAS WIDENED to the #270 two-draw form, one atomic change per kata
across every mirror, each five-way cross-validated by running all mirrors:

  137  5 mirrors, % 100000. Sink UNCHANGED at 79998760.
  260  5 mirrors, % 100000. Sink unchanged at 573145098.
  235  5 mirrors, TWO SITES — see below. Sink 198558594 (was stale everywhere).
  248  differential.kara/.py (bench mirrors were already clean, per the scope
       correction). 3000 cases, 0 mismatches on the widened space, both
       agree on new hash 933790874; README hash updated.

A SECOND NARROW SITE IN 235 THE CORRECTED SCAN ALSO MISSED: the query indices.
`pi = (y / 65536) % n` with n = 200000 draws 15-bit indices, so the modulus
never fires there either — 8M queries only ever touched the FIRST 32,768 of
200,000 nodes; 84% of the tree was built and never searched. Both sites are
widened. The predicate lesson compounds: the corrected scan keyed on the
modulus literal being "wide", and 200000 appears as `% n`, not as a literal —
a scan for this class has to resolve the modulus, not pattern-match it.

WHY NO SINK EVER CAUGHT 137/260, recorded because it bounds what
cross-validation can promise: both katas' answers depend ONLY on the loner
values, which the generator change does not touch. The sink pins
cross-language agreement and algorithm correctness while being completely
blind to the input distribution — the two properties this row is about are
exactly the ones it cannot see. 235's sink does depend on the data, which is
why its M5 staleness is self-evident (recorded sink no longer matches the
sources) while 137/260's is not; each README note says which case it is in.

MEASURED SHAPE CHANGES (generator replicated in python, distribution and BST
build measured directly):

  137/260 values:  19,421 -> 25,996 distinct of 30,000 draws; max 32,766 -> 99,999
  235 build keys:  32,696 -> 181,331 distinct of 200,000; the README's claimed
                   "depth ~35" was FALSE FOR BOTH distributions — measured 48
                   narrow, 43 wide. Replaced with the measured number.

DONE: source widening (25 files), five-way sink validation per kata, 137 kara
A/B/auto-par parity (79998760 all three; 260/235's interp lanes are
impractical at bench iteration counts — the five-way cross-language sink is
the stronger oracle there), container-x86 re-bench of all three benchmarked
katas from the post-fix revision (BENCH_JSON=1, python parity lane included),
README notes under each bench-staleness block naming this row.

REMAINING, and why the row stays OPEN: the canonical M5 `results.json` lanes
for 137, 260 and 235, plus each README's quoted runtime table, predate the
widening and must be re-measured from bb43ae5 or later on the reference host.
That is owner-machine work by definition of the lane. Everything else in this
row is closed.

One environment note for whoever benches in a container next: `mem_peak`
needs GNU time at /usr/bin/time (`apt-get install time`) — absent in a fresh
container, and bench.sh's compile-memory section exits 127 without it.

FIXED ACROSS ELEVEN KATAS, in two commits by two sessions. kara-katas bb43ae59
took the four whose bound was a LITERAL above 32768 (137, 235, 248, 260);
62fea61c took the seven whose bound is SYMBOLIC and therefore invisible to a
line-level scan (135, 236, 252, 253, 257, 261, 287). 3b3f0d45 re-measured the M5
lane for all ten benchmarked ones.

The two sessions widened the four overlapping katas independently and produced
BYTE-IDENTICAL sinks — 79998760, 198558594, 933790874, 573145098 — which is a
better check on the transform than either derivation alone.

FINAL SCOPE, after the count was wrong three times:

  135-candy               % cap, cap = 100000 on one of two workloads
  137-single-number-ii    % 100000
  235-lca-bst             % 1000000 and query indices % 200000
  236-lca-binary-tree     query indices % 100000
  248-strobogrammatic-iii differential only, % 100000
  252-meeting-rooms       Fisher-Yates % (k+1) over 120,000
  253-meeting-rooms-ii    Fisher-Yates % (k+1) over 150,000
  257-binary-tree-paths   % open.len(), peak 83,155 (simulated)
  260-single-number-iii   % 100000
  261-graph-valid-tree    % i over 100,000 and Fisher-Yates over 99,999
  287-find-the-duplicate  Fisher-Yates % (k+1) over 200,000

Confirmed CLEAN with bounds read from source, not assumed: 132 (alpha <= 26),
134 (cap <= 110), 240 (maxv+2 = 7994), 243/244/245 (vocab_n = 256), 246
(len = 32), 250 (alphabet = 3), 269 (alpha = 8), 270 (already two-draw).

WHAT THE WORKLOADS ACTUALLY WERE. 235's queries reached only the first 32,768 of
200,000 nodes, so 84% of the tree was never searched — re-measured, every
language got 24-36% slower. 287's Fisher-Yates kept the whole pointer-chase
inside the low 32k of a 200k array, so its locality was an artifact — every
language 49-53% slower. 137/260 confined values to [0, 32768), leaving bits
15..31 always zero, so seventeen of thirty-two bit-planes never incremented;
that shows up only in the overflow-checked Rust lane, +7.5%. No published RATIO
moved materially in any of the ten (largest: 236, and that one is not this bug).

TWO APPLICATION ERRORS, both caught by checks rather than by reading, and both
worth recording because the checks are the transferable part:

  * OVER-application. 252, 253 and 261 each carry a differential with the same
    one-draw form, and all three were widened before their bounds were read.
    They draw n = ...%9, %11, %12+1 — bounds under 13, where the modulus always
    fired. Reverted. Caught by MIRROR-PARITY: a kata's mirrors implement one
    algorithm, so they must end up with the same number of widened draws, and
    261 came out 10 kara against 8 python.
  * UNDER-application. 257's Go lane spells its bound `% int64(len(open))`,
    whose leading cast kept it out of the inventory while its four siblings were
    widened — a Go lane silently generating different data from the other four.
    Caught by asking which mirrors of a TOUCHED kata went untouched, which
    mirror-parity cannot see because it only compares files that changed.

AND ONE FINDING THAT IS NOT THIS BUG. #236's kāra lane moved +14.5% in the
re-bench while C/Rust/Go stayed within 3.6%. Holding karac fixed and varying
only the data gives 0.140 s both ways, ratio 1.000 — the widening costs that
kata nothing. Filed as [[B-2026-08-17-36]]: a kāra-only regression between
2026-07-27 and 689dadd6, unbisected. It surfaced only because the re-bench was
read per-lane: a data change feeds every lane, so the question worth asking is
whether the lanes moved TOGETHER, and nine did while one did not.

THE LESSON THIS ROW ACTUALLY CARRIES, given it was re-scoped twice before being
fixed: a scan is a claim about a corpus and deserves the same falsification
effort as a performance claim. Four predicates were used here — literal-only,
mask-spelling-only, .kara-only, and allow-list-by-modulus-text — and every one
of them looked correct against the examples in front of it while being silently
wrong elsewhere. What finally bounded the problem was not a better regex but two
CONSISTENCY checks that need no bound analysis at all: mirrors of one kata must
agree, and a touched kata must not have untouched mirrors.

title: Text-mode `karac check` silently DROPS the whole `TypeCheckResult::warnings` channel: every `type_lint_warning` lint (`deprecated`, `unstable_api`, `map_value_clone_reinsert`, ...) renders in `--output=json` and prints NOTHING in plain text mode — `All checks passed.` on a program whose JSON surface carries a warning.
detail:
FOUND while probing B-2026-08-17-2: the map_entry lint's canonical fixture — the exact program its own unit test asserts fires — printed nothing through `karac check`, which looked like the walk hole being probed but discriminated to a different mechanism: the lint DID fire (present in --output=json), and `render_text_diagnostics` simply has no loop over `t.warnings`. Ownership warnings print because they ride a different channel (`pipeline.ownership.errors` with an advisory split).

CONSEQUENCE: a human running plain `karac check` never sees a deprecation, an unstable-API use, or the quadratic-map hint; the Mend loop (JSON) was never affected, which is why it survived this long.

DISCRIMINATOR: `karac check <canonical map_entry fixture>` -> 'All checks passed.' only; same file with --output=json -> diagnostics[0].lint_name = map_value_clone_reinsert.
investigation: 2026-08-17. Found, discriminated from B-2026-08-17-2, and fixed in the same session (281a257).
