(2) `i32::MIN` IS REACHABLE AS A PRODUCT though its magnitude is not reachable as a positive one; the checked multiply tests against the bound for the RESULT's sign, and the magnitudes are carried unsigned precisely because `-i32::MIN` would itself overflow. Pinned.

`gpu.dot` — checks the per-element product AND every accumulation, because either overflows ALONE: `65536 * 65536` leaves i32 in a single term with nothing yet accumulated, so checking only the running sum would let a wrapped product through. The consequence is that the identity `gpu.dot(a, b) == gpu.sum(a * b)` extends over integers to WHICH PROGRAMS TRAP, not merely to what the successful ones return. The twin is written as products-then-`tree_reduce_i32` rather than as a fused loop, so that holds BY CONSTRUCTION — a fused loop would be a second implementation to keep in step. Operands must SHARE an element type: a mixed pair has no single overflow rule, and for integers the rule decides the trap set.

`gpu.matmul` — equals `a.matmul(b)` TRAP FOR TRAP, the sharper form of the float promise recorded in the ninth batch. That one said tiling preserves the naive k-ascending ORDER; the integer form's consequence is stronger, because identical order means identical INTERMEDIATES, and overflow is a property of the intermediates. So reordering the tile loop would break the trap agreement EVEN WHERE IT PRESERVED EVERY RETURNED VALUE — a performance change that looks value-preserving and is not. One unrepresentable output cell traps the whole product; a matrix with a wrapped entry is not an answer.

TWO SHADER-LEVEL FACTS THAT ARE EASY TO GET WRONG AND HARD TO SEE:
  * A PADDED LANE MUST NEVER RAISE THE FLAG. Lanes past m, n or k stage zeros and multiply them; if they were allowed to accumulate, an edge workgroup on a perfectly valid matrix would trap on arithmetic that is not in the data. Only a lane holding a real output cell accumulates.
  * THE FLAG BUFFER IS INDEXED BY THE FLATTENED WORKGROUP ID. Matmul's grid is genuinely 2-D (unlike every other kernel here, whose y axis is an overflow lane for x), so a `wid.x`-only index would have edge rows silently overwrite each other's flags — losing a trap rather than adding one.

PREREQUISITE, filed and fixed separately as B-2026-08-20-27: an integer `Tensor.matmul` never overflow-checked AT ALL — `karac build` silently wrapped, `karac run --interp` returned a value outside the element type, and neither trapped, though the ELEMENT-WISE `a * b` over the same tensors trapped on both. `gpu.matmul` cannot promise to equal `a.matmul(b)` including the traps while the CPU form does not trap, so that had to land first.

THREE TESTS ASSERTED THE OLD REFUSALS and now assert the new contract (`checked_int_emitter_refuses_prod...` → `..._supports_prod...`, the u32 tree's refusal set, and the typechecker's "refuse what has not been decided"). That is the change being deliberate rather than a regression, and the renamed tests carry the reason.

VERIFIED across all three surfaces (`run --interp`, `run`, `build`) on lavapipe, at 17x17x17 for matmul — straddling the 16-wide tile in all three dimensions at once, so every edge guard and the k-padding are exercised together; a matmul whose dimensions are all tile multiples exercises no padding at all.

THIS ROW IS NOW COMPLETE. Nothing is open, nothing is blocked, and no decisions remain. Shipped over `Vec[f32]`: sum / prod / min / max / mean / dot / argmin / argmax / variance / stddev / prefix_sum. Over `Vec[i32]` and `Vec[u32]`: sum / prod / min / max / mean / dot / argmin / argmax / variance / stddev, the last of these EXACT. Plus a tiled `matmul` over rank-2 `Tensor[f32]` / `Tensor[i32]` / `Tensor[u32]`, equal to `a.matmul(b)` bit-for-bit and trap-for-trap. The only deliberate gap left is integer `prefix_sum`, which is not a decision or a block but simply unwritten: it needs the overflow flag carried through every lane rather than only the one that writes the result, which is ordinary work on the pattern `emit_int_reduce_kernel` already establishes.

PROGRESS 2026-08-20 (thirteenth batch) — INTEGER `prefix_sum` (d3cadc9f), the one gap the twelfth batch left named. It closed as predicted — ordinary work on the established pattern — but the work turned up one fact worth more than the feature.

WHY THE OVERFLOW FLAG COULD NOT BE INHERITED. Every checked integer op before this one CONVERGES: only lane 0 survives a reduction, a lane above the stride holds a partial nobody reads, and `ovf[0]` after the fold is the whole story. A SCAN WRITES ALL n VALUES, so an overflow in ANY lane is an overflow in the answer. The emitted shader ORs the flag across the whole workgroup. Reusing the reduction's lane-0 habit would have silently dropped overflows in exactly the elements the caller asked for — which is the plausible-wrong-number shape this family exists to refuse, arrived at by copying working code rather than by any new mistake.

PADDED LANES ARE CHECKED TOO, and that is not conservatism. A lane past the buffer starts at the identity, but the scan sweeps real values into it, so by the last step it holds the CHUNK TOTAL — which phase 2 folds and every later chunk's offset depends on. Excluding padded lanes is the obvious "only real elements matter" shortcut and it drops a real quantity.

THE PHASE-3 OFFSET ADD IS CHECKED, and it is the step most easily forgotten: phases 1 and 2 look like THE ARITHMETIC while shifting a chunk looks like BOOKKEEPING. `scanned[i] + offset` adds two real values and is precisely where a long buffer's total finally leaves the range — it is the only place a late chunk meets an early chunk's sum. Its E2E fixture is built so that NEITHER per-chunk scan overflows, so only the offset add can raise the flag; a fixture that also overflowed in phase 1 would pass whether or not phase 3 were checked at all.

THE FINDING: THE SPECIFIED ORDER DECIDES WHETHER AN INTEGER SCAN TRAPS, not merely what it returns. This is the prefix sum's version of what this row already records for the reductions (the tree-vs-line trap table), and it is SHARPER here, because Hillis-Steele forms WINDOW SUMS that a sequential scan never forms at all. With MAX = i32::MAX:

  | buffer            | running total          | gpu.prefix_sum |
  |-------------------|------------------------|----------------|
  | [-MAX, MAX, MAX]  | -MAX, 0, MAX (in range)| TRAPS          |

The first Hillis-Steele step computes prev[2] + prev[1] = MAX + MAX. All three surfaces trap on it, because the interpreter reproduces the device's step order — so this is SPECIFIED BEHAVIOUR, not a divergence. But it means replacing a running total with `gpu.prefix_sum` is NOT a pure speedup on integer data: it can introduce a trap that was not there. Pinned as a test that FIRST asserts every running total is in range, so the fixture cannot quietly rot into an ordinary overflow case and keep passing for the wrong reason.

Note this is strictly stronger than the reduction table above. There the tree and the line form different GROUPINGS of the same total; here the scan forms sums of interior sub-ranges the sequential form never computes, so the trap sets are not merely different orderings of the same intermediate set.

VERIFIED across all three surfaces at 1, 3, 5, 65 and 4097 elements. 4097 is the load-bearing length: past 64*64 the chunk totals THEMSELVES need more than one workgroup, so a host loop written for a single level is correct up to 4096 and wrong after, passing every short fixture — the same failure shape this family keeps designing against.

THE ROW IS NOW COMPLETE WITH NO GAPS AT ALL, deliberate or otherwise. Over `Vec[f32]`: sum / prod / min / max / mean / dot / argmin / argmax / variance / stddev / prefix_sum. Over `Vec[i32]` and `Vec[u32]`: THE SAME ELEVEN, with variance / stddev exact and every integer op trapping rather than wrapping. Plus a tiled `matmul` over rank-2 `Tensor[f32]` / `Tensor[i32]` / `Tensor[u32]`, equal to `a.matmul(b)` bit-for-bit and trap-for-trap.
fix: FIXED across thirteen batches, closing with d3cadc9f (integer prefix_sum). See detail for the per-batch record.

title: NO `shared struct` OR `par struct` COULD SATISFY ANY TRAIT BOUND ANYWHERE -- `impl_table_key` had no `Type::Shared` arm, so `type_satisfies_bound` answered `false` for every trait, and the diagnostic contradicted itself in one sentence: "`ParS` does not implement `Doer`; trait `Doer` is implemented by: ParS".
detail:
MEASURED while probing B-2026-08-19-11. `fn run[T: Doer](p: ref T)` called with a `shared struct` or `par struct` value that HAS an `impl Doer for` it is rejected, and the rejection names the type as an implementor in its own "implemented by:" list.

ROOT CAUSE, one missing match arm. A `shared struct S` / `par struct S` value carries `Type::Shared(S)`, deliberately distinct from `Type::Named { name: "S" }` so consumers can match shared-ness off the type (see `Type::Shared`'s doc). `impl_table_key` (src/typechecker/types.rs) mapped Named / Ref / MutRef / Slice / Refinement / primitives and fell through to `None` on `Shared` -- and `None` means `type_satisfies_bound` returns `false` before ever consulting the impl table.

WHY IT SURVIVED THIS LONG: `receiver_for_method_lookup`, defined TWENTY LINES BELOW `impl_table_key` in the same file, DOES collapse `Type::Shared(name)` to the nominal name. So `s.go()` resolved correctly and only the trait-BOUND path failed. Every ordinary use of a shared struct works; the failure needs a generic bound to show up, which is why no kata caught it.

SCOPE. `shared enum` / `par enum` are NOT affected -- enums carry `Type::Named` and always keyed correctly. Confirmed by matrix: plain struct, plain enum, shared enum all satisfied the bound; only the two struct forms failed.

THE CATCH-22 THIS PRODUCED ON THE PROVIDER SURFACE. `with_provider` rejects a `shared struct` provider with `E_NOT_CROSS_TASK` whose fix-it reads "replace `SharedDB` with the `par` form of the same type". Following that fix-it produced a NEW error from `check_provider_satisfies_declared_bound` -- "provider of type 'ParDB' does not implement `DbProvider`" -- because that check reaches the impl table through `type_satisfies_bound`. The compiler's own suggested repair produced a program the compiler rejected, and there was NO way to write a reference-semantics provider at all.

FIX: add the `Type::Shared(name) => Some((name, vec![]))` arm, mirroring `receiver_for_method_lookup`. Shared structs are non-generic at v1, so there are no args to carry. Tests pin both halves (method call AND bound) in one program so the two paths cannot drift apart again.

fix: f4340ba
title: the `providers { R => p } in { .. }` block form NEVER checked the declared provider trait -- a provider implementing nothing at all passed `karac check` clean, because B-2026-08-19-4 wired the check into the `with_provider(..)` call form only.
detail:
MEASURED while probing B-2026-08-19-11. `providers { UserDB => NotAProvider { data: 100 } } in { .. }`, where `NotAProvider` has no `impl DbProvider` whatsoever and `effect resource UserDB: DbProvider;` declares one, reported "All checks passed." The identical program in `with_provider[UserDB](NotAProvider { .. }, || ..)` form was correctly rejected.

The two forms are the same thing: design.md § Provider-Rooted Resources says `providers {}` DESUGARS to `with_provider`, and codegen builds the same resource vtable from the same bound's methods either way. B-2026-08-19-4 added `check_provider_satisfies_declared_bound` at the call-form site in expr_call.rs and did not reach the `ExprKind::Providers` arm in exprs.rs, which carried a comment stating that provider-trait conformance "remains deferred" -- accurate when written, stale the moment -19-4 landed.

NOT SYMMETRIC WITH THE CROSS-TASK CHECK, which is what makes this easy to miss on a read: the `Providers` arm DID already run `is_cross_task_safe_with` on each binding. One of the two provider obligations was enforced in both forms and the other in only one, so the arm looks checked at a glance.

CONSEQUENCE: a resource call inside the block dispatches through a vtable built from a trait the provider does not implement. The block form is the shape design.md's own multi-resource examples use.

FIX: call `check_provider_satisfies_declared_bound` per binding in the `Providers` arm (widening it to `pub(super)`), and correct the stale comment.

fix:
FIXED by c88b51b. `register_items` now binds each user-enum unit variant under BOTH `First.A` and the bare `A`, which is what the two neighbouring registration paths already did -- the prelude `Ordering` / `MemoryOrdering` loop binds both spellings, and the baked-stdlib `Item::EnumDef` arm ~40 lines above binds the qualified one. User enums were the single path that bound only the bare name.

That mattered because `eval_expr`'s `ExprKind::Path` arm tries `env.get("First.A")` first and, on a miss, falls back to the LAST SEGMENT ALONE. With no qualified key ever registered, every `First.A` in the language took that fallback and read `env["A"]` -- a slot both enums had written, last declaration winning.

The bare binding is deliberately kept. The pattern matcher classifies a bare PascalCase identifier as a unit-variant pattern only when `env.get(name)` returns a unit `EnumVariant` (documented at the `Ordering` registration); dropping it would turn every bare match arm into a catch-all binding, which is bug-ledger B-2026-06-30-14.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces -- `run --interp`, `run` (JIT), `build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` -- across six programs: colliding unit variants direct and through a let, colliding tuple variants, colliding struct variants, and the unambiguous bare-name case. All agree and all are correct. Four regression tests in tests/interpreter.rs, including one pinning that non-unit variants keep working (they were always correct -- constructed at call sites where the enum name is in hand) and one pinning the bare-name path against the B-2026-06-30-14 regression.
title: `First.A` EVALUATED TO A `Second` VALUE under `karac run` whenever two enums shared a unit-variant name -- user enums registered their unit variants under the BARE name only, so the later declaration overwrote the earlier and the qualified path fell through to it; the wrong `enum_name` then rode the value into method dispatch and called the other enum's impl
detail:
MEASURED while probing B-2026-08-19-11 (pre-existing; reproduced on clean `main` at 47df5f5 via `git stash`, so it is NOT caused by the B-2026-08-19-13 fix that shares the session).

REPRO, self-contained:

    enum First { A, B }
    enum Second { A, B }
    impl First { fn tag(ref self) -> i64 { 1 } }
    impl Second { fn tag(ref self) -> i64 { 2 } }
    fn main() {
        println(First.A.tag());   // prints 2 -- WRONG, expected 1
        println(Second.A.tag());  // prints 2 -- correct
    }

Both lines print `2`. The later-declared enum's impl wins for both.

THE TYPE IS RIGHT, WHICH IS THE DANGEROUS PART. `let d = First.A; describe(d)` where `describe(x: Second)` is correctly rejected with "expected 'Second', found 'First'" -- so the binding really does carry type `First`, and it is METHOD/IMPL SELECTION that ignores the qualifier, not variant resolution producing the wrong value. That means the usual downstream guards (assignment checks, exhaustiveness, effect inference) all see a well-typed program and pass. The wrong answer is silent.

With DISTINCT variant names (`First { Gamma }` / `Second { Alpha }`) both dispatch correctly, so the trigger is specifically the shared variant NAME, not the two-enum shape.

RENAMES ARE A TRAP HERE: two enums with no overlap today start miscompiling the moment someone adds a colliding variant to either one, at a call site in neither file.

NOT INVESTIGATED: whether the interpreter and codegen agree (measured under `--interp` only; this container has no runtime archives built), and whether a trait-bound generic call (`run[T: Doer]`) misdispatches the same way -- it did in the original matrix probe, which is how this was noticed.

Whoever picks this up: start at the impl-table lookup for a unit-variant receiver, and check whether the enum name is being carried into the key at all.

DIAGNOSIS CORRECTION (2026-08-19, at close). The row filed this as a `miscompile` affecting method dispatch, and recorded "NOT INVESTIGATED: whether the interpreter and codegen agree". They did not: this was a RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE, and codegen was the correct side throughout. `karac build` printed the right answer before the fix and after it; only `karac run` was wrong. The class is corrected to `run-vs-build` accordingly.

The row also mis-located the defect. It said "start at the impl-table lookup for a unit-variant receiver, and check whether the enum name is being carried into the key at all" -- the enum name WAS carried into the key correctly, and the impl table was never at fault. Instrumenting the dispatch key settled it in one run: the receiver arrived already stamped `Second`. Dispatch faithfully used the identity the VALUE carried; construction had put the wrong one there.

Two things made it look like a dispatch bug from the outside, and both are worth remembering because they will mask the next one of these:
  - A `match` arm compares only the VARIANT name, so `match First.A { First.A => .. }` matched a value whose `enum_name` was `Second`. The match appearing to work is what pointed the original investigation away from construction.
  - The STATIC type was right (`First`), confirmed by a passing type error against a `Second` parameter. So the typechecker agreed with the author, codegen agreed with the typechecker, and only the interpreter's value disagreed with everyone -- with no phase in a position to notice.

SCOPE, measured rather than assumed: only UNIT variants were affected. Tuple (`First.W(7)`) and struct (`First.S { v: 7 }`) variants are constructed at call sites that have the enum name in hand and never consult the bare env binding; both were already correct and are now pinned.

REMAINDER, split out as its own row rather than buried here: the BARE ambiguous form `let x = A;` is still wrong, and is a live run-vs-build divergence today. See B-2026-08-19-17.

fix:
FIXED by a94038e (a) + 15b8dc7 (b), in two parts, deliberately separable.

(a) INTERPRETER COMPLIANCE -- the actual bug, zero breakage. `register_items` binds a bare variant name by plain last-write-wins, so the later-declared enum owned `env["A"]` for the whole program. The typechecker does not resolve it that way and codegen follows the typechecker, so the interpreter was the odd one out. Rather than reimplement the precedence in a second place -- two copies of a rule is exactly how these backends drifted apart -- `retag_bare_unit_variant` reads the enum the typechecker already recorded in `expr_types` for that span and adopts it. Agreement is then true by construction; this is the same channel B-2026-08-13-8 used to hand codegen's winning impl to the interpreter. It is silent when the value is not a unit variant, when `expr_types` has no entry (it is sparse), or when the enum already matches, so the non-colliding case costs one map lookup.

(b) REJECT THE AMBIGUITY -- the language change. A bare variant name declared by two or more USER enums is now `E0279 AmbiguousBareVariant`, naming both enums and offering both qualified forms. Scoped precisely to the case with no chosen winner; three collisions that DO have one are deliberately still accepted:
  - user enum shadowing a stdlib/prelude one -- the two-tier scan favours the user on purpose, so `MyIoErr.Other` is not hijacked by the seeded `IoError.Other`;
  - `Some` / `None` / `Ok` / `Err`, pinned to their builtin owner so a user enum cannot capture a bare `None`;
  - PATTERN position, which is scrutinee-typed and correct on every backend -- `match c { Less => ... }` after `.cmp()` is idiomatic and must keep working.

The diagnostic sits on the bare-identifier arm of `infer_expr`, not inside `resolve_identifier_type`, for the reason B-2026-08-11-6 recorded when it put the type-name-in-value-position diagnostic in the same place: that helper is also the speculative first-segment fallback for `resolve_path_type`, so a hard error inside it fires on paths that go on to resolve fine. The resolved winner is returned after the diagnostic, so an ambiguous name costs ONE error instead of a cascade of "expected X, found Error" at every downstream use.

WHY REJECTING COSTS NOTHING THE AUTHOR COULD HAVE WRITTEN. Expression position has no type-direction at all: `let x: Second = A;`, `fn f() -> Second { A }` and `want_second(A)` are ALL rejected today with "expected 'Second', found 'First'". The losing enum is not merely deprioritized, it is unreachable by bare name even deliberately. So the choice was never the author's to make, and picking one silently was the worst of the available behaviours.

MEASURED BREAKAGE: none. The full suite is 122 targets / 9288 passing with (b) in place -- no test in the repo uses a colliding bare variant in expression position. The programs (b) newly rejects are exactly those that were already either divergent or correct only by coincidence (when the alphabetical winner happened to also be the last declared).

FORWARD-COMPATIBLE: an error can later be relaxed into type-directed resolution without breaking anyone, whereas blessing a winner now would make changing it a breaking change.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (`run --interp`, `run`, `build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`) across eight programs; 7 new tests (5 typechecker, 2 interpreter); both clippy legs and fmt clean.
title: A BARE AMBIGUOUS UNIT VARIANT PICKED A DIFFERENT ENUM IN EACH BACKEND -- `karac build` printed First's answer and `karac run` printed Second's, with no diagnostic. Fixed in two parts: the interpreter now adopts the enum the typechecker recorded (it was the one backend never given the resolution order), and a bare variant declared by two USER enums is now rejected outright instead of resolved by an alphabetical tie-break nobody chose.

fix:
FIXED by ba484b53. `program_declares_gpu_kernel` is now one half of `program_uses_gpu_runtime`; the other half is a source scan for the reduction spellings (`gpu.sum(`, `gpu.prod(`, `gpu.min(`, `gpu.max(`, `gpu.dot(`), the same cheap form the Arrow IPC gate beside it already uses. A false positive only routes a non-GPU program to the correct-if-slower interpreter, so the scan is safe to keep broad.

THE TEST HOLE MATTERED MORE THAN THE BUG. `tests/gpu_e2e.rs` compared `karac run --interp` against `karac build` — and `--interp` is PRECISELY the lane the routing is supposed to select, so the comparison ran straight through the defect and reported green. The A/B rule in kara-katas/CLAUDE.md is `run` == `build`, and `run` means the DEFAULT lane, which has been the JIT since LLJIT slice 6c. `assert_gpu_reduce_matches_interp` now asserts all three surfaces agree (`run --interp`, `run`, `build`). Reverting the one-line detection makes it fail with the original symbol error, so the new leg is not vacuous — checked.

GENERALIZABLE LESSON: any future opt-in runtime feature (the `gpu`, `regex` and `arrow` archives are all on this axis) needs its JIT-routing gate keyed on what the PROGRAM REACHES, not on a syntactic marker that happens to correlate with it today. And an A/B harness that pins only the fallback lane cannot see a routing bug at all.
title: `karac run` FAILED on every GPU reduction program while `karac build` answered correctly — `JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ karac_runtime_gpu_reduce_f32 ]`. A run-vs-build divergence shipped in the reduction slice and live on main until the same day.
detail:
FOUND 2026-08-19 while wiring `gpu.dot`, by running a fixture through `karac run` by hand rather than through the E2E suite — which was green throughout.

MECHANISM. The sibling `karac_jit_runner` links the runtime WITHOUT the opt-in `gpu` feature (the heavy wgpu/Metal backend), so the LLJIT `dlsym` generator cannot resolve `karac_runtime_gpu_*` and `main` fails to materialize. That is known and handled: B-2026-07-10-6 routes such programs to the tree-walk interpreter. The routing predicate was `program_declares_gpu_kernel`, an AST walk for a `#[gpu]` fn.

WHY THE PREDICATE MISSED. A reduction has no kernel. `gpu.sum(v)` names the OPERATION instead of taking a combiner, deliberately: a user-supplied fold would have to be associative for a tree reduction to mean anything and nothing in the language can check that, so naming the op moves the obligation to the compiler. The very property that makes the surface safe is what made it invisible to a gate that looks for `#[gpu]`. Every reduction program therefore took the JIT lane and died.

SEVERITY. High rather than medium: it is not a wrong answer but a total failure of the DEFAULT execution path for a whole feature family, and it shipped green because the test that exists to catch exactly this class was comparing the wrong two lanes.

fix:
FIXED by 6716341. Root cause was one step before the packer, which is why five plausible fixes downstream of it all failed. `coerce_enum_payload_scalar` coerces a variant argument to the width its variant DECLARES; seeded `enum Option[T] { Some(T) }` declares `T`, which lowers to the all-i64 generic base. That base is a placeholder, not a target, so the i128 was narrowed to i64 before `coerce_to_payload_words` ever ran. The coercion is now skipped when the declared payload type is the enum's own generic parameter — a concretely declared payload (the B-2026-08-13-18 class-mismatch case it exists for) still coerces.

With that removed the two halves are symmetric: `coerce_to_payload_words` splits a wider-than-a-word integer into little-endian words, and `reconstruct_payload_value` rejoins them. What tells the unpack the binding is 128 bits wide is `pattern_binding_types`, which had no entry at all — `method_callee_type_name`'s per-width list was missing its 128-bit arms, and its `_ => None` fallthrough made the omission invisible to the compiler.

Lifting the refusal made three further 128-bit defects reachable for the first time:
  - `checked_*` builds its `Option[Self]` inline via phis over i64 words, so a 128-bit result failed module verification ("PHI node operands are not the same type as the result"). It now routes through the same splitter the ordinary `Some(x)` path uses, so both producers of an `Option[i128]` emit the identical word pair.
  - `wrapping_*` carried a stale per-width allowlist omitting the 128-bit arms — "no method 'wrapping_mul' on type 'i128'" — though both backends already handled the width.
  - `saturating_*` was wrong in BOTH backends, differently. Codegen computed the signed bounds as `((1u128 << (bits - 1)) - 1) as u64`, whose cast truncates: at 128 bits SMAX came out `u64::MAX` and SMIN came out `0`. It now builds them by bit pattern (`all_ones >> 1`, then `+1`), correct at every width. The interpreter clamped by OPERATION (`sub` → MIN, else MAX) rather than by result sign, so an overflowing NEGATIVE product saturated to `i128::MAX`.

Plus one run-vs-build divergence: every UNSIGNED 128-bit overflow-family call fell through to a generic tail whose `(a as u64) as i128` truncates the operand to 64 bits, so `(2^100 as u128).checked_mul(2)` answered `0` in the interpreter and 2^101 compiled. It now reinterprets the carrier's bits as `u128`, the same trick the 64-bit-unsigned branch plays with i64/u64.

VERIFICATION. Byte-identical across all four surfaces — `karac build`, `karac build` with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, `karac run` (JIT), `karac run --interp` — on the seeded `Option`/`Result` (both arms), a user enum, a variant whose 128-bit field is followed by a 64-bit one (so the word cursor must advance by two), negatives, `u128`, arithmetic on the bound value, and `None`. Every asserted value is one a 64-bit answer gets wrong; 2^100 is used throughout because its low word is ZERO, which is what made the original bug print `0` rather than something visibly corrupt. Tests: `a_128bit_enum_payload_type_checks` (tests/typechecker.rs, replacing the refusal test), `e2e_128bit_enum_payload_round_trip` and `e2e_128bit_saturating_clamps_toward_the_result_sign` (tests/codegen.rs), and the interpreter twins `a_128bit_enum_payload_round_trips_in_the_interpreter` and `the_128bit_overflow_families_are_width_correct_in_the_interpreter` (tests/interpreter.rs). Gates: fmt, both clippy legs, default suite (106 targets), codegen 3074 and memory_sanitizer 1130 under KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1.

METHOD NOTE, since it reversed the outcome: five fixes read out of the code (word count, slot size, pack, unpack, match side) were all applied and all failed, and were reverted rather than shipped half-applied into machinery 3000+ codegen tests depend on. Tracing the actual IR found the real site in one step. Read the IR before reading more code.

REMAINDER, split out rather than buried here: the upper half of `u128` (values above `i128::MAX`) and `i128::MIN`'s literal magnitude are still unreachable, because the interpreter's value carrier is a signed `i128`. Codegen is unaffected. Filed as B-2026-08-19-23.
title: A 128-bit scalar cannot be carried in an ENUM PAYLOAD: an Option/Result payload word is 64 bits and `i128`/`u128` needs two, which the pack/unpack machinery has no case for. Refused loudly at type-check for now (`Option[i128]`, `Result[i128, E]`, and `checked_*` which returns `Option[Self]`); everything else about 128-bit works.
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-19-8 stage 5, which lifted the 128-bit rejection everywhere else. This is the one shape that could not go with it.

WHY IT IS REFUSED RATHER THAN LEFT: unchecked it MISCOMPILES SILENTLY. `Option[i128]` holding 2^100 read back as 0, because `coerce_to_payload_words` took the one-word scalar fast path and `coerce_to_i64` kept only the low half — and 2^100's low word is zero, so the wrong answer looked like a plausible one. That is precisely the defect class B-2026-08-19-6 was filed for, so it may not ship silently.

ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED, with the layers written down so the next attempt starts informed. A first cut fixed five sites and was STILL wrong, which is why it was backed out rather than pushed through — a half-applied change to payload machinery that 3000+ codegen tests depend on is worse than none. The layers found, in the order they surfaced:
  1. `llvm_type_word_count` returns 1 for EVERY `IntType`, so an i128 payload counted as one 64-bit word and took the scalar fast path.
  2. `payload_word_count_for_type_expr` lists the single-word primitives and has no 128-bit entry.
  3. `coerce_to_payload_words`'s scalar fallback pushes ONE word, so `out.len() == num_words` and neither the inline nor the oversize-boxing path notices the loss.
  4. `rebuild_value_from_payload_words` zero-extends word 0 alone (it already receives w0/w1/w2, so the fix is local).
  5. `reconstruct_payload_value`'s match-side binding does the same, and after fixing 1-4 the match arm STILL read 0 — so there is at least one more site, and the model of this path was incomplete. That is where it was stopped.
Boxing is NOT the shortcut it looks like: the unpack and drop sites recompute `llvm_type_word_count(T) > area` independently, and with area=3 for Option a 2-word payload is not oversized, so pack-side boxing would desynchronise from an inline-reading unpack.

SCOPE OF THE REFUSAL: `Option[i128]` / `Result[i128, E]` written as an annotation (caught in `lower_type_expr`), and `checked_*` on a 128-bit receiver (caught in `method_numeric.rs` — its `Option[Self]` is INFERRED, never written, so the annotation guard cannot see it; without that second guard the program reached codegen and failed module verification with a `phi i64` fed an i128, which is loud but is an internal LLVM message and a run-vs-build divergence, since the interpreter answers correctly). `saturating_*` / `overflowing_*` / `wrapping_*` return `Self` or a tuple and are unaffected.

COST OF THE GAP: design.md § method families promises all four on `i128`, and `checked_*` is the one that cannot ship. Its own note now records the exception. Deleting that note is what closing this row looks like.
tracker: src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs::coerce_to_payload_words; src/codegen/calls.rs::rebuild_value_from_payload_words; src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs::reconstruct_payload_value; src/codegen/declarations.rs::{llvm_type_word_count,payload_word_count_for_type_expr}; docs/spikes/oversized-enum-payload.md; the guards in src/typechecker/lowering.rs and src/typechecker/method_numeric.rs

fix:
FIXED by 9298b98.

(1) THE PRESENTATION SPLIT. Refusals now travel the interpreter's ordinary runtime-error channel (`record_runtime_error`): a span-carrying diagnostic with an error return trace, exit 1, matching `karac build`. Previously `karac run` printed `thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/interpreter/helpers.rs:491` plus a full Rust backtrace and exited 101 -- compiler internals surfacing for an ordinary empty-input mistake, and a different exit code for any harness keying on one.

(2) THE `stddev` MISLABEL, WHICH THIS ROW HAD BACKWARDS -- see the correction in `detail`. It was a codegen-only defect and therefore a THIRD divergence, not shared wrong text. `stats_variance` now takes the caller-facing name so `stddev` names itself.

ONE POLICY FUNCTION, NOT DUPLICATED GUARDS. `stats_trap_message` is now the single source of truth for which calls refuse and what they say, consulted once at the shared call site before dispatch. The f64 and i64 dispatchers are separate functions, and letting each carry its own copy of the message is exactly how the `stddev` half drifted into codegen in the first place. The in-dispatcher `panic!`s became `unreachable!` naming the missing pre-check, so a genuine internal-invariant violation (a future caller dispatching without pre-checking) stays loud while the user-facing panic is gone.

VERIFIED on both legs for all five functions and both element axes: identical messages, exit 1 on both, interpreter output carrying `at <file>:<line>:<col>`. Tests: 3 in tests/interpreter.rs (the five refusals as runtime errors, the i64 axis, the percentile range) and 1 codegen E2E pinning that `stddev` names itself rather than `variance`.
title: `Stats.*` empty-input refusals presented DIFFERENTLY on the two legs -- the interpreter raw-`panic!`ed (Rust backtrace, exit 101) where `karac build` emitted a clean Kara panic with a span (exit 1) -- across FIVE functions and both element axes; and `Stats.stddev([])` reported itself as `Stats.variance()` under `karac build` ONLY, so the two legs named different functions for one program.
detail:
FOUND 2026-08-19 while deciding what `gpu.mean` should do with an empty buffer — i.e. by consulting the existing precedent rather than by testing Stats itself. The DECISION the two legs make is identical and correct (refuse; do not invent a value), so this is a presentation divergence, not a wrong answer. It is still a run-vs-build divergence of the kind CLAUDE.md calls non-negotiable, and the interpreter's half also violates the standing rule that every phase emits structured diagnostics with source spans and never just panics.

MEASURED, all four on `let v: Vec[f64] = []`:

  Stats.mean(v)      interp: thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/interpreter/helpers.rs:473:17: Stats.mean() called on empty slice   (+ full Rust backtrace, exit 101)
                     build:  panic at s_mean.kara:3:27 in main: Stats.mean() called on empty slice                              (exit 1)
  Stats.median(v)    interp: helpers.rs:500 ; build: clean panic at the span
  Stats.variance(v)  interp: helpers.rs:482 ; build: clean panic at the span
  Stats.stddev(v)    interp: helpers.rs:491 ; build: clean panic at the span

TWO DEFECTS, ONE ROW because they are the same four call sites:

  1. THE PRESENTATION SPLIT. `eval_stats_fn` (`src/interpreter/helpers.rs`) uses `panic!` where the interpreter's runtime-error channel is what the AOT path effectively uses. A user comparing `karac run` to `karac build` on the same program sees a compiler-internals backtrace on one and a language-level diagnostic on the other, with different exit codes (101 vs 1) — so a test harness or CI script keying on the exit code will disagree about what happened.

  2. `stddev` MISLABELS ITSELF as `variance`, on BOTH legs (so this half is not a divergence, just wrong text). `stddev` is implemented as the sqrt of `variance` and inherits its guard's message, which sends the reader to the wrong function name.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. The empty-slice guard is the one place these functions talk to the user, and it is the case a caller is most likely to hit from real data. It is also the precedent anyone reaching for 'what should my new reduction do on empty?' will read — as this session did. A precedent that behaves differently depending on which backend you happen to be running is a poor one to copy.

SHAPE OF THE FIX (not attempted, out of scope for the slice that found it): route the four guards in `eval_stats_fn` through the interpreter's `record_runtime_error` (span-carrying) instead of `panic!`. `eval_stats_fn` is a free helper, so it may need the error channel threaded in or the guards hoisted to the calling arm in `eval_call.rs` — check which is smaller before committing to one. Give `stddev` its own message while there.

title: Set/SortedSet `contains` and `remove`, and both `binary_search` arms, REJECTED a borrowed needle — `s.contains(w)` for a `w: ref String` failed with "expected 'String', found 'ref String'" against a spec that reads `val: ref T`
detail:
Found writing kata #288 (Unique Word Abbreviation), whose counts-indexed solver asks `idx.words.contains(word)` for a `word: ref String` — the natural phrasing, and the one design.md's Set table sanctions: `fn contains(ref self, val: ref T) -> bool` (line 1744), with `remove` at 1743 and `binary_search`'s `needle: ref T` at 3165 saying the same. 

THIS IS THE MISSED-SIBLING HALF OF B-2026-08-15-22. That bug established the rule and the fix for `Vec`/`VecDeque`'s `contains`: a probe SCANS for its needle and never keeps it, so a borrowed needle is exactly as usable as an owned one, and the assignability comparison must peel `Ref`/`MutRef` first. The fix was inlined at the two arms it was reported against. Every other probe in the stdlib kept comparing the raw type. 

SCOPE, measured with a probe matrix rather than assumed from the one failing call: `Vec.contains`, `VecDeque.contains`, `Map.contains_key`, `SortedMap.contains_key` and `Map.get` already accepted a ref; `Set.contains`, `SortedSet.contains`, `Set.remove`, `SortedSet.remove`, `Vec.binary_search` and `Slice.binary_search` all rejected one. Six sites, each contradicting its own written signature. 

CAUSE IS STRUCTURAL, which is why the earlier fix did not reach them: the set arms group `"contains" | "insert" | "remove"` into a single match arm, so the two probes inherited `insert`'s ownership requirement. `insert` genuinely does store its argument — design.md gives it `val: T`, owned — so the grouping had to be SPLIT rather than patched, and a fix that simply peeled for the whole arm would have wrongly let `Set.insert(borrowed)` through.
fix:
Named the rule once as `peel_probe_ref` in `src/typechecker.rs` instead of inlining the peel a fifth time, with the owning-vs-probing distinction written down — that distinction IS the rule, and re-deriving it per site is how the first six sites were missed. Split `"contains" | "remove"` out of the `insert` arm in both `stdlib_map.rs` set arms (hashed and sorted) and applied the peel there; applied it to both `binary_search` arms in `stdlib_seq.rs`. The peel is for the ASSIGNABILITY comparison only — the three numeric coercion checks keep the raw type, so a borrowed numeric needle behaves exactly as before and no coercion is recorded against a reference. 

VERIFIED: all six sites accept a ref; `Vec.contains`/`Map.contains_key` unchanged; `Set.insert(ref)` and `SortedSet.insert(ref)` still correctly REJECT, so the ownership requirement survives where the spec really asks for it. The B-2026-08-14-1 narrowing guards on the same arms still fire (`Set[u8]` + a `300i64` VARIABLE is still rejected for contains, insert and remove alike) — note the guard probe must use a variable, not a literal, as that test's own doc-comment warns, since a literal is range-checked by a different path.

title: REFUTED: `String` DOES have indexed character access -- `s.char_at(i) -> Option[char]`, specced at design.md:4541 and implemented across all three backends, and the `s[i]` diagnostic names it directly. The allocation-free spelling the row asks for already exists; and rewriting the repo's own #288 benchmark to use it measured NO speedup (0.25s both ways), so the performance rationale does not reproduce either.
detail:
Kata #288 abbreviates a word as first-letter + middle-length + last-letter. Every mirror language spells that in constant time — Python `w[0]`/`w[-1]`, Rust `w.as_bytes()[0]`, Go `w[0]`/`w[len(w)-1]`, C `w[0]`/`w[n-1]`. Kara's String table (design.md line 1806) offers `len`, `push_char`, `push_str`, `chars`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `trim`, `split`, `replace`, case conversion and `+` — no indexed access and no `first`/`last` char. The natural Kara phrasing is therefore `let cs: Vec[char] = w.chars().collect();` followed by `cs[0]` / `cs[n-1]`, which allocates a whole Vec[char] to read two characters. 

COST, measured on the #288 bench (3000-word dictionary, 1M is_unique punches, container x86_64): the `collect()` phrasing runs 274.6 ms +/- 15.6; the same program with `abbrev` rewritten to walk `chars()` once tracking first/last in flight, allocating nothing, runs 212.0 ms +/- 26.5 — a 1.30x +/- 0.18 speedup from deleting the allocation alone. 

NOT THE WHOLE STORY, stated explicitly so the number is not over-read: Kara is 2.76x slower than Go on this workload, and removing the allocation closes only part of that. The remaining ~2x is undiagnosed — plausibly String hashing and the per-query abbreviation String construction, but that has NOT been measured and should not be assumed. 

Note the UTF-8 caveat that makes this a design question rather than an oversight: byte indexing is O(1) but not character indexing, and `chars()` is the only currently-correct answer for non-ASCII. A `first_char`/`last_char` pair returning `Option[char]` would be O(1) and O(1)-from-the-end on UTF-8 respectively, and would cover this case without promising general indexed access.
fix:
CLOSED AS INVALID -- the premise was refuted by running the compiler, and the proposed remedy was then measured and did not help.

WHAT THE ROW CLAIMS: "no indexed access and no first/last char", so "the natural Kara phrasing is therefore `let cs: Vec[char] = w.chars().collect();` followed by `cs[0]` / `cs[n-1]`, which allocates a whole Vec[char] to read two characters."

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. `s.char_at(i) -> Option[char]` — specced at design.md:4541 ("the i-th Unicode scalar value. O(n); no panic on out-of-bounds"), listed in `STRING_BUILTIN_METHODS`, implemented in the typechecker (`stdlib_seq.rs`), the interpreter (`method_call_seq.rs`) and codegen (`vec_method.rs`, via `karac_runtime_string_char_at`). The `s[0]` compile error names it in its own help text: "use s.char_at(i) for the i-th character (O(n)) — it returns Option[char]". Verified running: `w.char_at(0)` and `w.char_at(w.char_count() - 1)` on "hello" print `h` and `o`.

The row's String inventory is drawn from a design.md table it cites as line 1806 — which is a BLANK LINE in the current file. It reads the spec, and an outdated part of it, rather than the compiler; `char_at` appears five times in design.md today and `char_count` once.

THE PERFORMANCE RATIONALE DOES NOT REPRODUCE VIA `char_at`. Rewriting `bench/uniqueabbr.kara`'s `abbrev` to `char_count()` + two `char_at` calls — allocation-free, byte-identical output — measured 0.25s before and 0.25s after (best of 5, container x86_64). No speedup. The kata change was therefore REVERTED rather than committed: trading readable `cs[0]` / `cs[n-1]` for two `match` arms is a real cost in a corpus whose job is to stay idiomatic, and it buys nothing measurable here.

A CAUTION ABOUT ONE OF MY OWN NUMBERS. A first microbenchmark — 400k calls of `abbrev` on one 20-char string — showed `char_at` 18x faster than `chars().collect()` (0.36s vs 0.02s). That number is an ARTIFACT and must not be quoted: hammering one short string makes the per-call `Vec[char]` allocation the entire workload, which is not what the kata does (build a 3000-word dictionary once, then punch it 1M times). The real benchmark is the honest measurement, and it says 1.00x.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is narrower than the row: there is no O(1) LAST character. `char_at(n-1)` walks, and `char_count()` walks again, so "last char" is two O(n) passes where UTF-8 permits O(1) (step back over continuation bytes). The row's own suggestion — `first_char`/`last_char` returning `Option[char]` — remains the right shape IF someone wants it. It is deliberately NOT filed as open work: the only motivation on record is this row's performance argument, and that argument did not survive measurement. Anyone reaching for it should produce a workload where the walk actually costs, first.

ALSO NOT REPRODUCED, and left alone: the row reports Kara 2.76x slower than Go on this kata with "~2x undiagnosed". Nothing here touches that, and it remains unexplained.

title: The UPPER HALF of `u128` (values above `i128::MAX`) is unreachable end-to-end: the interpreter's value carrier is a signed `i128`, so such a value is stored as a negative bit pattern. `340282366920938463463374607431768211455u128` is REJECTED at parse; a value reached by arithmetic (`0u128.wrapping_sub(1u128)`) prints `-1` under `karac run --interp` while `karac build` prints the correct 3.4e38 — a run-vs-build divergence. `-170141183460469231731687303715884105728i128` (i128::MIN) is rejected for the same reason: its magnitude `2^127` exceeds `i128::MAX`.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-19-19's enum-payload fix across the full 128-bit surface; split out rather than folded in because it is not a payload defect — it reproduces on a plain `let`.

CODEGEN IS CORRECT AND UNAFFECTED. It lowers to LLVM's real `i128` and picks unsigned ops from the static type, so every u128 value including the upper half compiles and prints correctly. The gap is entirely on the interpreter/front-end side, which is why it presents as run-vs-build.

FOUR SYMPTOMS, ONE CAUSE (`Value::Int(i128)` is signed):
  1. PARSE. `parser/exprs.rs`'s `IntegerOutOfRange` arm does `i128::try_from(m)` for a 128-bit suffix; a u128 above `i128::MAX` fails it and falls through to the i64 error message, which is also misleading (it suggests a `u64` suffix for a value that needs u128).
  2. `i128::MIN`'s LITERAL. `-170141183460469231731687303715884105728i128` lexes as a positive magnitude `2^127` under a unary minus. `2^127 > i128::MAX`, so it is rejected before the minus is folded. The i64 sibling (`-9223372036854775808`) has a dedicated fold at `parse_prefix`; the 128-bit case needs the same shape.
  3. DISPLAY. `span_type_is_unsigned64` — the predicate that selects the unsigned reading — matches `U64`/`Usize` only, so an upper-half u128 renders with its signed reading (`-1` for `u128::MAX`).
  4. RANGE CHECK. `span_int_bounds` gives `U128` a ceiling of `i128::MAX` rather than `u128::MAX`, with a comment saying exactly why.

NOT FIXED BY WIDENING THE BOUND. The ceiling in (4) is a consequence, not the defect: raising it to `u128::MAX` cannot help while the carrier cannot hold the value. The real fix is for the carrier to carry signedness — either a `Value::UInt(u128)` sibling or a signedness tag on `Value::Int` — after which (1), (3) and (4) follow from it and (2) is an independent parser fold.

WHAT DOES WORK, so the scope is clear: every u128 value at or below `i128::MAX` is fully correct on all four surfaces (verified in B-2026-08-19-19's commit — arithmetic, `checked_*`/`wrapping_*`/`saturating_*`/`overflowing_*`, enum payloads, printing). The 128-bit overflow families were separately made bit-exact for unsigned in that commit, so the ARITHMETIC on upper-half values is already right; it is the literal and the rendering that are not.

WHY MEDIUM, NOT HIGH: it is loud at the literal (a parse error, not silent), and the arithmetic-reached case is a `karac run --interp` display divergence rather than a wrong compiled answer. Nothing miscompiles.

CORRECTION (2026-08-19, from B-2026-08-19-27's work): this row widened three sibling "which widths may appear here" lists to the 128-bit pair and MISSED a fourth — `display_field_is_leaf` in src/codegen/synth_display.rs, which gates the field types a `#[derive(Display)]` struct may carry. A `u128` field therefore still refused to compile ("whose Display is not yet supported under `karac build`") even though `emit_display_fn_for_type` behind it had already gained its 128-bit arm here. Fixed in d888846. The lesson for the next such sweep: grep the whole `"u8" | "u16" | "u32" | "u64"` family and check each hit individually — this class of list is duplicated across codegen, and the four sites found here were not all of them.
fix:
FIXED by d0b8bdf. The row's own hypothesis — "the carrier must grow an unsigned half" — was wrong, and measuring first is what showed it. The carrier model was already right: an unsigned value is held as its two's-complement bit pattern, sign-extended into the signed carrier, which is how `u64` past `i64::MAX` has always ridden a signed `i64`. What was missing is that every CONSUMER of that model had 64 baked in, from the era when `u64` was the only unsigned width whose top half did not fit. No new variant, no carrier change.

FRONT END. The literal could not be written: a `u128` magnitude in `(i128::MAX, u128::MAX]` had no positive form, and `i128::MIN`'s magnitude `2^127` is one past `i128::MAX` so `Neg(Integer(n))` could not carry it either. The `u128` band now takes the wrapped bit pattern the 64-bit band has always used; `i128::MIN` gets the unary-minus fold `i64::MIN` has had since B-2026-08-06-13. The out-of-range message for a 128-bit suffix no longer advises adding a `u64` suffix.

Range-checking that literal needed a SEAM, not a wider bound: no `(min, max)` pair of `i128` can express `u128`, so raising the ceiling was never going to work. `check_int_literal_fits` now takes the literal's own suffix; a `u128`-suffixed literal is accepted on the strength of the lexer having parsed its magnitude with `u128::from_str_radix`, while a genuine negative — which never carries the suffix, because a unary minus makes it `Neg(Integer(n))` — still has to clear `min`. `-1u128`, `-1i128` and `let x: u128 = -1` are rejected exactly as before, asserted by `a_negative_still_cannot_initialize_u128`.

INTERPRETER. The bool `span_type_is_unsigned64` became `span_unsigned_int_width` returning `Some(64)` / `Some(128)` / `None`, and every one of its ~17 consumers now dispatches on the width: the ordered comparisons, division, remainder, `>>`, the add/sub/mul overflow boundary (a new `eval_binary_u128` mirroring `eval_binary_u64`), `to_string` / `println` / f-strings, and the `sort` / `min` / `max` comparators for `Vec`, `Column` and `Tensor`. The 64-bit-only predicate was DELETED rather than kept alongside, so the assumption cannot quietly return. Before this: `2e38 > 5` answered false, `2e38 / 3` trapped as "integer overflow", `u128::MAX` printed `-1`, and a `Vec[u128]` sorted its largest elements first.

CODEGEN needed four fixes, three of them 128-bit gaps rather than signedness ones, and all found by running the probe rather than by reading:
  - `type_to_type_expr` had no 128-bit arms, so a 128-bit type round-tripped as `TypeKind::Error`. That is why `println(o)` on an `Option[i128]` was refused with "bind a struct literal to a `let` first" — about a plain variable. Found by instrumenting the display registration after five minutes of reading the display lists had produced nothing; the trace printed `pte=Error` immediately.
  - `emit_display_fn_for_type` had no 128-bit arm and PANICKED the compiler ("type_name 'u128' not yet supported") on `println` of a `Vec[u128]`.
  - `rebuild_value_from_payload_words` zero-extended word 0 for anything wider than a word, keeping the LOW half — the same defect B-2026-08-19-19 fixed in the sibling match-arm reconstruction, here in the Display reconstruction. 2^100's low word is zero, so it would have rendered `Some(0)`.
  - the `Vec` sort thunk, the `karac_sortcmp_<T>` family and the element-comparison helper listed the unsigned widths by name without `u128`.

Also fixed here because it is the same hardcoded 64: `span_int_width` had no 128-bit arms, so `1i128 << 100` was rejected against a 64-bit bound, and `shift_at_width` computed on a `u64` carrier where a 128-bit result cannot exist.

REGRESSION CAUGHT AND FIXED IN FLIGHT. Widening `truncate_to_width` to a 128-bit carrier silently changed how a `u64` at or above 2^63 is encoded (zero-extended positive instead of wrapped negative), and the existing `test_interp_u64_*` tests caught it via the `narrow_to_i64` hard check. That encoding is load-bearing — `eval_binary_u64`, `literal_as_i128` and the `%llu` display path all assume the wrapped form — so the 64-bit arm is now explicit and every width below 128 behaves as it did. Worth remembering: widening a carrier helper is not a no-op for the widths it already served.

VERIFICATION. Byte-identical across `karac build`, that build with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, `karac run` (JIT) and `karac run --interp`, over display, comparison, div/rem, shift, arithmetic, bit ops, the overflow-aware method families, enum payloads, casts, struct fields, function parameters and returns, `Vec` elements, sorting, and both literal boundaries. Every asserted literal is above `i128::MAX`, where a signed reading flips the SIGN rather than merely losing precision — `u128::MAX` reads as `-1`. Tests: `the_128bit_literal_boundaries_are_writable` and `a_negative_still_cannot_initialize_u128` (tests/typechecker.rs); `the_upper_half_of_u128_is_correct_in_the_interpreter`, `a_u128_vec_sorts_by_magnitude` and `shifts_run_at_the_values_own_width` (tests/interpreter.rs); `e2e_upper_half_of_u128_end_to_end`, `e2e_128bit_shift_amounts_reach_the_full_width` and `e2e_128bit_display_inside_containers_and_payloads` (tests/codegen.rs). Gates: fmt, both clippy legs, default suite (106 targets), codegen 3079 and memory_sanitizer 1130 under KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1.

SPLIT OUT, both found by this row's measurement and neither belonging to it: B-2026-08-19-26 (a shift takes its width and signedness from the AMOUNT — a silent miscompile on plain `i64`, fixed in bb3eeb7) and B-2026-08-19-27 (the interpreter's `display_render` renders a nested unsigned value signed; reproduces identically on `u64`, so it predates 128-bit entirely).
tracker: src/parser/exprs.rs::parse_prefix (the i64::MIN unary-minus fold, which the 128-bit case needs a sibling of); src/parser/exprs.rs IntegerOutOfRange arm (`i128::try_from(m)`); src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs::type_is_unsigned64; src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs::span_int_bounds (the U128 ceiling and its comment); src/interpreter/value.rs::Value::Int
