fix:
FIXED by 1464a6f. The range-index arm of `infer_expr` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) stamped every `v[a..b]` `Slice { mutable: false }` unconditionally. It now upgrades to `mut Slice[T]` when the parameter is a mutating slot and the base admits it.

BASE ADMISSIBILITY IS ASKED WITH `types_compatible` AGAINST THE VERY SLOT TYPE THE UPGRADE PRODUCES, rather than by re-listing the sources the coercion table already lists. That is the same predicate the argument is checked against a moment later, so the upgrade cannot admit anything the assignability table would reject and the two cannot drift apart: a `ref Vec[T]` base and a read-only `Slice[T]` base both decline, and still report the read-only type they actually have.

KEYED ON THE PARAMETER, NOT ON THE CALL-SITE `mut` MARKER, even though the marker is what the spec line writes. The marker rule is a free-function rule (design.md Feature 4 Part 1½ -- "method calls never mark"), so keying the upgrade on the marker would have left a METHOD taking `mut Slice[T]` in exactly this dead end with no legal spelling at all. Marker discipline stays where it already lives, in `check_call_site_marker`.

THAT REQUIRED NARROWING `is_arg_forwarded` (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs), and this is the half that is easy to miss. Its arm (A) asks whether the argument's own type is already `mut ref T` / `mut Slice[T]`; with the upgrade in place it read the type the upgrade had just minted and concluded the argument arrived already-mutable. The first build therefore answered the spec's own line with "this argument is already a mut-ref; drop the `mut` marker" -- and dropping it made the sub-range read-only again, an unbroken loop. A RANGE INDEX is now exempt from arm (A) specifically: its mut-ness is a borrow taken AT this call boundary, so the argument is fresh and the marker rule applies to it exactly as to a bare `mut v`. Arm (B), the place-root walk, still sees through the index, so a genuinely forwarded sub-range (`s[1..2]` over a `mut Slice[T]` binding) still needs no marker -- and still refuses a redundant one.

MEASURED, byte-identical across interp / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT. The spec line itself: `sort_in_place(mut v[1..4])` over `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]` gives `3 1 1 4 5`. Offset: `poke(mut w[2..4])` writing index 0 lands on `w[2]` (`1 2 99 4`). Array base: `poke(mut a[1..3])` gives `1 99 3 4`. Forwarded two frames down: `middle(mut v[1..5])` then `poke(s[1..3])` writes `v[2]`. The untouched endpoints are the assertion that matters -- a header built over a COPY, or at the wrong offset, would still print plausible-looking numbers.

REJECTIONS ALL HOLD, each with its specific diagnostic rather than a blunt fallback: unmarked `bump(v[1..3])` gets the marker diagnostic ("requires a `mut` marker"), a `ref Vec[T]` base and a read-only `Slice[T]` base get "expected 'mut Slice[i64]', found 'Slice[i64]'", a marked forward gets "already a mut-ref; drop the marker", and `sum(v[1..3])` is unchanged.

Pinned by eight tests in tests/typechecker.rs (`test_mut_slice_accepts_a_marked_sub_range` and siblings -- the three accepting ones fail without the fix; the marker test additionally asserts the redundant-marker message is ABSENT, which is what makes it guard the `is_arg_forwarded` half rather than just the type) and two E2E in tests/codegen.rs (`test_e2e_mut_sub_range_slice_writes_through_to_the_backing_buffer`, `test_e2e_mut_sub_range_of_a_mut_slice_forwards`).
title: A MUTABLE SUB-RANGE slice cannot be formed at a call site -- design.md § Slices' own second example is rejected. The spec's block reads `sort_in_place(mut v);` then `sort_in_place(mut v[1..4]);  // sub-range mutable slice`. The first works on all three backends; the second fails `karac check` with `expected 'mut Slice[i64]', found 'Slice[i64]'`, so a range-indexed argument produces a READ-ONLY slice header even under a `mut` marker. There is no alternative spelling: `let s = mut v[1..4];` is `error[parse]: 'mut' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier`. The read-only half of the same feature is fine -- `sum(v[1..3])` gives 5 on interp and JIT alike.
detail:
Probe: domain-22 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d22/{sl1,sl2,sl2b,sl3,sl4,st5}.kara.

EVERYTHING AROUND IT WORKS, which is what makes this a narrow gap rather than a missing feature area. Whole-collection mutable coercion: `sort_in_place(mut v)` sorts in place on both backends. `split_at_mut` -- the spec's "foundational primitive for safe parallel writes into a shared buffer" -- is correct: `let mut halves = v.split_at_mut(2); halves.0[0] = 90; halves.1[0] = 91;` yields 90 and 91 in the backing array. `Slice[T]` is implicitly Copy as specified (passing the same slice to two calls leaves the binding live, and `.len()` still answers afterwards). Every read-only coercion in the § Slices example block is right: `Vec[T]` -> 10, `Array[T, N]` -> 60, sub-range -> 5, `.as_slice()` -> 10.

SO THE MISSING PIECE IS EXACTLY ONE EDGE: range-index in argument position under a `mut` marker must synthesize a `mut Slice[T]` header rather than a shared one. The spec calls this shape out explicitly in the coercion paragraph -- "`ref mut Vec[T]` and `ref mut Array[T, N]` coerce to `mut Slice[T]` at call boundaries" -- and the sub-range case is the example line under it.

FOLLOW-ON SPLIT OUT: B-2026-08-21-7 -- a call-site `mut` marker bypasses the `let mut` requirement entirely, so `bump(mut x)` mutates a binding declared without `mut` while `x = x + 1` on that same binding is correctly refused. Pre-existing and independent of this fix (its repros are whole-collection and scalar forms that predate it): local mutability is an OWNERSHIP-phase rule and the call-argument path never asks it. This fix inherits the hole symmetrically rather than widening it -- `touch(mut v[1..3])` over a non-`mut` `v` is now accepted exactly as `touch(mut v)` already was, and both should start being refused by the same check.

fix:
FIXED by 537a237. `last` now takes an optional end-relative index on every sequence receiver -- `Vec`, `Slice` and `Array` -- across typecheck, the interpreter, and both codegen paths.

WHAT THE SPEC ASKED FOR AND WHAT SHIPPED. design.md § Numeric Semantics rules out Python-style wrap-around (`-1` as an index is always a bug, and panics) and names the replacement in the same breath: "For end-relative access, use `.last(n)` where `n` defaults to 0". The no-argument half shipped; the argument half did not. The diagnostic made it worse by stating the shipped half as the intended surface -- `Vec.last() takes no arguments` reads like a rule rather than a gap.

ONE DEVIATION FROM THE SPEC SENTENCE, DELIBERATE AND NOW WRITTEN INTO IT. That paragraph ends "Negative or out-of-bounds `n` panics", and this returns `None` instead. The panic clause reads `last(n)` as an INDEXING form, but the shipped `last()` is on the other side of the very split the paragraph draws: `v[i]` panics (measured: both `v[-1]` and `v[9]` panic), while `v.get(i)`, `v.first()` and `v.last()` return `Option` (measured: `v.get(9)` -> None, `v.last()` on an empty Vec -> None). Since `n` DEFAULTS TO 0, honouring the panic clause literally would make `v.last()` on an empty sequence panic where it has always returned `None` -- breaking a working API and splitting `last` from `first`, which returns `Option` too. The Option contract is the only reading under which `last()` and `last(0)` can agree, so that is what landed, and design.md's sentence has been corrected to state it (with a parenthetical recording what it used to say, so the change is not silent).

CODEGEN IS WHERE THE REAL RISK WAS, and the E2E test exists because of it: the first build ACCEPTED `v.last(2)`, type-checked it, and returned the last element on every call while the interpreter walked back correctly -- a silent run-vs-build divergence that only differing element values expose. Two separate lowerings had to learn the offset, because `Vec`/`Slice` share a length-driven arm while `Array` indexes a static length through its own. The Array arm needs no range test of its own: `(n - 1) - k` against an UNSIGNED bounds compare rejects both directions for free, since `k >= n` wraps the subtraction to a huge unsigned value and `k < 0` pushes the index past `n - 1`.

The argument is evaluated BEFORE the branch in the Vec/Slice arm, unconditionally, so a side-effecting `n` runs exactly once on every path including the empty receiver -- sinking it into the taken branch would have made the effect depend on the length.

MEASURED on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT), byte-identical: `v.last()`/`last(0)`/`last(1)`/`last(2)` over `[10,20,30]` -> 30/30/20/10; `last(3)` and `last(-1)` -> None; the same sweep on a `Slice` and on an `Array[i64,3]`; an empty `Vec` -> None at every arity; a RUNTIME `n` driven by a loop counter that walks off the front; and a `String` element, whose multi-word Option payload rides the same path.

Pinned by five tests, all failing without the fix: `last_accepts_an_optional_end_relative_index`, `last_rejects_two_args_and_a_non_integer_index`, and `first_still_takes_no_arguments` (tests/typechecker.rs -- the last of these because `first` and `last` were ONE match arm before this change, so splitting them could have widened both), plus `test_e2e_last_takes_an_end_relative_index` and `test_e2e_last_end_relative_carries_a_heap_element` (tests/codegen.rs).

SCOPED TO SEQUENCES. `Iterator.last()` keeps its no-argument arity: an iterator has no random access, so an end-relative index would mean buffering the tail, which is a different feature and not what the spec paragraph is about (it is written about ARRAY INDEXING).
title: `v.last(n)` -- the END-RELATIVE ACCESS design.md prescribes as THE replacement for negative indexing -- takes no argument: `v.last(1)` is rejected with `Vec.last() takes no arguments`. § Numeric Semantics, in the same breath as ruling out Python-style wrap-around: "Negative indices are out-of-bounds errors — they panic at runtime... No Python-style wrap-around; `-1` as an index is always a bug. FOR END-RELATIVE ACCESS, USE `.last(n)` WHERE `n` DEFAULTS TO 0: `v.last()` returns the last element, `v.last(1)` the second-to-last, etc. Negative or out-of-bounds `n` panics." So the spec closes one door and points at another that is not there -- `v.last()` works, `v.last(1)` does not, and the diagnostic states the no-argument form as though it were the intended surface rather than an unimplemented half.
detail:
Probe: domain-22 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d22/nu3.kara. Diagnostic source: src/typechecker/stdlib_iter.rs:655 ("Iterator.last() takes no arguments"; reported against a Vec receiver as "Vec.last()").

CONTEXT -- THE REST OF § Numeric Semantics IS EXEMPLARY, which is why this one stands out. Measured correct on both backends: truncated division (`-7/2 == -3`, `7/-2 == -3`, `-7/-2 == 3`), modulo taking the dividend's sign (`-7%2 == -1`, `7%-2 == 1`, `-7%-2 == -1`), `div_euclid`/`rem_euclid` (-4 and 1), arithmetic right shift on signed (`(-8i32) >> 1 == -4`), unsigned comparison (`0xFFFFFFFFu32 < 1u32 == false`), all four overflow families on `i64.MAX` (checked -> None, wrapping -> i64.MIN, saturating -> i64.MAX, overflowing -> (i64.MIN, true)), `iN::MIN / -1` trapping as "integer overflow", division by zero as its own distinct "division by zero" message, `<< 32` on an i32 as "shift amount out of range", and the full float-literal grammar including underscores in mantissa and exponent (`1_000.000_5`, `1e1_000`, `2.5E+6_f32`).

fix:
FIXED by bc2a768. Codegen's index dispatch gained a `Slice` sibling to the inline-temp `Vec` arm it already had -- `inline_index_recv_slice_te` + `compile_inline_temp_slice_index` in `src/codegen/collections.rs`, dispatched immediately after the Vec arm. The identifier-keyed slice path fires only for a NAMED binding, so the `{ptr, len}` header a slice-producing expression evaluates to fell through to the generic tail, which handles only `ArrayType` / `VectorType` -- hence "Index operator applied to non-array type". The new arm materializes the header into a synth slice local, registers it through the same `register_var_from_type_expr` every other synth-binding arm uses, and recurses, so `compile_slice_index` lowers the read (bounds check included) unchanged.

Its own arm rather than a widening of the Vec one, because the two differ in both layout and ownership: a slice is a 16-byte `{ptr,len}` with no `cap` word to read, and it is ALWAYS a borrow -- so nothing is dropped and no element is deep-cloned. Dropping here would free the receiver's buffer out from under the live binding that owns it.

The element type comes from `slice_elem_type_expr_from_rhs`, the SAME resolver the `let b = s.bytes()` binding path uses. That makes the two-step spelling -- which always worked -- the oracle rather than a second implementation: `s.bytes()[i]` and `let b = s.bytes(); b[i]` now read the same byte by construction.

Measured on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT), byte-identical: `s.bytes()[1]` -> 101, the same index inside an f-string -> 111, accumulated over a while loop -> 532, `v.as_slice()[2]` -> 30, `c"abc".as_bytes()[2]` -> 99, a field-rooted receiver `w.s.bytes()[3]` -> 108, and a heap element `hs.as_slice()[1]` -> "cd". An out-of-range index panics on every backend rather than reading past the storage.

Pinned by `test_e2e_index_slice_temporary_matches_the_bound_spelling` and `test_e2e_index_slice_temporary_bounds_checked` (tests/codegen.rs) and `asan_index_into_slice_temporary_frees_nothing` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs -- LSan-clean over 60 iterations of a heap-element read, pinning the frees-nothing choice from both sides). All three fail without the fix.

`s.bytes()[a..b]` never reaches the new arm and is unchanged: a range slice of a temporary escapes its statement and the ownership checker rejects it upstream with "bind the receiver to a local first".
title: `s.bytes()[i]` -- the byte-access form design.md documents for protocol and binary-format parsing -- is check-clean and interp-correct but has NO CODEGEN: `karac run` and `karac build` both die with `codegen failed: Index operator applied to non-array type`. § Strings, Internal representation bullets: "Byte access: `s.bytes()[i]` returns `u8`, panics on out-of-bounds (same as any slice). Use for protocol/binary format parsing, not text processing." Measured on `let s = "hello"; println(f"byte0 = {s.bytes()[0]}")`: `karac check` -> All checks passed; `karac run --interp` -> byte0 = 104; `karac run` and `karac build` -> the codegen failure above. So the documented binary-parsing primitive is available only under the interpreter, which is now the opt-in backend.
detail:
Probe: domain-22 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d22/sx1.kara.

LOUD, NOT SILENT -- the build fails with a diagnostic rather than miscompiling, so there is no wrong-answer risk; the cost is that a spec-documented API is unreachable from both compiled backends after a clean check.

THE REST OF THE § Strings API SURFACE IS CORRECT on all three backends, which bounds this to the index form: byte length vs codepoint count on a multi-byte string (`"héllo"` -> len 6, char_count 5), `char_at(1)` -> 'é', `char_at(99)` -> None with no panic, `s[i]` correctly a COMPILE error carrying the O(n)-scan rationale the spec gives for it, saturating `substring` bounds (out-of-range start -> empty, end past length -> clamped), the codepoint-boundary panic for a cut inside a multi-byte character, and the whole `StringSlice` borrowed-view example (`find` + `slice` + `.to_string()`) verbatim from the spec.

SMALL PARITY NIT, not worth its own row: the boundary-panic message differs between backends -- interp says "end byte index 2 is not a UTF-8 codepoint boundary in a 6-byte string", the JIT drops the two numbers.

FOLLOW-ONS SPLIT OUT rather than folded in, because both are distinct root causes with their own failure modes:

- B-2026-08-21-4 -- a free function DECLARED to return `Slice[T]` produces a garbage header at the return boundary (`pick(v).len()` prints a pointer-sized number instead of 3). A Call arm for the two element-type resolvers was written, MEASURED, and reverted here: with the element type visible, `pick(v)[2]` returned 3 instead of 30 and the bound spelling printed garbage -- so registering the type converts a loud failure into a silent one. The value crossing the return is already wrong; that has to be fixed first.

- B-2026-08-21-5 -- `c.len()` on a `ref CStr` PARAM panics codegen through an inkwell unwrap. Found while probing the `as_bytes` receiver shapes here; the literal receiver (`c"abc".as_bytes()[1]`) is correct on every backend.

fix:
FIXED by 410d6f5 — IMPLEMENTED, on the owner's call, rather than narrowing the sentence. `String.normalize(form)` and the `NormalizationForm` prelude enum now exist, so the remedy the Equality bullet names is real on every surface.

THE ROW LEFT THE CHOICE OPEN BECAUSE IT COSTED IT AS "pulls in Unicode tables (a real dependency decision)". Measured, it is much cheaper than that reads:

  crate                          stripped fat-LTO staticlib   already in a graph?
  icu_normalizer 2.2             +99 KB                       YES — `karac` already
                                                              has it via
                                                              ureq -> url -> idna ->
                                                              idna_adapter
  unicode-normalization 0.1.25   +136 KB                      no

So the INTERPRETER half cost zero new crates — naming `icu_normalizer` directly only pins a version. The AOT half is an eighth OPT-IN archive (`libkarac_runtime_unicode.a`, +161 KiB on the archive), auto-selected only when the emitted object references `karac_unicode_*`, exactly like `gpu` / `regex` / `arrow`; nothing else links the tables. Both halves link the SAME crate and version, which is what makes interpreter and codegen byte-identical by construction rather than by convention — the Arrow IPC twin's rule.

THE SPEC'S SPELLING WAS NOT EXPRESSIBLE, which this row did not catch and which no amount of implementing could have satisfied as written. `s.normalize(NFC)` violates design.md's OWN naming rule CN-4 (acronyms as words: `HttpClient` not `HTTPClient`, `IoError` not `IOError`), and the identifier-class check enforces CN-4 — an all-caps enum variant is a hard parse error in the baked stdlib and in user code alike. The bullet named an API that could not have been declared in the language it documents. Corrected to `s.normalize(Nfc)`, with the four variants `Nfc` / `Nfd` / `Nfkc` / `Nfkd` visible unqualified like `Ordering`'s `Less` and `MemoryOrdering`'s `Relaxed`.

TWO CODEGEN DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED ON THE WAY, both discovered by verifying the four surfaces rather than by reading:

1. BAKED-STDLIB ENUM VARIANTS LOWERED THEIR TAG TO 0, SILENTLY. `declare_enums` walks only the user's `program.items`, so a `STDLIB_PROGRAMS` enum absent from user source had no layout and every variant expression compiled to the FIRST variant with no diagnostic. Measured: `let f = Nfd; s.normalize(f)` normalized as `Nfc` — AOT answered 2 where `--interp` answered 3. Fixed by seeding the layout, and the fifteen hand-rolled seeds already in `declarations.rs` (Ordering, VarError, SeekFrom, …) gained a `seed_unit_enum` helper so a sixteenth cannot repeat the four-map transcription by hand. Pinned by `normalize_form_reaches_codegen_bare_qualified_and_bound`, which fails with the seed removed.

2. A NON-IDENTIFIER RECEIVER HAD NO DISPATCH. `"literal".normalize(f)` fell through to "no handler for method on non-identifier receiver"; `normalize` needed adding to the String-only name list that materializes such a receiver, and to the two heap-String classifiers (`expr_is_string_like`, `closure_body_produces_heap_string`) so the fresh allocation is cleaned up once.

Verified byte-identical on --interp / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT across all four forms, the spec's own `e`+U+0301 vs U+00E9 hazard, both length directions (composition shrinks 3->2, decomposition grows 2->3), the compatibility pair doing what the canonical pair does not (U+FB01 -> `fi`), all three ways the form reaches the call (bare, qualified, bound), a literal and a binding receiver, chaining onto the result, and the empty / pure-ASCII identities. `karac run` routes a normalizing program to the interpreter (the regex / Arrow JIT posture, since the JIT runner does not build the opt-in feature).

ARCHIVE SELECTION VERIFIED THREE WAYS, not assumed: hiding the archive produces the actionable "build `libkarac_runtime_unicode.a`" error; a non-normalizing program still links lean and `nm` finds zero `karac_unicode_*` in it; a normalizing binary has them.

Twelve tests — 2 typechecker, 5 interpreter, 5 codegen — plus 4 runtime unit tests and an ASAN fixture pinning that the malloc'd result has exactly one owner across a bare temporary, a live binding, and a chain.
title: `String.normalize` and the `NFC` constant DO NOT EXIST, so the remedy design.md gives for its own Unicode-equality hazard is unwritable. § Strings, Equality bullet: "`String` equality (`==`) compares raw UTF-8 bytes. Two strings with identical visual appearance but different Unicode normalization forms (e.g., NFC vs NFD) are **not** equal. USE `s.normalize(NFC)` FOR NORMALIZATION-AWARE COMPARISON." Measured: `a.normalize(NFC)` -> `error[resolve]: undefined name 'NFC', did you mean 'Neg'?`; the no-argument form `a.normalize()` -> `error[typecheck]: no method 'normalize' on type 'String'`. Neither `normalize` nor `NFC` appears anywhere in `src/`. The hazard the bullet describes is real and reproduces -- `"e\u{0301}" == "\u{00e9}"` is false, exactly as documented -- so the paragraph correctly warns about a trap and then names an escape that was never built.
detail:
Probe: domain-22 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d22/{sx2,sx4}.kara.

DETECTION: `grep -rn '"normalize"\|NFC' src/` returns nothing at all -- not a wiring gap between phases, simply absent.

WHICH SIDE MOVES IS THE OWNER'S CALL. Implementing normalization pulls in Unicode tables (a real dependency decision, and there is no other consumer in the language today), so the cheaper repair may be to narrow the sentence -- state the byte-equality rule and the NFC/NFD hazard, and say normalization-aware comparison is not in v1, rather than naming an API. What should not survive is the current form, where the spec hands the reader a call that does not resolve.

SEE ALSO the sibling `Hash` claim in the same bullet -- "`Hash` is consistent with `==` — it hashes raw bytes" -- which does hold: the byte-equality half of the paragraph is correct throughout.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S COSTING AND ITS SPELLING CLAIM, both measured while fixing it.

The row read the dependency as the expensive half and suggested narrowing the sentence as "the cheaper repair". Neither premise held. `icu_normalizer` was ALREADY in the compiler's dependency graph (via `ureq -> url -> idna -> idna_adapter`), so the interpreter cost zero new crates, and the AOT tables went into an opt-in archive that only normalizing programs link — a pattern this repo already had three instances of. The measured sizes are in the fix.

The row also said "there is no other consumer in the language today". There is: `String.to_lowercase` / `to_uppercase` are full-Unicode already (`karac_string_to_lowercase` uses Rust `str::to_lowercase`). They are free only because std ships case-mapping tables — and std ships NO normalization tables, which is the actual reason this one needed a crate and `to_lowercase` did not. That distinction, not "no consumer", is what made the dependency question real.

Finally, and most consequentially: the row treated `s.normalize(NFC)` as a valid call that simply had no implementation. It is not valid Kāra under any implementation — an all-caps variant name breaks design.md's own CN-4 and the identifier-class check rejects it outright. The bullet was wrong twice over, and only one of the two errors was the missing API.

title: `String.push(char)` emits an OUT-OF-LINE call to `karac_string_encode_char` per character, ~1.3 ns each; the runtime function already tests ASCII first, so the cost is the call itself. Inlining the `cp < 0x80` fast path (as Rust's String::push does) should recover most of it -- worth ~40% of a string-building kata's total runtime
detail:
Found while asking whether kata #293's 3.25x gap to C was expected. It is, in the sense that nothing is BROKEN -- but the gap decomposes into one addressable piece and two that are already fine, and the addressable piece is a codegen decision rather than a language property.

THE KATA NUMBER: 40,000 boards x 3 densities x 64 chars, one owned String per result (2,510,273 of them). Kara 528.2 ms, C 162.4 ms, Rust 493.3 ms, Go 555.5 ms.

RULED OUT -- ALLOCATION. An LD_PRELOAD counter gives Kara 2,739,223 malloc / 255,809 realloc against C's 2,510,274 / 0, i.e. ~1.09 malloc and 0.10 realloc PER STATE. The presize pass is working. Confirmed independently: rewriting `String.new()` as `String.with_capacity(n)` produces BYTE-IDENTICAL allocation counts (2510276 malloc, 0 realloc, same total bytes) and identical time (264.0 ms vs 266.0 ms, within noise). The idiom leaves nothing on the table and this is not a repeat of B-2026-08-20-3.

RULED OUT -- THE READ SIDE. A probe doing only the 160M `Vec[char]` indexed reads, with no String built, runs in 55.9 ms -- about 0.35 ns per read, so bounds-check elision is doing its job.

THE COST IS THE PUSH. The same probe plus `String.push` per character and a cheap consume runs 264.9 ms, so the pushes account for 264.9 - 55.9 = 209 ms over 160M characters: ~1.3 ns each, roughly 4 cycles, against a C byte store at well under one.

AND THE PUSH IS A CALL. `objdump -d` on the probe shows `karac_string_encode_char` as a call inside main's hot loop -- one per character, not inlined. The runtime implementation (`runtime/src/clone.rs:731`) ALREADY opens with `if cp < 0x80 { *out = cp as u8; 1 }`, so the ASCII path is a compare, a byte store and a length bump; what the program pays on top is call/return, argument setup and the compiler's inability to see through the boundary (no register allocation across it, no hoisting of the capacity check, no vectorisation of a run of ASCII pushes).

PROPOSED FIX, and the precedent for it: emit the `cp < 0x80` test INLINE at the push site -- store one byte and bump the length -- and keep the call only for the multi-byte and surrogate arms. This is exactly the shape of Rust's `String::push`, which inlines the ASCII case and defers to `encode_utf8` otherwise, and it is why the Rust mirror in this kata (493.3 ms) sits where it does despite building strings the same way.

EXPECTED WIN, stated as an estimate and not a measurement: the 209 ms of push time is ~40% of the kata's 528 ms. Removing the call overhead while keeping the same encode logic should take a large fraction of that, which would move Kara past Rust on this workload and to roughly 2x of C rather than 3.25x. The honest caveat is that I have not built the inlined version, so the win is inferred from the call being the only unexplained component, not demonstrated.

NOT A CORRECTNESS ISSUE. Every surface agrees; the kata verifies clean across run / interp / build / auto-par-off, and the sink matches C, Rust and Go exactly. This is purely about how much the per-character boundary costs.
fix:
CLOSED AS INVALID -- the premise was refuted by reading the codegen and then measuring. The optimization this row proposes ALREADY EXISTS and already works.

WHAT THE ROW CLAIMED: that `String.push(char)` emits an out-of-line call to `karac_string_encode_char` per character, and that inlining a `cp < 0x80` fast path (as Rust's String::push does) would recover ~40% of kata #293's runtime.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. `src/codegen/vec_method.rs:2377`, the `"push" if string_vars.contains(var_name)` arm, computes the UTF-8 length INLINE with no runtime call and stores the single byte directly on the ASCII path -- its own comment says so, and says why: "a pure-ASCII push needs neither an encode call (`karac_string_encode_char`) nor a variable-length `memcpy` -- which LLVM lowers to a libc `memmove` call even for one byte, the dominant cost on string-build workloads (kata:38 profile: memmove/memcpy ~40%, encode ~20% of the hot time). Only the rare multibyte path pays the call + copy." The proposed fix is a description of the existing code.

MEASURED, and the measurement is unambiguous. Two probes, 160M pushes each, identical apart from the character pushed: pushing '+' (1-byte) takes 94.9 ms +/- 1.3; pushing 'é' (2-byte) takes 1.163 s +/- 0.004. The ASCII path is 12.25x +/- 0.18 faster. If both routed through the same out-of-line call the two would be within a small constant of each other; a 12x split is exactly the signature of an inlined fast path beside an out-of-line slow one.

HOW I GOT IT WRONG, since the method is the reusable part. I ran `objdump -d` and grepped for calls across the WHOLE of `main` -- `awk '/<main>:/,/^$/'` -- then reported `karac_string_encode_char` as being "in the hot loop". It is in `main`, but the loop is not the only thing in `main`: the probe ends with `println(f"acc {acc}")`, and f-string char rendering routes through `emit_codepoint_to_utf8`, which is the documented caller of that helper. One static occurrence of a symbol in a function is not evidence that it executes per iteration, and I treated it as though it were. The behavioural probe above is what should have been run first: it needs no disassembly reading and cannot be misattributed.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE from the row, and is worth keeping: allocation is NOT the cause of kata #293's gap to C (~1.09 malloc and 0.10 realloc per state against C's 1.00/0.00, and `String.with_capacity(n)` measures byte-identical to `String.new()`), and the read side is NOT the cause (160M `Vec[char]` indexed reads run at ~0.35 ns each, so bounds-check elision is working). Those two eliminations stand on their own measurements and are unaffected by this refutation.

WHAT IS NOW UNEXPLAINED, stated as such rather than replaced with a fresh theory: with allocation, the read side, and the encode call all ruled out, kata #293's remaining 3.25x to C is not attributed to anything. A separate row should be opened for it only after someone profiles the binary properly -- `perf record` on the real bench, not a hand-read disassembly -- because the one thing this episode demonstrates is that guessing at the mechanism from static inspection produced a confident and wrong answer.

RESOLVED as a work item: six of the eight lints B-2026-08-20-36 found registered
with no emit site are now WIRED, and the two that remain are not wiring problems
— each needs a decision, and each is now its own row so the decision has
somewhere to live. `KNOWN_UNWIRED` in `src/lints.rs` still names both, so
`every_registered_lint_is_emitted_or_declared_unwired` keeps them honest.

THE SIX, in the order they landed:

  redundant_suffix       (B-2026-08-20-36)
  module_mut_binding     17ff5c0  — per-binding suppression via the cascade frame
  mutual_recursion_note  2a12881  — only the NOTE was missing; the JSON field
                                    had been populated all along
  pure_loop_in_par       fe3b242  — unwritable until a codegen defect under it
                                    was fixed: every arithmetic op in a `par`
                                    branch was emitting a cancel check
  repr_c_layout_ignored  666d3d41 — and its `pub` sibling, an ERROR
  float_in_serialized_type 666d3d41 — per-field

THE TWO THAT REMAIN, split out per the ledger's live-remainder rule:

  * B-2026-08-22-7 — `f16_software_emulated`. The trigger is well defined and
    decidable from real data (`combined_features()` already merges a per-target
    baseline with `--target-features`), but the baseline table lives in
    `src/codegen/driver.rs`, behind `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`. The typechecker
    — where the other five live and where `#[allow]` cascades for free — cannot
    reach it without breaking codegen containment; codegen can, but no codegen
    site reads `#[allow]` today. It is a placement decision with a real
    trade-off either way. Also measured: under every current default baseline
    (`+v8a` on aarch64, the x86_64 baseline, wasm `+simd128`) there is NO native
    f16, so the lint would fire on essentially all f16 arithmetic until someone
    widens the baseline — worth deciding on before building the plumbing.
  * B-2026-08-22-8 — `implicit_clone`. Cannot be resolved in the compiler at all:
    design.md defines no trigger for it, and `starter_set_covers_spec_listed_lints`
    pins the registration because the spec lists it, so de-registering needs a
    design.md edit first.

WHAT THIS ROW COST, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Every slice of it turned up
something the registry itself was lying about:

  * THE DESCRIPTION IS NOT A RELIABLE STATEMENT OF THE TRIGGER. Twice measured
    on this row — `module_mut_binding`'s described a different lint entirely,
    and `pure_loop_in_par`'s described an unimplementable rule ("a loop whose
    body has no parallelisable work") where the spec's actual trigger is
    CANCELLABILITY. Read the spec section, never the registry blurb.
  * ONE-LINE SUMMARIES HIDE SPLIT RULES. `repr_c_layout_ignored` read as one
    lint and was two rules: a suppressible warning for a private struct AND a
    hard error for a `pub` one, because a `pub` `#[repr(C)]` type's field order
    is an FFI contract. Neither existed. Wiring only the lint would have left
    the error missing and looked complete.
  * "DEFERRED" IS NOT THE SAME AS "UNFIREABLE". `float_in_serialized_type`'s
    derive machinery is deferred post-v1, which reads like grounds for wontfix.
    The ATTRIBUTE parses and typechecks today, so the trigger is decidable and
    the promise is already being made.
  * ADDING A SEVERITY BAND BREAKS OPEN-CODED SEVERITY TESTS. The `note` band
    broke seventeen sites that had spelled "is this advisory" as
    `!= FfiLintHint`; the `warn` band needed a third. Both are now single hoisted
    predicates (`kind_is_note`, `kind_is_lint_warning`, `resolve_kind_is_note`)
    precisely so the next band does not repeat it.
  * THE GUARD PROVES A NAME, NOT A BEHAVIOUR. `every_registered_lint_is_emitted_
    or_declared_unwired` only checks that a lint NAME appears outside lints.rs.
    It cannot see that an emit has the wrong SEVERITY or that its `#[allow]` is
    inert — which is how `layout_unassigned_fields` sat "wired" while being a
    hard error whose suppression was never read (filed and fixed separately).
    The other 'wired' lints are still worth spot-checking on that axis.

A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN TEXT, recorded because it propagated: it claimed
these lints are "advertised by `karac lint --list`". THERE IS NO `karac lint`
COMMAND (measured: `error: unknown command 'lint'`). The real exposure is
narrower and still real — `#[allow(<name>)]` is accepted rather than reported as
`unknown_lint`, `#[deny(<name>)]` passes vacuously, and only `#[expect(...)]`
tells the truth, which is how B-2026-08-20-36 found the class to begin with.
title: SIX OF THE EIGHT REGISTERED-BUT-UNWIRED LINTS ARE NOW WIRED (`redundant_suffix`, `module_mut_binding`, `mutual_recursion_note`, `pure_loop_in_par`, `repr_c_layout_ignored`, `float_in_serialized_type`); the last two are not wiring problems but DECISIONS -- `f16_software_emulated` needs a placement call (its target baseline is only reachable behind the llvm feature gate) and `implicit_clone` needs a design.md edit -- and are split to B-2026-08-22-7 and B-2026-08-22-8
detail:
SEVEN INDEPENDENT DETECTION PASSES, not one fix -- they share only the shape of the omission (registered name + level + description, no trigger ever written). Rough read of what each needs, from its registry description and the design.md section that names it:

  * `module_mut_binding` -- design.md § Module-Level State gives it the most surface of the seven, including the exact suppression form (`#[allow(module_mut_binding)]` is per-binding, not module-wide) and an alternative menu (context struct, Mutex, Atomic, #[thread_local], LazyLock, OnceLock) that the diagnostic is supposed to surface. Probably the next-best slice for the same reason `redundant_suffix` was the first: the spec describes behaviour that does not exist.
  * `implicit_clone` -- fires where the compiler inserts a copy the author did not write. Overlaps the existing `rc_fallback` machinery (`ownership.rs`), which is live, so the trigger may be reachable from the same analysis rather than a new one.
  * `pure_loop_in_par` -- a `par` block whose body has no effects worth parallelising. The auto-par analysis already computes what it would need.
  * `mutual_recursion_note` -- note-severity; the effect checker already runs SCC iteration over the call graph, which is exactly where mutual recursion is visible.
  * `repr_c_layout_ignored` / `float_in_serialized_type` / `f16_software_emulated` -- the three with the least spec surface; each needs its trigger condition PINNED DOWN before it can be written, and one of them may deserve `wontfix` rather than an invented rule.

WHY THIS IS NOT LOW SEVERITY DESPITE FIRING NOTHING: the failure is a false promise rather than a wrong answer. `karac lint --list` advertises all seven, `#[allow(...)]` accepts them, and a user who writes `#[deny(pure_loop_in_par)]` gets a build that passes for the wrong reason. `#[expect(...)]` is the one surface that tells the truth -- it reports `unfulfilled_lint_expectation` -- which is how B-2026-08-20-36 found the class.

SOURCE NOTE: split from B-2026-08-20-36 rather than buried in its close, per the ledger's live-remainder rule. That row's detection method (`rg -l --glob '!src/lints.rs' '\b<name>\b' src/`) is now a test, so this list cannot silently grow while it sits open.

PROGRESS (17ff5c0): `module_mut_binding` is now WIRED and drops out of KNOWN_UNWIRED (7 -> 6). It emits from `check_module_binding` in the typechecker, not from the effect checker's `modbind_synth`, because the spec's PER-BINDING suppression needs the binding's own `lint_overrides` on the innermost cascade frame; the frame is pushed around the emit alone so the function's early returns cannot leak it. Codes W0281 / E0281.

SCOPE NOTE for whoever takes the rest: design.md's profile table names FOUR profiles (`lib`, `app`, `embedded`, `gpu`) but `CompileProfile` has only `Default`, `Embedded`, `Kernel` -- there is NO `app` profile. The table's `app` row is a hard ERROR rather than this lint, so it was left unimplemented rather than approximated, and the lint stays silent under `embedded`, which permits module-level `let mut` outright (MMIO / DMA / static buffers). The missing `app` profile is a separate gap, not part of this row.

SECOND DEFECT FIXED IN PASSING: the registry description for `module_mut_binding` described a DIFFERENT lint entirely ("shadows a value that the resolver would otherwise rebind"), so `karac lint --list` advertised the wrong meaning. Worth checking the remaining six descriptions against their spec sections before wiring each one -- the description is not a reliable statement of the trigger.

PROGRESS (2a12881): `mutual_recursion_note` is now WIRED; KNOWN_UNWIRED 6 -> 5. Only HALF the spec sentence was missing: the `--output=json` `mutual_recursion_groups` field had been populated all along, so the gap was the NOTE alone -- which is exactly why `#[allow]` had nothing to suppress and `#[deny]` passed vacuously. Emitted from the effect checker (codes L0002 / note severity), with `#[allow]` read straight off the declaration as `ownership.rs` does for `rc_fallback`, since that phase has no access to the typechecker's cascade.

LESSON FOR THE REMAINING FIVE: adding a second ADVISORY effect kind broke seventeen sites that had open-coded "is this a note" as `!= FfiLintHint`. Do not reach for `kind_blocks_production` as the note test -- `TargetGateViolation` does not block production but IS an error that `check` reports and tests assert on; conflating them makes every target-gate test stop seeing its diagnostic (measured). Use the hoisted `kind_is_note`.

NOISE OBSERVATION, not yet a defect: the self-hosted compiler emits ELEVEN of these notes (a recursive-descent parser and a recursive emitter are legitimately mutually recursive -- one cycle spans 20 `Parser.*` functions). That is what design.md prescribes and it is non-blocking, so the behaviour is left as specified; if the volume proves unwanted the lever is the registered default LEVEL, not the emit site.

IMPLICIT_CLONE: RECOMMEND wontfix / de-register, do NOT wire it. Measured, not assumed. design.md defines NO trigger for it: the name appears only in a Tier-3 suppression list, a cascade example, and the starter-set roster. The spec states "No implicit clones" for compiled code, and the ONE auto-clone feature that exists (`karac repl --auto-clone`) is spec'd to emit a DIFFERENT diagnostic, `perf[auto-clone-in-repl]`. The only place compiled Kara gains a copy the author did not write is codegen's use-after-move defensive copy -- and those sites ALREADY emit `warning[ownership]` at the same span with actionable help (measured: `let a = consume(v); let b = v.len();` warns, builds, and runs). Wiring `implicit_clone` there would double-report one span. It cannot simply be removed either: `starter_set_covers_spec_listed_lints` pins it because design.md lists it, so de-registering needs a spec edit. Leave it registered and in KNOWN_UNWIRED until that spec question is settled.

FOUND WHILE PROBING IT: `layout_unassigned_fields` -- a lint NOT on this row's list, because the guard counted it wired -- was emitted as a hard ResolveError, so a spec-legal program failed to compile, and its `#[allow]` was never read. Filed and fixed as its own row. The guard only proves a lint NAME appears outside lints.rs; it cannot see that the emit has the wrong SEVERITY or that its suppression is inert. Worth spot-checking the other 'wired' lints on that axis.

PROGRESS (fe3b242): `pure_loop_in_par` is now WIRED; KNOWN_UNWIRED 5 -> 4. It could NOT be wired alone -- the slice turned up a CODEGEN DEFECT underneath it, and the lint was unwritable until that was fixed, because "this loop has no effect boundary" was never true of any loop.

THE CODEGEN DEFECT. Lowering rewrites `a + b` on a numeric primitive into `Call(Path(["i64","add"]), ...)`, and codegen recovers exactly that `i64.add` key to narrow the par-branch cooperative cancel check. Nothing ever put such a key in `callee_effectful` -- builtins have no declaration to infer from -- so EVERY arithmetic operation inside a `par` branch read as an unclassifiable callee and had a cancel check emitted before it. Measured on a branch whose body is `while i < 1000 { acc = acc + i; i = i + 1; }`: SIX cancel checks, two of them INSIDE the loop (`while.cond`, `while.body`), so the flag was loaded and tested twice per iteration of pure arithmetic. After the fix: ZERO in the loop, branch-entry check correctly retained.

design.md is explicit that this must not happen -- "inserting preemption points into pure computation would defeat the single-pass compilation and zero-runtime-tax goals", and "the compiler does not automatically insert effect-boundary checks at loop backedges". So this was a live perf defect in its own right, not merely a blocker for the lint.

THE DESCRIPTION WAS WRONG AGAIN. The registry read "a loop whose body has no parallelisable work" -- a different and unimplementable rule. design.md's trigger is CANCELLABILITY: a loop with no effect boundary cannot observe the cancel flag. That is the SECOND confirmed case of a registry description misstating its own trigger, after `module_mut_binding`. Treat the description as unreliable for each of the remaining four and read the spec section instead -- this is now a measured pattern, not a caution.

ONE CLASSIFIER, TWO CONSUMERS: `effect_set_is_effectful` is hoisted out of `build_callee_effectful_table` so the lint and the checks actually emitted answer one question one way. A lint that disagreed would be worse than none -- it would report a loop as uncancellable while codegen had placed a check inside it.

A THIRD SEVERITY BAND was required. The renderers were binary, note-or-error, so a `warn[...]` diagnostic printed `error[effect]` AND counted toward the exit code -- which would have made every Mend / `karac fix` cycle treat an intentionally bounded loop as a failure. `kind_is_lint_warning` is hoisted for the same reason `kind_is_note` was.

NOTE FOR THE REMAINING FOUR: this row's own text says these lints are "advertised by `karac lint --list`". THERE IS NO `karac lint` COMMAND (measured: `error: unknown command 'lint'`). The real exposure is narrower and still real -- `#[allow(<name>)]` is accepted rather than reported as `unknown_lint`, `#[deny(<name>)]` passes vacuously, and only `#[expect(...)]` tells the truth. Worth correcting wherever else that claim appears.

PROGRESS (666d3d41, 6ff52c3d pre-rebase): `repr_c_layout_ignored` and `float_in_serialized_type` are now WIRED; KNOWN_UNWIRED 4 -> 2. Both were straightforward once the trigger was read off the spec rather than the registry — which is the third and fourth confirmation of this row's own warning that the description is not a reliable statement of the trigger, though here the descriptions happened to be right.

REPR_C_LAYOUT_IGNORED WAS TWO MISSING RULES, NOT ONE, and the row's one-line summary hid that. design.md § Interaction with layout blocks splits by VISIBILITY:

  * private `#[repr(C)]` + layout -> WARNING listing the ignored groups, suppressible.
  * `pub` `#[repr(C)]` + layout -> COMPILE ERROR, "a `pub` type may be consumed by FFI code that depends on the exact field order".

Neither existed. A `#[repr(C)]` struct with a layout block compiled in SILENCE on both paths, so the layout looked effective and was not — the same false-promise shape as the unwired lint, one severity band up. The `pub` half is a separate `ResolveErrorKind` deliberately: `#[allow(repr_c_layout_ignored)]` must not reach it, or an FFI field-order contract becomes opt-out. That case has its own assertion in the test.

FLOAT_IN_SERIALIZED_TYPE is PER-FIELD and that is the whole design of it — a type may carry one float the author has reasoned about beside another they have not. A per-struct implementation is the obvious shortcut, silences both, and the pin fails it.

ITS DERIVE MACHINERY IS DEFERRED POST-V1, which is presumably why nobody wrote it and is worth stating so the next reader does not re-derive it: it does NOT make the lint vacuous. `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` parses and typechecks today (the name is in the known-derive set), so the trigger is decidable from the AST now. Anyone tempted to call this one `wontfix` on deferral grounds should note the attribute is already accepted, so the promise is already being made.

TWO PREDICATES HOISTED RATHER THAN COPIED, the reusable part of this slice. `Attribute::is_repr_c` now backs both `cheader.rs` and this check: one decides a struct crosses the C ABI and the other decides that struct's layout block is therefore ignored, so a drifted copy would let one act on a repr the other did not see. `extract_derived_traits` became `pub(crate)` so the resolver reads derives through the typechecker's parser instead of a second one that could disagree about the call-form (`Display(snake_case)`) spelling.

THE RUSTFMT DIAGNOSTIC HAZARD BIT AGAIN, within a day of being filed as B-2026-08-21-45: both new messages shipped in draft with 30-space runs mid-sentence, because rustfmt rejoined their `\`-continued literals and kept the indentation as real spaces. Rendered output is the only way to catch it — the source looks correct and `cargo fmt --check` is clean. Both are now built with `concat!`. Anyone wiring the remaining two should write the message that way from the start.

REMAINING: `f16_software_emulated` and `implicit_clone`. `implicit_clone` still carries this row's earlier recommendation of wontfix / de-register pending a spec edit, and nothing found here changes it. `f16_software_emulated` has a real spec trigger (design.md:2347, :13794 — "on targets without native `f16`/`bf16` hardware, LLVM promotes operations to `f32`"), so it is wireable, but it is the only one of the seven whose condition depends on the TARGET rather than on the source alone, which is why it is left for a slice that can decide where target capability is known.

title: MEASURED NEGATIVE RESULT -- hoisting the ASCII test to the top of the `String.push` codegen arm removes 34% of the program's retired instructions and makes it 10% SLOWER; the string-build inner loop is latency-bound, not instruction-bound, so instruction-count reasoning does not predict its wall time
detail:
SUBJECT. `src/codegen/vec_method.rs`'s `"push" if string_vars` arm computes the UTF-8 encoded length (1/2/3/4) up front, because the capacity check `len + enc_len > cap` needs it, and only tests for ASCII afterwards at the store. LLVM lowers that length computation to a branchless cmp/cmov ladder, so every ASCII push pays it. The obvious optimization is to split on `cp < 0x80` FIRST, give the fast side the constant length 1, and leave the ladder + encode + memcpy on the cold multibyte side. It was implemented in full (both sides sharing a new `emit_string_grow_geometry` helper so the growth geometry stays identical) and MEASURED. It is a regression. Reverted; not landed.

THE MEASUREMENT (callgrind + hyperfine, this container, x86_64, 4 cores; workload = kara-katas leetcode/201-300/293-flip-game/bench/flipgame.kara, 160,657,472 one-byte pushes). Retired instructions fell from 6,594,311,973 to 4,359,668,709 -- a 33.9% cut, and the hot loop shrank from 33 instructions per push to 21, exactly as the static reading predicted. Wall clock went the OTHER WAY: 492.9 ms +/- 28.3 -> 542.7 ms +/- 13.4 over 40 runs each, both binaries built by the same compiler modulo this one arm. A 10% slowdown for a third fewer instructions.

WHY. The disassembly names the mechanism. Before the split the source array's base pointer lives in a register across the loop (`mov 0x0(%r13,%r12,4),%r13d` -- one load in the critical path). After it, the arm's extra basic blocks raise register pressure in the ENCLOSING loop and the base gets spilled, so each iteration reloads it and then loads through it: `mov 0x58(%rsp),%rax` followed by `mov (%rax,%r12,4),%r15d` -- two dependent loads where there was one. The removed instructions were ILP-friendly filler the core was retiring for free (old IPC ~3.2, new ~2.0); the added load is on the dependency chain and is not free. A control confirms the split is not itself harmful: an isolated 2.5M x 64-char string-build micro with almost nothing else live measures 237.2 ms vs 236.5 ms, dead neutral. The cost only appears when `push` is inlined into a loop that already needs its registers.

WHY wontfix RATHER THAN open. There is no defect here -- the shipped code is the faster of the two -- and the question the row exists to close is whether this optimization is worth building. It has been built and measured; it is not. Reopening it needs a NEW mechanism (e.g. a way to get the constant-length fast path without adding basic blocks), not another attempt at this one.

SOURCE NOTE / METHOD. This is the second theory about kata #293's gap to C to be refuted by measurement, after B-2026-08-21-1 (which claimed an out-of-line encode call per character that does not exist). Both were derived by reading disassembly and reasoning about instruction counts. The standing lesson is in the numbers above: on this workload a 34% instruction cut bought a 10% SLOWDOWN, so retired-instruction counts do not order these variants and must not be quoted as if they do.

WHAT THE PROFILE DID SETTLE, and it reframes the gap. Retired instructions, same workload: C 1,656,729,972; rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on 5,181,589,940; karac 6,594,311,973. Wall: 162.3 / 403.0 / 521.0 ms. Kara is 3.98x C in instructions and 3.21x in wall -- but only 1.27x and 1.30x of RUST, which implements the identical algorithm with the identical growable-String abstraction and is itself 2.48x C. Kara's malloc-side instruction counts match Rust's to five significant figures (`_int_malloc` 326,836,831 vs 326,836,911). So most of the distance to the C mirror is the cost of a length-and-capacity-tracked heap String against C's raw fixed `malloc(65)` with no bookkeeping -- an abstraction difference both safe languages pay -- and the Kara-specific remainder over Rust is ~1.3x, not ~3.2x.

PRIOR ART, and why this looked like a sure thing. B-2026-07-18-8 (fixed) is the same optimization shape applied to `String.push_str`: a length that reaches codegen as a RUNTIME value forces a branchy variable-length copy, and const-folding the length-1 case collapsed it to a single store, closing a 1.15-1.56x instruction gap to equal-safety Rust across a cluster of char-append katas. `push`'s enc_len ladder is visibly the same defect, and the same remedy removes the same proportion of instructions -- it simply does not make this workload faster, because push_str's gap was real front-end work and push's ladder is not. Two identical-looking instruction-count wins, opposite outcomes; only the stopwatch told them apart.

fix:
FIXED by b538966 (header from the receiver's place) and c5469bb (method-return element type).

Two defects, both in codegen's Slice[T] lowering.

(1) `as_slice` built the returned header from the receiver's SLOT rather than
its PLACE. For a `ref Vec[T]` receiver the slot holds a POINTER to the vec, so
the emitted header took its data/len from the pointer's own storage — garbage.
Reading the receiver's place first makes the header describe the vec itself.

(2) The element type of a `-> Slice[T]` value was resolved only through a free
function's declared return; a method returning `Slice[T]` fell through to the
default and lowered its elements at the wrong width.

The method arm must sit LAST among the method arms: the fixed-element arms
(`bytes` / `as_bytes`) are more specific, and an earlier insert silently
shadowed `CStr.as_bytes()` — caught by clippy's unreachable-pattern lint.

Verified on both twins (--interp and codegen) for: a free-fn return
(`pick(v).len()` -> 3), iteration (`for x in s` -> 10 20 30), indexing
(`pick(v)[2]` -> 30), a ref param (`probe(ref)` -> 3), and the method sibling
(-> 9 3 3). Six E2E cases added; all pass.
title: A free function DECLARED to return `Slice[T]` hands back a GARBAGE header in codegen while `--interp` is correct, and MOST uses of it are SILENT. `fn pick(v: ref Vec[i64]) -> Slice[i64] { v.as_slice() }` over `let v: Vec[i64] = [10, 20, 30]`, measured on the JIT: `println(pick(v).len())` prints a pointer-sized number (140208557007525) instead of 3; `let s = pick(v); println(s.len())` the same; `for x in s` floods hundreds of garbage words instead of 10 20 30. No diagnostic, exit 0. Only the INDEX paths fail loudly -- `pick(v)[2]` and `let s = pick(v); s[2]` both report `codegen failed: Index operator applied to non-array type`, because the callee's `Slice[T]` return is never registered as an element type anywhere. So one family reads as a wrong answer or a hard stop purely by which method you call on it.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-20-40 (inline index of a slice temporary), probing whether that fix should extend to a Slice-returning call.

MEASURE-FIRST RESULT, AND THE REASON THIS IS ITS OWN ROW. The obvious fix looked like an element-type gap: `infer_slice_elem_from_rhs` / `slice_elem_type_expr_from_rhs` (src/codegen/types_lowering.rs) resolve a slice binding's element from `as_slice` / `bytes` / `as_bytes` / range-index receivers and have no `Call` arm, so a call result has no element type anywhere. A `Call` arm reading the callee's declared return from `fn_sig.fn_return_type_exprs` (plus a shared `call_slice_return_te` excluding `ref Slice` returns, which arrive as a bare ptr) was written and MEASURED -- and REVERTED, because it makes things worse: with the element type visible, `pick(v)[2]` returned 3 instead of 30 and `let s = pick(v); s[2]` printed 3 as well. It converts the last loud failure in the family into a silent one.

SO THE ELEMENT TYPE IS NOT THE DEFECT. `pick(v).len()` needs no element type and was ALREADY a silent miscompile before any change -- as were `let s = pick(v); s.len()` and `for x in s`. The value crossing the return boundary is itself wrong, and the loud index failures were merely the one path that happened to notice. Fix the return of a `Slice[T]`-typed value first; the element-type arm can be re-landed on top of it afterwards and is small (about 15 lines in each helper plus the shared resolver).

THE METHOD SIBLING FAILS LOUDLY IN BOTH SPELLINGS, so it is either the same root cause caught before it can produce a value, or a separate registration gap: `struct Buf { v: Vec[i64] }` + `impl Buf { fn view(ref self) -> Slice[i64] { self.v.as_slice() } }` gives `b.view()[2]` -> `Index operator applied to non-array type` and `let s = b.view(); s.len()` -> `no handler for method 'len' on variable 's'`, while `--interp` prints 9 and 3. Worth re-measuring once the free-fn boundary is fixed.

NOT the inline-index gap B-2026-08-20-40 closed: that one was about a slice-valued expression having no NAMED binding to dispatch on, and its fix (a synth slice local) is deliberately gated on the element resolvers above, so it cannot fire for a call and cannot mask this.
tracker: src/codegen/types_lowering.rs::llvm_return_type (how a `Slice[T]` return is typed at the call boundary — start here, the returned VALUE is what is wrong); src/codegen/functions.rs::compile_function (the return emission that feeds it); src/codegen/types_lowering.rs::infer_slice_elem_from_rhs + ::slice_elem_type_expr_from_rhs (the two element-type resolvers whose missing `Call` arm is the SECOND half, deliberately not landed — see detail); src/codegen/collections.rs::inline_index_recv_slice_te (the B-2026-08-20-40 sibling that must not be widened to a `Call` until the boundary is fixed)

fix:
FIXED by 5b895aa.

Root cause was upstream of the panic. `CStr` was missing from BOTH LLVM
type-lowering entry points -- the `TypeKind::Path` arm of
`llvm_type_for_type_expr` and the name-keyed `llvm_type_for_name` -- so it
fell through to the unknown-name `i64` default. A `ref CStr` PARAM then
registered an 8-byte `inner_ty`, and `load_variable`'s ref-param deref
loaded a scalar word where the method expected the `{ptr, i64}` aggregate;
`into_struct_value` panicked on it. That is why only the PARAMETER spelling
crashed: a literal or owned receiver never crosses that deref.

Both entry points now map `CStr` to `slice_struct_type()`, keeping them in
agreement as the B-2026-08-11-34 comment requires. The owning `CString`
keeps its distinct `{ptr,len,cap}` vec shape.

The unwrap is ALSO replaced with a structured `Err` carrying the receiver
offset, which the row asked for independently of the lowering fix: the root
fix should make it unreachable, but no phase may abort with a Rust
backtrace (CLAUDE.md § Coding Standards), and it now guards any future
non-aggregate receiver shape.

Verified on all THREE backends -- --interp, AOT build, and JIT -- for
`len`, `is_empty`, and `as_bytes()[i]` on a `ref CStr` param: 3 false true
97 99, identical everywhere. That includes the `c.as_bytes()[i]` shape from
the originating B-2026-08-20-40 probe. One regression test added, using the
STRICT assert form so a missing runtime archive cannot make it pass
vacuously.
title: `compile_cstr_method` PANICS on a `ref CStr` PARAMETER receiver instead of emitting a diagnostic: `fn look(c: ref CStr) -> i64 { c.len() }` aborts karac with `Found IntValue(... %c.deref = load i64, ptr %c1 ...) but expected the StructValue variant` at src/codegen/method_call_ffi.rs:34 (inkwell `BasicValueEnum::into_struct_value`). `--interp` prints 3. Any CStr method on that receiver shape hits it -- `len`, `as_bytes` measured.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while probing receiver shapes for B-2026-08-20-40 (`c.as_bytes()[i]`).

BOUNDED TO THE `ref CStr` PARAM. A literal or owned receiver is correct on every backend: `c"abc".as_bytes()[1]` -> 98, `let b = c"abc".as_bytes(); b[1]` -> 98, both matching `--interp`. Only the parameter spelling reaches the unwrap, and the panic text names the value it got -- `%c.deref = load i64` -- so the receiver is being loaded as a scalar word where the method expects the CStr aggregate.

VIOLATES THE STANDING RULE that every phase emits a structured diagnostic with a span rather than panicking (CLAUDE.md, Coding Standards). Even before the receiver lowering is fixed, the unwrap should become a `Err(...)` carrying the receiver span, so the failure reads as an unsupported form rather than a compiler abort with a Rust backtrace.
tracker: src/codegen/method_call_ffi.rs::compile_cstr_method (the `recv.into_struct_value()` unwrap at the top of the fn — the panic site, and the place a structured Err belongs regardless); src/codegen/functions.rs (where a `ref CStr` param's slot is set up — the receiver arrives as a loaded i64 rather than the `{ptr, i64}` aggregate); tests/codegen.rs::test_e2e_cstr_len_is_empty_as_bytes (the literal-receiver coverage that passes, showing the gap is param-only)

fix:
FIXED by 8c3c8d6 (this commit) on top of 59c8d30, which landed defects 1 and 2.

FIXED IN THREE PARTS, one per defect, plus the fallout the third one exposed.

(1) THE HASH ITSELF, ONCE, SHARED. New `karac-hash` crate (`hash/`) implements
SipHash-1-3 with a 128-bit key. The interpreter calls it directly; codegen emits
`call @karac_hash_bytes` (a `karac-runtime` shim over the same crate) in place of
the FxHash byte loop it used to inline into every per-type `hash_fn`. One
implementation, so the two backends agree by construction rather than by
convention -- the rule the Arrow IPC twin and `String.normalize` already follow.
Zero dependencies, `no_std`-clean, because it has to cross wasm32-wasip1,
wasm32-wasip1-threads and the embedded targets. Verified against an ORACLE
rather than transcribed constants: Rust's `DefaultHasher` IS SipHash-1-3, so the
test compares against it for every length 0..=40, which catches a transposed
rotation constant that copied vectors would only catch if the copying were
itself right.

(2) THE SEED, PER PROCESS. `hash/src/seed.rs` draws a key once per process from
ASLR + clock + thread id. `KARAC_HASH_SEED=<n>` (decimal or `0x`; `0` is a legal
pin) reproduces a run exactly, which is what lets the suites and the kata A/B
harness compare output at all. The interpreter had a second, separate half of
this defect: it hashed nothing observable -- it walked `entries` in INSERTION
order -- so `MapData`/`SetData` grew an `iter_observable()` that orders by the
seeded hash, and every observable walk now goes through it (`for` loops,
`.iter()`, `.keys()`, `.values()`, `Display`, `debug_fmt`, and the separate
`println` formatter in `builtin.rs`, which was its own missed path).

(3) THE THIRD PARAMETER. `Map[K, V, H]` / `Set[T, H]` accept exactly two
selectors -- `SipHash13BuildHasher` (default) and `FxBuildHasher` (unkeyed,
floodable, stable across runs of one binary) -- declared as zero-field structs
in `runtime/stdlib/hash.kara` and prelude-visible, since design.md writes the
spelling bare in its own prose. Anything else in that slot is now a compile
error naming both, as is a hasher on `SortedMap`/`SortedSet` (ordered
containers compare; they never hash). `FxBuildHasher` routes to
`karac_hash_bytes_fx` -- FxHash living in the same shared crate, so the fast
path is a second entry point rather than a second implementation.

WHERE THE THIRD PART GOT INTERESTING, and the reason the parser is involved.
The obvious shape -- leave `Map[K, V, H]` in the AST -- is wrong, and quietly
so. Codegen and the interpreter recognize a `Map` by matching the head name AND
requiring EXACTLY two generic arguments (`extract_map_kv_types`,
`map_kv_type_exprs`, `extract_set_elem_type`, and every drop / clone / layout
path funnelling through them). A three-argument `Map` fails all of those tests,
so it is not a `Map` to any of them -- not "a Map with a different hasher" but a
different and WRONG answer about how to free the thing. Measured directly: with
the argument left in place, `Map[String, i64, FxBuildHasher]` compiled and ran,
but `nm` on the binary showed no `karac_hash_bytes_fx` at all; the annotation
had not been recognized as a Map anywhere, and the program only worked because
inference re-registered it from `Map.new()`. Relaxing each arity gate is a hunt
across 564 `args.len()` sites with no way to prove it finished.

So the PARSER deletes the argument and records the choice on
`Program::container_hashers`, keyed by the container path's span (the
`freeze_spans` / `stmt_lint_overrides` precedent). After the parse, the AST of
`Map[K, V, FxBuildHasher]` is byte-identical to `Map[K, V]` -- no later phase
can tell them apart, so none can get it wrong -- and one bit of difference lives
in a table that exactly two places read: codegen's `container_hasher_for` and
the interpreter's `new_hash_container`. Only a RECOGNIZED selector in the
trailing position is stripped, so misspellings keep their argument and still
reach the typechecker's diagnostic.

Codegen selects at CONSTRUCTION and stores the chosen `hash_fn` in the control
block `karac_map_new` returns, so every later insert/get uses it without
re-deciding; the synthesized per-key-type symbol carries a `_fx` suffix, without
which the second map would silently reuse the first's function. The interpreter
stamps `MapData`/`SetData` at `Map.new()` / `Set.new()`, reading the same table
off the same span, through the existing `pending_let_ty` channel -- extended to
struct-literal fields so it covers the two positions codegen reads (a `let`
annotation and a field's declared type).

FALLOUT, and the part worth remembering. Six tests in the compiler's own suite
asserted `Map`/`Set` iteration order, and FIVE OF THEM PASSED on the run that
introduced the seeding -- a two-key map has a 50% chance of looking stable, so
"the suite is green" proved nothing. They surfaced one at a time across runs
under different seeds. All six now compare CONTENTS (sorted) and keep exact
ordering only for the statements around the walk. The lesson is written into
CLAUDE.md with the sweep that finds them:
`for seed in 1 2 3 5; do KARAC_HASH_SEED=$seed cargo test; done`.

TESTS. `hash/`: oracle agreement over lengths 0..=40, the length byte (so `"a"`
and `"a\0"` cannot collide), the key actually keying, Fx pinned to constants --
which is what proves Fx is UNSEEDED, since the test binary seeds itself randomly
and a pinned digest would fail on almost every run otherwise. `tests/cli.rs`:
two subprocess tests, because both properties are about what differs between one
process and the next -- the default varies and a pin reproduces; an
`FxBuildHasher` map's order does NOT move across six processes while the default
map in the SAME program does, asserted under `--interp` and against a compiled
binary. `tests/codegen.rs`: the two hashers order the same ten keys differently
in ONE process (the symbol-mangling pin -- reverting `runtime_symbol()` fails
it), and Fx maps/sets still find, remove and dedupe. `tests/typechecker.rs`:
both spellings accepted, an opted-out map still assignable to `Map[K, V]`, and
each of the three refusals. Non-vacuity checked by reverting each half and
watching the matching test fail.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, and recorded in design.md rather than implied: the
`Hasher` and `BuildHasher` traits are still not baked, so the two names are
type-level SELECTORS, not user-implementable hashers. A user naming their own
type in that slot is rejected with a diagnostic that says exactly this. That is
a separate feature -- an ordinary trait with default method bodies, dispatched
per hash -- not a widening of this parameter.

CROSS-BACKEND ORDER, stated plainly so the "one shared implementation"
sentence above is not over-read. The two backends share the HASH FUNCTION,
not the walk: the interpreter orders its observable walk by the seeded hash
of each key, while the compiled backends walk an open-addressed table's
buckets. Measured under one pinned seed (`KARAC_HASH_SEED=7`, same program):

    interp {alpha: 1, mike: 2, bravo: 3, charlie: 5, zulu: 0, yankee: 4}
    AOT    {yankee: 4, alpha: 1, mike: 2, charlie: 5, zulu: 0, bravo: 3}

Both are reproducible under that pin within their own backend, and both vary
without it. design.md leaves the order unspecified, so this is conformant --
but a reader should not expect `karac run` and `karac build` to emit the same
permutation, and no test should be written as if they would.
title: `Map`/`Set` DO NOT USE THE SPEC'S DEFAULT HASHER: design.md mandates `SipHash13BuildHasher` seeded from a per-process random source, codegen emits FxHash with a COMPILE-TIME-CONSTANT seed and the interpreter hashes not at all -- so there is no hash-flooding resistance, iteration order is fully deterministic across runs (design.md says it must vary), the two backends order differently from each other, and `Map[K, V, FxBuildHasher]` -- design.md's own spelling -- does not resolve, so there is no opt-in either way
detail:
WHAT THE SPEC SAYS, twice and unambiguously. design.md § `Hash` and `Hasher`, "Default hasher for v1": "`Map[K, V]` and `Set[T]` without an explicit hasher use `SipHash13BuildHasher`, seeded from a per-process random source." And § Map, on iteration: "Iteration order is unspecified and varies across process runs -- the default hasher is DoS-resistant and seeded fresh per process ... so bucket placement and therefore iteration order differ from one run to the next." The stability policy paragraph names the reason: "the overwhelmingly common attack vector is hash-flooding from adversarial input."

WHAT IS IMPLEMENTED. `src/codegen/synth.rs` emits FxHash -- per byte, `h = h.rotate_left(5) ^ byte; h *= FXHASH_SEED` -- where `FXHASH_SEED: u64 = 0x517c_c1b7_2722_0a95` is a Rust `const`. There is no per-process seed anywhere in the emitted hash or in the runtime that installs one. The choice is documented and was made deliberately on speed grounds (the `bench/hash_quality/` investigation, 2026-05-15: geometric mean 0.56x of the FNV-1a baseline across 18 cells); what the comment does not mention is that design.md requires a different default.

MEASURED, three ways.
(1) Same AOT binary, ten string keys, run three times: Map and Set iteration order is BYTE-IDENTICAL every run. The spec says it must differ.
(2) Same source, three surfaces: `karac run --interp` iterates in INSERTION order (`zulu alpha mike bravo yankee charlie xray delta whiskey echo` for that insertion sequence), while `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` both iterate in FxHash bucket order (`delta alpha charlie mike echo bravo yankee whiskey zulu xray`). Two different orders, each deterministic. A program that leans on iteration order therefore gives one answer under the interpreter and another under codegen, and no amount of re-running will reveal it -- which is precisely the failure mode per-process seeding exists to make loud. (This is adjacent to B-2026-08-01-17, the fixed Set/SortedSet Drop-order divergence, and to B-2026-08-17-38's `TreeMap` row, but neither covers the hasher itself.)
(3) `let mut m: Map[String, i64, FxBuildHasher] = Map.new();` -- the three-parameter spelling design.md uses in its own prose, twice -- fails with `error[resolve]: undefined type 'FxBuildHasher'`. So a user can neither opt IN to a fast hasher nor opt OUT of the weak one; the third type parameter does not exist.

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST A DOCUMENTATION FIX. The security property is load-bearing for a language whose spec calls hash-flooding the common attack vector, and `Map[String, _]` keyed on request data is the shape that matters. Separately, the determinism silently converts "unspecified order" from a rule the implementation enforces into a rule nothing checks -- every program that accidentally depends on order will pass its tests indefinitely and break on the next hasher change, which design.md explicitly reserves the right to make ("may change in future Kara versions").

ON THE SPEED ARGUMENT, measured rather than assumed. kata #294's bench (900 memoized game-tree searches, `Map[String, bool]` keyed on 22-byte boards, ~1.4M lookups) was used to price the difference by transplanting Kara's exact emitted hash function into the Rust twin, leaving its `HashMap` otherwise identical: Rust with SipHash-1-3 measured 669.7 ms +/- 14.1 and Rust with Kara's hash 675.4 ms +/- 31.4 over 20 runs -- INDISTINGUISHABLE. On short string keys the weaker default bought nothing observable in that setting. CAVEAT, because it cuts against the measurement: the transplant is byte-at-a-time to stay faithful to Kara's emitted loop, whereas rustc-hash processes 8-byte chunks, so this prices Kara's hash FUNCTION, not the best available fast hash. It is evidence that the current default is not obviously worth its cost, not proof that a fast hasher never is -- which is an argument for shipping the spec's seeded default WITH the `Map[K, V, H]` opt-in, rather than for silently keeping the fast one.

REPRO. `Map[String, i64]` with keys `zulu alpha mike bravo yankee charlie xray delta whiskey echo`, iterate `m.keys()` and print; compare `karac run --interp`, `karac run` and `karac build` against each other and each against itself across runs.
