title: A call-site `mut` MARKER BYPASSES THE `let mut` REQUIREMENT, so a binding declared without `mut` can be mutated through any mutating parameter while direct assignment to that same binding is correctly refused. Measured on all three backends, `karac check` clean: `fn bump(n: mut ref i64) { n = n + 1; }` + `let x: i64 = 1; bump(mut x);` prints 2; `fn push_one(v: mut ref Vec[i64])` + `let v: Vec[i64] = [1]; push_one(mut v);` leaves 7 at index 1; `fn touch(xs: mut Slice[i64]) { xs[0] = 9; }` + `let v: Vec[i64] = [1,2,3]; touch(mut v);` prints 9. The SAME binding rejects `v[0] = 9` with `error[ownership]: cannot assign through 'v' -- 'v' is declared without 'mut' at line 2:5`, help `change the declaration to 'let mut v'`. So the marker -- whose stated job is to make the mutation VISIBLE at the call site -- is the one spelling that escapes the check the declaration is supposed to enforce.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-20-38 (mut sub-range slice at a call site), probing which phase enforces base mutability. It is not that fix's doing and predates it: all three repros above are whole-collection / scalar forms that shipped long before.

WHERE IT LIVES. Local mutability is an OWNERSHIP-phase rule, not a typechecker one -- the typechecker has no `let mut` bit, which is why `v[0] = 9` is caught by `error[ownership]` and not `error[typecheck]`. The call-argument path never asks the question: the typechecker checks assignability (owned `Vec[T]` fills a `mut Slice[T]` / `mut ref Vec[T]` slot -- correct at the type level) and `check_call_site_marker` checks only that the marker is PRESENT, never that the marked place is mutable. Nothing downstream re-asks.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. `let` vs `let mut` is the reader's contract that a binding does not change; every mutation of it is supposed to be announced twice, at the declaration and at the call. Today the second announcement silently substitutes for the first, and the declaration's guarantee is worth nothing to anyone who does not also read every call the binding is passed to.

B-2026-08-20-38 INHERITS THIS SYMMETRICALLY AND DOES NOT WIDEN THE CLASS: with the sub-range upgrade landed, `touch(mut v[1..3])` over a non-`mut` `v` is accepted exactly as `touch(mut v)` already was. Both should start being refused by the same check, in one place.

CLASSIFIED `false-positive` FOR THE INVERSE REASON THE NAME SUGGESTS -- this is the checker failing to fire where it should (a false NEGATIVE of the ownership rule), which the controlled vocabulary has no separate value for; `soundness` overstates it, since no memory rule is broken and every write is to storage the caller owns. The cost is a broken source-level guarantee, not a broken program.
tracker: src/ownership.rs (the `cannot assign through` check that fires for `v[0] = 9` -- the rule that already exists and the natural home for the argument-position twin); src/typechecker/expr_call.rs::check_call_site_marker (sees the marker and the argument's place expression, but deliberately asks only about presence -- it has no `let mut` bit to consult, which is why the fix belongs in ownership); src/typechecker/exprs.rs::param_mutates_through (the shared predicate naming the three parameter spellings that must all be covered: `mut ref T`, `mut Slice[T]`)

fix:
FIXED by 04ed765. `Value::Map` and `Value::Set` are now `Arc<RwLock<MapData>>` / `Arc<RwLock<SetData>>` — insertion-ordered storage with a hash index beside it — where they were a bare `Vec<(Value, Value)>` / `Vec<Value>`.

MEASUREMENT CORRECTED THIS ROW'S CAUSE ANALYSIS, and the correction is the useful part. The row attributes the quadratic behaviour to the association list's linear scan. That scan is real, but it is the SMALLER half. Two measurements separate them:

  - INSERT-ONLY is quadratic on its own -- 0.19 s / 0.64 s / 2.40 s at n = 1000 / 2000 / 4000, ratios 3.3x and 3.8x -- in a program that performs no lookups at all.
  - `Vec.push` over the same lengths is LINEAR: 0.088 / 0.094 / 0.130 / 0.192 s at n = 1000..8000.

The difference between those two loops is representation, not algorithm. `Env::get` ends in `other.clone()`, so materializing a method's receiver DEEP-COPIES the whole container before the method body runs. `Value::Array` was already `Arc<RwLock<Vec<Value>>>`, so its clone is a refcount bump; `Value::Map` was by-value, so every `insert` / `get` / `len` copied the map. An index alone would have left that untouched and the curve would have stayed quadratic -- the fix had to move the representation first.

BOTH HALVES LANDED, because either alone is insufficient: Arc-backing removes the O(n) clone but leaves an O(n) scan, and the index removes the scan but not the clone.

MEASURED, same program as the row's (insert n keys, then look up all n):

  n        before      after     speedup
  1000     0.48 s      0.123 s     3.9x
  2000     1.84 s      0.179 s      10x
  4000     7.31 s      0.281 s      26x
  8000    27.61 s      0.473 s      58x

Per-doubling ratios go from 3.8x / 4.0x / 3.8x (quadratic) to 1.46x / 1.57x / 1.69x (linear, with the interpreter's constant factor). `Set` is the same story: 0.33 / 1.08 / 4.33 s (3.3x, 4.0x) becomes 0.115 / 0.170 / 0.263 s (1.5x). Map and Set EQUALITY also drop from O(n^2) to O(n) as a side effect -- both were a nested scan and now probe the index.

ITERATION ORDER IS UNCHANGED, deliberately. design.md § Map states iteration order is unspecified and the two backends already disagree (interpreter insertion-ordered, codegen bucket-ordered) -- that divergence is B-2026-08-21-6's subject, not this row's, so keeping the interpreter's insertion order makes this a complexity fix with nothing observable riding on it. `entries` is walked directly by every read path exactly as the `Vec` was; the index only answers "where is this key".

ONE OBSERVABLE CHANGE, stated rather than buried: `Set.remove` used `swap_remove`, which moved the last element into the hole, and now preserves order like every other container. Both are legal under the unspecified-order rule and order-preserving is what `Map` and `Vec` already do.

CORRECTNESS OF THE INDEX rests on one asymmetric obligation: `a == b` implies equal hashes, but NOT the converse -- every candidate the hash suggests is confirmed with `==`. That is what lets `hash_value` be written conservatively: anything whose equality is subtle (every float carrier, `SharedStruct`, channel ends, closures) hashes to its DISCRIMINANT ALONE, so those keys share one bucket and degrade to a linear scan -- which is exactly the behaviour being removed here, so an under-hashed key type is slow, never wrong. Only OVER-hashing could lose an entry, so no arm hashes anything the matching arm of `PartialEq for Value` does not compare. Floats are the sharpest case (IEEE equality: `NaN != NaN`, `0.0 == -0.0`) and are unreachable as keys anyway -- `Map[f64, _]` is rejected at typecheck as not `Hash`. `Struct` fields and `EnumData::Struct` payloads live in a `HashMap`, so their per-field hashes are XOR-combined to stay order-independent.

REGRESSION SURFACE MEASURED, because Arc-backing changes how storage is shared and only `deep_clone_value` at binding sites keeps two bindings independent. Both full suites are green (`cargo test` and `cargo test --features llvm`, zero failures). A 40-file interp-vs-JIT parity sweep over map/set-using katas agrees 26/26 on every file that completes under both backends; the 14 that do not are BENCH files whose interpreter arm still exceeds 40 s, and the 15 apparent "divergences" in a first pass were an artifact of that sweep masking `timeout`'s exit status behind a pipe -- re-run with the status checked, nothing diverges. A baseline sweep on the pre-change compiler produced the identical set, confirming none of it is new.

HOW MUCH THIS ROW'S OWN EXAMPLE GAINS, measured rather than assumed, because the row's "WHY IT MATTERS" leans on it: kata #294's differential runs 234 s before and 168 s after on the same machine -- a real 1.4x, not an order of magnitude. Its memo map holds ~1492 entries over ~8900 calls, so the scan was never where its time went; that kata is dominated by general tree-walk overhead. The 58x figure above is what MAP-BOUND work gains. The row's claim that "essentially all of that difference is memo lookups scanning a list" does not survive measurement, and the coverage that kata cut (exhaustive band 14 -> 12) is not restored by this fix alone.

Pinned by nine E2E tests in tests/interpreter.rs -- insertion order, overwrite-keeps-position, survivors-findable-after-remove (the case a stale index breaks silently), value-semantics for `Map`, `Set`, and a map inside a struct field, the `entry`/`or_insert` slot chain, distinct tuple keys sharing a bucket, and a 400-key volume case -- plus four unit tests in src/interpreter/value.rs, of which `hash_value_agrees_with_equality` is the one guarding the whole design.
title: THE INTERPRETER'S `Map`/`Set` ARE ASSOCIATION LISTS, so every `get`/`insert`/`contains` is a LINEAR SCAN and any map-keyed program is QUADRATIC under `karac run --interp` -- measured 4x per doubling against codegen's flat line, and design.md documents O(1) lookup
detail:
REPRESENTATION. `src/interpreter/value.rs`: `Map(Vec<(Value, Value)>)`. Lookup is `entries.iter().find(|(k, _)| *k == idx)` (`eval_expr.rs`) and insert is `m.iter().position(|(k, _)| *k == key)` (`method_call_map.rs`) -- an association list, no hashing at all. `Set` shares the shape. Codegen, by contrast, emits a real open-addressed table with a per-key hash fn (`src/codegen/synth.rs`, `maps.rs`).

MEASURED. Insert n integer keys, then look up all n. Interpreter: n=1000 0.65 s, n=2000 2.02 s, n=4000 7.16 s, n=8000 27.51 s -- ratios 3.1x, 3.5x, 3.8x per doubling, converging on the 4x that means quadratic. The same program built with `karac build` reports 0.00 s at n=8000. So this is not the interpreter's usual constant factor; it is a different complexity class, and the gap widens without bound.

WHAT THE SPEC SAYS. design.md § Map, on `Entry[K, V]`: "`entry` provides O(1) lookup with an in-place update path that avoids double-hashing and key cloning" -- double-hashing being a cost the interpreter cannot incur, because it never hashes once.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND SPEED. `karac run --interp` is one of the four surfaces every kata must agree on (kara-katas CLAUDE.md: run vs build vs auto-par build, and the tree-walk arm is the diligence lane). A quadratic `Map` silently caps what that surface can verify: kata #294's differential -- memoized game-tree search keyed by board string -- had to have its exhaustive band cut from length 14 to length 12 (32,767 boards to 8,191) purely to finish under the interpreter, and the single-run spine trimmed from 22 to 18. The interpreter run costs ~3 minutes where the compiled one costs 1.4 seconds, and essentially all of that difference is memo lookups scanning a list. Every memoization kata pays this, and each one quietly shrinks its own coverage to compensate.

SCOPE / SEVERITY. No wrong answers -- the association list is correct, just slow -- so this is `perf`, not `miscompile`. Medium rather than low because it is a complexity-class divergence from both the spec and the other backend, and because it degrades a mandated verification surface rather than merely a convenience one.

RELATED. B-2026-08-21-6 covers a different divergence in the same pair of implementations -- codegen's hasher is not the spec's seeded SipHash13, and the interpreter's insertion-ordered iteration falls out of exactly the association list documented here. One fix (give the interpreter a real hash map with the spec's default hasher) would close both, but they are separate defects and either could be fixed without the other.

CORRECTION (at fix time): the cause analysis above is half right. The linear scan is real but secondary; the DOMINANT cost was `Env::get`'s deep clone of the whole container on every method-receiver read, which made insert quadratic with no lookups involved. See the fix note for the two measurements that separate them.

CORRECTION (2026-08-21, after the fix landed). This row's claim that kata #294's differential bands were cut "purely to finish under the interpreter, and essentially all of that time is memo lookups scanning a list" is REFUTED by measurement. The FIX ITSELF IS REAL AND IS NOT IN QUESTION — the integer-keyed probe this row was filed on goes from 27.51 s to 0.62 s at n = 8000. What is wrong is the attribution of the KATA's cost to it. Re-running kata #294's differential unchanged against the fixed interpreter:

    band 12/10/18/16, before the fix   191.60 s
    band 12/10/18/16, after  the fix   215.28 s
    band 13/10/18/16, after  the fix   440.92 s

(The two 12-band runs are from different container instances; read them as unchanged, not as a regression.) The bands could not be restored and were left at 12/10/18/16. What dominates that file under the tree-walk interpreter is `next_states` building a fresh successor `String` per node, which no map change touches. The same holds for the kata's bench workload, which still exceeds ten minutes under `--interp` after the fix.

The note is appended here rather than left in the kata alone because a closed row is read later as evidence, and this one carried a causal claim nobody had tested. kata #294's README and its differential and bench headers have been corrected to match.

title: design.md WRITES SYNTAX THE PARSER HAS NO PRODUCTION FOR, in two places syntax.md also disagrees with: the inline associated-type binding `Trait[Assoc = T]` (43 lines of design.md, and syntax.md's own comment at :650) has no form in `TRAIT_BOUND = PATH [ "[" TYPE_LIST "]" ]`, and an effect clause on an impl header (`impl From[E] for A with writes(Log) {`) has no form at all
detail:
FOUND BY the new design.md conformance sweep (scripts/design-conformance.py), which feeds every ```kara block in the spec to `karac check`. Both of these are parse-phase rejections of syntax the spec writes as ordinary v1 surface.

(1) INLINE ASSOCIATED-TYPE BINDING. design.md writes `Iterator[Item = T]` throughout -- 43 lines, including the Vec/Map/SortedMap stdlib method tables (`fn extend[I: Iterator[Item = T]](...)`, `fn keys(ref self) -> impl Iterator[Item = ref K]`). syntax.md's own commentary uses it too, at :650 (`trait IteratorOver[T] = Iterator[Item = T];`). But syntax.md:2168 defines `TRAIT_BOUND = PATH [ "[" TYPE_LIST "]" ]` -- a plain type list, with no `IDENT = TYPE` production -- and the parser rejects the form with `Expected RightBracket, found Equal`. The sanctioned spelling is the WHERE-CLAUSE constraint at syntax.md:375 (`TYPE "." IDENT "=" TYPE`), and it works: `fn take_all[I: Src](it: I) -> i64 where I.Item = i64` is accepted. So three artifacts disagree -- design.md and syntax.md's prose use the inline form, syntax.md's grammar does not define it, and the compiler implements the grammar. Either the grammar gains the production or design.md's 43 lines are rewritten; the row exists because right now no two of the three agree.

(2) EFFECT CLAUSE ON AN IMPL HEADER. design.md:3817 writes `impl From[ParseError] for AppError with writes(Log) {`. The parser rejects it with `Expected LeftBrace, found With` -- there is no effect clause in the impl-header production. Reduced: `impl From[A] for B with panics { fn from(a: A) -> B { return B {}; } }` fails the same way.

NOT DEFERRED. deferred.md's two `Item =` hits are both about GENERIC TAITs (`type Iter[T] = impl Iterator[Item = T];`), a different feature; nothing defers the bound form or the impl-header effect clause. Trait aliases, by contrast, ARE handled as deferred.md promises -- `trait Sortable[T] = Ord + Clone;` parses, so that half of the section is fine.

REPRO. `scripts/design-conformance.py --only 'Iterator[Item ='` and `--only 'impl From[ParseError]'`.

TWO MORE OF THE SAME SHAPE, added after triaging the conformance baseline. Both are forms design.md writes and syntax.md's grammar does not define, so the parser rejecting them is consistent with the grammar and inconsistent with the prose:

(3) `_` IN TYPE-ARGUMENT POSITION. design.md writes `x as Tensor[f32, _]`, `y as Tensor[bf16, _]` (:2340, :2343), `Map[F64, _]` (:2289) and `.collect[Vec[_]]()` (:1898). syntax.md:2060's TYPE production lists PATH_TYPE / TUPLE_TYPE / POINTER_TYPE / FUNCTION_TYPE / DYN_TYPE / `Never` / `ref T` / `mut ref T` / `weak T` / `()` -- no `_`. Probed: `let v: Vec[_] = [1i64, 2i64];` gives `Expected type, found Underscore`.

(4) `=>` AS LOGICAL IMPLICATION IN A CONTRACT. design.md:4215 writes `impl invariant not self.stops.is_empty() => self.direction != Direction.Idle`. syntax.md's CONTRACT production (:407) is `requires EXPR | ensures ( IDENT ) EXPR`, and its predicate grammar (REFINEMENT_PRED / PURE_EXPR, :982) has arithmetic, comparison and `&&`/`||` but no implication; `=>` appears in the grammar only in match arms (:1307) and provider bindings (:1048). Probed: the same invariant WITHOUT the `=>` clause parses and reaches the typechecker, so it is the operator and not the `impl invariant` form that is missing.

THREE MORE, moved here from B-2026-08-21-11 when its doc bugs were fixed and the leftovers turned out not to be doc bugs:

(5) `ref` AS AN EXPRESSION PREFIX. design.md's Temporary Lifetime Rules write `let r = ref some_function();` for the binding-extension rule. syntax.md has `"ref" TYPE` (:2066) and `ref` as a CAPTURE_MODE (:1612) -- no expression form -- and the parser rejects it.

(6) `ref` IN A PATTERN. design.md documents it twice -- `Foo { ref name, score }` for partial moves in match arms, and `ref x @ PATTERN` -- but syntax.md:1344's PATTERN and :1355's FIELD_PATTERN have no `ref` alternative, and the parser rejects it.

(7) `get_unchecked`'s RETURN TYPE, and the missing way to build a `ref`. design.md's bounds-check section calls it "an `unsafe fn` returning `ref T`" and its example writes `unsafe { &*ptr.offset(n as isize) }`. Probed: the implementation returns `T` (`unary '*' ... found 'i64'`), and `&` is not an operator -- `*p.offset(n)` is accepted, `&*p.offset(n)` is `Expected expression, found Amp`. So neither half of the documented shape can be written, and which half is wrong is a language decision: either `get_unchecked` returns `ref T` and the language needs a reference-forming expression, or the doc should say `T`.

TWO MORE, from the signature rung added for B-2026-08-21-28 -- the first pass that fed design.md's bodiless declaration tables to the compiler instead of setting them aside:

(8) `with` BEFORE `->`. design.md's Return-position `impl Trait` section writes the effect clause ahead of the return type, and annotates the two lines as meaning different things:

        fn iter_lines(path: String)
            with allocates(Heap)                       // execution effects
            -> impl Iterator[Item = String] with reads(FileSystem) panics

    Reduced, with nothing else in play: `fn f(x: i64) with panics -> i64 { x }` is `Expected LeftBrace, found Arrow`; `fn f(x: i64) -> i64 with panics { x }` is accepted. syntax.md is consistent with the parser -- every signature it writes puts `->` first (:444, :454, :688, :712, :996, :1552) -- so this is design.md alone. Both blocks in that section (:6864, :6912) are written the failing way, and the prose depends on the split: the `with` line is described as the function's own effects and the `->` line's trailing `with` as the existential's method-use effects. Reordering to `-> R with E1 with E2` has no obvious meaning, so the fix is a decision about the grammar, not a mechanical doc edit.

(9) AN OPAQUE FOREIGN TYPE MUST CARRY THE C NAME, AND THE NAMING RULE FORBIDS IT. design.md:12998 writes the canonical libc example:

        unsafe extern "C" { type FILE; fn fopen(...) -> *mut FILE ... }

    Probed: ``FILE` is Const-class but opaque foreign type names must be Type-class (PascalCase); consider renaming to `File``. The same block with `File` compiles. But an opaque FOREIGN type is not Kāra's to name -- it stands for a C library's `FILE`, and the suggestion to rename it silently proposes a different C symbol. The casing lint is right for Kāra-declared types and wrong here; either `extern` type declarations are exempt, or the language needs a link-name attribute so the Kāra-side name can differ from the foreign one. design.md documents neither.

fix:
FIXED by 5fee766 (`is_sorted`), 820175a (`Vec.from_fn`), 87a90e6 (`to_ne_bytes`) and 41f7b70 (`.discriminant()`).

All four entry points implemented, each through typecheck + the interpreter + codegen, and each verified byte-identical on interp / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT.

`Vec.is_sorted()` (5fee766) -- also on `Slice` and `Array`. Non-strict ascending; 0 or 1 elements is vacuously sorted. Codegen compares adjacent pairs through the same `karac_cmp_<T>` family `sort` uses rather than an open-coded `<=`, which is what keeps the answer from drifting from the interpreter's `value_compare` OR from the order `sort` just produced: an open-coded signed compare reads `[1u64, u64::MAX]` as descending. The close-paren element stash `sort`/`sorted` used gained a `Slice` and an `Array` leg it never had -- `sort` only reorders in place, so `is_sorted` is the first sequence method whose ANSWER depends on element signedness, and both receivers answered `false` for an ascending `u64` pair before the stash. An IEEE float element is refused as `sort` refuses it, with a measured `is_sorted`-specific note: with the gate lifted, `[1.0, NaN].is_sorted()` answered TRUE on all four surfaces while `a[0] <= a[1]` on the same pair answered false. design.md's contracts example -- `requires haystack.is_sorted()` and `invariant self.data.is_sorted()` -- now compiles and runs.

`Vec.from_fn(n, f)` (820175a). The index parameter is seeded as `i64` before the function argument is inferred, or the spec's own `|i| i * 2` fails inside its body; the element type is then the function's RETURN. Codegen must settle the element type BEFORE the allocation, since the buffer is sized and strided at `sizeof(elem)` -- an annotation wins, otherwise `infer_expr_llvm_type` answers or declines. A heap element also needed the f-string accumulator disarmed, exactly as `Vec.push` disarms it: without that the last iteration's allocation had two owners ("free(): double free detected in tcache 2" under AOT and JIT, correct under `--interp`), pinned under ASAN with the disarm removed as a positive control. Only the INLINE-closure form lowers, the same deferral `Vec.retain` reports.

`to_ne_bytes()` (87a90e6) -- on every integer scalar, not just `u16`. Returns `Array[u8, N]`, not `Vec[u8]`, which is what makes design.md's `Hasher` body work as written: the fixed array coerces to the `ref Slice[u8]` that `write` declares, and allocates nothing. Codegen lowers it as store-then-reload, so the answer IS native order by construction and no endianness constant is baked in. Three codegen gaps had to close for the value to be usable, all about a fixed array that is not a named binding: an unannotated `let b = n.to_ne_bytes()` had no registered element type and striding at the i64 default SEGFAULTED when handed to a slice parameter; a fixed-array RVALUE at a call boundary reached the callee as a raw `[N x i8]` and failed module verification; and `arg_is_array_source` recognized only named bindings, so B-2026-06-19-1's `ref Slice[T]` carve-out skipped every temporary.

`<enum>.discriminant()` (pre-rebase) -- on C-like (payload-free) enums, returning the repr type: `u8` for `#[repr(u8)]`, `i32` for `#[repr(i32)]`, conservative `u32` with no `#[repr]`. THE ANSWER IS NOT THE TAG: codegen lays these enums out at declaration positions 0/1/2 (design.md is explicit that declared discriminants are not layout commitments at v1), so `UsbClass { Audio = 0x01, Hid = 0x03, MassStorage = 0x08 }` must answer 1/3/8 from tags 0/1/2. Both backends map tag to declared value; the values are folded ONCE, in the typechecker (`TypeCheckResult::enum_discriminants`), because a declared discriminant may be a constant expression and two independent folds is exactly how the backends would come to disagree. Payload enums are excluded -- the spec's own v1 restriction -- with a diagnostic that names the reason and the hand-written `fn tag(ref self)` remedy design.md recommends.

FOUND BY the design.md conformance sweep. These are defects in the SPEC's examples, not in the compiler -- in each case the compiler is right and the prose is wrong -- but they are worth a row because design.md is the authoritative artifact and a reader copying these lines gets a parse error.

(1) HARD KEYWORDS USED AS IDENTIFIERS. syntax.md §1.1 lists `lock` under Ownership and `group` under Layout, and says at :129 that all keywords are reserved without the `r#` escape. design.md then writes `mu.lock().get(key)` in four blocks (:2554, :2569, :2583, :10005 -- the temporary-lifetime rules for `if let` / `let...else` / `while let`) and `let group = TaskGroup.new()` in two (:9228, :9601). Neither can be written. `lock` in particular is not an accident of reservation: syntax.md:1577 defines `LOCK_EXPR = "lock" IDENT [ IDENT ] BLOCK`, so `lock mu { ... }` IS the language's lock form and `mu.lock()` is Rust idiom that leaked into the spec's own worked examples for a different feature.

(2) `=` FOR A LABELED ARGUMENT. design.md:2090 writes `raw_prices.fillna(0.0, treat_nan_as_null = true)`. design.md:8773 states the rule: "both arguments use Kara's labeled-argument shape, not Rust's `=`". Probed: `f(1i64, flag: true)` is accepted, `f(1i64, flag = true)` is `Expected RightParen, found Equal`. The doc contradicts itself in the same file.

(3) RUST IDIOMS THE LANGUAGE DOES NOT HAVE. design.md:4634 writes `let eth_ether_type: [u8; 2] = b"\x08\x00"` -- the array type here is `Array[u8, 2]` (syntax.md:927, :1802), and the line is also missing its terminating `;`. :12993 writes `if !ptr.is_null(self.raw())`; the language spells negation `not`, and the compiler has a targeted diagnostic that says exactly that. :11919 writes `unsafe { &*ptr.offset(n as isize) }` -- `&` is Rust's reference operator and does not exist here. :8437, :8449 and :8467 write `AstNode.Lit { value: v * 2, .. }` with a BARE `..`, where syntax.md:1774's STRUCT_LITERAL requires `"." "." EXPR` -- a base value to take the remaining fields from. (The functional-update feature is separately broken even when written correctly -- see B-2026-08-21-12.)

(4) COMMA-SEPARATED EFFECT ITEMS. :10385, :10409 and :13139 write `with reads(UserStore), writes(Display)` and `with sends(Network), receives(Network), suspends`. Effect items are space-separated; the compiler's diagnostic is `effect items are space-separated, not comma-separated; remove the ','`.

(5) EXAMPLES THAT DO NOT TYPECHECK AS WRITTEN. :11300's bounds-check-elision example mixes `i64` and `usize` in `xs[i]` and applies unary `*` to a non-pointer. :12662's `pub extern "C" fn double` has a body that panics and a signature with no `with panics`, which the effect checker requires -- the block exists to explain panic semantics across the C boundary, and cannot be compiled to demonstrate them. :8575 carries a stray double semicolon (`let c = Mutex(Counter { val: 0 });;`) and a trailing `;` on a `par struct` declaration. :4296 writes `({ balance: self.balance - amount }, amount)` -- an anonymous record literal; struct literals here are `Name { ... }`.

WITHDRAWN FROM THIS ROW. An earlier revision listed design.md:13651's `let pattern = r"\d{3}-\d{4}";` as a fifth doc bug, on the grounds that :4649 says `r` is "reserved but not yet implemented". That was wrong: :13651 sits under design.md's own **Deferred Items** section, under the heading `Raw String Literals`, with `**Why deferred:**` and `**Design shape:**` markers. Illustrating future syntax in a roadmap section is not a defect. The conformance suite now classifies every block under a Deferred-Items heading as `deferred` rather than as a divergence, which removed 13 blocks from the failing set.

MINOR, NOT FILED SEPARATELY: design.md:4649 also specifies the wording of that lex error as `string prefix 'r' is reserved but not yet implemented`; the lexer emits `string prefix 'r"..."' is reserved for future use; only f"..." and c"..." are recognized in v1`. The implemented message is arguably the better one, so this is noted rather than filed.

Each of these blocks is recorded in docs/design-conformance-baseline.json with reason `DOC BUG`, so fixing the prose clears them from the baseline.

CLOSING NOTE -- the auto-triage that produced this row's list was too eager. It keyed on the compiler's `'X' is a reserved keyword` diagnostic and called every hit a doc bug, without asking whether the keyword was being used AS THE LANGUAGE INTENDS. Seven of the 29 were not doc bugs at all: four inline-assembly blocks documenting reserved-for-future syntax, and three writing forms syntax.md has no production for. Both are legitimate things for a spec to contain, and editing them would have deleted documented features to satisfy a parser. Each was checked against syntax.md's grammar before being touched, and the seven were moved rather than rewritten.

title: FOUR FORMS syntax.md OR design.md DEFINES THAT THE FRONT END REJECTS -- `let...else` (a named production, LET_ELSE_STATEMENT), struct functional update `Name { f: v, ..base }` (in the STRUCT_LITERAL production; it PARSES and the typechecker then ignores the base), lint-level attributes on a statement (`#[expect(deprecated)] old_api();`), and a sub-range mutable slice argument (`f(mut v[1..4])`, design.md's own § Slices line)
detail:
FOUND BY the design.md conformance sweep and each confirmed with a reduced probe. These differ from B-2026-08-21-9: there the grammar does not define the form either, so at least the documents are only in a two-way disagreement. Here syntax.md or design.md DOES define it and the implementation does not have it.

(1) `let...else`. syntax.md:1115: `LET_ELSE_STATEMENT = "let" [ "mut" ] PATTERN "=" EXPR "else" BLOCK ";"`, listed at :1098 as a STATEMENT alternative, and design.md gives it a section heading of its own ("`if let` and `let...else`"). Probe:
    let Ok(config) = load(p) else { return Err(CErr.Missing); };
  -> parse: Expected expression, found Semicolon
`if let ... else` is fine; it is the `let`-statement form that is missing.

(2) STRUCT FUNCTIONAL UPDATE. syntax.md:1774: `STRUCT_LITERAL = IDENT "{" FIELD_INIT { "," FIELD_INIT } [ "," ] [ ".." EXPR ] "}"`. Probe:
    let b = P { x: 5i64, ..a };
  -> typecheck: missing field 'y' in struct 'P'
This one is the interesting failure of the four: it PARSES. The `.. EXPR` tail is consumed and then dropped, so the typechecker sees a literal with a missing field. A form that parses and is silently discarded is worse than one that is rejected -- there is no diagnostic pointing at the unimplemented feature, only a confusing complaint about the field the base was supposed to supply.

(3) LINT-LEVEL ATTRIBUTES ON A STATEMENT. design.md documents `#[allow(<lint>)]` as per-binding and per-statement in several places (e.g. :1444 and :1453, `#[allow(module_mut_binding)]` "per-binding, not module-wide") and has a § Lint Level Attributes. Probe:
    fn migrate_caller() { #[expect(deprecated)] old_api(); }
  -> parse: attribute `#[expect]` is not valid on a loop expression; only `#[par_order_free]` is recognized
The parser accepts an attribute block only immediately before a `while` / `for` / `loop`, so no lint level can be set on a statement or a binding at all.

(4) SUB-RANGE MUTABLE SLICE ARGUMENT. design.md § Slices writes both lines verbatim:
    sort_in_place(mut v);            // ref mut Vec[i64] coerces to mut Slice[i64]
    sort_in_place(mut v[1..4]);      // sub-range mutable slice
The first is accepted. The second gives `expected 'mut Slice[T]', found 'Slice[i64]'` -- the range index produces a shared slice, and the `mut` marker does not carry through it.

SCOPE. None of the four is under design.md's Deferred Items section, and none appears in deferred.md. Each is reachable from ordinary code: (1) and (3) are everyday ergonomics, (2) is a silent-drop hazard, and (4) is the documented way to sort part of a vector in place.

ITEM (4) IS ALREADY FIXED, detected automatically. On the next `git pull` the conformance gate reported `FIXED 4602 [Module-Level Bindings > Slices] — remove from the baseline`, and a reduced probe confirms it: `sort_in_place(mut v[1..4])` is now accepted. The block has been dropped from docs/design-conformance-baseline.json (94 -> 93 entries). The row stays OPEN for items (1) `let...else`, (2) struct functional update, and (3) statement lint attributes.

Worth recording as the suite's first live catch: the block was not re-probed by hand or remembered by anyone — the gate noticed a baseline entry had started passing and said so.

ITEM (1) IS FIXED — and the diagnosis in this row was half wrong, which is worth recording. `let...else` is not missing: it is FULLY IMPLEMENTED, with 210 handling sites across the compiler and its own behaviour tests in `tests/interpreter.rs` and `tests/codegen.rs`. The parser simply stopped at the else block's closing brace and never looked for the `;`, so the spelling BOTH documents write failed with `Expected expression, found Semicolon` while the undocumented semicolon-less form compiled and ran. A feature implemented end to end and unreachable as written down — which is why the row read as "the front end rejects it".

THE FIX ACCEPTS BOTH SPELLINGS rather than requiring the `;`, deliberately. syntax.md:1115 writes it as required, so matching the grammar exactly would mean REJECTING the form this compiler's own tests are written in (`test_let_else_match_and_diverge`, `test_e2e_let_else_binds_then_else_diverges`). Whether a block-tailed binding takes a terminator is a language decision, not a defect, and it is not one to make by breaking the authors' own tests in a bug-fix commit. Accepting both removes the divergence without deciding it; tightening to required later is a one-word change in `src/parser/stmts.rs` plus those two tests, and the code comment there says so.

The conformance gate confirmed it without being asked: `FIXED 2530 [Module-Level Bindings > `if let` and `let...else`] — remove from the baseline`. Baseline 93 -> 92. Items (2) struct functional update and (3) statement lint attributes remain open; item (4), the sub-range mutable slice, was fixed upstream earlier.

ITEM (2) — THE SILENT DROP IS CLOSED; THE FEATURE IS NOT. `P { x: 1, ..base }` now gets one targeted diagnostic instead of a misleading `missing field 'y'`:

    error[E_STRUCT_LITERAL_SPREAD_UNSUPPORTED]: struct 'P' literal has a spread base
    (`..base`), which is parsed but NOT applied — no field is copied from the base.
    copy the remaining field explicitly instead: `y: <base>.y`.

The message names each absent field so the rewrite is mechanical, and the missing-field cascade is suppressed so one mistake produces one error. With every field already explicit the base is inert rather than lossy, and the message says that instead ("the base has no effect — drop it"); it is still an error, because accepting it would keep implying the base means something.

WHY A DIAGNOSTIC AND NOT AN IMPLEMENTATION. The phases disagree, and dangerously: the PARSER stores the base (`ExprKind::StructLiteral { spread: Option<Box<Expr>> }`), the INTERPRETER fully implements the copy (`eval_struct_literal`, including `SharedStruct` and weak-handle re-storing), and CODEGEN binds `{ path, fields, .. }` and never reads it. Fixing only the typechecker would therefore have turned a compile error into a RUN-VS-BUILD MISCOMPILE — `karac run --interp` copying the base while `karac build` left those fields unwritten. Today there is no such divergence only because the form is unreachable unless it is redundant: `P { x: 1, y: 2, ..a }` typechecked and both surfaces printed the same thing because every field was explicit. Verified before changing anything.

Implementing it properly means codegen emitting the base and copying the unmentioned fields, which is an OWNERSHIP question (who owns a spread heap field, when is the base dropped, what happens to an RC field) — the exact territory this ledger's double-free rows come from. That is a feature slice, not a bug fix, and it should not ride in on a diagnostic change. The row stays OPEN for it, and for item (3), statement lint attributes.

Tests: `tests/typechecker.rs` gains three — the spread diagnostic fires and names the field, the all-explicit case reports inertness, and a literal with NO spread still reports plain missing fields (the regression guard for the suppression).

ITEM (3) IS FIXED, AND THE ROW IS CLOSED. Statement-position lint attributes now parse and take effect: `#[allow(lint)] stmt;` pushes a lint frame around exactly that statement and pops it after, so the override covers the statement and its subexpressions and nothing following. `#[expect]` participates in the end-of-typecheck unfulfilled sweep on the same terms as an item-level one — without that, an unfulfilled statement-level expectation would have been silently accepted, which is the single outcome `#[expect]` exists to rule out.

TWO IMPLEMENTATION NOTES worth keeping. The overrides live on `Program::stmt_lint_overrides`, keyed by the statement's span, rather than on `Stmt`: `Stmt` is constructed at 191 sites across the parser, desugarer, lowering and codegen, none of which have an opinion about lints, and `Program::freeze_spans` already established the side-table pattern for exactly this reason. And the dispatch had to change in `is_statement_start`, not just `parse_statement` — a block asks that predicate first, and `#` was not a statement start, so attributed statements never reached the statement parser at all. It now scans past the attribute block: a loop keeps the expression-position path (it owns `#[par_order_free]` and a trailing `for` needs no `;`), and so do misplaced loop attributes and codegen hints, whose targeted diagnostics would otherwise have to be duplicated.

Item (2), struct functional update, is SPLIT OUT to its own row: its silent drop is fixed (3b4b97d) and what remains is implementing the feature in codegen, which is an ownership question rather than a defect. This row is closed on items (1), (3) and (4).

title: EVERY `gpu.*` REDUCTION SILENTLY DROPPED every element past 4,194,240. The twelve reduce/scan shaders recovered the thread index as `gid.x` alone and wrote their per-workgroup partial to `output[wid.x]`, but `run_compute` caps a dispatch's X extent at 65535 workgroups and spreads anything longer across grid ROWS. So above 65535*64 elements row 0 was the only row read, and the rows that did run overwrote each other's partial slots. Measured: `gpu.sum` of 5,000,000 ones answered `4194240` (exactly one row); `gpu.max` answered `1` and `gpu.argmax` `0` with the true maximum 7.0 planted in the LAST element. A wrong number with no error, on the input size the GPU path exists to serve.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while designing resident-buffer reductions (`gpu.sum(buf.field)` on a GpuBuffer handle) — reading how the reduce shader binds its input surfaced that it indexes 1-D while the dispatch core it shares is 2-D. Not reachable from any existing test: every reduction fixture in the suite is small, and the failure begins above four million elements.

WHY IT HID. The convention was already written down, on `DISPATCH_X_SPAN` in src/gpu_wgsl.rs: 'every kernel entry recovers the flat thread index as `gid.y * DISPATCH_X_SPAN + gid.x`'. The three MAP kernels (`emit_kernel`, `emit_kernel_soa`, `emit_kernel_stencil`) honour it. The reduction family added under B-2026-08-19-13 did not — its dispatches LOOK 1-D at the call site, so the 2-D spreading is an invisible consequence of the shared core rather than a visible property of the op. The tiled matmul, whose 2-D-ness IS visible, got the identical hazard right in the same work and even carries the comment '`wid.x`-only index would collide across rows' — so the knowledge was present and simply not applied where the geometry was implicit.

THE FIX is uniform across all twelve emitters: recover the flat thread index, and bind a flat workgroup number `wg = wid.y * DISPATCH_X_WORKGROUPS + wid.x` for every per-workgroup output (reduction partials, scan chunk-totals, overflow flags). Both forms degenerate to the old ones when `wid.y == 0`, so a single-row dispatch is unchanged and small buffers keep their exact previous tree order — the fix adds coverage without touching float association.

TESTS, two kinds. (1) A structural gate over every reduce/scan emitter (`every_reduction_shader_indexes_the_full_2d_dispatch_grid`) asserting both flat forms and — the load-bearing half — that NOTHING indexes by a bare `wid.x`. It counts DISTINCT emitters and fails at 12, so a new emitter cannot silently dodge it. (2) An end-to-end gate at 5,000,000 elements. It is build-only on purpose: a dispatch grid exists only on the device path, and the oracle needs no interpreter twin because every partial sum stays under 2^24, making the sum exact in f32 regardless of tree order — so it tests element COVERAGE, not association. Its three lines fail differently: the sum catches a dropped COUNT, max/argmax catch dropped DATA. Costs 0.56s.

NOT AFFECTED: `gpu.matmul` (computes its own grid via `run_compute_grid`), and the three map/dispatch/stencil kernels.

ONE CORRECTION WORTH KEEPING. The first version of the structural test demanded the flat workgroup number of ALL twelve emitters, and that rule was itself wrong: `emit_scan_offset_kernel` writes `output[i]` per THREAD and binds no `workgroup_id` at all (its int twin binds one only for the overflow flag, which the f32 form has no need of), so forming `wg` there emitted a reference to an unbound `wid` and the shader failed naga validation on the device. The E2E suite caught it; the structural test could not, because it was the thing asserting the wrong rule. The rule is now conditional — a shader must form the flat number IF it binds a workgroup id, and must never index by a bare `wid.x` either way. Worth recording because it is the general shape: a text-level gate cannot check that the text it demands is legal, so it needs an execution gate behind it.
tracker: src/gpu_wgsl.rs::DISPATCH_X_WORKGROUPS (the new constant + the rule); the twelve emitters emit_reduce_kernel / emit_int_reduce_kernel / emit_arg_kernel / emit_scan_kernel / emit_scan_offset_kernel / emit_int_scan_kernel / emit_int_scan_offset_kernel / emit_deviation_kernel / emit_int_deviation_kernel / emit_wide_fold_kernel / emit_dot_kernel / emit_int_dot_kernel; runtime twin runtime/src/gpu.rs::run_compute (x = wg.min(65535)); tests/gpu_e2e.rs::a_reduction_past_one_dispatch_row_still_sees_every_element

fix:
FIXED by c6ac12f. The warning now carries a machine-applicable DELETION of the suffix, so `karac fix` removes it.

THE CHANNEL WAS ALREADY THERE AND ALREADY READ. `cmd_fix` has consumed the WARNING fix-it channel since B-2026-08-03-9 (`src/cli/fix_cmds.rs`, the `t.warnings.iter().filter_map(|e| e.fix_it...)` arm, whose comment says a warning's fix "is by definition optional-but-safe ... which is exactly what `fix` is for"). Nothing about `karac fix` needed changing. The producer was missing for one reason: `type_lint_warning` hardcodes `fix_it: None`, so NO lint routed through it could ever advertise a fix. Split it into `type_lint_warning_with_fix`, with the old name delegating and `None`, so no other call site moved and the next lint that wants a fix has somewhere to put it.

THE EDIT IS DERIVABLE WITHOUT RE-LEXING, which is why this is small: `warn_redundant_suffix` already receives the literal's whole token span (`42i64`, `1_000i64`, `0xFFi64`, `3.14f64`) and the suffix is its tail, so the edit is the last `suffix.len()` bytes with an empty replacement. Both suffixes this lint fires on are ASCII, so byte and character length agree and the arithmetic cannot land mid-character. Guarded rather than assumed: a span not longer than the suffix would mean the token span is not what the arithmetic takes it for, and a wrong deletion is worse than none, so that case emits the warning with no fix.

SAFE BY THE LINT'S OWN PREDICATE. It fires only when the suffix names the type the literal would have had anyway, so the unsuffixed spelling infers identically. The shape worth checking was a method call on a literal -- `1i64.to_string()` becoming `1.to_string()`, where `1.` might plausibly have lexed as a float -- and it parses correctly. The float form cannot lose its point (`1f64` is already a parse error; only `3.14f64` reaches the lint), so removing `f64` leaves a float.

VERIFIED ON THE EXACT CORPUS THIS ROW MEASURED, not on a sample. Re-measuring first reproduced the row's numbers to the digit: 914 files, 853 carrying warnings, 26,094 warnings. Then every one of those 853 files was copied, fixed, and re-checked:

    853 files fixed, 26,094 suffixes deleted, 0 broke compilation, 0 warnings left

and on the 24 of them fast enough to run under the interpreter inside the harness timeout, output was byte-identical before and after. So the fix is complete over the corpus and semantics-preserving where semantics could be compared.

Pinned by three tests, all of which fail without the fix: `redundant_suffix_carries_a_suffix_deleting_fix` and `redundant_suffix_fix_spans_every_literal_spelling` (tests/typechecker.rs) assert the EDIT rather than its presence -- they read the cut back out of the source and check the byte before it is still part of the number, because an off-by-one here silently eats a digit and changes the program's value -- and `test_fix_deletes_redundant_literal_suffixes` (tests/cli.rs) drives `karac fix` end to end over underscored, hex, negative, float and in-loop literals, then asserts the rewritten file still CHECKS CLEAN, since a fix that produced a broken file would still have "applied".

THE ROW'S DEFERRED QUESTION IS STILL DEFERRED, and correctly so: whether kara-katas drops its suffixes or carries `#[allow(redundant_suffix)]` is a content decision for that repo. It is now a one-command decision rather than 26,094 hand edits, which is what this row was for. Nothing in kara-katas was changed here.
title: THE NEWLY-WIRED `redundant_suffix` LINT SHIPS WARN-BY-DEFAULT WITH NO MACHINE-APPLICABLE FIX, so `karac fix` reports `no fixable diagnostics` on a file carrying 14 of them -- and the kata corpus went from warning-clean to 26,094 warnings across 853 of its 914 `.kara` files the moment it landed
detail:
MEASURED right after `17ff5c0` / the `redundant_suffix` wiring landed (B-2026-08-20-36 -> B-2026-08-21-2). Every `.kara` file under kara-katas `leetcode/`, `bespoke/`, `backend/` and `oracle/` was run through `karac check`:

    914 files, 61 warning-clean, 26,094 `redundant_suffix` warnings

Per-file counts run 14 to 140. The corpus is written with explicit `0i64` / `1i64` suffixes throughout -- that is the house style in kara's own CLAUDE.md examples and in every kata -- so essentially none of it is warning-clean any more.

THE LINT IS NOT THE PROBLEM. It is correct: `i64` IS the default for an unsuffixed integer literal, and design.md § Numeric Semantics is what it enforces. The problem is that there is no mechanical way to act on it.

    $ karac check fixtest.kara   | grep -c redundant_suffix   ->  14
    $ karac fix   fixtest.kara                                ->  (no fixable diagnostics)
    $ karac check fixtest.kara   | grep -c redundant_suffix   ->  14

The emitted diagnostic carries `code: W0280`, `lint_name: redundant_suffix`, `class: LINT_WARNING` and NO fix/suggestion field, so `karac fix` has nothing to apply. This is not a limitation of `karac fix` in general -- earlier the same day it applied 4 fixes to kata #294's differential for the `this argument is already a mut-ref; drop the mut marker` diagnostic. The machinery works; this lint just does not feed it.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. kara's CLAUDE.md and kara-katas' CLAUDE.md both make `karac fix` the PRIMARY fix path of the Mend loop -- "apply `karac fix` for machine-applicable diagnostics as the primary fix path, feed the rest back". A lint that fires 26,094 times and is machine-applicable in principle (delete four characters at a known span) but carries no fix sends all 26,094 into the feed-it-back-to-a-model path. That is the single worst ratio of mechanical work to model work the loop has yet been handed, and it is exactly the case the fix channel exists for.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, since the span is already exact: attach a `remove-span` fix covering the suffix token. The `-D`/`#[deny]` escalation path at `src/cli/diag_json.rs:1651` already knows how to reach this diagnostic, and `src/typechecker/exprs.rs:3303`'s `warn_redundant_suffix` has the `Span` in hand.

SEPARATE QUESTION, NOT FILED HERE: whether the kata corpus should be swept to drop the suffixes or should carry `#[allow(redundant_suffix)]`. That is a content decision for kara-katas and should follow the fix landing, not precede it -- rewriting 26,094 literals by hand before a machine fix exists would be doing the compiler's work in the wrong repo.

SECOND-ORDER EFFECT, hit immediately. The corpus's standard four-surface check compares `karac run --interp` / `karac run` / `karac build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` by hashing each one's output with `2>&1` — stderr merged in, because a diagnostic that appears on one surface and not another IS a divergence worth catching. Since this lint landed, the two `karac run` surfaces emit compile warnings on stderr and the two prebuilt-binary surfaces do not, so every kata in the corpus now reports a false run-vs-build divergence under that idiom. Observed on kata #294's differential: `2>&1` gave jit=c33f7563… against build=seq=84d2b0bf…, and stdout-only gave all three identical. The check has to be narrowed to stdout, which costs the surface-specific-diagnostic signal it was merging stderr to get.

fix:
FIXED by 2a12881 (same commit that surfaced it).

The gate now filters with the hoisted `kind_is_note`, so note-severity effect findings never fail a multi-file build.
title: The MULTI-FILE build gate failed the build on ANY effect-checker entry, including NOTE-severity ones: `run_multi_file_codegen` tested `!e.errors.is_empty()` with NO kind filtering at all, so an advisory finding aborted the build with `error[effect]` and `1 error(s) found`. Latent since `FfiLintHint` existed -- that hint would have tripped it too -- and unhit only because no multi-file fixture declares an `extern` that triggers one.
detail:
FOUND BY the self-host oracle (`selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run`) while wiring `mutual_recursion_note` (B-2026-08-21-2), NOT by a targeted probe. The self-hosted compiler is full of legitimate mutual recursion -- a recursive-descent parser and a recursive emitter -- so the new note fired ELEVEN times across `parser.kara` and `codegen.kara`, every one rendered `error[effect]`, and the port-regression check reported "self-hosted emitter FAILED TO COMPILE".

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE NEW LINT: the single-file paths all filtered advisory kinds; only the multi-file path did not. So the same program could pass `karac check` as one file and fail to build as a package, purely on a diagnostic that is documented as "never a compile error". That is a run-vs-build-class divergence in the shape B-2026-08-05-17 and B-2026-07-31-29 each fixed for a different phase.

SOURCE NOTE: the pre-existing half of the seventeen-site `!= FfiLintHint` duplication catalogued in B-2026-08-21-2. The other sixteen were merely inconsistent; this one was WRONG on its own terms before any change in that commit.

fix:
FIXED by fa8a940.

The resolver had no notion of a non-fatal diagnostic -- every `ResolveError` was fatal -- so a diagnostic the spec calls a warning could only be spelled as an error. Adds `resolver::resolve_kind_is_note` (the resolver twin of `effectchecker::kind_is_note`) plus a `LayoutUnassignedFields` kind, and routes EVERY gate through the one predicate: `has_resolve_errors`, `total_errors`, the text renderer (`warning[resolve]`), the JSON code table (W0150), and `resolve_ok` in the test harness. The emit site now also reads `#[allow(layout_unassigned_fields)]` off the layout item's attributes, the way `ownership.rs` reads `rc_fallback`.

W0150 is the resolver's FIRST warning code, which broke two explain band checks asserting resolver codes start with `E01`/`E08` -- an encoding of "the resolver only mints errors". The band exists to stop numeric collision with the typechecker's E02xx, and W0150 is in the resolver's own 01xx band, so both checks now accept `W01` and the code is catalogued so `karac explain W0150` answers.

Verified: unannotated -> `warning[resolve]`, check and build exit 0, binary produced and runs; annotated -> silent. Two regression tests.
title: A SPEC-LEGAL PROGRAM FAILED TO COMPILE: `layout_unassigned_fields` was emitted as a hard `ResolveError`, so any `layout` block not naming every field made `karac build` exit 1 with NO binary -- though design.md defines unlisted fields as collecting into an implicit trailing hot group and calls the diagnostic a WARNING. The `#[allow(layout_unassigned_fields)]` escape hatch the diagnostic's OWN suggestion text named was never read, so it did nothing.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while evaluating `implicit_clone` for B-2026-08-21-2, not by a targeted probe -- the first layout fixture written to test a DIFFERENT lint failed to compile.

BOTH HALVES WERE KNOWN AND UNIMPLEMENTED: `src/resolver/collect.rs` carried `// TODO: Implement proper warning severity and #[allow(layout_unassigned_fields)].` directly above the emit. The user-visible effect is worse than a missing lint -- the compiler printed a suggestion telling the user to apply an attribute that had no effect, so following the diagnostic's own advice did not unblock the build.

WHY HIGH: it makes a DOCUMENTED language affordance unusable. design.md's implicit-trailing-hot-group rule cannot be relied on at all -- every layout block must enumerate every field or the program does not build, and no suppression works.

CLASS NOTE: `false-positive` -- a diagnostic firing at a severity the spec does not assign to it, rejecting a legal program.

fix:
FIXED by 3e84931.

`selfhost/src/lexer.kara` gains the `b"` arm, `selfhost/src/token.kara` the
`Token.ByteString(Vec[u8])` variant, and `selfhost/src/main.kara` the

boundary and the record of committing it was lost, so a later attempt to
