checked against a concrete slot (so `Vec.new()` in a generic enum variant
could infer its element). Worth doing if that shape ever shows up.

FIXED by 69be64c.

FIXED IN TWO PLACES, because the bound turned out to be undischarged from TWO
call paths and the second one is where the spec's own motivating example lives.

(1) THE MISSING CONSTRAINT ARM. `discharge_assoc_type_eq_bounds` in
`typechecker/exprs.rs`, called from `discharge_type_bounds` right beside the
`ProjectionBound` sibling the row's reading pointed at. Its shape is that
sibling's, deliberately: build the projection the constraint names
(`AssocProjection { param: "I", assoc: "Item" }`), substitute the call's
solutions into it -- which rewrites the receiver from the type-param name to
the concrete type's bare name, via the `AssocProjection` arm of
`substitute_type_params` that already existed for GAT slice 5 -- resolve it
through `impl_assoc_types`, and compare. Only the last step differs: an
equality constraint compares TYPES (`types_compatible`) where a projection
bound asks `type_satisfies_bound`.

Two details worth keeping. The REQUIRED side is lowered against the function's
FULL type-param list, not just the solved ones: `solutions` holds only the
params inference pinned, so a reference to an as-yet-unsolved sibling would
lower as an undefined type and emit a spurious diagnostic on a line the user
did not write. And either side that has not bottomed out in a concrete type
(an unresolved projection, a bare param, an inference var, an error) is
SKIPPED rather than reported -- the sibling's "discharge only when fully
resolvable" rule. An unsolved receiver already has the unsolved-`T`
diagnostic, and an impl-table miss means the `I: Src` bound itself failed and
has its own error; reporting here too would only cascade.

The diagnostic names both sides, because "bound not satisfied" alone leaves
the reader to go find the impl:

  error[E_WHERE_CLAUSE_ASSOC_TYPE_EQ_NOT_SATISFIED]: associated-type bound
  `I.Item = i64` is not satisfied; `Ss` has `Item = String`

When the required side is a type parameter solved from another argument
(`where I.Item = T`), the message renders the SOLVED type, not `T` -- which is
the more useful half of the pair.

(2) THE METHOD CALL PATH, which discharged NOTHING. Fixing (1) and re-probing
showed `h.take(Ss {})` still accepted. The cause is not specific to this
constraint: `method_user_impl.rs` called the thin
`check_call_args_with_substitution` wrapper, which passes `None` for the
callee's where clause -- so a method discharged no bound of ANY class. Plain
`T: Marker`, projection bounds, const predicates and this row's assoc-eq alike
were all unenforced on a method call while the free-function path
(`expr_call.rs`, which always passed its clause) rejected the same program.
MEASURED as its own defect before fixing:

  fn free[T: Marker](x: T) -> i64 { 0 }                   // rejects NotMarked
  impl Holder { fn take[T: Marker](ref self, x: T) -> i64 { 0 } }
  h.take(NotMarked {})                                    // ACCEPTED

The wrapper call is now `check_call_args_with_substitution_full` with
`sig.where_clause` and `sig.generic_params`, both already on `FunctionSig` and
already in scope at that site. `apply_call_site_marker` stays `false` (the
`mut` marker rule is free-function-only per design.md) and
`explicit_generic_args` stays `None` (no turbofish surface on this dispatch).

WHY BOTH LANDED TOGETHER rather than the second being deferred. design.md's
motivating spelling for this bound is `fn extend[I: Iterator[Item = T]]` -- a
METHOD. Fixing only free functions would have left the constraint unenforced
in exactly the position it is written, which is the shape of a fix that reads
as complete and is not. The second defect is filed as its own row
(B-2026-08-22-9) because its evidence, class and blast radius are its own.

BLAST RADIUS, measured rather than assumed, since this tightening turns
previously-accepted programs into errors: the full default suite is 0 failures
and all 917 `.kara` files in the kata corpus still typecheck clean. That the
compiler's own corpus never leaned on the hole is the reason both halves could
land in one commit.

TESTS (`tests/typechecker.rs`), each in both directions -- satisfied accepted,
violated rejected: the row's verbatim repro; the diagnostic naming both sides;
the inline `Src[Item = i64]` spelling (through the `*_desugared` helpers,
since `desugar_program` is what rewrites it onto this constraint); a type-param
RHS solved from a sibling argument; a generic RHS (`Vec[i64]` vs
`Vec[String]`, so the comparison is structural rather than by name); and both
halves on the method path. Non-vacuity checked by reverting each half
independently: dropping the discharge fails all six assoc-eq tests and leaves
the pre-existing acceptance test green; dropping only the method wiring fails
exactly the two method tests and no others.
title: AN ASSOCIATED-TYPE-EQUALITY BOUND IS NEVER DISCHARGED AT CALL SITES -- `where I.Item = i64` is validated at the DECLARATION and then ignored, so a call passing an `I` whose `Item` is `String` is accepted; the bound does not bind

fix:
FIXED by 02e73282.

`TypeKind::ImplTrait` and `TypeKind::Dyn` gain an `assoc_bindings: Vec<AssocBinding>` field, kept separate from `args` for the same reason `TraitBound::assoc_bindings` is: a binding is not a positional argument. The parser reaches it through `parse_trait_path_with_bindings` (src/parser/types.rs), which wraps `parse_path_type` in the same save/enable/drain dance `parse_trait_bound` uses -- so the form is legal exactly where a TRAIT is named and `Vec[Item = i64]` stays the parse error it was. A binding's RHS gets the `NestedGenericArg` block, so `Src[Item = impl Foo]` is rejected like `Vec[impl T]`.

The two positions are DIFFERENT MECHANISMS, which is what the row asked to settle:

  - ARGUMENT position lowers onto the existing where-clause machinery. `desugar_impl_trait_args_in_function` is already giving the parameter a name, and a binding on a named parameter IS `WhereConstraint::AssocTypeEq` -- emitted directly rather than left on the synthetic bound, because `hoist_assoc_bindings_in_program` is the FIRST pass in `desugar_program` and has already run. Measured equivalent to the explicit `where T.Item = i64` spelling, including where both are still lax (that laxness is B-2026-08-22-3's, not this row's).

  - RETURN position has no name to constrain, so the binding rides the existential: `Type::Existential` gains `assoc_bindings: Vec<(String, Type)>`. It does two things, one per side of the abstraction barrier. CALLER side it de-opaques the projection -- `dispatch_trait_assoc_fn` substitutes `Self -> TypeParam(target)`, so a method declared `-> Self.Item` comes back as `Src.Item`, keyed on the TRAIT, which resolves to nothing; measured, `let x = make().get()` was `cannot infer type parameter 'Src'` and the ONLY workaround was annotating the binding site. `substitute_existential_assoc_bindings` (src/typechecker/types.rs) supplies the missing fact. DEFINITION side it is an obligation: `existential_binding_mismatch` resolves the concrete witness's own `Assoc` through the ordinary projection machinery and `is_subtype_with_projections` rejects a witness that contradicts it, with a distinct `E_IMPL_TRAIT_ASSOC_MISMATCH` -- folding it into `E_IMPL_TRAIT_MISSING_BOUND` would have sent the reader to add an impl that is already there.

Four walks that previously visited only `args` now visit the bindings too, each because a binding is the one place design.md's own Map table puts the thing being looked for: the CAPTURE SET (`walk_for_impl_trait`, typechecker/items.rs -- `fn keys(ref self) -> impl Iterator[Item = ref K]` has its `ref` nowhere else, so the existential was being recorded as capturing no input borrow), VARIANCE occurrences, SCOPE-LOCAL escape, and public-signature VISIBILITY. Name resolution (`resolve_refs.rs`) and cross-module path rewriting (`module_binding.rs`, which runs BEFORE desugar and so still sees bound-position bindings) walk them as well.

A binding naming no associated type of the trait is rejected at the binding (`E_UNKNOWN_ASSOC_TYPE_BINDING`), listing the ones the trait does declare; deduped on span because a signature's return type is lowered more than once.

syntax.md gains an `IMPL_TRAIT_TYPE` production (the TYPE grammar had none at all) and both it and `DYN_TYPE` take `BOUND_ARG`; design.md's `impl Trait` section states the two-sided meaning.

Tests: 8 in tests/typechecker.rs (projection resolution + its no-binding control, the witness-mismatch rejection, the missing-bound error staying distinct, the typo rejection, argument-vs-where equivalence, and both capture-set halves), 6 in tests/parser.rs (return/argument/mixed-positional AST shape, ordinary-path rejection, nested-`impl` rejection, formatter round-trip), 1 codegen E2E for the argument-position half across all surfaces.

NOT CLOSED HERE, and split out rather than buried: a method call through a RETURN-position existential has no codegen dispatcher at all, with or without a binding -- filed as B-2026-08-22-10.
title: AN INLINE ASSOCIATED-TYPE BINDING IS STILL REJECTED IN `impl Trait` TYPE POSITION -- `fn keys(ref self) -> impl Iterator[Item = ref K]` (design.md's own Map method table) fails to parse, though the same binding now works in every BOUND position

fix:
Fixed in 70168ff -- but NOT by adding the production the row asked for.
The row's premise is refuted: the construct is not in the language, and
three independent parts of the spec already said so.

  syntax.md IMPL_BLOCK ......... grammar has NO effect clause on the header
  syntax.md "Trait impl with     puts the effects on the METHOD, with a
    effects" example ........... plain `impl Processor for RemoteProcessor {`
  design.md, 12 lines below      "impl-level effect syntax is not valid v1 ...
    the cited example .......... the compiler rejects it with a diagnostic
                                 suggesting the trait-method `with _`"

design.md:3819 was the LONE outlier in the whole spec -- a single
occurrence -- and its header clause was redundant with the very next
line's `fn from(...) -> AppError with writes(Log)`. An authoring slip, not
a specified feature. So the "what needs deciding first" the row raised
(default row vs upper bound vs documentation) did not need deciding: the
reading was already settled, in the negative, immediately below the
example that misled the reader.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY BROKEN was the diagnostic the spec promises. The parser
fell through to `expect(LeftBrace)`:

    error[parse]: Expected LeftBrace, found With
    error[parse]: Expected expression, found RightBrace   <- CASCADE

Two diagnostics from one mistake, the second pointing at the block's
closing brace on an unrelated line, and neither mentioning effects or the
remedy. Now: the clause is parsed with the real effect-list grammar and
reported as `ParseErrorKind::ReservedSyntax` (E0005) -- "not yet", not
"nonsense", which is what design.md's "reserved for future relaxation"
warrants. Consuming the clause is what removes the cascade.

MACHINE-APPLICABLE. `karac fix` deletes the clause. Safe precisely BECAUSE
the position carries no meaning -- there is no effect information to
relocate, unlike a genuine syntax error where deleting would lose intent.
Verified end to end: fix rewrites the header, spacing stays correct
(`impl From[ParseError] for AppError {`, not a doubled space), the file
then checks clean.

REMEDY TAILORED PER SHAPE. An INHERENT impl (`impl S with panics {`) has
no trait to carry `with _`, so it gets "put the effects on the impl's own
methods instead" rather than being told to edit a trait that does not
exist. One string for both shapes would have been a diagnostic that lies
in one of them.

The effect-VARIABLE spelling `impl[T, with E] ...` is untouched and keeps
its existing resolver diagnostic (E0110); `tests/resolver.rs` already
covers it.

DOCS BROUGHT INTO LINE, since the doc is what generated this report:
design.md's example restored to the shape its own prose describes, its
normative paragraph extended to name the concrete-clause spelling and both
diagnostic codes, and the IMPL_BLOCK production in syntax.md annotated
with the rejection -- following the E_MARKER_IMPL_HAS_METHOD convention
already used there.

CLASS NOTE: filed `missing-feature`, which survives only on a reading
where the missing feature is the DIAGNOSTIC. The syntax is correctly
absent and stays absent; nothing was added to the language.

Tests: exactly-one-diagnostic (the cascade guard), the two per-shape
remedies, all four effect spellings (`writes(Log)` / `panics` / `_` /
`blocks`), and the applied fix edit. Full suite 109 binaries, 14838
passed, 0 failed; fmt clean; clippy clean on both feature legs.
title: AN EFFECT CLAUSE ON AN IMPL HEADER IS CORRECTLY ABSENT FROM THE GRAMMAR -- but the parser rejected it with a generic `Expected LeftBrace, found With` PLUS a cascaded second error, instead of the targeted "declare the trait method `with _`" diagnostic design.md promises; design.md:3819's own example wrote the clause, which is what made it look like a missing production
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-21-9, item 2. Its item 1 (the inline associated-type binding) is fixed for bound positions; this half was never a grammar gap alone.

  impl From[A] for B with panics { fn from(a: A) -> B { return B {}; } }
  -> error[parse]: Expected LeftBrace, found With

WHAT NEEDS DECIDING FIRST, which is why this is not simply a parser change: design.md writes the clause but does not say what it MEANS. Candidate readings -- (a) a default effect row every method in the block inherits unless it declares its own; (b) an upper bound each method must stay within, checked per method; (c) documentation with no checking. They differ observably for a method that declares fewer effects than the header, and (a) and (b) disagree about whether the header can ADD effects a method did not declare. Effects drive conflict analysis and scheduler placement, so guessing here would bake a semantics into the parser that the effect checker would then have to live with.

Recommend settling the reading in design.md first, then the parser and effect-checker changes are small and obvious.

fix:
CLOSED `wontfix` -- REAL AND REPRODUCIBLE, measured to a standstill, no
caller. THERE IS NO FIXING COMMIT, because nothing was built; 8fcfb64d is
cited as the commit that CHANGED THIS ROW'S STATUS rather than one that
closed it. That commit (B-2026-08-22-19) fixed the verb lattice so that
every pair of channel communication verbs is Safe, which is precisely what
left per-value identity with nothing to buy. This is the outcome the row's own scoping pass specified: "Anyone
picking this up should first establish a CONCRETE caller that the collapse
still hurts; if none exists, `wontfix` is the honest close, not a feature
build." That search was run and came back empty.

THE GAP IS REAL, and reproduces. Two functions declaring `writes` on two
DISTINCT channels serialize, where two distinct DECLARED resources fan out
(`karac build --concurrency-report`):

  two distinct `resource` decls, writes ... parallel_group
                                            "independent effects on
                                             different resources"
  the same resource twice, writes ......... <no parallelization> (correct)
  two distinct CHANNELS, writes ........... <not co-grouped>  <- the collapse

Both channel calls report `writes(Channel)` -- one identity for two values --
so the analyzer cannot tell them apart and declines the fan-out the
distinct-resource control gets.

BUT NO IDIOMATIC SPELLING IS AFFECTED. The verbs design.md actually uses on
channels are unhurt, because after B-2026-08-22-19 (8fcfb64d) fixed the verb lattice
every pair of communication verbs is Safe on any resource:

  sends(tx1) + sends(tx2), distinct channels ......... co-grouped
  sends(tx1) + receives(rx2), distinct channels ...... co-grouped

So identity would buy conflict analysis nothing on the idiomatic path, which
is what retires the original motivation for the whole row.

CORPUS SEARCH, 1228 files -- `runtime/stdlib`, `examples`, `tests`, and the
903-file kata repo. Every fn declaring a channel-typed parameter with an
effect clause was extracted and bucketed by verb:

  sends ...... 9        writes ..... 2
  receives ... 4        reads ...... 0

Eleven of the thirteen are `sends`/`receives`. The only two `writes(tx)`
uses in the entire corpus are in ONE test,
`test_channel_relaxation_is_scoped_to_the_communication_verbs`, which exists
to assert that `writes`+`writes` on a channel MUST still conflict -- and it
passes the SAME channel to both calls, so it is a same-resource pair that
per-value identity would leave conflicting exactly as it does today. It is
not a caller the collapse hurts; it is a caller that WANTS the conflict.

So the residual behavioural cost is confined to a spelling that design.md
never uses, that nothing in the corpus uses, and whose one appearance
depends on the opposite outcome. Building alias/region reasoning to reach it
is not a trade worth making.

THE BASIS FOR CLOSING IS ALREADY PINNED, which is what makes `wontfix` safe
rather than a shrug: `test_channel_sends_on_distinct_channels_fan_out` and
`test_channel_multiple_consumers_fan_out` assert the idiomatic fan-outs, and
the narrowness control above asserts `writes` still conflicts. If someone
later breaks the first, this close's premise fails LOUDLY instead of rotting
quietly. All four channel tests green.

REOPEN CONDITION, stated so this is not a permanent dead end: a concrete
program that (a) declares `writes` or `reads` on two DISTINCT channels and
(b) measurably loses parallelism because of it. Absent that, the spec-fidelity
gap against design.md:6049 ("each channel is its own effect resource") stands
as documented-but-unimplemented, which is the honest state.

DO NOT re-derive the "cheaper middle grounds" the original row listed --
per-construction-site and per-parameter identity. Both targeted the
conflict-analysis motivation that measurement has removed.
title: CHANNEL EFFECT RESOURCES HAVE NO PER-VALUE IDENTITY -- every channel collapses to the single `Channel` resource. The conflict-analysis motivation this row was filed on has since been REFUTED by measurement (the producer/consumer case already worked; two-producer serialization was a verb-lattice defect, fixed separately) -- what remains is a narrow spec-fidelity gap against design.md:6049, where only the NON-communication verbs on distinct channels over-serialize
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-21-32, which landed the accept-the-syntax half (6efbaa0) under an explicit owner decision to defer this half rather than block on it.

WHAT IS TRUE NOW. `with sends(tx)` on a `tx: Sender[T]` parameter resolves, and the four spec'd `Sender`/`Receiver` declaration forms compile and run. But every value-rooted channel resource canonicalizes to ONE identity, so two functions with different channel parameters both report `sends(Channel)`.

WHY THAT WAS THE RIGHT INTERIM. The collapse is the SOUND direction: all channels being one resource means two channel-touching tasks always conflict, so conflict analysis OVER-reports (refuses to parallelize something it could) rather than UNDER-reporting (parallelizing two tasks that genuinely share a channel). The alternative available without this feature -- keying the resource on the parameter NAME -- is unsound in the dangerous direction, since `sends(tx)` and `sends(out)` would be disjoint resources for what may be the same channel.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING, and it is the interesting half. design.md:6049 says "each channel is its own effect resource", and the conflict table at :6095 reasons about "two tasks sharing a channel [having] `sends` and `receives` on the *same* resource". The safety argument for parallelizing a producer against a consumer rests on that PER-VALUE identity. Today the compiler cannot state it: it cannot distinguish two channels, so it cannot prove two branches touch DIFFERENT ones, and it therefore refuses the parallelization the spec advertises rather than permitting it unsoundly.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY TAKES -- this is a type-system feature, not a parse fix, which is what kept it out of -32. Resource identity has to be carried by the VALUE, which means mapping call-site arguments to resource identities and reasoning about aliasing: `snd(tx, 1)` and `snd(tx2, 2)` must yield different resources, `snd(tx, 1)` twice must yield the same one, and a channel reached through a struct field or a `ref` must resolve to the channel it borrows. That is alias/region reasoning. Scope it before starting.

CHEAPER MIDDLE GROUNDS WORTH EVALUATING FIRST: (a) identity per SYNTACTIC channel construction site, which would distinguish two `Channel.new()` results without full alias analysis and covers the common producer/consumer shape; (b) identity per parameter WITHIN one signature's conflict check only, which is where :6095's argument actually lives, leaving cross-function identity collapsed. Either is strictly better than today and much smaller than the general feature.

DO NOT re-key on the parameter name as a shortcut -- see the soundness note above; that is the one direction that is worse than the current collapse.

=== SCOPED AND RE-MEASURED 2026-08-22 -- THE STATED MOTIVATION IS REFUTED ===

This row asked for per-VALUE channel identity and justified it with
design.md:6095's producer-against-consumer parallelization argument, calling
that argument "not backed by the compiler". Scoping it as the row instructed
("Scope it before starting") measured both halves of that claim, and the
motivation does not hold up.

1. THE PRODUCER/CONSUMER CASE ALREADY WORKED. `sends` + `receives` was the
   ONE communication row `ConcurrencyChecker::two_effects_conflict` had
   right (`(Sends, Receives) => false`). Measured: a `sends(tx)` statement
   and a `receives(rx)` statement co-group into one parallel group. So
   :6095's argument WAS backed; this row's title said otherwise.

2. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY BROKEN was two PRODUCERS: `(Sends,Sends)` and
   `(Receives,Receives)` were coded as CONFLICT against design.md:5813's
   table, which lists both as Safe. Filed and fixed separately as
   B-2026-08-22-19 (fix 8fcfb64d) -- that is a verb-lattice defect, not an
   identity one.

3. PER-VALUE IDENTITY WOULD NOT HAVE FIXED IT ANYWAY -- and this is the part
   that retires the conflict-analysis motivation entirely. design.md:6109
   blesses multiple producers on the SAME channel, which is a same-resource
   pair under ANY identity scheme, so identity cannot reach it. Conversely,
   once the lattice matches the table, EVERY pair of channel communication
   verbs is Safe regardless of which channel each touches -- so telling
   `tx1` from `tx2` buys conflict analysis exactly nothing.

A THIRD GAP found in the same pass, filed as B-2026-08-22-20: the BUILTIN
channel methods carry no `sends`/`receives` effect at all, so only
user-DECLARED channel effects exist today.

WHAT REMAINS, and why this row stays open rather than being closed
`invalid`: the SPEC STATEMENT is still unimplemented. design.md:6049 says
"each channel is its own effect resource", and the compiler still collapses
every one to `Channel`. The residual BEHAVIOURAL consequence is now narrow
and confined to the NON-communication verbs: `writes(tx1)` and `writes(tx2)`
on two distinct channels collapse to one resource and over-serialize.
design.md spells channels only with `sends`/`receives`, so that shape is
unidiomatic and has no known real-world caller -- which is why severity drops
from medium to low.

DO NOT re-derive the "cheaper middle grounds" the original row listed
((a) per-construction-site identity, (b) per-parameter within one signature).
Both were aimed at the conflict-analysis motivation that measurement has now
removed. Anyone picking this up should first establish a CONCRETE caller that
the collapse still hurts; if none exists, `wontfix` is the honest close, not
a feature build.

fix:
FIXED by 840f95ef. `Hasher` and `BuildHasher` are baked, and the trailing slot of
`Map[K, V, H]` / `Set[T, H]` now accepts ANY type that implements
`BuildHasher`, dispatched through the user's own methods on both backends.

WHAT SHIPPED, against the (a)-(e) plan this row's scoping pass left:

(a) `runtime/stdlib/hash.kara` declares both traits verbatim from design.md --
`Hasher` with `write` / `finish` plus ten default-bodied `write_*` convenience
methods, `BuildHasher` with `type Hasher: Hasher` and `build`. The `H: Hasher`
bound is restored on `Hash.hash`. Both names join the prelude scope-0 list next
to the two selectors, for the same reason they are there: a user hasher is
named inline in a type annotation, so its impl blocks would otherwise be the
one part of the feature needing an import.

(b) `HasherKind::User(String)` carries the BUILDER's type name. The enum loses
`Copy` (a `String`-carrying variant cannot keep it); the fallout was ~20
mechanical `.copied()` / field-move sites across `codegen`, `codegen/maps`,
`interpreter/eval_call` and `interpreter/value`. `runtime_symbol` becomes
`Option<&'static str>` -- `None` for a user hasher, which is not a gap but the
whole point: its permutation is user code, so there is no runtime entry point
to name. `mangle_suffix` returns `Cow` and folds the builder name in, so two
builders in one program get two synthesized `hash_fn`s instead of colliding in
the cache.

(c) The whitelist is gone, but NOT where this row expected. The check could not
stay in `take_hasher_type_arg`, because the PARSER strips the argument before
the typechecker ever sees it, and the parser has no impl table -- it cannot
tell `MyBuildHasher` from `i64`. So `take_container_hasher_arg` now strips ANY
bare trailing path and records the name, and validation moves one phase later
to `TypeChecker::check_recorded_container_hasher`, which reads the same impl
table both backends dispatch through. Leaving unknown names in place was the
alternative and is worse: it would make a legitimate `Map[K, V, MyBuildHasher]`
stop being a `Map` to every later phase, which is the exact failure the
deletion exists to prevent.

(d) `emit_hash_bytes_call` gains a user arm emitting three direct calls --
`B.build()` -> `S.write(bytes)` -> `S.finish()` -- around one stack slot for
the state and one for the `Slice[u8]` header. The row's read of the codegen
side was right: this is ONE emit site, and the map's calling convention is
untouched, because `karac_map_*` was already reaching the hash through a
function pointer. The builder -> state-type hop comes from a new plain-data
`Codegen::user_hasher_states` table read off the AST in `compile_program`,
beside `container_hashers` and for the same reason.

(e) The interpreter twin is a new module, `interpreter::user_hasher`, and it is
the part this row's scoping did not anticipate. `MapData::hash_key` is a
`&self` method reached through an `RwLock` guard: there is no interpreter in
scope and no way to thread one in without changing the signature of every map
and set operation in the tree. It therefore keeps its own -- a leaked
`&'static Program` / `&'static TypeCheckResult` (one clone per process,
installed from `Interpreter::new` only for a program that names a user hasher)
and a per-thread sub-`Interpreter`. Leaking is what makes the sub-interpreter
storable in a `thread_local` at all, and it is bounded and one-shot. The two
alternatives are both worse: a raw pointer to the live interpreter hands out a
second `&mut` to a value already borrowed up the stack, and rebuilding an
interpreter per key hash puts `Interpreter::new` + `register_items` on the map
hot path. `TypeCheckResult` gained `Clone` (and `UnionInfo` with it) for this.

ONE COMPILER BUG HAD TO BE FIXED TO SHIP (a), not worked around. design.md
writes `Hasher.write_u8`'s default body as `self.write([n])`, and baking that
made EVERY user `impl Hasher` fail module verification -- "Call parameter type
does not match function signature" -- while `karac check` accepted the program
and `--interp` ran it. The spec's own text was the reproducer. It is the
METHOD-CALL half of B-2026-08-21-24: that row spilled the synthesized
`{ptr, i64}` header for a `ref Slice[T]` slot on the free-function path and
never on this one, the same "landed on two of the three call paths" shape as
B-2026-06-19-1, B-2026-08-05-41 and B-2026-08-21-39 before it. Mapped over a
3x2x2 matrix (free fn / inherent method / trait default body) x (ref Slice /
bare Slice) x (literal / call result): exactly the two method-receiver cells
with a `ref Slice` slot and a literal argument failed, and all twelve pass
after the fix. Filed as B-2026-08-22-26, fixed in this commit, with a
regression test covering both receiver shapes. Writing the stdlib body as
`n.to_ne_bytes()` instead would have made the suite green and left the bug in
the compiler for the next caller.

TWO RESTRICTIONS, both reported rather than silently accepted:

  * THE BUILDER MUST BE A FIELDLESS STRUCT. The slot names a TYPE, so there is
    nowhere for per-table configuration to come from and both backends
    construct the builder themselves. A seed goes inside `build()`.
  * THE STATE TYPE MUST IMPLEMENT `Hasher`, checked HERE rather than left to
    the general GAT-bound machinery -- which does not discharge a bound
    declared on a STDLIB-baked trait (B-2026-08-22-28). Unchecked this is
    the worst available outcome: codegen finds no symbol and degrades to a
    constant digest while the interpreter raises a missing-method error, so the
    two backends disagree on a program `karac check` accepted.

THE ROW'S "ONE UNMEASURED RISK" IS ANSWERED: NO HOISTING NEEDED. Measured on
the arm64 box this row was pinned to, `--release`, 200 000 `String` inserts
plus 1 000 000 lookups, five rounds interleaved round-robin after a warm-up,
1-minute load average under 2:

    default SipHash13BuildHasher   0.09 s   (0.08-0.09 across all five)
    user FNV-1a hasher             0.09 s   (0.08-0.09 across all five)
    FxBuildHasher                  1.23 s   (1.22-1.24 across all five)

The per-key `build` / `write` / `finish` frames disappear into the map
operation around them -- a user hasher is at parity with the builtin it
replaces, so the per-key construction this row flagged needs no hoisting. The
`bench/hash_quality/` crate the row pointed at was not the right instrument:
it compares hash FAMILIES in Rust, not the Kara-level dispatch cost, so the
measurement above is a fresh three-variant Kara bench instead.

That run also surfaced two pre-existing `FxBuildHasher` defects, both
reproduced on a clean `main` and neither introduced here: a compiled
`Map[i64, V, H]` under any non-default hasher stops growing and silently drops
every key past the last resize (B-2026-08-22-27, high), and `FxBuildHasher` is
13.7x SLOWER than the default it is advertised as a fast alternative to on
`String` keys (B-2026-08-22-29).

TESTS. 5 in `tests/typechecker.rs` (accepted shape, type identity preserved,
the two refusals, and the once-per-write diagnostic), 3 in
`tests/interpreter.rs` (finds/removes, two hashers order differently, set +
struct key), 4 in `tests/codegen.rs` (the same three compiled, plus the
`ref Slice` method-call regression), 4 unit tests on the byte encoding in
`user_hasher.rs`, and 1 in `tests/cli.rs` that is the one no single-process
assertion can replace: across six SUBPROCESSES on BOTH surfaces, the
user-hashed map's order must be FIXED while the default map's keeps moving, and
must not be INSERTION order -- which is what a hasher that never ran, or one
whose digest collapsed to a constant, leaves behind.

DOCUMENTED IN design.md, including the property a user should know before
writing one: the byte image `write` receives is backend-specific. A compiled
binary feeds the key's memory image; the interpreter feeds a canonical
flattening of the key `Value`. So a user hasher fixes the order across
PROCESSES -- which is what a test-deterministic hasher is for -- but does not
give the same digest under `--interp` as under a compiled binary. That is
within the existing contract; the two builtins already differ between backends
the same way, for the same reason.
title: The `Hasher` and `BuildHasher` TRAITS are not baked, so a user cannot write their own hasher: `Map[K, V, H]` accepts only the two compiler-known selectors `SipHash13BuildHasher` / `FxBuildHasher`, and design.md's "User-extensible hashers" paragraph describes a surface that does not exist
detail:
WHAT IS MISSING. design.md § `Hash` and `Hasher` declares two traits in full --

    trait Hasher {
        fn write(mut ref self, bytes: ref Slice[u8]);
        fn finish(ref self) -> u64;
        fn write_u8(mut ref self, n: u8)   { self.write([n]) }
        ...
    }
    trait BuildHasher { type Hasher: Hasher; fn build(ref self) -> Self.Hasher; }

-- and a paragraph titled "User-extensible hashers" that says "`Hasher` is an
ordinary trait. Users implement it for FxHash-style speed, for content-addressed
hashes ... or for test-deterministic hashers." NEITHER trait is baked into the
stdlib. `runtime/stdlib/hash.kara` declares only `trait Hash { fn hash[H](ref
self, hasher: mut ref H); }`, and its own comment has said since CR-202 slice 5e
that "the actual `Hasher` trait is not yet baked, so this declaration omits the
`H: Hasher` bound".

WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD (B-2026-08-21-6, `59c8d30`+). The `Map[K, V, H]` /
`Set[T, H]` parameter is real and both backends honour it, but `H` must name one
of exactly two compiler-known types -- `SipHash13BuildHasher` or
`FxBuildHasher`, declared as zero-field structs and used as type-level
SELECTORS, not as `impl BuildHasher` sites. Anything else is a hard error whose
message says so ("A user-written hasher is not supported yet -- the
'BuildHasher' trait is not implemented"), and design.md now carries a paragraph
marking the extensible surface as intended rather than shipped. So this is a
KNOWN, DIAGNOSED and DOCUMENTED gap, not a silent one -- which is why it is
filed separately rather than left inside the closed row.

WHY IT IS NOT A TRIVIAL WIDENING. Today the hasher choice reduces, in codegen,
to which runtime entry point the synthesized per-key-type `hash_fn` calls
(`karac_hash_bytes` vs `karac_hash_bytes_fx`), and in the interpreter to which
`core::hash::Hasher` impl `hash_value_with` instantiates. A user-written
`Hasher` is a different shape entirely: the per-hash state becomes a user value
with user methods, so codegen must emit a call into user code per key rather
than a call into the runtime, and the interpreter must run a user `write` /
`finish` pair per key. That also drags in the `Hasher` trait's DEFAULT METHOD
BODIES (`write_u8` and friends, which call `to_ne_bytes`) and `BuildHasher`'s
ASSOCIATED TYPE, so it is a trait-machinery slice, not a table-widening one.

WHERE TO START. `runtime/stdlib/hash.kara` (bake both traits, restore the
`H: Hasher` bound on `Hash.hash`), `src/hasher_kind.rs` (the plain-data enum
would gain a third, user-typed variant carrying the impl's name),
`src/typechecker/lowering.rs::take_hasher_type_arg` (accept any type that
implements `BuildHasher` instead of the two-name whitelist), and the two
construction sites in `src/codegen/maps.rs` plus
`src/interpreter/eval_call.rs::new_hash_container`.

=== SCOPED 2026-08-22 -- THE TWO THINGS THIS ROW CALLS HARD ARE ALREADY BUILT ===

Claimed this to implement, measured the two obstacles it names, and both are
already present. Nothing changed in the compiler; the row stays open, but its
cost estimate should come down and its starting point moves.

1. "IT IS A TRAIT-MACHINERY SLICE" -- the machinery exists and runs. The row
rests on `BuildHasher`'s ASSOCIATED TYPE and the `H: Hasher` bound being the
hard part. Measured with a structural stand-in for exactly that shape -- a
bounded associated type, an impl supplying it, and a method returning
`Self.Made` whose result is then mutated and read:

    trait Sink { fn put(mut ref self, n: u8); fn done(ref self) -> u64; }
    struct Acc { total: u64 }
    impl Sink for Acc { ... }
    trait Build { type Made: Sink; fn make(ref self) -> Self.Made; }
    struct AccBuilder { }
    impl Build for AccBuilder { type Made = Acc; fn make(ref self) -> Acc { ... } }

`karac check` passes and all three backends agree (`--interp` 7, `karac run`
7, `karac build` 7). So a bounded associated type, `Self.Assoc` in return
position, and per-instance mutation through a trait are all working today.
Baking `Hasher` / `BuildHasher` is a DECLARATION job in
`runtime/stdlib/hash.kara`, not a language-feature build.

2. "CODEGEN MUST EMIT A CALL INTO USER CODE PER KEY RATHER THAN A CALL INTO
THE RUNTIME" -- true, but not the structural change it reads as, because the
dispatch is ALREADY indirect. `karac_map_*` receives the per-key-type hash as
a FUNCTION POINTER (`hash_fn_ptr`, src/codegen/maps.rs:119/224), and
`src/codegen/synth.rs` already documents the property: "the `karac_map_*`
table was already calling its `hash_fn` through a function POINTER, so this
adds a call frame, not a new indirection class." Swapping a builtin hasher for
a user one therefore changes the BODY of the synthesized `hash_fn`, at ONE
emit site -- `synth.rs::emit_hash_bytes_call`, whose whole builtin-specific
content is `self.hash_hasher.runtime_symbol()` at line 81 -- plus the
interpreter twin. The map's calling convention is untouched.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT, in the order it should be done:
  (a) declare both traits in `runtime/stdlib/hash.kara` and restore the
      `H: Hasher` bound on `Hash.hash`;
  (b) a third `HasherKind` variant carrying the impl's type name -- note this
      enum is plain data shared with the interpreter, so the variant must not
      carry anything LLVM-shaped;
  (c) `take_hasher_type_arg` / `is_hasher_selector`: replace the two-name
      `HASHER_SELECTORS` whitelist with "any type implementing BuildHasher";
  (d) `emit_hash_bytes_call`: for the user variant, construct via
      `BuildHasher.make()`, drive `write` over the key bytes, read `finish`;
  (e) the interpreter twin in `hash_value_with` / `new_hash_container`.

THE ONE UNMEASURED RISK, and it is a perf question rather than a correctness
one: (d) constructs a hasher instance PER KEY HASH, on the map hot path. The
builtin path is a single call to `karac_hash_bytes`. Whoever builds this
should bench a user hasher against the builtins before deciding whether the
per-key construction needs hoisting -- `bench/hash_quality/` already exists
for exactly this comparison.

NOT ATTEMPTED beyond the scoping above: (a)-(e) is still a stdlib +
typechecker + codegen + interpreter + tests slice, which wants its own run
rather than the tail of another. But it starts from a much better place than
this row implies.

WHERE TO VERIFY THIS ONE, decided 2026-08-22: on the local arm64 macOS box,
not in a cloud container. Two of the checks this change needs are ones a
shared 4-core container cannot answer honestly.

  * LEAKS. (d) adds a hasher CONSTRUCTION per key hash, on the path every map
    and set operation takes. Leaks are not always architecture-independent
    here -- B-2026-07-12-29 was an arm64-ONLY RC leak that x86 LSan reported
    clean -- so a green x86 `memory-sanitizer` run does not clear this class.
    `scripts/lsan-local.sh` is native arm64 and is the right gate.
  * PERF. The builtin path is one `karac_hash_bytes` call; the user path
    constructs, drives `write`, then reads `finish`. Whether that needs
    hoisting is a measurement, and `bench/hash_quality/` is the existing
    comparison -- but only on a quiet machine. Numbers taken under a
    saturated 4-core container (load ~4.5, which is what the scoping run had)
    are not worth acting on.

Correctness alone -- (a) through (e) plus tests -- is portable and could be
built anywhere; it is these two gates that pin the work to the arm64 box.

fix:
FIXED by 289bc8a3, wiring the lint in the TYPECHECKER, with the capability question
answered WITHOUT the backend -- which is what dissolved the placement
dilemma this row was filed on.

THE ROW FRAMED IT AS typechecker-vs-codegen, and both options looked bad
because each phase holds half of what is needed: the typechecker owns the
`#[allow]` cascade (`effective_lint_level`) but not the target; codegen owns
the target but has no `#[allow]` reader and no diagnostics channel at all
(measured: no `warnings`/`Diagnostic` producer under `src/codegen/driver.rs`),
and a codegen-only lint would be silently absent from a default `karac check`.

The way out is that the capability question does not actually need LLVM.
`target::target_has_native_f16()` answers it from `(cpu, features)` alone:
`baseline_cpu_and_features()` classifies the native target from
`std::env::consts::ARCH`/`OS` (not from a triple, which only the LLVM driver
resolves), then two MEASURED CPU lists plus the explicit feature flags decide.
Nothing crosses the containment boundary.

EVERY TABLE ENTRY IS MEASURED, with `llc -mcpu=... ` on `fadd half` (LLVM 18) --
native emits `fadd h0, h0, h1` (AArch64) or `vaddsh` (x86), emulated emits
`fcvt` promotion, and wasm emits `__extendhfsf2`/`__truncsfhf2` libcalls:

  apple-m1                                   NATIVE
  sapphirerapids                             NATIVE
  generic +v8a,+outline-atomics              emulated
  x86-64 / -v2 / -v3 / -v4                   emulated
  core2, generic                             emulated
  generic +v8.2a / +v8.4a / +v8.6a           emulated
  generic +v8a,+fullfp16                     NATIVE
  x86-64 +avx512f,+avx512vl,+avx512fp16      NATIVE
  wasm32-wasip1 (+simd128 or not)            emulated (libcalls)

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ROW, both from that table -- see the appended
"RE-SCOPED" section for the full write-up:
  * `apple-m1` IS native, so "under EVERY current default baseline there is
    no native f16" was wrong, and the feature-string check this row specified
    would have been a FALSE POSITIVE on Apple Silicon (that baseline is
    `("apple-m1", "")` -- an empty feature string).
  * `+avx512fp16` alone does NOT enable it; it needs `+avx512f,+avx512vl`
    too. Naming it prerequisite-less under-reports, which is the safe
    direction, but the row's one-flag framing was incomplete.

A THIRD CORRECTION, found only by running the thing: the fail-open rule for
an unmeasured CPU was first written as "unreachable without an explicit
`--target-cpu`". That is false -- `karac build` ALWAYS installs a CPU
override, because `resolve_native_cpu_baseline` applies `cpu-baseline = "v3"`
by default. The first implementation therefore went silent on every ordinary
build. Caught by testing `karac build` rather than only `karac check`; fixed
by adding the measured `CPUS_WITHOUT_NATIVE_F16` list so every CPU the
default path can install is decided by measurement, and pinned by
`every_default_baseline_cpu_is_measured`.

TESTS. Six in tests/typechecker.rs (fires on f16 and bf16; quiet on f32/f64
and on an f16 COMPARISON, which is not promoted arithmetic; `#[allow]`
cascades; the message names the cpu it judged) and three unit tests in
`target.rs`, including `native_baseline_matches_the_codegen_table`, which
pins the new baseline classifier against
`codegen::driver::default_cpu_and_features` so the two producers cannot
drift. Removed from `KNOWN_UNWIRED` in `src/lints.rs`, so
`every_registered_lint_is_emitted_or_declared_unwired` now holds it to being

REMAINING, and deliberate: an unmeasured user-named `--target-cpu` fails OPEN
(no lint). A false "your f16 is emulated" on hardware that runs it natively
sends someone rewriting code that was already fast, which is worse than a

title: `f16_software_emulated` IS THE ONE STARTER-SET LINT WHOSE TRIGGER DEPENDS ON THE TARGET -- and the blocker is NOT the placement this row was filed on: the specified feature-string check reads only the `features` half of `default_cpu_and_features`, so it is blind to CPU-implied support (`aarch64-apple-darwin` resolves to `("apple-m1", "")`), and no inkwell/LLVM-C call reports a CPU's resolved subtarget features to fix that
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-21-2 when the other six of that row's eight were wired.
It is not a wiring gap of the same kind, which is why it outlived them.

THE TRIGGER IS WELL DEFINED. design.md:2347: "On targets without native
`f16`/`bf16` hardware, LLVM promotes operations to `f32` automatically. The
compiler emits a `#[allow(f16_software_emulated)]`-suppressible lint so the
performance cost is never silent." Repeated at :13794. So: an `f16`/`bf16`
OPERATION, on a target lacking native support.

IT IS ALSO DECIDABLE FROM REAL DATA, not an invented capability table. The
compiler already models target features -- `combined_features()` in
`src/codegen/driver.rs` merges a per-target default baseline with the user's
`--target-features`, and `default_cpu_and_features(triple)` holds the defaults.
Checking that string for `+fullfp16` / `+avx512fp16` answers the question with
the compiler's own source of truth.

THE PROBLEM IS WHERE THE EMIT GOES, and both options cost something:

  * TYPECHECKER -- where the other five wired lints live, and where `#[allow]`
    cascades for free. It cannot reach `default_cpu_and_features`: `src/codegen`
    is `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`, and CLAUDE.md's codegen-containment invariant
    forbids upstream phases from depending on the backend. Reaching it would
    mean lifting the baseline table upstream or duplicating it -- and a
    duplicated baseline table is exactly the producer/consumer drift this
    codebase keeps paying for.
  * CODEGEN -- where the target machine actually is, so containment holds. But
    NO codegen site reads `#[allow]` today (measured: `is_bare("allow")` appears
    in `ownership.rs` and the typechecker, nowhere under `src/codegen/`), so
    suppression is new plumbing. And the lint would then exist only in
    `--features llvm` builds, so `karac check` on a default build would not
    report it.

MEASURED, AND IT CHANGES THE PRIORITY: under EVERY current default baseline
there is no native f16. aarch64 defaults to `("generic", "+v8a,+outline-atomics")`
-- ARMv8.0, which predates `+fullfp16`; the x86_64 baseline carries no
`+avx512fp16`; wasm is `+simd128`. So on today's defaults the answer is always
"emulated", and the lint would fire on essentially every `f16`/`bf16` arithmetic
program. That is what the spec asks for and it is not wrong, but it means the
feature-string check is inert until someone passes `--target-cpu` /
`--target-features` to widen the baseline. Anyone wiring this should decide
whether a lint that fires on all current targets is the intended user
experience before building the suppression plumbing for it.

STILL VISIBLE IN CODE: it remains in `KNOWN_UNWIRED` in `src/lints.rs`, so
`every_registered_lint_is_emitted_or_declared_unwired` keeps it honest -- the
list cannot go stale while this sits open.

=== RE-SCOPED 2026-08-22: THE PROPOSED CHECK IS UNSOUND, AND THE REAL
    OBSTACLE IS NOT PLACEMENT ===

Picked this up to wire, and stopped before building it: the check this row
specifies would be WRONG on at least one shipped target, and the API needed to
make it right does not exist. Both are measured below. Nothing was changed in
the compiler; the row stays open with a corrected design.

1. THE FEATURE-STRING CHECK READS HALF THE SOURCE OF TRUTH.
`default_cpu_and_features(triple)` returns a PAIR -- `(cpu, features)`. This
row proposes "Checking that string for `+fullfp16` / `+avx512fp16`", i.e.
reading only the `features` half. But the aarch64 macOS arm returns

    (true, false, true, false) => ("apple-m1", "")

-- an EMPTY feature string, with the whole hardware capability carried by the
CPU NAME. Any CPU whose implied subtarget features include half-precision is
therefore reported as "software emulated" no matter what it supports. The
same hole applies to any user-supplied `--target-cpu` (e.g. `apple-m2`,
`sapphirerapids`), not just the defaults.

This also corrects this row's own measurement. It states "under EVERY current
default baseline there is no native f16", supporting that with the aarch64
LINUX default (`("generic", "+v8a,+outline-atomics")`, correctly pre-fullfp16).
It does not account for the aarch64 DARWIN default, where the CPU is
`apple-m1` and the feature string is empty. Whether `apple-m1`'s LLVM subtarget
enables FullFP16 was NOT verifiable from this container (the CPU listing is
native-target-only and `--target=` does not retarget it), so it is flagged, not
asserted -- but the conclusion does not depend on it: either apple-m1 has
native f16 and the check is a FALSE POSITIVE on Apple Silicon, or it does not
and the check is right by accident while still blind to every CPU-implied
feature. Resolve it on an arm64 macOS host before building anything.

2. LLVM CANNOT ANSWER THE CORRECTED QUESTION. Measured against
inkwell 0.9's `TargetMachine` surface, there is no call that reports the
RESOLVED subtarget feature set for a given CPU:

  * `get_feature_string()` (LLVMGetTargetMachineFeatureString) echoes back the
    string the machine was CONSTRUCTED with -- it does not expand the CPU.
  * `get_host_cpu_features()` describes the HOST, which is authoritative only
    for a native build and simply wrong under cross-compilation.
  * There is no `has_feature` / CPU-expansion entry point at all. This is the
    same gap this file already documents for CPU listing, where the workaround
    is capturing an LLVM stderr dump from a child process -- and that dump
    lists the available features, not which ones a given CPU turns on.

3. WHAT THIS DOES TO THE PLACEMENT QUESTION. The row frames typechecker-vs-
codegen as a trade between `#[allow]` cascade and containment. Correctness
settles it more sharply: the typechecker cannot be right, because the missing
knowledge is CPU -> implied features, which is LLVM's, and duplicating LLVM's
subtarget tables upstream is far worse drift than the baseline table this row
worried about. Note also that `default_cpu_and_features` is a pure
`&str -> (&'static str, &'static str)` map with NO LLVM types, so LIFTING it
out of `src/codegen/` is clean and drift-free -- this row treats "lifting or
duplicating" as one option, and they are not the same. But lifting alone does
not rescue the typechecker, because the table is not the missing piece.

4. THE TRACTABLE DESIGN, for whoever takes this next:
  (a) NATIVE build (no target override): `get_host_cpu_features()` IS
      authoritative -- parse it for `+fullfp16` / `+avx512fp16`. This is the
      common case and the one where a wrong answer is most visible.
  (b) CROSS build: the explicit `--target-features` string, plus a small
      EXPLICIT cpu->fp16 table covering the handful of CPUs
      `default_cpu_and_features` can return. Unknown CPU must pick a
      documented direction; suggest NOT linting (a missing perf note is
      cheaper than a false one on hardware that is fine).
  (c) Emit from codegen, and accept the two costs this row already names: new
      `#[allow]` plumbing (no site under `src/codegen/` reads it today), and
      the lint being absent from a default `karac check`.

5. THE UX QUESTION THIS ROW RAISES SURVIVES, and is now sharper: with the
correction above, the lint would fire on every f16 program on x86_64 and on
aarch64 LINUX, but possibly NOT on aarch64 macOS. So it is not uniformly
noisy -- it is platform-dependent in a way that will read as inconsistent
unless the message says which target it judged. Any implementation should
name the target and CPU in the diagnostic.

NOT A VACUOUS TARGET: `f16`/`bf16` is a real implemented surface (83 `f16` and
133 `bf16` references in `src/`, genuine `context.f16_type()` / `bf16_type()`
lowering, and coverage across nine test files), so the lint has real programs
to fire on. This is worth doing -- just not with the check as specified.

=== IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-22 -- WHAT THE RE-SCOPE ABOVE GOT RIGHT AND WRONG ===

The re-scope section above was written before building anything, and building
it settled two of its open questions and refuted one of its conclusions.

SETTLED: `apple-m1` HAS native f16. The re-scope flagged this as unverifiable
from the container and refused to assert it. It is verifiable -- just not
through the compiler's own CPU listing (which is native-target-only). `llc`
ships with the AArch64 backend registered, so `llc -mtriple=aarch64-apple-darwin
-mcpu=apple-m1` on `fadd half` answers directly: it emits `fadd h0, h0, h1`,
a hardware half-precision add, where `-mcpu=generic` emits the `fcvt`->`fadd s`
->`fcvt` promotion. So the false-positive-on-Apple-Silicon hazard was REAL,
not hypothetical, and this row's "under EVERY current default baseline there
is no native f16" is wrong for aarch64 macOS.

SETTLED: `+avx512fp16` alone is not sufficient -- it needs `+avx512f,+avx512vl`
alongside it, or LLVM keeps promoting. With them (or with `-mcpu=sapphirerapids`)
it emits `vaddsh`. The one-flag framing in this row was incomplete. The
failure direction is safe (under-report), so the shipped check keeps the
simple flag test.

REFUTED: "LLVM cannot answer the corrected question, therefore codegen is the
only placement that can be correct." The premise is true -- no inkwell/LLVM-C
call expands a CPU to its resolved subtarget features -- but the conclusion
does not follow, because the question does not have to be answered AT COMPILE
TIME BY LLVM. It can be answered once, offline, by measurement, and carried
as a table. That is what `target::target_has_native_f16` does, which puts the
whole decision upstream of the backend and lets the lint live in the
typechecker where the `#[allow]` cascade already works.

That also retires the placement dilemma this row was filed on, rather than
choosing a side of it: the reason codegen looked mandatory was an assumed
dependency on LLVM that turned out to be avoidable.

STILL TRUE from the re-scope: reading only the feature half of
`(cpu, features)` is unsound, `default_cpu_and_features` is LLVM-free and
liftable, and codegen has no `#[allow]` reader. The last of those is now a
reason the typechecker WINS rather than a cost to absorb.

fix:
Resolved in 85ce532 by option (a) -- `implicit_clone` REMOVED from the v1

BOTH OF THIS ROW'S PREMISES WERE WRONG, and the removal is right anyway --
for a stronger reason than the row gave.

  1. "The spec states 'No implicit clones' for compiled code." That sentence
     is REPL-SCOPED (design.md:11469). It sits in the REPL section
     contrasting default strictness against `karac repl --auto-clone`, and
     says REPL strictness is identical to compiled code -- not that compiled
     code has been given a no-implicit-clones guarantee.

  2. "The only place compiled Kara gains a copy the author did not write is
     codegen's use-after-move defensive copy -- and those sites ALREADY emit
     `warning[ownership]` at the same span, so wiring here would
     double-report." That site DOES NOT ALLOCATE. Measured with the ASAN
     allocation counter against a non-reusing baseline:

       move, no reuse ....................... 10 / 13 allocations
       move + reuse via `v.len()` ........... 13   (same as baseline)
       move + reuse via `v[0].len()` ........ 13   (same as baseline)
       owned param as a literal element ..... 10   (same as baseline)

     The fourth shape is one this row never considered:
     `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg`, the mechanism added by B-2026-07-18-38
     to fix a real double free. `fn dup(x: String) -> Vec[String] { [x] }`
     allocates exactly as its baseline does.

to report. The real case is that the lint NAMES SOMETHING THAT DOES NOT
OCCUR. That distinction matters for the decision: a merely redundant lint
can be worth keeping, while a vacuous one is a false promise, because
`#[deny(implicit_clone)]` passes and reads as a guarantee of no hidden
allocations in a hot path.

title: `implicit_clone` HAS NO TRIGGER IN THE SPEC AND CANNOT BE DE-REGISTERED WITHOUT A design.md EDIT -- the one starter-set lint whose resolution is a SPEC decision, not a compiler change
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-21-2, carrying forward that row's measurement unchanged
because nothing found since has altered it.

THE MEASUREMENT (from -2, re-stated here so this row stands alone): design.md
defines NO trigger for `implicit_clone`. The name appears only in a Tier-3
suppression list, a cascade example, and the starter-set roster. The spec states
"No implicit clones" for compiled code, and the ONE auto-clone feature that
exists (`karac repl --auto-clone`) is spec'd to emit a DIFFERENT diagnostic,
`perf[auto-clone-in-repl]`. The only place compiled Kara gains a copy the author
did not write is codegen's use-after-move defensive copy -- and those sites
ALREADY emit `warning[ownership]` at the same span with actionable help
(measured: `let a = consume(v); let b = v.len();` warns, builds, and runs).
Wiring `implicit_clone` there would double-report one span.

WHY IT CANNOT SIMPLY BE REMOVED: `starter_set_covers_spec_listed_lints` pins it
because design.md lists it in the v1 starter set (:11664). De-registering the
lint therefore requires editing that list in the spec first. That is a language
decision, not a compiler cleanup, which is why it is filed rather than done.

THE DECISION, stated so whoever holds it can just answer it: either
  (a) design.md drops `implicit_clone` from the v1 starter set, the registry
      entry goes, and `KNOWN_UNWIRED` shrinks by one; or
  (b) design.md gains a trigger for it that does NOT duplicate the existing
      `warning[ownership]` on defensive copies.

RECOMMENDATION: (a). The spec's own "No implicit clones" stance and the
already-shipped ownership warning together leave the lint nothing to name.

WHY IT IS LOW RATHER THAN MEDIUM despite being a false promise: the exposure is
narrow and now well understood -- `#[allow(implicit_clone)]` is accepted rather
than reported as `unknown_lint`, and `#[deny(implicit_clone)]` passes vacuously.
There is no `karac lint` command (B-2026-08-21-2 measured that too), so it is
not advertised in a listing the way that row originally claimed.

The wrapper itself is DELETED rather than left unused: its whole body was a call to `_full` with three `None`s, and the third is the bug -- with no wrapper to reach for, a future call site has to pass the where clause or write `None` where it is visible in the diff.
