title: THE BLESSED EXPLICIT SPELLING DID NOT WORK FOR BUILTIN TYPES -- `Vec[i64].new()` / `Map[K, V].new()` / `Channel[T].new()` all reported "no method 'new'", because the qualified form parses as a METHOD CALL resolved against `env.impls` while the unqualified `Vec.new()` is a CALL answered by a special-case constructor arm; fixed by routing the first to the second on both backends
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-21-53, and PROMOTED by its decision. That row settled
that Kara has no call-site type application and that explicit selection is by
QUALIFYING THE RECEIVER -- `Vec[i64].new()`. The parser and typechecker do
route that shape (it reaches `try_path_receiver_method`), and after
B-2026-08-21-53's fix it works end to end for USER types on every surface.
It does not work for the BUILTINS:

  let v = Vec[i64].new();            // no method 'new' on `Vec[…]`
  let m = Map[String, i64].new();    // no method 'new' on `Map[…]`
  let (tx, rx) = Channel[i64].new(); // no method 'new' on `Channel[…]`

READING. The arm resolves through `env.impls`. Builtin collections dispatch
through special-case infer paths rather than an impl-table entry, and the arm
says so itself -- its fall-through comment reads "Built-in types (Vec, Option,
etc.) whose methods dispatch through special-case infer paths rather than
`env.impls` are out of scope for this slice". That scoping was harmless while
the qualified form was a niche spelling. It is not harmless now that the form
is the documented answer to "how do I pin the type".

SEVERITY. High, on IMPACT rather than breakage: nothing miscompiles, but the
spec (as of B-2026-08-21-53) now tells users to write a form that fails on
`Vec`, `Map` and `Channel`. Today the only way to pin those is an annotation
(`let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();`), which works but is not what the spec says,
and does not cover argument position without a temporary binding.

FIX SKETCH, not attempted: give the type-path arm a builtin fall-through that
re-dispatches `Vec`/`Map`/`Set`/`Channel`/`Option`/`Result` constructors to the
same special-case infer paths the unqualified `Vec.new()` uses, carrying the
path's generic args as the instantiation instead of leaving them to inference.
The user-type half of this is already done and its tests
(`type_qualified_assoc_call` in tests/codegen.rs) are the shape to mirror.

fix:
Fixed in 1b75e99, and the ROOT CAUSE IN THE FILED ROW WAS WRONG in both
halves. The row read the IR's three cleanup blocks as "the callee frees the
whole array including the element it returned, and the caller frees it
again." Reading the actual IR:

  * the CALLEE emits no frees at all -- it loads element 0 and returns it;
  * the two extra cleanups are not on the array. They are on `%fstr.acc` and
    `%fstr.acc2`, the F-STRING ACCUMULATOR temporaries that built the two
    elements.

So nothing about owned-`self`, partial moves, or an array ABI is involved.
`compile_array_literal` simply never suppressed an element's independent
scope-exit cleanup once the array took ownership of its buffer, so that free
and the array's owner released the same pointer.

That makes this a missing MEMBER of an existing family rather than a new
defect class: the Vec literal and the tuple literal both call
`suppress_fstr_acc_if_moved_out(e)` immediately after `compile_expr(e)`, and
both carry comments explaining that the call must sit exactly there, while
`last_fstr_acc` still holds THIS element's accumulator rather than the next
one's (the slot is single and overwritten per element). The array literal was
the one aggregate that never joined. The fix is that one call, in that
position.

SIBLING CHECKED, not assumed: the Vec path carries a SECOND protection for
this class (B-2026-07-18-38, an owned caller-retains param used as a literal
element). Probed `fn dup(x: String) -> Array[String, 1] { return [x]; }` --
already balanced, so there is no second gap on the array path.

WHY THE LITERAL FORM LOOKED FINE. `["xx", "yy"]` never reproduced it: static
string literals carry `cap == 0`, so the owned-heap predicate is false and no
free is emitted either way. Only a heap-constructed element (an f-string)
exposes it, which is why the shape had to be built deliberately.

TESTS. `asan_array_elem_moved_out_of_an_owned_param_is_balanced` is the
repro, landed RED and `#[ignore]`d one commit earlier so the finding could
not be lost, un-ignored here. Its sibling
`asan_struct_field_moved_out_of_owned_self_is_balanced` is the passing
CONTRAST that localizes the defect to the array path -- kept precisely so a
later reader does not go looking for it in the struct path, which was clean
all along.

A NOTE ON THE MEASUREMENT, because it nearly produced a much worse row.
Three probes appeared to fail together, which read as a broad
owned-self-extraction bug. One of those "failures" was a wrong expected value
in the probe itself -- 50 f-strings `a0..a49` total 140 bytes, not 150. The
control and the real defect are distinguishable only by FAILURE MODE:
"unexpected stdout (ASAN passed)" versus an explicit `ERROR:
AddressSanitizer`. Grepping only for `test result` hides that difference.
Full suite after the fix: 109 binaries, 14855 passed, 0 failed.
title: MOVING A HEAP ELEMENT OUT OF AN OWNED `Array[T, N]` PARAMETER DOUBLE-FREES IT -- `fn take_first(a: Array[String, 2]) -> String { return a[0]; }` frees the returned buffer at the callee's exit AND again in the caller; `karac check` is clean, the program prints the right answer, and only ASAN sees it
detail:
FOUND while measuring B-2026-08-21-43 (a user impl on a non-scalar `Array`
head, called on a temporary). NOT caused by that arm and not fixed by it --
filed separately because it is the more serious defect and it BLOCKS -43.

REPRO (either spelling; the free fn is the smaller one):

  fn take_first(a: Array[String, 2]) -> String { return a[0]; }
  fn mk(i: i64) -> Array[String, 2] { return [f"a{i}", f"b{i}"]; }
  // ... last = take_first(mk(i)); in a loop
  -> AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free

  impl Tag for Array[String, 2] { fn take_first(self) -> String { return self[0]; } }
  -> same

SILENT. `karac check` passes, the program prints the correct string, and it
exits 0 without a sanitizer. The heap corruption is invisible to every gate
the suite runs except ASAN, which is why 14838 passing tests did not catch it.

READING: the callee frees the whole array at exit, including the element it
just returned, so the caller's own free of the returned String is the second
one. Moving out of one element has to suppress that element's drop -- the
partial-move bookkeeping a struct field already gets.

LOCALIZED, not assumed. The STRUCT analogue of exactly the same move is
CLEAN:

  struct Pair { a: String, b: String }
  impl Pair { fn take_a(self) -> String { return self.a; } }   // ASAN clean

So this is not a general hole in owned-param drop tracking -- it is specific
to moving out of a FIXED ARRAY. Both tests are in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs:
`asan_array_elem_moved_out_of_an_owned_param_is_balanced` (the repro, marked
`#[ignore]` because it is red on main -- un-ignore with the fix) and
`asan_struct_field_moved_out_of_owned_self_is_balanced` (the passing contrast
that keeps the localization honest).

CONTROLS RUN, so the repro is not a harness artifact: a plain loop String
reassign, a single-shot field extract, and a `ref self` field read are all
ASAN-clean. (An earlier read of this as a general owned-self extraction bug
was WRONG -- three probes appeared to fail together, but one of those
failures was a bad expected value in the probe itself, not a sanitizer abort.
The distinction is visible only in the failure MODE: "unexpected stdout"
versus an explicit `ERROR: AddressSanitizer`.)

WHY IT BLOCKS B-2026-08-21-43. That row wants the temporary-receiver arm to
admit non-scalar `Array` heads. Measured: with the scalar gate removed,
`mk().tag()` works and is ASAN-clean, and `mk().take_first()` double-frees --
but so does the BOUND spelling `let a = mk(); a.take_first()`, which needs no
change from -43 at all. So widening that gate does not introduce the
unsafety, it only adds a second spelling that reaches it. Fix this first and
-43's widening becomes unconditionally safe; the two ASAN tests above are
already the shape its close needs.

fix:
FIXED by 8fcfb64d. Guard the `(Sends,Sends)` / `(Receives,Receives)` conflict arms in
`ConcurrencyChecker::two_effects_conflict` (src/concurrency/conflicts.rs) with
`a.resource == crate::ast::CHANNEL_RESOURCE_CANONICAL`, so the channel
resource follows design.md:5813's table (Safe) while `Network` keeps the
conservative shared-socket behaviour. All three concurrency-side wrappers
(`effects_conflict`, `effects_conflict_excluding_network`, `conflict_detail`)
funnel through this one predicate, so the diagnostic path inherits the fix
with no second site to keep in sync. Four pins in tests/concurrency.rs:
distinct-channel sends fan out, multi-producer on ONE channel fans out,
multi-consumer fans out, and `writes`+`writes` on a channel still conflicts
(the narrowness control).
title: TWO SENDS ON A CHANNEL SPURIOUSLY SERIALIZE -- `ConcurrencyChecker::two_effects_conflict` codes `(Sends,Sends)` and `(Receives,Receives)` as a CONFLICT on EVERY resource, contradicting design.md:5813's table (both Safe), :6109's multi-producer/multi-consumer statement, and the compiler's own `effectchecker::effects_conflict`, which transcribes the table correctly -- so the two lattices disagree and the one driving auto-parallelization is the wrong one
detail:
FOUND WHILE SCOPING B-2026-08-21-52, which asked for per-VALUE channel
resource identity and named this behaviour as its motivation. The motivation
turned out to be a different, much smaller defect -- this one -- so it is
filed separately rather than buried in that row.

design.md:5813's conflict table is explicit, and all three communication rows
say the same thing:

  | `sends` + `sends`       | Safe | Safe |
  | `sends` + `receives`    | Safe | Safe |
  | `receives` + `receives` | Safe | Safe |

design.md:6109 then spells out WHY, for channels specifically: "multiple
producers and multiple consumers are both valid channel patterns" -- a
channel is an MPMC queue that synchronizes internally.

`ConcurrencyChecker::two_effects_conflict` implemented two of those three
rows backwards:

  (Sends, Sends) => true,          // CONFLICT
  (Receives, Receives) => true,    // CONFLICT
  (Sends, Receives) => false,      // Safe -- the only one that matched

The compiler's OWN second lattice, `effectchecker::effects_conflict`
(src/effectchecker.rs:2848), transcribes the table correctly -- all three
false. So the two lattices disagreed with each other, and the one that
actually drives auto-parallelization was the wrong one.

MEASURED, before the fix, with two sends on two DIFFERENT channels:

    fn push_a(tx: Sender[i64]) -> i64 with sends(tx) { return 1; }
    fn push_b(out: Sender[i64]) -> i64 with sends(out) { return 2; }
    fn main() { let c1 = 0; let c2 = 0;
                let x = push_a(c1); let y = push_b(c2); }

  parallel_groups: [{[0,1] "pure computations"}]      <- stmts 2,3 NOT grouped

The producer/consumer pair (`sends` + `receives`) DID group, so B-2026-08-21-52's
title claim -- that design.md:6095's producer-against-consumer argument is not
backed by the compiler -- is not what was broken. Two PRODUCERS were.

WHY THE CONSERVATIVE ARMS EXIST, AND WHY THEY STAY. The deviation is not
sloppiness: it is load-bearing for `Network`. Two `sends(Network)` on a
POSSIBLY-SHARED socket interleave and corrupt the stream, and this pass
carries no connection identity to tell one socket from another, so it
conflicts and relaxes only for provably-ephemeral pairs
(`is_ephemeral_network_fanout`). `test_a2b2_borrow_param_network_sends_
receives_stays_serial` pins exactly that. The bug is that a
socket-motivated rule was applied to EVERY resource, including the one
resource the spec singles out as safe.

THE FIX keys the relaxation on the RESOURCE, not the verbs: the two
conservative arms are guarded by `a.resource == CHANNEL_RESOURCE_CANONICAL`,
so a channel follows the table as written while `Network` keeps its
conservative behaviour untouched. Deliberately narrower than "the channel
resource never conflicts": `writes(Channel)` + `writes(Channel)` still
conflicts, since the table only blesses the communication verbs. A
narrowness-control test pins that, and was verified to FAIL against a
deliberately over-wide `if a.resource == CHANNEL { return false }` variant
before being kept.

NOTE FOR THE PER-VALUE-IDENTITY ROW: per-value identity would NOT have been
sufficient here. It fixes two sends on two DIFFERENT channels (they become
different resources), but design.md:6109 also blesses multiple producers on
the SAME channel, which stays a same-resource pair under any identity scheme.
Only the lattice fix covers both.

SPEC OBSERVATION, not fixed here and not a defect in this row's sense:
design.md:5813's table has NO socket exception, so the `Network`
serialization the compiler performs (and which
`test_a2b2_borrow_param_network_sends_receives_stays_serial` pins as
required for soundness) is undocumented in the table it appears to
contradict. The two conflict lattices also still disagree for `Network`
specifically -- `effectchecker::effects_conflict` says Safe, the concurrency
one says Conflict -- which is pre-existing and deliberate (one drives
diagnostics, the other parallelization), but nothing in design.md records
either. Worth a spec sentence; left alone here to keep this fix scoped.

fix:
FIXED by e576a8c.

ONE SEEDING BLOCK in `effectchecker.rs`, modelled on the `sends(Network)` block
this row identified as the only such construction in the compiler:

  Sender.send       + sends(Channel)
  Receiver.recv     + receives(Channel)
  Receiver.try_recv + receives(Channel)

Measured before and after with `query effects`, which is also how the row's
own claims were verified before any code was written:

  tx.send(1)     [allocates Heap]           -> + sends(Channel)
  rx.recv()      [allocates Heap, suspends] -> + receives(Channel)
  rx.try_recv()  [allocates Heap]           -> + receives(Channel)

THE RESOURCE IS THE COLLAPSED `Channel`, and choosing it was the one real
design question. The row correctly framed per-value identity as out of scope
(B-2026-08-21-52), but that leaves "seed WHAT resource?" open. Answered by
measurement rather than by picking: a hand-declared `with sends(tx)` ALREADY
canonicalizes to `sends(Channel)` today, so seeding the same name makes the
builtin call and the user's wrapper agree, instead of introducing a second
spelling that per-value identity would later have to reconcile. When
B-2026-08-21-52 lands, both move together. The collapse remains the SOUND
direction meanwhile — one shared resource means two channel-touching tasks
always conflict, over-reporting rather than under-reporting.

MERGED, NOT INSERTED. The seeding idiom next door is `insert`, and these two
keys were already owned by the `allocates(Heap)` and `suspends` seeds — a
copy of the neighbouring pattern would have silently dropped both. The block
uses `entry().or_default()` and adds; that both survivals hold is ASSERTED in
the tests, not assumed.

`try_recv` additionally needed a `STDLIB_METHOD_MAP` entry. Without the
method-name-to-qualified-name routing its seed is unreachable, so the row's
list of three would have silently been a list of two.

`try_send` and `recv_blocking` are spec'd at design.md:6070 but DO NOT EXIST
as methods today ("no method 'try_send' on type 'Sender'"), so they are not
seeded — seeding a name nothing resolves to is inert, and a missing method is
a different gap from a missing effect. Split out as B-2026-08-22-21.

THE PUBLIC-BOUNDARY TIGHTENING, which is what the row meant by "not a
one-liner", behaves as intended and is pinned in both directions:

  public function 'push' performs sends(Channel) but does not declare it
  (via call to 'Sender.send' at line 2)

and the spec's own `with sends(tx)` satisfies it.

BLAST RADIUS, measured because this converts previously-accepted programs into
errors — which was the row's stated reason for deferring it. A per-file
error-count diff over all 194 `.kara` files in `examples/` + `runtime/stdlib/`
is IDENTICAL before and after; 917 kata files typecheck clean; full default
suite 0 failures; `--features llvm` suite 0 failures. The predicted breakage
did not materialize because the affected surface is small (4 example files, 5
stdlib files, 0 katas reference the channel methods at all) and those callers
either are not public or already declare their effects.

NOT ADDRESSED, and left as the row recorded it: the
`channel_param_names` program-wide-name looseness noted at the end of the row
is untouched and still accurate.

TESTS in tests/effectchecker.rs: `test_channel_send_infers_sends_channel` and
`test_channel_recv_infers_receives_channel` (each also asserting the
pre-existing `allocates`/`suspends` seed survived the merge), and
`test_public_fn_must_declare_channel_send` for both boundary directions.
Non-vacuity: reverting the seed fails all three and leaves the four
pre-existing channel tests green.
title: THE BUILTIN CHANNEL METHODS CARRY NO `sends`/`receives` EFFECT -- `Sender.send` is seeded `allocates(Heap)` and nothing else, and the ONLY `EffectVerbKind::Sends` construction in the whole compiler is the `sends(Network)` block, so a real `tx.send(v)` is invisible to conflict analysis, `karac explain` and `query effects`; design.md:6070 declares it `with sends(tx) allocates(Heap)`
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING the channel conflict lattice (the B-2026-08-21-52 scoping
pass). Independent of that fix, and it bounds how much of the channel effect
surface is reachable at all today.

design.md:6070 declares the channel methods with per-value channel effects:

    fn send(self, tx: Sender[T], val: T)     with sends(tx) allocates(Heap)
    fn try_send(...) -> Result[...]          with sends(tx) allocates(Heap)
    fn recv(self, rx: Receiver[T]) -> T      with receives(rx) suspends
    fn recv_blocking(...)                    with receives(rx) blocks
    fn try_recv(...) -> Option[T]            with receives(rx)

MEASURED: the compiler seeds `Sender.send` with `allocates(Heap)` ONLY
(src/effectchecker.rs:1199, in the shared allocates seed list). Grepping
every `verb: EffectVerbKind::Sends` construction in the compiler returns
exactly ONE site -- the `sends(Network)` / `receives(Network)` seeding block
at src/effectchecker.rs:1316. There is no site anywhere that produces a
`sends`/`receives` effect on a CHANNEL resource.

CONSEQUENCE. A real `tx.send(v)` contributes no channel effect, so the whole
channel surface is invisible to conflict analysis, to `karac explain`, and to
`query effects` -- the same hole the comment at src/effectchecker.rs:1305
describes for the network surface ("Without these, the whole network surface
is invisible to network-effect conflict analysis, `karac explain` / `query
effects` ...") and fixes there, but never fixed for channels.

Channel effects therefore only exist today when a user DECLARES them on their
own wrapper (`fn push(tx: Sender[i64]) with sends(tx)`), which is the form
B-2026-08-21-32 made resolve and the form the conflict-lattice fix operates
on. That form works; the builtin call does not produce the effect.

NOT ATTEMPTED, and it is not a one-liner: seeding a `sends` effect on a
builtin every channel program calls changes PUBLIC-BOUNDARY effect
verification for every such program (a public fn calling `tx.send` would then
have to declare it), so it needs its own slice with the declared-vs-performed
surface measured first. Note `recv` additionally carries `suspends`, and
`suspends`-carrying statements are excluded from auto-parallelization upstream
by `effects_mark_coroutine_boundary` before the conflict lattice is reached --
so seeding `receives` on `recv` would not by itself change any
parallelization decision; `try_recv` (no `suspends`) is the one that would.

SEPARATE LOOSENESS NOTED WHILE READING THIS CODE, not fixed and not the
subject of this row: `EffectChecker::channel_param_names` is a PROGRAM-WIDE
set of NAMES, collected from every function/trait/impl signature up front
(src/effectchecker.rs:990). `canonical_resource_name` then rewrites any bare
single-segment resource whose name is in that set. So a bare `with sends(tx)`
written in a function that has NO `tx` parameter still canonicalizes to the
channel resource, as long as SOME other function in the program happens to
declare a channel-typed parameter named `tx`. Pre-existing, orthogonal to the
missing builtin effect, and low-impact (the resolver has already rejected
every other reading of a bare name by that point) -- recorded so the next
person to touch this does not rediscover it.

fix:
FIXED by bde5935.

BOTH METHODS IMPLEMENTED end to end — typecheck, interpreter, runtime,
codegen, effect seeds — plus the `SendError[T]` type design.md's `try_send`
signature names but never defined.

  tx.try_send(v)      -> Result[(), SendError[T]]   sends(Channel) allocates(Heap)
  rx.recv_blocking()  -> T                          receives(Channel) blocks

Effects measured with `query effects`, which is also how the row's own claims
were checked before any code was written. `recv_blocking` carries `blocks` and
NOT `suspends`, asserted in both directions — the two execution verbs are the
entire observable difference between it and `recv`, which lowers to the same
runtime entry and returns the same value (`karac_runtime_channel_recv` already
parks on a condvar on every threads-target, so `recv_blocking` is honest about
what happens now while `recv` keeps the forward-looking verb).

`SendError.Closed` IS DELIBERATELY UNREACHABLE ON BOTH BACKENDS, and this was
the one real design decision. The compiled runtime CAN detect a dropped
receiver — receivers are `total - senders` in its live-end counters — and an
earlier draft did exactly that. Measured against the interpreter, it produced a
RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE:

  fn orphan() -> Sender[i64] { let (tx, rx) = Channel.new(); ...; return tx }
  orphan().try_send(9)   ->  karac build: "closed 9"   --interp: "sent"

because the interpreter's `ChannelBuf` is one `Arc` shared by both ends with no
per-end liveness; giving it that means deterministic drop semantics for
`Value::Receiver`, which a tree-walk evaluator with freely-`Clone`d values does
not have. This project does not accept a run-vs-build divergence — the same
rule that made the bounded `send` fail fast instead of park (B-2026-08-22-16,
whose reasoning reads identically) — so the receiver check was REMOVED rather
than kept. Both backends now agree on `Ok` and `Full`, and design.md § Channel
lifetimes says so explicitly instead of claiming a panic that does not happen.
Split as B-2026-08-24 below.

THREE DEFECTS FOUND ON THE WAY IN, each pinned by a test that fails without it:

1. PRE-EXISTING, and the reason `try_send` could not work on a heap payload at
   all. `infer_channel_method` recorded `channel_elem_types[span]` BEFORE the
   per-method arm ran, and on an unannotated `Channel.new()` the element is
   still `?T0` at that point — the arm's `pin_channel_elem_from_arg` is what
   solves it, from the first send's argument. So the first send recorded a
   1-word placeholder and codegen sized a 24-byte `String` at 8 bytes.
   MEASURED ON CLEAN `main`, before any of this row's work:

     let (tx, rx) = Channel.new(); let a = "alpha"; tx.send(a);
     println(f"got {rx.recv()}")
       --interp     -> "got alpha"
       karac build  -> "got "            (silently dropped payload)
       karac run    -> abort: "receiver elem_size 24 exceeds sent blob 8"

   Every pre-existing String-channel test ANNOTATES its pair, which is exactly
   why none of them could see it. Fixed by re-recording the element after the
   arm has pinned it; the dispatch-gate write stays unconditional, because
   codegen's channel dispatch keys on an entry being PRESENT.

2. `try_send` is the only channel method that BOTH pins the element from its
   argument AND returns a type mentioning it, so it handed a match a
   `Result[(), SendError[?T0]]` scrutinee. The payload binding then had no
   recorded type and surfaced far downstream as `codegen: no handler for method
   'len' on variable 'v'`. Only visible when the match is on the FIRST
   `try_send` in the function — a preceding bare `let r = tx.try_send(x)` pins
   the element and hides it entirely.

3. LEAK, found by the ASAN fixture and fixed rather than filed. A hand-seeded
   generic enum has ONE layout for every `T`, so unlike a monomorphized user
   enum it has no per-instantiation drop kind, and an oversize payload's
   heap box has no owner. The seeded `SendError` payload area is therefore
   sized from the program's own channel element types (floor 3 words) instead
   of a bare `T`'s 1, so the payload is inline and no box exists. LSan before:
   24 bytes per rejected `String` send (2400 in 100 objects), 48 per struct
   (4800 in 100). A `NestedStruct`-style drop kind derived the same way WAS
   tried and changed nothing measurable, so it was dropped rather than landed
   as plausible dead code.

ALSO: `SendError[+T]` is covariant, like `Option[+T]`/`Result[+T, +E]` — `T`
occurs only in producer position. Caught by the stdlib variance hygiene gate,
which is the gate doing its job.

BLAST RADIUS. Per-file error-count diff over all 194 `.kara` files in
`examples/` + `runtime/stdlib/`: ONE line changed, `runtime/stdlib/channel.kara`
0 -> 1, and it is not a regression — checking a baked stdlib file as a loose
user file rejects its variance marker (`E_VARIANCE_USER_DECL_NOT_YET`), which
is why `option.kara` already reported 1 and `result.kara` 2 in the SAME
baseline. `channel.kara` joined that by-design set by gaining a marker. 917
kata files typecheck clean. Full default suite 0 failures; full `--features
llvm` suite 0 failures under KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1 (codegen 3181,
memory_sanitizer 1146, par_codegen 267, cli 651); both clippy legs and fmt
clean.

TESTS. `tests/codegen.rs`: `e2e_channel_try_send_and_recv_blocking` (scalar
Ok/Full round-trip, heap payload on an unannotated pair, and a typed-payload
case calling a method on the bound payload) and
`e2e_channel_unannotated_heap_send_pins_element_size` (defect 1, with the
annotated pair as the control). `tests/effectchecker.rs`:
`test_try_send_and_recv_blocking_effects`. `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`:
`asan_channel_try_send_heap_payload_both_arms_no_double_free` (String payload,
both arms, 100 iterations; plus a 4-word scalar struct that pins the dynamic
sizing — without it, 3200 bytes leak). Non-vacuity: each of the five pieces
reverted independently fails its own test and nothing else.
title: `Sender.try_send` AND `Receiver.recv_blocking` ARE SPEC'D BUT DO NOT EXIST -- design.md:6070 declares both with effects, and each is "no method '<name>' on type '<Sender|Receiver>'"
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-22-20, which seeded the channel communication effects
and could only seed the methods that exist. Recorded because that row's fix
covers three of the five methods design.md:6070 declares, and the gap should
not be inferred from the seed list's shape.

MEASURED, each as a standalone program with an annotated
`(Sender[i64], Receiver[i64])` binding:

  tx.send(1i64)        OK
  rx.recv()            OK
  rx.try_recv()        OK
  tx.try_send(1i64)    error: no method 'try_send' on type 'Sender'
  rx.recv_blocking()   error: no method 'recv_blocking' on type 'Receiver'

design.md:6070 declares them as:

    fn try_send(...) -> Result[...]  with sends(tx) allocates(Heap)
    fn recv_blocking(...)            with receives(rx) blocks

so each is a missing METHOD, not a missing effect — the effect seeding is
mechanical once the method resolves (add the qualified name to the block
B-2026-08-22-20 added, plus a `STDLIB_METHOD_MAP` entry, which is what
`try_recv` needed there).

RE-MEASURED AFTER B-2026-08-22-16 LANDED (`Channel.bounded`, 555495c9), because
`try_send` is the non-blocking send on a BOUNDED channel and the two overlap by
construction — `try_send`'s `Result` return only means anything when a channel
can be full. That work did NOT introduce either method: both still report "no
method" against a `Channel.bounded(2)` endpoint as well as a `Channel.new()`
one. So this row stands on its own and is not waiting on anything.

(Also checked while there, and NOT a defect: `Channel.bounded(cap)` infers its
element type fine unannotated, exactly as `Channel.new()` does. An explicit
`(Sender[i64], Receiver[i64])` annotation on it reports `found
'(Sender[?T0], Receiver[?T0])'`, which is the annotation fighting inference
rather than a gap in the new surface.)

`recv_blocking` does not have that overlap: it is the `blocks`-flavoured
sibling of `recv`'s `suspends`, and is independent of capacity. Note the
`blocks` vs `suspends` distinction is load-bearing for scheduler placement
(design.md's two execution verbs), so it is not a synonym for `recv`.

RE-MEASURED AND CORRECTED WHILE FIXING: the row's closing note that the effect
seeding is "mechanical once the method resolves" held for `recv_blocking` but
UNDERSTATED `try_send`. The method resolving was the small half; the return
type `Result[(), SendError[T]]` needed a stdlib enum, a prelude registration, a
codegen enum layout (the first payload-carrying channel seed), a new runtime
entry point, and it exposed three separate defects — one of them a pre-existing
run-vs-build divergence in plain `send`. The row's own framing of `try_send` as
the interesting half of the pair was right; its estimate of the cost was not.

fix:
FIXED by d80540b6, by widening the key set from six to sixteen so the
coincidence the assertion trips on becomes combinatorially negligible.

The detector is "SipHash13 and Fx produce different iteration orders", and
SipHash13 is seeded per process. Six keys admit 720 orderings, so the seeded
order coincides with Fx's now and then. Measured directly by running the
compiled test binary 400 times, each a fresh process and therefore a fresh
seed: 0 failures, consistent with the ~1/720 estimate. (The first attempt at
that measurement was VACUOUS -- `--exact` with a bare test name filtered all
1362 tests out, so every run "passed" without running anything. Caught by
checking the "N passed" line rather than the exit code.)

Sixteen keys admit ~2e13 orderings. This is a probability argument, not a
proof, and the comment now says so along with the alternative that was
rejected: pinning the expected Fx walk as a constant would be fully
deterministic but would couple the test to the index's bucket layout, which
is what the order comparison was written to avoid.

BOTH ASSERTIONS ARE LOAD-BEARING, established by simulating each regression
rather than assuming. An index built under the wrong hasher while `get` uses
the right one is caught by the LOOKUP assertion ("Fx map lost key zulu"). A
selector ignored CONSISTENTLY -- index and `get` both on the default -- keeps
every lookup working and is caught ONLY by the ORDER assertion. So the flaky
assertion could not simply be deleted in favour of the deterministic one.
title: FLAKY TEST -- `a_map_hashes_through_the_hasher_it_was_built_with` asserts that SipHash13 and Fx produce DIFFERENT iteration orders over six keys, but SipHash13 is seeded per process, so the two orders coincide on some runs and the `assert_ne!` fires with two identical vectors
detail:
FOUND AS A ONE-OFF FAILURE during an unrelated full `--lib` run, then
isolated: it is a genuine flake, not a regression.

  ---- interpreter::value::map_data_tests::a_map_hashes_through_the_hasher_it_was_built_with
  panicked at src/interpreter/value.rs:2492:
  assertion `left != right` failed: both hashers produced the same order
    left:  ["charlie", "yankee", "mike", "bravo", "alpha", "zulu"]
   right:  ["charlie", "yankee", "mike", "bravo", "alpha", "zulu"]

WHY IT IS FLAKY BY CONSTRUCTION. The test builds the same six string keys
into two `MapData`s -- one `HasherKind::SipHash13`, one `HasherKind::Fx` --
and asserts their `iter_observable()` orders DIFFER, as a proxy for "the
hasher selector actually reaches the index". SipHash13 is seeded per process,
so its bucket order is not fixed across runs; Fx's is. Six keys admit 720
orderings, so on some fraction of runs the seeded order coincides with Fx's
and the `assert_ne!` fires with two identical vectors -- exactly what the
output above shows.

MEASURED: 5/5 passes in isolation and 3/3 passes of the full `--lib` suite
(1362 tests) on the same commit that produced the failure, plus a pass on the
parent commit. So it is low-frequency rather than load-dependent, and NOT
caused by the change that happened to be in the tree when it fired.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS RATE SUGGESTS: it fails in the `--lib` target,
which every `cargo test` run includes, and it fails with a message that reads
like a real defect ("the selector is not reaching the index"). A reviewer who
hits it will reasonably suspect whatever they were working on -- which is
precisely what happened here, costing a bisect against the parent commit to
clear.

THE FIX IS SMALL and should not weaken what the test checks. The property it
wants is "the two hashers produce different BUCKET ASSIGNMENTS", and asserting
that through observable ITERATION ORDER is what introduces the coincidence.
Options, cheapest first: (a) assert on the hashed index/bucket values
directly rather than on iteration order; (b) keep the order comparison but
use enough keys that a coincidence is negligible (720 orderings is not);
(c) seed SipHash13 deterministically in the test. (a) is the honest one --
it tests the selector rather than a downstream shadow of it.

fix:
FIXED by 0e5dca3.

ONE CHANGE, in `compile_channel_try_send`: WHERE the move-suppression is
emitted now depends on the payload kind, because who owns a rejected value
does.

MEASURED under LSan, and both directions are wrong in different ways:

  payload        reject path              disarming the source gives
  -------------  -----------------------  ---------------------------------
  String / Vec   ARM BINDING owns it      correct (leaving it armed = DOUBLE FREE)
  struct+heap    SOURCE BINDING owns it   LEAK (1480 bytes / 200 objects)

Both are internally consistent — exactly one owner each — they just put the
owner in different places, and an ordinary `fn f(x: T) -> Result[(), E[T]]`
call shows the SAME split. So this is not channel semantics; it is the
language's existing convention, and `try_send` now follows it instead of
copying `send`.

`send` never had to choose: it ALWAYS moves into the queue and has no reject
path, so its unconditional disarm (B-2026-07-13-16) is right for it and wrong
here. The suppressors write a runtime `cap = 0` into the source's slot, so
they are position-dependent — the fix is which basic block they land in, not
new machinery. `NestedStruct` is precisely "an inline user struct whose own
drop fn frees its heap", so the classifier that decides enum payload drops
decides this too, rather than a second hand-rolled type test drifting from it.

THE MAP/SET HALF STAYS UNCONDITIONAL and that is deliberate: it edits the
compile-time cleanup QUEUE (Map cleanup is queue-driven — no in-slot sentinel
for a walker to skip), so it cannot be branch-conditional at all. On the Ok
path the queue owns the handle and a second free would be a double free; on
the reject path the cost is a leaked handle. Wrong-free versus leak, and it
picks leak.

TWO THINGS TRIED, MEASURED, AND REMOVED rather than landed as plausible dead
code:

  * Deriving the payload's `EnumDropKind` from the channel element types, the
    way the payload WIDTH already is. With the payload inline and the
    suppression split by kind, the value already has exactly one owner, and
    arming the enum's own drop on top turned the `String` case into a DOUBLE
    FREE. (An earlier attempt at this looked inert; that measurement was
    CONFOUNDED — the seed ran before `register_struct_metadata`, so it scored
    every user struct at the unknown-name default and derived nothing. Moving
    the seed made the derivation real, and only then could it be measured
    honestly. Recorded because "I tested it and it changed nothing" was true
    of the experiment and false of the claim.)
  * A `seeded_enum_variant_field_type_exprs` override so
    `emit_enum_drop_switch`'s `NestedStruct` arm could resolve the payload's
    concrete struct name instead of the declaration's bare `T` — real (the arm
    emits a GEP and NO call without it, which is a genuine hole for any future
    seeded generic enum that needs a drop), but unreachable once the drop kind
    is `None`. Removed with the derivation it existed to serve.

HOW IT WAS FOUND — the diagnosis that actually mattered, since three plausible
mechanisms were wrong first. The IR of a leaking program was diffed against
the same program written through a helper function (`fn mk(x: Big, n: i64) ->
Result[(), SendError[Big]]`), which is ASAN-clean. The clean version emits
`__karac_drop_struct_Big(ptr %y)` on the SOURCE at scope exit and never emits
an enum drop at all; the leaking one emits the same call but the source's
fields were already zeroed by the disarm. That is what identified the owner as
the source binding rather than anything about the enum.

THE `Closed` ARM is covered by the same rule and is verified separately: it
became reachable only with B-2026-08-22-24 (landed while this was in flight),
so the split had never been measured on it. It rides the reject-path rule, and
that falls out of placing the struct disarm on the OK branch rather than on
"not Full" — which is why the split is written that way.

TESTS in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs, all inside
`asan_channel_try_send_heap_payload_both_arms_no_double_free`: the
struct-with-heap payload (the leak), the `Vec` payload (the double free the
first fix attempt caused), and the `Closed` arm with a struct payload.
Non-vacuity in BOTH directions: collapsing the split to always-disarm leaks
1480 bytes on the struct case; collapsing it to Ok-branch-only double-frees on
the String and Vec cases. Four-surface parity (`--interp` / JIT / `build` /
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`) re-checked on eight channel programs including the
`Closed` orphaned-sender shape.

Full default suite 0 failures; full `--features llvm` suite 0 failures under
KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1; both clippy legs and fmt clean; 917 kata
files typecheck clean; per-file error-count diff over `examples/` +
`runtime/stdlib/` identical to the B-2026-08-22-21 baseline.
title: A STRUCT-WITH-HEAP CHANNEL PAYLOAD LEAKS ITS OWN `String`/`Vec` FIELDS ON `try_send`'S REJECT PATH -- the `SendError.Full(v)` binding frees a String or Vec payload correctly, but a struct CARRYING them leaks each field; the identical user-generic-enum program is ASAN-clean
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-22-21, which implemented `try_send` and closed the
larger half of this class. Filed rather than folded into that row because it
survives the fix that closed the others and has a different mechanism.

MEASURED under LSan, 100 iterations, `struct Big { a: String, b: String }` sent
over a bounded channel and rejected by `try_send`:

  1480 bytes leaked in 200 objects   (790 + 690 -- the two `String` buffers of
                                      each rejected `Big`)

WHAT IS ALREADY CLEAN, which is what makes the remainder small and specific:

  String payload        try_send both arms, 100 iters  -> clean
  Vec[i64] payload      try_send both arms, 100 iters  -> clean
  4-word scalar struct  try_send both arms, 100 iters  -> clean
  struct-with-heap      PLAIN send + recv, 100 iters   -> clean

So it is not the channel transport, not the enum payload BOX (B-2026-08-22-21
removed that by sizing the seeded `SendError` payload area from the program's
channel element types -- before that sizing this same program leaked an
ADDITIONAL 4800 bytes in 100 objects, one 48-byte box per rejected send), and
not heap payloads generally. It is a struct payload's OWN heap fields, on the
arm that hands the value back.

THE CONTROL IS THE INFORMATIVE PART. The identical program with a user generic
enum in place of `SendError` --

  struct Big { a: String, b: String }
  enum W[T] { A(T), B(T) }
  fn mk(x: Big, n: i64) -> Result[(), W[Big]] { if n > 0 { return Err(W.A(x)); } return Ok(()); }
  match mk(y, 1) { Ok(u) => .., Err(W.A(v)) => v.a.len() + v.b.len(), .. }

-- is ASAN-CLEAN. `W[Big]` is MONOMORPHIZED, so `declare_enums` computes its
layout against a concrete `Big` payload; a hand-seeded stdlib enum has exactly
ONE layout for every `T` and cannot. That is the same root cause as the box
B-2026-08-22-21 fixed, showing up in the second of the two things a layout
carries.

NOT FIXED BY THE OBVIOUS MOVE, and this was measured rather than assumed:
deriving the payload's `EnumDropKind` from the program's channel element types
-- the same trick that sizes the width one line above it -- produced
BYTE-IDENTICAL LSan output. So the leak is not reached through the enum's drop
kind at all, and that derivation was dropped rather than landed as
plausible-looking dead code. The likely owner is the ARM BINDING's scope
cleanup (`try_send` suppresses the source's cleanup on both paths, since the
value leaves the caller either way -- into the queue or into the `SendError`),
but that was not confirmed and should not be assumed by whoever picks this up.

BOUNDED: a leak, never a double free or a wrong answer, on a shape (sending a
struct that owns heap over a channel AND using `try_send` rather than `send`)
that no example, stdlib file or kata uses today. The ASAN fixture for it is
NOT checked in as an `#[ignore]`d test -- the shipped fixture covers the clean
shapes -- so reproducing means writing the program above.

fix:
FIXED by d6fe527. The row's central claim -- that the interpreter CANNOT
model receiver liveness -- is refuted; it can, and the mechanism is about
twenty lines.

WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED: "deterministic drop semantics for `Value::Receiver` in
a tree-walk evaluator whose values are freely `Clone`d ... a per-end counter
inside `ChannelBuf` plus a real drop hook on the two endpoint `Value`
variants", explicitly flagged as "not a small slice".

WHAT IT ACTUALLY TOOK: the per-end counter, and the drop hook is just `Drop`
on a newtype. `Value::Sender(Arc<ChannelBuf>)` becomes
`Value::Sender(SenderHandle)`, where `SenderHandle`'s `Clone` and `Drop` are
the only things that move `ChannelBuf::senders`; same for the receiver. The
row is right that `Arc::strong_count` cannot answer the question -- both ends
hold the same `Arc` -- but a count only the handle touches can.

THE PART THE ROW TREATED AS THE HARD ONE TURNED OUT NOT TO BE. A tree-walk
evaluator drops the `Receiver` value when its scope is torn down, which is
exactly the moment the compiled backend drops its own end. No new drop
discipline, no region analysis. The row's own repro was the test:

  fn orphan() -> Sender[i64] { let (tx, rx) = Channel.new(); ...; return tx }
  orphan().try_send(9)

  before:  karac build -> "closed 9"   --interp -> "sent"     (the divergence)
  after:   interp / JIT / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build -> "closed 9"

BLAST RADIUS: 20 call sites across 5 files, all mechanical (`h.buf()` where
the code had an `Arc`). The one that mattered was `Sender.clone()`, which had
to become a HANDLE clone rather than an `Arc::clone` -- a cloned sender is a
second live endpoint and the count has to say so.

THREE THINGS MOVED TOGETHER, as the row specified. The compiled check went
back into `karac_runtime_channel_try_send`, ahead of the capacity arm (a
receiver-less channel is closed whether or not it is also full; reporting
`Full` would invite a retry that can never succeed). `send` gained its spec'd
panic on both backends. design.md's "v1 status of the no-receiver case"
paragraph is gone, replaced by a statement of what now holds.

ONE EXISTING ASAN FIXTURE CHANGED, and the reason is worth keeping. `asan_
channel_end_explicit_return_single_free` returned a SENDER from `mk` and then
did `s.send(22)` in `main` -- on a channel whose receiver had died with `mk`'s
frame. It was depending on the unspecified behaviour this row removes. Its
subject is the `ExprKind::Return` drop suppression, not send semantics, and
its own comment already described returning `rx` while the code returned
`tx`; the fixture had drifted from its description. It now returns the
receiver, matching both its comment and its sibling
`asan_channel_end_returned_from_fn_single_free`, with both sends made while
`rx` is alive. All ten channel ASAN fixtures green.

TESTS pair the two backends on purpose, because their AGREEMENT is what makes
the behaviour shippable at all: four in tests/interpreter.rs -- `Closed`, the
live-receiver control (an always-zero count would satisfy the first and break
every real program), `send`'s error, and a sender-CLONE case that one shared
count would pass and a per-end one must not -- plus `e2e_channel_closed_when_
the_receiver_is_gone` as the compiled twin. A regression on either side now
fails a test.

Full suite: 109 binaries, 14888 passed, 0 failed. fmt clean; clippy clean on
both feature legs and on the wasm32-wasip1 arm (the runtime changed).
title: THE INTERPRETER CANNOT MODEL RECEIVER LIVENESS, SO `SendError.Closed` AND `send`'S NO-RECEIVER PANIC ARE BOTH UNREACHABLE -- the compiled runtime has the counters and had to give them up to keep run == build
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-22-21. That row implemented `try_send`; this is the
capability its `Closed` variant is waiting on, and it also covers a spec claim
about plain `send` that predates it.

design.md declares two behaviours that depend on knowing whether any receiver
is still alive:

  fn send(...)      // "panics if all receivers are dropped"
  fn try_send(...)  // Err when "no receiver exists"  -> SendError.Closed(v)

NEITHER IS IMPLEMENTED. `send` does not consult receiver liveness at all (it
never has), and `try_send`'s `Closed` is produced only for a null channel
handle, which nothing a Kara program can write produces.

THE COMPILED SIDE COULD DO IT TODAY -- receivers are `total - senders` in
`KaracChannel`'s live-end counters -- and B-2026-08-22-21's first draft did.
MEASURED, that alone is worse than not doing it:

  fn orphan() -> Sender[i64] { let (tx, rx) = Channel.new(); ...; return tx }
  orphan().try_send(9)   ->  karac build: "closed 9"   --interp: "sent"

The interpreter's `ChannelBuf` is a single `Arc` shared by BOTH ends with no
per-end liveness, so it cannot tell a dropped receiver from a live one. This
project does not accept a run-vs-build divergence -- the same rule that made
the bounded `send` fail fast instead of park (B-2026-08-22-16) -- so the
compiled check was removed and both backends now agree by construction.
design.md's Channel section states the v1 hold explicitly rather than claiming
a panic that does not happen.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE, and why it is not a small slice: deterministic drop
semantics for `Value::Receiver` in a tree-walk evaluator whose values are
freely `Clone`d. `Arc::strong_count` on the shared `ChannelBuf` does not
answer it either -- both ends hold the same `Arc`, so the count cannot
distinguish a live sender from a live receiver. It needs a per-end counter
inside `ChannelBuf` plus a real drop hook on the two endpoint `Value`
variants.

WHEN IT LANDS, three things move together: the compiled receiver check goes
back into `karac_runtime_channel_try_send` (the code is described in its doc
comment), `send` gains its spec'd panic, and design.md's "v1 status of the
no-receiver case" paragraph comes out.

fix:
Fixed in 098daf6. `0_i64` -> `0` and `1_000_i64` -> `1_000`; `42i64` -> `42`
was already right and stays so.

WHERE IT IS FIXED IS THE ONE INTERESTING PART, because the obvious place does
not work. `warn_redundant_suffix` derives the deletion as the last
`suffix.len()` bytes of the literal token, and to widen it over the separator
it would have to look at the byte before -- which it CANNOT SEE:
`typecheck(program, resolve_result)` takes no source text, and the token
carries a numeric VALUE plus a suffix enum rather than the author's digits, so
`0_i64`, `0i64` and `0x0i64` are indistinguishable there. Threading source
through every caller of `typecheck` to recover one underscore is not a trade
worth making for a cosmetic defect.

`Pipeline` already holds the text for exactly this purpose. Its `source`
field's own doc says "Span-driven lints need the author's own spelling", and
the `map_value_clone_reinsert` lint one block above already reads it the same
way; the widening runs immediately after, in the same place and pattern.

THAT ALSO SERVES BOTH CONSUMERS FROM ONE PLACE, which a fix inside `cmd_fix`
would not have. `karac fix` and `--output=json`'s `fix_it` object read the
same span, so correcting only the CLI would have left every IDE applying the
published edit still producing `0_`. There is a test pinning the JSON offset
and length for that reason, separate from the CLI one.

WHY WALKING BACK CANNOT OVER-DELETE: an underscore directly abutting the
suffix can only be the attaching separator, because a digit separator has a
digit after it. `1_000_i64` keeps its digit separators and loses only the
attaching one -- asserted, not assumed, since that is the case a careless
"strip trailing underscores" would get wrong.

COSMETIC CONFIRMED, NOT ASSUMED: the tests assert the rewritten file still
runs and prints the same values (`0 1000 42`), which is what keeps this low
severity. It is worth fixing because `karac fix` is the primary fix path the
Mend loop tells authors to trust, and a rewrite that emits syntax nobody would
write undermines exactly the surface it sells.

THE LIVE REPRODUCTION IS CLEANED UP. The row left six dangling literals in
kara-katas bespoke/word-frequency/word_frequency.kara deliberately, as the
in-tree repro; that is now redundant with the tests, and `karac fix` cannot
remove them (there is no suffix left to delete), so they were hand-edited in
kara-katas 19484c5. Verified byte-identical before and after on all three
surfaces -- `run --interp`, `build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` -- with
KARAC_HASH_SEED pinned because the kata walks a Map, and all three agree.

METHOD NOTE, because the first A/B run reported a difference that did not
exist: the comparison harness redirected `karac build` to /dev/null, the
`karac` under test had been built WITHOUT `--features llvm` so `build` fell
back to type-check and emitted no binary, and the script then hashed bash's
"./before: No such file or directory" -- which differs from the `after`
message by the filename alone. Every "before != after" number in that pass was
an artifact of the two file names. Rebuilding with `--features llvm` gave
identical output on all three surfaces. Do not swallow the build output of a
comparison harness.

Full suite after rebasing onto B-2026-08-22-6's hasher work: 109 binaries,
14907 passed, 0 failed. fmt clean; clippy clean on both feature legs.
title: `karac fix`'s `redundant_suffix` DELETION SPAN IS ONE CHARACTER SHORT ON THE UNDERSCORE-SEPARATED SUFFIX FORM: `0_i64` is rewritten to `0_`, leaving the separator that existed only to attach the suffix
detail:
B-2026-08-21-14 gave the `redundant_suffix` warning a machine-applicable deletion so `karac fix` could remove the suffix. The deletion covers the suffix TEXT but not the optional `_` that separates it from the digits, so the two literal spellings are not handled alike:

    let a = 0_i64;        ->  let a = 0_;          WRONG
    let b = 1_000_i64;    ->  let b = 1_000_;      WRONG
    let c = 42i64;        ->  let c = 42;          right

REPRODUCE: put the three lines above in a file, `karac fix` it. All three warnings are reported and 'applied 3 fix(es)'.

IMPACT IS COSMETIC, NOT SEMANTIC, and that is measured rather than assumed. The rewritten form still lexes as an integer literal: the file passes `karac check` afterward and prints `0 1000 42`, the same values as before. So this is a code-quality defect in a rewrite the user is invited to apply en masse, not a miscompile -- hence low severity.

The trailing separator is nevertheless not something a human would write, and `karac fix` is the primary fix path the Mend loop tells authors to trust, so a fix that leaves behind syntax nobody would author undermines exactly the surface it is meant to sell.

SOURCE NOTE: found by sweeping `karac fix` across the whole kara-katas corpus (914 `.kara` files, 848 changed, 25,925 `redundant_suffix` removals). Exactly one file in the corpus uses the underscore-separated form -- bespoke/word-frequency/word_frequency.kara -- and it produced five `0_` / `1_` / `10_` literals. The sweep was verified by building and running every file before and after with KARAC_HASH_SEED pinned (908 comparable, 908 byte-identical), which is how a purely cosmetic defect was separated from a semantic one. The dangling literals were originally left in place in that repo as a live reproduction; kara-katas 19484c5 has since hand-patched them away, so the in-tree repro is GONE and the three-line snippet above is the reproduction. Noted because the earlier wording pointed a future reader at a file that no longer demonstrates anything.

fix:
FIXED by 840f95ef, in the same commit as B-2026-08-22-6, by giving the method-call argument
loop the arm the free-function path has had since B-2026-08-21-24: when the
parameter is `ref`, spill `coerce_to_slice`'s synthesized header through
`materialize_rvalue_for_ref_arg` and pass its address instead of the value.
Three lines, reusing the existing helper rather than inventing a second
materialization -- the same shape the free-function fix took.

Regression test `e2e_collection_literal_into_a_ref_slice_param_of_a_method` in
`tests/codegen.rs`, covering BOTH receiver shapes (a trait default body
monomorphized into the impl, and an ordinary inherent method) with the
by-value `Slice[T]` control beside each, since that spelling always worked and
a regression confined to the `ref` slot would otherwise hide behind it.
title: A collection literal passed to a `ref Slice[T]` parameter through a METHOD CALL fails LLVM module verification -- `coerce_to_slice` builds the `{ptr, i64}` header as a value and the method-call arg loop pushes it into a `ptr` slot. `karac check` accepts the program and `--interp` runs it. The method-call half of B-2026-08-21-24, which fixed the same shape on the free-function path only; design.md's own `Hasher.write_u8` body (`self.write([n])`) is the reproducer
detail:
WHAT HAPPENED. A collection literal passed to a `ref Slice[T]` parameter
THROUGH A METHOD CALL ON THE RECEIVER produced a module that fails LLVM
verification. `karac check` accepted the program and `--interp` ran it
correctly, so it was a build-only failure on a checked program:

    trait Sink {
        fn write(mut ref self, b: ref Slice[u8]);
        fn put(mut ref self, n: u8) { self.write([n]) }
    }
    // karac build:
    //   codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Call parameter type does
    //   not match function signature!
    //     %slice.len = insertvalue { ptr, i64 } %slice.ptr, i64 %lit.len, 1
    //     call void @Acc.write(ptr %self.ref.ptr, { ptr, i64 } %slice.len)"

`coerce_to_slice` builds the `{ptr, i64}` header as a VALUE; a `ref` slot
declares a `ptr`. The method-call argument loop in `src/codegen/method_call.rs`
pushed the header straight into that slot.

IT IS THE METHOD-CALL HALF OF B-2026-08-21-24, which fixed exactly this on the
free-function path (`call_dispatch.rs`) and never on this one -- the same
"landed on two of the three call paths" shape as B-2026-06-19-1 (Array into a
ref-slice param), B-2026-08-05-41 (a field place into a `mut ref` slot) and
B-2026-08-21-39 (Array into an associated fn's `mut Slice`). Four rows in this
family now; the call paths keep drifting because each fix is applied where the
reproducer happened to be written.

MEASURED over a 3 x 2 x 2 matrix -- (free fn, inherent method on self, trait
DEFAULT body on self) x (`ref Slice[u8]`, bare `Slice[u8]`) x (`[n]` literal,
`n.to_ne_bytes()` call result). Exactly two cells failed, and they are the two
that combine a method receiver, a `ref` slot, and a literal:

    free fn                      ref Slice   literal      ok
    free fn                      ref Slice   to_ne_bytes  ok
    free fn                      bare Slice  literal      ok
    free fn                      bare Slice  to_ne_bytes  ok
    inherent method on self      ref Slice   literal      CODEGEN FAIL
    inherent method on self      ref Slice   to_ne_bytes  ok
    inherent method on self      bare Slice  literal      ok
    inherent method on self      bare Slice  to_ne_bytes  ok
    trait DEFAULT body on self   ref Slice   literal      CODEGEN FAIL
    trait DEFAULT body on self   ref Slice   to_ne_bytes  ok
    trait DEFAULT body on self   bare Slice  literal      ok
    trait DEFAULT body on self   bare Slice  to_ne_bytes  ok

All twelve pass after the fix. The literal is the discriminating input because
it owns no storage the pointer fast-paths above can borrow; a call result is
classified by `arg_is_array_source` and takes the earlier carve-out, and a
by-value `Slice[T]` slot wants the header as a value anyway.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, and why that matters. design.md § `Hash` and `Hasher` writes
`Hasher.write_u8`'s default body as literally `self.write([n])`. Baking that
trait for B-2026-08-22-6 therefore made EVERY user `impl Hasher` fail to
compile -- the spec's own text was the reproducer, and the trait had no user
before that row. Writing the stdlib body as `n.to_ne_bytes()` would have made
the suite green in one character and left the bug in the compiler for the next
caller.

fix:
FIXED by bab8cf2.

TWO LINES OF MECHANISM: the monomorphized `Map[K, V]` bodies now LOAD the
map's stored `hash_fn` pointer from its control block and call it indirectly,
instead of calling a `karac_hash_<K>` symbol baked in at emission time.

THE FIX WAS ALREADY WRITTEN, in the same file, for the sibling containers. The
Set monos (`emit_mono_set_contains_body` / `_insert_body`) and the String-key
Map get read `KARAC_MAP_HASH_FN_OFFSET`, and the comment above the Set one
states the rule the Map bodies broke, verbatim: "the buckets were filled with
this exact function ... so hardcoding one here would probe the wrong bucket for
a Set whose stored hash differs." The Map bodies were never brought along.

That is also exactly why the reported symptom was `Map[i64, i64, H]` and
nothing else. MEASURED, all at N=200000 with FxBuildHasher:

  Map[i64, i64, Fx]     3391 missing   <- the two baked-hash bodies
  Set[i64, Fx]          0 missing      <- loads the stored fn
  Map[String, i64, Fx]  0 missing      <- loads the stored fn

WHY THE HASHER MATTERED, which the row correctly flagged as the strange part
since the resize trigger cannot see a hash. It is not the trigger. The hasher
is a CONSTRUCTION-time decision: `Map.new` synthesizes the hash fn for the
declared `H` and stores the pointer, and every erased-path operation --
`contains_key`, `get`, and crucially `resize`/`rehash_from` -- calls through
it. The mono fast path called the DEFAULT hash instead. So a non-default map
FILED keys under one hash and PROBED under another.

THE ROW'S INFERRED DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, and it is worth saying so plainly
because it is the natural reading of the numbers: nothing "stops growing", and
`find_insert_slot`'s "Should not reach here" fallback is not involved. The
table resizes normally throughout. What produces the contiguous tail is that
each resize takes the SLOW path, which rehashes the whole table through the
stored fn and thereby REPAIRS every previously-misfiled key. Only the keys
inserted since the last resize stay lost -- hence a tail, and hence one
beginning at exactly the 3/4 threshold. The row's own control (the default
hasher never loses a key) is explained by the baked hash being the correct one
there.

MUCH WORSE THAN THE ROW RECORDED, and this is the correction that matters:
it is NOT a large-N phenomenon, and it is not only `Map[i64, V]`. Measured on
the unfixed compiler:

  Map[i64, i64, Fx]   n=16 -> 3 missing   n=64 -> 15   n=100 -> 3   n=1000 -> 231
  Map[char, i64, Fx]  62 keys -> 13 missing

A SIXTEEN-KEY map already loses keys, and `char` keys share the same emitted
body (`char` lowers to LLVM i32), so that family was equally broken and shows
it at 62 keys. The comment the fix deleted had justified sharing one body
between `char` and `i32` because "both are FNV-1a over 4 bytes and produce
identical output for identical input" -- true of the default hasher and of
nothing else. The row's "196609 at N=200000" framing
made it look like something you reach only at scale; the defect is present
from the first resize onward, i.e. essentially always. Severity `high` was
right for a different reason than the one given.

WHY LOADING THE POINTER BEATS MANGLING THE SYMBOL. The obvious alternative --
put the hasher in `mono_map_cache_key` so each hasher gets its own symbol
family -- is strictly worse. The mono family is `linkonce_odr` and SHARED by
every `Map[i64, i64]` in the module, so a program holding one default and one
Fx map of the same K/V would still need the body to be correct for both, which
a baked symbol cannot be. Reading the pointer makes the shared symbol correct
for every hasher at once, needs no cache-key change, and closes the class:
no future hasher can desync it. Pinned by
`two_maps_with_different_hashers_share_one_mono_symbol_safely`.

COST, measured rather than waved at. The hash becomes the one indirect call in
the probe (eq and the bucket walk stay inlined; the erased path this family
replaces pays an FFI boundary per operation, and the Set monos already pay
exactly this). On a `Map[i64, i64]` DEFAULT-hasher insert+get loop, 300k
entries x 6 rounds, 11 interleaved reps of each binary:

  baseline median 207 ms  (min 200, max 237)
  fixed    median 212 ms  (min 204, max 231)   +2.4%

Interleaving matters: naive back-to-back runs read +10%, which was machine
drift, not the change.

TESTS in tests/codegen.rs: `an_fx_hashed_i64_map_finds_every_key_across_resizes`
(n = 16/64/100/1000, asserting presence AND value AND len) and
`two_maps_with_different_hashers_share_one_mono_symbol_safely`. Non-vacuity
measured for EACH HALF SEPARATELY, since either alone still desyncs the pair:
reverting only the insert body gives 504/115 bad, reverting only the get body
gives 1180/500.

WHY THE EXISTING HASHER TESTS MISSED IT, worth knowing before adding the next
one: every pre-existing `FxBuildHasher` test uses `String` keys (a different,
already-correct lowering) with three entries. The mono `Map[i64, V]` family
and a resize were both required, and no test had either.

Full default suite 0 failures; full `--features llvm` suite 0 failures under
KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1 with `--no-fail-fast`; both clippy legs and
fmt clean; 917 kata files typecheck clean and four map-heavy katas verified
byte-identical across `--interp` / `build`.
title: A COMPILED `Map[i64, V, H]` under any NON-DEFAULT hasher stops growing after one resize and silently drops every key past it: `len` still counts them, `contains_key` cannot find them, and the missing keys are the contiguous tail starting at exactly 3/4 of the stalled capacity (196609 at N=200000, 393217 at 400000, 786433 at 800000). `--interp` is correct, so it is a run-vs-build divergence; the default hasher never loses a key at any N
detail:
WHAT HAPPENS. A COMPILED `Map[i64, V, H]` whose `H` is anything other than the
default hasher stops growing after one particular resize. Every insert past
that point still increments `len`, so the map reports the right size -- and
every one of those keys is then unfindable. `contains_key` / `get` return
"missing" for a contiguous SUFFIX of the inserted keys, silently.

REPRODUCED, `karac build --release`, arm64 macOS, on `3efbe0a7` (i.e. WITHOUT
the user-hasher change that surfaced it -- this is not that feature's bug):

    fn main() {
        let mut m: Map[i64, i64, FxBuildHasher] = Map.new();
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < 200000 { m.insert(i, i); i = i + 1; }
        println(m.len());                     // 200000  -- correct
        let mut missing = 0; let mut j = 0;
        while j < 200000 {
            if not m.contains_key(j) { missing = missing + 1; }
            j = j + 1;
        }
        println(missing);                     // 3391    -- WRONG, want 0
    }

The missing keys are exactly `196609 ..= 199999` -- a contiguous tail, not a
scatter, which is what rules out a hash-distribution explanation.

THE PATTERN IS EXACT, and it is a capacity boundary. Sweeping N against the
default hasher as the control:

    N        default        FxBuildHasher
    200000   0 missing      3391 missing, first = 196609 = 3/4 * 2^18 + 1
    400000   0 missing      6783 missing, first = 393217 = 3/4 * 2^19 + 1
    800000   0 missing     13567 missing, first = 786433 = 3/4 * 2^20 + 1

3/4 is `KaracMap::insert`'s resize trigger (`runtime/src/map.rs`: "Resize when
(occupied + tombstones) / capacity > 3/4"), so the boundary is that threshold
exactly, at the capacity one growth short of what N needs.

INFERRED FROM THAT, NOT YET MEASURED: the table reaches capacity C, fills to
its resize threshold, and the growth that should follow does not happen -- after
which every further insert falls through `find_insert_slot`'s
`for i in 0..capacity` loop to its `(first_tombstone.unwrap_or(0), false, ctrl)`
fallback, whose own comment reads "Should not reach here if resize policy is
respected." That fits every number above, but it has not been confirmed against
the emitted code; treat it as the first thing to check, not as the diagnosis.

WHAT IS RULED OUT ALREADY:
  * NOT hash quality. A user-written FNV-1a hasher fails at the SAME count
    (196609) as FxHash. Two different permutations producing an identical
    boundary is structural, not distributional.
  * NOT the control-byte tag. `KARAC_MAP_TAG=1` and `KARAC_MAP_TAG=0` both
    produce 196609.
  * NOT `ctrl_of` colliding with a sentinel: it sets `BUCKET_OCCUPIED_BIT`, so
    an occupied byte can never read as `BUCKET_EMPTY` / `BUCKET_TOMBSTONE`.
  * NOT the interpreter. `karac run --interp` finds all 200000. This is a
    RUN-VS-BUILD divergence, compiled side wrong.
  * NOT `String` keys, at least not at this size: `Map[String, i64,
    FxBuildHasher]` with 200000 keys loses none (it is merely very slow -- its
    own row).

WHERE TO LOOK. The hasher-dependence is the strange part, since the resize
trigger reads only `len` / `tombstones` / `capacity` and cannot see the hash.
That points at the two paths differing in WHICH insert runs: codegen
monomorphizes map operations (`src/codegen/mono.rs`), and a non-default hasher
changes the synthesized `hash_fn`'s symbol (`HasherKind::mangle_suffix`), so
the two spellings may not be taking the same emitted insert at all. Confirm
first which insert each one lowers to, before reading `resize` / `rehash_from`.

SEVERITY. High: a compiled program silently loses map lookups on a shipped,
documented spelling, with `len` still reporting the entries as present. It is
also the whole failure mode `Map` exists to not have.

fix:
Fixed in d0ced1a, following the row's own plan, which was accurate in every
particular -- including why it was not a one-liner.

`TraitInfo` carried `assoc_types: Vec<String>`: names only, enough to answer
"does this trait have an assoc type called X" and useless for discharging

ONE DESIGN DETAIL THE ROW DID NOT ANTICIPATE: the map had to become OWNED.
The user-program half can hand out `&'a AssocTypeDecl` tied to
`self.program`, but the baked half borrows `self.env`, and the per-binding
discharge loop below needs `self` mutably. Cloning a handful of small decls
per impl is the cheap way to hold both sources in one map; the alternative is
threading two differently-lifetimed maps through the loop for no gain.

THE WORKAROUND IT REPLACES IS GONE, and the reason to remove it was measured

title: An associated-type bound declared on a STDLIB-BAKED trait is never discharged at an impl site: `trait_assoc_decls` finds the trait declaration only by scanning `program.items`, and a baked trait lives in `env.traits` instead -- so `impl BuildHasher for B { type Hasher = <a type with no Hasher impl> }` type checks, while the same shape on a user-declared trait is correctly rejected with E_GAT_BOUND_NOT_SATISFIED
detail:
WHAT IS MISSING. A GAT / associated-type bound declared on a trait that is
BAKED FROM STDLIB SOURCE is never discharged at an impl site. The same bound on
a trait declared in the user's own program IS discharged, and reports
`E_GAT_BOUND_NOT_SATISFIED` correctly.

MEASURED, side by side. This is rejected, correctly:

    trait Sink { fn put(mut ref self, n: u8); }
    struct NotASink { }
    trait Build { type Made: Sink; fn make(ref self) -> Self.Made; }
    struct B { }
    impl Build for B { type Made = NotASink; fn make(ref self) -> NotASink { NotASink { } } }
    // error[E_GAT_BOUND_NOT_SATISFIED]: binding `type Made = NotASink` does not
    // satisfy declared GAT bound `Made: Sink`

Naming the associated type the same as its bound trait (`type Sink: Sink`, the
shape design.md's `BuildHasher` uses) changes nothing -- still rejected. But
the identical shape against the STDLIB `BuildHasher` is ACCEPTED:

    struct NotAHasher { h: u64 }
    struct BadBuild { }
    impl BuildHasher for BadBuild {
        type Hasher = NotAHasher;              // NotAHasher does not impl Hasher
        fn build(ref self) -> NotAHasher { NotAHasher { h: 0u64 } }
    }
    // "All checks passed."  <- should be E_GAT_BOUND_NOT_SATISFIED

WHY. `src/typechecker/items.rs`'s `trait_assoc_decls` finds the trait's
declaration by scanning `self.program.items` for a matching `Item::TraitDef`.
A stdlib-baked trait is registered into `env.traits` and is NOT in
`program.items`, so the lookup misses, `trait_assoc_bounds` comes back empty,
and the per-binding discharge loop below it never runs. The comment at that
site already narrows itself to "the user-program surface where program.items
carries the decl" -- the gap is known to the code and simply never closed.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX. `env.traits`' `TraitInfo` carries
`assoc_types: Vec<String>` -- NAMES only, no bounds. The discharge loop wants
`&AssocTypeDecl` (it also reads `generic_params` and `where_clause` further
down), so closing this means `TraitInfo` growing a bounds/decl table populated
in `env_build`, and `trait_assoc_decls` falling back to it. That is a real
slice with its own test surface, which is why it is filed rather than folded
into the row that found it.

WHAT THIS COST IN THE MEANTIME. B-2026-08-22-6 needs the `type Hasher: Hasher`
bound to actually hold -- both backends call `write` / `finish` on whatever
`build()` returns -- so it carries its own focused check in
`check_recorded_container_hasher` rather than relying on this machinery. That
check should be deleted when this row lands, and its test
(`a_builder_whose_state_type_is_not_a_hasher_is_refused` in
`tests/typechecker.rs`) kept, since it would then be covering the general
mechanism instead of a local workaround.

SEVERITY. Medium, and the class is `soundness` rather than `diagnostics`
because the bound is ACCEPTED AND DOCUMENTED, then silently unenforced -- which
is worse than rejecting it, since every impl downstream is entitled to rely on
it. Every stdlib trait with a bounded associated type is exposed; `BuildHasher`
is simply the first one to have had a user-facing impl surface.

fix:
FIXED by d7cc9cfd. A five-op avalanche (`moremur`) applied to every
`fx_hash_bytes` digest. One file.

REPRODUCED FIRST, on different hardware than the row: this container is Linux
x86-64, the row measured arm64 macOS. Same program, ~11x there vs the row's
13.7x -- so the defect is algorithmic, not an arm64 artifact. Both binaries
printed the same 1000000 throughout, so no keys were ever lost; this was purely
throughput.

    before   default 0.37-0.41s   fx 4.16-4.75s   (~11x slower)
    after    default 0.44s        fx 0.38s        (0.87x -- FASTER)

THE ROW'S MECHANISM WAS RIGHT IN KIND AND UNDERSTATED IN DEGREE, which is the
part worth keeping. It said the low bits are "weakly mixed for keys sharing a
prefix". Measured, it is not a thin spread but a CEILING: un-finalized Fx yields
about 1000 distinct low-bit values for `key-N` keys NO MATTER how wide the mask.

        keys / mask      raw Fx   finalized
       4096 / 12-bit        985        2597
      16384 / 14-bit       1033       10341
     200000 / 18-bit       2057      126663

So past ~1024 buckets a growing table cannot spread these keys at all, and every
further insert lengthens a probe chain. That is why the slowdown scales with map
size, and it is why the row saw 13.7x at 200k rather than something mild.

THE ROW'S PROPOSED FIX WAS THE WRONG LEVER. It suggested indexing from the HIGH
bits (fibonacci/multiply-shift). That is a codegen ABI change: the bucket
encoding is replicated in `src/codegen/mono.rs`, `control_flow_for.rs` and
`runtime.rs`, and `runtime/src/map.rs`'s own module docs say the failure mode of
disagreement is a lookup that misses a present key -- a silent wrong answer.
Worse, the control byte's tag is drawn from the HIGH bits precisely BECAUSE the
index uses the low ones, so moving the index there would have to move the tag
too. Fixing the hash instead is one place, changes no ABI, and both backends
already funnel every leaf hash through `fx_hash_bytes` (codegen and the runtime
via the `karac_hash_bytes_fx` extern, the interpreter via `FxHasher`), so they
stay in lockstep by construction.

CONFLICT CHECK, because this row shares a suspect with B-2026-08-22-27, which
landed (bab8cf2) while this was in progress. That fix is confined to
`src/codegen/mono.rs` -- mono probes loading the map's stored hasher pointer
instead of a symbol baked in at emission time. It touches neither the hash nor
`synth.rs`. The ledger's "separate failure modes, shared suspect" framing held.

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE FROM rustc-hash. karac's Fx digest no longer matches it
byte for byte, and the four KATs are updated with a note saying so. That is the
point rather than a cost: rustc-hash is fine in rustc, whose table indexes from
the high bits; karac's indexes from the low ones, so byte-identical FxHash is
the wrong hash for this table. `b""` still hashes to 0 -- the avalanche fixes 0,
the one value it cannot improve -- a pre-existing wart of the empty key,
unchanged.

THE FIRST REGRESSION TEST WAS VACUOUS, and catching that produced the sharper
mechanism above. It asserted low-bit spread over 1024 keys and PASSED with the
mixer removed, because at that scale the two are indistinguishable (644 vs 632).
The shipped test uses 16384 keys over a 14-bit mask, where un-finalized Fx gives
1033 and a mixed digest gives ~10300; it is verified in BOTH directions (FAILED
at 1033 with the finalizer stashed, ok restored). The measurement table is in
the test's own comment so the next reader cannot repeat the small-N trap.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED, and measured rather than assumed. Codegen's
combiners for Vec elements / struct fields / tuple fields (`src/codegen/synth.rs`)
end in the same rotate-xor-multiply and were left alone. They consume FINALIZED
leaves now, and the shape most likely to expose a weak combiner -- tuple keys
sharing a field, `Map[(i64, i64), i64]` with a constant first element -- measures
FASTER under Fx than the default (0.10s vs 0.18s median). No remainder to file.

GATES. fmt clean; clippy clean on BOTH legs; `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1
cargo test --features llvm --no-fail-fast` = 125 binaries, 14853 passed, the only
failures being the 60 in `tests/gpu_e2e.rs` at the opt-in GPU archive gate (all
one line, none reaching a shader); `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` clean, quarantine
matched exactly. The full suite mattered more than usual here: changing the
digest changes Map ITERATION ORDER for every `FxBuildHasher` map, and CLAUDE.md
records that four order-asserting tests once passed on the very run that
introduced the hash seeding. Nothing moved.
title: `FxBuildHasher` WAS 13.7x SLOWER than the default on `String` keys because an Fx digest's low bits -- the ones karac's table takes its bucket index from -- hit a CEILING of ~1000 distinct values regardless of table size; fixed with a final avalanche in `fx_hash_bytes`, making Fx 0.87x the default (faster), and deliberately diverging karac's Fx digest from rustc-hash's
detail:
WHAT HAPPENS. `FxBuildHasher` -- documented in `runtime/stdlib/hash.kara` as
"FxHash ... Faster on short keys" and offered as the opt-out for people who
want speed over DoS-resistance -- is 13.7x SLOWER than the default
`SipHash13BuildHasher` on `String` keys, compiled.

MEASURED, arm64 macOS (Apple M5 Pro), `karac build --release`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, five rounds interleaved round-robin after a warm-up run,
1-minute load average under 2. Identical program in all three, differing only
in the trailing hasher: 200 000 `f"key-{i}"` inserts, then 5 x 200 000
`contains_key` over the same keys. All three print the same 1000000, so the
work is identical and no keys are lost:

    Map[String, i64]                    0.09 s   (0.08 0.09 0.09 0.09 0.09)
    Map[String, i64, FxBuildHasher]     1.23 s   (1.23 1.22 1.24 1.24 1.22)
    Map[String, i64, <user FNV-1a>]     0.09 s   (0.09 0.09 0.09 0.09 0.08)

The spread is tight and reproducible -- this is not noise, and the user FNV-1a
column is the control that shows a NON-default hasher is not inherently slow.

WHY IT PROBABLY HAPPENS, unverified. `karac_map_*` is open-addressed with
linear probing, and takes the bucket index from the LOW bits of the digest
(`(hash as usize) & (self.capacity - 1)`). karac's Fx byte loop is
`h = rotl(h, 5) ^ b; h *= SEED` per byte, whose low bits are weakly mixed for
keys sharing a prefix -- which `key-0 .. key-199999` all do. Long probe chains
would explain a 13.7x on lookups while leaving correctness intact, which is
exactly the shape observed. The standard fix for that shape is to index from
the HIGH bits (fibonacci/multiply-shift) rather than to change the hash.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND SPEED. The stdlib comment and design.md both present the
Fx opt-out as a speed/safety trade. On this key shape it is neither: slower AND
floodable. Until this is understood, that documentation is selling something
the implementation does not deliver, and a reader following it lands 13.7x
slower than doing nothing.

NOT THE SAME BUG as the compiled non-default-hasher key loss filed alongside
this: that one is a correctness failure on `i64` keys past a capacity
boundary, this one is a pure throughput result on `String` keys with every
lookup answering correctly. They were surfaced by the same bench run and share
a suspect (the table's use of the digest's low bits), but they are separate
failure modes and should be measured separately.

FIXED by 6cf7be8e. The row asked which half was wrong -- the tests or
the CPU table -- and the honest answer turned out to be "the tests, for `f16`;
the LINT, for `bf16`". The first half was already fixed upstream while this row

    triple / cpu                          f16              bf16
    arm64-apple-macosx apple-m1           fadd h0, h0, h1  Cannot select
    aarch64 generic +v8a                  fcvt/fadd s/fcvt Cannot select
