`apple-m1` in neither `CPUS_WITH_NATIVE_F16` nor `CPUS_WITHOUT_NATIVE_F16` and

karac does not hand bf16 arithmetic to LLVM. `codegen/expr_ops.rs` widens it to

The consequence: on every CPU in `CPUS_WITH_NATIVE_F16` -- `apple-m1`,

returned. Confirmed on this box: `test_ir_f16_bf16_arithmetic_lowers_to_half_and_bfloat`
passes here (so the widening IS emitted), while `karac check` on a bf16 add

`cf2c4f84` did not introduce that -- the conflation predates it -- but it
ENSHRINED it: `bf16_arithmetic_warns_too` was given the same host gate as its

The test then passed by asserting the bug.

TESTS. `bf16_arithmetic_warns_too` becomes `bf16_is_emulated_on_every_target`

title: Three `f16_software_emulated` lint tests fail on EVERY aarch64 macOS machine on a clean `main`: the tests assert the emulation warning fires, while `baseline_cpu_and_features` resolves Apple Silicon to `apple-m1`, which `target_has_native_f16` answers `true` for -- so the lint correctly stays quiet. CI is x86_64 and green, leaving a permanently-red local suite
detail:
WHAT HAPPENS. Three tests in `tests/typechecker.rs` fail on EVERY aarch64 macOS
machine, on a clean checkout of `main`, with no local changes:

    bf16_arithmetic_warns_too
    f16_arithmetic_warns_that_it_is_software_emulated
    the_f16_lint_names_the_cpu_it_judged

    thread 'the_f16_lint_names_the_cpu_it_judged' panicked:
      the diagnostic must name the cpu it judged (apple-m1), got []

Verified on `3efbe0a7` with the working tree stashed, so it is not a local
artifact: `cargo test --test typechecker -- f16 bf16` gives 7 passed, 3 failed.

WHY. `target::baseline_cpu_and_features` maps `("aarch64", "macos")` to
`("apple-m1", "")`. `target_has_native_f16` then finds `apple-m1` in neither
`CPUS_WITH_NATIVE_F16` nor `CPUS_WITHOUT_NATIVE_F16` and takes the
fail-open default, `true` -- so the lint correctly does NOT fire, and three
tests that assert it fires cannot pass. CI is x86_64 Linux, which resolves to
`x86-64`, which IS in `CPUS_WITHOUT_NATIVE_F16`, so the lint fires there and
the suite is green.

The tests know this. `the_f16_lint_names_the_cpu_it_judged`'s own comment says
"aarch64 macOS resolves to `apple-m1`, which IS native" -- and then asserts the
emulation warning is present anyway. The three assertions and that comment
cannot both be right.

WHICH HALF IS WRONG IS AN OPEN QUESTION, and worth answering before touching
the tests:
  * If Apple Silicon DOES execute `f16` arithmetic natively (`fadd h`), the
    tests are wrong and should gate on `target_has_native_f16()` instead of
    asserting unconditionally -- there is already a host-independent sibling,
    `f16_is_quiet_where_the_target_has_hardware_support`, to model on.
  * If it does NOT, then `apple-m1` belongs in `CPUS_WITHOUT_NATIVE_F16` and
    the lint has been silently missing on every Apple dev machine. B-2026-08-22-7
    settled the x86 side of this by MEASUREMENT with `llc`; the same
    measurement on aarch64 answers this one.

Either way the current state is the worst of the two: a red suite on a whole
class of developer machines, which trains everyone who runs `cargo test`
locally to ignore three failures -- and the next real regression in that file
hides behind them.

SEVERITY. Medium. Nothing shipped is wrong (the lint's failure direction is
under-report, which B-2026-08-22-7 already reasoned about and accepted), but a
permanently-red local suite has a cost that compounds.

fix: Fixed in 6c3957cf. An owned by-value Array[T, N] whose element owns heap (Array[String, N]) had NO scope-exit element drop registered at any binding site -- no CleanupAction, no synthesize_array_drop_fn, no track_*_array. So every element buffer leaked. Invisible at the default -O2 (the buffers are provably dead and LLVM deletes them) and on macOS ASAN (no LeakSanitizer); caught only by the Linux memory-sanitizer -O0 leg. Modeled the fix on the tuple owned-aggregate machinery but with array-index ([i]) GEP: (1) synthesize_array_drop_fn_te (runtime.rs) emits a drop fn freeing each of the N elements via the element type's own cap-guarded drop; (2) make_array_param_callee_owned (param_own.rs) registers it for an owned Array[heap, N] param/self -- note Array[T,N] parses as Path("Array") with generic args [Type(T), Const(N)], NOT TypeKind::Array (the [T;N] sugar), which is why the first attempt's TypeKind::Array arm never fired; (3) TRANSFER ownership, not deep copy -- the callee is sole owner, so the caller does not also free, which is what the measured single-element (a[1]) leak in take_first(mk(i)) confirmed (a[0] returned had its single owner in last); (4) suppress_array_elem_move_source (param_own.rs) cap-zeros a constant-index element moved out via return a[k] so the array drop skips the returned buffer (else double-free); (5) suppress_array_binding_move_arg retracts the caller's array drop when the whole array is passed by value into another callee (move_declined_copy_struct_arg choke point) so nested passing fn g(a){h(a)} does not free the shared buffers twice. Scalar-element and ref/mut ref array params are untouched. Verified: the three B-2026-08-22-18 fixtures plus a new nested-passing fixture (asan_array_owned_param_moved_into_nested_call_is_balanced) all clean under Linux LSan at -O0; codegen array E2E suite green.
title: Owned Array[T, N] with heap elements leaks its element buffers at -O0 -- no scope-exit element drop was ever registered (the -O0 remainder B-2026-08-22-18 surfaced by combining a fixed String array with f-string elements under LSan)
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the memory-sanitizer -O0 CI job after B-2026-08-22-18 (9d53994) removed the scalar-element gate on Array-temporary method calls and d5cf0d09 added the three Array[String,2] LSan fixtures. Those fixtures pass at -O2 (dead-store elimination deletes the never-freed buffers) but leak at -O0 where no pass pipeline runs -- exactly the class the asan-o0-leg guards. Not a regression from a specific commit: the array element drop never existed; the fixtures were simply the first heap-bearing fixed arrays exercised under LSan. REPRO: fn take_first(a: Array[String, 2]) -> String { return a[0]; } called in a loop over mk(i)=[f"a{i}", f"b{i}"] leaks the sibling element b{i} once per iteration (LSan: 137 bytes / 49 objects).

WHAT LANDED IS (a) ALONE: `is_heap` learns the `Array[T, N]` PATH spelling.
Only the `[T; N]` sugar reached the `TypeKind::Array` arm; the path form parses
as `Path("Array", [Type(T), Const(N)])` and fell through to the unknown-named-
type `false`. `generic_type_args` already drops the const arg, so the two
spellings now agree by construction.

(b) WAS NOT NEEDED -- the row's point 2 is REFUTED. It predicted that even with
`is_heap` corrected the let/value analysis would schedule zero drops for a
bound `let a: Array[String,2] = [..]`. Measured: it schedules `a` immediately.
`bind_pattern`'s `Binding` arm makes any binding Owned when its ANNOTATED type
is heap, and the array was only ever unscheduled because the path spelling
scored POD. So one line closed both (a) and (b).

That means THE RISK THIS ROW WAS FILED FOR IS CLOSED. The oracle no longer
believes a fixed array owns nothing, so a codegen refactored to CONSUME the
schedule will emit an array drop rather than silently dropping the element
frees on the floor -- which was the whole stated consequence.

THE ROW'S MODEL OF CODEGEN WAS ALSO WRONG, and this is the finding worth
carrying forward. Scope (b) says to model the local array's ownership "to match
codegen's synthesize_array_drop_fn_te + suppress_array_elem_move_source +
suppress_array_binding_move_arg". Those are the PARAM mechanisms:
`synthesize_array_drop_fn_te` has exactly ONE caller in the tree, and it is
`make_array_param_callee_owned`. For a LOCAL array codegen emits no array-keyed
cleanup action at all -- the elements are discharged through whatever owns them
individually. Dumped from `drop_obs` on three shapes:

  let a: Array[String,2] = ["lit".to_string(), ...]  -> codegen records NOTHING
  let a: Array[String,2] = [f"..", f".."]            -> records `fstr.acc`, `fstr.acc3`
  let x = mk(); let y = mk(); let a = [x, y]         -> records `x`, `y`
  (oracle records `a` in every case)

NOT A LEAK, verified under LSan on four shapes: f-string elements, named
bindings moved in, call-result elements, and an array RETURNED out of its
function (which also rules out the use-after-free the source-owns model would
invite if the escape suppression were missing). All clean.

SO THE DIVERGENCE IS A PLACE-KEY MISMATCH, not a missing drop, and comparing by
name would false-positive on every local fixed array. Added as differential
ALIGNMENT RULE 4 (`is_fixed_array_render`, matching both `Array[T]` and the
sugar's `[T]` rendering), documented explicitly as a KNOWN GAP rather than a
genuine ownership difference like rules 1-3 -- because it is codegen owning
local arrays element-wise where it owns param arrays whole, not two correct
models disagreeing.

(c)/(d) ADJUSTED TO WHAT IS TRUE. The boundary test is retargeted rather than
merely tightened from `== 0` to `>= 1`: `drops_checked` stays 0 (rule 4 filters
the place), and the test now asserts against the ORACLE DIRECTLY that its
schedule contains `a`. That is the half that is newly true; asserting `>= 1` on
the differential would have been asserting something rule 4 makes false.
Non-vacuity: reverting the `is_heap` case leaves the schedule `[]` and the
assertion fails with the rendered drop list.

Full ownership + drop_differential suites green (14/14); default suite 0
failures; `--features llvm` 109 targets, 0 failures under
KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1 with `--no-fail-fast` (only the known
missing-GPU-archive job); both clippy legs and fmt clean.

TWO REMAINDERS SPLIT OUT rather than folded in: B-2026-08-23-4 (codegen should
own local arrays whole, which is what lets rule 4 come out) and B-2026-08-23-5
(the drop_fuzz differential corpus is not at the 0 divergences its module doc
claims -- found while validating this row, pre-existing, identical before and
after this change).
title: Ownership oracle does not model fixed-array (Array[T,N]) ownership, so the drop-differential is blind to the array-element-drop class and the planned codegen-consumes-oracle refactor would regress B-2026-08-23-1
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while hardening B-2026-08-23-1 (owned Array[String,N] element leak, fixed in codegen at 6c3957cf). The cheap in-process oracle<->codegen drop-differential (tests/drop_differential.rs, src/drop_differential.rs, src/ownership_oracle.rs) is the standing gate for the whole drop class and the down-payment on the 'codegen consumes the oracle' refactor. It NEVER caught the array leak because the ownership oracle does not model fixed arrays end-to-end:

  1. `is_heap`/`is_heap_builtin` (ownership_oracle.rs): the `Array[T,N]` GENERIC spelling parses as Path("Array", [Type(T), Const(N)]) and falls through the Path arm to `false` (POD). Only the `[T;N]` sugar hits the `TypeKind::Array` arm. A one-line Path("Array") case makes is_heap correct (verified: returns true), but is NOT sufficient (next point) and touches the oracle's violation analysis too, so it must land with the full model.
  2. Local drop SCHEDULING: even with is_heap corrected, the oracle's let/value analysis schedules ZERO local drops for a bound `let a: Array[String,2] = [..]` (its ArrayLiteral value modelling, grouped with Tuple, and the let-binding heap inference do not emit an array drop obligation).
  3. The differential intentionally EXCLUDES param drops (drop_differential.rs line ~166, 'discharged caller-side'), so the owned Array PARAM case B-2026-08-23-1 actually fixed cannot be gated by this differential at all -- only the LSan memory_sanitizer fixtures gate it.
  4. The differential CORPUS had no fixed-array case.

CONSEQUENCE / RISK: today the codegen fix (6c3957cf) frees array elements and the LSan -O0 leg gates the leak, so there is no live leak. But the oracle -- the single source of truth the mechanization is converging on -- believes a fixed array owns nothing and schedules no drop. When codegen is refactored to CONSUME the oracle's schedule, it would stop emitting the array element frees and reintroduce B-2026-08-23-1's leak. This is the leak class hiding inside the safety net meant to prevent it.

SCOPE TO CLOSE: (a) teach `is_heap` the Path("Array") spelling (heap iff element is heap); (b) teach the oracle to SCHEDULE a fixed-array local drop and model its element move-out (return a[k]) and pass-by-value transfer to match codegen's synthesize_array_drop_fn_te + suppress_array_elem_move_source + suppress_array_binding_move_arg; (c) add fixed-array cases to the differential corpus and tighten tests/drop_differential.rs::owned_fixed_array_of_string_is_an_oracle_boundary from `== 0` to `>= 1`; (d) validate the full ownership_oracle + drop_differential suites (the is_heap change alone shifts violation analysis). Belongs in the ownership-model-mechanization workstream, not a rushed inline edit -- a half-taught oracle (is_heap true, scheduling still 0) is inconsistent and was deliberately NOT landed.

title: `f16_software_emulated` asked ONE capability question for TWO widths, so `bf16` arithmetic warned nowhere on a native-`f16` CPU (`apple-m1`, `sapphirerapids`) -- yet karac widens bf16 to `f32` UNCONDITIONALLY on every backend (LLVM 18's AArch64 ISel cannot select scalar `bfloat`), so the cost was always real and always silent. The same diagnostic also named the baseline CPU rather than the `--target-cpu` one its decision judged
detail:
WHAT HAPPENED. `f16_software_emulated` asked ONE capability question for TWO
widths, so on every CPU in `CPUS_WITH_NATIVE_F16` -- `apple-m1`,
`sapphirerapids` -- a `bf16` program paid the software-emulation cost and got
no warning at all. Every Apple developer machine, since the lint landed in
B-2026-08-22-7.

WHY THE TWO WIDTHS ARE NOT ONE QUESTION.

`f16` is a target capability, and the table is right about it. Measured with
`llc` 18.1.8 (the version karac links) on a bare `fadd half`:

    arm64-apple-macosx apple-m1      fadd h0, h0, h1        NATIVE
    aarch64 generic +v8a             fcvt / fadd s / fcvt   promoted
    aarch64 generic +v8a,+fullfp16   fadd h0, h0, h1        NATIVE
    x86_64 x86-64                    __extendhfsf2 libcall  promoted

`bf16` is not on that axis at all, because karac never hands it to LLVM.
`codegen/expr_ops.rs` widens bf16 arithmetic to `f32` and rounds back with the
RNE sequence UNCONDITIONALLY -- there is no target test anywhere in that path --
since LLVM 18's AArch64 ISel cannot select scalar `bfloat` arithmetic
(B-2026-07-22-1) and taking the same path on both architectures is what keeps
them bit-identical. Measured the same way: `fadd bfloat` at `-mcpu=apple-m1`
dies with `LLVM ERROR: Cannot select: bf16 = fadd`. So NO CPU makes bf16
native, and asking the CPU about it was answering a question with one answer
everywhere.

CONFIRMED ON THE BOX, before the fix, both halves of the contradiction at once:
`test_ir_f16_bf16_arithmetic_lowers_to_half_and_bfloat` passes on this
apple-m1 machine -- so the widen-compute-round sequence IS what gets emitted --
while `karac check` on a `bf16` add printed nothing.

HOW IT SURVIVED A TEST SUITE. `bf16_arithmetic_warns_too` asserted the lint
fires. On aarch64 macOS it did not, so the test was RED -- which is what
B-2026-08-22-30 was filed on. `cf2c4f84` then made the f16/bf16 tests
host-aware, correctly for `f16` (the CPU table is right, the tests were wrong)
and by extension for `bf16`, which gave the bf16 test the same host gate. The
suite went green by asserting the bug: on a native-f16 host the test now
required the bf16 lint to stay quiet. The conflation predates that commit; what
it changed was that a red test stopped pointing at it.

A SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME DIAGNOSTIC, found while verifying the f16 half: it
named a CPU it had not judged. `target_has_native_f16` resolves the
`--target-cpu` override; the message read `baseline_cpu_and_features()`
directly. Measured: `karac build --target-cpu generic` on this Apple box
correctly FIRES the lint (generic promotes f16) and then reports "cpu
`apple-m1`" -- the host baseline, whose real answer is the opposite. A
diagnostic that names the wrong target is worse than one that names none,
because it reads as a fact about this build; that is exactly what
`the_f16_lint_names_the_cpu_it_judged` was written to prevent, and it could not
catch this because it never sets an override.

Fixed in 7102243. A local fixed array now registers the same array-keyed

exactly one owner remains, and alignment rule 4 is gone -- the class is gated

PART, which was WHERE. An attempt earlier in this session implemented both

ALLOCATION COUNTS. That reads as "no double free, change is sound" and is in

no-ops for those shapes (fresh temps carry no independent cleanup, and an

That is also why the rewritten test asserts `assert_clean(&src) > 0` rather

replaces the rule-4 exclusion test with its inverse, keeping the oracle-side
assertion because the two sides agreeing proves they MATCH, not that either
models the array (two empty sets agree too). Four ASAN shapes land as

title: Codegen owns a LOCAL fixed array element-wise but a PARAM fixed array whole, so the drop-differential cannot gate the array class by place name and needs alignment rule 4 to exclude it
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-23-2, which taught the ownership oracle to model fixed
arrays and then could not gate the class because of this.

MEASURED with `drop_obs` on three shapes (oracle schedules `a` in all three):

  let a: Array[String,2] = ["lit".to_string(), ...]  -> codegen records NOTHING
  let a: Array[String,2] = [f"..", f".."]            -> records `fstr.acc`, `fstr.acc3`
  let x = mk(); let y = mk(); let a = [x, y]         -> records `x`, `y`

`synthesize_array_drop_fn_te` -- the array-keyed drop -- has exactly ONE caller
in the tree, `make_array_param_callee_owned`. So a PARAM array is owned whole
(one `StructDrop` keyed on the array slot, with the element move-out and
call-site source suppression that `owned_array_params` drives), while a LOCAL
array's elements stay owned by whatever produced them.

NOT A LEAK, and not unsound: verified under LSan across four shapes -- f-string
elements, named bindings moved in, call-result elements, and an array RETURNED
out of its function. The last one matters: it rules out the use-after-free the
element-wise model would invite if the escape suppression were missing.

WHY IT IS WORTH CLOSING ANYWAY. It is an inconsistency between two paths that
should be one, and it costs the mechanization its gate: the differential
compares by PLACE NAME, so an oracle-scheduled `a` against codegen-recorded
`x`/`y`/`fstr.acc` is a false positive on every local fixed array.
B-2026-08-23-2 had to add alignment rule 4 to exclude them, documented there as
a KNOWN GAP rather than a real ownership difference (unlike rules 1-3, which
each record two correct models legitimately disagreeing).

SCOPE: make a local `let a: Array[T, N]` register the same `StructDrop` the
param path does, and suppress the element sources so exactly one owner remains.
The suppression is the risky half -- `[x, y]` copies the `{ptr,len,cap}`
headers, so arming the array drop without disarming `x`/`y` is a DOUBLE FREE,
not a leak. When it lands, delete `is_fixed_array_render` and rule 4 from
`src/drop_differential.rs` and the class becomes gated by name like every other;
`tests/drop_differential.rs::owned_fixed_array_of_string_schedules_and_is_excluded_by_rule_4`
should then assert a non-zero `drops_checked` instead of asserting against the
oracle directly.

=== ATTEMPTED 2026-08-23, NOT LANDED — THE REGISTRATION SITE IS THE HARD PART ===

An attempt implemented both halves the SCOPE paragraph names and reverted them,
because the drop registration never fired. Recording what it cost, so the next
attempt starts past it.

WHAT WAS TRIED. (a) The element-source suppression was added to
`compile_array_literal`, bringing it to parity with the Vec literal: the three
calls it was missing (`maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg`,
`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`, and the Map-source suppression), in the
Vec path's order — defensive copy BEFORE the cap-zero, so it reads the
source's real `cap`. (b) The local `let` was taught to call
`make_array_param_callee_owned` with the element `TypeExpr` and `N`.

WHY (b) DID NOT FIRE, and this is the finding worth keeping: the natural-looking
hook in `stmts.rs` -- the `!borrow_elided && !matches!(slot_ty, ArrayType(_))`
guard that visibly SKIPS arrays, which reads exactly like the place the array
case was excluded from -- sits inside a region already gated on
`self.var_types.vec_elem_types.get(var_name)`. A fixed-array local has no entry
there, so the whole region is unreachable for it and a branch added inside is
dead code. The array registration needs a site OUTSIDE that gate.

A second, smaller trap on the way: the element `TypeExpr` must come from the
ANNOTATION for `let a: Array[String, 2] = ...`. `array_elem_type_exprs` is the
UN-annotated path's side table and holds nothing for an annotated binding. The
destructure to use is the one `functions.rs` already applies to array PARAMS
(`GenericArg::Type` + `GenericArg::Const`, `n > 0`).

MEASUREMENT NOTE, because it is how the dead code went unnoticed for a while:
all four ASAN shapes stayed clean and at IDENTICAL allocation counts after the
change. That reads as success and is actually the signature of an INERT change
-- the suppressions added in (a) are no-ops for these shapes (fresh temps carry
no independent cleanup, and an f-string accumulator is already neutralized by
B-2026-08-22-18), and (b) never ran. The differential is the only thing that
showed it: `owned_fixed_array_of_string` still reported `place: "a"` missing
from codegen after rule 4 was removed. So DO NOT take ASAN cleanliness as
evidence the registration landed -- check the differential, which is the
instrument that distinguishes "correct" from "absent".

Rule 4 and `is_fixed_array_render` are therefore still in place, and the test
still asserts the exclusion. They come out together with a registration that
actually fires.

fix:
FIXED by f0a55a6.

Two defects, disjoint and both necessary. Measured by reverting each
independently against the corpus: codegen-only 6, oracle-only 88, both 0,
neither 94 -- a clean partition, so no edit is redundant.

1. CODEGEN -- an EMITTING path that never RECORDED. `fire_due_user_drops`
   fires a binding's cleanup at its NLL live-range end and RETIRES the action
   from the frame, so the scope-exit funnel (`emit_cleanup_action_at`, which
   records) never sees it. Its `RcDec` arm already recorded, with a comment
   naming this exact hazard -- "retiring the action here without recording
   would present a *retimed* drop to the differential as a MISSING one" -- but
   the `UserDrop` arm directly beside it did not. That arm fires for every
   binding whose type carries an `impl Drop`, which is why an entire class was
   invisible: 88 phantom divergences. Recorded directly via `drop_obs::record`
   rather than by rebuilding a `CleanupAction` for `record_drop_obs`, so the
   production path (sink never armed) allocates nothing -- the cost `armed()`
   exists to avoid. Emission stays open-coded: `emit_cleanup_action`'s
   `UserDrop` arm also flushes `pending_box_field_zeroes` (B-2026-08-18-4),
   scope-exit-ordered work this early fire must not do.

2. OWNERSHIP ORACLE -- a move it did not model. `Some(t)` parses as
   `ExprKind::Call`, so it took the free-call caller-retains default and READ
   its argument, where `Tuple` / `StructLiteral` / `MapLiteral` all Move
   theirs. An enum-variant constructor is an aggregate literal: the argument
   escapes into the enum, which then owns it. Reading it left the source
   binding Owned alongside the enum, so ONE value carried TWO scheduled drops
   (`let o = Some(t)` scheduled `o` AND `t`), and codegen -- which keys the
   drop on the enum binding -- read as missing one. 6 divergences. `TypeDb`
   now collects every payload-carrying variant name (user enums in both bare
   and qualified spelling, plus the prelude's `Some`/`Ok`/`Err`); unit variants
   are excluded, since they take no argument to consume. Only heap bindings are
   disarmed by a Move, so `Some(n)` on an i64 is unaffected.

NEITHER WAS A LEAK. Every divergent shape is LSan-clean and runs its `Drop`
body exactly once on interp, JIT and AOT alike. Confirmed BEFORE either fix by
building each shape with `-fsanitize=address` and running under
`detect_leaks=1`. The reports were fidelity failures in the differential, not
memory bugs -- which is what the row asked to be determined first.

WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED, the part worth keeping: the curated standing gate
`tests/drop_differential.rs` had NO case declaring an `impl Drop` -- zero
across all 14 shapes -- and an `impl Drop` is precisely what routes a binding
onto the unrecorded firing path. The corpus was red and the gate was green
because the gate could not reach the class at all. Four Drop-bearing cases
added, each pinned by reverting the fix it covers: two go red on the codegen
revert, three on the oracle revert, none survive both.

MEASURED: corpus 94 -> 0 at the default size, 186 -> 0 at `--count 400`.
`drops checked` falls 779 -> 771 (1553 -> 1531 at 400): that is the
double-schedule correction showing up in the count, not lost coverage.
Non-vacuity re-proved with `KARAC_DROPOBS_SILENCE=1` -- 771/771 divergences
reported with the recorder silenced. Oracle self-check clean over 400 programs
/ 4461 scheduled drops, 0 invariant violations.

DOCS CORRECTED, since the stale number is what let this sit: the
`drop_differential.rs` module header and
`docs/spikes/ownership-model-mechanization.md` both claimed 0 while the corpus
read 94. Both now state that a zero is a measurement rather than a property,
that it has gone red once, and that when a curated gate and the corpus
disagree the corpus is the one to believe.
title: The drop_fuzz oracle-codegen differential corpus reports 94 divergences at the default size (186 at --count 400), against a module doc that states the corpus reached 0 -- so the corpus-level leak gate is red while the curated 14-shape gate is green
detail:
FOUND WHILE VALIDATING B-2026-08-23-2 (the row's item (d) asks for the full
suites to be validated, which is what surfaced this). Filed rather than fixed:
it is pre-existing and orthogonal to that row's change.

MEASURED, on `main`:

  ./target/debug/drop_fuzz --differential              -> 186 programs, 779 drops, 94 divergences
  ./target/debug/drop_fuzz --differential --count 400  -> 375 programs, 1553 drops, 186 divergences

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-23-2: the numbers are IDENTICAL with and without that
change (375/1553/186 both ways), which also confirms its alignment rule 4 is
neutral on this corpus.

THE CLAIM IT CONTRADICTS. `src/drop_differential.rs`'s module header documents
three alignment rules "each pinned by a false positive it removed (the corpus
went 792 -> 392 -> 111 -> 0 divergences as they went in)", and describes the
differential as checking "100% of generated programs (no capture skip)". The
corpus is not at 0 today.

WHAT IS STILL GREEN, so this is a gap in coverage rather than a live leak
report: `tests/drop_differential.rs` -- the curated 14-shape standing gate --
passes, as do the LSan `memory_sanitizer` fixtures that gate the actual leaks.
The divergent places are fuzzer-generated names (`mo5`, `mo13`, `t11`, `t4`),
i.e. the generator's move-out and temporary bindings, concentrated in `main`.

TO DETERMINE FIRST, before treating any of it as a leak: whether these are real
missing drops or a fourth class of false positive (the three known ones were
all alignment, not codegen bugs). The report at `target/drop-fuzz/differential.md`
lists every `(seed, function, place)`, and `drop_fuzz --seed <s> --count 1`
plus `differential_explain` reproduces one in isolation. If they are false
positives the module doc needs a fourth rule; if any is real it is a leak class
the curated gate does not cover.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN FRAMING. The row asked whether the 94 were real
missing drops or "a fourth class of false positive (the three known ones were
all alignment, not codegen bugs)". Both horns were wrong. They were false
positives -- nothing leaked -- but NOT an alignment mismatch to be excluded by
a fourth rule, and one of the two causes WAS in codegen: a firing path that
emitted a drop without recording it. So the answer is a third shape the row did
not anticipate, and the fix removes the divergences at their source rather than
filtering them. No fourth alignment rule was added; the four that exist are
unchanged.

The row's other premise held: the reported places really were concentrated in
`main` and really were the generator's move-out (`mo*`) and temporary (`t*`)
bindings -- but that was incidental. `mo`/`t` are simply the fuzzer's names for
`Tracked` locals, and `Tracked` is its only `impl Drop` type; the prefix was a
proxy for "has a Drop body", which is the actual predicate.

fix:
FIXED by 550eeef.

Two defects in the same mechanism, both necessary and disjoint. Measured by
reverting each against a 16-program matrix (8 body shapes x explicit-vs-omitted
annotation, plus method / fn-value / call-site / owned-locals shapes):
types_lowering-only leaves 2 failing, exprs-only leaves 15, both leave 0.

1. THE ROW'S BUG. `-> ()` parses as its OWN `TypeKind::Unit` variant, NOT as
   the empty `Tuple` that `llvm_return_type` already mapped to void. It fell to
   the wildcard, lowered through `llvm_type_for_type_expr`, and landed on the
   i64 default -- so the function carried an i64 LLVM return type while its
   body emitted `ret void`. Added the missing `TypeKind::Unit => None` arm,
   which routes an explicit `-> ()` down the IDENTICAL path as an omitted
   return type -- the one-character-different program that was always correct.
   `compile_closure_fn_type` has carried the same `Unit`-is-void arm since
   closures were added; this is that rule finally reaching the free-function
   and method signature.

   The row's diagnosis was right in full, including the detail that made it
   findable: with an explicit `return;` the verifier caught the mismatch, and
   without one nothing did.

2. A SECOND, PRE-EXISTING DEFECT the fix surfaced. `return <unit-valued expr>;`
   inside a VOID function emitted a value return. The TAIL-return site in
   `functions.rs` has carried a `fn_returns_void` guard for exactly this since
   it was written (its comment describes the identical verifier message); the
   explicit-`return` site in `exprs.rs` never got one.

   NOT INTRODUCED BY (1), and worth stating precisely because the sequence
   looks like a regression: `fn g() { return f(); }` with the annotation
   OMITTED failed module verification identically BEFORE any change here, so it
   was never about `-> ()`. What (1) changed is that the ANNOTATED spelling
   `fn g() -> () { return f(); }` stopped silently miscompiling and started
   hitting that same pre-existing refusal -- a silent miscompile converted into
   a loud build error, then fixed. Ordered after the `sret` arm for the reason
   the tail site gives: an sret function's signature is also void, but the
   struct must be stored through the result pointer first. No cleanup call in
   the new arm -- `emit_scope_cleanup` has already run above the chain, and a
   second walk would double free every owned local (checked under ASAN with a
   `Drop`-bearing local and an owned String: one `D5`, no leak, no double free).

WHY A HIGH-SEVERITY MISCOMPILE SURVIVED THIS LONG -- the part worth keeping.
`-> ()` is documented in design.md (§ First-Class Functions' `fn save(u: User)
-> () with writes(UserDB)`, which is what the probe was transcribing when it
found this) and used by ZERO `.kara` files anywhere: 0 of 427 in this repo, 0
of 917 in kara-katas. A spec'd surface with no corpus coverage at all. The
regression tests added here are its first coverage.

The body matrix also mattered for a second reason: ONE shape masked the bug.
`if true { println("x"); }` supplied the missing terminator and was GREEN
before the fix, so a single-shape test had roughly a 1-in-8 chance of proving
nothing. That shape is kept in the test deliberately.

MEASURED: all 16 programs byte-identical across interpreter, JIT, AOT and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`; ASAN+LSan clean on the owned-locals path. Four regression
tests in `tests/codegen.rs`, each pinned by reverting the fix it covers (all
four fail on the types_lowering revert; the two return-of-unit-call tests fail
on the exprs revert; none survives both). Each `-> ()` case additionally
asserts its output equals the annotation-dropped control, so the tests check
the two spellings AGREE rather than just matching a literal.
title: ANY non-`main` function declared with an EXPLICIT `-> ()` return type miscompiles into UNBOUNDED RECURSION on both compiled backends. `fn f() -> () { println("x"); }` + `fn main() { f(); }` prints `x` ONCE under `--interp` and prints it forever under `karac run` until the stack guard aborts (exit 134); the AOT binary SIGSEGVs (exit 139). `karac check` reports "All checks passed." The control one character away is clean: DROP the `-> ()` and the identical program is correct on all three backends. ROOT CAUSE IS VISIBLE IN THE ONE SHAPE THAT FAILS LOUDLY -- give the body an explicit `return;` and the LLVM verifier catches it: `codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Function return type does not match operand type of return inst!\n  ret void\n i64"`. So codegen gives the function an i64 LLVM return type while emitting `ret void`; without an explicit `return` the mismatch is not caught and control runs off the end of the function. `fn main() -> ()` is UNAFFECTED (main is lowered separately), which is why this survives every hello-world smoke test.
detail:
Probe: domain-23 spec-transcription pass (found while transcribing § First-Class Functions' `fn save(u: User) -> () with writes(UserDB)` example). Repro /tmp/.../hunt/d23/pf/{u1,u3,q1,q3,r1,r4,s1..s8}.kara.

BODY MATRIX -- `fn f() -> () { BODY }` called once from main, `karac run`:
  `println("x");`                 -> CRASH 134 (x printed repeatedly)
  `let a = 1;`                    -> CRASH 134
  <empty>                         -> CRASH 134 (fatal runtime error: stack overflow)
  `let a = 1; println(f"{a}");`   -> CRASH 139
  `println("x"); println("y");`   -> CRASH 134
  `return;`                       -> build refused, LLVM verifier message above
  `let a = 1; return;`            -> build refused, same
  `if true { println("x"); }`     -> OK (the if's terminator masks the missing return)

IT IS NOT ABOUT FUNCTION VALUES, though that is how I found it: `let g = f; g(7)` and a direct `f(7)` fail identically, and a `Fn(i64) -> ()` PARAMETER TYPE is fine (`fn run(f: Fn(i64) -> ()) { f(1); }` runs correctly on both backends). Methods are hit too -- `impl S { fn show(ref self) -> () { println("m"); } }` stack-overflows.

WHAT THE RECURSION ACTUALLY IS: with `fn f() -> () { println("x"); }` and a main that prints before and after the call, `karac run` emits `before x before x before x ...` -- so control returns to the TOP OF MAIN, not to f's caller. The frame is being resumed at the wrong address, not looping inside f.

ARCHIVES WERE REBUILT before the AOT leg was measured (the tree had gained runtime/src/stack_guard.rs and the on-disk archives were two weeks stale, which first presented as `undefined reference to karac_runtime_install_stack_guard` -- the documented stale-archive signature, not this bug).

fix:
FIXED by 67e0e1f. Root cause: the effect model is NAME-BASED -- effects flow along call-graph edges keyed by function symbol -- so a function reached as a VALUE left the model entirely and its declared effects reached nobody. `extract_callee_name` resolves the callee of `f(7)` to the symbol `f`, which names no function, so `callee_effect_sets` found nothing and contributed no effect.

Fix: a mention of a free function in VALUE position now contributes that function's effects to the enclosing function, through a synthetic call edge on the same channel the `__modbind_*` keys already use. Implemented by giving `modbind_synth.rs`'s shadow-aware walker a second table (`fn_value_ref_syms`). That walk was REUSED rather than duplicated because it already has the two properties this rule needs and a fresh 85-arm walker would have had to re-earn: a shadow stack covering every binding form (let / parameter / closure param / match arm / for pattern), and an EXHAUSTIVE `walk_expr` with no catch-all, so a future `ExprKind` is a compile error rather than a silently unwalked path that leaks an effect.

Edges are computed once per function (`fn_value_ref_calls`) and consumed in THREE places. `infer_function_effects` is the obvious one. `build_call_graph` is the non-obvious one and is required: a single-member SCC is inferred in ONE pass on the premise that every callee sits in an earlier SCC and is already resolved, so an edge missing from the GRAPH loses the effect of any mentioned function whose own effects are INFERRED rather than declared (a declared-effect callee is seeded up front and would have masked the bug -- the returned-function test is the shape that pins it). `check_one_par_block` is the third: a par block that reaches a module-binding writer through a function value is the same 1328 conflict, and was missed for exactly the reason the public-boundary check was.
title: A declared effect is LOST when a function is reached through a LET BINDING or a CONTAINER ELEMENT, so a public function's effect declaration -- "guaranteed semantics" per § Specification Layers -- is bypassable in two lines. design.md § First-Class Functions: "**Effects carry through.** A function with effects produces a typed function value that includes those effects: `let f = save;  // f: Fn(User) -> () with writes(UserDB)` -- calling f carries the writes(UserDB) effect, SAME AS CALLING SAVE DIRECTLY." Measured against a `fn save(n: i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB)`: `pub fn direct() -> i64 { save(7) }` correctly errors `public function 'direct' performs effects [writes(UserDB)] but has no effect declaration`; `pub fn via_value() -> i64 { let f = save; f(7) }` reports "All checks passed." A second hop (`let f = save; let g = f; g(7)`) also passes. The CONTAINER leg is worse than silent -- `let mut v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(save); v[0](7)` reports a PARTIAL set, `performs effects [panics]`, naming the indexing panic while dropping the callee's declared `writes(UserDB)`, so the diagnostic reads as an authoritative effect list that is wrong.
detail:
Probe: domain-23 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d23/pf/{e1,e2,e3,e4,c2,c3,c4,c5}.kara -- one path per file.

THE MACHINERY EXISTS AND MOSTLY WORKS, which is what makes this a hole rather than an absent feature. Correctly caught: the direct call (e1); passing the function as an ARGUMENT -- `apply(save, 7)` errors with the well-aimed `argument 1 has effect writes(UserDB) not declared in slot [pure]` (e4); an immediately-invoked closure `(|n| save(n))(7)` (c2); a closure inside an iterator chain `v.iter().map(|n| save(n)).fold(...)` (c3). Correctly ACCEPTED when the effect IS declared (e3). Only the binding path and the container-element path leak.

WHY SOUNDNESS AND NOT FALSE-POSITIVE: design.md's § Contracts section leans on this exact guarantee to justify NOT having a `forbids(verb)` predicate -- "omitting `writes(R)` from a public function's declaration is the commitment that the function does not write to `R`, and the effect checker verifies it statically against the body... Mismatch is a compile error". A caller reading a `pub fn` signature with no `writes` clause is entitled to conclude no write happens; today a one-line rebind makes that conclusion false with no diagnostic anywhere.

NOTE ON MEASUREMENT: my first probe of this used `-> ()` on the effectful function and was re-run without it, because `-> ()` independently miscompiles (B-2026-08-23-6) and would have contaminated the result. Every leg above is measured on `-> i64` signatures.

FIX NOTE (2026-08-23) -- SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN THIS ROW RECORDED. The row named two leaking paths; measurement found six, plus two that reported a partial set. LEAKED (0 errors, now caught): `let f = save; f(7)`; `let f = save; let g = f; g(7)`; `let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB) = save` -- the HONEST annotation leaked too, so "write the effect into the type" was never a workaround; `let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 = save`; `Holder { f: save }` then `(h.f)(7)`; `fn get() -> Fn(i64) -> i64 { save }` then `let f = get(); f(7)`. PARTIAL, now complete: the Vec-element leg went `[panics]` -> `[panics, writes(UserDB)]`, and likewise with an honest element type. ALREADY CORRECT pre-fix, measured rather than assumed by capturing a stashed-fix baseline: the direct call; `apply(save, 7)` against a pure slot; and `let f = P.bump` -- a METHOD reference as a value, which I had expected to be a hole and which the baseline showed was already handled.

WHY OVER-APPROXIMATION RATHER THAN PRECISION. `Type::Function` carries no effect row (131 sites across 27 files), so design.md's `f: Fn(User) -> () with writes(UserDB)` is not representable and effects cannot be propagated through the value's TYPE. The rule therefore attributes at the MENTION: `let f = save;` contributes even if `f` is never called. That direction is the safe one -- over-declaration is accepted (verified directly: a `pub fn` declaring an unperformed `writes(UserDB)` passes), so a spurious attribution costs an annotation, while a missing one costs the public-boundary guarantee this row is about. The type-level remainder is split out rather than buried here.

FALSE-POSITIVE SURFACE MEASURED. Attribution is by NAME, so a local shadowing a function name is the risk the rule creates. All five binding forms are tested, with a non-vacuity anchor (`test_unshadowed_mention_is_attributed`): without it the five shadow cases would also pass with attribution disabled entirely. The guard needed that anchor -- a refactor that moved the shared shadow check into the modbind half left the function-value half unguarded, and the shadow tests caught it. Corpus: 94 kara examples + 917 kara-katas = 1011 real Kara files, ZERO new-class diagnostics; the 7 examples that error are all pre-existing KNOWN_BROKEN_FILES entries with unchanged first errors.

PERF -- TWO WRONG GUESSES, BOTH CAUGHT BY MEASURING. (1) The naive version cost 15-47% of effectcheck time; caching the edges per function did NOT recover it. (2) The actual cause: `walk_expr`'s `Call` arm walks the callee, so every DIRECT call was also emitting a redundant function-value edge, roughly doubling the call graph. `walk_callee` now routes a bare-name callee past the value rule (a correctness no-op -- the ordinary call graph already holds that edge). Measured as a share of front-end time, the metric that cancels machine-load variance between runs: mesh n=1000 went 22.43% pre-fix -> 27.67% naive -> 22.82% final.

ACCEPTED BEHAVIOURS. `apply(save, 7)` against a pure slot now reports TWO errors rather than one; verified as two genuinely distinct required fixes rather than one mistake reported twice, by checking that an HONEST slot still leaves the caller error standing alone. Two functions that merely MENTION each other as values now form an effect-inference cycle and draw the "mutual recursion group" note though neither calls the other -- a note, suppressible, program still passes; filed separately.

fix:
FIXED by 72b91bb. Root cause: the built-in primitive resources simply had no seeds in `inferred_effects`. The seeding machinery was mature -- `File.*`, `BufReader.*`, `BufWriter.*`, `DataFrame.*`, the whole `Network` surface and `Env.set` were all hand-seeded -- but the console, stdin, the env READ half, `Clock`, `RandomSource` and the free `fs` functions were absent, so they contributed nothing to any effect set. A second, independent hole compounded it: the effect walker's lowercase ambient-module map routed only `env` / `stdin` / `critical_section`, so `fs.` / `clock.` / `rand.` / the explicit `stdout.` / `stderr.` forms never reached a seed key even where one existed.

The fix has four parts, and each is FORCED by the one before it -- seeding alone would have been a silent regression:

1. Seed the missing builtins, under BOTH key forms: the bare free-function name (`println`, keyed exactly as `panic` / `todo` already are) and the qualified resource method (`Stdout.println`). Same bridge-the-`with`-clause-into-inference rationale as the `File.*` block -- the baked-stdlib clauses on these `#[compiler_builtin]` stubs are documentation, not the propagation mechanism.

2. Generalize the ambient-module map to the canonical seven (`env/clock/rand/stdin/stdout/stderr/fs`), matching the typechecker's, the interpreter's and codegen's copies of the same table.

3. Carve the console out of BOTH concurrency decisions, via one shared `is_console_resource` predicate. The auto-par design DELIBERATELY relies on console output carrying no resource effect: `find_parallel_groups` fans print statements out because `karac_par_run` captures each branch's output and replays it in source order, which is the documented reversal of B-2026-06-13-18's blanket suppression. Seeding `writes(Stdout)` made two prints conflict (killing that parallelism) AND made a print count as "meaningful work" in the cost model (so a group of nothing but prints stopped being trivial and would pay ~70us of spawn to run two `println`s in parallel). Both halves are needed; each was measured to be independently necessary by reverting it alone.

4. Let a `Console`-providing target satisfy `Stdout` / `Stderr` in the target gate. design.md's table gives `wasm_browser` `Console` and deliberately not `Stdout` -- a browser has no file descriptors -- but `println` is a builtin on every target and the browser glue implements it as exactly that: `fd_write` routes fd 1 to `console.log` and fd 2 to `console.error`. Every printing browser program built fine before only because the gate never saw a console effect; the inconsistency predates the seeding and this reconciles it. WRITE sinks only -- `console.log` has no input side, so `Stdin` stays unprovided.
title: BUILT-IN PRIMITIVE RESOURCE effects are never inferred -- stdout, stdin, stderr, env and the filesystem contribute NOTHING to any effect set, so design.md's own two I/O skeletons report the wrong answer and a `pub fn` that does I/O needs no declaration. § Standard I/O Surface states the results outright for its guessing-game skeleton ("The inferred effect set: `reads(Stdin), writes(Stdout), panics`") and its CLI skeleton ("Inferred effects: `reads(Env), reads(FileSystem), writes(Stdout), writes(Stderr), panics`"). Transcribed VERBATIM, both check clean and `karac check --output=json` reports `program_effects: []` for the first and `['panics()']` for the second. The enforcement half is missing in step: `pub fn emit() -> i64 { println("hi"); 1 }`, `pub fn read_it() { stdin.read_line(); }`, `pub fn envy() { env.args(); }` and `pub fn err_it() { eprintln("e"); }` ALL pass with no effect declaration, while the identical shape over a USER-DEFINED resource is correctly refused (`public function 'p' performs effects [writes(UserDB)] but has no effect declaration`).
detail:
Probe: domain-23 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d23/pf/{io1,io2,ef1,ef2,ef3,ef4,ef5}.kara.

SPEC IS EXPLICIT THAT THESE PROPAGATE, in more than one place. § Entry Point: "CLI arguments are read via `env.args()` (stdlib), which carries `reads(Env)` and PROPAGATES INTO `main()`'s inferred effect set AUTOMATICALLY -- the programmer never writes the annotation." § Built-in Primitive Resources defines the resource set these belong to.

SCOPE OF THE CONSEQUENCE: `writes(Stdout)` and `reads(Stdin)` are the effects that appear in almost every real program, so the effect system's public-boundary guarantee is absent exactly where it would be exercised most. It also means the effect-conflict analysis that auto-concurrency rests on sees no I/O effects at all -- worth checking whether two tasks that both write stdout are considered non-conflicting.

RELATED BUT SEPARATE: B-2026-08-23-7 is a hole in how effects PROPAGATE through function values; this row is about built-in resource effects never being ATTRIBUTED in the first place. Different halves -- a fix to either leaves the other standing.

CONTROLS: `main()`'s four allowed return types all behave exactly as § Entry Point specifies -- `()` -> 0, `Result[(), E]` -> `Error: boom` on stderr with exit 1, `ExitCode.from(3)` -> exit 3, `ExitCode.SUCCESS` -> exit 0, and `fn main() -> i64` correctly refused with E_MAIN_RETURN_TYPE.

FIX NOTE (2026-08-23). MEASURED SURFACE. Eleven builtin forms went from contributing nothing to reporting the right effect: `println` / `print` / `Stdout.println` / `stdout.flush` -> writes(Stdout); `eprintln` -> writes(Stderr); `stdin.read_line` / `read_to_string` -> reads(Stdin) + blocks; `env.args` / `env.var` -> reads(Env); `clock.now` (and `Clock.now`) -> reads(Clock); `RandomSource.next_u64` -> reads(RandomSource); `fs.read_to_string` -> reads(FileSystem); `fs.write` -> writes(FileSystem). `env.set` already worked and was the tell that the machinery existed rather than being absent.

design.md's TWO SKELETONS now report what the doc says. The CLI skeleton matches exactly -- all five of `reads(Env), reads(FileSystem), writes(Stdout), writes(Stderr), panics` -- against the `['panics()']` this row recorded. The guessing-game skeleton exposed a DOC ERROR rather than an implementation gap: it reports `reads(Stdin), writes(Stdout), blocks` and NOT `panics`, and isolating each construct showed `panics` comes from INDEXING (which the CLI skeleton has via `args[1]` and this one does not -- `i64.parse` returns an Option the `match` handles exhaustively, and `?` propagates rather than panicking). design.md was corrected to match, and the test pins both skeletons in both directions.

CORPUS FALLOUT WAS ONE FILE. 94 examples + 917 katas + 12 packages: a single `pub fn send_all` in a Mend solution that prints, plus two `pub fn` in the game_of_life package -- all three correct, all three now declare `writes(Stdout)`. The kata corpus was untouched (0 of 917). NOTE: my first package sweep was VACUOUS -- it passed a `--manifest-path` flag `karac` does not have, so every invocation errored and matched nothing; the "all packages clean" it appeared to show was worthless. The real signal was the `example_packages` test, which is what caught game_of_life; the sweep was redone by cd-ing into each package.

THE TEST-PROGRAM FALLOUT IS THE INTERESTING PART, because two of the three cases are the new rule working. `run(f)` where `fn run(g: Fn(i64) -> ())` became an E0404 -- passing a now-effectful `f` into a slot that declares PURITY -- which is the same rule B-2026-08-23-7's own control demonstrates, and that test program was only ever legal because `println` had no effect. A `pub fn main() with writes(Console)` that also printed had to declare `writes(Stdout)`. A wasm target-gate test's `pub fn paint()` likewise. All three test PROGRAMS were fixed; no compiler behaviour was relaxed to accommodate them.

FOUND WHILE MEASURING, NOT CAUSED BY THIS ROW: `eprintln` writes to stderr under the interpreter and is silently DROPPED ENTIRELY under both JIT and AOT -- not misrouted to stdout, lost. Confirmed identical on a stashed-fix build, so it predates this change. Filed separately as a run-vs-build divergence. Also checked and NOT a bug: the interpreter's `_ => ("Stdout", "print")` catch-all looks like it would route `eprint` to stdout, but `eprint` is not a builtin at all (`karac` rejects it as an undefined name), so that arm only ever receives `print`. The dead `eprint` seed I had written was dropped.

fix:
FIXED by 9c95c06, on the INTERPRETER side, and the row's supporting citation needs a correction.

WHAT THE ROW CITED, AND WHY IT WAS THE WRONG LINE. The row justified "the compiled backends are right" by quoting design.md's sentence that errdefer fires on "an explicit tail value of an `Err`-typed expression". That sentence (line 914) governs **`defer`/`errdefer` inside a `try` block** -- and `try` is parser-only at v1 (line 920: use sites emit E_TRY_BLOCK_NOT_IMPLEMENTED_YET). The FUNCTION-scope rule is lines 837 and 866, and both enumerate the non-success paths as `?`-propagating Err, `?`-propagating None, explicit `return Err(...)`, explicit `return None` (866 adds panic). NEITHER mentions a tail expression. So the spec does not actually settle this at function scope; it is silent, and its one sentence on the subject is about a construct that does not exist yet.

WHAT SETTLED IT INSTEAD: `tests/codegen.rs::test_e2e_errdefer_fires_on_tail_err_expression`, which has pinned the compiled behaviour since Phase 7 and documents the mechanism ("when the function's final expression is syntactically `Err(...)` ... `compile_function`'s tail emitter routes through `emit_scope_cleanup_for_error_path`"). The compiled behaviour is deliberate and tested; the interpreter simply had no equivalent. The row's CONCLUSION was right even though its citation was not.

THE FIX. `eval_body_growing` -- the documented single chokepoint every function/closure/method body invocation routes through -- sets `next_block_is_fn_body`, and `eval_block_inner` TAKES it on entry. Taking rather than reading is what makes nesting correct: the body's own block consumes the flag, so every block inside it reads false, which matches codegen applying the rule to `func.body.final_expr` and nowhere else. At the tail, a function body whose final expression satisfies the error-exit predicate classifies via the new `ExitPath::classify_tail_value` and runs the errdefer phase before the drop+defer drain.

ONE PREDICATE, NOT TWO. The rule is SYNTACTIC -- `Err(e)` fires, `if c { Err(e) } else { Ok(v) }` does not -- and the temptation was to reimplement it in the interpreter from the runtime value instead. That would have been WORSE THAN THE BUG: it would fire on the four tail shapes codegen does not (`if`, `match`, a tail call returning Err, a nested-block tail), creating a fresh divergence in the opposite direction. So codegen's `is_error_exit_value` was extracted to `ast::is_error_exit_value` -- a plain AST predicate, no backend types, so codegen containment holds -- and both backends now read the same function. Same rule as the SipHash and Arrow twins: agree by construction, not by convention.

The interpreter is also more precise than codegen here for free: it binds an `errdefer(e)` payload from the ALREADY EVALUATED tail value, so the payload expression is never run twice.

MATRIX, all three backends, before -> after. Sixteen programs covering every exit path and payload shape; interp/JIT compared pairwise, AOT spot-checked.
  tail Err  / tail None / tail Err with two errdefers   DIVERGED -> agree
  `?` prop / explicit return Err / tail Ok               agreed  -> agree (unchanged)
  tail `if`, `match`, call, nested block that evaluate to Err   agreed (none fires) -> agree, unchanged
  errdefer(e) with an impure payload                     DIVERGES -> STILL DIVERGES, filed separately

CORPUS IMPACT: none, and it is the same story as the two rows before it. Exactly three `.kara` files in the repo contain the string `errdefer`, and all three are the SELF-HOSTED COMPILER recognizing the keyword (`"errdefer" => Token.ErrDefer`), not using it. No program in the repo or in kara-katas uses `errdefer` at all, so nothing changes behaviour and the construct has no dogfooding -- which is why a missing cleanup path survived.

CHECKED AND NOT REPRODUCED: `selfhost/src/ast.kara` renames its error-recovery variant from `Err` to `Error` with a comment saying `is_error_exit_value` "would mis-stage errdefer cleanup and panic on the shared-enum return value" -- i.e. a false positive on a USER enum with a variant named `Err`. Probed four shapes (plain and `shared` enum, tail and explicit-return) on both backends: all correct, no panic. Either it was fixed since or the shape is narrower than the comment describes. Not filed, since a hazard that will not reproduce is not a bug report; recorded here so the next reader does not take the comment as current.
title: The INTERPRETER SKIPS an `errdefer` block when the function's `Err` comes from its TAIL EXPRESSION, while both compiled backends run it. `fn work() -> Result[i64, String] { errdefer { println("failed"); } defer { println("always"); } Err("bad".to_string()) }` prints `always | err bad` under `karac run --interp` and `failed | always | err bad` under `karac run` (JIT) and the AOT binary alike -- so the cleanup that the shipped binary performs is silently absent under the interpreter. `karac check` is clean. The divergence is specific to the tail-expression form: an `Err` reached via `?` short-circuit and an explicit `return Err(...)` both run the `errdefer` correctly on ALL THREE backends, and the `Ok`-from-tail control correctly skips it on all three.
detail:
Probe: domain-23 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d23/pf/{df2,df3,df4,df5}.kara -- one exit path per file.

PATH MATRIX, `errdefer` + `defer` in the same function:
  Err from tail expression   -> interp: always | err bad          JIT/AOT: failed | always | err bad   DIVERGES
  Err via `?` short-circuit  -> all three: rollback | err inner                                        agree
  Err via `return Err(..)`   -> all three: rollback | err explicit                                     agree
  Ok from tail expression    -> all three: always | 1 (errdefer correctly skipped)                     agree

WHICH SIDE IS RIGHT: the compiled backends. design.md describes `errdefer` as firing "only when the block exits via the `Err` path (a `?` short-circuit, OR AN EXPLICIT TAIL VALUE OF AN `Err`-TYPED EXPRESSION — though the latter shape is rare since `?` is the canonical early-exit mechanism)". The spec names the exact shape and says it fires; the interpreter is the outlier.

SEVERITY REASONING: rare shape by the spec's own admission, and it fails toward LESS cleanup under the interpreter rather than toward a wrong value -- but `errdefer` exists to run rollback logic, so a silent skip in the backend used for `--interp` debugging is the wrong direction for the one construct whose entire job is to run on failure.

UNRELATED OBSERVATION, deliberately NOT filed: under AOT the "Error return trace:" lines interleave differently with the printed output than under interp/JIT. That is stdout-vs-stderr buffering, not an ordering defect.

fix:
FIXED by 54548e0. title: `Type::Function` carries NO EFFECT ROW, so design.md § First-Class Functions' `let f = save;  // f: Fn(User) -> () with writes(UserDB)` is not representable and a function value's effects cannot propagate through its TYPE. NARROWED 7e7972b: the IMPRECISION this caused -- a function value that is bound and never called still demanding the enclosing function declare its effects -- is FIXED, in the effect checker and without the type row (bind-an-alias, attribute-at-every-other-mention). What remains is representability only, and the prescription in the original title does not work as written: the typechecker cannot populate an effect row, because `effectcheck` runs after `typecheck` AND consumes its output, so inferred effects at typecheck time would need a cycle. Read the detail before picking this up.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-23-7 rather than buried in it, per the live-remainder rule.

SIZE: 131 `Type::Function` sites across 27 files, plus 86 `Type::OnceFunction`. Adding an effect row touches unification, compatibility, substitution, display, codegen and the interpreter -- a design change, not a bug fix, which is why -7 shipped the over-approximation instead.

WHAT IT WOULD BUY: precision (no spurious attribution for a function value that is never called), and the ability to CHECK a binding's declared effect type rather than only to attribute at the mention -- see the sibling row on `let`-annotation slots, which is the smaller half of the same gap and may be fixable first.

NOTE ON THE SPEC: design.md's behavioural sentence -- "calling `f` carries the `writes(UserDB)` effect, SAME AS CALLING SAVE DIRECTLY" -- is TRUE as of -7. It is the TYPE spelling in the same example's comment that is still aspirational.

PARTIAL FIX LANDED (7e7972b): the IMPRECISION half is fixed; the
representability half -- the effect row itself -- is what this row now
tracks, and the size estimate above understates it. See below.

THE ROW'S PRESCRIPTION DOES NOT WORK AS WRITTEN. An effect row on
`Type::Function` has to be POPULATED by the typechecker, and the
typechecker cannot know a function's effects. `effectcheck` runs AFTER
`typecheck` and CONSUMES its output -- `effectcheck_with_typecheck_data`
takes `method_callee_types` and `call_type_subs` to resolve method callees
-- so making the typechecker know inferred effects requires the reverse
edge, i.e. a cycle. DECLARED effects (`with writes(UserDB)`) are syntactic
and available at typecheck; INFERRED effects for private fns are not, and
inferring those is the whole point of the effect system. A row populated
for declared functions and "unknown" everywhere else is worse than no row,
because the unknown cases are exactly the ones a consumer would most want
to trust. The 131 + 86 sites are real but they are the cheap part; the
phase order is the expensive part, and this row did not previously say so.

WHAT WAS FIXED INSTEAD, AND WHY IT NEEDED NEITHER. The harm the row
describes -- `let f = save;` with no call still demanding the declaration
-- is not caused by the missing type row. It is caused by -7 attributing at
the MENTION. The fix is one rule in the effect checker's body walker
(`src/effectchecker/modbind_synth.rs`): `let f = save;` binds an ALIAS and
attributes nothing; EVERY other mention of the alias attributes, including
the callee of a direct call. "Used at all, other than being bound" is a
sound over-approximation of "escapes or is called", and the walker's
`walk_expr` is exhaustive with no catch-all, so it visits every mention.

That is why NO ESCAPE ANALYSIS was needed either -- the pre-fix plan was to
reuse `src/result_escape.rs`, and it turned out the walker's existing
`walk_callee`-vs-`walk_expr` split already draws the only line that
matters. The alias rides the SHADOW STACK (a new `ShadowEntry.fn_alias`)
rather than a side map, so scoping is innermost-wins for free: an inner
`let f = 5` hides an outer `let f = save` while its block is open, and the
alias is live again after it closes. A flat map gets that second half
wrong.

MEASURED, before -> after, `pub fn holder() { let f = save; }`:
  before  error[effect]: public function 'holder' performs effects
          [writes(UserDB)] but has no effect declaration
  after   clean
and every escape shape still demands it: called, returned, passed as an
argument, stored in a struct field, captured by a closure, pushed into a
container. Reassignment attributes the NEW value at the assignment, so
`let mut f = save; f = pure_fn;` with no call is now clean while
`let mut f = pure_fn; f = save;` is caught.

TEST-SUITE NOTE worth reading before touching this again: exactly ONE
existing test failed, `test_unshadowed_mention_is_attributed`, and it
failed CORRECTLY -- it pinned the retired behaviour (`let other = save; 5 +
1` was attributed). It exists as the non-vacuity anchor for the shadowing
test next to it, so it was repointed to a shape the rule still covers
(`other(7)`) rather than deleted. The other 470 passed untouched, including
every -7 soundness pin, which is the evidence that the precision win did
not cost a real effect.

STILL OPEN, and all this row now means: design.md § First-Class Functions
spells a function value's type as `f: Fn(User) -> () with writes(UserDB)`.
That spelling is still not representable -- `Type::Function` has no effect
row -- so effects still do not propagate through the TYPE, only along the
name-keyed edges the effect checker maintains. The behavioural sentence in
the same paragraph ("calling `f` carries the `writes(UserDB)` effect, same
as calling save directly") remains TRUE. Anyone picking this up should
start from the phase-order finding above, not from the site count.

DESIGN QUESTION RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -> docs/spikes/function-type-effect-row.md.
Read the spike before touching this row; the three conclusions it reaches
change what the work IS.

1. The phase-order blocker recorded above DISSOLVES. The typechecker never
   needed to KNOW effects -- it needs to carry a `Concrete | Var` ROW and let
   the effect checker solve it, which is what the language's existing
   `with E` effect parameters and the existing positional solver
   (`build_fn_effect_var_positions` / `compute_call_var_bindings`) already
   do at parameter positions. No cycle. Do NOT attempt to populate the row
   with inferred effect SETS at typecheck time.

2. NOTHING TODAY DEPENDS ON IT. Every path a function value can take was
   re-measured at current HEAD -- through a `let`, through a container,
   through an effect-variable parameter, and across a `pub` boundary -- and
   all four demand the declaration. The B-2026-08-23-7 mention rule closes
   them without a type row.

3. The reason (1) and (2) can both be true is that V1 HAS NO SEPARATE
   COMPILATION: design.md 1115 says `[dependencies]` is "ignored, not
   rejected". design.md 6297's firewall -- public boundaries use DECLARED
   effects -- only bites once packages ship, and at that point a downstream
   consumer sees only the signature and the row becomes load-bearing.

SO: this is a PACKAGE-MANAGER PREREQUISITE, to be scheduled with that work
rather than before it. The real cost is replacing the index-keyed positional
effect-variable solver with structural unification over the row; the 217
`Type::Function` sites are the cheap part, and `lower_type_expr_inner`
already parses the row and drops it (one `..`).

A separate diagnostics bug found during this investigation is filed as
B-2026-08-24-12 (a public function returning an `Fn` cannot follow the
compiler's own suggested fix).

RE-MEASURED 2026-08-25 at HEAD 0cb0b27 (`target/debug/karac`, `karac check`).
Finding 2 STILL HOLDS -- all four paths a function value can take demand the
declaration, so there is still no measured hole and the scheduling answer is
unchanged. Re-run because the spike's measurement dated 2026-08-24 and main
had advanced.

  let f = save; f(7)                          demands writes(UserDB)
  effect var at a param position, via a let   demands
  Vec[Fn(..) with E] container param          demands
  across a pub boundary (pub fn get -> Fn)    demands

THE CONTROLS ARE THE POINT -- an error nobody can clear would prove nothing:
  - `pub fn holder() { let f = save; }` (bound, never used) is CLEAN, so the
    B-2026-08-23-7 precision win survives and the four demands above are real
    escapes rather than blanket over-attribution.
  - Adding the suggested `with writes(UserDB)` clears shapes 1-3.
  - Shape 4 emits B-2026-08-24-12's parenthesised-return-type guidance, and
    following it VERBATIM (`-> (Fn(i64) -> () with writes(UserDB)) with
    writes(UserDB)`) compiles clean -- that row's fix is doing its job.
  - Shape 4 also fires B-2026-08-24-1's slot check, `returned value has effect
    writes(UserDB) not declared in slot [pure]`.

Verdicts stable over 8 runs each (shapes 1/1/1/2 errors, controls exit 0), so
B-2026-08-24-22's `karac check` nondeterminism does not reach this surface --
that one is rc-fallback diagnostics, and these programs produce none.

Programs are four `resource UserDB; fn save(u: i64) with writes(UserDB)`
variants; reconstructing them from this note takes about a minute, which is
why they are described rather than pasted.

STATUS CORRECTED wontfix -> relocated (2026-08-25). This row was briefly

fix:
FIXED by 4f67f9d1. Root cause: `check_subtyping_in_stmt`'s `Let` arm (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs) walked the VALUE for nested calls and dropped the binding's `ty` on the floor -- so the one thing that makes a `let` a slot, the declared `Fn(..)` annotation, was never compared against anything. `check_call_args_subtyping` already held the entire rule; it was simply unreachable from a binding.

THE FIX is two new methods in the same impl block plus two rewritten stmt arms:

  * `fn_annotation_slot_effects` resolves an explicit `Fn(..)` / `OnceFn(..)` annotation to the effect set it admits. It returns None -- "no check here" -- for a non-function type, for `with _`, and for a named effect VARIABLE. That last case is the one judgement call and is deliberate: `with E` is bound per CALL SITE by `compute_call_var_bindings`, which needs a callee symbol and an argument list, and a binding annotation has neither. Resolving `E` against no bindings yields the EMPTY set, which would reject every effectful value assigned to a legitimately polymorphic slot, so the check fails OPEN. `test_let_annotation_effect_variable_slot_is_not_checked` pins that rather than leaving it to be "fixed" into a false positive later.

  * `check_binding_annotation_subtyping` runs the same comparison the argument path runs, emitting the same `EffectSubtypeViolation` kind with the same `EffectSubtypeTrace`, so `karac explain` renders it identically. The wording is parallel too -- `binding `f` has effect writes(UserDB) not declared in slot [pure]` beside the existing `argument 1 has effect ...` -- so a reader who has seen one recognises the other.

`Let` and `LetElse` both route through it. `LetUninit` has no value to check at the declaration.

MEASURED SCOPE CORRECTION, recorded because it nearly went the other way. The row's "NOT A SOUNDNESS HOLE AS OF -7" claim is CONFIRMED -- but the first pass appeared to REFUTE it: a stale `target/debug/karac` (built 08-22, before -7 landed on 08-23) reported "All checks passed" for `pub fn hand_out() -> i64 { let f = save; f(7) }`, which would have made this a soundness hole and a much larger bug. After a rebuild every one of those shapes errors at the public boundary; -7's mention rule fires everywhere, annotated or not, and the residual really was only the unchecked annotation. A binary older than the fix under discussion is indistinguishable from a compiler bug -- check `ls -la target/debug/karac` against the fix date before trusting a green.

ALSO FIXED, same function family, found while writing the tests: the rendered slot list was built by iterating a `HashSet<Effect>`, so a slot declaring two or more effects printed them in per-process-random order -- measured 14 vs 16 out of 30 runs for a two-element set, i.e. a coin flip in shipped diagnostic text and in any snapshot of it. Both slot paths now sort before joining, and `test_multi_effect_slot_renders_in_a_stable_order` pins the exact rendering.

TESTS: 14 in tests/effectchecker.rs. The load-bearing one is `test_let_annotation_slot_and_parameter_slot_agree`, which puts the same function into the same declared slot at both positions and requires the same verdict -- an argument-only regression passes every other test in the group. Around it: exact-match, wider-slot, pure-value, polymorphic and effect-variable negatives; `let else`; an effectful closure; `OnceFn`; the resource-less-verb (`panics`) pair guarding the B-2026-08-05-18 class at the new site; and two controls proving an UNANNOTATED `let` and a non-function annotation are not slots -- the shape a naive "check every let" fix would break.

GATES: 9806 tests pass (0 failed), fmt clean, clippy clean on both feature legs.

REMAINDER: the same slot is still unchecked at four other positions -- see B-2026-08-24-1, filed with this fix.
title: A `let` binding's `Fn(...)` TYPE ANNOTATION is never checked against the assigned function's effects, so `let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 = save;` -- a slot that declares PURITY -- silently accepts an effectful `save`, while the IDENTICAL parameter slot is rejected. Measured against `fn save(n: i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB)`: `fn apply(f: Fn(i64) -> i64, n: i64)` called as `apply(save, 7)` errors `argument 1 has effect writes(UserDB) not declared in slot [pure]`, but `let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 = save;` in a caller that declares `with writes(UserDB)` reports NOTHING. The same E0404 rule, applied at one site and not the other.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-23-7; split out rather than folded in, since -7's fix does not address it.

NOT A SOUNDNESS HOLE AS OF -7: the caller still acquires `writes(UserDB)` from the MENTION of `save`, so the public boundary holds and a `pub fn` cannot hide the effect. What survives is that the annotation itself is a lie nobody diagnoses -- the binding claims a pure `Fn(i64) -> i64` and is handed something that writes.

WHERE: `check_call_args_subtyping` (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs) drives the slot rule off `TypeKind::FnType`'s `effect_spec` and is reached only from the `Call` / `MethodCall` arms of `check_subtyping_in_expr`. `StmtKind::Let`'s arm walks the VALUE for nested calls but never compares the binding's declared type against the value's effects, so a `let` with an explicit `FnType` annotation is an unchecked slot. The machinery to check it already exists and has the arg-position diagnostic to copy.

RELATED: the general inability to carry effects in `Type::Function` is the larger sibling row; this one needs only the AST-level annotation, which already carries `effect_spec`, so it is likely fixable on its own.

fix: FIXED by 249f165. `emit_mutual_recursion_notes` now asks a narrower question than inference does, and uses a narrower graph to answer it. `build_call_graph` gained an `EdgeKinds` parameter plus a `build_call_graph_calls_only()` sibling that omits the `fn_value_ref_calls` edges; the note re-runs Tarjan on that graph and counts a member as mutually recursive only if it sits in a call-only SCC of size >1. Three renderings result: every member call-recursive -> "mutual recursion group ...", byte-identical to before; none -> "effect-inference cycle ... Every cycle here passes through a function-as-value reference, so no member is mutually recursive with another."; mixed -> "mutual recursion group ...; joined by function-as-value reference: ...", because naming a value-joined member inside a mutual recursion group is the same false statement in miniature. The second graph is built only when `fn_value_ref_calls` is non-empty, so a program that never mentions a function as a value pays nothing. `#[allow(mutual_recursion_note)]` and the `mutual_recursion_groups` JSON field are both unchanged. Tests: 4 in tests/effectchecker.rs (value-only rewording, with a non-vacuity assert that the note still FIRES; genuine-recursion wording unchanged; mixed partition; suppression) -- the two bug-pinning ones were confirmed to FAIL against a pre-fix binary. Corpus: 1111 .kara files swept with pre- and post-fix binaries, output multiset identical (see the CORRECTION for the one apparent diff, which reproduced on the pre-fix binary too and is filed separately).
title: The mutual-recursion NOTE now fires for two functions that merely REFERENCE each other as VALUES, calling them a "mutual recursion group" though neither calls the other. `fn p(n: i64) -> i64 { let f = q; n + 1 }` + `fn q(n: i64) -> i64 { let g = p; n + 2 }` reports `note[effect]: mutual recursion group resolved by fixed-point inference: \`p\` (no effects), \`q\` (no effects)`. The program passes and the note is suppressible with `#[allow(mutual_recursion_note)]`, so this is diagnostic wording, not a check failure -- but "mutual recursion" is a false statement about the program.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: introduced by B-2026-08-23-7, which adds function-as-value edges to `build_call_graph` so effects propagate through a mentioned function. Those edges are real EFFECT-DEPENDENCY edges -- p's inferred effects genuinely depend on q's -- so Tarjan sees a true cycle and the fixed-point loop is doing the right thing; only the note's WORDING assumes every graph edge is a call.

DOES NOT AFFECT: correctness of inference (the cycle converges), and the note is already gated behind `mutual_recursion_allow`.

LIKELY FIX: distinguish call edges from value-reference edges when rendering the note (either exclude value-only cycles, or word it as an effect-inference cycle rather than mutual recursion). The edge kind is not currently recorded -- `build_call_graph` returns bare `(Symbol, Span)` -- so this needs a tag on the edge.

FREQUENCY: requires two functions to mention each other as values; zero occurrences across the 1011-file corpus swept for -7.

CORRECTION (at fix time): the repro recorded in this row no longer reproduces, and that is not a regression -- it was never quite the right program. `fn p(n) { let f = q; n + 1 }` binds `q` to a name that is then never used, and a DEAD function-as-value binding contributes no edge. That is correct precision rather than a hole: `let f = writer; f(n)` and `let f = writer; take(f)` BOTH propagate (verified against a `pub fn` missing the declaration, which is rejected in both), and so do the return, argument and `v.push(..)` mention forms. Only the never-used binding is silent. So the two-dead-lets program produces no SCC and no note at all.
The bug itself is real and was reproduced with a LIVE mention -- two functions that each stash the other in a struct field:
    struct Holder { f: Fn(i64) -> i64 }
    fn p(n: i64) -> i64 { let h = Holder { f: q }; n + 1 }
    fn q(n: i64) -> i64 { let h = Holder { f: p }; n + 2 }
-> `note[effect]: mutual recursion group resolved by fixed-point inference: \`p\` (no effects), \`q\` (no effects)`, with neither function calling the other. That is the program the regression test uses.
REMAINDER: the `--output=json` `mutual_recursion_groups` field still carries a value-only cycle under a name that says "mutual recursion". Not folded in here, because narrowing that field's membership is a documented-contract change (design.md 6374 names the field; tests/effectchecker.rs pins it as "a separate promise" that stays populated when the note is suppressed) and design.md describes no kind discriminator. Split out as its own open row.

fix:
FIXED by 5786ab6. Two edits, each independently necessary (each was reverted alone and the gate failed).

(1) `src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs` — `eprintln` now joins `println` / `print` on the `compile_print` intercept. It is a prelude FREE function, so no later arm ever claimed it; without the intercept it reached the unknown-callee constant-0 fallback and lowered to nothing at all.

(2) `src/codegen/control_flow.rs` — `compile_print` computes `to_stderr = name == "eprintln"` once and threads it into all 22 write sites: 10 `emit_nul_safe_write` calls plus 12 String/collection arms. The stdout-defaulting wrapper `emit_print_and_free_string` was DELETED rather than extended, so every arm now names its stream explicitly and a print arm added later has to decide rather than inherit stdout by omission — the omission is what this bug was.

No new machinery was needed on either side. `emit_nul_safe_write` already took a `to_stderr` flag (`Stderr.println` used it), `stdio_stream` already selected the `stderr` global, and the runtime's auto-par capture already recorded a per-segment `stream` and replayed per stream — its header comment names `eprintln` explicitly. The path existed; nothing was routed into it.
