So only the lookahead was missing, and the "blast radius across every `[`-suffixed expression followed by a brace" the row worried about is bounded by that existing flag plus the type-start guard. Pinned by a regression test over subscript-then-brace shapes (`if f[i] { .. }`, `while f[i] { .. }`, `match v[i] { .. }`, `for x in g[r] { .. }`, and the single-identifier body that the restriction must still claim).

KNOWN BOUNDARY: the SELF-HOST Kara parser (`selfhost/src/`) does not parse this form. No divergence results -- the Rust-side sexp renderer in `tests/selfhost_parser.rs` does not emit `generic_args`, and no corpus program uses the syntax -- so the self-host oracle is unaffected; self-host parity for the new form is ordinary phase-12 lag, not a regression introduced here.
title: A STRUCT LITERAL WITH EXPLICIT GENERIC ARGUMENTS (`Connection[Disconnected] { socket: ... }`) does not parse in ANY expression position, so design.md § Typestate via Phantom Type Parameters line 8756 -- the line that demonstrates the wrong-state compile error -- cannot be written as the spec writes it. `let c = C[S] { fd: 1 };` -> `Expected Semicolon, found LeftBrace`; the same literal as a tail expression -> `Expected expression, found Colon`. Annotating the binding and using the bare name (`let c: C[S] = C { fd: 1 };`) works.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-23-10, which makes the two lines ABOVE this one (the `struct Disconnected;` / `struct Connected;` markers) parse. Reproduces IDENTICALLY with braced `struct Disconnected {}` markers, so it is independent of that row's sugar and was not introduced by it.

MEASURED, all with the same `struct C[T] { fd: i64 }`:
  let, no annotation   `let c = C[S] { fd: 1 };`            -> error[parse]: Expected Semicolon, found LeftBrace
  tail expression      `fn mk() -> C[S] { C[S] { fd: 1 } }` -> error[parse]: Expected expression, found Colon
  WORKS (workaround)   `let c: C[S] = C { fd: 1 };`            annotate the binding, use the bare name
  WORKS                non-generic `P { x: 1 }`

CAUSE is the classic `expr [ index ] {` ambiguity: after `C[S]` the parser holds an index expression and reads the following `{` as a BLOCK, so the field list is parsed as statements. That is why the two positions report DIFFERENT errors -- the `let` form wants its `;` and finds `{`, while the tail position tries to parse `fd: 1` as an expression and trips on the `:`. Kara has no turbofish (design.md: "`[T]` not `<T>`. No turbofish"), so there is no `::<>` spelling to disambiguate with.

TWO FIX SHAPES, both real decisions rather than mechanical: a restricted-expression rule (no struct literal in the `if` / `while` condition or `match` scrutinee position, which is how Rust resolves the same ambiguity), or a bounded lookahead that commits to a struct literal when `[` ... `]` is followed by `{` IDENT `:`. Either has a blast radius across EVERY `[`-suffixed expression followed by a brace, which is why this is filed rather than folded into B-2026-08-23-10.

SCOPE is small and localized -- same family as B-2026-08-23-10 and B-2026-08-20-37's `[u8; N]` leg: the form appears in design.md EXACTLY ONCE (line 8756, the line demonstrating the wrong-state compile error that the whole Typestate section builds to) and ZERO times in the `.kara` corpus. The workaround is a single type annotation. Low severity on that measurement, but it is the reason § Typestate via Phantom Type Parameters still cannot be transcribed end to end.

fix:
FIXED by de0fee9. `eval_par_block`'s join now harvests the branch interpreter's DIAGNOSTIC PAYLOAD alongside the four things it already took. `BranchResult` gained two elements -- `runtime_errors` and the `(error_trace, error_trace_truncated)` pair -- and the join merges them into the parent in source order, next to the console replay and BEFORE the control-flow check that returns early on the first error.

TWO VECS, NOT ONE. The row named `runtime_errors`; the RETURN TRACE is a second vec on the branch interpreter and died the same way. Harvesting only the first would have left the par diagnostic missing the `Error return trace:` section that the identical fault outside `par` prints -- a partial landing of exactly the kind this cluster keeps producing. The trace is taken only when the branch actually recorded an error: a SUCCESSFUL branch can still have pushed frames (a `?` propagating an `Err` is ordinary control flow, not a fault), and those would otherwise render under a sibling's error as if they belonged to it.

THE BAR IS PARITY WITH THE SAME FAULT OUTSIDE `par`, not a new par-specific rendering, and that is now exact -- same message, same trace section, same exit status. Measured after the fix, `panic()` in a branch: `runtime error: died` / `at p1.kara:1:38` / `Error return trace:` / exit 101, character-for-character the non-par baseline modulo the span. A clean par block still exits 0.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ROW, both measured:
  (1) EXIT CODE. The row records JIT/AOT exiting 1. They exit 101 now -- B-2026-08-23-17's fix (`c12de8f`, panics to stderr + exit 101) landed after this row was filed. The assert shape still exits 1 under JIT because it takes the `KARAC_TEST_FAILURE` path, and that difference is PRE-EXISTING and identical outside `par` -- not something this fix changes or should.
  (2) "THE STATEMENTS AFTER THE JOIN ARE SKIPPED" is true for the `panic()` and bare-index shapes but NOT for `return v[99]`, which prints `joined 0 ()` -- the post-join `println` runs with a FABRICATED `()` where an `i64` belongs. That is a second, independent defect, filed as B-2026-08-24-7: it reproduces with no `par` in sight, so it is not the join's doing. After this fix the par case matches the non-par case exactly, including that residue.

SCOPE NOTE ON FAIL-FAST: with two failing branches, WHICH error is reported is nondeterministic (measured 3/8 vs 5/8 over eight runs) because the pre-start cancellation check means a branch may never run at all. That is the existing `cancel` design, unchanged here, and it is why every regression test uses exactly ONE failing branch -- asserting on both would be flaky by construction, the same discipline the Map/Set iteration-order rule enforces.
title: A RUNTIME ERROR inside a `par {}` branch is swallowed WHOLE by the interpreter -- no message on stderr, exit code 0, and the statements after the join are skipped -- so a program that died halfway reports SUCCESS. JIT and AOT both print the error and exit 1. Measured on three unrelated error shapes (`panic("...")`, a Vec index out of bounds, a failed `assert`), all three identical: `karac run --interp` prints NOTHING and exits 0 where `karac run` and the compiled binary print `panic at c2.kara:1:51 in boom: vec index out of bounds` and exit 1.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while measuring B-2026-08-23-15's crash-visibility question (does buffering a par branch's stderr for join-replay lose it when the branch dies?). The answer there was no -- the join replays output BEFORE it propagates the error -- but the program written to ask it exposed this, which is a bigger and unrelated problem. NOT caused by that fix: verified by stashing it, rebuilding, and reproducing exit 0 identically.

SCOPE: `par {}` ONLY. The same `panic()` at top level is reported correctly and exits 1 (`runtime error: plain` plus an `Error return trace:`), so the error machinery works end to end; it is the join that drops the payload.

MEASURED, three backends x three error shapes:
  panic("branch died")   interp [nothing] exit 0 | jit `panic at crash.kara:1:47 in boom: branch died` exit 1 | aot same as jit
  Vec index out of range interp [nothing] exit 0 | jit `panic at c2.kara:1:51 in boom: vec index out of bounds` exit 1 | aot same
  assert(1 == 2, "...")  interp [nothing] exit 0 | jit `KARAC_TEST_FAILURE {...}` with message `assert died` exit 1 | aot same
The `panic()` case does still emit the branch's own earlier `eprintln` output, because the join replays console segments before propagating -- so the program looks like it ran and simply stopped early, with nothing indicating anything went wrong.

CAUSE, confirmed by reading the join: a branch runs on its OWN `Interpreter` (`eval_par_block`, `src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs`), and `record_runtime_error` (`src/interpreter.rs`) pushes the `RuntimeError` -- message, span, trace -- onto THAT interpreter's `runtime_errors` vec. The join harvests exactly four things per branch: `defined_vars`, the console segments, the dbg lines, and `cf_result`. `runtime_errors` is not among them -- the identifier does not occur anywhere in `eval_stmt.rs` -- so the populated vec is dropped with the branch interpreter. What reaches the parent is the bare `ControlFlow::RuntimeError` marker, which `ExprKind::Par`'s arm faithfully re-raises via `set_cf` (that part is correct, and is why the statements after the join are skipped). The CLI then finds the parent's `runtime_errors` EMPTY, has nothing to render, and exits 0.

LIKELY FIX: harvest `branch_interp.runtime_errors` as a sixth element of `BranchResult` and extend the parent's vec in source order, next to the existing console replay. The error VALUE already propagates correctly, so this is about carrying the DIAGNOSTIC PAYLOAD across the join, not about control flow.

WHY HIGH: silent success on a failed run is the worst shape a divergence can take -- worse than a wrong answer, because nothing signals the answer should be doubted. It also breaks any CI or script gating on `karac run --interp`'s exit status, and `karac test` runs the interpreter.

fix:
FIXED by 5a585d8. The retraction already existed -- `suppress_array_binding_move_arg` (`src/codegen/param_own.rs`) removes an owned `Array[T, N]` binding's array-keyed `StructDrop` from the cleanup frame -- but it was hooked ONLY at the by-value CALL-ARGUMENT choke point (`move_declined_copy_struct_arg`). Neither RETURN position called it, so a returned array's slot drop fired in the callee while the caller freed the same element buffers. Hooked at both return sites now.

TWO SITES, AND EACH COVERS A SHAPE THE OTHER DOES NOT -- established by revert-discrimination, not by reading:
  `src/codegen/exprs.rs`, the `ExprKind::Return` arm  -> `return a;` as the last statement AND a mid-body/conditional `return a;`
  `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` (`call_dispatch.rs`) -> a bare TAIL expression `a` with no `return` keyword
Removing the exprs.rs hook alone fails the `returned_out` and `conditional_return` fixtures while the tail one stays green; removing the tail hook alone fails only the tail fixture. Note this CORRECTS the natural reading of `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`, whose `from_last_stmt` branch destructures `ExprKind::Return` and so looks like it owns `return a;` as the final statement -- it does not; that shape reaches the `exprs.rs` arm first. Hooking one site and trusting it to stand for both would have left the other shape corrupting memory with no failing test.

THREE STANDING FIXTURES, one per return shape (`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`): the pre-existing `..._returned_out_...`, plus `..._tail_expression_...` and `..._conditional_return_...`. The full `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` leg is GREEN at 1151 passed / 0 failed (was 1148 / 1), and `drop_differential` is 19/19 -- the retraction removes a drop, so a leak is the natural way to over-correct, and the Linux LSan half of the same run is what rules it out.

WHY IT SURVIVED, and the general lesson: the origin commit `71022437` DID add an escape fixture, and its message states the intent exactly -- "an array returned out must NOT have its slot drop fire, which would be a use-after-free rather than a leak". That fixture could not fail at the gate that ran it. At the default -O2 the array in `mk` is provably dead, so LLVM deletes the allocation and the double free with it; only the -O0 leg, where no pass pipeline runs, executes the allocation the program actually writes. A fixture asserting a memory property is only as good as the opt level it runs at.

OLDER AND BROADER THAN THE LOCAL-ARRAY FRAMING -- answering the question this row left open, and correcting a first answer. The obvious reading is that `71022437` introduced it, since the second free is the array-keyed `StructDrop` on the LOCAL's slot and that registration is what the commit added. That is true of the local shape but is NOT the whole defect: `make_array_param_callee_owned` has armed the same slot drop for array PARAMS since well before that commit, and an owned param returned straight back out (`fn pass(a: Array[String, 2]) -> Array[String, 2] { return a; }`) reaches the identical missing retraction by the older route. Measured, not reasoned: with both hooks removed that shape double-frees under ASAN at -O0; with them it is clean. So `71022437` WIDENED the set of arrays the gap applies to (locals joined params) rather than creating it, and the param leg has been corrupting memory for longer. It is now a fourth standing fixture, `asan_owned_array_param_returned_out_is_not_dropped_twice`, so the two legs cannot regress independently.
title: `asan_local_fixed_array_returned_out_is_not_dropped_twice` DOUBLE-FREES at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, so `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` is RED on main and reports the fixture as a new unquarantined failure. The fixture PASSES at the default -O2, which is the classic -O0-only shape: at -O0 no pass pipeline runs so the allocation the fixture intends actually happens, while at -O2 LLVM deletes the provably-dead buffer along with the evidence.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by running the asan -O0 gate over an unrelated interpreter fix (B-2026-08-23-15) and getting a failure that had nothing to do with it. Attribution was verified, not assumed: with that fix STASHED and the tree rebuilt from clean `origin/main`, the same fixture double-frees identically, so this is pre-existing and belongs to main rather than to the change that found it.

MEASURED at b8ddc469, x86_64 Linux, both archives rebuilt lean-then-full:
  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 cargo test --features llvm --test memory_sanitizer
  -> 1148 passed, 1 failed. ASAN: `SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: double-free ... in free`, the buffer `previously allocated by thread T0 here: #1 ... in mk`.
The DEFAULT -O2 run of the same suite is green -- the full `cargo test --features llvm` sweep over the same tree was 125 binaries / 14907 passed with the only 60 failures all being the expected `gpu_e2e.rs:372` opt-in-archive gate. So this is invisible to every gate except the -O0 leg.

ORIGIN: `71022437` ("fix(codegen): own a local fixed array whole, like a param one; retire rule 4", 2026-08-23 12:51) is the commit that added this fixture, and 10 commits have landed on main since, so the authoring session has moved on and the failure is unowned. Whether the commit introduced the double-free or added a fixture that exposes an older one is not established here -- the sibling `6c3957cf` ("free elements of an owned Array[T,N] with heap elements") is the other half of that pair and is the natural first place to look.

DELIBERATELY NOT QUARANTINED. `tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt` is empty by design and its header says the list ONLY SHRINKS; adding a 15-hour-old double-free to it would convert a loud regression into a permanent allowlist entry, which is precisely the decay the file warns against. Leaving the leg red keeps the signal where it can be acted on.

WHY HIGH: a double-free is memory corruption in emitted code, not a test artifact -- the -O2 pass only hides it by deleting the allocation. `local fixed array returned out` is an ordinary shape (build an `Array[T, N]` in a function, return it), so this is not an exotic corner.

fix:
FIXED by 7d0a582. `dbg` of a `shared enum` now lowers on both compiled backends, rendering byte-identically to the interpreter across every variant shape -- one-word tuple, two-word tuple, unit, and a struct-variant whose `String` payload spans three words. SELF-REFERENTIAL shared enums are refused instead, and that half is filed separately.

THE LAYOUT COINCIDENCE THE ROW ASKED ME TO VERIFY HOLDS, and verifying it was the right call because it is what makes the whole approach a wrapper rather than a rewrite. A shared enum's box is `{ i64 strong, <enum words...> }`, so the aggregate `emit_enum_display_fn` already switches on IS the box's tail. MEASURED on a four-variant enum with a String payload: `heap_type` is 6 x i64 and the enum's own `llvm_type` is 5 x i64 -- every word an i64 on both sides, so no padding can differ. `emit_shared_enum_debug_display_fn` now ASSERTS that relation (length and word-for-word type equality) at synthesis time, so a future layout that breaks it fails the build instead of silently reading the tag from the wrong offset. The renderer is then ~20 lines: load the handle, GEP past the control header, call the existing enum renderer.

CACHE ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING AND ONLY ONE DIRECTION WORKS -- I measured both. Both functions key on the bare enum name. Registering the wrapper FIRST makes `emit_enum_display_fn`'s own entry check find the wrapper and emit a self-call: `karac build` succeeds and the binary never terminates (measured, `timeout` kill). So the inner is synthesized first and the wrapper takes the key over afterwards.

THAT SAME COLLISION IS ALSO A MISCOMPILE FOR A SELF-REFERENTIAL SHARED ENUM, WHICH IS NOW REFUSED. While the inner renderer is being synthesized, a payload of the enum's OWN type resolves -- through the dispatcher's `module.get_function` fallback -- to that inner, the AGGREGATE-taking function, and is handed a word holding a HANDLE. MEASURED on `shared enum T2 { Node(i64, T2), Leaf(i64) }` nested twice:
  interpreter: Node(3, Node(7, Leaf(99)))
  AOT:         Node(3, Leaf(139898617069619))
  JIT:         Node(3, Leaf(5))
The garbage word read as a tag, so the failure is a WRONG VARIANT, not a crash -- exactly the failure mode the row predicted for a layout mismatch, arriving from a different cause.

I ALMOST SHIPPED THIS. A single-level `shared enum Tree { Node(Tree), Leaf }` rendered `Node(Leaf)` CORRECTLY on all three backends, because the garbage happened to match the unit variant's tag and a unit variant has no payload to be wrong about. Only pushing to two levels with a payload-bearing variant exposed it. The lesson worth carrying: a recursive-shape test needs depth AND a payload, or it certifies nothing.

THE REFUSAL IS SCOPED BY MEASUREMENT, not by caution. A payload of a DIFFERENT shared enum (`Outer.Wrap(Inner.X(42))`) and a payload of a shared STRUCT (`Outer.Holds(P { n: 5 })`) both resolve to that type's own wrapper and render correctly on both backends -- so only self-reference (and cycles) are refused, via a DFS over shared-enum payload types.

TESTS (`tests/cli.rs`), both verified to FAIL against the pre-fix build:
  - `test_dbg_of_a_shared_enum_renders_the_same_on_all_three_backends` -- all four variant shapes, three backends.
  - `test_dbg_of_a_self_referential_shared_enum_refuses_but_siblings_render` -- the cyclic refusal, the interpreter still rendering it, and the two sibling shapes still compiling.
The second test initially passed against the pre-fix build and was VACUOUS: its sibling half fell into the same `if built.success() { ... } else { skip }` soft-skip that a missing runtime archive uses, so a build that REFUSED those shapes looked identical to one that could not link. It now asserts the refusal text is absent before allowing that skip, and fails pre-fix as it should.

The two tests that use an unlowerable `dbg` shape as their fail-closed trigger moved for the THIRD time (`dbg(1)` -> shared struct -> shared enum -> cyclic shared enum), as their own notes asked.
title: `dbg(x)` where `x` is a `shared ENUM` still REFUSES to compile -- "codegen: `dbg` at L:C cannot render a value of type `Shape` yet" -- while `karac run --interp` renders it (`Circle(5)`). B-2026-08-24-2 gave the shared STRUCT a Debug renderer and left this half deliberately failing closed, per that cluster's rule that a partly-landed renderer must NAME what it cannot draw rather than print a placeholder. A HEADERLESS shared struct refuses for a separate and more interesting reason, below.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-24-2 rather than left implied by it, the same way that row was split out of B-2026-08-23-18. The struct half is done and tested on all three backends; this is the remainder.

TWO SHAPES STILL REFUSE, and they are not the same problem.

(1) SHARED ENUM. A shared struct's fields sit in the RC box at known offsets, which is what made its renderer a field walk. A shared enum's payload sits behind a VARIANT TAG in that box, so rendering it needs the tag dispatch the plain-enum renderer already does, applied one indirection down. MEASURED and encouraging: a shared enum DOES have an `enum_layouts` entry (`Shape` -> tags `{Circle: 0, Rect: 1, Empty: 2}`, with `field_word_offsets`), and its heap box is 4 fields wide against 5 for a 4-field shared struct -- consistent with `{ i64 strong, <enum words...> }`. So the likely shape of the fix is small: GEP past the refcount word and hand the resulting pointer to `emit_enum_display_fn`, IF the enum's LLVM aggregate is laid out identically to the box's tail. That last clause is the part to verify rather than assume -- a padding difference between the two would read the tag from the wrong place, and the failure would be a wrong VARIANT NAME rather than a crash.

The interpreter half is already correct and deterministic (it renders `Circle(5)` -- variant name and payload, no enum-name prefix), so unlike the struct case there is no oracle work to do first.

(2) HEADERLESS SHARED STRUCT. This one is a real design constraint, not an unwritten arm. The headerless niche drops the refcount word, so user field 0 moves to heap index 0 -- and `headerless_here` answers PER FUNCTION (it reads `fn_ctx.current_fn_name`), while a synthesized renderer is emitted once and cached program-wide. One cached function cannot hold both layouts, so `dbg_unsupported_shape` refuses a type that is headerless at the call site rather than emit a renderer that reads every field at the wrong offset somewhere else. Fixing this properly means either keying the renderer cache on (type, layout) and emitting both variants, or hoisting the headerless decision to a whole-program property. `synth_drop` sidesteps the same funnel for the same reason and records it. Note this arm is currently UNREACHED by any test -- no measured program has been observed hitting it -- so it is a guard against a hazard rather than a fix for an observed failure.

NOT URGENT, deliberately: the failure mode is a compile-time diagnostic that names the type and points at `--interp`, not a miscompile or a crash. The `tests/cli.rs` tests `test_dbg_of_an_unrenderable_shape_refuses_and_names_it` and `test_unlowerable_defer_body_refuses_instead_of_vanishing` both use a shared enum as their unlowerable trigger and will need retargeting again when this lands -- that trigger has now moved twice (`dbg(1)` -> shared struct -> shared enum), so move it a third time rather than deleting either test.

RESOLUTION NOTE (2026-08-24): the row's hoped-for shape was right -- a shared enum's box really is the control header plus the enum's own words, and reusing `emit_enum_display_fn` on the box tail works. The thing it flagged to verify (a padding difference reading the tag from the wrong place) does NOT occur, and is now asserted at synthesis time rather than assumed. A DIFFERENT path to the same "wrong variant name" symptom did occur, from a cache-key collision between the wrapper and the inner renderer on a self-referential enum; that half is refused and filed as its own row. The headerless remainder this row also described is untouched and moves to that new row.

fix:
FIXED by b964f37. `Interpreter::set_cf` (src/interpreter.rs) — the single funnel every `return` / `break` / `continue` goes through — now DECLINES to write `pending_cf` when an unwind is already in flight. A new `ControlFlow::is_unwind()` (src/interpreter/exec.rs) names the four unwind variants (`RuntimeError`, `ExitUnwind`, `Cancelled`, `TimedOut`) — exactly the set `call_function`'s propagate arm already groups — so a fault, a `process::exit`, a `par` cancellation or a test deadline all outrank a statement that is merely carrying a value out of the expression it faulted inside of.

`record_runtime_error` and its `assert`-style sibling write `pending_cf` DIRECTLY and are deliberately left unguarded: a fault must still be recordable while another unwind is pending. The guard governs the statement-level funnel alone, which is where the downgrade happened.
title: A RUNTIME ERROR inside `return <expr>` is OVERWRITTEN by the return's own control flow, so the interpreter KEEPS EXECUTING after the fault and hands the caller a FABRICATED value. `fn boom() -> i64 { let v = Vec[1, 2]; return v[99] }` called from `main` prints `got ()` -- a Unit where an `i64` belongs -- and only then reports the error; the compiled backends abort at the fault and print nothing else. Not `par`-specific: reproduces at top level with no `par` in the program.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-24-4 (a par branch's diagnostic dropped at the join). That row recorded "the statements after the join are skipped", which holds for `panic()` and for a bare `let x = v[99];` but NOT for `return v[99]` -- that shape printed `joined 0 ()`. Isolating why showed the cause has nothing to do with `par`, so it is filed separately rather than folded into that fix.

MEASURED, same program, no `par` anywhere:
  fn boom() -> i64 { let v = Vec[1, 2]; return v[99] }
  fn main() { let x = boom(); println(f"got {x}"); }
  interp -> `got ()` THEN `runtime error: index 99 out of bounds (len 2)` + trace, exit 101
  jit    -> `panic at t.kara:1:48 in boom: vec index out of bounds`, exit 101, NOTHING else
The interpreter runs `main` to completion on a value that does not exist; the compiled backend never reaches the `println`.

CONTRAST, the same fault NOT in return position:
  fn boom() -> i64 { let v = Vec[1, 2]; let x = v[99]; x }
  interp -> error + trace only, exit 101, no `got` line. Correct.
So the defect is specific to `return <erroring expr>`.

CAUSE, from reading the two sites: `record_runtime_error` (`src/interpreter.rs`) sets `self.pending_cf = Some(ControlFlow::RuntimeError)` and returns `Value::Unit` as the expression's value. The `return` statement then evaluates its operand, gets that `Unit`, and sets `pending_cf = Some(ControlFlow::Return(value))` -- OVERWRITING the RuntimeError marker that was already there. The fault is downgraded to an ordinary return of `()`, and execution resumes in the caller. The error survives only because it is ALSO recorded in `runtime_errors`, which the CLI drains at exit -- which is why the message still appears and the exit code is still 101, and why this reads as "extra output" rather than a silent wrong answer.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE STRAY LINE: statements that the compiled backends never execute DO execute in the interpreter after a fault. If any of them writes a file, sends on a channel, or mutates shared state, the two backends have performed different side effects for the same program -- a run-vs-build divergence in what the program DID, not merely in what it printed. Severity is medium rather than high only because the failure is loud (the message still prints, the exit status is still nonzero), so nothing gates on a false success; raise it if a side-effecting repro is found.

LIKELY FIX: make `pending_cf` refuse to be overwritten while it holds `RuntimeError` -- a fault outranks a `return` / `break` / `continue` that is merely carrying its value. Check the guard against the sibling family that has already been through this area (B-2026-07-15-7 spurious cascade, B-2026-08-09-18 / -19 faulted-receiver and faulted-operand ICEs, B-2026-08-18-37 nested faulting subscript): those fixed the interpreter CRASHING on a faulted operand, and this is the same "what does a faulted sub-expression mean to its parent" question one level up, at the statement.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW, from measuring before fixing: the row concluded "the defect is specific to `return <erroring expr>`". It is NOT. `break <erroring expr>` downgrades a fault identically — `fn boom() -> i64 { let v = Vec[1, 2]; let r = loop { break v[99] }; r }` printed `got ()` from its caller exactly as the `return` shape did. Both statements carry a value through the same `set_cf` funnel, which is why the fix is one guard there rather than a change to either statement. The row's CONTRAST section stands: a fault NOT in a value-carrying position was already correct.

Also fault-kind-agnostic, contrary to the index-OOB framing: divide-by-zero (`return 10 / d`), `unwrap` of `None` (`return o.unwrap()`) and a FAULTING CALLEE (`return inner()`, where `inner` faults and `call_function`'s propagate arm sets the marker) all reproduced, because every one of them routes through `record_runtime_error` to the same marker. Five shapes total, all verified fixed against the compiled backends, all five failing again when the guard alone is reverted.

SEPARATE DEFECT FOUND WHILE TESTING, filed as its own row rather than folded in: a tail-position `loop` drops its break value in BOTH backends. `fn pick() -> i64 { let mut i = 0; loop { i = i + 1; if i == 3 { break i * 10 } } }` prints `()`, while the `let r = loop { … }; r` and `return loop { … }` spellings of the same loop both print `30`. It is not a run-vs-build divergence (interp and JIT agree) and it predates this fix — it surfaced only because the inverse-failure half of this row's test suite used a tail `loop` to exercise the healthy `break` path.

fix:
FIXED by 40c6c13, option (a): `panics` joins the transparent set
FOR SLOT SUBTYPING ONLY.

`is_slot_transparent_verb` (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs) is the ordinary
transparent set plus `panics`, and the six slot comparisons now call it.
Scoped deliberately: `panics` is still inferred, still declared on
functions, still verified on public signatures, still reported by
`karac explain`. Only the value-against-slot comparison ignores it. A slot
may still DECLARE `with panics`; it is simply not a requirement the value
has to meet.

`blocks` and `suspends` stay CHECKED, and that asymmetry is the whole
design: they drive scheduler placement rather than falling out of
arithmetic, so "this callback must not block" is a constraint worth
expressing and cheap to honor. The consequence, stated plainly in design.md,
is that v1 has no way to say "this callback must not panic" -- consistent
with the absence of a `forbids(verb)` predicate elsewhere.

WHAT SETTLED THE DECISION was the standard library, not the ergonomics
argument in the row. 27 of the stdlib's 33 `Fn(..)` slots are bare --
`Vec.map(f: Fn(T) -> T)`, `Pool.new(create_fn: Fn() -> T)`,
`Once.get_or_init(init: Fn() -> T)`, `autograd.grad(f: Fn(Var) -> Var)` --
and NONE was written with `panics`. Under the old rule a callback as
ordinary as `|w, i| w[i]` could fill none of them. That is the language's
own API surface disagreeing with its own rule, which is stronger evidence
than "users will cargo-cult the annotation".

A CORRECTION TO THE RECORD. While proposing this it was argued that a bare
slot "was never a deliberate way" to forbid panics. That was WRONG, and the
test suite said so: THREE tests from B-2026-08-05-18 -- the fixed row about
resource-less verbs being dropped in list-to-set conversion -- assert
exactly that a `panics` value must not satisfy a pure slot
(`test_undeclared_resource_less_verb_in_slot_still_rejected`,
`test_wrong_resource_less_verb_in_slot_still_rejected`,
`test_let_annotation_resource_less_verb_follows_the_slot`). So the old
behaviour was deliberate and tested, and this row is a reversal of a prior
decision rather than the fixing of an oversight. Whoever revisits it should
know that.

Those three guards were RE-POINTED, not deleted. Each exists to prove a
resource-less verb survives the list-to-set conversion and that verb
identity is respected -- purposes entirely independent of WHICH
resource-less verb carries them. They now run on `blocks` (and `blocks`
into a `suspends` slot for the identity one), which is still checked, so
B-2026-08-05-18 remains guarded at full strength. Deleting them would have
dropped a real regression guard; leaving them on `panics` would have
asserted the behaviour this row removes.

ALSO REVERTED: `tests/codegen.rs`'s `test_e2e_closure_over_builtin_
predicates_and_handle_refs` had `with panics` added to its `vecat` slot
under B-2026-08-24-1 to get the suite green. That was the workaround the
row was filed about, and it is now back to the idiomatic bare spelling --
which is the observable proof of this fix, since that test program is
exactly the shape that provoked the row.

MEASURED after the change:
  bare slot, panicking closure   let / return / argument   all clean
  bare slot, `blocks` value      returned value has effect blocks() not declared in slot [pure]
  bare slot, `suspends` value    returned value has effect suspends() not declared in slot [pure]
  bare slot, `writes(UserDB)`    returned value has effect writes(UserDB) not declared in slot [pure]
title: A BARE `Fn(..)` SLOT IS IMPRACTICAL BECAUSE `panics` IS INFERRED FROM ORDINARY INDEXING and is not a transparent verb, so a closure as plain as `|w, i| w[i]` does not fit `Fn(ref Vec[u8], i64) -> u8` and must be spelled `Fn(ref Vec[u8], i64) -> u8 with panics`. Measured identical at all FIVE slot positions -- argument, `let` annotation, assignment, return, struct field -- so this is one rule applied consistently, not a defect in any one of them. The question is whether a bare `Fn(..)` should mean "pure INCLUDING panics" at all, given that indexing, division and (on some shapes) arithmetic all infer it: as it stands, `with panics` becomes boilerplate on nearly every non-trivial function value, which is the shape of an annotation users cargo-cult rather than read.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by B-2026-08-24-1, which wired the four remaining slot positions. The FIRST program in the existing test suite to be rejected by the newly-wired return position was `tests/codegen.rs`'s `test_e2e_closure_over_builtin_predicates_and_handle_refs`, on `fn vecat() -> Fn(ref Vec[u8], i64) -> u8 { |w, i| w[i] }` -- a line nobody would look at twice.

NOT A DEFECT IN -1, and the measurement is the point. The same closure in the same slot is rejected identically at the argument position (the ORIGINAL E0404 rule, shipped long before), at the `let` annotation (B-2026-08-23-12) and at the return position (B-2026-08-24-1):
  q_arg_panics    argument 1 has effect panics() not declared in slot [pure]
  q_let_panics    binding `f` has effect panics() not declared in slot [pure]
  q_ret_panics    returned value has effect panics() not declared in slot [pure]
So the rule was already load-bearing at two positions; -1 made it visible at three more. Reverting any one of them would restore the inconsistency B-2026-08-23-12 existed to remove.

WHAT TO DECIDE. Either (a) `panics` joins the transparent verbs for SLOT-SUBTYPING purposes -- it is already filtered by `is_transparent_verb` in `check_binding_annotation_subtyping`, so this is a one-line policy change, not new machinery -- or (b) the spec says a bare `Fn(..)` slot admits `panics` implicitly and only the RESOURCE verbs are checked, or (c) the status quo is correct and `with panics` is the honest spelling users should write. This row exists to make that a decision rather than an accident; do not "fix" it by weakening one position.

WORTH NOTING for whoever takes it: `panics` is the verb the auto-par conflict rule deliberately treats as NON-conflicting (src/concurrency/conflicts.rs), on the grounds that a Kāra panic is a process exit rather than an unwind. That is a precedent for treating it differently from the other five resource verbs, though it is a different question.

REPRO: three-line programs over `fn vecat() -> Fn(ref Vec[u8], i64) -> u8 { |w, i| w[i] }`, one per position, each with `with panics` on the ENCLOSING function so the slot rule is what fires rather than the public-effect rule.

fix:
FIXED by 0ee3e15, along the exact line the row predicted: `emit_enum_display_fn` gained an explicit cache-key suffix, the two renderers stopped colliding, and the cycle guard was DELETED rather than kept. Net -62 lines.

THE CONTRADICTION AND WHY SPLITTING THE KEY DISSOLVES IT. The wrapper takes a HANDLE and `emit_enum_display_fn` takes the AGGREGATE -- two functions rendering one enum with different first parameters, sharing one cache key (the bare enum name, which is also what `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` looks up). Inner-first: a payload of the enum's own type resolved to the inner and was handed a handle word. Wrapper-first: the inner's own entry check found the wrapper and emitted a self-call. Now `emit_enum_display_fn_keyed(enum_name, args, key_suffix)` appends the suffix to BOTH the cache key and the symbol name while `enum_name` keeps driving every layout and AST lookup, so the two concerns -- which enum's variants, and who owns the cache slot -- come apart. The wrapper registers under the bare name FIRST and emits the inner under `<Enum>__agg`; a nested lookup then resolves to the wrapper, which is right, because that payload IS a handle. Only three call sites existed, and the other two pass `""` and are bit-identical.

VERIFIED ON THE PROGRAM THAT MISCOMPILED. All three backends now print `Node(3, Node(7, Leaf(99)))` for `shared enum T2 { Node(i64, T2), Leaf(i64) }` nested twice -- against `Node(3, Leaf(139898617069619))` (AOT) and `Node(3, Leaf(5))` (JIT) before. The refusal is gone, not relocated.

TWO ADJACENT DEFECTS FELL OUT OF READING THE SAME CODE, both fixed here.

(1) `emit_enum_display_fn` inserted into `display_fn_cache` UNCONDITIONALLY while its lookup used the mode-aware `disp_cache_get`. So a renderer synthesized in DEBUG mode was filed under the DISPLAY map, where a later `println` of the same enum would find it and render Debug's quoted leaves -- a `"s"` where Display owes `s`. Latent only because nothing had reached both modes for one enum; a genuine run-vs-build hazard the moment something did. Now routed through `disp_cache_put`.

(2) `dbg` of a FUNCTION VALUE had no entry in `dbg_unsupported_shape`, so it fell through to `emit_display_fn_for_type` and PANICKED the compiler: `type_name 'unknown' not yet supported`. A compiler crash is precisely what this cluster exists to convert into a diagnostic, so this was the rule being broken in the module that enforces it. It now refuses by name (`Fn(..)`). That shape is unrenderable in PRINCIPLE, not merely unimplemented: the interpreter prints the callee's name (`<fn add>`) and a compiled function value is a bare code pointer carrying none.

THAT ALSO GIVES THE FAIL-CLOSED TESTS A TRIGGER THAT SHOULD LAST. Theirs has moved four times -- `dbg(1)` -> shared struct -> shared enum -> cyclic shared enum -> function value -- once per renderer landing, because every previous choice was a shape that was merely NOT YET WRITTEN. A function value is different in kind, so the churn should stop.

A TEST THAT COULD NOT FAIL, FOUND IN THE VACUITY CHECK: `test_unlowerable_defer_body_refuses_instead_of_vanishing` asserted only that the build fails and mentions `dbg`. A compiler PANIC satisfies both -- so against the pre-fix build, where this shape panicked, the test passed while witnessing exactly the outcome it exists to prevent. It now also asserts the output contains no "panicked", and fails pre-fix as it should. All three touched tests were verified failing pre-fix and passing post-fix.

REMAINDER: the headerless / weak-headered shared type. Untouched, still refused, still unreached by any measured program. Split into its own row rather than left inside this one.
title: `dbg(x)` where `x` is a SELF-REFERENTIAL `shared enum` (`shared enum T2 { Node(i64, T2), Leaf(i64) }`) REFUSES to compile. Not a missing arm: the shared-enum wrapper and the inner `emit_enum_display_fn` share ONE cache key (the bare enum name), so a payload of the enum's own type resolves to the aggregate-taking inner and is handed a handle. Refusing is the new behaviour; before the guard it MISCOMPILED, printing a wrong variant. A HEADERLESS or weak-headered shared type refuses for its own separate reason, below.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-24-6, which landed the shared-enum renderer for every non-cyclic shape. The headerless remainder described in that row moves here too, since -6 is now closed.

(1) SELF-REFERENTIAL SHARED ENUM -- a cache-key collision, not an unwritten renderer.

`emit_shared_enum_debug_display_fn` is a wrapper (load the handle, GEP past the control header, delegate) over `emit_enum_display_fn`. BOTH key their cache on the bare enum name, which is also the key `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` looks up before it reaches the shared arm. Neither order is safe:
  - inner first, wrapper takes the key after (what ships): while the INNER is being synthesized, a payload of the enum's own type resolves through the dispatcher's `module.get_function` fallback to the inner, which expects a pointer to the AGGREGATE and gets a word holding a HANDLE.
  - wrapper first: `emit_enum_display_fn`'s own entry check finds the wrapper and emits a self-call. MEASURED: `karac build` succeeds and the binary never terminates.

MEASURED MISCOMPILE, before the guard, on `shared enum T2 { Node(i64, T2), Leaf(i64) }` nested twice:
  interpreter  Node(3, Node(7, Leaf(99)))
  AOT          Node(3, Leaf(139898617069619))
  JIT          Node(3, Leaf(5))
The garbage word read as a tag, so the symptom is a WRONG VARIANT rather than a crash.

A TEST-DESIGN WARNING WORTH KEEPING: the single-level `shared enum Tree { Node(Tree), Leaf }` rendered `Node(Leaf)` CORRECTLY on all three backends against the broken renderer -- the garbage matched the unit variant's tag, and a unit variant prints no payload to be wrong about. A recursive-shape test needs DEPTH and a PAYLOAD-BEARING variant or it certifies nothing.

LIKELY FIX: give `emit_enum_display_fn` an explicit cache-key parameter (defaulting to the enum name) so the inner can be registered under a distinct key -- e.g. `<Enum>__agg` -- leaving the bare name free for the handle-taking wrapper. Then both orders are safe and the cycle guard can be deleted. The guard itself is `shared_enum_is_cyclic` in `src/codegen/dbg.rs`, a DFS over shared-enum payload types.

SCOPE, measured and pinned by test: only SELF-reference is affected. A payload of a DIFFERENT shared enum (`Outer.Wrap(Inner.X(42))`) and of a shared STRUCT (`Outer.Holds(P { n: 5 })`) each resolve to that type's own wrapper and render correctly.

(2) HEADERLESS / WEAK-HEADERED SHARED TYPE -- carried over from B-2026-08-24-6, still unreached by any measured program.

The headerless niche drops the refcount word, so user field 0 moves to heap index 0 -- and `headerless_here` answers PER FUNCTION (it reads `fn_ctx.current_fn_name`) while a synthesized renderer is emitted once and cached program-wide. One cached function cannot hold both layouts, so `dbg_unsupported_shape` refuses a type that is headerless at the call site. Fixing it properly means keying the renderer cache on (type, layout) and emitting both variants, or hoisting the headerless decision to a whole-program property; `synth_drop` sidesteps the same funnel for the same reason and records it. The weak-headered (base-2) arm is excluded on the narrower ground that nothing sets `has_weak_header` today -- weak fields are declaration-only in codegen -- so that path has never been exercised end to end.

NOT URGENT: the failure mode is now a compile-time diagnostic that names the type and points at `--interp`. That is a strict improvement on where this started, which was a silent wrong answer.

NOTE FOR WHOEVER LANDS THIS: `tests/cli.rs`'s `test_dbg_of_an_unrenderable_shape_refuses_and_names_it` and `test_unlowerable_defer_body_refuses_instead_of_vanishing` both use a cyclic shared enum as their deliberately-unlowerable trigger. That trigger has now moved THREE times (`dbg(1)` -> shared struct -> shared enum -> cyclic shared enum). Move it a fourth time rather than deleting either test -- the property they check is fail-closed propagation, not anything about `dbg`.

RESOLUTION NOTE (2026-08-24): fixed exactly as the row proposed -- an explicit cache-key parameter on `emit_enum_display_fn` -- and the cycle guard the row described was deleted rather than kept, so a self-referential shared enum now RENDERS instead of being refused. The row's two warnings both earned their place: the recursive test does need depth and a payload-bearing variant (the single-level shape renders correctly against the broken renderer), and the fail-closed trigger did need moving a fourth time. The headerless / weak-headered half of this row is untouched and moves to its own row.

fix:
FIXED by 787c355. THREE DEFECTS, one per phase, and a single explanation for all three backend behaviours.

1. PARSER, `is_block_expr` (src/parser/stmts.rs). `Loop` was listed with `While`/`WhileLet`/`For` as an expression "always treated as a statement (not final_expr)", so a trailing `loop` never became a block's value and the function fell off its own end. `Loop` is removed; the other three stay, because design.md gives them type `()` unconditionally and there is nothing to carry out. That was the interpreter's `()`.

2. TYPECHECKER, `ExprKind::Loop` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs). It inferred `Type::Never` unconditionally, ignoring every `break <value>`; `Never` is the bottom type, so the declared return type was never enforced. It now pushes a collector frame and returns `lub_block_type(Never, &break_values)` — `Never` only when no value-break exists, keeping `loop {}` genuinely divergent.

THE HANG AND THE STACK OVERFLOW WERE THE SAME BUG AS (2), and the IR shows it. With the loop typed `Never`, the exit block was emitted as:

    loop.exit:                          ; preds = %mul.ovf.ok
      %loop.val = load i64, ptr %loop.result
      unreachable                       ; where `ret i64 %loop.val` belonged

The `break` was always correct — it stores the value and branches here. But `unreachable` is UB, so LLVM deleted the edge reaching it and the loop became genuinely infinite: the AOT binary hung, the JIT died of a stack overflow under a different pass pipeline. That also explains the row's HONESTY NOTE about the JIT printing `()` once and overflowing three times later — two builds of identical source making different choices about the same UB. Fixing the type made the exit reachable and the `ret` appear.

3. CODEGEN, the `break`-value slot (src/codegen/control_flow.rs) — found only because (1) and (2) made it reachable, and a genuine SILENT MISCOMPILE in its own right. `compile_loop` pre-allocated `loop.result` as a bare `i64` ("i64 by default; refined if used" — the refinement was never written) and `compile_break` stored only `if val.is_int_value()`. So `fn f() -> f64 { loop { break 2.5 } }` stored NOTHING and loaded whatever the slot held: 0 from AOT, 94219697698608 from the JIT, against 2.5 from the interpreter — no diagnostic on any path. The slot is now allocated LAZILY by the first stored value, at that value's own type, and read back at the same type. `compile_labeled_block` shares the mechanism and had the identical bug (`break found 3.5` printed 0).

A `loop` that nothing breaks out of is divergent (design.md rule 0), so its exit block has no predecessors; it is now terminated with `unreachable`, which is what lets the enclosing `get_terminator().is_none()` guards skip a follow-on `ret`. Without that, a `-> Vec[String]` function ending in a `loop` that exits only via `return` emitted `ret i64` against a `{ptr, i64, i64}` return type — caught by the existing `test_e2e_value_fn_loop_tail_terminates_with_unreachable`, which pinned exactly this shape.

NON-SCALAR BREAK VALUES ARE REFUSED, NOT COMPILED. A `String`/`Vec` break value is a `{ptr, i64, i64}` header whose buffer has an owner; copying it through the slot gives it a second owner and both the loop body's scope cleanup and the receiving binding free it — a measured double free ("free(): double free detected in tcache 2"), strictly worse than the module-verification error the i64 slot used to raise. Correctness needs the move-aware suppression `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` already performs for function tails, applied at every break site; that is its own slice, filed separately. Until then codegen fails closed with an actionable message naming the reason and the workaround.

THE FRAME MODEL. `break_value_types` was a label-keyed list only labeled BLOCKS pushed to, so unlabeled breaks — and breaks targeting a labeled LOOP — matched nothing and were dropped. It is now a stack of `BreakFrame`s that every break target pushes: `loop` collects values, `while`/`while let`/`for` push VALUELESS frames, labeled blocks collect by name. The valueless frames are load-bearing: without them a bare `break` inside a `while` nested in a `loop` would resolve to the outer loop and contribute `()` to its LUB.

THREE design.md RULES NOW HOLD that did not: the LUB itself; "a type mismatch across `break` sites is a compile error" (`check_break_values_agree` — `lub_block_type` silently picks a candidate, and that silence is what let this surface rot); and "`while` and `for` loops always have type `()`", so a value-carrying break out of one is rejected rather than discarded.
title: A TAIL-POSITION `loop` DROPS ITS BREAK VALUE and the declared return type is NEVER CHECKED, so one program behaves THREE DIFFERENT WAYS: `fn pick() -> i64 { let mut i = 0; loop { i = i + 1; if i == 3 { break i * 10 } } }` prints `()` and exits 0 under the interpreter, STACK-OVERFLOWS the JIT, and HANGS FOREVER as an AOT binary. `karac check` reports "All checks passed." -- even for `fn pick() -> i64 { loop { break "a string" } }`, a String break in an i64 function.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the inverse-failure tests for B-2026-08-24-7 (a fault must not be downgraded by the statement carrying it). That row's guard needed a test proving a HEALTHY `break` still carries its value; the tail-`loop` spelling of that test failed, and reverting the guard did not change it -- so it predates that fix and is unrelated to it. The B-2026-08-24-7 test suite uses the `let r = loop { .. }; r` spelling instead, with a comment pointing here.

MEASURED, current `main` + 8c93983, all deterministic (JIT 3/3, AOT 2/2):
  fn pick() -> i64 { let mut i = 0; loop { i = i + 1; if i == 3 { break i * 10 } } }
  fn main() { println(pick()); }
    karac check          -> "All checks passed.", exit 0
    karac run --interp   -> prints `()`, exit 0        <- silent wrong answer, no diagnostic
    karac run  (JIT)     -> "fatal runtime error: stack overflow", exit 134
    karac build (AOT)    -> HANGS FOREVER (killed at 8s and at 10s)
Three backends, three behaviours, and the one that "succeeds" returns a Unit where an `i64` was declared.

HONESTY NOTE ON ONE MEASUREMENT: an earlier probe in the same session recorded the JIT printing `()` for this program. That does NOT reproduce -- three consecutive runs against a freshly built `karac` all stack-overflow. The earlier reading is recorded here rather than dropped, because a backend that gave two different answers for one program across two builds of the same source is itself worth pinning; whoever fixes this should confirm which is current before trusting either.

CONTRAST -- the same loop in any OTHER position is correct on every backend:
  let r = loop { .. break i * 10 }; r   -> 30
  return loop { .. break i * 10 }       -> 30
  fn pick() -> i64 { if true { 42 } else { 0 } }  -> 42   (tail `if` is fine)
  fn pick() -> i64 { let mut i = 0; { i = 7; i } } -> 7   (tail block is fine)
So this is specific to a `loop` as the FINAL EXPRESSION of a block.

CAUSE, two independent defects that compound:
1. PARSER, `is_block_expr` (src/parser/stmts.rs:415). `While` / `WhileLet` / `For` / `Loop` are forced to be STATEMENTS, never a block's `final_expr`. The comment there says so outright: "These are always treated as statements (not final_expr / implicit return). For `loop` with break-value, use `let x = loop { ... };` pattern." So the function falls off the end and yields Unit. That is a deliberate rule, and the `let` workaround it names does work -- but nothing TELLS the user, which is defect 2.
2. TYPECHECKER, `ExprKind::Loop` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs:5016) infers `Type::Never` UNCONDITIONALLY -- it walks the body and ignores `break <value>` entirely. `Never` coerces to anything, so `-> i64` is satisfied by a tail `loop` and the declared return type is never enforced. This is what makes the String-break program compile clean. The sibling `ExprKind::LabeledBlock` arm directly below it does it correctly: it pushes a `break_value_types` frame, collects the break values, and computes `lub_block_type(tail_ty, &frame)`. The unlabeled `loop` arm is missing exactly that machinery.

SUGGESTED FIX: give `ExprKind::Loop` the `LabeledBlock` treatment -- collect `break <value>` types and infer `Never` only when there are none (which keeps `loop {}` as a genuine divergent expression). That alone turns the String-break program into a type error and makes the i64 case a checkable mismatch. Whether to ALSO let a tail `loop` be a block's value (relaxing `is_block_expr`) is a separate design call; if it stays a statement, the typechecker should then reject `-> i64` with a tail `loop` that breaks with a value, rather than silently returning `()`.

The JIT stack overflow and the AOT hang are almost certainly downstream of the same lowering -- a `break` whose value is dropped appears not to take the loop-exit edge -- but that was not traced, and a fix should re-measure all three backends rather than assume the type rule alone closes them.

WHY IT SURVIVED THIS LONG — measured, not guessed: a sweep of every `.kara` file in kara/ and kara-katas/ found ZERO value-carrying `break`s. All 542 lines containing "break" are bare `break;` / `break label;` or English prose in comments. The `loop`-as-expression feature was entirely undogfooded, so nothing in the corpus, examples, stdlib or self-host set ever exercised it — which is also why the `while`/`for` prohibition landed with no migration cost.

The typechecker field doc had recorded the gap as deliberate: "loop-LUB inference is a separate slice that will reuse the same machinery once the design entry promotes (out-of-scope here)". The design entry is present and fully specified, so the deferred slice was simply due; this is that slice. The parser carried the matching workaround in a comment — "For `loop` with break-value, use `let x = loop { ... };` pattern" — and that workaround was ITSELF broken for any non-i64 value, which no one had noticed because nothing used it.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW: it recorded the JIT/AOT symptoms as "almost certainly downstream of the same lowering ... but that was not traced, and a fix should re-measure all three backends rather than assume the type rule alone closes them." Traced now, and right for a more specific reason than supposed — not a mis-lowered break edge but `unreachable` emitted from the `Never` type and then exploited by LLVM. All three backends were re-measured, not assumed. The row also under-counted the blast radius: it described a parser+typecheck defect, and a third, independent SILENT MISCOMPILE in codegen (the hardcoded-i64 break slot) sat behind it, reachable today via `let x = loop { break 2.5 }` and `break label 3.5` without any of this row's other conditions.

SEPARATE HARDENING, NOT THE CAUSE. `compile_break` and `compile_continue` were found to FAIL OPEN while tracing: `if let Some(frame) = frame { ... }` with no `else`, so a break matching no frame emitted NO branch and silently became a no-op. Both now return `Err`. This was NOT the cause here — the guard was added first as a diagnostic and did not fire, which is what ruled the hypothesis out and sent the investigation to the IR. It is kept because a missing frame is a compiler bug that should refuse to emit rather than produce a silently looping binary.

fix:
FIXED by 2193636.

`check_annotation_slots` (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs) descends a
declared annotation and its literal initializer together, calling the
existing `check_binding_annotation_subtyping` at every level. The `let` and
`let else` positions use it; assignment, return and struct-field positions
keep the flat check, since each of those is a single slot.

Covered, each asserted to report EXACTLY ONCE:
  Vec literal        binding `v` element 0
  Array literal      binding `a` element 0
  repeat literal     binding `v` element
  Option payload     binding `o`
  tuple element      binding `t` element 0
  map value          binding `m` value 0
  nested Vec[Option] binding `v` element 0
plus two controls: a pure function in a pure element slot is clean, and an
honest element slot (`Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB)]`) accepts the
effectful one.

Map KEYS are checked alongside values -- a function value is a legal map
key, and checking only the value would have been an assumption rather than
a decision.
title: The `Fn(..)` EFFECT SLOT INSIDE A CONTAINER is never checked, so an effectful function placed in a pure-declared element slot is accepted in silence: `let v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = [save, dbl];` declares each element pure and `save` writes. Measured silent for Vec, Array, Option payload, tuple element, map value and repeat literals, and for the nested `Vec[Option[Fn(..)]]`. This is B-2026-08-24-1's stated deferral ("container elements and map values ... unmeasured -- worth its own probe rather than an assumption folded in"), now measured: the five positions -1 wired all read a slot whose annotation is an `Fn(..)` at the TOP, and nothing looked one level in.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the deferral named in B-2026-08-24-1's detail, promoted to its own row and fixed in the same session. Filed and closed together because the measurement IS the row -- leaving it open for a week would have been bookkeeping, not information.

THE TRAP, and the reason this is worth reading rather than just a wiring gap. The obvious implementation matches `ExprKind::ArrayLiteral` against a `Vec[E]` annotation, which is what the PARSED AST holds and what a debug dump of `karac::parse` shows. It covers nothing. `lower` runs BEFORE the effect checker and rewrites a bare `[..]` initializer into `PrefixCollectionLiteral { type_name: "Vec", .. }` when the annotation is Vec/Set/Map -- while leaving an `Array[T, N]`-annotated one an `ArrayLiteral`. So the half-right walk passes an Array test and silently misses every Vec, the commonest container in the language. Both spellings are now listed in one arm with a comment saying why. Measuring against the REAL pipeline rather than the parsed AST is what caught it: `Array` fired and `Vec` did not, from two source lines of identical shape.

The descent is STRUCTURAL, not type-directed: it pairs an annotation shape with the literal shape that matches it and recurses, so `Vec[Option[Fn(..)]]` works without a case of its own, and a mismatch (annotation says Vec, value is a call) simply stops the walk. It must never be the thing that REJECTS a shape -- the typechecker owns "does this value fit this type"; this pass only finds slots to compare.

NOT COVERED, measured and deferred again rather than guessed: `v.push(save)` and `m.insert(k, save)`. They carry the same slot but read it off the RECEIVER, which needs a per-method map from argument position to generic argument (`Vec.push` arg 0 to param 0, `Map.insert` arg 1 to param 1). That is stdlib knowledge the effect checker does not otherwise hold, and baking a table of it into this pass is a different design question from reading an annotation. The B-2026-08-24-1 scope stack does make it reachable -- the receiver's declared `TypeExpr` is already in hand -- so whoever takes it starts from `SubtypingWalk::slot`, not from scratch.

SOUNDNESS UNCHANGED throughout, as with every row in this family: B-2026-08-23-7 makes the MENTION of `save` contribute its effects to the enclosing function, so a `pub fn` could never hide the write through a container. What was missing was any complaint about the ANNOTATION being a lie.

fix:
FIXED by 05a5108.

The suggested-fix text is now return-type-aware. When the declared return
type is an `Fn(..)` / `OnceFn(..)`, the advice names the PARENTHESISED
spelling and renders the real return type, so it can be copy-pasted:

  Add: with writes(UserDB) after a PARENTHESISED return type —
  `-> (Fn(i64) -> i64) with writes(UserDB)` — because a `with` written
  directly after an `Fn` return type binds to that type, not to the function

Every other return type keeps the original wording verbatim; the special
case is exactly one shape wide, and a test pins that.

DELIBERATELY NOT THE FULLY-DOUBLED SPELLING. This diagnostic knows the
FUNCTION's effects; it does not know whether they come from the returned
value. Suggesting `-> (Fn(..) with E) with E` would be a guess that is wrong
whenever the function performs the effect in its own body and returns a pure
function. Following the advice given now moves the user from the loop to a
DIFFERENT, actionable error -- the return-slot check from B-2026-08-24-1
asking for the row when the value really carries one. Two accurate messages
beat one guessed message, and the test asserts the second message is not the
first repeated.

BLOCKED ON A SECOND BUG, fixed in the same commit and filed separately as
B-2026-08-24-14: rendering the return type concretely requires
`formatter::render_type_expr`, and that printer was emitting `fn(i64) -> i64`
for an `Fn` type -- lowercase, which does not parse in type position. The
first version of this fix therefore produced advice that was copy-pasteable
and still wrong. Fixing the printer was a precondition, not a detour.
title: THE COMPILER'S OWN SUGGESTED FIX IS UNFOLLOWABLE for a public function that RETURNS an `Fn(..)` value. `pub fn get() -> Fn(i64) -> i64 { save }` errors with "public function 'get' performs effects [writes(UserDB)] but has no effect declaration. Add: with writes(UserDB) to the function signature" -- and doing EXACTLY that reproduces the SAME error, because a `with` clause after an `Fn` return type binds to the RETURN TYPE, not to the function. The one spelling that compiles is `pub fn get() -> (Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB)) with writes(UserDB) { save }` -- parenthesised AND doubled -- which the diagnostic never mentions and which no user would guess. Measured on all four spellings.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while resolving B-2026-08-23-11's design question (see docs/spikes/function-type-effect-row.md). Not part of that question -- a self-contained diagnostics bug in the suggested-fix text.

MEASURED, four spellings of the same intent:
  pub fn get() -> Fn(i64) -> i64 { save }
      error: ... has no effect declaration. Add: with writes(UserDB) to the function signature
  pub fn get() -> Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB) { save }        <- the literal advice
      error: ... has no effect declaration. Add: with writes(UserDB) ...   (IDENTICAL)
  pub fn get() -> (Fn(i64) -> i64) with writes(UserDB) { save }
      error: returned value has effect writes(UserDB) not declared in slot [pure]
  pub fn get() -> (Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB)) with writes(UserDB) { save }
      All checks passed.

WHY IT LOOPS. `with` after a return type is ambiguous between the function's own effect clause and the returned `Fn` type's effect row, and the parser resolves it toward the TYPE. So the advice text -- which is generated by the public-effect rule, and is correct for every return type that is not an `Fn` -- lands in the one place where following it changes nothing. The user sees a compiler that repeats itself.

NOT A REGRESSION from B-2026-08-24-1. Verified: the fourth spelling compiled before that row and still does. What -1 added is the third line of the table (a bare return slot is now caught), which is correct and is what makes the doubled spelling the RIGHT answer rather than merely one of two.

FIX SHAPE, in increasing order of ambition. (a) Make the suggested-fix text return-type-aware: when the return type is an `FnType`, emit the parenthesised-and-doubled spelling instead of the bare one. Cheapest, and turns an unfollowable message into a copy-pasteable one. (b) Additionally warn on the ambiguous spelling itself -- `-> Fn(..) with E` almost certainly means the type and almost never means what a user writing it expects. (c) Reconsider the grammar so the binding is explicit. (c) is a design change and should not be done for this row alone.

REPRO: /tmp/.../ev/{g_firewall_bare,h_suggest,i_parens,j_both}.kara, four three-line programs over `effect resource UserDB;` + `fn save(n: i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB) { n * 2 }`.

fix:
FIXED by 758bf19. `compile_break` now disarms the source's scope-exit free BETWEEN the store and the drain — the break-site twin of what `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs) does for a function tail — so the value leaves the loop owned exactly once and struct-typed break values travel the slot.

TWO SUPPRESSORS ARE NEEDED, because the buffer has two possible owners:
  * `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg` for a tracked BINDING (`break s`) — a runtime `store cap, 0` that makes the queued `FreeVecBuffer` no-op;
  * `rhs_stages_fstr_acc` + `zero_vec_alloca_cap` for an F-STRING or `.to_string()` value (`break f"got{i}"`), where the buffer belongs to the interpolation accumulator and there is no binding to disarm.
The first cut had only the former. It fixed `break s` and `break [i, i*2, i*3]` while every f-string carrier still double-freed — which is how the second suppressor was found rather than reasoned about. `rhs_stages_fstr_acc` is deliberately the same predicate the let-binding and tail-return paths use: it covers `.to_string()` as well as a literal `f"…"`, and the narrower `InterpolatedStringLit` match missed exactly that shape once before (B-2026-07-12-17).

ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: after the store, because zeroing before the value is read corrupts what the receiver gets (B-2026-06-12-6); before `emit_scope_cleanup_from`, because that drain is what is being disarmed.

STILL SKIPPED, each for its own reason rather than as a leftover: POINTERS (a `shared` handle needs a matching retain, not a cap-zero), ARRAYS (`Array[T, N]` drops elementwise via `StructDrop`, a different suppressor), and the EMPTY STRUCT — `break outer ()` is a VALUELESS break per design.md § `break expr` ("Plain `break` (or `break ()`) is valid in any loop form"), so there is nothing to carry and a slot would only invent one.

THE COMPILE-TIME QUEUE-RETRACTING SUPPRESSORS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT REUSED (Map/Set's `suppress_map_cleanup_for_tail_identifier`, the boxed-enum payload retraction). A `break` is CONDITIONAL and sits inside a loop that may iterate many times without taking it, so a flow-insensitive retraction would disarm the cleanup on the iterations that do NOT break — trading this double free for a leak. That is the exact bargain the tail-return code warns against in its own comments, and it is why a `Map` / `Set` / boxed-enum break value still takes the skip path. Filed as the remaining surface rather than attempted.
title: A NON-SCALAR `break` VALUE (String / Vec / struct) cannot travel through the compiled backends' break-value slot: `fn pick() -> String { loop { break f"x" } }` and the labeled-block twin `found: { break found f"x" }` both FAIL AT MODULE VERIFICATION (`ret i64` against `{ptr, i64, i64}`), while the interpreter returns the value. Storing the header instead is a DOUBLE FREE, measured -- so the slot deliberately refuses it.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-24-10 rather than folded in. That row made `loop` an expression valued by its breaks (787c355), which typed the break slot by the VALUE instead of a hardcoded `i64` and fixed the float case (`break 2.5` had silently produced 0 from AOT and a garbage integer from the JIT). Aggregates are the remainder: they need ownership work the type fix does not supply.

MEASURED on 787c355:
  fn pick() -> String { loop { break f"x" } }            interp: got2   AOT/JIT: module verification error
  fn pick() -> String { let s = loop { break f"x" }; s } interp: got2   AOT/JIT: module verification error
  fn pick() -> f64    { loop { break 2.5 } }             interp: 2.5    AOT/JIT: 2.5   <- fixed by 787c355
  let r = found: { break found f"deep" };                interp: deep   AOT/JIT: module verification error
The `let x = loop { … }` spelling fails identically, so this is NOT specific to the tail position and PREDATES 787c355 — the old parser comment recommended exactly that spelling as the "value-producing form" for `loop`, and it was already broken for any non-i64 value. Nothing in the corpus used it (a sweep found zero value-carrying breaks in 542 `break` lines), which is why it went unnoticed.

WHY IT IS REFUSED RATHER THAN COMPILED. An intermediate cut of 787c355 stored the value unconditionally. A `String`/`Vec` value is a `{ptr, i64, i64}` header whose buffer already has an owner; copying it into the slot and loading it at the exit creates a SECOND owner, and the loop body's scope cleanup plus the receiving binding both free it. Measured: "free(): double free detected in tcache 2" on `str_break`, `str_let` and `lb_str`. Silent heap corruption is worse than a loud verification error, so `store_in_frame_at` (src/codegen/control_flow.rs) stores only `is_int_type() || is_float_type()` and leaves everything else unstored — which keeps the single owner.

Note the store must stay SILENT rather than erroring: a first attempt returned `Err` for every non-scalar and broke two existing tests that legitimately write `break outer ()`, the unit literal being a valueless break per design.md § `break expr` ("Plain `break` (or `break ()`) is valid in any loop form"). Any fix must keep unit breaks working.

LIKELY FIX: apply the move-aware cleanup suppression the function tail already performs — `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` (src/codegen/functions.rs), which zeroes the source's `cap` field so the queued `FreeVecBuffer` no-ops and the receiving binding becomes the unique owner — at every break site that carries an aggregate. The `{ptr, i64, i64}` slot itself is already correctly typed by the lazily-allocated `result_ty`; only the ownership half is missing. Verify under `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` (and the Linux/LSan CI leg, since a macOS asan run does not detect leaks) rather than by output alone — the failure mode here is a free, not a wrong value.

VERIFIED, all on 758bf19. Eight carrier shapes byte-identical across `karac run --interp` and `karac build`: f-string (`break f"got{i}"`), tracked binding (`break s`), Vec literal (`break [i, i*2, i*3]`), struct with a String field (`break Row { name: f"r{i}", n: i*5 }`), two breaks of the same type on different guards, `break outer <String>` from inside a nested `while`, plus the scalar shapes from B-2026-08-24-10. All clean under ASAN with LeakSanitizer live at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` — the level that actually runs the allocations, since -O2 folds several of these fixtures to nothing (B-2026-08-04-17). The nested case allocates 15 times and is clean.

THE LEAK DIRECTION IS TESTED, NOT ASSUMED. `asan_loop_break_binding_value_frees_unbroken_iterations` allocates a fresh String on EVERY iteration and breaks on a later one, so the fall-through iterations must still free theirs. That is the mirror-image bug this fix could have introduced, and it is the one a compile-time retraction would have caused.

TEST PAIRING NOTE, deliberate and documented in the fixture block: `assert_clean_asan_run` SKIPS when setup fails, so the three ASAN fixtures alone would pass VACUOUSLY if aggregates ever regressed to being refused at codegen. The compile-path half is guarded in tests/codegen.rs, whose `run_program` PANICS on a codegen failure — `test_e2e_loop_break_string_value_round_trips` and its Identifier sibling. Both halves are needed: one asserts the value arrives, the other that it arrives owned once.

fix:
FIXED by 05a5108.

`src/formatter/types.rs`'s `TypeKind::FnType` arm now destructures
`effect_spec` and `is_once` instead of matching them away, and writes the
correct head:

  Fn(...)         / OnceFn(...)      -- head, was lowercase `fn(`
  ... with _                          -- polymorphic row, was dropped
  ... with writes(D)                  -- concrete row, was dropped

MEASURED, `karac fmt` on one source line holding all three:
  before   let f: fn(i64) -> i64 = save;      <- from `Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB)`
           let g: fn(i64) -> i64 = save;      <- from `OnceFn(i64) -> i64`
  after    let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(UserDB) = save;
           let g: OnceFn(i64) -> i64 = save;

and the formatted output now round-trips (`karac check` on it reports only
the effect error the ORIGINAL source has) and is a fixpoint under a second
format pass. Before, feeding `karac fmt`'s own output back in failed with
`error[parse]: Expected type, found Fn`.

WHY THE SEVERITY IS NOT HIGHER THAN IT LOOKS. Two of the three losses --
the effect row and once-callability -- are silent weakenings of a declared
guarantee, which is the class `no_effect_attribute_keeps_its_verbs` exists
to guard ("formatting must never be able to weaken a guarantee"). They were
saved from being silent CORRUPTION only by the third defect: the lowercase
head made the output unparseable, so the damage surfaced at the next parse
instead of quietly changing two types. `karac fmt` also prints to stdout
rather than rewriting in place, so the blast radius is whoever pipes it back
over their source -- the obvious workflow, and what a `--write` flag or an
editor format-on-save integration would do.

The regression test lives next to the `#[no_effect]` one it mirrors and
pins the same two properties: the output parses, and a second pass is a
fixpoint.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-24-12, whose fix renders a return
type into a suggested-fix string and so could not be correct until this was.
title: `karac fmt` EMITS UNPARSEABLE SOURCE for any `Fn(..)` / `OnceFn(..)` type annotation, and silently drops two declarations doing it. One `TypeKind::FnType` arm in src/formatter/types.rs matched `effect_spec` and `is_once` away with `..` and wrote a LOWERCASE head, so `Fn(i64) -> i64 with writes(D)` printed as `fn(i64) -> i64` -- the effect row GONE -- and `OnceFn(i64) -> i64` printed as the same text, once-callability GONE, making two different types indistinguishable in the output. Feeding `karac fmt`'s own output back in fails with `error[parse]: Expected type, found Fn`. The two silent weakenings are the class `no_effect_attribute_keeps_its_verbs` exists to guard ("formatting must never be able to weaken a guarantee"); they escaped being silent CORRUPTION only because the unparseable head made the damage surface at the next parse.

fix:
Fixed in 114a9d2. One `icmp` + branch per call site in
`src/codegen/vec_method.rs`, via a new `emit_vec_mutation_bounds_check`
helper that mirrors what `emit_split_bounds_check` already does for plain
indexing.

THE PREDICATE DIFFERS BETWEEN THE THREE, which is the only subtle part:
`insert` compares UGT because `idx == len` is a legal APPEND, while `remove`
and `swap_remove` compare UGE. Using UGE for `insert` would turn a
memory-safety fix into a broken `push`, so the in-range test pins
insert-at-len and insert(0)-into-empty explicitly.

The unsigned compare covers negative indices for free: a negative `i64`
reinterpreted as unsigned exceeds any representable length, so one compare
catches both halves. That is the same trick indexing already used, and it is
why this costs one compare rather than two.

All three now panic with exit 101 and a located message on `karac run` and
`karac build` alike, matching `--interp`:

    panic at m4.kara:168:23 in ss_add: Vec.insert index out of bounds

TWO REGRESSION TESTS, and the first was verified to fail without the fix by
stashing the codegen change and re-running (it went red; the in-range test
stayed green, which is correct — its job is to catch a wrong predicate, not
the missing check). The out-of-range test pins the message AND exit 101 for
all three methods at a positive and a negative index; pinning the code is
what separates "panics" from "dies somehow", since the bug produced 134 for
insert/remove and 0 for swap_remove.

VERIFICATION: codegen 3197 passed / 0 failed and memory_sanitizer 1158
passed / 0 failed, both under KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1 so no case
green-skipped; all default-feature suites green; `cargo clippy --all
--all-targets -D warnings` clean on BOTH the default and `--features llvm`
legs; `cargo fmt --all --check` clean.

NOTE ON THE FIRST TEST RUN, which showed 7 then 9 unrelated failures: those
were a STALE runtime archive (the container's archives predated 52 pulled
commits) plus the absent optional `unicode` / `regex` / `arrow` archives, not
this change. Rebuilding all five archives took the suite to fully green. The
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` gate is what turned the optional-archive
cases from silent skips into visible failures, which is exactly its purpose.
title: `Vec.insert` / `Vec.remove` / `Vec.swap_remove` HAVE NO CODEGEN BOUNDS CHECK: an out-of-range index CORRUPTS THE HEAP (insert/remove) or SILENTLY RETURNS GARBAGE AND DROPS AN ELEMENT (swap_remove) on both compiled backends, where the interpreter panics and design.md says "panics if out of bounds"

fix: Fixed in 776680a (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs). Three changes. (1) The `StmtKind::Assign` / `CompoundAssign` arm now calls the DESCENDING `check_annotation_slots` instead of the top-level-only `check_binding_annotation_subtyping` it wraps -- the same upgrade B-2026-08-24-11 made to the `let` arm, which the assignment arm never received. (2) New `check_stored_arg_slots` + the `stdlib_stored_arg_slots` table, called from the `MethodCall` arm: it reads the element slot off the RECEIVER's declared `TypeExpr` (already in hand on the B-2026-08-24-1 scope stack) rather than off the callee's parameter list, and hands it to the same descending walk, so `vv.push([save])` on a `Vec[Vec[Fn(..)]]` works for free. (3) New `check_generic_param_slots`, also from the `MethodCall` arm: it maps a user method's bare type-parameter mention to its index in the inherent impl header's generic list and reads the receiver's type argument there. Six new tests in tests/effectchecker.rs, half of them all-clean false-positive guards.
title: A declared `Fn(..)` EFFECT SLOT is checked only when the value arrives in the DECLARING statement, so the same annotation gives two different answers depending on which statement fills it: `let v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = [save];` is caught while `v.push(save)` one line later is silent, and `let o: Option[Fn(i64) -> i64] = Some(save);` is caught while `o = Some(save);` is not. Three distinct causes -- the assignment position never got B-2026-08-24-11's DESCENDING walk; a baked stdlib store carries its slot on the RECEIVER, which the callee-parameter check cannot see; and a user generic method's `value: T` parameter is a slot only after the receiver's type argument is substituted in.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the deferral named in B-2026-08-24-11's detail ("NOT COVERED,
measured and deferred again rather than guessed: `v.push(save)` and
