`m.insert(k, save)`"), now measured and closed, plus two neighbouring gaps the
same probe turned up. Filed and closed together because the measurement IS the
row.

THE UNIFYING SHAPE. Every position B-2026-08-24-1 and -11 wired reads the slot
off a DECLARATION and compares it against the value written in that same
statement. A value that reaches the slot LATER was never compared to it, so one
annotation gave two different answers depending on which statement filled it:

    let o: Option[Fn(i64) -> i64] = Some(save);   // caught since -11
    let mut o: Option[Fn(i64) -> i64] = None;
    o = Some(save);                                // silent
    let mut v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = [save];      // caught since -11
    let mut v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = [dbl];
    v.push(save);                                  // silent

THREE FIXES, and they are genuinely three -- different reasons, not one gap
seen three ways.

(1) ASSIGNMENT, pure wiring. The `let` position was upgraded to the DESCENDING
walk by -11 and the assignment position was left on the top-level-only check it
wraps. `check_annotation_slots` is a strict superset -- it checks this level and
then recurses -- so the fix is the call it should always have been. Covers
`o = Some(save)`, `v = [save]`, `t = (save, 2)`.

(2) BAKED STDLIB STORES, and the one place the effect checker now holds stdlib
knowledge. `v.push(save)` carries the element slot on the RECEIVER, and
`check_call_args_subtyping` cannot find it because it reads slots off the
CALLEE's parameter list -- which `Vec.push` does not have. `runtime/stdlib/
vec.kara` declares the SHAPE only (`struct Vec[=T] { }`); the method surface is
hand-written match arms in the typechecker (`infer_vec_method`,
`method_vec_mutation.rs`). There is no `TypeExpr` for `push`'s parameter
anywhere in the program, so "argument 0 lands in slot T" cannot be derived --
only stated. `stdlib_stored_arg_slots` states it for Vec.push, Vec.insert,
VecDeque.push_back/push_front, Map.insert and SortedMap.insert.

THE HEURISTIC THAT WAS REJECTED, because it is the obvious shortcut and it is
wrong: "check every argument against the receiver's sole `Fn`-typed generic
argument". On a `v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64]`, a call like `v.map(g)` passes a
function value that is NOT stored in the element slot, and flagging it is a
FALSE POSITIVE -- the one failure mode this family must not acquire. Naming the
storing methods explicitly is both safer and more honest about what is known.

SET and SORTEDSET are absent by measurement, not oversight: the element must be
`Hash + Eq` / `Ord` and a function type is neither, so `Set[Fn(i64) -> i64]` is
rejected by the TYPECHECKER before the effect checker runs ("element type does
not implement `Hash + Eq`"). `Map`'s KEY slot is listed anyway, for the same
reason in reverse -- the table describes what the METHOD stores, which stays
true, rather than what happens to be reachable today, which would rot silently
if function types ever gain a hash.

(3) USER GENERIC METHODS, and this half needs no table at all. For
`impl[T] Holder[T] { fn set(mut ref self, value: T) }`, the parameter's written
type is `T`, which is not an `FnType`, so `check_call_args_subtyping` stops --
but on a `Holder[Fn(i64) -> i64]` receiver the parameter IS a pure
`Fn(i64) -> i64` after substitution. Resolved by mapping the parameter's bare
type-parameter mention to its position in the impl header's generic list and
reading the receiver's type argument there.

Note this half needs NO notion of which arguments are STORED: a parameter's
substituted type constrains its argument whether the callee keeps the value or
merely calls it, exactly as a directly-written `Fn(..)` parameter does. Storage
only mattered for the baked containers, whose parameters have no written type to
substitute into. Inherent impls only -- a TRAIT impl's method parameters are
typed by the TRAIT's generics, so indexing into the impl header's list would be
reading the wrong list.

FALSE-POSITIVE EVIDENCE, since all three fixes make the compiler REJECT
programs it used to accept. 594 `.kara` files swept -- 400 in kara-katas, 194 in
`examples/` + `runtime/stdlib/` -- and NOT ONE new slot violation. The full
suite is green on both legs: 8357 tests under `--features llvm` with
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, and the non-codegen suite besides. Six
negative cases are pinned as tests: a slot that DECLARES the effect, a pure
value, a non-`Fn` element, a `panics` value (transparent per B-2026-08-24-8), a
non-storing method, and an UNANNOTATED receiver (no declaration, so no slot to
lie about -- silence there is correct, not a miss).

STILL NOT COVERED, measured and left rather than half-wired. A receiver that is
not a plain named binding: `self.items.push(save)` carries the same element slot
on a struct FIELD, and the walk reads the receiver's type off the scope stack by
NAME. Reaching it means resolving a receiver EXPRESSION to a declared type,
which is a different job from looking one up -- filed as its own row rather than
guessed at here.

SOUNDNESS UNCHANGED throughout, as with every row in this family: B-2026-08-23-7
makes the MENTION of `save` contribute its effects to the enclosing function, so
no `pub fn` could ever have hidden the write through any of these paths. What
was missing, and is now present, is a complaint about the ANNOTATION being a
lie.

fix:
Fixed in a9d540b (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs). The receiver lookup stops
being a name lookup and becomes a resolution: `receiver_declared_type` walks a
receiver expression to the type someone actually WROTE for it, and every slot
check downstream is unchanged.

FOUR receiver shapes now resolve, where only a plain named local did before.

1. `self` -- from the enclosing method's `method_bodies` key (`"Registry.add"`
   -> `Registry`), threaded onto the walk as `SubtypingWalk::self_type`. The
   name-keyed slot stack cannot hold this, which is why the row existed.
2. A FIELD ACCESS -- resolve the object, then read the field's declared type off
   the struct via the existing `struct_field_type`. It recurses, so
   `self.inner.items` works without a case of its own.
3. An INDEX -- `indexed_element_type` off the container's own annotation.
4. A PARAMETER -- see the separate note below; this was not in the row and turned
   out to be the widest of the four.

Plus `peel_borrow`: a receiver held as `mut ref Vec[Fn(..)]` names the same
element slot as `Vec[Fn(..)]`. Only RECEIVER resolution peels -- a
`let f: ref Fn(..)` annotation is still compared exactly as written, because
there the wrapper is part of the thing being declared.

Five new tests in tests/effectchecker.rs, one of them the all-clean
false-positive guard covering both deliberate boundaries.
title: A declared `Fn(..)` element slot on a receiver that is NOT a plain named binding is still unchecked: `self.items.push(save)` carries the same slot as `items.push(save)` -- on a struct FIELD rather than a local -- and is silent. B-2026-08-24-16 reads the receiver's declared type off the walk's scope stack, which is keyed by NAME, so any receiver that is an EXPRESSION (field access, index, method chain) has no entry.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the remainder named in B-2026-08-24-16's detail, split out rather than buried in the closed row, per the live-remainder rule.

WHY IT WAS NOT FOLDED IN. `SubtypingWalk::slot` is a stack of (binding name, declared TypeExpr) pushed at each `let` with an annotation, and -16's receiver lookup is a lookup in that stack. `self.items` names no binding, so there is nothing to look up. Reaching it means resolving a receiver EXPRESSION to a declared type -- walking `self` to the enclosing impl's target type, then that struct's field list to `items`'s annotation -- which is a different job from looking a name up, and one with its own failure modes (shadowed `self`, a field whose type is itself a type parameter, a receiver that is an index or a method chain). Guessing at it inside -16 would have put a half-checked path next to a checked one with no test able to tell them apart.

PARTIAL MACHINERY EXISTS: `struct_field_type` (added by B-2026-08-24-1 for the struct-field slot position) already maps a struct name + field name to the declared `TypeExpr`. What is missing is the step before it -- deciding which struct a receiver expression names.

SOUNDNESS UNCHANGED, as everywhere in this family: B-2026-08-23-7's mention rule makes the enclosing function declare the effect regardless. This is about diagnosing a lying ANNOTATION, not about letting an effect escape.

FIXED 2026-08-24. Three notes worth keeping, because two of them are traps and
one is a gap this row did not know it had.

TRAP 1 -- `self` IS NOT AN IDENTIFIER. It has its own AST node,
`ExprKind::SelfValue`, and never parses as `Identifier("self")`. The obvious
arm -- `ExprKind::Identifier(name) if name == "self"` -- compiles, reads
correctly, and covers NOTHING. It was written that way first and shipped past a
build; what caught it was the probe having a local-field receiver next to the
`self` one, so `r.items.push(save)` fired while `self.items.push(save)`, one
line up and structurally identical, stayed silent. Exactly the shape of
B-2026-08-24-11's `ArrayLiteral` / `PrefixCollectionLiteral` trap, caught by
exactly the same discipline: put the two spellings side by side in one probe
and make the pipeline tell you which one is real. A test pins the live arm as
the non-vacuity anchor.

TRAP 2 -- A RESOLVER AND ITS DIAGNOSTIC NAME MUST BE WIRED TOGETHER. The index
arm was added to `receiver_declared_type` and fired for nothing, because the
call site pairs it with `receiver_subject` in one `if let (Some, Some)` and the
SUBJECT renderer had no `Index` case. A resolver that can name a shape its
renderer cannot is silently dead. The two now share `receiver_place`, so a
shape either resolves and renders or does neither.

THE GAP THE ROW DID NOT KNOW ABOUT -- PARAMETERS. The slot stack was filled only
by `let`, so a parameter -- a declared slot written just as plainly, one line
further up -- had no entry at all. `fn f(v: mut ref Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64]) {
v.push(save) }` was silent, and so was every field or index reached through a
parameter. This is not a receiver-expression problem and was missed by every
position in this family since B-2026-08-23-12, not just by the receiver lookup;
it was found only because a probe of parameter-receiver shapes was written to
check the field path and came back entirely clean. Parameters are now seeded
into the stack at the top of each body walk, which also gives the ASSIGNMENT
position (`f = save` on an `Fn`-typed parameter) its slot for free.

STDLIB KNOWLEDGE STAYS EXPLICIT. `indexed_element_type` lists the heads whose
index semantics are known and returns `None` for everything else. `Map` is why
the direction matters: `m[k]` yields the VALUE, so reading generic argument 0
would compare against the KEY slot. A user type with its own `Index` impl can
yield anything at all, so guessing argument 0 there is how a false positive gets
in -- the same discipline as `stdlib_stored_arg_slots`, and the same reason.

FALSE-POSITIVE EVIDENCE. Every change here makes the compiler REJECT programs it
used to accept, and PARAMETER seeding widens the slot stack for every function
body in every program, so that is the real exposure. 1111 `.kara` files swept
with the final binary -- 917 in kara-katas, 194 in `examples/` +
`runtime/stdlib/` -- and NOT ONE new slot violation. Full suite green on both
legs.

STILL NOT COVERED, and split out as its own row rather than buried here: a
METHOD-CHAIN receiver (`hand_out().push(save)`). Its type is a RETURN type, not
a written annotation, and this pass holds no return types. The all-clean test
pins that silence deliberately, so wiring it later is a visible change to an
assertion rather than a quiet widening.

fix:
CLOSED wontfix by 0c1f009, which lands the MEASUREMENT and its regression tests rather than an implementation -- the close this row itself named as the honest one if the niche turned out to be unreachable.

MEASURED: the headerless arm cannot fire. `dbg(x)` hands `x` itself to a call, which is exactly the escape the headerless purity gate demotes on, so a type can be headerless or it can be `dbg`-able, never both. 16 probe programs, instrumented at the codegen reconcile to print both headerless sets: every one that named a shared value in a `dbg` argument emptied BOTH sets, and every matching control WITHOUT the `dbg` kept them. Zero refusals across the sweep. Coverage: both arms (program-wide `headerless_types` and per-fn `headerless_fns`), free fns and impl methods, and the bare member / `Option[member]` / link-field-of-member / tuple-containing-member argument positions. The complement holds too -- `dbg` of a SCALAR field (`x.val`) leaves both sets intact and never consults the shared arm -- which is what makes the exclusion structural rather than a property of one syntactic shape.

WHY NOT IMPLEMENT. No program can reach the arm, so a renderer for it would be GEP-offset code that no test can exercise -- the same reason this row already gave for excluding the weak-headered half ("keeps it failing closed rather than shipping untested"). That reasoning applies to the headerless half as well.

WHY NOT DELETE THE GUARD. It is insurance with a plausible trigger: `dbg` returns its argument, so modelling it as a borrowing/summarized intrinsic (to skip the owned copy) is a natural future optimization -- and that is exactly the change that would stop it demoting. Deleting the guard would turn that optimization into a silent miscompile, every field read landing one word off. So the guard stays and the exclusion is now PINNED instead of assumed: `tests/elision.rs` asserts `dbg` of a member demotes both sets, each with a control asserting the same program IS headerless without the `dbg` (without that half the assertion passes for any of the many reasons a program fails the gate -- a vacuous green); `tests/cli.rs` asserts the chain COMPILES AND RENDERS identically on interp/JIT/AOT. All three assertions were mutation-tested: a non-demoting expression, a scalar substituted for a member, and a forced `headerless_here == true` each fail the suite, the last with the exact refusal diagnostic.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS -- it was half wrong, and the wrong half is the load-bearing one. This row said the headerless base "is a PER-FUNCTION property while a synthesized renderer is cached program-wide". `headerless_here` in fact answers from TWO sets and only one is per-function. `headerless_types` (Phase C2b) is PROGRAM-WIDE and returns true in every fn -- for a type in it the base is uniform, so a program-wide cached renderer is exactly the right shape and would need only its base taken from the same funnel, not a keyed cache. Only `headerless_fns` (Phase D, keyed per `(fn, type)`) is the half a single cached renderer genuinely cannot serve. So the "LIKELY FIX: key the renderer cache on (type, base)" above overstates the work for one arm and is right only for the other. The source comments in `src/codegen/dbg.rs` and `src/codegen/synth_display.rs` carried the same conflation and are corrected in this commit.

The WEAK-HEADERED half is unchanged and still correct as filed: `has_weak_header` is false for every type today, so that path has never been exercised end to end; build it with the weak-field codegen slices, not before.
title: `dbg(x)` REFUSES for a HEADERLESS or WEAK-HEADERED `shared` type -- the last two shapes in the shared family the compiled `Debug` renderers do not cover. MEASURED UNREACHABLE and closed without an implementation: `dbg(x)` hands `x` to a call, which is exactly the escape the headerless purity gate demotes on, so a type can be headerless or `dbg`-able but never both (16 probe programs, both arms, controls green). `has_weak_header` is false for every type today. The guard is KEPT as insurance -- making `dbg` a borrowing intrinsic would stop it demoting and turn the arm into a silent one-word field-offset miscompile -- and the exclusion is now pinned by tests instead of assumed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-24-9, which fixed the self-referential shared enum and deleted its cycle guard. The shared family otherwise renders end to end now: `shared struct` / `par struct` (B-2026-08-24-2), `shared enum` (-6), self-referential `shared enum` (-9).

(1) HEADERLESS. The headerless niche drops the refcount word, so user field 0 moves from heap index 1 to index 0. `headerless_here` (`src/codegen.rs`) answers PER FUNCTION -- it reads `fn_ctx.current_fn_name` and consults `target_abi.headerless_fns` -- while `emit_shared_struct_debug_display_fn` emits ONE function cached program-wide. Baking either base into that shared function makes every field read land at the wrong offset in the other kind of function, so `dbg_unsupported_shape` refuses when the type is headerless at the call site. `synth_drop` sidesteps the same funnel for the same reason and records it at `src/codegen/synth_drop.rs`.

LIKELY FIX: key the renderer cache on (type, base) and emit both variants on demand, or hoist the headerless decision to a whole-program property. The first is contained -- `emit_enum_display_fn_keyed`'s suffix parameter (added by -9) is the same mechanism, and the struct renderer would need the equivalent.

(2) WEAK-HEADERED. `has_weak_header` gives a `{ strong, weak, fields... }` box and base 2. It is `false` for every type today -- weak fields are declaration-only in codegen -- so that path has never been exercised end to end, and the renderer excludes it rather than shipping an untested arm. This one resolves itself when the weak-field codegen slices land: build it together with them, not before.

HOW TO TELL WHETHER (1) IS REACHABLE AT ALL, which is the first thing to establish and was NOT established when this was filed: no probe has produced a program where `dbg` of a headerless shared type is refused. Every shared-struct shape tried during -2 and -9 (flat, `mut` fields, self-referential `Option[shared]` linked lists, `Vec[shared]` elements, `par struct`) reported `headerless_program_wide=false`. If the niche turns out to be unreachable for any type `dbg` can name, the honest close is `wontfix` with that measurement recorded, not an implementation.

NOT URGENT: the failure mode is a compile-time diagnostic naming the type and pointing at `--interp`.

fix:
PARTIALLY FIXED by d9b5ea0 — the Map/Set half only. The `shared` half is NOT fixed and is split to its own row; see below, and do not read this row as clearing it.

MAP / SET, fixed. Their cleanup is queue-driven (`FreeMapHandle`) with no in-slot sentinel like Vec/String's `cap = 0`, which is why the existing move suppressor (`suppress_map_cleanup_for_tail_identifier`) disarms by editing the cleanup queue at COMPILE time. That is right for a function tail, which runs once, and wrong at a `break`: a break is conditional and sits inside a loop that may iterate many times without taking it, so retracting the action would disarm the free on every non-breaking iteration too — a leak in place of a double free.

`disarm_moved_handle_by_zeroing` (src/codegen/control_flow.rs) instead stores null into the binding's slot, so the disarm executes only on the path that actually breaks. That required making `FreeMapHandle` uniformly null-tolerant: the three `karac_map_free*` entry points already no-op on a null handle, but the codegen-side rc_dec / drop-fn walks ABOVE them read bucket bytes off the handle at fixed offsets and would fault for `Map[K, shared V]`. The action now null-guards, mirroring the `BoxedEnumDrop` arm — which records the same flow-insensitivity reasoning, for the same reason, in its own comment.

A pointer enters the loop's result slot only against PROOF that ownership was taken (the `owned_ptr` flag), never as a type test. The LLVM type is an opaque `ptr` shared by every handle kind, so a Map and a `shared` struct are indistinguishable from the value alone; the cleanup queue is the only witness to which is which.

MEASURED on d9b5ea0: `loop { ...; let mut m = Map.new(); m.insert(f"k{i}", i*7); if i == 3 { break m } }` returns 21 from the interpreter and from an AOT binary, and is clean under ASAN with LeakSanitizer at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (27 allocations for the multi-iteration shape, no leak — so the two non-breaking iterations still free their own maps).
title: A `Map` / `Set` BREAK VALUE could not leave a loop on the compiled backends: `loop { ...; let mut m = Map.new(); ...; break m }` FAILED AT MODULE VERIFICATION while the interpreter returned it. Their cleanup is QUEUE-DRIVEN (`FreeMapHandle`, no in-slot sentinel), so the existing move suppressor retracts the queued action at COMPILE time -- flow-insensitive, and at a conditional `break` that would disarm the free on every NON-breaking iteration, leaking instead of double-freeing.

fix:
Fixed in ba5b136 (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs, tests/effectchecker.rs).

THE ROW'S BLOCKER WAS WRONG, and the correction is the useful part. This row
argued a chained receiver's type could only be recovered from the TYPECHECKER,
whose `Type::Function` carries no effect row (B-2026-08-23-11) -- so a recovered
return type would arrive with the `with` clause already erased, every chained
receiver would read as a PURE slot, and the check would become a
false-positive generator strictly worse than silence.

The typechecker was never needed. A callee's return type is an AST `TypeExpr`
-- the annotation its author WROTE, `with` clause intact -- sitting on the
declaration the effect checker already holds. `check_call_args_subtyping` has
been reading exactly that, four lines of `function_bodies.get(..).return_type`,
since long before this row was filed. Erasure happens at
`lower_type_expr_inner`, which this side of the compiler never goes through.

That is the same shape as B-2026-08-23-11's own dissolved blocker: a real
constraint on ONE route, mistaken for a constraint on the goal, because the
route already in the file was not checked.

New `callee_return_type` does the two-table lookup; `receiver_declared_type`
gains a `Call` arm (via `extract_callee_name`) and a `MethodCall` arm (via
`resolve_method_callee_key`). An UNDECLARED return type yields `None` and the
walk stops -- correct, since there is then no annotation to call a lie -- and a
generic return resolves to the unbound parameter and is a silent no-op, exactly
as a generic struct field is. Both pinned by tests.
title: A METHOD-CHAIN receiver's declared `Fn(..)` element slot is still unchecked: `hand_out().push(save)` carries the same slot as a bound `v.push(save)`, but the receiver's type is the callee's RETURN type rather than a written annotation, and the slot walk holds no return types. The last of the four receiver shapes B-2026-08-24-17 named; the other three (`self`/field, index, parameter) are closed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the remainder named in B-2026-08-24-17's detail, split out rather than buried in the closed row, per the live-remainder rule.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT FROM THE THREE THAT CLOSED. `receiver_declared_type` resolves a receiver to a type SOMEONE WROTE: a `let` annotation, a parameter's declared type, a struct field's declaration, or a container's element argument. Every one of those is a `TypeExpr` sitting in the AST. A call's result has no such thing at the call site -- the type is the CALLEE's return annotation, which means resolving the callee first. For a free function that is a `function_bodies` lookup and genuinely cheap; for a method it needs `resolve_method_callee_key`, and for a chain it needs the whole thing recursively, at which point the pass is doing type inference the typechecker already did and threw away.

THE HONEST ROUTE is probably not to rebuild it here but to read it off the typechecker's side tables, the way `check_call_args_subtyping` already reads `call_type_subs` and `method_callee_types`. That is blocked on the same thing B-2026-08-23-11 tracks: the typechecker's `Type::Function` carries NO EFFECT ROW, so a return type recovered from it would say `Fn(i64) -> i64` with the `with` clause already erased -- a PURE slot, no matter what was written. Recovering the type without the row would make every chained receiver look like a pure slot and turn this into a false-positive generator, which is strictly worse than the current silence.

SO: schedule this WITH B-2026-08-23-11's effect row, not before it. Until then the silence is deliberate and pinned by the all-clean test `the_new_receiver_shapes_do_not_over_fire`, so wiring it is a visible change to an assertion rather than a quiet widening.

SOUNDNESS UNCHANGED, as everywhere in this family: B-2026-08-23-7's mention rule makes the enclosing function declare the effect regardless. This is about diagnosing a lying ANNOTATION, not about letting an effect escape.

FIXED 2026-08-24, same day, and the row's recorded reasoning is RETRACTED --
see the fix field. Two things came out of it worth more than the fix.

THE PINNED TEST DID ITS JOB. B-2026-08-24-17 closed with
`the_new_receiver_shapes_do_not_over_fire` asserting this silence deliberately,
so that wiring it later would be "a visible change to an assertion rather than a
quiet widening". That is exactly what happened: the assertion failed the moment
the arm landed, and moving it into a positive test was the deliberate act the
pin was there to force. Worth repeating for the next deferral in this family --
pin the silence, and the flip announces itself.

THE TEST HARNESS WAS PARTLY VACUOUS, which is the bigger find. `slot_violations`
ran `parse` + `effectcheck` and nothing else. Two consequences, both invisible
while the code happened to handle the other spelling too:

  - `lower` never ran, so a `Vec`-annotated `[..]` initializer stayed an
    `ArrayLiteral` instead of becoming the `PrefixCollectionLiteral` production
    sees. That is the EXACT rewrite B-2026-08-24-11 was caught by -- so the
    tests guarding that fix were exercising the arm that was already working,
    not the one that had been broken.
  - `typecheck` never ran, so `method_callee_types` was empty and every check
    reached through `resolve_method_callee_key` silently found nothing. This
    surfaced here as a concrete failure: `r.part().push(save)` fired under
    `karac check` and stayed silent in the unit test, which is what exposed the
    gap.

The helper now runs parse -> resolve -> typecheck -> lower ->
effectcheck_with_typecheck_data, and EVERY slot test in the file was routed
through it. All 501 passed unchanged, so the fidelity cost nothing -- but "they
pass either way" was precisely the property that hid the hole. It does not
assert `typed.errors.is_empty()` on purpose: several cases are about the effect
checker's opinion of a program the typechecker also has opinions about, and
coupling them would make an unrelated type-error change fail this file.

FALSE-POSITIVE EVIDENCE, as for every row in this family: 1111 `.kara` files
swept with the final binary (917 kara-katas, 194 `examples/` +
`runtime/stdlib/`), zero new slot violations. Both clippy legs and `cargo fmt
--check` clean.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE. B-2026-08-23-11 stays exactly where its spike put it
-- a package-manager prerequisite. Nothing here needs the type row; it needs the
declaration's own annotation, which is a different object that happens to
describe the same function. The lesson is narrower than "the row is unblocked":
before deferring on a dependency, check whether the thing you actually need is
already in hand under another name.

fix:
FIXED by 54fcfd3, and the fix is much smaller than this row assumed — the whole change is to PERMIT the pointer store in `store_in_frame_at` and emit nothing extra.

AN RC'D VALUE MOVES OUT BY RETAIN, NOT BY SUPPRESSION. The IR of the working function-tail path — `fn f() -> Node { let n = ...; n }`, which has always compiled — settles it:

    %move.rc.load = load ptr, ptr %n
    %rc_inc = add i64 %rc, 1          ; retain at the move
    store i64 %rc_inc, ptr %rc_ptr2
    ...                                ; the source's queued RcDec STILL FIRES
    ret ptr %n1                        ; net +1, which the receiver releases

The source is not disarmed; a balancing `+1` is added against its still-live dec. That retain already lives inside `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` under the `apply_shared_transfer` flag, and `compile_break` has been calling that helper since B-2026-08-24-13. So the transfer was already correct at the break site; the only thing blocking it was `store_in_frame_at` refusing pointers.

THIS ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, and correcting it is the useful part. It recorded that "disarming the source is evidently NOT sufficient for an RC'd value" and listed three candidate causes. The real cause was ORDERING, and it was self-inflicted: the failed attempt's zero-store ran BEFORE the retain, so `move.rc.load` read null out of the slot and `emit_refcount_inc` incremented through it. That is the bus error, and the hang is the same write landing in malloc's bookkeeping. Nothing about RC semantics was the obstacle — two things written in the wrong order were.

The row's suggested remedy ("needs a matching RETAIN rather than a cap-zero") was directionally right for the wrong reason: no new retain was needed, only the removal of the zeroing that broke the existing one.

MAP AND `shared` NOW TAKE OPPOSITE TREATMENTS THROUGH THE SAME FUNCTION — Map/Set disarm by zeroing, `shared` deliberately does not — so both mechanisms and the reason they differ are written at `disarm_moved_handle_by_zeroing`. The trap that makes the wrong one look right is that `RcDec` is ALREADY null-guarded, for the unrelated case of a body-local slot whose `let` never ran.

STILL REFUSED, unchanged: an RVALUE source (`break Node { v: 11 }`) has no binding to retain against, exactly as `break Map.new()` has none to disarm. Both fail loudly at module verification rather than being half-supported.
title: A `shared` STRUCT OR ENUM BREAK VALUE cannot leave a loop on the compiled backends, and the OBVIOUS FIX MAKES IT WORSE: `loop { ...; let n = Node { v: i }; break n }` fails at module verification today (interpreter returns it), but disarming the source binding the way Map/Set now does -- which LOOKS correct, because `RcDec` is already null-guarded -- was MEASURED to HANG for a `shared struct` and to die with a BUS ERROR for a `shared enum`.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split from B-2026-08-24-19 at close time. That row fixed the `Map`/`Set` half (d9b5ea0) by disarming the source binding's queued cleanup with a RUNTIME zero-store, path-sensitively. The `shared` half is not the same problem and is filed here with the failed attempt recorded, because the attempt is the useful part.

THE TRAP, and it is a real one. `CleanupAction::RcDec` is ALREADY null-guarded (src/codegen/runtime.rs) — for an entirely unrelated reason: a body-local shared slot whose `let` never executed carries a null sentinel from `track_rc_var`, so the dec has always had to skip it. Reading that guard, extending `disarm_moved_handle_by_zeroing` to `shared` looks like adding one match arm next to the `FreeMapHandle` one. It compiles, it typechecks, and every `shared` fixture that previously failed loudly now builds.

MEASURED WITH THAT ARM IN PLACE, default opt level, on top of d9b5ea0:
  shared struct Node { v: i64 }
  fn pick() -> Node { let mut i = 0; loop { i = i + 1; let n = Node { v: i * 11 }; if i == 3 { break n } } }
      interp: 33    AOT: HANGS (killed at 8s, exit 124)
  shared enum Tree { Leaf(i64), Node(i64, i64) }
  fn pick() -> Tree { let mut i = 0; loop { i = i + 1; let t = Tree.Node(i, i * 2); if i == 2 { break t } } }
      interp: 6     AOT: Bus error (exit 135)
Both are memory corruption — strictly worse than the module-verification error they replaced — so the arm was reverted before landing. `shared` break values still take the skip path and still fail loudly, which is the correct state until this is understood.

WHAT IT MEANS, stated as the open question rather than a conclusion: disarming the source is sufficient for a Vec buffer (one owner, ownership moves) and for a Map handle (same), but NOT for an RC'd value. A `shared` binding holds a +1 that does not simply transfer by nulling the slot; something else — a retain on the breaking path, the receiving binding's release registration, or the per-iteration scope frame's interaction with the result slot — is also involved. WHICH of those was NOT diagnosed. Anyone picking this up should start by asking whether the receiving binding registers a release for a loop's value at all: if it does not, a retain alone converts the corruption into a leak rather than fixing it.

The same warning is duplicated in the `disarm_moved_handle_by_zeroing` doc comment, because the misleading part (RcDec's existing null guard) lives in the code, not in the ledger.

RVALUE SOURCES are a separate sub-case, untested here: `break Node { v: 11 }` has no binding to disarm at all, so whatever mechanism fixes the Identifier case may or may not cover it.

CORPUS IMPACT: none. The sweep during B-2026-08-24-10 found zero value-carrying `break`s anywhere in kara/ or kara-katas/.

VERIFIED on 54fcfd3. `shared struct` -> 33 and `shared enum` -> 6, byte-identical across `karac run --interp` and `karac build`; the Map/Set carriers from B-2026-08-24-19 still return 14 and 21. All clean under ASAN with LeakSanitizer at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (13 and 12 allocations).

BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE TESTED, which matters more for an RC change than for a buffer one: `asan_loop_break_shared_struct_releases_unbroken_iterations` allocates a `Node` on EVERY iteration and breaks on the third, so too few decs leaks the two that fell through and too many frees the one that escaped. Only LeakSanitizer catches the first, and only on Linux (CLAUDE.md: a green macOS asan run is silent about leaks).

The ASAN fixtures do NOT guard the compile path — `assert_clean_asan_run` skips when setup fails, so a regression to refusing aggregates would make them pass vacuously. The paired `tests/codegen.rs` round-trips are the loud half; `run_program` panics on a codegen failure. Both halves are needed and the pairing is noted in the fixture block.

fix:
FIXED by 9628ede. TWO INDEPENDENT ROOT CAUSES, not one -- the row filed a
single symptom with two faces, and each needed its own fix, both in
`src/ownership.rs`'s `record_rc_and_uam_witnesses`.

(1) DIFFERING WITNESS. `rc_witnesses` is a `HashMap` keyed by the CFG
builder's MANGLED name, and `demangle_binding` collapses two distinct
bindings in one function that share a spelling (`ename@arm1` /
`ename@arm2`, different scopes) onto one key. The `.insert` was
unconditional, so the survivor was whichever the per-process hash walk
reached last. Now keeps the FIRST witness in source order -- the rule the
UseAfterMove arm immediately below already applied, and the key
`emit_rc_fallback_notes` already sorts on.

(2) EMIT ORDER. `uam_witnesses` is likewise a `HashMap`, pushed into
`self.errors` in iteration order, so the warning SET was stable but the
SEQUENCE differed every run. Now sorted on the same key. This half was
INVISIBLE to the first measurement, which sorted before hashing and so saw
only a stable set; it took an unsorted diff to surface it.
title: `karac check` IS NOT DETERMINISTIC: the same binary on the same unchanged input emits a DIFFERENT rc-fallback diagnostic run to run. On runtime/stdlib/protobuf.kara the `ename` note cites `consume at 1630:59, other use at 1650:59` in some runs and `consume at 1750:57, other use at 1763:59` in others -- measured 9/11 and 11/9 over two 20-run batches of ONE binary. Diagnostic ORDER is unstable too: 200 differing lines across a 1111-file sweep of one binary against itself, same files and same exit codes throughout.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping the corpus to verify B-2026-08-23-13 changed nothing. The apparent old-vs-new diff turned out to reproduce on the PRE-FIX binary against itself, which is how the nondeterminism surfaced at all; -13 is not the cause and is not implicated.

NOT the language's Map/Set hasher, and NOT pinnable the usual way. `KARAC_HASH_SEED=7` does NOT stabilise it (7/5 split over 12 pinned runs) -- that variable seeds `karac-hash`, which is the hasher for the LANGUAGE's `Map`/`Set`. This is the COMPILER's own internals: ~140 files under src/ use `std::collections::HashMap`/`HashSet`, whose `RandomState` is seeded from the OS per process, so any diagnostic whose order or witness selection falls out of iterating one of those varies per run with no way to pin it.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED. Established: same binary, same input, two different diagnostic SETS at roughly even odds (not merely reordered -- runs emit exactly two rc-fallback notes and the second one's site flips between two candidates, so one whole note is present in one run and a different one in another); and separately, unstable ordering across the corpus. NOT established: whether generated CODE differs. Both variants promote the same binding `ename`, so the likely reading is that only the cited WITNESS varies, but that was not verified -- `ownership.rs` derives `use_after_move_consume_sites` (codegen's defensive-copy set) FROM the diagnostics, so a run-varying diagnostic set is exactly the shape that could reach codegen. Anyone picking this up should settle that FIRST, since it decides whether this is cosmetic or a reproducibility defect in the build.

WHERE TO LOOK: `src/ownership/rc_promote.rs`'s `emit_rc_fallback_notes`, and the `rc_values` / `arc_values` `HashMap`s it walks. Note the precedent in that exact function -- B-2026-08-14-34 leg B already fixed the sibling half of this (two notes coming out in either order) by flattening and SORTING before rendering, with a comment recording 16/4 over 20 runs. The ordering was fixed there; WHICH witness survives per (fn_key, binding) was not.

WHY IT MATTERS beyond tidiness: `--output=json` is what the Mend loop diffs (the same argument B-2026-08-14-34 made), and an expected-output test over any affected program is latently flaky -- it passes or fails on a coin flip, which is the failure mode hardest to attribute. The general class is wider than this one note: 140 files can leak per-process hash order into output.

FREQUENCY: one binding in the 1111-file corpus produces the differing-witness form; the ordering instability touched 200 lines across the same sweep.

CLOSED 2026-08-25 by 9628ede.

THE ROW'S OPEN QUESTION -- "whether generated CODE differs" -- IS SETTLED:
IT DOES NOT. Measured, not argued. `load_rc_fallback` (src/codegen.rs)
consumes only `rc_map.keys()`, i.e. the binding NAMES, and discards the
`RcEntry` spans; both colliding entries are named the same, so the key set
is identical whichever wins. Empirically: 20 builds of a program
exhibiting the flip produced ONE byte-identical binary while the note
variant moved 12/8 across the same runs (with a 12/8 split, the odds of 20
builds all hitting one variant are ~7e-5, so both variants demonstrably
produced the same output). The row named
`use_after_move_consume_sites` as the likely path to codegen; that set is
derived from the UseAfterMove ERRORS, not from the rc-fallback notes, and
is a `HashSet` of `(offset, length)` -- order-independent and stable. So
this was a diagnostics defect, correctly severity-medium, not a
build-reproducibility one.

MEASURED, before -> after:
  protobuf.kara rc-fallback note SETS, 40 runs   2 (11/9 split)  -> 1
  protobuf.kara UAM warning ORDERINGS, 15 runs   15              -> 1
  1232-file corpus, two sweeps of ONE binary     204 differing   -> 0 lines

REGRESSION TESTS (tests/ownership.rs), both confirmed NON-VACUOUS at
12/12 failures against reverted source:
  rc_fallback_witness_survives_deterministically_on_a_name_collision
    -- pre-fix kept the LATER witness, (11, 12) instead of (6, 7)
  use_after_move_warnings_are_emitted_in_source_order
    -- pre-fix offsets came out [220, 278, 104, 162], not sorted
The ordering test asserts ASCENDING OFFSETS rather than a fixed
permutation, so it pins the property (a reader scans top-down) without
pinning span arithmetic an unrelated parser change would shift.

VERIFIED: full `--features llvm` suite, 125 suites / 15107 tests, 0
failures; fmt; clippy on both feature legs.

CAUTION FOR THE NEXT SESSION, learned the hard way here and NOT a property
of this bug: an earlier full-suite run reported 3 codegen failures
(`test_e2e_loop_break_*_rvalue_round_trips`, a `ret i64 0` vs `ptr` module
verification error) that were an artifact of running `git fetch` / `rebase`
/ `push` WHILE the suite was compiling against the working tree -- the
rebase pulled a sibling session's commit in mid-run and the suite built a
mixed tree. Both controls cleared it (the three tests pass with this fix
applied AND reverted, 3/3 each way) and a re-run on a stable tree was
green at 125/15107. Do not mutate the working tree while a test run reads
it, and do not attribute a failure from such a run to either the local
change or the sibling commit without re-running clean.

title: The `--output=json` `mutual_recursion_groups` field still reports a VALUE-ONLY cycle as a mutual recursion group, the same false claim B-2026-08-23-13 fixed in the terminal note. Two functions that each stash the other in a struct field, neither calling the other, appear in that array under a name asserting they mutually recurse.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the deliberate remainder of B-2026-08-23-13. That row rewrote the NOTE to distinguish call cycles from function-as-value cycles; the JSON channel carries the same claim and was left alone on purpose.

WHY IT WAS NOT FOLDED IN. Narrowing the field's membership is a documented-contract change, not a wording fix. design.md 6374 names the field in the same sentence as the note; tests/effectchecker.rs pins it as "a separate promise" that stays populated even when `#[allow(mutual_recursion_note)]` suppresses the note, so a consumer may reasonably be reading it independently. Dropping value-only cycles from it would also LOSE true information -- that a fixed point was needed over that cycle at all, which is what the `resolution_trace` describes.

LIKELY FIX, and it needs a spec decision first: add a `kind` discriminator to `MutualRecursionGroup` ("mutual_recursion" | "value_reference_cycle"), which is ADDITIVE -- existing fields and existing consumers are untouched -- and add the corresponding sentence to design.md. The classification itself is already computed and free to reuse: `call_only_recursive_members()` in src/effectchecker/bounds.rs, added by -13. The work is the contract, not the analysis.

DOES NOT AFFECT: correctness of inference, the terminal note (fixed), or suppression.

FREQUENCY: requires two functions to mention each other as values; zero occurrences across the 1111-file corpus.

fix: FIXED by 0892679. An rvalue carrier needs NO ownership action -- only permission to store. `compile_break`'s `owned_ptr` now accepts a second proof beside the binding disarm: `break_value_is_fresh_owned_handle`, an ALLOWLIST of the two forms that manufacture ownership -- a `shared` struct literal (mallocs its own box, stores rc = 1) and a call / method call that is not declared to return a borrow (reusing `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, which already carves that exception out). `shared enum` variant construction parses as a call, so it arrives through the second arm. `store_in_frame_at`'s pointer gate is unchanged; only the supply of proofs grew.
title: An RVALUE `break` value that owns heap is still refused: `break Node { v: 11 }` (shared), `break Map.new()`, and `break f"x"` in a labeled-block TAIL position have no source BINDING to retain against or disarm, so they fail at module verification while the interpreter returns them. Loud, not silent -- but a spec-legal program that does not compile.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the remainder left by B-2026-08-24-13 (String/Vec), -19 (Map/Set) and -21 (shared). Each of those fixed the IDENTIFIER carrier, because every mechanism they use is keyed on a source binding: `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg` looks up a tracked variable, `disarm_moved_handle_by_zeroing` needs a slot to null, and the shared retain reads the handle back out of that slot. An rvalue has none of those.

MEASURED on 54fcfd3:
  shared struct Node { v: i64 }
  fn pick() -> Node { let mut i = 0; loop { i = i + 1; if i == 2 { break Node { v: i * 11 } } } }
      interp: 22    AOT/JIT: codegen failed: Module verification failed
  fn pick() -> Map[String, i64] { loop { ...; break Map.new() } }   -- same shape, not separately measured
The f-string case (`break f"x"`) is NOT in this row: it works, because `rhs_stages_fstr_acc` keys on the staged ACCUMULATOR rather than a binding. That is the hint for the fix — an rvalue's heap does have an owner, just not a named one.

WHY IT IS LOW: the workaround is to bind first (`let n = Node { … }; break n`), which is one line and arguably clearer; the failure is a compile error, not a wrong answer or a corruption; and a corpus sweep during B-2026-08-24-10 found zero value-carrying breaks anywhere in kara/ or kara-katas/, so nothing in-tree hits it.

LIKELY SHAPE OF THE FIX: an rvalue that owns heap is already a temporary with exactly one owner and (for `shared`) rc == 1, so it may need NO ownership action at all — only permission to enter the result slot. If so the work is finding the right predicate for "this value is a fresh temporary whose ownership transfers", not new emission. Verify against `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` rather than output alone; and note that permitting a pointer store without proof of ownership is exactly what the `owned_ptr` flag exists to prevent, so whatever predicate is chosen has to be as trustworthy as a binding lookup.
CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S SCOPE. It listed `break f"x"` as working and implied String/Vec rvalues were part of the remainder; measured, the STRUCT-typed carriers all already worked -- `break "hello"`, `break f"x{i}"` and `break [1, 2, i]` round-trip on every backend on 54fcfd3. They lower to a `{ptr, i64, i64}` header, which the slot has accepted since B-2026-08-24-13. The gap was exactly the HANDLE types, which lower to a bare pointer and so meet the `owned_ptr` gate: `shared struct`, `shared enum`, `Map` and `Set`. A regression test now pins the String/Vec half so the pointer-gate story is not mistaken for the whole story.

THE DIAGNOSIS CAME FROM THE `return` TWIN, not from reading the break path. `return Node { v: i * 11 }` in the same loop already compiled, and its IR is the entire argument: a `malloc`, a `store i64 1` into the refcount, and a bare `ret ptr` -- no retain, no dec, nothing queued in any cleanup frame. `return make_map(n)` is the same shape one level up (`%call = call ptr @make_map` then `ret ptr %call`). The temporary is born owned and the drain has nothing to say about it, so the row's "LIKELY SHAPE OF THE FIX" was right: permission, not emission.

THE PREDICATE IS AN ALLOWLIST BY CONSTRUCTION, which is the part worth defending. The tempting shape is a negative test -- "this is not obviously a borrow" -- and it is wrong, because the forms that must keep failing are PLACE reads: `break o.inner`, `break vs[0]`, `break self.head` hand out a handle the container still owns, with no retain behind it. Admitting one costs a use-after-free; refusing an unfamiliar form costs a compile error. `tests/codegen.rs::test_loop_break_borrowed_field_stays_refused` pins the borrowed-field refusal so a later simplification to the negative test fails a test rather than shipping.

MEASURED on this fix, all three backends agreeing: shared struct rvalue 22, shared enum rvalue 6, Map-via-call 14, Set-via-call true, call-returning-shared 22, and the three struct-typed carriers unchanged. Three ASAN fixtures cover it bidirectionally -- each allocates a scratch handle on EVERY iteration that the break path must still drain while carrying an unrelated one out, so too few decs leaks the scratches and too many frees what escaped. Verified non-vacuous by raising a `min_allocs` floor and watching it fail.

STILL REFUSED, and left open as B-2026-08-25-6: a BRANCHING carrier, `break if c { Node { v: 4 } } else { Node { v: 5 } }`. Each tail is a fresh temporary but the `If` itself is not, and widening the allowlist to branches needs an ALL-tails rule (one place-reading tail would be enough to make it unsound), which is a bigger claim than this row's evidence supports.

NOTE: a struct-literal `spread` (`Node { v: 42, ..base }`) needs no gate here -- the typechecker rejects it outright with E_STRUCT_LITERAL_SPREAD_UNSUPPORTED, so it never reaches codegen.

fix:
FIXED by d7bd8ac9 (body half; the layout half landed earlier in 77799b8). Calling a `std.cli` method now builds and runs. The row's own three-line repro -- `let a = Arg.string(); let b = a.required();` -- compiles, and a full builder chain plus `parse()` produces byte-identical output on all FOUR surfaces: `karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`, `karac run` (JIT), and `karac run --interp`.

THE GATE IS SEMANTIC, NOT SYNTACTIC, and the row's own plan for it was wrong. The previous detail block specified "a program-level expression walker" to detect cli CALLS, and named the absence of one as the blocker. Writing it would have been wasted work: a call is precisely the form that CANNOT be recognized from the AST. `p.parse()` names no type, and `p`'s type lives in the typechecker's tables, not in the tree. Any walk would have had to chase bindings back to their definitions -- reimplementing inference badly.

What the gate uses instead already existed. Every route to a cli value passes through a cli TYPE, because the module's only entry points are the associated fns `Parser.new` / `Arg.string` and every builder hop returns a cli-typed value. So "some expression in this program has a cli type" is IMPLIED BY "this program calls a cli method", which is all a gate needs. `TypeCheckResult.expr_types` already holds the inferred type of every expression, so `lower_program` folds the named-type heads onto a new `Program.referenced_type_names`, riding the same forward as the four tables it already hands codegen so codegen need not take a `TypeCheckResult` (`question_conversions`, `question_ok_payload_types`, `wp_result_types`, the callee-key table). No new walk, and no syntactic position can be missed as the grammar grows.

It OVER-approximates on purpose: a program that only NAMES `Parser` in a field or signature also compiles the bodies. That direction costs dead IR the linker strips (measured: a cli-using and a cli-free binary came out the same size, 336896 bytes); the opposite direction costs a failed build.

THE GATE IS REQUIRED, NOT PRECAUTIONARY -- measured, by registering cli unconditionally and running the suite. `test_ir_return_struct_field_vec_element_emits_clone` and `wrapping_arith_lowers_without_overflow_trap` BOTH FAIL that way, because cli's ~600 lines emit `karac_clone_String` calls and checked-overflow intrinsics into every module that compiles them. Unlike protobuf's, they are not rescued by the zero-use fixpoint prune: cli's parse loop and its helpers call each other, so no member of the group ever reaches zero uses. That is the same mutual-recursion argument `program_uses_protobuf` was written on.

`std.cli` is now in BOTH module lists and never in both at once: when the gate fires it is a fully compiled module carried by `compiled_stdlib_programs`, and `layout_only_stdlib_programs` returns empty so its layouts are not declared twice. Layouts stay unconditional either way -- the asymmetry the layout half was landed on (a missing layout is SILENT, a missing body is LOUD) is unchanged, and is why only the body half is gated at all.

NO STACK OVERFLOW. An earlier attempt at this row recorded a compiler stack overflow on registering cli, and a copy-support cycle guard as the suspected fix. Re-measured on current `main`: registering cli's bodies unconditionally builds clean, and both a cli-using and a cli-free program compile and run. Whatever produced that overflow was fixed by something else in the interim (8a04107's layout ordering is the likeliest candidate); no cycle-guard change was needed or made.

MEMORY. cli's bodies had NEVER been AOT-compiled before this commit, so every heap path in them is newly exercised machine code -- and this module already produced two memory-corruption rows (B-2026-08-25-15, a borrowed match payload double-freeing on the compiled side only; and B-2026-08-25-13's four borrowed-String-into-owned-field stores). `asan_stdlib_cli_builder_and_parse_are_clean` runs the builder chain, `parse()`, and `help_text()` three times under ASAN+LSan: clean. LSan was confirmed live on the host first with a deliberate 1234-byte C leak, which it reported -- a green ASAN run means nothing otherwise.

TESTS. `stdlib_cli_method_call_reports_the_uncompiled_body_gap` asserted the OPPOSITE of this fix (that the call failed loudly, naming the gap). It was correct for the layout-only state and is now false by construction, so it is REPLACED, not deleted quietly, by `stdlib_cli_method_call_compiles`. `stdlib_cli_bodies_stay_out_of_a_cli_free_program` asserts the gate's own decision by name -- the two IR-shape tests catch a widened gate only indirectly, through a missing clone call and a missing overflow trap. `e2e_stdlib_cli_parses_and_reports_end_to_end` deliberately ROUND-TRIPS String values back out, because this row's earlier probes gave false negatives when nothing read a field back.

VERIFICATION: llvm 15138 passed / 0 failed / rc 0 across 109 targets under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` (15135 baseline, minus 1 replaced test, plus 4 new = 15138, reconciled exactly); default leg green; clippy clean on both feature legs; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
title: `std.cli` IS NOT AOT-COMPILABLE: every pure-Kāra INSTANCE method on its types (`Arg.required`, `Parser.about`, ... ) dies in codegen with `no handler for method '<m>' on variable '<v>'`, so `karac check` passes and `karac build` fails -- while roadmap.md marks the feature `[x]` done and deferred.md ships it at v1
detail:
REPRODUCE, three lines, no subcommands needed:

    fn main() { let a = Arg.string(); let b = a.required(); println("ok"); }

`karac check` -> All checks passed. `karac build` -> `error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method 'required' on variable 'a' (method dispatch fell through; this is a codegen bug -- add a dispatch...)`. `karac run --interp` works. So the whole module is INTERPRETER-ONLY today.

THE SPLIT IS STATIC-vs-INSTANCE, and it is clean:

    Arg.string()      static/associated fn   BUILDS
    Parser.new(name)  static/associated fn   BUILDS
    a.required()      instance method        NO CODEGEN
    a.help(s)         instance method        NO CODEGEN
    p.about(s)        instance method        NO CODEGEN

IT IS NOT THE SIGNATURE SHAPE. A user-defined struct with the identical shape -- by-value `self` returning Self, including `Vec[Struct]` fields, the exact builder pattern `Parser` uses -- compiles and runs correctly. Three variants tested (String fields only / `Vec[i64]` field / `Vec[Struct]` field); all three build and print the right answer. So the defect is about these types, not about builder methods.

THE CONTRAST THAT NAMES THE CLASS: `Interner.intern` is a PRELUDE stdlib instance method and it builds fine -- because it carries `#[compiler_builtin]`, i.e. a codegen intrinsic. `std.cli`'s methods have no such hook, and cli.kara's own header states that as a design property: "Pure-Kāra implementation: methods are inferred through the impl-table dispatch path; no compiler intrinsic hooks are required for any of these methods." That claim holds for the INTERPRETER and is false for CODEGEN, which is the whole bug in one sentence.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and deliberately not claimed: whether this generalizes to EVERY pure-Kāra prelude instance method or is specific to `std.cli`'s types. The obvious second sample, `BufWriter`, is a placeholder stub (its bodies return `Err(IoError.Other("placeholder"))`), so it cannot discriminate. Whoever picks this up should determine the true blast radius first -- if it is the general case, this row is much bigger than std.cli.

WHY HIGH: the docs promise this feature as shipped. roadmap.md:531 marks the argument parser `[x]` under "`std.cli` (v66 graduation, 2026-05-11 -- P1 v1)", and deferred.md § std.cli says "Ship `std.cli` at v1 (P1, Phase 8 floor)" with the rationale that "a meaningful fraction of v1 user code will be CLI tools". A CLI tool is precisely the program a user AOT-compiles and ships as a binary, so the one execution mode this module needs is the one it does not have. The docs are corrected in the same commit as this row rather than left asserting a working feature.

SOURCE NOTE: found while auditing the FR4 chained-field-receiver deferral. `runtime/stdlib/cli.kara` was the ONLY file in the compiler's 194-file Kāra corpus to hit FR4 (6 read-only occurrences), which looked like evidence that FR4 blocked shipping code -- until building a program that uses std.cli showed it fails far earlier, on this. FR4 is not the binding constraint on std.cli; this is.

--- 2026-08-25 INVESTIGATION (row stays OPEN; see the four layers below) ---

BLAST RADIUS -- the question this row left explicitly open ("whether this generalizes to EVERY pure-Kara prelude instance method or is specific to std.cli's types") is now ANSWERED: it does NOT generalize. `std.cli` is the only baked module that fails, because three independent escape hatches cover everything else. Measured, all four AOT-built and run:
  volatile_cell  ambient, GENERIC type,  unregistered -> WORKS (prints 42)   monomorphization inlines the body into the user program
  binary_heap    ambient, GENERIC type,  unregistered -> WORKS               same
  autograd       GATED (`import std.autograd`), concrete -> WORKS (prints 3) import injects the items as user items
  ordering / process / protobuf / tracing  ambient, concrete, REGISTERED -> WORK
  cli            ambient, concrete, UNREGISTERED -> FAILS
So the failing class is "ambient prelude module + CONCRETE type + not in `compiled_stdlib_programs`", and `std.cli` is its only member. (`json`'s `to_json` is a TRAIT declaration, not an inherent impl -- an earlier count of it here was a regex artifact. `Option[Ordering].is_lt` is not reachable from user code: there is no `partial_cmp` on f64.)

FOUR LAYERS, each hiding the next. Registering cli in `compiled_stdlib_programs` (the "obvious fix" this row already warned about) peels them one at a time:
  1. cli absent from `compiled_stdlib_programs`  -> the reported "no handler for method".
  2. Registering it -> COMPILER STACK OVERFLOW, on `hello world`, not just on a cli program. Root-caused and FIXED separately: a MUTUAL type cycle through a `Vec` had no cycle guard (B-2026-07-28-3 guarded only the direct cycle). This is a general compiler crash on 6 lines of user code, reproduced on pristine main with no stdlib involved -- filed and fixed as its own row.
  3. With the emission terminating, cli.kara's OWN cycle is still fatal: `Parser.subcommands: Vec[Subcommand]` and `Subcommand.parser: Parser`. Declining the copy (the correct termination fix) leaves a by-value `Parser` param caller-retains, and own-by-transfer excludes self-referential structs by design (B-2026-08-05-33) -- so `Parser.parse(self)`, which moves fields out of `self`, SEGFAULTS where the interpreter prints "parsed".
     RECIPE (tried, works, deliberately NOT landed while this row is open): flatten `Subcommand` to `{ name, about_text, args, flags }` and build it from the sub-parser's fields in `Parser.subcommand`. The cycle buys nothing -- v1 is one level of subcommand depth, the nested Parser's own `subcommands` are never read, and `SubcommandResult` is already flat for exactly this reason. Only `.args` / `.flags` / `.about_text` are ever read off it (grep `.parser` in cli.kara). With the flattening, `p.parse()` on the FULL builder surface (about / version / arg / flag / subcommand / required-arg checking) builds AND runs correctly.
  4. TWO DEFECTS REMAIN behind that, and they are why this row is not closed:
     (a) A user fn whose declared return type is a baked stdlib struct gets an `i64` signature: `fn build() -> Parser { ... }` fails module verification with "Function return type does not match operand type of return inst". NOT cli-specific and NOT new -- `fn mk() -> Command` (process) and `fn mk() -> Regex` (regex) fail identically on today's main, and both modules have been registered for months. Mechanism, from the source: stdlib struct layouts are declared at src/codegen.rs:7512 (`for tp in compiled_stdlib_programs`), but user FREE-FN signatures at src/codegen.rs:7289 -- earlier -- so the return type resolves against an empty `struct_types` and falls back to i64. A CLI tool's natural shape is a `build_parser()` helper, so this blocks the feature even once cli compiles.
     (b) Destructuring `Ok(a)` where `a` is cli's `Args` SEGFAULTS under AOT while the interpreter prints correctly. `let r = p.parse();` alone is fine; entering the `Ok(a)` arm is what crashes. `Args` carries `sub: Option[SubcommandResult]`. Not yet root-caused.

WHY THE REGISTRATION WAS NOT LANDED: with (a) and (b) live, registering cli trades a LOUD compile-time "no handler for method" for a SILENT segfault at runtime. That is strictly worse for a user, so the registration, and the cli.kara flattening that only matters alongside it, are held until (a) and (b) are fixed. The flattening was additionally not landable on its own: `karac`'s own CLI consumes `--help` / `--name` before the program sees them, so the module's INTERPRETED behaviour -- the one mode std.cli works in today -- could not be A/B'd end to end.

--- 2026-08-25 UPDATE 2 (8a04107); row STAYS OPEN, now blocked on B-2026-08-25-12 ---

DEFECT (a) FROM THE PREVIOUS UPDATE IS FIXED (8a04107) and was BROADER than that update said. Baked stdlib LAYOUTS were declared after the user's layout + signature passes, so any user item NAMING a stdlib struct resolved against a `struct_types` the module was not in yet and took `llvm_type_for_name`'s silent `i64` fall-through. The previous update recorded only the return-type shape; a user struct FIELD is equally affected -- `struct Holder { c: Command }` laid the field out AS `i64`, making the struct `{ i64, i64 }` and its literal's `insertvalue` invalid -- which is why the fix hoists the layout pass ahead of `build_struct_types`, not merely ahead of signatures. Pinned by two E2E tests; `run_program` panics on codegen failure, so neither can pass vacuously.

DEFECT (b) IS ROOT-CAUSED, AND THE PREVIOUS UPDATE'S CHARACTERISATION OF IT WAS WRONG ON BOTH COUNTS. It is not the `Ok(a)` destructure as such, and `Option[SubcommandResult]` is irrelevant. Filed as B-2026-08-25-12: a `match` on a `Result` whose Ok payload is a struct carrying THREE OR MORE `Vec` fields segfaults the compiled binary. Reduced to 10 lines of ordinary user code with NO stdlib involvement and confirmed on PRISTINE main, so it is neither cli-specific nor caused by this session's work. The threshold is sharp (1-2 Vecs pass, 3-4 fault, with and without a trailing Option), and `let r = s.go()` on the identical program is clean. `Args` carries exactly three Vecs, which is the whole reason `match p.parse()` faults.

A THIRD, SEPARATE DEFECT WAS FOUND AND FIXED IN 8a04107: cli.kara stored a BORROWED `String` into an owned `String` field at four sites (`val` / `token` bound out of an `Option` by `argv.get(i)` is a `ref String`). User code cannot compile that; the baked copy could, because `lower_stdlib_source` discards its typecheck errors -- filed as B-2026-08-25-13. Codegen moved the borrowed buffer into the new owner, so a compiled `parse()` DOUBLE-FREED (`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`) as soon as a `--name value` pair was actually parsed, while the interpreter stayed correct. Cloning at the four sites fixes it, verified by running the compiled parser across the argv matrix.

cli.kara IS NOW `karac check` CLEAN (0 errors): the 4 type errors above, plus the 6 `chained_field_receiver` FR4 lint errors that the `Parser`/`Subcommand` flattening removes. The flattening landed as prerequisite work; it is behaviour-preserving under the interpreter (verified across the argv matrix, byte-identical before and after).

REGISTRATION IS STILL NOT LANDED, for the reason this row already gave, now attached to a different blocker. It was implemented and measured: with cli registered, the full builder surface compiles and `p.parse()` runs -- but `match p.parse() { Ok(a) => .. }` segfaults via B-2026-08-25-12, so registering would still trade a LOUD "no handler for method" compile error for a SILENT segfault. cli AOT behaviour is therefore unchanged from main. THIS ROW CLOSES when B-2026-08-25-12 is fixed and the registration can land behind it; the flattening it needs is already in.

--- 2026-08-25 UPDATE 3 (443a902); row STAYS OPEN, blocker moves to B-2026-08-25-15 ---

B-2026-08-25-12 IS FIXED (443a902), and with it the `match p.parse() { Ok(a) => .. }` segfault is gone. Registering `std.cli` was then re-attempted and MEASURED end to end: the entire builder surface compiles and runs under `karac build` and matches the interpreter — `Arg.string().required()` (this row's original three-line repro), a `fn build() -> Parser` helper, `Parser.new(..).about(..).version(..).flag(..).arg(..).subcommand(..)`, and the `Ok(a)` destructure. `hello world` is unaffected.

ONE PATH STILL CORRUPTS, so the registration is again NOT landed: `args.get_string(name)` double-frees when the argument was actually supplied — a 2-byte `karac_string_clone` buffer freed twice, both frees in `main`, under ASAN. `parse()` alone is CLEAN under ASAN with the same argv, so the trigger is `get_string`'s `return Ok(pv.value)` — a `String` field read out of a BORROWED payload and returned as owned. Filed as B-2026-08-25-15 with the ASAN report and four failed reduction attempts recorded.

The standard is unchanged from every earlier stage of this row: registering today would hand a user a CLI parser that silently corrupts the heap the first time an argument is read back, which is strictly worse than the loud "no handler for method" compile error they get now. The registration diff is one `LazyLock` plus one `compiled_stdlib_programs` entry — trivially re-applied once B-2026-08-25-15 closes, which is now the ONLY thing between this row and done.

--- 2026-08-25 UPDATE 4: the get_string double free is FIXED in cli.kara, and REGISTRATION IS MEASURED TO NEED A CONDITIONAL GATE ---

WITH B-2026-08-25-15's three sites cloned in cli.kara (`get_string` on `Args` and on `SubcommandResult`, plus `subcommand_name`'s `Some(s.name)`), `std.cli` compiles AND RUNS CORRECTLY under `karac build`, memory-clean. Measured with the registration applied locally, every case byte-identical to the interpreter:
  - the builder surface (`about` / `version` / `flag` / `arg` / `subcommand`), `Arg.string().required()`, and a `fn build() -> Parser` helper;
  - `match p.parse() { Ok(a) => .. }`, `get_string`, `get_flag`, `subcommand_name`, positionals, and the `--help` / `--version` / error paths;
  - ASAN with LSan LEFT ON (no `detect_leaks=0`): clean, exit 0, on the argv matrix including `--name x` and `add --file f.txt` — the exact inputs that previously double-freed.

BUT UNCONDITIONAL REGISTRATION BREAKS TWO STRUCTURAL TESTS, and they are right to break. Both assert the ABSENCE of something in a program's pre-optimization IR, and registering `cli` compiles cli.kara's bodies into EVERY module:
  - `test_ir_return_struct_field_vec_element_emits_clone` — asserts a `Vec[i64]`-only program emits NO `karac_clone_String`. cli's String handling emits one.
  - `wrapping_arith_lowers_without_overflow_trap` — asserts no checked-overflow intrinsic. cli's `i = i + 1` emits one.
Relaxing either guard to accommodate the registration would be the wrong trade: they are flagging real pollution. `cli.kara` is ~600 lines that every user's compile would now carry through codegen, and the "always present" modules (`ordering`, `mem`) are tiny ones whose bodies prune to nothing.

SO THE REGISTRATION MUST BE CONDITIONAL, exactly like `protobuf` (`program_uses_protobuf` exists for precisely this reason — a module that "can't rely on the prune"). The remaining work is a `program_uses_cli(user: &Program)` detector, and there is ONE non-obvious requirement:

    The detector MUST fire on a TYPE reference, not only on a call. `compiled_stdlib_programs` is consumed by the hoisted LAYOUT pass as well as the declare/compile passes (the fix for this row's defect (a), 8a04107), so a program with `fn build() -> Parser` and no `Parser.new` call still needs cli's layouts — without them the return type resolves against an empty `struct_types` and silently lowers to `i64`, which is the very bug that fix closed.

Over-inclusion is safe (it only registers a module that then prunes); under-inclusion silently reintroduces either "no handler for method" or the `i64` layout bug. `src/codegen/consume_class.rs`'s `walk_exprs` is the existing expression walker to build on; the type side needs its own pass over signatures, `let` annotations and struct fields.

THE REGISTRATION IS THEREFORE STILL NOT LANDED, for the third distinct reason in this row's history — but note the reason has changed CATEGORY: it is no longer a correctness blocker (no crash, no corruption, ASAN/LSan clean), only a scoping one. What remains is a bounded, well-specified piece of work, and the cli.kara half of it is landed and independently correct.

--- 2026-08-25 THE CORRECTNESS BLOCKER IS CLEARED; WHAT REMAINS IS SCOPING ---

B-2026-08-25-15 — the borrow-payload double free that `get_string` tripped — is FIXED in 55f16cb, at the compiler rather than in cli.kara. That matters for this row in two ways.

First, the whole `std.cli` surface is now AOT-correct on its own terms: builder, parse, get_string, get_flag, subcommand_name, and the help/version/error paths all match the interpreter byte-for-byte and run ASAN/LSan-clean.

Second, it removed a hidden hazard this row would otherwise have shipped. `runtime/stdlib/cli.kara` has FIVE instances of that shape, not the three 427f899 hand-cloned: `flags_set.push(fentry.name)` and `sub_flags_set.push(fentry.name)` inside `fn parse(ref self)` are on the FLAG path, which no earlier ASAN run exercised. Registering cli before the compiler fix would have shipped two live double frees. The three explicit `.clone()`s are now redundant (harmless — a `.clone()` receiver is a MethodCall, not a FieldAccess, so the copier declines and there is no double copy); removing them belongs to this row's slice, where cli can finally be AOT-tested directly instead of through a mirror program.

SO THE ONLY REMAINING WORK IS THE USAGE GATE, unchanged from the entry above: a `protobuf`-style `program_uses_cli(user: &Program)` in `compiled_stdlib_programs`, because unconditional registration compiles cli's ~600 lines into every module and breaks two structural guards (a `Vec[i64]` program must emit no `karac_clone_String`; a `wrapping_*` program must emit no checked-overflow intrinsic). Those guards are correct; the gate is what makes them stay true. The detector MUST fire on a TYPE reference and not only on a call — `fn build() -> Parser` with no `Parser.new` call still needs cli's layouts, because the layout hoist consumes the same list, and without them the return type resolves against an empty `struct_types` and silently lowers to `i64` (the bug 8a04107 closed).
--- 2026-08-25 THE LAYOUT HALF IS LANDED; THE ROW STAYS OPEN ON THE BODY HALF ---

THE PLAN IN THE ENTRY ABOVE — one `program_uses_cli` detector gating all four registration passes — IS SUPERSEDED, because measuring the two halves showed they have OPPOSITE failure modes and only one of them is safe to gate:

  LAYOUTS.  A missing layout is SILENT. `llvm_type_for_name` falls through to `i64`, so `fn mk() -> Parser` takes an `i64` signature while its body stores a real six-field struct; the damage surfaces far from the cause as a module verification failure, or not at all. Gating layouts on a syntactic detector means a detector MISS IS THE MISCOMPILE — and any AST-walk detector is an approximation. Layouts declare types and emit no IR, so carrying an unused module's layouts costs nothing; that is the same argument `regex` and `mem` already ship on. They are now UNCONDITIONAL, via a new `layout_only_stdlib_programs()` list consumed by the layout hoist alongside `compiled_stdlib_programs`.

  BODIES.  A missing body is LOUD — the call fails at dispatch or at link. That half can be gated, and must be: cli's ~600 lines are real Kāra whose bodies emit `karac_clone_String` calls and checked-overflow intrinsics into every module that compiles them, which is what broke `test_ir_return_struct_field_vec_element_emits_clone` and `wrapping_arith_lowers_without_overflow_trap` when unconditional registration was tried.

So the `i64` hazard is now closed BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by the accuracy of a detector, and the detector is needed only where a miss is loud.

MEASURED, by stashing the change and rebuilding:

    struct Holder { p: Parser, n: i64 }
    fn mk(nm: String) -> Parser { return Parser { program_name: nm, ... }; }
    fn name_of(h: Holder) -> String { return h.p.program_name; }

  BEFORE: `karac check` -> All checks passed; `karac build` -> `codegen: cannot resolve field 'program_name' on this receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen)`; `--interp` correct.
  AFTER:  builds, and `demo/abt/1.0` is byte-identical across `--interp`, `karac build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`.

A FALSE-NEGATIVE TRAP, recorded because two probes fell into it before the real one was written: a program that NAMES `Parser` but never reads a field back builds and prints correctly EVEN AGAINST THE BROKEN COMPILER. Every reference is `i64`-wide and consistently so, so the collapse is unobservable — the same shape as B-2026-08-25-15's string-literal trap. Any repro for this class MUST round-trip a field's value.

ONE DELIBERATE REGRESSION, from silent-wrong to loud. A program CALLING a cli associated fn (`Parser.new(..)`) previously built and ran: the call took `compile_assoc_call`'s last-resort `i64 0`, `mk()` was declared `-> i64`, and the whole chain was consistently `i64`-wide, so it silently produced a binary holding a fake, empty `Parser`. With the layout registered those widths no longer agree, so it would now fail module verification hundreds of lines from the cause. Rather than leave that, the dispatcher's fall-through now reports the real gap for any type in a layout-only module:

    error: codegen failed: codegen: `Arg.string` is not compiled — `std.cli`'s type
    layouts are registered but its method bodies are not, so only programs that NAME
    its types (fields, signatures, bindings) build today. Run with `--interp` (or
    `KARAC_RUN_JIT=0`); tracked as B-2026-08-25-2.

The `i64 0` default itself is UNCHANGED for every unrecognized name — the guard keys on `layout_only_stdlib_type_names()`, derived from the layout-only programs' own items, so it cannot affect a type it does not own.

WHAT REMAINS, and it is this row's headline: CALLING a `std.cli` method still does not build. The body half needs (a) a usage gate over the user program and (b) the three body-compiling passes wired behind it. The gate's detector only has to catch CALLS — layouts being unconditional means a type mention needs nothing — and a miss is the loud error above rather than a miscompile. The blocker is that no program-level expression walker exists today: `walk_exprs` (src/codegen/consume_class.rs) covers a single expression tree and is private, with no statement/block/item driver, and `span_visitor.rs` walks the whole program but yields only `Span`s, not names. Writing that driver is the next slice.

REGRESSION PINS: `e2e_stdlib_cli_type_named_but_uncalled_lowers_at_real_layout` (reads three fields back, so the collapse is observable) and `stdlib_cli_method_call_reports_the_uncompiled_body_gap` (asserts the error names both the call and this row), both in tests/codegen.rs.

  end-to-end          : 5,300 guard-test iterations x 6 programs = 31,800

CANDIDATE (b) IS THEREFORE REFUTED AT ITS PREMISE on this architecture, not
merely rate-bounded. It decomposes into (b1) "codegen sometimes emits no check"
-- contradicted by 415/415 byte-identical artifacts -- and (b2) "the check is
emitted but sometimes does not fire" -- contradicted by 20,000/20,000 exit 101.

A REAL COVERAGE HOLE IN THE GUARD ITSELF, found on the way and now closed. The
E2E guard `vec_mutation_methods_bounds_check_out_of_range_index` DOES NOT
EXERCISE A RUNTIME BOUNDS CHECK. Its indices are LITERALS on a Vec whose length
is provable, so LLVM settles the comparison at compile time. Measured:
`v.insert(7i64, ...)` emits an unconditional panic and DELETES the
`println("survived")` fall-through -- the string is absent from the binary --
while `v.insert(1i64, ...)` drops the panic message entirely. The test's
`!stdout.contains("survived")` assertion is thus discharged by dead-code
elimination, not by a check firing. This surfaced as two DIFFERENT out-of-range
literals compiling to BYTE-IDENTICAL binaries (`insert(7)` and `insert(3)`,
identical SHA-256), which was initially mistaken for a broken determinism
detector. The structural guard
`vec_mutation_bounds_checks_survive_into_emitted_object` keeps its index opaque
but asserts only PRESENCE in the object, and its index (`env.args().len()`, a
stable 1) is IN RANGE -- so it never fires either. Nothing covered the case real
code actually hits: an index computed at run time that turns out to be out of
range. Verified by hand across all three backends (`(env.args().len() as i64) +
6i64` against a length of 2 panics with exit 101 under --interp, JIT and AOT
alike) and now pinned by
`codegen_tests::vec_mutation_bounds_check_fires_for_a_runtime_opaque_index`.

STRUCTURAL GUARD FOR THE DETERMINISM PROPERTY, in the same spirit as this row's
`..._survive_into_emitted_object`: sampling bounds a rate, an assertion removes
the question. `cli::build_output_is_byte_reproducible_across_processes` builds
one source TWICE IN TWO PROCESSES and asserts the artifacts are byte-identical,
then rewrites the same file with one changed index and asserts the bytes move.
It covers a bug class wider than this row -- nondeterministic emission order,
the classic HashMap-iteration leak -- which no existing test covered (the repo's
other "determinism" tests pin diagnostic ties, cache keys and render order, not
emitted artifacts). MUTATION-TESTED, and the first attempt was a FALSE PASS
worth recording: mutating the second build to `insert(3i64, ...)` left the test
green, because another out-of-range literal folds to the same unconditional
panic. Only an IN-RANGE index (`insert(1i64, ...)`) is a real mutation; it fails
with "artifacts of different SIZE (345312 vs 345352 bytes)".

WHAT IS PROVEN AND WHAT IS NOT, stated separately on purpose. Proven: on x86_64
at this commit, codegen is byte-reproducible for this program and the emitted
check fires deterministically, including for a run-time-opaque index. NOT
proven: that the leaked-artifact exec (candidate (a)) produced the ONE observed
