fix:
FIXED by 803d173, BY NARROWING THE SPEC, and the row's own gating question is what decided it. It asked, correctly, that supersession be settled BEFORE implementing. It is settled: `Box` / `Rc` / `Arc` are superseded, and the evidence is the compiler's own teaching rather than an inference from absence.

MEASURED on 363d579, one program per claim:
  * All six constructors and all three type positions fail at resolve, as filed
    (`undefined name 'Box'`, `undefined type 'Rc'`, ...).
  * `shared struct Node { value: i64 }` + `let b = a;` leaves BOTH `a` and `b`
    readable -- reference semantics with RC, no move error. So the `Rc` use case
    is covered under another spelling, which is exactly what the row said it had
    not measured.
  * `par struct Shared { value: i64 }` constructs and reads back. That is the
    `Arc` use case -- design.md § item 61 already calls `par struct` the
    language-level "this type crosses tasks" marker.
  * A self-referential `enum Tree { Leaf(i64), Node(Tree, Tree) }` is rejected
    with a diagnostic that NAMES THE REPLACEMENTS: "either flatten the variant,
    mark the inner enum as `shared` (RC pointer) or `par` (cross-task pointer --
    use this one if the value must cross a task boundary), or wrap it in a
    `Vec` / collection layer". The compiler already teaches Kara's indirection
    vocabulary at the exact moment a user would reach for `Box`.

THE STRUCTURAL REASON THERE IS NOTHING TO IMPLEMENT: in Kara, indirection is a property of the TYPE DECLARATION (`shared` / `par` keywords) rather than a wrapper applied at each use site. So there is no per-allocation constructor for the fallible-allocation table to give a `try_` twin to -- which is why that table now has no row for them rather than a row marked "not yet".

CORRECTED IN design.md: the fallible-allocation table's `Box[T] / Rc[T] / Arc[T] | new(t) | try_new(t)` row (deleted, with a note recording why there is no row rather than a deferred one); the `Box[=T]` variance-table row; `Box.new` / `Rc.new` / `Arc.new` in the alloc-bearing-method list, the indirect-allocator rejection list, and the `panic_on_alloc_failure` list. `karac check` on every fenced `kara` block still passes (`scripts/design-conformance.py --check`).

THE `par { }` ESCAPE LIST WAS WORSE THAN THE ROW KNEW, and this is the part worth reading. The row flagged one site naming `Arc[shared struct S]`. There are THREE (design.md:1339, :1341, :1463), and each also named `RwLock[T]` -- which does not exist either (`undefined type 'RwLock'`, no stdlib file, no `PRELUDE_TYPES` entry; the only `RwLock` text in the tree is Rust-side comments describing the runtime's internal `Arc<RwLock<...>>` storage). The compiler's own `par { }` ERROR was already accurate ("wrap in Atomic[T], Mutex[T], or use #[thread_local]"); it was the prose that had drifted. All three lists now match the diagnostic.

A THIRD ABSENT NAME IN THE SAME LISTS turned out to be a live defect rather than doc drift, and is split to B-2026-08-26-3 rather than buried here: `LazyLock[T]` PASSES `karac check` and then fails on every execution backend, and the `module_mut_binding` warning was recommending it by name.

NOT DONE, and deliberately left for an owner call rather than decided here: roughly nine further `Box[T]` / `Rc[T]` / `Arc[T]` mentions remain in design.md, all of them CONCEPTUAL rather than promises of API -- Rust's vocabulary used as shorthand while explaining a concept (the cross-task-safe closed enumeration at :3605 and :9084, the `!Send` examples at :9828 and :9838, `Clone` shallow-vs-deep semantics at :8994 and :9011, cancellation-safety at :9457, the RC-flavor note at :178). title: The ENTIRE `Box` / `Rc` / `Arc` smart-pointer family is UNDEFINED -- all six of `Box.new`, `Box.try_new`, `Rc.new`, `Rc.try_new`, `Arc.new`, `Arc.try_new` fail at RESOLVE with `undefined name`, and `Box[T]` in type position is `undefined type 'Box', did you mean 'Hex'?`. design.md carries them in three separate places as shipped surface: § Type Inference's variance table has `Box[=T] | invariant | Owned heap pointer; consuming `Box[T]` yields `T`...`; § Fallible Allocation's table has the row `Box[T] / Rc[T] / Arc[T] | new(t) | try_new(t)`; and § Fallible Allocation's indirect-allocator rules name `every `Box.new(...)` literal` as one of the sites that must be rejected under a no-panic profile. `Arc` is additionally LOAD-BEARING FOR A DOCUMENTED CONCURRENCY RULE -- § Module-Level Bindings says a `let mut` binding may be written from inside `par { }` only when its type is `Atomic[T]`, `Mutex[T]`, `RwLock[T]`, or `Arc[shared struct S]`, so one of the four sanctioned escapes cannot be spelled.
detail:
Probe: domain-24 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d24/{bx,t2}.kara -- the six constructor forms enumerated one per compile.

THE NAME IS KNOWN TO THE IMPLEMENTATION BUT NOT BOUND: `"Box"` appears in src/ownership_oracle.rs:321 (alongside String / Vec / Map / Set / VecDeque / Slice / Rc / Arc in a heap-type list), src/typechecker/env_build.rs:855 (a comment about `impl[T] Box[T]`) and src/typechecker/derives.rs:1561. So downstream phases are written to expect these types; nothing declares them.

DID NOT MEASURE whether an equivalent exists under another spelling -- `shared struct` covers the RC use case in Kara's ownership model, so it is possible `Box`/`Rc`/`Arc` were superseded by design and the spec text is the stale half. That is the first thing to settle before implementing: if they are superseded, three doc sites need correcting (including the `par { }` escape list, which would then name a type the language does not have); if they are not, this is a missing prelude family.

fix:
FIXED by 2242d1c (the Vec half; the remainder is split out to B-2026-08-26-22 rather than left buried here).

LANDED: `Vec.capacity()`, `Vec.reserve(n)`, `Vec.reserve_exact(n)`, `Vec.resize(n, val)`, `Vec.append(other)` across typecheck + interpreter + codegen, plus the `Vec.try_reserve` / `Vec.try_reserve_exact` companions with real `karac_alloc_fallible` lowering. Every one verified on BOTH backends against the interpreter as oracle, not against a hardcoded string.

THE ROW'S OWN CORRECTION WAS RIGHT AND IS WHAT MADE THIS TRACTABLE: the missing half was the PANICKING BASE, not the companion layer. `src/fallible_alloc.rs` derives every `try_X` by recursing into `X` for argument validation and return-type synthesis, so `try_reserve` could not exist until `reserve` did. Registering the two companions afterward was a two-line edit to `TRY_ALLOC_INSTANCE_BASES` plus one codegen arm — the deferral rule in that module working exactly as written rather than an exception to it. Its header no longer lists `Vec.reserve`/`Vec.reserve_exact` as deferred, and now says why `Box.new`/`Rc.new` will never join the list at all (B-2026-08-25-19: Kara spells heap indirection with `shared`/`par` type declarations, so there is no per-allocation constructor to twin).

`capacity()` LANDED WITH THE FAMILY, on the row's own recommendation, because without it `reserve` is unobservable from Kara and no test can tell `v.reserve(1000)` from a no-op.

WHAT `capacity()` MEANS, decided rather than inherited, and written into design.md's Vec table: it is a LOWER-BOUND query, not an allocator promise. Guaranteed `capacity() >= len()`, and `capacity() >= len() + n` after `reserve(n)`; the exact value is Reported behavior. The two backends genuinely differ — the interpreter grows a host `Vec<Value>` on Rust's policy, codegen grows on `max(4, cap * 2)` — so twinning the NUMBER would have meant either pinning something neither backend promises or hand-rolling codegen's growth curve inside the interpreter to make a promise nobody asked for. Every test therefore asserts `>=`. This is a deliberate exception to the byte-identical-twins rule the Arrow IPC and `String.normalize` surfaces follow, and the reason is that those twin an OUTPUT while this reports an allocator detail.

TWO SEMANTIC CHOICES design.md left open, both now documented in its Vec table:
  * `reserve(additional)` takes Rust's argument convention — room for that many MORE elements, not a target capacity. The surrounding names (`reserve_exact`, `resize`, `append`) are already Rust spellings, so matching the convention avoids a surface where the names are Rust's and the meanings are not. Non-positive is a no-op, matching `truncate`'s clamp.
  * `append(other)` takes its source BY VALUE, unlike Rust's `&mut Vec<T>`. Kara call sites never write `mut` on a method argument (design.md Feature 4 Part 1.5), so a borrow-and-drain spelling would leave `other` silently emptied with nothing at the call site to say so. Consuming it makes the transfer an ordinary move, and using the source afterward becomes the ordinary use-after-move error.

THE BUG I INTRODUCED AND CAUGHT, worth recording because the fixture that guards it had to move files to be real. Landing `resize`/`append` WITHOUT seeding them receiver-mutating in `effectchecker.rs` made an `a.append(b)` LATER in a body corrupt an EARLIER `v[4]` read on an UNRELATED Vec -- `vec index out of bounds` at -O2, because `method_effects_imply_receiver_mutation` saw `append` as read-only and the auto-parallelizer co-grouped the statements around a stale `{ptr,len,cap}` branch-capture header. That is the standing B-2026-07-14-17 rule ("every builtin in-place mutator must be seeded or the auto-par gate silently races it") collecting a fourth victim. Seeded, and `Vec.append` added to `ownership.rs`'s MutRef receiver table beside `Vec.resize`.

THE FIXTURE FOR IT LIVES IN `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`, NOT `tests/codegen.rs`, AND THAT MATTERS BEYOND THIS ROW: `run_program_capturing` passes `None` for the concurrency analysis, so auto-par NEVER RUNS under the codegen E2E harness and no fixture there can catch this class. The first draft of the guard was written in that file and passed against the unseeded compiler -- measured, then moved. The ASAN harness passes `Some(&analysis)`, so it sees what `karac build` sees; the moved fixture was then verified RED with the seed removed and green with it restored.

DELIBERATELY NOT LANDED, and NOT half-landed: `try_resize` / `try_append` are absent rather than registered-without-codegen. Adding a name to `TRY_ALLOC_INSTANCE_BASES` without a matching `CODEGEN_FALLIBLE_INSTANCE_BASES` entry produces a method that passes `karac check` and fails `karac build` -- the run-vs-build shape -- and this change declined to add two new instances of it. `String.reserve`, `Map.reserve` and `Vec.from_iter` have no base at all. All five re-measured one-per-compile on the closing commit and carried into the follow-up row with their exact diagnostics.

TESTS: 6 in `tests/interpreter.rs` (reserve/reserve_exact/resize/append/heap-element resize/try_* derivation), 2 twin comparisons in `tests/codegen.rs` driven off `run_program_full` as oracle, 3 in `tests/typechecker.rs` (accepted signatures; arity and element-type rejections for all five methods), and the auto-par ASAN guard above.

SEPARATELY, the same section specifies "The `Display` formatting names the failed operation's byte size on the `OutOfMemory` arm and \"capacity overflow\" on the `CapacityOverflow` arm" -- measured, `f"{e}"` renders `CapacityOverflow` and `OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: 4096 }`, which is the DEBUG form for both arms.

THE SURFACE THAT EXISTS IS CORRECT, which is what makes the gaps worth naming rather than the feature immature: `Vec.try_with_capacity(1024)? + try_push(42)?` runs clean end to end and the `AllocError` enum has exactly the two specified variants with the specified payload (`OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: usize }`, `CapacityOverflow`), reachable from the prelude with no import as the spec requires.

THE DISPLAY LEG IS THE MORE LIKELY TO BITE: `AllocError` is an error type, so its `Display` is what reaches users through `main() -> Result[(), E: Display]`'s `Error: {e}` line and through any log statement. Debug-shaped output there leaks the field name and braces into an end-user message.

fix:
FIXED by 0fcc886. `m.try_insert(k, v)?;` no longer warns; `m.insert(k, v);` was already exempt and is unchanged.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS THE NATURAL READING AND IT WAS WRONG, in a way that matters for anyone touching this code. The title says the exemption "is keyed to the panicking spellings and does not follow through the `try_*` twin", which reads as: add the twins to `displaced_value_exempt`'s list. That fix would have changed NOTHING. Instrumenting the predicate showed the list is never reached.

MEASURED, by dumping the callee key the lint actually sees:

    m.try_insert(1, 2)?    method=try_insert   method_callee_types=Some("Map.insert")
    h.try_insert()?        method=try_insert   method_callee_types=Some("Holder.try_insert")

For a BUILTIN fallible twin the typechecker canonicalizes the callee key to the PANICKING handler (`Map.try_insert` routes to `compile_map_method`'s `insert` arm, per `src/fallible_alloc.rs`), so the table holds `"Map.insert"` while the source text says `try_insert`. `is_displaced_value_discard`'s guard is `callee_method == method`, i.e. `"insert" == "try_insert"` -- false, return false, list never consulted. A USER method is not canonicalized and keeps `"Holder.try_insert"`.

So there were TWO defects, and the diagnostic pointed at neither:

  1. THE GUARD. Both sides are now normalized to the panicking spelling before comparison. The guard's actual purpose -- stopping a STALE inner entry from a chained span (`"VecDeque.pop_front"` recorded under an outer `.try_insert`) from exempting an unrelated call -- is preserved, because the normalized names must still correspond.

  2. THE `?` NODE. The discarded expression is `ExprKind::Question`, not the `MethodCall` inside it; the predicate matched only `MethodCall` and bailed immediately. It now looks through `Question` and keys the side-table lookup on the INNER call's span, since `method_callee_types` holds nothing under the `?`.

A PLEASANT CONSEQUENCE of the canonicalization: the receiver-scoping the exemption already intended falls out for free. A user's `try_insert` keeps its own spelling, so it stays un-exempt with no special case -- which is exactly what design.md's "a user-defined `insert` returning `Option` still warns" asks for.

THE `try_` STRIP INSIDE `displaced_value_exempt` IS BELT-AND-BRACES, NOT THE MECHANISM, and is documented as such at the function so the next reader is not misled the way this row's title was. It makes the predicate correct whichever spelling it is handed, covering a future twin that does not get canonicalized.

SCOPE, against the row's "whichever of those grow `try_*` twins needs the same treatment". The normalization is generic -- it strips `try_` and matches the panicking name -- so it needs no second list and cannot drift out of sync with the first. A future `Vec.try_pop` or `SortedMap.try_remove` is exempt the day it lands. Surveying what exists today: `try_insert` is the ONLY `try_*` method in the family whose `?`-unwrapped type is an `Option`. `Set.try_insert` / `SortedSet.try_insert` return `Result[bool, AllocError]` (`?` yields `bool`, never category 1), and `try_push` / `try_push_back` / `try_push_front` / `try_push_str` / `try_extend_from_slice` / `try_with_capacity` return `Result[(), AllocError]`. So `Map.try_insert` is the whole of today's surface, and the rule is what covers tomorrow's.

WHAT DELIBERATELY STILL WARNS, each pinned by a test that passes with AND without the fix, so an over-broad exemption fails it:
  - `m.try_insert(k, v);` with NO `?` -- the discarded type is the `Result` and the abandoned branch is an OOM, not a displaced value. The exemption is consulted only when the discarded type is `Option` (`check_discard`), so this path was never at risk, and the test keeps it that way.
  - A user-defined `try_insert` of identical shape through `?` -- receiver not a stdlib container.
  - A non-exempt `Option` reached through `?` -- looking through the `?` must not blanket-exempt everything so reached; the base name still has to be in the list. `Process.try_wait()?` is the real-world case: it yields `Option[ExitStatus]` where the `Option` IS the result (did the child exit?), and `("Process", "wait")` is absent, so it warns.

NON-VACUITY: `test_discarded_map_try_insert_through_question_does_not_warn` was verified RED against the unfixed source (57 passed / 1 failed with the fix stashed). The other three pass either way by design, as above.

title: `m.try_insert(k, v)?;` as a statement warns `discarded 'Option' value`, though the displaced-value must-use exemption exists precisely for that shape on `Map.insert`. `Map.try_insert` returns `Result[Option[V], AllocError]` -- so `?` unwraps the alloc failure and leaves the DISPLACED VALUE `Option[V]`, which the implicit-`Option` must-use lint then flags. design.md § `#[must_use]`'s "Displaced-value exception to category 1" makes `Map.insert` / `Map.remove` / `Vec.pop` and friends exempt on exactly this reasoning: "the mutation is the operation's purpose and the `Option` is an ancillary report; discarding it is the dominant correct idiom (`map.insert(k, v);` as a statement is the shape virtually every map user writes). Warning here would train users to reflexively scatter `let _ =`, eroding the lint's signal where it matters." The exemption is keyed to the panicking spellings and does not follow through the `try_*` twin, so the fallible form of the same call carries a warning the panicking form does not.
detail:
Probe: domain-24 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d24/{al3,mi}.kara.

THE RETURN SHAPE ITSELF LOOKS RIGHT, and this row is not asking for it to change: `Result[Option[V], AllocError]` reports both the allocation outcome and the displaced value, which is strictly more informative than the spec's blanket "`try_insert` returns `Result[(), AllocError]`" sentence. The defect is that the exemption list was not extended to match.

EXACT MEASUREMENT of the return type, since the warning alone is ambiguous: matching `m.try_insert(1, 2)` against `Some`/`None` reports `the scrutinee has type 'Result[Option[i64], AllocError]'`.

SCOPE TO CHECK WHEN FIXING: the exemption covers `Map.insert`, `TreeMap.insert`, `Map.remove`, `TreeMap.remove`, `Vec.pop`, `Vec.remove_first`, `VecDeque.pop_front`/`pop_back`. Whichever of those grow `try_*` twins needs the same treatment; only `Map.try_insert` was measured here.

fix:
FIXED by 44851f9, BY SHIPPING THE NAMESPACE, not by narrowing the sentence -- and the choice is worth recording, because the row itself flagged narrowing as the cheaper repair and an owner call.

WHY IMPLEMENT RATHER THAN NARROW. The stability paragraph is not decoration: it exists because `Map`/`Set` hash under a per-process RANDOM key (B-2026-08-21-6), so it tells a user who needs a digest to survive a restart NOT to use `Hash` -- and then named a replacement that was never built. Narrowing the sentence would have DELETED THE ONLY ESCAPE HATCH and left those four use cases (content addressing, on-disk indexes, snapshot tests, distributed sharding) with no supported option at all -- strictly worse than if the warning had never been written, because the warning is correct. Shipping one function makes the escape hatch real; what remains unbuilt is then a performance nicety and a separate module, not a trap. (This is where it differs from the sibling B-2026-08-20-41 shape the row cites: there the warning had a workaround, here it had none.)

WHAT SHIPS. `StableHash.siphash24(bytes: Slice[u8], k0: u64, k1: u64) -> u64` -- SipHash-2-4 over `bytes` under the caller's 128-bit key, reading no process state. `StableHash` is a namespace struct nobody constructs, the shape `Base64` / `Hex` / `Url` already use (`runtime/stdlib/stable_hash.kara`, registered in `STDLIB_SOURCES` + `PRELUDE_TYPES`). Kara has no `mod` -- its module tree comes from the directory layout and the stdlib is a flat baked prelude -- so a literal `hash.stable` submodule was never on the table.

TWO DELIBERATE DEPARTURES FROM THE SPEC TEXT, both now recorded in design.md rather than left as silent drift:
  - `::` -> `.`, the row's own spelling note. `hash::stable::siphash24` could never have parsed.
  - `key` -> `k0, k1`. SipHash-2-4 takes a 128-BIT key; Kara has no `u128`, and expanding one `u64` into two halves would have been an invented convention under a name that promises interoperability -- karac's `siphash24` would then disagree with every other implementation of `siphash24`, destroying the one property the function exists for. The arity moved to match the algorithm.

WHY A SECOND SIPHASH. `hash_bytes` is SipHash-1-3 and is deliberately UNSTABLE (per-process key); 2-4 is the round count the paper specifies as default and therefore the one another language's `siphash24` computes. `State` is now generic over both counts (`State<C, D>`), so the permutation, the block split, the little-endian word decode and the length byte exist exactly ONCE and each variant still monomorphizes to straight-line unrolled code.

AGREEMENT BY CONSTRUCTION ACROSS BACKENDS. The interpreter calls `karac_hash::siphash24` directly; codegen lowers to `karac_stable_siphash24`, a thin shim over the same fn. Neither open-codes the permutation -- the Arrow-IPC / `String.normalize` rule, and load-bearing here rather than tidy: a digest advertised as stable across machines is ALREADY BROKEN if `karac run` and `karac build` disagree about it, and a user storing one to disk has no way to notice. The symbol sits in the DEFAULT runtime feature set (`runtime/src/hashing.rs`), not an opt-in archive, so lean / full / wasm / wasm-threads all carry it and the JIT resolves it from the sibling runner via the keep-list.

VERIFICATION IS ORACLE-BASED, NEVER SELF-TAKEN -- which matters more here than usual, since a pin taken from our own output would confirm only self-consistency while the function's entire value is that someone else's `siphash24` agrees. `std`'s deprecated `SipHasher` IS SipHash-2-4: `hash/src/lib.rs::agrees_with_stds_siphash24` runs it over 4 keys x 41 lengths, and EVERY pinned constant in the language-level tests was computed with it before being written down. (The first draft of those pins was invented and the test caught it immediately -- exactly the failure mode the crate's existing KAT comment warns about.)

MEASURED, beyond the unit oracle: the digest is byte-identical across interp / JIT / AOT for five byte-source shapes -- `String.bytes()`, a named `Vec[u8]`, a bare array literal (no alloca), the empty input (`(null, 0)` at the FFI boundary), and a non-zero 128-bit key; and it is identical under three different `KARAC_HASH_SEED` pins while a `Map`'s iteration order visibly moves under the same pins (`dcba` vs `dabc`) -- the contrast the feature exists for, in one measurement. Both are pinned as tests (`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_stable_hash_siphash24_agrees_with_the_interpreter` as a TWIN comparison against the in-process interpreter oracle rather than a shared constant, so the two cannot drift together; `tests/cli.rs::stable_hash_digest_does_not_move_with_the_process_hash_seed` in a subprocess, since the property is about what differs between processes).

The paragraph's closing promise is reachable too: `karac explain --concept=stable-hash` is the page it says users are pointed at, and `tests/cli.rs::test_stable_hash_page_claims_match_the_compiler` compiles each thing the page calls absent and fails if it ever ships, so the page cannot quietly start lying.

NOT CLOSED BY THIS, split to B-2026-08-26-2: the same paragraph's `xxh3` and `crypto` promises.
title: The STABLE-HASH module does not exist, so the escape design.md prescribes for every use case where `Hash` is explicitly the wrong tool is unavailable. § `Hash` and `Hasher`, stability policy: hash values are "not stable across runs, not stable across Kara versions, not stable across targets", and therefore "Code that needs stable digests (content addressing, on-disk indexes, snapshot tests, distributed sharding) does **not** use `Hash`. Kara's stdlib SHIPS explicit, versioned functions for that purpose -- `hash::stable::siphash24(bytes, key)`, `hash::stable::xxh3(bytes)`, and the `crypto` module for cryptographic hashes." Neither `siphash24` nor `xxh3` appears anywhere in `src/` or `runtime/stdlib/`, and there is no `hash.stable` namespace to call. The paragraph's closing promise is unreachable too: "Users who reach for `Hash` for stability are pointed at the stable-hash module by a `karac explain` page" -- see B-2026-08-25-23 for the state of `karac explain --concept=`.
detail:
Probe: domain-24 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d24/h4.kara.

THE REST OF § Hash AND Hasher IS FULLY IMPLEMENTED, which is why this stands out as an omission rather than an unfinished area: `#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]` on a struct with a String field works as a `Map` key on both backends; a USER `impl Hasher` with only `write` and `finish` defined correctly inherits the default-bodied convenience methods (`h.write_u64(42)` then `h.finish()` returns the mixed value on interp and JIT alike); and `Map[i64, i64, FxBuildHasher]` -- the third type parameter the spec introduces to make the hasher a property of the table -- typechecks and runs.

SPELLING NOTE, not a separate defect: the spec writes the module path with Rust's `::` separator (`hash::stable::siphash24`), which would not parse in Kara even if the module existed -- paths use `.`. Worth fixing in the same edit.

SAME SHAPE AS B-2026-08-20-41 (`String.normalize` / `NFC`): the spec correctly identifies a hazard, warns the reader off the wrong tool, and names a replacement that was never built. Both are cases where the cheaper repair may be to narrow the sentence rather than implement the API -- an owner call.

fix:
FIXED by 7472e06 for the two pages that can exist today. `--concept=` now serves `closures`, `operators` and `module-state`; the unknown-name hint is derived from an `ALL_CONCEPTS` slice rather than a hand-written string, so a future page cannot be added to the enum and forgotten in the hint that advertises it. Both new pages are reachable by the bare-name form too (`karac explain module-state`), which also exercises the shape classifier against a hyphen.

THE STABLE-HASH PAGE IS NOT INCLUDED and is not being quietly dropped: it explains a module that does not exist, so it rides on B-2026-08-25-22. That row already cross-references this one. Writing the page first would produce exactly the failure this ledger keeps recording -- documentation for surface that was never built.

WRITTEN AGAINST MEASURED BEHAVIOUR, NOT THE SPEC, and that turned out to matter. The operators page's stated job (design.md: it "documents the full desugaring table so that users can see why a given operator call fails and which trait they would need") is only served by wording that matches what the user actually saw in their terminal. Probing every rule in § Operator Traits found FOUR divergences, filed as B-2026-08-25-29 (behaviour) and B-2026-08-25-30 (diagnostics). A page transcribed from design.md would have told users that `(x: i32) + (y: i64)` widens (it is rejected), that `==` needs `PartialEq` (the diagnostic demands `Eq`), that `vec1 + vec2` names a trait and points at `.concat` (it names neither), and that `not` works on integer primitives (it does not). Instead the page teaches the real rejection wording with the real fix for each, and carries a short "where the implementation differs from design.md today" section so a user is not left thinking the spec lied.

THE MODULE-STATE PAGE NEEDED NO SUCH HEDGING -- that surface is implemented well, which is worth recording since this row's neighbours are all spec-ahead-of-implementation. Measured working as specified: the compile-time initializer rule and its three error codes (E_MODULE_BINDING_EFFECTFUL_INIT, E_MODULE_BINDING_HEAP_TYPE, E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING), E_ONCE_CELL_AT_MODULE_SCOPE, the synthetic per-binding effect resource, per-binding `#[allow(module_mut_binding)]` suppression, and the `par { }` write rule -- which is genuinely effect-set-based, firing through a call to a helper carrying the effect, not just on a syntactic assignment. `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `LazyLock`, `OnceLock` and `#[thread_local]` all work at module scope. Two details the page records that the spec does not: `RwLock` is in design.md's supported-paths list but `RwLock.new(0)` is rejected at module scope as an effectful initializer, and the `app` / `gpu` hard-error profile rows are deliberately unimplemented because no such `CompileProfile` variant exists (see the comment on `warn_module_mut_binding`).

TESTS ARE DRIFT GUARDS, NOT SNAPSHOTS. `test_operators_page_quotes_live_diagnostics` and `test_module_state_page_quotes_live_diagnostics` compile each failing program and assert BOTH that the compiler still emits the fragment AND that the page still quotes it, so improving any of these messages fails the test until the page moves with it. That coupling is deliberate: the existing closures-page tests pin strings by hand, which drifts silently because nothing links the two. Also added: a width bound (concept pages are read in a terminal, so every line must fit 78 columns or the tables destroy themselves at 80), JSON-envelope coverage for every page, bare-name lookup for every page, and a check that the `module_mut_binding` warning's six-item menu matches what the page it points at actually explains.

`karac explain --help` now lists all three concepts with a one-paragraph summary each, so the pages are discoverable without reading design.md.

GATES: 9918 tests pass (0 failed), fmt clean, clippy clean on both feature legs.

ENVIRONMENT NOTE for whoever runs the llvm leg next in a cloud container: `/usr/lib/llvm-18` shipped with `bin`/`lib`/`share` but NO `include`, so `cargo clippy --features llvm` died in the `llvm-sys` build script on a missing `llvm-c/Target.h`. `apt-get update && apt-get install -y llvm-18-dev` restores it -- the bare `install` fails first with a 404 on a stale `libxml2-dev` pin until the index is refreshed.
title: `karac explain --concept=` supports exactly ONE concept, `closures`, and it is not one of the pages design.md names. The error message self-documents the gap: `error: unknown concept 'operators'. Supported: closures.` design.md names two pages by exact flag -- `karac explain --concept=operators`, which § Operator Traits says "documents the full desugaring table so that users can see why a given operator call fails and which trait they would need", and `karac explain --concept=module-state` -- plus a stable-hash page referenced in prose (§ Hash stability policy: "Users who reach for `Hash` for stability are pointed at the stable-hash module by a `karac explain` page"). None of the three exists. The document makes 36 references to `karac explain` overall, so the surface is load-bearing for the AI-first diagnostics story.
detail:
Probe: domain-24 spec-transcription pass; measured by invoking `karac explain --concept=operators` and reading the supported list off the rejection.

LOW SEVERITY BECAUSE IT IS ADDITIVE and fails loudly with an accurate list -- no user is misled about what happened, they simply cannot get the page. It is filed because the missing pages are the ones diagnostics are supposed to hand off to: an operator-desugaring failure and a reach-for-`Hash`-for-stability mistake are both cases where the compiler is specified to point somewhere, and today it points at nothing.

SEE ALSO B-2026-08-25-22 -- the stable-hash page cannot be written until the module it explains exists, so that one is downstream.

fix:
FIXED by 733c0f2. ROOT CAUSE: both diagnostic renderers labelled a resolve diagnostic by PHASE. `src/cli.rs` formatted `"{sev}[resolve]"` unconditionally, and since the message text does not repeat the lint name either, a reader who saw the warning had nothing to pass to `#[allow(...)]` -- for `layout_unassigned_fields`, an attribute design.md § Layout Rules prescribes BY NAME and which does work. The row's diagnosis was exactly right.

The rule was already settled elsewhere in the same file: the typecheck renderers use `err.lint_name.as_deref().unwrap_or("typecheck")` and carry a comment saying why -- "the bracket is the actionable label", because that is what `-A <name>` takes. Only the resolve lane had not been given it.

FIX: added `resolve_kind_lint_name(kind) -> Option<&'static str>` beside the existing `resolve_kind_is_note` in src/resolver.rs, following the one-predicate discipline that function documents (the effect side accumulated seventeen open-coded copies before that rule was adopted). Both renderers consult it, so text and JSON cannot drift apart. `None` for an ordinary hard error, which keeps its phase label.

THE SWEEP THE ROW ASKED FOR, done: there are exactly THREE note-severity resolve kinds and all three are lint-backed -- `LayoutUnassignedFields`, `LayoutReprCIgnored`, `FloatInSerializedType`. `repr_c_layout_ignored` had the identical defect and is fixed and tested alongside, so this is a class fix rather than one string.

SECOND DEFECT FOUND, NOT IN THE ROW, fixed here because it is the same root cause on the other lane: `src/cli/diag_json.rs` hardcoded `severity: "error"` and `lint_name: None` for every resolve diagnostic. So `karac check --output=json` reported `"severity": "error"` for a diagnostic the text lane prints as a warning, that exits 0, and whose own `code` in the SAME record is `W0150`. That divergence lands on the Mend path, where the JSON is the interface -- an agent reading it would see a hard error where the compiler reports a warning. Both fields now read the same two predicates.

VERIFIED:
  text  warning[resolve]           -> warning[layout_unassigned_fields]
  text  warning[resolve]           -> warning[repr_c_layout_ignored]
  json  severity "error"           -> "warning", lint_name populated
  control: `#[allow(layout_unassigned_fields)]` still suppresses (exit 0, silent)
  control: a hard resolve error keeps error[resolve] / "severity": "error" / exit 1

REGRESSION TEST: `lint_backed_resolve_warnings_name_their_lint_on_both_lanes` in tests/cli.rs. It asserts both lanes, both note kinds, and -- the part that makes it more than a string check -- that the name printed in the bracket is the one that ACTUALLY silences the warning, by running the suppressed twin. The hard-error control is what proves the fix did not simply relabel everything. Verified RED pre-fix on the first assertion.
title: The unassigned-layout-fields warning renders as `warning[resolve]` instead of `warning[layout_unassigned_fields]`, so the suppression design.md prescribes cannot be discovered from the message. § Layout Rules: "The compiler emits a warning once per layout block listing the unassigned fields — suppress with `#[allow(layout_unassigned_fields)]` when the omission is intentional." The warning fires correctly and the allow DOES suppress it -- `#[allow(layout_unassigned_fields)]` on the layout block turns `warning[resolve]: layout 'ps': fields not assigned to any group or cold section: b. These will be placed in an implicit trailing hot group.` into "All checks passed." But the rendered tag names the PHASE, not the lint, and the message text never states the lint name either, so a user who sees the warning has nothing to pass to `#[allow(...)]`. Sibling lint-backed diagnostics render with their own name -- `warning[deprecated]: use of deprecated item 'old_api'` and `warning[must_use]: discarded 'C' value` in the same compiler, on the same surface.
detail:
Probe: domain-24 spec-transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d24/{ly2,ly4,ly5,cmp}.kara -- ly4 shows the warning, ly5 the same file with the allow, cmp the two siblings that render correctly.

LAYOUT BLOCKS ARE OTHERWISE SOUND, measured against § Feature 1's worked example verbatim: the full seven-field `Entity` block with two `group`s and a `cold` section checks clean and reads back `entities[0].position.x`; a field listed in two groups is correctly rejected (`field 'a' appears in multiple sections in layout 'ps'`); and `align(64)` on a group parses and checks.

WORTH A SWEEP RATHER THAN A ONE-LINE FIX: whatever renders this warning is emitting through the phase-tagged path rather than the lint path, so any other lint-backed diagnostic raised from the resolver will have the same problem. I did not enumerate which others are affected.

fix: 8d32a0d
title: An ASSOCIATED fn in a GENERIC impl that binds a struct LITERAL to a local and calls a MUTATING sibling through it dispatches to the UNMANGLED base prototype: `fn build(v: Vec[T]) -> Bag[T] { let mut b = Bag { xs: v }; b.arrange(); b }` SEGFAULTS at a heap-carrying `T` under JIT and AOT while the interpreter is correct; `T = i64` is silently fine

fix:
FIXED by 40a54f6. Two of the row's three defects are closed; the third (the span) is split out as its own row rather than buried here -- split to B-2026-08-25-31; see the REMAINDER note below.

ROOT CAUSE: A GUARD THAT ALREADY EXISTED ONE FILE OVER. An un-inferred type argument becomes `Type::Error` and then flows into every downstream bound check. The bound-discharge path in `src/typechecker/exprs.rs` (~2345) already skips it, with the comment "Unresolved metavar / propagating-param / already-error -- upstream diagnostics handle. Avoid noise." The `bound_gate` in `src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs` (~719) was never given the same guard, so it rendered `Type::Error` through `render_unsatisfied_bound_message` and produced the row's three defects at once: it blamed the BOUND rather than the inference failure, printed `<error>` as though it were a type name, and appended "trait `Ord` is implemented by: Bf16, F16, ..." -- a list in which the fix does not appear. This was never a design gap; one path had learned a lesson the other had not.

IT COULD NOT SIMPLY COPY THE `continue`. Measured: the two spellings of the empty literal differ in whether anything upstream reports them.
    W.from(Vec[])   -> E_EMPTY_PREFIX_LITERAL_NEEDS_ANNOTATION at the LITERAL's own span (7:20), correct and actionable
    W.from([])      -> nothing reported at all; `Vec[Type::Error]` is returned silently
So skipping outright would have left the bare form with NO diagnostic and accepted a broken program in silence -- strictly worse than the wrong message. The gate now stays quiet only when the root cause is already on the record (new `TypeChecker::reported_uninferrable_empty_literal`, set by `report_empty_prefix_literal`), and otherwise emits a message that names the inference failure and prescribes the annotation.

AN UNADVERTISED SECOND BUG, FIXED IN PASSING: the prefix form emitted TWO diagnostics -- the accurate literal-anchored one, immediately followed by the contradictory `<error>` restatement at the use. A reader who trusted the second went looking for a missing `Ord` impl. It now emits exactly one. This is what `empty_prefix_literal_reports_once_at_the_literal` pins, and it failed RED against the unfixed source alongside the bare-form regression.

NO CHANGE TO WHAT COMPILES, and this was checked against the spec rather than assumed. design.md § Collection Literals titles its rule "**Empty prefix-literal requires an annotation**" and gives `let y = Array[]` as the erroring example; it states no rule for the bare `[]` form. This row is class `diagnostics`, severity `low` -- rejecting more programs is a language change it does not ask for. Measured before/after on six programs: `W.from([])` with no use, the annotated form, and the unbounded `impl[T] W[T]` control all still pass; `unbounded_impl_with_empty_literal_is_unchanged` pins the last of those.

FIVE TESTS, and the split matters:
  - `empty_bare_literal_reports_inference_failure_not_a_bound_failure` -- REGRESSION, verified RED. Asserts the message names the inference failure AND, separately, that it contains none of `<error>` / "is not satisfied" / "is implemented by", so each of the row's three message defects regresses legibly on its own.
  - `empty_prefix_literal_reports_once_at_the_literal` -- REGRESSION, verified RED. Exactly one error, and it is the literal-anchored one.
  - `annotated_empty_literal_still_typechecks` -- CONTROL. The prescribed fix must actually work, or the diagnostic is a lie.
  - `unbounded_impl_with_empty_literal_is_unchanged` -- CONTROL. Pins that the fix did not start rejecting the accepted case.
  - `a_genuinely_unsatisfied_bound_still_names_the_bound` -- CONTROL. The guard keys on the ERROR type specifically; a real bound failure on a CONCRETE type (`Vec[f64]` against `T: Ord`) must keep its original message, implementors list included, because there the list IS the fix.
The three controls pass with and without the fix by design -- they exist to fail if the guard is ever widened.

REMAINDER, SPLIT TO ITS OWN ROW (B-2026-08-25-31): the row's defect 3, the caret pointing at the first USE rather than at the literal, is NOT fixed. `Type::Error` is a payload-free variant, so nothing links it back to the span it originated from; carrying one would touch every match site across the typechecker. The cheap alternative -- pointing at the "nearest" or "only" empty literal -- can attribute the error to an UNRELATED literal whenever the error type arose from some other inference failure, and a confidently wrong caret reads worse than a correct-but-distant one. The new message compensates in words ("annotate the value it came from, e.g. `let v: Vec[i64] = [];`") but the caret is unchanged, and p3_far_apart still shows a four-line gap between literal and report.

VERIFIED: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; BOTH clippy legs clean; `tests/typechecker.rs` 2490/2490; full `--features llvm` suite green.
title: An un-inferrable `T` from an EMPTY array literal is reported as a BOUND failure naming `<error>` as the type, pointed at a later method call rather than at the literal: `W.from([])` on `impl[T: Ord]` says "trait bound `T: Ord` is not satisfied; `<error>` does not implement `Ord`"
detail:
REPRODUCE, no stdlib involved:

    struct W[T] { xs: Vec[T] }
    impl[T: Ord] W[T] {
        fn from(v: Vec[T]) -> W[T] { W { xs: v } }
        fn size(ref self) -> i64 { self.xs.len() }
    }
    fn main() { let g = W.from([]); println(g.size()); }

    error[typecheck]: 8:13: method 'size' is not callable on this `W`: trait bound `T: Ord` is not
    satisfied; `<error>` does not implement `Ord`; trait `Ord` is implemented by: Bf16, F16, ...

THREE THINGS ARE WRONG WITH THE MESSAGE, and the underlying compile is right to fail:
  1. It blames the BOUND. The actual problem is that `T` cannot be inferred from `[]`; the bound is
     merely what noticed. A reader goes looking for a missing `Ord` impl.
  2. It prints `<error>` as if it were a type name, then helpfully lists every type implementing
     `Ord` -- none of which is the fix. The fix is an annotation on the empty literal.
  3. It points at line 8 (`g.size()`), not line 7 (`W.from([])`) where the un-inferrable literal is.
     The span is on the first USE, so the further apart the two are the worse it reads.

NOT A SOUNDNESS BUG, and deliberately not filed as one. The UNBOUNDED control -- the same program with
`impl[T] W[T]` -- COMPILES and RUNS CORRECTLY, printing 0 on the interpreter and on an AOT binary
alike. An empty `Vec` of an un-inferred element type has no observable element behaviour, so accepting
it is defensible; it is only when a bound has to be discharged that the un-inferred `T` becomes
visible, and then it is reported as the wrong problem.

SUGGESTED SHAPE: detect that the type argument resolved to the error type BEFORE running the bound
check, and emit a distinct "cannot infer the element type of this empty collection literal -- add an
annotation, e.g. `let v: Vec[i64] = [];`" diagnostic anchored at the literal's own span.

SOURCE NOTE: hit while writing the E2E parity tests for `PriorityQueue`, where the empty-queue case
was first written `PriorityQueue.from([])`. The repo's `karac check` test gate rejected it, which is
the gate working; the annotated form `let empty: Vec[i64] = []` is what shipped.

fix: Fixed in 14c6d32.
title: SIX `let`-RHS forms bound a generic-struct value with NO recorded instantiation, so the sibling call dispatched to the unmangled base prototype and SEGFAULTED at a heap-carrying `T`: identifier copy, free-fn call, assoc fn returning Self, method returning Self, block expression, index into `Vec[Bag[T]]`

fix:
Fixed in 5fa76a7. Resolved on the RECEIVER side, in `enum_inst_type_of_expr`, since no binding-site arm could reach a nameless temporary.

Three changes, one rule -- an instantiation record is only useful if its params are CONCRETE:
  1. A struct-literal receiver reconstructs its type arguments from the struct's DECLARED generic parameter names and resolves them through the active monomorph's substitution. Factored out as `struct_literal_generic_inst`, shared with the `let`-site arm that B-2026-08-25-25 added.
  2. A CALL receiver resolved to the callee's DECLARED return type, which for a generic callee is the GENERIC form (`Bag[T]`) -- the identical "holds the generic form, which is worse than holding nothing" defect as B-2026-08-25-27, just on the receiver side. Resolved through the same substitution.
  3. The span fallback gets that resolution too, for the same reason.

TWO FORMS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL REPORT are also covered and now pinned by the regression test: a CHAINED temporary (`Bag { xs: v }.dup().inner()`) and an ASSOCIATED-FN temporary (`Bag.make(v).inner()`).

SCOPE CORRECTION worth recording, because the original row did not state it. The defect required the temporary to be INSIDE A GENERIC CONTEXT, where `T` is a parameter of the enclosing impl. From a non-generic caller the receiver's concrete type is inferable by other means, which is why the stdlib's own `PriorityQueue.from(v).into_sorted_vec()` -- the same syntactic shape, called from `main` -- was correct throughout, and why the design.md example never exhibited it. The blast radius was therefore generic library code, not application code.

REGRESSION TEST `e2e_generic_method_call_on_temporary_receiver` (tests/codegen.rs) table-drives four temporary forms plus a NAMED-binding control, each at both `i64` and `String`. The control was correct before the fix, so it pins the diagnosis: the defect was the absence of a NAME, not the value. The `String` leg is what fails pre-fix; `i64` is silently correct, as everywhere in this family.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT STANDS. Six arms had accumulated on the `let`-site chain, four of them reactively after an escape; this case proved a seventh could never have been enough, because `enum_inst_var_types` is name-keyed and a temporary has no key. Both halves are now fixed by the same rule applied at two sites (binding and receiver) rather than by enumerating RHS shapes. If a further case in this family appears, prefer extending that rule over adding an arm.
title: A method call whose receiver is an unnamed TEMPORARY inside a generic impl dispatches to the unmangled base prototype and SEGFAULTS at a heap-carrying `T`: `Bag { xs: v }.inner()` and `mkbag(v).inner()` crash where `let q = Bag { xs: v }; q.inner()` is correct

fix:
FIXED by 297ef4f, which corrected design.md and the `explain --concept=operators` page rather than the compiler.

BOTH HALVES WERE DESIGN.MD DEFECTS, NOT IMPLEMENTATION GAPS. This row assumed the spec was ahead of the compiler and asked which side should move; measuring the spec against itself answered it. The implementation was right both times and design.md was corrected.

HALF 1 -- WIDENING. design.md CONTRADICTED ITSELF, and the row cited only the losing side. Sec Operator Traits ("Homogeneous signatures in v1") said `(x: i32) + (y: i64)` is valid and widens. Sec Numeric types ("Literal-involved promotion in binary operators") says the opposite, and says it with everything a spec decision normally carries:

  * the stated rationale -- literal promotion covers the 95% case "without opening the door to implicit widening between typed variables";
  * a stated invariant -- "two typed expressions always follow the same rules everywhere ... There is no numerics dialect where typed variables silently widen";
  * an explicit deferral -- "safe widening between variables can be revisited as a targeted follow-up; v1 stops at literals";
  * and a WORKED EXAMPLE of the exact case the other section calls valid:
        let n: i32 = 10;
        let k: i32 = n + x;   // compile error: cannot mix i32 and i64 without `as`

The compiler agrees with the section that has the reasoning. The widening sentence in sec Operator Traits was an aside inside a paragraph about signature homogeneity, and it is the one that was rewritten -- it now states the no-widening rule, points at the literal-promotion section, and keeps the true part (mixed KINDS such as `i64 + f64` stay errors under any future relaxation, because that conversion is not in the widening table at all).

HALF 2 -- `Not`. THE ROW HAD THE OPERATOR WRONG. Kara has TWO complements where Rust spells one `!`, and I only measured one of them: `not a` is logical and takes `bool`; `~a` is bitwise, takes an integer, and complements every lane of an integer-lane `Vector[T, N]`. `~` is a real token in the lexer, sits at precedence level 12 in syntax.md beside `not`/`-`/`*`, and is implemented in the typechecker and both backends. So "bitwise `Not` on integer primitives is not available" was false -- it is available, under a spelling sec Operator Traits never mentions. That section's Bitwise row said `not a` -> `Not.not(a)` and now says `~a` -> `Not.not(a)`.

A THIRD DEFECT SURFACED IN THE SAME BULLET, unmeasured by the row: sec Operator Traits also claimed the BINARY bitwise traits ship "on integer primitives and `bool`". `bool & bool` is rejected -- `error[typecheck]: bitwise operator requires integer type, found 'bool'`. The stdlib-impl bullet was split in two and corrected: `& | ^ << >>` on integers only, `Not` on integers via `~` and on `bool` via `not`, with neither spelling accepting the other's operand type.

THE PAGE ROTTED THE WAY NEGATIVE CLAIMS DO. `karac explain --concept=operators` carried this row's divergence bullets, and one of them was ALREADY STALE before this work started: B-2026-08-25-30 rewrote the arithmetic rejection into trait language but left behind the bullet asserting the compiler "currently reports arithmetic operator requires numeric type" -- a page telling users the compiler does something it no longer did, shipped by the same commit that made it untrue. The quotes-live-diagnostics test could not catch it, because it asserts each current wording is PRESENT and never that a dead one is ABSENT. `test_operators_page_carries_no_superseded_wording` now closes that half: it pins the six retired wordings as forbidden, and holds the one surviving divergence bullet (`Vec.concat`, B-2026-08-26-1) to a live program so it fails loudly when that row closes. The `not`/`~` pair moved from the divergence section to rejection 5, since both diagnostics are correct behaviour rather than gaps, and both are now pinned to compiled programs.

FOUND WHILE MEASURING, FILED SEPARATELY: `~` computed at the carrier width rather than the declared width, so every narrow unsigned integer was wrong in both backends and wrongly in two different ways. Fixed in the same commit. Its root cause -- an unsuffixed narrow local getting an i64 alloca, which also leaves B-2026-08-06-7's shift fix incomplete in the common spelling -- and the interpreter's narrow-lane vector arithmetic are filed as their own rows.


FILED FROM THIS WORK: B-2026-08-26-6 (the `~` miscompile, fixed in the same commit), B-2026-08-26-7 (its codegen root cause -- an unsuffixed narrow local allocated at i64, which also leaves B-2026-08-06-7 shift fix incomplete in the ordinary spelling), B-2026-08-26-8 (the interpreter narrow-lane vector arithmetic divergence). B-2026-08-26-1, filed by this row work and cited in the page divergence section, was closed independently by another session in 5964c16.
title: TWO CLAIMS in design.md § Operator Traits contradicted the implementation, and BOTH TURNED OUT TO BE SPEC DEFECTS rather than the missing features this row first reported. (1) IMPLICIT WIDENING AT OPERATOR BOUNDARIES: § Operator Traits said `(x: i32) + (y: i64)` widens and is valid; § Numeric types says the opposite -- with a rationale, an invariant ("there is no numerics dialect where typed variables silently widen"), an explicit v1 deferral, and a worked example of that exact expression as a compile error. design.md contradicted ITSELF and the compiler matched the section carrying the reasoning, so § Operator Traits was corrected. (2) BITWISE `Not`: this row reported it "not available on integer primitives" after measuring only `not a`. Kāra has TWO complements where Rust spells one `!` -- `not a` (logical, `bool` only) and `~a` (bitwise, integers and integer-lane `Vector[T, N]`) -- and `~` works; § Operator Traits simply never mentioned the operator, writing the Bitwise desugaring as `not a` -> `Not.not(a)`. A THIRD, unreported defect in the same bullet: it claimed the binary bitwise traits ship on `bool`, but `bool & bool` is rejected. FIXED BY CORRECTING THE SPEC in all three places, plus the `explain --concept=operators` page whose divergence section had gone stale.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the `karac explain --concept=operators` page for B-2026-08-25-23. The page's stated job (design.md: it "documents the full desugaring table so that users can see why a given operator call fails and which trait they would need") forced a measurement of every operator rule against the implementation rather than a transcription of the spec, which is what surfaced these.

MEASURED, one program per claim, on 67c2a3a-era `main`:
  i32 + i64   -> error[typecheck]: cannot mix integer types 'i32' and 'i64' in arithmetic
  u8  + u32   -> error[typecheck]: cannot mix integer types 'u8' and 'u32' in arithmetic
  f32 + f64   -> error[typecheck]: cannot mix float types 'f32' and 'f64' in arithmetic
  i64 + f64   -> error[typecheck]: cannot mix integer and floating-point operands  (CORRECT -- spec agrees this stays an error)
  (x: i32) + 2 -> accepted                                                          (literal widening works)
  not (a: i64) -> error[typecheck]: unary '!' requires 'bool', found 'i64'
  not (a: u8)  -> error[typecheck]: unary '!' requires 'bool', found 'u8'
  not (b: bool)-> accepted

WHICH SIDE MOVES IS THE OWNER'S CALL, and the two halves may go different ways.

The WIDENING half is the consequential one. design.md ties it to an existing mechanism -- "the same implicit lossless widening at operator boundaries that it applies at assignment boundaries", with eligibility limited to the implicit-widening table -- so the table and the assignment-boundary coercion already exist; what is missing is applying them at the operator. Note the spec is careful that the trait signatures stay homogeneous (`Self, Self`) and the coercion is inserted by the compiler at the call site, so this is not the heterogeneous-`Rhs` extension, which the same paragraph explicitly defers.

The `Not` half is smaller and may simply be a spec overreach: `not` reads as a boolean keyword, and a language that spells bitwise complement `not` invites `not 0` meaning -1 rather than `false`. If the decision is that integers keep no complement operator, the § Operator Traits bitwise rows and the stdlib-impl bullet both need narrowing.

RELATED SPELLING DEFECT, filed separately as a diagnostics row: the typecheck message for this case says `unary '!' requires 'bool'` -- spelling the operator with Rust's `!`, which the PARSER already rejects with `the \`!\` operator is not used in Kara; use \`not\` instead`. So a user who writes `not a` on an integer is told about an operator the language does not have.

NOT A REGRESSION: no evidence either behaviour ever worked. This is spec-ahead-of-implementation, the same shape as B-2026-08-25-19 (Box/Rc/Arc) and B-2026-08-25-22 (stable hash).

DOCUMENTED IN THE MEANTIME: `karac explain --concept=operators` carries a "Where the implementation differs from design.md today" section naming both, so a user hitting the cast requirement is not left thinking the spec lied to them. That section must be updated or dropped when this row closes -- `tests/cli.rs::test_operators_page_quotes_live_diagnostics` compiles each case and asserts the page still quotes the live wording, so it will fail loudly if the behaviour changes without the page.

RECLASSIFIED AT CLOSE. This row was filed as class `missing-feature` / surface `typecheck`, because it read the two divergences as the compiler lagging the spec. Both turned out to be defects in design.md itself, and nothing in typecheck changed -- so the original labels assert exactly the thing the close refutes, that a feature was missing. Corrected to `other` on both axes; the resolution was a documentation change.

fix:
FIXED by 3964ede. All three wording defects the row measured are fixed, and the `explain --concept=operators` page moved in lockstep as the row predicted it would have to.

  arithmetic   arithmetic operator requires numeric type, found 'Vec[i64]'
            -> type 'Vec[i64]' does not implement trait Add; there is
               deliberately no `impl Add for Vec[T]` -- use `a.extend(b)` to
               append b's elements to a
  distinct     (same operator-language message)
            -> type 'UserId' does not implement trait Add; add
               #[derive(Arithmetic)] to 'UserId' to use arithmetic operators
               between two 'UserId' values, or unwrap explicitly
  equality     does not implement Eq; add #[derive(Eq)] ...
            -> does not implement PartialEq; add #[derive(PartialEq)] ...
  ordering     does not implement Ord; add #[derive(Ord)] ...
            -> does not implement PartialOrd; add #[derive(PartialOrd)] ...
  unary not    unary '!' requires 'bool', found 'i64'
            -> unary 'not' requires 'bool', found 'i64'

The Eq/Ord correction was already latent in the code rather than a judgement call: the guards are `type_supports_partial_eq` / `type_supports_partial_ord`, so the predicate and the message it emitted disagreed about which trait was required. Verified by measurement that `#[derive(PartialEq)]` and `#[derive(PartialOrd)]` each compile ALONE, on a struct and on a distinct type.

A DEFECT IN THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS FIX, caught by the suite and recorded because the failure mode is instructive: rewriting the catch-all arm to "type 'T' does not implement trait Add" made the message FALSE for `String`. `String + String` is accepted several branches earlier, so String DOES implement Add; `s + 1` reaches the arm because the RIGHT operand is wrong. The old vague wording was unhelpful but made no claim about impls -- the new one asserted something untrue, which is worse. That case now reports `'+' on 'String' requires a 'String' right operand, found 'i64'`, while `String - String` still reports a missing `Sub` impl, which is true. A confident rewrite of a diagnostic can regress it below the vague message it replaces; only running the existing assertions caught it.

DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM THE SPEC SENTENCE, measured before deviating: design.md offers "`vec.concat(other)` or `vec.extend(other)`", but `Vec.concat()` here takes ZERO arguments and is `Vec[String]`-only -- it joins the receiver's own elements into one String. Quoting the spec verbatim would have sent a `Vec[i64]` reader to "Vec.concat() requires String elements", a worse dead end than the message being replaced. The diagnostic names only `extend`, the explain page records the divergence, and the spec/implementation gap is filed as B-2026-08-26-1 rather than silently absorbed.

COUPLING, as the row anticipated: `tests/cli.rs::test_operators_page_quotes_live_diagnostics` went red the moment the messages improved and stayed red until the page moved. It grew from five cases to NINE -- adding the Vec redirect, the distinct-type derive, the `not` spelling, and the two derive-advice fragments -- so all three defects are now pinned by the page-quotes-compiler contract rather than the two that were.

SIX OTHER TESTS pinned the old strings across tests/typechecker.rs and the explain-page width check; all were updated to the new wording (the assertions' intent is unchanged in every case). Two of them carried a SECOND stale case that only surfaced after the first was fixed, so the old strings were swept for globally rather than fixed one failure at a time.
title: OPERATOR-FAILURE DIAGNOSTICS DO NOT SPEAK THE TRAIT LANGUAGE design.md § Operator Traits mandates, and two of them NAME A TRAIT THE USER DOES NOT NEED. The spec is explicit: "Diagnostics for a missing impl (e.g., `vec1 + vec2`) speak the trait language -- \"type Vec[T] does not implement trait Add\" -- not operator language -- \"+ is not defined for Vec[T]\"", and § Notably absent adds that `vec1 + vec2` gets "a diagnostic pointing at `vec.concat(other)` or `vec.extend(other)`". Measured, `[1,2] + [3,4]` reports `arithmetic operator requires numeric type, found 'Vec[i64]'` -- operator language, no trait named, no method redirect. Separately, `==` on a struct reports `does not implement Eq; add #[derive(Eq)]` and `<` reports `does not implement Ord; add #[derive(Ord)]`, but the desugaring runs through `PartialEq` / `PartialOrd` and `#[derive(PartialEq)]` / `#[derive(PartialOrd)]` ALONE is sufficient to compile -- so the message names the total trait when the partial one is what is required. The spec states the `Eq` marker "is never named by the desugaring".
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found alongside the sibling behaviour row while writing the `karac explain --concept=operators` page for B-2026-08-25-23; split from it because these are DIAGNOSTIC-WORDING defects with no behaviour change, and the fixes are independent.

MEASURED:
  [1,2] + [3,4]                    -> arithmetic operator requires numeric type, found 'Vec[i64]'
  UserId(3) + UserId(1)            -> arithmetic operator requires numeric type, found 'UserId'
  struct Q; a == b, no derive      -> type 'Q' does not implement Eq; add #[derive(Eq)] to use == or !=
  struct Q; a <  b, no derive      -> type 'Q' does not implement Ord; add #[derive(Ord)] to use <, <=, >, or >=
  #[derive(PartialEq)] only, a == b -> ACCEPTED   (so `Eq` in the message is not what was needed)
  #[derive(PartialOrd)] only, a < b -> ACCEPTED   (so `Ord` in the message is not what was needed)
  not (a: i64)                     -> unary '!' requires 'bool', found 'i64'

THREE DISTINCT WORDING DEFECTS, in rough order of user cost:

(1) THE ARITHMETIC REJECTION NAMES NO TRAIT AND NO ALTERNATIVE. "requires numeric type" tells a user what the compiler checked, not what they can do. For `Vec` the spec already knows the answer -- `.concat` / `.extend` -- and § Notably absent says the whole reason `impl Add for Vec[T]` does not exist is to force that explicit method name, which only works if the diagnostic actually says it. For a `distinct` type the answer is `#[derive(Arithmetic)]`, which is likewise unmentioned. Both redirects are cheap: the type is in hand at the rejection site.

(2) THE EQ/ORD MESSAGES OVER-PRESCRIBE. Telling a user to add `#[derive(Eq)]` when `#[derive(PartialEq)]` suffices is not merely imprecise -- for a type containing an `f32`/`f64` field it prescribes a derive the language deliberately does NOT offer on floats (design.md: floats are `PartialEq + !Eq` because `NaN != NaN` breaks reflexivity). A user with a float field who follows the message is sent toward a dead end, and the message never mentions the trait that would have worked.

(3) THE `not` MESSAGE SPELLS THE OPERATOR `!`. The parser rejects `!` with `the \`!\` operator is not used in Kara; use \`not\` instead`; the typechecker then describes the very operator the user DID write correctly as `unary '!'`. One of the two spellings is wrong and it is not the parser's.

WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, so this is a wording fix rather than a plumbing one: the user-defined-impl rejection already speaks trait language perfectly -- `user-defined \`impl Add for P\` is not supported in v1; operator traits are stdlib-only` -- and the Eq/Ord messages already name a trait and a machine-applicable derive. The dispatch surface knows the trait; the arithmetic arm just does not reach for it.

DOCUMENTED IN THE MEANTIME: `karac explain --concept=operators` teaches the ACTUAL wording of all four rejections plus the fix for each (including that the partial derive is enough), and `tests/cli.rs::test_operators_page_quotes_live_diagnostics` compiles each case and asserts the page still quotes what the compiler emits -- so improving any of these messages fails that test until the page moves with it. That is the intended coupling, not an obstacle.

fix:
FIXED by a54d41d. The caret now lands on the `[]` itself whenever the origin is known exactly, and falls back to the pre-fix call span whenever it is not.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE OBSTACLE AND WRONG ABOUT WHERE IT SITS. `Type::Error` is indeed payload-free (677 mentions across src/), and putting a span on it is indeed out of scope. But provenance does not have to live on the type: the `let` that binds the literal's type has BOTH halves in hand at once -- the initializer expression, and the inferred type that came out of it. Recording the link there costs one side table and no change to `Type`.

WHAT LANDED:
  * `TypeChecker::uninferrable_binding_origins: FxHashMap<String, Span>` -- binding name -> the bare `[]` span that left its type un-inferrable.
  * `record_uninferrable_binding_origin`, called from BOTH the `Let` and `LetElse` arms of `check_stmt_inner` (the un-annotated branch), gated on the inferred type actually mentioning `Type::Error` -- note `matches!(ty, Type::Error)` is NOT the test, since the error is nested inside `Vec[..]`; a `type_mentions_error` walk is.
  * At the consumption site in `method_user_impl.rs`, an `ExprKind::Identifier` receiver looks its name up and the diagnostic is anchored on the recorded span; anything else keeps `*span`.

THE ROW'S WARNING ABOUT A WRONG CARET IS HONOURED BY CONSTRUCTION, not by care. `sole_bare_empty_literal_span` returns `Some` only when the initializer contains EXACTLY ONE bare empty literal; two candidates return `None` because nothing distinguishes them. And a binding that fails that test REMOVES any stale entry under its name rather than leaving one behind.

THAT REMOVAL IS LOAD-BEARING AND WAS MEASURED, not assumed. With the `None` arm temporarily deleted and the compiler rebuilt, this program:

    fn helper() { let g = P.from([]); println("z"); }
    fn main()   { let g = P.pair([], []); println(g.size()); }

reported the error for `main` while underlining the literal inside `helper` -- a confidently wrong caret in a DIFFERENT FUNCTION, which is strictly worse than the distant-but-correct caret being fixed. Restored, it falls back to the call span. `a_stale_origin_is_not_reused_by_a_later_binding` pins it.

ONLY THE BARE FORM IS TRACKED, deliberately. `Vec[]` already reports at its own span via `E_EMPTY_PREFIX_LITERAL_NEEDS_ANNOTATION`, so counting prefix literals in the scan would let a prefix literal claim a bare literal's diagnostic. Pointing the bare form at its own literal is what makes the two halves of ONE rule agree -- the row framed this as moving a caret, but it is really the bare form catching up to its sibling.

A PRECEDENT WORTH RECORDING, since it looked at first like a reason NOT to do this. `check_unsolved_type_param` deliberately defers for raw pointers, citing design.md § "Method dispatch on raw pointers requires a known pointee": "the diagnostic underlines the read site, not the construction". That is a real convention and it argues for keeping the RAISE POINT at the use -- which this fix does not change. What it does not argue for is keeping the CARET away from the fix site when the fix site is known exactly. The two are separable and only the second was wrong here.

WHAT WAS NOT DONE, and why it is not a live remainder: the message still reads "annotate the value it came from, e.g. `let v: Vec[i64] = [];`" rather than naming the binding and its inferred shape. Doing better needs either source access in the typechecker (it holds none -- spans become line:col only in the CLI renderer) or a secondary-span/note channel on `TypeError` (which has `message`/`span`/`kind`/`lint_name`/`fix_it` and no note field). Both are diagnostics-INFRASTRUCTURE features well beyond this row; with the caret now on the literal, the sentence is read next to the thing it describes, which is what it needed.

TESTS: four in tests/typechecker.rs, asserting on the UNDERLINED SOURCE SLICE rather than a line number so a regression prints what it actually underlined -- the literal is underlined; two candidate literals fall back without guessing; a stale origin is not reused across functions; a healthy binding records nothing and still compiles.

GATES: 9927 tests pass (0 failed), fmt clean, clippy clean on both feature legs.
title: The un-inferrable-type-argument diagnostic points at the first USE, not at the empty literal that caused it, because `Type::Error` carries no provenance. B-2026-08-25-26 fixed the message (it now names the inference failure instead of blaming a bound, and no longer prints `<error>` or an irrelevant implementors list) but left the SPAN, which is the third of that row's three defects.

fix:
FIXED by e2673b8. `PriorityQueue[T: Ord]` gains

    fn peek(ref self) -> Option[T]

in `runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara`, as a real Kāra body like the rest of
that module -- both directions keep their winner at index 0, so it is one index
and no comparisons, and `None` when empty. The row's exact repro now prints `3`.

THE SHAPE IS NOT THE ONE THE ROW SUGGESTED, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. The row
proposed `fn peek(ref self) -> Option[ref T]`, citing `Map.get` / `SortedSet.min`
as precedent. `Option[ref T]` occurs in the stdlib in exactly one place --
`once.kara`'s `OnceCell.get` / `OnceLock.get` -- and both are
`#[compiler_builtin]` stubs whose bodies are never-evaluated placeholders. A real
Kāra body CANNOT INHABIT the type: there is no way to spell `Some(<a reference
into self>)`, and `None` is an `Option[T]`. Probed directly, on a user struct
outside the stdlib:

    fn peek(ref self) -> Option[ref T] { ... Some(self.xs[0]) }
    -> error[typecheck]: expected 'Option[ref T]', found 'Option[T]'   (x2, on
       the `None` return and on the `Some`)

so the suggested signature is unwritable except by moving `PriorityQueue` onto
the compiler intercept the module's header explicitly argues against. `peek`
therefore returns `Option[T]` and COPIES the root: free for a scalar `T`, a
clone for a heap-carrying one, non-disturbing to the queue either way. That is
weaker than Rust's `BinaryHeap::peek` (`Option<&T>`) and the header's complexity
table now says so rather than claiming a bare O(1).

design.md WAS NOT SILENT ON THIS, contrary to the row. The row states that the
spec "does not list `peek` either, so the spec and the impl AGREE and only the
file's own documentation block is wrong." In fact § `PriorityQueue[T]` carried a
"**Not provided:**" paragraph naming `peek` first, with the reason -- "it would
have to hand back an `Option[ref T]`, which needs a compiler intercept rather
than a Kāra body -- see `OnceCell.get`". The row's author read the method table
and not the prose above it. That matters because it inverts the finding: this
was not an undocumented omission, it was a DELIBERATE omission resting on a
premise -- that peek "would have to" return `Option[ref T]` -- which is false.
`Option[T]` is a legitimate shape, it is expressible in a Kāra body, and it
delivers the O(1) root read the archetypal use case needs. The paragraph has been
replaced with one that states what `peek` returns and what the copy costs, the
method table and the summary table (§ Collections) gained rows, and the worked
example now shows peek-then-pop.

VERIFIED, four surfaces byte-identical (`run` JIT / `run --interp` / `build` with
auto-par ON / `build` with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), on the row's repro and on a
15-assertion program covering: empty -> None; min-first and max-first roots;
`from` / `max_first_from` heapify-then-peek; `String` elements; and the
non-disturbance properties that are the whole point of a peek -- peek twice
returns the same element, `len` does not move, and the following `pop` returns
exactly what `peek` promised.

THE ROW'S CENTRAL CLAIM IS NOW EXECUTABLE. The two-heap streaming median (kata
295) runs as a test: a max-first queue over the lower half, a min-first over the
upper, median = the two roots read without removing. Its ten medians are
cross-checked against an independent oracle (Python `bisect.insort` + midpoint
over the same feed) and match exactly -- 5, 10, 5, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 7 -- and the
trailing `lo.len() + hi.len()` is 10, proving twenty `peek` calls removed nothing.

LEAK/UAF ORACLE. `peek` copies an element out of a container behind a `ref`
receiver, which is the exact shape behind several of this repo's ownership
defects -- a shallow copy double-frees, an orphaned original leaks.
`asan_priority_queue_peek_copies_a_heap_root_without_disturbing_it`
(`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`) runs `PriorityQueue[String]` through repeated peeks
and a full drain under `-fsanitize=address`; this container is Linux, so LSan is
live and the run is clean.

TESTS (5 live, all verified RED against the unfixed source, plus 1 deferred):
  - `tests/interpreter.rs` x2 and `tests/codegen.rs` x2 -- twin pairs asserting
    the SAME expected string, which is the parity property this module's real
    Kāra bodies exist to keep honest.
  - `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` x1 -- the LSan oracle above.
  - `asan_priority_queue_peek_drop_count_is_one_per_returned_copy` is written and
    `#[ignore]`d against B-2026-08-25-35; see below.

TWO THINGS FOUND ALONG THE WAY, both filed rather than folded in:

1. B-2026-08-25-35 (new, high) -- `PriorityQueue[T]` is UNINSTANTIABLE FOR EVERY
   USER TYPE. The drop-count ASAN fixture needs a `T` that is both `Ord` (to go
   in the queue) and `Drop` (to count drops), and no user struct can be both:
   `#[derive(Ord)]` makes `<`/`>` work but does NOT satisfy the `T: Ord` bound
   (the candidate list the error prints is primitives only), while a hand-written
   `impl Ord` DOES satisfy the bound but leaves `<`/`>` a hard error inside
   `outranks`. The operator path and the bound path recognize disjoint sets of
   implementations and the two spellings fail at opposite ends. Independent of
