title: `PriorityQueue` HAS NO `peek`: there is NO non-destructive way to read the root, so the archetypal two-heap median use case cannot read a queue's head at the O(1) its own doc comment advertises -- and `runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara`'s header promises `peek / len O(1)` for a method that does not exist in the file or in design.md
detail:
REPRODUCE:

    fn main() {
        let mut q: PriorityQueue[i64] = PriorityQueue.max_first();
        q.push(3);
        match q.peek() { Some(v) => { println(f"{v}"); } None => {} }
    }

-> `error[typecheck]: no method 'peek' on type 'PriorityQueue'`, on all three
surfaces.

THE FILE ADVERTISES IT. `runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara`'s header carries a
complexity table reading:

    push / pop      O(log n)
    peek / len      O(1)
    from            O(n)      -- Floyd heapify, not n pushes
    into_sorted_vec O(n log n)

so the one operation named at O(1) alongside `len` is the one the type does not
have. design.md's method table (§ `PriorityQueue[T]`) does not list `peek`
either, so the spec and the impl AGREE with each other and only the file's own
documentation block is wrong. That makes this two defects with one fix: add the
method, or delete the row -- and deleting the row is the wrong call, for the
reason below.

THERE IS NO WORKAROUND AT THE RIGHT COMPLEXITY. The full surface is new /
max_first / from / max_first_from / push / pop / len / is_empty / clear /
into_sorted_vec. Reading the root without removing it therefore costs either
`pop` + `push` (O(log n) twice, and it MUTATES, so it needs `mut ref` where a
reader wants `ref`) or `into_sorted_vec` (O(n log n) AND consumes the queue).
Neither is a peek.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING CONVENIENCE. The canonical use of a pair of
priority queues is the streaming median (LeetCode 295, kata 295 in kara-katas):
hold a max-first queue over the lower half and a min-first queue over the upper
half, and THE MEDIAN IS THE TWO ROOTS. That query is O(1) precisely because
reading a root is O(1). Without `peek` the textbook algorithm cannot be written
at its textbook cost in Kara, which is a strange thing to be true of a
freshly-landed `PriorityQueue`. Rust's `BinaryHeap::peek`, Java's
`PriorityQueue.peek`, Python's `heap[0]`, C++'s `priority_queue::top` all
provide it.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, matching the file's existing conventions:

    fn peek(ref self) -> Option[ref T]

`ref self` (a reader, unlike push/pop), and `Option[ref T]` rather than
`Option[T]` so it does not clone -- the same choice `Map.get` and
`SortedSet.min` / `.max` already make in this stdlib, and `SortedSet.min` is the
closest existing precedent for 'read the extreme without removing it'.

SOURCE NOTE: found immediately after `PriorityQueue` landed (the
binary_heap.kara -> priority_queue.kara rename), while checking whether kata
295 should stop hand-rolling its heap and use the stdlib type. It cannot,
yet -- not because the type is missing, but because the one operation its
headline algorithm needs on every query is the one absent from it.
tracker: runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara (header complexity table promises `peek`); design.md § `PriorityQueue[T]` method table needs the row too

fix:
FIXED by 7d20106.

Fixed by zero-initializing the synthetic Display accumulator at the ENTRY
block, not only at its use site — one call to the existing
`zero_init_str_acc_at_entry` helper, added to `render_via_display_fn`
(`src/codegen/synth_display.rs`).

ROOT CAUSE, and it is not the `?` desugaring the title suspected. The
entry-point wrapper renders `Error: {e}` through a synthetic accumulator
`cd.acc`, a `{ptr,len,cap}` alloca hoisted to the entry block whose
`{null,0,0}` init was emitted at the USE site — deliberately, so a loop
re-renders from empty. That is correct for the use site and wrong for every
path that never reaches it, because `emit_main_result_err_exit` registers the
accumulator for FUNCTION-scope cleanup via its f-string bridge. The scope-exit
drain therefore ran on the SUCCESS path too, read an uninitialized `cap`, saw
garbage > 0 and called `free` on a garbage pointer. gdb, on the row's own
repro: `free(mem=0x5)` inside `karac_free_buf`, called directly from `main`.

The helper that fixes it already existed and its doc comment already described
this exact failure mode — it was written for the f-string accumulator after
the same bug bit `std.tracing`'s exporter bodies. `render_via_display_fn` is
the second alloca of the same shape and was simply never wired to it. Two
sites, one contract, one of them unenrolled.

THE ROW'S "run-vs-build" FRAMING IS RIGHT AS AN OBSERVABLE AND WRONG AS A
DIAGNOSIS, which matters for anyone who meets this class again. Nothing about
the JIT is broken: both backends emit the identical uninitialized read, and
the IR is the same. AOT survives because `main`'s frame lands on fresh,
zeroed kernel stack pages, so `cap` reads 0 and the `cap > 0` guard skips the
free. Under the JIT `main` runs nested inside the runner, on stack the LLVM
compilation machinery has already dirtied. Measured: 0 failures across 40 AOT
runs at varying stack offsets (env padding 97..3880 bytes), against 5/5
segfaults under the JIT. So AOT is not correct here, it is structurally
lucky, and the bug was always latent in the compiled output.

WHY THE PAYLOAD REPRESENTATION LOOKED LIKE THE DISCRIMINATOR. The row's
measured table (inline scalar crashes, `String` payload and all-unit do not)
is real but incidental: those shapes route through different Display
renderers, and only the ones reaching `render_via_display_fn` allocate the
accumulator at all. The discriminator is which renderer runs, not how the
payload is held.

SCOPE — the function-scope hoist is what makes `main` special. The same
accumulator inside an `if` branch is cleaned up in that branch's own scope, so
it is initialized on exactly the paths that free it; verified by inspecting
the emitted IR for `fn show(v, flag) { if flag { println(f"{v}") } }`, where
the cleanup sits in the `then` block. Only the entry-point wrapper hoists the
cleanup above the branch that initializes it.

VERIFIED across 11 error-type shapes — the row's six (struct-payload,
tuple-payload, payload-variant-last, `AllocError`, all-unit, `String`-payload)
plus a taken-`Err` arm, a 3-word and a 4-word inline payload, the tail
`return Err(…)` spelling, and the original repro — each byte-identical under
`karac run`, `karac run --interp`, `karac build`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`. Regression test
`test_main_question_mark_success_path_does_not_free_uninit_display_acc`
(tests/cli.rs) runs the repro five times, since a single clean run proves
nothing about a fault that depends on stack residue; it segfaults 5/5 at the
parent commit. No ASAN test accompanies it: an uninitialized READ is MSan's
territory, not ASAN's, and the AOT binary ASAN would instrument is the leg
whose zeros make the free benign.
title: `?` in `main()` SEGFAULTS under `karac run` (the default JIT executor) whenever main's error type is an enum with an INLINE SCALAR payload -- `AllocError` included -- while `--interp`, `karac build` and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` all produce the correct output. Minimal repro allocates nothing and never takes the `Err` arm: `fn ok() -> Result[i64, AllocError] { return Ok(7); }` + `fn main() -> Result[(), AllocError] { let x = ok()?; println(x); return Ok(()); }` gives rc=139 with no output, 5/5 runs. An all-unit error enum works, and a `String`-payload error enum (`IoError`) works, so the discriminator is the payload REPRESENTATION, not its presence. `?` in a non-main function is fine, and `main -> Result` without `?` is fine -- it takes both. This silently breaks the fallible-allocation API as design.md spells it, since `v.try_push(x)?` inside `fn main() -> Result[(), AllocError]` is the spec's own example.
detail:
Found while working B-2026-08-25-20; NOT caused by it -- confirmed on clean
`main` (81c3989) with the session's edits stashed and both bins rebuilt.
Deterministic: 5/5 runs segfault.

MINIMAL REPRO -- allocates nothing, and the `Err` arm is never taken:

    fn ok() -> Result[i64, AllocError] { return Ok(7); }
    fn main() -> Result[(), AllocError] {
        let x = ok()?;
        println(x);
        return Ok(());
    }

`karac run` -> rc=139 (SIGSEGV), no output. `karac run --interp` -> `7`.
`karac build` -> `7`. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` -> `7`. So three of the
four surfaces are correct and the DEFAULT executor is the broken one.

WHAT ACTUALLY DISCRIMINATES -- measured one enum shape per compile. It is the
error type's PAYLOAD REPRESENTATION, not the presence of a payload:

  CRASHES (rc=139):
    enum { Oom { bytes: usize }, Over }     struct payload, inline scalar
    enum { A(i64), B }                      tuple payload, inline scalar
    enum { NotFound, Other(i64) }           payload variant last -- order is
                                            not the variable
    AllocError                              the prelude type, same shape
  WORKS (rc=0):
    enum { A, B }                           all-unit
    enum { Other(String), NotFound }        String payload
    IoError                                 units + `Other(String)`

So an inline SCALAR payload (i64/usize) crashes and an out-of-line String
payload does not, which points at the entry-point wrapper codegen emits for
`main() -> Result[(), E]` mis-handling the inline-payload enum layout rather
than at anything in the `?` desugaring itself.

NARROWING THAT RULES THINGS OUT:
  * `?` in a NON-main function with the same error type: fine. It is the
    entry-point wrapper specifically.
  * `main() -> Result[(), AllocError]` with `return Ok(())` and NO `?`: fine.
    Both halves are needed.
  * `.unwrap()` instead of `?`, with `main() -> ()`: fine.
  * Unaffected by KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, KARAC_BUF_CACHE=0,
    KARAC_RC_ELIDE_REF_PARAMS=0.
  * `karac_alloc_fallible` is present and exported in `karac_jit_runner`
    (`nm` confirms `T karac_alloc_fallible`), and is declared with the same
    `malloc_type` signature as `karac_alloc_or_panic`, so this is NOT the
    stale-runner / missing-keep-list class in CLAUDE.md.

WHY IT LOOKED LIKE AN ALLOCATOR BUG AT FIRST, worth recording so the next
reader does not repeat the detour: every early repro reached it through a
`try_*` method (`Vec.try_with_capacity(64)?` alone segfaults; the panicking
`Vec.with_capacity(64)` does not), which reads as "fallible allocation is
broken under the JIT". It is not -- the `try_*` methods are simply the
idiomatic reason a program writes `?` in `main` with an `AllocError` error
type. The allocation is incidental.

BLAST RADIUS: every program whose `main` propagates a scalar-payload error
with `?`. That includes the entire fallible-allocation API as design.md
spells it (`v.try_push(x)?` inside `fn main() -> Result[(), AllocError]` is
the spec's own example at design.md:1870), which is why no existing test
caught it -- `tests/codegen.rs` and `tests/interpreter.rs` both exercise
`try_*` through `match`, never through `?` in `main`.

fix:
FIXED by 7553a08.

Fixed in three layers, because the row's core finding was right: the visible
defect could not be fixed without first fixing the thing that would have
hidden a half-fix.

LAYER 1 -- THE FAIL-OPEN, WHICH HAD LIVE VICTIMS TODAY. The row predicted
this as a hazard of the half-done state; it was already reachable on current
main. `emit_main_result_err_exit` compiled `f"Error: {e}\n"` and, on ANY
codegen failure, silently emitted the bare prefix instead. Measured before
touching anything: `fn main() -> Result[(), (i64, i64)]` printed
`Error: (1, 2)` under `--interp` and `Error: ` under BOTH compiled backends.
Same for `(i64, String, bool)`, `(i64,)`, and `Option[(i64, i64)]`. That is a
run-vs-build divergence on a four-line program, and the fallback is what made
it silent -- the ONLY thing that line carries is the error, so dropping it
turns a compiler gap into a program that reports failure and says nothing
about it. It also made `E_MAIN_ERR_NOT_DISPLAY` a lie downstream: a type that
PASSES that typecheck could still reach codegen unrenderable. The arm now
propagates, with a diagnostic naming the type and saying the exit line would
print nothing.

LAYER 2 -- WHY THE TUPLES WERE UNRENDERABLE. Not a missing renderer: the
entry point's Display operand is SYNTHESIZED, so it carried
`Span::default()`, and every span-keyed Display table (`display_tuple_types`,
`display_option_result_types`, `display_vec_types`, the Map/Set pair,
`display_generic_enum_types`) missed. Shapes with a second, NAME-keyed
registration -- `Vec`, `Map`, `Set`, `Option`-of-scalar, via
`register_var_from_type_expr` -- survived on that; a tuple has no name-keyed
twin, so it fell through to the value-kind arms, which cannot tell a tuple
from a struct. Fixed by seeding the same span-keyed tables at the operand's
own span (`seed_synthetic_display_tables`) rather than growing a name-keyed
twin per shape, so the entry point renders whatever a real `f"{x}"` renders.
The operand's span is now `usize::MAX`-offset so the key cannot collide with
a real expression's -- the previous `Span::default()` was not "absent", it was
the perfectly ordinary key `(0, 0)`. All three tuple shapes now agree across
`--interp` / JIT / AOT; `Option[(i64,i64)]` is now a HARD BUILD ERROR, which
is what the same operand already got in an ordinary `f"{o}"`, so the entry
point and the rest of the language finally agree.

LAYER 3 -- THE ALLOCERROR PROSE ITSELF. `#[derive(Display)]` dropped,
hand-written `impl Display` added, per § `#[derive(Display)]` on enums'
sanctioned escape. `Debug` stays derived and still renders the struct-variant
shape (asserted as the control). Two codegen changes make a PRELUDE manual
impl reachable at all:

  (a) `alloc_error` registered in `compiled_stdlib_programs`, so codegen
      compiles the impl body and `AllocError.to_string` exists in the module.
      Unconditional, like `ordering`: the body calls nothing that calls it
      back, so the zero-use prune removes it whole from programs that never
      display an `AllocError`. MEASURED: an `AllocError`-free binary is
      336896 bytes before and after -- byte-identical -- so no usage gate is
      warranted (`protobuf`/`cli` need theirs only because their bodies are
      mutually recursive and survive the prune).

  (b) `baked_display_enum_names` now admits a baked enum with a MANUAL
      `impl Display`, not only a derived one. The set's job is "this enum's
      Display goes through the value/user path", which is a property of
      HAVING a Display, not of how it was spelled; recognising only the derive
      is what dropped a prelude enum out of every codegen Display path the
      moment it took design.md up on its own override advice.

All three Display paths -- `e.to_string()`, `f"{e}"`, and the entry-point
`Error: {e}` line -- now render `out of memory: 4096 bytes` /
`capacity overflow` identically on `--interp`, `karac run` (JIT), `karac build`
and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

A FIFTH INSTANCE OF B-2026-08-25-33 FELL OUT. Routing `AllocError` to the
user-impl arm made `fn main() -> Result[(), AllocError] { let x = ok()?; }`
SEGFAULT under `karac run` on the SUCCESS path (5/5 runs) -- caught by that
bug's own regression test, which happens to use `AllocError`. Same defect,
new site: `fstr_render_part`'s `fstr.ud.acc` is an entry-hoisted alloca
stored at the USE site and registered for FUNCTION-scope cleanup, so the
drain read an uninitialized `cap` on paths that never rendered. Guarded with
`zero_init_str_acc_at_entry`, and its unguarded twin `fstr.str.acc` in the
same function guarded alongside it rather than left as the next instance.
The wider class -- ~16 further `create_entry_alloca` + `track_vec_var` pairs
with no entry init -- is filed separately rather than swept here.

TESTS. Three in `tests/cli.rs`, each verified to FAIL on the unfixed compiler
and pass on the fixed one (`git stash push -- src runtime`, rebuild, run):
`test_alloc_error_displays_its_specified_prose_on_every_backend` (every
Display path, both variants, all three backends, with `dbg` as the
Debug-unchanged control), `test_main_result_error_never_prints_a_bare_prefix`
(ten `E` shapes spanning both lookup routes, each compared against the
interpreter oracle -- and asserting the ORACLE itself printed something, so a
silently-empty oracle cannot make the comparison vacuous), and
`test_unrenderable_main_error_is_a_build_error_not_an_empty_message`.

ONE EXISTING TEST HAD PINNED THE BUG. `alloc_error_prelude_type_usable_
without_import` asserted `"CapacityOverflow"` -- the derived shape -- so it
passed for the whole time design.md's sentence was false. Corrected to
`"capacity overflow"` with the history recorded at the assertion.

Docs: phase-8-stdlib-floor.md's entry named this exact follow-up ("Display
currently uses the default ... rendering, not the design's custom wording")
and quoted the now-stale derive list; both updated. design.md needed no
change -- its § Fallible Allocation sentence is simply true now.

Gates, re-run on merged main (this landed on top of ~950 lines from four
sibling sessions): llvm suite 15306 passed / 0 failed across 126 targets,
default suite 9995/0 across 124 targets, clippy 0 on BOTH feature legs with
--all-targets, cargo fmt clean. The first post-merge run failed one E2E case
on `undefined reference to karac_map_reserve` -- a STALE archive, from the

title: `AllocError`'s `Display` renders the Debug form (`OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: 4096 }`) into the user-facing `Error: {e}` entry-point line, and the spec-sanctioned fix -- a manual `impl Display`, per § `#[derive(Display)]` on enums' "Implement `Display` manually to override" -- CANNOT LAND without codegen work: a prelude impl lives in `STDLIB_PROGRAMS`, which codegen does not walk, so the impl reaches the interpreter only. Registering the module as a compiled stdlib program fixes `.to_string()` under AOT but leaves `f"{e}"` and the entry-point line unfixed. Worse, the half-done state FAILS OPEN: dropping the derive without teaching codegen about the impl makes `karac build` emit `Error: ` with an EMPTY message rather than erroring, because the typechecker sees the impl and codegen does not.
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-25-20(2), whose Display leg is not the one-line edit
it reads as. Measured end to end.

THE DEFECT AS REPORTED IS REAL and the damage is user-facing: `AllocError`
reaches end users through design.md:6413's `Result[(), E: Display]` entry-point
contract, which prints `Error: {e}` to stderr. Today that line reads
`Error: OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: 4096 }` -- the Debug form, field name
and braces included -- on all three backends.

THE SPEC CONFLICT RESOLVES CLEANLY, so this is not a spec question.
design.md § Fallible Allocation pins prose ("names the failed operation's byte
size on the `OutOfMemory` arm and \"capacity overflow\" on the
`CapacityOverflow` arm") while § `#[derive(Display)]` on enums pins the derived
shape. The derive section names the escape itself: "Implement `Display`
manually to override the derived representation entirely." So the intended fix
is a MANUAL `impl Display for AllocError`, with `Debug` left derived. Note the
derived shape is NOT itself wrong here: `src/typechecker/derives.rs:1308` says
both backends deliberately agree on `Variant { name: v }` for a struct variant,
so the derive needs no change.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE EDIT -- all measured on a real build of the change:

  1. A manual `impl Display` in `runtime/stdlib/alloc_error.kara` reaches the
     INTERPRETER but not CODEGEN. Prelude impls live in `STDLIB_PROGRAMS`,
     which `src/codegen.rs:8432` documents codegen does NOT walk. With just
     the `.kara` edit: interpreter and the entry-point `Error:` line render
     the new prose correctly, while `karac build` fails outright on
     `println(f"{e}")` and `e.to_string()` ("no handler for method
     'to_string'").

  2. Registering `alloc_error` in `compiled_stdlib_programs` (gated on use via
     `Program.referenced_type_names`, the B-2026-08-25-2 mechanism) fixes
     `.to_string()` under AOT -- verified printing `capacity overflow` -- but
     NOT the other two Display paths. `f"{e}"` still fails with "Display of a
     struct in an f-string is supported when the interpolated expression is a
     variable or field access" even though the operand IS a plain variable,
     and the entry-point line still does not consult the impl. Both need
     codegen work: `user_display_impl_type` (src/codegen/synth_display.rs:1914)
     resolves a user impl by looking up `<Type>.to_string` in the module, and
     the enum-name predicate feeding it does not admit a prelude enum.

  3. THE HALF-DONE STATE FAILS OPEN, which is the part that makes this worth
     its own row. Removing `#[derive(Display)]` without teaching codegen about
     the manual impl leaves the entry-point path emitting an EMPTY message:
     `karac build` succeeds and the program prints `Error: ` with nothing after
     it. The typechecker accepts `main() -> Result[(), AllocError]` because it
     DOES see the impl; codegen then renders nothing. A missing Display under
     codegen should be a hard error, not an empty string -- that fail-open
     behaviour is independent of `AllocError` and is the more dangerous finding
     here.

The session reverted the change rather than ship (2) or (3): under codegen (2)
turns a working `println(f"{e}")` into a compile error and (3) turns a wrong
message into a silent one. Both are strictly worse than the reported bug.

fix:
FIXED by 5964c16, narrowing the spec sentence to the method that exists, and by deleting two STALE entries from `karac explain --concept=operators`'s divergence list -- one of which this fix itself invalidated.

MEASURED on 0398a18, one program per claim. The row is accurate except for one detail, corrected below:
  a + b        (Vec[i64])  -> type 'Vec[i64]' does not implement trait Add;
                              there is deliberately no `impl Add for Vec[T]` --
                              use `a.extend(b)` to append b's elements to a
  a.concat(b)  (Vec[i64])  -> Vec.concat() requires String elements
  a.concat("-")(Vec[i64])  -> Vec.concat() requires String elements
  a.concat("-")(Vec[String])-> Vec.concat() expects 0 argument(s), found 1
  a.append(b)              -> no method 'append' on type 'Vec'
  a.extend(b)              -> accepted
  v.concat()   (Vec[String])-> accepted, yields String

CORRECTION TO THE ROW: it attributes `Vec.concat() expects 0 argument(s), found 1` to `a.concat("-")` on a `Vec[i64]`. Measured, that receiver reports `requires String elements` -- the element-type check fires before the arity check. The arity message appears on a `Vec[String]` receiver. Both messages are real; only which receiver produces which was swapped.

THE DIAGNOSTIC WAS ALREADY RIGHT. B-2026-08-25-30 (3964ede) had already made `vec1 + vec2` speak trait language and name `a.extend(b)` alone, and left a NOTE at `src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs::arithmetic_rejection_message` explaining why `concat` is deliberately not named there. So nothing in the compiler needed changing -- this row was the design.md sentence still promising what the diagnostic had stopped promising.

WHAT THE SENTENCE NOW SAYS: it quotes the live diagnostic verbatim, states that `Vec.concat()` is a different already-shipped operation (zero-argument `Vec[String]` join -- `join` with an empty separator), states that `append` does not exist, and -- the part a reader actually needs -- states the SEMANTIC CONSEQUENCE the old sentence hid: `extend` is in-place and requires a `mut` receiver (`cannot call `extend` on `a` -- `a` is declared without `mut``), while `vec1 + vec2` asks for a VALUE. There is no producing two-`Vec` concatenation, and the obvious name for one is taken by the `String`-joining `concat()`. That is a real gap, stated rather than papered over; adding a producing form is an API decision, not a bug fix, so it is not made here.

TWO STALE BULLETS REMOVED from the `operators` explain page's "Where the implementation differs from design.md today" list, both verified stale by compiling the case:
  * "Missing-impl diagnostics speak OPERATOR language ... it currently reports
    'arithmetic operator requires numeric type, found Vec[i64]' and names no
    trait or method" -- FALSE since 3964ede. The page's own main body already
    taught the corrected wording, so the page CONTRADICTED ITSELF: a reader who
    got the trait-language message and then consulted the page was told the
    compiler does not emit it. Left behind when -30 closed.
  * "design.md offers `vec.concat(other)` as one of the two redirects" --
    invalidated by this commit's own design.md edit. Removing it in the same
    commit is the point: a divergence note that outlives its divergence is the
    same defect as the one it documented.
The two remaining bullets (operator-boundary widening, bitwise `Not` on
integers) were re-measured and are STILL TRUE, so they stay; they are
B-2026-08-25-29's, in flight in another session, and were deliberately not
touched.

GUARD: `tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs::operator_traits_vec_redirect_names_only_extend` reads the shipped `docs/design.md` and fails if the paragraph names `concat` as a redirect again. It is a PROSE guard, which is the point -- the claim lives in a sentence, not a fenced block, so `scripts/design-conformance.py` (which lints only code blocks) could never have caught it, and did not. The compiler half was already pinned by `tests/cli.rs::test_operators_page_quotes_live_diagnostics`'s "vecredirect" case, so spec and implementation are now pinned from both ends.

The guard caught its own author on the first run: the replacement note originally QUOTED the old wording ("an earlier draft offered `vec.concat(other)`"), which a substring check cannot distinguish from offering it. Reworded the note rather than weakening the assertion.
title: design.md § Operator Traits § Notably absent prescribes `vec.concat(other)` as one of the two redirects for `vec1 + vec2`, but `Vec.concat()` in this implementation is a DIFFERENT operation: zero-argument and `Vec[String]`-only, joining a Vec's own String elements into one String. There is no two-Vec concatenation method at all -- `a.concat(b)` on a `Vec[i64]` reports `Vec.concat() requires String elements`, `a.concat("-")` reports `Vec.concat() expects 0 argument(s), found 1`, and `append` does not exist. Only `extend` (in-place, any element type) does what the spec sentence promises.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-25-30, which rewrote the `vec1 + vec2` diagnostic to name a redirect. The spec sentence was the obvious text to quote; measuring it first is what stopped a diagnostic from pointing users at a method that errors.

MEASURED, on a fresh build:
  [1,2].concat([3,4])      -> Vec.concat() requires String elements
  ["x","y"].concat("-")    -> Vec.concat() expects 0 argument(s), found 1
  [1,2].append([3])        -> no method 'append' on type 'Vec'
  let mut c = [1,2]; c.extend([9,10]); c.len()  -> 4     (works, any element type)

So `Vec.concat()` is Rust's `Vec<String>::concat()` -- a join of the receiver's own elements -- not `a.concat(b)`. The spec sentence reads as though it were the latter.

DECIDED IN -30, AND WORTH RE-DECIDING HERE RATHER THAN INHERITING: the diagnostic names only `extend`, and the `karac explain --concept=operators` page records the divergence. Emitting the spec's wording verbatim would have been actively harmful -- a `Vec[i64]` user following `vec.concat(other)` lands on "requires String elements", which is a worse dead end than the vague message the fix replaced.

THE FIX IS A CHOICE, NOT A LOOKUP, which is why this is its own row:
  (a) amend design.md to say `extend` only -- smallest change, and arguably
      what the spec meant, since `extend` is the operation that exists;
  (b) add a two-Vec `concat(other) -> Vec[T]` returning a new Vec, which is
      what the spec sentence promises and what a reader expects from the name.
      Note this would COLLIDE with the existing zero-arg `Vec[String].concat()`
      unless that one is renamed (`join`?) or the two are distinguished by
      arity -- the collision is the real design question, and it is why (b) is
      not obviously right despite matching the prose.
Whoever takes this should decide (a) vs (b) deliberately; -30 deliberately did not, since a diagnostic must name a method that exists TODAY either way.

SEVERITY: low. Nothing miscompiles and no user is misled by the compiler any more -- the diagnostic and the explain page both name only `extend`. What remains is that design.md, the authoritative spec, describes a method surface that does not exist, which will mislead the next person transcribing that section.

fix:
FIXED by 7da2bfe, narrowing the spec, and the reason is better than the one this row recorded when it was filed.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW, which I filed and which overstated its own case. It says "there is NO cryptographic hash anywhere in the stdlib: no sha256, no blake3, no `crypto` namespace" and treats that as an over-promise the spec makes and does not keep. The first half is true and still is. The framing is not: `std.crypto` is COMMITTED AND SCHEDULED, not undesigned. `docs/deferred.md § std.crypto` carries a full design section with an algorithm table whose committed choices include BLAKE3 for general hashing (chosen over SHA-2 precisely so callers do not need HMAC wrapping), and `docs/roadmap.md:1060` places the module at Phase 11+ (P1), blocked on FFI stabilisation (Phase 9) so the primitives delegate to a vetted C library rather than being reimplemented in Kara. I did not check either tracker before filing.

So the crypto half was never a promise with nothing behind it — it was a promise whose backing the § Hash paragraph failed to POINT AT. It now does: the paragraph names `deferred.md § std.crypto`, names BLAKE3, gives the phase and the blocker, and says outright that the honest answer until then is an external library. The substitution warning that made this row worth filing at all -- do not reach for `siphash24`, it is a keyed PRF and not collision-resistant -- is unchanged and now sits next to the pointer.

THE `xxh3` HALF IS DROPPED RATHER THAN TRACKED, on a stronger argument than the one in this row's detail. That argument was "we cannot implement XXH3 safely without the reference 192-byte secret and official KAT vectors". True, but it is an argument about difficulty, and difficulty is not why it should not ship. The real reason is REDUNDANCY: the use case xxh3 was named for -- a fast digest for content addressing -- is better served by BLAKE3, which the committed `std.crypto` set above already carries, which is in the same speed class, and which is collision-resistant as well. Shipping XXH3 alongside it would leave three overlapping stable-hash options where the third is the ONLY one that is neither DoS-resistant nor collision-resistant: a choice every user would have to get right, for no capability they would not already have. design.md now says this in those terms.

THE EXPLAIN PAGE'S DIVERGENCE SECTION IS RETIRED, which is the other half of the fix and the easy half to forget. `karac explain --concept=stable-hash` carried a "Where the implementation differs from design.md today" list naming `hash.stable.xxh3` (a spelling B-2026-08-25-22 had already superseded) and the `crypto` module. After this edit the spec and the implementation AGREE on both, so a divergence section describing their disagreement would be exactly the defect B-2026-08-26-1 was filed for -- a note that outlives its divergence. It is replaced by "What this namespace does NOT give you", which states the same two absences as deliberate, with the tracker pointer for one and the supersession reason for the other.

GUARDS. `tests/cli.rs::test_stable_hash_page_claims_match_the_compiler` still compiles a program per absent facility and fails if either starts resolving, so the day `std.crypto` lands the page cannot keep saying it has not; its assertions were retargeted from the old wording to the new. A new prose guard, `tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs::hash_section_points_the_crypto_gap_at_its_tracker`, pins that the stability paragraph keeps naming `deferred.md § std.crypto`, names BLAKE3, and keeps the "not a collision-resistant hash" warning -- a prose guard because the claim lives in a sentence, where `scripts/design-conformance.py` (code blocks only) cannot see it.

NOTHING IS STRANDED BY THE NARROWING, which is what made it the right call rather than the cheap one: `StableHash.siphash24` (B-2026-08-25-22) already gives every caller a working stable digest. That is the test this row's sibling B-2026-08-25-22 failed -- there, narrowing would have deleted the only escape hatch, so the facility had to be built. Here the escape hatch exists and the two remaining names were a scheduled module and a redundant one.
title: TWO MORE FACILITIES design.md § `Hash` and `Hasher`'s stability paragraph NAMES AS SHIPPED DO NOT EXIST, after B-2026-08-25-22 built the third. (1) `xxh3(bytes)` -- a faster UNKEYED stable digest; nothing in `src/`, `runtime/` or `hash/` implements XXH3, and there is now no fast stable option at all (`StableHash.siphash24` is the only one, and it is the keyed, slower one). (2) "the `crypto` module for cryptographic hashes" -- there is NO cryptographic hash anywhere in the stdlib: no sha256, no blake3, no `crypto` namespace. The second is the consequential one, because `siphash24` is now sitting where a user looking for a digest will find it, and SipHash is a fast keyed PRF, NOT collision-resistant -- a user who substitutes it for a cryptographic hash (signatures, dedup against an adversary, anything where a chosen collision matters) gets something that looks like it works.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-25-22 rather than left inside it, per the "if a closed-out investigation leaves a live remainder, split it into its own open row" rule -- -22 shipped `StableHash.siphash24` and closed; these two are what its paragraph still over-promises.

MITIGATED, NOT HIDDEN, IN THE MEANTIME. `karac explain --concept=stable-hash` carries a "Where the implementation differs from design.md today" section naming both as DOES NOT EXIST, and spelling out why `siphash24` is not a substitute for the crypto half. `tests/cli.rs::test_stable_hash_page_claims_match_the_compiler` compiles a program using each and asserts the compiler still rejects it, so the day either ships the test fails and the page must be updated with it. design.md § `Hash` and `Hasher` carries the same "Not yet shipped, and not to be improvised around" note.

WHY XXH3 WAS NOT HAND-ROLLED ALONGSIDE SIPHASH-2-4, which is the useful half of this row for whoever picks it up. SipHash-2-4 was ~15 lines on top of machinery `hash/src/lib.rs` already had (the permutation, generic now over its two round counts) AND had an exact in-tree oracle: `std`'s deprecated `SipHasher` IS SipHash-2-4, so correctness was checkable over 4 keys x 41 lengths without transcribing a single constant. XXH3 has neither property. It is ~500-700 lines with distinct code paths for lengths 0, 1-3, 4-8, 9-16, 17-128, 129-240 and >240, and it is parameterized by `kSecret`, a fixed 192-BYTE table. There is no oracle for it in `std` and no vetted dependency that clears `karac-hash`'s zero-dependency bar (that bar is load-bearing: the crate is linked into the runtime's wasm32-wasip1, wasm32-wasip1-threads and Cortex-M archives). A hand-rolled XXH3 whose secret table or long-input path is subtly wrong produces digests that CLAIM to be XXH3 and are not -- which is strictly worse than not shipping it, because the entire reason to pick XXH3 over `siphash24` is agreeing with other implementations of XXH3. So the work item is not "write XXH3": it is "vendor the reference secret and the official KAT vectors, or admit a dependency and justify it against the target matrix".

THE CRYPTO HALF IS A DIFFERENT AND LARGER DECISION -- a cryptographic hash in the stdlib means a constant-time implementation, a versioning/deprecation policy for the algorithms, and probably a dependency; it is not a slice of this row so much as a roadmap entry that this paragraph is currently writing cheques for.

WHICH SIDE MOVES IS STILL THE OWNER'S CALL, and unlike -22 the "narrow the sentence" option is now genuinely available: with `StableHash.siphash24` shipped, the paragraph's warning against `Hash` has a working escape hatch, so deleting the `xxh3` and `crypto` promises would no longer strand anyone. That was the argument that forced implementation for -22 and it does not apply here.

title: `PriorityQueue[T]` IS UNINSTANTIABLE FOR EVERY USER TYPE, because the OPERATOR path and the TRAIT-BOUND path recognize DISJOINT sets of `Ord` implementations: `#[derive(Ord)]` makes `<`/`>` work but does NOT satisfy a `T: Ord` bound, while a hand-written `impl Ord` DOES satisfy the bound but leaves `<`/`>` a hard error. Neither spelling reaches a working `PriorityQueue[UserType]`, and the operator diagnostic actively misdirects: it tells the hand-impl author to `add #[derive(Ord)]`, which then fails at the bound instead.
detail:
MEASURED on 00db404-era `main` (i.e. AFTER 3964ede, the B-2026-08-25-30 operator-diagnostic
rewrite) + the B-2026-08-25-32 `peek` commit, one program per claim,
all four surfaces (`run`, `run --interp`, `build`, `build` with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 -- they agree):

  A. `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct Item { id: i64 }`, bare `a < b`
     -> ACCEPTED, builds and runs.

  B. the SAME derived struct, `let mut q: PriorityQueue[Item] = PriorityQueue.new(); q.push(..)`
     -> error[typecheck]: method 'push' is not callable on this `PriorityQueue`: trait bound
        `T: Ord` is not satisfied; `Item` does not implement `Ord`; trait `Ord` is implemented
        by: Bf16, F16, F32, F64, String, bool, char, i16, i32, i64, i8, isize, u16, u32, u64,
        u8, usize
     Note the candidate list: PRIMITIVES ONLY. `#[derive(Ord)]` registers nothing the bound
     checker can see.

  C. hand-written `impl Ord for Item { fn cmp(ref self, other: ref Item) -> Ordering {..} }`
     (plus PartialEq/Eq/PartialOrd), bare `a < b`
     -> error[typecheck]: type 'Item' does not implement PartialOrd; add #[derive(PartialOrd)]
        to use <, <=, >, or >=
     The operator path does not see the `impl` block either -- note the program declares
     `impl PartialOrd for Item` on the line above and is told it does not implement PartialOrd.
     The suggestion is the defect's sharpest edge: following it lands the author in case B.

  D. the SAME hand-impl struct in a `PriorityQueue` -> the BOUND IS SATISFIED (push/pop/peek
     all resolve), and the failure moves INTO the stdlib body, at
     `runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara`'s `outranks`, which compares elements with `>` / `<`:
       build: error: codegen failed: Unsupported struct binary op: Gt
       run --interp: runtime error: operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type 'Struct'
                     and 'Struct' (this is a type error the typechecker reports as a hard error;
                     it reached the interpreter only because `karac run` executes despite
                     typecheck errors)

So the two registries are DISJOINT, and the two spellings fail at OPPOSITE ends: derive is
stopped at the call site, impl is stopped inside the stdlib body. There is no third spelling.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A HIGH. `PriorityQueue[T: Ord]` is documented in design.md § `PriorityQueue[T]`
and in the module header as a generic collection over any `T: Ord`, and `Ord` is a user-
implementable trait -- design.md § Operator Traits presents both `#[derive(Ord)]` and a manual
`impl` as ways to get one. In practice the type only works for the built-in `Ord` primitives and
`String`. A user with a `Task { priority, name }` -- the single most obvious reason to reach for a
priority queue at all -- cannot use it, and the compiler tells them to do the one thing that
makes it worse. The same disjointness should be checked on `SortedSet[T]` / `SortedMap[K, V]`
and on `Vec.sort()`, which carry the same bound; this row measured only `PriorityQueue`.

NOT A REGRESSION OF B-2026-07-03-7, THOUGH IT LOOKS LIKE ONE. That row (fixed, ba67416e) reported
the same two error strings -- 'operator Lt is not defined for operands of type Struct and Struct'
and 'Unsupported struct binary op' -- for a `#[derive(Ord)]` struct. Its fix made the DERIVE case
work, which is exactly what measurement A above confirms still holds. What was never covered is
the hand-written `impl Ord`, which reaches the identical two messages by the other route (D). Do
not close this by re-testing the derived case: that half is green and has been since ba67416e.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while writing the leak/drop-count ASAN oracle for B-2026-08-25-32
(`PriorityQueue.peek`). The natural way to count drops is a `T` with a `Drop` body, and a `T` in a
`PriorityQueue` must be `Ord`, so the fixture needs a user struct that is BOTH -- which this
defect makes unconstructible. `asan_priority_queue_peek_drop_count_is_one_per_returned_copy` in
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` is written and carries `#[ignore]` naming this row; un-ignoring it is
the acceptance test for the fix. The `peek` leak oracle over `PriorityQueue[String]` is unaffected
and runs clean under LSan.

DIAGNOSTIC WORDING RE-MEASURED AFTER 3964ede. An earlier draft of this row quoted case C as
"does not implement Ord; add #[derive(Ord)]", which is what the compiler said before
B-2026-08-25-30's fix landed mid-investigation. The message now names PartialOrd on both
halves. Only the wording moved: all four measurements above were re-run against the
rebased tree and the behaviour is unchanged, so the finding is not a consequence of that
fix and is not fixed by it.
fix:
FIXED by 8af03a8 -- the DERIVE half. A `#[derive(Ord)]` user type is now usable in a
`PriorityQueue` and in any bounded generic impl, end-to-end, with the two backends
byte-identical. The HAND-WRITTEN-IMPL half is deliberately NOT fixed and moves to
B-2026-08-26-7; the reason is measured and is the more important half of this close.

THE ROW'S TWO-REGISTRY DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, AND THE CORRECTION MATTERS. It described
"the OPERATOR path and the TRAIT-BOUND path" as recognizing disjoint sets. There are
THREE paths, and the bound is checked by two DIFFERENT ones with different powers:

  type_supports_partial_ord   the `<` operator                  derive only
  type_satisfies_bound        bound on a FREE generic fn         derive + impl table
  Env::bound_satisfied        bound on a GENERIC IMPL's method   impl table only

So the row's clean "derive fails the bound / impl satisfies the bound" split is not
the shape of it. A derive satisfies the bound on a free generic fn and fails it on a
generic impl's method -- the SAME type, the SAME bound, two answers decided by which
side of the call the bound was written on. Measured:

  fn free[T: Ord](a: T) -> i64                     + #[derive(Ord)] Item -> ACCEPTED
  impl[T: Ord] Holder[T] { fn tag(ref self) .. }   + #[derive(Ord)] Item -> REJECTED

PriorityQueue's whole surface is the second kind, which is why the row's headline
symptom looked total.

WHAT LANDED, two halves both required:

1. Env::bound_satisfied consults the derive tables. Its own comment asserted that
   named-type derive satisfaction "stays with the richer type_satisfies_bound, which
   this env gate cannot reach" -- that is false: TypeEnv owns `structs`/`enums`. The
   per-trait derive names mirror the type_supports_* helpers exactly, supertrait
   closure included, so #[derive(Ord)] answers a PartialOrd query.

2. A monomorph substitution in codegen. With the bound open, `outranks` still failed:
   it compares two INDEXED elements (`self.xs[i] > self.xs[j]`), and resolving that
   element's type name walked the DECLARED field type -- `Vec[T]` on
   `struct PriorityQueue[=T]` -- yielding `T`, the impl's type PARAMETER rather than
   the monomorph's argument. `T` names no struct, so the ordered-comparison dispatch
   declined and codegen reported "Unsupported struct binary op: Gt". Same class as
   B-2026-08-25-28. Note the row's own case D attributed that error to the hand-impl
   spelling; it was actually the monomorph blindness, and it hit the derive spelling
   identically once the bound let it through.

WHY THE HAND-IMPL HALF MUST NOT BE FIXED THE SAME WAY. Four helpers lack the user-impl
fallback that type_supports_ord has (partial_ord, partial_eq, eq, hash), and adding it
is one line each. That change was written, measured, and REVERTED. It does not make the
operator call the user's body; it makes the compiler apply DERIVE machinery to a type
whose author asked for something else:

  - `impl Ord` whose `cmp` REVERSES the order: `a < b` evaluated by DECLARATION ORDER,
    contradicting the body. A PriorityQueue[Item] holding ids 1/3/2 popped 1, where the
    user's cmp demands 3. Silent wrong answer, both backends would agree on it.
  - the same path in `if a < b { .. }` did not even produce a bool --
    "Module verification failed: Branch condition is not 'i1' type!  br i64 0" -- and
    `f"{a < b}"` printed `0`, the raw comparator i64. The interpreter reported
    "path 'Item.lt' has no interpreter evaluation rule", i.e. the desugaring targets a
    method the user never wrote and nothing supplies.
  - `impl PartialEq` comparing ONLY `id` on a two-field struct: both backends printed
    NOT-equal for two values the user's `eq` calls equal. They AGREE with each other, so
    the A/B rule cannot catch it -- the quietest of the four.
  - `impl Hash` hashing only `id`, as a Map key: `m.len()` was 2 where the user's hash
    collides to 1.

The derive-only gate is PROTECTIVE, not an oversight: it is what stands between a user
and those silent wrong answers. It stays until operator-trait dispatch actually calls
user bodies. B-2026-08-26-7 carries all four measurements plus the self-contradicting
diagnostics ("`Item` does not implement `Hash`; trait `Hash` is implemented by: Item"),
and `hand_written_partial_ord_impl_still_does_not_enable_the_operator` in
tests/typechecker.rs pins the rejection with the reasoning inline so it is not "fixed"
later by relaxing it.

The same finding forced a gate on the codegen half: the `<`/`>` dispatch now requires a
DERIVE, not mere membership in `ord_orderable_types` (which deliberately includes
hand-written impls). Without it the monomorph fix let hand-impl types reach the
declaration-order comparator in AOT while the interpreter still errored -- converting
"both backends fail loudly" into a run/build divergence with a silent wrong answer on
one side. `Vec.sort()` keeps the wider set; only the operator dispatch narrows.

A REGRESSION THE TARGETED RUN MISSED. The float wrappers F32/F64/F16/Bf16 are seeded in
codegen from hard-coded shapes rather than walked out of the prelude AST, so
register_ord_orderable_types never saw their real
#[derive(Eq, Ord, Hash, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Copy)] and the new derive gate declined on
them: `iter.max()` / `.min()` over an F64 failed with the very error this row removes.
Registered explicitly. Two codegen tests caught it in the FULL suite after the targeted
run was green -- the gate was correct, the population was incomplete.

A DEFECT THIS FIX MAKES REACHABLE, filed as B-2026-08-26-6 (high). With derived types
finally admitted, an element carrying `impl Drop` exposes that PriorityQueue.push runs
the drop glue for its by-value parameter on a value it has ALREADY MOVED into the backing
Vec: it drops once at push and again at pop, AOT only (the interpreter drops once), and
LSan reports 31 bytes leaked in 8 allocations once the element also owns a String.
Pre-existing and previously unreachable, since no user type could enter a PriorityQueue
at all. Its ASAN oracle is written and #[ignore]d against that row, with the CORRECT
expected sequence rather than current output.

TESTS: 3 in tests/typechecker.rs -- two verified RED against the unfixed tree, one the
deliberate-non-fix pin -- plus 2 codegen E2E (RED) and 2 interpreter twins. The
interpreter twins are PARITY tests and are labelled as such in their doc comments: they
do NOT go red, because that harness's run() does not assert the typecheck is clean and
`karac run` demotes typecheck errors to warnings, so the tree-walker never enforced the
bound at all. Calling them regression oracles would have overstated the coverage.

GATES: full --features llvm suite 15,207 passed / 0 failed / 19 ignored across 110
targets, KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1, zero skip notices. fmt clean; clippy clean on
both the default and --features llvm legs.

BOTH FOLLOW-UP ROWS WERE RENUMBERED from -3/-4 to -6/-7 during the final rebase: another
session allocated -3/-4 for unrelated bugs while this was in verification.

FIXED by 3988b47. `LazyLock[T]` ships: prelude type, interpreter arms, and
codegen, verified byte-identical under `--interp`, `karac run`,
`karac build` and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`.

The row framed the remaining work as an owner call between shipping the
specification and deleting design.md's tables, and priced shipping as "real
work across three phases". It was cheaper than that, because the engine
already existed: `OnceLock`'s `get_or_init` runs a closure exactly once
behind a thread-safe guard, which IS `LazyLock`'s mechanic — the two differ
only in where the closure comes from. So the work was wiring a new front end
onto a proven back end, not building one.

  * Stdlib: `struct LazyLock[=T] { handle_id: i64 }` plus
    `#[compiler_builtin] new(init: Fn() -> T)` and `get(ref self) -> ref T`,
    sharing `once.kara` and `OnceLock`'s handle space. `get` returns `ref T`
    rather than `Option[ref T]` because there is no unfilled state a caller
    can observe — design.md's family table already said "Method surface:
    `get` only".
  * Interpreter: `lazy_init_table` holds the closure from `new`; the first
    `get` runs it and caches into the existing `once_table`, so a second
    `get` short-circuits before the closure is even looked up.
  * Codegen: `LazyLock.new` is a recognized module-binding initializer form,
    so the closure is statically known at every `get` site — it is recorded
    in `lazy_var_inits` and `X.get()` compiles as
    `X.get_or_init(<that closure>)`, reusing `compile_once_get_or_init`
    whole. No function pointer in read-only data was needed, which is the
    one place the implementation is simpler than the spec's sketch.

SCOPE NOTE — the LOCAL form ships too. design.md's table covers module scope
and `par struct` fields and says nothing about
`let c: LazyLock[T] = LazyLock.new(|| ...)` inside a function. Leaving it
unlowered would have shipped a FRESH run-vs-build divergence (the
interpreter accepts it; codegen fell through method dispatch, and an
uninitialized cell segfaulted), which is the defect class this row exists to
remove, so the local `let` site records its closure the same way the module
registrar does.

TWO SPECIFIED RULES ARE STILL UNENFORCED, split into their own rows rather
than buried here, and named in `karac explain --concept=module-state` and
design.md rather than left silent:

  * B-2026-08-26-15 — the capture restriction ("may only capture other
    module-level compile-time bindings; captures of runtime state are a
    compile error"). Measured to be a missing RESTRICTION, not a correctness
    hazard: a closure capturing a local is accepted and produces identical
    results on all three backends, and a per-iteration cell in a loop gives
    the expected fresh value each time.
  * B-2026-08-26-16 — effect attribution to the calling function. This one
    has teeth: `pub fn peek() -> i64 { return CACHE.get(); }` whose closure
    calls a `with reads(Db)` function passes `karac check` clean, while the
    direct-call control is correctly rejected. Undeclared effects escape
    through `get()`.

A THIRD DEFECT CAME OUT OF THE SAME GUARD — B-2026-08-26-17, a module-scope
`Atomic[T]` failing both compiled backends with "has no slot". The row
credited `tests/cli.rs::
every_type_the_module_mut_binding_warning_names_actually_runs` with running
programs, which is why a check-only recommendation could not re-enter the
menu. It did not: it ran `karac check` only, so it would NOT have caught the
defect it is named for. It now runs each probe, and the first execution
surfaced `Atomic` — the entry listed ABOVE the one under investigation.
title: `LazyLock[T]` IS A CHECK-ONLY PHANTOM: `let TABLE: LazyLock[i64] = LazyLock.new(|| 40 + 2);` passes `karac check` cleanly and then fails on EVERY execution backend -- `--interp` dies with "path 'LazyLock.new' has no interpreter evaluation rule", and `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` both reject `TABLE.get()` with "codegen: no handler for method 'get'". It is not a type outside that one special-cased module-binding form either: `fn f(x: LazyLock[i64])` is `undefined type 'LazyLock'`. Until this was found, the live `module_mut_binding` WARNING recommended it by name ("Prefer a context struct, `Mutex`, `Atomic`, `#[thread_local]`, `LazyLock`, or `OnceLock`"), so following the compiler's own advice produced a program that checks and then cannot be run or built.
detail:
Found while settling B-2026-08-25-19 (Box/Rc/Arc), by auditing every type design.md's module-state escape lists name rather than only the three the row cited.

MEASURED, one program per phase, on 363d579:
  let TABLE: LazyLock[i64] = LazyLock.new(|| 40 + 2);
  fn main() { println(TABLE.get()); }
    karac check        -> All checks passed.
    karac run --interp -> runtime error: internal: path 'LazyLock.new' has no
                          interpreter evaluation rule (accepted by the
                          typechecker but not wired in the tree-walk
                          interpreter) -- please report this
    karac run  (JIT)   -> error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method
                          'get' on variable 'TABLE'
    karac build        -> same codegen error
  fn f(x: LazyLock[i64]) { }  -> error[resolve]: undefined type 'LazyLock'

WHY IT CHECKS AT ALL: `src/typechecker/items.rs` special-cases `LazyLock.new(|| ...)` as a recognized module-binding initializer form (the `"LazyLock" => args.len() == 1 && matches!(args[0].value.kind, ExprKind::Closure { .. })` arm), and module-scope type annotations are matched structurally rather than resolved against the type namespace -- a bogus annotation surfaces as a typecheck MISMATCH (`expected 'NopeNotTaken', found 'i64'`), not as `undefined type`. So the initializer grammar shipped without the type, the interpreter arm, or the codegen arm.

FIXED IN THIS COMMIT, the half that actively misleads: the `module_mut_binding` warning no longer names `LazyLock`. `docs/design.md`'s supported-paths list no longer names it either, and `karac explain --concept=module-state` now states what it actually does instead of listing it as an option with a method surface. `tests/cli.rs::every_type_the_module_mut_binding_warning_names_actually_runs` compiles a module-scope program per recommended TYPE, so a recommendation that only survives `karac check` cannot re-enter that menu -- a name-resolves check would NOT have caught this one, which is the whole reason the guard runs programs.

STILL OPEN, and an owner call: design.md § Module-Level Bindings specifies `LazyLock[T]` in DETAIL -- a three-row family-comparison table (Initializer / Concurrency / Module-scope / `par struct` field / Method surface), a "picking the right primitive" guide contrasting it with `OnceLock` and `OnceCell`, and the entire rightmost column of the profile-gating table (`let X: LazyLock[T]` across lib / app / embedded / gpu). Either that specification ships (prelude type + interpreter eval + codegen for `new`/`get`), or those tables come out. Shipping it is the more useful direction -- `OnceLock` covers late-bound values but not "derive this from module constants on first use", which is the regex/lookup-table case the spec calls canonical -- but it is real work across three phases, not a doc edit.

NOT THE SAME AS `RwLock[T]`, which the same lists also named: that one is absent outright (`undefined type 'RwLock'`, no stdlib file, no prelude entry) and has no partial implementation behind it. It was removed from the design.md lists in the same commit.

fix:
FIXED by 5a7e985. Rewrote § Conversion Traits' canonical `?` example over APIs
that exist, and added a regression test that pins the section's blocks to the
compiler.

Fix shape (a) from the row, for the reason the row gave: it keeps the section
teaching what it is for and does not commit the language to a second parse
surface. `input.parse_i64()?` became `parse_setting(input)?` -- a user-defined
`Result[i64, ParseError]` step, symmetric with the `store(n)?` line that was
already user-defined and already fine.

Also added the piece whose absence CAUSED the error, rather than only deleting
the error: a short block showing how a propagable `Result` is built on the real
`i64.parse` --

    fn parse_setting(input: String) -> Result[i64, ParseError] {
        match i64.parse(input.trim()) {
            Some(n) => Ok(n),
            None => Err(ParseError { input: input }),
        }
    }

The row's core complaint was that the document contained both parse forms and
only one was real. Deleting the unreal one leaves a reader who wants an error
value exactly where the row's author started; showing the lift closes it. The
prose says plainly that the built-in parse returns `Option`, not `Result`, and
that `?` needs an error VALUE to convert.

REGRESSION TEST: `design_md_question_operator_example_is_realizable` in
tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs. It typechecks the section's own blocks --
EXTRACTED from design.md, not restated in the test, so it cannot drift from
what it guards -- concatenated with a preamble supplying only the user-level
names the section leans on but never defines (`ParseError`, `DbError`,
`AppError`, `log_error`, `store`, the `From[DbError]` impl).

That split is the actual rule being enforced, and it is why this is not simply
"the block parses": a spec fragment may legitimately name types and functions
the reader will write -- a fragment that defined them would stop being a
fragment -- but it may NOT call a method on a BUILT-IN type that does not
exist. Everything unresolved after the preamble is a call into the language.

Verified in both directions rather than assumed: with the old line restored the
test fails with exactly `["no method 'parse_i64' on type 'String'"]`, and with
the current line it passes. Full design_md_code_blocks file green (12 tests).

TWO MEASUREMENTS MADE WHILE FIXING, both of which shaped the preamble and are
recorded so the next editor does not rediscover them:

  * `ParseError` cannot be an ENUM. The section's own `AppError.Parse(e)` makes
    `AppError` an enum whose variant carries `ParseError`, and v1 allows only
    one level of enum nesting -- an `enum ParseError` there is rejected with
    E_ENUM_NESTED_ENUM_PAYLOAD (unless marked `shared`/`par`). A struct is the
    shape the section is already committed to.
  * `log_error` must take `ref`. The doc's `From` body logs the error and THEN
    moves it into `AppError.Parse(e)`; an owned parameter moves it twice and
    draws an ownership warning on design.md's own example.

Both are consistent with the section as written -- neither required changing
it -- so the doc was left alone on those two points.

NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately so: the corrected example does not RUN
correctly, for reasons that have nothing to do with the names this row is
about. The section's shape -- two `impl From[X] for AppError` for one target --
silently dispatches to the wrong impl on both backends, filed as
B-2026-08-27-1 (high, miscompile). That is why the regression test asserts the
example TYPECHECKS rather than that it produces the right answer; asserting
behaviour today would either fail or, worse, bake in the wrong answer. The
scope split is intentional: this row was filed as a documentation defect and is
closed as one.
title: design.md's CANONICAL `?`-operator example calls `input.parse_i64()?` and names `ParseError` -- NEITHER EXISTS: the real API is `i64.parse(s) -> Option[i64]`, which cannot be used with `?` the way the example shows
detail:
design.md § `?` operator and cross-error-type propagation is the section that
teaches how `?` converts between error types, and its worked example is:

    fn parse_and_store(input: String) -> Result[(), AppError] {
        let n = input.parse_i64()?;   // ParseError -- requires From[ParseError] for AppError
        store(n)?                    // DbError    -- requires From[DbError] for AppError
        Ok(())
    }

Two of those names do not resolve:

    input.parse_i64()  ->  error[typecheck]: no method 'parse_i64' on type 'String'
    ParseError         ->  error[resolve]: undefined name 'ParseError'

`parse_i64` exists in the tree only as the INTERNAL runtime symbol
`karac_runtime_parse_i64` (src/codegen.rs), never as a user-facing method.

THE REAL API IS SHAPED DIFFERENTLY, not just spelled differently, which is why
this is worth a row rather than a rename. design.md's OWN main example (§ the
guessing-game program) uses the actual form:

    match i64.parse(line.trim()) {
        Some(guess) => println(f"You guessed {guess}"),
        None => println("not a number"),
    }

-- a STATIC method on the type returning `Option[i64]`, verified working. So the
document contains both forms and only one of them is real. An `Option` return
cannot demonstrate what the broken example is there to demonstrate: there is no
error VALUE to convert, so `From[ParseError] for AppError` has nothing to
convert from, and the section's entire point -- cross-error-type propagation
through `?` -- needs a different example or a fallible-parse API that returns
`Result`.

WHY LOW: it is illustrative prose, not a spec table, and the working form is
documented elsewhere in the same file, so nothing is BLOCKED. Why it is worth
filing anyway: it is the canonical example for a core language feature, it is
the first thing a reader copies when learning `?`, and both names failing means
the copy does not merely misbehave -- it does not compile.

FIX SHAPE, one of: (a) rewrite the example over two APIs that do return
`Result` and exist, which keeps the section teaching what it is for; or (b) add
the fallible-parse API the example assumes. (a) is the smaller change and does
not commit the language to a second parse surface.

SOURCE NOTE: found while checking how to parse integers for kata 297
(serialize/deserialize a binary tree, which parses its own wire format). The
kata uses the working `i64.parse` form; nothing is blocked.

fix:
FIXED by 06880a4. build the word list from `inner_word_count` and pass
it to `rebuild_value_from_payload_word_slice`. Verified across 11 error-type
shapes on all four surfaces (`run`, `--interp`, `build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0
build`), including 1-, 2-, 3- and 4-word payloads and both the `?` and tail
spellings. Regression test
`test_main_question_mark_err_renders_every_payload_word` (tests/cli.rs), which
fails at the parent commit with `Error: W(1,2,3,140723206629624)`.
title: `?` in `main() -> Result[(), E]` reconstructed `E` from only its first THREE payload words, so any error held inline in four or more words rendered garbage for the rest on EVERY compiled backend (`Error: W(1,2,3,140723206629624)` under JIT, `Error: W(1,2,3,0)` under AOT, against `W(1,2,3,4)` under `--interp`). Third and last site of a three-word cap already lifted twice elsewhere.
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-25-33 (the `?`-in-`main` segfault); a distinct
defect at a distinct site, and NOT caused by that fix — reproduced at the
parent commit with the fix stashed.

REPRO (4-word inline struct payload, propagated with `?`):

    struct Wide { a: i64, b: i64, c: i64, d: i64 }
    impl Display for Wide {
        fn to_string(ref self) -> String { f"W({self.a},{self.b},{self.c},{self.d})" }
    }
    fn bad() -> Result[i64, Wide] { return Err(Wide { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4 }) }
    fn main() -> Result[(), Wide] { let x = bad()?; println(x); return Ok(()) }

  --interp     -> Error: W(1,2,3,4)          (correct)
  karac run    -> Error: W(1,2,3,<garbage>)
  karac build  -> Error: W(1,2,3,0)

An ENUM error type shows it one word earlier, since the tag consumes a word:
`enum E { W(i64,i64,i64), B }` propagated with `?` gives `W(1,2,50)` under AOT.

THE SITE. `src/codegen/exprs.rs`, the `?` branch guarded by
`current_fn_name == "main" && main_result_err_te.is_some()`, called
`rebuild_value_from_payload_words(e_ty, w0_i, w1_i, w2_i)` — the fixed-arity
three-word wrapper. Its width-general sibling
`rebuild_value_from_payload_word_slice` already existed and is what the other
two sites use.

WHY IT SURVIVED TWO PRIOR FIXES OF THE SAME CAP. B-2026-08-04-12 lifted it off
the fn-level `Err` aggregate by building a full `ret_words` vector;
B-2026-08-23-20 lifted it off the tail `return Err(…)` exit by switching that
site to the slice form. Both landed in this area and neither touched this
branch, so the tail spelling of a wide error printed correctly while the `?`
spelling of the SAME error type did not — which is what makes it easy to miss.

A NOTE FOR WHOEVER TOUCHES THIS NEXT, because the obvious fix is wrong.
Reusing the `ret_words` vector already computed a few lines above does NOT
work: that vector is additionally clamped to `outer_word_count`, derived from
the ENCLOSING function's return enum — and `main`'s LLVM signature is the C
entry `i32`, not a `Result` aggregate, so the clamp collapses the list and
even a ONE-word payload comes back garbage (measured: `A(42)` became
`A(140737171092712)`). The words must be taken from `inner_word_count`, the
callee's own aggregate width.

fix:
297ef4f

Both backends drop the declared width at the SAME place: `~x` lowers to a `T.not(x)` assoc call (lowering.rs `rewrite_unary`), and each backend's `not` arm re-synthesizes a bare unary op from the value, discarding the `type_name` that carries the width. The sibling `neg` arm one block above already range-checks at the declared width -- this is the same shape as B-2026-08-06-7's negate and shift legs, at the one operator that fix did not reach.

Codegen (`assoc_call.rs`): re-narrow with `truncate_to_narrow_width`, the helper B-2026-08-06-7 added for exactly this, whose doc-comment already claimed the invariant "a narrow-typed value always fits its declared width" that `~` was violating. Its visibility widened from private to `pub(super)`.

Interpreter (`eval_ops.rs`): complement on the u128 carrier and re-narrow through `truncate_to_width` at `span_int_width`'s `(bits, is_unsigned)`, mirroring `shift_at_width`.

`span_int_width` additionally learned to peel `Type::Vector` to its lane type, since lane ops recurse carrying the CONTAINER's span. Peeled THERE and not in `narrow_oob` on purpose: `span_int_width`'s only two callers are `~` and the shifts, where codegen's real `<N x iX>` lanes are the oracle; `narrow_oob` governs lane `+`/`-`/`*`, where codegen WRAPS rather than traps, so peeling there would have traded one divergence for another.

THE TEST SPELLING IS LOAD-BEARING AND THE FIRST DRAFT GOT IT WRONG. A suffixed initializer (`let a: u8 = 5u8`) gives the local a real `i8` alloca, so `xor i8` was already correct in codegen; only an UNSUFFIXED one (`let a: u8 = 5`) leaves it in the i64 carrier. The first regression test used suffixed literals throughout, passed with the fix stashed, and proved nothing. Both spellings are now pinned in both backends' tests. The interpreter, having no notion of storage width, was wrong for both spellings.
title: `~` COMPLEMENTS AT THE CARRIER WIDTH, NOT THE DECLARED WIDTH, so every narrow UNSIGNED integer gets a wrong value and the two backends disagree on which wrong value. `~(5u8)` is 250; the compiled backends produced 18446744073709551610 (2^64-6) and the interpreter produced -6 -- a value a `u8` cannot represent at all. Measured across every width: `u8`/`u16`/`u32` wrong in BOTH backends, `i8`..`i64` and `u64` correct in both (signed `~x == -x-1` never leaves a narrow signed range; 64 IS the carrier width). Also fixed on integer-lane `Vector[T, N]`, where the interpreter gave -6 per lane against codegen's correct 250.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while measuring B-2026-08-25-29 half 2, which claimed bitwise `Not` on integers "is not available". It IS available -- spelled `~`, which that row never tried -- and measuring it turned up this instead.

CROSS-REFS: B-2026-08-26-7 (the codegen root cause this fixes at the operator rather than at the source), B-2026-08-26-8 (the lane arithmetic left divergent), B-2026-08-06-7 (the negate/shift siblings this mirrors).

fix:
FIXED by 08410c2.

The slot is now sized from the ANNOTATION for both directions, and the literal suffix is finally inert.

ROOT CAUSE. `const_int_for_suffix` derives an integer literal's LLVM type from its SUFFIX alone -- no suffix means the default i64, whatever the binding is annotated. `bind_pattern` then allocas at `val.get_type()`, so `let b: u8 = 200` produced an i64 slot for a `u8` binding while `let b: u8 = 200u8` produced a real i8 one. Every width-sensitive operation on the binding inherited that width.

THE FIX IS THE INTEGER TWIN OF A LEG THAT ALREADY EXISTED. `widen_let_value_to_annotation` (B-2026-08-13-15) already re-sized a `let` value to its annotation, and B-2026-08-14-11 had already added a float arm to it, narrowing an unsuffixed float literal so `let a: f32 = 0.1` equals `let a: f32 = 0.1f32`. The integer arm was missing, and the function's doc comment asserted it was unnecessary: "Narrowing at a `let` is already handled (an out-of-range literal is a typecheck error, and an in-range one is range-checked and packed by the literal path)". The first half is true and is exactly what makes the truncation safe; the second half was false, and this row is what it cost. Renamed to `fit_let_value_to_annotation`, since it now does both directions and the old name asserted otherwise.

Gated on the LITERAL rather than on the value, copying the float leg's reasoning verbatim: an i64-typed VALUE at a `u8` annotation is an implicit narrowing between two DECLARED types, which the language refuses, and silently truncating it here would hide a diagnostic instead of fixing a bug.

THE NEGATED LITERAL NEEDED A SECOND SHAPE, and a first pass at the fix missed it. `-100` parses as `Neg(Integer(100))`, but `lowering.rs` rewrites every unary operator to its trait method, so at a typed `let` it reaches codegen already desugared into a CALL -- `i8.neg(100)` -- and that assoc-call arm deliberately widens to i64 for its range check. Matching only the `Unary` spelling left `let a: i8 = -100; a << 1` at -200, a value an `i8` cannot hold. Both shapes are matched now; the `Unary` one still occurs when lowering declines to rewrite.

A SECOND, PRE-EXISTING BUG HAD TO BE FIXED FOR THIS TO LAND, and it is the more interesting half. The auto-par return-slot sizer's `-> Self` arm (`infer_expr_llvm_type`, the `abs`/`sqrt`/transcendental case) accepted an i64 receiver ONLY, with a comment stating the invariant it relied on: "codegen widens every integer local to i64 in both storage and value flow ... That i64-backing is why a source-level narrow annotation (`let n: i32`) still resolves here: its slot IS i64." That invariant was ALREADY FALSE -- `let base: i32 = 7i32` has always produced a real i32 slot -- and such a receiver fell through to `None`, dropping the slot, so the branch body failed to compile at all: `codegen failed: Undefined variable 'x'`. A HARD ERROR on a valid program, standing in `main` for however long, and invisible because every par test in the file writes its literal without a suffix and that spelling compiled at i64. `test_e2e_par_join_branch_narrow_int_method` is named for the narrow case and was covering the i64 path twice.

Verified as pre-existing rather than caused here: with this row's change stashed, `let base: i32 = 7i32` in a par block already failed the same way. The guard now accepts the real integer widths (8/16/32/64/128). It was never a narrowing exclusion but a receiver-SHAPE filter, and it keeps that role: `bool` is i1 and stays out, and although `char` is also i32, the typechecker rejects `c.abs()` / `c.sqrt()` outright (`no method 'abs' on type 'char'`), so no non-numeric receiver can reach the arm with one of these methods -- measured, not assumed. A struct receiver lowers to a StructType and misses regardless.

SCOPE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED. The row warned that "every operator whose correctness depends on the operand's LLVM width is a candidate". Fixing the slot width fixes them all at once, so the remaining question was whether other POSITIONS shared the hole. They do not: a struct-literal field, a `Vec` element, an `Array` element, a tuple element, a function argument and a function return all already narrowed an unsuffixed integer literal correctly, measured on both backends. That is the same list the float leg's comment gives for floats -- the annotated `let` was the last position out of step, for integers exactly as it had been for floats.

WHY THE ORIGINAL ROW'S OPTION (a) IS WHAT LANDED, in the narrow form. The row offered (a) allocate narrow locals at their declared width, "largest blast radius", versus (b) re-narrow at each width-sensitive operator, "a list that must be kept complete". (a) is what this is, but it turned out not to need the feared refactor: `fit_let_value_to_annotation` is one function on the one path that sizes a let slot, and the target IR -- a narrow alloca -- was already produced and exercised by the suffixed spelling. The change makes the two spellings converge on the path that was already tested, which is why the blast radius resolved to a single pre-existing par bug rather than a wave of them.

The pre-existing auto-par return-slot defect that had to be fixed for this to land is filed separately as B-2026-08-26-14.
title: A NARROW LOCAL INITIALIZED FROM AN UNSUFFIXED LITERAL IS ALLOCATED AT i64 IN CODEGEN, so every width-sensitive operation on it runs at 64 bits and can produce a value the declared type cannot represent. The literal suffix -- which ought to be semantically inert once the binding carries an explicit type annotation -- decides the storage width: `let a: u8 = 200u8` gets a real `i8` alloca, `let b: u8 = 200` stays in the i64 carrier. MEASURED in AOT, against `karac run --interp` which is correct in every arm: `b << 4` is 3200 (should be 128), and `let d: i32 = 1; d << 31` is 2147483648 -- a value an `i32` cannot hold. THAT LAST CASE IS THE SOUNDNESS HOLE B-2026-08-06-7 CLAIMS TO HAVE CLOSED: its regression tests assert exactly `1i32 << 31 == -2147483648`, but spell the literal WITH a suffix, so the fix was only ever exercised on the path that allocates `i32` and the ordinary spelling still miscompiles. `~` had the identical hole and was fixed at the operator (B-2026-08-26-6) rather than at this root; every operator whose correctness depends on the operand's LLVM width is a candidate, and only shifts and `~` have been checked.
detail:
A NARROW LOCAL INITIALIZED FROM AN UNSUFFIXED LITERAL IS ALLOCATED AT i64 IN CODEGEN, so every width-sensitive operation on it runs at 64 bits and can yield a value the declared type cannot represent. The literal suffix -- which should be semantically inert once the binding carries an explicit type annotation -- decides the storage width:

  let a: u8 = 200u8;  ->  %a = alloca i8   ->  shl i8   ->  a << 4 == 128   (correct)
  let b: u8 = 200;    ->  %b = alloca i64  ->  shl i64  ->  b << 4 == 3200  (WRONG)

MEASURED on 4e3215d-era main, `karac build` (AOT), against `karac run --interp` which is correct in every arm:

  let a: u8  = 200u8; a << 4u8    -> 128           interp 128     CORRECT
  let b: u8  = 200;   b << 4      -> 3200          interp 128     WRONG
  let c: i32 = 1i32;  c << 31i32  -> -2147483648   interp same    CORRECT
  let d: i32 = 1;     d << 31     -> 2147483648    interp same    WRONG

THE LAST ROW IS THE SOUNDNESS CASE B-2026-08-06-7 CLAIMS TO HAVE CLOSED. That row's own summary is "narrow `<<` additionally computes at i64 so an `i32` binding can hold a value out of its declared range", and its regression tests (`e2e_shift_runs_at_declared_width`, `test_shift_runs_at_declared_width`) assert exactly `1i32 << 31 == -2147483648`. Both spell the literal WITH a suffix, so the fix was only ever exercised on the path that allocates i8/i32 -- and the unsuffixed spelling, which is how the same program would ordinarily be written, still produces 2147483648 in a binding typed `i32`. The interpreter half of that fix is complete; only codegen has the hole.

SCOPE IS WIDER THAN SHIFTS. `~` had the identical hole and was fixed at the operator (B-2026-08-26-6) rather than at the root, precisely because the root fix is not local: `compile_narrow_int_binop` and `widen_int_to_i64` exist because "an i64-canonical local vs an i8 buffer element of the same Kara type" both occur today, so changing which one a `let` produces moves every narrow-integer path at once. Any operator whose correctness depends on the operand's LLVM width is a candidate; shifts are proven, `~` was proven, the rest are unaudited.

TWO POSSIBLE FIXES, and the choice is a real one:
(a) Allocate narrow locals at their DECLARED width, so the suffix stops mattering. Fixes the whole class at the root; largest blast radius.
(b) Re-narrow at each width-sensitive operator, as `~` now does and as the shift path already tries to. Contained per operator, but it is a list that must be kept complete, and the shift's existing attempt shows how a gap survives when the test picks the wrong spelling.

NOT A REGRESSION IN `~`'s FIX: `~` is correct in both spellings now. This row is the remaining root cause, and shifts are the proven live instance.

CROSS-REFS: B-2026-08-26-6 (the `~` instance, fixed at the operator), B-2026-08-06-7 (the shift fix this leaves incomplete), B-2026-08-25-29 (the row being worked when this surfaced).

fix:
FIXED by ff403a3. The row deferred pending "a design.md decision on narrow-lane overflow semantics"; the decision is WRAP, and design.md § Portable SIMD now says so outright.

WHAT DECIDED IT, since the row's own framing leans the other way:

  * The premise "design.md does not say" was too strong in one direction and not strong enough in another. `Column[T]` / `Tensor[T, S]` element ops DO trap at the element width, in BOTH backends, pinned by `test_column_narrow_element_binop_overflow_traps` — measured live, interp and AOT both raise `integer overflow` on `Column[i32]` at i32::MAX + 1. So there IS a precedent; the row did not weigh it.
  * But it does not carry. `Column` / `Tensor` are data-frame types: the user asked for a column of i32. design.md § Portable SIMD defines `Vector[T, N]` as lowering "to the widest available primitive on the target" — its contract IS machine lane semantics, and no SIMD ISA traps. Trapping needs a per-operation cross-lane reduction to decide whether to fault, plausibly costlier than the arithmetic, on the one type whose purpose is arithmetic throughput.
  * THE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLED IT: codegen wraps UNIFORMLY at N = 4 and N = 64.
