The concern that the scalar-fallback path (lane counts no native vector unit covers) inherits the scalar trap rule — which would make correctness vary across targets and break § Portable SIMD's "performance, not correctness, is what varies" — does not occur. Codegen is internally consistent, so WRAP moves exactly one non-perf-critical backend and breaks no stated invariant, while TRAP would move codegen for every lane op on every integer lane type plus regress all SIMD throughput plus need a `wrapping_*` escape hatch that does not exist.

THE INTERPRETER WAS BUGGY EITHER WAY, which is worth separating from the semantics question: 400 is neither the wrap (144) nor the trap. The row treats the fix as blocked on the decision; only the TARGET VALUE was blocked.

HOW, and why not the one-liner the row warned against: `settle_int_binop` and `vector_lane_wrap` are siblings of `narrow_oob`, not a peel inside it. The row is right that peeling `Vector` in `narrow_oob` is wrong — that function answers "which range TRAPS", so an entry there would make the interpreter reject a lane sum codegen wraps, trading a wrong-value divergence for a trap-vs-wrap one. The arithmetic arms now consult the wrap first and fall through to the unchanged trap path for every other width.

VERIFIED in both backends, values agreeing exactly: u8 200+200 -> 144; i8 100+100 -> -56 (two's complement, not saturating); u8 5-10 -> 251; i16 300*300 -> 24464; and u8 200+200 at N = 64 -> 144. `tests/codegen.rs::e2e_vector_lane_arithmetic_agrees_with_the_interpreter` is a TWIN comparison against the in-process interpreter oracle rather than shared constants, so the two backends cannot drift together; `tests/interpreter.rs` pins the exact values.

GUARDED AGAINST THE OBVIOUS REGRESSION: `wrapping_vector_lanes_did_not_stop_columns_or_scalars_trapping` asserts `Column[i32]` element ops and plain scalar `i32` still trap. The risk in this change is widening the exception into the trapping widths it sits beside, so that is the thing pinned.

design.md § Portable SIMD carries the exception explicitly — including WHY it departs from the `Column` precedent — because a reader who meets the wrap and knows the trap rule should find reasoning rather than conclude it was forgotten.
title: INTERPRETER `Vector[T, N]` LANE ARITHMETIC IGNORES THE LANE WIDTH, so a narrow-lane vector computes on the i128 carrier and diverges from codegen, whose lanes are a real `<N x iX>`. MEASURED with `Vector[u8, 4]` lanes of 200: `v + v` is 400 in the interpreter and 144 in AOT (144 is correct -- 400 truncated to `u8`). The `~` and `<<` arms of the same divergence were fixed by teaching `span_int_width` to peel `Type::Vector` to its lane type; the ARITHMETIC arms route through `narrow_oob` instead and are still divergent. LEFT DELIBERATELY, because the obvious one-line extension is wrong: `narrow_oob` is a TRAP predicate, so peeling `Vector` there would make the interpreter raise `integer overflow` on a lane sum of 400 while codegen WRAPS it to 144 -- trading a wrong-value divergence for one backend rejecting a program the other runs. Needs a design.md decision on narrow-lane overflow semantics first.
detail:
INTERPRETER `Vector[T, N]` LANE ARITHMETIC IGNORES THE LANE WIDTH, so a narrow-lane vector computes at the i128 carrier and diverges from codegen, whose lanes are a real `<N x iX>`. MEASURED with `Vector[u8, 4]` lanes of 200:

  v + v    -> interp 400   AOT 144   (144 is correct: 400 truncated to u8)
  v << n   -> interp 144   AOT 144   (FIXED by the followup row's Vector peel)
  ~v       -> interp 250   AOT 250   (FIXED by the followup row's Vector peel)

The `~` and `<<` arms were fixed by teaching `span_int_width` to peel `Type::Vector` to its lane type -- its only two callers. The ARITHMETIC arms (`+ - * / %`) route through `narrow_oob` instead, which peels `Column` and `Tensor` but not `Vector`, and they are still divergent.

THE ARITHMETIC HALF WAS DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE, because the obvious one-line extension is wrong. `narrow_oob` is a TRAP predicate: adding a `Vector` peel there would make the interpreter raise `integer overflow` on a lane sum of 400, while codegen WRAPS it to 144. That trades a wrong-value divergence for a trap-vs-wrap divergence, which is worse -- one backend rejecting a program the other runs.

So the open question is which behaviour is specified for narrow-lane vector arithmetic on overflow, and design.md does not say. The two candidates:
(a) WRAP, matching codegen and ordinary SIMD expectations -- then the interpreter needs a lane-width truncation that is NOT the trapping `narrow_oob` path.
(b) TRAP, matching Kara's scalar integer-overflow rule ("traps at the declared width") -- then codegen is the side that moves, and every lane op needs an overflow check.

design.md's SIMD section should answer this before either backend changes. Note (b) is the answer consistent with the scalar rule, and (a) is the answer consistent with what SIMD hardware does and what codegen already emits -- which is exactly why this needs a decision rather than a patch.

CROSS-REFS: B-2026-08-26-6 (the `~`/`<<` lane arms, fixed by the `Type::Vector` peel in `span_int_width`), B-2026-08-26-7 (the codegen-side narrow-width root cause).

── INVESTIGATION 2026-08-26 (Group D): THE PREMISE "design.md does not say" IS TOO STRONG ──

The row defers on the grounds that narrow-lane overflow semantics are unspecified, so neither backend can move. Measured, Kara HAS already answered this question for the sibling container types, in both backends, with a regression test pinning it:

  Column[i32] at i32::MAX, `c + 1`:
    karac run --interp -> runtime error: integer overflow
    karac build        -> panic ...: integer overflow
  Vector[u8, 4] lanes of 200, `v + v`:
    karac run --interp -> 400        (no width applied at all)
    karac build        -> 144        (wraps)

`span_int_bounds` says so in its own comment, added by B-2026-07-01-3: element-wise `Column[T] / Tensor[T, S]` ops peel to the element "so a narrow-element container op range-checks exactly like the scalar op (codegen ALREADY TRAPS at the element's LLVM width; the interpreter silently produced out-of-range values)". `tests/interpreter.rs::test_column_narrow_element_binop_overflow_traps` pins it. design.md's GPU section carries the same discipline into lane-parallel code at deliberate cost -- checked integer ops, an overflow flag OR-ed across the whole workgroup, and an explicit note that padded lanes must not trap on data that is not there.

So the shape of the question changes. It is not "two candidates, no precedent". It is: `Vector` is the ONE container type whose codegen wraps where its siblings trap, and the interpreter is wrong under BOTH candidate semantics -- 400 is neither the trap nor the wrap. Whichever way the decision goes, the interpreter's 400 is a bug.

WHAT THE ROW GETS RIGHT, and what is still a real decision: `Vector[T, N]` is an explicit PERFORMANCE primitive in a way `Column` and `Tensor` are not. Per-lane overflow checks cost exactly what the type exists to buy, and no SIMD ISA traps. That is a genuine argument for (a) WRAP that the row does not state, and it is why this is not simply "codegen is out of line with its siblings and should be fixed".

RECOMMENDATION, for whoever takes the decision: (a) WRAP, with the divergence closed on the INTERPRETER side (make lane arithmetic truncate to the lane width rather than route through the trapping `narrow_oob`), and design.md's Portable SIMD section stating outright that `Vector[T, N]` lane arithmetic wraps -- explicitly departing from the scalar trap rule, with the performance reason recorded so the departure reads as deliberate rather than as the `Column` precedent being forgotten. The alternative, (b) TRAP, is more consistent but makes explicit SIMD pay a per-lane check, which is a language-level performance commitment rather than a bug fix.

NOT ACTED ON, deliberately: either direction is a semantics commitment across two backends, so it is an owner call rather than something to settle from inside a bug fix. The measurements above are the decision inputs; the row stays open.

fix:
FIXED by d9c520e, which teaches the caller-drops convention its SECOND escape route.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is one rule short rather than a `PriorityQueue` bug. Kara
passes a by-value argument under a CALLER-DROPS convention: a fresh temporary
is dropped by the caller after the call and the callee registers nothing for
it. Correct whenever the value dies inside the call, and codegen already
carved out the one escape it knew about -- the callee RETURNING the parameter
(`fn_returns_param` / `fn_returns_param_payload`, the "does it leave through
the return value" question, asked at two depths). It never modelled the other
way out: the callee STORING the parameter into a place the CALLER STILL HOLDS.
`fn push(mut ref self, x: T) { self.xs.push(x); }` leaves the value alive in
the caller's own queue when the call returns, so the caller's temp drop and
the container's element drain were two owners for one value.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AND THE CORRECTIONS MATTER
MORE THAN THE PATCH.

  1. It is NOT in `push`. `PriorityQueue.push$Item`'s emitted body contains no
     call to `Item.drop` at all -- the extra drop is a `karac_drop_Item` in
     MAIN, on a `%__owned_agg_tmp` the CALLER allocated for the argument. The
     row named the callee; the defect is entirely caller-side.

  2. It is NOT specific to `PriorityQueue`, to the stdlib, to generics, or to
     `push`. Measured on a plain user struct with no derives and no stdlib
     involvement:
       struct Bag { xs: Vec[Item] }
       impl Bag { fn add(mut ref self, x: Item) { self.xs.push(x); } }
     double-drops identically. So does `self.one = x` (a field ASSIGNMENT, no
     container). A direct `v.push(Item { .. })` in `main` -- same push, no
     intervening user function -- is CLEAN. The intervening by-value parameter
     is the whole trigger.

  3. It is NOT AOT-only, and this is the part with teeth. The row says "AOT
     only; the interpreter drops once", true of the METHOD shape it measured
     because the interpreter runs its fresh-temp argument drops on the
     free-function path only. On a FREE function --
       fn add_to(v: mut ref Vec[Item], x: Item) { v.push(x); }
     -- BOTH backends printed `drop 7` twice. Both wrong, so they agreed, so
     the kata A/B rule (`run` == `build`) reports a pass. A defect that hides
     from the project's main correctness check by being wrong on both sides is
     worth more than the one that announced itself.

THE FIX. A third sibling to the two existing escape predicates, in the same
file and the same shape: `ast::fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place(f, i)` --
does `f` move by-value parameter `i` into a place rooted at `self` (under a
BORROWED receiver only; an owned `self` dies with the frame) or at one of
`f`'s own `ref`/`mut ref` params? Sinks are a method call on such a place with
the param among its args, and an assignment into such a place. Conservative
toward TRUE, the direction both siblings already document: over-answering
leaks a drop, under-answering double-frees, and only the first is recoverable.

Wired at the three call sites that reach the same registrar, each of which
needed its own key and none of which the other two cover:
  - free fn      (`call_dispatch`, arg loop)
  - concrete method (`method_call`, arg loop)
  - monomorphized generic impl method (`mono::compile_generic_call`) -- the leg
    `PriorityQueue.push` takes.

TWO INDEXING TRAPS, both silent. `find_function_ast` returns a `Function`
whose `params` EXCLUDE the receiver, but the method site counts `self` as
argument 0 and `compile_generic_call` receives a desugaring that moves the
receiver INTO `params[0]` and empties `self_param`. An index one off simply
reads a parameter that is not there and answers `false` -- the gate stops
existing with no error. Normalized inside one helper on a `receiver_counted`
flag rather than at each site. And the stdlib is BAKED, so
`find_function_ast(user_program, "PriorityQueue.push")` finds nothing; the
resolution falls back to `mono_state.generic_fns`, which is where every
generic callee including stdlib actually lives.

THE HALF THAT MUST NOT BE SUPPRESSED. The first version skipped the caller's
registration outright and traded the double body for a 9-byte leak: `push`
DEFENSIVE-COPIES the element's `String`, so the caller's original buffer is
orphaned and is still the caller's to free. Codegen already models exactly
this split for the return-passthrough route -- bodies to the value's new
owner, memory for the orphaned original stays here -- so the fix folds into
that existing flag rather than adding a parallel one, and the flag is renamed
`arg_escapes_frame` because `arg_flows_into_return` is no longer what it
means. LSan confirms: 40 bytes / 11 allocations with both halves suppressed,
back to the pre-existing 31 / 8 with only the body half.

ORACLES. Three E2E cases in `tests/codegen.rs` (free fn, concrete method,
monomorphized `PriorityQueue`) plus interpreter twins, all verified RED with
the predicate stubbed to `false` and green with it live. The interpreter's
free-fn twin is a REAL regression oracle (that backend was wrong on its own);
the method twin is labelled a PARITY pin, since the interpreter passed it
before the fix for the wrong reason. A NEGATIVE case on each backend pins the
other direction -- a callee that only READS its by-value param must still let
the caller drop it -- so a future widening of the predicate to key on the
receiver's mode alone fails loudly. Under ASAN: three new leak-clean fixtures
covering all three legs.
title: `PriorityQueue.push` RUNS THE DROP GLUE FOR ITS BY-VALUE PARAMETER ON A VALUE IT HAS ALREADY MOVED into the backing `Vec`, so an element type with `impl Drop` drops ONCE AT PUSH AND AGAIN AT POP on the compiled backend -- the interpreter drops once. LSan: 31 bytes leaked in 8 allocations once the element also owns a `String`.
detail:
MEASURED on the B-2026-08-25-35 tree, `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct Item`
with an `impl Drop`:

  A. Item WITHOUT a heap field (`struct Item { id: i64 }`), push 3 then push 1, then drain:
       AOT:    drop 3 | drop 1 | built | pop 1 | drop 1 | pop 3 | drop 3
       INTERP: built | pop 1 | drop 1 | pop 3 | drop 3
     The two leading drops are the defect: each pushed value is dropped AT PUSH, and the
     copy living in the queue is dropped again at pop. A/B divergence, AOT-only.

  B. Item WITH a heap field (`{ id: i64, name: String }`), 3 pushes + 2 peeks + drain:
       AOT fires 8 drops where 5 are correct (3 elements + 2 peek copies).
       Under `-fsanitize=address` on Linux (LSan live):
         Direct leak of 22 byte(s) in 5 object(s) ... in karac_string_clone
         Direct leak of  9 byte(s) in 3 object(s) ... in PriorityQueue.push$Item
         SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 31 byte(s) leaked in 8 allocation(s).

  C. The SAME struct WITHOUT `impl Drop` -> AOT and interpreter agree exactly, LSan clean.
     So the trigger is `impl Drop` on the element, not the heap field; the heap field only
     turns the extra drop into an observable leak.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-25-35, MADE REACHABLE BY IT. Before that fix no derived user type
satisfied the `T: Ord` bound on `impl[T: Ord] PriorityQueue[T]`, so no user type -- and
therefore no `impl Drop` type -- could be placed in a `PriorityQueue` at all. The defect
sits in `push`'s by-value parameter handling, which is generic stdlib code that predates
the bound fix; it was simply unreachable.

`PriorityQueue.push` is `fn push(mut ref self, x: T)`, and its body does `self.xs.push(x)`.
The value is MOVED into the backing vector, so the parameter slot must not be dropped on
return. Whether the same shape affects other by-value stdlib params over a generic `T`
(`Vec.push` itself, `VecDeque.push_back`, `Map.insert`) was NOT measured here -- `Vec.push`
with a Drop element is the obvious next probe, and if it diverges the scope is much wider
than `PriorityQueue`.

ACCEPTANCE TEST ALREADY WRITTEN. `asan_priority_queue_peek_drop_count_is_one_per_returned_copy`
in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` is the oracle, currently `#[ignore]`d naming this row. Its
expected sequence is the CORRECT one -- do not relax it to match current AOT output.
Un-ignoring it is the acceptance test.

CORRECTION (2026-08-26, at fix time). The LSan figure in the report --
"31 byte(s) leaked in 8 allocation(s)" -- is NOT caused by the double drop and
does not go away with it. Measured after the drop sequence was made correct on
both backends: the same fixture still leaks 31/8. Bisected:
  - the same struct with `impl Drop` REMOVED leaks too (19/5), so `Drop` is not
    the trigger -- which contradicts this row's own case C;
  - a plain `Vec[Item]` holding that same `String`-bearing struct is CLEAN;
  - `PriorityQueue[String]` (element IS the String) is CLEAN.
So the residual is `PriorityQueue` of a STRUCT CARRYING A HEAP FIELD, split out
as B-2026-08-26-18. This row's acceptance test bundled the two and stays
`#[ignore]`d against -15; the drop-count half it was written for is now covered
by heap-free fixtures that run live.

fix:
Fixed in 095087d (hashing) + c39362a (equality), which had to ship together.

The two halves are one mechanism. Hashing a key through a user impl while
comparing it structurally places the key by one rule and looks it up by another,
which loses entries rather than merely reordering them — so the hashing commit
alone deliberately left a no-derive key REJECTED, and the equality commit is what
lifted that.

WHAT THE DESIGN TURNS ON. design.md § `Hash` and `Hasher` splits two questions:
`Hash` decides WHICH BYTES a value contributes, `BuildHasher`/`Hasher` decides
how those bytes become a digest. Implementing that split is what makes a user
`impl Hash` COMPOSE with a user `BuildHasher` instead of overriding it — pinned
by a test that puts both in one program.

`Hash.hash` is generic over the hasher, so calling it needs a monomorph bound to
a concrete `H`. Codegen's monomorphizer is driven from CALL SITES, so requesting
an instance from inside the synthesized LLVM hash function — below the AST —
would have meant reimplementing that inference at the wrong layer. `desugar.rs`
emits one ordinary Kāra function per implementing type instead:

    fn karac_hash_bytes_of_T(k: ref T) -> Vec[u8] {
        let mut s = KeyByteSink { bytes: [] };
        k.hash(s);
        return s.bytes;
    }

Resolve, typecheck and mono then see a normal call and produce
`T.hash$KeyByteSink` with no new machinery, and BOTH BACKENDS RUN THE SAME BODY.
That last part is a strict improvement on what the spec records for the user-
`BuildHasher` path, where a compiled binary feeds the key's memory image and the
interpreter feeds a canonical `Value` flattening and the two deliberately differ:
once the impl decides the bytes there is nothing left to disagree about.

FOUR THINGS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, each of which would have shipped a
defect:

  * The sink's `write_u8`/`write_i64`/… are spelled out in its impl rather than
    inherited. `synthesize_trait_default_methods` runs over the USER program, so
    a baked stdlib impl never passes through it, and both backends key off the
    impl's own item list — "method 'write_i64' not found on type 'KeyByteSink'".
  * `hash.kara` is compiled only for a program that has a user `impl Hash`.
    Unconditional inclusion emitted checked-overflow intrinsics from the sink's
    loop into every module and failed
    `wrapping_arith_lowers_without_overflow_trap` — the hazard the `cli` entry in
    that list already documents.
  * The synthesized hash function installs itself as `current_fn` while emitting;
    the Vec-buffer free appends basic blocks there, and leaving the outer
    function installed produced "Referring to a basic block in another function!".
  * THE HASHER WORLD IS NOW PER-THREAD AND PER-PROGRAM. It was set-once: one
    process runs many programs, so a `#[derive(Hash, Eq)]` map run after an
    unrelated program with a hand-written `impl Hash` was hashed and compared
    through THAT impl, collapsing two keys the derive keeps distinct. Making it
    refreshable then exposed the second half — the suites run in PARALLEL, and a
    single mutable global thrashes between programs. Both were latent in the
    pre-existing user-`BuildHasher` path this shares; per-thread state closes
    them for both. Caught by the derived-key CONTROL, not by the feature's own
    assertions, which is the argument for writing the control.

VERIFIED across the whole container surface — insert, overwrite, get,
contains_key, remove, and `Set` dedup — with impls that key on ONE field while
another varies, so every assertion fails under structural hashing or structural
equality. Identical on both backends. A derived-key control asserts the
structural answers are undisturbed, and an ASAN fixture pins the per-key-hash
sink buffer being freed, since that free is on the map's hot path.

THE REJECTION SURVIVES FOR A PARTIAL SET — `Hash` without `Eq`, or `PartialEq`
without the `Eq` marker — which is the easy mistake once these are hand-written,
and the message now names the missing half. It previously said key hashing "does
not dispatch to a hand-written body": true when written, the opposite of true now.

FOUND ALONGSIDE, NOT CAUSED BY THIS: `Map.get` with an inline TEMPORARY struct
key that owns heap leaks the temporary, on the derived path just as much. Filed
as B-2026-08-26-32.
title: `Map` HASHING NEVER CALLS A HAND-WRITTEN `impl Hash`: with the derive absent the key is REJECTED, and with `#[derive(Hash)]` present alongside the impl the program checks clean and the DERIVE SILENTLY WINS. The COMPARISON half is fixed and now matches design.md -- `==` and `< <= > >=` dispatch to a user body on all three backends, ordering desugars through `PartialOrd.partial_cmp` as specified, and the generic-body / shared-struct surfaces are closed on B-2026-08-26-24 and -25.
detail:
This is the half of B-2026-08-25-35 that was DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED, and the measurements
below are why -- the one-line "make the predicates agree" change was written, measured, and
reverted.

The typecheck gate that rejects `<` on a hand-written `impl PartialOrd`
(`type_supports_partial_ord`, derive-only) looks like a simple oversight next to
`type_supports_ord`, which already has a `has_user_impl_ord` fallback. Adding the same
fallback to `type_supports_partial_ord` / `_partial_eq` / `_eq` / `_hash` makes every
rejection go away. What it does NOT do is make the operator call the user's body:

  1. ORDERING -- `struct Item { id: i64 }` with an `impl Ord` whose `cmp` REVERSES the
     order (smaller id is Greater). With the gate relaxed, `a < b` compiled and evaluated
     by DECLARATION ORDER, contradicting the body. In a `PriorityQueue[Item]` holding
     ids 1/3/2, `pop` returned 1 -- the declaration-order minimum -- where the user's
     `cmp` demands 3. Silent wrong answer.

  2. ORDERING, worse -- in a plain `if a < b { .. }` the relaxed path did not even
     produce a bool:
       error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
              "Branch condition is not 'i1' type!  br i64 0, label %then, label %else"
     and `println(f"{a < b}")` printed `0`, the raw comparator i64, not `true`/`false`.
     The interpreter meanwhile reported `internal: path 'Item.lt' has no interpreter
     evaluation rule (accepted by the typechecker but not wired in the tree-walk
     interpreter) -- please report this`, i.e. the desugaring targets an `Item.lt` the
     user never wrote and nothing supplies.

  3. EQUALITY -- `struct Item { id: i64, tag: i64 }` with an `impl PartialEq` comparing
     ONLY `id`. Two Items with equal ids and different tags: both backends printed
     `eq=FALSE`, i.e. structural comparison including `tag`. Consistent across backends,
     so no A/B check catches it -- the quietest failure of the three.

  4. HASHING -- the same struct with an `impl Hash` hashing only `id`, used as a `Map`
     key. Two Items with equal ids and different tags produced `m.len() == 2` on both
     backends; the user's `hash` would have collided them to 1.

So the derive-only gate is PROTECTIVE, not a bug: these predicates ask "does the DERIVE
machinery support this type", and answering yes for a hand-written impl makes the compiler
apply derive machinery to a type whose author asked for something else. The genuine defect
is one level down -- operator-trait dispatch does not exist for user bodies -- and closing
it means wiring `==` / `<` / `Map` hashing to call `eq` / `partial_cmp` / `cmp` / `hash`
on both backends, then relaxing the gate as the LAST step.

THE DIAGNOSTICS ARE A SEPARATE, SMALLER DEFECT and can be fixed independently. They are
self-contradicting today, because the "implemented by:" candidate list is built from the
impl table while the verdict comes from the derive table:

    trait bound `T: Hash` is not satisfied; `Item` does not implement `Hash`;
    trait `Hash` is implemented by: Item

    trait bound `T: Eq` is not satisfied; `Item` does not implement `Eq`;
    trait `Eq` is implemented by: Bf16, F16, F32, F64, Item, String, bool, ...

and the operator message tells the author of an `impl PartialOrd` to `add
#[derive(PartialOrd)]` -- which would compile, and then ignore the body they wrote. A
correct message would say that the operator requires a derive because it lowers to a
declaration-order comparator, and that their impl cannot be dispatched to yet.

REGRESSION PIN: `hand_written_partial_ord_impl_still_does_not_enable_the_operator` in
`tests/typechecker.rs` asserts the gate still rejects, with the reasoning inline, so this
is not "fixed" later by relaxing it.

=== DIAGNOSTICS HALF FIXED by 3b1865d; THE ROW STAYS OPEN FOR DISPATCH. ===

THE TITLE OVERSTATES ONE CASE, and the correction is load-bearing for anyone who picks this up.
"OPERATORS NEVER CALL A HAND-WRITTEN OPERATOR-TRAIT BODY: `==` uses structural comparison" is
true ONLY for an `impl PartialEq` written WITHOUT the `Eq` marker. MEASURED on all three
backends with an `eq` that returns `false` for two IDENTICAL values (so structural and
hand-written answers are opposites, which an `eq` that merely ignores a field cannot
distinguish):

  impl PartialEq alone                -> `==` REJECTED by the gate
  impl PartialEq + impl Eq for T {}   -> `==` prints false / `!=` prints true  == THE USER'S BODY
  (gate relaxed, impl PartialEq alone) -> `==` prints true                     == structural

So equality DOES dispatch today, through the `Eq` marker. The original measurement 3 was taken
under the relaxed-gate experiment and then generalized into the title.

THE MECHANISM, which the row did not name and which is where the remaining work is.
`target_type_name` in `lowering.rs` decides whether an operator lowers to a user method, and it
looks the type up by TRAIT NAME:

    BinOp::Eq | BinOp::NotEq            -> "Eq"
    BinOp::Lt | BinOp::LtEq | Gt | GtEq -> "Ord"

then emits `T.<method>` where method is `eq` / `lt` / `le` / `gt` / `ge`. That explains both
halves at once:

  * EQUALITY works because the emitted method is `eq`, which is exactly what a user
    `impl PartialEq` provides. `!=` is desugared to `not eq(a, b)` a few lines below, which is
    why the marker-gated path is complete rather than half-wired.

  * ORDERING CANNOT WORK AS WRITTEN, because it emits `T.lt` / `T.le` / `T.gt` / `T.ge` --
    methods NO user impl defines and nothing supplies. design.md specifies the desugaring as
    `PartialOrd.partial_cmp(a, b).is_lt()`, not `lt`. This is the concrete reason the row's
    measurement 2 saw `internal: path 'Item.lt' has no interpreter evaluation rule`: the
    lowering targets a method that does not exist. The `Ordering` helpers it should be routing
    through (`is_lt` / `is_le` / `is_gt` / `is_ge`) are already specified and present.

So the ordering fix is NOT "wire up dispatch from scratch" -- it is: emit
`T.cmp(a, b).is_lt()` (or `partial_cmp(...).is_lt()`) instead of `T.lt(a, b)`, and gate on the
user impl. Whoever takes that should re-measure the row's case 1 (an `impl Ord` whose `cmp`
REVERSES the order) against `PriorityQueue`, because that is the assertion that proves the body
is really being called rather than the declaration-order comparator.

WHAT LANDED. Only the diagnostics, which the row itself carves out as independently fixable.
The two rejection messages denied an impl the author is looking at and prescribed a derive that
compiles and then silently discards it. They now differ by family, because what the two families
can honestly offer differs:

  equality -> names the impl and gives the workaround that WORKS ("add 'impl Eq for T {}'"),
              verified end to end by a codegen E2E test so the advice cannot rot into a lie;
  ordering -> says dispatch to hand-written ordering impls is not implemented, and that the
              derive would compare by DECLARATION ORDER rather than calling the impl. No
              workaround is invented, because none exists.

A type with NO operator impl keeps the plain derive advice; a regression test pins that the new
message does not swallow the common case.

THE GATE IS UNCHANGED and the row's protective reasoning stands. The one-line relaxation was
re-run here on the EQUALITY predicate (`type_supports_partial_eq` accepting `has_impl("PartialEq")`)
and reproduced the silent structural answer exactly as the row predicted for ordering, so it was
reverted. `hand_written_partial_ord_impl_still_does_not_enable_the_operator` still pins the gate,
now asserting the new wording, and its prose carries the `==`/`Eq` correction above.

STILL OPEN, unchanged: `<` `<=` `>` `>=` do not dispatch to a user `impl Ord`/`impl PartialOrd`
(the `T.lt` dead end above), and `Map` ignores a user `impl Hash`. The self-contradicting
trait-bound message ("`Item` does not implement `Hash`; trait `Hash` is implemented by: Item")
is also untouched -- it is generated elsewhere than the operator path fixed here.

=== ORDERING DISPATCH + THE SELF-CONTRADICTING BOUND MESSAGE FIXED
=== (f53241e lowering+codegen, f03364a docs, 178df9c bound message, 6c69abd Map message,
===  f8b0d4d + 82d6d91 gate corrections -- see GATE HOLES below).
=== THE ROW STAYS OPEN FOR ONE THING ONLY: `Map` HASHING. ===

WHAT LANDED, and the correction that made it possible. The row diagnosed the
ordering failure as "the lowering targets `T.lt`, a method no user impl provides"
-- correct, and the fix is the one it names: `a < b` now lowers to
`T.cmp(a, b).is_lt()`. Verified on all three backends with a `cmp` that REVERSES
the order, so declaration order and the body give opposite answers on every one of
`<` `<=` `>` `>=`; also across a two-field struct compared by its SECOND field, a
heap-bearing struct compared in reverse, and a unit-only enum whose `cmp` is
unconditionally `Greater`. `#[derive(Ord)]` still compares by declaration order.

Lowering alone would still have produced a WRONG ANSWER in compiled output, which
the row did not anticipate. codegen's builtin `method == "cmp"` arm runs BEFORE
user-impl dispatch, and its own comment asserted "user-struct `.cmp` is rejected at
typecheck and never arrives" -- untrue since `type_supports_ord` grew its
`has_user_impl_ord` fallback. A single-field struct lowers to a bare int, so a user
`.cmp` matched that arm's `(IntValue, IntValue)` case and was answered by a
DECLARATION-ORDER integer compare. Measured with a `cmp` returning
`Ordering.Greater` unconditionally: `--interp` said `is_lt() == false` (the body),
the compiled binary said `true` (the field). Silent, compiled-only, invisible to
any single-backend test. That arm now declines when a user impl owns `cmp`.

THE GATE WAS NOT RELAXED -- the row's central warning is intact.
`type_supports_partial_ord`, the DERIVE-support predicate, is untouched. Acceptance
comes from a separate predicate asked only at the operator's own gate, which accepts
exactly the shapes lowering can route. `hand_written_partial_ord_impl_still_does_
not_enable_the_operator` was REPLACED rather than deleted, by acceptance plus
execution tests that a reversing body really is what answers the operator on each
backend -- the assertions the pin was standing in for.

`cmp`, NOT design.md's `partial_cmp`. `Option[Ordering].is_lt()` is unimplemented
in codegen -- not merely for a synthesised receiver but for a plain
`let o: Option[Ordering]` local, which builds nowhere and runs fine under
`--interp`. Desugaring through it would have traded a clean rejection for a
run-vs-build divergence. `Ord: PartialOrd` is enforced at impl registration, so the
only shape excluded is an `impl PartialOrd` with NO `impl Ord`; that keeps its
rejection, and the message now prescribes the `impl Ord` that works instead of the
derive that silently discards the body. Divergence recorded in design.md
§ Comparison Traits and in `karac explain operators`; the codegen gap is its own row.

THE SELF-CONTRADICTING BOUND MESSAGE is fixed (178df9c). `trait bound `T: Hash` is
not satisfied; `Item` does not implement `Hash`; trait `Hash` is implemented by:
Item` was two tables disagreeing in one sentence -- the verdict from
`type_satisfies_bound` (derive tables, for the derive-backed traits) and the
candidate list from the impl table. The failing type is split out of its own list
and answered directly.

STILL OPEN, and now measured precisely rather than inferred -- the row's Map claim
needed the same correction its `==` claim did:

  * WITHOUT a derive, `Map[Item, i64]` with a user `impl Hash` is REJECTED, not
    silently structural: "key type does not implement `Hash + Eq`". The row's
    measurement 4 (`m.len() == 2` on both backends) was taken under the RELAXED-GATE
    experiment, exactly as its measurement 3 was.

  * WITH `#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]` AND a hand-written `impl Hash for Item`,
    the program CHECKS CLEAN and the DERIVE SILENTLY WINS. An `impl Hash` collapsing
    every key to one bucket still gave `m.len() == 2` for two keys differing only in
    a field the body ignores. This needs no gate relaxation at all -- writing both is
    the natural thing to do, since `Map` demands the derive -- so it is the live
    silent-wrong-answer path and the reason this row stays open.

  * The asymmetry is the point: with BOTH a derive and a hand-written impl present,
    `==` and `< <= > >=` now let the USER'S BODY win (verified on both backends with
    an `eq` returning `false` for identical values and a `cmp` returning `Greater`
    unconditionally: `false false`). Only `Hash` still lets the derive override.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: making `#[derive(Hash)]` + `impl Hash` a coherence error.
It would convert the silent path into a loud one, but it rejects programs that
compile today and would have to be undone the moment real dispatch lands. The
remaining work is dispatch -- routing `Map`/`Set` key hashing to the user's `hash`
on both backends, which means calling user code from a path that today hashes raw
bytes through `karac_hash_bytes`.

GATE HOLES FOUND AND CLOSED AFTER THE FIRST FIX (f8b0d4d, 82d6d91). Recorded
because both were introduced by the fix itself and both are the exact failure
mode this row warns about -- a rejection traded for a broken program -- so the
next person widening this gate should know what the two sides must agree on.

The gate accepts a type for the WHOLE `< <= > >=` surface at once; lowering picks
its target PER OPERATOR. Two ways that went wrong:

  1. Accepting on ANY of `cmp`/`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` let an impl defining only `lt`
     pass `karac check`, after which `a < b` reached the real `P.lt` and `a > b`
     reached a `P.gt` nobody wrote -- dying with `path 'P.gt' has no interpreter
     evaluation rule`, i.e. this row's own symptom, reintroduced by its own fix.
     The gate now requires `cmp` (which covers all four by construction) or ALL
     FOUR direct methods.

  2. Asking a LOOSER question than `target_type_name` does. That function resolves
     a user operand only when `trait_impls` carries `("Ord", name)`, and reads
     methods from `trait_impl_methods`, which is built from TRAIT impls alone. A
     `cmp` in an INHERENT `impl P` block alongside an `impl PartialOrd` satisfied
     the gate without satisfying either, so lowering emitted NOTHING and both
     backends failed ("operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type
     'Struct'" / "Unsupported struct binary op: Lt"). Both halves of the gate now
     mirror `target_type_name` exactly.

Neither was visible in the diff; both came from sweeping the shape space. The
sweep that settled it -- and the one to re-run after any change here -- covers:
`impl Ord{cmp}`, all-four direct methods, partial direct methods, inherent `cmp`,
`partial_cmp` alone, no impl, derive only, derive + impl, and multi-field /
heap-bearing / enum receivers. Every program that passes `check` must then RUN on
the interpreter AND BUILD. The only shape that still violates that is a
`shared struct`, which predates this work and is B-2026-08-26-25.

=== THE COMPARISON HALF IS NOW COMPLETE AND MATCHES design.md (483fef4). ===
=== STILL OPEN FOR `Map` HASHING ONLY. ===

The desugaring is the SPECIFIED one now. This row's earlier update recorded that
`<` routed through `Ord.cmp` rather than design.md's
`PartialOrd.partial_cmp(a, b).is_lt()`, because `Option[Ordering].is_lt()` had no
codegen lowering — accepting the spec's form would have traded a clean rejection
for a run-vs-build divergence. B-2026-08-26-23 closed that gap, so 483fef4
switched the preference to `partial_cmp` and the divergence note beside
design.md's table is gone. The rejection it forced went with it: an
`impl PartialOrd` with NO `impl Ord` now drives all four operators on both
backends, verified with a comparator that reverses the order.

One thing tightened rather than carried over: the direct `lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` form
is taken only when an impl supplies ALL FOUR. With a partial set the operators
split across two comparators — `a < b` calling a hand-written `lt` while `a > b`
went through the comparator — so a disagreeing pair could report both `a < b` and
`a > b` true. That split predated this work.

THE OTHER TWO SURFACES the comparison half was missing are closed on their own
rows, both found by sweeping shapes rather than reading diffs:
  * B-2026-08-26-24 — a comparison inside a GENERIC body never reached the
    element's impl (`PriorityQueue` the casualty). Note this row's acceptance
    test named `PriorityQueue`; that test now passes.
  * B-2026-08-26-25 — a `shared struct` was admitted by the typechecker and
    implemented by neither backend. Its equality half turned out silently wrong
    in the same way this row's title describes: `==` compared structurally and
    never reached the `impl PartialEq`, while the diagnostic promised it would.

WHAT REMAINS HERE, unchanged and still the reason this row is open: `Map` hashing
never calls a hand-written `impl Hash`. Without the derive the key is REJECTED;
with `#[derive(Hash)]` present alongside the impl the program checks clean and the
DERIVE SILENTLY WINS (an `impl Hash` collapsing every key to one bucket still
gives `m.len() == 2` for two keys differing only in an ignored field). That needs
no gate relaxation, which is what makes it the live hazard. The end state is
dispatch — routing `Map`/`Set` key hashing to the user's `hash` on both backends,
which means calling user code from a path that today hashes raw bytes through
`karac_hash_bytes`. The diagnostics around it are already honest (6c69abd): the
rejection names the impl it is overriding and says the derive will be used
instead.

fix:
FIXED by 0564ee2. Took the row's recommended option (a) -- rename the table row to `push`, keep the description -- because the rest of design.md had already made that choice without the table noticing.

THE DOCUMENT ALREADY AGREED WITH THE COMPILER, in two places, which is what settled (a) over (b) beyond the row's own reasoning. The fallible-alloc table lists `String` -> `push(c)` -> `try_push(c)`, and the OOM-default prose names `String.push` alongside `String.push_str`. So `push_char` was a single stale outlier in a document that otherwise documented `push` correctly; adding `push_char` as a real method (option (b)) would have made the spec MORE inconsistent, not less. `Vec.push` sharing the name and shape is the third corroboration the row already noted.

VERIFIED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING: `s.push_char('a')` reports `no method 'push_char' on type 'String'`; `s.push('a')` works on interpreter and JIT; `push_char` appears nowhere in `src/` or `runtime/`. The description was also checked rather than copied -- `s.push('e-acute'); s.push('CJK-ri')` yields `len=5` (2 + 3 bytes), so "encodes to UTF-8 in-place" is accurate and `len()` is a byte count.

TWO ADJACENT DOCS ASSERTED THE SAME FALSE THING, both reached by following the cross-references out of the table, and both corrected in the same commit because leaving them would have re-taught the error this row exists to remove:

  * `docs/implementation_checklist/phase-7-codegen.md`'s `push_char`/`push_byte` fast-path entry claimed "today appending one character to a `String` goes through `push_str` of a 1-byte slice" and that "`push_char` is already spec'd at design.md:1809 (the method exists in the language surface; only codegen is missing)" -- citing the exact line this row is about. Both claims are false. `vec_method.rs`'s `"push" if ... string_vars` arm computes the UTF-8 length INLINE (no `karac_string_encode_char` call) and takes an ASCII fast path that stores the single byte directly, skipping the slice round-trip entirely -- which is precisely the lowering that entry asked for. Its own code comment cites the kata:38 profile (memmove/memcpy ~40%, encode ~20%) that motivated the work, and E2E coverage exists as `test_e2e_string_push_char_{ascii,multibyte_utf8,mixed_with_push_str}`. The typechecker test comment dates it: "Shipped 2026-05-25 as the kata-71 follow-up". Entry now marked scalar-half-done, with `push_byte` (single-byte append, no UTF-8 boundary check) correctly left as genuinely unshipped new surface.

  * `examples/game_of_life/src/display.kara`'s GAP-K said a `StringBuilder` or `String.with_capacity(n)` + repeated `push_char` "would fix this" and that "without it, we fall back to per-cell println, which issues one write syscall per cell". Both halves exist today. The comment now records that accurately. The renderer itself STILL USES THE PER-CELL FALLBACK and was deliberately not rewritten: that is a behaviour change needing its own expected-output oracle, not a doc correction, so folding it in would have been scope the row did not ask for. Flagged in the comment as a separate pass rather than silently left or silently done.

THE REGRESSION TEST IS A LINT OVER THE WHOLE TABLE, not an assertion about one row, because a single-row test would not have caught this row's sibling if the next stale entry lands elsewhere in the same table. `design_md_string_table_names_only_methods_that_exist` (tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs -- the file that already exists to lint design.md against the compiler) extracts every method name from the `String` table and fails if the compiler does not have it. It probes by CALLING each name and distinguishing "no method 'x'" / "no associated function 'x'" from an argument complaint, so it never has to parse the signature column -- only an existing method can complain about its arguments. It asserts a floor on the number of extracted names so a moved table or a broken parser cannot make it pass over an empty set. Confirmed to FAIL, naming `push_char`, when the original row is restored.

FOUND WHILE BUILDING THAT LINT, FILED SEPARATELY as B-2026-08-26-40: a wrong-ARITY call to an associated function is reported as if the function did not exist. `String.with_capacity()` and `String.with_capacity(1i64, 2i64)` both give `no associated function 'with_capacity' on type 'String'` -- identical to the message for a genuinely absent name -- while `String.with_capacity(8i64)` typechecks. Instance methods get this right (`s.push()` -> `'push' expects 1 argument, found 0`), so it is specific to the static path. Its first practical cost was inside this very lint: a zero-arg probe reported `with_capacity` as missing, and the probe had to be widened to several arities before it worked. That is also the reason the lint's arity loop exists and should not be simplified away until B-2026-08-26-40 is fixed.

VERIFICATION. 109 suites green under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, so no E2E soft-skips. `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy --all --all-targets -D warnings` clean on both feature legs. The only non-green suite is `gpu_e2e`, whose 60 failures are the optional GPU archive being absent in this container; it soft-skips without the strict flag and is unrelated. No compiler code changed in this commit -- the fix is documentation plus one new lint.
title: design.md's `String` METHOD TABLE names the char-append method `push_char`, which DOES NOT EXIST -- the working method is `push(c: char)`, and the table has NO ROW FOR IT, so the documented spelling fails and the real one is undocumented
detail:
let mut s = String.new();
    s.push_char('a');   // error[typecheck]: no method 'push_char' on type 'String'
    s.push('a');        // works

design.md § `String` lists:

    | `push_char` | `fn push_char(mut ref self, c: char)` | Appends a single Unicode scalar; encodes to UTF-8 in-place |
    | `push_str`  | `fn push_str(mut ref self, s: ref String)` | Appends a string slice in-place |

`push_str` exists and works. `push_char` does not exist anywhere -- no
typecheck arm, no codegen handler, no stdlib definition. And the table contains
NO ROW for `push`, which is the method that actually appends a char.

SO BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE BROKEN, which is what separates this from a rename: a
reader following the spec writes `push_char` and gets a typecheck error, and a
reader looking for how to append a char finds no documented way to do it. The
working spelling is discoverable only from existing `.kara` sources.

THIS IS A NORMATIVE TABLE, not illustrative prose -- the difference from
B-2026-08-26-4, filed the same day, which is a broken worked EXAMPLE in the `?`
section. A method table is the surface a user is expected to program against,
which is why this is medium and that one is low. Both are the same underlying
failure: design.md describing an API the compiler does not have.

FIX SHAPE, one of: (a) rename the row to `push` and keep the description, which
matches the implementation and costs nothing; or (b) add `push_char` as the
documented name and keep `push` as it is. (a) is smaller and does not grow the
surface. Note `Vec.push` already exists with the same name and shape, so `push`
on `String` is the CONSISTENT choice rather than merely the incumbent one.

SOURCE NOTE: found writing kata 297's parenthesized codec, which assembles an
integer literal character by character while scanning. The kata uses `push`;
nothing is blocked.

fix:
FIXED by 3454927. The if-expression was never the subject: ANY value-position branch leaf that hands an `Option[shared T]` binding to an owned consumer handed out an UNCOUNTED alias. Measured red before the fix and green after, all on the same program shape: the `if`-expression arm, a `match`-expression arm, a bare `{ a }` block, an `else if` chain, a nested `if` inside an arm, and a `let bound = if ... ;` RHS. Only the direct `show(a)` control was ever green.

MECHANISM, read out of the emitted IR for the repro and its control side by side. A `shared` value moves out of a binding by RETAIN, not by suppression: the source keeps its queued scope-exit dec and the escaping value takes an independent `+1`. For a bare-Identifier call argument that retain is emitted at the CALL SITE by `share_option_shared_ref_for_arg` (the `opt.arg.inc.*` blocks), which is why `show(a)` is green. For a plain `shared Node` it is emitted at the LEAF, per-arm, inside each branch's own basic block (`move.rc.load` + `rc_inc`, via `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`'s shared arm) -- which is why the same program with `shared Node` instead of `Option[Node]` is green through an if-expression. The `Option[shared]` shape reached NEITHER: the call-site companion bails on anything that is not a bare Identifier, and the leaf retain declines because the binding's slot is an Option aggregate, so `var_type_names` names it `Option` and the `shared_types` lookup misses. So `make(s)` allocated at rc 1, the branch loaded the Option struct with no inc, the callee's param `RcDecOption` took it to 0 and freed it -- and then the caller's own still-armed `RcDecOption` decremented THROUGH the freed box.

WHY THE SYMPTOM LOOKS LIKE AN ALLOCATOR FAULT, and why two iterations are needed. There is no second `free`: the stray dec turns 0 into -1, not into another zero. It writes `0xFFFF...F` at offset 0 of a freed chunk, which is where glibc keeps the tcache `fd` pointer, so the corruption is silent until the NEXT `malloc` walks that list -- one more loop iteration -- and aborts with `malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected`. That is the whole reason the row reads as a heap-allocator bug rather than an ownership one.

FIX -- two leaf hooks, both per-arm and flow-sensitive, mirroring exactly what the plain-`shared` leaf already does:
  * `compile_block_with_frame` (src/codegen/stmts.rs), beside the existing `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` call: retain an `Option[shared]` Identifier tail. This is the value-position-block hook, so it covers `if`/`if let` arms, bare `{ }` blocks and every nesting of them, for EVERY consumer -- a call argument, a `let` RHS, anything -- because it fires at the leaf rather than at the consumer.
  * `compile_match`'s arm-tail block (src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs), beside the sibling Vec/Map/boxed-payload neutralizers, for a bare-Identifier arm body.
Both reuse `share_option_shared_ref_for_arg` unchanged, which self-gates on `var_option_shared_heap`, so every other tail shape is a no-op -- including a `Some(..)`/call leaf, which already carries its producer's `+1`.

BOTH HOOKS ARE GATED AGAINST DOUBLE-COUNTING the function-tail path, which compensates the same leaves through `tail_ret_inner` -> `compile_tail_final_expr`. The block hook reads `fn_ctx.tail_ret_inner` at entry, BEFORE `compile_block` `take()`s it; the match hook gates on the `tail` it already holds. Without the gate a `fn f() -> Option[Node] { if c { a } else { a } }` would retain twice and leak -- the inverse failure, and the one the LSan fixture below exists to catch.

PER-ARM IS LOAD-BEARING, not a stylistic choice. `take(if s < 2 { d } else { make(9) })` has two arms that need OPPOSITE treatment: `{ d }` hands out a borrowed binding and needs the retain, `{ make(9) }` carries `make`'s own `+1` and must not take a second. A single retain at the phi is wrong in both directions -- omit it and the borrowed arm double frees, add it and the fresh arm leaks. Emitting into each arm's own basic block is what satisfies both, and the mixed-arm leg of the new tests is what holds that honest.

THE ROW'S "ASAN DOES NOT REPRODUCE IT" IS CORRECT, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL, NOT LUCK -- worth recording because it bounds what the ~1200-fixture `memory_sanitizer` corpus can ever gate. `link_executable_with_sanitizer` passes `-fsanitize=address` to `cc` at LINK time only; neither the runtime archive nor the Kāra-emitted object is INSTRUMENTED, and ASAN's shadow-memory checks live in instrumented code. So the harness gates precisely the faults that cross the allocator boundary -- double free, invalid free, leaks -- and is blind to a use-after-free ACCESS from emitted code. This bug produces no second `free`, so there is nothing at that boundary to see. Measured rather than assumed: an ASAN fixture written for this exact program passes against the UNFIXED compiler (verified by stashing the fix and re-running). `link_executable_with_sanitizer`'s doc comment said the harness "focuses on codegen-emitted heap operations", which reads as the opposite of the truth on this point; it now states the limit and names this row.

TESTS. `tests/codegen.rs::option_shared_through_if_expression_survives_a_rebinding_loop` -- the `#[ignore]`d acceptance test that landed with this row -- is un-ignored and green. Beside it, `option_shared_through_every_branch_leaf_form_survives_a_rebinding_loop` covers the whole family in one program (if-arm, match-arm, bare block, mixed arms, nested if, else-if chain, `let`-bound if) and twins its output against the interpreter rather than a hardcoded string. Both verified RED against the unfixed compiler and green after; the pre-existing `option_shared_without_an_if_expression_survives_a_rebinding_loop` control stays green on both sides, so the delta stays attributable. `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_option_shared_through_branch_leaf_into_owned_param_no_double_free` is added as the LEAK half only -- its doc says so, and says it was measured green against the unfixed compiler -- because over-retaining a leaf is the obvious wrong fix for the mixed arm and LSan is what catches it.
title: HEAP CORRUPTION ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS: an `if`-EXPRESSION whose arms yield an `Option[shared]` binding, passed BY VALUE to a function inside a loop that rebinds it, aborts with glibc's `malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected` on the SECOND iteration -- `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` alike, with or without auto-par -- while `--interp` prints the correct answer. Replacing the if-EXPRESSION with `show(a)` (one token) makes it green, and so does an if-STATEMENT around two calls, so the defect is the if as a value-producing form. ASAN DOES NOT REPRODUCE IT, which is why ~1200 `memory_sanitizer.rs` fixtures never saw the class.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO -- 13 lines, and its one-token CONTROL:

    shared struct Node { val: i64 }
    fn make(n: i64) -> Option[Node] { return Some(Node { val: n }); }
    fn show(t: Option[Node]) {
        match t { None => { } Some(n) => { println(f"v {n.val}"); } }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut s = 0;
        while s < 2 {
            let a = make(s);
            show(if s == 0 { a } else { a });   // <-- CRASHES
            // show(a);                          // <-- the control: GREEN
            s = s + 1;
        }
    }

MEASURED on 4ff8ab1-era `main`, all four surfaces:

    karac run --interp     ->  v 0 / v 1              exit 0   CORRECT
    karac run   (JIT)      ->  malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected
    karac build            ->  malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected, exit 134 (SIGABRT)
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build ->  same abort, exit 134

Note the crash beats the FIRST `println` to stdout: nothing is printed at all,
so the corruption is detected on an allocation that precedes the first output.

BISECTED -- each ingredient removed individually makes the program green, so
all four are required:

  1. `shared` -- the same program over a PLAIN `struct Plain { val: i64 }` in
     an `Option` is green. Reference semantics (the RC control block) is what
     is being mishandled.
  2. `Option[T]` -- the same program over a BARE `shared` value (`fn make(n) ->
     Node`, `fn show(t: Node)`, no `Option` anywhere) is green. The niche-ABI
     `Option[shared]` representation is implicated, not `shared` alone.
  3. THE IF-EXPRESSION -- that is the control above, and it is a single token's
     difference. Rewritten as an if-STATEMENT around two calls
     (`if s == 0 { show(a); } else { show(a); }`) it is also green, so the
     defect is in the if as a VALUE-producing form, not in the branch.
  4. AN OWNED PARAMETER -- consuming the same if-expression with an INLINE
     `match` instead of a function call is green, and so is passing it to a
     `fn show(t: ref Option[Node])`. The bad accounting happens where the
     if-expression's value is transferred into a by-value parameter.

Plus one loop condition:

  5. TWO OR MORE ITERATIONS of the loop that rebinds `a`. A single iteration is
     green, and so is the same body with no loop at all (two straight-line
     if-expressions). This is what makes it look like an RC balance that is
     off by one per iteration rather than a one-shot bad pointer -- the first
     pass survives, the second one frees something the first pass already
     released.

The two arms need NOT name different bindings: `if c { a } else { a }` -- both
arms the SAME binding -- crashes, which rules out any explanation resting on
merging two distinct handles at the phi.

WHY THE ASAN CORPUS NEVER CAUGHT THIS, measured rather than assumed. Linking
the identical program with `-fsanitize=address` through
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s harness produces a run that is CLEAN under ASAN
*and prints the correct output* -- no double-free report, no bad-free report,
no leak. So `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` cannot host the regression test for
this class at all: ~1200 fixtures there are blind to it. The reproducing
harness is the ordinary E2E one in `tests/codegen.rs` (real `cc` link, glibc
allocator), which is where the test below lives. That ASAN's interposed
allocator hides it is itself a hint about the shape: the corruption is not a
free of an obviously-invalid pointer (ASAN checks that) but something whose
damage depends on glibc's chunk layout.

TEST LANDED WITH THIS ROW, verified RED:

fix:
RELOCATED by 5858a19 to docs/roadmap.md § Phase 7.3 stdlib, the `StringSlice`
item, which that commit expanded to carry the remaining work in full (the measured state, what is blocked and
why, and the open decision). Nothing here is refuted -- the 3-4x deficit
against borrowed-view languages is real and the row's benchmarking is sound --
but the framing needs three corrections, and after them there is no action item
that does not first require an owner decision.

1. THIS IS SPECIFIED BEHAVIOUR, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. design.md's String method
   table already reads `split ... -> Vec[String]` with the note "v1: owned
   copies; zero-copy `StringSlice` views are v2", and § StringSlice states the
   v1/v2 boundary outright: the zero-copy split form "is v2 ... The v2 work is
   split-yielding-views (a borrow flowing through a collection), not the core
   view type." So the API's return shape was chosen deliberately and the fix is
   already scheduled. roadmap.md's `StringSlice` item is its canonical home.

2. THE PROPOSED FIX SHAPE (a) CONTRADICTS design.md. The row offers
   `split_slices` / `split_ref` returning `Vec[Slice[u8]]`. design.md § Strings
   is explicit that "a `StringSlice` is *not* a `Slice[u8]` -- the UTF-8
   invariant is carried by the type, not the element kind". A borrowing split
   must yield `StringSlice`, not `Slice[u8]`, or it hands back something that
   has dropped the invariant the type system exists to keep.

3. THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS TOO STRONG, and correcting it is what changed the
   disposition. The row says "there is no spelling of tokenize-this-string-and-
   read-the-fields in Kara today that does not allocate per field", and treats
   hand-rolled `Slice[u8]` scanning as the only workaround. But `Vec[StringSlice]`
   being rejected does NOT mean views cannot be produced -- only that a
   COLLECTION of them cannot. A cursor returning `Option[(StringSlice, i64)]`,
   or a lazy iterator struct holding a `StringSlice` and yielding
   `Option[StringSlice]`, needs no collection of borrows at all. Both typecheck
   and both run.

   They did NOT compile, which is why the row's author reasonably concluded
   otherwise: reading the view back out of the `Option` is a match binding, and
   a match-bound `StringSlice` had lost its method dispatch under `karac build`
   (every method but `to_string` hard-errored, while `--interp` ran it). That is
   filed and FIXED as B-2026-08-26-38.

MEASURED after that fix -- the same 9,600,024 tokens, identical output from
both spellings, container x86-64, best of 3:

    s.split(",")            owned Vec[String]     0.404 s    53.1 MiB peak RSS
    borrowing SplitIter     zero-copy             0.045 s    10.3 MiB peak RSS

9.0x faster, 5.2x smaller. So the language already reaches the zero-copy tier;
the floor this row measured has moved. What is left is exactly an API-shape
question: getting that 9x costs every caller a hand-rolled ~12-line iterator,
which is not something to teach.

WHY RELOCATED RATHER THAN FIXED OR WONTFIX. Fixing it means ADDING A STDLIB API,
and which one is an unmade design decision with a real fork:

  * design.md commits to `split` ITSELF yielding views, which is v2 and gated on
    a lifetime feature ("a borrow flowing through a collection") that does not
    exist and is not a small piece of work;
  * a cursor/iterator form needs none of that and could ship immediately -- but
    doing so either introduces a SECOND borrowing spelling that v2 will later
    duplicate, or amounts to deciding that the iterator IS the borrowing form
    and `split` stays owned permanently.

Picking between those is an owner call, not a bug fix, so the row would sit
`open` as a permanent non-action-item -- which is what the `relocated` status
exists to prevent. `String.split_whitespace` and `String.lines` carry the same
shape and should move with whatever is chosen; this row measured only `split`.

SEVERITY was medium and that still holds for the API gap. Nothing is blocked,
and the workaround is now materially better than the row could have known:
9x, on both backends, in ~12 lines rather than a hand-written `Slice[u8]` lexer.
title: `String.split` HAS NO BORROWING FORM: it returns `Vec[String]`, so tokenizing costs one heap allocation and one byte copy PER FIELD, and there is no slice-returning variant to reach for. Measured at 0.67 s where C's in-place split is 0.03 s and Rust's `Vec[&str]` is 0.18 s -- but Kara BEATS Rust's same-semantics `Vec[String]` version (1.17 s) by 1.7x, so the implementation is fine and the API's return shape is the entire gap.
detail:
MEASURED, four implementations of the SAME micro-benchmark -- split a 3.2 MB
comma-separated string (400,001 seven-byte tokens) 24 times and count the
tokens. Container x86-64, all compiled at their normal optimization:

    C, split in place (no copies)                      0.03 s
    Rust, split(',').collect::<Vec<&str>>()  borrowed  0.18 s
    KARA,  s.split(",")                                0.67 s
    Rust, split(',').map(String::from).collect() owned 1.17 s

THE IMPLEMENTATION IS NOT THE PROBLEM -- READ THE LAST TWO ROWS. Against the
version with the SAME semantics (one owned, heap-allocated token per field),
Kara's `split` is 1.7x FASTER than Rust's. What costs the 3.7x against
borrowed Rust is entirely the API's return type: `String.split` yields
`Vec[String]`, so every token is a fresh allocation and a byte copy, and there
is no slice-returning variant to reach for when the tokens are only going to be
read.

WHERE IT SHOWS UP IN REAL CODE. Kata 297's benchmark lane (200k-node tree, 24
chained serialize/deserialize round trips) is 2.2x slower than C, and ablating
the compiled binary one stage at a time attributes essentially all of it here:

    serialize + hash, no deserialize     0.82 s
    serialize + deserialize, no hash     2.31 s
    all three                            2.57 s

-- deserialize is ~1.9 s of a 2.57 s run, three quarters of the total, and the
tokenizer is the whole of that. Peak RSS tells the same story: 73.6 MiB against
C's 14.2 MiB and Rust's 25.8 MiB, because ~400k owned token Strings are live
across every deserialize. Note Python, which also allocates owned copies, is
15x slower than C on the same workload; Go and Rust both hand back views into
the original buffer. Kara is the only COMPILED language in the corpus's
five-way mirror that copies.

WHY THIS IS A LANGUAGE-SURFACE ROW AND NOT A PERF ROW. There is no spelling of
"tokenize this string and read the fields" in Kara today that does not allocate
per field. `Slice[u8]` scanning exists and is what `codec_paren.kara` uses, but
that is writing a lexer by hand, not splitting a string -- it is the workaround,
not the API. The gap is a MISSING RETURN SHAPE.

FIX SHAPE, one of: (a) add a borrowing sibling -- `split_slices` /
`split_ref` returning `Vec[Slice[u8]]` or a lazy iterator of subslices tied to
the receiver's lifetime, leaving `split` as it is; (b) make `split` itself lazy
and yield borrowed views, and have the owning form be an explicit
`.map(String.from)` collect, which is Rust's arrangement and the one that
composes best but is a breaking change to every existing caller; (c) leave it
and document the cost. (a) is additive and does not disturb the ~40 katas
already calling `split`. Whichever is chosen, `String.split_whitespace` and
`String.lines` carry exactly the same shape and should move together --
this row measured only `split`.

SEVERITY medium, not high: nothing is BLOCKED, every program that needs the
tokens owned is already paying the right price, and the workaround (hand-rolled
`Slice[u8]` scanning) exists and is used in the corpus. What earns the row is
that the default, idiomatic, taught spelling is the allocating one, with no
non-allocating alternative to graduate to -- so text-processing code in Kara
starts at a 3-4x deficit against every other compiled language for a reason
that has nothing to do with codegen quality.
