fix:
FIXED by 08410c2, alongside B-2026-08-26-7, which is what surfaced it.

The guard carried a comment stating the invariant it depended on: "codegen widens every integer local to i64 in both storage and value flow ... That i64-backing is why a source-level narrow annotation (`let n: i32`) still resolves here: its slot IS i64." That invariant was ALREADY FALSE when written, because a SUFFIXED narrow literal (`let base: i32 = 7i32`) has always produced a real i32 slot. Only the UNSUFFIXED spelling compiled at i64 -- and that is the spelling every par test in `tests/par_codegen.rs` uses, including `test_e2e_par_join_branch_narrow_int_method`, which is NAMED for the narrow-receiver case and was in fact covering the i64 path a second time. So the arm's one intended regression test could never fail.

B-2026-08-26-7 made the unsuffixed spelling narrow too, which routed that test onto the broken path and turned this from invisible into a suite failure. Confirmed pre-existing rather than caused by it: with that change stashed, the suffixed program above already failed identically.

The guard now accepts the real integer widths (8/16/32/64/128). It was never a narrowing exclusion but a receiver-SHAPE filter, and it keeps that role -- `bool` is i1 and stays out, and although `char` is also i32, the typechecker rejects `c.abs()` / `c.sqrt()` outright (`no method 'abs' on type 'char'`, measured), so no non-numeric receiver can reach this arm with one of these methods. A struct receiver lowers to a StructType and misses regardless.

`test_e2e_par_join_branch_suffixed_narrow_int_method` pins the spelling that was broken all along, beside the unsuffixed one, so the pair cannot collapse onto a single path again.

LESSON WORTH THE ROW: a test named for an edge case is not evidence the edge case is covered. This one asserted the right answer for years while exercising the wrong path, because the value under test was normalized away before it reached the code being tested.

COVERAGE STRENGTHENED by 3d31b1f, because the fix as landed repeated this row's own mistake in miniature: the guard was widened to the integer widths but verified on i32 alone, leaving the width list pinned by a commit message rather than a test. `test_e2e_par_join_branch_narrow_int_method_every_width` now asserts i8/i16/i32/i64/i128 through the arm, and it is meaningful rather than vacuous: reverting the guard to i64-only fails it loudly, since a dropped slot panics `run_program` with `Undefined variable 'x'` instead of returning a wrong answer. `test_e2e_par_join_narrow_slots_through_other_sizer_arms` additionally covers a struct field, a Vec index and a user `impl` method at narrow widths -- these were never broken and the test passes with the guard reverted, so it is NOT a guard pin; it exists because B-2026-08-26-7 made narrow slots the common case in branch bodies where they had been rare, changing which path those arms take.

AUDIT OF THE CLASS, done at the same time and finding nothing further: unsigned receivers cannot reach the arm at all (`no method 'abs' on type 'u8'`), an annotated `f32` receiver through the float leg works, and the struct-field / Vec-index / user-impl arms all handle narrow slots. The `-> Self` arm was the only one carrying this defect.
title: A `par` BRANCH WHOSE BODY CALLS A VALUE-PRESERVING SCALAR METHOD (`abs` / `sqrt` / a `float_math` transcendental) ON A NARROW-INTEGER RECEIVER FAILS TO COMPILE AT ALL -- `error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'x'` on a valid program. The auto-par return-slot sizer's `-> Self` arm (`infer_expr_llvm_type`, `src/codegen/stmts.rs`) accepted a receiver whose inferred LLVM type was EXACTLY i64; a narrow one returned `None`, the slot was dropped, and the branch body then referenced a binding that no longer existed. MEASURED: `fn main() { let base: i32 = 7i32; let total = par { let x = base.abs(); let y = base + 100i32; x + y }; println(total); }` -> `codegen failed: Undefined variable 'x'`, on 7c7d4eb-era main with no other change.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while fixing B-2026-08-26-7 -- that change made the unsuffixed literal spelling narrow, which routed the existing par test onto this already-broken path. Verified pre-existing by reproducing with the B-2026-08-26-7 change stashed.

fix:
FIXED by bd68c8a. The rejection the spec promises now exists; no behaviour was repaired, because none was broken.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING. The row measured this correctly and it is worth restating, because it determines the shape of the fix: the capturing form produced identical, correct results on `--interp`, `karac run` and `karac build`. Nothing miscompiled and no backend disagreed. So this change ADDS a compile error to a program that previously worked; it does not change any accepted program's meaning.

THE WALKER THE ROW POINTED AT WAS NOT THE RIGHT ONE, and this is the substantive deviation. The row nominated `gpu_safe.rs`'s `check_gpu_closure_captures` ("the walk is already written and already proven on the GPU rule"). It is written and proven, but it is specialized: `note_capture` filters each captured name through `gpu_unsafe_reason` and emits `(name, GpuUnsafe)`. Reusing it needed either threading a predicate through its exhaustive ~200-line match (a large mechanical edit across ~50 recursive call sites) or handing it a synthetic `outer` map typed so that every entry reads as GPU-unsafe. The second is the tempting one and it is a trap: the rule would then depend on `gpu_unsafe_reason`'s behaviour, so a future change to what counts as GPU-safe would silently stop this rule firing, with no test tying the two together.

`cross_task_check.rs`'s `collect_captures_expr` -- used by the `spawn` / `tg.spawn` / `par {}` boundary checks -- is already the general version: a free-standing pure AST function (it does not take `&TypeChecker`), shadow-aware, filtered only on presence in the supplied `outer` map. It also returns each capture's FIRST-REFERENCE span, which the GPU walk does not, so the diagnostic anchors inside the closure body at the offending identifier instead of at the closure as a whole:

    3 |     let BAD: LazyLock[i64] = LazyLock.new(|| runtime + 1i64);
      |                                              ^^^^^^^

It was module-private; it is now `pub(super)`. No behavioural change to the cross-task sites.

HOOKED beside the `spawn` check in `infer_call`, and deliberately at that exact point rather than anywhere else in the function: that site's own comment records why, and the reason applies unchanged here -- the outer-scope snapshot has to be taken BEFORE the closure body's typecheck pushes the closure's params onto the local scope, or the params themselves would read as enclosing locals.

THE HALF THAT MAKES IT CORRECT RATHER THAN MERELY PRESENT is what it declines to reject, and each of these would have been a regression of the feature's primary use:

  * a module-level `let TABLE: LazyLock[i64] = LazyLock.new(|| …)` -- the form design.md actually documents; inert because the local snapshot is empty;
  * a LOCAL cell capturing a MODULE-level binding -- precisely what the spec permits ("may only capture other module-level compile-time bindings"), and it stays legal because module bindings are not in `flatten_local_scope_snapshot`;
  * a closure param, or an inner `let`, shadowing an outer local of the same name -- not a capture, handled by the walker's shadow stack;
  * a free-function reference -- not in the snapshot, so not a capture.

All four are pinned by `lazylock_init_closure_accepts_module_bindings_and_shadows`, alongside `lazylock_init_closure_rejects_a_captured_local`, which covers the row's two measured cases (a plain local, and the loop variable in the fresh-cell-per-iteration shape) plus a capture sitting below an inner `let`, which a walker that stopped at the first binding form would miss.

DIAGNOSTIC CODE: E0284, not the E0259 first chosen. E0259 is free in `CODE_TABLE` but already assigned to a LINT, in a separate registry the table does not list. `lint_codes_do_not_collide_with_the_code_table` and `code_table_has_no_cross_phase_collisions` both caught it -- worth recording, because "grep CODE_TABLE for a free number" is the obvious and insufficient way to pick one.

VERIFICATION. 109 suites green under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, so no E2E soft-skips; `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy --all --all-targets -D warnings` clean on both feature legs. The only non-green suite is `gpu_e2e`, whose 60 failures are the optional GPU archive being absent in this container; it soft-skips without the strict flag and is unrelated.

LEFT ALONE DELIBERATELY, per the row's own note: design.md's family table still does not document the LOCAL `let c: LazyLock[T] = …` form, which B-2026-08-26-3 shipped to avoid a run-vs-build divergence. This change polices captures WITHIN that form; it does not decide whether the form should exist. If the local form is later declared illegal, this rule becomes redundant and can go with it -- that is a spec decision, not one to make from inside a capture check.
title: `LazyLock.new`'s closure-capture restriction is UNENFORCED: design.md says the closure "may only capture other module-level compile-time bindings; captures of runtime state are a compile error", but a closure capturing a function local is accepted silently. Measured to be a missing RESTRICTION rather than a correctness hazard -- the capturing form produces identical, correct results on `--interp`, `karac run` and `karac build` -- which is why it is split out of B-2026-08-26-3 rather than blocking it.

fix:
FIXED by b77511f. `collect_lazy_lock_inits` records each module binding's
initializer closure by name, and the `MethodCall` arm of
`collect_calls_in_expr` recurses into it at a `get()` site, so the closure's
calls land in the calling function's effect set exactly as a direct call
would. Regression test
`tests/cli.rs::test_lazy_lock_get_attributes_init_effects_to_the_caller`.

THE SCOPE WAS NARROWER THAN THIS ROW IMPLIED, and measuring that first is
what shaped the fix. Two neighbouring forms were ALREADY correct:

  * a LOCAL `let c: LazyLock[T] = LazyLock.new(|| ...)` — its closure is a
    sub-expression of the enclosing function body, so the ordinary walk
    already descends into it;
  * `cell.get_or_init(|| load())` — its closure is a syntactic argument at
    the call site, same reason.

Both work because the closure is REACHABLE FROM THE CALL SITE BY STRUCTURAL
DESCENT. A module-level `LazyLock`'s closure is not: it lives at the
binding, outside any function body, and `LazyLock.get` is a
`#[compiler_builtin]` with no `with` clause, so there was nothing at the
`get()` site to walk and no callee effects to inherit. That, precisely, was
the defect — not the primitive as a whole.

So the fix supplies the one missing edge. The map is the effect-checker twin
of codegen's `lazy_var_inits` and the interpreter's `lazy_init_table`; all
three exist because the same closure has to be found again from the
binding's NAME rather than from the syntax around the call.

TWO THINGS THE OBVIOUS VERSION GETS WRONG, both caught while building it:

  * Keying on the RECEIVER'S NAME taints an unrelated method. A local
    `let CACHE: Map[String, i64] = Map.new()` shadowing a module-level
    `CACHE: LazyLock[i64]` inherited `reads(Db)` onto its `Map.get` — the
    exact `map.get()` taint the precise-resolution comment in
    `inference.rs` already warns about. Re-gated on the TYPECHECKER's
    resolved callee key, which separates `LazyLock.get` from `Map.get` by
    type instead of by spelling.
  * Two `LazyLock`s whose closures call each other's `get()` form a cycle
    through the BINDING TABLE that the AST does not contain, so structural
    descent alone would not terminate. A `RefCell` visited-set guards it;
    the mutual pair and the self-cycle both terminate and still attribute.

ATTRIBUTED AT EVERY `get()`, NOT JUST THE FIRST. Which call actually runs
the initializer is a runtime race, so the static answer has to hold for all
of them. That over-approximates for callers that hit the cache, which is the
sound direction, and it is the same answer `get_or_init` already gives.

TEST SITED END-TO-END ON PURPOSE. The fix keys off the typechecker's callee
table, and the effectchecker unit harness (`effectcheck_with_profile_config`)
builds a checker with that table EMPTY — a unit-level test would have
exercised none of it and failed for the wrong reason. The production paths
(`check` / `run` / `build`) all populate it; the not-typechecked path is the
one `cli.rs` already documents as producing no codegen anyway.

CORPUS IMPACT: none. Nothing outside `runtime/stdlib/once.kara` mentions
`LazyLock`, so the stricter rule newly rejects nothing that passed before.

ONE CLAIM IN THIS ROW WAS CHECKED AND NOT UPHELD AS STATED. The row said
effect sets drive conflict analysis, so an invisible effect is one the
scheduler cannot conflict-check. True in principle, but the demonstration
does not land: two `par` branches both performing `writes(Log)` through
`get()` are accepted — and so is the DIRECT-CALL control, so that shape is
not conflict-rejected regardless and nothing regressed. The honest
criterion, and the one every probe now satisfies, is PARITY WITH THE
EQUIVALENT DIRECT CALL.

SPUN OUT: B-2026-08-26-19, a general `ref T` -> `T` coercion gap in
closure-tail position, found while writing the cycle probe. Not
LazyLock-specific — `OnceLock.get_or_init` predates `LazyLock` and shows it
too.
title: UNDECLARED EFFECTS ESCAPE THROUGH `LazyLock.get()`: design.md says the effect system attributes first-access initialization to the CALLING function, but a `pub fn` whose only effectful work is a `LazyLock.get()` running an effectful closure passes `karac check` clean, while the identical direct call is correctly rejected. The public-function effect-declaration rule is bypassed.
detail:
Split from B-2026-08-26-3, which shipped `LazyLock[T]` itself. This is the
remainder with teeth -- its sibling B-2026-08-26-15 is a missing restriction
with no correctness consequence; this one lets a public function perform
effects it does not declare.

design.md § Module-Level Bindings, `LazyLock[T]` paragraph: "the effect
system attributes the first-access initialization to the *calling* function,
not to the module."

MEASURED on 3988b47. The `LazyLock` path is accepted:

    resource Db;
    fn load() -> i64 with reads(Db) { return 5; }
    let CACHE: LazyLock[i64] = LazyLock.new(|| load());
    pub fn peek() -> i64 { return CACHE.get(); }
    fn main() { println(peek()); }
      karac check -> All checks passed.

The direct-call control, same shape, is correctly rejected:

    resource Db;
    fn load() -> i64 with reads(Db) { return 5; }
    pub fn peek() -> i64 { return load(); }
      karac check -> error[effect]: public function 'peek' performs effects
                     [reads(Db)] but has no effect declaration.
                     Add: with reads(Db) to the function signature

So the effect walk does not see through `get()` to the stored closure. The
consequence is not confined to a missing diagnostic: effect sets drive
conflict analysis and auto-parallelization, so a `reads`/`writes` that the
checker cannot see is a `reads`/`writes` the scheduler cannot conflict-check
either.

WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM AN ORDINARY MISSING ARM: the closure is
stored at the module binding and run at an arbitrary later call site, so
attribution has to travel from the binding to each `get()` caller -- which is
precisely what the spec sentence asks for and why it is called out
explicitly there. The interpreter and codegen already resolve the closure
per `get` site (`lazy_init_table` / `lazy_var_inits`), so the binding->site
mapping the effect walk needs already exists in both backends.

fix:
FIXED by f79cefd. `resolve_atomic_storage` falls back to
`mod_bindings.module_bindings` when the receiver is not a local: the global
IS the storage, the same posture `get_data_ptr` already documents for the
Vec/Map/Set method paths, so it substitutes for the alloca directly and
`ModuleBindingInfo` supplies both the pointer and the element type.

Verified `let COUNTER: Atomic[i64] = Atomic.new(0)` with `store`/`load`
identical under `--interp`, `karac run` and `karac build`. Regression test
`tests/cli.rs::test_module_scope_atomic_lowers_on_every_backend`.
title: A MODULE-SCOPE `Atomic[T]` failed BOTH compiled backends with `codegen: Atomic receiver 'X' has no slot` while `--interp` was correct -- and module scope is exactly the placement the `module_mut_binding` warning recommends it for, so the compiler steered users into a program it could not build. `resolve_atomic_storage` consulted only local allocas, never the module-binding global.
detail:
Found while shipping `LazyLock[T]` (B-2026-08-26-3), by a route worth
recording because the guard that found it was supposed to have found it
already.

That row credited `tests/cli.rs::
every_type_the_module_mut_binding_warning_names_actually_runs` with
compiling and running one module-scope program per recommended TYPE, and
argued that a name-resolves check would not have caught the `LazyLock`
phantom "which is the whole reason the guard runs programs". The guard did
NOT run programs -- it called `check_source_output`, which shells out to
`karac check` and nothing else. So its name and the reasoning built on it
were both wrong, and the property it was believed to enforce was never
enforced.

Making it actually run its probes (parent commit 3988b47) surfaced this on
the FIRST execution -- `Atomic`, the entry listed above the one under
investigation:

    let COUNTER: Atomic[i64] = Atomic.new(0);
    fn main() {
        COUNTER.store(7, MemoryOrdering.SeqCst);
        println(COUNTER.load(MemoryOrdering.SeqCst));
    }
      karac check        -> All checks passed.
      karac run --interp -> 7
      karac run  (JIT)   -> error: codegen failed: codegen: Atomic receiver
                            'COUNTER' has no slot
      karac build        -> same

Confirmed pre-existing at the parent commit with the session's edits
stashed. `Mutex` and `OnceLock` module bindings were unaffected -- they route
through their own handle lowerings, which already consult the module-binding
globals.

fix:
FIXED by 54c5421. The row's diagnosis was wrong about the locus, and the
correction is most of the value here: this is NOT a `PriorityQueue` defect, not
a generics defect, and not a stdlib defect.

ROOT CAUSE, one line: an index-assign whose container is reached through a
field of `self` never released the element it overwrote.
`emit_displaced_index_elem_drop` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`) is the pass that
frees a displaced element's heap fields, and its field-rooted arm opened with

    let ExprKind::Identifier(root) = &inner.kind else { return; };

`self` parses as `ExprKind::SelfValue`, which is its own AST node and not an
`Identifier`, so EVERY self-rooted element store returned early and its
displaced element's buffer was orphaned. The sibling STORE path
(`compile_index_store`, `src/codegen/collections.rs`) already normalises
`SelfValue` to a synthetic `Identifier("self")` and carries a comment
explaining why — so the store half had been taught about `self` and the
release half never was. The store landed correctly; the free went missing.

BISECTED to that single statement, 21 ASAN probes, each leg measured:

  LEAKS   `self.xs[0] = Item { .. }`         (fresh literal, through `self`)
  CLEAN   `b.xs[0]    = Item { .. }`         (same statement, NAMED root)
  CLEAN   `v[0]       = Item { .. }`         (same statement, local `Vec`)
  CLEAN   `let t = self.xs[0]`               (the READ side is fine)
  CLEAN   `self.xs[0] = f"z{9}"`             (`String` element, through `self`)
  CLEAN   free fn taking `mut ref Vec[T]`, generic and non-generic alike

So: not generics (a non-generic `Bag { xs: Vec[Item] }` with a `mut ref self`
method leaks identically), not the stdlib (same), not `PriorityQueue` (it is
merely the first caller — `swap`'s three self-rooted stores are how the stdlib
hit it), and not `String` elements (a `String` element slot is a
`{ptr,len,cap}` vec-struct, which the release helper's FIRST arm handles
without needing the displaced-drop pass at all — which is exactly why the row's
own case C, `PriorityQueue[String]`, looked clean and misdirected the search).

CONFIRMED IN THE EMITTED CODE, not just by LSan: pre-fix the leaking and clean
binaries differed by exactly one `karac_free_buf` call; post-fix the counts
match.

THE SECOND HALF IS MANDATORY, AND IT IS WHERE THE DANGER IS. Normalising the
receiver alone would have turned a leak into a DOUBLE FREE. The alias guard
gating this release is keyed on the container's NAME and opens with
`expr_mentions_name_deep(rhs, container)` — a walk with no `SelfValue` arm at
all. For a self-rooted container it therefore reports "no mention" for EVERY
rhs, `self.xs[j]` included, and answers "safe to release" unconditionally: the
guard would not merely fail to catch the aliasing store, it would be fully
disarmed. `expr_contains_self_value` is the narrow stand-in for that mention
test, so an aliasing self-rooted rhs declines exactly as a named root's does.
`asan_self_rooted_index_assign_from_sibling_element_is_not_double_freed` is
the oracle for that leg specifically.

BODIES vs MEMORY. The helper emits two halves — the user `Drop` BODIES and the
cap-guarded memory release. The self-rooted arm takes the MEMORY half only
(`run_bodies: false`). This is not timidity: turning bodies on was measured,
and it breaks `asan_priority_queue_push_drops_a_drop_element_exactly_once` by
printing `drop 1 / drop 3` at every push — because `swap` RELOCATES the
displaced element rather than destroying it, and a relocated value's `Drop`
body must not run. Since a self-rooted store previously emitted NEITHER half,
memory-only fixes this row's leak while changing no observable behaviour. The
relocation defect itself is real and PRE-EXISTING on the named-root arm —
verified by stashing this fix and reproducing byte-identically on main — and is
filed as B-2026-08-26-21 rather than folded in here.

ORACLES. Four ASAN fixtures, each verified RED with the normalisation stubbed
and green with it live: the minimal self-rooted shape, the aliasing sibling
store (the double-free direction), the `PriorityQueue`-of-heap-bearing-struct
sift, and this row's own acceptance test, now UN-IGNORED. A fifth, the
named-root twin, was already green and is kept deliberately as a CONTRAST
oracle: it pins the asymmetry that located the bug, so a future change that
regresses the named path fails loudly instead of quietly making both roots leak
and leaving the pair looking consistent.
title: A `PriorityQueue[T]` whose element T is a STRUCT CARRYING A HEAP FIELD leaks that field's buffer -- 31 bytes in 8 allocations on the three-push fixture. Independent of `impl Drop`; a plain `Vec[T]` holding the same struct is clean, and `PriorityQueue[String]` is clean, so the gap is specifically the generic queue's handling of a struct element's interior heap.
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-26-9, which reported this leak as a symptom of its
drop-count defect. It is not: the drop sequence is now byte-identical on both
backends and the leak is unchanged at 31 bytes / 8 allocations.

MEASURED (Linux, LSan live), fixture = the `#[ignore]`d
`asan_priority_queue_peek_drop_count_is_one_per_returned_copy` in
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`, `struct Item { id: i64, name: String }`, three
pushes + two peeks + drain:

    Direct leak of 22 byte(s) in 5 object(s) ... in karac_string_clone
    Direct leak of  9 byte(s) in 3 object(s) ... in PriorityQueue.push$Item
    SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 31 byte(s) leaked in 8 allocation(s).

The 9/3 is one leaked buffer per push -- the defensive copy `push` makes of the
element's `String` -- so the copy that lands in the backing `Vec` is never freed
by the drain.

BISECTED, and every leg of this contradicts -9's case C, which claimed the
no-`Drop` variant was LSan-clean:

  A. Same struct, `impl Drop` REMOVED       -> STILL LEAKS (19 bytes / 5 allocs
                                               on a two-push variant). `Drop` is
                                               not the trigger.
  B. `Vec[Item]` instead of PriorityQueue,
     same struct, same `impl Drop`          -> CLEAN.
  C. `PriorityQueue[String]` (element IS
     the String)                            -> CLEAN
                                               (`asan_priority_queue_string_drain_no_leak`).
  D. `PriorityQueue[Item]` where
     `Item { id: i64 }` -- no heap field    -> CLEAN
                                               (`asan_priority_queue_push_drops_a_drop_element_exactly_once`).

So the trigger is the pair: the generic queue AND a struct element with interior
heap. B is the useful contrast -- `Vec` and `PriorityQueue` hold the same element
in the same backing buffer, so whatever the `Vec` drain does for a struct
element's fields, the queue's path does not.

`PriorityQueue` is the only stdlib collection written in real Kara bodies rather
than as a Rust twin, so the likely locus is the `.kara` source's own
push/pop/sift path (or its monomorphization) rather than a runtime entrypoint --
but that is a hypothesis, not a measurement, and it has not been narrowed
further.

ACCEPTANCE TEST ALREADY WRITTEN.
`asan_priority_queue_peek_drop_count_is_one_per_returned_copy` is `#[ignore]`d
naming this row. Its stdout expectations are already met exactly; ONLY the LSan
result blocks it, so un-ignoring it is this row's acceptance test. Do not relax
its expectations.

fix:
FIXED by fa5e169, in two halves — the second of which the row did not
anticipate and which is the reason a check-only fix would have been worse
than the bug.

THE RULE IS NARROWER THAN THIS ROW STATED. The title called it a
"`ref T` -> `T` coercion". `check_assignable` actually performs a ONE-LEVEL
SCALAR peel (B-2026-07-15-3), gated on `scalar_reads_as_value` =
Int | UInt | Float | Bool | Char. So `ref String` -> `String` is rejected in
EVERY position, return included, and that is correct rather than a second
defect. The row's own probes could not distinguish "Copy-gated" from
"scalar-gated" — `String` is neither — and only reading the source settled
it. Worth recording because the wrong reading would have produced a fix that
lets you obtain an owned `String` by reading a borrow.

TYPECHECK HALF. On the expected-type closure path (`typechecker/exprs.rs`),
the body is checked with `check_expr(body, expected_ret)` — which ALREADY
accepts a `ref i64` body against an `i64` expectation via that peel. But
`body_ty` kept the borrow, so the closure's type became `Fn() -> ref i64` and
the trailing `check_assignable(expected, &actual)` rejected a body the same
function had just approved one line earlier. The coercion was permitted and
never written back; the fix writes it back, under a condition copied verbatim
from `check_assignable` so the two cannot drift.

This also explains the asymmetric diagnostics that made the defect look
stranger than it was: `ref String` fails the INNER check and reports at the
body ("expected 'String', found 'ref String'"), while `ref i64` passes the
inner check and dies at the OUTER one ("expected 'Fn() -> i64', found
'Fn() -> ref i64'"). One defect, two error shapes.

CODEGEN HALF — MANDATORY, AND FOUND BY RUNNING RATHER THAN CHECKING. With
only the typechecker fixed, the annotated-let case passed `karac check` and
then died in LLVM's module verifier:

    Function return type does not match operand type of return inst!
      ret ptr %usermethod
     i64

The tail handed back the pointer; nothing performed the read. So the
"trivially worked around, rejects a legal program" framing in this row would
have held only until someone fixed the half the row named — the false
rejection was, in effect, load-bearing. `compile_closure` now emits the load
before the cleanup drain (the pointer may address storage the frame is about
to release), keyed on the actual LLVM shapes rather than on a Kāra type,
which makes it self-limiting: a closure whose value already matches its
declared return is untouched by construction, so no program that compiles
today can be perturbed.

SURFACE. Not stdlib-specific, as the row suspected: user methods declared
`-> ref T`, `ref` PARAMETERS used bare as a closure tail, and both the
argument-position and annotated-`let` forms were all affected. Verified fixed
across i64 / f64 / bool / u8 under `--interp`, `karac run`, `karac build` and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`, all byte-identical, plus the `ref String`
rejection pinned so the peel cannot be widened later without a test failing.

The two probes that originally motivated this row (`take(|| cell.get_or_init(..))`
and its user-method twin) now clear typecheck and stop at a DIFFERENT,
later-phase diagnostic — ownership rejecting a `ref`-capturing closure that
escapes its scope. That is a separate question about closure capture escape,
not this coercion, and it is left alone.

SEPARATE PRE-EXISTING DEFECT FOUND AND FILED: B-2026-08-26-20 — a `char`
returned through ANY closure prints as its code point under the compiled
backends (`let c: char = 'z'; let f: Fn() -> char = || c; println(f())` gives
`z` interpreted, `122` compiled). No `ref` anywhere, so it is unrelated to
this row; confirmed pre-existing by stashing all `src/` changes, rebuilding
clean HEAD and re-running. Deliberately excluded from this row's regression
test — asserting it there would pin that defect rather than this one — and
the test says so at the exclusion.
title: A `ref T`-returning method is accepted in a plain value position but REJECTED as a closure tail against `Fn() -> T`: `|| cell.get_or_init(|| 7)` fails with "expected 'Fn() -> i64', found 'Fn() -> ref i64'" while `println(cell.get_or_init(|| 7))` and `return cell.get_or_init(..)` from an `i64`-returning fn both coerce fine. The `ref T` -> `T` coercion applies in return and argument position but not in closure-tail position.
detail:
Spun out of B-2026-08-26-16, found while writing a cycle probe for that
row's regression test. NOT `LazyLock`-specific: `OnceLock.get_or_init`
predates `LazyLock` entirely and shows the same thing, which is what makes
this a general coercion gap rather than a wrinkle of the new type.

MEASURED on b77511f:

    fn take(f: Fn() -> i64) -> i64 { return f(); }
    fn main() {
        let cell: OnceLock[i64] = OnceLock.new();
        println(take(|| cell.get_or_init(|| 7)));
    }
      -> error[typecheck]: expected 'Fn() -> i64', found 'Fn() -> ref i64'

The same call in a plain value position is fine:

    fn main() {
        let cell: OnceLock[i64] = OnceLock.new();
        println(cell.get_or_init(|| 7));       // All checks passed.
    }

and so is `return CACHE.get();` from a `-> i64` function, where `get`
likewise yields `ref i64` (verified while closing B-2026-08-26-16).

So the deref/copy coercion that fires at a return site and an argument site
does not fire when checking a closure body against an expected `Fn() -> T`.
The workaround is to force a value expression in the tail (`... + 1`,
binding to a `let` first), which is exactly the kind of contortion that
should not be needed.

WHY LOW: it rejects a legal program rather than accepting an illegal one, it
is trivially worked around, and it needs a deliberate combination (a
`ref`-returning stdlib method used bare as a closure tail against an
explicitly-typed `Fn`). Filed rather than folded into -16 because the cause
is in the closure-vs-expected-type check, nowhere near that row's effect
walk, and because the surface is every `ref T`-returning method — `get`,
`get_or_init`, and any user method declared `-> ref T` — not just the two
observed.

fix:
FIXED by d3b3053, at the mechanism rather than at the instance.

THE ROW'S GUESS AT THE CAUSE WAS RIGHT IN SHAPE AND WRONG IN SCOPE. It
suspected "the closure's return value reaches the `println` dispatch with its
Kāra type recorded as the integer". The value is fine; the QUESTION was being
asked of the wrong thing. `expr_is_char` (codegen/expr_ops.rs) decided
char-ness by matching on SYNTACTIC FORM -- one arm per construct that can
yield a char -- so any form without an arm answered `false`, silently, in the
direction that prints an integer where a glyph belongs.

That is a fail-open allowlist, and it had already failed four times: the
function's own comments say "Fourth instance of this function's recurring
gap" and "a cast ... was simply never added", and two `MethodCall` arms
record the same symptom twice ("77 instead of 'M'"). A closure call was the
fifth. Adding a fifth arm would have fixed the reported program and left the
generator of these bugs running.

So the question now goes to the phase that already knows. `lowering.rs`
derives focused span-sets from `TypeCheckResult.expr_types`
(`string_typed_exprs`, `borrow_vec_typed_exprs`, `iterator_typed_exprs`,
`fn_value_typed_exprs`), and the comment beside them invites precisely this:
"Add other small focused side-tables here if future codegen paths need to
identify other shape-sharing types." `char` lowers to a bare `i32`, so it is
that problem exactly -- the same reason `string_typed_exprs` exists to
separate `String` from the other 3-word shapes. `char_typed_exprs` joins
them; `expr_is_char` consults it FIRST.

The syntactic arms are kept as a FALLBACK, not as the mechanism: some spans
never reach `expr_types` -- desugared and codegen-synthesized nodes carry
spans the typechecker never saw -- so deleting them outright would trade this
gap for a different one.

SURFACE MEASURED BEFORE FIXING. The RENDERING sites lost char-ness
(`println`, `to_string`, f-string; annotated and inferred closures alike),
while `f() == 'z'` and `show(f())` with `show(c: char)` were already correct
-- the callee's declared type answers those, so they never consulted the
predicate. That split is what identified the predicate as the culprit rather
than the closure lowering.

A TEST HAD PINNED THIS DEFECT AS THE SPECIFICATION, and this is the part
worth remembering. `tests/repl_jit.rs::repl_jit_snapshot_covers_f64_bool_char`
asserted `107` under the comment:

    // Kāra's `println` on a `char` value prints the Unicode codepoint
    // as an integer (107 == 'k'), not the glyph.

That was never the language's behaviour -- `println('k')` prints `k`, and the
interpreter prints `k` in that same test. The author had hit this very defect
(the REPL's global-load replay is another form with no arm), concluded it was
the rule, and wrote it down. The test then passed for the wrong reason and
would have blocked the fix: it failed the moment the behaviour became
correct. Corrected to expect the glyph, with the history recorded at the
assertion so it is not "re-fixed" back.

FALSE-POSITIVE CHECK (the risk a span-keyed table carries): `c as i32` still
prints `122`, `b as char` prints the glyph, `Vec[char]` indexing and
`.chars()` iteration are unchanged. The regression test sweeps RENDERING
SITES rather than char-producing forms -- the point being that the answer no
longer depends on which syntax reached the renderer -- and includes the
cast-away case, which a fix that rendered everything char-shaped as a glyph
would break.

VERIFIED: llvm 15,276 / 0, default 9,979 / 0, both clippy legs and fmt clean.
title: A `char` returned through a CLOSURE prints as its integer code point under both compiled backends while the interpreter prints the character: `let c: char = 'z'; let f: Fn() -> char = || c; println(f())` gives `z` under `--interp` and `122` under `karac run` / `karac build`. No borrow involved — the same `char` printed directly, or returned from a plain function, renders correctly on every backend.
detail:
Found while testing the scalar matrix for B-2026-08-26-19 and confirmed
PRE-EXISTING: all `src/` changes stashed, clean HEAD rebuilt, same divergence.
It is unrelated to that row's `ref` peel — the repro below contains no `ref`
at all.

MEASURED (clean HEAD, and again on fa5e169):

    fn main() {
        let c: char = 'z';
        let f: Fn() -> char = || c;
        println(f());
    }
      --interp    -> z
      karac run   -> 122
      karac build -> 122

CONTROLS, both correct on all three backends — which is what isolates the
closure return as the culprit rather than `char` printing generally:

    fn main() { let c: char = 'z'; println(c); }              -> z / z / z

    struct Box { v: char }
    impl Box { fn peek(ref self) -> ref char { return self.v; } }
    fn main() { let b = Box { v: 'z' }; println(b.peek()); }  -> z / z / z

So `println` renders `char` correctly, and a `ref char` method result renders
correctly; only a `char` that arrives as a CLOSURE's return value loses its
char-ness and is formatted as the underlying integer.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE OUTPUT SUGGESTS: this is the A/B rule in
kara-katas ("every kata must produce identical output under `karac run` and
`karac build`") failing on a two-line program. The likely mechanism is that
the closure's return value reaches the `println` dispatch with its Kāra type
recorded as the integer the `char` is lowered to, so the formatter picks the
integer arm — meaning any other type-directed dispatch on a closure result
(Display, comparison, `to_string`) is worth checking for the same loss, not
just printing.

Deliberately EXCLUDED from B-2026-08-26-19's regression test, with a comment
at the exclusion saying why: `char` is in the scalar set that row's peel
covers, so including it there would have pinned this defect under that row's
name.

fix:
LANDED 2026-08-27.

`v[i]` is a BORROW — design.md's `Index.index` is `fn index(ref self, idx) -> ref T` — so binding one in value position reads THROUGH a reference and obeys the same rule as `*r`: it requires `T: Copy`. Underneath is that a container is not partially movable: there is no `Vec` with a hole in it, and Kāra has no per-slot drop flags. `let t = v[i]` and `v[i] = v[j]` on a non-`Copy` element are now `E0285` / `E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY`, run-fatal so the interpreter cannot run what codegen refuses. The divergence this row reported — a swap written through index reads printing a different `Drop` sequence under `karac run` than under `karac build` — is gone because neither backend is asked the question any more.

THE RULE NEEDED NARROWING FIVE TIMES, every time because a fixture was right and the rule was wrong. Not every `expr[i]` names a stored element:

  1. CONSTRUCTED reads — a range slice (`s[6..11]`, `v[a..b]`), a `Column` positional read (`c[i] -> Option[T]`), a `weak` upgrade (`w[i] -> Option[T]`). Each BUILDS a value instead of naming one. Marked positively in index inference via a span-keyed side set, so an index path nobody classified goes unmarked and is simply not rejected.
  2. `shared` handles — reading one retains it and leaves the slot intact. Extended twice: first for `Type::Shared`, then for a shared type still spelled `Type::Named` (a `shared enum` element of a `Vec`), and the lookup had to move to the type ENV because a shared type is usually declared in a different module from where it is read. That second miss was rejecting all six of the self-hosted compiler's `Vec[TypeExpr]` reads.
  3. SoA layouts — the element has no contiguous existence at all.
  4. Function values — a fat-pointer copy.

Those took the default leg from 14 failures to 3 BEFORE a single fixture was touched.

THE MIGRATION is the bulk of the work: 78 stdlib sites, ~90 codegen fixtures, ~130 ASAN sites across 46 fixtures, the self-hosted compiler (11) and its 210-program oracle corpus (14 programs + 12 derives), 2 book snippets and their prose, 2 examples, 10 auto-par sites. `ref` where the binding is read, `.clone()` where it escapes, `.swap(i, j)` where the shape was a swap. The split was derived from the compiler — apply `ref` everywhere, then read off the `expected 'T', found 'ref T'` errors, which name the escaping bindings exactly — never chosen by eye.

TWO LANGUAGE GAPS had to be closed first, both filed and fixed on the way: tuples and `Option[shared T]` had no `.clone()` (B-2026-08-27-23), and an index store whose RHS is a clone leaked the displaced element.

WORTH RECORDING, because the rule paid for itself while being migrated:
  - `examples/heap.kara`'s `swap` lost a `Copy`-element constraint its own comment conceded, so a `Heap[T: Ord]` is now genuinely generic.
  - `embeddings.kara`'s similarity scan stopped copying a tensor row view per element.
  - `proto_atoi` / `proto_pascal_case` now take `ref String`; five call sites got faster and none needed a copy.
  - The SoA-borrow guard added for this rule immediately caught a latent miscompile in `examples/slipstream` that an earlier pass of this same work had introduced.

Six unrelated bugs surfaced during the migration and are filed separately: B-2026-08-27-20 (nested index store from a named local double-frees), -21 (borrowed element loses its method surface), -22 (`.clone()` on an SoA element miscompiles), -23 (fixed), -29 (a clone passed directly as a call argument leaks).

Landed in 6a73afd.
title: A RELOCATING element store (`b.xs[i] = b.xs[j]`, then `b.xs[j] = t`) runs the displaced element's user `Drop` BODY, even though the value is being moved to another slot rather than destroyed. A two-element swap of a `Drop` type prints FIVE drop bodies, all during the swap and none at scope exit; the correct sequence is one body per element when it finally dies.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-26-18, and PRE-EXISTING — not introduced by it.
Verified by stashing that fix, rebuilding, and re-running the fixture: the
output is byte-identical, so this is main's behaviour on a path -18 does not
touch.

MEASURED. `struct Item { id: i64 }` with `impl Drop`, held in
`struct Bag { xs: Vec[Item] }`, swapped from `main` (a NAMED root):

    let t = b.xs[0];
    b.xs[0] = b.xs[1];
    b.xs[1] = t;

    got:      built, drop 1, drop 2, drop 1, drop 2, drop 1, swapped
    expected: built, swapped, drop 2, drop 1

Six `Drop` bodies for two elements, every one of them fired DURING the swap,
and none at scope exit. ASAN/LSan is CLEAN throughout — the memory side is
balanced, so this is a pure observable-behaviour defect, which is why no leak
gate catches it.

WHY IT HAPPENS. `emit_displaced_index_elem_drop` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`)
emits two halves for the element a store displaces: the user `Drop` BODIES,
and the cap-guarded MEMORY release. That is right when the displaced value is
being destroyed and wrong when it is being RELOCATED — `b.xs[i] = b.xs[j]`
does not kill the old `b.xs[i]`, it overwrites a slot whose contents the
program is in the middle of moving elsewhere. The alias guard in front of it
asks whether the RHS can carry the container's heap (a memory-safety
question) and nothing asks whether the displaced value is dying (a semantics
question), so the bodies fire on a live value.

The `let t = b.xs[0]` leg is the sharpest: `t` is a local, so the guard sees no
mention of the container at all and cannot decline even in principle.

SCOPE. Named roots only, today. The self-rooted arm added by B-2026-08-26-18
deliberately passes `run_bodies: false` for exactly this reason — a self-rooted
store emitted NEITHER half before, so restoring the memory release alone fixes
that leak without importing this defect into `PriorityQueue.swap`. Turning
bodies on there was measured and DOES import it: it breaks
`asan_priority_queue_push_drops_a_drop_element_exactly_once`, whose
one-body-per-element-at-pop sequence is the correct semantics.

THE FLIP SIDE, and why this is not simply "turn bodies off". A self-rooted
store now skips bodies unconditionally, so a genuine destroying overwrite
(`self.xs[i] = Item { .. }`, fresh literal) does NOT run the displaced
element's `Drop` body. That is the status quo for self-rooted stores rather
than a regression, but it is the missing half of the same question: codegen
needs to distinguish DESTROY from RELOCATE, and today neither root does. A
real fix gives both arms that distinction and then runs bodies exactly on the
destroy leg.

ACCEPTANCE TEST. Not yet written — the shape above is the whole fixture, and
its expected sequence is `built / swapped / drop 2 / drop 1`. Note that a
correct fix must keep `asan_priority_queue_push_drops_a_drop_element_exactly_once`
and the four B-2026-08-26-18 oracles green.


RE-MEASURED 2026-08-26 on current main, and the row UNDERSTATED it in two ways.

  1. It is ALSO a run-vs-build divergence. The row measured AOT only. Both
     backends are wrong AND they disagree with each other:

       AOT     built, drop 1, drop 2, drop 1, drop 2, drop 1, swapped
       interp  built, drop 2, drop 2, drop 1, swapped
       spec    exactly one body per value

  2. The count in the title is wrong: FIVE bodies, not six. Recount from the
     same output.

THE MODEL-INDEPENDENT VIOLATION, which is what makes this a bug regardless of
the unsettled timing question below: `let t = b.xs[0]` clones, so at most TWO
objects with `id == 1` ever exist, and AOT ran `drop 1` THREE times. design.md
§ Drop pins "a value is dropped exactly once, at the scope exit of its final
owner", so a third body is impossible under any reading.

PARTIAL FIX LANDED (see the commit): the displaced element's `Drop` BODIES are
now gated on a DESTROY-vs-RELOCATE test — `Self::store_destroys_displaced`,
true only for an rhs that constructs a new value (aggregate literal or call),
false for `b.xs[i] = b.xs[j]` and `b.xs[j] = t`. The memory half stays
unconditional. AOT drops from five bodies to three and the impossible third
`drop 1` is gone; a genuinely destroying overwrite (`b.xs[0] = Item { .. }`)
still runs the displaced body on both backends.

STILL OPEN, which is why this row is not closed: the two backends print
different IDENTITIES for the three remaining bodies (AOT `1,2,1`; interp
`2,2,1`). The interpreter half is untouched. Settling it needs the semantics
question below answered first, because the correct expected sequence depends on
it.

THE TIMING QUESTION THIS ROW ORIGINALLY LEANED ON IS SETTLED, and settling it
was part of this work. The sequence the row first quoted assumed SCOPE-EXIT
drop timing, which is not what the language specifies. design.md pins LIVE-RANGE
END twice, at length and with worked examples -- § defer/errdefer rules
("Destructors fire at each binding's live-range end, not at lexical scope end,
per the non-lexical-lifetime rule") and § Drop ordering within a branch ("A
value whose last use is in the middle of a branch has its drop inserted at that
mid-branch point and does not appear in the end-of-branch cleanup stack at
all"). Both backends already do live-range end; measured, an unused
`let a = Item { id: 7 }` prints its body before the next statement on both.

Two sentences in § Part 8 `Drop` still said "scope exit" and contradicted that,
and the stale phrasing had already cost a wrong fix direction: B-2026-07-21-1
(fixed, 7c4bf90) cited "design.md § Drop: 'the compiler calls drop at scope
exit'" as "the spec'd semantics" and moved the INTERPRETER toward scope-exit
timing, while B-2026-08-09-3 (fixed, e9e3807) cited the normative rule and moved
CODEGEN toward live-range end. Both cited the same document for opposite
answers. The two stale sentences are corrected in this commit, so the document
now says live-range end everywhere and no future row can cite the other answer.
No behaviour change -- the implementation was already on the normative side.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY STILL OPEN HERE. Two things, neither of them timing:

  1. The two backends print different IDENTITIES for the three remaining
     bodies (AOT `1,2,1`; interp `2,2,1`). The interpreter half of the
     destroy-vs-relocate gate is untouched.

  2. Whether `let t = b.xs[0]` on a non-`Copy` element CLONES (creating a third
     object, which would make more than one body per id legitimate) or should
     be rejected outright is not stated anywhere in design.md. The expected
     sequence for this fixture depends on that answer, so this row does not
     pin one yet.


DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED 2026-08-26, and the row's own headline was wrong about
WHICH value was firing twice. The extra body did not come from the DISPLACED
element. It came from the MOVED-FROM SOURCE: a local moved into a container's
element slot (`b.xs[j] = t`) kept its own `UserDrop` registration, so `t` ran
its `impl Drop` body a second time at the binding's live-range end even though
the container's element already owned the value and would run the body when the
container dropped. `zero_struct_move_caps` had disarmed that source's MEMORY
cleanup back in B-2026-08-12-22 but left its BODIES registration armed — the
two halves of one move, only one of which had been done.

That half is FIXED, under B-2026-08-26-31 (see that row for the one-line change
and its fixtures). It was never the destroy-vs-relocate question this row spent
its length on, which is why the gate landed earlier did not close it: the gate
was a real improvement to a different axis, not the fix for this symptom.

WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS is a MODEL DISAGREEMENT between the two backends, and it
is not a patch to either one until an upstream question is answered.

Reading an element CLONES. Measured: after

    let t = b.xs[0];
    b.xs[2] = t;

the vector reads `1,2,1` — slot 0 still holds its original value. (Confirmed
independently by this session's `asan_local_moved_into_struct_elem_slot_is_not
_double_freed` fixture, which asserts exactly that.) So the interpreter treats
the store as DESTROYING the displaced value, while codegen's
`store_destroys_displaced` treats it as a RELOCATION. Both are internally
coherent; they are answers to a question nobody has decided.

BOTH FIX DIRECTIONS WERE TRIED AND MEASURED, and each breaks the other's shape
(measured by the session that filed this correction, not re-run here):

  - Removing codegen's gate makes a three-element `PriorityQueue` drain print
    ELEVEN `Drop` bodies for three elements.
  - Giving the interpreter the relocation model makes the self-store
    `b.xs[0] = b.xs[0]` print NO body, where codegen correctly prints one.

So this row now wants an upstream DECISION, not an implementation: what does
`let t = v[i]` MEAN for a non-`Copy` element — a move, a clone, or a compile
error? design.md does not say, and the correct expected sequence for every
fixture on this row depends on the answer. Do not patch either backend toward
the other until that is settled; the two current behaviours are the settled
halves of an unsettled question, and `test_e2e_local_moved_into_elem_slot
_drops_once` deliberately pins codegen's side ONLY, with a doc comment saying
so.

The FIVE-not-six recount recorded above stands and is unchanged by this.

DECISION MADE 2026-08-26 (owner-ratified). The upstream question this row was
waiting on — what `let t = v[i]` MEANS for a non-`Copy` element — is answered:
it is a COMPILE ERROR. design.md now states it normatively in § Part 1, "The
index operator (`expr[i]`)", written as the indexing peer of the existing
dereference rule.

The decision was not a new invention. Four existing commitments already implied
it, and the behaviour accepted until now was the one thing contradicting all
four:

  1. `Index.index` is `fn index(ref self, idx: i64) -> ref T` — an index
     expression produces a BORROW, not a value (design.md, Core Collections).
  2. "Deref is not a consume": `*r` in expression position requires `T: Copy`;
     non-`Copy` values are read through a reference only via `.clone()` or field
     projection (design.md § The dereference operator).
  3. `Index.index_set` is `fn index_set(mut ref self, idx: i64, val: T)` — it
     takes the incoming value BY VALUE, which a `ref T` cannot supply, so
     `v[i] = v[j]` falls to the same rule.
  4. `runtime/stdlib/mem.kara` states in its own doc comment that moving a value
     out without running its destructor "cannot be written in safe Kāra source
     (you cannot move out of a `mut ref`)" — which is why `mem.swap` /
     `mem.replace` are `#[compiler_builtin]` intrinsics at all.

WHY THIS DISSOLVES THE ROW RATHER THAN ARBITRATING IT. The programs on which the
two backends disagreed (AOT `1,2,1`, interp `2,2,1`) STOP COMPILING. The only
element-store form surviving for a non-`Copy` `T` is `v[i] = <fresh owned
value>`, which `index_set` gives exactly one meaning: the displaced element is
destroyed in place and its `Drop` body runs there. BOTH BACKENDS ALREADY
IMPLEMENT THAT. It is the decisive property of this option — the only one of the
three requiring no behavioural change to code that currently works, and no
arbitration between two internally coherent models.

The two rejected alternatives, for the record:
  - MOVE is not representable. There is no `Vec` with a hole in it and Kāra has
    no per-slot drop flags. Rust rejects the same construct (E0507) for the same
    reason.
  - CLONE was the tempting option and loses on Kāra's own stated philosophy: a
    bare `[i]` that silently deep-copies a heap-bearing struct is an invisible
    allocation, in a language that bans implicit coercions, keeps `*`
    "load-bearing rather than redundant", and requires `Clone` to be called by
    name. It also silently perturbs `Drop` counts — which is how this bug arose.

ROOT CAUSE, restated. The stdlib's own `PriorityQueue.swap`
(`runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara:127`) hand-writes the exact operation
`mem.kara` declares unwritable in safe source. Both backends then improvised
semantics for an unsanctioned program, and improvised differently. The front end
letting it through is the defect; the backend divergence was the symptom.

MEASURED BLAST RADIUS (non-`Copy` elements only — `Copy` scalars are untouched,
which is the overwhelming majority of index reads):
  - `runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara:129` — the ONE element-to-element store
    in the entire stdlib. Rewrites to `self.xs.swap(i, j)`.
  - `runtime/stdlib/autograd.kara` TensorTape — `values` / `grads` are
    `Vec[Tensor[f32, [?]]]`, and `Tensor` is not `Copy`; ~8 sites in the 380-460
    range read elements by value (`let v = tp.values[self.idx]`). These are the
    real migration, and THIS IS A FINDING, NOT ONLY A COST: each such read is
    today a silent full-tensor deep copy inside a reverse-mode autograd hot
    loop. Most want `let v = ref tp.values[i]`; the rule forces the choice to be
    made explicitly either way. Worth its own perf row once measured.
  - kara-katas: 109 element-to-element stores in total, but only ~2 on plainly
    non-`Copy` element types. APPROXIMATE — counted by element-type spelling,
    not by typechecking.

IMPLEMENTATION REMAINING — this row stays OPEN until it lands:
  1. Add `Vec.swap(mut ref self, i: i64, j: i64)`. REQUIRED, not optional:
     `mem.swap` cannot express an intra-container exchange, because it needs two
     `mut ref` into one `Vec` and design.md's aliasing rule forbids that (the
     same reason Rust needs `slice::swap` alongside `mem::swap`). Without it the
     rule outlaws the pattern and leaves no way to write a heapsort. Spec'd in
     the Vec method table in this commit; the implementation (interpreter +
     codegen, with the no-`Drop`-body guarantee) is NOT written.
  2. Reject `let t = v[i]` and `v[i] = v[j]` for non-`Copy` `T` with
     `E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY` and the three fix-its the spec block pins (`ref`
     borrow / `.clone()` / `.swap`). Machine-applicable — suits `karac fix`.
  3. Migrate `PriorityQueue.swap` to `self.xs.swap(i, j)` and re-derive this
     row's fixtures, whose expected sequence becomes "does not compile" for the
     swap-through-index shape.
  4. Confirm the four B-2026-08-26-18 oracles and
     `asan_priority_queue_push_drops_a_drop_element_exactly_once` stay green.

Step 2 makes previously-accepted programs fail to compile. That is the intent of
the decision, but it is a SOURCE-BREAKING change and must land together with the
fix-its working, not ahead of them.

IMPLEMENTATION ATTEMPTED 2026-08-26; PARTLY LANDED, REJECTION BLOCKED.

LANDED (4d75c59): `Vec.swap` now works on BOTH backends. It had no codegen arm
at all (B-2026-08-26-34) and silently ignored out-of-range indices in the

NOT LANDED: the `E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY` rejection itself. It is written and

THE BLOCKER, and it was not visible from the spec. The rejection's fix-it set

THE BLAST RADIUS WAS MEASURED WRONG in the decision above, by 8x. That

    autograd.kara       67     protobuf.kara        9
    embeddings.kara      2     priority_queue.kara  2      TOTAL 80

No false positives — `Vec[f64]` / `Vec[i64]` element reads are correctly

STILL TRUE from the decision above: rejecting the form dissolves this row's

The decision is not in question — only its prerequisite, which is now filed.

REMAINING WORK, in order: B-2026-08-26-36 (`ref` bindings — the interpreter
half is the real cost, see that row), then unpark the rejection, then migrate

PARKED PATCH: `docs/wip/b-2026-08-26-21-index-move-rejection.patch` (applies

through a borrowed Vec element), so the rejection's fix-it is now SATISFIABLE

THE 78-SITE STDLIB MIGRATION STILL DOES NOT LAND. Bisected to

THE FIXTURE COST WAS MEASURED and is the other half of why this is not close:

68 `memory_sanitizer`, 62 `codegen`, 8 `par_codegen`, plus `book_snippets`.
All but one are test PROGRAMS that use the rejected form and no longer

PROGRESS 2026-08-27 — implemented and migrated; blocked on B-2026-08-27-23.

The rejection itself is written and works, and it needed NARROWING FOUR TIMES, every time because a fixture was right and the rule was wrong. WHAT IS LEFT is fixture migration in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` — about 11 sites the automated pass could not reach: chained indexes (`m[i][j]`), slice temporaries (`names.as_slice()[i]`), fn-returned receivers (`names()[0]`), a `T: Clone` bound a generic-mono fixture needs, and a couple of duplicate lines the scoped matcher declines to touch. That is work, not a blocker.

A WARNING FOR THAT WORK, learned the expensive way here: an ASAN fixture migration must be verified WITHOUT the rules applied as well as with them. A pass that looked right under the rules broke five fixtures on a clean compiler — `.clone()` on a type with no `Clone` is a hard error either way, and `#[derive(Clone)]` added to a fixture's struct changes what that fixture measures. Both legs, every time.

Do NOT migrate by matching on TEXT SHAPE. An earlier blanket regex appended `.clone()` to 94 sites matched by shape rather than by diagnostic, silently touching `Copy` elements that were never rejected, and broke five passing tests. Take the sites from the compiler.

fix:
FIXED by 4c3da28, completing the fallible-allocation surface design.md § Fallible Allocation's panicking/fallible table specifies. The one remainder -- a fallible `collect`, which `Vec.try_from_iter` cannot honestly be built without -- is split out to B-2026-08-26-27 rather than left buried here.

WHAT LANDED, against the five items this row named:
  * `Vec.try_resize` / `Vec.try_append` -- real fallible codegen arms, then registered. Both ALL-OR-NOTHING, and the ordering is what buys it: the fallible allocation happens before anything is mutated, so an `Err` leaves the receiver's buffer, length and contents untouched. `try_append` additionally disarms its SOURCE's cleanup only on the success path, so on OOM the source still owns its elements and its binding frees them exactly once -- disarming up front (which the infallible `append` can do, because it cannot fail) would leak every element on the OOM path.
  * `String.reserve` across all three phases; `String.try_reserve` derived for free.
  * `Map.reserve` + `Map.try_reserve`, and `Set.reserve` + `Set.try_reserve` as well -- a `Set` is a `Map[T, ()]` over the same runtime table, which is what design.md's "where applicable" was pointing at. New runtime entry points `karac_map_reserve` / `karac_map_try_reserve` (plus a shared `KaracMap::reserve_additional`), keep-listed so the JIT runner can `dlsym` them.
  * `Vec.from_iter` -- the panicking base only; see the deferral below.

THREE ACCESSORS DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED, each for a different measured reason, recorded so they are not "filled in" later as oversights:
  * NO `String.capacity()`. `Vec.capacity()` is sound because the interpreter mutates a `Value::Array` in place through its `Rc`, so a reservation survives. A `Value::String` is CLONE-ON-WRITE -- every mutating arm clones and calls `write_back_receiver` -- so a reservation is discarded by the next `push_str` while codegen's `{ptr,len,cap}` keeps it. The accessor would be a guaranteed run-vs-build divergence. Held by tests/typechecker.rs::string_has_no_capacity_accessor.
  * NO `Map.capacity()` / `Set.capacity()`. Different reason: the bucket count is an implementation detail of the probing scheme (a power of two sized off a 3/4 load factor, counting tombstones). Publishing it would make that scheme observable behaviour; `len()` is what user code has business reading.
  * NO `Vec.try_from_iter`. `from_iter` lowers to `iter.collect()`, and `collect`'s codegen grows its accumulator through the PANICKING allocator -- so a companion built on that rewrite would return `Ok` unconditionally and abort inside `collect` on real OOM. A companion that LIES about being fallible is worse than one that does not exist. It typechecked briefly during this work; the registration was backed out rather than shipped. Held by tests/typechecker.rs::vec_try_from_iter_stays_absent_until_collect_can_fail.

`Vec.from_iter` IS `iter.collect()`, not a second implementation of it. The typechecker types it by building a synthetic `<iter>.collect()` and inferring THAT, and `lowering.rs` rewrites the call to the same thing -- so the two spellings cannot drift in element type, in accepted iterator shapes, or in diagnostics, and both backends run one code path. Same "exact alias" discipline `Vec.extend` / `extend_from_slice` already follow. It is strictly better than bare `collect()` at one point: `let d = Vec.from_iter(0..3)` needs no type annotation, because the element type comes from the iterator rather than from context. A test compares the two spellings directly on both backends, so a future "optimisation" cannot quietly give `from_iter` its own path.

ONE BUG I INTRODUCED AND CAUGHT, worth recording because the type system could not: `karac_map_reserve`'s `additional` parameter was first typed `u64`. Kara integers arrive as `i64`, and `reserve` treats a non-positive argument as a no-op (Vec and String clamp it in codegen), so `m.reserve(-5)` was reinterpreted as a reservation of 18 quintillion entries -- the capacity search saturated and the process aborted with `panic: out of memory`. The FFI boundary is exactly where a sign disappears silently. The parameter is now `i64` and clamps at the runtime, which is the single point both the panicking and fallible entry points share; `a_negative_reserve_is_a_no_op_on_every_collection` covers Vec, String, Map and Set in one program so the four cannot drift apart again.

AND ONE PRE-EXISTING BUG FOUND ALONG THE WAY, filed and fixed separately as B-2026-08-26-26: every instance `try_*` companion consumed with `?` failed `karac build` under the auto-parallelizer, verified on clean HEAD with `try_push`.

TESTS: 6 in tests/interpreter.rs (String.reserve as a hint; the Vec/String arm-shadowing guard; try_resize/try_append; Map+Set reserve; negative reserve across all four collections; from_iter across iterator shapes), 4 twin comparisons in tests/codegen.rs driven off `run_program_full` as oracle plus a from_iter-vs-collect equivalence test, 8 in tests/typechecker.rs (accepted signatures, arity rejections, and the two deliberate absences), and the auto-par ASAN guard from -26.
title: The fallible-allocation table's REMAINING gaps, after B-2026-08-25-20 landed the Vec capacity family: `try_resize` / `try_append` have panicking bases now but no fallible codegen arm and so are NOT registered; `String.reserve`, `Map.reserve` and `Vec.from_iter` still have no base at all. Measured one per compile on the commit that closed -20: `v.try_resize(4, 0)` -> `no method 'try_resize' on type 'Vec'`; `v.try_append(b)` -> `no method 'try_append'`; `s.reserve(16)` -> `no method 'reserve' on type 'String'`; `m.reserve(16)` -> `no method 'reserve' on type 'Map'`; `Vec.from_iter(0..4)` -> `no associated function 'from_iter' on type 'Vec'`. design.md's panicking/fallible table names all five.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-25-20 at its close rather than left buried in it, so the remainder stays on the work queue as its own row (the CLAUDE.md rule about a closed investigation's live remainder).

WHAT -20 DID LAND, so this row is scoped to the actual remainder: `Vec.capacity()`, `Vec.reserve`, `Vec.reserve_exact`, `Vec.resize`, `Vec.append` across typecheck + interpreter + codegen, plus `Vec.try_reserve` / `Vec.try_reserve_exact` with real `karac_alloc_fallible` lowering. That closed the row's headline `try_reserve`, and it closed the reason the other companions could not exist: `fallible_alloc.rs` DERIVES every `try_X` from its panicking `X`, so the base always had to come first.

TWO DIFFERENT KINDS OF GAP REMAIN, and they are not the same amount of work.

(a) `try_resize` / `try_append` — BASE EXISTS, COMPANION DELIBERATELY UNREGISTERED. Registering a companion in `TRY_ALLOC_INSTANCE_BASES` without a matching `CODEGEN_FALLIBLE_INSTANCE_BASES` entry gives a method that typechecks and then fails `karac build` loudly — the run-vs-build shape. -20 declined to add two new instances of it, so the names simply do not resolve today. The work is a fallible codegen arm each, modelled on the `try_reserve` arm that landed (same capacity arithmetic; `karac_alloc_fallible` + memcpy + free in place of `karac_realloc_or_panic`, and `build_alloc_oom_result` on null). `try_append` has the extra wrinkle that its source is already consumed by the time the allocation can fail, so the Err path must still leave the source's elements owned by exactly one side.

(b) `String.reserve` / `Map.reserve` / `Vec.from_iter` — NO BASE AT ALL. `String` shares the `{ptr,len,cap}` layout and has `emit_string_buffer_grow`, so its `reserve` is close to the Vec one. `Map.reserve` is the odd one out: the Map is a runtime handle behind FFI, so it needs a `karac_map_reserve` entry point rather than inline capacity arithmetic, which is the same reason `Map.try_insert` still routes through `compile_map_method`. `Vec.from_iter` is a CONSTRUCTOR via `FromIterator` and is the largest of the three — design.md's own fallible-alloc prose leans on it (`let v = Vec.try_from_iter(0..1024)?` is the sanctioned replacement for a rejected `.collect()` under `panic_on_alloc_failure = false`), so it is the one with a spec consumer already pointing at it.

WHY THIS IS MEDIUM AND NOT HIGH: nothing here miscompiles or corrupts. Every missing name is a clean `no method` diagnostic at typecheck, and the `panic_on_alloc_failure = false` profile flag that would make the fallible surface load-bearing is itself not implemented yet, so no user program can currently be forced onto these methods.

PROGRESS (aae805f, 2026-08-26). THREE OF THE FIVE ITEMS LANDED; this row stays OPEN for the other two. Done: `try_resize` and `try_append` now have real fallible codegen arms and are registered companions (both all-or-nothing — the allocation precedes any mutation, and `try_append` disarms its source's cleanup only on the success path, so an `Err` leaves the source still owning its elements); `String.reserve` lands across all three phases and `String.try_reserve` derives from it for free. REMAINING: `Map.reserve` (needs a `karac_map_reserve` runtime entry point — the Map is a handle behind FFI, so there is no inline capacity arithmetic to write; `KaracMap::resize`/`try_resize` and the shared `rehash_from` are the pieces to build it from) and `Vec.from_iter` / `try_from_iter` (a `FromIterator` CONSTRUCTOR, the largest of the five, and the one with a spec consumer already pointing at it — design.md's fallible-alloc prose offers `Vec.try_from_iter(0..1024)?` as the sanctioned replacement for a rejected `.collect()`). ONE DECISION MADE ALONG THE WAY, recorded so it is not re-litigated: there is NO `String.capacity()` and there should not be. `Vec.capacity()` is sound because the interpreter mutates a `Value::Array` in place through its `Rc`; a `Value::String` is clone-on-write, so a reservation is discarded by the next `push_str` there while codegen keeps it — the accessor would be a guaranteed run-vs-build divergence. `tests/typechecker.rs::string_has_no_capacity_accessor` holds that. ALSO FOUND, and fixed in the same commit: B-2026-08-26-26, a PRE-EXISTING run-vs-build failure on every `try_*` companion consumed with `?`, verified on clean HEAD with `try_push`.

fix:
Fixed in 4e75708 (all three shapes) — three separate defects wearing one error
message ("no handler for method 'is_lt'").

The two `cmp` shapes were a MISSING RETURN-TYPE RECORD. Method dispatch recovers
the receiver's type name, and codegen's builtin `cmp` arm materializes its
`Ordering` aggregate inline without declaring anything, so nothing named the
result. A user `impl Ord`'s `cmp` IS a declared function with a
`fn_return_type_names` entry — which is exactly why that shape always worked and
hid this. `type_name_of_expr` now answers `Ordering` for a `cmp` the builtin arm
will handle, mirroring that arm's own condition so it cannot claim the name for a
call the builtin declines; an inherent `fn cmp` returning something else is a
user impl by that test and keeps its declared type. The let-binding path needed
the same widening: its method-call arm filtered on `struct_types`, and `Ordering`
is an ENUM, so the name was computed and then dropped on the floor.

`Option[Ordering]` was a MISSING DECLARATION. Its five predicates lived in
`option.kara`, which codegen does not compile. Adding that file to
`compiled_stdlib_programs` was tried and is NOT the fix — it re-declares
`enum Option[+T]`, replacing the builtin two-word `{tag, payload}` layout;
`build_option_some_via_phis` panicked with `ExtractOutOfRange` and three Map/Set
codegen tests failed. Relocating just the impl block into `ordering.kara`, which
is already compiled and declares no Option, gets the five methods with no second
layout. A note at the new site records the measurement so the discarded approach
is not retried.

Verified across the full matrix: `Some(Less)` / `Some(Equal)` / `Some(Greater)` /
`None` against all five predicates — 20 values, byte-identical between the
interpreter and the compiled binary, including `None` answering false to
everything per design.md's "incomparable" rule.

CONSEQUENCE. This was the gap that forced the ordering operators to desugar
through `Ord.cmp` instead of design.md's specified
`PartialOrd.partial_cmp(a, b).is_lt()`. With it closed, 483fef4 switched the
desugaring to the specified form and lifted the rejection of an `impl PartialOrd`
with no `impl Ord`. The divergence note that stood beside design.md's table is
gone.
title: `Ordering`'s PREDICATE METHODS (`is_lt` / `is_le` / `is_gt` / `is_ge` / `is_eq`) fail to BUILD whenever codegen cannot name the receiver's type -- a chained `a.cmp(b).is_lt()` on a PRIMITIVE, and EVERY `Option[Ordering]` receiver including a plainly-annotated local. All three shapes run correctly under `--interp`, so this is a run-vs-build divergence, and it is what forced the ordering operators to desugar through `cmp` instead of design.md's specified `partial_cmp`.
detail:
Found while implementing B-2026-08-26-10's ordering-operator dispatch; measured
with that fix STASHED, so all three shapes are pre-existing and independent of it.

WHAT WORKS. A plain `Ordering` local builds and runs:

    let o: Ordering = Ordering.Greater;
    println(o.is_lt());          // interp: false   build: false   OK

So does the chained form when the receiver is a USER `impl Ord`'s `cmp`:

    a.cmp(b).is_lt()             // Item has `impl Ord`   -> builds, correct

THREE SHAPES THAT DO NOT BUILD, all `--interp`-green:

  A. `Option[Ordering]`, even as an annotated local -- nothing to do with
     chaining:
       let o: Option[Ordering] = Some(Ordering.Greater);
       println(o.is_lt());
     -> codegen: no handler for method 'is_lt' on variable 'o'
     (`--interp` prints `false`.)

  B. a chained `.cmp(...)` on a PRIMITIVE receiver:
       let a: i64 = 1; let b: i64 = 5;
       println(a.cmp(b).is_lt());
     -> codegen: no handler for method 'is_lt' on non-identifier receiver
     (`--interp` prints `true`.)

  C. the same primitive comparator bound to a local first -- so the failure is
     not about the receiver being an expression:
       let o = a.cmp(b);
       println(o.is_lt());
     -> codegen: no handler for method 'is_lt' on variable 'o'
     (`--interp` prints `true`.)

TWO DISTINCT CAUSES, which is why they are one row but not one fix.

  * B and C are a MISSING RETURN-TYPE RECORD. Method dispatch recovers the
    receiver's type name via `type_name_of_expr` / `var_type_names`, and the
    BUILTIN `cmp` lowering (`method == "cmp"` in `src/codegen/method_call.rs`)
    builds an `Ordering` aggregate inline without ever registering "Ordering"
    as the call's result type name. A user `impl Ord` works precisely because
    its `Item.cmp` IS a declared function, so the name is recoverable and
    `try_compile_freshtemp_user_method` resolves `Ordering.is_lt`. The
    annotated-`Ordering` local works for the same reason from the other
    direction: the `let` annotation seeds the record.

  * A is a MISSING DECLARATION. `Ordering`'s own impl block reaches codegen
    because `ordering_stdlib_program()` is in `compiled_stdlib_programs`;
    `impl Option[Ordering]` lives in `runtime/stdlib/option.kara`, which is
    not, so no `Option[Ordering].is_lt` symbol is ever declared. Note this is
    the args-aware impl (`impl Option[Ordering]`, not `impl Option[T]`), so
    whatever declares it has to carry the instantiation into the symbol name.

WHY THIS COST SOMETHING CONCRETE. design.md § Comparison Traits specifies
`a < b` as `PartialOrd.partial_cmp(ref a, ref b).is_lt()` and says the operators
go "through `PartialOrd`, never `Ord` directly". Shape A makes that unimplementable
in codegen today, so B-2026-08-26-10 desugars user-type ordering through
`Ord.cmp` instead, and an `impl PartialOrd` with NO `impl Ord` is REJECTED at
typecheck rather than accepted into a program that would check, interpret, and
then fail to build. The divergence is recorded in design.md § Comparison Traits
and in `karac explain operators`; closing shape A is what would let the specified
form be preferred and that rejection be lifted.

fix:
Fixed in 191dc02, and it needed a DIFFERENT fix in each backend.

This row expected a deferred-rewrite pass or a mono-time comparison path, because
lowering runs before monomorphization and `T` is genuinely unknown there. Neither
was needed. A METHOD call dispatches on the RECEIVER, so `a.cmp(b).is_lt()`
requires no `T` substitution and one emitted AST works in the tree-walk and in
every monomorph. Confirmed by hand before writing any of it: that spelling
already ran and built correctly inside a `T: Ord` body, which is what made this
small rather than structural.

The comparator is chosen by the BOUND, not by preference. Supertrait methods do
not re-export through the requiring trait (design.md § "Constraints and method
resolution"), so `T: Ord` cannot call `partial_cmp` and `T: PartialOrd` cannot
call `cmp` — emitting the wrong one gives "no method 'partial_cmp' on type
parameter 'T'". Bounds are threaded from the enclosing IMPL BLOCK as well as the
function, since `impl[T: Ord] PriorityQueue[T]` is where the shipping case lives.

THE HALF THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN MISSED. Fixing lowering alone left the two backends
DISAGREEING — worse than the shared failure it replaced. codegen lowers its
stdlib from source (`lower_stdlib_source`) and got the right answer; the
interpreter's baked stdlib is signature-registered and never type-checked in the
user's pipeline, so `expr_types` is empty for it and the rewrite is skipped
entirely. `PriorityQueue`'s `self.xs[i] < self.xs[j]` is exactly that body. The
interpreter now dispatches to a hand-written comparator at RUNTIME, placed ahead
of the derived-order arm so it wins the same way lowering makes it win for a type
it can see; `partial_cmp` returning `None` answers false to every predicate.

Pinned in both backends with a REVERSING comparator (so declaration order and the
impl disagree) plus a derive control asserting 1/2/3 where the impl gives 3/2/1 —
a regression that quietly falls back to declaration order fails these rather than
passing them.

NOTE ON THIS ROW'S CLAIM ABOUT B-2026-08-26-10. It said that row's stated
acceptance test could not be satisfied by fixing operator dispatch alone. That
was correct, and both are now closed.
title: A COMPARISON OPERATOR INSIDE A GENERIC BODY never dispatches to the element's user `impl Ord`: operator lowering resolves only CONCRETE operand types, so `a < b` on a `T: Ord` stays unlowered and dies with `operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type 'Struct'` / `Unsupported struct binary op: Gt`. `PriorityQueue[T]` is the shipping casualty -- it works for `#[derive(Ord)]` and fails for every hand-written impl.
detail:
Found while implementing B-2026-08-26-10 and measured with that fix STASHED, so
it is pre-existing. It is also the reason that row's own stated acceptance test
("re-measure case 1 ... against `PriorityQueue`") CANNOT be satisfied by fixing
operator dispatch alone -- the row assumed one fix would cover both, and it does
not. Worth knowing before picking either up.

REPRO. A struct whose `cmp` reverses the order, in a `PriorityQueue`:

    struct Item { id: i64 }
    impl PartialEq for Item { fn eq(ref self, other: ref Item) -> bool { self.id == other.id } }
    impl Eq for Item {}
    impl PartialOrd for Item { fn partial_cmp(ref self, other: ref Item) -> Option[Ordering] { Some(other.id.cmp(self.id)) } }
    impl Ord for Item { fn cmp(ref self, other: ref Item) -> Ordering { other.id.cmp(self.id) } }
    fn main() {
        let mut q: PriorityQueue[Item] = PriorityQueue.new();
        q.push(Item { id: 1 }); q.push(Item { id: 3 }); q.push(Item { id: 2 });
        while q.len() > 0 { match q.pop() { Some(it) => println(it.id), None => {} } }
    }

  --interp: runtime error: operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type
            'Struct' and 'Struct'   (at priority_queue.kara:124)
  build:    error: codegen failed: Unsupported struct binary op: Gt

The SAME program with `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]` and no impls
prints 1 / 2 / 3 on both backends. So the container is fine; what fails is
reaching a hand-written impl from inside it.

CAUSE. `rewrite_binary` in `src/lowering.rs` asks `target_type_name(lhs_ty, ..)`,
which returns a name only for a concrete `Type::Named` (or a primitive). Inside
`PriorityQueue[T]`'s sift loops the operand type is `Type::TypeParam("T")`, so
no lowering is emitted at all and the raw `BinOp::Lt` survives to both backends,
where a struct operand has no comparison rule. The derive path escapes this
because it does not go through operator lowering -- derived ordering reaches the
declaration-order comparator (`karac_cmp` / `value_compare`) directly.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE EXTENSION. Lowering runs BEFORE monomorphization, so at
the point `target_type_name` is asked there is no instantiation to look up --
`T` is genuinely unknown there, not merely unresolved. A fix has to either (a)
