defer the operator rewrite for type-param operands until the mono pass has bound
`T`, or (b) give the backends a `T: Ord` comparison path that consults the bound
impl at monomorphization time. Both are bigger than the concrete-operand fix that
landed for B-2026-08-26-10.

SCOPE. Not specific to `PriorityQueue` -- any generic body comparing two `T: Ord`
values with `< <= > >=` has it, including user-written generic functions. The
`Ord`-bounded stdlib free functions (`min` / `max` / `clamp` in
`runtime/stdlib/ordering.kara`) are UNAFFECTED because they were already written
against `a.cmp(b)` and a `match`, not the operators -- which is the shape of the
workaround for user code until this is fixed.

fix:
Fixed in 47a6810, together with an equality defect found beside it.

ORDERING was the filed run-vs-build divergence. Both branches of the operator
gate test `Type::Named`, and a shared type presents as `Type::Shared`, so it fell
through both. `target_type_name` had the same blind spot, so even a shared type
with a real `impl PartialOrd` lowered to nothing.

Both sides moved together, which this row warned was necessary: widening only the
gate would have converted the divergence into a rejection while leaving a
legitimate impl unreachable, and widening only lowering would have left the
underived case still admitted.

THE DERIVE CASE IS REFUSED, deliberately. The new arm does not consult
`type_supports_partial_ord` the way its sibling does, because that predicate
accepts a `#[derive(Ord)]` and a derived ordering on a shared type has no
lowering on either backend — measured, the derive alone fails identically to no
derive at all. Accepting on that basis would have preserved the divergence.

EQUALITY, which this row flagged as unmeasured, turned out worse than a
divergence: silently wrong, and contradicting a diagnostic. `==` on a shared
struct compared structurally and never reached the `impl PartialEq`, while the
typechecker's own message told the author that adding the `impl Eq` marker would
make it dispatch. It now does.

That fix has two halves and the first attempt shipped only one — recorded here
because the failure was instructive. Resolving the type name for equality while
the `!=` rewrite still tested `Type::Named` alone made `a != b` lower to a
`T.ne(a, b)` nobody defines: the interpreter reported `path 'Node.ne' has no
interpreter evaluation rule` and the compiled binary printed a raw `0` instead of
`true`. Caught by probing the shape space, not by reading the diff.

Both regression tests use comparators that DISAGREE with the structural answer —
an `eq` returning false for two equal-field nodes, and a reversing `partial_cmp`
— so a structural or declaration-order result fails them rather than passing.
title: ORDERING OPERATORS ON A `shared struct` ARE ADMITTED BY THE TYPECHECKER AND IMPLEMENTED BY NEITHER BACKEND: `a < b` on a shared struct passes `karac check` with NO derive and NO impl at all, then fails with `operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type 'SharedStruct'` under `--interp` and `Binary op Lt: left operand has non-comparable type PointerType` at build. Adding `#[derive(Ord)]` does not help.
detail:
Found while implementing B-2026-08-26-10's ordering dispatch, and measured to be
INDEPENDENT of hand-written impls: a shared struct with NO derive and NO impl at
all also passes `karac check` and then fails on both backends. So this is not the
user-impl question -- the ordering gate simply does not cover shared operands.

REPRO, the minimal form:

    shared struct Node { id: i64 }
    fn main() {
        let a = Node { id: 1 };
        let b = Node { id: 5 };
        println(a < b);
    }

  karac check   -> All checks passed.
  --interp      -> runtime error: operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of
                   type 'SharedStruct' and 'SharedStruct' (this is a type error
                   the typechecker reports as a hard error; it reached the
                   interpreter only because `karac run` executes despite
                   typecheck errors)
  karac build   -> error: codegen failed: Binary op Lt: left operand has
                   non-comparable type PointerType(...) (likely a typechecker
                   gap -- `assert_eq` and `==` should reject mismatched operand
                   types before reaching codegen)

Both backends' own error text says a typechecker gap is the cause, and they are
right. Adding `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]` does NOT help -- it
checks clean and fails identically at run time, so the whole ordering surface is
unavailable on `shared struct`, derived or not.

CAUSE. The ordering gate in `src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs` has two branches, and
both test `Type::Named`:

    matches!(cmp_left, Type::Named { name, .. } if self.env.distinct_types.contains_key(name))
    matches!(cmp_left, Type::Named { name, .. } if self.env.structs.contains_key(name)
                                                || self.env.enums.contains_key(name))

A `shared struct` presents as `Type::Shared(name)`, so neither branch fires and
the operator is admitted unconditionally, returning `Type::Bool`. This is the
same shape as the pre-B-2026-07-03-7 hole for plain structs -- silently admitted
at typecheck, no lowering downstream, error at run/build -- which that row fixed
for `Type::Named` only.

FIXING IT IS A TWO-SIDED CHANGE, and doing one side alone makes things worse.
Widening the gate to `Type::Shared` turns the current run-vs-build divergence into
a clean rejection for the underived case, but `target_type_name` in `lowering.rs`
ALSO resolves only `Type::Named`, so a shared struct with a real `impl Ord` would
be accepted by the widened gate and then still emit nothing -- moving the
divergence rather than closing it. Both must move together:

  * `type_supports_partial_ord` / `type_supports_ord` already have `Type::Shared`
    arms reading `derived_traits`, so the DERIVED case needs only the gate widened
    plus a backend comparison path for a shared receiver;
  * the hand-written case needs `target_type_name` to resolve `Type::Shared`, at
    which point `ordering_dispatch_comparator`'s existing (currently unreachable)
    `Type::Shared` arm starts doing its job -- a note at that arm points here.

The `==` / `!=` side of the same gate should be checked in the same pass; it was
not measured here.

fix: FIXED by aae805f. See the detail — root cause, the one-line matching rule that missed, why the second `Vec` binding is required to reproduce, and the regression test (verified red with the seeds removed).
title: RUN-VS-BUILD ON EVERY FALLIBLE `try_*` COMPANION CONSUMED WITH `?`: the auto-parallelizer hoists the call into a worker function, which returns void, so the `?` failure path's `ret {i64, i64}` fails module verification and `karac build` REFUSES a program `--interp` runs correctly. Measured on clean HEAD with `try_push`, a companion that has shipped since phase-8-stdlib-floor item 8: two `v.try_push(1)?` calls plus ONE unrelated second `Vec` binding is the whole repro -- `error: codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Found return instr that returns non-void in Function of void return type! ret { i64, i64 } %q_ret_val"`, while `karac run --interp` prints the right answer and exits 0.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while landing B-2026-08-26-22's `try_resize` / `try_append` arms, but NOT caused by them -- confirmed by stashing every source change, rebuilding, and reproducing with `try_push` alone.

ROOT CAUSE, one line of matching. `method_effects_imply_receiver_mutation` (src/concurrency/reads.rs) decides whether a method call writes its receiver by scanning the effect checker's seed table for `key == method || key.ends_with(".<method>")`. Every INSTANCE `try_*` companion was seeded under the single shared key `__builtin_try_alloc` (`fallible_alloc::TRY_ALLOC_EFFECT_KEY`), which matches neither form, so all of them read as NON-mutating to the auto-parallelizer -- even though that seed gives them a real `allocates(Heap)` effect for the effect checker's own purposes. The static CONSTRUCTOR companions were never affected: they are seeded under fully-qualified names (`Vec.try_with_capacity`, `Vec.try_from_slice`, ...) that the suffix match does find.

WHY THE SECOND `Vec` IS REQUIRED, and why this went unnoticed. The analyzer only forms a parallel group when it has independent work to hoist; a lone binding gives it nothing. The second, entirely unrelated `Vec` is what supplies it. That is the same ingredient B-2026-08-25-20's `Vec.resize`/`Vec.append` seeding bug needed, which suggests the shape rather than the individual method is what to test for.

FAILURE MODE IS A REFUSAL, NOT A MISCOMPILE, which is the one piece of good news: the module verifier catches it, so no wrong-answer binary ships. It is still a run-vs-build divergence on a documented feature -- design.md § Fallible Allocation's whole point is that `v.try_push(x)?` is "always available at every call site".

FIXED IN THE SAME CHANGE that found it (B-2026-08-26-22's commit): the mutating instance companions now carry fully-qualified seed keys (`Vec.try_push`, `Vec.try_insert`, `Vec.try_extend`, `Vec.try_extend_from_slice`, `Vec.try_reserve`, `Vec.try_reserve_exact`, `Vec.try_resize`, `Vec.try_append`, `String.try_push_str`, `VecDeque.try_push_back`, `VecDeque.try_push_front`). Suffix matching makes these name-based rather than type-based, so one key per method name answers for every receiver type -- `Vec.try_insert` also covers `Map` / `Set` / `SortedSet`. `try_clone` is deliberately excluded: it allocates but does not mutate its receiver, and seeding it would over-serialize every clone for nothing.

REGRESSION TEST: tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_fallible_companions_are_seeded_against_the_auto_parallelizer, verified RED with the seeds removed and green with them restored. It lives in the ASAN suite rather than tests/codegen.rs because `run_program_capturing` passes `None` for the concurrency analysis -- auto-par never runs under the codegen E2E harness, so no fixture there can reach this class at all. That is the second time in two rows the same harness hole has decided where a guard has to live (see B-2026-08-25-20), which is worth treating as a standing fact about the two harnesses rather than a per-bug surprise.

fix:
FIXED by c5da7e8. `collect` now has a fallible lowering, and `Vec.try_from_iter` is registered on top of it.

THE LOWERING. `try_compile_iter_adaptor_collect_to_vec` gained an `_ex` entry taking a `fallible` flag, and `build_body` an `err_name: Option<&str>` threaded to the leaf. Infallible, `err_name` is `None` and not one byte of the emitted block changes -- the point of routing the companion through the SAME engine rather than giving it a parallel lowering that would drift. Fallible, three things differ:

  * the leaf append becomes `match <acc>.try_push(<cur>) { Ok(_) => {} Err(e) => match e { AllocError.OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: b } => { <err> = b } _ => { <err> = 0 } } }`;
  * the block gains `let mut __icerr_N: i64 = -1;` at the head and `if <err> >= 0 { break }` at the head of the fused loop body;
  * the tail swaps from `__icv_N` to `if <err> >= 0 { Result.Err(AllocError.OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: <err> }) } else { Result.Ok(__icv_N) }`.

THE PARTIAL CONTAINER UNWINDS FOR FREE. This row expected the hard part to be a bespoke unwind that drops each already-collected element before the `Err` escapes. It is not needed: on the `Err` tail `__icv_N` is simply never moved out, so it dies as an ordinary block-local and the existing scope-exit cleanup runs every element's drop. Because `collect` is a codegen-time SOURCE-LEVEL desugaring rather than a hand-written IR loop, the accumulator is a real `let` binding subject to the same cleanup as any other -- the desugaring is what makes the unwind path free, and it is worth naming because the row was filed expecting the opposite.

BAILING ON THE FIRST FAILURE IS NOT AN OPTIMIZATION. Once the accumulator has refused to grow it refuses for every element left in the source, so without the `break` an OOM at element 3 of 10_000 runs 9_997 more `try_push` calls that cannot succeed -- and each remaining element is still MATERIALIZED by the adaptor chain and moved into a `try_push` that stores nothing, so a heap-bearing element type leaks one buffer per remaining element instead of one in total. The guard is `<err> >= 0`, a plain i64 compare.

WHY THE FLAG IS AN i64 AND NOT AN `Option[AllocError]`. Both nicer shapes were tried against real codegen and both were REFUSED, because there is no re-typecheck after lowering and so a synthetic local carries no type side-table: `__icerr_N.is_none()` gives "no handler for method 'is_none' on variable '__icerr_0'", and a `Some(x)` pattern over a synthetic `Option[AllocError]` gives "Undefined variable '__iceo_0'". Primitives need no side-table, so the flag carries the byte count directly (`-1` = no failure) and the enum is rebuilt at the tail -- `requested_bytes` still reaches the caller intact. The nested match that recovers the count DOES bind, because its scrutinee is a real call rather than a synthetic local.

REGISTRATION, once the lowering existed, was the four-line change the row predicted: `"from_iter"` back into `TRY_ALLOC_STATIC_BASES`, `("Vec", "from_iter")` into `CODEGEN_FALLIBLE_STATIC`, `"from_iter" => coll == "Vec"` re-admitted in the typechecker's static-companion gate, and a `Vec.try_from_iter` arm in `assoc_call.rs` calling the `_ex` entry. The typechecker records `Vec[U]` at the derived synthetic span (`usize::MAX - offset - 1`, the `method_call_iter.rs` convention) so codegen can read the element type back. The interpreter gets a dedicated arm that evaluates the same synthetic `arg.collect()` and wraps it via `result_ok` -- identical to how `try_with_capacity` / `try_from_slice` already behave there, since the interpreter has no allocation-failure path.

A SECOND, UNRELATED BUG WAS FOUND AND FIXED IN THE SAME CHANGE, and it is the more interesting half. `Vec.try_from_iter(..)?` inside an auto-parallelized loop crashed `karac build` with `Found return instr that returns non-void in Function of void return type! ret { i64, i64 }` -- the SAME crash B-2026-08-26-26 had just fixed by seeding each fallible companion NAME as receiver-mutating. That fix worked for those names and left the invariant unstated, so the next `?`-bearing call to arrive walked straight back into it: `try_from_iter` is a CONSTRUCTOR (no receiver to mark) and reductions are a different path from par-groups, so neither half of the previous fix applied. The property that actually holds is about `?`, not about which function is spelled with it: `x?` returns from the ENCLOSING function on its failure arm, and a parallel worker returns void. So `ExprKind::Question` now answers `true` in the early-exit walker, and the loop-REDUCTION path (`recognize_reductions_in_block`), which had no early-exit gate at all, gained one.

THE GATE HAD TO BE NARROWER THAN THE EXISTING PREDICATE. Gating reductions on the full `stmt_has_early_exit` de-parallelized working code -- `test_ir_reduction_fires_with_break_in_nested_loop` caught it -- because `break`/`continue` jump to the nearest enclosing loop and inside a NESTED one never leave the body being lowered. The walker is now parameterized on a `loop_jumps` flag, with `block_escapes_enclosing_fn` (`loop_jumps = false`, `return`/`?` only) as the reduction gate and `stmt_has_early_exit` (`loop_jumps = true`) unchanged for par-groups. A `break` that DOES escape the parallelized loop is still rejected downstream by the depth/label-aware `reduce::block_has_early_exit`.

VERIFICATION. Both backends agree across `0..4`, `(0..6).map(..)`, `src.iter().map(..)` chains and heap `Vec[String]` elements; `Vec.try_from_iter` matches its panicking base output-for-output; the interpreter and codegen tests are paired. The ASAN fixture is Linux/LSan-authoritative and non-vacuous -- 588 allocations against the 3-allocation baseline under `KARAC_ASAN_ALLOC_AUDIT=1` with `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` set, so it linked and ran a real binary. `tests/typechecker.rs`'s `vec_try_from_iter_stays_absent_until_collect_can_fail` -- the guard the base row left behind asserting the name must NOT exist -- was replaced by `vec_try_from_iter_is_registered_now_that_collect_can_fail`, which is the honest inversion rather than a deletion.

WHAT IS NOT COVERED. The OOM path itself has no executable test: triggering a real allocation failure in-process would require exhausting container memory, so the `Err` branch is verified structurally (it is the same `alloc_fallible` + `build_alloc_oom_result` shape as the `try_reserve` / `try_resize` / `try_append` arms landed in B-2026-08-26-22) rather than by execution. The one element in flight when `try_push` refuses is still moved into a call that stores nothing; whether codegen's `try_push` frees it on its `Err` path is a property of `try_push` itself and identical for a hand-written `v.try_push(s)?`, so it was left alone rather than folded into this row.
title: `Vec.try_from_iter` CANNOT BE REGISTERED UNTIL `collect` HAS A FALLIBLE LOWERING: its base `Vec.from_iter` lowers to `iter.collect()`, whose codegen grows the accumulator through the PANICKING allocator, so a companion built on that rewrite would return `Ok` unconditionally and then abort inside `collect` on real OOM. design.md § Fallible Allocation names `try_from_iter` in its table AND leans on it in prose -- `let v = Vec.try_from_iter(0..1024)?` is the sanctioned replacement for a `.collect()` rejected under `panic_on_alloc_failure = false` -- so this is the one row in that table with a spec consumer already pointing at it. Measured on the commit that closed B-2026-08-26-22: `Vec.try_from_iter(0..4)` reports `no associated function 'try_from_iter' on type 'Vec'` at typecheck, identically under `karac check` and `karac build`.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-26-22 at its close. Four of that row's five items shipped complete; this is the fifth's fallible half, and it is a genuinely different piece of work from the other four rather than a leftover.

WHY IT WAS NOT SHIPPED WITH THE BASE. `from_iter` was implemented as an exact alias of `collect` — the typechecker types it by inferring a synthetic `<iter>.collect()`, and `lowering.rs` rewrites the call to that same expression, so both backends run one implementation. Registering `try_from_iter` on top of that alias was tried and BACKED OUT: the fallible-companion machinery would have wrapped an infallible `collect` in `Result.Ok`, producing a method whose type says it can fail and whose body cannot. Under actual allocation failure it would abort inside `collect` rather than return `Err(AllocError.OutOfMemory{..})`. A companion that lies about being fallible is worse than one that does not exist, so the name is absent at BOTH check and build rather than half-present.

WHAT THE WORK ACTUALLY IS: a fallible lowering for `collect` itself. Codegen builds the accumulator by repeated growth through `karac_realloc_or_panic`; a `try_collect` shape needs that loop to grow through `karac_alloc_fallible` and to bail out with `Err(bytes)` on a null, freeing the partial accumulator on the way out. The `try_reserve` / `try_resize` / `try_append` arms landed in B-2026-08-26-22 are the closest models — same fallible-alloc + memcpy + free-old shape, same `build_alloc_oom_result` on null — but none of them has to unwind a PARTIALLY BUILT container, which is the new part here: the elements already collected must be dropped (not just their spine freed) before the `Err` escapes, or a heap-bearing element type leaks on every OOM.

ONCE THAT EXISTS the registration is small, and deliberately so: add `"from_iter"` back to `TRY_ALLOC_STATIC_BASES`, add the `("Vec", "from_iter")` pair to `CODEGEN_FALLIBLE_STATIC`, and re-admit `"from_iter" => coll == "Vec"` in the recognized-companion gate in `src/typechecker/expr_call.rs`. All three edits were made and reverted during B-2026-08-26-22, so the shape is known.

GUARDED IN THE MEANTIME by tests/typechecker.rs::vec_try_from_iter_stays_absent_until_collect_can_fail, which asserts the name stays rejected. That test is the thing to DELETE when this row is fixed — it exists to stop the companion being re-registered on the panicking base, not to keep the feature out forever.

SEVERITY: medium and not higher, on the same grounds as its parent row. Nothing miscompiles; the missing name is a clean `no associated function` diagnostic, and the `panic_on_alloc_failure = false` profile flag that would make the fallible surface load-bearing is itself not implemented yet, so no user program can currently be forced onto this method.

title: A NESTED `Result` AS `main`'s ERROR TYPE LOSES BOTH ITS TAG AND ITS PAYLOAD on every compiled backend: `main() -> Result[(), Result[A, B]]` returning `Err(Ok(3))` prints `Error: Ok(3)` under `--interp` and `Error: Err(0)` under JIT and AOT -- the WRONG variant with a zeroed payload, not merely an unrendered one. Reproduced on `Result[i64, i64]` (both `Ok` and `Err` inner values collapse to `Err(0)`), `Result[bool, bool]` (`Err(false)`) and `Result[i64, String]` (`Err()`), so the inner discriminant is dropped unconditionally rather than truncated by width.
repro:
fn main() -> Result[(), Result[i64, i64]] { return Err(Ok(3)); }

  karac run --interp m.kara         # Error: Ok(3)     <- oracle
  karac run          m.kara         # Error: Err(0)
  karac build        m.kara && ./m  # Error: Err(0)

Also measured: Err(Err(9)) -> Err(0); Result[bool, bool] Err(Ok(true)) ->
Err(false); Result[i64, String] Err(Ok(3)) -> Err().
detail:
Found while sweeping every `E` shape `type_supports_display` admits, for
B-2026-08-25-34's entry-point Display work. Distinct from that row's
fail-open and NOT fixed by it: this path emits a renderer and the renderer
runs -- it just renders a value that was reconstructed wrong. The output is
PLAUSIBLE (`Err(0)` is a well-formed `Result`), which makes it worse than the
empty message the fail-open produced: nothing about the line says the error
was lost.

SUSPECTED SITE, NOT CONFIRMED. `emit_main_result_return` reconstructs `E`
from the outer aggregate's payload words (fields 1..n) via
`rebuild_value_from_payload_word_slice`. An inner `Result[A, B]` is itself a
`{tag, w0, w1, w2}` aggregate, so it needs a word for its own tag plus its
payload, and the outer `Result[(), E]` would have to be wide enough for all
of them -- the B-2026-08-23-20 / B-2026-08-26-5 width family. But
`Option[i64]` as `E` renders CORRECTLY (`None`, `Some(5)`), and that is the
near-miss control: same 4-field enum shape, so a pure width-shortfall story
does not explain why `Result` loses its tag while `Option` keeps its. Check
the Result tag convention (Ok == 1, Err == 0) against what the reconstruction
writes into field 0 before assuming width.

Not common, but not academic: a `Result` inside a `Result` is what a `main`
whose error type is an alias over a fallible result produces, or an
unflattened `?`-chain. Medium because the failure is silent and
always-wrong rather than shape-dependent.
fix:
FIXED by c9db880. The suspected site was right and the reasoning that dismissed it was wrong.

MECHANISM. `Result`'s payload area is a FIXED five words. An inner `Result[A, B]` is itself a six-word `{tag, w0..w4}` aggregate, so it does not fit, and `coerce_to_payload_words` heap-BOXES it with the box pointer in word 0. `emit_main_result_return` rebuilt `E` straight from the payload words, so that pointer was read as `E`'s FIELD 0 -- for a nested `Result`, its inner TAG. A heap address is never 1, so the variant always decoded as `Err`; the payload words past the five-word area read as zero. Hence `Err(0)`, uniformly, for every inner value and both inner variants -- which is exactly the "dropped unconditionally rather than truncated by width" signature the row recorded.

WHY THE CONTROL MISLED. The row set width aside because `Option[i64]` as `E` renders correctly, reasoning that it is the "same 4-field enum shape". That is the measurement that needed one more step: `Option[i64]` IS four words, which is precisely why it fits the five-word area and never boxes. `Result[i64, i64]` is six. The control was not a same-width comparison at all -- it was the case on the other side of the threshold, so it confirmed the width story instead of refuting it. Measured directly: outer aggregate 6 fields / 5 payload words; `Option[i64]` e_ty `{i64,i64,i64,i64}` (4); `Result[i64,i64]` e_ty `{i64,i64,i64,i64,i64,i64}` (6).

The row's other instruction -- check the Ok==1 / Err==0 tag convention against what the reconstruction writes into field 0 -- was the right question, and the answer is that nothing wrote a tag there at all: field 0 received a POINTER.

TWO SITES, WHICH IS THE PART THAT NEARLY GOT MISSED. `main`'s error value is rebuilt independently in two places: the tail `return Err(..)` path (`emit_main_result_return`, `functions.rs`) and the `?`-propagation branch (`exprs.rs`, the `q_main_wider` word gather). Only the first is what the row reproduced. The second had the identical gap and was found by inspecting the sibling call sites rather than by the repro: `fn inner() -> Result[i64, Result[i64,i64]]` returning `Err(Ok(3))`, propagated out of `main` with `?`, printed `Error: Ok(3)` under `--interp` and `Error: Err(0)` under JIT and AOT. That is the shape the row's own detail anticipates ("an unflattened `?`-chain"), so fixing only the reproduced site would have closed the row while leaving the bug reachable through the other door.

A THIRD SITE ALREADY HAD THE CHECK: the errdefer staging helper (`exprs.rs`) deboxes on `llvm_type_word_count(e_ty) > payload_area`, and the match-arm unpacker `reconstruct_payload_value` has always done the same for boxed variant payloads. So the predicate was never in doubt -- it is the unpack mirror of pack's `out.len() > num_words` -- it simply existed in two places and was absent from the two that rebuild `main`'s error. It is now stated once, in `rebuild_payload_deboxing_if_spilled` (`calls.rs`), and shared by both main-return sites, so they agree by construction rather than by copy.

VERIFICATION. Every shape the row names now agrees across interpreter / JIT / AOT: `Result[i64,i64]` (`Ok(3)` and `Err(7)`), `Result[bool,bool]` (`Ok(true)` and `Err(false)`), `Result[i64,String]` (`Err("boom")` and `Ok(42)`), with the `Option[i64]` and scalar controls unchanged and the error exit still code 1. The `Ok` path still prints normally and exits 0.

Regression tests are in `tests/cli.rs`: `test_main_result_error_nested_result_keeps_tag_and_payload` (six shapes, interpreter as oracle, JIT and AOT strictly equal to it) and `test_main_result_error_nested_result_survives_question_propagation` (the `?` door). Both were confirmed to FAIL on the parent commit with exactly the reported symptom -- `left: "Error: Err(0)"`, `right: "Error: Ok(3)"` -- so they are genuine regression tests rather than tests written to pass. The nested cases were also added to B-2026-08-25-34's shared shape list, whose AOT half soft-skips; the two dedicated tests instead ASSERT the build succeeds, since these are shapes codegen must render and a build failure is the regression rather than a reason to pass vacuously.

Suite: 109 suites green under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, so no E2E soft-skips -- `codegen` 3281, `cli` 716, `interpreter` 1737, `memory_sanitizer` 1196 (Linux, so LeakSanitizer is live), `par_codegen` 270. `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy --all --all-targets -D warnings` clean on both feature legs. The only non-green suite is `gpu_e2e`, whose 60 failures are all the optional GPU archive being absent in this container; it soft-skips without the strict flag and is unrelated to this change.

NOT COVERED. Triple nesting (`Result[(), Result[i64, Result[i64,i64]]]`) is refused at build time by B-2026-08-25-34's fail-closed diagnostic, naming the f-string renderer rather than this reconstruction. Verified byte-identical before and after this fix, so it is a pre-existing renderer gap and untouched here. The heap box itself is still not freed on the error-exit path; that allocation predates this change (previously the box was never even read) and the process exits immediately after, so it is out of scope for this row rather than introduced by it.

title: A MANUAL `impl Display` IS IGNORED AS SOON AS THE VALUE IS NESTED: an enum with a hand-written `Display` renders through its impl at top level (`f"{e}"` -> `aye 7`) and through the DERIVED/Debug shape one level down (`f"{[e]}"` -> `[A { n: 7 }, B]`, `f"{Some(e)}"` -> `Some(A { n: 7 })`). So the ONE mechanism design.md offers for overriding a rendering silently stops applying inside a container, and a type whose `Display` exists to hide its internals leaks them from inside any `Vec` or `Option`. The interpreter does this consistently; codegen cannot render the `Option` case at all, which is the run-vs-build half.
detail:
Measured on CLEAN main (`git stash`, rebuild) and on a plain USER enum, so it
is neither caused by nor confined to B-2026-08-25-34's prelude work. It
surfaced there because `AllocError` gained a manual `Display` and promptly
showed the same split: `println(e)` / `e.to_string()` / `f"{e}"` give the new
prose, `f"{vec_of_alloc_errors}"` gives the Debug shape.

WHAT NEEDS DECIDING FIRST, and why this is filed rather than fixed. design.md
does not say which trait a CONTAINER's element rendering dispatches through.
Rust sidesteps the question entirely (there is no `Display for Vec`), so
there is no precedent to copy. Two coherent answers: (a) elements render
through `Display`, making the override transitive and the impl the single
source of truth for how a value looks; or (b) container rendering is
explicitly Debug-shaped, in which case the spec should SAY so and `f"{v}"`
should arguably require `Debug` on the element rather than `Display`.
Today's behaviour is neither -- (a) at depth 0 and (b) at depth 1, with
nothing written down. Answering that is the first task on this row; the code
change is downstream of it.
fix:
FIXED by 59d6568. Both backends now dispatch a container's ELEMENT rendering through the
element's own `Display`, so a hand-written `impl Display` wins at every depth
rather than only at depth 0.

WHAT THE ROW ASKED TO DECIDE FIRST WAS ALREADY DECIDED -- twice, in writing and
in code, which is the finding that turned this from a policy question into a
straightforward alignment:

  * design.md § Strings already committed to option (a) for `Option`/`Result`
    ("renders its payload through the payload's own `Display`"), and gave a
    rationale that is container-agnostic by construction: "`println(p)` on the
    bare payload already routes through `Display`, so wrapping it in an
    `Option` must not change how it renders." A `Vec` wraps exactly as an
    `Option` does. That same paragraph named the field-name rendering "a
    `Debug`-in-`Display` bug to be aligned to this rule".
  * The TYPECHECKER already enforces option (a)'s contract: `f"{v}"` on a
    `Vec[P]` whose `P` has no `Display` is rejected outright ("type 'Vec[P]'
    does not implement Display"). So a container is interpolable exactly when
    its elements are `Display` -- which REFUTES option (b) (that container
    rendering is Debug-shaped and should require `Debug` on the element).
    The gate demanded `Display` and the renderer then ignored it.

So the two coherent answers the row posed were not symmetric: one was already
the written and enforced rule, and the renderers simply did not implement it.

INTERPRETER (`src/interpreter/builtin.rs`). `render_typed_mode` -- the shared
walker behind `display_render_typed` / `debug_render_typed` -- now consults
`user_display_impl_to_string_key` at every recursive position and calls the
user body, but ONLY when `debug` is false: `Debug` is a different trait and
keeps the field-name shape, which is what `dbg()` reports. Calling user code
from the walker requires `&mut self`, so the three renderers took that receiver
and the eight closure-based recursion sites became plain loops; every caller
was already in a `&mut self` context, so nothing rippled outward.

`Set`, `SortedSet` and `SortedMap` needed arms of their own. The walker never
destructured those three, so they fell to a catch-all that formats through
`Value`'s RUST `Display`, a renderer that cannot reach a user impl. Codegen's
Set renderer recurses through the shared dispatcher and therefore picked the
impl up for free the moment the arm below landed — so leaving the interpreter
alone would have produced `Set{B}` against `Set{bee}`, converting a
consistent-but-wrong rendering into a genuine run-vs-build divergence. This is
the one place the fix had to ADD coverage rather than redirect it. Punctuation
is copied verbatim from the `Value` `Display` arms they replace; `debug` keeps
the old path, since routing them through the typed walker there would also
start quoting their leaves — an improvement, but a separate change.

`user_display_impl_to_string_key` gained `SharedStruct`, which turned out to
be a run-vs-build divergence at DEPTH 0 that predated this row entirely. The
helper matched `Struct` and `EnumVariant` only, so the interpreter ignored a
`shared struct`'s `impl Display` EVERYWHERE — including a bare `println(a)`
and an explicit `a.to_string()` — while codegen resolved it through
`expr_user_struct_name` (shared types are registered in `struct_field_names`)
and honored it. `println(a)` on a `shared struct Sh` printed `sh(1)` under
`karac build` and `Sh { v: 1 }` under `--interp`. The depth dispatch would
have widened that to containers, so it had to be closed here; the fix closes
the depth-0 half with it. A shared ENUM was never affected (it rides as a
`Value::EnumVariant`, already matched) and is asserted as the control.

Each container arm now copies its elements OUT of the `RwLock` guard before
recursing. That is not incidental tidying: a user `to_string` runs arbitrary
Kāra code that may touch the very container being printed, and holding a read
guard across that call would deadlock on a write. The `SharedStruct` arm reads
each field out of its cell for the same reason.

CODEGEN (`src/codegen/synth_display.rs`). `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` is
the single choke point every container element, struct field and enum payload
already routes through, so one arm covers all of them: when the module carries
a compiled `<T>.to_string` (the discriminator -- built-ins are named
`karac_display_<T>`), emit a `karac_display_<T>` wrapper that calls the user
method and appends the returned String to the accumulator. Placed AHEAD of the
shared / enum / struct arms, which claim a type by name and would otherwise
emit the built-in shape without ever asking whether the user wrote an impl.

The wrapper's free is guarded on `cap > 0`. `cap == 0` means non-owning, and a
`to_string` returning a string LITERAL (`match self { B => "bee" }`) points at
a read-only global -- freeing it aborts. Same invariant and same guard as
`emit_write_and_free_string`. The ASAN fixture exercises both payload shapes in
one program for exactly this reason: the f-string arm leaks without the free,
the literal arm aborts with an unguarded one.

MEASURED, before -> after, both backends byte-identical in each state:

  f"{[Ue.A{n:7}, Ue.B]}"   [A { n: 7 }, B]            -> [aye 7, bee]
  f"{Some(p)}", p: Point   Some(Point { x: 3, y: 4 }) -> Some((3, 4))

The second line is design.md's OWN canonical example, and its previous output
was the `Debug`-in-`Display` bug that paragraph was written against -- so this
also closes that documented item. design.md attributed it to the interpreter;
it was both backends, and the note has been corrected to say so.

A SWEEP of every wrapper shape against a user impl backs the claim that the
surface is now uniform. Agreeing on both backends: `Vec`, nested `Vec`, tuple,
`Option`, `Result`, struct field, `Map` key and value, `Set`, enum payload,
shared struct, shared enum. Interpreter-only (codegen refuses the key type for
an unrelated reason): `SortedSet` / `SortedMap`. Pre-existing AOT refusal that
reproduces with a DERIVED struct and no user impl, so out of scope here: a
`Slice` of any struct in an f-string.

Two halves of the row's repro were NOT this bug and are unchanged: `karac
build` refusing `f"{Some(enum_value)}"`, and refusing a `#[derive(Display)]`
struct with a payload-bearing enum field. Both reproduce identically with a
DERIVED Display and no user impl anywhere, so they are the pre-existing
compound-payload codegen gap, not the override-at-depth question. The second
is now filed as its own row.

design.md § `#[derive(Display)]` on enums gained "The override applies at every
depth" -- the sentence the row's tracker asked for -- stating the rule, its
grounding in the typechecker gate, and that `Debug` is unaffected.

A LATE REGRESSION worth recording, because the coverage that caught it was not
mine. Codegen's dispatcher serves `Debug` and `Display` alike — the two
families differ only by `disp_sym_prefix` and the per-mode cache — so the new
arm captured `dbg()` too until it was gated on `display.debug_render`, the
exact analogue of the interpreter's `debug` flag, which the interpreter half
had had from the start. `dbg(e)` on an `AllocError` reported its Display prose
instead of `OutOfMemory { requested_bytes: 4096 }`. The E2E oracle in
`tests/codegen.rs` could not see it: `run_program` captures stdout and `dbg`
writes to stderr. It was caught by B-2026-08-25-34's CLI test, which asserts
that stderr line as a CONTROL. A user-type equivalent has been added beside it
so the gap is covered on purpose rather than by luck.

Tests: 6 in `tests/interpreter.rs` (depth sweep across Vec / nested Vec /
Option / Result / tuple / struct field / Map value / `.to_string()`; Set +
SortedSet + SortedMap; shared struct at depth 0 and nested; `dbg` keeps the Debug shape; a derived-Display control
that must not shift; design.md's `Some((3, 4))` example), 5 E2E in
`tests/codegen.rs` mirroring the same bytes as the run-vs-build oracle, 1 ASAN
leak fixture, and 1 CLI test asserting `dbg` across all three backends. `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`e2e_compound_struct_payload_display_matches_interpreter` (B-2026-07-08-18)
pinned the old shape and was updated: that row closed the DIVERGENCE by
teaching codegen to emit what the interpreter emitted, which agreed on the
shape design.md called a bug. Its doc comment said the payload renders "NOT the
struct's own Display impl" and would have been actively misleading left in
place, so it was rewritten rather than just renumbered.
tracker: docs/design.md § `#[derive(Display)]` on enums — needs a sentence saying which trait a container's ELEMENT rendering dispatches through

title: SWEEP THE REMAINING ENTRY-HOISTED-ALLOCA / CONDITIONAL-STORE / SCOPE-TRACKED SITES. The shape behind B-2026-08-25-33 -- and behind a fifth instance found in B-2026-08-25-34 -- is `create_entry_alloca` plus a store emitted at the USE site plus `track_vec_var`, whose function-scope drain then reads an uninitialized `cap` on any path that skipped the store and frees a garbage pointer. A mechanical scan finds ~16 further `create_entry_alloca`-then-track pairs with no `zero_init_str_acc_at_entry`; each needs classifying as genuinely unconditional (safe) or conditional (a latent free-of-garbage).
repro:
The two confirmed instances, both fixed in B-2026-08-25-34, show the shape:

  src/codegen/runtime.rs  fstr.ud.acc   (segfaulted 5/5 under `karac run`)
  src/codegen/runtime.rs  fstr.str.acc  (same fn, guarded alongside it)

The scan that produced the candidate list -- every `create_entry_alloca` with
a `track_vec_var`/`track_string_var` within 25 lines and no zero-init:

  runtime.rs:2524 __owned_tmp | method_call.rs:9923 __vrecv_tmp,
  10017 __owned_tmp | collections.rs:3830/3834/3951/3955 v/shfld.read.* |
  stmts.rs:10591, 11558 | control_flow_match.rs:10872 __whilelet_miss_scrut |
  method_call_ffi.rs:318 fu8.tmp | mono.rs:2473 |
  synth_display.rs:3171/3401/3456 *.disp.tmp | pattern_binding.rs:287

(Line numbers are as of 7553a08 and will drift; the pattern is the anchor.)
detail:
Filed rather than swept because the sweep is a different job from the row
that exposed it: each site needs its own reachability argument -- is the
store actually conditional? -- and, where it is, a program that reaches the
skipping path. The fault is INVISIBLE without one: AOT survives on fresh
zeroed kernel stack pages while the JIT faults on stack the LLVM compilation
machinery has already dirtied. That asymmetry is why this class keeps
recurring -- a latent site passes every AOT test and every ASAN run that does
not go through the JIT.

THE STRUCTURAL FIX WORTH PRICING FIRST: make `track_vec_var` itself zero-init
the alloca at entry, so registering for cleanup and being safe to clean up
become the same act. It has 39 call sites; for a slot that IS unconditionally
stored the extra entry store is dead (the real store dominates it), so the
cost is IR noise rather than semantics. The reason not to do it blind is
SHAPE: the helper GEPs with `vec_struct_type()`, so any tracked alloca that
is not `{ptr,len,cap}`-shaped would be miscompiled by the guard rather than
protected by it. Verifying that invariant across the 39 sites is exactly the
work this row is for.

Four rows have now paid for this shape one site at a time: the
f-string-in-a-loop double free, B-2026-08-25-33, and the two fixed under
B-2026-08-25-34.
fix:
FIXED by 225e233c. Swept structurally rather than site by site, and the row's blocking question turned out to have a cheaper answer than 39 case analyses.

THE ANSWER TO "IS THE SHAPE INVARIANT SAFE TO ASSUME". The row's reason not to fix this blind was that the guard GEPs with `vec_struct_type()`, so a tracked alloca of some other shape would be miscompiled by the guard rather than protected by it. But the DRAIN already GEPs the very same pointer with the very same type -- `emit_cleanup_action`'s `FreeVecBuffer` arm reads field 2 as `cap` and field 0 as `data` via `build_struct_gep(vec_ty, *vec_alloca, ..)`, and every caller of `emit_cleanup_action` binds `vec_ty = self.vec_struct_type()`. So `{ptr, len, cap}` is not a new requirement the guard imposes; it is a load-bearing invariant of `FreeVecBuffer` that predates it. A site violating it is ALREADY miscompiled today by the cleanup itself, guard or no guard. That reduces "verify the invariant across 39 sites" to "the invariant is already required by the existing code", which is a proof rather than an enumeration.

WHERE THAT ARGUMENT STOPS. It covers READS; the guard also WRITES, which the drain does not. So the guard carries two checks the drain does not need: the pointer must be an `alloca` INSTRUCTION (a GEP or a parameter names storage that may already hold a live value, and storing `{null, 0, 0}` over it would destroy that value), and its ALLOCATED TYPE must actually be the vec struct. Anything else is declined, not guessed.

MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. `KARAC_TRACKED_SLOT_CENSUS=1` makes codegen classify every tracked slot and attribute it to its tracking site via `#[track_caller]`. Across every `.kara` file in the repo that compiles -- 51 programs, 2064 tracked slots -- EVERY slot was a vec-shaped alloca: zero non-alloca, zero wrong-shape, zero missing-type. The distribution also shows where the volume is: `exprs.rs:204` (the f-string accumulator, 911), `stmts.rs:6844`/`6846` (let bindings, 1038), `runtime.rs:2552` (69), with single digits from `pattern_binding.rs:705`, `control_flow_match.rs:4696`, `control_flow_for.rs:1312` and others.

THE FIX. Zero at the TRACKER, not at each use site, so registering a slot for cleanup and making it safe to clean up become the same act -- a future tracking site cannot reintroduce the class by forgetting a separate guard call, which is exactly how the four prior instances happened. The store is emitted immediately after the alloca instruction, which dominates every use of that slot by definition, and `cap == 0` makes the drain's existing owned-heap test skip the free. All four scope-registration entry points are wired: `track_vec_var` plus the `track_vec_of_{aggs,maps,tensors}_var` siblings.

TWO SITES DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE, both of which push `FreeVecBuffer` but are not this class. `emit_owned_vec_element_release_on_overwrite` emits its cleanup IMMEDIATELY at an overwrite point that is dominated by the store it overwrites, so there is no unconditional-drain-versus-conditional-store mismatch. `task_group.rs`'s capture re-registration targets a different pointer (the task wrapper's copy, stored unconditionally as part of capture packing), which is a separate mechanism.

NO USER-VISIBLE BEHAVIOUR CHANGED, and this is the honest headline. Every one of the remaining sites the row's mechanical scan flagged turned out to be already-guarded (`exprs.rs:204` is the f-string accumulator, protected since the original double free), unconditionally stored (the `stmts.rs` let-binding sites), or registered into a scope frame that only drains on the path that stores. The match-arm binding sites -- `pattern_binding.rs:705`, `control_flow_match.rs:4696` -- looked like the obvious conditional-store candidates and are NOT: their cleanup lands in the ARM's scope frame, which is drained inside the arm's own basic block, so a non-taken arm neither stores nor drains. Five hand-built programs aimed at those shapes (never-taken match arm binding a `Vec` payload and a `String` payload, zero-trip `for` with an f-string body, untaken `if` binding a `Vec`, `None` arm of a `Option[Vec]` match) all behaved identically on a pre-fix and post-fix compiler under both JIT and AOT. A corpus-wide pre-fix/post-fix JIT diff over every `.kara` file in the repo found no behavioural difference attributable to this change either.

So the classification the row asked for came back: SAFE, all of them, today. That is a real result and not a reason the work was pointless -- the class recurred four times because each new tracking site had to remember an independent guard, and what the fix removes is that possibility, not a live crash.

THE REGRESSION TEST GUARDS THE PREMISE, NOT AN OUTPUT, which is the only honest thing to test given the above. `test_every_tracked_vec_slot_is_a_vec_shaped_alloca` (tests/cli.rs) compiles a program spanning many tracking sites -- plain/nested/`String` vec bindings, an f-string accumulator in a loop, a never-entered loop, a match with a never-taken heap-payload arm -- with the census on, and fails if any tracked slot is not a vec-shaped alloca. It has teeth: flipping the shape check to `slice_struct_type()` makes it fail and NAME the offending sites (`stmts.rs:6846`, `exprs.rs:204`, ...). It also asserts a floor on the number of census rows, so the test cannot silently pass over an empty set if the census or the tracking path is ever rewired.

VERIFICATION. 109 suites green under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, so no E2E soft-skips -- `codegen` 3281, `cli` 717, `interpreter` 1737, `memory_sanitizer` 1196 (Linux, so LeakSanitizer is live and this is the authoritative gate for the free-of-garbage class this row is about), `par_codegen` 270. `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy --all --all-targets -D warnings` clean on both feature legs. The only non-green suite is `gpu_e2e`, whose 60 failures are the optional GPU archive being absent in this container; it soft-skips without the strict flag and is unrelated.

FOUND WHILE SWEEPING, FILED SEPARATELY: B-2026-08-26-39 -- the `Error return trace` section is nondeterministic on the compiled backends (same binary, same input, same pinned hash seed, 0/1/3/4 frames across 20 runs) while `--interp` is stable. It reproduces identically on a pre-fix compiler, so it is not related to this change.

title: A local MOVED into a container's struct element slot (`b.xs[j] = t`) kept its own `UserDrop` registration, so its `impl Drop` body ran a SECOND time at the binding's live-range end even though the container now owns the value. The memory half of the same move was already disarmed, so ASAN stayed silent and only the observable body count showed it.
detail:
FOUND while re-measuring B-2026-08-26-21, whose diagnosis this corrects: the
duplicated `Drop` body on that row's swap fixture came from the MOVED-FROM
SOURCE, not from the displaced element the row spent its length on.

THE TWO HALVES OF ONE MOVE. An index store of a named local into a container's
element slot (`b.xs[j] = t`, where the element type is a struct with a live
heap field) MOVES the source's field pointers into the slot. B-2026-08-12-22
made that safe on the MEMORY axis by calling `zero_struct_move_caps` on the
source, so the source's heap cleanup no-ops and the container's element drain
is the only thing that frees the buffer.

It left the BODIES axis alone. The source binding's `UserDrop` cleanup action
stayed armed, so at the binding's live-range end `t` ran its `impl Drop` body a
SECOND time — once via the container's element (correct, the container owns the
value now) and once via its own stale registration (the bug).

WHY NO SANITIZER CAUGHT IT. The memory half was already correct, so there is no
double free and no leak behind this: ASAN and LSan are clean on the fixture
before AND after the fix. Only the observable body count shows it. That is why
both new `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` fixtures assert a clean run on both sides
of the change rather than a behaviour delta — they exist to keep the memory
half from regressing while the bodies half is edited, since only one of the two
halves has a sanitizer behind it.

MEASURED. `struct Item { id: i64, tag: String }` with `impl Drop` printing
`D{id}`, two elements in a `Vec[Item]`, the swap rotation:

    let t = b.xs[0];
    b.xs[0] = b.xs[1];
    b.xs[1] = t;

    got (pre-fix):   built, 21, D2, D1, D1
    got (post-fix):  built, 21, D2, D1
    two live values -> exactly two bodies

THE FIX is one statement in the `ExprKind::Index` assignment arm of
`src/codegen/stmts.rs`, in the same `if let Some(sname) = elem_struct.filter(
|_| container_owns)` block that B-2026-08-12-22 added:
`self.suppress_user_drop_for_var(src)`. Same helper and same reasoning as the
by-value call-arg move in `call_dispatch.rs` (B-2026-07-30-11); this arm is the
index-store peer that never got it. The interpreter is already correct here and
is untouched.

NOT AN A/B ORACLE, deliberately. The interpreter still prints an extra `D2` for
the element `b.xs[0] = b.xs[1]` displaces, because it treats an element read as
clone-then-destroy while codegen's `store_destroys_displaced` treats the same
store as a relocation. That divergence is the OPEN remainder of B-2026-08-26-21
and is a model question design.md does not answer. The new codegen fixture pins
codegen's side only and says so in its doc comment; when the model question is
decided, its expectation and the interpreter's must be re-derived together.
fix: 0af8b28

FIXED by b46cb47.

THE ROW MEASURED ONE SHAPE; THE DEFECT HAD NINE. Every lookup entry point that
takes a key it does not retain leaked a fresh owned struct temporary, not just
`Map.get`. Measured under LSan before the fix (x86_64 Linux, where LSan actually
runs -- the arm64 macOS host that filed the row could not have measured this
locally, since `-fsanitize=address` there has no LeakSanitizer):

  Map.get, inline struct literal (the row's repro) 135 B / 5 allocations
  Map.get, key produced by a CALL                  135 B / 5
  Map.get, key whose heap is a Vec field           160 B / 5
  Map.get_or                                       135 B / 5
  Map.remove + contains_key                        216 B / 8
  Set.contains                                     135 B / 5
  Set.remove                                       135 B / 5
  SortedMap.floor (pivot)                          108 B / 4
  Map.get, ENUM-variant key owning heap            135 B / 5  (valgrind)

All nine are clean after the fix, and the row's three narrowing claims still
hold as CONTROLS: a bound key, an `insert`, and a `Map[String, _]` looked up with
a temporary f-string were clean before and remain clean.

THE FIX IS THE AGGREGATE SIBLING OF A HELPER THAT ALREADY EXISTED, which is also
the explanation for the row's most informative clue. `free_fresh_owned_str_arg`
was already called at each of these lookup sites, and it is exactly why a
`Map[String, _]` key was clean while a struct WRAPPING a String was not: the
String path had a free, the aggregate path had none.
`free_fresh_owned_struct_key_arg` is its counterpart -- same call sites, same
freshness gate, `emit_struct_drop_synthesis` instead of the string buffer free.
`insert` is untouched, because there the key is MOVED into the collection and the
collection's drop reclaims it; freeing it at the call would double-free.

THE ENUM LEG WAS FOUND WITH A SECOND INSTRUMENT, not by reasoning from the
struct fix. With the struct leg landed, valgrind (independent of the ASAN
harness, and available here because this is Linux) reported the fixed struct
program losing 0 bytes while the same program with an ENUM key still lost
135 B / 5. `free_fresh_owned_enum_key_arg` covers it through
`emit_enum_drop_switch`. Its shape gate is ordered deliberately: `enum_name_of_expr`
ALSO resolves a bare `Identifier`, so consulting it before checking the
expression shape would free a let-bound enum whose drop belongs to its binding —
the very double free the struct leg avoids by matching only `StructLiteral` and
call return types. `asan_map_get_with_bound_enum_key_is_clean` is that control.

THE DROP IS IMMEDIATE, NOT SCOPE-EXIT, and that choice is load-bearing rather
than stylistic. The row points at `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`, the
ordinary call-argument path, and registering the key there would have been the
obvious move. It would also have been wrong: that helper hoists ONE entry alloca
and frees it once at function exit, so inside a loop -- which is where lookups
live, and what the row's own repro does -- it frees the LAST key and leaks every
earlier one. That is the entry-alloca/scope-cleanup shape of B-2026-08-25-33 and
B-2026-08-26-30. Storing and dropping adjacently in a single basic block is
correct per iteration and lets the hoisted slot be reused safely.

`Identifier` keys are deliberately not matched, which is what keeps the row's
documented workaround (`let probe = Item { .. }; m.get(probe)`) from becoming a
double free: a let-bound key is owned by its binding and freed at its scope exit.

VERIFIED: the full memory_sanitizer suite is green post-fix, so no pre-existing
double-free/UAF guard regressed; and the row's repro is byte-identical across
`--interp`, JIT, `build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

A NOTE ON HOW THE PRE-FIX NUMBERS WERE OBTAINED, because a leak table is worth
nothing if the runs were vacuous. Each was measured by stashing the fix,
rebuilding both `karac` AND the test binary (the harness links the compiler as a
library, so rebuilding only `karac` measures the wrong thing), and re-running.
The three sites with no prior measurement -- `get_or`, `Set.remove`,
`SortedMap.floor` -- were each confirmed to leak before being claimed as fixed,
rather than assumed to leak because they share a code path.

TRAP, worth recording because it produced a full table of false CLEANs on the
first attempt: these tests live in `mod memory_sanitizer_tests`, so a filter of
the bare function name matches NOTHING, and `--exact` on no match prints
`test result: ok. 0 passed` -- which a "did it pass" grep accepts. Every one of
the eight leaking shapes was scored CLEAN by that detector minutes after it had
been seen failing. Require `ok. 1 passed`, and use the full `mod::name` path.
This is trap 4 from docs/spikes/b-2026-08-25-3-x86-handoff.md, hit again.

CROSS-REF: B-2026-08-26-10 (whose ASAN fixture surfaced this),
B-2026-08-25-33 / B-2026-08-26-30 (the entry-alloca shape this fix avoids).
title: `Map.get` WITH AN INLINE TEMPORARY STRUCT KEY THAT OWNS HEAP LEAKS THE TEMPORARY -- one allocation per lookup. Binding the key first is clean, a `Map[String, _]` looked up with a temporary f-string is clean, and INSERT is unaffected (the key is moved into the map); it is specifically a borrowed-then-discarded struct key on the lookup path. NOT specific to hand-written impls -- the `#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]` path leaks identically.
detail:
Found while building an ASAN fixture for B-2026-08-26-10's user-`impl Hash`
dispatch, and confirmed PRE-EXISTING by measuring the derived path beside it —
this is not specific to hand-written impls.

REPRO. The temporary is the key expression itself:

    #[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
    struct Item { id: i64, name: String }
    fn main() {
        let mut m: Map[Item, i64] = Map.new();
        m.insert(Item { id: 1, name: f"a-padding-padding-padding" }, 1);
        let mut j = 0;
        while j < 5 {
            match m.get(Item { id: j, name: f"b-{j}-padding-padding-padding" }) {
                Some(v) => { println(v); } None => {}
            }
            j = j + 1;
        }
        println(m.len());
    }

  LeakSanitizer: 108 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocation(s), allocated in `main` —
  one per `get` whose key temporary was built inline.

WHAT NARROWS IT.

  * The KEY must be an inline temporary. Binding it first
    (`let probe = Item { .. }; m.get(probe)`) is clean, which is the workaround
    and what the B-2026-08-26-10 fixture uses.
  * The key must be a STRUCT that owns heap. A `Map[String, i64]` looked up with
    a temporary f-string (`m.get(f"b-{j}-...")`) is clean, so the one-level
    String path already drops its temporary; it is the struct wrapper that does
    not.
  * INSERT is unaffected: 40 inserts of the same inline temporaries leak
    nothing, because the key is MOVED into the map and the map's drop frees it.
    Only the lookup path, where the temporary is borrowed and then discarded,
    loses it.
  * Hand-written impls are NOT required. Measured on both: 5 leaks with
    `impl Hash` + `impl PartialEq`/`Eq`, 4 with `#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]`
    on the identical program shape. The derived count is lower only because one
    lookup hits and takes a different arm.

WHY IT WAS NOT VISIBLE BEFORE. Nothing here is new; the shape is just rare in the
suite, which mostly looks up by a bound key or by a primitive. It surfaced now
because B-2026-08-26-10's fixture reached for the most natural spelling of a
lookup.

WHERE TO LOOK. `compile_call`'s inline-owned-aggregate arg tracking
(`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`) drops an inline struct/tuple temp passed to
a callee that does not forward it; the map lookup path reaches
`karac_map_get` through a different route and appears not to register the temp.
`remove` and `contains_key` take a key the same way and should be checked in the
same pass — this row measured `get` only.

title: A `#[derive(Display)]` STRUCT WITH A PAYLOAD-BEARING ENUM FIELD IS REFUSED BY `karac build` -- and the refusal is INVERTED with respect to difficulty: the same struct renders fine NESTED IN A `Vec` (`f"{[h]}"` -> `[Dh { u: B }]`), and the field renders fine ON ITS OWN (`f"{h.u}"` -> `A { n: 4 }`), but interpolating the struct itself (`f"{h}"`) fails the whole compile with "field 'u' has a type (...) whose Display is not yet supported under `karac build`". The interpreter renders all three. An ALL-UNIT enum field is the working control, so the gap is exactly the payload-bearing case.
detail:
Codegen has TWO renderers for the same derived-Display struct and only one of
them is restricted:

  * `emit_struct_debug_display_fn` -- the by-pointer, buffer-append form used
    whenever the struct is NESTED (a collection element, an enum payload,
    another struct's field). It renders each field through
    `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr`, which handles any type that dispatcher
    knows, payload enums included. This is why `f"{[h]}"` works.
  * `build_struct_display_parts` -- the f-string-lowering form used when the
    struct is interpolated DIRECTLY. It classifies each field with
    `display_field_is_leaf`, a hand-maintained name list (the integer widths,
    `f32`/`f64`/`bool`/`char`/`String`, plus all-unit enums via
    `enum_unit_variants`), and returns a hard error for anything else.

So the restriction is a property of the spelling, not of the type -- which is
what makes the difficulty inversion above possible.

`display_field_is_leaf`'s list has needed widening before for exactly this
reason: B-2026-08-19-23 widened three sibling lists to the 128-bit widths and
missed this one, so a `u128` field went on being refused after the feature
otherwise landed. That is the same failure mode as this row: a capability
exists one layer down and the leaf list does not know about it.

LIKELY CHEAP. `P::Expr(field_expr)` -- what the leaf branch emits -- is
precisely the `f"{h.u}"` spelling that already works for a payload enum on
both backends, so admitting enums registered in `enum_layouts` to the leaf
predicate may be the whole fix. Wants checking against the `Secret` redaction
arm above it and against a field whose enum is generic (B-2026-08-19-28 passes
use-site generic args through the nested path; the leaf path has no equivalent).

PRE-EXISTING, and NOT caused by B-2026-08-26-29's override-at-depth work: the
repro above carries no hand-written `impl Display` anywhere. A user impl on the
field type hits the same refusal by the same route, which is how this was
found while bounding that row's codegen half.
fix:
FIXED by 7b5f733. `display_field_is_leaf` now admits any NON-GENERIC enum
registered in `enum_layouts`, so a `#[derive(Display)]` struct with a
payload-bearing, tuple-variant or `String`-payload enum field — and one whose
field type carries a hand-written `impl Display` — renders on both backends
instead of failing the compile.

WHY THE REFUSAL WAS INVERTED, which is the part worth keeping. Codegen has TWO
renderers for the same derived-Display struct and only one was restricted:

  * `emit_struct_debug_display_fn` — the by-pointer, buffer-append form used
    whenever the struct is NESTED (collection element, enum payload, another
    struct's field). It renders each field through
    `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr`, which knows payload enums. Hence
    `f"{[h]}"` worked.
  * `build_struct_display_parts` — the f-string-lowering form used when the
    struct is interpolated DIRECTLY. It classified fields with
    `display_field_is_leaf`, a hand-maintained NAME LIST (integer widths,
    `f32`/`f64`/`bool`/`char`/`String`, plus all-unit enums), and hard-errored
    on anything else.

So the restriction was a property of the SPELLING, not of the type. That is
what produced the difficulty inversion: `f"{[h]}"` (struct nested in a Vec)
rendered, `f"{h.u}"` (the field alone) rendered, and `f"{h}"` — the simplest
of the three — killed the compile. And because the error is raised at emission
for the struct, a file whose only offending line was `f"{h}"` failed even
where the working spellings were the ones actually used.

The fix is small because the capability was already there: the leaf branch
emits `P::Expr(field_expr)`, which IS the `f"{h.u}"` spelling, and that
spelling already rendered these fields identically on both backends. The
predicate was the only thing refusing them.

design.md § Strings already claimed both backends "cover a struct field of enum
type". That was false for a payload-bearing enum, so this makes an existing
spec claim true rather than adding a capability.

NON-GENERIC IS LOAD-BEARING, and the first cut of the fix got this wrong. The
leaf branch synthesizes its field expression with the CONTAINING STRUCT's span,
so nothing downstream can recover the field's own instantiation — the nested
renderer threads use-site generic args explicitly (B-2026-08-19-28) and this
path has no equivalent. Measured on the over-broad version:

  * a generic enum field (`struct H { u: O2[i64] }`) PANICKED the compiler —
    `emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'T' not yet supported` — which is
    strictly worse than the refusal it replaced;
  * an `Option[i64]` field (seeded in `enum_layouts`, so it qualified) stopped
    hitting this function's accurate "field 'u' has a type … not yet
    supported" and fell through to the f-string path's misleading "bind a
    struct literal or call result to a `let` first", advice that does not
    apply to a field access.

Both now stay on the clean error, and `test_generic_and_collection_display_
fields_stay_a_clean_error` pins all three deferred shapes (generic enum,
`Option`, `Vec`) against both regressions — a panic, or the wrong message.

design.md's follow-on sentence named only collection-typed fields. It now names
the generic-enum and `Option[T]` cases as well, and records that a non-generic
enum field does render, so the deferral is described by what actually blocks it
(carrying an instantiation into the direct-interpolation path) rather than by
an out-of-date list.

Tests: 2 in `tests/codegen.rs` — one E2E covering struct-variant,
tuple-variant, `String`-payload, unit-variant and user-`impl Display` enum
fields, and the boundary guard above. Gates: codegen 3281 passed, cli 714,
interpreter 1737, typechecker 2519, memory_sanitizer 1196, fmt and both clippy
legs clean.

NOTE ON THE ORIGINAL ROW: it framed the bug as the payload-bearing enum field
only. Probing during the fix showed `Option[T]`, generic-enum and collection
fields were refused by the same predicate, so the surface was wider than
filed — but the three that remain refused are refused for a DIFFERENT reason
(no instantiation channel), which is why they are deferred here rather than
carried along.

title: `Vec.swap` HAD NO CODEGEN ARM: `karac build` hard-errored "Vec/String method 'swap' is not yet supported in codegen" on a program `karac run` executed correctly. The method was wired through the typechecker, ownership, effectchecker and the interpreter, so it looked implemented everywhere except the one backend that compiles.
detail:
FOUND while implementing B-2026-08-26-21's resolution, which names
`Vec.swap` as the sanctioned replacement for the rejected
`let t = xs[i]; xs[i] = xs[j]; xs[j] = t` spelling. The replacement was
itself a run-vs-build divergence, which is the same failure class -21 is
about.

MEASURED before the fix:
  karac run --interp   built / 21 / D2 / D1   (correct)
  karac build          error: codegen failed: Vec/String method 'swap'
                       is not yet supported in codegen

WHY IT LOOKED IMPLEMENTED. `"swap"` is in `ast.rs`'s mutation-method list,
`"Vec.swap"` is in the effectchecker's in-place-mutator seed set and in
`ownership.rs`, and `src/interpreter/method_call_seq.rs` has a working arm.
Only `src/codegen/vec_method.rs` had no `"swap"` case, so it fell through to
the catch-all error. A grep for the method name finds five hits and suggests
full support; only running it under both backends shows the gap.

FIX. `karac_vec_swap` in the runtime (a `ptr::swap_nonoverlapping` of two
element slots) plus a codegen arm modelled on `reverse`, and the keep-list
entry the JIT runner needs. Neither value is destroyed by a swap — it is a
pure relocation of two live values — so no user `Drop` body runs and no RC
traffic is emitted; that guarantee is what makes the method a sound
replacement for the rejected form, so it is pinned by
`test_e2e_vec_swap_relocates_without_running_drop_bodies` rather than left to
inspection. Verified byte-identical across `karac run --interp`, the default
auto-par build, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

title: `Vec.swap` with an out-of-range index SILENTLY DID NOTHING in the interpreter: `v.swap(0, 99)` on a two-element Vec left the vector untouched and exited 0. Negative indices were swallowed the same way, by an `as usize` cast that wrapped them out of range. Every sibling in the family (`v[i]`, `insert`, `remove`, `swap_remove`) panics.
detail:
FOUND while adding the codegen arm for B-2026-08-26-34, by checking what the
two backends should agree on at the boundary rather than only in the middle.

The arm read `if i < guard.len() && j < guard.len() { guard.swap(i, j) }`
with no `else`, so an out-of-range swap was a silent no-op. Because the
indices are cast `i_val as usize`, a NEGATIVE index wrapped to a huge value
and took the same path — where design.md § Array indexing pins negative
indices as runtime panics ("`-1` as an index is always a bug").

WHY IT MATTERED NOW. Codegen's new arm emits a real bounds check (reusing
`emit_vec_mutation_bounds_check`, the same helper `insert` / `remove` /
`swap_remove` use since B-2026-08-24-15). Leaving the interpreter permissive
would have made the two backends disagree on the same program — a fresh
run-vs-build divergence introduced by the fix for one.

BOTH NOW PANIC with the same message shape and exit 101. Regression cases
extend `vec_mutation_methods_bounds_check_out_of_range_index` rather than

fix:
Landed in three commits.

`ref` in expression position (`let r = ref v[i]`) parses, typechecks, interprets and compiles. v1 scope is deliberately ONE operand shape — an index into a sequence — because that is the only shape both backends alias identically: the interpreter binds `Value::ElemRef` over the container's `Arc`, codegen a pointer into the same buffer. Every other operand is rejected in the typechecker with `E_REF_OPERAND_UNSUPPORTED`, run-fatal, so `karac run` cannot execute what `karac build` refuses; before that guard, `let r = ref make()` printed `3` under the interpreter and failed to compile.

Two codegen gaps were closed behind it.

A borrowed VEC element (0eb4e2f) needed two registrations, and either alone still produced the SAME error text, which is what made it hard to read from the diagnostic. Found by tagging all three sites that emit that string rather than guessing a second time.

A borrowed TENSOR element (fe964f0) is bound by its BLOCK POINTER, not as a ref shim. Tensors use the by-value ref ABI, so a `Vec[Tensor]` slot holds the control-block pointer and a tensor binding's alloca is expected to hold that pointer directly — which is how the existing `ref Tensor` accessor path (`let r = h.view()`) already binds one. Registering `tensor_var_infos` ON TOP OF a `ref_params` shim, the obvious-looking fix, leaves one indirection too many: `tensor_ptr_for_var` loads through the shim via `get_data_ptr` and then loads again, reading the control block's first word as a pointer. It does not fail loudly. It compiles and returns denormal garbage — `test_e2e_autograd_mse_loss` printed `0.000…15956413663` where it expects `10 / 2 / 4`. That attempt was reverted and the mechanism worked out instead. The regression test asserts VALUES (`2 4 8`), because a test checking only that the program builds would have passed on the broken version.

One shape is rejected rather than supported (d676cac): an element of an SoA-laid-out container. Under a `layout` block the element has no contiguous storage — its fields live one buffer per group and `entities[i]` is materialised, not named — so there is no address a borrow can hold. Codegen did not notice, and borrowed the group base: against an AoS baseline of `40 / 500 / 5000 / 3 30 300 3000` it returned `145 / 200 / 2000 / 0 0 0 0`. Now a typecheck error naming both ways out.

Known remaining gap, filed separately: `.clone()` on an index THROUGH a `ref` binding segfaults. Each half works alone.
title: `ref` IN EXPRESSION POSITION IS SPECIFIED BUT UNIMPLEMENTED: design.md shows `let r = ref some_function();` (§ Binding-extension exception) and `let p: ref i32 = ref 42;`, and the parser rejects both with "'ref' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier". This BLOCKS the B-2026-08-26-21 index-move rejection, whose only fix-it for a `Clone`-less element type is the borrow spelling.
detail:
MEASURED. All three documented spellings fail at PARSE, not typecheck:
    let r = ref make();            -> 'ref' is a reserved keyword ...
    let p: ref Item = ref it;      -> same
    let v = ref tp.values[i];      -> same
design.md renders the first two inside fenced `kara` blocks (§
Binding-extension exception), so the spec presents as a working form.

WHY IT BLOCKS -21. That row's resolution rejects `let t = v[i]` for a
non-`Copy` element and offers three fix-its: `ref` borrow, `.clone()`, and
`Vec.swap`. `.clone()` is withheld for types that do not have one (the
B-2026-07-29-31 rule — a confident wrong steer is worse than no suggestion),
and `Tensor` is such a type. Measured blast radius across `runtime/stdlib`:
80 rejected sites in 4 files, of which `autograd` contributes 67, ALL of them
`Vec[Tensor[f32, [?]]]` element reads with no `.clone()` available. Landing
the rejection first would hand those 67 sites a diagnostic they cannot
satisfy.

HOW FAR IT GOT (parked, patch preserved; NOT landed). Parser and typechecker
are written and working — `ref expr` parses as a new `UnaryOp::Ref`, and
`let r = ref b.xs[0]` typechecks as `ref Item` with `karac check` clean.
Deliberately NOT landed, because parse+typecheck alone is WORSE than the
status quo: today the form fails cleanly at parse; half-implemented it would
compile and then die in codegen.

THE REAL COST IS THE INTERPRETER, and it is not a small patch. `Value` has
no reference, place, or slot variant; `mut ref` PARAMETERS are simulated by
WRITE-BACK at call boundaries, a mechanism that cannot express a binding
living for a scope. `Value::Array(Arc<RwLock<Vec<Value>>>)` shares the
vector, but an element read hands back a CLONED `Value`, not an alias into
it. A faithful `ref` therefore needs a new representation (something like
`Value::ElemRef(Arc<RwLock<Vec<Value>>>, usize)`) plus deref handling at
every read site, codegen needs address computation per place form
(`lower_indexed_elem_ptr_vec` covers the index case only), and ownership
needs borrow-liveness enforcement or the two backends diverge the moment a
container mutates during a live borrow.

REJECTED SHORTCUT, recorded so it is not re-proposed: making `ref` a
SNAPSHOT in both backends. They would agree, and for legal programs it is
observationally equivalent (mutating a container during a shared borrow is
already illegal). It is still wrong — design.md sells the borrow at "cost:
none", and the entire value of `ref` for the 67 autograd sites is avoiding a
full-tensor deep copy per read. A `ref` that silently copies is worse than
no `ref`.

PARKED PATCH: `docs/wip/b-2026-08-26-36-ref-bindings.patch` (applies cleanly to
5686fcb). Parser + typechecker only — `ref expr` as a new `UnaryOp::Ref`, the
typing rule (`T` -> `ref T`, idempotent on an existing `ref`, narrowing a
`mut ref`), and the ten match sites the exhaustiveness check flagged. Do NOT
land it alone: parse+typecheck without backends is worse than today's clean
parse error, because the form would compile and then die in codegen.

One trap it already avoids, for whoever picks it up: the new `Token::Ref` arm
must carry a negative lookahead for `|` / `||`. `parse_prefix` already has a
guarded `Token::Ref` arm for the Rule 2½ closure capture-mode prefix
(`ref |x| ...`) FURTHER DOWN the same match, so an unguarded arm placed earlier
silently shadows it and parses the capture mode as a borrow of a closure.

IMPLEMENTED AND LANDED 2026-08-26 — this row's headline is now WRONG in the
useful direction: `ref` in expression position is no longer unimplemented.

  f545357  `ref <sequence>[i]` — parser, typechecker, both backends.
  0eb4e2f  indexing THROUGH a `ref` binding, for a borrowed Vec element.

WHAT v1 SUPPORTS, measured rather than assumed:

    r.field          OK      r.method()       OK      r + x            OK
    r[j]  (Vec elem) OK      r[j] (Tensor)    COMPILE ERROR — see below

The aliasing is the contract and it holds on both backends: the interpreter
binds `Value::ElemRef { arr, idx }` over the container's own `Arc`, codegen
binds a pointer into the same buffer, and a read through the borrow observes a
mutation made while it is live. A snapshot on either side would restore the
divergence B-2026-08-26-21 exists to close, so `E_REF_OPERAND_UNSUPPORTED`
(E0283) rejects every operand shape the two backends cannot alias identically,
in the TYPECHECKER, before either backend sees it.

THE INDEX-THROUGH-BORROW FIX NEEDED TWO REGISTRATIONS, and either alone still
failed with the SAME message, which is why the diagnostic could not be read
straight: the value-based index path claimed the shim (a borrow must never be
synthesised or freed as a temporary), and with that excluded the named-Vec
path still did not fire because it gates on `vec_elem_types`, which the shim
had not registered. Found by TAGGING all three sites that emit "Index operator
applied to non-array type" and re-running — after a first fix that "should
have worked" did not.

DO NOT REGISTER `tensor_var_infos` FOR A BORROWED TENSOR ELEMENT the way
0eb4e2f registers `vec_elem_types`. It was tried and REVERTED: the program
then COMPILES and MISCOMPILES, returning denormal garbage
(`0.000…15956413663`) where `test_e2e_autograd_mse_loss` expects `10 / 2 / 4`.
Cause looks like a double-deref — `tensor_ptr_for_var` calls `get_data_ptr`
and then loads, correct for a normal tensor variable whose alloca holds a
control-block pointer, but for a shim `get_data_ptr` has ALREADY loaded, so
the second load reads the control block's first word as a pointer. A loud
compile error beats a silent wrong number; fix the indirection before
re-attempting.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE 78-SITE STDLIB MIGRATION (see B-2026-08-26-21): it does
NOT land yet. Bisected to its first breaking line — `autograd.kara:398`,
`let g = ref tp.grads[self.idx];`. That line is TEXTUALLY IDENTICAL to
line 389, which passes; the difference is the USE — 389 does `g + 0.0`
(arithmetic, fine) and 398 does `g[i]` (index through a borrowed Tensor).
`protobuf`'s 9 sites are unaffected: they migrate to `.clone()`, not `ref`,
because their values are consumed as owned `String`.

REMAINING WORK: the Tensor indirection above, then re-run the migration. The
`embeddings` sites index borrowed rows too and will follow the same fix.

fix:

A CALL ARGUMENT is a value position exactly as a `let` initializer is, so the index-move rule applies there too. Implemented as a third call site for `reject_index_move_non_copy`, in `check_call_args_with_substitution_full` where an argument meets its parameter type, and it discriminates on the PARAMETER: rejected only when the parameter is BY VALUE. Handing `v[i]` to a `ref T` / `mut ref T` / `Slice[T]` parameter is a borrow, and a borrow is the remedy the rule points at rather than the offence. Measured on this row's own repro: `take(b.xs[0])` rejected, `peek(b.xs[0])` accepted.

BLAST RADIUS was far smaller than this row estimated ("a much larger blast radius than the two pinned forms"): 3 stdlib sites, 1 selfhost, 4 codegen fixtures, 10 auto-par sites, plus a share of the ASAN corpus. Nothing else.

THE MIGRATION SHAPE IS THE INTERESTING HALF, and it is the argument for the rule rather than against it: the right answer is usually that THE CALLEE SHOULD HAVE BORROWED. `proto_atoi` and `proto_pascal_case` only read their `String`, so making them take `ref String` fixed five call sites with two signature changes and no copies at all. A call argument is a value position exactly as a `let` initializer is, so

title: A `StringSlice` BOUND BY A MATCH PATTERN LOST EVERY METHOD BUT `to_string` under `karac build` -- `match head(s) { Some(v) => v.len() }` over an `Option[StringSlice]` ran under `--interp` and failed the compile with "no handler for method 'len' on variable 'v'".
