The SAME view reached through a `let`, a tuple element or a struct field compiled, so the defect was specific to the pattern-binding path. This blocked the one zero-copy tokenizing spelling the language can express today (a cursor/iterator yielding `Option[StringSlice]`), on the backend where avoiding the per-token allocation is the whole point.
detail:
CAUSE. In `src/codegen/pattern_binding.rs` a single `if` did two unrelated
jobs, gated on `String`/`CString`: it inserted `vec_elem_types` -- the side
table METHOD DISPATCH reads to pick the String-shaped arm -- and it set
`bound_vec_elem`, which schedules the end-of-arm `track_vec_var` buffer free.
`StringSlice` was excluded from that `if`, with a comment explaining the
exclusion in terms of the FREE only ("a borrow, `cap == 0`, nothing to free"),
which is correct and remains so. What the comment did not notice is that the
same `if` was also the only thing registering dispatch, so excluding the free
silently excluded the dispatch.

The two are separable, and the let-binding path already treats them that way:
`stmts.rs`'s `surface == "String" || surface == "StringSlice"` arm registers
BOTH tables for a view, arguing the free is `cap > 0`-guarded to a no-op. The
fix registers the dispatch half at the pattern-binding site and deliberately
does NOT set `bound_vec_elem`, so this path keeps its stricter no-free choice.

SAME SHAPE AS B-2026-08-05-8, which fixed exactly this for `String` and left a
comment saying String "was the one payload kind that got the free but not the
dispatch". `StringSlice` is the next one and arrives from the opposite
direction: it gets NEITHER, and only one of those omissions was intended. Worth
recording as a pattern -- a payload kind's free and its dispatch are decided by
one predicate, so any type that legitimately opts out of the free silently opts
out of dispatch too.

WHY THIS WAS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN DEFERRING, and how it was found. It came
out of bounding B-2026-08-26-13 (`String.split` allocates per field). That row
states "there is no spelling of tokenize-this-string-and-read-the-fields in
Kara today that does not allocate per field". That is not quite right, and this
bug is why it looked true: `Vec[StringSlice]` is indeed rejected at typecheck
(design.md pins it as v2 -- "a borrow flowing through a collection"), but a
CURSOR or lazy ITERATOR yielding `Option[StringSlice]` needs no collection of
borrows and typechecks fine. It simply could not be COMPILED, because reading
the view back out of the `Option` is a match binding. Under `--interp` it ran
the whole time.

MEASURED once it compiled -- same workload, 9,600,024 tokens, identical output
from both spellings, container x86-64, best of 3:

    s.split(",")          owned Vec[String]     0.404 s    53.1 MiB peak RSS
    borrowing SplitIter   zero-copy             0.045 s    10.3 MiB peak RSS

9.0x faster and 5.2x smaller. So the language can reach the zero-copy tier
today; what B-2026-08-26-13 is really about is that the stdlib offers no such
API and the user must hand-roll a ~12-line iterator. That row is relocated to
the roadmap on those terms.

TESTS. `test_e2e_match_bound_string_slice_keeps_method_dispatch` in
`tests/codegen.rs` with its byte-identical oracle twin
`a_match_bound_string_slice_keeps_its_methods` in `tests/interpreter.rs` --
both exercise `len` and `slice` on a match-bound view plus a full lazy
`SplitIter`. Plus `asan_match_bound_string_slice_is_not_freed`, which pins the
half deliberately left out: re-conflating dispatch with the free would free the
SOURCE string's buffer once per token, and the fixture tokenizes 20k times so
that is immediate rather than probabilistic.

GATES: codegen 3282, interpreter 1738, cli 716, typechecker 2519,
memory_sanitizer 1196 -- all 0 failed; fmt and both clippy legs clean.
fix: Fixed by d5056cd. `pattern_binding.rs` now registers a match-bound `StringSlice` in `vec_elem_types` for METHOD DISPATCH while deliberately leaving `bound_vec_elem` unset, so no end-of-arm buffer free is scheduled for a borrow. Mirrors the let-binding path's dispatch registration without adopting its (no-op) free.

title: THE `Error return trace` SECTION IS NONDETERMINISTIC ON THE COMPILED BACKENDS: the same AOT binary, same input, same pinned `KARAC_HASH_SEED`, emits a DIFFERENT NUMBER OF FRAMES run to run -- and sometimes omits the section entirely -- while `--interp` emits the same four frames every time. Measured on `examples/json.kara`, 20 consecutive AOT runs at `KARAC_HASH_SEED=7`: 4 runs printed 0 frames, 1 run printed 1, 11 printed 3, 4 printed 4. The interpreter printed 4 frames in 6/6. The program's own stdout (the parsed JSON and the `ERROR:` lines) is byte-identical across all runs -- only the trace varies.
detail:
FOUND while sweeping B-2026-08-26-30 (the entry-hoisted-alloca class), by
diffing every `.kara` file in the repo between a pre-fix and post-fix
compiler under the JIT. `examples/json.kara` differed -- but it also differs
from ITSELF: the pre-fix compiler produced three distinct outputs across six
runs at a pinned seed, so this is not a regression from that work and is
unrelated to it. Filed separately rather than folded in.

NOT MAP-ORDER NOISE, which is the first thing to rule out in this repo.
`Map`/`Set` iteration order is random per process by design, but
`KARAC_HASH_SEED` pins it, and the compiled runtime DOES honor the pin --
verified directly: a five-key `Map[String, i64]` walked under
`KARAC_HASH_SEED=7` printed `epsilon alpha gamma delta beta` on 6/6 AOT runs.
So the seed is doing its job and the program's control flow is deterministic;
the JSON output and error messages confirm it by being byte-identical. Only
the trace section moves.

(Noted in passing, NOT part of this row: at the same pinned seed the
interpreter walked that same map as `alpha beta delta gamma epsilon` -- a
different order from AOT. Iteration order depends on table layout as well as
the hash, and design.md only promises the two backends share the HASH, so
this is probably by design. It is recorded here because it looks alarming
next to the sentence "the two backends agree by construction" and someone
should decide explicitly whether cross-backend order parity is intended.)

WHERE TO LOOK. The compiled trace is a single global `Mutex<ErrorTraceState>`
ring buffer in `runtime/src/lib.rs` (`karac_error_trace_push` /
`karac_error_trace_clear`, printed from an `atexit` handler). Codegen emits a
push at every `?` failure site and a CLEAR at every `?` success site, so what
survives to exit is a function of the interleaving of successes and failures
-- `json.kara` parses several inputs, some of which succeed. Three candidates
worth separating before assuming:

  1. the `atexit` printer racing or running after some state is torn down --
     the file notes TLS destructors were deliberately avoided here for
     exactly that reason, so the ordering hazard was already known;
  2. `if let Ok(mut state) = ERROR_TRACE.lock()` SILENTLY DROPS the frame on
     a poisoned lock, so any panic-while-holding turns every later push into
     a no-op -- that would explain whole-section omissions, though it should
     be sticky rather than intermittent;
  3. a genuinely uninitialized read somewhere in the push path.

WHY IT MATTERS. The trace is a diagnostic surface a user reads to locate a
failure, and design.md pins its format. An error report that silently loses
frames -- or the entire section -- on some runs is worse than one that never
prints it, because nothing distinguishes "no propagation happened" from "the
frames were dropped this time". It also makes any test asserting trace
content flaky by construction, which is how it stayed invisible: the E2E
suite has no test pinning a multi-frame trace on a compiled backend.

REPRO. `karac build examples/json.kara -o /tmp/j && for i in $(seq 1 20); do
KARAC_HASH_SEED=7 /tmp/j 2>&1 | grep -c 'json.kara:'; done | sort | uniq -c`
-- expect a single count, observe a spread. `karac run --interp
examples/json.kara` is the oracle at 4 frames. Reconfirmed on b9b2a9d.
fix:
Fixed by 7c10fdf.

ROOT CAUSE: auto-parallelization, plus a trace buffer that was global where
design.md says it must be per-thread.

design.md § Error return traces specifies the implementation as "a THREAD-LOCAL
fixed-depth ring buffer". The runtime had a single shared
`Mutex<ErrorTraceState>`. That is indistinguishable from the spec on a
sequential program and wrong the moment two `?` chains are live at once,
because codegen emits a PUSH at every `?` failure site and a CLEAR at every `?`
success site: with one buffer, a task that succeeds wipes the frames a
concurrently-running task just pushed.

WHAT MADE IT SURPRISING is that `examples/json.kara` contains no `par`, no
`spawn` and no `TaskGroup` -- `main` is 17 straight-line `roundtrip` calls.
AUTO-PAR still ran its `?` sites across five threads. Instrumenting
push/clear with the thread id showed the same four pushes landing on threads
{1,2,5}, {2,3,5} and {1,5} on consecutive runs of ONE binary. So the row's
three candidate causes -- atexit racing, a poisoned lock, an uninitialized read
-- were all wrong; nothing was corrupted and nothing raced inside the runtime.
The buffer faithfully recorded an interleaving that was itself nondeterministic.

Confirmed by ablation before touching anything: `KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1` pinned the
output to exactly 3 frames on 12/12 runs, single-threaded. With auto-par: 7
distinct traces over 30 runs, 0 to 4 frames. ASLR was ruled out separately
(`setarch -R` still varied), which is what excluded the uninitialized-read
hypothesis.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ROW.

  * "the interpreter emits the same FOUR frames every time" -- it emits THREE,
    the same three the fixed AOT binary emits. The row's counting command,
    `grep -c 'json.kara:'`, also matched the effect NOTE line
    (`examples/json.kara:203:5: mutual recursion group resolved ...`) that the
    interpreter prints and the compiled backend does not. There was never a
    frame-count divergence between the backends.
  * The row's parenthetical about `Map` iteration order differing between
    backends at a pinned seed is unrelated to this row and is untouched here;
    it still deserves its own decision.

FIX, in two parts.

1. PER-THREAD BUFFERS (spec compliance). `ERROR_TRACES` is now a
   `Mutex<Option<HashMap<ThreadId, ErrorTraceState>>>`; push and clear only
   ever touch the current thread's entry, so no chain can be interleaved with
   or cleared by another. A `HashMap` keyed by thread rather than an actual
   `thread_local!` because the printer runs from an `atexit` handler, and the
   runtime already documents (on `CURRENT_FRAME`) why that rules TLS out: TLS
   destructors run during thread shutdown, BEFORE the C runtime's atexit
   handlers, so a TLS read inside `atexit` panics. A plain global map has no
   destructor-ordering hazard and gives the same isolation.

2. AN HONEST NOTE INSTEAD OF A FRAGMENT. Isolation alone does NOT make the
   output deterministic, and measuring showed why: with per-thread buffers the
   spread narrowed from 7 outputs to 2, because whether all of a chain's
   pushes happen to land on the exiting thread still varies. So when the
   program dispatched to the worker pool at all, the printer now emits

       Error return trace: unavailable — the `?` chain was split across
       parallel tasks (cross-task propagation is not yet tracked).
       Rebuild with KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1 for a complete trace.

   This follows the row's own argument: an error report that silently loses
   frames is worse than one that never prints them, "because nothing
   distinguishes 'no propagation happened' from 'the frames were dropped this
   time'". The note distinguishes them.

   The discriminator is a `PAR_DISPATCHED` flag set in `karac_par_run_pooled`,
   NOT "did another thread record frames". That choice is the whole reason the
   result is deterministic: which thread runs a branch is decided by a
   work-helping join and varies, whereas WHETHER the pool was used is a
   property of the call structure (`karac_par_run_auto` picks pooled vs
   sequential on a fork-depth check, not on timing). `seq_par_run`, the
   sequential fallback, deliberately does not set it -- it runs branches on the
   calling thread, so those chains stay intact and must keep printing.

MEASURED AFTER, same binary, same pinned seed:

    auto-par ON     40/40 runs identical (the note)
    KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1   12/12 runs identical (the complete 3-frame trace,
                         byte-identical to `--interp`)

TESTS, in `tests/cli.rs`. `test_error_return_trace_is_deterministic_across_runs`
builds `examples/json.kara` -- the measured repro, and the program known to
reach the pool -- runs it 12 times at a pinned seed and asserts every run's
stdout AND stderr match run 0. It asserts the property the row is about rather
than pinning a particular trace, which is what let the bug hide: the E2E suite
had no test pinning a multi-frame trace on a compiled backend. A/B VERIFIED:
reverted the runtime fix, rebuilt both archives, and the test FAILS ("run 1:
stderr differs from run 0"); restored, it passes.

A first attempt at that test used a hand-written loop and was VACUOUS -- it
neither ended on a failing `?` nor triggered auto-par, so it printed empty
stderr on every run and would have passed against the unfixed compiler. That
is recorded in the test's own comment, because the same trap is waiting for the
next person who writes a trace test.

`test_error_return_trace_is_complete_without_the_pool` is the companion guard:
determinism alone is satisfiable by printing nothing, so it pins that a
sequential chain still yields its COMPLETE trace (2 frames, no note). It passes
both before and after, which is correct -- the sequential path was never the
broken one.

design.md § Error return traces gains the rule as a new bullet next to the
existing "No async interaction yet" deferral, since this IS that deferred case,
made legible rather than silent. When Phase 6 lands and the trace travels with
the error across tasks, the note goes away.

GATES: codegen 3282, cli 719, interpreter 1738, memory_sanitizer 1197,
par_codegen 270 -- all 0 failed; fmt, both native clippy legs, and BOTH wasm
clippy legs clean. The wasm legs earned their keep: the first cut put `HashMap`
on a pool-gated import line, which native clippy cannot see and which broke the
sequential-wasm build.

FIXED by 9d530ad. The row asked for the blast radius to be measured before fixing, and measuring it CORRECTED the row's own diagnosis in two ways.

THE ROW SAID "the associated-function/static path". THAT IS TOO BROAD. User-defined `impl` statics were never affected: `Point.at(1i64)` against a two-parameter `at` already reported `expected 2 argument(s), found 1`, and a genuinely absent `Point.nope()` correctly reported `no associated function 'nope' on type 'Point'`. Instance methods were correct on both sides too (`s.push()` -> `'push' expects 1 argument, found 0`). The defect is specific to the BUILTIN/baked-stdlib static path, which is what makes the fix a local one rather than surgery on the shared catch-all -- and is why the fix must NOT be applied there, since that catch-all serves the user-impl path correctly today.

THE BLAST RADIUS WITHIN THAT PATH IS EVERY BUILTIN STATIC, not just `String`: measured on `String`, `Vec`, `VecDeque`, `Map`, `Set`, `SortedSet`, `SortedMap` -- `Vec.new(1i64)`, `Map.new(1i64)`, `Set.new(1i64)`, `Vec.filled(1i64)`, `VecDeque.with_capacity()` all reported absence for what was purely an arity mistake.

MECHANISM. The builtin statics have no signature the typechecker can consult; each is an ad-hoc arm in `infer_call` guarded on an exact `args.len()` (`segments[1] == "with_capacity" && args.len() == 1`). An arity mismatch matches no arm, falls out of `infer_call` to `infer_expr(callee)` -> `resolve_path_type`, and lands in the catch-all that emits "no associated function". Both the genuine-typo case and the wrong-arity case reach the SAME site, which is exactly why they were indistinguishable -- confirmed by temporarily marking the two candidate emit sites and observing both inputs arrive at `expr_ops.rs`'s.

A SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME MESSAGE, found while fixing the first and not in the filed row at all: a fallible companion was reported under a name the user never wrote. `Vec.try_with_capacity()` said `no associated function 'with_capacity' on type 'Vec'`. `infer_call` resolves a companion by cloning the callee, rewriting `segments[1]` to the BASE name, and RECURSING, so any diagnostic raised inside that recursion has already lost the `try_` prefix. A user reading it is told that a function they did not call does not exist. The arity check therefore runs at the companion site, before the rewrite, and reports the name as spelled; the first attempt put it only at the outer site and still printed the base, which is how the recursion was found.

THE FIX is a diagnostic-only arity table for the builtin statics, consulted at two points in `infer_call`: at the companion site (before the `try_` rewrite) and just before the generic fallthrough to `resolve_path_type`. It never admits a call -- it only decides which MESSAGE a call that has already failed to match every arm receives.

WHY A HAND-MAINTAINED TABLE IS ACCEPTABLE HERE, since that is the obvious objection. Drift is bounded by construction and asymmetric. A MISSING row degrades to the previous behaviour (the catch-all message), so an omission costs nothing that was not already wrong. A WRONG row is the only harmful case -- it would announce an arity for a function that genuinely is not there, turning a correct absence diagnostic into a confident lie -- and `builtin_assoc_fn_arity_table_matches_the_compiler` calls every row at its listed arity and fails if the compiler disagrees. Verified to have teeth: adding a bogus `("String", "bogus_not_real", &[1])` row makes it fail, naming the row. The table was also not transcribed from the arms by hand; it was MEASURED by probing each candidate name across arities 0..=3 against the real typechecker and recording which the compiler accepts.

NOT EVERY BUILTIN STATIC NEEDED A ROW, and the ones that did not are worth naming so nobody adds them redundantly: `Vec.from_fn()` already had its own arity message ("Vec.from_fn expects 2 arguments (n, f), found 0"), and so did `String.from_utf8()` and `Result.Ok()`. `Option.new` was checked and reports absence at arities 0, 1 and 2 alike -- it genuinely does not exist, so its "no associated function" is CORRECT and this change leaves it alone.

THE ABSENCE MESSAGE IS NARROWED, NOT REMOVED. It is load-bearing: it exists (per its own comment, from 2026-05-22) to stop an unknown `Type.method` propagating a permissive sentinel into codegen, where it resurfaces as a misleading "no handler for method 'unwrap' on variable 'x'" and sends the reader chasing a phantom codegen bug. `a_genuinely_absent_associated_function_still_reports_absence` pins that half.

VERIFICATION. Four tests in `tests/typechecker.rs`: the arity-not-absence case across seven builtin shapes, the `try_`-prefix-preserved case, the table-drift guard, and the still-reports-absence guard. 109 suites green under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, so no E2E soft-skips; `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy --all --all-targets -D warnings` clean on both feature legs. Re-verified after rebasing onto the `ref`-bindings feature (B-2026-08-26-36), which landed mid-work and touched the typechecker. The only non-green suite is `gpu_e2e`, whose 60 failures are the optional GPU archive being absent in this container; it soft-skips without the strict flag and is unrelated.

PROVENANCE NOTE: this row was filed from a false positive it caused in the `String`-method-table lint that closed B-2026-08-26-11 -- a zero-arg probe reported `with_capacity` as MISSING, and the probe had to be widened to several arities before the lint worked at all. That arity loop can be simplified now, but it is harmless and documents why it exists, so it was left in place.


UNRELATED RED MAIN FIXED ALONGSIDE (ba3abca, its own commit). While running the verification suite, `origin/main` was found red on the DEFAULT no-feature leg: `code_table_catalogues_every_code_in_a_covered_band` failed with `numbered codes the emitter mints with no CODE_TABLE row: ["E0283"]`. E0283 is `TypeErrorKind::RefOperandUnsupported`, landed by the `ref`-bindings feature (f545357, B-2026-08-26-36) -- minted in the typechecker and numbered in `diag_json.rs`, but with no row in `CODE_TABLE`, which is exactly the gap that test exists to catch. Confirmed pre-existing by checking out `origin/main` detached, with none of these commits present, and observing the identical failure. Fixed in a SEPARATE commit so it can be reverted or superseded independently if the owning session lands its own; a cross-session message would have been preferable but no peer was reachable from this container. Verified after rebase that only one E0283 row exists, so nothing was duplicated.
title: A WRONG-ARITY CALL TO AN ASSOCIATED FUNCTION IS REPORTED AS IF THE FUNCTION DID NOT EXIST: `String.with_capacity()` and `String.with_capacity(1i64, 2i64)` both report `no associated function 'with_capacity' on type 'String'` -- byte-identical to the message for a name that genuinely is not there -- while `String.with_capacity(8i64)` typechecks fine. INSTANCE methods get this right (`s.push()` reports `'push' expects 1 argument, found 0`), so the defect is specific to the associated-function/static path and shows up as an asymmetry between the two call forms.
detail:
FOUND while building the `String`-method-table lint that closed
B-2026-08-26-11: the lint probes each documented name by CALLING it and
telling "no method 'x'" apart from an argument complaint. A single zero-arg
probe reported `with_capacity` as MISSING, which it is not -- the probe had
to be widened to several arities to work at all. So this bug's first
practical cost was a false positive in a tool written to catch exactly the
"documented but absent" class.

MEASURED (all four on the same build):

    s.push()                        -> 'push' expects 1 argument, found 0     CORRECT
    s.push('a', 'b')                -> 'push' expects 1 argument, found 2     CORRECT
    String.with_capacity()          -> no associated function 'with_capacity' WRONG
    String.with_capacity(1i64,2i64) -> no associated function 'with_capacity' WRONG
    s.definitely_not_a_method()     -> no method 'definitely_not_a_method'    (control)

`String.with_capacity(8i64)` typechecks, so the function plainly exists; and
a wrong ARGUMENT TYPE is reported correctly too (`String.with_capacity("x")`
-> `expected 'i64'`). It is specifically arity on the static path that
collapses into a does-not-exist message.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE SEVERITY SUGGESTS. "No associated function 'x'"
is a claim about EXISTENCE, and a user who miscounted arguments on a
constructor is told the constructor is not there. The likely next move is to
go looking for the right NAME -- rename the call, search the docs, file a
"documented method missing" bug -- when the name was right all along and only
the argument count was wrong. That is the same wasted trip B-2026-08-26-11
sent a reader on, arriving from the opposite direction, which is why it is
worth a row rather than a shrug. It also makes the diagnostic actively
misleading for the AI-first wedge: a model reading this error will rewrite
the call site rather than fix the arity.

Kept at LOW because nothing is miscompiled, no program is blocked, and the
correct call always works -- it is a wrong message on an already-failing
compile.

FIX SHAPE. The instance-method path already produces the right message, so
the arity check exists and just is not reached on the associated-function
path: that resolution appears to key the lookup on (name, arity) and report a
miss as absence, rather than resolving on name first and then checking arity.
Resolving by name, then reporting arity separately, would make the two call
forms agree. Worth confirming whether the same collapse affects associated
functions on OTHER types (`Vec.with_capacity`, `Map.new`, user `impl` statics)
before fixing -- the probe here only covered `String`, so the blast radius is
unmeasured and may well be every static in the language.

fix:
FIXED by 34c3f54. A user `impl Drop` on a Map KEY type now runs, exactly once, at every
site that destroys an entry — on both backends, in the same order, at the same
point in the program.

WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT, AND TWO THINGS IT DID NOT.

  * Right: the headline. `emit_map_val_user_drop_bodies_fn` had no key twin,
    keys had only `emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk` (memory, no bodies), and
    design.md § Drop owes the body -- "the compiler invokes `drop` at the end
    of each value's live range", and a key stored in a map is a value whose
    live range ends when the map is destroyed.
  * "NEVER fires" is too strong. It never fires for an INLINE TEMPORARY key,
    which is what the repro uses. For a BOUND-LOCAL key it DID fire, at the
    move site:
        let k = K { s: "kk" };
        m.insert(k, 1);        # dropK kk -- here, before insert returns
  * That fire was ALSO a run-vs-build divergence the repro cannot reach: the
    compiled backend ran the body over a MOVED-FROM slot and printed `dropK `
    with an EMPTY string where `--interp` printed `dropK kk`. Same
    body-over-a-zeroed-source symptom B-2026-08-02-22 fixed for VALUES. Keys
    were one step behind values, not merely missing a walk.

THE STATE WAS A DELIBERATE PAIR, which is why neither half could move alone.
`disarm_moved_value_arg_user_drops` said so in its own doc comment: "Key args
stay on the container-only disarm: no container walk covers keys, so a key
source's own body firing once is today's (leak-free) behavior." Measured both
ways: the walk alone double-fires a bound-local key (once at the move site over
a moved-from slot, once at teardown); the strong disarm alone stops an RAII key
releasing at all.

THE FIX, five parts.

  1. `emit_map_key_user_drop_bodies_fn`. Needed almost no new machinery:
     `at_key_half` ALREADY existed because `Set`/`SortedSet` elements live in
     the key half, and the loop already computes a Map's stride as
     `key_size + val_size`. So the twin is that same configuration under a
     distinct symbol (`__karac_dropkeys_` vs `__karac_dropelems_`) -- distinct
     because a Map whose key AND value both drop needs both walks live at once.
     The shared body takes a `key_half` flag and declines for Set/SortedSet,
     whose one element is already the value walk.
  2. Admission to `is_container_elem_bodies_fn`. THIS was the part that looked
     like a blocker and was not. That predicate is a prefix test on the drop
     FUNCTION's name, and it is the first disjunct of the NLL gate in
     `fire_due_user_drops` -- so a container-bodies walk is NLL-eligible
     regardless of its empty `type_name`. Matching only `__karac_dropelems_`
     left the new key walk on the scope-exit funnel while the value walk fired
     at the binding's live-range end, which the interpreter (NLL for both)
     turned into a timing divergence. Widening the prefix test fixed it.
     Recorded because the reading that stalled this row for a session was that
     empty-`type_name` registrations "stay at scope exit" -- true for
     par-branch registrations, and the container-bodies disjunct is the
     exception that carries both map walks.
  3. The strong disarm on the key expr at the three `Map.insert` sites in
     `maps.rs` (OWNING path only -- a borrowed key is not moved in), and
     `record_ctor_arg_moves(&args[..2])` instead of `&args[1..2]` in the
     interpreter twin.
  4. The interpreter's registration gate qualified on the VALUE arg alone, so
     `Map[K, i64]` with a dropping K never armed and the new walk had nothing
     to resolve -- the gate-before-walk shape of B-2026-08-02-24 and
     B-2026-08-03-1. It now qualifies on EITHER half. Codegen needs no
     equivalent: `register_map_val_bodies` tries both emitters and each
     declines on its own.
  5. The three sibling sites where the VALUE walk was invoked and the key had
     no counterpart, each of which would otherwise have just moved the gap:
     `m.clear()`, a Map held in a struct FIELD, and a Map reached as a
     container ELEMENT -- in both backends.

ORDER WITHIN AN ENTRY: KEY then VALUE. An entry's halves drop in the order
`Map[K, V]` declares them, the rule a struct's fields already follow. It also
falls out of codegen for free -- `fire_due_user_drops` drains a frame in
reverse-introduction order and the value walk is registered first -- so the
interpreter calls `run_map_key_user_drops` before `run_map_val_user_drops` to
agree. design.md fixes no order; what matters is that it is fixed and matched,
because the bodies are observable.

MEASURED: 15 probe shapes byte-identical across `--interp` and `karac build`
-- inline-temp key, bound-local key, key-only map, value-only map, both-drop
map, Set element, `clear`, struct field, nested block, map read after insert,
and the row's own repro -- and the six shapes that exercise the new walks
re-checked across ALL THREE backends (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac
build`), which is the check Group A's confirmation note above shows is the one
that separates a real fix from a part-1-only one (it measured --interp 1 vs
JIT/AOT 2).

TWO THINGS FROM THAT CONFIRMATION NOTE, both of which the landed fix already
satisfies, recorded so the reasons stay attached:

  * "Any future attempt should put a bound-local key in the FIRST test it
    writes." Both regression tests do
    (`a_moved_map_key_runs_its_drop_body_exactly_once` and
    `test_e2e_moved_map_key_drop_body_fires_once`), and they assert the
    String field's CONTENT as well as the count -- the count alone passes a
    body that ran over a moved-from slot.
  * The symbol-name collision (one name for both halves makes `get_function`
    return the value walker for a key request -> every value body twice, no key
    body, a double free for heap-owning V). The half is in the symbol
    (`__karac_dropkeys_` vs `__karac_dropelems_`), and the E2E test's exact
    expectation catches a regression: the collision reads as a repeated
    `dropV` with `dropK` missing. Its doc comment now says so, since the
    naming looks like an arbitrary detail worth "simplifying".

TESTS. Two in `tests/interpreter.rs` and two E2E twins in `tests/codegen.rs`
asserting the same bytes (four destruction sites in one program; and the
moved-local key firing ONCE, with its String field intact -- the content
assertion is what catches a body run over a moved-from slot, which a count
assertion alone would pass). Plus `asan_map_key_user_drop_bodies_fire_once`,
the keys twin of the existing values fixture: a `String`-bearing key over 30
build-and-tear-down rounds, asserting `fired=300` exactly. The COUNT is the
oracle a sanitizer cannot give -- a double fire is not a memory error, so ASAN
passes it silently, which is precisely how the values leg needed its own
count-based fixture.

GATES: codegen 3286, interpreter 1741, memory_sanitizer 1211, cli 719,
typechecker 2526 -- all 0 failed; fmt and both clippy legs clean.

RESIDUAL, filed separately: `m.remove(k)` still runs no key body. The removed
VALUE is moved out into the returned `Some(old)` and its body runs at the
caller, which is correct; the stored KEY is destroyed in place (the runtime
frees its buffer via the `drop_key` flag) and its body is owed. It needs the
body to run BEFORE that buffer free and there is no existing hook at that
point, so it is a more delicate change than the five above -- and, unlike the
teardown gap, it is parity-clean today, so it was not worth rushing into this
commit.
title: A USER `impl Drop` ON A MAP **KEY** TYPE NEVER FIRES, while the same impl on the VALUE type does. B-2026-07-30-11 shipped the Map-VALUES drop-body leg (`emit_map_val_user_drop_bodies_fn`); keys have only `emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk`, which reclaims memory and runs no user bodies. Identical under `--interp` and `build`, so it is a resource-cleanup gap for RAII key types rather than a run-vs-build divergence.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-26-32 (the borrowed key-temporary leak), probing whether a key temp's Drop body should run.

REPRO. Two identical types, one used as the key and one as the value:

    #[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
    struct K { id: i64 }
    struct V { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for K { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dropK {self.id}"); } }
    impl Drop for V { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dropV {self.id}"); } }
    fn main() {
        let mut m: Map[K, V] = Map.new();
        m.insert(K { id: 1 }, V { id: 1 });
        println("inserted");
    }

  --interp AND build both print:
      dropV 1
      inserted
  `dropK` never appears, on either backend.

TWO SEPARATE OBSERVATIONS, and they should not be conflated.

  (a) THE KEY'S BODY NEVER RUNS AT ALL. This is the headline. An RAII key --
      a file handle, a lock guard, a connection -- silently never releases.
      The asymmetry is visible in the codegen surface itself:
      `emit_map_val_user_drop_bodies_fn` (synth_drop.rs) has no key twin, and
      `emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk` (runtime.rs) is a MEMORY walk only. So this
      looks like a known-shaped omission from B-2026-07-30-11's values leg
      rather than a deliberate semantic choice, and design.md settles it:
      SS Drop, "The compiler invokes `drop` at the end of each value's live
      range." A key stored in a map is a value whose live range ends when the
      entry (or the map) is destroyed, so its body is owed. The fix is the keys
      twin of the values walk. NOTE that the Map method table's `clear` says
      only "Removes all entries" where PriorityQueue's says "Drops every
      element"; the general rule carries it, but that table would be clearer if
      it said so too.

  (b) THE VALUE'S BODY RUNS AT INSERT TIME, not at map teardown -- `dropV 1`
      prints BEFORE `inserted`. That is the moved-from SOURCE temporary being
      dropped after its buffer moved into the map, and the map's own copy then
      never runs a body at teardown. Whether that is correct depends on the
      same design.md question as (a); `asan_map_value_user_drop_bodies_fire_once`
      pins that it fires exactly ONCE, which is the property that test was
      written to protect, and this observation does not contradict it. Do not
      'fix' (b) by suppressing the source drop without first answering (a),
      or an RAII value stops releasing too.

NOT A PARITY BREAK. Both backends agree exactly, which is why this is filed as
missing-feature rather than run-vs-build. It is also why it is invisible to the
A/B kata rule: no output differs between surfaces.

NOT A MEMORY LEAK. The key's memory IS reclaimed (`emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk`
does that, and B-2026-08-26-32's ASAN fixtures are clean). What is lost is the
user-visible SIDE EFFECT of the drop body, which no sanitizer can see -- so a
test for this has to assert on stdout, not on LSan.

CROSS-REF: B-2026-08-26-32 (the sibling key-temporary leak, fixed),
B-2026-07-30-11 (the values leg this is the missing twin of),
tests/memory_sanitizer.rs `asan_map_value_user_drop_bodies_fire_once`.

RE-VERIFIED 2026-08-26 on a tree rebased past 19 sibling commits (including 59d6568 'honor a user impl Display at every depth' and 4d75c59 Vec.swap, with the runtime archives rebuilt for the new karac_vec_swap symbol): the repro is unchanged, dropV fires and dropK does not, on both backends.

FILED UNDER -41, NOT -33. This row was drafted as B-2026-08-26-33; while its parent fix was being verified, another session filed AND closed a different B-2026-08-26-33 (3636fcd files it, 2cc9eb2 closes it). That is the id-allocation race CLAUDE.md documents -- ids are computed from the highest in the file, so two sessions drafting in the same window pick the same number. Recomputed immediately before the write, per the same rule.

── INVESTIGATION 2026-08-26 (Group C). A working two-part fix exists and is
   NOT landed, because it would trade this row's parity-clean gap for a
   run-vs-build TIMING divergence. Patch preserved at
   `docs/wip/b-2026-08-26-41-map-key-drop-bodies.patch`; apply with
   `git apply`. What follows is what it does, what it fixes, and the one
   thing that blocks it.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ROW'S OBSERVATIONS.

  * "A user `impl Drop` on a map KEY type NEVER fires" is too strong. It never
    fires for an INLINE TEMPORARY key, which is what the repro uses. For a
    BOUND-LOCAL key it DOES fire — at the move site, before the insert
    returns:

        let k = K { s: "kk" };
        m.insert(k, 1);          # --interp: dropK kk   (here, at the move)
        println("--after-insert--");

  * That bound-local fire is ALSO a run-vs-build divergence, which the row
    did not spot because its repro cannot reach it. The compiled backend runs
    the body over a MOVED-FROM slot and prints `dropK ` with an EMPTY string
    where `--interp` prints `dropK kk`. That is the same
    body-over-a-zeroed-source symptom B-2026-08-02-22 fixed for VALUES; keys
    are exactly one step behind.

THE CURRENT STATE IS A DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED PAIR, not an oversight in two
places. `disarm_moved_value_arg_user_drops` says so in its own doc comment:
"Key args stay on the container-only disarm: no container walk covers keys, so
a key source's own body firing once is today's (leak-free) behavior." So the
weak disarm and the missing walk hold each other up, and NEITHER can move
alone: the walk alone double-fires a bound-local key (measured), and the
strong disarm alone stops an RAII key releasing at all.

THE FIX, both halves together.

  1. `emit_map_key_user_drop_bodies_fn` — the keys twin. It needed almost no
     new machinery: `emit_map_val_user_drop_bodies_fn` ALREADY walks the key
     half, because that is how `Set`/`SortedSet` elements are handled
     (`at_key_half`), and the loop already computes the Map stride as
     `key_size + val_size`. So the twin is that same configuration with a
     distinct symbol name; the shared body takes a `key_half` flag and
     declines for Set/SortedSet (whose one element is already the value walk).
  2. The strong disarm on the key expr at the three `Map.insert` sites in
     `maps.rs` (on the OWNING path only — a borrowed key is not moved in), and
     `record_ctor_arg_moves(&args[..2])` instead of `&args[1..2]` in the
     interpreter twin.
  3. The interpreter's registration gate qualified on the VALUE arg alone, so
     `Map[K, i64]` with a dropping K never armed and the new walk had nothing
     to resolve — the gate-before-walk shape of B-2026-08-02-24. It now
     qualifies on either half. Codegen needs no equivalent: its
     `register_map_val_bodies` tries both emitters and each declines on its own.

MEASURED WITH THE PATCH APPLIED — 7 of 9 probe shapes agree exactly across
backends, including every shape the row names:

    inline-temp key      --interp / build   dropK fires once, at teardown
    bound-local key      --interp / build   dropK fires ONCE (double gone),
                                            correct field data on both
    Map value            unchanged
    Set element          unchanged
    Map[K,V] both drop   both backends: dropV then dropK

WHAT BLOCKS IT. The remaining two shapes differ in WHEN, not whether: with the
patch, codegen fires the key walk at SCOPE EXIT while the interpreter fires it
at the binding's LAST USE. Both run the body exactly once. It shows up only
when a map's last use precedes its scope end:

    { let mut m: Map[K, i64] = Map.new();
      let k = K { id: 7 };
      m.insert(k, 1);
      println("--in-scope--"); }        # interp: dropK 7 BEFORE --in-scope--
                                        # build:  dropK 7 AFTER  --in-scope--

The cause is understood and is NOT incidental. `fire_due_user_drops`
(runtime.rs) implements design.md's NLL placement — "destructors fire at each
binding's live-range end, not lexical scope end" — and its doc comment states
the gate: it is "gated to non-shared STRUCT user-drops", because their let-path
registration "is mutually exclusive with every other cleanup action", and
registrations with an EMPTY `type_name` "stay at scope exit — a conservative
residual, never a double-fire". Both map walks register with an empty
`type_name`, so both are scope-exit by construction. The VALUE walk looks
early only because in those programs the early body is the moved-from LOCAL's
own NLL drop, not the walk.

So making the key walk NLL-placed means giving a map-handle registration a
non-empty `type_name` and thereby opting it into a channel whose stated
precondition — mutual exclusivity with every other cleanup action — a map
handle does NOT satisfy (it also carries `FreeMapHandle`). That is a
double-fire / use-after-free risk on the map's memory, so it was not attempted
blind. THAT is the piece of design work this row now needs, and it is a
question about the NLL channel's gate, not about keys.

ALSO FOUND, unfixed, and part of the same twin-shaped omission — each is a
site where the VALUE walk is invoked and the key walk has no counterpart:

    maps.rs `m.clear()`            runs value bodies, no key bodies
    synth_drop.rs (Map as a struct FIELD)      value bodies only
    synth_drop.rs (Map as a container ELEMENT) value bodies only

A complete fix should sweep all three alongside the binding-death path, or the
gap simply moves.

NOT ATTEMPTED: observation (b) in the original detail (a value's body running
at insert time). With the patch, `Map[K,V]` teardown fires `dropV` then
`dropK`, and the ordering is arbitrary-but-fixed; design.md constrains neither.


── INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION 2026-08-27 (Group A). Part 1 alone was built a
   second time, from the row's own diagnosis and without reference to the
   patch above, and it hit exactly the blocker documented here. Recording it
   because the trap is evidently easy to walk into: the keys twin looks
   self-contained, the inline-temporary repro the row leads with passes, and
   nothing fails until a BOUND-LOCAL key is tried.

   Measured with part 1 only (no strong disarm, no interpreter gate change),
   `let k = K { id: 7 }; m.insert(k, 1);`:

       --interp   dropK x1
       JIT        dropK x2
       AOT        dropK x2

   Two things worth adding to the note above. First, part-1-only is not merely
   a double fire, it is also a RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE (1 vs 2) — so landing it
   would trade this row's parity-clean gap for a parity break immediately, not
   only at the NLL-timing stage. Second, the shape is invisible to an
   inline-temporary test suite: a three-backend regression test over
   `m.insert(K { id: j }, V { id: j })` passes at dropK 3 / dropV 3 with the
   defect present. Any future attempt should put a bound-local key in the
   FIRST test it writes.

   Also independently confirmed while measuring: giving the key and value
   walkers one LLVM symbol name (both halves mangle the same `map_te`) makes
   `get_function` return the value walker for a key request, running every
   VALUE body twice — dropV x6, dropK x0. The half has to be in the symbol
   name. That is a double free for a heap-owning V, and it is silent unless a
   Set control is measured alongside.

fix:
FIXED by 0dffbc0. An impl's dispatch IDENTITY now carries the implemented
trait's own arguments, so two `impl From[X] for T` are two names.

WHERE THE FIX WENT, and why it is not a new mechanism. `src/impl_dispatch.rs`
already existed for this exact failure on a DIFFERENT axis (B-2026-08-13-8: two
impls for two instantiations of one target, same erased `Head.method`, same
interpreter-keeps-LAST / codegen-keeps-FIRST split). This row is that module's
axis with the arguments moved from the target to the trait, so the repair
widens the identity it computes rather than adding a second scheme:

    render_impl_identity(imp) = render_impl_target(target)
                                + "@" + trait-with-args, when the trait has any

`AppError@From[ParseError].from` and `AppError@From[DbError].from`. The `@` is
chosen so the segment stays dot-free — dispatch keys are split on the LAST `.`
to recover the method, which the module header calls out.

The module had explicitly reasoned that two impls rendering the same target are
a COHERENCE question and left them alone. That holds for an argument-less trait
(`Ord` + `Display` on one type), and does not for a parameterized one:
`From[A]` and `From[B]` are distinct trait instances the language supports
together, and `find_from_impl` already told them apart by matching the source
type against `from`'s first parameter. Nothing was ambiguous except the name.

NEITHER BACKEND NEEDED A CHANGE. Both already register through
`impl_dispatch_segment` (the interpreter in `register_impl_methods`, codegen at
`src/codegen.rs`'s two `dispatch_head` sites), so both picked the new names up
for free. What changed instead is what the CALL SITES are told: the conversion
side-tables (`question_conversions`, `into_conversions`, `try_into_conversions`)
now record the RESOLVED impl's dispatch segment rather than the bare target
name, via `TypeChecker::resolved_impl_dispatch_segment`. That is the structural
half of the fix — the choice the typechecker already made is now the choice both
backends execute, so they cannot re-derive different answers from a shared name.

THE DIRECT-CALL SPELLING NEEDED ITS OWN REPAIR (symptom 1). `resolve_path_type`
returns the FIRST impl whose target matches and that declares the member, with
no argument context at all — its own comment says so. That made the second impl
unreachable: `AppError.from(db_err)` was rejected as "expected 'ParseError',
found 'DbError'", naming a type the author never wrote. The METHOD-call spelling
already resolved correctly by argument type
(`try_identifier_receiver_method`'s `from` arm), but a CAPITALIZED receiver
parses as a two-segment PATH call and never reaches it — so the two spellings of
one call disagreed. `infer_multi_impl_conversion_call` gives the path spelling
the same argument-directed lookup and records the winner in a new
`assoc_conversion_dispatch` table, which lowering applies to the path head. A
genuinely absent impl now reports which source types DO convert, instead of
presenting one arbitrary impl's parameter as the only option.

CONSERVATIVE WHERE IT CANNOT BE EXACT. If a CONST argument appears in the
trait's arguments there is no faithful spelling to name the impls apart with, so
the identity DECLINES and the group is refused through the existing
`E_IMPL_TARGET_NOT_DISTINGUISHABLE` rather than silently collapsed. This was
found while fixing the main case and is not hypothetical: `impl
From[Array[i64, 3]] for T` alongside `impl From[Array[i64, 5]] for T` converted
an `Array[i64, 3]` value through the `[i64, 5]` impl, with `karac check` silent.
The `TraitAxis` enum exists to keep "the trait has no arguments" distinct from
"its arguments cannot be rendered" — conflating those two collapses the second
back onto the bare target, which restores the original bug in a corner behind a
name that looks disambiguated. The diagnostic's wording was widened to say the
const may sit in the target OR in the trait's arguments, since either half can
now be the unrenderable one.

ADDITIVE. A qualified name is minted only for a group that genuinely collides; a
lone `impl From[X] for T` is not a group and keeps the symbol it owns today; and
the baked stdlib defines NO `From` impls at all (its numeric conversions are
compiler builtins), so nothing outside an already-broken program moves. Verified
directly rather than assumed — an inherent `fn from` sitting alongside a
`From` impl also still works, because the bare-head member of a qualified group
keeps its head name, so the inherent one holds `T.from` and the trait impl moves.

TESTS. Five integration tests plus five unit tests, all verified to FAIL with
the fix reverted:

  * `two_from_impls_dispatch_by_source_type` (interpreter) and
    `test_e2e_two_from_impls_dispatch_by_source_type` (codegen) run `?`,
    `.into()` and a direct `AppError.from(x)` in ONE fixture, in BOTH impl
    ORDERS. The order parameter is the point: the two backends were wrong in
    OPPOSITE directions, so any single-order fixture passes on one backend by
    luck and proves nothing. The two error payloads are deliberately different
    shapes (`String` vs `i64`), which is what makes a wrong dispatch a type
    confusion rather than merely a wrong answer.
  * `a_direct_from_call_resolves_by_argument_across_two_impls` and its
    `try_from` twin (typechecker) pin symptom 1 in both conversion traits.
  * `a_from_call_with_no_matching_impl_names_the_types_that_do_convert` is the
    half that keeps the widening from becoming a hole — resolution considering
    every impl must not make it accept anything.
  * `conversion_impls_that_cannot_be_named_apart_are_refused` pins the const-arg
    corner as a REFUSAL, one error per member.

Full `--features llvm` suite green under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`
(codegen 3288, cli 719, interpreter 1743, typechecker 2530, lib 1374); both
clippy legs and `cargo fmt --check` clean.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS. The row said a real fix "needs the
impl's source type in the registered NAME ... applied consistently across
lowering, the interpreter's function environment, codegen's module symbols, and
the typechecker's direct-call resolution". The name change was right; the list
was too long. Because both backends already funnel their registration through
one shared renderer, neither the interpreter's env nor codegen's symbols needed
touching — the module was built so that widening the identity reaches every
phase at once. The actual work was the two the row did not name: teaching the
side-tables to carry the RESOLVED impl instead of the target, and giving the
path spelling of a direct call the argument-directed lookup the method spelling
already had.
title: TWO `impl From[X] for T` FOR THE SAME TARGET SILENTLY RUN THE WRONG ONE: `?` and `.into()` resolve the conversion by target name only (`T.from`), so selection falls to impl ORDER -- interpreter takes the last, codegen the first, and the two backends disagree on the same program. Mismatched payloads give an interpreter `unreachable!` or a silent AOT type confusion that prints a raw heap pointer. This is the shape design.md's canonical `?` example teaches
detail:
When a target error type has MORE THAN ONE `impl From[X] for T`, every phase
that resolves the conversion keys on the TARGET name alone (`"{target}.from"`)
and loses the source type. The typechecker's own lookup is correct --
`env.find_from_impl(source, target, args)` matches the `from` method's first
parameter against `source`, and its doc comment says so explicitly -- but the
selection it performs is then DISCARDED: `question_conversions` records only
`SpanKey -> target_name` (a `FxHashMap<SpanKey, String>`, src/typechecker.rs),
so both backends re-derive the callee by name and pick whichever impl their
own table happens to hold.

They do not agree on which one that is. MEASURED, same program, only the
ORDER of the two impl blocks swapped:

    impl order          interpreter picks     AOT/JIT codegen picks
    (Parse, Db)         From[DbError]         From[ParseError]
    (Db, Parse)         From[ParseError]      From[DbError]

The interpreter takes the LAST registered (`Interpreter::call_function` ->
`self.env.get("AppError.from")`, a flat name-keyed environment, last write
wins); codegen takes the FIRST (`self.module.get_function("AppError.from")`,
src/codegen/exprs.rs:2104 -- LLVM renames the second definition, so the
unsuffixed name resolves to the first). Neither consults the source type.
Both are wrong half the time, and they are wrong in opposite directions, so
`karac run` and `karac build` disagree about the same source.

THREE SYMPTOMS, in increasing order of severity.

(1) FALSE-POSITIVE TYPE ERROR on a direct call. With both impls in scope,

        let a = AppError.from(parse_err);   // OK
        let b = AppError.from(db_err);      // error[typecheck]: expected 'ParseError', found 'DbError'

    -- the second is rejected although `impl From[DbError] for AppError` is
    right there. `T.from` resolves to a single signature.

(2) SILENT WRONG ANSWER when the payloads are structurally compatible. Two
    error structs that are both `{code: i64}` convert without complaint into
    the WRONG `AppError` variant, running the wrong impl's body (including its
    effects -- a logging `From` silently does not log, or logs the wrong
    error).

(3) TYPE CONFUSION when they are not. `struct ParseError { tag: String }`
    fed to `fn from(e: DbError)` where `DbError` is `{a: i64, b: i64, c: i64}`:

      * interpreter: internal panic, not a diagnostic --
        `unreachable!` at src/interpreter.rs:2375, "field 'a' not found on
        struct 'ParseError' ... either an interpreter codepath constructed the
        struct without this field or the typechecker accepted access to a
        missing field".
      * AOT: no error at all. The `String`'s three words are reinterpreted as
        the three `i64` fields and printed --
        `CONVERTED DbError a=94475988951040 b=4 c=0`, where `a` is the raw heap
        POINTER (an ASLR disclosure), `b` the length. Exit status 0.

`.into()` IS AFFECTED THE SAME WAY, through the blanket `Into` impl: with the
two impls above, `fn h1(e: ParseError) -> AppError { e.into() }` and
`fn h2(e: DbError) -> AppError { e.into() }` BOTH dispatch to the same impl --
`FROM DbError` twice on the interpreter, `FROM ParseError` twice on AOT. So the
defect is not specific to `?`; it is in how a `From` impl is named and looked
up, and `?` is merely its most-documented user.

`TryFrom` CARRIES IT TOO -- measured, not inferred. `find_tryfrom_impl` has the
identical shape (matching `try_from`'s first parameter, then discarding the
choice), and with `impl TryFrom[A] for T` and `impl TryFrom[B] for T` both in
scope, `T.try_from(b)` is rejected with `expected 'A', found 'B'` -- symptom (1)
again. So the fix has to cover both conversion traits, not just `From`.

WHY HIGH: this is a documented core feature, and the shape that breaks it is
the shape design.md TEACHES. § Conversion Traits' canonical `?` example names
exactly two impls for one target in its own two comment lines ("requires
From[ParseError] for AppError" / "requires From[DbError] for AppError"), which
is the two-impl configuration above. A single-impl program is accidentally
correct, which is why this survived: the bug appears exactly when a reader
follows the spec's own example far enough to add the second error type.

WHY THE FIX IS NOT SMALL. The lookup that is already correct cannot simply be
threaded through, because the two impls are not DISTINGUISHABLE at the point
of call: both register a function literally named `AppError.from`, in a flat
name-keyed environment (interpreter) and a single LLVM module (codegen). A
real fix needs the impl's source type in the registered NAME -- a mangling
change -- applied consistently across lowering, the interpreter's function
environment, codegen's module symbols, and the typechecker's direct-call
resolution for `T.from(x)` (symptom 1). Carrying the source type in
`question_conversions` is necessary but not sufficient on its own.

REPRODUCTION: the minimal program is the two-impl example above; the type-
confusion variant differs only in giving the two error structs different
field shapes. Both are order-sensitive, so a repro must pin the impl order to
state which backend it is exercising.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-26-4 (design.md's `?` example named
`parse_i64`/`ParseError`, neither of which existed). Rewriting that example
over APIs that DO exist meant actually running it, and the corrected example
-- being the spec's own two-error-type shape -- ran the wrong conversion. The
doc repair and its regression test landed separately; this row is the
implementation defect underneath, and is why that test asserts the example
TYPECHECKS rather than that it produces the right answer.

title: `Map.remove(k)` DESTROYS AN ENTRY'S KEY IN PLACE AND RUNS NO `Drop` BODY FOR IT. B-2026-08-26-41 gave map keys their drop-bodies walk and wired it into every site that destroys an entry -- binding death, `clear()`, a map in a struct field, a map as a container element -- but `remove` was left out deliberately, as the one site whose fix is not the same shape. Identical on both backends, so it is a resource-cleanup gap rather than a parity break.
detail:
`Map.remove(k)` DESTROYS AN ENTRY'S KEY IN PLACE AND RUNS NO `Drop` BODY FOR
IT. B-2026-08-26-41 gave map keys their drop-bodies walk and wired it into
every site that destroys an entry -- binding death, `clear()`, a map in a
struct field, a map as a container element -- but `remove` was left out
deliberately, as the one site whose fix is not the same shape. This is that
remainder.

REPRO (identical on both backends, so it is a resource-cleanup gap, not a
parity break -- which is why it was not rushed into -41's commit):

    #[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
    struct K { s: String }
    struct V { s: String }
    impl Drop for K { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dropK {self.s}"); } }
    impl Drop for V { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dropV {self.s}"); } }
    fn main() {
        let mut m: Map[K, V] = Map.new();
        m.insert(K { s: "kk" }, V { s: "vv" });
        println("--before-remove--");
        m.remove(K { s: "kk" });
        println("--after-remove--");
        println(f"len={m.len()}");
    }

    --interp AND build:
        --before-remove--
        dropV vv          <- correct: see below
        --after-remove--
        len=0

    `dropK kk` never appears on either backend.

WHY THE VALUE IS ALREADY RIGHT AND THE KEY IS NOT. The two halves leave a
`remove` by different routes. The VALUE is MOVED OUT into the returned
`Some(old)`, so the map stops owning it and its body runs wherever that
`Option` dies -- here, immediately, because the result is discarded. That is
correct and must not be touched. The KEY is destroyed IN PLACE: the bucket is
tombstoned and the runtime frees the key's heap buffer via `karac_map_remove`'s
`drop_key` flag (set from `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct(key_ty)`). Memory is
reclaimed; the user body is owed and never runs.

WHY IT IS NOT A COPY OF -41's FIX. The four sites -41 covered all destroy
every entry at once, so each could simply call the whole-table walk
(`emit_map_key_user_drop_bodies_fn`) before the memory work. `remove` destroys
ONE entry, and the body has to run on THAT key while its fields are still
live -- i.e. after the bucket is located and before `drop_key` frees the
buffer. There is no hook at that point today: the location and the free both
happen inside the runtime's `karac_map_remove`, and codegen never sees the
bucket. Plausible shapes, none obviously best:

  (a) have codegen look the key up first (`karac_map_get`-style probe into a
      key-sized scratch), run the body on the copy, then call remove -- the
      pattern the SORTED walk in `emit_map_val_user_drop_bodies_fn` already
      uses, and body-only, so running it on a copy is exactly as observable;
  (b) pass a per-key body fn pointer into `karac_map_remove` alongside
      `drop_key`, so the runtime invokes it between locating the bucket and
      freeing;
  (c) return the old KEY as well as the old value, making the caller the owner
      the way the value already is -- a public API change to `remove`, so the
      largest of the three and one design.md would have to speak to.

SECOND, SMALLER CASE, same site: the LOOKUP key argument. `m.remove(K { s:
"kk" })` builds a temporary purely to hash and compare; codegen frees it via
`free_fresh_owned_struct_key_arg` and runs no body. Whether a lookup temporary
OWES a body at all is a real question -- it is a value whose live range ends at
the call, so design.md § Drop says yes -- but it is a different question from
the stored key's, and answering one does not answer the other. `contains_key`
and `get` take the same temporary and have the same question.

SEVERITY medium, matching its parent: nothing leaks (memory is reclaimed on
both paths), nothing diverges between backends, and the workaround is to hold
the key elsewhere. What is lost is an RAII key's release on the one operation a
program uses to retire a single entry, which is exactly the shape -41 was filed
about.
fix:
FIXED by eca034b, across all four containers.

WHY IT NEEDED A DIFFERENT SHAPE FROM B-2026-08-26-41, which is the whole reason
it was split off. The four sites that row covered all destroy every entry at
once, so each could call the whole-table walk before doing its memory work.
`remove` destroys ONE entry, and the body has to run on THAT key while its
fields are still readable: after the bucket is located, before the buffer is
freed. Codegen never sees the bucket -- `lookup` and `free_stored_key` both
happen inside the runtime -- so there is no point in the emitted code where the
body could go.

The body therefore travels INTO the runtime as a function pointer, which is not
a new idea here: `karac_map_free_with_val_drop_fn` already takes an
`Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(*mut c_void)>` and calls it on a blob in place.
`karac_map_remove_old_with_key_drop_fn` is the same shape for the key half,
invoking the callee between `lookup` and `free_stored_key`.

`emit_map_key_one_drop_body_fn` emits that callee: the same two calls the table
walk makes per element -- the type's own `<K>.drop` and its
`emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn` field bodies -- applied to a single key blob.
Body-only, so the memory stays the runtime's to release through `drop_key`. It
returns `None` when the key type runs no body at all, and that `None` is the
signal to keep calling the plain `karac_map_remove_old` with no pointer, so
nothing changes for the overwhelming majority of maps.

A SEPARATE SYMBOL, not a fifth parameter on `karac_map_remove_old`. Widening a
signature keeps the name, so an archive built before the change still LINKS and
is handed one argument too few -- silent garbage, and exactly the failure mode
CLAUDE.md § "A STALE archive is not a missing archive" exists to make loud. A
new name turns that same staleness into an undefined-reference the E2E harness
already reports with a rebuild recipe. Both new symbols were added to
`__preserve_no_mangle_symbols`, without which the JIT fails with "Symbols not
found" while AOT links fine (the B-2026-07-12-22 class).

SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN THE ROW STATED. The row was written about `Map.remove`.
Measured, all four containers were affected and all four are fixed:

    Map.remove          dropV only  ->  dropK then dropV
    SortedMap.remove    dropV only  ->  dropK then dropV
    Set.remove          NOTHING     ->  the element's body
    SortedSet.remove    NOTHING     ->  the element's body

The Set pair ran NO body at all because a Set's element IS the key half -- the
same reason `Set` shares the key-side walk. Both lower to the same `remove_old`
entry point (a Set is `Map[T, ()]` removed through a dummy out slot), so one
runtime variant serves all four.

Interpreter side: `MapData::remove` already returned the stored key and the
call site discarded it (`Some((_, v))`). `SetData` gained the symmetric
`remove_entry`; `SortedMap` and `SortedSet` moved from `remove` to
`remove_entry` for the same reason -- `BTreeMap::remove` drops the key on the
floor.

KEY BEFORE VALUE IS A CONSEQUENCE HERE, not an imposed order: the key dies at
the call and the value moves out into the returned `Some(old)`, dying wherever
that lands. It happens to match the order B-2026-08-26-41 had to choose
deliberately.

VERIFIED on all three backends (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac build`)
across the four containers plus the eight shapes B-2026-08-26-41 established.

A SEPARATE LEAK FOUND WHILE BUILDING THE ASAN FIXTURE, filed as its own row.
The obvious fixture -- a `String`-bearing struct key -- leaks that String on
EVERY remove, and it is nothing to do with drop bodies: `drop_key` is
`llvm_ty_is_vec_struct(key_ty)`, which is FALSE for a struct, so the runtime
frees a bare `String`/`Vec` key and never a struct key's inner buffers.
Measured 4490 bytes over 200 removals, IDENTICAL with the key's `impl Drop`
deleted, and a bare `Map[String, V]` doing the same 200 removals is clean. The
landed fixture uses a scalar-field key and says why in place, because a
heap-field key there would assert someone else's bug and mask this row's.

TESTS: one in `tests/interpreter.rs` and its byte-identical E2E twin in
`tests/codegen.rs`, both covering all four containers in one program, plus
`asan_remove_key_drop_body_runs_before_the_free` asserting `fired=400` exactly
over 200 insert/remove pairs -- the count is the oracle a sanitizer cannot
give, since a double body is not a memory error.

GATES: codegen 3287, interpreter 1742, memory_sanitizer 1212, cli 719 -- all 0
failed; fmt, both native clippy legs, and both wasm clippy legs clean.

STILL OPEN at this site, unchanged and parity-clean: the LOOKUP key argument.
`m.remove(K { .. })` builds a temporary purely to hash and compare, and no body
runs for it on either backend. Whether a lookup temporary owes a body is a real
question -- design.md § Drop says a value's body runs at the end of its live
range, which ends at the call -- but it is a different question from the stored
key's, and `contains_key` / `get` take the same temporary and raise it
identically. Deliberately not answered here.

title: `Map.remove` LEAKS A STRUCT KEY'S HEAP FIELDS -- one allocation per removal. The runtime's `drop_key` flag is `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct(key_ty)`, true for a BARE `String`/`Vec` key and FALSE for a STRUCT key, so `Map[String, V]` frees the stored key on remove and `Map[K, V]` where `K { s: String }` never frees `s`. Nothing to do with `Drop` bodies: measured identically with the key's `impl Drop` deleted.
detail:
FOUND while building the ASAN fixture for B-2026-08-27-2 (the key/element
`Drop` body on remove). The obvious fixture for that row is a `String`-bearing
struct key; it leaked, and the leak turned out to be someone else's.

RULED OUT, in this order, before filing:

  * Not the new key-body path. Deleting `impl Drop for K` entirely -- so the
    body machinery is never engaged and codegen takes the plain
    `karac_map_remove_old` -- leaks the SAME 4490 bytes in the SAME 200
    allocations.
  * Not the lookup TEMPORARY. Binding the probe key to a local
    (`let probe = K { .. }; m.remove(probe);`) leaks identically, so this is
    not the B-2026-08-26-32 shape.
  * Not remove-in-general. A bare `Map[String, V]` over the same 200
    insert/remove pairs is clean.

CAUSE. `karac_map_remove_old`'s `drop_key` parameter is codegen-set from
`llvm_ty_is_vec_struct(key_ty)` -- "the key IS a heap `{ptr,len,cap}`". That is
true for `Map[String, V]` / `Map[Vec[T], V]` and FALSE for a struct key, even
one whose fields own heap. The runtime then frees the stored key's buffer only
in the bare case; a struct key's inner buffers are never walked, and the
tombstone orphans them. The comment on `karac_map_remove_old` states the
contract accurately ("nonzero = key is a heap `{ptr,len,cap}` Vec/String") --
the flag is doing what it says. What is missing is a path for the OTHER key
shape.

WHY THE MAP'S OWN TEARDOWN DOES NOT COVER IT: teardown walks OCCUPIED slots,
and `remove` has already vacated this one. That is the same reasoning the
existing comment gives for why `drop_key` exists at all ("the tombstone would
otherwise orphan the stored key buffer, since `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec`
only walks OCCUPIED slots") -- it is just not carried through to struct keys.

FIX SHAPE. The machinery to walk a struct's heap fields exists on the value
side: `karac_map_free_with_val_drop_fn` takes a per-blob drop function and the
codegen emitters that produce one already exist. The key side needs the same --
a per-key MEMORY drop fn (distinct from B-2026-08-27-2's per-key BODY fn, which
is deliberately body-only) threaded through the remove entry points. Whether to
add a second function pointer or to fold both into one that does bodies then
memory is the open design call; folding is tempting but the two have different
ordering requirements against `free_stored_key`.

SIBLINGS TO CHECK when fixing -- each is a site where a struct key is destroyed
and the same flag governs: `Set.remove` / `SortedSet.remove` (element is the
key half), `m.clear()`, and map teardown for a struct key. Only `remove` has
been measured here.

SEVERITY medium, not high: it is a steady leak rather than a corruption, it
needs a struct key that owns heap AND a remove-heavy workload, and the
interpreter is unaffected (its value model owns the memory), so it is
compiled-backends-only and shows up as growth rather than as a wrong answer.
fix:
Fixed in 0170c65. The row was right about the mechanism and understated the
blast radius: EIGHT shapes leaked, not one, and one of them is not about
struct keys at all.

THE FIX. The row's "FIX SHAPE" guessed a new per-key MEMORY drop fn was
needed. It was not — that fn already existed. `map_val_drop_fn_for_type_expr`
synthesizes a per-blob `karac_drop_<K>`, and `emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk`
applies it to every occupied bucket at TEARDOWN. The remove/clear sites
simply never asked for it. They now do, resolved by receiver name through
two new helpers (`map_key_te_for_var`, `map_key_mem_drop_fn_for_var`) that
read the same side tables teardown reads.

The row's open design question -- one function pointer or two, and whether
folding is safe against `free_stored_key`'s ordering -- dissolved once the
exclusion was noticed. The two cases are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, and that rule
was already written down three times: `emit_free_one_map_handle` and both
`track_map_var_with_val_drop` call sites force `key_is_vec = false` whenever
a key drop fn exists, because the fn owns the WHOLE key side including the
outer buffer. So `drop_key` and the fn never both fire, no ordering question
arises, and one pointer suffices. The runtime is UNCHANGED — B-2026-08-27-2's
`karac_map_remove_old_with_key_drop_fn` carries the extra work, so this fix
adds no symbol and cannot go stale against an archive.

Getting that exclusion wrong is the fix's one real hazard, and it has a
witness: `Map[Vec[String], V]`. The flag and the fn each see a
`{ptr,len,cap}` there, so a careless version double-frees the outer buffer.
`asan_map_remove_releases_a_vec_string_keys_elements` covers it, and
`asan_map_remove_with_a_bare_string_key_stays_clean` covers the other
direction (a bare `String` key that must STAY on the flag).

WHAT LEAKED, all measured under LSan on Linux, all now clean:

  Map.remove / SortedMap.remove   a struct key's heap fields
  Set.remove / SortedSet.remove   a struct element's heap fields
  Map.clear                       a struct key's heap fields
  Set.clear                       BARE `String` elements, and struct ones
  Map.remove                      a `Vec[String]` key's ELEMENTS
  Map.remove                      a `shared` key -- the whole control block

TWO OF THESE ARE WIDER THAN THE ROW.

  `Set.clear` called plain `karac_map_clear`, which zeroes the status bytes
  and does nothing else. It released no element memory -- including the BARE
  `String` element the `drop_key` flag has always covered at every other site
  -- and it ran no element `Drop` BODIES. The missing bodies are the
  B-2026-08-26-41 family, not this one, and were a run-vs-build divergence:
  the interpreter ran them, the compiled backends did not. Fixed here rather
  than filed, because they are one arm's worth of missing work and each half
  is invisible to the other's test -- a sanitizer never sees a skipped body,
  and a `println` never sees a leak.

  A `shared` KEY leaked its entire control block plus everything under it.
  This is the one key shape whose release is a REFCOUNT DEC rather than a
  drop fn: `map_val_drop_fn_for_type_expr` declines for a shared half on
  purpose, because teardown and `clear` give the count back through
  `emit_map_shared_half_rc_dec_walk` and a drop fn there would double-dec.
  `remove` runs no walk, so nothing gave it back at all. The dec is therefore
  confined to the SINGLE-ENTRY destructor and deliberately NOT added to
  `map_key_mem_drop_fn_for_var`, which the clear arms use.

TWO MISTAKES WORTH RECORDING, both caught by measurement rather than review:

  1. The first shared-key dec passed the key BLOB ADDRESS to
     `emit_refcount_dec_by_type`. That function geps field 0 of the heap type
     off what it is handed, so it decremented the map's own bucket bytes: the
     leak did not move and the table was being quietly corrupted. The blob
     HOLDS the rc pointer; it is not the rc object. `emit_map_shared_half_rc_
     dec_walk` loads before deccing for exactly this reason, and the only
     signal that anything was wrong was that the leak total stayed identical.

  2. The first version called the key's `drop` BODY beside the dec. The body
     already runs INSIDE `emit_rc_dec`, on the zero edge, via
     `__karac_rc_drop_<K>` -- so it printed twice. Beside-the-dec is also
     wrong on the semantics, not just the count: with a live alias the body
     must wait for that alias's end, and an unconditional call would fire it
     early over a still-referenced object. Both directions are now asserted
     in `test_e2e_remove_releases_a_shared_key_through_the_refcount`.

A THIRD FINDING, filed separately as B-2026-08-27-4 rather than fixed here:
building the shared-key fixture surfaced that the compiled backends match a
`shared` key by POINTER IDENTITY while the interpreter matches it
STRUCTURALLY. `m.contains_key(twin)` answers true on `--interp` and false on
both compiled backends. That is a silent wrong ANSWER, not a leak, and has
nothing to do with drops.

`__karac_dropkey1_` is renamed `__karac_keydtor1_`. It is no longer a member
of the body-only `dropelems`/`dropkeys` family, and keeping their name is
what would invite the next reader to assume memory is handled elsewhere --
which is the exact assumption that produced this bug.

Tests: 9 ASAN fixtures including the two controls above, plus three-backend
parity tests for the `Set.clear` bodies and the `shared` key. Gates green:
codegen 3291, memory_sanitizer 1222, interpreter 1745, cli 719, par_codegen
270, drop_differential 19, lljit_e2e 16, example_corpus 2; fmt and both
clippy legs clean. The runtime crate is untouched, so the wasm legs are
unaffected.

title: A `shared` STRUCT USED AS A MAP/SET KEY IS MATCHED BY POINTER IDENTITY ON THE COMPILED BACKENDS AND STRUCTURALLY BY THE INTERPRETER. `m.contains_key(twin)` answers `true` on `--interp` and `false` on both `karac run` and `karac build`, for a `twin` with identical field values and a `#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]` on the shared struct. `remove` and `get` follow: the compiled lookup silently misses an entry that is present. A wrong ANSWER, not a leak.
detail:
FOUND while building the `shared`-key ASAN fixture for B-2026-08-27-3. The
first draft of that fixture inserted and removed structurally-equal twins and
reported `len=20` where it expected `0` -- ASAN itself was clean, because the
removal never happened. The leak fixture was retargeted to the same-binding
form (which does remove on every backend) and this was split out.

WHICH SIDE IS RIGHT. The interpreter, on the reading that `#[derive(Hash, Eq,
PartialEq)]` means what it says: the derive is written on the type and asks
for structural equality over its fields. `shared` governs the STORAGE
discipline -- reference semantics, RC -- and design.md does not say it
silently reinterprets a derived `Eq`. If pointer identity is wanted for a
shared key, that is what a hand-written `impl Eq` is for, and the compiled
behaviour would then be reachable deliberately rather than by surprise.

Worth confirming against design.md before fixing, because the opposite
resolution is defensible and would make this a SPEC + interpreter bug rather
than a codegen one. Either way the two backends must agree, which is the part
that is not in question.

BLAST RADIUS is every keyed lookup over a shared key: `get`, `contains_key`,
`remove`, `entry`, and the `Set`/`SortedSet` equivalents. Not measured
individually; the three above are.

SEVERITY high despite the narrow shape. It is a silent wrong answer that
differs BETWEEN BACKENDS, which is the class this project treats as its
hardest invariant -- a program tested under `--interp` and shipped through
`karac build` changes behaviour with no diagnostic. It is also
self-concealing: the compiled lookup MISSES, so the map keeps growing and the
symptom reads as a logic bug in the caller.

NOT A DROP/LEAK DEFECT and not caused by B-2026-08-27-3's fix -- measured on
the same commit both before and after it. Filed separately for that reason.
fix:
Fixed in 393424d. design.md settles the open question the row left: the
INTERPRETER was right.

    § Equality: "`==` always means structural equality. Structural equality is
    defined by the `Eq` trait ... The `Eq` trait determines `==` REGARDLESS of
    whether the compiler chose RC or owned representation. There is no
    reference-identity short-circuit for implicitly RC'd values."

and the table two lines down makes the intent unmistakable by naming the
other behaviour separately: `ref_eq(a, b)` on `shared struct` | OK --
reference identity is meaningful HERE. `ref_eq` carries a `shared` bound
precisely so identity is reachable, deliberately, under its own name. A
`shared` key silently becoming identity-matched is that feature arriving
without being asked for. So this is a codegen bug, not a spec question.

CAUSE. The struct arms of `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` and
`emit_hash_fn_for_type_expr` both carry `&& !shared_types.contains_key(...)`.
A shared key therefore fell to the byte-compare / byte-hash fallback, and a
shared key's stored blob IS a pointer -- so the fallback compared and hashed
POINTER IDENTITY. Same exclusion, same line, in both.

FIX. A shared arm in each dispatcher, and a pair of emitters implementing one
rule: A SHARED KEY BEHAVES AS ITS NON-SHARED TWIN WOULD. Load the pointer,
then apply to the pointee what the unshared path applies. A shared struct
walks its fields through the same per-field child comparators the plain
struct walk uses (so a `String` field recurses rather than comparing headers);
a shared enum compares its user AREA, which is what a plain enum key does.

EQ AND HASH HAD TO MOVE TOGETHER. Equal keys that hash differently never land
in the same bucket, so an equality-only fix leaves every lookup missing
exactly as before -- while looking correct in any test that compares two keys
directly. The `dedup` and `removed` assertions in the parity tests are what
actually hold that pairing.

FIVE SHAPES MEASURED, all three backends, before -> after:

    shared struct, scalar fields        false -> true
    shared struct, `String` field       false -> true
    shared struct, nested shared field  false -> true
    shared enum                         false -> true
    Set[shared] dedup                   len=2 -> len=1

THREE THINGS THE EMITTERS GET RIGHT ON PURPOSE, each a way to get it wrong:

  * USER AREA ONLY, never the rc header -- it differs between two
    structurally-equal boxes, so including it makes every distinct pair
