    unequal and looks exactly like the bug being fixed. Offsets come from
    `shared_gep_layout`, the centralized funnel, so a weak-targeted type's
    two-word header is picked up for free. A map key can never be headerless
    (the purity gate excludes any collection mention), so the base is
    layout-stable across functions and one synthesized fn is safe.
  * NO POINTER FAST PATH. `pa == pb -> true` is tempting, and it would also
    terminate a cyclic comparison, but it is OBSERVABLE: an `f64` NaN field
    makes a value structurally unequal to ITSELF, so the fast path would
    answer `true` where the interpreter answers `false`. The null test is a
    guard, not a fast path -- it fires only where a field walk would fault.
  * NICHE `Option[shared Inner]` FIELDS store a bare pointer (null = None),
    not the conventional 4-i64 Option layout, so the `Option` child fn reads
    the wrong shape. The inner type's own shared comparator reads exactly
    that slot instead. Both fns are declared into the module BEFORE their
    bodies are emitted, so a self-referential `Node { next: Option[Node] }`
    finds itself and terminates rather than recursing forever in the emitter.

TWO ADJACENT DIVERGENCES FOUND AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED HERE. Both are
pre-existing, live in different emitters, were measured on this commit BOTH
BEFORE AND AFTER, and are neither caused nor worsened by this change:

  * B-2026-08-27-5 -- `==` on a shared struct with a niche `Option[shared T]`
    field compares raw pointers. `try_compile_struct_eq_typed` routes a
    struct with a Vec field to the type-directed comparator and carries the
    same `|| shared_types.contains_key(...)` exclusion this row was about;
    the shape-directed walk it falls back to does not know the niche layout.
    Worth noting that this fix makes the inconsistency VISIBLE where it was
    previously uniform: in one program `m.contains_key(b)` is now true while
    `a == b` is still false. Uniformly wrong is not better than half right,
    but the pair should be closed.
  * B-2026-08-27-6 -- a plain ENUM key with a heap-bearing payload
    (`enum S { A { s: String } }`) compares its payload words rather than
    recursing. Nothing `shared` involved; it is why the shared-enum leg here
    aims at parity with the plain enum rather than at correctness beyond it.

Tests: three-backend parity over the four emitter paths a shared key can
take, plus Set dedup and remove, with negative (`-ne`) cases so an
always-true comparator cannot pass. Gates: codegen 3292, interpreter 1746,
memory_sanitizer 1222, cli 719, par_codegen 270, drop_differential 19,
lljit_e2e 16, example_corpus 2 -- zero failures; fmt and both clippy legs
clean. The runtime crate is untouched, so the wasm legs are unaffected.

title: `==` ON A `shared struct` WITH A NICHE-ENCODED `Option[shared T]` FIELD COMPARES RAW POINTERS, so two structurally-equal values answer `false` on the compiled backends and `true` on the interpreter. `try_compile_struct_eq_typed` routes a struct to the TYPE-directed comparator only when it has a Vec field AND is not shared; everything else falls to the SHAPE-directed field walk, which does not know a niche slot holds a bare pointer instead of the 4-i64 Option layout.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-4, and measured on that commit BOTH BEFORE
AND AFTER it: `eq=false` either way, so this is pre-existing and was neither
caused nor worsened there.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-27-4. Same exclusion, different emitter.
`try_compile_struct_eq_typed` (B-2026-08-12-5) carries
`|| self.type_decls.shared_types.contains_key(name)` for the same reason the
key comparators did -- a shared value is a pointer and the type-directed
comparator was written for inline structs. B-2026-08-27-4 fixed the KEY path
by teaching the comparators to deref; this is the `==` OPERATOR path, which
still falls back to `compile_struct_eq`'s shape-directed per-field walk.

That walk dispatches on LLVM SHAPE, and a niche `Option[shared Inner]` field
is a bare `ptr` (null = None) where the conventional layout is
`{tag, w0, w1, w2}`. Shape dispatch therefore sees two pointers and compares
them.

CONSEQUENCE WORTH STATING PLAINLY: after B-2026-08-27-4 the inconsistency is
VISIBLE where it used to be uniform. In one program `m.contains_key(b)` now
answers true while `a == b` still answers false, for the same pair. Uniformly
wrong was not better than half right -- the map path is the one users hit
first, and it is now correct -- but the pair should be closed.

FIX SHAPE. `emit_eq_fn_for_shared` (added by B-2026-08-27-4) already handles
niche fields correctly: it calls the inner type's own shared comparator on
the field slot, which is null-guarded and reads exactly that shape. So the
work is to ROUTE the `==` operator at a shared struct to that existing fn
rather than to the shape-directed walk -- lifting the `shared_types`
exclusion in `try_compile_struct_eq_typed` and pointing it at
`emit_eq_fn_for_shared`. Check the Vec-field gate at the same time: it exists
so the ordinary walk cannot regress, and a shared receiver may want a
different gate.

SEVERITY medium, not high: it needs a shared struct with a niche
`Option[shared T]` field AND a direct `==` between two distinct instances --
the recursive-data shape design.md steers away from anyway ("Recursive type
representations use `Pool[T]`, not `shared struct` + `weak`"). It is still a
silent wrong answer that differs between backends.
fix:
Fixed in 41b233c. The row's diagnosis of WHERE was wrong, and the mechanism
turned out to be sharper than "compares raw pointers".

WHERE. The row blamed `try_compile_struct_eq_typed`'s `shared_types`
exclusion and the shape-directed `compile_struct_eq` fallback. Neither is
involved: `compile_struct_eq` takes `StructValue` operands, and a shared
struct's operand is a POINTER, so it never reaches that path at all. `==` on
a shared struct has had its own type-directed comparator all along --
`emit_shared_struct_eq_fn` / `karac_sheq_<T>` -- which walks fields through
`shared_gep_layout` and recurses per declared field TypeExpr. It is a good
comparator. It had one blind spot.

WHAT. A niche-encoded `Option[shared T]` field stores a BARE pointer (null =
None), ONE word. For that field the walk falls to
`emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr(Option[T])`, which builds a comparator for the
CONVENTIONAL `{tag, w0, w1, w2}` -- FOUR words -- whose general-case body is a
byte loop over `size_of(key_ty)`. So it reads 32 bytes out of an 8-byte slot.
Confirmed directly rather than inferred: an instrumented build printed
`slot_llvm=ptr` alongside `key_ty={ i64, i64, i64, i64 }` for the same field.

The clearest evidence is the shape where the bug does NOT show:

    shared struct Padded { v: i64, next: Option[Padded], p1: i64, p2: i64, p3: i64 }

The surplus 24 bytes land on p1/p2/p3, and the compiled answer came out RIGHT
purely because those happened to be equal. Move the niche field LAST and the
read leaves the object, and two `None`s compare UNEQUAL. Both shapes are now
asserted, because a fix that merely RELOCATED the over-read would satisfy a
test written around the last-field shape alone.

ON THE OUT-OF-BOUNDS QUESTION, stated carefully because it is tempting to
overclaim: the surplus bytes ARE read (the `Padded` result proves the read
leaves the field), and for a last-field niche the observed `false` can only
come from bytes past the object. But ASAN reports NOTHING -- at -O0 and -O2,
with a 16-byte box against a 32-byte read, over 50 iterations. So this is
recorded as a wrong answer, not a proven OOB. Whatever the surplus lands in,
the sanitizer considers it valid memory.

THE FIX needed no new machinery. `emit_eq_fn_for_shared` (added by
B-2026-08-27-4) takes a SLOT, loads it, and null-guards -- both null equal,
one null unequal -- before walking, which is exactly the niche encoding's
three cases. The niche arm is checked BEFORE the bare-shared-field arm, since
a niche field's TypeExpr is `Option[Inner]`, not `Inner`, so that arm never
sees it.

THE DEEPER DEFECT, and the reason this is more than a one-arm patch: THERE
WERE TWO INDEPENDENT STRUCTURAL COMPARATORS FOR ONE SHARED TYPE.
`karac_eq_<T>` (map keys, which B-2026-08-27-4 added -- without noticing
`karac_sheq_` already existed) and `karac_sheq_<T>` (`==`). Only one knew
about niches. That is not an incidental duplication: it is exactly how
`contains_key(b)` and `a == b` came to answer differently for the same pair,
which is the inconsistency the -4 row flagged as this row's motivation. They
are ONE implementation now -- the key comparator is a slot adapter over the
`==` walk (load, null-guard, delegate), and a test asserts the two agree.
Shared enums keep their user-area compare, since that walk is struct-only.

Registering each fn into the module BEFORE emitting its body is what makes
the resulting MUTUAL recursion terminate: a niche field sends the `==` walk
back into the key comparator for the inner type, and a self-referential
`Node { next: Option[Node] }` closes that loop on itself. A 5-link chain is
asserted so this cannot pass by luck.

A CAUTION FROM B-2026-08-27-4 IS RETIRED RATHER THAN PROPAGATED. That fix
avoided `karac_sheq_`'s pointer fast path, reasoning that an `f64` NaN field
makes a value structurally unequal to itself, so `pa == pb -> true` would be
observable. The typechecker rejects the premise: `#[derive(Eq)]` on a struct
with an `f64` field is refused outright ("struct 'F' derives Eq but field 'x'
has non-Eq type 'f64'"). The case cannot arise for a derived comparator, so
unifying on the fast-path implementation is sound. Measured both ways: `a ==
a` on a NaN-bearing struct answers `true` on the interpreter too.

ONE ADJACENT DIVERGENCE FOUND AND NOT FIXED, filed as B-2026-08-27-9: under
`#[derive(PartialEq)]` alone -- which DOES admit a float field -- two
distinct structs holding the same NaN compare `true` on the compiled backends
and `false` on the interpreter. Different path (float field comparison, not
the niche slot), and unrelated to `shared`.

Tests: three-backend parity over none/none, some/some, some/none, a 5-link
chain, and the trailing-field `Padded` case, plus an explicit assertion that
`contains_key` and `==` agree on one pair. The `deep` operands are BOUND
rather than inline `chain(4) == chain(4)`: comparing two call results is a
separate, already-diagnosed codegen gap, and letting it fire would mean the
test never reached the comparator. Gates: codegen 3294, interpreter 1747,
memory_sanitizer 1223, cli 719, par_codegen 270, drop_differential 19,
lljit_e2e 16, example_corpus 2, map_entry_lint 9 -- zero failures; fmt and
both clippy legs clean. The runtime crate is untouched, so the wasm legs are
unaffected.

title: A PLAIN (non-shared) ENUM USED AS A MAP/SET KEY WITH A HEAP-BEARING PAYLOAD COMPARES ITS PAYLOAD WORDS INSTEAD OF RECURSING, so `Map[S, V]` where `enum S { A { s: String } }` misses a structurally-equal key on the compiled backends and finds it on the interpreter. `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` has arms for tuples, `Vec`, and STRUCTS, but none for enums -- an enum key falls to the byte-compare fallback, which for a `String` payload compares two distinct heap POINTERS.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-4 and measured independently of it -- nothing
`shared` is involved. Filed separately for that reason, and because it is why
B-2026-08-27-4's shared-ENUM leg aims at PARITY WITH THE PLAIN ENUM rather
than at correctness beyond it: a shared enum key now behaves exactly as its
non-shared twin does, which is right by that fix's rule and still wrong by
this one.

CAUSE. `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` (and its hash twin) dispatch per shape:
tuple, `Vec`, struct, else the byte fallback. Structs recurse per declared
field TypeExpr, which is why a `struct K { s: String }` key works. Enums have
no arm at all, so an enum key is byte-compared over its inline
`{tag, w0, w1, w2}` area -- and a `String` payload stores a `{ptr,len,cap}`
in those words, so the comparison reads two distinct heap pointers.

RELATED, ALREADY KNOWN. B-2026-08-26-32's enum-key ASAN fixture
(`asan_map_get_with_inline_temporary_enum_key_is_clean`) asserts `hits=0` --
that is, it encodes the MISS as expected. That test is about a leak, not
about matching, so it is not wrong; but it is where the symptom has been
sitting in plain sight, and it will need its expectation updated when this is
fixed.

FIX SHAPE. An enum arm in both dispatchers, walking tag first and then the
active variant's declared field TypeExprs through the same child comparators
the struct arm uses. `enum_variant_field_type_exprs` already supplies the
per-variant field list. The hash twin must move WITH it, for the reason
B-2026-08-27-4 records: equal keys that hash differently never meet in the
same bucket, so an equality-only fix changes nothing observable.

SEVERITY medium: a silent wrong answer that differs between backends, but it
needs an enum key whose payload owns heap, and the scalar-payload enum key --
the common case -- is correct today.
fix:
FIXED by a35c3f5. `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` and `emit_hash_fn_for_type_expr` gained an
ENUM arm, both keyed on one shared `enum_structural_key_plan(enum_name)` so the
two cannot drift: compare tags, then switch on the tag and walk the LIVE
variant's declared payload fields through the same child comparators the struct
arm uses. The hash seeds its digest with the tag (as the `Vec` arm seeds with
`len`) and folds each field in through the same FxHash tail-mix, which is what
keeps two variants carrying identical payload WORDS from colliding.

WHAT MADE THIS A KEY-ONLY DEFECT, which the row did not say and which is the
clearest way to see it: this compiler has TWO enum comparators. The `==`
OPERATOR site already routed a heap-payload enum to `compile_enum_eq`
(`exprs.rs`), which walks the tag and rebuilds each payload from its words --
generic substitution included, so `Option[String] == Option[String]` has always
been right. The KEY/collection family (`emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` and its hash
twin, consumed by `Map`/`Set`) had no enum arm at all. So `x == y` and
`m.contains_key(y)` answered differently about the same two values, and only
the second was wrong. The regression tests assert both in one program for that
reason: the two paths agreeing is the property, not just the key lookup
answering `true`.

WHAT THE ROW'S FIX SHAPE DID NOT NAME, and the real content of the fix: a
payload word is not a memcpy of the field. `coerce_to_payload_words` writes one
i64 stream per source field, so the payload area is a word-EXPANDED image. A
narrow scalar arrives widened into a whole word -- harmless, since its
comparator loads only its own width from the low end and both sides were
widened identically -- but a `struct { a: i32, b: i32 }` spends TWO words where
its LLVM value is eight bytes, and every field after the first then sits at the
wrong offset. So "walk the declared field TypeExprs through the same child
comparators" is sound only where the word image IS the LLVM layout.
`payload_words_match_llvm_layout` is that predicate; it checks real
`TargetData` offsets for a struct payload rather than re-deriving LLVM's
packing rules. Where it says no the enum keeps the byte compare, declining
per-ENUM and never per-field, because a walk that skipped one field it could
not read would answer `true` for two values differing only there -- a worse
answer than the byte compare it replaces.

THE SHARED-ENUM LEG MOVED WITH IT. B-2026-08-27-4 defines a shared key as
behaving "exactly as its NON-SHARED twin does", so repairing the plain enum
alone would have broken that rule in the other direction. Measured before the
change: `Map[shared enum Node { Named { s: String } }, i64].contains_key(twin)`
= `false` on AOT, `true` on the interpreter. A shared enum's user area has the
same `{tag, w0, w1, ...}` shape as a plain enum's value, so both legs now share
one `emit_enum_area_{eq,hash}_fn` parameterised by which struct type to GEP
through.

CORRECTION TO THE ROW. Its RELATED note said
`asan_map_get_with_inline_temporary_enum_key_is_clean` "asserts `hits=0` -- that
is, it encodes the MISS as expected ... it will need its expectation updated
when this is fixed". It does not: that test inserts `a-padding-...` and probes
with `b-{j}-padding-...`, keys that genuinely differ, so `hits=0` is correct
under structural equality too. It passes unchanged, as do all 1223 ASAN tests.
The real gap there was the opposite one -- neither it nor its
`asan_map_get_with_bound_enum_key_is_clean` control ever ran a MATCHING inline
temporary, so the successful-lookup path had never been under ASAN at all.
Added as `asan_map_get_with_a_matching_inline_temporary_enum_key_is_clean`.

TESTS. Three, each confirmed to fail with the fix reverted (the interpreter
twin is the oracle and passes both ways by design):
`test_e2e_an_enum_key_with_a_heap_payload_is_matched_by_content` (codegen),
`an_enum_key_with_a_heap_payload_is_matched_by_content` (interpreter), and the
ASAN test above. The E2E program covers eight variant shapes -- unit, scalar,
struct-variant `String`, two-field tuple variant, `Vec` payload, nested
heap-owning struct, widened narrow scalar, and a shared enum -- plus `Set`
dedup and `remove`, which is what actually checks that hash moved with eq
(equal keys that hash differently never meet in the same bucket), a `-ne` line
per shape so an always-true comparator cannot pass, two variants carrying
identical payload words under different discriminants, and the `==` pair that
pins the two comparators together. Reverted, it prints `text=false pair=false
items=false nested=false dedup=2 removed=8 shared=false` while every
scalar/unit control stays correct.

REMAINDER, measured and filed rather than left implicit in a predicate: the two
shapes the plan declines -- a GENERIC enum key (`Map[Option[String], _]`) and
an enum whose payload struct has two consecutive sub-word fields ahead of a
heap field -- are both shapes `compile_enum_eq` already handles on the operator
side, so the same divergence survives in miniature. Filed with that as the fix
shape. Separately, `Vec.contains` reaches NEITHER comparator (it calls
`compile_binop` on loaded values, so `enum_name_of_expr` has no operand
expression to resolve) and compares an enum element's raw words; filed too.

RESOLVED by 478fef6 as option (c) PLUS the interpreter half of (b): destruction
order in an UNORDERED container is specified as unspecified -- the same rule
iteration already follows -- and the interpreter stops presenting a stable order
the spec does not promise. SortedMap/SortedSet are the escape hatch and were
MEASURED to already deliver it.

THE ROW'S OWN RECOMMENDATION WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED HERE. It said "(b) is
the smallest change that makes the two backends agree by construction". It is
not: (b) hash-orders the interpreter's drop walk, but the interpreter sorts by
seeded hash while the compiled table walks bucket placement, so the two remain
DIFFERENT permutations of each other. That is visible in the row's own
non-affected-iteration table, where interp and build disagree at a pinned seed --
the evidence was already on the page and was read the wrong way round. (b) buys
self-consistency, not agreement, and it is worth landing for that reason alone.

WHAT WAS MEASURED, freshly built at 67e9737, six shapes x three seeds:

  Map[K,i64] K:Drop   seed 1/3/7  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6  build 4 2 5 3 6 1 / 6 1 2 4 5 3 / 2 1 4 3 6 5
  Map[i64,V] V:Drop   seed 1/3/7  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6  build 4 5 6 1 3 2 / 6 4 3 5 1 2 / 2 3 5 1 4 6
  Set[E]     E:Drop   seed 1/3/7  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6  build 4 2 5 3 6 1 / 6 1 2 4 5 3 / 2 1 4 3 6 5
  SortedMap keys      seed 1/3/7  interp == build == 1 2 3 4 5 6   (identical, every seed)
  SortedMap values    seed 1/3/7  interp == build == 6 5 4 3 2 1   (identical, every seed)
  SortedSet elements  seed 1/3/7  interp == build == 1 2 3 4 5 6   (identical, every seed)

JIT == AOT on every shape, so the split is interpreter-vs-compiled, not
three-way. The SortedMap/SortedSet rows are the load-bearing new fact: the
escape hatch design.md already points at for iteration ALSO holds for
destruction, seed-independently and across backends. That is what makes "use a
sorted container" real advice rather than a deflection, and it is why (c) is
adequate rather than merely cheap.

THE INTERPRETER WAS CONTRADICTING ITSELF IN A SINGLE RUN, which is the part
that turned this from a spec question into a fix. One program, one map:

  iter 1 iter 3 iter 5 iter 6 iter 4 iter 2      <- for (k, v) in m
  drop 1 drop 2 drop 3 drop 4 drop 5 drop 6      <- the same map dying

Two walks of one container, two orders. The drop walk called `MapData::iter`
(raw insertion-ordered STORAGE); every other read path goes through
`iter_observable`, the seeded permutation B-2026-08-21-6 added on 2026-08-22.
The walk's own comment -- "Insertion order ... the two differ exactly as
`for (k, v) in m` already does" -- was TRUE when written (last touched
2026-08-17) and became false five days later when the seeding landed. This is a
migration miss, not a design choice: nobody decided the drop walk should keep
storage order, it was simply not converted.

The damage was the STABILITY, not the disagreement. Unspecified-and-varying is
what the spec says and what the compiled backends do; the interpreter handed out
a stable insertion order instead, so a program that came to depend on it looked
correct under `karac run` and reordered under `karac build`. Routing the two
walks (binding death and struct-field death) through `iter_observable` makes the
interpreter agree with ITSELF and vary per process, so the dependency surfaces
on the first pair of runs instead of at the backend boundary.

WHY NOT (a), INSERTION ORDER IN CODEGEN -- priced, not waved off. The runtime
map is open-addressed with two parallel arrays (`status`, `kv`) and no insertion
index, so this needs a third: a per-entry sequence number, `karac_map_new`
variant to allocate it, maintenance on every insert and resize, and a sort at
teardown. The cost is not the memory (~8 B/bucket, and only for Drop-bearing
maps); it is that `src/codegen/mono.rs` emits its OWN copies of the probe and
insert loops -- three sites -- so the array would have to be maintained
identically in two places that already carry this exact hazard. map.rs's header
states the failure mode of runtime/codegen disagreement: "a lookup that misses a
present key -- a silent wrong answer, not a crash". Adding a second parallel
array doubles that surface to buy an order the spec does not require.

WHY NOT (d), A SORT-BY-HASH DROP WALK IN CODEGEN -- the option the row did not
list, and the closest call. `hash_fn` is already in the map control block, and
only ONE emitted walker is observable (`emit_map_half_user_drop_bodies_fn`; the
other status-array walks are memory release, iteration and lookup), so it is
genuinely contained: one runtime helper returning slots sorted by hash, one loop
rewrite, plus (b) on the interpreter. It would make all three surfaces
byte-identical AT A PINNED SEED, which would let E2E tests assert exact drop
sequences -- closing the coverage hole B-2026-08-27-8 names, where every walker
test asserts counts and an order regression is therefore invisible.

It was rejected because the capability it buys is one this project's own
conventions forbid using. CLAUDE.md SS `Map`/`Set` iteration order: "Compare
CONTENTS: sort the walked lines, or compare as a set". A test asserting a
hash-derived sequence -- even under `KARAC_HASH_SEED` -- pins an implementation
detail of the hasher and the table, and breaks on any future change to either.
Paying for a capability the guidance says not to exercise is not a trade worth
making. If that guidance is ever revisited, (d) is the option to revisit with
it, and this row is the pricing.

WHAT LANDED

  * design.md SS Map, after the existing iteration-order paragraph: element
    destruction order in an unordered container IS that same unspecified order,
    with the two guarantees that do hold spelled out -- each live element's body
    runs exactly once, and SortedMap/SortedSet destroy in key order,
    seed-independently and identically on every backend. Keys before values.
  * `src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs`: `run_map_half_user_drops` and
    `run_field_map_half_user_drops` walk `iter_observable` (Map) /
    `SetData::iter_observable` (Set) instead of storage. Both stale comments
    replaced -- the one that had gone false, and the SortedMap aside that framed
    key order as a wart rather than as the escape hatch.
  * CLAUDE.md (kara) SS `Map`/`Set` iteration order, and kara-katas' A/B rule:
    the precondition written down. The reason this hides is specific and is
    stated: with `for (k, v) in m` the author chose to observe the order and can
    sort at the use site; drop bodies are sequenced by the runtime with NO use
    site to intervene at, so a kata that prints from a container element's Drop
    breaks A/B with nothing in the source that looks order-dependent.

TESTS -- and the shape matters, because the obvious test is forbidden.
`container_element_drop_order_is_the_containers_own_iteration_order` compares
the program's OWN two walks (iterate the map, then let it die) and asserts they
are equal. Self-relative, so it pins no hash order and holds on every seed and
every run -- which is what makes it runnable at all under the no-asserting-order
rule. Eight elements, so a regression survives only the 1-in-40320 of seeds
whose hash order happens to equal insertion order. NEGATIVE-CONTROLLED: with the
fix reverted it fails 5/5 across seeds 1-5.

`a_sorted_container_destroys_its_elements_in_key_order` and its E2E twin
`test_e2e_sorted_container_destroys_in_key_order` pin the escape hatch with
exact literals -- legitimate here because key order is seed-independent --
covering SortedMap keys, SortedMap values and SortedSet elements, measured
identical on interp, JIT and AOT at seeds 1 and 7. Keys are inserted DESCENDING
so key order and insertion order disagree; ascending inserts would let a walk
that ignored the ordering pass.

NOT A LEAK AND NOT A DOUBLE FIRE, unchanged from the filing: every element's
body runs exactly once on both backends. The full `--features llvm` suite is
green.

REMAINDER, stated rather than buried: the compiled backends and the interpreter
still produce DIFFERENT permutations at the same pinned seed, for drop order and
for ordinary iteration alike. That is now within spec on both counts instead of
within spec on one and undocumented on the other, and it is the pre-existing,
larger fact -- map ITERATION order has always disagreed across backends, and
this row's drop walk was one instance of it, not a separate defect.
title: CONTAINER ELEMENT `Drop` BODIES FIRE IN A DIFFERENT ORDER ON THE TWO BACKENDS: the interpreter walks INSERTION order (deterministic across seeds and runs), the compiled backends walk BUCKET order (a different permutation per `KARAC_HASH_SEED`). Affects all three walks -- Map values, Map keys, Set elements. Ordinary `for (k, v) in m` iteration is NOT affected: it is hash-ordered and run-to-run random on BOTH backends, exactly as design.md specifies. So this is the drop walk alone, and it breaks the A/B rule for any RAII element type.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while thinking through B-2026-08-26-41's blocker, and
re-measured with FRESHLY REBUILT archives at 8b39686 after a stale archive had
already produced one false finding in the same session (see below).

MEASURED, 6 elements inserted 1..6, `KARAC_HASH_SEED` pinned:

    Map[K, i64], K: Drop        seed=1  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6 | build 4 2 5 3 6 1
                                seed=2  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6 | build 4 6 3 2 1 5
                                seed=7  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6 | build 2 1 4 3 6 5
                                seed=11 interp 1 2 3 4 5 6 | build 6 4 2 5 3 1
    Map[i64, V], V: Drop        seed=3  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6 | build 6 4 3 5 1 2
    Set[E],      E: Drop        seed=3  interp 1 2 3 4 5 6 | build 6 1 2 4 5 3

  The interpreter is 1..6 on EVERY seed and on every unpinned run -- it is not
  merely a different order, it is INSERTION order and fully deterministic. The
  compiled backends produce a distinct permutation per seed.

WHAT IS *NOT* AFFECTED, which is what localizes this. Ordinary iteration:

    for (k, v) in m { println(f"{k}:{v}"); }

  interp seed=1  1 3 5 4 2      build seed=1  4 5 1 3 2
  interp seed=2  5 1 2 3 4      build seed=2  2 5 4 1 3
  and unpinned, BOTH backends vary run to run.

  That is hash order on both sides, unspecified and randomized -- precisely what
  design.md SS `Hash` and `Hasher` and CLAUDE.md's "never assert Map/Set
  iteration order" describe. User-visible iteration conforms. Only the DROP
  WALK diverges, and only in the interpreter's direction: it walks the
  order-preserving `MapData` (B-2026-08-21-6's hash-indexed, insertion-ordered
  store) raw, while user-facing iteration deliberately presents hash order.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT INTRODUCED BY THE KEY WALK. The Map-VALUE and Set-ELEMENT
walks both date from B-2026-08-26-11 (B-2026-07-30-11's values and Set-elements
legs) and both diverge identically, measured above. 34c3f54's key walk simply
joins them.

WHY IT MATTERS. kara-katas' A/B rule is "every kata must produce identical
output under `karac run` and `karac build`", and any program whose container
elements have an observable `Drop` violates it today. It is invisible to the
existing suites because no fixture prints from a container element's drop body
and then compares backends -- the tests added for the three walks all assert
COUNTS, deliberately, because Map order is documented as unspecified.

THE DESIGN QUESTION, which is what this row is really for. design.md fixes no
order for container element destruction; it says only that `drop` runs "at the
end of each value's live range". Three coherent answers, and picking one is the
work:
  (a) SPECIFY insertion order and make codegen match. Deterministic and
      debuggable, and the interpreter already does it -- but it costs codegen an
      insertion-order index it does not currently keep, i.e. real per-entry
      memory in every Drop-bearing container.
  (b) SPECIFY that the order is unspecified, and make the INTERPRETER hash-order
      its drop walk to match its own iteration. Cheap, self-consistent, and
      kills the parity break -- at the price that a program's drop output
      legitimately varies run to run, which the A/B kata rule then has to carve
      out explicitly rather than silently.
  (c) Leave it, and state in design.md that container element drop ORDER is
      unspecified and must not be observed. Zero cost, but it makes the A/B
      rule conditional, and a rule with an unwritten exception is how this
      class hides.

  (b) is the smallest change that makes the two backends agree by construction,
  which is the property the Arrow/normalize/hash twins are all built on. (a) is
  the only one that makes RAII output reproducible, which is what someone
  debugging a resource leak actually wants. This is a spec call, not a codegen
  call.

NOT A LEAK AND NOT A DOUBLE FIRE. Every element's body runs exactly once on
both backends; only the sequence differs. The full memory_sanitizer suite is
green.

CROSS-REF: B-2026-08-26-41 / 34c3f54 (the key walk), B-2026-07-30-11 (the value
and Set-element legs), B-2026-08-21-6 (the per-process hashing this interacts
with), CLAUDE.md SS "`Map` / `Set` iteration order is random per process".

fix:
FIXED by a74acc3, as the row specified: `CleanupAction::UserDrop` now CARRIES the answer and
`is_container_elem_bodies_fn` is deleted. The new field is a three-valued
`UserDropKind` (`OwnWrapper` / `ContainerElemBodies` / `StructFieldBodies`)
rather than the row's `bodies_only: bool`, because the same variant had a SECOND
name-prefix predicate reading it -- see SCOPE below.

THE HAZARD IS LIVE, NOT THEORETICAL -- MEASURED BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING. On
`b669c21`, `Map[K, V]` with both halves dropping and the map's last use at
`m.len()` prints `len 1 / dropK 1 / dropV 1 / MARKER` on all three backends:
NLL-placed, interpreter and codegen agreeing. Renaming the key-half walker from
`__karac_dropkeys_map_*` to `__karac_dropkbodies_map_*` -- six characters in one
`format!`, no behavioural edit anywhere -- and rebuilding gives
`len 1 / dropV 1 / MARKER / dropK 1` under `karac build` while `--interp` is
unmoved. A run-vs-build divergence produced by the spelling of a symbol, with no
error, no warning and a green suite. That is exactly the shape the row describes
as having cost a session on B-2026-08-26-41.

WHAT THE FIX IS. `track_user_drop_var_with_fn` takes `kind` as a REQUIRED
argument at all 21 call sites; `track_user_drop_var` passes `OwnWrapper`
(it sources the fn from `user_drop_wrapper_fns`, so the kind is certain) and
`track_container_elem_bodies_before_own` passes `ContainerElemBodies` (its whole
purpose). Seven consumers now read the field instead of the symbol:
`fire_due_user_drops`'s NLL admission, `armed_container_elem_bodies_action`,
`has_armed_container_elem_bodies`, `has_armed_own_user_drop`, the `own_idx`
search in `track_container_elem_bodies_before_own`, and both
`suppress_*_bodies_for_var` retractions. Requiredness is structural, not a
convention: `CleanupAction::UserDrop` has no default, so a new registrar that
omits the kind does not compile -- which is precisely what a name-prefix test
cannot be, and is the property the row asked for.

TWO SITES COULD NOT TAKE A CONSTANT, AND BOTH ARE THE INTERESTING ONES.
`call_dispatch.rs`'s discarded-owned-return site builds `bodies_fn` on two
branches -- `emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn` (a container walk) on the
enum leg, `field_bodies_fn_for_owned_temp` (a field walk) on the struct leg --
and registers both through one call, so the kind travels WITH the function as
`Option<(FunctionValue, UserDropKind)>`. `par_blocks.rs`'s write-back
reconstructs a `UserDrop` from an action it sampled off the frame, so it
PROPAGATES the sampled kind via `SlotOwnership::User`. Hard-coding either as
`OwnWrapper` would have retimed a real walk; the comment there previously said
the empty `type_name` kept the entry off the NLL gate, which was only true when
the sampled fn happened not to be a `dropelems` one.

HOW THE 21 CLASSIFICATIONS WERE VERIFIED RATHER THAN GUESSED. Each site's
`drop_fn` was traced to its emitter and the emitter to its `format!` -- six
emitters spell `__karac_dropelems_*` (one of them spelling `__karac_dropkeys_*`
on its key leg, via a computed infix), and three spell `__karac_dropbodies_*`. Then a temporary `assert_eq!` inside the registrar
compared the declared `kind` against the old name-prefix classification on every
registration, and the full `--features llvm` suite was run with it armed: zero
mismatches, so the refactor is behaviour-identical at every site the suites
reach. The assertion was deleted before commit. (A first attempt at this census
used `eprintln!` + `#[track_caller]` and produced nothing -- the test harness
captures stderr for passing tests. An assertion has no such hole, since a panic
fails the test.)

THE ROW'S OWN AUDIT UNDERCOUNTS, AND ITS SEVERITY ARGUMENT RESTS ON THAT COUNT.
It says "Seven sites call `track_user_drop_var_with_fn` with an empty
`type_name`; three are statement-temporaries … and the four that register NAMED
bindings all pass a covered prefix". Counted on `b669c21`: there are ELEVEN
empty-`type_name` sites, three statement-temporaries and EIGHT named-binding
registrations. The four the row missed are `stmts.rs`'s tuple-element and
Option/Result-payload walks and BOTH `pattern_binding.rs` re-home sites.

Seven of those eight are `__karac_dropelems_*` and were NLL-placed, so the row's
conclusion -- nothing mis-placed on `main` today -- survives the correction for
the container class it was about. The eighth does not fit that sentence:
`pattern_binding.rs`'s second re-home registers `__karac_dropbodies_only_<S>`, a
struct bodies-only walk, against a NAMED binding with an empty `type_name`, so
neither the container clause nor the type-keyed clauses admit it and it drains
at scope exit. This refactor preserves that exactly (`StructFieldBodies`). It is
NOT claimed here as a bug: whether a re-homed field-bodies walk should be
NLL-placed is a question the row did not ask and this session did not measure.
It is recorded because it is the one bodies-only walk on a named binding that is
not NLL-placed, which makes it the obvious first place to look if this class
resurfaces.

SCOPE: THE ROW NAMED ONE PREDICATE; THERE WERE TWO. `is_struct_field_bodies_fn`
tests `__karac_dropbodies_` on the SAME field for the SAME kind of decision
(which retraction family a moved-out field's walk belongs to), and its failure
mode is worse than misplacement -- a field-bodies walker spelled outside that
prefix escapes `suppress_struct_field_bodies_for_var` entirely, so a moved-out
field's body runs a second time rather than at the wrong time. Fixing one and
leaving the other would also have left the tree in its most confusing state:
an action carrying an explicit semantic kind that one consumer trusts and
another ignores in favour of a string test. Both are deleted; the enum has three
variants because the two predicates cut three ways, and `has_armed_own_user_drop`
depends on that (a field-bodies walk counts as "own" there, an element walk does
not) -- a two-valued `bodies_only` would have silently merged those.

THE MISSING TEST THE ROW ASKED FOR, ON BOTH BACKENDS.
`test_e2e_container_bodies_walks_fire_at_the_nll_point` (tests/codegen.rs) and
`container_bodies_walks_fire_at_the_nll_point` (tests/interpreter.rs) print a
`|marker` after each binding's last use and assert the SEQUENCE across six
walker families at once: Vec elements, tuple elements, enum payload,
Option payload, map values and map keys (two walkers under one binding), and Set
elements. Asserting sequence is a deliberate departure from every other walker
test in the tree, which asserts counts -- and counting is what let this class
hide, since a demoted walker still fires each body exactly once. Order-safety is
bought by ONE entry per container: a single element has a single permutation, so
this pins placement without pinning the unspecified iteration order
(B-2026-08-27-7). The enum case is load-bearing in a second way -- `e` is never
used after its `let`, so its body must land BEFORE the `[enum]` line, which
scope-exit placement cannot produce.

NEGATIVE CONTROL, on the NEW mechanism rather than the old one. Declaring the
map key-half registration `OwnWrapper` -- leaving its symbol name untouched, so
only the new channel can notice -- makes the codegen fixture fail with
`… [map 1] V5 |map K5 [set 1] …` against the interpreter twin's
`… [map 1] K5 V5 |map [set 1] …`: the key body demoted past the marker, the same
signature the pre-fix rename produced. Run twice, once with the equivalence
assertion armed (it fires first, naming the symbol) and once with it disabled,
so the FIXTURE is shown to catch the demotion on its own rather than the
assertion catching it. Restored, both green.

MEASURED NOTE, filed here rather than as its own row because it is inert and the
code now says so at the site: `emit_discarded_tuple_elem_bodies_fn` spells its
symbol `__karac_dropbodies_tuple_te_*` -- a TUPLE-ELEMENT walk named in the
struct-field family. The old name test therefore classified it as
`StructFieldBodies`, and the new argument preserves that exactly. It is
harmless because the action registers under `__disc_tup_tmp`, a statement
temporary that `drain_statement_temp_user_drops` retires at statement end, so it
reaches neither an NLL last-use map nor either retraction helper. It is worth
recording as the one place in the tree where the two conventions were already
crossed -- and as the reason the fix is a required argument rather than a
longer prefix list.
title: NLL DROP PLACEMENT IS DISPATCHED ON AN LLVM SYMBOL-NAME PREFIX. `is_container_elem_bodies_fn` decides whether a cleanup action fires at the binding's last use or at scope exit by testing `starts_with("__karac_dropelems_")` (plus `__karac_dropkeys_` since 34c3f54). A bodies-only walker whose emitter picks any other prefix is silently demoted to scope exit — a run-vs-build divergence with no error, no warning and no failing test. NO LIVE INSTANCE TODAY: all four named-binding walkers are covered. This is the latent hazard, and it has already cost one session.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while working through B-2026-08-26-41's stated blocker; that
row is fixed (34c3f54) and this is the mechanism it turned on, filed separately
because it is a refactor rather than a defect.

WHAT THE CHANNEL LOOKS LIKE. `fire_due_user_drops` (runtime.rs) implements
design.md's NLL placement — bodies fire at a binding's live-range end rather
than lexical scope end. Its admission test is three clauses; the first is a
STRING PREFIX on the emitted function's name, and it is the only clause a
container walker can satisfy, because those walkers register through
`track_user_drop_var_with_fn("", …)` with an EMPTY `type_name` and the other
two clauses both key on `type_name`.

HOW IT COST A SESSION, measured 2026-08-26/27. B-2026-08-26-41 needed a Map
KEY-half bodies walk. Two implementations were written independently:

  * one named it `__karac_dropelems_mapkey_<te>` — matched the prefix, was
    NLL-placed, agreed with the interpreter;
  * one named it `__karac_dropkeys_map_<te>` — missed the prefix, was demoted
    to scope exit, and DISAGREED with the interpreter.

The second was read as evidence of a deep problem: its investigation concluded
that NLL-placing the key walk would require giving a map-handle registration a
non-empty `type_name`, thereby opting it into a channel whose stated
precondition (mutual exclusivity with every other cleanup action) a map handle
does not satisfy, since it also carries `FreeMapHandle` — a double-free / UAF
risk, correctly refused blind. A two-part patch was parked unlanded at
`docs/wip/` with that as the blocker.

None of it was true. The empty `type_name` was never what pinned the walk to
scope exit — the VALUE walk carries the same empty `type_name` and is NLL-placed
(measured: `Map[i64, V]` with the map's last use at `m.len()` fires `dropV`
there on both backends). The whole difference was six characters of symbol name.
Renaming the walker into the `dropelems` family made all of that row's blocker
shapes agree; 34c3f54 landed the equivalent fix by widening the predicate
instead. Either works. Neither removes the hazard.

WHY IT IS SEVERITY LOW RATHER THAN HIGHER — CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED. Seven sites
call `track_user_drop_var_with_fn` with an empty `type_name`; three are
statement-temporaries that drain through `drain_statement_temp_user_drops`
instead, and the four that register NAMED bindings all pass a covered prefix:

    runtime.rs:8151   `__karac_dropelems_map_…`     map values
    runtime.rs:8169   `__karac_dropkeys_map_…`      map keys      (via 34c3f54)
    control_flow…7641 `__karac_dropelems_tuple_…`   tuple elements
    stmts.rs:6999     `__karac_dropelems_enum_…`    enum payloads

  So nothing is mis-placed on `main` today. The cost is entirely in what the
  next walker does. There are 18 distinct `__karac_drop*` families in
  src/codegen; two of them are admitted. A new emitter that names itself after
  any of the other sixteen conventions gets silent scope-exit placement.

THE FIX IS TO STOP INFERRING. `CleanupAction::UserDrop` should carry the answer
— a `bodies_only: bool` (or an enum distinguishing a bodies walk from a
wrapper) set by the registrar, which knows it for certain — and
`is_container_elem_bodies_fn` should be deleted. The predicate is asking "is
this function bodies-only, so that firing it early frees nothing early?", which
is a property of the REGISTRATION, not of the spelling of a symbol. Widening a
prefix list is the same mistake with a longer list.

  Cheap: one field, four registration sites, one predicate deleted. The risk is
  the reverse of the current one — a registrar that forgets the flag demotes its
  walk — so the field should be a required constructor argument rather than a
  defaulted one, which is exactly what a name-prefix test cannot be.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT NOTICEABLE IN THE MEANTIME: no test asserts that a bodies
walker is NLL-placed. The three walks each have tests, and all of them assert
COUNTS (deliberately — Map order is unspecified, see B-2026-08-27-7), so a
demoted walker still fires exactly once and every test stays green. A single
A/B fixture per walker, printing a marker between the binding's last use and
scope end, would catch the whole class.

CROSS-REF: B-2026-08-26-41 / 34c3f54 (the row this came from, and the widened
predicate), B-2026-08-27-7 (the count-not-sequence test convention that hides
this), design.md SS Drop (NLL placement).

title: A FLOAT FIELD OF A `shared struct` IS COMPARED BY BITS, NOT BY IEEE SEMANTICS, so `==` is wrong in BOTH directions on the compiled backends: `0.0` vs `-0.0` answers `false` (should be true) and NaN vs NaN answers `true` (should be false). The interpreter is right in both. `emit_eq_fn_for_type` has arms for integers and `String` and a byte-loop fallback for everything else; a `FloatType` gets the byte loop. The PLAIN-struct `==` path is unaffected -- it compares floats properly -- so this is specific to the shared walk.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-5, and measured independently of it: it
reproduces on that fix's commit both before and after, and nothing about the
niche-field path is involved.

CAUSE. `emit_shared_struct_eq_fn`'s field walk routes each field through
`emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr`, which for `f64` falls to `emit_eq_fn_for_type`'s
general case -- a byte-by-byte loop over `size_of(key_ty)`. Bit equality is
not float equality, and it differs from it in exactly the two places IEEE
defines specially: `-0.0` and `0.0` are numerically EQUAL with different bit
patterns, and NaN is numerically UNEQUAL TO ITSELF with identical ones. The
byte loop gets both backwards.

`emit_eq_fn_for_type` already has an `IntType` arm that loads and compares
directly; there is simply no `FloatType` arm beside it.

WHY THE PLAIN STRUCT IS FINE: a non-shared struct's `==` goes through
`compile_struct_eq`, which extracts each field as a value and recurses through
`compile_binop` -- so a float field gets a real float comparison. Only the
shared walk, which works from pointers and per-field comparator functions,
reaches the byte loop.

REACHABILITY. `-0.0` is the practically important half. It arises from
ordinary arithmetic (negation, `x * -1.0`, underflow of a negative quantity,
many accumulations) with nothing exotic in the program, and the failure is a
`==` that answers `false` for two values every other part of the language
agrees are equal. NaN needs a deliberate `0.0 / 0.0` or a domain error.

NOTE THE `#[derive(Eq)]` BOUNDARY, which is why this is not a MAP-key bug:
the typechecker refuses `#[derive(Eq)]` on a struct with an `f64` field
("struct 'S' derives Eq but field 'x' has non-Eq type 'f64'"), and a Map key
needs `Eq`. So a float can only reach a comparator through `#[derive(PartialEq)]`
and the `==` operator. That same boundary is what makes
`emit_shared_struct_eq_fn`'s POINTER FAST PATH sound (B-2026-08-27-5 measured
it: `a == a` on a NaN-bearing struct answers `true` on the interpreter too),
so the fast path is NOT implicated here.

FIX SHAPE. A `FloatType` arm in `emit_eq_fn_for_type`, beside the `IntType`
one: load both and `build_float_compare(OEQ, ..)`, which gives `-0.0 == 0.0`
true and NaN false -- the IEEE semantics the interpreter and the scalar `==`
operator already implement. Check `Vec[f64]` at the same time: element
comparison routes through the same `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr`, so
`Vec[f64] == Vec[f64]` is likely to carry the identical defect (not measured).

SEVERITY medium: a silent wrong answer that differs between backends, and the
`-0.0` half is reachable from ordinary arithmetic; but it needs a `shared`
struct with a float field compared by `==`, and the plain-struct case -- the
common one -- is correct.
fix:
Fixed in cac21aa. The row's diagnosis was right and its SCOPE was wrong in
both directions -- too narrow about what was broken, and silent about what
must NOT change.

THE FIX is the arm the row predicted: a `FloatType` case in
`emit_eq_fn_for_type` beside the `IntType` one, comparing with `OEQ`
(ordered-and-equal). Not `UEQ`, which is true when either operand is NaN.

TOO NARROW. The row asserted "the PLAIN-struct `==` path is unaffected". That
holds only for a DIRECT float field. Per B-2026-08-12-5 a struct carrying a
Vec field is routed to the TYPE-DIRECTED comparator, so
`struct Pv { v: Vec[f64] }` was broken exactly like the shared cases. Four
routes reach the comparator family and all four were affected:

    shared struct, direct float field
    `Vec[f64]` ELEMENT (via the vec comparator)
    PLAIN struct with a Vec[f64] field
    plain struct nested inside a shared one

plus `f32` alongside `f64`. The row's suspicion that `Vec[f64] == Vec[f64]`
carried the same defect turned out to be unreachable for a different reason
-- see B-2026-08-27-10 -- but `Vec[f64]` AS A FIELD is reachable and was
broken.

TOO BROAD, and this is the half that mattered. A TOTAL-ORDER WRAPPER
(`F32`/`F64`/`F16`/`Bf16`) compares its float field BY BITS deliberately and
oppositely: two canonicalized NaNs are EQUAL, `-0.0` and `+0.0` are DISTINCT.
That is the entire reason those types exist -- bit equality is what gives
floats a total order, which is what lets one be a `Map` key or be sorted at
all -- and their hash hashes the same bits.

Widening the IEEE arm over them SPLIT HASH FROM EQ: two canonical-NaN keys
stopped comparing equal while still hashing together, so a `Map[F64, V]`
silently grew a second entry for one key. Measured precisely -- `m.len()`
1 -> 2 and `m.get(r)` 2 -> -1, with every other line of that program
unchanged, because the wrapper's `==` OPERATOR has its own bit-level lowering
and only its KEY comparator goes through the generic struct walk.

`test_e2e_total_order_wrapper_nan_canonicalized` caught it, doing exactly
what its own comment predicted: "a site that forgot would fail SILENTLY, with
equal keys hashing apart." `emit_eq_fn_for_struct` now diverts a wrapper's
field to an integer compare of matching width (reusing the existing `IntType`
arm -- the float slot reinterpreted at that width IS the bit pattern), and a
new test asserts the IEEE and bit behaviours side by side in ONE program so
the contrast cannot drift apart.

That also corrects a claim made while fixing B-2026-08-27-5: that floats can
never reach a hash/eq pairing because the typechecker refuses `#[derive(Eq)]`
on a float-bearing type. True of a BARE float, false in effect -- the wrapper
is `Eq`, is a legal key, and recurses into a float field. The code comment
asserting otherwise has been corrected rather than left to mislead.

TWO TEST-CONSTRUCTION HAZARDS, both hit here, both now documented in the
tests themselves because either one silently produces a passing test that
proves nothing:

  1. CONSTANT FOLDING. With `0.0 / 0.0` written inline, LLVM folds the whole
     comparison and yields the RIGHT answer without the emitted comparator
     ever running. The first draft of this fix looked correct for that reason
     while the runtime path was untouched; it only showed up when the NaN came
     from an opaque function. Operands now come from `nan64` / `negzero`.

  2. `0.0 - 0.0` IS `+0.0`, NOT `-0.0`. The first `negzero` helper was
     `return 0.0 - z`, so every negzero assertion compared `0.0` to `0.0` and
     held whatever the comparator did. The A/B against the unfixed compiler is
     what caught it -- those lines PASSED before the fix. It is `return -z`
     now, and the A/B re-run shows every assertion failing without the fix.

A THIRD FALSE LEAD, recorded because it cost time: a probe using struct names
`F32`/`F64` reported a divergence that was really a NAME COLLISION with the
prelude wrappers, not a float defect. Filed as B-2026-08-27-11 -- a user
struct named `F64` gets the wrapper's single-field comparison and answers
`true` for values differing in a second field. Renaming the probe made the
"divergence" vanish.

Tests: three-backend parity across the four routes and both widths, the
half-precision wrappers, and the wrapper-vs-plain contrast. A/B verified
against the unfixed compiler. Gates: codegen 3297, interpreter 1748,
memory_sanitizer 1223, typechecker 2530, cli 719, par_codegen 270,
drop_differential 19, lljit_e2e 16, example_corpus 2 -- zero failures; fmt
and both clippy legs clean. The runtime crate is untouched, so the wasm legs
are unaffected.

title: `Vec[T] == Vec[T]` IS ACCEPTED BY `karac check` AND `karac build`, EXECUTED BY BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS, AND REJECTED AT RUNTIME BY THE INTERPRETER -- which reports it as a type error the typechecker was supposed to have caught. Worse, the compiled answer is WRONG for heap elements: two `Vec[String]` with identical contents compare `false`. So the same program either dies on `--interp` or silently answers incorrectly under `karac build`.
detail:
FOUND while checking B-2026-08-27-9's suspicion that `Vec[f64] == Vec[f64]`
carried the float defect. It does not, because the comparison is not a
supported operation at all -- but the way it is unsupported is the bug.

THREE THINGS ARE WRONG AT ONCE, and they should be resolved together because
each one alone has an obvious but incompatible fix:

  1. The INTERPRETER's diagnostic asserts a fact that is false: it says "the
     typechecker reports as a hard error", and `karac check` on the same file
     prints "All checks passed." Either the typechecker lost the check or the
     message was written against an intended behaviour that never shipped.
  2. `karac build` ACCEPTS it. Whatever the answer to (1), build and check
     must agree with each other and with the interpreter about whether this
     program is legal.
  3. Codegen EXECUTES it and gets heap elements WRONG. `Vec[String]` with
     equal contents answers `false`, which means the emitted comparison is not
     `emit_eq_fn_for_vec` (that recurses per element into `karac_eq_String`)
     but something comparing the `{ptr,len,cap}` headers.

WHICH WAY IT SHOULD RESOLVE is a real design question, not obvious: design.md
§ Equality says `==` means structural equality via `Eq`, and a `Vec[T]` where
`T: Eq` has a perfectly good structural equality -- `emit_eq_fn_for_vec`
ALREADY IMPLEMENTS IT for Set/Map element use (B-2026-06-20-15). So "make
`Vec == Vec` legal and route it there" is at least as defensible as "reject
it in check and build". What is not defensible is the current state, where
the three components disagree.

SEVERITY high: it is a silent wrong ANSWER under `karac build` for the heap
case, and a run-vs-build split for every case. A program tested under
`--interp` cannot even reach the bug (it dies), so the failure mode is
"worked in testing, wrong in production" -- inverted from the usual.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-27-9: measured on that fix's commit both before and
after, and the `Vec[i64]` leg has no float in it.
fix:
RESOLVED by a7512aa in the direction design.md already specified: `Vec[T] == Vec[T]`
is LEGAL and compares CONTENTS. § Conditional `impl` Blocks gives the semantics
outright -- `impl[T: Eq] Eq for Vec[T] { self.len() == other.len() and
self.iter().zip(other.iter()).all(|(a, b)| a == b) }` -- so "reject it in check
and build", the row's other candidate, would have removed a capability the spec
grants and both backends already had.

THE ROW'S GUESS AT THE MECHANISM WAS WRONG, AND THE TRUTH MADE THE FIX SMALLER.
It read "something comparing the {ptr,len,cap} headers". It was not the headers:
`compile_binop`'s struct path dispatches on LLVM FIELD COUNT, and `String` and
`Vec` are both `{ ptr, i64, i64 }`, so a `Vec == Vec` landed in
`compile_string_binop` and was compared AS A STRING -- `len_eq &&
memcmp(min(len))` over the ELEMENT buffer, reading `len` BYTES of what are `len`
ELEMENTS. That single mechanism explains both symptoms the row filed as separate
puzzles: `[1,2] == [1,9]` answered TRUE (the leading two bytes of both i64
buffers are `01 00`), and two `Vec[String]` with equal contents answered FALSE
(it compared the low bytes of two heap pointers). A header comparison would have
answered FALSE to the first, which is what makes the distinction load-bearing
rather than pedantic.

THE DECISIVE MEASUREMENT: wrapping the SAME vec in a one-field
`#[derive(PartialEq)]` struct answers CORRECTLY on all three backends. The
struct-field path routes through `emit_eq_fn_for_struct` -> `emit_eq_fn_for_vec`,
which is the spec's comparator; the interpreter's derived-struct path uses
`Value`'s own element-wise `PartialEq`. So the correct comparator already
existed in BOTH backends and was already reachable one layer up -- only the bare
operator missed it. That reframes the fix from "implement Vec equality twice" to
"route two operator sites to what they already had", which is why it is ~40 lines
of routing and no new comparison logic.

WHAT LANDED, per component of the row's three-way disagreement:

  (1) The INTERPRETER's false diagnostic. It had no `Array` arm at all, so
      `Vec == Vec` fell to the catch-all whose message asserts "this is a type
      error the typechecker reports as a hard error". `karac check` printed "All
      checks passed." on the same file. The message was the wrong half: the
      typechecker has ADMITTED a `Vec` operand since B-2026-08-18-6
      (`type_supports_partial_eq` recurses into the element), deliberately and
      in line with the spec. Added the `Eq`/`NotEq` `Array` arms, which delegate
      to `Value`'s `PartialEq` -- the same comparator the `SharedStruct` arms
      directly above use, and the same one the derived-struct path already
      reached.

  (2) `karac build` ACCEPTING it. It still accepts it, because that is correct;
      what changed is that it now computes the right answer.

  (3) Codegen executing it wrongly. A type-exact intercept ahead of
      `compile_binop` routes a `Vec`-typed operand to `karac_eq_Vec_<T>`.

A SECOND MISS, FOUND ONLY BY PROBING PAST THE ROW: `ref Vec[T] == ref Vec[T]`
stayed silently wrong after the first cut of the fix -- still answering `true`
for differing contents. The first cut read `owned_temp_drops`, which keys on
`Type::Named{"Vec"}` and so has no entry for a `ref` param (`Type::Ref(Vec)`).
Widening THAT table was not an option: it drives scope-exit drops, so teaching
it about borrows would free a buffer the borrow does not own. The fix is a
dedicated `vec_eq_elem_types` span table that peels `ref`/`mut ref` exactly as
the typechecker's own `Eq` arm does (`strip_refs_for_compare`), so the borrowed
and owned shapes are one case in codegen because they are one case in the type
rule. Type-exactness is also what makes the intercept safe to place ahead of
`compile_binop`: an LLVM-shape test cannot tell a `Vec` from a `String` (that IS
this bug), and `var_elem_type_exprs` cannot tell a `Vec` from a `Slice` or a
`VecDeque`, so neither was usable.

A LEAK THE FIX ITSELF INTRODUCED, CAUGHT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. Returning early from
the intercept skipped the fresh-owned operand frees the fall-through path runs
for a String-shaped `Eq` (B-2026-08-11-24) -- and a `Vec` IS String-shaped, so
`ids() == ids()` leaked both element buffers: 192 bytes in 2 allocations under
LSan, where the pre-intercept build was clean. Mirroring the two
`free_fresh_owned_str_arg` calls in the intercept closes it. Worth recording as
a shape rather than an incident: an early return past a fall-through cleanup is
invisible to every correctness test, and the ASAN fixture is the only thing that
saw it.

VERIFIED on interp, JIT and AOT, byte-identical across all three: same-contents,
differing-contents, differing-length, empty-vs-full, self, `!=`, `ref` param,
nested `Vec[Vec[i64]]`, `Vec[f64]`, `Vec[bool]`, `Vec[char]`, `Vec[String]`, and
a `Vec` of a `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq)]` struct -- plus `String == String`
unchanged, since the intercept declines a non-`Vec` operand. Negative-controlled:
with the fix reverted the codegen fixture fails 4 of its 8 assertions, and the
interpreter fixture dies on the false diagnostic.

THREE SIBLINGS FOUND AND FILED SEPARATELY, not folded in: `Slice[T] == Slice[T]`
(check accepts, interpreter repeats the same false claim, codegen refuses as a
reference type), `Array[T, N] == Array[T, N]` (check accepts, interpreter answers
correctly, codegen refuses with a non-comparable `ArrayType`), and a PRE-EXISTING
element leak in `free_fresh_owned_str_arg` -- a fresh-temporary `Vec[String]`
operand leaks its element Strings (26 bytes in 4 allocations), measured
IDENTICALLY with this fix reverted, so it is that helper's buffer-only shape and
not this change.

title: A USER STRUCT NAMED `F64` / `F32` / `F16` / `Bf16` SILENTLY INHERITS THE PRELUDE TOTAL-ORDER WRAPPER'S COMPARISON, which compares ONE float field and ignores every other field -- so `F64 { x: 1.0, tag: 1 } == F64 { x: 1.0, tag: 2 }` answers `true` on the compiled backends and `false` on the interpreter. A FALSE-POSITIVE equality: the compiler reports two distinguishable values as equal. Affects plain and `shared` structs alike. The type's LAYOUT is correctly the user's (field reads return the user's fields), so only comparison is captured.
detail:
FOUND while probing B-2026-08-27-9: a fixture that happened to name its
structs `F32`/`F64` reported a float divergence that vanished on rename. The
false lead was worth the time -- the real finding is worse than the one being
probed.

CAUSE. The total-order wrapper machinery keys off the type NAME.
`is_total_float_wrapper_te` and `total_float_wrapper_widths` both match on the
bare strings "F32" | "F64" | "F16" | "Bf16" with no check that the type is the
PRELUDE one, so a user declaration of that name is treated as the wrapper by
every comparison site that consults them. The wrapper is a single-field
`{ float }` struct, so its comparison reads one float and stops -- which is
why a second field is ignored entirely.

WHY IT IS NOT CAUGHT BY THE EXISTING SHADOWING TEST.
`user_struct_shadowing_a_prelude_type_name_keeps_its_own_layout` asserts the
LAYOUT survives, and it does -- field reads are correct here too. Shadowing is
therefore a supported feature that is honoured in one subsystem and silently
overridden in another; the test covers exactly the half that works.

SEVERITY high. A false-positive equality is worse than a false negative: it
reports two distinguishable values as the same, so a dedup, a cache hit, a
`Map` key, or a guard clause silently takes the wrong branch rather than
merely doing redundant work. It needs an unlucky type name, but nothing warns
-- there is no diagnostic on redefining a prelude name.

FIX SHAPE. Two candidate directions, and the choice is a language decision
rather than a codegen detail:
  (a) Make the wrapper checks identity-based rather than name-based -- resolve
      to the prelude declaration and compare against it, so a user type of the
      same name is simply a different type. This preserves shadowing as the
      layout test already implies it is supported.
  (b) REJECT redefinition of a prelude type name with a diagnostic. Simpler
      and arguably kinder, but it contradicts the existing shadowing test and
      would be a breaking change for any code relying on it.
Whichever is chosen, the two subsystems must stop disagreeing about whether
shadowing is allowed.
fix:
Fixed in 374a8a3. The row posed the fix as a language decision between two
options; design.md had already decided it, and the implementation turned out
to be three holes behind one symptom rather than the single name test the row
described.

WHICH OPTION. design.md § Module System settles it against the row's option
(b): "Users can shadow prelude names in their own code (THE LANGUAGE DOES NOT
RESERVE THEM), though a lint warning flags the most-likely-unintended cases."
Prelude items are the lowest precedence level and "any explicit import or
wildcard import shadows a prelude name WITHOUT ERROR". So rejecting the
declaration was never on the table, and option (a) -- make the checks
identity-based -- is the only one consistent with the spec and with the
existing layout test.

THE MECHANISM WAS ALREADY BUILT. `user_shadowed_prelude_types` exists for
precisely this, separating a user declaration from the stdlib's own via
`stdlib_origin`, and `F32`/`F64`/`F16`/`Bf16` were already in
`PRELUDE_TYPES`. `types_lowering` even states the intended contract: "make the
user's type behave like the type they wrote ... refuse to run built-in
machinery over a user value, and stop describing a user value with built-in
machinery's layout." The wrapper sites simply never asked. All nine of them
now route through one `is_prelude_total_float_wrapper` predicate, so the fix
reaches comparison, `Display`, the sort comparator, `F64.from` and the iter
reduce path together rather than one symptom at a time.

THREE HOLES, each found only by testing the next declaration kind. Each alone
would have left the row half-fixed while the headline repro passed:

  1. THE SHADOW WAS NEVER RECORDED FOR A `shared struct`. The insert sat in
     the PLAIN branch of the struct-declaration split, under a comment calling
     itself "the one place that sees the override happen". So a
     `shared struct F64` was invisible to the set -- and not just here: every
     consumer (the built-in refusals, the `types_lowering` layout path, the
     HTTP client) was equally blind to a shared user shadow. Hoisted above the
     split.

  2. `vec_method` DID `.expect("F32/F64/F16/Bf16 have wrapper widths")` on a
     name-matched arm. The moment the predicate learned to decline, that
     `expect` would turn a legal program into a COMPILER PANIC. Now declines.

  3. DECLINING IS ONLY HALF THE FIX, and this is the part the row did not
     anticipate. `rewrite_binary` rewrites `a == b` into `T.eq(a, b)` whenever
     an impl table says `T: Eq` -- and that table is NAME-KEYED, so the
     stdlib's own `#[derive(Eq, Ord, Hash, ...)] struct F64` answers for a
     user `struct F64` that has no such impl. The call therefore still arrives
     in `compile_assoc_call`, and with the wrapper arm now declining it fell
     through to the unknown-callee tail and yielded a const `i64` 0. That is
     exactly the failure `rewrite_binary`'s own comment records ("the compiled
     binary printed a raw `0` instead of `true`"), and it printed as a
     plausible-looking `false` -- so the row's inequality repro looked FIXED
     while equality was silently broken.

     A lowered comparison on any shadowed prelude type is now compiled as what
     the source actually said, by REBUILDING THE BINARY EXPRESSION. Not by
     compiling both operands to values and calling `compile_binop`: a
     `shared struct` comparison resolves its type from the operand
     EXPRESSIONS, and two bare pointers carry no name -- that spelling was
     measured and reported the "structural `==` on this reference type is not
     yet supported" gap for a shape the unlowered operator compiles fine.

     Keyed on the shadow set rather than on the four float names, since any
     prelude type whose stdlib declaration carries a comparison derive can
     reach the same tail.

THE REAL WRAPPER IS UNCHANGED and is asserted alongside the fix rather than
left to its own tests: bit-level equality (two canonicalized NaNs EQUAL),
sorting, a `Map[F64, V]` where both NaN keys collide into one entry, and a
`Display` that prints the wrapped float rather than a struct form. With nine
name tests replaced at once, a predicate that is too eager silently demotes
the wrapper to an ordinary struct at any one of them, and that is not a
failure any wrapper test would attribute to this change.

NOT FIXED, and worth stating plainly: the ROOT is that the typechecker's impl
table is name-keyed, so the stdlib's impls answer for a user type of the same
name. This fix corrects the observable behaviour at the codegen boundary; it
does not make the impl table identity-aware. A user `struct F64` still
type-checks as though it had `Eq`/`Ord`/`Hash`/`Copy` it never declared, which
is why the lowered-call fallback has to exist at all. Filed as
B-2026-08-27-14.

Also noted while measuring: `karac check` emits NO diagnostic for a
declaration that shadows a prelude type name, though design.md promises "a
lint warning flags the most-likely-unintended cases" and refers to "the
standard prelude-shadow lint" in three places. Filed as B-2026-08-27-15.

Tests: three declaration kinds (plain, `shared`, `#[derive(Eq)]`) across three
backends, plus the wrapper-integrity guard. A/B verified against the unfixed
compiler -- the shadowed test fails there, and the guard passes both ways by
design, which is what a guard is for. An EQUALITY assertion sits beside the
inequality ones specifically because the const-0 tail prints as `false`.
Gates: codegen 3300, interpreter 1750, memory_sanitizer 1223, typechecker
2530, cli 719, par_codegen 270, drop_differential 19, lljit_e2e 16,
example_corpus 2 -- zero failures; fmt and both clippy legs clean. The runtime
crate is untouched, so the wasm legs are unaffected.

FIXED by 51d68e9. The declines are gone: the walk now RESOLVES a payload's
type and READS it correctly instead of pointer-casting into the words and
refusing wherever that is invalid.

Reading a payload is the entire fix, and there are three ways the words are
not the value. Each gets a read mode, chosen per field at plan time:

  Direct   the words ARE the value -- every scalar, `String`/`Vec`/`Slice`, a
           Map/Set handle, a `shared` pointer, and any struct whose fields land
           on word boundaries. A pair of GEPs, exactly as before, so the common
           key pays nothing for the new coverage.
  Rebuild  `struct { a: i32, b: i32, s: String }` spends three word runs where
           LLVM packs the two `i32`s into eight bytes, shifting every field
           after the first. Load the words and rebuild through
           `reconstruct_struct_from_words` -- the maintained reader for this
           stream, shared with match-arm binding -- into an entry-block slot.
  Boxed    NOT ANTICIPATED BY THE ROW, and the reason the generic leg is more
           than substitution: `enum Box1[T] { One(T) }` allots `T` ONE word
           from its erased layout, so a `String` argument does not fit and
           construction heap-BOXED it. The word holds a box pointer, and the
           box holds the value at its real LLVM type, so deboxing IS the field
           pointer -- no rebuild needed.

Generic payload types resolve by substituting the instantiation, so the plan is
keyed on the full `TypeExpr` rather than a bare name. That forced the
comparator's NAME to carry the instantiation too, which the row did not
foresee: `mangled_type_name` drops generic arguments, so `Option[String]` and
`Option[i64]` would have shared one `karac_eq_Option` and whichever was emitted
first would have answered for both. `display_mangle_te` renders a non-generic
enum as its bare name, so concrete enums keep the symbol they had.

WORD OFFSETS COME FROM THE ERASED LAYOUT, not from recomputed resolved widths.
The row's fix shape pointed at `compile_enum_eq`, which recomputes them
sequentially; that is right only while every field fits its allotment. The
erased table is what CONSTRUCTION wrote against, and a field overflowing its
allotment there is precisely the boxing signal `reconstruct_payload_value`
unpacks with, so the same table answers both questions.

CORRECTION TO THE ROW, measured after the fix landed. It said both shapes were
ones "`compile_enum_eq` ALREADY HANDLES ON THE `==` SIDE". Only half true:

  * The sub-word struct leg is wrong on the `==` side too. `compile_enum_eq`
    rebuilds a field only when it occupies <= 3 words and otherwise falls to a
    best-effort word-wise compare, and `{ i32, i32, String }` is five. So
    `x == y` on that shape answered `false` as well -- the divergence the row
    described (`==` right, `contains_key` wrong) does not exist there.
  * The generic leg is worse than wrong on the `==` side: `Box1[String] ==
    Box1[String]` PANICS THE COMPILER, because the sequential offsets walk off
    the end of the erased area and `build_extract_value` is unwrapped. Filed
    separately with its own repro; it predates this fix (the only change to
    `expr_ops.rs` here is one visibility widening).

TESTS. An E2E/interpreter pair, both confirmed to fail with the fix reverted:
`test_e2e_a_generic_or_sub_word_enum_key_is_matched_by_content` and
`a_generic_or_sub_word_enum_key_is_matched_by_content`. They cover all three
read modes, both generic forms (single-field boxed, multi-field boxed),
`Option`/`Result`, scalar and payload-free controls that were already correct,
a `-ne` line per shape, and `Set` dedup plus `remove` for the hash twin. Two
LIVE INSTANTIATIONS of one generic enum in one program is the line that catches
the shared-symbol collision -- reverted, the fixture prints every heap-bearing
case `false` and `dedup=2 removed=1` while `opt-none`, `res-err`, `scalar` and
the scalar instantiation stay correct.
title: THE MAP/SET ENUM KEY COMPARATOR DECLINES TWO PAYLOAD SHAPES THAT `compile_enum_eq` ALREADY HANDLES ON THE `==` SIDE, so `Map[Option[String], V]` and an enum whose payload struct has two consecutive sub-word fields ahead of a heap field still miss a structurally-equal key on the compiled backends while `x == y` on the same two values answers `true`. B-2026-08-27-6 closed the general case; `enum_structural_key_plan` returns `None` for both of these, leaving them on the byte compare.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-6 and measured after it landed -- this is what
that fix's two declines leave behind, filed rather than left implicit in a
predicate.

CAUSE, one per leg, and they are the same cause seen twice: the key comparator
reads a payload by POINTER-CASTING into the payload words, which is only valid
where the word image is the value.

  * GENERIC. `enum_structural_key_plan` bails whenever
    `enum_generic_param_names` is non-empty: the payload's declared type is the
    parameter `T`, and resolving that name anyway would find a USER type that
    happens to share it -- the B-2026-08-03-5 hazard the drop walker guards
    identically.
  * SUB-WORD STRUCT. `payload_words_match_llvm_layout` bails because
    `coerce_to_payload_words` writes one i64 stream per source field, so
    `{ i32, i32, String }` spends three word-runs where LLVM packs the two
    `i32`s into eight bytes. Field 1 is at byte 4 and word offset 8; every
    field after it is misread.

FIX SHAPE, and the reason these are ONE row rather than two: `compile_enum_eq`
(`expr_ops.rs`, the `==` operator's enum path) already solves both. It
substitutes generic params through `enum_param_subst` + `subst_type_params`,
and it does not pointer-cast -- it REBUILDS each payload from its word run, the
same way a match arm binds one. Teaching the key comparator to read payloads
that way (reconstruct into an alloca, then hand the alloca to the child
comparator) would retire `payload_words_match_llvm_layout` for aggregate
payloads and the generic decline in one move; the scalar / String / Vec /
shared cases stay direct, where the word image genuinely IS the value. Eq and
hash must move together, as everywhere else in this family.

SEVERITY medium. The generic leg is the more common shape by some distance --
`Option[String]` and `Result[String, E]` are ordinary map keys where a user
`enum E[T]` is rare -- and the divergence is the awkward kind: the same two
values compare equal with `==` and fail to find each other in a `Map`, in one
program, on one backend.

fix:
FIXED by 6aead97. `Vec.contains` now compares through the ELEMENT'S OWN
comparator -- `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr`, the one `Map` and `Set` already use
-- instead of `compile_binop` on two loaded aggregates. The element is already
addressable inside the buffer, so only the needle needs a stack slot; the
comparator is emitted before the loop blocks because synthesis moves the
builder's insert point. An element with no recorded `TypeExpr` keeps the old
value-wise path.

Routing EVERY element type through one comparator was the choice rather than
teaching `compile_struct_eq` to recognise an enum: at that point it holds LLVM
values with no type name and no variant list to walk. The side benefit is that
`shared` and GENERIC elements come along for free -- both now reach the same
fixed comparator instead of each needing an arm here.

SCOPE SWEEP, which the row left open ("other value-wise comparison sites
reached the same way ... only `contains` is measured here"). Every
`compile_binop(&BinOp::Eq, ...)` call site outside `expr_ops.rs` was checked:

  * `Vec.contains` -- this row, fixed.
  * `Array.contains` (`method_call.rs`) -- same shape in codegen, but
    UNREACHABLE from the surface language: the typechecker answers "no method
    'contains' on type 'Array'". No user program can hit it, so nothing was
    changed there.
  * `assert_eq` / `assert_ne` (`test_assert.rs`) -- SAME DEFECT, and confirmed
    live: two structurally-equal enums with `String` payloads pass on the
    interpreter and FAIL the assertion on the compiled backends. That is the
    worst member of the family, since it silently flips a test's verdict.
    Filed separately; not folded in here because it has the operand
    EXPRESSIONS available and so wants the `compile_enum_eq` interception
    rather than this fix's pointer route.
  * `control_flow_match.rs`'s literal compare -- scrutinee against a LITERAL
    pattern, which is never an enum aggregate. Not affected.

So the row's guess at a family was right, but not in the shape it guessed:
`index_of` / `position` / `SortedVec`-style search do not exist as separate
value-wise sites, and the real sibling was the assertion helper.

TESTS. An E2E/interpreter pair, confirmed to fail with the fix reverted:
`test_e2e_vec_contains_matches_an_enum_element_by_content` and
`vec_contains_matches_an_enum_element_by_content`. Struct-variant, tuple-
variant, unit-variant, generic (`Option[String]`), and `shared` elements, with
`String` / struct / `i64` controls that were already correct and a `-ne` line
per shape. EVERY PAYLOAD IS BUILT BY A FUNCTION CALL rather than a literal:
two identical string literals can fold to one global, which would let a
pointer compare answer `true` and hide the defect, so distinct allocations are
what make the test able to fail.
title: `Vec.contains` COMPARES AN ENUM ELEMENT'S RAW PAYLOAD WORDS, reaching NEITHER of the compiler's two structural enum comparators, so `vec![E.A(f"yy")].contains(E.A(f"yy"))` is `false` on the compiled backends and `true` on the interpreter. It calls `compile_binop` on LOADED VALUES, so the `==` operator's `enum_name_of_expr` interception has no operand expression to resolve and the aggregate falls to `compile_struct_eq`'s field-wise i64 compare over `{tag, w0, w1, ...}`.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-6, and measured to PREDATE it: the same program
gives the same wrong answer with that fix reverted, so this is an independent
gap rather than a remainder of it.

CAUSE. `Vec.contains` (`vec_method.rs`) loads `data[i]` and the needle as SSA
values and calls `compile_binop(&BinOp::Eq, elem_val, needle_val)`. Both of the
