compiler's structural enum comparators are out of reach from there:
`compile_enum_eq` is selected at the `==` OPERATOR site in `exprs.rs` by
running `enum_name_of_expr` over the operand EXPRESSIONS, which this call site
does not have; and `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` (the Map/Set family, which grew
its enum arm in B-2026-08-27-6) takes pointers, not values. So the aggregate
falls through to `compile_struct_eq`, whose per-field recursion over an enum's
`{tag, w0, w1, ...}` compares payload words as i64s -- a heap pointer compare
for any payload that owns heap.

FIX SHAPE. `Vec.contains` already knows the element's `TypeExpr` (it is a Vec
method on a tracked variable), so the direct repair is to stop comparing loaded
values: spill the needle and the element to stack slots and call
`emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr(&elem_te)` on the two pointers, exactly as `Set` and
`Map` do. That makes it structural for EVERY element type in one move rather
than enum by enum, and it inherits the enum arm already there. The narrower
alternative -- teach `compile_struct_eq` to recognise an enum aggregate -- is
worse: it has only LLVM values at that point, with no type name and no variant
list to walk.

SCOPE NOT YET SWEPT: other value-wise comparison sites reached the same way
(`Vec.index_of` / `position` / `remove_item`-family, `Slice` equivalents, and
any `SortedVec`-style search) plausibly share this, since the shape is "compare
two loaded aggregates without their TypeExpr". Only `contains` is measured
here; the fix above would cover the family if they route through one helper.

SEVERITY medium: a silent wrong `false` from an ordinary collection query, on
one backend only, with the interpreter disagreeing.

title: THE IMPL TABLE IS NAME-KEYED, so a user type that shadows a prelude name SILENTLY INHERITS THE STDLIB TYPE'S TRAIT IMPLS. A user `struct F64 { x: i64, tag: i64 }` with NO derives passes `karac check` and compiles `a == b`, while the identical `struct Other` is correctly rejected with "type 'Other' does not implement PartialEq; add #[derive(PartialEq)]". The compiler then attributes the borrowed impl TO THE USER: the Map-key diagnostic reads "you have written `impl Eq for F64`" for an impl they never wrote.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-11, and it is that row's ROOT. The fix there
corrects the observable behaviour at the codegen boundary -- a shadowing type
now gets its own comparison rather than the total-order wrapper's -- but it
could not make the impl table identity-aware, and the fallback it had to add
(`compile_assoc_call` recompiling a lowered `T.eq(a, b)` as an ordinary
comparison) exists ONLY because this row is open. Closing this one should
make that fallback dead code; check it at the same time.

NOT LIMITED TO THE FLOAT WRAPPERS. The mechanism is `rewrite_binary`'s gate
in `src/lowering.rs`, which asks whether the impl table lists `T: Eq` /
`T: PartialOrd` for the NAME, and the same name-keying is what lets the
typechecker accept `==` in the first place. Every prelude type with a
declared impl can lend it: measured on `F64`, and the shape generalizes to
any `PRELUDE_TYPES` entry whose stdlib declaration carries a derive.

WHY THIS IS `soundness` RATHER THAN `diagnostics`. The program is accepted
with a capability it never declared, and the capability is then EXERCISED --
the comparison runs. Before B-2026-08-27-11 it ran the stdlib type's
comparator over the user's layout, which is where the false-positive equality
came from. The diagnostic that mis-attributes the impl is a symptom, not the
defect.

design.md § Module System is unambiguous that the declaration itself is
legal: "Users can shadow prelude names in their own code (the language does
not reserve them), though a lint warning flags the most-likely-unintended
cases." So the fix is not to reject the program -- it is for the impl lookup
to resolve the type IDENTITY, not its name, so a user `F64` simply has no
`Eq` until the user derives one.

FIX SHAPE. The typechecker needs the same discrimination codegen already has
in `user_shadowed_prelude_types` (populated from `stdlib_origin`, so it
already distinguishes a user declaration from a spliced stdlib one). Either
carry that set into the impl-table lookup, or key the table on a resolved
type id rather than a bare name. The second is the real fix and is the same
change `types_lowering`'s comment calls for: "The real fix is
module-qualified stdlib types (`http.Response` as a distinct type)" --
already tracked in that form as B-2026-08-02-13, which this row shares a root
with.

SEVERITY high: a program is accepted and run with trait behaviour it never
asked for, silently, and the compiler's own diagnostic tells the author they
wrote code they did not write -- which is the worst kind of wrong, because it
sends them looking for an impl that does not exist in their source.
fix:
Fixed in e17ecdf. The row's diagnosis was right and its FIX SHAPE named the
wrong layer -- it proposed carrying `user_shadowed_prelude_types` into the
impl-table lookup, and lookup is exactly where the fix does NOT work.

WHERE THE IMPLS COME FROM. Not from the stdlib source at all, which is what
the row assumed. `runtime/stdlib/f64.kara`'s `#[derive(Eq, Ord, Hash, ...)]`
is a red herring: native derives are skipped by `expand_derives` and
synthesize no impl. The `Eq`/`Ord` impls for `F32`/`F64`/`F16`/`Bf16` are
seeded in RUST, in `register_stdlib_impls`, on the same list as the integer
and `String` builtin operator impls. That list is keyed on bare names, and
those four are ordinary struct names a user may take.

WHY LOOKUP-TIME FILTERING IS NOT ENOUGH, measured rather than reasoned. The
first attempt did exactly what the row proposed -- skip a compiler-internal
impl (`target_span == None`) in `Env::find_impl` when the target is
user-declared. It fixed the typecheck error and NOTHING ELSE, because
`env.impls` feeds four consumers and `find_impl` is one:

    has_impl            the typecheck gate           (fixed)
    trait_impls         `rewrite_binary`'s gate      (still live)
    trait_impl_methods  the same lowering pass       (still live)
    find_method         method resolution            (still live)

So `a == b` was still rewritten into a `T.eq(a, b)` nothing implements, which
reaches codegen's unknown-callee tail as a const `i64` 0 -- and prints as a
plausible-looking `false`, which is how that half hides. Filtering the two
lowering sets as well worked, but at that point the fix was three filters
maintaining one invariant.

SKIPPING AT THE SEEDING is one place and covers all four by construction. The
recipe is not new: `register_baked_stdlib` already computes exactly this set
-- `self.program.items` filtered on `!stdlib_origin`, guarded by
`compiling_stdlib` -- to drop stdlib source items a user redefines, under a
comment stating the rule this row needed all along: "the user's definition
(and its impls) must own the name". The Rust-seeded impls were simply outside
that skip.

A SECOND DISCRIMINATOR THAT LOOKED RIGHT AND IS NOT. `StructInfo` carries
`defining_stdlib_origin`, and the obvious move is to key off it. Measured: it
is `false` for the STDLIB'S OWN `F32`/`F64`/`F16`/`Bf16`, so a filter built on
it strips the real wrapper's impls too -- five wrapper tests failed, including
`test_e2e_total_order_wrapper_nan_canonicalized`. The flag is unreliable for
spliced prelude declarations; `self.program.items` + `stdlib_origin` is the
one that holds.

THIS RETIRES B-2026-08-27-11's CODEGEN FALLBACK, as that row predicted. The
`compile_assoc_call` arm that recompiled a lowered `T.eq(a, b)` as an ordinary
comparison existed only because this row was open. Verified by DISABLING it
and re-running that row's fixtures -- all correct -- before deleting the 54
lines, rather than assuming deadness from the argument.

WHAT THE USER SEES NOW. A user `struct F64` with no derives gets the same
diagnostic as an identically-shaped `struct Other`: "type 'F64' does not
implement PartialEq; add #[derive(PartialEq)]". The mis-attributing clause is
gone -- the Map-key diagnostic no longer claims "you have written `impl Eq for
F64`" about source that does not exist. Deriving `PartialEq` on the shadowing
type makes `==` legal exactly as on any other name, which is the half a
too-broad fix would have broken and which has its own test.

NOT CHANGED, and worth being explicit since the row called this the root: the
impl table is still NAME-keyed. What changed is that the compiler no longer
SEEDS a builtin impl under a name the user has taken. A user `impl Eq for
F64` they write themselves still registers and still applies -- `target_span`
is what separates a real impl from a seeded one, and only seeded ones are
skipped. Module-qualified stdlib types (B-2026-08-02-13's "real fix") remain
the general answer.

Tests: the shadowed/control pair asserting IDENTICAL diagnostics for two
declarations differing only in NAME -- the property, so either side drifting
is the bug returning -- plus the derive guard. A/B verified against the
unfixed compiler. Gates: typechecker 2534, codegen 3306, interpreter 1754,
memory_sanitizer 1224, cli 719, par_codegen 270, example_corpus/packages,
book_snippets, design_md_code_blocks -- zero failures; fmt and both clippy
legs clean. The runtime crate is untouched.

title: THE PRELUDE-SHADOW LINT DOES NOT EXIST. design.md refers to it in three places as shipped behaviour -- "a lint warning flags the most-likely-unintended cases", "the standard prelude-shadow lint", "the lint flagged at § Module System — Prelude catches accidental shadowing" -- but declaring `struct F64`, `struct Map` or `struct Option` produces NO diagnostic: `karac check` prints "All checks passed."
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-11. Not the cause of anything there -- the
shadowing declaration is LEGAL by design ("the language does not reserve
them") and the bug was that codegen ignored the shadow. But the lint is the
mechanism design.md relies on to make the legality safe, and it is absent, so
a shadowing that is about to behave surprisingly arrives with no warning at
all.

WHAT design.md CLAIMS, verbatim, in three separate places:

  § Module System — Prelude: "Users can shadow prelude names in their own code
  (the language does not reserve them), though A LINT WARNING FLAGS THE
  MOST-LIKELY-UNINTENDED CASES."

  § Module System, stdlib modules row: "Local bindings can shadow them with
  THE STANDARD PRELUDE-SHADOW LINT."

  § Raw Pointer Construction: "The cost — `ptr` becomes a prelude module name
  that local bindings can shadow — is minor; THE LINT FLAGGED AT § Module
  System — Prelude catches accidental shadowing of prelude items."

The third sentence is the one that matters most: a design decision is
justified BY the lint's existence. That justification is currently unbacked.

SCOPE NOT MEASURED. This row tests TYPE names only. design.md's wording
covers local BINDINGS shadowing prelude module names (`ptr`, `env`, `fs`)
too, and those are not checked here -- a fix should establish which cases the
lint is meant to cover before deciding what "most-likely-unintended" means.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING WARNING USUALLY WOULD: the codebase
already carries several bugs whose whole shape is "a name-keyed built-in path
captured a user type of the same name" -- B-2026-08-02-13 (HTTP `Response` /
`HttpError` double-free), B-2026-08-15-12 (a shadowed enum), and
B-2026-08-27-11 (the float wrappers). Each was found by someone tripping over
it. The lint is the cheap general defence, and it is the one part of the
design that was never built.

SEVERITY low: it is a missing warning on a legal program, not a wrong answer.
Filed because design.md states it as shipped in three places, so the gap is a
spec/implementation divergence rather than an unimplemented idea -- and
because the sentence in § Raw Pointer Construction leans on it as
justification.
fix:
Fixed in e17ecdf. The lint now exists, is on by default, and is suppressible
per declaration with `#[allow(prelude_shadow)]`.

WHAT IT DOES. A user `struct`/`enum` declaration whose name is in
`PRELUDE_TYPES` emits `warning[prelude_shadow]` at the declaration, naming the
consequence -- built-in paths keyed on that name no longer apply to this type
-- and stating plainly that the declaration is legal. Skips `stdlib_origin`
declarations and stdlib self-compiles, or every spliced prelude source would
flag itself.

THE SUPPRESSION IS THE PART THAT NEEDED CARE. `type_lint_warning` consults the
lint-override cascade, and the declaration's own `lint_overrides` frame has to
be pushed for the emit or `#[allow(prelude_shadow)]` parses and is SILENTLY
IGNORED. That failure mode is worse than having no lint at all: the author
writes the documented suppression, gets the warning anyway, and has no way to
tell whether the attribute or the lint is broken. The first cut had exactly
that bug; `warn_module_mut_binding`'s push/pop shape is what fixes it, and a
test asserts both directions.

SCOPE, WHICH THE ROW LEFT OPEN. It noted that design.md says "most-likely-
UNINTENDED cases" without defining them, and that a fix should establish which
cases the lint covers before deciding. Measured across the corpus rather than
argued:

    94 example programs, 9 warn
    Response x4 · Request x2 · Stats · Parser · Json · Entry · Command

Every one is an APPLICATION-DOMAIN NOUN. ZERO examples shadow core vocabulary
-- nothing in the corpus declares `Vec`, `Option`, `Map`, `Set` or `Result`.
That is the answer to the row's question: a general lint costs ~10% of
examples in noise, all of it deliberate domain shadowing, and it costs nothing
on the structural types where an accidental shadow would actually be
surprising.

So the lint stays GENERAL (any `PRELUDE_TYPES` name) and the nine deliberate
shadows are annotated with `#[allow(prelude_shadow)]` plus a one-line reason.
The alternative -- narrowing the warn-set to a hand-drawn "core vocabulary"
list -- was rejected because the partition would be my taxonomy rather than
the spec's, and `Response` is precisely the name that caused B-2026-08-02-13's
double free, so silencing it by category is the wrong default. Narrowing
remains a one-line change if the noise proves unwelcome; the measurement above
is what that decision should be made against.

SCOPE NOT COVERED, restated so it is not mistaken for done: this warns on TYPE
declarations only. design.md's wording also covers local BINDINGS shadowing
prelude MODULE names (`ptr`, `env`, `fs`) -- the case § Raw Pointer
Construction leans on the lint for -- and that is untouched here. It needs a
different emission site (binding introduction, not item declaration) and a
different name set (`PRELUDE_MODULES`, not `PRELUDE_TYPES`).

Registered as `E0282`/`W0282` in the JSON diagnostic map, alongside the other
lint kinds.

Tests: the firing set (asserting exactly the two PRELUDE names in a
three-declaration program warn, so a lint that fires on everything fails) and
the suppression. A/B verified against the unfixed compiler. Gates: typechecker
2534, codegen 3306, interpreter 1754, memory_sanitizer 1224, cli 719,
example_corpus/packages, book_snippets, design_md_code_blocks -- zero
failures; fmt and both clippy legs clean.

FIXED by 752e0b9, together with B-2026-08-27-17 (one commit: the second row is
what happens when the decision this one fixes has two copies).

THE CRASH. `compile_enum_eq` packed per-field offsets sequentially from the
RESOLVED field widths, which holds only while every field still fits the
allotment the ERASED layout reserved. When it does not,
`coerce_to_payload_words` heap-BOXED the field into one word at construction,
so the sum indexed past an area that never held those words and
`build_extract_value` returned an unwrapped `Err`. Offsets now come from the
erased table -- what construction actually wrote against -- and a field
overflowing its allotment there is precisely the boxing signal
`reconstruct_payload_value` unpacks with. Same rule `enum_structural_key_plan`
follows, which is the point: the two enum comparators now answer the layout
question the same way.

THE WIDE-PAYLOAD LEG. Every field is now materialised as a POINTER and handed
to `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` -- the family Map/Set keys go through -- instead
of being rebuilt into a VALUE and passed to `compile_binop`. That fixes the
>3-word word-wise compare the row named, and it removes a dependency that
turned out to be a trap: `compile_binop` dispatches an aggregate by FIELD
COUNT, so a three-field user struct is indistinguishable there from a
`String`'s `{ptr,len,cap}` and lands in `compile_string_binop`, which reads
field 0 as a pointer and PANICS. The first version of this fix hit exactly
that. Filed separately; this route no longer depends on its outcome.

A SOUNDNESS FIX THE ROW DID NOT ANTICIPATE, and the reason to read this entry.
The payload walk is now GATED ON TAG EQUALITY. The switch dispatches on the
LEFT tag, so with mismatched tags it still entered that variant's block and
read the RIGHT operand's words as that variant's payload. That was harmless
while those reads were integer extracts feeding an `icmp` -- the tag
conjunction discarded the answer -- but this fix DEREFERENCES a field: a boxed
payload is `inttoptr` + load, and a rebuilt one is loaded through by its own
comparator. An uninitialised word from a unit variant is then a wild pointer.
`Box1.One(s) == Box1.Nil` SEGFAULTED under the JIT and read out of bounds
under AOT. Caught only because the fixture compared a payload-carrying variant
against a payload-free one on all three backends; the AOT leg alone did not
fault. Every `-tag` line in the regression test exists for this.

CORRECTION TO THE ROW. Its "SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME FUNCTION" named
`struct { a: i32, b: i32, s: String }` as an example of the `n <= 3` rebuild
gate. Wrong attribution: that enum never reaches `compile_enum_eq` at all.
`enum_drop_kind_for_type_expr` refuses to classify a payload struct
`NestedStruct` unless it is word-ALIGNED, so a struct with two consecutive
sub-word fields classifies `None`, `enum_has_heap_payload` reports false, and
the operator site never selects the structural comparator. The `n <= 3` gate
IS real and IS fixed -- `struct Big { a: i64, b: i64, s: String }` (five words,
word-aligned) is the shape that actually exercises it, and it is in the test.
The alignment gate is filed as its own row.

TESTS. An E2E/interpreter pair confirmed to fail with the fix reverted:
`test_e2e_enum_eq_handles_a_boxed_or_wide_generic_payload` and
`enum_eq_handles_a_boxed_or_wide_generic_payload`. Single-field boxed
(`Box1[String]`), multi-field boxed (`Pair2[String]`), the word-aligned wide
struct payload, `Option[String]`, a scalar-payload control that was already
correct, a `-ne` line per shape, and one `-tag` line per READ MODE, since each
dereferences differently. Every payload is built by a function call so no
literal folding can let a pointer compare pass.
title: `==` ON A GENERIC ENUM WHOSE ARGUMENT OVERFLOWS ITS ERASED PAYLOAD ALLOTMENT PANICS THE COMPILER, so `Box1[String] == Box1[String]` for `enum Box1[T] { One(T) }` aborts `karac build` with an unwrap failure in `compile_enum_eq` instead of compiling. The function recomputes per-field word offsets SEQUENTIALLY from the resolved field widths, but the enum's payload AREA is sized from the erased parameter (one word for `T`), so a three-word `String` walks `build_extract_value` straight off the end of the aggregate.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-12, and measured to PREDATE it: the only
change that row made to `expr_ops.rs` is widening `enum_param_subst` to
`pub(super)`, so the crash is reachable on `main` before and after.

CAUSE. `compile_enum_eq` deliberately does NOT read
`layout.field_word_offsets`, and its comment explains why -- a seeded generic
layout records a variant's whole payload span as one entry, which says nothing
about where a field begins once `T` is known. It packs sequentially from word 0
by each RESOLVED field's own width instead. That is correct exactly while every
field still FITS the allotment the erased layout reserved. When it does not,
`coerce_to_payload_words` heap-BOXES the field into a single word at
construction, so the value in the area is one box pointer -- while the
sequential walk believes three inline words are there and indexes
`build_extract_value(lhs, start + 1 + j)` past the aggregate's field count. The
result is an unwrapped `Err`, i.e. a compiler panic rather than a wrong answer.

FIX SHAPE, and it is already written down next door: B-2026-08-27-12 solved the
same question for the map/set comparator. Take offsets from the ERASED table
(what construction actually wrote against), and treat a field whose resolved
width EXCEEDS its allotment as boxed -- load the word, `inttoptr`, and the box
holds the value at its real LLVM type, which is how `reconstruct_payload_value`
already reads one back. The two comparators would then agree by construction
instead of by coincidence.

SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME FUNCTION, worth fixing in the same pass: a field
occupying MORE THAN THREE words falls to a best-effort word-wise compare
(`n <= 3` gates the rebuild). For a payload struct that owns heap -- e.g.
`struct { a: i32, b: i32, s: String }`, five words -- that compares the
`String`'s heap POINTER, so `x == y` answers `false` for equal contents. No
crash, just a silent wrong answer, and the same rebuild the map/set side now
does would close it.

SEVERITY high: a compiler crash on a legal program is worse than a wrong
answer, since no workaround exists short of not writing the comparison.

fix:
FIXED by 752e0b9, alongside B-2026-08-27-16.

The decision "does this compiled `==` on two enum operands take the structural
comparator" now lives in ONE function, `try_compile_enum_operand_eq`, called by
both `compile_expr`'s `Binary` arm and `test_assert.rs`. That is the whole fix:
the operator site had the structural path all along, and the assertion helper
simply never consulted it -- it compiled its operands and called
`compile_binop`, which dispatches an aggregate by shape and sent the enum to
the word-wise `compile_struct_eq`, comparing a heap-owning payload's POINTER
words.

As the row predicted, this site differs from `Vec.contains` (B-2026-08-27-13)
in what it can reach: `assert_eq` HAS the operand expressions, so
`enum_name_of_expr` can name the type and the operator's own path applies,
where `Vec.contains` held only loaded values and had to be routed to the
pointer comparator instead.

Also as the row predicted, the target inherited whatever `compile_enum_eq` got
wrong -- which is why the two were fixed in one commit rather than in sequence.
An `assert_eq` over `Box1[String]` would have hit -16's compiler panic on the
way to being correct.

TESTS. An E2E/interpreter pair confirmed to fail with the fix reverted:
`test_e2e_assert_eq_compares_an_enum_by_content` and
`assert_eq_compares_an_enum_by_content`. Struct-variant, tuple-variant and
unit-variant payloads, a cross-TAG `assert_ne`, a generic enum
(`Option[String]`), and struct / string / int controls that were already
correct. Both directions are asserted -- `assert_eq` on equal values and
`assert_ne` on different ones -- because the defect flips a verdict, so a test
that only checked one direction could pass on a comparator that answered a
constant. Every payload is built by a function call rather than a literal:
folded string globals would let a pointer compare answer `true` and hide it.
title: `assert_eq` / `assert_ne` COMPARE AN ENUM'S PAYLOAD WORDS INSTEAD OF ITS CONTENTS, so a Kara test asserting two structurally-equal enums with heap payloads PASSES on the interpreter and FAILS on the compiled backends. `test_assert.rs` calls `compile_binop` on two already-compiled VALUES, which cannot reach `compile_enum_eq` (selected at the `==` operator site from the operand EXPRESSIONS) nor `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` (which takes pointers), so the aggregate falls to `compile_struct_eq`'s field-wise i64 compare over `{tag, w0, w1, ...}`.
detail:
FOUND during the scope sweep for B-2026-08-27-13, which fixed the same defect
at `Vec.contains`. Filed separately rather than folded in because the fix is
different in kind: `Vec.contains` had no operand expressions and had to be
routed to the POINTER comparator, while `assert_eq` holds `args[0].value` and
`args[1].value` and can reach the structural `==` path directly.

WHY THIS IS THE WORST MEMBER OF THE FAMILY. Every other site returns a wrong
value that a program might notice. This one flips a TEST VERDICT: an assertion
over enums silently reports failure where the language says the values are
equal, so a correct program looks broken and -- for `assert_ne` -- a broken one
looks correct. It also lands on exactly the code most likely to be written
while dogfooding the language.

FIX SHAPE. Lift the operator-site enum interception out of `exprs.rs` (the
`enum_name_of_expr` + `enum_inst_type_of_expr` + `enum_has_heap_payload` block
that routes to `compile_enum_eq`) into a helper taking the two operand `Expr`s
and their compiled values, and call it from both `exprs.rs` and
`test_assert.rs`. That keeps ONE definition of "how a compiled `==` on an enum
is decided", which is the property whose absence produced this row. Note the
target inherits whatever `compile_enum_eq` itself gets wrong -- see the
generic-overflow crash and the >3-word word-wise fallback filed alongside this
-- so the two are best fixed in one pass.

SCOPE. `assert_ne` shares the code path and the defect (verified in the same
program). The sweep found no other live site: `Array.contains` has the same
shape in codegen but is unreachable from the surface language, and
`control_flow_match.rs`'s use compares a scrutinee against a LITERAL pattern,
never an enum aggregate.

SEVERITY high: silently wrong test results, on the compiled backends only,
with the interpreter disagreeing.

fix:
RESOLVED by 9b8d435. The row's diagnosis of the CAUSE was exactly right --
`compile_binop` asks "is this a String/Vec?" by counting fields, and
`{ptr, i64, i64}` has three -- and its prescribed FIX SHAPE ("decide by TYPE,
not by field count ... route a named user struct to `emit_eq_fn_for_struct`")
is what landed. Two things it got wrong are worth recording, because both
change what the fix had to be.

(1) THE SEVERITY STORY IS UNDERSTATED. The row says "a compiler crash on a
legal, ordinary program", and the crash is the LOUD half. There is a silent
half: a three-field struct whose FIRST FIELD IS A POINTER compares WRONG and
says nothing. Measured --

    #[derive(PartialEq, Eq)] shared struct Node { v: i64 }
    #[derive(PartialEq, Eq)] struct T3 { h: Node, a: i64, b: i64 }
    T3 { h: Node { v: 1 }, a: 5, b: 6 } == T3 { h: Node { v: 1 }, a: 5, b: 9 }

    karac run --interp   false      (correct -- `b` differs)
    karac build          true       (WRONG)

-- because the string comparator read field 0 as the data pointer, field 1
(`a` = 5) as the length, and memcmp'd five bytes of two RC blocks that happen
to match. `b` is never looked at. A `shared` field is the ordinary way for a
user struct to begin with a pointer, so this is not an exotic shape.

(2) THE ROW'S NARROWER STOPGAP CANNOT WORK, AND NOT FOR THE REASON GIVEN. It
proposes "require the three field TYPES to match `{ptr, i64, i64}` before
taking the string path", and expects that to still misroute
"`{ i64, i64, String }`-shaped structs whose first field is a pointer". The
real obstacle is sharper: user structs get LITERAL, structurally-uniqued LLVM
struct types, so a struct whose first field is a pointer lowers to THE SAME
`{ptr, i64, i64}` type object as a `String` -- `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct`, which
compares by type identity, returns TRUE for it. No shape test can separate the
two, at any precision. Only the operand's Kāra type name can. (The row's own
example, `{ i64, i64, String }`, is not the hazard it names: measured, that one
PANICS like the rest, because field 0 extracts as an `i64`.)

WHAT LANDED. `try_compile_struct_eq_typed` already existed -- B-2026-08-12-5
built it for exactly this class, when a `Vec` FIELD was misrouted to the string
comparator -- and it was gated to structs that contain a Vec, deliberately, "so
the ordinary scalar/String struct comparison keeps its existing inline field
walk and this cannot regress it". That gate is what left the three-field case
open, because the confusion was never confined to Vec fields. The fix removes
it: every registered non-shared user struct now routes to the type-directed
`karac_eq_<S>`. The caller's `!llvm_ty_is_vec_struct(lhs.get_type())` guard
came off for the same reason -- it was excluding precisely the pointer-first
structs of (1), and it was redundant anyway, since the helper keys on the
operand's type name and declines a real `String`/`Vec`.

That is a widening of an existing route, not a new comparator:
`emit_eq_fn_for_struct` is what `Set`/`Map` keys of arbitrary struct type have
always used, and it dispatches per field on the declared `TypeExpr`, so nesting
is correct BY CONSTRUCTION. That matters here, because the row's blast-radius
note was if anything too modest: `compile_struct_eq` recurses per field through
`compile_binop`, so a three-field struct nested inside a TWO-field one crashed
too, with neither struct three fields at the top level.

VERIFIED byte-identical on interp, JIT and AOT across seven shapes -- three
i64s, String-first, String-last, shared-first (the silent case), nested, and
two- and four-field controls -- with the compiled answer matching the
interpreter's on every row. Negative-controlled: reverted, the E2E fixture
panics at `expr_ops.rs`'s `into_pointer_value()`. An ASAN fixture covers the
ownership question the widening raises, since routing every user struct through
a pointer-taking comparator spills operands that own heap: clean on bound and
temporary operands, with a `shared` field to pin that the comparison neither
retains nor releases. Suites: llvm 15443 passed / 0 failed; default 10047
passed / 0 failed; clippy clean on both legs.
title: `==` ON A USER STRUCT WITH EXACTLY THREE FIELDS PANICS THE COMPILER, so `struct S3 { a: i64, b: i64, c: i64 }` and `S3 { .. } == S3 { .. }` aborts `karac build` with an unwrap failure in `compile_string_binop`. `compile_binop` dispatches an aggregate by FIELD COUNT -- `field_count == vec_struct_type().count_fields()` -- and a `String`'s `{ptr, len, cap}` also has three, so any three-field struct is routed to the string comparator, which reads field 0 as a pointer.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-16, and measured to PREDATE it: the same
program panics at the same site with that fix reverted, and neither commit
touches `compile_binop`'s struct dispatch.

CAUSE. `compile_binop_typed`'s struct arm asks "is this a String/Vec?" by
COUNTING FIELDS:

    let field_count = ls.get_type().count_fields();
    let vec_fields = self.vec_struct_type().count_fields();   // 3
    if field_count == vec_fields { return self.compile_string_binop(op, ls, rs); }

That is a shape test standing in for a type test, and three-i64 is not a
String. `compile_string_binop` then does
`build_extract_value(lhs, 0).unwrap().into_pointer_value()` on an `i64` and
inkwell panics. A struct of `{ i64, i64, {ptr,i64,i64} }` -- three fields, one
of them a String -- lands there too.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE DIRECT `==`. Any comparator that REBUILDS an
aggregate and hands it to `compile_binop` inherits this. B-2026-08-27-16's
first attempt did exactly that for a wide enum payload and hit the panic
through `enum Holder { W(Big) }` with `struct Big { a: i64, b: i64, s: String }`;
it was rerouted through `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` (the pointer comparator)
specifically to stop depending on this dispatch. So the blast radius is wider
than "someone wrote a three-field struct".

FIX SHAPE. Decide by TYPE, not by field count. The value-side dispatch has no
type name, so the honest fix is to stop asking `compile_binop` this question:
route a named user struct to `emit_eq_fn_for_struct` (via
`emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` on stack slots) at the operator site, where the
operand EXPRESSIONS are still available to name the type -- the same move
B-2026-08-27-13 made for `Vec.contains` and B-2026-08-27-17 for `assert_eq`.
A narrower stopgap would be to require the three field TYPES to match
`{ptr, i64, i64}` before taking the string path, which fixes `S3` but still
misroutes `{ i64, i64, String }`-shaped structs whose first field is a
pointer.

SEVERITY high: a compiler crash on a legal, ordinary program, with no
workaround other than not comparing the struct or padding it to four fields.

fix:
FIXED by d6cb5222. `enum_payload_needs_structural_eq` now gates the `==`
structural path, replacing the `enum_has_heap_payload` fold that the row
identified as the wrong question asked of the wrong table.

THE ROW'S FIX SHAPE WAS RIGHT AND IS WHAT LANDED: do not widen the drop
classifier. Its `None` for a non-word-aligned payload struct is load-bearing --
its own comment records that classifying one the entry-copy cannot duplicate
turns a status-quo leak into a DOUBLE FREE -- so the drop side keeps saying
exactly what it said. The new predicate asks equality's own question instead:
can these bytes be compared as opaque WORDS? That is independent of whether the
drop path can free them or the entry-copy can duplicate them, which is the
decoupling the row asked for.

A SECOND SYMPTOM OF THE SAME GATE, not named by the row and worth reading
before assuming the fix is only about heap: FLOATS. A float payload owns no
heap, so no drop classification would ever have routed it to the structural
path -- yet bit equality is not IEEE equality in exactly the two places the
standard defines specially. Measured before the fix:
`Num.F(0.0) == Num.F(negzero())` answered FALSE and
`Num.F(nan()) == Num.F(nan())` answered TRUE. Both backwards, and both are the
errors B-2026-08-27-9 fixed for the type-directed comparators; the enum
operator path simply never reached them. The predicate covers it because the
question it asks is about the bytes, not about ownership -- which is the
argument for phrasing it that way rather than as "transitively owns heap", the
phrasing the row proposed.

The old predicates are kept as extra disjuncts rather than replaced. They fold
over a classification the type walk cannot see, so a payload kind recorded
there but unknown to the walk still routes correctly; the new one only ever
widens.

SCOPE HELD: integers, `bool` and `char` keep the cheaper word compare, so an
all-scalar enum is unchanged. The regression test's control is deliberately a
struct of three `i32`s -- also NOT word-aligned, so it demonstrates that the
predicate keys on what the bytes MEAN rather than on the alignment property
that produced the bug.

TESTS. An E2E/interpreter pair confirmed to fail with the fix reverted:
`test_e2e_enum_eq_is_not_gated_on_a_drop_classification` and
`enum_eq_is_not_gated_on_a_drop_classification`. Reverted it prints
`subword=false zeros=false nan=true` -- the three wrong answers -- while
`scalarstruct`, `floats`, `ints` and every `-ne` line stay correct. The float
operands come from opaque functions so LLVM cannot constant-fold the
comparison and answer correctly without running the emitted code (the trap
B-2026-08-27-9's own test records). The `-tag` lines carry forward
B-2026-08-27-16's dereference guard: the payload walk must not run when tags
differ, since a unit variant's uninitialised words become a wild pointer once
a field is read through.

NOTE ON THE ROW'S "RELATED, NOT ASSERTED HERE". It recorded that the same
`None` classification also means the payload struct's `String` is not freed at
enum drop, flagged as the deliberate status-quo leak rather than a finding.
That is unchanged by this fix and remains true: equality no longer consults
the drop classification, but the drop classification itself was not touched.
title: AN ENUM WHOSE PAYLOAD STRUCT IS NOT WORD-ALIGNED IS TREATED AS HAVING NO HEAP PAYLOAD, so `==` on it silently compares payload WORDS: `enum Holder { W(TwoNarrow) }` with `struct TwoNarrow { a: i32, b: i32, s: String }` answers `false` for two structurally-equal values on the compiled backends and `true` on the interpreter. `enum_drop_kind_for_type_expr` requires `struct_payload_word_aligned` before classifying a struct payload `NestedStruct`, so a struct with two consecutive sub-word fields classifies `None`, and `enum_has_heap_payload` -- which gates the structural `==` path -- then reports false.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-16 and measured after it landed. That row named
this exact shape as its second defect and attributed it to the `n <= 3`
rebuild gate in `compile_enum_eq`; that attribution was WRONG. The gate is
upstream of the comparator entirely -- `compile_enum_eq` is never called for
this enum -- so fixing the wide-payload rebuild (which is done) does not reach
it. Filed as its own row for that reason.

CAUSE, a chain of three. `enum_drop_kind_for_type_expr` classifies a named
non-shared struct payload `NestedStruct` only when
`aggregate_param_copy_supported_struct` AND `struct_payload_word_aligned` hold;
`{ i32, i32, String }` fails the second, because the word stream spends one
word per field while LLVM packs the two `i32`s into eight bytes. It therefore
classifies `None`. `enum_has_heap_payload` is a fold over
`field_drop_kinds` asking whether any kind `is_heap_bearing()`, so the enum
reports FALSE. And `compile_expr`'s `Binary` arm gates the structural
comparator on exactly that predicate, so `==` falls through to the word-wise
`compile_struct_eq` -- which compares the `String`'s heap POINTER.

THE CLASSIFIER'S `None` IS DELIBERATE and must not simply be widened. Its own
comment records why: the drop side and the deep-copy-on-entry must stay
symmetric, and classifying `NestedStruct` for a struct the entry-copy cannot
duplicate turns a status-quo LEAK into a DOUBLE FREE. So the drop
classification is load-bearing for ownership and is not the thing to change.

FIX SHAPE. Stop asking a DROP classification an EQUALITY question. The `==`
gate wants "would a word compare give the wrong answer for this enum" -- i.e.
does any payload field transitively own heap -- which is independent of
whether the drop path can free it or the entry-copy can duplicate it. A
predicate of its own (or simply routing every enum with a non-empty payload to
`compile_enum_eq`, which is correct for scalar payloads too, just more IR)
would decouple them. Note the doc on `enum_drop_switch_does_work` already
flags this coupling as a hazard -- "that predicate also picks
`compile_enum_eq`'s variant-aware comparison path, and widening it would
change `==` semantics" -- so the two questions were known to be entangled;
this row is what the entanglement costs.

RELATED, NOT ASSERTED HERE: the same `None` classification means the payload
struct's `String` is not freed at enum drop. The classifier comment calls that
the status-quo leak it is deliberately preserving, so it is recorded as context
rather than claimed as a new finding -- it has not been measured under LSan
here.

SEVERITY medium: a silent wrong answer that differs between backends, bounded
to an enum whose payload struct has two consecutive sub-word fields ahead of a
heap-owning one.

title: A NESTED index store whose RHS is a named local double-frees under codegen (`d[0][1] = x`), while the same store from a temporary (`d[0][1] = f"zz"`) is clean and the interpreter is correct in both. One binding is the whole difference.
detail:
A nested index store whose RHS is a NAMED LOCAL double-frees under codegen, while the same store from a TEMPORARY is fine and the interpreter is correct in both cases. The two programs differ by one binding:

    let mut d: Vec[Vec[String]] = Vec.new(); d.push(r);
    let x: String = f"zz";
    d[0][1] = x;                 // build: free(): double free detected in tcache 2
    d[0][1] = f"zz";             // build: fine

Both print `zz` under `karac run --interp`. The temporary form is what `test_e2e_nested_index_store_releases_the_displaced_element` already covers, which is why this has stayed invisible: every existing fixture for the nested-store release path stores a temporary.

Read as: the store releases the displaced element and then the local's own scope-end cleanup releases the same buffer again — the move into the slot does not appear to clear the source's ownership for a nested (two-level) index destination. A single-level `v[i] = x` from a named local does not reproduce.

Found while migrating fixtures for B-2026-08-26-21; unrelated to that rule (this program is not rejected by it — the RHS is a local, not an index read). Pre-existing on main.
fix:
FIXED by cd032829. The row's reading was right — "the move into the slot does
not appear to clear the source's ownership for a nested (two-level) index
destination" — and the cause is one match arm.

CAUSE. The move-suppression that stops a source binding from freeing a buffer
the container now owns is selected by matching the assignment target's OBJECT:

    ExprKind::Identifier(container) => ...    // `v[i] = x`
    ExprKind::FieldAccess { .. }    => ...    // `h.xs[j] = t`
    _ => false,

For `d[0][1] = x` the object is ITSELF an `Index`, so it fell to `_ => false`
and `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg` never ran. The single-level form is
safe only because the `Identifier` arm happens to cover it, which is exactly
the asymmetry the row measured.

WHY IT HAD NO TEST LOOKING AT IT, beyond the row's own note that existing
fixtures store a temporary: a temporary is the one RHS shape that CANNOT expose
this. It owns nothing, so there is nothing to suppress and no second free. The
bug needs a named local, and the nested-store fixtures never used one.

FIX. A third arm reusing the field-rooted arm's predicate and
`vec_index_elem_type_expr`, which already peels one Vec layer per index level.
That generality was verified rather than assumed: a fix that special-cased two
levels passes the filed repro and still aborts on `top[0][0][0] = y`, so the
three-level form is in the test.

TESTS. Three, all confirmed to fail with the fix reverted:
`test_e2e_nested_index_store_from_a_named_local_is_balanced` (codegen), its
interpreter oracle twin, and
`asan_nested_index_store_from_a_named_local_is_balanced`.

THE ASAN TEST LOOPS THE STORE FIVE TIMES, and that is the part worth keeping.
A suppression fix can fail in two OPPOSITE directions and a single store cannot
distinguish them: suppress too little and the buffer is freed twice (ASAN),
suppress too much and every stored local leaks (LSan — which runs on Linux CI
but NOT on macOS, so a green local Mac run would not have seen the second).
Five iterations each move a fresh local in and displace the previous one, so a
leak accumulates to five blocks instead of hiding as one. Both directions are
green: the full ASAN suite passes 1227.

The E2E controls pin that the new arm neither under- nor over-reaches: a
scalar element (`Vec[Vec[i64]]` — nothing owned, so over-suppression would be
invisible without it) and a whole-inner-Vec replacement (`outer[0] = nb`,
which already took the working `Identifier` arm). Every payload is built by a
function call rather than written as a literal, since two identical literals
can fold to one global and a double free of a shared global need not abort.

title: A `ref` element binding did not dispatch methods like the value it borrows, in two independent ways: `.clone()` on an element read THROUGH one (`let row = ref d[0]; row[0].clone()`) SEGFAULTED, and a `ref` binding to a STRING element (`let s = ref names[i]`) had no String method surface at all — every method on one fell through to "no handler", while the interpreter ran all of them.
detail:
`.clone()` on an index THROUGH a `ref` binding segfaults under codegen. Both halves work alone; only the combination fails:

    let row = ref d[0]; println(row[0]);        // ok, both backends
    let x: String = r[0].clone();               // ok, both backends (no ref binding)
    let row = ref d[0]; let x = row[0].clone(); // interp: "aa"; build: SIGSEGV

`karac check` passes, and the interpreter is correct, so this is a run-vs-build divergence that crashes rather than diverging quietly.

The `ref`-binding element read (`row[0]`) reaches the buffer through `get_data_ptr`, which loads through the shim; the method-call path for an indexed receiver lowers the index to an element pointer and synthesizes an identifier for it. The two are presumably disagreeing about how many derefs the shim implies — the same class as the borrowed-Tensor double-deref fixed in fe964f0, but on the method-dispatch path rather than the tensor path.

Matters more than a normal codegen gap because `.clone()` on an index read is exactly what B-2026-08-26-21's fix-it tells users (and `karac fix`) to write, so a borrowed row plus the recommended repair is a plausible shape, not a contrived one.

Found while migrating fixtures for B-2026-08-26-21.
fix:
FIXED by 367edc1 (2026-08-27). Two independent gaps in `try_compile_ref_binding`'s registration (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`), both about the shim being registered as something other than the value it borrows. The row filed them as one symptom because both were found through the same `.clone()` probe.

LEG 1 — a WRONG entry, and the segfault. The binding writes two element tables and they disagreed: `vec_elem_types[row]` correctly held the INNER element type (`String`), while `var_elem_type_exprs[row]` — the TypeExpr twin of that table, whose contract is likewise the binding's ELEMENT type — held the binding's OWN type (`Vec[String]`). The reader that consumes the TypeExpr half is `compile_indexed_receiver_method`, which registers the synth receiver for `row[0]` from it, so the synth for a `String` element was registered as a `Vec[String]` over a slot pointing at the String's `{ptr, len, cap}`. `clone` read "aa"'s header AS a Vec header, took `len = 2` as an element COUNT, and cloned two `String`s out of the letter bytes — SIGSEGV inside `karac_string_clone`. Fixed at the WRITE site, so all ~170 readers of that table see a consistent entry rather than one reader being patched.

The row's guess ("the two are presumably disagreeing about how many derefs the shim implies — the same class as the borrowed-Tensor double-deref fixed in fe964f0") was wrong: the pointer arithmetic was correct throughout. `get_data_ptr` loads through the `ref_params` shim exactly once and the GEP lands on the right element. What was wrong was the TYPE the synth receiver was registered under, which is why the failure was inside a runtime clone rather than at the load.

LEG 2 — a MISSING entry, and the dispatch fall-through. A `ref` binding to a STRING element registered no `string_vars` at all, so String method dispatch had no entry for it. Adds the same two registrations `register_var_from_type_expr` makes for a String binding (`vec_elem_types = i8`, `string_vars`). Deliberately NOT a wholesale delegation to that registrar, which would have been the tidier-looking change: its Column/DataFrame arms register CLEANUP trackers, and queuing a free on a borrow whose buffer the container owns is a double free.

TITLE CORRECTED at close. The original conflated the two legs, reading as though every String method failed on the shape the example showed. Measured: through a Vec-element borrow (`row[0].m()`), `.len()`, `.starts_with()`, `.substring()` and `.to_string()` all returned CORRECTLY and only `.clone()` crashed — none of the others reads the element TypeExpr, and Vec's `len` happens to load the same word String's does. The blanket "every String method falls through" is true only of leg 2's direct String borrow. They are asserted alongside `clone` in the regression test so a future break there is not mistaken for this row.

Tests: `test_e2e_method_on_an_element_through_a_ref_binding` and `test_e2e_string_methods_through_a_ref_binding` (`tests/codegen.rs`) for value parity; `asan_clone_of_element_through_ref_binding_is_clean` and `asan_string_methods_through_ref_binding_are_clean` (`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`) for memory. The ASAN half is not decorative here — the borrow aliases a buffer the container owns, so a spurious free from either registration would be a double free rather than a wrong value, and leg 2's fix is exactly the kind of registration that could have queued one.

Gates: codegen 3316/0, memory_sanitizer 1237/0, par_codegen 270/0, selfhost_codegen 1/0, default suite 108 result lines all ok, both clippy legs and `cargo fmt --check` clean. ASAN runs under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`.

title: `.clone()` on an element of an SoA-laid-out container returns the wrong data under codegen — element 5 reads back the cold group at indices 1 and 2 (`100 1000 200 2000` for `5 50 500 5000`). The interpreter and the AoS build are both correct.
detail:
`.clone()` on an element of an SoA-laid-out container returns the wrong data under codegen. Same program with and without the `layout` block:

    let c = entities[5].clone(); println(f"{c.x} {c.y} {c.vx} {c.vy}");

    AoS  interp 5 50 500 5000   build 5 50 500 5000
    SoA  interp 5 50 500 5000   build 100 1000 200 2000   <-- wrong

The returned values are the COLD group (`vx`, `vy`) at indices 1 and 2 rather than element 5 — i.e. it reads a group buffer directly instead of materialising the element.

Cause is structural: a method call on an index receiver lowers the index to a single element pointer and synthesizes an identifier bound to it (`compile_indexed_receiver_method`). An SoA element has no single pointer — its fields live one buffer per `layout` group, and reading one requires `compile_soa_index_read`'s reassembly. The lowering has no SoA arm, so it GEPs into whichever buffer it landed on.

The sibling `ref entities[i]` shape has the same root cause and is now REJECTED in the typechecker (d676cac) rather than miscompiled; this is the method-call half of that, still silent. Direct field access (`entities[i].x`) is correct in both layouts and is the working spelling.

Found while migrating fixtures for B-2026-08-26-21. Caught only because `test_e2e_soa_whole_element_matches_aos` runs one body under both layouts and compares.
fix:
FIXED by 56985ec7. The row's cause analysis was exactly right — "a method call
on an index receiver lowers the index to a single element pointer and
synthesizes an identifier bound to it ... an SoA element has no single pointer"
— and the fix is the arm it proposed: materialise the element through
`compile_soa_index_read`, the same reassembly `entities[i].x` already uses, and
bind the synth to THAT. The rest of the indexed-receiver flow then sees an
ordinary contiguous struct and is unchanged.

WIDER THAN `.clone()`, WHICH THE ROW DID NOT SAY. Every method on an SoA
indexed receiver read the wrong data, not just the cloning one — a `ref self`
reader returned garbage from the same wrong buffer (`entities[5].sum()` gave
3300 for an element summing to 5555).

AND THE MUTATING CASE NEEDS MORE THAN THE READ FIX, which is the part worth
reading before assuming the row scoped the work. A materialised element is a
COPY, so a `mut ref self` method writes into the copy and the container never
sees it. `entities[3].bump()` was a silent no-op before this, and would have
REMAINED one under a read-only fix while every read went correct — the failure
would have looked fixed. The AoS path avoids this only because it hands the
method the element's real storage. The copy is therefore scattered back through
`compile_soa_index_store` when the receiver is `MutRef`, and only then: a
read-only receiver needs no write-back, and doing one anyway would store a
stale copy over anything the call itself changed.

KNOWN COST, recorded rather than hidden: the scatter re-evaluates the index
expression, so a side-effecting index (`entities[next()].bump()`) would advance
it twice. That is the same re-evaluability requirement `emit_displaced_index_
elem_drop` already documents for the AoS displaced-element path, so the
constraint is not new to this site.

TESTS. `test_e2e_soa_element_method_matches_aos` runs ONE body under both
layouts and compares, like `test_e2e_soa_whole_element_matches_aos` — the
differential the row credits with catching this. That structure is load-bearing
here: every line passes under AoS, so a single-layout fixture would assert
nothing about the bug. It covers the clone at two indices, a `ref self` reader,
the mutation, two NEIGHBOUR reads and a direct field read past the cap 0→4→8
realloc boundary (the write-back's blast radius — writing a whole materialised
element back through group buffers is exactly the operation that could smear
across neighbours, and a mis-strided store shows there first).

Reverted, it prints `clone5 100 1000 200 2000` — the row's measurement to the
digit — plus `clone3 0 0 0 0`, `read5 3300`, `read0 11`, and
`mut4 4 40 400 4000` for the lost mutation, while every neighbour and direct
field line stays correct.

ALSO CORRECTED: `test_e2e_soa_whole_element_matches_aos`'s comment, which
documented this miscompile as a standing limitation ("NEITHER replacement for
it works here ... `entities[i].clone()` MISCOMPILES under SoA"). Half of that
is now false and would have misled the next reader into a workaround.

title: A tuple (`(i64, String)`) and `Option[T]` have NO `.clone()`, so the index-move rejection outlaws reading such an element by value with no replacement available. This is the remaining blocker on landing B-2026-08-26-21.
detail:
A TUPLE (`(i64, String)`) and `Option[T]` have no `.clone()`, so B-2026-08-26-21's index-move rejection outlaws reading such an element by value while offering no replacement for it. This is the remaining blocker on landing that rule.

MEASURED, both on current main:
    let v: Vec[(i64, String)] = [...]; let t = v[0].clone();   // no method 'clone' on type '(i64, String)'
    let w: Vec[Option[N]] = [...];     let t = w[0].clone();   // no method 'clone' on type 'Option'

The rejection's three offered remedies all fail for these element types:
  - `.clone()` does not exist (above).
  - `ref v[i]` is only a borrow, so it does not help when the binding ESCAPES into a by-value position — which is what these sites do (`out.push(t)`, a call argument).
  - `v.swap(i, j)` applies only when the shape is a swap.

So the program has no legal spelling at all. Eleven `memory_sanitizer.rs` fixtures are left on the old form for exactly this reason (five of them for this one; the rest hit already-filed codegen gaps).

WHY IT IS THE RULE'S PROBLEM RATHER THAN THE FIXTURES'. The rule is right that reading a `(i64, String)` element out by value MOVES it, and a container cannot hold a hole. The gap is that the language gives no way to take an independent copy of a tuple or an `Option`, which every other non-`Copy` element type has (a struct derives `Clone`; `String` and `Vec` have one).

Two ways out, and the choice is a design decision rather than a bug fix: give tuples and `Option[T]` a `Clone` (structural, following their components), or let the rule keep accepting a by-value read where no `Clone` exists — which reintroduces the divergence it was written to close, so probably not.

SOURCE NOTE: found by migrating the ASAN corpus for B-2026-08-26-21. Every other corpus (stdlib, codegen fixtures, selfhost + its 210-program test corpus, the book, examples, GPU) migrated cleanly; this is the one shape with no answer.
fix:
Fixed. Less was missing than this row assumed: `type_supports_clone` ALREADY accepted `Type::Tuple` structurally and `clone_receiver_self_type` already handled `Option[T]`, so a `T: Clone` bound discharged against a tuple while `t.clone()` on the same value reported `no method 'clone'`. The bound was decorative, exactly as B-2026-08-17-33 describes for user types. Four narrow fixes rather than a new capability.

1. A `shared` handle now always clones. `clone_receiver_self_type` had always answered `Some` for one — `clone` on a shared handle IS the refcount bump — while `type_supports_clone` demanded `#[derive(Clone)]`. The two disagreed, and the disagreement is what broke `Option[shared N]`: `n.clone()` compiled, but the same handle inside an `Option` did not, because the payload check ran through the stricter of the two. A derive cannot be what decides whether a refcount can be incremented.
2. A tuple arm on `clone_receiver_self_type`.
3. The interpreter's clone dispatch gained `Value::Tuple`; `deep_clone_value` already had the arm and only the dispatch list was missing it.
4. Codegen resolves both receivers through an INDEX READ, which is the shape that mattered — a tuple in a local already cloned. `aggregate_clone_fn_for_receiver` turned tuples away at a `Path`-only guard, and an `Option` element had no resolvable type at all, because `register_var_from_type_expr` records a payload only when it can RECONSTRUCT IT FOR DISPLAY, which a `shared struct` payload fails.

THE ADMITTED TUPLE COMPONENT CLASS IS MEASURED. Each shape was run before being admitted, and it is deliberately NARROWER than `Result`'s equivalent (which admits `Vec`):

    (i64, String)  (String, String)  (i64, i64)  (i64, Option[T])   correct on both backends
    (i64, Vec[i64])        DOUBLE FREE, once the Vec owns real heap
    (i64, (i64, String))   SILENT MISCOMPILE — `94711002536753` where the interpreter printed `32`
    (i64, SomeStruct)      already a loud codegen error

Both bad shapes fail ONLY through an index-read receiver — the same tuple in a local clones correctly — and the typechecker cannot see the receiver's shape, so the class excludes nested containers and nested tuples outright. They now report a clean `no method 'clone'`. Admitting them to look more complete would have traded a clear error for a double free and a wrong number.

Also fixed on the way: the indexed-element synth cleanup removed a dozen registrations but never the three TUPLE ones, so `__indexed_elem_N` stayed registered as a tuple past its lifetime.

EFFECT ON THE ROWS THIS BLOCKED: the codegen leg is 3306/3306 GREEN WITH BOTH RULES APPLIED, where it previously could not compile the two `Option`-element fixtures at all. B-2026-08-26-21 and -37 are no longer blocked on a language gap; what remains for them is fixture migration in `memory_sanitizer.rs` (11 sites the automation could not reach — chained indexes, slice temporaries, fn-returned receivers), which is work, not a blocker.

Fixed in de92164.

RESOLVED by 30420faf, together with B-2026-08-27-25.

CODEGEN: `emit_eq_fn_for_vec` is generalized over the header layout into
`emit_eq_fn_for_ptr_len_header`, and `emit_eq_fn_for_slice` calls it with
`slice_struct_type()` instead of `vec_struct_type()`. A `Slice` is
`{ptr, i64 len}` and a `Vec` is `{ptr, i64 len, i64 cap}` -- the data pointer
and the length sit at the same two fields, so the comparison ("equal lengths,
then equal elements") is one body with one parameter. The row anticipated this
("would need `emit_eq_fn_for_vec` generalized over the two layouts, which is a
real change, not a routing one") and that is what it cost: the emitter split,
plus a `slice_elem_te_of_operand` oracle and a `compile_slice_eq` that
normalizes the two forms a slice operand arrives in (a local is the ADDRESS of
its `{ptr,len}` slot; a parameter is the fat struct BY VALUE).

Sharing the emitter is the point rather than an economy: it is what makes
`v.as_slice() == w.as_slice()` agree with `v == w` by construction instead of by
two implementations that happen to match.

INTERPRETER: the `Value::Slice` arm the row predicted would be nearly free was
nearly free -- `Value`'s `PartialEq` already compares slices by content, which is
why a slice-typed struct FIELD worked and only the bare operator did not.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE ROW, in the interpreter's favour rather than against it:
that `PartialEq` took TWO read locks when both slices view the same storage
(`v[0..2] == v[2..4]`), and `RwLock::read` is not documented to be reentrant --
recursively acquiring a read lock the current thread already holds may deadlock.
It did not deadlock on this platform (glibc's pthread rwlock grants a second
reader when no writer is queued), but the bare operator makes that pair an
ordinary comparison rather than a rarity reached only through a derived struct,
so the same-storage case now takes one lock. The regression tests use
same-buffer ranges deliberately for this reason.

MEASURED, all three backends byte-identical on one program: content equality
over `Slice[i64]` and `Slice[String]`, differing lengths, same-buffer ranges,
self-comparison, a `Slice` param and a `mut Slice` param, a slice over a stack
`Array`, and two empty slices. LSan-clean, including the case that matters most
for a slice -- it OWNS NOTHING, so any free at all on this path would be a
double-free of the viewed buffer.

NOT COVERED, and the row did not claim it: `mut Slice[T] == Slice[T]` is
rejected by the typechecker ("cannot compare 'mut Slice[i64]' and 'Slice[i64]'")
because `strip_refs_for_compare` does not strip slice mutability. Same-mutability
comparison works in both directions. Left as-is -- it is a typechecker question,
not this one.

TESTS: `test_e2e_slice_equality_compares_contents` (codegen, 11 legs),
`slice_equality_is_content_equality_in_the_interpreter` (oracle),
`asan_slice_and_array_equality_are_ownership_neutral`. All three fail on the
pre-fix tree (verified by stashing `src/` and re-running); the array half of the
interpreter oracle passes there, which is expected and documented -- the
interpreter was already right for `Array`.
title: `Slice[T] == Slice[T]` IS ACCEPTED BY `karac check`, DIES IN THE INTERPRETER WITH A DIAGNOSTIC THAT BLAMES THE TYPECHECKER, AND IS REFUSED BY CODEGEN AS "a reference type" -- the same three-way disagreement B-2026-08-27-10 fixed for `Vec`, on the sibling type, and unfixed by that work.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-10, by probing the neighbouring shapes that
share the `{ptr,len,...}` hazard rather than stopping at the row's own case.

MEASURED on one binary, `let s1: Slice[i64] = a[0..2]; let s2 = c[0..2];
s1 == s2`:

  karac check        All checks passed.
  karac run --interp runtime error: operator 'Eq' is not defined for operands
                     of type 'Slice' and 'Slice' (this is a type error the
                     typechecker reports as a hard error ...)
  karac build        error: structural `==`/`!=` on this reference type is not
                     yet supported under `karac build` (codegen); it works
                     under `karac run --interp`.

Three components, three answers. The interpreter's message repeats the same
FALSE CLAIM B-2026-08-27-10 corrected for `Vec` -- `karac check` passes, and it
passes deliberately: `type_supports_partial_eq` has a `Type::Slice` arm that
recurses into the element, right beside the `Vec` arm. Codegen's message is
also wrong in its specifics: it says the gap is "a `shared enum`, or a `shared
struct` nested inside a by-value struct", and a `Slice` is neither.

NOT FIXED BY B-2026-08-27-10 and deliberately not folded into it. That fix
routes a `Vec`-typed operand to `karac_eq_Vec_<T>`, which walks a
`{ptr,len,cap}` control block; a `Slice` is a different shape and reaches
`compile_binop` as a POINTER value, not a struct value, so it takes a different
branch entirely. Sharing the comparator would need `emit_eq_fn_for_vec`
generalized over the two layouts, which is a real change, not a routing one.

WHICH WAY IT SHOULD RESOLVE has the same answer as -10 did: design.md § Slices
gives a slice value semantics over a borrowed range, and the typechecker
already admits the operand, so making it work is more defensible than
retracting it. The interpreter arm is nearly free (`Value::Slice` already has a
content-comparing `PartialEq`, used by the derived-struct path); codegen is the
work.

fix:
RESOLVED by 30420faf, together with B-2026-08-27-24.

The row's own case is the smallest part of what was wrong. Its prescription --
"elementwise comparison over the fixed extent (N is a compile-time constant, so
it unrolls or emits a counted loop with no control block to read)" -- is exactly
what `emit_eq_fn_for_array` does: a counted loop to N with no length word and no
length check, since two arrays that reach it have the same type. The routing is
a third oracle (`array_te_of_operand`) beside the `Vec` and `Slice` ones.

WIDER THAN THE ROW RECORDED, in three ways found by probing rather than by
argument, all fixed and all pinned:

1. `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr` had NO `Array` arm at all, so an array-typed
   struct FIELD and an array MAP KEY fell to the byte-loop fallback. That is
   accidentally right for a scalar element and WRONG for a heap one:
   `#[derive(PartialEq)] struct Ws { a: Array[String, 2] }` compared two equal
   values UNEQUAL under `karac build` while the interpreter said equal, and
   `Map[Array[String, 2], _]` grew a second entry for one key. Both silent, both
   older than the row's loud failure, and neither reachable by a routing-only
   fix. The hash twin (`emit_hash_fn_for_array`) lands with the eq one on the
   rule B-2026-08-27-4 and -6 both turn on: a structural eq without a structural
   hash puts equal keys in different buckets, where they never meet to be
   compared.

2. The fallback NAMED ITSELF from `mangled_type_name`, which is a bare "Array"
   for every instantiation -- so the first `Array[_, _]` in a program supplied
   the comparator for all the others. `display_mangle_te` had the same hole one
   level down: it filtered CONST generic args out of the mangle, so
   `Array[i64, 2]` and `Array[i64, 3]` produced one name fragment. Const args are
   now part of the mangle (a type whose identity includes an extent has one
   layout per N), and the array dispatch is checked AHEAD of the shallow cache
   lookup rather than after it.

3. `llvm_type_for_type_expr` had no arm for `TypeKind::Array`, the form
   `TypeChecker::type_to_type_expr` rebuilds from inference (a source-written
   annotation parses as `Path("Array", ..)` and was fine). It fell to the
   `_ => i64` default, so the ELEMENT type of a nested
   `Array[Array[i64, 2], 2]` lowered to a scalar word and the walk strode wrong
   -- `n2 == m2` on values differing in one inner element answered TRUE.

ONE THING THE ROW GOT EXACTLY RIGHT and worth repeating: the diagnostic
misdiagnosed itself. "likely a typechecker gap ... should reject mismatched
operand types" fired on two operands of identical type. That message is still
there for genuine mismatches; `Array` no longer reaches it.

MEASURED, all three backends byte-identical: bare `==`/`!=` at extents 0, 2 and
3, `Array[String, N]`, a struct field, two nesting depths at two inner extents,
and `Map` keys at both element kinds. LSan-clean for bound operands, slices and
map keys.

NOT FIXED, filed as B-2026-08-27-30: a fresh-TEMPORARY array operand
(`mk(2) == mk(2)`) leaks its element Strings, 26 bytes in 4 allocations -- the
same signature B-2026-08-27-26 measured for the `Vec` shape and not covered by
its fix, because an array operand never reaches `free_fresh_owned_str_arg` at
all. Honest framing: the program did not compile before this fix, so the leak
surface is new behind it rather than a regression in working code.

TESTS: `test_e2e_array_equality_compares_contents` (codegen, 14 legs including
the field, the mangler and both `Map` shapes),
`array_equality_is_content_equality_in_the_interpreter` (the oracle -- the
interpreter was already right, which is the whole shape of a run-vs-build
split), `asan_slice_and_array_equality_are_ownership_neutral`.
title: `Array[T, N] == Array[T, N]` IS ACCEPTED BY `karac check`, ANSWERS CORRECTLY UNDER THE INTERPRETER, AND FAILS TO COMPILE: codegen reports "left operand has non-comparable type ArrayType" and blames a typechecker gap that is not one.
detail:
FOUND alongside B-2026-08-27-24 while probing the shapes neighbouring
B-2026-08-27-10.

MEASURED on one binary, `let x: Array[i64, 2] = Array[1, 2]; let y = Array[1,
9]; x == y`:

  karac check        All checks passed.
  karac run --interp array diff false   array same true      (both correct)
  karac build        error: codegen failed: Binary op Eq: left operand has
                     non-comparable type ArrayType(... "[2 x i64]") (likely a
                     typechecker gap -- `assert_eq` and `==` should reject
                     mismatched operand types before reaching codegen)

DIFFERENT SHAPE FROM -24 AND FROM -10, which is why it is a separate row: this
one has a WORKING interpreter and a build that refuses. The failure is loud, so
it is not a wrong-answer bug -- but a program that runs under `karac run` and
cannot be built is still a run-vs-build split, and it is the shape that costs
most late (it surfaces at ship time).

THE DIAGNOSTIC MISDIAGNOSES ITSELF. It guesses "likely a typechecker gap ...
should reject mismatched operand types", and the operand types are not
mismatched -- both sides are `Array[i64, 2]`. `type_supports_partial_eq` has a
`Type::Array` arm that recurses into the element, so acceptance is deliberate,
exactly as it is for `Vec` and `Slice`. The message sends a reader to the wrong
phase.

CHEAPEST HONEST FIX is probably elementwise comparison over the fixed extent (N
is a compile-time constant, so it unrolls or emits a counted loop with no
control block to read) -- strictly simpler than the `Vec` case, which had to
load a length at runtime.

fix:
RESOLVED by e57bc89, along the line the row itself prescribed: give the
temporary a drop that walks elements rather than a bare free of the outer
buffer, using the element `TypeExpr` that B-2026-08-27-10's `vec_eq_elem_types`
table now supplies at this site. That table is what made the fix small -- the
call site had the operand EXPRESSION all along but no way to name its element
type.

THE ROW UNDER-SCOPED ITS OWN FINDING. It measured the `Vec[String]` case (26
bytes in 4 allocations) and described the defect as that shape's. It is the
element TYPE's: a fresh `Vec[Vec[i64]]` operand loses 64 bytes in 2 allocations
-- the two inner buffers -- by the identical mechanism, and a `String` operand
is clean, because for a `String` the outer buffer IS the whole allocation. Any
heap-owning element type leaks; the fix is keyed on `vec_element_drain_fn`
returning `Some`, so it covers all of them and leaves `Vec[i64]` on the cheap
buffer free it has always had.

SHAPE OF THE FIX. The whole-`Vec` drop REPLACES the buffer free rather than
running before it. `karac_drop_Vec_<T>` releases the buffer as well as the
elements, so emitting both would double-free -- which is why the `String`
control leg is load-bearing in the fixture and not decoration: a regression
that re-added the buffer free shows up there as a double-free rather than as a
leak. Resolving through `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr` -- the memory-side family
every other element drain funnels through -- is what makes a nested
`Vec[Vec[T]]` recurse correctly without a case of its own, and keeps user
`Drop` bodies on the NLL channel where they belong.

THE DOUBLE-FREE RISK THE WIDENING RAISES WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED.
`free_fresh_owned_str_arg` has 30 call sites, and the ones that matter are
those where the argument does NOT die at the call: `push` MOVES its argument
into the container and a map key is moved by `insert`. Both are in the fixture
and both are clean, which is what pins that this fires only where the temporary
genuinely dies. Negative-controlled: reverted, the fixture leaks 103 bytes in 8
allocations.

ONE SITE IS STILL LEAKING AND IT IS A DIFFERENT BUG -- filed separately.
`Vec.contains` with a fresh `Vec` needle leaks the needle ENTIRELY (202 bytes
in 4 allocations for two calls), and reverting this fix changes that number not
at all, so the free does not fire there at all rather than firing and missing
elements. Same symptom class, opposite cause, different site.

Suites: llvm 15444 passed / 0 failed; default 10047 passed / 0 failed; clippy
clean on both legs.
title: `free_fresh_owned_str_arg` FREES A FRESH TEMPORARY OPERAND'S BUFFER BUT NOT ITS ELEMENTS, so a `Vec[String]` temporary compared with `==` leaks every element String -- measured 26 bytes in 4 allocations under LSan, IDENTICALLY before and after B-2026-08-27-10.
detail:
FOUND while adding B-2026-08-27-10's ASAN fixture, and separated from it by
measurement rather than by assumption: the identical leak reproduces with that
fix REVERTED, so it belongs to the helper, not to the new intercept.

REPRO under `assert_clean_asan_run`:

  fn ids(n: i64) -> Vec[String] {
      let mut v: Vec[String] = Vec.new();
      v.push(f"item{n}");
      v.push(f"item{n + 1}");
      return v;
  }
  fn main() { println(f"{ids(1) == ids(1)}"); }

  SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 26 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocation(s)

Four allocations = the four element Strings. Swap the `f"item{n}"` elements for
STRING LITERALS and the run is clean, because a literal's bytes are rodata --
which is why the sibling fixture in the same file passes and why this was
invisible until an element was genuinely heap-allocated.

MECHANISM: `free_fresh_owned_str_arg` (B-2026-08-11-24, the `Eq` sibling of
B-2026-07-21-12's concat free) frees the operand's BUFFER with a `cap > 0`
guard. For a `String` operand that is the whole allocation. For a `Vec[T]` with
a heap `T` the buffer is only the outer array; each element owns its own
allocation and nothing frees them. The helper's gate is shape-based
(`llvm_ty_is_vec_struct`), so it cannot tell the two apart -- the same
String/Vec shape confusion that caused B-2026-08-27-10, in a second place.

THE FIX IS NOT "free harder". The right operation for an owned temporary with
heap elements is the one B-2026-08-11-33 chose for its struct sibling:
give it an owner (`track_fresh_struct_temp_operand`) so the registered drop
walks elements at scope exit, rather than emitting a bare `free` of the outer
buffer. Doing that for the Vec case needs the element `TypeExpr`, which
B-2026-08-27-10's `vec_eq_elem_types` table now supplies at exactly this site.

SCOPE: any fresh-temporary `Vec[String]`-shaped operand of `==` / `!=` /
`String` concat that reaches the surface-`Binary` path. Bound operands are
unaffected (their bindings own the elements and drop them correctly -- measured
clean).

fix:
Fixed in dc939a8. The row's measurement was exact; what it left open ("whether
`check` skips the pass outright or runs a single-module variant") has a third
answer, and the gap is one pass wider than the row states.

WHAT `check` DID. `package_check_on` ran resolve and typecheck PER MODULE and
returned. It did not run a single-module variant of the effect check and it did
not skip a call -- the pass it was missing has no per-module form. The
cross-module effect check exists only on the FLATTENED super-program, and
`run_multi_file_codegen` was the only thing that built one. So `check` was not
mis-configured; it never reached the pass at all.

WIDER THAN THE ROW: THE OWNERSHIP HALF DIVERGES IDENTICALLY, from the same
early return. Measured on the same shape:

    fn take(v: Vec[i64]) -> i64 { return v.len(); }
    pub fn run() -> i64 with allocates(Heap) {
        let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
        v.push(1);
        let a = take(v);
        let b = take(v);          // use after move
        return a + b;
    }

    karac check   All checks passed.
    karac build   error[ownership]: multi-file ownership failed:
                    src/helper.kara:6:18: value 'v' moved here, used again here

Concurrency and the `has_fatal_errors` gate were in the same position. All of
them now run, because they are one block in `build` and were extracted as one
block.

HOW. `run_multi_file_late_phases` is that block, lifted out of
`run_multi_file_codegen` and shared rather than reimplemented -- the two
commands cannot answer differently again, which is what
`package_check_on`'s own comment already claimed ("Answering differently here
would reintroduce the very divergence this function exists to remove").

Deliberately NOT `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`, unlike its parent: `karac check`
has to work in the default build and none of these passes needs a backend.
`format_pipeline_errors` was llvm-gated for the same accidental reason and is
un-gated too -- the default leg failed to compile until it was, which is how
the coupling surfaced.

STRUCTURED OUTPUT, which is the half that matters for the row's own argument.
The row's "WHY THIS MATTERS" is that `karac check --output=json` is the Mend
loop's entry point and `karac fix` consumes its diagnostics. A pre-rendered
blob would satisfy every text assertion and still be useless there, so the
renderer was split: `collect_pipeline_diags` produces `{file, line, column,
message}` per finding and the text formatter sits on top of it. One traversal,
so JSON and text cannot drift, and `build`'s text output is byte-identical to
before. `check --output=json` now emits

    {"severity":"error","phase":"effect","file":".../helper.kara",
     "line":2,"column":5,"message":"public function 'run' performs
     writes(Stdout) but does not declare it (via call to 'println' at line 3)"}

A THIRD COMMAND WAS AFFECTED AND IS EASY TO MISS. `karac run` on a package
gates through the same `PackageCheck` (`gate_run_on_package_check`), so it
inherited the refusal the moment `has_errors()` learned to count the late
failure -- but its TEXT arm renders each diagnostic kind explicitly, so
without a matching line `karac run` exited 1 having printed NOTHING. Caught by
running it; the JSON arms of that function were patched by the same edit and
the text arm was not.

COST. `karac check` on `examples/slipstream` (6 modules): 0.33s. The added
passes are the same ones `build` already ran, so a project that builds pays
them once either way.

Tests: an effect pair and an ownership pair, each asserting that `check` and
`build` AGREE rather than merely that `check` fails -- each one asserts the
build still fails FIRST, so a check failing for an unrelated reason cannot
satisfy it -- plus the JSON shape and a control that a correctly-declared
package still passes. A/B verified against the unfixed compiler: all three bug
tests fail there, the control passes both ways.

NOT INVESTIGATED, restated from the row so it is not mistaken for done:
whether other build-only passes have the same shape. The extraction makes the
answer cheap for the next person -- anything `build` gates on before codegen
now lives in one function, and adding it there reaches `check` for free.

Gates: cli 723, codegen 3307, interpreter 1757, typechecker 2534,
memory_sanitizer 1225, example_packages/example_corpus/manifest -- zero
failures; fmt and both clippy legs clean. The runtime crate is untouched.
title: `karac check` ON A PROJECT DOES NOT RUN THE MULTI-FILE EFFECT CHECK THAT `karac build` RUNS, so a project prints "All checks passed." and then fails to build with an undeclared-effect error -- measured with ONE binary on `examples/slipstream`.
detail:
FOUND while repairing `examples/slipstream` (see the commit restoring its two
SoA element reads). Not a Vec-equality finding; filed separately because it is
a much broader hazard than the example that exposed it.

MEASURED with a single `--features llvm` `karac`, in `examples/slipstream`,
with `pub fn run()` declaring `panics` but not `writes(Stdout)`:

  karac check    All checks passed.            (exit 0)
  karac build    error[effect]: multi-file effect failed:
                   src/host_linux.kara:41:5: public function 'run' performs
                   writes(Stdout) but does not declare it (via call to
