                   'println' at line 46)

Same binary, same directory, same sources, opposite verdicts. Adding
`writes(Stdout)` makes both pass.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE ONE EXAMPLE: `karac check --output=json` is the
entry point of the Mend loop -- CLAUDE.md § "Developing Kāra code" makes it the
authority a model iterates against, and `karac fix` consumes its diagnostics.
An error class that `check` cannot see is an error class Mend cannot converge
on: the loop reports success, and the failure appears only at build. That
inverts the wedge's central promise.

BLAST RADIUS is every PUBLIC function in a multi-module project whose declared
effect set is incomplete -- the check exists precisely because public effects
are declared-and-verified rather than inferred (design.md § Effects). Single-
file programs are not obviously affected; the failing pass is named
"multi-file effect".

NOT INVESTIGATED HERE: whether `check` skips the pass outright or runs a
single-module variant of it, and whether the same gap covers other build-only
passes. The measurement above is the whole of what was established.

fix:
RESOLVED by 4af0901. The row's central claim -- that the free "does not fire
there at all rather than firing and missing elements" -- was right, and the
mechanism is simpler than the row allowed for. It offered two candidates ("the
freshness predicates reject a `Vec`-typed Call result, or that call is on a
branch this shape does not take"); neither is true. THE ARM NEVER CALLED THE
HELPER. `Set.contains` (B-2026-06-20-12), `Map.contains_key` (B-2026-06-20-9),
`starts_with` and `binary_search` all free their borrowed argument;
`Vec.contains` was the one lookup that did not, and had not since it was
written.

THE ROW UNDER-SCOPED IT, in the same way B-2026-08-27-26's did. It names a
fresh `Vec` needle, because that is the shape the -26 verification sweep
happened to probe. A fresh `String` needle leaks too, by the identical
mechanism:

    Vec[String].contains(mk_string())        10 B / 2 allocations (2 calls)
    Vec[Vec[String]].contains(mk_vec())     202 B / 4 allocations (2 calls)

Any heap-owning needle type leaks. This is worth stating because the row's
"SCOPE" paragraph reads as though a container-typed argument were the
condition; the condition is only that the needle be fresh-owned and own heap.

WHAT LANDED: the two free helpers the `Set.contains` site already pairs -- the
String/Vec one plus the aggregate sibling that covers a fresh STRUCT needle.
The `Vec`-needle leg COMPOSES with B-2026-08-27-26 rather than duplicating it:
this row restores the call, and that fix is what makes the call drain the
needle's own elements once it fires. Neither alone closes the `Vec` case.

THE NON-FRESH LEGS ARE WHERE THE RISK LIVES, and the fixture is built around
them rather than around the leak. A bound needle is owned by its binding, a
place expression by its container, a literal by rodata -- freeing any of them
here is a double-free or a free of static memory. Each is read back AFTER the
lookup so that a would-be double-free surfaces as an observable
use-after-free; without those legs a fix that freed unconditionally would pass
the leak assertions cleanly. Negative-controlled: reverted, the fixture leaks
111 bytes in 4 allocations.

Suites: llvm 15452 passed / 0 failed; default 10050 passed / 0 failed; clippy
clean on both legs.

SEPARATELY, and unrelated to this row: verifying it found `main` RED on CI's
default leg -- both `test_check_project_reports_the_multi_file_*_error_build_
reports` tests (landed with B-2026-08-27-27's fix) fail there on their own
anti-vacuity assert, because a no-llvm `karac build` exits SUCCESS with
"requires the llvm feature" and never reaches the pass they compare against.
Gated on `llvm` in the same push.
title: `Vec.contains(<fresh Vec temporary>)` LEAKS THE NEEDLE ENTIRELY -- buffer and elements -- because `free_fresh_owned_str_arg` does not fire at that call site at all, unlike the `==` operand path where it fires and misses only the elements (B-2026-08-27-26).
detail:
FOUND while verifying B-2026-08-27-26's fix did not double-free at the other
29 call sites of `free_fresh_owned_str_arg`. Five of the six probed shapes were
clean; this one leaked, and the measurement separates it from -26 cleanly.

MEASURED under LSan, `outer: Vec[Vec[String]]`, `ids(n) -> Vec[String]`:

    outer.contains(ids(1));
    outer.contains(ids(9));

    SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 202 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocation(s)

Four allocations for two calls = each needle's outer buffer PLUS its element
string. The whole needle survives, not just its elements.

WHY IT IS NOT -26. That row is about a free that FIRES and releases only the
outer buffer, so its signature is "elements leak, buffer does not". Here both
leak, and the number is IDENTICAL with -26's fix reverted (202 B / 4 either
way) -- so the free is not reached at this site at all. Same symptom class,
opposite cause.

NOT INVESTIGATED: which of the guards declines. `vec_method.rs` does call
`free_fresh_owned_str_arg(&needle_arg.value, needle_val)` on the `contains`
path, so either the freshness predicates reject a `Vec`-typed Call result, or
that call is on a branch this shape does not take. The measurement above is
the whole of what was established.

SCOPE: a lookup-style method that BORROWS a container-typed argument. `insert`
and `push` MOVE theirs and are correctly untouched (measured clean).

title: A STRUCT `.clone()` passed DIRECTLY as a call argument was never freed — `take(a.clone())` leaked its temporary once per call, unbounded in a loop, while `take(mk())` and `let c = a.clone(); take(c)` were both clean. Struct-specific (the original title over-generalised): a `String` / `Vec` clone in the same position was always clean, because only an aggregate param's callee entry-copy orphans the caller's value.
detail:
A `.clone()` result passed DIRECTLY as a call argument is never freed. The temporary leaks once per call, and it is not about indexing — a plain local leaks identically.

MEASURED under LSan, three shapes side by side:

    fn take(x: It) -> i64 { return x.name.len(); }

    while i < 20 { t = t + take(mk()); }            clean
    while i < 20 { t = t + take(a.clone()); }       LEAKS 680 bytes / 20 allocations
    while i < 20 { t = t + take(v[0].clone()); }    LEAKS 680 bytes / 20 allocations
    while i < 20 { let c = v[0].clone(); take(c); } clean

So: a fresh temporary from an ordinary call is freed, and a clone BOUND TO A LOCAL first is freed, but the clone passed inline is not. One allocation leaked per call, unbounded in a loop.

PRE-EXISTING, and verified as such: the plain-local form reproduces on a clean checkout of `origin/main` with no local changes applied. It is old — `a.clone()` as an argument has always been expressible — and it was invisible because no ASAN fixture used that spelling; every one of them bound the clone first or passed a fresh call result.

READ AS: the caller materialises the clone into a temporary for the argument slot and never registers that temporary for cleanup, while a call-returned temporary IS registered. The callee takes the parameter by value, so ownership was meant to transfer; whichever side is meant to free it, neither does.

MATTERS MORE THAN A NORMAL LEAK because `.clone()` on an argument is exactly what B-2026-08-26-21's diagnostic tells users (and `karac fix`) to write when a call argument reads a non-`Copy` element: `take(v[i].clone())` is the fix-it's own suggested spelling. Four `memory_sanitizer.rs` fixtures hit it during that migration and had to bind the clone to a local instead.

WORKAROUND until fixed: bind first — `let c = x.clone(); f(c)`.

SOURCE NOTE: found while migrating the ASAN corpus for B-2026-08-26-21, by probing why four fixtures leaked after an otherwise-correct `.clone()` migration.
fix:
FIXED by 9f3f4fe (2026-08-27).

THE ROW'S TITLE WAS TOO BROAD AND IS CORRECTED HERE: the leak is
STRUCT-SPECIFIC. Both repro shapes in the original measurement passed a
struct (`It { id: i64, name: String }`), and a probe of the neighbours it
never ran shows why that matters — `take_s(a.clone())` over a `String` and
`take_v(b.clone())` over a `Vec[i64]` are both CLEAN, and always were. A
`String`/`Vec` argument passes its `{ptr,len,cap}` header by value and the
callee frees it directly; there is no second copy for the caller's original
to be orphaned behind. The corrected title says so, and
`asan_string_and_vec_clone_call_arguments_stay_clean` pins it so the fix
cannot quietly widen.

MECHANISM. An owned by-value aggregate param is callee-owned by ENTRY COPY
(`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst`, `param_own.rs`): before the body
runs, the callee duplicates the struct's heap fields into its own frame and
registers the drop that frees THAT copy. So the caller's argument value is
never taken — it is copied from — and whoever owns it caller-side must free
it. For every other fresh-temp spelling somebody does:
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` has an arm for a struct LITERAL
(`f(S { .. })`), for a fn-call temp (`f(mk())`), and for a variant ctor
(`f(E.V(..))`), and a let-bound clone is freed by its binding's own
`let`-path drop. A top-level `.clone()` matched NONE of them: it is a
`MethodCall`, and the arm dispatch enumerates `Call | Path | StructLiteral |
Tuple`. So the clone's deep copy of the receiver's heap had no owner at all.

THE FIX is that missing arm, and it is a name lookup rather than new
ownership policy: `owned_struct_temp_arg_name` answers the struct name for a
struct literal (as before) OR for a `recv.clone()` whose receiver is an
identifier of known struct type or an element read (`v[i].clone()`). The
registration body underneath is UNCHANGED — the same `needs_memory_drop`
gate, so the same `callee_owns_by_transfer` exclusion (B-2026-08-07-15) and
the same shared/copy-support reasoning apply to the clone temp as to the
literal. That is deliberate: the clone temp IS a fresh owned struct value in
argument position, so the question of who frees it has one answer, not two.

MEMORY ONLY FOR THE CLONE SHAPE, and the reason is parity rather than
caution. A clone temp runs no user `Drop` body on EITHER backend today: this
arm's body registrations are literal-shaped, and the interpreter's twin
(`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`) resolves a type name for a struct literal / fn
call / variant ctor and returns `None` for a method call. The two therefore
AGREE, and registering the body on the codegen side alone would have traded
this leak for a run-vs-build divergence — the strictly worse defect, and the
exact class B-2026-08-26-21 spent a session on. Verified rather than
assumed: `#[derive(Clone)] struct G` with an `impl Drop` printing its id
prints `drop 1` exactly once under `--interp` and under `karac build` alike,
before and after. Whether a clone temp SHOULD run a body is a separate
question about a shape both backends currently skip; the free is not.

MEASURED. `take(a.clone())` over 20 iterations: 680 bytes in 20 allocations
before (34 bytes each — the cloned `String`), zero after. The index-receiver
spelling `take(v[0].clone())` measured identically and is fixed by the same
arm. Three fixtures pin the three answers
(`asan_struct_clone_call_argument_frees_temp`,
`asan_struct_clone_of_element_call_argument_frees_temp`, and the String/Vec
control above); the 39-test `clone` family of `memory_sanitizer.rs` stays
green, as does the suite.

PRE-EXISTING, as the row said: `a.clone()` in argument position has always
been expressible, and it was invisible because no ASAN fixture used the
inline spelling — every one bound the clone first or passed a fresh call
result. B-2026-08-26-21's migration is what produced the spelling in
quantity, since `.clone()` is one of the two remedies its diagnostic names.

RESOLVED by c1c1f35, along the line the row prescribed: give the temporary an
element-walking owner, since there is no buffer for a free to hang off. The row
is unusually accurate about its own cause -- "an `Array[T, N]` is a by-value
`[N x T]` with no `{ptr, len, cap}` buffer ... there is NO cleanup on the path"
-- and the fix follows it directly.

WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT AND IS WORTH KEEPING: the honest framing of provenance.
Before B-2026-08-27-25 this program did not compile, so making it compile
created the leak surface; the fix is right and this is a new gap behind it, not
a regression. That is the correct way to read it and it is why the severity is
medium rather than high.

WHERE IT DIFFERS FROM THE FIX AS BUILT. The row suggests registering the drop
"as a scope-exit action the way B-2026-08-11-33 does for a struct temporary".
The drop is emitted IMMEDIATELY instead, for the reason
`free_fresh_owned_struct_key_arg` records: a scope-exit registration hoists one
entry alloca and frees only the LAST value when the comparison sits in a loop,
which is the B-2026-08-25-33 shape. Adjacent store-and-drop in one basic block
is correct per iteration.

The element policy is not new either: `vec_element_drain_fn` decides WHETHER an
element needs dropping, so `Array[i64, N]` emits nothing here exactly as it
frees nothing on the `Vec` path, and `Array[Vec[i64], N]` is covered with no
case of its own -- verified, since a fix keyed on `String` would pass every
other row of the fixture and fail that one.

THE ROW'S SCOPE PARAGRAPH IS TOO PESSIMISTIC IN ONE DIRECTION AND TOO OPTIMISTIC
IN ANOTHER, and both halves were measured rather than reasoned about. It says
"an array temporary in any OTHER position was never freed either". Not so for a
BY-VALUE CALL ARGUMENT: `take(mk(3))` is clean, because the callee owns the
parameter and drops it at its own scope exit. But an INDEXED temporary,
`mk(4)[0]`, does leak -- 13 bytes in 2 allocations -- which the row does not
mention. Filed separately.

A THIRD LEAK, unrelated to temporaries and found by probing the non-fresh
controls: a struct FIELD of array type with heap elements is never dropped
(`struct Holder { a: Array[String, 2] }`, 13 bytes in 2 allocations, no
comparison anywhere in the program). Also filed separately. Both reproduce
identically with this fix reverted.

VERIFIED under LSan across fresh-vs-fresh, `!=`, a `Vec` element type, rodata
literals on both sides, literal-vs-fresh, and bound operands read back after the
comparison. The literal-vs-fresh row is the one that matters most: it puts one
rodata operand and one heap operand in a SINGLE comparison, so an implementation
that dropped "both operands" rather than "each fresh operand" frees static
memory there and nowhere else. Negative-controlled: reverted, the fixture leaks
193 bytes in 14 allocations. Suites: llvm 15463 passed / 0 failed; default 10053
passed / 0 failed; clippy clean on both legs.
title: A fresh `Array[String, N]` TEMPORARY compared with `==` leaks every element -- 26 bytes in 4 allocations under LSan, the same signature B-2026-08-27-26 measured for the `Vec` shape and NOT covered by its fix.
detail:
FOUND while adding B-2026-08-27-25's ASAN fixture, and separated from
B-2026-08-27-26 by measurement rather than by assumption: this reproduces ON
TOP OF that row's fix (`e57bc89`), unchanged.

REPRO under `assert_clean_asan_run`:

  fn mk(n: i64) -> Array[String, 2] {
      return Array[f"item{n}", f"item{n + 1}"];
  }
  fn main() { println(f"{mk(2) == mk(2)}"); }

  SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 26 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocation(s)

Four allocations = the four element Strings of the two temporaries. Every
neighbouring shape is CLEAN and was measured so in the same run: two BOUND
`Array[String, 2]` values compared (`let p = mk(1); let q = mk(1); p == q`), a
bound array moved into a `Map` key on a duplicate insert, and both
`Slice[String]` legs -- so the defect is the TEMPORARY, not the comparator and
not the type.

WHY -26's FIX DOES NOT REACH IT. That fix drains a fresh Vec temporary's
elements before freeing its buffer, hooked on `vec_elem_te_of_operand` inside
`free_fresh_owned_str_arg`. An array operand never reaches that helper at all:
`compile_array_eq` returns early from the Binary arm, exactly as
`compile_vec_eq` does, and an `Array[T, N]` is a by-value `[N x T]` with no
`{ptr, len, cap}` buffer for a buffer-free to hang off. So there is no
partial free to widen here -- there is NO cleanup on the path.

PRE-EXISTING? No, and this is worth stating plainly: before B-2026-08-27-25 the
program did not compile (`karac build` reported "left operand has non-comparable
type ArrayType"), so making it compile is what created the leak surface. That is
the honest framing -- the fix is right and the leak is a new gap behind it, not
a regression in previously-working code.

SHAPE OF THE FIX. The same one -26 chose, one type over: give the temporary an
owner rather than emitting a free. The operand type is already available at the
site (`array_te_of_operand`), so `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr` on the array type
-- which walks the elements -- is the operation, registered as a scope-exit
action the way B-2026-08-11-33 does for a struct temporary.

SCOPE: any fresh-temporary `Array[T, N]` operand of `==` / `!=` whose element
owns heap (`String`, `Vec`, a struct with either). A scalar element is clean by
construction. Nothing outside the surface-`Binary` path is implicated -- an
array temporary in any OTHER position was never freed either, but that is the
general fresh-temporary question, not this one.

fix:
FIXED by 9c06c13.

RESOLVED along the line the row prescribed, and the caveat it flagged -- "taking
care that the EXTRACTED element is not dropped with it" -- turned out to have a
settled answer already in the tree rather than needing a new policy.

`compile_inline_temp_vec_index_ex` is the `Vec` peer of this site and has been
clean on the identical program since B-2026-06-14-32. Its recipe is: read the
element, DEEP-CLONE it, then drop the whole temporary. The clone is what makes
dropping the indexed element safe -- the load shallow-aliases that element's
buffer for a non-Copy element type -- and it is also what the INTERPRETER does,
which is the oracle here: indexing does not consume, so `v[i]` stays valid and
the read is a copy. So the array arm is that recipe applied at the array's own
lowering (`compile_index`'s "arbitrary expression" branch, where a temporary is
already materialized into `arr.tmp` for the GEP), with
`emit_drop_fn_for_array` -- the operation B-2026-08-27-30 added -- as the drop.

THE FIX IS TWO HALVES AND THE SECOND IS NOT OPTIONAL. Dropping the temporary
alone moved the fixture from 13 bytes in 2 allocations to 6 in 1: the elements
were freed but the CLONE then leaked, because it has no consuming binding and
no scope-exit cleanup of its own. That is the same gap
`expr_is_inline_temp_vec_heap_index` exists to close for the Vec shape, so the
array case was added to that one predicate rather than to any of its five
consumers -- print args, by-value user-fn args, map keys, method args, return
all ask the same question and now get the same answer.

SCOPE, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The row's `let s = mk(4)[0]` sibling is
NOT part of this: `karac check` rejects it with E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY, exactly
as it rejects the `Vec` spelling, so the shape is not in the language. It looked
like a live leak only because the ASAN harness compiles in-process without the
ownership gate -- worth knowing before trusting any harness-only repro.

Two adjacent shapes were measured and are NOT covered, deliberately. An
`Array[Vec[..], N]` temporary cannot be indexed at all in v1 (a nested index or
an indexed-receiver method call, both separate codegen gaps), so the fixture
covers that element type as a struct FIELD instead, reaching the same
`emit_drop_fn_for_array` with the same element policy. And an array LITERAL
temporary -- `Array[f"a{n}", f"b{n}"][0]` -- still leaks, because
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` admits only `Call`/`MethodCall`; it reproduces
byte-identically with this fix reverted, so it is pre-existing rather than a
residue. Filed separately with its own measurement (the leak there is the
INDEXED element specifically -- 5 bytes indexing element 0, 2 bytes indexing
element 1 of the same array -- so the non-indexed elements already have an
owner and it is a different mechanism from this row).

VERIFIED under LSan across both index positions, an `Array[i64, N]` control
(clones nothing, drops nothing), a 3-iteration loop, and a BOUND array read back
twice afterwards -- the control that would surface a wrong drop as a
use-after-free rather than a leak. Negative-controlled: with the fix reverted the
fixture leaks 60 bytes in 9 allocations. All three backends agree byte-for-byte
on the fixture (interp == jit == aot).
title: An INDEXED `Array[String, N]` temporary leaks its elements -- `mk(4)[0]` loses 13 bytes in 2 allocations -- a different position from B-2026-08-27-30's `==` operand and not covered by its fix.
detail:
FOUND while probing the positions B-2026-08-27-30's scope paragraph left as an
open question. That row states "an array temporary in any OTHER position was
never freed either, but that is the general fresh-temporary question". Measured,
that is half right, and the half it gets wrong is the useful half.

MEASURED under `assert_clean_asan_run`, with
`mk(n) -> Array[String, 2]` returning `Array[f"item{n}", f"item{n + 1}"]`:

  println(mk(4)[0]);                    13 B / 2 allocations   LEAKS
  println(f"{take(mk(3))}");            clean                  (by-value param)
  let p = mk(1); ... p == q             clean                  (bound)

So the by-value CALL ARGUMENT position is already covered -- the callee owns
the parameter and drops it at its own scope exit -- and it is the INDEX that
leaks. The two allocations are the array's two element strings; indexing reads
one element out and the array itself is then unreachable with nothing to drop
it.

NOT B-2026-08-27-30. That row is the `==` operand position and its fix
(`c1c1f35`) drops each fresh operand inside `compile_array_eq`. This shape never
reaches that function, and the leak reproduces identically with that fix
reverted.

FIX SHAPE is likely the same operation at a different site:
`emit_drop_fn_for_array` now exists and walks the elements, so the index
lowering needs to drop the temporary after extracting the element -- taking care
that the EXTRACTED element is not dropped with it, which is the difference from
the `==` case where nothing escapes.

fix:
FIXED by 9c06c13.

RESOLVED. The row's hypothesis -- "whether the walk simply has no `Array` case
was not established here" -- is confirmed, and the answer is that it has no
array case in TWO independent classifiers, which is why nothing caught it.

`emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl` classifies each field twice over. The
name-based pass reads `struct_field_type_names`, which is the last path segment
of the field's `TypeExpr`; an array is `TypeKind::Array { element, size }`, not
a `Path`, so the recorded name is `None` and no arm matches. The type-driven
nested-aggregate pass then destructures the field's LLVM type as a `StructType`
and `continue`s on anything else; an array lowers to `ArrayType`, so it never
gets asked. A `Vec[String]` field is caught by the first and a nested struct by
the second, which is exactly why the row's "LIKELY ADJACENT" guess was right:
the gap is the `Array[T, N]` arm specifically.

Fixed with a third classification pass, running last so it only promotes fields
every other pass left `None`, routed through the field's own
`karac_drop_Array_<T>_<N>` (`emit_drop_fn_for_array`, from B-2026-08-27-30).
Classified only when that returns `Some`, so an `Array[i64, N]` field adds
nothing -- the element policy is `vec_element_drain_fn`'s, shared with the `Vec`
drain, so `Array[Vec[i64], N]` is covered with no case of its own.

THE DROP ALONE IS A USE-AFTER-FREE, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH READING. This
codebase states the pairing rule in several places -- widening a drop obliges
the move sites to widen with it -- and here it was not theoretical. With the
classification landed by itself, `fn take(h: Holder) -> String { return
h.a[0]; }` turned this row's 13-byte leak into a heap-use-after-free: the
callee's scope-exit drop freed the very element it had just handed back. The
paired half is `vec_index_elem_type_expr`'s `FieldAccess` arm, which resolved a
`Vec[E]` field to `E` and returned `None` for an array; widening it is what
makes `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg` deep-clone the read in return and
owned-sink position. The `Vec` spelling of that same program was already clean,
through exactly that resolver -- so the fix is again "do what the Vec field
already does", not a new mechanism. That leg is in the fixture permanently
because it fails LOUDLY (a nonzero exit, not a leak count) if the two halves
ever drift apart again.

VERIFIED under LSan across: the field read three times over (a drop at the read
would surface as a use-after-free), the by-value-param field return above, a
MOVED-OUT field (`let taken = h.a;` -- the other direction of the pairing, where
`h`'s drop must not free what was moved), an `Array[i64, 2]` field control, an
`Array[Vec[i64], 2]` field for the element policy, and a `Vec[Holder]` so the
field drop is reached through a container's element drain rather than only a
bare scope exit. Negative-controlled: with the fix reverted the fixture leaks
124 bytes in 11 allocations. All three backends agree byte-for-byte on the
fixture (interp == jit == aot).
title: A struct FIELD of type `Array[T, N]` with heap elements is never dropped: `struct Holder { a: Array[String, 2] }` leaks 13 bytes in 2 allocations with no comparison, index or temporary anywhere in the program.
detail:
FOUND while probing the NON-FRESH control legs for B-2026-08-27-30's fix -- the
shapes that must NOT be dropped at the `==` site. The place-expression leg
(`h.a == b`) leaked, and isolating it showed the comparison was irrelevant.

MINIMAL REPRO under `assert_clean_asan_run` -- note there is no `==` in it:

  fn mk(n: i64) -> Array[String, 2] { return Array[f"item{n}", f"item{n + 1}"]; }
  struct Holder { a: Array[String, 2] }
  fn main() {
      let h = Holder { a: mk(7) };
      println(h.a[0]);
  }

  SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 13 byte(s) leaked in 2 allocation(s)

Two allocations = the field's two element strings. `h` goes out of scope and its
struct drop does not walk an ARRAY field's elements.

WHY IT IS ITS OWN ROW. B-2026-08-27-30 and -31 are both about a fresh TEMPORARY
with no owner. Here there IS an owner -- the binding `h` -- and its drop is
incomplete, which is a different defect in a different place
(`emit_struct_drop_synthesis`'s field walk) and reproduces with -30's fix
reverted, unchanged.

LIKELY ADJACENT: the same field walk presumably handles a `Vec` or `String`
field correctly (those are the shapes it was built for), so the gap is the
`Array[T, N]` field arm specifically. `emit_drop_fn_for_array` (added by
`c1c1f35`) is the operation that arm would need; whether the walk simply has no
`Array` case was not established here.

fix:
FIXED by 01d6784. `Env::bound_satisfied` -- the gate METHOD RESOLUTION uses -- now composes the eight derive-only builtins (`Copy` / `Clone` / `Debug` / `PartialEq` / `PartialOrd` / `Eq` / `Ord` / `Hash`) structurally over a tuple, a fixed array and a SIMD vector, and admits `()` alongside the scalars. Three lines of dispatch; the recursion goes back through `bound_satisfied` itself, so the float carve-out above it composes rather than being restated.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is one line of the row's own guess made precise: `impl_table_key` returns `None` for a tuple BY CONSTRUCTION -- `env_add_impl` deliberately never keys tuples or arrays, and there is no surface syntax for `impl Ord for (i64, i64)` -- so the impl-table walk that `bound_satisfied` ends in answered `false` for EVERY trait at those shapes, not just `Ord`. The sibling gate on the free-fn side (`type_satisfies_bound`) delegates to `type_supports_*`, which has recursed through `Type::Tuple` since long before this row. Two hand-rolled tables, one of them missing the aggregates. This is the THIRD patch of that shape to the same function: primitives first, then `#[derive]`d named types (B-2026-08-25-35, whose comment already names the pattern -- "the same type, the same bound, two answers decided by which side of the call the bound was written on"), now the structural shapes.

MEASURED, one build, impl gate vs free-fn gate: REJECT/OK for tuples under `Ord`, `Eq`, `Hash`, `Clone` and `PartialOrd`; for a nested tuple; for `(String, i64)`; for `Array[i64, 2]`; and for `()`. Both gates already AGREED on `(i64, f64)` and `Array[f64, 2]` under `Ord` (rejected -- design.md § Float semantics), and still do. `Default` is deliberately excluded from the composition set: the sibling `type_supports_default` has no aggregate arm at all, so composing it would have invented an answer the free-fn side does not give -- a fresh divergence in the opposite direction.

THE ROW'S SECOND SYMPTOM IS NOT FIXED, and it turned out to be the load-bearing half. `.cmp()` on a tuple has no dispatch on ANY surface, and a comparison written against the type PARAMETER inside a bounded impl (`fn beats(x: T, y: T) -> bool { x < y }`) lowers to `T.cmp` -- so the bound now admits the tuple and the body then fails to lower. Filed as its own row. That is also why `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]`, the row's motivating spelling, still does not work on the compiled backend: every `PriorityQueue` method lives on `impl[T: Ord]`, and `outranks` orders through `T`.

TWO PRE-EXISTING DEFECTS FOUND WHILE VERIFYING THIS, both filed separately and both reproducing with the bound REMOVED (`impl[T] W[T]`), so neither is caused by this fix. First, tuple comparison never lowered at all: `karac check` accepted `a < b` on two tuples and then the interpreter died on its catch-all arm while `karac build` refused with "Unsupported struct binary op: Lt" -- fixed here too, in the same commit, since admitting the bound while `<` cannot lower would have shipped a program that compiles and refuses to run. Second, and worse: a tuple type ARGUMENT does not survive the monomorphization substitution channel, which is name-keyed. That one is a silent miscompile and is the reason `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]` printed garbage rather than an error.
title: A `T: Ord` bound on a GENERIC IMPL rejects a tuple that the IDENTICAL bound on a free fn accepts: `impl[T: Ord] W[T]` refuses `W[(i64, i64)]` with "`(i64, i64)` does not implement `Ord`", while `fn pick[T: Ord](a: T, b: T)` takes the same tuple and may even call `.cmp()` on it
detail:
REPRODUCE, no stdlib involved:

    struct W[=T] { v: Vec[T] }
    impl[T: Ord] W[T] { fn add(mut ref self, x: T) { self.v.push(x); } }
    fn main() { let mut w: W[(i64, i64)] = W { v: Vec.new() }; w.add((1, 2)); }

    error[typecheck]: method 'add' is not callable on this `W`: trait bound `T: Ord` is not
    satisfied; `(i64, i64)` does not implement `Ord`

THE SAME BOUND ON A FREE FN IS ACCEPTED, which is what makes this a bound-checking inconsistency rather than a plain missing impl:

    fn pick[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> T { match a.cmp(b) { Ordering.Less => a, _ => b } }
    fn main() { let r = pick((1, 2), (1, 3)); println(r.0); }   // All checks passed

Note that free fn even calls `.cmp()` on the tuple and is accepted, while `.cmp()` on a CONCRETE tuple (`(1,2).cmp((1,3))`) is rejected -- so the two sites disagree in both directions.

MEASURED BOUNDARY (all on one build):
  OK        tuple `<` / `>` / `==`
  OK        `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort()` and `.sort_by(...)`
  OK        `SortedSet[(i64,i64)]` -- and SortedSet's element bound IS `T: Ord`
  OK        free fn `[T: Ord]` with a tuple arg, including one that calls `.cmp()`
  OK        generic impl with NO bound (`impl[T] W[T]`) at a tuple
  OK        generic impl `[T: Ord]` at `i64` and at `String`
  REJECTED  generic impl `[T: Ord]` at `(i64, i64)` and at `(i64, i64, i64)`
  REJECTED  `.cmp()` on a concrete tuple
  REJECTED  `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]`

So it is specific to the bound check at a GENERIC IMPL METHOD, and specific to tuples: the same impl accepts scalars, and dropping the bound accepts tuples. `SortedSet` passing is the sharpest control -- it carries the same `T: Ord` element bound and is satisfied by a tuple, but it is a compiler builtin rather than a Kāra-source generic impl.

CONSISTENT ACROSS BACKENDS: `karac check` and `karac run --interp` both reject, so this is a front-end false-positive and not a codegen divergence. Nothing is miscompiled; correct programs are refused.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW: `PriorityQueue[T: Ord]` is the first STDLIB type written as a Kāra-source generic impl with an `Ord` bound -- every earlier ordered collection (`SortedMap`, `SortedSet`) is a builtin, whose bound goes through the path that already accepts tuples. So this was reachable before but had no stdlib caller to hit it.

SOURCE NOTE: found writing kata 347's bounded-heap variant, where `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]` is the obvious spelling for a (count, value) entry. The kata did NOT work around it silently: it carries a `Weakest` struct with a hand-written PartialEq/Eq/PartialOrd/Ord chain, and its header states the rejection and points here. That chain is independently worth keeping -- the answer orders by (count DESC, value ASC), two keys disagreeing on direction, which no DERIVED ordering can express -- so the kata is not merely a workaround. But the tuple spelling should compile.

fix:
FIXED by c56e598. Two defects in the same family, and they are not
separable: the second is unreachable until the first is fixed, and becomes a
live use-after-free the moment it is.

ROOT CAUSE, one step earlier than this row's own framing. The row reads the
symptom as "the branch-leaf retain is emitted once per binding, not once per
use", which is how it looks from outside and which predicts the boundary
correctly. Instrumenting `share_option_shared_ref_for_arg` shows the mechanism
is upstream of that: the consuming binding `t` is never registered in
`var_option_shared_heap` AT ALL.

    [DBG] retain emitted for: a     <- then-arm leaf  (B-2026-08-26-12)
    [DBG] retain emitted for: b     <- else-arm leaf
    [DBG] DECLINED (unregistered): t   x3   <- every `show(t)` call site

Both leaf retains fire exactly as B-2026-08-26-12 intended. All three call-site
retains DECLINE, because the call-site companion self-gates on the same
`var_option_shared_heap` registration, and `t` has none. So `t` gets neither the
per-USE retains a registered binding gets nor its own scope-exit `RcDecOption`,
and the single leaf retain is standing in for the whole of `t`'s ownership. One
`+1` covers exactly TWO consumptions -- which is why the boundary is exact at
the third, and why two reads look green rather than merely lucky.

The registration is refused by `control_flow_owned_option_shared`, case (g) of
the `let`-RHS cascade in `stmts.rs`. It counts a branch leaf as owning a `+1`
only when the leaf is a PRODUCER -- a `Some(..)` literal, a call returning
`Option[shared]`, or `None` -- and a bare binding handed out of an arm is none
of those. That was correct when it was written and stopped being correct when
B-2026-08-26-12 taught the leaf itself to retain: from that commit on, a bare
`Option[shared]` binding handed out of an arm DOES carry an independent `+1`.
The two mechanisms simply never met. Fix: an `Identifier` arm in
`control_flow_owned_option_shared` keyed on `var_option_shared_heap` -- the SAME
predicate the emission self-gates on, so the registration cannot drift from
whether the retain was actually emitted.

SECOND DEFECT, found by the fix and fixed with it: `if let`'s THEN arm never had
a leaf hook. B-2026-08-26-12's message states its `compile_block_with_frame`
hook covers "if/if let arms". It covers `if`, and an `if let`'s ELSE branch,
which routes through that helper -- but an `if let`'s THEN arm hand-rolls its
frame drain against a plain `compile_block` (`control_flow.rs`), carries the
plain-`shared` suppressor, and never reaches the `Option[shared]` retain. The
gap was invisible while the consuming binding went unregistered, because no
retain and no dec is balanced by accident. Registering the binding makes the
missing `+1` load-bearing: the new owner's scope-exit dec frees a box the leaf
never retained, and the source's own dec then runs through it. Measured
`if let Some(x) = o { a } else { b }` with three consumptions: BEFORE the fix
`/ 0 0` on AOT and JIT plus a `malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected`;
with the case-(g) fix alone the values became correct but the JIT still aborted;
with the `if let` hook added, clean on all three backends. Gated on
`tail.is_none()` like the `match` sibling, so a function-tail `if let` does not
take a second retain -- verified by a fixture that returns one.

VERIFICATION. `option_shared_from_a_branch_leaf_survives_a_third_consumption`
(the `#[ignore]`d acceptance test that landed with this row) is un-ignored, and
`option_shared_from_every_branch_leaf_form_survives_repeated_consumption` covers
twelve legs at three-plus consumptions each: both `if` arms, both `if let` arms,
a `match` arm, a bare block, an else-if chain, a nested `if`, both directions of
the MIXED borrowed/fresh shape, a five-use leg, and a `None` arm. Both verified
RED against the unfixed compiler; the pre-existing no-branch control stays
green. Twinned against the interpreter, which was correct throughout, and
`option_shared_branch_leaf_survives_repeated_consumption` in
`tests/interpreter.rs` pins that oracle on the DEFAULT feature leg -- without it
the semantics have no coverage under a plain `cargo test`, since `tests/codegen.rs`
is entirely `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`.

`asan_option_shared_branch_leaf_repeated_consumption_is_clean` is the LEAK half
and its doc says so: measured GREEN against the unfixed compiler, exactly as
this row and B-2026-08-26-12 predict, because the sanitizer is linked in rather
than compiled in and a stray dec writes `-1` instead of calling `free` twice.
It gates the obvious WRONG fix instead -- the defect is a missing `+1`, so
retaining harder makes the symptom go away, and a retain at the phi or on an
arm whose producer already carries its own `+1` leaks. Its mixed-arm leg takes
each direction on alternating iterations so either error accumulates into a
leak LSan reports.

REMAINDER, split out rather than buried here: an arm-LOCAL binding as the leaf
(`let t = if c { let u = make(1); u } else { b };`) is still wrong, unchanged by
this fix in both directions -- measured `/ 0 0` on AOT and JIT before and after,
`1 1 1` on the interpreter. Different mechanism: `u`'s leaf retain DOES fire,
but `u`'s own scope-exit dec inside the arm cancels it, and `u` is out of the
name env by the time case (g) runs, so `t` cannot be registered from it. Filed
as B-2026-08-27-43.
title: 3454927 (B-2026-08-26-12) EMITS THE BRANCH-LEAF RETAIN ONCE PER BINDING, NOT ONCE PER USE, so the THIRD consumption of an `Option[shared]` selected by a value-position branch reads through a freed box. Eight lines, no loop: `let t = if true { a } else { b };` then three `show(t)` calls prints `1 1 1` under `--interp` and `1 1 <garbage>` under `karac build` -- WHICH EXITS 0. Two uses are balanced and green; the boundary is exactly the third. The fix's own fixtures all consume the value once, so the axis was never covered.
detail:
EIGHT LINES, NO LOOP, AND THE COMPILED ANSWER IS SILENTLY WRONG:

    shared struct Node { val: i64 }
    fn make(n: i64) -> Option[Node] { return Some(Node { val: n }); }
    fn show(t: Option[Node]) -> i64 {
        match t { None => { return 0; } Some(n) => { return n.val; } }
    }
    fn main() {
        let a = make(1);
        let b = make(2);
        let t = if true { a } else { b };
        println(f"{show(t)} {show(t)} {show(t)}");
    }

MEASURED on 89c16d8 (i.e. AFTER 3454927, the B-2026-08-26-12 fix):

    karac run --interp  ->  1 1 1                              exit 0   CORRECT
    karac build         ->  1 1 -4404075218272500113           exit 0   WRONG, SILENT
    karac run (JIT)     ->  1 1 -7168264928796111300  then
                            malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected

The garbage word differs run to run, which is what a read through a reclaimed
box looks like. THE AOT BINARY EXITS 0 -- there is no abort, no diagnostic, and
nothing in the exit status to notice. That is the whole reason this is filed
high rather than as a leftover of the row it follows: B-2026-08-26-12 announced
itself by killing the process, and this does not.

CONTROL, identical but for the branch leaf -- `let a = make(1); println(f"{show(a)}
{show(a)} {show(a)}");` -- prints `1 1 1` on all four surfaces.

THE BOUNDARY IS THE THIRD USE, and it is exact:

    2 consumptions of the selected value   ->  green on every surface
    3 consumptions                         ->  third one reads freed memory
    4 consumptions                         ->  same

That boundary IS the diagnosis. 3454927 taught a value-position branch leaf to
emit a retain when it hands an `Option[shared]` binding to an owned consumer,
which took the count from 1 to 2 and made the two-use case balance exactly.
The retain is emitted ONCE for the binding, not once per USE, so a third
consumer decrements a box already at 0. The fix was correct in kind and short
by a factor: per-binding where it needed to be per-use.

WHY IT SURVIVED THE FIX'S OWN TEST SUITE. Every fixture landed with 3454927 --
the `if` arm, the `match` arm, the bare block, the `else if` chain, the nested
`if`, the `let` RHS -- consumes the selected value EXACTLY ONCE, inside a loop
that runs twice. Two iterations x one use is a different axis from one
iteration x three uses, and the retain-per-binding accounting is correct on the
first and wrong on the second. `option_shared_from_a_branch_leaf_survives_a_third_consumption`
(landed with this row, `#[ignore]`d and verified RED) is the missing axis, with
`option_shared_read_three_times_without_a_branch_leaf` beside it as the green
control so the failure stays attributable to the leaf.

ASAN STILL DOES NOT REPRODUCE IT, for the reason recorded on B-2026-08-26-12:
`-fsanitize=address` is linked in, never compiled in, so it sees allocator-level
faults and cannot see a use-after-free ACCESS from the uninstrumented Kara
object. Here the access IS the bug -- the AOT run does not even reach an
allocator fault -- so the E2E harness remains the only place this can be gated.

SOURCE NOTE: kata 297's `differential.kara` still aborted after 3454927, with a
different allocator message than before (`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
rather than `malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected`). Bisected to its P5
block, where the selected tree is consumed four times -- once for the expected
fingerprint and once per codec arm. Dropping any one of the three arms makes it
green, and duplicating one arm instead of adding a distinct one crashes just the
same, which is what showed the count rather than the arms to be the variable.
Per the katas' never-route-around rule the differential is not being rephrased;
it stays as the witness and cites this row.

fix:
FIXED by 5313f90, along the line the row prescribed for the drop but NOT the
one it prescribed for the fix shape -- and its measurement turned out to be an
optimizer artifact, which is the part worth keeping.

THE MECHANISM IS -31's AFTER ALL. The row read the leak as "only the INDEXED
element leaks, so the literal's other elements already have an owner", and
proposed the consumer half alone (`expr_is_inline_temp_vec_heap_index`) rather
than -31's pair. They have no owner. At `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` the same program
loses BOTH elements -- 7 bytes in 2 allocations for
`println(Array[f"aaaa{n}", f"b{n}"][0])` -- and the IR shows why: every
element's independent cleanup is suppressed by `compile_array_literal` (the
f-string accumulator's cap is zeroed, a bound source's cap is zeroed by the
move) and nothing takes over, because only a BOUND literal arms the
array-keyed drop (B-2026-08-23-4). At the default -O2 the non-indexed element
is dead and LLVM removes its `malloc`, so exactly one leak is reported and it
is whichever element was read. That is the whole of the asymmetry the row
inferred ownership from. Anyone re-measuring a temporary-elements leak should
pin `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` first; the default level hides the dead half.

So the fix is -31's pair, gated one expression kind wider:
`compile_index` clone-then-drops the temporary, and
`expr_is_inline_temp_vec_heap_index` admits the shape so the consuming site
frees the clone. The two gates are now the same predicate by construction --
a shape the lowering drops but the consumer refuses trades N leaked elements
for one leaked clone, which is the failure -31 documents between its halves.

The predicate is NEW rather than a widening of `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`,
exactly as the row argued: that one is asked by many unrelated sites and a
rodata literal (`Array["aa", "bb"]`) is not a droppable fresh owned temp in
their sense. `expr_is_fresh_owned_array_temp` is `Call`/`MethodCall` plus
`ArrayLiteral`, used only by the array sites, whose free runs through
`vec_element_drain_fn`'s `cap > 0` guard.

THE `==` OPERAND POSITION CAME WITH IT. B-2026-08-27-30's site had the
identical Call-only gate and the identical leak, and it is NOT hidden by -O2
there because the comparator reads every element:
`Array[f"aaaa{n}", f"b{n}"] == Array[f"cccccc{n}", f"d{n}"]` lost all four
elements, 16 bytes in 4 allocations. Moved to the same predicate here rather
than filed as a second row for a one-word change.

SCOPE, MEASURED. Rodata elements are the control the widening is riskiest
against and they are now dropped: `Array["aa", "bb"][0]` and the `==` spelling
that B-2026-08-27-30's fixture already carried as a must-not-drop shape both
reach `emit_drop_fn_for_array` and stay clean through the cap guard. The
bound-source leg is the other direction -- `let s = f"s{n}"; Array[s, t][0]`
MOVES both bindings into the literal (their caps are zeroed), so the array is
the only owner and the drop is not a double-free. A scalar element
(`Array[n, n + 1][1]`) drops nothing: `vec_element_drain_fn` returns None and
no drop fn is emitted.

VERIFIED under LSan at BOTH optimization levels (`asan_indexed_array_literal_
temp_drops_its_elements`, `asan_array_literal_eq_operand_drops_its_elements`),
plus a codegen E2E value test that is not decoration: the fix DEEP-CLONES the
element before freeing the array around it, and the wrong order prints freed
memory while still exiting 0, which no leak count would catch. All four
surfaces -- `karac run --interp`, `karac run` (JIT), `karac build`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` -- print byte-identical output. Full gates:
memory_sanitizer 1241/0, codegen 3319/0, par_codegen 270/0, selfhost_codegen
1/0, default suite 108 result lines all ok, both clippy legs and
`cargo fmt --check` clean.
title: An array LITERAL temporary leaks ALL of its elements -- indexed (`Array[f"a{n}", f"b{n}"][0]`, 7 bytes in 2 allocations) and as an `==` operand (16 bytes in 4) -- the same mechanism as B-2026-08-27-31 one expression kind over, not the different one this row was filed as.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-31, as the producer shape its gate does not
reach. That row covers a fresh array temporary from a CALL (`mk(4)[0]`); this is
the same expression over an array LITERAL, and the two are separated only by
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, which admits `Call`/`MethodCall` and nothing
else.

MEASURED under `assert_clean_asan_run`:

  let n = 3;
  println(Array[f"a{n}", f"b{n}"][0]);        2 B / 1 allocation   LEAKS

PRE-EXISTING, not a residue of -31's fix: it reproduces byte-identically with
that fix stashed (2 B / 1 allocation, same figure), so nothing about the new
clone-then-drop path created or widened it.

THE MECHANISM IS NOT -31's, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART OF THIS ROW. Under -31 the
whole array was unowned and EVERY element leaked (13 B / 2 allocations for a
2-element array). Here only ONE element leaks, and it is the INDEXED one. Probed
with deliberately unequal element lengths to identify it rather than infer it --
`Array[f"aaaa{n}", f"b{n}"]` leaks 5 bytes when indexed at 0 and 2 bytes when
indexed at 1, i.e. whichever element is read out. So the literal's other elements
already have an owner that frees them; what has no owner is the value handed to
the consumer. That is the shape `expr_is_inline_temp_vec_heap_index` exists for
(a read-out element with no consuming binding), not the shape
`emit_drop_fn_for_array` exists for.

FIX SHAPE, therefore, is probably the consumer half alone rather than -31's
pair: admit an array-literal-rooted index to the fresh-owned-arg predicate so
the consuming site frees the read value. Widening `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`
itself is the wrong lever -- it is asked by many unrelated sites, and an
`ArrayLiteral` of rodata elements (`Array["aa", "bb"][0]`) must not become
droppable there; B-2026-08-27-30's fix records the same hazard for the `==`
operand position.

SEVERITY medium and not high on the same reasoning B-2026-08-27-30 was: an array
literal indexed inline is a small surface, the loss is bounded by the element
size, and there is no correctness consequence -- the value read is correct on all
three backends.

CORRECTION (at close, 5313f90). The measurement above -- "only ONE element
leaks, and it is the INDEXED one", "so the literal's other elements already
have an owner" -- is an artifact of the DEFAULT optimization level, and the
conclusion drawn from it is wrong. At `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` the same program
loses BOTH elements (7 bytes in 2 allocations), and the emitted IR shows every
element's independent cleanup suppressed by `compile_array_literal` with
nothing taking over. At -O2 the non-indexed element is dead and LLVM removes
its `malloc`, which is the entire asymmetry -- including the "probed with
deliberately unequal element lengths" result (5 bytes indexing 0, 2 indexing
1): whichever element is READ is the one that survives DCE.

So the fix shape is B-2026-08-27-31's pair after all, not "the consumer half
alone". The row's other reasoning holds and was followed: the widening does
NOT go into `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`.

fix:
FIXED by ce72041. The row asked for three sites to be cleared with a probe that had been VALIDATED
against a known-positive control, rather than on the bad evidence that made the first
attempt useless. That was done, and it changed the answer: ONE OF THE THREE REPRODUCED.

  for-loop binding      CLEAR    -- already covered by B-2026-08-25-28's span-fallback

  match pattern binding DEFECTIVE -- the family reproduces. SEGFAULT at `T = String`,

                                    is a different class and is filed as its own row.

THE PROBE, and why its negative readings are now evidence. Two changes to the one the row
recorded as useless. First, the `mut`-in-binding-position obstruction (`for mut b`,

the row's own suggestion. Second, and what actually settles it, a DIRECT STRUCTURAL
ORACLE alongside the crash: `nm` on the AOT binary, asking whether the sibling method was
emitted as `$i64` / `$struct` monomorph siblings or as one bare prototype. That is the
defect itself rather than a downstream symptom, so it does not depend on the corruption
becoming observable.

VALIDATION, the step whose absence voided the first probe. B-2026-08-25-28's resolution
was temporarily removed from `enum_inst_type_of_expr` (the `.map(|i|
concrete_generic_struct_inst(&i)...)` on the span fallback) and the probe re-run:

  site                fix present            fix removed
  let (control)       ok                     ok                      -- own `let`-site arm
  for-loop binding    ok                     SEGV + bare prototype   -- probe SEES it here
  tuple destructure   dispatch ok            SEGV + bare prototype   -- probe SEES it here
  match binding       SEGV + bare prototype  SEGV + bare prototype   -- covered by nothing

The middle column is the finding; the right column is what makes the middle column mean
something. The probe demonstrably detects the defect at the for-loop and tuple sites, so
"ok" there is a measurement. At the match site it is positive either way -- that site is
reached by no covering arm at all.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is this family's own rule broken one more time.
`src/codegen/pattern_binding.rs` ALREADY had a payload-binding arm recording a generic
struct's instantiation (added for `.field` GEPs, B-2026-07-12-2). It read
`pattern_binding_inner_types`, which is a PRE-monomorphization span table, so inside
`impl[T: Ord] Bag[T]` it holds the GENERIC form `Bag[T]`. The gate
`is_generic_named_struct_type_expr` accepts that -- it only asks for a known generic
struct with at least one arg -- so `enum_inst_var_types["b"] = Bag[T]` went in unresolved.

That is B-2026-08-25-27's "holds the generic form, which is worse than holding nothing",
except one level more damaging: `enum_inst_var_types` is the FIRST and authoritative arm
of `enum_inst_type_of_expr`, so a generic record there satisfies the chain and stops the
search BEFORE the span fallback -- the single arm that does resolve through the
substitution. The match site was therefore not merely uncovered by -28's fix, it was
actively immunised against it. That is the whole reason the for-loop binding, which falls
through to that fallback, was already correct while its sibling was not.

FIX: resolve through the active monomorph's substitution before inserting, via the same
`concrete_generic_struct_inst` the `let` site and the receiver side already use --
`.unwrap_or(full_te)`, so an already-concrete record passes through untouched and the arm
is inert outside a monomorph. One line of logic, the family's standing rule applied at the
one site that had been left out of it: A RECORD IS ONLY USEFUL IF ITS PARAMS ARE CONCRETE.

TESTS. `tests/codegen.rs::e2e_generic_non_let_binding_instantiation_across_sites` sweeps
the for-loop and match sites at BOTH `i64` and `String`, sibling to the existing
`..._let_binding_instantiation_across_rhs_forms`; the scalar leg is not decoration, since

title: A MATCH-ARM payload binding inside a generic impl recorded the PRE-monomorphization `Bag[T]` into the name-keyed instantiation table, poisoning the FIRST arm of the lookup chain so the sibling call dispatched to the unmangled base prototype and SEGFAULTED at a heap-carrying `T` (`T = i64` silently correct); the for-loop and tuple-destructure sites were already clear
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-25-28 (fixed, 5fa76a7) per the ledger convention that a closed-out investigation's live remainder gets its own OPEN row rather than being buried in the closed one. The remainder was written into -28's closing note, which is not the work queue -- so nothing tracked it. This row is that fix.

WHAT IS UNVERIFIED. The B-2026-08-25-25/-27/-28 family is 'a generic-struct value whose concrete instantiation is not recorded, so a method call through it dispatches to the UNMANGLED base prototype and segfaults at a heap-carrying `T`'. The audit swept and fixed the `let`-RHS forms (-27: identifier copy, free-fn call, assoc fn returning Self, method returning Self, block expression, index into a Vec of them) and the temporary-receiver site (-28). It did NOT clear these three, which bind a generic-struct value without a `let`:
  - a `for` loop binding:      `for b in bags { b.method(); }`
  - a `match` pattern binding: `match opt { Some(b) => { b.method(); } None => {} }`
  - a tuple destructure:       `let (b, _n) = pair; b.method();`

WHY THEY WERE NOT CLEARED, which is the part worth keeping. Reproducing this family needs a MUTATING sibling call through the binding (`mut ref self`), because the corruption only becomes observable once a wrongly-strided write lands. All three sites REJECT `mut` in the binding position (`for mut b in ...`, `Some(mut b)`, `let (mut b, _)` are parse errors: "'mut' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier"). The workaround probe used a `ref self` sibling chain instead -- and that probe reports OK on a form ALREADY PROVEN BROKEN (the free-fn-call `let` RHS, which segfaults under the mutating probe). A probe that cannot detect the defect on a known-positive control cannot clear anything, so these three read 'ok' for a reason unrelated to whether they are correct. Recording that explicitly so the next session does not mistake three OK rows for coverage and close this on the same bad evidence.

SUGGESTED PROBE: route the mutation through a BY-VALUE method so the binding itself need not be `mut` -- e.g. `fn arranged(self) -> Self { let mut s = self; s.arrange(); s }`, called as `b.arranged()` from an immutable binding. Note that shape contains `let mut s = self`, which is B-2026-08-25-7's own form, so the probe must be validated against a known-positive control BEFORE its negative results are trusted -- exactly the step whose absence made the first probe useless.

SEVERITY: filed MEDIUM because it is UNCONFIRMED, not because the impact would be moderate. Every confirmed member of this family is HIGH -- a silent segfault at a heap-carrying `T` with the interpreter correct and `T = i64` masking it completely. If any of these three reproduces, it is high and should be refiled as such. If none does, close this row as `not-reproduced` WITH the validated probe recorded, so the clearing is evidence rather than assumption.

CLASS `other` deliberately: this is a VERIFICATION GAP, not a demonstrated defect. Filing it as `miscompile` would assert a bug nobody has shown to exist.

fix:
FIXED by bd5dbc2. `compile_mono_function`'s owned-param arm was gated
`matches!(&param.ty.kind, TypeKind::Path(_))`, so a by-value TUPLE param of a MONOMORPH
fell straight through it: the mono got NEITHER an entry-copy NOR a scope-exit drop, where
`compile_function` gives a non-generic callee both (#21, `make_tuple_param_callee_owned`).

The caller's tuple-literal arm (`call_dispatch.rs`) is not gated on genericity and registers
its temp's drop either way, on an assumption it states outright: "the callee now entry-copies
a heap-bearing tuple param, so this caller temp is an INDEPENDENT buffer that must free its
own heap." For a mono that sentence was false. Caller temp and callee param aliased ONE
buffer, so `let (b, _n) = p; b.xs` handed that buffer out as the result AND left the caller's
temp drop to free it.

This is B-2026-07-08-6's rule, one param shape further. That row added the mono entry-copy
for named aggregates and its comment already says the invariant: the callee-side copy and the
caller-side drop of the original "MUST stay paired". The pairing was implemented for
`TypeKind::Path` params and never extended to `TypeKind::Tuple`.

THE FIX has two halves and the second is what makes it do anything. Adding the tuple arm
alone is inert: `make_tuple_param_callee_owned` bails at its first gate,
`any(type_expr_has_drop_heap)`, and inside a generic impl the declared element is the GENERIC
form `Bag[T]`, which reads as heapless because `T` is erased. So the elements are resolved
through the active monomorph's substitution (`concrete_generic_struct_inst`, `.unwrap_or` the
declared form) BEFORE the ownership call -- the same "a record is only useful if its params
are CONCRETE" rule this area keeps needing.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, since the row recorded ASAN as not yet run. Under `-fsanitize=address` at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` the two frees separate cleanly:

  legitimate:  free directly in `main`            -- `r`'s drop of the Vec it now owns
  the bug:     main -> __karac_drop_tuple_te_Bag_ -> __karac_drop_struct_Bag

on a 48-byte region: two 24-byte String control blocks, i.e. the Vec's element buffer. At
`-O2` both frames collapse into `main` and say nothing; at `-O0` `take$struct$T_ct_String` is
a separate symbol and there is still no `take` frame, which is what identifies the caller's
temporary rather than the callee's param as the second owner.

A REFUTED HYPOTHESIS, recorded because it is the plausible one and it is wrong. The obvious
suspect was `field_copy_supported` declining for a generic-erased `T` -- the codebase's own
`struct_is_self_referential` doc lists "a generic-erased `T`" among the declines. Instrumenting
both gates showed `make_tuple_param_callee_owned` is NEVER ENTERED for a mono: the non-generic
build prints the entry and "COPIED", the generic build prints nothing at all. The decline is one
level up, in the param loop, not inside the copy-support walk. Anyone re-deriving this should
check entry before checking gates.

VERIFICATION. All eleven variants of the row's measured matrix are now correct on interpreter,
JIT and AOT -- including the two the row flagged as JIT-only (`Vec[i64]`, and a field that never
escapes), which is the evidence that the fix is the shared cause rather than an AOT-shaped
patch. Under ASAN with LSan on, the repro exits 0 with empty stderr: the double free is gone and
did NOT become a leak, which is the failure mode a wrong fix here produces.

WHAT THIS FIX EXPOSES, and it is the part worth reading before extending it. Removing the
alias means the generic path stops MASKING a pre-existing leak. Two shapes, both of which let
the tuple value ESCAPE the caller's frame, now leak the caller's original 48-byte buffer:

    fn passthru[T](p: (Bag[T], i64)) -> (Bag[T], i64) { p }   // param returned whole
    use2(mk(["x", "y"]))                                      // call-temporary argument

On the escape path the caller registers NO drop for its original (measured: the tuple arm in
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` is not even REACHED, so this is not a gate that
declined). Pre-fix the callee aliased that same buffer and handed it back out, so nothing
leaked; post-fix the callee owns a copy and the original is orphaned -- exactly the
"entry-copy passthrough leaves the ORIGINAL orphaned" situation B-2026-08-01-14 fixed for
ENUM args, never done for tuples.

THIS IS NOT A REGRESSION INTRODUCED HERE, and that was measured rather than argued. The
IDENTICAL NON-GENERIC spelling of both shapes leaks the same 48 bytes on an UNMODIFIED tree,
and the non-generic path is untouched by this change:

    shape                     fix reverted   fix applied
    passthrough, generic      clean          48 B leak
    passthrough, NON-generic  48 B leak      48 B leak     <- untouched by this fix
    call-temp,   generic      clean          48 B leak
    call-temp,   NON-generic  48 B leak      48 B leak     <- untouched by this fix

So the defect already exists on the non-generic path; the generic path was clean only BECAUSE
of the aliasing that made it double-free. The trade is deliberate and worth stating plainly: a
HIGH-severity double free (memory corruption, silent, wrong results) is fixed, and an
already-present 48-byte LEAK becomes visible on one more spelling instead of being masked by
corruption. The two paths are now consistent, which is the precondition for fixing the leak
once rather than twice. Filed as its own row.

TESTS. `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_generic_struct_destructured_from_a_tuple_param_frees_once`
covers struct-first, struct-second, both-slots-structs, the `Vec[i64]` scalar-element leg and
the named-binding argument; the two escape shapes above are deliberately NOT guarded there,
with the measurement recorded in the test so nobody reads their absence as an oversight;
`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_generic_struct_destructured_from_a_tuple_param_frees_once` runs both
element types; `tests/interpreter.rs::generic_struct_destructured_from_a_tuple_param_round_trips`
is the oracle twin. Negative control: with the fix reverted the ASAN test FAILS with exactly
this double free, and passes with it restored.

ALSO CLOSED THE LOOP ON B-2026-08-27-36. Its
`e2e_generic_tuple_destructure_binding_dispatches_to_the_monomorph` was deliberately pinned
through a NON-CONSUMING chain, with a comment saying to rewrite it to the consuming shape once
this row landed -- because pinning the natural shape then would have encoded this bug. It is now
the consuming shape, so all three non-`let` binding sites are covered by one oracle.
title: Destructuring a GENERIC struct out of a TUPLE PARAM and consuming its heap-carrying field DOUBLE-FREES under JIT and AOT while the interpreter is correct: `fn take[T](p: (Bag[T], i64)) -> Vec[T] { let (b, _n) = p; b.xs }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. Not the wrong-monomorph family -- it fires at `T = i64` too and `nm` confirms the right monomorph was selected. A non-generic struct, a LOCAL tuple, and a direct non-tuple param are all clean; the JIT is strictly more sensitive than AOT
detail:
FOUND BY the B-2026-08-27-36 audit, at one of the three binding sites that row exists to
clear. Filed separately because it is a DIFFERENT CLASS: -36 is the wrong-monomorph
dispatch family (a segfault, masked at `T = i64`), this is a double free that fires at
`T = i64` too. Their independence is measured, not inferred -- `nm` on the AOT binary of a
crashing program shows `Bag.arrange$i64` AND `Bag.arrange$struct$T_ct_String`, i.e.
dispatch already selected the correct monomorph. -36's fix does not touch this.

MINIMAL REPRO -- three lines, no impl, no method call, nothing but Vec:

    struct Bag[T] { xs: Vec[T] }
    fn take[T](p: (Bag[T], i64)) -> Vec[T] { let (b, _n) = p; b.xs }
    fn main() { let r = take((Bag { xs: ["x", "y"] }, 0)); println(f"len={r.len()} [{r[0]}]"); }

`karac check` passes. `karac run --interp` prints `len=2 [x]`. `karac run` (JIT) and
`karac build` both abort with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (rc=134).

MEASURED MATRIX. Every row is a variant of the repro above, run on all three backends. The
interpreter is correct in EVERY row and is omitted.

  variant                                                      jit      aot
  the repro, as written                                        DOUBLE   DOUBLE
  `struct Bag { xs: Vec[String] }` -- NON-generic               ok       ok
  `let p = (Bag { xs: v }, 0)` -- tuple is a LOCAL, not a param  ok       ok
  `fn take[T](b: Bag[T])` -- direct param, no tuple              ok       ok
  `struct Bag[T] { a: T }`, `b.a` -- no heap-carrying field      ok       ok
  `(i64, Bag[T])` -- struct in the SECOND slot                  DOUBLE   DOUBLE
  `(Bag[T], Bag[T])` -- both slots structs                      DOUBLE   DOUBLE
  `let (b, n) = p; println(n); ...` -- second slot USED         DOUBLE   DOUBLE
  `let v = b.xs; v` -- moved to a local, then returned          DOUBLE   DOUBLE
  `Vec[i64]` field instead of `Vec[String]`                     DOUBLE   ok
  `b.xs.len()` -- field read, never escapes                     DOUBLE   ok

SO THE CONDITIONS ARE: a GENERIC struct, DESTRUCTURED OUT OF A TUPLE PARAM, whose
heap-carrying field is then consumed. Non-generic is clean, a LOCAL tuple is clean, and the
same struct passed as a direct param is clean -- it is specifically the tuple-param
destructure. Tuple POSITION is irrelevant and so is whether the other slot is used; both
were wrong guesses on a first pass and are recorded here as refuted so nobody re-derives
them.

THE JIT IS STRICTLY MORE SENSITIVE THAN AOT, which is the useful diagnostic handle: JIT
fires on a `Vec[i64]` field and on a field that never leaves the function, where AOT needs a
heap-carrying ELEMENT that escapes. Any fix should be verified on BOTH, and the JIT leg is
the one to reproduce against.

MEASUREMENT HAZARD, worth a line because it silently produced a wrong first characterisation
of this bug. `karac build` from a binary NOT built with `--features llvm` does not fail --
it prints `note: karac build requires the llvm feature; falling back to type check` followed
by `All checks passed.`, and emits no executable. A harness that greps for a crash string
therefore reports every variant as "ok". Confirm the binary is an llvm build before trusting
any negative row in a matrix like the one above.

NOT VERIFIED UNDER ASAN. The abort is glibc's own tcache check, so the specific allocation
freed twice has not been identified; `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s harness should name the
site outright and is the obvious first step.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption, no diagnostic and no warning, on a shape reachable
from ordinary code (destructure a tuple of value-plus-count, move the value's buffer out).
The interpreter is correct throughout, so it is also a run-vs-build divergence.

REGRESSION TEST PLACEHOLDER: `tests/codegen.rs::e2e_generic_tuple_destructure_binding_dispatches_to_the_monomorph`
pins the tuple site through a NON-CONSUMING chain precisely because the consuming shape
crashes here. When this row is fixed, rewrite that test to the consuming shape so the tuple
site is covered by the same oracle as its for-loop and match siblings.

fix:
FIXED by 01d6784. Interpreter: `Value::Tuple` arms for `Lt`/`LtEq`/`Gt`/`GtEq` (through `value_compare`, the same comparator the derived-`Ord` aggregate arm beside them uses) and for `Eq`/`NotEq` (through `Value`'s own `PartialEq`, the same one the `Vec` and `Slice` arms use). Codegen: the `<`-family dispatch in `exprs.rs` now looks the operand up as a TUPLE before it looks it up by NAME, and `lowering.rs` fills the span-keyed operand table for tuple-typed expressions so there is something to look up.

The comparator was already there and already ordering these exact tuples: `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` has had a `TypeKind::Tuple` arm all along, which is why `Vec[(i64, i64)].sort()` has always worked on both backends while the bare operator did not. What was missing was only the operator DISPATCH -- it resolves an operand's type by name, and a tuple has none. Because both halves now route through that one comparator (`karac_cmp_<T>` compiled, `value_compare` interpreted, which its own doc records as the same total order), the two backends agree by construction rather than by convention.

Ordering is gated on every leaf carrying a TOTAL order -- `value_is_totally_ordered` in the interpreter, `te_is_totally_ordered` in codegen, and the two accept the same set deliberately, since a backend that lowered where the other declined would answer a program the other refuses to run. A BARE float declines on both: `value_compare` and `karac_cmp_<T>` both order floats by `total_cmp` (NaN last) because every one of their other callers is a sort key, and that is not what `<` means on an `f64`. The `F32`/`F64`/`F16`/`Bf16` wrappers, whose whole purpose is to be totally ordered, do qualify. Equality has no such gate -- it is IEEE element-wise, which is both what design.md § Float semantics requires and what AOT already did.

Regression tests: `tuple_comparison_and_equality_in_the_interpreter` (tests/interpreter.rs) and `test_e2e_tuple_comparison_and_equality` (tests/codegen.rs), kept row-for-row so each is the other's oracle. Verified identical on `karac run --interp`, the JIT, and `karac build`.
title: Tuple comparison operators NEVER LOWERED on either backend, while `karac check` accepted them: `let a = (1, 2); let b = (1, 3); a < b` passed the typechecker, then the interpreter died on its catch-all arm (whose message claims the typechecker rejects this -- it does not) and `karac build` refused with "Unsupported struct binary op: Lt"

fix:
FIXED by 01d6784. `compile_tuple_eq_te` -- field-wise `==` / `!=` driven by the tuple's own `TypeExpr`, intercepted in `exprs.rs`'s Binary arm before `compile_binop` can apply its field-count heuristic.

Recursing on the element `TypeExpr` rather than on `compile_binop` (as `compile_struct_eq` does) is what makes NESTING correct by construction: a three-element tuple sitting inside a two-element one walks straight back into the same collision otherwise, which is exactly the leg B-2026-08-27-18's `Nested` row pins for structs. A NON-tuple element still delegates to `compile_binop`, where the field-count heuristic is right -- a `String` element really is that header, and `("a", 1, 2) == ("b", 1, 2)` must reach the byte comparator for field 0.

Pinned by the `t3` / `n3a` / `f3a` rows of `test_e2e_tuple_comparison_and_equality`, which vary tuple ARITY for this reason: a fixture built only from pairs passes against the bug.
title: A THREE-element tuple `==` PANICS THE COMPILER: `(1, 2, 3) == (1, 2, 4)` lowers to `{i64, i64, i64}`, structurally the same LLVM object as the `{ptr, i64, i64}` String/Vec header, so `compile_binop`'s field-COUNT dispatch sent it to the String byte-comparator, which extracted field 0 as a pointer
detail:
REPRODUCE (pre-existing on ae55c85; `karac build` only, the interpreter is correct):

    fn main() { let a = (1, 2, 3); let b = (1, 2, 4); println(f"{a == b}"); }

    thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/codegen/expr_ops.rs:8162:
    Found IntValue(... "%l.ptr = extractvalue { i64, i64, i64 } %a1, 0" ...)
    but expected PointerValue variant

EXACT SIBLING OF B-2026-08-27-18, which is this collision for a three-FIELD user struct and whose fix note already states the general rule: user structs and tuples get LITERAL, structurally-uniqued LLVM types, so anything shaped `{ptr-or-i64, i64, i64}` is indistinguishable from a `String` by shape alone, and the dispatch has to be by TYPE.

WHY IT HID: arity-selective. Two- and four-element tuples miss the collision entirely and have always compiled, so every existing tuple fixture in the tree is built from pairs. Nested `((1,2,3), 4)` crashes too, one level down, even though neither tuple is three-wide at the top level.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the B-2026-08-27-33 follow-up fixture, which varied tuple arity to check the new ordering path and hit this on the equality path instead.

fix:
FIXED by 3cfbd1e. Fixed entirely in codegen's monomorphization substitution channel (`src/codegen/mono.rs`, +275 lines): six new helpers, one new arm on an existing one, and four edits inside `compile_generic_call`. No other module is touched — in particular the typechecker is not, which is the first thing the row's own diagnosis gets wrong.

THE CHANNEL WAS NOT THE ONE THE ROW NAMED. See the DIAGNOSIS CORRECTION appended to `detail`: `call_type_subs` is EMPTY at these spans in BOTH the broken (tuple) and the working (i64) case, so `record_call_type_subs` could not be the difference and the typechecker needed no change at all. The binder is codegen-side and one level down: `method_call.rs` derives EXPLICIT generic args for an impl-method call from the receiver's recorded instantiation, and `compile_generic_call`'s explicit-args loop lowers any `TypeExpr` into the LLVM subst but records the NAME only under `if let TypeKind::Path`. A tuple has no name, so it fell out of the name channel there — and the name channel is what `concrete_generic_struct_inst` reads to re-render `self`'s instantiation for the NEXT call.

THE FIX carries a nameless type argument in the ELEMENT-AWARE channel (`subst_type_exprs` -> `mono_state.type_subst_type_exprs`) instead, which can express it. That channel already existed for Vec/VecDeque elements (B-2026-07-13-2/-3), and its two consumers already PREFER it over the head-only name map: `concrete_generic_struct_inst` (B-2026-08-25-11) and `subst_monomorph_type_params`. So one insert propagates through both and no consumer needed widening -- `Bag[T]` re-renders as `Bag[(i64, i64)]`, `enum_inst_var_types["self"]` records it, and the nested `self.sw(..)` gets the tuple back as its own explicit arg. Three levels of nesting are covered by the fixture.

FOUR PIECES:
1. `type_expr_is_structural_type_arg` -- the predicate for "the name channel structurally cannot carry this". `Tuple` ONLY, deliberately: `Array` is the near neighbour but also reaches codegen through the const-generic size axis, so it needs its own measurement rather than an argument by analogy (B-2026-08-27-42); `FnType`/`Pointer`/`Frozen` have no monomorph-key convention at all.
2. The explicit-args loop's `else if` -- captures the receiver-derived tuple that the `Path` arm drops.
3. `resolve_structural_param_substs` -- the FREE-FUNCTION leg, which the row did not report and which the method fix alone left standing. `pick[T](a: T, b: T)` has no receiver, so it binds through `infer_type_args`, which sees only the LLVM shape -- and every tuple lowers to the same opaque `struct` there. Recovers the argument's type from `seq_eq_operand_types`, the span-keyed table lowering fills from `tc.expr_types` for every typed expression. Measured before and after: `pick((1, 2), ..)` beside `pick((1.5, 2.5), ..)` failed module verification on `pick$struct` and now runs.
4. `append_structural_type_param_mangle` + a `TypeKind::Tuple` arm on `mono_mangle_token_for_type_expr` -- the mangle axis (`$T_st_tup_i64_i64`), which is repro B.

5. The FORWARDING leg, found by probing rather than reported: `outer[U](a: U, b: U)` whose body calls `pick(a, b)`. Neither source above can reach it -- the argument's static type is the CALLER's own type param, so there is no receiver instantiation and no tuple in `expr_types`. `infer_type_args` binds `T` from the LLVM value, so the body was always right and only the SYMBOL collided (module-verifier reject, not a wrong answer). Closed with an LLVM-SHAPE fallback on the same mangle axis (`$T_st_sh2_i64_i64`), gated to fire only when the `subst_names` entry does not RESOLVE to a type. "Absent" was the obvious gate and it was wrong, which measurement showed: on this path the name channel records the caller's own param spelling (`T -> "U"`, because flattening `U` through an empty `type_subst_names` leaves it as itself), so the gate never fired until it asked whether the name resolves. The fallback is deliberately weaker than the `TypeExpr` source and documented as such: `(i64, i64)` and `(u64, u64)` share one LLVM shape and would still collide, which is the same erasure `llvm_type_to_mangle_str` has everywhere else and is unreachable on the direct path. The named-type control (`outer("aa", "bb")` beside `outer(1, 2)`) has always worked and still does. The token spelling matches the typechecker's `type_to_mono_mangle_token`, which has rendered `tup_<a>_<b>` over `Type` all along; the two are twins and now agree. No pre-existing symbol changes: all three resolvers that write `subst_type_exprs` require a `TypeKind::Path` on the value they record, so none of them could ever produce a tuple, and the gated set was empty before this row.

MEASURED PRE-FIX, per shape, against the same compiler with only this diff stashed -- four distinct failure modes, no single one of which would have caught the others:
  - `(i64, i64)`         wrong answer: `10:1 2:20` for `2:20 1:10`
  - `(i64, i64, i64)`    wrong answer: `2,1,3 4,5,6` for `4,5,6 1,2,3` (arity-selective -- three scalars are the `{ptr,i64,i64}` String-header shape)
  - `(String, i64)`      SEGFAULT at run time
  - `((i64, i64), i64)`  wrong answer through a nested tuple
  - all four in ONE file  compiler panic, `ExtractOutOfRange` at expr_ops.rs:3555 (three tuple instantiations of `Bag` collide on one symbol before anything runs)
  - repro B              module verification: `Call parameter type does not match function signature ... W.add$struct`
Post-fix all six are correct and BYTE-IDENTICAL across interp, JIT and AOT.
