TESTS: `test_e2e_tuple_type_arg_survives_a_nested_generic_call` (codegen) with `tuple_type_arg_through_a_nested_generic_call_in_the_interpreter` as its verbatim oracle; `test_e2e_two_tuple_instantiations_of_one_generic_get_distinct_symbols` (both call shapes); `asan_tuple_type_arg_with_a_heap_element_through_a_nested_generic_call` for the row that segfaulted, which is also the LSan gate on the heap-owned element. `test_e2e_ord_bound_on_generic_impl_admits_a_tuple` (B-2026-08-27-33) is widened to TWO tuple instantiations and its "one instantiation, deliberately" paragraph corrected -- that restriction existed only because of this row's repro B.

ONE NEIGHBOUR PROBED AND DELIBERATELY LEFT: a container param bound to a FIELD-ACCESS argument (`swap01(mut self.xs)` from inside a generic-impl method) still loses its element -- silently for a tuple, as a SEGFAULT for a String. It is filed separately and NOT under this row because it is not tuple-specific: the identical shape breaks at `Bag[String]` too, so the cause cannot be "the name channel has no name for a tuple". It is that the element resolvers key on the argument's BINDING NAME and a field access is not an identifier. The control that pins the split is a plain `let mut t: Vec[(i64, i64)]` identifier argument to the same callee, which is correct on AOT for both element types.

STILL OPEN AND NOT THIS ROW: `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]` no longer miscompiles, and it is no longer this row's problem, but it still does not BUILD. It fails loudly with "no handler for method 'cmp' on variable '__indexed_elem_3'" -- an INDEXED-ELEMENT receiver, which is a fourth shape of B-2026-08-27-47's family ("codegen's `.cmp()` receiver surface is narrower than the typechecker admits"), alongside the struct-literal, call-result and `Option[T]` receivers that row lists. B-2026-08-27-41 landed `.cmp()` on a tuple VALUE while this row was in flight and is what moved the blocker there; recorded here because the row -47 does not name this receiver shape, and `sift_up` reaching `outranks` through `self.heap[i].cmp(..)` is how every `PriorityQueue[T]` hits it.

Going from silent garbage to a named error is the whole of this row's contribution to that shape, and it is worth stating plainly: the three rows -33, -40 and -41 have each removed one obstacle in front of `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]`, and one remains.
title: A TUPLE TYPE ARGUMENT does not survive the monomorphization substitution channel, which is keyed by type NAME. A nested generic call silently loses the binding and erases `T` to the i64 default -- SILENT WRONG ANSWER on the compiled backend, correct under the interpreter -- and two distinct tuple instantiations of one generic collide on a single mono symbol

fix:
Fixed in 31cf904: three missing dispatch arms, one per surface. Every comparator
involved already existed -- `type_supports_ord` has recursed through
`Type::Tuple` all along, `value_compare` orders `Value::Tuple`
lexicographically, and `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` has had a `TypeKind::Tuple`
arm since before B-2026-08-27-33 (which is why `Vec[(i64, i64)].sort()` always
worked). Nothing needed to be written except the routing.

TYPECHECKER (`method_nominal_tail.rs`): the `cmp` intercept was gated to a
`Type::Named` receiver, so a tuple fell past it to the tuple no-method arm and
was refused with "no method 'cmp' on type '(i64, i64)'". Added a `Type::Tuple`
leg. No derive gate carries over: `!has_user_impl_ord` exists on the Named leg
so a hand-written `impl Ord` is not overruled by the declaration-order
comparator, and a tuple is structural -- there is no name to hang an impl on, so
there is nothing to overrule. Left-to-right IS the language's tuple order, the
same reasoning the operator path records for skipping its own derive check.

INTERPRETER (`method_call.rs`): the `cmp` arm listed Struct / SharedStruct /
EnumVariant receivers and no tuple. Added `Value::Tuple`, gated on
`value_is_totally_ordered` (promoted to `pub(super)`).

CODEGEN (`expr_ops.rs`, `method_call.rs`): `compile_user_cmp_to_ordering` was
keyed by type NAME, which a tuple does not have. Split out a `TypeExpr`-keyed
core, `compile_cmp_to_ordering_te` -- exactly the split
`compile_ordered_user_cmp` / `compile_ordered_cmp_te` already carries for the
OPERATOR spelling, and for the same reason. The dispatch site now takes the
receiver's `TypeExpr` from the span-keyed operand table, runs it through the
active monomorph substitution, and routes a totally-ordered tuple to that core
ahead of the name lookup.

THE SUBSTITUTION STEP IS LOAD-BEARING, not decorative, and this was measured
rather than assumed: `fn pick[T: Ord](a: (T, i64), b: (T, i64))` compiles with
it and declines without it (A/B'd by deleting the call and rebuilding). It fails
CLOSED -- `te_is_totally_ordered` rejects the unresolved `T` leaf -- so the
failure is a build error, never a comparison against the wrong layout.

BOTH BACKENDS GATE ON THE SAME PREDICATE (`te_is_totally_ordered` /
`value_is_totally_ordered`) so the method spelling accepts exactly the set the
operator spelling accepts. That gate is why the interpreter declines a tuple
carrying a bare float or a struct leaf even though `value_compare` would happily
answer: answering where codegen refuses would have manufactured a run-vs-build
split out of a fix whose whole point is closing one. The boundary was measured
against the operator first -- a named-struct leaf is check-green and refused by
both backends, a bare-float leaf likewise -- and the fix reproduces it rather
than widening or narrowing it. (A float leaf is in fact rejected one step
earlier for `.cmp`, at typecheck, since `type_supports_ord` says no.)

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLOSE, and the row's own NOTE anticipated it: a receiver
typed as a BARE `T` (`fn smaller[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> bool { a < b }`). Its
written type carries no tuple at all, so nothing reaches the span-keyed table,
and the mono channel that would supply the binding drops tuple type arguments
outright -- B-2026-08-27-40, still open. Probed directly: at `T = P` the channel
carries `type_subst_names = {"T": "P"}`; at `T = (i64, i64)` it is EMPTY. The
interpreter answers that spelling now (it is untyped at runtime, so `a` simply
IS a `Value::Tuple`); both compiled backends still decline it, loudly, with "no
handler for method 'cmp' on variable 'a'". So the remaining split is check-green
+ interp-correct + build-refused, which is strictly better than the
check-green + interp-runtime-error + build-refused it replaced.

TESTS: six new. `tests/typechecker.rs` -- `test_tuple_cmp_method_resolves_to_-
ordering` and the negative `test_tuple_cmp_rejected_when_an_element_is_not_ord`.
`tests/interpreter.rs` -- `tuple_cmp_dispatches_through_value_compare` and
`tuple_cmp_through_a_bare_type_parameter` (the interpreter-only leg; it exists
because `tests/codegen.rs` is entirely `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`, so without it
the semantics has NO coverage on the default `cargo test` leg).
`tests/codegen.rs` -- `test_e2e_tuple_cmp_to_ordering`, twinned against the
interpreter rather than pinned to a literal since the defect was the two
backends disagreeing about whether the program exists at all, and
`test_e2e_tuple_cmp_through_a_tuple_of_type_params` for the monomorph leg.

FIVE of the six confirmed RED against the unfixed compiler (src reverted, tests
kept). The sixth is the float-leaf negative, which passes on both sides by
design -- it guards the boundary against a future widening, not this fix.

The codegen fixture deliberately carries its NEIGHBOURS: a `#[derive(Ord)]`
struct, `String`, `i64`, `char`, and a hand-written `impl Ord` whose `cmp`
REVERSES the order -- the B-2026-08-26-10 shape, which must keep answering
`Greater` for `Rev{1}.cmp(Rev{2})` rather than being taken over by the
structural comparator. The intercept this widened is the same one that gates
those.

TWO ADJACENT DEFECTS were found while checking that the neighbouring receiver
kinds were untouched, and both are filed separately rather than folded in: an
enum-variant LITERAL receiver answers a constant `Ordering` under the
interpreter (silent, high), and codegen's `.cmp` receiver surface refuses a
struct-literal / call-result / `Option[T]` receiver the checker admits (loud,
medium). Both reproduce identically on the unfixed compiler. They are why the
new codegen fixture binds its `P` and `Rev` receivers to locals instead of
writing them inline.
title: `.cmp()` on a tuple has no dispatch on ANY surface -- the typechecker refuses `(1, 2).cmp((1, 3))` outright, and both backends fall through their method dispatch. This is what a comparison written against a bounded type PARAMETER lowers to, so `fn beats[T: Ord](x: T, y: T) -> bool { x < y }` fails at a tuple even though `(1, 2) < (1, 3)` now works directly
detail:
REPRODUCE, three ways, all on the same build:

    (1, 2).cmp((1, 3))
      error[typecheck]: no method 'cmp' on type '(i64, i64)'

    fn smaller[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> bool { return a < b; }
    smaller((1, 2), (1, 3))
      karac check         All checks passed.
      karac run --interp  runtime error: method 'cmp' not found on type 'unknown'
                          (no interpreter dispatch arm)
      karac build         error: codegen failed: no handler for method 'cmp' on variable '...'

    struct Bag[=T] { xs: Vec[T] }
    impl[T: Ord] Bag[T] { fn less(ref self, i: i64, j: i64) -> bool { self.xs[i] < self.xs[j] } }
      same two failures at Bag[(i64, i64)]

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE METHOD SPELLING: `<` written against the type PARAMETER inside a bounded generic does not lower to a comparison, it lowers to `T.cmp` -- so this gap, not the operator, is what stands between B-2026-08-27-33's bound fix and `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]`, whose `outranks` is exactly `self.xs[i] < self.xs[j]`.

WHERE THE THREE ARMS GO. Typechecker: the `cmp` intercept in `method_nominal_tail.rs` is gated to `Type::Named` receivers and needs a `Type::Tuple` leg (no `has_user_impl_ord` check applies -- a tuple cannot carry one). Interpreter: a `Value::Tuple` arm in the `cmp` dispatch, over `value_compare`, which already orders tuples lexicographically. Codegen: `compile_user_cmp_to_ordering` is name-keyed and needs the `TypeExpr` split its ordering sibling `compile_ordered_cmp_te` already got, over `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr`, which already has a `TypeKind::Tuple` arm. All three comparators exist; this is dispatch, not algorithm.

NOTE that fixing this does NOT by itself make `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]` work -- the monomorph substitution channel loses a tuple type argument entirely (its own row, filed the same day), which is a silent miscompile sitting behind this one.

SOURCE NOTE: the second half of B-2026-08-27-33's own MEASURED BOUNDARY ("REJECTED `.cmp()` on a concrete tuple ... so the two sites disagree in both directions"). That row's fix closed the bound half only.

fix:
Fixed in b356e808. The row's diagnosis was exactly right, including its reading
of why this outlived the tuple sibling: the fix is an EMITTER, not a dispatch
line. `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` gains an `Array` arm and the interpreter
gains the dispatch arm its already-present `value_compare` Array leg
(B-2026-06-30-15) was waiting for.

The comparator is the `VecLike` body with both length halves deleted: N is a
compile-time constant and two arrays that reach it have the SAME type, so
there is no length word to load and no length tiebreak. It is keyed on
`array_elem_and_len` -- the recognizer `emit_eq_fn_for_array` already uses, and
the one that accepts both surface spellings (`Path("Array", [T, N])` from an
annotation, `TypeKind::Array` from inference) -- so ordering and equality agree
about what an array IS by sharing the recognizer rather than restating it. A
COUNTED loop, unlike the tuple arm's unrolled chain: an array's extent is
arbitrary and every element shares one comparator, so unrolling would emit N
copies of one call.

Three smaller pieces went with it: `compile_ordered_cmp_te` now types its
spill slots off the VALUE rather than `into_struct_value()` (which panicked on
an ArrayValue before the dispatch could be reached) and declines a pointer
operand rather than silently comparing addresses; the operator dispatch is its
OWN block rather than a line in the struct-operand one, because an array
lowers to `[N x T]` and `is_struct_value()` skipped that block entirely --
which is also why this row's error came from a different place than the
tuple's.

A CONSEQUENCE THE ROW DID NOT PREDICT, worth recording: `Vec[Array[i64, 2]]
.sort()` did not work either. The row frames this as an operator gap, and it
reads that way because the tuple sibling's sort DID work throughout. But
`sort()` routes to the same `karac_cmp_<T>` family, so with no array
comparator it had nothing to route to. Operator and sort were one gap and are
closed by the one arm; the E2E fixture pins the sort as well.

THE GATE IS PER-ELEMENT, NOT ON THE CONTAINER, and that is the one design
decision here. In the interpreter `Value::Array` represents a `Vec` as well as
an `Array[T, N]`, and no value-shape test separates them -- so an arm in
`value_is_totally_ordered` would make a tuple holding a `Vec` orderable there
while codegen's `te_is_totally_ordered` still declines a `Vec`, manufacturing
a divergence out of the fix. Asking each ELEMENT instead makes the two gates
accept exactly the same set. Measured symmetric on every boundary shape:

    Array[(i64, i64), N]   lowers on both, agrees
    Array[f64, N]          declines on both (the tuple row's float carve-out:
                           `total_cmp` is a sort key's order, not `<`'s)
    Array[Array[i64,2],2]  declines on both  <- REMAINDER, see below
    (Array[i64, 2], i64)   declines on both, unchanged by this fix

THE NESTED-ARRAY REMAINDER is deliberate and symmetric, not an oversight.
Supporting it would require the interpreter to accept a `Value::Array`
ELEMENT, which is precisely the Vec-ambiguity above; codegen declines it by
the same construction so the two stay aligned. Both fixtures pin it, so a
later widening has to be deliberate and has to move both backends together.

A SIBLING GAP WAS FOUND AND NOT FIXED HERE: `Slice[T]` ordering has the
identical shape (`type_supports_ord` has a `Type::Slice` arm too; `karac
check` passes, the interpreter dies on its catch-all, `karac build` refuses
with "Unsupported struct binary op: Lt"). Filed as B-2026-08-27-45 rather than
folded in, since it is a different comparator over a borrowed range and this
row is scoped to `Array`.

Tests: `test_e2e_array_ordering_and_equality` (heap `String` elements, so the
comparator must route per element rather than compare pointer words;
first-differing-element-decides; tuple elements, crossing the two comparators;
the newly-working sort) and `array_ordering_in_the_interpreter`, which
additionally pins the two declined shapes. Both verified RED against the
unfixed compiler.

Gates: codegen 3327/0, memory_sanitizer 1243/0 under LSan, par_codegen 270/0,
selfhost_codegen 1/0, default `cargo test` all green, both clippy legs and
`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean. All four surfaces byte-identical.
title: `Array[T, N]` ORDERING operators never lower, while `karac check` accepts them: `a < b` on two `Array[i64, 2]` passes the typechecker and then fails on both backends. `Array` EQUALITY was fixed by B-2026-08-27-25; the `<` family is the half that was left
detail:
REPRODUCE:

    fn main() {
        let a: Array[i64, 2] = Array[1, 2];
        let b: Array[i64, 2] = Array[1, 3];
        println(f"{a < b}");
    }

    karac check         All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  runtime error: operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type
                        'Array' and 'Array' (this is a type error the typechecker reports as
                        a hard error; it reached the interpreter only because `karac run`
                        executes despite typecheck errors)
    karac build         error: codegen failed: Binary op Lt: left operand has non-comparable
                        type ArrayType(...) (likely a typechecker gap -- `assert_eq` and `==`
                        should reject mismatched operand types before reaching codegen)

Both messages blame the typechecker for admitting this. It admits it deliberately: `type_supports_ord` has a `Type::Array` arm beside its `Type::Tuple` one, and B-2026-08-27-33 extended the generic-impl bound gate to match, so `impl[T: Ord] W[T]` now accepts `W[Array[i64, 2]]` too.

THE TUPLE SIBLING WAS FIXED the same day; the array was left because the machinery differs. `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` has a `TypeKind::Tuple` arm and a `Vec`/`VecDeque` arm but NO `Array` arm, so unlike the tuple case there is no existing comparator to route to -- the fix is an emitter, not a dispatch line. The interpreter needs the matching arm over `value_compare`.

LOW because both backends fail LOUDLY and agree, so nothing is silently wrong; it is a shape the checker calls legal that neither backend runs.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while verifying B-2026-08-27-33's cross-backend sweep.

fix:
Fixed in 9f62ac6. The row's own diagnosis was right in every part, including
that no refinement of case (g)'s static re-derivation could reach this shape,
and its suggested remedy is what landed: an EMISSION-DRIVEN record.

`share_option_shared_ref_for_arg` now records the SPAN of each expression it
actually retains, keyed to that leaf's inner shared heap layout
(`BorrowVars::option_shared_leaf_retains`, cleared per function alongside
`var_option_shared_heap`). `control_flow_owned_option_shared`'s `Identifier`
arm consults that record when the name lookup misses — which is exactly the
arm-local case, where `compile_block_with_frame` has reverted the arm's env
before the consuming `let` classifies its RHS. Both sources stay fail-closed:
no live binding and no record means no retain was emitted, so the value is a
bare alias and registering a scope-exit dec against it would double-free.

Asking the emission what it did is exact by construction rather than by
convention, which is what makes it close the whole leaf-form axis at once: any
future leaf shape that takes a retain is registered by the same lookup, with
no second predicate to keep in sync. That is the property the row asked for.

WHY REGISTRATION IS THE WHOLE FIX, arithmetically. The escaping `+1` is the
same object in both halves of the family, reached two ways. In
B-2026-08-27-34's shape it is the leaf retain itself, taken on top of a
binding whose own dec fires later at function scope. Here the leaf retain is
cancelled inside the arm by the arm-local's scope-exit dec — but that dec was
the arm-local's OWN accounting, so what it cancels is its own ownership and
the value still escapes at rc 1 with nobody holding it. Either way exactly one
ref is orphaned, and registering the consuming binding is what adopts it: the
binding gets a scope-exit dec and a per-use retain, so the count stops
depending on how many times it is consumed. No retain was added or removed by
this fix.

MEASURED, on the row's own repro, all four surfaces byte-identical after the
fix (`--interp`, JIT `run`, `build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` all `1 1 1`),
against `/ 0 0` on the two compiled surfaces before.

The regression fixture takes eleven arm-local legs at three-plus consumptions
(both `if` arms; both arms local; an arm-local ALIASING an enclosing binding,
which pins that the adopted ref is the arm-local's own and not the source's; a
five-use leg; a `match` arm; a nested block; an else-if chain; a `None` arm; an
`if let` then arm; a leg inside a loop) plus the enclosing-binding leg as a
control. Against the unfixed compiler all eleven are RED and all exit 0 — `/ 0
0` and garbage words — and the control is GREEN, which is what attributes the
failure to the arm-LOCAL shape rather than to branch leaves at large.

The row's note that no fixture was landed with it is now closed: the shape it
wrote out verbatim is leg 1.

HONEST LIMIT on the ASAN half. `asan_option_shared_arm_local_branch_leaf_is_balanced`
is RED pre-fix, but by the OVERFLOW PANIC the garbage read produces when folded
into the accumulator — not by an LSan report. The fault is a read, and the
process dies on the arithmetic before any leak check runs, so the sanitizer
never sees this bug (same reason as the sibling row's fixture). Its standing
value is the balance check on the two wrong fixes: register too eagerly and the
scope-exit dec double-frees, retain too eagerly and the count never reaches
zero. Its doc comment says so rather than implying LSan coverage it does not
have.

Gates: memory_sanitizer 1243/0 under LSan (Linux), codegen 3326/0, par_codegen
270/0, selfhost_codegen 1/0, default `cargo test` 108/108 result lines green,
both clippy legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
title: AN ARM-LOCAL BINDING HANDED OUT OF A BRANCH LEAF LOSES ITS OWNER, so the FIRST consumption of the selected `Option[shared]` reads through a freed box. `let t = if c { let u = make(1); u } else { b };` prints `1 1 1` under `--interp` and `/ 0 0` under `karac build` -- WHICH EXITS 0. Split out of B-2026-08-27-34, whose fix moves it in neither direction: the leaf retain fires, but the local's own scope-exit dec cancels it inside the arm and the name is gone from the env before case (g) can register the consumer.
detail:
AN ARM-LOCAL BINDING HANDED OUT OF A BRANCH LEAF LOSES ITS OWNER, so the FIRST
consumption of the selected `Option[shared]` already reads through a freed box.
Split out of B-2026-08-27-34, whose fix does not move it in either direction.

    shared struct Node { val: i64 }
    fn make(n: i64) -> Option[Node] { return Some(Node { val: n }); }
    fn show(t: Option[Node]) -> i64 {
        match t { None => { return 0; } Some(n) => { return n.val; } }
    }
    fn main() {
        let b = make(2);
        let t = if true { let u = make(1); u } else { b };
        println(f"{show(t)} {show(t)} {show(t)}");
    }

MEASURED, both before and after B-2026-08-27-34's fix -- identical output on
each side, so this is neither caused nor masked by it:

    karac run --interp  ->  1 1 1      exit 0   CORRECT
    karac build         ->  / 0 0      exit 0   WRONG, SILENT
    karac run (JIT)     ->  / 0 0      exit 0   WRONG, SILENT

The delta from B-2026-08-27-34's own repro is one line: the then-arm binds a
LOCAL and hands the local out, instead of handing out a binding from the
enclosing scope. Replace `{ let u = make(1); u }` with an outer `a` and the
program is green on all three backends.

MECHANISM, instrumented at `share_option_shared_ref_for_arg`:

    [DBG] retain emitted for: u     <- the arm-local leaf DOES retain
    [DBG] retain emitted for: b
    (no `t` retains -- `t` is unregistered)

So the leaf hook fires, but `u`'s own scope-exit `RcDecOption` drains with the
arm's frame and cancels it, leaving the value escaping at rc 1 with nobody
owning it. `t` is not registered because `control_flow_owned_option_shared`
(case (g)) runs AFTER the RHS compiles, by which point `compile_block_with_frame`
has reverted the arm's name env and `u` is gone from `var_option_shared_heap` --
so the Identifier arm B-2026-08-27-34 added correctly declines rather than
registering a binding whose retain was already cancelled. Both halves are
individually right; the escaping value simply has no owner between them.

WHY THE BOUNDARY IS THE FIRST USE HERE, not the third as in B-2026-08-27-34:
there the leaf retain survived, so the box reached the uses at rc 2 and paid for
two of them. Here it is cancelled inside the arm, so the box arrives at rc 1 and
the first callee's param dec already frees it.

FIXING IT NEEDS A DIFFERENT MECHANISM than case (g)'s static re-derivation,
which cannot see a name that no longer exists. The shape that would work is
emission-driven: have the leaf hooks record the SPAN of each leaf they retained
(and its heap type), then have case (g) match the RHS's own leaves against that
record rather than re-deriving ownership from the leaf's syntactic form. That is
exact by construction and would close the arm-local case and any future leaf
form at once -- but it is new machinery with its own test surface, which is why
it is filed rather than folded into B-2026-08-27-34.

SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-27-34's fix across the branch-leaf
family, not reported from a kata. No fixture is landed for it -- adding an
`#[ignore]`d one would have been the pattern, but the shape is already written
out above verbatim and runs as-is.

fix:
FIXED by 4efd5ab.

TWO gaps, not the one the row predicted, and the row's SUGGESTED FIX addressed only
the first. Both were confirmed by instrumenting the decision points rather than read
off the source, because the row's own "not REACHED AT ALL" note left open which of
several sites was declining.

GAP 1 -- the ADMISSION test, which is what the row half-found. `compile_call`'s arg
loop admits an argument to `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` when
`!flows_into_return || arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct(..) || arg_is_entry_copied_heap_enum(..)`.
There is no TUPLE sibling, so `passthru((Bag { .. }, 7))` -- which DOES flow into the
return -- was excluded before the registrar ran. The probe prints it outright:

    [B44 gate] callee=passthru arg#0 kind=Tuple flows_into_return=true escapes=true
               entry_struct=false entry_enum=false => ADMIT=false

So the registrar's tuple arm was never at fault; nothing ever asked it.

GAP 2 -- the REGISTRAR's arm, which the row missed entirely because it only measured
the passthrough shape. `use2(mk(["x","y"]))` does NOT flow into a return, so it was
admitted, entered the registrar, and matched NO arm at all: not the enum arm
(`enum_name_of_expr` = None), not the tuple arm (which tested `ExprKind::Tuple`, a
LITERAL, while this is an `ExprKind::Call`), and not the named-struct arm
(`owned_struct_temp_arg_name` answers only for a struct literal or a `.clone()`).

    [B44 gate] callee=use2 arg#0 kind=Call flows_into_return=false => ADMIT=true
    [B44 registrar] ENTER kind=Call enum_name=None owned_struct_temp=None

A tuple return has no NAME, which is precisely why every name-keyed arm missed it.

THE FIX. `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_tuple` is the third entry-copy sibling, mirroring
the callee's own `make_tuple_param_callee_owned` gate (some element owns drop-bearing
heap AND every element is copy-supported) so caller and callee stay in the lockstep
B-2026-07-08-6 requires. It is wired into BOTH admission gates -- `compile_call`'s and
`compile_mono_call_args`' -- and the registrar's tuple arm now keys on
`tuple_arg_elem_type_exprs`, which answers for a tuple literal AND for a call whose
declared return type is a tuple.

TWO LOOKUPS HAD TO BE WIDENED, and each was found only by measuring after the obvious
version of the fix left half the matrix red:

  * The scalar `7` DEFEATED the predicate. `infer_arg_elem_te` names an element by
    resolving an EXPRESSION and cannot name an integer literal, so it yields an empty
    path, `field_copy_supported` rejects it, and the `all(..)` conjunct failed on the
    SCALAR while the callee -- which sees the declared `(Bag, i64)` -- entry-copied.
    The lockstep was being broken by an artifact of inference. Fixed by filling only
    the UNRESOLVED positions from the callee's declared param type, which keeps the
    caller's view authoritative where it has one (it is the view carrying the concrete
    instantiation at a generic call site). Measured: `elem Path([""]) drop_heap=false
    copy_sup=false`.

  * A GENERIC callee is in NEITHER `fn_sig.fn_asts` NOR `fn_sig.fn_return_type_exprs`
    -- measured, `passthru[T]` reports `in_fn_asts=false`. Both lookups now fall back
    to `mono_state.generic_fns`, the same two-map pattern `mono_call_arg_moves_into_self`
    already uses. Without this the two GENERIC cells stayed red after the two
    non-generic ones went green, which is what surfaced it.

MEASURED, before -> after, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` + valgrind (this container is Linux, so
LSan/valgrind leak detection is live):

    shape                                   unfixed        fixed
    passthru, generic                       48 B lost      clean
    passthru, NON-generic                   48 B lost      clean
    call-temp, generic                      48 B lost      clean
    call-temp, NON-generic                  48 B lost      clean
    passthru with a bare String element       3 B lost      clean
    two call temps in one expression        72 B / 2 blk    clean

The last two were NOT in the row -- they were found by sweeping a wider shape matrix
and are the same defect at a different element type and at multiplicity 2 (the
registration is per-argument, not once per function).

NO OVER-FREE. The dangerous direction for a leak fix is registering a caller free for
a buffer the callee took, so a 10-shape matrix was run against an UNFIXED control
binary built from the same tree. Every shape that was clean before is clean after,
every shape that leaked before leaks less or not at all, and no shape gained an
invalid-free or double-free on any of the three backends:

    01 consume / 02 bound-identifier arg / 04 nested tuple / 05 all-String tuple /
    08 (Vec[i64], i64) / 10 generic consume    -- clean before AND after
    06 String passthru / 07 two call temps     -- leaked before, clean after
    03 user-Drop element                       -- unchanged (see the split-out row)
    09 Map element                             -- unchanged: 1 B + 48 B, and a BARE
                                                  `Map` param leaks the same 48 B on
                                                  the control, so it is not tuple-related

The predicate is fail-CLOSED by construction: when neither the caller's inference nor
the callee's declaration resolves an element it stays an empty path, which reads as
no-drop and not-copyable, so the predicate declines and the shape degrades to the
pre-existing leak rather than to an over-free.

The bodies walk stays LITERAL-only, deliberately. Its gate is per-ELEMENT freshness,
which needs the element EXPRESSIONS; a call returning a tuple has none to inspect, so
there is no way to tell a fresh element from a place element whose body belongs to its
own binding. Memory-only there matches what the interpreter twin
(`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`) already does for that spelling, so widening the memory
registration does not open a run-vs-build divergence.

NOT DONE, and left visible rather than guessed at: the mono admission gate still has
no ENUM sibling. B-2026-08-01-14 added `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_enum` to the free-fn
gate only, so whether a generic ENUM argument leaks the same way is unmeasured, and
putting a caller-side free on an unmeasured path is how a leak fix becomes a double
free. A comment at that gate says so.

TESTS. `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_generic_struct_destructured_from_a_tuple_param_frees_once`
gains the six guards this row asked for when it was filed -- both escape shapes in
both spellings, plus the String-element and two-call-temp shapes -- replacing the
deferral comment that named them. Twins:
`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_heap_tuple_arg_escaping_the_frame_is_freed_once` and
`tests/interpreter.rs::heap_tuple_arg_escaping_the_frame_round_trips`.
NEGATIVE-CONTROLLED: with the three source files stashed and the tests kept, the ASAN
test FAILS with `ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks` on
`escape-passthru-generic` -- so it gates the fix rather than passing either way.

SPLIT OUT: the 10-shape sweep turned up an unrelated INTERPRETER defect -- a user
`Drop` body firing TWICE for a struct destructured out of a tuple param. Identical on
the unfixed control, so it is pre-existing and not this fix's doing. Filed separately.
title: A heap-bearing TUPLE argument whose value ESCAPES the caller's frame LEAKS the caller's original buffer, because the callee entry-copies but the caller registers no orphan-free: `fn passthru(p: (Bag, i64)) -> (Bag, i64) { p }` and `use2(mk([...]))` each leak 48 bytes under LSan while printing the right answer. The enum sibling of this arm got the `arg_escapes_frame` orphan-free in B-2026-08-01-14; the tuple arm never did. Pre-existing on the NON-generic path, and unmasked on the generic one by B-2026-08-27-37
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-27-37, and PRE-EXISTING to it -- the non-generic spelling leaks
on an unmodified tree, and -37 touches only `compile_mono_function`. It is filed separately
because it is a different defect with a different owner: -37 is the mono's MISSING entry-copy,
this is the caller's MISSING orphan-free on the escape path.

REPRO (a): the param returned whole.

    struct Bag { xs: Vec[String] }
    fn passthru(p: (Bag, i64)) -> (Bag, i64) { p }
    fn main() { let (b, n) = passthru((Bag { xs: ["x", "y"] }, 7)); println(f"{n} {b.xs.len()} {b.xs[0]}"); }

REPRO (b): a call temporary as the argument.

    struct Bag { xs: Vec[String] }
    fn mk(v: Vec[String]) -> (Bag, i64) { (Bag { xs: v }, 3) }
    fn use2(p: (Bag, i64)) -> i64 { let (b, n) = p; b.xs.len() + n }
    fn main() { println(f"{use2(mk(["x", "y"]))}"); }

Both print the right answer and exit 0. Under `-fsanitize=address` (Linux, LSan on) both
report `Direct leak of 48 byte(s) in 1 object(s)` -- the Vec's element buffer, two 24-byte
String control blocks.

MECHANISM. The callee entry-copies a heap-bearing by-value tuple param
(`make_tuple_param_callee_owned`, #21), so caller and callee hold INDEPENDENT buffers and each
must free its own. When the tuple value ESCAPES the caller's frame the caller registers no drop
for its original, and the copy is what flows onward -- so the original is orphaned. Measured,
not inferred: instrumenting `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` shows its tuple arm is not
REACHED AT ALL on the escape path (the probe prints for the consuming call and prints nothing
for the passthrough), so this is not a gate that declined -- the escape path never gets there.

This is precisely the case B-2026-08-01-14 fixed for ENUM arguments, and its comment states the
rule in general terms: "entry-copy passthrough (`pass2(E2.B(..))` where the callee returns its
param): the callee deep-copies the payload at entry and the COPY flows out to the result's
consumer, so the ORIGINAL aggregate here is orphaned -- free it, MEMORY ONLY". That arm exists
for enums (`if arg_escapes_frame { ... track_enum_var(slot) ... }`) and has no tuple sibling.

MEASURED MATRIX -- the four cells that establish it is pre-existing and not -37's doing:

    shape                     -37 reverted   -37 applied
    passthrough, generic      clean          48 B leak
    passthrough, NON-generic  48 B leak      48 B leak    <- -37 cannot touch this path
    call-temp,   generic      clean          48 B leak
    call-temp,   NON-generic  48 B leak      48 B leak    <- -37 cannot touch this path

The generic column was clean before -37 only BECAUSE the mono skipped the entry-copy and
aliased the caller's buffer -- the very aliasing that made -37 a double free. Removing the
alias unmasks this leak on the generic spelling; the non-generic spelling has always had it.

SUGGESTED FIX: give the tuple arg arm the `arg_escapes_frame` branch its enum sibling already
has -- register a MEMORY-ONLY free of the caller's original when the value escapes, with the
bodies staying with the result's consumer. The obstacle to verify first is that the tuple arm
is not reached on that path at all, so the branch may need to live wherever the escape path
routes instead; find that site before writing the arm.

SEVERITY medium, not high: a leak, bounded by the number of such calls, with no corruption and
no wrong output -- unlike the double free it was masking. It is Linux-CI-visible (the
`memory-sanitizer` job runs LSan; a local macOS asan run will NOT catch it, per CLAUDE.md).

WHEN FIXED: `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_generic_struct_destructured_from_a_tuple_param_frees_once`
carries a comment naming both shapes and saying to add them as guards there; do that, in BOTH
the generic and non-generic spellings.

fix:
Fixed in 8cfae471. The row's own "what the fix needs" held in full, including
that the comparator is the `Vec` walk parameterized by the header and that the
interpreter needed only a dispatch arm.

CODEGEN. `Body::VecLike` gains a `header_llvm` field and the `Path` head match
gains a `"Slice"` arm; the walk reads fields 0 and 1, which a
`{ptr, len, cap}` and a `{ptr, len}` share, so ONE body serves both. That is
the same parameterization `emit_eq_fn_for_ptr_len_header` performs for
equality, which is what makes a slice's ordering and its equality read a
header the same way rather than by two conventions that could drift.

`compile_slice_ord` is the entry point, and it is its own function rather than
a call to `compile_ordered_cmp_te` for two reasons that are properties of a
slice:

  * A slice operand arrives as a bare `ptr` when it is a LOCAL (the address of
    its header slot) and as the fat struct BY VALUE when it is a PARAMETER.
    `operand_as_ptr` normalizes the two, exactly as `compile_slice_eq` does;
    `compile_ordered_cmp_te` deliberately declines a pointer operand, because
    for every other shape reaching it a pointer would mean comparing
    addresses. The same fact puts the dispatch AHEAD of the array block and
    outside the struct-operand one -- a slice local is neither an array value
    nor a struct value, so it would otherwise fall past every ordered arm to
    the "Unsupported struct binary op" this row reported.
  * The comparator is keyed on a CANONICAL `Slice[T]` rebuilt from the
    element, not on the operand's own type. A `mut Slice[T]` operand is a
    `TypeKind::MutSlice`, which `display_mangle_te` renders "unknown", so
    every element type would collapse onto one `karac_cmp_unknown` -- the
    collision B-2026-08-27-25 records for the bare `"Array"` name. It is
    SILENT here, since every comparator in the family has the same
    `(ptr, ptr) -> i64` signature and a shared symbol produces wrong answers
    rather than a verifier error. Rebuilding also makes the two spellings name
    one function, so `v[0..2] < s` agrees with the `mut` form.

ONE THING THE ROW DID NOT NAME, and the sharpest edge here: the LENGTH
TIEBREAK must be kept. Adapting the array comparator -- whose extent is fixed,
so it has neither a length load nor a tiebreak -- is the obvious move and is
wrong: two slices differ in length routinely, and without the tiebreak a
PREFIX compares EQUAL to the slice containing it. Every other row of a natural
fixture still passes with it dropped, so the fixture pins it explicitly.

INTERPRETER: a dispatch arm only. `value_compare` has had a `Slice` arm,
comparing the viewed ranges, as long as its `Vec` one.

THE PER-ELEMENT GATE from B-2026-08-27-42 is reused rather than re-derived,
which is what the row asked for and what keeps the two backends accepting the
same set -- the interpreter's gate can only ask a slice's elements, so asking
the container in codegen would diverge. `slice_elems_totally_ordered` asks only
the VIEWED range, not the whole backing store: the range is what the
comparison reads. Measured symmetric on every boundary shape:

    Slice[(i64, i64)]   lowers on both, agrees
    Slice[f64]          declines on both (the float carve-out: `total_cmp` is
                        a sort key's order, not `<`'s)
    Slice[Vec[i64]]     declines on both -- what the per-element gate is for

Tests: `test_e2e_slice_ordering` and `slice_ordering_in_the_interpreter`. The
prefix row pins the tiebreak; the `show(...)` / `cmp2(...)` rows pin the
pointer/by-value normalization and the `mut Slice` spelling; the heap rows are
BUILT rather than written as literals so element 0 of each slice is
content-equal but a DISTINCT allocation -- a comparator reading the pointer
word returns there with an arbitrary answer instead of walking on, and two
string literals would likely share one rodata address and let that pass. Both
element types appear in one program so a symbol collision surfaces as a wrong
answer. Both fixtures verified RED against the unfixed compiler.

THE FAMILY IS NOW CLOSED: tuple (B-2026-08-27-33), array (B-2026-08-27-42),
slice (this row). `Vec[T] < Vec[T]` was never part of it and remains correctly
rejected -- a `Vec` operand is a `Type::Named`, which the comparison gate holds
to a `PartialOrd` derive, while the other three are their own `Type` variants
and fall through it. The one remainder across the family is a NESTED sequence
(an array of arrays, a slice of Vecs), which declines on both backends by
construction and is pinned in the fixtures of both rows.

Gates: codegen 3329/0, memory_sanitizer 1244/0 under LSan, par_codegen 270/0,
selfhost_codegen 1/0, default `cargo test` all green, both clippy legs and
`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean. All four surfaces byte-identical.
title: `Slice[T]` ORDERING operators never lower, while `karac check` accepts them -- the last member of the tuple/array family: `a < b` on two `Slice[i64]` passes the typechecker, then dies on the interpreter's catch-all and on `karac build`'s "Unsupported struct binary op: Lt". Slice EQUALITY was fixed by B-2026-08-27-24; the `<` family is the half that was left
detail:
REPRODUCE:

    fn main() {
        let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(1); v.push(2); v.push(3);
        let a: Slice[i64] = v[0..2];
        let b: Slice[i64] = v[1..3];
        println(f"{a < b}");
    }

    karac check         All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  runtime error: operator 'Lt' is not defined for operands of type
                        'Slice' and 'Slice' (the message claims the typechecker reports
                        this as a hard error; it does not, and did not)
    karac build         error: codegen failed: Unsupported struct binary op: Lt

THE THIRD MEMBER of the family B-2026-08-27-33 (tuple) and B-2026-08-27-42
(array) closed, and the last one left. `type_supports_ord` and
`type_supports_partial_ord` each carry a `Type::Slice` arm right beside their
`Type::Tuple` and `Type::Array` ones, so `karac check` admits the operand
deliberately -- the gap is in the two lowerings, which makes it a run-vs-build
failure rather than an honest rejection.

`Vec[T] < Vec[T]` is NOT in this family and is correctly rejected today
("type 'Vec[i64]' does not implement PartialOrd"), because a `Vec` operand is
a `Type::Named` and the comparison gate holds a named type to a `PartialOrd`
derive. A slice and an array are their own `Type` variants, so they fall
through that gate entirely. Worth stating because it is what makes the three
rows a family and `Vec` not a fourth.

WHAT THE FIX NEEDS, by analogy with the two that landed. Codegen: the
comparator half already exists in part -- `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` has a
`Vec`/`VecDeque` arm that walks a `{ptr, len, cap}` header, and a slice is the
same walk over a `{ptr, len}` one, which is exactly the parameterization
`compile_slice_eq` / `karac_eq_Slice_<T>` already performs for EQUALITY
(B-2026-08-27-24). Plus the operator dispatch, which for a slice operand has
the extra wrinkle the equality path already handles: a slice LOCAL compiles to
the address of its header slot while a slice PARAMETER arrives as the fat
struct by value, so the operand must be normalized (`operand_as_ptr`) before
the comparator sees it. Interpreter: a dispatch arm only -- `value_compare`
has had a `Value::Slice` arm (comparing the viewed ranges) since the same
commit that gave it the `Vec` one.

The per-element gate B-2026-08-27-42 settled on carries over unchanged and
should be reused rather than re-derived: gate on the ELEMENT's total order
(`te_is_totally_ordered(elem)` / `value_is_totally_ordered` per element), never
on the container, so the two backends accept the same set. A slice element that
is itself a slice or a Vec must decline on both, for the reason recorded there.

LOW for the same reason B-2026-08-27-42 was: both backends fail LOUDLY and
agree, so nothing is silently wrong. It is a shape the checker calls legal that
neither backend runs.

SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-27-42's fix -- probing which other
`type_supports_ord` arms the comparison gate lets through. Not caused by that
fix; measured identical before and after it.

fix:
FIXED by 87210fe. The row's diagnosis was right and its scope was one shape
of four.

It says the receiver "is evidently not arriving at that arm as an EnumVariant at
all, and the call is being answered somewhere else; the arm itself is not the
suspect." Both halves hold, with one correction: the receiver DID arrive at the
`cmp` arm as an `EnumVariant`, but as the WRONG ONE. Measured with a probe on
the arm:

    obj = EnumVariant { enum_name: "Ordering", variant: "A", data: Unit }

The variant survived; the ENUM NAME was replaced. `value_compare` then ordered
that against a well-formed `E.B`.

WHY THAT PRODUCES A CONSTANT rather than merely a mis-ordering -- the row noted
the invariance but not its cause. `value_compare`'s two-`EnumVariant` arm is
`an.cmp(bn).then_with(variant order).then_with(payload)`: the ENUM NAME is the
primary key, and the variant order is only consulted when the names are EQUAL.
Once the receiver is retagged, the two names never match, so the comparison is
decided entirely by `"Ordering".cmp("E")` -- Greater, for every operand pair.
That is the measured `2 2 2` exactly. It also explains the row's observation
that the constant differs between programs while staying operand-independent:
the value is just the lexicographic order of the retagged name against the real
one, so a program whose retag target sorts BEFORE its enum answers a constant
Less (`0 0 0`) instead.

MECHANISM — a synthesized AST node reusing a source span, read back through a
span-keyed channel that was written for a different node.

`lowering.rs`'s `rewrite_enum_literal_method_call` (B-2026-07-13-4) materializes
a literal receiver into an identifier receiver:

    E.A.cmp(other)   ->   { let __karac_elm_N = E.A; __karac_elm_N.cmp(other) }

and gives the synthesized `Identifier` node `callee.span` — the span of the
ORIGINAL three-segment path `E.A.cmp`. The typechecker had recorded the
enclosing CALL's RESULT type at that same span. `retag_bare_unit_variant`
(B-2026-08-19-17 (a)) reads `expr_types[span]` on every identifier evaluation
and adopts the recorded enum, so it read `Ordering`, missed on
`env["Ordering.A"]` (no such variant), and fell through to its in-place retag —
producing a variant the target enum does not declare. Probe output, unfixed:

    ident-retag name="__karac_elm_224_12" val=E.A recorded=Named{"Ordering"}   <- wrong
    ident-retag name="a"                  val=E.A recorded=Named{"E"}          <- right

That second line is why a BOUND receiver was always correct, and why `<` was
correct in either spelling: neither goes through a synthesized node.

THE BUG WAS NEVER ABOUT `cmp`. The trigger is a method on a unit-variant literal
whose RETURN TYPE IS `Named`, because that is what makes the recorded type
survive the `Type::Named` filter. Measured, one program per return type:

    return type              unfixed                          fixed
    Ordering  (`cmp`)        SILENT: constant `2 2 2`          `0 2 1`
    another enum declaring   LOUD: "method 'to_fruit' not      correct
      the same variant         found on type 'Fruit'"
    a struct                 ICE: "internal error: entered     correct
                               unreachable code: field access
                               ...: receiver was Value::Unit"
    i64                      correct (not `Named`, no retag)   correct

So three of the four sibling shapes were broken, and one of them PANICS the
interpreter with a message that blames the typechecker — a violation of the
never-panic diagnostics rule on top of the wrong answer. The primitive-return
row is also why this survived since B-2026-07-13-4: that commit's own fixture
returns `i64`, the one return type the retag declines.

THE FIX gates the retag on the identifier being SPELLED as the variant name
(`name != variant` -> return unchanged). That is the entire set
`register_items`' last-write-wins can get wrong — the collision is over
`env["A"]`, so the identifier being read has to BE `A`. Every other identifier
holds a value produced by an expression that already took its own trip through
the retag, or came from a qualified `Enum.Variant` path, which is unambiguous by
construction; adopting a span-recorded type there can only overwrite a correct
answer. Gating on the spelling closes the class rather than the one lowering
that exposed it: a synthesized node stays free to reuse a source span, because
this channel no longer reads one it was not written for.

A second, independent guard rejects a recorded enum that does not DECLARE the
variant. It is deliberately decisive only for a KNOWN enum, so the prelude's
`Option`/`Result` (which need not appear in `enum_info`) keep the pre-existing
behaviour and the builtin case the retag was built for is not withdrawn.

THE RETAG STILL FIRES where it should — checked, not assumed. Both of
B-2026-08-19-17's own regression tests pass unchanged
(`bare_variant_resolution_matches_the_typechecker_not_declaration_order`,
`user_enum_does_not_hijack_the_builtin_bare_none`, the latter being a bare
`None` where `name == variant`), as does B-2026-07-13-4's
`test_method_on_enum_unit_variant_literal`. Those tests are the guard in the
opposite direction: they fail if a future change removes the retag outright.

SCOPE CHECK on the sibling lowering. `rewrite_shared_index_match_scrutinee` also
synthesizes an identifier over a `let`, but keys it to the SCRUTINEE's own span,
at which the recorded type IS the scrutinee's — so it never aliased another
node's type and needed no change. `rewrite_enum_literal_method_call` was the one
site whose reused span belonged to a different expression.

PINNED by four tests in `tests/interpreter.rs`
(`variant_literal_cmp_receiver_is_not_retagged_to_the_call_result_enum`,
`..._survives_a_method_returning_a_colliding_enum`,
`..._with_a_struct_returning_method_does_not_ice`,
`..._with_a_primitive_returning_method_still_works`) and one twin in
`tests/codegen.rs` (`test_e2e_method_on_enum_variant_literal_receiver`). The
first three and the codegen twin were stash-proven RED against the unfixed
compiler; the primitive-return test passes both ways by design and is kept as
the boundary marker that stops a future narrowing from looking complete. The
interpreter tests are deliberately on the DEFAULT `cargo test` leg, since
`tests/codegen.rs` is entirely `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`.

ONE ADJACENT DEFECT FOUND AND NOT FOLDED IN: `Color.Red.to_tag().n` — a field
read on a struct returned by a method on a variant literal — fails `karac build`
with "codegen: cannot resolve field 'n' on this receiver". Measured identically
on the unfixed and fixed compilers, so it is neither caused nor masked by this
change; the bound-receiver spelling of the same read compiles and runs. Filed
separately rather than widened into this row. Loud, never silent.
title: `.cmp()` WITH AN ENUM-VARIANT LITERAL AS THE RECEIVER answers a CONSTANT under the interpreter, independent of both operands -- `E.A.cmp(E.B)`, `E.B.cmp(E.A)` and `E.A.cmp(E.A)` all return the SAME `Ordering`, while both compiled backends return Less/Greater/Equal correctly. Silent wrong answer, no diagnostic on any surface. Binding the receiver first (`let a = E.A; a.cmp(E.B)`) is correct, and so is the `<` operator in either spelling, so only the literal-receiver method spelling is affected.
detail:
`.cmp()` WHOSE RECEIVER IS A BARE ENUM-VARIANT LITERAL answers a CONSTANT under
the interpreter -- the same `Ordering` for every operand pair -- while both
compiled backends answer correctly. A silent wrong answer with no diagnostic on
any surface: `karac check` passes, `karac run --interp` prints the wrong thing
and exits 0.

    #[derive(Ord, Eq)]
    enum E { A, B }
    fn tag(o: Ordering) -> i64 {
        if o.is_lt() { return 0; }
        if o.is_eq() { return 1; }
        return 2;
    }
    fn main() {
        println(f"{tag(E.A.cmp(E.B))} {tag(E.B.cmp(E.A))} {tag(E.A.cmp(E.A))}");
    }

MEASURED:

    karac run --interp  ->  2 2 2      WRONG (constant Greater)
    karac build         ->  0 2 1      CORRECT
    karac run (JIT)     ->  0 2 1      CORRECT

The constant is not a fixed value -- it is whatever the mis-dispatch happens to
produce, and it varies between programs. A three-variant enum measured `0 0 0`
(constant Less) for `Low.cmp(High)` / `High.cmp(Low)` / `Mid.cmp(Mid)`, and a
program declaring two enums answered `0 0 0` for BOTH while the two-variant
program above answered `2 2 2`. What is invariant is that the answer does not
depend on the operands, which is what makes it a wrong answer rather than a
mis-ordering.

THE BOUNDARY IS THE RECEIVER SPELLING, and only the receiver:

    let a = E.A;  a.cmp(E.B)   ->  correct on every backend
    E.A.cmp(b)                 ->  WRONG under interp   (literal receiver)
    a.cmp(E.B)                 ->  correct              (literal ARGUMENT is fine)
    E.A < E.B                  ->  correct on every backend (operator spelling)

So a literal in argument position is fine and the operator spelling is fine; it
is specifically a variant literal in RECEIVER position of the method spelling.
The interpreter's `cmp` arm (`interpreter/method_call.rs`) requires `obj` to be
a `Value::EnumVariant`, and `value_compare` orders those correctly by variant
index -- which the bound-receiver row proves. So the receiver is evidently not
arriving at that arm as an `EnumVariant` at all, and the call is being answered
somewhere else; the arm itself is not the suspect.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-27-41. Measured on the unfixed compiler as well as the
fixed one, identical output on both sides; that commit's interpreter change is a
`matches!` -> `match` rewrite over the same three receiver arms plus a new tuple
arm, and touches no enum path.

SOURCE NOTE: found while checking that B-2026-08-27-41's widening of the `cmp`
intercept left the neighbouring receiver kinds untouched. It is the reason that
row's fixture binds its `P` and `Rev` receivers to locals rather than writing
them inline -- the inline spelling is a different, pre-existing defect on a
different receiver kind, and folding it in would have hidden this.

fix:
Fixed in fa6d35a. Two independent defects behind the one symptom, exactly as
the row separated them.

(1) AND (2) -- THE RECEIVER WITH NO NAME. Codegen resolved the `.cmp`
receiver through `inferred_receiver_type`, which reads `var_type_names` and
so answers only for an `Identifier` or `self`. The fix falls back to
`type_name_of_expr`, the wider sibling that ALREADY types a struct literal
(its `StructLiteral` arm) and a call result (its `Call` arm, via
`fn_return_type_names`) -- so this is a fallback onto an existing resolver,
not a new one. It runs SECOND because `inferred_receiver_type` carries a
`Slice` fallback the wider helper lacks, which keeps every receiver that
resolved before on exactly its old path.

The row measured two shapes; the fix turns out to close four, because they
all fail for the one reason. An INDEX receiver (`v[0].cmp(v[1])`) and a
TUPLE-ELEMENT receiver (`t.0.cmp(t.1)`) were equally nameless and equally
broken, and both now lower -- `type_name_of_expr` has arms for them already.
A FIELD CHAIN (`h.p.cmp(q)`) likewise.

Additive by construction rather than by inspection: the name only reaches
`compile_user_cmp_to_ordering`, which routes to `emit_cmp_fn_for_struct` /
`_enum`, and both decline unless the type is in `ord_orderable_types`. A
name that is not an orderable aggregate yields `None` and falls through to
the same "no handler" error as before.

The `user_owns_cmp` guard above this dispatch already consulted
`type_name_of_expr`, which is what makes the fix safe on the one axis that
matters: a user `impl Ord` still wins over the builtin from a LITERAL
receiver, not just from a bound one. Verified with a `Rev` whose
hand-written `cmp` reverses the order -- the structural comparator would say
Less where the impl says Greater, which is the B-2026-08-26-10 shape (a
silent wrong answer in compiled output only). Both spellings report Greater
on both backends.

(3) THE GENERIC AGGREGATE -- and the row's "prior question", answered.
`Option` was not special. Measured on the unfixed compiler, all check-green
and interp-green and build-refused: `Option[i64]`, `Result[i64, i64]`, a
user `enum MyOpt[T]`, a user `struct Pair[T]`, and -- transitively -- a
non-generic `#[derive(Ord)]` struct holding an `Option[i64]` field
("Unsupported struct binary op: Lt"). The class is `.cmp` on a generic
aggregate, not a missing Option arm.

Why neither backend can lower it is structural, not an oversight:
`emit_cmp_fn_for_enum` reads payload `TypeExpr`s by enum NAME, so inside
`Option` it sees the parameter `T` and never the instantiation, and
`emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` refuses a `Path` carrying `generic_args` for
that reason. The interpreter's `aggregate_is_orderable` independently
requires `generic_params.is_empty()` and says so in its own comment. So the
`<` spelling was ALREADY refused by both backends -- agreeing, which is why
`<` never split. Only `.cmp` did, because it consulted that gate on neither
side: the typechecker asked only whether the derive was present (never about
the arguments), and the tree-walker answered straight out of
`value_compare`, which has runtime values and so can order what no static
comparator can.

So the answer to "should Option be ordered at all" is: not by a DERIVED
comparator, and both backends had already decided that -- the typechecker
simply had not been told. `type_supports_ord` / `type_supports_partial_ord`
now require the aggregate to be non-generic. That is the direction this file
already takes for this exact shape: `type_supports_display` rejects
`Type::Unit` precisely so a meaningless interpolation cannot render
differently per backend.

The `PartialOrd` twin is narrowed in step, deliberately.
`register_ord_orderable_types` admits a `#[derive(PartialOrd)]` aggregate
into codegen's comparator family on equal footing with `Ord`, so narrowing
only the `Ord` spelling would have moved the split one derive over rather
than closing it -- `#[derive(PartialOrd)] struct S { x: Option[i64] }` was
verified to be the same defect.

A user `impl Ord` still wins, generic or not, and that escape hatch is
PRESERVED BEHAVIOUR rather than a defensive clause: a hand-written
`impl[T] Ord for W[T]` is a declared function, dispatches through the
ordinary user-impl path, and was measured working on BOTH backends. Gating
it out would have broken code that compiles today, so it is pinned by its
own fixture.

DIAGNOSTIC. The `<` spelling on a generic aggregate now errors at check
instead of at run/build, which is a strict improvement (it failed on both
backends before), but it inherited advice that is actively wrong here: the
prelude's `Option` already carries `#[derive(Ord, PartialOrd)]`, so "add
#[derive(PartialOrd)]" sends the reader after a derive that is present.
`ordering_unsupported_because_generic` replaces it with what is true -- the
derive is there, the derived comparator cannot order a type-parameter
payload -- and names the `impl Ord` escape hatch that does work.

NOT FIXED, and filed as B-2026-08-27-51: `Vec[Option[i64]].sort()` remains
check-green, sorted correctly under `--interp`, and refused by
`karac build`. It is the same family but a different mechanism --
`Vec.sort()`'s codegen element-type dispatch has its own gate, independent
of `type_supports_ord` (deliberately: B-2026-08-11-7 records that gating
sort on `type_supports_ord` broke `Vec[Vec[String]].sort()`), so this fix
does not reach it and widening that gate is its own measurement.

Making the DERIVED generic case work is a feature, not this fix: it needs a
monomorphized comparator per instantiation. When it lands, the gate here
widens and nothing else has to move.

FIXTURES, all verified RED against the unfixed compiler except where noted:
`test_e2e_cmp_on_a_non_identifier_receiver` (tests/codegen.rs, 10 rows,
fails pre-fix with the row's exact "no handler for method 'cmp' on
non-identifier receiver"), `test_generic_aggregate_ordering_rejected_on_both_spellings`
and `test_derive_ord_rejected_when_a_field_is_a_generic_aggregate`
(tests/typechecker.rs, both RED),
`test_generic_ordering_gate_spares_what_both_backends_lower`
(tests/typechecker.rs -- green pre-fix by design; it is the guard that the
narrowing did not overshoot), and
`cmp_on_a_non_identifier_receiver_under_the_tree_walker` (tests/interpreter.rs
-- also green pre-fix, since the tree-walker was already right). That last
one exists because the E2E TWINS against the interpreter: without a
literal-pinned oracle on the default `cargo test` leg, both backends could
later agree on a new wrong answer and the twinned assertion would still
pass.

GATES (re-run after rebasing onto 3cfbd1e / 87210fe / 4efd5ab, which touched
codegen and the interpreter): codegen 3337/0, memory_sanitizer 1245/0 under
LSan, par_codegen 270/0, selfhost_codegen 1/0, default leg green, both
clippy legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean. All four surfaces
byte-identical on every fixed shape.
title: CODEGEN'S `.cmp()` RECEIVER SURFACE IS NARROWER THAN THE TYPECHECKER ADMITS: a struct LITERAL receiver (`P { .. }.cmp(q)`), a CALL-RESULT receiver (`mk(1).cmp(mk(2))`) and an `Option[T]` receiver (`x.cmp(y)`) all pass `karac check` and run correctly under `--interp`, and all three refuse to build. Loud, not silent -- `karac build` errors -- but a run-vs-build split in a shape the checker calls legal.
detail:
CODEGEN'S `.cmp()` RECEIVER SURFACE IS NARROWER than what the typechecker admits
and what the interpreter answers. Three receiver shapes measured, all
check-green, all interp-correct, all refusing to build.

    #[derive(Ord, Eq)]
    struct P { a: i64, b: i64 }
    fn mk(a: i64) -> P { return P { a: a, b: 0 }; }
    fn main() {
        println(f"{P { a: 1, b: 2 }.cmp(P { a: 1, b: 3 }).is_lt()}");   // (1)
        println(f"{mk(1).cmp(mk(2)).is_lt()}");                          // (2)
        let x: Option[i64] = Some(1);
        let y: Option[i64] = Some(2);
        println(f"{x.cmp(y).is_lt()}");                                  // (3)
    }

MEASURED, each shape on its own:

    (1) struct literal   check OK   interp true   build: no handler for method 'cmp' on non-identifier receiver
    (2) call result      check OK   interp true   build: no handler for method 'cmp' on non-identifier receiver
    (3) Option[i64]      check OK   interp Less   build: no handler for method 'cmp' on variable 'x'

Two distinct causes behind one symptom. (1) and (2) are the identifier-keyed
receiver: codegen resolves the `.cmp` receiver through `inferred_receiver_type`,
which reads `var_type_names` and so only sees an `Identifier` / `SelfValue`
receiver -- the same class of gap as B-2026-06-13-17 / B-2026-07-11-11 for other
methods. Binding first (`let p = P { .. }; p.cmp(q)`) compiles and is correct, so
the comparator and the lowering are both fine; only the receiver resolution is.
(3) IS an identifier, but `Option` has no arm in codegen's `cmp` dispatch at all.

(3) also carries an INTERNAL inconsistency worth recording, independent of the
backend split: `x.cmp(y)` on an `Option[i64]` is answered by the interpreter
(`Less`) while `x < y` on the same two values is REFUSED by it ("operator 'Lt' is
not defined for operands of type 'EnumVariant' and 'EnumVariant'") -- and codegen
refuses both. So the method and operator spellings disagree on Option in the
interpreter, in the opposite direction from the tuple case B-2026-08-27-41 fixed.
Whether Option should be ordered at all is the prior question; `type_supports_ord`
currently returns `true` for it by falling through its Named arm's `else`, which
is why the typechecker admits both spellings.

LOUD, NOT SILENT, on every shape here -- `karac build` errors and emits no
binary, so nothing ships a wrong answer. That is why this is medium and its
sibling row (the enum-literal receiver, which answers a wrong constant under
interp) is high.

SOURCE NOTE: found while checking that B-2026-08-27-41's tuple `.cmp` arm left
the neighbouring receiver kinds untouched. All three shapes reproduce identically
on the unfixed compiler -- none is caused or masked by that commit, whose codegen
change is guarded on `TypeKind::Tuple`.

fix:
FIXED by b0dac13. `PatternKind::Tuple` now joins `Struct` /
`TupleVariant` on the `let_destructures_owned_param` gate
(`src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs`), so `let (r, n) = p;` over an owned tuple
param binds param VIEWS and registers no Drop slots — leaving the caller's
single fire, which is what both compiled backends already ran.

DIAGNOSIS CONFIRMED, MECHANISM ONE LEVEL DOWN FROM THE ROW'S WORDING. The row
guessed "the param's own drop and the binding's drop both fire"; the count and
the neighbourhood are right, the attribution is not. Backtraces name the two
sites exactly: the EXTRA fire is `run_cleanup` ->
`invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` inside the CALLEE's block — the slot the
pattern's BINDING registered — and the surviving one is
`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` -> `run_discarded_value_user_drops` in the CALLER.
The tuple param itself never had a slot at all.

IT IS NOT THE ONE-LINE GATE WIDENING IT LOOKS LIKE. A retraction is a HAND-OFF:
correct exactly when someone else fires. Adding a bare `| PatternKind::Tuple(_)`
and stopping there turns a GREEN shape RED, because one frame kind has no-one
else — `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` is wired into `eval_call` alone, so an impl
method's arguments reach no caller-side fire. Measured on that first attempt:
`impl W { fn take(ref self, p: (R, i64)) { let (r, n) = p; … } }` went from one
body to ZERO against one on both compiled backends. The gate now bails on a
method frame (`owned_param_frame_is_method`, pushed beside
`owned_param_names_stack` at both call sites).

REPAIRS A SHAPE THE ROW DID NOT NAME. That same bail fixes the STRUCT leg's
method form, broken since B-2026-08-01-12 landed the free-fn gate without the
distinction: `let Holder { r } = h;` inside a method fired ZERO bodies against
one on both compiled backends. Measured on an UNMODIFIED binary before any of
this landed, so it is pre-existing and was not introduced here.

A SECOND, PRE-EXISTING DEFECT HAD TO BE FIXED FOR THE FIRST TO BE MEASURABLE AT
ALL, and it is the more interesting half. `moved_out_container_bodies_bindings`
and its two per-element siblings (`moved_out_tuple_elem_bodies`,
`moved_out_struct_field_bodies`) were keyed by bare NAME with NO frame scoping —
the exact hole B-2026-08-09-10 closed for the other three sets, with these three
left out. So a callee acting on its own param silently disarmed an unrelated
CALLER binding that happened to share the spelling. Measured, one variable
renamed and nothing else changed:

    fn take(p: (R, i64)) { let (r, n) = p; println(f"got {r.id} {n}"); println("after") }
    fn main() { let p = (R { id: 5 }, 1); take(p); println("end") }   -> 1 body
    fn main() { let q = (R { id: 5 }, 1); take(q); println("end") }   -> 2 bodies

The collision was CANCELLING this row's double fire, so the shape read as
correct whenever the author happened to reuse the name. That is also why a first
pass at the fix looked like it regressed the place-argument shapes to zero: the
control programs were themselves collided, and the "0" was two defects
interacting, not one. The three sets now join the `std::mem::take` isolation in
`eval_call`. Without that, no consistent rule exists — the same source shape
wants opposite answers depending on an unrelated identifier.

SCOPE, measured across 31 destructure shapes on all three backends (interp /
LLJIT / AOT), each shape a separate program:
  * FIXED here, previously interp=2 vs compiled=1 — tuple param destructure
    (the row's repro); both elements Drop-bearing; nested tuple pattern;
    element moved into a further call; whole-move rebind then destructure;
    generic fn; two tuple params in one signature; destructure inside a branch;
    tuple literal argument with a place element; a param forwarded from another
    fn; and every place-argument form (statement call, nested in a `println`,
    let-bound result), which is the collision-masked family above.
  * FIXED here, previously interp=0 vs compiled=1 — struct destructure and
    tuple destructure inside an impl method.
  * ALREADY correct and still correct — bare struct param, tuple param read by
    FIELD (no destructuring), wildcard element, struct-pattern destructure of a
    struct param, free-fn struct destructure with literal and with place arg.

The ORDERING difference the row set aside is unchanged and out of scope: the
interpreter runs the body at the callee's NLL point, the compiled backends after
the call. It is present in the already-correct bare-param control too, so it
belongs to drop placement generally, not to this row. Both regression tests are
written so the three backends agree byte-for-byte, which is why they can share
one expected string.

NOT FIXED, and filed separately rather than folded in — three neighbours found
by the same sweep, each with a control proving it is a different defect:
B-2026-08-28-1 (compiled backends run NO body for a tuple destructured from a
non-param source), B-2026-08-28-2 (body runs TWICE on ALL THREE backends when
a destructured element is returned), B-2026-08-28-3 (codegen cannot compile a
tuple rebuilt from destructured elements).

Regression tests: `tests/interpreter.rs`'s
`test_tuple_param_destructure_single_caller_fire` (three argument shapes,
including the collided one, so the isolation fix is pinned) and
`test_method_param_destructure_single_caller_fire` (tuple and struct legs, so
the method bail is pinned), each with a same-source same-string codegen E2E twin
in `tests/codegen.rs`.

ALSO REPAIRED, measured pre/post against a b510b81 interpreter after the rebase
(these were not in the original sweep and are not in the counts above):
RECURSION through a tuple param went 8 bodies -> 4 (AOT 4); a NESTED call chain
went 4 -> 2 (AOT 2); and a whole-move rebind of an owned param INSIDE A METHOD
(`let h2 = h;`) went 0 -> 2 (AOT 2), the same zero-fire the method bail fixes for
the direct destructure.

NOT FIXED, and filed as B-2026-08-28-4: the same destructure inside a CLOSURE
still runs two bodies on the interpreter and ZERO under `karac build`. Verified
UNCHANGED by this fix (2 before, 2 after, on a pre-fix binary built from
b510b81): `owned_param_names_of_fn` resolves against `program.items`, a closure
matches no top-level function, so a closure frame contributes the empty set by
construction and the gate never fires there.
title: The INTERPRETER fires a user `Drop` body TWICE for a struct DESTRUCTURED out of a TUPLE PARAM, where the compiled backends fire it once: `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { let (r, n) = p; r.id + n }` prints `drop 41` twice under `karac run --interp` and once under `karac build`. Isolated to the destructuring -- a bare struct param and a tuple param read by FIELD are both correct -- so the param's own drop and the binding's drop both fire. The interpreter-side twin of B-2026-08-27-37, which was codegen's DOUBLE FREE on the same source shape
detail:
The INTERPRETER fires a user `Drop` body TWICE for a struct DESTRUCTURED out of a
tuple param, where both compiled backends fire it once -- a run-vs-build divergence
AND a violation of drop-exactly-once on the interpreter side.

REPRO:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { let (r, n) = p; r.id + n }
    fn main() { println(f"{take((R { id: 41 }, 1))}") }

    karac run --interp   ->   drop 41 / drop 41 / 42      <-- body runs TWICE
    karac build          ->   42 / drop 41                <-- once

Only ONE `R` is ever constructed, so the two prints are one object's body running
twice, not two objects.

ISOLATED to the destructuring. Two neighbours, same struct, same user `Drop`, both
correct on the interpreter:

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { r.id + 1 }                       // bare struct param  -> once
    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { p.0.id + p.1 }            // tuple param, field access, no
                                                            // destructuring       -> once

So it is specifically `let (r, n) = p` over a tuple PARAM: the param's own drop and
the binding's drop both fire. Presumably the destructuring binds the element out
without disarming the tuple param's element drop.

NOT the same defect as B-2026-08-27-37, though it is the same SHAPE. That row was
codegen's DOUBLE FREE of the heap buffer for a struct destructured out of a tuple
param; this is the interpreter running a user Drop BODY twice for that shape. The
memory half and the body half are separate channels, and this half is on the other
backend -- worth noting that a single source shape had a defect on both.

PRE-EXISTING, and independent of B-2026-08-27-44's fix: an UNFIXED control binary
built from the same tree prints the identical `drop 41 / drop 41 / 42`. Found while
sweeping a 10-shape safety matrix for that row rather than by a targeted probe.

SEPARATE, NARROWER OBSERVATION not claimed as part of this bug: the interpreter runs
the body BEFORE the `println` while the compiled backends run it after. That ordering
difference is also present in the correct bare-struct-param case, so it is a broader
question about drop placement relative to a tail expression and does not belong to
this row. The COUNT is what makes this one a defect.

SEVERITY medium: a user-visible run-vs-build divergence on a documented-once
guarantee, but confined to the interpreter (the shipped compiled backends are
correct), and a Drop body running twice is an observable-effects bug rather than
memory corruption.

ALL THREE BACKENDS, measured on a freshly-built `karac` + `karac_jit_runner` PAIR:

    karac run --interp   ->   drop 41 / drop 41 / 42      <-- TWICE
    karac run  (LLJIT)   ->   42 / drop 41                <-- once
    karac build  (AOT)   ->   42 / drop 41                <-- once

So the JIT sides with AOT and the interpreter is the outlier. Worth stating because
an earlier reading of this same shape had the JIT agreeing with the INTERPRETER, and
that reading was an artifact of a STALE `karac_jit_runner`: a `cargo test` run against
a stashed tree had rebuilt both bins, and later builds refreshed only `karac`. That is
exactly the staleness footgun CLAUDE.md documents for `karac run`. Re-measured after an
explicit `cargo build --features llvm --bin karac --bin karac_jit_runner`, which is
what the numbers above come from -- do the same before trusting any JIT reading here.

fix:
FIXED by 152f30f.

CONFIRMED as reported, and the mechanism is one step past where the row left
it. Codegen COMPILES the block receiver correctly — instrumented, it hands back
a proper `{ i64 }` StructValue for `Tag`. What it cannot do is NAME that value's
type, so `field_index_for` finds no field layout and the loud guard fires.

`type_name_of_expr` had no block arm, as the row diagnosed. But adding the
obvious one is not merely insufficient, it is a MISCOMPILE. Measured, with the
naive arm installed:

    struct Other { a: i64, n: i64 }
    struct Tag   { n: i64, a: i64 }
    let x = Other { a: 5, n: 42 };
    println({ let x = make(); x }.n);   // make() -> Tag { n: 7, a: 99 }

    naive block arm  ->  99      (WRONG, silent)
    fixed            ->   7

The reason is `compile_block_with_frame`: per B-2026-07-13-6's lexical scoping
it reverts the whole per-variable env at scope exit, so by the time ANY consumer
asks for the block's type, the tail's binding is gone. Re-deriving the tail
there resolves the identifier `x` against the OUTER `x`, which the block-local
shadows — and since both structs declare an `n`, at different indices, that is
not a build error but a read of Tag's storage at Other's index, landing on
`Tag.a`. Trading the loud gap for a silent wrong answer would have been strictly
worse than the bug. `compile_block_with_frame`'s own comment already names the
rule ("the consuming let/arm re-derives its own metadata from the typechecker's
type, not from a block-local tail's name entry"); nothing enforced it.

THE FIX records the tail's type name one line BEFORE the revert, while the
block's own scope is still live, keyed by the block's span, and reads it back
from a new `Block | Seq | Unsafe` arm in `type_name_of_expr`. The capture POINT
is the load-bearing part, not the arm, so `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`test_e2e_block_receiver_tail_is_typed_in_the_blocks_own_scope` pins the
shadowing fixture above specifically — no other fixture can distinguish the two
implementations. An unrecorded block reads back None and keeps the pre-existing
loud error, so the channel is fail-closed and never guesses.

Span-keying is safe here despite `type_name_of_expr` being deliberately
structural (the parser aliases spans across chained postfix): the table is only
ever written and read under a BLOCK's span, so a block cannot be confused with
the field access wrapping it. Recording — rather than reading the typechecker's
type for the block — is also what makes the enum-lowering case work at all:
lowering runs AFTER typecheck, so a synthesized block has no `expr_types` entry.

A SECOND DEFECT the fix exposed, and fixed. Making the shape buildable made its
ownership reachable for the first time, and it LEAKED:
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` — the gate on `track_freshtemp_field_access_object`
— admits `Call` and `MethodCall` and NOT `Block`, so the temp aggregate had no
owner and its heap fields were never freed, including the ones the read never
names (the B-2026-07-22-2 shape reached through a different receiver kind). LSan
exits 23 on a two-`String` fixture without it. A value-position block hands its
tail to the consumer by neutralizing the tail's own cleanup
(`suppress_block_tail_cleanup`), so the consumer IS the owner; the fresh-temp
registration is widened at that one call site via a separate predicate, following
the array-literal sibling B-2026-08-27-35 rather than widening the shared one.
Gated by `test_block_receiver_heap_field_read_is_leak_free` in
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`.

VERIFIED across all six consumer positions — println / let / argument / assign /
binop / if-condition — all previously failing, all now building and agreeing with
the interpreter on all three backends (interp, JIT, AOT). The row's own four
spellings pass, as do a nested field (`.inner.m`), a method call on a block
receiver, a nested block tail, a bare struct-literal tail, and the motivating
`Color.Red.to_tag().n`. All three new tests were proven RED against the unfixed
compiler by stashing only `src/`.

NOT COVERED, filed as B-2026-08-28-7 — two receiver shapes measured while
scoping this, both still `run-vs-build` on the same resolution surface. (1) A
`shared struct` block receiver (`{ let n = make(); n }.v`) is consulted through
`shared_type_for_expr`, which runs BEFORE the block is compiled and so cannot see
the recording; it declines, and the generic tail's StructValue guard misses
because a shared receiver compiles to a pointer. (2) An `if`-expression receiver
(`if c { make(1) } else { make(2) }.n`) is a different node kind with no arm at
all. Both are separate mechanisms from the one fixed here, so they are their own
row rather than a silent remainder in this one.
