title: A FIELD READ ON A BLOCK-EXPRESSION RECEIVER never lowers: `{ let x = make(); x }.n` fails `karac build` with "codegen: cannot resolve field 'n' on this receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen)", while `karac check` accepts it and the interpreter answers it. Binding the block to a local first (`let t = { ... }; t.n`) builds and runs. It reaches ordinary source through a LOWERING: `rewrite_enum_literal_method_call` rewrites `Color.Red.to_tag().n` into exactly this shape, so a program containing no block at all fails to build with a diagnostic naming a receiver the author never wrote.
detail:
A FIELD READ WHOSE RECEIVER IS A BLOCK EXPRESSION fails `karac build`, while
binding the same block to a local first compiles and runs. `karac check` accepts
both and the interpreter answers both, so this is a run-vs-build split on a
shape the front end admits.

    struct Tag { n: i64 }
    fn make() -> Tag { return Tag { n: 7 }; }
    fn main() {
        println({ let x = make(); x }.n);
    }

MEASURED, four spellings of the same read:

    let t = { let x = make(); x }; t.n      ->  builds, prints 7        OK
    { let x = make(); x }.n                 ->  BUILD FAILS, interp 7
    { let x = make(); x }.n + 1             ->  BUILD FAILS, interp 8
    let t = { let x = make(); x }; t.n + 1  ->  builds, prints 8        OK

    error: codegen failed: codegen: cannot resolve field 'n' on this receiver
    (its type was not recorded for codegen); this is a compiler gap — run with
    `--interp` (or `KARAC_RUN_JIT=0`) and please report it

So the boundary is the RECEIVER being a block, not the field, the field type, or
the enclosing expression. Codegen's field-receiver type resolution
(`type_name_of_expr` / the `compile_field_access` receiver walk) has arms for
identifier, index, call and method-call receivers; a BLOCK receiver has none, so
the receiver's type is never recorded and the guard fires. Same family as
B-2026-08-06-19 / B-2026-08-12-28 / B-2026-08-14-5 — one more unhandled receiver
shape on that one resolution surface.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE HAND-WRITTEN SPELLING SUGGESTS: a lowering
synthesizes this shape from source that contains no block at all.
`lowering.rs`'s `rewrite_enum_literal_method_call` (B-2026-07-13-4) rewrites a
method call on a unit-variant literal into exactly this form, so

    Color.Red.to_tag().n        // `to_tag` returns a struct

becomes `{ let __karac_elm_N = Color.Red; __karac_elm_N.to_tag() }.n` and fails
to build, with a diagnostic naming a receiver the author never wrote. The
bound-receiver spelling `let c = Color.Red; c.to_tag().n` builds and runs. That
is how this was found, and it is the reason to fix the general block-receiver
arm rather than special-case the enum path: any future lowering that
materializes a receiver into a block inherits the same gap.

LOUD, NEVER SILENT. Every failure is codegen's own "cannot resolve field ...
please report it" guard, which exists precisely so this class cannot fall
through to the `i64 0` placeholder B-2026-07-20-9 removed. Hence medium: the
build stops, and the workaround (bind the receiver to a local) is mechanical.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-27-46, whose repro used the
struct-returning leg of the variant-literal shape. On the pre-fix compiler the
interpreter ICE'd on that leg before codegen was ever reached, which is what hid
this. NOT CAUSED BY that fix: `karac build` was measured on the UNFIXED compiler
and produced the byte-identical error, and the fix touches only
`src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs`. The hand-written block spelling above reproduces
with no enum in the program at all, which is the proof it is not an enum bug.

title: A GENERIC FN'S CONTAINER PARAM BOUND TO A FIELD-ACCESS ARGUMENT loses its ELEMENT TYPE, because every resolver that recovers an element keys on the argument's BINDING NAME and a field access has none. `swap01(mut self.xs)` from a generic-impl method swaps 8 bytes of a 16-byte tuple element -- SILENT wrong answer on the compiled backends, correct under the interpreter -- and SEGFAULTS at a String element. NOT tuple-specific, which is what separates it from B-2026-08-27-40
fix:
FIXED in 4e5bdc0. Two name-keyed resolvers plus one contract repair.

ROOT CAUSE, as the row diagnosed it: every codegen resolver that recovers a container argument's ELEMENT keys on the argument's BINDING NAME to index a var side-table, and a field access has no name, so each declined and `T` stayed unbound -- falling to the `i64` unknown-name default. Two of them matter for this shape, and they must move together:

  * `augment_subst_from_arg_elem_types` binds the element's LLVM TYPE. Its `Vec`/`VecDeque` arm reads `var_types.vec_elem_types[name]`; its `Slice` arm reads `infer_elem_from_source` / `fresh_container_arg_elem_llvm`. All name-gated.
  * `resolve_container_param_elem_substs` binds the element's NAME and `TypeExpr`, through `arg_container_elem_type_expr`, whose arms were Identifier / `.clone()` / a named Vec-returning Call.

Instrumented on the failing and working programs, the decline is exact: for `swap01(mut self.xs)` both resolvers report `arg_kind=Discriminant(20)` (FieldAccess) and produce nothing; for the identifier control both report `Discriminant(9)` and bind.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE MECHANISM AND TOO STRONG ABOUT THE TRIGGER. It concluded "the trigger is the ARGUMENT SHAPE -- a field access -- not the element type, not the impl, and not the generic nesting", on the strength of a control that used an IDENTIFIER argument. A field access is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT: the TYPECHECKER's `call_type_subs` frame also binds `T`, and where it does, a field argument was always fine. Measured, printing the frame at each mono call:

  struct     element   call site       call_type_subs      AOT
  ---------- --------- --------------- ------------------- ----------------
  (none)     tuple     main (ident)    --                  correct
  plain      String    main            {"T": "String"}     correct
  generic    String    main            {"T": "String"}     correct
  plain      tuple     main            None                WRONG, silent
  generic    tuple     main            None                WRONG, silent
  generic    tuple     generic impl    None                WRONG, silent
  generic    String    generic impl    None                SEGFAULT (139)

So the frame is empty in exactly two situations, and EITHER ALONE is enough: the element type is NAMELESS (a tuple -- the B-2026-08-27-40 channel limit), or the call sits inside a GENERIC IMPL, where the binding is self-referential and deliberately dropped by `record_call_type_subs`. That is why `Bag[String]` breaks inside an impl method and the same `Bag[String]` from `main` does not, and it corrects the row's "not the element type, not the impl" to "either one, independently". The receiver's own genericity is NOT a factor -- a plain `struct Bag { xs: Vec[(i64, i64)] }` miscompiles identically, which the row did not have.

FIX (src/codegen/mono.rs):

  1. `arg_container_elem_type_expr` gains a `FieldAccess` arm that DELEGATES to `vec_index_elem_type_expr`. That helper already resolves this exact shape for an INDEX read (`self.xs[i]`): receiver's struct type, the field's declared `Vec[E]`, `resolve_generic_field_te` through the receiver's recorded instantiation for a generic field, then one Vec (or Array) peel. `self.xs` as an ARGUMENT wants the identical answer, so delegating -- rather than restating the resolution -- is what keeps the two from drifting.

  2. `field_arg_container_elem_llvm`, the LLVM twin, resolves THROUGH that same helper rather than from a parallel lookup, so the NAME and TYPE this argument binds for `T` come from one source and cannot disagree. That split is the documented failure mode of this whole family: name bound with the type still defaulted gives `Function return type does not match operand type of return inst`; type bound with the name still the literal `"T"` gives a shared `karac_clone_T` specialized to whichever mono lowered first.

  3. Wired into the `Vec`/`VecDeque` and `Slice` arms as a last-resort `or_else`, so an identifier argument keeps its exact previous binding and only a shape that previously bound NOTHING is affected.

  4. CONTRACT REPAIR, found by probing rather than by reading: `fresh_container_arg_elem_llvm` delegates to `arg_container_elem_type_expr` and excluded only `Identifier`, so the new arm leaked through and made a BORROWED FIELD answer as a "fresh rvalue". Its single caller reads only the TYPE, so the leak was harmless today -- but the next caller to ask that helper the OWNERSHIP question it is named for would get a wrong answer whose direction is a caller-side free of a buffer the struct still owns. `FieldAccess` is now excluded there explicitly, with the reasoning recorded at the guard.

MEASURED, all three backends byte-identical where they build:

  shape                                    before (AOT)          after
  ---------------------------------------- --------------------- ---------
  tuple elem, generic impl                  `10:1 2:20` (silent)  `2:20 1:10`
  String elem, generic impl                 SEGFAULT, exit 139    `bb aa`
  tuple elem, plain struct, from main       `10:1 2:20` (silent)  `2:20 1:10`
  tuple elem, generic struct, from main     `10:1 2:20` (silent)  `2:20 1:10`
  returning `first(self.xs)`                module verify FAIL    `1:10`
  identifier-arg control                    correct               correct

TESTS: `e2e_container_param_bound_to_a_struct_field_argument` (tests/codegen.rs, six cases including the two controls that pin the diagnosis), `container_argument_from_a_struct_field_round_trips` (tests/interpreter.rs -- the A/B oracle; every case was already correct under the tree walk, which is what made this a run/build divergence), and `asan_container_param_bound_to_a_struct_field_argument` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs). NEGATIVE-CONTROLLED: with the fix reverted and the tests kept, the codegen cases fail and ASAN reports `allocation-size-too-big` on the String element -- the 8-byte swap leaves a garbage length in the 24-byte control block, so the corruption is real memory damage and not merely a wrong print.

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, both confirmed PRE-EXISTING against an unfixed control binary built from the same tree, and neither caused by this fix:
  * B-2026-08-27-52 (fixed in the same push) -- a read-only `ref` container param given a struct-field argument double-frees, because the mono path computes an in-place place pointer only for `mut ref`. This fix makes the returning-callee shape BUILD, which is how that one became reachable there; it already aborted on its own shapes with no involvement from this row.
  * B-2026-08-27-53 (open) -- a `Slice[T]` param given a struct-field Vec argument still fails module verification. Loud, unchanged by this fix, byte-identical error on the unfixed control.

Fixed in 12b88f9, by narrowing the CHECK to what both backends lower rather
than widening codegen -- the same direction B-2026-08-27-47 took, and for the
same reason.

THE GATE HAD THE RIGHT NAME AND THE WRONG BODY. `require_ord_element` is
called at every site that needs an ordered element (Vec/Slice `sort`,
`sorted`, `is_sorted`, `binary_search`, Array `is_sorted`), but since
B-2026-08-11-7 it checked ONLY for a reachable IEEE float. Nothing ever asked
whether the element was orderable at all, so every non-float element type
passed regardless of what codegen could do with it.

MEASURED on the unfixed compiler -- all check-green, all sorted correctly
under `--interp`, all refused by `karac build`:

    Vec[Option[i64]]         "Vec.sort() in codegen supports integer, String,
    Vec[Result[i64, i64]]     float, tuple, and nested-Vec element types"
    Vec[Plain]               (a struct with NO #[derive(Ord)])
    Vec[Sh]                  (a #[derive(Ord)] SHARED struct)

and `sorted()` / `is_sorted()` split identically on each. So the row's
`Option` framing was one member of a class, exactly as -47's `Option` was.

The shared-struct member is the sharpest, because the language had ALREADY
decided it: `x < y` on a `#[derive(Ord)] shared struct` is rejected at check
with a purpose-written message ("`#[derive(PartialOrd)]` does not order a
shared type -- add `impl PartialOrd for S`"). Only the sort gate had not
heard, so the same type that cannot be compared with `<` could be handed to
`sort()`.

WHY NOT `type_supports_ord` -- the trap this row was filed pointing at.
B-2026-08-11-7's first version gated on it and broke `Vec[Vec[String]].sort()`,
whose recursive lexicographic comparator has worked since B-2026-06-30-15,
and it left a standing instruction: check what the comparators support, not
what the predicate says. That warning is LIVE, not historical -- re-measured
before writing a line of the fix, `#[derive(Ord)] struct Z { x: Vec[String] }`
is still rejected today.

The cause is worth recording because it looks like a bug that was already
fixed: `type_supports_ord` HAS a `Type::Vector { element } => recurse` arm
that appears to cover this, but `Type::Vector` is the SIMD `Vector[T, N]`, an
unrelated type. `Vec[String]` is `Type::Named { name: "Vec" }` -- a baked
stdlib struct carrying no `#[derive(Ord)]` -- so it reaches the `Named` arm
and is judged as a user type.

SHAPE OF THE FIX. `element_default_order_is_lowerable` is stated as
`type_supports_ord` plus exactly three corrections, and keeping it a short
DIFF rather than a fresh enumeration is deliberate: restating the whole
comparator family in the typechecker is what would let the copy drift again.
Each correction stays individually arguable.

  1. `Vec`/`VecDeque`/`Slice` elements recurse (the `Vec[Vec[String]]` case).
  2. `Shared` is false -- codegen's `emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` excludes
     shared types outright and `<` already rejects them.
  3. `Float` is TRUE here, so `reachable_ieee_float` stays the only voice on
     floats. It already names the NaN harm and the `F64` remedy; a second,
     vaguer error for the same cause would be a regression. Pinned by an
     assertion that a bare `f64` element produces exactly ONE diagnostic.

Where the predicate is uncertain it answers true, and the asymmetry is the
whole design: a wrong `false` rejects a program that compiles and runs today,
while a wrong `true` merely leaves the pre-existing loud build error in place.
Unknown names, type parameters and exotic shapes are therefore admitted and
left to the backend.

The diagnostic names the obstacle that actually applies -- a derive fixes the
underived struct and CANNOT fix the generic or the shared one. Pointing at the
wrong remedy is precisely the failure -47 had to correct on the `<` operator's
message, so the three cases are pinned separately.

THE ANTI-DRIFT TABLE, which is half the fix. Two encodings of one question in
two files (`require_ord_element` in the typechecker,
`emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` in codegen/vec_method.rs) drifted once already; a
comment cannot hold them in step, but a table that fails when either side
moves can. `test_e2e_sort_element_gate_matches_codegen_support` asserts that
every element type the CHECKER admits also BUILDS and matches the interpreter;
`test_sort_element_gate_rejects_what_codegen_cannot_lower` and
`..._spares_what_codegen_lowers` pin the rejected and accepted sets. Widen
codegen without widening the gate and the rejected table fails; narrow codegen
and the compiled one does.

It earned its keep on first run, finding a defect of a HIGHER class than the
one it was written for: `Vec[bool].sort()` sorts DESCENDING on all three
compiled surfaces while the interpreter sorts ascending, and `false < true`
answers `false` when compiled. Both trace to bool lowering as a SIGNED `i1`,
so `true` is -1 and every bool comparison inverts. That is a SILENT wrong
answer where this row is a loud refusal; it reproduces identically before this
change; it is filed as B-2026-08-28-5. The `bool` row is held OUT of the table
with a comment saying why, because an entry there today would assert the bug.

NOT ADDRESSED, deliberately: `binary_search` shares the `require_ord_element`
call site and so inherits the new gate, but its codegen support is genuinely
narrower still (integer and String only, not the comparator family), so
`Vec[(i64, String)].binary_search(..)` remains check-green and build-refused.
Its own error already admits the divergence in as many words ("it works under
`karac run --interp`"). Filed as B-2026-08-28-6 rather than widened here,
because closing it means teaching binary_search the comparator family, not
moving a gate.

VERIFIED: the reproducer fixture is RED pre-fix. The two guard fixtures are
green pre-fix BY DESIGN and are recorded that way rather than counted as
reproductions -- they exist to catch over-rejection and drift, not this bug.
No kata regressed: 22 of 935 kata files use sort/sorted/is_sorted and none is
newly rejected.

GATES: codegen 3338/0, memory_sanitizer 1245/0 under LSan, par_codegen 270/0,
selfhost_codegen 1/0, default leg green, both clippy legs and
`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
title: `Vec[Option[T]].sort()` IS CHECK-GREEN, SORTS CORRECTLY UNDER `--interp`, AND REFUSES TO BUILD -- `Vec.sort()`'s codegen element-type dispatch has its own gate, independent of `type_supports_ord`, so B-2026-08-27-47's narrowing does not reach it. Loud, not silent.
detail:
`Vec.sort()` on a generic-aggregate element is a run-vs-build split that
B-2026-08-27-47 measured but deliberately did not close, because it is a
different mechanism.

    fn main() {
        let mut v: Vec[Option[i64]] = Vec.new();
        v.push(Some(2));
        v.push(None);
        v.push(Some(1));
        v.sort();
        for x in v {
            match x { Some(n) => println(f"Some({n})"), None => println("None"), }
        }
    }

MEASURED (on fa6d35a, i.e. WITH -47's fix in):

    check   OK
    interp  Some(1) / Some(2) / None   -- declaration order, Some before None
    build   error: codegen failed: Vec.sort() in codegen supports integer,
            String, float, tuple, and nested-Vec element types; use
            sort_by(|a, b| ...) for other element types

Why -47's fix does not reach it. That fix narrowed `type_supports_ord` so a
GENERIC aggregate is no longer Ord, which closed the `.cmp` and `<`
spellings on `Option[i64]`. `Vec.sort()` does not gate on
`type_supports_ord`: B-2026-08-11-7 records that gating it there was tried
and REVERTED, because `type_supports_ord` answers `false` for
`Vec[Vec[String]]` (a baked stdlib struct carrying no `#[derive(Ord)]`)
while `Vec[Vec[String]].sort()` is supported and tested. So sort's
typecheck-side gate is scoped to `reachable_ieee_float` only, and everything
else is left to the backends -- where the interpreter's `value_compare`
orders anything and codegen's element dispatch orders a fixed list.

That asymmetry is the bug: the two backends disagree about which element
types `sort` accepts, and the typechecker admits the union.

LOUD, NOT SILENT -- `karac build` errors and emits no binary, and the error
even names the workaround (`sort_by`). Hence medium, not high.

Two candidate fixes, and picking between them is the work:
  (a) teach codegen's `Vec.sort()` element dispatch to route an unsupported
      element type through the same `karac_cmp_<T>` comparator family the
      `<` operator uses, which would ALSO have to decline the generic
      aggregate -- leaving the check-side gap open; or
  (b) give sort a typecheck-side gate that matches what codegen actually
      implements, without re-breaking `Vec[Vec[String]]` the way
      B-2026-08-11-7 measured. That means the gate has to be "what the
      comparator family covers", not "what derives Ord" -- the two are
      genuinely different sets, which is precisely why the first attempt
      failed.

SOURCE NOTE: found while closing B-2026-08-27-47, checking whether narrowing
`type_supports_ord` reached every surface that had been ordering `Option`.
It did not, and the residual is recorded here rather than left implicit in
that row's fix prose.

fix:
FIXED in `383a723` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`).

ROOT CAUSE. `track_destructure_leaf_cleanup` — the shared per-leaf cleanup
registrar for a tuple destructure — ended in a bare `track_struct_var` with no
`drop_method_keys` check. `track_struct_var` is the MEMORY field-walk, so a leaf
whose type declares `impl Drop` had its buffers freed and its user body silently
dropped on the floor. That is precisely the reported signature: RSS flat, body
gone.

The simple-`let` path a few thousand lines up has a THREE-WAY cascade for the
same decision, and the destructure helper implemented only its third arm:

  1. an own `impl Drop`      -> `track_user_drop_var` (the `karac_drop_<T>`
                                WRAPPER: body + fields + memory in ONE action);
  2. no own Drop but a
     Drop-bearing FIELD      -> `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn` on the
                                `UserDrop` channel PLUS the ordinary memory drop;
  3. anything else           -> memory only.

Arm 1 must REPLACE the memory registration rather than join it — registering
both frees the same buffers twice. Arm 2 is additive because a type that merely
CONTAINS a dropper has no wrapper to hang off (nothing builds one for a type
with no Drop), so its bodies and its memory are disjoint work on one slot. The
fix transplants the cascade verbatim, and gives the helper's ENUM arm the
payload-bodies walker that the simple-`let` enum site already pairs with
`track_enum_var`. `UserDrop` is the channel and not `StructDrop` because only
`UserDrop` fires at the binding's NLL live-range end, which is where the
interpreter places the body; on `StructDrop` it would print after the statements
following the leaf's last use, a fresh run-vs-build divergence in the same
output the parity gate compares.

THE ROW'S CHARACTERISATION WAS RIGHT BUT ITS SCOPE WAS TOO NARROW. "A tuple that
is NOT a param" is the correct boundary, and the field-read control correctly
isolated the destructuring `let`. Widening the shape matrix past the row's two
sources found four more shapes on the same root, all 1/0/0 before the fix:

  * a tuple LITERAL RHS (`let (r, n) = (R { id: 41 }, 1)`) — the most common
    spelling of the repro, and it failed for a DIFFERENT reason: it reached
    neither branch of the destructure finisher, being neither "fresh" by
    `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` (Call/MethodCall only) nor a place by
    `place_root_ident`. Its leaves registered no cleanup at all. Admitted at
    this site only, for the reason `expr_is_fresh_owned_array_temp` gives for
    its own split: the general predicate is asked by many unrelated sites and a
    tuple literal is not universally a fresh owned temp to them (`("aa", 1)`
    holds a rodata element). The leaf frees here are cap-guarded, so a rodata
    element is a no-op — pinned by a test.
  * a leaf that declares no Drop but OWNS a Drop-bearing field (arm 2);
  * a nested tuple pattern and an ENUM leaf, both from a fresh source;
  * a leaf inside a nested block.

`match` and `for` destructure were measured CORRECT throughout, which is what
pins the defect to the `let` destructure path rather than to destructuring.

THE REGRESSION THE FIRST CUT SHIPPED, and the reason the param control is
load-bearing. An unconditional leaf registration made a tuple-PARAM destructure
print the body TWICE: `make_tuple_param_callee_owned` deep-copies each element
at entry and registers a tuple drop that already runs their bodies, so the
source genuinely owns them there. The tuple LOCAL has no such owner, which is
why the identical leaf needs the body in one case and must not have it in the
other. `owned_struct_params` cannot tell them apart — it is populated for
`Path`-typed params only, so a tuple param is absent from it and both sources
read identically through it (measured: `own_armed=false elem_bodies_armed=false`
for BOTH). The gate is `current_fn_param_names`. The regression test asserts
ONE body, not a non-empty output, so a future re-widening fails here.

MEASURED, at 50 iterations with a heap `String` field, drop-body counts
interp/jit/build:

    shape                unfixed        fixed
    tuple local          50 / 0 / 0     50 / 50 / 50
    call result          50 / 0 / 0     50 / 50 / 50
    tuple literal        50 / 0 / 0     50 / 50 / 50
    field-bearing leaf   50 / 0 / 0     50 / 50 / 50
    tuple param          50 / 50 / 50   50 / 50 / 50   <- control, unchanged

All five valgrind-clean (`--leak-check=full --errors-for-leak-kinds=definite`,
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`): 0 errors, 0 definite leaks. The unfixed column is from a
control binary built from the same tree with only `src/codegen/stmts.rs`

TESTS. `tests/interpreter.rs::user_drop_body_fires_once_for_a_let_destructure_leaf`
(the oracle — every case already passed, and still passes with the fix reverted,
which is the point of an oracle),
`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_user_drop_body_runs_for_a_let_destructure_leaf` (10 rows
including both controls), and
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_user_drop_body_on_a_let_destructure_leaf`

NOT FIXED, filed separately, all five found by this row's shape matrix:

  * B-2026-08-28-9  — an enum leaf from a tuple LOCAL (its element `TypeExpr`

title: BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS RUN NO USER `Drop` BODY AT ALL for a struct DESTRUCTURED out of a tuple that is NOT a param -- a tuple LOCAL or a CALL RESULT: `let p = (R { id: 41 }, 1); let (r, n) = p;` prints `drop 41` under `karac run --interp` and NOTHING under `karac run` or `karac build`. Measured 0 of 40 bodies over a loop. The BUFFERS are still freed (peak RSS flat at ~2.3 MB across 300k iterations, matching the non-destructuring control), so this is the OBSERVABLE-EFFECTS half of drop only -- and it is the SHIPPED path that is wrong, which is the exact reason B-2026-08-27-48 stayed medium and this does not
detail:
BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS SKIP THE USER `Drop` BODY for a struct destructured out
of a tuple whose source is NOT a parameter. The interpreter is correct here; the
shipped compiled path is the broken one.

REPRO (tuple LOCAL):

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    fn main() { let p = (R { id: 41 }, 1); let (r, n) = p; println(f"{r.id + n}") }

    karac run --interp   ->   42 / drop 41        <-- correct
    karac run  (LLJIT)   ->   42                  <-- body never runs
    karac build  (AOT)   ->   42                  <-- body never runs

The CALL-RESULT source is the same defect:

    fn make() -> (R, i64) { (R { id: 41 }, 1) }
    fn main() { let (r, n) = make(); println(f"{r.id + n}") }   -- same 1 / 0 / 0

ISOLATED by a control that differs in one token -- the same local, read by FIELD
instead of destructured, is correct on all three backends:

    fn main() { let p = (R { id: 41 }, 1); println(f"{p.0.id + p.1}") }
                                                      -- 1 / 1 / 1, all agree

So it is the destructuring `let`, not the tuple, not the local, and not the
struct.

AT SCALE: a 40-iteration loop building `(R { id: i, name: f"payload-{i}" }, 1)`
and destructuring it runs 40 bodies on the interpreter and 0 under `karac build`.

THE MEMORY HALF IS FINE, and that is worth stating because it is what keeps this
out of the leak class. Peak RSS over 300,000 iterations with a heap `String`
field: 2296 KB destructuring vs 2284 KB for the field-read control -- flat, and
indistinguishable. Codegen frees the buffers and skips only the user body, so the
failure is silent RAII: a `Drop` that closes a file, releases a lock, decrements
a counter or logs simply does not happen under the compiled backends.

SEVERITY high, and deliberately one step above B-2026-08-27-48's medium. That row
justified medium with "confined to the interpreter (the shipped compiled backends
are correct)". This is the mirror image: the interpreter is right and the two
SHIPPED backends are wrong, so the same reasoning puts it higher. No memory
unsafety and no leak, which is why it is not `high` for the usual reason.

NOT the same defect as B-2026-08-27-48, whose fix landed alongside this filing:
that was the INTERPRETER firing twice for a tuple PARAM, and the param source is
exactly the case this row EXCLUDES -- with the fix in, a tuple param destructure
now reads 1 / 1 / 1 on all three backends while this local-source shape still
reads 1 / 0 / 0. Two sources, opposite directions, opposite backends.

SOURCE NOTE: found by sweeping a 31-shape destructure matrix across all three
backends while fixing B-2026-08-27-48, not by a targeted probe. Every other shape
in that matrix now agrees; this one and its call-result sibling do not.

fix:
Fixed in d5d7421 by making both caller-side tuple-argument Drop-body walks
filter per ELEMENT instead of per argument.

DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED. The row's title and its "likely shape of the fix" both
name the destructure — "an element destructured out of it and then returned",
with the `fn_returns_param` passthrough guard as the suspected gap. The guard
half is right; the destructure half is not the axis. Measured on the pre-fix
compiler, `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { p.0 }` — no `let` anywhere — is the
same defect at the same count (2/2/2), and so is the `return r;` spelling. What
the three share is that the escaping value is a PART of the param. A fix aimed
at the destructure alone would have repaired one of three spellings.

MECHANISM. The caller's fresh-temp argument walk fires the user `Drop` body of
every element of a tuple-LITERAL argument, on the theory that the whole temp
dies inside the call. Its only escape hatch is `fn_returns_param`, which asks a
WHOLE-param question: is the param handed back bare (or moved bare into a
returned aggregate literal)? A returned part answers no, so the walk fired the
element's body at the call AND the result's owner fired it again at the
binding's live-range end. The control `fn take(r: R) -> R { r }` was correct
throughout, which is what pins the gap to the guard rather than to the walk.

WHY NOT SIMPLY SUPPRESS THE WALK. Because that is a different soundness hole,
not a fix. Measured on `fn take(p: (R, R)) -> R { let (a, b) = p; a }`, where
both elements carry Drop and only element 0 escapes: pre-fix 3 bodies (41
twice, 42 once); with an argument-wide suppression, 1 (42 lost entirely).
Post-fix 2, one per object. That shape is now a row of both behavioural tests
precisely because it fails on any version that is not element-precise.

THE FIX. `fn_returns_param_parts` (src/ast/items.rs) reports which top-level
tuple elements / struct fields of a param reach a return site — through a
direct projection, a one-level destructure leaf, a `let` alias chain, or a
returned aggregate literal. `fn_returns_param` itself is deliberately NOT
widened: eight codegen ownership sites read it, several documented as turning a
leak into corruption if its answer moves, and none of them asked for a finer
answer. The new predicate UNDER-approximates, the opposite of its sibling's
conservatism and for a different reason: a missed escape leaves the
pre-existing double body (no worse), while a false escape would suppress the
only body that runs. Nested destructures, projections of projections and
container escapes therefore report nothing and behave exactly as before.

Both twins consume it: `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`' tuple arm (interp) and
`track_discarded_tuple_elem_bodies` (codegen). The emitted walker is cached by
symbol name, so the skip set is part of that name; an empty skip appends
nothing, leaving every pre-existing symbol byte-identical.

Verified across 14 shapes on interp / LLJIT / AOT. Nine-row tests in
tests/interpreter.rs (`test_returned_tuple_param_element_user_drop_body_runs_once`)
and tests/codegen.rs (`e2e_user_drop_body_of_a_returned_tuple_param_element_runs_once`),
with controls for the other element returned, the bare param, and nothing
escaping. Full codegen (3352), memory_sanitizer (1252), interpreter (1787) and
drop_differential green; fmt and both clippy legs clean.

THE ASAN QUESTION THE ROW ASKED IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS TWO-PART.
For the row's own repro the second body was bodies ONLY: the destructure
spelling with a `String` field is clean under ASAN+LSan on a compiler built
WITHOUT this fix as well as with it (measured by stashing src/ and rebuilding),
so the memory side was balanced throughout and this was a wrong side-effect
count, never corruption. New fixture
`asan_returned_tuple_param_element_drop_body_is_memory_balanced` pins that.

The `p.0` spelling is a different story and is NOT fixed here: at a
heap-carrying element it is a hard `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
abort under both compiled backends. It reproduces identically pre-fix, and it
fires with NO `impl Drop` anywhere in the program, so it is a pure memory
defect that this row's machinery cannot reach. Filed separately rather than
folded in, and deliberately left out of the ASAN fixture so this test is not
red for another row's bug.
title: A user `Drop` body runs TWICE FOR ONE OBJECT on ALL THREE BACKENDS when a struct destructured out of a tuple param is RETURNED: `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { let (r, n) = p; r }` prints `drop 41` twice under `--interp`, LLJIT and AOT alike. Only one `R` is ever constructed. Backend-CONSISTENT, which is why no run-vs-build parity test can see it -- the whole destructure matrix agrees here, at the wrong number
detail:
A user `Drop` body runs TWICE for a SINGLE object when a struct destructured out
of a tuple param is RETURNED from the callee. All three backends do it, so
drop-exactly-once is violated everywhere rather than divergently.

REPRO:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { let (r, n) = p; r }
    fn main() { let x = take((R { id: 41 }, 1)); println(f"{x.id}") }

    karac run --interp   ->   drop 41 / 41 / drop 41
    karac run  (LLJIT)   ->   41 / drop 41 / drop 41
    karac build  (AOT)   ->   41 / drop 41 / drop 41

Exactly one `R` is constructed, so both prints are one object's body running
twice -- not two objects each running once.

WHY IT HID: every parity harness in the tree compares the backends against each
other, and here they AGREE. The 31-shape destructure matrix swept for
B-2026-08-27-48 flags this shape as "OK" on a pure interp-vs-AOT comparison; it
takes counting the CONSTRUCTIONS to see it. Any bug of this form -- consistently
wrong on both sides -- is invisible to the run-vs-build gate that catches most of
this class, which is the general point worth keeping.

WITH A HEAP FIELD the body still runs twice and the program exits 0:

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    ... -> `drop 41 n41` twice, exit 0

so this is not (visibly) a double free; the memory half appears balanced and only
the body count is wrong. Not confirmed under ASAN -- worth an
`asan_`-prefixed fixture in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` to settle whether the
second body run is accompanied by a second release on some shape of `R`.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT: B-2026-08-27-48 is the interpreter firing twice for a tuple
param destructure whose element is NOT returned -- fixed, and this shape is
unaffected by that fix (it read 2/2/2 both before and after, measured). The
returning callee is a separate ownership question: the element flows out through
the return value, so the callee's fire and the caller's fire both claim it. The
existing `fn_returns_param` passthrough guard in `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`
covers a param returned WHOLE, not an element destructured out of it and then
returned -- that gap is the likely shape of the fix.

SOURCE NOTE: found by sweeping a 31-shape destructure matrix across all three
backends while fixing B-2026-08-27-48.

fix:
FIXED by 0f058f1.

CONFIRMED exactly as reported, on all three spellings and both directions:
`let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); q.0.id + q.1` built and printed 42, while
`let q = make(); q.0.id + q.1` and `make().0.id` both failed `karac build` on
the loud "cannot resolve field 'id' on this receiver" guard and both answered
under `--interp`.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT. `type_name_of_expr`'s `TupleIndex` arm resolves
the element's struct name from two sources -- a PLACE chain
(`place_chain_tuple_tes`, for `h.ps.0`) and the per-variable
`tuple_var_elem_type_names` registry -- and the let-binding site populates that
registry from exactly two sources of its own: a tuple ANNOTATION, or a tuple
LITERAL on the RHS. A tuple that came from a CALL matches none of the four,
which is why the boundary was the initializer of `q` and not the spelling of
the read. This is the same resolution surface as B-2026-08-27-49 and
B-2026-08-14-5, one node kind over.

THE FIX adds the callee's DECLARED return type as a third source, through one
new helper (`call_return_tuple_tes`, keyed exactly like its `Slice` and `Array`
siblings so a free fn, an associated fn and a method all resolve). It is
consumed in the two places the two failing spellings need:

  - the let-binding site, so `let q = make(); q.0.id` registers `q`'s element
    names the same way an annotation would. Recording at the BINDING rather
    than looking the callee up at the read site is what makes shadowing correct
    for free -- `shadow.rs` already snapshots and restores this registry, and a
    fixture where a call-bound `x` shadows an outer tuple local of a DIFFERENT
    struct proves the restore.
  - the `TupleIndex` arm, for an UNBOUND result (`make().0.id`), which has no
    binding to key on.

A declared return type is full-fidelity by construction, the same standard the
annotation source already meets, so this is a fourth source of the same quality
rather than an inference.

FAIL-CLOSED, WHICH IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART. B-2026-08-27-49 measured that the
naive version of its own fix traded a loud gap for a SILENT WRONG ANSWER, which
is strictly worse than the bug. The same trap is live here: a generic callee's
`-> (T, i64)` yields the bare parameter name, and had that been recorded, a
read of a field that some unrelated struct also declares would have resolved to
that struct's layout. Both new sources therefore accept an element only when it
names a type codegen has a layout for, and record `None` otherwise -- so a
generic callee keeps refusing loudly (measured: `fn firstof[T](x: T) -> (T,
i64)` still fails to build, filed as B-2026-08-28-28). The E2E fixture is built
to be able to fail rather than merely refuse: `Other` and `Tag` both declare an
`n`, at DIFFERENT indices, so a mis-resolution prints 99 or 42 instead of 7.

A SECOND DEFECT THE FIX EXPOSED, AND FIXED -- the same one B-2026-08-27-49 hit,
and for the same reason. Making the shape resolve made it compile for the first
time, which made its OWNERSHIP reachable for the first time, and nothing owned
it. Measured on the emitted IR: `println(make(1).0.name)` emitted NO drop at
all, against the sibling `println(plain(1).name)`'s `__freshtemp_fldobj` slot
plus `__karac_drop_struct_Person`; under LSan it lost the read field's buffer on
every read (3 bytes per `.name`, 6 per `.note`, additive when both are read).
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` -- the gate on
`track_freshtemp_field_access_object` -- asks what KIND of expression produced
the value, and a `TupleIndex` is a PROJECTION rather than a producer, so it
declined. A separate predicate at that one call site asks the same question one
hop down at the base, following the array-literal sibling B-2026-08-27-35 rather
than widening the shared predicate (a tuple-index place rooted at a BINDING is
emphatically not a fresh owned temp -- the binding owns it and already drops
it). `test_heap_field_read_on_a_fresh_tuple_temp_is_leak_free` gates it, and
gates the leak half specifically: with the resolution fix in and only this
predicate reverted, it loses 27 bytes in 6 allocations.

NOT COVERED, filed as B-2026-08-28-27. A fresh tuple temp's OTHER heap elements
-- the ones the projection does not name -- still leak, because this fix drops
the projected element and nothing owns the tuple. That is PRE-EXISTING and
independent: measured on unmodified main, where the shape compiles without any
struct field read at all, `println(twoheap(1).1)` over `-> (Person, String)`
loses 24 bytes in 6 allocations across two calls at -O0. Its own row rather
than a silent remainder here.

VERIFIED on all three backends (interp, JIT, AOT), which agree on all 13 rows of
the E2E matrix: the row's own three spellings, the shadowing fixture and its
restore, a second-field read, a NESTED read (`deep().0.inner.m`, where this arm
types the receiver of the second hop), and the method-call and
associated-function callee spellings. Heap-field, `shared struct` and enum
elements were checked separately and all build and agree. Both new tests were
proven RED against the unfixed compiler by stashing only `src/`.
title: A STRUCT FIELD READ THROUGH A TUPLE ELEMENT never lowers when the tuple came from a CALL: `let q = make(); q.0.id` (and `make().0.id`) fail `karac build` with "codegen: cannot resolve field 'id' on this receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen)", while the SAME read on a tuple LITERAL local (`let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); q.0.id`) builds and runs. `karac check` accepts both and the interpreter answers both. One more unhandled receiver shape on the surface B-2026-08-27-49 is open against
detail:
A FIELD READ THROUGH A TUPLE ELEMENT fails `karac build` when the tuple's value
came from a CALL, and succeeds when the identical read is done on a tuple literal
bound to a local. `karac check` accepts both; the interpreter answers both.

MEASURED, three spellings, no `Drop` impl anywhere (so this is unrelated to the
drop work it was found beside):

    struct R { id: i64 }
    fn make() -> (R, i64) { (R { id: 41 }, 1) }

    let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); q.0.id + q.1   ->  builds, prints 42      OK
    let q = make(); q.0.id + q.1              ->  BUILD FAILS, interp 42
    make().0.id                               ->  BUILD FAILS, interp 41

    error: codegen failed: codegen: cannot resolve field 'id' on this receiver
    (its type was not recorded for codegen); this is a compiler gap -- run with
    `--interp` (or `KARAC_RUN_JIT=0`) and please report it

So the boundary is where the TUPLE's value came from, not the receiver syntax:
`q.0.id` is spelled identically in the passing and failing lines, and only the
initializer of `q` differs. That points at the element type of a tuple local
never being recorded when the local is initialized from a call, rather than at a
missing receiver arm.

DESTRUCTURING the same returned tuple is a working control:

    let (a, b) = take((R { id: 41 }, 1)); a.id + b     ->  builds

SAME FAMILY AS B-2026-08-27-49, NOT THE SAME CASE. That row is the BLOCK-
expression receiver (`{ let x = make(); x }.n`) and states codegen's receiver walk
"has arms for identifier, index, call and method-call receivers"; this is a
TUPLE-INDEX receiver whose base is a call-initialized local, which those arms do
not cover. Both land on the same `cannot resolve field ... its type was not
recorded` guard, alongside B-2026-08-06-19 / B-2026-08-12-28 / B-2026-08-14-5 --
worth fixing as one resolution surface rather than one arm at a time, and worth
checking whether -49's fix already covers this before starting.

LOUD, NEVER SILENT: the build stops on codegen's own guard, and the workaround
(destructure, or bind the element first) is mechanical. Hence medium.

SOURCE NOTE: found by sweeping a 31-shape destructure matrix across all three
backends while fixing B-2026-08-27-48; it was initially mistaken for a defect
about REBUILDING a tuple from destructured elements, which a fresh-tuple control
refuted -- the rebuild is fine, the field read is not.

fix:
FIXED by c4d53de (the interpreter half; the codegen half the row recorded was
already gone by the time this was picked up — see below).

The let-destructure gate resolved the callee's owned params through
`owned_param_names_of_fn`, which searches `program.items`. A CLOSURE matches no
top-level `Item::Function`, so it contributed the EMPTY set by construction --
exactly as the row diagnosed. The gate could not fire inside a closure body, its
destructure leaves kept their Drop slots, and the element's body ran once from
the callee's slot and once from the caller's fresh-temp argument walk, which
fires for a closure call exactly as it does for a free fn.

The closure's `param_patterns` and `closure_env` are already destructured in
scope at the frame push, so the fix reads them there rather than looking the
callee up by name. A name lookup could never have worked: the callee value is
`Value::Function { name: "<closure>", .. }`, so the frame push was being handed
the literal string `<closure>` -- which is why the first attempt at this fix,
keyed on `self.env.get(fn_name)`, silently did nothing.

A closure's params are `Pattern`s carrying no recorded type, so `ref`/`mut ref`
cannot be filtered out the way the fn path filters them. Only plain `Binding`
patterns are collected, and the borrow-typed case is pinned by a measured
control instead of by a filter this shape cannot express.

MEASURED, body counts interp / jit / build, pre-fix -> post-fix:

    |p: (R, i64)| { let (r, n) = p; r.id + n }   2/1/1 -> 1/1/1   full parity
    |p: (R, R)|   { let (a, b) = p; a.id + b.id } 4/2/2 -> 2/2/2
  CONTROLS, unchanged:
    the same body as a FREE FN                   1/1/1
    |r: ref R| { r.id }                          1/1/1

THE ROW'S CODEGEN HALF WAS ALREADY FIXED when this was picked up, and the row is
stale on that point: it recorded `karac build` at ZERO for the tuple-param
shape, and AOT now runs ONE. Other destructure work landed between the filing
and this fix. So the "one row with two sides" framing turned out to be a
snapshot rather than a standing fact, and only the interpreter side needed
doing.

WHAT REMAINS ON THE COMPILED SIDE IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE, which the row did not
name and which this fix does not touch: a closure's by-value STRUCT param runs
ZERO bodies on both compiled backends while the interpreter runs one --

    |w: W| { let W { r, n } = w; r.id + n }      1 / 0 / 0   (post-fix)
    |r: R| { r.id }        (no destructure)      1 / 0 / 0

The TUPLE-param spelling is correct compiled, which is what localizes it to the
struct case rather than to closures generally. Filed as B-2026-08-28-38: it is
codegen declining to own a closure's by-value struct param, a different
mechanism from the gate repaired here.

Tests: `test_closure_param_destructure_user_drop_body_runs_once`
(tests/interpreter.rs, 4 rows), verified RED pre-fix on the exact double fire.
title: A tuple-param destructure inside a CLOSURE is wrong on BOTH backends and in OPPOSITE directions: `let f = |p: (R, i64)| { let (r, n) = p; r.id + n };` runs the user `Drop` body TWICE under `karac run --interp` and ZERO times under `karac build`, for one object. The free-fn spelling of the same body is correct (1/1/1) after B-2026-08-27-48, which is what makes the closure the variable
detail:
A TUPLE-PARAM DESTRUCTURE INSIDE A CLOSURE is wrong on both backends, in
opposite directions, for a single object.

REPRO:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    fn main() {
        let f = |p: (R, i64)| { let (r, n) = p; r.id + n };
        println(f"{f((R { id: 41 }, 1))}");
        println("end");
    }

    karac run --interp   ->   drop 41 / drop 41 / 42 / end    <-- TWICE
    karac build  (AOT)   ->   42 / end                        <-- ZERO

CONTROL, and it is what isolates the closure: the identical body as a FREE FN
is correct on all three backends (1 / 1 / 1) as of B-2026-08-27-48's fix.

    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { let (r, n) = p; r.id + n }

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-27-48'S FIX, and not fixed by it either. That fix routes
through `owned_param_names_of_fn`, which resolves a name against
`program.items`; a closure matches no top-level `Item::Function`, so it
contributes the EMPTY set by construction (documented at
`owned_param_names_stack`: "a closure ... contributes an empty set, so the gate
never fires inside closures"). The gate's final predicate is therefore false for
a closure frame both before and after the change -- the interpreter's two fires
are the pre-fix behaviour, preserved.

WHY IT NEEDS BOTH HALVES FIXED. Teaching the interpreter's destructure gate about
closure params would take the interpreter from 2 to 1 and still not reach parity,
because the compiled backends are at 0 -- codegen appears not to treat a closure's
by-value param as a param for drop purposes at all. So this is one row with two
sides, not an extension of the free-fn gate.

RELATED: B-2026-08-27-48 (interpreter double fire, free-fn and method tuple
params -- fixed) and its sibling filed the same day for compiled backends running
NO body for a tuple destructured from a non-param source. The zero-fire half here
may share a root with that one; the two should be checked together, since both
are codegen declining to own a destructured tuple element.

SOURCE NOTE: found probing recursion / nesting / closure frames for regressions
from B-2026-08-27-48's frame-isolation change. Recursion and nested calls came
back clean (4 and 2 bodies, matching AOT); the closure did not.

title: A READ-ONLY `ref` CONTAINER PARAM OF A GENERIC CALLEE, GIVEN A STRUCT-FIELD ARGUMENT, DOUBLE-FREES the field's buffer: the mono argument path computes an in-place place pointer only when the param is `mut ref`, so `vlen(self.xs)` against `v: ref Vec[T]` aborts with glibc `free(): double free detected` on both compiled backends while the interpreter is correct. The MONO half of B-2026-07-12-1, which fixed exactly this for the non-generic call path

A `Slice[T]` PARAM GIVEN A STRUCT-FIELD `Vec` ARGUMENT from a generic-impl method fails MODULE VERIFICATION: the Vec-to-Slice coercion declines on a field access, so a 3-word `{ptr,len,cap}` is passed to a 2-word `{ptr,i64}` formal. Loud, not silent -- the third name-keyed blind spot in the family of B-2026-08-27-50
fix:
FIXED by 6bbb01a. `coerce_to_slice`'s place arm now resolves the Vec
header through a BORROWED root: `place_vec_header_ptr` falls back to a new
`borrowed_place_chain_ptr` (`src/codegen/expr_ops.rs`) that loads the pointer
out of a `ref`/`mut ref` slot and GEPs each field hop, so the callee receives a
real `{ptr,i64}` slice header over the caller's buffer.

THE ROW'S CAUSE IS RIGHT; ITS SCOPE IS NOT. The row names a "generic-impl
method" and reads as a monomorphization problem. Genericity is not the axis, and
four controls settle it -- the failing set is exactly the BORROWED bases:

    head(a.xs)            owned local                     builds  (already did)
    go(b: Bag)            owned param, generic or not     builds  (already did)
    go(b: ref Bag)        ref param, NON-generic          FAILED
    go(b: ref Bag[T])     ref param, generic              FAILED
    go(b: mut ref Bag)    mut ref param                   FAILED
    impl Bag { go(ref self) }        NON-generic impl     FAILED
    impl[T] Bag[T] { go(ref self) }  generic impl         FAILED  <- the row

A plain `impl` and a plain `ref` param fail identically to the generic ones, and
an OWNED param of the same struct builds. So the row's repro is one member of a
larger family, and a fix aimed at monomorphization would have missed most of it.

WHY IT DECLINED, measured rather than inferred. Instrumenting the two halves of
`place_vec_header_ptr` on all four failing shapes gives the same answer every
time: `arg_is_vec_header_place` = TRUE (the type test passes -- it is pure
resolution and reads the field type fine through a borrow), and
`field_chain_place_ptr` = None. That bail is deliberate and correct for its
OTHER callers -- they suppress move-outs, and writing through a borrow the
callee does not own is what corrupted neighbouring locals in B-2026-07-21-5/-6 --
and its doc already names the way out for a caller that needs a real place
through a borrow: load the slot explicitly, as `mem_place_ptr_and_value`'s
ref-param arm does. This is that caller. Building a slice header READS two words
and writes nothing, so the hazard the bail exists for cannot arise here.
`field_chain_place_ptr` is therefore left exactly as it was; the new path is
consulted only after it declines.

RECURSIVE, because one hop would have been an arbitrary stopping point: the
owned root already walks `o.inner.xs` through `field_chain_place_ptr`, so
stopping at a single hop would leave the borrowed spelling of a shape that
already builds still failing verification. Measured both ways -- two-hop chain
with an owned root built before this fix and still does; with a borrowed root it
failed and now builds. Field hops only; an `Index` hop is excluded for the same
purity reason `field_chain_place_ptr` gates its own `Index` arm on, and no
measurement backs answering that question here.

VERIFIED across 15 shapes on all three backends (interp / LLJIT / AOT), each its
own program: the seven borrowed spellings above, plus the owned controls, plus
`mut Slice[i64]` writes through both `mut ref self` and a named `mut ref` param,
a `shared` receiver (the B-2026-08-06-4 arm, untouched and still working), a
`ref Slice[T]` formal (the borrow path that never reaches this coercion), a
two-field struct, and `.len()` on the coerced slice. All agree except one
pre-existing defect filed separately (below).

THE WRITE HALF IS LOAD-BEARING and is why the regression test mutates before it
reads: a header built over a COPY of the borrowed struct would compile and read
back correctly while silently dropping every write. `bump` adds 100 to element 0
through `mut ref self` and again through a named `mut ref` param; the printed
101 then 201, with element 1 still 2, is what proves the header points at the
caller's real buffer at the right offset.

NOT FIXED, filed separately as B-2026-08-28-NEW: moving a `Vec` OUT of a field of
a borrowed binding inside a GENERIC fn or impl (`let v = self.xs;`) double-frees
the buffer under both compiled backends -- `karac check` clean, interpreter
correct, JIT and AOT abort with SIGABRT. Found in the same sweep; the
non-generic spelling is correct, which is the control that isolates it, and it
involves no `Slice` and no coercion, so it is not this row.

Regression tests: `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`e2e_slice_param_from_a_borrowed_field_place` (generic impl receiver, generic
`ref` param, both element types, two-hop chain) and
`e2e_mut_slice_param_from_a_borrowed_field_place` (the write leg), each with a
same-source same-string interpreter twin. Both fail on a pre-fix binary with
`Module verification failed`, measured.

Fixed in 45d2e1b. The row's diagnosis was right about the mechanism and wrong
about the extent: it named two sites and one symptom, and there were FIVE
lists and four symptoms, spanning BOTH backends.

ROOT CAUSE, one sentence: `bool` is an unsigned 1-bit integer, but every
codegen site that asks "compare and widen this as signed or unsigned?" carried
its OWN enumeration of the unsigned type names, and only one of the five had
`bool` in it.

An `i1` holds one bit, so "signed i1" is an interpretation, not a storage
difference: the set value reads as `-1`. That localizes the damage precisely --
only sites that COMPARE or WIDEN an `i1` can be wrong, which is why `==`,
`if b { }`, printing and storage were all correct throughout, and why the
class is enumerable rather than open-ended.

MEASURED on 7ff292e, interpreter vs all three compiled surfaces (jit / build /
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` build agreed with each other and disagreed with the
tree-walker in every case):

    false < true, <=, >, >=      true              -> false     (all four ops)
    Vec[bool].sort() / sorted()  false false true  -> true true false
    false.cmp(true)              Less              -> Greater
    true as i64 / as u8 / as i32 1 / 1 / 1         -> -1 / 255 / -1

The row had the first two. The `.cmp` and the CAST are new here, and the cast
is the one with the most realistic blast radius: `flag as i64` is an ordinary
thing to write and yields -1.

THE FIX IS ONE SHARED PREDICATE, NOT FOUR PATCHED LISTS. `helpers::
primitive_name_is_unsigned` is now the single answer, consulted by the lowered
binop dispatch (assoc_call.rs), both `Vec.sort` thunk lists and the comparator
family's `signed` flag (vec_method.rs), and the `expr_is_unsigned_int`
syntactic walk (expr_ops.rs). Patching each list in place would have fixed the
same four symptoms and left the shape that produced them intact; five copies of
one predicate is the defect, and the symptom is downstream of it.

The comparator family is the reason this reads as drift rather than as a design
decision: it is the ONE list that already had `bool`, so a bool ordered
correctly through a tuple, a nested `Vec` or a derived struct field and
inverted everywhere else. Its arm keeps its own name SET (which element types
get a comparator body at all -- a different question) and now derives only the
`signed` flag from the shared predicate, so folding them together changes no
behaviour.

`char` is folded in for uniformity and is NOT a live defect, and the argument
is a proof rather than a spot-check: `char` lowers to `i32`, and the ONLY way
to obtain one is a literal, a `String` walk, or `char.try_from` -- an
`i64 as char` cast is rejected outright with `E_INT_AS_CHAR` ("not every
integer is a valid Unicode scalar"), which is what forecloses a negative bit
pattern. So every `char` value is at most `0x10FFFF`, and signed and unsigned
agree on all of them. Confirmed empirically too: `'a' < 'b'` and
`Vec[char].sort()` were correct before this change and are correct after.

`.cmp` WAS A DIFFERENT DEFECT WEARING THE SAME SYMPTOM, and it is the half
worth reading. That site did not have a stale list; it had NO signedness input
at all -- `IntPredicate::SLT` / `SGT`, hardcoded -- while its `<` / `.lt`
sibling has carried operand signedness since B-2026-07-04-8. So it was wrong
for every unsigned integer whose value sets the top bit of its width, not only
for bool:

    (200u8).cmp(100u8)            Greater  -> Less
    (4000000000u32).cmp(1u32)     Greater  -> Less

Fixing bool's `.cmp` means giving that site a flag; once the flag exists these
are fixed by construction. There is no version of this fix that repairs bool
and leaves them, short of writing a bool special-case into a signedness
decision -- which is how the five lists happened.

THE INTERPRETER HAD THE SAME `.cmp` GAP, and it is the genuinely interesting
finding, because NO differential could have caught it. Codegen's `.cmp` was
signed and the tree-walker's `.cmp` called `value_compare` with no unsigned
hint, so BOTH BACKENDS AGREED ON THE WRONG ANSWER: `u64.MAX.cmp(1u64)` and
`(2^63 as usize).cmp(1)` answered `Less` on every surface. run-vs-build sees
nothing; the A/B rule sees nothing; only an oracle sees it. It surfaced here
only because fixing the compiled half made the twin fail -- i.e. correcting one
backend is what exposed the other, and had I stopped at codegen I would have
INTRODUCED a run-vs-build divergence while closing one.

The interpreter half now routes through `eval_binary` with the same
`span_unsigned_int_width` hint the `.lt` arm uses, rather than reimplementing
the comparison: `.cmp` and `<` share one implementation and cannot drift apart
again. Gated on a hint being present, so String, floats, signed ints and bool
keep `value_compare` untouched.

NOT ADDRESSED, deliberately: `emit_binary_search_cmp` (vec_method.rs) has a
sixth unsigned list, and it is the one place I did NOT route through the shared
predicate. It is not a live miscompile -- `bool` is absent from its SIGNED list
too, so `Vec[bool].binary_search(..)` errors at build rather than inverting --
and its `is_uint` doubles as the "which element types are supported" set, so
folding it in would silently WIDEN binary_search to bool and char. That is
B-2026-08-28-6's work (teaching binary_search the comparator family), not this
row's, and doing it here would have shipped an untested feature inside a
miscompile fix. Left with a comment naming the predicate and the reason.

VERIFIED. Three fixtures, each RED before the fix and each pinned to LITERAL
expected output rather than twinned against a backend -- twinning is exactly
what failed to catch the `.cmp` half, so a fix for it must not rely on the
mechanism it defeated. Per-half RED evidence, measured by reverting one
directory at a time:

  - reverting src/codegen/ alone: every row of the new E2E fixture wrong except
    equality and branching ("01 false false false false / 03 2 0 1 /
    04 true true false false / 05 0 / 06 0 / 07 0 / 08 -1 255 -1").
  - reverting src/interpreter/ alone: the tree-walk fixture gives "2 0 0 ..."
    where "2 2 2 ..." is correct -- the u64/usize rows.
  - the restored `bool` row in the sort table: "true true false" vs
    "false true true".

The `bool` row is back in `test_e2e_sort_element_gate_matches_codegen_support`
with the hold-out comment replaced by a note on why it was held out; that table
(added for B-2026-08-27-51) is what found this bug on its first run.

The tree-walk fixture also carries a SIGNED row (`(-5).cmp(1)` must stay
`Less`), because the failure mode of this fix is over-correction -- making
every integer unsigned would satisfy every other row in it.

GATES, all on the REBASED tree (main gained four commits under this fix, two of
them codegen, so the pre-rebase green did not carry): codegen 3348/0,
interpreter 1785/0, memory_sanitizer 1249/0 under LSan with
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` (so no soft-skip could report green
vacuously), par_codegen 270/0. Pre-rebase additionally: selfhost_codegen 1/0
and the default leg at 58 suites / 5154 passed / 0 failed. Both clippy legs
(`--all --all-targets`, with and without `--features llvm`) exit 0, and
`cargo fmt --all -- --check` is clean.

A NOTE ON THE GATE RUNS THEMSELVES, because two of them lied: the container
filled its disk twice mid-build, and BOTH times the shell reported exit code 0
while the suite had never compiled ("No space left on device", visible only in
the log body). A green that came from a build which did not run is worth
nothing, so both were discarded and re-run after clearing ~20 GB and rebuilding
with debug symbols off. Worth recording next to this repo's existing
stale-archive warnings: exit status is not evidence that a gate executed.

KATA A/B: all 23 katas using `.cmp` are byte-identical under `karac run
--interp` and `karac build`. The `Vec[bool]` sweep is NOT reported as evidence
-- it returned pass=0 fail=0 skip=52 because the snapshot binary it invoked was
deleted mid-run to free disk, which is a vacuous pass of exactly the shape
CLAUDE.md warns about, not a result.
title: EVERY `bool` COMPARISON INVERTS IN COMPILED CODE: `false < true` answers FALSE and `Vec[bool].sort()` sorts DESCENDING on jit/build/auto-par, while the interpreter is correct -- bool lowers as a SIGNED `i1`, so `true` is -1. SILENT wrong answer; the comparator family in the same file already treats bool as unsigned.
detail:
`false < true` answers TRUE in the interpreter and FALSE compiled, and
`Vec[bool].sort()` sorts DESCENDING compiled while the interpreter sorts
ascending. Silent wrong answers -- no diagnostic, no crash, no refusal.

MEASURED (b510b81, before B-2026-08-27-51's gate landed, so this predates it
and is unrelated to it):

    fn main() {
        let mut v: Vec[bool] = [true, false, true, false];
        v.sort();
        for e in v { println(f"{e}"); }
        println("--");
        println(f"{false < true}");
    }

    interp  false false true true  --  true      <- correct
    jit     true true false false  --  false     <- WRONG, both lines
    build   true true false false  --  false     <- WRONG, both lines
    nopar   true true false false  --  false     <- WRONG, both lines

So all three COMPILED surfaces agree with each other and disagree with the
tree-walker, which is why the usual run-vs-build differential over compiled
backends would not see it either.

SUSPECTED ROOT CAUSE -- one cause, two sites. `bool` lowers to LLVM `i1`, and
a signed `i1` has values 0 and -1, so `false`(0) `<` `true`(1 as signed i1 =
-1) is FALSE and the whole order inverts. Read in the source, not measured:

  1. `src/codegen/expr_ops.rs` (~6137) picks `IntPredicate::SLT` vs `ULT` from
     `is_unsigned`, which comes from `expr_is_unsigned_int` -- a predicate
     about unsigned INTEGER types, which a `bool` operand is not. Hence the
     signed compare.
  2. `src/codegen/vec_method.rs`, the `"sort"` arm: the unsigned-thunk list is
     `Some("u8"|"u16"|"u32"|"u64"|"u128"|"usize"|"uint")` -- `bool` is absent,
     so `emit_default_sort_thunk` is asked for a SIGNED comparator.

Note the near miss that makes this a drift bug rather than an oversight: the
COMPARATOR FAMILY in the same file already gets it right --
`emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr` maps `"u8" | ... | "bool" | "char"` to
`IntScalar { signed: false }`. So bool is correctly unsigned on the path that
`Vec[Vec[bool]].sort()` and tuple elements take, and incorrectly signed on the
direct scalar path. Two lists, one of them stale.

`char` is in the comparator family's unsigned list and likewise absent from
the sort arm's, but is BENIGN in practice: every valid code point is below
2^31, so signed and unsigned `i32` compares agree. Worth fixing for uniformity
while in there, not a live defect.

HARM. Any `bool` comparison in compiled code is inverted: `a < b`, `a > b`,
sorting, and anything that folds through them. The realistic shape is
partitioning or ranking on a boolean key -- `flags.sort()` to group false
before true, or a `sort_by` whose comparator compares two bool fields --
where the output is silently reversed and nothing reports it. `Vec[bool]` is
uncommon; a bool comparison inside a larger comparator is less so.

FIX SHAPE. Make both sites treat `bool` as unsigned, matching the comparator
family that already does. Then add the `bool` row back to
`test_e2e_sort_element_gate_matches_codegen_support` in tests/codegen.rs --
it is currently held out with a comment naming this id, precisely so the
table does not assert the bug -- and add a `false < true` E2E row, since the
comparison half is not covered by the sort table at all.

SOURCE NOTE: found by the anti-drift differential table added for
B-2026-08-27-51, on its first run. That table exists to compare the sort
gate against codegen's comparator support; it caught a miscompile in a
supported element type instead, which is a different and higher-severity
class than the loud run-vs-build gap it was written for.

fix:
Fixed in 09913ea, by the direction this row named: teach `binary_search` the
comparator family rather than narrow the check to its current support. The
row was right that narrowing would be the wrong direction -- it would reject
`Vec[P]` programs the interpreter runs correctly and `sort` already handles.

WHAT THE ROW HAD, AND WHAT IT MISSED. It recorded a LOUD element-coverage gap
in codegen. There were in fact THREE defects, and the third is silent and lives
in BOTH backends.

1. ELEMENT COVERAGE (the row). Measured on 5ed5f6c, every one check-green and
   correct under `--interp`:

       Vec[bool]           build refused
       Vec[char]           build refused
       Vec[(i64, String)]  build refused
       Vec[Vec[String]]    build refused
       Vec[P]              build refused   (#[derive(Ord)] struct)
       Vec[Suit]           build refused   (#[derive(Ord)] enum)
       Vec[F64]            build refused

   `bool` and `char` are NEW here -- the row listed tuples, nested Vec, Array,
   derived structs/enums and F64, but not those two. They are exactly what
   B-2026-08-28-5 predicted in the comment it left on this function: that row
   deliberately did not fold the shared unsigned predicate into `is_uint`
   because doing so would widen support as a side effect of a signedness fix.
   This row is where that widening belongs, so the predicate is folded in now
   and the comment is replaced by the widening it was deferring.

2. TWO EXITS, NOT ONE -- the row noticed this and it turned out to matter. The
   tuple failed EARLIER than the rest, at `vec_elem_type_name`, with "could not
   resolve the element type": a tuple has no plain named type, so it never
   reached the supported-type dispatch at all. Resolving the element TYPE EXPR
   (what the comparator family keys on) instead of the NAME (which only selects
   the two inline fast paths) closes that exit; the name is now allowed to be
   empty. Both the Vec and the Slice receiver paths had the same shape.

3. `binary_search` DID NOT ORDER LIKE `sort`, AND NOTHING COULD SEE IT. Not in
   the row, found while checking whether the inline integer path could stay.
   It widened to i64 and compared SIGNED -- correct for u8..u32, which
   zero-extend into the positive half, and wrong for u64/usize/u128, where the
   widening is a no-op and the top of the range rides as a negative i64. The
   old doc comment asserted the opposite ("uint values are non-negative i64").

   The result is a SILENT wrong answer on a Vec that `sort` ITSELF produced:

       let b: Vec[u64] = [1u64, 2u64, 18446744073709551615u64];
       b.is_sorted()                  -> true    (sort's order, unsigned)
       b.binary_search(2u64)          -> None    <- present at index 1
       b.binary_search(u64.MAX)       -> None    <- present at index 2

   So three methods on one Vec disagreed about its order. And the INTERPRETER's
   `binary_search` had the identical gap -- its `sort` has used
   `value_compare_u64` since B-2026-07-04-8 while its `binary_search` arm still
   called the signed `value_compare` -- so BOTH BACKENDS RETURNED THE SAME
   WRONG `None`. No run-vs-build differential, and no A/B kata check, could
   have caught it. This is the second time in two rows that fixing one backend
   is what exposed the other; it is worth treating as the standing lesson
   rather than a coincidence.

THE FIX. Codegen's `emit_binary_search_cmp` keeps its two inline fast paths
(integer, String) and its `else` now calls the comparator family --
`emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr`, the same `karac_cmp_<T>` functions `Vec.sort()`
lowers to. Operands spill to entry allocas because those take pointers, and
the family already returns the -1/0/+1 i64 this function is contracted to
produce, so the bisection loop is untouched. The integer path's compare now
takes its predicate from the element's own signedness.

Sharing the family rather than extending the inline compare is the point: a
second hand-rolled ordering is what let the two methods drift apart, and
extending it would have meant re-deriving lexicographic tuple order,
nested-Vec order and declaration-order struct comparison -- all of which
already exist there, and all of which the interpreter's `value_compare`
already agrees with.

The interpreter half takes the unsigned dispatch its own `sort` arm uses. Note
the spelling differs from `sort`'s and the difference is load-bearing: `sort()`
is typed `Unit`, so it reads the element type off the non-aliased close-paren
leaf, but `binary_search` returns `Option[i64]`, which the close paren carries
and which peels to nothing. Copying `sort`'s spelling verbatim left the arm
signed and the reproducer unchanged -- measured, not reasoned -- so it reads
the RECEIVER span first and falls back to the close paren.

WHAT IS STILL REFUSED, and now for the same reason as `sort`: the `else` is
reached only when the comparator family itself declines the element type, so
the two methods fail together rather than at different boundaries. Its message
no longer claims "Integer and String element types are supported", which
stopped being true.

VERIFIED. Both halves RED independently, by reverting one directory at a time:

  - reverting src/codegen/ alone: the element table fails on the `char` row
    ("not yet supported under `karac build`"), and the signedness fixture gives
    "02 true absent / 03 absent" where "02 true 1 / 03 2" is correct.
  - reverting src/interpreter/ alone: the tree-walk fixture gives
    "true absent absent 1 0" against "true 1 2 1 0".

The element-coverage half is pinned by EXTENDING B-2026-08-27-51's anti-drift
table rather than by a new one: every row now runs `sort` AND `binary_search`,
so the assertion is the row's own title -- binary_search accepts every element
type sort does. Widen or narrow either method alone and a row fails. The
signedness half is pinned to LITERAL expected output in both backends, because
a twin against the interpreter would have certified the shared wrong answer,
which is exactly how it survived. Both fixtures carry a SIGNED row as the
over-correction guard, and the E2E additionally pins the duplicate-key index
(std's branchless variant picks a specific index among equal keys), which the
fix had to preserve while swapping the comparator underneath -- confirmed for
the integer, String and tuple paths.

Also verified across all four surfaces (`--interp`, JIT, `build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`): F64, a Slice receiver with a tuple element, absent
elements, and an empty receiver.

GATES, on the REBASED tree (main gained a codegen commit under this fix):
codegen 3351/0, interpreter 1786/0, memory_sanitizer 1251/0 under LSan with
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, par_codegen 270/0. Pre-rebase additionally:
selfhost_codegen 1/0 and the default leg at 70 suites / 7177 passed / 0 failed.
Both clippy legs (`--all --all-targets`, with and without `--features llvm`)
exit 0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.

KATA SWEEP: 35 katas using `Vec[bool]` or `binary_search` are byte-identical
under `karac run --interp` and `karac build`; 0 divergences. A further 19 are
`differential.kara` harnesses that exceed a 90s timeout by design, not
failures.

A METHODOLOGY NOTE THAT COST REAL TIME, worth leaving for the next session.
An earlier version of that sweep reported EIGHT divergences, all of them
false. It had been running concurrently with a `cargo` rebuild of `karac`, and
a momentarily NON-LLVM `karac build` exits 0 while emitting no binary -- so the
script's `build && run` succeeded, the missing binary produced a shell error
into the "compiled output" file, and that got diffed against real interpreter
output and scored as a wrong answer. All eight are byte-identical when
re-checked against a stable binary. Two lessons: never run a kata A/B against
`target/debug/karac` while any cargo command may rewrite it (copy the binary
first), and have the harness distinguish NO-BINARY from DIVERGE, because
otherwise a build that produced nothing is indistinguishable from a
miscompile.
title: `Vec.binary_search` ACCEPTS EVERY ELEMENT TYPE `sort` DOES BUT LOWERS ONLY INTEGER AND String -- tuples, nested Vec, Array, derived-Ord structs/enums and `F64` are check-green, work under `--interp`, and refuse to build. It inherited B-2026-08-27-51's gate but its own support is narrower still.
detail:
`Vec[(i64, String)].binary_search(needle)` is check-green, works under
`karac run --interp`, and is refused by `karac build`. Its own error says so
in as many words:

    codegen failed: `Vec.binary_search` on element type `<T>` is not yet
    supported under `karac build` (codegen); it works under
    `karac run --interp`. Integer and String element types are supported.

WHY IT SURVIVED B-2026-08-27-51. That row gave `sort` / `sorted` /
`is_sorted` an element gate keyed on what codegen's comparator family
(`emit_cmp_fn_for_type_expr`) lowers, wired into `require_ord_element`.
`binary_search` shares that call site, so it INHERITED the new gate and no
longer accepts `Option[i64]`, an underived struct, or a shared struct.

But binary_search's codegen support is narrower STILL: it does not route
through the comparator family at all -- it has a hand-rolled integer/String
comparison and an `else` that errors. So every element type between the two
levels stays split: tuples, nested `Vec`, `Array`, derived-`Ord` structs and
enums, and the `F64` wrapper all sort fine and cannot be binary-searched.

MEASURED after 12b88f9 (all three: `karac check` clean, `--interp` prints
`true`, `karac build` refuses):

    Vec[(i64, String)]   codegen failed: Vec.binary_search: could not resolve
                         the element type
    Vec[Vec[String]]     codegen failed: `Vec.binary_search` on element type
                         `Vec` is not yet supported under `karac build`
                         (codegen); it works under `karac run --interp`.
                         Integer and String element types are supported.
    Vec[P]               same message, element type `P`
                         (P is a `#[derive(Ord)] struct P { a: i64 }`)

The tuple lands on a different message than the other two -- it fails earlier,
at element-type resolution, rather than at the supported-type `else`. Same
split, and worth knowing there are two exits to close rather than one.

NOT FIXED WITH -51 deliberately: closing this means teaching binary_search the
comparator family (emit a `karac_cmp_<T>` call in place of the hand-rolled
compare), not moving a gate. Narrowing the check to binary_search's current
support instead would be the wrong direction -- it would reject `Vec[P]`
programs that the interpreter runs correctly and that `sort` already handles,
trading a loud build error for a compile error on working code.

LOUD, NOT SILENT -- and the message already names the workaround surface --
so medium, not high.

SOURCE NOTE: identified while closing B-2026-08-27-51, when checking whether
the new gate reached every method sharing its call site. It reached
binary_search but did not close it, and the residual is recorded here rather
than left implicit in that row's fix prose.

title: TWO MORE RECEIVER SHAPES the block-receiver fix does not reach, both still `karac check`-clean and interpreter-correct but failing `karac build` with codegen's "cannot resolve field ... on this receiver" guard: (1) a `shared struct` block receiver (`{ let n = make(); n }.v`), whose type is consulted through `shared_type_for_expr` BEFORE the block is compiled, so the block-tail recording B-2026-08-27-49 added cannot be there yet; and (2) an `if`-expression receiver (`if c { make(1) } else { make(2) }.n`), a different node kind with no arm at all. Same resolution surface as B-2026-08-27-49 / -08-06-19 / -08-12-28 / -08-14-5.
detail:
Two receiver shapes measured while fixing B-2026-08-27-49, both left OPEN there
on purpose rather than folded in: each fails through a DIFFERENT mechanism from
the one that fix addresses, so neither is a remainder of it.

LEG 1 — a `shared struct` block receiver.

    shared struct Node { v: i64 }
    fn make() -> Node { return Node { v: 11 }; }
    fn main() { println({ let n = make(); n }.v); }

    check: All checks passed.   interp: 11
    build: error: codegen failed: codegen: cannot resolve field 'v' on this
           receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen); this is a compiler
           gap - run with `--interp` (or `KARAC_RUN_JIT=0`) and please report it

The NON-shared spelling of exactly this program builds and runs since
B-2026-08-27-49. The difference is WHICH call site asks for the receiver's type.
A plain struct receiver is typed by `field_index_for` -> `type_name_of_expr`,
which runs AFTER `compile_expr(object)` has compiled the block, so the tail-type
recording is in place by then. A shared receiver is typed by
`shared_type_for_expr` (src/codegen/types_lowering.rs:3182), consulted BEFORE
