`compile_expr` because the shared path needs to know it is emitting a GEP
through an RC pointer rather than extracting from a struct value. At that point
the block has not been compiled, so nothing is recorded and no amount of
recording could be: the ordering, not the table, is the obstacle. Having
declined, the shared branch falls to the generic tail, where `compile_expr`
yields a POINTER and the `StructValue` guard misses -> the loud guard.

Fixing it means either resolving a block's type STATICALLY (which must not
resolve the tail against the enclosing scope - see B-2026-08-27-49's measured
99-instead-of-7 miscompile, where an outer binding of the same name shadows the
block-local), or restructuring `compile_field_access` to compile a block
receiver ONCE up front and dispatch on the resulting value. The latter is the
cleaner shape but duplicates a subset of a ~600-line function that also handles
weak fields, FFI unions, niche Options and `ref` fields; a block receiver could
legitimately need any of them, so a partial duplicate would diverge. Deferred
deliberately rather than rushed.

LEG 2 — an `if`-expression receiver.

    struct Tag { n: i64 }
    fn make(k: i64) -> Tag { return Tag { n: k }; }
    fn main() { let c = true; println(if c { make(1) } else { make(2) }.n); }

    check: All checks passed.   interp: 1
    build: same "cannot resolve field 'n'" error

`ExprKind::If` is a different node kind from `ExprKind::Block` and
`type_name_of_expr` has never had an arm for it. Its branches ARE blocks, so the
B-2026-08-27-49 recording already covers them and an `If` arm delegating to the
then-branch's recorded entry is likely most of the fix - but it would need the
matching ownership work (`value_block_hands_out_its_tail` widened to `If`, or
the temp aggregate's heap fields leak exactly as the block receiver's did before
that fix, LSan exit 23) plus its own leak gate, and a `match`-expression
receiver is the obvious next sibling after it. That is a shape's worth of work,
not a line, which is why it is a row.

BOTH LOUD, NEVER SILENT - every failure is codegen's own "please report it"
guard, the one that exists so this class cannot reach the `i64 0` placeholder
B-2026-07-20-9 removed. Hence medium: the build stops and the workaround (bind
the receiver to a local first) is mechanical and already the spelling most
programs use.

SOURCE NOTE: measured on the post-B-2026-08-27-49 compiler; leg 2 is
independent of that fix and reproduces before it as well.
fix:
FIXED by dac56eb. Both legs, by different means, because they fail for
different reasons.

LEG 2 (`if` / `if let` receiver) was the small one. `compile_if` already routes
BOTH branches through `compile_block_with_frame`, so B-2026-08-27-49's tail-type
recording covers them already and the `if` only has to read the THEN branch's
entry — the typechecker has made the branches agree, so one answers for both. An
`if let` needed one extra line: its then-arm hand-rolls its frame against a plain
`compile_block` (an asymmetry `control_flow.rs` already documents at
B-2026-08-27-34) and so never reaches that recording site, so it records its own,
with the arm's pattern bindings still live for the same reason the block sibling
records before its revert.

Ownership had to move with it: `value_block_hands_out_its_tail` now admits an
`if`/`if let` with both arms present. Whichever branch runs, its tail's cleanup
was neutralized, so the consumer owns the aggregate — and without registering the
drop its heap fields leak, exactly as the block receiver's did. Gated by
`test_if_expression_receiver_heap_field_read_is_leak_free`.

LEG 1 (`shared struct` block receiver) is the interesting one, and it is NOT a
missing arm. Every shared field path gates on knowing the receiver's type BEFORE
`compile_expr` runs, because it has to decide it is emitting a GEP through an RC
pointer rather than extracting from an aggregate. A block cannot answer then: its
type is its tail's, and the tail is typed in the block's own scope, which is
recorded only as the block compiles. So the ordering, not the table, was the
obstacle — no amount of recording reaches a gate that runs first.

The fix adds one branch in the generic tail, where `compile_expr(object)` has
already run and therefore already recorded: if the compiled receiver is a
POINTER and its (now nameable) type is a shared struct, GEP the field. It sits
after every other path has declined and immediately before the loud "please
report it" error, so it can only turn a failing build into a working one and can
never reroute a receiver an earlier branch claimed.

Ownership reuses the CALL-result receiver's path rather than restating it: the
bug-#8 branch's body is extracted as `load_owned_shared_temp_field` and shared.
Both are fresh temporaries holding one ref nothing else will free, so their
`Option[shared]` compensation and their final release have to stay identical, and
now cannot drift. Gated by
`test_shared_block_receiver_scalar_field_read_is_refcount_balanced`, which pins
balance in both directions — one dec too few leaks the box, one too many frees it
under the live bound alias in the same program.

A PHASE-D LAYOUT HAZARD found while doing that, and closed. The extracted body
hard-coded the headered layout (`heap_type`, field base 1). `shared_gep_layout`'s
doc lists `sh_call_` as a deliberate exception to the "every member-field GEP
routes through one place" invariant, on the grounds that a call-returned type can
never be headerless — the purity gate excludes any type a declared fn signature
mentions. That argument is sound for a CALL and says nothing about the new
caller, whose tail can be a cluster-member literal built in the very function
that owns the cluster; a headered GEP on a headerless object reads at the wrong
offset, silently. The helper now routes through `shared_gep_layout`, which is
byte-identical wherever the old premise held and correct where it does not, and
the invariant's doc is updated so the exception list shrinks to `sh_idx_` rather
than growing on trust.

SCOPED OUT, DELIBERATELY: a `String`/`Vec` field on a shared TEMPORARY receiver.
Making leg 1 accept it produced a heap-use-after-free — `exprs.rs`'s
`clone_shared_struct_heap_field_read` deep-copies the field AFTER
`compile_field_access` returns, i.e. after this branch released the temp's last
ref and its recursive drop freed the buffer. That is not this row's bug: the
CALL spelling `make().tag` LEAKS the same buffer on a compiler with none of this
(5 bytes, LSan, measured on the stashed tree), so the clone/release protocol for
a shared temporary receiver is already broken. The branch therefore DECLINES a
field the cloner would want to copy, leaving the honest loud gap instead of
trading it for a memory error, and the protocol bug is filed as
B-2026-08-28-14. The bound spelling (`let b = make(); b.tag`) is clean and
stays clean — it is in the leg-1 ASAN fixture for exactly that reason.

VERIFIED: both legs across interp / JIT / AOT on every shape measured — plain
`if`, `if`-with-the-else-branch-taken, else-if chain, `if let`, nested field,
method call on the receiver, `let`-consumer, arithmetic consumer, and for leg 1
the scalar shared block receiver, a shared `if` receiver, a second shared struct,
and the pre-existing bound receiver alongside. All four new tests proven RED
against the unfixed compiler by stashing only `src/`.

FIXED by 919f31e.

Fixed in TWO parts, and the measurement that separates them is the useful part of
this row: the walker arm the title asks for fixes NOTHING on its own.

The row's diagnosis of the symptom was exact -- `finish_place_source_tuple_destructure`'s
per-leaf loop opened with `let PatternKind::Binding(name) = &pat.kind else { continue; };`
and a nested `((r, m), n)` has `PatternKind::Tuple` at index 0, so the inner leaf
was never reached. It was also right that the arm alone is not enough, and named
both missing pieces correctly: the nested leaf needs its own element `TypeExpr`
and a cap-zero of the source at a NESTED index.

What the row did not have is which of those is load-bearing. Measured by
stashing each half independently, on this HEAD, all three surfaces:

    walker recursion only   -> nested-from-local 0 bodies, enum-from-local 0   (fixes nothing)
    registry lookup only    -> nested-from-local 0 bodies, enum-from-local 1   (fixes B-2026-08-28-9 only)
    both                    -> nested-from-local 1 body,   enum-from-local 1   (both fixed)

The recursion is unreachable without the type fix, because the element type of a
tuple LOCAL was resolved through `tuple_var_elem_tes` (call_dispatch.rs), whose
only non-annotation source is `tuple_var_elem_type_names` -- a
`Vec<Option<String>>`. A name cannot spell `(R, i64)` at all, so `((R, i64), i64)`
came back as a single EMPTY path and the new arm's `TypeKind::Tuple` test could
never fire. That is the same erasure B-2026-08-28-9 reports from the other side
(an enum constructor has no recorded name either), which is why one change closes
both rows.

THE READER, NOT THE RECORDER. The row expected the fix to live "wherever a tuple
local's element `TypeExpr`s are recorded". They were already recorded correctly:
the let-site stores exact element TEs in `var_types.tuple_var_elem_tes` via
`tuple_binding_elem_tes` -> `refined_tuple_literal_elem_te`, which has a nested-
tuple arm and falls back to `infer_arg_elem_te` for an enum constructor. The gap
was in the LOOKUP: `tuple_var_elem_tes()` checked the annotation table, then went
straight to the lossy names synthesis without ever consulting that record.

The function carried a comment describing precisely the missing lookup --
"the let-site's own record (`tuple_binding_elem_tes` ...) beats the names-derived
synthesis below, which renders an `Option[Res]` element as an EMPTY path" --
sitting directly on top of the names fallback with no code between them. This
checkout is shallow (237 commits, earliest 9aa0fd3, itself a file split), so
whether the code was dropped in a refactor or never landed cannot be determined
from here.

AND THE COMMENT IS NOT THE WHOLE STORY -- "beats" is WRONG AS WRITTEN, which
this fix's first cut had to learn the expensive way. Implementing it literally
(prefer the record wholesale) leaked 2 bytes in
`asan_tuple_index_assignment_heap_elems_freed` and broke `example_corpus`. That
regression is already documented, at the OTHER end of the same relationship:
`suppress_tuple_index_move_source` applies the record only to the degenerate
case and says why -- "the names-derived spelling is left alone everywhere else,
because it is the one the Vec/String arms were tuned against (an f-string
element's inferred TE spells `str`, and preferring it wholesale regressed
`asan_tuple_index_assignment_heap_elems_freed`)". So a previous session ran this
same experiment, hit this same test, and left the finding one call site away
from the comment that invites the mistake.

The two registries are NOT ordered by accuracy, which is what makes "beats"
wrong. Instrumented on the regressing program, `let mut t = (f"a{1}", 2)` gives:

    names-derived   Path { segments: [] }     -- zero segments
    recorded        Path { segments: [""] }   -- one segment, the empty string

Neither names anything. They merely fail DIFFERENTLY, and arms downstream branch
on `segments.last()`, which is `None` for one and `Some("")` for the other.

So the rule landed here is a PER-ELEMENT MERGE, not a preference: an element
keeps its names spelling wherever that spelling says anything at all, and takes
the record only where the names spelling is degenerate (an absent name, i.e. an
empty path). That is exactly the narrow rule `suppress_tuple_index_move_source`
already applied locally, lifted into the shared function so every reader of
`place_chain_tuple_tes` gets it instead of one site. It buys precisely the two
shapes a NAME cannot express -- a nested tuple and an enum constructor -- and
moves nothing else, which is why the Vec/String arms tuned against the names
spelling stay put. `tuple_elem_te_is_informative` is the predicate; it rejects
both the empty segment list and the single empty segment, since `infer_arg_elem_te`
produces the latter when every inference it tries declines.

NO WIDENING OF `zero_tuple_elem_cap_at` WAS NEEDED, against the row's expectation
that this was the measured change gating the fix. That function already has a
`TypeKind::Tuple` arm and is parameterised on (base_ptr, tuple_ty, idx), so
GEP'ing to the nested element and calling it one level down cap-zeroes at a
nested index with the function untouched. Its documented narrowness (#21:
"Vec/String/i64 leaves keep the proven source-owns model untouched") is therefore
still intact -- no leaf kind changed hands.

The cap-zero half is load-bearing even though the pre-fix count was 0, and a
control now pins it: `let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1);` with NO destructure runs
the body on all four surfaces (measured), so the source's own walk does reach a
nested leaf. Registering the leaf's body without also cap-zeroing the source
would therefore print it TWICE -- the exact regression the tuple-param control in
this test exists to catch. The leaf takes the body only by taking the memory.

Fixtures: `e2e_user_drop_body_runs_for_a_let_destructure_leaf` gains
`nested-from-local` (the repro), `nested-from-literal` (the fresh-path sibling
that was already correct), `nested-no-destructure-control` (the cap-zero guard
above) and `enum-leaf-from-local` (B-2026-08-28-9's repro). RED-verified: with
both source hunks stashed the test fails at `nested-from-local`.

A SEPARATE SHAPE FOUND AND NOT FIXED HERE, filed as its own row: a tuple-typed
BINDING leaf -- `let (inner, n) = p;` where `p: ((R, i64), i64)`, so `inner`
binds the whole nested tuple rather than destructuring it -- still prints the
body under `--interp` and nothing compiled, after this fix. It reaches the same
walker but exits at the `TypeKind::Path` test rather than the pattern test, and
closing it needs the tuple element-bodies channel
(`emit_tuple_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn`), not the enum/nested-struct channel this
walker registers through -- a different mechanism, so a different row.
title: A NESTED TUPLE PATTERN never runs its inner leaf's user `Drop` body when the source is a tuple LOCAL: `let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1); let ((r, m), n) = p;` prints `drop 41` under `karac run --interp` and NOTHING under `karac run` / `karac build`. The place-source destructure walker visits only `PatternKind::Binding` leaves and `continue`s past a nested `Tuple` pattern outright, so the inner leaf is never reached. The SAME shape from a CALL or a tuple LITERAL is correct -- B-2026-08-28-1's fresh path already recurses through nested patterns
detail:
Measured on `383a723` (B-2026-08-28-1's fix in place), drop-body counts
interp / jit / build:

    let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1); let ((r, m), n) = p;   -> 1 / 0 / 0   <- this row
    fn make() -> ((R, i64), i64) { ... }  let ((r,m),n) = make();
                                                          -> 1 / 1 / 1   <- correct
    let ((r, m), n) = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1);             -> 1 / 1 / 1   <- correct

So the defect is the SOURCE, not the nesting: a tuple LOCAL routes through
`finish_place_source_tuple_destructure` (stmts.rs), whose per-leaf loop reads

    let PatternKind::Binding(name) = &pat.kind else { continue; };

and a nested `((r, m), n)` has `PatternKind::Tuple` at index 0. The fresh path
(`track_tuple_destructure_leaf_cleanups`) has a `PatternKind::Tuple(inner)` arm
that recurses, which is why the call and literal sources are right.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED WITH B-2026-08-28-1. Recursing the PLACE path needs more
than the pattern arm: each nested leaf also needs its own element `TypeExpr` and
a nested `zero_tuple_elem_cap_at` to cap-zero the source at a nested index. That
function's narrowness is deliberate and documented as double-free motivated (#21:
"Vec/String/i64 leaves keep the proven source-owns model untouched"), so widening
it is a measured change in its own right rather than a rider on a body-registration
fix.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-1's shape matrix past the two sources
its row named, not by a targeted probe.

fix:
FIXED by 919f31e.

Fixed together with B-2026-08-28-8 by one change, in the place the row pointed at
but on the other side of it.

The row's instrumentation was right and reproduced exactly: the per-leaf
`TypeExpr` for an enum element arrives with EMPTY path segments, so
`p.segments.last()` is `None` and the leaf `continue`s before the `is_enum` /
`enum_layouts` lookup can run. Its caveat was worth having too -- the sibling
`i64` element prints `path []` as well, so an empty segment list is only
load-bearing for a leaf that needs a NAME to be classified.

WHERE THE ROW WAS WRONG: it called this "an upstream RECORDING gap ... the tuple
local's element type for an enum-constructor initializer is never resolved to
`E`", and put the fix "wherever a tuple local's element `TypeExpr`s are
recorded". The recording is fine. The let-site already stores exact element TEs
in `var_types.tuple_var_elem_tes` (via `tuple_binding_elem_tes`), and for an enum
constructor `refined_tuple_literal_elem_te` declines -- its Call arm handles only
`Option`/`Result` ctors -- and the fallback `infer_arg_elem_te` resolves `E`
correctly. The record was there and correct all along.

The gap was in the READER. `tuple_var_elem_tes()` (call_dispatch.rs), which
`place_chain_tuple_tes` calls for an Identifier source, consulted the annotation
table and then fell through to synthesising TEs from
`tuple_var_elem_type_names` -- a `Vec<Option<String>>`, where a `None` name
becomes the empty path the row measured. It never read
`var_types.tuple_var_elem_tes` at all, despite a comment inside the function
describing exactly that lookup and asserting it "beats the names-derived
synthesis below". Comment present, code absent.

The record is consulted PER ELEMENT and only where the names spelling is
degenerate -- NOT preferred wholesale, which the comment's "beats" invites and
which regresses two suites. See B-2026-08-28-8 for the measurement and for the
prior session's finding at `suppress_tuple_index_move_source`, which had already
established the narrow form. For an enum element the names spelling is an empty
path and the record says `E`, so the merge takes the record and the leaf
classifies -- which is what closes this row.

That the same erasure also blocked a NESTED TUPLE element -- a name cannot spell
`(R, i64)` under any circumstances -- is what ties this row to B-2026-08-28-8;
see that row for the per-half measurement showing the registry lookup fixes this
one alone, while the nested case additionally needs the walker's pattern arm.

Measured after the fix, drop-body counts interp / jit / build / nopar:

    let p = (E.A(R { id: 41 }), 1); let (e, n) = p;   -> 1 / 1 / 1 / 1

RED-verified on this HEAD before the change (1 / 0 / 0 / 0), and pinned by the
new `enum-leaf-from-local` row of
`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_user_drop_body_runs_for_a_let_destructure_leaf`, sitting
next to the `enum-leaf-from-call` row that passed throughout -- which is what
holds the source asymmetry the row identified.
title: An ENUM leaf destructured out of a tuple LOCAL never runs its live variant's payload `Drop` body: `enum E { A(R), B }  let p = (E.A(R { id: 41 }), 1); let (e, n) = p;` prints `drop 41` under `karac run --interp` and NOTHING compiled. The place-source walker's per-leaf `TypeExpr` arrives with EMPTY path segments for an enum element, so its `is_enum` test can never fire and the leaf is skipped before any registration. Same shape from a CALL or a tuple LITERAL is correct
detail:
Measured on `383a723` (B-2026-08-28-1's fix in place), drop-body counts
interp / jit / build:

    let p = (E.A(R { id: 41 }), 1); let (e, n) = p;   -> 1 / 0 / 0   <- this row
    fn make() -> (E, i64) { ... }  let (e, n) = make();
                                                      -> 1 / 1 / 1   <- correct
    let (e, n) = (E.A(R { id: 41 }), 1);              -> 1 / 1 / 1   <- correct

So the enum ARM added by B-2026-08-28-1 works; what fails is reaching it from a
place source. Instrumented `finish_place_source_tuple_destructure`: for the
struct-leaf repro the per-leaf `TypeExpr` prints `path ["R"]`, and for this enum
repro it prints `path []` -- an empty segment list. `place_chain_tuple_tes`
therefore hands back a `TypeKind::Path` with nothing in it, `p.segments.last()`
is `None`, and the leaf `continue`s before the `is_enum` /
`enum_layouts` lookup ever runs.

That makes this an upstream RECORDING gap, not a cleanup-registration gap: the
tuple local's element type for an enum-constructor initializer is never resolved
to `E`. The fix belongs wherever a tuple local's element `TypeExpr`s are recorded,
which is why it is not a one-line addition to the destructure walker.

NOTE the non-enum element in the same tuple ALSO prints `path []` (the `i64` in
the struct repro does), so an empty segment list is not by itself proof of the
gap -- it is only load-bearing for a leaf that needs a name to be classified.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-1's shape matrix, not by a targeted
probe.

fix:
FIXED by f723dde.

TWO OF THE ROW'S THREE HALVES WERE ALREADY GONE by the time it was worked, which
is worth recording because the row reads as one defect and is three:

  * the CALL source ("does not run AT ALL") was closed by B-2026-08-28-29's root
    (b), which gave the bound leaf a user-`Drop` body it never had. Measured
    `42 / drop 41` on all three backends before this commit;
  * the by-value PARAM source, which this row's repro does not name but the
    shape matrix reaches, is B-2026-08-28-19's caller-side-vs-scope-exit
    ordering. Deliberately left alone, and the source gate is written so it
    stays that way;
  * the LOCAL source is what remained, and is what this fixes.

IT IS WORSE THAN THE PLACEMENT ERROR THE ROW MEASURED, and the heap-carrying
shapes are what show it. The row says "one body, attributed to the wrong owner
and therefore placed before the statements that read the leaf" -- exactly right
about the mechanism, and it understates the consequence. The body was running on
the SOURCE, which `bind_pattern` had already moved out of, so with a `String`
field it printed `drop 41 ` against the interpreter's `drop 41 n41`. A `Drop`
body observing an EMPTIED field is a wrong-value defect, not only an early one,
and no count-based or order-based check would have distinguished them.

THE FIX IS A TRANSCRIPTION. `let x = w.r` is the same move and was already
correct on every backend: `disarm_struct_field_move_bodies` masks the field out
of `w`'s walk and the destination registers its own. The destructure spelling
never did that. Three steps carry over per bound leaf -- disarm the source's
bodies at that field, suppress its memory for that field, register the leaf's
own drop -- and `field-access-model` is a row in both fixtures so the two
spellings cannot drift apart again.

FOUR MEASURED CORRECTIONS, each a different failure and none of them predictable
from reading the code. This is the part the row's "separate measured change"
estimate was right about and understated:

  1. body moved, memory left with the source -> USE-AFTER-FREE. The body now
     outlives the source's free, which fires at the destructure statement.
  2. memory moved with `zero_struct_field_move_cap` -> still a DOUBLE FREE. That
     helper reaches only DIRECT Vec/String/Map/Option fields; a nested STRUCT
     field's own heap survived it. The field-access twin routes through
     `suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal`, whose nested-aggregate arm
     recurses into the moved-out struct's leaves -- it gains a by-name entry
     point here, since a destructure has no `FieldAccess` node to hand over.
  3. both moved correctly, but the `callee_owned_src` arm FURTHER DOWN THE SAME
     LOOP then registered its own `track_struct_var` on the leaf -> DOUBLE FREE
     again. Invisible in the source and obvious in the emitted IR, as
     `__karac_drop_struct_R` sitting beside `karac_drop_R`; a scratch IR dumper
     is what found it, after three wrong hypotheses reasoned from the source.
  4. a leaf that declares no `Drop` of its own has no wrapper to take, so the
     chain's memory registration stands and its field-bodies walk must be
     registered AFTER it. The frame drains LIFO, so "runs before the free" means
     "registered later" -- the opposite of the intuitive placement.

THE SOURCE GATE IS A POSITIVE SIGNAL, and that too is measured. A first cut
excluded `ref` params, `owned_struct_params` and the current function's
parameter names, and STILL doubled the body on two shapes that are none of
those: a CLOSURE parameter (`|w: W| { let W { r, n } = w; .. }`) and a rebound
param VIEW, whose bodies are owned caller-side under caller-retains.
`var_owns_struct_field_bodies` asks whether the source is currently RUNNING the
walk, which answers for every such shape at once -- there is nothing to transfer
unless the source holds it. Both regressions were caught by existing fixtures
(`e2e_closure_by_value_struct_arg_runs_its_drop_body`,
`e2e_param_view_rebind_single_caller_fire`), which is what a positive gate is
for.

FINAL MEASUREMENT, interp / jit / build identical on every row and memory-clean
under valgrind and ASAN: place source, two Drop-bearing fields, a consumed leaf,
a heap-carrying field's VALUE, a field-only-`Drop` leaf, and the field-access
model. Unchanged: unread leaves and wildcard leaves (where both placements
coincide), the call and tuple sources, the closure-param source, and the
by-value param source that remains B-2026-08-28-19.
title: A STRUCT-PATTERN destructure leaf's user `Drop` body is wrong in TWO OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS depending on the source: from a LOCAL it runs TOO EARLY (`drop 41` then `42`, against the interpreter's `42` then `drop 41`), and from a CALL it does not run AT ALL. `struct W { r: R, n: i64 }  let W { r, n } = w;` -- the struct twin of B-2026-08-28-1, whose helper `track_owned_destructure_field_cleanup` ends in the same bare `track_struct_var` tail with no `drop_method_keys` check
detail:
Measured on `383a723` (B-2026-08-28-1's fix in place, which touched only
the TUPLE helper). Full stdout, interp vs the three compiled surfaces:

    LOCAL source
      let w = W { r: R { id: 41 }, n: 1 }; let W { r, n } = w; println(f"{r.id + n}");
        interp                 42 / drop 41        <- correct
        jit / build / nopar    drop 41 / 42        <- body runs, at the WRONG TIME

    CALL source
      fn make() -> W { ... }  let W { r, n } = make(); println(f"{r.id + n}");
        interp                 42 / drop 41        <- correct
        jit / build / nopar    42                  <- body never runs

The LOCAL case is not a second body: it is the SOURCE `w`'s field-bodies walk
firing at `w`'s own live-range end (which is the destructure statement, since `w`
is not used again), while the leaf `r` is registered for MEMORY only and never
gets a body of its own. So one body runs, attributed to the wrong owner and
therefore placed before the statements that read the leaf.

ROOT CAUSE is the struct twin of B-2026-08-28-1: `track_owned_destructure_field_cleanup`
(stmts.rs) ends in

    if struct_types.contains_key(seg) && !shared_types.contains_key(seg) {
        self.track_struct_var(seg, alloca);
    }

-- the MEMORY field-walk, with no `drop_method_keys` check and so no route to the
`karac_drop_<T>` wrapper that runs the body. Identical shape to the tuple helper's
tail before `383a723`.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED ALONGSIDE. The tuple fix was additive because the tuple
place-source path already cap-zeroes the source element, so the source's body was
NOT firing and the leaf could simply take it. Here the source's body IS firing
(the LOCAL row above), so registering the leaf without also suppressing the
source produces TWO bodies -- exactly the regression the tuple-param control in
`e2e_user_drop_body_runs_for_a_let_destructure_leaf` exists to catch. The struct
fix therefore needs a source-suppression half that the tuple fix did not, and
that is a separate measured change.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-1's shape matrix, not by a targeted
probe.

fix:
FIXED by 821d5ab, for all three sources this row measured. The row's READ of the
mechanism was right — an empty substitution makes `type_runs_user_drop_mono`
judge `Box2 { v: T }` Drop-free through a bare `T` — and its guess at the single
site was not, because the arguments are erased THREE times over and each fix is
necessary while none is sufficient:

  * `infer_arg_elem_te` rebuilds every tuple element's type from its NAME and
    always emits `generic_args: None`, so the literal's own `Box2[R]` was
    erased before anything recorded it. A struct literal SPELLS its
    instantiation, so that arm now returns the literal's path verbatim.

  * `tuple_var_elem_tes` then preferred the name spelling over the recorded
    `TypeExpr`, because a name is "informative" and this erasure is invisible:
    `Box2` meaning `Box2[R]` and `Box2` meaning nothing in particular are the
    same string. Its per-element merge rule now also takes the record where the
    name is provably lossy.

  * and the leaf recorded no instantiation at all — the site the row named.
    Fixing only that changes nothing, which is what the first attempt measured.

THE GUARD IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART, and getting it wrong is worse than the bug.
`concrete_generic_struct_inst` RESOLVES type parameters through the active
monomorph substitution and answers `None` when there is nothing to resolve, so
an already-concrete `Box2[R]` needs the `let` site's `unwrap_or(te)` fallback.
Applied without checking the ARGUMENTS, that fallback records `Bag[T]` — the
shape a generic callee's declared return type produces, read from a caller with
no active substitution — which is precisely the record B-2026-08-27-36 forbids:
it satisfies the instantiation lookup and stops it before the arm that would
have resolved `T`. That did not merely lose a body. It made
`e2e_heap_tuple_arg_escaping_the_frame_is_freed_once` print a dangling pointer
where `x` belonged: an OVER-FREE of the caller's buffer, caught by the full
suite and not by any fixture written for this row. Every argument must name a
real type; a bare parameter disqualifies the record.

RESIDUAL, split out rather than left implicit: the GENERIC-CALLEE spelling
`fn src[T](x: T) -> (Box2[T], i64)` destructured at the call site is still
silent on both compiled backends, because the element type there IS the bare
`Box2[T]` and binding `T` needs the CALL SITE's substitution — the
B-2026-08-28-28 machinery, not this one. Filed as B-2026-08-28-61. It is
deliberately not forced through the fallback above, since that is the harmful
non-answer this fix's guard exists to reject.

VERIFIED on an eight-row matrix, identical across interp / jit / build: the
three sources, a leaf that is READ, a two-parameter generic, the non-generic
control, and — the row that pins precision rather than presence —
`non-drop-param`, where a fix that recorded ANY instantiation rather than the
right one would run a body the interpreter does not. Fixture:
`e2e_generic_tuple_destructure_leaf_runs_its_field_body`, proven RED by stashing
only `src/`.
title: A GENERIC struct leaf destructured out of a tuple never runs its Drop-bearing field's body on ANY source path -- local, call result and tuple literal all print it under `karac run --interp` and nothing compiled: `struct Box2[T] { v: T }  let (b, n) = (Box2[R] { v: R { id: 41 } }, 1);`. The leaf has no recorded instantiation, so the field-bodies substitution is empty and `Box2 { v: T }` is judged Drop-free through a bare `T`
detail:
Measured on `383a723` (B-2026-08-28-1's fix in place), drop-body counts
interp / jit / build, all three sources:

    let p = (Box2[R] { v: R { id: 41 } }, 1); let (b, n) = p;   -> 1 / 0 / 0
    fn make() -> (Box2[R], i64) { ... }  let (b, n) = make();   -> 1 / 0 / 0
    let (b, n) = (Box2[R] { v: R { id: 41 } }, 1);              -> 1 / 0 / 0

Uniform across sources, which distinguishes it from the place-source-only
siblings and points at the SUBSTITUTION rather than at reachability. The
non-generic control `struct W { r: R }` in the same position is correct on all
three (it is a passing row of
`tests/codegen.rs::e2e_user_drop_body_runs_for_a_let_destructure_leaf`), so the
field-bodies arm itself works -- it is the generic resolution that fails.

MECHANISM (read, and consistent with the measurement, but not instrumented to the
line): the arm resolves its substitution through

    self.type_decls.enum_inst_var_types.get(name)

keyed on the LEAF binding, and a destructure leaf appears to carry no recorded
instantiation there. With an empty subst, `type_runs_user_drop_mono("Box2", {})`
sees the declared field type as a bare `T`, concludes the type owns no
Drop-bearing field, and skips the walk. This is the same mono-awareness gap
B-2026-08-02-14 fixed for the simple-`let` path, reappearing at the destructure
leaf because the leaf's instantiation is recorded (if at all) by a different
route than a `let` binding's.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-1's shape matrix, not by a targeted
probe.

fix:
FIXED by 429977d.

Wildcard destructure leaves now run the discarded value's user `Drop` body,
across both backends and all four source kinds.

THE HOLE. A wildcard binds no name. The interpreter's `push_drops_for_stmt`
registers a Drop slot per BOUND name, and codegen's leaf walkers key off a
binding name too, so a wildcard leaf reached no owner on either backend and the
body ran ZERO times -- against design.md § Drop's "a value is dropped exactly
once, at the live-range end of its final owner". Codegen's tuple `Wildcard` arm
did exist, but only freed a direct `{ptr,len,cap}` element; it never ran a body.

THREE SITES, each answering a different ownership question:

  * interpreter (`run_wildcard_destructure_leaf_user_drops`, called from the
    `let` arm beside the whole-pattern discard fire): pulls each wildcard
    position's value out of the bound `Value` and runs
    `run_discarded_value_user_drops` on it, at the destructure point.
  * codegen fresh-tuple path (`track_tuple_destructure_leaf_cleanups`): the
    `Wildcard` arm gains the body half it never had. Element `TypeExpr`s come
    from `tuple_arg_elem_type_exprs`, which answers for both fresh spellings
    this path admits (a tuple literal and a call returning a tuple).
  * codegen place-tuple path (`finish_place_source_tuple_destructure`): the
    loop bound names and `continue`d past everything else; a `Wildcard` arm now
    fires bodies, gated on the SAME `owner_runs_bodies` question the binding arm
    already asks.
  * codegen fresh-struct path (`finish_owned_struct_destructure`): a wildcard
    field over a fresh source, gated to `fresh` only -- see the asymmetry below.

Emitted as a DIRECT CALL at the destructure point rather than a scope-exit
registration: the discarded value is dead the moment the pattern binds nothing
to it, and the interpreter fires there too, so deferring would have agreed on
the count while disagreeing on the ORDER -- reintroducing this family's one
run-vs-build split from the other side.

THE PARAM GATE IS THE CONSTRAINT, not a detail. A by-value param source
(`fn take(p: (R, i64)) { let (_, n) = p; }`) was ALREADY correct at one body:
the caller owns the entry copy under caller-retains and fires it. Firing at the
leaf too would double it. Both backends reuse the gate they already apply to
BINDING leaves -- `let_destructures_owned_param` (interp) and
`owner_runs_bodies` (codegen) -- rather than introducing a second one. The
interp mirror deliberately omits that predicate's view-PROPAGATION side effect,
which runs once per statement in `eval_block_inner` afterwards.

MEASURED, body counts interp / jit / build, pre-fix -> post-fix:

    tuple place    let p = (R,1); let (_, n) = p;      0/0/0 -> 1/1/1  <- the row
    tuple literal  let (_, n) = (R, 1);                0/0/0 -> 1/1/1
    tuple call     let (_, n) = mk();                  0/0/0 -> 1/1/1
    struct call    let W { r: _, n } = mk();           0/0/0 -> 1/1/1
    struct place   let w = W{..}; let W{r:_,n} = w;    0/1/1 -> 1/1/1
    two droppers   let (_, b) = p;   (want 2)          1/1/1 -> 2/2/2
    both wildcards let (_, _) = p;   (want 2)          0/0/0 -> 2/2/2
  CONTROLS, unchanged and correct throughout:
    param tuple / param struct / match arm / wildcard-on-non-dropper /
    whole-pattern `let _` / no-destructure-at-all        all 1/1/1

`struct place` is worth singling out: it was the family's ONLY run-vs-build
split (interp 0, compiled 1, compiled correct). That is what made the family
findable at all -- every other row agreed at the wrong answer, which no A/B gate
can report. It is also why the struct arm fires for a FRESH source only: firing
it on a place source too would take the compiled backends to two and re-open the
split from the other direction.

THE MEMORY HALF, and the part that was not predictable. Adding the body alone
made `let (_, n) = (R { id, name: String }, 1)` LEAK 3 bytes under LSan where it
had been clean. Pre-fix nothing read the discarded `R`, so LLVM deleted its
`String` allocation as dead; a body that reads `self.name` makes the allocation
live and exposes a missing free underneath -- the wildcard arm's `track_vec_var`
covers only a DIRECT `{ptr,len,cap}` element, never a struct element with a heap
field. So the fresh-tuple site frees as well as running bodies.

The naive generalization of that -- "fresh means unowned, so always free" -- is
also wrong, and ASAN caught it: doing the same on the fresh STRUCT path
double-freed, because a fresh struct temp DOES carry its own whole-aggregate
drop where a fresh tuple temp does not. `free_memory` is therefore per-site
(fresh tuple TRUE, place FALSE, fresh struct FALSE), each value measured rather
than derived. Both halves are emitted separately -- bodies-only walker then
memory drop -- never the combined `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper, whose use here would
have produced exactly the double free.

STILL OPEN, filed rather than pinned wrong: a wildcard field over a struct
LITERAL source runs zero bodies compiled. It is blocked behind a larger separate
defect -- a fresh-struct-source destructure loses even a BOUND field's body,
because `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` admits only `Call`/`MethodCall` so a
struct literal reaches no leaf path at all. Filed as B-2026-08-28-29.

Tests: `e2e_wildcard_destructure_leaf_user_drop_body_runs_once` (tests/codegen.rs)
and `test_wildcard_destructure_leaf_user_drop_body_runs_once`
(tests/interpreter.rs), 13 rows each, both verified RED pre-fix; plus
`asan_wildcard_destructure_leaf_drop_body_is_memory_balanced`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), 5 shapes at a heap-carrying `R` under ASAN + LSan,
which is the fixture that caught both the leak and the double free above.
title: A tuple-element WILDCARD drops the element ZERO TIMES ON ALL THREE BACKENDS: `let (_, n) = p;` where element 0 declares `impl Drop` runs the body under NEITHER `karac run --interp` NOR `karac run` NOR `karac build`, against design.md's guarantee that a value is dropped exactly once at its final owner's live-range end. NOT a run-vs-build divergence -- all three agree, so no A/B gate can see it. The non-tuple control `let _ = R { .. }` is correct on all three
detail:
REPRO (measured on `383a723`):

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}"); } }
    fn main() { let p = (R { id: 41 }, 1); let (_, n) = p; println(f"{n}"); }

    interp / jit / build / nopar   ->   `1` on all four. No body, anywhere.

CONTROLS that bound it:

  * `let (r, _) = p;` -- the wildcard on the NON-dropping element -- is correct
    on all four (1 / 1 / 1 / 1). So it is the wildcard landing on the DROPPER,
    not the presence of a wildcard.
  * `let _ = R { id: 41 };` -- a wildcard `let` with no tuple -- is correct on
    all four. So it is not "wildcard bindings never drop".
  * `let p = (R { id: 41 }, 1);` with NO destructure at all is correct on all
    four, which rules out "a tuple local never drops its elements".

AGAINST THE SPEC. design.md § Drop ("Interaction with move semantics") states
"A value is dropped exactly once, at the live-range end of its final owner."
Zero is not once, whichever owner one picks: if `_` does not bind then the
element's final owner is still `p` and `p`'s drop should run it; if the
destructure moves the element out then the wildcard slot is the final owner and
IT should. Both readings demand one body; the implementation delivers none.

WHY THIS CLASS AND NOT `run-vs-build`. All three backends agree, so the A/B rule
the kata corpus and the parity gates rest on is satisfied while the guarantee is
broken -- which is exactly why this needs its own row rather than riding along
with the destructure-leaf family. It is also why it survived B-2026-08-28-1's
whole shape matrix as the one row that "passed" on every surface.

NOTE the memory half is NOT obviously broken: `track_tuple_destructure_leaf_cleanups`
has a `PatternKind::Wildcard` arm that frees a discarded `{ptr,len,cap}` element
through a synthetic slot. It is the user BODY that has no wildcard arm anywhere.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-1's shape matrix, not by a targeted
probe. Filed deliberately even though every backend "agrees", because agreement
on the wrong answer is the failure mode an A/B gate cannot report.

fix:
FIXED by e58aaef, in `src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs` (one substitution, 1 effective line
plus its comment) by substituting the ACTIVE MONOMORPH'S type arguments into the
field TypeExpr before the clone-support gate reads it.

THE OWNERSHIP QUESTION THE ROW RAISED IS SETTLED, AND THE ANSWER IS "LEGAL, AND
IT IS A COPY". The row suspected the front end should reject a whole-value move
out of a `ref` binding's field, and that `karac check` passing was itself
suspicious. It is not: the interpreter AND the non-generic compiled path had
already agreed for as long as both existed. Measured with a mutating probe --
`fn n(ref self) -> i64 { let mut v = self.xs; v.push(99); return v.len(); }` --
the local reports 3 while the caller's `a.xs.len()` is still 2, on the tree walk
and on the non-generic compiled path alike. The callee gets an independent deep
copy; the caller's field is untouched. So the fix was to make the generic
compiled path match the two backends that were already right, NOT to add a
diagnostic. This also makes the "should not accept it at all" branch of the
row's LIKELY SHAPE section moot, and no spec change was needed.

ROOT CAUSE. `clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs` (B-2026-07-21-11) exists for
exactly this hazard and its doc comment describes this bug: the field read
through a borrow bit-copy-aliases the caller's field while the `let` registers
an owned cleanup, so it deep-copies the compiled value in place. Every gate in
it PASSED on the generic path -- instrumentation confirmed `root=self`,
`in_sig_ref=true`, `leaf=Vec`, `obj_ty=Bag`, all identical to the working
non-generic compile, on the monomorph `Bag.n$i64` itself. The decline was one
step further down. The leaf's full TypeExpr is read from the struct DECLARATION
table (`struct_field_type_exprs`), which inside `impl[T] Bag[T]` still says
`Vec[T]`; `borrow_payload_clone_supported` then correctly refuses to synthesize
a clone for an unsubstituted type parameter and the function returned the value
UNCLONED -- silently, since declining is its normal no-op path. The emitted IR
is unambiguous: the non-generic `Bag.n` stores through
`karac_clone_Vec_i64(refchain.letmove.src, refchain.letmove.clone)`, while
`Bag.n$i64` bare-`store`s the aliased header and then `karac_free_buf`s it at
exit, against a caller that frees the same pointer.

The fix routes `fte` through `subst_monomorph_type_params` before that gate.
That is the SAME helper and the same precedence B-2026-08-25-11 landed on for
the sibling defect, and it is a documented no-op outside a monomorph
(`type_subst_names` and `type_subst_type_exprs` both empty), so the non-generic
path is bit-identical -- which the `control-nongeneric` row asserts.

THIS IS THE THIRD SITE IN ONE FAMILY. B-2026-08-25-10 (copy-depth on an owned
by-value aggregate param) and B-2026-08-25-11 (the receiver's concrete
instantiation) were the same erasure -- a generic field/element type read at its
declaration and never substituted -- at the OWNED-self sites. This is the
BORROWED-self site. The family is "a decision keyed on a field's declared type,
made inside a monomorph".

SCOPE IS WIDER THAN THE ROW'S TWO SHAPES, and the extra shapes were found by
sweeping rather than assumed. Measured 6 of 11 probes aborting pre-fix and all
11 correct post-fix, on all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0):
  - generic impl `ref self`                              (the row's repro) ABORT
  - generic free fn `ref` param                          (row's second)    ABORT
  - readback of the caller's field after the call                          ABORT
  - `Vec[String]` element                                                  ABORT
  - `mut ref` param (not just `ref`)                                       ABORT
  - a SECOND type parameter's field (`Pair[K, V]`, field `Vec[V]`)         ABORT
  - `T = Vec[i64]`, a param bound to a generic-args-carrying type          HANG
Two shapes were already correct and are the controls that isolate the trigger to
erasure: the non-generic twin, and a bare `String` field of a generic struct --
a type with NO parameter to substitute, which reached the clone all along.

THE `T = Vec[i64]` CASE PRESENTED AS A HANG, NOT AN ABORT. Under LLJIT it spun
until killed at 30s rather than aborting; AOT of the same program exited 0. Same
missing clone, different downstream symptom -- worth recording because a search
for this defect by its abort signature would have missed that shape entirely.

TESTS. Three, each verified against the reverted compiler:
  - `tests/codegen.rs` `e2e_generic_borrowed_field_move_out_is_a_copy_not_an_alias`
    -- 10 rows incl. both controls and the `mutate` copy-semantics row. FAILS
    reverted.
  - `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`
    `asan_generic_borrowed_field_move_out_does_not_double_free` -- 6 cases.
    FAILS reverted with a MEMORY ERROR (the harness reports exit code `None`,
    i.e. death by signal), not an output mismatch. Elements are built through
    `env.args().len()` and read back BY BYTE, per the harness's own warning that
    a constant-seeded `.len()`-only fixture folds away at -O2 and asserts
    nothing; String elements are f-string-built because literals are rodata with
    cap 0, which would make the second free a silent no-op (the false negative
    B-2026-08-25-10's notes record).
  - `tests/interpreter.rs` `generic_borrowed_field_move_out_yields_a_copy` --
    PASSES reverted BY DESIGN. Every case was already correct under the tree
    walk; it is the oracle the codegen twin is asserted against, so a future
    change that "resolves" a divergence by moving the interpreter fails here

GATES, all re-measured ON THE PUSHED BASE after a mid-task rebase onto six
commits (one of them another drop-ownership codegen fix, d5d7421): fmt clean;
clippy clean on BOTH legs; default suite 108 targets / 10089 passed / 0 failed
/ 3 ignored / exit 0; llvm suite under KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1
110 targets / 15559 passed / 0 failed / 18 ignored / exit 0.

like a red suite. The first exhausted the container's disk allowance while

The rebase also conflicted in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`, where another

SIBLING BRANCHES PROBED AND CLEAN -- no follow-up rows from them. The same

and both were measured rather than assumed: a generic STRUCT leaf
(`let i = self.inner` where `inner: Inner[T]`, whose clone te is built from the

title: MOVING A `Vec` OUT OF A FIELD OF A BORROWED BINDING inside a GENERIC fn or impl DOUBLE-FREES the buffer under both compiled backends: `impl[T] Bag[T] { fn n(ref self) -> i64 { let v = self.xs; return v.len(); } }` runs correctly under `--interp` and ABORTS (SIGABRT, `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`) under `karac run` and `karac build`, on a program `karac check` passes clean. The NON-GENERIC spelling of the same method is correct, which is the control that isolates it -- no `Slice`, no coercion, no call required
detail:
MOVING A `Vec` OUT OF A FIELD OF A BORROWED BINDING, inside a GENERIC function
or impl, DOUBLE-FREES the buffer under both compiled backends. `karac check`
passes, the interpreter is correct, and both compiled backends abort.

REPRO -- 9 lines, no `Slice`, no coercion, no call to anything:

    struct Bag[=T] { xs: Vec[T] }
    impl[T] Bag[T] {
        fn n(ref self) -> i64 { let v = self.xs; return v.len(); }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut a: Bag[i64] = Bag { xs: Vec.new() };
        a.xs.push(1); a.xs.push(2);
        println(f"{a.n()}");
    }

    karac check          All checks passed.
    karac run --interp   2                                    <- correct
    karac run  (LLJIT)   free(): double free detected in tcache 2
    karac build  (AOT)   free(): double free detected in tcache 2   (SIGABRT, rc=134)

THE CONTROL THAT ISOLATES IT is the same method with the generic dropped --
`struct Bag { xs: Vec[i64] }` and `impl Bag` -- which prints 2 on all three
backends. Genericity is the whole difference; nothing else in the program moves.

A GENERIC FREE FN with a `ref` param fails identically, so it is not about the
`self` receiver:

    fn n[T](b: ref Bag[T]) -> i64 { let v = b.xs; return v.len(); }   -> double free

ELEMENT TYPE IS IRRELEVANT: `Vec[i64]` and `Vec[String]` both abort, so what is
freed twice is the Vec BUFFER, not the elements. The borrowed field's buffer ends
up owned by both the callee's local `v` and the caller's still-live `a.xs`.

READING THE FIELD BACK afterwards aborts too (`println(f"{a.xs[0]}")` after the
call), so the caller's binding is genuinely left pointing at freed memory rather
than the two frees merely racing at exit.

NOT REQUIRED: a call, a `Slice` parameter, or a coercion. The first sighting was
`let v = self.xs; return head(v);` with `head(s: Slice[T])`, which made it look
like part of B-2026-08-27-53; stripping the call to a bare `v.len()` reproduces
it unchanged, so the slice coercion is a bystander.

LIKELY SHAPE OF THE FIX: the front end arguably should not accept a whole-value
move out of a field of a `ref` binding at all -- the callee does not own it --
and `karac check` passing is itself suspicious. If the move IS to remain legal
(a copy for the callee), then codegen owes the local a COPY rather than a
borrowed alias of the caller's header, and the generic path is where that copy
goes missing since the non-generic path already does the right thing. Whichever
way it is resolved, the ownership-checker question should be settled first,
because it decides whether codegen needs a copy or the program needs a
diagnostic.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption reachable from a `karac check`-clean
program, on the shipped compiled path, with the interpreter disagreeing. Not
merely loud-failing like B-2026-08-27-53, whose fix this was found alongside.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping the borrow axis for B-2026-08-27-53 (a
`Slice[T]` param fed from a borrowed field). It was in the very first control
batch for that row and survived every narrowing -- it is unaffected by that fix,
measured before and after.

title: A `String` / `Vec` FIELD READ ON A SHARED-STRUCT TEMPORARY RECEIVER LEAKS THE BUFFER: `make().tag` where `make() -> shared Node` prints correctly and leaks 5 bytes under LSan, because the deep-clone that gives the read its own copy (`clone_shared_struct_heap_field_read`, in `exprs.rs`'s FieldAccess arm) runs AFTER `compile_field_access` has already released the temporary's last ref. The BOUND spelling (`let b = make(); b.tag`) is clean. The same ordering makes the block/`if` receiver spelling a heap-use-after-free, which is why B-2026-08-28-7 declines that field shape rather than compiling it.
detail:
The clone-and-release protocol for a shared-struct TEMPORARY receiver is
ordered wrongly, and the two spellings of the same read show it as two different
memory errors.

MEASURED, on a compiler with none of B-2026-08-28-7's changes (stashed tree),
via `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s `assert_clean_asan_run`:

    shared struct Node { v: i64, tag: String }
    fn make(k: i64) -> Node { return Node { v: k, tag: "hello".to_string() }; }

    fn main() { println(make(1).tag); }
        -> prints "hello"
        -> ERROR: LeakSanitizer: 5 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s)

    fn main() { let b = make(1); println(b.tag); }
        -> clean

    fn main() { println({ let n = make(1); n }.v); }        // scalar field
        -> clean (since B-2026-08-28-7)

THE ORDERING. `exprs.rs`'s FieldAccess arm is

    let v = self.compile_field_access(object, field)?;
    let v = self.clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read(expr, v)?;
    self.clone_shared_struct_heap_field_read(expr, v)

For a TEMPORARY receiver `compile_field_access` takes the bug-#8 call-result
branch, which loads the field and then `emit_refcount_dec_by_type`s the temp —
"the field value has been read into a register and no longer depends on the heap
object", which is true for a SCALAR field and false for a heap one. The
`{ptr,len,cap}` just loaded still points into the box. `clone_shared_struct_heap_field_read`
then deep-copies from that pointer, one step too late.

Which memory error you get depends on whether the release actually took the box
to zero. On the CALL spelling it evidently does not free before the clone reads
(the clone succeeds and prints correctly) but nothing ends up owning the copy —
a leak. On a BLOCK receiver, where the block retains the tail out and its frame
drain then decs, the release does take it to zero and the clone reads freed
memory: `ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free ... in memcpy`, through
`karac_string_clone`. That is measured, not predicted — it is what an ungated
B-2026-08-28-7 leg-1 branch produced, and it is why that fix declines exactly
the fields this cloner would want to copy (`is_string_type_expr(fte) ||
extract_vec_elem_type(fte).is_some()`) and leaves the loud "cannot resolve
field" gap in place instead.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE. The copy has to be taken before the release, not after.
The obstacle is that moving it into `compile_field_access` collides with the
existing cloner, which would then copy a second time — the "first of two clones,
leaving this buffer with no owner" hazard `clone_shared_struct_heap_field_read`'s
own borrowed-receiver gate documents (B-2026-07-29-21's family). So the two sites
have to agree explicitly: either the temp-receiver path clones and marks the read
as already-copied, or the release is deferred past the clone. Either way it is a
protocol change across two files, which is why it is a row and not a rider on
B-2026-08-28-7.

WHY MEDIUM RATHER THAN HIGH: the reachable spelling LEAKS but computes the right
answer, and it leaks once per read of a heap field off a temporary rather than
unboundedly per element. It is not a miscompile and not a crash. The
use-after-free half is NOT reachable from source today — it only appears if the
block/`if` receiver is allowed through, which B-2026-08-28-7 deliberately does
not do.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-28-7 leg 1, whose ASAN gate carries the
clean bound-receiver spelling (`let b = make(4); println(b.tag);`) so the
boundary between the working and broken shapes stays pinned while this is open.
fix:
FIXED by e17e361. The row's diagnosis was WRONG ON MECHANISM, and the real one is
worse: the ordering it blamed is a real defect but only the SECOND of two, and it
was invisible until the first was fixed.

WHAT ACTUALLY LEAKED. `emit_rc_dec` dispatches to the per-struct recursive drop
fn `__karac_rc_drop_<Name>` only when one has ALREADY been synthesized for the
heap type, and falls back to a plain `free(ptr)` otherwise — releasing the BOX
and none of the String / Vec / Map / inner-shared buffers it owns. Synthesis is
lazy and driven by `track_rc_var`: by a BINDING. A temporary has no binding, so
nothing had ever established that precondition at the temp-receiver release, and
EVERY field read on a shared temporary shallow-freed its receiver. The emitted
IR for `make(1).tag` is four instructions of refcount and then a bare
`call void @free(ptr %call)` — no field walk anywhere.

So the leaked 5 bytes were the ORIGINAL buffer inside the box, not the clone the
row assumed, and the clone was reading LIVE memory the whole time — which is why
the call spelling leaked instead of crashing.

THE TELL, and the reason this is worth reading rather than just fixing: the same
expression's memory behaviour depended on an unrelated statement elsewhere in the
program. With no `Node` binding anywhere, `println(make(1).tag)` leaks. Add
`let w = make(9);` on any line — a statement that touches nothing the read
touches — and that same read becomes `heap-use-after-free` in
`karac_string_clone` instead, because the binding synthesized the drop fn, which
made the release deep, which freed the buffer under the clone. Both measured. A
diagnosis taken from one of those two programs generalizes to the wrong bug,
which is what happened when this row was filed from the block-receiver spelling
(whose inner `let` warms the drop fn, so it presented as the use-after-free).

THE FIX IS BOTH HALVES, and each alone is a memory error:

  1. Synthesize the recursive drop fn before releasing, so the release is DEEP.
     Alone: turns the leak into a use-after-free.
  2. Defer the release past the deep copy, so the copy is taken from a buffer the
     box still owns. Alone: the release stays shallow and the leak stands.

(1) is one memoized, idempotent call — the same one `track_rc_var` makes, so the
temp site now establishes the precondition every other dec site already
establishes, rather than depending on some other statement to have done it. It is
also not a new idea: `emit_vec_elem_rc_dec_fn` (runtime.rs) already force-
synthesizes the element type's drop fn before its dec, with a comment naming this
exact failure — "rather than falling to a plain `free` that strands them" — after
a `Vec[Expr]` element's shared children leaked for the same reason. The temp
receiver was simply never given the same treatment.
It also makes the `Option[shared]` compensation directly above it correct for
the first time: that inc is emitted to be cancelled by the recursive drop's dec,
which the comment already asserted and the emitted code did not keep whenever the
drop fn was missing.

(2) moves the RELEASE rather than the clone, deliberately. Cloning inside the
release path instead would make it the first of two clones — the "leaving this
buffer with no owner" hazard `clone_shared_struct_heap_field_read`'s
borrowed-receiver gate already documents for B-2026-07-29-21's family. Deferring
keeps ONE clone site. The pending release is set immediately before
`compile_field_access` returns and drained immediately after the cloners run;
both of its two callers drain, and a `debug_assert` at the set site turns a
forgotten drain in a future third caller into a loud overwrite rather than a
silently dropped release.

A THIRD DEFECT FELL OUT OF (1) AND IS FIXED HERE TOO. Making the release deep
broke a shape that had worked: `make_outer(12).inner.tag`, where `inner` is a
bare `shared` field, printed `t12` before and garbage after on BOTH compiled
backends, because the now-recursive drop dec's the inner box while the loaded
pointer still aliases it. A bare `shared T` field is the same alias one level
down as the `Option[shared T]` field beside it, so it gets the same +1
compensation, and the two are exclusive by construction
(`shared_heap_type_for_type_expr` keys on the head segment, so `Option[Node]`
never reaches the bare arm). Caught by the interpreter oracle, not by reasoning —
it is row 11 of the E2E fixture for exactly that reason.

SCOPE IS WIDER THAN THE ROW STATES: the leak is not specific to heap-field reads.
A SCALAR read on a shared temporary — `println(make(1).v)` — leaks the receiver's
String just as surely, since the shallow free walks nothing. It reads clean at
-O2 only because the untouched buffer is a provably dead allocation LLVM deletes
outright (the hazard `assert_clean_asan_run`'s alloc-audit doc warns about); at
-O0 it leaks 4 bytes, measured. One fix at the release covers both, because both
go through the same helper.

B-2026-08-28-7's DELIBERATE DEFERRAL IS LIFTED. That fix declined a `String`/`Vec`
field on a block / `if` receiver rather than compiling it into a use-after-free,
and pointed here. With the protocol fixed there is no longer a field shape to
decline, so the branch is unconditional and the loud "cannot resolve field" gap
for that spelling is closed.

VERIFIED across interp / JIT / AOT on eleven receiver shapes, all three backends
agreeing line for line: call result, value block, `if` with each branch taken,
`Vec` field, scalar field, a `let` consumer, a bound receiver, `.len()` on the
read, the nested bare-`shared` hop, and concatenation. Both new tests proven RED
against the unfixed compiler by stashing only `src/`.

KNOWN REMAINDER, filed as B-2026-08-28-20 rather than buried here: the
nested `make_outer(12).inner.tag` hop still leaks the inner node's 3-byte buffer.
That leak is UNCHANGED by this fix — 3 bytes before, 3 bytes after, measured on
both compilers — because the +1 restores the pre-existing balance rather than
improving on it; the consumer of a bare-`shared` field read off a temporary never
takes ownership of it.

FIXED by 0944166. The premise the row reasoned from — that `p.0` yields a
shallow copy the destructure path avoids — was measurably wrong in an
instructive way: BOTH spellings produce the same `extractvalue` of the element.
What differs is not the extraction but the CONSUMING POSITION, and the row's
"the destructure spelling is clean" control is what made that invisible.

MECHANISM, read out of the emitted IR for the row's own repro against its own
control. Both compile the tuple param's entry deep-copy (`dcopy.*`, from
B-2026-08-28-2's fix) and both register the callee-side
`__karac_drop_tuple_te_R_i64(ptr %p)` that copy earns. The destructure then
emits the move-suppression `smv.f1.cap`/`smv.f1.len` stores that zero the
element's `{ptr,len,cap}` in `%p`, so the tuple's drop no-ops and the returned
value is the buffer's sole owner. The projection emits NO zeroing at all: it
frees `%p`'s element and returns a struct still pointing at it. ASAN reports
`heap-use-after-free` in the caller's `memcpy` of the returned aggregate,
exactly as the row recorded — the copy reads the control block after the free.

The machinery was all present and correct. `zero_tuple_elem_cap_at` even
documents itself as "used at a single-element move-out — `let x = t.0`", and it
routes a user-struct element through `zero_struct_move_caps` properly.
`suppress_tuple_index_move_source` was simply hooked at the two `let`-statement
positions in `stmts.rs` AND NOWHERE ELSE, so every ESCAPING position — where
the element actually leaves the frame and the suppression matters most — went
unsuppressed. The `owned_struct_params` bail inside that helper, which looked
like the culprit, is inert here: it is `TypeKind::Path`-gated at registration,
so a tuple param never enters the set.

SCOPE, and it is wider than the row on three axes. Eleven shapes abort pre-fix,
against three clean controls (measured on 381384f, all four surfaces):

  * POSITION, not extraction: fn tail, explicit `return`, early `return` in a
    branch, and an aggregate-LITERAL field (`H { r: p.0 }`) all abort. The
    `let` and call-argument positions are clean — the argument one not by
    suppression but because the callee entry-copies.
  * SOURCE, not parameters: a tuple LOCAL (`let p = (...); p.0`) aborts
    identically, as does a tuple held as a struct field moved off `self`. The
    row read this as tuple-PARAM specific; it is not.
  * ELEMENT: `.1` aborts as well as `.0`, and a `Vec` payload aborts as well as
    a `String`. The `Vec` row is also the run-vs-build witness within this bug:
    pre-fix it aborted under LLJIT while the -O2 AOT build happened to survive,
    so a `karac build`-only check would have called that shape clean.

TWO PEERS SHARED THE HOLE, found by probing the neighbouring suppressors rather
than assuming they were sound, and both are fixed in the same commit because
one hook set covers all three:

  * `suppress_place_field_struct_move_source` — the deeper place `p.0.name`, a
    heap field INSIDE the element. Hooked at four `let` positions, no escaping
    hook, same failure.
  * `suppress_array_elem_move_source` — `a[0]`. This one WAS wired at both
    return positions but not at the aggregate-literal field, so
    `H { r: a[0] }` double-freed while `return a[0]` was clean. That asymmetry
    is the tell that the hook set, not the helper, was the defect.

THE FIX is three hook sites and no new logic: `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
(fn tail), the explicit-`return` arm in `exprs.rs`, and the struct-literal
field-init loop. Each gets the tuple-index and deeper-place peers; the literal
site additionally gets the array peer it was missing. +37 lines, all of it
comment except six calls.

VERIFICATION. Codegen E2E `e2e_tuple_elem_moved_out_at_an_escaping_position_is_
not_double_freed` (18 rows: 11 shapes + 7 controls) and ASAN
`asan_tuple_elem_escaping_the_frame_is_freed_exactly_once` (10 cases). Reverted,
the E2E fails at `[tail-param]` and the ASAN fixture dies on a MEMORY ERROR
(exit 23, `heap-use-after-free ... in memcpy`) rather than an output mismatch —
worth stating because a signal death is what a revert of this looks like, not a
wrong string. The interpreter oracle
`tuple_elem_moved_out_at_an_escaping_position_yields_a_live_value` PASSES
against the unfixed compiler by design: it pins the semantics the compiled twin
is asserted against so a later change cannot move the oracle to meet a broken
backend.

THE CONTROLS EARN THEIR PLACE because the fix ADDS cap-zeroing, whose
over-firing failure mode is a LEAK, which no exit code shows. A `ref` tuple
param (callee does not own the caller's storage), a source read again after the
move, and the already-correct `let` position are all asserted, and the ASAN
fixture carries them so LSan on the Linux CI leg covers the leak direction.

NOT FIXED, and separate: `v[0].0` — a tuple element off a CONTAINER element —
double-frees both before and after this change, and unlike everything above it
fails at the `let` position too. That is an index-rooted chain, which the
suppressors deliberately decline (B-2026-08-12-27: the read must be deep-CLONED,
because the container still owns the element); the clone path
`clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read` covers `v[0].name` but not `v[0].0`. Missing
clone, not missing suppression — filed as its own row rather than folded in
here.

ALSO NOT FIXED, and separate: a heap field read through a DEEPER place rooted at
a `ref` binding and returned DIRECTLY -- `fn peek(w: ref W) -> String { w.r.name }`,
its `ref self` twin, and the tuple-hop `p.0.name` -- double-frees on both compiled
backends. Depth ONE (`fn peek(r: ref R) -> String { r.name }`) is clean, and so is
the depth-two `let s = w.r.name; s` spelling, so it is specifically the deeper
place returned with no intervening `let`. Confirmed pre-existing by building the
parent commit and measuring the identical abort, which is the only reason it is
not attributed to this change: the new tail hook fires on exactly these
expressions. It wants the deep CLONE that B-2026-08-28-13 gave the depth-one
`let` position (`clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs`), not a suppression -- a `ref`
binding does not own the caller's storage, so cap-zeroing it would strand that
buffer. Filed as its own row.
title: PROJECTING A HEAP-CARRYING STRUCT ELEMENT OUT OF A TUPLE PARAM AND RETURNING IT DOUBLE-FREES: `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { p.0 }` where `struct R { id: i64, name: String }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (rc 134) under BOTH `karac run` and `karac build`, while `karac check` passes and `--interp` is correct. Fires with NO `impl Drop` anywhere, so it is pure memory. Four controls bound it to exactly this shape: the `let (r, n) = p; r` DESTRUCTURE spelling is clean, a STRUCT param's `w.r` projection is clean, a scalar-only `R` is clean, and a bare `String` element is clean
detail:
REPRO (measured on d5d7421, and identically on the commit before it):

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { p.0 }
    fn main() { let x = take((R { id: 41, name: f"n{41}" }, 1)); println(f"{x.id} {x.name}") }

    karac check          ->  All checks passed.
    karac run --interp   ->  `41 n41`                       <- correct
    karac run  (LLJIT)   ->  free(): double free detected in tcache 2, rc 134
    karac build  (AOT)   ->  free(): double free detected in tcache 2, rc 134

Under ASAN it reports as `heap-use-after-free` on a 3-byte region inside
`memcpy` -- the projected copy reads the element's control block after the
source tuple has freed the buffer -- which is the same defect seen earlier by
the allocator.

FOUR CONTROLS, each flipping ONE dimension, all clean (rc 0):

  * SPELLING -- `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { let (r, n) = p; r }`. The
    destructure form of the same extraction is correct. So it is the
    PROJECTION, not the extraction.
  * PARAM SHAPE -- `struct W { r: R, n: i64 }  fn take(w: W) -> R { w.r }`.
    A struct param's field projection is correct. So it is TUPLE-param
    specific, not aggregate-param general.
  * ELEMENT HEAP -- `struct R { id: i64 }` with the same `p.0`. Correct. So
    the heap field is required.
  * ELEMENT SHAPE -- `fn take(p: (String, i64)) -> String { p.0 }`. Correct.
    So the element must be a STRUCT that CARRIES heap, not a bare heap value.

NOT A `Drop` BUG, and that is the isolating fact. The repro above declares no
`impl Drop` at all; adding one changes nothing but the printed output (`drop 41
n41` before the abort). B-2026-08-28-2 -- the double user-`Drop`-body row this
was found under -- is therefore a separate defect on a separate mechanism: that
one is caller-side BODY registration, this one is buffer ownership, and
d5d7421's element-precise body filter is provably inert here because a program
with no `Drop` impl emits no bodies walker for it to filter.

LIKELY SHAPE. `p.0` on an owned tuple param appears to yield a shallow copy of
the element struct -- control block included -- while the source tuple keeps
its own cleanup, so both the returned value's owner and the param's cleanup
free the same buffer. The destructure path does not do this, which suggests the
projection is missing whatever move-out suppression `finish_place_source_tuple_-
destructure` applies to a destructured leaf.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption on both shipped backends from a
`karac check`-clean program, with the interpreter disagreeing (so the
run-vs-build gate would catch it if the corpus had this shape -- it does not).

SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the ASAN fixture B-2026-08-28-2's row asked
for, by widening that row's repro to a heap-carrying element.

fix:
FIXED by 44ebce6.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS CORRECT AND ITS SCOPE ESTIMATE WAS TOO LARGE. It says
closing this "needs partial-move tracking on the local (element 0 moved out,
element 1 not), which is a different mechanism from an argument-site skip list".
The first half is exactly right. The second half suggested new machinery, and
none was needed: partial-move tracking on a tuple local ALREADY EXISTS on both
backends, built for `let x = t.N` (B-2026-08-03-3) -- the interpreter's
`moved_out_tuple_elem_bodies` set, which `run_array_element_user_drops` consults
to skip exactly those indices, and codegen's `disarm_tuple_elem_bodies_at`,
which re-registers the element walk with the index masked. And
`fn_returns_param_parts` already reported WHICH parts escape, for the literal
spelling. The fix is one hook per backend joining two existing pieces.

The framing that makes it a two-line change rather than a new analysis: a callee
that returns element N is the SAME MOVE as `let x = q.N`, reached through a call
instead of a projection. Recording it as a per-element move-out on the local,
rather than as a skip at the argument site, is what lets the local's own cleanup
do the rest unchanged.

PER-ELEMENT, NOT PER-ARGUMENT, and the fixtures pin it. In
`local-arg-two-droppers` (`fn take(p: (R, R)) -> R { let (a, b) = p; a }` called
on a local) only element 0 escapes; element 1 dies inside the call and its body
must still run caller-side. Masking the local's whole walk -- the obvious
coarser fix -- loses `drop 42`, which is the identical constraint
B-2026-08-28-2 measured on the literal side.

TOP-LEVEL elements only, matching the literal filter: a deeper path names
something INSIDE an element, which a per-element mask cannot express
(B-2026-08-28-23).

VERIFIED on six shapes across all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), byte-identical on each: both escaping spellings (destructure
and `p.0`) now at one body, the two-dropper row at one body EACH in the right
order, and the row's own three controls unchanged -- the callee returning the
other element, no call at all, and the literal-argument spelling d5d7421 fixed.

FIXTURES extend the B-2026-08-28-2 twins in all three suites rather than adding
parallel tests, and are RED-verified pre-fix in each. The ASAN rows deliberately
OMIT the `p.0` projection spelling at a heap-carrying `R`: that shape is a
pre-existing use-after-free filed on its own row, and the existing fixture's doc
already explains why it is excluded there -- adding it would make the test red
for a different bug. The behavioural twins cover that spelling at a scalar `R`,
where no buffer exists to dangle, which keeps the body-count claim complete
without dragging the memory defect in.

Gates on the landed tree: codegen 3379, memory_sanitizer 1282 under LSan with
KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1, interpreter 1801, par_codegen 270, selfhost 1,
default leg green, both clippy legs and fmt clean. Re-run after rebasing onto
821d5ab and 3e4a63b, both drop fixes that landed mid-flight.
title: The B-2026-08-28-2 double `Drop` body SURVIVES when the tuple argument comes from a LOCAL instead of a literal: `let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); let x = take(q);` still prints `drop 41` twice on all three backends after d5d7421. Same escaping-part asymmetry, different caller-side site -- the fresh-temp walk never sees a place argument, so this is the moved-out LOCAL's own cleanup firing alongside the result's. The control `-> i64` (returning the other element) is correctly 1
detail:
Measured on d5d7421 (B-2026-08-28-2's fix in place), user `Drop` body counts
interp / jit / build:

    let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); let x = take(q);        -> 2 / 2 / 2   <- this row
      (where `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> R { let (r, n) = p; r }`)

    CONTROL, same callee returning the OTHER element:
    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { let (r, n) = p; n }
    let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); let x = take(q);        -> 1 / 1 / 1   <- correct

    CONTROL, no call at all:
    let q = (R { id: 41 }, 1); println(f"{q.1}");      -> 1 / 1 / 1   <- correct

So the asymmetry is exactly B-2026-08-28-2's -- one body when the element dies
inside the callee, two when it escapes through the return -- reached through a
different caller-side owner.

WHY d5d7421 DOES NOT COVER IT. That fix filters the FRESH-TEMP argument walk,
which is gated on `ExprKind::Tuple` (interp) / `discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr`
(codegen). A bare identifier argument is a PLACE, so it never enters that walk
at all -- the second body here is the local binding `q`'s own cleanup firing at
its live-range end, on an element that has been moved out through the callee's
return. Suppressing it needs partial-move tracking on the local (element 0 moved
out, element 1 not), which is a different mechanism from an argument-site skip
list and deliberately out of that fix's scope.

BACKEND-CONSISTENT, like its parent row: all three agree at 2, so no
run-vs-build gate can see it.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-2's repro past the literal-argument
spelling its row named.

fix:
FIXED by f697522.

Per-FIELD caller-side masking, the struct twin of B-2026-08-28-2's per-element
tuple fix, and it reuses that fix's analysis unchanged: `fn_returns_param_parts`
already emitted `ParamPart::Field(name)` for a field returned out of an owned
struct param, through either spelling. What was missing was a SITE to apply it
at, exactly as the row predicted.

Two sites, one per backend, and both had a masking precedent already in the tree
so neither needed new machinery:

  * codegen (`call_dispatch.rs`, the named-struct arm of
    `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst`) now resolves the escaping
    `ParamPart::Field` names against the struct's declared field order

title: A tuple param returned WHOLE and then destructured AT THE CALL SITE loses its element's user `Drop` body on both compiled backends: `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> (R, i64) { p }  let x = take((R { id: 41 }, 1)); let (r, n) = x;` prints `drop 41` under `--interp` and NOTHING under `karac run` / `karac build`. The whole-param passthrough guard correctly hands ownership to the caller, and the caller's destructure of a CALL-RESULT LOCAL then registers no body for the leaf
detail:
Measured on d5d7421, user `Drop` body counts interp / jit / build:

    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> (R, i64) { p }
    fn main() { let x = take((R { id: 41 }, 1)); let (r, n) = x; println(f"{r.id}") }
