title: The caller-side fresh-temp argument `Drop` walk fires AT THE CALL in the interpreter and at SCOPE EXIT in both compiled backends, so a tuple-literal argument whose element dies inside the callee prints its body in a different ORDER on the two surfaces: `fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { let (r, n) = p; n }` gives `drop 41 / 1` under `--interp` and `1 / drop 41` compiled. Counts agree (1/1/1) -- only sequence differs, which is why every count-based check in this family missed it
detail:
Measured on d5d7421, full stdout:

    fn take(p: (R, i64)) -> i64 { let (r, n) = p; n }
    fn main() { let x = take((R { id: 41 }, 1)); println(f"{x}") }
      interp            drop 41 / 1
      jit / build       1 / drop 41

    fn take(p: (R, R)) -> R { let (a, b) = p; a }
    fn main() { let x = take((R { id: 41 }, R { id: 42 })); println(f"{x.id}") }
      interp            drop 42 / 41 / drop 41
      jit / build       41 / drop 41 / drop 42

PRE-EXISTING and older than B-2026-08-28-2's fix, which is what the second row
shows: `drop 42` is the element that dies INSIDE the call, it is not one the
fix removes from the walk, and it moves position between backends both before
and after. The first row is untouched by that fix entirely (nothing escapes the
callee, so nothing is skipped) and diverges identically.

MECHANISM. `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` runs the walk immediately as the call
returns; codegen's twin registers the bodies as a cleanup ACTION on the
caller's scope frame, so it drains at scope exit. Both fire exactly once, so
every assertion in this family -- which counts bodies -- is satisfied.

WHICH IS CORRECT is a real question, not a formality, and is why this is filed
rather than fixed on sight. The value provably dies inside the callee, so the
interpreter's placement reads as the intended one; but moving codegen to fire
at the call site means emitting the walk before the result is materialized, on
a path whose LIFO drain order is load-bearing for the memory registrations that
share the frame (see `track_discarded_tuple_elem_bodies`' comment on ordering).
Severity low: a side-effect ordering difference, no memory consequence, and no
count changes.

`load_owned_shared_temp_field` bumps the loaded inner handle's refcount — the

title: A BARE-`shared` FIELD READ OFF A SHARED TEMPORARY RECEIVER LEAKS THE INNER OBJECT'S PAYLOAD: `make_outer(12).inner.tag` prints `t12` on all three backends and leaks 3 bytes under LSan, because the `+1` that keeps the inner box alive across the outer temporary's recursive drop is never released by the consumer — and the BOUND spelling (`let h = make_outer(12).inner;`) leaks the same 3 bytes, so the binding's RC cleanup is not pairing with it either. Measured IDENTICALLY before and after B-2026-08-28-14, which added the `+1` only to restore the balance that fix's deep release would otherwise have broken.
detail:
A bare-`shared` field read off a shared TEMPORARY receiver leaves the inner box
with one ref nobody will ever release, so the inner object's heap payload leaks.

MEASURED, identically on the pre- and post-B-2026-08-28-14 compilers, via
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s `assert_clean_asan_run`:

    shared struct Node { v: i64, tag: String }
    fn make(k: i64) -> Node { return Node { v: k, tag: f"t{k}" }; }
    shared struct Outer { id: i64, inner: Node }
    fn make_outer(k: i64) -> Outer { return Outer { id: k, inner: make(k) }; }

    fn main() { println(make_outer(12).inner.tag); }
        -> prints "t12" (correct, on all three backends)
        -> ERROR: LeakSanitizer: 3 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s)

    fn main() { let h = make_outer(12).inner; println(h.tag); }
        -> same: correct, 3 bytes leaked

NOT A REGRESSION, and that is the point of filing it separately.
B-2026-08-28-14 made the temporary's release a DEEP recursive drop, which
dec's this inner box — so it had to add a compensating `+1` on the loaded
pointer, or the read dangled (it did: `t12` before, garbage after, on both
compiled backends). The `+1` restores exactly the pre-existing balance and no
more: before the fix the inner box was never dec'd at all (shallow free walked
no fields), after it the drop dec's 2 -> 1. Either way the last ref is never
released. 3 bytes before, 3 bytes after.

WHY THE BOUND SPELLING DOES NOT SAVE IT. `let h = make_outer(12).inner;` looks
like it should: the binding registers an RC cleanup and should take the `+1`
over. It leaks the same 3 bytes, so something on that path is not pairing the
binding's dec with this read's inc — which is the specific thing to chase first,
since a working bound spelling would make the temporary one a much smaller
question.

WHY LOW: bounded and non-corrupting. It is one leaked inner payload per read of
a bare-`shared` field off a temporary receiver, the output is correct on every
backend, and the shape is uncommon — the usual spelling binds the outer
(`let o = make_outer(12); o.inner.tag`), which does not go through the
temporary-receiver release at all. It is a leak, never a miscompile and never a
use-after-free.

fix:
FIXED by 56e6493, on both backends, and it cost far less than this row priced
it at — which is the part worth recording, because the row's own analysis is
what would have deterred the next reader.

THE ROW'S "WHAT IT WOULD TAKE" IS WRONG. It reads `karac_drop_<T>` as an
indivisible unit -- "user body, then the field walk, then the field FREES,
emitted as ONE cached symbol" -- and concludes a mask needs a variant wrapper
built from scratch with a body/free split to get right. The wrapper is ALREADY
three separate `build_call`s in exactly that order, and the middle one is the
same maskable walker B-2026-08-28-17 uses. So the variant is those three calls
with one argument changed: `emit_user_drop_wrapper_skipping` is ~30 lines and
reuses `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping` verbatim. The interpreter
decomposes identically -- `run_user_drop_body_on_value` is literally
`run_user_drop_body_only` followed by the field walk, and the fix calls the two
halves separately instead of masking the helper's input.

WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT is the constraint: only the BODY step may be masked. The
escaping field's memory is still the caller temp's to release, since the callee
received a copy of the aggregate and not its allocation, so a mask reaching
`emit_struct_drop_synthesis` trades the double body for a silent leak. That is
why the parent's own body still sees the WHOLE value too -- it may read the
field it is about to hand back -- and why the ASAN fixture gives every dropper a
`String` and reads each escaping value afterwards, so a mask that went the
other way surfaces as a use-after-free rather than staying latent.

PER-FIELD, NOT WHOLESALE. `karac_dropnf_<T>` already existed for the
moved-out-field shape and drops the body step entirely; on `struct Two { a: R,
b: R }` returning `a` it takes `b`'s body from one to zero. The masking walker's
`$keep…` suffix keeps a masked wrapper from aliasing the full one, and the full
wrapper's cache entry is deliberately untouched -- it is one symbol shared by
the let-path, container elements and every other owner in the module, and only
this caller knows a field escapes.

THE FN-CALL ARM WAS THE HALF THIS ROW DID NOT MENTION, and shipping without it
would have been worse than leaving the row open. `take(mk())` registers the
identical wrapper through the other arm of the same helper. With only the
struct-literal arm fixed, the interpreter got that shape right and both compiled
backends still doubled -- a run-vs-build divergence in place of a uniform wrong
answer. Found by widening the shape matrix past the row's own repro.

ONE RESIDUAL, SPLIT OUT RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT. `take(W { .. });` with the
result discarded now runs each body exactly once on every backend, but the two
compiled backends emit the field's body BEFORE the parent's while the
interpreter emits the parent's first, which is the order design.md § Drop
ordering specifies. Verified pre-existing by stashing `src/`: pre-fix compiled
output was `drop 47`, `drop W5`, `drop 47` against the interpreter's `drop W5`,
`drop 47`, `drop 47`. Filed as B-2026-08-28-53. The E2E fixture deliberately
omits that shape rather than pinning whichever order is wrong; the interpreter
twin pins the correct one.

title: A PARENT STRUCT THAT DECLARES ITS OWN `Drop` still double-runs a returned field's user `Drop` body: with `impl Drop for W` added, `fn take(w: W) -> R { let W { r, n } = w; r }` prints `drop 41` twice for one `R` on all three backends. B-2026-08-28-17's per-field mask is structurally unreachable here -- both backends dispatch a parent that owns a `Drop` to the full `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper and never reach the maskable bodies walker, and only the wrapper's BODY half may be masked since its field frees must still run
detail:
Measured on the B-2026-08-28-17 fix commit, user `Drop` body counts
interp / jit / build, and IDENTICAL on a compiler built without that fix
(verified by stashing `src/` and rebuilding), so this is neither caused nor
repaired by it:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct W { r: R, n: i64 }
    impl Drop for W { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop W{self.n}") } }
    fn take(w: W) -> R { let W { r, n } = w; r }
    fn main() { let x = take(W { r: R { id: 41 }, n: 1 }); println(f"{x.id}") }
                                                       -> 3 / 3 / 3

Output on every backend: `drop W1`, `drop 41`, `41`, `drop 41`. `drop W1` is
correct (`W` is consumed and dies inside the call) and the trailing `drop 41` is
correct (`x` at its last use). The MIDDLE `drop 41` is the defect -- exactly one
`R` is constructed, and its body runs twice.

WHY B-2026-08-28-17's FIX DOES NOT REACH IT, which is the whole content of this
row. That fix masks the escaping field out of the caller-side FIELD-BODIES walk.
That walk is only registered when the parent declares NO `Drop` of its own -- on
both backends the dispatch is an if/else, not a sequence:

  * interp (`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`): the masked
    `drop_user_drop_fields_of_value` call sits under
    `if !self.program.drop_method_keys.contains_key(&tn) && ...`. A parent WITH
    a `Drop` impl takes the earlier `run_user_drop_body_on_value` branch instead,
    which runs the body and walks the fields itself.
  * codegen (the named-struct arm of `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst`):
    a parent with a user `Drop` registers `track_user_drop_var` and RETURNS
    before reaching the `field_bodies_fn_for_owned_temp_skipping` call.

So the mask is structurally unreachable for this shape, not merely ineffective.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE, and why it is a separate change rather than a rider. The
registration here is the full `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper -- user body, then the
field walk, then the field FREES -- emitted as ONE cached symbol shared by the
let-path, container elements, and every other owner in the module. Masking a
field out of it means emitting a mask-keyed variant wrapper, and only the BODY
half may be masked: the escaping field's memory is still this buffer's to
release, so a mask that reached the frees would leak. The bodies-only walker
B-2026-08-28-17 masks has no such split to get wrong (it frees nothing, which is
what made that fix purely additive). Same reasoning the parent row used to defer
the struct leg from B-2026-08-28-2.

NOT a memory defect: the same shape with a heap-carrying
`R { id: i64, name: String }` exits 0 with correct field contents, so this is a
duplicated side effect, not corruption -- matching B-2026-08-28-17, and unlike
the tuple-projection double free B-2026-08-28-15.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-17's shape matrix to a parent that
declares its own `Drop`. Deliberately excluded from that row's regression
fixtures (documented in
`e2e_user_drop_body_of_a_returned_struct_param_field_runs_once`) so they pin
only counts that are actually correct.

fix:
FIXED by 7c0569a on all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), for the WHOLE-PARAM channel and free functions. The row's
headline program now prints `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99`; both of its controls
are unchanged.

WHAT THE ADDENDUM GOT RIGHT, and what it missed. The addendum names the fix
exactly -- "(a) the coroutine-style ownership flip ... plus (b) a per-path
escape flag" -- and calls it "a scoped design slice, not an ABI project". That
held. What it did not notice is that (b) ALREADY EXISTED when it was written:
B-2026-08-28-51's `74223ee` had built the per-path conditional-move flag for
LOCALS -- `note_escaping_site` as a shared classification, `cond_move_drop_flags`
+ `emit_user_drop_call_guarded` in codegen, `record_conditional_move_tail` +
`moved_out_user_drop_bindings` in the interpreter -- and documented it as
deliberately NOT touching the three `has_armed_*` predicates. So this row needed
only (a), pointed at that machinery. The union answer is untouched; nothing that
depends on it moved.

THE TWO CONSTRAINTS, both found by measuring a wrong version rather than by
reasoning. Either one omitted turns this row into a worse defect than the one it
closes.

  1. BODIES ONLY. The obvious registration is the coroutine precedent verbatim
     -- `track_user_drop_var`, which installs the binding's OWN wrapper. That
     wrapper frees the fields as well as running the body, and an owned
     by-value param is caller-drops for MEMORY whoever runs the body. Measured
     on a param with a `String` field: `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
     under the JIT. `emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn` frees nothing, which
     is the split this row's own text describes from the other side ("NOT a
     memory defect on any of the three: these channels register BODIES only").
     An `i64`-only payload has nothing to double-free, so the unsafe version
     passed every body-count fixture in the tree -- which is why the ASAN
     fixture added here carries `String` fields on purpose.

  2. ADMITTED ONLY WHERE THE FLAG CAN CLEAR. `fn_returns_param` is true for an
     AGGREGATE-LITERAL return (`if k { H { r: r } } else { .. }`) because its
     `expr_is_ident` recurses into struct and tuple literals; the flag clears
     only on a BARE identifier at an escaping arm tail. Registering on the bare
     `fn_returns_param` therefore left the callee running a body for a value
     that had left the frame: measured `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41` on all three
     compiled backends -- a double body PLUS a read of the dropped value, i.e.
     precisely the failure this row argues the union answer exists to avoid.
     The new `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` (src/ast/items.rs) declines
     it, along with anything else it cannot see: `may_mention` answers TRUE for
     any expression shape it does not explicitly recognize, so an unhandled
     shape declines the fix rather than admitting an unseen escape.

DECLINED, MEASURED, AND FILED rather than guessed at:

  * METHODS -> B-2026-08-28-70. `method_call.rs`'s argument handling does not
    stand down for a conditionally-returned arg the way `call_dispatch.rs`
    does, so the callee-side flip double-fires there: measured `drop 41` /
    `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99` on all three compiled backends for
    `impl B2 { fn pick(ref self, r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } } }`.
    The flip is only ever sound where the caller has already stood down, so the
    method half needs its caller audited first. NOTE, separately measured: that
    same method program is a PRE-EXISTING run-vs-build divergence -- the
    interpreter loses the body while all three compiled backends run it --
    verified identical with this fix stashed, so it is not introduced here.

  * GENERICS -> B-2026-08-28-71. Monomorphs have their own param loop
    (`compile_mono_function`), the same reason B-2026-08-05-7 gives for its own
    duplicate registration there. Adding this one passed every body-count case
    but printed a CORRUPTED name for a heap-carrying param -- `drop dr` where
    `drop i1` was due, all three compiled backends -- so the mono param slot
    does not hold what the bodies-only walker expects (the value appears to

    generic by its declared name and would otherwise have applied the fix
    alone, converting a shared bug into a run-vs-build divergence. Four-surface

  * A `return` operand inside a branch. Codegen clears the flag at match arms
    and block tails but suppresses a `return` statically instead, so that route
    is outside this mechanism -- B-2026-08-28-65 / -52's shape, and untouched

STILL OPEN, and the row's own framing of it stands. The PARTS channel (a tuple
element or struct field pulled out of an owned param -- `fn take(w: W, k: bool)
-> R { let W { a, b } = w; if k { a } else { b } }`) and the PAYLOAD channel are

and after).

TWO FIXTURE CASES PINNED THIS ROW'S DEFECT AS INTENDED BEHAVIOUR. B-2026-08-28-51

title: ALL THREE interprocedural escape predicates UNION over a callee's return sites, so a BRANCHY callee loses the user `Drop` body of whichever value actually died in the call: `fn take(r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } }` called with `k = false` never runs R{41}'s body on any backend. Long-standing and deliberate rather than a regression -- `fn_returns_param_payload` documents the trade in as many words, and the whole-param leg predates the tuple/field part channel that inherited it from B-2026-08-28-2/-17
detail:
The three interprocedural escape predicates in `src/ast/items.rs` --
`fn_returns_param` (whole param), `fn_returns_param_payload` (a value bound out
of an enum param), and `fn_returns_param_parts` (a tuple element / struct field)
-- all answer over the UNION of a callee's return sites. A callee whose branches
yield DIFFERENT values therefore reports every one of them, the caller suppresses
its side of the drop for all of them, and whichever value actually died inside
the call loses its user `Drop` body.

MEASURED, body counts interp / jit / build. Two objects are constructed in each
program and only one body runs:

    // parts channel, struct (on the B-2026-08-28-17 fix commit)
    fn take(w: W, k: bool) -> R { let W { a, b } = w; if k { a } else { b } }
    take(W { a: R { id: 41 }, b: R { id: 42 } }, true)
                                    -> 1 / 1 / 1   (prints `41`, `drop 41`)
    // parts channel, tuple -- the masking here is d5d7421's (B-2026-08-28-2,
    // already on main) and is untouched by the -17 commit measured on
    fn take(p: (R, R), k: bool) -> R { let (a, b) = p; if k { a } else { b } }
                                    -> 1 / 1 / 1   (same shape, same loss)
    // whole-param channel -- FAR older than either (B-2026-07-01-7 era), and
    // the reason this is a family row rather than a regression report
    fn take(r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } }
    take(R { id: 41 }, false)       -> 1 / 1 / 1   (prints `99`, `drop 99`;
                                       R{41} dies in the callee, body lost)

ISOLATED with two controls on that last program, which between them rule out
"the caller-side walk simply does not fire for this shape":

    fn take(r: R, k: bool) -> i64 { if k { 1 } else { 2 } }   // never returns r
    take(R { id: 41 }, false)       -> 1 / 1 / 1   `drop 41`, `2`   CORRECT
    fn take(r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } }
    take(R { id: 41 }, TRUE)        -> 1 / 1 / 1   `41`, `drop 41`  CORRECT

The second control is the SAME PROGRAM as the failing one with `k` flipped. The
callee, the argument and the predicate's answer are all identical; only which
branch executes differs. That is what makes this a static-vs-dynamic mismatch
rather than a missing case somewhere.

The whole-param case is untouched by any recent work and predates the part
channel entirely, so the union is the channel's LONG-STANDING behaviour rather
than something the B-2026-08-28-2 / -17 fixes introduced. Those fixes inherited
it by building on the same shape of predicate.

IT IS ALSO THE DELIBERATE TRADE, which is why this is filed rather than
hot-fixed. `fn_returns_param_payload`'s doc states it in as many words:
CONSERVATIVE-TRUE on a mixed-path callee, accepting "a missed body, never a
double drop, and never a memory fault, since nothing here frees." Intersecting
across return sites instead would restore the DOUBLE body on exactly these
shapes -- the defect B-2026-08-28-2 and -17 were filed for -- so the choice is
between two wrong counts in opposite directions, and the tree has already picked
one. Any change here must move all three predicates together, or the part
channel ends up out of step with the whole-param one it is layered on.

NOT a memory defect on any of the three: these channels register BODIES only,
and the memory registrations are independent of them. Confirmed on the parts
channel by the ASAN + LSan fixtures for B-2026-08-28-2 and -17, both clean.

WHAT A REAL FIX LOOKS LIKE, if the trade is ever revisited: the caller registers
ONE cleanup action per call site and has no runtime knowledge of which return
site fired, so no purely static answer is precise here. Closing it properly
means a callee-side signal -- the callee taking ownership of the parts it did
not return, or a returned discriminant the caller's cleanup can switch on --
which is a calling-convention change, not a predicate tweak. That is the honest
reason this sits open rather than being a small omission.

SOURCE NOTE: found by auditing `fn_returns_param_parts` while fixing
B-2026-08-28-17; the doc comment on that fn claimed under-approximation without
qualifying the multi-return-site case, and was corrected in the same commit to
state both directions and point here.

RECONFIRMED on cca1ae2, all five programs, all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT /
AOT / AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) — every count matches the row exactly, so
nothing since has changed it. Both controls still hold, including the
same-program-`k`-flipped one.

MECHANISM PINNED IN THE IR, which the row inferred but did not show. The
callee's `take` for the whole-param repro emits NO drop of `r` on EITHER path:

    then:                              ; the escaping path
      %r2 = load { i64 }, ptr %r
      %smv.f0.p = getelementptr ... ptr %r, i32 0, i32 0
      br label %ifmerge
    else:                              ; the path where R{41} dies
      br label %ifmerge                ; <- empty. no body, no free.

So it is not that the callee drops on the wrong path — it never registers a
drop for the param at all, and the caller has suppressed its own. That is the
whole loss, visible in four instructions.

WHY THE CALLEE HAS NOTHING TO EMIT, and this is the part that reframes the cost
estimate. An owned by-value param is CALLER-DROPS by design: `compile_function`
does not register a `UserDrop` for one. There is exactly ONE exception in the
tree, and it is a working precedent for the ownership flip this row calls a
calling-convention change — `is_coroutine_compiled` gates a
`track_user_drop_var(struct_name, &param_name, alloca)` on the owned param,
with the comment "Every caller of a coroutine fn suppresses its own drop of the
owned arg ... keeping it a single drop". Callee-owned param, caller always
suppresses, NO signature change, NO returned discriminant, no ABI change of any
kind.

SO THE REMAINING GAP IS NARROWER THAN "A CALLING-CONVENTION CHANGE". Applying
that same flip to a conditionally-returned param leaves one problem, and it is
the same one this row is about, moved inside the callee:
`suppress_user_drop_for_var` (runtime.rs) REMOVES the action from
`scope_cleanup_actions` outright, so the one branch that returns the param
disarms the body on every path. What is actually needed is:

  (a) the coroutine-style ownership flip for params where the predicate is
      conservative-true, plus
  (b) a per-path escape flag — a callee-local `i1`, set where the param is
      returned, tested at the exit — so the callee's own disarm stops being
      flow-insensitive.

Both are callee-local. Neither changes the signature, the return value, or the
caller (which already suppresses unconditionally for these params).

STILL NOT ATTEMPTED HERE, deliberately, and the reasons are about risk rather
than mechanism:

  * The failure mode of getting (b) wrong is a DOUBLE body — precisely the
    defect B-2026-08-28-2 and -17 were filed for — while the current trade's
    failure mode is a missed body with no memory fault. The safe direction is
    the one already chosen, so a half-verified change here is worse than none.
  * All three channels must move together (the row's own point, unchanged), and
    the parts channel is layered on the whole-param one.
  * It must land in the INTERPRETER simultaneously. All four surfaces currently
    agree, so a codegen-only fix would convert a soundness bug into a
    run-vs-build divergence — which the kata corpus treats as a harder failure
    than the one it replaces.

WHAT THIS ADDENDUM CHANGES: not the disposition, only the price. The row read as
"needs a calling-convention change", which reads as out of scope indefinitely.
It needs a callee-local ownership flip that already exists for coroutines, plus
a one-bit flag, done across three channels and two backends at once. That is a
scoped design slice, not an ABI project.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while auditing this row for fixability; no code change was
made and no other row was touched.


CORRECTION 2026-08-28 -- THIS ROW'S CENTRAL PREMISE IS REFUTED. The row argues
the disposition from a claimed invariant: the tree has "already picked" the safe
horn, so a fix "would restore the DOUBLE body on exactly these shapes" and the
choice is "between two wrong counts in opposite directions". The double body is
ALREADY PRESENT on an adjacent shape, on all four surfaces, together with a read
of an already-dropped value -- filed as B-2026-08-28-51:

    fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } }
    take(true)   -> `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41`     2 bodies for one object

Same conditional move, same missing runtime bit; the only difference is that the
value is a LOCAL rather than a param. So there is no safe status quo being
protected here, and "a missed body, never a double drop" describes this row's
own channel rather than the compiler.

THE MECHANISM IS ALSO ONE LEVEL LOWER THAN THIS ROW PLACES IT. The predicates
are not the origin -- they are one consumer of a compiler-wide policy of
resolving conditional moves statically, which has two horns and no arbiter:

  * OVER-SCHEDULE: `merge_outer_states` (`src/ownership_oracle.rs`) merges a
    conditionally-moved place back to `Owned` because "codegen's runtime cap/null
    guard makes the over-scheduled conditional drop correct". That guard is a
    MEMORY guard; a user `Drop` BODY has no null to test, so the body re-runs.
  * UNDER-SCHEDULE: the `suppress_user_drop_for_var` family REMOVES the action.
    `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` states the consequence itself -- "Static
    and flow-insensitive like every sibling -- a conditional return disarms on
    all paths, which can only under-fire." This row's shapes.

Which horn a shape lands on is decided by whether its move site is RECOGNIZED,
not by its semantics: `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` reads only
`body.final_expr` / the last statement and never descends into `if` arms, so a
bare-identifier branch tail is not seen as a move at all. B-2026-08-28-52 is the
consequence -- ONE program wrong in OPPOSITE directions on the two backends,
interp over-scheduling and codegen under-scheduling the same binding.

WHAT THIS CHANGES FOR THE FIX. The row's addendum already names the right
primitive (a per-path escape flag); the correction is that it must be scoped by
an analysis rather than applied uniformly, for a reason the addendum does not
mention. Three COMPILE-TIME predicates read frame membership as a proxy for
ownership -- `has_armed_user_drop`, `has_armed_own_user_drop`,
`has_armed_container_elem_bodies` (`src/codegen/runtime.rs`) -- and drive
unrelated decisions from it; `has_armed_user_drop`'s doc gives the case
(B-2026-07-30-11's displaced-value leg, whose failure shape is
B-2026-07-31-38's double body). Retaining flag-guarded actions makes all three
answer true where they answered false. So "never remove, always guard" is not a
drop-in, and the flag has to be restricted to bindings an analysis marks
conditionally-moved while unconditional moves stay on today's static removal.

AND THERE IS NO NARROW FIX, which is worth recording before the next attempt.
Teaching `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` to descend into branch arms stops
B-2026-08-28-51 double-firing and immediately converts it into B-2026-08-28-52's
codegen bug, because the suppression it would then perform is the
flow-insensitive removal. Moving a shape between horns is not progress.

RECONFIRMED on 6085d46: all five of this row's programs and both controls
reproduce exactly as written, on all four surfaces.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while auditing this row for fixability. No code change was
made; two new rows were filed (B-2026-08-28-51, -52) and this addendum added.

fix:
FIXED by 4d37d4e, on both backends, by widening the analysis and BOTH
caller-side masks together -- which is what this row predicted, and it is worth
recording that the second half turned out to be the larger one.

THE PREFIX IS NOT AN APPROXIMATION OF THE PATH. That is the constraint that
shapes the whole change and the reason the widening could not stop at the
analysis. Reporting `Field("inner")` for `w.inner.r` -- the obvious way to make
an existing top-level mask do something -- would mask the entire subtree, and a
SIBLING field of `inner` that really does die inside the call would lose its
only body. That is a false escape, the direction this analysis is explicitly
built to avoid, so the prefix is a different and WRONG answer rather than a
coarser one. Measured: `struct I2 { r: R, s: R }` returning `w.inner.r` must
still print `s`'s body at the call, and it does.

SO THE MASKS GAINED THE SHAPE OF THE PATH. `ParamPath` is a path from the
parameter inwards. `FieldSkipTree` is the codegen counterpart -- fields skipped
at this level, plus a sub-mask for the walker each SURVIVING field recurses
into -- and the walker's symbol suffix folds in the whole tree, so two masks
that keep the same top-level fields and differ one level down cannot alias. The
interpreter's value mask gained the same two arms: a length-1 path REMOVES the
field, a longer one REPLACES it with a masked copy of itself, so the walk still
reaches its siblings.

THE NESTED DESTRUCTURE CAME ALONG FOR FREE, and the row anticipated it ("the
same limit applies to ... a nested DESTRUCTURE"). Carrying paths through the
alias table fixes both spellings with one change: `let W { inner, n } = w; let
I { r } = inner; r` now has the second `let` extend the first's path instead of
failing a whole-param gate. Pinned in both fixtures.

THE TUPLE SPELLING `p.0.1` IS STILL DECLINED, deliberately and for a different
reason than before: the analysis now reports it, but the tuple channel's skip
list is a FLAT element index list with nowhere to put a deeper answer, so it
keeps only length-1 tuple paths and leaves that shape at its pre-existing
behaviour -- the same safe direction, now enforced at the caller rather than at
the analysis. A tuple skip tree is the obvious follow-on and is NOT filed,
because no measurement of that shape exists; the row itself notes it was never
separately measured.

THE FLAT `fn_returns_param_parts` AND `escaping_field_indices` ARE REMOVED
rather than kept as thin wrappers. Every caller now reads the path form, and a
dead top-level-only answer sitting beside the real one is exactly how the next
reader masks a prefix by accident.

VERIFIED on a six-row matrix, identical across interp / jit / build: the row's
repro, the sibling row above, the nested destructure, an INTERMEDIATE that
declares its own `Drop` (whose body must still fire -- the mask removes a leaf,
not the level it hangs off), the one-level `w.inner` control the widening had to
leave untouched, and a `-> i64` control where nothing escapes. Both fixtures
proven RED by stashing only `src/`.
title: A NESTED PROJECTION out of an owned struct param still double-runs the field's user `Drop` body: `fn take(w: W) -> R { w.inner.r }` prints `drop 41` twice for one `R` on all three backends. This is `fn_returns_param_parts`' DOCUMENTED under-approximation working as designed -- it classifies a projection only off the WHOLE param and declines a projection-of-a-projection by construction, which leaves the pre-existing double body (the safe direction) -- so closing it widens the ANALYSIS, not the two caller-side sites B-2026-08-28-17 finished
detail:
Measured on the B-2026-08-28-17 fix commit, user `Drop` body counts
interp / jit / build:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct I { r: R }
    struct W { inner: I, n: i64 }
    fn take(w: W) -> R { w.inner.r }
    fn main() { let x = take(W { inner: I { r: R { id: 41 } }, n: 1 });
                println(f"{x.id}") }
                                                       -> 2 / 2 / 2

One `R` is constructed and its body runs twice -- the same defect
B-2026-08-28-17 fixed for a ONE-level field, at a two-level projection.

THIS IS THE DOCUMENTED UNDER-APPROXIMATION, working as designed rather than
failing. `fn_returns_param_parts` classifies a projection only off the WHOLE
param: `denote` answers `Some(Some(Field("inner")))` for `w.inner`, and a
projection of an already-projected part returns `None` by construction, with a
comment saying so. Reporting nothing leaves the shape exactly as it behaved
before that analysis existed -- the pre-existing double body -- which is the
SAFE direction on this channel, since a wrongly-reported part would suppress the
only body that runs.

So closing this is a widening of the analysis (model one more level of nesting,
and correspondingly teach both caller-side sites to mask a NESTED field rather
than a top-level index), not a bug fix in the sites. The two are separable and
the sites are the finished half.

The same limit applies to the tuple spelling (`p.0.1`) and to a nested
DESTRUCTURE, both of which the analysis declines for the same reason; they were
not separately measured for this row.

NOT a memory defect (bodies only; nothing on this channel frees).

fix:
FIXED by 0723acf.

CONFIRMED exactly as reported, on all four surfaces, and both controls held:
`fn take(v: Vec[(R, i64)]) -> R { v[0].0 }` aborted with `free(): double free
detected in tcache 2` (rc 134) under `karac run` and `karac build` alike while
`--interp` printed `41 n41`; the `let`-bound spelling aborted identically; and
the all-FieldAccess spelling `v[0].name` was clean. The row's diagnosis was
right in full -- a missing CLONE, not a missing suppression -- and the fix is
the one it names.

THE ONE THING THE ROW COULD NOT SAY IS WHERE THE CLONE GOES, and getting that
wrong looks like a working fix for five of the eight positions. Cloning at the
CONSUMERS -- the route `clone_owned_vec_index_element` takes for the WHOLE
element, and the first thing tried here -- was measured to fix `let`, `return`,
an argument, an assignment and a branch tail, and to leave STRUCT-LITERAL FIELD,
`Vec.push` and TUPLE CONSTRUCTION still aborting, because those three consume
without routing through it. Cloning at the READ, which is what the FIELD sibling
`clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read` does and why that spelling passes all eight,
reaches every destination through the single takeover
`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` already funnels ~87 call sites into.
So the fix is a tuple-index sibling of that function, called from the
`TupleIndex` arm exactly as the two field cloners are called from the
`FieldAccess` arm.

TWO ELEMENT SHAPES, TWO OWNERSHIP CONTRACTS, and conflating them would corrupt
memory rather than merely leak. A `{ptr,len,cap}` member takes the sibling's
full mechanism -- its own scope cleanup so a non-consuming read
(`println(v[0].0)`, `v[0].0.len()`) does not leak, registered in
`vec_elem_field_clone_slots` so a consuming destination takes it over by
zeroing the clone's `cap`. A STRUCT member must NOT go in that table: the
takeover zeroes field 2 of a `{ptr,len,cap}` at the recorded slot, and doing
that to a struct slot writes over an unrelated field. It follows
`clone_owned_vec_index_element`'s contract instead -- hand back a fresh value,
let the consumer own it -- which is the contract the whole-element read it is
projecting out of has always had.

A SECOND DEFECT, INDEPENDENT OF ANY CONTAINER, found because one position kept
failing after the clone was right. `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` has arms for an
f-string, an identifier, a FIELD (B-2026-08-06-8) and a nested block, and fell
through to `_ => {}` on a TUPLE-INDEX tail -- so the block frame dropped the
owner of the very value the block was handing to its consumer. Both sources it
can name were measured aborting on both compiled backends: this row's
`if c { v[0].0 } else { … }`, and a plain tuple LOCAL with no container in
sight (`let x = { let t = (f"a{1}", 2); t.0 };`). One arm, routed to the same
suppressor as its two siblings, fixes both -- the suppressor already holds the
right neutralizer for each source (the tuple-field move-out cap-zero for the
local, the clone takeover for the container element).

NOT by extending the move-out suppressors, exactly as the row insists.
B-2026-08-12-27 taught them to DECLINE index-rooted chains on purpose, and
recorded the cost of having done otherwise. The E2E test pins the semantics no
sanitizer can see: `let mut w = v[0].0; w = w + "X";` then reading `v[0].0`
must still print the value, which is what separates the clone from the
cap-zeroing that also silences the abort.

VERIFIED across interp / JIT / AOT on a 28-fixture sweep -- every consuming
position (let, return, argument, struct-literal field, `Vec.push`, tuple
construction, field assign, index assign, `if` tail, match arm, block tail),
every non-consuming read, a Copy member as the must-not-clone control, and the
container re-read after each consumer -- plus the same matrix over a struct
member. Two tests, both proven RED by stashing only `src/`: the LSan gate
(`test_tuple_element_of_a_container_element_is_cloned_not_aliased`, clean at
both -O2 and -O0) and the copy-semantics oracle
(`test_e2e_tuple_element_of_a_container_element_is_a_copy`).

THREE THINGS NOT COVERED, each filed rather than left as a silent remainder:

  * B-2026-08-28-32 -- a consumer that is itself an UNBOUND TEMPORARY
    (`println(Box2 { w: v[0].0 }.w)`, `println((v[1].0, 9).0)`, printing an
    `if`/`match`/block value without binding it) leaks the read. PRE-EXISTING
    and not this row's: the already-working FIELD spelling leaks the same
    shapes for the same byte counts, measured side by side.
  * B-2026-08-28-33 -- a cloned STRUCT member passed DIRECTLY as an owned
    argument (`takes_r(w[1].0)`) leaks 3 bytes, because an owned aggregate
    param is callee-owned by entry copy and nothing owns the caller's clone.
    This is a trade this fix makes knowingly: the same expression DOUBLE-FREED

  * B-2026-08-28-34 -- `v[0].0.id` (a field read through a tuple element OF a
    container element) still fails `karac build` on the loud "cannot resolve

ALSO FOUND AND FILED, same class one node kind over: B-2026-08-28-35 --
`let e = q[1].r` where `q: Vec[Q]` and `Q { r: R }` DOUBLE-FREES today, because
the field sibling clones only `{ptr,len,cap}` fields and declines a
struct-valued one.
title: A TUPLE ELEMENT PROJECTED OUT OF A CONTAINER ELEMENT (`v[0].0`) IS NEVER CLONED AND DOUBLE-FREES ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS, AT EVERY POSITION INCLUDING `let` -- `fn take(v: Vec[(R, i64)]) -> R { v[0].0 }` where `struct R { id: i64, name: String }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (rc 134) under `karac run` and `karac build` alike, while `karac check` passes and `--interp` prints `41 n41`. The all-FieldAccess spelling of the same read, `v[0].name`, is CLEAN, which is what isolates the tuple-index hop.
detail:
MEASURED on 381384f (all four surfaces: interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0):

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    fn take(v: Vec[(R, i64)]) -> R { v[0].0 }
    fn main() { let x = take([(R { id: 41, name: f"n{41}" }, 1)]);
                println(f"{x.id} {x.name}") }

    karac check          ->  All checks passed.
    karac run --interp   ->  `41 n41`                        <- correct
    karac run  (LLJIT)   ->  double free, rc 134
    karac build  (AOT)   ->  double free, rc 134  (also with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0)

TWO CONTROLS bound it:

  * POSITION IS IRRELEVANT -- `fn take(v: Vec[(R, i64)]) -> R { let x = v[0].0;
    x }` aborts identically. This is what separates it from B-2026-08-28-15,
    whose whole shape was "the `let` position is covered and the escaping ones
    are not". Here NO position works, so it is not a missing hook.
  * THE FIELD SPELLING IS CLEAN -- `fn take(v: Vec[R]) -> String { v[0].name }`
    is correct on all four surfaces. So the container-element read has a
    working path; the TUPLE-INDEX hop is the one that misses it.

WHY IT IS A MISSING CLONE, NOT A MISSING SUPPRESSION, and why this must not be
"fixed" by extending the move-out suppressors. An index-rooted place reads out
of a CONTAINER ELEMENT whose heap the container still owns and will free.
B-2026-08-12-27 established exactly this and made the suppressors DECLINE such
chains (`place_chain_is_index_rooted`, param_own.rs), because cap-zeroing the
element would trade a double free for a leak -- and it recorded the cost of
having done otherwise: `let mut w = ps[0].word; w = w + "X";` then reading
`ps[0].word` printed garbage. The correct treatment is the one the field
spelling already gets: DEEP-CLONE the read so the binding owns a copy and the
container keeps its own buffer. `clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read` does that for
`v[0].name`; nothing does it for `v[0].0`.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption on both shipped backends from a
`karac check`-clean program, with the interpreter disagreeing. Same class and
same reachability as B-2026-08-28-15, and indexing a Vec of tuples is an
ordinary thing to write.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-28-15, by probing whether the new
escaping-position hooks introduced a regression on container-element sources.
They did not -- this shape was already broken at every position before that
change and is unchanged by it, verified by measuring it against both the
stashed and restored fix. Filed separately rather than folded into that row
because the root cause is a different mechanism (missing clone vs. missing
suppression hook) and the two fixes do not overlap.

fix:
FIXED by d4da426.

CONFIRMED exactly as reported, on all four surfaces, and all three controls
held: `fn peek(w: ref W) -> String { w.r.name }`, its `ref self` twin and the
tuple-hop `p.0.name` all abort with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
(rc 134) under `karac run` and `karac build`; depth ONE, the depth-two `let`
spelling, and a scalar leaf through the same deeper place are all clean; and
`--interp` prints the field TWICE, which is the oracle.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT, and one hop off on the location. It named
`clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs` (B-2026-07-21-11) as the helper the return
position never reaches, which is true — but that helper is the `let`-position
cloner, and the return position already HAS one for depth one:
`maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg`'s borrowed-receiver arm, which is exactly why
`fn peek(r: ref R) -> String { r.name }` was clean. The defect is in that arm,
not in the absence of a cloner: it names the receiver with

    match &object.kind {
        ExprKind::SelfValue => Some("self".to_string()),
        ExprKind::Identifier(n) => Some(n.clone()),
        _ => None,
    }

so it recognises the receiver only when the receiver IS the root. At two hops
the object is itself a `FieldAccess`/`TupleIndex`, the match answers `None`, and
the arm declines — the read hands out an alias of the borrowed struct's buffer
and the caller's drop frees it a second time.

THE FIX walks the place chain to its root and admits it when that root is a
`ref` param, then resolves the receiver's type through `place_chain_type_name`
as a fallback (ordered so the depth-one path is bit-identical to before). The
walk is deliberately NOT `place_root_ident`: that one also walks through an
`Index` hop, and a container element is a different owner with its own cloner
one arm above, so admitting it would clone the same read twice.

A CLONE, NOT A SUPPRESSION, as the row insists, and the direction matters more
here than for an owned source. A `ref` binding does not own the caller's
storage, so cap-zeroing it would strand the caller's buffer with no owner AND
leave the caller reading a field it no longer holds. The E2E oracle pins that:
`let mut s = peek(v); s = s + "X";` then reading `v.r.name` must still print the
value.

RESTRICTED TO A `ref`-PARAM ROOT, unlike the three root classes the depth-one
gate admits. The other two (`for_loop_owned_agg_vars`,
`borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars`) are left at the depth they were measured at;
widening them is a separate question with the opposite failure mode — a clone
nothing takes over is a leak — and nothing in this row needed it.

VERIFIED across interp / JIT / AOT on a 14-shape sweep: the row's three
spellings, all three of its controls, depth THREE, the tail spelling, `mut ref`,
a struct-valued leaf, an ARGUMENT position, a `Vec.push` position, and an owned
(non-`ref`) receiver as the must-not-change control. Two tests, both proven RED
by stashing only `src/`: the LSan gate
(`test_ref_rooted_deep_place_heap_read_is_cloned_not_aliased`, clean at both -O2
and -O0, and carrying the argument and push rows because this helper also runs
at argument positions, where an unclaimed clone would surface as a leak rather
than an abort) and the copy oracle
(`test_e2e_ref_rooted_deep_place_heap_read_is_a_copy`).

NOT COVERED, filed as B-2026-08-28-37: a TUPLE-INDEX LEAF through the same
borrowed place — `fn peek(t: ref Wt) -> String { return t.pair.0; }` where the
field is a `(String, i64)` — still double-frees. This arm matches only a
`FieldAccess` at the outermost position, so a tuple-index leaf never reaches it
at all; that is a different resolution path (the leaf type comes from the
tuple's element `TypeExpr`, not a struct field table), pre-existing and
unchanged by this fix.
title: A HEAP FIELD READ THROUGH A DEEPER PLACE ROOTED AT A `ref` BINDING AND RETURNED DIRECTLY IS NEVER CLONED AND DOUBLE-FREES: `fn peek(w: ref W) -> String { w.r.name }` (and its `ref self` twin, and the tuple-hop `p.0.name`) aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (rc 134) under `karac run` and `karac build`, while `karac check` passes and `--interp` prints the field TWICE -- once from the callee, once from the caller reading it back -- which is the oracle: the read must be a COPY. DEPTH ONE is clean and so is the depth-two `let` spelling, which is what isolates it.
detail:
MEASURED on 0944166 (all four surfaces: interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0). Every program prints `n41` twice under `--interp`:

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    struct W { r: R, n: i64 }

    fn peek(r: ref R) -> String { r.name }              -> clean, all four
    fn peek(w: ref W) -> String { let s = w.r.name; s } -> clean, all four
    fn peek(w: ref W) -> String { w.r.name }            -> rc 134 compiled
    impl W { fn peek(ref self) -> String { self.r.name } }
                                                        -> rc 134 compiled
    fn peek(p: ref (R, i64)) -> String { p.0.name }     -> rc 134 compiled

So neither the `ref` mode nor the depth alone is the variable: it is a DEEPER
place (two or more hops) rooted at a `ref` binding, consumed at a RETURN
position with no intervening `let`. A scalar field through the same deeper place
(`fn peek(w: ref W) -> i64 { w.r.id }`) is clean, as expected -- there is no
buffer to free twice.

THE FIX WANTED IS A CLONE, NOT A SUPPRESSION, and getting that backwards would
turn this into a leak. A `ref` binding does not own the caller's storage: the
caller still holds the buffer and still frees it, and it can still read the
field afterward (the interpreter proves both). Cap-zeroing the source here would
strand the caller's buffer with no owner. What the compiled backends need is the
deep copy that B-2026-08-28-13 gave the DEPTH-ONE `let` position --
`clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs`, which deep-copies a heap field read through a
`ref`/`mut ref` binding so the binding and the caller's struct-drop own
independent buffers. That helper is hooked at the `let` positions; the return
position at depth >= 2 reaches no cloner at all.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption on both shipped backends from a
`karac check`-clean program, with the interpreter disagreeing. `fn peek(w: ref W)
-> String { w.r.name }` is about as ordinary an accessor as Kara has.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-28-15, by probing whether that row's
new escaping-position hooks over-fired on `ref` roots -- the failure mode a
suppression fix has to be checked against, since over-firing produces a leak
rather than an abort. They do not: this shape was already broken before that
change, confirmed by building the PARENT commit and measuring the identical
abort on all three compiled surfaces. Worth stating explicitly because the new
tail hook does fire on exactly these expressions, so "the hook caused it" was
the obvious hypothesis and is wrong. Filed separately because the mechanism is a
missing clone, not a missing suppression hook.

fix:
FIXED by 72b6f1c.

The row's diagnosis was exact on both counts: the leaf exits at
`place_source_tuple_leaf_cleanups`' `TypeKind::Path` test, one step past where
B-2026-08-28-8's nested-PATTERN spelling failed; and it needs the TUPLE channel
rather than the enum / nested-struct one, because
`track_destructure_leaf_cleanup` dispatches off the String/Vec/Map/Set/struct
side-tables and a tuple leaf is none of them. Both landed as written —
`emit_tuple_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` on the `ContainerElemBodies` channel over
`synthesize_tuple_drop_fn_te` for the memory, with the cap-zero the row calls
for.

THE MEMORY HALF IS NOT OPTIONAL, and the first cut proved it rather than
predicting it. The row asks for "the matching cap-zero of the source element so
the body is not run twice", which is right and incomplete: the cap-zero hands
this element's ownership AWAY from the source, so a bodies-only leaf leaves
nobody freeing it. Measured at 3 bytes leaked on a heap-carrying element. Memory
is registered BEFORE the bodies, so the LIFO drain runs the bodies against live
buffers.

PLACEMENT, which the row asked be settled with the fix rather than after it: the
body lands at the leaf's NLL end on every backend, matching the interpreter in
both directions. With the bound leaf UNREAD it prints before the following
statement (`drop 41` / `1`); with the leaf READ it prints after (`3` /
`drop 41`). That is the `ContainerElemBodies` channel doing what the row
required, and both spellings are pinned.

BOTH SOURCE KINDS, which the row's matrix does not cover. Its repro is a tuple
LOCAL; the fresh tuple-literal and call sources reach the identical hole through
a different function (`track_tuple_destructure_leaf_cleanups`, whose
`PatternKind::Binding` arm calls the same side-table dispatch). Fixing only the
place spelling would have left `let (inner, n) = ((R { .. }, 2), 1)` silent
beside a repaired `let p = ...; let (inner, n) = p`. The fresh path takes no
cap-zero — there is no named source to disarm, the same reason its own comment
gives for passing `register_user_bodies = true`.

MEASURED, interp / jit / build identical and valgrind-clean on every row: place
source with the leaf unused and used, fresh literal source, call source, two
Drop-bearing elements inside the bound tuple, and a triple-nested tuple bound at
the middle level. Unchanged: the nested-PATTERN spelling (B-2026-08-28-8) and
the undestructured control, the latter being what proves the source's own walk
does reach this element and therefore that the leaf can only take the body by
taking the element with it.

A RESIDUAL IS FILED SEPARATELY. A tuple-typed leaf whose element type has NO
`Drop` still gets no owner, on either source — 98 bytes on a fresh literal and 2
on a place source, measured with a runtime-built `Vec[String]` that the
optimizer cannot fold away. That is the B-2026-08-28-50 family one container
over (a leaf with no body to hang a walker off gets no memory owner either), not

fix take four corrections.
title: A TUPLE-TYPED BINDING LEAF loses its inner element's user `Drop` body when the source is a tuple LOCAL: `let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1); let (inner, n) = p;` prints `drop 41` under `karac run --interp` and NOTHING under `karac run` / `karac build`. The leaf is a `PatternKind::Binding` whose element `TypeExpr` is a `TypeKind::Tuple`, so it clears the place-source walker's PATTERN test and then exits at its `TypeKind::Path` test -- one step past where B-2026-08-28-8's nested-PATTERN spelling failed
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-28-8, by widening that row's shape matrix to the
spelling where the nested tuple is BOUND rather than destructured. Distinct from
-8 in both the failing test and the channel a fix needs, which is why it is a
separate row rather than a rider on that fix.

Measured AFTER -8's fix (the nested-PATTERN spelling is green there), drop-body
counts interp / jit / build / nopar:

    let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1); let ((r, m), n) = p;   -> 1 / 1 / 1 / 1   <- B-2026-08-28-8, fixed
    let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1); let (inner, n) = p;    -> 1 / 0 / 0 / 0   <- this row
    let p = ((R { id: 41 }, 2), 1); println(f"{p.1}");     -> 1 / 1 / 1 / 1   <- control, no destructure

So it is the BINDING of a tuple-typed element that loses the body, not the
nesting: the same source, undestructured, runs it on every surface.

MECHANISM. `place_source_tuple_leaf_cleanups` (stmts.rs) now recurses through a
nested `PatternKind::Tuple`, but this leaf is a `PatternKind::Binding`, so it
falls through to the classification below, which opens

    let TypeKind::Path(p) = &te.kind else { continue; };

and the leaf's `te` is a `TypeKind::Tuple`. The leaf is therefore skipped for the
same reason -8's was, one test later.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE ARM. The walker registers through the enum /
nested-struct channel (`register_var_from_type_expr` +
`track_destructure_leaf_cleanup`), and a TUPLE leaf is none of the kinds that
channel keys on -- `track_destructure_leaf_cleanup` dispatches off the
String/Vec/Map/Set/struct side-tables. Running a tuple leaf's element bodies
needs the tuple channel instead (`emit_tuple_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` /
`synthesize_tuple_drop_fn_te`, the pair the let-site uses for a tuple BINDING),
plus the matching cap-zero of the source element so the body is not run twice --
the source's own walk does reach it, per the control above. That is a different
mechanism from the one -8 needed, and a measured change in its own right.

NOTE ON ORDERING, worth settling with the fix rather than after it: the
interpreter prints `drop 41` BEFORE `1` here (the leaf `inner` is never used, so
its live range ends at the destructure), whereas for `let ((r, m), n) = p` with
`r` used it prints the body last. Whichever backend is taught this shape must
match the interpreter's NLL placement, not merely its count.

SOURCE NOTE: found by widening B-2026-08-28-8's shape matrix during that row's
fix, not by a targeted probe.

fix:
FIXED by 1aeaddc.

CONFIRMED as reported, with the IR making the mechanism unambiguous. Against
the BOUND spelling — which stores the tuple into a slot and calls
`__karac_drop_tuple_0(ptr %t)` — the UNBOUND `println(twoheap(1).1)` emits
neither the store nor the drop. Nothing owns the temporary, so every heap
element leaks: 12 bytes in 3 allocations per call at -O0 (`ada` + `unread` +
`sib`). The B-2026-07-22-2 family, reached through the one aggregate kind with
no fresh-temp registration.

THE FIX is the registration the bound case already has — materialize the temp
into a slot and `track_tuple_var` it — plus the takeover that has to come with
it. Both halves were measured failing alone, in this order:

  1. Registering a drop for the WHOLE tuple and excluding the projected element
     up front (zero its cap at materialization) fixes every CONSUMING position
     and leaves the NON-consuming ones leaking the element they hand out:
     `println(twoheap(1).1)` still lost `sib`, `twostr(1).0.len()` still lost
     its string.
  2. Covering the whole tuple with NO exclusion fixes those and double-frees at
     `let` / `Vec.push` / an argument, because the consumer already owned that
     element — measured before any change: `let w = twoheap(1).1` leaked
     `ada`+`unread` and NOT `sib`.

So the element handed out is owned by the temp's drop by default, and a
CONSUMING destination takes it over — `freshtemp_tuple_elem_slots` keyed by the
read's span, zeroed through `take_over_freshtemp_tuple_elem`, reached from
`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` for the return / argument /
struct-literal / push / block-tail positions and called directly from the `let`
arm, which does not route through that funnel. The same two-sided shape
`vec_elem_field_clone_slots` and `container_elem_struct_clone_slots` use, and
it is a third instance of the same lesson rather than a new invention.

THE COMPOSITION WITH B-2026-08-28-3 IS THE PART THAT WOULD HAVE BITTEN. That
fix registers the PROJECTED element when the projection is a struct whose field
is then read (`structpair(1).0.name`). With the tuple temp now owning
everything, both registrations covered the same buffers and the shape went from
leaking to `attempting double-free` — measured, on exactly the three fixtures
where both fire and nothing else. The resolution is that the -3 registration IS
a consuming destination in the takeover's sense, so it hands its element over
like any other. That also closes the leak -3 left behind, which its own row
names: reading `.0.name` out of a `(Person, String)` reclaimed the `Person` and
leaked the sibling `String`.

Needs the callee's declared element `TypeExpr`s to name the projected element
(`call_return_tuple_tes`, added by B-2026-08-28-3). Without them the exclusion
cannot be emitted, so the whole registration is skipped rather than risking the
double free — fail-closed to the pre-existing leak.

VERIFIED across interp / JIT / AOT on a 15-shape sweep, all clean at both -O2
and -O0: non-consuming reads of a heap element and of a Copy member, `let`,
`Vec.push`, an argument, both elements read from separate temps, the bound and
discarded controls, and the three -3 composition shapes. Every fixture set from
B-2026-08-28-3, -24, -25, -35 and -37 was re-run in full with no regressions.

title: A FRESH TUPLE TEMP IS NEVER DROPPED, so every heap element it owns leaks: `println(twoheap(1).1)` where `twoheap -> (Person, String)` loses the whole tuple -- the read element's own `String` included -- 24 bytes in 6 allocations across two calls at -O0. Pre-existing and independent of B-2026-08-28-3, which fixed only the PROJECTED element; measured RED on unmodified main, on a shape that needs no struct field read at all. Binding the tuple is clean.
detail:
A FRESH TUPLE TEMP IS NEVER DROPPED, so every heap element it owns leaks:
`println(twoheap(1).1)` where `twoheap -> (Person, String)` loses the WHOLE
tuple -- the read element's `String` included -- and no spelling of the read
changes it. Pre-existing and independent of the tuple-element field read
B-2026-08-28-3 fixed beside it; measured RED on unmodified main.

MEASURED under LSan at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (at -O2 the optimizer deletes the
dead allocations and the fixture asserts nothing -- the B-2026-08-04-17
hazard):

    struct Person { name: String, note: String, age: i64 }
    fn twoheap(k: i64) -> (Person, String) {
        return (
            Person { name: "ada".to_string(), note: "unread".to_string(), age: k },
            "sib".to_string(),
        );
    }

    println(twoheap(1).1); println(twoheap(2).1);
      -> 24 bytes leaked in 6 allocations

Twelve bytes in three allocations per call: `"ada"` (3), `"unread"` (6) and
`"sib"` (3). That is the entire tuple, so nothing owns the temporary at all --
not the projected element, not the siblings.

THE PLAIN-STRUCT SIBLING OF THIS IS ALREADY FIXED, which is what makes the gap
legible. B-2026-07-22-2 taught `compile_field_access` to materialize a fresh
CALL-RESULT STRUCT temp into a slot and register its struct drop
(`__freshtemp_fldobj` + `__karac_drop_struct_Person`, visible in the emitted IR
of `println(plain(1).name)`). B-2026-08-28-3 extended that registration to a
struct PROJECTED out of a fresh tuple, so `make().0.name` now drops the
projected element. Neither covers the tuple AGGREGATE: the remaining elements
have no owner, and a tuple temp with no struct field read anywhere in the
program -- the shape measured above, which has always compiled -- has no owner
either.

WHY IT IS ITS OWN ROW rather than a remainder in B-2026-08-28-3: that fix made
one spelling COMPILE for the first time, and the leak below it predates the
spelling. The shape above needs no struct field read at all and is RED on
unmodified main, so this is a distinct defect on a distinct mechanism (the
tuple temp's ownership, not the field resolution) and closing -3 does not
close it.

SEVERITY medium: silent, unbounded in a loop, and reachable from ordinary code
(any function returning a tuple with a `String`/`Vec` element, consumed without
binding). It is bounded in the other direction by how easily it is avoided --
binding the tuple (`let q = twoheap(1);`) is clean, measured -- and by x86 -O2
DCE hiding it in exactly the programs where the elements go unread.

TWO SEPARATE HOLES, and the row named only the second. It is worth recording
because the first is what made the shape unfixable by the route the row
proposed.

  1. A GENERIC CALLEE HAS NO `fn_return_type_exprs` ENTRY AT ALL. That table is
     populated by `declare_function`, which never runs for a generic function —
     only for its monomorphs. So `call_return_tuple_tes` answered `None` before
     it could even look at the element, and no amount of substitution
     downstream would have helped. Measured directly with an instrumented
     lookup: `key=firstof present=false`. The generic AST is available under the
     same name in `mono_state.generic_fns`, which is where `compile_generic_call`
     itself reads it, so the declared return type was never missing — it was
     being looked for in the one table that by construction cannot hold it.

  2. THE ELEMENT IS THE TYPE PARAMETER. With the return type in hand, `(T,
     i64)`'s element 0 is `T`, which B-2026-08-28-3 deliberately refused to
     record: taking a bare parameter name at face value resolves a field read
     against whatever unrelated struct also declares that field, the
     silent-wrong-answer trade B-2026-08-27-49 measured and rejected. `T` is now
     bound for THIS CALL from `call_type_subs`, the typechecker's per-call-site
     record, flattened through the active monomorph's `type_subst_names` so a
     generic call nested inside a monomorph resolves the outer parameter too.
     That is the same table and the same flattening `compile_generic_call` uses
     to select the monomorph, so the name resolved here is by construction the
     one whose layout the call actually runs against.

NOT `subst_monomorph_type_params`, which the row's own "fix shape is known"
note pointed at. It substitutes the ENCLOSING function's parameters, so it
would answer with the CALLER's binding for a same-named parameter — right only
by coincidence, and wrong exactly when both are generic. The row said as much;
this records which table replaced it.

PER-CALL BINDING IS WHAT THE E2E FIXTURE PINS. `Tag` and `Other` both declare
an `n` at DIFFERENT indices and both are passed to the same `firstof`, so a
resolution that bound `T` once — last writer wins, which is the failure
`emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr` actually had under B-2026-07-12-16 — prints one
of them wrong rather than refusing. Nothing else in the fixture would catch it.

STILL FAIL-CLOSED at every step: an unrecorded call site, an unbound parameter,
or a binding naming no known layout all yield `None` and the shape keeps
refusing loudly. A parameter bound to a builtin (`firstof(5)`) resolves to no

The non-generic control B-2026-08-28-3 fixed builds. Deliberate: the declared return type is `(T, i64)`, and recording the bare param name would resolve the read against an unrelated struct -- the silent-wrong-answer trade B-2026-08-27-49 measured and rejected.
detail:
A GENERIC callee's tuple element still cannot be named, so a struct field read
through it keeps refusing loudly: `fn firstof[T](x: T) -> (T, i64)` followed by
`let q = firstof(Tag { n: 9 }); q.0.n` fails `karac build` with "codegen: cannot
resolve field 'n' on this receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen)",
while `karac check` accepts it and the interpreter prints 9.

MEASURED, against a NON-generic control that B-2026-08-28-3 fixed:

    struct Tag { n: i64 }
    fn firstof[T](x: T) -> (T, i64) { return (x, 1); }
    fn make() -> (Tag, i64) { return (Tag { n: 9 }, 1); }

    let q = make();            q.0.n   ->  builds, prints 9      OK
    let q = firstof(Tag {..}); q.0.n   ->  BUILD FAILS, interp 9

DELIBERATE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT, and the reason is worth keeping: B-2026-08-28-3's
new sources read the callee's DECLARED return type, which for a generic callee
is `(T, i64)` -- the type PARAMETER, not the monomorph's argument. Recording
`"T"` would name no struct, and a consumer that took it at face value would
resolve a field read against whatever unrelated struct happens to declare that
field name. B-2026-08-27-49 measured exactly that outcome from the naive
version of its own fix and called it strictly worse than the bug, so both new
sources gate on the element naming a type codegen has a layout for and record
`None` otherwise. This row is the cost of that gate, made visible rather than
left implicit.

SAME CLASS AS B-2026-08-25-35 and B-2026-08-25-28: a type expression left in
terms of a type PARAMETER inside a monomorph. The fix shape is known -- the
`Index` arm of `type_name_of_expr` already calls `subst_monomorph_type_params`
for precisely this -- but that helper substitutes the ENCLOSING function's
parameters, and what is needed here is the CALLEE's, bound at the call site.
That is a different lookup and does not exist yet, which is why this is a
follow-up rather than a line in -3.

LOUD, NEVER SILENT, and the workaround is mechanical (destructure the tuple, or
bind the element). Hence medium.

FIXED by 05fefaa.

The row's analysis was right in every particular that could be settled by
reading code — two separable roots, each named exactly, each leaving half the
surface broken if fixed alone — and its one open question is the one that took
the work: "any fix here must answer 'who already frees this' per source kind
rather than assuming freshness implies unowned."

ROOT (a), the struct LITERAL source, took the widening the row prescribed: the
tuple path's `|| matches!(&value.kind, ExprKind::Tuple(_))`, in its struct
spelling, restricted to a plain non-shared struct literal.

ROOT (b), the bound leaf's missing body, took the tuple path's cascade — but
SHARED rather than transplanted a second time. `track_destructure_leaf_cleanup`'s
struct arm is now `track_destructure_struct_leaf_user_drop`, called from both
paths, with an `owns_memory` parameter. That parameter exists because the
own-`Drop` wrapper is body + fields + memory in ONE action and must REPLACE a
memory registration rather than join it; the helper returns whether it took the
memory so each caller can skip its own.

THE OWNERSHIP ANSWER IS NOT UNIFORM ACROSS THE ARMS, and both errors were
reached before the split settled. Measured under valgrind on a heap-carrying
field:

    BOUND leaf, literal source, memory left on the narrow flag
                                                3 bytes LEAKED
    UNBOUND field, literal source, both the discard walker and the
      unbound-field arm claiming it             12 frees / 11 allocs, ABORT

So the BOUND-leaf arms take the widened `fresh` and the UNBOUND-field arm stays
on `fresh_call`. A bound leaf moves the field out and nothing follows it; an
unbound one is already claimed by the discard walker one arm up.

WHAT MADE THE LITERAL LOOK UNIFORMLY OWNED is worth recording, because it is the
same mask B-2026-08-28-12's row names and it fooled this fix's first cut. These
programs are leak-clean while the leaf goes unused — LLVM deletes the whole dead
allocation chain — so an early measurement read "in use at exit: 0" and was
written up as "the literal temp already carries its own whole-aggregate drop".
It carries nothing. Registering a `Drop` body is what makes the buffer live
enough for the real answer to appear, which is how a bodies-only first cut
produced a fresh 3-byte leak. The measurement that settles it uses NO `Drop`
anywhere, so no body is in play:

    BOUND leaf, literal source, no Drop, heap field   3 bytes LEAKED
    BOUND leaf, call source                           clean
    BOUND leaf, place source                          clean

That pre-existing leak is closed by the same widening.

FINAL MEASUREMENT, interp / jit / build, all 1/1/1 and all memory-balanced:

    let W { r, n } = mk();                       1/0/0 -> 1/1/1
    let W { r, n } = W { r: R { .. }, n: 1 };    1/0/0 -> 1/1/1
    let W { r: _, n } = W { r: R { .. }, n: 1 }; 1/0/0 -> 1/1/1
    field-only-Drop leaf, call source            1/0/0 -> 1/1/1

CONTROLS, unchanged at one body: place, param and tuple sources, the wildcard
leaf over a CALL source (B-2026-08-28-12's own fix), and the field-only-Drop
leaf over a place source.

ALSO CLOSES B-2026-08-28-45 — the enum-typed field of the same fresh literal,

row hours earlier, from a different repro, and turns out to be root (a) seen

A RESIDUAL, unchanged by this and filed separately: an UNBOUND field whose type
has NO `Drop` gets no walker here and so no owner on the literal source —
measured at 98 bytes on a runtime-built `Vec[String]`, identical before and
after (verified by stashing `src/` and rebuilding).
title: A destructure of a FRESH STRUCT source loses user `Drop` bodies on BOTH compiled backends while the interpreter runs one: `let W { r, n } = mk()` and the struct-literal spelling both print nothing where one `drop 41` is due. Two separable roots -- `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` admits only `Call`/`MethodCall`, so a struct LITERAL never reaches the leaf path at all (the tuple literal got exactly this widening in B-2026-08-28-1 and the struct spelling never did), and even on the admitted call spelling the BOUND leaf registers memory cleanup but no user body. PLACE, PARAM and TUPLE sources are all correct, which is what localizes it
detail:
Measured on the B-2026-08-28-12 fix commit, user `Drop` body counts
interp / jit / build. Identical on a compiler built WITHOUT that fix (verified
by stashing `src/` and rebuilding), so this is neither caused nor repaired by
it:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct W { r: R, n: i64 }
    fn mk() -> W { W { r: R { id: 41 }, n: 1 } }

    BOUND leaf, fresh CALL source:
      let W { r, n } = mk();                          -> 1 / 0 / 0
    BOUND leaf, fresh LITERAL source:
      let W { r, n } = W { r: R { id: 41 }, n: 1 };   -> 1 / 0 / 0
    WILDCARD leaf, fresh LITERAL source:
      let W { r: _, n } = W { r: R { id: 41 }, n: 1 };-> 1 / 0 / 0

CONTROLS, all correct on all three backends, which is what localizes this to a
FRESH STRUCT source rather than to struct destructures generally:

    BOUND leaf, PLACE source:  let w = W { .. }; let W { r, n } = w;   1/1/1
    BOUND leaf, PARAM source:  fn take(w: W) { let W { r, n } = w; }   1/1/1
    BOUND leaf, TUPLE local:   let p = (R, 1); let (r, n) = p;         1/1/1
    WILDCARD leaf, fresh CALL: let W { r: _, n } = mk();               1/1/1
                               (that last one is B-2026-08-28-12's fix)

RUN-VS-BUILD, with the INTERPRETER on the correct side -- one body for one
object -- and both compiled backends silent.

TWO ROOTS, and they are separable. `finish_owned_struct_destructure` gates its
whole leaf-cleanup path on `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, which admits only
`Call` / `MethodCall`. So:

  (a) a struct LITERAL is not admitted at all, and the destructure reaches
      neither branch -- the exact hole B-2026-08-28-1 fixed for the TUPLE
      literal by widening at the call site (`|| matches!(&value.kind,
      ExprKind::Tuple(_))`); the struct spelling never got the equivalent. This
      is why the WILDCARD leg fails on the literal but not on the call: the
      B-2026-08-28-12 arm is inside that gate and never runs.

  (b) even when the gate DOES admit the source (the call spelling), the BOUND
      leaf registers memory cleanup but no user `Drop` BODY -- `bound_name`'s
      arm chain has no equivalent of the tuple path's
      `track_destructure_leaf_cleanup(.., register_user_bodies = true)`.

Fixing (a) alone would close the wildcard-literal leg and leave both bound legs
broken; fixing (b) alone would close the call-source bound leg and leave the
literal spelling untouched. Both are needed for the surface.

NOT a memory defect in the shapes measured: the same programs with a
heap-carrying `R { id: i64, name: String }` exit 0 with correct output. But note
the ADJACENT measurement from B-2026-08-28-12's own fix, because it is the
likeliest trap for whoever takes this: adding a body to a discarded fresh struct
element WITHOUT checking ownership produced an ASAN `double-free`, since a fresh
struct temp -- unlike a fresh TUPLE temp -- already carries its own
whole-aggregate drop. Any fix here must answer "who already frees this" per
source kind rather than assuming freshness implies unowned.

MECHANISM, enum half: `run_discarded_leaf_user_drop_bodies` (stmts.rs) opens with

    if self.type_decls.shared_types.contains_key(&name)
        || !self.type_decls.struct_types.contains_key(&name) { return; }

the one the BINDING-leaf arm of `track_destructure_leaf_cleanup` already uses for

each correct alone. 919f31e (B-2026-08-28-8) made codegen's place-source walker
recurse through nested tuple patterns; 429977d then added a `Wildcard` arm INSIDE
that walker, so on a place source the arm fires at nested depth. Its interpreter
twin (`run_wildcard_destructure_leaf_user_drops`) collects only TOP-LEVEL wildcard
positions, so it does not. On the FRESH path the same commit passes `None` for the
nested element TypeExprs -- documented there as "a recorded residual" -- so the
literal source runs no body on either side and the two agree on the wrong answer.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE COUNT SUGGESTS: B-2026-08-28-12 existed because all
three backends agreed on zero, which no A/B gate can report. These two shapes
took that same family and turned it into a real divergence in BOTH directions at
once, which means a kata exercising either spelling now fails the A/B rule for a
reason no ledger row described.

A THIRD SHAPE of the same family is measured and NOT fixed here, filed as its
own open row (B-2026-08-28-31): an enum that declares
its OWN `impl Drop`. The interpreter runs the enum's own body and skips the
payload, so the payload walker this row wires is the WRONG body there, not a
partial one -- and the right one lives on the wrapper, which also frees. Split
out rather than buried here, so the remainder stays on the work queue.

fix:
FIXED by d283401.

The row's diagnosis of the SYMPTOM was exact and its prescription was not, in a
way worth recording because it made the fix look larger than it is.

It expected the remedy to live on the combined `karac_drop_<E>` wrapper (body
AND memory), and therefore to need "the `free_memory` question answered for
enums first". Both halves turned out to be already available:

  * the right walker is the BODIES-ONLY one the STRUCT leaf already uses.
    `emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn` is named for structs, but for an ENUM
    name it finds `owns_body` true and the struct field-bodies walk `None`, so
    it emits a walker that calls `<E>.drop` and nothing else — no payload walk,
    no frees. Exactly the "bodies-only entry point for an own-Drop enum" the row
    asked for, already written.
  * `free_memory` is already answered for enums at this site: the memory branch
    routes a non-struct through `emit_enum_drop_switch`, so the per-site split
    B-2026-08-28-12 established (fresh tuple frees, place source does not)
    applies unchanged.

So the whole change is one more arm in the walker selection.

ONE BODY IS THE TARGET, NOT TWO, and the row did not have the measurement that
settles it. The same enum discarded through a STRUCT pattern's wildcard field --
`let W { e: _, n } = w` -- ALREADY ran `drop E` and only that, on all three
backends, before this fix. Making the tuple leaf run two would have put it out
of step with its own sibling. The row's worry that the payload walker prints
`drop R41` "instead of" `drop E` is right about which body is wrong, and this
takes the other one.

MEASURED, body counts interp / jit / build, pre-fix -> post-fix:

    let p = (E.A(R{..}), 1); let (_, n) = p;   1 / 0 / 0  ->  1 / 1 / 1
    let (_, n) = (E.A(R{..}), 1);              1 / 0 / 0  ->  1 / 1 / 1
    let p = (E.B, 1); let (_, n) = p;          1 / 0 / 0  ->  1 / 1 / 1
      (a PAYLOADLESS variant, which shows the compiled zero was about the OWN
       body and not about failing to reach a payload)
  CONTROLS, unchanged:
    payload-only enum, no own Drop             1 / 1 / 1   (B-2026-08-28-30)
    the STRUCT-pattern wildcard field sibling  1 / 1 / 1
    the same enum BOUND rather than discarded  2 / 2 / 2
    the same enum as a fresh ARGUMENT          2 / 2 / 2
