title: A CONTAINER-ELEMENT HEAP READ CONSUMED BY AN UNBOUND TEMPORARY LEAKS: `println(Box2 { w: p[0].word }.w)`, `println((p[1].word, 9).0)`, and printing an `if`/`match`/block value without binding it all lose the deep clone the read emits -- 3 bytes in 1 allocation each under LSan. Pre-existing on the already-working FIELD spelling, which leaks the same shapes for the same byte counts; the BOUND form of every one is clean. The consuming temporary takes the clone over and then dies without freeing it.
detail:
A CONTAINER-ELEMENT HEAP READ CONSUMED BY AN UNBOUND TEMPORARY LEAKS: reading
`ps[0].word` (or the tuple spelling `v[0].0`) into a struct literal, a tuple, or
a branch value that is PRINTED rather than BOUND loses the deep clone the read
emits, because nothing owns the temporary that consumed it. Pre-existing on the
already-working FIELD spelling, and independent of B-2026-08-28-24, which fixed
the tuple hop's double free beside it.

MEASURED under LSan, both spellings side by side, same byte counts -- which is
what identifies the temporary rather than the hop as the cause:

    struct P { word: String, n: i64 }
    struct Box2 { w: String }
    fn mkp() -> Vec[P] { return [P { word: f"a{1}", n: 1 }, ...]; }

    println(Box2 { w: p[0].word }.w);              -> 3 bytes in 1 allocation
    println((p[1].word, 9).0);                     -> 3 bytes in 1 allocation
    println(if c { p[0].word } else { p[1].word }) -> 3 bytes in 1 allocation
    println(match c { true => p[1].word, ... })    -> 3 bytes in 1 allocation
    println({ let q = P { word: f"t{1}", n: 2 }; q.word })
                                                   -> 2 bytes in 1 allocation

    let b = Box2 { w: p[0].word }; println(b.w);   -> CLEAN

The BOUND form of every one of them is clean, and so is the tuple spelling's
bound form -- so the read and the clone are both fine, and the leak is that the
consuming TEMPORARY has no owner to hand the clone's cleanup to. The read
registers the clone in `vec_elem_field_clone_slots` precisely so a consuming
destination can take it over by cap-zeroing it; a destination that is itself
unowned takes it over and then dies without freeing it.

SAME FAMILY AS B-2026-07-22-2 and B-2026-08-28-27 -- an aggregate temporary that
nothing owns, reached through one more expression kind. The difference from
those two is which side is missing: there the temp's own heap fields were never
freed, here the temp took over a clone's cleanup and then was not freed itself.

SEVERITY low: a leak, not corruption, bounded by the size of the read value, and
every one of these shapes is clean the moment the consumer is bound. It is
unbounded in a loop, which is why it is not `wontfix`.

The bound form is clean. A knowing trade made by B-2026-08-28-24 -- the same expression DOUBLE-FREED before it -- filed so the remainder is visible; the fix needs a struct-shaped takeover in `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex`, and registering the cleanup without it turns the leak back into a double free at `let`.
detail:
A CLONED CONTAINER-ELEMENT STRUCT PASSED DIRECTLY AS AN OWNED ARGUMENT LEAKS 3
BYTES: `takes_r(w[1].0)` where `w: Vec[(R, i64)]`, `R { id: i64, name: String }`
and `fn takes_r(r: R) -> i64`. The bound form (`let e = w[1].0;
takes_r(e);`) is CLEAN.

MEASURED under LSan at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:

    println(takes_r(w[1].0));            -> 3 bytes leaked in 1 allocation
    let e = w[1].0; println(takes_r(e)); -> clean

A KNOWING TRADE MADE BY B-2026-08-28-24, not a regression: that same expression
DOUBLE-FREED before it, on both compiled backends. The row is filed so the
remainder is visible rather than implied.

THE MECHANISM is the collision of two correct rules. B-2026-08-28-24 clones a
tuple member at the READ, because that is the only place that reaches all eight
consuming destinations. A STRUCT member's clone deliberately gets no scope
cleanup -- it follows `clone_owned_vec_index_element`'s contract, where the
consumer owns what it receives -- because the `{ptr,len,cap}` takeover it would
otherwise register (`vec_elem_field_clone_slots`) zeroes field 2 of a Vec header
at the recorded slot and would scribble on a struct. But an owned aggregate
PARAM is callee-owned by ENTRY COPY (`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned`,
caller-retains): the callee duplicates the heap fields into its own frame, so
the caller's clone is never taken over by anyone, and at an unbound call site
there is no binding to own it either.

THE FIX SHAPE IS KNOWN AND IS WHY THIS IS DEFERRED RATHER THAN GUESSED AT: the
struct clone needs a scope cleanup (`track_struct_var`) plus a struct-shaped
takeover in `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex`, zeroing every heap field's
cap rather than a Vec header's. That funnel already makes the exact distinction
required -- it skips a caller-retains `owned_struct_params` source, which is
what an owned aggregate param is -- so the caller would keep its cleanup here
and cede it at `let` / `push` / a struct literal. Registering the cleanup WITHOUT
the takeover is not a partial fix: it turns this leak back into a double free at
`let`, measured.

SEVERITY low: a leak bounded by the struct's heap, in one position, strictly
better than the double free it replaced, and clean the moment the argument is
bound first.

detail:
A STRUCT-VALUED FIELD READ OFF A CONTAINER ELEMENT IS NEVER CLONED AND
DOUBLE-FREES: `let e = q[1].r` where `q: Vec[Q]`, `struct Q { r: R, n: i64 }`
and `struct R { id: i64, name: String }` aborts under ASAN with `attempting
double-free`. The exact sibling of B-2026-08-28-24, one node kind over -- that
row was the TUPLE-INDEX hop, this is the FIELD hop when the field's type is a
STRUCT rather than a `{ptr,len,cap}`.

MEASURED under ASAN:

    let q = mkq(); let e = q[1].r; println(e.name);
        -> ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free

    let q = mkq(); println(takes_r(q[1].r));      -> CLEAN

The argument position is clean for a reason that makes the `let` failure sharper
rather than milder: an owned aggregate param is callee-owned by ENTRY COPY, so
the callee never frees the caller's alias. A BINDING has no such protection --
it registers its own drop over a buffer the container still owns, and both free
it.

THE MECHANISM is a gate, one line long. `clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read` is the
read-side cloner for a heap field of a container element, and it declines
anything that is not a `{ptr,len,cap}`:

    if !(self.is_string_type_expr(&fte) || self.extract_vec_elem_type(&fte).is_some())

A struct-valued field is exactly what that rejects, so the read hands back a
shallow alias of the element's storage with no clone anywhere.

WIDENING THE GATE IS NOT THE WHOLE FIX, which is why this is its own row rather
than a line in B-2026-08-28-24. A struct clone cannot be registered in
`vec_elem_field_clone_slots` -- the takeover there zeroes field 2 of a Vec
header at the recorded slot and would scribble on a struct -- so it needs the
struct-shaped ownership contract worked out in B-2026-08-28-33, and the two
should land together.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption on the compiled backends from a `karac
check`-clean program, same class and same reachability as B-2026-08-28-24, and a
struct field inside a Vec element is an ordinary thing to write.

agrees across all three backends, which is exactly why this needs its own entry:
agreement on the wrong number is the failure mode an A/B gate cannot report.

      let p = (E.A(R { id: 41 }), 1); let (_, n) = p;      1 / 1 / 1

      let W { e: _, n } = w;                                1 / 1 / 1

      take(E.A(R { id: 41 }))                               2 / 2 / 2

Two objects are constructed in every one of those programs -- the enum and its
payload -- and design.md § Drop requires each to be dropped exactly once at its
final owner's live-range end. The two DISCARD paths run one body; the two
non-discard paths run two. The discard paths are the ones losing a body, and
they lose the same one: the payload's.

design -- `emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn` for an own-`Drop` enum

reintroduce exactly the double free the per-site `free_memory` split exists to
avoid (measured in B-2026-08-28-12 and again in B-2026-08-28-36).

    `discarded_owned_temp_tail`, a `Self::`-static, purely SYNTACTIC predicate
    matching `Call` / `MethodCall` / a block tail of one. A unit variant never
    entered the arm at all, and so never reached the cleanup battery inside it;
    the enum registrar within was never the thing declining. Deciding a unit
    variant needs the enum tables, so the fix adds a `&self` sibling rather than
    widening the static predicate.

MEASURED, body counts interp / jit / build, pre-fix -> post-fix:

    let _ = E.B;                        0 / 0 / 0  ->  1 / 1 / 1
    let _ = S.X;   (an enum whose variants are ALL payloadless)
                                        0 / 0 / 0  ->  1 / 1 / 1
  CONTROLS, unchanged throughout:
    let e = E.B;                        1 / 1 / 1   BOUND
    take(E.B)                           1 / 1 / 1   fresh ARGUMENT
    let p = (E.B, 1); let (_, n) = p;   1 / 1 / 1   wildcard LEAF
    let _ = E.A(R { .. })               2 / 2 / 2   B-2026-08-28-39's shape

THE BARE SPELLING IS NOT FIXED, and its absence is a decision rather than an
oversight. `let _ = B` is already correct on the interpreter -- the `Identifier`
arm admitted it all along, which is exactly what made this family look
spelling-dependent rather than site-dependent -- and still runs ZERO compiled.
The aggregate registrar the codegen arm feeds never matches an `Identifier`
argument, because a let-bound enum's drop belongs to its binding and registering
a second caller-side drop over it would be a DOUBLE FREE rather than a missing
body. An earlier cut of this fix did admit it: it bought nothing (the registrar
declined anyway) and implied a support that is not present, so it was removed.
Filed as B-2026-08-28-43.

ALSO STILL OPEN, and a different site again: the BARE-STATEMENT spelling
`E.B;` (no `let _ =` at all) runs 0 / 0 / 0. Not this arm -- it is the
statement-expression discard, which has its own dispatch. Filed with
B-2026-08-28-43.

title: A PAYLOADLESS VARIANT OF AN OWN-`Drop` ENUM, DISCARDED BY `let _ =`, RUNS ZERO BODIES ON ALL THREE BACKENDS: `let _ = E.B;` where `impl Drop for E` prints nothing under `karac run --interp`, `karac run` and `karac build` alike, against design.md's "dropped exactly once at the live-range end of its final owner". Three controls isolate the discard site as the culprit -- the same value drops correctly when BOUND (`let e = E.B`), as a fresh ARGUMENT (`take(E.B)`), and through a tuple wildcard LEAF, all 1/1/1
detail:
Measured on 4997b9f, drop-body counts interp / jit / build. All three agree at
ZERO, which is why no parity gate reports it.

    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("drop E") } }
    fn main() { let _ = E.B; println("end"); }
      -> `end` on all three backends            0 / 0 / 0     <- this row

CONTROLS, all correct, and between them they rule out every explanation except
the discard site:

    let e = E.B; println("mid");             1 / 1 / 1   BOUND
    fn take(e: E) -> i64 { 7 }  take(E.B)    1 / 1 / 1   fresh ARGUMENT
    let p = (E.B, 1); let (_, n) = p;        1 / 1 / 1   tuple wildcard LEAF
                                                         (B-2026-08-28-31)

So it is not "a payloadless variant never drops", and not "an own-`Drop` enum is
skipped": the same value, the same type, drops exactly once in every other
position. Only `let _ =` loses it.

MECHANISM, on the interpreter side and confirmed by reading:
`discard_rhs_produces_owned_value` decides whether the discard fires at all, and
its arms are `StructLiteral`, `Identifier`, `Tuple`, `Call` and `MethodCall`. A
UNIT variant is none of those -- `E.B` is a bare `ExprKind::Path` -- so the gate
answers false and no body fires. The neighbouring `E.A(R { .. })` is a `Call`,
which is how the payload-bearing spellings reach the site at all
(B-2026-08-28-39 fixed what happens once they do).

The compiled backends are at zero too, so this needs its own answer on that side
rather than the interpreter simply being taught to match: both are wrong against
the bound/argument/leaf behaviour they themselves implement.

fix:
FIXED by ed405c3.

CONFIRMED as reported, and the identifier-rooted control held: `let s =
h.xs[0].name` and `impl H { fn peek(ref self) -> String { self.xs[0].name } }`
both abort with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (rc 134) on both
compiled backends, while the identical read off a bare local `Vec[R]` is clean
and the interpreter prints the field twice.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS EXACT — one gate, `ExprKind::Identifier` on the
container in `clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read` — and the fix is the one it
proposes: answer the gate's real question from the FIELD's declared type.

    let ExprKind::Identifier(cname) = &container.kind else { return Ok(val) };
    if !slice_elem_types.contains(cname) && !map_key_types.contains(cname)
        && !vec_elem_types.contains(cname) { return Ok(val); }

That pair asks "is this an owning Vec / Slice / Map, so the element's heap has
an owner that will free it". For a bare local the answer is a per-variable
registry keyed on the name; for a field it is the field's own type, which
`vec_index_elem_type_expr` already resolves (its `self.toks[i]` arm, with
monomorph substitution) and which the very next statement requires to succeed.
So the container shape now admits a FieldAccess, the registry check stays
scoped to the identifier case, and a field that is not a collection still
declines a few lines down — fail-closed, with no second copy of the rule.

WIDENED IN LOCKSTEP WITH THE TUPLE-INDEX SIBLING. The same Identifier-only gate
is duplicated in `clone_vec_elem_tuple_index_read` (B-2026-08-28-24), and
`h.ps[0].0.name` over a `Vec[(R, i64)]` FIELD has the identical hole. Fixing
one and not the other would leave the two spellings of one read disagreeing
about which containers own their elements — the asymmetry this family has
produced at every other layer, so it is closed here rather than filed.

CONSUMING POSITIONS ONLY, as measured. `let`, a struct-literal field,
`Vec.push` and `return` aborted; an ARGUMENT position and every non-consuming
read were already clean, because an owned aggregate param is callee-owned by
entry copy and a borrow frees nothing. Those rows are in the fixture as the
opposite direction: this clone carries its own scope cleanup, so they are what
fails if a future change registers the clone without the takeover.

VERIFIED across interp / JIT / AOT on seven shapes plus the tuple spelling, and
every fixture set from B-2026-08-28-3, -24, -25, -27, -34, -35 and -37 re-run
in full with no regressions.
`test_field_rooted_container_heap_field_read_is_cloned` gates it, clean at both
-O2 and -O0 and proven RED by stashing only `src/`
(`heap-use-after-free` in memcpy).

title: A HEAP FIELD READ OFF A FIELD-ROOTED CONTAINER IS NEVER CLONED AND DOUBLE-FREES: `h.xs[0].name` where `struct H { xs: Vec[R] }` and `struct R { id: i64, name: String }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (rc 134) on both compiled backends, and so does the `ref self` twin `self.xs[0].name`, while `karac check` passes and `--interp` prints the field twice. The IDENTIFIER-rooted spelling of the same read is CLEAN, which is what isolates the container ROOT: `clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read` requires `ExprKind::Identifier` for the container.
detail:
A HEAP FIELD READ OFF A FIELD-ROOTED CONTAINER IS NEVER CLONED AND
DOUBLE-FREES: `h.xs[0].name` where `struct H { xs: Vec[R] }` and
`struct R { id: i64, name: String }` aborts with `free(): double free detected
in tcache 2` (rc 134) on both compiled backends, while `karac check` passes and
`--interp` prints the field twice. The IDENTIFIER-rooted spelling of the same
read (`v[0].name` over a local `Vec[R]`) is clean.

MEASURED on unmodified main (0dbf4bd), both roots:

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    struct H { xs: Vec[R] }

    let v: Vec[R] = [...]; let s = v[0].name;          -> clean
    let h = H { xs: [...] }; let s = h.xs[0].name;     -> rc 134
    impl H { fn peek(ref self) -> String { self.xs[0].name } }
                                                       -> rc 134

THE MECHANISM is one gate in `clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read`, the read-side
cloner for a heap field of a container element:

    let ExprKind::Identifier(cname) = &container.kind else { return Ok(val); };
    if !slice_elem_types.contains(cname) && !map_key_types.contains(cname)
        && !vec_elem_types.contains(cname) { return Ok(val); }

A FIELD-rooted container (`h.xs`, `self.xs`) is not an identifier, so the
cloner declines and the read hands out a shallow alias of the element's buffer
— which every owning destination then frees alongside the container.

RESOLUTION IS NOT THE PROBLEM HERE, which is what makes this a narrow fix.
`vec_index_elem_type_expr` already resolves a FieldAccess-rooted index (its
`self.toks[i]` arm, with monomorph substitution), and `place_chain_type_name`
does too. Only the container-shape gate and the registry lookup that follows it
assume a bare name. What the gate is really asking — "is this an owning Vec, a
Slice or a Map, so the element's heap has an owner that will free it" — has to
be answered from the FIELD's declared type instead of from a per-variable
registry keyed on an identifier.

SEVERITY high: silent memory corruption on both shipped backends from a
`karac check`-clean program, with the interpreter disagreeing, and a `Vec`
field inside a struct read through an accessor is entirely ordinary code — it
is the shape the self-hosted parser is written in (`self.tokens[self.pos]`).

SOURCE NOTE: found while gating B-2026-08-28-34, whose fixture used
`self.xs[0].0.name` for the `self`-rooted row. That row's own fix (a tuple hop
in the cloner's walk) did not help, and dropping the tuple hop entirely still
aborted — so the container ROOT, not the hop, was responsible. Confirmed
pre-existing by rebuilding at stashed `src/` and re-running both spellings.

fix:
FIXED by d5dbdcb.

THE ROW UNDERSTATED ITS OWN SCOPE BY A FACTOR OF FOUR, and finding that out is
most of the work. It filed two spellings; widening its repro across positions
showed the BARE form is a weaker path at every fresh-temp position, while the
QUALIFIED form is correct at all of them. Drop-body counts interp / jit / build,
measured on b75a1f0:

    let _ = B;                        1/0/0   vs  E.B  1/1/1   (the row)
    take(B)                           0/0/0   vs  E.B  1/1/1   (new)
    let p = (B, 1); let (_, n) = p;   1/0/0   vs  E.B  1/1/1   (new)
    let (_, n) = (B, 1);              1/0/0   vs  E.B  1/1/1   (new)
    B;  /  E.B;                       0/0/0   both spellings   (the row)

Fixing only the row's first line would have left `take(B)` at 0/0/0 next to a
repaired `let _ = B` — an arbitrary place to stop, and one that would have read
as deliberate. The struct-FIELD wildcard (`W { e: B, .. }` destructured) is the
one fresh-temp position the bare form already reached; it is pinned as a control
so the fix cannot regress it while moving its siblings.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS OF THE BLOCKER WAS EXACT: "the aggregate registrar never
matches an `Identifier` argument, since a let-bound enum's drop belongs to its
binding and a second caller-side drop would be a double free", and "closing this
means distinguishing an `Identifier` that names a VARIANT and is not a local
from an `Identifier` naming a local, inside a registrar whose current invariant
is never-an-`Identifier`". That is exactly what landed, and the invariant is
intact: `fresh_bare_unit_variant_enum` answers only for a name that no local,
const-generic substitution or module binding shadows -- MIRRORING
`compile_expr`'s `Identifier` resolution order rather than approximating it --
and `enum_name_of_expr` is deliberately not used for this shape, because its
`Identifier` arm resolves through `var_type_names`, i.e. precisely the local
case.

THREE CAUSES, one per surface, and only the first is the one the row named:

  * The codegen REGISTRAR, as above.
  * The tuple LEAF's element type. `infer_arg_elem_te` asks
    `enum_name_of_expr` first, which answers `None` for a non-local
    `Identifier`, so a bare-variant element resolved to the EMPTY type name and
    the discarded leaf was classified as nothing at all. The bare-variant leg is
    asked there rather than inside `enum_name_of_expr`, whose twenty other
    callers really are asking about a local.
  * The INTERPRETER's argument walk, which is the one that had already been
    written for this shape and still could not see it. It excluded a named
    binding with `env.get(v).is_none()` -- but the item pass seeds EVERY unit
    variant into the OUTERMOST scope as a constant, so that test answers `Some`
    for the variant exactly as it does for a local, and the exclusion meant for
    bindings swallowed the variant whole. `Env::is_outermost_only` asks whether
    an INNER scope binds the name, which is the question that separates them.
    The row's note that "the interpreter is already correct here" held for
    `let _ = B` and not for `take(B)`.

The two backends restrict the admission to USER-declared enums, which makes them
agree BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by convention -- the Arrow-twin rule: the
interpreter's `find_enum_for_variant` scans `program.items`, which carries no
baked stdlib, and codegen filters `seeded_enum_names`. A bare `None` is what
this excludes in practice, and `Option`'s payload cleanup stays with its own
machinery at every one of these sites.

CONTROLS, all measured, all unchanged at ONE body -- these are the double-free
direction the registrar's invariant exists to guard: a BOUND local, a bound
local PASSED ON, a PASSTHROUGH callee, and a LOOP (one body per iteration, not
an accumulating registration). Two enums with distinct bare variant names each
resolve to their own enum. An enum with no user `Drop` stays silent. A shared
enum is untouched (and diverges identically in both spellings -- filed
separately). A local cannot in fact shadow a variant name, since `let B = ...`
is rejected as a refutable pattern; the shadowing guard stays anyway, because
`fresh_bare_unit_variant_enum` is a general predicate and the parameter and
const-generic cases are not covered by that syntax rule.

The ASAN fixture measures the double-free direction directly rather than
inheriting it, on an enum whose OTHER variant carries a `String`: admitting an
`Identifier` at all is what the registrar declined to do, so a spurious second
owner would run the drop switch twice over a live heap word.

FOUR NEIGHBOURS were isolated by the same sweep and filed separately rather than
folded in, each with a control proving it is NOT spelling-dependent and so not
this row: a fresh struct-literal wildcard destructure (interp 1 / compiled 0), a
bound struct holding a unit variant (interp 0 / compiled 1, the opposite
direction), a bound TUPLE holding one (0/0/0), and a discarded payload-bearing
ctor STATEMENT (interp 1 / compiled 2).
title: TWO MORE SPELLINGS OF A DISCARDED PAYLOADLESS OWN-`Drop` ENUM VARIANT STILL RUN NO BODY: `let _ = B;` (the BARE spelling) is interp 1 / compiled 0, and the bare STATEMENT `E.B;` is 0/0/0. B-2026-08-28-41 fixed the qualified `let _ = E.B` on both backends; the bare `let` spelling is blocked by a deliberate invariant -- the aggregate registrar never matches an `Identifier` argument, since a let-bound enum's drop belongs to its binding and a second caller-side drop would be a double free -- and the bare statement is a different dispatch entirely
detail:
Measured on b75a1f0 (B-2026-08-28-41's fix in place), drop-body counts
interp / jit / build:

    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("drop E") } }

    let _ = B;      (BARE spelling of the same discard)   1 / 0 / 0
    E.B;            (bare STATEMENT, no `let _ =`)        0 / 0 / 0

    FIXED by -41 and shown for contrast:
    let _ = E.B;                                          1 / 1 / 1

CONTROLS, all correct, same as the ones that localized -41: the value drops
exactly once when BOUND, as a fresh ARGUMENT, and through a tuple wildcard LEAF,
on every backend.

TWO DIFFERENT CAUSES, which is why this is one row with two rows' worth of care
rather than a re-file of -41:

  * `let _ = B` -- the interpreter is already correct here (its
    `discard_rhs_produces_owned_value` `Identifier` arm admitted the bare
    spelling all along; that asymmetry is precisely what made the family look
    spelling-dependent). Compiled is zero, and the blocker is DELIBERATE: the
    aggregate registrar the discard arm feeds never matches an `Identifier`
    argument, because a let-bound enum's drop belongs to its binding and
    registering a second caller-side drop over the same value is a double free,
    not a missing body. Closing this means distinguishing "an `Identifier` that
    names a VARIANT and is not a local" from "an `Identifier` naming a local",
    inside a registrar whose current invariant is "never an `Identifier`" --
    a measured change against the double-free direction, not a widened match arm.
    An attempt to admit it during -41 was removed for exactly this reason: it
    bought nothing, since the registrar declined anyway.

  * `E.B;` -- a bare statement-expression, which does not reach the wildcard-let
    discard arm at all; that dispatch is separate and needs its own answer.

fix:
FIXED in two commits, one per half: 6ca7ed6 for the tuple literal, bb6f7df for
the branch value.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS OF THE SECOND HALF WAS WRONG, and correcting it is most of
what this fix is. The row asserts that "the `if` spelling of the identical match
program is CLEAN, so the two branch forms already disagree, and that asymmetry
is the thing to resolve". Re-measured on the row's own fixtures, the split ran
the OTHER way -- `println(if …)` leaked and `println(match …)` was clean -- and
once the CONSUMER is held fixed there is no split at all. Both branch forms
behave identically; which one LSan flags on a given fixture is a stack-layout
accident, not a codegen difference. Their IR is identical modulo block naming
and ordering, with the same clone, cap-zero and free counts and the same
allocation profile at exit.

THE REAL AXIS IS THE CONSUMER, measured at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0:

    println(if c { p[0].word } else { p[1].word })    -> 3 bytes, 1 alloc
    println(match c { true => p[0].word, ... })       -> 3 bytes, 1 alloc
    use_it(if c { … })  /  use_it(match c { … })      -> 3 bytes, 1 alloc
    let d = <either>                                  -> clean
    out.push(<either>)                                -> clean
    <either> as a discarded statement                 -> clean

`println` borrows and never takes the clone over; a by-value call argument
leaves the caller owning the buffer under this codegen and so does not either.
A `let` init and a `Vec.push` argument do -- which is why they were already
clean, and why they are the shapes a naive fix breaks. The by-value call
argument was NOT in the row at all; it is the same defect one consumer over.

THE MECHANISM, correctly stated. The read deep-clones and registers the clone's
own cleanup so a non-consuming read does not leak. An arm tail is a CONSUMING
position, so the arm-tail suppressor neutralizes that cleanup -- correct, the
arm's slot must not free what escaped it. Nothing at the merge then owned the
escaping value. So it is the same two-sided shape as B-2026-08-28-32 and
B-2026-08-28-27: an owner is missing, not an owner being wrongly removed, which
is the opposite of what the row says about the match arm.

THE FIX registers an owner for the merged value and records it under the branch
NODE's span, so every destination that DOES take ownership takes it over
through the funnel the ~87 other consuming positions already use. Without that
second half it trades the leak for a double free on `let`, `push` and `return`.
Four small pieces support it: the element type each clone was tracked with is
recorded beside its slot (a `String` drains as `i8`, a `Vec[U]` by its inner
shape); the funnel signals when it neutralizes a clone; `compile_expr` stashes
the branch node's span, because `compile_if` / `compile_match` are handed the
condition and the arms but never the node -- the same reason
`discarded_branch_spans` is keyed on the condition; and each merge arms the
owner only when an arm actually took a clone over.

THE TUPLE-LITERAL HALF (6ca7ed6) is the shape the row describes accurately, and
the row's account of WHY it declined is right: `track_freshtemp_tuple_object`
resolves the projected element's `TypeExpr` from `call_return_tuple_tes`, and a
literal has no callee. What that `TypeExpr` is FOR is the exclusion -- zeroing
the projected element's cap -- and for a `{ptr,len,cap}` member the LLVM shape
answers that as well as a name would, since `String` and `Vec` are zeroed
identically. A struct member still declines, because guessing a `TypeExpr`
there would zero the wrong bytes. `value_block_hands_out_its_tail` also had to
admit a tuple literal, one aggregate kind over from the struct literal -32
added. The SCALAR projection is the third case and the one that made the first
attempt wrong: `(p[1].word, 9).1` has nothing for a consumer to take over, so
declining it outright left the tuple's OTHER member with no owner; it now
registers the drop and records no takeover entry.

VERIFIED at both -O2 and -O0 and proven RED by stashing only `src/` (18 bytes
in 6 allocations for the branch fixture, 3 bytes in 1 for the tuple one). The
discard rows are kept in the fixture even though they need nothing: an owner
armed on a discard would free a buffer the container still holds, which the
trailing reads of `p` would surface as a use-after-free rather than a leak.
title: TWO SHAPES OF THE B-2026-08-28-32 FAMILY STILL LEAK: a container-element heap read consumed by an unbound TUPLE LITERAL (`println((p[1].word, 9).0)`), and one handed out of ANY BRANCH VALUE -- `if` and `match` alike -- into a consumer that does not take ownership, which is `println(...)` or a by-value call argument -- 3 bytes in 1 allocation apiece at -O0. FILED CLAIMING an if-vs-match asymmetry (`if` clean, `match` leaking); re-measurement refutes it in both directions -- the two forms emit identical IR and identical allocation profiles, and the real axis is the CONSUMER, with `let`, `Vec.push` and `return` already clean because they take the clone over.
detail:
TWO SHAPES OF THE B-2026-08-28-32 FAMILY STILL LEAK, each on its own mechanism
rather than on the one that row's fix addressed. A container-element heap read
consumed by an unbound TUPLE LITERAL or handed out of a MATCH ARM loses the
clone: 3 bytes in 1 allocation apiece, measured under LSan at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (at -O2 the optimizer deletes the dead allocation and the
fixture asserts nothing).

    struct P { word: String, n: i64 }
    fn mkp() -> Vec[P] { return [P { word: f"a{1}", n: 1 }, ...]; }

    println((p[1].word, 9).0);                             -> 3 bytes, 1 alloc
    println(match c { true => p[1].word, false => p[0].word });
                                                           -> 3 bytes, 1 alloc

    println(Box2 { w: p[0].word }.w);                      -> fixed (-32)
    println(if c { p[0].word } else { p[1].word });         -> clean
    println({ let q = P { word: f"t{1}", n: 2 }; q.word }); -> clean
    let d = if c { p[0].word } else { p[1].word };          -> clean

WHY THEY ARE NOT THE SAME FIX. B-2026-08-28-32 widened
`value_block_hands_out_its_tail` to admit a struct literal, which is the gate
that arms a fresh-temp drop for a FIELD-ACCESS RECEIVER. Neither remaining shape
goes through that gate:

  * The TUPLE LITERAL is a projection, not a receiver — it would route through
    `track_freshtemp_tuple_object` (B-2026-08-28-27), which declines because it
    resolves the projected element's `TypeExpr` from
    `call_return_tuple_tes` and a literal has no callee to read it from. It
    needs the element types derived from the literal's own elements, and the
    takeover cannot be emitted without them.

  * The MATCH ARM is the opposite problem: nothing is missing an owner, an owner
    is being REMOVED. `compile_match`'s per-arm
    `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg(&arm.body)` hits the
    `vec_elem_field_clone_slots` takeover and cap-zeroes the clone — correct
    when the match's value is consumed by something that owns it, a leak when
    the consumer is `println`. The `if` spelling of the identical program is
    clean, so the two branch forms already disagree, and that asymmetry is the
    thing to resolve.

SEVERITY low, for the reasons the parent row gives: a leak rather than
corruption, bounded by the read value, and clean the moment the consumer is
bound. Unbounded in a loop, which is why it is not `wontfix`.

    enum E { A(R), B }   impl Drop for E { println("drop E") }

FIXED by 9727cdb. Both this row and B-2026-08-28-47 are one gap seen from two
positions, fixed together because the two backends had to move in step.

CODEGEN kept the enum out of the tuple-element walker deliberately:
`elem_te_runs_user_drop` admitted a `Path` head only when it named a user
STRUCT, on the stated grounds that enum bodies "ride the enum-payload walker".
That is true for a BOUND local, and true for a struct FIELD since
B-2026-08-28-40 gave the field walker its own enum arm -- but nothing registers
such a walker for a tuple ELEMENT, which is why -47 was silent on all three
backends. The fix admits a non-shared user enum and gives
`emit_slot_drop_bodies_at` an enum leg mirroring that field arm instruction for
instruction: the enum's own body, then its live variant's payload bodies.
Option/Result keep the exclusion -- their payload level is the
`optres_payload_heads` leg, and admitting them twice would double-fire.

THE INTERPRETER needed the same arm at FOUR positions whose dispatch was
struct-shaped and fell through: the binding-level element loop
(`run_array_element_user_drops`), the struct-field walk
(`drop_user_drop_fields_of_value` -- this row), `run_tuple_item_user_drops`,
and the tuple-FIELD arm. Its doc had justified the omission as "codegen's pass
is struct-field-only, and matching its scope exactly is what keeps the two
backends in step"; that reasoning had gone stale when codegen gained the field
arm, which is precisely how this row came to be a divergence in the
interpreter-silent direction.

commit. That predicate does not only select walks -- it gates the move-out
bookkeeping. With it false, `struct W { e: E }` was not drop-relevant, so
destructuring `w` never marked it moved and the parent's field walk still ran
at `w`'s death. The first cut therefore printed `E`'s body TWICE on
`let W { e: _, n } = w`, a control that had been correct. Instrumenting the
walk's entry showed the difference plainly: the struct analogue enters the walk
with the discarded LEAF's value, this one entered with the whole parent.

codegen's selection rule (it reaches an enum member only through
`type_runs_user_drop`, which answers for an enum via `drop_method_keys` alone).
Ungated, the interpreter also fired for an enum with NO own Drop but a
Drop-bearing payload, and for a Vec element of any own-Drop enum -- both silent
on every backend today. Measured against a stashed build: each case turned a
both-backends-silent shape into a fresh run-vs-build divergence, i.e. the exact
failure this row is about, newly created one position over. Both shapes are
real and are filed separately rather than fixed here, because closing them
means widening CODEGEN first.

KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), byte-identical on each: the five target shapes now correct,

`tests/interpreter.rs` and `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`, and pin the exclusions
AS SILENCE so a later widening cannot land on one backend only. The ASAN test

title: A STRUCT HOLDING A UNIT VARIANT OF AN OWN-`Drop` ENUM DIVERGES IN THE INTERPRETER-SILENT DIRECTION when it is never destructured: `let w = W { e: E.B, n: 1 }; println(w.n)` runs `drop E` on both compiled backends and NOTHING in the interpreter -- the opposite direction from every neighbouring row in this family
detail:

    enum E { A(R), B }   impl Drop for E { println("drop E") }
    struct W { e: E, n: i64 }

    NEVER destructured:
      let w = W { e: E.B, n: 1 }; println(f"{w.n}");   0 / 1 / 1
      let w = W { e: B,   n: 1 }; println(f"{w.n}");   0 / 1 / 1
    DESTRUCTURED (the control, correct):
      let w = W { .. }; let W { e: _, n } = w;         1 / 1 / 1

interpreter-fires / compiled-silent; this one is compiled-fires /
interpreter-silent, and the compiled answer is the RIGHT one -- `w` owns an `E`,

interpreter gap: a struct field holding an own-`Drop` ENUM does not reach the
binding's drop walk, while the same field destructured out DOES.

destructure family: the value here is never destructured at all.

title: A TUPLE HOLDING A UNIT VARIANT OF AN OWN-`Drop` ENUM RUNS NO BODY ON ANY BACKEND when it is never destructured: `let p = (E.B, 1); println(p.1)` is 0/0/0, while the same tuple DESTRUCTURED through a wildcard leaf is 1/1/1 -- backend-consistent, so no parity gate can report it
detail:
Measured on d5dbdcb, drop-body counts interp / jit / build.

    enum E { A(R), B }   impl Drop for E { println("drop E") }

    NEVER destructured:
      let p = (E.B, 1); println(f"{p.1}");             0 / 0 / 0
      let p = (B,   1); println(f"{p.1}");             0 / 0 / 0
    DESTRUCTURED through a wildcard leaf (the control, correct):
      let p = (E.B, 1); let (_, n) = p;                1 / 1 / 1

ALL THREE BACKENDS AGREE ON ZERO, which is the failure mode no A/B gate can
report and the reason this is a soundness row rather than a parity one. The
tuple owns the enum and dies at scope exit; `E.drop` must run exactly once, and
the DESTRUCTURED sibling proves the machinery to run it exists and is reached
one statement later.

The STRUCT analogue is the opposite shape and is filed separately
(B-2026-08-28-46, where the compiled backends are right and the interpreter is
silent). Here neither is right.

Both spellings agree, so this is not B-2026-08-28-43.

FIXED by 4190c0a. The third site in the sequence B-2026-08-28-39 opened and
B-2026-08-28-40 continued, and it took the same treatment, exactly as this row
predicted it would.

THE PAYLOAD WALK IS SITE-LOCAL. `run_discarded_value_user_drops` has ~31
callers, and the CALL-source discard sits in the very next arm of this same
`match` -- `mk();` where `mk` returns the enum, which BOTH compiled backends
deliberately run at one body. Widening the shared walker fixes this site and
breaks that one, which is the trade the row warned against; the fix instead adds
the walk beside the `run_discarded_value_user_drops` call, gated on the enum
declaring its own `Drop`, and `call-source-stmt-control` in the fixture is the
row that holds the line.

No inline-construction gate is needed here, and that is the one difference from
the `let _ =` twin. That twin needs to distinguish `let _ = E.A(..)` from
`let _ = mk()` because both are `Let` statements; in STATEMENT position the two
already take different arms of the callee match, so a `Path` callee IS the
inline construction by construction.

A SECOND DEFECT AT THE SAME SITE, found by the shape matrix and worse than the
one filed. The BARE UNQUALIFIED spelling `A(R { id: 41 });` ran NOTHING -- 0
against compiled's 2, where this row's qualified spelling was 1 against 2:

    QUALIFIED   E.A(R { id: 41 });     interp 1 -> 2   (this row)
    BARE        A(R { id: 41 });       interp 0 -> 2   (found here)

THERE: the discard gate's `Identifier` callee arm looks for a program FUNCTION,
and a variant name is not one, so the discard is declined outright rather than

treatment, so the two statement kinds agreed for the qualified spelling and

fix:
FIXED by 5885ba5. BOTH residuals, with one predicate — because they were never
two defects.

THE ROW'S TWO RESIDUALS ARE ONE DEFECT SEEN THROUGH TWO BLIND SPOTS OF THE
MEASUREMENT, and establishing that is most of what this close is worth:

  * "the bound spelling leaks at -O2 and is CLEAN at -O0" — it leaks at BOTH.
    At -O0 the pointer is still sitting in the binding's alloca in a live stack
    frame at exit, so LSan classifies it REACHABLE rather than leaked; -O2 drops
    the alloca and the same leak becomes visible. Proven directly rather than
    argued: `LSAN_OPTIONS=use_stacks=0` reports 44 bytes in 2 allocations for
    the very program this row calls clean.

  * "one temp-read binding is clean; a second binding leaks exactly one box; the
    count does not scale with the reads" — every temp-read binding leaks its own
    box. Adding any second shared binding perturbs the frame enough for LSan to
    see one of them, which is exactly what made the count look flat and sent the
    row's own analysis after "a single slot or a once-only emission being
    reused". With the reads visible the count scales normally: three bindings,
    three boxes.

THE MECHANISM. `load_owned_shared_temp_field` emits a `+1` on the loaded inner
pointer so the receiver's recursive drop cannot free it out from under the
reader, and its comment states the contract: the consumer "takes ownership of
the +1". The `Option[shared T]` arm does exactly that. The BARE `shared T` arm
(B-2026-08-28-14) never taught the let site, so the binding took its OWN ref on
top — two increments against one release. The suppression reuses the predicate
B-2026-08-28-20 added to `shared_type_for_call_like`, so the retain half and the
release half cannot drift apart.

THREE HYPOTHESES REFUTED ALONG THE WAY, all recorded here because each was
plausible enough to cost the next reader an hour:

  1. `deferred_shared_temp_release` (the row's own) — already ruled out in an
     earlier update; that slot is only armed for a `String`/`Vec` leaf.
  2. The cleanup REGISTRATION being displaced when a second action is registered
     (the first update's conclusion, and where it told the next session to
     start) — instrumented at `track_rc_var`, `emit_cleanup_action`'s `RcDec`
     arm and the `DueDrop::Rc` path: the binding's `RcDec` is registered and
     emitted in BOTH programs, at scope exit, never through the NLL early path.
  3. A missing decrement — the leaking program emits MORE decrements than the
     clean one (3 vs 2), and every one of them is correct. Counting decrements
     could never have found this, because the imbalance was on the RETAIN side.

The IR is what settled it: two increments on the inner box against one release,
visible in the clean program as plainly as in the leaking one — which is the
tell that the measurement, not the program, was the thing differing between
them.

FIXTURE: `asan_bound_shared_temp_field_read_releases_once`, nine programs, each
in its own `main` for the reason this row already documented. It leads with the
TWO-BINDING shape rather than the row's own repro, because that is the shape the
harness's default LSan configuration can see; the one-binding row is kept beside
it and its doc is explicit that it asserts less. Three controls keep the fix
from being a blanket suppression — an IDENTIFIER receiver never takes the read's
`+1` and must keep its own inc, where suppressing would be a use-after-free.

Proven RED by stashing only `src/` (44 bytes / 2 allocations at -O0, 4 bytes / 1
at -O2) and verified clean on ten programs across both opt levels and both LSan
stack-scanning modes.

A NOTE FOR THE CORPUS, not for this row: `use_stacks=0` found a real leak that
the default configuration reports as clean. Any fixture whose leaked pointer is

suite under that option is not attempted here, since it would also surface

experiment for anyone auditing this class.

(2) A program with MORE THAN ONE shared-temp field read leaks exactly ONE box regardless of how many: one read is clean, two leak 42/2, three still leak 42/2, and a three-iteration loop leaks 84/4. detail:
TWO RESIDUALS OF B-2026-08-28-20, both pre-existing and both measured identical
before and after that row's fix (which closed only the UNBOUND chain).

ONE — THE BOUND SPELLING, which B-2026-08-28-20 itself named as the thing to
chase first:

    shared struct Node { v: i64, tag: String }
    shared struct Outer { id: i64, inner: Node }
    fn make(k: i64) -> Node { return Node { v: k, tag: f"t{k}" }; }
    fn make_outer(k: i64) -> Outer { return Outer { id: k, inner: make(k) }; }

    let h = make_outer(14).inner; println(h.tag);
        -> -O2: 3 bytes leaked in 1 allocation
        -> -O0: CLEAN

The opt-level split is the clue and is worth keeping: at -O0 the binding's RC
cleanup pairs with the read's `+1` and the box is reclaimed, so the whole
mechanism is present and works. At -O2 the payload survives — 3 bytes, the
`String` — while the box does not leak. That is the shape of a cleanup that runs
but does not walk the field, not of a missing dec.

TWO — MORE THAN ONE SHARED-TEMP FIELD READ IN ONE PROGRAM leaks exactly one box,
and the count does not scale with the reads:

    let a = make_outer(1).inner; println(a.tag);                  -> clean
    … two such bindings                                           -> 42 bytes, 2 allocs
    … three such bindings                                         -> 42 bytes, 2 allocs
    … three iterations of a loop doing one                        -> 84 bytes, 4 allocs

One read is clean; two, three, or a mix of bound and unbound reads all leak ONE
box; a loop leaks one per two iterations. A count that is flat in the
straight-line case and grows in the loop is not "each read leaks" — it points at
a single slot or a once-only emission being reused, which is the first thing to
look for. `deferred_shared_temp_release` is a single `Option` slot with a
`debug_assert!` guarding exactly that reuse, and it is the obvious suspect to
rule in or out first.

SEVERITY low, on the same grounds as the parent row: bounded, non-corrupting, the
output is correct on every backend, and the usual spelling (`let o =
make_outer(k); o.inner.tag`) does not go through the temporary-receiver path at
all. Unbounded in a loop, which is why it is not `wontfix`.

SOURCE NOTE: split out while gating B-2026-08-28-20. Its fixture puts every
shape in its OWN program for this reason — combined into one `main`, these two
residuals mask all eight rows and the fixture passes for the wrong reason.

--- MEASUREMENT UPDATE (2026-08-28, investigated but not fixed) ---

THE HYPOTHESIS THIS ROW OFFERED IS REFUTED. It pointed at
`deferred_shared_temp_release`, a single `Option` slot with a `debug_assert!`
guarding reuse, as the first thing to rule in or out. Ruled OUT: the assert
does not fire on the two-binding repro, and it could not — that slot is only
armed for a `String`/`Vec` leaf, while `.inner` is a bare `shared` field and
never defers. Recording the refutation because the guess was plausible enough
to cost the next reader the same hour.

THE EMITTED CODE IS SYMMETRIC, which is what makes this subtle. On the
two-binding program at -O0: the inc/dec pairs, the `__karac_rc_drop_*` call
count and the cleanup BLOCK structure all scale exactly 2x from the clean
one-binding program (`rc_cleanup_do` → `rc_free` → `rc_done` → `rc_cleanup_join`
per binding, both drops present and reachable). So this is not a missing
operation and not an unreachable drop.

THE SHARPENED REPRO, which is the useful part and supersedes the counts above:

    let a = make_outer(1).inner; println(a.tag);              -> CLEAN
    … and a second temp-read binding                          -> 42 bytes / 2
    … the two in SEPARATE BLOCK SCOPES                        -> 84 bytes / 4
    … both bindings first, then both prints                   -> 40 bytes / 1
    … a temp-read binding + an unrelated `let c = make(2);`   -> 42 bytes / 2
    two plain `let a = make(1);` bindings, no temp read        -> CLEAN

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE LAST PAIR, and it was not in the original row. A
temp-read binding alone is fine. A temp-read binding plus ANY OTHER shared
binding leaks one box — the other binding need not be a temp read, need not
share a type, and need not touch the same object. Two plain shared bindings with
no temp read anywhere are clean. So the defect needs exactly one temp-read
binding and at least one more RC cleanup action in the function; separate scopes
make it worse (one box per binding) rather than better, which rules out a
scope-exit ordering effect and points at the cleanup REGISTRATION — one action's
target being displaced when a second is registered.

That is where to look next: the RC cleanup action list and `track_rc_var`'s
registration, not the release site this row was filed against.

STILL OPEN. The B-2026-08-28-20 fix (9cc5fb1) closed the unbound chain and is
unrelated to either residual here — every figure above is identical before and
after it.


NARROWED AGAIN 2026-08-28, by instrumenting the RC cleanup registration the
previous update pointed at. Three things are now ruled out or established, and
none of them is where the row or its first update expected to land.

WHICH BOX LEAKS: the TEMP-READ binding's, not the added one. With the two tags
made different lengths (`tag1` vs `tag2222222`) the indirect leak is 4 bytes —
`a`'s payload. So the added binding does not leak; its mere PRESENCE makes `a`'s
box leak.

`a`'s DECREMENT IS EMITTED, in both programs. Traced at `track_rc_var` and at
`emit_cleanup_action`: the clean one-binding program registers and emits exactly
one `RcDec` for `a`; the leaking two-binding program registers and emits BOTH,
`c` first then `a` (registration-LIFO at scope exit). Neither fires through the
NLL early path — the `DueDrop::Rc` arm never runs for either. So this is not a
missing action, not a retracted one, and not an NLL retiming.

THE ACTION'S POINTER IS AN SSA VALUE, NOT A SLOT: `a`'s `RcDec` carries
`%inner = load ptr, ptr %sh_call_inner` — the pointer LOADED at the read — where
an ordinary binding carries its alloca. That is worth recording as the structural
oddity of this path even though it is not by itself the defect (the clean
one-binding program carries the same shape and is clean).

COUNTS IN `main`, from the emitted IR: the clean program has 2 inline
increments and 2 decrements; the leaking one has 2 increments and 3 decrements,
with `__karac_rc_drop_Node` called twice rather than once. MORE decrements, not
fewer — so the imbalance is not a dropped release, and the next step is to
attribute each of the three decrements to an object rather than to count them.

WHAT IS LEFT: work out which object each emitted decrement targets in the
two-binding program. The shape of the answer is either an extra retain on `a`'s
node that the counts above hide, or one of the three decrements targeting the
wrong box. Both are readable from the IR with the boxes distinguished; that is
where the next session should start, rather than at the registration.

The row named the mechanism and the fix shape exactly: "closing this means
SEPARATING the two claims -- the walker owning Drop-bearing types and the
unbound-field arm owning the rest -- rather than widening either gate on its

resolution and drift from it. So `run_discarded_leaf_user_drop_bodies` now
RETURNS whether it took the memory, and the unbound-field arm claims a
struct-literal source's field exactly when it did not.

A field ABSENT from the pattern entirely -- dropped by `..` rather than bound to
`_` -- never reaches the walker at all, so it answers false and this arm owns it.
That is the correct answer and it falls out of the same signal rather than
needing its own case.

The Drop-BEARING boundary in the same position stays at one free, which is what

leak-clean in this shape only because LLVM deletes the dead allocation chain
whole -- the DCE mask B-2026-08-28-12 and -29 both record -- so a fixture

title: AN UNBOUND DESTRUCTURE FIELD WHOSE TYPE HAS NO `Drop` LEAKS ON A STRUCT-LITERAL SOURCE: `let W { r: _, n } = W { r: R { .. }, n: 1 }` where `R` carries a `Vec[String]` and declares no `Drop` loses 98 bytes on both compiled backends, while the same field over a CALL source or a PLACE source is clean -- the source axis B-2026-08-28-29 fixed for BODIES, still open for the memory of a Drop-free type
detail:
Measured on 05fefaa (B-2026-08-28-29's fix in place) and identical on the
commit before it -- verified by stashing `src/` and rebuilding -- so this is
neither caused nor repaired by that work.

    struct R { id: i64, tags: Vec[String] }        // NO impl Drop
    struct W { r: R, n: i64 }
    fn mkv(n: i64) -> Vec[String] { let mut v = Vec[String].new(); v.push(f"t{n}"); v }

    UNBOUND field, struct-LITERAL source:
      let W { r: _, n } = W { r: R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, n: 1 };
                                              98 bytes definitely lost
    UNBOUND field, CALL source:
      let W { r: _, n } = mk();               clean
    UNBOUND field, PLACE source:
      let w = W { .. }; let W { r: _, n } = w;  clean

THE `Vec` MATTERS TO THE REPRO, not to the defect. A bare `String` field is
leak-clean in the same shape only because LLVM deletes the whole dead allocation
chain -- the DCE mask B-2026-08-28-12 and -29 both record. `mkv` builds its
buffer through a runtime `push`, which the optimizer cannot fold away, so the
leak becomes observable. Any non-DCE-able heap in that position leaks the same
way.

WHY B-2026-08-28-29 DOES NOT COVER IT. That fix established, by measurement,
that a struct-literal source owns nothing and that its BOUND leaves must own
their fields; it widened the bound-leaf arms accordingly. An UNBOUND field over
that source has exactly one owner today -- the discard walker
(`run_discarded_leaf_user_drop_bodies`), which frees when
`free_memory` is true. That walker returns early for a type with no `Drop`,
because it has no body to run, so a Drop-FREE type gets no owner at all. The
unbound-field arm lower in the loop is the natural second candidate, and it is
deliberately held at `fresh_call`: admitting the literal there while the walker
also claims a Drop-BEARING field aborts at 12 frees for 11 allocs (measured on
that row). So closing this means separating the two claims -- the walker owning
Drop-bearing types and the unbound-field arm owning the rest -- rather than
widening either gate on its own.

SOURCE NOTE: found by sweeping B-2026-08-28-29's ownership matrix past the
Drop-bearing shapes its own fix is about, specifically to find what the new
per-arm split does NOT cover.

fix:
FIXED by 74223ee for the OVER-FIRE horn — the high-severity half, a double body plus a
read of the already-dropped value — on all four surfaces. Both backends now
carry the runtime bit the row said they lacked, each in its own idiom, driven
by ONE shared syntactic classification so they agree by construction.

THE CLASSIFICATION. `note_escaping_site` (character-for-character the same rule
in `Interpreter` and `Codegen`) records the spans of expressions sitting in an
ESCAPING position — a value handed to an owner rather than discarded — seeded
at exactly three sites: a function body's tail, a `return` operand, and a `let`
initializer. It then pushes that property down through branch structure, so
each arm tail of an escaping `if` / `if let` / `match` / block is escaping too.
Escaping-ness is a STATIC property of a syntactic site, so seeding lazily as
compilation/evaluation reaches each site is equivalent to a precomputed set and
needs no full AST walker. A DISCARDED `if` (or `match`) STATEMENT is
deliberately not a seed, which is what keeps the boundary the investigation
identified.

THE BIT, INTERPRETER. It evaluates only the TAKEN arm, so reaching an arm's
tail IS the proof that this path moved the value; `record_conditional_move_tail`
marks the binding in `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` there. Deliberately skips a
binding the current block OWNS — that one is the ordinary tail move the static
`suppress_tail_expr_user_drop` already handles, and its scoping is exactly why
it never needed a runtime bit.

THE BIT, CODEGEN. It emits both arms, so it cannot use evaluation as evidence.
`arm_conditional_move_tail_flag` instead clears a per-binding `i1` alloca in the
ARM'S OWN basic block; `emit_user_drop_call_guarded` tests it. The flag and its
`true` init go in the function's ENTRY block, which dominates every path, so
allocating LAZILY at the move site is correct even though the `let` that
registered the action compiled long before — that is what removes the need for a
pre-pass. BOTH firing channels route through the guard: the scope-exit drain and
`fire_due_user_drops`' NLL live-range-end fire. The second is not optional —
`let y = if k { r } else { s };` makes the branch each local's last use, so the
conditionally-moved binding lands there rather than at scope exit, and guarding
only the drain left that shape wrong on the compiled backends while the
interpreter was right: a divergence the fix would have INTRODUCED.

WHY THIS STAYS OFF THE PREDICATE QUESTION the row warns about. Only a binding
actually reached as an escaping branch-arm tail gets a flag, and the action stays
ARMED either way — a guard is added to a drop that already exists, no action is
retained that was previously removed. `has_armed_user_drop`,
`has_armed_own_user_drop` and `has_armed_container_elem_bodies` therefore answer
exactly as before. The 2026-08-28 investigation's separability claim held.

A CLOSURE BODY IS THE THIRD ESCAPING SITE, and it is the one place this fix
briefly made things WORSE rather than better — worth recording because the
suites did not catch it and no shape in the row's own matrix has it. The
interpreter reaches a closure body through `next_block_is_fn_body`, which covers
"function/closure/method body", so the interpreter half fixed
`|| { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } }` for free. Codegen
compiles a closure body in `closures.rs`, NOT through `compile_function`, so it
never saw the seed — and an aligned-WRONG program (both backends double-firing)
became a run-vs-build DIVERGENCE. Fixed by planting the same seed at the closure
body's tail. The flag map is also saved/cleared/restored around that body, since
a closure is its own LLVM function and an entry-block `i1` alloca is not
addressable from outside it. Methods needed nothing: codegen compiles them
through `compile_function` like any other function, which the `method-branch-tail`
test row pins so the closure row is not mistaken for covering every non-free
function body.

MEASURED, 22 shapes x 4 surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0),
byte-identical across all four unless noted. 21 of 22 aligned AND correct:

  branch-tail-moved (the row's repro)  `drop 41`/`41`/`drop 41` -> `41`/`drop 41`
  branch-tail-not-moved (k=false)      unchanged, still 1 body in the callee
  two-locals-merge                     3 bodies/2 objects -> 2/2
  match-arm                            3 bodies/2 objects -> 2/2  (was aligned-WRONG)
  closure-branch-tail, both directions correct (see above)
  method-branch-tail                   correct, needed no change
  return-in-branch (shape B, k=true)   interp 2 -> 1, now agrees with codegen's 1
  else-if-chain, nested-if-arm         correct
  if-let arm tails, both directions    correct
  a call inside the arm before its tail correct (the seed survives the call)
  heap-field husk                      interp `drop forty-one` / codegen `drop `
                                       -> both `drop forty-one`, no husk read
  discarded-if-statement               1 body, UNCHANGED (the boundary)
  discarded-match-statement            1 body, UNCHANGED (the boundary)
  straight-line / param branch tails    correct before and after (controls)

STILL OPEN, and it is the row's other horn, not a residue of this fix:
`fn take(k) -> R { let r = R{41}; if k { return r; } R{99} }` with k=false still
loses `r`'s body on all three COMPILED backends (interp `drop 41`/`99`/`drop 99`,
LLJIT and AOT alike `99`/`drop 99`) — measured byte-identical before and after
this commit. That is the UNDER-fire horn: `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
statically REMOVES the action, and un-removing it is precisely the change that
makes the three predicates above answer differently. Filed separately rather
than left inside a closed row.

Regression tests: `tests/interpreter.rs`'s
`test_conditionally_moved_local_user_drop_body_runs_once` and `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`e2e_conditionally_moved_local_user_drop_body_runs_once`, 16 rows each, sharing
their expectations verbatim so a future divergence fails one of the two against a
common constant. The two `discarded-*-statement` rows are the ones that constrain
the fix rather than reproduce the bug: their arm tails are the same bare `r`, so
any version keying on shape instead of on an escaping position takes them from
one body to zero.
title: A CONDITIONALLY-MOVED LOCAL RETURNED FROM A BRANCH TAIL RUNS ITS `Drop` BODY TWICE AND IS THEN USED AFTER THE DROP, on all four surfaces: `fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } }` with `k = true` prints `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41`. This is the OVER-SCHEDULE horn of B-2026-08-28-22's mechanism -- `merge_outer_states` deliberately re-marks a conditionally-moved place `Owned` and relies on a runtime cap/null guard that exists for MEMORY and does not exist for a user `Drop` BODY -- and it refutes that row's premise that the tree uniformly picked the missed-body direction
detail:
The escaping path runs the callee's scope-exit body on a value it has
already handed to the caller, and the caller then reads it and drops it
again. The middle `41` in the output is a READ OF AN ALREADY-DROPPED
VALUE.

FULL MATRIX, user `Drop` body counts on all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT
/ AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), measured on 6085d46. Exactly ONE `R` reaches the
caller in every program; correct is one body per constructed object.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }

  A. LOCAL, branch TAIL     fn take(k) -> R { let r = R{41}; if k { r } else { R{99} } }
       k=true  (r escapes)  -> 2/2/2/2  `drop 41` `41` `drop 41`   WRONG, double
       k=false (r dies)     -> ok       `drop 41` `99` `drop 99`
  B. LOCAL, `return r`      fn take(k) -> R { let r = R{41}; if k { return r } R{99} }
       k=true               -> interp 2, codegen 1                 WRONG in interp
       k=false              -> interp ok, codegen MISSES 41's body  WRONG in codegen
  C. PARAM, branch tail     fn take(r: R, k) -> R { if k { r } else { R{99} } }
       k=true               -> ok
       k=false              -> 1/1/1/1, 41's body lost             WRONG (= B-2026-08-28-22)
  D. PARAM, `return r`      fn take(r: R, k) -> R { if k { return r } R{99} }
       k=true               -> ok
       k=false              -> 1/1/1/1, 41's body lost             WRONG (= B-2026-08-28-22)

CONTROLS, both correct on all four surfaces: the straight-line local
(`let r = R{41}; r` -> 1 body) and a callee that never returns the param
(`fn take(r: R, k) -> i64` -> 1 body, `drop 41` first).

ROOT CAUSE, one mechanism, two horns. A value that is moved on SOME paths and
dies on others needs runtime knowledge at the drop point, and neither backend
has any. Each channel resolves that statically, and they do not agree on which
way:

  * The OVER-SCHEDULE horn is documented policy. `merge_outer_states`
    (`src/ownership_oracle.rs`) merges a conditionally-moved place back to
    `Owned` -- "any disagreement ... yields `Owned`, so the drop is scheduled
    and codegen's runtime cap/null guard makes the over-scheduled conditional
    drop correct." That guard is a MEMORY guard. A user `Drop` BODY has no null
    to test, so an over-scheduled body simply runs a second time. Shape A.
  * The UNDER-SCHEDULE horn is the move-suppression family
    (`suppress_user_drop_for_var` and the ~20 sites that call it), which
    REMOVES the cleanup action outright. `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
    says so in as many words: "Static and flow-insensitive like every sibling
    -- a conditional return disarms on all paths, which can only under-fire."
    Shapes C and D, and the codegen half of B.

Which horn a shape lands on is decided by whether the move site is RECOGNIZED,
not by anything about the shape's semantics. `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
inspects only `body.final_expr` / the last statement and never descends into
`if` arms, so a bare-identifier BRANCH TAIL is not seen as a move at all (horn
1, shape A) while the identical value reached by an explicit `return r` IS seen
(horn 2, shape B/D). That is why one program, shape B, is wrong in OPPOSITE
directions on the two backends.

VISIBLE IN THE OUTPUT, which is how the husk was identified without an IR
dump. With a heap field the spurious body reads moved-from bits and the two
backends disagree about what it sees:

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.name}") } }
    fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41, name: "forty-one" };
                            if k { r } else { R { id: 99, name: "ninety-nine" } } }
    fn main() { let x = take(true); println(f"{x.id} {x.name}") }

    interp   -> `drop forty-one` / `41 forty-one` / `drop forty-one`
    jit/AOT  -> `drop `          / `41 forty-one` / `drop forty-one`

So codegen zeroes the moved-from slot (the empty name is the husk) while the
interpreter's first body still sees the live value -- a run-vs-build
divergence riding on top of the double body. Exit code 0 and the caller's
field contents are correct, so the MEMORY side is intact: the cap/null guard
does its job and there is no double free. Only the side effect is wrong,
which is exactly why the guard was thought sufficient.

WHY NO NARROW FIX EXISTS, which is the part worth recording. Teaching
`suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` to descend into branch arms makes shape A
stop double-firing -- and immediately converts it into shape B's codegen bug,
because the suppression it would then perform is the flow-insensitive REMOVAL.
The two horns are the same missing runtime bit seen from either side; moving a
shape from one to the other is not progress. Any real fix has to introduce that
bit (a per-binding drop flag: alloca `i1`, armed at registration, cleared at the
move site, tested at the drain) in BOTH backends together.

AND THE UNIFORM FORM OF THAT FIX IS NOT A DROP-IN, which is the trap. "Stop
removing the action, always guard it with a flag" is wrong: three COMPILE-TIME
predicates read frame membership as a proxy for ownership --
`has_armed_user_drop`, `has_armed_own_user_drop`,
`has_armed_container_elem_bodies` (`src/codegen/runtime.rs`) -- and drive
unrelated decisions from it. `has_armed_user_drop`'s own doc gives the case: the
displaced-value leg (B-2026-07-30-11) runs a reassigned binding's old body only
when the binding still owns it, "a value moved out earlier ... had its action
retracted, and firing on the stale slot would read moved-from bits
(B-2026-07-31-38's repro shape prints the payload's body twice)". Retaining
flagged actions makes all three answer true where they used to answer false, so
the flag must be scoped to bindings an ANALYSIS marks conditionally-moved,
leaving unconditional moves on today's static removal.

SOURCE NOTE: found while auditing B-2026-08-28-22 for fixability, by asking
whether the same shape works for a LOCAL instead of a param. No code change
was made. Filed separately from -22 because it is the OPPOSITE failure
direction (a double body plus a use-after-drop, versus a missed body) and is
the more severe of the two.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
INVESTIGATION 2026-08-28 (no code change). Matrix re-measured on e799916 and
confirmed unchanged. The row's analysis holds in every particular; what follows
narrows its "no narrow fix exists" conclusion, which is stronger than the
evidence requires.

THE OVER-FIRE HORN CAN BE FIXED WITHOUT TOUCHING THE THREE PREDICATES, and that
is the useful correction. The row's "not a drop-in" warning is about
`has_armed_user_drop` / `has_armed_own_user_drop` /
`has_armed_container_elem_bodies` answering true where they used to answer
false, once flagged actions are RETAINED instead of removed. That hazard is real
for the UNDER-schedule horn (shapes B-codegen / C / D), where the fix means
keeping an action the move-suppression family currently deletes.

It does not apply to shape A. Nothing is suppressed there today -- the action is
ALREADY ARMED, which is exactly why it double-fires. Adding a runtime guard to
an action that already exists changes no membership, so all three predicates
answer precisely as they do now. Shape A is therefore separable: a first slice
can introduce the drop flag for the over-fire horn alone, leave every
suppression site untouched, and close the high-severity half (a double body plus
a read of the dropped value) without going near the predicate question.

WHERE THE INTERPRETER HALF FAILS, precisely, since the row does not say. Its
`suppress_tail_expr_user_drop` IS already called for the arm block -- every
block tail reaches it (`eval_stmt.rs`, the block-tail path) -- and it is a no-op
for this shape for one reason: it retracts from THAT block's `cleanup` vector,
while `r` lives in the enclosing function block's. The arm has nothing of `r`'s
to retract. So the interpreter is one frame away, not one feature away.

AND WHY THE OBVIOUS INTERPRETER FIX IS WRONG. Redirecting that retraction to the
runtime `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` set would be flow-sensitive by
construction (only the taken arm's block is evaluated) and fixes shape A. It
also breaks a shape that is correct today:

    let r = R { id: 41 }; let k = true;
    if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } };      // DISCARDED if-statement
                                          // 1/1/1 today: `drop 41` / `end`

Here the taken arm's tail is the same bare `r`, the value is discarded rather
than moved, and marking it moved takes that program from one body to ZERO. So
the marking cannot key on "block tail is an identifier"; it needs the enclosing
`if` to be in RETURN position, which is context the block-tail path does not
currently carry.

SHAPES RE-MEASURED, both backends, to keep the boundary exact:

    let y = if k { r } else { s };  (both arms LOCAL bindings)
      interp and AOT alike -> `drop 99` `drop 41` `41` `drop 41`
      Two objects, three bodies: `s` dies correctly, `r` fires spuriously at the
      merge and again at `y`'s death. Same single defect as shape A with a
      second local present, NOT a distinct one -- recorded so it is not filed
      twice.

    with a heap field, the husk divergence reproduces here too:
      interp -> `drop 41 n41` (live value)   AOT -> `drop 41 ` (moved-from)

    the DISCARDED if-statement above -> 1/1/1, correct, and is the boundary the
    interpreter fix must not cross.

STILL OPEN, and deliberately so: the fix is a drop flag in both backends, and
even the narrowed first slice touches the drain path that every cleanup action
in the compiler goes through. Left for a session that can carry the full-suite
verification budget that change deserves, with the scope now reduced to the
over-fire horn alone.

fix:
FIXED by f94c75c, completing a repair that took two commits because the row
documented two horns of one mechanism and each needed its own.

This row's subject is SHAPE B —
`fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { return r; } R { id: 99 } }`
— the one program that was wrong in OPPOSITE directions on the two backends:
the interpreter double-ran the body when the branch was taken (`drop 41` /
`41` / `drop 41`, the middle `41` a read of an already-dropped value), and
codegen LOST the body when it was not (`99` / `drop 99`). Both are now
correct, and all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) agree on both `k` values:

    k = true    41 / drop 41                  (was: interp ran 2 bodies)
    k = false   drop 41 / 99 / drop 99        (was: codegen ran 1, not 2)

The interpreter's OVER-fire half went with B-2026-08-28-51 (74223ee), which
gave a conditionally-moved binding a per-path mark so a body fires only on
the path that owns the value. The codegen UNDER-fire half is
B-2026-08-28-65, fixed here: the static frame removal at a nested `return`
is replaced by a runtime guard on the already-armed action, gated on the
action living in an enclosing frame so an unconditional `return r;` keeps
today's behaviour.

THE ROW'S CENTRAL CLAIM HELD UP AND IS WHY THIS WORKED. It said no narrow
fix exists, because teaching the tail-return suppression to descend into
branch arms would move shape A onto shape B's horn rather than repairing
anything, and that any real fix must introduce the missing runtime bit — "a
per-binding drop flag: alloca `i1`, armed at registration, cleared at the
move site, tested at the drain" — in BOTH backends together. That is exactly
what the two commits did, in that order. It also warned that the uniform
form is not a drop-in, because three compile-time predicates read frame
membership as a proxy for ownership; that warning was right too, and the
scoping it demanded (flag only bindings an analysis marks conditionally
moved, leave unconditional moves on the static removal) is the shape both
fixes took.

WHAT THE ROW GOT WRONG, recorded because it cost time: it attributed
codegen's recognition of the move to `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`.
For this program the body's `final_expr` is `R { id: 99 }`, so that walk
never sees `r`; the removal comes from the `ExprKind::Return` compile arm in
`src/codegen/exprs.rs`. The row's REASONING about which spellings land on
which horn is unaffected — codegen does recognize an explicit
`ExprKind::Return` as a move and the interpreter does not — only the named
function was off by one call site.

SHAPES C AND D (the PARAM forms, both spellings, `k = false`) are UNCHANGED
and remain aligned-wrong on all four surfaces, which is what this row always
said they were: B-2026-08-28-22's subject, not this one's. An owned
by-value param is caller-drops, so there is no callee-side action to retain
and nothing for a flag to guard; closing that needs the callee-owned-param
