title: ONE PROGRAM, WRONG IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS ON THE TWO BACKENDS: a local moved out by an explicit `return r` inside a branch (`fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { return r } R { id: 99 } }`) double-runs the body in the INTERPRETER when the branch is taken, and LOSES the body in CODEGEN when it is not. The interpreter is on the over-schedule horn of B-2026-08-28-22's mechanism and codegen is on the under-schedule horn, for the same binding
detail:
Both backends resolve the same conditional move statically and pick
DIFFERENT horns, so neither `k` value agrees across surfaces:

    fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { return r } R { id: 99 } }

    k = true   correct: `41` / `drop 41`
      interp   -> `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41`   double body + use-after-drop
      jit/AOT  -> `41` / `drop 41`               CORRECT

    k = false  correct: `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99`
      interp   -> `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99`   CORRECT
      jit/AOT  -> `99` / `drop 99`               41's body lost

AOT and AOT-with-KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 agree with the JIT throughout.

FULL MATRIX, user `Drop` body counts on all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT
/ AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), measured on 6085d46. Exactly ONE `R` reaches the
caller in every program; correct is one body per constructed object.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }

  A. LOCAL, branch TAIL     fn take(k) -> R { let r = R{41}; if k { r } else { R{99} } }
       k=true  (r escapes)  -> 2/2/2/2  `drop 41` `41` `drop 41`   WRONG, double
       k=false (r dies)     -> ok       `drop 41` `99` `drop 99`
  B. LOCAL, `return r`      fn take(k) -> R { let r = R{41}; if k { return r } R{99} }
       k=true               -> interp 2, codegen 1                 WRONG in interp
       k=false              -> interp ok, codegen MISSES 41's body  WRONG in codegen
  C. PARAM, branch tail     fn take(r: R, k) -> R { if k { r } else { R{99} } }
       k=true               -> ok
       k=false              -> 1/1/1/1, 41's body lost             WRONG (= B-2026-08-28-22)
  D. PARAM, `return r`      fn take(r: R, k) -> R { if k { return r } R{99} }
       k=true               -> ok
       k=false              -> 1/1/1/1, 41's body lost             WRONG (= B-2026-08-28-22)

CONTROLS, both correct on all four surfaces: the straight-line local
(`let r = R{41}; r` -> 1 body) and a callee that never returns the param
(`fn take(r: R, k) -> i64` -> 1 body, `drop 41` first).

ROOT CAUSE, one mechanism, two horns. A value that is moved on SOME paths and
dies on others needs runtime knowledge at the drop point, and neither backend
has any. Each channel resolves that statically, and they do not agree on which
way:

  * The OVER-SCHEDULE horn is documented policy. `merge_outer_states`
    (`src/ownership_oracle.rs`) merges a conditionally-moved place back to
    `Owned` -- "any disagreement ... yields `Owned`, so the drop is scheduled
    and codegen's runtime cap/null guard makes the over-scheduled conditional
    drop correct." That guard is a MEMORY guard. A user `Drop` BODY has no null
    to test, so an over-scheduled body simply runs a second time. Shape A.
  * The UNDER-SCHEDULE horn is the move-suppression family
    (`suppress_user_drop_for_var` and the ~20 sites that call it), which
    REMOVES the cleanup action outright. `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
    says so in as many words: "Static and flow-insensitive like every sibling
    -- a conditional return disarms on all paths, which can only under-fire."
    Shapes C and D, and the codegen half of B.

Which horn a shape lands on is decided by whether the move site is RECOGNIZED,
not by anything about the shape's semantics. `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
inspects only `body.final_expr` / the last statement and never descends into
`if` arms, so a bare-identifier BRANCH TAIL is not seen as a move at all (horn
1, shape A) while the identical value reached by an explicit `return r` IS seen
(horn 2, shape B/D). That is why one program, shape B, is wrong in OPPOSITE
directions on the two backends.

WHY THIS SHAPE SPLITS THE BACKENDS while shape A (the branch TAIL, filed as
B-2026-08-28-51) does not: codegen recognizes an explicit `ExprKind::Return`
as a move and applies the static removal, so it lands on the under-schedule
horn; the interpreter does not recognize it and leaves the drop scheduled, so
it lands on the over-schedule horn. Change the `return r` to a bare branch
tail and codegen stops recognizing it too, which is why all four surfaces
then agree -- on the wrong answer.

WHY NO NARROW FIX EXISTS, which is the part worth recording. Teaching
`suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` to descend into branch arms makes shape A
stop double-firing -- and immediately converts it into shape B's codegen bug,
because the suppression it would then perform is the flow-insensitive REMOVAL.
The two horns are the same missing runtime bit seen from either side; moving a
shape from one to the other is not progress. Any real fix has to introduce that
bit (a per-binding drop flag: alloca `i1`, armed at registration, cleared at the
move site, tested at the drain) in BOTH backends together.

AND THE UNIFORM FORM OF THAT FIX IS NOT A DROP-IN, which is the trap. "Stop
removing the action, always guard it with a flag" is wrong: three COMPILE-TIME
predicates read frame membership as a proxy for ownership --
`has_armed_user_drop`, `has_armed_own_user_drop`,
`has_armed_container_elem_bodies` (`src/codegen/runtime.rs`) -- and drive
unrelated decisions from it. `has_armed_user_drop`'s own doc gives the case: the
displaced-value leg (B-2026-07-30-11) runs a reassigned binding's old body only
when the binding still owns it, "a value moved out earlier ... had its action
retracted, and firing on the stale slot would read moved-from bits
(B-2026-07-31-38's repro shape prints the payload's body twice)". Retaining
flagged actions makes all three answer true where they used to answer false, so
the flag must be scoped to bindings an ANALYSIS marks conditionally-moved,
leaving unconditional moves on today's static removal.

NOT a memory defect on either backend: exit 0, correct field contents at the
caller, and the same cap/null guard cited above covers the frees. Bodies only.

fix:
FIXED by 43e93bc. The site is the ONE-SHOT DISCARD FRAME, not the NLL fire.

The previous narrowing correctly ruled out `drain_statement_temp_user_drops`
by instrumentation and concluded the bodies must therefore come through
`fire_due_user_drops`. The first half holds and the second does not. Dumping
what that drain actually fires shows it firing exactly `karac_dropnf_W` in the
BOUND spelling and nothing at all in the discarded one -- so the instrumented
"no whitelisted action" result was real, but it was a statement about the
DISCARDED spelling only, and the drain is doing the work one spelling over.

What the discarded statement does instead is push its OWN frame
(`track_discarded_temp_cleanup`'s caller: "the caller has already pushed the
one-shot discard frame"). Both temporaries land on it -- the ARGUMENT while
`compile_expr` ran, the RESULT when the cleanup battery ran after -- and
`drain_top_frame_with_emit` walks the whole frame in reverse index order, so
the later-pushed RESULT fires first. Six instructions of `main` show it:

    store W-literal -> %__owned_agg_tmp        ; argument temp
    %call = call @take(...)
    store %call     -> %__owned_agg_tmp1       ; result temp
    call @karac_drop_R(%__owned_agg_tmp1)      ; result FIRST
    call @karac_dropnf_W(%__owned_agg_tmp)     ; argument SECOND

THE ROW'S OWN GROUNDING CORRECTION IS WHAT MADE THIS TRACTABLE and is
confirmed verbatim: the applicable rule is design.md § Drop ordering's
LIVE-RANGE end, not parent-before-fields (the callee moves `r` out of `w`, so
no parent/child relation survives into the caller) and not LIFO (which, read
as LIFO-by-introduction, would make the compiled order right). The argument
temporary's last use is the call; it dies there, before the result exists, so
the two live ranges do not overlap and LIFO never gets to arbitrate. The bound
spelling recorded as the behavioural target is exactly the oracle it was
predicted to be.

THE FIX is `drain_discard_frame_args_first(mark)`, a sibling of
`drain_top_frame_with_emit` that splits the frame at the argument/result
boundary -- `mark` is the frame length captured immediately after
`compile_expr` -- and drains the two halves in order, each LIFO within itself.
Order WITHIN each group is untouched, so the registrars' "memory BEFORE
bodies" frame discipline still holds for the battery's own registrations.
Wired at all three discard sites: the bare statement (`take(..);`), the
wildcard let (`let _ = take(..);`), and the struct/tuple-tail arm. The first
is the one the row's repro takes; the second had the identical inversion and
is pinned so the two spellings cannot drift.

NO REORDERING OF THE EXISTING DRAIN was possible, as the previous narrowing
said -- but the reason it gave ("getting it to fire first means firing it at
the call") turns out to overstate the cost. The argument temp does not have to
MOVE to the call; it only has to be retired ahead of a result that did not
exist when it died. Both bodies still emit at the `;`, so nothing changes about
when memory is released relative to the call, and the change is contained to
one drain function plus three call sites.

THE HAZARD THIS ROW WAS LEFT UNATTEMPTED FOR DOES NOT MATERIALIZE, and the
bound spelling is the proof rather than an argument. Reordering moves the
parent's heap free AHEAD of the returned field's body, and the result is
routinely a field moved OUT of that parent -- the one thing that could turn an
ordering fix into a use-after-free. But the bound spelling ALREADY ran in this
order, over exactly that shape, before this change: `fn take(w: W) -> R`
returning a `String`-carrying field measured 15 allocs / 15 frees, 0 errors
under valgrind. The moved-out field is masked out of the parent's wrapper
(`karac_dropnf_<T>` -- user body plus field-heap synthesis, with the moved
field's step dropped), so the parent never frees what it handed on.

MEASURED, four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0):

    take(W { r: R { id: 47 }, n: 5 });      before  interp drop W5/drop 47
                                                    compiled drop 47/drop W5
                                            after   all four drop W5/drop 47

and on the heap-carrying variant, after the fix: the discarded form 14 allocs
/ 14 frees and the bound form 15/15, both ERROR SUMMARY 0 under valgrind at
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0.

TESTS: `e2e_discarded_own_drop_parent_temp_orders_its_body_first`
(tests/codegen.rs, 5 rows -- both discard spellings, the `bound` oracle, and
two controls: a parent with no `Drop` of its own and one whose moved-out field
is scalar, both byte-identical before and after, which a fix that reordered
the frame wholesale rather than at the boundary would fail); its verbatim
interpreter twin `test_discarded_own_drop_parent_temp_orders_its_body_first`,
pinning the oracle order so the legs cannot drift; and
`asan_discarded_own_drop_parent_temp_order_is_memory_balanced`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs, 3 rows) for the memory half, whose `Drop` bodies
READ their heap field deliberately -- a literal-printing body lets LLVM delete

title: A DISCARDED own-`Drop` parent temp runs its FIELD's `Drop` body BEFORE its own on the two compiled backends and AFTER it in the interpreter: `take(W { r: R { id: 47 }, n: 5 });` with the result thrown away prints `drop 47` / `drop W5` under jit and build and `drop W5` / `drop 47` under the interpreter. design.md § Drop ordering specifies parent first, so the interpreter is the correct leg. COUNTS are right on all three (one body each) -- this is ordering alone, and it is confined to the DISCARDED-result shape: the same program binding the result agrees on all three backends.
detail:
A DISCARDED own-`Drop` parent temp orders its own body against its FIELD's
body differently on the interpreter than on the two compiled backends. Split
out of B-2026-08-28-21 when its shape matrix was widened; that row fixed the
COUNTS for this shape and this is the ordering remainder, measured after the
fix and confirmed pre-existing before it.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct W { r: R, n: i64 }
    impl Drop for W { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop W{self.n}") } }
    fn take(w: W) -> R { let W { r, n } = w; r }
    fn main() { take(W { r: R { id: 47 }, n: 5 }); println("end"); }

    interp  ->  drop W5 / drop 47 / end        <- correct per design.md
    jit     ->  drop 47 / drop W5 / end
    build   ->  drop 47 / drop W5 / end

design.md § Drop ordering specifies the parent body first, then the fields die,
which is also the order `karac_drop_<T>` emits internally (own body, then the
field-bodies walk, then the frees) and the order every BOUND spelling of this
program produces on all three backends. So the interpreter is the correct leg
and the compiled ones are wrong, and the defect is specific to the result being
DISCARDED rather than to the own-`Drop` parent as such.

PRE-EXISTING, verified by stashing `src/` and rebuilding on the pre-fix
compiler: it printed `drop 47`, `drop W5`, `drop 47` against the interpreter's
`drop W5`, `drop 47`, `drop 47` -- the same inversion, under the extra body
B-2026-08-28-21 removed. So -21 neither caused nor repaired it; removing the
double is what made it visible, since before that the field body appeared on
both sides of the parent's.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT: counts are one per body on every backend after -21, and
the heap-carrying variant is clean under LSan
(`asan_own_drop_parent_masking_a_returned_field_frees_it`). It is an
observable-side-effect ordering divergence, in the same family as
B-2026-08-28-19.

SEVERITY low: the counts are right, the shape is a discarded result, and a
program whose meaning depends on this order is already relying on unspecified
sequencing between two independent `Drop` bodies. It is a run-vs-build
divergence, though, which is the class this project treats as a bug regardless
of severity.

SOURCE NOTE: found while pinning B-2026-08-28-21's fixtures -- the
`result-discarded` row failed on ORDER after the counts were fixed, and was
left out of the E2E fixture rather than pinned in the wrong direction. The
interpreter twin pins the correct order today, so a fix that moved the compiled
backends into line would make the two fixtures agree; that is the acceptance
test for this row.


NARROWED 2026-08-28, and one hypothesis REFUTED by instrumentation rather than
by reading. Re-measured on 8888f9f (after B-2026-08-28-19 moved the caller-side
argument walk to statement end): the divergence is unchanged, `drop 47` /
`drop W5` compiled against the interpreter's `drop W5` / `drop 47`, so -19 is
not the root and the two rows are separate as filed.

THE OBVIOUS SUSPECT IS NOT INVOLVED. The natural reading is that both temporaries
-- the argument `W { .. }` and the DISCARDED result `R` -- land on the
statement-end drain, which fires LIFO (`drain_statement_temp_user_drops`,
"the last-materialized temp's body runs first"), and that LIFO is what puts the
later-created result ahead of the argument. Instrumented: for this program that
drain fires ZERO times. Neither body goes through it.

Both bodies nonetheless run BEFORE the following `println("end")`, so they are
not at scope exit either. That leaves the NLL live-range-end firing
(`fire_due_user_drops`) as the site, with both temporaries' last use falling at
the same statement.

WHAT THAT CHANGES FOR A FIX. The interpreter gives the two temporaries DIFFERENT
live-range ends -- the argument's at the call, the result's after it -- and the
compiled backend collapses both to one point and then orders them among
themselves. So the question is not "which order should the drain use" but
"should the argument temporary die at the call", which is the same question
B-2026-08-28-19 answered yes for the tuple-element BODIES channel. Extending
that to the whole `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper of an own-`Drop` argument is a change
to when MEMORY is freed, not just a body's position, which is why it was not
attempted under this row's low severity.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while auditing this row for fixability immediately after
landing B-2026-08-28-19. No code change was made; the trace was removed.
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-28 on c8b0734. Divergence unchanged (`drop 47` /
`drop W5` compiled against interp's `drop W5` / `drop 47`), and the previous
narrowing's central claim independently CONFIRMED: instrumenting
`drain_statement_temp_user_drops` to dump its tail shows no whitelisted
`UserDrop` action for this program on either spelling -- only memory-channel
entries -- so the statement-end drain is not the site.

TWO THINGS THIS ADDS.

1. CODEGEN CONTRADICTS ITSELF, which is a sharper framing than
   "interpreter vs compiled" and gives the fix a local oracle. The BOUND
   spelling of the same program agrees on all three backends AND agrees with
   the interpreter's discarded order:

       let x = take(W { r: R { id: 47 }, n: 5 });   interp/jit/AOT
                                                    -> drop W5 / drop 47
       take(W { r: R { id: 47 }, n: 5 });           interp -> drop W5 / drop 47
                                                    jit/AOT -> drop 47 / drop W5

   So codegen already produces the correct order one spelling over. Whatever
   makes the argument temp die at the call in the bound case is absent in the
   discarded one, and that difference -- not the interpreter -- is the thing
   to chase.

2. THE GROUNDING IS THE LIVE-RANGE RULE, NOT "PARENT FIRST". This row cites
   design.md's parent-before-fields ordering, but that rule does not actually
   reach this program: `fn take(w: W) -> R { let W { r, n } = w; r }` MOVES
   `r` out of `w` inside the callee, so by the time either body runs in the
   CALLER there is no parent/child relation left -- they are two independent
   values. Read that way the applicable rule is design.md § Drop ordering's
   LIFO-by-introduction, which would put the later-created result FIRST and
   make the compiled order right.

   The interpreter is still the correct leg, but for the other rule in the
   same section: destructors fire at each binding's LIVE-RANGE end, and the
   argument temporary's last use is the call itself. It dies there, before the
   result exists -- so `drop W5` precedes `drop 47`, and LIFO never gets to
   arbitrate because the two live ranges do not overlap. This matters for the
   fix: the target is "the argument temp dies at the call", not "reorder the
   drain", and it is what the bound spelling already does.

NO CHEAP REORDERING EXISTS, checked rather than assumed. Both bodies come
through the NLL path (`fire_due_user_drops`), which walks the frame in
REVERSE-INTRODUCTION order; the argument temp is introduced first, so it
necessarily fires last from there. Getting it to fire first means firing it at
the call, which is the same conclusion the previous narrowing reached -- a
change to when the own-`Drop` argument's MEMORY is released, not a body
position. Left unattempted under this row's low severity, now with the bound
spelling recorded as the behavioural target and local oracle for it.

fix:
FIXED by 0e872dd. The last of the three enum-member rows, and the one that sat a
level below the other two.

NOT THREE GAPS BUT ONE PREDICATE, which is why the fix adds no per-position
code. Every walker reaches an enum member through `type_runs_user_drop`, and
every leg of that function reads `struct_field_type_names` /
`struct_field_type_exprs` -- the struct field tables. None of them can see a
VARIANT payload, so an enum answered true only via `drop_method_keys`, i.e. only
when it declared its own `Drop`. `enum E2 { A(R), B }` was therefore invisible in
all three member positions at once. Giving the predicate an
`enum_variant_field_type_exprs` leg closed the struct field, the tuple element
and the Vec element together, and the fixtures assert all three for that reason
rather than out of thoroughness.

Two exclusions carried over from the payload walker, for its stated reasons: a
generic enum's payload TE is the type PARAMETER itself, so admitting generic
params would make `Option[T]` look like it carries a Drop-bearing payload for
every `T`; and `Option`/`Result` are excluded outright because their payload
level is already covered by the `optres_*` legs, where admitting them here would
double-count.

THE INTERPRETER HALF is two changes that had to move together, and the coupling
is the same one 9727cdb recorded when it created this row's exclusion. The
payload walk at the four member arms becomes UNCONDITIONAL while the own body
stays gated on `drop_method_keys` -- but `field_value_carries_user_drop` also had
to admit a payload-carrying variant, because that predicate gates the MOVE-OUT
BOOKKEEPING as well as the walks. Widen the walks alone and a value the
bookkeeping does not consider drop-relevant is never marked moved by a
destructure, so the owner's walk still runs at its death and the body fires
twice. That is exactly the failure the -46 fix hit and fixed; the two predicates
have to describe the same set.

WHY IT WAS DEFERRED RATHER THAN DONE WITH -46/-47, and the deferral was correct.
The interpreter half alone is a one-line change and was MEASURED at the time: it
makes the interpreter print `drop R5` while both compiled backends stay silent
-- a fresh run-vs-build divergence manufactured one position over from the one
-46 was filed to remove. The order was forced: widen codegen's predicate first,
then remove the interpreter's gate in the same commit. That is what happened.

VERIFIED on 14 shapes across all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), byte-identical on each: the three payload-only positions now
run `drop R5`, every own-`Drop` shape from -46/-47/-55 still correct, and the

title: AN ENUM WITH NO OWN `Drop` BUT A DROP-BEARING PAYLOAD RUNS NO BODY ON ANY BACKEND when held as a struct field or tuple element: `enum E2 { A(R), B }` (no `impl Drop`) in `let p = (E2.A(R { id: 5 }), 1)` is 0/0/0, though `R`'s body runs when the same value is BOUND directly. The deliberate exclusion of B-2026-08-28-46/-47's fix, because closing it means widening `type_runs_user_drop` to look inside an enum's variants -- a CODEGEN change that must land before the interpreter's
detail:
Measured on 9727cdb, body counts interp / jit / build / build with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. `R` declares a `Drop`; `E2` does not.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop R{self.id}") } }
    enum E2 { A(R), B }        // no `impl Drop`

    tuple element   let p = (E2.A(R { id: 5 }), 1); println(f"{p.1}")
                                            -> 0 / 0 / 0 / 0
    struct field    struct W3 { e: E2, n: i64 }
                    let w = W3 { e: E2.A(R { id: 5 }), n: 1 }; println(f"{w.n}")
                                            -> 0 / 0 / 0 / 0

One `R` is constructed in each program and its body never runs. The
OWN-`Drop` sibling of both shapes (`enum E { A(R), B }` WITH an
`impl Drop`) runs `drop E` then `drop R` on every backend as of 9727cdb,
so the machinery to reach the payload exists and is one predicate away.

Both backends agree, so no A/B or kata parity gate can report it -- the
agree-on-zero shape, the same class as the row this was found beside.

MECHANISM, and it is one line in each backend rather than a missing walk.
CODEGEN reaches an enum member in these positions only through
`type_runs_user_drop`, which answers for an ENUM via `drop_method_keys` alone:
it has legs for a struct's fields, a Vec element, a Map/Set value and a tuple
element, but none that looks INSIDE an enum's variants. So an enum with no own
`Drop` is invisible to `elem_te_runs_user_drop` and to the struct-field
selector, whatever its payload holds. THE INTERPRETER matches that rule
deliberately as of 9727cdb: its enum arms are gated on `drop_method_keys` for
exactly this reason.

WHY IT WAS EXCLUDED RATHER THAN FIXED with -46/-47, which is the part
worth keeping. The interpreter half alone is a one-line change -- drop the
`drop_method_keys` gate on those arms and the payload walk runs. It was
written that way first and MEASURED: it makes the interpreter print
`drop R5` while both compiled backends stay silent, which is a fresh
run-vs-build divergence manufactured one position over from the one -46
was filed to remove. So the order is forced -- widen codegen's selector
first, then remove the interpreter's gate in the same commit.

NOT a memory defect: exit 0 and correct field contents throughout. The
payload's heap is freed by the owner's own drop on both backends; only the
side effect is missing. Bodies only.

fix:

part. The row said `emit_vec_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` "has no enum leg". That

to register the walker at all -- the `elem_struct_name` filter in `stmts.rs`
tested `struct_types.contains_key`, so `Vec[E]` registered nothing and the
walker was never reached.

both backends with the SAME inferred spelling. So the cause is not element-type
inference, which was the other live hypothesis, and not the walker's body. Three

annotated `let mut v: Vec[E]`, and the array literal `[E.B]` -- which also

first: the walker's `field_bodies` comes from `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn`,

holds -- the same asymmetry B-2026-08-28-40 fixed for a struct field and
B-2026-08-28-47 for a tuple element. Both halves land here: the selector admits

`emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn` after the own body.

title: A `Vec` ELEMENT OF AN OWN-`Drop` ENUM RUNS NO BODY ON ANY BACKEND: `let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(E.B)` is 0/0/0 while the TUPLE element of the same enum now runs it -- `emit_vec_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` has no enum leg, the gap B-2026-08-28-47 closed for its tuple sibling
detail:
Measured on 9727cdb, body counts interp / jit / build / build with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0:

    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("drop E") } }

    Vec element    let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(E.B); println(f"{v.len()}")
                                            -> 0 / 0 / 0 / 0
    tuple element  let p = (E.B, 1); println(f"{p.1}")
                                            -> 1 / 1 / 1 / 1   (since 9727cdb)

`v` owns the enum and dies at scope exit, so `E.drop` must run exactly
once. The tuple row is the same value in the sibling container position
and now runs it, which is what makes this a gap rather than a policy.

Both backends agree, so no A/B or kata parity gate can report it -- the
agree-on-zero shape, the same class as the row this was found beside.

MECHANISM, and it is one line in each backend rather than a missing walk.
CODEGEN reaches an enum member in these positions only through
`type_runs_user_drop`, which answers for an ENUM via `drop_method_keys` alone:
it has legs for a struct's fields, a Vec element, a Map/Set value and a tuple
element, but none that looks INSIDE an enum's variants. So an enum with no own
`Drop` is invisible to `elem_te_runs_user_drop` and to the struct-field
selector, whatever its payload holds. THE INTERPRETER matches that rule
deliberately as of 9727cdb: its enum arms are gated on `drop_method_keys` for
exactly this reason.

The container walkers are separate symbols with separate coverage:
`emit_tuple_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` gained an enum leg with
B-2026-08-28-47; `emit_vec_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` has none. The
interpreter serves BOTH shapes from one element loop
(`run_array_element_user_drops`), so its enum arm is gated on the
binding's shape (`is_tuple`) purely to stay level with codegen -- remove
that gate alone and the Vec case becomes an interp-1 / compiled-0
divergence. Measured; that is why the gate is there and commented.

So the fix is the Vec-walker peer of -47's tuple work: give
`emit_vec_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` the same enum leg
(own body, then `emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`), then drop the
`is_tuple` gate in the interpreter in the same commit. `VecDeque` shares
the walker and was not separately measured.

NOT a memory defect: exit 0, no leak reported. Bodies only.

FIXED by 3e4a63b.

The row named the mechanism exactly — B-2026-08-28-26's registration is gated on
the bodies walker existing, an element type with no `Drop` produces no walker,
and the memory half went with the skipped registration — and prescribed the
repair: "this needs the equivalent" of B-2026-08-28-50, where a discarded field
with no `Drop` got no walker and therefore no owner. That is what landed. The
two halves are resolved independently, and the cap-zero on the place path
follows whether EITHER half was taken, since either one makes the leaf an owner
the source must stop competing with.

Both source paths took the same change (`place_source_tuple_leaf_cleanups` and
`track_tuple_destructure_leaf_cleanups`), for the reason -26's own fix needed
both: they are different functions with the identical hole.

A NEW, DISTINCT LEAK WAS ISOLATED WHILE WRITING THE FIXTURE, and it is worth
recording how. The obvious ASAN control — the same tuple never destructured —
FAILED, and the first reading was that the fix had broken it. It had not:
measured against a stashed `src/`, that shape leaks the same 2 bytes before and
after this commit. The tuple binding's own aggregate drop does not reach the
nested struct's `Vec` elements the way the leaf's `TypeExpr`-driven
`synthesize_tuple_drop_fn_te` does, so the undestructured spelling loses the
inner `String` while the destructured one no longer does. Filed on its own row;
the control is deliberately absent from the fixture with the reason stated
there, because asserting it clean would assert something false.

MEASURED. Fresh literal 98 bytes -> 0; place source 2 bytes -> 0. The
Drop-BEARING boundary in the same position stays at one body and one free —
that leaf IS claimed by the bodies walker, and the independence of the two
halves must not turn into a second claim. All twelve shapes from
B-2026-08-28-26's matrix remain backend-identical and valgrind-clean, with every
drop-body count unchanged: this fix moves memory ownership only.

The `Vec` stays in the fixture for the reason B-2026-08-28-50's does: a bare
`String` element is leak-clean here only because LLVM deletes the whole dead
allocation chain, so a fixture written the obvious way would pass against the
broken compiler. The pre-fix run reports exactly "98 byte(s) leaked in 2
allocation(s)".
title: A TUPLE-TYPED DESTRUCTURE LEAF WHOSE ELEMENT TYPE HAS NO `Drop` GETS NO MEMORY OWNER, on either source: `let (inner, n) = ((R { .. }, 2), 1)` where `R` carries a `Vec[String]` and declares no `Drop` loses 98 bytes on a fresh literal and 2 on a tuple LOCAL, while the same tuple left undestructured is clean -- the B-2026-08-28-50 family one container over, and the half B-2026-08-28-26's fix does not reach
detail:
Measured on 72b6f1c (B-2026-08-28-26's fix in place) and identical on the
commit before it, so this is neither caused nor repaired by that work.

    struct R { id: i64, tags: Vec[String] }        // NO impl Drop
    fn mkv(n: i64) -> Vec[String] { let mut v = Vec[String].new(); v.push(f"t{n}"); v }

    FRESH tuple-literal source:
      let (inner, n) = ((R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1);
                                              98 bytes definitely lost
    PLACE source:
      let p = ((R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1); let (inner, n) = p;
                                              2 bytes definitely lost
    UNDESTRUCTURED control:
      let p = ((R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1); println(f"{p.1}");
                                              clean

THE `Vec` IS THE REPRO, NOT THE DEFECT, exactly as on B-2026-08-28-50: a bare
`String` element is leak-clean in the same shape only because LLVM deletes the
whole dead allocation chain. `mkv` builds its buffer through a runtime `push`
the optimizer cannot fold, which is what makes the bytes observable. Any
non-DCE-able heap in that position leaks the same way.

WHY B-2026-08-28-26 DOES NOT COVER IT, and why the two must not be merged. That
row is about the missing BODY, and its fix registers the tuple channel --
`emit_tuple_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` for the bodies, `synthesize_tuple_drop_fn_te`
for the memory -- gated on the bodies walker existing. A leaf whose element type
declares no `Drop` produces no bodies walker, so the whole registration is
skipped and the memory half goes with it. Same shape as B-2026-08-28-50, where a
discarded struct FIELD with no `Drop` got no walker and therefore no owner; the
fix there was to let the second candidate arm claim exactly what the walker
declined, and this needs the equivalent for the tuple leaf.

The two sources leak different amounts because they lose different things: the
fresh literal has no owner for the element at all (98 bytes -- the `Vec` buffer
and its element), while the place source's own walk still frees most of it and
loses only the inner `String` (2 bytes).

fix:
FIXED by e615cce, and the row's diagnosis needed revising in one important
way before it could be.

WHAT THE ROW SPLIT INTO (a) AND (b) WAS ONE DEFECT. The row read the compiled
`dE dE` as a correct-count/wrong-placement problem plus a separately missing
payload body. Both halves had the same cause: those `dE`s were coming from the
MEMORY channel, which reached the body only because `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`
handed it the user-drop WRAPPER for a Drop-bearing enum. Scope exit is simply
where the memory channel drains, and the wrapper runs the enum's own body but
not its payload's -- which is exactly the `mid end dE dE` the row recorded.

B-2026-08-28-58 (033eafc) closed that wrapper hole. Re-measured immediately
after it, the compiled side ran NO array element bodies at all:

    let a: Array[E, 2] = [E.B, E.A(R { id: 3 })]; println("mid"); println("end");
      interp   dE dE dR3 mid end
      jit      mid end
      build    mid end

MEASURING THE SURFACE THEN SHOWED THE ROW UNDERSTATED IT. `Array` had no
element-bodies walker at all, so a STRUCT element never ran its body on the
compiled backends either -- the wrapper was already excluded for structs by
B-2026-07-30-11, so nothing ever leaked through for them. Baseline, 12 shapes,
11 diverged (only the no-Drop boundary agreed), including `Array[R, 2]` of a
plain Drop-bearing struct and `Array[S, 2]` whose elements own heap. The enum
was just the one element type whose body reached the output by accident, which
is what made this look like a placement bug rather than a missing walker.

FIX. `emit_array_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn` -- the array peer of the tuple
(B-2026-07-30-11) and `Vec` (B-2026-08-28-55) walkers. Bodies-only: it calls
`emit_slot_drop_bodies_at` per element and frees nothing, with the array's
storage still owned by the scope-exit `__karac_drop_array_te_*` registered
beside it. A separate emitter rather than a reuse of the tuple one because an
array lowers to an `ArrayType`, which `build_struct_gep` cannot index; every
element shares one `TypeExpr`, so the walk is straight-line over `0..n`.

SECOND HALF, found by the matrix rather than by the row. A bare rebind
`let b = a;` carries no annotation, so the destination could not resolve its
element type and registered nothing while the move disarmed the source: bodies
in the interpreter and on neither compiled backend. Type-agnostic (it failed
identically for `Array[R, 2]`) and invisible with an annotation on the
destination, which already worked. Fixed with an `array_var_elem_te` source
record, the array twin of `tuple_var_elem_tes` / `optres_var_payload_tes`.

THE TRAP IN THAT SECOND HALF, and why it is worth reading before touching this
code. The obvious spelling is to widen `arr_parts`, the existing resolution
chain -- but `arr_parts` feeds `make_array_param_callee_owned`, the MEMORY
registration, as well as the new bodies one. Widening it gave `b` a second
memory drop over elements `a` still owns: ASAN reported `attempting double-free`
on `let a: Array[S, 2] = [..]; let b = a;`. The bodies resolution therefore runs
on its own chain and leaves `arr_parts` untouched. Bodies follow the move;
memory does not. The `moved-on` ASAN row exists to hold that line.

MEASURED, 12 shapes, interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, all four
byte-identical after the fix (baseline in parens where it differed):

    Array[E,2] mixed        dE dE dR3 mid        (compiled: nothing)
    Array[E,1] unit         dE                   (compiled: nothing)
    Array[H,1] payload-only dR4                  (compiled: nothing)
    Array[R,2] struct       dR1 dR2              (compiled: nothing)

    Array[E,2] moved on     dE dE moved          (compiled: nothing)
    Array[R,2] moved on     dR1 dR2 moved        (compiled: nothing)
    Array[E,2] moved+annot  dE dE moved          (compiled: nothing)
    Array[E,2] indexed      dE dE dR7 read       (compiled: nothing)
    nested scope            dE inner outer       (compiled: nothing)
    Array[J,2] no drop      (nothing)            unchanged boundary

`memory_sanitizer::asan_fixed_array_element_bodies_are_memory_balanced`, both

title: AN `Array[E, N]` OF AN OWN-`Drop` ENUM DIVERGES TWICE OVER: the interpreter runs both bodies IMMEDIATELY and the compiled backends run them at SCOPE EXIT, and the compiled side additionally LOSES the payload body -- `let a: Array[E, 2] = [E.B, E.A(R{3})]` is interp `dE dE dR3 mid end` vs compiled `mid end dE dE`
detail:
Measured on 1de8459 (i.e. AFTER B-2026-08-28-55's `Vec` fix, 0ad7a39),
drop-body counts and ORDER, interp / jit / build.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }

      let a: Array[E, 2] = [E.B, E.A(R { id: 3 })];
      println("mid"); println("end");

        interp:   dE | dE | dR3 | mid | end
        jit:      mid | end | dE | dE
        build:    mid | end | dE | dE

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS IN ONE SHAPE, and they need separating before either is
fixed:

  (a) PLACEMENT. The interpreter fires both bodies at the binding's NLL end --
      which is immediately, since `a` is never read again -- and both compiled
      backends fire at SCOPE EXIT, after `end`. Same count, different observable
      position, so this is a live run-vs-build divergence even where the counts
      agree. design.md § Drop ordering puts the body at the final owner's
      live-range end, which is the interpreter's answer.

  (b) MISSING PAYLOAD BODY ON THE COMPILED SIDE. The compiled backends print
      `dE dE` and never `dR3`: the enum's own body runs for each element but the
      live variant's PAYLOAD walk does not. The interpreter runs both. This half
      is a missing body, not a mis-timed one.

RELATIONSHIP TO THE NEIGHBOURS. Before B-2026-08-28-46/-47 (9727cdb) this shape
was interp 0 / compiled 1 -- silent in the interpreter, which is the direction
-46 fixed for struct fields. That fix deliberately scoped its interpreter
element leg to TUPLES via an `is_tuple` flag precisely because `Vec`/`Array`
behaved differently on the compiled side; B-2026-08-28-55 then fixed `Vec`
(0ad7a39) and `Array` came along for the interpreter half only, which is what
produced today's placement split. So this row is the residual of that scoping
decision, and it is the shape to check FIRST when the `is_tuple` guard is
eventually lifted.

The `Option[E]` sibling is filed separately and fails differently again
(silent on all three).

re-measured against current main after two sibling sessions fixed the tuple,

fix:
FIXED by 033eafc. TWO defects, and neither could land alone.

(1) MISSING BODY, both backends. `emit_optres_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`'s
target filter demanded `struct_types`, so a user-enum payload got no walker
emitted and the binding took no `UserDrop` registration at all. It now admits a
non-shared user enum (Option/Result excluded — a nested built-in rides its own
walker) and runs the enum's own body followed by its live variant's payload
walk, the order every sibling walker in this family uses.

(2) MISPLACED BODY, compiled only — the half the row did not have, found while
reproducing it. `emit_user_drop_wrappers` mints `karac_drop_<T>` for EVERY type
in `drop_method_keys`, enums included, and `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`'s
B-2026-07-30-11 guard (which exists precisely to stop the memory channel
picking up that wrapper) covered `struct_types` only. So for a Drop-bearing
ENUM the module lookup handed the memory channel the WRAPPER and the body ran
at scope exit: `let r: Result[E, i64] = Ok(E.B);` printed `dE` AFTER the last
statement on jit and build while the interpreter printed nothing. The struct
guard's own comment had noted the `Result` sibling was safe "because its admit
is narrower" — true for structs, and exactly what left the enum uncovered.

The two are coupled: fixing (1) alone makes `Result` run the body TWICE. The
guard therefore gains an enum leg routing to the memory-only
`emit_enum_drop_switch`, with the same `$mem` fallback name the struct twin
needed for B-2026-08-03-10 (`emit_primitive_drop_fn` reopens the very lookup
the guard exists to bypass).

INTERPRETER, both halves. `run_optres_payload_user_drops` bound the payload as
`Value::Struct` and returned on anything else. And `type_name_runs_user_drop` —
the gate that arms the registration at all — recursed only through `StructDef`,
so `Option[H]` for a payload-only enum never qualified; that leg is the
interpreter twin of the one B-2026-08-28-54 added to codegen's
`type_runs_user_drop`.

MEASURED, twelve shapes, interp / jit / build (+ KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), all now
byte-identical with the body at the binding's live-range end:

    Option[E] Some(E.B)          0/0/0 -> dE
    Option[E] Some(E.A(R))       0/0/0 -> dE dR
    Result[E,i64] Ok(E.B)        0/dE(late)/dE(late) -> dE
    Result[E,i64] Ok(E.A(R))     0/dE(late)/dE(late) -> dE dR
    Result[i64,E] Err(E.B)       0/dE(late)/dE(late) -> dE
    Option[G] Some(G.A(str))     0/0/0 -> dG          (G carries heap)
    Result[G,i64] Ok(G.A(str))   0/dG(late)/dG(late) -> dG
    Option[H] Some(H.A(R))       0/0/0 -> dR          (H has no own Drop)
    Result[H,i64] Ok(H.A(R))     0/0/0 -> dR
    Option[J] Some(J.A(str))     0/0/0 -> 0           (boundary, unchanged)
    Option[None]                 0/0/0 -> 0           (boundary, unchanged)
    CTRL Option[struct R]        dR/dR/dR             (unchanged)

Move-out is unchanged and was re-measured across nine consumption shapes
(consuming match / if-let / no-bind arm / rebind / from-call / passthrough /
discarded temp / nested scope): all four surfaces identical, no double fire.

FIXTURES, all three suites, each RED-verified against the unfixed tree:
`codegen::e2e_own_drop_enum_as_optres_payload_runs_its_body`,
`interpreter::own_drop_enum_as_optres_payload_runs_its_body`,
`memory_sanitizer::asan_own_drop_enum_as_optres_payload_is_memory_balanced`.
The codegen rows pin ORDER, not just count, because that is where defect (2)
lived.

TWO SEPARATE FINDINGS came out of this and are filed on their own rows rather
than folded in here: B-2026-08-28-63 (a consuming `match`/`if let` arm that
binds an enum payload out runs NO body for it, while the same arm binding a
STRUCT payload runs one — pre-existing, measured identical before this fix) and
B-2026-08-28-64 (`Option[K]` never frees a heap-carrying nested-struct payload,
where `Result[K, i64]` does). The second is why the ASAN fixture excludes that
one shape and says so.

CORRECTION to this row as filed: it predicted the fix would be "on the
Option/Result payload leg on both sides, not in the user-enum arms", via
`value_runs_user_drop` classifying a bare `Value::EnumVariant` as drop-free.
The payload leg was indeed one half, but the diagnosis missed the compiled
memory-channel defect entirely (the row recorded `Option` as 0/0/0 and did not
measure `Result`, which it noted as untested) — and `Result` is where the
run-vs-build divergence was hiding.
title: AN `Option[E]` HOLDING AN OWN-`Drop` ENUM RUNS NO BODY ON ANY BACKEND -- `let o: Option[E] = Some(E.B)` is 0/0/0 and the payload variant loses `dR` too; the `Option` sibling of B-2026-08-28-55's `Vec` element, still open after that fix
detail:
Measured on 1de8459 (AFTER B-2026-08-28-55's `Vec` fix, 0ad7a39),
drop-body counts interp / jit / build.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }

      let o: Option[E] = Some(E.B);            0 / 0 / 0
      let q: Option[E] = Some(E.A(R{id:4}));   0 / 0 / 0   (no `dE`, no `dR4`)

    CONTROLS on the same build, all correct:
      let e = E.B;                             1 / 1 / 1
      let p = (E.B, 1);                        1 / 1 / 1   (B-2026-08-28-47)
      let w = W { e: E.B, n: 1 };              1 / 1 / 1   (B-2026-08-28-46)
      let v = [E.B];                           1 / 1 / 1   (B-2026-08-28-55)

ALL THREE BACKENDS AGREE ON ZERO, so no A/B gate can report it -- the same
reason B-2026-08-28-47 sat open, and why this is classed soundness rather than
run-vs-build. The `Option` owns the `E`, the binding dies at scope exit, so
`E.drop` must run exactly once and the payload's body with it.

WHY IT SURVIVED THE SWEEP. `Option`/`Result` are built-ins with no source
`EnumDef`, so every declared-type-driven walk in this family short-circuits them
into `run_discarded_value_user_drops` / the tag-guarded
`emit_optres_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn` before the user-enum arms are reached
(the `enum_name == "Option" || enum_name == "Result"` guard that opens each of
those arms). Those Option paths in turn recurse through `value_runs_user_drop`
on the PAYLOAD, which classifies a bare `Value::EnumVariant` of a user enum as
drop-free -- the payload-level twin of the gap B-2026-08-28-46 closed one
container level up. So the fix is on the Option/Result payload leg on both
sides, not in the user-enum arms.

`Result[E, _]` is untested here and should be measured with it.

registration itself." That is precisely it.

third has to add work rather than re-claim heap: the `karac_drop_<E>` wrapper's

title: A NAMED TUPLE-DESTRUCTURE LEAF OF ENUM TYPE LOSES THE ENUM'S OWN `Drop` BODY ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS while the interpreter runs it: `let (gv, gn) = (E.A(R{5}), 6);` is interp 1 / jit 0 / build 0, and the compiled side still runs the PAYLOAD body, so it is the enum's own body alone that is lost
detail:
Measured on 1de8459, and separately BEFORE and AFTER the
B-2026-08-28-46/-47 fix (9727cdb) -- byte-identical on each, so this is
pre-existing and untouched by that row. Drop-body counts interp / jit / build.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"r{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("e") }

    PAYLOAD variant:
      let g = (E.A(R { id: 5 }), 6); let (gv, gn) = g;
        interp:   e | r5 | g=6 | end
        compiled: ---- | r5 | g=6 | end        <- `e` missing, `r5` present
    UNIT variant:
      let g = (E.B, 6); let (gv, gn) = g;
        interp:   e | g=6 | end
        compiled: ---- | g=6 | end

THE SPLIT IS THE DIAGNOSTIC. In the payload case the compiled backends still run
the PAYLOAD body (`r5`) and lose only the enum's OWN (`e`), so the leaf IS
reached and walked -- what is missing is the `<E>.drop` call that should precede
the payload walk, not the registration itself. The unit case has no payload to
hide behind and shows the loss bare.

The interpreter is right: `gv` binds the `E`, owns it, and dies at scope exit.

DISTINCT FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS, which are all a different leaf: B-2026-08-28-10 is
a STRUCT-pattern leaf, B-2026-08-28-11 a GENERIC struct leaf out of a tuple,
B-2026-08-28-12 a WILDCARD leaf (and aligned-silent, not divergent). This is a
NAMED leaf of ENUM type.

fix:
FIXED by 6c0a296.

THE CORRECTION ABOVE IS THE ROW'S REAL CONTENT, and it landed as corrected: an
arm on `tuple_elem_needs_deep_drop`, not a change of drop strategy at the
binding site. The originally-filed mechanism was inferred from the symptom and
was wrong; that is recorded in the row rather than quietly overwritten, because
the same inference is available to the next reader.

THE NEW ARM IS NARROWER THAN THE OBVIOUS ONE, deliberately.
`contains_vec_of_heap_elems` answers only "does this transitively contain a
`Vec` whose ELEMENTS own heap" -- precisely what the LLVM-type walk under-frees,
since it reaches the `{ptr,len,cap}` buffer and cannot see whether what is
behind it is scalars or `String`s. Reaching for the existing
`type_expr_has_drop_heap` would have been a one-liner and wrong in the
permissive direction: it answers true for ANY heap-owning type, so a struct
whose only heap is a direct `String` field -- which the LLVM walk frees
correctly today -- would have been moved onto a different drop strategy for no
reason. This predicate selects that strategy for EVERY tuple binding in the
program, so the width of the arm is the whole risk, and `direct-string-field` is
a fixture row holding the boundary.

BLAST RADIUS MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED. The shapes the widening newly moves
are all clean: the element read through the tuple, the element MOVED OUT to a
callee (the move neutralizer still works against the newly selected drop), a
Drop-BEARING struct element (one body, heap fully freed), and the same `Vec`
reached through two struct levels. The full suite was run on the change before
it was committed, not only the three heavy targets, for the same reason.

MEASURED: struct-wrapped `Vec` 2 bytes -> 0; two struct levels -> 0; the
direct-`Vec` spelling unchanged and clean, which is the row that showed the gate
was the axis in the first place -- one ownership question answered two ways,
differing only in whether a struct sits between the tuple and the `Vec`.

The `Vec` is the repro rather than the defect here as in B-2026-08-28-50 and
-56: `mkv` builds its buffer through a runtime `push` the optimizer cannot fold.
The pre-fix run reports exactly "2 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s)".
title: AN UNDESTRUCTURED TUPLE LOSES THE INNER HEAP OF A NESTED STRUCT ELEMENT: `let p = ((R { tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1); println(p.1)` where `R` declares no `Drop` leaks the `Vec`'s inner `String` -- the tuple binding's own aggregate drop frees the outer buffer but not its elements, where the DESTRUCTURED spelling of the same tuple is now clean (B-2026-08-28-56)
detail:
Measured on 3e4a63b and identical on the commit before it -- verified by
stashing `src/` and rebuilding -- so this is neither caused nor repaired by
B-2026-08-28-56.

    struct R { id: i64, tags: Vec[String] }        // NO impl Drop
    fn mkv(n: i64) -> Vec[String] { let mut v = Vec[String].new(); v.push(f"t{n}"); v }

    UNDESTRUCTURED:
      let p = ((R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1); println(f"{p.1}");
                                              2 bytes definitely lost
    DESTRUCTURED (clean since B-2026-08-28-56):
      let p = ((R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1); let (inner, n) = p;   clean
      let (inner, n) = ((R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 2), 1);              clean

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE DIAGNOSIS. Two spellings of one ownership question now
answer differently, and the destructured one is right. A destructure leaf
registers `synthesize_tuple_drop_fn_te`, which is `TypeExpr`-driven and descends
into the nested struct's `Vec` to free its elements. An undestructured tuple
BINDING registers its drop through the LLVM-type-driven path
(`track_tuple_var` -> `synthesize_aggregate_drop_fn`), which frees the `Vec`'s
outer `{ptr,len,cap}` buffer -- 96 of the 98 bytes -- and does not reach the
element `String` inside it. The 2 bytes are exactly that one element.

That is the same declared-name-erasure class B-2026-08-02-26 records for tuple
LITERAL element inference: an LLVM-type walk cannot see that a `{ptr,len,cap}`
holds `String`s rather than scalars, so it stops one level short. The fix
direction is presumably to give the tuple binding the same `TypeExpr`-driven
drop the leaf now gets, using `tuple_var_elem_tes` (which B-2026-08-28-26's fix
already populates for leaves) -- but the binding site has its own callers and
its own ownership contracts, so it is a measured change rather than a
substitution.

WHY IT IS FILED RATHER THAN FIXED ALONGSIDE -56: it is a different site
(the binding's drop synthesis, not the destructure leaf's registration), it
predates that row, and mixing an ownership repair with a drop-synthesis
deepening is what made B-2026-08-28-29's own fix take four corrections.

SOURCE NOTE: found because it was written as the obvious ASAN control for
B-2026-08-28-56's fixture and FAILED. The first reading was that the fix had
broken it; measuring against a stashed `src/` showed it identical before and
after. The control is deliberately absent from that fixture, with the reason
stated inline, because asserting it clean would assert something false.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
CORRECTION 2026-08-28, before any fix attempt. THE MECHANISM ABOVE IS WRONG and
is retained only so the correction is legible.

It states that the undestructured tuple binding "registers its drop through the
LLVM-type-driven path (`track_tuple_var` -> `synthesize_aggregate_drop_fn`)".
That was inferred from the symptom, not read. The binding site ALREADY has the
`TypeExpr` path, added by B-2026-08-02-26 for exactly this class:

    let deep_elem_tes = self.tuple_binding_elem_tes(ty.as_ref(), value)
        .filter(|tes| tes.iter().any(|e| self.tuple_elem_needs_deep_drop(e)));
    if let Some(elem_tes) = deep_elem_tes {
        if let Some(drop_fn) = self.synthesize_tuple_drop_fn_te(agg_ty, &elem_tes) { ... }

What declines is the GATE. `tuple_elem_needs_deep_drop` (synth_drop.rs) admits a
`TypeKind::Tuple` by recursion, and a `TypeKind::Path` only when the element is
ITSELF a `Vec[<heap>]` (`vec_inner_type_expr`) or an `Option`/`Result` whose
payload qualifies. A `Path` naming a STRUCT that merely CONTAINS a `Vec[heap]`
field answers false, so the tuple takes the LLVM-type drop -- which frees the
`Vec`'s outer buffer and cannot see that its elements are `String`s.

ISOLATED, and the repro is simpler than the one above -- no nesting is needed:

    fn mkv(n: i64) -> Vec[String] { let mut v = Vec[String].new(); v.push(f"t{n}"); v }

    let p = (mkv(3), 1);                    println(f"{p.1}")   clean
      (a DIRECT `Vec[String]` element -- the gate admits it)
    struct R { id: i64, tags: Vec[String] }        // no impl Drop
    let p = (R { id: 41, tags: mkv(3) }, 1);  println(f"{p.1}")   2 bytes lost
      (a STRUCT element carrying the same `Vec` -- the gate declines it)

So the fix is an arm on `tuple_elem_needs_deep_drop` for a struct element that
transitively owns heap the LLVM walk cannot reach, NOT a change of drop
strategy at the binding site.

THAT GATE SELECTS BETWEEN TWO WHOLE DROP STRATEGIES for every tuple binding in
the program, which is why this stays filed rather than fixed on sight: widening
it moves tuples that are correct today onto a different drop, and the blast
radius wants the full suite, not the three heavy targets. The narrowest form is
an arm that answers true only when the struct element transitively contains a
`Vec[<heap>]` -- precisely the case the LLVM walk under-frees -- rather than for
any heap-owning struct.

SEVERITY unchanged at low: 2 bytes per binding, no divergence (both backends
leak it), and the destructured spellings are correct since B-2026-08-28-56.

title: A GENERIC CALLEE'S tuple element still loses its Drop-bearing field's body when destructured at the call site: `fn src[T](x: T) -> (Box2[T], i64)` with `let (b, n) = src(R { id: 47 });` prints `drop 47` under `--interp` and nothing on either compiled backend. The three CONCRETE sources B-2026-08-28-11 measured are fixed; this one is not, because the element type read from the callee's declaration IS the bare `Box2[T]` and binding `T` needs the CALL SITE's substitution -- the B-2026-08-28-28 machinery rather than -11's.
detail:
A GENERIC CALLEE'S tuple element still loses its Drop-bearing field's body.
Split out of B-2026-08-28-11 rather than left implicit: that row's three
sources -- a tuple local, a call result and a tuple literal, all spelling a
CONCRETE `Box2[R]` -- are fixed by 821d5ab, and this fourth source is not.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct Box2[T] { v: T }
    fn src[T](x: T) -> (Box2[T], i64) { return (Box2[T] { v: x }, 1); }

    fn main() { let (b, n) = src(R { id: 47 }); println(f"{n}") }
                                                   -> 1 / 0 / 0

Measured on 821d5ab, drop-body counts interp / jit / build, in the same
eight-row matrix whose other seven rows agree on all three.

WHY -11's FIX DOES NOT REACH IT, which is the whole content of this row. That
fix carries an instantiation to the destructure leaf from wherever the element
type is SPELLED concretely -- a struct literal's own `Box2[R]`, or a callee
whose declared return type says `(Box2[R], i64)`. Here the callee's declared
return type says `(Box2[T], i64)`, and `T` is bound only at the CALL SITE.

AND FORCING IT IS WORSE THAN LEAVING IT, which is measured rather than assumed.
-11's fallback (`concrete_generic_struct_inst(te).unwrap_or(te)`) would happily
record `Box2[T]` here. That record satisfies the instantiation lookup and stops
it before the arm that would have resolved `T` -- the hazard B-2026-08-27-36
documents -- and when the same fallback was applied without an argument check
during -11's development it did not merely lose a body: it made
`e2e_heap_tuple_arg_escaping_the_frame_is_freed_once` print a dangling pointer
where `x` belonged, an OVER-FREE of the caller's buffer. So -11's guard rejects
a bare-parameter record by design, and this row is what that rejection costs.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE: the per-call-site binding `call_type_subs` holds, flattened
through the active monomorph's `type_subst_names` -- the same table and the same
flattening B-2026-08-28-28 used to name a generic callee's tuple ELEMENT, one
question over (that row asked for the element's type NAME; this one needs the
whole instantiation `Box2[R]`). Both the caller-side leaf recorders -11 touched
would then consult it before falling back.

NOT a memory defect: bodies only, and the leaf's memory is registered
independently. SEVERITY medium on the same footing as its parent -- a `Drop`
that closes a file or releases a lock simply does not happen once compiled, and
run-vs-build divergence is the class this project treats as a bug regardless.

fix:
FIXED by 5ce2a57, by modelling the route rather than by patching a symptom —
which is what the row's own "what it would take" proposed, and it held up.

`fn_returns_param_via_call(program, f, i)` asks whether `f` hands parameter `i`
to another CALL whose result reaches a return site. It is a separate,
PROGRAM-AWARE entry point rather than a widening of `fn_returns_param`, for the
reason that predicate's own doc gives: eight codegen ownership consumers read it
and several are documented as turning a leak into corruption if its answer
moves. Only the two caller-side Drop-BODY walks ask this one.

INTERPROCEDURAL BY NECESSITY. Passing the param to a call proves nothing:
`fn consumer(y: R) -> i64 { return uses(y); }` genuinely consumes it, so a
predicate keyed on "the param appears as an argument at a return site" would
take that value's ONLY body away. The CALLEE's own `fn_returns_param` answer is
what decides, which is exactly the precision the two existing routes already
demand and the reason the fixture's `callee-consumes` row exists.

ONE LEVEL, BARE ARGUMENT — the conservative direction the row prescribed. A
missed escape keeps a double body; a false one loses the only `Drop`. TWO SHAPES
THEREFORE STAY DOUBLED, measured and named rather than quietly dropped:

    fn mid(x: R) -> (BoxR, i64) { return outer2(x); }      -> 2  (two hops)
    fn wrapped(y: R) -> (BoxR, i64) { return (src2(y).0, 9); }
                                                          -> 2  (forwarded into
                                                                 a PROJECTION)

Admitting either means proving the value survives two frames rather than one.
They are documented in the fixture's doc comment instead of pinned, so it
asserts only counts that are correct, and they are not filed separately because
they are the same route under-approximated by design — the pattern
`fn_returns_param_parts`' own doc already follows for its limits.

NEITHER BACKEND WAS RIGHT, which is why no run-vs-build gate ever saw this: the
interpreter doubled too. That makes the interpreter twin here a regression test
rather than the oracle, unusually for this family.

VERIFIED on a six-row matrix identical across interp / jit / build. Fixtures:
`e2e_param_escaping_through_a_forwarded_call_drops_once` and
`test_param_escaping_through_a_forwarded_call_drops_once`, both proven RED by
stashing only `src/`. The generic spelling is pinned beside the plain one
because it is how the row was found — B-2026-08-28-61 removed the cancelling
half of a two-bug coincidence there, and re-measuring the non-generic twin is

title: A BY-VALUE PARAM THAT ESCAPES THROUGH A CALL in return position runs its `Drop` body TWICE on all three backends: `fn outer(y: R) -> (BoxR, i64) { return src(y); }` with `let (d, n) = outer(R { id: 49 });` prints `drop 49` twice for one `R`. `fn_returns_param` models the param used BARE at a return site and the param moved into a returned aggregate LITERAL; a param handed to another CALL whose result is returned is a THIRD escape route it does not model, so the caller-side walk fires alongside the eventual owner's. Backend-consistent, and independent of genericity -- the generic and non-generic spellings double identically.
detail:
A BY-VALUE PARAM THAT ESCAPES THROUGH A CALL in return position runs its user
`Drop` body twice for one object, on every backend.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct BoxR { v: R }
    fn src2(x: R) -> (BoxR, i64) { return (BoxR { v: x }, 1); }
    fn outer2(y: R) -> (BoxR, i64) { return src2(y); }
    fn main() { let (d, n) = outer2(R { id: 49 }); println(f"{n}") }

    interp / jit / build  ->  2 / 2 / 2

One `R` is constructed. `drop 49` prints twice, then `1`.

THE ROUTE IS THE POINT. Kara passes a by-value argument under a CALLER-DROPS
convention -- the caller drops a fresh temporary after the call and the callee
registers nothing -- and codegen carves out the escapes it knows about:
`fn_returns_param` recognizes the param used BARE at a return site or moved into
a returned aggregate LITERAL (`(r, 9)`, `Holder { r }`), and B-2026-08-26-9
added the STORE-into-self-or-a-ref-param route. A param handed to ANOTHER CALL
whose result is returned is a third route, and none of the three predicates
model it. So `outer2`'s caller-side walk fires `y`'s body while the value is in
fact still travelling out through `src2`'s return, to be dropped again by
whoever owns the result.

INDEPENDENT OF GENERICITY, which is what makes it a route rather than a
substitution gap: the generic spelling
`fn outer[U](y: U) -> (Box2[U], i64) { src(y) }` doubles identically, and both
were measured side by side.

VISIBLE ONLY SINCE B-2026-08-28-61, and that is a disclosure rather than a
regression. Before that fix the GENERIC spelling was silent here -- right by
accident, because the missing destructure-leaf body cancelled the extra
caller-side one -- while the non-generic spelling already doubled. -61 removed
the cancelling half, so the two spellings now agree with each other and are both
wrong in the same way. Fixing the route corrects both in one move.

NOT a memory defect: bodies only, and it is backend-consistent, so no
run-vs-build gate sees it. SEVERITY medium on the same footing as the rest of
this family -- a `Drop` that closes a file or releases a lock runs twice.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE: teach `fn_returns_param` (and the parts sibling) the
call-forwarding route -- a param passed as an argument to a call whose value
reaches a return site. The conservative direction is the usual one for this
family: reporting the escape suppresses the caller-side fire, and a MISSED
escape keeps today's double while a FALSE one would suppress the only body that
runs, so the route should be admitted only where the argument is the param
BARE, matching the precision the two existing routes already demand.

SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-28-61, by widening its matrix to a
generic wrapper and then re-measuring the non-generic twin to determine whether

title: A CONSUMING `match` / `if let` ARM THAT BINDS AN ENUM PAYLOAD OUT RUNS NO `Drop` BODY FOR IT ON ANY BACKEND, while the same arm binding a STRUCT payload runs one -- `match o { Some(e) => ... }` for `Option[E]` prints `got` and nothing else
detail:
Measured on 033eafc (i.e. AFTER B-2026-08-28-58's fix), drop-body output,
interp / jit / build. All three agree, which is why no A/B gate reports it.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }

      let o: Option[E] = Some(E.A(R { id: 1 }));
      match o { Some(e) => { println("got") } None => { println("none") } }

        interp / jit / build:   got          <- expected `got dE dR1`

    if let Some(e) = o { println("got") }           same: `got`

CONTROL, same program shape one type over, correct on all three backends:

      let o: Option[R] = Some(R { id: 1 });
      match o { Some(r) => { println("got") } None => { println("none") } }
        interp / jit / build:   got dR1                       <- correct

      if let Some(r) = o { println("got") }
        interp / jit / build:   got dR2                       <- correct

So the machinery is present and works; it is blind to an ENUM payload
specifically. `e` is an owned `E` local with a live range ending at the arm's
end, so its `Drop` body must run exactly once there, and its live variant's
payload body with it.

The arm's move-out bookkeeping is correct and is NOT the bug: the SOURCE
`Option`'s payload walk is retracted exactly as it should be (verified — no
double fire, and the memory side is balanced under LSan, `consuming-match-
moved-out` in `asan_own_drop_enum_as_optres_payload_is_memory_balanced`). What
is missing is the DESTINATION half: the arm binding never registers a body for
the enum it now owns. So this is an under-drop with no double-drop hiding
behind it -- the safe direction, but still a body the language promises.

PRE-EXISTING, and deliberately established as such rather than assumed:
measured identical on the tree with B-2026-08-28-58's fix STASHED (`got`, all
three backends, both spellings). The -58 work does not touch arm bindings.

WHY IT SURVIVED THE CONTAINER SWEEP. -46/-47/-54/-55/-58 all closed the
position where the enum is a MEMBER of something that dies -- struct field,
tuple element, `Vec` element, `Option`/`Result` payload -- i.e. the owner's
walk. A `match` arm is the opposite direction: the payload stops being a member
and becomes a binding in its own right, which is a different registration site
(`pattern_binding.rs`) that the sweep never touched. The struct control passing
is what localizes it there rather than in any walker.

SOURCE NOTE: found while building the move-out regression matrix for
B-2026-08-28-58 -- the nine consumption shapes were there to prove the fix did
not double-fire, and two of them turned out to fire zero times for a reason
that predates it.
fix:
FIXED by f862656.

CODEGEN. An inline `Option`/`Result` enum payload bound out by a consuming arm
was registered with `track_enum_var`, which covers the payload's MEMORY and
nothing else. It now also registers `emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn` on
the `UserDrop` channel; that emitter is name-driven and has answered for enums
since B-2026-08-28-40, so it runs the enum's own body followed by its live
variant's payload walk and frees nothing -- which is what lets it sit beside the
`EnumDrop` on the same slot.

INTERPRETER. The gate was the same struct-only bind in THREE copies -- the
`match` arm stash in `pattern_match.rs` and the `if let` / `while let` stashes
in `eval_expr.rs`. All three had to move together: leaving one behind makes the
same program print differently depending on which spelling consumed the payload,
which is why `if-let` is a fixture row beside `match` rather than a footnote.

TWO THINGS THE REPRODUCTION FOUND THAT THE ROW DID NOT HAVE.

(1) A BOXED enum payload takes a different branch. An enum wider than the
`Option` payload area (`enum G { A(String), B }` is 4 words against 3) is
heap-boxed, so the inline arm declines on word count. That branch admitted
STRUCTS only. Fixing just the inline arm made the interpreter fire the body
while both compiled backends stayed silent -- converting the row's agreed
silence into a live run-vs-build divergence, which is strictly worse than the
bug being fixed. Measured before the boxed leg went in:
`match o { Some(g) => .. }` for `Option[G]` was interp `got dG` / jit `got` /
build `got`. The boxed branch now admits a non-shared user enum.

(2) An arm that CONSUMES its binding gives the body two owners. With a real
registration on the arm binding, `let k = match o { Some(e) => { e } .. }` runs
the body once for the arm and once for `k`: measured `dE dE kept` on all four
surfaces against the interpreter's `dE kept` before the gate. The registration
is therefore gated on the arm's consumption classifier
(`consume_class::binding_only_borrowed`), per BINDING rather than per arm --
a multi-binding pattern can borrow one payload and move another -- populated at
the `match` arm loop and at the `if let` / `while let` bind sites. The boxed leg
carries the same gate for its enum half.

THE STRUCT SIBLING IS NOT FIXED HERE, DELIBERATELY, and this is the part worth
reading before anyone tries. The struct spelling of (2) has the same double
fire and predates all of this work: `let k = match o { Some(r) => { r } .. }`
for `Option[R]` prints `dR1 dR1 kept` on both compiled backends against the
interpreter's `dR1 kept`. Applying the identical gate to the struct arm was
tried, and it suppressed THREE bodies that must run --
`e2e_let_else_moved_payload_single_drop`,
`e2e_owned_self_enum_receiver_single_fire` and
`test_e2e_result_struct_payload_field_freed_and_single_body` -- because the
classifier calls "consuming" several shapes that transfer nothing (a free-fn
call arg is entry-copied, so `f(r)` is not a transfer) and because `let ... else`
never populates the borrowed-only set at all, leaving every binding there
blocked. So the gate is correct for a NEW registration and wrong as a retrofit
onto an old one; the struct half needs the classifier's false-consuming cases
closed first. Filed as B-2026-08-28-66.

MEASURED, interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, all four byte-identical
after the fix (before, where different, in parens):

    match o { Some(e) => .. }      Option[E]     got dE dR1   (all: got)
    if let Some(e) = o             Option[E]     got dE       (all: got)
    match r { Ok(e) => .. }        Result[E,i64] got dE       (all: got)
    match o { Some(h) => .. }      Option[H]     got dR4      (all: got)   payload-only
    match o { Some(g) => .. }      Option[G]     got dG       (all: got)   boxed
    match o { Some(r) => .. }      Option[R]     got dR2      unchanged control
    let k = match o { Some(e)=>{e} }              dE kept     (gate; ungated dE dE)
    match o { Some(e) => sink(e) }                sank dE     (all: sank)
    match o { Some(_) => .. }                     some dE dR1 unchanged boundary
    match o { Some(x) => .. }      Option[J]     got          unchanged boundary

FIXTURES in all three suites, each RED-verified against the unfixed tree:
`codegen::e2e_consuming_arm_runs_the_bound_enum_payloads_drop_body`,
`interpreter::consuming_arm_runs_the_bound_enum_payloads_drop_body`,
`memory_sanitizer::asan_consuming_arm_enum_payload_bodies_are_memory_balanced`.

TWO B-2026-08-28-58 ROWS UPDATED. Its `consuming-match-does-not-double-fire`
(interpreter) and `consuming-match-moved-out` (ASAN) pinned `got` with no body,
and both said in their own comments that the consuming arm losing the body was a
separate row -- this one. Their claim is unchanged (exactly one fire); only the
count they measure against moved from zero to one.

A SECOND FINDING came out of this and is filed separately: B-2026-08-28-67, an
ORDERING divergence on `match e { E.A(r) => .. }` over a bare user enum, where
the interpreter runs the payload body before the enum's own and both compiled
