title: `Option[K]` NEVER FREES A HEAP-CARRYING NESTED-STRUCT PAYLOAD while `Result[K, i64]` DOES: the plain `let` site calls `track_inline_result_payload_var` with no `Option` sibling for a struct/enum payload -- masked entirely by dead-malloc removal until some body reads the buffer
detail:
Measured on 033eafc under LSan (Linux `memory-sanitizer` harness). Seven
shapes, ONE leaks:

    enum K { A(R2), B }
    struct R2 { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for R2 { println(f"d{self.name}") }

      let o: Option[K]      = Some(K.A(R2 { id: 5, name: f"n{5}" }));   LEAK 2 B
      let o: Result[K, i64] = Ok(K.A(R2 { id: 5, name: f"n{5}" }));     clean

    and the five other cells of the matrix, all clean:
      Option[K] with a DIRECT `String` payload + own `Drop` on K         clean
      Option[R2]           (struct payload, same struct, same body)      clean
      Option[K] nested struct with NO heap                               clean
      let h = K.A(R2 { .. })   (direct enum binding, no Option)          clean
      Option[K] direct String, Drop elsewhere                            clean

The `Option` / `Result` pair is the whole finding: same enum, same nested
struct, same body, same walker, one frees and one does not.

MECHANISM. The plain `let` registration site (`stmts.rs`, the Call-shaped-RHS
block) calls `track_inline_option_payload_var`, `track_inline_result_payload_var`
and `track_inline_option_map_payload_var`. The `Result` one reaches
`result_inline_payload_struct_drops` -> `inline_struct_payload_drop`, which is
gated on `type_expr_has_drop_heap` -- true for `K`, since its `field_drop_kinds`
carry `NestedStruct` -- and registers `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr(K)`. The
`Option` one only covers the inline `{ptr,len,cap}` `String`/`Vec` overlay, and
`option_inline_payload_elem` returns `None` for a struct/enum payload
(instrumented: `elem=false` for both `Option[R2]` and `Option[K]`). The
struct/enum sibling `track_inline_option_agg_payload_var` EXISTS and does
exactly the right thing -- `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok` admits an
enum via `enum_layouts`, then `emit_option_drop_fn` -- but it is only ever
called from the two destructure-LEAF sites (`stmts.rs:11813`, `12011`), never
from a plain `let`. Confirmed by instrumentation: it is not invoked for this
binding.

`Option[R2]` (the struct-payload control) is clean for an unrelated reason and
should not be read as the `Option` path working -- it takes no registration at
that site either; its buffer is reclaimed elsewhere. So the missing sibling is
the gap, not a mis-set gate.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE, and the part worth carrying forward. Nothing observed the
payload's buffer, and LLVM removes an unread `malloc` outright, so the program
allocated nothing and LSan reported nothing. Making a `Drop` body READ the
buffer is what turns it into a reportable leak. Proven rather than argued: with
the same fix in place but the walk emitted EMPTY (body suppressed), the shape is
clean; with the walk running a body that reads `self.name`, it leaks 2 bytes;
with a body that reads only `self.id`, it is clean again. Same registrations in
all three (verified by instrumenting every registrar) -- only observability
differs. This is the same masking B-2026-08-28-12's note describes from the
other direction, and it means a green LSan run over a corpus whose `Drop` bodies
happen not to touch their heap does NOT clear this class.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE B-2026-08-28-58 FIXTURE. That fix makes the body run, so it
is what unmasks this. Its ASAN fixture therefore pins the `Result` half of this
exact shape (`result-nested-struct-heap`) and excludes the `Option` half,
naming this row -- rather than pinning a leak as if it were the intended
behaviour.

NOT FIXED HERE DELIBERATELY. The one-line-looking fix is to call
`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var` beside its `Result` peer at the plain
`let` site. That changes drop registration for EVERY `Option[struct]` and
`Option[enum]` plain `let` in the language, and the suppression family keyed on
`inline_option_agg_payload_vars` (match arms, rebinds, passthrough aliases,
moved-arg disarms) all has to be re-checked against it or the leak becomes a
double free -- the ledger's own bar has that trade the other way round. It
wants its own slice with the full LSan corpus behind it, not a tail-end
addition to a body fix.

SOURCE NOTE: found because B-2026-08-28-58's ASAN fixture went red on exactly
one row; scoped by a seven-cell matrix and by instrumenting each registrar to
show the `Option`/`Result` asymmetry directly.

CORRECTION (2026-08-28, at fix time). The mechanism above — and this row's
TITLE — are wrong, and the proposed one-line fix is a double free. Calling
`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var` at the plain `let` site was built and
measured: `Option[K]`'s payload is heap-BOXED, a `BoxedEnumDrop` already owns
the box, and `emit_option_drop_fn` frees it a second time. It presented as
CLEAN at the default -O2 (10 allocs / 10 frees, 0 errors) and aborted only at
-O0/-O1 and under the JIT.

The real predictor is payload BOXEDNESS, which cuts across `Option` and
`Result` alike: `Result[K, i64]` is clean only because `K` fits `Result`'s
5-word area and stays inline, and `Result[K, Wide]` — same enum, same nested
struct, same body — leaks the identical 2 bytes. The gap is in
`boxed_enum_payload_variants`, whose payload-name filter admitted structs
only, so a boxed ENUM payload got no inner drop and its interior was never
walked. See the `fix` field.

The row's "seven shapes, ONE leaks" matrix is still accurate as DATA; it is
the inference drawn from it that does not hold, because every clean cell in it
happens to be inline and the single leaking cell is the only boxed one.
fix:
Fixed in 77729f2f by admitting a user ENUM to `boxed_enum_payload_variants`'s
payload-name filter (`src/codegen/types_lowering.rs`) and resolving that name
through `emit_enum_drop_switch` in `track_boxed_enum_var`
(`src/codegen/runtime.rs`).

THE ROW'S MECHANISM WAS WRONG, and the correction is the useful part. The row
reads the shape as an `Option`/`Result` asymmetry — "the `Option` sibling
`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var` is never called from a plain `let`" —
and proposes calling it beside its `Result` peer. That fix was built and
MEASURED, and it is a double free: `Option[K]`'s payload is heap-BOXED, a
`BoxedEnumDrop` already owns the box, and `emit_option_drop_fn` frees it a
second time. Valgrind on the emitted binary named the block as 40 bytes (the
box) rather than the 2-byte `String`, freed once inside a called drop fn and
once directly in `main`.

That fix also LOOKED clean, which is the trap worth recording. At the default
-O2 it reported 10 allocs / 10 frees and 0 errors; only -O0 and -O1 aborted
with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. An -O2-only reading would
have landed a double free as a leak fix. The `karac run` JIT aborted at every
level, which is what exposed it.

THE ACTUAL PREDICTOR IS BOXEDNESS, not which enum wraps the payload. The
control that settles it: `Result[K, i64]` is clean because `K` (40 B) fits
`Result`'s 5-word area and stays INLINE, where
`track_inline_result_payload_var` already walks it. Widen the OTHER half so
the payload boxes — `Result[K, Wide]`, same `K`, same `R2`, same body — and
the `Result` leaks the identical 2 bytes. The asymmetry the row names is a
consequence of the two seeded areas (Option 3 words, Result 5), not of a
missing `Option` registrar.

MECHANISM. `boxed_enum_payload_variants` returns
`(enum_name, payload_variant, inner_struct_name)`, and `inner_struct_name`
filtered on `struct_types.contains_key(n)` alone. A boxed payload that is a
user ENUM matched nothing, so `track_boxed_enum_var` derived
`inner_drop_fn = emit_struct_drop_synthesis(None) = None` and `BoxedEnumDrop`
freed the box over an unwalked interior. The field's own doc said as much —
"names a user struct payload ... or `None` for tuples / scalars" — an enum was
never considered. Instrumented directly: `Option[K]` registers
`inner_struct=None drop_resolved=false`; `Result[K, Wide]` registers only for
the `Err`/`Wide` side.

The enum arm resolves `emit_enum_drop_switch` rather than going through
`emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`, because that dispatcher's `karac_drop_<T>`
module lookup can return the user-drop WRAPPER for a `Drop`-bearing enum and
run the body a second time on the memory channel — B-2026-08-28-58 leg A, this
row's parent, verbatim. `Option`/`Result` payloads stay excluded: a boxed
payload that is itself one of them is the envelope-chain shape
(`deeper_tags`, B-2026-08-07-6), whose walk is mutually exclusive with an
inner payload drop and whose let-site branch would otherwise be bypassed.
Structs are ordered first and keep the exact fn they resolved before.

MEASURED, valgrind at -O0/-O1/-O2, five shapes fixed and every control
unmoved:

    plain `let`                     2 B lost -> clean
    wildcard `match`                2 B lost -> clean
    consuming `match`               2 B lost -> clean
    by-value call                   2 B lost -> clean
    rebind move (`let p = o;`)      2 B lost -> clean
    envelope chain Option[Option[Option[i64]]]   clean -> clean
    `None`                                       clean -> clean
    `Result[K, i64]` (inline)                    clean -> clean

Drop bodies fire exactly once and identically on interp / LLJIT / AOT for
every shape above.

RESIDUE, split out rather than folded in: a `Result` with ONE side boxed loses
the OTHER side's inline walk, because `track_inline_result_payload_var`'s
name-keyed `boxed_enum_payload_vars` early return is per-BINDING while the
boxing is per-SIDE. Not enum-specific — `Result[R2, Wide]` with a plain struct
`Ok` leaks the same 2 bytes while `Result[R2, i64]` is clean. Filed as
B-2026-08-28-68.

REGRESSION TEST `asan_boxed_enum_option_payload_interior_is_walked`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), RED against the pre-fix compiler at every opt
level. Its `Drop` body READS the payload buffer (`contains` scans its bytes)
and the payload is seeded from the opaque `env.args().len()`: with the body
suppressed, or reading only the scalar `self.id`, nothing observes the buffer,
LLVM deletes the `malloc` outright and the shape passes against the BROKEN
compiler — the same mask the row itself documents. The body prints a
seed-INDEPENDENT result so the expectation cannot drift with the harness's
argv. A consuming `match` arm is deliberately absent from the fixture: it ran
no body at all when this was written (B-2026-08-28-63, fixed concurrently in
f862656), and pinning that count would have broken the moment that row landed.

FIXED by f94c75c. The removal was `suppress_user_drop_for_var` in the
`ExprKind::Return` arm of `src/codegen/exprs.rs` — a compile-time frame
retraction, so it disarmed the binding on EVERY path, not the one that
returns. The row named `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` as the site; that
was imprecise. For this repro the body's `final_expr` is `R { id: 99 }`, so
the tail walk never sees `r` at all. The `return r;` nested in the `if`
reaches the removal through the `ExprKind::Return` compile arm instead. Same
family, same flow-insensitivity, one function over.

The fix keeps the action ARMED and clears B-2026-08-28-51's per-binding `i1`
flag at the `return`. Both firing channels already route through
`emit_user_drop_call_guarded` (the scope-exit drain and the NLL
live-range-end fire), so the body is skipped on the returning path and runs
on every other. `guard_user_drop_for_nested_return` is gated on the action
living in an ENCLOSING frame, which is exactly the test for "this `return`
is nested": an unconditional `return r;` at the body's top level finds the
action in the innermost frame, declines the guard, and keeps today's static
removal. Only the conditional case changes behaviour.

THE ROW CALLED THIS A CALLING-CONVENTION-SIZED CHANGE AND IT WAS NOT — but
the reason is worth recording, because the same argument does NOT rescue
B-2026-08-28-22. Two runtime-sentinel siblings already sit in this exact
`return` arm for the memory half of the identical problem:
`suppress_boxed_enum_payload_cleanup_for_owner` ("runtime word-0 zero, not a
queue retract, so a binding returned on one path and consumed on another
still frees its box on the consuming path") and
`neutralize_moved_soa_groups_slot` ("use a runtime `cap = 0` sentinel, not
the tail path's compile-time frame removal: the early-return cleanup frame
is shared with the fall-through path, where `a` is NOT returned and must
still be freed — frame removal would leak it there"). Bodies were the only
channel with no sentinel, and -51 built one. This slice just spends it.

THE PREDICATE RISK THE ROW FLAGGED IS REAL AND RESOLVES THE OTHER WAY.
Retaining the action makes `has_armed_user_drop`, `has_armed_own_user_drop`
and `has_armed_container_elem_bodies` answer `true` where they answered
`false`, and the first gates the displaced-value leg (B-2026-07-30-11) that
runs a reassigned binding's OLD body. Firing that on a moved-from slot is
B-2026-07-31-38's shape. Control flow makes the ownership proxy exact for
this shape: if the `return` had executed the function would have LEFT, so
every path that reaches a later reassignment or scope exit is a path where
the `return` did not run and the binding still owns its value. Measured, not
assumed — `s10` (`let mut r = R{41}; if k { return r; } r = R{99}; r`, k
false) went from `99` / `drop 99` to the interpreter's `drop 41` / `99` /
`drop 99`. The predicate change FIXES a second missing body rather than
introducing a stale-slot read, and `displaced-fallthrough` pins it.

The argument requires the frame stack to be per-function. It is:
`compile_closure_body` `mem::take`s `scope_cleanup_actions` (and, since -51,
`cond_move_drop_flags`), so an enclosing function's frames are never visible
from inside a closure whose `return` exits only the closure. That was the
one shape that could have broken the invariant, and it is excluded
structurally rather than by a check.

MEASURED, 17 shapes x 4 surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), before and after on the same binaries: 7 shapes FIXED
(the repro; the `match`-arm spelling; two levels of nesting; a `return`
inside a loop; the displaced-value leg; a heap-carrying local; a second
local that is never returned), 8 unchanged-correct including the
unconditional-return boundary, and 2 byte-identical. Every changed line is a
compiled surface GAINING the missing body; no interpreter line moved
anywhere, which is what a codegen-only fix should look like.

A 14-shape edge sweep adds the spellings the suites do not cover: closure
(the shape that regressed during -51 and is now correct in both directions),
method, generic, `defer` in scope, three exit paths, `Vec`, `String`, and
`shared` locals. 13 of 14 correct on all four surfaces.

THE ONE THAT IS NOT FIXED, deliberately: the PARAM spellings
(`fn take(r: R, k) -> R { if k { return r; } R { id: 99 } }` and the generic
`pick[T](k, a, b)`) are byte-identical before and after and remain
aligned-wrong on all four surfaces. An owned by-value param is caller-drops

no action to retain and nothing for a flag to guard. That is
B-2026-08-28-22's channel (the interprocedural escape predicates unioning
over return sites), and it needs the callee-owned-param flip that row
describes, not this one's. Both param shapes are pinned as fixtures
(`param-nested-return`) so that fixing -22 is NOTICED here rather than
silently changing an untested expectation.

`test_nested_return_local_user_drop_body_runs_on_the_fallthrough`, so a

plus `asan_nested_return_local_drop_body_is_memory_balanced`

GATES on the rebased tree: fmt clean; clippy clean on BOTH legs; llvm suite

title: A `return <local>` NESTED IN A BRANCH LOSES THE LOCAL'S `Drop` BODY ON THE PATH THAT NEVER TAKES THE RETURN, on all three COMPILED backends while the interpreter is correct: `fn take(k) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { return r; } R { id: 99 } }` with `k = false` prints `99` / `drop 99` compiled and `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99` under --interp. This is the UNDER-FIRE horn of B-2026-08-28-51's mechanism -- `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` statically REMOVES the action, disarming on every path including the ones that never reach the `return` -- and it is the half that row's fix deliberately did not touch, because un-removing an action is what changes the three frame-membership predicates
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-28-51 when that row's OVER-fire horn was fixed, so the
remaining half does not disappear inside a closed row.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}"); } }
    fn take(k: bool) -> R { let r = R { id: 41 }; if k { return r; } R { id: 99 } }
    fn main() { let x = take(false); println(f"{x.id}"); }

    interp                       -> `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99`  CORRECT
    LLJIT / AOT / AOT AUTO_PAR=0 -> `99` / `drop 99`              `r`'s body LOST

`k = false` never takes the `return`, so `r` dies in the callee and must run
its body there. All three compiled backends lose it. Measured byte-identical
before and after the -51 fix commit, on the same binaries — this is not a
residue of that change, it is the horn that change deliberately did not touch.

MECHANISM, already diagnosed in -51 and restated here so this row stands alone.
`suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` inspects the last statement of the body and,
on seeing `return <identifier>`, REMOVES the binding's cleanup action outright.
The removal is static and flow-insensitive — it disarms on every path, including
the ones that never reach the `return`. Its own doc says so: "Static and
flow-insensitive like every sibling — a conditional return disarms on all paths,
which can only under-fire." The interpreter's twin
(`suppress_return_stmt_user_drop`) retracts from the CURRENT block's cleanup
vector, which for a nested `return` does not hold the binding, so the retraction
silently no-ops and the interpreter stays correct here by accident of scoping.

WHY -51's FIX DOES NOT REACH IT, which is the useful part. That fix adds a
runtime guard to an action that is ALREADY ARMED — nothing is retained that was
previously removed — which is exactly why it left `has_armed_user_drop`,
`has_armed_own_user_drop` and `has_armed_container_elem_bodies` answering as
before. Fixing THIS shape means the opposite: keeping an action the suppression
family currently deletes, and then guarding it. All three predicates read frame
membership as a proxy for ownership, so a retained-but-flagged action makes them
answer true where they answer false today. `has_armed_user_drop`'s own doc gives
the concrete casualty: the displaced-value leg (B-2026-07-30-11) runs a
reassigned binding's old body only while the binding still owns it, and firing on
a stale slot reads moved-from bits (B-2026-07-31-38's shape prints a payload's
body twice).

title: A CONSUMING ARM THAT HANDS ITS BOUND STRUCT PAYLOAD ON RUNS THAT PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `let k = match o { Some(r) => { r } .. }` is interp `dR1 kept` vs compiled `dR1 dR1 kept`; the enum sibling is gated, the struct one cannot be with today's classifier
detail:
Measured on f862656, interp / jit / build.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }

      let o: Option[R] = Some(R { id: 1 });
      let k = match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { R { id: 0 } } };
      println("kept");

        interp:   dR1 kept
        jit:      dR1 dR1 kept
        build:    dR1 dR1 kept

The arm's VALUE is the binding, so the match's result owns it and `k`
registers its own drop; the arm's `track_user_drop_var` wrapper then runs the
body a second time over the same value. PRE-EXISTING -- it predates
B-2026-08-28-63 by a long way and was measured identically before that work.

A SECOND SHAPE, same cause, opposite visible direction:

      let o: Option[R] = Some(R { id: 1 });
      match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { R { id: 0 } } };   // result discarded
      println("dropped");

        interp:   dropped
        jit:      dR1 dropped
        build:    dR1 dropped

Here the compiled body is the ONLY one, and the interpreter runs none -- so the
same defect reads as a doubled body when the result is bound and as a
missing-interpreter body when it is discarded.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW. B-2026-08-28-63 gave the ENUM spelling of that arm a body
for the first time, which made the shape testable one type over and put the
struct number beside it. Nothing about the struct path changed.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG, MEASURED. -63 gates its NEW enum registration on
`consume_class::binding_only_borrowed` -- if the arm consumes the binding,
whoever took it owns the body. Applying that same gate to the struct arm
suppressed THREE bodies that must run:

    codegen::e2e_let_else_moved_payload_single_drop
    codegen::e2e_owned_self_enum_receiver_single_fire
    codegen::test_e2e_result_struct_payload_field_freed_and_single_body

Two reasons, both in the classifier rather than in the arm:

  * `has_consuming_sink` treats a FREE-FUNCTION call argument as NON-consuming
    on purpose ("entry-copied args: a derived arg is fine"), so `f(r)` is not a
    transfer -- correct for the by-value entry-copy model, and it means
    "consuming" is not the same question as "someone else now owns the body".
  * `let ... else` never populates the borrowed-only set at all (its bind site
    is a third caller that -63 deliberately left alone, since a let-else binding
    lands in the ENCLOSING scope rather than an arm), so every binding there
    reads as consumed and loses its body.

So the gate is sound for a registration that did not exist before and unsound
as a retrofit onto one that did. Closing this needs the classifier to answer
"does another owner now hold this value's Drop body" -- which is the same
question B-2026-08-28-22's escape predicates ask -- rather than "is this
syntactically a consuming position".

RELATED, NOT THE SAME. `let k = match o { Some(e) => { id(e) } .. }` where `id`
returns its param prints `dE dE` on ALL FOUR surfaces. That is the entry-copy
model showing through (two values, two bodies) and the backends agree, so it is
not this row.

WHAT THE ROW GOT WRONG. Its stated defect (a DOUBLED BODY, `dR1 dR1 kept`) is
real but needs shape B -- the match as a function's returned value. Its quoted
repro is shape A, which at HEAD agrees across all three backends on the body
count. With a scalar payload A is clean outright; with a HEAP payload A is a
DOUBLE FREE, which is memory-safety rather than a body count and is invisible
at the default -O2. So the row's title understates its own repro.

ONE ROOT, TWO CHANNELS. Both A and B are the arm registering an owner for a
value another owner also takes -- the arm's `track_user_drop_var`
(`pattern_binding.rs`, the struct arm) beside the destination's own drop. They
differ only in WHICH channel doubles: in A the body count happens to come out
right and the MEMORY is freed twice; in B the memory balances and the BODY runs
twice. That is why a scalar payload shows B but not A -- with no heap there is
nothing for A to double.

SEVERITY. Raised to HIGH: shape A heap is a double free (`free(): double free
detected in tcache 2` under `karac run`, `Invalid free()` under valgrind on the
AOT binary at -O0), not the medium run-vs-build divergence this was filed as.

at all -- so none of the three tests the naive gate broke are in its

title: A `match` OVER A BARE USER ENUM RUNS THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY AND THE ENUM'S OWN IN OPPOSITE ORDERS ON THE TWO BACKENDS -- `match e { E.A(r) => .. }` is interp `dR5 dE` vs compiled `dE dR5`; same count, different sequence
detail:
Measured on f862656, interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }

      let e = E.A(R { id: 5 });
      match e { E.A(r) => { println("got") } E.B => { println("b") } }

        interp:            got  dR5 dE
        jit / build / np:  got  dE  dR5

The NESTED spelling behaves the same way, which is how it was first seen:

      let o: Option[E] = Some(E.A(R { id: 3 }));
      match o { Some(e) => { match e { E.A(r) => { println("inner") } E.B => {} } }
                None => {} }

        interp:            inner dR3 dE
        jit / build / np:  inner dE  dR3

COUNTS AGREE -- one body each -- so this is purely a sequence divergence, which
is why it is `low` and why it survived every count-based fixture in the
-46/-47/-54/-55/-57/-58/-63 family.

WHICH IS RIGHT is a real question, not a formality. The compiled order (own body
first, then the payload's) is what every other walk in the family produces and
what a direct `let x = E.A(R { .. });` prints on all three backends -- so the
compiled side is self-consistent with the rest of the tree. The interpreter's
order comes from the arm binding `r` dying at the arm's end BEFORE the scrutinee
`e`'s own body fires, which is defensible on live-range grounds and is what
design.md's NLL rule would give if `r` is read as an ordinary local. Fixing this
means picking one and stating it, not just making the two match.

PRE-EXISTING and untouched by B-2026-08-28-63: measured identical with that
fix stashed (interp `got dR5 dE` / compiled `got dE dR5`). The only thing -63
changed here was making both sides run a body at all in the `Option[E]`
spelling, which is what put the two orders side by side.

SOURCE NOTE: found in the B-2026-08-28-63 shape matrix as the one row that
stayed DIVERGE after every count was fixed.
WHICH ORDER IS RIGHT: SETTLED 2026-08-28. The row asks this explicitly and
leaves it open; it is the COMPILED order (`dE` then `dR5`), on three
independent grounds.

1. THE SPEC SAYS SO. design.md § Part 8 (`Drop`), on why `Drop` is not
   derivable: "'drop each field in order' is what the compiler already does
   automatically AFTER THE USER'S DROP BODY RETURNS". Own body first, fields
   second. `dE` then `dR5`.

2. THE INTERPRETER CONTRADICTS ITSELF. A direct
   `let x = E.A(R { id: 5 });` prints `dE` / `dR5` on ALL THREE backends,
   including the interpreter. Only the `match` spelling flips it there, so
   this is not a coherent interpreter policy being weighed against codegen's
   — it is one interpreter path disagreeing with the other.

3. THE MOVE-OUT READING THE INTERPRETER IMPLEMENTS IS THE ONE design.md
   REJECTS. Its order comes from treating the arm binding as having MOVED the
   payload out of `e`, so `r` dies at the arm's end before `e`'s body runs.
   design.md § Part 8 (Interaction with move semantics): "Partial moves out of
   a struct field are rejected if the struct has a `Drop` impl: the drop body
   assumes all fields are present". `E` HAS a `Drop` impl here, so its payload
   is not available to be moved out from under its destructor.

TWO CONTROLS that locate the divergence precisely (all measured
interp / jit / AOT):

    arm does NOT consume the binding      `E.A(r) => { println("got") }`
        interp `dR5 dE`   compiled `dE dR5`        DIVERGE  <- this row
    arm DOES consume it                   `E.A(r) => { keep(r) }`
        interp `dR5 dE`   compiled `dR5 dE`        AGREE
    enum with no own `Drop`               `enum E { A(R), B }`
        interp `dR5`      compiled `dR5`           AGREE

So the divergence is exactly: a NON-consuming arm over a scrutinee whose enum
has its own `Drop`. The consuming case already agrees, and agrees on the
move-out order — which is correct there, because a consumed binding really
does take the body with it.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG, MEASURED. The interpreter stashes the payload
binding as a real Drop slot in `pattern_match.rs`
(`arm_moved_user_drop_payload_bindings`, under the `consuming_scrutinee`
gate), which is what makes it die at the arm's end. Gating that stash on the
arm not consuming the binding — the same question codegen's
`pattern_binding_arm_borrowed_only_names` asks — was built and it LOSES
BODIES rather than reordering them:

    bare      `got dE`     (dR5 gone)
    nested    `inner`      (both gone)
    noEdrop   `got end`    (dR5 gone)
    consumed  `k5 dE end`  (dR5 gone)

Two separate reasons, both worth carrying forward:

  * SKIPPING THE STASH DOES NOT HAND THE PAYLOAD BACK TO THE SCRUTINEE. The
    disarm that retracts `e`'s own payload walk runs regardless of whether the
    stash fired, so the body ends up owned by nobody. A fix has to move BOTH
    — leave the walk armed exactly when it declines to stash — and those two
    decisions live in different places.
  * THE AVAILABLE CLASSIFIER ANSWERS THE WRONG QUESTION. `binding_only_borrowed`
    called `keep(r)` borrowed-only, so even the genuinely-consuming control
    lost its body. That is the same free-function-argument weakness
    B-2026-08-28-66's row documents ("`has_consuming_sink` treats a
    free-function call argument as NON-consuming ... by the by-value
    entry-copy model"), hit from the other side.

only the sequence differs.

FIXED by dcf4891.

THE ROW'S OWN "SETTLED" SECTION WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE ANSWER AND RIGHT ABOUT WHY
THE OBVIOUS FIX FAILS, so this is mostly the mechanism it asked for. The
compiled order (own body, then the payload's) stands; the interpreter moved.

WHAT THE ARM IS ACTUALLY BEING ASKED. The failed first attempt gated the arm
stash on the `binding_only_borrowed` consumption classifier and lost bodies.
Re-measuring the whole arm-body matrix on a HEAD build shows why, and it is not
the classifier being merely imprecise -- it is answering a DIFFERENT QUESTION.
Measured, interp vs compiled, `enum E { A(R), B }` with own `Drop`:

    r.id                     interp dR5 dE   compiled dE dR5    DIVERGE
    r not mentioned          interp dR5 dE   compiled dE dR5    DIVERGE
    r.get()   (ref self)     interp dR5 dE   compiled dE dR5    DIVERGE
    r.eat()   (owned self)   interp dR5 dE   compiled dE dR5    DIVERGE
    keep(r)   (free-fn arg)  interp dR5 dE   compiled dR5 dE    agree
    let m = r;               interp dR5 dE   compiled dR5 dE    agree
    v.push(r)                interp dR5 dE   compiled dR5 dE    agree
    W { r: r }               interp dR5 dE   compiled dR5 dE    agree

The split is not "does ownership transfer away" -- `keep(r)` transfers nothing
under the entry-copy model, and every backend still gives the ARM the body. It
is "is the binding MATERIALIZED AS A VALUE anywhere, or only READ THROUGH?"
Projections, method receivers (either receiver mode -- `r.eat()` takes `self` by
value and is still on the read-through side), and no mention at all are reads;
a bare mention in any value position is a materialization. That is exactly the
question `consume_class::binding_only_borrowed` does NOT answer, because it
models a free-fn argument as entry-copied and therefore non-consuming --
correctly, for its own callers. So the fix is a NEW predicate, not a reuse, and
`binding_use::tests::disagrees_with_binding_only_borrowed_on_a_free_fn_argument`
pins the disagreement so a later "why are there two of these?" cleanup cannot
quietly collapse them.

THE PLUMBING NOTE TURNED OUT NOT TO APPLY. The row suggests moving
`codegen::consume_class` to a shared top-level module first, since the
interpreter cannot reach it. That refactor was not needed: the predicate the
interpreter needs is not in that module and would have had to be written
anyway. `src/binding_use.rs` is new, plain-AST, 300 lines, and both backends can
reach it. (`mod consume_class` did become `pub(crate)`, for the cross-check test
above and nothing else.)

WHY THE WALK IS EXHAUSTIVE, WHICH IS NOT A STYLE CHOICE. The verdict SUPPRESSES
drop bookkeeping, so an occurrence the walk fails to see reads as "no mention"
= read-through -- the unsafe direction. `consume_class`'s `walk_exprs` has a
`_ => {}` fallback and does not descend into `InterpolatedStringLit`, so
`f"{keep(r)}"` -- the single commonest way a kata touches a payload -- would
have been invisible and scored read-through. `binding_use`'s match is exhaustive
over all 56 `ExprKind` variants with no catch-all, so a new variant is a compile
error rather than a silent under-count. `interpolation-hole` is a fixture row
for exactly this.

BOTH DECISIONS MOVE TOGETHER, and getting that wrong is how the first attempt
failed. The disarm (`disarm_moved_out_enum_payload`, which retracts the
scrutinee's payload walk) and the arm stash (which gives the binding a real Drop
slot) now consult the same gate, so a read-through arm retracts nothing and
stashes nothing.

GATED ON THE ENUM HAVING ITS OWN `Drop`, which is the principle and not just a
narrowing. design.md Part 8: "Partial moves out of a struct field are rejected
if the struct has a `Drop` impl: the drop body assumes all fields are present."
With no own body there is no destructor to strand, the move-out is legitimate,
and the two orders coincide anyway -- `enum H { A(R), B }` with no `impl Drop`
measured `v5 dR5` on all four surfaces before and after. This also means

both are the row's own lesson -- "the two decisions live in different places" --

named binding whose walk could be handed the payload back -- so standing the
stash down hands the body to nobody. Measured `v7 dE`, with the payload's `dR7`
gone outright, against `v7 dR7 dE` before. The gate is now additionally

    match e { E.A(r) if r.id == 1i64 => { let m = r; println(f"m{m.id}") }
              E.A(r) => { println(f"v{r.id}") }  E.B => {} }

title: A `Result` WITH ONE SIDE BOXED LOSES THE OTHER SIDE'S INLINE PAYLOAD WALK: `track_inline_result_payload_var`'s name-keyed `boxed_enum_payload_vars` early return is per-BINDING while boxing is per-SIDE, so `Result[R2, Wide]` leaks the inline `Ok` payload's heap while `Result[R2, i64]` is clean -- not enum-specific, and masked entirely until a `Drop` body reads the buffer
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-28-64 when that row's boxed-ENUM-interior half was
fixed (d4f565d); this half is untouched by it and was measured identical
before and after.

    struct R2 { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for R2 { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.name}") } }
    struct Wide { a: i64, b: i64, c: i64, d: i64, e: i64, f: i64 }

      let o: Result[R2, i64]  = Ok(R2 { id: 5, name: f"n{5}" });   clean 10/10
      let o: Result[R2, Wide] = Ok(R2 { id: 5, name: f"n{5}" });   LEAK 2 B, 10/9

Same `Ok` payload, same struct, same body. The ONLY difference is the `Err`
half: widen it past `Result`'s 5-word area so the `Err` side boxes, and the
`Ok` side -- still inline, still needing its walk -- silently loses it.

NOT ENUM-SPECIFIC, which is what separates this from its parent row. The
parent was about a boxed payload that is a user ENUM; this reproduces with a
plain STRUCT `Ok` payload and no enum anywhere. The enum spelling leaks too
(`Result[K, Wide]` with `enum K { A(R2), B }`, 10 allocs / 9 frees), but the
enum is incidental.

MECHANISM. `track_inline_result_payload_var` (`src/codegen/runtime.rs`) opens
with a name-keyed early return:

    if self.payload_vars.boxed_enum_payload_vars.contains(var_name) { return; }

That set records the BINDING, not the side. When either half of a `Result`
boxes, the let site registers a `BoxedEnumDrop` and inserts the binding into
that set, so this registrar returns before reaching EITHER side's walk --
including the side that is inline and whose payload nothing else frees.

The guards immediately below it are already per-side and were made so
deliberately: B-2026-08-06-26 replaced the name-keyed reasoning with a
TYPE-keyed `result_payload_is_boxed` computed independently for `ok_boxed` and
`err_boxed`, and its comment states the intent in as many words -- "the two
sides are gated INDEPENDENTLY so a boxed `Ok` beside an inline-heap `Err`
keeps the `Err` drop it still needs". That is exactly this shape with the
sides swapped. The per-side gates are correct; the name-keyed return above
them fires first and makes them unreachable.

So the fix direction is to narrow the early return rather than delete it. It
still has a job -- the original B-2026-08-06 measurements show that registering
an INLINE overlay over a BOXED payload reads the box POINTER as the payload's
first word and frees whatever follows it -- but that hazard is per-side too,
and the per-side gates below already express it. The likely shape is to drop
the name-keyed return and let `ok_boxed` / `err_boxed` carry the whole
decision, which requires checking that `boxed_enum_payload_vars` membership
never carries information the type-keyed predicate lacks (B-2026-08-06-26's
own note says the reverse -- the name set knows only bindings the compilation
SAW being boxed, so the type predicate is the STRICTER of the two).

MASKED BY DEAD-MALLOC REMOVAL, same as the parent. The leak is observable only
because the `Drop` body READS `self.name`; with the body suppressed, or
reading only the scalar `self.id`, LLVM removes the unread `malloc` and the
shape reports clean. A corpus whose `Drop` bodies do not touch their heap will
not catch this.

Measured at -O0/-O1/-O2 under valgrind, on d4f565d; the leak is opt-level
independent. Drop bodies fire once and identically on interp / LLJIT / AOT in
every cell -- this is a pure leak, not a run-vs-build divergence, so the
parity gates cannot see it either.
NARROWED 2026-08-28 (same session, after the obvious fix was built and
REJECTED by measurement). Recording this so the next attempt does not repeat
it.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG, and the row's own "likely shape" above names it:
drop the name-keyed early return and let the per-side `ok_boxed` / `err_boxed`
type gates carry the decision. Built as a narrowing that keeps the early
return only when the sides cannot be resolved
(`Self::result_payload_tes(result_te).is_none()`). It fixes all five reported
shapes -- `Result[R2, Wide]`, the mirror `Result[Wide, R2]`, both-heap-one-
boxed, and the two controls stay put -- clean at -O0 and -O2, bodies firing
once and identically on interp / LLJIT / AOT.

It also REGRESSES `asan_boxed_result_payload_no_inline_cleanup`, the fixture
that pins B-2026-08-06-26. Reduced to the minimal shape, the trigger is
CONDITIONAL CONSTRUCTION + A CONSUMING MATCH, with no move anywhere:

    let m: Result[Wide, String] =
        if i % 2 == 0 { Ok(Wide { .., s: mk(n+i) }) } else { Err(mk(n+i)) };
    match m { Ok(x) => { x.s.contains(..) } Err(t) => { t.contains(..) } }

      pre-fix   31 allocs / 31 frees          clean
      post-fix  31 allocs / 27 frees          128 direct + 64 indirect lost

Bisected against two controls that stay clean under the same build: the same
conditional with NO match (30/30), and a move-and-match with NO conditional
(29/29). So it is not the move -- the first hypothesis, and it was wrong.

MECHANISM OF THE REGRESSION. The 128 direct bytes are 2 blocks of 64, which is
exactly `Wide` (5 x i64 + a 3-word String) -- the BOX, unfreed on the two `Ok`
iterations. Registering the `Err`-side inline action puts the binding into
`inline_result_payload_vars`, so the consuming arm now runs
`suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup` on it, which disarms by storing 0 into
the layout's field 3 (the inline overlay's `cap` word). On the `Ok` side that
same binding's payload is a BOX owned by a `BoxedEnumDrop`, and the disarm
neutralizes it.

So the guard's real job is BROADER than its comment claims. The comment
describes only a REGISTRATION hazard (an inline overlay read over a box
pointer), which the per-side type gates do subsume. What it is also doing is
keeping the whole inline BOOKKEEPING -- registration AND the suppression's
zeroing -- away from a binding that carries a box on any side. The suppression
is per-BINDING in exactly the way the registration was, and making the
registration side-aware without making the disarm side-aware moves the bug
rather than fixing it.

WHAT A REAL FIX NEEDS: `suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup` (and the
siblings that zero `cap` to disarm) taught which SIDE the consuming arm
actually took, so an `Ok`-arm consumption cannot disarm an `Err`-side inline
action and vice versa -- and, on a binding whose other side is boxed, cannot
touch the box's bookkeeping at all. The two actions are already mutually
exclusive at runtime by tag; it is only the compile-time disarm that conflates
them. That is a change to the suppression family, not to this registrar, and
it wants its own slice with the full LSan corpus behind it.

The five reported shapes and their two controls are all plain `let` bindings
with no consuming match, which is why the narrowing looked complete against
them. Any future attempt should carry the conditional-plus-match shape above
as a REQUIRED control alongside them.
fix:
Fixed in c886f1e. TWO halves, and either one alone is a regression -- which is
why the earlier narrowing on this row concluded the obvious fix was wrong. It
was: it is only half.

HALF 1 -- the reported leak. `track_inline_result_payload_var`
(`src/codegen/runtime.rs`) opened with a name-keyed early return on
`boxed_enum_payload_vars`. That set records the BINDING, and the let site
inserts it as soon as EITHER half boxes, so a `Result` with one boxed half
returned before reaching either side's walk -- including the inline half whose
payload nothing else frees. The per-side gates immediately below
(`ok_boxed` / `err_boxed`, B-2026-08-06-26) already express the hazard
correctly and per side; the binding-keyed return fired first and made them
unreachable. That row's own note is the mirror of this bug -- "the two sides
are gated INDEPENDENTLY so a boxed `Ok` beside an inline-heap `Err` keeps the
`Err` drop it still needs" -- and that exact program leaked 2 bytes.

The return is kept only as the fallback for a `result_te` whose sides cannot be
resolved at all, where the per-side gates would read `false` for both and
reinstate the original hazard.

HALF 2 -- the disarm, which is what the previous attempt hit and mis-diagnosed.
A consuming arm's `suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup`
(`src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs`) disarms by calling
`zero_result_payload_area`, which zeroes fields `1..n` -- EVERY payload word,
including word 0, where a boxed side keeps its box POINTER. Nulling it makes
the `BoxedEnumDrop` tag/pointer guard skip, so the box and its interior leak.
Its own doc calls whole-area zeroing a "safe superset"; it is, while both sides
are INLINE.

CORRECTION to this row's earlier narrowing, which named the wrong write: it
said the disarm "stores 0 into the layout's field 3 (the inline overlay's `cap`
word)". That is the `_for_moved_arg` sibling. The consuming-arm suppressor
calls `zero_result_payload_area` and zeroes the WHOLE area, which is what
reaches word 0. The conclusion drawn there was right -- the disarm neutralizes
the box -- but the mechanism as written would not have done it, and the
arithmetic (field 3 is the overlay's `cap`, the box pointer is word 0) is what
exposed the slip.

So the disarm is now per-side as well: a boxed side has no inline action to
disarm -- its payload belongs to the `BoxedEnumDrop` -- so the suppression is a
no-op there and the correct move is to leave the slot untouched.

READ OFF THE ARMED ACTION, not re-derived. The matched side's boxedness is
determined by looking for a `BoxedEnumDrop` on this slot guarded on this
variant's discriminant. That action's existence IS the statement "this side is
boxed and owned elsewhere", so registration and disarm cannot drift apart: if
the registration ever declines to box, there is no action to find and the
zeroing resumes.

ZEROING ONLY THE `cap` WORD IS WRONG, measured rather than reasoned. It was the
obvious narrower disarm and it produced an ASAN double-free: a
struct-with-heap inline payload cap-guards on the CONCRETE struct's own field
offsets -- precisely why the whole area is zeroed -- so disarming only `cap`
left that walk armed beside the arm's binding.

NOT ENUM-SPECIFIC, which is what separates this from its parent
B-2026-08-28-64: every fixture here has a plain STRUCT payload and no user enum
anywhere. Boxedness of the OTHER side is the whole trigger.

MEASURED, valgrind at -O0:

    Result[R2, Wide]   (inline Ok + heap, boxed Err)   10/9  -> 10/10
    Result[Wide, R2]   (boxed Ok, inline Err + heap)   10/9  -> 10/10   [mirror]
    Result[R2, W2]     (heap both sides, one boxed)    10/9  -> 10/10
    Result[R2, i64]    (neither boxed)                 10/10 -> 10/10   [control]
    Err-taken boxed                                     9/9  -> 9/9     [control]
    conditional + consuming match                      31/31 -> 31/31   [half 2]
    move + match                                       29/29 -> 29/29

`asan_boxed_result_payload_no_inline_cleanup`, which the first half alone
broke, passes.

REGRESSION TEST `asan_result_with_one_boxed_side_keeps_the_other_sides_walk`,
RED pre-fix with `LeakSanitizer: 80 byte(s) leaked in 16 allocation(s)` -- two
leaking arms over eight iterations. It carries four arms so both halves are
pinned: the neither-boxed control, the reported shape, the mirror, and a
CONSUMING arm over a one-side-boxed `Result`, which is the arm that drives the
disarm and the one that regressed under half 1 alone.

title: A DISCARDED `match` WHOSE ARM YIELDS ITS BOUND PAYLOAD RUNS NO `Drop` BODY IN THE INTERPRETER while both compiled backends run exactly one -- `match o { Some(r) => { r } .. };` in statement position is interp `dropped` vs compiled `dR1 dropped`; a discarded CALL result and a read-only arm both run it, so the loss is specific to the arm handing the binding on
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-28-66's "second shape" and measured on its own, because
it is the OPPOSITE direction from that row (the interpreter under-fires here,
codegen over-fires there) and lives on a different backend, so no fix to the
codegen arm registration can reach it.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

    fn main() {
      let o: Option[R] = Some(R { id: 1 });
      match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { R { id: 0 } } };   // result DISCARDED
      println("dropped");
    }

      interp            -> `dropped`            NO body
      jit / AOT         -> `dR1` / `dropped`    exactly one -- CORRECT

Exactly one `R` is constructed and nothing takes it, so it dies at the
statement and must run its body once. The compiled backends do; the
interpreter runs none.

TWO CONTROLS, both correct on all three backends, which localize it to the arm
handing the binding on rather than to discarded temporaries generally:

    fn mk() -> R { R { id: 1 } }
    fn main() { mk(); println("dropped"); }
      -> `dR1` / `dropped` everywhere.  A discarded CALL result runs its body
         in the interpreter, so the discarded-temp machinery works.

    match o { Some(r) => { println(f"saw{r.id}") } None => { .. } };
      -> `saw1` / `dR1` / `dropped` everywhere.  An arm that only READS the
         binding runs the body in the interpreter, so arm bindings are not
         broadly missing their bodies.

So the loss needs BOTH a discarded match result AND an arm whose VALUE is the
bound payload. The interpreter's consuming-arm stash hands the payload to the
arm's value and the discarded-statement path does not pick it back up, so the
value falls between the two owners.

HEAP MAKES NO DIFFERENCE to this cell: the same program with
`struct R { id: i64, name: String }` is 11 allocs / 11 frees under valgrind on
the compiled side and still silent in the interpreter, so this is a missing
BODY only -- the memory is reclaimed either way. That is what keeps it medium
rather than high, and it is also why an ASAN/valgrind corpus cannot find it:
only an A/B output comparison can.

Measured on 82c26b7 with a snapshot binary verified at that revision
(`karac 0.1.0-dev.shallow+g82c26b7d9`).

SOURCE NOTE: found while re-measuring B-2026-08-28-66, whose headline shape did
not reproduce at HEAD; the six-cell matrix built to re-scope that row separated
this cell from the two codegen ones.
NARROWED 2026-08-28 (same session, after the interpreter-only fix was built
and REJECTED by measurement). The row's premise -- "the compiled backends are
right, so this is an interpreter fix" -- holds for the cell it reports and
NOT for its neighbours, and fixing the interpreter alone makes the tree worse.

THE ONE-ARM FIX. The statement-position discard dispatch in
`eval_stmt_cf` (`src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs`, `StmtKind::Expr`) matches on
`ExprKind::Call` / `MethodCall` / a unit-variant `Path` / a bare unit-variant
`Identifier`, and has no `Match` arm, so a discarded match's value never
reaches `run_discarded_value_user_drops`. Adding

    ExprKind::Match { .. } => self.run_discarded_value_user_drops(discarded),

does exactly what this row asks: the reported cell goes from interp-silent to
`dR1` / `dropped`, matching both compiled backends. No new gate is needed for
the shapes that must stay silent, because the walker is value-driven -- a
read-only arm yields `Unit`, for which the walker is a no-op (verified).

WHY IT WAS REVERTED. It converts TWO cells of AGREED SILENCE into new
divergences. Measured on the same build, all three backends:

                                              before          after
  A. braced arm yields binding, discarded
     `match o { Some(r) => { r } .. };`   interp - / compiled dR1   ALL dR1
  B. BARE arm yields binding, discarded
     `match o { Some(r) => r, .. };`      ALL silent          interp dR1,
                                                              compiled silent
  C. arm yields a FRESH LITERAL, discarded
     `match n { 1 => { R { id: 7 } } .. };` ALL silent        interp dR7,
                                                              compiled silent

A is this row and is genuinely fixed. B and C are cells where BOTH sides are
wrong today -- one body is correct in each, since exactly one `R` is
constructed and nothing takes it -- and the interpreter-only change makes the
interpreter right while leaving codegen silent. That is the trade
B-2026-08-28-63's commit message explicitly calls out as "worse than the bug",
and it degrades the A/B oracle that is the only thing able to see this class
at all (memory is balanced in every cell -- 9/9, 10/10, 11/11 -- so no
ASAN/LSan corpus can reach any of it).

THE CODEGEN HALF, located but not built. Codegen's discard machinery is
gated by `Self::discarded_owned_temp_tail` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`), which
returns `Some` only for a `Call` or `MethodCall` tail, recursing through
blocks. A `Match` tail returns `None`, so `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp`
and every sibling discarded-temp tracker are never even consulted for a
discarded match. That is why cells B and C are silent compiled.

Cell A is compiled-correct for an unrelated reason -- the braced arm's
boxed-payload-view registration survives into the discard, which is also why A
alone is sensitive to the braces. So codegen's own behaviour across A/B/C is
inconsistent in a way that has nothing to do with the interpreter.

WHAT A REAL FIX NEEDS: the two halves landing TOGETHER -- codegen's
discarded-temp tail admitting a `Match` whose arms yield an owned Drop-bearing
value, and the interpreter's one-arm dispatch above. Either alone moves the
divergence rather than removing it. The codegen half is the larger one: a
match has several arms with different values, so admitting it is not the
one-line tail-recursion the `Call`/`MethodCall` shapes get.

The scope is therefore wider than this row was filed as: it is A + B + C on
BOTH backends, not "the interpreter misses A".
fix:
FIXED by 16a8791, BOTH HALVES TOGETHER, which is what the row's own reverted
attempt established was necessary.

THE ROW'S MATRIX HAD DRIFTED, and re-measuring it first is what kept the fix
correctly scoped. It was measured at 82c26b7; 22 codegen commits have landed on
`src/codegen` since. Current state before this fix, all four surfaces:

  cell                                   interp     compiled
  A  braced arm yields the bound payload  silent     dR1       divergent
  B  bare arm yields the bound payload    silent     dR1       divergent  <<<
  C  arm yields a fresh literal           silent     silent    agreed, both wrong

The row records B as one of its two cells of AGREED SILENCE. It is not one any
more -- the compiled backends fire there and only the interpreter is silent, so
B is the same shape as A rather than a cell needing a codegen change. Taking the
recorded matrix as given would have mis-scoped this.

CELL C IS WIDER THAN THE ROW HAD IT. It is silent compiled in EVERY spelling,
including one the row never tried: arms that are CALLS (`match n { 1 => mk(7),
_ => mk(0) };`). So "the braced arm's boxed-payload-view registration" is not
what separates the cells; the fresh-value case simply never registered at all.

THE CODEGEN HALF IS IN A DIFFERENT PLACE THAN THE ROW LOCATED IT, and is
smaller. The row points at `Self::discarded_owned_temp_tail` returning `None`
for a `Match`, and estimates the work as teaching it several arms. But a
`discarded_match_value_tail` gate already exists at the bare-statement discard
site and already admits this shape. Two things below it declined:

  1. `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp` resolves `ret_ty_name` only from a
     `Call` (fn return type) or a `MethodCall` (receiver.method). A `Match` tail
     matched no arm, so the name was `None` and the whole battery below it --
     which is otherwise driven purely by that name and the compiled value -- was
     skipped. Added a `Match` arm: all arms yield the match's own type, so the
     FIRST arm's tail decides it, resolved through a struct literal or the same
     call shape.
  2. `discarded_match_value_tail`'s per-arm gate calls
     `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, which recognizes only `Call`/`MethodCall`,
     so a STRUCT LITERAL arm was rejected before the tracker was ever consulted.
     Admitted in that gate rather than by widening the predicate, which has many
     other consumers whose freshness question is a different one (entry-copy
     depth, RC transfer).

THE INTERPRETER HALF is the one-arm dispatch the row already identified, added
verbatim, and the row's note that it needs no extra gate holds: the walker is
value-driven and a read-only arm yields `Unit`.

A REGRESSION WAS INTRODUCED AND CAUGHT MID-FIX, which is worth recording
because it is exactly the failure the row warns about. With only the tracker's
`Match` arm in place, the call-arm cell fired compiled while the interpreter
stayed silent -- a NEW divergence in a cell that had been agreed. The remaining
two edits closed it. Neither half is landable alone.

MEASURED, all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`),
identical in every cell and each firing exactly ONE body:

  braced arm yields the bound payload   dR1 / dropped
  bare arm yields the bound payload     dR1 / dropped
  braced arm yields a fresh literal     dR7 / dropped
  bare arm yields a fresh literal       dR7 / dropped
  arm yields a call result              dR7 / dropped

CONTROLS, unchanged and still one body each on every surface -- these are what
show the change did not widen into discarded temporaries generally or into arm
bindings generally: a discarded CALL result (`mk();`) and a READ-ONLY arm
(`Some(r) => { println(f"saw{r.id}") }`).

Pinned by `test_discarded_match_arm_value_runs_its_drop_body_once` (5 rows) with
`test_discarded_match_controls_keep_their_single_body`, and their codegen twin
`e2e_discarded_match_arm_value_runs_its_drop_body_once` (5 rows + both
controls). Verified NON-VACUOUS in the right places: on the pre-fix tree the
interpreter twin fails on the bound-payload arm and the codegen twin on the
fresh-literal arm. The row's observation that memory is balanced in every cell
holds, so no ASAN/LSan corpus can reach this class -- the A/B pair is the only
thing that can, which is why both twins exist.

SPLIT: the `let _ = match …` spelling is a DIFFERENT site (the wildcard-let arm
of `compile_stmt` / `discard_rhs_produces_owned_value`) with its own state, and
is untouched here -- measured byte-identical before and after this fix. It has
its own open cells and is filed separately.

title: A CONDITIONALLY-RETURNED owned param of a METHOD loses its `Drop` body IN THE INTERPRETER while all three compiled backends run it -- and the callee-side flip that fixed the free-function twin (B-2026-08-28-22) DOUBLE-FIRES here, because `method_call.rs`'s argument handling does not stand down the way `call_dispatch.rs`'s does
detail:
Two findings about the same shape, one pre-existing and one a measured
constraint on the fix that closed its free-function twin.

THE SHAPE, the method sibling of B-2026-08-28-22's headline program:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct B2 { n: i64 }
    impl B2 { fn pick(ref self, r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { r } else { R { id: 99 } } } }

      let b = B2 { n: 1 };
      let x = b.pick(R { id: 41 }, false);   println(f"{x.id}")

        interp:            99 / drop 99          R{41}'s body LOST
        jit / build / np:  drop 41 / 99 / drop 99   correct

(1) IT IS A PRE-EXISTING RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE. Measured identically with
B-2026-08-28-22's fix stashed, so nothing in 7c0569a introduced or moved it. The
three compiled backends already run the body where the value dies; the
interpreter does not. That makes this the INTERPRETER's half of -22's mechanism,
surviving on the method path only -- the free-function path is now correct on
all four surfaces.

(2) THE OBVIOUS FIX IS MEASURED WRONG, which is why -22 declined to extend to
methods. Applying -22's callee-side ownership flip to a method param -- the same
registration, same guard, same shared predicate -- gives TWO bodies for one
object on the compiled backends:

      jit / build / np:  drop 41 / drop 41 / 99 / drop 99

The flip is only ever sound where the CALLER has already stood down, and the
method caller does not: `method_call.rs` and `call_dispatch.rs` are separate
argument paths, and only the latter declines the body drop for a
conditionally-returned arg. So the callee-side registration lands on top of a
caller drop that is still armed. The index is NOT the problem and should not be
re-investigated: at `compile_function` a method is named `Type.method` with
`self` occupying param 0, so `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare(func, i)`
already answers on the right parameter (verified by instrumentation --
`B2.pick i=1 param=r pred=true`).

WHAT CLOSING THIS NEEDS, in order: audit `method_call.rs`'s argument handling to
find whether it declines the body drop for a conditionally-returned arg at all,
and if not, make it stand down exactly where `call_dispatch.rs` does. Only then
does the callee-side flip become available -- at which point it is the one-line
gate removal in `src/codegen/functions.rs` (drop the `!func.name.contains('.')`
clause) plus its interpreter twin in `cond_returned_param_drop_names`. Doing the
callee half first, in either backend alone, is the double free above or a fresh
divergence.

The conservative direction is unchanged while this is open: a missed body in the
interpreter, never a double drop, never a memory fault.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-28-22, by probing the method sibling of
its headline program before assuming the free-function result generalized. Both
measurements above are from that session; no code change was made for this row.
fix:
FIXED by 277621a, giving a method's owned argument exactly one Drop owner, on both
backends at once.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE ORDERING AND WRONG ABOUT THE SCOPE, and
the correction is what made the fix tractable. It reported an interpreter-only
loss on a CONDITIONALLY-returned param, and prescribed auditing
`method_call.rs`'s argument handling before touching the callee-side flip. The
audit found the gap it predicted, plus two the row did not see:

  * The loss is not specific to conditional returns. A method param that is
    NEVER returned lost its body in the interpreter too --
    `impl B2 { fn eat(ref self, r: R) -> i64 { 7 } }` over `b.eat(R { id: 41 })`
    printed `7` alone against `drop 41` / `7` on all three compiled backends.
    The row's shape is one member of that wider class.
  * The compiled backends have the OPPOSITE defect on the same surface, and it
    was live on main: because the method caller ALWAYS fired, a param the method
    hands back ran its body twice.
    `impl B2 { fn id(ref self, r: R) -> R { r } }` over `let x = b.id(R { id: 41 });`
    printed `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41` -- two bodies for one object -- against
    a correct one in the interpreter.

The free-function twin is what settles which count is right rather than leaving
it a preference: `fn id2(r: R) -> R { r }` and `fn eat2(r: R) -> i64 { 7 }` are
unanimous at ONE body on all four surfaces. Both method behaviours are defects
measured against it, in opposite directions.

WHY THE TWO BACKENDS FAIL OPPOSITELY: the method-argument path carries neither
half of the ownership protocol the free-function path has. Codegen's caller
never consulted an escape predicate at all -- the free-fn registrar computes
`escapes_frame = flows_into_return || moves_into_outliving_place` and the method
registrar simply omitted the first term -- so it fired unconditionally, which is
right when the callee discards the value and a double body when it hands it
back. The interpreter has no caller-side fire for methods by design
(`owned_param_frame_is_method`), and the frame did not own its params either, so
nobody fired.

THE FIX, three parts:

  * `fn_always_returns_param` (src/ast/items.rs), a new predicate asking whether
    the callee hands the param back on EVERY exit: every leaf tail yields it and
    every `return` the walker sees yields it too, "yields" matching
    `fn_returns_param`'s own notion (bare, or an aggregate literal that moves it
    in).
  * codegen/method_call.rs stands the caller down where some OTHER owner is
    certain -- that predicate, or `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare`, which is
    the same admission rule the callee-side flip uses, so the two agree by
    construction rather than by convention. codegen/functions.rs drops its
    free-functions-only gate accordingly: the precondition it was explicitly
    waiting on ("only ever sound where the caller has already stood down") now
    holds on this path.
  * the interpreter's method frame owns the `Drop` body of every owned param
    that dies inside it, since it is the only owner there is. Wider admission
    than the free-fn sibling for exactly that reason.

THE PREDICATE HAD TO BE THE "EVERY EXIT" ONE, AND THIS IS THE MEASUREMENT WORTH
KEEPING. A first draft reused `call_arg_flows_into_return` -- i.e.
`fn_returns_param`, the UNION over return sites. It fixed every double body and
introduced a fresh loss: `fn early(ref self, r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return
R { id: 98 }; } r }` at `k = true` lost R{22}'s body on all three compiled
backends, where the pre-existing always-fire had it right. "Escapes somewhere" is
not "someone else owns it". Every shape the narrow predicate declines keeps
today's behaviour, so no shape can newly lose a body through this edit -- which
is the property that makes it safe to land at all. The regression was caught only
because the baseline was measured before the fix rather than assumed; it is now
pinned by the `return-stmt-other-value-keeps-caller-fire` case in both suites.

ALSO FIXED, found while probing and required for the above to be sound: the
interpreter's method path did not isolate the callee frame's moved-out sets, as
`eval_call` does for a free fn. They are keyed by BINDING NAME with no frame
qualifier, so a mark left by one method leaked into the next frame reusing the
name -- `Box3.add`'s `r` (legitimately marked, it goes into `self.xs`)
suppressed an unrelated later method's `r`, and renaming that param to `q` was
enough to make the body reappear. Pre-existing, but invisible until the frame
started owning its params. The snapshot is taken AFTER B-2026-08-01-7's
owned-enum-receiver insert, deliberately: that insert names a CALLER-scope
binding and must ride out on the saved copy.

GENERICS are admitted on the caller-side leg, which needs no callee cooperation,
and that alone brings a generic method's dying param from zero bodies to one.
Their conditionally-returned leg stays declined on BOTH backends: codegen cannot
hand that to the callee (B-2026-08-28-71's corrupted mono param slot), so fixing
the interpreter alone would convert a shared gap into a run-vs-build divergence.

FIXTURES in all three suites, each RED-verified against the pre-fix compiler
case by case rather than in aggregate: 8 cases red in
tests/interpreter.rs, 5 in tests/codegen.rs, every substantive case red on at
least one backend. The two free-function oracles are green on both by design --
they are the controls that would catch a change which "fixed" methods by moving
free functions. The ASAN twin pins the memory side, where the caller's new
stand-down would be a leak rather than a wrong line of output if the result
binding did not in fact own the value; it was red pre-fix with four doubled
bodies (`drop b1`, `drop d1`, `drop e1`, `drop h1`), and ASAN itself stayed
clean throughout, consistent with this family registering bodies only.

RESIDUE, both filed rather than folded in: B-2026-08-29-3 (a GENERIC method that
ALWAYS returns its param still doubles on the compiled backends -- the
monomorph path does not reach the method-argument site this fixed) and
B-2026-08-29-4 (a HIGH-severity double free on the method inline-Option channel,
found by reading the same argument loop: an off-by-one on the param index).

Gates: interpreter 1809, codegen 3392, memory_sanitizer 1297, non-llvm suite all
green; fmt clean; clippy clean on both feature legs.

title: A GENERIC callee's monomorph param slot does not hold what a bodies-only user-`Drop` walker expects: registering B-2026-08-28-22's conditionally-returned-param body walk in `compile_mono_function` printed a CORRUPTED field value (`drop dr` where `drop i1` was due) for a heap-carrying param, so the fix is declined on both backends for generics
detail:
B-2026-08-28-22 gives a callee back the `Drop` BODY of an owned param it returns
on some tail paths and not others. Monomorphs have their own param loop
(`compile_mono_function`), so the registration needs a second site there -- the
same reason B-2026-08-05-7 states for its own duplicate registration a few lines
away ("`compile_function`'s sibling registration never runs for a mono body --
mono has its own param loop").

Adding it there is WRONG, and quietly so:

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.name}") } }
    fn genf[T](r: R, k: bool, t: T) -> R { if k { r } else { R { id: 96, name: f"n96" } } }

      let h = genf(R { id: 1, name: f"i1" }, false, 7);   println(f"{h.id}")

        interp:            drop i1 / 96 / drop n96     correct
        jit / build / np:  drop dr / 96 / drop n96     CORRUPTED

`dr` is not a truncation of `i1` -- it is other memory read as a `String`
{ptr,len}. The body fires the right number of times on the right paths, so every
body-COUNT case passes; only a field READ inside the body shows it. The
non-heap version of the same program (`struct R { id: i64 }`, printing
`self.id`) is entirely correct, which is why this survived the first pass of
probes.

WORKING HYPOTHESIS, not yet confirmed: the mono param arrives INDIRECTLY, so the
`create_entry_alloca(fn_val, &param_name, param_val.get_type())` slot holds a
POINTER rather than the struct, and `emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn` --
which expects a pointer to the struct -- reads the pointer's own bytes as the
{ptr,len,cap} of `name`. That would explain both the garbage and why an
`i64`-only payload looks fine (an `i64` field read from a wrong-but-mapped
address prints a plausible number rather than a visibly broken string; it was
not checked whether the number was right). Confirming it means dumping the mono
param's LLVM type at that site and comparing with `compile_function`'s.

DECLINED ON BOTH BACKENDS, deliberately. The interpreter resolves a generic by
its declared name and so applied -22's fix without any of this; leaving it there
while codegen declined would have converted a shared, symmetric bug into a
run-vs-build divergence -- which the kata corpus treats as the harder failure.
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` is gated on `generic_params.is_none()` in
both backends, so a generic callee keeps -22's original defect (a MISSED body,
no memory fault) identically on all four surfaces. The
`generic-callee-declined` case in each of the three -22 fixtures pins that.

WHAT CLOSING THIS NEEDS: establish how an owned struct param is actually passed
to a monomorph, then either load through the slot before handing it to the walker
or register against the right pointer. It is a contained question about one
site, not a design question -- the guard machinery and the predicate are already
built and proven on the non-generic path.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-28-22, by re-running its probe set with
a `String` field added after the `i64`-only generic case passed. The two-character
garbage is what made it visible; a wider field would have printed something
harder to notice.
fix:
FIXED by 907b378, on all five surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 / AOT at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0), for generic FREE FUNCTIONS and
generic METHODS alike. The row's headline program now prints `drop i1` / `96` /
`drop n96`, matching its non-generic twin exactly.

THE ROW'S HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED, and that matters because it named the wrong
half of the machinery. It read the corruption as an ABI question -- "the mono
param arrives INDIRECTLY, so the slot holds a POINTER rather than the struct" --
and set as the closing condition "establish how an owned struct param is
actually passed to a monomorph". Instrumentation at that exact site answers:

    [B71] mono=genf$i64 param#0=r declared=R has_user_drop=true
          param_val_ty={ i64, { ptr, i64, i64 } }  alloca_ty=ptr

The struct BY VALUE, the same shape `compile_function` sees, into an ordinary
opaque-pointer alloca. There is no indirection to unwrap. `compile_function`
does have three ABI adjustments the mono lacks (`arm64_coerced_struct_params`,
`indirect_struct_params`, the `Option[shared]` niche) and an sret index shift,
and any of them WOULD produce this shape -- but the first two are empty on
x86-64, where the row was measured, and monos are never sret. The hypothesis was
plausible and checkable, and checking it cost one eprintln.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING: two halves of B-2026-08-28-51's per-path guard that
`compile_function` sets up in its prologue and `compile_mono_function` did not.

  1. THE ESCAPING SITE. `note_escaping_site(func.body.final_expr)` is the first
     of the three escaping sites and the only one seeded per FUNCTION -- `let`
     initializers and `return` operands are seeded per statement in
     `compile_stmt`, which a mono body shares, so those two were fine and the
     omission was invisible until a TAIL-returned param needed it. A generic
     body never passes through `compile_function` (both top-level loops in
     `codegen.rs` skip a generic item), so nothing had ever seeded it. With the
     site unseeded, `arm_conditional_move_tail_flag` early-returns on the
     returning arm, the flag never clears, and the body fires on the path that
     RETURNED the value as well. That is the whole of the `drop dr` the row
     measured: a second body reading a struct whose field had been handed on,
     printing the format literal's own bytes. Reproduced exactly in this shape
     while building the fix -- with the param registration in place and this one
     line absent, the escaping call `genf(R { id: 1, name: f"i1" }, true, 7)`
     printed `drop ` / `1` / `drop i1`.
  2. THE FLAG MAP. `cond_move_drop_flags` holds ALLOCAS, and a mono is compiled
     NESTED inside its caller's body, so the map has to be isolated per mono or
     a mono's guard loads the CALLER's stack slot for a same-named binding.
     `compile_function` clears it for exactly this reason; both mono call sites
     now save and restore it around the nested compile, mirroring
     `scope_cleanup_actions`.

With those two in place the registration itself is the non-generic site's,
verbatim: BODIES ONLY (`emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn` -- the caller
still owns the memory, and the mono additionally holds an ENTRY DEEP-COPY from
`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst`, so a wrapper that freed fields would
be freeing the copy it had just run the body on), guarded per path, and gated on
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` + `!fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place`.

THREE ADMISSION GATES CAME OFF WITH IT, all three naming this row: the
interpreter's free-function exclusion (`cond_returned_param_drop_names`), its
method exclusion (`method_param_drop_names`), and the `generic_params.is_none()`
leg of the caller-side stand-down in `compile_generic_call`. That last one is
the one that decides the generic METHOD case, and it is easy to miss: a generic
FREE function stands down through `call_arg_flows_into_return`'s union, whose
scan is `Item::Function`-only and so answers `false` for a `Type.method` key. It
was found by measurement, not by reading -- with every other half of the fix in
place, `impl T { fn pick[U](ref self, r: R, k: bool, u: U) -> R }` still ran the
body twice on all three compiled backends while the free-function twin was
already correct. The fourth gate, `compile_function`'s own
`func.generic_params.is_none()`, is left in place and re-documented as a no-op
belt: that fn is never called with a generic item.

A CORRECTION TO THE ROW'S SCOPE. It states that a generic callee "keeps -22's
original defect (a MISSED body, no memory fault) identically on all four
surfaces". That held for a generic FREE function; it did NOT hold for a generic
METHOD, which was a run-vs-build divergence in BOTH directions at once --
measured pre-fix on the six-call probe program: the interpreter missed the body
on the dying path (`drop e1` absent) while all three compiled backends ran it
TWICE on the escaping path (`drop g1` twice). So the "identical on every
surface" reading that justified declining on both backends was true of half the
shape only.

MEMORY, measured rather than argued. Under valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` the
probe program goes 44 allocs / 44 frees pre-fix to 45 / 45 post-fix, ZERO errors
either way -- the net +1 is two recovered bodies' format strings less the one
removed duplicate, so the extra body was spurious and never a double free (the
same discrimination B-2026-08-29-14 needed, and the reason a non-allocating drop
body is the right instrument when an allocation delta is ambiguous). Every
generic probe matches its NON-GENERIC twin exactly on both counts: 14/14 for the
dying path, 12/12 escaping, 18/18 for the `match` spelling, 13/13 for the
store-into-self shape the predicates decline.

FIXTURES. Four cases added to each of the codegen and interpreter -22 suites
(dying and escaping paths, `i64`-only and `String`-carrying), plus
`asan_generic_conditionally_returned_param_bodies_are_memory_balanced` covering
a generic free fn, a generic `match` callee additionally instantiated at
`U = String`, and a generic method, with distinct param names per callee for
B-2026-08-29-11's reason. The DYING-path cases are RED-verified against a
compiler built at the parent commit; the ESCAPING-path cases are honest
CONTROLS -- already correct pre-fix -- and they earn their place by failing
against the INTERMEDIATE version of this fix (registration in place, escaping
site unseeded), which is the state the row's own measurement describes.

Gates: fmt clean; clippy clean on BOTH feature legs; codegen 3404,
memory_sanitizer 1311, par_codegen 270, interpreter 1819, ownership 481,
typechecker 2543, cli 723, lib 1374, plus the full default suite -- zero
failures, with `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` on the archive-linking suites
and the archives rebuilt (lean then full) after `7a8107c` touched
`runtime/src/lib.rs` mid-session.

title: A `match` THAT IS A FUNCTION'S RETURNED VALUE RUNS THE YIELDED PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `fn take(o: Option[R]) -> R { match o { Some(r) => { r } .. } }` is interp `dR1` vs compiled `dR1 dR1`; memory stays balanced and NO pattern-binding registration fires, so it is not the arm registration B-2026-08-28-66 turned out to be
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-28-66 when that row was re-measured. It is the DOUBLED
BODY that row's title describes; the shape its repro actually printed was a
double free through a different channel, fixed in 0e6f200. This half is
untouched by that fix and was measured identical before and after it.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

    fn take(o: Option[R]) -> R { match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { R { id: 0 } } } }
    fn main() { let o: Option[R] = Some(R { id: 1 }); let k = take(o); println("kept"); }

      interp            -> `dR1` / `kept`               CORRECT
      jit / AOT         -> `dR1` / `dR1` / `kept`       body twice

Exactly one `R` is constructed and one reaches `k`, so one body is correct.

INDEPENDENT OF THE BRACES, which is what separates it from -66. That row's
defect turned on `Some(r) => { r }` being a Block where `Some(r) => r` is an
Identifier; here BOTH spellings double identically (`s_fn` and `s_fn_bare`,
`dR1 dR1` each). So the arm-tail neutralizer family is not involved.

MEMORY IS BALANCED, unlike -66: 10 allocs / 10 frees with a scalar payload and
12 / 12 with `R { id: i64, name: String }`, valgrind-clean at -O0. Only the
BODY doubles. That also means an ASAN/LSan corpus cannot find it -- it is
visible only to an A/B output comparison.

NOT A PATTERN-BINDING REGISTRATION. Instrumented every `track_user_drop_var` /
`track_user_drop_var_with_fn` call site in `pattern_binding.rs` while compiling
this program: NONE fires. (For contrast, -66's shape fires exactly one, at the
boxed-payload-view site.) The struct arm's own registration is gated on
`!pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`, and `o` IS an owned param of
`take`, so that site routes to `track_struct_var` -- memory only -- by design.

WHERE THE SECOND BODY COMES FROM, hypothesis not yet confirmed: the
caller-retains model (B-2026-08-01-13). A payload bound out of an owned-param
scrutinee is a view of the callee's entry copy, so its body is deliberately
left to the CALLER's fire. Here the callee also RETURNS that payload, so the
caller ends up firing both for the entry copy it retained and for the returned
value bound to `k`. If that is right, the fix has to notice that the callee
handed the payload back out rather than dropping it, which is the same
"does another owner now hold this body" question B-2026-08-28-22's escape
predicates ask -- and the reason -66's row said closing it needs the
classifier rather than a syntactic gate.

RELATED, NOT THE SAME, carried over from -66 and re-confirmed:
`let k = match o { Some(e) => { id(e) } .. }` where `id` returns its param
prints two bodies on ALL FOUR surfaces. The backends AGREE there, so that is
the entry-copy model showing through rather than a divergence.

Measured on 0e6f200; identical on a snapshot binary built at 82c26b7, before
the -66 fix.
