                                                  38 B / 1 object   LEAKS

    struct D { s: String }                        38 B / 1 object   LEAKS
    let vv: Option[D] = Some(D { s: <38 B> });
    if let Some(d) = vv { d };

    CONTROL -- bound and USED, not handed out:    clean
    if let Some(s) = vv { println(f"{s.len()}"); }

So the trigger is a TAIL-POSITION hand-out whose result is discarded. All three
leaking spellings are single statements; no loop, no store, no second binding.

WHERE TO LOOK. This is the population `branch_value_is_owned` names -- the
guard that stops `suppress_boxed_payload_view_move` from neutralizing the
source when nothing downstream owns the branch's value. That guard is correct
and load-bearing (B-2026-08-28-75 measured it: removing it leaks 68 B on the
boxed twin, and the `match` site's own comment predicts the same). The question
this row asks is the next one along: the guard correctly declines to hand
ownership to a destination that does not exist, but nothing then frees the
value at the end of the discarded construct either. The arm binding appears to
take the payload out of the slot regardless of whether the result is kept.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT. B-2026-08-28-44 fixed the leak where a container-element
READ handed out of a branch value had no owner at the merge; that row's answer
was to give the escaping value an owner. This is the mirror case -- the value
escapes into nothing at all -- and the answer is more likely a drop at the
discard point than an owner at a merge.

SOURCE NOTE: found while building B-2026-08-29-1's boundary matrix. It was
filed there as `discarded-iflet` on the assumption that it was a boundary the
fix had to avoid breaking; it was already RED, which is how it was noticed.
It is NOT in that row's fixture -- a fixture cannot carry a row it does not
fix.
fix:
FIXED by a86e5d1. TWO mechanisms, not one, and the row's "WHERE TO LOOK" named
only the first of them. Its guess was right about where the answer lived --
the `branch_value_is_owned` population -- and wrong about the shape: the
answer is not "a drop at the discard point" but "STOP TAKING THE DROP AWAY",
for the half of the corpus that had an owner all along.

MECHANISM 1 -- the arm tail names something that ALREADY HAS AN OWNER.
`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` at an arm tail is a HANDOVER: it
takes the tail's buffer away from whatever owns it (a pattern binding, a local
in scope) so the branch's consumer can own it instead. A DISCARDED branch has
no consumer, so the handover strands the buffer. B-2026-08-29-13 had already
gated ONE channel of that call on `owns_result` (the bare-`shared` transfer
inc) with exactly this reasoning; the fix gates the WHOLE call, at both arm-tail
sites (`compile_match`, `compile_if_let`).

That covers `match` and `if let`. A plain `if` reaches the same suppressor
through `compile_block_with_frame`, which is shared with value-position blocks,
`let` initializers and call arguments and holds no condition at all -- so it
cannot ask `branch_value_is_owned` itself. `compile_if` (and an `if let`'s ELSE
arm, which routes there too) now carries the answer in through a one-shot
`branch_arm_value_discarded`, `take`n at that function's entry so only the block
it was set for reads it and a nested value-position block inside the arm gets
the ordinary treatment.

MECHANISM 2 -- the arm tail MINTS its value. There is no owner to leave armed;
nothing ever held it, so mechanism 1 buys nothing. The fix REGISTERS one, in
the arm's own frame, gated on `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` so an aliasing
place-expr tail is never freed out from under its binding.

WHY IN THE ARM AND NOT AT THE STATEMENT. `discarded_match_value_tail` already
covered mechanism 2 for `match` alone, at the statement site, and extending it
to `if`/`if let` does not work: a no-`else` branch hands its arm's value to the
statement NOT AT ALL. `compile_if`'s merge yields a const-0 placeholder when
`else_val` is `None`, so by the time the statement site sees anything the
buffer is already unreachable. `if let Some(s) = vv { s };` -- the row's
headline spelling -- is exactly that shape.

WHAT THE ROW MISSED. Filed as three spellings of one bug; it is two mechanisms
across five spellings, and the row's own three all sit in mechanism 1. Found
while narrowing: `if seed() > 0 { a } else { b };` over two plain locals leaks
identically with no pattern and no payload anywhere, which is what showed the
population is "a discarded branch tail", not "a bound payload handed out".

SLICE 5's DEFERRAL IS LIFTED. `test_ir_discarded_branching_tail_temp_not_tracked`
asserted the leak -- "a safe leak, deferred" -- because a branching tail could
not be routed through the statement chokepoint without double-freeing an
aliasing place-expr branch. Registering inside the ARM under a freshness
predicate is what makes that safe, so the test now asserts the temp IS tracked
and a new sibling pins the aliasing half staying untracked.

MEASURED (`asan_discarded_branch_frees_the_value_its_arm_hands_out`, 18 rows):
12 leak rows RED and 6 control rows GREEN against the unfixed compiler at
`-O0`; all 18 green after. The controls are the real gate -- each is a shape
where an over-eager free is a DOUBLE FREE rather than a leak, including the
aliasing `let k = if c { a } else { b }` the deferral was protecting.

FIXTURE NOTE, worth more than the fix. Six of these rows passed against the
UNFIXED compiler when written directly in `main`, while valgrind reported
`definitely lost` on every one: LeakSanitizer scans the live stack
conservatively, so a leaked buffer whose `{ptr,len,cap}` is still sitting in
`main`'s frame reads as REACHABLE and goes unreported. Every case now runs in a
`go()` helper, which puts the stale slot below the stack pointer before LSan
looks. This is a second way an ASAN fixture passes vacuously, alongside the
known `-O2` folding one, and it is invisible in exactly the same way.

At `-O2` only `source-survives-the-discard` stays RED (the others' allocations
are dead and LLVM deletes them) -- the same `-O0`-detects/`-O2`-passes split the
B-2026-08-29-2 and -18 fixtures carry.

ADJACENT ROWS THIS DOES NOT TOUCH, both measured rather than reasoned about:

  * B-2026-08-29-25 -- a discarded `if` whose arm is a STRUCT LITERAL runs no
    user `Drop` body. Unchanged here: the fresh-tail owner is gated on
    `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, which admits `Call`/`MethodCall` only, so
    a struct-literal arm never reaches it. Re-measured after this fix: all
    three backends still print only `end`.

  * The tail temp of a value-position BLOCK or BRANCH consumed by a position
    that registers no owner -- a method receiver or a free-fn argument -- still
    leaks. Byte-identical before and after (36 B / 1 block on each of four
    spellings). Filed separately; the value there is consumed, not discarded,
    so every mechanism added here is correctly inert on it.

title: A passthrough call used DIRECTLY AS A MATCH SCRUTINEE (`match take(s) { .. }`, the result never bound) DOUBLE-FREES the inline `Option`/`Result` payload on all three compiled backends -- for a FREE FUNCTION as well as a method, so it is not the method-path gap B-2026-08-29-4 closed
detail:
The scope remainder of B-2026-08-29-4, and a wider defect than that row: this
one reproduces on the FREE-FUNCTION path too, so it is not about methods.

MEASURED on 8d8d1b4 (the -4 fix commit) and identically on its parent, so the
fix neither introduced nor addressed it:

    fn takef(o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o }
    fn main() {
        let n = 1;
        let s = Option.Some(f"a{n}");
        match takef(s) { Option.Some(v) => { println(f"got {v}"); }
                         Option.None => { println("none"); } }
    }

        interp:            `got a1`     CORRECT
        jit / build / np:  `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`

    The METHOD spelling of the same program behaves identically:

    impl Bx { fn take(ref self, o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o } }
      match b.take(s) { Option.Some(v) => { println(f"got {v}"); } ... }
                       -> same abort on the same three backends

THE CONTRAST THAT LOCALIZES IT is the `let`-bound spelling of the very same
call, which is CLEAN on all four surfaces since B-2026-08-29-4:

    let o = takef(s);
    match o { Option.Some(v) => { println(f"got {v}"); } ... }   -> `got a1`

So the payload is owned correctly when the passthrough result is BOUND, and
doubly owned when it is consumed as a temporary. B-2026-08-29-4's fix records
the ownership alias at the `let` site (`passthrough_owner_alias`); a scrutinee
temporary never passes through that site, so the source stays armed and the
match's own consumption frees the same buffer.

The relevant machinery for the temp path appears to be the discarded-temp
registrars, which consult `call_passthrough_armed_any_source` (runtime.rs) --
the superset detector that also covers boxed payloads. Whether that path is
simply not reached for a match scrutinee, or is reached and does not disarm the
source, has NOT been established: no instrumentation was run on it, and this row
deliberately does not guess. B-2026-08-29-4 is a cautionary precedent here --
that row was filed with a confidently-worded root cause inferred from reading
the same family of code, and the mechanism was refuted by a one-line
instrumentation once the fix was attempted.

Payloads must be built with an INTERPOLATED f-string to reproduce: a plain
literal is rodata with `cap == 0` and is never freed, so `f"a1"` silently tests
nothing. An earlier comparison in the -4 investigation drew a wrong conclusion
from exactly that.

WHAT CLOSING IT NEEDS: instrument the scrutinee-temp path first to establish
which registrar sees the call and what it does with the source, then fix at that
site, then a RED-verified ASAN fixture in BOTH spellings (free function and
method) plus a no-passthrough control -- a fix that disarms the source
unconditionally would strand a freshly produced payload with no owner, which is
the failure direction the -4 fixtures already guard against on the `let` path.

SOURCE NOTE: found while writing B-2026-08-29-4's ASAN fixture. Every shape had
passed individually in the `let`-bound form; writing the fixture in the
inline-scrutinee form made four of them abort at once, which is what exposed
this as a separate defect rather than a gap in that fix.
fix:
FIXED by d1db93d, by classifying a passthrough match scrutinee as source-retaining
and stopping the fresh-temp inline-`Result` registrar from claiming it.

INSTRUMENTED BEFORE DIAGNOSING, deliberately: B-2026-08-29-4 in this same family
was filed with a confidently-worded root cause inferred from reading, and it was
refuted the moment a fix was attempted. The trace here showed
`fresh_owned_temp=true` and `passthrough=Some("s")` while all three fresh-temp
scrutinee registrars DECLINED the scrutinee -- which ruled them out as the second
owner and pointed at the ARM BINDING instead. The row's own "WHERE TO START"
guess (the discarded-temp registrars) was wrong; those cover statement position,
not a scrutinee.

TWO HALVES, each measured independently necessary by removing it and re-running
the fixture, in both directions:

  * the match's scrutinee site now classifies a passthrough call as
    source-retaining -- the flag whose own comment states the rule: "the source
    keeps it, so the arm binding must not register a free and the suppressors
    must not disarm the source". This alone fixes every `Option` spelling.
  * `track_freshtemp_inline_result_scrutinee` declines a passthrough, for the
    same reason it already declines a borrow-returning scrutinee. `Result` needs
    this IN ADDITION, because that registrar claims a `Result` temp where no
    registrar claims an `Option` one.

The second half was found only by bisecting the shapes individually after a
combined fixture still aborted with the first half in place -- each shape had
passed on its own, so the combination is what exposed it.

NARROWING the arm binding rather than zeroing the source, the direction this
family already settled: B-2026-08-06-21 tried the zeroing form and turned a clean
program into a leak. Leaving the source sole owner cannot leak (it is still
armed), and the arm reads the payload before the source's scope-exit free.

Confirmed on all four surfaces and valgrind-balanced: free-function and method
spellings, `Option` and `Result` payloads, `mut ref self`, two-argument callees
returning either argument, and the combined program (26 allocs, 26 frees).

FIXTURES in all three suites, RED-verified: the ASAN twin aborts pre-fix and
carries a no-passthrough control (a fix that declined unconditionally would
strand the freshly produced payload with no owner) and a `let`-bound control
(both routes must classify the same call alike). The interpreter cases are
controls -- that backend was already correct, so they pin that codegen moved onto
its answer rather than both moving.

Gates: codegen 3394, memory_sanitizer 1301, interpreter 1812, non-llvm suite all
green; fmt clean; clippy clean on both feature legs.

title: An `Option` MATCH ARM THAT REBINDS ITS HEAP PAYLOAD TO A LOCAL AND RETURNS IT IS A DOUBLE FREE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `match b { Some(r) => { let k = r; return k; } .. }` over `Option[Res]` with `Res { id, name: String }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` where the interpreter prints correctly; the `Result` twin, the value-enum twin, and the scalar-payload twin are all CLEAN, and so is the same arm without the intermediate `let`
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-28-72, and NOT caused by it. Measured identical with
that row's caller-side retraction ON and OFF (a temporary `KARAC_B72_OFF=1`
hatch over the one changed gate, so a single binary answered both
directions): `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` either way. It is
pre-existing and orthogonal.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id} {self.name}") } }

    fn take(b: Option[Res]) -> Res {
        match b {
            Some(r) => { let k = r; return k; }
            None    => { return Res { id: 0, name: f"z" }; }
        }
    }
    fn main() {
        let b: Option[Res] = Some(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" });
        let r: Res = take(b);
        println(f"got {r.id}");
    }

      interp     -> `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`                    CORRECT
      jit / aot  -> `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, exit 134

THE ARM-LOCAL REBIND IS THE TRIGGER. `Some(r) => { return r; }` -- the same
program without the intermediate `let` -- is CORRECT on all three backends
(post -72). Adding `let k = r;` between the binding and the return is the
whole difference.

valgrind at -O0 names the block: `Invalid free() ... Address 0x4b90a30 is 0
bytes inside a block of size 2 free'd`. Size 2 is `f"e7"`, the payload
struct's `name` buffer. One free comes through a function called from `main`
(the callee) and one directly from `main`, so both owners are live at once.

THREE CONTROLS, all clean, which is what makes this narrow rather than a
general property of the alias:

    Option[Res], `let k = r; return k;`   HEAP payload    DOUBLE FREE
    Result[Res, i64], same alias          HEAP payload    clean
    enum Box2 { Full(Res), Empty }, same  HEAP payload    clean
    Option[R],  same alias                SCALAR payload  clean

So it needs all three of: `Option` (not `Result`, not a user value enum), a
payload that OWNS heap, and the intermediate rebind. The `Result` control is
the surprising one -- the two built-ins share the erased `{tag, w0, w1, w2}`
layout and the same `FreeInlineOptionPayload` / `FreeInlineResultPayload`
family, so whatever asymmetry admits this is in one of the per-type gates,
not in the layout.

WHERE TO START. `callee_optres_param_entry_copied` (call_dispatch.rs) decides
whether the caller keeps its own `FreeInlineOptionPayload` or zeroes the slot
as a move; it answers from the param TYPE alone, so it is identical for the
clean `return r` shape and this one. That means the divergence is downstream,
in what the CALLEE does with the rebind -- the natural suspects are the
`let`-site re-registration for `k` and whether `r`'s own registration is
retracted by the rebind rather than by the return.

SOURCE NOTE: found while building the guard-rail matrix for B-2026-08-28-72.
Not reachable from that row's own repro, which has no intermediate binding.

CORRECTION (2026-08-29, at close). Two claims in this row were wrong, and both
came from reasoning about the CALLER when the whole defect is in the callee's
arm.

(1) "WHERE TO START" pointed at `callee_optres_param_entry_copied` and
    reasoned that since it answers from the param TYPE alone it is identical
    for the clean `return r` shape and this one, so the divergence must be
    downstream in what the callee does with the rebind. The first half is
    true and the conclusion is not: `main`'s emitted IR is BYTE-IDENTICAL
    between the two programs. Nothing caller-side differs, so nothing
    caller-side needed to.

(2) The three controls were recorded as an unexplained asymmetry -- "whatever
    admits this is in one of the per-type gates". There is no per-type gate.
    `Result` and the value enum put the payload where this box mirror is not
    the owner, and a SCALAR payload fits `Option`'s 3-word area so no box
    exists to leave live. The controls are all consequences of BOXEDNESS,
    which the row had already observed ("a payload that OWNS heap") without
    connecting it to the mechanism.

What the row got right and what made the fix findable: the reduction to
exactly three requirements (`Option`, a heap-owning payload, the intermediate
rebind) and the observation that the same arm without the `let` is clean.
Diffing the emitted IR of those two programs is what named the missing store
in one step.
fix:
FIXED by 905d73f in codegen, by carrying the payload BOX POINTER across a
whole-value rebind.

THE ROW'S "WHERE TO START" WAS WRONG and is corrected here. It pointed at
`callee_optres_param_entry_copied` and guessed the divergence was downstream
in what the callee does with the rebind. The caller is not involved at all:
`main`'s IR is BYTE-IDENTICAL between the double-freeing program and the clean
one. The entire difference is inside the callee's arm.

THE MECHANISM. `Res { id: i64, name: String }` is 4 words against `Option`'s
3-word payload area, so the payload is heap-BOXED and the box's owner is the
CALLER. B-2026-08-06-10's whole-payload mirror zeroes the box's interior
alongside the escaping value's own copy -- that mirror is what stops the
caller's `__karac_drop_struct_Res(box)` from freeing a buffer the return value
carried away. It is keyed by SLOT
(`payload_vars.deboxed_payload_box_ptrs: HashMap<PointerValue, PointerValue>`),
recorded for the arm binding at bind time.

`let k = r;` gives the escaping value a NEW slot, which that map has never
heard of, so the mirror silently skipped the box:

    CLEAN   `Some(r) => { return r; }`
        store i64 0, ptr %smv.f1.cap        ; the copy   %r
        store i64 0, ptr %smv.f1.cap14      ; the BOX    %enumbox.mv

    BUGGY   `Some(r) => { let k = r; return k; }`
        store i64 0, ptr %smv.f1.cap        ; the copy   %k
        (no box zero -- %enumbox.mv is computed and never written)

The box therefore kept a live `{ptr,len,cap}` and the caller freed the
`String` a second time. valgrind at -O0: `Invalid free() ... Address ... is 0
bytes inside a block of size 2 free'd` -- size 2 is `f"e7"`, the payload's
`name` buffer.

THE FIX is four lines of bookkeeping at the `let` site (stmts.rs, the
`StmtKind::Let` arm): when the RHS is an identifier whose slot carries a box
pointer, insert the same pointer under the DESTINATION slot. The existing
mirror then fires unchanged. Propagate rather than move the entry -- `r` may
still be read after the rebind, and a second zero of the same box is a
repeated store of 0, not a double free.

MEASURED, every shape that was reduced for the row:

    Option, `let k = r; return k;`   HEAP payload   DOUBLE FREE -> correct
    Option, `let k = r; k` (tail)    HEAP payload   DOUBLE FREE -> see below
    Option, `let mut k = r; ...`     HEAP payload   DOUBLE FREE -> correct
    Option, `let k = r; let m = k;`  two levels     DOUBLE FREE -> correct
    GUARD  Option, `return r;`       no rebind      correct     -> correct
    CONTROL Result, same rebind                     correct     -> correct
    CONTROL value enum, same rebind                 correct     -> correct
    CONTROL Option, SCALAR payload                  correct     -> correct
    CONTROL local scrutinee (no param)              correct     -> correct

The three controls the row listed as "surprising" are explained by the
mechanism rather than by a per-type gate: `Result[Res, i64]` and the
value-enum spelling put the payload somewhere this box mirror is not the
owner, and a SCALAR payload fits the 3-word area so there is no box at all.
That is why the row's guess at a per-type asymmetry found nothing.

ONE SHAPE IMPROVES WITHOUT BECOMING CORRECT. The BLOCK-TAIL spelling
(`Some(r) => { let k = r; k }`) no longer double-frees, but still prints the
payload's `Drop` body twice -- the second fire reads the neutralized copy and
prints an empty name. That remainder is B-2026-08-29-8, filed before this fix
and measured identical with it: a memory fault became an already-tracked body
double, which is a strict improvement and not a new defect.

TWO PINS, and they are not redundant. The ASAN fixture
`asan_rebound_boxed_option_payload_returned_is_owned_once` catches the double
free (RED pre-fix: `AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free`). The codegen
output pin `test_e2e_rebound_boxed_option_payload_returned_drops_once` catches
the BODY COUNT, which ASAN cannot see; pre-fix it fails with `left: Some("")`
because the aborting binary prints nothing. It carries the two-level rebind
and the no-rebind guard rail as separate assertions.

Verified: codegen, interpreter, memory_sanitizer, drop_differential all green;
asan-o0 leg matches its quarantine list exactly; both clippy legs and fmt
clean.

title: A MATCH ARM THAT REBINDS ITS PAYLOAD TO A LOCAL AND YIELDS IT AS THE ARM'S BLOCK TAIL RUNS THE `Drop` BODY TWICE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `Box2.Full(r) => { let m = r; m }` is interp `dR1` vs compiled `dR1 dR1`, the extra fire at the ARM BLOCK's exit for a value that escapes; the `return` spelling of the same arm is correct, and value enums and `Option` carry it alike
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-28-72 as a residual it does not cover. Measured
identical with that row's retraction ON and OFF, and it reproduces on a USER
VALUE ENUM as readily as on `Option`, which places it outside the
caller-retains family -72 and B-2026-08-09-15 belong to.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum Box2 { Full(R), Empty }

    fn take(o: Box2) -> R {
        match o { Box2.Full(r) => { let m = r; m } Box2.Empty => { R { id: 0 } } }
    }
    fn main() { let o: Box2 = Box2.Full(R { id: 1 }); let k = take(o); println(f"C k={k.id}"); }

      interp     -> `C k=1` / `dR1`              CORRECT
      jit / aot  -> `dR1` / `C k=1` / `dR1`      body twice

THE BLOCK TAIL IS THE TRIGGER, not the rebind by itself. The `return`
spelling of the same arm (`Box2.Full(r) => { let k = r; return k; }`) is
CORRECT on every backend. Only yielding the local as the arm's tail doubles.
That is the same Block-vs-Identifier split B-2026-08-28-66's arm-tail
neutralizer family turns on -- `{ m }` is a Block, and the four neutralizers
in `compile_match` key on `arm.body` being `ExprKind::Identifier` -- so the
first thing to check is whether `Self::block_tail_expr` is being consulted
here at all.

WHERE THE SECOND BODY FIRES. Instrumented with markers inside the callee:

      [take:enter]
      dR7            <- at the ARM BLOCK's exit, for the local that escapes
      [take:before-return]
      C k=7
      dR7            <- the caller's binding, CORRECT

The local `m` is dropped at the arm block's scope exit even though its value
IS the match's result and leaves the frame. The interpreter retracts it.

MEMORY IS BALANCED -- only the body doubles -- so an ASAN/LSan corpus cannot
see this class and neither can the run-vs-build parity oracle's memory half.
An output pin is the only signal, as it was for -72 and B-2026-08-09-15.

`Option` carries it identically (`Some(r) => { let m = r; m }`), and there
the count went 3 bodies -> 2 across -72's fix: that row removed the
caller-side duplicate and left this one standing.

SOURCE NOTE: found while building the guard-rail matrix for B-2026-08-28-72.
fix:
FIXED by 077a6bd in codegen, by giving the value-position block-tail suppressor
the USER-DROP channel its function-body sibling has had since B-2026-07-22-2 --
scoped to the innermost frame.

THE HOLE. `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` (stmts.rs) neutralizes an Identifier
tail through two channels: `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg` (memory) and
`suppress_boxed_enum_payload_cleanup_for_owner` (boxed payload). It never
touched the `UserDrop` action. Its function-body twin
`suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` (call_dispatch.rs) ends its Identifier arm
with exactly the missing call, and says why: "the source binding's value is
moved out as the function return value ... the caller will fire it when its own
binding for the returned value goes out of scope". A value-position block tail
is the same move to the same effect.

THE IR NAMES IT IN ONE LINE. Buggy `{ let m = r; m }` vs clean
`{ let m = r; return m; }`, same program otherwise:

    BUGGY  match.body0:  ... call void @karac_drop_R(ptr %m)   <- the escaping local
    CLEAN  match.body0:  ... (no such call)

The `return` spelling was already correct because it routes through the
function sibling instead.

WHY THE THREE CONTROLS BEHAVE AS THEY DO -- this is what makes the shape narrow
rather than "block tails are broken":

    `{ let m = r; m }`          REBIND + block tail   DOUBLED  -> fixed
    `{ let m = r; return m; }`  REBIND + return       correct (function sibling)
    `{ r }`                     no rebind, tail       correct
    `{ let m = r; m.id }`       REBIND, no escape     see the residual below

`{ r }` is correct for a reason worth keeping: a payload bound out of an
OWNED-PARAM scrutinee registers memory-only under caller-retains
(`pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`), so there is no `UserDrop` to
retract. It is specifically the REBIND that mints a genuinely owned local, and
the block tail that hands it out.

THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG AND THE MEASUREMENT CAUGHT IT. Calling
`suppress_user_drop_for_var` directly fixes every shape above and REGRESSES a
different one, because that helper walks EVERY live frame:

    let a = R { id: 1 }; let b = R { id: 2 };
    let k = if a.id > 0 { a } else { b };

    before the fix   `dR2` / `k=1` / `dR1` / `end`    correct, and what interp prints
    over-broad fix   `k=1` / `dR1` / `end`            `b`'s body LOST

`b` dies in place on the path not taken, and a static retraction cannot tell
the two branches apart. That is precisely the split B-2026-08-28-51 already
drew, and `emit_user_drop_call_guarded`'s doc states the rule this fix now
obeys: "the innermost frame is the ordinary tail-move the static suppressor
already handles correctly, and its scoping -- the retraction only reaches the
frame that owns the action -- is exactly why that case never needed a runtime
bit." An ENCLOSING-frame binding is the runtime per-path flag's business
(`arm_conditional_move_tail_flag`, armed on the line immediately above this
one); an INNERMOST-frame binding cannot be conditional, because the frame it
lives in is the one being handed out.

So the shipped form retains only in `scope_cleanup_actions.last_mut()`. `m` is
in that frame; `a` and `b` are not.

CLOSES THE RESIDUALS LEFT ON TWO EARLIER ROWS. B-2026-08-29-7's fix (905d73f)
turned its block-tail spelling from a double free into a doubled body and
recorded that as this row; B-2026-08-28-72's own `q2` probe still printed two
bodies after that row landed. Both now agree at one, along with every other
fixture from that investigation (11 programs re-run, all AGREE).

ONE RESIDUAL SPLIT OUT, and it is NOT this defect: `{ let m = r; m.id }` --
the rebind WITHOUT an escape -- runs the body TWICE on ALL THREE backends
(`dR1 dR1 v=1`). They AGREE, so no A/B gate can see it, and the interpreter
doubling it is proof this fix is not involved (codegen-only change). Measured
identical before and after. Filed as B-2026-08-29-17.

TWO PINS IN ONE TEST, and the guard rails are the point. The test is RED
against the UNFIXED compiler (`dR1 / C k=1 / dR1`, the doubled body) AND RED
against the OVER-BROAD first attempt (`k=1 / dR1 / end`, the lost `dR2`), so it
discriminates the two failure modes rather than merely detecting one. No ASAN
fixture: the retraction frees nothing, memory is balanced on both sides, and
the parity oracle's memory half cannot see this class -- the output pin is the
only signal.

title: REGRESSION (277621a): A METHOD that RETURNS a payload bound out of its owned enum / `Option` param now runs that payload's `Drop` BODY TWICE IN THE INTERPRETER -- `impl T { fn take(ref self, b: Box2) -> Res { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } .. } } }` was interp-and-compiled `drop 7 e7` at 277621a^ and is interp `drop 7 e7 / got 7 / drop 7 e7` vs compiled `got 7 / drop 7 e7` at main; the FREE-FUNCTION spelling is correct on both
fix:
FIXED by 1167db7, by REVERTING 277621a's method-frame moved-out isolation. The row
is mine and its attribution was correct.

CONFIRMED THE ATTRIBUTION INDEPENDENTLY before acting -- `git checkout 277621a^
-- src` plus a full rebuild gave `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`, agreeing with AOT, so
the regression is 277621a's and not something it merely exposed.

THEN BISECTED WITHIN THE COMMIT, which is the part that decided the fix. 277621a
made two interpreter changes: the method frame started OWNING its params (the
B-2026-08-28-70 fix proper), and the callee frame's moved-out sets were ISOLATED
(mirroring `eval_call`). Disabling each independently:

    param registration OFF, isolation ON   -> double body REMAINS
    param registration ON,  isolation OFF  -> correct

So the registration -- the part that fixed -70 -- is not implicated and stays.
This matters: the row's own "WHERE TO START" pointed at the ownership move and
suggested the escaping case needs `fn_returns_param_payload`. That was a
reasonable reading and it is not where the defect is. Adding those exclusions
was tried first and changed nothing (the predicate answered `payload=true`, so
the registration was already declining), which is what forced the bisect.

WHY THE ISOLATION BREAKS IT. The moved-out sets are keyed by BINDING NAME with no
frame qualifier. Nothing inside the callee marks an escaping payload moved-out --
the suppression comes entirely from the CALLER's mark on the argument leaking
into the callee under the shared name. Isolating the frame removed that leak and
with it the only suppression this shape had, so the callee fired the payload's
body at its own exit and the caller's binding fired it again.

The accidental leak is therefore LOAD-BEARING today. That is an unpleasant thing
to restore deliberately, and it is still the right call: the defect it hides is a
MISSED body (one method's mark suppressing an unrelated later method's
identically-named param), and a missed body is strictly less harmful than a
double one. Isolation remains the right end state, but only once the callee marks
an escaping payload itself -- a scoped slice, not a line. Filed as
B-2026-08-29-11.

THE -70 FIXTURE CASE that depended on the isolation was REMOVED from the
interpreter suite rather than re-pinned to the regressed output: re-pinning would
make the fixture assert a defect as expected behaviour. Its codegen twin keeps
the case, because that backend is correct there; the resulting one-sided
divergence is exactly what the new row tracks.

A RED-verified interpreter fixture for the returned-payload shape is added in
both the user-enum and `Option` spellings, and its doc records the bisect --
specifically that the param registration is NOT implicated -- so the next reader
does not re-land the isolation without the callee-side marking, or strip the
registration looking for this.

Gates: codegen 3397, memory_sanitizer 1302, interpreter 1814, non-llvm suite all
green; fmt clean; clippy clean on both feature legs.

title: A METHOD whose owned `Option[T]` param has its payload bound out and NOT returned MISSES the payload's `Drop` body under CODEGEN -- interp `drop 7`/`v=7` vs compiled `v=7`. The USER-ENUM half of this row is FIXED (a method frame's owned-param scrutinee is now consuming); what remains is codegen arming the payload-bodies walk only for a tracked VALUE enum, so an `Option` argument never gets one
detail:
SPLIT OUT of the sibling regression row, and the opposite half of it. Also
found while building B-2026-08-28-72's method-spelling guard rail.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct T { n: i64 }
    impl T {
        fn take(ref self, b: Option[Res]) -> i64 {
            match b { Some(r) => { return r.id; } None => { return 0; } }
        }
    }
    fn main() {
        let t = T { n: 1 };
        let b: Option[Res] = Some(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" });
        let v: i64 = t.take(b);
        println(f"v={v}");
    }

      interp -> `drop 7` / `v=7`      CORRECT
      aot    -> `v=7`                 body MISSED

The payload is bound out and NOT returned, so the callee is its sole owner and
one body is due. The VALUE-ENUM twin of the identical program (`enum Box2 {
Full(Res), Empty }`) is CORRECT on both backends, which is what makes this an
`Option`-specific hole rather than a general property of the method path.

CODEGEN'S MISS IS PRE-EXISTING, measured at 277621a^ and at main: `v=7` with
no body, both times. What CHANGED at 277621a is the interpreter, which used to
miss it too (`v=7` at 277621a^) and now runs it correctly. So that commit did
not introduce this defect -- it made it VISIBLE by fixing one side of an
agreed silence, which is the good direction and the reason this row can be
filed at all. Before it, no A/B gate could have seen this.

Not a memory fault: a missed `Drop` BODY is a lost side effect, and the
payload's buffer is still freed (LSan-clean).

WHERE TO START: `callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` / the method path at
`method_call.rs:7196` is where the caller decides whether to keep its own
payload-bodies walk for a method argument. The value-enum twin working means
the plumbing is right and something in the `Option` leg of the METHOD index
shift (the receiver occupies slot 0 for `fn_param_ref` but not in the AST --
the `ast_i` adjustment `callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` documents) is
answering differently than for a user enum.

CORRECTION 2026-08-29 -- THIS ROW'S MEASUREMENTS ARE SUPERSEDED, and the reason
matters more than the numbers: they were taken while 277621a's method-frame
moved-out ISOLATION was on main, and that isolation was reverted in 1167db7
(B-2026-08-29-9, a high-severity double body it caused). The interpreter
behaviour this row recorded was an ARTIFACT of it.

Specifically, the row states "interp `drop 7` / `v=7` CORRECT" for the `Option`
program and "the VALUE-ENUM twin of the identical program is CORRECT on both
backends". Neither holds now, and neither held before 277621a either --
re-measured at 277621a^ with `git checkout <sha> -- src` and a full rebuild, the
two agree with today exactly. So the isolation briefly made the interpreter fire,
which is what the row caught.

RE-MEASURED on 343cd10, all four surfaces (interp / jit / AOT / AOT with
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), with FREE-FUNCTION oracles added -- they are what fixes one
body as the right answer rather than a preference:

    // payload bound out and NOT returned; `-> i64` so nothing escapes
    method + Option[Res]   interp `v=7`            aot `v=7`             0 / 0
    method + user enum     interp `v=7`            aot `drop 7` / `v=7`  0 / 1
    free fn + Option[Res]  interp `drop 7`/`v=7`   aot same              1 / 1  ORACLE
    free fn + user enum    interp `drop 7`/`v=7`   aot same              1 / 1  ORACLE

So the corrected picture is THREE gaps, not one, and only one of them is a
run-vs-build divergence:

  (i)   method + `Option`, INTERPRETER  -- body missed
  (ii)  method + `Option`, CODEGEN      -- body missed  (the row's original find;
                                           unanimous with (i), so A/B-invisible)
  (iii) method + user enum, INTERPRETER -- body missed  (the divergence)

The row's framing of an "`Option`-specific hole" is therefore half right: the
`Option` leg is missed on BOTH backends, while the user-enum leg is missed on the
interpreter alone. What the two legs share is the METHOD path; what the value-enum
twin actually shows is not that the plumbing is right, but that codegen has one
leg the interpreter lacks.

ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED, recorded so the next attempt does not repeat it. The
interpreter's method frame already owns its owned params since 277621a
(`method_param_drop_names`), and that registration admits only `Value::Struct`.
Extending it to `Value::EnumVariant` -- with the `fn_returns_param_payload`
exclusion B-2026-08-29-9 proved mandatory -- REGISTERS correctly and changes
nothing: instrumentation shows `val=EnumVariant(Option.Some) payload_esc=false`
and the name pushed, yet no body runs. So the frame's `CleanupAction::Drop` does
not walk an enum value's payload bodies, and the registration alone is not the
missing piece. The change was reverted rather than left in as dead weight.

WHERE THE OWNER ACTUALLY IS on the working free-function path:
`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` calls `run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` for a user
enum arg, and that walk is wired into `eval_call` ALONE -- a method frame reaches
no caller-side fire at all (`owned_param_frame_is_method`). Note that walk
explicitly excludes `Option`/`Result` ("Option/Result stay with their own
machinery"), which is consistent with the `Option` leg being missed on both
backends rather than only one.

WHAT CLOSING IT NEEDS: the method path needs the payload walk the free-fn caller
runs -- either by firing it after the method body for owned enum args that do not
escape, or by teaching the frame's drop action to walk an enum payload -- plus
the `Option` leg on the codegen side. The guards are already established and must
be carried over: `fn_returns_param_payload` (the double body of B-2026-08-29-9)
and `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` (B-2026-08-26-9).

Not a memory defect on any leg: bodies only, the payload's buffer is still freed.

SOURCE NOTE: re-measured while picking this row up, after noticing its numbers
could not be reproduced. No code change landed for it.

UPDATE 2026-08-29 (57bfb26) -- THE USER-ENUM HALF IS FIXED; the `Option` half is
what remains, and this row is re-scoped to it.

The gate was `scrutinee_expr_is_consuming` (src/interpreter/pattern_match.rs),
which declines an owned-param scrutinee on the ground that the payload's `Drop`
observability "belongs to the CALLER (caller-retains)". That hand-off is real
for a FREE FUNCTION and vacuous for a METHOD, whose arguments reach no
caller-side fire -- the same asymmetry `owned_param_frame_is_method` already
records for the `let`-destructure gates, and the same one B-2026-08-28-70 turned
on. A method frame's owned-param scrutinee is therefore consuming, and the arm
stash now fires.

MEASURED after, all four surfaces:

    method + user enum   interp `drop 7`/`v=7`   aot same     1 / 1  FIXED
    method + Option      interp `drop 7`/`v=7`   aot `v=7`    1 / 0  REMAINS
    free fn + user enum  1 / 1   unchanged (the oracle)
    free fn + Option     1 / 1   unchanged (the oracle)

The B-2026-08-29-9 boundary was checked rather than assumed: where the arm
RETURNS the payload, the caller's binding owns it and the stash must stay
silent. It does -- the dynamic move-out disarm still retracts it -- so making
the scrutinee consuming does not resurrect that double body. Both shapes are
pinned by the new fixture.

WHAT REMAINS, and it is CODEGEN-side now rather than shared: the `Option`
spelling's body is missed by codegen. The caller arms the payload-bodies walk
(`track_container_elem_bodies_before_own`, src/codegen/stmts.rs) only when the
binding is a tracked VALUE enum; `Option`/`Result` are excluded because they
carry their own payload machinery, which is the same split the interpreter's
`run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` states in prose. So the walk is never armed
for an `Option` argument and the suppressor at `method_call.rs` -- which the
row originally pointed at -- never gets the chance to matter. That pointer was
reasonable and is not where the gap is.

NOTE THE DIRECTION CHANGE, deliberately: before this commit the `Option` case
was an AGREED SILENCE (0 bodies on both backends), invisible to any A/B gate.
It is now a run-vs-build divergence with the interpreter correct. That is the
good direction -- it is what makes the remaining gap reportable at all -- but it
is a NEW divergence and is recorded here rather than left to be tripped over.
Widening the codegen arming to `Option` is a separate slice with this family's
characteristic double-free risk (arm a walk where a second owner already
exists and the leak becomes a double free), so it was measured and left rather
than half-done.

WHAT CLOSING IT NEEDS: arm the payload-bodies walk for an `Option`/`Result`
argument whose payload type carries a user `Drop`, or route that case through
the machinery those types already have. Whichever way, the guards this family
has established must come with it: `fn_returns_param_payload` (B-2026-08-29-9's
double body) and `callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` (B-2026-08-09-15's, already
consulted at both argument sites).

SHA NOTE: this update first cited `f6d1aae`, the commit's identity before a
rebase onto five sibling Drop-family commits that landed while this session
could not push. That SHA is orphaned and unreachable from `main`; the live
commit is `57bfb26`. Worth knowing that `bug-lint.sh` cannot catch this class —
its fix-SHA resolvability check is skipped on the shallow clone these sessions
run in ("WARN shallow clone"), so a stale pointer lints clean.
fix:
FIXED in 28ab271, and the row's own diagnosis was wrong in a way worth recording.

THE ROW SAID the caller arms the payload-bodies walk only for a tracked VALUE
enum, so an `Option` argument never gets one. It does get one. `let b:
Option[R] = Some(..)` registers a `ContainerElemBodies` action at its let site
(stmts.rs, via `emit_optres_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`), and a frame trace
shows that action ARMED and DUE at the call statement in the failing program.
What kills it is that the method path calls
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` on the argument in between, zeroing
the source slot, so the walker reads an already-cleared tag and runs nothing.

The free-function path does not zero, and the reason is a guard it has and the
method path lacked: B-2026-08-06-31's `boxed_struct_binding` carve-out — a
binding whose box carries a user STRUCT interior keeps its cleanup across a
by-value call, because the zero is a MOVE and nothing takes the box over. That
carve-out landed on `call_dispatch.rs` only. Adding it to `method_call.rs` is
the whole codegen fix.

PRECONDITION worth knowing before writing a fixture: the payload must carry
HEAP. With `struct R { id: i64 }` the binding is not in
`boxed_struct_payload_vars`, no zero happens, and the pre-fix compiler is
already correct. A first draft of the fixture used exactly that and passed
against the unfixed compiler; the row's own `Res { id, name: String }` is what
makes it bite.

MEASURING IT AT ALL needed a callee LOCAL between the two candidate firing
points (`let loc = R { .. }` used after the match). Without one, a body fired at
the arm and a body fired in the caller are indistinguishable in the output. Six
free-function cells then fix the oracle unanimously, on all four surfaces: the
argument's payload body fires ONCE, in the caller, AFTER the callee's scope
exit. The rule is that every method cell prints what its free-function twin
prints.

Against that oracle three method cells were wrong, not one:

  method + Option, payload bound out   compiled 0 bodies   (this row)
  method + Option, never matched       compiled 0 bodies   (not recorded here)
  method + enum,   payload bound out   interp fired at the ARM, not the caller

THE THIRD IS 57bfb26's, i.e. this row's own previous update, and it is retracted
here. That commit made a method frame's owned-param scrutinee "consuming" so the
arm would fire, on the premise that a method frame's arguments reach no
caller-side fire. False: a method whose owned enum param is never matched has
always run its body in the caller, on every surface. The fire looked absent
because the callee frame's moved-out mark on its own parameter leaked out and
disarmed a CALLER binding that shared the name — and the probe spelled both `b`.
Two defects cancelled. Rename the caller's binding to `carg` and the same
program printed the body TWICE on the interpreter against once compiled. So
57bfb26 traded a missed body for a name-dependent double one, and the reason it
measured clean is that it had neither a rename control nor a placement marker.

CONVERGENCE WITH b04cf10. That commit (B-2026-08-29-11) landed on this exact
code minutes before this one and reached the same leak from the other side. Its
frame isolation is kept unchanged and its fixtures still pass. What is narrowed
is `record_method_arg_moves`, which stood the caller down on EVERY by-value
argument on the rule "if the payload dies inside, the frame's arm stash fires
it". That holds only when there IS an arm. Measured on main at b08caec: a method
that never matches its owned enum param went from one body to ZERO, against one
on all three compiled backends — a missed body introduced by that commit and
invisible to its probes, which all match on the param. The stand-down now
applies only where the value LEAVES the callee: `fn_returns_param`,
`fn_returns_param_payload`, or `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` (that row's
own repro, `add(r)` pushing into `self.xs`, is the third). b04cf10 tried this
narrowing and rejected it for double-firing the dies-inside case; it double-fired
because the arm was still firing too, and with 57bfb26 reverted the caller is the
single owner.

RESULT: all 20 probe cells agree across interp / JIT / AOT / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0,
and every method cell is byte-identical to its free-function twin. Valgrind-clean
throughout; this was a bodies-only defect on every leg, as the row said.

Fixtures RED-verified against the pre-fix compiler --- codegen
`mid9 dR9 v8 post` (the missing body) and interpreter
`dR8 mid9 dR9 dR8 v8 post` (the double) --- each shape carried in both namings,
because until now a rename was a semantic change.

RESIDUALS split out rather than folded in, both agreed-wrong on all four
surfaces and so not A/B divergences: B-2026-08-29-48 (an assign-then-return arm
doubles the payload body) and B-2026-08-29-49 (a payload moved into a `mut ref`
param runs one body too many).

title: The interpreter's method frames SHARE one moved-out name space, so one method's legitimately-marked param suppresses an unrelated LATER method's identically-named param and loses its `Drop` body -- the accidental leak cannot simply be closed, because it is currently the ONLY thing suppressing a payload bound out of an owned enum param and returned (B-2026-08-29-9)
detail:
The trade B-2026-08-29-9 was forced to make, recorded so the next attempt starts
from the measurements rather than re-deriving them.

THE MISSED BODY. The interpreter's `moved_out_*` sets are keyed by BINDING NAME
with no frame qualifier, and the METHOD path does not isolate a callee frame's
copies the way `eval_call` does for a free fn. So a mark one method makes
outlives its frame and suppresses an unrelated later frame that happens to reuse
the name:

    struct Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }
    impl Box3 { fn add(mut ref self, r: R) { self.xs.push(r); } }
    struct G2 { n: i64 }
    impl G2 { fn eat(ref self, r: R) -> i64 { 3 } }

      let mut bx = Box3 { xs: Vec.new() };
      bx.add(R { id: 11 });  println("added");
      let g = G2 { n: 1 };  let v = g.eat(R { id: 12 });  println(f"{v}")

        interp:            drop 11 / added / 3               `drop 12` LOST
        jit / build / np:  drop 11 / added / drop 12 / 3      correct

`add`'s `r` is LEGITIMATELY marked -- it moves into `self.xs` -- and that mark is
what suppresses `eat`'s unrelated `r`. RENAMING the second param to `q` makes the
body reappear, which is how the name-keying was identified rather than inferred.

WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY FIXED, and this is the whole point of the row. 277621a
isolated the method frame's sets, which closes exactly this. It also caused a
DOUBLE `Drop` body (B-2026-08-29-9, high): nothing inside a callee marks an
escaping payload moved-out, so a method that returns a payload bound out of its
owned enum / `Option` param relies entirely on the CALLER's mark leaking in under
the shared name. Isolating removed the leak and with it the only suppression that
shape had. Bisected within the commit: with the param registration disabled the
double body remained, with the isolation disabled it went away.

So the accidental leak is LOAD-BEARING, and the isolation was reverted because a
missed body is strictly less harmful than a double one.

WHAT CLOSING IT NEEDS, in order -- the isolation is the second step, not the
first:

  1. Make the CALLEE mark an escaping payload moved-out itself, inside its own
     frame, so the shape does not depend on a caller mark arriving through a name
     collision. `fn_returns_param_payload` already answers the static question
     (verified true for the shape by instrumentation); what is missing is a
     registration, not a predicate.
  2. Only then re-land the frame isolation, which at that point removes a genuine
     leak rather than a load-bearing one.

Attempting (2) alone is exactly what regressed, and adding
`fn_returns_param_payload` exclusions to the frame's OWN registration is NOT (1)
-- that was tried and changed nothing, because the registration was already
declining for this shape.

NOT a memory defect: bodies only, LSan-clean, consistent with the rest of this
family. The codegen side is correct throughout, so the whole cost is a
run-vs-build divergence.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while reverting B-2026-08-29-9. The fixture case that
covered this in the interpreter suite was removed rather than re-pinned to the
regressed output; the codegen twin keeps its case, so the divergence has a
one-sided pin until this row closes.

UPDATE 2026-08-29 (64e3e90) -- ONE NARROW LEG CLOSED, THE ROW'S OWN SHAPE
UNCHANGED. B-2026-08-29-21 admitted a new kind of mark into this shared set: once
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` started accepting the `return` spelling, a
method's escaping path disarms its own param by marking it, and that mark outlived
the call and silenced the NEXT call's identically-named param. Measured: one
method called three times, escaping in the middle, ran `drop 4` / `drop 3` /
nothing in the interpreter against `drop 4` / `drop 3` / `drop 5` on all three
compiled backends.

64e3e90 saves and restores ONLY the membership of the names in
`method_param_drop_names`, rather than isolating the whole set. That deliberately
sidesteps the trade this row exists to record: a caller's PRE-EXISTING mark on one
of those names is preserved exactly, so the load-bearing leak B-2026-08-29-9
measured is untouched, and what is undone is only a mark the frame itself
introduced.

THIS ROW'S CANONICAL REPRO STILL DIVERGES, verified at 64e3e90: `Box3.add(r)`
followed by `G2.eat(r)` prints `drop 11` / `added` / `3` in the interpreter
against `drop 11` / `added` / `drop 12` / `3` compiled. `add`'s `r` moves into
`self.xs`, so it is excluded from `method_param_drop_names` by
`fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` and the narrow save/restore never sees it.
The two-step plan above is unchanged and is still what closing this needs.
fix:
Fixed in b04cf10. Two changes, both in the interpreter's method-call path, and
they are one idea: a method frame owns its arguments, so its marks belong to it
and the caller must stand down.

WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT AND WHAT IT GOT WRONG. The missed body is exactly as
described -- `Box3.add(r)` then `G2.eat(r)` printed `drop 11 / added / 3` in the
interpreter against `drop 11 / added / drop 12 / 3` on all three compiled
backends, and the frame isolation closes it. The two-step plan was wrong, and
so was the premise under it.

THE LEAK WAS NOT LOAD-BEARING. It was load-bearing for one SPELLING. The row
records that isolating the frame turns the escaping shape -- a method returning
a payload bound out of its owned enum param -- into a double `Drop` body, and
that this is why 277621a was reverted. That measurement was taken on
`test_method_returned_enum_param_payload_body_runs_once`, whose caller writes
`let b: Box2 = ...; t.take(b)` -- the same name as the callee's param. Rename
the caller's binding to `qq`, change nothing else, and the double body is
already there with the leak fully intact:

    impl T { fn take(ref self, b: Box2) -> Res
             { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } .. } } }

      let b  = Box2.Full(Res { id: 7, .. }); t.take(b)    got 7 / drop 7 e7
      let qq = Box2.Full(Res { id: 7, .. }); t.take(qq)   drop 7 e7 / got 7 / drop 7 e7

measured on main at 0814cc2, against `got 7 / drop 7 e7` on all three compiled
backends for both. So the leak was not protecting the shape; it was protecting
the shape's fixture. Step 1 of the plan -- "make the callee mark an escaping
payload moved-out itself" -- was aimed at the wrong side of the call.

WHAT ACTUALLY OWNS THE SUPPRESSION. Instrumenting the firing point rather than
reasoning about it: in the renamed program the extra body fires on `qq`, the
CALLER's binding, through `fire_due_drops` -> `run_enum_payload_user_drops`
after the call returns. The caller was still walking a payload it had handed
away. Nothing on the method path had ever marked it -- the callee's own mark
leaked back OUT under the shared name and did the job by accident.

That gap has a name already. `eval_call` has run `record_passthrough_arg_moves`
for free fns since B-2026-08-02-23, and codegen has had the METHOD twin since
B-2026-08-09-15 (`callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` in its own `method_call.rs`).
The interpreter's method path had neither.

The method rule is WIDER than the free-fn one, and this is the part worth
keeping. A free fn follows caller-retains: its owned-param scrutinee is
non-consuming and the CALLER fires the payload body, so only the passthrough
subset may be disarmed. A method frame is declared to own its arguments
(`owned_param_frame_is_method`, B-2026-08-29-10), so for a method the caller
stands down on EVERY by-value arg. One rule covers both destinations: if the
payload dies inside, the frame's arm stash fires it; if it is handed back, the
caller's binding for the RESULT fires it. Narrowing this to the passthrough
subset was tried first and fails `payload-dies-inside-method` with a double
body, which is the fixture case that pins the width.

So the fix is `record_method_arg_moves` (new, `eval_call.rs`) called after the
frame restore, plus the blanket isolation in `method_call.rs` -- 277621a's
change, re-landed now that the caller no longer depends on its leak. Borrowed
params are excluded (a view is not a move) and `record_container_move_source_name`
carries the existing narrowing, so an own-`Drop` struct param stays armed
because a by-value struct param is entry-copied and the two frames hold
genuinely distinct values.

THREE THINGS THE PLAN CALLED FOR THAT MEASURED UNNECESSARY, each built and then
removed after the probes showed it changed nothing:

  - a per-frame set of params whose payload escapes (`fn_returns_param_payload`),
  - a carve-out standing the arm stash down for those params, and
  - a callee-side mark disarming the param's own payload walk.

The first two are what the row's step 1 asked for. They are redundant because
B-2026-08-28-51's per-path flag already disarms the stash at the `return` that
hands the payload out -- and it does so PATH-SENSITIVELY, where a
`fn_returns_param_payload` gate is conservative-true and would have lost the
body on a run that took a non-escaping arm. Not adding it is strictly better,
not merely smaller. The third is redundant because
`disarm_moved_out_enum_payload` already retracts the param's walk whenever an
arm consumes. Removing all three took the diff from 231 lines to 106.

64e3e90's narrow save/restore of `method_param_drop_names`' membership is
subsumed and gone: restoring the whole set undoes every mark the frame made,
that one included.

FIXTURES. `test_method_frame_marks_do_not_leak_across_frames` (interpreter, 8
cases) and `e2e_method_frame_marks_do_not_leak_across_frames` (codegen, 6). The
interpreter test is RED on 0814cc2 at the row's own repro. The codegen twin
passes before and after by design -- the whole defect was interpreter-side, so
its job is to pin the oracle. It carries the renamed spelling too, because the
compiled answer being name-independent is what made the interpreter's
name-dependent one a divergence rather than a convention. Controls: both free-fn
oracles (caller-retains must not move onto the method rule), the
payload-dies-inside case (which pins the caller stand-down's width), and the
renamed twin of the row's own repro (which passed before the fix, so it proves
the gap was closed rather than relocated).

`test_method_returned_enum_param_payload_body_runs_once`'s doc-comment is
rewritten in place: it asserted the leak was load-bearing and the fix was a
revert, and both halves are now known to be false.

Gates: fmt clean, both clippy legs clean, full `--features llvm` suite green.
No ASAN fixture -- the change is interpreter-only and the interpreter frees
nothing, consistent with the row's own "bodies only, LSan-clean".

title: A `Tensor` FIELD OF A STRUCT IS NEVER FREED -- 72 B per struct, with no ref return, no method and no read of the field anywhere; the parent row's "tensor ref-return" framing is wrong, and a one-line classifier arm would convert the leak into a DOUBLE FREE because there is no tensor deep-copy peer (measured: 9 allocs on a by-value pass vs a `Vec` field's 10)
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-28-74, whose "leak 2" this is. That row framed it as "a
tensor ref-return (72 B), in asan_tensor_ref_return_borrow_clean" and left it
uninvestigated. The framing is wrong in the same shape as that row's leak 1
was: neither the ref return, nor the method, nor any READ of the field is part
of the trigger.

MINIMIZED. Measured under plain valgrind at -O0 (see the observability note
below for why -O0), allocs/frees:

    struct Holder { t: Tensor[i64, [2, 3]] }
    fn main() {
        let h = Holder { t: Tensor.from([[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60]]) };
        println(7);                      // the tensor is never touched
    }                                    9/8, 72 B definitely lost

  and the controls that localize it:

    let t = Tensor.from(...); println(t[1, 2]);        9/9   clean
      -- a BARE tensor binding is freed; the field is not
    struct Holder { t: Tensor, n: i64 }, read only `n`  9/8   72 B lost
      -- an unrelated second field changes nothing
    fn mk() -> Holder { ... }  let h = mk();           9/8   72 B lost
      -- also leaks when the struct is returned from a fn
    fn firstrow(t: ref T) -> ref T  over a BARE tensor  9/9   clean
      -- the free-fn `ref Tensor` return the row blamed is CLEAN on its own

So: a `Tensor` FIELD of a struct is never freed, full stop. The original
fixture reached it only because `struct Holder { t: Tensor }` happened to be
how it held the tensor it was taking a view of.

MECHANISM. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis`'s field classifier (the `FieldDrop`
enum in `src/codegen/synth_drop.rs`) has no Tensor arm, so a `Tensor` field
classifies as `FieldDrop::None` and the drop walk skips it. The block itself is
a plain null-guarded `free` of the `[rank][dims][data]` pointer — the same one
`CleanupAction::FreeTensor` emits for a bound tensor — so the emit side is
trivial. Note the classifier already carries `FileHandleClose` (B-2026-08-09-20)
and `GpuBufferFree` (GPU-SLIP-4b-4), each added when that particular opaque
handle was separately discovered to leak as a field; `Tensor` is the next one
of that family. `Column` / `DataFrame` fields were NOT checked here (no
`Column.from` constructor to build one with) and are neither claimed clean nor
claimed broken.

A ONE-LINE CLASSIFIER ARM IS NOT ENOUGH, and the reason is measured rather than
argued. There is no tensor deep-COPY peer, so adding the drop alone converts
this leak into a double free:

    struct Holder { t: Tensor[i64, [2, 3]] }
    fn take(h: Holder) -> i64 { ... }   let h = ...; take(h);    9 allocs
    let g = h;                                                   9 allocs
    struct Holder { t: Vec[i64] }  (the CONTROL)                10 allocs

The Vec-field control allocates one MORE block on the by-value pass — the
buffer is cloned — which is exactly why a `Vec` field can safely carry a drop.
The tensor block is not cloned in either spelling, so a drop registered on both
`h` and `g` (or on `h` and the callee's copy) would free one pointer twice.
`synth_drop.rs`'s existing `Vec[Tensor]` field arm records this same constraint
in prose: it deliberately scopes itself to the SHARED-struct drain and declines
to widen `elem_te_needs_direct_recursive_drain`, because that predicate also
gates the owned-param deep-copy and "there is no tensor-element clone, so
widening it would unbalance copy-depth vs drop-depth (double-free) for a VALUE
struct field."

So the fix is a PAIR — a tensor field clone on the copy path and a tensor field
drop on the drop path, landed together — or a narrower scoping that provably
never sees a copied struct. That is why this is split rather than folded into
B-2026-08-28-74's fix.

OBSERVABILITY. Reproduces under plain valgrind, and under LSan only with
`LSAN_OPTIONS=use_stacks=0`, which is how the parent row found it. It is an
-O0-visible leak: at -O2 LLVM promotes the never-freed block away and every
spelling above reports clean. The parent row's "-O2 sweep shows ZERO real
leaks" carries the same caveat for the same reason. The named fixture
(`asan_tensor_ref_return_borrow_clean`) asserts CLEANLINESS and passes today,
so nothing flags this.
fix:
FIXED by 4b0a560.

ROOT CAUSE. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis`'s field classifier (the `FieldDrop`
enum in `src/codegen/synth_drop.rs`) had no `Tensor` arm, so a `Tensor` field
classified `FieldDrop::None` and the drop walk skipped it. Added
`FieldDrop::TensorFree`, which frees the `[rank][dims][data]` block exactly as
`CleanupAction::FreeTensor` already does for a BOUND tensor: null-guard, free,
null the field.

THE FIX IS A PAIR, AND THE SECOND HALF WAS FOUND BY MEASUREMENT. A `"Tensor"`
arm in `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` nulls the source on a whole-struct move.
Without it, adding the drop CONVERTS THIS LEAK INTO A DOUBLE FREE: `let g = h;`
arms both structs against one block, measured as `free(): double free or
corruption` and, under ASAN, an `attempting double-free` abort. That is the
same field-the-drop-frees-but-the-move-does-not-neutralize shape the Map/Set
arm beside it exists to prevent, and it is why the two halves land together.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW AS FILED. The row said a one-line classifier arm would
double free "because there is no tensor deep-copy peer (measured: 9 allocs on a
by-value pass vs a `Vec` field's 10)", and concluded the fix must be a
COPY/drop pair. The allocation counts are right; the conclusion drawn from them
was wrong. A tensor-bearing struct is NOT copy-supported —
`field_copy_supported` has no `Tensor` arm and falls to its `_ => false`
default — so a by-value struct param stays CALLER-RETAINS and the callee never
mints a second owner. The missing clone is therefore not a hazard; it is the
reason there is no hazard on that path. This is the established
not-copy-supported-but-still-dropped pairing a `Map`/`Set` field already has,
which `struct_heap_copyable_or_handle` documents as the two properties coming
apart. Verified against a live `Map`-field control whose numbers are
byte-identical across this change, and pinned by the `tensor-field-by-value-param`
row, which is clean before AND after.

The row's inference came from `synth_drop.rs`'s `Vec[Tensor]` field comment,
which declines to widen `elem_te_needs_direct_recursive_drain` for exactly the
copy/drop-balance reason quoted. That comment is about the SHARED-struct drain,
where the predicate it names also gates the owned-param deep-copy. It does not
transfer to a plain value struct's field classifier, which has no such coupling.
The real hazard was on the MOVE path, not the copy path.

RE-SCOPE (as filed, and confirmed). Not a "tensor ref-return" — the parent row
B-2026-08-28-74's framing for its leak 2. No ref return, no method, and no read
of the field are needed; `asan_tensor_ref_return_borrow_clean` reached the leak
only because it held its tensor in a `struct Holder`. That fixture asserts
cleanliness BY NAME and passed throughout: 12 allocs / 11 frees with 72 B lost,
now 12/12 clean.

MEASURED, valgrind at -O0, allocs/frees before -> after:

  field never read (`println(7)`)          9/8  -> 9/9
  field read (`h.t[1, 2]`)                 9/8  -> 9/9
  second scalar field, only `n` read       9/8  -> 9/9
  struct returned from a fn                 9/8  -> 9/9
  the move `let g = h;`                    9/8  -> 9/9
  by-value param `take(h)`                 9/8  -> 9/9
  `Vec[H]` of two                          11/9 -> 11/11
  `Map`-field control (all 3 spellings)    unchanged

Thirteen shapes, valgrind ERROR SUMMARY 0 on every one, and output
byte-identical across interpreter, JIT, AOT and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

OBSERVABILITY, and why the test fixtures look the way they do. As the row
noted, this is -O0-visible: at -O2 LLVM promotes the never-freed non-escaping
block out of existence and every FLAT spelling above drops to 8 allocations and
reports clean. `memory_sanitizer` compiles at -O2 (`read_opt_level_env`
defaults to `2`), so both load-bearing rows of
`asan_struct_tensor_field_is_freed` hold their tensors in a `Vec`, where the
optimizer cannot promote them. Verified non-vacuous against BOTH halves: with
no fix the `tensor-field-in-vec` row reports 144 B leaked in 2 allocations;
with the drop arm alone `tensor-field-moved-into-vec` aborts on a double free
while the flat move row still passes. The flat rows are kept as the minimal
statements of the bug and do their work under the -O0 leg
(`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`), with a deliberately low `min_allocs` floor.

NOT INVESTIGATED: `Column` / `DataFrame` fields. The classifier's history
(`FileHandleClose`, B-2026-08-09-20; `GpuBufferFree`, GPU-SLIP-4b-4; and now
`TensorFree`) is one opaque-handle field type discovered leaking at a time, so
a sweep of the remaining ones is worth someone's time. No `Column.from`
constructor exists to build a fixture with, so nothing is claimed either way.

title: A `match` ARM THAT YIELDS A SHARED CHILD INTO A BINDING LEAKS THAT CHILD'S BOX -- `let keep = match t { Bin(l, r) => l };` over a recursive `shared enum` is 11 allocs / 10 frees, 32 B lost, IDENTICALLY for a bound and a fresh-temp scrutinee, so it is not a freshness bug; returning the child instead of binding it is clean
detail:
Found while adversarially probing B-2026-08-28-74's fix (the fresh-temp
shared-enum scrutinee release) for a double free it might introduce. It does
not introduce one; this leak was already there, and it is NOT a fresh-temp
issue at all — the bound-scrutinee spelling leaks identically.

REPRO. Measured under plain valgrind at -O0, allocs/frees (see the
observability note):

    shared enum E { Num(i64), Bin(E, E) }
    fn mk() -> E { return E.Bin(E.Num(1), E.Num(2)); }
    fn main() {
        let t = mk();
        let keep = match t { Num(a) => E.Num(a), Bin(l, r) => l };
        println(9);
    }                                          11/10, 32 B definitely lost

`mk()` builds three boxes: the outer `Bin` and its two `Num` children. The arm
yields the CHILD `l` into `keep`, so `keep` and the outer box's tag-switched
drop walk are both owners of that child's box, and exactly one of the three
boxes goes unfreed.

NOT A FRESHNESS BUG — this is the part worth recording, because the shape looks
like B-2026-08-28-74's and is not. Every spelling below is 11 allocs / 10 frees
and loses the same 32 B, on both the pre- and post- trees of that row's fix:

    let t = mk(); let keep = match t { … => l };   bound scrutinee, result bound
    let t = mk(); let keep = match t { … => l };   + never reading `keep`
    let keep = match mk() { … => l };              fresh-temp scrutinee (post-fix)

The third row is the one -74's fix moved: it was 11 allocs / 8 frees before, so
that fix recovered two of the three missing frees and brought the fresh-temp
spelling to exactly its bound oracle. The residue is this row, and it sits
below both spellings equally.

WHAT IS NOT AFFECTED, which localizes it to the BINDING of the arm's value:

    fn pick() -> E { return match mk() { … => l }; }  … 11/11 clean
      -- handing the child out as a RETURN is clean (post -74 fix)
    match mk() { A(s) => s, … }  over `shared enum W { A(String) }`
      returned from a fn                              … 10/10 clean
      -- a heap STRING payload out of the same shape is clean

So the leak needs all of: a `shared` enum, an arm yielding a `shared` CHILD
(not a Vec/String/Map payload — those are covered by
`suppress_shared_enum_payload_move_out`, which only zeroes `VecOrString` and
`Map`/`Set` field words), and the match's VALUE bound to a local rather than
returned. A shared child field has no `cap` word to zero, so that suppressor
has nothing to disarm and the accounting has to come from an inc/dec instead.

LIKELY DIRECTION, unverified: the bare-`shared` peer of the arm-tail retain.
`control_flow_match.rs`'s arm-tail block already carries an
`Option[shared T]` arm-tail retain (B-2026-08-26-12) next to
`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`; there is no bare `shared T` sibling, and
the missing +1 on the escaping child is consistent with one box surviving with
a count that never reaches zero. That is a guess from the neighbourhood, not a
measurement -- the next session should instrument before acting on it.

OBSERVABILITY. -O0 only under valgrind / LSan-with-`use_stacks=0`; at -O2 LLVM
promotes the unfreed box away and every spelling reports clean, the same caveat
B-2026-08-28-74 carries. A regression test for this must therefore use a
RECURSIVE shared enum built recursively (the one shape -O2 cannot elide), which
this repro already is.
fix:
FIXED by 9e337a9.

ROOT CAUSE, and it REFUTES THIS ROW'S OWN FILED HYPOTHESIS. The row guessed
"the bare-`shared` peer of the arm-tail retain ... there is no bare `shared T`
sibling" of `share_option_shared_ref_for_arg`, and flagged that as a guess from
the neighbourhood to be instrumented before acting on. Instrumented: the retain
is NOT missing. It fires, from `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex`'s shared
arm, and it is correct — that arm balances the source's queued dec with a fresh
inc so, in its own words, "consumer becomes the new owner of one ref".

What was missing is the OTHER half: the `block_tail_shared_transfer` record the
let site reads to SKIP its own receive-inc. That record existed for a direct
`shared` FIELD tail (B-2026-08-06-15, whose doc states the rule exactly: "the
consumer's let-site receive-inc must then be skipped -- taking one would strand
the count at 1 forever") and for nothing else. So a bound shared identifier
handed out of a match arm or an if-let branch got counted twice.

Traced at the emission sites for `let keep = match t { .. Bin(l, r) => l };`
over a recursive `shared enum`:

  INC  l    pattern_binding.rs:256   arm binding receives      rc 1 -> 2
  INC  l    call_dispatch.rs:8464    the TRANSFER retain       rc 2 -> 3
  DEC  l                             arm scope exit            rc 3 -> 2
  INC  keep stmts.rs:6079            the let receive-inc <<<   rc 2 -> 3
  DEC  keep                          keep's scope exit         rc 3 -> 2
  DEC  t                             parent's drop walk        rc 2 -> 1

Three incs, three decs, birth 1 -> final refcount 1, one box lost. The RETURN
spelling is clean for a reason that made this look like a freshness bug when it
is not: a `Call` RHS is fresh, so the caller's binding never takes the extra
inc. The BOUND and FRESH-TEMP scrutinee spellings leak identically, exactly as
the row said.

THE FIX IS RECORDED, NOT RE-DERIVED, so the flag and the inc cannot drift
apart. The predicate stays in the one helper all ~87 call sites funnel through
(`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` sets `shared_transfer_applied` where
it emits the inc); only the TAIL sites read it back. Reading it anywhere else
would be wrong: `let x = { v.push(n); other };` applies a transfer for the push
that has nothing to do with what the block hands out.

THREE LEAF SITES need the raise, and the third is the one a narrower fix misses:
`compile_match`'s arm tail, `suppress_block_tail_cleanup`'s Identifier arm, and
an if-let's THEN branch. The last is compiled in `compile_if_let` and reaches
NEITHER of the others -- the same "third leaf hook" gap B-2026-08-27-34 records
for `Option[shared T]`, whose comment sits three lines from where this raise had
to go: `compile_block_with_frame` covers plain `if` and an if-let's ELSE branch,
never its THEN.

A SECOND, DISTINCT CAUSE, which the row did not have. A DISCARDED construct has
no consumer at all, so the transfer inc is never spent -- `match t { Bin(l, r)
=> l };` in statement position leaked the same 32 B for the opposite reason
(too many incs with nothing to take them, rather than one consumer too many).
Both discarding sites now gate the inc on `branch_value_is_owned`, the predicate
the boxed-payload neutralizer a few lines away already uses for "a DISCARDED
match result has no destination at all". Only the shared arm is gated; every
other suppression those calls perform still runs.

The row's scoping also needed widening on two counts, both measured: the
DISCARDED spelling leaks (the row said "the match's VALUE bound to a local
rather than returned"), and it is not enum-specific -- a shared STRUCT child
(`shared enum W { A(N) }`, `shared struct N`) leaks its 16 B box the same way.

MEASURED, valgrind at -O0, allocs/frees before -> after:

  match, bound scrutinee, result bound        11/10 -> 11/11
  ... result bound AND read                   11/10 -> 11/11
  match, FRESH-TEMP scrutinee, result bound   11/10 -> 11/11
  `if let`, result bound                      11/10 -> 11/11
  block-wrapped match, result bound           11/10 -> 11/11
  match DISCARDED                             11/10 -> 11/11
  `if let` DISCARDED                          11/10 -> 11/11
  shared STRUCT child, result bound           10/9  -> 10/10
  child RETURNED (control)                    11/11    unchanged
  arm yields a FRESH value (control)          12/12    unchanged
  shared-struct child returned (control)      10/10    unchanged

ERROR SUMMARY 0 on all eleven, output byte-identical across interpreter, JIT,
AOT and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`. The two controls are the rows that would fail if the
record over-reached and suppressed a genuinely needed inc.

UNLIKE B-2026-08-28-74 AND B-2026-08-29-12, THIS LEAK SURVIVES -O2 on the
recursive shape: measured pre-fix at 11 allocs / 10 frees with 32 B lost at the
level `memory_sanitizer` compiles at. So
`asan_branch_tail_shared_transfer_is_not_double_counted` (8 rows) asserts in the
default suite with no container needed to defeat the optimizer -- verified
non-vacuous, 32 B leaked in 1 allocation on the pre-fix tree. Only the
non-recursive shared-struct-child shape is elided at -O2, which is why the
recursive spine is used throughout.

title: A METHOD that returns its owned param with `return r;` (rather than as a BLOCK TAIL) runs the param's `Drop` body TWICE under codegen for a FRESH-TEMP argument -- interp `got 7 / drop 7 e7` vs aot `drop 7 e7 / got 7 / drop 7 e7`; the block-tail spelling of the identical method is correct on both (277621a fixed that cell and left this one), and both free-function twins are correct
detail:
Sibling of B-2026-08-29-9's matrix, and the cell 277621a did NOT move: measured
identical at 277621a^ and at main, so PRE-EXISTING rather than a regression.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id} {self.name}") } }
    struct T { n: i64 }
    impl T { fn take(ref self, r: Res) -> Res { return r; } }
    fn main() {
        let t = T { n: 1 };
        let r: Res = t.take(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" });
        println(f"got {r.id}");
    }

      interp -> `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`                 CORRECT
      aot    -> `drop 7 e7` / `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`   body twice

THE `return` SPELLING IS THE TRIGGER. The identical method written with a
BLOCK TAIL (`fn take(ref self, r: Res) -> Res { r }`) is correct on both
backends -- and it is correct BECAUSE of 277621a, which fixed exactly that
cell (it doubled under aot before). So the two spellings were both broken, one
got fixed, and this is the leftover.

The free-function twins of BOTH spellings are correct, which is what makes one
body the right answer rather than a preference.

WHY THE TAIL WAS FIXED AND THE `return` WAS NOT, most likely: 277621a's
caller-side stand-down is gated on `fn_always_returns_param` or
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare`. The latter "declines `return`
statements outright" by its own doc (codegen clears its per-path flag at match
arms and block tails but NOT at a `return` operand), and if the former also
reasons over tail expressions then a `return`-only callee is admitted by
neither -- so the caller keeps firing while the result binding also owns the
value. That is a reading, not a measurement; the measurement is the two rows
above.

A FRESH-TEMP argument is what this shape needs. With a NAMED caller binding
the same callee doubles on BOTH backends instead (an agreed double, filed as B-2026-08-29-15) -- so the arg form and the callee spelling are independent axes and
the four combinations do not behave alike.

SOURCE NOTE: found while mapping the method-path ownership matrix for
B-2026-08-29-9.


CORRECTION 2026-08-29 -- MEASURED FURTHER, and the divergence has a sharper
cause than "the aot doubles". Allocation counts under valgrind at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, compiled:

    fresh temp + block tail `{ r }`     12 allocs    1 body
    fresh temp + `return r;`            13 allocs    2 bodies

Same callee semantics, same argument, different SPELLING -- and the `return`
form allocates one more `Res`. That extra allocation is a callee ENTRY COPY the
block-tail form does not make, and the second body is codegen faithfully running
one body per object. The interpreter makes no such copy, which is where the
divergence comes from.
