So the defect to fix is the SPURIOUS ENTRY COPY on the `return` spelling, not
the body count that follows from it: removing a body while its buffer exists
would trade a divergence for a leak. The block-tail spelling of the identical
program is correct at one object and one body on all four surfaces, which is
what shows the copy is unnecessary rather than inherent.

See B-2026-08-29-15's correction for the named-argument half of the same
measurement, where BOTH backends make the copy and the count question becomes a
design question instead.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while picking up B-2026-08-29-15. No code change was
made.


CORRECTION 2026-08-29 (SECOND) -- THE FIRST CORRECTION'S ROOT CAUSE WAS WRONG,
and it argued AGAINST the fix that turned out to be right.

It read the `return` spelling's extra allocation (13 vs 12 under valgrind at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`) as a callee ENTRY COPY, and concluded that "the defect to
fix is the SPURIOUS ENTRY COPY, not the body count", because "removing a body
while its buffer exists would trade a divergence for a leak".

There is no entry copy. Rerun with a drop body that does NOT allocate
(`println("bodyfired")`, a rodata literal), both spellings allocate
IDENTICALLY -- 10 allocs / 10 frees each -- while the `return` form still runs
the body twice. The 13th allocation was the SECOND BODY'S OWN format string:
`f"drop 7 e7"` is 9 characters and the measured delta was exactly +1 alloc and
+9 bytes, which the payload `"e7"` (2 bytes) cannot account for.

So the two bodies ran on ONE object whose single heap buffer was freed exactly
once -- no leak and no double free, which is why valgrind reported 13/13 with
zero errors and nothing looked wrong on the memory side. Removing a body was
therefore safe, and post-fix the `return` spelling measures 12 allocs / 12
frees: the SAME count as the block-tail and free-function forms of the
identical program. A fix that had instead removed an entry copy would have
left the count at 13 minus a payload allocation; a fix that leaked would have
shown frees below allocs. Neither is what happened.

The lesson worth keeping is about the measurement, not the conclusion: an
allocation delta measured with an ALLOCATING drop body cannot distinguish "an
extra object exists" from "an extra body ran", because the body itself
allocates. Isolate by making the body allocation-free before attributing a
delta to the object.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing this row, by re-deriving the measurement rather
than trusting the earlier note.


NOTE 2026-08-29 -- A MINIMAL REPRODUCER FOR B-2026-08-29-11 FELL OUT OF THIS
WORK, recorded here because it is small enough to be worth having.

A composite fixture exercising several methods of one type lost `Drop` bodies
under `--interp` that every compiled backend ran. In ISOLATION each method was
correct on both backends; only the combination diverged. The trigger is the
PARAMETER NAME:

    impl T1 {
        fn take(ref self, r: R) -> R { return r; }                  // returns it
        fn swapout(ref self, r: R) -> R { ...; return R { .. }; }   // param dies
    }

Call `take` then `swapout` and the interpreter loses `swapout`'s body. Rename
ONLY `swapout`'s parameter to `q`, change nothing else, and it is correct --
which is B-2026-08-29-11's shared moved-out name space exactly: `take`'s
legitimate move-out of `r` leaves a mark that a LATER frame's `r` reads as
already moved. Unchanged pre- and post-fix here, so it is that row's defect
and not this one's. `asan_return_spelling_method_param_is_memory_balanced`
names every parameter distinctly on purpose to keep it out of this fixture.
fix:
FIXED by 7df22de, in `src/ast/items.rs`, by admitting a `return`-only callee in
`fn_always_returns_param`'s NO-TAIL arm, which previously declined outright.

The caller-side stand-down asks two predicates and this shape was admitted by
NEITHER. `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` declines `return` statements
outright (its own doc says so). `fn_always_returns_param` declined any body
with no `final_expr`, with a comment saying such a body was "left to the
`return` channel" -- a channel that does not accept it. So the caller kept
firing while the result binding also owned the value. That reading was the
one the row itself proposed, and it holds.

The no-tail arm now admits when THREE conditions hold: the function declares a
return type, at least one visible `return` yields the param, and no visible
`return` fails to. The first two are load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces,
and this was verified by DELETING them rather than argued: a body with no
`return` at all (a unit-returning method whose owned param dies inside) then
reads as "always returns the param" for want of a counter-example, the caller
stands down, and NOBODY owns the body -- measured as `saw 41` / `after` with
the `drop 41` gone, on every backend. That case is pinned in both fixtures,
and it is the ONLY case in either that those two conditions decide; the other
boundary cases are declined by the no-bad-return test alone, so they stay
green with the guards deleted and would not have caught the over-admission.

The two `bad_return_*` walkers are folded into one `return_operands`
collector. The no-tail arm needs two facts about the same set of returns, and
two traversals that must stay in lockstep can drift apart. Folding them also
closed a coverage hole in the old walk, which visited only `Expr` and `Let`
statements: `let ... else { return; }` -- the language's most common bare
`return` -- was invisible to it, as were the assignment forms and `defer` /
`errdefer` blocks. A missed bad return is the dangerous direction now that the
walk is the primary evidence rather than a secondary check. The collector does
not descend into closure bodies, whose `return` returns from the closure.

TWO NEIGHBOURING SHAPES FIXED AS A CONSEQUENCE, both measured pre/post and
pinned as cases:

  - an AGGREGATE return, `return Hh { r: r };` -- an AGREED DOUBLE on both
    backends (so not a divergence, and invisible to the run-vs-build rule)
    now one body, matching its free-function oracle.
  - a GENERIC method with the `return` spelling -- interp 1 / compiled 2,
    now one body on all surfaces.

VERIFICATION: five surfaces per case (interp, jit, build, nopar, build at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`), each against its free-function twin. Fixtures
`e2e_return_spelling_method_returned_param_body_runs_once` (tests/codegen.rs),
`test_return_spelling_method_returned_param_body_runs_once`
(tests/interpreter.rs) and `asan_return_spelling_method_param_is_memory_balanced`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), all RED-verified against the pre-fix compiler.
Gates: fmt clean, clippy clean on BOTH feature legs, 108 default suites plus
codegen 3404 / memory_sanitizer 1310 / par_codegen 270 / interpreter 1819 /
ownership 481 / typechecker 2543 / cli 723 / lib 1374, zero failures.

title: A NAMED struct binding passed by value to a function that returns it runs the `Drop` body TWICE on all four surfaces -- for a FREE FUNCTION as well as a method, and for a block tail as well as `return r;`. NOTE: the row's free-function oracle and its `return`-vs-tail framing are both REFUTED, and the second body tracks a second real allocation (the callee's entry copy), so 'one body is due' is a design question rather than a measured defect -- see the CORRECTION
detail:
Found while mapping the method-path ownership matrix for B-2026-08-29-9, and
the one cell in that matrix where BOTH backends are wrong the same way -- so no
A/B gate can see it and only an absolute expectation catches it.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id} {self.name}") } }
    struct T { n: i64 }
    impl T { fn take(ref self, r: Res) -> Res { return r; } }
    fn main() {
        let t = T { n: 1 };
        let a = Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" };
        let r: Res = t.take(a);
        println(f"got {r.id}");
    }

      interp -> `drop 7 e7` / `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`
      aot    -> `drop 7 e7` / `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`
      AGREE, and both wrong: one `Res` is constructed and one reaches `r`, so
      exactly one body is due.

PRE-EXISTING: measured identical at 277621a^ and at main.

The FRESH-TEMP spelling of the same call (`t.take(Res { id: 7, .. })`) diverges
instead -- interp correct, aot doubling -- and is filed as B-2026-08-29-14. That
pair is the useful part: the same callee, the same one-body answer, and the arg
form alone decides whether the defect is a divergence an A/B gate reports or an
agreement it cannot.

The free-function twin (`fn take(r: Res) -> Res { return r; }` over a named
binding) is correct on both backends, so this is specific to the method path
and one body is the established answer rather than a preference.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ONE SHAPE: this is a worked example of the class the
kata A/B harness is structurally blind to. B-2026-08-28-63 and B-2026-08-28-72
were both found only because something OTHER than parity was looking. A
method-path fix that repairs the divergent cells without an absolute
expectation on this one would leave it silently doubling.

SOURCE NOTE: found while mapping the method-path ownership matrix for
B-2026-08-29-9.

CORRECTION 2026-08-29 -- THE SUPPORTING CLAIM IS REFUTED AND THE COUNT QUESTION
IS NOT SETTLED. Two measurements change what this row says.

(1) THE FREE-FUNCTION TWIN IS NOT CORRECT. The row rests its "one body is the
established answer rather than a preference" on it. Measured on de34d25 and
identically at 277621a^, all four surfaces:

    fn takef(r: Res) -> Res { return r; }
      let a = Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" };  let r: Res = takef(a);
        interp / jit / build / no-par -> `drop 7 e7` / `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`

Two bodies, exactly like the method spelling. So the oracle this row cites does
not hold, and the defect is not specific to the method path.

(2) THE DECIDING FACTOR IS THE ARGUMENT FORM, NOT `return`. Replacing `return r;`
with the block tail `{ r }` changes nothing for a NAMED argument -- still two
bodies on all four -- while a FRESH-TEMP argument with a block tail is one body
on all four. So `return` versus tail is not the axis the row identifies it as;
named-binding versus fresh-temp is.

(3) AND THE COUNT TRACKS REAL OBJECTS, which is why this must not simply be
"fixed" to one. Allocation counts under valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:

    fresh temp + block tail    12 allocs    1 body   (compiled)
    fresh temp + `return r;`   13 allocs    2 bodies
    named      + block tail    13 allocs    2 bodies
    named      + `return r;`   13 allocs    2 bodies

Every compiled case runs exactly as many bodies as there are `Res` buffers. The
extra allocation is the callee's ENTRY COPY, and `call_dispatch.rs` documents
that model in as many words -- "for a struct-literal arg the callee entry-copies
... the copy flows out (freed via the result binding), this drops the original"
-- and reasons explicitly that "the own-wrapper case keeping two bodies is
consistent with its two frees".

So "exactly one body is due" assumes the entry copy is NOT observable through
`Drop`, and the tree has already taken the opposite position. That is a
LANGUAGE-DESIGN question (should a move that is implemented as a defensive copy
run the original's `Drop`?), not a defect measurement, and it is not this row's
to settle unilaterally. Removing a body while its buffer still exists would turn
this into a leak.

WHAT REMAINS GENUINELY WRONG, and is worth a separate look: the number of
OBJECTS depends on the spelling of the callee. `fn take(r: Res) -> Res { r }`
over a fresh-temp argument allocates 12 and `{ return r; }` allocates 13, for
the same callee semantics. The spurious entry copy on the `return` spelling is
the defect here rather than the body count that follows from it -- and it is
also what makes B-2026-08-29-14 a divergence, since the interpreter makes no
such copy.

STILL TRUE AND STILL VALUABLE: the row's wider point stands unaltered. This is a
cell where both backends agree and both are questionable, so no A/B gate can see
it, and only an absolute expectation would.

SOURCE NOTE: re-measured while picking this row up. No code change was made.
fix:
FIXED by baf2338. The row's ORIGINAL claim was right and its own CORRECTION was
wrong: exactly one `Drop` body is due here, and the second one was spurious.

WHAT THE CORRECTION GOT WRONG. It rescued the two-body behaviour by arguing the
count "tracks real objects" -- a callee entry copy -- and warned that "removing a
body while its buffer still exists would turn this into a leak". Its evidence was
an allocation table in which the named spelling allocated 13 against the
fresh-temp's 12. That extra allocation is not a copy of the payload; it is the
SECOND BODY'S OWN FORMAT STRING, which is exactly what `7df22de` had already
recorded when it closed B-2026-08-29-14 ("both spellings allocate identically
there"). A non-allocating drop body settles it, and a large field settles it
beyond argument:

    struct Res { id: i64, xs: Vec[i64] }   // 256 elements
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("d") } }

    named argument   11 allocs, 11 frees, 10,269 bytes   TWO bodies
    fresh temp       11 allocs, 11 frees, 10,269 bytes   ONE body

Byte-for-byte identical. A deep copy of a 256-element `Vec[i64]` cannot hide in
that. One object, one buffer set, freed once, with the body run twice.

The same false premise was written into THREE places in the tree and is corrected
in all of them: `call_dispatch`'s container-only narrowing ("an own-`Drop` struct
param is ENTRY-COPIED by the callee ... Two entry-copied values genuinely
exist"), `record_passthrough_arg_moves`' doc, and `record_method_arg_moves`' doc.

WHAT THE ROW ITSELF GOT WRONG, as its CORRECTION already established and this
re-measurement confirms on all 8 cells: the defect is neither method-specific nor
`return`-specific. Free function and method, `return r;` and block tail, all four
doubled for a NAMED argument and all four were correct for a fresh temp. The
deciding axis is the ARGUMENT FORM alone.

THE FIX. `fn_always_returns_param_bare` (src/ast/items.rs) is a strict sibling of
`fn_always_returns_param`, sharing its walker with a `bare_only` flag rather than
duplicating it -- the lesson `7df22de` recorded when it folded this family's two
mirrored traversals into one. It drops the aggregate-literal recursion from the
"yields" test, which is the distinction the looser predicate cannot draw: both
`fn take(r) -> Res { r }` and `fn mk(r) -> Bx { Bx { r: r } }` let the value cross
the frame boundary, but only in the first is the caller's result binding THE
ARGUMENT ITSELF. Only that licenses retracting the caller's owner.

Wired into four places, two per backend, so the backends move together:
`record_passthrough_arg_moves` (free fn) and `record_method_arg_moves` (method)
in the interpreter, both routing to a new `record_returned_arg_user_drop_move`
that reuses the existing `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` channel -- the same
own-`Drop` widening B-2026-08-02-22 already applies for aggregate args; and the
argument loops of `compile_call` / the method path in codegen.

A LEAK THE FIRST FORM INTRODUCED, AND WHY THE FINAL FORM DOES NOT. Codegen's
`suppress_user_drop_for_var` retracts the whole `karac_drop_<T>` action, which is
body + fields + MEMORY. Standing the caller down with it took the bare cases from
13 allocs / 13 frees to 12 / 11: the body correctly gone, and a `String` buffer
orphaned with it. So the CORRECTION's *conclusion* about ownership was right even
though its reasoning was not -- the caller's slot is the sole MEMORY owner of a
by-value struct argument, and the result binding does not free it.

`suppress_user_drop_body_keeping_memory` (src/codegen/runtime.rs) therefore
DOWNGRADES rather than removes: the `UserDrop` action's wrapper is swapped for the
field-cleanup-only `__karac_drop_struct_<T>` that wrapper would itself have
called, against the same alloca. A struct with no heap-owning fields synthesises
no such function, and there plain removal is correct. Post-fix the bare cases read
12 allocs / 12 frees, 0 valgrind errors, no definite loss -- the same count as the
fresh-temp control, which is the shape of a removed body rather than a new leak.

A SECOND REGRESSION THE SUITE CAUGHT, AND THE GUARD IT FORCED. Standing the
caller down is wrong when the callee's result is stored BACK INTO the argument's
own binding: `let mut e = mk_loud(7); e = pass(e);`. There `e` does not die at the
call -- it goes on to own the returned value -- so retracting its action leaves
that value with no owner at all. Measured: the struct spelling lost `loud drop` /
`drop 7 l7` outright, and the enum spelling ABORTED before flushing any output.
`DropRc::assign_ident_target` records the bare-identifier target of the statement
being compiled (reset at the top of every `compile_stmt`, so it cannot outlive
it) and `suppress_user_drop_body_keeping_memory` declines on a match. A stale
value there could only make the suppression more conservative -- a kept double
body, never a lost one.

THREE FIXTURE EXPECTATIONS WERE STALE AND ARE CORRECTED, not worked around.
`field-returning-free-fn` and `tuple-returning-free-fn` (tests/codegen.rs) and
the interpreter twin asserted `k8 / dR8 / dR8 / dE / post` -- two payload bodies
for one object -- justified in a comment as "under the entry-copy model `keep`
returns an independent value, so `k` and the arm binding both own one". That is
the same refuted premise. Their own neighbours are the oracle: `field-let-rebind`
and `tuple-let-rebind` run `let m = r;` over the identical object flow and assert
ONE body. Measured with a heap payload, the call form and the rebind form are
both valgrind-clean and balanced (12 allocs / 12 frees and 11 / 11, 0 errors, no
definite loss), and both backends now agree at one body -- so this was an AGREED
wrong count, not a divergence, and correcting it removes an asymmetry rather than
introducing one.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED, and is filed as B-2026-08-29-50 (double bodies) and B-2026-08-29-51 (the block-wrapped self-assignment leak): the AGGREGATE shape
(`fn wrapf(r: Res) -> Hh { Hh { r: r } }`) and the CONDITIONAL callee still run
two bodies for one object. Both are declined on purpose here. The 3-byte definite
leak `call_dispatch`'s note records for the aggregate is real and is what the
strict predicate preserves; the conditional shape is declined by both escape
predicates and its k=true path depends on the caller still firing.

VERIFICATION. RED-verified: all five defect cells print `drop 41` / `41` /
`drop 41` on the pre-fix compiler and `41` / `drop 41` after, on interp, JIT and
AOT alike. The four boundary controls (aggregate, tuple-aggregate, dies-inside,
conditional) are byte-identical before and after, so the change moves only the
bare hand-back. Fixtures in tests/interpreter.rs
(`test_named_arg_returned_bare_user_drop_body_runs_once`), tests/codegen.rs
(`e2e_named_arg_returned_bare_user_drop_body_runs_once`, run under
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`) and tests/memory_sanitizer.rs
(`asan_named_arg_returned_bare_is_memory_balanced`, which pins BOTH directions --
the bare cases balanced and the declined aggregate still owning its buffer, so a
later loosening of the predicate is caught as a leak). The behaviour fixtures
deliberately assert nothing about the aggregate's body count, since that count is
still wrong.

This is the class the row was right to emphasise: both backends agreed, at the
wrong number, so no A/B gate could report it and only an absolute expectation
could.

FIELD NOTE: this row's `class` reads `run-vs-build`, which its own body already
contradicted and this fix confirms — every cell AGREED across interpreter, JIT
and AOT, before and after. `miscompile` is the accurate class. Left as filed
rather than rewritten on close, since the discrepancy is recorded here and
silently editing a taxonomy field is how the field rotted the first time; noted
so a later reader searching `run-vs-build` for real divergences knows why this
one is in the set.

title: A GENERIC method that returns its owned param CONDITIONALLY is wrong in BOTH directions and diverges both ways -- param dies: interp 0 bodies / compiled 1; param escapes: interp 1 / compiled 2 -- and neither side can be corrected alone, because the callee-side flip that would settle it is declined for generics (B-2026-08-28-71)
detail:
The one shape B-2026-08-29-3 could not settle, split out with its measurements
rather than pinned in a fixture to either backend's answer.

MEASURED on 7f5d6f9 (the -3 fix commit), all four surfaces (interp / LLJIT / AOT
/ AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0). Exactly one `R` reaches the caller's binding in
each program, so ONE body is correct in every row:

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}"); } }
    struct G1 { n: i64 }
    impl G1 { fn gm_pick[T](ref self, r: R, k: bool, t: T) -> R
                { if k { r } else { R { id: 99, tag: f"z" } } } }

      g.gm_pick(R { id: 41, .. }, false, 5)   // param DIES inside
        interp   `99` / `drop 99`                      0 bodies for R{41}
        compiled `drop 41` / `99` / `drop 99`          1   CORRECT

      g.gm_pick(R { id: 41, .. }, true, 5)    // param ESCAPES
        interp   `41` / `drop 41`                      1   CORRECT
        compiled `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41`          2

    // the generic FREE-FUNCTION twin, for contrast
      gf_pick(R { id: 41, .. }, false, 5)     0 / 0   both lose it (the
                                                      documented B-2026-08-28-22
                                                      trade for generics)
      gf_pick(R { id: 41, .. }, true,  5)     1 / 1   correct

So the METHOD spelling diverges in BOTH directions, and in opposite senses: the
interpreter under-fires where the value dies, codegen over-fires where it
escapes. The free-function twin is at least self-consistent.

WHY NEITHER SIDE IS FIXABLE ALONE. Codegen's caller fires unconditionally for
this leg, which is right on the dying path and a double body on the escaping
one; standing it down would swap those, not fix them. The static answer cannot
be precise -- which path runs is a runtime fact -- so the resolution is the
callee-side per-path flag (B-2026-08-28-51's), which `compile_mono_function`
declines to install for generics because the mono param slot does not hold what
the bodies-only walker expects (B-2026-08-28-71, measured there as a CORRUPTED
name rather than a wrong count). The interpreter, symmetrically, declines to
claim the param for the same reason B-2026-08-28-70 gave.

THAT REASON IS ITSELF PARTLY REFUTED, and worth recording. B-2026-08-28-70's
interpreter gate declines a generic conditional param on the stated ground that
"codegen's caller keeps firing, so claiming it here would fix the interpreter
alone and turn a shared gap into a run-vs-build divergence". Codegen's caller
does fire -- but the interpreter claiming NOTHING is precisely what makes the
dying direction diverge (0 vs 1). The two do not cancel; the gap was already a
divergence when that comment was written.

A MEASURED CANDIDATE, not applied: removing that interpreter gate (letting the
frame claim a generic conditional param, with the per-path flag disarming on the
escaping tail) would give interp 1 on BOTH paths -- fixing the dying direction
to agree with codegen at the correct count, and leaving the escaping direction
divergent at interp 1 / compiled 2, which is codegen's pre-existing double. That
is a strict improvement on one direction and no change on the other. It was NOT
applied here because it is a partial fix to a shape whose real resolution is
B-2026-08-28-71, and this session had already taken one regression from a change
whose reasoning outran its measurements (B-2026-08-29-9).

WHAT CLOSING IT NEEDS: B-2026-08-28-71 first (the mono param slot, so the
callee-side flip becomes installable for generics), then the caller stand-down
on the conditional leg at BOTH method argument sites -- `method_call.rs` and the
monomorph loop -- exactly as the non-generic path already does. The candidate
above is available as an interim if the divergence proves to matter before then.

NOT a memory defect: bodies only, valgrind-balanced at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` on
the surrounding method matrix.

title: ALL THREE BACKENDS run a match-arm payload's `Drop` body TWICE when the arm REBINDS it to a local that does NOT escape -- `Box2.Full(r) => { let m = r; m.id }` prints `dR1 dR1 v=1` where one body is due; the same arm without the rebind is correct everywhere, and the ESCAPING spelling of this rebind was B-2026-08-29-8 (which DIVERGED, so parity caught it -- this one agrees and parity cannot)
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-8, and NOT that defect. Measured identical before
and after its fix (077a6bd), which is a CODEGEN-only change -- and the
interpreter doubles here too, so it cannot be involved.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum Box2 { Full(R), Empty }
    fn take(o: Box2) -> i64 {
        match o { Box2.Full(r) => { let m = r; m.id } Box2.Empty => { 0 } }
    }
    fn main() {
        let o: Box2 = Box2.Full(R { id: 1 });
        let v = take(o);
        println(f"v={v}");
    }

      interp / jit / aot -> `dR1` / `dR1` / `v=1`     ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong

Exactly one `R` is constructed and nothing escapes the callee, so exactly ONE
body is due. All three backends run two.

THE REBIND IS THE TRIGGER. The identical arm WITHOUT it
(`Box2.Full(r) => { r.id }`) is correct on every backend: `dR1` / `v=1`. So
`let m = r;` inside a match arm mints a SECOND owner of the payload -- `r`'s
registration and `m`'s both fire -- where the arm binding alone had one.

THE AGREEMENT IS THE INTERESTING PART, and it is why this needs its own row
rather than a note on the parent. B-2026-08-29-8 was the ESCAPING spelling of
the same rebind (`{ let m = r; m }`), and it DIVERGED -- interp one body,
compiled two -- so the A/B gate could see it. Take the escape away and both
backends double together, so nothing reports it. The pair is a clean worked
example of the class parity is structurally blind to, alongside
B-2026-08-29-15 and B-2026-08-28-63.

WHERE TO START. The escaping spelling was fixed by retracting the tail
identifier's `UserDrop` in the innermost frame. Here there is no tail
identifier to key on -- the tail is `m.id`, a `FieldAccess` -- so the question
is upstream of that site: why does `let m = r;` register a drop for `m`
WITHOUT retracting `r`'s, when the same statement at the top level of a
function body is an ordinary whole-value move that does disarm its source?
The `let`-site move-suppression path (`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`
and the `UserDrop` sibling around it) is the place to instrument, with the
arm-binding registration in `pattern_binding.rs` as the other end: an arm
binding out of an OWNED-PARAM scrutinee is memory-only under caller-retains,
so `r` should have no `UserDrop` at all -- yet two bodies fire, so one of the
two assumptions is wrong and instrumenting which is the first step.

Not a memory fault: a doubled `Drop` BODY is a repeated side effect, and the
payload here owns no heap (`R { id: i64 }`). A heap-carrying payload should be
checked before assuming the memory side is balanced.

SOURCE NOTE: found as the failing GUARD RAIL while pinning B-2026-08-29-8 --
the assertion was written expecting one body, and it reported two against a
compiler that had just been fixed. Worth keeping as a pattern: a guard rail
that fails on first run is either a wrong expectation or a second bug, and
here the three-way agreement settled which.
fix:
FIXED by 8bc9955 on BOTH backends, by propagating the VIEW-NESS of a payload
bound out of an owned-param scrutinee to a rebind of it.

THE BIND WAS ALREADY RIGHT. Under caller-retains (B-2026-08-01-13) a payload
bound out of an owned param is a VIEW of the callee's entry copy: codegen
registers it memory-only (`track_struct_var`, gated on
`pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`) and the interpreter registers
nothing (`scrutinee_expr_is_consuming` answers false for an owned param). The
CALLER fires the body. What was missing is that the view-ness did not
PROPAGATE: `let m = r;` inside the arm minted a genuinely owned local, which
registered its own body and ran the one the caller was already going to run.

B-2026-08-01-15 ESTABLISHED EXACTLY THIS RULE ONE LEVEL UP -- `let h2 = h;`
over the PARAM ITSELF propagates, and that shape is correct on every backend
(pinned as a control). This row is the same rule for a payload bound out of
the param, and both backends already had the machinery: codegen's
`param_view_locals` (whose doc says "a destructure or match on one is a
param-view bind exactly like the direct param case") and the interpreter's
`owned_param_names_stack`, which B-2026-08-01-15 propagates into directly.
Neither had the payload case. Three inserts, one per binding path.

MEASURED, every shape reduced for the row:

    owned param, `{ let m = r; m.id }`        dR1 dR1  ->  dR1     FIXED
    owned param, `Option[R]` payload          dR1 dR1  ->  dR1     FIXED
    owned param, two levels of rebind         dR1 dR1  ->  dR1     FIXED
    owned param, `if let` spelling            dR1 dR1  ->  dR1     FIXED
    owned param, `while let` spelling         dR1 dR1  ->  dR1     FIXED
    owned param + a SECOND unmatched param    dR1 dR2 dR1 -> dR2 dR1   FIXED (3->2, and 2 is right)
    GUARD local scrutinee + rebind            dR1      ->  dR1     unchanged
    GUARD fresh-temp scrutinee + rebind       dR1      ->  dR1     unchanged
    GUARD rebind ESCAPES as return value      dR1      ->  dR1     unchanged
    GUARD `let h2 = h;` over the param        dR1      ->  dR1     unchanged

THE `if let` LEG NEEDED ITS OWN INSERT, and the `while let` leg a third: they
are separate binding paths in the interpreter, so the `match` spelling went
green while `if let` still doubled. That is the same spelling-dependent split
B-2026-08-28-63 had to close once already for this family, which is why all
three are pinned.

BOTH BACKENDS AGREED ON THE WRONG ANSWER. That is what kept this invisible --
no A/B gate can report a defect both sides share -- and it is why the fix had
to land on both halves in one commit. Measured mid-fix: with only the codegen
half applied, the shape became an interp-vs-compiled DIVERGENCE, which is the
worse failure and exactly what B-2026-08-28-69's principle warns against.

A LEAD FOR B-2026-08-29-11. `tests/interpreter.rs` records that the
interpreter's name-keyed moved-out set leak is currently "load-bearing -- it is
the only thing suppressing a payload bound out of an owned enum param and
returned", which is why 277621a's frame isolation was reverted in
B-2026-08-29-9. This fix suppresses that class on purpose rather than by
accident, so the isolation may now be re-landable. NOT verified here -- that is
-29-11's row and its own measurement.

ONE RESIDUAL, NOT THIS DEFECT: wrapping the rebind into a fresh enum and
re-matching it (`let m = r; let w = W.One(m); match w { W.One(z) => z.id }`)
still runs two bodies for one value, on all three backends, measured IDENTICAL
before and after. Filed as B-2026-08-29-19.

ONE EXISTING PIN CHANGED, deliberately and with the oracle behind it.
`asan_let_aliased_enum_param_payload_frees_once` (B-2026-08-09-16) pinned its
case 4 -- which is THIS row's shape with a heap-carrying payload -- at TWO
bodies, justified as "the callee's param is entry-copied, so caller and callee
hold genuinely distinct buffers ... each buffer runs one body". Its own doc
added that this was "pinned as observed rather than as preferred, so a later
change to that shape shows up here instead of passing silently". It did.

The free-function ORACLE refutes the two-buffer reading. Strip the enum wrapper
and change nothing else about the ownership:

    fn take_keep(p: Res) -> i64 { let k: Res = p; k.id }

Same owned param, same entry copy, same heap payload, same rebind, same
non-escape. Measured with a binary verified newer than the source at each end:

    case 4 (payload rebind)   PRE two bodies   POST one
    oracle (param rebind)     PRE one body     POST one

If entry-copying implied two bodies the oracle would print two, and it never
has. So the expectation is now one, and ASAN is clean on both sides of the
change -- the frees were balanced before and after, so this line was never a
memory question, only a body count.

PINS IN BOTH SUITES, carrying the same cases with the same expected output, and
both RED against the pre-fix compiler. The guard-rail test is red pre-fix too --
on the unmatched-second-param case, which was three bodies before this and is
