both sides, so the output pins are the only signal.

title: THE OUTER-`Result` SPELLING OF THE NESTED-ENVELOPE LEAK: `Result[Option[Wide], i64]` and `Result[Option[String], i64]` still strand the innermost payload's heap on plain scope exit (38 B each), because their `NestedBoxedEnumDrop` DIRECT registration passes `box_contents: None` at the let site so the leaf-drop resolver that fixed the outer-`Option` half has nothing to see
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-2, whose outer-`Option` half is fixed by c876e64.
This is the same defect reached through a different cleanup action, and it needs
work that fix does not do.

WHY THE OUTER SHAPE CHANGES THE ACTION. `Option`'s inline payload area is 3
words and `Result`'s is 5. So in `Option[Option[Wide]]` the inner `Option[Wide]`
(4 words) does not fit and is BOXED -- a `BoxedEnumDrop`, which c876e64 now
resolves a leaf drop for. In `Result[Option[Wide], i64]` that same
`Option[Wide]` DOES fit inline, and only the `Wide` inside it boxes -- a
`NestedBoxedEnumDrop`, a separate action with a deliberately box-only rule.

MEASURED at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 against c876e64 (i.e. WITH the outer-`Option` fix
in), payload runtime-derived via `env.args().len()`:

    Result[Option[Wide], i64]            38 B / 1     still leaks
    Result[Option[String], i64]          38 B / 1     still leaks
    Result[Option[Option[String]], i64]  38 B / 1     still leaks, no arm

    Option[Option[Wide]]                 clean        fixed by c876e64
    Result[Wide, i64]                    clean        flat, always correct

THE BLOCKER IS UPSTREAM OF THE DROP, and it was instrumented rather than
inferred. `track_nested_boxed_enum_var_at_field` takes a `box_contents:
Option<TypeExpr>`, and printing it for `Result[Option[Wide], i64]` shows
`contents=None`. Only the struct-FIELD half of that family carries a contents
type (B-2026-08-12-18); the DIRECT half hardcodes `None` at the let site in
`stmts.rs`. So a resolver keyed on the contents type -- the whole mechanism of
c876e64 -- has nothing to resolve, and widening it alone changes nothing.

WHAT IT NEEDS, in order:

  1. Plumb the contents type through the DIRECT half's registration.
  2. Give the action a leaf drop field, resolved the same way (mutually
     exclusive with the existing narrow `inner_payload_free` arm so the two can
     never both free one interior).
  3. Its own ownership story. The box-only rule exists for a measured reason and
     the arm-bind disarm this family already has
     (`suppress_struct_field_boxed_payload_arm_bind`) is gated on
     `struct_field_boxed_payload_vars` -- the struct-FIELD population -- and
     zeroes the whole box word, which for the DIRECT half would strand the
     ENVELOPE rather than just standing the interior down. The instrument this
     half wants is c876e64's `retract_boxed_leaf_drop_for_consuming_pattern`,
     which clears the interior drop and leaves the envelope free armed.

THE DEPTH RULE FROM c876e64 CARRIES OVER AND IS THE PART NOT TO RE-DERIVE: only
a pattern binding at the OWNING DEPTH retracts (an intermediate envelope binding
does not take the leaf over, and a wildcard names no owner at all), and a
STRUCT/ENUM leaf takes no retraction because an arm binding it gets the header
rather than the fields' heap. Both halves were forced by failing measurements;
see that row.

ONE ADDITIONAL SHAPE IS ALREADY KNOWN TO NEED THE ARM-AWARE HALF, and it is the
counter-example to any unconditional fix here:
`Result[Option[Option[String]], i64]` matched `Ok(o) => .. Some(s) => ..` is
CLEAN today because the arm's binding owns and frees the String. An interior
drop added without the retraction double-frees it -- the same trap that made the
first attempt at the outer-`Option` half abort two existing fixtures.

SOURCE NOTE: found while narrowing B-2026-08-29-2; these are that row's `n01`-`n04`,
`p01`, `p04`, `p09`, `p10` and `z02` probes, the ones that stayed red when every
outer-`Option` shape went green.

CORRECTED 2026-08-29 on the mechanism count: it is TWO, not one. The row was
written from `Result[Option[Wide], i64]` and generalized from there, but
`Result[Option[String], i64]` boxes NOTHING — its `Option` is 4 words and
`Result`'s inline payload area is 5, so the emitted function contains no box at
all and the leak is a missing inline-payload drop rather than a missing box
interior. The step list on the row (plumb `box_contents`, add a leaf drop, give
it an ownership story) is correct for the boxed half and simply does not apply
to the inline one.
fix:
FIXED by c794214.

IT IS TWO MECHANISMS, NOT ONE, and that is the correction the row most needs.
It was filed as a single boxed-payload gap on the strength of
`Result[Option[Wide], i64]`; the emitted IR for `Result[Option[String], i64]`
contains no box anywhere. The difference is pure layout arithmetic, since
`Result`'s inline payload area is 5 words where `Option`'s is 3:

  * `Result[Option[String], i64]` -- the `Option[String]` is 4 words, so it sits
    INLINE and nothing boxes at any level. The Ok payload simply had no drop.
  * `Result[Option[Wide], i64]` -- `Wide` is 7 words, so the `Option[Wide]`
    still sits inline and only the `Wide` boxes. This is the
    `NestedBoxedEnumDrop` half the row described.

HALF ONE, THE INLINE PAYLOAD. `inline_struct_payload_drop` declined an
`Option`/`Result` Ok/Err payload because `type_expr_has_drop_heap` answers a
flat `false` for both. That predicate has 36 callers, so the question is asked
at the one site that needs a different answer rather than changed there --
`inline_struct_payload_drop` has exactly two callers, both in the `Result`
inline registration, so the change cannot reach anything else.

GATED ON THE PAYLOAD NOT BOXING ITSELF, and the gate is the difference between
a fix and a worse bug. `Result[Option[Option[String]], i64]` puts an
`Option[Option[String]]` inline whose OWN payload boxes, so word 1 holds a BOX
POINTER rather than a `{ptr,len,cap}` -- and `emit_option_drop_fn` reads that
overlay directly (its doc says the caller must gate boxed payloads out).
Admitting it freed a pointer as a buffer: measured as an AddressSanitizer
DOUBLE FREE before `boxed_enum_payload_variants(arg).is_empty()` was added.

HALF TWO, THE NESTED BOX. Its DIRECT registration passed `box_contents: None`
at the let site, on the recorded reasoning that "this half NEVER takes an
interior free" because an arm can bind the interior out (`Ok(Some(Some(t)))`)
and owns it. That is true of an arm that DOES bind it and says nothing about the
programs that do not -- construction alone leaks 38 B. What was missing was not
the caution but the instrument, and B-2026-08-29-2 had since built it:
`retract_boxed_leaf_drop_for_consuming_pattern` stands the drop down for exactly
the arms that own the value, so the contents can now be handed over.

THE NESTED FAMILY RETRACTS ON ANY BINDING, not at a measured depth, and the
asymmetry with B-2026-08-29-2's rule is a property of what the source can NAME
rather than a loosening. For a DIRECT box every level between the binding and
the leaf is a `coerce_to_payload_words` envelope the program cannot name, so an
intermediate binding hands nothing over and only a binding at the owning depth
is an owner. For a NESTED box the inline payload IS an `Option`/`Result` the
program names directly: `match vv { Ok(o) => .. }` binds it and `o` carries the
box POINTER with it, so that one binding takes over the box and everything under
it. Measured -- `Result[Option[Option[String]], i64]` matched
`Ok(o) => match o { Some(i) => match i { Some(s) => .. } }` is clean on an
unmodified tree because the arm chain owns and frees the `String`, and keeping
the leaf drop armed there is a double free. Retracting on any binding can only
ever leave the pre-existing leak, never add a free.

ONE MORE GAP FELL OUT, and it is worth naming because it was invisible from the
row: `payload_te` at the boxed let site comes from
`option_generic_arg_type_expr`, which is `Option`-ONLY. A `Result` whose boxed
payload is itself heap-bearing (`Result[Result[String, i64], i64]`) arrived with
no payload type at all and could resolve nothing -- so it leaked even after
B-2026-08-29-2's outer-`Option` fix, through the DIRECT box action. The
resolution falls back to the generic arg the boxed VARIANT names (`Ok` is arg 0,
`Err` arg 1) rather than widening that shared helper, whose other consumers in
the same block are deliberately `Option`-shaped.

MEASURED at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, ASAN + LSan, payload runtime-derived through
`env.args().len()`:

    Result[Option[String], i64]              38 B / 1  -> clean   INLINE half
    Result[Option[Vec[i64]], i64]            80 B / 1  -> clean   INLINE half
    Result[Option[Option[String]], i64]      38 B / 1  -> clean   inline, gated
    Result[Option[Wide], i64]                38 B / 1  -> clean   NESTED half
    Result[Result[String, i64], i64]         38 B / 1  -> clean   DIRECT box
    Result[i64, Option[String]]              38 B / 1  -> clean   Err side

    HAZARDS -- clean BEFORE and after; red only if a retraction stops firing
    `Ok(o)` / `Ok(Some(s))` / the arm chain / the `if let` -- all clean
    AXES -- flat `Result[String, i64]`, flat `Result[Wide, i64]`, a POD payload,
    and an inner wildcard: correct before and after

COVERAGE. `memory_sanitizer::asan_nested_result_payload_frees_its_leaf`,
14 rows, RED-verified against the unfixed tree. `-O0` ONLY, for the reason
`asan_nested_option_envelope_frees_its_leaf_payload` states at length: every
leaking row builds a nested value and drops it, and at `-O2` the local
non-escaping structure is scalarized and the allocation removed outright.
`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` is the gate.

WITH THIS THE FAMILY IS CLOSED. B-2026-08-29-2 fixed the outer-`Option` shapes,
B-2026-08-29-1 the flat `Option`/`Result` reassignment shapes, and this row the
outer-`Result` ones through both of their mechanisms.

title: ALL THREE BACKENDS run a `Drop` body TWICE when a match-arm payload is rebound, RE-WRAPPED into a fresh enum and matched again -- `Full(r) => { let m = r; let w = W.One(m); match w { W.One(z) => z.id } }` prints `dR1 dR1 v=1` where one body is due; the same rebind without the re-wrap is correct (B-2026-08-29-17), and the backends AGREE so no A/B gate can see it
fix:
FIXED by a865ed6. Propagates a param view's Drop-body ownership ACROSS A
VARIANT CONSTRUCTOR, the one move position the caller-retains rule had never
covered.

THE ROW'S FRAMING WAS INCIDENTAL, in both halves, and the measurements are
worth keeping because the title still reads the old way.

  * The REBIND and the SECOND MATCH are red herrings. The whole defect is

        fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let w = W.One(r); 7 }      -> dR1 dR1

    no rebind, no re-match, no enum payload, no `match` anywhere. The row's
    `let m = r; let w = W.One(m); match w { .. }` is that shape with three
    inert decorations on top; `let m = r; let m2 = m; m2.id` (rebind chain,
    no wrap) is correct, and `let m = R { .. }; let w = W.One(m); match w`
    (wrap + rematch, no view) is correct. Only the wrap of a VIEW is wrong.

  * The "WHERE TO START" hypothesis -- that the aggregate/variant-ctor
    move-out retraction may not run for a binding that is a param VIEW,
    "since it may be gated on the binding having a registration to retract,
    and a view has none" -- is right about the mechanism and wrong about the
    consequence. Traced at the registration channel, the three shapes read:

        let m = r            caller __owned_agg_tmp/karac_dropnf_R           = 1
        let w = W.One(m)     m/karac_drop_R RETRACTED by the wrap; w walker  = 1
        let w = W.One(r)     caller __owned_agg_tmp/karac_drop_R + w walker  = 2

    The retraction runs and correctly finds nothing, because a view never had
    a registration. The surplus is not a missed retraction -- it is the
    WRAPPER's `__karac_dropelems_enum_W` walk being armed at all, on top of a
    caller fire that was always going to happen. (`karac_drop_R` vs
    `karac_dropnf_R` differ only in the nested-FIELD step, and `R` has no
    Drop-bearing field, so the caller's fire is one body either way.)

THE RULE. B-2026-08-01-15 established that `let h2 = h;` over an owned param
makes `h2` a view too, and B-2026-08-29-17 that a match-arm rebind of a
payload does the same. A CONSTRUCTOR is the same move one level up: the value
stored into `W.One(..)` is still the caller's to destroy, so the fresh binding
must not arm a walk of its own -- and must itself become a view, or the next
`let w2 = w;` re-arms what the wrap just withheld.

THE FIX, four pieces:

  * `Codegen::expr_is_param_view` (src/codegen/runtime.rs) -- names the test
    the let/assign rebind paths already spelled inline, needed here per
    ARGUMENT rather than once per statement.
  * `Codegen::enum_ctor_payload_bodies_are_caller_owned` -- true when every
    payload the walker would visit is a view. Its per-field admission test is
    character-for-character `emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`'s, so
    "all visited payloads" means the same thing on both sides.
  * The enum let-registration site (src/codegen/stmts.rs) withholds the
    walker and marks the binding a view instead. It also takes the bare
    `expr_is_param_view(value)` case -- see the divergence below.
  * `Interpreter::let_ctor_payloads_are_param_views` (eval_stmt.rs), wired
    into `let_destructures_owned_param`. Its admission test is
    `value_runs_user_drop` over the BOUND value, which is exactly what this
    backend's walker (`run_enum_payload_user_drops_value`) visits. Each side
    asking the question its OWN walker asks is what makes them agree by
    construction; a narrower question here would over-suppress and lose a
    body codegen still runs.

A SECOND DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED: `fn take(w: W) -> i64 { let w2 = w; 7 }`
-- a bare rebind of an owned ENUM param -- was a run-vs-build DIVERGENCE, the
interpreter already at one body and both compiled backends at two. The
interpreter was right; codegen armed a second walker for `w2` because the RHS
is an Identifier, not a Call, so the constructor predicate declined it. Hence
the `|| self.expr_is_param_view(value)` leg. Covered as case 4.

A DIVERGENCE CREATED AND BACKED OUT, recorded because the reasoning is not
obvious from the result: the interpreter predicate initially admitted
`let q = Some(r);` and fixed it to one body -- correctly -- while both
compiled backends stayed at two, because `Option`'s payload TypeExpr is the
enum's own generic parameter, which `emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`
skips, so there is no codegen walker to withhold. A one-sided correction
turns an agreed defect into a run-vs-build split, which is the worse of the
two, so `Option`/`Result` are now excluded on the interpreter side to hold
parity. Pinned at the defect in the interpreter suite so the exclusion is
visible rather than silent.

THE MEMORY QUESTION THE ROW LEFT OPEN IS ANSWERED: ASAN/LSan are clean on a
HEAP-CARRYING payload, before the fix as well as after. Pinned as
`asan_wrapped_param_view_payload_frees_once`, because the obvious reading of
the shape says the opposite -- the callee's `w` and the caller's entry copy
hold the same String buffer, which looks exactly like a double free and is
not one. Severity therefore stays medium: this was only ever a body count.

DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED, and pinned at the defect rather than left to drift:
a MIXED wrap (`W2.Two(r, R { id: 2 })`) shares ONE walker between a view and
a fresh payload, so withholding it wholesale would trade this double for a
MISSING body -- the same severity, the other direction. That needs a per-slot
masked walker (the enum sibling of `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping`).
Struct-literal / tuple / Vec / `Some` wraps double identically and are
untouched here. Both are B-2026-08-29-24, filed with these measurements.

Tests: `test_e2e_wrapped_param_view_payload_drops_once` (codegen, 9 cases, 4
of them guard rails), `test_wrapped_owned_param_payload_drop_body_runs_once`
(interpreter, 9 cases), `asan_wrapped_param_view_payload_frees_once` (2
cases). Both behavioural suites RED-verified against the pre-fix tree.

title: THE `let _ = match …` SPELLING OF A DISCARDED MATCH RUNS NO `Drop` BODY IN THREE CELLS while its call twin (`let _ = mk();`) is correct on both backends -- two cells are agreed-but-wrong and one is a run-vs-build divergence; a different site from B-2026-08-28-69's bare-statement discard, and measured byte-identical across that fix
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-28-69, whose fix covers the BARE-STATEMENT discard
(`match o { … };`) and deliberately does not touch this one. Measured
byte-identical before and after that fix, so this is pre-existing and
independent.

`let _ = <match>` is a different site on both backends: codegen's wildcard-let
arm of `compile_stmt` (gated on `discarded_owned_temp_tail` /
`discarded_unit_variant_tail`, neither of which admits a `Match`), and the
interpreter's `discard_rhs_produces_owned_value`. The bare-statement site got
`discarded_match_value_tail` and the interpreter's `StmtKind::Expr` `Match` arm;
this one got neither.

MEASURED, all four surfaces, with the same `struct R` + `impl Drop` fixture the
parent row uses. Exactly one `R` is constructed and nothing takes it, so the
correct answer is one body in every row:

  let _ = match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { R { id: 0 } } };
      interp silent / compiled silent      AGREED, BOTH WRONG
  let _ = match o { Some(r) => r, None => R { id: 0 } };
      interp silent / compiled dR1         DIVERGENT
  let _ = match n { 1 => { R { id: 7 } } _ => { R { id: 0 } } };
      interp silent / compiled silent      AGREED, BOTH WRONG

  and the control that shows the site works for a non-match RHS:
  let _ = mk();
      interp dR1 / compiled dR1            correct on both

So the wildcard-let spelling of a discarded match is wrong in all three cells
while its call twin is right, and one of the three is additionally a
run-vs-build divergence.

WHY IT WAS NOT FOLDED INTO THE PARENT FIX. The interpreter predicate here
carries a doc contract the parent site does not: "Codegen twin: the same match
in `compile_stmt`'s wildcard-let path; the two must stay identical or the
backends fire on different shapes." Its `ExprKind::Identifier(_) => true` arm is
MORE permissive than codegen's freshness gate, so admitting a `Match` by
recursing through it would fire the interpreter on arm shapes codegen rejects --
re-creating the divergence one spelling over. Any fix here has to decide the
per-arm predicate for both backends at once, which is a separate design
decision from the parent's.

OBSERVABILITY: same as the parent -- memory is balanced in every cell, so only
an A/B output comparison can see this. No ASAN/LSan corpus reaches it.
fix:
FIXED by e88b7bf, for the FRESH-VALUE arms only. Three of the row's cells move
from zero bodies to one on all three backends; the other three do not, and the
reason is a genuine boundary rather than an omission -- see the split below.

THE DEFECT WAS A MISSING LINE, and the row located it correctly. Codegen's
BARE-STATEMENT discard arm has chained three sibling gates since
B-2026-08-28-69:

    let tail = Self::discarded_owned_temp_tail(expr)
        .or_else(|| self.discarded_unit_variant_tail(expr))
        .or_else(|| self.discarded_match_value_tail(expr));      // <-- the third

and its comment states that the two discard spellings "cannot drift apart"
because they share the same `&self` siblings. They had. The WILDCARD-LET arm
chained only the first two, and neither admits a `Match`, so the whole
statement fell through to the general arm and registered no discard cleanup at
all. The fix is that `.or_else` leg plus the matching disjunct in the arm's
guard. The interpreter's `discard_rhs_produces_owned_value` was missing the
same thing -- it had no `ExprKind::Match` arm -- so both backends were silent
together and only an absolute expectation could see it.

MEASURED, before -> after, all three backends, one body due in every row:

    let _ = match n { 1 => { R { id: 7 } } _ => { R { id: 0 } } };   0 -> 1
    let _ = match n { 1 => R { id: 7 }, _ => R { id: 0 } };          0 -> 1
    let _ = match n { 1 => mk(7), _ => mk(0) };                      0 -> 1
    let _ = mk();                             (control)              1 -> 1

WHAT DID NOT MOVE, AND WHY IT IS A SPLIT RATHER THAN A SHORTFALL. The row's
other two cells, plus the enclosing-local boundary, are all arms that HAND OUT
A BINDING instead of minting a value:

    let _ = match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { R { id: 0 } } };    0 / 0
    let _ = match o { Some(r) => r, None => R { id: 0 } };           0 / 1  DIVERGENT
    let r = R { id: 41 }; let _ = match n { 0 => r, _ => R { id: 9 } };  0 / 0

That is exactly B-2026-08-29-5's population -- "a discarded match / if let
whose arm hands the bound payload out as the construct's value" -- reached
through the `let _ =` spelling rather than the bare statement. It is a
different question from this row's: not WHETHER the discard site is armed, but
WHO owns a value the arm took out of somewhere else. The cells are now pinned
as measured in both behavioural suites and cross-referenced there, so -29-5's
fix will show up as those rows failing.

AND THE PERMISSIVENESS TRAP THE ROW WARNED ABOUT IS REAL -- it decides the
shape of the interpreter half. The row noted that
`discard_rhs_produces_owned_value`'s `ExprKind::Identifier(_) => true` arm is
more permissive than codegen's freshness gate, so recursing through a `Match`
with the whole predicate would fire the interpreter on arm shapes codegen
rejects. Confirmed by the second cell above: compiled prints `dR1` there
(through the general match lowering's arm-scope drop, not through any gate)
while the interpreter prints nothing. Admitting a bare identifier at an arm
tail would fix THAT cell and simultaneously break the FIRST one, where
compiled is silent -- moving the divergence one row over at no net gain. So
the `Match` arm peels each arm with `arm_tail_expr` and excludes `Identifier`
explicitly, and the divergence stays put, owned by -29-5.

MEMORY. Balanced before and after, verified rather than assumed: the widened
gate now routes heap-carrying arm values through the discard battery, which
FREES as well as running bodies, so widening it is precisely the change that
converts a leak into a double free if the value was not the discard site's to
own. `asan_discarded_let_wildcard_match_frees_once` pins both directions on a
String payload. Its second case is the enclosing-local boundary, and it is
LSan-CLEAN -- so that cell was never a leak, only a missing body, which is
what distinguishes it from -29-5's String repro and is worth knowing before
anyone fixes them together.

TWO MORE GAPS FOUND WHILE BOUNDING THIS, NEITHER FIXED (B-2026-08-29-25):
the `if` spelling of the same discard is silent in BOTH statement forms -- so
that one predates this row and sits at the parent's site too, not only here --
and a block-WRAPPED match (`let _ = { match .. };`) is missed because
`discarded_match_value_tail` requires the expression itself to be a `Match`
while its two siblings recurse through block wrappers.

Tests: `e2e_discarded_let_wildcard_match_runs_its_drop_body_once` (codegen)
and `test_discarded_let_wildcard_match_runs_its_drop_body_once` (interpreter),
each a row-for-row sibling of the parent row's table with the three moved
cells and the three pinned ones labelled as such, plus both controls; and
`asan_discarded_let_wildcard_match_frees_once`. Both behavioural suites
RED-verified against the pre-fix tree, failing on the fresh-literal row.

title: A NON-GENERIC method whose owned param is returned CONDITIONALLY, with BOTH exits spelled as `return` statements, runs the param's `Drop` body TWICE under all three compiled backends on the ESCAPING path -- interp `got 7 / drop 7 e7` vs aot `drop 7 e7 / got 7 / drop 7 e7`; the free-function twin is correct on every surface, and the DYING path already agrees
detail:
Sibling of B-2026-08-29-14, and the case its fix deliberately does NOT
cover. Measured identical before and after 7df22de, so PRE-EXISTING rather
than a regression from it.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id} {self.name}") } }
    struct T { n: i64 }
    impl T {
        fn take(ref self, r: Res, k: bool) -> Res {
            if k { return r; }
            return Res { id: 98, name: f"e98" };
        }
    }
    fn main() {
        let t = T { n: 1 };
        let a: Res = t.take(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" }, true);   // ESCAPING path
        println(f"got {a.id}");
    }

      interp -> `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`                 CORRECT
      jit    -> `drop 7 e7` / `got 7` / `drop 7 e7`   body twice
      build  -> same as jit
      nopar  -> same as jit
      O0     -> same as jit

THE FREE-FUNCTION TWIN IS CORRECT on all five surfaces (`got 7` / `drop 7 e7`),
which is what makes one body the right answer rather than a preference. The
DYING path (`k = false`) already agrees everywhere at one body for the param
plus one for the replacement, so this is the escaping direction only.

WHY B-2026-08-29-14'S FIX DOES NOT REACH IT, and why widening it would be
wrong: `fn_always_returns_param` requires that NO visible `return` fails to
yield the param, and here `return Res { id: 98, .. };` plainly does not. That
condition is what keeps the caller firing on the DYING path, where nothing
else owns the value -- relaxing it to a union over return sites is exactly the
trade B-2026-08-28-22 was filed for and measured to lose a body. So the caller
must keep firing on both paths, and the escaping path's second owner has to be
disarmed on the callee side instead.

THE CALLEE-SIDE CHANNEL EXISTS BUT DECLINES THIS SPELLING.
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` is the predicate for precisely this
shape -- a param returned on some paths and not others -- and hands ownership
to a per-path flag (B-2026-08-28-51) that disarms on the escaping path. Its
own doc says it "declines `return` statements outright": codegen clears the
flag at match arms and block tails but NOT at a `return` operand. So the
BLOCK-TAIL spelling of this same method is handled and the `return` spelling
is not.

Consistent with that reading, the mixed spelling
`fn take(ref self, r: Res, k: bool) -> Res { if k { return r; } Res { id: 98, .. } }`
is worth measuring as part of any fix: the escaping exit is still a `return`,
so the flag has the same nowhere to clear.

LIKELY FIX: teach the conditional channel's per-path flag to clear at a
`return` whose operand yields the param, the same way it clears at a block
tail -- i.e. the codegen counterpart of the walk B-2026-08-29-14 added on the
predicate side. That keeps the caller firing (so the dying path is unchanged)
and disarms the callee's registration on the escaping path.

The GENERIC version of this shape is B-2026-08-29-16, which is wrong in BOTH
directions and cannot use the callee-side flip at all (B-2026-08-28-71). This
row is the NON-generic one, where the flip is available.

SOURCE NOTE: found as a boundary control while fixing B-2026-08-29-14 --
`c2` in that session's matrix. Confirmed pre-existing by measuring the same
program against a compiler built at that fix's parent.

CORRECTION 2026-08-29 -- TWO CLAIMS IN THIS ROW ARE REFUTED AT HEAD (59df774), and
the scope is wider than "non-generic".

(1) RETRACTED 2026-08-29, same day. An earlier revision of this correction
claimed "the dying path already agrees everywhere" was FALSE, on a measurement of
interp 0 bodies / compiled 1. That measurement was an ARTIFACT of the probe
program, not of the dying path: every callee in it reused the parameter name `r`,
and an ESCAPING call earlier in the same program left a mark in the interpreter's
name-keyed `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` that silenced the later dying call
(B-2026-08-29-11's shared name space). Re-measured with an ISOLATED dying call at
the same commit: `drop 7` / `got 98` / `drop 98` on interp and all three compiled
backends alike. So this row's original claim was RIGHT and the correction was
wrong. Recorded rather than deleted because the failure mode is worth knowing:
a probe that reuses one parameter name across several callees silently couples
its cells, and the coupling looks exactly like a spelling-dependent defect.

(2) "THE GENERIC VERSION OF THIS SHAPE IS B-2026-08-29-16" IS NO LONGER RIGHT, on
two counts. -16's program is the if/else BLOCK-TAIL spelling, not the `return`
spelling, and it is now FIXED on all five surfaces by 907b378. The generic
`return`-spelling method is a distinct cell and it is still broken here -- escaping
gives compiled 2 bodies / interp 1, exactly like the non-generic one this row
covers. Its dying leg, unlike the non-generic one, is CORRECT on both backends
(interp 1 / compiled 1), because 907b378 lifted the interpreter's generic gate. So
the generic and non-generic `return` spellings now differ on the dying path and
agree on the escaping one, and both belong to this row rather than to -16.

(3) THE FREE-FUNCTION `return` TWIN IS NOT A CLEAN ORACLE ON THE DYING PATH. This
row cites the free-function twin as correct, which holds for the ESCAPING path
(`got 15` / `drop o`, all five surfaces, generic and non-generic). On the DYING
path both backends run ZERO bodies -- that is the already-pinned
`return-in-branch-declined` boundary (B-2026-08-28-65 / -52), an agree-wrong cell
rather than an oracle. Use the `match`-spelling free-function twin instead, which
is correct in both directions.

SOURCE OF THE CORRECTION: the 16-cell spelling matrix run while closing
B-2026-08-29-16 -- {method, free fn} x {generic, non-generic} x {`return`, `match`}
x {dying, escaping}. The `match`-spelling method dying cell is its own gap and is
filed as B-2026-08-29-26.
fix:
FIXED in 64e3e90. The row's own LIKELY FIX was right about the mechanism and
wrong about where the work was: it proposed teaching the per-path flag to clear
at a `return` whose operand yields the param. The flag already did.
B-2026-08-28-65 added `guard_user_drop_for_nested_return`, which stores `false`
into exactly that flag at a nested `return`, and `note_escaping_stmt_sites`
already seeds a `return` operand on both backends. What was still refusing was
the PREDICATE: `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` declined the whole function
the moment any `return` mentioned the param (its condition 4), on the stated
ground that codegen "clears the flag at match arms and block tails but NOT at a
`return` operand" -- a sentence that had been true when written and was not any
more.

So the fix is to collect each `return` operand's leaves alongside the body tail's
and run the same yields-bare / yields-nothing / no-other-mention analysis over
the union. Condition 3 still rules out an aggregate-literal escape, now at a
`return` as well as at a tail. It also drops the requirement that the body HAVE a
tail: a function whose exits are all `return` statements has none, which is why
this row's own program could never have been admitted by the old shape of the
code.

MEASURED over a 16-cell spelling matrix -- {method, free fn} x {generic,
non-generic} x {`return`, `match`} x {dying, escaping} -- on all five surfaces
(interp / LLJIT / AOT / AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 / AOT at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0).
The predicate change alone fixed four cells:

    method  + `return` + escaping, NON-generic   compiled 2 bodies -> 1   (this row)
    method  + `return` + escaping, GENERIC       compiled 2 bodies -> 1
    free fn + `return` + dying,    GENERIC       both backends 0 -> 1
    free fn + `return` + dying,    NON-generic   both backends 0 -> 1

The last two are the PARAM analogue of B-2026-08-28-65 / -52, which fixed the
LOCAL spelling; the param one had stayed open behind the same condition 4.

TWO FURTHER CHANGES were needed to land it without trading one defect for
another, and both are worth recording because neither is visible from the row:

(1) THE INTERPRETER NEVER SAW A TAIL-POSITION `return`. In `if k { return r }`
    with no semicolon the `return` is the block's FINAL EXPRESSION, not a
    statement, so neither `note_escaping_stmt_sites` nor the statement-loop
    `record_conditional_move_tail` reached it. Admitting the mixed spelling
    without fixing that ran the body TWICE on the returning path -- `drop a` /
    `got 1` / `drop a`, a double plus a read of the dropped value -- against one
    body on all three compiled backends, whose guard is reached from the `return`
    expression itself and so never had the gap. Seeding and recording on the
    operand at the block-tail site closes it.

(2) A METHOD FRAME'S MARK ON ITS OWN PARAM OUTLIVED THE CALL. Once the predicate
    started admitting these shapes, the escaping path's disarm became a mark in
    `moved_out_user_drop_bindings`, which is keyed by bare NAME with no frame
    qualifier and which the method path deliberately does not isolate
    (B-2026-08-29-9 measured that isolation as load-bearing). The mark then
    silenced the NEXT call's identically-named param: one method called three
    times, escaping in the middle, ran `drop 4` / `drop 3` / nothing in the
    interpreter against `drop 4` / `drop 3` / `drop 5` on all three compiled
    backends. Saving and restoring ONLY these param names' membership -- rather
    than the whole set -- fixes it while preserving a caller's pre-existing mark
    exactly, so the load-bearing leak is untouched. This is a narrow leg of
    B-2026-08-29-11, which stays OPEN: its canonical repro marks a param that
    moves into `self`, a name `method_param_drop_names` excludes, and it still
    diverges at 64e3e90 (verified).

WHAT THIS ROW GOT RIGHT, AND ONE THING IT DID NOT. Its refusal to widen
`fn_always_returns_param` was correct and is untouched -- the caller still fires
on both paths and the callee still disarms per path. Its escaping-path
measurement reproduces exactly. Its claim that the DYING path "already agrees
everywhere" is also CORRECT for an isolated call, and an earlier correction
appended to this row saying otherwise has been retracted -- see the RETRACTION
below.

THE METHOD MIXED SPELLING WAS THE WORST CELL AND NOTHING WAS WATCHING IT.
`impl T { fn take(ref self, r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return r } R { .. } } }`
ran TWO bodies on all five surfaces before this, AGREEING across them, so no A/B
gate could report it; it took an absolute expectation to see. Two fixtures that
pinned the old counts as "NOT FIXED, pinned deliberately" and "the predicate
declines it" now assert the correct one -- both were explicit tripwires for this
gap and both fired.

NOT a memory defect, as the row said: bodies only. Valgrind at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0
over the three probe programs is 31/31, 28/28 and 88/88 allocs/frees with zero
errors.

title: EVERY COMPILED macOS BINARY THAT RECORDS AN ERROR-RETURN-TRACE FRAME ABORTS AT EXIT -- SIGABRT / exit 134 and a raw Rust panic (`use of std::thread::current() is not possible after the thread's local data has been destroyed`) in place of the `Error return trace:` section. macOS-only; kept `main` red for two days.
detail:
FOUND by reading CI, not by a kata: the `Codegen E2E (macOS arm64, LLVM 18)`
job had been the sole red leg on `main` since 2026-08-27, failing 8 of 3404
tests in `tests/codegen.rs` -- the four `test_e2e_question_trace_*` cases,
the three `test_error_trace_*_format*` cases, and
`test_e2e_main_result_question_and_returns`. Every one carried the same
stderr.

NOT A TEST-HARNESS ARTIFACT, and not toolchain drift. Local rustc is
1.94.1 (e408947bf), byte-identical to the pin CI runs, and a four-line `?`
program built with the installed `karac` reproduces it directly:

    fn boom() -> Result[i64, i64] { Err(7_i64) }
    fn caller() -> Result[i64, i64] { let _ = boom()?; Ok(0_i64) }
    fn main() { match caller() { Ok(_) => println(0_i64), Err(e) => println(e) } }

    $ ./trace_fmt_default
    thread '<unnamed>' panicked at .../thread/current.rs:315:9:
    use of std::thread::current() is not possible after the thread's local
    data has been destroyed
    7
    exit=134

The program's own stdout is correct; the trace section never prints and the
process aborts instead of exiting 0. So this is a SHIPPED-BINARY defect, not
a test-only one -- any user program that propagates an `Err` through `?` on
macOS died this way.

MECHANISM. `print_trace_at_exit` keyed `ERROR_TRACES` with
`std::thread::current().id()`. The comment on `ERROR_TRACES` records exactly
why a global map replaced a `thread_local!` there: TLS destructors run during
thread shutdown, BEFORE the C runtime drains its `atexit` handlers, so a TLS
read from inside `atexit` is unsound. But `std::thread::current()` is ITSELF
TLS-backed -- the lookup KEY walked back into the hazard the map had just
dodged. Since 1.83 std panics on that access rather than minting a fresh
handle, and the panic unwound out of an `extern "C"` handler, hence the
abort. Linux drains `atexit` before destroying the main thread's TLS, which
is why the two Linux legs stayed green and only the macOS arm64 leg went red.

REGRESSION FROM 7c10fdf25 (2026-08-26), the fix for B-2026-08-26-39 -- the
commit that introduced the `ThreadId`-keyed map. Its landing date matches the
CI red start date exactly.

FIX. Read the thread identity on the PUSHING thread, at the moment the
`atexit` handler is registered, into a `TRACE_OWNER: OnceLock<ThreadId>`.
First-push is the correct thread to capture: when the pool never dispatched,
every `?` site runs on the calling thread, so the first pusher IS the thread
that returns from `main`; when it did, `PAR_DISPATCHED` short-circuits the
printer before the key is read at all, so the `map.get` moves below that
check.

VERIFIED. All three trace formats (text / json / jsonl) print and exit 0 on
the repro; `cargo test --features llvm --test codegen` is 3404 passed / 0
failed (was 3396 / 8); the JIT, auto-par and producer-mode legs of the same
CI job are green.

title: EVERY SCALAR `bf16` OPERATION ABORTED ISel ON arm64 AND wasm32 -- `LLVM ERROR: Cannot select`, exit 134, no program output. The `==` comparator emitted a raw `fcmp oeq bfloat`, and five more sites (contains / abs / clamp / sort+Map NaN canonicalization / min+max via `llvm.minnum.bf16`) did the same. NOT JIT-only and NOT macOS-only as first filed: AOT escaped only because the row's probe compared LITERALS the O2 pipeline folds away; with runtime operands `karac build` dies too. x86_64 legalizes all of it, which is why it was invisible here.
detail:
FOUND while verifying B-2026-08-29-22: the macOS arm64 CI job's SECOND leg
(`Codegen E2E via LLJIT`, `KARAC_TEST_JIT=1`) fails
`test_e2e_narrow_float_fields_compare_by_ieee`, which asserts
`Some("")` != the expected six lines. CI has not reached that step since
2026-08-27 because the AOT leg above it aborted the job first, so the failure
was MASKED, not new.

NOT CAUSED BY THE B-2026-08-29-22 FIX. Verified by stashing that change and
re-running the single test on an otherwise clean tree: it fails identically,
same assertion, same empty output. It is also on an unrelated path -- narrow-
float comparison, nothing to do with error traces.

REPRODUCED standalone, and the JIT's real error is louder than the test's
empty-string assertion shows:

    $ karac run narrowfloat.kara
    LLVM ERROR: Cannot select: 0x70ef49230: i32 = setcc 0x70ef4d8c0,
      0x70ef49930, setoeq:ch
        0x70ef4d8c0: bf16,ch = load<(load (s16) from %ir.0)> ...
        0x70ef49930: bf16,ch = load<(load (s16) from %ir.1)> ...
    In function: karac_eq_bf16
    exit=134

    $ karac build narrowfloat.kara && ./narrowfloat
    f32-negzero=true / f32-nan=false / f16-eq=true / f16-ne=false /
    bf16-eq=true / bf16-ne=false
    exit=0

So the comparator IR is the same on both backends and only the JIT's
instruction selector rejects it: a bare `setcc` on two `bf16` loads has no
legal arm64 pattern. `f16` in the same program is fine -- only the `bf16`
leg fails -- which points at the target features (or the lack of scalar bf16
compare legalisation) on the LLJIT's target machine differing from the one
`karac build` configures for the AOT path. The fix is presumably to promote
the operands to `f32` before the compare in `emit_eq_fn_for_type_expr`'s
`bf16` arm, so neither backend depends on a scalar bf16 setcc being
selectable -- but that is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

SCOPE. `bf16` equality is unusable under `karac run` / the REPL on arm64;
AOT is unaffected. Aborting with `LLVM ERROR` and no output is also a bad
failure mode in its own right -- a user sees a compiler-internal message,
not a diagnostic.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN FRAMING (2026-08-29, at close). Three of the
claims above were measured false while fixing it, and the corrected shape is
in the `fix` prose:

  * "on arm64" -> aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu fails identically, and so does
    wasm32. Not a macOS matter.
  * "AOT is unaffected" / class `run-vs-build` -> AOT is affected. The probe
    in this row compares the LITERALS `1.5bf16` / `2.5bf16`, which the
    `default<O2>` IR pipeline folds away before ISel (1 `fcmp oeq bfloat`
    before `opt -O2`, 0 after). With runtime operands the compare survives
    O2 and `karac build` aborts on arm64 as well. The row's `class` is left
    as `run-vs-build` only because `bug-close.py` has no `--class` flag;
    read it as `codegen-gap`.
  * "the target features ... differing" -> the actual mechanism is the OPT
    LEVEL: `llc -O0` selects a scalar bf16 compare on aarch64 (it emits
    `fcvt s0,h0; fcvt s1,h1; fcmp s0,s1`), `-O1` and above do not.
fix:
FIXED by 7ba9c46. Every `bf16` operation now lowers through `f32`; codegen emits no
native `bfloat` node beyond a bare copy, and a module-level guard rejects one
on EVERY host so the class can no longer hide on x86.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE INSTRUCTION AND WRONG ABOUT THE
SCOPE, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Re-measured with llc-18 from an x86_64 container
(the `-mtriple` override reproduces arm64 ISel exactly; the abort text is
byte-identical to the one the row quotes):

  * NOT macOS-specific. `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` fails identically, on
    `-mcpu` in {generic, apple-m1, apple-m2, neoverse-v1, cortex-a72}.
  * NOT JIT-only, so NOT `run-vs-build` -- the row's headline claim
    ("`bf16` equality is unusable under `karac run` ... AOT is unaffected")
    is false. It looked true because the row's probe compares the LITERALS
    `1.5bf16` / `2.5bf16`, which the AOT `default<O2>` IR pipeline folds away
    before ISel ever sees them: 1 `fcmp oeq bfloat` before `opt -O2`, 0 after.
    Give the same program RUNTIME operands (`env.args().len()`) and the
    compare survives O2 (1 -> 2, via inlining) and `karac build` dies on
    arm64 too. AOT was never safe; it was lucky. The opt-level difference is
    also the real mechanism behind the run/build split the row observed --
    not the "target features" its hypothesis names.
  * ALSO BREAKS wasm32, an AOT target we ship (`--target=wasm_wasi`).
  * `f16` is genuinely fine everywhere -- that half of the row holds.

ONE SITE IN THE ROW, SIX IN THE CODE. Probing each bf16 operation and
grepping the emitted IR found the scalar `==` comparator
(`synth.rs`, the row's `karac_eq_bf16`) plus: `Vec.contains`; `.abs()`
(`fcmp olt` + `fneg`); `.clamp()`; the NaN canonicalization behind
`sort` / `Map` on the `Bf16` wrapper (`fcmp uno`); and `.min()` / `.max()`,
which emit the `llvm.minnum.bf16` INTRINSIC -- a native bf16 op wearing a
call's clothing, and the one that survived the first round of fixes and
still killed wasm32. All six now widen to f32. The scalar operators and
binary arithmetic were already correct: `expr_ops.rs` has widened those
since the `f16_software_emulated` lint was written, which is what made the
comparator's divergence from house style visible as a defect at all.

THE COMMENT THAT CAUSED IT. `build_float_cast_bf16_safe` -- the helper an
earlier fix (B-2026-07-22-1) added for exactly this hazard -- asserted that
"bf16 *arithmetic* (`fadd`/`fcmp`/`fneg`) legalizes fine, only the conversion
nodes are gapped". That is false on the very CPUs its own text names:
`fadd`/`fsub`/`fmul`/`fdiv`/`fneg`/`fcmp` on `bfloat` all die with the same
"Cannot select", operands loaded from pointers so nothing crosses a call
boundary. Only `alloca`/`load`/`store`/`bitcast` survive. The sentence is
corrected in place, because a wrong comment next to the right helper is what
let the comparator sit on the generic float path for a year.

A SIGN-BIT XOR DOES NOT WORK, WHICH IS THE NON-OBVIOUS PART. Negating a bf16
is one bit-flip, so the natural lowering is bitcast-i16 / xor 0x8000 /
bitcast-back: exact, integer-only, and it selects fine in isolation.
DAGCombine then folds `bitcast(xor(bitcast x, signmask))` STRAIGHT BACK into
`fneg x`, reintroducing the unselectable node from IR that does not contain
it -- measured on the real `.abs()` lowering, which selects at `-O0` and dies
at `-O1`+ with `Cannot select: bf16 = fneg`. (`and` with the inverted mask is
folded to `fabs` the same way, so the whole family is out.) `-O0` selecting
and `-O1` not is the inverse of the usual direction and is worth remembering.
The f32 round-trip survives because the round-back is the rounding-bias +
NaN-quieting sequence, which no combine recognizes as an `fptrunc`.

That also means the unary-minus site, which B-2026-07-22-1 wrote as exactly
this XOR, was only ever safe BY CONSUMER: its result is immediately re-widened
for formatting, which collapses the bitcast pair before any fold sees a float.
Measured: that shape selects, and the `.abs()` shape -- same XOR, result feeding
a `select` on `bfloat` -- does not. It is unified onto the helper.

FAIL CLOSED, BECAUSE THE REAL DEFECT IS THAT x86 HIDES IT.
`verify_no_native_bf16_ops` walks the finished module before
`Module::verify` and rejects any native `bfloat` arithmetic, comparison,
conversion, or `llvm.*` intrinsic, naming the function and the helper to
route through. x86_64 legalizes every one of these happily, so a bad site is
invisible on the machines this compiler is developed and CI-tested on and
shows up only as an `LLVM ERROR` abort with no program output on someone
else's arm64 or wasm build. The guard makes it a deterministic compiler error
wherever the code is built. Both arms were validated against known-positive
controls (revert the comparator -> caught; disable the min/max widening ->
caught), not merely observed not to fire.

THE GUARD'S OWN FIRST DRAFT CRASHED THE COMPILER, which is worth recording
because the failure mode was the one thing a diagnostic pass must never do.
It walked operands with inkwell's `InstructionValue::get_operand`, which
routes through `BasicValueEnum::new` and is `unreachable!()` for an operand
that is not a basic value. The coroutine intrinsics carry token and metadata
operands, so every `async` and wasm-threads build panicked inside the check
(`test_coro_frame_malloc_matches_frame_sizeof` and
`wasm_threads_instantiate_threaded_export_taskgroup_e2e`, caught by the full
suite, not by the targeted tests). It now reads the instruction's PRINTED
form instead, which has no such hazard, and skips `<N x bfloat>` so the
vector path stays out of scope. Both arms plus a `Vector[bf16, N]` NEGATIVE
control were re-validated after the rewrite -- the detection logic changed
completely, so the earlier validation did not carry over.

VERIFIED. 13 bf16 programs (the row's own repro, a runtime-operand variant,
and 11 shape probes) are byte-identical across all four surfaces --
`--interp`, JIT, AOT, AOT with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` -- and every one now
SELECTS under llc-18 for aarch64 both unoptimized (the JIT's path) and after
`opt -O2` (AOT's), and for wasm32. Two regression tests: an IR-level one
asserting no native bf16 node (with an anti-vacuity check that the fixture
still produces bf16 at all), and a behavioural one pinning the answers.
The pair was RED-verified together against a deliberately regressed
comparator WITH THE GUARD DISABLED -- the true pre-fix state -- and the
result is the point of the whole row: the OUTPUT test PASSED and only the IR
test failed, printing `%feq = fcmp oeq bfloat %fva, %fvb`. An output-based
test on x86 cannot see this bug, which is precisely how it shipped.

NOT FIXED HERE, FILED AS B-2026-08-29-34: `Vector[bf16, N]` lane ops. The
vector legalizer scalarizes `<4 x bfloat> fadd` back into a scalar `bf16
fadd` and then cannot select it (wasm32 dies on `fp_to_bf16`), so the SIMD
path has the same disease -- but through ~18 vector-typed sites needing
`<N x float>` widening, a different fix. The guard is scalar-only on purpose:
rejecting the vector form without fixing it would turn code that works on x86
today into a hard compile error everywhere.

title: A param VIEW wrapped into a MIXED-payload enum, or into a STRUCT / TUPLE / VEC / `Some`, still runs its `Drop` body TWICE -- `let w = W2.Two(r, R { id: 2 })` prints `dR1 dR2 dR1` where `dR1 dR2` is due, and `let s = S { r: r }` prints `dR1 dR1`; B-2026-08-29-19 fixed only the SINGLE-payload enum wrap, because the shared walker cannot be withheld per slot and `Option`'s generic payload has no walker at all
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-19, whose fix covers the SINGLE-PAYLOAD enum wrap
only. Everything here is the same root cause -- a param VIEW moved into a
fresh owner, whose Drop body the caller still runs -- reached through a
constructor that fix deliberately declines. Every shape below was measured
IDENTICAL before and after B-2026-08-29-19's fix, on all three backends.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum W2 { Two(R, R), None3 }
    struct S  { r: R }
    struct S2 { r: R, k: i64 }
    struct S3 { a: R, b: R }

  A. MIXED PAYLOADS -- one view, one fresh, sharing a single walker.
     fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let w = W2.Two(r, R { id: 2 }); 7 }
       interp / jit / aot -> `dR1 dR2 dR1 v=7`   ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong
     Due: `dR1` once and `dR2` once. The struct-field twin is the same:
     fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let s = S3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }; 7 }
       -> `dR2 dR1 dR1 v=7`

  B. NON-ENUM WRAP KINDS, all single-payload, all doubling `dR1`:
     let s = S { r: r };        -> `dR1 dR1 v=7`   struct literal
     let s = S2 { r: r, k: 9 }; -> `dR1 dR1 v=7`   struct literal + inert field
     let t = (r, 5);            -> `dR1 dR1 v=7`   tuple
     let v2 = [r];              -> `dR1 dR1 v=7`   Vec literal
     let q = Some(r);           -> `dR1 dR1 v=7`   Option/Result

WHY (A) WAS NOT FIXED WITH ITS SIBLING. `__karac_dropelems_enum_<E>` is
declared-type-driven and walks EVERY payload slot of the live variant, so it
can only be armed or withheld whole. Withholding it for a mixed wrap trades
this double for a MISSING body on the fresh payload -- the same severity, the
other direction -- so B-2026-08-29-19 requires ALL visited payloads to be
views and declines otherwise. The fix is a per-slot MASKED walker, the enum
sibling of `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping` (B-2026-08-28-17/-23),
keyed on (variant, field index); the interpreter twin masks
`run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` the same way. Both backends must land
together -- see below.

WHY (B) WAS NOT FIXED WITH IT. Each wrap kind registers its cleanup at a
different site, and `Some`/`Ok` do not go through the enum walker at all:
`Option`'s payload TypeExpr is the enum's own generic parameter, which
`emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn` skips, so those payloads ride the
`optres_*` machinery instead and there is no walker for a suppression to
withhold.

THE ORDER OF OPERATIONS IS LOAD-BEARING, and it was measured the hard way on
the parent row: the interpreter half of the `Some(r)` case alone is easy and
CORRECT in isolation, and landing it turned an agreed defect into a
run-vs-build divergence (interp 1, both compiled backends 2). An agreed
defect is the better of the two, so the parent excludes Option/Result on the
interpreter side purely to hold parity. Whoever fixes (B) must land the
`optres_*` codegen leg in the SAME commit and delete that exclusion, not
before.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT. ASAN/LSan are clean on these shapes including a
heap-carrying payload -- verified for (A) as case 2 of
`asan_wrapped_param_view_payload_frees_once`. The surplus is a body, not a
free, and the pins exist so a future fix cannot let it become one.

AGREED ACROSS ALL THREE BACKENDS, so no A/B parity gate can see any of it;
absolute expectations are the only signal. Currently pinned AT THE DEFECT in
three places, so a fix will show up as those tests failing and must update
them: `test_e2e_wrapped_param_view_payload_drops_once` case 7 (codegen),
`test_wrapped_owned_param_payload_drop_body_runs_once` cases
`guard-mixed-payloads` and `guard-option-wrap` (interpreter), and
`asan_wrapped_param_view_payload_frees_once` case 2.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-29-19 -- the mixed case as the
guard rail that forced its all-payloads-must-be-views condition, the wrap
kinds as a boundary sweep once the minimal shape was known.
fix:
FIXED by 2ce3507. Every wrap kind the row lists is now correct on all
three backends -- except the `Vec` literal, which the measurements below show
was never this bug at all.

FOUR LEGS LANDED, each the maskable form of a walker that used to be
all-or-nothing. The row's own design was right about the shape of the fix and
about which mechanism each half needed.

  * ENUM, the row's part (A) -- `emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn_skipping`,
    new, keyed on (variant, declared payload index): the enum sibling of
    `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping` the row named. The old boolean
    `enum_ctor_payload_bodies_are_caller_owned` is now the `views == visited`
    case of a per-slot `enum_ctor_param_view_payload_slots`, and the let-site
    registers the masked walker instead of the full one. The interpreter twin is
    `moved_out_enum_payload_slots`, consumed by BLANKING the masked slots to
    `Value::Unit` before the walk rather than by threading a gate through it --
    the walk skips a slot that is not a `Value::Struct`, and blanking keeps the
    index alignment with the declared payload list that removing an item would
    destroy. That is `moved_out_struct_field_bodies`'s own idiom one container
    over.
        W2.Two(r, R { id: 2 })          dR1 dR2 dR1  ->  dR2 dR1

  * STRUCT LITERAL, part (B) and part (A)'s twin -- no new walker needed:
    `disarm_struct_field_bodies_at` (B-2026-08-03-8) already retracts and
    re-emits with a field masked, so `mask_param_view_struct_literal_fields`
    calls it once per view-initialized field. Interpreter twin:
    `moved_out_struct_field_bodies`, the set that route was built for. When
    EVERY visited field is a view the binding is itself marked a param view, so
    a later `let s2 = s;` inherits the withholding rather than re-arming a full
    walk over the fields just masked -- B-2026-08-01-15's propagation reached
    through a literal.
        S { r: r }                      dR1 dR1      ->  dR1
        S2 { r: r, k: 9 }               dR1 dR1      ->  dR1
        S3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }     dR2 dR1 dR1  ->  dR2 dR1
        S { r: r }; let s2 = s;         dR1 dR1      ->  dR1

  * TUPLE, part (B) -- the same shape again through
    `emit_tuple_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn_skipping` and
    `moved_out_tuple_elem_bodies`, both of which already existed for move-outs.
        (r, 5)                          dR1 dR1      ->  dR1
        (r, R { id: 2 })                dR1 dR2 dR1  ->  dR2 dR1

  * OPTION / RESULT, part (B) -- the leg the row said must land IN THE SAME
    COMMIT as the interpreter's exclusion, and it does. Codegen's `optres_*`
    let-site now withholds through `optres_ctor_payloads_are_all_param_views`,
    and `let_ctor_payloads_are_param_views`'s `Option`/`Result` bail -- added by
    B-2026-08-29-19 purely to hold parity while no codegen leg existed -- is
    deleted here.
        Some(r)                         dR1 dR1      ->  dR1

A FIFTH SHAPE THE ROW DID NOT LIST, found by sweeping the wrap kinds against a
struct that has its OWN `impl Drop`: `Sd { r: r }` where `struct Sd { r: R }`
doubled the same way (`dSd dR1 dR1`). It needed a different mechanism, because
such a struct has no per-binding field walker at all -- its field bodies run
inside the type-level `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper, shared by every binding of the
type. The route is `disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field`'s wholesale
wrapper swap (`emit_user_drop_wrapper_without_field_bodies`), which is sound
here exactly when every visited field is a view. Its own body still fires.
        Sd { r: r }                     dSd dR1 dR1  ->  dSd dR1

THE `Vec` LITERAL IS NOT THIS BUG, and the row's (B) list is wrong to include
it. `let v = [r];` does double -- but so does

    fn take() -> i64 { let m = R { id: 4 }; let v = [m]; 7 }        dR4 dR4

with no param anywhere, and

    fn take() -> i64 { let v = [R { id: 4 }]; 7 }                   dR4

is correct. So the cause is a moved-in BINDING whose ownership the element walk
does not take over -- a move-suppression hole -- not caller-retains. An
`ArrayLiteral` arm was written for the shared predicate and then REMOVED: it
would have fixed the half whose source happens to be a param and left the
identical local-source double standing, which is a worse state than either. All
three spellings are pinned in both behavioural suites, because it is the triple
that identifies which bug it is. Split out as B-2026-08-29-45.

TWO SHAPES THIS FIX CORRECTED THAT NOBODY HAD MEASURED, both found by probing
the new mask against adversarial neighbours and both verified against a
stashed-`src` pre-fix build:

  * `fn take(r: R, q: R) { let s = S3 { a: r, b: q }; }` -- TWO views into one
    literal ran FOUR bodies (`dR2 dR1 dR1 dR2` interp, `dR2 dR1 dR2 dR1`
    compiled), and now runs two.
  * `fn take(r: R) { let s = S3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }; let x = s.b; }` was a
    run-vs-build DIVERGENCE (interp `dR2 dR1`, both compiled backends
    `dR2 dR1 dR1`) and is now agreed at `dR2 dR1`.

NOT A MEMORY CHANGE, as the row predicted and as the pins now enforce. Only body
walkers are masked; no memory registration is touched on either backend.
`asan_wrapped_param_view_payload_frees_once` gained five heap-carrying cases
covering the struct, tuple, `Option` and both mixed wraps, and case 2's
expectation moved from three bodies to two -- the frees were balanced before and
after, which is the whole reason that case exists.

ONE MEASUREMENT WORTH RECORDING SO THE NEXT READER DOES NOT ATTRIBUTE IT HERE:
two owned params dropped by the caller print in OPPOSITE ORDER on the two
backends -- `fn take(r: R, q: R) -> i64 { 7 }` gives `dR1 dR2` under `--interp`
and `dR2 dR1` under JIT and AOT. No wrap is involved, it reproduces on a
pre-fix build, and it is untouched by this commit. Filed as B-2026-08-29-46.

A SECOND PRE-EXISTING SHAPE, same provenance and same treatment: moving a param
view back OUT of the struct it was just wrapped into
(`let s = S { r: r }; let x = s.r;`) doubles, while the LOCAL-source twin
(`let s = S { r: R { .. } }; let x = s.r;`) is correct. The move-out hands the
body to `x` properly; what is missing is that `x` inherits nothing about the
field having been a view. Measured identical pre-fix, pinned beside its correct
twin in both suites, filed as B-2026-08-29-47.

DELIBERATELY DECLINED, pinned at the defect in both behavioural suites rather
than left to drift, and AGREED across all three backends in each case:

  * a MIXED literal of a struct with its own `impl Drop`
    (`Sd3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }`). Codegen can only swap that wrapper for one
    that drops ALL field bodies, so masking one slot there would cost the fresh
    field's body -- the exact trade this row exists to avoid. The interpreter
    COULD mask it per field and declines on purpose, because doing so alone
    turns an agreed defect into a run-vs-build divergence, which B-2026-08-29-19
    already had to back out once for `Option`. B-2026-08-29-43.
  * a whole-value REBIND after a MIXED wrap (`let w = W2.Two(r, …); let w2 = w;`)
    re-arms the full walk: the mask is keyed on the binding and the destination
    registers afresh. The ALL-views case propagates view-ness instead, which is
    why `S { r: r }; let s2 = s;` is fixed and this is not. B-2026-08-29-44.

Tests: `e2e_wrapped_param_view_nonenum_and_mixed_wraps_drop_once` (codegen, 9
fixed cases + 8 guard rails + 5 pinned declines) and
`test_wrapped_param_view_nonenum_and_mixed_wraps_drop_once` (interpreter, the
same cases with the same expected output, which is the point -- every one of
these AGREED across backends while wrong, so only an absolute expectation
catches a regression). B-2026-08-29-19's three pins are updated in place:
codegen case 7, and the interpreter's `guard-mixed-payloads` / `guard-option-wrap`
which are no longer guard rails and are renamed accordingly.

title: A DISCARDED `if` RUNS NO `Drop` BODY IN EITHER STATEMENT FORM -- `if c { R { .. } } else { .. };` and `let _ = if c { .. };` are both silent on all three backends where one body is due, because `discarded_match_value_tail` is `Match`-only and has no `If` sibling at either discard site; the same gate also misses a BLOCK-WRAPPED match (`let _ = { match .. };`) that its two sibling gates would have recursed into
detail:
FOUND WHILE BOUNDING B-2026-08-29-20, which fixed the `let _ = <match>`
discard gate. These are the two shapes the same gate family still misses.
Both are AGREED ACROSS ALL THREE BACKENDS, so no A/B parity gate can see
either; absolute output expectations are the only signal.

Fixture throughout:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

  A. THE `if` SPELLING, in BOTH statement forms. One body is due in each.

     let _ = if n == 1 { R { id: 7 } } else { R { id: 0 } };
         interp / jit / aot -> silent      ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong
     if n == 1 { R { id: 7 } } else { R { id: 0 } };
         interp / jit / aot -> silent      ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong

     THE SECOND LINE IS THE IMPORTANT ONE: it is the BARE-STATEMENT form, so
     this gap PREDATES B-2026-08-29-20 and sits at B-2026-08-28-69's site as
     well as at the one just fixed. `discarded_match_value_tail` is
     `Match`-only -- it opens with `let ExprKind::Match { arms, .. } = ..
     else { return None }` -- and there is no `If` sibling anywhere, so
     neither discard site has ever admitted an `if`. The corresponding
     `match` spellings of both lines are correct today, which is what
     identifies this as the predicate's shape coverage rather than anything
     about discards.

  B. A BLOCK-WRAPPED MATCH at the wildcard-let site.

     let _ = { match n { 1 => { R { id: 7 } } _ => { R { id: 0 } } } };
         interp / jit / aot -> silent      ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong

     `discarded_owned_temp_tail` and `discarded_unit_variant_tail` both
     recurse through Block / Seq / Unsafe / LabeledBlock wrappers to find
     their tail; `discarded_match_value_tail` does not, so one pair of braces
     hides an otherwise-admitted match from the gate.

LIKELY ONE FIX FOR BOTH. Give `discarded_match_value_tail` the block recursion
its two siblings already have, and generalize its arm walk to the then/else
tails of an `If` -- the per-arm predicate itself (fresh owned temp / string /
struct literal) needs no change, and the interpreter's `Match` arm in
`discard_rhs_produces_owned_value` takes the mirror-image widening.

LAND BOTH BACKENDS IN ONE COMMIT. B-2026-08-29-20 measured what happens
otherwise: an arm shape admitted on one side only converts an agreed silence
into a run-vs-build divergence, and an earlier interpreter-only attempt at the
PARENT row (B-2026-08-28-69) was reverted for exactly that. Whatever widening
lands here must keep the interpreter's `Identifier`-at-arm-tail exclusion, or
it will fire on the hand-out-a-binding population that B-2026-08-29-5 owns and
codegen is silent for.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT, as far as measured: the sibling shapes that DO fire are
ASAN/LSan-clean through the discard battery
(`asan_discarded_let_wildcard_match_frees_once`), and these simply never reach
it. A fix must re-check under the sanitizer anyway, since routing a value into
that battery frees it as well as running its body.

SOURCE NOTE: found as boundary probes while fixing B-2026-08-29-20 -- (A) by
asking whether the `if` spelling shared the `match` spelling's gap, and (B) by
asking whether the gate recursed through block wrappers the way its siblings do.
fix:
FIXED by fd4e80f. Three changes, landed in one commit because any one of
them alone converts an agreed silence into a run-vs-build divergence -- the
measurement that got an earlier interpreter-only attempt at the parent row
(B-2026-08-28-69) reverted, and that this row's own text warned about.

  * `discarded_match_value_tail` (codegen) gained an `If` leg and the block
    recursion its two siblings (`discarded_owned_temp_tail`,
    `discarded_unit_variant_tail`) have always had. Its per-arm fail-closed
    test moved out into a shared `discard_arm_tail_qualifies`, so the `Match`
    and `If` legs cannot admit different shapes; a nested `Match`/`If` at an

  * `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp` (codegen) gained the matching `If`
    arm, resolving the branch type through a new shared
    `discard_branch_tail_type_name`.

    THIS WAS THE HALF THE ROW DID NOT PREDICT, and it is why "give
    `discarded_match_value_tail` the block recursion and generalize its arm
    walk to an `If`" was a correct but incomplete diagnosis. Opening the gate

  * the interpreter's TWO discard sites, mirroring both of the above: an `If`

MEASURED, interp / jit / aot, on the row's own fixture. Each program
constructs exactly one `R` that nobody takes, so one body is due:

  let _ = if n == 1 { R { .. } } else { .. };        0/0/0 -> 1/1/1
  if n == 1 { R { .. } } else { .. };                0/0/0 -> 1/1/1  (A, bare)
  let _ = if n == 1 { mk(7) } else { mk(0) };        0/0/0 -> 1/1/1
  if n == 1 { mk(7) } else { mk(0) };                0/0/0 -> 1/1/1
  let _ = if .. else if .. else { .. };              0/0/0 -> 1/1/1

  let _ = { match n { 1 => { R { .. } } .. } };      0/0/0 -> 1/1/1  (B)

  { mk(7) };                    0/1/1 -> 1/1/1
  let _ = { R { id: 7 } };      0/1/1 -> 1/1/1

THE LIVENESS GATE ON THE NEW `If` ARM IS LOAD-BEARING, verified by removing

IT COLLIDED WITH B-2026-08-29-5, WHICH LANDED MID-FLIGHT, AND THE COLLISION

STATEMENT-LEVEL owner. With both, a branch whose arms are fresh calls was

THE TWO NOW PARTITION THE SHAPE rather than overlapping. `compile_if` asks

(the merge yields a placeholder, so the statement site never sees the value)
and an arm tail naming an existing binding.

Both directions are measured, not reasoned about. Against a tree carrying -5's

ZERO bodies on all three backends -- the arm-level owner frees the buffer but
