concretely: `reduce_sum` folds lanes through the SCALAR path, so a vector
rounding that disagreed with the scalar one would make the operation disagree
with itself.

SCALAR HALF, WHICH THE ROW DID NOT KNOW ABOUT. B-2026-08-29-23 fixed the
plain-instruction sites and `min`/`max` and stopped there, leaving `sqrt`,
`exp`, `ln`, `log2`, `log10`, `exp2`, `sin`, `cos`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`,
`trunc`, `signum`, `recip`, `to_degrees`, `to_radians` and `fract`
instantiating overloaded intrinsics at `bfloat`. Every one aborts ISel off x86
(measured: `bf16 = fsqrt`, `bf16 = fexp`, `bf16 = ffloor`).
`build_float_intrinsic_bf16_safe` plus `widen_bf16_scalar` /
`narrow_bf16_scalar` route them, at the shared `float_math` call rather than
per-method.

MEASUREMENT. 23 programs sweeping the whole `Vector[bf16, N]` surface plus the
scalar math methods: ZERO native bfloat nodes (scalar or vector) in the emitted
IR, and every one now selects on `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`,
`aarch64-apple-darwin` and `wasm32-unknown-wasi` under llc-18 -O2. Values are
unchanged from what the native bf16 ops produced on x86 before the guard
started rejecting them (checked against a guard-disabled build), and `karac run`
now agrees with `karac run --interp` on every scalar method at all four float
widths and on every vector op but one (see B-2026-08-29-40).

THE GUARD IS WIDENED IN THIS COMMIT, as the row asked. Its second pass now
matches `<N x bfloat>` as well as scalar `bfloat`.

title: THE THREE `let`-FORM LEGS NEVER RAN THE PROJECTION-PLACE PAYLOAD SUPPRESSOR, so `if let E.A(r) = s.e { let m = r; .. }` over a HEAP payload FREES THE BUFFER TWICE -- no program output at all, valgrind reporting an invalid read of a freed block, while the `match` spelling of the same code is clean
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-29-33; measured on 0814cc2 (i.e. PRE-EXISTING,
not introduced by that work -- confirmed by measuring the same program with the
fix stashed) and on jit / build alike.

    struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}:{self.s}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }
    struct S { e: E }

      let s = S { e: E.A(R { id: 8, s: f"n8" }) };
      if let E.A(r) = s.e { let m = r; println(f"m{m.id}:{m.s}") }
      println("post")

        interp:            m8:n8 dR8:n8 dE dR8:n8 post
        jit / build:       <NO OUTPUT>
        valgrind:          Invalid read of size 2 ... 0 bytes inside a block of
                           size 2 free'd

The `match` spelling of the same program was clean at the same commit
(`m8:n8 dR8:n8 dE dR0: post` -- a doubled BODY, which is B-2026-08-29-33, but no
memory error). The TUPLE spelling `if let E.A(r) = t.0 { … }` fails identically.

CAUSE. `suppress_destructured_struct_field_enum_cleanup` -- the projection-place
source suppressor, which cap-zeroes the enum field inside the OWNING struct so
its synthesized drop skips the buffer the binding now owns -- has been called
from the `match` arm loop since #15. The `if let`, `while let` and `let … else`
legs each call only the IDENTIFIER-place `suppress_destructured_enum_payload_
cleanup` beside it, so a projection scrutinee left the source fully populated
while `m` took the payload, and both freed it.

FIXED by 9f3e2cb, alongside B-2026-08-29-33: all three legs now call it, and
because that function also carries the BODIES half as of the same commit, the
two move together -- the B-2026-08-28-67 lockstep rule.

Fixture rows `heap-payload-field` and `heap-payload-if-let-field` in
`codegen::e2e_materializing_arm_over_a_projection_owns_the_payload_once`, both
RED against the unfixed tree (they fail by producing nothing at all).

FILED SEPARATELY rather than folded into -33's prose because the severity is
different in kind: -33 is a doubled `Drop` body, this is a double free, and a
ledger that hides a high-severity memory bug inside a medium row's fix text
cannot be counted.
fix: FIXED by 9f3e2cb — see the detail above; the fix and the finding are the same commit.

title: A TWO-HOP PROJECTION (`match w.s.e { .. }`) STILL RUNS A MATERIALIZING ARM'S PAYLOAD BODY ON THE ZEROED SLOT -- compiled `m8 dR8 dE dR0` vs interp `m8 dR8 dE dR8`, where the ONE-hop spelling now gives `m8 dR8 dE` on both
detail:
Measured on 9f3e2cb (the B-2026-08-29-33 fix), interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. PRE-EXISTING and unchanged by that commit -- verified
byte-identical with it stashed.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }
    struct S { e: E }     struct W { s: S }

      let w = W { s: S { e: E.A(R { id: 8 }) } };
      match w.s.e { E.A(r) => { let m = r; println(f"m{m.id}") } E.B => {} }

        interp:            m8 dR8 dE dR8       <- two bodies
        jit / build / np:  m8 dR8 dE dR0       <- two bodies, second on the
                                                  cap-zeroed slot

The ONE-hop spellings (`s.e`, `t.0`) print `m8 dR8 dE` on all four surfaces
after -33, so this is exactly the shape that fix scoped out.

WHY IT IS SEPARATE AND WHAT IT NEEDS. -33's payload mask is applied by
`disarm_projection_enum_payload_bodies`, which resolves `<ident>.<field>` and
`<ident>.<index>` -- the places whose OWNER has a walk it can re-register. A
two-hop chain needs the mask threaded one level down, through
`FieldSkipTree::nested` against the intermediate field's walker: the shape
`nested: { idx_of_s: { payload_here: { idx_of_e } } }`, which the tree already
supports and nothing yet builds. The interpreter needs the matching change, and
its mask is currently a flat `(var, field)` pair -- it would have to become a
PATH, with `pending_payload_masked_fields` re-seeded for the nested call rather
than taken once.

The MEMORY half already handles arbitrary depth (`suppress_destructured_struct_
field_enum_cleanup` walks the chain through `field_chain_place_ptr`), which is
exactly why the compiled second fire reads a ZEROED object rather than a live
one: the source was emptied, and only the bodies half stopped at one hop.

SEVERITY low: no memory error (valgrind clean), same body COUNT on both
backends, and a two-hop projection scrutinee is rare next to the one-hop forms.

SOURCE NOTE: found in the B-2026-08-29-33 shape probe as one of the two rows
that stayed DIVERGE after the 24-cell matrix went green.
fix:
FIXED by 4843ffe7. The payload mask is now a PATH on both backends, so a projection scrutinee of
ANY depth masks the arm-materialized payload at the level that actually owns
the enum.

WHAT IT WAS. B-2026-08-29-33 keyed the mask on a SINGLE field index, so
`match w.s.e { .. }` resolved to nothing and the owner's walk stayed unmasked:
the payload body fired a SECOND time after the arm already ran it. One defect,
two symptoms -- an extra body on every backend, and a run-vs-build divergence
in what that body PRINTED, since the compiled backends read the slot the
move-out had cap-zeroed (`dR0`) where the interpreter still saw the live
object (`dR8`). The row's own framing was exact and its diagnosis held up.

THE FIX, both halves.

  * CODEGEN: `struct_moved_field_payload_bodies` holds `Vec<usize>` PATHS
    instead of a bare index; `projection_field_index_path` resolves a chain of
    field accesses rooted at an identifier (using `place_chain_type_name` for
    every hop past the first); `FieldSkipTree::from_payload_paths` turns a
    one-element path into `payload_here` and a longer one into `nested`, one
    level per intermediate field.

  * INTERPRETER: `moved_out_struct_field_payload_bodies` holds `(var, Vec<
    field name>)`; `pending_payload_masked_fields` holds paths; and
    `drop_user_drop_fields_of_value` RE-SEEDS the mask, head stripped, before
    recursing into a nested struct field. The mask is deliberately TAKEN at
    entry so a nested walk cannot inherit it by name collision, and a deeper
    path is exactly the case where it SHOULD travel -- so the re-seed is
    explicit rather than a widened borrow. Names where codegen uses indices,
    because this backend walks a field MAP; same path in each backend's
    currency.

THE ROW'S "WHERE TO START" WAS CORRECT, including the part I initially
doubted: `FieldSkipTree::nested` HAS been consumed by the emitter since
B-2026-08-28-23 (`skip.nested.get(&field_idx)`, handed to the recursive
`emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping`). Only the BUILDING side was
missing. A first reading of mine said the field was dead because a truncated
grep cut off the consumption site; re-checked and corrected before writing any
code.

MEASURED, 16 programs on all four surfaces (interp / jit / aot /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), valgrind clean throughout. Six shapes went from divergent
to correct: two-hop, three-hop, two-hop with an own-`Drop` intermediate,
two-hop with sibling fields still owed, the `if let` spelling, and a two-hop
with a statement following. Four controls unchanged: the one-hop form, a
NON-consuming arm (payload not taken, so the owner still owes that body), a
payload-less `E.B` arm, and one-hop with a trailing statement.

COMPOSITION was the half most likely to go wrong quietly, so it is pinned
rather than argued: masking an inner `s.e` leaves an outer `e`'s payload
firing and vice versa (same field NAME at both levels), a one-hop and a
two-hop mask on one variable compose, and two sibling subtrees stay
independent whether one or both are masked.

A MERGE THE REBASE FORCED, and it is load-bearing. B-2026-08-31-30 landed
mid-row and added `struct_moved_nested_field_bodies` -- nested struct
SUB-PATTERN masks that also feed `FieldSkipTree::nested`. Two rows now write
one tree from opposite directions (whole inner fields vs a payload N levels
down), and every site here calls `replace_user_drop_fn_for_var`, which swaps
the walker WHOLESALE -- so a site assembling only its own row's half silently
drops the other's, with the outcome depending on which arm compiled last.
Taking either side of the conflict would have been wrong. All three
mask-building sites now go through one `field_skip_tree_for_var` builder that
merges both sources; before this, only the site the conflict happened to touch
knew about -30's map at all.

TESTS: `codegen::e2e_deep_projection_scrutinee_runs_one_payload_body` and
`interpreter::test_deep_projection_scrutinee_runs_one_payload_body` carry the
same 14 shapes in the same order, the twin generated mechanically from the
codegen source so the two cannot drift. Both RED-verify against the stashed
compiler with the defect's exact signature (`left: "m8\ndR8\ndE\ndR8\n"`). No
ASAN fixture: the row is body-count and divergence only -- valgrind was clean
before the fix as well as after, and a fixture that passes in both directions
is noise, not a gate.

ONE GAP FOUND AND NOT FIXED, filed as B-2026-08-31-43: a `self`-ROOTED
scrutinee is unmasked at EVERY depth, so the payload body doubles. It is the
ROOT-KIND axis, not the depth axis this row fixed -- the proof being that the
ONE-hop `self.e` doubles identically to `self.s.e`. Both backends agree, so it
is an agreed gap rather than a divergence, and it is byte-identical against
the pre-fix compiler. Pinned in both tests so a one-sided fix fails loudly.

title: A `ref self` METHOD WHOSE MATCH MOVES `self.e`'s PAYLOAD OUT RUNS THE ENUM'S OWN `Drop` BODY TWICE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `dR8 dE n8 dE dR8` vs interp `dR8 n8 dE dR8`, the extra `dE` firing INSIDE the callee on the caller's struct
detail:
Measured on 9f3e2cb (the B-2026-08-29-33 fix), interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. PRE-EXISTING and unchanged by that commit -- verified
byte-identical with it stashed.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }
    struct S { e: E }
    impl S {
        fn grab(ref self) -> i64 {
            match self.e { E.A(r) => { let m = r; return m.id } E.B => { return 0i64 } }
        }
    }

      let s = S { e: E.A(R { id: 8 }) };
      println(f"n{s.grab()}");

        interp:            dR8 n8 dE dR8
        jit / build / np:  dR8 dE n8 dE dR8      <- `dE` TWICE

The receiver is `ref self`, so the callee owns nothing: the caller's `s` is the
sole owner and its walk (`dE dR8`, after `n8`) is the whole story. The compiled
backends run an EXTRA `dE` inside `grab`, before the call returns -- the enum's
own body firing on a struct the callee only borrows.

NOT the payload half. The payload's body count is right on both sides (one
`dR8` from the moved-out `m` at the arm's end, one from the caller's walk); it
is specifically the enum's OWN body that doubles, and only under a borrowed
receiver. A `match s.e` at the same place in a free function is clean on all
four surfaces (`m8 dR8 dE`), which is what makes the receiver mode the variable
rather than the projection.

WHAT WAS RULED OUT. B-2026-08-29-33's payload disarm deliberately does NOT
register a walk when it finds none to replace, precisely because inventing one
here made the caller's struct fire inside the callee -- that path was measured
and removed before landing, and this row's numbers are from the tree WITHOUT it,
and identical to the pre-fix tree. So the spurious `dE` predates all of that
work and belongs to whatever arms an own-body action against a borrowed `self`.

SOURCE NOTE: found in the B-2026-08-29-33 shape probe as the second of two rows
that stayed DIVERGE after the 24-cell matrix went green.

CORRECTION (2026-08-31, at close): the "NOT the payload half" scoping above is
right, but the "A `match s.e` at the same place in a free function is clean on
all four surfaces" sentence is NOT -- and it is what pointed this row at the
receiver mode. Re-measured on a full own / ref / mut ref x method / free-fn
matrix, `fn f(s: ref S)` diverges IDENTICALLY to `ref self` (`dR4 dE n4 dE dR4`
vs interp `dR4 n4 dE dR4`), while an owned RECEIVER `fn m(self)` is clean exactly
as an owned free-fn param is. The variable is not method-vs-free-function; it is
whether the matched place is reached through a BORROW, which is what puts the
scrutinee on the defensive-clone path. The free-function shape quoted in the
SOURCE NOTE (`m8 dR8 dE`) is a different program from the one measured here.
fix:
FIXED by fddafe3. `materialize_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee` (src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs)
registered BOTH halves of the enum's drop on the `__freshtemp_enum_scrut` alloca
it stages the scrutinee into: the memory glue `__karac_drop_<E>` AND the user
body `karac_drop_<E>`. Registering the body is right for the one population the
registration was written for -- a GENUINE FRESH TEMP (`match mk() { ... }`,
B-2026-07-11-26): nobody else owns it, so its `Drop` runs there or nowhere. It
is wrong for the other population that reaches the same code, which arrives
through the `force` / `heap_index` doors: a DEFENSIVE COPY of a place the source
still owns. Those clones exist so a consuming arm's binding gets an independent
buffer; the original is untouched and runs its own body at its own death, so
running the clone's body too makes the count depend on a codegen internal.

The fix hoists `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` out of the entry gate (it was
already computed there) and conditions ONLY the user-body registration on it.
The memory registration is unchanged for both populations, because the clone
really does own duplicated buffers -- and `__karac_drop_<E>` frees them without
running any user body (it recurses into `__karac_drop_struct_*`, which only calls
`karac_free_buf`), so the two halves separate exactly along the line that
matters: the copy is freed, the copy is not mourned.

THE ROW'S SHAPE WAS ONE OF FOUR, and the receiver mode was not the variable.
The row read the difference as `ref self` vs an owned receiver, having measured a
free function as clean. It is not the receiver: `fn f(s: ref S)` diverges
identically (`dR4 dE n4 dE dR4` vs interp `dR4 n4 dE dR4`), and an owned
RECEIVER `fn m(self)` is clean for the same reason an owned free-fn param is --
neither is in `signature_ref_params`, so no clone is minted. What decides is
whether the scrutinee's place is reached through a borrow. Widening from there
found three more legs on the same registration, two of them doubling the body
outright:

    for p in v { match p { E.A(r) => ... } }   dE dE   (interp dE)  <- B-2026-07-14-1's clone
    match v[0] { E.A(r) => ... }               dE dE   (interp dE)  <- the heap_index leg
    match <refparam>.f { E.A(r) => ... }       dE inside the callee (interp: none)
    match mk() { E.A(r) => ... }               dE      -- CORRECT, the control

The live-local leg (B-2026-08-08-25 leg 3) was already clean, and for an
instructive reason: `enum_payload_clone_is_faithful` refuses to clone when the
payload is a `NestedStruct`, precisely because "a clone is a compiler-internal
artifact the source language never asked for" (B-2026-08-09-9). That is the same
rule as this fix, one level down -- it is about the PAYLOAD's body, and nothing
had ever asked the question about the ENUM'S OWN body. The remedy differs
because declining to clone is not available at this site: the ref-chain, loop-
element and index legs exist to fix real double-frees (B-2026-07-21-5/-6,
B-2026-07-14-1), so this keeps the clone and withholds the body instead.

VERIFIED three-way byte-identical (interpreter / LLJIT / AOT `karac build`) on a
fixture carrying all four legs, and the control leg pins B-2026-07-11-26 so an
over-reach that silenced a real fresh temp fails loudly. Tests:
`e2e_defensive_scrutinee_copy_does_not_rerun_the_enum_own_drop_body` and its IR
guard `ir_defensive_scrutinee_copy_keeps_memory_cleanup_and_drops_the_user_body`
(tests/codegen.rs), the interpreter oracle twin
`test_scrutinee_clone_does_not_rerun_the_enum_own_drop_body`
(tests/interpreter.rs), and `asan_ref_chain_enum_scrutinee_clone_frees_once`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) for the leak the memory half would have become. The
IR guard is the anti-vacuity pairing: the E2E asserts an ABSENCE, so it would
also pass if the defensive clone simply stopped being emitted -- which would
silently re-open the double-frees the clone legs exist to fix -- so the guard
asserts the clone and its memory cleanup are still there alongside the missing
body, with a fresh-temp function as the paired positive.

title: A method's FRESH-TEMP argument whose value is handed back out runs its `Drop` body TWICE on both compiled backends against once in the interpreter -- the passthrough guard that would suppress the caller-side temp drop is gated on `ExprKind::Identifier`, which a temp never is
detail:
A METHOD arg with no caller binding gets the caller-side temp drop AND the
returned value's own body, so one value runs two. The passthrough guard that
exists for exactly this on both codegen call paths is written
`if let ExprKind::Identifier(var_name) = &a.value.kind`, and a fresh temp is not
an identifier, so it never applies:

    src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs:2209   free-fn leg   (B-2026-08-09-15)
    src/codegen/method_call.rs:7196     method leg    (B-2026-08-09-15)

Both compute the right answer -- `flows_into_return ||
callee_returns_enum_arg_payload(..)` is true for these programs -- and then
discard it because the arg has no name to suppress.

TWO SPELLINGS, both measured at 0814cc2 and unchanged by B-2026-08-29-11 (that
row's fix is interpreter-only):

  (1) payload bound out of a fresh-temp ENUM arg, handed back

      impl T { fn take(ref self, b: Box2) -> R
               { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } .. } } }
        let r = t.take(Box2.Full(R { id: 7 })); println(f"got {r.id}")

          interp:            got 7 / drop 7                  correct
          jit / build:       drop 7 / got 7 / drop 7         DOUBLE

  (2) fresh-temp STRUCT arg escaping bare into a returned `Option`

      impl K { fn f(ref self, r: R, keep: bool) -> Option[R]
               { if keep { return Option.Some(r); } return Option.None; } }
        k.f(R { id: 3 }, false); k.f(R { id: 4 }, true); k.f(R { id: 5 }, false)

          interp:            drop 3 / a / drop 4 / b / drop 5 / c          correct
          jit / build:       drop 3 / a / drop 4 / drop 4 / b / drop 5 / c DOUBLE

The three-call shape is worth keeping: only the ESCAPING call doubles, so the
two non-escaping calls are their own in-program control and rule out "fresh temp
args double-fire generally".

The interpreter is correct on both, which is what makes this a run-vs-build
divergence rather than a shared gap. It is a BODY count, not a free -- `Drop`
bodies here only print -- so it is not by itself a memory fault; whether the
second body accompanies a second free of the payload's heap was not measured and
should be, since case (1)'s `R` is returned to a live binding.

NOT the same defect as B-2026-08-29-11, and the distinction matters for whoever
takes this: that row was the interpreter losing a body because two frames shared
a name space; this is codegen running one too many because a guard is keyed on a
syntactic form the argument does not have. The fix is presumably to give the
fresh temp's drop the same passthrough gate the named-binding path gets, at both
sites, rather than to widen the identifier match.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while fixing B-2026-08-29-11 -- these were the two probes
in that session's matrix that did not converge once the interpreter was
repaired.
fix:
FIXED by fc379153. The METHOD leg's fresh-temp spelling now runs ONE body, converging on the
interpreter. The row's diagnosis was exactly right, including both code
pointers.

THE FIX IS ONE PREDICATE. `escapes_frame` at the method-call registrar
(`method_call.rs`) carried `fn_always_returns_param || fn_conditionally_-
returns_param_bare || call_arg_moves_into_outliving_place`, but NOT
`callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` -- the route the sibling named-binding guard
a few hundred lines up already consults. Adding it reaches the temp precisely
because `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` keys on the VALUE, not on a name,
which is what the identifier-gated guard could never do. So the fix is not
"widen the identifier match" (the row's own suggested shape) but "feed the
answer to the registrar that does not need a name" -- same conclusion, better
lever.

MEASURED, ten programs on interp / jit / aot, `R { id, name: String }` so the
payload carries heap:

    let r = t.take(Box2.Full(mk(7)));            2 bodies -> 1, agrees
    ... with the result read twice                2 bodies -> 1, agrees
    CONTROL named binding `t.take(b)`             1 body, unchanged
    CONTROL `k.g(mk(7))` consumes, returns scalar 1 body, unchanged

THE ROW'S OPEN MEMORY QUESTION, ANSWERED: it asked whether the second body
came with a second free, since case (1)'s `R` is returned to a live binding.
It does NOT. Valgrind on all four affected programs at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:
0 errors and no definite loss, BEFORE the fix as well as after. This channel
runs bodies and frees nothing, so the defect was a transcript defect only.

SCOPED TO THE METHOD LEG ON PURPOSE. The row names both sites, but the FREE-FN
spelling doubles on BOTH backends (measured: `freefn_take(Box2.Full(mk(7)))`
prints two bodies under `--interp` too). Fixing codegen there alone would take
an agreed gap and make it a divergence -- the trade this repo explicitly
refuses. The free-fn leg needs both backends moved together and is not this
row's fix.

THE SECOND SPELLING IS SPLIT OUT, NOT FIXED (B-2026-08-31-46), and the
reason is worth recording because the obvious fix is WRONG. Case (2) is a temp
escaping inside a returned `Option.Some(r)` rather than as the bare param.
`fn_returns_param` requires the return operand to be the parameter's bare
identifier, so the wrapped form is invisible to it -- but these predicates are
documented CONSERVATIVE-TRUE, and in the row's own three-call program the two
NON-escaping calls (`keep = false`) correctly print their bodies today. A
conservative-true answer would skip the caller-side drop on ALL THREE calls,
turning one doubled body into two LOST bodies and a leak. The wrapped form
needs the per-path callee-side ownership flip that
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` already has for the bare form, which is
feature-sized rather than a predicate edit.

TWO MORE SHAPES FOUND, both filed and both measured byte-identical at
`c4af3243` (before this session's discard-path work), so neither is a
regression from it:
  * B-2026-08-31-47: a method enum-temp arg whose payload the arm BINDS but
    does NOT return (`fn keep(..) -> i64 { match b { Box2.Full(r) => return
    r.id } }`) runs NO body on the interpreter against one compiled -- the
    opposite direction to this row.
  * the same row's second shape: the BARE-STATEMENT discard of a method call
    returning `Option[R]` loses the body on the interpreter where the
    `let _ =` spelling keeps it, so the two discard spellings disagree.

TESTS: `codegen::e2e_method_fresh_temp_arg_handed_back_runs_one_body` and
`interpreter::test_method_fresh_temp_arg_handed_back_runs_one_body`. The
codegen one RED-verifies against the stashed compiler with the exact defect
signature (`drop 7 h7 / got 7 / drop 7 h7` against `got 7 / drop 7 h7`); the
interpreter twin was already correct on the fixed spelling and pins that it
stays so. Both carry the two shapes that REMAIN divergent, each pinning its
OWN backend's current output rather than a shared expectation -- which is what
makes a one-sided fix of either fail loudly instead of silently converging one
half.

FIXED by c793ad0. The root cause is one step upstream of this row's framing,
and the correction matters because the row's own title names the wrong
mechanism.

NOT "classified as non-RC for life". The ownership pass never decided anything
about RC here. The TYPECHECKER recorded the wrong TYPE for the RHS, and every
downstream conclusion followed correctly from it. Measured, dumping
`expr_types` for the two spellings side by side:

    let x: Option[Node] = None;                     -> Named { name: "Option", args: [TypeParam("T")] }
    let x: Option[Node] = Some(Node { .. });        -> Named { name: "Option", args: [Shared("Node")] }

`check_expr(value, &declared)` verifies a bare `None` against the annotation
but does not re-record it, so the polymorphic literal keeps its uninstantiated
type. `use_classifier`'s Let arm keys `local_types` off `expr_types[value.span]`
-- the RHS, read as the BINDING's type -- and `is_copy_type` answers
`Option[T]` by asking whether every argument is `Copy`. A bare `TypeParam` is
not, so the binding scored non-`Copy`, every later use became a Consume, and
the UAM predicate fired. `Type::Shared(_)` already has its own `Copy` arm,
which is why the `Some(..)` spelling and a bare `shared` binding were both
always clean. The initializer, not the type, was the variable -- exactly what
the row's four-way table showed, for a reason the row misattributed.

THE `help` TEXT FOLLOWED FROM THE SAME WRONG TYPE rather than being a second
defect. `moved_type_supports_clone` saw `Named { name: "Option" }` with a
non-clonable argument and correctly said so; it was answering about a type the
program does not have.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN SEVERITY ARGUMENT: "`karac check` returns EXIT 1
on it" IS FALSE. Re-measured deliberately: an ownership UAM warning alone
prints under `warning[ownership]`, ends with "All checks passed.", and exits 0
-- for this shape and for a genuinely-moving plain struct alike. The exit 1
observed while filing came from TWO UNRELATED typecheck errors in the same file
(`this argument is already a mut-ref; drop the `mut` marker` at kata 298's
`differential.kara:253-254`), which were fixed separately in the same session.
The row's "fails a Mend loop or a CI gate" justification does not hold. What
does hold is the rest: a false positive on the standard accumulator shape
(`let mut acc: Option[T] = None;` filled in a loop), reported through
`karac check --output=json`, which the Mend loop reads and acts on. Medium
stands on that; it never rested on the exit code, and the claim should not have
been made without measuring it.

THE FIX records the declared type at the RHS span when the annotation is fully
concrete and the recorded type is not, so it can only ever replace an
unresolved type with the resolved one the annotation already committed to. A
generic annotation (`let v: Vec[T] = Vec.new()` inside `fn f[T]`) is left
alone. Deliberately at the recording site rather than in `is_copy_type`: the
wrong type would otherwise keep flowing to every other consumer of
`expr_types`, and the next symptom would look unrelated to this one.

TESTS, in `tests/ownership.rs`, the first two verified RED before the fix:
  option_shared_binding_initialized_to_none_is_not_use_after_move
  option_shared_binding_initialized_to_none_then_reassigned_is_not_use_after_move
  option_of_a_moving_payload_initialized_to_none_still_reports_the_move
The third is the guard that earns the fix its narrowness: `Option[String]` and
`Option[Vec[i64]]` under the same `None` initializer STILL report their reuse,
so the change narrows classification to the annotation rather than suppressing
the diagnostic for `Option` generally.

GATES: default suite 108/108 green; `--features llvm` codegen 3415, memory
sanitizer 1316, par_codegen 723, cli 1827, interpreter 481, typechecker 2543,
ownership 270 -- all green; clippy clean on BOTH feature legs; fmt clean.
title: A BINDING INITIALIZED TO `None` IS CLASSIFIED AS NON-RC FOR THE REST OF ITS LIFE, so reusing an `Option[shared T]` after passing it by value is reported as a move-after-move -- and `karac check` EXITS 1. `let mut x: Option[Node] = None;` warns on two `f(x)` calls; the identical program with `let mut x = make(0);` is clean. Later reassignment does not rehabilitate it. The `help` gives the game away by asserting the value "has no `.clone()` -- that exists only on ... RC types" when `.clone()` compiles and runs, so the pass has concluded the binding is not RC at all.
detail:
FOUR PROGRAMS, ONE VARIABLE -- THE INITIALIZER -- AND NOTHING ELSE:

    shared struct Node { val: i64, mut left: Option[Node] }
    fn f(t: Option[Node]) -> i64 { match t { None => { return 0; } Some(n) => { return n.val; } } }
    fn make(v: i64) -> Option[Node] { return Some(Node { val: v, left: None }); }

    fn main() {
        <BINDING>
        println(f"{f(x)} {f(x)}");
    }

    let mut x: Option[Node] = None;   x = make(1);   -> WARNED
    let mut x: Option[Node] = None;                  -> WARNED
    let mut x = make(0);              x = make(1);   -> clean
    let mut x: Option[Node] = make(0); x = make(1);  -> clean

Every one of the four is the same TYPE, the same callee, the same two uses. The
two that are warned are the two whose declaration initializer is `None`. Adding
an explicit type annotation does not change it; reassigning afterwards does not
change it; whether the later value came from a call or a struct literal does not
change it. The initializer is the whole variable.

THE WARNING:

    warning[ownership]: value 'x' moved here, used again here (moved at line N)
      help: declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads, or restructure
            to avoid reuse ('x' has no `.clone()` -- that exists only on
            `String`, the built-in heap collections and RC types)

IT IS A FALSE POSITIVE, and measured as one. `Option[shared Node]` is an RC
type: passing it by value retains, so a second use is legal and does the right
thing. Both warned programs print the correct answer on ALL FOUR surfaces
(`run --interp`, `run` JIT, `build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`, exit 0), and
`karac build` emits a working binary. Nothing is unsound; the report is simply
wrong.

THE `help` TEXT IS WRONG TOO, AND IN THE SAME DIRECTION -- WHICH IS THE TELL.
It states the value "has no `.clone()` -- that exists only on ... RC types".
`Option[shared Node]` IS an RC type and `x.clone()` compiles and runs
(`f(x.clone())` twice prints `2 2`). So the pass is not merely mis-scoring a
use; it has concluded the binding is not RC AT ALL, and the help text is
faithfully reporting that wrong conclusion. That points at classification by
INITIALIZER: `None` carries no heap payload, so a binding initialized from it
is typed as non-RC and every later use is scored as a plain move -- which is
exactly the four-way split above.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A STRAY WARNING. `karac check` returns EXIT 1 on it, so
it fails a Mend loop, a CI gate, or any `karac check`-clean policy. And the
shape it rejects is the standard accumulator:

    let mut acc: Option[TreeNode] = None;
    while ... { acc = node(v, acc, None); }
    if arm_a(acc) != s or arm_b(acc) != s { ... }

which is how one builds a spine, a list, or any linked structure in a loop.
There is no natural rewrite: initializing to a dummy `Some(..)` to dodge it is
worse code, and the `.clone()` the help text says is unavailable is in fact the
only thing that silences it.

SOURCE NOTE: found writing kata 298's differential, whose P5 block builds
ascending and descending spines with exactly the accumulator above and then
hands each to three arms. The kata keeps the natural spelling and cites this
row.

title: A REDUCED-PRECISION RECEIVER (`f16` / `bf16`) CALLED THE DOUBLE-PRECISION libm SYMBOL and got silent garbage -- `x.tan()` returned `x`, `x.hypot(y)` returned 2.4e16. Wrong answers on EVERY target including x86, with no diagnostic. Ten methods affected.
detail:
FOUND while verifying B-2026-08-29-34's fix by A/B-ing every scalar float
method against the interpreter at all four float widths. It is NOT the same
class as that row: nothing aborts, nothing fails to select, and x86 is affected
just as much as arm64. The program simply computes the wrong number.

THE MECHANISM IS ONE LINE. `tan` / `atan2` and the inverse-trig / hyperbolic set
have no LLVM-18 intrinsic, so codegen calls libm directly and picked the symbol
with:

    let is_f32 = fty == self.context.f32_type();

A BINARY test. `f16` and `bf16` are neither f32 nor f64, so they took the f64
arm: they called `tan` rather than `tanf`, and then DECLARED it with the
receiver's own type -- `declare bfloat @tan(bfloat)`, a signature libm does not
have. libm read a double out of 16 bits of stack and returned whatever was
there.

MEASURED (x86_64, `karac run` vs `karac run --interp`, receiver 2.0):

    method   interp          codegen (before)
    tan      -2.1875         2                 <- returned the receiver
    atan      1.109375       2
    asin      NaN            2
    acos      NaN            0.0000000000086
    sinh      3.625          2
    cosh      3.765625       0
    ln_1p     1.1015625      2
    exp_m1    6.375          2
    atan2     0.58984375     -5.4e-39
    hypot     3.609375       24769797950537730

f32 and f64 agree exactly, which is what localizes the bug to the width test.
Both half formats are affected identically.

FIXED by e860b90: a half format has no libm entry point of its own, so
it now widens to f32, calls the `f`-suffixed symbol, and rounds back -- which is
also what the reduced-precision semantics ask for (compute in f32, round once).
The widening is scoped to the libm branch: an earlier draft hoisted it above the
branch, where it silently reached the INTRINSIC path too and made
`build_float_intrinsic_bf16_safe` see an already-f32 receiver, decide no
narrowing was due, and leak f32 precision out of a bf16-typed expression
(`a.exp()` printing 7.389056205749512 instead of 7.375). The interp-vs-codegen
sweep caught that regression; reasoning about the diff did not.

Regression test: `e2e_half_precision_libm_calls_use_the_f32_symbol` in
tests/codegen.rs, which asserts the VALUES rather than that it compiles -- an
"it builds" test passes against this bug.
fix: FIXED by e860b90, in the same commit as B-2026-08-29-34. See the detail field for the mechanism, the measured before/after table, and the scoping regression the first draft introduced.

title: The INTERPRETER's `Vector[bf16, N]` unary math never rounds lanes back to the element width -- it computes every lane in f64 and keeps the excess precision, so `a.sqrt().reduce_sum()` disagrees with codegen. The other eight methods agree BY LUCK OF THE INPUTS, not by correctness.
detail:
FOUND while A/B-ing B-2026-08-29-34's fix. Codegen is the CORRECT half here;
the interpreter is the one to change.

REPRODUCTION (x86_64, current main + B-2026-08-29-34's fix):

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let s: bf16 = (n as f32) as bf16;
        let t: bf16 = ((n + 1) as f32) as bf16;
        let a: Vector[bf16, 4] = Vector[bf16, 4](s, t, s, t);
        println(f"{a.sqrt().reduce_sum()}");
    }

    karac run --interp   4.84375
    karac run            4.8125

WHY CODEGEN IS RIGHT. design.md's rule (and the `f16_software_emulated` warning
codegen itself emits) is that each operation widens to f32 and ROUNDS BACK.
Under that rule sqrt(2) rounds to the bf16 1.4140625, and folding the four lanes
through the scalar bf16 add gives 4.8125. 4.84375 is what you get by keeping
sqrt(2) at f32 precision (1.4142135) and rounding only at the end. The
interpreter's own SCALAR path agrees with codegen -- `one + two.sqrt() + one +
two.sqrt()` prints 4.8125 under `--interp` -- so the interpreter disagrees with
ITSELF between its scalar and vector paths.

THE SITE. src/interpreter/method_call_seq.rs, the
`"sqrt" | "exp" | "ln" | "tanh" | "sigmoid" | "floor" | "ceil" | "round" | "trunc"`
arm: it maps each `Value::Float(x)` lane through the f64 libm function and
rebuilds the vector, with no narrowing to the receiver's element width. The
width IS available at this site -- the neighbouring `to_bits` arm reads it from
`typecheck_result.vector_method_receivers`, keyed by the call span.

THE TRAP FOR WHOEVER FIXES THIS: the other eight methods in that arm currently
AGREE with codegen, and they agree BY LUCK -- their f64 results happen to round
to the same bf16 as the properly-rounded ones for the inputs tried. They are
equally unrounded. So a fixture that pins only `exp` would pass before and after
and prove nothing; the fixture has to be `sqrt`, or a swept set of inputs.

Only `sqrt` diverges today. Arithmetic (`+ - * /`), `dot`, `reduce_*`, and the
lane-shuffling methods all agree.

CORRECTION (2026-08-29, on fixing) -- THIS ROW UNDERSTATED ITS OWN BLAST RADIUS.

The paragraph above ends "Only `sqrt` diverges today", and the one before it
warns that the other eight methods in the arm "AGREE BY LUCK OF THE INPUTS".
The first sentence is false and the second is half right, in a way that matters
for whoever writes the fixture.

Measured on `Vector[bf16, 4]` lanes of 1/2/3/7 and of 1/3, 1/7, 5/3, 1/9,
against all three compiled surfaces: `exp`, `ln`, `tanh` and `sigmoid` diverge
as well -- on inputs that ordinary, not on anything contrived. Five of the nine
methods were wrong, not one.

The four that DID agree are `floor` / `ceil` / `round` / `trunc`, and they agree
STRUCTURALLY rather than by luck: an integral result of a narrow-format input
already sits exactly on the narrow grid, so rounding it is a no-op. No choice of
inputs makes them diverge. So the trap this row flagged is real but was aimed at
the wrong four methods -- a fixture pinning `floor` would indeed have proved
nothing, while one pinning `exp` would have caught the bug immediately.

The row is also narrower than the defect in a second way: it is not bf16-only.
`Vector[f32, 4].sqrt()` had the same divergence (interpreter
1.4142135623730951, every compiled backend 1.4142135381698608). The arm's own
doc comment had declared that f32 gap acceptable, which is why it went unnoticed
-- the comment was describing the bug.

Finally, "Codegen is the CORRECT half here" is confirmed, with one caveat worth
recording: codegen is right about the WIDTH, which is what this row is about,
but the two backends still disagree in the last bit or two on
`exp`/`ln`/`tanh`/`sigmoid` at every width INCLUDING f64, where rounding is the
identity. That residual is codegen's Cephes polynomial against the interpreter's
exact libm -- a separate, long-documented question, untouched by the fix.
fix:
FIXED by 5f226ed. The interpreter's vector unary-math arm now rounds each
lane back to the receiver's ELEMENT width, which is what the scalar path has
done since B-2026-08-14-7.

THE FIX. In `src/interpreter/method_call_seq.rs`, the
`"sqrt" | "exp" | "ln" | "tanh" | "sigmoid" | "floor" | "ceil" | "round" | "trunc"`
arm now reads the receiver's element type ONCE from `vector_method_receivers`
(keyed by the call span -- the collision-proof channel the neighbouring
`to_bits` arm already used, and the right one here because the method-call node
has already overwritten this span in `expr_types` with the call's RESULT type),
then routes each lane's f64 result through the existing
`round_float_to_declared_size`. No new rounding code: that helper and the
`round_f64_via_bf16` / `round_f64_via_f16` it delegates to are the same ones the
narrowing CASTS use, which is what makes a value reaching a narrow lane by
computation and one reaching it by an explicit `as` land on the same bits.

This is the FOURTH site of one pattern, and the last one holding f64 bits in a
narrower slot: B-2026-07-22-4 took the narrowing casts, B-2026-08-05-31 the
tensor element-wise path (`round_tensor_elems`), and B-2026-08-14-7 the scalar
arithmetic plus scalar `sqrt` / `float_math`.

THE ROW UNDERSTATED THE BLAST RADIUS -- CORRECTED. It said "Only `sqrt` diverges
today" and warned that the other eight methods "AGREE BY LUCK OF THE INPUTS".
Measured on `Vector[bf16, 4]` lanes of 1/2/3/7 and of 1/3, 1/7, 5/3, 1/9:
`exp`, `ln`, `tanh` and `sigmoid` diverge too, on inputs that ordinary. Only
`floor`/`ceil`/`round`/`trunc` agreed, and they agree STRUCTURALLY rather than
by luck -- an integral result of a narrow-format input already sits exactly on
the narrow grid, so rounding it is a no-op. The trap the row warned about was
therefore real but aimed at the wrong four methods: a fixture pinning `floor`
would have proved nothing, while one pinning `exp` would have caught this. The
regression test pins all five non-integral methods.

NOT bf16-ONLY, either. The row's repro is bf16, but f32 had the same defect --
`Vector[f32, 4].sqrt()` returned the f64 1.4142135623730951 where every compiled
backend gives the f32 1.4142135381698608. The arm's own doc comment had declared
that gap acceptable ("an `f32` vector's low-order bits can differ, as for the
other float ops"); that sentence was describing the bug, and is now gone.

MEASUREMENT. A generated sweep of all nine methods over two 4-lane vectors at
each of bf16 / f16 / f32 / f64, compared across `karac run --interp`,
`karac run` (JIT), `karac build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` -- lines
on which the interpreter disagreed with the compiled backends:

    bf16   12 -> 0     (all four surfaces byte-identical)
    f16    13 -> 4
    f32    10 -> 7
    f64     4 -> 4     (untouched, by design -- see below)

The three COMPILED surfaces were byte-identical to each other before and after,
at every width; only the interpreter moved.

WHAT THE RESIDUAL IS, AND WHY IT IS NOT THIS BUG. The remaining f16/f32/f64
lines are `exp`/`ln`/`tanh`/`sigmoid` disagreeing in the last bit or two. That
is codegen's hand-written Cephes polynomial against this arm's exact f64 libm --
the gap the arm's doc comment has always described -- and it is independent of
width: it is the WHOLE of the f64 residual, where rounding is the identity and
cannot have changed anything. Narrowing merely hides it at bf16 (8 mantissa bits
swamp a 1-ULP f64 difference) and leaves it visible at f32. Closing it would
mean changing which approximation one of the two backends computes, a different
decision from carrying the right width, so it is deliberately left alone.

THE REGRESSION TEST AND ITS NEGATIVE CONTROL.
`tests/interpreter.rs::test_vector_unary_math_rounds_lanes_to_element_width`
pins the five non-integral methods at bf16 plus an f32 line and an f64 line --
the two boundaries, since f32 must round and f64 must NOT (a fix that
over-rounded would show as an f64 lane losing digits). With the fix stashed it
fails on 7 of its 8 lines, the f64 line being the one that correctly does not
move. `tests/codegen.rs::test_e2e_vector_unary_math_lane_width_matches_the_interpreter`
is its character-identical compiled twin; it does not fail without the fix
(codegen was right all along) and exists so the two halves cannot drift apart
again.

FILED SEPARATELY, NOT FOLDED IN -- both confirmed on a genuine `--features llvm`
build: B-2026-08-29-52 (printing a `Vector[T, N]` gives three different answers across
the three backends) and B-2026-08-29-53 (compiled `Vector[f16, N].tanh()` returns NaN
above ~5.5).

A VERIFICATION HAZARD MET TWICE IN ONE SESSION, both times the same shape -- a
measurement taken against a binary that was not the one under test:
  1. At the start `karac run` AGREED with `--interp`, appearing to refute the
     row outright. `karac_jit_runner` was 24 minutes older than `karac` (a
     `--bin karac`-only rebuild), so the JIT half was running pre-fix codegen.
     Rebuilding both bins reproduced the row exactly.
  2. Later a bare `cargo test` (no `--features llvm`) rebuilt
     `target/debug/karac` WITHOUT llvm, after which `karac build` silently fell
     back to type-check and `karac run` silently used the tree-walk. Two probes
     taken in that window were interpreter-vs-interpreter and showed spurious
     agreement. The tell was printed and initially skimmed past: "note: karac
     build requires the llvm feature; falling back to type check".
Both point at one rule: before believing an A/B result, confirm that the
binaries being compared are the ones you think they are AND that each is
actually the backend you named it.

title: The INTERPRETER computes `to_degrees` / `to_radians` / `cosh` at f64 and returns an f64-precision value whatever the receiver's width, so all three disagree with codegen on f32, f16 and bf16. `to_degrees` prints the same 17 digits for every width.
detail:
FOUND while A/B-ing B-2026-08-29-34's fix; PRE-EXISTING, and confirmed against a
pristine build of main with that fix stashed (identical values), so it is not
introduced by it. Codegen is the correct half.

MEASURED (x86_64, receiver 2.0, `karac run --interp` vs `karac run`):

    width  method       interp                    codegen
    f32    cosh         3.762195587158203         3.7621958255767822
    f32    to_degrees   114.59155902616465        114.59156036376953
    f32    to_radians   0.03490658503988659       0.03490658476948738
    f16    to_degrees   114.59155902616465        114.5625
    bf16   to_degrees   114.59155902616465        114.5
    f16    to_radians   0.03490658503988659       0.034912109375
    bf16   to_radians   0.03490658503988659       0.034912109375

The tell is in the left column: the interpreter prints THE SAME 17-digit value
for f32, f16 and bf16, i.e. the result never touches the receiver's width at
all. f64 agrees (there is nothing to round).

`cosh`'s f16/bf16 rows are absent above because codegen was returning garbage
for them until B-2026-08-29-42 was fixed in the same commit; they agree now.
`cosh` at f32 is a slightly different shape from the other two -- interp goes
through f64 `cosh` then rounds, codegen calls `coshf` -- so it is a last-ULP
disagreement rather than a missing narrowing, and may want a different answer
(decide which backend defines the result before changing either).

Low severity: the affected values are correct to within a rounding step, unlike
B-2026-08-29-42's garbage. It is still an A/B-rule violation, which the project
treats as non-negotiable, and a kata using `to_degrees` on an f32 would fail its
run-vs-build check today.
fix:
FIXED by 7c552c7. A scalar float method is now COMPUTED at the receiver's
declared width, not computed in f64 and rounded into it afterwards.

WHY ROUNDING WAS NOT ENOUGH -- THE ROW'S THREE METHODS SPLIT INTO TWO MECHANISMS.

  * `to_degrees` / `to_radians` never touched the width at all. Their arm
    (`recip` | `to_degrees` | `to_radians` | `fract` in
    `src/interpreter/method_call.rs`) returned a bare `Value::Float`, and its
    comment asserted codegen "replicates the same `fdiv`/`fmul` and constants,
    so `run == build` is bit-exact" -- true only at f64. That comment was
    describing the bug, the same way B-2026-08-29-40's arm comment did.
  * `cosh` DID round: it goes through `float_math`, which has called
    `round_float_to_span_width` since B-2026-08-14-7. Its residual is a SECOND
    mechanism -- computing in f64 and rounding to f32 is not the same as
    computing in f32, because two roundings are not one.

So the fix has to be "compute at the width", and rounding is then just the last
step. `eval_at_span_width` / `eval_at_span_width2` (src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs)
take the f64 and f32 function for one method and pick by the declared width;
`span_float_width` was split out of `round_float_to_span_width` (now a thin
wrapper on it) so callers can ask for the width rather than only for a rounding.
Every arm names both functions once -- `at_width!(cosh)` expands to
`f64::cosh` / `f32::cosh` -- so the two width paths cannot drift apart.

f16 / bf16 route through the f32 function and are then rounded to their own
width, which is exactly what codegen does for a half format (B-2026-08-29-42
sends them to the `f`-suffixed libm symbol). The two agree by construction
rather than by coincidence -- the structural-mirror rule B-2026-08-29-40 used.

THE ROW'S SET WAS INCOMPLETE, AND ONE MISS WAS THE LUCK-OF-THE-INPUTS TRAP.
`recip` shares the unrounded arm with `to_degrees`/`to_radians` and is equally
broken, but the row missed it: its receiver made `1/x` exactly representable.
Measured at 1/3 and 1/7 it diverges at bf16, f16 AND f32. That is the same trap
B-2026-08-29-40's row warned about and then fell into itself. `fract` and
`signum` share the arm too and are STRUCTURALLY exact -- `x - trunc(x)` of a
representable `x` is representable -- so they were never visibly wrong; they are
routed through the same helper anyway, so the arm no longer depends on which of
its methods happen to be exact.

The second mechanism also reached further than `cosh`: `sinh`, `log10` and
`atan` had the identical 1-ULP gap.

MEASUREMENT. 36 scalar float methods x 4 widths, and separately 23 unary methods
x 60 f32 inputs, across `karac run --interp` / `karac run` / `karac build` /
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`:

    surface sweep      before                                   after
    bf16               recip to_degrees to_radians               (none)
    f16                recip to_degrees to_radians               (none)
    f32                log10 recip to_degrees to_radians         asinh acosh atanh
    f64                (none)                                    (none)

    f32 x 60 inputs    32 diverging of 1380                      18 of 1380

All seven values the row tabulated now agree, and the interpreter prints exactly
the row's codegen column. The three compiled surfaces were identical to each
other before and after; only the interpreter moved.

WHICH BACKEND DEFINES THE RESULT -- THE ROW ASKED, AND IT IS ANSWERABLE.
The row said `cosh` at f32 "may want a different answer (decide which backend
defines the result before changing either)". Codegen does, on the measurement:
`rustc`-computed f32-native values match `karac run`'s output on 40 of 40 f32
samples across eight methods (the two apparently-differing lines are `0.0` vs
`0` formatting, not value), where f64-then-round matched 13 of 40. design.md's
rule -- operations happen at the declared width -- points the same way. So the
interpreter was the half to change, and no judgement call was left over.

WHAT REMAINS, AND WHY IT IS NOT THIS BUG. `asinh` (13/60), `acosh` (4/60) and
`atanh` (1/60) still differ at f32, and NEITHER path fixes them: against codegen,
f32-native scores 47/56/59 of 60 and f64-then-round scores 50/55/55. Rust's std
implements the inverse hyperbolics as Rust formulas rather than as libm calls, so
its `f32::asinh`, its `f64::asinh` and the `asinhf` codegen calls are three
different algorithms and no interpreter-side choice reproduces the third. Filed
as B-2026-08-29-60 rather than papered over with a per-method exception that would buy 3
matches in 180 and add a drift trap. The uniform rule is kept.

ALSO FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, FILED SEPARATELY: B-2026-08-29-61 -- `karac build`
constant-folds a compile-time-known f32 `cosh`/`sinh`/`log10` at a different
precision from the runtime call, so ONE AOT BINARY returns two different answers
for the same value.

AND A CROSS-REFERENCE FOR B-2026-08-29-56, recorded here because that row belongs
to another live session and must not be edited underneath it. The `--features
llvm` gate for this fix caught `selfhost_parser_matches_rust_parser_items`
failing with a double free. It is NOT caused by this work -- it fails identically
with `src/interpreter/` stashed -- and it is the same red oracle B-2026-08-29-56
already reports. What that row does not yet name is the culprit, so: BISECTED TO
c793ad0 (the B-2026-08-29-39 fix, "an annotated `let` records the binding's type,
not the literal's"). Each of the four upstream code commits was checked out and
rebuilt in turn -- `git checkout`, not `git archive`, so mtimes stamp and the
rebuild is real:

    2ce3507  PASS   fix(drop): mask a param view's Drop body per slot ...
    28ab271  PASS   fix(drop): a method's owned enum/Option arg drops ...
    c793ad0  FAIL   fix(typecheck): an annotated `let` records the binding's type
    baf2338  FAIL   fix(drop): one Drop body for an argument the callee hands back

The drop-family commits either side are clean, so it is not the drop work. The
mechanism is plausible: a binding's recorded type is what codegen consults to
decide whether a value is RC-managed and where its release goes, so changing
which type an annotated `let` records moves those decisions for any binding whose
annotation and initializer disagree.

FIXED by 131957b3. Both backends now mask exactly the param view's body and keep the fresh field's,
and the two legs landed in ONE commit as this row required.

THE DECLINE WAS CORRECT WHEN WRITTEN AND IS NOW OBSOLETE -- that is the whole
of the fix. B-2026-08-29-24 declined this shape because an own-`Drop` struct's
field bodies run inside the type-level `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper, and the only
surgery on it was `emit_user_drop_wrapper_without_field_bodies`, the
all-or-nothing variant. Masking a MIXED literal with that would have traded the
view's doubled body for the fresh field's MISSING one, the same severity in the
other direction.

`emit_user_drop_wrapper_skipping` is the per-field variant, and it has existed
since B-2026-08-28-21 -- it masks only the BODY step, leaving the parent's own
body and every field's MEMORY where they were. It was built for the caller-side
temp path and simply never wired to the let-path binding. So the fix adds a
`disarm_user_drop_field_bodies_masked` swap alongside the existing whole-wrapper
one and calls it for `owns_body && !all_views`. No new mechanism; the row's
premise had merely gone stale.

BOTH LEGS TOGETHER, WHICH THE ROW MADE A CONDITION. The interpreter's mask is
per field and always COULD have fixed this shape alone; it declined on purpose,
because doing so turns an agreed defect into a run-vs-build divergence -- the
trade B-2026-08-29-19 already had to back out once for `Option`. Its
`!all_views && has_own_drop` bail comes out in the same commit as codegen's
masked wrapper, so the two move together and never diverge in between.

MEASURED, 10 shapes on interp / jit / aot, `R { id, name: String }` so the
payload carries heap; valgrind 0 errors on every one:

    let s = Sd3 { a: r, b: mk(2) }        dSd3 dR2 dR1 dR1 -> dSd3 dR2 dR1
    let s = Sd3 { a: mk(2), b: r }        (order reversed) same
    3 fields, 1 view + 2 fresh            both fresh bodies survive
    3 fields, 2 views + 1 fresh           the fresh body survives
    view beside a NON-Drop field          dMix dR1
    read of the masked binding            rd2 dSd3 dR2 dR1
    two mixed literals in one frame       separate masks, no cross-talk

    BOUNDARIES, all unchanged: ALL-views (the shape -24 fixed), ALL-fresh
    (nothing masked), and MIXED over a struct with NO own `Drop` (the
    per-field path this fix does not touch).

Every row pins BOTH halves -- the view fires once AND the fresh field fires
once -- because the failure mode a fix here can introduce is the fresh body
going missing, not the view firing again. A fixture that only counted the view
would pass a fix that silenced everything.

MEMORY: unchanged and clean, as the row predicted ("the surplus is a body, not
a free"). The masked wrapper deliberately does not touch `emit_struct_drop_-
synthesis`, so every field's buffer is still released exactly once; valgrind
confirms it across all ten shapes.

TESTS: the two pins that held this shape at the defect --
`e2e_wrapped_param_view_nonenum_and_mixed_wraps_drop_once` and its interpreter
twin, case `pin-owndrop-mixed` -- FLIP, and their comments are rewritten rather
than deleted: what they recorded was true when written, and the reason it
stopped being true is the useful part. New coverage is
`codegen::e2e_mixed_owndrop_literal_masks_only_the_view_body` and
`interpreter::test_mixed_owndrop_literal_masks_only_the_view_body`, same 10
shapes in the same order. All FOUR red-verify against the stashed compiler --
both new tests and both flipped pins, on both backends -- so none of them is a
tautology.
title: A MIXED STRUCT LITERAL over a struct with its OWN `impl Drop` still runs a param view's `Drop` body TWICE -- `let s = Sd3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }` prints `dSd3 dR2 dR1 dR1` where `dSd3 dR2 dR1` is due; B-2026-08-29-24 fixed every other mixed wrap, and declined this one because such a struct's field bodies run inside the TYPE-LEVEL `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper, which can only be swapped for a variant that drops ALL of them
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-24, which fixed the mixed enum, mixed struct and
mixed tuple wraps and this one shape's ALL-VIEWS sibling.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    struct Sd3 { a: R, b: R }
    impl Drop for Sd3 { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dSd3") } }

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let s = Sd3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }; 7 }
      interp / jit / aot -> `dSd3 dR2 dR1 dR1 v=7`   ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong
    Due: `dSd3` once, `dR2` once, `dR1` once.

WHY IT WAS DECLINED. Every other mixed wrap has a PER-BINDING walker that
B-2026-08-29-24 could re-emit with one slot masked. A struct with its own
`impl Drop` has none: its field bodies run inside `karac_drop_<T>`, a
type-level function shared by every binding of the type, and the only existing
surgery on it is `emit_user_drop_wrapper_without_field_bodies` -- a variant
that drops ALL field bodies. That is what the ALL-VIEWS case uses
(`let s = Sd { r: r }` is fixed), and it is exactly wrong for a MIXED literal:
it would trade the view's doubled body for the fresh field's missing one, the
same severity in the other direction.

THE INTERPRETER DECLINES ON PURPOSE, and that is the part not to undo casually.
Its mask is per field, so `mask_param_view_struct_literal_fields` COULD fix
this shape on that backend alone -- and doing so turns an agreed defect into a
run-vs-build divergence, which is the worse of the two. B-2026-08-29-19 already
made and backed out that exact trade for `Option`. Whoever fixes this must land
the codegen leg -- a per-field masked WRAPPER variant, the
`emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping` treatment applied one level up -- in
the SAME commit as the interpreter's `!all_views && has_own_drop` bail.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT: the surplus is a body, not a free. ASAN/LSan clean.

Pinned at the defect in both suites, so a fix shows up as those failing:
`e2e_wrapped_param_view_nonenum_and_mixed_wraps_drop_once` and
`test_wrapped_param_view_nonenum_and_mixed_wraps_drop_once` (case
`pin-owndrop-mixed`).

fix:
FIXED by 6bf48fbc. The STRUCT and TUPLE spellings now inherit the wrap's mask across a rebind, on
both backends in one commit. The ENUM-CTOR spelling is deliberately left
agreed-but-wrong and filed separately -- see the trade below.

ATTEMPT-1'S RECORD WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE SHAPE AND WRONG ABOUT THE SITE, and
correcting that is what unblocked this. It concluded that the
`emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn` registration in `stmts.rs` "NEVER RAN" for the
destination, and pointed the next attempt at the OTHER call sites. Instrumenting
`track_user_drop_var_with_fn` with `#[track_caller]` shows the destination
registering at `stmts.rs:9087` -- the very site attempt 1 instrumented:

    [UD] var=s  fn=__karac_dropbodies_S3           @ stmts.rs:9087
    [UD] var=s  fn=__karac_dropbodies_S3$keep1$s0  @ control_flow_match.rs:8828
    [UD] var=s2 fn=__karac_dropbodies_S3           @ stmts.rs:9087   <- unmasked

So attempt 1's PREFERRED approach ("mask-aware registration is the right
shape") was correct as written and needed no new site. Its other dead end is
confirmed and preserved: disarm-after-register does not work at a `let`,
because the disarm helpers re-register rather than replace.

THE FIX. `transfer_move_masks_on_rebind` (both backends) copies the source
binding's masks to the destination -- copies, not moves, since the source is
still live for its own scope-exit walk. The struct site then builds its walker
through `field_skip_tree_for_var`, which B-2026-08-29-36 had already made the
single builder for all three mask kinds, so the walker is emitted ALREADY
masked. The tuple literal computed its view set from the expression and stored
nothing per variable; it now records as well as uses, which is what gives a
tuple rebind something to inherit.

SCOPED TO A BARE-IDENTIFIER RHS, and this is the half that had to be measured.
The first cut consulted the mask maps at EVERY struct `let`. Those maps are
name-keyed and accumulate across a whole function, so a FRESH binding inherited
a stale mask from an earlier move-out of the same name and silently lost a
body -- three existing move-out tests went red
(`test_e2e_struct_field_move_out_single_body_fire`,
`..._result_struct_payload_field_freed_and_single_body`,
`..._mixed_halves_result_struct_field_freed`). Gating on a rebind restores all
three. A name-keyed map read outside the one site that knows the names are
related is the general hazard here.

THE ENUM-CTOR SPELLING, AND WHY IT IS NOT FIXED. Transferring
`moved_out_enum_payload_slots` on a rebind makes the interpreter print the due
`dR2 dR1` for `let w = W2.Two(r, mk(2)); let w2 = w;`. Codegen cannot follow:
it derives a constructor's view slots from the ctor EXPRESSION at the `let` and
stores nothing per variable, so a rebind there has no mask to inherit. Landing
the interpreter half alone was MEASURED during this fix and produced
`dR2 dR1` against `dR1 dR2 dR1` -- an AGREED defect converted into a
run-vs-build divergence, the trade B-2026-08-29-19 was backed out for and the
one this row's own text forbids. Withheld, with the numbers recorded at the
withhold site so the absence reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

MEASURED, 8 shapes on interp / jit / aot, `R { id, name: String }` so the
payload carries heap; valgrind 0 errors on every one:

    let s = S3 { a: r, b: mk(2) }; let s2 = s;   dR2 dR1 dR1 -> dR2 dR1
    let t = (r, 5); let t2 = t;                  dR1 dR1     -> dR1
    ... rebound twice (s -> s2 -> s3)            dR2 dR1 dR1 -> dR2 dR1
    let w = W2.Two(r, mk(2)); let w2 = w;        dR1 dR2 dR1, UNCHANGED, agreed

    CONTROLS, unchanged: the same struct and tuple wraps WITHOUT a rebind, the
    ALL-VIEWS struct wrap WITH one (correct via view-ness propagation, the
    mechanism the mixed case lacks), and the enum wrap without a rebind.

TESTS: `codegen::e2e_whole_value_rebind_inherits_the_wrap_mask` and
`interpreter::test_whole_value_rebind_inherits_the_wrap_mask`, same shapes in
the same order, both RED-verified against the stashed compiler with the exact
signature (`dR2 dR1 dR1` against `dR2 dR1`). Each pins the enum shape at its
CURRENT agreed output, so a one-sided enum fix fails loudly on the other
backend instead of silently converging half the family.
title: A WHOLE-VALUE REBIND AFTER A MIXED WRAP RE-ARMS THE WALK THE MASK JUST WITHHELD -- `let w = W2.Two(r, R { id: 2 }); let w2 = w;` prints `dR1 dR2 dR1` where `dR2 dR1` is due, because B-2026-08-29-24's per-slot mask is keyed on the BINDING and the destination registers afresh with no mask
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-24. The ALL-VIEWS case has no such hole: it marks
the binding a param view, and view-ness propagates through a rebind
(B-2026-08-01-15), so `let s = S { r: r }; let s2 = s;` is correct. Only the
MIXED case, whose binding is not a view, loses its mask.

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let w = W2.Two(r, R { id: 2 }); let w2 = w; 7 }
      interp / jit / aot -> `dR1 dR2 dR1 v=7`   ALL THREE AGREE, all wrong
    Due: `dR2 dR1`.

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let s = S3 { a: r, b: R { id: 2 } }; let s2 = s; 7 }
      -> `dR2 dR1 dR1 v=7`, same shape through the struct literal.

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let t = (r, 5); let t2 = t; 7 }

Fixed in aa33534. TWO HALVES, matching the row's own split, on BOTH backends.

existing binding into a container literal armed the container's element-body
walk without retracting the source's own ownership, so the body ran at the
source's NLL death AND again through the walk. The `let` registration now
retracts each bare-identifier element source with the STRONG disarm
(`suppress_user_drop_for_var`), for the reason the aggregate arms of

`r` is a param VIEW whose body the CALLER runs, so the container must arm no

SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-24, whose row listed `let v2 = [r];` beside the
struct / tuple / `Some` wraps as another instance of the caller-retains
double. IT IS NOT ONE, and the triple below is what separates them:

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let v = [r]; 7 }                      -> dR1 dR1
    fn take() -> i64 { let m = R { id: 4 }; let v = [m]; 7 }     -> dR4 dR4

anywhere, so the cause cannot be caller-retains: it is a MOVE-SUPPRESSION hole

fix:
FIXED by 33f8781. One character of behaviour -- the argument walk in
`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` now runs `.rev()` -- and the rest of the work was
establishing that this is the direction design.md already requires, and that the
two neighbouring divergences it does NOT close are different bugs.

THE ROW ASKED FOR A SPEC DECISION THAT WAS ALREADY MADE, and its instinct about
which side to change was backwards. It says "deciding which is correct is a
design.md Drop ordering question and should be settled there before either side
is changed -- reversing the interpreter to match codegen is not obviously right,
since forward argument order is what a reader expects." design.md settles it in
two pieces that have to be read together, which is presumably why the row
reached for a new decision instead:

  * Temporary Lifetime Rules, the position table: "Function/method call argument
    | After the call returns". Both temps have the SAME live-range end, so the
    table alone cannot order them -- and it does not try to.
  * Drop ordering within a branch, rule 1: the unified drop+defer stack is "a
    single LIFO stack ordered by program-order of introduction". That is the rule
    that sequences co-expiring values, and the same section's Composition with
    drop ordering paragraph points at it explicitly ("this section determines
    WHEN a temporary's live range ends; drop ordering determines HOW multiple
    expiring temporaries are sequenced relative to each other").

Arguments are introduced left to right, so they pop right to left. The compiled
backends were right, no spec change was needed, and the "forward is what a reader
expects" intuition is the same one that would argue a block's `let` bindings
should drop in declaration order -- which rule 1 also rejects.

THE INTERPRETER WAS OUT OF STEP WITH ITSELF, WHICH IS THE STRONGER EVIDENCE. Its
own METHOD path was ALREADY reverse: `h.take(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 })` printed
`dR2 dR1` on all three backends before this commit, because a method's arguments
are claimed by the callee frame through `method_param_drop_names` and never reach
this walk (that asymmetry is why `owned_param_frame_is_method` exists). So the
divergence was not "the interpreter has a different ordering policy" -- it was one
walk, in one path, disagreeing with the same backend's other path. Pinned as the
`guard-method-*` cases, which were green before and after.

SCOPE IS NARROWER THAN THE LOOP SUGGESTS. `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` skips
identifier arguments outright -- a named binding drops through its own owner -- so
only calls with TWO OR MORE FRESH-TEMP arguments change. A mixed call is sequenced
by the two owners' relative program order and was already correct in both
directions, which is the point of the two `guard-mixed-*` cases:

    let a = R { id: 1 }; take(a, R { id: 2 })   ->  dR2 dR1   (reverse)
    let b = R { id: 2 }; take(R { id: 1 }, b)   ->  dR1 dR2   (FORWARD)

The second is not a bug and must not be "fixed": `b` is introduced first, so it
pops last. A blanket reverse-by-argument-position would break it, and a case list
of all-temp calls would not have noticed. The loop's non-firing bookkeeping (the
`moved_out_tuple_elem_bodies` inserts) is set-valued and order-independent, so
reversing it changes nothing there.

MEASURED, interp/jit/aot agreeing at each line after the fix and the interpreter
alone differing before it:

    take(R{1}, R{2})                         dR1 dR2      ->  dR2 dR1
    take3(R{1}, R{2}, R{3})                  dR1 dR2 dR3  ->  dR3 dR2 dR1
    fn take(r,q) { let z = R{3}; 7 }         dR3 dR1 dR2  ->  dR3 dR2 dR1
    take(mk(1), mk(2))                       dR1 dR2      ->  dR2 dR1

The callee-local case is the one that localizes the fault: `z`'s position was
already right and only the two params were forward, so a single walk was at
fault rather than the whole cleanup order.

NOT A MEMORY CHANGE. Only a body walk was reordered; no cleanup registration
moved. `asan_owned_param_temps_free_once` runs the two-, three- and mixed-argument
shapes with heap on every payload under LSan (live on Linux) and reports clean.

TWO NEIGHBOURING DIVERGENCES THIS DOES NOT CLOSE, both found while sweeping the
argument surface, both measured identical before and after this commit, and both
pinned on BOTH sides so each pair records the divergence rather than one backend's
half:

  * A STATIC (associated) function's fresh-temp arguments run NO body at all on
    JIT and AOT -- `H.s2(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 })` prints `v=7` alone against
    this backend's `dR2 dR1 v=7`. That is a lost body, strictly worse than a
    misordering, and a different mechanism: those temps never reach the caller

    and LSan is clean -- so the memory registration fires and only the user body
    is absent, the same body-vs-memory split B-2026-08-29-24 measured from the
    other direction. B-2026-08-29-54.
  * TIMING rather than order: the position table ends an argument temporary's
    live range "After the call returns", so in `take(R{1}, R{2}) + take(R{3},
    R{4})` the first call's temps must die before the second call's are built.
    The interpreter now does exactly that (`in-take dR2 dR1 in-take dR4 dR3`);
    the compiled backends hold all four to the statement's `;` (`in-take in-take
    dR4 dR3 dR2 dR1`), extending a temporary past the position rule's ceiling --
    the very thing the section's "NLL never EXTENDS a temporary's live range past
    the position-specific end" sentence forbids. Note this fix is what made the
    number diagnosable: before it, both backends were wrong in different ways and
    the shape read as more of the same ordering noise. B-2026-08-29-55.

title: TWO OWNED PARAMS' `Drop` BODIES RUN IN OPPOSITE ORDER ON THE TWO BACKENDS -- `fn take(r: R, q: R) -> i64 { 7 }` called with two fresh temps prints `dR1 dR2` under `--interp` and `dR2 dR1` under JIT and AOT; the COUNT is right on both, so only an output-order comparison sees it
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-24, and explicitly NOT caused by it -- the
divergence reproduces on a stashed-`src` pre-fix build, and the repro has no
wrap of any kind in it.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    fn take(r: R, q: R) -> i64 { 7 }
    fn main() { let v = take(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 }); println(f"v={v}"); }

      karac run --interp  -> `dR1 dR2 v=7`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `dR2 dR1 v=7`
      karac build         -> `dR2 dR1 v=7`

Both bodies fire at the same program point on both backends (after the call
returns, before the next statement), so this is not the sanctioned
NLL-vs-scope-exit timing difference B-2026-07-01-8's fix note set aside -- it is
the order WITHIN one drop point, forward on the interpreter and reverse on the
compiled backends.

parity gate is built to catch, and any kata whose two arguments both carry a
`Drop` body would differ between `karac run --interp` and `karac build`. It has
presumably survived because two owned Drop-bearing params in one call is rare
in the corpus.

WHERE TO START. The interpreter fires these from `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` in

question and should be settled there before either side is changed -- reversing
the interpreter to match codegen is not obviously right, since forward argument
order is what a reader expects.

fix:
FIXED by eec415a4. `let x = s.r` reads a caller-owned value back OUT of the place a
wrap put it into, and neither backend ever asked whether the DESTINATION should
register a `Drop` body. The move-out machinery was never the missing half: it
retracts the SOURCE correctly (B-2026-08-03-8), which is why the same statement
over a LOCAL source was already right. What was missing is that `x` inherits
nothing about the value being a param VIEW, so the caller's fire and `x`'s fire
were two.

WIDER THAN THE ROW, and measured so. `fn take(o: O) { let x = o.r; }` -- a field
read straight off a by-value param, no wrap anywhere -- doubles identically, as
does the two-hop `w.o.r`. So the subject is view-ness, not the wrap, and the fix
is stated at the chain ROOT rather than at the wrap.

BOTH BACKENDS, ONE COMMIT, and one of them was already split. The METHOD-frame
spelling was a live run-vs-build DIVERGENCE before this: the interpreter printed
the due `dR1` while all three compiled surfaces printed `dR1 dR1`, because a
method's arguments reach no caller-side fire (`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` is
wired into `eval_call` alone), so the interpreter's slot was the only one.
Fixing codegen converges it; the interpreter's arm inherits
`let_destructures_owned_param`'s existing method-frame bail, which is what keeps
that single body from going to zero. Landing the interpreter half without the
bail was measured here and gave ZERO bodies in a method frame.

MECHANISM. Each backend gains one record and one predicate:

  * `param_view_struct_fields` -- codegen's in `payload_vars` (name -> field
    names), the interpreter's a `(binding, field)` set -- written where the
    B-2026-08-29-24 wrap masker already computes its view set, and written
    BEFORE that masker's three branches return, since they mask by three
    different routes and only this record is common to all of them.
  * `field_move_out_source_is_param_view` / `let_reads_param_view_field` --
    walk the initializer's chain to its root and answer: is the ROOT a param
    view (which settles ANY depth, since everything reachable through a view is
    a view), or was the FIRST hop off it recorded above? The second arm is what
    covers the two wraps that never become views themselves -- a MIXED literal,
    which still owns its fresh fields, and a wrap over a struct with its own
    `impl Drop`, whose body is the binding's own.

The retraction routes differ because the backends' registrations do: codegen
calls `suppress_user_drop_for_var` (which retracts the `UserDrop` action alone,
leaving every memory action in place), while the interpreter returns `true` from
`let_destructures_owned_param` so `push_drops_for_stmt` never registers. Both
also propagate view-ness onto the destination, so a later `let y = x;` inherits
the withholding instead of re-arming it.

MEASURED, four surfaces x fifteen shapes (`e2e_param_view_field_moved_back_out_runs_one_body`
and its interpreter twin). The row's own shape and nine relatives go from two
bodies to the due one; five controls over a LOCAL source, and the one that
matters most -- moving the FRESH field out of a mixed wrap -- are unchanged,
which is what keeps the fix from being a blunt instrument. Valgrind clean before
and after: this was always a body count, never a memory defect.

TWO REMAINDERS, both filed rather than folded in. The TUPLE spelling
(`let t = (r, 5); let x = t.0;`) still doubles on all four surfaces -- agreed,
so a gap and not a split -- because a tuple literal masks per index and never
marks its binding a view, leaving the predicate nothing to find; it needs the

still divergent, the interpreter losing the fresh field's body to a coarse
whole-walk disarm that shadows its own per-field mask; that split PREDATES this
fix and is strictly narrower after it (i[`dR1 dR1`] vs c[`dR1 dR2 dR1`] became
i[`dR1`] vs c[`dR2 dR1`]).
title: MOVING A PARAM VIEW BACK OUT OF THE STRUCT IT WAS JUST WRAPPED INTO DOUBLES ITS `Drop` BODY -- `let s = S { r: r }; let x = s.r;` prints `dR1 dR1` where one is due, because the move-out destination registers its own body while the caller still fires; the same shape with a LOCAL source is correct
