One `Res { id: 7 }` exists and its body runs twice: once caller-side at the
argument's live-range end, once at `v`'s. (`drop 0` is the displaced
initializer and is correct.)

The DIRECT spelling is right, which is what localizes it:

    match b { Full(r) => { return r; } Empty => { .. } }   ->  one body

So the escape predicates -- `fn_returns_param_payload` and codegen's
`callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` -- recognize a payload returned STRAIGHT out
of the arm and miss one that reaches the return through an intervening local.
The caller therefore keeps its walk while the result's binding also owns the
value.

Agreed on both backends, so this is invisible to the A/B rule and was found
only by asking whether the COUNT was right, not whether the two agreed. Worth
noting as a method for this family: unanimity is not correctness.

Not a memory defect -- bodies only, valgrind-clean.

WHERE TO START: `crate::ast::fn_returns_param_payload` matches an arm whose
TAIL or `return` is the bound payload. It needs the dataflow one step further:
a payload assigned to a local that is itself returned. `fn_returns_param` has
the same shape for the whole-param case and should be checked for the same
hole.

ID NOTE: first filed as B-2026-08-29-43, which a sibling session had already
taken while this one was running its gates. Renumbered before the push; no
other row cites the old id.
fix:
FIXED in d135d02. The row's diagnosis was RIGHT, and its pointer
(`fn_returns_param_payload` needs the dataflow one step further) was the fix
almost verbatim -- which is worth saying, because the two rows before it in this
family both had to be retracted.

WHAT THE PREDICATE COULD NOT SEE, and why it is scope rather than oversight.
`grow_aliases` already follows a payload out of an arm through a `let`
(`let k = r; return k;`). The assignment spelling defeats it because BOTH ENDS
of the route sit outside the arm: `out` is declared before the `match` and the
`return out;` comes after it, while the walk only ever looks inside the arm
body. So the arm's assignment TARGETS now come back out to the caller, which
asks the whole function body whether their roots leave
(`assigned_roots` / `escapes_by_assignment`). Place roots are followed through
field, tuple-index and index projections, so `h.inner = r` escapes when `h`
does; `MultiAssign` needs no handling because desugar rewrites it into `let`
temps plus single `Assign`s before any consumer sees the program.

ONE PREDICATE, BOTH BACKENDS. Codegen reaches it through
`callee_returns_enum_arg_payload`, so the single change moves method and free
function, user enum and `Option`, together: all four combinations measured at
two bodies before and one after, byte-identical to the direct `return r`
spelling of the same callee. The `if let` leg got the same treatment as
`match`, and is pinned.

THE ROW'S SCOPE WAS NARROWER THAN THE DEFECT. It presents the shape as a
method (`impl T { fn take(ref self, b: Box2) -> Res }`), and the FREE-FUNCTION
twin doubles identically -- so this never was a method-path defect, and the
method framing would have sent the next reader to `method_call.rs` as
B-2026-08-29-10's did. Both spellings are rows in both fixtures.

MEASURING IT NEEDED A CALLEE LOCAL. `let loc = R { .. }` used after the match
sits between the two candidate firing points, so the fixtures pin the PLACE and
not only the count -- a body fired at the arm lands before `mid9`, one at callee
scope exit between `mid9` and `dR9`, and the caller-side fire after `dR9`. The
payload must also carry HEAP for the codegen leg to bite, the same precondition
B-2026-08-29-10 recorded.

THE CONSERVATIVE-TRUE COST IS UNCHANGED AND SHARED. On a callee that returns
the payload on one path and a fresh value on another, the caller now stands
down on both, so the die-inside path loses the body. That is the union trade
`fn_returns_param_payload` has always documented, and it was measured on the
DIRECT spelling too before accepting it here: `fn d(b: Box2, flag: bool) -> Res
{ if flag { return Res { id: 5, .. }; } match b { Full(r) => { return r } .. } }`
called with `flag = true` loses the argument's body on every surface, exactly as
the assign spelling now does. So this fix does not widen that class -- it makes
the two spellings agree, including where the union is already known to
over-approximate.

THE BOUNDARY IN THE OTHER DIRECTION is pinned as
`control-assigned-but-not-returned`: a payload assigned to an outer local the
callee does NOT return dies inside, and the callee's own scope drop is the
single body. The predicate must stay false there and does.

Valgrind-clean throughout -- bodies only, as the row said.

FIXTURES RED-VERIFIED against the pre-fix compiler: codegen
`dR0 mid9 dR9 dE dR8 v8 dR8 post` and interpreter the same string, each with
the extra `dR8` this fix removes.

RESIDUALS split out rather than folded in, both found while building the
controls: B-2026-08-29-57 (`return out` as a block's FINAL EXPRESSION, with no
trailing semicolon, makes the interpreter run the returned local's body twice --
the same function with `return out;` is correct, and so is the bare tail) and
B-2026-08-29-58 (a payload assigned to an outer local the callee does not return
runs one extra body on the interpreter). B-2026-08-29-59 is not a defect in this
family at all but the reason the row's "all four surfaces" phrasing needs care:
`karac run` does not reach the JIT lane in this container, so it is a second
interpreter reading rather than a third backend.

SHA NOTE: this note first cited `a6f6572`, the commit's identity before a
rebase onto the sibling commits that landed while these gates ran. That SHA is
orphaned; the live commit is `d135d02`. `bug-lint.sh` cannot catch this class --
its fix-SHA resolvability check is skipped on the shallow clone these sessions
run in, so a stale pointer lints clean.

title: An argument the callee STORES into an outliving place (`fn take(sink: mut ref Vec[Res], r: Res) { sink.push(r); }`) runs the value's `Drop` body ONE TIME TOO MANY when the argument is a NAMED BINDING -- the fresh-temp spelling of the same callee, compiled once, is correct, so one call site's spelling decides it. NOT method-specific and not about enums, as filed: a second, independent hole makes `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` blind to a payload bound out of the param by a `match`, which is what breaks the enum and method spellings (and even the fresh-temp one). Unanimous on all four surfaces, so A/B-invisible
detail:
The other control that came out of B-2026-08-29-10's boundary set.

    impl T { fn take(ref self, sink: mut ref Vec[Res], b: Box2) {
        match b { Full(r) => { sink.push(r); } Empty => { } }
    } }
    // caller: t.take(mut sink, carg); println(f"pushed {sink.len()}");

      all four surfaces -> `drop 7` / `pushed 1` / `drop 7`

The payload is pushed into `sink` and lives on -- `sink.len()` is 1 -- so the
FIRST body runs over a value that did not die. The second, at `sink`'s own
drain, is the correct one.

`fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` is the predicate meant to cover exactly
this (B-2026-08-26-9), and B-2026-08-29-10 wired it into the METHOD caller's
stand-down. The stand-down is evidently reached -- without it the count would
be higher -- so the remaining fire is the PAYLOAD walk rather than the
whole-arg one: the argument is disarmed as a value while the walk over its
payload still runs.

Unanimous across interp / jit / AOT / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, so no A/B gate reports
it; found by counting against the free-function oracle instead. MEASURE THE
FREE-FN SPELLING FIRST -- if it is also 2, this is not method-specific and the
row should be rescoped.

Not a memory defect -- bodies only, valgrind-clean.

ID NOTE: first filed as B-2026-08-29-44, which a sibling session had already
taken while this one was running its gates. Renumbered before the push; no
other row cites the old id.
fix:
FIXED by 0343db57.

RESCOPED FIRST: not method-specific. The row's own instruction -- "MEASURE THE
FREE-FN SPELLING FIRST -- if it is also 2, this is not method-specific and the
row should be rescoped" -- fires. The free-function spelling counts 2
identically on all four surfaces, and so does a shape with no enum in it at all
(`fn take(sink: mut ref Vec[Res], r: Res) { sink.push(r); }`).

TWO INDEPENDENT HOLES, both ending in a second body over a value that did not
die. Neither is the mechanism the row guessed ("the argument is disarmed as a
value while the walk over its payload still runs").

HOLE 1 -- an IDENTIFIER argument never consulted the escape predicate.
`fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` has existed since B-2026-08-26-9 and says
exactly the right thing about the callee above. Only the FRESH-TEMP registrar
ever asked it. An identifier arg is skipped by `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` ("the
caller binding's own NLL drop covers those") and drops through its own binding,
which consulted nothing -- so ONE callee, compiled ONCE, gave two answers
depending on how the argument was SPELLED at the call:

    take(mut sink, Res { id: 1 });      `pushed 1 | drop 1`             one body
    let c = Res { id: 2 };
    take(mut sink, c);                  `drop 2 | pushed 1 | drop 2`    two

Both call sites in ONE program is the sharpest form: the extra body lands
between the two markers, where only the named call could have produced it.

HOLE 2 -- the predicate is blind to a payload bound OUT of the param. `moves()`
matches by NAME, so `match b { Full(r) => sink.push(r) }` stores `r` and never
`b`, and the predicate answered false for a value that plainly escapes. With it
blind, even the FRESH-TEMP enum spelling ran two bodies -- so hole 1's fix alone
leaves the row's own repro broken, which is why the two are recorded separately
and have separate regression legs.

The row's METHOD repro fails by a THIRD route built out of hole 2: the method
caller already stands down on every by-value arg (B-2026-08-29-11), so there it
is the callee FRAME that fires -- `method_param_drop_names` skips a param only
where the predicate is true, and hole 2 made it false. The row's reading that
"the stand-down is evidently reached ... so the remaining fire is the PAYLOAD
walk" is right about the method and wrong about the free function, where no
stand-down is reached at all; that split is what made one mechanism look like a
method-only defect.

WHOSE BODY IT IS was settled by printing at the callee's exit and after the
call. `callee-end | drop 7 | after-call` puts the extra fire in the CALLER's
post-call argument drop, and the fresh-temp spelling of the same callee has
none -- which is what rules out every callee-side explanation.

THE FIX -- five edits, symmetric across both backends:
 * `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` (src/ast/items.rs) gains
   `stores_via_destructure`: an arm's payload binding counts as the param when,
   and only when, the scrutinee is the BARE param. `if let` likewise. A
   projection (`match b.inner`) does not, the same line `moves` already draws.
 * `compile_call`'s identifier-arg gate (call_dispatch.rs) admits the
   store-into-an-outliving-place route beside the two return routes.
 * `callee_takes_over_arg_drop_body` admits it too -- the value's new HOME is
   the other frame that runs the body, the same guarantee the two return
   predicates give.
 * `record_passthrough_arg_moves` (interpreter) gains the same route, and it
   licenses the WHOLE-VALUE disarm, not only the container-walk one.
 * the method spelling of the container-walk disarm (method_call.rs) matches.

MEASURED, 17 shapes x {interp, JIT, AOT, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0}: all four surfaces
agree on every shape, and every unconditional-store shape runs exactly one body.
Heap-carrying payloads (`Res { id: i64, tag: String }`), free-fn and method
alike, are valgrind-clean -- 0 errors, no definite or indirect loss.

A DOUBLE THE ROW DID NOT NAME is fixed with it: a CONDITIONAL store, on the path
where it FIRES (`if r.id > 100 { sink.push(r); }`, id=200), printed
`drop 200 | pushed 1 | drop 200` for the named spelling -- a genuine double body
over an object living in `sink` -- while the temp spelling of the same callee
was already correct.

RESIDUAL, split out rather than buried: on the path where a conditional store
does NOT fire, the body is now LOST, on both spellings. No per-callee static
predicate can be right on both paths, and the predicate documents the
leak-over-double-free lean it answers with. Before this the two spellings were
wrong in OPPOSITE directions -- named DOUBLED when the store fired, temp LOST
when it did not -- so the change makes them uniform in the documented direction.
Measured pre-fix: the temp spelling already lost that body (pre-existing since
B-2026-08-26-9), the named spelling did not (new here).
 Split out as B-2026-08-30-28,
which carries the measurement table for both sides of the fix and the shape a
real per-path fix needs.

title: A param moved into a RETURNED AGGREGATE (`fn wrapf(r: Res) -> Hh { Hh { r: r } }`), and a CONDITIONALLY-returned param on BOTH its paths, still run the user `Drop` body TWICE for one object -- the two shapes B-2026-08-29-15's bare hand-back fix deliberately declined. Both AGREE across interp/JIT/AOT, so no A/B gate can see either
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-29-15 rather than buried in it: that row fixed the BARE
hand-back (`fn take(r: Res) -> Res { r }` / `{ return r; }`) and deliberately
declined these two neighbours, so the remainder needs its own queue entry.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }

    // (A) AGGREGATE RETURN
    struct Hh { r: Res }
    fn wrapf(r: Res) -> Hh { return Hh { r: r }; }
    fn main() { let a = Res { id: 41, name: f"e" }; let h = wrapf(a);
                println(f"{h.r.id}"); }
      interp / jit / aot -> `drop 41` / `41` / `drop 41`   AGREE, two bodies
                                                          for ONE object.

    // (B) CONDITIONAL CALLEE -- doubles on BOTH paths, for different reasons
    fn pick(r: Res, k: bool) -> Res { if k { return Res { id: 98, name: f"z" }; } r }
    fn main() { let a = Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" }; let x = pick(a, true);
                println(f"{x.id}");
                let b = Res { id: 5, name: f"e5" }; let y = pick(b, false);
                println(f"{y.id}"); }
      interp / jit / aot, all three identical:
        `drop 7` `drop 7` / `7 -> 98` / `drop 98` / `drop 5` / `5` / `drop 5`
      k=true  (param dies inside): the CALLER fires and the callee's own
              registration fires -- two bodies.
      k=false (param handed back):  the CALLER fires and the RESULT binding
              fires -- two bodies, the same shape B-2026-08-29-15 fixed for an
              unconditional callee.

Both AGREE across backends and both are at the wrong count, so the kata A/B gate
is structurally blind to them -- the same point B-2026-08-29-15 was right to
emphasise, and the reason these are worth a row rather than a footnote.

WHY -15 DECLINED THEM, and what has changed since.

(A) was declined because `call_dispatch`'s container-only narrowing records a
MEASURED 3-byte definite leak for exactly this shape when the caller's whole
`karac_drop_<T>` action is retracted: the param acquires a NEW owner (`Hh`), the
caller's slot is still the sole MEMORY owner, and removing the action removes the
free along with the body. `fn_always_returns_param_bare` therefore declines any
aggregate, which is what keeps that leak avoided.

That obstacle is now smaller than it was. B-2026-08-29-15 added
`suppress_user_drop_body_keeping_memory` (src/codegen/runtime.rs), which
DOWNGRADES the action to the field-cleanup-only `__karac_drop_struct_<T>` instead
of removing it -- body gone, memory kept. It was written for the bare case, where
the same leak appeared (13 allocs / 13 frees to 12 / 11 under the removing form,
back to 12 / 12 under the downgrade). Whether it transfers to the aggregate case
is NOT MEASURED and must not be assumed: the aggregate's field cleanup runs
through the CONTAINING struct's drop, so the two owners are nested rather than
parallel, and a downgrade could double-free where it merely un-leaked before. The
experiment is cheap -- widen the gate at the two arg loops from
`fn_always_returns_param_bare` to `fn_always_returns_param`, then re-run
`asan_named_arg_returned_bare_is_memory_balanced`, whose `wrap` case exists
precisely to catch this.

(B) is declined by BOTH escape predicates and that is load-bearing, not an
oversight. `fn_always_returns_param` sees the `return Res { id: 98 }` and answers
false; `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` needs some leaf tail that does NOT
mention the param, and this body's only tail IS the param, so it answers false
too. The caller consequently keeps firing on every path. That is what makes the
`k = false` path a duplicate against the result binding; on `k = true` the
duplicate is against the CALLEE's own registration instead, since a callee no
predicate admits keeps its param in `cond_returned_param_drop_names` and fires it
when the param dies inside. So both paths double, by two different second owners
-- which is why neither "stand the caller down" nor "stop the callee registering"
fixes this alone. Doing the first unconditionally would trade the `k = true`
double for a LOST body, the exact regression B-2026-08-28-22 documents with a
measurement. A fix plausibly needs the per-path flag (B-2026-08-28-51) extended to
a callee whose escaping path is a block TAIL and whose dying path is a `return` --
the combination `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` explicitly declines today
(its condition 2 wants some leaf tail that does not mention the param, and here
the only tail IS the param).

NOT MEASURED, and stated rather than implied: whether either double body is
accompanied by a second FREE. Both programs are valgrind-clean at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (A: 13 allocs / 13 frees, 0 errors; B: 20 / 20, 0 errors), so
neither is a double free today -- but that is a measurement of the current
lowering, not a proof that the extra body is harmless, and a user `Drop` body with
side effects runs twice either way.

SOURCE NOTE: found and measured while fixing B-2026-08-29-15; the four boundary
controls there are byte-identical before and after that fix, so these two counts
are pre-existing and unmoved by it.
fix:
FIXED by 7b23317. Both shapes now run exactly one `Drop` body per object
on interp, JIT and AOT alike, and BOTH of this row's stated obstacles turned out
to be wrong -- one about memory, one about what a predicate answers.

(A) THE AGGREGATE. This row said the downgrade's transfer to the aggregate was
"NOT MEASURED and must not be assumed", because "the aggregate's field cleanup
runs through the CONTAINING struct's drop, so the two owners are nested rather
than parallel, and a downgrade could double-free where it merely un-leaked
before". Measured, they are PARALLEL. The reason is a fact neither -15 nor this
row had established: passing an own-heap struct BY VALUE already deep-copies its
heap fields. With a 256-element `Vec[i64]` field, against the same program with
no call at all (10 allocs / 8,218 bytes):

    param dies inside the callee    11 allocs / 10,266 bytes
    bare hand-back                  11 allocs / 10,266 bytes
    moved into a returned aggregate 11 allocs / 10,266 bytes   (+2,048 each)

So the caller's slot holds its OWN buffer, distinct from the one the returned
`Hh` owns, and the downgraded field cleanup frees exactly that. Post-fix the
aggregate reads `13 allocs / 13 frees, 0 errors, no definite loss` under
valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` -- byte-identical to the bare spelling's
`13 / 13` -- and passes ASAN+LSan. The 3-byte leak this row cites is real and
belongs to the REMOVING form (`suppress_user_drop_for_var`); the stand-down has
downgraded rather than removed since -15, so it no longer applies.

(B) THE CONDITIONAL. This row said `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` "needs
some leaf tail that does NOT mention the param, and this body's only tail IS the
param, so it answers false too", and built its whole suggested approach on that
(extending the per-path flag of B-2026-08-28-51). It answers TRUE. The predicate's
condition 4 collects every `return` OPERAND as an additional exit leaf, so
`return R { id: 98 }` is the non-mentioning leaf the row thought was missing.
Checked directly against the parsed AST rather than reasoned about:

    pick: returns=true always=false cond_bare=TRUE payload=false outliving=false

That inverts the fix. The callee ALREADY owns the body on the dies-inside path
(`cond_returned_param_drop_names`, gated on this same predicate); the caller was
simply firing on top of it. So no new per-path machinery was needed -- the caller
stands down on exactly the set the callee picks up.

THE FIX, one rule replacing two. The caller's own `Drop` body stands down when
SOME OTHER FRAME is guaranteed to run it on EVERY path, which is the union of:

  * `fn_always_returns_param` -- every exit hands the argument back, so the
    RESULT BINDING owns it. Bare or wrapped in a returned aggregate alike.
  * `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` -- some exits hand it back (result
    binding owns it), the rest let it die inside (CALLEE FRAME owns it).

Exactly one owner either way, which is what keeps this clear of B-2026-08-28-22:
an UNCONDITIONAL stand-down loses the dies-inside body, and this is not that.

`fn_always_returns_param_bare` is REMOVED and the family folds back to one
predicate. It was introduced by -15 to keep the aggregate out, its documented
justification was the 3-byte leak, and that justification no longer describes the
code. Leaving a `pub` predicate whose only stated reason is a superseded
measurement is worse than deleting it. Four call sites -- two per backend --
now ask the union: `record_passthrough_arg_moves` / `record_method_arg_moves` in
the interpreter, and `callee_takes_over_arg_drop_body` (renamed from
`callee_always_returns_arg_bare`) at the free-fn and method arg loops in codegen.

A THIRD DEFECT FOUND WHILE PINNING THIS, AND FIXED HERE: a RUN-VS-BUILD
divergence, the one shape in this family an A/B gate CAN see. `may_mention`
answered its conservative `true` for `ExprKind::SelfValue`, so a method whose
non-param exit merely interpolates a field of self --
`return R { name: f"z{self.n}" }` -- was declined by the predicate. Measured on
the PRE-FIX compiler, that shape already split: the interpreter ran two bodies
for the dies-inside path where the compiled backends ran one. A method's
receiver is never one of `f.params`, so `SelfValue => false` is sound by
construction; with it, both paths of that method run one body and all three
backends agree. Pinned in `asan_conditionally_returned_arg_is_memory_balanced`,
whose `T4.pick` interpolates `self.n` for exactly this reason -- drop the
`SelfValue` arm and the interpreter and AOT legs disagree again.

AN OVERREACH IN -15's OWN PROSE, CORRECTED IN FOUR PLACES. That row's fix, and
the comments it wrote into `call_dispatch.rs`, `record_method_arg_moves`,
`tests/codegen.rs` and `tests/interpreter.rs`, concluded from the named-vs-fresh-temp
byte-identity that "there is no entry copy". The identity is real and the
conclusion drawn from it -- that the copy cannot be what makes the two spellings'
body counts differ -- is right, but "no entry copy exists" is not: the measurement
above shows every by-value call makes one. The accurate argument, now written in
all four places, is that the FRESH-TEMP control entry-copies identically and has
always run ONE body, and nobody has called that wrong -- so the copy is a
lowering artifact of a move, not a second user-visible object for `Drop` to
observe. The tree models that copy extensively (`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct`,
`consume_class`'s non-consuming classification), which is why leaving "no entry
copy exists" standing would have misled the next reader of any of them.

VERIFICATION. RED-verified on the pre-fix compiler: all five new behaviour cases
(aggregate free / aggregate method / aggregate TUPLE / conditional free /
conditional method) printed two bodies on interp, JIT and AOT alike, and all
three AGREED while wrong -- so no A/B gate could have reported any of them.
Post-fix all five print one, on all three. Fixtures:
`test_named_arg_returned_bare_user_drop_body_runs_once` (tests/interpreter.rs)
and `e2e_named_arg_returned_bare_user_drop_body_runs_once` (tests/codegen.rs),
sharing expectations verbatim; memory pinned by
`asan_conditionally_returned_arg_is_memory_balanced` (new) and by the corrected
`wrap` row of `asan_named_arg_returned_bare_is_memory_balanced`, whose
two-body expectation this row's fix inverts. That ASAN row still fails in the
LEAK direction if the stand-down is ever widened back to the removing form.
The tuple case is there because `yields` recurses into tuple literals as well as
struct ones, so a `StructLiteral`-only fix passes the other two aggregate rows.

NOT FIXED, and filed rather than buried: the by-value deep copy itself
(B-2026-08-29-63). It is orthogonal to the body count -- present with and
without a `Drop` impl, and on callees that return the param, wrap it, or just
read a field -- but it is a real per-call cost in a move language and this row is
where it was measured.

title: A self-assignment whose RHS is a BLOCK ending in a passthrough call leaks the argument's heap -- `e = { let z = 1; pass(e) };` loses the `String` (13 allocs / 12 frees, 2 bytes definitely lost) while the unwrapped `e = pass(e);` is clean. PRE-EXISTING (identical at d90b61f), and invisible to the A/B gate twice over: both backends agree AND the printed output is correct
detail:
PRE-EXISTING, and confirmed so by direct measurement rather than assumed: the
same program leaks identically at d90b61f (before B-2026-08-29-15) and after it.

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    fn pass(r: R) -> R { return r; }
    fn main() {
        let mut e = R { id: 7, name: f"e7" };
        e = { let z: i64 = 1; println(f"z{z}"); pass(e) };
        println(f"use {e.id}");
    }

    valgrind --leak-check=full, KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0:
      13 allocs, 12 frees, ERROR SUMMARY: 1, definitely lost: 2 bytes in 1 block
    Output `z1 / use 7 / drop 7` is CORRECT -- one body for one object. Only the
    heap is wrong: the `String` "e7" is never freed.

The control is the same assignment WITHOUT the block wrapper, which is clean:

    e = pass(e);          ->  12 allocs, 12 frees, 0 errors, no loss

So the block is the whole difference. Both spellings store the callee's result
back into `e`, and both print one body; only the wrapped one strands the buffer.

WHY IT IS WORTH A ROW. The leak is small and the shape is uncommon, but the two
programs are semantically identical and one of them is right, so this is a
lowering discrepancy rather than a design question -- the kind that is cheap to
fix once someone knows where to look and expensive to rediscover. It is also
invisible to the A/B gate twice over: both backends agree, AND the observable
output is CORRECT on both. Only a memory check finds it, which is why it survived
until a leak sweep ran across this shape.

WHERE TO LOOK, from the neighbouring work rather than from a diagnosis (this was
NOT root-caused -- stated plainly so nobody treats the pointer as a finding):
B-2026-08-29-15 established that for a by-value struct argument the CALLER's slot
is the sole memory owner, and that a self-assignment must keep its cleanup action
because the binding goes on to own the returned value. `DropRc::assign_ident_target`
is set by an assignment and inherited by the statements compiled inside its RHS,
so the guard itself reaches the block form -- verified: the fixed compiler
produces exactly the pre-fix numbers here, so the suppression is NOT firing and
the leak predates and outlives that mechanism. The likelier neighbourhood is the
block-tail cleanup path (`suppress_block_tail_cleanup` and the tail-temp handling
around it), where the block's own frame drains between the tail's value being
produced and the assignment's store.

NOT MEASURED: whether the same leak appears for a `let` (rather than an
assignment) whose RHS is a block ending in a passthrough call, and whether an
enum or container payload leaks the same way or more.

SOURCE NOTE: found while checking whether B-2026-08-29-15's self-assignment guard
survived a statement nested inside an assignment's RHS. It does; this leak is a
different and older defect that the probe happened to walk into.
fix:
FIXED by 2378582, which makes `assign_rhs_is_owned_user_call` match the RHS's
VALUE-PRODUCING TAIL rather than only a bare `Call` at the root:

    let ExprKind::Call { callee, .. } = &value.kind else { return false };

`e = { let z = 1; pass(e) };` arrives as an `ExprKind::Block`, so that `else`
fired, `roundtrip_frees_old` was false, and -- because `rhs_mentions_lhs` is
true -- the caller's ENTIRE overwrite-cleanup branch
(`(!rhs_mentions_lhs || roundtrip_frees_old)`) was skipped. The old value's
field heap was never freed. A new `assign_rhs_value_tail` peels `Block` / `Seq`
/ `Unsafe` to their final expression, recursively.

The IR says it in two lines. Control (`e = pass(e)`), correct:

    %call = call @pass(%e4)
    call void @__karac_drop_struct_R(ptr %e)
    store %call, ptr %e

Block form, pre-fix:

    %call = call @pass(%e19)
    store %call, ptr %e                  <- no drop of the overwritten value

The row's own pointer was to `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` and the block-tail
cleanup path; it is honestly labelled a guess ("this was NOT root-caused") and
it was the wrong neighbourhood. The block frame drains fine -- the assignment
simply never asks for the cleanup, because a one-line pattern match does not see
through a wrapper. Recorded because the row's advice would have sent a reader to
the wrong file.

BOTH "NOT MEASURED" ITEMS ANSWERED, with valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:

  * A `let` (rather than an assignment) whose RHS is a block ending in a
    passthrough call does NOT leak -- 12 allocs / 12 frees. It creates a new
    binding, so there is no old value to free and nothing to skip.

  * An enum payload leaks the same way, and a multi-field struct leaks MORE --
    one lost block PER heap field. Pre-fix / post-fix:

        two `String` fields   14/12, 2 errors  ->  14/14, 0
        enum `String` payload 10/9,  1 error   ->  10/10, 0
        no `impl Drop` at all 11/10, 1 error   ->  11/11, 0

    The last one also widens the row: the leak is not limited to Drop-declaring
    types, which the fixture's `impl Drop` made easy to assume.

THE LEAK IS OPTIMIZATION-DEPENDENT, which the row did not state and which
explains both its low severity and its survival. The test fixture loses 7 blocks
at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (36 allocs / 29 frees) and is CLEAN at the default `-O2`
(22/22), where LLVM deletes the redundant allocation outright. A release build
never showed it. The regression test therefore carries its MEMORY assertion on
the `-O0` leg (`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`, B-2026-08-04-17) -- verified red there
pre-fix with `ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks` and green after --
while the default `-O2` leg still asserts the OUTPUT, so a leak traded for a
lost or doubled `Drop` body fails at either level. Worth knowing before writing
any leak fixture in this family: at `-O2` it would have passed pre-fix and
proved nothing.

A SIBLING IS LEFT UNFIXED AND IS FILED SEPARATELY, not folded in: an `if` /
`match` RHS leaks identically (`e = if c { pass(e) } else { pass(e) }`, 12 allocs
/ 11 frees) and is UNTOUCHED by this change -- measured byte-identical before and
after, so it is neither regressed nor helped. Those forms have several tails that
need not agree (`e = if c { pass(e) } else { mk() }`), so admitting them means
deciding what to do when the arms disagree, which is a different question from
this one.

title: Printing a `Vector[T, N]` gives THREE DIFFERENT ANSWERS -- the interpreter renders the lanes, the JIT prints a raw POINTER (the same one for two different vectors), and AOT prints one stray lane. `karac check` accepts it with no diagnostic.
detail:
FOUND while A/B-ing B-2026-08-29-40's fix, on a genuine `--features llvm` build
(both `karac` and `karac_jit_runner` freshly rebuilt).

REPRODUCTION:

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let a: i32 = n as i32;
        let v: Vector[i32, 4] = Vector[i32, 4](a, a + 10, a + 20, a + 30);
        println(f"iv {v}");
        let g: Vector[f32, 4] = Vector[f32, 4](1.5f32, 2.5f32, 3.5f32, 4.5f32);
        println(f"fv {g}");
    }

    karac run --interp     iv Vector(1, 11, 21, 31)
                           fv Vector(1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5)
    karac run   (JIT)      iv 140157074695024
                           fv 140157074695024
    karac build (AOT)      iv 21
                           fv 1

Three backends, three answers, and no diagnostic anywhere: `karac check` prints
"All checks passed."

TWO DETAILS THAT IDENTIFY THE GARBAGE. The two JIT lines print the SAME number
for two DIFFERENT vectors of different element types, which is what marks it as
an address rather than any function of the data. On the AOT side `21` is lane 2
of the i32 vector and `1` is a truncation of the f32 lane 0, so the compiled
formatter is reading a single scalar out of a place that holds a vector instead
of walking the lanes.

Element type is not the variable: seen at i32 and f32 here, and at every float
width (bf16 / f16 / f32 / f64) during the B-2026-08-29-40 sweep, where a
whole-vector `println` was the first thing tried and had to be abandoned for
per-lane reads before that row's real question could even be measured.

SEVERITY. High rather than medium because it is SILENTLY WRONG OUTPUT from a
program the compiler accepts, in both compiled backends, on the most ordinary
thing anyone does with a value -- print it. It is also exactly the shape
kara-katas' A/B rule exists to catch, so any kata that prints a vector will
report a spurious run/build divergence and send someone hunting the wrong bug.

WHERE TO LOOK. The interpreter already has the correct behaviour --
`src/interpreter/value.rs`'s `Value::Vector` arm renders `Vector(l0, l1, ...)`.
The compiled side needs the matching formatter. The JIT/AOT difference in WHICH
garbage appears is the two backends reading a different place, not two separate
bugs; one formatter fixes both.

WORTH CHECKING AT THE SAME TIME whether the right answer is a formatter or a
REJECTION: if interpolating a whole vector is not meant to be supported, the
typechecker should say so, and today it says nothing at all. Either resolution
closes the divergence; silently printing a pointer is the only outcome that
cannot be right.
fix:
FIXED by 60465148. Both compiled backends now render a whole `Vector[T, N]` as
`Vector(l0, l1, ...)`, byte-identical to the interpreter.

FORMATTER, NOT REJECTION -- the row's open question, answered. The interpreter
already renders vectors, and design.md § Portable SIMD promises "the user's
source program is identical across targets -- performance, not correctness, is
what varies", so the interpreter is the reference and the compiled side is what
was missing. Rejecting `f"{v}"` would have removed a working capability from one
of three backends to make the other two agree, which is the wrong direction; and
`println` on a value is the most ordinary thing a program does.

ROOT CAUSE. `fstr_render_part` dispatches an interpolation part through a chain
of type-keyed arms (user Display, struct, enum, collection, Vec, Map/Set,
Option/Result, tuple) before a scalar fallback. There was no arm for an LLVM
`<N x T>`, so a vector reached the fallback, which had nothing to distinguish
the aggregate from a String, a struct or a pointer -- and the two backends
happened to guess differently, which is the whole reason one row reported three
answers. `compile_print` had the same gap.

THE BARE-`println` HALF WAS NOT IN THE ROW, and it failed WORSE. `println(v)`
printed NOTHING AT ALL on both compiled backends -- the line simply vanished
from the output while the interpreter printed the vector:

    println("before"); println(v); println("after");
    interp   before / Vector(1, 2, 3, 4) / after
    JIT      before / after
    AOT      before / after

An f-string at least printed something wrong; this dropped the statement. Both
spellings now route through one renderer, so they cannot drift apart.

THE FIX, in three plain-data pieces:

  * `Program::vector_typed_exprs` (src/ast.rs, populated in src/lowering.rs from
    `TypeCheckResult.expr_types`) -- the PRESENCE sibling of the existing
    `unsigned_vector_exprs`, which records only the unsigned-element subset and
    so cannot answer "is this a vector at all". The arm has to decide before
    compiling the part: once the scalar path has run there is no way back. Plain
    span data, no LLVM type crossing the boundary -- the codegen-containment
    rule.
  * `try_compile_vector_display` (src/codegen/synth_display.rs) -- walks the
    lanes of the compiled `<N x T>`, appending into a scope-tracked String
    accumulator. Lane count and element kind come from the LLVM vector type;
    SIGNEDNESS cannot (an `iN` is signless) and comes from
    `unsigned_vector_exprs`, the table the SIMD reduce/compare paths already
    trust for that question. Floats go through `format_f64_to_stack_buf`, the
    same shortest-round-trip helper the scalar and struct-field renderers use,
    so a lane and a bare float of equal value cannot print differently; it
    widens f32/f16/bf16 itself, bf16 via f32 per B-2026-07-22-1. 128-bit lanes
    use the runtime's own formatter rather than the `%lld`/`%llu` path, which
    would truncate.
  * The arm is wired into BOTH `fstr_render_part` (src/codegen/runtime.rs) and
    `compile_print` (src/codegen/control_flow.rs), ahead of every value-kind
    arm.

DELIBERATELY NOT FOLDED IN: `vector_method_receivers`. `unsigned_vector_exprs`
folds it because a `MethodCall` shares its receiver's span and that table wants
the RECEIVER's element signedness. Here the question is the expression's own
type, and `v.reduce_min()` is an `f32` -- folding receivers in would make the
renderer treat a scalar call result as a vector.

MEASURED after, all three backends identical on: i32 / u8 / i64 / f64 / f32 /
f16 / bf16 lanes, non-power-of-two `N`, an unbound expression (`f"{v + v}"`), a
call result, two vectors plus text in one f-string, a vector printed inside a
loop, and the bare-`println` spelling of each. Memory: valgrind over 50
iterations of both spellings reports 0 errors and `in use at exit: 0 bytes in 0
blocks`.

ONE SHAPE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT MATCH THE INTERPRETER, and it is the
interpreter that is wrong. An unsigned lane above `i64::MAX` renders as the
value here and as a signed reinterpretation there:

    let u: Vector[u64, 2] = Vector[u64, 2](18446744073709551615u64, 1u64);
    println(f"scalar {s}");   18446744073709551615      (both)
    println(f"lane0 {u[0]}"); 18446744073709551615      (both)
    println(f"whole {u}");    interp Vector(-1, 1) / compiled Vector(1844...5, 1)

`Value::Vector` holds untyped `Value::Int` lanes, so its Display cannot recover
a signedness the interpreter's own INDEXED read gets right -- the same program
prints both answers. Reproducing that here to keep the twin green would write a
known-wrong sign convention into new compiled code and make it harder to remove,
so the compiled side is correct and the interpreter half is filed separately.

TESTS: two in tests/codegen.rs. The twin (`..._agrees_with_the_interpreter`)
asserts AOT against the interpreter AND against pinned text -- the twin alone
would pass if both sides drifted together, the pin alone would not catch a
backend that stopped matching the reference. It covers both spellings, since
they failed differently. The second test pins the wide-unsigned case against the
correct value rather than twinning it, so it keeps passing when the interpreter
half lands. RED verified by stashing src/: `left: "139900053902362\n"`.

title: Compiled `Vector[f16, N].tanh()` returns NaN for x above ~5.5 -- the exp-derived formula computes e^(2x), which overflows f16's exponent range. The SCALAR `x.tanh()` on the same value in the SAME binary returns the correct 1.
detail:
FOUND while A/B-ing B-2026-08-29-40's fix. Confirmed on a genuine
`--features llvm` build; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` (AOT) agree with
each other here, so this is codegen, not a JIT/AOT split.

REPRODUCTION:

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let a: f16 = ((n + 3) as f32) as f16;   // 4
        let b: f16 = ((n + 5) as f32) as f16;   // 6
        let c: f16 = ((n + 6) as f32) as f16;   // 7
        let d: f16 = ((n + 19) as f32) as f16;  // 20
        let v: Vector[f16, 4] = Vector[f16, 4](a, b, c, d);
        println(f"vec  tanh {v.tanh()[0]} {v.tanh()[1]} {v.tanh()[2]} {v.tanh()[3]}");
        println(f"scal tanh {a.tanh()} {b.tanh()} {c.tanh()} {d.tanh()}");
    }

    karac run --interp        vec  tanh 0.99951171875 1 1 1
                              scal tanh 0.99951171875 1 1 1
    karac run / karac build   vec  tanh 1 NaN NaN NaN
                              scal tanh 0.99951171875 1 1 1

THE COMPILED BACKEND DISAGREES WITH ITSELF: `v.tanh()[i]` is NaN where
`v[i].tanh()` on the same value in the same binary returns the correct 1. That
self-disagreement is what makes this a defect rather than a precision choice --
there is no reading under which one function of one value has two answers inside
one program.

MECHANISM. `tanh` is derived from `exp` (the unary-math arm in
`src/interpreter/method_call_seq.rs` records the same for the compiled side:
"`sigmoid`/`tanh` are derived from `exp`"), as a function of e^(2x). f16's
largest finite value is 65504 and e^(2x) crosses it at x ~= 5.545; above that
the intermediate is +inf and the ratio inf/inf is NaN. The measured threshold
matches to the value:

    x = 5      tanh 1      (e^10  = 22026,  fits)
    x = 5.5    tanh 1      (e^11  = 59874,  fits)
    x = 6      tanh NaN    (e^12  = 162754, overflows)

`v.exp()` is itself CORRECT at x = 6 (prints 403.5 = e^6), which rules out a
general exp bug and pins it on the DOUBLED exponent specifically.

SCOPE. f16 only, among the widths tried. bf16 has f32's exponent range (max
~3.4e38) and showed no NaN anywhere in the B-2026-08-29-40 sweep; f32 would need
x > 44. `sigmoid` was NOT observed to fail -- it is 1/(1 + e^-x), whose
intermediate underflows toward 0 rather than overflowing -- but it is derived
from the same `exp` and was only probed over -6..7, so it is NOT cleared.

FIX SHAPE (not attempted here). Codegen already widens `bf16` vector lanes to
f32 for this family of reasons (B-2026-08-29-34). Doing the same for f16 `tanh`
removes the overflow with no threshold logic at all, since e^(2x) over f16's
whole input range sits comfortably inside f32. The alternative -- the standard
saturation identity, returning sign(x) for |x| past a cutoff -- also works but
adds a constant that has to be right per width.

SCOPE CORRECTION (2026-08-30, on fixing) -- THE TITLE UNDERSTATES THIS ROW IN
THREE WAYS, and the first is the one that would mislead someone re-deriving
scope from the index line alone.

The NaN is the VISIBLE half; there is a quiet half that returns a plausible
wrong number. At x = 4 -- comfortably under the ~5.5 threshold, and the FIRST
LANE OF THIS ROW'S OWN PRINTED REPRO -- the compiled vector gave exactly 1
where the answer is 0.99951171875, because both `e^2x +/- 1` round to the same
f16 and the quotient cancels. The repro above shows it ("vec tanh 1 NaN NaN
NaN" against "scal tanh 0.99951171875 1 1 1"); only the prose misses it. A
fixture written to catch NaN would have passed over it.

`sigmoid` IS affected. This row hedged correctly ("NOT observed to fail ... but
it is NOT cleared") and the reasoning for why it might be safe is right -- it
underflows toward 0 rather than overflowing. It still lost an f16 ULP to the
same missing widening: 0.88037109375 against the interpreter's 0.880859375 at
x = 2, and 0.9970703125 against 0.99755859375 at x = 6.

And it is not confined to `Vector`. `apply_vector_float_unary` has a second
caller -- the tensor-map vectorizer -- so `t.map(|x| x.tanh())` over a
`Tensor[f16, ...]` carried the identical NaN, measured at both a 4-element and
a 16-element tensor.

Everything else in this row held up: the mechanism, the measured threshold, the
`v.exp()` control that rules out a general exp bug, the f16-only width scope,
and the fix shape it recommended over the saturation identity.
fix:
FIXED by 2e5490d. `apply_vector_float_unary`
(`src/codegen/method_call_vector.rs`) now widens BOTH half formats to f32 for
the whole body and rounds once at the end, instead of widening bf16 alone.

THE FIX. A new `widen_reduced_float_vector` / `narrow_reduced_float_vector`
pair (`src/codegen/expr_ops.rs`) -- the vector twin of the existing
`widen_reduced_float_scalar` pair, which has covered both half formats since
B-2026-08-29-42 ("Neither half format has a libm entry point of its own, so
both widen to f32, call the `f`-suffixed symbol, and round back"). bf16 still
routes through the integer-shift emit (`fpext bfloat` is unselectable on LLVM
18 aarch64); f16 uses a plain `fpext`/`fptrunc`. One site, so all nine arms
and both callers are fixed at once.

WHY f16 WAS LEFT NARROW, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. The widening this
function already had was added for SELECTABILITY (B-2026-08-29-34): aarch64
and wasm32 cannot select `<N x bfloat>` lane ops. f16 selects fine, so under
that reason there was nothing to do for it -- and the arm looked deliberate
rather than incomplete. But the reason that MATTERED here was never selection.
These arms are multi-step formulas and it is the INTERMEDIATES that overflow.
Two adjacent facts, one true and one irrelevant, are what kept this open: a
fix aimed at the original reason would never have covered f16.

THE ROW'S MECHANISM IS EXACTLY RIGHT. `tanh` is `(e^2x-1)/(e^2x+1)`, f16's
largest finite value is 65504, `e^2x` crosses it at x ~= 5.545, and above that
the ratio is `inf/inf` = NaN. The measured threshold in the row (5.5 fine, 6
NaN) matches to the value. Its FIX SHAPE suggestion -- widen like bf16 rather
than add a per-width saturation cutoff -- is the one taken, for the reason it
gave plus one more: the cutoff would have fixed `tanh` and left every other
multi-step f16 lowering to be found one at a time.

THE ROW'S SCOPE IS NARROWER THAN THE DEFECT, IN THREE WAYS.

1. NOT ONLY THE NaN. At x = 4 -- comfortably UNDER the threshold, and the
   first lane of the row's own printed repro -- the compiled vector returned
   exactly 1 where the answer is 0.99951171875. Both `e^2x +/- 1` round to the
   same f16, so the quotient is 1 by cancellation. The row's output shows this
   ("vec tanh 1 NaN NaN NaN" against "scal tanh 0.99951171875 1 1 1") but its
   prose reads as a NaN bug, and a fixture written to catch NaN alone would
   have missed the half that returns a plausible wrong number.

2. `sigmoid` WAS AFFECTED. The row says it "was NOT observed to fail ... but
   it is NOT cleared", and the reasoning for why it might be safe is right
   (1/(1+e^-x) underflows toward 0 rather than overflowing). It still lost an
   f16 ULP for the same missing widening: at x = 2 the compiled binary gave
   0.88037109375 against the interpreter's 0.880859375, and at x = 6
   0.9970703125 against 0.99755859375. Both are pinned now.

3. THE TENSOR MAP PATH CARRIED IT TOO. `apply_vector_float_unary` has a second
   caller -- the tensor-map vectorizer -- so `t.map(|x| x.tanh())` over a
   `Tensor[f16, ...]` produced the identical NaN. Measured pre-fix at both a
   4-element and a 16-element tensor ("map tanh 1 NaN NaN NaN" either way),
   which also rules out "it only bites when the map fails to vectorize".

MEASUREMENT. A generated sweep of all nine unary methods over three 4-lane
vectors at each of f16 / bf16 / f32 / f64, across `karac run --interp`,
`karac run` (JIT), `karac build` (AOT) and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` --
lines where the interpreter disagreed with the compiled backends:

    f16    10 -> 0
    bf16    0 -> 0     (byte-identical, before and after)
    f32     8 -> 8     (untouched)
    f64     3 -> 3     (untouched)

And the row's own self-contradiction argument, counted directly -- lines where
`v.m()[i]` disagreed with `v[i].m()` INSIDE ONE AOT BINARY:

    f16     8 -> 0
    f32     3 -> 3
    f64     3 -> 3

Only the f16 COMPILED surfaces changed at all: bf16, f32 and f64 are
byte-identical on all four surfaces before and after, and the f16 interpreter
output never moved (it was the oracle throughout).

THE f32/f64 RESIDUAL IS NOT THIS BUG. Those remaining lines are
`exp`/`ln`/`tanh`/`sigmoid` differing in the last bit or two -- codegen's
Cephes polynomial against the interpreter's exact libm, the gap
B-2026-08-29-40 documents and deliberately left alone. It is independent of
width (it is the WHOLE of the f64 residual, where rounding is the identity),
so widening cannot touch it.

THE ONE ARM WHERE WIDENING COULD HAVE COST ACCURACY IS `sqrt`, whose native
`<N x half>` form is correctly rounded while a trip through f32 rounds twice.
It cannot: f32's 24 significand bits meet the 2p+2 condition for f16's 11
exactly. Verified exhaustively rather than cited -- over all 31745 finite
non-negative f16 inputs, `f16(f32(sqrt x))` and `f16(sqrt x)` agree on every
one. The four rounding arms are exact for the same reason an integral result
is: it already sits on the narrow grid.

TESTS. Three in `tests/codegen.rs`, one oracle twin in `tests/interpreter.rs`.
`test_e2e_vector_f16_transcendentals_match_the_scalar_and_the_interpreter` is
the value test and carries the scalar answers on the same line as the vector
ones, because the self-disagreement is the argument -- pre-fix it fails with
`vt 1 NaN NaN NaN` and `sg 0.88037109375 0.9970703125` while its `ve`/`se`/`bf`
/`f32` control lines hold steady.
`test_e2e_tensor_map_f16_transcendental_matches_the_interpreter` covers the
second caller. `test_ir_vector_f16_unary_math_computes_in_f32` is structural:
it asserts the `fpext`/`fptrunc` pair and the ABSENCE of `fdiv <4 x half>`,
which is where the NaN was born -- a value test alone would pass on a
`tanh`-only saturation cutoff. All three are RED pre-fix. The interpreter twin
`test_vector_f16_transcendentals_are_computed_without_overflowing_the_lane`
passes either way by design; it freezes the oracle so the two halves cannot
drift apart the way the bf16 pair did.

FILED SEPARATELY, both found while measuring this and both confirmed
INDEPENDENT of it (identical before and after the fix): B-2026-08-30-24 (no f16
program can be linked for a wasm target -- `__extendhfsf2` / `__truncsfhf2`
are undefined, and a bare runtime `as f16` conversion is enough to trigger it)
and B-2026-08-30-25 (the typechecker accepts ANY method name on an `f16`/`bf16`
receiver, because `method_callee_type_name` has no arm for either width).

FIXED in 5962bb9. The assoc-call arm now registers a caller-side owner for its
by-value arguments, which it never did at all.

THE ROW'S LOCALIZATION WAS EXACTLY RIGHT AND ITS GRADING WAS NOT. "It is the
static-call arm specifically, not method calls in general" is the finding, and
it holds literally: `src/codegen/assoc_call.rs`'s user-impl-block arm compiles
each argument and pushes it into `compiled_args` without ever calling
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`, the registrar the free-function arm
(`compile_call`) and the instance-method arm (`compile_method_call`) have both
called for months. Three dispatch arms, two of them registering an owner. The
row's guess that `method_param_drop_names`' free-fn-vs-method asymmetry "is
likely the wrong frame to reason in" was also right, and for a sharper reason
than it gives: the method arm is the CLOSER sibling, because both are keyed by
the same `Type.method` string, so `find_function_ast` resolves the callee
identically and the escape predicates take the same form. The one real
difference is the parameter index -- a static function has no `self_param`, so
the source argument `i` IS the declared parameter index where the method arm's
`pidx = i + 1` steps past the receiver.

IT IS A LEAK TOO, and the row says twice that it is not. "NOT A LEAK, and the
distinction is measured rather than assumed" rests on a clean LeakSanitizer run
in `asan_owned_param_temps_free_once`. The run was clean; the inference was
wrong. That harness builds at `-O2`, where the only consumer of the argument's
allocation is a callee that ignores its parameter, so LLVM deletes the
allocation and LSan is handed a program with nothing to lose. Rebuilt at `-O0`,
the pin's OWN source leaks 16 bytes in 2 blocks before this commit and is clean
after it. This is precisely the population B-2026-08-04-17 named -- "fixtures
that allocate nothing at `-O2` and so assert nothing" -- reached this time
through a fixture that looked like it carried heap on purpose, since
`f"heap-one"` is an f-string and reads as a heap payload.

Measured at `-O0`, valgrind `--leak-check=full`, before -> after:

FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-46, by sweeping the argument-drop surface for
shapes the ordering fix did not reach, and NOT caused by it -- the missing bodies
reproduce on a pre-fix build.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    struct H { n: i64 }
    impl H { fn s2(a: R, b: R) -> i64 { 7 } }
    fn main() { let v = H.s2(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 }); println(f"v={v}") }

      karac run --interp  -> `dR2 dR1 v=7`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `v=7`
      karac build         -> `v=7`

ONE ARGUMENT IS ENOUGH -- `impl H { fn s1(a: R) -> i64 { 7 } }` called as
`H.s1(R { id: 1 })` gives `dR1 v=7` against `v=7`, so this is not an arity or an
ordering effect. It is specific to a FRESH TEMP: the same static function called
with MOVED LOCALS (`let x = R { id: 1 }; let y = R { id: 2 }; H.s2(x, y)`) runs
both bodies on all three backends, in the right order.

registration fires and only the user body is absent -- the same body-vs-memory
split B-2026-08-29-24 established from the other direction. The consequence is
still real: a `Drop` impl that closes an fd, releases a lock, or decrements a
counter simply does not run.

`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`; codegen's caller-side equivalent registers the temps

that never performs that registration. Note the neighbouring shapes that DO work
and bound the search: a free function's fresh-temp args work on all three
backends, and an INSTANCE method's do too (`h.take(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 })` ->

interpreter side). So it is the static-call arm specifically, not method calls in

CORRECTION (2026-08-30, at close): the row's "NOT A LEAK" grading is wrong, and
the way it went wrong is worth keeping because the evidence looked strong. The
row says the distinction is "measured rather than assumed" and cites a clean
LeakSanitizer run over a pin whose payloads are `f"heap-one"` / `f"heap-two"`.
LSan was clean and the pin does carry f-strings; what neither fact establishes is
that anything was ALLOCATED. `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` builds at `-O2`, the
callee ignores both parameters, so the allocations have no live consumer and LLVM
deletes them. Rebuilt at `-O0` the same source leaks 16 bytes in 2 blocks
pre-fix. Across the fifteen shapes in the fix note the leak runs 64-225 bytes per
call and 15,780 bytes in 200 blocks over a 100-iteration loop.

So the defect was a lost body AND an orphaned buffer, and the second half was
invisible to the instrument used to rule it out. `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s own
harness comment names this population (B-2026-08-04-17, "fixtures that allocate
nothing at `-O2` and so assert nothing"); the general rule is that a leak
measurement on an argument whose callee ignores it must be taken at `-O0`, or
taken with an allocation floor, because `-O2` will delete the thing being
measured. The pin now carries that floor.

fix:
FIXED by 4b73d1e2.

The drain POINT moved and nothing else did, which is what the row asked for and
also the only change that could be made without re-opening B-2026-08-29-46.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Argument temporaries were registered on the enclosing
STATEMENT's cleanup frame and drained at its `;`. design.md
(§ Temporary Lifetime Rules) gives an argument its own position row --
"Function/method call argument | After the call returns" -- and the neighbouring
row it was actually getting, "Statement-position expression (`expr;`) | At the
`;`", is strictly longer. The section's composition-with-NLL paragraph names
that direction explicitly as the forbidden one: "NLL never EXTENDS a
temporary's live range past the position-specific end -- that direction would
invalidate the lock-eagerness guarantee."

THE FIX is a per-call window: `call_arg_temp_mark()` records the frame length
before a call's arguments are lowered, and `drain_call_arg_temp_user_drops`
fires exactly the temps pushed during that call once it has been emitted. The
hooks sit at the three `compile_expr` dispatch arms (`Call`, `MethodCall`, and
the pipe desugar's `Call`); the assoc path needs no hook of its own because
`compile_call` reaches `compile_assoc_call` from inside the window.

THE DRAIN ITSELF IS UNTOUCHED, deliberately -- the row warned that "anything
that reorders the drain instead will re-open that row", and it would have.
Within one window the temps still pop LIFO, which is what makes two arguments
run right-to-left (B-2026-08-29-46; design.md's "single LIFO stack ordered by
program-order of introduction"). `drain_statement_temp_user_drops` and the new
per-call drain are now two calls into one core with a `call_return_only` flag;
re-running the statement drain after a call window is free, since the entries
are retired and `frame.len() <= mark` short-circuits.

THE FLAG NARROWS THE NAME SET, and that narrowing is load-bearing. The statement
drain fires five synthetic names; only three are ARGUMENTS (`__owned_agg_tmp`
from `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst`, `__refarg_tmp` from
`queue_ref_rvalue_arg_cleanup`, and `__disc_tup_arg`). The fresh-temp RECEIVER
(`__urecv_drop_tmp`) and the fresh-temp SCRUTINEE (`__freshtemp_enum_scrut`)
each have their OWN row in the position table with a different end and are not
arguments, so a per-call drain must not claim them -- they stay on the statement
frame, unchanged. `__owned_agg_tmp` is shared with the DISCARD registrar
(`try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp`), which would have made the name ambiguous
inside a call window; it is called only from `stmts.rs`, outside every window,
so it cannot land in one.

THE ROW'S EXPLANATION OF WHY THIS SURVIVED IS WRONG, AND THAT IS THE MOST
USEFUL THING THE FIX TURNED UP. The row reasons: "A single-call statement cannot
show it (the `;` follows the call return immediately with nothing in between),
which is presumably why it has survived." Only the first clause is true, and
only for a statement whose ENTIRE expression is the call. Any enclosing
expression that runs after the call re-opens the gap -- and the commonest
spelling in the whole test corpus does exactly that:

    fn main() { println(f"{take(R { id: 41 })}") }

Here the body belongs BEFORE the printed value (the temp dies when `take`
returns; `println` runs after), and the compiled backends put it after. So the
bug was NOT rare -- it was everywhere, in the single-call shape, and it survived
for the opposite reason to the one the row gives: EIGHT existing control cases
had the compiled-side-only ordering baked in as their expected value, while
`--interp` printed the body first the whole time. They were recording the
divergence as intent. Corrected here, each with the reason at the site:
`struct-arg`, `struct-arg-destructured`, `free-fn-control`,
`closure-param-source-control` (codegen), `argument-control`,
`param-source-control`, `param-tuple-control`, `param-struct-control`,
`callee-consumes`, and the two asan twins. One of them carried the comment "the
row is here so a future ownership change cannot move the compiled side without
someone noticing" -- which is precisely what happened, working as designed.

Two neighbouring controls were checked and deliberately NOT changed, because
they are not arguments and must keep the longer live range:
`no-destructure-control` (`let p = (R { id: 41 }, 1); println(f"{p.1}")`, a
local binding dropping at scope exit) and `tuple-arg-control` /
`two-dropper-tuple-control`, which already expected body-first.

MEASURED, all four surfaces (`--interp`, JIT, AOT, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`)
unanimous after the fix and the compiled three differing before it:

    take(R{1},R{2}) + take(R{3},R{4})    in-take in-take dR4 dR3 dR2 dR1
                                      -> in-take dR2 dR1 in-take dR4 dR3
    h.take(...) + h.take(...)            same shape, method spelling
    H.s2(...) + H.s2(...)                same shape, assoc spelling
    one(mk(one(mk(1)) + 1))              in-one in-one dR2 dR1
                                      -> in-one dR1 in-one dR2
    println(f"{take(R{41})}")            41 drop 41  ->  drop 41 41

The fourth is the shape that pins the WINDOW rather than the drain: an argument
that is itself a call must drain inside the outer call's window, interleaved
with it, not batched at the end.

ATTRIBUTION IS FROM A REAL PRE-FIX BASELINE, not from assumption -- the tree was
stashed, rebuilt, and re-measured. Of the twelve probe shapes, exactly the four
two-call/nested ones changed; the other eight (nested single call, identifier
argument, mixed identifier+temp, discarded call, `ref`-param fresh rvalue,
single-call statement, early return, loop body) were already unanimous before
the fix and are unanimous after it. That baseline is also what proves the one
remaining divergence in the probe is NOT mine: an `if`/`else` in argument
position (`one(if c { mk(1) } else { mk(2) })`) runs NO Drop body on ANY
backend, before and after, so it is invisible to an A/B parity gate and is filed
separately.

NOT A MEMORY CHANGE. Only the point at which a body runs moved; no cleanup
registration was added, removed, or re-homed. valgrind `--leak-check=full`
reports zero errors and zero leaks on every probe program, including the
String-carrying payloads, and the LSan-bearing `memory_sanitizer` suite is green
(its two corrected fixtures assert ORDER, not count -- ASAN passed before and
after; only the stdout line order moved).

Tests: the two pins the row planted are now LIVE cases asserting the same
byte-identical strings on both backends -- `two-calls-one-statement-free`,
`-method`, `-assoc` and `deep-nest-inner-call-drains-first` in
`e2e_owned_param_temps_drop_in_reverse_argument_order` (codegen) and
`test_owned_param_temps_drop_in_reverse_argument_order` (interpreter). Absolute
expectations on both sides are the only thing that can hold this: every body ran
exactly once on both backends before the fix and only the point differed, so no
count-based assertion and no A/B parity gate could see the row.
RED-verified: with `src/` stashed and the new tests in place, the codegen leg
fails at `case two-calls-one-statement-free`,
`left: Some("in-take\nin-take\ndR4\ndR3\ndR2\ndR1\nv=14\n")`.
title: ARGUMENT TEMPORARIES ARE HELD TO THE END OF THE STATEMENT ON THE COMPILED BACKENDS INSTEAD OF DYING WHEN THE CALL RETURNS -- `take(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 }) + take(R { id: 3 }, R { id: 4 })` runs all four bodies after BOTH calls, so the first call's guard is still live while the second runs; design.md's position table and its no-extension rule both say otherwise, and `--interp` matches them
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-46 and NOT caused by it -- the compiled
behaviour is identical on a pre-fix build. What the fix changed is that this
became DIAGNOSABLE: before it both backends were wrong in different ways here,
and the shape read as more of the same ordering noise.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    fn take(r: R, q: R) -> i64 { println("in-take"); 7 }
    fn main() {
        let v = take(R { id: 1 }, R { id: 2 }) + take(R { id: 3 }, R { id: 4 });
        println(f"v={v}")
    }

      karac run --interp  -> `in-take dR2 dR1 in-take dR4 dR3 v=14`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `in-take in-take dR4 dR3 dR2 dR1 v=14`
      karac build         -> same as JIT

The interpreter's line is what design.md requires and the compiled one is not.
Two rules compose to fix it, and neither alone is enough:

  * Temporary Lifetime Rules, the position table: "Function/method call argument
    | After the call returns". The FIRST call's temps therefore die before the
    SECOND call's are constructed -- `R { id: 3 }` does not exist yet at the point
    `R { id: 1 }` must be gone.
  * The same section's Composition with NLL: "the position-specific live-range
    end is the LATEST drop point for the temporary ... NLL never EXTENDS a
    temporary's live range past the position-specific end -- that direction would
    invalidate the lock-eagerness guarantee".

Holding all four to the statement's `;` is exactly that forbidden direction. The
compiled backends are applying the statement-position rule ("Statement-position
expression (`expr;`) | At the `;`") to values the argument row governs, which
is a strictly longer live range.

WHY IT MATTERS beyond the printed order: this is the held-too-long footgun the
tail-expression rule was written against, one position over. A `Lease` or a
`MutexGuard` passed as an argument stays checked out for the remainder of the
enclosing statement instead of being released when the call it was built for
returns -- and in a statement containing a second call, that second call runs
while the first's guard is still live. A single-call statement cannot show it
(the `;` follows the call return immediately with nothing in between), which is
presumably why it has survived.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT: every temporary is freed exactly once on both backends;
only the point at which the body runs differs.

WHERE TO START. Codegen registers argument temps on a caller cleanup frame that
is drained at statement end. The frame's drain order is correct and must not
change -- it is what makes B-2026-08-29-46's reverse order fall out -- so the fix
is the drain POINT, not the drain: a per-call sub-frame drained as the call
returns, with the LIFO discipline preserved within it. Anything that reorders
the drain instead will re-open that row.

PINNED AT THE DEFECT ON BOTH SIDES: `pin-arg-temps-held-to-statement-end` in
`e2e_owned_param_temps_drop_in_reverse_argument_order` (codegen) and
`pin-arg-temps-die-at-call-return-not-statement-end` in
`test_owned_param_temps_drop_in_reverse_argument_order` (interpreter), so a fix
to either side shows up as its own pin failing.

fix:
FIXED by bc1c37c.

Hooked `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` at the two RETURN
positions it had never been called from: the tail-return retraction list in
`suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` (`src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs`) and the
explicit-`return` list in `src/codegen/exprs.rs`. Both are needed — a `return`
nested in an `if` is not the body's tail, so the tail walk never sees it — and
both run AFTER the return value is loaded, per B-2026-06-12-6: zeroing the
source slot first corrupts the value the caller receives.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is a hole rather than a wrong rule. `let buf = Some(<heap>)`
arms a `FreeInlineOptionPayload` on the binding, cap-guarded at the option's
word 2. The helper that retracts it when the binding is moved away already
existed and was hooked at SEVENTEEN consuming positions — struct-literal
fields, call arguments, method receivers, channel sends, a `let` RHS — and at
no ESCAPING one. So the callee freed the payload on its way out and the caller
freed the same buffer again. This is the same hole shape B-2026-08-28-15 found
for the tuple-index peer ("hooked at the four `let` positions and nowhere
else"), and it is the INLINE sibling of the heap-BOXED payload disarm that
B-2026-08-07-1 added to these very lists and stopped at.

The disarm is a RUNTIME whole-slot zero, not a compile-time queue retract, so a
binding returned on one path and consumed on another still frees its payload on
the consuming path. That is not a stylistic choice: a static retraction would
strand the payload on the consuming path, trading this double free for a leak.
Both directions are pinned by the `cond-returned` / `cond-consumed` fixture
rows, and valgrind is clean on each.

TRIGGER SET RE-MEASURED, and TWO OF THE REPORTED CONDITIONS WERE WRONG.

  * "The caller must CONSUME the payload" — FALSE. `let r = collect();
    println("held")` aborts, and so does a bare `collect();` with no binding at
    all. The second free is the CALLEE's own, so the caller needs to do nothing
    but exist. Both are now fixture rows (`caller-holds`, `caller-discards`)
    precisely because the report called them clean.
  * It is `Option`-specific, not "any heap-carrying local returned". A user
    enum with the identical payload (`enum E { A(String) }`; `let buf =
    E.A(f"zz"); buf`) was ALWAYS clean, as were a plain returned `String`, a
    returned tuple, and a returned struct wrapping a String — different drop
    channels. Kept as `user-enum-control`.

Confirmed correct in the report: the payload must be heap (scalar is clean),
the value must be bound to a local (a bare-tail temporary registers no binding
cleanup and was always clean), it must cross a function boundary, and `mut` /
reassignment are not ingredients. Also verified not `String`-specific:
`Option[Vec[i64]]` and `Option[<struct with a String>]` double identically.

THE SELF-HOST ORACLE IS NOT FIXED BY THIS, AND THE REPORT'S ATTRIBUTION OF IT
WAS WRONG. `selfhost_parser_items` stays red. Measured on both sides of this
commit rather than argued: with the fix reverted and re-applied, the oracle's

does change is the failure MODE — SIGABRT on heap-corruption detection becomes

plain `//` comment is clean; `"/// d\nstruct Q {}"` is the minimal input). That
routes through `Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments`, whose shape is this

That is the self-host differential -- the only test that runs two independent
implementations of the parser against each other -- and CI's `codegen-e2e` job
runs it. Found while gating B-2026-08-29-46; verified NOT caused by that work by
re-running with `src/` stashed.

MINIMAL REPRO -- no annotation, no `mut`, no reassignment, no loop:

    fn collect() -> Option[String] {
        let buf = Some(f"zz");
        buf
    }
    fn main() {
        match collect() {
            Some(s) => println(f"[{s}]"),
            None => println("none"),
        }
    }

      karac run --interp  -> `[zz]`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, SIGABRT
      karac build         -> same

Deterministic: 3/3 aborts.

THE TRIGGER SET IS NARROW, and each of these was measured rather than reasoned:

  * The payload must be HEAP. `Some("zz")` with a plain string literal is clean
    (that is a static `StringSlice`), `Some(f"zz")` aborts. `Option[i64]` is
    clean. `Option[B]` for `struct B { s: String }` aborts, so it is the heap
    behind the payload and not `String` specifically.
  * The `Option` must be BOUND TO A LOCAL and that binding returned.
    `fn collect() -> Option[String] { Some(f"aa") }` -- the same value as a bare
    tail -- is clean, and so is `fn make() -> Option[String] { let s = f"x";
    Some(s) }`, which binds the PAYLOAD instead of the option. Only `let buf =
    Some(<heap>); buf` aborts.
  * It must cross a FUNCTION BOUNDARY. The identical statements inlined into
    `main` are clean.
  * The caller must CONSUME the payload. `let r = collect(); println("held")`
    is clean; `match`, `if let`, and `.unwrap()` all abort. So the second free is
    the caller's, on a buffer the callee's return path already freed.

`mut` and reassignment are NOT ingredients -- they were in the shape this was
found through and drop out of the minimal form.

LONG-STANDING, NOT PART OF THE 2026-08-29 DROP SERIES. Bisected: the repro aborts
at `7a8107c` (2026-08-29 14:12 UTC), which predates every `fix(drop)` commit of
that day, and at `2ac067e`, `9f3e2cb`, `b04cf10`, `a865ed6`, `fd4e80f` in
between. Going further back was not attempted because `7a8107c` is the last
`runtime/src` change, so an older `src/` would link a NEWER archive and the
measurement would be about the wrong pair (CLAUDE.md's staleness rule, applied in
reverse).

WHY IT ONLY NOW TURNED CI RED, and this is the part worth reading before blaming
a recent commit. `c793ad0` ("an annotated `let` records the binding's type, not
the literal's", closing B-2026-08-29-39) did not create this. It WIDENED THE
SPELLINGS THAT REACH IT. Measured on both sides of that commit:

    fn collect() -> Option[String] {          fn collect() -> Option[String] {
        let mut buf: Option[String] = None;       let mut buf = Some(f"zz");
        buf = Some(f"aa");                        buf = Some(f"aa");
        buf                                       buf
    }                                         }
    27aa72f: clean   c793ad0: ABORT          27aa72f: ABORT   c793ad0: ABORT

The right-hand column is this bug and predates the commit. The left-hand column
is the spelling the self-host parser actually uses -- `let mut buf:
Option[String] = None;` appears ~18 times across `selfhost/src/parser.kara` --
and it was clean only because the annotated `None` RHS recorded
`Option[TypeParam("T")]` rather than `Option[String]`, so codegen never took this
path. `c793ad0` correctly recorded the concrete type, and the previously-shielded
spelling landed on the existing defect. So a REVERT is the wrong reflex twice
over: it would re-open B-2026-08-29-39 (a false `karac check` error on a program
every backend runs correctly) and would only re-hide this, not fix it.

WHERE TO START. The callee's return path and the caller's consume path both free
the payload. `let buf = Some(<heap>); buf` is the "conditionally / unconditionally
returned local" shape the caller-retains machinery has been reworked around all
week (`fn_returns_param`, `cond_returned_param_drop_names`, the
`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` passthrough guards), except the value here is a LOCAL
rather than a param, so none of those predicates look at it. The bare-tail case
being clean says the return-value ownership transfer is right when the value is a
temporary and wrong when it is a named binding -- which points at the local's own
scope-exit cleanup not being retracted by the move into the return slot.

NOT AN INTERPRETER BUG: `--interp` is correct on every shape above.

title: `return out` as a block's FINAL EXPRESSION -- no trailing semicolon -- makes the INTERPRETER run the returned local's `Drop` body TWICE, once at callee scope exit and again at the caller's binding. `return out;` as a STATEMENT and the bare tail `out` are both correct, on every backend. Compiled output is correct in all three spellings, so the semicolon alone is the whole difference
detail:
Found while building B-2026-08-29-48's fixtures, and it is why those
fixtures spell every return with a semicolon: the first draft used the
`return out }` form the sibling fixtures use, and one row failed for a reason
that had nothing to do with the fix under test.

MINIMAL REPRO -- three functions that differ only in how the local leaves:

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

    fn tail_ret(k: i64) -> R { let out: R = R { id: k, tag: f"t" }; println("mid"); return out }
    fn stmt_ret(k: i64) -> R { let out: R = R { id: k, tag: f"t" }; println("mid"); return out; }
    fn bare_tail(k: i64) -> R { let out: R = R { id: k, tag: f"t" }; println("mid"); out }

    fn main() {
        let a: R = tail_ret(1); println(f"v{a.id}");
        let b: R = stmt_ret(2); println(f"v{b.id}");
        let c: R = bare_tail(3); println(f"v{c.id}");
    }

      interpreter  -> tail_ret `mid dR1 v1 dR1`   TWO bodies for one value
                      stmt_ret `mid v2 dR2`       one
                      bare_tail `mid v3 dR3`      one
      karac build  -> `mid v1 dR1` / `mid v2 dR2` / `mid v3 dR3`   all one
      same with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0.

So the interpreter drops the local at the callee's scope exit AND hands it to
the caller, whose binding drops it again. The extra body lands BEFORE the
caller's `v1`, which is what identifies it as the callee's scope drop rather
than a second caller-side fire.

The trigger is purely the parse shape: `Return(out)` reached as the block's
`final_expr` instead of as `StmtKind::Expr`. Nothing about the value or the type
changes between the two, and the compiled backends treat them identically.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT: valgrind on the compiled binary is clean (0 errors, all
blocks freed), and the extra run is a body, not a free. The interpreter has no
sanitizer peer, but the doubled body is observable directly.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT: B-2026-08-29-56 is also about a local returned from a
function, and points the opposite way -- there the COMPILED backends double-FREE
a heap `Option` bound to a local and returned, while the interpreter is correct.
The two are not the same defect and should not be merged: this one is
interpreter-only, bodies-only, and keyed on the semicolon; that one is
compiled-only, a real double free, and clean in the bare-tail spelling that this
one is also clean in.

WHERE TO START: whatever marks a returned binding as moved-out in the
interpreter is reached on the `StmtKind::Expr(Return(..))` path and missed when
the same `Return` arrives as a block's `final_expr`. The bare-tail case being
correct says the final-expr path itself is handled -- it is specifically
`Return` nested inside it that is not.
fix:
FIXED in fc450fe, together with a SECOND defect of the same shape one level up
that the row did not know about and that no A/B gate could have found.

THE ROW'S HALF, and its pointer was right. The block-exit hook drives
`suppress_tail_expr_user_drop` and its container twin
(`record_container_bodies_move_sources`), both of which match on `Identifier`.
Handed the `Return` node itself they silently did nothing, so the callee
dropped the local at its own scope exit as well as handing it to the caller.
The statement loop's `suppress_return_stmt_user_drop` already unwraps the
`Return` before calling the same helper, which is exactly why `return out;` was
correct and `return out` was not. B-2026-08-29-21 added that same unwrap at this
site for `note_escaping_site` and `record_conditional_move_tail` and stopped
there; this is the rest of that hook.

THE SECOND DEFECT, found by the probe matrix built to bound this fix's blast
radius and filed as B-2026-08-29-65: a returned PARAM doubled its body on EVERY
backend, not just the interpreter.

    fn f(r: R) -> R { println("mid"); return r }     -> `mid dR5 v5 dR5`  TWO
    fn f(r: R) -> R { println("mid"); return r; }    -> `mid v5 dR5`      one

`fn_always_returns_param` collects the body's leaf tails and requires each to
YIELD the param. A tail `return r` reached that walk as the `Return` node,
yielded nothing, and the predicate declined for a body whose only exit hands the
param back -- so the caller kept firing beside the result binding. The
semicolon spelling has no tail expression at all and takes the no-tail arm
B-2026-08-29-14 added, which is why it was correct. `leaf_tails` now descends
