through a `Return` operand; a bare `return;` still declines, correctly, because
it yields nothing.

Worth noting where that leaves B-2026-08-29-15: its fix (baf2338) closed the
`return r;` spelling and the tail spelling stayed broken, agreed on both
backends and therefore invisible to the A/B rule that row was argued on.

BLAST RADIUS MEASURED, NOT REASONED. Against a 14-shape probe the interpreter
change removes exactly eight bodies -- every one a tail-`return` duplicate --
and changes nothing else. Post-fix every cell's interpreter count matches the
compiled count.

THE WIDENED LEAF-TAIL WALK IS GUARDED FROM BOTH SIDES, because its failure
direction flips: a too-permissive walk stands the caller down and LOSES a body
rather than duplicating one. `branch-*` keeps a sibling local that is not
returned dying inside the callee (`if flag { return a } else { return b }`,
which also exercises the walk descending through `If`); `param-dies-*` keeps the
predicate declining when no `return` yields the param.

Fixtures RED-verified against the pre-fix compiler, and each half fails its own
row first: codegen on `param-tail-return` (`mid dR6 v6 dR6`) and the interpreter
on `local-tail-return` (`mid dR1 v1 dR1`). Every tail-`return` row has its
`return x;` twin beside it and the two assert the same string, in both suites.
Valgrind-clean.

RESIDUALS, both compiled-side, both pre-existing (measured with this commit's
`src` reverted) and neither related to the semicolon: B-2026-08-29-66 (a struct
wrapping a `Vec` of `Drop` elements, built in a callee and returned, runs the
element body on FREED memory when the caller's `let` is not the first statement
of its block -- valgrind Invalid read, a garbage id that differs between runs)
and B-2026-08-29-67 (a `Vec` returned from a callee runs its element body BEFORE
the caller's use on the compiled backends, after it on the interpreter).

SOURCE NOTE: `selfhost_parser_items` is red at HEAD throughout this work, which
is B-2026-08-29-56. Verified red with this commit's `src` reverted, and its
repro is unaffected by either half of this fix.

title: A `match` arm that ASSIGNS the param's payload to an outer local the callee does NOT return runs the payload's `Drop` body ONE TIME TOO MANY on the interpreter -- the callee's own scope drop fires and the caller's argument walk fires too. All three compiled surfaces run it once. The `let`-bound twin (`let inner = r;`) is correct everywhere
fix:
FIXED in e7c7d44. The row's diagnosis was right and its WHERE-TO-START was
nearly the fix verbatim: `rearm_container_bodies_for_name` is indeed called on
an assignment target for the FRESH value, and the SOURCE side of the same
assignment was indeed the gap.

THE GATE. `record_assign_of_param_view` (src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs) mirrors
the binding leg of `let_destructures_owned_param`: when an assignment's RHS is
an identifier already in the owned-param VIEW set, the target joins that set
(so a later `let z = out;` inherits the ownership story) and is silenced through
`moved_out_user_drop_bindings`. It is called from the `Assign` arm immediately
AFTER the existing re-arm, and that order is load-bearing -- the re-arm clears
this very set, so taking the record first would have it wiped by the statement
that establishes it.

SILENCING THROUGH THE WHOLE-BINDING SET IS WHAT MAKES THE REPEATED-ASSIGNMENT
SHAPE WORK, and it was not the obvious choice. `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` is
consulted at TWO fire sites, not one: `invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` (the
target's own slot) and the displaced-value drop the `Assign` arm runs before
overwriting. So `out = r1; .. out = r2;` runs a displacement body for the value
the target genuinely owned (`R{0}`) and none for the view it later held
(`R{8}`), which is exactly what codegen produces. A narrower silencer aimed only
at the slot would have left the displacement body firing and doubled `R{8}`
again one statement later.

WHICH BACKEND WAS RIGHT WAS NOT OBVIOUS, and the row asserts it without showing
the work, so here is the work. Two conventions coexist and they disagree:

    fn f(a: R) { let mut out = R{0}; out = a; .. }      -> body fires CALLEE-side
    match b { E.A(r) => { let inner = r; .. } }         -> body fires CALLER-side

Both backends AGREE on each of those, which is what makes them oracles rather
than opinions. A whole param moved into a local is owned by the local; an arm
payload bound out of an owned param is a VIEW whose owner is still the caller.
`out = r` is the second shape, so the caller-side firing codegen already did is
the convention and the interpreter's extra callee-side body is the anomaly. The
fix therefore removes a body rather than moving one, and the compiled output is
untouched.

PINNED BY PLACE, NOT ONLY BY COUNT. `assign-place-pinned` puts a callee local
(`dR9`, dead at its last use) and a `pre-ret` / `post-call` bracket between the
three candidate firing points, so a body fired at the arm, at the callee's own
slot, and at the caller's walk land in three distinguishable positions. Without
it a fix that reached one body by disarming the CALLER instead would pass just
as well while producing the opposite order.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ROW, both found while building its controls.

(1) "The `let` TWIN IS CORRECT, which is what localizes it" holds for FREE
FUNCTIONS ONLY. Inside a method frame the `let` spelling doubles identically
(`dR8 m dE dR8 v8` against `m dE dR8 v8` compiled), so the twin localizes the
defect to the assignment path only in the frame the row measured. The method
leg of both spellings is filed as B-2026-08-30-55.

(2) The row's measurements are labelled `interpreter`, and reproducing them
needs `karac run --interp` SPECIFICALLY. In this container a bare `karac run`
reaches the JIT lane and prints the COMPILED answer, so the row looks
not-reproduced when measured that way -- this session recorded exactly that
reading before catching it. B-2026-08-29-59's note that `karac run` does not
reach the JIT here is no longer true of this environment, whatever it was when
that row was written.

THE METHOD-FRAME EXCLUSION IS LOAD-BEARING, not defensive boilerplate copied
from `let_destructures_owned_param`. Retraction is a hand-off, and a method's
FRESH-TEMP enum argument has nobody to hand off to: `t.take(E.A(R{..}))` runs
the payload body exactly ONCE today, from the very slot this gate would retract,
so retracting there takes the count to zero. Measured before the guard was
written rather than after.

TESTS. `test_arm_payload_assigned_to_outer_local_drop_body_runs_once`
(tests/interpreter.rs, 12 cases) and its codegen oracle twin
`e2e_arm_payload_assigned_to_outer_local_drops_once` (11 -- the twin omits the
arm-not-taken case, which is a compiled-side defect filed as B-2026-08-30-53 and
would have to be written into an expectation to be shared). RED-verified against
the pre-fix compiler: `left: "dR0\nmid\ndR8\ndE\ndR8\nv8\n"` on the first case.
Guard rails cover a fresh-value assignment, a LOCAL scrutinee, a fresh-temp
scrutinee, an unmatched second owned param, and B-2026-08-29-48's
assigned-AND-returned boundary; the `let` twin is carried as a control so a
change that "fixed" the assignment spelling by moving the `let` one fails.

Valgrind-clean throughout -- bodies only, as the row said.

RESIDUALS, all three found while building the controls and split out rather than
folded in: B-2026-08-30-53 (the same statement with the arm NOT taken loses the
target's own initializer body on both compiled backends -- the mirror-image
defect, and the reason the two test files do not share that case),
B-2026-08-30-54 (the FIELD-target spelling `h.f = r`, where the interpreter doubles
exactly as here AND codegen permanently disarms the field so a later fresh value
assigned to it loses its body -- both backends wrong, in different directions,
so neither is an oracle and this fix deliberately does not extend there), and
B-2026-08-30-55 (method frames do not participate in the ENUM-param ownership
protocol at all).

title: `karac run` does NOT reach the JIT lane -- it runs the tree-walk interpreter, despite the JIT being the documented default since LLJIT slice 6c. Measured two ways: hiding `karac_jit_runner` entirely changes nothing (the lane would abort with 'karac_jit_runner not found'), and a 20M-iteration loop that a JIT finishes instantly did not complete in 10 MINUTES. Every ledger row whose evidence cites `karac run` as a 'JIT surface' has therefore been reading the interpreter twice
detail:
Found while re-checking B-2026-08-29-48's surface matrix, after `karac run`
sided with `--interp` on two programs where the compiled binary differed. The
expectation (CLAUDE.md, and `src/cli/run_check_cmds.rs`'s own comment block) is
that `karac run` defaults to LLJIT and `--interp` opts out.

TWO INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENTS, because the first alone is circumstantial:

  1. `mv target/debug/karac_jit_runner target/debug/karac_jit_runner.bak`, then
     `karac run prog.kara` -- ran the program normally. The JIT lane calls
     `locate_karac_jit_runner()` and, on `None`, prints
     `error: karac_jit_runner not found` and returns. It printed nothing.
     (Setting `KARAC_JIT_RUNNER` to a bogus path is NOT sufficient: that helper
     falls back to the sibling binary when the env path does not exist, which is
     why the first attempt at this test was inconclusive.)
  2. A pure compute loop -- `while i < 20000000 { acc = acc + i % 7; i = i + 1 }`
     -- did not finish under `karac run` within a 10-minute cap. Native code
     runs that in well under a second whatever the opt level.

Both against a `karac` built `--features llvm` (the same binary's `karac build`
succeeds, so the feature is on) and a `karac_jit_runner` rebuilt in the same
`cargo build --features llvm` invocation, so this is not the stale-runner
footgun CLAUDE.md documents.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A SLOW `run`. The four-surface protocol this repo's
drop-family rows use is interp / JIT / AOT / AOT-with-KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, and it
is the evidence standard those rows are argued on. If `karac run` is the
interpreter, that matrix has THREE distinct surfaces, not four, and the JIT is
unverified by every one of those measurements -- including the ones in this
session's own rows, whose phrasing is corrected in B-2026-08-29-48's fix note.
An A/B divergence that exists only between the JIT and AOT would currently be
invisible to all of them.

NOT YET DIAGNOSED, deliberately: the gate at `run_check_cmds.rs` reads
`output == OutputMode::Text && timeout.is_none() && !interp && !program_uses_gpu
&& !program_uses_arrow_ipc && KARAC_RUN_JIT != "0"`, and every conjunct looks
satisfied for a plain `karac run file.kara` with no env set. Either an enclosing
condition or a different dispatch path is taking these programs, and finding
which is the first step. No environment variable was set in the measuring shell
(`env | grep -i karac` is empty).

Severity high on consequence rather than on user-visible breakage: programs
still run and still produce correct output. What is broken is a verification
channel several open rows depend on.
fix:
INVALID by bc1c37c's session — the premise is refuted. `karac run` DOES reach
the JIT lane; both measurements in this row were artifacts of a stale,
non-llvm `karac` binary.

Re-measured, and the discriminator is a program on which the two backends
genuinely disagree (B-2026-08-29-56's minimal repro, which aborts under the JIT
and is correct under `--interp`):

    ./target/debug/karac run --interp min.kara   -> [zz]
    ./target/debug/karac run          min.kara   -> free(): double free detected

If `karac run` were the tree-walk interpreter, those two could not differ. They
do, deterministically.

The row's own first measurement then reproduces CORRECTLY against a properly
built binary: with `target/debug/karac_jit_runner` moved aside, `karac run`
fails with `error: karac_jit_runner not found — set KARAC_JIT_RUNNER, or
install karac with --features llvm`, and restoring the runner restores the
JIT behaviour. That is exactly the abort this row claimed did not happen.

WHY IT WAS MISMEASURED, since the trap is documented in CLAUDE.md and still
caught someone. A plain `cargo test` (no `--features llvm`) overwrites
`target/debug/karac` with a NON-LLVM build. That binary never looks for the
runner at all — it prints "requires the llvm feature; falling back to type
check" for `build` and routes `run` to the tree-walk interpreter — so hiding
the runner changes nothing (measurement 1) and a 20M-iteration loop is
interpreter-slow and times out (measurement 2). Both readings are consistent
with "no JIT lane" and both are really "no llvm in this binary". The session
had run `cargo test` between building and measuring.

CONSEQUENCE for the rows this session filed around it: the retraction it
prompted was itself wrong. Measurements described as a "JIT surface" in
B-2026-08-29-10, -48 and -57 were JIT readings after all, provided the
`--features llvm` build was current at the time — which is the same staleness
question every AOT measurement in this repo carries, and is checked the same
way (rebuild both bins, then measure).

PRACTICAL RULE, worth more than this row was: before concluding anything about
`karac run`'s backend, prove the binary is an llvm build — the cheapest proof
is that `karac run` and `karac run --interp` DIFFER on a known
divergent program, not that some timing looks slow.

title: `asinh` / `acosh` / `atanh` diverge between `run` and `build` at f64 as well as f32 -- Rust std implements the inverse hyperbolics as formulas rather than libm calls, so the interpreter ran a different ALGORITHM from the `asinh` / `asinhf` codegen emits, which no choice of width or rounding could reconcile.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-29-41, which made every other scalar float method
agree between the interpreter and codegen at every width. These three are what is
left, and unlike the rest they are NOT a missing-narrowing or wrong-width bug:
no interpreter-side choice fixes them.

MEASURED (x86_64, f32 receivers, 60 inputs of i/7 for `asinh`, 1 + i/7 for
`acosh`, i/61 for `atanh`; `karac run --interp` vs `karac run`):

    method   diverging   f32-native == codegen   f64-then-round == codegen
    asinh      13/60              47/60                    50/60
    acosh       4/60              56/60                    55/60
    atanh       1/60              59/60                    55/60

The middle column is what the interpreter does today; the right column is what it
did before B-2026-08-29-41. NEITHER is right. For comparison, the methods that
row fixed sit at 60/60 in the middle column (`to_degrees`, `to_radians`) or 40/40
(`cosh`, `sinh`, `log10`, `atan`, `exp`, `ln`, `sqrt`, `tan`).

MECHANISM. Rust's std does not delegate the inverse hyperbolics to libm the way
it does `cosh`/`log10`/`atan`; it implements them as formulas
(`asinh` as `(x + (x*x + 1).sqrt()).ln()` and friends). So three different
algorithms are in play for one function:

    Rust `f32::asinh`   -- an ln/sqrt formula evaluated in f32
    Rust `f64::asinh`   -- the f64 formula, then rounded to f32
    codegen             -- a call to the platform's `asinhf`

The interpreter can pick either of the first two. Codegen calls the third. That
is why both columns above fall short, and why this is not closable by choosing a
width -- the width is already right.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT (none attempted here, in rough cost order):

  1. Have the interpreter call the SAME `asinhf` / `acoshf` / `atanhf` codegen
     calls, via `libc` or a small `extern "C"` block. Exact by construction, and
     the same "one implementation, both backends" rule the `karac-hash` crate and
     the Arrow IPC twin already follow. Costs a libc dependency on a path that
     currently has none, and needs a decision about platforms whose libm differs.
  2. Have CODEGEN stop calling libm and emit the same formula the interpreter
     evaluates. Removes the platform dependence entirely (today the compiled
     answer varies with the host libm), but changes compiled numerics for a
     function people may already depend on.
  3. Declare the inverse hyperbolics accurate-to-1-ULP rather than bit-exact and
     write that into design.md, so the A/B rule has a stated exception with a
     bound instead of an undocumented one.

SEVERITY low, for the same reason the parent row was: the values are correct to
within a rounding step. It is still an A/B-rule violation, which the project
treats as non-negotiable, so it is filed rather than absorbed. Note that the
1/60 for `atanh` makes this exactly the kind of gap a small fixture will miss --
see the parent row's luck-of-the-inputs correction.
fix:
FIXED by cc4f0c6. It routes the interpreter's `asinh` / `acosh` / `atanh` to the SAME libm
entry points codegen calls -- option 1 of the three the row listed -- via a
small `extern "C"` block and six safe shims in `src/float_math.rs`, consumed by
a second `at_width_libm!` macro in the interpreter's float-math arm that names
the f64 and f32 symbol for each method so the two width paths cannot drift.
Zero new dependencies: `libc` is gated behind the `llvm` feature and the
interpreter must build on the default leg, so the six C99 symbols are declared
directly.

WHY THAT OPTION, MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED. Over 720 values (3 methods x 2
widths x 120 inputs) the compiled output equalled libm's value on EVERY line
and the interpreted output equalled Rust's formula on EVERY line; the
formula-vs-libm difference counts reproduced the observed interp-vs-codegen
divergence exactly in all six cells (f64 14/17/3, f32 10/12/12 of 120). So the
gap was not a rounding step that could be tuned -- it was two different
algorithms -- and calling libm closes it by CONSTRUCTION, the same
"one implementation, both backends" rule the `karac-hash` crate and the Arrow
IPC twin follow. Option 2 (codegen emits Rust's formula) was rejected as the
larger and less consistent change: it would leave these three as the only
float-math methods NOT calling libm, against the twenty that do, and would
change compiled numerics people may already depend on. Option 3 (declare a
1-ULP tolerance in design.md) is moot once the answer is exact; design.md's one
relevant sentence, "Math (`sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, etc.) via libm", is now more
true than it was, so no spec change was needed.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ROW'S OWN MEASUREMENTS.

(1) NOT f32-only. f64 diverges too, at a comparable rate: 14/17/3 of 120 for
    `asinh`/`acosh`/`atanh`, against this row's implicit claim that the f64
    column was clean. Rust implements the inverse hyperbolics as formulas at
    BOTH widths, so f64 was never in a different position -- the parent row
    (B-2026-08-29-41) had sampled only two receivers per width and neither
    happened to expose it. That is precisely the luck-of-the-inputs trap this
    row's closing paragraph warns about, landing on this row's own claim.

(2) The frequency is much higher than the row's 60-input table suggested. On a
    400-point series spanning negatives, the `acosh` boundary at 1.0 and
    `atanh` near +/-1, Rust's formula differs from libm on up to 137/400 (34%)
    of f64 inputs and 148/400 (37%) of f32 inputs for `acosh` -- not the 4/60
    the row tabulated. Severity stays LOW because each individual value is
    still correct to within a rounding step, but this was a common case, not a
    rare one.

WHY IT SHIPPED. `float_math.rs`'s own `classify` doc already names this exact
hazard -- it explains that `cbrt` is deliberately EXCLUDED from the language
because "Rust's `f64::cbrt` is an in-Rust implementation, not a libm call, and
it disagrees with the system libm `cbrt` this table would lower to ... which
would break `run == build`". The three inverse hyperbolics sit in that same
class and were admitted into the table below that comment without anyone
noticing. The hazard was documented; the membership test was never applied.

WHY f16 AND bf16 NEVER SHOWED IT, before or after. Both widths were 0/120 on
every surface even with the bug present. The formula-vs-libm gap is about one
ULP at f32 (~2^-24 relative), and narrowing the f32 result to f16's 11-bit or
bf16's 8-bit mantissa absorbs it: both backends round to the same reduced-
precision value. So the divergence is visible only at the two widths where the
final rounding is not coarse enough to hide it -- f32 and f64 -- which is the
complete explanation of the width pattern, and another reason a fixture built
from a couple of reduced-precision receivers proves nothing here.

VERIFIED. 4 widths x 4 surfaces (`run --interp`, `run` JIT, `build` with
auto-par, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`), on both the 120-point and the 400-point
series: 32 and 31 diverging lines at f32/f64 before, ZERO after, at every
width on every surface. The full 36-method float sweep from B-2026-08-29-41 is
also clean at all four widths, so nothing else moved. Regression tests are an
oracle pair -- `tests/interpreter.rs::
test_inverse_hyperbolics_agree_with_the_libm_symbols_codegen_calls` and
`tests/codegen.rs::test_e2e_inverse_hyperbolics_agree_with_the_interpreter` --
whose expectations are COMPUTED from libm rather than hardcoded, so they pin
the actual invariant ("both backends call the same symbol") against whatever
libm the host has instead of freezing one platform's bits into the suite.
Negative control: with the routing reverted, all 16 of 16 lines fail.

ONE THING NOT VERIFIED HERE. The six symbols are C99 7.12.5 and are exported by
glibc, musl, macOS libSystem and the Windows UCRT alike, but this container has
no MSVC toolchain and the Windows CI job runs the DEFAULT leg only
(`cargo build --all` / `cargo test --all`, no `--features llvm`) -- so codegen
has never linked `asinhf` there either, and the interpreter's `extern "C"`
block is genuinely the first thing to require these symbols on that platform.
The exposure is bounded and loud: a missing symbol is a link error on the
Windows `test` job, not a wrong answer, and the new interpreter test is
self-consistent on any libm (it compares the interpreter against the same
symbols the test binary links), so it cannot fail merely for computing
different bits than glibc does.

TITLE CORRECTED on close. The original said the divergence was "at f32" and
that "no interpreter-side choice reproduces the third" algorithm. The first is
wrong (f64 diverges too, see above). The second is refuted by this fix:
calling libm from the interpreter IS an interpreter-side choice, and it
reproduces codegen exactly. The row had implicitly limited the interpreter to
picking between Rust's own f32 and f64 implementations, which is what made the
problem look unsolvable from that side.

title: ONE AOT BINARY RETURNS TWO ANSWERS FOR THE SAME VALUE: `karac build` constant-folds a compile-time-known f32 `cosh`/`sinh`/`log10` in double precision while the runtime call uses the f32 symbol, so `lit.cosh()` and `dyn.cosh()` differ even though the binary prints `lit == dyn` as true. Breaks run == build.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-29-41. Independent of that fix, which is
interpreter-only: this is entirely codegen-side and reproduces on a HEAD build
either way.

ONE AOT BINARY RETURNS TWO DIFFERENT ANSWERS FOR THE SAME VALUE.

    fn main() {
        let lit: f32 = 2.0f32;                  // compile-time known
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let dyn32: f32 = ((n + 1) as f32);      // runtime-derived, same 2.0
        println(f"lit  cosh {lit.cosh()}");
        println(f"dyn  cosh {dyn32.cosh()}");
        println(f"equal {lit == dyn32}");
    }

    karac run --interp    lit 3.7621958255767822   dyn 3.7621958255767822
    karac run   (JIT)     lit 3.7621958255767822   dyn 3.7621958255767822
    karac build (AOT)     lit 3.762195587158203    dyn 3.7621958255767822
    (all three print `equal true`)

`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` is identical to the default build, so this is not
an auto-par effect.

The binary agrees that the two receivers are equal and then computes `cosh` of
them differently. That self-contradiction is what makes it a defect rather than a
precision preference -- the same shape as B-2026-08-29-53, where a compiled
`Vector[f16, N].tanh()` disagreed with its own scalar `tanh`.

MECHANISM. LLVM's constant folder evaluates a libm call on a constant argument
using the HOST's double-precision function and rounds the result to f32; the
runtime call goes to `coshf` directly. Two roundings versus one -- the same
double-rounding that B-2026-08-29-41 fixed on the interpreter side, appearing
here inside codegen and gated on whether the argument happens to be known at
compile time.

SCOPE, measured over four f32 receivers (2, 3, 5, 7) x 19 unary methods,
comparing the folded literal against the runtime call in the SAME binary:

    cosh    2/4 inputs   e.g. folded 3.762195587158203  runtime 3.7621958255767822
    log10   1/4          e.g. folded 0.4771212637424469 runtime 0.4771212339401245
    sinh    1/4          e.g. folded 548.3161010742188  runtime 548.316162109375

Everything else agreed on those inputs; the sample is small and the affected set
is likely wider, so treat these three as a lower bound rather than the list.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ULP. Two consequences are worse than the size of the
error suggests. First, it breaks `run == build`, which kara-katas treats as
non-negotiable and which is the project's main cross-backend safety net. Second,
it means constant-folding is not semantics-preserving here: the same expression
changes value when a binding becomes compile-time known, so an unrelated edit
that lets a value fold can silently move a result.

A TESTING NOTE WORTH KEEPING. This is why the B-2026-08-29-41 sweeps derived
their receivers from `env.args()`. A fixture built from literals measures the
FOLDED path, not the runtime one, and the two are not the same program -- the
mirror image of the vacuity trap in B-2026-08-29-34, where a folded probe
reported health because the operation never reached ISel.

WHERE TO LOOK. The fold happens in LLVM, so the lever is on the emission side:
either mark these calls so the folder leaves them alone, or make the folder's
precision match the runtime call. Worth checking first whether the JIT escapes
purely because it optimizes less -- if so, the same divergence is latent there at
a higher opt level rather than absent.
fix:
FIXED by d95d6f7.

A float method whose result is not exactly representable at the receiver's
width is now marked `nobuiltin` at its LLVM call site, so the constant folder
leaves it alone and the value is produced by the target's libm on every path --
folded or called, native or cross-compiled.

MECHANISM, CONFIRMED RATHER THAN INHERITED FROM THE ROW. The row named LLVM's
constant folder; three measurements pin it:

  * `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` builds AGREE (both columns 3.7621958255767822). O1, O2
    and O3 all diverge. So it is the mid-end pipeline, not ISel and not the
    front end.
  * `main`'s disassembly holds exactly ONE `coshf` call for a program that
    writes two. The literal receiver never reaches a call at all.
  * The JIT escapes for a stronger reason than the row guessed. It asked
    whether the JIT merely "optimizes less", and whether the divergence is
    latent there at a higher opt level. It is not: the JIT runs NO mid-end
    pipeline -- `codegen.rs`'s JIT path calls `run_passes` with
    `coro-early,coro-split,coro-cleanup` and nothing else -- and
    `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL` moves nothing there (measured identical at 0/1/2/3
    against an AOT build that diverges at 1/2/3). The divergence would appear
    the day the JIT gained the mid-end, not at a knob that exists today.

THE ROW'S SET WAS A LOWER BOUND, AS IT SUSPECTED: three methods named, SEVEN
affected. Sweeping all 27 `float_math` methods over 20 receivers each at all
four float widths, comparing the folded column against the runtime column IN
ONE BINARY (2160 rows per pass):

    width   before                                              after
    f32     18/540   asin atan tanh cosh(3) log10(4)
                     sinh(4) atan2(4)                           0/540
    f64      0/540                                              0/540
    f16      0/540                                              0/540
    bf16     0/540                                              0/540

f64 is clean because the fold and the call are the same host `cosh`; it would
diverge on a cross-compiled target, which is why the rule is not restricted to
f32. f16 and bf16 are clean because the fold's second rounding lands on the
same 11- or 8-bit value. After the fix all four widths are also byte-identical
across `--interp`, `karac run`, `karac build` and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac
build` -- 2160 rows, four surfaces.

THE LEVER: `nobuiltin` ON THE CALL SITE. `canConstantFoldCallTo` returns false
for a no-builtin call before it inspects anything else, and does so for an
overloaded intrinsic (`llvm.log10.f32`) exactly as for a named symbol
(`coshf`) -- which matters because karac emits these two different ways
depending on whether the LLVM-18 pin has an intrinsic for the method, and both
arms fold. Putting it on the CALL and not on the declaration is what keeps the
cost to the fold alone: LLVM's library-attribute inference still runs on the
`coshf` declaration, so the call keeps its `memory(read)` / `nounwind` and
stays hoistable; only the fold and the libcall-simplifier rewrites are given
up.

WHY NOT FOLD IT CORRECTLY INSTEAD. karac could evaluate the constant itself
with Rust's `f32::cosh` and emit the result. That fixes the native case and
RE-CREATES the bug for a cross-compiled one, because the fold would then be the
HOST's libm and the call the TARGET's (wasm's wasi-libc). Suppressing the fold
makes the value come from one implementation on every path by construction,
rather than by the host and the target happening to agree -- the same rule the
`karac-hash` crate and the Arrow IPC twin follow.

FIVE METHODS KEEP THE FOLD, and that exemption is the half most worth stating.
`floor` / `ceil` / `round` / `trunc` return a value exactly representable at
the receiver's width and `copysign` only moves a sign bit, so for these the
wider computation and the narrow one agree on every input and the fold is free.
`float_math::constant_fold_is_exact` is the single table, placed next to
`classify` for the same anti-drift reason that module exists, and a unit test
pins every one of the 27 names to a side. Non-vacuity confirmed on the
disassembly: a program of `(2.7f32).floor()` and `.ceil()` links no `floorf` or
`ceilf` at all, so those are still folded rather than merely still correct.
(`sqrt` is not in the table but belongs on the exact side for a subtler reason
recorded in the doc comment: rounding a binary64 square root to binary32 is
correctly rounded because 53 >= 2*24 + 2. That is a property of `sqrt` alone.)

WHAT THE FIX COSTS, MEASURED. Only the fold. For a RUNTIME receiver the emitted
binaries are BYTE-IDENTICAL before and after (checked for `cosh` and `log10`).
For a compile-time-known receiver inside a loop, an intrinsic-family method is
still hoisted out by LICM -- `log10f` called once above the loop, the body an
unrolled `vaddss` chain -- while a direct-libm-family method is not, so
`(2.0f32).cosh()` in a 1000-iteration loop went from a folded constant to a
per-iteration call. That asymmetry is PRE-EXISTING rather than introduced here:
pre-fix, a RUNTIME-receiver `cosh` was already called inside the loop, and the
pre/post binaries for that program are identical. Filed as B-2026-08-30-27.

SCOPE: THE SCALAR PATH IS THE WHOLE SURFACE, checked rather than assumed. The
only other place codegen lowers a transcendental is the SIMD path
(`method_call_vector.rs`), and it is not exposed: `Vector.exp` / `ln` / `tanh` /
`sigmoid` are built from `fmul` / `fadd` / `fdiv` on the vector type rather than
from a libm call, and LLVM folds plain FP arithmetic with APFloat at the
operand's own semantics -- there is no host-double detour to double-round. The
five vector ops that DO use an intrinsic (`sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`,
`trunc`) are exactly the five on the exact side of the table. `float_math` has
one codegen consumer, `method_call.rs:3869`, and both of its emission arms are
covered.

SCOPE: THE SCALAR PATH IS THE WHOLE SURFACE, checked rather than assumed. The
only other place codegen lowers a transcendental is the SIMD path
(`method_call_vector.rs`), and it is not exposed: `Vector.exp` / `ln` / `tanh` /
`sigmoid` are built from `fmul` / `fadd` / `fdiv` on the vector type rather than
from a libm call, and LLVM folds plain FP arithmetic with APFloat at the
operand's own semantics -- there is no host-double detour to double-round. The
five vector ops that DO use an intrinsic (`sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`,
`trunc`) are exactly the five on the exact side of the table. `float_math` has
one codegen consumer, `method_call.rs:3869`, and both of its emission arms --
the direct libm call and the overloaded intrinsic -- are covered.

FIXTURE. `e2e_compile_time_known_float_math_is_not_folded_at_double_precision`
is built from all 18 measured pre-fix divergences plus four exact-op controls,
and asserts that the two columns AGREE rather than that either matches a
literal -- the value is the host libm's and differs across platforms, but a
fold and a call on one machine must not. RED-verified: against the pre-fix
compiler it fails on its first row (`asin` of 0.8, folded 0.9272952675819397 vs
called 0.9272952079772949). A fixture built from the three methods the row
named would have missed `atan2`, `tanh`, `atan` and `asin`.

ALSO FOUND WHILE SWEEPING, FILED SEPARATELY: B-2026-08-30-26 -- `n as bf16` from an
integer compiles under the interpreter and is REFUSED by both compiled
backends, which is what stopped the bf16 leg of the sweep until it was routed
through f32.

WONTFIX -- real, reproducible, fully explained, and NOT decidable by any static
rule.

NO FIX COMMIT, deliberately: nothing in the compiler changes for this row, so
the SHA recorded against it is 7a10c4e -- B-2026-08-30-6's fix, the last commit
to touch this recogniser and the one whose side effect (the difference form now
accepts `>> 1`) retired this row's own leading hypothesis. The re-measurement
below is against that commit, i.e. current `main`.

MECHANISM, now identified exactly. The cliff is LLVM's `X86CmovConversion`
pass, which rewrites a `cmov` BACK into a branch when it judges the `cmov` to
sit on a loop-carried dependency chain short enough that a predicted branch
would be cheaper. Proof: rebuilding the `>> 1` lane with
`KARAC_LLVM_ARGS="-x86-cmov-converter=false"` yields byte-for-byte the same
branchless loop the `/ 2` lane gets -- identical `cmovge`/`cmovl`, 41 `cmov` in
`main` against 39 -- minus the sign correction, and it is then the FASTEST build
of all at 634.9 ms.

So the `/ 2` spelling was never "better". Signed division by 2 truncates toward
zero, which costs a three-instruction sign correction (`shr $0x3f; add;
sar $1`); that dead weight lengthens the chain just enough to tip the pass's
arithmetic and leave the `cmov` in place. The correct, cheaper `>> 1` spelling
loses the branchless form precisely BECAUSE it is cheaper. The 1.67x is the
price of an accident, not of the shift.

WHY IT IS STILL NOT FIXABLE HERE. karac recognises this idiom syntactically
(`control_flow_bce.rs` § midpoint), so it CAN annotate the comparison branch
`!unpredictable`, which suppresses the pass. That was implemented, and it works:
kata #300 went 1187 -> 639.0 ms, 1.86x, with `/ 2` unchanged (713.9 -> 713.6)
and all gates green. It was REVERTED, because on kata #275's h-index search the
same annotation is 2.02x SLOWER (454.0 -> 916.0 ms). The marking was precise --
`cmov` in `main` went 70 -> 72, exactly the one comparison -- so this is not a
targeting bug. The premise is simply false: a binary search's comparison is NOT
unpredictable by construction.

THE DECIDING MEASUREMENT. Same program, same spelling, same compiler; only the
DATA changed (kata #300's values from uniform-random to a ramp):

    values      branchy (default)   branchless (forced)   winner
    random          1187 ms             639.0 ms          branchless 1.86x
    ramp             416.7 ms           480.1 ms          branchy     1.15x

The sign flips on the input distribution alone. Which lowering is right is a
property of the data, not of the source, so no static rule -- in karac or in
LLVM -- can choose correctly. Cache residency was tested as a rival explanation
and refuted: kata #275's search shrunk to 512 elements (4 KiB, L1-resident)
still prefers the branch, 162.8 vs 190.2 ms.

WHAT IS AVAILABLE TO A USER WHO KNOWS THEIR SEARCH IS UNPREDICTABLE: the
existing lever, no new surface needed --
`KARAC_LLVM_ARGS="-x86-cmov-converter=false"` (634.9 ms, matching the reverted
annotation's 639.0 within noise).

C CONTRAST, re-measured, and sharper than the row and kata README had it. clang
emits ZERO `cmov` in `main` for EVERY spelling, so it never makes this
if-conversion decision at all; in C the spread is pure instruction cost:
signed `long / 2` 1.206 s, `long >> 1` 927.7 ms, `size_t / 2` 933.1 ms. Adding
`__builtin_unpredictable` to the comparison -- the C spelling of the annotation
above -- takes clang to 663.7 ms, 1.40x, confirming the mechanism is LLVM-wide
and not a karac artifact. Note where that leaves the corpus: karac's default
`/ 2` lane at 713.9 ms already beats every unannotated clang build here, WHILE
still carrying a bounds check clang does not emit.

SUPERSEDES the "surviving overflow checks" hypothesis recorded below. That
patch is now effectively landed -- 7a10c4e's fix taught the difference form to
accept `>> 1` as a side effect -- and the cliff is unchanged at 1.67x on current
`main`, measured, which retires the hypothesis on landed code rather than on a
reverted patch.
title: Spelling a binary-search midpoint `lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1)` instead of `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` costs 1.67x on current main: LLVM's X86CmovConversion rewrites the branchless loop back into a branch, and only `/ 2`'s signed sign-correction lengthens the dependency chain enough to stop it -- so the "slower" spelling wins by accident. NOT statically decidable: forcing the branchless form is 1.86x FASTER on this kata and 2.02x SLOWER on kata #275, and flipping only the input data from random to a ramp reverses the sign within this one program
detail:
REPRO: kara-katas leetcode/201-300/300-longest-increasing-subsequence/bench/lisscan.kara, a patience-sorting LIS over 3000 arrays x 512 elements x 24 passes. The ONLY difference between the two binaries is one character on line 67:

    let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;        709.1 ms +/- 3.0
    let mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1);    1144   ms +/- 5.0     1.61x +/- 0.01

Both print checksum 122670492. hyperfine, 10 runs, 3 warmup, x86-64 container (4-core Xeon @ 2.80 GHz), karac 0.1.0-dev, default build. KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 reproduces the same ratio, so auto-par is not involved (the `/ 2` build measures 713.8 ms default vs 716.3 ms with auto-par off -- 1.00x, and user time tracks wall in both, i.e. single-threaded either way).

MECHANISM, MEASURED rather than read off the disassembly (cachegrind --branch-sim=yes, workload shrunk to 200 arrays x 2 passes so the simulation terminates):

                      / 2            >> 1          delta
  I refs        18,459,532      17,082,883         -7.5%
  Branches       2,952,946       5,793,071        +96.2%
  Mispredicts      178,447         700,820       +292.7%
  Mispred rate         6.0%           12.1%

The `>> 1` build executes FEWER instructions and is 1.61x slower. Instruction mix in `main` agrees on the cause: the `/ 2` build carries `cmovge` + `cmovl` for the search's compare and the `>> 1` build carries NEITHER, gaining `jge` in their place (and `jo` 1 -> 3). So `if tails[mid] < x { lo = mid + 1 } else { hi = mid }` is if-converted to branchless conditional moves when the midpoint is written `/ 2`, and is left as a real branch when it is written `>> 1`. On a data-dependent binary search that branch is close to a coin flip, and the mispredict rate doubles.

WHY THIS IS FILED EVEN THOUGH KARA WINS THE LANE. With `/ 2` kara is the FASTEST mirror on this workload -- 709 ms against clang -O3's 950 ms (size_t indices) and 1.249 s (long indices), rustc -O 1.072 s, go 1.046 s. Nothing is broken. What is filed is a CLIFF: a one-character, semantics-preserving rewrite that a performance-minded programmer is likely to reach for precisely because they believe a shift is cheaper than a divide, and which costs 61%. The two spellings are indistinguishable in the source and in the language reference; only the stopwatch separates them.

RULED OUT, each measured: NOT the shift operator's own cost -- an isolated tight loop `acc = acc + (i / 2)` vs `(i >> 1)` over 3e8 iterations measures 101.2 ms vs 101.4 ms, dead level, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 (the first attempt at this control was auto-parallelized -- user 219 ms against wall 60 ms -- and had to be redone). NOT bounds checks: the two `main` disassemblies are 6258 and 6261 lines with 5 panic calls each. NOT signed-division semantics: kara's `/` truncates toward zero exactly like C and Rust (-3/2 = -1, -7/2 = -3, -7%4 = -3) on both the interpreter and codegen backends, so the `/ 2` form is not winning by being wrong.

CONTRAST WITH THE C MIRROR, which is the mirror-image defect and is worth recording next to this one because the two point in opposite directions. In C the SAME source-level choice runs the other way: `long lo, hi; ... lo + (hi - lo) / 2` costs clang 1.249 s and rewriting it as `>> 1`, or as `size_t`, or as `unsigned long` all land at ~950 ms (949.9 / 950.2 / 963.3). There the signed `/ 2` pays a sign-correction sequence that the shift avoids. So the identical micro-decision is worth -31% in C and +61% in kara, in opposite directions. `restrict` on the data pointer changes nothing (963.3 ms), ruling out aliasing on the C side.

PRIOR ART. B-2026-08-13-10 (fixed) is the same if-conversion class from the other side -- LLVM declining to if-convert a reduction karac emits, where rustc/clang did -- and its fix was to widen a full-unroll hint. This row is the reverse: if-conversion FIRES for the natural spelling and is LOST for an equivalent one, so the lead is whatever in the emitted IR differs between `sdiv by 2` and `ashr 1` such that the former keeps the select and the latter does not. B-2026-08-21-3 (wontfix) is the standing warning that retired-instruction counts do not order variants on this codebase; this row is another instance -- fewer instructions, materially slower -- and was measured with a branch simulator for that reason rather than argued from a disassembly read.

WHERE TO LOOK: what karac emits for `ExprKind::Binary` `Shr` against `Div` by a constant 2 on i64, and whether the overflow-check scaffolding around `>>` (the extra `jo`) introduces a basic block that makes SimplifyCFG's if-conversion look unprofitable for the enclosing compare. NOT VERIFIED -- the `jo` delta is suggestive but the causal direction between the shift's checks and the lost select has not been established.d.

=== INVESTIGATION 2026-08-30 -- STILL OPEN. Three hypotheses refuted by
measurement, and the cause localised to LLVM rather than to karac. ===

THE DIVERGENCE IS NOT IN WHAT KARAC EMITS. At `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` both
spellings produce the SAME number of overflow-check branches in `main` (12
`jo` each). At O1/O2/O3 the div build keeps 1 and the shift build keeps 3.
karac hands LLVM equivalent IR and LLVM discharges two more checks for one
spelling than the other, so nothing in codegen's own lowering distinguishes
them. This retires the row's original "WHERE TO LOOK" note.

REFUTED (1) -- the shift-amount range check. The row supposed
`emit_shift_amount_check`'s two basic blocks plus conditional branch split the
block and deterred if-conversion. Implemented the obvious fix (constant-fold
the check when the amount is a compile-time constant, emitting nothing) and
measured: NO change, 1.62x before and after. The string "shift amount out of
range" is absent from the pre-fix binary too -- LLVM was already folding those
blocks away. Reverted.

REFUTED (2) -- the surviving overflow checks. Extended the binary-search
midpoint recogniser (`control_flow_bce.rs` § midpoint) to accept `>> 1`
alongside `/ 2`, which is sound for the difference form and does what the row
predicted to the code: `jo` in `main` went 3 -> 1, matching the div build
exactly. The cliff did NOT move. Worse, interleaved A/B over 20 runs put the
patched build at 1.159 s -> 1.192 s, i.e. 1.03x +/- 0.02 SLOWER on 39 fewer
disassembled lines. That is the B-2026-08-21-3 pattern again -- fewer
instructions, slower wall -- and the change was reverted rather than landed.
The `/ 2` build was byte-for-byte unaffected (719.8 vs 719.0 ms), confirming
the patch touched only the shift path.

REFUTED (3) -- SimplifyCFG's two-entry-phi cost model.
`KARAC_LLVM_ARGS=-two-entry-phi-node-folding-threshold=` at 2, 4 and 8 leaves
the cmov count in `main` at 39 in every case. Whatever declines the
if-conversion is not that threshold, so it is happening below IR level
(ISel / early-ifcvt / MachineBlockPlacement) rather than in SimplifyCFG.

WHAT IS LEFT, and it is now a single difference. With the overflow checks
equalised the two inner loops are instruction-identical up to the compare; the
ONLY remaining distinction is the three-instruction sign-correction sequence
(`shr $0x3f; add; sar $1`) that signed `/ 2` carries and `>> 1` does not. The
div loop if-converts both assignments (`cmovge` / `cmovl`); the shift loop
keeps `jge`. So the working hypothesis is now that the correction's presence
is what tips a machine-level if-conversion decision -- NOT VERIFIED, and the
next step is to confirm it by constructing a shift-spelled loop carrying an
equivalent-cost dead sequence and checking whether the cmov returns.

SPUN OUT: B-2026-08-30-6, a HIGH-severity miscompile in the same recogniser,
found while reading it for hypothesis (2). `(lo + hi) / 2` truncates toward
zero, so its `assume(mid < hi)` is `assume(false)` for a negative odd sum, and
a bisection over negative bounds SIGBUS'd compiled while running correctly
interpreted. Fixed in 7a10c4e. The two rows are the same spelling-sensitivity
seen from opposite sides: this row is a spelling that is sound but
unrecognised; that one was a spelling recognised but unsound.

title: Passing an own-heap struct BY VALUE deep-copies its heap fields at every call, even though the argument is MOVED -- measured at exactly N*8 extra bytes for an N-element `Vec[i64]` field at N=256/1024/4096, on callees that return the param, wrap it, or just read a field and drop it, and with or without a `Drop` impl
detail:
Found and measured while fixing B-2026-08-29-50, whose analysis turned on whether
the caller and the callee's result own the same buffer. They do not, and the
reason is this: passing an own-heap struct BY VALUE deep-copies its heap fields
at the call, even though the argument is MOVED and the caller can never observe
it again.

    struct Res { id: i64, buf: Vec[i64] }
    fn mkres(n: i64) -> Res { ... buf of N elements ... }
    fn eatf(r: Res) -> i64 { return r.id; }        // param DIES inside
    fn main() { let a = mkres(41); let n = eatf(a); println(f"{n}"); }

Total bytes allocated, valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, against the identical
program with the call removed (`let n = a.id;`):

    N elements    with call    no call    delta      N * 8
       256          10,266      8,218     2,048      2,048
     1,024          22,554     14,362     8,192      8,192
     4,096          71,706     38,938    32,768     32,768

The delta is exactly the element buffer, at every size -- a full deep copy, not a
header or a rounding artifact. Allocation counts go 10 -> 11 in every case: one
extra buffer, freed once, so the program stays balanced and valgrind-clean. It is
a COST, not a leak, which is why nothing has caught it.

NOT SPECIFIC TO ANY OF THE THINGS IT COULD PLAUSIBLY BE SPECIFIC TO. Measured at
+2,048 (N=256) for all of:

  * a callee that just reads a field and drops the param (`eatf` above),
  * a callee that hands the param straight back (`fn takef(r: Res) -> Res { r }`),
  * a callee that moves it into a returned aggregate (`Hh { r: r }`),
  * the same struct WITHOUT a `Drop` impl at all.

So it is the by-value argument passing itself, not `Drop` registration, not the
return path, and not the aggregate.

WHY IT MATTERS. Kara is a move language: `eatf(a)` is documented and checked as a
MOVE, `a` is dead afterwards, and the ownership tiers exist precisely so that a
caller who wants to keep the value writes `ref`. A move that silently costs
O(size-of-heap-fields) defeats that -- a 4,096-element buffer costs 32 KB of
memcpy per call, and a hot loop pays it per iteration. The interpreter does not
copy, so this is also a compiled-vs-interpreted PERFORMANCE gap, not just an
absolute one.

THE TREE MODELS THIS DELIBERATELY, which is why the row is filed rather than
fixed here. `binding_use.rs` ("models a free-function argument as entry-copied
and therefore NON-consuming"), `codegen/consume_class.rs`, and
`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` all encode the entry copy, and a family of
ownership decisions is built on top of it -- B-2026-08-06-9, B-2026-08-06-31 and
the `optres_param_entry_copied` path all reason from "the callee's copy is
independent". Removing the copy is therefore not a local change: it is a move to
true move-semantics for by-value struct params, and every one of those decisions
has to be re-derived against it. That is a slice of its own, and plausibly a
design note before it is a patch.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: whether the copy survives at higher
optimisation levels. All figures above are `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, chosen so the
lowering is visible; LLVM may well elide some of these memcpys at -O2, which
would change the practical cost without changing the lowering that produces it.
That check is the first thing the fixing slice should do, because if -O2 already
elides the common cases the priority drops sharply.

SOURCE NOTE: measured while establishing that B-2026-08-29-50's aggregate case
has two PARALLEL owners rather than nested ones -- the copy is exactly what makes
them parallel, and it is why the caller's downgraded field cleanup is correct
there rather than a double free.

UPDATE 2026-08-29 (same session that filed the row). The row's own stated first
step is DONE, and its answer is the OPPOSITE of what the row expected. Two
further things are now measured that the row did not know: what the copy is FOR,
and what removing it costs and breaks.

(1) -O2 DOES NOT ELIDE IT. The row said "LLVM may well elide some of these
memcpys at -O2 ... if -O2 already elides the common cases the priority drops
sharply." It does not. With the buffer genuinely READ, the deltas are unchanged
from -O0 at every size:

    N          O0 delta   O2 delta      N*8
      256        2,048      2,048     2,048
    1,024        8,192      8,192     8,192
    4,096       32,768     32,768    32,768

THE NAIVE VERSION OF THIS CHECK LIES, AND IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION. Run
against this row's own reproduction -- where nothing reads `buf` -- the call and
no-call variants are byte-identical at -O1 and above (9 allocs / 6,170 bytes
both). That looks exactly like "-O2 elides the copy" and is not: LLVM
dead-code-eliminated the BUFFER in both variants, so they matched trivially while
each allocating 2,048 FEWER bytes than at -O0. The tell is that the CONTROL moved
too. Any re-check of this must keep the buffer live.

(2) COST: 1.96x ON A HOT LOOP, and the copy is the whole of it. 200,000 calls
passing a 1,024-element `Res`, against the identical program whose callee takes
`ref Res` (same output, 19999900000):

    by value   10.8 ms   400,047 allocs   3,276,809,723 bytes
    by ref      5.5 ms   200,047 allocs   1,638,409,723 bytes

Exactly 2x the allocations and 2x the bytes. With the copy removed (prototype
below) the by-value form runs in 5.6 ms and allocates 200,047 /
1,638,409,723 -- INDISTINGUISHABLE from the `ref` version. So the entire gap is
this copy, and closing it is worth ~2x on by-value-struct-passing code.

(3) WHAT THE COPY IS FOR -- the part this row got wrong by omission. It framed
the copy as pure cost. It is not: it is the mechanism implementing the
DELIBERATELY NON-FATAL `UseAfterMove` promise at CALL-ARGUMENT sites.
Use-after-move is a WARNING, not an error (`kind_blocks_production`,
src/ownership.rs): `karac check` on `let a = mk(); f(a); println(a.buf[1]);`
prints `warning[ownership]` and then `All checks passed`, and `karac build`
emits a working binary. That is documented and intentional, on the promise that
"codegen defensive-copies the reuse, so the binary is memory-safe".

But the TARGETED mechanism for that promise (`uam_consume_sites` /
`uam_defensive_copy`, B-2026-08-10-21) has exactly THREE call sites -- two
struct-literal field inits and one let-stmt value -- and NONE is a call argument.
Measured: the use-after-move program above allocates 11 buffers, the SAME as the
non-reusing call, not 12. There is no second copy at an argument because the
ENTRY copy is already the defensive one. Remove it and that program is a
use-after-free plus a double free (measured below). This row's framing -- "a move
that silently costs O(size-of-heap-fields) defeats [move semantics]" -- still
holds, but the copy is currently load-bearing for a shape the compiler ACCEPTS.

(4) PROTOTYPE, and the exact obstacle set. Env-gated
(`KARAC_MOVE_STRUCT_PARAMS=1`), two edits: the callee prologue
(`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst`, src/codegen/param_own.rs) skips
`deep_copy_struct_heap_fields_in_place`, and `move_declined_copy_struct_arg`
(src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs) widens its retraction to copy-supported structs.
That is the copy-UNSUPPORTED path (B-2026-08-05-33 / B-2026-07-28-4) applied to
copy-supported types -- own by TRANSFER, caller gives up its drop. Built and
measured, then REVERTED; the tree carries none of it.

    shape                                O2 stock      O2 transfer
    identifier, not reused               11 allocs     10, clean, correct
    method arg (`s.eat(a)`)              10            9,  clean, correct
    nested forward (`outer` -> `inner`)  10            9,  clean, correct
    identifier REUSED after the move     11, clean     use-after-free + double free
    fresh call temp `eat(mkres(41))`     10, clean     double free
    fresh struct literal `eat(Res{..})`  10, clean     double free
    field arg `eat(h.r)`                 10, clean     double free

The three winning rows are the payoff; the four failing rows are ONE root cause.
The callee's decision is PER-FUNCTION (type-level -- it compiles one prologue for
every call site), while the caller's retraction is PER-SITE and narrow
(Identifier only, and it must not fire for a reused binding without stranding the
reuse). Wherever the two disagree, both frames free the same buffer.

(5) WHAT A REAL FIX HAS TO LOOK LIKE. The uniform version makes the callee
UNCONDITIONAL -- always transfer, never copy -- and moves every decision to the
caller, the only side that can see the argument's shape:

    identifier, not reused  -> hand over the original, retract the drop  (the win)
    identifier, reused      -> hand over a defensive copy, KEEP the drop
    fresh temp (call / lit) -> hand over the original, and do NOT also free it
                               caller-side (`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct`
                               must then answer false)
    field / index place arg -> hand over a defensive copy; parent keeps ownership

Coherent, and with no caller/callee disagreement left -- but not a local change,
and the dependent surface is LARGER than this row first listed. Besides
`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` there are two siblings that must move in
lockstep -- `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_enum` (B-2026-08-01-14) and
`arg_is_entry_copied_heap_tuple` (B-2026-08-27-44) -- plus the Option/Result
family (`optres_param_entry_copied` / `callee_optres_param_entry_copied`, five
sites across functions.rs, call_dispatch.rs and method_call.rs). Each is a
documented fix carrying its own measurement, and each must be re-derived against
"there is no copy". Re-deriving four families at once in the subsystem with the
most bug history in the tree is how a silent double-free class lands, so this
session deliberately did NOT attempt it -- consistent with this row's own
"a slice of its own, and plausibly a design note before it is a patch".

(6) THE DESIGN QUESTION THAT GATES IT, filed as B-2026-08-29-64. Everything above
is downstream of one decision that is not codegen's to make: is use-after-move an
ERROR or a WARNING? If it becomes an error, the reused-binding row drops out of
the obstacle set entirely and the caller-side defensive copy is never needed --
the fix gets materially smaller. design.md is currently self-inconsistent on
exactly this point, which is why it is a row and not a footnote.
fix:
FIXED by 8b0ad9e. The copy is gone wherever removing it is unobservable, and the
row's own section (5) is what landed -- but reached through a whole-program GATE
rather than the caller-side defensive copies that section proposed, which is what
kept the dependent surface from having to move at all.

(1) WHAT THE GATING QUESTION TURNED OUT TO BE. B-2026-08-29-64 is FIXED, and it
did NOT flip use-after-move to an error: it established that the two surfaces
genuinely differ on purpose (the REPL rejects the cell, `karac build` accepts the
program) and corrected the documentation that denied it. So the compiled surface
keeps the non-fatal warning, the entry copy still has something to protect, and
this row lands in its HARDER form -- the one where a reused binding must keep
working.

(2) THE MECHANISM: A WHOLE-PROGRAM PERMISSION, NOT A PER-SITE REPAIR. The row's
section (5) made the callee unconditional and moved every decision to the caller,
which needs a caller-side defensive copy for reused bindings, field places and
fresh temps -- and re-derives `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_{struct,enum,tuple}` plus
the five-site Option/Result family against "there is no copy". That is the
re-derivation the row warned lands a silent double-free class.

The asymmetry it is fighting is real but it has a second resolution. The callee's
decision is PER-FUNCTION because one body is emitted; the safe shape is a
property of the CALL SITE. So compute the fact the way `bce_interproc` computes
its bounds precondition (new `src/codegen/param_transfer.rs`): a param is
transfer-owned only when EVERY call site in the program passes it safely, and one
site that cannot be proven disqualifies it outright. There is then no
disagreement to repair, because there is no site on the transfer path that wanted
the old behaviour. Every predicate above keeps its exact meaning: a disqualified
param is entry-copied, and `arg_is_entry_copied_heap_struct` still answers true
about it. NONE of the four families moved.

A site is safe when the argument is a plain `Identifier` that names a binding the
frame OWNS -- a `let`, or an own-mode param; never a `ref`/`mut ref` one, never a
name a PATTERN introduces, and never one that is REASSIGNED anywhere in the frame
-- and is NOT in `use_after_move_consume_sites`. Everything else disqualifies: a fresh temp
(whose caller-side cleanup `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` registers), a field
or index place (whose parent keeps ownership), a labelled argument (no positional
mapping attempted), a defaulted param, and any function whose name is ever
mentioned outside direct-callee position -- it may be reached through a call the
walk cannot see. `pub` fns and `main` are excluded for that same reason: their
callers need not be in this program.

(3) THE TYPE HALF, AND THE ONE EXCLUSION THE ROW DID NOT ANTICIPATE. A user
`Drop` ANYWHERE IN THE TYPE declines, and it is about observable ORDER rather than
memory. Transfer moves the value's death from the caller's frame into the
callee's, so a `Drop` body that ran after the call returns now runs before it.
Measured: `println(f"eat={eat(a)}")` over a `Res` with an `impl Drop` prints
`eat=11` then `drop 10` under the entry copy -- AND THE INTERPRETER AGREES WITH
THE ENTRY COPY -- while transfer printed them the other way round. Both orderings
are defensible; only one is what `karac run` does, and a compiled backend that
reorders a user-visible side effect away from the interpreter is a run-vs-build
divergence, which this repo treats as a compiler bug rather than a trade. The
test is transitive and conservative in the declining direction (an unresolvable
field type answers "has a drop"), because a wrong `false` reorders a side effect
and a wrong `true` only misses an optimisation.

That exclusion costs nothing measured. The cost this row is about is the
field-buffer memcpy, and the row's own measurement recorded the same `N * 8`
delta "with or without a `Drop` impl".

Both halves live in ONE predicate, `struct_param_transfer_eligible`
(param_own.rs), read by all three sites that must agree -- the callee prologue,
the caller's drop retraction, and the caller's fresh-temp registrar gate. Sharing
it is the safety argument: a condition that drifted between two of them would
leave one frame freeing a buffer the other had taken. Both failure directions
were MEASURED while building this, not reasoned about -- see (5).

(4) RESULT. Hot loop, 200,000 calls passing a 1,024-element `Res`, same binary,
`KARAC_MOVE_STRUCT_PARAMS=0` vs default:

    entry copy (=0)   400,051 allocs   3,276,809,851 bytes   47 ms
    transfer          200,047 allocs   1,638,409,723 bytes   33 ms
    the same fn taking `ref Res`
                      200,047 allocs   1,638,409,723 bytes   29 ms

Exactly 2x the allocations and 2x the bytes removed, and the by-value form is now
allocation-identical to the `ref` form -- which is what the row's prototype
predicted and is the whole of the gap it measured. Per-call, on the row's own
256-element reproduction: 11 allocs / 10,266 bytes -> 10 / 8,218, and the
two-hop `outer -> inner` shape 12 / 12,314 -> 10 / 8,218 (BOTH hops elided).

(5) THE FOUR BUGS THIS WENT THROUGH, recorded because each is a site the row did
not list and none is reachable by reading the callee's arm. The last two were
found by the GATE, not by reasoning, which is the argument for running it:

  * A type with an `impl Drop` DOUBLE-FREED (`double free detected in tcache 2`,
    11 allocs / 12 frees). The caller's cleanup for such a type is a `UserDrop`
    action, not the `StructDrop` the retraction scanned for -- and B-2026-08-29-15
    may already have DOWNGRADED its wrapper while leaving it a `UserDrop`. Then,
    with that fixed, the caller's fresh-temp registrar still materialized an
    `__owned_agg_tmp` and hung the full `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper off it, on the
    stated premise that "this caller temp is an INDEPENDENT buffer ... never the
    callee's" -- true under the copy, false under transfer.
  * Fixing those the OTHER way lost the body entirely: with the caller retracting
    and the callee registering only the field walk (`track_struct_var_inst`), no
    frame ran `drop 41` at all. Under transfer the callee owns body AND memory, so
    it registers the wrapper INSTEAD of the field walk (never as well -- the
    wrapper calls it internally).

The first two are moot on the landed patch, which declines `Drop` types outright
for the ordering reason in (3); they are recorded because they are what a future
widening hits first. The next two are LIVE exclusions, and both were caught by
`cargo test --features llvm`, not by inspection:

  * SELF-ASSIGNMENT DOUBLE-FREED. `p = remake(p);` does not kill `p` at the call
    -- it goes on to own the returned value -- and the assignment FREES THE
    DISPLACED ORIGINAL, which under transfer the callee has already freed:
    `AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free`, caught by the pre-existing
    `asan_roundtrip_reassign_frees_displaced_original`. Retracting the caller's
    drop instead merely trades it for a LEAK of the returned value (measured, in
    that order), which is what settled where the fix belongs: the PREPASS, so the
    callee keeps its entry copy and the two sides cannot disagree. Any binding
    reassigned anywhere in its frame is now declined.
  * A PATTERN-BOUND NAME CAN BE A BORROW VIEW. `match r { S { f } => g(f) }` over
    a `ref` scrutinee binds `f` to a field of memory another frame owns. The
    caller-side retraction cannot see that -- it removes a `StructDrop` keyed by
    the binding's slot, finds none, and silently no-ops while the callee frees the
    borrowed buffer. Reachable only through a name COLLISION with a same-named
    `let`, since the walk has no scoping; every pattern-introduced name now joins
    the never-admit set, collected by a `PatternKind`-exhaustive walk.

Both were fixed by NARROWING the admission set rather than by repairing a
caller/callee pair -- which is the practical payoff of the whole-program gate over
section (5)'s design, and worth more than the shapes it gives up.

(6) SOUNDNESS OF THE WALK. A MISSED call site is the unsound direction -- it
leaves a param admitted that another frame still owns -- so the walk matches every
variant of `ExprKind`, `StmtKind` AND `Item` with no `_` catch-all, and a variant
added later fails the build here instead of silently admitting a transfer. The
`Item` arm is not decoration: enumerating "items with bodies" from memory misses
`TestCase` (carries a `Block`) and `ConstDecl` / `ModuleBinding` (carry an
initializer `Expr`), none of which look like function definitions. The sibling
`bce_interproc::all_bodies` this was modelled on walks only the three fn-shaped
items and so has that same gap; it is not touched here, but the gap is real.

VERIFICATION. Twelve probe programs covering every shape in the row's obstacle
table plus a MIXED callee (one safe site and one field-place site on the same
param, which must disqualify it) and a recursive one, each checked on FOUR
surfaces -- `run --interp`, `run` (JIT), `build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` -- plus a fifth comparison against
`KARAC_MOVE_STRUCT_PARAMS=0` to prove the transfer changes no OUTPUT anywhere.
All agree; all valgrind-clean with 0 errors. The four shapes that must decline
(reused binding, fresh call temp, fresh struct literal, field place) allocate
exactly what they did before.

Two regression tests in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs. The first is RED-verified by
COUNT, since the pre-fix program was correct and clean and only the cost differed:
251 malloc calls with the transfer off, 131 with it on, asserted against a 180
ceiling that sits between them with headroom on both sides
(`KARAC_MOVE_STRUCT_PARAMS=0` reproduces the pre-fix number exactly and is how it
was verified). The second pins the DECLINING direction -- field place, fresh temp,
reused binding and `Drop`-bearing type -- and it is the one that fails if the
transfer is ever widened past what the prepass admits.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; BOTH clippy legs clean; the full
`--features llvm` suite 12,504 passed / 0 failed. (The five `normalize_*` codegen
tests fail on any tree without the opt-in `libkarac_runtime_unicode.a`, which
CLAUDE.md says to skip unless doing normalization work; building it makes all five
pass, which is how they were cleared rather than assumed.) Re-verified AFTER the
rebase onto a `main` that had advanced by ~1,580 lines across 14 files including
`src/codegen.rs`: `codegen` 3,511, `memory_sanitizer` 1,349, `interpreter` 1,884,
`cli` 731, all green.

NOT DONE, stated rather than implied. Only the STRUCT family transfers. Enums,
tuples and the Option/Result family keep their entry copy, and their caller-side
predicates keep their exact meaning -- deliberately, so this slice re-derives
none of them. Methods and associated calls are not admitted either: the prepass
keys on free-function names, so a method param is never a candidate and its call
sites need no gate. The row's win table listed `s.eat(a)` as a winner; it is not
one here. A monomorph body carries a mangled `func.name` that is not a key in the
set, so a generic fn misses the optimisation rather than taking it unsoundly.

title: design.md's REPL section states use-after-move is a blocking `error[E0382]` with "strictness identical to compiled code"; the compiler emits code E0500 as a NON-BLOCKING warning -- `karac check` prints `warning[ownership]` then `All checks passed`, and `karac build` produces a working binary and exits 0
detail:
Found while working B-2026-08-29-63, whose whole design question turns on this:
the by-value entry copy exists to honour the promise that use-after-move is safe
because it is NON-FATAL. Whether that promise should exist at all is a language
decision, and the spec currently gives two different answers.

WHAT THE COMPILER DOES. `UseAfterMove` is advisory by construction --
`kind_blocks_production` (src/ownership.rs) lists it, alongside `RcFallbackNote`,
as a kind that does NOT block production. Measured on:

    struct Res { id: i64, buf: Vec[i64] }
    fn eatf(r: Res) -> i64 { return r.buf[0]; }
    fn main() {
        let a = mk(41);
        let n = eatf(a);
        println(f"n={n} after={a.buf[1]}");   // `a` was moved on the line above
    }

  * `karac check` prints `warning[ownership]: ... value 'a' moved here, used
    again here (moved at line 6:18)` and then `All checks passed.`
  * `karac build` produces a binary; it prints `n=7 after=8` and is
    valgrind-clean. Interpreter and JIT agree.

That behaviour is deliberate and documented at the definition: codegen
defensive-copies the reuse, so the binary is memory-safe, and the diagnostic
carries a machine-applicable `.clone()` fix "precisely because the program
compiles and runs".

WHAT design.md SAYS, in two places that disagree with it and with each other.
The REPL section (§ Ownership across cells, around line 11692) shows

    print(v.len());  // use-after-move error

and renders it as

    error[E0382]: use of moved value `v`

then states "The error is correct and identical to the error the same code would
produce in a `.kara` file" and "Strictness is identical to compiled code; only
the diagnostic presentation is notebook-aware." Both sentences are false against
the measurement above: in a `.kara` file it is a warning, checking passes, and a
binary is produced.

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS, one of which is a wrong constant:

  * SEVERITY. "error" / "strictness identical to compiled code" describes a
    blocking diagnostic. The implementation is non-blocking by design.
  * THE CODE ITSELF. `error[E0382]` is not this compiler's code for it. Both
    `src/cli/diag_json.rs` and `src/cli/explain.rs` map
    `OwnershipErrorKind::UseAfterMove` to **E0500**, and design.md's OWN
    diagnostic-schema section (lines 11158 and 11200) uses E0500 for the same
    diagnostic, with the example message "`user` moved on line 38, used again
    here." E0382 is Rust's code for use-of-moved-value; it appears exactly once
    in design.md, in this one passage, and nowhere in the compiler. So the
    passage is internally inconsistent with the spec's own registry, not just
    with the implementation. A reader who trusts it will `karac explain E0382`
    and get nothing.

WHY IT IS WORTH A ROW RATHER THAN A SILENT DOC EDIT. The severity half is not
obviously a documentation bug -- it may be the SPEC that is right and the
implementation that is provisional. The advisory status is justified at its
definition on the strength of the defensive copy, and B-2026-08-29-63 measures
what that copy costs: 1.96x on a by-value-struct hot loop, and it is the entire
gap between passing by value and passing by `ref`. So the two rows are the two
halves of one decision:

  * If use-after-move BECOMES an error, the defensive copy at call arguments has
    nothing left to protect, and -63's fix loses its hardest case (a reused
    binding) along with the caller-side copy that case requires.
  * If it stays a warning, design.md's REPL passage needs correcting to say so,
    and -63 must keep a defensive copy on exactly the reuse path.

Either way the E0382/E0500 mismatch is a plain error and should be fixed
regardless of which way the severity question goes.
