title: A PARAM returned by a TAIL `return r` -- no trailing semicolon -- runs its `Drop` body TWICE on EVERY backend, while the same function written `return r;` runs it once. Agreed-wrong, so no A/B gate sees it. The remaining half of B-2026-08-29-15, whose fix closed the statement spelling only
detail:
Found while bounding B-2026-08-29-57's blast radius: the same semicolon axis as
that row, one level up, and on both backends rather than the interpreter alone.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

    fn f(r: R) -> R { println("mid"); return r }     // tail, no semicolon
    fn g(r: R) -> R { println("mid"); return r; }    // statement

    fn main() {
        let p: R = R { id: 5, tag: f"t" };
        let v: R = f(p);
        println(f"v{v.id}");
    }

      f  -> `mid dR5 v5 dR5`   TWO bodies for one R, interp AND compiled
      g  -> `mid v5 dR5`       one, both

One `R` is constructed and one reaches `v`, so exactly one body is due.

MECHANISM: `fn_always_returns_param` (src/ast/items.rs) collects the body's LEAF
TAILS and requires every one to YIELD the param -- the bare identifier or an
aggregate literal around it. A tail `return r` reached that walk as the `Return`
NODE, which yields nothing, so condition 1 failed and the predicate declined for
a body whose only exit hands the param back. The caller then kept firing beside
the result binding. The semicolon spelling has NO tail expression at all, so it
takes the no-tail arm B-2026-08-29-14 added, which is why it was already
correct.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-29-15: that row is the same double body for a named struct
argument returned by value, and its fix (baf2338) closed the `return r;`
spelling. The tail spelling stayed broken -- agreed on both backends, so the A/B
rule that row was argued on could not see the remainder. This is why an absolute
expectation, not parity, is what catches this family.

FIXED in fc450fe alongside B-2026-08-29-57: `leaf_tails` now descends through a
`Return` operand. A bare `return;` still pushes the node and so still declines,
correctly -- it yields nothing.

The widened walk is guarded from both sides in the fixtures, because its failure
direction is the opposite one: too permissive means the caller stands down and a
body is LOST rather than duplicated. `branch-*` keeps a sibling local that is not
returned dying inside the callee; `param-dies-*` keeps the predicate declining
when no `return` yields the param.
fix: FIXED in fc450fe. See B-2026-08-29-57, which this landed with; the mechanism and the guards are recorded there and in the detail above.

title: A struct WRAPPING a `Vec` of `Drop` elements, built in a callee and returned, runs the element's `Drop` body on FREED memory in the compiled backends -- printing a garbage id that differs between runs, with a valgrind `Invalid read of size 8`. The trigger is positional: it happens when the caller's `let` is NOT the first statement of its block, and disappears when it is. The interpreter is correct either way
detail:
Found while bounding B-2026-08-29-57's blast radius, from a probe row that was
meant to be a control.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    struct Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }

    fn build(k: i64) -> Box3 {
        let mut v: Vec[R] = Vec.new();
        v.push(R { id: k, tag: f"t" });
        let bx: Box3 = Box3 { xs: v };
        println("mid");
        return bx
    }

    fn main() {
        println("lead");                    // <-- REMOVE THIS AND IT IS CORRECT
        let a: Box3 = build(14);
        println(f"v{a.xs[0].id}");
        println("post");
    }

      karac build -> `lead mid v14 post dR94159984916049`
      --interp    -> `lead mid v14 dR14 post`

      valgrind: `Invalid read of size 8`, 1 error. The printed id differs on
      every run and between auto-par on and off, which is the tell that it is
      read from freed memory rather than merely misplaced.

WITHOUT the leading statement the compiled output is `mid v14 dR14 post`,
valgrind-clean. So the defect is not in the callee or the type -- it is the
caller's binding position, which is what moves the element body from its
live-range end to after the block's last statement, by which time the buffer is
gone.

THE RETURN SPELLING IS IRRELEVANT, which is worth stating because this was found
next to a semicolon-sensitive bug and is NOT one. All four spellings behave
identically, clean as the first statement and faulting after a leading one:
`return bx`, `return bx;`, the bare tail `bx`, and `return Box3 { xs: v }`
built directly at the return site.

The direct spelling carries a SECOND, separate defect visible in the same runs:
it prints an extra `dR14` before the caller's use (`mid dR14 v14 dR14 post` as
the first statement), so the element body fires once too many there even when no
fault occurs.

RELATED, NOT THE SAME: B-2026-08-29-56 is also a callee-built heap value
returned and then consumed, and also compiled-only. That one aborts with
`free(): double free detected` on an `Option[String]` bound to a local, needs no
leading statement, and is clean in the bare-tail spelling. This one never
aborts, needs the leading statement, and is spelling-independent. Whether they
share a root cause is worth checking early -- if they do, one fix closes both.

PRE-EXISTING: measured identical with B-2026-08-29-57's fix reverted, so neither
half of that commit is implicated.

WHERE TO START: the element-bodies walker for a struct FIELD that is a
container, and where its firing point is chosen relative to the binding's NLL
live-range end. The interpreter fires at the live-range end in both positions;
the compiled backend fires at the live-range end only when the binding leads its
block.

UPDATE 2026-08-30 — CAUSE LOCATED, NOT FIXED. Row stays open. The trigger named
above is a SYMPTOM of the real one, and one of the row's measurements is wrong.

THE TRIGGER IS AUTO-PAR, NOT BINDING POSITION.

    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build lead.kara -o l && ./l
    lead mid v14 dR14 post          <- correct, and valgrind-clean (0 errors,
                                       "in use at exit: 0 bytes in 0 blocks")

So the row's "the printed id differs ... between auto-par on and off" is a
CORRECTION: auto-par OFF is not merely different, it is CORRECT. That is also
the workaround for anyone who hits this before it is fixed.

Binding position matters only because it decides whether a parallel group FORMS.
`karac build --concurrency-report` on the two variants:

    with the leading println      with no leading statement
    parallel_group {              <no parallelization opportunities detected>
      [14] println(...)
      [15] build(...)
      reason: no data or effect dependencies
    }

The `let a = build(14);` statement is INSIDE the group, so it is lifted into a
`__par_branch_*` worker function. That is what a leading statement buys: a
second statement for the group to form around. A leading `let z: i64 = 1;` does
NOT trigger it (measured) because it does not group; any non-binding statement
does -- expression statement, bare call, `if`, `while`, `let _ = ...`.

THE MECHANISM, and it is an OWNERSHIP handshake rather than a firing-position
one. par_blocks.rs's slot-publish loop already implements the right protocol for
this class -- when a branch publishes a binding to the parent, the branch's
cleanup action is REMOVED from its frame and its metadata surfaced through
`slot_ownership`, and the parent re-registers the equivalent against its own
alloca (`register_slot_ownership`, stmts.rs's auto-par dispatch). Its comment
names the original instance: "the `Map.new()`-in-a-branch UAF". Two shapes slip
through it, and they fail differently:

  1. `Vec[R]` bound DIRECTLY in a group (`let v: Vec[R] = mk();`) -- the
     publish loop's `frame.retain` never sees ANY action for `v` (instrumented:
     zero transfer records for that slot, while the `Box3` case records two).
     So the branch's element-bodies walk is not retired and runs at BRANCH exit.
     Result is an ORDERING defect only, valgrind-clean:

         interp  lead 3 dR3 post
         AOT     lead dR3 3 post

     The element `Drop` bodies run before the parent's first use. The buffer
     itself is fine -- the parent re-tracks it via `track_vec_var`.

  2. `Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }` -- the struct case from this row's repro. Here the
     actions ARE transferred (instrumented: `UserDrop(a, Box3,
     StructFieldBodies)` plus one more, both `transferred=true`), and the result
     is still a use-after-free plus a 2,112-byte / 23-block leak. So for this
     shape the transfer is incomplete or the re-registration against the
     parent's alloca is not equivalent -- the strong candidate is the Vec
     BUFFER free for the `xs` FIELD, which is keyed on a pointer that is not the
     struct binding's `local_ptr` and so is not captured, leaving the branch to
     free it at branch exit while the parent's transferred bodies walk it later.
     Not yet confirmed; confirming it is the next step.

NOTE the kind is `StructFieldBodies`, not `ContainerElemBodies` as this row's
"WHERE TO START" guessed. Both are `UserDrop` kinds and both are transferable in
principle; the gap is not the kind's eligibility.

WHY THIS WAS NOT FIXED IN THE SAME PASS: the two shapes need different repairs
in the branch-publish handshake, and this is the subsystem where a partial fix
converts a use-after-free into a double free rather than into correctness. The
diagnosis is recorded so the next session starts from a located mechanism.

CHECKED AND RULED OUT along the way: the NLL last-use map. `compute_block_last_use`
and `compile_block`'s firing loop agree on statement indices, and instrumenting
both showed `main` never reaching that loop at all -- an auto-par body compiles
its top-level statements through `compile_function_body`'s own loop
(stmts.rs:1186), not `compile_block`. Anyone re-deriving this should instrument
the loop at stmts.rs:1717, not the one at 456.

ALSO MEASURED, bounding the class: a `String` binding in the same position forms
no group and is fine; a `Vec[i64]` binding DOES group, is published, and is
correct and valgrind-clean. So the defect needs a `Drop`-bearing element type,
not merely a heap-owning binding lifted into a branch. The related
B-2026-08-29-56 (now fixed) is a different mechanism -- it needed no group.
fix:
FIXED by fa0f33fe, together with B-2026-08-29-67 — one mechanism, two
rows.

THE TRIGGER THIS ROW NAMES IS A SYMPTOM. The caller's binding position only
decides whether an auto-par GROUP forms around the `let`; it is not what
breaks. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` is correct in BOTH positions and valgrind-clean,
which also CORRECTS this row's "the printed id differs ... between auto-par on
and off": auto-par off is not merely different, it is right — and it was the
workaround while this was open. A leading `let z: i64 = 1;` does not trigger it
(it forms no group); any non-binding statement does.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN 2026-08-30 UPDATE: the "2,112-byte / 23-block
leak" attributed to the `Box3` shape is NOT a leak. It is the auto-par worker
pool's baseline — a `Vec[i64]` program with no `Drop` type anywhere reports
byte-identical numbers (2,112 bytes / 23 blocks / one "possibly lost"
pthread-DTV record from `_dl_allocate_tls`). `definitely lost` was 0 before the
fix and is 0 after. The real defect was the use-after-free alone.

THE MECHANISM is the branch-publish ownership handshake in
`src/codegen/par_blocks.rs`, and it had three independent holes. All three end
the same way — a `Drop`-bodies walk running after the memory it reads is freed
— and each needed its own repair, which is why this was not fixed in the
diagnosis pass.

1. A PUBLISHED STRUCT SLOT lost its NLL eligibility in transit.
   `register_one_slot_ownership` re-registered the branch's transferred
   `UserDrop` with `type_name: String::new()`, on the stated grounds that "no
   Kāra type name in scope here". One IS in scope — on the action being
   sampled — and blanking it demoted the parent's copy out of
   `fire_due_user_drops`' TYPE-keyed early-fire clauses. A `StructFieldBodies`
   walk has no other route into NLL placement (unlike `ContainerElemBodies`,
   which the kind clause admits on its own), so the demoted copy fell through
   to the scope-exit drain, where LIFO ran it AFTER the `StructDrop` that frees
   `xs`. `SlotOwnership::User` now carries `type_name` and the registrar uses
   it — the same "carry it over rather than assume it" rule B-2026-08-27-8
   established for the sibling `kind` field, applied to the field that was
   still being assumed.

2. A PUBLISHED VEC SLOT never reached the transfer scan at all. A Vec-shaped
   slot suppresses its own buffer free by zeroing `cap` and then `continue`d
   straight past the rest of the publish loop — including the ownership
   transfer at the end of it. So a `Vec[T]` of `Drop` elements left its
   `ContainerElemBodies` walker in the BRANCH frame, where it ran at branch
   exit, ahead of the parent's first read. `cap = 0` does not stop that walker:
   it reads `data`/`len`, which stay live precisely so the parent can use them.
   The `continue` is now a flag that skips only the RC / inline-payload
   suppression block (the part that is genuinely Vec-inapplicable); the
   transfer scan always runs. This is the whole of B-2026-08-29-67.

3. AN UNPUBLISHED BRANCH-LOCAL BINDING never had an NLL fire at all. When the
   lifted binding is never read again, every statement joins the group and the
   binding is not a slot — so (1) and (2) have nothing to hand over. A branch
   fn compiles exactly ONE statement and therefore has no statement loop, and
   nothing in it ever called `fire_due_user_drops`; the bodies walk fell to the
   branch's own scope-exit drain and LIFO put it after the `StructDrop`.
   Measured `A callee-end dR22978400716 B` against a correct `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`
   run of the same program. A branch-local binding's entire live range IS that
   one statement, which is exactly the sequential path's
   `last_use[name] == this stmt`, so the branch now makes that call for any
   `let` binding it did not publish.

Also changed, as the safety net under (1): `register_slot_ownership` used to
replay the branch frame's push order verbatim. That is right for every pair the
branch pushes memory-first, and wrong for the one it does not — a struct
binding pushes `UserDrop`(field bodies) BEFORE its `StructDrop`, because the
sequential path never drains that pair at scope exit (NLL fires the bodies
early and retires the action). Replaying that order into a frame that DOES
drain it inverts the intent. Re-registration is now a stable memory-first /
bodies-last split, so the parent's LIFO drain walks before it frees even when
no parent statement is left to fire at. B-2026-07-31-40's Drop-valued `Map` —
the shape that pinned the old ordering — is unaffected: the branch already
pushes that pair memory-first, so the split is a no-op for it, and a test now
guards that.

MEASURED, 14 shapes x {interp, AOT, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, JIT}: every
use-after-free is gone and auto-par output now equals auto-par-off output on
all 14. Valgrind on every compiled shape: 0 invalid reads/writes, 0 definitely
lost, 0 indirectly lost. Fixed here: this row's `Box3` repro, the `Vec[R]`
direct shape (-67), two Vec slots in one group (was `lead dR1 dR2 1 2 post`),
and the unpublished branch-local struct.

REGRESSION TESTS: five in `tests/par_codegen.rs` (published struct slot,
published Vec slot, two Vec slots, unpublished branch-local, and the
Drop-valued-Map ordering guard on the re-registration split) and one two-shape
case in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` under the auto-par ASAN/LSan entry point.
The four new behavioural ones were verified RED on 93c6cc86 before the fix.

SPLIT OUT, still open: this row's "SECOND, separate defect" — `return Box3 { xs: v }`
built directly at the return site runs the element body ONCE TOO MANY — is
NOT auto-par's and is not fixed here. It reproduces identically with
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, and the discriminator is the return spelling alone:
`return <StructLiteral>` doubles, while `let bx = ...; return bx` and the bare
tail `Box3 { xs: v }` are both correct on every backend. Filed as
B-2026-08-30-18. Before this fix that extra body was the one landing on
freed memory in the never-used-again shapes, which is why the two looked like
one bug.

title: A `Vec[T]` of `Drop` elements returned from a callee runs the element's `Drop` body BEFORE the caller's first use of the vector on the compiled backends, and AFTER it on the interpreter -- `m3 dR3 v3` against `m3 v3 dR3`. Right count, wrong place, and the compiled read lands on an element whose body has already run
fix:
FIXED by fa0f33fe, as hole (2) of B-2026-08-29-66 — the same mechanism,
and the reason the two rows are closed together.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S MEASUREMENT: "Same under `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`" is wrong.
The sequential build of this exact program prints the interpreter's order,
`start m3 v3 dR3 post`, on 93c6cc86 — measured directly. Only the default
(auto-par) build diverged. This is the same error B-2026-08-29-66 made in the
opposite direction, and it is why both rows read as "not auto-par" and were
filed apart.

THE CAUSE: a Vec-shaped slot published out of an auto-par branch suppresses its
own buffer free by zeroing `cap`, and then `continue`d past the rest of the
publish loop — including the ownership-transfer scan at the end of it. So the
`UserDrop`/`ContainerElemBodies` walker for a `Vec[T]` of `Drop` elements stayed
in the BRANCH frame and ran at branch exit, before the parent's first read.
`cap = 0` does not stop that walker: it reads `data`/`len`, which stay live
precisely so the parent can use them. The parent, meanwhile, re-takes the
buffer via `track_vec_var`, which is why this was valgrind-clean — right count,
right memory, wrong place.

The `continue` is now a flag that skips only the RC / inline-payload
suppression block, which is the part genuinely inapplicable to a Vec-typed
local; the transfer scan always runs, so the walker reaches the parent and
fires at the binding's real last use.

This row's own observation that "an A/B kata WOULD catch this one, unlike its
siblings in this batch" held: the two backends printed different strings, and
the regression test
(`test_e2e_auto_par_vec_of_drop_elems_slot_bodies_run_at_parent_last_use` in
`tests/par_codegen.rs`) pins exactly that, verified RED on 93c6cc86.

title: The DEFAULT (JIT) REPL lane silently discards every cross-cell mutation -- `let mut n: i64 = 0;` then `n = 5;` reads back 0, a String reads back EMPTY, and Vec/Map mutations vanish -- while `--interp` is correct on all four; this is B-2026-07-29-20's headline case, which is marked fixed, live again on the lane a user gets by default
detail:
The DEFAULT REPL lane silently discards every mutation a cell makes to a binding
declared in an earlier cell. No error, no warning -- the next cell simply reads the
binding's ORIGINAL initializer value. `--interp` is correct on every case below, so
the two REPL backends disagree with each other, and the wrong one is the default.

Measured on one session, `karac repl` (JIT, the default when built with `llvm`)
against `karac repl --interp`, same input on both:

    cells                                     JIT     --interp   correct
    let mut n = 1;  n = n + 5;  n             1       6          6
    let mut s = f"a";  s = s + f"b";  s       (empty) ab         ab
    let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
        v.push(7);  v.len()                   0       1          1
    let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new();
        m.insert(f"k", 3);  m.len()           0       1          1

So it is not the container tier, and not heap types: a plain `i64` REASSIGNMENT is
lost too, and a `String` reads back EMPTY rather than merely stale.

THIS IS B-2026-07-29-20's HEADLINE CASE, LIVE AGAIN ON THE DEFAULT LANE. That row
(status `fixed`, sha 8172bae, severity high) is titled "REPL cross-cell value
snapshot was taken at each binding's INITIALIZER, so EVERY in-cell mutation was lost
crossing to the next cell -- on both lanes and for every type, not just the
container tier: `let mut n: i64 = 0; n = 5;` read back 0." Running that exact
snippet today:

    karac repl            n=0     <- the pre-fix value the row quotes
    karac repl --interp   n=5

The row also notes that "the JIT lane's `is_mut` container exclusion ... was itself
what turned the loss into a silent empty read", which is exactly the `String` row
above. The interpreter lane honours the fix; the JIT lane does not.

NOT DETERMINED, and stated rather than guessed: whether this is a REGRESSION after
8172bae or a fix that never fully covered the JIT lane despite the row's "on both

fix:
FIXED by 80bb5ec6. The JIT lane's cross-cell snapshot global was written EXACTLY ONCE, by the
cell that declared the binding, so every later cell could read it but never write
it back.

ROOT CAUSE. `compute_snapshot_sets_for_cell` (src/repl.rs) sorts each top-level
`let` in the cell's synthetic main into a `replay` set (load the value from
`__karac_repl_snapshot_<name>` instead of re-running the RHS) or a `capture` set
(run the RHS, then store the bound value into that global). The two were treated
as MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE -- a name already carrying a global went into `replay` and
`continue`d, so it never entered `capture`, and `emit_pending_snapshot_captures`
iterates `capture` only. Cell 1 wrote the global; cells 2..N loaded it, mutated a
local copy, and dropped the result on the floor.

REGRESSION OR NEVER-COVERED: NEVER-COVERED, determined from history rather than
guessed (this container's clone was shallow when the row was filed; `git fetch
--unshallow` made 8172bae reachable). 8172bae fixed WHEN the capture fires --
moving it from the `let` to end of cell -- which covers a mutation made in the
DECLARING cell, the shape all 13 of its probed rows exercise. It left the replay
classification exclusive, so a mutation made in any LATER cell was still lost.
Only three commits have touched src/repl.rs since 8172bae (2f8aa271, c12de8f6,
04ed765f) and none of them touch this classification, so the gap dates to slice
B.5.1, not to a later regression. The row's "this is -20's headline case live
again" reading was right about the symptom and wrong about the cause: -20's
headline snippet has the mutation in a SEPARATE cell, which its own fix never
reached.

MEASURED, both lanes, cell 1 declares / cell 2 mutates / cell 3 reads:

    shape                       JIT (before)   JIT (after)   --interp
    let mut n: i64 = 0; n = 5        0              5            5
    let mut f: f64;    f = 2.5       0              2.5          2.5
    let mut b: bool;   b = true      false          true         true
    let mut c: char;   c = 'z'       a              z            z
    let mut s = f"a";  s = s + f"b"  (freed heap)   ab           ab
    String.new(); s.push_str("hi")   (empty)        hi           hi
    Vec[i64].new();    v.push(7)     0              1            1
    Map[i64,i64].new(); m.insert     1              1            1   <- correct before
    Set[i64].new();     q.insert     1              1            1   <- correct before

WHY MAP AND SET WERE ALREADY CORRECT, and why that mattered: their snapshot global
holds an opaque HANDLE POINTER, so an in-place `insert` through the replayed handle
is visible through a global that was never refreshed. The seven by-value shapes
store the value itself (or, for String/Vec, a `{ptr,len,cap}` triple) and had no
such aliasing. So the container tier looked healthy while the scalar tier was
broken, which is the opposite of the usual polarity and is why this survived a
suite with four dedicated container tests.

THE TWO HEAP KINDS DID WORSE THAN GO STALE -- they read FREED memory, which the row
did not identify:

  * String: a later-cell `s = s + f"b"` frees the buffer the global points at.
    `let mut s = f"abcdefghij";` then `s = s + f"KLM";` printed len=10 (the stale
    length) with bytes `A\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\xf3\x0f`.
  * Vec: a later-cell push past `cap` reallocates and frees the old buffer. Four
    elements in cell 1 (cap exactly 4), five more in cell 2, and cell 3 read
    len=4 with v[0] = 94542648599680 -- a raw pointer value, not 1. A push that
    stays inside `cap` is merely stale.

That upgrades this from a lost-update bug to a memory-safety one on the default
interactive lane.

FIX (two lines of behaviour, in the two places that own the halves):

  * src/repl.rs -- a replayed name now enters `capture` as well as `replay`, so
    the end-of-cell write-back refreshes the global every cell. Idempotent for an
    unmutated binding: the slot still holds what the load produced.
  * src/codegen/stmts.rs -- `emit_snapshot_capture_for_name` takes the DECLARE
    form of the global when the name is also in `snapshot_replay`. The defining
    copy already lives in the runner's JITDylib; emitting a second definition
    would install a duplicate. (`get_or_define_snapshot_global` happens to return
    the declaration the replay path already put in the module, but that is an
    emission-order accident -- the choice belongs on the classification.)

The "mutually exclusive" invariant was stated in three doc comments
(`compile_to_ir_for_repl_cell_with_snapshots`, and both field docs on `Codegen`);
all three now say the sets overlap and why.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN MEASUREMENT. The filed table's Map row used
`Map[String, i64]`, whose String key is NOT snapshot-eligible
(`snapshot_kind_for_type` accepts primitive keys only). That row was measuring the
B.5.3d aggregate-type pass-through, not this bug, and it still diverges after this
fix -- filed separately rather than folded in here, since the mechanism is
different (the RHS re-runs) and so is the remedy.

--interp was correct throughout and is unchanged: it re-captures every watched
binding at each scope exit (`capture_watched_bindings`) rather than keying on a
first-binding set, which is exactly the property the JIT lane was missing.

TESTS: four new in tests/repl_jit.rs, all RED before the fix (verified by stashing
the two source files and re-running: 4/4 fail, `left: "0" right: "5"` on the i64
case) and green after. A nine-shape matrix across declare/mutate/read cells with
Map and Set as controls; one test each pinning the String and Vec freed-buffer
shapes by asserting ELEMENTS and not just length (a stale length and a freed read
are otherwise indistinguishable); and a chained case mutating in two successive
cells, which is what pins the write-back as REPEATING rather than merely moved --
a one-shot capture and a per-cell capture agree on a single mutation.

FIXED in c935db1, for the population the row measured: a value-position block or
branch whose tail hands out a binding THAT OUTLIVES THE HAND-OUT. The row's
proposed direction — a per-arm owner — is right; which arms may take one, and
which frame it goes in, is the whole content of the fix, and both boundaries
were found by things breaking rather than by reasoning.

WHAT THE ROW HAD RIGHT, and it is load-bearing: a consumer-side free is not
available. `let a = { loc }.contains("p"); println(loc)` prints `loc` correctly,
so the wrapper disarms the binding's cleanup without ending its readable
lifetime, and the gates B-2026-08-29-27 widened free IMMEDIATELY at the use
site. Confirmed in the IR rather than inferred: the tail value is LOADED before
`move.cap.p` is zeroed, so what escapes carries the ORIGINAL `cap` and is a
genuine owning header with nobody holding it.

THE MECHANISM. `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` records that it zeroed a
Vec/String binding's `cap` AND WHICH FRAME held that binding's `FreeVecBuffer`
(`vecstr_source_disarmed`); the value-block tail raises it
(`block_tail_binding_unowned`); the escaping value then gets an owner registered
IN THAT FRAME and recorded in `branch_tail_owner_slots`, so the owning
destinations take it over through the funnel B-2026-08-28-44 already built. A
STANDALONE block registers its own after its frame drains; an ARM reports
instead (`arm_pending_tail_owner`) and its branch compiler registers.

THE FRAME IS THE DESIGN, and it sets the boundary in both directions.

  Too INNERMOST and it frees too early. `track_vec_var` pushes onto the
  innermost frame, and a transient call-ARGUMENT frame pops as soon as the call
  returns: `println({ loc }); println(loc)` freed the buffer between the two
  statements and printed garbage on the second — 14 valgrind errors, a
  use-after-free introduced by the fix itself.

  If NO LIVE FRAME holds that cleanup there is nothing to replace, and
  registering anyway is a double free. That is the case of a tail naming a
  binding declared INSIDE the block handing it out — which is exactly what every
  codegen-internal desugar synthesizes. `Vec.sorted()` lowers to
  `{ let mut __srt = recv.clone(); __srt.sort(); __srt }`; the iterator
  adaptors, `collect` into a non-Vec target, the nested-Vec index bind and the
  generic-enum payload bind all build the same shape, and each already arranges
  its own ownership at the producer. A draft without that check took out 11
  codegen and 12 memory-sanitizer tests at once, `let s: Vec[i64] = v.sorted()`
  segfaulting among them.

THE MINTING ARM OF A MIXED BRANCH IS NOT FIXED, and this is the correction to
the row's framing that cost the most to find. Its text names the shape without
drawing the conclusion ("with the then-arm taken, `mk(n)`'s temp escapes"), and
it is real: B-2026-08-29-27's gates require EVERY tail to mint, so a branch with
one binding arm declines and the other arm's fresh temp is left unowned too. A
draft gave it an owner via `materialize_owned_temp` and every sweep fixture went
green — and the SELF-HOST SEED-RUN ORACLE went red. Reducing that gave a
one-line difference: `fn f() -> String { { match .. } }` double-freed while the
same `match` unwrapped was clean. The minting arm has no source binding to take
a frame from, so it lands in the innermost frame, and with a wrapper that is the
WRAPPER's frame, which drains before the value escapes. It is the same frame
question as the binding case with no answer available locally; filed rather than
guessed at, with the sibling binding arm's frame as the lead.

Three more things were measured failures of simpler drafts:

  AN ARM CANNOT REGISTER ITS OWN. `compile_match` keeps a PER-ARM frame standing
  around the body, so an owner registered from inside a brace-wrapped arm is
  freed at the end of that arm — before the merge, before any consumer. `let g =
  match e { A(x) => { let p = f"[{x}]"; p }, B => "z" }` aborted with a double
  free while the `if` spelling of the same block was clean, the whole difference
  being that one frame. The block reports and the branch compiler registers,
  each after ITS own drain.

  NESTING. `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` recurses through a block tail, so
  `{ { t } }` re-emits the cap-zero and the outer block cannot tell that from a
  first disarm — it registered a second owner and double-freed. The outer now
  adopts the inner's slots, COPIED under its own key rather than moved: a
  consumer looks up whichever span IT holds, and a function tail return holds
  the body's tail expression, so re-keying made that takeover miss instead.

  LOOPS. A per-arm owner slot is stored into on one path only, so
  `track_vec_var`'s once-per-call entry-block zero is not enough: on the next
  pass an arm that did not run still holds the previous pass's already-freed
  header. `while i < 3 { let t = mkB(i); if i > 0 { mkA(n) } else { t }.len(); }`
  double-freed until the slot was also reset in the block that dominates the
  arms and re-executes per pass.

`compile_if_let` needed one more thing, worth recording because it was silent:
`compile_expr` stashes `current_branch_expr_span` for `If` and `Match` and never
did for `IfLet`, so the takeover key was `None` and an if-let arm registered
nothing at all.

Two neighbours had to be kept out, both measured double-freeing against an
earlier draft: an ALL-MINT construct, whose value a consuming gate still frees at
the use site (B-2026-08-29-27), and a DISCARDED branch, whose source is
deliberately left armed (B-2026-08-29-5). An arm can see neither, so the branch
compilers pass both down in a one-shot `arm_tail_owner_ctx` alongside the
takeover key — the BRANCH's span, not the arm block's, an owner filed under
which is invisible to a consumer and so a double free rather than a miss.
`branch_tail_owner_slots` is now a LIST per span for the same reason, and is
cleared per function: it holds allocas, and a Vec accumulating across monomorphs
of one generic body would let a takeover zero the previous function's slot.

The loop row is the mixed case in miniature: the iteration that took the binding

Regression test `asan_branch_tail_binding_handout_frees_once`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), under LSan. Every receiver row uses `.contains()`

title: A VALUE-POSITION BLOCK OR BRANCH WHOSE TAIL HANDS OUT A BINDING RATHER THAN MINTING A TEMP LEAKS IT, AND CANNOT BE FIXED AT THE CONSUMER -- `{ loc }.contains("x")` strands 32 B and `loc` is STILL READABLE afterwards, so the immediate free the widened consuming gates emit would DANGLE that read rather than merely double-free; the mixed-arm spelling shows the ownership is per-path, so the answer is a per-arm owner at the merge, not a wider consumer-side predicate
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the deliberate remainder of B-2026-08-29-27, split out rather than
buried in that row. It widened seven consuming gates to admit a value-position
block or branch whose EVERY tail MINTS a fresh owned temp; this is the
population it fails closed on, and the failing-closed is measured-correct rather
than merely cautious.

MEASURED (KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and 2, valgrind, runtime-derived payload via
`env.args().len()` so nothing folds; `mk(n) -> String` returns a 32 B buffer):

    let loc = mk(n);
    let a = { loc }.contains("payload");        32 B / 1 object   LEAKS
    println(f"a={a} loc={loc}");                <-- `loc` STILL PRINTS CORRECTLY

    let loc2 = mk(n);
    let b = if c { mk(n) } else { loc2 }.contains("payload");
                                                32 B / 1 object   LEAKS

    CONTROL -- every tail mints a temp:         clean since B-2026-08-29-27
    let d = if c { mk(n) } else { mk(n + 1) }.contains("payload");

WHY THE CONSUMER CANNOT FIX IT, which is the whole content of this row. The
wrapper DOES disarm the binding's own scope cleanup on the way out -- that is
what makes this a leak today rather than a double free -- but it does not end
the binding's readable lifetime, and the `loc` print above is the proof. Several
of the gates B-2026-08-29-27 widened free IMMEDIATELY at the use site
(`free_str_vec_buffer_if_heap` at both method-receiver sites,
`free_fresh_owned_str_arg` at the borrow-consuming-operand chokepoint), so a
consumer-side free here would DANGLE that later read: a use-after-free, strictly
worse than the leak it replaces. So this is not "the predicate is one arm kind
too narrow" -- widening it is the wrong fix, not merely an unfinished one.

THE MIXED SPELLING ADDS THE SECOND HALF OF THE ARGUMENT. The disarm is emitted
in the ARM'S OWN basic block, so it executes only when that arm runs. With the
then-arm taken, `mk(n)`'s temp escapes and `loc2` is freed by its own cleanup;
with the else-arm taken, `loc2`'s cleanup is disarmed and `loc2` escapes.
Exactly one buffer leaks on either path and nothing double-frees -- so the
ownership is genuinely PER-PATH, which a single predicate asked once at the
merged value cannot express regardless of how it is written.

WHERE TO START: a per-arm owner at the merge -- the direction
`own_branch_merged_clone` / `branch_tail_owner_slots` already took for the
container-element clone (B-2026-08-28-44). Register an owner in the arm that
needs one, and let a consuming destination take it over through the existing
funnel. That machinery is keyed on a container-element clone
(`vec_elem_field_clone_slots`) and so does not reach a binding hand-out today.
The takeover half is not optional: a `let`, a `Vec.push` argument, a `return`
and an assignment all own the merged buffer, and B-2026-08-29-27's
`asan_branch_tail_owned_temp_frees_once` already carries those four as
tripwires.

SEVERITY: one leak per evaluation, unbounded in a loop; no double free and no
wrong answer, so it is a leak-only class. Pinned at its current leaking value by
`asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free` under the leak-tolerant
ASAN runner, so a future fix that turns it into a memory error fails loudly
rather than trading one class for a worse one.

CORRECTION (2026-08-30, at close). This row's measurements were all of a tail
naming a binding that OUTLIVES the hand-out, and that population is fixed. Two
neighbouring shapes it does not measure turned out to belong to different fixes,
and both were found by breaking things rather than by reading:

  - the MINTING arm of the same mixed branch, which this row's own text names in
    passing ("with the then-arm taken, `mk(n)`'s temp escapes"). It leaks for a
    related reason and needs a frame no arm can see. B-2026-08-30-11.
  - a tail naming a binding declared INSIDE the block handing it out. Admitting
    it is a DOUBLE FREE, because it is the shape every codegen-internal desugar
    synthesizes; and unlike this row it has no dangling hazard, so it belongs to
    the consuming gate rather than to an owner. B-2026-08-30-12.

fix:
FIXED by a0619a88, in three parts. The row's own half is ONE LINE -- admit an
`InterpolatedStringLit` tail to `branch_tail_mints_fresh_owned_temp_inner`
(src/codegen/stmts.rs), the leaf behind `expr_is_fresh_owned_branch_tail`. The
other two close a SEPARATE pre-existing leak in the same family, found while
verifying the first and measured at HEAD.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND ITS POPULATION WAS 4.5x TOO SMALL. It measured
two spellings; NINE are closed by that line. One fixture per shape, valgrind,
`f"x{n}"` a 2 B buffer:

    shape                          pre -O0   pre -O2   post (both)
    b   receiver `if`              2 B       2 B       clean
    d   by-value call argument     2 B       clean     clean
    p1  bare block                 2 B       2 B       clean
    p2  nested block               2 B       2 B       clean
    p3  `match`                    2 B       2 B       clean
    p4  `else if` chain            2 B       2 B       clean
    p5  `len` fast path            2 B       clean     clean
    p6  f-string interpolation     2 B       2 B       clean
    p7  concat operand             2 B       2 B       clean
    v.push  (OWNING destination)   clean     clean     clean
    p8  `let`     (OWNING)         clean     clean     clean

Whole-fixture: 35 allocs / 26 frees -> 35 / 35 at -O0, 33 / 26 -> 35 / 35 at
-O2. SEVEN OF THE NINE LEAK AT -O2, so the ordinary memory-sanitizer leg gates
this; the row's single opt-level note (`d` is -O0-only) reads like the whole
population is, and `p5` is the second such spelling.

THE OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED: INERT. The row held this back on whether the
call-argument gate's `rhs_stages_fstr_acc` / `last_fstr_acc` staging survives
the arm-tail suppressor. It never engages -- that predicate matches a DIRECT
`InterpolatedStringLit` (or a struct/enum `.to_string()`), never a branch
WRAPPING one -- so the `!rhs_stages_fstr_acc` term is vacuously true here and
the argument is materialized exactly once. `d` clean under ASAN is the
measurement.

WHY NO DANGLING HAZARD: the accumulator registers its own scope cleanup and
`suppress_block_tail_cleanup` zeroes that alloca's `cap` leaving the arm.
Correct in itself -- the value escapes, the arm's frame must not free it -- and
exactly what leaves the merged value owned by nobody. A disarm with no
counterpart is the hole a use-site free fills, and an f-string temp has no later
reader, unlike the binding tail whose sibling row needs a per-arm owner.

THREE MORE SPELLINGS, A DIFFERENT MECHANISM, ALSO FIXED. A DISCARDED
value-block with an f-string tail leaked 2 B per evaluation AT HEAD, at every
nesting depth: `{ f"b{n}" };`, `{ { f"c{n}" } };`, `{ { { f"e{n}" } } };`.
`compile_block_with_frame` computes `consumer_frees` from "does my tail mint?",
which is really "will a use-site gate free this?" -- a question presupposing a
use site. A discarded block has none, so the frame must keep its own owner. It
stayed hidden because every OTHER tail shape reaching that question is also
owned by the statement site (`stmt_owns_block_tail`), which suppresses the
discard leg entirely; an f-string tail is the first owned by neither. Two gaps
fed it, both in `compute_discarded_branch_spans`:

  1. THE TWO SPELLINGS OF ONE DISCARD DISAGREED. `let _ = { .. };` recorded a
     value-position block by its own span (`record_discarded_let_rhs`); the bare
     `{ .. };` statement did not. Measured: `let _ = { f"d{n}" };` clean,
     `{ f"b{n}" };` leaking -- the same program, the other spelling. The
     statement position now uses the same recorder.
  2. THE RECORDER TOOK ONLY THE OUTERMOST BLOCK. Discard is inherited through a
     single-tail wrapper exactly as `record_discarded_branch` documents for a
     branch, and each block is compiled by its OWN `compile_block_with_frame`
     looking up its OWN span. Now recursive; verified to three levels.

A MEASUREMENT ERROR IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE IT ALMOST WROTE THE WRONG STORY.
An intermediate draft concluded the widening had INTRODUCED the discard leak and
narrowed the predicate with an extra parameter to "fix" it. Both were wrong. The
pre/post harness ran a pre-fix compiler built in a separate worktree whose
`CARGO_TARGET_DIR` held no runtime archive, so every "pre" build FAILED at link
and the script -- which read a missing leak line as "clean" -- scored a failed
build as a clean run. With `KARAC_RUNTIME` pointed at the real archive and the
build exit status checked, the same shapes leak at HEAD. The extra parameter was
then measured to make no difference on any shape and removed. Two lessons worth
the words: a pre/post script must assert the build SUCCEEDED before scoring it,
and a compiler built in a foreign target dir needs `KARAC_RUNTIME`.

TRIPWIRES, measured pre/post across the whole discard matrix with zero invalid
frees: a discarded block with a CALL tail, with a BRANCH tail, with a string
LITERAL tail, and both `let _ =` spellings, plus a user-`Drop` struct literal
whose body must still fire exactly once. Those are owned by the statement site
and must NOT acquire a second owner here -- that failure is a double free, not a
leak. All unchanged, output identical.

THE TWO OWNING DESTINATIONS in the consuming fixture (`Vec.push`, a `let` read
twice) were already correct and are controls, not coverage.

A STRING-LITERAL ARM IS DELIBERATELY STILL DECLINED, so `if c { f"i{n}" } else
{ "lit" }` still leaks 2 B when the f-string arm runs. The free would be a
runtime no-op -- the site branches on `cap > 0` and rodata has `cap == 0` -- but
that is measured for ONE of the seven gates, and the real cost is to the
fail-closed quantifier: "every tail MINTS" is what keeps an aliased-place arm
out, and weakening it to "mints or is harmless" puts every future candidate up
for re-argument at seven sites. Split to B-2026-09-01-9 with the measurement.

TESTS. `asan_branch_tail_fstring_arm_frees_once` asserts the nine consuming
shapes clean plus the two owning controls, with a 20-allocation floor via
`assert_clean_asan_run_min_allocs` so a future pipeline change cannot make the
clean-run assertion vacuous (35 measured under the audit, 3 of them ASAN's own
startup). `asan_discarded_value_block_keeps_its_owner` covers the discard half
and its tripwires. `test_e2e_branch_tail_fstring_arm_values_round_trip` and its
interpreter oracle pin the VALUES, because the way a use-site free fails is
reading freed memory. `asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free`
loses its `b`/`d` rows and keeps a pointer to where they went, including the
reasoning that was correct and still led away from the fix ("the owner cannot
stand in, it keys off the Vec/String MOVE neutralizer") -- true, and beside the
point, because the gap was in the consuming GATE, not the producer.
title: A VALUE-POSITION BRANCH WHOSE ARM TAIL IS AN F-STRING LEAKS THE ACCUMULATOR -- `if c { f"x{n}" } else { f"y{n}" }.contains("x")` and the call-argument spelling each strand the 2 B buffer while the UNWRAPPED f-string is clean at both positions; the acc registers its own cleanup and the arm-tail suppressor then neutralizes it, so unlike the binding-tail sibling there is no dangling hazard here -- only a disarm with no counterpart at the merge
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the second deliberate remainder of B-2026-08-29-27, split out
rather than buried in it. That row widened seven consuming gates to admit a
value-position block or branch whose every tail mints a fresh owned temp via a
CALL; an f-string arm is a fresh owned temp produced a different way, and its
leak has a different cause and a different fix.

MEASURED (KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, valgrind; `f"x{n}"` is a 2 B buffer):

    let b = if c { f"x{n}" } else { f"y{n}" }.contains("x");
                                                2 B / 1 object   LEAKS
    let d = use_it(if c { f"x{n}" } else { f"y{n}" });
                                                2 B / 1 object   LEAKS

    CONTROL -- the same f-strings unwrapped:     clean
    let d2 = use_it(f"x{n}");
    let e = f"y{n}".contains("y");

    CONTROL -- string-LITERAL arms:              clean
    let g = if c { "lit1" } else { "lit2" }.contains("lit");
        (rodata, cap == 0; there is nothing to free, so no gate is needed)

WHY IT IS A DIFFERENT FIX FROM ITS BINDING-TAIL SIBLING (the other
B-2026-08-29-27 remainder). There the tail hands out storage that stays readable
after the wrapper, so a consumer-side free would dangle and the fix has to be a
per-arm owner. Here there is no such hazard: the f-string accumulator DOES
register its own scope cleanup (`track_vec_var` on the `fstr.acc` alloca), and
the arm-tail suppressor then neutralizes it on the way out -- correct in itself,
the value escapes the arm and the arm's frame must not free it -- leaving
nothing at the merge. It is a disarm with no counterpart, not an ownership
ambiguity.

WHY IT WAS HELD BACK ANYWAY: admitting an `InterpolatedStringLit` tail into
`expr_is_fresh_owned_branch_tail` is one line, but the call-argument gate
additionally consults `rhs_stages_fstr_acc` / `last_fstr_acc` -- staging that
exists precisely so a DIRECT f-string argument is not materialized twice against
the accumulator's own cleanup. Whether that staging is inert once the arm-tail
suppressor has already fired is the question this needs answered, and answering
it by measurement rather than by argument is worth its own row. The
discard-position sibling `discard_arm_tail_qualifies` already admits the shape,
which is a hint that it is admissible here too -- but the discard frame is the
only owner there, so it is not evidence.

SEVERITY: one small leak per evaluation, unbounded in a loop; no double free and
no wrong answer. Low rather than medium because the leaked buffer is the
rendered f-string, typically tens of bytes. Pinned at its current leaking value
by `asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free`.

CORRECTION (at close): two claims above did not survive measurement, and a
third population turned up that the row does not mention at all.

1. THE CONSUMING POPULATION IS NINE SPELLINGS, NOT TWO. The row measured the
   receiver and call-argument forms. A bare block, a nested block, the `match`
   form, an `else if` chain, the `len` fast path, an f-string interpolation and
   a concat operand all leaked the same 2 B, and all nine fell to the same line.
   The per-shape table is in the `fix` field. Not a criticism -- the row
   measured what it needed to file -- but a reader sizing the test from the two
   listed shapes would under-scope it.

2. "Pinned at its current leaking value by
   `asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free`" is now stale: the
   `b`/`d` rows were removed from that fixture and re-asserted, clean, in
   `asan_branch_tail_fstring_arm_frees_once`.

3. A DISCARDED value-block with an f-string tail leaks by a DIFFERENT mechanism
   and is not in this row's framing at all. `{ f"b{n}" };` and its nested
   spellings each lost 2 B at HEAD, through `compile_block_with_frame`'s
   `consumer_frees` rather than through any of the seven consuming gates. Fixed
   here because it is the same value and the same family, with its own fixture;
   see `fix`.

The row's own diagnosis was otherwise exactly right, including the part that
made this cheap: it identified the disarm-with-no-counterpart mechanism, said
the fix differs from its binding-tail sibling's per-arm owner, and named the one
thing it had not checked (`rhs_stages_fstr_acc` staging). That question is
answered in `fix` -- inert, because the predicate matches a direct f-string and
not a branch wrapping one.

One thing the row's framing DID cost. Calling this "a PRODUCER-side gap" (in the
pinning test's doc) points at the f-string accumulator, and the accumulator is
correct at every step: it registers its cleanup, the suppressor disarms it, the
value escapes. The gap is in the CONSUMING gate, which never recognized the
shape as minting. That distinction is why the fix is one line in a predicate
rather than new ownership machinery, and why B-2026-08-30-2's owner "cannot
stand in" -- true, and beside the point, since no owner was needed.

title: `cbrt` can now be admitted to the float-math table -- the libm-shim mechanism added by B-2026-08-29-60 removes the exact `run == build` obstacle that `float_math.rs`'s own `classify` doc cites for excluding it.
detail:
`cbrt` was excluded from the float-math table for exactly the reason
B-2026-08-29-60 has now removed. `src/float_math.rs`'s `classify` doc states
the exclusion and its rationale verbatim: "Rust's `f64::cbrt` is an in-Rust
implementation, not a libm call, and it disagrees with the system libm `cbrt`
this table would lower to (e.g. `27.0.cbrt()` is `3.0000000000000004` in the
interpreter but `3.0` from libm), which would break `run == build`."

That obstacle was real, and it was the SAME mechanism that B-2026-08-29-60
found in `asinh`/`acosh`/`atanh` -- Rust-implemented rather than
libm-delegating. Closing that row added the mechanism the exclusion lacked: an
`extern "C"` shim block in `float_math.rs` letting the interpreter call the
very symbol codegen emits, so a method in this class now agrees by
construction instead of being kept out of the language.

So the exclusion note is now stale as a permanent verdict, and `cbrt` /
`cbrtf` can be admitted the same way the three inverse hyperbolics were: add
`cbrt` to `classify` as Unary, add `("cbrt", false) => Some("cbrt")` /
`("cbrt", true) => Some("cbrtf")` to the codegen `libm_sym` table (it has no
LLVM-18 intrinsic either, so it takes the direct-libm path its neighbours
take), and route the interpreter arm through `at_width_libm!` with a
`cbrt_f64`/`cbrt_f32` shim pair. The row's own worked example is the natural
first test: `27.0.cbrt()` should print `3` on BOTH backends afterwards, where
today the interpreter would print `3.0000000000000004` if the method existed.

Filed rather than folded into B-2026-08-29-60 because it is a FEATURE
addition, not part of closing an A/B divergence -- `cbrt` is absent today, so
nothing is currently wrong. Severity low; it is a small gap in the float-math
surface (design.md's "Math (`sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, etc.) via libm") with a
now-unblocked, mechanical fix. Note also that a `cbrt` shim is the point at
which the shim block stops being a three-method special case and becomes the
general answer for this class, so it is worth doing for the shape as much as
for the function.
fix:
Fixed in f8045545. `cbrt` is admitted and all four surfaces agree --
`karac run --interp`, `karac run` (JIT), `karac build`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` -- on 60 f64 and 60 f32 inputs spanning both
signs, plus the row's own `27.0`, byte-identical.

The row's four-part recipe was applied as written: `classify` gains `cbrt` as
Unary, codegen's `libm_sym` gains `("cbrt", false) => Some("cbrt")` /
`("cbrt", true) => Some("cbrtf")`, `float_math.rs` gains a `c_cbrt`/`c_cbrtf`
shim pair beside the inverse hyperbolics, and the interpreter arm routes
through `at_width_libm!`. That much was mechanical and correct. Two things the
row records were not, and both trace to one fact neither it nor the doc it
quotes accounts for: `compiler_builtins` -- linked into every Rust binary and
every Rust staticlib -- ships its OWN weak `cbrt`/`cbrtf`, and that definition
wins over the platform libm's wherever a Rust object is in the link.

PREMISE INVERTED. The row, quoting `classify`'s own doc, says `27.0.cbrt()` is
`3.0000000000000004` in the interpreter and `3.0` from libm. On x86-64 glibc
with rustc 1.94.1 it is the reverse: glibc's `cbrt` answers
`3.0000000000000004`; Rust answers `3`. And Rust's `f64::cbrt` is not a
separate implementation from the symbol codegen emits at all -- measured
bit-for-bit over 2000 inputs at both widths, `f64::cbrt` and a Rust binary's
`extern "C" cbrt` are the same function, 0 differences, because std routes to
the compiler_builtins definition. So the interpreter shim is NOT load-bearing
for `cbrt` on this host; it is what keeps the two backends tied together if a
future toolchain stops routing there, which is a fact about a Rust version
rather than an invariant. Landed anyway, for that reason and for the shape the
row asks for, but documented as such -- `classify`'s doc has been corrected in
place rather than left to be re-quoted by the next row.

THE ACTUAL BREAK WAS ONE LANE OVER, and the row does not mention that lane.
Admitting `cbrt` as specified made `karac run` -- the DEFAULT executor --
disagree with `karac build` and `karac run --interp`: `3.0000000000000004`
against `3`, and on 224 of 400 sampled f64 inputs, 121 of 2000 at BOTH widths.
Ruled out in order: not constant folding (an opaque receiver diverges
identically), not an optimisation level (KARAC_OPT_LEVEL 0/1/2/3 agree within
each lane and differ across them), not a stale `karac_jit_runner`. The cause is
that the runner references no `cbrt`, so nothing pulls the compiler_builtins
member into it, and ORC's process-symbol generator resolves the emitted call
through `dlsym` -- which cannot see an archive symbol that arrived with LOCAL
linkage -- landing on glibc's. The interpreter (inside `karac`) and an AOT
binary (which links `libkarac_runtime.a`) both land on compiler_builtins'.

That is the same shape as B-2026-08-20-5 one class over, and it reuses that
row's mechanism: `__muloti4` is published because `dlsym` finds NOTHING;
`cbrt`/`cbrtf` are published because `dlsym` finds the WRONG ONE.
`LLJITEngine::define_compiler_rt_builtins` now hands the JIT the address
`float_math`'s own `c_cbrt` resolves to, so every lane calls one
implementation.

SCOPE, measured rather than assumed. `compiler_builtins` shadows 20 of the 64
libm names codegen can emit on this host. Eighteen are exactly specified by
IEEE 754 -- `sqrt`, `fabs`, `copysign`, the four integral roundings, `fmod`,
`fma` and their `f` forms -- so two implementations cannot disagree, which is
why nothing had gone wrong before: `%` on f64 was checked across all four lanes
and is identical. `cbrt` is the only INEXACT member of the shadowed set, which
is why the exclusion this row lifted only ever had one member.

Tests: three fixtures and one guard.
`tests/interpreter.rs::test_cbrt_agrees_with_the_libm_symbol_codegen_calls` and
`tests/codegen.rs::test_e2e_cbrt_agrees_with_the_interpreter` are the twinned
A/B pair, computing expectations from the linked symbol rather than freezing
one host's bits (the rule the inverse-hyperbolic pair set). The codegen half
also runs on the JIT lane under CI's `KARAC_TEST_JIT=1`, and
`tests/lljit_e2e.rs::jit_e2e_cbrt_resolves_the_implementation_the_other_lanes_link`
pins that lane unconditionally -- both were verified RED with the publication
removed and GREEN with it. Inputs after the first differ between the two
implementations at BOTH widths, found by sweeping k/10 for k in 1..=2000
against a C program linked with `-lm`.
`tests/lljit_e2e.rs::jit_e2e_every_shadowed_libm_symbol_is_exact_or_published`
is the structural half: it walks every libm name codegen can emit, finds the
ones whose static resolution differs from `dlsym`'s, and requires each to be
either IEEE-exact or listed in the new `codegen::PUBLISHED_LIBM_SYMBOLS`. That
turns "only `cbrt` is shadowed today" from a measurement into a guard, so if a
future toolchain ships its own `sin` or `log` a test names it instead of a
value coming out different on one of four lanes with nothing failing anywhere.

title: `to_degrees` / `to_radians` on an `f16` receiver disagree between the interpreter and every compiled surface on ~25% of inputs -- codegen rounds 180/pi INTO f16 before multiplying, because the block's opening widen covers bf16 only.
detail:
`to_degrees` / `to_radians` on an `f16` receiver disagree between the
interpreter and both compiled backends, on roughly a quarter of inputs. Found
by the whole-table sweep run while closing B-2026-08-29-60; it is a DIFFERENT
mechanism from that row (which was formula-vs-libm on the inverse hyperbolics)
and touches different methods, so it is filed rather than folded in.

MEASURED (x86_64, 150 inputs per method per width, `karac run --interp` vs
`karac run` vs `karac build` vs `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`, all three
compiled surfaces agreeing with each other and differing from the
interpreter):

    width   to_degrees   to_radians
    bf16       0/150        0/150
    f16       38/150       41/150
    f32        0/150        0/150
    f64        0/150        0/150

    e.g. `to_radians` at one f16 receiver: interp -0.1844482421875,
         compiled   -0.1845703125   (about 1 ULP at f16 near 0.18)

MECHANISM, and it is entirely on the CODEGEN side. `src/codegen/method_call.rs`
handles `recip`/`to_degrees`/`to_radians`/`fract` in one block that begins with
`widen_bf16_scalar`, which widens **bf16 only** -- f16 is a type LLVM can do
native arithmetic on, so it is left alone. The arm then builds its constant
with `fty.const_float(57.29577951308232)`, and at `fty == half` that rounds
180/pi INTO f16 before the multiply: f16's ULP near 57.3 is 0.03125, so the
constant itself carries ~2.7e-4 of relative error before any multiplication
happens. The interpreter computes the same expression at f32
(`eval_at_span_width` maps F32/F16/BF16 to the f32 path) and rounds once at
the end, so it multiplies by a constant that is right to ~1e-8.

WHAT ISOLATES IT TO CODEGEN, decisively and without a bisect: bf16 and f16 take
the IDENTICAL interpreter path -- the same `eval_at_span_width` arm, the same
f32 computation, the same final narrowing -- and differ only in that codegen
widens bf16 and not f16. bf16 shows 0/150; f16 shows 38 and 41. The one
asymmetry between them lives in `widen_bf16_scalar`, so that is the cause.
It also means the bf16 leg is only correct BY ACCIDENT: the widening was added
for B-2026-08-29-34, because native bfloat ops are unselectable off x86, and it
happened to fix the constant's precision as a side effect. Nobody chose the
accurate constant for bf16; f16 simply never got the same treatment.

NOT INTRODUCED BY B-2026-08-29-41 (which reworked the interpreter half of this
same arm) NOR BY B-2026-08-29-60. The error is dominated by codegen's
f16-rounded constant, and that code is untouched by both; the interpreter-side
change in -41 (f64-then-round to compute-at-f32) cannot move an f16 result,
because a product that coarse rounds to the same f16 either way.

LIKELY FIX: widen f16 through the same path bf16 takes -- i.e. make the block's
opening widen any reduced-precision receiver rather than bf16 specifically, so
the constant is materialized at f32 and the multiply happens there, with one
rounding at the end. That makes f16 agree with bf16, with the interpreter, and
with the "compute in f32, round once" rule the codegen comments elsewhere in
this file already state for reduced-precision receivers.

THE OTHER TWO METHODS IN THE SAME BLOCK ARE FINE, and for a reason worth
recording, because it says what the bug actually is. `recip` and `fract` take
the identical un-widened f16 path and were exercised 150 times each by the same
sweep: 0/150 both. `fract` is x - trunc(x), exact at any width. `recip` is
1.0/x, and 1.0 is exactly representable at every width, so codegen's constant
carries no error; what remains is a double rounding (f32 divide, then narrow)
against codegen's single f16 divide, and that is SAFE here by the 2p+2 rule --
f16 needs 2*11+2 = 24 intermediate bits and f32 has exactly 24, the same
argument B-2026-08-29-41 used to justify compute-at-width for + - * / and sqrt.

So this bug is NOT the double-rounding hazard that rule governs; it is upstream
of it. `to_degrees`/`to_radians` are the only two members of the block whose
constant is irrational, so they are the only two where `const_float` at `half`
destroys precision before the arithmetic starts. No amount of intermediate
width protects a multiply whose multiplicand was already wrong.

SEVERITY medium: it is a live `run == build` violation, which the project
treats as non-negotiable, and unlike B-2026-08-29-60's last-ULP gap the
compiled side here is the LESS accurate one -- it is throwing away most of the
precision of a mathematical constant, not choosing a different correctly-
rounded algorithm.
fix:
FIXED by 42e103d. The block's opening widen now covers EVERY reduced-precision
receiver instead of bf16 specifically, so `to_degrees` / `to_radians` build
their constant at f32 and multiply there, with a single rounding back to f16 at
the end -- the interpreter's arithmetic exactly, not an equivalent of it.

`src/codegen/expr_ops.rs` gains `widen_reduced_float_scalar` /
`narrow_reduced_float_scalar` beside the existing bf16 pair, returning the
`FloatType` to round back to rather than a bool, and
`src/codegen/method_call.rs`'s `recip` / `to_degrees` / `to_radians` / `fract`
block calls them. The two pairs are kept SEPARATE and documented as answering
different questions: the bf16 pair exists for a SELECTABILITY problem (LLVM 18
cannot select native `bfloat` arithmetic off x86, B-2026-08-29-34) and is used
by `build_float_intrinsic_bf16_safe` and friends, where widening f16 would
change results for no reason; the new pair exists for an ACCURACY one, and f16
needs it despite selecting natively everywhere.

WHY THIS IS EXACT AND NOT MERELY CLOSER. The two backends spell the constants
differently -- codegen builds `to_radians` from `std::f64::consts::PI / 180.0`
in f64, Rust's `f32::to_radians` from `f32::consts::PI / 180.0` in f32 -- so
"compute at f32" only makes them agree if the two spellings land on the same
f32. They do, both of them: f32(57.29577951308232) and
f32(57.2957795130823208767981548141051703) are the same float, and
f32(f64_PI/180) == f32(f32_PI/180) == 0.01745329238474369. So after the widen
codegen is not approximating the interpreter, it is running the same multiply
on the same bits. That is what the pre-existing 0/2400-divergence f32 column
was already evidence for, and it is why the fix needed no constant tuning.

THE ROW'S MECHANISM CONFIRMED EXACTLY, not inferred. Over 300 f16 receivers,
with both models computed independently in Python (f32 via `struct`, f16 by
explicit round-to-nearest-even at 11 bits):

    interpreter output == "constant at f32, multiply at f32, round once" 300/300
    compiled  (before)  == "constant rounded INTO f16, multiply at f16" 300/300
    compiled  (before)  == the interpreter's model                      132/300
    compiled  (after)   == the interpreter's model                      300/300

The IR names the culprit outright: before the fix the emitted instruction is
`%to_deg = fmul half %a4, 0xH5329`, and `0xH5329` is 57.28125 -- 180/pi after
f16 rounding, 2.5e-4 of relative error against the ~1e-8 the interpreter
multiplies by. As the row said, no intermediate width recovers a multiplicand
that was already wrong.

MEASURED, four surfaces (`karac run --interp` vs `karac run` vs `karac build`
vs `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`), before -> after:

    fixture                                     before        after
    4 block methods x 600 inputs, f16          344 lines     0
    34-method table x 150 inputs, f16           79 lines     0
    both fixtures at bf16 / f32 / f64             0           0

The row's own 150-input figures (38 and 41) reproduce exactly on its fixture;
on a wider input spread the rate is higher still -- 206/600 `to_degrees` and
138/600 `to_radians` -- because the constant's error is a fixed fraction of an
f16 ULP, so how often it flips the final rounding is a property of the input
distribution, not a fixed 25%.

THE ROW'S OTHER CLAIMS ALL HELD at 4x its sample: `recip` and `fract` are
0/600 each at f16 both before and after (1.0 is exact at every width; x -
trunc(x) is exact), and bf16 / f32 / f64 are 0/600 throughout. The bf16 path is
byte-identical before and after -- the new helper does exactly what the old one
did for a bf16 input -- so its correctness stays where it was, but the reason is
now written down instead of being the accident the row identified.

NO VECTOR TWIN, which is worth recording so nobody re-runs the sweep to find
out: the vector receiver surface is `sqrt | exp | ln | sigmoid | tanh | floor |
ceil | round | trunc` only, so the two methods that carry an irrational
constant do not exist there. The vector splats that do exist use 1.0 and 2.0
(exact at every width), and the `exp` / `ln` polynomials -- the one place
vectors do carry irrational coefficients -- are guarded to f32, with f16 and
bf16 falling back to the intrinsic. A sweep of every `const_float` call site in
`src/codegen/` finds no other inexact constant that can be materialized at a
reduced-precision type: `stats.rs` and `column.rs` build theirs at an explicit
`f64_type`, and `types_lowering.rs` is source literals, which are supposed to
round to their declared width.

TESTS, and a verified negative control. `tests/codegen.rs` gains an E2E pin
over all four block methods at all four widths, whose ten f16 receivers were
chosen BY THE ORACLE as values where the two models disagree on both methods
(so twenty values fail if the widen ever stops covering f16), plus an IR test
asserting no `half` arithmetic survives the block. `tests/interpreter.rs` gains
the same fixture with the same expected text, so the pair is the run==build
assertion split across the two suites -- a future "fix" that moved the
interpreter to match a broken codegen would fail there rather than pass
quietly. With the two source hunks reverted and the tests kept, both codegen
tests FAIL (the E2E on 11 of 26 lines, the IR test naming `fmul half`) and the
interpreter test still PASSES, which is the correct signature for a
codegen-only bug.

Bit-exact string pins are portable here, unlike the libm transcendentals
`tests/interpreter.rs`'s `approx_line` helper exists for: an fmul by a
constant, an fdiv by 1.0 and `x - trunc(x)` are IEEE-exact on every platform.

PROVENANCE, which the row reasoned to correctly and git now confirms. The
block shipped in `ce982ad` (2026-08-17) with `const_float` at the receiver
width and NO widen at all, so the same hazard structurally applied to bf16 as
well. `e860b90` (2026-08-29, B-2026-08-29-34) added `widen_bf16_scalar` here
for the SELECTABILITY reason and removed the bf16 half as a side effect twelve
days later -- the "correct by accident" the row identified, now with the two
commits named. Neither B-2026-08-29-41 nor B-2026-08-29-60 touched this code,

FIXED by 7a10c4e. The sum form now requires a FLOORING halve: `(lo + hi) >> 1` is recognised, `(lo + hi) / 2` is not. The difference form `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` is untouched and keeps both assumes, because its dividend `hi - lo >= 1` is positive under the dominating strict guard and the two roundings agree on every non-negative value -- which is precisely the proof `docs/investigations/bce_monotonic_assume.md` states, for signed FLOOR. The sum form had been added alongside it without a matching proof.

Narrowed rather than dropped, deliberately: `lo <= floor((lo+hi)/2) <= hi-1` follows from `lo < hi` alone, negative sums included, so the flooring spelling is sound and stays supported. A fix that merely deleted the arm would read as "the sum form is unsupported" and invite a later session to restore it as a missing feature.

COST OF THE NARROWING, measured: a 1M-element Vec binary search spelled `(lo + hi) / 2` loses the assumes and runs 1.01x +/- 0.08 -- nothing measurable, 12 runs interleaved.

  test_ir_binsearch_sum_midpoint_floor_shift_keeps_assume

title: A bisection over NEGATIVE bounds miscompiles: `(lo + hi) / 2` truncates toward zero, so the midpoint recognizer's `assume(mid < hi)` is `assume(false)` at `hi == lo + 1`, and the compiled program runs on injected UB (SIGBUS) where the interpreter is correct

The JIT REPL's B.5.3d PASS-THROUGH silently REVERTS every mutation to a `let mut` binding whose type is not snapshot-eligible, and re-runs its RHS (side effects included) on every cell -- `Map[String, i64]`, `Vec[String]` and `Option[i64]` all read back their initializer in the next cell even when the mutation was made in the SAME cell, and a side-effecting initializer printed 3 times across 4 cells; `--interp` is correct on both counts, and the deferral is documented as giving "correct (re-evaluating) semantics", which holds only for an immutable binding with a pure RHS
detail:
The JIT REPL snapshots a cross-cell `let` into an LLVM global only for a
closed tier of types (`snapshot_kind_for_type`, src/repl/util.rs): i64, f64, bool,
char, String, `Vec[primitive]`, `Map[primitive, primitive]`, `Set[primitive]`.
Everything else -- struct, enum, tuple, `Option`, `Rc`/`Arc`, closure, `SortedSet`,
and any `Vec`/`Map`/`Set` whose element or key is not one of the four primitives --
takes the B.5.3d PASS-THROUGH: no global, and the replayed `let`'s original RHS is
re-lowered and re-run in every subsequent cell.

phase-7-codegen.md's B.5.3d entry says of that fallback: "the v1 source-replay
fallback gives correct (re-evaluating) semantics -- the let RHS re-runs on each cell
rather than reading from a snapshot global." That is only true for an IMMUTABLE
binding whose RHS is PURE. Neither half holds in practice, and both failures are
silent.

(1) MUTATIONS ARE REVERTED. Because the RHS re-runs, cell N+1 rebuilds the binding
from its initializer and the mutation is gone. Measured, `karac repl` (JIT default)
vs `karac repl --interp`, same input:

    shape                                            JIT   --interp
    Map[String,i64].new(); insert in a LATER cell     0        1
    Map[String,i64].new(); insert in the SAME cell    0        1
    Vec[String].new(); push in a LATER cell           0        1
    Option[i64] = None; `o = Some(4)` in a LATER cell false    true

Note the second row: unlike B-2026-08-30-1, this loses a mutation made in the
DECLARING cell too, because the loss happens when the NEXT cell re-evaluates the
RHS -- not when the current one fails to write a global.

(2) SIDE EFFECTS RE-EXECUTE. The whole point of the snapshot tier (per B.5.1's own
doc: "`let log = read_file(\"big.json\")` should not reread the file on every cell")
is not to re-run a side-effecting initializer. Pass-through does exactly that.
Measured over a 4-cell session whose cell 2 is `let mut v: Vec[String] = mk();`
where `mk()` prints:

    karac repl            SIDE EFFECT / SIDE EFFECT / cell 3 / SIDE EFFECT / cell 4
    karac repl --interp   SIDE EFFECT / cell 3 / cell 4

Three executions vs one. The same program with `Vec[i64]` (an ELIGIBLE type) prints
it once on both lanes, which isolates the cause to snapshot eligibility rather than
to anything about the function.

WHY `--interp` IS RIGHT ON BOTH: its `let_snapshots` cache is a
`HashMap<String, Value>` with no type tier at all -- every watched top-level binding
is captured at each scope exit, whatever its type. The JIT lane's tier is a codegen
limitation (each type needs its own storage format + ownership handshake for the
global), and the tier boundary is exactly where the two lanes part company.

WHY HIGH. It is the default backend on the REPL/notebook surface; it is silent, with
a plausible wrong value rather than an error; the affected type surface is far LARGER
than the eligible one (`Option` and struct payloads are the common shapes in
interactive exploration -- B.5.3d's own text names them as the most REPL-relevant);
and it contradicts design.md § Interactive Evaluation Model > Cell Scope, which
specifies the session's accumulated content as "the body of an implicit
`fn main()`". Under that model a mutation in cell 2 is simply a statement earlier in
one function body, and no reading of it permits cell 3 to see the initializer.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-30-1 (fixed, 80bb5ec6). Same user-visible symptom, different
mechanism, disjoint type surface. -1 was the ELIGIBLE tier: the global existed and
was never written back after the declaring cell. This is the INELIGIBLE tier: there
is no global, and the RHS re-runs. Fixing -1 does not touch this, and the check that
separates them is whether `snapshot_kind_for_type` accepts the binding's type. The
row for -1 was filed with a `Map[String, i64]` in its measurement table, which is
this bug rather than that one -- corrected in place there, and split out here rather
than folded in, since the remedies differ.

WHAT THE FIX WOULD BE, so the next session does not re-derive it: this is B.5.3d,
already on phase-7-codegen.md as a deferred item ("REPL value-snapshot for
non-primitive aggregates"), and the work is per-type storage + ownership handshakes.
What this row adds is that the deferral's stated justification is FALSE -- the
fallback is not "correct but slower", it is silently wrong for any mutated binding
and for any impure initializer -- so the deferral needs either the implementation or,
in the interim, a diagnostic: a REPL note when a cell binds a `let mut` of an
ineligible type, saying the binding will not carry mutations across cells. A silent
wrong answer is the part that makes this worth a row rather than a checklist line.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: whether a `struct`/`enum`-typed binding
behaves identically (only `Map[String,i64]`, `Vec[String]` and `Option[i64]` were
probed); whether the RHS re-execution can also produce a DOUBLE FREE when the
re-evaluated initializer transfers ownership of something the previous cell's copy
still owns; and whether the browser playground and the Jupyter kernel, which share
this backend, show the same two divergences.

REPRODUCTION (any llvm build; rebuild BOTH `karac` and `karac_jit_runner` first):

    printf 'let mut v: Vec[String] = Vec.new();\nv.push(f"a");\nprintln(f"{v.len()}");\n' | karac repl
    printf 'let mut v: Vec[String] = Vec.new();\nv.push(f"a");\nprintln(f"{v.len()}");\n' | karac repl --interp
