an ineligible Map key, so verifying that row's own numbers surfaced this as the
separate thing it was measuring.

UPDATE 2026-08-30 — the SILENCE is fixed; the DIVERGENCE is not. Row stays open,
severity high -> medium. Landed in 25e982c2.

WHAT LANDED. A cell that declares a top-level `let` the JIT lane cannot snapshot
now emits a note naming the binding, its type, and the lane that is correct:

    warning[repl-jit-no-snapshot]: `v` (Vec[String]) is rebuilt from its
    initializer in every later cell -- the JIT REPL has no cross-cell snapshot
    for this type, so a mutation will not survive the cell boundary and a
    side-effecting initializer runs again each time. `karac repl --interp`
    carries this binding correctly (B-2026-08-30-7).

`--interp` still answers correctly; the JIT lane still answers wrongly. What
changed is that the wrong answer is no longer unannounced, and the user is told
which lane to use. `Session::passthrough_divergence_notes` (src/repl.rs).

WHERE IT FIRES, and why there. At the cell that DECLARES the binding, not the
one that loses the value. That is the actionable moment -- the user learns the
binding will not persist before building on it -- and it fires exactly once with
no dedup state, because from the next cell onward the name is in
`persistent_lets` and the walk skips it.

WHEN IT FIRES, and why not always. Only when harm is possible: `let mut` (Kara's
prerequisite for mutating at all, so an immutable binding cannot hit the
mutation failure), or an initializer that is a direct call to a session-defined
free function (the `let log = read_file(...)` shape, and the one that
re-executes). Deliberately NOT for an immutable binding with a
constructor-shaped initializer -- `let p = Point { x: 1 };` is the common shape
in an interactive session, re-running it is observationally identical, and
warning there would bury the real cases under noise on every ordinary cell.
A constructor (`Vec.new()`, a struct literal) is a MethodCall / StructLiteral
rather than a Call through an identifier, so it does not trip the second
condition.

WHY THE SEVERITY DROPS TO MEDIUM. `high` was justified by SILENT wrong answers
on the default lane -- a plausible wrong number with nothing to indicate it. The
user now gets the wrong number WITH an explanation and a working alternative,
which is the difference between a trap and a documented limitation. It is not
`low`: the default lane still computes wrong values, and a user who ignores the
note gets them.

WHAT REMAINS, unchanged: the snapshot tier itself (B.5.3d). Each type needs its
own storage format and cross-cell ownership handshake -- that is the deferred
work this row's first half describes, and it is tracked at
docs/implementation_checklist/phase-7-codegen.md § B.5.3d, whose entry now
carries this row's measurements and the correction below. Kept OPEN rather than
relocated because the divergence is live and user-visible, and `relocated` is
for a row with no action item today; extending the tier is an action item, just
a large one.

ALSO CORRECTED: the B.5.3d entry claimed the pass-through fallback "gives
correct (re-evaluating) semantics". That was the sentence which made the
deferral look safe, and it is false for any mutated binding or impure
initializer. Corrected in place with both measurements.

NOT ADDRESSED, stated rather than implied: the note keys on `let mut` and on a
direct call to a session fn. A binding mutated only through a `mut ref` method
on an immutable-looking receiver, or an initializer whose impurity is reached
through a method call (`obj.load()`) or a nested call rather than a direct one,
will not warn. Both are narrowings of a warning, not of the underlying bug, and
neither makes the JIT lane any less correct than it already was.

UPDATE 2026-09-01 — the BY-VALUE half of the tier LANDED; the heap-carrying
half is what remains. Row stays open, severity unchanged at medium.

WHAT LANDED. `SnapshotPrimKind::ByValue` — a seventh snapshot kind covering
every type whose lowered representation holds no heap pointer and no
refcount. The premise the deferral rested on is that "each of those types
would need its own cross-cell ownership story"; that is true of the
heap-carrying ones and was over-generalized to the whole remainder. For a
by-value type there is NO ownership story to write: copying the binding's
slot into the snapshot global is a COMPLETE transfer, because nothing behind
a pointer is being shared. So capture is a plain `store`, replay a plain
`load`, and — unlike String/Vec (which zero the slot's `cap`) or Map/Set
(which skip `track_map_var`) — neither side suppresses a cleanup, because
there is no cleanup to suppress.

The class:
  - every scalar width the language has. The original tier admitted only
    i64/f64/bool/char and said so ("Adding width-correct lowering for
    i8/i16/i32/u*/etc. is mechanical follow-up work"); `i32`, `u8` and `f32`
    bindings were silently reverting on the same mechanism as the row's
    measured cases.
  - `Option[T]` / `Result[T, E]` over by-value payloads. Both lower to the
    SEEDED `{ i64 tag, i64 w0, i64 w1, i64 w2 }` shape, a fixed constant, so
    the global's width cannot drift between the cell that defines it and a
    cell that loads it — the property that makes a cross-module global safe
    at all.
  - tuples of by-value elements.
  - a user `struct` / `enum` that is neither `shared` nor `par`, carries no
    user `impl Drop`, is not generic, and whose every field / variant payload
    is itself by-value (recursively; the walk is depth-bounded because a
    declaration cycle would otherwise not terminate).

MEASURED, `karac repl` vs `karac repl --interp`, mutation made in the cell
AFTER the declaring one (the row's own table shape):

    shape                                  before      after    --interp
    Option[i64], o = Some(4)               false       true     true
    i32,         n = 5                     0           5        5
    (i64, bool), t = (7, true)             1 false     7 true   7 true
    struct P{x,y}, p.x = 9                 1 2         9 2      9 2
    enum E{A,B(i64)}, e = E.B(3)           0           3        3

And the side-effect half, a 4-cell session whose cell 2 is
`let mut o: Option[i64] = mk();` where `mk()` prints:

    before   SIDE EFFECT / SIDE EFFECT / cell 3 / SIDE EFFECT / cell 4
    after    SIDE EFFECT / cell 3 / cell 4          (== --interp)

The `warning[repl-jit-no-snapshot]` note stops firing for these shapes, which
is the right coupling: it keys on `snapshot_kind_for_type` returning None, so
it narrows exactly as the tier widens.

HOW REPLAY REBUILDS DISPATCH, and why not by hand. The four existing kinds
each poke their own side-tables in the replay path (`string_vars`,
`vec_elem_types`, `map_key_types`, …). That does not generalize to an
open-ended class: `println(o)` needs `var_option_payload_te`, `t.0` needs
`tuple_var_elem_type_names`, `p.x` needs `var_type_names`, and a generic
field needs the instantiation record. So the by-value arm calls
`register_var_from_type_expr` — the SAME registrar the ordinary `let` arm
uses — which makes a replayed binding indistinguishable from a freshly-bound
one rather than approximately so. Safe there for the reason the other arms
skip `track_vec_var`: that registrar writes dispatch metadata only and never
queues a cleanup action.

The `TypeExpr` it needs rides in `Codegen::snapshot_value_types`, keyed by
binding name, because the variant itself carries no payload (keeping
`SnapshotPrimKind: Copy`, which several call sites rely on). The REPL
persists the DECLARING cell's `TypeExpr` in `Session::jit_snapshot_value_types`
rather than re-deriving it per cell: the global was sized by that cell, and a
later cell that inferred a different type for the same name would load it at
the wrong width.

A NAMED TYPE MUST BE DECLARED IN THE SESSION'S OWN SOURCE, and this is not
tidiness — it is a regression this work introduced and then had to fix.
Several baked stdlib types are OPAQUE HANDLES whose declared shape is a lie
about their storage: `struct DataFrame { … }` and `Interner` walk as by-value
fields, so the field-shape rule admits them, and codegen then lowers each to
a bare `ptr` whose pointee the slot's scope-exit cleanup frees. Snapshotting
one copies the pointer, the original is freed at end of cell, and the next
cell loads a dangling handle: measured, `karac repl` died with "JIT runner
subprocess died mid-cell" on `DataFrame.new()` + `d.height()` where
`--interp` printed `0`. Nothing in the `Type` says so, and
`StructInfo::defining_stdlib_origin` does NOT answer for those two, so
provenance is taken from the one source that cannot be wrong about it —
whether the declaration is among the session's own `program.items` with
`stdlib_origin == false`. `tests/repl_jit.rs`'s
`repl_jit_by_value_tier_excludes_an_opaque_handle_type` pins it.

The cost of that whitelist, stated rather than implied: a STDLIB VALUE ENUM
is genuinely by-value and stays on pass-through anyway. Measured: `Ordering`,
mutated in a later cell, still reads back its initializer on the JIT lane
(`false` vs `--interp`'s `true`) and still warns. Admitting it needs a rule
that can tell a stdlib value type from a stdlib opaque handle — codegen has
exactly that list (`builtin_opaque_ptr_handle`), but it is `pub(super)` inside
codegen and inverting the guard to a blacklist would make correctness depend
on that list being exhaustive, which the whitelist does not.

A `Drop`-carrying struct is excluded too, for a different reason: capture
hands the value to a global nobody tears down, so its destructor would never
run — trading this row's divergence for a new one. The exclusion is by name,
scanned from the session's `impl Drop` blocks, because `TypeCheckResult`
exposes the shapes and not the impls.

WHAT REMAINS, and it is the same kind of work the row's first half describes,

the primitive-element cases the bespoke kinds already cover — including the
row's own `Map[String, i64]` and `Vec[String]` measurements, which are

WHAT LANDED. `VecElemKind::String` — the four bespoke container kinds
(`Vec`, `Map` key, `Map` value, `Set`) now admit a `String` component, so
`Vec[String]`, `Map[String, V]`, `Map[K, String]` and `Set[String]` snapshot
instead of falling through to pass-through. `Vec[String]` and
`Map[String, i64]` are the two shapes THIS ROW's opening table measured, so
the row's headline divergence is closed; `Set[String]` and
`Map[String, String]` come along by the same argument.

WHY THE DEFERRAL'S REASON DOES NOT HOLD, which is the whole content of the
fix. The tier's own comment deferred these on the ground that "Vec[String] /
Vec[<user struct>] would need per-element drop accounting and stay in
pass-through", and the Map arm says the same of aggregate keys. That is the
requirement for FREEING the container. Capture does not free it. It
suppresses the slot's cleanup WHOLESALE, and the drain's ENTIRE per-element
walk sits inside the branch that suppression turns off — the `FreeVecBuffer`
arm's own comment says so in as many words: "Guarded by the same `cap > 0`
branch, so a moved-out Vec skips per-element drops too." So the transfer to
the snapshot global is COMPLETE for the whole tree, buffer and elements
alike: no second owner, nothing freed, and the storage is reclaimed when the
JITDylib is torn down. That is not a new policy invented for this fix — it is
exactly what `String` and `Vec[i64]` have done since B.5.2 ("option (a) leak
the buffer"). The deferral generalized a freeing requirement onto a path that
does not free, the same shape of over-generalization the by-value half
corrected in the previous update.

WHAT LANDED. `SnapshotPrimKind::InlineEnvelope` — an eighth snapshot kind for
an `Option[T]` / `Result[T, E]` whose lowered slot is the seeded inline
`{ i64 tag, i64 w0, i64 w1, i64 w2 }` envelope and whose heap payload is a

named as "the nearest adjacent one" and left open, so this closes that item

THE PREVIOUS UPDATE'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND ITS REMEDY WAS INCOMPLETE, which
is the part worth reading. It said storage was not the obstacle — a
`{ptr,len,cap}` payload fits the seeded envelope exactly — and that only
suppression was, "since `zero_vec_alloca_cap` GEPs a vec struct and an enum

arm verbatim (the envelope is a fixed 32-byte constant, so the global's width
cannot drift between cells), and suppression is
`retract_inline_envelope_payload_cleanup`: the Map/Set RETRACTION shape rather
than the String/Vec cap-sentinel shape, dropping the queued
`FreeInline{Option,Result}Payload` for the slot. Retraction is a complete
transfer for the same reason it is on the container tier — the overlay action
is the only thing that would free the payload buffer, so removing it leaves
the snapshot global as the sole owner, reclaimed at JITDylib teardown.

What the diagnosis did not reach is that suppression is not the whole handshake
for this kind. See the regression below.

And the side-effect half, a 4-cell session whose cell 2 is
`let mut o: Option[String] = mk();` where `mk()` prints:

    before   SIDE EFFECT / SIDE EFFECT / cell 3 / SIDE EFFECT / cell 4

update is longer than the shape count justifies. Retraction alone turned a
WRONG ANSWER into a DEAD RUNNER — strictly worse than the divergence being

The mechanism: `inline_{option,result}_payload_vars` is an input to a match
arm's BORROW-VS-CONSUME classification (`scrutinee_is_inline_optres_local`).
A REPLAYED binding never entered those sets — replay defers to
`register_var_from_type_expr`, which writes dispatch metadata and nothing else
— so `match o { Option.Some(s) => println(s) }` over a replayed envelope was
classified CONSUMING and freed the payload buffer at arm exit, while the
snapshot global still pointed at it. Measured on the retraction-only version:

    cell 1  let mut o: Option[String] = Option.Some(f"alpha");
    cell 2  match o { Option.Some(s) => println(s), … }   ->  alpha
    cell 3  match o { Option.Some(s) => println(s), … }   ->  JIT runner
                                                              subprocess died
                                                              mid-cell
    cell 4  (fresh runner, replays from scratch)          ->  alpha

The SAME two matches as one AOT `.kara` program are clean under valgrind and
print `alpha` twice, which is what localizes this to the REPL rather than to
the arm: in a program `o` is a real local the classification can see is still
live, and it borrows. `--interp` prints `alpha` three times.

`register_replayed_inline_envelope_payload` is the fix — the METADATA half of
`track_inline_{option,result}_payload_var` without its queued action. It states
the true thing about a snapshotted binding: it is NEVER dead at end of cell,
because the global outlives the frame. So the arm borrows, nothing is freed,
and the next cell's load is valid. Queueing the action itself would be wrong
for precisely the reason capture retracts it — a second owner is what this tier
exists to avoid.

fix:
FIXED by d825ba93, the fourth and final landing: `SnapshotPrimKind::SlotTransfer`, the
GENERAL kind that closes the rest of the tier at once instead of a bespoke kind
per shape.

THE DEFERRAL ASKED THE WRONG QUESTION, and that is the whole content of this
close. Every previous update chipped at the framing this row inherited -- "each
of those types would need its own cross-cell ownership story (the global holds a
heap pointer; who runs the destructor? when?)" -- by showing one more type did
not, in fact, need one. The by-value half showed it for types with no heap; the
container half showed it for `Vec[String]` / `Map[String, V]`; the
inline-envelope half showed it for `Option[String]`. Each correction was local.
The general statement is that the question is not what a type's cleanup DOES,
it is whether that cleanup is REACHABLE FROM THE BINDING'S SLOT -- and it always
is, because every action that frees a local's value is registered by a `track_*`
call taking that local's slot. So the entire handshake for the remainder is one
`retract_all_cleanup_for_slot(slot)` at capture.

`Codegen::cleanup_action_slot` states that invariant as an exhaustive match over
all 34 `CleanupAction` variants -- 30 name a slot, and the four that do not
(`UserDefer`, `UserErrDefer`, `ProviderPop`, `ReleaseMutex`) own no value a
binding could hand to a global. It is shared with `record_drop_obs`, which had
been carrying its own copy of the same match for diagnostics, so the two cannot
drift; and because the snapshot use is a CORRECTNESS one, a future
`CleanupAction` variant is now a compile error until its slot is declared.

MEASURED, `karac repl` vs `karac repl --interp`, mutation in the cell AFTER the
declaring one. Every row is a shape this row's own remaining-work list named:

    shape                                  before   after   --interp
    Vec[Vec[i64]]        v.push(...)       0        1       1
    Vec[Vec[String]]                       0        1       1
    Map[i64, Vec[i64]]   m.insert(...)     0        1       1
    Vec[<user struct>]   v.push(...)       0        1       1
    SortedSet[i64]       s.insert(3)       0        1       1
    SortedMap[i64,i64]   m.insert(3,4)     0        1       1
    SortedMap[String,i64]                  0        1       1
    Ordering             o = Greater       false    true    true
    Option[<struct w/ heap>]               false    true    true
    Option[Option[String]]                 false    true    true
    (i64, String)        t = (2, f"b")     1        2       2
    closure              f(1) in cell 2    ok       ok      ok

THE FRONTIER WAS THE BUG, not the general rule. `Vec[Vec[i64]]` stayed on
pass-through even after `SlotTransfer` existed to take it, and the cause had
nothing to do with ownership: `snapshot_kind_for_type` was one `match`, so the
bespoke `Vec` arm MATCHED on the head name and returned `None` from its inner
element classification -- consuming the outer arm and never reaching the later
tiers. The classifier is now a sequence of four questions, each of which may
answer `None` and fall through. Asking a tier a question it is allowed to
decline is what makes tiers compose; a `match` arm cannot decline.

THE `Ordering` CLASS IS CLOSED TOO, by the mechanism the previous update said it
would need. That update recorded a stdlib VALUE enum as genuinely by-value yet
kept out, because the session-declared rule could not tell one from a stdlib
OPAQUE HANDLE, and noted that inverting to codegen's `builtin_opaque_ptr_handle`
blacklist "would make correctness depend on that list being exhaustive, which
the whitelist does not". `SLOT_TRANSFER_STDLIB_TYPES` is the whitelist answer:
the containers, the two built-in envelopes, and `Ordering`. An unlisted stdlib
name fails CLOSED, back to pass-through -- so `DataFrame` and `Interner` (opaque
handles) and anything holding an OS resource whose release is observable stay
out by construction rather than by remembering.

EXCLUSIONS, each with its own reason rather than a blanket deferral, and each
pinned by a test:
  - a user `impl Drop` ANYWHERE inside the type, including behind a field of a
    container element. Retraction means the destructor never runs, where
    `--interp` keeps a real `Value` and drops it. This is a permanent,
    structural exclusion, not a deferral.
  - a stdlib name off the whitelist (above).
  - a BORROW -- `ref` / `mut ref` / `Slice` / `Pointer` / `Weak`. The referent
    is owned by a different slot, so there is nothing here to retract and the
    global would hold a pointer whose owner dies at end of cell. This is the one
    shape where the transfer argument fails outright rather than being merely
    unproven.
  - a GENERIC type: no single lowered layout to size a global with.
  - a binding whose OWN type is `shared` -- see the split-out row below.

MEMORY-CHECKED, and the check itself needed fixing first. `valgrind
--trace-children=yes karac repl` traces ONE process: the JIT lane runs in the
`karac_jit_runner` subprocess and memcheck was not following it, so a "clean"

Under that: across a 30-statement session exercising nine of the newly-admitted
shape families, including three repeated reads through each transferred value,
ZERO invalid reads / writes / frees, zero double frees, zero uninitialised
reads.

THE ACCEPTED LEAK, measured for the first time. Every update since B.5.2 has
recorded the "leak into the JITDylib until teardown" policy as unmeasured in
absolute terms. That session leaks 1131 bytes total (6 records / 482 B
definitely lost, 5 records / 649 B possibly lost). Small, but it is now a number
rather than an assurance, and it scales with the number of DISTINCT snapshotted

ALSO ADMITTED AND MEASURED, beyond the list above: `Array[String, N]` (repeated
element reads across cells agree with `--interp`).

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLOSE, split into its own rows rather than buried here:
B-2026-09-01-36 (a binding whose own type is `shared` reads garbage if
admitted -- a replay-registration gap, not a transfer one) and B-2026-09-01-37
(a struct literal as a call argument, alone in a REPL cell, fails to resolve on

FIXED by 10018b3. The escape disarm was reaching the return sites and being VETOED there.


`bc1c37c` (B-2026-08-29-56) hooked `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move`
at the two return positions, which was the right place, but it reused the
CONSUMING-position helper and so inherited that helper's veto: a source that a
read-only `match` arm left owning its payload sits in
`drop_rc.inline_optres_retained_sources` and is skipped outright.

The veto is correct where it was written. A consuming-position disarm rests on
"a callee already took the buffer", which a BORROWING arm never did, so zeroing
the sole owner's slot there would leak -- that is B-2026-08-08-25 leg 1, and it
was measured: the earlier attempt at the zeroing form turned a clean program
into a leak. A RETURN has the opposite premise and needs no such argument:
handing the header out IS the transfer, so exactly one owner remains either way.

FIX. Split the helper into a shared impl plus two entry points --
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` (consuming, unchanged) and
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_escape` (returning) -- and let the
escaping one override the retention veto. The override is narrowed to the
BARE-IDENTIFIER shape: `<src>.map(f).unwrap_or(d)` in return position is still a
consuming expression whose read-only source may legitimately have kept its
buffer, so it keeps the veto and reaches the caller through the chain's own
value rather than through this slot. The two call sites in `call_dispatch.rs`
(body tail) and `exprs.rs` (explicit `return`) now use the escaping entry point.

MECHANISM CONFIRMED, NOT ASSUMED. The row hypothesised that the consuming arm
disarms by zeroing the cap word at runtime and that a later ASSIGNMENT silently
re-arms it. That is not what happens. Instrumenting the veto branch and building
each shape showed an exact correlation over six variants: every body whose
source hit the veto aborted, every body that reached the disarm was clean, and
nothing else moved. There is no re-arming step.

TWO OF THE ROW'S THREE "REQUIRED INGREDIENTS" ARE REFUTED, and both are now
fixture rows for that reason.

  * A REASSIGNMENT of the local is NOT required. `readonly-arm-returned` has
    none -- `let mut buf = Some(f"a"); match buf { Some(prev) => println(prev) };
    buf` -- and aborted pre-fix exactly like the row's own repro. The row
    reported this shape clean.
  * The arm need not be read-only in the source-level sense.
    `arm-escapes-payload` MOVES the payload out and puts a new one back
    (`Some(prev) => { let mut j = prev; j.push_str("!"); buf = Some(j); }`) and
    aborted too: the `Some(prev)` binding is enough to put the local on the
    retained list.

What is actually required is only that a `Some(prev)`-shaped arm classify the
local as a retained source, and that the local then ESCAPE. `Some(_)` binds
nothing, so it never joins the list and was already correct; consuming the local
in place instead of returning it is clean for the same reason bc1c37c's own rows
were -- nothing escapes.

WHY THE SELF-HOST PARSER HIT IT, and the oracle it was failing:
`Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments` (selfhost/src/parser.kara:322) accumulates
into an `Option[String]` across a loop and returns it, which is the

`cargo test --features llvm --test selfhost_parser_items` was RED on `main` and
is green with this commit.

FIXTURES. `tests/codegen.rs` gains 13 rows, ten of them RED pre-fix (each
aborted, so `run_program` returned `None` against its expected string). Three
`*-control` rows were green on both sides and guard the two directions this fix

needed) and `map-chain-return-control` (the chain whose source kept its buffer).
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` gains the LSan half, which is the only gate that

`tests/interpreter.rs` gains a parity mirror; the interpreter was correct on

title: A CONSUMED-THEN-REASSIGNED-THEN-RETURNED `Option` LOCAL IS FREED TWICE -- a `match` arm that binds the payload out disarms the binding's scope-exit free by zeroing its cap, a later assignment silently re-arms it, and the return then hands the same buffer to the caller. All three are required; removing any one is clean, and the arm that actually executes is irrelevant. THIS, not B-2026-08-29-56, is what `selfhost_parser_matches_rust_parser_items` has been dying on -- bisected to `///` doc comments, i.e. `Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments`
detail:
MAIN IS RED ON A REQUIRED ORACLE, AND THIS ROW — NOT B-2026-08-29-56 — IS WHY.
`cargo test --features llvm --test selfhost_parser_items` fails at HEAD. That
row was reported as the oracle's cause; it is a real defect and is now fixed
(bc1c37c), but it is NOT what the oracle dies on. Measured on both sides of
that commit: the oracle's first valgrind error is byte-identical before and
after, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` yields the same 83 lines of output either way.
The fix changes only the failure MODE (SIGABRT on heap-corruption detection ->
SIGSEGV), which is exactly the kind of change that reads as progress on a
re-run and is not.

MINIMAL REPRO (9 lines, no loop, no `mut ref self`, no generics):

    fn collect() -> Option[String] {
        let mut buf: Option[String] = Some(f"a");
        match buf {
            Some(prev) => { println(f"saw {prev}"); buf = Some(f"z"); }
            None => { buf = None; }
        }
        buf
    }
    fn main() {
        match collect() { Some(x) => println(f"[{x}]"), None => println("none"), }
    }

      karac run --interp  -> `saw a` / `[z]`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
      karac build         -> same

THREE INGREDIENTS, ALL REQUIRED. Each was removed independently and the program
is clean without it, so this is a conjunction and not a family of three bugs:

  1. a CONSUMING arm — a `match`/`if let` on the local that binds its payload
     out (`Some(prev)`). With `Some(_)` instead, clean.
  2. a REASSIGNMENT of that same local afterwards. Without it, clean. It does
     NOT have to be inside the arm — moving `buf = Some(f"z")` to after the
     whole `match` aborts identically — and the assigned value may be a fresh
     temporary, so it is not a move-suppression gap on the RHS.
  3. the local is RETURNED. Consume it locally instead of returning it and the
     program is clean, which is what makes this compiled-only and invisible to
     any test that does not hand the value out.

The arm that DOES execute is irrelevant: a variant where only the `None` arm is
ever taken at runtime still aborts. So the disarm being undone is applied
statically, on a path the program does not run.

MECHANISM, hypothesised and not yet confirmed — the next reader should verify
rather than assume. The consuming arm disarms the binding's
`FreeInlineOptionPayload` by ZEROING the cap word at runtime
(`suppress_inline_option_payload_cleanup`), so the scope-exit free skips and the
arm binding owns the buffer. A subsequent assignment writes a fresh header into
that same slot, silently RE-ARMING the cleanup; the return then hands the same
payload to the caller. Two owners, one buffer. If that is right, the fix belongs
wherever an assignment to a previously-disarmed Option local re-establishes
ownership, not at the return sites bc1c37c hooked.

WHY THE SELF-HOST PARSER HITS IT. Bisected the oracle's 108 inputs to the first
failing one, then reduced: a `///` DOC COMMENT on any item triggers it, and a
plain `//` comment does not. `"/// d\nstruct Q {}"` alone aborts;
`"pub struct Q { x: i64 }"` alone is clean. That routes through
`Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments` (selfhost/src/parser.kara:322), which is
this shape almost verbatim:

    fn collect_leading_doc_comments(mut ref self) -> Option[String] {
        let mut buf: Option[String] = None;
        loop {
            ...
            match buf {
                Some(prev) => { let mut joined = prev; ...; buf = Some(joined); }
                None => { buf = Some(line); }
            }
        }
        buf
    }

A direct 33-line Kara transcription of that method reproduces on its own. The
free-function twin reproduces too, so `mut ref self` is not an ingredient.

VERIFIED PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by bc1c37c: with that commit stashed, all
of `doc`, `docfree`, `docnoloop`, `doconce` abort identically. What bc1c37c does
repair is the sibling spelling `docoverwrite` (loop + plain reassignment, no
consuming arm), which the selfhost parser happens not to use.

NOT AN INTERPRETER BUG: `--interp` is correct on every shape above.

CORRECTION (at close). The title above overstates the trigger and misnames the
mechanism; both were measured wrong, and the row is left as filed rather than
rewritten so the correction is legible.

  * "CONSUMED-THEN-REASSIGNED-THEN-RETURNED" -- the REASSIGNMENT is not an
    ingredient. `let b: Option[String] = Some(f"a"); match b { Some(p) =>
    println(p) }; b` has none and aborts identically. The row's own
    "removing any one is clean" test must have varied something else.
  * "disarms the binding's scope-exit free by zeroing its cap, a later
    assignment silently re-arms it" -- there is no re-arming step. The disarm
    at the return site is VETOED and never runs at all, because bc1c37c reused
    the consuming-position helper whose `inline_optres_retained_sources` check
    skips exactly the sources a read-only arm left owning their payload.
  * The arm need not be read-only in the source-level sense either: an arm that
    MOVES the payload out and puts a new one back aborts too, because the
    `Some(prev)` binding alone is what puts the local on the retained list.

What IS required is a `Some(prev)`-shaped arm plus an ESCAPE. Both refuted
claims are now fixture rows (`readonly-arm-returned`, `arm-escapes-payload`)
precisely because the row asserted them clean.

The row's remaining claims all held: `///` doc comments as the selfhost
trigger, `Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments` as the site, the arm that
executes being irrelevant, `--interp` being correct throughout, and the defect
being pre-existing rather than introduced by bc1c37c.

title: The INTERPRETER renders an unsigned `Vector` lane above `i64::MAX` as a SIGNED reinterpretation -- `Vector[u64, 2]` holding `u64::MAX` prints `Vector(-1, 1)` while the SAME program's scalar and INDEXED-lane reads of the same value both print 18446744073709551615, and both compiled backends now print the unsigned value too; `Value::Vector` holds untyped `Value::Int` lanes, so its Display cannot recover a signedness the index path gets right
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-29-52 (the compiled backends printed an address /
a stray lane / nothing for a whole `Vector[T, N]`). Establishing the interpreter
as the reference for that fix meant checking its rendering at every lane type,
and this is the one where the reference is itself wrong.

MEASURED, one program, `karac run --interp`:

    let s: u64 = 18446744073709551615u64;
    let u: Vector[u64, 2] = Vector[u64, 2](18446744073709551615u64, 1u64);
    println(f"scalar {s}");    18446744073709551615     <- right
    println(f"lane0 {u[0]}");  18446744073709551615     <- right
    println(f"whole {u}");     Vector(-1, 1)            <- WRONG
    let b: Vector[u8, 4] = Vector[u8, 4](200u8, 1u8, 2u8, 3u8);
    println(f"u8whole {b}");   Vector(200, 1, 2, 3)     <- right

So it is not "the interpreter renders vectors wrong". Three of the four lines
are right, including the INDEXED read of the very lane that renders wrong one
line later. The failure needs an unsigned lane whose value exceeds `i64::MAX`,
which in practice means `u64` (and presumably `u128`, not probed): `u8`/`u16`/
`u32` values all fit in the positive `i64` range and render correctly by
accident.

ROOT CAUSE. `Value::Vector(Vec<Value>)` (src/interpreter/value.rs) holds plain
`Value::Int(i128)` lanes with no element type attached, and its `Display` arm
writes each lane with `write!("{}", v)`. The scalar and indexed paths get the
right answer because the f-string interpolation layer reinterprets by the
expression's STATIC type; the whole-vector Display has no per-lane type to
consult, so it prints the carrier as signed. The lane is stored already wrapped
into the signed domain -- `18446744073709551615u64` arrives as `-1` -- which is
why the carrier being an i128 wide enough to hold the value does not save it.

DIRECTION OF THE DIVERGENCE IS NOW INVERTED, and that is deliberate. Before
60465148 the compiled backends printed garbage for every vector, so this case
was invisible. They now render lanes correctly, including this one, so the
remaining disagreement is `--interp` against BOTH compiled backends, with the
compiled side right. That was a considered choice in 60465148: matching the
interpreter here would have written a known-wrong sign convention into the new
formatter and made it harder to remove. `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`e2e_vector_display_renders_wide_unsigned_lanes_as_unsigned` pins the compiled
value, and the sibling twin test excludes this shape, so fixing this row makes
the twin absorb the case with no test churn.

WHY MEDIUM rather than high. The value is wrong and silent, which argues high;
against that, it needs `u64`/`u128` lanes carrying values above `i64::MAX`, the
compiled backends -- what ships -- are correct, and the scalar and indexed reads
a program is far more likely to use are correct on every backend. It is a real
wrong answer in a narrow corner, not a trap across the surface.

FIX SHAPE, so the next session does not re-derive it. Two options, and the
choice is a design call rather than a bug hunt:

  (a) Attach the element type to `Value::Vector` -- e.g. `Vector { lanes,
      elem: NumKind }` -- and have Display consult it per lane. Correct for
      every current and future lane type, and gives the Display arm the same
      information the index path effectively has. Costs a variant change and
      every construction site (eval_call.rs's `Vector[T, N](..)` arm,
      eval_ops.rs's element-wise arms, method_call.rs's splat / from_array).
  (b) Stop wrapping unsigned lanes into the signed domain at construction, so a
      `u64` lane holds `18446744073709551615i128` and prints correctly with no
      Display change. Narrower to write, but it changes the carrier invariant
      the element-wise arithmetic arms rely on -- lane arithmetic WRAPS per
      design.md § Portable SIMD and B-2026-08-26-8, and that wrap is currently
      expressed in the signed domain, so this option needs that rule re-checked
      at every unsigned width rather than assumed.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: `u128` lanes (the same argument
applies but was not run); whether `:type`, `%show`, `karac test` failure
rendering or the Jupyter kernel's value display reach the same Display arm and
inherit the same wrong text; and whether an unsigned lane that reaches
`Vector`'s Display through a container (`Vec[Vector[u64, 2]]`) renders the same
way.

REPRODUCTION:

    printf 'fn main() {\n  let u: Vector[u64, 2] = Vector[u64, 2](18446744073709551615u64, 1u64);\n  println(f"lane0 {u[0]}");\n  println(f"whole {u}");\n}\n' > /tmp/v.kara
    karac run --interp /tmp/v.kara      # lane0 18446744073709551615 / whole Vector(-1, 1)
    karac build /tmp/v.kara -o /tmp/v && /tmp/v   # both unsigned

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-29-52; that row's fix had to decide
whether to reproduce this or diverge from it, and chose to diverge.
fix:
FIXED by 69708f4, which gives the interpreter's TYPE-DIRECTED renderer a `Value::Vector` arm
(`render_typed_mode`, src/interpreter/builtin.rs). Three lines of logic: peel
the element type with the existing `display_element_type`, recurse per lane,
join as `Vector(a, b)`.

THE ROW'S ROOT CAUSE WAS CLOSE BUT NOT RIGHT, and the correction is what made
the fix small. It said `Value::Vector` "holds untyped `Value::Int` lanes, so its
Display cannot recover a signedness the index path gets right", and proposed two
fixes on that basis: (a) attach a `NumKind` to the variant, touching ~30
construction sites, or (b) stop wrapping unsigned lanes into the signed domain,
which changes a carrier invariant the lane-arithmetic arms depend on.

Both were unnecessary. `Display` in value.rs is indeed type-blind, but it is NOT
the path a printed value takes: `println` / f-string / `dbg` all go through
`Interpreter::render_typed_mode`, which threads the STATIC type down and already
has the exact `Value::Int` arm that reads a carrier back through
`type_unsigned_int_width`. That is how a `Vec[u64]` holding `u64::MAX` prints
correctly today -- MEASURED, and it is the observation that unlocks this: the
carrier there is `-1` too, and the container arm recursing with the element type
is the only reason it renders right.

So the missing piece was not information, it was an ARM. `render_typed_mode` had
arms for `Array`, `Slice`, `Map`, `Tuple`, `Struct`, `EnumVariant` and
`SharedStruct` but none for `Vector`, so a vector fell past all of them to the
untyped catch-all. Both helpers it needs were already vector-aware --
`type_unsigned_int_width` and `display_element_type` each list
`Type::Vector { element, .. }` alongside `Array` and `Slice` -- so the fix
consumes machinery that was already in place and waiting.

The lesson generalizes past this row: the carrier convention (an unsigned value
at or above 2^63 is STORED as its negative reinterpretation, deliberately, per
`truncate_to_width`'s comment) means EVERY renderer of an integer must be
type-directed. Any future `Value` variant that holds numbers and gets its own
rendering needs an arm here, or it inherits exactly this bug.

MEASURED after, `karac run --interp`, all previously wrong and now matching both
compiled backends byte for byte:

    whole Vector(18446744073709551615, 1)   was Vector(-1, 1)
    u128  Vector(3402823669...11455, 1)     was Vector(-1, 1)
    bound Vector(9223372036854775808, 1)    was Vector(-9223372036854775808, 1)
    invec [Vector(18446744073709551615, 1)] was [Vector(-1, 1)]
    intup (Vector(18446744073709551615, 1), 7)
    inopt Some(Vector(18446744073709551615, 1))
    bare println(u) -> Vector(18446744073709551615, 1)

and unchanged, as controls: `signed Vector(-1, 1)` (an i64 -1 must stay -1) and
`narrow Vector(200, 1, 2, 3)`.

THE ROW'S OWN "NOT MEASURED" LIST, now measured. `u128` lanes: wrong in exactly
the same way, now fixed. Container-nested (`Vec` / tuple / `Option` of a
vector): all three were wrong, all three now correct, and they came right for
free because the container arms recurse INTO the new arm -- which is the
evidence the fix sits at the recursion point rather than at depth 0. `dbg()`:
same path, same fix. Exactly 2^63 (the first value that misses the carrier) was
not on the row's list and is now a pinned case, because a fix special-casing the
all-ones pattern would pass a `u64::MAX`-only test.

FIXTURES. `tests/interpreter.rs::vector_display_renders_wide_unsigned_lanes_as_unsigned`
asserts `u[0]` and `u` IN ONE PROGRAM -- the self-contradiction is the bug, and
either line alone looks correct. RED-verified: 9 of 11 rows flip when the arm is
reverted, and the two controls hold identical across the flip, so no half of it
is vacuous.

The codegen side needed no fix and no new test -- it ABSORBED the case, which is
what the row's author designed for. `e2e_vector_display_renders_wide_unsigned_lanes_as_unsigned`
existed only to pin the compiled value while the interpreter disagreed, with a
comment saying the twin could take it over once this row closed. The four
unsigned rows (u64::MAX f-string, u64::MAX bare `println`, 2^63, u128::MAX) now
live in `e2e_vector_display_agrees_with_the_interpreter` and the pinned test is
deleted: the twin strictly subsumes it, asserting interpreter AND compiled
against one text instead of the compiled side alone. Also RED-verified.

FOUND WHILE FIXING, filed as B-2026-08-30-39: the compiled backends cannot
render a nested vector AT ALL, and fail by PANIC rather than diagnostic --
`emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Vector_u64_2' not yet supported`, no span.
`dbg(v)` at any depth and any container layer over a vector in an f-string abort
`karac build`; depth-0 `println(v)` / `f"{v}"` are fine. That is why the nested
rows above are pinned in the interpreter fixture with NO codegen twin -- a twin
would not compile. When -37 closes, they can gain one.

FIXED by ff99609. The rule was "does any arm bind anything?". It is now "does
any arm MOVE what it bound?".

Binding a payload out is not by itself a move of the scrutinee. What moves it is
the arm going on to hand that binding somewhere -- a consuming call, a container
push, the match's own value, a return. An arm that only READS what it bound
leaves the scrutinee whole, which is the semantics the interpreter implements
and the borrow classification codegen has used since B-2026-08-08-25.

FIX. `use_classifier.rs`'s `ExprKind::Match` arm now walks the ARMS FIRST and
asks, per arm, whether any name the pattern bound was recorded as a `Consume`
inside that arm's body; the scrutinee is classified `Consuming` only if one was.
The answer is derived from the classifier's OWN notion of a consume -- a small
`arm_consumed_names` stack fed from `record_named`, the single point every
identifier leaf passes through -- rather than from a second, parallel escape
analysis, so the two cannot drift as new consuming positions are added. Walking
the arms first is safe because `classification.kinds` is span-keyed, so insertion
order does not affect the result, and an arm body cannot introduce a type the
scrutinee expression depends on.

MEASURED, before and after, on six read-only shapes and three moving ones:

  shape                                    warn before   warn after   program
  Option[String]                                1            0        correct
  Result[String, i64]                           1            0        correct
  Option[Vec[i64]]                              1            0        correct
  user enum E { A(String) }                     1            0        correct
  Option[(String, i64)]                         1            0        correct
  Option[i64] (scalar control)                  0            0        correct
  arm calls eat(p)                              1            1        correct
  arm does out.push(p)                          1            1        correct
  arm yields p as the match value               1            1        correct

"correct" = interpreter, JIT, default AOT and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT all agree
byte-for-byte, valgrind-clean under `--leak-check=full`. So every suppressed
warning was on a program with nothing wrong with it, and every retained one is
on a genuine move.

`if let` / `while let` are NOT touched and stay unconditionally reading. That
asymmetry -- `if let Some(p) = b { .. }` never warned where the identical `match`
did -- is what ruled out a deliberate strict-move rule when this was filed, but
closing it would ADD diagnostics to existing code, which is a different change
from removing ones that were never true. It is a false NEGATIVE in an advisory
diagnostic, and it is left as one deliberately, noted at the code site.

THE LEGACY WALKER (`ownership/expr_check.rs`) CARRIES THE SAME "any arm binds"
RULE and is deliberately left alone: the warning is emitted from the CFG /
`rc_predicate` path that `use_classifier` feeds, and after this change the
reported count is zero for every read-only shape above, so nothing reaches the
user through the other path. Changing the legacy walker's `ValueState` tracking
would move dataflow that no measurement here calls for.

ONE FINDING NOT FIXED HERE, filed as its own row: `Option[S]` where `S` is a
STRUCT with a `String` field is a genuine use-after-free -- a read-only arm, then
a second read, prints garbage under the JIT and both AOT legs while `--interp` is
correct, and valgrind reports an invalid read of a freed block. It is a residual
of B-2026-08-08-25, whose borrow classification admits only a DIRECT
`{ptr,len,cap}` payload (`String` / `Vec`), and it is the one shape whose warning
this commit removes while the program stays broken. That trade is deliberate: the
warning was not protecting anyone (it is advisory, the build proceeds, and
"value 'b' moved here, used again here" does not describe a use-after-free), and
the checker's job is to state the language's semantics, not to mirror codegen's
current capability table.
title: A READ-ONLY `match` ARM IS REPORTED AS A MOVE OF ITS SCRUTINEE, so an `Option[String]` read once and then returned draws `value 'b' moved here, used again here` on a program every backend compiles and runs correctly. B-2026-08-08-25 deliberately classifies such an arm as a BORROW in codegen; `ownership.rs` still records it as a move. The `if let` spelling of the same thing does NOT warn, which is what rules out a deliberate strict-move rule. Diagnostics-only, and the help text it prints is unactionable
detail:
THE OWNERSHIP CHECKER AND BOTH BACKENDS DISAGREE ABOUT WHETHER A READ-ONLY
`match` ARM CONSUMES ITS SCRUTINEE. Same disagreement shape as B-2026-08-18-32
(`String +`), and like that one the backends are the side that matches the
language's intent.

    fn c() -> Option[String] {
        let b: Option[String] = Some(f"a");
        match b { Some(p) => { println(p); } None => {} }
        b
    }

      warning[ownership]: value 'b' moved here, used again here (moved at ..)
        help: declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads, or
              restructure to avoid reuse ('b' has no `.clone()` -- that exists
              only on `String`, the built-in heap collections and RC types)

The program is CORRECT and runs correctly on all four surfaces. B-2026-08-08-25
deliberately classifies an arm that only READS its bound payload as a BORROW of
the scrutinee -- `scrutinee_is_readonly_inline_optres_local` in
`src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs` -- precisely so the source stays live and
usable afterwards. `ownership.rs` never got that memo and still records the
`Some(p)` binding as a move of `b`.

SHAPES MEASURED (`karac check`, warning count):

  match + read-only arm, Option[String]      1   <- false positive
  match + read-only arm, Result[String, i64] 1   <- false positive
  match + read-only arm, Option[Vec[i64]]    1   <- false positive
  `if let Some(p) = b { .. }` then `match b` 0   <- inconsistent with the above
  `Some(_)` (binds nothing)                  0   correct
  a reassignment between the two uses        0   correct (reassign reinitializes)

The `if let` row is the sharpest evidence that this is not a deliberate strict
move rule: the two spellings have identical semantics and only the `match` one
warns.

IMPACT is diagnostics-only -- it is a warning, `All checks passed.` still
prints, and every backend compiles and runs the program correctly. But it fires
on ordinary idiomatic code (an `Option[String]` read once and then returned),
and existing fixtures in the tree already trip it, so it is noise on exactly the
shape B-2026-08-08-25 went out of its way to make legal.

THE HELP TEXT IS ALSO WRONG HERE, independently of the false positive. There is
no callee, so "declare the callee parameter `ref`" is unactionable, and the
parenthetical asserts `b` has no `.clone()` when `Option[String]` is not one of
the listed types for a reason the reader cannot act on either. No
machine-applicable fix is offered (E0500 carries no `fixes`), so `karac fix`
leaves it alone -- correctly, since any edit it made would be wrong.

FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-30-8, whose repro emits this warning on every
shape; it is NOT the cause of that double free and is filed separately because
it is a different surface with a different failure mode.

fix:
FIXED by 1c0b4d5f. The row's own prescription — borrow the SIBLING
binding arm's frame — implemented as written, including its warning about
which frame not to use.

WHAT CHANGED. Arm-owner registration is DEFERRED until every arm of a branch
has been compiled, and an arm that MINTS its value but reported no pending
record takes the frame from a sibling arm that did. `mixed_branch_arm_owner`
(src/codegen/runtime.rs) is the whole rule; `register_pending_arm_owner_at` /
`own_escaping_tail_value_at` add an explicit block for the ownership store, so
deferring the DECISION does not move the IR: each store still lands in its own
arm's end block, which is what keeps ownership per-path. Three call sites: the
plain `if`, the `if let`, and `compile_match`'s arm loop.

The order obstacle the row identified is exactly why the deferral is needed —
"registration is per-arm and emitted in that arm's own basic block, while the
sibling's frame is not known until every arm has been compiled". Of the two
routes it offered, this is the first (defer the stores, using the arm-end
blocks the compilers already capture) rather than the pre-created shared slot,
because it leaves B-2026-08-30-2's per-arm slot semantics untouched: an arm
that does not run still leaves `cap == 0` and its cleanup still skips.

MEASURED (valgrind, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `2` identical; per-arm payload
sizes chosen so the leaked block identifies which arm produced it):

    shape                                              before   after
    `if c { mkA(n) } else { t }.contains("aaa")`        15 B     clean
    `match n { 1 => mkA(n), _ => t }.contains("aaa")`   15 B     clean
    `f"[{if c { mkA(n) } else { t }}]"`                 15 B     clean
    CONTROL every arm mints                             clean    clean
    CONTROL both arms hand out bindings                 clean    clean
    CONTROL owning destination (`let s = if …`)         clean    clean

No invalid read, write or free in any row at either level, and the sibling
binding still prints correctly after the branch — the borrowed frame's exit is
after any later read of it, which is the property that makes borrowing it
sound rather than merely convenient.

THE FRAME THE ROW WARNED ABOUT is not used, and the fixture that catches it is
in the test. An owner in the INNERMOST live frame lands in the wrapper's frame
when the branch is itself wrapped, and that drains before the value escapes —
the draft that did this double-freed on `selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run`,
with the unwrapped spelling clean, which is why a single-level fixture misses
it. `asan_mixed_branch_minting_arm_frees_once`'s `w1` row is that nesting: the
branch sits inside a block inside a function whose caller consumes the result.

WHAT IS NOT CLOSED, split out as B-2026-09-01-23 rather than left implicit.
The `while` row of the table above is IMPROVED BUT STILL LEAKING: three
iterations went from 57 B in 3 blocks to 42 B in 2, five from an unmeasured
baseline to 72 B in 4. The owner slot now exists, but it is ONE PER CONSTRUCT
and `reset_vec_slot_at_block_end` makes it mean "this pass's escaping value",
while the frame holding its cleanup drains once — after the loop. Each pass
therefore overwrites the previous pass's header and only the survivor is
freed, so the count is `iterations - 1`. That is a frame-GRANULARITY defect,
not the owner-ABSENCE one this row is about, and it has its own control: the
same branch with the sibling binding declared INSIDE the loop body is clean,
because the borrowed frame is then the body's and drains every pass.

TESTS. `asan_mixed_branch_minting_arm_frees_once` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs)
asserts a clean LSan run over all six rows above; it fails on the pre-fix
compiler with `SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 30 byte(s) leaked in 2
allocation(s)`. `asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free` is GONE:
its `m1` / `m2` rows were this row's population and are now clean, and its
`m3` row went with B-2026-08-30-12 — the test existed only to pin those three
at their leaking values, so nothing was left for it to assert.
`asan_loop_arm_owner_slot_keeps_only_the_last_pass` replaces it, pinning the
remainder under B-2026-09-01-21 with the same leak-tolerant runner and the
same purpose: a future fix that turns the leak into a memory error fails
loudly rather than trading one class for a worse one.

A NOTE ON THE FIRST TEST DRAFT, because it is the failure mode CLAUDE.md warns
about and it happened here: the fixture used `!c` for negation, which Kāra
spells `not`. The harness reported a parse error and SKIPPED, so the test
passed both before and after the fix. It was caught by running the RED check
rather than by reading the green result — the same reason the check is worth
its cost.
title: THE MINTING ARM OF A MIXED BRANCH HAS NO OWNER EITHER -- `if c { mkA(n) } else { t }.contains("aaa")` strands the 27 B `mkA` temp on the `c` path while the `t` path is clean, because B-2026-08-29-27's gates need EVERY tail to mint and B-2026-08-30-2's owner needs a source binding to inherit a FRAME from; the innermost frame is wrong (a wrapping block's drains before the value escapes -- caught by the self-host seed-run oracle, not by any sweep), so the lead is the SIBLING binding arm's frame
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the deliberate remainder of B-2026-08-30-2, split out rather than
buried in it. That row gave an owner to a value-position block or branch whose
tail hands out a BINDING; this is the sibling arm of the same construct.

MEASURED (valgrind, KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and 2, identical; per-arm payload sizes
chosen so the leaked buffer identifies which arm produced it):

    let t = mkB(n);                             // 27 B
    let k = if c { mkA(n) } else { t }.contains("aaa");
                                                27 B  LEAKS  <- mkA's temp
    let k = match n { 1 => mkA(n), _ => t }.contains("aaa");
                                                27 B  LEAKS
    let s = f"[{if c { mkA(n) } else { t }}]";  27 B  LEAKS
    while i < 3 { .. if i > 0 { mkA(n) } else { t } .. }
                                                54 B / 2 blk  (the two mint iterations)

    CONTROL -- the BINDING arm of the same constructs: clean since B-2026-08-30-2.
    CONTROL -- EVERY arm mints:                 clean since B-2026-08-29-27.

WHY IT IS NEITHER OF THOSE. B-2026-08-29-27's consuming gates require EVERY tail
to mint, so one binding arm declines the whole construct and no gate frees the
merged value. B-2026-08-30-2's owner replaces the cleanup a disarmed SOURCE
BINDING gave up, and a minting arm has no source binding, so there is nothing
for it to replace and no frame to inherit.

WHY A DRAFT THAT "FIXED" IT WAS WRONG, which is the useful part of this row. An
owner via `materialize_owned_temp` lands in the INNERMOST live frame. At an arm's
registration point that is whatever encloses the branch -- and when the branch is
itself wrapped, that is the WRAPPER's frame, which drains before the value
escapes. Measured: `fn f(n: Node) -> String { { match n.tok { Num(v) =>
"num".to_string(), Named(v, s) => s, Blank => "b".to_string() } } }` freed the
arm's temp at the end of `f`'s inner block and the caller freed it again --
`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, with valgrind reporting invalid reads
before it. The same `match` WITHOUT the wrapping braces was clean, which is the
whole difference and the reason a single-level fixture misses this. Every
fixture in B-2026-08-30-2's own sweep went green on that draft; the SELF-HOST
SEED-RUN ORACLE (`selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run`, corpus[199]) is what caught
it, on a nested `match` over a `shared enum`.

WHERE TO START: the frame. The sibling BINDING arm of the same construct reports
one (`vecstr_source_disarmed` carries it), and by construction it outlives the
branch -- the binding was declared before it. Both arms yield one Kāra value with
one lifetime, so using the sibling's frame for the minting arm is the principled
choice; freeing later than necessary is a delay, never a use-after-free. The
obstacle is ORDER: registration is per-arm and emitted in that arm's own basic
block, while the sibling's frame is not known until every arm has been compiled.
Either defer both stores to after the arms (re-positioning the builder at each
arm's end block, which `compile_if` already captures as `then_end_bb` /
`else_end_bb`), or pre-create one slot per construct before the branch and have
each arm store into it -- the latter also subsumes the per-pass reset
B-2026-08-30-2 needs a separate store for.

SEVERITY: one leak per evaluation, unbounded in a loop; no double free and no
wrong answer, so it is leak-only. Pinned at its current leaking value by
`asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free` (rows `m1`, `m2`) under the
leak-tolerant ASAN runner, so a future fix that turns it into a memory error
fails loudly rather than trading one class for a worse one.

fix:
FIXED by cdb844d4. The row's own prescription, and it was right on every count including
the one that made it cheap: this belongs to the CONSUMING GATE, not to
B-2026-08-30-2's owner.

WHAT CHANGED, and it is one line of routing. `expr_is_fresh_owned_branch_tail`
— the predicate the seven B-2026-08-29-27 gates hold — now calls
`branch_tail_mints_fresh_owned_temp_local` instead of the narrow
`branch_tail_mints_fresh_owned_temp`. The widened inner predicate already
existed (B-2026-08-30-38 built it for `fresh_owned_branch_tail_repr`), and its
own doc comment named this row's work: "Widening them looks right — `{ let t =
mk(5); t }.contains("x")` still strands its buffer — but that is a leak at
seven sites with their own frees, measured separately." This is that
measurement.

The seven call sites are BYTE-IDENTICAL to before; only what the predicate
means changed. The narrow wrapper became dead once they all routed to the
widened one, so the two wrappers are now one. The narrow INNER predicate
stays — `control_flow.rs`, `control_flow_match.rs` and `stmts.rs:1010` have
three callers asking a different question, and folding those would be a
different row.

WHY THE WIDENING IS SOUND HERE and not at the gates' usual population. Those
gates free IMMEDIATELY at the use site, and their fail-closed rule exists
because a tail handing out a binding leaves that binding READABLE afterwards —
freeing it would dangle, which is worse than the leak. That reasoning is
entirely about a binding declared OUTSIDE the wrapper. One the wrapper
declares ITSELF has no later reader by construction: the block ends at the
tail. `block_local_binding_tail_rhs` is what separates the two, by requiring a
`let` in THIS block that binds the tail name (a destructuring or `let else`
binder declines, since neither gives a single producer expression), so an
outer-binding tail keeps declining exactly as before.

MEASURED (valgrind, one fixture per row, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `2`
identical):

    shape                                          before    after
    `{ let t = mkB(n); t }.contains("bbb")`         27 B     clean
    `println({ let u = mkB(n); u })`                27 B     clean
    `{ let t = mkB(n); t }.len()`                   27 B     clean
    `let s = { let t = mkB(n); t }` (OWNING)        clean    clean
    `{ loc }.contains("bbb")` + later `loc` read    clean    clean, still prints
    `v.sorted().len()` / `let s = v.sorted()`       clean    clean

No invalid read, write or free at either optimization level in any row.

THE DANGER THE ROW FLAGGED, checked rather than assumed. It warned that a
block whose tail names its own binding "is the shape every codegen desugar
synthesizes" — `Vec.sorted()` lowers to `{ let mut __srt = recv.clone();
__srt.sort(); __srt }` — and that each already arranges ownership at the
producer, so a second owner is a double free; an earlier draft took out 11
codegen and 12 memory-sanitizer tests, `let s: Vec[i64] = v.sorted()`
segfaulting among them. That draft registered a replacement OWNER in the
innermost live frame, which is a different mechanism. These desugars are built
inside codegen (`src/codegen/vec_method.rs`), not as user-visible AST blocks,
so they never reach an AST-level consuming gate at all — and the `sorted` rows
above are clean at both spellings and both optimization levels. The tripwire is
pinned in the new test rather than left as reasoning.

TESTS. `asan_block_local_tail_frees_once` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) asserts a
clean LSan run over all six shapes above. It fails on the pre-fix compiler with
`SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 54 byte(s) leaked in 2 allocation(s)`. The `m3`
rows in `asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free`, which pinned
this shape AT ITS LEAKING VALUE, are removed — the same treatment
B-2026-08-30-3's `b`/`d` rows got when they were fixed — and that test's doc
now points here. `asan_branch_tail_binding_handout_frees_once`'s `i*` rows are
untouched and still pass: they pin the OWNER's decline, which this does not
change.

NOT ADDRESSED, stated rather than implied: B-2026-08-30-11, the sibling
remainder (the MINTING arm of a MIXED branch), is untouched — it needs a frame,
not a predicate, and its row records why the innermost one is wrong. The three
remaining callers of the narrow inner predicate were not re-examined; whether
any of them wants the widened rule too is a separate question this row does not
answer.
title: A VALUE-POSITION BLOCK WHOSE TAIL NAMES A BINDING IT DECLARED ITSELF LEAKS IT IN A READ-ONLY CONSUMER -- `{ let t = mkB(n); t }.contains("bbb")` strands 27 B while the OWNING spelling is clean; B-2026-08-30-2's owner declines it because there is no live frame to replace and admitting it double-freed 23 tests (it is the shape every codegen desugar synthesizes), but unlike that row the source cannot be read again, so this one belongs to `expr_is_fresh_owned_branch_tail` and the seven gates B-2026-08-29-27 wired
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the second deliberate remainder of B-2026-08-30-2.

A value-position block whose tail names a binding declared INSIDE it leaks that
binding's buffer when the consumer is read-only:

    let k = { let t = mkB(n); t }.contains("bbb");     27 B  LEAKS
    println({ let u = mkB(n); u });                    27 B  LEAKS
    CONTROL -- an OWNING consumer (`let s = { let t = mkB(n); t }`): clean.

`suppress_block_tail_cleanup` disarms `t` before the block's frame drains, which
is required (the frame is about to free it and the value must survive to its
consumer), and nothing then owns it unless the consumer does.

WHY B-2026-08-30-2 DECLINES IT, and why the decline is not merely cautious. That
fix registers a replacement owner in the frame that held the SOURCE's cleanup;
here that frame has already drained, so there is nothing to replace. Registering
in the innermost frame instead is a DOUBLE FREE, because this is precisely the
shape every codegen-internal desugar synthesizes -- `Vec.sorted()` lowers to
`{ let mut __srt = recv.clone(); __srt.sort(); __srt }`, and the iterator
adaptors, `collect` into a non-Vec target, the nested-Vec index bind and the
generic-enum payload bind all build it. Each already arranges ownership at the
producer. A draft that admitted this shape took out 11 codegen and 12
memory-sanitizer tests at once, `let s: Vec[i64] = v.sorted()` segfaulting among
them.

WHY THIS ONE IS THE CONSUMING GATE'S, NOT THE OWNER'S -- the difference from
B-2026-08-30-2's population, and the reason it can be fixed the cheap way. That
row could not be fixed at the consumer because the source binding is still
READABLE after the hand-out, so the immediate free those gates emit would dangle
a later read. A block-local tail has no later reader: the binding dies with the
block. So `expr_is_fresh_owned_branch_tail` (src/codegen/stmts.rs) can simply be
widened to admit a tail that is an Identifier naming a binding the block itself
declared, and the seven gates B-2026-08-29-27 wired will free it at the use site
exactly as they do a minted temp.

THE CARE NEEDED IS IN THE PREDICATE, not the gates. It must admit ONLY a binding
local to the block being handed out -- a tail naming an OUTER binding is
B-2026-08-30-2's population and must keep declining, or the widened gates dangle
the outer binding's later read. The information is available at the same place
B-2026-08-30-2 gets it: `vecstr_source_disarmed` records which frame held the
source's cleanup, and "the block's own frame" is exactly the distinguishing
answer. The predicate is syntactic today and would need that flow fact, which is
the design question this row is really about.

SEVERITY: one leak per evaluation, unbounded in a loop; no double free and no
wrong answer. Pinned at its current leaking value by
`asan_branch_tail_declined_shapes_do_not_double_free` (row `m3`).

fix:
FIXED by bd00968b. The row's own reading was right on the first try and
wrong on the second: it IS one RHS shape missing the old-value drop rather than
a missing mechanism, but the missing hook is not on the Assign arm's drop path
at all -- it is in the arm's RHS CLASSIFICATION, one step earlier.

`compile_stmt`'s Assign arm frees the target's displaced buffer from a single
gate, `trigger_eager_free`, which requires `lhs_is_tracked_vec` and then one of
six RHS shapes. Two of those six are computed by matching on `value.kind`
DIRECTLY:

    let rhs_is_self_alias  = matches!(&value.kind, Identifier(n) if n == name);
    let rhs_is_moved_alias = matches!(&value.kind, Identifier(n) if n != name
                                        && vec_elem_types.contains_key(n));

A value-position block wraps the identifier one level deeper, so `s = { t };`
was neither, the gate never fired, and the displaced buffer was orphaned. The
fix peels the wrapper before classifying, via the already-existing
`Self::block_tail_expr` (`Block` / `Seq` / `Unsafe`, recursively):

    let rhs_tail = Self::block_tail_expr(value);

and matches on `rhs_tail.kind` in both predicates. Three lines.

WHY THIS IS A ONE-SHAPE GAP AND NOT A MISSING MECHANISM -- the evidence, not the
assertion. The third admission shape, `rhs_is_fresh`, is computed by
`rhs_yields_fresh_ref`, which ALREADY peels exactly these wrappers. So
`s = { mkB(n) };` was clean the whole time, at both opt levels, and only the
alias spellings leaked. The two classifications had simply drifted apart; this
puts them back in agreement.

BOTH PREDICATES PEELED TOGETHER, and that pairing is the load-bearing half of a
three-line change. Widening `rhs_is_moved_alias` alone -- the change that makes
the reported leak go away -- makes `s = { s };` free the very buffer it is about
to store back, trading a leak for a use-after-free. `s = { s }` is clean today
(10 allocs / 10 frees) and is pinned as a control in the regression fixture for
exactly that reason.

`block_tail_expr` peels `Block` / `Seq` / `Unsafe` and deliberately NOT
`LabeledBlock`: a labeled block's value can also arrive from a `break`-with-value
that the tail expression does not name, so its tail is not the sole answer to
"what gets stored". Leaving it out keeps the pre-fix (leaking, but safe)
behaviour there rather than guessing.

MEASURED, on the combined regression fixture, valgrind and ASAN agreeing. At
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`: pre-fix 30 allocs / 23 frees, **138 B definitely lost in 7
blocks**; post-fix 30 / 30, clean. The 138 B decomposes exactly as the shapes
predict -- 15 B for the displaced String, 40 B for a displaced `Vec[i64]`, and
83 B across a five-iteration loop's displaced generations (15 + 4x17), which is
the "unbounded in a loop" the row called out. All four surfaces (interp / JIT /
build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) print identical output before and after.

THE -O2 LEG HAS NO MEMORY COVERAGE HERE AND THE FIXTURE SAYS SO. Pre- and
post-fix are both 20 allocs / 20 frees at the default `-O2` -- LLVM folds every
one of those allocations away, and a loop with an opaque bound was tried
specifically to defeat that and does not. So the memory half of
`asan_block_rhs_assignment_frees_the_value_it_overwrites` is carried entirely by
the `-O0` leg (`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`), where it fails pre-fix with
"138 byte(s) leaked in 7 allocation(s)"; at `-O2` it asserts only the
accumulated output, which still catches a leak traded for a wrong value or a
use-after-free. Verified RED at `-O0` against the stashed fix and GREEN with it,
rather than inferred from a green run.
title: AN ASSIGNMENT WHOSE RHS IS A VALUE-POSITION BLOCK DOES NOT FREE THE VALUE IT OVERWRITES AT -O0 -- `let mut s = mkA(n); s = { t };` strands 15 B while `s = mkB(n)` and `s = t` are both clean at BOTH opt levels, so it is one RHS shape missing the old-value drop rather than a missing mechanism; clean at -O2, which is the default, so a default build hides it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found sweeping the neighbourhood of B-2026-08-30-2; unrelated to it
and IDENTICAL before and after that fix, which is how it was identified as
pre-existing rather than a regression.

An assignment whose RHS is a value-position BLOCK does not free the value it
overwrites, at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0:

    let t = mkB(n);
    let mut s = mkA(n);        // 15 B
    s = { t };
    println(f"s={s}");          15 B LEAKS at -O0, clean at -O2

Both neighbouring spellings are clean at BOTH opt levels, which is what makes
this a block-RHS gap rather than an assignment gap:

    s = mkB(n);                 // assignment from a call        clean
    s = t;                      // assignment from a binding     clean

The -O0/-O2 split says the buffer really is unreferenced at -O0 and the optimizer
happens to eliminate the allocation (or fold the store) at -O2 -- it is not
evidence that only the unoptimized path is wrong. `--release` is -O2 by default
(see `karac build --release`), so a default build hides it.

WHERE TO START: the assignment statement's own drop of the previous value.
`compile_stmt`'s Assign arm frees the target's old buffer before storing the new
one for the call and identifier RHS shapes; the block RHS reaches a different
path (the block's value is an already-loaded SSA value by the time the store
happens) and the old-value free is skipped. The `let`-with-block-RHS sibling is
clean, so the machinery exists — this is a missing hook on one RHS shape rather
than a missing mechanism.

SEVERITY: one leak per assignment, unbounded in a loop; no double free and no
wrong answer.

title: THE INTERPRETER SILENTLY DISCARDS `return` / `break` / `continue` INSIDE A MATCH ARM WHEN THE SCRUTINEE IS A FRESH TEMP WHOSE ENUM HAS ITS OWN `impl Drop` -- the statement after the `return` runs, the loop never breaks, and a `return v` yields UNIT; both compiled backends are correct
detail:
Measured on d7ee19d + the B-2026-08-29-28 fix, interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, fresh binaries and archives. The fix is codegen-only and
changes nothing here: every line below is byte-identical with it stashed.

    enum E { A(i64), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> E { return E.A(n) }

      match mk(7) { E.A(n) => { println(f"v{n}"); return } E.B => {} }
      println("AFTER-RETURN")

        interp:            v7 AFTER-RETURN      <- the `return` did not happen
        jit / build / np:  v7 dE                <- returned, body ran

THREE SHAPES, ONE CAUSE. `break` and `continue` are lost the same way, and a
`return` WITH A VALUE returns unit instead:

    break     while i < 3 { match mk(7) { E.A(n) => { println(f"v{n}"); break } .. }
                            println("AFTER-BREAK"); i = i + 1; }
                interp `v7 AFTER-BREAK v7 AFTER-BREAK v7 AFTER-BREAK done`
                compiled `v7 dE done`
    continue  interp runs the rest of the body twice; compiled continues
    value     fn f() -> i64 { match mk(7) { E.A(n) => { return n } E.B => { return 0 } } }
                `println(f"t{f()}")` prints interp `t()`, compiled `t7`
                -- a WRONG VALUE, not just wrong sequencing

ISOLATED TO ONE GATE, by bisecting the program rather than the source. Four
variants of the same match, `return` in the arm each time:

    no Drop at all                      AGREE    v7
    payload struct has Drop, enum does not   AGREE    v7 dR7
    ENUM has its own Drop                    DIVERGE  interp `v7 AFTER-RETURN`
    both have Drop                           DIVERGE  interp `v7 dR7 AFTER-RETURN`

and the scrutinee's SHAPE is the second half of the gate:

    let e = mk(7); match e { .. return .. }   AGREE    v7 dE
    match mk(7) { .. return .. }              DIVERGE
    if let E.A(n) = mk(7) { .. return }       DIVERGE

So the trigger is exactly: a FRESH-TEMP scrutinee (a `Call`/`MethodCall`, not a
named binding) whose enum carries its own `impl Drop`, with a diverging
statement in the arm. A named scrutinee of the same enum is fine, which is what
makes this narrow enough to have escaped every existing fixture -- the
-46/-47/-54/-55/-57/-58/-63/-67 family is written against `let e = ..; match e`.

WHY IT IS HIGH AND NOT A SEQUENCING ROW. Every other row in this family is a
Drop-ORDER divergence with counts agreeing. This one changes CONTROL FLOW: a
loop that should run once runs to completion, statements after a `return`
execute, and a value-returning `return` yields unit. A program can compute the
wrong answer, and `karac run` is the DEFAULT executor, so this is what a user
sees first. The enum's own body is also lost outright on the interpreter side
(`dE` never appears), which is a second, quieter defect riding the same path.

POINTER FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT. `eval_match` in `src/interpreter/pattern_match.rs`
ends `self.env.pop_scope(); return result;` and hands the arm's result back
faithfully, so the signal is not lost THERE -- look at the fresh-temp
scrutinee's own-body path that runs around it (the caller in
`src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs`, near the two
`arm_moved_user_drop_payload_bindings` call sites). The gate above says the
guilty path is the one reached only when `drop_method_keys` contains the
scrutinee's enum AND the scrutinee is a fresh temp; a fix should make that path
propagate a diverging result instead of consuming it, and the four-variant
table above is the regression fixture.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping scrutinee shapes for B-2026-08-29-28 -- the
`return`/`break`/`continue` rows were added to probe codegen's terminator paths
(an arm that diverges never reaches the merge block), and the INTERPRETER was
the side that failed.
fix:
FIXED by facec84.

THE ROW POINTED AT THE RIGHT NEIGHBOURHOOD AND THE WRONG LEVEL. Its pointer
says the signal "is not lost THERE" in `eval_match` and to look at the
fresh-temp scrutinee's own-body path around it -- correct, and that is where
the SYMPTOM lives. But the defect is one level down and is not
scrutinee-specific at all: it is in `run_user_drop_body_only`
(`src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs`), the shared runner that EVERY drop-body hook
in the interpreter funnels through.

THE MECHANISM IS TWO LINES. The block evaluator drains a raised signal into
its own `Result` -- `let cf_opt = match stmt_result { Ok(_) => self.pending_cf.take(), .. }`
-- and `run_user_drop_body_only` ends with `let _ = self.eval_body_growing(&body);`.
So running a `Drop` body while a `return` / `break` / `continue` was still
sitting in `pending_cf` handed that signal to the body's own block, which
drained it and dropped it on the floor. The enum's body vanished in the same
motion and for the same reason: `eval_call` short-circuits on a set
`pending_cf` immediately after evaluating the callee and BEFORE dispatching it
(`eval_call.rs:2008`), so every `println` inside the body returned without
emitting. One cause, both symptoms -- which is why `dE` never appeared AND
the statement after the `return` did.

THE INVARIANT IS "A DROP BODY IS TRANSPARENT TO A SIGNAL ALREADY IN FLIGHT",
and every other drop-body site in the interpreter already satisfied it by
CONSTRUCTION rather than by intent: `run_cleanup` is reached only after the
block evaluator has taken the signal OUT of `pending_cf`, so bodies run there
with it clear. The fresh-temp scrutinee hooks in `eval_expr.rs` are
where that stops being true -- measurably the `match` and `if let` ones, since
the `while let` spelling of the same program stayed correct throughout (see
below). The fix brackets `eval_body_growing` with a save/restore of
`pending_cf` at that single choke point -- ~45 call sites funnel through it --
rather than patching the three hooks, so a fourth caller cannot forget it. It
is a no-op wherever the signal is already clear, which is everywhere else.

THE PRECEDENCE GUARD IS DELIBERATELY NOT LOAD-BEARING, and the comment says so
rather than implying otherwise. `eval_body_growing` bottoms out in
`eval_block_inner`, which drains ANY signal the body itself raised into the
discarded `Result`, so `pending_cf` is None at the restore and the
`ControlFlow::is_unwind` test cannot fire today. It is kept as a guard for the
day that changes, encoding the precedence `call_function` already applies. It
is NOT extended into "propagate a panic raised inside a drop body", because
design.md 9165 requires the effect checker to REJECT such a program outright
("This is a static rule, not a runtime one -- there is no 'abort on panic in
drop' fallback to discover at runtime"). Teaching this path to propagate one
would be implementing the fallback the spec forbids instead of fixing the
missing static check; that check's absence is filed as <<PANICFREE>>.

MEASURED across interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 on a 21-shape matrix
(return / return-value / break / continue / labeled-break / question-mark /
nested-match / return-in-nested-block / if-let / if-let-else / while-let-return /
while-let-break / let-else / struct-scrutinee / drop-body-panics / plain-no-flow
plus the row's own four and the two-part gate), with the fix STASHED and
REBUILT for the baseline rather than remembered:

    pre-fix    7 AGREE / 14 DIVERGE
    post-fix  19 AGREE /  2 DIVERGE

THE TWO RESIDUALS ARE NOT THIS ROW. `struct-scrutinee` is B-2026-08-30-15 --
the compiled backends run no body at all there, and this fix corrects only the
interpreter's CONTROL FLOW on that shape (`v7 AFTER done` -> `v7 dS7 done`
against a compiled `v7 done`). `drop-body-panics` is the ill-formed program
design.md 9165 says must be rejected, so its divergence is downstream of
<<PANICFREE>> and not something to reconcile.

TWO THINGS THE ROW UNDERSTATED, both found by sweeping rather than by reading:

  * THE GATE IS "SCRUTINEE HAS ITS OWN BODY", NOT "SCRUTINEE IS AN ENUM". The
    row's isolation table varies the Drop across an enum and its payload and
    concludes the enum must carry it. A fresh-temp STRUCT scrutinee with its
    own `Drop` lost the `return` identically (`v7 AFTER done`) -- the row never
    tested that shape because its table only varied enums.

  * `?` IS AFFECTED, AND IT IS THE WORST SPELLING. `?` desugars to an early
