    return and was discarded the same way, so a function that should propagate
    `Err("big")` returned `Ok(0)` instead: interp `v7 AFTER ok0` vs compiled
    `v7 dE errbig`. That is a WRONG VALUE out of the idiomatic error-propagation
    operator, on the default executor. The row lists only `return` / `break` /
    `continue`.

WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT: pre-existence (re-confirmed -- the matrix above was
taken on 27a7730 with the fix stashed and rebuilt), the two-part gate as far as
it went (a NAMED scrutinee is fine, a fresh temp is not), that the enum's own
body is lost as a second symptom, and the severity call. This is a control-flow
defect on `karac run`, the default executor, not the drop-ORDER kind the rest of
this family is made of.

TWO BOUNDARIES DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED, both measured identical before and after
and both pinned as fixture rows: a NAMED scrutinee (`let e = mk(7); match e`)
never reached the interrupted path, and a type with no `Drop` of its own has no
body to run into the signal.

A THIRD THING THE SWEEP TURNED UP, and it cuts the other way -- the `while
let` SPELLING WAS NEVER AFFECTED. `match` and `if let` over the same fresh-temp
scrutinee both lost the `return`; `while let` did not (`v7 dE done` on all four
surfaces, before and after). So the three sibling constructs did NOT behave
alike here, which is worth recording in a family where the recurring lesson has
been the opposite -- B-2026-08-28-63's whole point was that the three spellings
must move together. It is pinned as a fixture row so a later unification cannot
silently regress the one that was already right.

FIXTURES. `interpreter::diverging_arm_over_a_freshtemp_scrutinee_keeps_its_control_flow`
(12 rows) and `interpreter::diverging_arm_over_a_freshtemp_struct_scrutinee_keeps_its_control_flow`
are the REGRESSION half -- NINE of the twelve rows measured RED on the unfixed
tree (the three exceptions being `while-let` and the two boundaries), and the
test fails pre-fix on its first row with exactly `v7 AFTER done` where
`v7 dE done` is due. The compiled twin
`codegen::e2e_diverging_arm_over_a_freshtemp_scrutinee_keeps_its_control_flow`
is the ORACLE: green before and after, because the fix is interpreter-only.
That is the MIRROR of B-2026-08-29-28, where the interpreter was the oracle and
codegen was moved onto it -- worth recording, because it means "the interpreter
is the reference" is not a rule in this family, only a case-by-case finding.

The struct row is interpreter-only ON PURPOSE and kept as its own test rather
than a table row, so that closing B-2026-08-30-15 is a one-line move of the
shape into the shared table instead of an archaeology exercise.

ONE STALE COMMENT CORRECTED. B-2026-08-29-28's `arm-returns-fires-on-that-edge`
row was written codegen-only BECAUSE of this bug, and said so by id. That shape
now measures `v10 dR10 dE` on all four surfaces, so the comment's stated reason
no longer holds; it now records that -14 fixed it and points at the
four-surface coverage. The row itself stays, because what it pins is
codegen-specific (the arm's cleanup is emitted on the arm's own edge and never
reaches the merge block).

NO design.md CHANGE. The compiled behaviour was already correct and the spec
never described the interpreter's; only the implementation disagreed.

title: A FRESH-TEMP STRUCT SCRUTINEE'S OWN `Drop` BODY NEVER RUNS AT ALL ON EITHER COMPILED BACKEND -- `match mkS() { S { r: r } => .. }` is interp `v7 dS dR7` vs compiled `v7 dR7`, with `dS` missing outright rather than misplaced
detail:
Measured on d7ee19d + the B-2026-08-29-28 fix, interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. Byte-identical with that fix stashed -- it is enum-only and
does not touch this.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    struct S { r: R }
    impl Drop for S { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dS") } }
    fn mkS() -> S { return S { r: R { id: 7 } } }

      match mkS() { S { r: r } => { println(f"v{r.id}") } }
      println("s1"); println("s2")

        interp:            v7 dS dR7 s1 s2
        jit / build / np:  v7 dR7 s1 s2        <- `dS` never runs

NOT A PLACEMENT DIVERGENCE. B-2026-08-29-28's whole family is "same count,
different point"; this one is a MISSING BODY. The payload's `dR7` fires on every
backend, so the enclosing struct's own destructor is the only thing dropped, and
a `Drop` impl that releases something real -- a lock, a file handle, a
connection -- simply never releases it under `karac build`.

WHY: `materialize_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee`
(`src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs`) is the single site that mints an owner for
a fresh-temp scrutinee, and it bails at `variant_pattern_enum_name(pattern)?`,
which returns `None` for a struct pattern. Nothing downstream picks the struct
temp up, so no `UserDrop` action is ever registered for it -- there is no
placement to get wrong. This is the STRUCT sibling of the gap B-2026-07-11-26
closed for all-scalar user-Drop ENUMs, and the code comment at that bail
("a fresh-temp enum scrutinee whose type has a user `impl Drop` must RUN that
Drop ... exactly as a bound `let s = <expr>` binding would") states the rule
this violates for structs.

THE BOUND SPELLING IS THE ORACLE and is clean: `let s = mkS(); match s { .. }`
runs `dS` on all four surfaces. So the two spellings of the same program
disagree, which is the same shape of argument B-2026-08-28-74 used for the
shared-enum tracker.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping scrutinee shapes for B-2026-08-29-28. Every
shape in that row is an ENUM scrutinee; adding the struct row to the matrix was
what surfaced this.
fix:
FIXED by ed13ce30, with two corrections to the row and one gap left open
and pinned.

THE MECHANISM IS THE ONE THE ROW NAMED. `materialize_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee`
bails at `variant_pattern_enum_name(pattern)?`, which is `None` for a struct
pattern, and no sibling picked the value up -- so a fresh-temp struct scrutinee
had NO OWNER AT ALL. Added `materialize_freshtemp_struct_scrutinee`, the struct
member of the same family as `track_freshtemp_shared_enum_scrutinee` /
`track_freshtemp_boxed_enum_scrutinee` / `track_freshtemp_inline_result_
scrutinee`: gate on `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` + non-borrow, resolve the
struct name from the arm pattern (`struct_pattern_names_a_user_struct`, which
already distinguishes a real struct pattern from an enum STRUCT-VARIANT
pattern) or else from the callee's declared return type, and register the
type's `karac_drop_<S>` wrapper via `track_user_drop_var`. Wired into all four
constructs -- `match`, `if let`, `let...else`, `while let` -- plus the
statement-end drain allowlist, which is what puts the body at the point
design.md's Temporary Lifetime Rules table specifies rather than at the
enclosing scope's exit.

CORRECTION 1 -- THE ROW UNDERSTATED THE DEFECT, and the missing half is memory.
It measured only the DESTRUCTURING arm, where the moved-out binding happens to
carry the field's body and buffer, which is exactly what hid the rest. Measured
pre-fix, compiled vs `--interp`:

    match mkS() { S { r: r } => .. }   v7 dR7            vs  v7 dS dR7
    match mkS() { S { r: _ } => .. }   v                 vs  v  dS dR7
    match mkS() { s          => .. }   v7                vs  v7 dS dR7
    match mkSc() { Sc { n } => .. }    v7                vs  v7 dSc
    match mkSh() { Sh { s, n } => .. } v7[pay]           vs  v7[pay] dSh
    if let S { r: _ } = mkS() { .. }   v                 vs  v  dS dR7
    let S { r: _ } = mkS() else { .. } (nothing)         vs  dS dR7
    while .. { match mkS() { .. } }    (nothing, per it) vs  dS dR7 per it

Every arm that moves nothing out loses BOTH bodies and LEAKS the payload --
9 allocs / 8 frees, 15 B definitely lost for a one-`String` payload (valgrind,
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`); 60 B in 4 allocations for the looped regression fixture
under LSan. All eight rows above now match the interpreter byte-for-byte on all
four surfaces (interp / JIT / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), and the leak is gone
(10 allocs / 10 frees).

CORRECTION 2 -- "THE BOUND SPELLING IS THE ORACLE AND IS CLEAN" IS NOT TRUE, and
the row leans on it. `let s = mkS(); match s { S { r: r } => .. }` measures
`v7 dR7 dS dR7` compiled against the interpreter's `v7 dS dR7`: `R`'s body runs
TWICE and the two legitimate bodies come out in the reverse order. That is
B-2026-08-31-31, filed later and independently, and it is the same shape the
argument was resting on -- so the two spellings do not disagree in the way the
row says; the fresh-temp one was simply worse.

THE DESTRUCTURING ARM IS DECLINED, DELIBERATELY, and that is the row's own
headline repro. `track_user_drop_var` registers `karac_drop_<S>` -- body, then
field bodies, then memory, as ONE action -- so when an arm binds a Drop-bearing
field the wrapper re-runs a body the binding already owns. Registering it anyway
was measured: `match mkS() { S { r } => .. }` becomes `v7 dR7 dS dR7`. The
missing `dS` appears and `dR7` runs twice, which for a `drop()` that closes a
handle is a DOUBLE CLOSE -- a regression on a shape that is correct today, not a
partial fix. The codebase's own bar says which side of that trade to be on: "an
under-suppressed field drop double-frees; an over-suppressed one leaks." The
per-arm `suppress_destructured_struct_pattern_cleanup_at` cannot rescue it: it
zeroes the moved field's CAP, which stops the second FREE and not the second
BODY. Masking the body needs the per-variable wrapper variant B-2026-08-31-31
already scopes, so that row now closes this remainder for the bound and the
fresh-temp spelling at once. The decline is pinned as
`destructuring-arm-boundary` in the regression fixture so it cannot be dropped
silently.

The decline gate is narrowed to fields whose type actually RUNS a body, and that
narrowing is load-bearing rather than an optimisation: gating on "binds any
field" cost `Sc { n }` its `dSc` for an `i64` that moves nothing droppable
(measured -- it regressed that row from parity back to missing). A `String`/`Vec`
field is likewise admitted, because the cap-zeroing suppressor already protects
its memory and `String` runs no body.

UNTOUCHED BOUNDARY, verified rather than assumed: a struct with NO `Drop` of its
own is unchanged at `v7 dR7`, where the INTERPRETER is the one running no body
(`v7`). That is B-2026-08-31-32, an interpreter-side row, and it is pinned as
`no-own-drop-boundary` so a future widening of this path cannot perturb it from
the codegen side.

title: A FRESH-TEMP `shared enum` SCRUTINEE'S OWN `Drop` BODY STILL RUNS AT THE ENCLOSING SCOPE'S EXIT -- `match mkSe() { .. }` is interp `v1 dSe s1 s2` vs compiled `v1 s1 s2 dSe`; the value-enum half of this was fixed by B-2026-08-29-28, the shared half rides a different channel
detail:
Measured on d7ee19d + the B-2026-08-29-28 fix, interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0.

    shared enum Se { A(i64), B }
    impl Drop for Se { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dSe") } }
    fn mkSe() -> Se { return Se.A(1) }

      match mkSe() { Se.A(n) => { println(f"v{n}") } Se.B => {} }
      println("s1"); println("s2")

        interp:            v1 dSe s1 s2
        jit / build / np:  v1 s1 s2 dSe

design.md § Temporary Lifetime Rules is as explicit here as it is for a value
enum -- "Match-expression scrutinee | Through every arm body (the scrutinee is
live across all arms; drops at match exit)" -- and the same section's
composition-with-NLL paragraph forbids extending past that end. So this is the
same defect as B-2026-08-29-28, on the one enum flavour that fix does not reach.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED THERE, and why it is not a one-line follow-on. The two
flavours reach the drop through DIFFERENT CHANNELS:

  * A VALUE enum goes through `materialize_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee`, which
    registers a `CleanupAction::UserDrop` -- a body call and nothing else. That
    is what B-2026-08-29-28 moved to the construct's exit, and moving a
    body-only action early is safe because it frees nothing.
  * A SHARED enum goes through `track_freshtemp_shared_enum_scrutinee`
    (B-2026-08-28-74), which registers an `RcDec` via `track_rc_var`. The user
    body is not a separate action at all -- it runs from inside the RC drop fn
    when the count reaches zero. Placing the body earlier therefore means
    RELEASING A REFERENCE earlier, and if an arm binding aliases into the box
    that is a use-after-free, not a reordering.

Codegen's own rule for this channel is stated in `fire_due_user_drops`:
"Memory-only drops (no user body) also stay at scope exit: with no observable
side effects, scope-exit free is equivalent to NLL free." The rationale is sound
and it is exactly what breaks here -- a shared enum WITH a user `impl Drop` does
have an observable side effect on that channel, so the class it was filed under
no longer describes it.

LOW because counts agree on every surface (one `dSe`, no leak, no double free --
B-2026-08-28-74 established the release itself is correct); only the point
differs. Whoever takes this should decide first whether the body can be split
off the RcDec into its own `UserDrop` action fired at match exit with the
release left at scope exit, which would make it the value-enum case exactly;
that is a design question, not a placement tweak.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping scrutinee shapes for B-2026-08-29-28 -- the
shared-enum row was added to the matrix to check the fix's boundary and stayed
DIVERGE after it landed.
fix:
FIXED by 1de3bd88. The row's diagnosis was exactly right, including its reason
for not folding this into B-2026-08-29-28, and its stated objection turned out
to be answerable rather than blocking.

THE CHANNEL SPLIT IS AS THE ROW DESCRIBES. A VALUE enum's `Drop` body is a
standalone `CleanupAction::UserDrop`, which -28 moved to the construct's exit
via `fire_freshtemp_scrutinee_body_at_exit`. A SHARED enum's body runs from
inside `__karac_rc_drop_<E>` when the count reaches zero, so there is no body
action to move -- the only way to move the body is to move the DECREMENT.
`track_freshtemp_shared_enum_scrutinee` now returns the box pointer it
registered, and `compile_match` releases it at the merge block through
`fire_freshtemp_shared_scrutinee_dec_at_exit`, which removes the `RcDec` from
its frame first so the scope-exit drain cannot dec a second time.

THE ROW'S OBJECTION, AND WHY THE MERGE BLOCK IS THE SAFE POINT. It argued that
moving a dec is not the same as moving a body -- a dec that reaches zero FREES
the box, so an arm binding aliasing into it would be a use-after-free rather
than a reordering. Three things answer it, and the third is the one that
matters:

  * A MOVED-OUT payload is already excluded. B-2026-08-28-74's
    `suppress_shared_enum_payload_move_out` zeroes the consumed field's words in
    the box, so the binding owns that payload outright and the box no longer
    references it.
  * A READING arm binding holds its own `+1`, taken at the bind and released by
    the ARM's frame -- which drains on the arm's own edge, strictly before the
    merge block. A count of 2 at the dec leaves 1 and frees nothing.
  * A DIVERGING arm never reaches the merge block and emits its cleanup on its
    own edge with the action still registered; retirement happens after every
    arm is compiled, so it cannot take the action from an arm that already
    emitted it. Same structural argument the value-enum sibling documents.

MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED. The regression fixtures are that objection turned
into tests: `escaping-payload` in `codegen::e2e_freshtemp_shared_enum_scrutinee_
releases_at_construct_exit` and the whole of
`memory_sanitizer::asan_freshtemp_shared_enum_scrutinee_release_at_match_exit`
have every arm MOVE its heap payload out and read the value AFTER the dec. Clean
under valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and under LSan at both levels. Five shapes
-- scalar payload, heap payload, escaping payload, nested matches, loop --
now match `--interp` byte-for-byte on all four surfaces; pre-fix the compiled
three printed `v1 s1 s2 dSe` against `v1 dSe s1 s2`.

Firing an `RcDec` at a chosen point is not new machinery: `fire_due_user_drops`
already does it for NAMED shared bindings at their NLL live-range end, under the
same retire-what-you-fired rule its own comment states ("retiring an action that
did not fire is not a retiming, it is a dropped decrement, i.e. a leak"). This
applies it to the one owner with no name to compute a live range from.

INCIDENTAL FINDING, SPLIT OUT: writing the ASAN fixture surfaced a 15 B leak
when the same match sits in a NESTED EXPRESSION position (an f-string, a call
argument) instead of being let-bound. It is not this row's -- identical before
and after this fix, and it reproduces on a VALUE enum -- so it is filed as
B-2026-09-01-26 and that shape is deliberately excluded from the fixture here,
with the exclusion and its reason recorded in the test's doc comment.

title: AN `if let` MISS DROPS THE SCRUTINEE TEMPORARY *AFTER* THE `else` ARM ON BOTH BACKENDS, WHERE design.md SAYS BEFORE IT -- `els dE` vs the specified `dE els`; the two backends AGREE, so no A/B gate can see it
detail:
Measured on d7ee19d + the B-2026-08-29-28 fix, interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 -- all four byte-identical, which is the point.

    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn mkB() -> E { return E.B }

      if let E.A(r) = mkB() { println(f"v{r.id}") } else { println("els") }
      println("s1"); println("s2")

        all four backends:  els dE s1 s2
        design.md:          dE  els s1 s2

design.md § `if let` and `let...else`, "Scrutinee temporary scope", second
bullet: "In the **`else` arm of `if let`**: scrutinee temporaries have already
been dropped *before* the arm body begins. The else arm does not see the
scrutinee's temporaries -- they fired the moment the match decision routed
control to the else path." The section says in as many words that this "closes
the lock-held-during-else-branch footgun", and § Temporary Lifetime Rules'
table repeats it: "Scrutinee of `if let` / `while let` / `let-else` | Before the
non-matching arm runs (on miss)".

The scrutinee here IS covered by the rule rather than adjacent to it: § Bindings
vs. temporaries defines the governed set as "the scrutinee expression's
anonymous intermediates: function-call results not bound to a name", which is
exactly `mkB()`.

WHY IT SURVIVES EVERY GATE. The two backends agree, so the four-surface A/B rule
reports green; the counts are right, so no leak or double-free check fires; and
the deviation is from a SPEC SENTENCE, which nothing in the suite asserts. It is
findable only by reading the table against a measurement, which is how it turned
up.

PRE-EXISTING AND NOT INTRODUCED BY B-2026-08-29-28. Before that fix the
interpreter already printed `els dE` and codegen printed `els s1 s2 dE`; the fix
moved codegen onto the interpreter's placement, which is correct for parity and
inherits the interpreter's deviation from the spec. Fixing this one means moving
BOTH backends, and it is the miss edge specifically -- the hit path
(`if let` over a matching value) is already correct on both.

LOW: nothing leaks and the two backends agree, so the only cost is the footgun
design.md names -- a `Lease`/lock temporary staying checked out across the
`else` branch.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping scrutinee shapes for B-2026-08-29-28; the
miss-path row was in the matrix as a boundary check and turned out to disagree
with the spec on both backends rather than between them.
fix:
FIXED by f7a9f48e. Both backends moved together, which is what this row
said the fix would require.

WHAT LANDED. The scrutinee temporary's user `Drop` now fires PER EDGE rather
than at the point where the two edges rejoin:

  - `if let` MISS: at the TOP of the `else` arm, before any of its code.
  - `if let` HIT: unchanged, at the end of the then arm.
  - `let…else` MISS: at the top of the divergent else block.
  - `let…else` HIT: unchanged.

design.md § `if let` and `let...else` > "Scrutinee temporary scope" specifies
exactly this asymmetry, and the section states that the else-edge half is what
"closes the lock-held-during-else-branch footgun" — so the ORDER is the
feature, not an incidental. Its worked example is a `Lease` whose `Drop`
returns a pooled connection: it must be back in the pool before the else arm
logs and retries.

MEASURED, all four surfaces (`run --interp`, `run`, `build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`) byte-identical before AND after — which is the point,
since the two backends agreeing is why no A/B gate could see this:

    shape                          before        after (== design.md)
    if let MISS                    els dE s1     dE els s1
    if let HIT                     v7 dE s1      v7 dE s1     (unchanged)
    if let MISS, no else arm       dE s1         dE s1        (unchanged)
    if let HIT, then arm returns   v7 dE         v7 dE        (unchanged)
    if let MISS inside a loop      els dE ×2     dE els ×2
    let…else MISS                  els dE        dE els
    let…else HIT                   dE v7 end     dE v7 end    (unchanged)

THE ROW UNDERSTATED ITS SCOPE: `let…else` is wrong in the same way and the row
names only `if let`. design.md's third bullet covers it in as many words ("In
the **`else` block of `let...else`**: same rule — scrutinee temporaries are
dropped before the divergent else block runs"), and the interpreter's own
comment at that site documented the old order as deliberate — "on the miss edge
AFTER the else block runs (matching codegen's drop-during-return order)" — which
was an accurate description of codegen and a deviation from the spec. Both
halves had to move or the two backends would have split, which they briefly did
mid-fix: with only the interpreter moved, `let…else` measured `dE els` on
`--interp` against `els dE` on all three compiled surfaces. That intermediate
state was strictly worse than the bug, and is the reason the `let…else` half is
in this fix rather than deferred to its own row.

HOW, and why it is not just "move the call". The drop was left queued as a
`UserDrop` cleanup action for the enclosing statement's drain, which sits after
the merge block and therefore after BOTH arms. Firing it earlier at that single
site is impossible — there is only one site, and the two edges need different
placements. `take_freshtemp_scrutinee_drop` retracts the queued action once and
hands back `(slot, drop_fn)`; `emit_taken_scrutinee_drop` emits it at a given
insert point. The `if let` path emits at the end of the then arm and at the top
of the else arm; `let…else` at the top of the else block and, on the match edge,
at the very end of `compile_let_else` — after every suppressor has zeroed the
caps/tags of what the pattern moved out, so the drop frees only the residue,
exactly as the queued action would have.

EXACTLY ONCE PER RUNTIME PATH, by construction rather than by check: the action
is retracted once, and each of the two IR emission sites sits on a different
edge. The then-arm emission is skipped when that arm diverges, because a
`return` there already drained the frame through `emit_scope_cleanup` while the
action was still queued — pinned by the `if-let-hit-then-returns` row.

MEMORY-CHECKED, since emitting one drop at two IR sites is exactly how a double
free gets written. A heap-carrying version (`E.A(R { name: String })` /
`E.B(String)`, mixing hit, miss and a three-iteration loop) is clean under
valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `2`: no invalid reads/writes, no double
free, and no definitely-lost bytes.

TESTS. `codegen::e2e_if_let_miss_drops_the_scrutinee_temp_before_the_else_arm`
(7 rows) and its interpreter twin, both RED on pre-fix `src` (`els\ndE\npost`
against the specified `dE\nels\npost`). They assert ABSOLUTE expected output
rather than backend parity, because parity was already green — a spec deviation
shared by both backends is invisible to the four-surface rule, which is the
whole reason this row existed. The HIT rows are boundaries: the spec asks for
the opposite placement there, so a fix that simply moved the drop earlier
everywhere would have broken them.

`while let` WAS CHECKED AND IS CORRECTLY ORDERED — `v0 dE v1 dE after`, each
iteration's temporary dropping at the end of that iteration's body, which is
design.md's fourth bullet. But the same probe turned up a DIFFERENT defect in
it: the loop-exit miss runs no body at all. Two scrutinee temporaries created,
one `dE` printed, on all three surfaces, where the identical miss through
`if let` prints it. That is a missing body rather than a misplaced one, so it is
filed as B-2026-09-01-42 rather than folded in here.

NOT ADDRESSED, stated rather than implied: `else if let` chains are named in the
same design.md bullet as `if let` and were not probed separately (they lower
through the same `compile_if_let`, so they are expected to follow, but expected
is not measured); and the fix covers the fresh-temp ENUM and STRUCT scrutinee
slots, not the boxed-enum or inline-Result staging slots, which register
different actions and were not measured for this ordering.

title: A struct literal built DIRECTLY at a `return` site, whose field is a `Vec` of `Drop` elements, runs the element's `Drop` body ONCE TOO MANY on every compiled backend -- `mid dR14 v14 dR14 post` against the interpreter's `mid v14 dR14 post`. The two working spellings both route the value through a named binding first (`let bx = ...; return bx`) or omit `return` entirely (the bare tail), so the return-position literal is the whole trigger; a non-container `Drop` field is correct in all three spellings
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-29-66, which recorded it as "a SECOND, separate defect
visible in the same runs" while that row was being fixed for its use-after-free.
The two are genuinely different: -66 was auto-par's branch-publish ownership
handshake, this one has nothing to do with auto-par and reproduces identically
with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`. Splitting it out now because -66's fix removes the
memory fault that was masking it -- before the fix, in the shapes where the
returned binding is never read again, THIS extra body was the one landing on
freed memory and printing garbage, so the two looked like one bug.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    struct Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }

    fn build(k: i64) -> Box3 {
        let mut v: Vec[R] = Vec.new();
        v.push(R { id: k, tag: f"t" });
        println("mid");
        return Box3 { xs: v }          // <-- THE WHOLE TRIGGER
    }

    fn main() {
        let a: Box3 = build(14);
        println(f"v{a.xs[0].id}");
        println("post");
    }

      --interp     -> `mid v14 dR14 post`      one body
      karac build  -> `mid dR14 v14 dR14 post` TWO, the first before the use
      same with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, and same on the JIT.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE RETURN SPELLING ALONE, and it is clean. Holding
everything else fixed and varying only how the value leaves `build`:

    return Box3 { xs: v }              TWO bodies      <- struct literal AT the return
    let bx: Box3 = Box3 { xs: v };
    return bx                          one body, correct
    Box3 { xs: v }                     one body, correct   (bare tail, no `return`)

So it is not the struct literal and not the return -- it is a struct literal
built directly in `return` position. Note this is the OPPOSITE polarity to
B-2026-08-29-57, where the semicolon on a `return` mattered and the value was a
bare local; here the spelling of the VALUE matters and the semicolon does not.

A CONTAINER FIELD IS REQUIRED. `struct W { r: R, note: String }` -- a
Drop-bearing field that is not a container -- is correct in all three spellings
(`mid v14 dR14 post`). Adding a second, non-Drop container field
(`struct S { names: Vec[String], xs: Vec[R] }`) still doubles, so it is the
`Vec`-of-`Drop`-elements field that carries it, not the field count or a
String field.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT ON ITS OWN: valgrind on the compiled binary is clean --
0 errors, 0 definitely lost, 0 indirectly lost. The extra run is a BODY, not a
free, and the buffer is still intact when it runs, which is exactly what makes
it quiet. A user `Drop` with an observable side effect (a close, a release, a
decrement, a log) would fire it twice.

WHERE TO START: the fresh-temp / return-position registration for a struct
literal whose field is a container of Drop-bearing elements. The working
spellings both route the value through a named binding first, so the suspicion
is that the return-position literal registers its element-bodies walk TWICE --
once as an owned temp at the construction site and once for the returned value
-- where the let-bound form registers it once and the bare tail suppresses it
for the caller. `karac build --emit-llvm` on the three spellings side by side
should show the extra `__karac_dropelems_*` call directly.

PRE-EXISTING: measured identical on 93c6cc86, before B-2026-08-29-66's fix.
fix:
FIXED by 8b463471.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is a hook-set asymmetry rather than a missing analysis. Two
sites handle a value leaving a function: `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return`
(`src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs`) for the bare tail, and the `ExprKind::Return`
arm in `src/codegen/exprs.rs` for the explicit spelling. They are supposed to
carry the same set of disarms. They did not: B-2026-08-02-23 leg 2 -- the
AGGREGATE-LITERAL source disarm, which walks a returned struct/tuple literal and
retracts the Drop-BODIES action of every binding named inside it -- was added to
the tail site only. The explicit-`return` arm had the memory-half transfer
(`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`, which does recurse into literal fields)
and the fresh-temp field move, but nothing for the bodies half.

So `return Box3 { xs: v }` over `struct Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }` left `v`'s
`UserDrop{ContainerElemBodies}` armed. It fired at the callee's exit and again at
the caller's binding death:

    karac build / karac run / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0   mid dR14 v14 dR14 post
    --interp                                     mid v14 dR14 post

The two spellings the row records as working were working for a reason, not by
luck, and that is what localised this: `let bx = Box3 { xs: v }; return bx`
reaches the explicit-return arm as a bare Identifier, which the arm already
disarms; the bare tail `Box3 { xs: v }` reaches leg 2 itself. The return-position
literal was the only spelling with no owner for the bodies half.

THE FIX is four lines at the explicit-`return` site, immediately after
`consume_freshtemp_field_move`: if the returned expression is a `StructLiteral`
or `Tuple`, run `collect_aggregate_literal_sources` over it and
`suppress_user_drop_for_var` each name -- the same helper pair leg 2 uses, so the
two sites now genuinely carry the same set.

WHY THIS SAT QUIET FOR SO LONG, and it is the general lesson: the MEMORY and
BODIES halves of a container's cleanup are separate actions with separate
suppression channels. The memory half was already transferred here, so the
buffer had exactly one owner -- valgrind reported 0 errors and 0 leaked bytes at
both `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `=2`. Nothing crashed. What doubled was the
observable side effect: a `Drop` that closes a file, releases a lock or logs ran
twice. Only a fire-COUNT oracle sees that, which is why the row was originally
recorded as an aside inside B-2026-08-29-66's use-after-free and only became
visible as its own defect once -66's fix removed the memory fault that was
printing garbage over it.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`), which now agree exactly, across four shapes --
each of which doubled pre-fix and fires once now:

    return Box3 { xs: v }                   struct literal at the return  (the row)
    return (v, 7)                           tuple literal, same position
    return Two { xs: a, ys: b }             two independent sources, one literal
    if k > 0 { return Box3 { xs: v } } ...  conditional return, every path

    pre-fix  aot: mid dR14 v14 dR14 A dR20 t7 dR20 B dR31 dR30 w3031 dR31 dR30 C dR40 c40 dR40 D
    post-fix all: mid v14 dR14 A t7 dR20 B w3031 dR31 dR30 C c40 dR40 D

The conditional row is the one worth stating explicitly: the disarm is STATIC
and flow-insensitive, like every sibling in both hook sets, so it retracts on all
paths whether or not a given path returns. That direction can only under-fire,
never double-fire, and the `named-binding-then-return` / `bare-tail-literal`
boundary rows in the interpreter twin are there to catch an over-disarm showing
up as a MISSING body.

REGRESSION TESTS: `codegen::test_e2e_aggregate_literal_at_explicit_return_single_fire`
(all four shapes, absolute expected output, RED-checked against a stashed `src/`
-- the pre-fix line above is that measurement) and its oracle twin
`interpreter::aggregate_literal_at_explicit_return_fires_element_bodies_once`,
which was already green and is pinned so a future "reconciliation" cannot move
the reference instead of the backend.

FIXED by 4f02313.

`pattern_binds_direct_inline_heap_payload` now admits a user STRUCT that
transitively owns heap, not only a direct `String` / `Vec` payload, so the
read-only arm is classified as the borrow B-2026-08-08-25 intended and the
source keeps its payload.

A `shared struct` PAYLOAD IS EXCLUDED, and the first version of this fix did not
exclude it. `Option[Inner]` over a `shared struct Inner` is an RC box, a
different ownership regime from the value payloads B-2026-08-08-25's borrow
model is about: a field read off one is DEEP-CLONED (B-2026-08-13-6) precisely
because the box may have other handles. Classifying that arm as a borrow drops
an owner the RC path still expects, and it is not a theoretical worry -- the
first version turned `asan_shared_struct_heap_field_read_cloned_not_aliased`
(whose program matches exactly this shape) into an ASAN memory error, while
every value-struct shape stayed correct and the whole rest of the suite passed.
The full-suite gate is what caught it; the 13-shape boundary table did not,
because none of its shapes was shared. `Option[shared struct]` is now a pinned
control in both fixtures so the exclusion cannot be lost by accident.

A `len()`-SHAPED PROBE HIDES THIS BUG, which is the other thing worth carrying
forward. Probing `Option[S { v: Vec[i64] }]` through `q.v.len()` reads a length
field that survives the free and answers correctly on all four surfaces,
valgrind included; through `q.v[0]` the same program is an invalid read. The
row's own boundary table was right and a first re-measurement of it through
`len()` was wrong.

MEASURED, on the read-then-read shape, each program across `--interp` / JIT /
default AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT plus `valgrind --leak-check=full`:

    shape                          before                     after
    Option[S { s: String }]        garbage, VG invalid read   correct, vg clean
    Option[S { v: Vec[i64] }]      garbage, VG invalid read   correct, vg clean
      (only through `v[i]`; `v.len()` looked correct before the fix too)
    Option[Outer{Inner{String}}]   garbage, VG invalid read   correct, vg clean
    Result[S { s: String }, i64]   prints EMPTY, VG CLEAN     correct, vg clean
    Option[S { n: i64 }]           correct                    correct (control)
    Option[shared struct]          correct                    correct (control)
    Option[String] / [Vec] /
      [(String,i64)] / [i64],
      Result[String,i64],
      enum E { A(String) },
      enum E { A(S) }              correct                    correct

THE NESTED CASE IS NOT IN THE ROW and is why the predicate is transitive rather
than one hop: `Outer { i: Inner { s: String } }` fails identically, and a check
that looked only at `Outer`'s immediate field types would have left it broken
while every listed shape passed.

THE `Result` LEG IS FIXED TOO, and the row was right to insist it be checked
separately: it fails valgrind-CLEAN, printing empty, because the payload is
moved out and zeroed rather than freed-then-read. A fix verified against the
`Option` leg and a sanitizer alone would have looked complete while that stayed
broken -- the sanitizer has nothing to report there.

SCOPE IS THE STRUCTS THAT ARE BROKEN, NOT ALL STRUCTS. `named_struct_owns_heap`
answers false for a struct with only scalar fields, so `Option[S { n: i64 }]`
keeps the path it already takes correctly; the change is confined to payloads
that own heap. A cycle (`struct A { b: Option[B] }` / `struct B { a: Option[A] }`)
is bounded by fuel, and exhausting it answers "owns heap" -- the conservative
direction, since being wrong that way costs a missed optimization rather than a
dangling read.

FIXTURES. `e2e_optres_struct_payload_read_only_arm_does_not_take_the_payload`
(codegen) pins all four broken shapes plus the scalar-struct control, and
`asan_optres_struct_payload_read_only_arm_is_a_borrow` (memory_sanitizer) is the
one that catches the actual defect: an output assertion only fails a
use-after-free when the freed block happens to have been reused, while ASAN
fails on the read. RED-verified -- pre-fix the ASAN twin reports
`ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free ... in memcpy` and the E2E twin
fails on the second read. The ASAN twin also guards the opposite error: these
arms are borrows now, so an owner that went missing would leak, which the Linux
CI leg's LeakSanitizer fails on.
title: THE STRUCT-PAYLOAD RESIDUAL OF B-2026-08-08-25: a read-only `match` arm over an `Option[S]` / `Result[S, E]` whose STRUCT payload carries heap still takes the payload, so a later read of the source is a use-after-free that prints garbage on the JIT and both AOT legs while `--interp` is correct. The borrow classification admits only a DIRECT `{ptr,len,cap}` payload (`String` / `Vec`), and a struct that merely CONTAINS one is not admitted. The same struct inside a USER enum variant is correct, so it is the built-in `Option`/`Result` channel specifically; the `Result` leg fails differently (valgrind-clean, second read empty)
detail:
THE STRUCT-PAYLOAD RESIDUAL OF B-2026-08-08-25. That row made a read-only
`match` arm over a live `Option`/`Result` local a BORROW, so the source keeps
its payload and a later read is valid. The classification admits only a DIRECT
`{ptr,len,cap}` payload -- `pattern_binds_direct_inline_heap_payload` requires
the bound type to be `String` or `Vec`. A STRUCT payload that merely CONTAINS a
`String` is not admitted, so the arm still takes the payload, the source is left
dangling, and the second read is a use-after-free.

    struct S { s: String }
    fn main() {
        let b: Option[S] = Some(S { s: f"hello" });
        match b { Some(p) => { println(p.s); } None => {} }
        match b { Some(q) => println(q.s), None => println("n") }
    }

      karac run --interp   ->  hello / hello        (correct)
      karac run (JIT)      ->  hello / <garbage>
      karac build          ->  hello / <garbage>
      KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0     ->  hello / <garbage>

    valgrind: Invalid read of size 2 in memmove, "Address .. is 0 bytes inside
    a block of size 5 free'd" -- the `String` buffer of `S.s`, freed by the
    first arm and read by the second.

SO IT IS A SILENT WRONG ANSWER, not a crash: the program prints, exits 0, and
the second line is whatever was left in the freed block. All three COMPILED
backends agree with each other and disagree with the interpreter, which is the
run-vs-build signature.

THE BOUNDARY, measured on the same read-then-read shape (each program: interp vs
JIT vs default AOT vs `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` AOT, plus valgrind `--leak-check=full`):

    Option[String]              correct         Option[(String, i64)]  correct
    Result[String, i64]         correct         Option[i64]            correct
    Option[Vec[i64]]            correct         enum E { A(String) }   correct
    enum E { A(S) }             correct         Option[S{n: i64}]      correct
    Option[S{s: String}]        USE-AFTER-FREE (valgrind invalid read)
    Option[S{v: Vec[i64]}]      USE-AFTER-FREE (valgrind invalid read)
    Result[S{s: String}, i64]   WRONG OUTPUT (prints empty; valgrind CLEAN)

Two things that boundary settles. It is the WRAPPING that matters, not the
struct: the same struct inside a USER enum variant is correct, so only the
built-in `Option`/`Result` channel is affected. And a struct payload with no
heap in it is fine, so the trigger is a heap-owning FIELD reached one hop below
the bound payload rather than the payload itself.

The `Result` leg fails DIFFERENTLY -- valgrind-clean, second read empty -- so it
is the payload being moved out and zeroed rather than freed-then-read. Same
root (the arm is not a borrow) but not the same failure, and a fix should be
checked against both legs rather than the `Option` one alone.

FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-30-10, which removed the (unrelated, and wrong)
`value 'b' moved here, used again here` warning this program used to draw. That
warning was NOT a guard: it is advisory, the build proceeds regardless, and its
text describes a move rather than a use-after-free -- but it does mean this shape
is now silent at check time as well as at run time, which is why the row is
filed high rather than medium.

fix:
FIXED by f1bb1102, together with its sibling B-2026-08-30-21 -- same root, one
table over.

`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`'s fn-call arm matched a bare
`ExprKind::Identifier` callee only, exactly as the row predicted, so
`s1(H.mkr(1))` -- a two-segment `Path` callee -- matched nothing and the
argument was classified as carrying no user `Drop`. `declare_function` already
keys impl fns as `Type.method` in the very table the arm reads, so only the KEY
had to be built from the qualified spelling.

FIXED ON THE INTERPRETER TOO, which the row's "ALL THREE BACKENDS AGREE" makes
necessary rather than optional. The interpreter's fn-returned Drop-temp
classifier had the same hole one arm over: its `Path` arm recognised a qualified
UNIT VARIANT (`Sig.B`) but not an associated fn, so it also gave the argument no
owner. A codegen-only fix was measured mid-work and did exactly what the row
implies it would -- JIT and AOT started printing `dR1` while `--interp` stayed
silent, converting a uniform wrong answer into a run-vs-build divergence. The
new `assoc_fn_return_type_name` resolver is fail-closed on an ambiguous
`Type.method` (two impls, or a non-path target), matching the sibling lookups in
that file: running a `Drop` body against the wrong type is worse than the leak
it would paper over.

MEASURED: `v=7` with no body on all four surfaces before, `dR1 v=7` on all four
after, identical to the free-producer oracle. Valgrind at `-O0`: 76 bytes
definitely lost before, 0 errors after. The `-O0` qualifier is the row's and it
is right -- at `-O2` the callee ignores its parameter and LLVM deletes the
allocation, so the leak is invisible in an optimized measurement.

Twinned in both test files, which is possible precisely because all four
surfaces agree once both halves land -- unlike its sibling, whose interpreter
half is still held by B-2026-08-30-22.
title: AN ARGUMENT PRODUCED BY AN ASSOCIATED CALL HAS NO OWNER ON ANY BACKEND -- `s1(H.mkr(1))` where `H.mkr` is an `impl` block's associated fn runs NO `Drop` body on interp, JIT and AOT (the free-function producer `s1(mkr2(1))` runs it) and leaks the payload at -O0; all three backends agree, so only an absolute expectation against the free-fn spelling sees it
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-54, by sweeping the argument-ownership surface
for shapes that fix does NOT reach, and measured identical before and after it.

    struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> String { f"pay-{i}-aaaa...(78 bytes)" }
    struct H { n: i64 }
    impl H { fn mkr(i: i64) -> R { R { id: i, s: mk(i) } } }
    fn s1(a: R) -> i64 { 7 }
    fn main() { let v = s1(H.mkr(1)); println(f"v={v}") }

      karac run --interp  -> `v=7`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `v=7`
      karac build         -> `v=7`   + 78 bytes definitely lost at -O0

The FREE-FUNCTION producer is clean on all three: replacing `H.mkr(1)` with a
plain `mkr2(1)` gives `dR1 v=7` and no leak. So this is the PRODUCER, not the
callee -- and note the callee here is a free function, so it is not the
B-2026-08-29-54 arm reappearing. `H.s1(mkr(1))` (assoc callee, free producer) is
also clean post-fix. Only an argument PRODUCED BY an associated call has no
owner.

ALL THREE BACKENDS AGREE on the missing body, so no A/B parity gate and no
run-vs-build comparison can see it; only an absolute expectation against the
free-function spelling can. The leak is compiled-only and `-O0`-only -- at `-O2`
the callee ignores its parameter, so LLVM deletes the allocation and the leak
disappears from the measurement (the same masking that mis-graded
B-2026-08-29-54; measure this class at `-O0`).

WHERE TO START. `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`'s fn-call arm resolves the
producing function's return type through
`self.fn_sig.fn_return_type_names.get(fn_name)`, keyed on an `ExprKind::Call`
whose callee is a bare `ExprKind::Identifier`. `H.mkr(1)` is neither -- it is the
qualified spelling -- so the arm matches nothing and the argument is classified
as carrying no user `Drop`. The fix is presumably to resolve the qualified
`Type.method` key the same way (`find_function_ast` already does, and
`fn_return_type_names` is populated for impl-block methods under that key), but
the interpreter loses the body too, so its twin
(`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`' type-name resolution) needs the same widening or
the fix opens a divergence in the other direction.

fix:
FIXED by f1bb1102, together with its sibling B-2026-08-30-20 -- one root in two
tables: the qualified `Type.method` callee spelling is not resolved where a bare
identifier is.

The let-binding type hint's UFCS arm read `segments[0]`, the type the fn is
DECLARED ON, and accepted it whenever that type's LLVM shape matched the value's.
That is a CONSTRUCTOR assumption -- `Type.new()` does return `Type` -- and for
`impl H { fn id(a: R) -> R }` the two are unrelated, so the shape test is a
COINCIDENCE FILTER. When it passed, the binding was recorded as the HOLDER `H`,
which is why symptom 1 reads "cannot resolve field 'id'": `H` genuinely has no
`id`. When it failed, nothing was recorded and symptom 2's body was lost. Both
fall out of consulting `fn_return_type_names` for the callee's declared return
type, which `declare_function` already keys as `Type.method`.

THIS ROW'S STATED GATE IS WRONG, and the correction is the useful part.
"ALL-SCALAR IS THE GATE" and "give `R` a single heap field and BOTH symptoms
vanish" are both reproducible and both mis-generalized. Measured:

    R { id: i64 }   beside  H { n: i64 }    -> FAILS
    R { id: i64 }   beside  H { n: f64 }    -> WORKS  (same R, same all-scalar)
    R { f: f64 }    beside  H { n: f64 }    -> FAILS  (not about i64)
    R { a, b: i64 } beside  H { p, q: i64 } -> FAILS  (not about field count)

The real gate is an LLVM-SHAPE COLLISION between the returned struct and any
other registered struct: on a collision the holder guess fires and records the
wrong type; without one it declines and the ambiguity-limited shape fallback
(B-2026-07-20-9) refuses to guess, leaving the binding unregistered. The row's
heap-field experiment worked only because it moved `R`'s shape away from `H`'s
-- it changed the field COUNT, not the heap-ness. That is the same confound as
B-2026-08-31-20's `Vec.push` control, which is worth noting as a pattern: a
control that varies two things at once confirms whichever one the author had in
mind.

SYMPTOM 2 IS THE SERIOUS HALF and is now covered: a `Drop` impl that closes an
fd or releases a lock ran not at all, with no diagnostic. The fix restores it,
verified against the free-function spelling (`dR1 mid`) on all three compiled
surfaces.

INTERPRETER NOT TWINNED, deliberately. `--interp` runs an EXTRA body for this
shape -- B-2026-08-30-22, open, and measured identical before and after this
change -- so a twinned fixture would pin that defect's output. The E2E states
the free-function oracle's answer and asserts the compiled surfaces only; the
pair goes from (interp 2 / compiled 0) to (interp 2 / compiled 1), so -22 is now
the only thing keeping them apart.

The CONSTRUCTOR path the old heuristic existed for is kept as a fallback for
callees that never reach `fn_return_type_names` (compiler builtins such as
`Stats.min`), and `P.new() -> P` is pinned in the fixture.
title: AN ASSOCIATED CALL RETURNING AN ALL-SCALAR STRUCT RECORDS NO TYPE FOR ITS RESULT: a field read off it is a HARD `karac build` failure (`cannot resolve field 'id' on this receiver`) and the result binding's own `Drop` body is silently LOST -- both vanish the moment the struct gains one heap field, and the free-function spelling is correct throughout
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-54 and measured identical before and after it.
TWO SYMPTOMS, one root: an associated call returning an ALL-SCALAR struct
records no type for its result binding.

Symptom 1 -- a HARD `karac build` failure on a field read:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    struct H { n: i64 }
    impl H { fn id(a: R) -> R { a } }
    fn main() { let x = H.id(R { id: 1 }); println(f"x={x.id}") }

      karac run --interp  -> `dR1 dR1 mid`-class output, runs fine
      karac build         -> error: codegen: cannot resolve field 'id' on this
                            receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen)

Symptom 2 -- the result binding's own `Drop` body is LOST, same shape without
the field read:

    fn main() { let x = H.id(R { id: 1 }); println("mid") }

      karac run --interp  -> `dR1 mid`
      karac build         -> `mid`          (no body at all)

The FREE-FUNCTION spelling is correct for both: `fn idf(a: R) -> R { a }` called
as `idf(R { id: 1 })` builds, and prints `dR1 mid`.

ALL-SCALAR IS THE GATE, which is what makes this easy to miss. Give `R` a single
heap field (`s: String`) and BOTH symptoms vanish -- the field read compiles and
the body runs on every backend. A heap field is what causes the binding's type to
be recorded, so the defect only shows for structs made entirely of scalars, i.e.
the shape least likely to be reached for while chasing memory bugs.

Symptom 1 is LOUD -- codegen's own "please report it" guard, which exists so this
class cannot fall through to an `i64 0` placeholder (B-2026-07-20-9) -- and joins
a long-standing family of the same message (B-2026-08-12-28, B-2026-08-14-5,
B-2026-08-28-34 among others), each of which was one unrecorded receiver source.
Symptom 2 is SILENT and is the more serious half: a `Drop` impl that closes an fd
or releases a lock simply does not run, with no diagnostic.

WHERE TO START. Whatever populates the let-binding's type for a call result --
the same table the free-function path fills from `fn_return_type_names` -- is not
filled from the `Type.method` arm of `compile_assoc_call` for a struct with no
heap field. Both symptoms should fall out of recording it there; check the
Drop-registration half explicitly, since a resolver-only fix would make the field
read compile while the body stays lost.

fix:
FIXED by 491dd0e5. The row's "WHERE TO START" was right about the function and
right to warn about the three-way asymmetry.

`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` fires a fresh-temp argument's body as the call
returns and suppresses that when the callee can RETURN the parameter. Both of
its guards -- the B-2026-07-01-7 passthrough guard and the B-2026-08-26-9
outliving-place guard -- searched `Item::Function`, i.e. FREE functions only.
`Value::Function` carries just the BARE name, so an associated callee arrives as
`id` rather than `H.id` and matches nothing: no suppression, so the temp's body
ran at the call and the result binding's ran at scope exit.

THE THREE ROUTES ARE THE EVIDENCE, and the row was right to say to check which
one the assoc arm uses before widening anything. Measured: free-fn correct,
METHOD correct, associated wrong. The method path claims its arguments through
the callee frame (`method_param_drop_names`) and so never consults these guards
at all -- the assoc arm is a genuine third case, exactly as B-2026-08-29-46's
note recorded, not a variant of either neighbour.

THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE ROOT, in three different tables, all landed this session:
B-2026-08-30-21 read the HOLDER as a call's return type; B-2026-08-30-20 matched
only a bare `Identifier` callee in the argument-owner tracker; this row searches
only free functions. Each produced a different wrong answer -- wrong binding
type, missing owner, duplicated body -- for the same `Type.method` spelling.

RESOLUTION IS STRICTLY ADDITIVE. A free function of the name still wins, so no
existing resolution changes; an inherent-impl method is consulted only when no
free function claims the name AND exactly one impl offers it. Ambiguity yields
`None`, leaving the guards at today's answer rather than guessing: suppressing
against the wrong candidate would STRAND the body instead of duplicating it,
which trades a double-run for a leak. That direction matters here because a
duplicated `Drop` is the more visible failure and the easier one to be tempted
into over-fixing.

CLOSES THE SPLIT B-2026-08-30-21 LEFT. That row's programs went from (interp 2 /
compiled 0) to (interp 2 / compiled 1) when it landed, and now agree 1/1 on all
four surfaces. Its fixture comment, which said this row was open and that
twinning would pin its output, is corrected in the same commit.
title: THE INTERPRETER RUNS AN EXTRA `Drop` BODY FOR AN ASSOCIATED-FN PASSTHROUGH ARGUMENT -- `let x = H.id(R { .. })` where `fn id(a: R) -> R { a }` prints `dR1 x=1 dR1` under `--interp` against `x=1 dR1` on JIT and AOT; here the COMPILED backends are the oracle (they match the free-function spelling on all three) and the interpreter double-fires
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-54 and measured identical before and after it --
the fix is on the compiled side and the compiled side is the one that is RIGHT
here, which is why this is filed rather than folded in.

    struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> String { f"pay-{i}-aaaa...(78 bytes)" }
    struct H { n: i64 }
    impl H { fn id(a: R) -> R { a } }
    fn main() { let x = H.id(R { id: 1, s: mk(1) }); println(f"x={x.id}") }

      karac run --interp  -> `dR1 x=1 dR1`     TWO bodies for ONE object
      karac run (JIT)     -> `x=1 dR1`
      karac build         -> `x=1 dR1`         + valgrind clean

The FREE-FUNCTION spelling is correct on all three (`x=1 dR1`), so this is the
associated-call arm of the interpreter specifically. The callee hands its
argument straight back, so the caller's RESULT binding owns it and exactly one
body is due; the interpreter fires the argument temporary's body at the call AND
the binding's at scope exit.

THE COMPILED BACKENDS ARE THE ORACLE HERE, unusually for this family. Both agree
with the free-function spelling on both backends, and the memory is provably
single-free (valgrind clean, 0 errors). A duplicated `Drop` body is not a
harmless print: the same body that double-prints would double-release a lock,
double-decrement a refcount, or close an fd twice.

WHERE TO START. The interpreter's `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` fires a fresh-temp
argument's body as the call returns. For a passthrough callee the free-function
path suppresses that (the value flows out to the caller's binding); the
associated-call path evidently does not consult the same predicate. Note the
interpreter's own METHOD path takes a third route again -- arguments are claimed
by the callee frame through `method_param_drop_names` -- so check which of the
three the assoc arm is actually using before widening anything;
B-2026-08-29-46's fix note records that this three-way asymmetry is real and
that the assoc arm is a third case rather than a variant of the other two.

fix:
FIXED by 92b3a50 for eleven of the twelve cells on the compiled backends and ten
of twelve under `--interp`. TWO INTERPRETER-ONLY CELLS REMAIN, both on the
ASSOCIATED spelling, and they are recorded below rather than closed over.

THE ROW'S PLAN IS REFUTED A SECOND TIME, and in the cheaper direction. The
2026-09-01 investigation correctly refuted the ORIGINAL prescription (a
predicate swap) and replaced it with "extend B-2026-08-28-51's per-path flag to
`return`-borne escapes ... in both `arm_conditional_move_tail_flag` (codegen)
and `record_conditional_move_tail` (interpreter), and then relax condition 4."
No part of that was needed:

  * CONDITION 4 WAS ALREADY RELAXED. `collect_return_leaves` folds every
    `return` operand into the leaf set, so the `return` spelling is analysed
    exactly like the block-tail one. The doc comment still described the old
    behaviour, which is what the plan was written against; it is corrected in
    place.
  * THE PER-PATH FLAG ALREADY REACHES THESE SHAPES. Nothing in either backend's
    flag machinery was touched.

WHAT ACTUALLY DECLINED THE ROW'S OWN REPRODUCER was condition 3, via
`may_mention`'s catch-all. That helper answers "might this leaf mention the
parameter", conservatively `true` for any shape it does not recognise -- and it
did not recognise a CALL. The row's `pick` has `mk(98)` in the arm that does NOT
hand `a` back, so the leaf whose whole job is to not mention `a` was read as
possibly mentioning it, and the whole function was declined.

THE ONE-LINE EXPERIMENT THAT LOCALISED IT, worth repeating before trusting any
diagnosis in this family: replace `mk(98)` with a string literal and change
nothing else. Both directions then print correctly on all four lanes with no
compiler change at all. That is what moved the search from the flag machinery
(two backends, a documented double-free failure mode) to a predicate helper.

THE FIX, two parts:

  1. `may_mention` (src/ast/items.rs) gains `Call` and `MethodCall` arms: a call
     mentions the parameter exactly when its callee expression or one of its
     arguments does. Faithful rather than permissive -- `consume(a)` and
     `a.take()` still recurse to the bare identifier and still decline, so no
     escape the flag cannot clear is admitted. Every other shape keeps the
     catch-all.
  2. `compile_assoc_call` gains the BINDING-argument body retraction that
     `compile_call` and `compile_method_call` have had for months. That arm had
     NONE of the three (`callee_takes_over_arg_drop_body`,
     `suppress_user_drop_body_keeping_memory`,
     `suppress_container_elem_bodies_for_var`) -- the same third-dispatch-arm
     omission B-2026-08-29-54 records for the registrar beside it.

THE ROW'S MATRIX WAS WRONG IN THREE CELLS, re-measured on current `main` before
any change. It reported `free/named/k=false` and `assoc/named/k=false` as
"correct, all 4"; both were DOUBLED. It reported `method/named/k=true` as
doubled under `--interp`; it was correct. Its headline cell was accurate. This
is not drift from the intervening commits -- the same three cells measure
identically at `02814a8`, yesterday's tip, so the matrix was mis-recorded rather
than overtaken.

MEASURED, twelve cells x four lanes, before -> after (correct is one body per
object: at k=true `d<arg>` before the caller's print, at k=false the print then
`d<arg>`):

    free  / fresh / true     body LOST, all 4      -> correct
    free  / named / false    DOUBLED, all 4        -> correct
    method/ fresh / false    DOUBLED, compiled     -> correct
    method/ named / false    DOUBLED, all 4        -> correct
    assoc / named / false    DOUBLED, all 4        -> correct on compiled;
                                                     STILL DOUBLED under --interp
    assoc / named / true      correct              -> correct
    assoc / fresh / true     LOST under --interp   -> unchanged
    the other five cells      correct              -> correct

Fixtures: `codegen_conditional_return_param_drop_matrix` (tests/codegen.rs) pins
all twelve cells on the compiled lanes, and
`test_conditional_return_param_drop_matrix` (tests/interpreter.rs) pins ten of

pre-fix.

STILL OPEN, the two interpreter-only associated cells:
`H.apick(R { .. }, true)` runs NO body for the dying argument, and
`H.apick(r, false)` runs TWO for the returned one. Compiled lanes are correct

ONE DEAD END RECORDED so it is not repeated: `cond_returned_param_drop_names`
(src/interpreter/eval_call.rs) early-returns for any dotted callee, commented
"free functions only". Lifting that for associated functions specifically --

title: THE FREE-FUNCTION SPELLING OF A CONDITIONAL RETURN LOSES THE DYING PARAMETER'S `Drop` BODY on all three backends -- `fn pick(a: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return R { id: 98 }; } a }` at `k = true` never runs `a`'s body, while the METHOD and ASSOCIATED spellings of the same function do; the free-fn arm is the last one still gated on the union-over-return-sites predicate
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-54, which fixed this shape for the ASSOCIATED
spelling and left the free-function one behind. Measured identical before and
after that commit.

    struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> String { f"pay-{i}-aaaa...(78 bytes)" }
    fn pick(a: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return R { id: 98, s: mk(98) }; } a }
    fn main() { let x = pick(R { id: 1, s: mk(1) }, true); println(f"x={x.id}") }

      karac run --interp  -> `x=98 dR98`
      karac run (JIT)     -> `x=98 dR98`
      karac build         -> `x=98 dR98`   + valgrind clean

`a` is NOT returned on this path -- `k` is true, so the callee returns a freshly
built `R { id: 98 }` and `a` dies at the callee's scope exit. Its `Drop` body
must run. No backend runs it.

THE METHOD AND ASSOCIATED SPELLINGS OF THE SAME FUNCTION BOTH DO, on all three
backends, which is what localizes this to the free-function arm rather than to a
policy about conditional returns:

    impl H { fn pick(ref self, a: R, k: bool) -> R { ... } }   -> `dR1 x=98 dR98`
    impl H { fn pick(a: R, k: bool) -> R { ... } }             -> `dR1 x=98 dR98`

A LOST BODY, NOT A LEAK -- deliberately distinguished rather than assumed.
Valgrind at `-O0` is clean for all three spellings, so `a`'s buffer is freed on
every one of them; the free-function spelling frees it without running the user
body. That is the same body-vs-memory split B-2026-08-29-24 and B-2026-08-29-54
both turned on.

WHERE TO START. `compile_call`'s registrar gates on
`call_arg_flows_into_return`, the union over return SITES, which answers true for
a parameter returned on ANY path -- so the caller stands down even on the path
where the parameter dies, and nothing else picks it up. The method arm was moved
off that predicate by B-2026-08-28-70 onto the pair
`fn_always_returns_param || fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare`, whose second leg
hands ownership to the callee-side per-path flip (B-2026-08-28-51); the
associated arm was built on that same pair by B-2026-08-29-54. The free-function
arm is the last one still on the union predicate. That row's note already
records the measurement -- standing the caller down on the union "measurably
lost `fn early(ref self, r: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return R { id: 98 }; } r }`'s
body for `r` at `k = true`" -- so this is that exact defect, left in place on the
one arm the row was not about.

ALL THREE BACKENDS AGREE, so no A/B parity gate can see it; it needs an absolute
expectation, ideally asserted against the method and associated spellings of the
same source so the three arms cannot drift again.

MEASURED 2026-09-01, AND THIS ROW'S PRESCRIPTION IS REFUTED. Do not implement
it: moving the free-fn arm onto `fn_always_returns_param ||
fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` trades a LOST body for a DOUBLED one,
because the method arm it names as the model has the complementary defect.

THE FULL MATRIX. Same callee body in all six cells --
`fn pick(a: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return R { id: 98, s: mk(98) }; } return a; }`
-- varying only the call spelling and the ARGUMENT shape, which this row does
not vary at all. Correct is `dR1 x=98 dR98` at k=true and `x=1 dR1` at k=false.

    spelling  argument     k=true (a dies)          k=false (a is returned)
    --------  -----------  -----------------------  ------------------------
    free      fresh temp   body LOST, all 4 lanes   correct, all 4
    free      named local  correct, all 4           correct, all 4
    assoc     fresh temp   body LOST under --interp correct, all 4
                           only; compiled lanes ok
    assoc     named local  correct, all 4           correct, all 4
    method    fresh temp   correct, all 4           body DOUBLED on JIT/AOT
                                                    (`dR1 x=1 dR1`), interp ok
    method    named local  body DOUBLED under       correct, all 4
                           --interp (`dR1 dR1 ...`)

So three of six cells are wrong, in TWO directions, and the row's claim that
"the METHOD AND ASSOCIATED SPELLINGS ... both do, on all three backends" holds
only for the argument shape it happened to test. The free-fn cell it reports is
real; the model it points at is not a model.

WHY THE NAMED SPELLING LOOKS RIGHT, which is what hid this: the caller's own
local binding has an independent drop that fires regardless of the argument
protocol. It covers the free-fn loss by accident, which is why the row's
reproducer needed a fresh temp to show anything.

THE ACTUAL MECHANISM, instrumented rather than inferred. For this `pick`:

    fn_always_returns_param(f, 0)              = false
    fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare(f, 0)  = false
    fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place(f, 0)  = false

Both legs of the pair are FALSE, so the pair does not mean "the callee owns
it" here -- it means "nobody has claimed it". The two arms then pick opposite
defaults from that same non-answer: the free-fn arm consults
`call_arg_flows_into_return` (the union over return sites), gets true, and
stands the caller down with no other owner -> LOST. The method arm consults the
pair, gets false, and registers the caller unconditionally -> DOUBLED wherever
the callee really does hand the param back. Neither is per-path, which is the
only thing that would be right.

`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` declines by DESIGN, and its own doc says
why -- condition 4: "No `return` statement anywhere in the body mentions the
parameter. Codegen clears the flag at match arms and block tails but NOT at a
`return` operand (it suppresses those statically instead), so a `return`-borne
escape is outside this mechanism's reach. That shape is B-2026-08-28-65 / -52
and is deliberately left to them." Both of those rows are CLOSED, so the shape
has no owner anywhere. The tail spelling `{ if k { return .. } a }` is declined
too, by condition 2: its tail expression has a single leaf, so there is no
"other leaf tail that does not mention the parameter".

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT: extend B-2026-08-28-51's per-path conditional-move
flag to `return`-borne escapes -- clear it at a `return <param>` operand in both
`arm_conditional_move_tail_flag` (codegen) and `record_conditional_move_tail`
(interpreter) -- and then relax condition 4, which is the single line keeping
this shape out of the mechanism built for it. Once the callee-side flip owns the
param per path, BOTH arms can stand down on the pair and all six cells follow.
The risk is the interaction the doc flags in passing ("it suppresses those
statically instead"): a static suppression plus a dynamic flag on the same exit
is how a double free gets built, so the two have to be reconciled rather than
stacked, and every cell above needs re-measuring at k=true AND k=false.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE. This is a mechanism extension across two backends with a
double-free failure mode, not the predicate swap the row describes, and shipping
the swap would have moved the defect rather than removed it. Severity stays
soundness: a `Drop` body that never runs is an unreleased lock or an unclosed fd,
and the doubled cells are the same body running twice on one object.

fix:
FIXED by 240919c. `runtime/src/f16.rs` defines the two missing
compiler-rt builtins for wasm targets, so an f16 program links and runs.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS HELD, AND ITS PROPOSED "SMALLER CHANGE" DOES NOT EXIST.
It offered two shapes: supply the builtins to the wasm link, or give f16 the
integer-shift treatment bf16 has, and called the first smaller. The first is
smaller, but not in the form the row imagined -- there is no archive to add.
Measured with `llvm-nm`, `__extendhfsf2` / `__truncsfhf2` are in NONE of:
the wasm runtime archive, Rust's `libcompiler_builtins` rlib for
`wasm32-wasip1` (which does ship a builtins set -- `__absvdi2`, `__muldc3`
and friends are all present, just not the f16 family), or wasi-libc's
`libc.a`. There is no `libclang_rt.builtins-wasm32.a` in the rustup
self-contained sysroot either. So "add it to the link line" had nothing to
point at, and the fix is to DEFINE them.

The second shape was rejected for a reason worth recording: it does not
work. Emitting the conversions inline in codegen would not remove the
libcall, because LLVM legalizes f16 ARITHMETIC into the same two calls on
its own (see the `llc` output in the sibling row below). Avoiding them
entirely would mean widening every f16 op on wasm — a far larger change than
the one the linking bug needs, and a second f16 semantics path alongside the
native one.

THE ABI WAS READ, NOT GUESSED. `llc-18 -mtriple=wasm32-unknown-wasi` on a
two-line `.ll` declares `__truncsfhf2 (f32) -> (i32)` and `__extendhfsf2
(i32) -> (f32)` in the object's type section: the half travels as its 16-bit
pattern widened into an i32, and a `half` ARGUMENT arrives already widened to
f32 (an `fpext half to float` on wasm compiles to nothing at all). Worth
knowing that this differs from the x86-64 host, where `__extendhfsf2` takes
`_Float16` in an SSE register -- so a native harness CANNOT call the host
builtin to cross-check that direction. Calling it with a `u16` returns 0.0
for every input, which looks like a broken implementation rather than a
broken call.

THE ROUNDING IS THE INTERPRETER'S ALGORITHM, AND THAT IS NOW A MEASURED
CLAIM RATHER THAN AN INTENTION. `f32_to_f16_bits` is copied from
`src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs`, and before copying it, it was compared
against the HOST's compiler-rt `__truncsfhf2` over ALL 2^32 f32 bit
patterns, NaN payloads included: ZERO differences. So agreeing with the
interpreter and agreeing with every native target are the same thing here,
and the wasm backend now joins both by construction.

THE EXTEND DIRECTION WAS WRONG IN THE FIRST DRAFT, AND ONLY THE EXHAUSTIVE
CHECK CAUGHT IT. `f16_bits_to_f32`'s subnormal renormalization had the
exponent and the mantissa shift each off by one. It was correct on all 63490
normal / Inf / NaN patterns and wrong on all 2046 subnormal ones -- the
smallest subnormal came out at half its value. Every hand-picked spot check
would have passed; the 2^16 sweep against an independent arithmetic
derivation failed 2046 times and named the branch. It now reports zero
mismatches on all three checks (value, round-trip through the trusted host
`__truncsfhf2`, and signed zero).

VERIFICATION, END TO END. `node`'s `node:wasi` runs a preview-1 module, so
this was checked by RUNNING and not only by linking. A 22-line f16 sweep
(conversions at the normal, subnormal, overflow and negative-zero branches,
plus arithmetic, comparisons, vector ops and reductions) is byte-identical
between the native binary, `karac run --interp`, and the wasm module under
node -- on 21 of its 22 lines. The 22nd is the sibling row below.
Both wasm legs link: `--target=wasm_wasi` and `--target=wasm_browser`,
including the dual-artifact `--features=wasm-threads` build, since the
builtins are gated on `target_family = "wasm"` and land in both archives.

TESTS. Three unit tests in `runtime/src/f16.rs`: the 2^16 exhaustive extend
check (with a deliberately different, arithmetic derivation as the oracle),
the round-trip over the whole domain, and a table of the boundaries a
round-trip cannot reach (ties in both directions, the overflow edge at
65520, both ends of the subnormal range, negative zero, NaN quieting).
`tests/cli.rs::wasm_f16_conversion_build_and_run_e2e` is the end-to-end
half: it builds for `wasm_wasi` and runs under `node:wasi`, asserting the
native output. Pre-fix it FAILS -- checked by stashing the module, rebuilding
the archive and running it -- rather than skipping, because an
undefined-symbol link error is not one of the infrastructure walls
`failed_wasm_build_skip_reason` treats as a skip.

Its receiver derives from `env.args().len()` for a load-bearing reason: with
a literal, LLVM folds the conversion, emits no libcall, and the module links
whether or not the fix is present. That is not hypothetical -- the first
`wasm_browser` probe taken while filing this row used literals, linked
cleanly, and briefly suggested the bug was `wasm_wasi`-only.

FILED SEPARATELY: B-2026-08-30-32. Once programs could link, a second defect
became observable underneath this one -- LLVM-18 promotes f16 ARITHMETIC to
f32 on wasm32 and never rounds the result back, so `65504 * 3` yields a
finite 196512 where f16 must overflow to `inf`. It is not caused by this fix
(nothing linked before it, so nothing could have observed it) and not fixed
by it.
title: NO `f16` PROGRAM LINKS FOR A WASM TARGET: LLVM lowers `half` to the `__extendhfsf2` / `__truncsfhf2` compiler-rt builtins and the wasm link line has neither, so a bare runtime `as f16` conversion fails `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` with a raw rust-lld undefined-symbol dump. `bf16` links fine, because its conversions are emitted as integer shifts instead
detail:
NO `f16` PROGRAM CAN BE LINKED FOR A WASM TARGET. The compiler emits the
promotion libcalls LLVM lowers `half` to, and the wasm link has neither of
them:

    karac build --target=wasm_wasi --bindings none prog.kara
    rust-lld: error: undefined symbol: __extendhfsf2
    rust-lld: error: undefined symbol: __truncsfhf2

REPRODUCTION -- a bare CONVERSION is enough; no arithmetic, no vectors:

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let a: f16 = ((n + 3) as f32) as f16;
        println(f"{a}");
    }

    karac build                                     works, prints 4
    karac build --target=wasm_wasi --bindings none  undefined __extendhfsf2 / __truncsfhf2

The value must be RUNTIME-derived. With literals (`let a: f16 = 4.0f16;`) LLVM
folds the conversion away, no libcall is emitted, and the link SUCCEEDS -- so a
probe built from constants reports health here. That is the same vacuity trap
B-2026-08-29-34 and B-2026-08-29-61 describe, and it is why this went unnoticed:
`env.args()` is not available on `--target=wasm_browser`, so the obvious opaque
seed is unavailable on the target where one would reach for it.

SCOPE, measured on `--target=wasm_wasi --bindings none`:

    f16  scalar conversion  `((n+3) as f32) as f16`      FAILS
    f16  scalar arithmetic  `a + b`                      FAILS
    f16  vector unary math  `Vector[f16,4].tanh()`       FAILS
    bf16 scalar arithmetic  `a + b`                      LINKS
    f32  scalar arithmetic  `a + 1.0f32`                 LINKS

bf16 is the instructive contrast and points straight at the fix. It links
because codegen never emits an `fpext bfloat` at all: `emit_bf16_to_f32` /
`emit_f32_to_bf16` do the conversion with pure integer shifts (added for LLVM
18's aarch64 ISel, B-2026-08-29-34/-42). f16 has no such path, so LLVM's
legalizer emits the compiler-rt builtins -- which are simply not in the wasm
link line, though they ARE in the native one (an x86-64 baseline calls
`__extendhfsf2` too, per `src/target.rs`'s measured table, and links fine
because the system toolchain supplies compiler-rt/libgcc).

THE COMPILER ALREADY KNOWS. `warning[f16_software_emulated]` fires on this
build and says LLVM "promotes each operation to `f32` and rounds back";
`src/target.rs:92` and `src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs:1939` both name
`__extendhfsf2` / `__truncsfhf2` as the wasm lowering by name. The diagnostic
describes the mechanism and the link then fails on it, which is a good sign
this is an omission rather than a decision.

FIX SHAPE (not attempted). Either supply the two builtins to the wasm link --
they are compiler-rt symbols, and the wasm runtime archive is already built
separately for this target -- or give f16 the integer-shift treatment bf16 has
(narrower, but f16's round-to-nearest with subnormals is more work than bf16's
high-half truncation). The first is the smaller change; the second removes a
link-line dependency on every target.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-29-53's fix, and not fixed by it: measured identical
before and after, on all five shapes above. Found while checking that the
widening that fix introduces did not add a wasm dependency -- it does not, and
in fact emits FEWER of these libcalls (one pair per body instead of one pair
per op).

SEVERITY. `f16` is documented as a supported element type and `wasm_wasi` /
`wasm_browser` as supported targets; their intersection is empty and fails at
link time with a raw linker message rather than a diagnostic. Whether that is
medium or low depends on whether f16-on-wasm is meant to work in v1 -- if it is
deliberately out of scope, the actionable half is a `karac build` diagnostic
saying so, not a `rust-lld` undefined-symbol dump.

fix:
FIXED by d4cda14. Two arms in `method_callee_type_name`
(src/typechecker/types.rs) plus the exhaustiveness measure the row asked for.

THE FIX ITSELF is exactly the two lines the row identified: `Type::Float(F16)`
and `Type::Float(BF16)` now return their names instead of falling to
`_ => None`, so the `if let Some(prim)` guard in `method_user_impl.rs` runs the
existence check for them as it already did for `f32` / `f64`. `karac check` now
reports `no method 'completely_bogus' on type 'f16'` where it printed "All
checks passed."

WHY TURNING THE CHECK ON IS SAFE, which was the one thing worth verifying
before touching it: the real narrow-float methods never reach this lookup.
`sqrt` / `floor` / `ceil` / `round` / `abs` / `ln` / `exp` / `sin` / `cos` /
`trunc` / `signum` / `to_string` are intercepted STRUCTURALLY on
`Type::Float(_)` in `method_numeric.rs`, well ahead of the name-keyed
`find_methods_with_args`. So the only names that arrive here are ones nothing
recognises. Measured all twelve on both `f16` and `bf16`, before and after: none
regressed, and they are now pinned by a test of their own rather than left to
the next reader to re-derive.

Distinct from `primitive_type_name` in `src/lowering.rs`, which B-2026-08-30-40
explicitly warns must NOT gain an `f16` arm (it would lower `a + b` to
`f16.add(a, b)` against an unreachable namespace). Different function, different
consumer, and that warning does not reach this one.

THE EXHAUSTIVENESS MEASURE, which is the part that outlives the two lines. The
row's closing argument was that a fix adding only the arms "leaves the next
instance to be discovered the same way", this being the THIRD instance of one
shape (B-2026-08-11-2 `char`/`bool`, B-2026-08-19-19 `i128`/`u128`, this row
`f16`/`bf16`). `every_primitive_receiver_rejects_an_invented_method` walks all
EIGHTEEN primitive receivers -- every integer width, every unsigned width, all
