four floats, `bool` and `char` -- and asserts an invented method is rejected on
each. It asserts the TYPE NAME in the message too, not merely that some error
fired, because an arm returning the wrong name would still reject the call while
naming a type the author never wrote -- which is the same defect one step over,
and is what the interpreter does today when it reports an `f16` receiver's
missing method "on type 'f64'".

A new primitive width added without an arm now fails immediately, and the
failure names the width. Measured: the sweep is RED on the pre-fix tree and
green after; the companion positive test
(`narrow_float_receivers_keep_their_real_methods`) passes on both, which is
correct -- it guards against the fix OVER-reaching, so it is not a witness for
the fix and must not look like one.

NOT FIXED HERE, and worth stating because the row's repro shows it: the
BACKEND messages remain wrong for a receiver whose method genuinely does not
exist. `karac build` still says "this is a codegen bug -- add a dispatcher arm
in `compile_method_call`", and `karac run --interp` still names type `f64` for
an `f16` receiver. Those are now unreachable through this door -- the
typechecker rejects first -- but they are reachable through any other primitive
hole of the same shape, and blaming the compiler for user error is its own
defect. Left alone rather than widened into: it needs a survey of which backend
messages are reachable at all now, which is a different piece of work.
title: THE TYPECHECKER ACCEPTS ANY METHOD NAME ON AN `f16` / `bf16` RECEIVER -- `karac check` prints "All checks passed." on `let s: String = a.completely_bogus();`, because `method_callee_type_name` has arms for F32 and F64 only and the `_ => None` fallthrough silently skips the existence check. The poisoned `Type::Error` then unifies with any use site, and the program dies in the backend with a message blaming the COMPILER
detail:
THE TYPECHECKER ACCEPTS ANY METHOD NAME ON AN `f16` OR `bf16` RECEIVER. Not a
missing method -- ANY name, including one that exists nowhere. `karac check`
prints "All checks passed." on this:

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let a: f16 = ((n + 1) as f32) as f16;
        let s: String = a.completely_bogus();
        let v: Vec[i64] = a.also_bogus();
        println(f"{s} {v.len()}");
    }

    karac check          All checks passed.
    karac build          error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method
                         'completely_bogus' ... (this is a codegen bug -- add a
                         dispatcher arm in `compile_method_call`)
    karac run --interp   runtime error: method 'completely_bogus' not found on
                         type 'f64' (no interpreter dispatch arm)

The SAME program with an `f32` receiver produces 2 typecheck errors, which is
the correct behaviour and the control.

Two consequences, and the second is the worse one. The return type poisons to
`Type::Error`, which is universally assignable -- so the invented call unifies
with `String` at one use site and `Vec[i64]` at the next, and neither is
flagged. And the failure the author eventually sees BLAMES THE COMPILER: the
codegen message tells them they have found a codegen bug and should go add a
dispatcher arm, and the interpreter message names type `f64` for an `f16`
receiver. A typo on an f16 method is user error and must not read as a compiler
defect.

MEASURED across the four float widths, with a real method the width does not
have (`sigmoid`, which is Vector/Tensor-only) and with an invented one:

    f32   .sigmoid / .not_a_real_method    typecheck REJECTS   (correct)
    f64   .sigmoid / .not_a_real_method    typecheck REJECTS   (correct)
    f16   .sigmoid / .not_a_real_method    typecheck ACCEPTS
    bf16  .sigmoid / .not_a_real_method    typecheck ACCEPTS

THE SITE, and it is two lines. `method_callee_type_name`
(`src/typechecker/types.rs:1081`) maps every primitive to its name for the
method-existence check in `src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs` -- and its
float arms are `Float(F32)` and `Float(F64)` only. `F16` / `BF16` fall to the
trailing `_ => None`, the `if let Some(prim)` guard skips the whole arm, and
the receiver drops onto the silent-poison fall-through.

THE GUARD ITSELF IS FINE -- `Type::Float(_)` in the `matches!` covers both
widths. It is only the name lookup inside it that comes back `None`.

THE SHAPE HAS RECURRED, which is the part worth acting on beyond the two lines.
A missing arm here is invisible to the compiler, so it is only ever found by
tripping over it:
  * B-2026-08-19-19 -- IN THIS FUNCTION: the `i128`/`u128` arms were missing,
    an `Option[i128]` payload binding got no width, and codegen bound the low
    word. The comment it left sits two arms above the float ones and says the
    `_ => None` fallthrough "made the omission invisible to the compiler".
  * B-2026-08-11-2 -- in the sibling GUARD, not this function, but the same
    silent-poison outcome: `char` and `bool` were "the ONLY receivers in the
    language that accepted any method name at all", with the same universally
    assignable `Type::Error` and the same you-found-a-codegen-bug message. Its
    fix comment is directly above the guard f16/bf16 now slip through.
  * this row -- `f16` / `bf16`.
A fix that only adds the two arms leaves the next instance to be discovered the
same way. Worth pairing with an exhaustiveness measure: replace the `_ => None`
with explicit arms for the `Type` variants that are enumerable, or add a test
that walks every primitive width and asserts an invented method is rejected on
each -- the latter is cheap and would have caught all three.

NOT related to B-2026-08-29-53's fix (typecheck vs codegen, and measured
identical before and after it). Found because a generated f16 sweep for that
row called `sigmoid` on a scalar and got a codegen error instead of the
typecheck error an f32 receiver would have produced.

title: An integer <-> `bf16` conversion is refused by BOTH compiled backends in every direction (`internal error: codegen emitted a native bfloat SIToFP/UIToFP`) while the interpreter performs it. `f16` is unaffected, and an explicit `f32` hop compiles -- so the four int-conversion opcodes are simply missing the widening the float-cast sites already have.
detail:
FOUND while sweeping B-2026-08-29-61: the bf16 leg of a four-width float-math
sweep would not build, and the cause was not the math at all but the
`(n as bf16)` used to derive a runtime-opaque receiver.

An integer <-> `bf16` conversion is REFUSED by both compiled backends in every
direction, while the interpreter performs it:

    shape                    karac run --interp    karac build / karac run (JIT)
    let x: bf16 = n as bf16       x 1              internal error: ... native `bfloat` SIToFP
    let x: bf16 = u8 as bf16      x 1              internal error: ... native `bfloat` UIToFP
    let x: i64  = b as i64        x 1              internal error: ... native `bfloat` llvm.*
    let x: f16  = n as f16        x 1              BUILDS -> x 1        (control)
    let x: bf16 = (n as f32) as bf16   x 1         BUILDS -> x 1        (workaround)

The message is the B-2026-08-29-23 / -34 guard firing, and it is accurate about
the cause -- LLVM 18 cannot select native bf16 -- so this is a MISSING WIDENING
at the int-conversion sites rather than a new hazard. The float-conversion sites
were routed through `build_float_cast_bf16_safe`; `SIToFP` / `UIToFP` / `FPToSI`
/ `FPToUI` with a `bfloat` end were not, which is why an explicit `f32` hop
compiles and the direct form does not.

Not a wrong answer: it is a clean refusal at build time, with a diagnostic that
names the mechanism. But it IS a run-vs-build divergence -- the interpreter
accepts a program both compiled backends reject -- and the fix is mechanical:
widen through f32 at the four integer-conversion opcodes the same way the
float-cast helper already does, which is also exactly what the workaround line
shows is correct.

`f16` is unaffected throughout: it selects natively on the targets that build
codegen, which is why the guard is bf16-only.
fix:
FIXED by 532549e.

`compile_cast`'s int->float and float->int lanes now widen through f32 when
either end is `bf16`, the way its float->float lane already did.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY BROKEN, AND IT WAS WIDER THAN THE ROW SAID. The row named
`i64 as bf16`, `u8 as bf16` and `bf16 as i64`. The real surface is all 16
shapes -- 8 integer widths x 2 directions -- and each fails on BOTH compiled
backends while the interpreter performs it:

    i8/i16/i32/i64 -> bf16   internal error: ... native `bfloat` SIToFP
    u8/u16/u32/u64 -> bf16   internal error: ... native `bfloat` UIToFP
    bf16 -> {i,u}{8,16,32,64}  internal error: ... native `bfloat`
                               llvm.fptosi.sat.iN.bf16
    all 16 under --interp      correct
    the same 16 with f16       correct on every surface (control)

THE FLOAT->INT HALF IS NOT THE OPCODE THE ROW NAMED. `f as iN` does not emit
`fptosi`; it emits `llvm.fptosi.sat.iN.fM` (the saturating cast design.md
requires -- out-of-range clamps to MIN/MAX, NaN -> 0). At bf16 that instantiates
as `llvm.fptosi.sat.i8.bf16`, which trips the guard's pass 1 (intrinsic NAME
contains "bf16") rather than its pass 2, so it is an intrinsic-shaped bf16 node,
not a plain conversion node. Reading the row's `FPToSI` at face value would have
sent a fix to the wrong place.

TWO CHOKEPOINTS, NOT SIXTEEN CALL SITES.
  * float->int: the widening goes INSIDE `emit_float_to_int_sat`, which all
    five float->int callers share (`f as iN`, `f.saturating_to_iN()`, and the
    round-trip range checks behind the checked/trunc/wrapping families). Fixing
    it there covers every one of them and they cannot drift apart.
  * int->float: a new `build_int_to_float_bf16_safe`, the int-side sibling of
    the existing `build_float_cast_bf16_safe`, used by `compile_cast`. The many
    int->float sites in `stats.rs` / `column.rs` are deliberately NOT routed
    through it -- they name `f64_type()` literally and cannot reach bf16 -- and
    the module-wide guard now names the helper, so a future site that can reach
    bf16 gets an actionable message rather than a puzzle.

BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE EXACT, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH PROVING RATHER THAN ASSUMING.
bf16->f32 widens a truncated f32, so it is lossless and the saturating cast sees
the identical number. int->f32->bf16 double-rounds, and double rounding is safe
here by the standard bound: rounding a real to p1 bits then to p2 agrees with
rounding it straight to p2 whenever p1 >= 2*p2 + 2, and f32's 24 >= 2*8 + 2.
That is why the compiled result matches the interpreter, whose own `i as bf16`
takes a DIFFERENT route (i -> f64 -> f32 -> bf16) -- the two agree by a theorem
rather than by sharing code, so the fixture pins both halves.

MEASURED: a 226-row sweep (every integer width x values chosen to exercise
bf16's 8-bit significand, plus saturation at both ends, negatives into unsigned,
and +-1e30) across `--interp` / `karac run` / `karac build` /
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`. Before: the compiled surfaces did not build at
all. After: 225 of 226 rows identical on all four.

THE ONE REMAINING ROW IS NOT THIS BUG AND NOT bf16. `u64::MAX as bf16` prints
-1 under the interpreter and 18446744073709552000 (correct) on all three
compiled surfaces. It reproduces identically for `as f64`, `as f32` and `as f16`
-- code this fix does not touch and that has compiled fine all along -- so it is
a general interpreter defect: `Value::Int`'s signed carrier holds u64 values
above 2^63 as their negative two's complement, and the float cast reads the
carrier. It is a residual of B-2026-07-04-8 (which built the interpreter's u64
model for printing and sorting and never mentions casts). Filed as B-2026-08-30-34
rather than worked around here; the fixture uses a u64 value below 2^63 so it
keeps real u64 coverage without asserting the broken case.

FIXTURES. `e2e_int_bf16_conversions_are_lowered_through_f32` (codegen) plus the
parity mirror `int_bf16_conversions_round_and_saturate` (interpreter). The
values are picked so a lowering that merely COMPILES cannot pass: `257 -> 256`
and `-12345 -> -12352` pin bf16's 8-bit rounding, `1000.0 as i8 -> 127` and
`-1000.0 as i8 -> -128` pin saturation at both ends, `-2.5 as u8 -> 0` pins the
unsigned clamp.

A NOTE ON THE FIXTURE'S SHAPE, because the first draft got it backwards. It was
written with `assert!(out.is_some())` and a comment claiming the pre-fix build
failure would otherwise pass vacuously through `if let Some(out)`. That is
false: `run_program` PANICS on a codegen error on purpose ("codegen failures are
also programming bugs -- surface them loudly") and soft-skips to `None` only for
link/exec failures. The assert added nothing and would have converted the
documented no-archive skip into a hard failure on any machine without the
runtime archive. The RED run is what exposed it -- it panicked where the comment
predicted a `None` -- and the fixture now uses the plain form with the real
reason recorded.

title: A loop-invariant DIRECT-LIBM float method (`cosh`/`sinh`/`tan`/`asin`/...) is not hoisted out of a loop, while the INTRINSIC-family ones (`log10`/`exp`/`sin`/...) are -- so an identical loop pays a call per iteration or not, decided only by whether the LLVM-18 pin happens to have an intrinsic for the method.
detail:
FOUND while measuring what B-2026-08-29-61's fix costs, and PRE-EXISTING rather
than caused by it: a loop-invariant `cosh` was already called once per
iteration BEFORE that fix whenever its receiver was runtime-derived, and the
pre-fix and post-fix binaries for that program are byte-identical.

The two lowering families for `float_math` methods optimize differently, and
which family a method lands in is an accident of the LLVM-18 pin (does an
intrinsic exist?) rather than anything about the method:

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let mut acc: f32 = 0.0f32;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < n * 1000 { acc = acc + (0.5f32).M(); i = i + 1; }
        println(f"acc {acc}");
    }

    M = log10 / exp / sin        (llvm.* intrinsic)  -> HOISTED: one `log10f`
                                 call above the loop, body an unrolled
                                 `vaddss` chain
    M = cosh / tan / asin        (direct libm call)  -> NOT HOISTED: `coshf`
                                 inside the loop body, accumulator spilled to
                                 the stack each iteration

Mechanism: the intrinsic declaration carries `memory(none)`, `speculatable`
and `willreturn`, so LICM can hoist it out. The direct-libm declaration is left
to LLVM's library-attribute inference, which gives `coshf` only
`memory(read)` -- errno-conservative -- and that is not enough for LICM to move
the call out of the loop.

Why it is worth a row now even though it predates the fix: while these calls
were constant-folded, a LITERAL receiver never reached a call at all, so the
gap was only visible for a runtime receiver. B-2026-08-29-61 (correctly)
stopped folding them, so `(2.0f32).cosh()` in a loop is now a per-iteration
call where it used to be a constant, and the asymmetry has a wider surface.

The fix is small and makes the two arms consistent: give the direct-libm
declarations karac creates the same attributes the intrinsics already carry
(`memory(none)` / `nounwind` / `willreturn`, and `speculatable` since these are
total functions). karac has no errno surface, and the intrinsic arm is already
effectively errno-free today, so this removes an inconsistency rather than
adding an assumption. It was deliberately left out of the -61 commit to keep
that diff about correctness only.

Low severity: it costs a call per iteration in a pattern (a compile-time
constant transcendental in a hot loop) that is rare and that a programmer would
normally hoist by hand.
fix:
FIXED by 9b5fce2.

The libm declarations karac creates now carry the same attributes LLVM's own
float intrinsics already carry, so the two `float_math` lowering families
optimize alike.

    fn_val: memory(none) nounwind willreturn mustprogress speculatable

MEASURED, on the 1000-iteration loop the row describes (`acc = acc + (0.5f32).M()`),
reading the disassembly of `main`:

    M                     before                     after
    log10 / exp / sin     HOISTED (1 call above the  HOISTED
    (llvm.* intrinsic)    loop, body an unrolled
                          vaddss chain)
    cosh / tan / asin /   IN-LOOP (call every        HOISTED (1 call, 8
    sinh / tanh / atan /  iteration, accumulator     unrolled vaddss)
    acos (direct libm)    spilled to stack each time)

The same holds for a RUNTIME receiver, which is the case that shows this was
never really about constant folding: pre-fix, a loop-invariant runtime `cosh`
was already called every iteration while the identical `log10` loop was hoisted.
Both are hoisted now.

WHY THE ATTRIBUTES WERE MISSING RATHER THAN WRONG. `llvm.log10.f32` is declared
`memory(none) speculatable willreturn nounwind` by LLVM itself. `coshf` was
declared by karac with NO attribute group at all, leaving it to LLVM's
library-attribute inference, which is errno-conservative: it grants
`memory(read)`, and a call that may read memory cannot be lifted out of a loop
that writes any. So the difference between the two families was never a decision
anyone made -- it is whichever side of the LLVM-18 intrinsic pin a method
happened to fall on.

`memory(none)` DISCOUNTS errno, and that is sound HERE rather than in general.
Kara has no errno surface; nothing in the language can observe it. And the
intrinsic half of this very table has been declared errno-free since it was
written. So this removes an inconsistency between two arms of one feature rather
than introducing a new assumption -- the same judgement `-fno-math-errno`
encodes, applied to the arm accidentally left out of it.

IT COMPOSES WITH B-2026-08-29-61 RATHER THAN UNDOING IT, which was the thing to
check: `memory(none)` makes a call hoistable and CSE-able, but
`canConstantFoldCallTo` still bails on the call site's `nobuiltin` before it
looks at anything else. Re-measured after this change: the fold-vs-runtime sweep
is still 0/540 diverging at f32, f64, f16 and bf16, and all four widths are
still byte-identical across `--interp` / `karac run` / `karac build` /
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`. The fix buys back the optimization without
buying back the wrong answer.

FIXTURE. `libm_math_declaration_attrs::direct_libm_calls_are_declared_as_optimizable_as_the_intrinsics`
asserts the DECLARATION, not the hoist -- deliberately. The attributes are the
fix; whether a given loop gets hoisted is LLVM's decision and would make the
test a hostage to pipeline changes. It resolves the `#N` attribute-group
reference from the `declare` line rather than assuming a group number, and it
asserts the INTRINSIC arm alongside: without that contrast a future change could
satisfy the test by making both families consistently pessimal. RED-verified --
pre-fix it reports "`coshf` is declared with NO attribute group at all".

title: A CONDITIONAL store of an owned param into a `mut ref` param -- `if c { sink.push(r); }` -- LOSES the payload's `Drop` body on the path where the store does NOT happen, on both argument spellings and all four surfaces. The priced remainder of B-2026-08-29-49, which traded a DOUBLE body over a live object for a LOST one over a dead object, in `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place`'s documented leak-over-double-free direction; a per-callee static predicate cannot answer a per-path question
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-29-49 while that row was being fixed, as the priced
remainder of its fix rather than a defect that fix introduced from nothing.

`fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` answers per CALLEE, statically. A
conditional store has two paths and needs two answers:

    struct Res { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }

    fn take(sink: mut ref Vec[Res], r: Res) {
        if r.id > 100 { sink.push(r); }        // stores on ONE path only
    }

      take(mut sink, Res { id: 200 });   stores  -> `pushed 1  drop 200`   correct
      take(mut sink, Res { id: 7 });     doesn't -> `pushed 0`             BODY LOST

The predicate is documented CONSERVATIVE-TRUE and says why: "Answering true too
often means the caller skips a drop that nothing else runs -- a leak. Answering
false too often means two owners free one value -- a double free. Only the first
is recoverable, so the predicate leans that way." This row is the cost of that
lean, recorded so the next reader does not rediscover it as a fresh bug.

WHAT CHANGED IN -49, measured on both sides of the fix:

                      store FIRES            store does NOT fire
    temp arg    pre:  correct           pre:  LOST      (pre-existing, B-2026-08-26-9)
                post: correct           post: LOST      (unchanged)
    named arg   pre:  DOUBLE (drop 200  pre:  correct
                       pushed 1 drop 200)
                post: correct           post: LOST      (new here)

So -49 traded a DOUBLE BODY over a live object for a LOST BODY over a dead one,
in the direction the predicate documents, and made the two argument spellings
agree -- they were previously wrong in OPPOSITE directions, which is precisely
what made the whole class hard to see. The named spelling's non-store path
regressed from correct to lost; the temp spelling's did not change.

Unanimous on interp / JIT / AOT / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, so no A/B gate reports it.
NOT a memory defect: the retraction is `suppress_user_drop_body_keeping_memory`,
so the buffer still has exactly one owner -- valgrind-clean, 0 errors, no
definite or indirect loss. What is lost is the user-visible SIDE EFFECT of the
`Drop` body (a close, a release, a decrement, a log).

WHAT A REAL FIX NEEDS: a per-path answer, not a per-callee one -- either a
`fn_always_moves_param_into_outliving_place` (the strict sibling of
`fn_always_returns_param`, standing the caller down only for an UNCONDITIONAL
store, which reinstates the double on the firing path) or, properly, the
callee-side per-path flag B-2026-08-28-51 already uses for the conditionally
returned param: the callee disarms at runtime on the path that stored, and the
owner is exact on both. The second is the shape that actually resolves it; the
first only moves the error.

DO NOT "fix" this by tightening the predicate alone. That reintroduces
B-2026-08-26-9's double free, which is the unrecoverable direction.
fix:
FIXED by fd205752.

The row asked for "the callee-side per-path flag B-2026-08-28-51 already uses",
and that was the right instruction: B-2026-08-28-65 is THIS DEFECT ONE ESCAPE
ROUTE OVER. There, `if k { return r; }` was disarmed by a compile-time frame
removal that applies to ALL paths, so the fall-through ran no body; here it is
`if c { sink.push(r); }`, the same nesting with a call argument in place of the
return. The mechanism it introduced -- a bool alloca, `true` in the entry block,
cleared on the moving path, read by `emit_user_drop_call_guarded` -- needed no
change at all.

WHAT THE ROW GOT SLIGHTLY WRONG, and it matters for where the fix goes. The
row's framing is that -49 "traded" a double for a lost body. The stand-down -49
installed is CORRECT: a by-value parameter belongs to the callee under Kara's
caller-drops convention, and the caller declining is what makes the container
the single owner on the storing path. The actual defect is that the CALLEE
registered nothing, because the same MAY-predicate that licenses the caller's
stand-down (`fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place`, `any` at every branch) also
gated the callee's parameter drop. So on the non-storing path the value had no
owner in either frame. Nothing needed to be traded back.

FIVE PIECES:

  * `fn_always_moves_param_into_outliving_place` -- the MUST sibling (`all` at
    branches, an `else`-less `if` is a non-storing path, a loop never counts).
    `conditional = may && !must`.
  * `compile_function`'s parameter loop registers a BODIES-ONLY drop guarded by
    the flag when the store is conditional -- mirroring, ten lines above it, the
    conditional-RETURN registration that has done exactly this since -51.
  * `arm_conditional_store_flag` clears the flag at the storing statement.
    DELIBERATELY NON-RECURSIVE: matching a store nested inside a branch would
    emit the clear in the block that evaluates the CONDITION and disarm both
    paths, which is the all-paths disarming this row exists to undo.
  * `suppress_user_drop_for_var` declines for these parameters. This was found
    by instrumentation, not by reading: the clear fired correctly and then the
    store site's retraction deleted the action outright. Keyed on a dedicated
    `cond_store_flag_params` set rather than on `cond_move_drop_flags`, so no
    pre-existing retraction changes behaviour.
  * Both interpreter registrars extended on the same two predicates, because a
    codegen-only fix left the interpreter still losing the body -- a run-vs-build
    divergence, and one the codegen tests alone would have passed.

THE ESCAPE-ROUTE GUARD IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF, and it exists because the
obvious version of this fix DOUBLES. A parameter that can also leave by being
RETURNED has a path on which the flag stays armed while another frame has taken
the value over. Measured with the guard absent, against a recorded pre-fix
baseline: `{ if .. { let w = W { r: r }; return Some(w); } if .. { sink.push(r); } }`
ran the body TWICE for the returned object on all four surfaces -- `drop 301 `
with the String already moved out, then the real one -- and the bare-return and
return-through-a-call spellings each doubled on at least one backend. So
`escapes_by_non_store_route` declines the registration whenever any non-store
route exists, conservative-decline on any unrecognized shape, exactly the trade
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare`'s condition 3 makes. Those shapes keep
today's behaviour bit-for-bit; the remainder is filed as its own row rather than
left implicit.

MEASURED, 4 surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), all unanimous:

    conditional store, MISSES      body LOST  ->  one body     (the row)
    conditional store, FIRES       one body   ->  one body
    unconditional / both-arms      one body   ->  one body
    method into `self.xs`, nested  body LOST  ->  one body
    param also returnable          one body   ->  one body     (declined, at baseline)

Valgrind clean on heap-carrying payloads, 0 errors. B-2026-08-29-49's own
19-shape matrix re-runs unanimous, with H and H2 -- its conditional-miss shapes --
flipping from `pushed 0` to `drop 7 | pushed 0` and the other 17 unchanged.


The declined shapes' remainder is split out as B-2026-08-30-33, which carries the
measurement table for both sides of the guard and the two clears a real fix
needs (a `let`/assign that binds the param into an escaping local, and the
interpreter twin of the return-operand clear).

title: THE EFFECT CHECKER DOES NOT ENFORCE design.md's "Drop bodies must not panic" RULE -- an `impl Drop` whose body calls `panic()`, indexes out of bounds, or calls a `panics` function is ACCEPTED by `karac check`, where the spec requires rejection at the definition site; the three shapes the spec itself enumerates all compile
detail:
design.md 9165 (§ Drop and Destructors) states the rule and its enforcement
point without ambiguity:

    **Drop bodies must not panic.** The effect checker requires `fn drop` to
    be inferred `panics`-free: if any expression in the drop body could panic
    (an index out of bounds, an integer overflow in `#[checked]` arithmetic,
    an explicit `panic!`, a call to a function whose effect set includes
    `panics`), the impl is rejected at the definition site. This is a static
    rule, not a runtime one -- there is no "abort on panic in drop" fallback
    to discover at runtime.

`karac check` accepts all three of the shapes that sentence enumerates.
Measured on 27a7730, `karac check <file>` printing "All checks passed." for
each:

    explicit panic   impl Drop for S { fn drop(mut ref self) { panic("boom") } }
    index OOB        ... { let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); println(f"{v[3]}") }
    calls a panicky  fn boom() { panic("inner") }
                     ... { boom() }

so the gap is TOTAL, not a partial coverage hole -- no shape in the spec's own
list is caught.

WHAT HAPPENS INSTEAD, and it is three different things. The accepted program
then behaves differently on each backend (measured interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, a `Drop` body that prints then panics, reached at a match
arm's exit):

    interp            v7 dE-start done  + "runtime error: boom" on stderr
                      -- the panic does NOT stop the program; `done` still runs
    jit/build/nopar   v7 dE-start       + "panic ... in E.drop: boom", aborts

The compiled halves match design.md 6075's double-panic prohibition closely
enough; the interpreter continues past a destructor panic, which nothing in
the spec permits. But BOTH are downstream of a program that should never have
compiled, which is why this is filed against the effect checker and not as a
run-vs-build row.

WHY IT MATTERS beyond conformance: the rationale in that same paragraph is that
destructors run during panic unwind, so a panic-during-unwind becomes a
double-panic process abort (design.md 874, exit 134) that destroys the original
failure's information. The static rule exists to remove that class of
heisenbug entirely; without it the class is live, and the failure it produces
is the one hardest to debug -- an abort whose reported panic is not the one
that actually broke the program.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-30-14's fix, and the acceptance half cannot be:
`karac check` never runs a drop body, so the three "All checks passed." results
above are independent of that change by construction rather than by
measurement.

The RUNTIME half did change, and honestly stated: before -14's fix the
interpreter printed `v7 AFTER done` -- it lost the body, the panic AND the
`return` together. After it, the body runs and the `return` happens, and what
remains is that the panic does not stop the program. That residual is left in
place DELIBERATELY: teaching the drop-body runner to propagate an unwind would
be implementing the runtime fallback this spec sentence forbids, instead of
adding the static check it requires. -14's code comment records that choice and
points here.

POINTER. The effect checker infers private-fn effects and verifies declared
public ones (`src/effectchecker.rs`); what is missing is a rule that treats
`fn drop` in an `impl Drop for T` as a site whose INFERRED effect set must not
contain `panics`, rejecting at the definition site with the impl's span. The
three shapes above are the regression fixture, and a fourth -- a drop body that
is genuinely panic-free -- is the negative control that must keep compiling.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping diverging-arm shapes for B-2026-08-30-14. A
`Drop` body that panics was written as a PRECEDENCE probe (does a fault raised
inside the body outrank the `return` it interrupted?); the answer turned out to
be that the program should not have compiled at all.
fix:
FIXED by 198b899.

design.md 9165 states the rule and its enforcement point without ambiguity --
"the impl is rejected at the definition site. This is a static rule, not a
runtime one" -- and the checker simply did not implement it. All three shapes
the sentence itself enumerates printed "All checks passed."

THE FIX is `verify_drop_bodies_are_panics_free` in
`src/effectchecker/verify.rs`, a structural sibling of
`verify_impl_trait_ceilings` and placed beside it: both walk `impl Trait for
Type` blocks and compare an impl method's INFERRED effects against a ceiling.
Here the ceiling is fixed by the language rather than declared by a trait.
Keyed on the inferred set because `fn drop` has no `with` clause to declare
anything on -- inference is the only thing that knows the body indexes a `Vec`
or calls a `panics` function. New diagnostic E0417 / `DropBodyMayPanic`,
catalogued in `cli/explain.rs` and mapped in `cli/diag_json.rs`; the
`code_table_class_matches_the_effect_and_ownership_classifiers` test carries a
row for it so the catalogue and the classifier cannot drift.

MEASURED BLAST RADIUS -- AND THE FIRST MEASUREMENT WAS TOO NARROW, which is
worth recording because the rule is a new REJECTION and a new rejection is only
safe if the corpus survives it. Checking `examples/*.kara` gave 0 of 13 newly
rejected, and the ~17 in-tree `impl Drop` blocks (10+ in the stdlib, compiled
into `karac` itself) all still build -- a clean `karac check` on any program
proves the stdlib half, since a rejected stdlib drop body would fail every
compilation.

TESTS WERE NOT IN THAT SAMPLE, and they are where it bit. SEVEN
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` ASAN fixtures share one probe line in a `Drop`
body:

    if self.buf[0] < 0i64 { println(self.buf[0]); }

`self.buf[0]` is precisely the "index out of bounds" the spec sentence
enumerates, so the rule rejects it correctly -- and the suite's own effect-gate
(`tests/common/mod.rs`, which asserts every ASAN program passes the effect
checker so codegen is never fed input production would not see) fired exactly
as designed. Nothing was grandfathered: all seven were rewritten to

    if let Some(v) = self.buf.first() { if v < 0i64 { println(v); } }

`first()` is panics-free and STILL READS ELEMENT 0, which is the whole point of
the probe -- a use-after-free on the element buffer must still be caught. A
`len()`-based rewrite would have passed the gate while quietly weakening all
seven fixtures, and that is the trap worth naming for whoever hits this rule
next: make the body panic-free without making it stop touching what it was
built to touch. `memory_sanitizer` is 1324/0 after the rewrite.

So the honest summary is: no production code changed, and seven test fixtures
had to -- the rule reaches idiomatic code, and `Vec` indexing in a destructor
is the shape it reaches first.

WHAT IT CATCHES, and the ONE SHAPE IT DOES NOT. All three spec shapes are
rejected when written normally:

    panic("boom")                          REJECTED
    boom()   // fn boom() { panic(..) }    REJECTED
    let x = v[3];                          REJECTED

The same index written INSIDE an f-string interpolation hole --
`println(f"{v[3]}")` -- is still accepted, and that is NOT a hole in this rule:
effects of expressions inside an interpolation hole are not attributed to the
enclosing function AT ALL. Measured directly, and it is not panics-specific:

    pub fn f() { println(f"{boom()}") }     inferred [writes(Stdout)]      panics LOST
    pub fn f() { let n = boom(); println(f"{n}") }
                                            inferred [panics, writes(Stdout)]
    pub fn f() { println(f"{touch()}") }    inferred [writes(Stdout)]      writes(Db) LOST
      // fn touch() -> i64 with writes(Db)

A call's DECLARED `writes(Resource)` is dropped exactly as readily as its
`panics`, so this is a general inference gap and is filed as B-2026-08-30-35. The
fixture pins the current behaviour of that shape rather than leaving it
unstated, so closing the gap flips a test loudly instead of silently widening
this rule's reach.

FIXTURES. `effectchecker::drop_body_that_can_panic_is_rejected_at_the_definition_site`
(the three spec shapes) and
`effectchecker::a_panic_free_drop_body_and_an_inherent_drop_are_left_alone`
(the boundaries: a clean drop body, an INHERENT `fn drop` the compiler never
calls as a destructor, and the interpolation-hole shape). RED-verified by
disabling the verifier call: the rejection test fails, the boundary test still
passes -- which is the right pair, since the boundaries were never about this
rule.

title: `process.exit(code)` WORKS ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS AND RAISES AN INTERNAL "this is a compiler bug" RUNTIME ERROR ON THE INTERPRETER -- the interpreter already HAS a correct `process.exit` arm, but it is keyed on `ExprKind::Path` and the callee arrives as a bare `Identifier`, so it never fires; no other spelling is accepted
detail:
`process.exit(code: i32)` is specified -- design.md 6531 gives it a full
paragraph ("Available as a stdlib function when returning `ExitCode` from deep
in the call stack would require threading the exit decision through many
frames"), and design.md 6073 lists it in the `catch_panic` table as the one
thing that propagates straight through. The compiled backends implement it.
The interpreter reports an INTERNAL COMPILER BUG on the same source:

    fn main() { println("before"); process.exit(3); println("after") }

    karac check         All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  before
                        runtime error: internal: name 'process' resolved but
                        has no binding at run time. This is a compiler bug
                        (the resolver should have rejected or bound it) --
                        please report it with the source.
                          at pex.kara:1:32
    karac run (JIT)     exits 3
    karac build         exits 3

IT IS NOT UNIMPLEMENTED -- THAT IS THE INTERESTING PART. `src/interpreter/
eval_call.rs:476` has a hardcoded `"process.exit"` arm that does exactly the
right thing (`self.pending_cf = Some(ControlFlow::ExitUnwind { code })`, with
the comment "Run all pending defers via ExitUnwind propagation"). It never
fires, because it is guarded on the callee being `ExprKind::Path { segments }`
and this callee is not one: the diagnostic above is raised from the
`ExprKind::Identifier` arm of `eval_expr.rs:364`, so `process` reached the
evaluator as a BARE IDENTIFIER -- the receiver of a field/method access -- and
the path-keyed dispatch was never consulted. So the defect is in how the
callee is formed or classified upstream, not in a missing builtin.

`eval_expr.rs:350`'s own comment predicts this exact case: it says the arm
"stays reachable from any future resolver hole of the same kind" after an
earlier hole (a builtin name outside call position) was closed. This is that
next hole.

NO OTHER SPELLING WORKS, so there is no workaround and no "you held it wrong":

    process.exit(3)       accepted; compiled OK, interp internal error (above)
    std.process.exit(3)   error[resolve]: undefined name 'std', did you mean 'Add'?
    import std.process;   error[resolve]: unknown module `std.process`

The bare form is the only spelling the front end accepts, and it is the one
that diverges. (`runtime/stdlib/process.kara` is the child-process
`Command`/`Child` surface -- unrelated to `process.exit`, despite the shared
prefix. The only `process.exit` strings elsewhere in the repo are JAVASCRIPT
inside `tests/cli.rs`'s Node harness scripts, so no Kara program in-tree
exercises this and nothing was going to catch it.)

SEVERITY medium, not high: the interpreter reports rather than mis-executing,
which is the right failure direction. But `--interp` is the documented fallback
for every feature the JIT gates (regex, Arrow IPC, `String.normalize`,
`gpu.dispatch` all route there), so a program using `process.exit` has no
working interpreter path at all, and the message tells the user they have hit a
compiler bug rather than an unimplemented builtin.

PRIOR ART, adjacent and not this: B-2026-08-06-24 fixed the same "internal ...
this is a compiler bug" message for `extern` calls under `--interp` and settled
the principle -- an operation the tree-walk backend cannot support BY DESIGN
should refuse cleanly and name itself. `process.exit` is not in that category
at all: the interpreter can support it and already contains the code to.

RELATED BUT SEPARATE: B-2026-08-30-31 covers the COMPILED half's own defect
(buffered stdout written before the exit is lost). Different fix in a different
place -- callee classification here, an exit-path flush there -- so they are
filed apart rather than as one "process.exit is broken" row.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping diverging-arm shapes for B-2026-08-30-14 --
`process.exit` inside a match arm was written to probe a third kind of
terminator alongside `return` / `break` / `continue`.
fix:
FIXED by 198b899.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND THE FIX IS ONE ARM. The interpreter's
`process.exit` handler was keyed on `ExprKind::Path`, and the parser never
produces one here: `process.exit(3)` arrives as a METHOD CALL on the `process`
pseudo-receiver, so evaluation fell through to the `Identifier("process")` arm
of `eval_expr` and reported an internal "this is a compiler bug" error on a
program both compiled backends ran correctly.

`codegen/method_call.rs` had already hit this and its comment says so verbatim
-- "the interpreter (eval_call.rs) handles it as a path-call, but the parser
hands codegen a method call with `process` as a (pseudo-variable) identifier
receiver". So the shape was known; only the interpreter had not been taught it.

RATHER THAN ADD A SECOND COPY, the existing path-arm body was extracted into
`eval_process_exit` and both spellings now call it, so the two cannot drift.
The new method-call arm sits with the other pseudo-receiver dispatches (`ast`,
`compiler`, `gpu`) in `interpreter/method_call.rs` and carries the same
"`process` is not a real binding" guard codegen uses -- without it the two
backends would disagree about a user binding named `process` instead of about
this.

MEASURED, interp / jit / build, `println("before"); process.exit(3)`:

    before        exit 3   on all three   (was: interp printed the internal
                                           compiler-bug error and did not exit 3)

NO WORKAROUND EXISTED, which is why this was not merely cosmetic: the bare form
is the only spelling the front end accepts (`std.process.exit` is
`error[resolve]: undefined name 'std'`, `import std.process;` is `unknown
module`), so a program using `process.exit` had no working `--interp` path at
all -- and `--interp` is the documented fallback for every feature the JIT
gates.

FIXTURE: `cli::test_process_exit_keeps_prior_output_and_status_on_every_surface`
asserts stdout, exit status, AND the absence of the "this is a compiler bug"
string on the interpreter, across three statement shapes. Shared with
B-2026-08-30-31, whose auto-par half the same test covers.

title: AUTO-PAR RUNS `process.exit(code)` BEFORE THE `println`s THAT PRECEDE IT WHENEVER ANY STATEMENT FOLLOWS THE EXIT, silently discarding ALL prior stdout on a default build -- `println("a"); process.exit(3); println("z")` emits NOTHING where `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` emits "a"; `concurrency::predicates::expr_exits` did not recognize the exit as an early exit, and console writes are deliberately non-conflicting, so nothing ordered them against a process-terminating call
detail:
Output already written by `println` before a `process.exit(code)` is SILENTLY
LOST on both compiled backends. Measured on 27a7730 with a control that
isolates the exit as the only difference:

    fn main() { println("before"); process.exit(3); println("after") }
      karac build -> ./pex  ->  exit 3, stdout 0 bytes      <- "before" gone
      karac run   (JIT)     ->  exit 3, stdout 0 bytes

    CONTROL, same program without the exit:
    fn main() { println("before"); println("after") }
      karac build -> ./pex2 ->  exit 0, stdout "before after"

The exit CODE is correct (3, per design.md 6531); it is the buffered stdout
that never reaches the fd. Verified by redirecting to a file rather than a
pipe, so it is not a shell or tty artifact: `wc -c` on the redirected stdout
is 0.

WHY IT IS A REAL DEFECT AND NOT A BUFFERING TECHNICALITY. design.md 6531
specifies `process.exit` as "a controlled stack unwind that runs all pending
`defer`/`errdefer` blocks before terminating, identical to panic unwinding but
with a defined exit code". A path that runs user cleanup but discards output
the program already produced is losing the diagnostic the cleanup exists to
report -- the canonical use is exactly `println("fatal: ..."); process.exit(1)`
from deep in a call stack, which is the shape that emits nothing at all today.

The interpreter DOES print "before" (it fails afterward for its own reason --
B-2026-08-30-30), so the two backends also disagree here, but the compiled
behaviour is wrong on its own terms and would be wrong even if the interpreter
did not exist.

SCOPE NOTE, deliberately unmeasured: whether `panic()` and the `?`-in-`main`
error path share the flush gap was NOT tested, so this row claims only what it
measured -- `process.exit`. Both are plausible siblings and worth a sweep when
this is taken; a fix that flushes on one exit path and not the others would
leave the class open.

POINTER. `process.exit` lowers through the runtime; the fix is to flush the
console buffer before the process terminates on that path (and to check the
same for whatever other paths call the underlying exit). The E2E shape above,
asserted with the control beside it, is the regression fixture -- the control
matters, because a test that only checks "exit code is 3" passes today.

SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping diverging-arm shapes for B-2026-08-30-14 --
`process.exit` inside a match arm was written to probe a third kind of
terminator, and the missing "before" line was visible in the A/B output.
fix:
FIXED by 198b899.

THIS ROW'S ORIGINAL CHARACTERIZATION WAS WRONG, and the correction is the most
important thing in it. It was filed as "stdout is lost when the program ends
via `process.exit`", with the canonical `println("fatal: ..");
process.exit(1)` given as emitting nothing. That exact program WORKS. What was
actually measured, on re-checking with fresh archives:

    println("a"); process.exit(3)                       "a"  exit 3   CORRECT
    println("a"); process.exit(3); println("z")         ""   exit 3   WRONG
    println("a"); println("b"); process.exit(3)         "a b" exit 3  CORRECT
    println("a"); println("b"); process.exit(3); ..     ""   exit 3   WRONG

The trigger is A STATEMENT FOLLOWING THE EXIT, not the exit itself -- and when
it fires it discards ALL prior output, not just the last line. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`
was correct in every case, which is what named the cause.

HOW THE ORIGINAL ROW WENT WRONG is worth recording. Its measurement was taken
with a STALE runtime archive and only the with-tail shape was tried, so a
general claim was written from a single data point. Two of this repo's
documented traps at once: the archive-staleness rule in CLAUDE.md, and
generalizing from one shape without varying it. The `exit-last` row now in the
fixture exists precisely because varying that one thing is what found the truth.

THE REAL BUG, and it is a miscompile rather than a flush problem. Auto-par
decides what may move into workers, and `concurrency::predicates::expr_exits`
is the predicate that says "this statement transfers control out". It knows
`return`, `break`, `continue` and `?` -- the `?` arm was itself added late,
B-2026-08-26-27, for this same class of omission -- but `process.exit` reaches
it as a METHOD CALL on the `process` pseudo-receiver rather than as a jump
expression, so the generic `MethodCall` arm walked the receiver and args and
answered `false`. Auto-par then hoisted the surrounding statements into
workers, and the process terminated before the console writes landed.

Nothing else in the analysis was going to catch it: console writes are
DELIBERATELY non-conflicting for auto-par, so there was no dependency edge
between the prints and the exit to order them.

THE FIX is one arm in `expr_exits` recognizing `process.exit` as an early exit,
guarded on `process` not being a real binding -- the same guard
`codegen/method_call.rs` and `interpreter/method_call.rs` carry. All three must
agree on when that name means the pseudo-module, or a user binding called
`process` would be ANALYZED as an exit while the backends treat it as an
ordinary method call.

AFTER, all six probe shapes agree across interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, with exit code 3 preserved on every one.

SEVERITY RAISED to high from the filed medium. Silent, total output loss on a
default build, on the idiomatic "report then exit" path, with the
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` leg correct -- so an A/B check that only compares the two
compiled surfaces to each other would still have caught it, but any test
asserting only the exit code would not.

FIXTURE: `cli::test_process_exit_keeps_prior_output_and_status_on_every_surface`
asserts stdout AND exit status under both `KARAC_AUTO_PAR` settings and on
`--interp`, across `exit-last` / `stmt-after-exit` /
`two-writes-then-exit-then-stmt`. The `exit-last` row is what keeps the trigger
honest: without it, a regression that simply stopped parallelizing anything
would still pass. Shared with B-2026-08-30-30, whose interpreter half it also
covers.

Fixed in c1a9f3e. Codegen now widens f16 arithmetic to f32 and rounds
the result back ITSELF on wasm targets, instead of leaving a native `half` op
for a backend that does not round it, and a post-optimization guard rejects any
that slips through.

ROOT CAUSE, from the backend's own output. LLVM 18 has TWO legalizations for
`half` and they are not interchangeable. `SoftPromoteHalf` -- x86_64, aarch64
-- widens each operand, computes in f32 and ROUNDS THE RESULT BACK after every
operation. `PromoteFloat` -- wasm32 -- keeps the value in an f32 carrier and
rounds only where the narrow type is forced. `llc-18` on a two-op chain
`(a+b)*b`:

    x86_64                          wasm32
      __extendhfsf2 x2                f32.add
      addss                           f32.mul       <- no round between them
      __truncsfhf2                    __truncsfhf2
      __extendhfsf2
      mulss
      __truncsfhf2

aarch64 matches x86 (`fcvt h,s` after each op). The missing intermediate round
is the bug.

THE ROW'S PROPOSED FIX SHAPE DOES NOT WORK, and measuring that first is what
made the rest of this tractable. The row said to apply "the bf16 treatment"
-- widen to f32 and round back -- ideally unconditionally. Emitting
`fptrunc (binop (fpext a) (fpext b))` is undone by the optimizer: InstCombine
shrinks it straight back to `binop half` whenever the wide type is exact for
the narrow one, and f32 is exact for f16 (24 significand bits >= 2*11 + 2,
Figueroa's condition). MEASURED at `default<O2>`, the pipeline karac runs: all
five of fadd/fsub/fmul/fdiv/frem fold back. bf16 escapes this only because its
conversions are emitted as INTEGER bit manipulation (`emit_f32_to_bf16`), so
there is no fpext/fptrunc pair for the fold to match -- a property of bf16's
unselectability workaround, not a property of the recipe. A fix in the obvious
shape would have passed an un-optimized IR test and shipped the bug.

THREE OPAQUE NARROWINGS WERE MEASURED; the third is what landed.

  * `llvm.experimental.constrained.fptrunc` survives the optimizer and then
    dies at ISel with `LLVM ERROR: Cannot select: strict_fp16_to_fp` -- the
    same hard abort with no diagnostic that bf16 gives. It trades a wrong
    answer for a compiler crash.
  * An inline integer round-to-nearest-even sequence, bf16's shape, would
    avoid a call. bf16's version is a bias-add on the top 16 bits because a
    bf16 IS a truncated f32; f16 has a different exponent width, so the same
    job needs overflow-to-inf and subnormal renormalization written out --
    new, unvalidated IEEE rounding code in the one place where a mistake is
    itself a fresh miscompile.
  * An explicit call to `__truncsfhf2`, which is what landed. It is opaque to
    the fold, it is EXACTLY what x86_64 emits after every `fadd half`, and it
    resolves to `runtime/src/f16.rs`'s definition -- whose rounding was
    validated against host compiler-rt over all 2^32 f32 bit patterns while
    fixing B-2026-08-30-24. So wasm, native and the interpreter agree by
    construction rather than by measurement, the rule the Arrow IPC twin and
    `String.normalize` follow. It costs nothing extra on this target: the
    wasm backend already calls `__truncsfhf2` for every f16 STORE.

  (A `store half` / `load half` round-trip also rounds correctly at ISel, and
  is useless in the mid-end, which forwards the store to the load and leaves
  the `fptrunc` exposed to the fold.)

TARGET-GATED, NOT UNCONDITIONAL -- a deliberate departure from the row, which
argued unconditional "keeps ONE f16 semantics path" and costs nothing "since
the explicit round is what they emit anyway". The second half is true and the
conclusion still does not follow: x86_64 and aarch64 already round correctly,
so widening them would only add IR for InstCombine to shrink back to what
codegen would have emitted anyway. The divergence surface the row worried about
is covered structurally instead, by the guard below.

VECTORS TOO. `Vector[f16, N]` lane arithmetic carried the identical defect
through a different path -- the vector legalizer scalarizes the lane op into
the same scalar `half` nodes -- and `Vector[f16, 4]` multiplication returned a
finite 196512 on wasm. Only the ROUNDING is per-lane; the arithmetic stays a
`<N x float>` vector op, which wasm does have.

AND THE MATH INTRINSICS, which is the row's scope being narrower than the
defect and was nearly missed. An intrinsic is a native f16 op wearing a call's
clothing: `llvm.sqrt.f16` looks like a call, not like an `fmul`, so the opcode
sweep that found everything above walks straight past it. It was caught only
because a probe written to check the fix covered struct fields and function
boundaries happened to print `65504f16.sqrt()`, which came back as the
unrounded f32 255.93748474... where both other backends give 255.875 (the
correctly-rounded f16: the exact root 255.937484... sits just below the
midpoint of 255.875 and 256.0). Measured over the fourteen f16 math methods --
sqrt, sin, cos, exp, exp2, ln, log2, log10, pow, floor, ceil, round, trunc,
copysign -- 9 of 11 printed lines differed from native. The two that agreed
were exactly `floor`/`ceil`/`round`/`trunc` and `copysign`, the families that
are exact at any width; that prediction is what the guard's allow-list rests
on, so it is pinned as a test.

All fourteen route through one helper (`build_float_intrinsic_bf16_safe`), so
they are fixed at that single choke point. bf16 was immune to this by ACCIDENT
rather than design: `verify_no_native_bf16_ops`'s first pass matches
intrinsics BY NAME and every `llvm.*.bf16` contains "bf16", so bf16 was forced
down the widened path from the moment that guard landed. Nothing matched
`llvm.sqrt.f16`.

THE GUARD RUNS AFTER OPTIMIZATION, where its bf16 sibling runs before it, and
the difference is the whole point. `verify_no_native_bf16_ops` asks what
CODEGEN EMITTED, which is right for bf16: the ops it forbids are unselectable,
so no LLVM transform can introduce one. For f16 the optimizer is precisely the
thing that can undo the fix, so a pre-pipeline check would pass on IR the
pipeline then breaks. `verify_no_native_f16_arith` therefore runs last, after
every pass, and asks the only question that matters: is the module the BACKEND
receives free of unrounded f16 arithmetic? It covers two failure modes rather
than one -- a codegen site that forgets to widen, and a future LLVM that learns
to see through the call, which is one TargetLibraryInfo entry away.

It has TWO PASSES for the two spellings. Pass 2 sweeps opcodes
(FAdd/FSub/FMul/FDiv/FRem at `half` or `<N x half>`); pass 1 reads intrinsic
DECLARATION NAMES, because that is the spelling an opcode sweep cannot see --
the same reason the bf16 guard's first pass reads names, and reading names
rather than call operands is also what keeps it safe on coroutine intrinsics.
Pass 1 is an ALLOW-LIST (`fabs` / `minnum` / `maxnum` / `minimum` / `maximum` /
`copysign` / `fmin` / `fmax` -- each returns one of its operands or moves a
sign bit, so none can leave the f16 grid) so that a newly-emitted inexact
intrinsic fails closed instead of slipping through.

Both passes are proven to fire, not assumed to. With the arithmetic widening
disabled the guard reports "a native `half` FAdd survived into the wasm
backend in `main`"; with the intrinsic widening disabled, "the inexact f16
intrinsic `llvm.sqrt.f16` survived into the wasm backend". Verified not to
false-positive across all eight fixtures used here, including vector
reductions and `dot` -- which emit no `v4f16` at all, having already been
widened to `<4 x float>` by earlier work.

MEASURED. A generated sweep -- 14 receivers, every ordered pair, all five
operators, plus compound assignment, unary negation, an accumulation loop, an
overflow product loop, vector lane ops, reductions, sqrt/tanh and `Vec[f16]`
storage; 195 printed lines -- compared across a native binary, `karac run
--interp` and the wasm module under `node:wasi`:

    pre-fix    185 of 195 lines differ from native
    post-fix     0 of 195

The regression fixture is 6 lines chosen for the four ways an unrounded
intermediate becomes visible (overflow that must saturate to inf, a
non-representable quotient, an underflow that must flush to zero, and
compounding drift), plus the vector form. All 6 differed pre-fix.

CORRECTIONS TO THIS ROW, all three found by measuring what it asserted.

  * The row located the defect at the ABI boundary -- "adds in f32, and
    returns the f32 unrounded", "the missing final `__truncsfhf2` IS the bug".
    Measured, a STORE does round (`f32.add; __truncsfhf2; i32.store16`). The
    defect is BETWEEN chained arithmetic ops, which is a broader claim than
    the row made, and it is why the accumulation loop drifts.
  * The row left the comparison operators as an open question, correctly
    flagging that the pairs it tried were "agrees by luck of the inputs". The
    answer is that the operators themselves are fine: the wasm backend
    normalizes each operand through f16 before comparing it, so a compare
    self-corrects. What was broken was comparing an unrounded arithmetic
    RESULT, which the arithmetic fix cures. `fneg` and `fabs` are likewise
    exact and need nothing, which is why the guard's opcode list omits all
    three.
  * The row measured "8 of 8 f16 lines diverge". Over the broader sweep it is
    185 of 195 for arithmetic, plus 9 of 11 for the math methods the row did
    not consider at all.

design.md's reduced-precision section said only that "LLVM promotes to `f32`
for computation", omitting the rounding; it now carries an erratum naming both
legalizations and which targets use them. That is the same conclusion the bf16
erratum (B-2026-08-29-23) reached from the other direction -- bf16 could not be
SELECTED, f16 selects fine and was not ROUNDED -- so the erratum states the
general rule both point at: a reduced-precision format's semantics are
codegen's responsibility on every target, and "LLVM handles it" needs a
per-target measurement before it may be written down.

FILED, NOT FIXED HERE: B-2026-08-30-36 — `f16` and `bf16` implement none of
the six arithmetic operator traits, so neither satisfies a generic `T: Add`
bound. Found by a probe written to check this fix covered a generic
instantiation; it does not arise there because the instantiation is rejected
before codegen sees it. Separate surface (typechecker), separate cause (one
list in `env_build.rs` that omits both widths), and the operators work when
spelled directly — which is why every f16 test in the tree passes over it.

Tests: `wasm_f16_arithmetic_build_and_run_e2e` (tests/cli.rs) builds for
wasm_wasi and runs under node:wasi, asserting output byte-identical to native;
`wasm_f16_arithmetic_rounds_through_an_unfoldable_call`,
`wasm_f16_vector_lane_arithmetic_rounds_per_lane` and
`wasm_f16_math_intrinsics_are_widened_and_rounded` (tests/wasm_codegen.rs) pin
the emitted IR -- the CALL rather than the widening, because the widening alone
is what the optimizer removes; `test_f16_arithmetic_results_are_representable_in_f16`
(tests/interpreter.rs) is the oracle twin, seeded with a literal 1 because an
in-process interpreter test reads the test binary's argv.
title: LLVM-18 PROMOTES f16 ARITHMETIC AND MATH METHODS TO f32 ON wasm32 AND NEVER ROUNDS THE RESULT BACK, so a wasm module holds values the type cannot represent: `65504f16 * 3f16` is a finite 196512 where it must overflow to `inf`, `65504f16.sqrt()` is the unrounded f32 255.93748474... where the f16 answer is 255.875, and every inexact quotient keeps f32 precision. Native and the interpreter both round; bf16 is unaffected because codegen widens and rounds it ITSELF rather than trusting the backend
detail:
LLVM-18 PROMOTES f16 ARITHMETIC TO f32 ON wasm32 AND NEVER ROUNDS THE RESULT
BACK, so a compiled wasm module carries values no `f16` can hold. The native
backend and the interpreter both round; wasm is the odd one out.

FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-30-24, and only observable BECAUSE of it: no f16
program linked for a wasm target before that fix, so nothing could run to
disagree. Not caused by it -- the codegen is unchanged either way -- and not
fixed by it.

THE HEADLINE CASE IS NOT A ROUNDING NUANCE. With `a = 65504` and `b = 3` at
f16 (receivers derived from `env.args()` so nothing folds):

                              native / --interp      wasm under node:wasi
    a * b                     inf                    196512
    a + b                     65504                  65507

65504 is the largest finite f16. The product must overflow to `inf` and the
sum must round back down to 65504; on wasm both come out as finite values
that are not representable in the type they are typed as.

MEASURED over eight receiver pairs x {add, sub, mul, div}, comparing a native
binary, `karac run --interp`, and the wasm module run under `node:wasi`:

    f16    8 of 8 lines diverge      (native == interp on every one)
    bf16   0 of 4 lines diverge      (the control -- see below)

Every `div` diverges, because a quotient is rarely f16-representable:
`3.5 / 1.25` gives the f16 2.80078125 natively and the f32 2.799999952316284
on wasm. `add`/`sub`/`mul` diverge exactly when their exact result is not
f16-representable -- `0.1 + 0.3` is 0.39990234375 natively and
0.4000244140625 on wasm.

THE MECHANISM, FROM THE BACKEND'S OWN OUTPUT. `llc-18` on a bare
`fadd half`:

    x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu        wasm32-unknown-wasi
      call __extendhfsf2              call __truncsfhf2 / __extendhfsf2  (arg)
      call __extendhfsf2              call __truncsfhf2 / __extendhfsf2  (arg)
      addss                           f32.add
      call __truncsfhf2               <nothing>

x86 widens both operands, adds, and rounds the result back. wasm normalizes
each incoming operand through f16 (its ABI passes a `half` as an f32), adds
in f32, and returns the f32 unrounded. The missing final `__truncsfhf2` IS
the bug.

bf16 IS THE CONTROL, AND IT POINTS AT THE FIX. The same eight-pair sweep at
bf16 shows zero divergence, because codegen does not emit native `bfloat`
nodes at all: it widens every bf16 arithmetic op to f32 and rounds back
itself (B-2026-08-29-23/-34), with `verify_no_native_bf16_ops` rejecting any
module that reintroduces one. f16 was left to the backend because f16 IS
selectable everywhere -- which is true, and is not the same as being
correctly rounded.

design.md ALREADY SAYS THIS, ABOUT THE OTHER WIDTH. Its § reduced-precision
erratum (B-2026-08-29-23) reads: "this paragraph used to say LLVM performs
that promotion automatically. It does not, and relying on it produced a
shipped bug." That erratum was written about bf16 selectability. The same
sentence is now true of f16 ROUNDING on wasm, and design.md's line 14079
("On targets without native support, LLVM promotes to `f32` for computation")
is, read as a claim about wasm f16, false in its second half -- it promotes
and does not round back.

FIX SHAPE (not attempted here). The bf16 treatment, narrowed to what f16
needs: have codegen widen f16 arithmetic to f32 and round back explicitly,
rather than emitting a native `half` op and trusting the backend. Doing it
unconditionally (as bf16 does) keeps ONE f16 semantics path and costs
nothing on targets that already round, since the explicit round is what they
emit anyway; doing it only for wasm is smaller but creates a second path and
a divergence surface between targets. A `verify_no_native_f16_arith_ops`
sibling to the bf16 verifier would keep the class closed. Whether the
comparison operators need the same treatment was NOT measured -- `a < b`
agreed on every pair tried, but every pair tried had operands that were
already f16-representable, so that is the "agrees by luck of the inputs"
trap B-2026-08-29-40 documents rather than a clearance.

SEVERITY. The values are wrong rather than imprecise (a finite 196512 where
the type tops out at 65504), it breaks `run == build` across targets, and it
is silent. Against that: it needs the wasm target AND f16, a combination that
could not be built at all until now, so nothing shipped can have hit it.

SCOPE NOTE (added at close). This row's measurements were sound and its
mechanism was right, but its scope was narrower than the defect in three ways,
all corrected in the `fix` field:

  * The defect is not at the ABI boundary. This entry says wasm "returns the
    f32 unrounded" and calls the missing final `__truncsfhf2` the bug. A STORE
    does round (`f32.add; __truncsfhf2; i32.store16`); what is missing is the
    round BETWEEN two chained arithmetic ops, which is a broader claim and is
    why an accumulation loop drifts.

  * MATH METHODS ARE AFFECTED TOO, and are not mentioned here at all.
    `65504f16.sqrt()` returned the unrounded f32 255.93748474... where the f16
    answer is 255.875; over the fourteen f16 math methods, 9 of 11 printed
    lines differed from native. They reach the backend as `llvm.sqrt.f16`-style
    intrinsics -- a native op wearing a call's clothing -- which is exactly
    what an opcode sweep for `fmul half` cannot see.

  * The comparison operators, left open here as "not measured", are FINE. The
    wasm backend normalizes each operand through f16 before comparing, so a
    compare self-corrects. What was broken was comparing an unrounded
    arithmetic RESULT, which the arithmetic fix cures. `fneg` and `fabs` are
    likewise exact.

The proposed remedy in FIX SHAPE does not work as written, which is the
substantive correction: emitting the widened form unconditionally, as bf16
does, is undone by InstCombine at `default<O2>` for all five operators. See
the `fix` field.

title: A by-value param with TWO exits -- conditionally STORED into a `mut ref` place and also RETURNED on another path -- runs NO `Drop` body on the path where it dies inside the callee. The shape B-2026-08-30-28's per-path flag deliberately DECLINES: nothing clears the flag on a non-store exit, so admitting it DOUBLES the body instead (measured, all four surfaces). Unanimous across backends, so no A/B gate reports it
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-30-28 while that row was being fixed, as the shape its
fix deliberately DECLINES rather than a defect the fix introduced. Measured
identical before and after (baseline recorded on the pre-fix compiler by
stashing the change, rebuilding, and re-running the same program).

-28 gives a conditionally-stored by-value parameter a per-path drop flag: armed
on entry, cleared at the store, read at scope exit. That works because the store
is the only way the value leaves. A parameter that can ALSO be returned has a
second exit, and nothing clears the flag there -- so the callee's guarded body
and the caller's result binding both fire for one object:

    struct Res { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id} {self.tag}") } }
    struct Wrap { r: Res }

    fn via_let(sink: mut ref Vec[Res], r: Res) -> Option[Wrap] {
        if r.id > 200 { let w: Wrap = Wrap { r: r }; return Some(w); }   // escapes
        if r.id > 100 { sink.push(r); }                                  // stores
        return None;                                                     // dies here
    }

Ungated, that printed `drop 301 | drop 301 ret` on all four surfaces -- the first
with the String already moved into the wrapper, which is what a body running over
a moved-out value looks like. The bare-return (`return Some(r)`) and
return-through-a-call (`return inner(r)`) spellings each doubled on at least one
backend; codegen's return-operand clear happens to cover those two and the
interpreter's does not, so they were also a run-vs-build split.

So `outliving_store::escapes_by_non_store_route` declines the registration
whenever any non-store exit exists, conservative-decline on any shape it does not
recognize. THE COST IS THIS ROW: for a parameter with two exits, the path where
the value dies inside the callee runs no body at all -- exactly the -28 defect,
surviving on the narrower shape.

    via_let(mut s, Res { id: 6, tag: "dies" })   ->   (no output)

Unanimous across interp / JIT / AOT / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, so no A/B gate reports
it. NOT a memory defect: the registration is bodies-only
(`emit_struct_user_drop_bodies_only_fn`), so the buffer keeps exactly one owner
either way -- valgrind-clean, 0 errors. What is lost is the user-visible SIDE
EFFECT of the `Drop` body.

WHAT A REAL FIX NEEDS: the flag cleared at EVERY exit, not just the store. The
return-operand clear already exists in codegen (`arm_conditional_store_flag`
matches `Return(Some(inner))` and recurses through aggregates and call
arguments); what is missing is (a) the same clear on a `let`/assign that binds
the parameter into a local which then escapes -- which needs the local's own fate
tracked, not just the statement -- and (b) the interpreter twin of the
return-operand clear. Do BOTH or neither: clearing on one backend only is how the
`call-ret` spelling became a run-vs-build split in the first place.

DO NOT "fix" this by loosening `escapes_by_non_store_route` alone. The guard is
what holds the count at one; without it this shape DOUBLES, which is the
unrecoverable direction. `e2e_a_param_that_can_also_be_returned_is_not_given_a_store_flag`
pins that and will fail if the guard is relaxed without the clears landing first.
fix:
FIXED by f77f6a4b.

The row's own prescription was implemented as written -- "clear at EVERY exit,
not just the store" and "do BOTH or neither" -- and both halves mattered.

  * codegen's `arm_conditional_store_flag` widened from a statement EXPRESSION
    to a whole statement, so a `let`, an assignment and a `return` disarm the
    per-path flag the same way a store does. Moved to `compile_stmt_inner`'s
    head, beside the escaping-site seeding that already ran there. Still
    NON-RECURSIVE, which is the same correctness argument B-2026-08-30-28 makes:
    the clear has to land in the block the statement compiles into, not the one
    evaluating an enclosing condition.
  * the interpreter twin, `disarm_cond_store_param_on_handover`. Its existing
    `record_conditional_move_tail` matches only a BARE identifier at an escaping
    site, which is exactly why `return Some(r)`, `return inner(r)` and
    `let w = W { r: r };` all slipped past it. That gap was also a run-vs-build
    split on its own: `return inner(r)` ran TWO bodies in the interpreter
    against ONE in codegen, because codegen's return-operand clear recurses
    through call arguments and the interpreter had no clear at all.
  * the guard loosened to admit exactly the cleared routes, and RENAMED
    `escapes_by_non_store_route` -> `escapes_by_unclearable_route`. The store
    stopped being the only exit that clears the flag, so a name built around
    "non-store" had stopped describing the question; what decides admission is
    whether BOTH backends disarm at the exit, not which exit it is.

MEASURED -- three callee shapes (`return Some(r)`, `let w = W { r: r }; return
Some(w)`, `return inner(r)`) x three paths (escapes / stores / dies inside), on
interp / JIT / AOT / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, all four unanimous:

    escapes       one body  ->  one body
    stores        one body  ->  one body
    dies inside   NO body   ->  one body      (this row)

Valgrind clean, 0 errors. B-2026-08-30-28's and B-2026-08-29-49's shape matrices
re-run unanimous with no count changing except the three that were zero.

TWO THINGS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, both recorded because the answer was
"no defect" and that is worth knowing:

  * The new per-frame set is name-keyed with no frame qualifier, the same shape
    that made B-2026-08-29-11 and B-2026-08-29-9 leak marks between frames. A
    probe with a CALLER binding spelled the same as the callee's parameter
    measured IDENTICAL before and after, so no leak was observable -- but the
    save/restore was added anyway, because every neighbour in that block is
    isolated and a set outliving its frame is a hazard whether or not one
    program has found it yet.
  * A `let w = W { r: r };` runs the payload's body at the LET rather than when
    `w` dies. That looked like fallout from the new `let` clear; it is not.
    Stashing the change and rebuilding measures the same placement on both
    backends, so it predates this row entirely and is left alone here.

B-2026-08-30-28's guard test was REWRITTEN rather than left passing under a
false name: it asserted the shape "is not given a store flag", which this row
makes untrue. It now pins all three paths in one program, since they fail in
opposite directions -- the escaping path doubles, the dying path loses -- and a
test covering one would pass a fix that broke the other.

title: A `u64` value >= 2^63 converts to EVERY float type as its negative two's-complement under the interpreter (`u64::MAX as f64` prints -1) while all three compiled surfaces print the correct 18446744073709552000. `Value::Int`'s signed carrier is converted instead of the value -- the cast-path residual of B-2026-07-04-8, whose u64 model covered printing, comparison and sorting but never mentions casts.
detail:
FOUND while sweeping B-2026-08-30-26's int <-> bf16 conversions across four
surfaces: 225 of 226 rows agreed, and the one that did not turned out to have
nothing to do with bf16.

    let a: u64 = 18446744073709551615u64 ...   (u64::MAX, opaque to the compiler)

    surface           a as f64                a as f32                a as bf16
    karac run --interp  -1                      -1                      -1
    karac run (JIT)     18446744073709552000    18446744073709552000    18446744073709552000
    karac build         18446744073709552000    18446744073709552000    18446744073709552000

The compiled backends are correct; the interpreter is wrong, for EVERY float
target, and `as f16` gives `inf` compiled against `-1` interpreted. It also
reproduces at 2^63 exactly (interp -9223372036854776000, compiled
9223372036854776000) and is correct for every value below 2^63, which locates it
precisely: `Value::Int`'s signed i128 carrier stores a u64 above 2^63 as its
negative two's-complement image (`int_from`'s u64 arm is
`((i as u64) as i64).into()`), and the float arm then converts the CARRIER
(`Value::Float(i as f64)`) instead of the value.

This is a residual of B-2026-07-04-8, which built the interpreter's u64 model --
its title is "the tree-walk interpreter has NO u64 model: Value::Int(i64) is
signedness-blind, so every u64 value >= 2^63 is handled as its negative i64
two's-complement" -- and fixed printing, comparison and sorting. Its prose does
not contain the words "cast", "float", "as f64", "sitofp" or "uitofp" anywhere,
so the conversion path was never in scope rather than having regressed.

NOT caused by B-2026-08-30-26 and not fixable there: `as f64` and `as f32` have
compiled and diverged this way all along, and they never touch the bf16 lanes
that fix changes. The bf16 leg merely made a fourth surface available to compare
against.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINER. The cast site (`eval_expr.rs`'s `int_from`) receives
the i128 carrier and the TARGET type name, and has no idea whether the SOURCE
was unsigned -- which is the whole B-2026-07-04-8 problem in miniature. Fixing
it needs the source's signedness threaded to the cast, the same way that row
threaded an `unsigned` flag through the sort keys, so it wants its own slice
rather than a graft.

Exotic in practice for the same reason B-2026-07-04-8 records: the lexer rejects
integer literals above i64::MAX unless suffixed, so a u64 >= 2^63 is reachable
only through a deliberate `u64` suffix or shift-constructed high bits.
fix:
FIXED by 74f6989.

Every route by which an integer reaches a float slot in the interpreter now
converts the VALUE rather than the signed `i128` carrier, using the source's
recorded unsigned width.

THE SURFACE WAS TEN SITES, NOT ONE. The row recorded `as f64` / `as f32` /
`as f16` / `as bf16`, which is where it was found. Probing each way an integer
can land in a float slot found every one of them converting the carrier
independently:

    as-cast (all four float widths)   `mx as f64`            -1
    to_f32 / to_f64 methods            `mx.to_f64()`          -1
    float-annotated let                `let x: f64 = mx;`     -1
    call argument                      `takef(mx)`            -1
    method argument                    `s.setm(mx)`           -1
    function tail expression           `fn f(v: u64) -> f64 { v }`        -1
    explicit return                    `fn f(v: u64) -> f64 { return v; }` -1
    struct-literal field               `S { f: mx }`          -1
    field assignment                   `s.f = mx`             -1
    Vec[f64] element store             `vf.push(mx)`          -1

against 18446744073709552000 on `karac run` (JIT), `karac build`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` alike. Measured over a 9-value x 10-shape sweep:
45 of 90 rows diverged before, 0 of 90 after, on all four surfaces.

THREE SEPARATE CONVERSION MECHANISMS had to be taught the same fact, which is
why the site count is what it is:
  * `cast_value` (the `as` cast) — gained a `src_unsigned_width` parameter,
    supplied at the cast site from the OPERAND's own leaf span (the `Cast`
    node's span covers `x as T`, a different key).
  * `coerce_int_value_to_declared_float` (the implicit widening at let / arg /
    field / return positions) — same parameter, threaded from each caller's
    source expression. `assign_to_place` needed it too, for `s.f = mx`.
  * `float_coerced_arg_sites` (the typechecker's record of an integer sitting
    in a float slot, consumed at container stores and the assign RHS) — both
    consumers converted the carrier.
All three now go through one helper, `carrier_to_f64`.

THE RETURN POSITION NEEDED A DIFFERENT SHAPE OF FIX, and it is the interesting
one. The caller-side widening in `eval_call` sees only a `Value` and cannot tell
a `u64` past 2^63 from the negative `i64` it shares a carrier with — the
information is gone by then. Converting at the call site is therefore impossible
in principle, not merely awkward. So the conversion moved to where the returned
expression is still in hand: the `ExprKind::Return` operand and the block TAIL,
both via `coerce_float_assign_rhs`, which is inert unless the typechecker
flagged that exact span. That covers a `return` nested inside a branch, which a
tail-expression-only fix would have missed — verified with
`fn f(v: u64, k: bool) -> f64 { if k { return v; } v }` on both paths.

`u64 as u128` WAS ALSO SIGN-EXTENDING, and that is a second defect this found
rather than a consequence of the first. `18446744073709551615u64 as u128` stored
-1, so the `u128` was already wrong before anything read it as a float — the
