    (`w => format!("i{}", w)`), and LLVM's `IntType` carries no signedness, so
    `i128` and `u128` both answer "i128". It structurally cannot tell them
    apart.
  * `is_scalar_primitive_mangle_name` is the NAME channel that exists to correct
    exactly this erasure — its own comment says narrow ints are "WIDENED to i64
    before the call, so `token` is 'i64' for every narrow width … Append the
    exact declared name instead" (B-2026-07-03-24). Its list runs
    `i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 | u8 | u16 | u32 | u64 | usize | isize | f16 | bf16 |
    f32 | f64 | bool | char` — `i128` and `u128` are absent, so the correction
    never fires for them and the erased token stands.

THE FIX IS TWO STRINGS, and the evidence that it is sufficient is program B
above: a `u128`-only monomorph is ALREADY CORRECT, so giving `u128` its own
symbol is all that is needed — nothing about 128-bit code generation itself is
broken. Adding `"i128" | "u128"` to `is_scalar_primitive_mangle_name` is the
whole change. Note `llvm_type_to_mangle_str` CANNOT be fixed instead: signedness
is not recoverable from an `IntType`, so the name channel is the only one that
can carry it.

DELIBERATELY NOT FOLDED INTO B-2026-08-30-36. That row is about `f16`/`bf16`
satisfying the arithmetic operator traits; this is a different type family whose
own reachability story differs (`i128`/`u128` implement none of the six
arithmetic traits either — the same `env_build.rs` omission, one list over — so
a BOUNDED generic cannot reach them at all today, and the repro above needs an
unbounded `[T]`). Filing it separately keeps that row reviewable and leaves this
one a turnkey change with its own regression test to write.

WHOEVER ENABLES `i128`/`u128` IN THE OPERATOR-TRAIT LISTS MUST LAND THIS FIRST.
`env_build.rs`'s `signed_ints`/`unsigned_ints` stop at 64 bits, so
`fn g[T: Add](a: T, b: T)` at `i128` is rejected today with "`i128` does not
implement `Add`". Adding the widths there without this makes every bounded
128-bit generic share one signedness — which is precisely the trap
B-2026-08-30-36 measured for `f16`/`bf16` and is why that row's fix is three
changes and not the one line it was filed with.

title: A READ-ONLY `match` ARM OVER AN `Option`/`Result` WHOSE PAYLOAD IS A HEAP-OWNING NON-STRUCT STILL TAKES THE PAYLOAD -- six shapes, three failure modes: `Option[Map]`/`[Set]`/`[SortedMap]` read back as `None`, `Result[E]` prints empty, and `Option[E]` / `Option[Option[String]]` abort with a double free. A seventh, `Result[Map]`, SEGFAULTED and is fixed. B-2026-08-30-19 reached the STRUCT payload only
detail:
FOUND by a second-pass audit of B-2026-08-30-19's own fix. That row extended
`pattern_binds_direct_inline_heap_payload` from a DIRECT `{ptr,len,cap}` payload
to a user struct that transitively owns heap, and its prose says the change is
"confined to the shapes that are broken today". It was not: six more shapes were
broken and stayed broken.

MEASURED on `main`, 13 shapes, each a two-read program (`match x { Some(p) =>
read; ... }` twice) against `--interp` as the reference:

  BROKEN
    Option[Map[i64, String]]      1 then `no-b`   -- source reads back as None
    Option[Set[String]]           1 then `no-b`
    Option[SortedMap[i64,String]] 1 then `no-b`
    Result[E, i64] (E owns heap)  `re` then EMPTY -- moved out and zeroed
    Option[E]      (E owns heap)  double free detected in tcache 2 (SIGABRT)
    Option[Option[String]]        double free detected in tcache 2 (SIGABRT)
  CORRECT (controls)
    Option[Vec[String]]           -- `Vec` was always admitted
    Option[(String, i64)]         -- tuple payloads have their own gate
    Option[F] (enum, no heap)     -- must STAY out
    Option[Option[i64]]           -- must STAY out
    Option[i64], Option[u8]       -- scalars, no owner
    Option[shared struct]         -- RC box, must STAY out (B-2026-08-13-6)

All four modes reproduce identically on JIT, AOT and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, and
`--interp` is correct for every row -- the run-vs-build signature.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT CAUSED BY -19, and measured rather than argued: rebuilding
with -19's admission line reverted to `t == \"String\" || t == \"Vec\"` leaves
`Option[Map]`, `Option[E]` and `Option[Option[String]]` failing IDENTICALLY,
while the shape -19 did fix regresses to garbage. So -19 is neither cause nor
cure here.

TWO DISTINCT MECHANISMS, which is why this is not a one-line extension of -19.

  (a) The CLASSIFIER's entry point was struct-only while its own field walker
      one level down was already conservative: `named_struct_owns_heap` answers
      `false` for any name that is not a known struct, whereas
      `field_te_owns_heap` answers `true` for anything that is neither a scalar
      nor a known heap-free struct. A payload the walker would call heap-owning
      as a FIELD was called heap-free as the payload ITSELF.

  (b) The GATE in front of the classifier requires membership in
      `inline_{option,result}_payload_vars`, and
      `track_inline_option_payload_var` registers nothing unless the payload is
      an inline heap `Vec`/`String` (`option_inline_payload_elem`). So
      `Option[Map]`, `Option[E]` and `Option[Option[String]]` never reach the
      classifier at all, and their double frees come from a different owner --
      the enum/aggregate drop synthesis -- not from this borrow decision.

PARTIAL FIX ALREADY LANDED (f29da14) for (a) only: `binding_type_name_owns_heap` /
`named_type_owns_heap` / `named_enum_owns_heap` replace the struct-only entry
point and teach the walker to resolve a user ENUM, so the two ends of one
judgement can no longer drift apart. That flips `Result[Map[i64, String]]` from
a SEGFAULT to correct, and holds every one of the six controls above. It is
landed because the asymmetry is a latent defect on its own terms, not because it
closes this row. The six shapes listed BROKEN remain broken and need (b).

NEXT STEP for whoever takes this: (b) is the load-bearing half. The question to
settle first is whether these payloads SHOULD be registered as inline (making
the existing borrow machinery apply) or whether the read-only-arm borrow needs a
second, representation-independent path. Do not extend the classifier further
without answering that -- (a) is already as far as the classifier alone reaches.

A CONSERVATIVE DEFAULT IS NOT SAFE HERE, measured the hard way, and it is the
first thing to know before touching the classifier. "Conservative" in this code
usually means "answer owns-heap when unsure", on the reasoning that a wrong
`true` costs a missed optimization while a wrong `false` dangles. That reasoning
does NOT hold at the binding entry point, because `true` here classifies the arm
as a BORROW, and a borrow DROPS an owner whenever the payload turns out to own
itself. Both answers are unsafe for some shape.

The first version of `binding_type_name_owns_heap` fell through to `true` for
any unresolved name, partly on the strength of a comment in this same file
asserting that a whole-tuple binding has no `pattern_binding_types` entry. It
has one: `bind_pattern_types` records a `Type::Tuple` binding under the literal
name `"Tuple"` (`typechecker/patterns.rs`), which the conservative arm then
admitted. `e2e_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` produced NO OUTPUT AT
ALL -- the same signature B-2026-08-08-25 recorded when it first drew this line,
reproduced by rediscovering the same hazard from the other side. The landed
version is an explicit allow-list (`String`, `Vec`, `Map`, `Set`, `SortedMap`,
`SortedSet`) plus the resolved struct/enum/shared answers, with `"Tuple"`
excluded by name; the stale comment has been corrected in place.

sites through one `carrier_to_f64` helper and measured 0 of 90 rows diverging
over a 9-value x 10-shape sweep. The sweep was over the ten shapes it had

  let a: Array[f64, 2] = [u, 1.0]    -1 / ...992          ...992   CONVERTED, WRONG WIDTH

fix:
FIXED by b554da2, in `src/codegen/control_flow.rs` + `src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs`
by giving the branch merge a MIXED int/float arm reconciliation, the
cross-KIND sibling of the two width reconciliations it already had.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is one line of omission rather than a wrong computation.
The `if` / `if let` / `match` merges each build a phi only when every arm's
LLVM type agrees, and otherwise fall through to a const-`i64 0` placeholder --
a fallback whose comment reads "otherwise the `if` is in statement position
(unit value)". Two helpers existed to make the types agree:
`unify_int_branch_widths` (int-vs-int) and `unify_float_branch_widths`
(float-vs-float), each of which returns its arguments UNTOUCHED when the pair
is not of its kind. So an `i64` arm beside a `double` arm passed through both
untouched, failed the all-same-type check, and took the whole construct to the
placeholder. The `0` in the row's table is that placeholder, not a bad
conversion; nothing ever attempted the int->float conversion at all.

That also explains the row's own observation that BOTH arms fail. The
placeholder replaces the whole `if`, so the float arm is lost with the integer
one -- confirmed here: the `return-position-if` shape prints `0` for the `n`
arm AND `0` for the `0.5` arm.

THE FIX adds `unify_int_float_branch_values` (two-arm) and
`unify_int_float_match_arm_values` (N-arm), each converting the INTEGER side to
the float sibling's type in that arm's own predecessor block, so the result
dominates the phi's incoming edge -- the placement rule every neighbouring
helper already follows. Routed through `build_int_to_float_bf16_safe` so a
`bf16` target cannot emit an aarch64-unselectable `sitofp .. to bfloat`. Runs
LAST, after the two width passes, so each side is already at the width it will
keep.

THE DIRECTION IS FORCED, NOT CHOSEN. A mixed pair can only reach the merge
having already been unified by the typechecker to ONE Kara type, and an integer
arm beside a float arm unifies to the FLOAT (Kara widens int->float at an
annotation boundary and never narrows float->int implicitly). So the integer
side is the one that converts.

SIGNEDNESS is read from the arm's TAIL EXPRESSION, peeled through any block
wrapper (`branch_tail_value_expr`), via the existing `expr_is_unsigned_int`.
This is load-bearing, not defensive: `let a: f64 = if true { u } else { 0.0 }`
with `u: u64 = u64::MAX` prints 18446744073709552000 under `uitofp` and

fix:
FIXED by 76677be1.

NOT THE FIX THE ROW PREDICTED. It called for building a per-branch drop flag;
B-2026-08-28-51 had already built one, and the whole defect was that its seeding
never reached argument position. `note_escaping_site` marks the tails of a
wrapper in escaping position so the taken arm's tail disarms the binding it hands
over -- an `i1` flag cleared in that arm's basic block on the compiled backends,
a `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` insert in the interpreter. It recursed through
wrapper tails but NOT into a call's argument list, and ran only for `let` and
`return` statements.

So a by-value call argument becomes the fourth escaping position, seeded from
`let`, `return`, an assignment RHS, and a call in STATEMENT position. That last
one needed care: a discarded CALL still consumes its arguments, so its wrapper
arguments are seeded like a `let`'s, while a discarded `if` stays excluded --
its arm tails have no consumer, and marking them takes a program that runs one
body today to zero. With the binding disarmed on the path that hands it over,
the argument temp is the single owner there, and the body that runs on the other
path belongs to a second object rather than being a duplicate.

SEEDED ONLY WHERE SOME TAIL MINTS. The gate is load-bearing, and it was measured
rather than reasoned: the seed disarms, and the registration that must replace it
needs a minting tail to name a type from. An ALL-PLACES wrapper
(`one(if c { a1 } else { a2 })`) has none, so seeding it disarmed the taken
binding with nothing taking over and the value's body VANISHED on all three
compiled surfaces while the interpreter still ran it -- a regression this fix
introduced and then closed. Unseeded, both backends keep their prior correct
behaviour: each binding armed, dying in place.

A SECOND SELF-INFLICTED BUG, same root: `first_branch_tail` handed the registrar
the FIRST tail, which for a mixed construct is the place tail -- a binding the
registrar's arms cannot classify -- so it registered nothing and the fix added no
body at all. It now prefers the first MINTING tail. Both were caught by probing
shapes the row did not name, not by the suite.

Both admissions are gated on the SEEDING rather than on shape -- codegen on the
conditional-move flag existing for that binding
(`arg_producer_mints_fresh_owned_temp`), the interpreter on the tail's span being
a marked site (`cond_moved_place_tail_type_name`) -- so the disarm and the
registration cannot drift apart. That coupling is the safety argument: an
identifier tail somewhere the seeding does not reach keeps its binding armed, and
admitting it there would be the double fire again.

VERIFICATION: seven cases per backend pin mixed-fresh-taken, mixed-binding-taken
(the double-fire direction), all-places, statement position, method calls, a
passthrough callee, and a match arm; RED-verified -- reverting `src` fails both
at `mixed-wrapper-arg-fresh-branch-taken` with the missing body. Six probe

every one, the check that matters when the risk is an extra drop. Full gates:
llvm 15839/0, default 10176/0, both clippy legs and fmt clean.

SCOPE CONFIRMED WIDER THAN FILED, in the row's favour: the same seeding fixes the

reach.
title: A MIXED CONTROL-FLOW ARGUMENT LOSES THE FRESH BRANCH'S `Drop` BODY when that branch is the one taken -- `one(if false { k } else { mk(31) })` runs `k`'s body and never `mk(31)`'s, on all four surfaces; the SAME construct let-bound runs both, so this is argument-position-specific
detail:
LEFT OPEN BY B-2026-08-30-38 DELIBERATELY, not missed by it. That row taught
both backends to resolve a wrapper argument through its tails, but only when
EVERY tail mints a fresh owned temp (`expr_is_fresh_owned_branch_tail`, the
fail-closed rule B-2026-08-29-27 established). A MIXED construct -- one tail
naming a binding, another minting -- is declined, and the decline is required
rather than merely cautious: the binding keeps its own name-keyed drop, so
claiming the merged value would run one body TWICE. Widening the predicate is
therefore the WRONG fix; this needs a per-branch drop flag.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}"); } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> R { R { id: n } }
    fn one(r: R) -> i64 { println("  in-one"); r.id }
    fn main() {
        let k = mk(30);
        let m1 = one(if false { k } else { mk(31) });   // dR30 only -- dR31 LOST
        println(f"  m1={m1}");
        let j = mk(40);
        let m2 = one(if true { j } else { mk(41) });    // dR40 -- correct
        println(f"  m2={m2}");
        let q = mk(50);
        let m3 = if false { q } else { mk(51) };        // dR50 AND dR51 -- correct
        println(f"  m3={m3.id}");
    }

M3 IS THE CONTROL AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT: the identical construct bound to a
`let` runs both bodies. So the LET path already models the conditional move
correctly and only ARGUMENT position does not -- which is what says the missing
piece is a per-branch flag at the argument window, not a defect in the ownership
model. `k`'s own body firing at the merge is correct (it genuinely dies there,
under NLL); the value actually passed to the call is what has no owner.

Measured identical on a pre-fix build (`git stash` of `src`, rebuilt), so this
is NOT fallout from B-2026-08-30-38 -- it is the part of that bug its fix could
not reach. All four surfaces agree (`--interp`, JIT, AOT, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`),
so no A/B parity gate and no kata can see it, and valgrind `--leak-check=full`
is clean: the memory channel fires and only the user body is lost. Same
body-vs-memory split as B-2026-08-29-24 / -54 / -38.

WHERE TO START. The two admission points are codegen's
`branch_tail_mints_fresh_owned_temp_inner` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`) and the
interpreter's `wrapper_tail_arg_type_name` (`src/interpreter/eval_call.rs`).
Both currently require ALL tails to resolve. Closing this means registering the
temp per BRANCH with a flag the minting tails set and the binding tails clear,
drained on B-2026-08-29-55's per-call argument window
(`call_arg_temp_mark` / `drain_call_arg_temp_user_drops`) -- NOT on the
statement frame, or the live-range extension that row closed comes back. Note
codegen already has conditional-disarm machinery from B-2026-08-30-33 to model
on. The interpreter needs the same treatment: it loses the body too.

fix:
FIXED by 07dc9e76.

MECHANISM CONFIRMED as the row suspected. The interpreter's cleanup slots are
NAME-KEYED (`CleanupAction::Drop { name }`) and resolve through the env when they
fire; two `let`s of one name push two slots with the same key, and by drain time
the env holds only the survivor, so both fired on it. The compiled backends key
on the SLOT, which is why they were already right.

THE FIX is `CleanupAction::DropShadowed { name, value }`, which freezes the
shadowed value into its slot at the shadowing `let` and drops it through the
value-based walk `let _ = …` already uses. That is sound for exactly the reason
the bug existed: the name that addressed the value is gone, so nothing can reach
it again. The trace keeps the SOURCE name, so existing drop-order assertions read
unchanged.

ORDERING IS THE CORRECTNESS ARGUMENT, in both directions, and it is the part a
re-implementation is most likely to get wrong. The freeze runs AFTER every
move-suppression helper, which is what keeps `let z = z;` at ONE body -- those
helpers have already retracted the source's slot, so there is nothing left to
freeze and the single object keeps its single owner. It runs BEFORE
`push_drops_for_stmt`, because once the fresh slot exists a slot bearing that
name is ambiguous between the two generations. It also converts the LAST matching
slot, not the first, so repeated shadowing does not re-freeze an already-frozen
generation.

A SECOND NAME-KEYING FLAW one level up, found by the same probes and fixed with
it: `compute_block_last_use`'s never-read fallback kept the FIRST `let` for a
shadowed name. That endpoint precedes the surviving slot's existence, so the
survivor never fired by NLL and drained at scope exit instead -- measured as
`let b = E.V(mk(3)); let b = E.V(mk(4));` running the second body at the end of
`main` while both compiled backends ran it at the shadowing `let`. The LAST `let`
wins now; a real read still wins over both, which is what the original
`or_insert` was protecting.

VERIFICATION: nine cases per backend, byte-identical across the pair
(`test_shadowed_binding_drops_its_own_value` / `e2e_shadowed_binding_drops_its_own_value`)
-- unread-first, read-before-shadow, three-deep, neither-read, nested block, loop
body, a Drop-bearing field, a shadowed param, and `let z = z;` as the guard rail.
RED-verified: reverting `src` fails at `shadow-unread-first` with the row's exact
`dR2 dR2`. Gates: llvm 15843/0, default 10178/0, both clippy legs and fmt clean.

REMAINDER, filed as B-2026-08-30-57: with this backend fixed, the COMPILED ones
are now visibly wrong on two shadowing shapes -- a block-local shadowed binding
loses its body entirely, and a shadowed enum followed by a later `Vec[R]`
declaration defers its payload body to function exit. The two argument-position
pins deliberately DISAGREE now, each annotated, rather than being relaxed into

MEASUREMENT NOTE: an intermediate reading of this suggested a JIT-vs-AOT split.
It was a stale `karac_jit_runner` -- the footgun CLAUDE.md documents -- and
rebuilding both bins showed all three compiled surfaces agreeing. Recorded

non-existent backend divergence.
title: INTERPRETER: A SHADOWED BINDING'S `Drop` BODY NEVER RUNS AND THE SHADOWING VALUE'S RUNS TWICE -- `let t = mk(1); let t = mk(2);` prints `dR2 dR2` under `--interp` against `dR2 dR1` on every compiled backend, so one resource is released twice and another never
detail:
A RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE, and the interpreter is the wrong one.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}"); } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> R { R { id: n } }
    fn main() {
        let t = mk(1);
        let t = mk(2);
        println(f"  t={t.id}");           // --interp: dR2 dR2   JIT/AOT: dR2 dR1
        let v = { let u = mk(3); let u = mk(4); u.id };
        println(f"  v={v}");              // --interp: dR4 dR4   JIT/AOT: dR4 dR3
    }

BOTH HALVES ARE WRONG on this backend and they are different failures wearing
one symptom: the shadowed `R { id: 1 }`'s body NEVER runs (a resource never
released), and `R { id: 2 }`'s runs TWICE (a resource released twice -- an
unlock of an already-unlocked lock, a double close). The second is the more
serious: a `Drop` body is a user-visible effect, so double-running one is a
soundness break, not a tidiness issue.

MECHANISM (suspected, not yet confirmed): the interpreter's cleanup actions are
NAME-KEYED -- `push_drops_for_stmt` pushes `CleanupAction::Drop { name }` per
`let`, and the action resolves the name in the env when it fires. Two `let`s
binding the same name push TWO actions with the SAME key, and by the time either
fires the env holds only the surviving value, so both resolve to it. The
compiled backends key on the SLOT, not the name, which is why they are correct.
If that reading holds, the fix is to bind the value (or its slot identity) into
the action at push time rather than re-resolving at fire time.

BOTH the function body and a nested block reproduce it, so this is about
shadowing itself and not about block nesting.

FOUND while probing B-2026-08-30-38's block-local binding tail
(`one({ let t = mk(90); let t = mk(91); t }`), which is why the shadowing
spelling came up at all -- but it is INDEPENDENT of that row: the repro contains
no call argument of a `Drop` type, and it was measured byte-identical on a
pre-fix build (`git stash` of `src`, rebuilt). valgrind `--leak-check=full` is
clean on the AOT binary, which says nothing about the interpreter and is noted
only to head off the assumption that a memory tool would have caught this.

NOT PINNED YET -- no test asserts either spelling, which is presumably how it
survived: every existing shadowing test uses types with no user `Drop`.

022f07c — (b) IS FIXED, AND WITH IT THE WHOLE ROW.

detail:
FOUND while closing B-2026-08-30-47, and it is what the last three of that
row's shapes actually were. -47 attributed `Option[E]`,
`Option[Option[String]]` and `Result[E]` to the payload-representation gap it
named. Widening that gap fixed the `Map` family and left those three failing
identically, which is what prompted probing a shape -47 never tried: the same
payload types bound whole and read WITHOUT destructuring.

MEASURED on `main` (each program matches the same local twice, reading only):

  DESTRUCTURING ARM -- all broken
    Option[S { s: String }], `Some(S { s })`      `sd` then GARBAGE (UAF)
    Option[(String, i64)], `Some((s, n))`         double free (SIGABRT)
    Option[E] heap enum, inner `match p { A { s } }` double free (SIGABRT)
    Result[E, i64], inner `match q { A { s } }`   `re` then EMPTY
  WHOLE BINDING, NO DESTRUCTURE -- all correct, the controls
    Option[E] read via a method on the binding      1 then 1
    Result[E, i64] read via a method                1 then 1
    Option[Map] / [Set] / [SortedMap] via `.len()`  1 then 1

`--interp` is correct for every row; JIT, AOT and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` agree with
each other and disagree with it.

SO THIS IS NOT THE REPRESENTATION AXIS, which is why it needed its own row.
The struct and tuple rows are the proof: those payload types were never in
doubt -- `Option[S]` bound whole is the exact shape B-2026-08-30-19 fixed and
`Option[(String, i64)]` is a pinned control in
`e2e_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` -- and both fail as soon as the
arm destructures instead of binding. The axis is the PATTERN, not the payload.

ROOT CAUSE, read off the classifier rather than inferred:
`pattern_binds_direct_inline_heap_payload` requires every payload-consuming
sub-pattern to be `matches!(&p.kind, PatternKind::Binding(_))` -- a whole-payload
binding. Any destructuring pattern therefore fails the classifier BY
CONSTRUCTION, the arm is never classified a borrow, and the transfer path runs:
the bound leaf registers as an owner and frees at arm exit while the source's
own drop is still armed (double free), or the source is disarmed and a later
read runs off the freed block (garbage / empty). No widening of the payload-type
side reaches this -- that was measured, not assumed: B-2026-08-30-47's fix moved
none of these rows.

The inner-`match` spelling is the same defect one level down: the arm binds the
payload whole (so the OUTER classifier can fire), and then the inner `match` over
that binding destructures a heap field out of a value the source still owns. The
borrow-ness of the outer binding does not propagate into the inner pattern.

NEXT STEP for whoever takes this. The classifier's whole-binding restriction is
not arbitrary -- B-2026-08-08-25 recorded that a destructuring `Some((v, k))`
gives each heap element its OWN `track_vec_var`, so classifying that arm as a
borrow drops those owners, and that is the same hazard that emptied
`e2e_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` twice (once in B-2026-08-08-25,
once in B-2026-08-30-47's first attempt). So the fix is NOT to relax the
whole-binding test. It is to make a destructured leaf bound out of a
source-retained payload a BORROW ITSELF -- registering no owner, exactly as the
whole-payload binding does on the borrow path -- and to propagate that
borrow-ness through a nested pattern. Treat any patch that merely admits
destructuring patterns to the existing classifier as wrong until that test
passes.

PARTIALLY FIXED by d22cf63. Twelve of the shapes above are correct on
all four surfaces; two sub-mechanisms remain and the title has been rewritten

of the fixture:

  * `pattern_destructures_heap_payload` admits a destructuring payload pattern
    to the read-only classifier, judged from the SCRUTINEE'S INSTANTIATION
    rather than from the leaves. That detail is forced: a shorthand struct
    field (`S { s }`) carries no sub-`Pattern` at all -- the field name IS the
    binding -- so there is no span to look up in `pattern_binding_types` and no
    per-leaf type to read. The payload's own `TypeExpr` needs neither.
  * `scrutinee_is_boxed_optres_local` admits the HEAP-BOXED payload channel,
    which is the one most of these shapes actually ride: a payload wider than
    the payload words is boxed, so every multi-field struct and every tuple
    payload was failing the membership test before the pattern was even looked
    at.

The whole-binding test is NOT relaxed, which the row asked for explicitly: a
`Binding` sub-pattern is rejected by the new classifier and left to the sibling
one.

ADMITTING THE BOXED CHANNEL WHOLESALE IS UNSAFE, measured. The first version
added it to the shared membership predicate and broke five tests --
`e2e_named_optres_boxed_payload_arm_runs_user_drop_body`,
`test_e2e_user_drop_scrutinee_option_field_move_out_runs`, and three ASAN cases
including `asan_consuming_arm_boxed_payload_handed_on_is_freed_once` -- every
one of them a boxed payload bound WHOLE and then moved on or field-moved-out.
A box is a different ownership regime, like a `shared struct`. It is therefore
admitted only TOGETHER WITH a destructuring pattern; a whole-payload binding
over a boxed local keeps the path it takes today.

FIXED, all four surfaces: single- and multi-field struct destructure, `..` rest
patterns, tuple-payload destructure, nested (`Outer { i }`), the `Result`
Ok-destructure, the `if let` spelling, and a `Vec`-typed leaf. Controls held:
a heap-free payload stays off the borrow path, `Option[shared struct]` stays
out, and the whole-payload binding is unchanged.

STILL BROKEN -- two mechanisms, both narrower than this row's original claim:

  (a) AN ARM THAT USES TWO BOUND LEAVES IN ONE EXPRESSION. `S { v, n }` with
      `println(v[0] + n)` still reads back garbage, while `println(v[0] + 1)`
      on the identical pattern is correct -- so it is not the pattern and not
      the payload, it is the consume classifier counting the SCALAR leaf's use
      as an escape, which drops the whole arm off the read-only path. A scalar
      leaf has no owner to drop, exactly the argument
      `pattern_binds_scalar_variant_payload` already makes for a scalar
      PAYLOAD; the same reasoning has not reached a scalar LEAF inside a
      destructure.

  (b) AN INNER `match` OVER A WHOLE-BOUND PAYLOAD.
      `match a { Some(p) => match p { A { s } => println(s) } }` still double
      frees (and the `Result` twin prints empty). The outer arm binds `p`
      whole -- so the outer classifier can fire -- and the inner `match` then
      destructures a heap field out of a value the source still owns. The
      outer binding's borrow-ness does not propagate into the nested pattern.
      Two things were tried and MEASURED NOT TO FIX IT, so do not repeat them:
      teaching `scrutinee_is_borrowed_binding` about
      `borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars` (the names are registered, but the
      outer classifier never fires for these locals), and admitting the boxed
      channel to membership (the outer classifier still declines, because
      `no_arm_payload_escapes` counts the inner destructure as an escape).
      The load-bearing question is that escape analysis: it must see through a
      nested destructure whose leaves are themselves only read.


SUB-MECHANISM (a) IS ROOT-CAUSED AND MEASURED, AND A FIX FOR IT IS BLOCKED ON A
THIRD DEFECT. No code landed for it this round; what follows is the hand-off.

ROOT CAUSE. An arithmetic or comparison operator IS A CALL by the time the
escape walker runs: `n + 1` is desugared to `i64.add(n, 1)` (measured — the
callee is `Path(["i64", "add"])`). `borrow_binding_escapes`'s `Binary` arm,
which treats a bare operand as a BORROW, therefore never sees it, and the
operand falls to the generic "passed to a call means moved" rule. That is the
whole of why `println(v[0] + n)` differs from `println(v[0] + 1)`: nothing is
moved either way, only whether an operand happens to be a binding.

THE OBVIOUS FIX WORKS AND IS UNSAFE. Treating the args of a call whose callee is
`Path([<primitive>, _])` as borrow positions fixes every shape in (a) — all of
`v[0] + n`, `n + v[0]`, `n + 1`, and the `let x = v[0] + n` spelling, on all four
surfaces, with the fourteen controls holding. It also LEAKS: 3200 bytes in 200
objects (one per loop iteration) in
`asan_freshtemp_result_arm_binding_a_struct_payload_owns_it_once`, plus
`test_ir_structpat_boxed_destructure_suppresses_box_fields`.

SCOPING IT TO THE READ-ONLY CLASSIFIERS DOES NOT HELP, which was the obvious
containment and is worth recording as tried: a `pattern_state` flag set only
around `scrutinee_is_readonly_inline_optres_local` and its `if let` sibling
(the only two callers with a named-local source) leaves both tests failing
identically. The leak arises THROUGH that classifier, not through one of the
other eight `no_arm_payload_escapes` callers.

WHAT THE LEAK ACTUALLY IS. The relaxation flips this to the borrow path:

    let r: Result[i64, One] = g(i);          // One { msg: String }
    match r { Ok(v) => { n = n + v; } Err(e) => { ...reads e.msg... } }

Before, `v` (a SCALAR) counted as escaping through `n + v`, so the match stayed
on the transfer path. After, it is read-only, `r` is a borrow, and `r`'s `Err`
payload is never freed.

TWO CONTROL PROBES NARROW IT, and both were run under ASAN on the unmodified
compiler: the same read-only borrow over `Result[i64, One]` does NOT leak with
`Ok(_)`, and does NOT leak with `Ok(v)` bound-but-UNUSED. So the borrow path
frees an `Err` payload correctly in general; the leak needs the sibling arm's
scalar binding to be USED. That is a third defect, independent of this row's
subject, and it has to be understood before (a) can land — the relaxation is
merely what makes an existing hole reachable.

NEXT STEP: start from the two control probes above, find why a read-only
`Result` borrow stops freeing its `Err` payload once the sibling `Ok` arm's
scalar binding is used, fix that, and only then apply the operator relaxation
(with the fresh-temp ASAN test as the gate). Do NOT land the relaxation alone.


SUB-MECHANISM (a) IS FIXED by c64cbfd, and the third defect that blocked it is
B-2026-08-31-14, fixed in the same commit.

(a)'s FIX IS ONE LINE OF REUSE. The escape walker now asks
`consume_class::is_lowered_primitive_operator` — the predicate B-2026-08-05-3
added to the SIBLING classifier for this exact desugar, with the exact same
symptom there (a guard `Some(x) if x.1 == 5i64` scored "consumed" purely
because `==` had become a call, disarming the source and leaking a tuple
payload). `consume_class` has known about it since; `borrow_binding_escapes`
never learned. Two classifiers, one predicate, no drift.

THE EARLIER ATTEMPT'S LEAK WAS NOT WHAT THIS ROW GUESSED. The previous note
here recorded that a relaxation leaked 3200 bytes and blamed a read-only
`Result` borrow failing to free its `Err` payload. That was WRONG, and the
correction is worth keeping because the wrong answer was reached twice: every
single-match probe of that shape is clean, on stock and after. Bisecting the
failing program block by block showed the leak needs TWO matches in one
function, in a specific ORDER — a read-only borrow first, then a fresh temp
whose arm genuinely moves the payload out, both binding the same name. That is
B-2026-08-31-14, a pre-existing leak reproducible on an unmodified compiler,
which the relaxation merely lit from another direction. An earlier bisect
missed it because the harness emitted blocks in sorted order and happened to
put the borrow SECOND, where it is clean.

STILL OPEN, and now the only thing left on this row: (b), an inner `match` over
a whole-bound payload — `match a { Some(p) => match p { A { s } => .. } }`
double frees, and the `Result` twin prints empty. The outer arm binds `p` whole
so the outer classifier can fire; the inner `match` then destructures a heap
field out of a value the source still owns, and the outer binding's borrow-ness
does not propagate into the nested pattern. `borrow_binding_escapes`'s `Match`
arm calls a bare-`name` scrutinee a move outright ("conservative move" in its
own comment), so the outer classifier declines before anything else is asked.
The load-bearing question is whether that can be refined to "a move only if some
inner arm's bindings escape THAT arm" — `no_arm_payload_escapes` already answers
exactly that, recursively. Two things were measured NOT to fix it on their own
and should not be retried: teaching `scrutinee_is_borrowed_binding` about
`borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars`, and admitting the boxed channel to
membership.

title: The SAME `match` arm as B-2026-08-29-58 with the arm NOT TAKEN loses the assigned-into local's OWN initializer `Drop` body on both compiled backends -- `out` still holds the value it was declared with, nobody else owns it, and only the interpreter runs it. The mirror image of -58, which ran one too many on the taken path
fix:
FIXED by ed0a330b.

ROOT CAUSE exactly where the row said to look. `src/codegen/stmts.rs`'s Assign
arm has a `rhs_is_param_view` branch (B-2026-08-01-16) that fires when the RHS is
an owned param or a transitive view of one -- and a match-arm payload binding IS
such a view, inserted into `param_view_locals` by B-2026-08-29-17 in
`pattern_binding.rs`. That branch called `suppress_user_drop_for_var(target)`,
which is an ALL-PATHS removal of the target's `UserDrop` action.

The removal is right for the value the assignment STORES -- under caller-retains
the moved-in value's body is the caller's -- and wrong for the value the target
was INITIALIZED with, and those are two different values. Only the second
survives on a path where the assignment never ran, and there nobody else owns it:
the scrutinee is `E.B` and has no payload to walk. Both compiled backends printed
`mid dE v0` against the interpreter's `mid dR0 dE v0`, the interpreter being
path-sensitive for free.

THE FIX reuses B-2026-08-28-51's `cond_move_drop_flags`, applied to the
assignment TARGET rather than to a handed-over source: `cond_move_drop_flag_for`
allocates a bool in the ENTRY block initialized to `true` (dominating every
path), and the branch now stores `false` into it instead of retracting. That
store lands in the basic block the assignment compiles into, so it executes only
where the store did, and `emit_user_drop_call_guarded` already reads the flag at
BOTH fire sites -- the scope-exit drain and the NLL live-range end. The taken
path is therefore byte-identical to the retraction it replaces. It falls back to
the static retraction if no flag can be made (no current function / entry block),
which is the degenerate case only.

THE SECOND HALF, which the suite found and which is the more interesting one.
The retraction had a job beyond scheduling scope exit: the DISPLACEMENT fire at a
later assignment is gated on `has_armed_user_drop(name)`, so removing the action
also silenced it. That silence is required -- `assign-repeated` in
`e2e_arm_payload_assigned_to_outer_local_drops_once` assigns a param view TWICE,
and the second displacement must NOT fire, because by then the target holds a
view whose body is the caller's. With the action left armed the flag alone was
not enough and that case regressed to `dR0 m1 dR8 m2 ...` against its pinned
`dR0 m1 m2 ...`.

So the displacement's wrapper call now routes through
`emit_user_drop_call_guarded` as well, reading the SAME flag. The ordering makes
it fall out: the displacement is emitted before the store and the clear after it,
so the first assignment reads `true` and fires the target's genuinely-owned value
(`dR0`), and the second reads the `false` the first one wrote and skips. That is
the same answer the retraction gave, now also correct on a path where no store
ran. A binding with no flag takes the helper's unguarded call, byte-identical to
before.

The lesson worth keeping: replacing a static retraction with a runtime flag has
to find every consumer that was reading the retraction as a fact, not only the
one that fires the action.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`), which now agree exactly. Six shapes, with the
pre-fix column measured against a stashed `src/`:

    shape                                    pre-fix AOT        post-fix (all four)
    a  arm NOT taken (the row)                mid dE a0          mid dR0 dE a0
    b  arm taken                              dR0 mid dE dR5 b5  unchanged
    c  FRESH value assigned in the arm        dR1 dE c1          unchanged
    d  UNCONDITIONAL param-view assign        dR2 dR9 d9         unchanged
    e  the repro inside a `while` loop        dE e181            dR90 dR91 dE e181
    f  whole-param rebind `h2 = h`            dR1 dR4 v4         unchanged
    g  assigned TWICE (`assign-repeated`)     dR0 m1 m2 dE ...   unchanged

`e` is worth calling out: an in-loop declaration whose arm is never taken lost
BOTH iterations' bodies before and runs both now. `c`, `d`, `f` and `g` are the
boundaries -- `f` is B-2026-08-01-16's own shape and `g` is the existing suite
pin that forced the second half -- and none of them moved, which is what shows
the flag is a strict refinement of the retraction rather than a different rule.

VALGRIND at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `=2`: 0 errors on the row's repro and on the
in-loop shape, and no use-after-free anywhere. What remains is a pre-existing
`-O0`-only leak of ONE `String` per param-view assignment that actually runs
(2 bytes on the taken path here), unchanged in size by this fix -- and HALVED on
a program exercising both paths, 4 bytes/2 blocks -> 2 bytes/1 block, because the
not-taken call's body now runs. Filed separately as B-2026-09-02-5.

TWO REMAINDERS, split out rather than buried here:

  * B-2026-09-02-5 -- the `-O0` leak above.
  * B-2026-09-02-6 -- the flag is entry-block-initialized ONCE, so an assignment that
    runs on SOME iterations of a loop leaves it `false` for later ones. Measured
    on `if i == 0 { out = p; }` over a per-iteration `out`: the compiled output
    is `it0 dR90 it1 dR5 acc96` against the interpreter's
    `it0 dR90 it1 dR91 dR5 acc96` -- IDENTICAL pre- and post-fix, so this fix
    neither causes nor cures it, but the mechanism that now owns that path is
    this one. `cond_move_drop_flags` has carried the same limitation since
    B-2026-08-28-51.

REGRESSION TESTS:
`codegen::test_e2e_conditional_param_view_assign_keeps_target_body_per_path`
(all six shapes in one program, absolute expected output, RED-checked against a
stashed `src/` -- the pre-fix column above is that measurement) and its oracle
twin `interpreter::conditional_param_view_assign_keeps_the_targets_own_body`,
which was already green and is pinned so a future "reconciliation" cannot move
the reference instead of the backend.

CORRECTION, added after the close. The first cut (ed0a330b) carried a REGRESSION
that the suite did not catch, found while probing B-2026-08-30-54's field
spelling and fixed by b2122ccd.

The retraction this fix replaced had a THIRD job, beyond scheduling scope exit
and silencing a later displacement: `rearm_container_bodies_for_name` runs on
every assignment to a name and re-registers what a retraction removed, so a
target that held a param view and was then given a FRESH value got its body back
for free. The flag never removes the action, so nothing ever re-registers it, and
the stale `false` silenced the fresh value instead:

    let mut out: R = R { id: 0, tag: f"t0" };
    match b { E.A(r) => { out = r; } E.B => { } }
    println("m1");
    out = R { id: 5, tag: f"t5" };
    println("m2");
    return out.id

      before ed0a330b   dR0 m1 m2 dR5 dE dR8 v5   correct
      at     ed0a330b   dR0 m1 m2 dE dR8 v5       `dR5` LOST
      at     b2122ccd  dR0 m1 m2 dR5 dE dR8 v5   correct again

b2122ccd re-arms the flag (`store true`) on any assignment to a flagged name
whose RHS is NOT a param view, ordered after the store and after the displacement
fire so both halves stay right: the displacement reads the `false` the view
assignment left and correctly skips the caller's value, and only then does the
target become the owner of something of its own again. Confined to names that
ALREADY have a flag, so a program with no param-view assignment emits nothing new
— verified by instrumenting the arm on B-2026-09-02-1's auto-par repro, where it
never fires.

WHY THE SUITE MISSED IT, which is the part worth keeping: nothing in ~3,540
codegen E2E cases exercised "a target that held a param view is later given a
fresh value". `assign-repeated` in
`e2e_arm_payload_assigned_to_outer_local_drops_once` comes closest and assigns a
VIEW both times, which is the opposite half of the same question — and that pin
is what caught the displacement half of this fix, so the gap was one row wide.
The shape is now the `f` row of
`codegen::test_e2e_conditional_param_view_assign_keeps_target_body_per_path` and
`view-then-fresh-value` in the interpreter twin.

title: The FIELD-target spelling `h.f = r` of B-2026-08-29-58 is wrong on BOTH backends in different directions: the interpreter runs the payload's `Drop` body twice, and codegen disarms the field PERMANENTLY so a later fresh value assigned to `h.f` never runs its body at all. Neither side is an oracle, which is why -58's fix stops at a bare-identifier target
fix:
FIXED by 9a8b4616.

BOTH HALVES, as the row required -- fixing either alone would have turned an
agreed count of one on the first program into a divergence.

THE ORACLE THE ROW SAID DID NOT EXIST NOW DOES, and that is what unblocked this.
The row closed with "neither side is an oracle, which is why -58's fix stops at a
bare-identifier target". Since then the bare-identifier spelling was itself
fixed (B-2026-08-30-53, ed0a330b + b2122ccd) and agrees on all four surfaces, so
the field spelling has a reference: `h.f = r` must print exactly what
`out = r` prints. Every expectation below is the identifier test's own row with
`out` replaced by `h.f`, and the two now match line for line.

CODEGEN took the same shape as the identifier fix, which is the useful part of
the result -- the two legs are one mechanism rather than two rules.
`src/codegen/stmts.rs`'s field-target branch called
`suppress_user_drop_for_var(base)` (B-2026-08-01-19), an ALL-PATHS, PERMANENT
removal of the base's whole bodies action. It now clears a per-path
`cond_move_drop_flags` bool on the base instead, records which FIELD did it, and:

  * RE-ARMS (`store true`) when that same field later receives a value that is
    not a param view -- the base owns a body again. Only when that field is the
    ONLY one recorded, because the flag is per BINDING while the reason is per
    FIELD: re-arming while a sibling still holds a view would resurrect the
    view's body alongside the fresh one.
  * GUARDS the displaced-field emission (`emit_displaced_field_bodies`) with the
    same flag, and again only for the recorded field. Its `full_armed` gate
    reads the ACTION, which now stays armed while the flag carries the per-path
    answer, so without a guard the displacement fired for a value the base does
    not own. A COARSER version of this line was measured wrong before it went
    in: guarding a SIBLING field's displacement on the same flag deleted
    `g`'s initializer body outright.

`open_cond_move_guard` / `close_cond_move_guard` are new in `runtime.rs` -- the
run-of-calls form of `emit_user_drop_call_guarded`, which guards exactly one.

THE INTERPRETER half went through `moved_out_struct_field_bodies`, the PER-FIELD
mask `drop_user_drop_fields_of_binding` already consults, exactly as the row's

of `record_assign_of_param_view`, with that function's method-frame guard
verbatim; the same set now also gates the displaced-field fire, which is what
makes a repeated assignment agree with codegen. The per-field routing matters
rather than being a detail: the whole-binding set the identifier leg uses would
have taken every OTHER Drop-bearing field's body with it.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac build`,

    b  arm taken                 dR0 m dR8 dE dR8 b8   dR0 m dE dR8 b8    dR0 m dE dR8 b8

title: A METHOD frame does not participate in the owned-ENUM-param ownership protocol: a fresh-temp enum argument runs ZERO `Drop` bodies on the interpreter (neither the enum's own nor its payload's) against two compiled, and a NAMED one runs one too MANY. The free-fn twin and the struct-param twin are both correct, which localizes it to the intersection B-2026-08-28-70 did not reach
detail:
Found while deciding whether B-2026-08-29-58's fix could safely retract inside a
METHOD frame. It cannot, and the reason is this: a method frame does not
participate in the owned-ENUM-param ownership protocol at all, so the retraction
would have had nothing to hand off to.

The defect has TWO legs that look opposite and share one cause -- whether the
CALLER happens to have a fire of its own.

LEG 1, FRESH-TEMP argument: ZERO bodies on the interpreter.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    struct T { n: i64 }

    impl T { fn eat(ref self, b: E) -> i64 { return 3; } }
    fn main() { let t: T = T { n: 1 }; let v: i64 = t.eat(E.A(R { id: 8, tag: f"t8" })); println(f"v{v}") }

      karac run --interp -> `v3`          BOTH bodies lost -- the enum's and its payload's
      build / jit        -> `dE dR8 v3`

TWO CONTROLS localize it precisely, and both are correct on all four surfaces:

  * the FREE-FN twin of the identical program (`fn eat(b: E) -> i64`)
        -> `dE dR8 v3` everywhere
  * the STRUCT-param twin in the same method (`fn eat(ref self, r: R)`)
        -> `dR8 v3` everywhere

So it is neither "methods lose bodies" nor "enum args lose bodies" -- it is
exactly the intersection. B-2026-08-28-70 gave method frames ownership of their
by-value params, and that fix reaches a struct param and not an enum one.

LEG 2, NAMED argument: one body too MANY, because the caller's binding fires and
the method frame's slot fires as well.

    impl T { fn take(ref self, b: E) -> i64 {
        let mut out: R = R { id: 0, tag: f"t0" };
        match b { E.A(r) => { out = r; } E.B => { } }
        println("m"); return out.id;
    } }
    fn main() { let t: T = T { n: 1 }; let c: E = E.A(R { id: 8, tag: f"t8" });
                let v: i64 = t.take(c); println(f"v{v}") }

      karac run --interp -> `dR0 m dR8 dE dR8 v8`   TWO
      build / jit        -> `dR0 m dE dR8 v8`       one

The `let` spelling of leg 2 (`let inner: R = r;`) behaves IDENTICALLY, which is
what shows this is a frame-level gap and not an assignment-path one:
B-2026-08-29-17 fixed that spelling for free functions only, and B-2026-08-29-58
matched the assignment spelling to it in the same frames. Both are therefore
still doubled in a method frame today, together, by design -- neither fix could
retract there without turning leg 1 from one body into zero.

WHY THIS IS NOT B-2026-08-29-38: that row is the ESCAPING direction (a method's
fresh-temp arg HANDED BACK OUT runs two bodies on the compiled backends against
one in the interpreter). This is the opposite direction on the opposite backend
-- the value DIES INSIDE, and the interpreter is the one running too few. They
share the "method fresh-temp arg" phrase and nothing else.

Bodies only -- valgrind clean on the compiled binary -- and interpreter-only, so
`karac build` output is unaffected. Medium on those grounds, though note that
leg 1 losing a body is the direction that matters for a resource type: a `Drop`
that closes a handle simply never runs under `karac run --interp`.

WHERE TO START: `owned_param_frame_is_method` and the B-2026-08-28-70 machinery
it gates. The struct leg reaches an owner and the enum leg does not; the enum
shell's own body and its payload walk are both missing, so whatever registers a
method frame's param drops needs the enum arm the struct arm already has. Fixing
leg 1 is the precondition for retracting in method frames at all -- do it first,
then the `owned_param_frame_is_method` guards in `let_destructures_owned_param`
and `record_assign_of_param_view` can both be lifted and leg 2 closes with them.
fix:
FIXED by 3a09311 (leg 1) and 9082875 (leg 2 + the twinned fixtures). Both legs
close; a residue in one shape is split out as its own row rather than left
inside this one.

(1) THE DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND THE PRESCRIPTION WAS NOT. The row named the
site exactly -- `method_param_drop_names` admitted `Value::Struct` only, so a
method frame, which stands its caller down, left an owned ENUM argument with no
owner on either side. Its two controls localize it and both stay correct after
the fix: the free-function twin (whose caller still fires) and the fresh-temp
struct twin (which the existing arm admits).

Its instructions -- widen the arm, then "the `owned_param_frame_is_method`
guards in `let_destructures_owned_param` and `record_assign_of_param_view` can
both be lifted" -- are wrong in BOTH directions, and each wrong version looked
right until a test refuted it. All three are recorded because the plausible
version is the broken one every time:

  * WIDENING THE ARM UNCONDITIONALLY double-fires the NAMED spelling. For an
    argument that dies inside, the CALLER is deliberately the owner
    (B-2026-08-29-10 narrowed `record_method_arg_moves` to exactly that, after
    an unconditional stand-down left a method with no `match` arm with nobody to
    fire). Measured: `let c: E = ..; t.eat(c)` went from `dE dR8` to
    `dE dR8 dE dR8`.
  * NARROWING TO FRESH TEMPS instead breaks a NAMED argument RETURNED BARE,
    where the caller DOES stand down and the callee must claim it. Caught by
    `test_named_arg_returned_bare_user_drop_body_runs_once`, whose
    conditional-callee row is precisely that case.
  * THE `escapes` PREDICATE IS THE WRONG GATE, one step too wide. It stands the
    caller's CONTAINER walk down; the binding keeps its OWN `Drop` action unless
    the callee hands the value back AS ITSELF
    (`record_returned_arg_user_drop_move`'s narrower union). Measured on
    `fn assign_enum(b: E) -> R`, which returns a payload BOUND OUT of `b` -- so
    it escapes while `b` itself does not -- where the wider predicate had the
    caller and the frame both firing `dE`.

The rule that survives all three: THE FRAME CLAIMS WHAT THE CALLER IS NOT
FIRING, spelled with the same predicate the caller side uses so the two cannot
drift.

(2) LEG 2 IS THE SAME QUESTION, ASKED OF THE RETRACTION. Lifting the guards
outright fixes the named spelling and LOSES the payload body for a fresh temp --
exactly what `record_assign_of_param_view`'s own doc warned it would ("retracting
it would take that count to zero"). A retraction is licensed by some OTHER frame
owning the value, so both guards now ask
`method_frame_caller_retains_args`.

An intermediate version asked whether the frame had REGISTERED any slots, which
is a DIFFERENT question and also wrong: `fn tup(ref self, p: (Res, i64))` called
with a fresh temp registers nothing -- the registration admits structs and enums,
and a tuple is neither -- yet the frame is still the only owner. Retracting there
ran ZERO bodies against one on both compiled backends, and `strc(h: Holder)`,
whose `Holder` has no `Drop` of its own, failed identically. Caught by
`test_method_param_destructure_single_caller_fire`. One predicate now serves the
`let` and assignment spellings, which is what keeps them agreeing -- the property
B-2026-08-29-58 restored.

(3) A CORRECTION TO THE ROW AS FILED. It records the struct-param twin as
correct on all four surfaces. That holds only for the FRESH-TEMP spelling. The
NAMED struct twin -- `let c: R = R { .. }; t.eats(c)` -- ran `dR8` TWICE under
`--interp` against `dR8` compiled, before any change here, and the same rule
fixes it. So the defect was never enum-specific; it was enum-VISIBLE, because
the shape the row probed happened to be the one where the struct arm's
registration masked it.

VERIFICATION. Eight probe shapes across `--interp`, the JIT and `build`; seven
agree, against three before. The eighth is (4). Fixtures in
tests/interpreter.rs with CODEGEN TWINS sharing the expectations verbatim --
not ceremony, because this backend was already correct on every row, so an
interpreter-only fixture would keep passing while the two drifted, and
"they agree" is the property being restored. Full `--features llvm` suite
16,007 passed / 0 failed, re-verified after a rebase that brought in three
codegen fixes in this same drop-ownership family (cli 734, codegen 3,525,
interpreter 1,892, memory_sanitizer 1,355). Both clippy legs clean.

(4) RESIDUE, split out as B-2026-09-01-26 rather than left here. A FRESH TEMP
DESTRUCTURED inside the callee still differs, now in ORDER rather than count:
`dR0 m dR8 dE` under `--interp` against `dR0 m dE dR8` on both compiled
backends. Before this fix that shape was missing `dE` altogether, so it moved
from a wrong COUNT to a wrong ORDER — an improvement, and a different defect
from the one this row reports.

title: BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS BITCAST AN INTEGER INTO AN `Option` / `Result` PAYLOAD AND AN ENUM STRUCT-VARIANT FLOAT FIELD, so `let o: Option[f64] = Some(m)` reads back 4.45e-309 -- the raw integer bit pattern as a double. The user enum TUPLE-variant twin `T.W(m)` converts correctly, which is what localizes it
detail:
FILED to give this half its own id. B-2026-08-30-48's detail says the AOT
`4.45e-309` it measured "is a codegen miscompile in the same shapes and is
independent of signedness ... filed separately as B-2026-08-30-49". It was
not: B-2026-08-30-49 is about an integer arm of a float-typed BRANCH falling
to the const-0 placeholder, its fix touches only the `if`/`if let`/`match`
phi merges, and it says nothing about payload stores. So this defect was
pointed at a row that never described it and would have been lost when that
row closed.

MEASURED on `main` at b554da2 (i.e. WITH B-2026-08-30-49's fix in place, so
this is not that defect), `let m: i64 = 9007199254740993` -- the 2^53+1
conversion probe, which reads ...992 when converted and ...993 when not:

  shape                                    --interp   AOT
  let o: Option[f64] = Some(m)             ...993     4.4501477e-309   BITCAST
  enum S { V { f: f64 } }; S.V { f: m }    ...993     4.4501477e-309   BITCAST
  let r: Result[f64, i64] = Ok(m)          ...993     4.4501477e-309   BITCAST
  enum T { W(f64) }; T.W(m)                ...993     ...992           converts
  struct Plain { f: f64 }; Plain { f: m }  ...992     ...992           correct
  let v: Vec[f64] = [m]                    ...993     ...992           converts

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS SHARE THIS TABLE and only the AOT column belongs to this
row. The `--interp` ...993s are B-2026-08-30-48's half (the value stays a
`Value::Int` in a slot the program declared `f64`) and are NOT re-filed here.
This row is the AOT column: three shapes where the compiled backends write the
integer's BITS into a float slot.

`4.45e-309` is the tell and it is not a rounding artifact: 9007199254740993 as
a 64-bit pattern reinterpreted as an IEEE double is a subnormal near 4.45e-309.
So the store is a bitcast, not a bad conversion -- nothing attempted `sitofp`
at all.

WHAT LOCALIZES IT is the enum TUPLE-variant row. `T.W(m)` on a user enum with
a declared `f64` payload converts correctly, while `Some(m)` -- structurally
the same thing -- does not. So this is not "enum payloads are unconverted" as
a class; the user tuple-variant path already consults the declared payload
type and the `Option`/`Result` construction path and the enum STRUCT-variant
path do not. Any fix should start by finding why those two do not reach
whatever the tuple-variant path uses.

ROOT CAUSE, located but not fixed: `build_nonshared_enum_value`
(src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs) hands each payload value straight to
`coerce_to_payload_words`, which bitcasts into i64 words WITHOUT consulting
the variant's declared payload type. A fix needs the declared payload types
threaded to the constructor for the `Option`/`Result` and struct-variant
paths. Deliberately not folded into B-2026-08-30-49: different site,
different mechanism, and it would have landed untested under that row's
regression coverage.

SEVERITY high, on the same reasoning B-2026-08-30-49 carries: a silent wrong
answer with no diagnostic, `karac check` passes, and `let o: Option[f64] =
Some(n)` where `n` is an integer is ordinary code. It is also a run-vs-build
divergence, though note that BOTH backends are wrong here in different
directions -- neither is an oracle for this shape until -48's half lands too.

SCOPE NOTE: six shapes, chosen to bracket the boundary rather than to
enumerate. `Map` value, tuple element and `Array` element were probed under
B-2026-08-30-48 and are correct on AOT. Treat the list as a floor, per that
row's own lesson about this shape space.
fix:
FIXED by b9500f80. The AOT column of the row's table converges on the converted
value in all six shapes, plus two the table did not list.

ROOT CAUSE SHARPER THAN THE ROW STATED. The row placed it at
`build_nonshared_enum_value` handing payloads "straight to
`coerce_to_payload_words` WITHOUT consulting the variant's declared payload
type". Not quite: the tuple-variant path DOES consult it, through
`coerce_enum_payload_scalar` (B-2026-08-13-18), and that helper was already on
the `Some(..)` path too. It DECLINED. Three different reasons, which is why one
fix would not have covered them:

  * A GENERIC payload. `Option[T] { Some(T) }` declares its payload as a type
    PARAMETER, and the helper deliberately skips those -- coercing to the
    generic base's all-i64 placeholder NARROWS a wider payload, which is how
    `Option[i128]` printed 0 (B-2026-08-19-19). That skip covered every `Some`
    and `Ok` in the language. It now resolves the parameter through the
    construction site's recorded instantiation (`enum_inst_type_exprs`) first,
    and falls back to the skip when the site binds it to nothing concrete, so
    B-2026-08-19-19's reason still holds exactly where it applied.
  * An enum STRUCT-VARIANT never called the helper at all --
    `compile_enum_struct_variant_init` packs directly, on both the shared and
    non-shared paths. This one matches the row's description.
  * The QUALIFIED spelling of a generic user enum. `G.A(m)` routes through
    `compile_assoc_call`, which carried no span to look the instantiation up
    with, so it disagreed with its own bare sibling `A(m)` after the first half
    landed. That disagreement is the tell that this half was plumbing rather
    than a missing conversion.

WHAT THE ROW GOT EXACTLY RIGHT is the localizer: `T.W(m)` with a concretely
declared `W(f64)` converts and is structurally the same construction as
`Some(m)`. Following that difference is what led to the generic-parameter skip
rather than to the packer.

TWO SHAPES BEYOND THE TABLE, found by asking what else declares a payload
generically: a user generic enum in both its bare (`A(m)`) and qualified
(`G.A(m)`) spellings. Both were wrong; both are fixed and pinned. The row's own
"treat the list as a floor" note was right.

VERIFICATION: eight cases in `e2e_int_into_float_enum_payload_converts`, using
2^53+1 as the conversion probe -- it survives as itself when nothing converts
and lands on ...992 once it round-trips a double, so each case distinguishes a
correct store from BOTH a skipped `sitofp` and a bitcast. The concrete
tuple-variant, a plain struct field and a `Vec[f64]` literal are kept as
CONTROLS. RED-verified: reverting `src` fails at `option-generic-payload` with
the row's own 4.4501477e-309. Gates: llvm 15852/0, default 10180/0, both clippy
legs and fmt clean.

SCOPE NOTE, unchanged and worth repeating: this is the AOT column ONLY. The
`--interp` `...993`s in the row's table are B-2026-08-30-48's half and are
untouched, so the two backends still disagree on these shapes -- neither is an
oracle for them until that row lands.

FIXED by e59a31b, in the INTERPRETER -- and the row's title has the
direction backwards, which is worth stating plainly because it is what the fix
had to establish first.

THE COMPILED BACKENDS WERE RIGHT. Under caller-retains (B-2026-08-01-13), a
payload destructured from an owned by-value param is a VIEW of the callee's
entry copy: its `Drop` body belongs to the CALLER's fire, and the callee
registers nothing. So for one `R` value the correct total is ONE body, which is
what `karac build` and the JIT print (`in bound n5 dE dR5` -- the `dE dR5` is
the caller's walk). The interpreter printed `dR5` as well, i.e. TWO bodies for
one value. The row read the compiled column as "no body in the callee" and
called that a loss; it is caller-retains working as designed, and the surplus
was on the other side.

THE HOLE. B-2026-08-29-17 made a match-arm payload's view-ness PROPAGATE through
a rebind (`let m = r`), by inserting the arm's bindings into
`owned_param_names_stack` -- the interpreter's view set. It keyed that on the
scrutinee being a bare `ExprKind::Identifier` naming an owned param. A
PROJECTION of one, `match s.e { E.A(r) => … }` inside `fn take(s: S)`, binds out
of the SAME entry copy a bare `match s` would, but never matched the gate: `r`
stayed out of the view set, `let m = r` reached `let_destructures_owned_param`
whose `src_is_view` test consults exactly that set, and `m` registered a slot of
its own.

Codegen never had the hole. Its twin predicate,
`scrutinee_is_owned_param_binding`, walks FieldAccess / TupleIndex hops to the
root -- B-2026-08-03-3 leg B added that widening with the same reasoning, in
those words -- so the two sides were asking different questions about the same
program. They now ask the same one: a new `place_root_is_owned_param` mirrors
codegen's walk hop for hop, including its restriction (an `Index` or a call
anywhere in the chain stops it, because that is not a plain view of the entry
copy). One set does the work of codegen's two, since
`owned_param_names_stack` already holds both the parameter names and the locals
that inherited view-ness.

RESTRICTED TO VARIANT PATTERNS, and that restriction is load-bearing rather than
cautious. Codegen inserts into `param_view_locals` only for bindings in
`current_variant_payload_bindings`, so a plain TUPLE pattern over an owned
param's tuple field (`match s.t { (r, k) => … }`) keeps its slot there and both
backends run two bodies. Widening the new branch to every pattern kind would
have taken the interpreter to one and turned an AGREED answer into a fresh
divergence -- the worse of the two outcomes. The pre-existing bare-Identifier
branch keeps its wider pattern reach untouched; narrowing it is a separate
question with its own measurements, and it over-suppresses an owned TUPLE param
today (filed separately).

MEASURED, five cells moved and five controls did not, on all four surfaces
(interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0):

    user enum field   `match s.e`      dR dE dR  ->  dE dR
    Option field      `match s.o`      dR dR     ->  dR
    Result field      `match s.r`      dR dR     ->  dR
    two-hop chain     `match w.s.e`    dR dE dR  ->  dE dR
    struct-variant    `match h.v`      dR dSv dR ->  dSv dR

    tuple field / `ref` param / owned LOCAL projection / fresh temp / the same
    projection WITHOUT the rebind -- all unchanged, all still agreeing.

Tests: `test_owned_param_projection_payload_rebind_is_a_view` (interpreter) and
`e2e_owned_param_projection_payload_rebind_is_a_view` (codegen), one fixture
carrying all five fixed cells and all five controls, pinned to the same string
on both sides. RED-verified against the pre-fix tree: exactly five surplus `dR`
lines, one per fixed cell, with every control line identical -- so the fixture
cannot pass vacuously and cannot pass by over-reaching either, since silencing
a control would delete a line the expectation requires.
title: A MATCH ARM THAT MOVES AN OWNED STRUCT PARAM'S ENUM PAYLOAD INTO A FRESH LOCAL RUNS THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE UNDER `--interp` AND ONCE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `in bound dR5 n5 dE dR5` vs `in bound n5 dE dR5`; caller-retains makes the compiled column the correct one, so the surplus is the interpreter's (FILED WITH THE DIRECTION REVERSED -- see the CORRECTION in detail)
detail:
Measured on 8f138d7 and re-confirmed unchanged on d26995d (main immediately
before B-2026-08-29-37's fix landed), all four surfaces (interp / jit / build /
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0). PRE-EXISTING -- byte-identical against a compiler built with
B-2026-08-29-37's fix stashed out, so it is not that change's doing.

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }    impl Drop for E { println("dE") }
    struct S { e: E }

    fn take_own(s: S) -> i64 {
        println("in");
        match s.e { E.A(r) => { let m = r; println("bound"); return m.id } E.B => { return 0 } }
    }

      let s = S { e: E.A(R { id: 5 }) };
      println(f"n{take_own(s)}");

        interp:            start in bound dR5 n5 dE dR5 end
        jit / build / np:  start in bound     n5 dE dR5 end     <- NO `dR5` in the callee

`m` is a fresh OWNED local of the callee -- `let m = r` inside the arm -- so its
`Drop` body is due at the arm's end no matter what one concludes about the
scrutinee. The compiled backends run nothing there. The `dE dR5` both backends
print afterwards is the CALLER's walk (`s` is not treated as moved by either
side, which is its own question, and not this row's).

THE RECEIVER MODE IS THE WHOLE VARIABLE, which is what makes this the exact
complement of B-2026-08-29-37. That row's `ref self` / `ref S` shape mints a
defensive clone and used to run one body too MANY; this owned-param shape mints
no clone and runs one body too FEW. Both were on `main` at the same time, in
opposite directions, which is why fixing the first does not touch this.

SUSPECT (unverified): `scrutinee_is_readonly_owned_enum_projection` classifies
the arm binding as a BORROW when the root has a live bodies walk, and
`bind_pattern_values` then skips the binding's own drop registration -- correct
for a binding that stays a view, wrong once `let m = r` materializes it into a
local the arm owns. Worth checking whether the classifier should decline when an
arm body re-binds the payload by value.

SOURCE NOTE: found in the B-2026-08-29-37 receiver-mode matrix (own / ref /
mut ref x method / free fn), which the row's own "a free function is clean"
claim turned out to have mis-scoped -- see that row's fix note.

CORRECTION (2026-08-31, at close): the DIRECTION above is backwards. The
compiled backends are not losing a body -- under caller-retains they are
correct, and `in bound n5 dE dR5` is one body for one value, fired by the
caller. It is the INTERPRETER that runs one too many. The row was filed from a
receiver-mode matrix where the compiled column looked short next to the
interpreter's, and the extra `dR5` was read as the interpreter's baseline rather
than as the defect. The "exact complement of B-2026-08-29-37" framing survives
only in the weaker sense that both rows are about one backend running a surplus
body; the surplus is on the other side here.

fix:
INVALID -- the premise is refuted. The row's observation is real (`dR3 n3 dR3`
on every backend, ASAN/LSan clean) but its MECHANISM is misattributed. It is not
"the ownership checker declining to reject a move out of a borrowed place": the
compiler ACCEPTS `let m = s.r` off a `ref` param DELIBERATELY, and lowers it as
an implicit DEEP COPY. So the two `Drop` bodies are two VALUES destroyed once
each, not one value destroyed twice.

THE PROOF, and it is a one-command control the original investigation skipped:
mutate the callee's binding and read the caller's field afterwards.

    struct S { v: Vec[i64], name: String }
    fn steal(s: ref S) -> i64 {
        let mut m = s.v;   m.push(99);
        let n = s.name;
        return m.len()
    }
      let s = S { v: [1], name: "hi" };
      println(f"callee={steal(s)}");
      println(f"caller.len={s.v.len()} caller.name={s.name} caller.v={s.v}");

        interp / JIT / AOT, all three identical:
          callee=2
          caller.len=1 caller.name=hi caller.v=[1]

The callee's copy grew to 2 while the caller's `s.v` stayed `[1]` and `s.name`
survived. A move out of a borrow could not produce that; a copy is the only
reading. `dR{id}` firing twice for the same `id` is the copy's own destructor,
not a duplicated one -- which is also the explanation this row was missing for
its own ASAN/LSan-clean finding, recorded there as a puzzle.

WHERE THE BEHAVIOUR COMES FROM: B-2026-07-21-11, which fixed the very bug this
row believed it was seeing. Before that fix `let p = <refparam>.field`
bit-copy-ALIASED the caller's field while the binding got owned tracking, so both
freed the same heap -- a double-free abort on every compiled backend.
`clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs` (`src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs:4044`,
hooked at `src/codegen/stmts.rs:5478`) now deep-copies the RHS in place for every
heap-bearing leaf. Six regression tests pin it -- `test_e2e_ref_param_field_let_
move_all_leaves`, `e2e_borrow_payload_field_direct_consume_no_double_free`,
`e2e_generic_borrowed_field_move_out_is_a_copy_not_an_alias`,
`test_e2e_borrowed_tuple_member_leaf_is_a_copy`,
`test_e2e_match_bound_payload_vec_field_copy_over_ref_vec`, and
`e2e_generic_impl_field_keeps_the_declared_unsignedness` -- and one of them says
so in its name.

HOW THIS WAS ESTABLISHED, because the route matters more than the answer. A
rejection was actually BUILT and measured before being reverted: a typechecker
rule (`E_BORROW_MOVE_OUT` / `E0286`) beside `reject_index_move_non_copy`,
covering a projection or `*r` off a shared-borrow root in the same three value
positions. It swept CLEAN over 1154 `.kara` files -- `runtime/stdlib`,
`examples`, `selfhost`, `tests/` and `kara-katas` -- after two "defects" it found
were "fixed". Then the `--features llvm` suite failed those six codegen tests,
whose subject programs are `.kara` embedded in Rust source and therefore invisible
to a `.kara` corpus sweep. That is the same lesson B-2026-08-31-41 recorded --
"the corpus sweep was necessary but not sufficient; the one real false positive
lived in the test suite, not the corpus" -- and it is now the second time it has
been the deciding signal. Read the failing test NAMES before assuming they are
collateral: `..._move_out_is_a_copy_not_an_alias` states the language's answer
outright.

The two corpus "fixes" were consequently reverted too, since neither was a fix:
`runtime/stdlib/cli.kara`'s `let mut out: String = self.program_name` and
`selfhost/src/resolver.kara`'s seven `self.define(f.name, f.span)` calls are
implicit clones, not duplicated ownership. Making them explicit changes nothing
but the reader's expectations, and the selfhost one would have diverged the
oracle from its `src/resolver.rs` mirror.

WHAT SURVIVES AS A REAL QUESTION -> B-2026-09-01-4. The row's strongest point was
never the destructor count; it was the CONTRADICTION it noticed, and that stands:
`enum_payload_clone_is_faithful` (B-2026-08-09-9) refuses to clone a
`NestedStruct` payload because "a clone is a compiler-internal artifact the source
language never asked for", while this path mints exactly such a clone -- silently
allocating, and running a user `Drop` body the source never wrote. Split into its
own open row rather than buried here.

SEPARATELY LANDED (280ea02), in the same session and independently verified: the map-field
merge in `runtime/stdlib/protobuf.kara` used a read-modify-writeback
(`let t = self.f; t.insert(..); self.f = t;`) justified by a comment saying "a
mutating method on a `Map` FIELD through `mut ref self` does not persist". That is
no longer true -- measured, a direct `self.m.insert(k, v)` persists on all three
backends -- and under the deep-copy semantics above the workaround was copying the
whole map once per merged entry. Both callers now insert directly.
title: `let m = s.r` OFF A `ref` PARAM IS AN IMPLICIT DEEP COPY, NOT A MOVE OUT OF A BORROW -- the `dR3 n3 dR3` this row reported is TWO values destroyed once each, not one destroyed twice; premise misattributed, and the live remainder (an implicit clone runs a `Drop` body the source never wrote) is split to B-2026-09-01-4
detail:
Measured on 8f138d7 and re-confirmed unchanged on d26995d, all four surfaces,
and PRE-EXISTING (identical with B-2026-08-29-37's fix stashed out). NO `match` and no enum is involved -- this is
the plainest possible spelling:

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    struct S { r: R }

    fn steal(s: ref S) -> i64 {
        let m = s.r;        // moves a field OUT of a borrowed param
        return m.id
    }

      let s = S { r: R { id: 3 } };
      println(f"n{steal(s)}");

        karac check:  All checks passed.
        every backend: dR3 n3 dR3        <- ONE `R` value, TWO destructor runs

`s` is borrowed, so the callee owns nothing; `let m = s.r` nevertheless compiles
and produces an owned `m` whose body runs at the callee's end, while the caller's
`s` runs the same body again at its own death. Both backends agree, so this is
NOT a run-vs-build divergence -- it is the ownership checker declining to reject
a move out of a borrowed place, and the duplicate destructor is the consequence.

NOT A MEMORY BUG. Under ASAN + LSan (Linux) with a `Vec[String]` payload the same
program exits 0: no double free, no leak. So the cost is purely OBSERVABILITY --
a `Drop` body that logs, unlocks, decrements a counter or closes an fd runs twice
for one value.

    a borrow*, not a value."
  * § Match Arm Binding Modes: "If the scrutinee is a **`ref T`** borrow ...
    **no arm binding may consume a field**. All pattern bindings automatically
    become borrows."

container that still owns it. That is the same program `let t = v[0]` has been
rejected for since B-2026-08-26-21, one level up, and for the reason that
section states: "a container is not partially movable. There is no
representation for a `Vec` with a hole in it."

So the row's "which side is right" has a third answer: NEITHER, because the
program is not one the language sanctions. design.md makes that argument itself,
about this exact family, and it applies here verbatim: "That disagreement was not
a backend defect to arbitrate -- it was a program the language never sanctioned,
and each backend had filled the gap in good faith. Rejecting the form at the
front end removes the question instead of answering it."

index expression naming a borrowed element, an arm binding that is CONSUMED is

    `reject_index_move_non_copy` so the two rules ask one question. Every
    exemption that rule carries -- a range slice, an SoA layout, a `shared`
    handle, a function value, a `Copy` element -- is an exemption here.
  * CONSUMPTION is design.md's use-predicate table, via a new BORROW-AWARE
    variant of `binding_use::binding_only_read_through`. The existing walk is
    mode-BLIND -- every call argument counts as a use -- which is right for its
    own callers and wrong here, and `println(s)` is the shape that proves it:
    the single most common thing an arm does with a payload, and a consume under
    the blind walk. `binding_only_read_through_borrow_aware` takes an oracle
    (`callee`, `argument index`) -> "does that parameter borrow?", which the
    typechecker answers from `env.functions`. The table's own words: "`f(v)`
    where `f`'s parameter is declared `ref` or `mut ref` | read".

  * A callee the oracle cannot resolve answers BORROWS, and METHOD calls stay
    mode-blind. Both are the safe direction for a hard error: an under-fire
