title: A `match v[i]` ARM THAT MOVES ITS PAYLOAD INTO A BY-VALUE CALL RUNS THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON THE COMPILED BACKENDS AND ONCE IN THE INTERPRETER -- `got 3 dR3 dE dR3` vs `got 3 dE dR3`; the consuming call is the variable, not the index
detail:
Measured on all four surfaces (interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), on the
tree WITH B-2026-08-29-37's fix. PRE-EXISTING: on 8f138d7 and on d26995d the same program
already showed this `dR` asymmetry, alongside a doubled `dE` that -37 removed
(`got 3 dR3 dE dE dR3` there, `got 3 dR3 dE dR3` here). The `dE` half is fixed;
the `dR` half below is untouched by it and is what this row is about.

    struct R { id: i64, v: Vec[i64] }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }                 impl Drop for E { println("dE") }
    fn eat(r: R) -> i64 { return r.id }

      let mut v = Vec.new();
      v.push(mk(3));
      match v[0] { E.A(r) => { println(f"got {eat(r)}"); } E.B => { } }

        interp:            index got 3     dE dR3 index end
        jit / build / np:  index got 3 dR3 dE dR3 index end     <- `dR3` TWICE

The arm binds the element's payload and MOVES it into `eat`, which owns its
parameter and drops it -- so the compiled backends' first `dR3` is the callee's,
and their second is the container's element walk at `v`'s death. The interpreter
runs only the second: it hands `eat` a view rather than the value, so the payload
body never fires inside the callee.

THE CONSUMING CALL IS THE VARIABLE, not the index scrutinee. Spelling the same
arm as `let m = r; println(f"got {m.id}")` makes all four surfaces agree
(`got 3 dR3 dE dR3`, two `dR3` everywhere) -- so the divergence is specifically
that a by-value ARGUMENT out of a `v[i]` arm is a move on the compiled backends
and a borrow in the interpreter. `for p in v { match p { ... } }` over the same
data agrees on both sides with either spelling, which localizes this to the
heap-Vec-index scrutinee path.

Which side is right depends on the same unanswered question as the move-out-of-
borrow row filed alongside this one: `v[i]` is a place the container still owns,
so a consuming arm either duplicates the value (two bodies, the compiled answer)
or must be rejected (the interpreter is then merely lenient rather than correct).

title: A LOCAL WHOSE LAST USE IS A `ref` ARGUMENT TO A CALLEE RETURNING A HEAP VALUE IS DROPPED AT SCOPE EXIT INSTEAD OF ITS LIVE-RANGE END ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS, AGAINST design.md line 866 -- `str end dE` vs interp `dE str end`; an `i64` return is clean
detail:
Measured on 8f138d7 and re-confirmed unchanged on d26995d, all four surfaces,
and PRE-EXISTING (identical with B-2026-08-29-37's fix stashed out).

design.md line 866 is explicit: "Destructors fire at each binding's live-range
end, not at lexical scope end ... a value whose last use is mid-scope is dropped
at that use and does not appear in the end-of-scope stack at all." The
interpreter implements that. The compiled backends implement it too -- until the
callee's RETURN TYPE changes, which is the whole trigger:

    struct S { e: E }
    enum E { A(Vec[String]), B }  impl Drop for E { println("dE") }

    fn ret_i64(s: ref S) -> i64    { match s.e { E.A(v) => { let m = v; return m.len() } E.B => { return 0 } } }
    fn ret_str(s: ref S) -> String { match s.e { E.A(v) => { let m = v; return m[0] }    E.B => { return "n" } } }

    fn c_i64() { println("i64"); let s = S { e: E.A(mkv()) }; println(f"{ret_i64(s)}"); println("i64 end"); }
    fn c_str() { println("str"); let s = S { e: E.A(mkv()) }; println(f"{ret_str(s)}"); println("str end"); }

        interp:            i64 1 dE i64 end   str xyz dE str end   end
        jit / build / np:  i64 1 dE i64 end   str xyz str end dE   end
                                                            ^^^^ deferred

`s`'s last use is the `ret_str(s)` call in both columns. With an `i64` return the
compiled backends drop it right there, matching the interpreter and the spec.
With a `String` return -- a heap value derived from the payload the arm moved out
-- they defer the drop to the enclosing scope's exit instead.

CONSERVATIVE BUT OBSERVABLE, and observable in the direction design.md names: the
NLL drop rule exists partly to close the "lock-held-too-long footgun" (same
line), so a `Drop` that releases a lock or an fd is held past its live range for
exactly the shape where the callee hands back borrowed-derived data. Body COUNT
is right on both sides -- one `dE` -- so nothing leaks and nothing double-frees;
only the position moves.

SHAPE A, the lost body. A tail that hands out a binding is a MOVE, so the

sites -- `suppress_user_drop_for_var` and the inline `retain` in

dual registration intact as a unit (an enum binding registers an own-wrapper AND
a payload walk against one slot; retracting half a pair leaves a stale action).

drift. `suppress_user_drop_for_var` additionally narrows from "sweep every frame"
to "the innermost frame that holds one" -- the sweep still reaches an ENCLOSING
binding because the loop falls through when the inner frame has no match, and the
two differ only where an inner AND an outer frame both hold an action for the

(`src/codegen/stmts.rs`, two sites), so the change reached both backends.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}"); } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> R { R { id: n } }
    fn main() {
        let b = mk(3);
        let b = mk(4);
        println("  b-ok");            // note: `b` is never READ
        let c: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
        println(f"  c={c.len()}");
    }
    // 07dc9e76~1 (AOT): dR3 / dR4 / b-ok / c=0
    // 07dc9e76+  (AOT): dR4 / b-ok / c=0 / dR3     <- dR3 at function exit
    // --interp (post-fix): dR4 / dR3 / b-ok / c=0  <- correct, LIFO

is NEVER READ (so its endpoint comes from the fallback at all); a `Vec` binding
appears LATER in the same function; and the values carry a user `Drop`. It is not
about enums -- a shadowed struct reproduces it -- and not about the element type:
`Vec[i64]` is enough, elements need no `Drop`. Two shadowed values of DIFFERENT
types reproduce it too, so it is not the `(name, drop_fn)` retirement key.
Reading the shadowed name anywhere, putting the `Vec` FIRST, or using any
non-`Vec` later binding all make the backends agree.

the helper so codegen keeps the old first-`let`-wins fallback makes codegen WORSE

shared change produces) to `dR8 mid dR9`, one generation firing before the shadow
and the other at scope exit. The shared endpoint is right for both backends
everywhere except this `Vec` case, so the defect is in how codegen consumes it.

entries from the TOP FRAME ONLY (`scope_cleanup_actions.last()`) and filters on

and therefore the endpoint, so both should be collected at the shadowing `let`
and fire LIFO -- which is exactly what happens WITHOUT the `Vec`. Establish first

generation's action is still in the top frame at that moment, or whether the
`Vec` registration perturbs the frame the collection reads. The retirement key
`(binding_name, drop_fn)` was ruled out by the different-types probe above.

SEVERITY. The body still RUNS, so nothing leaks and no resource is released
twice; it runs LATE. That matters for a `Drop` that releases a lock or ends a
span, and it is a run-vs-build divergence, so a kata comparing the two backends
would see it -- unlike the lost-body defects around it, which were unanimous.

MEASURED 2026-08-31, by instrumenting `fire_due_user_drops` to dump the top
frame's `UserDrop` actions and their `last_use` lookup per statement. The two

    stmt=0  frame=[U:b@ptrA lu=Some(1)]                    (not due, 0 != 1)
    stmt=1  frame=[U:b@ptrA lu=Some(1), U:b@ptrB lu=Some(1)]  both due -> both fire

    stmt=0  frame=[U:b@ptrA lu=Some(1)]
    (no dump at stmt=1,2,3 for this instance)
    stmt=4  frame=[U:b@ptrA lu=Some(1), other]             still unfired

its endpoint still reading `Some(1)` -- an endpoint that has already gone by. The
collection is not rejecting it; it is never consulted at the statement where it
was due.

title: AN AUTO-PAR OUTLINED REGION SWALLOWS THE NLL DROP POINTS OF THE STATEMENTS IT SPANS -- `fire_due_user_drops` early-returns on the terminated insert block for exactly those indices, so a binding whose live-range end falls inside the region never fires there; the visible symptom today is that a NEVER-READ shadowed binding's `Drop` order is wrong in one direction without outlining and the other direction with it
detail:
THE DEFECT B-2026-08-31-5 EXPOSED, separated from the regression that exposed
it. That row is closed because the regression is gone; this is the thing that
made the regression possible, and it is older than both.

MECHANISM. `emit_par_run` outlines a statement range into a `__par_branch_*`
worker. While that region is emitted the builder's insert block is TERMINATED,
and `fire_due_user_drops` opens with an early return on exactly that condition.
So for every statement index the region spans, the NLL firing hook does not run.
A cleanup action whose live-range end lands on one of those indices has no
firing point at all and falls through to the scope-exit drain.

MEASURED by dumping the top cleanup frame per statement (instrumentation removed
before landing): `main` reached stmt 0 and stmt 4 and nothing between, with the
shadowed binding's action still pending at stmt 4 and its endpoint reading 1.
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` at COMPILE time makes the same program correct, which is what
localizes this to the outlining rather than to the endpoint computation.

THE FOUR-WAY TABLE, which is the part worth having. One program --
`let b = mk(3); let b = mk(4); println("mid"); let c: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();` --
under each `compute_block_last_use` never-read fallback, with and without
outlining. Correct is the interpreter's `dR4 dR3 mid c=0` (LIFO, both ahead of
the statement):

    fallback         auto-par OFF            auto-par ON (karac build default)
    first-`let`      dR3 mid c=0 dR4         dR3 dR4 mid c=0
    last-`let`       dR4 dR3 mid c=0  OK     dR4 mid c=0 dR3

NEITHER FALLBACK IS RIGHT IN BOTH, and that is the whole point: the last-`let`
endpoint is exactly right when nothing outlines and worst-of-four when something
does. Codegen therefore keeps the first-`let` fallback today, which is wrong in
a milder way in both columns. B-2026-08-31-5's claim that reverting was
"strictly worse" came from measuring only the auto-par-OFF column.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT THE FIX. A catch-up rule -- firing any action whose
endpoint has PASSED (`lu <= stmt_idx` instead of `==`) -- was implemented and
measured. It moves the body to the next LIVE statement, which is still after the
outlined region, so it recovers the count and not the position, and it widens
the firing rule everywhere to buy that. Reverted.

WHERE TO START. The outlined worker already computes its own `last_use` over its
own statement list and already calls `fire_due_user_drops` -- it is a real
block with a real frame. What is missing is that the ENCLOSING function's
actions for bindings whose statements were outlined are still registered in the
ENCLOSING frame, where no firing point remains. Either those actions move into
the worker's frame, or the enclosing loop fires the ones the region swallowed at
the region's boundary. The second is cheaper and probably enough for ordering,
since the boundary is a live insert point in the enclosing function.

SCOPE NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: only the never-read shadowed
shape was walked, because that is what made the swallowing visible. Any binding
whose NLL endpoint falls inside an outlined region should be affected --
ordinary non-shadowed locals included -- and that has NOT been probed. Nor has
whether a `par {}` block written explicitly (rather than auto-par's outlining)
takes the same path.

NOT VISIBLE TO `tests/codegen.rs`: that harness compiles SEQUENTIALLY, so its
pins only ever see the left column. A regression test for this belongs in
`tests/par_codegen.rs`, which is also why B-2026-08-31-5 shipped without one.

title: A TUPLE-PATTERN REBIND OVER AN OWNED TUPLE PARAM RUNS THE ELEMENT'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS AND ONCE UNDER `--interp` -- `b1 dR1 dR1` vs `b1 dR1`; the interpreter is the correct column, and the same arm WITHOUT the rebind agrees at one on every surface
detail:
Measured on 24abc95, all four surfaces (interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0),
and PRE-EXISTING -- byte-identical with B-2026-08-31-1's fix stashed out, and
that fix deliberately does not touch this shape (see its "RESTRICTED TO VARIANT
PATTERNS" note).

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }

    fn s1(t: (R, i64))  { match t { (r, k) => { let m = r; println(f"  b{m.id}"); } } }
    fn s1b(t: (R, i64)) { match t { (r, k) => {            println(f"  b{r.id}"); } } }

      s1   interp -> `b1 dR1`        jit / build / np -> `b1 dR1 dR1`
      s1b  interp -> `b2 dR2`        jit / build / np -> `b2 dR2`      AGREE

One `R` is constructed and passed by value, so ONE body is due, which makes the
INTERPRETER the correct column here and the compiled backends the surplus. The
control `s1b` -- the identical arm with the rebind removed -- agrees at one body
on every surface, so the trigger is precisely `let m = r`: the compiled side
arms a second body for the rebound local while the interpreter (whose
match-arm view propagation covers plain TUPLE patterns for an identifier
scrutinee) correctly withholds it.

WHY IT IS THE MIRROR OF B-2026-08-31-1 RATHER THAN THE SAME BUG. That row was
the interpreter running a surplus body because its view set did not reach
through a PROJECTION; codegen's did. This is the same disagreement one axis
over: for a TUPLE PATTERN the interpreter's view set is the WIDER of the two,
because codegen only view-marks bindings in `current_variant_payload_bindings`
and a tuple pattern's bindings are not variant payloads. Fixing -31-1 by
widening the interpreter to match codegen was therefore correct in that
direction and would have been wrong in this one, which is why the new gate is
restricted to variant patterns and this row exists separately.

NOTE THE THIRD CELL, which says the two are not simply "codegen is wrong":
`match s.t { (r, k) => { let m = r; … } }` over a tuple FIELD of an owned struct
param runs TWO bodies on every surface -- agreed, and by the one-value-one-body
rule agreed-and-wrong. So the tuple-pattern family currently holds one
divergence (this row) and one agreed surplus, and a fix should settle both
together rather than move the divergence around.

Bodies only: no memory fault is implied, and the payload here owns no heap. A
heap-carrying payload should be measured under LSan before assuming the memory
side is balanced.

SOURCE NOTE: found in the B-2026-08-31-1 nine-cell matrix, as the control that
was supposed to prove the new gate had not over-reached.

fix:
Fixed in 95fbe26 (fix) + 990cfed (twinned fixtures).

NOT THE `match` MACHINERY, WHICH IS WHERE THE ROW POINTED. Instrumenting every
decision in `handle_match` showed the struct-variant and tuple-variant spellings
reach IDENTICAL values for `arm_reads_through`, `consuming_scrutinee`,
`match_disarms_payload_walk` and `frame_is_sole_owner_of_param`. The pattern
machinery already handled `PatternKind::Struct` symmetrically at every site
(`arm_moved_user_drop_payload_bindings`, `pattern_consumes_user_drop_payload`,
`variant_payload_decls`, `run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` -- all inspected
and all correct). The loss was one level up, at the CALLER.

`eat(Sv.Hold { inner: R { .. } })` is spelled as an `ExprKind::StructLiteral`
whose path ends in the VARIANT, so `fresh_temp_arg_type_name`'s
`find_struct_def(path.last())` looked up `Hold`, found nothing, and the
fresh-temp argument walk claimed no owner at all -- so neither the enum's own
body nor its payload's ran. The tuple-variant twin `eatt(Tv.A(r))` is an
`ExprKind::Call` whose callee path resolves through the enum, which is exactly
why the row's control was correct and the spelling was the whole variable.

THE ROW'S OWN GUESS WAS RIGHT and its framing was too narrow: it suspected
"whether a struct-variant payload is simply absent from whatever the caller-side
fire enumerates, since the caller here passes a fresh temp and fires nothing".
That is precisely it -- but the `match` is incidental. An EMPTY-BODIED callee
reproduces the whole thing:

    fn eat(v: Sv) { println("e") }
    eat(Sv.Hold { inner: R { id: 1 } })   interp -> `e`   compiled -> `e dSv dR1`

which is what localized the fix.

THE FIX resolves the path through `qualified_struct_variant_enum_name`, a new
helper placed beside `qualified_enum_struct_variant_field_order` in
`interpreter.rs` and mirroring the resolution the VALUE-construction site a few
lines up already performs. Classifier and constructor now answer the same
question about the same path, which is what keeps them agreeing by construction.

QUALIFIED ONLY, deliberately. The unqualified spelling (`Hold { .. }`, equally
legal at that construction site) loses the same bodies on BOTH backends today;
claiming it in the interpreter alone would convert an agreed answer into a fresh
run-vs-build divergence -- the worse of the two, and the trade this family has
had to make before. Filed as B-2026-09-01-32.

MEMORY MEASURED, as the row asked. A heap-carrying payload (`String` + `Vec`)
agrees on all four surfaces, and `asan_fresh_temp_struct_variant_arg_payload_is_balanced`
pins it. That case was GREEN BEFORE THE FIX and the fixture says so: the fix is
interpreter-only and ASAN never runs the interpreter, so what it pins is the
compiled reference the interpreter now matches -- not a reproduction.

TWO NEIGHBOURS FOUND IN THE SAME MATRIX, both filed rather than folded in:
B-2026-09-01-31 (a DISCARDED struct-variant literal loses only the PAYLOAD body
under `--interp` -- a different site, still wrong after this fix) and
B-2026-09-01-33 (a PRODUCER-FN argument loses the payload body on both COMPILED
backends, the opposite direction). The latter is why the `producer-fn` case is
deliberately ABSENT from this row's twinned fixtures: pinning it would have
asserted one side of a live disagreement.

Verified: 16,027 passed / 0 failed on the full `--features llvm` suite, with
zero skip notices (so the E2E cases exercised real binaries); both clippy legs
and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
title: A STRUCT-VARIANT PATTERN OVER AN OWNED ENUM PARAM LOSES BOTH `Drop` BODIES UNDER `--interp` -- `b3` against `b3 dSv dR3` on all three compiled surfaces, with and without a rebind; the TUPLE-variant spelling of the identical program is correct everywhere
detail:
Measured on 24abc95, all four surfaces, and PRE-EXISTING (byte-identical with
B-2026-08-31-1's fix stashed out; that fix's new branch requires a PROJECTION
scrutinee and this one is a bare identifier, so it cannot reach this shape).

    struct R { id: i64 }         impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum Sv { Hold { inner: R }, Nil }
    impl Drop for Sv { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dSv") } }

    fn s2(v: Sv)  { match v { Sv.Hold { inner } => { let m = inner; println(f"  b{m.id}"); } Sv.Nil => { } } }
    fn s2b(v: Sv) { match v { Sv.Hold { inner } => {                println(f"  b{inner.id}"); } Sv.Nil => { } } }

      s2   interp -> `b3`      jit / build / np -> `b3 dSv dR3`
      s2b  interp -> `b4`      jit / build / np -> `b4 dSv dR4`

BOTH bodies vanish under `karac run --interp` -- the enum's own and its
payload's -- and the rebind is irrelevant: `s2b`, with no `let` at all, loses
them identically. This is the direction that matters for a resource type: a
`Drop` that closes a handle or releases a lock simply never runs on that
backend.

THE STRUCT-VARIANT PATTERN IS THE WHOLE VARIABLE. The TUPLE-variant spelling of
the same program (`enum E { A(R) }`, `match v { E.A(r) => … }`) is correct on
all four surfaces, one body each, with and without the rebind -- it is the
control that localizes this. The scrutinee is a bare owned enum param in both.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-30-55. That row is also "the interpreter runs zero bodies
for an owned enum param", but it is gated on a METHOD frame and its free-function
twin is explicitly correct. This one is a FREE FUNCTION, so whatever fix reaches
-30-55 through `owned_param_frame_is_method` will not reach this; the shared
symptom is a coincidence of two different holes. Worth checking whether a
struct-variant payload is simply absent from whatever the caller-side fire
enumerates, since the caller here passes a fresh temp and fires nothing.

Bodies only on the evidence to hand -- valgrind/LSan not run, and the payload
owns no heap, so a heap-carrying struct-variant payload should be measured
before assuming the memory side is balanced.

SOURCE NOTE: found in the B-2026-08-31-1 matrix while checking that the new
variant-pattern branch covered struct variants as well as tuple variants; the
PROJECTION spelling of this shape is fixed by that row, and this identifier
spelling was already broken underneath it.

fix:
FIXED by 86c9957. TWO defects with one symptom, and only one of them was the list
the row pointed at.

DEFECT 1, THE LIST. `display_field_is_leaf` (src/codegen/synth_display.rs) is
another longhand copy of the primitive widths, and it omitted `f16` and `bf16`.
A `#[derive(Display)]` struct with a NARROW-FLOAT field refused to compile —
which the row did not measure, having probed only `Vector`. It now reads
`PRELUDE_PRIMITIVES` first, the same anti-recurrence move B-2026-08-30-25 and
B-2026-08-30-40 made for their own copies of this list. That is four sibling
lists corrected in one night, all with the same `f32`/`f64` stop.

DEFECT 2, AND THE REASON `Vector` COULD NOT SIMPLY JOIN IT. Admitting `Vector`
as a leaf COMPILES and PRINTS THE WRONG THING: `f"{h}"` renders
`WithVec { v: 1, n: 1 }` — one stray lane, the exact B-2026-08-29-52 defect. The
parts path synthesizes each field's expression with the BASE's span, and a
vector interpolation resolves through the span-keyed `vector_typed_exprs` table;
the synthesized part therefore looks up a span belonging to the struct, misses,
and falls through to the scalar renderer. Measured, not reasoned about: the
one-line widening was applied and the wrong output recorded before it was backed
out.

So the vector case routes through the BY-POINTER renderer instead
(`emit_struct_debug_display_fn` + `render_via_display_fn`), which dispatches on
the field's `TypeExpr` and reaches the `Vector` arm B-2026-08-30-39 added. That
path needs no span at all.

THE APPROACH WAS ALREADY PROVEN ON THIS EXACT SHAPE, which is what made it the
small fix rather than a redesign: the SAME struct nested in a `Vec` renders
correctly today, because a container element goes through
`emit_struct_debug_display_fn`. Only the top-level spelling took the parts path.
The fix routes the top-level case to the path the nested one already took, and
the regression test asserts both spellings print the same struct identically —
which is the assertion that the two paths agree, not merely that both succeed.

THE GATE IS A POSITIVE TEST, NOT A CATCH-ALL. `struct_display_needs_type_directed_fn`
asks whether any field is a `Vector`, rather than falling back whenever
`build_struct_display_parts` returns `Err`. A catch-all would also swallow
genuinely unsupported field shapes, and `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` PANICS
rather than erroring for those — trading this row's clean (if ugly) diagnostic
for a compiler crash, which is the trade B-2026-08-30-39 was filed about.

THE ROW'S SECOND HALF — the diagnostic that dumps a Rust `{:?}` of the field's
TypeExpr, spans and all, into user-facing output — is UNCHANGED and still
reachable for the field shapes that remain unsupported (`Vec`, `Map`, `Set`,
tuple). It is no longer reachable for the two shapes this row reported. Left
alone deliberately: making that message readable means rendering a `TypeExpr`
back to source syntax, which is a formatting facility this file does not have
and which every unsupported-shape message in it would want. Filed separately
rather than half-done here.

MEASURED on all four surfaces (interp / jit / build / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0),
byte-identical:

    top    WithVec { v: Vector(1, -2, 3, -4), n: 1 }      (was: refused)
    nest   [WithVec { v: Vector(1, -2, 3, -4), n: 1 }]    (worked before; the control)
    float  WithVec { v: Vector(9, 8, 7, 6), n: 1 }        (call-result field value)
    narrow WithNarrow { a: 2.5, b: 3.5, c: 4.5 }          (was: refused)
    plain  Plain { n: 1, s: s, w: 3402823669...455 }      (parts path, unchanged)

Tests: the twins `test_derived_display_renders_vector_and_narrow_float_fields`
and `e2e_derived_display_renders_vector_and_narrow_float_fields`, pinned to one
string, RED-verified against the pre-fix tree with exactly the diagnostic this
row quotes.
title: A STRUCT FIELD OF `Vector[T, N]` TYPE HAS NO DERIVED-Display ARM UNDER `karac build`, AND THE REFUSAL DUMPS A RUST `{:?}` OF THE FIELD'S TypeExpr -- spans and all -- INTO THE USER-FACING ERROR; the same vector renders correctly at depth 0, in a `Vec`, in a tuple, as a `Map` value and under `dbg`, so the struct emitter is the one container that did not gain the recursion
detail:
Measured on 7e00ccd, `karac build` and `karac run` alike, WITH B-2026-08-30-39's
fix applied -- so this is what remains after the panic class it covers is gone,
and it is not that fix's doing (the same shape errors identically without it,
one line earlier in the same emitter's fall-through).

    #[derive(Display)]
    struct Holder { v: Vector[i32, 4] }

    fn main() {
        let h = Holder { v: Vector[i32, 4](1i32, -2i32, 3i32, -4i32) };
        println(f"{h}");
    }

      karac run --interp -> `Holder { v: Vector(1, -2, 3, -4) }`
      karac build        -> error, and the error is the problem:

    Display codegen for struct 'Holder': field 'v' has a type
    (Path(PathExpr { segments: ["Vector"], generic_args: Some([Type(TypeExpr {
    kind: Path(PathExpr { segments: ["i32"], generic_args: None, span: Span {
    line: 2, column: 27, offset: 45, length: 3 } }), span: Span { line: 2, ... }
    }), Const(Expr { kind: Integer(4, None), span: Span { ... } })]), span: Span
    { ... } })) whose Display is not yet supported under `karac build` (only
    primitives, String, and nested Display structs are supported;
    Vec/Map/Set/enum/tuple fields are tracked as subtask 5 follow-on)

TWO DEFECTS IN ONE LINE, and the second is the cheaper of the two to fix:

 1. A struct FIELD of vector type has no Display arm, while the same vector
    renders correctly at depth 0, inside a `Vec`, inside a tuple, as a `Map`
    value and under `dbg` (all of those landed with B-2026-08-30-39). The struct
    emitter is the one container that did not gain the recursion.

 2. The message DUMPS A RUST `{:?}` OF THE TypeExpr, spans and all, into
    user-facing output. Nothing in it names `Vector[i32, 4]` in source syntax,
    the line/column that would help are buried inside a Debug struct rather
    than attached as a span, and the closing advice lists the shapes that ARE
    supported without mentioning this one. A user reading it cannot tell which
    field of which struct to change.

NOT A PANIC -- it is a clean `Err` -- which is what keeps this medium rather
than the crash class its sibling row carried. `karac check` passes; only the
build fails.

SCOPE, measured: a field of `Vec[i64]` type in the same position fails with the
same message shape, so this is the general "compound field in a derived struct
Display" gap the message's own last clause admits ("Vec/Map/Set/enum/tuple
fields are tracked as subtask 5 follow-on"), and `Vector` simply joins that
list. What makes it worth its own row rather than a note on that backlog item is
that the vector case now DIVERGES from every other position the same value can
appear in, and that the diagnostic is unreadable.

SOURCE NOTE: found working B-2026-08-30-39's "NOT MEASURED" list, which asked
whether "struct FIELDS of vector type panic the same way". They do not panic --
they produce this.

fix:
FIXED by da529e8. Both halves the row asks for, plus a third the row did not see.

THE ROW'S PROPOSED CAPABILITY FIX MISPLACES THE DEFECT, and the correction is
the useful part of this entry. It says to route the Option/Result f-string part
"through `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` the way the `Vec`/`Map`/tuple parts
already go". It ALREADY went there: `try_compile_option_result_display` ->
`emit_option_display_te` -> `emit_enum_field_display` -> that dispatcher. What
stopped `Some([9])` was a GATE in front of it,
`is_reconstructable_display_payload`, which admitted primitives, `String`, and a
struct of at most three one-word scalars, and nothing else.

The gate was more conservative than the machinery it guarded, and the proof is
one program: a USER enum with the identical payload --
`#[derive(Display)] enum E { V(Vec[i64]) }` -- has always rendered `V([9])`,
because it reaches `emit_enum_field_display` WITHOUT passing this gate. That
renderer already deboxes a spilled payload (`want > num`) and dispatches
type-directedly, so everything needed was present. The oracle for widening the
gate was therefore "whatever a user enum can already print", and the fix is to
make the predicate say what the machinery can actually do:

  * handle-shaped stdlib collections (`Vec` / `Map` / `Set` / `SortedMap` /
    `SortedSet`) -- the payload is the same `{ptr, len, cap}` triple as
    `String`, which the predicate always admitted;
  * a `shared` type -- one RC pointer word, checked ahead of the by-value
    struct arm for the same reason `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` checks
    `shared_types` first: a shared type is in BOTH registries and the field
    walk is wrong for it;
  * a nested `Option` / `Result`, recursively;
  * a tuple, recursively over its fields;
  * a user struct, recursively over its fields -- replacing the "<= 3 one-word
    scalars" rule, which refused `P { x: i64, y: String }` and
    `Q { a, b, c, d: i64 }` even though `rebuild_payload_deboxing_if_spilled`
    handles both (measured: identical to the interpreter);
  * a user enum, whose own renderer walks its variants.

EVERY ONE OF THOSE WAS MEASURED against `--interp` before being admitted, and
two shapes were measured OUT again. `Option[Vector[i64, 4]]` compiled and
printed `Some(Vector(0, 94011124162560, 1, 0))` against the interpreter's
`Some(Vector(1, 2, 3, 4))`; `Option[Array[i64, 3]]` PANICKED the compiler
(`emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Array_i64_3' not yet supported`). Both
are pre-existing gaps one level down -- a user enum with a `Vector` payload
prints the same garbage today, and `match` on either binds a wrong value -- so
they keep the clean refusal rather than becoming a new way to reach a
miscompile. Filed as B-2026-08-31-18 (the reconstruction miscompile, which `match` shares)
and B-2026-08-31-19 (the `Array` display arm the dispatcher never grew).

THE ROW'S "NOT MEASURED" LIST, ANSWERED IN FULL:
  * `println(c)` has the same gap, through a different error site
    (`control_flow.rs`'s "Display of a struct argument ...").
  * a `Result` with a wide payload fails identically, in either position
    (`Result[Vec[i64], i64]` and `Result[i64, Vec[String]]`).
  * the layout boundary is NOT width. `Option[i128]`/`Option[u128]` (two payload
    words) and `Option[String]` (three) were already fine; the gate was a
    literal whitelist, not a size test.

AND WIDTH WAS NOT THE ONLY AXIS. `Option[f16]` and `Option[bf16]` -- ONE word,
narrower than the `i64` that works -- were refused too, because
`is_inline_displayable_payload` is a SIXTH hand-written primitive-width list
stopping at f32/f64 (after B-2026-08-30-25, B-2026-08-30-40, B-2026-08-31-9 and
the two before them). Widened to `crate::prelude::PRELUDE_PRIMITIVES`, which is
what every other module reads; `str` stays as the one extra name. That exposed a
SEVENTH: `emit_display_fn_for_type`'s `"f32" | "f64"` arm, whose absence turned
the newly-admitted `Option[f16]` from a clean error into a compiler PANIC. The
formatter widens any narrower float to f64 itself, so the arm needed no
width-specific work -- exactly as it needed none for f32.

THE DIAGNOSTIC, second half of the row. One string served two arrivals: an
f-string interpolating a struct LITERAL or call result, where "bind it to a
`let` first" is the fix, and an Option/Result PLACE EXPRESSION the synthesizer
declines -- already `let`-bound, so the advice was false as well as unhelpful,
which is what the row is about. `deferred_display_error` now names the type and
the offending payload for the second case and keeps the original text for the
first.

It prescribes NO rewrite, deliberately. The obvious one -- destructure with
`match`/`if let` and format the binding -- is itself WRONG for both shapes that
still reach it: `match` on an `Option[Array[i64, 3]]` prints `Some(1)` against
the interpreter's `Some([1, 2, 3])`, and an `Option[Vector[i64, 4]]` prints
`Some(0)` against `Some(Vector(1, 2, 3, 4))`. Advising it would trade a clean
compile error for silently wrong output. The message points at
`karac run --interp`, which does render both.

TWO REGRESSIONS THE FULL SUITE CAUGHT, both worth recording because they are the
shape a wider predicate takes:
  * `is_reconstructable_display_payload` recursed forever on a RECURSIVE type
    (`shared struct ListNode { val: i64, next: Option[ListNode] }`), overflowing
    the compiler's stack on a program that already compiled and rendered. Fixed
    with a seen-stack of struct names, plus the `shared` arm above, which
    answers that case before the field walk starts.
  * `test_unrenderable_main_error_is_a_build_error_not_an_empty_message`
    (B-2026-08-25-34) used `Option[(i64, i64)]` as its example of a shape
    codegen cannot render. It can now. The fixture moves to
    `Option[Vector[i64, 4]]` and KEEPS the old shape as a second row asserting
    it builds and matches the interpreter -- the retired example becomes a
    regression guard for the capability that retired it.

Tests: `e2e_option_result_display_multiword_payloads` +
`codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` (tests/codegen.rs),
`test_option_result_display_multiword_payloads` (tests/interpreter.rs, the
oracle), `asan_option_display_multiword_payload_frees_once`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs). The first and last were verified RED on the
unpatched tree; the interpreter twin never went red and says so.

A LEAK SURVIVES AND IS NOT THIS ROW'S. An Option/Result CALL RESULT interpolated
in an f-string (`f"{mk(n)}"`) leaks its payload buffer once per evaluation. It
is pre-existing, not introduced here: the same fixture with an `Option[String]`
return -- a shape admitted since B-2026-07-08-9 -- leaks 20 buffers under LSan
on the unpatched compiler. The widening does broaden its reach, so it is filed as
B-2026-08-31-17 and the ASAN fixture uses a `let`-bound spelling with a comment
naming that row.
title: AN `Option` WHOSE PAYLOAD LOWERS TO A MULTI-WORD STRUCT CANNOT BE INTERPOLATED IN AN F-STRING UNDER `karac build`, AND THE ERROR MISDESCRIBES ITS OWN CAUSE -- `Option[Vec[i64]]` is refused with "bind a struct literal or call result to a `let` first" when the expression is already a `let`-bound variable, while `Option[i64]` and `Result[i64, i64]` interpolate fine
detail:
Measured on 7e00ccd, `karac build` and `karac run`; PRE-EXISTING and unrelated to
B-2026-08-30-39, whose fix is applied here and changes none of these three rows.

    let a: Option[i64] = Option.Some(7i64);        f"{a}"  ->  Some(7)      OK
    let r: Result[i64, i64] = Result.Ok(3i64);     f"{r}"  ->  Ok(3)        OK
    let c: Option[Vec[i64]] = Option.Some([9i64]); f"{c}"  ->  ERROR        <-

      interp for all three: `Some(7)` / `Ok(3)` / `Some([9])`

    error: codegen failed: Display of a struct in an f-string is supported when
    the interpolated expression is a variable or field access (e.g. `f"{x}"`);
    bind a struct literal or call result to a `let` first (user-struct Display,
    subtask-5 follow-on)

THE MESSAGE IS WRONG ON ITS OWN TERMS, which is the half that costs a reader the
most time. The interpolated expression IS a variable -- `c`, bound by the `let`
on the line above -- and the value is not a struct. Following the advice cannot
help, because the advice is already satisfied. It comes from
`compile_fstr_part`'s final fall-through (src/codegen/runtime.rs), which reaches
"a struct value that isn't the String layout" and concludes user-struct; an
`Option` whose payload is wide enough to lower to a multi-word struct lands
there too, and nothing distinguishes the two.

THE VARIABLE IS THE PAYLOAD'S LAYOUT, not the payload's identity. `Option[i64]`
lowers to something the f-string path already handles and prints fine;
`Option[Vec[i64]]` does not. `Option[Vector[u64, 2]]` fails identically, which
is how this was found -- it was the seventh spelling in B-2026-08-30-39's table
and was read there as possibly a vector defect. It is not: the vector is
incidental, and that row's own note ("treat that message as a third defect
rather than assume it is accurate") was right to be suspicious of it.

TWO THINGS TO FIX, and they are separable:
  * the DIAGNOSTIC, which should name the actual shape and stop advising a
    `let` that is already there -- cheap, and it stops the next reader losing
    the time this cost;
  * the CAPABILITY: routing an Option/Result f-string part through
    `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` the way the `Vec`/`Map`/tuple parts already
    go, which is where the enum arm that would render `Some([9])` lives.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: whether `println(c)` (the non-f-string
spelling) has the same gap; whether a `Result` with a wide Ok payload fails
identically to the `Option`; and where exactly the layout boundary sits between
`Option[i64]` and `Option[Vec[i64]]`.

SOURCE NOTE: reduced from B-2026-08-30-39's `Option` row while closing it; the
three-way comparison above is what separates the payload-layout cause from the
vector one.

CLOSING NOTE (2026-08-31): one more divergence surfaced while measuring the
narrow-float half and is NOT this row's -- `let q: Option[f16] = Option.Some(0.1)`
prints `Some(0.1)` under `--interp` and `Some(0.0999755859375)` under
`karac build`, with codegen the correct side. Filed as B-2026-08-31-20.

title: A GENERIC CALLING ANOTHER GENERIC LOSES THE UNSIGNED READING ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS — `wrap[T](x) { show(x) }` prints `u64::MAX` as `-1` from JIT and AOT while the DIRECT `show(x)` at the same width is correct on both, and `--interp` is correct for both since B-2026-08-30-44
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-30-44, probing whether that row's interpreter fix
covered a generic that calls another generic. It does; the compiled backends do
not.

MEASURED on `main` with B-2026-08-30-44's fix in place:

    fn show[T](x: T) -> String { f"{x}" }
    fn wrap[T](x: T) -> String { show(x) }
    let big: u64 = 18446744073709551615u64;

    shape                          --interp   JIT   AOT
    wrap(big)   (transitive)       OK         -1    -1
    show(big)   (direct, CONTROL)  OK         OK    OK

Identical at `u128`. The direct row is what localizes it: the same callee, the
same width, the same interpolation — reached through one more generic frame.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-30-44'S FIX. The JIT/AOT columns are byte-identical
before and after that commit; only the `--interp` column moved (from `-1` to
correct). What the fix changed is VISIBILITY: the two backends previously agreed
on the wrong answer, so this shape passed an A/B comparison while being wrong on
every backend. It now fails A/B, which is the correct signal — the interpreter
matches what the same value prints outside a generic and the compiled side does
not.

WHY THIS IS NOT B-2026-08-30-45. That row was one monomorph SYMBOL serving two
widths, needed two instantiations in one program to show, and is fixed. This
needs a single width and one instantiation chain, and reproduces with `u64`
alone — no i128/u128 pair anywhere.

WHY THIS IS NOT B-2026-08-30-44 EITHER. That row is the tree-walk's signedness
recovery through `type_subs_stack`; this is the compiled side, which
monomorphizes and therefore has no such lookup to get wrong. The defect must be
in how the inner call's argument type is resolved when the caller is itself a
monomorph — i.e. `T` in `wrap$u64`'s body reaching `show`'s instantiation
machinery still spelled as a parameter rather than as `u64`. NOT diagnosed
further; that is a hypothesis from the shape, not a measurement.

SCOPE NOTE: only the display path was probed. Whether transitive-generic
ARITHMETIC is also affected on the compiled side is unmeasured — the analogous
interpreter half turned out to matter more than the display half
(B-2026-08-30-44's close records division and comparison both wrong), so that
is the first thing to check.
fix:
FIXED by d87ae4f. Codegen-only; the interpreter was already correct and is the
oracle, so every expected value in the tests is what `--interp` prints.

MECHANISM, confirmed rather than hypothesised. The row's own guess -- "`T` in
`wrap$u64`'s body reaching `show`'s instantiation machinery still spelled as a
parameter" -- is right in outline, and the precise site is
`infer_call`'s post-inference filter in src/typechecker/exprs.rs:

    if !matches!(&resolved, Type::TypeParam(n) if n == name) { solutions.insert(..) }

Inference resolves `show`'s `T` to the CALLER's `T`; the names are equal, so the
binding is dropped. That guard is deliberate and still wanted -- it is what
keeps the interpreter's substitution stack from seeing a `T -> T` entry that
shadows the outer frame which does know `T` (the B-2026-08-30-43 hazard). But
codegen reads the same table: `call_type_subs` is empty for the inner call,
`subst_names` stays unfilled, and `mangle_mono_name` falls back to
`llvm_type_to_mangle_str`, which carries a WIDTH and no SIGNEDNESS. So
`wrap$u32` called `show$i32`, and the body compiled at that signedness.

THE LOCALIZER is a one-token edit: spell the callee's parameter `U` instead of
`T` and the identical program is correct on every backend, emitting
`showU$u32`. The bug is the NAME COLLISION, not the nesting -- which is also
why the row's "reproduces with u64 alone, no i128/u128 pair" reasoning for
separating it from B-2026-08-30-45 holds.

FIX: `augment_subst_names_from_arg_type_names` in src/codegen/mono.rs, the
scalar twin of the existing container fallback `augment_subst_from_arg_elem_-
types` it runs beside. For a bare type-param param still unbound it takes, in
order: (1) the ARGUMENT's own registered concrete name from `var_type_names`,
which a monomorph fills for its params and locals -- direct evidence, and
enough for every binding-rooted argument; (2) for an INLINE expression
argument, which names no binding, the enclosing mono's binding for that SAME
NAME, which is sound because the only reason the entry is missing is the
collision above. Step 2 is guarded on `subst`'s slot being a scalar LLVM type:
the other way a binding can go missing is a solution
`type_to_concrete_or_param_name` cannot spell (a tuple, a function type), and
those lower to an aggregate. Both steps fill only a GAP -- a recorded binding
always wins -- so nothing that worked before changes.

CODEGEN CONTAINMENT held: no typechecker change was needed, and none was made.
Fixing the typechecker's filter instead would have been the wrong place twice
over -- it would re-open the interpreter hazard the filter exists for, and it
would add self-referential rows to `call_type_subs`, which
`karac query monomorphization` reads as its instantiation list.

WIDER THAN THIS ROW RECORDED, on both axes it flagged.

  * The SCOPE NOTE asks whether transitive-generic ARITHMETIC is affected. It
    is, and exactly as the note predicted from B-2026-08-30-44's precedent:
    `u64::MAX / 2` gave 0 and `u64::MAX < 2` gave true.
  * The row lists u64 and u128. EVERY unsigned width diverges -- u8 (255 read
    as -1), u16, u32, usize included. u32 is the sharpest, because a u32 fits
    non-negatively in the interpreter's i64 carrier, so `--interp` was correct
    there for a different reason than at u64 and the compiled side still was
    not.
  * Also diverging and not in the row: any nesting depth (a three-deep chain),
    a `ref T` parameter, and a program instantiating BOTH signednesses, which
    collapsed onto the signed body for both.

RED-VERIFIED as a clean partition on the pre-fix compiler: 15 of 22 shapes
diverged, 7 agreed. The 7 are the controls -- the renamed-parameter localizer,
the direct call, i32/i64/f64/String/bool. Post-fix all 22 agree across
`--interp`, JIT and AOT.

TESTS. `test_ir_transitive_generic_keeps_the_callee_at_the_declared_signedness`
asserts the emitted SYMBOLS (`show$u32` present, `show$i32` absent), because
the symbol is the mechanism and both monomorphs would take the same LLVM type
either way. `e2e_transitive_generic_keeps_the_declared_unsignedness` runs all
22 behavioural cases, and `interp_transitive_generic_is_the_codegen_-
unsignedness_oracle` in tests/interpreter.rs pins the same values on the
reference side, so an interpreter regression cannot silently move what the
codegen test is measured against. Both codegen tests pass under
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`, so they exercise real binaries.

title: A `u64` FIELD READ INSIDE A GENERIC `impl` PRINTS AS `-1` ON ALL THREE BACKENDS — `impl[T] Box[T] { fn get(ref self) -> String { f"{self.v}" } }` at `Box[u64]`, where the free-function spelling of the same interpolation is correct on all three since B-2026-08-30-44
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-30-44, probing whether that row's fix reached a
generic IMPL as well as a generic free function. It does not, and neither does
the compiled side — this is the one shape in the family where NO backend is
right, so there is no oracle for it today.

MEASURED on `main` with B-2026-08-30-44's fix in place:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    impl[T] Box[T] { fn get(ref self) -> String { f"{self.v}" } }
    fn show[T](x: T) -> String { f"{x}" }
    let big: u64 = 18446744073709551615u64;

    shape                                  --interp   JIT   AOT
    Box[u64] { v: big }.get()              -1         -1    -1
    show(big)          (free fn, CONTROL)  OK         OK    OK

The control is the same interpolation of the same value one construct over, so
the difference is the generic IMPL frame, not the width and not the
interpolation.

WHY IT IS FILED APART FROM B-2026-08-30-44. That row's fix resolves a
`Type::TypeParam` through `type_subs_stack`, which is pushed for a free-function
call. This shape's `T` comes from the IMPL's generic parameter, bound by the
receiver's type rather than by the call's arguments, so it is a different
binding channel — and the compiled backends being wrong too means the fix
cannot be interpreter-only the way that row's was. Both halves are needed here,
which is a materially different piece of work.

BOTH BACKENDS WRONG MEANS NO ORACLE. A/B agreement holds for this shape and
agrees on the WRONG value, so it will not surface as a run-vs-build divergence
and a kata using it would look clean. Whoever fixes this must pick the expected
value from the language definition (unsigned, i.e. 18446744073709551615) rather
than from either backend.

SCOPE NOTE: display only. Arithmetic on a `u64` field inside a generic impl is
unprobed and is the first thing to check, on the evidence of B-2026-08-30-44
where the arithmetic half was both unreported and more consequential than the
display half.

CORRECTION (2026-08-31, same session, after B-2026-08-30-43's fix landed at
8245dc9). The INTERPRETER HALF OF THIS ROW IS NOW FIXED. That row's missing
generic-substitution frame was the shared cause it predicted ("anything the
tree-walk resolves through `resolve_type_param` is affected inside a generic
impl method"), and pushing the frame makes `Box[u64] { v: n }.get()` print
18446744073709551615 under `--interp`.

WHAT REMAINS, and why this row stays OPEN: the compiled backends still print
`-1`. Re-measured on 8245dc9:

    shape                                  --interp   JIT   AOT
    Box[u64] { v: big }.get()              OK         -1    -1
    show(big)          (free fn, CONTROL)  OK         OK    OK

THE ROW'S FRAMING HAS CHANGED MATERIALLY and its original text should be read
with that in mind. It was filed as "wrong on all three backends, so there is no
oracle and A/B agreement hides it". That is no longer true: this is now an
ordinary run-vs-build divergence, it WILL surface in an A/B comparison, and the
interpreter is the reference to fix the compiled side against. The paragraph
below headed "BOTH BACKENDS WRONG MEANS NO ORACLE" is superseded — its advice
to pick the expected value from the language definition still gives the right
answer (unsigned), but it is no longer the only source.

The remaining half is plausibly the same defect as B-2026-08-31-11 (a generic
calling a generic loses the unsigned reading on both compiled backends), since
both are the compiled side failing to carry a concrete instantiation into a
body it did monomorphize. NOT measured as one; whoever takes either should
check the other first.
fix:
FIXED by 17279ac. The remaining compiled half is closed; the interpreter half was
already fixed by B-2026-08-30-43 (8245dc9), as this row's own CORRECTION
records, so the interpreter is the oracle and every expected value in the tests
is what `--interp` prints.

NOT THE SAME DEFECT AS B-2026-08-31-11, which this row named as the likely
shared cause and told whoever took either to check first. Checked: after -11's
fix landed (d87ae4f) this still reproduced unchanged, and the reason is visible
in the symbol table. -11's failure WAS the symbol -- `wrap$u32` called
`show$i32`. Here the symbol is right (`Box.get$u64`); the loss is inside a
correctly-monomorphized body. Two different mechanisms in the same family.

MECHANISM. `expr_is_unsigned_int` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) decides signedness
for the print / f-string path from the field's DECLARED type name. For
`struct Box[T] { v: T }` that name is `T`, which is not a uint name, so the read
fell through to signed and the snprintf widening sign-extended.

FIX: the three arms of that predicate which read a declared name -- the field
itself, a `Vec[T]` element reached through a local, and one reached through a
field -- resolve the name through the enclosing monomorph's `type_subst_names`
first (`resolve_mono_type_name`). That map is empty outside a monomorph and
holds no entry for an already-concrete name, so the resolution is the identity
in both cases and only bites for a name that IS a type parameter of the mono
being compiled.

THE SCOPE NOTE IS ANSWERED, AND IN THE NEGATIVE. It asks whether ARITHMETIC on
a `u64` field inside a generic impl is affected as well as display, on the
precedent of B-2026-08-30-44 where the arithmetic half mattered more. Measured:
it is not. `self.v / d` gave 9223372036854775807 and `self.v < o` gave false on
every backend before the fix. So did a method PARAM of type `T` and the field
copied to a local before use. The defect is narrower than "a generic impl" --
only a read that reaches `expr_is_unsigned_int` with the field's OWN declared
name.

WIDER IN ONE PLACE the row did not list: a `Vec[T]` ELEMENT inside a generic
impl (`f"{self.xs[0]}"` over `struct Bag[T] { xs: Vec[T] }`) fails identically,
through the two Index arms rather than the FieldAccess arm, and is fixed in the
same commit. And it is every unsigned width, not just u64 -- u8's 255 read as
-1 too.

RED-VERIFIED as a clean partition on the pre-fix compiler: 8 of 19 shapes
diverged, 11 agreed. Post-fix all 19 agree across `--interp`, JIT and AOT.

TESTS. `e2e_generic_impl_field_keeps_the_declared_unsignedness` (19 cases,
tests/codegen.rs) and `interp_generic_impl_field_is_the_codegen_unsignedness_-
oracle` (14 cases, tests/interpreter.rs) assert the same table on both sides.
Pinning both is deliberate given this row's history: it was filed as wrong on
all three backends, i.e. the case where A/B agreement HIDES a defect, so a
regression on either side must fail rather than restore the agreement on -1.
The codegen test passes under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`.

FIXED by 7bd0b04, and the row's hypothesis was right about WHERE to look and wrong
about WHAT to do there.

"WHERE TO START: whatever adjusts the expected argument count for a builtin
value-receiver call -- it is keyed on the method NAME somewhere." Found: the
adjustment is `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` in src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs,
`&["cmp", "eq", "ne", "lt", "le", "gt", "ge"]`, and its own comment had already
predicted this row -- "so is a `partial_cmp`/`total_cmp` surface, if one is
ever added."

"Adding `partial_cmp` beside `cmp` there is very likely the whole change."
MEASURED, AND IT IS THE WRONG CHANGE. The list is not an arity adjustment at
all: it ROUTES A CALL AWAY from the impl-table dispatch into a branch that
returns `Type::Error`. So `n.cmp(m)` was never really checked -- it was
POISONED, and `Type::Error` is universally assignable, so

    let s: String = n.cmp(m); println(s);      -->  prints Less

type-checks clean and runs, while the identical `a.cmp(b)` on a STRING receiver
is correctly rejected with "expected 'String', found 'Ordering'". Adding
`partial_cmp` to that list would have made a second method silently poisoned
rather than making it work.

THE REAL MECHANISM is one level down and structural, not name-keyed.
`register_builtin_impl`'s comparison signatures carry the RECEIVER in
`params` -- `param_names: [self, other]`, `params: [ty, ty]`. A USER impl does
not: its receiver rides `self_param` and never reaches `FunctionSig::params`,
which is why the "Check argument count (excluding self)" comment at the
value-receiver dispatch could be written and be right for every case that had
been exercised. For a baked signature it was not, so the dispatch expected 2
where 1 was given. `cmp` escaped only via the exemption above.

FIX: drop a leading `self` param at that dispatch when the signature names one.
Structural, so it covers every baked method with a `self` param at once and the
exemption list no longer has to grow an entry each time one is registered.

`partial_cmp` now types as `Option[Ordering]` and RUNS on all three backends
for i64, u64, f64, String, char and bool, bare and parenthesized. Including the
bare floats: `(0.0/0.0).partial_cmp(y)` answers `None`, which is the whole
reason `PartialOrd` is a separate trait and the population `cmp` cannot serve.
`f.cmp(g)` is and stays rejected (B-2026-08-11-9's float carve-out).

THE ROW'S VERIFICATION STEP is done and passes: "verify by checking that the
same spelling on a `String` and on a derived-`PartialOrd` struct also starts
working, since those reach the aggregate arm rather than the primitive one."
String works. And the row is right that the `T: PartialOrd` BOUND path was
never affected -- a type-param receiver resolves through
`dispatch_trait_assoc_fn`, not the concrete impl table -- which the tests keep
as a control.

REMOVING THE EXEMPTION ENTIRELY WAS TRIED AND MEASURED WRONG. Routing
`eq`/`ne`/`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` through the impl table makes them type-check and
run under `--interp` while `karac build` fails with "no handler for method 'eq'
on variable 'n'" -- codegen has no dispatcher arm for the value-receiver
spelling of those. Trading a silently-poisoned call for a check-green build-red
one is worse, so the exemption stays for those six until the arms exist, and the
code now records that measurement in place of the speculation it replaces.

THE `cmp` POISON IS A SEPARATE, LARGER FINDING and is filed as its own row
rather than closed silently here: it is a soundness hole (a `String`-annotated
binding accepting an `Ordering`), it predates this row, and closing it needs the
codegen dispatcher arms above first.

RED-VERIFIED: all 8 `partial_cmp` shapes were a typecheck rejection on all three
backends before and run identically on all three after; the 4 controls (`cmp`,
the `<` operator, the bound path, a `String` receiver) are unchanged.

TESTS. `partial_cmp_value_receiver_typechecks_while_float_cmp_stays_rejected`
(tests/typechecker.rs) makes the assertions only the checker can: that the call
types as `Option[Ordering]` rather than merely running, that a WRONG annotation
is rejected rather than absorbed by a poison `Type::Error` -- without that
assertion the test would pass on exactly the bug it is guarding -- and that the
float `cmp` carve-out survives. `interp_partial_cmp_value_receiver_resolves_on_-
a_concrete_type` and `e2e_partial_cmp_value_receiver_runs_on_a_concrete_type`
run the behaviour on both backends; the codegen one passes under
`KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`.
title: THE VALUE-RECEIVER SPELLING `x.partial_cmp(y)` IS REJECTED ON A CONCRETE RECEIVER WITH "expects 2 argument(s), found 1" WHILE THE IDENTICALLY-REGISTERED `x.cmp(y)` IS ACCEPTED — some receiver-arity adjustment is keyed on the method NAME and has not been told about the second one; the `T: PartialOrd` bound path is unaffected because a type-param receiver resolves by a different route
detail:
Measured on the tree WITH B-2026-08-30-41's fix, `karac check` alone (the
failure is at typecheck, so the backends never run).

    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let o = (n).cmp(n + 1);            // OK
        let p = (n).partial_cmp(n + 1);    // error: expects 2 argument(s), found 1
    }

      (n).cmp(n + 1)          All checks passed.
      (n).partial_cmp(n + 1)  error[typecheck]: method 'partial_cmp' expects
                              2 argument(s), found 1
      x.partial_cmp(x + 1.0)  same, on an `f64` receiver

Both methods are registered with the same `(self, other)` shape --
`register_builtin_impl("Ord", …, [("cmp", ord_sig(ty)), …])` and its new
`PartialOrd` sibling -- so the arity the checker counts is 2 for both. `cmp`
nonetheless accepts the value-receiver spelling and `partial_cmp` does not,
which means there is an adjustment somewhere that folds the receiver into the
count for `cmp` by name and has not been told about the second method.

NOT THE BOUND PATH, and that is what keeps this separate from the row it came
from. The form lowering emits for `a < b` under a `T: PartialOrd` bound is also
a value-receiver method call with one argument, and it works -- because a
TYPE-PARAM receiver resolves through a different route than a concrete one. So
the capability B-2026-08-30-41 restored is unaffected; this is the hand-written
spelling on a concrete receiver, and only that.

WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING ANYWAY: the two methods now sit side by side in the same
registration block, one callable and one not, with no rule a reader could infer
from either. And `partial_cmp` is the method design.md § Comparison Traits names
as the one the operators go through, so it is the more natural of the pair for
someone to reach for by hand.

WHERE TO START: whatever adjusts the expected argument count for a builtin
value-receiver call -- it is keyed on the method NAME somewhere, since the two
signatures are structurally identical. Adding `partial_cmp` beside `cmp` there
is very likely the whole change; verify by checking that the same spelling on a
`String` and on a derived-`PartialOrd` struct also starts working, since those
reach the aggregate arm rather than the primitive one.

SOURCE NOTE: found while closing B-2026-08-30-41, as the one spelling that
stayed broken after the six pieces that row needed.

fix:
FIXED by c64cbfd. `borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars` is snapshotted around
`compile_match`'s arm loop and restored per arm, so a registration lives exactly
as long as the arm that made it rather than until the end of the function.

The set's real consumer (`deep_copy_owned_struct_param_field_move`,
B-2026-07-17-20) runs INSIDE the arm that registered, so nothing it needs is
lost; what goes away is only the reach into later matches.

RED-verified by removing the restore: 2391 bytes in 50 objects, one per loop
iteration. GATES: fmt, both clippy legs, 105/105 targets and 14,485 tests under
`--features llvm` (memory_sanitizer 1328), plus the default leg.
title: A BORROW-MODE PAYLOAD BINDING NAME STAYED REGISTERED FOR EVERY LATER MATCH IN THE SAME FUNCTION -- `borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars` is keyed by BINDING NAME and cleared only per FUNCTION, so a read-only arm's registration was inherited by a later match that reused the name, which then stopped taking ownership of its own payload and leaked it. Needs two matches in one function IN ORDER (borrow first, then a fresh temp whose arm moves the payload out), both binding the same name
detail:
FOUND while working B-2026-08-30-52, and it is what blocked that row's
sub-mechanism (a). It is INDEPENDENT of -52 and reproduces on an unmodified
compiler.

MEASURED on stock `main` under ASAN/LSan -- 800 bytes in 50 objects, one per
loop iteration (2391 bytes on the padded fixture):

    let r: Result[i64, One] = g(i);            // One { msg: String }
    match r {                                  // READ-ONLY -> borrow.
        Ok(_) => { n = n + 1; }                //   registers `e`
        Err(e) => { if e.msg.contains(digits(i)) { n = n + e.msg.len(); } }
    }
    match g(i) {                               // FRESH TEMP, arm MOVES the payload
        Ok(v) => { n = n + v; }
        Err(e) => { let m: String = e.msg; ... }
    }

The second match must own its payload. The first match registered the name `e`
in `borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars` -- a set meaning "this binding aliases
storage someone else owns" -- and that set is cleared only per FUNCTION, so the
second match inherited the registration, treated its own `e` as an alias, and
nobody freed the buffer.

WHY IT SURVIVED THIS LONG, and the part worth reading before writing a probe for
anything in this family: EACH MATCH IS CLEAN ON ITS OWN, and the pair is clean
IN THE OTHER ORDER. A first bisect of the failing program reported "no
interaction" because the harness emitted blocks in sorted order and happened to
put the borrow SECOND. Only forcing the borrow first exposed it. A single-shape
probe -- the obvious thing to write -- cannot see this defect at all.

FIX: snapshot `borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars` around the arm loop in
`compile_match` and restore it per arm, so a registration lives exactly as long
as the arm that made it. The set's within-arm consumer
(`deep_copy_owned_struct_param_field_move`, B-2026-07-17-20) is unaffected --
it runs inside the arm that registered.

FIXTURE: `asan_borrow_mode_binding_name_does_not_leak_into_a_later_match`, whose
comment records the ordering that hides it. RED-verified: 2391 bytes in 50
objects with the restore removed.

NOT AFFECTED, measured: either match alone; the two in the opposite order; and
the whole `--features llvm` battery (105/105 targets, 14,485 tests,
memory_sanitizer 1328).

fix:
FIXED by 26e3508. Took the row's three-step plan, and step 1 turned out to be worth more than the
row credited it with.

THE ROW'S DEFERRAL REASON WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT. The row keeps the
exemption because "routing the six operator-named methods through the impl table
makes them type-check and then fail `karac build` with 'no handler for method
eq'; turning a silently-poisoned call into a check-green build-red one is the
worse trade". That premise was false: the divergence was ALREADY the state of
main, exemption or not. Measured across every receiver class that accepts them,
`eq`/`ne`/`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` were check-green, interp-working and build-failing
in 36 cells (6 methods x i64/u32/i8/bool/char/String). `String` is the
independent proof -- it is not in the exempted receiver gate at all, types
correctly as `bool` through the impl table, and still failed to build, with a
DIFFERENT message ("Vec/String method 'eq' is not yet supported in codegen").
So the gap was codegen's and never the exemption's, and step 1 fixes a live
36-cell run-vs-build divergence on its own account.

STEP 1 -- codegen (`method_call.rs`). A `VALUE_CMP_OPS` arm beside the existing
`cmp` arm, sharing its two operand shapes (an `IntValue` pair; a String
`{ptr,len,cap}` pair through the same `karac_string_cmp` the `<` operator uses)
and, deliberately, its `expr_is_unsigned_int` signedness rule. `.cmp` and `.lt`
answer the same question about the same pair, and B-2026-08-28-5 is the record
of what it costs when they derive signedness differently -- `.cmp` was hardcoded
signed while `<` was not, so `(200u8).cmp(100u8)` answered `Less`. Guarded on a
user impl exactly as `cmp` is.

STEP 2 -- typechecker (`method_user_impl.rs`). `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` and its
`is_exempt_builtin` gate are gone. The 28 poisoned cells (7 methods x
i64/u32/bool/char) now reject with the precise type: `let s: String = n.cmp(m)`
gets "expected 'String', found 'Ordering'", and the six get "found 'bool'",
matching what a String receiver always did.

THE FLOAT CARVE-OUT NEEDS NO CODE, and that is the part worth reading before
touching this again. `find_methods_with_args` returns empty for a bare float (no
baked Eq/Ord -- IEEE NaN), so the existing error branch already says "no method
'cmp' on type 'f64'". The first attempt kept a float arm of the old predicate,
which INVERTED its meaning -- the flag means "skip the table AND skip the error,
return poison", and floats had been OUTSIDE it, which is exactly what produced
the error -- and re-poisoned all seven float cells in one line. That is the
B-2026-08-11-9 reopening the old comment warned about; it was caught by re-running
the probe, not by reasoning, which is why the test now asserts the specific "no
method" wording rather than merely "some error".

A THIRD STEP THE ROW DID NOT ANTICIPATE, and the change is wrong without it.
Removing the exemption makes a user `impl i64 { fn lt(self, other: i64) -> String }`
REACHABLE for the first time -- the exemption short-circuited ahead of the impl
lookup, the same way the removed `"cast"` entry once made `impl i64 { fn cast }`
unreachable. Codegen honours it (its arm consults `user_impl_method_exists`,
reading the same static receiver type the typechecker did). The interpreter did
not, and printed the builtin's `true` where the compiled side printed `user`.

Fixing that exposed the real hazard. A gate keyed on the interpreter's own
`value_type_name` cannot work: it reads a type-ERASED `Value::Int`, which answers
`i64` for a receiver that is statically `u32`, so it applied the `impl i64`
method to a `u32` receiver -- `c.lt(d)` printed `user` under `--interp` against
`false` compiled, and the compiled side matched check, which types it `bool`. So
the gate reads the TYPECHECKER'S OWN DECISION instead, through
`method_impl_dispatch` -- the table B-2026-08-13-8 added for precisely this class
of "resolution neither runtime can redo". `method_user_impl.rs` now records the
winner there for a primitive receiver on these seven names.

`target_span.is_some()` is the USER-vs-BAKED discriminator on that record and is
load-bearing: `register_builtin_impl` puts the baked `Ord`/`Eq` through the same
`method_pick` branch with `target_type == "i64"`, so recording those too made the
interpreter's gate fire for EVERY primitive comparison and stand the builtin
aside with nothing behind it -- 40 of 41 cells went from agreeing to "method 'lt'
not found on type 'i64' (no interpreter dispatch arm)". A synthesized impl has no
source target to point at; a written one does.

MEASUREMENTS, all on x86-64 against the interpreter as oracle:
  - 28 poisoned cells before, 0 after; each now names the right type.
  - 36 build-failing cells before, 0 after; all agree with `--interp`.
  - `.cmp` (5 receiver classes) unchanged and still correct.
  - Signedness boundaries hold: `200u8 < 100u8` false, `4000000000u32 > 1u32`
    true, `false < true` true, negative i64 signed.
  - The operator and method spellings agree pair-for-pair on all of those.
  - 7 float cells reject as "no method"; `f64.partial_cmp` still resolves.
  - The user-impl pair: `impl i64` wins for an i64 receiver, loses for a u32 one.

TESTS. `comparison_methods_on_a_primitive_receiver_are_typed_not_poisoned`
(tests/typechecker.rs) is the row's own assertion, and it has to be the rejection:
this is invisible to an A/B kata, because the compiled backend refuses the
poisoned program outright and the two backends never disagree on a VALUE.
`e2e_value_receiver_comparison_methods_match_the_interpreter` (tests/codegen.rs)
covers the 36 cells plus the signedness and operator-agreement assertions;
verified non-vacuous -- with the codegen arm reverted it fails on the first case
with the "no handler" error. `value_receiver_comparison_prefers_a_user_impl_over_
the_builtin` (tests/interpreter.rs) pins the precedence and carries the u32
erasure control, which is the line only a typechecker-driven gate gets right.
title: A COMPARISON METHOD ON A PRIMITIVE RECEIVER IS SILENTLY POISONED, NOT CHECKED — `let s: String = n.cmp(m)` type-checks and PRINTS `Less` into the String slot, while the identical `a.cmp(b)` on a String receiver is correctly rejected; the name-keyed exemption that shields the seven comparison methods from a mis-count returns `Type::Error`, which is universally assignable
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-31-13, which is why that row's proposed one-line
fix was not taken: adding a name to this list makes a method poisoned, not
working.

MEASURED on `main` with B-2026-08-31-13's fix in place (the poison predates it
and is untouched by it):

    fn main() { let n: i64 = 3; let m: i64 = 4;
                let s: String = n.cmp(m); println(s); }

      --interp   prints `Less`
      karac check   All checks passed.

    fn main() { let a: String = "x"; let b: String = "y";
                let s: String = a.cmp(b); }

      error[typecheck]: expected 'String', found 'Ordering'      <-- correct

`let v: Vec[i64] = n.cmp(m);` also type-checks. So a PRIMITIVE receiver accepts
a comparison result into a binding of any type at all, and a String receiver
does not — the same call, the same method, one receiver class apart.

MECHANISM. `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` in src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs
(`&["cmp", "eq", "ne", "lt", "le", "gt", "ge"]`) exempts those names on a
non-float scalar receiver from the impl-table dispatch. The exemption exists for
a real reason — before B-2026-08-31-13 that dispatch mis-counted a baked
`(self, other)` signature's arity — but what it does is route the call into a
branch that type-checks the ARGUMENTS and returns `Type::Error`. That poison is
universally assignable, which is precisely the silent-poison class the same
function's comments record CLOSING for `char`/`bool` (B-2026-08-11-2) and for
the float receivers (B-2026-08-11-9). It survived here because the exemption
predates those and was read as an arity workaround rather than as a resolution
bypass.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED WITH B-2026-08-31-13, having been found there. That row's
fix makes the arity structural (drop a leading `self` param), which removes the
exemption's original justification — so removing the exemption was tried, and
MEASURED WRONG:

    fn main() { let n: i64 = 3; let m: i64 = 4; println(n.eq(m)); }

      --interp     false
      karac build  error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method 'eq'
                   on variable 'n' (method dispatch fell through …)

Same for `lt`. Routing the six operator-named methods through the impl table
turns a silently-poisoned call into a CHECK-GREEN BUILD-RED one, which is the
worse trade, so the exemption was left in place and this filed instead.

WHAT THE FIX NEEDS, in order:

  1. Codegen dispatcher arms for the value-receiver spelling of `eq`/`ne`/`lt`/
     `le`/`gt`/`ge` on a primitive receiver (`compile_method_call`). These are
     the operators' own comparisons, so the lowering already exists for the
     operator spelling — the method spelling just has no arm.
  2. Then delete `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` and its `is_exempt_builtin` gate
     entirely. With B-2026-08-31-13's `self`-param drop already in place, the
     impl-table dispatch types all seven correctly; `cmp` becomes `Ordering`
     and the six become `bool`, and `let s: String = n.cmp(m)` starts failing
     as it already does on a String receiver.
  3. Keep the FLOAT carve-out: bare floats have no baked `Eq`/`Ord` (IEEE NaN),
     so `f.cmp(g)` must still reach the "no method 'cmp' on type 'f64'" error
     rather than the impl table — B-2026-08-11-9 closed exactly that and an
     inversion of the gate silently reopened it during this session's
     experiment, which is worth knowing before touching the condition.

SEVERITY is medium rather than high because the wrong-typed binding is caught
by the next operation that cares — `println(s)` on the poisoned `String`
prints the Ordering rather than corrupting memory, and the compiled backend
refuses the interpolation outright. It is a checker soundness hole, not a
miscompile.

NOT A RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE, and so invisible to an A/B kata: the compiled
side refuses to build the poisoned program (`Display of a struct argument …`),
so the two backends never disagree on a value. Only a test that asserts the
REJECTION can catch it, which is why `partial_cmp_value_receiver_typechecks_-
while_float_cmp_stays_rejected` asserts a wrong annotation is rejected for
`partial_cmp` — the assertion this row's subject would fail.
