fix:
FIXED by 527bdf8. Six sites, one accounting rule: a `Vector[T, N]` costs
ONE WORD PER LANE and an `Array[T, N]` one per element -- the convention the
array pack side already used and nothing else agreed with.

  * `llvm_type_word_count` had no `VectorType` arm; its `_ => 1` catch-all
    called a 4-lane i64 vector a single word.
  * `payload_word_count_for_type_expr` -- the layout pass's sizing -- had
    neither a `"Vector"` path arm nor a `TypeKind::Array` arm, so both sized at
    the conservative 1. (It was also missing `f16`/`bf16` from its single-word
    primitive list; correct by accident through the same catch-all, now
    explicit.)
  * `coerce_to_payload_words` had no `VectorValue` arm, so a vector fell to
    `coerce_to_i64`, whose `_ => Ok(0)` default meant the payload was not
    truncated but ERASED.
  * `rebuild_value_from_payload_word_slice` had no vector arm and an ARRAY arm
    that returned an i64 zero under a comment calling the shape unexpected in
    v1.x workloads.
  * `pattern_payload_word_count` / `pattern_payload_llvm_type` /
    `reconstruct_payload_value` -- the match-arm unpack -- resolved neither name
    through `struct_types` nor `enum_layouts` and took the 1-word default.
  * `reconstruct_payload_value`'s struct-field loop and its
    `reconstruct_struct_from_words` sibling had no array/vector FIELD case;
    with the true width they reached the "unexpected multi-word non-struct"
    fallback, which keeps word 0 and `insertvalue`s an `i64` into a `<4 x i64>`
    slot -- invalid IR that fails module verification.

The typechecker half is two arms in `patterns.rs`: neither `Type::Array` nor
`Type::Vector` is a `Type::Named`, so no surface name and no inner `TypeExpr`
were ever recorded for such a binding, which is why codegen had nothing to size
from. They now record both, like the `Tuple` and `Map`/`Set` arms above them.

`emit_enum_field_display` needed widening too, and independently: it rebuilt
from a hardcoded `(w0, w1, w2)`, so with the word count fixed a 4-lane vector
rendered `Vector(1, 2, 3, 51)` -- three correct lanes and one undef. It now
passes the field's full word span, joining the contract
`rebuild_value_from_payload_word_slice` already had (B-2026-08-23-20 made the
same widening for the return path).

AN ALIGNMENT FAULT CAME WITH THE FIX AND IS THE PART WORTH READING. Giving
vectors their true width made them BOXABLE for the first time -- 4 lanes exceed
`Option`'s 3-word area -- and the boxing path is `malloc` + `build_store`. LLVM
gives that store the value's natural alignment, 32 for a `<4 x i64>`, and lowers
it to `vmovaps`; `malloc` guarantees 16. The result is a SIGSEGV whose faulting
instruction pair is unambiguous once seen:

    mov    $0x20,%edi
    call   malloc@plt
    vmovaps 0xa0(%rsp),%ymm0
    vmovaps %ymm0,(%rax)          <- faults on a 16-byte-aligned address

It is heap-state dependent, so it appeared and disappeared as unrelated
statements were added or removed -- removing ANY ONE of six statement groups
from the repro made it pass -- and ASAN masks it by changing the stack and heap
layout, so the sanitizer suite was green on the same program. The box store and
all four box consumers (`rebuild_payload_deboxing_if_spilled`,
`reconstruct_payload_value`'s debox, `emit_enum_field_display`'s debox, and the
`enumbox.uw.ld` unwrap site) are now emitted at alignment 8, which is always
valid and is what `malloc` actually promises.

MEASURED, all four surfaces byte-identical against `--interp` (`karac run`,
`karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`): 4-lane and 8-lane i64 vectors
(the latter inline in a user enum and BOXED in an `Option`, so the debox path is
exercised), i32 lanes (narrower than a word), f64 lanes, a 3-element array read
through an index, and a struct payload carrying both a vector and an array
field. Before the fix the same program printed `Vector(0, 0, 0, 0)`, bound `0`
or a box pointer in every match arm, and failed the build outright on `b[0]`
with "Index operator applied to non-array type".

TWO SHAPES ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT FROM THE FIXTURE, each for its own filed
reason. An `Array[T, N]` payload on a `#[derive(Display)]` enum still PANICS the
compiler (B-2026-08-31-19 -- and see the correction filed on that row: the array
Display gap is not only nested, `f"{a}"` on a bare `Array[i64, 3]` prints `1`
and `println(a)` prints nothing). And `Vec[Vector[T, N]]` faults on the same
alignment class one level out -- its element buffer is `malloc`ed and every
access to it (literal store, `push`, index read, `for`-in) is emitted at the
vector's natural 32 -- filed as B-2026-08-31-24.

WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS. B-2026-08-31-10 measured `Vector` and `Array` OUT of the
Option/Result Display gate precisely because of this row; that exclusion can be
lifted once B-2026-08-31-19 lands the missing array Display arm, which is the
only remaining reason for it.

Tests: `e2e_vector_array_enum_payload_round_trip` (tests/codegen.rs) +
`test_vector_array_enum_payload_round_trip` (tests/interpreter.rs, the oracle) +
`asan_vector_enum_payload_box_frees_once` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs, which
covers the box the width fix newly mints and the alignment relaxation with it).
The compiled and ASAN halves were verified RED on the unpatched tree.
title: A `Vector[T, N]` OR `Array[T, N]` ENUM PAYLOAD RECONSTRUCTS AS GARBAGE UNDER CODEGEN -- silently, in `match` as well as in Display, so a bound payload is a wrong VALUE and not merely wrong text: `match` on an `Option[Array[i64, 3]]` binds `1` where the interpreter binds `[1, 2, 3]`
detail:
Measured on the B-2026-08-31-10 tree (`karac build` and `--interp` agree with each
other everywhere except these rows), and PRE-EXISTING -- reachable today with no
part of that row's change applied.

DISPLAY, through a user enum, which needs no new capability to reach:

    #[derive(Display)] enum E { V(Vector[i64, 4]), N }
    let vv: Vector[i64, 4] = Vector[i64, 4](1, 2, 3, 4);
    let e = E.V(vv);
    f"{e}"   interp  V(Vector(1, 2, 3, 4))
             build   V(Vector(0, 140725430415224, 1, 0))     <- garbage, one word is a
                                                                stack address

    let c: Vec[Vector[i64, 4]] = [vv];
    f"{c}"   both    [Vector(1, 2, 3, 4)]                    <- CONTROL: the same value in
                                                                ELEMENT position is fine, so
                                                                the vector renderer is not
                                                                the defect

`match` IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS, because it produces a wrong value rather than
wrong text and nothing downstream can tell:

    let o: Option[Array[i64, 3]] = Some([1, 2, 3]);
    match o { Some(w) => println(f"Some({w})") None => {} }
             interp  Some([1, 2, 3])
             build   Some(1)                                 <- first element, not the array

    let ovv: Option[Vector[i64, 4]] = Some(vv);
    match ovv { Some(w) => println(f"Some({w})") None => {} }
             interp  Some(Vector(1, 2, 3, 4))
             build   Some(0)

LEAD, not a diagnosis. `llvm_type_word_count` (src/codegen/declarations.rs) has
no `VectorType` arm -- its `_ => 1` catch-all counts a 4-lane i64 vector as ONE
word, so `coerce_to_payload_words` believes it fits inline, never heap-boxes it,
and the unpack's `want > num` deboxing test never fires. `ArrayType` DOES have a
correct arm there (elem count x lanes), yet the Array case is wrong too, so the
array half is likely the other side: `rebuild_value_from_payload_word_slice`
(src/codegen/calls.rs) has arms for Int / Float / Pointer / the Vec and Slice
struct shapes / a generic struct, and none for `ArrayType` or `VectorType`.
`reconstruct_payload_value` (the match-arm unpacker) shares the contract and
shows the same symptom, which is consistent with the fault being in the shared
word accounting rather than in either consumer.

WHY THIS IS FILED SEPARATELY. B-2026-08-31-10 widened the Option/Result Display
gate to multi-word payloads and MEASURED THESE TWO SHAPES OUT again for exactly
this reason -- admitting them turned a clean compile error into the garbage
above. So the gate currently refuses `Option[Vector[...]]` / `Option[Array[...]]`
with a diagnostic that names the payload, and that refusal should be lifted as
part of fixing this row, not before it.

The refusal also means the OBVIOUS advice for the declined shapes -- destructure
and format the binding -- is wrong, which is why that row's new diagnostic
deliberately prescribes no rewrite and points at `karac run --interp` instead.

fix:
FIXED by c48c0fb. The row's title said the gap was NESTED; the
correction filed on it while working B-2026-08-31-18 was right that it is not,
and the full survey is what shaped the fix. Codegen had NO array Display at any
depth, and the failure mode varied by position and by element type:

    f"{a}"          Array[i64, 3]     interp [1, 2, 3]  build 1
    println(a)      Array[i64, 3]     interp [1, 2, 3]  build (nothing at all)
    f"{s}"          Array[String, 2]  interp [x1, y1]   build 93921800231728
    a.len() / a[0]                    both agree                    <- CONTROLS
    Vec[Array] elem / struct field / tuple field / enum payload / Map value
                                      interp renders    build PANICS the compiler

So the loud half was the nested one and the quiet half was the plain
interpolation, which reads backwards. The `Array[String, 2]` row is the worst of
the three: `93921800231728` is the first element's raw data POINTER, not a value
at all.

FOUR PARTS, and each answers one column of that table.

  * `emit_array_display_fn` / `emit_array_display_body` — the by-pointer
    renderer, sharing `emit_vec_display_body`'s text and loop shape because an
    array prints exactly like a `Vec` and the two must not drift. The layout
    differs in one way: an array's elements are INLINE at the value pointer
    rather than behind a `{ptr, len, cap}` data pointer, and its length is a
    constant. Element dispatch is one call to `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr`,
    which is what makes `Array[Vec[i64], 2]`, `Array[P, 2]` and nested arrays
    compose with no per-shape work.
  * `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` gains TWO arms, and that is the part worth
    remembering: `Array[T, N]` has two surface spellings that both reach this
    dispatcher. Source-written `Array[i64, 3]` parses as `TypeKind::Path` with
    generic args, while a `TypeExpr` synthesized from a `Type::Array` (the
    typechecker's `type_to_type_expr`) is `TypeKind::Array`. The path form is
    what a `Vec[Array[i64, 3]]` ELEMENT carries, so a fix covering only the
    other one still panicked there — measured, not reasoned.
  * `display_array_types` — a span-keyed table forwarded from `expr_types`,
    the array sibling of `display_vec_types`, carrying the WHOLE type because
    an array's identity includes its extent. `try_compile_array_display` reads
    it in the f-string part path and in `compile_print`, ahead of the
    value-kind arms that were misreading the aggregate.
  * `struct_display_needs_type_directed_fn` admits an array FIELD, in both
    spellings, exactly as B-2026-08-31-9 taught it to admit a `Vector` field.
    Without it the field-parts path refused the struct with a Rust `{:?}` dump
    of the field's `TypeExpr` while the same struct nested one level down
    rendered fine.

A LEAK CAME WITH THE NEW PATH AND IS FIXED IN IT. A fresh owned array temporary
(`f"{mk(n)}"`, an array literal) has no other owner and its ELEMENTS can own
heap — an `Array[String, 2]` is two `{ptr, len, cap}` triples inline — so the
first draft leaked both per evaluation: 40 allocations over a 20-iteration loop
under LSan. It reuses the array-temp drop the `==` operand path already emits
(`emit_drop_fn_for_array`, B-2026-08-27-30) behind the same
`expr_is_fresh_owned_array_temp` gate, so a bound array or a place expression is
untouched, and emits it AFTER the render and IMMEDIATELY rather than at scope
exit — a scope-exit registration hoists one entry alloca and frees only the last
value when the interpolation sits in a loop, which is the shape that surfaced
it. The `let`-bound spelling and the `Vec` call-result spelling were both
already clean, which is what localized it to the new code.

THIS CLOSES THE LOOP OPENED BY B-2026-08-31-10. That row measured `Vector` and
`Array` OUT of the Option/Result Display gate for two reasons: the payload word
accounting sized both at one word (B-2026-08-31-18) and this dispatcher had no
array arm. Both are now answered, so the exclusion is LIFTED here and
`Option[Array[i64, 3]]` / `Option[Vector[i64, 4]]` / `Result[Array[..], ..]`
render identically to the interpreter. `Slice[T]` stays out, and for a reason
that is now visible: it has no codegen Display AT ANY DEPTH either — a bare
`f"{s}"` on a slice is a hard error — so there is nothing to reconstruct into.
Filed as B-2026-08-31-25.

TWO FIXTURES MOVED WITH THE CAPABILITY, and each keeps its retired example
rather than deleting it:
  * `codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` (B-2026-08-31-10's
    diagnostic test) moves to `Option[Slice[i64]]` and now also asserts that

  * `test_unrenderable_main_error_is_a_build_error_not_an_empty_message`

The deferred-display diagnostic's rationale is corrected with them: it still
prescribes no rewrite, but the reason is now that destructuring a `Slice`

Tests: `e2e_array_display_renders_at_every_depth` (tests/codegen.rs) +
`test_array_display_renders_at_every_depth` (tests/interpreter.rs, the oracle) +
`asan_array_display_does_not_take_its_elements` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs).

title: `Array[T, N]` HAS NO Display UNDER CODEGEN AT ANY DEPTH, AND THE QUIET HALF IS THE PLAIN ONE -- nested (a `Vec` element, a struct field, a tuple field, an enum payload) it PANICS the compiler with `emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Array_i64_3' not yet supported`, while at depth 0 it is silent: `f"{a}"` prints `1`, `println(a)` prints nothing, and an `Array[String, 2]` prints its first element's raw data POINTER
detail:
Measured on the B-2026-08-31-10 tree; pre-existing and independent of it.

    let ar: Array[i64, 3] = [1, 2, 3];
    let mut v: Vec[Array[i64, 3]] = Vec.new();
    v.push(ar);
    f"{v}"   interp  [[1, 2, 3]]
             build   thread panicked at src/codegen/synth_display.rs:
                     emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Array_i64_3' not yet supported

This is B-2026-08-31-9's defect with `Array` in place of `Vector`.
`emit_display_fn_for_type_expr` routes by shape -- `Vec`, `Map`, `Set`,
`SortedMap`, `SortedSet`, `Vector` (added by that row), tuple, user enum, shared,
user struct -- and falls through to the by-NAME `emit_display_fn_for_type` for
anything else, whose catch-all panics. `Array[T, N]` has no arm, so every nested
spelling of an array reaches it: a `Vec` element, a struct field, a `dbg`
argument, a `Map` value. The remedy is the same one that arm took: give the
dispatcher an `Array` arm keyed on (elem, extent), since the const arg is part of
the type's identity (B-2026-08-27-25).

TWO NOTES ON SCOPE.

It is an ICE, not a diagnostic -- CLAUDE.md's "never just panic" rule -- so even
a deferral should turn the catch-all into an error before it becomes a shape the
renderer supports.

`Option[Array[i64, 3]]` reaches the same panic through the Option/Result
synthesizer. B-2026-08-31-10 keeps that shape on the DECLINED list partly for
this reason and partly because its payload also reconstructs wrong (B-2026-08-31-18); both have to be answered before the gate can
admit it.


CORRECTION (2026-08-31, while fixing B-2026-08-31-18): THE TITLE UNDERSTATES
THIS. The gap is not only nested — codegen has no `Array` Display at ANY depth,
and at depth 0 it is SILENT rather than a panic:

    let a: Array[i64, 3] = [n, n + 1, n + 2];
    println(f"a={a}");   interp  a=[1, 2, 3]
                         build   a=1              <- first element
    println(a);          interp  [1, 2, 3]
                         build   (prints nothing at all)

So the compiler-abort half is the one that fails LOUDLY and the plain
interpolation is a quiet miscompile, which is the wrong way round for how they
read. Whatever fixes the dispatcher arm has to cover both, and the depth-0
result is the one to pin a test on first.

fix:
FIXED by 4a58370. The `optres.disp.tmp` spill in
`try_compile_option_result_display` now registers the same inline-payload
cleanups a `let` of the same value would get --
`track_inline_option_payload_var` + `track_inline_result_payload_var` on the
spill slot -- so the temp is freed once at scope exit instead of never.

This is the row's own LEAD, confirmed and taken. It reuses the exact channel the
two sibling holes were fixed through: the bare-`String` spill (B-2026-07-15-12)
and the fresh-temp `Option` ARGUMENT spill (B-2026-08-12-1's
`track_optres_arg_temp`, which spills to an alloca and calls the same pair). That

and tag guards, which is what makes a `None`/`Err` temp a no-op rather than a

GATED ON FRESHNESS, via the Vec sibling's `print_vec_operand_is_owned_temp`, and
the gate is the load-bearing half rather than a precaution. Reaching that arm
means the expression is not a bare identifier -- but a PLACE is not an identifier

than inventing one.

MEASURED under Linux ASAN + LeakSanitizer.

  BEFORE: 5164 byte(s) leaked in 120 allocation(s)
  AFTER:  clean, and every render still produced

The fixture covers the whole class of non-place operand rather than the row's one
spelling: a direct call, a `Vec[String]` payload with depth (which leaked the
element buffer AND each `String` inside, so a fix freeing only the outer
allocation would still show), a `Result` in both its `Ok` and `Err` halves, two
calls interpolated in ONE f-string, and an inline `Some(f"...")` constructor.

THE THREE PLACE-EXPRESSION CONTROLS ARE THE OTHER HALF OF THE TEST, and they are
what a wrong fix fails rather than what a right one passes: a struct FIELD
(`h.o`, `h.r`), a `Vec` ELEMENT (`vo[0]`) and a TUPLE position (`t.0`), each
rendered TWICE. All three reach the same spill arm, none is owned by the frame,
and an unconditional registration would free the owner's buffer on the first

double free took. They pass, so the gate holds.

The sibling fixture `asan_option_display_multiword_payload_frees_once` carried a
comment saying the call-result spelling belonged in it once this landed. It is
better as its own fixture (this one needs the place-expression controls, which
have nothing to do with the multiword-payload widening), so that comment is

title: AN `Option`/`Result` CALL RESULT INTERPOLATED IN AN F-STRING LEAKS ITS PAYLOAD ONCE PER EVALUATION -- `f"{mk(n)}"` where `mk` returns `Option[String]` leaks 20 buffers over 20 iterations, while the `let`-bound spelling of the same value is clean
detail:
Measured under Linux ASAN + LeakSanitizer, on the UNPATCHED compiler (before
B-2026-08-31-10's widening), so it is pre-existing rather than introduced by it.

    fn mks(n: i64) -> Option[String] { return Some(f"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{n}") }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < 20 { println(f"call {mks(i + n)}"); i = i + 1; }
        println("end");
    }

    LeakSanitizer: 551 byte(s) leaked in 20 allocation(s)
      Direct leak of 524 byte(s) in 19 object(s)  <- one per iteration
      Direct leak of  27 byte(s) in  1 object(s)

With a `Vec[String]` payload it is 20 direct (the element buffer, through
`karac_realloc_or_panic`) plus 20 indirect (the `String`s inside), i.e. it scales
with the payload's depth as well as the iteration count.

THE `let`-BOUND SPELLING IS CLEAN, which localizes it:

    let o = mks(n); println(f"call {o}");     -> no leak (scope cleanup frees it)

LEAD. `try_compile_option_result_display` (src/codegen/synth_display.rs) spills a
non-place value into an `optres.disp.tmp` entry alloca so the by-pointer Display
fn has something to load from, and nothing ever drops it. The sibling
`try_compile_tuple_display` spills the same way. The bare-`String` version of
this exact hole was fixed by B-2026-07-15-12, which registers the fresh owned
temp via `track_vec_var` so scope exit frees it once -- gated on
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` precisely so a PLACE expression, owned elsewhere,
is not double-freed. The Option/Result spill wants the same treatment with the
enum's own memory-drop channel rather than the String one.

B-2026-08-31-10 does not cause this but does broaden its reach: every payload
shape that row newly admits now reaches the leaking spill, where before it failed
to compile. That row's ASAN fixture
(`asan_option_display_multiword_payload_frees_once`) therefore uses the
`let`-bound spelling and carries a comment pointing here; when this lands, the
call-result spelling belongs in it.

fix:
FIXED by f632ce30. One missing recursion, not one missing position.

An unsuffixed float literal takes its width from `round_float_to_span_width`,
which reads the type the TYPECHECKER recorded on the literal's span
(B-2026-08-14-11). So every position that agreed is one where
`record_narrow_float_literal` records, and every position that diverged is one
where it does not: it recursed through TUPLES ALONE. Two arms close the set --
a collection literal's elements against a `Vec` / `VecDeque` / `Array` /
`Slice` element type, and an `Option` / `Result` payload in all three
constructor spellings.

The `check_expr` Vec arm SYNTHESIZES its elements rather than checking them, so
nothing ever reached the literal holding the element type. That is the same
argument the existing tuple arm rests on, written in its own doc comment -- the
collection case was simply never added.

THE ROW NAMED ONE SPELLING; FIVE DIVERGED. Measured, 14 positions x 4 surfaces:

  DIVERGED (all now agree)     IN THE ROW?
    Option.Some(0.1)              yes
    bare Some(0.1)                no
    Ok(0.1)                       no
    Err(0.1)                      no
    let v: Vec[f16] = [0.1]       no
    let a: Array[f16,1] = Array[0.1]  no

  ALREADY AGREED (kept as controls)
    annotated let, fn arg, tuple elem, struct field, Vec.push, Option.Some(var),

FIXED IN THE TYPECHECKER, not at the interpreter's construction sites, because
the recorded type is what both backends read. Rounding an already-narrowed

`Vector[T, N]` is deliberately outside the sequence helper: nothing was measured
through it and its lane literal is a call, not a collection literal. Stated in

Both twins gain the six positions. On the NEW lines the codegen twin is the
ORACLE -- it was already right -- which is the mirror of the annotated `let`
that fixture was written for; pre-fix the interpreter half fails and the
compiled half passes. The over-reach guard
(`test_float_literal_width_respects_f64_slots_and_suffixes`) still passes, so

suffix CONTRADICTS the destination (`let d: Option[f32] = Option.Some(0.1f64)`)
still splits the backends. Measured pre-existing -- it diverges identically with

title: THE INTERPRETER DOES NOT NARROW A FLOAT LITERAL TO THE ANNOTATED PAYLOAD WIDTH INSIDE `Option.Some(...)` -- `let q: Option[f16] = Option.Some(0.1)` prints `Some(0.1)` under `--interp` and `Some(0.0999755859375)` under `karac build`, while every other position narrows on both backends
detail:
Found while measuring B-2026-08-31-10's narrow-float half; the codegen side is
the CORRECT one here, which is why it is filed against the interpreter.

    let q: Option[f16]  = Option.Some(0.1);   interp Some(0.1)
                                              build  Some(0.0999755859375)
    let r: Option[bf16] = Option.Some(0.1);   interp Some(0.1)
                                              build  Some(0.10009765625)

CONTROLS -- every one agrees on both backends, and agrees with the compiled
Option above:

    let a: f16  = 0.1;                        both   0.0999755859375
    let b: bf16 = 0.1;                        both   0.10009765625
    let mut v: Vec[f16] = Vec.new(); v.push(0.1);
                                              both   [..., 0.0999755859375]
    let a: f16 = 0.1; Option.Some(a)          both   Some(0.0999755859375)

So the narrowing happens correctly at a `let` with an annotation, at
`Vec.push`, and for an Option payload that arrives as an already-narrowed
VARIABLE. The one position that misses it is a float LITERAL passed directly to
an `Option.Some(...)` whose width comes from the binding's annotation -- the
interpreter keeps the value at f64 precision and prints the f64 shortest
round-trip.

`0.1` is chosen because it is not representable in either format, so the
narrowing is visible; `2.5` and `3.5` agree on every backend and would have
hidden it. Worth stating because the twinned display tests written for
B-2026-08-31-10 use exactly those exact values and pass either way.

fix:
FIXED by 964832d.

THE ALIASING QUESTION THIS ROW WAS HELD OPEN FOR IS ANSWERED BY THE MODEL THAT
ALREADY EXISTED, and measuring it is what unblocked the fix. The row asks
"whether the interpreter should model that as a refcount dec or as a body call,
and whether the two agree when a second reference is live". They are the same
thing and they do agree: the BOUND spelling already fires the body at the
0-transition -- `Env::drop_target` hands `invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` an
`Arc::strong_count` and it fires at `== 1`, deliberately reading the slot
WITHOUT cloning so the count stays live. Both new discard legs use that same
test, so "run the body at the discard" is not a new rule for `shared`: a value
reached with ONE reference is one nothing else can observe.

MEASURED, not assumed. `let a = S { .. }; let b = a;` runs exactly ONE body at
scope end, before and after this change. A discard beside a live alias
(`let a = ..; let b = a; let _ = S { .. };`) runs the discarded literal's body
and leaves the alias to die at its own scope end. And `let _ = a;` over a
still-live binding DECLINES in the new legs -- the binding holds the other
reference -- and keeps running through its own path, unchanged at one body.

THE POPULATION IS LARGER THAN FILED, and two of its cells were already
DIVERGENCES rather than agreed gaps: `let _ = mks(7)` (a shared value arriving
from a CALL) ran nothing on the interpreter and its body on both compiled
backends, and so did the two-tail branch this row names. The bare-statement call
spelling `mks(8);` was correct on all three throughout, which is what says the
gap was per-site rather than about calls.

WHY IT FELL THROUGH. A `shared` value is a bare RC pointer: exactly the kind the
aggregate registrar returns early on, and exactly the kind
`materialize_owned_temp` owns via `owned_temp_drops`. Every discard site ran one
or the other, never both, so the box had no owner anywhere. The two legs are
disjoint by construction, so running both at each site is safe and only one ever
claims a given value.

FIX, four sites. Codegen: the arm-level owner now admits the ADMITTED tail
rather than re-asking `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` (which recognizes only
`Call`/`MethodCall` and so declined a literal), and both discard sites' literal
arms gained the RC leg beside the aggregate registrar
(`shared_struct_literal_type`). Interpreter: `run_discarded_value_user_drops`
gained the `SharedStruct` arm it never had -- a shared value fell to `_ => {}` --
plus `run_discarded_shared_user_drop` for the three callers that hand that
walker a CLONE. That last part is the one subtlety: cloning bumps the `Arc` and
defeats the last-reference test, the same hazard `Env::drop_target`'s own doc
records for `get`, so those callers ask before cloning.

VERIFIED across 16 shapes on all three backends -- both direct spellings, the
no-`else` `if`, the two-tail `if`, the `match`, both bare-statement branch
spellings, the call spelling, and the alias/live-binding/no-`impl Drop`
controls. All 16 now agree; the enum branch discard is unaffected.

FIXTURES: `codegen::e2e_discarded_shared_literal_runs_its_drop_body` pins the
transcripts (interpreter and AOT asserted together) and
`memory_sanitizer::asan_discarded_shared_literal_frees_its_rc_box` pins the
leak, over a 20-iteration loop so the stranded box is work the optimizer cannot
fold away -- which is why the row could only measure it at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`. Both RED-verified.
title: A DISCARDED `shared` STRUCT LITERAL RUNS NO `Drop` BODY AND LEAKS ITS RC BOX ON ALL THREE BACKENDS -- `let _ = S { .. };`, `S { .. };` and the branch spellings are all silent and strand 41 B, while the same value BOUND (`let s = S { .. };`) is correct at one body and clean everywhere.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-29-30, as the one cell of that row's matrix whose
compiled half could be closed but whose interpreter half could not.

    shared struct S { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for S { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dS{self.id}") } }

                                        interp / jit / aot        leak (-O0)
    let _ = S { id: 1, name: f"a" };     silent / silent / silent   41 B / 2
    S { id: 2, name: f"b" };             silent / silent / silent   41 B / 2
    let s = S { id: 3, name: f"c" };     dS3    / dS3    / dS3      clean
    let _ = if c { S { .. } };           silent / silent / silent   41 B / 2
    let _ = if c { S { .. } } else { S { .. } };
                                         silent / dS4    / dS4      clean

The BOUND row is what says the discard site is the unit rather than shared
types generally, and the last row is a pre-existing run-vs-build DIVERGENCE
already: the two-tail `if` reaches the STATEMENT discard site, which frees the
box on both compiled backends, and the interpreter runs nothing.

THE COMPILED HALF IS ONE LINE AND WAS MEASURED. In B-2026-08-29-30's fix the
arm-level owner gates its `materialize_owned_temp` leg on
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` (Call/MethodCall), which declines a struct
literal. Passing the ADMITTED tail to that leg instead -- the admission gate
already requires an all-fresh literal, which is exactly the freshness that
function's contract asks of its callers -- makes the no-`else` row read
`dS14` on both compiled backends and clean under valgrind.

IT WAS DELIBERATELY REVERTED, and the reason is this row rather than caution.
`run_discarded_value_user_drops` in the interpreter has NO shared arm at all:
its `match` covers `Value::Struct`, `Value::Tuple` and `Value::EnumVariant`,
and a shared value falls to `_ => {}`. So the interpreter is silent for EVERY
row above, and landing the compiled half alone converts an agreed gap into a
divergence in one more shape -- the trade B-2026-08-29-30's own half A was held
back for two commits to avoid.

WHAT THE FIX NEEDS, and why it is not mechanical: a shared value can be
ALIASED, so "run the body at the discard" is not obviously right the way it is
for an owned struct. The RC dec is unambiguous (the discarded literal owns one
reference, and the body runs on the 0-transition, which is how the BOUND row
already works); what needs measuring is whether the interpreter should model
that as a refcount dec or as a body call, and whether the two agree when a
second reference is live. Both spellings of the DIRECT form and both branch
forms should be fixed together, since they are one population.

SOURCE NOTE: found by probing the boundary of B-2026-08-29-30's widened
admission gate -- the shared literal is admitted by `discarded_owned_literal_-
tail` and then declined by the aggregate registrar, which returns early for a
bare pointer. The leak numbers are valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`; at the
default `-O2` all rows are clean, the allocation being dead.

fix:
FIXED by a139cc1.

THE ROW'S COMPILED MEASUREMENT WAS STALE, and correcting it is what located the
real gate. It records `let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { E.B };` as running
NOTHING on jit/aot. That spelling was already correct on arrival -- and correct
BY ACCIDENT. `discarded_unit_variant_tail` is tried BEFORE
`discarded_match_value_tail` at both discard sites, and it peels an `if` down to
a unit arm's `Path`, so a construct with ONE unit arm was admitted through the
unit-variant gate. The registration is keyed on the MERGED value and dispatches
on its tag at runtime, so it was right for whichever arm ran. Give both arms a
payload and the accident disappears with the whole registration:

    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { E.B };          dE dR8   (already right)
    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { E.A(mk(9)) };   (nothing)
    let _ = match n { 0 => E.A(mk(8)) _ => E.B };      (nothing)

So the row's own repro was the one branch shape that WORKED, and the population
is larger than filed: every two-tail branch whose arms are enum ctors, in both
the `let _ =` and bare-statement spellings, on both compiled backends. All
measured pre-existing at 4ef5ff3.

TWO GATES, not one. The row names the first: each discard site's enum leg asks
`enum_name_of_expr` about the CONSTRUCT, which is neither a `Call` nor a `Path`,
so a two-tail branch registered nothing. It now asks a REPRESENTATIVE ARM TAIL
via `first_minting_branch_tail` -- the redirect the arg-position registrar
already performs at its head (B-2026-08-30-38) -- at BOTH sites, since the
`let _ =` and bare-statement twins have drifted apart on this trio before
(B-2026-08-29-20). The second gate is `discard_arm_tail_qualifies`, which had no
arm for a fresh UNIT variant: `E.B` is a `Path` and `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`
does not call one fresh, so a single `_ => E.B` declined the whole construct.
That is why the mixed `match` -- with no unit-variant peel to fall back on --
ran nothing at all while the mixed `if` worked.

THE INTERPRETER PEEL IS THE OTHER HALF AND COULD NOT HAVE LANDED FIRST, exactly
as the row says. `discard_producer_expr` deliberately refused to peel a two-tail
branch because compiled registered no payload walk there, so peeling alone would

title: A DISCARDED `if`/`else` WHOSE ARMS ARE OWN-`Drop` ENUM CTORS RUNS ONE BODY ON THE INTERPRETER AND NONE ON EITHER COMPILED BACKEND -- `let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { E.B };` prints `dE` under `--interp` and nothing under `karac run` / `karac build`, while stranding 6 B; the DIRECT spelling `let _ = E.A(mk(8));` is correct at `dE dR8` on all three.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-29-30, as a control in that row's matrix. It is a
live run-vs-build DIVERGENCE and PRE-EXISTING -- measured identical before and
after that fix, which does not touch a branch carrying an `else`.

    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

                                          interp    jit / aot    leak (-O0)
    let _ = E.A(mk(8));                   dE dR8    dE dR8       clean
    E.A(mk(8));                           dE dR8    dE dR8       clean
    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) };          dE dR8    dE dR8       clean   (-30)
    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { E.B };
                                          dE        (nothing)    6 B / 1

The third row is the shape B-2026-08-29-30 fixed, and it is what makes the
fourth legible: a no-`else` `if` is now owned INSIDE the arm, by the
arg-position aggregate registrar, whose enum leg registers the
`karac_drop_<E>` wrapper AND the `__karac_dropelems_enum_<E>` payload walk. An
`if` WITH an `else` takes the other path -- the STATEMENT discard site, via
`discarded_match_value_tail` -- and that site's enum leg asks
`enum_name_of_expr` about the construct it was handed, which for an `If` node
is `None`. So it registers neither, and the merged value is dropped with no
owner at all.

The interpreter's single `dE` comes from `run_discarded_value_user_drops`,
whose own-`Drop`-enum arm deliberately runs the OWN body alone; its payload
companion at the wildcard-let site is gated on `inline_ctor`, which asks about
the RHS node and so answers `false` for an `If`. B-2026-08-29-30 added
`discard_producer_expr` to peel a no-`else` `if` for exactly that question and
deliberately did NOT peel a two-tail `if`, because peeling it would move this
backend from agreeing with compiled at ONE body to disagreeing at TWO -- worse,
not better, until the compiled side owns the value.

SO THE FIX IS ON THE COMPILED SIDE FIRST: make the statement discard site
resolve the enum through the branch's ARM TAILS rather than through the `If`
node, the same representative-tail redirect
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` already performs at its head
(B-2026-08-30-38). Once it registers the wrapper and the payload walk, extend
`discard_producer_expr` to the two-tail `if` and the `match` in the same
commit, and all three land on `dE dR8`.

matrix, and confirmed pre-existing by running the same matrix against the
stashed pre-fix compiler. Leak measured with valgrind at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`.

fix:
Fixed in f6059cf. Two halves, both in `src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs`.

`suppress_boxed_payload_struct_destructure_at` resolved the payload pattern's

title: A NESTED `match` ARM THAT MOVES A HEAP LEAF OUT OF A WHOLE-BOUND *BOXED* `Option` PAYLOAD DOUBLE FREES -- the TRANSFER-path twin of B-2026-08-30-52 (b), which fixed the READ-ONLY path beside it. The JIT aborts on the bare shape while AOT prints the right answer; AOT joins in as soon as the arm's `if` CONDITION allocates. The `Result[E, i64]` twin (INLINE payload area) is clean, so this is the boxed channel specifically
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-30-52 (b), as the CONTROL that was supposed to
prove the read-only fix had not disturbed the transfer path. It had not: this
reproduces on an unmodified compiler, before and after that fix, and it is the
reason -52's ASAN fixture carries an UNCONDITIONAL control rather than the
natural conditional one (which would have pinned a permanent red).

MEASURED, `--interp` correct on every row below.

  THE BARE SHAPE -- JIT ONLY (AOT prints the right answer):

      enum E { A { s: String }, B }
      fn moved(i: i64) -> i64 {
          let a: Option[E] = Some(E.A { s: s_of(i) });   // BOXED: E is 4 words
          let mut r = 0;
          match a {
              Some(p) => { match p { E.A { s } => { let owned: String = s; r = owned.len(); } E.B => {} } }
              None => {}
          }
          return r;
      }

    `karac run` -> `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
    `karac build` and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` -> `5`, correct

  ADD AN ALLOCATING CONDITION AND AOT JOINS IN. Replacing the body with
  `if owned.contains(digits(i)) { r = owned.len(); }` -- where `digits`
  returns a fresh `String` -- aborts on ALL THREE compiled surfaces (JIT, AOT,
  `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`). Under ASAN: `attempting double-free`, 50 iterations,
  one per call. An f-string temp in the condition (`owned.contains(f"{i}")`)
  does it too, so it is the ALLOCATION and not the call.

  CONTROLS, all clean, each removing exactly one ingredient:

    `Result[E, i64]` instead of `Option[E]`     the INLINE channel -- clean
    a bare `let e: E = ...` local, no Option    clean
    single-level `Some(S { s, t })` destructure clean -- needs the NESTED match
    the same move with NO conditional           clean
    a conditional that does not allocate        clean (`if i > 0`, `if owned.len() > 3`)
    the leaf only READ, not moved               clean AFTER B-2026-08-30-52 (b);
                                                broken before it, which is that row

SO THE INGREDIENT LIST IS: a BOXED `Option` payload (wider than the 3-word
inline area), an outer arm that binds it WHOLE, an inner `match` that MOVES a
heap leaf out, and -- for the AOT half -- another heap allocation inside the
arm. Every one of those is load-bearing; dropping any one makes it clean.

WHY THE JIT/AOT SPLIT MATTERS FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS. It is not two bugs. The
bare shape's AOT run printing `5` is not evidence AOT is correct -- it is
evidence that whatever is double-freed there is not reached again before exit.
Adding an allocation makes the freed block get reused, and then AOT aborts too.
Write the probe with the allocating condition, or the AOT leg will look green.

NOT INVESTIGATED: which of the boxed channel's suppressors is the one that
double-arms. The read-only side of this shape was `pattern_binding_is_borrow`
not being raised (B-2026-08-30-52 (b)); this side is the opposite path, where
the arm genuinely owns the leaf and something else still frees it, so the
`retract_boxed_leaf_drop_for_consuming_pattern` /
`suppress_boxed_payload_struct_destructure` family is where to start.

REPRO FILES: the shapes above are `m9` / `n1` / `n3` / `q1` in the -52 session
notes; the minimal AOT-visible one is quoted verbatim above.

fix:
FIXED by 33f43c4. Took the row's SECOND remedy -- give the BUFFER the element's alignment -- and
the choice was settled by counting rather than by taste: the access sites that
would need relaxing number 229, the allocation sites 10. Relaxing accesses also
gives up the aligned-move selection that is the entire point of a SIMD element
type, and `vmovups`/`vmovaps` have been the same uop on an aligned address since
Sandy Bridge, so `vmovaps` costs nothing and is effectively an alignment
assertion. Fixing the allocator keeps the fast form and is one change.

RUNTIME (`runtime/src/alloc.rs`), two new entry points, both on the keep-list in
`lib.rs`:

  karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic(size, align)
      align <= 16 delegates to `karac_alloc_or_panic` verbatim, so nothing
      that malloc already satisfies pays for this. Otherwise
      `posix_memalign`, with size rounded up to a multiple of align (C11
      requires it of `aligned_alloc`; POSIX does not, but rounding keeps the
      two interchangeable). Deliberately BYPASSES the `buf_cache`: a parked
      buffer carries only malloc alignment, so serving an aligned request
      from it would reintroduce the crash intermittently -- the exact failure
      mode this row is about.

  karac_realloc_aligned_or_panic(ptr, new_size, align)
      Reallocs FIRST and re-aligns only if the result lands misaligned.
      Reshaped mid-implementation from `(ptr, old_size, new_size, align)`:
      the old capacity is not a live local at 4 of the 6 call sites, and the
      allocator already knows it, so realloc-then-check made every call site
      mechanical. POSIX makes plain `free` the correct deallocator for
      `posix_memalign` memory, so no free-side change was needed.

CODEGEN, one predicate and one helper in `vec_method.rs`:

  over_alignment_for_elem(elem_ty) -> Option<u64>   -- ABI alignment, > 16
  emit_vec_buffer_grow_alloc(elem_ty, data, bytes, name)

routed at 7 buffer-producing sites: the Vec literal (`collections.rs`, a
`malloc` rather than a realloc), the push grow, `insert`, `resize`, `append`,
`reserve` (`vec_method.rs`), and the STABILIZED PUSH LOOP in `reduce.rs`.

That last one is the one worth recording. `for i in 0..9 { v.push(a) }` is
rewritten into a bulk reserve + fill with its own emission path, so it survived
the first six routings untouched and kept crashing after the fix "landed". The
tell was in the disassembly, not the source: `mov $0x120,%esi; xor %edi,%edi;
call karac_realloc_or_panic` -- 288 = 9 x 32, a null pointer, and the PLAIN
entry point. A grep for `realloc_or_panic_fn_decl()` found it in `reduce.rs`
under a comment explaining that `realloc(NULL, n) == malloc`, which is exactly
why it did not look like an allocation site.

MEASUREMENTS. A 14-shape sweep (interpreter vs `karac build`, x86-64):
pre-fix 8 shapes SIGSEGV 40/40 runs -- for-in, push growth, i32x8, f64x4,
reserve, insert, nested Vec, and a struct whose only field is a vector (the
over-alignment travels through the struct's own ABI alignment). Post-fix all 14
agree with the interpreter. `objdump` confirms the mechanism: the vector
programs call the aligned entry points and the `Vec[i64]` control calls none.

THE ROW'S FOUR UNMEASURED QUESTIONS, now measured:
  - `Array[Vector[T, N], M]`  -- NOT affected. A fixed-size array is an
    alloca, which LLVM aligns to the element's natural alignment itself.
  - `Map`/`Set` VALUE of vector type -- NOT affected. Values live in the
    runtime's own allocation; clean at 200 entries (many rehashes).
  - `Tensor` of vectors -- not reachable to test; `Tensor` is numeric-scalar
    only, so there is no such program to write.
  - arm64 -- not run here (this container is x86-64). The row's hypothesis
    that AArch64's `ldr q`/`str q` tolerate the misalignment stands untested;
    if it holds, arm64 was never crashing and is now merely correct-by-
    construction rather than correct-by-luck.

TWO SHAPES RAN CLEAN PRE-FIX, deterministically (40/40): a literal read and a
push onto a literal. Their buffers happened to land on a 32-aligned malloc
result. They are not evidence of anything except that this crash is
alignment-of-the-day, which is also why the E2E test below is explicitly NOT
the guard.

TESTS. `test_ir_over_aligned_vec_element_buffer_uses_the_aligned_allocator` is
the real guard: 6 buffer-producing shapes must emit an aligned entry point, and
2 controls -- `Vec[i64]` and `Vector[i64, 2]`, the latter exactly 16 bytes,
proving the predicate is `> 16` and not `>= 16` -- must NOT. It fails on the
first case without the fix. `e2e_over_aligned_vec_elements_are_the_interpreter_
oracle` covers 14 shapes against the interpreter oracle and is a CORRECTNESS
check only: every one of them, including a shape engineered to walk the heap
offset through every residue mod 32 and which crashes 100% of the time under
`karac build`, ran clean inside the E2E harness even before the fix. The
harness compiles without the concurrency analysis and so emits a different
allocation sequence; a green run of it says nothing about alignment. Both test
doc-comments say so, so nobody reads that green as coverage it does not have.
title: EVERY ACCESS TO A `Vec[Vector[T, N]]` ELEMENT BUFFER IS EMITTED AT THE VECTOR'S NATURAL ALIGNMENT AGAINST `malloc` MEMORY, SO IT FAULTS ON `vmovaps` DEPENDING ON HEAP STATE -- a two-statement program SIGSEGVs or not according to what else allocated before it
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-31-18, and independent of it: reachable on the
unpatched compiler, and NOT fixed by that row (which relaxes the alignment of the
enum-payload BOX, a different allocation).

`malloc` / `karac_realloc_or_panic` guarantee 16-byte alignment. A
`Vector[i64, 4]` is `<4 x i64>` and wants 32. Codegen emits every buffer access
at the type's natural alignment, so x86-64 lowers them to `vmovaps` / `vmovaps`,
which FAULT on a merely-16-aligned address. Static survey of the emitted IR for a
program doing a literal, a push, an index read and a `for`-in:

    %vec.lit.buf = call ptr @malloc(...)
    store <4 x i64> %vv18, ptr %vec.lit.elem.0.ptr, align 32     <- literal
    %v.elem = load <4 x i64>, ptr %v.elem.ptr, align 32          <- index read
    %new_data = call ptr @karac_realloc_or_panic(ptr %data, ...)
    store <4 x i64> %vv212, ptr %elem.ptr, align 32              <- push
    %for.v.elem = load <4 x i64>, ptr %for.v.elem.ptr, align 32  <- for-in

(The `align 32` accesses to `%vv` / `%g` / `%x` in the same function are
ALLOCAS, which LLVM aligns correctly. Only the heap buffer is under-aligned.)

WHY IT IS A NIGHTMARE TO SEE. Whether a given `malloc` returns a 32-aligned
chunk depends on the heap's history, so the same statement faults in one program
and not in another. The reduction that found it had six statement groups and
removing ANY ONE of them made it pass; each group in isolation was clean. And
ASAN masks it outright -- it changes the allocator and the stack layout, so the
memory_sanitizer suite runs the crashing program green. The witness is the
disassembly at the faulting address:

    mov    $0x20,%edi
    call   malloc@plt
    vmovaps 0xa0(%rsp),%ymm0
    vmovaps %ymm0,(%rax)          <- SIGSEGV

TWO POSSIBLE REMEDIES, and the choice is the work. Relaxing every access to
alignment 8 (what B-2026-08-31-18 does for the enum box) is correct but is
whack-a-mole across the whole Vec surface and gives up the aligned-load codegen
that is the point of a SIMD type. Giving the BUFFER the element's alignment --
an aligned allocation path for over-aligned element types -- fixes every access
at once and keeps the fast form; it needs a `posix_memalign`/`aligned_alloc`
runtime entry point and a matching free, plus a sweep of the realloc path.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: whether `Array[Vector[T, N], M]`,
a `Map`/`Set` VALUE of vector type, or a `Tensor` of vectors have the same
shape; and whether any non-x86 target's aligned vector ops fault the same way
(AArch64's `ldr q`/`str q` do not require 16-byte alignment, so this may be an
x86-only crash with an arm64 silent-correctness twin).

SCOPE NOTE (2026-08-31, closing session). The row's four unmeasured questions
are now measured; see the fix field. One separate defect surfaced while
sweeping and is NOT this bug: `let g = ref arr[i]` on an `Array[Vector[i64,4], N]`
panics the compiler at `method_call_vector.rs:1196` ("expected the VectorValue
variant" -- `g` is loaded as `i64`), so the element type of a fixed-size Array
of vectors is lost on the ref-binding path. The interpreter runs the same
program correctly. Filed separately rather than folded in here.

DUPLICATE-FIX NOTE (2026-08-31). Two sessions fixed this row independently
and both fixes reached `main`: 33f43c4 (the one this row names) over-aligns
the ALLOCATION, and eee6e18 relaxed the ACCESSES to malloc's 16-byte
guarantee at ten emission sites. The second was reverted in 5441d4a
-- 33f43c4 is the fix that stands. Recorded here because `git log` on this
row's subject otherwise shows three commits with no way to tell which is
authoritative, and because the reasoning generalizes: relaxing an access
forfeits the aligned-move selection that is the point of a SIMD element
type, while the over-aligned buffer still pays for an alignment nothing
uses. The coverage question the duplicate raised was checked before the
revert rather than assumed: 33f43c4's predicate is
`get_abi_alignment(elem_ty) > 16`, so LLVM's own layout supplies the
structural recursion the duplicate hand-rolled, and `{<4 x i64>, i64}` (a
struct with a vector field) and `[2 x <4 x i64>]` (an Array element) both
answer 32 and take the aligned path. An IR trace of a fixture sweeping
those placements confirms it: all 19 remaining over-aligned accesses derive
from a Vec data buffer that took the aligned allocator, and the Map-value
and Option-payload spellings copy through an `alloca` (`%md.out_val`,
`%enum.field`), which LLVM aligns correctly. The duplicate's two
value-equality tests were kept for that wider shape coverage
(`e2e_vec_of_vector_operations_round_trip` and its interpreter twin).

CLAIM-PROTOCOL NOTE. The collision was not a protocol violation on either
side: the claiming session read a clean board, and the other session's fix
landed during its implementation window. The protocol's re-read step (step
3) only closes the window between tagging and starting, not the hours of a
long slice. A cheap mitigation for a multi-hour fix is to re-read the board
once more immediately before the pre-push rebase, which is where this
collision was in fact discovered -- one list call earlier would have saved
the work, not the duplicate commit.

fix:
FIXED by dc3b493 for the Display half; the Option/Result GATE half is NOT fixed
and is now B-2026-08-31-40 — read the last section before reopening this.

THE ROW'S OWN SURVEY WAS RIGHT AND SLIGHTLY UNDERSTATED. Ten positions diverged
from the interpreter, in three failure modes rather than the two the row named:

  REFUSE (fails closed)   depth-0 `f"{s}"`, depth-0 `println(s)`, and a
                          `mut Slice[i64]` param
  ICE the compiler        `dbg(s)`, tuple field, `Vec` element, `Map` value,
                          `derive(Display)` enum payload — all
                          `emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Slice_i64'`
  REFUSE with a `{:?}`    a `derive(Display)` struct FIELD, dumping the field's
                          Rust `TypeExpr`
  CONTROLS                `s.len()` and `s[0]` agreed throughout

Both of the row's NOT-MEASURED cases are now measured. `mut Slice[T]` does not
need an `as_mut_slice`: `show(mut v[0..2])` produces it, and it takes the same
route as the immutable spelling — mutability is not part of the rendering. A
slice as a `Map` value was one of the ICE positions.

THE FIX IS THE ARRAY ONE ONE STEP OVER, as the row predicted, with one
difference it did not.

  * `emit_slice_display_fn` shares `emit_vec_display_body` OUTRIGHT rather than
    copying it — same text, same loop, same per-element dispatch — with the
    2-word `{ptr, len}` header in place of `{ptr, len, cap}`. The body now takes
    its header struct as a parameter. The two field offsets coincide, so it
    could have kept reading `vec_struct_type()`; passing the real one keeps the
    code honest about which layout it walks and would catch a reordering.
  * ONE dispatcher arm, not two, and this is the part the row could not have
    known. B-2026-08-31-19 needed two arms for `Array` because a source-written
    `Array[i64, 3]` and a `TypeExpr` synthesized from a `Type::Array` arrive as
    different `TypeKind`s, and a fix covering one left the other panicking. I
    instrumented the fallthrough and ran all five ICE positions rather than
    reasoning about it: every spelling of a slice arrives as
    `Path(["Slice"], [T])`, differing only in whether the spans are real or
    synthesized. There is no `TypeKind::Slice`.
  * `display_slice_types` carries the ELEMENT type, not the whole type — a
    slice's length is a runtime field, so unlike the array table there is no
    extent to forward. `try_compile_slice_display` reads it from `compile_print`
    and the f-string part path.
  * `struct_display_needs_type_directed_fn` admits a slice field, in its one
    spelling.

NOTHING IS DROPPED, and the row was right about why: a slice BORROWS. The array
sibling needed a temp drop because a fresh `Array[String, N]` owns its elements
inline; a slice's buffer belongs to the `Vec` it came from, so registering the
temporary would schedule a free on live memory — the double free
B-2026-08-14-30 fixed on the `Vec` path. Verified under LSan with the rest of
the suite.

THE GATE HALF IS THE PART TO READ. The row asks whether this lets `Slice` leave
`is_reconstructable_display_payload`, since the stated reason for excluding it —
"nothing to reconstruct INTO" — is exactly what this fixes. I admitted it and
measured: ordinary interpolation is correct on every shape available.
`Option[Slice[i64]]` → `Some([1, 2])`, `None`, `Result[Slice, String]` →
`Ok([1, 2])`, `Option[Slice[String]]` → `Some([ab, cd])`, `Option[Option[Slice]]`,
a struct with a slice field inside an `Option`, and the `match o { Some(t) => … }`
destructure the row says "DOES NOT HELP" — which now does. All identical to the
interpreter.

Then the same predicate's OTHER consumer failed. It also gates `main`'s error
type, and there the admission converted a clean build error into a binary
printing `Error: Some([93867340896349])` — the slice's own data pointer rendered
as its first ELEMENT — where the interpreter prints `Error: Some([1])`. The
length was right and the pointer one indirection off. The bare
`Result[(), Slice[i64]]` spelling does the same once `seed_synthetic_display_tables`
is given a `Slice` arm. `Vec` in the same position is correct, so it is specific
to the two-word borrow shape.

So BOTH the gate admission and the seeding were reverted before landing. Trading
a refusal for a silent miscompile is the wrong direction and is the exact trade
B-2026-08-25-34 established fail-closed to avoid. Filed as B-2026-08-31-40 with
the boxing hypothesis named; both sites carry a comment pointing at it. `Slice`
therefore REMAINS the shape the two fixtures pin, and the row's prediction that
they would have to move was wrong for a reason worth recording: they keep their
subject, and only their RATIONALE changed — from "unrenderable at any depth" to
"the entry point mis-reconstructs it".

`deferred_display_error`'s doc is corrected for the same reason: it claimed
destructuring a declined payload hits the same refusal because slices have no
Display. They render now, so that reason is dead; the "prescribe no rewrite" rule
survives on its own merits, and the doc records all three shapes it has outlived.

A SECOND FINDING CAME OUT OF THE SWEEP FOR A REMAINING DECLINED SHAPE. Probing
whether anything else the gate declines is still reachable turned up an
unsubstituted generic `T`: an `Option[T]` inside `fn f[T: Display](x: Option[T])`
reaches the gate with the parameter unsubstituted, so `T = Vec[i64]` PANICS the
compiler and `T = Array`/`Slice` refuse naming `T`, while `T = i64`/`String`
build fine. Destructuring it is a silent miscompile. Confirmed pre-existing on a
clean 32d8186 build. Filed as B-2026-08-31-39.

TESTS. `e2e_slice_display_matches_the_interpreter_at_every_depth`
(tests/codegen.rs) covers all ten positions plus `Slice[String]`, the empty
slice, and the `mut` spelling, with the interpreter as the oracle throughout;
verified non-vacuous — with the dispatcher arm removed it fails on the original
`type_name 'Slice_i64' not yet supported`. The `dbg` case asserts the program
built and ran rather than its text, because `dbg` writes to stderr and the defect
was a compile-time panic.
title: `Slice[T]` HAS NO Display UNDER CODEGEN AT ANY DEPTH -- `f"{s}"` on a slice is a hard build error where the interpreter prints `[1, 2]`, and it is the last shape the Option/Result Display gate still has to decline
detail:
Measured on the B-2026-08-31-19 tree; pre-existing and independent of it.

    let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(1); v.push(2);
    let s: Slice[i64] = v.as_slice();
    f"{s}"        interp  [1, 2]
                  build   error: codegen failed: Display of this value is not yet
                          supported under codegen (user-struct Display, subtask-5
                          follow-on)
    println(s)    same refusal
    s.len()       both 2                                            <- CONTROLS
    s[0]          both 1

It FAILS CLOSED, which is why this is a `codegen-gap` and not a miscompile —
better than the sibling shapes it was found beside. `Array[T, N]` printed the
first ELEMENT for `f"{a}"` and its data POINTER for an `Array[String, N]`
(B-2026-08-31-19), and `Vector[T, N]` at one point printed a stack address
(B-2026-08-31-18). A slice simply refuses.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE DIRECT SPELLING. `Slice[T]` is the ONE payload shape
`is_reconstructable_display_payload` still declines, so it is what
`Option[Slice[i64]]` and `Result[Slice[..], ..]` fall over on, and it is the
subject two fixtures now pin BECAUSE it is the last unrenderable shape available
(`codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` and
`test_unrenderable_main_error_is_a_build_error_not_an_empty_message`). Fixing
this row therefore has to move those fixtures again, or admit there is no longer
a shape to pin them to and rewrite what they assert.

DESTRUCTURING DOES NOT HELP, which is worth stating because it is the obvious
workaround and the deferred-display diagnostic deliberately does not suggest it:
`match o { Some(s) => println(f"{s}") }` hits the same refusal one level down.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX is the array one, one step over. `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr`
needs a `Slice` arm feeding an `emit_slice_display_fn(elem_te)`, whose body is
`emit_vec_display_body` with a 2-word `{ptr, len}` header instead of the 3-word
`{ptr, len, cap}` one — the loop, the text and the per-element dispatch are all
already shared between the `Vec` and `Array` renderers. A span-keyed
`display_slice_types` sibling (the array one landed as `display_array_types`)
gives the depth-0 path its element type. Slices BORROW, so unlike the array temp
there is nothing to drop: a `mut Slice[T]` spelling should be checked to confirm
it takes the same route.

`dbg(s)` DOES NOT refuse -- it PANICS the compiler with
`emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Slice_i64' not yet supported`, the same
ICE the nested array positions gave before B-2026-08-31-19. So this row has both
halves too, and the loud one is again the nested position rather than the plain
one. A slice as a `#[derive(Display)]` struct FIELD is a third shape: it refuses
with a Rust `{:?}` dump of the field's `TypeExpr` (B-2026-08-31-16's subject),
which `struct_display_needs_type_directed_fn` will need to admit alongside
`Vector` and `Array`.

NOT MEASURED: `mut Slice[T]` (`Vec` has no `as_mut_slice` today, so the spelling
needs another producer), and a slice as a `Map` value.

title: BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS RUN A STRUCT FIELD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE WHEN A `match` ARM DESTRUCTURES A BARE STRUCT SCRUTINEE AND MOVES THE FIELD OUT -- the interpreter runs it once, which is correct
fix:
Fixed in 6673f7d, together with its twin B-2026-08-31-27 (the same fixture gates both).

ROOT CAUSE. `suppress_destructured_struct_pattern_cleanup` (codegen's #16) already
cap-zeroed each moved-out field's MEMORY in the source struct, which is why nothing
was ever freed twice and why ASAN saw nothing. The BODIES half had no counterpart:
the source's `__karac_dropbodies_*` walk still visited the moved-out field, so a
field type with a user `impl Drop` ran its body a SECOND time -- on the husk the
cap-zeroing had just left behind. Instrumented, that reads `dR47 dR0`, where `dR47`
is due and `dR0` is a body reading its own fields off a cleared object.

FIX. `disarm_arm_destructured_struct_field_bodies`
(`src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs`), called from the match-arm loop immediately
after #16 so the memory and bodies halves move in lockstep (the B-2026-08-28-67
rule). It masks each wholly-moved field index into `struct_moved_field_bodies` and
re-emits the walker through `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping`, reusing the
`FieldSkipTree` machinery `disarm_struct_field_bodies_at` already had for the
`let x = h.f` spelling (B-2026-08-03-8).

TWO DETAILS THAT ARE NOT OBVIOUS AND ARE BOTH LOAD-BEARING:

  * IN-PLACE SWAP, not retract-and-re-register. This runs inside a match ARM whose
    cleanup frame is inner to the owner's, so `track_user_drop_var_with_fn` would
    move the owner's whole walk into the arm and drain it there. It goes through
    `replace_user_drop_fn_for_var`, exactly as the payload sibling
    `disarm_struct_field_enum_payload_bodies_at` (B-2026-08-29-33) does and for the
    reason spelled out on it.
  * The `pattern_binding_is_borrow` gate. A read-only arm binds a VIEW and the
    source keeps ownership, so its walk must stay armed -- the invariant the whole
    read-only-arm family (B-2026-08-30-47 / -52) rests on. Without the gate this
    would have silently converted that family's fixtures into leaks.

SCOPE, MEASURED AND DELIBERATE. Three neighbouring shapes reproduce and are filed
rather than folded in, because each has a different carrier:

  * the `if let` / `let ... else` / NESTED-`match` spellings, which never reach #16
    at all and are a genuine DOUBLE FREE, not a duplicate body -- filed HIGH as
    B-2026-08-31-30;
  * the destructured struct having its own `impl Drop`, where the walk lives in the
    `OwnWrapper` (`karac_drop_H`) rather than a maskable `StructFieldBodies` action
    -- B-2026-08-31-31;
  * a fresh-TEMP struct scrutinee -- B-2026-08-31-32 (interpreter side).

FIXTURES. `e2e_destructuring_arm_runs_each_drop_body_exactly_once`
(tests/codegen.rs, 15 rows) asserts the exact output text on the interpreter and on
`karac build`, covering four -26 spellings (`..` rest, all fields named, renamed
binding, block arm body), six -27 shapes, and five controls. The interpreter is
explicitly NOT the oracle: it was the wrong one for ten of those rows, so every
expected value is what `karac build` printed, which is also what the five controls
agreed on before either fix.

WHY THE FIXTURE ASSERTS TEXT RATHER THAN SURVIVAL. Neither half is a memory error
-- -26 frees exactly once and -27 frees nothing extra -- so no ASAN fixture can see
either. A `Drop` body that logs, unlocks, decrements a counter or closes an fd was
running twice (or zero times) for one value, and only a body-COUNT assertion
catches that. This is the reason both bugs survived a tree with this much
sanitizer coverage.

RED-VERIFIED independently: with `src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs` alone reverted
the first row fails `left: "a\ndRa\ndR\nend\n"` against `right: "a\ndRa\nend\n"`;
with `src/interpreter/pattern_match.rs` alone reverted the fifth fails
`left: "a\nend\n"`.

GATES. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets
-- -D warnings` and the `--features llvm` leg both clean; full `cargo test
--features llvm` battery green.

title: THE INTERPRETER NEVER RUNS A FIELD'S `Drop` BODY WHEN A SINGLE-LEVEL `match` ARM DESTRUCTURES AN `Option`-WRAPPED PAYLOAD AND MOVES THE FIELD OUT -- both compiled backends run it once, which is correct
fix:
Fixed in 6673f7d, together with its twin B-2026-08-31-26 (the same fixture gates both).

THREE MECHANISMS, all in `src/interpreter/pattern_match.rs`. The row named the
`Option`-wrapped destructure; sweeping the shape space first showed the real axis is
wider -- a USER enum (`W.C(P { r, .. })`) and `Result` behave identically, so this is
about reaching through ANY container pattern, not about `Option`.

(a) `arm_moved_user_drop_payload_bindings` collected a payload binding only when the
    sub-pattern was a bare `PatternKind::Binding`. `Some(P { r, .. })`,
    `Some(E.A { r })` and `Some(T.A(r))` therefore contributed NOTHING, so no Drop
    slot was ever registered and no body ran. All three arms of that function (the
    Option/Result shape-only branch, the user-enum tuple-variant branch, and the
    struct-variant branch) now take the names the sub-pattern INTRODUCES, via
    `crate::cfg::pattern_bindings`. Over-approximating is safe and is already the
    documented contract there: the caller's runtime-value filter is what keeps a
    scalar binding silent, which is the same reason the bare spelling could be
    collected shape-only in the first place.

(b) `is_drop_binding`'s STRUCT arm asked `drop_method_keys.contains_key(&tn)` -- does
    this type declare a `Drop` of its OWN -- while the ENUM arm directly beside it
    asked the TRANSITIVE `type_name_runs_user_drop`. So `struct P { r: R }`, with no
    `Drop` of its own but a Drop-bearing field, registered nothing, while the same
    payload wrapped in an enum registered fine. The comment above the enum arm even
    records that it was widened for exactly this reason; the struct arm was left
    behind. It now asks `value_runs_user_drop`, the value-level twin.

(c) The NON-BLOCK arm body's drain had the matching hole: it ran the own body when
    the type declared one and nothing at all when it did not, so a payload
    registered by (b)'s widening would have been drained to silence. It now routes
    through `run_discarded_value_user_drops`, whose struct arm is exactly the
    own-body-else-field-walk pair and is already the documented twin of codegen's
    discard registrar. The BLOCK-body path needed no change --
    `invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` has handled the field-only struct since
    B-2026-07-29-39; it was never being reached.

BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS WERE CORRECT AT EVERY SHAPE HERE, so they are a complete
oracle and every expected value in the fixtures is what `karac build` prints.

FIXTURES. Two, deliberately:
  * `e2e_destructuring_arm_runs_each_drop_body_exactly_once` (tests/codegen.rs, 15
    rows) is the real gate -- it pins the two backends against each other, so a
    codegen regression cannot silently redefine the reference the interpreter is
    measured against.
  * `interp_a_destructuring_arm_runs_each_payload_drop_body_once`
    (tests/interpreter.rs, 10 rows) repeats the interpreter half on the DEFAULT leg,
    which CI runs on every push, so an interpreter regression does not have to wait
    for the `--features llvm` job.
Controls in both: a bare enum scrutinee, the nested whole-bound spelling, a payload
that IS the Drop type, and a binding of the non-Drop field -- each already agreed
with compiled before the fix and each is a path the widening must not disturb.

RESIDUAL, measured after the fix and filed rather than folded in: with an own
`impl Drop` on the payload struct, the interpreter runs the moved-out field's body
(fixed here) but still not the partially-moved residue's OWN body --
B-2026-08-31-33. That row deliberately does not propose a code change first,
because whether that body is due at all is the open design question
B-2026-08-31-2 raises. A fresh-TEMP struct scrutinee is a separate interpreter gap,
B-2026-08-31-32.

RED-VERIFIED: with `src/interpreter/pattern_match.rs` alone reverted, both fixtures
fail on the first `Option` + struct-payload row with `left: "a\nend\n"` against
`right: "a\ndRa\nend\n"`.

GATES. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both clippy legs clean; full
`cargo test --features llvm` battery green.

title: A BARE `match` ARM HANDING OUT A HEAP-CARRYING `Option` PAYLOAD RUNS NO `Drop` BODY ON EITHER COMPILED BACKEND -- `let _ = match o { Some(r) => r, None => .. };` where `Option[R]` and `R` carries a `String` prints `dR1` under `--interp` and nothing under `karac run` / `karac build`; the BRACED spelling of the same arm, the same bare arm over a USER enum, and the same bare arm over an `Option` whose payload carries no heap are all correct at one body on all three.
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-29-31, as the one cell of that row's matrix the
fix could not reach. PRE-EXISTING and confirmed so by measurement: the
BARE-STATEMENT spelling of the identical program diverged the same way against
the stashed pre-fix compiler.

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }        // heap-carrying
    impl Drop for R { .. }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> R { .. }

                                                     interp    jit / aot
    let _ = match o { Some(r) => r, .. };            dR1       (nothing)
    match o { Some(r) => r, .. };                    dR1       (nothing)
    let _ = match o { Some(r) => { r } .. };         dR1       dR1
    let _ = match e { E.A(r) => r, .. };  // user enum
                                                     dR1       dR1
    let _ = match o2 { Some(r) => r, .. }; // Option[R2], R2 all-scalar
                                                     dR1       dR1

THE THREE CONTROLS ARE THE WHOLE DIAGNOSIS. Braces fix it, a user enum fixes
it, and removing the heap field fixes it -- so the defect is not "bare arms",
not "match", and not "Option": it is the intersection, which is the
BOXED-`Option`-PAYLOAD channel. An `Option` whose payload carries heap is
boxed, and a bare (non-block) arm body never reaches
`compile_block_with_frame`, so whichever hook adopts the payload binding for a
braced arm is not reached for a bare one.

WHY IT IS VISIBLE NOW. B-2026-08-29-31 taught the interpreter to own an arm
tail naming a binding that has already left scope, which is what makes the
HEAPLESS spelling correct on all three (it was that row's "row 2 DIVERGENT",
compiled firing where the interpreter did not). The heap-carrying spelling then
became the only member of the family still split, in the opposite direction.
Admitting it was the right trade -- one narrower divergence in place of a wider
one -- but it is a divergence and it is this row.

WHERE TO START: `compile_match`'s bare-arm path, around
`suppress_boxed_payload_whole_binding` and the arm-scope drop registration.
The braced path adopts the payload binding through the arm's own frame; find
what the bare path does instead and give it the same adoption. Fixing it closes
BOTH statement forms at once, and lets the two pinned-divergent rows in
`e2e_wildcard_let_discard_owns_what_its_arm_hands_out` /
`test_wildcard_let_discard_owns_what_its_arm_hands_out` flip together.

SOURCE NOTE: probed as `p1`-`p4` plus `q1`/`q2` in B-2026-08-29-31's control
matrix; the pre-existence check is that matrix re-run against `git stash`ed
`src` with the binary rebuilt in between.

RE-MEASURED 2026-08-31 against `f6059cf6` ("disarm the box interior for a
consuming arm over a boxed ENUM payload"), which landed on `main` in this
same neighbourhood while B-2026-08-29-31 was in flight. It does NOT close
this: the bare `Option` arm is still silent on both compiled backends after
it, and all three controls above still read as tabulated. That commit fixed
the adjacent boxed-ENUM channel, which is consistent with this row's
diagnosis rather than contradicting it -- `E.A(r) => r` was already correct
here before it and remains so.
fix:
FIXED by 8ccadea. In `compile_match`'s per-arm code the memory and bodies
retractions sit two lines apart, and only the memory one was guarded:

    if self.branch_value_is_owned(scrutinee) {          // memory  -- gated
        self.suppress_boxed_payload_view_move(...);
    }
    if let ExprKind::Identifier(nm) = &arm.body.kind {  // bodies  -- UNGATED
        self.suppress_container_elem_bodies_for_var(&nm);
    }

The memory half took that guard in B-2026-08-28-66, whose comment states the
reason outright -- neutralizing assumes the destination registers a drop of
its own, and a DISCARDED match result has no destination at all. The bodies
half immediately below it never took it, so a discarded match still retracted
the source's bodies walk while handing the value to nobody, and the body ran
nowhere. That is the B-2026-08-28-67 lockstep rule broken in place: the two
halves of one handover must move together. Gating the bodies call on the
`owns_result` already computed a few lines above restores it, and closes BOTH
statement forms at once exactly as this row predicted.

THE ROW'S "WHERE TO START" WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE NEIGHBOURHOOD AND WRONG ABOUT
THE MECHANISM, and the difference matters for anyone reading it later. It said
the braced path "adopts the payload binding through the arm's own frame; find
what the bare path does instead and give it the same adoption" -- i.e. that
something is MISSING on the bare path. Nothing is missing. The braced arm is
correct because a `Block` is not an `ExprKind::Identifier`, so the retraction
above never fired for it and the source's walk still ran the body. The bare
path was not failing to adopt; it was actively DISARMING, and the fix is a
guard rather than an adoption. `suppress_boxed_payload_whole_binding`, the
row's other named suspect, was already correctly gated and is not involved.

THE THREE CONTROLS THE ROW TABULATED ALL FALL OUT OF THAT ONE SITE, which is
what confirms it: a braced arm is a `Block` (never an `Identifier`); a USER
enum is not in `boxed_enum_payload_vars`; an `Option` whose payload carries no
heap is not boxed at all. Only a boxed payload handed out of a bare arm
reaches the call.

A FOURTH CONTROL, measured while scoping and not in the row, narrows the
trigger further and is the reason the ownership axis is the right one rather
than a coincidence: an arm that BINDS the payload but yields something else
(`Some(r) => mk(5)`) was already correct on every surface, printing both
bodies. So the trigger is not "the arm binds a boxed payload" but "the arm's
tail IS that binding" -- precisely the handover case.

MEMORY IS UNCHANGED, as it must be, since only the bodies half moved.
`valgrind --leak-check=full` at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`: 13 allocs / 13 frees, 0
errors from 0 contexts, on the wildcard-`let`, the bare-statement, and the
stacked spellings alike.

VERIFIED across all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run`, `karac build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`) on an eleven-case matrix: the two broken
spellings plus nine cells that were already correct -- the braced arm, the
user enum, the heapless payload, the value CONSUMED rather than discarded, an
arm that binds but yields something else, a wildcard pattern, and a bare arm
whose value is consumed by a following use. No agreeing cell moved.

TESTS. The two pinned-divergent assertions this row predicted would flip both
did, and are now asserted as agreement rather than pinned:
`e2e_wildcard_let_discard_owns_what_its_arm_hands_out` (tests/codegen.rs)
carries both bare spellings in its table alongside the four controls that
localize the fix, and nothing is pinned divergent in that fixture any more;
`test_wildcard_let_discard_owns_what_its_arm_hands_out` (tests/interpreter.rs)
becomes an agreement assertion and gains the bare-STATEMENT spelling it did
not cover. The codegen fixture was verified to FAIL without the fix (`end`
alone on the first bare row) and pass with it. `asan_wildcard_let_discard_owns
_what_its_arm_hands_out` needed no change, which is the memory claim above
restated as a test.

title: `let g = ref arr[i]` ON AN `Array[Vector[T, N], M]` PANICS THE COMPILER -- the ref binding is loaded as the LANE type (`i64`) instead of the vector, and the next vector method call hits `into_vector_value` on an IntValue
detail:
Found while sweeping B-2026-08-31-24's blast radius, and NOT that bug: this one
is a compiler panic at build time on a legal program, not a runtime fault, and
it is specific to `Array` (the fixed-size, alloca-backed one). The identical
shape on a `Vec[Vector[i64, 4]]` compiles and runs correctly, which is what
separates the two.

    fn main() {
        let a: Vector[i64, 4] = Vector[i64, 4](1, 2, 3, 4);
        let arr: Array[Vector[i64, 4], 3] = Array[a, a, a];
        let g = ref arr[2];
        println(g.reduce_sum());
    }

    thread panicked at src/codegen/method_call_vector.rs:1196:47:
    Found IntValue(... llvm_value: "  %g.deref = load i64, ptr %g, align 8",
    llvm_type: "i64" }) but expected the VectorValue variant

The IR in the panic message is the whole diagnosis: `g` was emitted as a
`load i64`, so the Array's element type was resolved to the vector's LANE type
rather than the vector. `compile_vector_method` then unwraps the receiver as a
VectorValue and finds an integer. `karac run --interp` prints 10 -- the correct
answer -- so the interpreter half is fine and this is a codegen element-type
resolution gap.

TWO NEIGHBOURING SHAPES, for whoever picks this up:

  - `for e in arr { println(e.reduce_sum()); }` over the same array WORKS and
    prints correctly on all backends (it is a control in
    `e2e_over_aligned_vec_elements_are_the_interpreter_oracle`), so the
    for-in element path resolves the type the ref-binding path loses.

  - `let g: Vector[i64, 4] = arr[2];` is REJECTED at typecheck, with
    E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY telling you to borrow it (`ref arr[i]`) instead --
    which is the form that panics. So the diagnostic currently steers a user
    from a clean rejection into a compiler crash. Worth checking separately
    whether `Vector[T, N]` should be `Copy` at all; if it should, the move
    form is the natural spelling and this panic is on the recommended
    workaround for a rejection that should not happen either.

A COMPILER PANIC IS NEVER THE RIGHT OUTCOME. Even before the element type is
resolved correctly, the unwrap at `method_call_vector.rs:1196` should be a
structured diagnostic with a span -- every phase in this compiler is required
to emit one rather than panic.
fix:
FIXED by 73e6e86, which gives `try_compile_ref_binding`'s NAMED-LOCAL arm the container-class
dispatch it never had (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`). The arm called
`lower_indexed_elem_ptr_vec` unconditionally, so every non-Vec named local was
lowered as though its slot held a `{ptr, i64, i64}` Vec header. It now
