classifies exactly as `compile_indexed_receiver_method` (`calls.rs`) does, in
the same order -- Vec, then Slice, then an `ArrayType` slot -- and DECLINES
anything else, which is also what the sibling `FieldAccess` arm has always done
(`_ => Ok(None)`). The second half of the fix: an Array's element `TypeExpr`
comes from `array_elem_type_exprs`, not the `var_elem_type_exprs` the Vec/Slice
arms read; without it a field read through the borrow (`let r = ref pa[1]; r.a`)
failed with "cannot resolve field 'a' on this receiver". That table is
deliberately separate -- ~170 readers treat a `var_elem_type_exprs` entry as
"this binding is a Vec/Slice/Map" -- so the Array arm reads its own table rather
than widening that one.

THE ROW UNDERSTATED THIS, and the correction is the useful part of the entry.
It is filed as a compiler panic on `Array[Vector[T, N], M]`, which reads as a
narrow SIMD-adjacent gap. The panic is in fact the LUCKY case. The same shape on
`Array[i64, 3]` -- an unremarkable program -- BUILDS CLEANLY AND SEGFAULTS,
because nothing about the pun is vector-specific:

    %arr = alloca [3 x i64]                 ; [10, 20, 30]
    %len  = gep {ptr,i64,i64}, %arr, 0, 1    ; 20
    %data = gep {ptr,i64,i64}, %arr, 0, 0    ; 10
    %bounds = icmp uge i64 2, %len           ; 2 < 20, PASSES
    %e = gep i64, %data, i64 2               ; address 10 + 16
    %g.deref = load i64, ptr %e              ; SIGSEGV

Element 0 becomes the data pointer and element 1 the length, so the bounds check
is not merely useless -- it is DEFEATED, comparing the index against a payload
word, then dereferencing an address the array's own contents spell. On the
vector spelling the wrong element type (the vector's LANE) reaches
`compile_vector_method` and panics before that load is ever emitted, which is
why that spelling fails loudly at build time and the scalar one fails silently
at runtime. Real severity is therefore HIGH and the class is a type-confusion
miscompile with the panic as one symptom, not `crash`; the row is closed with
its filed severity left as recorded and this note as the correction.

The row's second ask is also done: `compile_vector_method`'s bare
`into_vector_value()` is now a structured `Err` naming the method and the kind
of value that arrived, with a helper that prints "an integer" rather than an
inkwell `Debug` dump of the whole `Value` struct. Nothing reaches it today --
the dispatch gap that did is closed -- so it stands as the guard for the next
such gap, which is the only thing that earns a defensive branch its place.

THE TWO NEIGHBOURING SHAPES the row flagged, both checked:

  - `for e in arr { ... }` was already correct and stays correct; it is a
    control line in the new test.

  - `let g: Vector[i64, 4] = arr[2];` is still rejected by E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY
    steering the user to `ref arr[i]`. That steer now leads somewhere that
    works, so the "diagnostic steers you into a compiler crash" half is
    resolved. Whether `Vector[T, N]` should be `Copy` -- which would make the
    move form the natural spelling and the rejection unnecessary -- is a
    language-design question this does not answer and is left open.

MEASURED (all four surfaces byte-identical, `scalar 30 / vector 10 / struct 3 4
/ alias 99 / vec 8`): `--interp`, `karac run` (JIT), `karac build`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`. The codegen E2E goes RED pre-fix with this row's
exact panic; the interpreter twin passes both before and after, which is what
makes it the oracle -- the interpreter was correct on every line throughout.

SoA NOTE, checked rather than assumed: the classification puts Vec FIRST, which
would be wrong if an SoA-laid-out `Vec` could reach it -- an SoA element has no
contiguous storage, so a pointer into the buffer is the exact silent-wrong-write
class `compile_indexed_receiver_method` materialises the element to avoid. It
cannot: the TYPECHECKER already rejects `ref` over an SoA container with
E_REF_OPERAND_UNSUPPORTED ("its fields live in one buffer per `layout` group, so
an element has no contiguous storage to borrow"), so the shape never reaches
codegen and the Vec-first order is safe.

SLICE NOTE: the Slice arm is behaviour-PRESERVING, not a fix, and it was worth
measuring rather than assuming. `Slice{ptr,len}` and `Vec{ptr,len,cap}` share
field offsets 0 and 1, so the old unconditional Vec path read a slice correctly
BY COINCIDENCE. Verified by stashing the fix: pre-fix and post-fix both print
30. The arm makes that principled instead of accidental.

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS FOUND WHILE SWEEPING, filed rather than folded in: the
interpreter binds the whole CONTAINER instead of the element for `ref s[i]` on a
Slice and `ref m[k]` on a Map, and a Map base now reaches a decline whose
message is an internal "unreachable: Ref handled in compile_expr". The second is
a strict improvement on what a Map base did before this fix -- it segfaulted the
same way the Array base did -- but an internal string with no span is not the
right end state.

title: THE `if let` / `let ... else` / NESTED-`match` SPELLINGS OF A STRUCT DESTRUCTURE DOUBLE FREE A MOVED-OUT HEAP FIELD ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- only the flat `match` spelling has the #16 source-field suppression
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-31-26, whose flat `match` spelling is the ONE member of this family that is safe. It is not that bug and not caused by its fix -- the three spellings below reproduce identically with `src/codegen/` checked out at the pre-fix parent.

`suppress_destructured_struct_pattern_cleanup` (codegen's #16) cap-zeroes each moved-out field in the SOURCE struct so the scrutinee's drop skips the buffer the arm's binding now owns. It has exactly ONE caller: the `match` arm loop in `control_flow_match.rs`. The `if let`, `while let` and `let ... else` legs in `control_flow.rs` run the whole neighbouring battery -- `suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup`, `suppress_destructured_struct_field_enum_cleanup`, `suppress_inline_option_payload_cleanup`, and a dozen more -- but never #16. A plain struct pattern in those positions therefore leaves the source field fully populated while the binding owns the same buffer, and both free it.

REPRO (payload padded past the short-string threshold so the block is real, and a second allocation after the arm so the freed block is reused -- without both, the second free lands on a block nothing reclaims and glibc stays quiet):

    struct R { s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.s.len()}") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }
    struct Q { h: H }
    // pad(t) returns a 47-byte String

  spelling                                          --interp                  karac build
  match h { H { r, .. } => .. }                     47 dR47 47 end            47 dR47 47 end   <- correct (#16)
  if let H { r, .. } = h { .. }                     47 dR47 47 end            DOUBLE FREE
  let H { r, .. } = h else { return };              dR47 47 dR47 47 end       DOUBLE FREE
  match q { Q { h: H { r, .. } } => .. }            47 dR47 47 end            DOUBLE FREE

Measured as `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` on `karac build`; the JIT aborts the same way. ASAN will report it as a double free rather than the silent duplicate-body of B-2026-08-31-26 -- these are memory errors, not observability ones, which is why this row is HIGH and that one is medium.

THE NESTED SPELLING IS A SEPARATE HALF from the two statement forms. `Q { h: H { r, .. } }` goes through the `match` arm loop and so DOES reach #16, but #16's `whole_move` gate skips a field whose sub-pattern is not a bare binding -- correctly, because the field itself is not moved, only something inside it. Nothing then descends to mask the INNER field. `FieldSkipTree` already carries a `nested` level for exactly this (the caller-side argument sites resolve a path through it), so the machinery exists and is simply not driven from here. The body-arity twin of the same gap shows up without a heap payload as `a dRa dRa` against the interpreter's `a dRa`.

THE `let ... else` SPELLING IS ALSO WRONG ON THE INTERPRETER, and in the other direction: it prints `dR47` TWICE (once before the binding is even used). That half is independent of the codegen double free and needs its own diagnosis.

FIX SHAPE, in the order the evidence supports: drive #16 (plus B-2026-08-31-26's bodies sibling `disarm_arm_destructured_struct_field_bodies`, which must move in lockstep with it -- the B-2026-08-28-67 rule) from the three `control_flow.rs` legs, then teach the `whole_move` gate to descend into a nested struct sub-pattern via `FieldSkipTree::nested`.
fix:
Fixed in ac28d68. THREE INDEPENDENT HALVES, each RED-verified on its own.

(1) THE THREE STATEMENT FORMS. `suppress_destructured_struct_pattern_cleanup`
(#16) cap-zeroes each moved-out field in the SOURCE struct so the scrutinee's
drop skips the buffer the binding now owns, and it had exactly ONE caller: the
`match` arm loop. The `if let` / `while let` / `let … else` legs in
`control_flow.rs` ran the entire neighbouring battery -- the enum-payload
disarm, the struct-field-enum disarm, the inline Option/Result suppressions, a
dozen more -- and never this one. All three now call it, together with
B-2026-08-31-26's bodies sibling `disarm_arm_destructured_struct_field_bodies`,
on the match edge only, so the memory and bodies halves move in lockstep (the
B-2026-08-28-67 rule). This is the same omission, one level up, that
B-2026-08-29-33 found for an enum-typed FIELD in these same three legs.

(2) THE NESTED SPELLING, a genuinely separate half. `match q { Q { h: H { r, .. } } }`
DOES reach #16, but its `whole_move` gate correctly declines to mask an outer
field whose sub-pattern destructures -- that field did not move, only something
inside it -- and nothing then descended to the inner field. #16 now RECURSES
into a nested struct sub-pattern against the field's own slot, so it composes to
any depth. The bodies twin needed new state: `struct_moved_nested_field_bodies`
(outer index -> inner indices), feeding `FieldSkipTree::nested`, which already
existed for the caller-side argument sites and simply was not driven from here.

(3) THE `let … else` INTERPRETER HALF, which the row recorded as wrong in the
other direction. `disarm_moved_out_enum_payload_one` runs at that site for an
ENUM payload and its comment describes this exact failure -- "the body runs
twice, once via the source's walk at its NLL death, before the binding is even
used, and once via the binding's own slot" -- but there was no STRUCT sibling,
so a bare struct pattern got precisely that: `dR47 47 dR47 47 end` against every
compiled backend's single body. The match edge now registers each wholly-bound
field into `moved_out_struct_field_bodies`, the per-field map
`drop_user_drop_fields_of_binding` has consulted since B-2026-08-03-8. Per
FIELD, not a wholesale retraction, so a field the pattern leaves unbound still
gets its body.

MEASURED, on the pre-fix compiler, with a payload padded past the short-string
threshold and a second allocation after the arm:

  spelling                                    --interp             karac build
  match h { H { r, .. } => … }                47 dR47 47 end       47 dR47 47 end   <- the only safe one
  if let H { r, .. } = h { … }                47 dR47 47 end       DOUBLE FREE
  let H { r, .. } = h else { … };             dR47 47 dR47 47 end  DOUBLE FREE
  match q { Q { h: H { r, .. } } => … }       47 dR47 47 end       DOUBLE FREE
  if let Q { h: H { r, .. } } = q { … }       47 dR47 47 end       DOUBLE FREE

Post-fix all five agree at one body on all three surfaces.

FIXTURES, two, because this half is a real memory error and the -26/-27 pair was
not. `e2e_every_struct_destructure_spelling_frees_once` (tests/codegen.rs) pins
the text; `asan_every_struct_destructure_spelling_frees_once`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) is the memory gate and carries a
`two_fields_one_taken` LEAK-direction control -- over-disarming a field the
pattern never bound is the opposite failure, the one both sibling disarmers were
fixed for (B-2026-08-04-6, B-2026-08-28-66), and LSan sees it only on the Linux
CI leg.

TWO FIXTURE TRAPS HIT AND RECORDED IN THE FIXTURES THEMSELVES:
  * The ASAN helper SKIPS on parse errors and reports the test as passing. The
    first version had assignment-as-block-tail bodies (`{ hit = … }` without a
    semicolon), so it never compiled a single program and went green in 0.07s.
    A `--nocapture` run is what exposed it; a plain `cargo test` cannot.
  * The allocation floor is per-fixture. Copying the sibling's 200 failed at a
    measured 99 -- a real count, not a vacuous run -- so the floor is set to 80.
    A floor above the true count fails every run; a floor of zero proves nothing.

NOT PART OF THIS ROW, measured while deriving the expected values:
  * Under the DEFAULT (auto-par) build the `let … else` row prints
    `47 47 end dR47` -- the binding's body slides to scope exit. That is
    B-2026-08-31-6 (an auto-par outlined region swallows the NLL drop points of
    the statements it spans), reproduces identically for a plain
    `let r: R = …` with no pattern at all, and is unrelated to anything here.
    The test harness builds with auto-par off, which is why its column is the
    NLL one.
  * `if let Some(H { r, .. }) = o` over an `Option`-wrapped struct payload runs
    NO body at all on either compiled backend. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING by
    rebuilding at the parent commit, and filed as B-2026-08-31-38 -- the `match`
    spelling of the same pattern is correct, so it is the `if let` leg alone.

title: WHEN THE DESTRUCTURED STRUCT HAS ITS OWN `impl Drop`, ITS WRAPPER STILL RUNS THE MOVED-OUT FIELD'S BODY ON THE HUSK -- the carrier is `OwnWrapper`, which B-2026-08-31-26's mask cannot reach
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residual of B-2026-08-31-26, measured after its fix landed and deliberately left out of it. That row's repro has no `impl Drop` on the destructured struct; adding one moves the field walk to a different cleanup action and the mask no longer applies.

REPRO -- identical to B-2026-08-31-26's except for the one added impl:

    struct R { s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR[{self.s}]") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }
    impl Drop for H { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dH") } }
    let h: H = H { r: R { s: "a" }, n: 4 };
    match h { H { r, .. } => println(r.s) }

    --interp     : a dH dR[a] end
    karac run    : a dR[a] dH dR[] end        <- `dR[]` is a body on a CLEARED object
    karac build  : a dR[a] dH dR[] end

TWO DEFECTS IN ONE LINE, and they should be split only if they turn out to have different causes:
  (1) the trailing `dR[]` -- the same husk body B-2026-08-31-26 fixed, surviving because the carrier       here is the `OwnWrapper` (`karac_drop_H`, body + fields + memory in one action) rather than a       separate `StructFieldBodies` action. Instrumentation confirms       `disarm_arm_destructured_struct_field_bodies` runs, masks every surviving field, and correctly       retracts the `StructFieldBodies` action -- there simply is not one carrying this walk. Masking       inside the wrapper needs a per-variable wrapper variant, which is why it was not folded into -26.
  (2) the ORDER of the two legitimate bodies is reversed between the backends: `dH dR[a]` on the       interpreter, `dR[a] ... dH` compiled. design.md fixes no order for a moved-out binding against       the residue's own body, but the bodies are observable, so it has to be fixed somewhere -- the       same argument the `Map` key-then-value order settled under B-2026-08-26-41.

NOT A MEMORY ERROR: the buffer is freed exactly once (the husk body reads a cleared `String`, printing empty), so ASAN/LSan stay silent. Only the observable body count and order are wrong.

The `let m = h.r` spelling of the same move is CORRECT on both backends (`dH a dR[a]`), which is the proof that a maskable path exists for an own-`Drop` struct and that only the match-arm route misses it.

RELOCATED to B-2026-09-01-38 (2026-09-01), after re-measuring on b14b45e.

Both defects reproduce exactly as filed, and a probe matrix added two findings
that decide where the row belongs.

THE ROW'S CONTROL IS NOT CORRECT. `let m = h.r` is recorded here as "CORRECT on
both backends (`dH a dR[a]`), which is the proof that a maskable path exists for
an own-`Drop` struct". The body COUNT matches, but the body's CONTENT does not:
with `H::drop` printing what it observes, the interpreter sees `r.s=b` and both
compiled backends see `r.s=` -- a cleared field. So there is no
already-correct path to copy; the compiled backend reads a husk in that spelling
too, and the control was passing only because its drop body never read the
moved field.

WHY THAT MAKES A LOCAL FIX THE WRONG MOVE. Masking the wrapper's field walk
would remove the trailing `dR[]` (defect 1) and leave `dH[sees r.s=]` -- still
a `Drop` body running against a half-cleared object, and still divergent from
the interpreter, so it would not even reach backend agreement. It would remove
one of two wrong things while reading as a resolution.

Both defects are manifestations of the shape design.md line 9240 forbids: a move
out of a struct that has its own `Drop`. B-2026-09-01-38 tracks that the rule is
unimplemented, and now carries both measurements, including the FULL-destructure
case (`H { r, n }`, every field bound) which the rule's wording may not reach --
the one shape here that could survive it. If -38 resolves in a way that leaves
the full destructure compiling, file a FRESH id for it citing this row rather
than reopening this one.

title: THE INTERPRETER RUNS NO `Drop` BODY AT ALL FOR A FRESH-TEMP STRUCT SCRUTINEE THAT AN ARM DESTRUCTURES -- `match H { .. } { H { r, .. } => .. }`; both compiled backends run it once
fix:
FIXED by 86e8d7a (fixtures in e0947f4).

THE GATE, and why the row's neighbour could not reach it. The arm-stash
registration read

    let consuming_scrutinee = !arm_reads_through
        && matches!(scrutinee, Value::EnumVariant { .. })
        && scrutinee_place.is_none_or(|sp| self.scrutinee_expr_is_consuming(sp));

so a STRUCT scrutinee never registered a slot for what its arm bound. That is
the exact mirror of B-2026-08-30-55, whose `method_param_drop_names` admitted
`Value::Struct` only and lost the enum -- one machinery, two opposite blind
spots, found a day apart from opposite directions.

It is also the precise reason B-2026-08-31-27 did not reach this, which the row
suspected without being able to say why: that fix widened the payload test
INSIDE this branch, and a struct literal never becomes a `Value::EnumVariant`,
so it never arrived at the branch at all.

THREE PARTS, each forced by a measurement rather than by reading the code:

  * A struct LITERAL has to count as ownerless. `scrutinee_expr_is_consuming`
    answered true for `Call` and fell through to `false` for `StructLiteral`.
    Adding it ALONE changes nothing, because the enum-only gate above still
    blocks it -- which made the first probe read as a refuted hypothesis when it
    was a half-applied one. Both halves are required.
  * ONLY where nothing else owns the value. Widening unconditionally made the
    `let`-bound control print its body TWICE (`dR[b] dR[b]` against one
    compiled). A struct has no `moved_out_enum_payload_bindings` equivalent, so
    there is nothing to retract a NAMED binding's field walk with -- which is
    exactly why the enum path may admit an identifier place here and this one
    may not. Restricted to a value built or returned AT the scrutinee.
  * The `if let` site computes `stash_names` BEFORE `bind_pattern`, so the
    filter I first wrote there consulted `env` before the names existed, every
    candidate answered `None`, and the stash came out empty -- the patch
    silently did nothing. The consumption loop already filters after binding, so
    the candidates go in unfiltered.

`if let` moves with `match` through ONE shared place test
(`struct_scrutinee_has_no_other_owner`) rather than a second copy: this family
has had to close a spelling-dependent split twice already (B-2026-08-28-63,
B-2026-08-29-17), and both times because the same rule was written out twice.

VERIFICATION. Five shapes on `--interp`, the JIT and `build`: a fresh literal, a
call temp, a `let`-bound control, a `..`-only arm and an own-`Drop` struct. All
agree, against three disagreeing cells before. Fixtures for both spellings, with
a CODEGEN TWIN sharing the `match` expectations -- that backend was correct on
every row, so an interpreter-only fixture would keep passing while the two
drifted, and "they agree" is the property. The `bound-local` and `no-binding`
rows are in the fixture precisely because they are what a later widening on
either side would break silently. Full `--features llvm` suite 16,022 passed /
0 failed; both clippy legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.

ON THE ROW'S CLOSING QUESTION -- "worth checking whether one fix reaches both"
(B-2026-08-30-15, the compiled backends losing the same scrutinee's OWN body).
It does not, and they are independent: -15 was fixed separately in ed13ce3 while
this was open, and this row's programs were re-measured against that tree before
any change here -- the interpreter still lost the FIELD body with -15 already
fixed. Two backends, two mechanisms, no shared fix.

FOUND, NOT FIXED, and split out as its own row rather than widened into here:
`if let` / `while let` over an `Option` with a STRUCT payload lose the body
where `match` runs it. MEASURED AGAINST THE PRE-FIX TREE so the attribution is
not a guess -- both were already broken before this change, so it is neither
fallout nor a regression. It is a different scrutinee shape (an enum whose
payload is a struct, not a struct scrutinee) reaching a different exclusion, and
folding it in would risk exactly the "moves the divergence rather than removing
it" trade this file records elsewhere.

title: THE INTERPRETER SKIPS THE PARTIALLY-MOVED RESIDUE'S OWN `Drop` BODY WHEN AN ARM DESTRUCTURES AN `Option`-WRAPPED PAYLOAD -- `Some(H { r, .. })` prints `dR[a]` where both compiled backends print `dH dR[a]`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residual of B-2026-08-31-27, measured after its fix landed. That fix made the interpreter run the moved-out FIELD's body (it previously ran nothing at all here); what it does not run is the payload struct's OWN body.

    struct R { s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR[{self.s}]") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }
    impl Drop for H { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dH") } }
    let o: Option[H] = Some(H { r: R { s: "a" }, n: 4 });
    match o { Some(H { r, .. }) => println(r.s), None => {} }

    --interp     : a dR[a] end
    karac run    : a dH dR[a] end
    karac build  : a dH dR[a] end

WHETHER `dH` IS DUE AT ALL IS THE REAL QUESTION, and it should be settled before either backend is changed. `H`'s `drop` body runs against a value one of whose fields has been moved out, so the body can observe a cleared field -- the hazard B-2026-08-31-2 raises for the `let m = s.r` spelling and that design.md does not currently answer. Two defensible resolutions: (a) both backends run it, and the interpreter is fixed to match compiled; (b) the ownership checker rejects a move out of a value with its own `impl Drop`, and the shape stops existing. Pick one in design.md first; the code change is small either way.

The whole-bound spelling `match o { Some(p) => println(p.n) }` runs `dH dR[a]` on EVERY backend, so the interpreter already agrees whenever nothing is moved out of the payload -- which is what makes this specifically about the partially-moved residue.

RELOCATED to B-2026-09-01-38 (2026-09-01). This row asked which backend is
right and noted the question "design.md does not currently answer". IT DOES
ANSWER, at line 9240 (Part 8: `Drop`, "Interaction with move semantics"):
partial moves out of a struct field are REJECTED when the struct has a `Drop`
impl, because the drop body assumes all fields are present. So neither backend
is right -- the program should not compile, and resolution (b) of the two this
row offered is the one the spec already picked.

Nothing enforces that rule today, which is what B-2026-09-01-38 tracks, together
with the sharper consequence found while checking this: the BARE spelling
`match h { H { r, .. } }` runs `R`'s drop body TWICE on both compiled backends,
the second time on the moved-from slot after zeroing (`dR[d:3]` then `dR[:0]`).

No action item here in the meantime, and deliberately so. Aligning the
interpreter to the compiled backends -- the small fix this row's divergence
invites -- would make BOTH backends run a `Drop` body against a partially-moved
value, which is the exact hazard the design.md sentence gives as its rationale,
and the work would be discarded when the rejection rule lands. When
B-2026-09-01-38 is resolved this shape stops existing and this divergence goes
with it; if the decision instead comes down the other way, file a FRESH id
citing this row rather than reopening it.

title: A STRUCT LITERAL WHOSE HEAP FIELD IS A PROJECTION OFF A FRESH TEMP DOUBLE-FREES ON AOT WHILE THE INTERPRETER IS CLEAN -- `let w = V { v: mkv(1).v, b: 1 };` where `mkv` returns a `V` carrying a `Vec[i64]` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` under `karac build` and prints normally under `--interp`; the `String` twin (`let w = P { a: mkp(1).a, b: 1 };`) behaves identically
detail:
MEMORY CORRUPTION AND A RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE IN ONE, in a plain `let` with
no discard, no branch and no `Drop` impl anywhere in the program.

    struct V { v: Vec[i64], b: i64 }
    struct P { a: String, b: i64 }
    fn mkv(n: i64) -> V { let mut q: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); q.push(n); return V { v: q, b: n }; }
    fn mkp(n: i64) -> P { return P { a: payload(), b: n }; }

                                              interp        jit / aot
    let w = V { v: mkv(1).v, b: 1 }; ..       (normal)      double free
    let w = P { a: mkp(1).a, b: 1 }; ..       (normal)      double free

    CONTROL -- the same read NOT consumed by a literal:  clean on both
    let q = mkv(1).v; ..
    let q = mkp(1).a; ..

THE CONTROL LOCALIZES IT. Reading a heap field off a fresh temp is handled
correctly on its own; it is consuming that read INTO A STRUCT LITERAL that
goes wrong. The field aliases the temp's buffer rather than copying it, the
temp keeps its own cleanup, and the literal's owner frees the same pointer
again. Same shape as the container-rooted family that B-2026-08-28-32 /
-33 / -42 closed (`ps[0].word` and friends), but rooted at a FUNCTION-RETURN
temp rather than a container element, which is why those fixes do not cover
it.

PRE-EXISTING, and the check is recorded because the row was found during a
neighbouring fix: measured byte-identical at `c4af3243`, the commit before
B-2026-08-29-31 taught the discard path to own an arm's value at all. Neither
that row nor B-2026-08-29-32 introduced it, and B-2026-08-29-32's guard exists
specifically to avoid making it worse -- registering the discarded-branch
spelling of the same literal turned a 38 B leak into this double free, which
is why that fix declines any field initializer it cannot prove is freshly
minted.

WHERE TO START: whatever clones a container-element heap read before it is
consumed by an owning aggregate, and why the fn-return-temp root does not
reach it. The interpreter is the oracle here -- it gets this right.

SOURCE NOTE: found as `C06`/`A01`/`A02` in B-2026-08-29-32's control matrix;
pinned in `codegen::e2e_discarded_branch_of_body_less_heap_literals_keeps_one_-
owner`'s neighbourhood only as the shape the guard declines, NOT as a passing
assertion -- this row's own shape has no test yet.
fix:
Fixed in 2b3b966. SIX MISSING CALL SITES OF A HELPER THAT ALREADY EXISTED.

ROOT CAUSE. `consume_freshtemp_field_move` (`src/codegen/expr_ops.rs`) is the
move-consumer companion of `track_freshtemp_field_access_object`: when a
consuming position takes exactly the staged field access, it zeroes that field's
heap in the temp's slot, so the temp's struct drop frees only the UNREAD
remainder. `let a = mkp(1).a;` has done this since B-2026-07-22-2.

It was hooked at the `let` / assign / `return` / fn-tail sites and at the
ORDINARY call-argument path -- and at NONE of the aggregate-literal consume
sites. So the identical read consumed by an owning aggregate left the temp's
cleanup armed while the aggregate took the same pointer, and both freed it. The
six sites now call it: the three struct-literal initializer loops
(`exprs.rs`), the two enum struct-variant initializer loops and the two
variant-constructor argument loops (`call_dispatch.rs`), the array and
vec-prefix literal element loops (`collections.rs`), and the tuple element loop
(`expr_ops.rs`). The helper self-gates on the staged slot matching the field
name AND the object span, so every other initializer no-ops.

THE ROW UNDER-DESCRIBED THE AXIS, and the probe matrix is why the fix is six
sites rather than one. The row recorded a struct literal. Measured on the
pre-fix compiler, ALL of these abort with `free(): double free detected in
tcache 2` on both compiled backends while `--interp` prints normally:

    P { a: mkp(1).a, b: 1 }        struct literal, String field
    V { v: mkv(1).v, b: 1 }        struct literal, Vec field
    W { a: mkp(1).a }              single-field struct literal
    [mkp(1).a]                     Vec literal element
    (mkp(1).a, 1)                  tuple element
    E.Ea { a: mkp(1).a }           enum struct-variant initializer
    T.Ta(mkp(1).a)                 enum tuple-variant ctor argument
    Some(mkp(1).a)                 Option ctor argument

and these were already correct, which is what localizes it to the DESTINATION's
kind rather than to the read:

    let t = mkp(1); P { a: t.a, b: 1 }    the read bound to a local first
    P { a: payload(1), b: 1 }             a DIRECT call as the initializer
    let a = mkp(1).a;                     the read at a plain `let`
    takes(mkp(1).a)                       an ORDINARY call argument

The row's "WHERE TO START" pointed at `clone_vec_elem_heap_field_read`, the
container-element cloner B-2026-08-28-32/-33/-42 built. That was the right
family to suspect and the wrong mechanism: that walker bails at `_ => return
Ok(val)` when the projection's root is a `Call` rather than an `Index`, and
CLONING is not what this shape needs anyway -- the temp is dying, so the read is
a MOVE and the existing takeover is both cheaper and already correct everywhere
else.

A SEVENTH SITE, FOUND BY THE GATE AND NOT BY REASONING, and it is the half of
this fix worth reading. The first cut passed both new fixtures and then failed
`asan_discarded_branch_of_body_less_heap_literals_frees_once` with
`LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks, 32 byte(s)` -- the LEAK direction, in the
one fixture built specifically to guard it.

B-2026-08-29-32's `field_init_aliases_a_temp` DECLINES to register a discarded
branch literal as an owner when it cannot prove a field initializer is freshly
minted, and `V { v: mkv(1).v }` was exactly such an initializer. Its doc comment
gives the reason: "the aliasing is PRE-EXISTING and is not this row's to repair
-- the `let`-BOUND spelling of the same literal already double-frees". That
premise is precisely what THIS row repaired. With the takeover in place the temp
no longer owns the field, and with the guard still declining, the literal did not
own it either: nobody freed it.

So the guard is narrowed to admit exactly what the takeover transfers -- a field
read whose object is a fresh owned temp, via the same `expr_yields_fresh_owned_-
temp` predicate `track_freshtemp_field_access_object` gates on. A place rooted at
a NAMED local (`P { a: t.a }`) still declines, which is the false negative that
guard's own history warns about at length.

The lesson generalizes past this row: a fix that TRANSFERS ownership has a second
failure mode that its own fixtures cannot see, because the transferred-from side
looks correct in isolation. Only a guard elsewhere that was declining ON THE
STRENGTH of the old aliasing will notice, and only under LSan.

FIXTURES, two, because this is a memory error and not only a text divergence.
`e2e_a_fresh_temp_field_read_consumed_by_an_aggregate_frees_once`
(tests/codegen.rs, 13 rows) pins the text over all eight broken shapes plus the
four controls; `asan_a_fresh_temp_field_read_consumed_by_an_aggregate_frees_once`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) is the memory gate and carries a
`two_fields_one_taken` LEAK-direction control. That control is the point of the
second fixture: the fix TRANSFERS ownership, so getting it wrong in the other
direction -- zeroing a field the aggregate never took -- leaks silently and
prints correctly. `mk2` returns a temp with two heap fields and the literal
takes one; the other must still be freed by the temp, which LSan checks on the
Linux CI leg only.

TWO FIXTURE-AUTHORING TRAPS HIT WHILE WRITING THIS, both mine and both worth
recording. A `struct V` in the prelude collided with an enum variant named `V`
-- the flat-namespace shadowing hazard the ledger tracks -- and the symptom was
not a name error but `codegen: no handler for method 'len' on variable 'a'`,
which reads like a codegen gap. And enum variant names are Type-class, so
`EA` / `TN` are rejected outright; the renames are `Ea` / `Tn`.

RED-VERIFIED: with all six sites reverted, the E2E fixture's first row fails
with `left: ""` (the process aborts before printing) and the ASAN fixture fails
outright.

GATES. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both clippy legs clean; full
`cargo test --features llvm` battery green.

title: A DISCARDED BRANCH WHOSE ARM LITERAL CONSUMES A LOCAL RUNS THAT LOCAL'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON ALL THREE BACKENDS -- `let t = mkd(7); let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } } else { .. };` prints `dD7` twice, once at the discard and once at the local's own scope end; the projected spelling (`W { r: t.r, .. }` over a local `W`) doubles identically
detail:
AN AGREED GAP, not a divergence: interpreter, JIT and AOT all print the same
doubled transcript, which is why no A/B parity gate has ever caught it.

    struct D { a: String, b: i64 }
    impl Drop for D { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dD{self.b}") } }
    struct W { r: D, b: i64 }

                                                          all three backends
    let t = mkd(7); let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } } else { .. };
                                                          dD7 dD7   (want dD7)
    let t = mkw(7); let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: t.r, b: 1 } } else { .. };
                                                          dD7 dD7   (want dD7)

    CONTROL 1 -- the same move, BOUND instead of discarded:  dD7 once, correct
    let t = mkd(7); let w = W { r: t, b: 1 }; println(f"b{w.b}");

    CONTROL 2 -- the arm MINTS its field instead of consuming a local:
    let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: mkd(7), b: 1 } } else { .. };   dD7 once, correct

    CONTROL 3 -- the field is projected off a fresh TEMP, not a local:
    let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: mkw(7).r, b: 1 } } else { .. }; dD7 once, correct

CONTROL 1 IS THE DIAGNOSIS. The bound spelling of the identical move retracts
the local's scope-end body correctly; only the DISCARDED spelling fails to,
so the discard path is registering an owner for the literal without marking
the consumed local moved-out. Controls 2 and 3 rule out "struct literals in
arms" and "projections" as the trigger -- it is specifically consuming a LIVE
LOCAL.

PRE-EXISTING: measured byte-identical at `c4af3243`, before B-2026-08-29-31
taught this path to own an arm's value, and on the interpreter -- which no
codegen-only change can reach -- so it predates both that row and
B-2026-08-29-32.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT from B-2026-08-31-34: that one is memory corruption in a
BOUND literal and diverges between backends; this one is a doubled BODY in a
DISCARDED literal and all backends agree. A fix for either should be checked
against the other's controls.

WHERE TO START: the moved-out marking B-2026-08-29-31 added for an arm tail
that NAMES a local (`discard_arm_tail_is_ownable` / `cond_move_escaping_sites`)
reaches a bare identifier tail but not a local CONSUMED BY A LITERAL in that
tail. Extending the same retraction through struct-literal field initializers
is the likely shape, on both backends together.

SOURCE NOTE: found as `Q1`/`Q3` in B-2026-08-29-32's control matrix. Pinned as
a KNOWN DEFECT (not asserted correct) in
`codegen::e2e_discarded_branch_of_body_less_heap_literals_keeps_one_owner` and
its interpreter twin, on both sides, so a one-sided fix fails loudly.

PROGRESS + CORRECTION (2026-09-01). The BOUND half of this family is fixed;
this row's own DISCARD repro is not, and stays open. The diagnosis above is
wrong in a way that matters, so it is corrected here rather than left to
mislead the next reader.

THE TRIGGER IS THE WRAPPER, NOT THE DISCARD. "CONTROL 1 IS THE DIAGNOSIS" reads
the bound spelling as correct and concludes "only the DISCARDED spelling fails
to [retract]". CONTROL 1 is the UNCONDITIONAL bound spelling, and it is the
only bound spelling that works. Measured on all three backends:

    let w = W { r: t, b: 1 };                          dD7        correct
    let w = { W { r: t, b: 1 } };                      dD7 dD7    doubled
    let w = if n == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } } else { .. } dD7 dD7    doubled
    let w = match n { 0 => { W { r: t, b: 1 } } .. }   dD7 dD7    doubled

A BARE BLOCK doubles with no branch anywhere in it, so the population is "an
aggregate literal at a value-position TAIL"; the branch arm and the discard are
members of it, not the axis. The unconditional `let` escapes only because
`stmts.rs` retracts its sources statically (the `struct_lit_sources` loop),
which a tail behind a wrapper cannot do -- one arm runs, and a static
retraction disarms on all paths or none.

THE PROJECTED SPELLING IS WORSE THAN FILED. This row records `W { r: t.r, .. }`
over a local `W` as doubling identically on all three. It doubles on the
INTERPRETER, but on JIT and AOT it is a DOUBLE FREE
(`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`), which glibc detects only
sometimes -- 1 run in 5 aborted, the rest printed `dD7 .. dD7` and exited 0.
Verified PRE-EXISTING by rebuilding at 64332f5, so it is not a consequence of
anything landed since; the intermittent detection is why it was recorded as a
doubled body.

WHAT LANDED. The per-path machinery already existed and reached one shape too
few: a bare IDENTIFIER tail (`if c { t } else { u }`) has been correct since
B-2026-08-28-51 via an `i1` drop flag cleared in the arm's own basic block, but
both backends' hooks matched `ExprKind::Identifier` and nothing else, so the
same move one aggregate deeper was invisible. Widened both to
`collect_aggregate_literal_sources` -- codegen
`clear_cond_move_flags_for_tail_sources`, interpreter
`record_conditional_move_tail`. Every bound spelling above is now one body on
all three backends, including the MIXED case (two arms consuming two different
locals) where the non-taken arm's source keeps its own body -- the case a
static retraction cannot express. Pinned as
`codegen::e2e_an_arm_literal_consuming_a_local_runs_one_body`, which asserts
the interpreter and AOT transcripts together so the two cannot drift apart.

WHAT REMAINS -- this row's own repro. `let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } }
else { .. };` still prints `dD7 dD7`, agreed on all three backends. It is not
reachable from the same hook: a discarded arm is deliberately NOT an escaping
site (`note_escaping_site`), so the flag is never cleared there. The two-tail
discard also yields its value to the STATEMENT-level site
(`try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp`) at the MERGE, where the taken arm is no
longer known, so the disarm has to be emitted in the arm and the decision to
register is made after it. A leg was written for the ARM-level owner
(`track_discarded_arm_owned_aggregate`) and REVERTED: it is reached only by the
no-`else` spelling, and no measurement attributed any change to it, so it was
not worth carrying unmeasured. Closing this needs either seeding the escaping
set for discarded arms whose registration is already decided, or moving the
two-tail discard onto the arm-level owner.

DO NOT decline the registration instead. Measured: declining at the merge loses
the ELSE arm's minted body -- `let _ = if false { W { r: t, .. } } else
{ W { r: mkd(9), .. } };` correctly prints `dD9 dD7` today, and a blanket
decline drops the `dD9`.

SOURCE NOTE: a `BARE if` with NO `else` in statement position was found to be a
PRE-EXISTING run-vs-build divergence in the same area (interpreter doubles,
both compiled backends run one body) -- confirmed on pristine `main`, so it
predates this work. Filed separately.
fix:
FIXED by e49a85f -- the WHOLE-LOCAL move, in every discarded spelling. The
PROJECTED spelling and the BLOCK-wrapper spellings remain and are filed as
B-2026-09-01-17 and B-2026-09-01-18.

THE GATE IS "DOES THIS DISCARD SITE OWN THE VALUE", and both backends already
had everything else. Each disarms an arm tail's aggregate-literal sources on
the path that hands them over -- codegen's
`clear_cond_move_flags_for_tail_sources`, the interpreter's
`record_conditional_move_tail`, both widened past a bare `Identifier` by this
row's earlier pass. What neither did was REACH that disarm for a DISCARDED
branch: a discarded statement is deliberately not an escaping site, on the
stated ground that "its arm tails go nowhere and marking them takes a program
that runs one body today to zero". That ground holds exactly when nothing owns
the result -- and `discarded_match_value_tail` is precisely the predicate for
when something does.

So the exclusion is readmitted on that condition and no wider. Codegen seeds
`note_escaping_stmt_sites` for a wildcard `let` and a bare statement when that
same predicate admits the construct, so seeding can never outrun registration.
The interpreter disarms the TAKEN arm's sources at the three sites that make
the ownership decision (`disarm_discarded_tail_sources`, keyed on
`taken_branch_tail` -- the per-path bit codegen expresses as an `i1` cleared in
the arm's own basic block).

An arm handing out a bare live local is declined by the predicate -- an
`Identifier` is not a fresh owned temp -- which is what preserves the
exclusion's own population unchanged.

DID NOT decline the registration instead, as the row's WHAT REMAINS note warns:
that loses the else arm's minted body. Pinned by the mixed-branch controls,
which still print `dD9 dD7` and `dR7 dR8`.

MEASURED, all four surfaces (`--interp`, JIT, `karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0
karac build`) byte-identical on every row:

                                                    before        after
    let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } } .. ;     dD7 dD7       dD7
    let _ = match n { 0 => { W { r: t, .. } } .. }; dD7 dD7       dD7
    if n == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } } .. ;             dD7 dD7       dD7
    ELSE taken (t never consumed)                   dD9 dD7       dD9 dD7
    mixed arms, two locals                          --            dR7 dR8
    bound spelling / all-mint arm / direct literal   one body      unchanged

THE PINNED PAIR MOVED TOGETHER. `codegen::e2e_discarded_branch_of_body_less_
heap_literals_keeps_one_owner` and its interpreter twin were pinned at the
doubled transcript on BOTH sides so a one-sided change fails loudly, and that
is exactly what happened while this was being written: the codegen half went
green and the interpreter twin failed the default leg, which is how the missing
interpreter half was found rather than shipped. Both now assert one body, and
five discarded cases were added to
`codegen::e2e_an_arm_literal_consuming_a_local_runs_one_body` -- verified RED
without the fix (`dR7 dR7` against `dR7`) and green with it.

VERIFIED: default `cargo test --no-fail-fast` 10219 passed / 0 failed;
`--features llvm` 15958 / 0; `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` 1346 passed / 1 failed,
matching its one-line quarantine exactly; fmt and both clippy legs clean.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN PROSE -- the projected spelling is NOT a double
free. The 2026-09-01 note records `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` on
JIT and AOT, glibc-detecting about 1 run in 5. Not reproducible: 0 non-zero
exits over 20 runs and valgrind-clean at the default -O2 AND at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, including a 5-iteration loop (10 bodies, 0 errors), on the
exact program the row prints. Also clean at `ebaacfc`, a tree predating both of
2026-09-01's discarded-branch commits, so nothing landed since is masking it.
The memory is balanced and the second body runs over the moved-from husk. The
doubled BODY reproduced exactly as filed; only the memory half does not.

title: THE INTERPRETER BINDS THE WHOLE CONTAINER, NOT THE ELEMENT, FOR `let g = ref c[i]` WHEN `c` IS A `Slice` OR A `Map` -- codegen and the typechecker both say `i64`, the interpreter says `Slice`
detail:
THE INTERPRETER BINDS THE WHOLE CONTAINER, NOT THE ELEMENT, FOR `let g = ref
c[i]` WHEN `c` IS A `Slice` OR A `Map` -- codegen reads the element, so the two
backends disagree on a spelling both accept.

Found while fixing B-2026-08-31-29 (the codegen half of the same spelling over
an `Array` base) and NOT that bug: this half is the interpreter's, and it is
wrong on container classes B-2026-08-31-29 left correct.

    fn main() {
        let v: Vec[i64] = [10, 20, 30];
        let s: Slice[i64] = v.as_slice();
        let g = ref s[2];
        println(g);          // interp: [10, 20, 30]   codegen: 30
    }

The binding is wrong, not the rendering -- `g` really is a `Slice`, which an
arithmetic use makes explicit:

    let t: i64 = g + 5;
    // runtime error: operator 'Add' is not defined for operands of type
    // 'Slice' and 'Int'

The `Map` spelling has the same shape (`let h = ref m[1]` on a
`Map[i64, i64]` holding `1 -> 42` prints `{1: 42}`, not `42`), and there the
divergence is currently masked because codegen DECLINES a Map base rather than
lowering it -- see the sibling row on that decline's message. So the live
run-vs-build divergence today is the SLICE one; the Map one becomes live the
moment a Map base gains a codegen lowering.

MEASURED -- THE TYPECHECKER IS NOT INVOLVED, and this is the part that makes
the row actionable. On the arithmetic program above, `karac check` reports "All
checks passed" and `karac build` produces 35 (30 + 5, correct). So the checker
types `g` as `i64`, agreeing with codegen, and the interpreter is alone in
binding the container. That also means the interpreter's own error text is
misleading: it says "this is a type error the typechecker reports as a hard
error; it reached the interpreter only because `karac run` executes despite
typecheck errors", and the typechecker reports no error here at all. Whatever
emits that note is inferring a typecheck failure it did not observe -- worth a
look while fixing this, though it is a separate thread.

NOT MEASURED:
  - `SortedMap` / `SortedSet` / `VecDeque` bases, and the `mut ref` spelling.
  - Whether the fix belongs at the interpreter's `ref` binding site or in
    whatever computes the index place for a non-Vec container.

The Vec and Array bases are correct on both backends and covered by
`e2e_ref_binding_over_an_array_base_reads_the_element` and its interpreter twin;
a fix here should extend that shared fixture rather than start a new one.
fix:
FIXED by 8ba5e95f. One arm was the whole cause: `eval_ref_borrow` matched
`Value::Array` alone and fell through to `return obj`, so every other container
base bound the CONTAINER rather than the element.

    if let (Value::Array(arc), Value::Int(i)) = (&obj, &iv) { ... ElemRef ... }
    return obj;                       // Slice and Map land HERE

A slice element IS an element of the backing array, so `Value::ElemRef`
represents it exactly -- same storage, index shifted by the window's start.
That equivalence is why the fix needs no new `Value` variant and why the
aliasing contract holds for free: a write through the parent `Vec` is visible
through the borrow, which is what the compiled backends already do.

THE MISSING BOUNDS CHECK IS HALF THE FIX, and the row did not have it.
`ref s[7]` on a two-element slice returned the container while all three
compiled surfaces panicked with "slice index out of bounds" -- so the old path
checked nothing at all for a slice. The new arm checks the WINDOW's length, not
the backing store's.

`Map` and `SortedMap` now DECLINE rather than binding the container. Returning
the map's value would read plausibly -- plain `m[1]` is 42 on every backend --
but it would be a `ref` that does not alias, and codegen refuses to build the
program regardless. An agreed refusal beats one backend inventing a
non-aliasing reference.

THE ROW'S "NOT MEASURED" LIST, ANSWERED:
  - `SortedMap` behaves exactly like `Map` (declines now, declined in codegen
    already), which widens the sibling row B-2026-08-31-37 to that class too.
  - `SortedSet` and `String` do not support indexing on ANY backend -- the
    typechecker rejects them before this code is reached.
  - `VecDeque` was already correct on all four surfaces.
  - `mut ref v[2]` is a PARSE ERROR on every base, `Vec` included ("'mut' is a
    reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier"). It is not an
    accepted `let` form, so that spelling has no divergence behind it.
  - The fix belongs at the interpreter's `ref` binding site, not in the index
    place computation -- the second of the row's two candidates.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SIBLING ROW. B-2026-08-31-37 proposes that codegen's
`Map`-base decline say "run with `--interp`" as the workaround. That wording is
now WRONG: the interpreter declines a `Map` element `ref` too, so it would send
a user to a backend that also refuses. The message should say the spelling is
unsupported on every backend and point at plain `m[k]`, which works everywhere.

MEASURED, seven container bases x four surfaces. `Vec` / `Array` / `VecDeque`
are unchanged; the arithmetic case (`g + 5`) goes from a hard "operator 'Add' is
not defined for operands of type 'Slice' and 'Int'" to the due 35 on all four.
Extends the shared `ref`-binding fixture in both test files rather than starting
a new one, as the row asked. Pre-fix the interpreter half fails and the codegen
half PASSES -- codegen was always right here, so its twin is the oracle.

The diagnostic is built with `concat!`: written as a `\`-continued literal,
rustfmt rejoins it and freezes the continuation indentation into the SHIPPED
text as 22 real spaces. `diagnostic_text_hygiene` caught exactly that here
(B-2026-08-21-45) -- the message had already been eyeballed and cleared before
the lint rejected it.

title: A `Map` BASE FOR `let g = ref m[k]` DECLINES WITH THE INTERNAL STRING `unreachable: Ref handled in compile_expr` -- no span, and the state is plainly reachable
detail:
A `Map` BASE FOR `let g = ref m[k]` DECLINES WITH AN INTERNAL MESSAGE --
`codegen failed: unreachable: Ref handled in compile_expr`, no span, no source
construct, and the word "unreachable" for a state that is plainly reachable.

Follow-up to B-2026-08-31-29, and a direct consequence of its fix. Before that
fix a Map base was lowered as though its slot were a `{ptr, i64, i64}` Vec
header and SEGFAULTED at runtime, exactly as the `Array` base did; the fix makes
the named-local `ref` arm classify the container and decline anything it has no
layout for. Declining is the right call -- `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_map` exists,
but the INTERPRETER binds the whole map for this spelling (sibling row), so
wiring codegen alone would convert a segfault into a run-vs-build divergence.
Trading a memory-safety bug for a loud build error is a strict improvement; the
message it lands on is not.

    fn main() {
        let mut m: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new();
        m.insert(1, 42);
        let g = ref m[1];
        println(g);
    }
    // error: codegen failed: unreachable: Ref handled in compile_expr

Two things are wrong with it. It is an INTERNAL invariant string leaking to a
user, and it is inaccurate: the arm is reached whenever `try_compile_ref_binding`
declines, which is now a normal, expected outcome rather than an impossible one.
A user reading it has no way to learn that the actual limitation is "a `ref`
binding over a Map element is not supported by the compiled backends".

The fix is a structured diagnostic with the operand's span, naming the container
class and saying `--interp` is the workaround -- the shape the neighbouring
codegen-gap messages already use (e.g. "cannot resolve field '{}' on this
receiver ... this is a compiler gap -- run with `--interp`"). Wiring the Map
lowering for real is the larger alternative and depends on the interpreter
question in the sibling row; the diagnostic is worth doing either way, because
it is also what a user hits for any FUTURE container class the arm declines.

NOT MEASURED: which other spellings reach the same `unreachable:` arm, and
whether the same string is emitted from other `Ref` paths.
fix:
FIXED by 15f91338, for the MESSAGE half. The span half is not done and is filed
separately -- see the end of this note.

`try_compile_ref_binding` returned `Ok(false)` at three sites it cannot lower,
and each fell through to `compile_unaryop`'s `UnaryOp::Ref` arm, which has
neither the operand nor a span and so could only print the invariant string.
Those sites now build the message themselves, where the container and the
expression are in hand.

TWO CASES, TWO MESSAGES, which is the substance rather than a rewording:

  * a `Map` element has no stable address to borrow -- a rehash moves it -- and
    the INTERPRETER declines the spelling too since B-2026-08-31-36. So
    `--interp` is NOT a workaround; the message says so and points at plain
    `m[k]`, which works on every backend.
  * any other base (a nested `ref v[0][1]`, a field base codegen could not
    type) IS handled by the interpreter, so the standard `--interp` pointer the
    neighbouring codegen-gap messages use is accurate there.

THIS ROW'S OWN PRESCRIPTION WAS STALE, which is worth recording because it was
correct when filed. The row asks for the `--interp` wording on the `Map`
message; B-2026-08-31-36 landed hours earlier and made the interpreter decline
that spelling, so following the row literally would have shipped advice sending
a user to a backend that also refuses.

The `unreachable:` arm was INACCURATE, not merely unhelpful -- it is reachable
from any `ref` outside the let-binding path -- so it now says that plainly
instead of asserting the state cannot happen.

A STALE COMMENT came with it. `try_compile_ref_binding` justified not wiring a
`Map` base by saying `let g = ref m[k]` binds the whole map under the
interpreter too. B-2026-08-31-36 changed that. The conclusion holds and the
REASON inverted: wiring codegen now would create the divergence in the opposite
direction, and a map element has no address to bind regardless. Corrected in
place, because a comment whose stated reason is false is worse than none.

MEASURED by execution, not by reading the source: `Map` and `SortedMap` get the
class-named message, a nested `ref v[0][1]` gets the `--interp` one, and the
`Vec` / `Slice` controls still build and print 30. The test asserts CONTENT --
internal string gone, class named, `--interp` present for exactly the case
where it is true -- so it survives rewording.

TWO HONEST LIMITS. The `Set` arm of the class predicate is deliberate but
UNREACHABLE today: `Set[i64]` rejects indexing at typecheck, so `ref s[i]` never
reaches codegen's decline. Only the `Map` path is exercised. And the SPAN half
of this row is not built: codegen's error channel is a bare `String` rendered as
`error: codegen failed: {e}`, with no span plumbing anywhere -- every
neighbouring codegen-gap message carries none either -- so a span needs the
channel itself reworked, which is a great deal larger than this row. Filed as
its own row rather than left implied here.

title: `if let Some(H { r, .. }) = o` OVER AN `Option`-WRAPPED STRUCT PAYLOAD RUNS NO `Drop` BODY AT ALL ON EITHER COMPILED BACKEND -- the `match` spelling of the same pattern is correct, so it is the `if let` leg alone
fix:
FIXED by 1849e2e. The `if let` / `while let` / `let ... else` legs called
`suppress_optres_payload_bodies_for_match` UNCONDITIONALLY. That retraction
disarms the SOURCE's `__karac_dropelems_opt_*` / `_res_*` action on the premise,
stated in its own doc, that "the arm's binding owns the resource from then on".
For a BORROW binding that premise is false -- nothing owns the payload -- so the
body was retracted with no owner to run it, and it ran nowhere. Gating all three
call sites on the `optres_bindings_owned` flag already computed a few lines
above them closes it; that is the same omission, in the same three legs, that
B-2026-09-01-10 fixed one call below for `suppress_boxed_payload_struct_
destructure`.

THE ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND ITS EXPLANATION OF THE `match` CONTROL WAS
NOT, which matters because the wrong half is what makes the fix look risky. The
row named `suppress_optres_payload_bodies_for_match` as "the first place to
look" and that was exactly right. But it said the `match` leg "reaches it
through the read-through gate" -- it does not reach it at all. Traced with the
call instrumented: for this program `pattern_binding_is_borrow` is TRUE on the
`match` leg, and its whole suppression battery sits behind
`scrut_ref_ptr.is_none() && !pattern_binding_is_borrow`, so the retraction never
fires there and the source's payload-bodies walk still runs the body. That is
why `match` was correct, and it is also the argument that the gate is right
rather than merely convenient: the fix gives the three `let`-family legs the
condition `match` has always had.

`let ... else` KEEPS FIRING, and measuring that was the difference between a
gate and a deletion. On the same program `optres_bindings_owned` is TRUE there
(`false` for `if let`), because a `let ... else` binding ESCAPES into the
enclosing scope and owns the payload; the retraction is correct on that leg and
the escaped binding's own drop runs the body. Deleting the call outright would
have doubled the body there. It is pinned as its own fixture row so a later
widening cannot quietly regress it.

THE ROW UNDER-REPORTED THE SURFACE BY ONE LEG. `while let Some(H { r, .. }) = q`
was broken identically and is closed by the same gate -- measured `44 end` (zero
bodies) on both compiled backends before, `44 dR44 end` after. The row recorded
`if let` only.

THE LEAK QUESTION THE ROW LEFT OPEN IS ANSWERED: NO LEAK, either way.
`valgrind --leak-check=full` at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` -- 11 allocs / 11 frees
pre-fix, 12 / 12 post (the extra pair is the restored body's own f-string), 0
errors from 0 contexts both times, on the `if let` and `while let` spellings
alike. The memory side was always balanced and only the user-visible body was
lost, so this stays a `run-vs-build` row and not a leak one, which is precisely
the determination the row asked for.

VERIFIED across all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run`, `karac build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`) on a 14-case matrix: five affected spellings
(`if let` with `..`, with every field named, with a renamed binding, over
`Result`, and `while let`) plus nine controls -- `let ... else`, the `match`
twin, a pattern binding nothing, a bare struct with no envelope, a user enum
wrapping the same payload, a payload that IS the `Drop` type, and the miss edge.

TESTS. `e2e_a_let_family_destructure_runs_the_payload_drop_body_once`
(tests/codegen.rs) carries the matrix, with SEPARATE interpreter and compiled
expectations so a known divergence is pinned deliberately rather than dropped
from the fixture. Verified to FAIL without the fix (`47 end` on the first row)
and pass with it. `asan_restored_let_family_payload_body_reads_live_memory`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) asks the question the E2E cannot: the restored body
dereferences `self.s`, so it proves the buffer it reads is still live and that
adding the body back introduces no second free. Its bodies are deliberately
CHATTY rather than silent for that reason, and it was checked against a
deliberately-wrong expectation to confirm ASAN really runs it rather than
skipping.

TWO PRE-EXISTING INTERPRETER FINDINGS came out of the matrix and are filed
rather than folded in, both confirmed against the stashed pre-fix compiler (and
neither reachable by this fix, which touches `src/codegen/control_flow.rs`
only):
  * B-2026-09-02-7 -- a `while let` arm that BINDS its payload runs the body
    TWICE per pass under `--interp` and once on both compiled backends; the
    surplus scales with the iteration count and the same loop binding nothing is
    correct everywhere.
  * B-2026-09-02-8 -- an `Option`-enveloped struct pattern binding only the
    NON-`Drop` field loses the body in the interpreter on BOTH the `if let` and
    `match` spellings, and the `let ... else` spelling of it loses the body on
    all four surfaces (agreed-and-wrong, so the A/B rule cannot catch that one).
Both are pinned as deliberately-divergent rows of the new fixture, so closing
either shows up here as a failure rather than passing unnoticed.

ID NOTE: those two were filed as B-2026-09-02-3 / -4 and renumbered to -7 /
-8 before landing, because a concurrent session published different bugs
under -3 and -4 while these were in flight. The ledger's id-allocation race,
exactly as CLAUDE.md describes it -- both sessions computed the same next id
from the same base, and the collision surfaced at the rebase rather than at
allocation.

title: AN `Option[T]` INSIDE A GENERIC FN REACHES THE DISPLAY GATE WITH `T` UNSUBSTITUTED, so an aggregate instantiation is declined or ICEs where the interpreter renders it -- `T = Vec[i64]` PANICS the compiler, `T = Array`/`Slice` refuse naming `T`, and DESTRUCTURING (the obvious workaround) is a SILENT miscompile printing `1` or nothing
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-31-25; PRE-EXISTING and independent of it --
confirmed on a clean 32d8186 build with none of that row's changes applied.

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) { println(f"{x}"); }

    show(Some(7))                    interp Some(7)      build Some(7)      <- CONTROL
    show(Some("hi"))                 interp Some(hi)     build Some(hi)     <- CONTROL
    show(Some(v))    T=Vec[i64]      interp Some([1])    build PANICS:
        emit_display_fn_for_type: type_name 'Vec' not yet supported
    show(Some(a))    T=Array[i64,2]  interp Some([1, 2]) build error: Display of
        `Option[T]` is not yet supported under codegen: its `T` payload cannot be
        reconstructed from the enum's inline payload words.
    show(Some(sl))   T=Slice[i64]    interp Some([1, 2]) same refusal

So the SCALAR instantiations monomorphize fine and the AGGREGATE ones do not:
the payload type reaching `is_reconstructable_display_payload` (and, for the
`Vec` case, `emit_display_fn_for_type_expr`) is the bare parameter `T`, not the
instantiated type. `T` is a `TypeKind::Path` with a segment matching no known
shape, so it falls to the predicate's final `enum_layouts.contains_key` and
answers false; the `Vec` spelling gets one step further and reaches the by-name
catch-all, which panics. The diagnostic naming "`T` payload" is the tell -- it
is printing the type parameter, which can never be a payload shape.

THE WORKAROUND IS WORSE THAN THE ERROR, which is what makes this more than a
missing feature. Destructuring inside the generic fn compiles and SILENTLY
MISPRINTS:

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) {
        match x { Some(t) => println(f"{t}"), None => println("n") }
    }
    T = Array[i64, 2]   interp [1, 2]   build 1          <- first element
    T = Vec[i64]        interp [1]      build (nothing)

Those are exactly the `Array`/`Vec` depth-0 failure modes B-2026-08-31-19 fixed
for the concrete spellings, so the generic path is reaching the pre-19 value-kind
arms -- more evidence that `T` is unsubstituted this far down rather than
substituted-but-unhandled.

TWO NOTES ON SCOPE. The `T = Vec` case is an ICE, not a diagnostic, so it
violates CLAUDE.md's "never just panic" rule even if the rest is deferred. And
`codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` (tests/codegen.rs) is the
fixture that will have to move when this is fixed: it currently pins its
diagnostic assertions on `Option[Slice[i64]]`, and if this row lands while
B-2026-08-31-40 also does, there may be no declined shape left to pin at all --
see that fixture's doc comment, which says what to do in that case.

NOT MEASURED: whether a generic METHOD (`impl S { fn show[T](...) }`) behaves the
same, and whether `Result[T, E]` in the same position differs from `Option[T]`.

DEPTH NOTE (2026-08-31, an investigating session that did NOT fix this). The
row's diagnosis is right -- the payload reaching the gate is the bare `T` -- but
the scope is understated, and the reason matters for whoever picks it up.

WHY THE SCALARS WORK, which the row could not explain: an `Option[T]` param is
displayed through the IDENTIFIER path (`try_compile_collection_display`), not
the span-keyed gate, and that path reads `var_option_payload_te`, registered in
the monomorph prologue from `subst_monomorph_type_params(param.ty)`. That
resolver has two channels and both are lossy in different ways, which is exactly
the observed split:

    T = i64, String      subst_names = {"T": "i64"}   works
    T = Vec[i64]         subst_names = {"T": "Vec"}   HEAD ONLY, element lost
                                                      -> by-name emitter ICEs
    T = Array[i64, 2]    subst_names = {}             NO ENTRY AT ALL
                                                      -> bare `T` reaches the gate

So `Vec` and `Array` fail for OPPOSITE reasons, and a fix must handle both.

WHAT WAS TRIED, and why it was reverted rather than landed. Adding a third
typechecker channel carrying the FULL resolved `TypeExpr` per param
(`call_type_subs_te`, built from `record_call_type_subs`'s `solutions` via
`type_to_type_expr`) and consulting it at the Display readers makes every
instantiation render correctly -- i64, String, Vec, Array, Slice, `Result[T,E]`,
and a generic METHOD (both of the row's NOT MEASURED items: both work). But it
also makes previously-REFUSED programs compile onto machinery that cannot carry
them, and each layer surfaced the next:

  1. Mono symbols collide for nameless type args, so two aggregate
     instantiations share one body -- `Array[2]` then `Array[3]` printed
     `[3, 4]` then `[7, 8]`, and an `Array` then a `Slice` printed
     `Some([94881993644816, 2])`, a raw pointer word rendered as an element.
     Filed as its own row; it is a LIVE bug today with no Display involved.
  2. Registering the param at its true instantiated type also reaches the
     DESTRUCTURING path, where the arm still unpacks an aggregate payload as one
     inline word. That turns this row's own noted silent miscompile (`d 3` for
     `[3, 4]`) into a SEGFAULT. The pattern tables are span-keyed and hold the
     uninstantiated `T` at 19 read sites.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, and the reason this is not a one-site fix: for a generic
function, EVERY span-keyed and binding-keyed type record in codegen holds the
uninstantiated `T`, and the monomorph's substitution channels are lossy. Making
one consumer correct exposes the next. A real fix is either (a) substituting the
type side-tables wholesale at monomorph entry, or (b) re-typechecking the
monomorph body -- both design changes rather than bug fixes, and both wanting
B-2026-08-31-48 landed first or alongside, or the Display fix trades a clean
refusal for silent garbage.

Everything above was measured, then the working tree was reverted; nothing from
this investigation is on `main`.

PARTIAL FIX, b2597b28 (2026-09-01) — the ICE half only; this row REMAINS OPEN.

The `T = Vec[i64]` instantiation no longer panics the compiler. It now takes the
same structured refusal its `Array` and `Slice` siblings take, so the
never-just-panic rule holds for this shape regardless of when the rest lands.

The cause was exactly as the DEPTH NOTE above diagnosed. The reconstructability
gate's handle-collection arm (`Vec | Map | Set | SortedMap | SortedSet`)
returned true on the SEGMENT NAME alone. For `T = Vec[i64]` the monomorph
records `{"T": "Vec"}` — head only — so a bare `Vec` path with no generic args
reached that arm, was admitted as a container, and went to the by-name emitter
with no element type to render, hitting its `panic!` catch-all. `Array`, having
no substitution entry, stayed a bare `T`, matched nothing and declined. The arm
now requires the generic args to be present: a head-only path is not something a
program can write, so no user spelling is affected, and the two instantiations
now fail the same way.

STILL OPEN, unchanged: rendering the aggregate instantiations at all. The depth
note's conclusion stands — substituting the monomorph's type side-tables
wholesale, or re-typechecking the body, wanting B-2026-08-31-48 alongside. The
narrow fix that was tried and reverted is still the wrong move for the reasons
recorded there.

ALSO STILL OPEN, and worth a separate look: the refusal's wording. It renders
the declined payload `TypeExpr`, which for a generic is literally `T`, so it
reads "its `T` payload cannot be reconstructed" — naming a type parameter as a
payload shape, which as this row says can never be one. Not chased here because
distinguishing an unsubstituted parameter from a user type named `T` needs a
heuristic that could misfire on legitimate declines, and the real fix removes the
message.

SECOND PARTIAL FIX, 78e1389 (2026-09-01) — the UNSOUND half; this row REMAINS OPEN.

The clean refusal this row treats as the safe status quo WAS NOT SAFE. It could
be bypassed, and what came through it was a silent miscompile or a segfault.

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) { println(f"{x}"); }

    show(Some(7));                      <- registers  x -> i64
    let v: Vec[i64] = vec![1];
    show(Some(v));                      <- DECLINED, inherits x -> i64

Measured pre-fix, interpreter correct on every line:

    i64 then Vec            build Some(94432365992720)   pointer word as i64
    i64 then Array          build Some(1)                first element
    i64 then Slice          build Some(94346364762896)
    String then Vec         build Some()                 control block as String
    String then Array       build <no output> rc=139     SEGFAULT
    all five in one program build <no output> rc=139     SEGFAULT
    Result, i64 then Vec    build Ok(94527773793040)
    generic METHOD, i64/Vec build 1:Some(93889133488912)

The last two answer both of this row's NOT MEASURED items: `Result[T, E]` in the
same position and a generic METHOD behave the SAME, and both were miscompiling
rather than refusing.

ORDER-DEPENDENT, which is the tell: reverse the two calls and `Vec` first
refuses cleanly, `i64` after it prints `Some(7)`. Each aggregate instantiation
ALONE also refuses. So the declined shape was never the damage — the entry left
behind by the previous instantiation was.

CAUSE. `var_option_payload_te` / `var_result_payload_te`
(`register_var_from_type_expr`, src/codegen/types_lowering.rs) are keyed by
BINDING NAME and outlive the function that registered them. When the payload is
not reconstructable the registration is declined — and, before this fix, nothing
retracted the entry a previous same-named binding had left, so
`try_compile_collection_display` found it and rendered THIS payload's words at
the PREVIOUS payload's type. Two monomorphs of one generic fn share their
parameter's name, which is what made it reachable without shadowing.

THE RULE ALREADY EXISTED, applied to one map and not these two. `slice_alias_md`
(src/codegen.rs) documents it outright -- "a name is dropped on any
re-registration (`register_var_from_type_expr`) so a shadowing local loses the
metadata". That is precisely the invariant these two tables needed and did not
have; the fix makes them consistent with it rather than inventing a policy.

This is also exactly the hole B-2026-08-31-49 closed, applied to one direction only.
That fix retracts the SIBLING map unconditionally (a stale `Result` entry
answering for an `Option` name) and its comment states the argument in full --
"when the payload is not reconstructable the registration below is declined, and
a stale entry ... then answered instead". The SAME-kind half was left registered,
and it is the half that segfaults. Both arms now retract both maps.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE ROW'S REMAINING WORK. It does not make a single aggregate
instantiation render; it makes the refusal hold. The depth note's conclusion is
untouched -- substituting the monomorph's type side-tables wholesale, or
re-typechecking the body, remains the real fix for the rendering half, and its
blocker B-2026-08-31-48 has since landed. What changes is the BASELINE that work
starts from: the depth note warned a narrow Display fix "trades a clean refusal
for silent garbage", and it was half right for a reason it did not know -- the
silent garbage was already there, reachable whenever a scalar instantiation
preceded an aggregate one.

Fixture: `codegen_declined_option_payload_does_not_inherit_a_stale_same_named_entry`
(tests/codegen.rs) -- five poisoned orderings asserted to take the structured
refusal, plus two controls: two DIFFERENT scalar instantiations must still both
render (the retraction must not clear an entry the current binding is about to
register successfully), and B-2026-08-31-49's own case must still pass. RED on
pristine main with "expected codegen to decline this program, but it compiled".

`codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` needs no move: the aggregates
are still declined, so its subject survives. Its standing instruction -- delete
the first assertion when -39 is fixed -- still refers to the RENDERING half.

STILL OPEN, unchanged: rendering the aggregate instantiations at all, and the
refusal's wording (it names the type parameter `T` as a payload shape).

THIRD FIX, def3015 (2026-09-01) — the RENDERING half. This row's headline
measurement is now closed; a NARROWER remainder is documented at the end.

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) { println(f"{x}"); }

Every instantiation in the row's opening table now renders, byte-identical
across all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT, `karac build`, and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`):

    T                 before                          after / interp
    i64               Some(7)                         Some(7)          (control)
    String            Some(hi)                        Some(hi)         (control)
    Vec[i64]          structured refusal              Some([1])
    Array[i64, 2]     structured refusal              Some([1, 2])
    Slice[i64]        structured refusal              Some([1, 2])

and so do six shapes the row never reached: `Vec[String]`, `Vec[Vec[i64]]`,
`Array[i64, 3]` beside `Array[i64, 2]` in ONE program, a TUPLE, `Result[T, E]`,
and a generic METHOD. The last two were this row's NOT MEASURED items; both
were miscompiling and both are fixed by the same change.

CAUSE, which is the DEPTH NOTE's diagnosis confirmed and given its missing
half. The note is right that the payload reaching the Display gate is the bare
`T`, and right that the two substitution channels are lossy in OPPOSITE ways
(`T = Vec[i64]` records the head `"Vec"` and drops the element; `T =
Array[i64, 2]` records nothing at all). What it does not say is that the gate
itself was never wrong. Every CONCRETE spelling of the same `Option` renders
correctly today on every surface — `Option[Vec[i64]]`, `Option[Array[i64, 2]]`,
`Option[Slice[i64]]`, in both the `f"{x}"` and the destructuring form —
measured before touching anything. So the machinery to render these payloads
already existed and was complete; it was being handed half a type.

That reframes the fix. The note's two candidates were "substitute the type
side-tables wholesale at monomorph entry" or "re-typecheck the monomorph body",
both design changes, and both aimed at making every span-keyed record concrete.
Neither is needed to close the rendering half, because only ONE resolver feeds
the Display path: `subst_monomorph_type_params`. Giving THAT function an exact
answer is a channel addition, not a rewrite.

THE FIX is a third per-call-site channel, `call_type_subs_te`, carrying the FULL
resolved `TypeExpr` the solver bound each type param to. It is built in
`record_call_type_subs` from the same `solutions` map the existing two channels
read, via `type_to_type_expr`, and threaded to
`mono_state.type_subst_call_te` alongside its two siblings.

Its PRECEDENCE is the whole design and is stated at the field. It OVERRIDES
`type_subst_names`, which is head-only and therefore WRONG rather than merely
incomplete — a bare `Vec` with no element is not a type any program can write.
It YIELDS to `type_subst_type_exprs`, which is equally exact and is written by
resolvers reading the caller's LIVE var side-tables; those see instantiations no
per-call record can, notably a nested generic call whose binding
`record_call_type_subs` deliberately drops as self-referential. So the new
channel fills gaps and corrects head-only entries, and changes nothing that was
already exact.

TWO SOLUTIONS ARE DELIBERATELY OMITTED from the channel. A bare `Type::TypeParam`
names no type — it is the propagated binding the name map already flattens
through the caller's substitution, and recording it would let `T -> T` shadow
that flattening. A `TypeKind::Error` round-trip is a LOST type that lowers to
`i64`, so an entry would be worse than the absence that makes consumers fall
back.

THE CHANNEL STOPS AT A BOUNDARY, and the boundary is measured rather than
cautious. It is consulted only for a type param that appears NESTED inside a
parameter's type; a param whose WHOLE declared type is the bare `T` (`x: T`,
`x: ref T`) keeps the resolution it had. The reason is an ownership convention
that turns out to depend on the element being UNKNOWN: a bare-`T` by-value param
enters `owned_vecstr_params` only if the mono prologue can see its element, and
for an argument the side-table resolvers cannot read (anything but a plain
identifier -- `x.clone()`, a literal, a call result) it could not, so the body
MOVED the buffer through instead of deep-copying it, and the caller-side
materialization gate is tuned against exactly that state.

Feeding those params the exact channel breaks the agreement, in both directions:
`fn echo[T](x: T) -> T { x }` called with `[r, r + 1, r + 2]` LEAKED one buffer
per call (the body now returns a deep copy and nothing owns the original --
72 B in 3 allocations over three iterations), and widening the materialization
gate to compensate turned `fn takeout[T](b: T) -> T { match b { v => return v } }`
into an ASAN DOUBLE-FREE, because a match-arm return still moves rather than
copies. The deep-copy is not uniform across return shapes, so no single
caller-side rule is right for both, and that is a separate defect: filed as
B-2026-09-01-30. Both were caught by the existing suite
(`asan_return_owned_generic_param_no_double_free`,
`asan_generic_unused_bare_type_param_temp_arg_no_leak`), which is the reason
they are recorded here as measurements rather than as a near miss.

THE MANGLE IS DELIBERATELY NOT WIRED TO IT, and that is a scope decision worth
