recording rather than an omission. Both mangle axes read `type_subst_type_exprs`
directly, and the typechecker already feeds them their own exact channel
(`call_type_subs_mangle`, widened to the nameless aggregates by B-2026-08-31-48,
which is why the seven-instantiation program above does not collide). Routing
the new map into those axes would change existing symbols for a fix that is
entirely about resolving types INSIDE a body.

THE DEPTH NOTE'S TWO BLOCKERS, re-measured rather than assumed. Its layer 1
(mono symbols collide for nameless type args) is GONE: B-2026-08-31-48 landed
in 007c279, and `Array[i64, 2]` beside `Array[i64, 3]`, and an `Array` beside a
`Slice`, both render correctly in one program. Its layer 2 (the destructuring
path segfaults once the param carries its true type) is REAL and was hit
head-on — see the remainder below.

78e1389's UNSOUNDNESS CLASS IS NOW UNREACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION, not merely
retracted. That fix stopped a DECLINED registration from inheriting a previous
same-named binding's payload type; it needed a decline to be reachable at all,
and no registration in those five programs is declined any more. All five
poisoned orderings, and their reverses, now render each instantiation at its own
payload type and match the interpreter exactly. The retraction stays in the
compiler and stays correct — it is what a future declined shape would rely on.

FIXTURES:

  * `codegen_generic_option_payload_renders_at_its_instantiation`
    (tests/codegen.rs) — one program, twelve lines, each a distinct LOSS
    CHANNEL rather than decoration: two `Vec` elements (head-only loss at two
    types, so a shared body prints one wrong), two `Array` LENGTHS side by side
    (nameless loss plus the -48 symbol collision), `Slice` and a tuple (the
    other nameless shapes), `Vec[Vec[i64]]` (the nested case a head name
    flattens), `Result[T, E]`, and a generic method. RED pre-fix as a COMPILE
    ERROR, not a wrong answer.
  * `codegen_option_payload_does_not_inherit_a_stale_same_named_entry` —
    RENAMED from `codegen_declined_option_payload_does_not_inherit_a_stale_
    same_named_entry` (the word "declined" stopped being true) and converted
    from five `codegen_error` refusal assertions to five `run_program` output
    assertions, which is exactly what its own NOTE ON SCOPE instructed. Reversed
    orderings added: aggregate-first always worked, so pre-fix it proved only
    that the stale entry was the damage; post-fix both directions must render.
  * `codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` — its standing
    instruction ("when -39 is fixed, DELETE the first assertion rather than
    hunting for a new victim") is carried out. The former declined subject is
    asserted as OUTPUT rather than deleted, so a regression that re-declines it
    fails on the fixture documenting why it was ever declined. Nothing now pins
    `deferred_display_error`'s declined-payload arm, and that is the honest
    state: every other `E` is rejected earlier by the typechecker.

NO ASAN FIXTURE, and the reason is a separate defect rather than an oversight.
The shape this row needs — a heap `Option` payload passed as a function
ARGUMENT — LEAKS, and it leaks identically for the plain non-generic spelling:
`fn show(x: Option[Vec[String]])` called in a 3-iteration loop leaks 333 B in 6
allocations, measured IDENTICALLY on pristine `src` and with this fix applied.
The `ref` spelling leaks too; the `let`-bound `println(f"{o}")` in `main` is
clean, which is the contrast that isolates it. Filed as B-2026-09-01-29. When
that lands, the aggregate-instantiation balance fixture this row wanted becomes
writable.

STILL OPEN, and narrowed to one thing. DESTRUCTURING a nameless aggregate
payload inside the generic fn:

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) {
        match x { Some(t) => println(f"{t}"), None => println("n") }
    }

    T                 interp      before        after
    i64 / String      7 / hi      7 / hi        7 / hi         (control)
    Vec[i64]          [1]         <nothing>     [1]            FIXED here
    Array[i64, 2]     [1, 2]      1             1              unchanged
    Slice[i64]        [1, 2]      [1, 2]        140727170663320  <- NEW measurement

The `Slice` row is this row's own data corrected: it recorded only `Array` and
`Vec` for the destructuring form, and `Slice` prints a raw pointer word, which
is the third failure mode and was never listed.

The obvious extension — widening
`record_mono_generic_enum_payload_types`'s two gates to consult the new channel,
three lines — WAS TRIED AND REVERTED, and it is the depth note's layer 2 exactly.
Measured with it applied: `Array` went from printing `1` to a SEGFAULT (rc 139)
and `Slice` from a pointer word to a compile refusal. The payload AREA of a
generic enum is sized for the erased `T` at declare time, so an aggregate is
stored boxed, and handing the pattern path the true type without also teaching
it that indirection makes it unpack a box that is not there. That is the
"pattern tables are span-keyed and hold the uninstantiated `T` at 19 read sites"
problem, and it is genuinely the design change the depth note described — for
the DESTRUCTURING path alone, which is now the row's whole remainder.

Also still open: the refusal's wording (it names the type parameter `T` as a
payload shape). Unchanged in reach — no generic `Option` Display reaches that
message any more — but the text is still there for whatever shape arrives next.

title: `main`'s ERROR PATH HANDS THE DISPLAY RENDERER A SLICE ONE INDIRECTION OFF -- the slice's own data POINTER is rendered as its first element (`Error: Some([93867340896349])` vs the interpreter's `Error: Some([1])`), which is why `Slice[T]` must stay out of `is_reconstructable_display_payload` even though ordinary interpolation now renders it correctly
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-31-25, and it is the reason that row could NOT
lift the `Slice` exclusion from `is_reconstructable_display_payload`.

That row gave codegen a slice Display at every ordinary depth. With it, admitting
`Slice` to the reconstruction gate makes plain interpolation correct --

    let o: Option[Slice[i64]] = Some(s);
    println(f"{o}")              interp Some([1, 2])   build Some([1, 2])   OK
    Result[Slice, String] Ok     interp Ok([1, 2])     build Ok([1, 2])     OK
    Option[Slice[String]]        interp Some([ab, cd]) build Some([ab, cd]) OK
    match o { Some(t) => f"{t}" } interp [1, 2]        build [1, 2]         OK

-- but the SAME predicate also gates `main`'s error type, and that path is wrong:

    fn main() -> Result[(), Option[Slice[i64]]] {
        let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(1);
        return Err(Some(v.as_slice()));
    }
    interp  Error: Some([1])
    build   Error: Some([93867340896349])       <- WITH the admission

The rendered "element" is a pointer value and the LENGTH is right (one element),
which localizes it: the renderer is reading the slice's `{ptr, len}` header
itself as the DATA, i.e. it was handed a pointer to the header where it expects
a pointer to the elements. `Vec` in the same position is correct
(`Error: [1]` / `Error: Some([1])` both match), so this is specific to the
two-word borrow shape, not to the entry point's payload machinery in general.

The bare spelling has the same fault and shows it is not the `Option` wrapper:
`main() -> Result[(), Slice[i64]]` builds and prints `Error: [94664940209587]`
once `seed_synthetic_display_tables` is given a `Slice` arm (without one it
declines, because the synthetic operand has no element type).

WHAT WAS DONE INSTEAD, and why. Both the gate admission and the synthetic-table
arm were REVERTED before landing B-2026-08-31-25, because each converts a clean
build error into a silent miscompile -- the wrong direction, and the exact
trade B-2026-08-25-34 established fail-closed to avoid. Both sites now carry a
comment naming this row and saying the admission waits on it. So `Slice` is
still the shape `codegen_declined_option_payload_names_its_shape` and
`test_unrenderable_main_error_is_a_build_error_not_an_empty_message` pin, but
for a NEW reason: not "unrenderable" (it renders) but "the entry point
mis-reconstructs it".

FIXING THIS IS THE WHOLE FIX. Once `main`'s path renders a slice correctly,
delete the `Slice` arm in `is_reconstructable_display_payload`, add the
`("Slice", 1)` arm to `seed_synthetic_display_tables`, and both fixtures need a
new subject or a rewrite.

NOT MEASURED: which of the two candidate sites is at fault -- the boxing in the
`Err` return (`emit_main_result_return`'s spill helper, which mallocs and stores
the aggregate, leaving a box pointer where the unpack may expect the value) or
`register_var_from_type_expr` computing a different LLVM type for the synthetic
slot than `err_val.get_type()`. The boxing hypothesis fits the observed
one-level-off symptom exactly and is where to look first.
fix:
INVALID by e363381 (2026-08-31): THE PREMISE WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT. Filed by the
B-2026-08-31-25 session, and corrected by the same session on the next pass.

The row claimed `main`'s error path hands the Display renderer a slice one
indirection off, on the evidence that admitting `Slice` to
`is_reconstructable_display_payload` turned a clean build error into
`Error: Some([93867340896349])`. The reconstruction is CORRECT. Instrumenting
the path shows `Slice[i64]` rebuilding as `{ptr, i64}` and `Vec[i64]` as
`{ptr, i64, i64}`, both from the same five payload words, both matching
`err_val.get_type()` -- so `llvm_type_for_type_expr` and
`rebuild_payload_deboxing_if_spilled` are both right, and neither of the two
hypotheses this row named was correct.

What the numbers actually were: the bytes of a `Vec` buffer the cleanup drain had
ALREADY FREED. Every repro in this row built its slice from a LOCAL `Vec`, and
the reading of the first element as "the slice's own data pointer" was pattern-
matching on glibc's freed-chunk contents, not evidence of an indirection.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, measured: an ARRAY-backed slice -- stack storage, never freed
-- renders `Error: [7, 8]` and `Error: Some([7, 8])` identically on both
backends at the entry point. And the failure is not entry-point-specific at all:
`fn f() -> Result[(), Slice[i64]]` returning `Err(v.as_slice())` for a local `v`
is equally wrong when matched in an ordinary caller, which is what shows `main`
was never the variable.

CONSEQUENCES. The `Slice` exclusion this row was created to justify has been
LIFTED (nine well-formed shapes measured identical to the interpreter:
`Some`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err`, a nested `Option`, a match destructure, an element type
that owns heap, a value crossing a function return, and the entry point), and the
`seed_synthetic_display_tables` arm is in. The real defect -- the ownership
checker admitting a slice that outlives the `Vec` it borrows, with `karac check`
reporting "All checks passed" -- is B-2026-08-31-41.

LESSON WORTH KEEPING: a garbage-looking value that happens to be pointer-shaped
is not evidence of a pointer bug. The cheap control that would have caught this
in one step is substituting storage that is never freed (an array for a `Vec`)
and re-measuring, which is now the first thing to try on any "renders garbage"
report.

title: A `Slice[T]` THAT BORROWS A LOCAL `Vec` ESCAPES INTO A RETURN VALUE WITH NO DIAGNOSTIC -- `karac check` says "All checks passed" on `fn f() -> Slice[i64] { let mut v = Vec.new(); ...; return v.as_slice() }`, and the compiled program then READS FREED MEMORY while the interpreter prints the live values, so it also reads as a run-vs-build divergence
fix:
FIXED by c5b5f6a. The rule was already NORMATIVE and simply unenforced: design.md
§ Slices, "Borrow rules" says "`Slice[T]` follows the same rules as `ref T` — it
cannot outlive the collection it borrows from". What was missing is that
`check_ref_return_source_pinning` early-returned on every `-> Slice[T]`
signature, because its slice recognizer (`type_expr_is_string_slice`) matched
`StringSlice` only.

ALL FOUR SHAPES ARE NOW REJECTED, and the corpus sweep found no legal program
that regressed.

THE FIX IS THE `StringSlice` TREATMENT ONE TIER OVER, which is the right shape
because the justification is the same sentence in the spec. Three parts:

  * `type_expr_is_vec_slice` covers BOTH spellings. `mut Slice[T]` is
    `TypeKind::MutSlice`, a distinct node from the `Path(["Slice"])` form, and
    covering only one would have left the `mut` escape unchecked — the same
    two-spellings trap B-2026-08-31-19 hit with `Array`.
  * A by-value `Slice` / `mut Slice` PARAMETER joins `ref` params and `ref self`
    as a valid source: it is a borrow handle whose backing belongs to the
    caller, exactly as a by-value `StringSlice` param already was.
  * Provenance is judged by the place chain's ROOT, not the whole expression.

THAT LAST PART WAS A FALSE POSITIVE I INTRODUCED AND THE TEST SUITE CAUGHT.
Reusing the `StringSlice` root classifier — which accepts only a bare identifier
or `self` — rejected `fn view(ref self) -> Slice[i64] { return self.v.as_slice() }`
as an unsupported form. That is sound code: `ref self` outlives the call, so a
slice of `self.v` does. It is the shape `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`e2e_as_slice_on_a_ref_receiver_and_a_slice_returning_call` exercises, and that
test failing is how it was found — not by reasoning about the classifier. The
new walk mirrors `borrow.rs`'s `place_expr_root` in which shapes count as
projections off a root (field access, index, tuple index, slice-of-slice).

A PRE-EXISTING FALSE POSITIVE CAME WITH IT and is fixed in the same commit,
because the new arm would have inherited it: a semicolon-less `return e` in tail
position was pushed as a return site TWICE — once as the inner expression by
`collect_return_exprs_in_block`, once as the raw `Return` node by the tail push
— and no classifier has an arm for a `Return`, so every one answered
`UnsupportedForm`. `fn f(x: ref S) -> ref S { return x }` was rejected while
`{ return x; }` and `{ x }` passed. Filed and closed as B-2026-08-31-45.

FALSE-POSITIVE SWEEP, run before landing because a new ownership rejection is
exactly the change that breaks legal code: 196 files across `examples/` and
`runtime/stdlib`, 935 across `kara-katas` — zero newly rejected. The full llvm
leg is green including `tests/ownership.rs` (488) and the codegen suite (3496).

WHAT IS NOT COVERED, deliberately. The rejection is at the RETURN boundary only.
The `Vec[Slice]`-outliving-its-backing shape measured in this row is an
intra-function escape through a container, which
`SliceConflictShape::DropOfBorrowed` already handles for the direct case but not
through a container element; that remains open. Unrecognized return forms answer
`UnsupportedForm` rather than being accepted — a clean error, never an unsound
accept, which is the trade every other classifier in this file makes.

TESTS. `slice_return_must_outlive_its_backing_owner` (tests/ownership.rs) pins
five rejected shapes (local Vec in both spellings, local Array, owned param,
field of a local struct) and six accepted ones (ref param, by-value Slice param,
mut Slice param, slice-local from a ref param, field through `ref self`, field
through a ref param). Verified non-vacuous: disabling the recognizer fails it.
detail:
Found while investigating B-2026-08-31-40, whose premise this REFUTES -- see
that row, now `invalid`.

    fn f() -> Slice[i64] {
        let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
        v.push(7);
        return v.as_slice()
    }
    fn main() { println(f"{f()}"); }

    karac check     All checks passed.          <- NO DIAGNOSTIC
    karac run       [7]
    karac build     [94926722142837]            <- freed-heap bytes

The slice borrows `v`'s heap buffer; `v` dies at `f`'s return and the buffer is
freed, so the caller renders freed memory. The interpreter keeps the data alive,
which is why this ALSO presents as a run-vs-build divergence -- and that is how
it was found, misattributed to the Display renderer.

THE SAME HOLE HAS A SHAPE WITH NO VISIBLE ESCAPE, and it is the one that misled
a whole investigation:

    fn main() -> Result[(), Slice[i64]] {
        let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(7); v.push(8);
        return Err(v.as_slice());
    }
    interp  Error: [7, 8]
    build   Error: [94468313997462, 3184667484397058355]

Here the slice never leaves `main`. It dangles anyway because the entry point's
cleanup drain runs BEFORE the `Error: {e}` line is rendered (documented at
`emit_main_result_err_exit`), so `v`'s buffer is gone by the time `E` is
formatted. Same defect -- the returned value borrows a local -- but nothing in
the source looks like an escape.

CONTROLS THAT ISOLATE IT. An ARRAY-backed slice has stack storage that is not
freed, and is correct on both backends in every one of these positions
(`Error: [7, 8]`, `Error: Some([7, 8])`). A `Vec` passed BY VALUE, or a slice of
a `Vec` that outlives the read, is correct too. So this is specifically
"the borrow outlives its owner", not anything about `Slice`'s layout, its
Display, or the `Option`/`Result` payload machinery -- all of which were
suspected first and cleared by measurement.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE OBVIOUS. `design.md`'s ownership tiers make `Slice[T]`
a borrow form, so an escape analysis for it is squarely in scope for the
ownership checker, which already has interprocedural escape predicates
(B-2026-08-28-22 works on exactly that machinery). The checker today accepts
the program silently, which is the worst of the three possible outcomes -- worse
than a false positive, and worse than a codegen refusal.

ALL THREE OF THE ORIGINALLY-UNMEASURED SHAPES ARE NOW MEASURED, and all three
are unsound. `karac check` passes every one; interp vs build:

    slice of a local Vec        [7]      vs [94372197060468]
    slice of a local ARRAY      [7, 8]   vs [94246293805856, 2]
    Vec[Slice] outliving a
      block-scoped backing Vec  [[7]]    vs [[94888445981279]]
    `mut` slice via `v[0..2]`
      escaping a return         [7, 8]   vs [93942219478550, 3184103439243621433]

The ARRAY case answers the open question in the affirmative: its stack storage
dies at the return just as the heap buffer does, and it survives ONLY in the
entry-point position, where the frame is still live when the error line prints.
That is what made the array a valid CONTROL for B-2026-08-31-40's refutation and
is NOT a contradiction: the array slice is sound exactly while its frame lives.

THE LEGAL CONTROL, which any fix must keep passing: a slice of a `ref`-parameter
`Vec` (`fn f(v: ref Vec[i64]) -> Slice[i64] { return v.as_slice() }`) is correct
on both backends, because the backing outlives the callee by construction.

title: AN AGGREGATE CONTAINING A `bf16` FIELD ABORTS THE WASM BUILD WITH `Cannot select: fp_to_bf16` WHEN IT CROSSES A NON-INLINED BOUNDARY BY VALUE -- a param or a return; the wasm ABI decomposes the struct into fields, so the `bfloat` field is promoted exactly as a bare param was, and B-2026-08-30-42's signature rewrite does not reach it. `ref self` builds (a pointer is not decomposed) and is a real workaround
detail:
An AGGREGATE containing a `bf16` field aborts the wasm build with
`LLVM ERROR: Cannot select: fp_to_bf16` when it crosses a function boundary
LLVM does not inline BY VALUE -- as a parameter or as a return. Same hard
process abort as B-2026-08-30-42 (exit 134, no span), different mechanism, and
NOT fixed by that row's signature rewrite.

Found while fixing B-2026-08-30-42 and deliberately not folded into it: that
row rewrites a bare `bf16` in a SIGNATURE to `i16`. This one is the wasm ABI
DECOMPOSING a small struct into its fields, so a `bfloat` field becomes a
`bfloat` register at the boundary and is promoted to `f32` exactly as a bare
parameter was.

MEASURED on `main` WITH B-2026-08-30-42's fix applied,
`--target=wasm_wasi --bindings=none`:

    pub fn f(b: Box) -> bf16   (by-value param)     ABORT
    pub fn f() -> Box          (by-value return)    ABORT
    pub fn f(b: Box) -> f32    (param, f32 return)  ABORT
    impl Box { pub fn f(ref self) -> bf16 }         Built
    fn f(b: Box) -> bf16       (PRIVATE, inlined)   Built

  where `struct Box { v: bf16 }`.

The two building rows are the shape of the answer. `ref self` builds because a
pointer is not decomposed -- so `ref` is a REAL WORKAROUND today, and worth
saying in the diagnostic if this is fixed by rejection rather than by lowering.
A private fn builds only because it is inlined away, which is the same fragile
accident B-2026-08-30-42 recorded: a struct too large to inline would fail
again.

TWO CANDIDATE FIXES, neither started:
  - Reinterpret the aggregate at the boundary: declare the wasm signature with
    a bf16-free twin type (`{ i16 }` for `{ bfloat }` -- identical size and
    layout) and store/reload through memory at both ends, which is exactly what
    `reinterpret_value_as` already does for the AArch64 `#[repr(C)]` coercion.
  - Pass it indirectly, reusing the `indirect_struct_params` machinery. That
    machinery is currently `is_export`-gated, so it would need widening.

NOT MEASURED: nested aggregates (a struct whose field is a struct with a bf16),
`Vec[Box]` / `Array[Box, N]` crossing a boundary by value, tuples containing
bf16, and whether an `Option[bf16]` payload hits the same node. All are the
same decomposition question and should be swept together with whichever fix is
chosen.
fix:
FIXED by b1be5b9. A wasm parameter whose lowered LLVM type carries a
`bfloat` ANYWHERE inside it is now declared as a bf16-free TWIN type -- every
`bfloat` leaf replaced by `i16`, identical size, alignment and field offsets --
and reinterpreted through memory back to the real type in the prologue, and from
the real type to the twin at each call site. No promotion is ever requested, so
`fp_to_bf16` is never formed.

This is the row's first candidate fix (the reinterpret one), and it is the
sibling of B-2026-08-30-42's contract exactly: that row rewrote a BARE `bf16` in
a signature to `i16` and bitcast at both ends; this one does the same one level
in, for the aggregate that CONTAINS one. Same recording shape (a per-function
map read by the prologue and by the four call surfaces), same principle -- the
body keeps the conventional shape and only the boundary moves.

The row's SECOND candidate (reuse `indirect_struct_params`) was rejected on
reading rather than on taste: that machinery is `is_export`-gated AND inserts the
function into `abi_adapted_export_names`, which makes `compile_call` REJECT an
internal Kāra call to it. A bf16-bearing aggregate is ordinary Kāra code that any
caller may call -- the row's own repro calls `f` from `main` -- so widening it
would have needed the internal call path built too, for a strictly larger change.

DETECTION IS ON THE LOWERED LLVM TYPE, not the source `TypeExpr`, and the two
predicates now sit side by side for opposite reasons.
`type_expr_is_bf16` (the scalar case) must key on SOURCE because `f16` also
lowers to a 16-bit float and is perfectly selectable -- a bit-width predicate
would rewrite `f16` signatures that have nothing wrong with them. The aggregate
case keys on the LOWERED type because the shapes reaching a parameter slot are
not all spelled in source: a monomorph's substituted struct, a `layout`-grouped
aggregate, a tuple, an `Array[T, N]`. `llvm_type_has_bf16` compares against
`context.bf16_type()` EXACTLY, so `half` is untouched either way; the
`Mix { h: f16, b: bf16, n: i16 }` case in the test is what pins that.

MEASURED, `--target=wasm_wasi --bindings=none`, on `main` with B-2026-08-30-42's
scalar fix already applied. The row listed four shapes as NOT MEASURED; all four
were measured, three of them abort, and one of the row's own claims does not
reproduce:

  ABORT (pre-fix)                                   after
    pub fn f(b: Box) -> bf16          by-value param  BUILT
    pub fn f(b: Box) -> f32                           BUILT
    pub fn f(o: Outer{Inner{bf16}})   NESTED  (new)   BUILT
    pub fn f(t: (bf16, i64))          TUPLE   (new)   BUILT
    pub fn f(b: Box{bf16, i64})       2-field (new)   BUILT
    pub fn f(b: Box{bf16, 5x i64})    6-FIELD (new)   BUILT
    pub fn f(a: Array[Box, 2])        ARRAY   (new)   BUILT
    impl Box { pub fn f(self) }       by-value self   BUILT

  BUILT before and after
    pub fn f() -> Box                 by-value RETURN
    pub fn f() -> Outer, -> (bf16,i64)
    impl Box { pub fn f(ref self) }
    pub fn f(b: ref Box)
    pub fn f(a: Vec[Box])
    pub fn f(o: Option[bf16])         (new)
    pub struct Box { v: f16 }         (new -- the f16 control)
    fn f(b: Box)                      PRIVATE, inlined away

CORRECTION TO THE ROW: it records the by-value RETURN as an ABORT. It is not,
and was not -- `pub fn f() -> Box`, `-> Outer` and `-> (bf16, i64)` all build on
`main` and print the native values. Only PARAMETERS were affected. The fix is
params-only for that reason, and the returns are in the regression test as
controls so a future return-side regression is caught rather than assumed absent.

CORRECTION TO THE ROW'S MECHANISM: it explains the abort as "the wasm ABI
DECOMPOSING a SMALL struct into its fields". Size is not the trigger. A six-field
struct (`{bf16, 5 x i64}`, 48 B) aborts exactly as the one-field struct does, so
a register-classification story predicts the wrong answer. The predicate is
therefore "the lowered type contains a `bfloat`", with no size term.

VERIFICATION. Building is not the property -- a bitcast ABI is exactly the kind
of change that compiles and computes garbage -- so every shape was run under
`node:wasi` and compared against the SAME program built natively. All 22 shapes
match, including three that a layout-preserving twin could plausibly break and a
naive one would: `bf16` at NON-FIRST field positions among `i64`/`i32`/`f64`
(a shifted offset would corrupt a neighbour), an `f16` and a `bf16` in ONE struct
(the twin must rewrite the `bfloat` and leave the `half`), and aggregates at
argument positions 1 and 3 with scalars between them (the pack must be positional
rather than uniform). Values that ROUND in bf16 are in there too --
`roundtrip(Box { v: 1.1 })` gives `1.1015625` on both -- because a "bitcast" that
had quietly become a conversion would not produce that.

`tests/cli.rs::wasm_bf16_aggregate_params_build_and_match_native` pins all of it.
Negative control run: with the fix stashed out, it fails with `exit=None`
(signal death, not an ordinary compile error) and `LLVM ERROR: Cannot select:
fp_to_bf16` in the message.

title: A `self`-ROOTED PROJECTION SCRUTINEE IS UNMASKED AT EVERY DEPTH, SO A MATERIALIZING ARM'S PAYLOAD `Drop` BODY RUNS TWICE -- `match self.e { E.A(r) => { let m = r; return m.id; } .. }` inside a `mut ref self` method prints `dR1` twice on all three backends, and the two-hop `self.s.e` doubles identically; the same code with the receiver bound to a LOCAL first runs one body
detail:
AN AGREED GAP, not a divergence: interpreter, JIT and AOT all print the same
doubled transcript, which is why no A/B parity gate sees it.

    struct R { id: i64 }   impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum E { A(R), B }     impl Drop for E { println("dE") }
    struct S { e: E }
    struct H1 { e: E }
    impl H1 { fn take(mut ref self) -> i64 { match self.e { E.A(r) => { let m = r; return m.id; } E.B => { return 0; } } } }
    struct H2 { s: S }
    impl H2 { fn take(mut ref self) -> i64 { match self.s.e { .. same .. } } }

                                        all three backends      want
      a.take()  // one hop,  self.e     dR1 1 dE dR1            dR1 1 dE
      b.take()  // two hops, self.s.e   dR2 2 dE dR2            dR2 2 dE

    CONTROL -- the identical match over a LOCAL rather than `self`:
      let s = S { e: E.A(R { id: 8 }) };
      match s.e { .. }                  m8 dR8 dE               correct

THE ROOT KIND IS THE WHOLE DIAGNOSIS, and the ONE-hop row is what proves it.
B-2026-08-29-36 generalized the mask from one hop to a path of any depth, and
that did not touch this: the one-hop `self.e` doubles exactly as the two-hop
`self.s.e` does, so the defect is not about DEPTH. Both backends resolve a
projection scrutinee only through an identifier root -- codegen's
`projection_field_index_path` and the interpreter's
`projection_field_name_path` both require `ExprKind::Identifier` -- and `self`
is its own expression kind (`ExprKind::SelfValue`, or an identifier that is
not in the variable-type table). The chain therefore resolves to `None` and
no mask is recorded at all.

WHY IT IS SEPARATE FROM THE ROW THAT FOUND IT: -36 is the depth axis and is
fixed; this is the root-kind axis and is untouched by it. Measured
byte-identical against the pre-`36` compiler, so it is neither caused by that
row nor reachable from it.

WHERE TO START: the `self` receiver already has a name in both backends' walk
machinery -- the interpreter's non-projection arm maps `ExprKind::SelfValue`
to the name `"self"`, and codegen's variable table holds the receiver under
that name for a `mut ref self` method. Teaching both path resolvers the same
`SelfValue -> "self"` base case is the likely shape. The caution recorded in
`disarm_struct_field_enum_payload_bodies_at` applies with full force here: for
a `ref self` receiver the CALLER owns the bodies walk, and registering one in
the callee made the caller's struct fire inside the callee (`dE` twice) when
that was last tried -- so the fix must confirm the action being replaced
actually belongs to this frame.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-29-36, as the one shape its matrix
could not bring into line. Pinned as a KNOWN GAP (not asserted correct) in
`codegen::e2e_deep_projection_scrutinee_runs_one_payload_body` and its
interpreter twin, on both sides, so a one-sided fix fails loudly.

title: B-2026-08-29-32'S FRESHNESS GUARD IS NOW OVER-CONSERVATIVE AND LEAKS 38 B PER EVALUATION IN TWO SHAPES THE UPSTREAM ALIASING FIX HAS SINCE MADE SAFE -- a discarded branch whose arm literal initializes a field from a LOCAL (`P { a: t.a, b: 1 }`, projected, or `P { a: s, b: 1 }`, moved in whole) still registers NO memory, because the guard that declines it was written against an aliasing double free that B-2026-08-31-34 has now fixed
detail:
WHY THE GUARD EXISTS. B-2026-08-29-32 taught a discarded branch to register
the memory of a body-less heap-carrying aggregate. Registering
unconditionally turned working programs into `free(): double free detected in
tcache 2`, because a field initialized from something that already had an
owner ALIASED it. The guard therefore admits only values MINTED at the literal
-- a call, a `.clone()`, literals, operator results -- and declines every
identifier and every place. Its own close records the trade explicitly: the
declined kinds keep their pre-existing leak, which is the better half of
leak-vs-double-free.

WHAT CHANGED. `2b3b9668` (closing B-2026-08-31-34, "an aggregate literal takes
the fresh-temp field it reads") fixed the aliasing itself. If a literal's
field no longer aliases the source, the reason to decline is gone and the
declined kinds can be admitted -- recovering 38 B apiece.

    let t = mkp(9);
    if seed() > 0 { P { a: t.a, b: 1 } } else { P { a: payload(), b: 2 } };
    <one more discard statement>                       38 B still leaked

MEASURE BEFORE WIDENING, and measure the STACKED form. The guard's first cut
was wrong precisely because a single-statement matrix said the shape was
clean: a local dies at its NLL last use when nothing follows it, so the alias
and the local's own cleanup never coexist and the double free cannot appear.
Add one more statement and it does. Any re-widening must be measured with a
following statement present, or it will reproduce that exact error.

WHERE TO START: `field_init_aliases_a_temp` in `src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs`
and its caller `discard_branch_tail_aliases_a_temp`. Re-measure the two
declined kinds against post-`2b3b9668` `main`, stacked; if clean, narrow the
guard to whatever aliasing remains, or drop it entirely if none does. The
existing ASAN fixture
`asan_discarded_branch_of_body_less_heap_literals_frees_once` already carries
both the admitted and declined kinds and is where the change gets proven.

SOURCE NOTE: raised by the author of B-2026-08-29-32 on noticing -34 close
upstream during the same session; NOT yet re-measured against the fixed tree,
which is the first step.

CORRECTION (recorded at close): this row's TITLE is half wrong, and the fix
prose is the accurate record. Two claims in it did not survive re-measurement.

(1) "IN TWO SHAPES THE UPSTREAM ALIASING FIX HAS SINCE MADE SAFE" -- only ONE
of the two named shapes was made safe. The bare binding (`P { a: s, b: 1 }`) no
longer aliases and is now admitted; the field projection (`P { a: t.a, b: 1 }`)
still does, and admitting it is still a double free in a loop whose source is
declared outside it. That half stays declined and is filed as its own row.

(2) The quoted repro is the STACKED form, which measures CLEAN on the tree this
row was filed against -- the 38 B figure was carried over unre-measured from
B-2026-08-29-32, as this row's own SOURCE NOTE says. The leak is real but lives
in the SOLO and LOOP forms.
fix:
FIXED by 1b5c026.

RE-MEASURED FIRST, AS THE ROW ASKED, AND THE PREMISE DID NOT SURVIVE INTACT.
The row's repro is the STACKED form -- a discard followed by one more
statement -- and that form is CLEAN on post-`2b3b9668` `main`, in every
spelling, for both named shapes. The 38 B figure it quotes was carried over
from B-2026-08-29-32's own pre-`-34` measurement and was never re-taken; the
row says so. The leak is real, but it lives in the two forms the row does not
name: SOLO (the discard is the last statement, nothing after it) leaks 38 B,
and a LOOP leaks 38 B per iteration -- 722 B over 19 of 20 iterations. That
inversion matters because the guard's own doc comment warns that a
one-statement matrix cannot see this class, and prescribes the stacked form as
the corrective; here the stacked form is the one that hides it.

MEASURED MATRIX (LSan, x86 Linux): 6 discard spellings (bare `if`, `let _ =
if`, bare `match`, `let _ = match`, over both named shapes) x 3 statement
forms (solo / stacked / loop) = 18 cells, plus 8 place kinds (local field,
nested field, `v[0]`, an owned param's field, a `ref` param's field,
`self.a`, a `shared struct` field, a bare binding) x 2 forms, plus 9 risk
shapes. Dropping the guard wholesale makes 44 of the 45 cells clean and turns
exactly ONE from clean into `double-free`.

WHAT THE ONE CELL IS, AND WHY IT KEEPS HALF THE GUARD. A FIELD projected off a
local declared OUTSIDE a loop -- `let t = mkp(9); while … { if c { P { a: t.a,
b: 1 } } else { … }; }` -- is moved once per iteration, but the move retraction
that would hand ownership over is STATIC and fires once. Admitting it frees the
same pointer five times. No statement-count matrix reaches this, which is the
same blind spot the guard's history describes, one level up: the corrective for
"a local dies at its NLL last use" is a following statement, and the corrective
for THIS is a loop.

SO THE GUARD SPLITS RATHER THAN DROPS. A BARE BINDING (`P { a: s, b: 1 }`) and
every non-field place (`v[0]`) no longer alias -- the whole-value move already
retracts the source's cleanup -- so declining them registered no owner at all
and WAS the leak. Those are now admitted, and are clean in all three statement
forms and in all nine risk shapes: a source read after the move, the arm NOT
taken (the source is never consumed, so its own cleanup must still be the one
that frees it), both arms consuming, a `mut` source reassigned afterwards, a
nested sibling field, and the loop-outer-source spelling. A FIELD PROJECTION
still aliases and stays declined.

THE FIELD HALF IS A REMAINDER, NOT A DEFERRAL BY TASTE, and it is filed
separately rather than buried here: closing it needs the move takeover
(`consume_freshtemp_field_move`) extended to NAMED LOCALS, which is a change to
the general aggregate-literal path and not to this discard site -- the
`let`-BOUND spelling does not transfer ownership either (`let p = P { a: t.a,
b: 1 }` leaves `t` freeing it at scope exit, measured clean over 5 loop
iterations precisely because `p` never owns it). Widening the discard site
alone cannot fix it without that.

FIX: `field_init_aliases_a_temp` (`src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs`) narrows from
"decline every identifier and every place" to "decline a FieldAccess whose
object is not a fresh owned temp". B-2026-08-31-34's fresh-temp exception is
unchanged and is now the only special case in the predicate.

FIXTURE: `asan_discarded_branch_literal_over_a_binding_frees_once`
(`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`) pins all three legs -- the admitted half in every
spelling and all three statement forms, the nine risk shapes, and the
loop-outer-field cell that must keep declining. RED-verified: 875 B leaked in
23 allocations with the fix reverted. All three carry allocation floors so the
cells cannot go vacuous. The sibling fixture's comment claiming BOTH kinds are
declined was corrected in the same commit.

title: A SEMICOLON-LESS `return e` IN TAIL POSITION IS REPORTED AS AN UNSUPPORTED BORROW-RETURN FORM -- `fn f(x: ref S) -> ref S { return x }` is rejected while the identical `{ return x; }` and `{ x }` spellings both pass; affects every borrow-return classifier (`ref T`, `StringSlice`, and the new `Slice[T]` arm)
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-08-31-41, and PRE-EXISTING to it -- reproduced on a
clean tree for `-> ref T` and `-> StringSlice`, neither of which that row
touches.

    struct S { a: i64 }
    fn f(x: ref S) -> ref S { return x }      error[ownership]: this borrow-return
                                              form is not yet supported
    fn f(x: ref S) -> ref S { return x; }     All checks passed.   <- IDENTICAL
    fn f(x: ref S) -> ref S { x }             All checks passed.   <- IDENTICAL

MECHANISM. `check_ref_return_source_pinning` collects return sites twice over
the body tail. `collect_return_exprs_in_block` already walks `final_expr` and
pushes the INNER expression of a `return`; the function then pushed the tail
AGAIN, unconditionally, as a raw `Return` node. No classifier has an arm for
`ExprKind::Return`, so every one of them fell to its catch-all and answered
`UnsupportedForm`. With a semicolon the `return` is a STATEMENT, collected once
and correctly, which is why the two spellings disagreed.

WHY IT SURVIVED. Every test and example in the tree writes the semicolon form,
so the shape was never exercised -- `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`fn pick(v: ref Vec[i64]) -> Slice[i64] { return v.as_slice(); }` family is
typical. It surfaced only because B-2026-08-31-41's new `Slice` arm would have
inherited it, turning a previously-unchecked signature into a false rejection.
fix:
FIXED by c5b5f6a, in the same commit as B-2026-08-31-41 because that row's new
arm would otherwise have inherited it.

The tail push now skips an expression that is itself a `Return` -- it is already
collected, by the walk immediately above it. Both call sites in
`src/ownership/ref_return.rs` are patched (the Tier-1 classifier and the
borrowed-collection one), each with a comment naming the double-push so the
next reader does not re-derive it.

Pinned by `a_semicolonless_tail_return_is_not_an_unsupported_borrow_form`
(tests/ownership.rs) across all three affected return types -- `ref T`,
`StringSlice` and `Slice[T]`. Verified non-vacuous: restoring the
unconditional push fails the test.

title: A FRESH-TEMP ARG ESCAPING INSIDE A RETURNED `Option.Some(r)` RUNS ITS `Drop` BODY TWICE ON THE COMPILED BACKENDS -- `let _ = k.f(mk(4), true);` over `fn f(ref self, r: R, keep: bool) -> Option[R] { if keep { return Option.Some(r); } return Option.None; }` prints the body twice under `karac run` / `karac build` and once under `--interp`; the NAMED-binding and FREE-FN spellings of the same shape print twice on BOTH backends
detail:
THE SECOND SPELLING OF B-2026-08-29-38, split out when that row's first was
fixed. The bare-param form (`return r`) is fixed; this wrapped-ctor form is
not, and the reason is that the obvious fix is WRONG rather than merely absent.

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }   impl Drop for R { .. }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> R { .. }
    struct K { n: i64 }
    impl K { fn f(ref self, r: R, keep: bool) -> Option[R] {
                 if keep { return Option.Some(r); } return Option.None; } }

      let _ = k.f(mk(3), false); println("a");
      let _ = k.f(mk(4), true);  println("b");
      let _ = k.f(mk(5), false); println("c");

        interp:        drop 3 / a / drop 4 / b / drop 5 / c          correct
        jit / build:   drop 3 / a / drop 4 / drop 4 / b / drop 5 / c DOUBLE

    The three-call shape is the in-program control: only the ESCAPING call
    doubles, so "fresh temp args double generally" is ruled out.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG, and this is the whole of the row. The passthrough
family (`fn_returns_param`, `fn_returns_param_payload`, ...) is documented
CONSERVATIVE-TRUE: when any return site passes the param through, the
caller-side temp drop is skipped for EVERY call. `fn_returns_param` requires
the return operand to be the param's BARE IDENTIFIER, which is exactly why
`return Option.Some(r)` is invisible to it. Extending it to see through the
ctor would answer true for this callee -- and then the two NON-escaping calls
above (`keep = false`), which print their bodies correctly today, would lose
them and leak, because on those paths nobody downstream owns the value. One
doubled body would become two lost bodies plus a leak.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY NEEDS: the per-path callee-side ownership flip that
`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` already has for the bare form -- the
callee takes the value over on the path that returns it and drops it on the
path that does not -- extended to a param returned WRAPPED in an `Option`/
`Result` constructor. That is feature-sized, which is why it is its own row.

NOTE THE OTHER TWO SPELLINGS ARE AGREED, NOT DIVERGENT, and must be moved
TOGETHER with any fix or the fix trades a gap for a divergence:

      let a1 = mk(4); let _ = k.f(a1, true);        both backends: 2 bodies
      let _ = freefn_opt(mk(4), true);              both backends: 2 bodies

So the correct end state is one body in all four spellings on both backends;
converging only the compiled side of the method spelling is what this row's
parent deliberately did NOT do.

SOURCE NOTE: measured as M03/M04/M08/M10 in B-2026-08-29-38's control matrix,
with a `String`-carrying payload. Valgrind clean throughout (0 errors, no
definite loss) -- bodies only, no memory fault. Pinned as a known divergence
in `codegen::e2e_method_fresh_temp_arg_handed_back_runs_one_body` and its
interpreter twin, each side pinning its own output.

title: THE INTERPRETER LOSES A `Drop` BODY THAT BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS RUN, IN TWO METHOD-ARG SHAPES -- a fresh enum temp whose payload an arm BINDS but does not return (`t.keep(Box2.Full(mk(7)))` over `fn keep(..) -> i64 { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r.id; } .. } }`) prints nothing under `--interp` against one body compiled; and the BARE-STATEMENT discard of a method call returning `Option[R]` loses the body where the `let _ =` spelling of the same call keeps it
detail:
TWO SHAPES, ONE DIRECTION: the interpreter runs FEWER bodies than compiled,
which is the opposite of B-2026-08-29-38 and its `Option.Some` sibling.

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }   impl Drop for R { .. }
    enum Box2 { Full(R), Empty }
    impl T { fn keep(ref self, b: Box2) -> i64 {
                 match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r.id; } Box2.Empty => { return 0; } } } }

      let n = t.keep(Box2.Full(mk(7))); println(f"n{n}");

        interp:        n7                     <- NO body; the temp's payload
                                                 is never dropped
        jit / build:   drop 7 h7 / n7         correct

    CONTROL -- the same method over a STRUCT temp rather than an enum one:
      let n = k.g(mk(7));            drop 7 h7 / n7 on all three, correct

    SECOND SHAPE -- the discard spelling disagrees with itself:
      k.f(mk(4), true);              interp loses the body
      let _ = k.f(mk(4), true);      interp runs it
    (compiled runs two in both, which is the -38 family, not this row)

WHY IT IS SEPARATE. B-2026-08-29-38 and its `Option.Some` sibling are codegen
running one body too MANY; these two are the interpreter running one too FEW,
and a fix for either family cannot produce the other. The `k.g` control rules
out "method temp args are dropped late generally" -- it is specific to an ENUM
temp whose payload an arm binds, and to the bare-statement discard.

PRE-EXISTING: measured byte-identical at `c4af3243`, before this session's
discard-path work (B-2026-08-29-30 / -31 / -32 / -36), so none of those rows
caused it. That check was run deliberately because -31 changed
`note_escaping_stmt_sites` and the interpreter's wildcard-`let` discard gate,
which is the same neighbourhood as the second shape here.

WHERE TO START: the interpreter's fresh-temp arg drop gate
(`run_fresh_temp_arg_drops`, which `fn_returns_param`'s doc names as the twin
of codegen's `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` gate -- the two are supposed to
agree by construction). For shape 1 ask why an enum temp whose payload is bound
but NOT returned is treated as handed off; for shape 2, why the bare-statement
and `let _ =` discards reach different gates.

SOURCE NOTE: measured as M05 and the `c2`/`c2b` pair in B-2026-08-29-38's
control matrix. Shape 1 is pinned as a known divergence in
`codegen::e2e_method_fresh_temp_arg_handed_back_runs_one_body` and its
interpreter twin, each side pinning its own current output.
fix:
FIXED by 30e0e5d (fixtures in bb7128c). Both shapes, and they turned out to be
ONE failure mode wearing two costumes: a RETRACTION whose premise is that some
other owner will run the body, made at a site where no other owner exists.

(1) SHAPE 1 -- a fresh-temp enum argument whose arm BINDS the payload.

Binding the payload sets `moved_out_enum_payload_bindings`, which disarms the
scrutinee's payload walk. That is a hand-off, and its recipient is the arm's new
owner. In a METHOD frame the arm does not take ownership --
`scrutinee_expr_is_consuming` answers false for an owned param, the
caller-retains carve-out B-2026-08-29-10 deliberately restored -- so the arm
defers to the caller; and a FRESH TEMP has no caller binding to defer to. Arm
defers, caller absent, walk disarmed: the body ran nowhere.

Isolated by three shapes measured side by side, which is what shows it is the
BINDING arm and not enum arguments or method frames generally:

    fn nomatch(ref self, b: Box2) -> i64 { return 1; }              correct
    fn wild(ref self, b: Box2) -> i64 { match b { Full(_) => .. } }  correct
    fn bind(ref self, b: Box2) -> i64 { match b { Full(r) => .. } }  ZERO bodies

The guard keeps the walk armed where this frame is the value's ONLY owner, and
that question has TWO halves. An earlier version had one and double-fired: where
the payload ESCAPES through the return -- `fn take(b: Box2) -> R { match b
{ Full(r) => return r, .. } }` -- the caller's RESULT binding owns it, and
arming the walk as well ran two bodies against one compiled. That is
`test_method_fresh_temp_arg_handed_back_runs_one_body`'s own first row, which
caught it.

(2) SHAPE 2 -- the two DISCARD SPELLINGS of one call disagreed.

    k.f(mk(4), true);            no body
    let _ = k.f(mk(4), true);    one body

A 2x2 probe -- (user enum, `Option`) x (bare, `let _`) -- leaves exactly ONE
failing cell, which is what turns this from "the bare discard is broken" into a
one-line diagnosis. The bare arm takes the DECLARED-TYPE payload walk, and
`Option`/`Result` are built-ins with no source-level `EnumDef`, so that walk
answers nothing for them. The `let _` spelling reaches the shared discard
walker, which carries its own value-driven `Option`/`Result` arm. The built-ins
now route there too; the user-enum sibling was correct on BOTH spellings and is
untouched.

(3) A SENTINEL FLIPS, as this row's own text anticipated. Shape 1 was pinned in
`test_method_fresh_temp_arg_handed_back_runs_one_body` as a known divergence,
"each side pinning its own current output". That case now asserts the shared,
correct result, and the pin's comment records what changed rather than being
deleted.

VERIFICATION. Fixtures for both shapes. The shape-1 one carries the isolation
above plus the handed-back guard, and has a CODEGEN TWIN sharing its
expectations: that backend was correct on every row, so a fixture on the fixed
side alone would keep passing while the two drifted, and "they agree" is the
property. Full `--features llvm` suite 16,019 passed / 0 failed; both clippy
legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.

NOT IN SCOPE, and the row says so itself: the COMPILED backends still run TWO
bodies for shape 2's escaping call. That is B-2026-08-29-38's family --
over-firing on the compiled side, the opposite direction -- and a fix for either
family cannot produce the other. Shape 2 therefore has no codegen twin: there is
no agreed answer to pin until that row closes.

title: TWO INSTANTIATIONS OF ONE GENERIC FN AT DIFFERENT `Array`/`Slice`/`Vector` TYPE ARGS COLLIDE ON ONE MONO SYMBOL AND FAIL MODULE VERIFICATION -- `fn ident[T](x: T) -> T` at `Array[i64,2]` and `Array[i64,3]` builds `call [2 x i64] @"ident$opaque"([3 x i64] ...)`; neither the head-name channel nor the element-aware mangle token can spell a nameless aggregate, so no disambiguating token is ever appended
detail:
Two instantiations of ONE generic function at different `Array` / `Slice` /
`Vector` type arguments collide on a single monomorph symbol, and the build
fails module verification. No Display, no traits, no nesting -- the smallest
generic function in the language:

    fn ident[T](x: T) -> T { return x }

    fn main() {
        let a2: Array[i64, 2] = Array[3, 4];
        let a3: Array[i64, 3] = Array[7, 8, 9];
        let r2: Array[i64, 2] = ident(a2);
        let r3: Array[i64, 3] = ident(a3);
        println(f"{r2[1]} {r3[2]}");
    }

    --interp   4 9
    build      error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
               "Call parameter type does not match function signature!
                  %a32 = load [3 x i64], ptr %a3, align 8
                 [2 x i64]  %call3 = call [2 x i64] @"ident$opaque"([3 x i64] %a32)"

`ident$opaque` is the tell: both instantiations mangled to the SAME symbol, the
first one emitted defined the signature, and the second was type-checked against
it.

ROOT CAUSE, traced. `mangle_mono_name` (`src/codegen/mono.rs`) appends a
disambiguating token only for params that clear a collision-class gate:

    let head = match subst_names.get(&param.name) {
        Some(h) => h.as_str(),
        None => continue,          // <- every nameless type argument exits here
    };
    let is_collision_class = matches!(head, "String" | "Vec" | "VecDeque") && ...;

Two independent reasons a nameless aggregate never gets a token:

  1. `type_to_concrete_or_param_name` cannot spell an `Array` / `Slice` /
     `Vector` / tuple, so `subst_names` has no entry and the `None` arm skips
     the param outright.
  2. `type_to_mono_mangle_token` (`src/typechecker/types.rs`), the ELEMENT-AWARE
     channel that exists precisely to disambiguate these, has no arm for
     `Type::Array`, `Type::Slice` or `Type::Vector` either -- all three fall to
     its `_ => None`.

So the type that most needs disambiguation (an `Array`'s LENGTH is part of its
size and stride) is the one type with no channel able to express it.

ATTEMPTED FIX, and why it is not attached. Adding `Array` / `Slice` / `Vector`
arms to `type_to_mono_mangle_token` and widening the gate's `None` arm to
`tokens.is_some_and(|t| t.contains_key(&param.name))` fixes the PAIRWISE cases
-- measured green on `Array[2]` vs `Array[3]`, `Slice` vs `Array`, and
`Vector[4]` vs `Vector[8]`. It does NOT fix three-way: adding a `Slice`
instantiation alongside the two arrays brings `ident$opaque` back for the
arrays. That was not understood at the time and the change was reverted rather
than landed half-understood on a shared `main`.

NOT MEASURED: why the third instantiation reverts the first two to the untokened
symbol (the obvious suspects are a `tokens` lookup that is absent for some call
spans, and `generated_monos` caching on a name that was minted before the token
was appended); whether tuples behave like the other three; whether an explicit
`ident[Array[i64, 2]](a)` differs from the inferred form; and whether the same
collision reaches a `#[repr(C)]` export.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-31-39: that row's aggregate `Option[T]` instantiations are
refused at the Display gate before they can reach codegen, which is what has
kept this collision mostly out of sight. Fixing that gate makes this one
reachable on every aggregate instantiation, so this should land FIRST or the two
should land together -- otherwise the Display fix trades a clean refusal for
silent garbage (measured: an `Array` then a `Slice` printed
`Some([94881993644816, 2])`, a raw pointer word rendered as an element).
fix:
FIXED by 007c279, which fixes it in the two places the row named, and the fix is exactly
the one the row sketched:

  * `type_to_mono_mangle_token` (`src/typechecker/types.rs`) gains `Array`,
    `Vector` and `Slice` arms. The LENGTH is part of the token because it is
    part of the identity -- two arrays of one element type and different lengths
    have different sizes and strides and must not share a body. A non-literal
    (const-param) length keeps `None` rather than minting a token two distinct
    instantiations could share: a wrong token is worse than no token, because
    the existing fallback at least fails loudly at the verifier instead of
    silently running the wrong body. `Slice` carries mutability, which is part
    of how the callee may write through the pointer.

  * `mangle_mono_name`'s collision gate (`src/codegen/mono.rs`) stops requiring
    a head NAME. It now keys the nameless case on a distinguishing TOKEN
    actually existing, which is precisely the condition for the append below it
    to produce distinct symbols; a param with no token keeps today's fallback.

THE ROW'S OWN "ATTEMPTED FIX" PARAGRAPH IS WRONG AND IS THE CORRECTION WORTH
RECORDING. It says this same change "does NOT fix three-way: adding a `Slice`
instantiation alongside the two arrays brings `ident$opaque` back for the
arrays", and that is why the change was reverted rather than landed. Re-measured
from a clean tree with the change applied, the three-way case builds and prints
`4 9 6`, matching `--interp` exactly. The original observation came from a
binary built during a stretch of repeated stash/re-apply cycles and was reading
a stale `karac`; nothing about three instantiations is special. A revert on a
false measurement is the expensive kind of caution, and the tell was available
-- the same fixture passed and failed within minutes without the source
changing.

MEASURED, all four surfaces byte-identical (`--interp`, `karac run` JIT,
`karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`):

    len 4 9 / elem 1 b / slice 6 z / vector 10 36 / tuple 1 3 / method 3 7
    / prior hi 8 k

Each line pins a different axis of the mono identity, because a token that
collapses any one of them reintroduces the bug: two LENGTHS at one element type,
two ELEMENT types at one length, the other two nameless aggregates, the tuple
(which has no head name for its own reason), and the same collision reached
through a generic METHOD rather than a free fn. `prior` is a regression guard
rather than decoration -- `String` / `Vec[i64]` / `Vec[String]` are the
collision class the gate already handled (B-2026-07-11-35), and widening it must
not disturb them.

The codegen half goes RED pre-fix with the row's exact module-verification
failure; the interpreter twin passes both before and after, which is what makes
it the oracle -- the interpreter has no monomorphization, so it was never
affected.

TWO FIXTURE TRAPS met while measuring, recorded so the next person does not
mistake either for a regression. Indexing a CALL RESULT (`ident(s)[0]`) is
unsupported on both backends ("Index operator applied to non-array type"),
pre-existing and unrelated -- bind through a `let` first, which is what the test
does. And `let r: mut Slice[i64] = ident(m); r[0] = 9;` is correctly rejected by
ownership (`r` needs `let mut`), identically on both backends.

SCOPE NOTE. The row predicted this would become reachable "on every aggregate
instantiation" once B-2026-08-31-39's Display gate is fixed, and asked for this
one to land first. That ordering now holds: -39 is still open, and this is on
`main` ahead of it.

title: A GENERIC `Result[T, E]` RENDERS WITH THE `Option` VARIANT TABLE WHEN A GENERIC `Option[T]` DISPLAY IS EMITTED FIRST -- `Ok(7)` prints `Some(7)` and `Err(9)` prints `None`, DROPPING THE PAYLOAD; order-dependent (reverse the two calls and both are correct), generic-only, and silent on both compiled backends
detail:
A generic `Result[T, E]` renders with the `Option` spelling -- `Ok(7)` prints as
`Some(7)` -- whenever a generic `Option[T]` Display is instantiated in the same
program. Silent, on the most ordinary type there is:

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) { println(f"o {x}"); }
    fn showr[T: Display](x: Result[T, i64]) { println(f"r {x}"); }
    fn main() { show(Some(7)); showr(Ok(7)); }

    --interp   o Some(7)   r Ok(7)
    build      o Some(7)   r Some(7)      <- WRONG VARIANT NAME

Reproduced identically at `T = String` (`r Ok(yo)` renders `r Some(yo)`), so it
is not scalar-specific. Both spellings compile and run today -- this needs none
of the aggregate machinery B-2026-08-31-39 is about, and was confirmed on a
PRISTINE tree at 8089970 with no local changes, then re-confirmed by stashing an
unrelated work-in-progress and rebuilding.

Found while working B-2026-08-31-39 and deliberately NOT folded into it: that
row is about an aggregate `T` reaching the Display gate unsubstituted, and this
reproduces at `T = i64` where nothing is unsubstituted and the gate is not
involved. Wrong output rather than a refusal or a crash, which is the worst of
the three, and it survives on shapes users write today.

MEASURED, and it localizes to ORDER between two GENERIC fns:

    showr ALONE                       r Ok(7)      CORRECT
    showr FIRST, then show            r Ok(7) / o Some(7)   BOTH CORRECT
    show FIRST, then showr            o Some(7) / r Some(7) WRONG
    non-generic show + showr          both correct
    show FIRST, then showr(Err(9))    o Some(7) / r None    WRONG

So it is not "Option always wins" and not generics alone -- it is
FIRST-EMITTED-WINS between two generic instantiations. Compile the `Option[T]`
Display first and the `Result[T, E]` one reuses it wholesale: `Ok` renders as
`Some` AND `Err` renders as `None`, which is Option's entire variant table
standing in for Result's. Reverse the two calls and both are correct.

That points at a key that does not distinguish the two enums for a GENERIC
instantiation while it does for a concrete one -- the display-fn cache
(`disp_cache_get`, keyed on a mangled type name built from the payload) and the
mono symbol are the two candidates, and the non-generic row above is what says
the payload spelling alone is not the whole key.

The `Err` case is the reason this is worse than a cosmetic naming bug: `Err(9)`
printing `None` DROPS THE PAYLOAD ENTIRELY, so an error value silently renders
as an absence.

NOT MEASURED: `Result[T, E]` with BOTH params generic; three or more
instantiations; whether a generic `Option` and a generic user enum collide the
same way; and which of the two candidate keys above is actually at fault.
fix:
Fixed in e5fd34f. A NINETEEN-LINE FIX, and finding it meant refuting the row's own
axis first.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, AND THAT IS THE MOST USEFUL PART OF THIS CLOSE.
It recorded the defect as generics-only and order-dependent "between two generic
instantiations", and pointed at the display-fn cache (`disp_cache_get`) and the
mono symbol as the two candidate keys. Neither is at fault, and generics are
incidental. Two measurements settle it:

    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]) …  fn showr[T: Display](y: Result[T, i64]) …
        GENERIC, DIFFERENT parameter names           -> both CORRECT

    fn show(x: Option[i64]) …            fn showr(x: Result[i64, i64]) …
        NON-GENERIC, SHARED parameter name `x`       -> `Ok(7)` prints `Some(7)`

Sharing a PARAMETER NAME is the whole condition. The row's non-generic control
read as clean only because it happened to use different names, which is what
sent the diagnosis to generics. This reaches ordinary non-generic code.

ROOT CAUSE. `var_types.var_option_payload_te` and `var_result_payload_te` are
keyed on the BARE variable name, and BOTH Display dispatch sites -- the
`compile_print` identifier arms (`control_flow.rs`) and the f-string
collection-display path (`synth_display.rs`) -- test the Option arm FIRST and
return. Neither map is cleared between functions, so an `Option` binding named
`x` in one function was still live when a `Result` parameter named `x` was
rendered in a later one, and Option's entire variant table stood in for
Result's. Instrumented, the second hole saw BOTH entries live for `x`
(`opt=true res=true`), which is what makes "Option is tested first" decisive.

THE FIX is at the registration, not the dispatch: `register_var_from_type_expr`
now retracts the sibling map entry when it sees a declared `Option` / `Result`.
Two details, both load-bearing:

  * UNCONDITIONAL, on the DECLARED type, rather than only on a successful
    registration. The payload-dropping `Err` case is exactly the one where the
    registration is DECLINED -- an `Err`-only instantiation leaves the Ok type
    param unsubstituted and the payload is not reconstructable -- so a version
    that retracted only on success left that case still answering through the
    stale entry.
  * At the registration rather than in the two dispatch sites, because generic
    MONO bodies are compiled without passing through the per-function state
    reset, so a fix that depended on that reset covers the non-generic half
    only.

MEASURED CLEAN afterwards on both orders, both variants, `T = i64` and
`T = String`, and four functions sharing `x` across two payload types.

A SECOND, NON-LOAD-BEARING FINDING, deliberately NOT included in the fix. These
two maps are the only per-function `var_types` maps that `functions.rs`'s reset
block never clears -- ~15 siblings including `optres_var_payload_tes` are
cleared there. Adding the clear is also correct and does fix the non-generic
half on its own, but RED-verification showed the fixture passes with it reverted
once the retraction is in place, so it was left out to keep the change minimal
and every line measured. Recorded here because the stale-per-function-state
hazard is real and the next reader of that block should know these two are
missing from it.

THE `Err` ROW IS ABSENT FROM THE FIXTURE ON PURPOSE, and its absence is a
finding rather than a gap. `showr(Err(9))` on a generic `Result[T, i64]` now
REFUSES to build ("its `T` payload cannot be reconstructed"). That refusal is
PRE-EXISTING: the same program with the preceding `show(...)` call removed
refuses identically on a pristine tree with this fix stashed out, so it belongs
to B-2026-08-31-39's unsubstituted-`T` territory. What changed is that the
collision used to MASK it -- preceded by a same-named `Option` binding, the
program printed `None` instead of refusing. Trading a silent payload drop for an
accurate refusal is the right direction, and it makes the shape behave the same
way with and without the neighbouring call.

FIXTURE. `e2e_option_and_result_displays_do_not_collide_on_a_shared_var_name`
(tests/codegen.rs, 8 rows: the non-generic control the row was missing, the
row's own generic repro, `T = String`, both variants in one program, four
functions sharing a name, plus the three controls that localize the cause to
the NAME -- Result-first, distinct names, and Result alone).

RED-VERIFIED: with the retraction reverted, the generic repro row fails
`left: "o Some(7)\nr Some(7)\n"` against `right: "o Some(7)\nr Ok(7)\n"`.

GATES. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both clippy legs clean; full
`cargo test --features llvm` battery green.

title: AN ENUM-CONSTRUCTOR MIXED WRAP LOSES ITS SLOT MASK ACROSS A WHOLE-VALUE REBIND, AND CODEGEN CANNOT INHERIT IT BECAUSE IT STORES NOTHING PER VARIABLE -- `let w = W2.Two(r, mk(2)); let w2 = w;` prints `dR1 dR2 dR1` where `dR2 dR1` is due, on all three backends; the STRUCT and TUPLE spellings of the same rebind were fixed by B-2026-08-29-44 and this one could not be, because `enum_ctor_param_view_payload_slots` derives the masked slots from the ctor EXPRESSION at the `let` and keeps no per-var record for a rebind to copy
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-29-44 when its struct and tuple halves landed. AGREED
across interpreter, JIT and AOT, so no A/B parity gate sees it.

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }   impl Drop for R { .. }
    enum W2 { Two(R, R), None2 }

      fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let w = W2.Two(r, mk(2)); let w2 = w; return 7; }
        all three backends -> `dR1 dR2 dR1 v=7`     (due: `dR2 dR1`)

      CONTROL, correct on all three: the same wrap with NO rebind
      fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let w = W2.Two(r, mk(2)); return 7; }  -> `dR2 dR1`

THE INTERPRETER HALF IS ALREADY WRITTEN AND WAS DELIBERATELY WITHHELD. Adding
`moved_out_enum_payload_slots` to `transfer_move_masks_on_rebind` makes this
backend print the due `dR2 dR1` -- measured during -44. It is NOT landed
because codegen cannot match it, and the result was measured too:
`dR2 dR1` against `dR1 dR2 dR1`, an agreed defect turned into a run-vs-build
divergence. That is the trade B-2026-08-29-19 was backed out for making, and
-44's own text forbids it. The withhold site in
`interpreter/eval_stmt.rs::transfer_move_masks_on_rebind` carries the numbers.

WHAT IT NEEDS, and why it is bigger than its siblings. The struct and tuple
masks are STORED per variable (`struct_moved_field_bodies`,
`tuple_moved_elem_bodies`), so -44's transfer had something to copy. The enum
ctor path computes its view slots from the constructor expression at the `let`
and stores nothing, so the prerequisite is a per-var map -- e.g.
`enum_ctor_moved_payload_slots: HashMap<String, HashSet<usize>>` populated where
`mask_param_view_enum_ctor_slots` currently applies the mask, then copied by
`transfer_move_masks_on_rebind` and consulted at the enum branch of the `let`
registration the same way the struct branch now consults
`field_skip_tree_for_var`.

MIND THE SCOPING TRAP -44 HIT. These maps are name-keyed and accumulate for a
whole function. Reading one at every `let` rather than only at a
bare-identifier REBIND makes a fresh binding inherit a stale mask from an
earlier move-out of the same name; that silently dropped a body in three
existing move-out tests during -44 and was caught only by the full suite. Any
enum-side store must be consulted under the same rebind gate.

BOTH BACKENDS MUST LAND TOGETHER, for the reason measured above.

SOURCE NOTE: measured as W01 in B-2026-08-29-44's control matrix (8 shapes,
interp/jit/aot, String-carrying payload, valgrind 0 errors). Pinned at its
current agreed output in `codegen::e2e_whole_value_rebind_inherits_the_wrap_-
mask` and its interpreter twin, so a one-sided fix fails loudly.

title: A SELF-ASSIGNMENT WHOSE RHS IS AN `if`/`match` LEAKS THE OVERWRITTEN VALUE -- `e = if c { pass(e) } else { pass(e) }` loses a block (12 allocs / 11 frees at -O0), the same shape B-2026-08-29-51 fixed for blocks and measured UNTOUCHED by it; MIXED arms leak identically, and like its sibling the leak is clean at -O2
detail:
A self-assignment whose RHS is an `if` or `match` (rather than a block) leaks the
value it overwrites, in exactly the shape B-2026-08-29-51 fixed for blocks:

    struct R { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    fn pass(r: R) -> R { return r; }
    fn main() {
        let mut e = R { id: 7, name: f"e7" };
        let c: bool = true;
        e = if c { pass(e) } else { pass(e) };
        println(f"use {e.id}");
    }

    valgrind --leak-check=full, KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0:
      12 allocs, 11 frees, ERROR SUMMARY: 1
    The `match` spelling (`e = match c { true => pass(e), false => pass(e) }`)
    measures identically. Output is CORRECT on both backends -- one body for one
    object -- so only the heap is wrong.

MEASURED UNTOUCHED by B-2026-08-29-51's fix: 12/11 both before and after that
change, so this is neither regressed nor helped by it. Filed separately at the
time rather than folded in.

SAME ROOT, DIFFERENT QUESTION. `assign_rhs_is_owned_user_call` decides whether
the assignment emits its overwrite cleanup, and B-2026-08-29-51 taught it to peel
`Block` / `Seq` / `Unsafe` to their single tail expression. An `if` / `match` has
SEVERAL tails that need not agree:

    e = if c { pass(e) } else { mk() };     // one arm roundtrips, one mints

so peeling is not the answer here -- the fix has to decide what the cleanup means
when the arms disagree. That is why the block fix stopped at the block forms.

THREE CANDIDATE RULES, none tried:
  * Require ALL arms to be owned user calls, and emit the cleanup once before the
    branch. Wrong if an arm returns the binding unchanged (`else { e }`), which
    is the shape the original probe used.
  * Emit the cleanup PER ARM, at each arm that roundtrips. Costs a duplicated
    call but is the only shape that is obviously right for mixed arms.
  * Decline mixed-arm branches entirely and keep today's behaviour for them,
    fixing only the all-arms-agree case. Smallest, and leaves a residue.

TWO THINGS MEASURED WHILE FILING, because both change how a fixture for this has
to be written:

  * MIXED ARMS LEAK IDENTICALLY. `e = if c { pass(e) } else { mk(9) }` -- one arm
    roundtrips, the other mints a fresh value -- measures 12 allocs / 11 frees,
    the same as the all-arms-agree case. So the mixed shape is NOT already
    handled somewhere else, and a rule that only fixes all-arms-agree leaves the
    larger half of the problem behind.

  * IT IS OPTIMIZATION-DEPENDENT, exactly as B-2026-08-29-51 was: 12/11 at
    `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and CLEAN at the default `-O2` (10/10), where LLVM
    deletes the redundant allocation. A fixture written for the ASAN suite will
    therefore PASS pre-fix at the default level and prove nothing -- its memory
    assertion has to ride the `-O0` leg (`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`), which is
    where B-2026-08-29-51's regression test carries its own.

NOT MEASURED: whether `if let` / `while let` spellings behave like `if`; and
whether a nested branch (a block whose tail is an `if`) leaks -- B-2026-08-29-51's
peel reaches the block but stops at the branch inside it, so that combination is
untested in either direction.

fix:
Fixed in 8a3f0a8.

The row's diagnosis was exact and is confirmed: `let x = s.a` runs two recorders
for one statement. `suppress_moved_out_drop_field` inserts a COARSE whole-walk
disarm keyed on the root name; the `let` arm inserts the PRECISE `(src, field)`
pair (B-2026-08-03-8). `drop_user_drop_fields_of_binding` tests the coarse set
FIRST and returns, so the precise mask was dead code for every depth-1 move and
the source's OTHER fields lost their bodies outright.

THE FIX is the shape the row proposed: depth 1 registers no coarse record. The
two conditions line up exactly -- the `let` arm's precise insert requires a bare
`Identifier` object, which is precisely what "depth 1" means in this branch --
so there is no shape that loses both records.

WIDER THAN FILED, and the control is what shows it. The row reports a "MIXED
WRAP" (a param view beside a fresh field) and reads as being about the view. It
is not: a literal whose fields are BOTH fresh (`S3 { a: mk(5), b: mk(6) }`,
`let x = s.a`) loses `dR6` identically, measured `dR5` against compiled's
`dR5 dR6`. And moving the LAST field (`let x = s.b`) only LOOKED correct --
the surviving field there is the param view, whose body another owner already
runs, so the coarse disarm had nothing left to lose. The axis is the shadowing;
the mixed wrap is just the shape it was found through.

THE ENUM LEG THE ROW ASKED FOR. It flagged that the walker's `Value::EnumVariant`
branch sits BEHIND the same early return, so narrowing could change an
enum-valued source. It cannot: BOTH inserts into `moved_out_drop_field_bindings`
are gated on a `Value::Struct` source -- this one requires the parent to be
`Value::Struct { .. }`, and the passthrough disarm's is inside a
`Some(v @ Value::Struct { .. })` arm -- and `rearm_container_bodies_for_name`
clears the record on rebind. Measured either way (`HasE { e: E.A(mk(4)), r: mk(5) }`,
`let x = s.r` -> `dR5 dR4` on all four surfaces before and after) and pinned as a
fixture row, so a later widening of either insert has to notice.

THE DEEP CHAIN KEEPS THE COARSE RECORD, deliberately. `let x = o.h.r` gets no
precise pair (the `let` arm needs a bare identifier object), so the root-coarse
disarm is the only mask it has, matching codegen's root-slot disarm as before.
Both backends UNDER-DROP it together -- `dR1` alone, with `q` and `k` losing
their bodies -- which is the trade the coarse record's own doc comment
describes. That is not this row, but it is two real lost bodies, so both
fixtures pin it on their side: closing that gap has to move both backends at
once rather than reintroducing a divergence here.

Note the doc comment's claim that the coarse record keeps "the two backends in
step either way" was FALSIFIED for depth 1 by this row's measurement, and is now
true again only for the deep chain, which is where the comment now applies.

Verified across `--interp` / JIT / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` on seven
shapes, and re-verified after rebasing onto 087e51c. RED-verified: pre-fix the
fixture yields exactly `dR1\n7\n` against `dR2\ndR1\n7\n`. Gates: both clippy
legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `tests/interpreter.rs` 1900 passed /
0 failed, `tests/codegen.rs` 3535 passed / 0 failed.
title: THE INTERPRETER LOSES A MIXED WRAP'S FRESH FIELD BODY WHEN THE VIEW FIELD IS MOVED OUT -- `let s = S3 { a: r, b: mk(2) }; let x = s.a;` prints `dR1` against every compiled backend's due `dR2 dR1`, because the COARSE whole-walk disarm short-circuits the per-field mask the same statement also registers
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-29-47 and PRE-EXISTING -- it was divergent before
that fix too, just more loudly (both halves wrong); the fix removed the shared
half and left this one exposed.

    struct S3 { a: R, b: R }
    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let s = S3 { a: r, b: mk(2) }; let x = s.a; return 7; }
      interp                 -> `dR1 v=7`
      jit / aot / aot-par0   -> `dR2 dR1 v=7`   DUE
    The fresh field `b` has no other owner, so its body is simply lost.

BEFORE B-2026-08-29-47 the same shape read i[`dR1 dR1`] vs c[`dR1 dR2 dR1`] --
divergent in the same direction, with an extra doubled `dR1` on both sides that
the fix removed from each. So this is strictly the NARROWER remainder, not a
new split.

CAUSE, and it is a shadowing rather than a missing mask. `let x = s.a` runs two
recorders in `eval_stmt.rs` for one statement:

  * `suppress_moved_out_drop_field` inserts the ROOT name into
    `moved_out_drop_field_bindings` -- a WHOLE-walk disarm, documented as
    deliberately coarse ("for a multi-field one it under-drops, which is the
    safe side of the trade -- the two backends stay in step either way").
  * the Let arm inserts the precise pair `(src, field)` into
    `moved_out_struct_field_bodies`, which masks exactly the moved field.

`drop_user_drop_fields_of_binding` tests the COARSE set first and returns, so
the precise mask is dead for this shape and the doc's "stay in step" claim is
falsified by the measurement above -- codegen's twin
(`disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field` plus the per-field
`emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping`) is per field and keeps `b`.

WHERE TO START. Skipping the coarse insert when the chain is DEPTH 1 -- exactly
where the Let arm registers the precise pair -- is the obvious shape of the fix,
but the coarse set also guards the ENUM branch of
`drop_user_drop_fields_of_binding` (its early return precedes the
`Value::EnumVariant` test), so an enum-valued source would change behaviour too.
Measure that leg before narrowing.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT: a body count, valgrind clean.

title: THE TUPLE SPELLING OF B-2026-08-29-47 STILL DOUBLES A PARAM VIEW'S `Drop` BODY -- `let t = (r, 5); let x = t.0;` prints `dR1 dR1` where one is due, agreed by all four surfaces, because the per-field param-view record that fix added has no tuple peer
detail:
FILED BY B-2026-08-29-47, which fixed the STRUCT spelling and pinned this one at
the defect in both new tests (`e2e_param_view_field_moved_back_out_runs_one_body`
/ `test_param_view_field_moved_back_out_runs_one_body`).

    fn take(r: R) -> i64 { let t = (r, 5); let x = t.0; return 7; }
      interp / jit / aot / aot-par0 -> `dR1 dR1 v=7`   ALL FOUR AGREE, all wrong
    Due: `dR1` once -- the caller runs it.

AGREED, so it stays a gap rather than a divergence; that is the only reason it
was not folded into -47.

WHY THE -47 FIX DOES NOT REACH IT. That fix answers "is this leaf caller-owned?"
two ways: the chain ROOT is a param view, or the FIRST hop is recorded in the
new `param_view_struct_fields` (a store of that name on each backend). A TUPLE
literal satisfies neither. `tuple_literal_param_view_elems` masks the view
ELEMENTS per index and the binding is never marked a param view (the mask is
per slot, so the all-views propagation the struct path uses does not fire), so
`t` is not a view and there is no `(t, 0)` record for `t.0` to find.

WHERE TO START. The tuple peer of the two stores added by -47 --
`param_view_tuple_elems` in `payload_vars` beside `param_view_struct_fields`,
and a `(binding, index)` set beside the interpreter's -- written where
`tuple_literal_param_view_elems` / `mask_param_view_tuple_literal_elems` already
compute the view set, and consulted from a `TupleIndex` arm of
`field_move_out_source_is_param_view` / `let_reads_param_view_field`. Both
backends must move in ONE commit: the interpreter can do it alone, and doing so
would turn this agreed gap into a run-vs-build split.

NOT A MEMORY DEFECT: a body count, valgrind clean.

fix:
FIXED by e207be3. The row asked for a DECISION between (a) document, (b) warn and
(c) reject. The answer is (a) + (b) now and (c) later, and the reason (c) is not
available today is not a cost judgement -- it is that the fix-it it would point
at does not exist.

(1) WHAT SETTLED IT. The row's own framing says (c) "matches the spec sentence
and the index rule". It does, and that is exactly why it cannot land yet: the
index rule got to be an ERROR because it had a zero-cost fix-it, `ref v[i]`.
This shape has none. MEASURED, not assumed: `let m = ref s.r;` is
`error[E_REF_OPERAND_UNSUPPORTED]: only `ref <sequence>[i]` is supported in v1`,
and `.clone()` exists only on a type that has one -- the row's own `R` does not.

design.md had already ruled on this exact question and the row did not have the
ruling, because the paragraph stating it was stale in BOTH directions. It read
"this rule is NOT yet enforced ... the parser does not yet accept `ref` in
