expression position", of the INDEX rule; both halves have since landed
(B-2026-08-26-36 then B-2026-08-26-21), which is why the row recorded the index
rule as enforced while the document denied it. What that paragraph got right is
the part worth keeping, and it is now the governing precedent here:

    Rejecting the form before the borrow spelling works would leave those sites
    with a diagnostic and no way to satisfy it, so the rejection is gated on the
    borrow form landing first.

A rule whose fix-it does not exist is not enforceable, whatever the spec says.
So the same gate applies one level up, and (c) is scheduled rather than
declined: when `ref` accepts a place expression, this becomes an error with
`ref s.r` as its fix-it. The stale paragraph is corrected in the same commit.

(2) WHAT LANDED. A new `borrow_projection_copy` lint (warn by default), emitted
through `type_lint_warning_with_fix` at the SAME two value positions the sibling
`E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY` covers -- a `let` initializer and an assignment RHS --
with `.clone()` as a machine-applicable fix where the type has one. It rides the
existing lint plumbing, so `#[allow(borrow_projection_copy)]`, the `--output=json`
`lint_name`/`fix_it` fields and `karac fix` all work with no new channel.

It sits in the TYPECHECKER rather than in a standalone `src/*_lint.rs` because
it needs no source text: detection reads the declared parameter mode, and the
fix is a zero-length insertion at the end of the read's span. The standalone
lints must read `self.source`, which is why `map_value_clone_reinsert` sits out
project mode entirely (B-2026-08-04-7); this one covers it.

Roots are the signature's borrows -- every `ref T` / `mut ref T` param plus
`self` under `ref self` / `mut ref self` -- collected per-function and
saved/restored around the body check on the same terms as
`current_fn_frozen_params`. It reads the DECLARED MODE and not the root
expression's inferred type on purpose: `expr_types` is keyed by span and a
projection's root shares its start offset with the whole chain, so `s` in `s.r`
reads back as the type of `s.r` (the overwrite hazard `map_entry_lint` documents
for the same reason).

(3) THE THREE EXEMPTIONS, one of which the lint got WRONG first. `Copy`,
`Error`/`Never`, `shared`, and function values follow the sibling rule. An
unsubstituted type param declines too: a `T: Copy` instantiation of the same
body does not copy, so firing would put a false claim on it.

The shared test had to look THROUGH `Option` / `Result` / tuples, which the
sibling rule never needs to: an indexed element IS the handle (`Vec[shared T]`),
whereas a FIELD routinely wraps one. `mut next: Option[Node]` over a
`shared struct Node` is the canonical linked-list link, and `let cur = self.head;`
there copies a HANDLE -- no second node, no second `Drop` body. The first draft
fired on three such sites in `examples/tangle/src/doubly_linked.kara`, where its
message was simply false. Caught by the corpus sweep, not by review.

TWO FALSE-POSITIVE CLASSES were found by RUNNING the lint rather than by reading
it, and both are recorded because neither is visible from the rule as stated:

  * The `Option[<shared>]` link above. Three sites in
    `examples/tangle/src/doubly_linked.kara`, found by the corpus sweep.
  * SHADOWING. The signature's borrow set is not the same question as "is this
    name a borrow HERE": an inner `let s = S { .. };` inside `fn f(s: ref S)`
    rebinds the name to an owned value whose projection is a MOVE. The first
    draft warned on it. The root test now requires the name to be a borrow in
    the signature AND to resolve to a `Ref`/`MutRef` in the local scope at the
    read. Both tests stay rather than just the scope one, because `self` is
    bound under its bare type rather than a `Ref` and the scope test alone
    would drop the `ref self` case.

(4) WHAT THE LINT ACTUALLY CLAIMS, and how each half was checked. `let m = s.r;`
over `s: ref S` neither moves (the caller still owns `s.r`) nor borrows (no
spelling); both backends COPY -- deep for a heap-bearing field
(`clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs`), bitwise otherwise. Note the row's `R { id: i64 }`
has no heap at all, so the doubling it reports is NOT that function: it is the
plain bit-copy plus owned tracking on the binding. The lint keys on `!Copy`,
which covers both and is what the spec sentence says.

  * The doubled `Drop`: `d3 3 d3 7 d7 end` on ALL FOUR surfaces (`--interp`,
    JIT, `build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`), byte-identical. The same program's
    OWNED-root spelling moves and runs the body once -- the contrast is the
    point, since the read's meaning is set by the root's parameter mode and
    nothing at the read shows which is in force.
  * The silent allocation: a `Vec[i64]` field read once per loop iteration, AOT.
    72 ms at n=16,000 and 302 ms at n=32,000 -- 4.2x for a 2x input, so
    quadratic -- against 5 ms for the same loop with the read hoisted out. 60x
    at n=32,000 and widening.

(5) SCOPE, and the one position deliberately left out. A CALL ARGUMENT
(`eat(s.r)`) is NOT reported. The sibling rule excludes the same position for
blast radius; here the reason is stronger and was measured: that shape mints no
copy at all and runs the `Drop` body EXACTLY ONCE, on all three surfaces, so a
warning there would be a false claim rather than a wider net.

(6) NOISE. 1 hit across 1,146 corpus files -- `runtime/stdlib`, `examples` and
all 950 `.kara` files in kara-katas, 512 of which use a `ref` parameter. The
single hit is a true positive (`cli.kara`'s `help_text` copies the whole
`program_name` String out of `ref self`) and is migrated in this commit by
`karac fix` itself, which is also how the fix-it was verified end to end:
output byte-identical before and after.

Worth recording for whoever lands (c): the `chained_field_receiver` lint's
fix-it text tells authors to "bind the inner field to a temporary first --
`let tmp = s.r;`", which is precisely the shape this one reports when the root
is a borrow. That is not a conflict today (one is a suggestion, the other a
warning, and both are true), but it becomes one the moment this is an error.

(7) NOT DONE, stated rather than implied. The copy is not ELIDED, and eliding it
was considered: every one of the six B-2026-07-21-11 regression programs binds
its copy READ-ONLY, so none of them wants a copy -- the copy is what codegen
improvised because the borrow spelling was missing. Eliding where the binding is
provably a non-escaping read-only view would remove both symptoms with no new
syntax, but it CHANGES OBSERVABLE `Drop` COUNTS on both backends, which is a
language decision this row is not the place to take unilaterally. It belongs
with the `ref <place>` work, and (c) is the cheaper end of it.
title: READING A NON-`Copy` FIELD OUT OF A `ref` PARAM MINTS AN IMPLICIT DEEP COPY -- silently allocating and running a user `Drop` body the source never wrote, which is exactly what `enum_payload_clone_is_faithful` refuses to do one level down
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-31-2, which is INVALID as filed (it read this copy as a
duplicated destructor on ONE value; it is one destructor on each of TWO values).
The contradiction that row noticed, though, survives its own refutation, and this
is it.

THE TWO POSITIONS, both deliberate, both landed, and in conflict.

(1) B-2026-07-21-11 made `let p = <refparam>.field` a DEEP COPY.
`clone_ref_chain_field_move_rhs` (`src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs:4044`,
hooked at `src/codegen/stmts.rs:5478`) deep-copies the RHS in place for every
heap-bearing leaf -- user struct, user enum, String, `Vec[i64]`, `Vec[String]`,
`Option[String]`. It fixed a real double-free (before it, the binding
bit-copy-aliased the caller's field and both freed the same heap). Six codegen
regression tests pin it; one is named
`e2e_generic_borrowed_field_move_out_is_a_copy_not_an_alias`.

(2) B-2026-08-09-9 (`enum_payload_clone_is_faithful`) REFUSES to clone a
`NestedStruct` payload, on the stated ground that "a clone is a
compiler-internal artifact the source language never asked for" -- i.e.
duplicating a value must not duplicate its `Drop` body.

Position (1) mints precisely the artifact position (2) forbids. Observable:

    struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    struct S { r: R }
    fn steal(s: ref S) -> i64 { let m = s.r; return m.id }
      let s = S { r: R { id: 3 } };
      println(f"n{steal(s)}");

        every backend: dR3 n3 dR3

Two values, one destructor each -- correct FOR A COPY. But the program never
asked for a copy. A `Drop` body that logs, unlocks, decrements a counter or
closes an fd runs twice for what the author wrote as one value, and the
allocation is invisible at the use site. `String`/`Vec` fields carry the same
silent cost: measured, `s.v` read out of a `ref` param deep-copies the buffer,
so a read-modify-writeback over a `Map` field copies the whole map per entry
(this was live in `runtime/stdlib/protobuf.kara`'s map merge until it was
rewritten to insert directly).

WHAT THE SPEC SAYS, and it currently agrees with NEITHER implementation.
design.md ss "The dereference operator (`*expr`)": "**Deref is not a consume.**
`*r` reads the referent; it does not move out of the reference (which would be
unsound -- the caller still owns the underlying value). `*r` in expression
position therefore requires `T: Copy` -- non-`Copy` values can be read *through*
the reference only via methods (`.clone()`, field projection, etc.)." Read
strictly, `let m = s.r` for non-`Copy` `R` should be an ERROR; the compiler
accepts it and clones. The sibling `E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY` rule DOES enforce the
strict reading for `v[i]`, so the two implicit-reference producers currently
disagree with each other as well as with the spec.

THREE WAYS TO SETTLE IT, in increasing cost:

  a. DOCUMENT the clone. Amend design.md to say a projection off a borrow is an
     implicit deep copy, note that it runs `Drop` per copy, and reconcile that
     with B-2026-08-09-9's principle (probably by scoping that principle to
     clones codegen mints for its OWN convenience, not ones a read implies).
     Cheapest, and makes the tree self-consistent.
  b. WARN. Keep the clone, add a lint at the read site so the allocation and the
     extra `Drop` are visible, with `.clone()` as the machine-applicable fix-it
     that silences it. Preserves every existing program.
  c. REJECT, matching the spec sentence and the index rule. MEASURED COST: a
     rejection was built and swept -- clean over 1154 `.kara` corpus files, but
     it breaks the six B-2026-07-21-11 regression tests, whose subject programs
     are embedded in Rust source and so are invisible to a `.kara` sweep. That
     is not a small revert; it reopens the shape B-2026-07-21-11 fixed unless
     every affected site migrates to an explicit `.clone()` first.

Do not pick (c) without reading those six tests: they encode the language's
answer as of 2026-07-21, and this row exists to decide whether that answer is
still the one wanted -- not to assume it is not.

title: A DISCARDED BRANCH LITERAL WHOSE FIELD IS A PROJECTION OFF A NAMED LOCAL STILL STRANDS 38 B -- `P { a: t.a, b: 1 }` is the half of B-2026-08-29-32's guard that B-2026-08-31-44 could NOT admit, because the aggregate-literal move takeover does not extend to named locals and admitting it double-frees in a loop
detail:
THE HALF OF B-2026-08-29-32'S GUARD THAT STILL HAS TO DECLINE, and the reason
it cannot be fixed at the discard site. B-2026-08-31-44 re-measured that guard
and split it: a bare binding and every non-field place no longer alias and are
now admitted, while a FIELD PROJECTION off a named local -- `P { a: t.a, b: 1 }`
-- still does and stays declined, keeping its 38 B-per-evaluation leak.

MEASURED (LSan, x86 Linux, post-B-2026-08-31-44):

    let t = mkp(9);
    if seed() > 0 { P { a: t.a, b: 1 } } else { P { a: payload(), b: 2 } };
                                       38 B leaked in 1 allocation

    // the same, one more statement after it            clean
    // the same, `let t` INSIDE a 20-iteration loop     722 B in 19 allocations

Same leak through `n.inner.a`, through an owned param's field, through a `ref`
param's field, through `self.a` in a method, and through a `shared struct`'s
field (39 B there). Every one of those is CLEAN if the guard is simply dropped.

WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY DROPPED. Exactly one shape turns from clean into
`double-free` when it is:

    let t = mkp(9);
    let mut i = 0i64;
    while i < 5i64 {
        if seed() > 0 { P { a: t.a, b: 1 } } else { P { a: payload(), b: 2 } };
        i = i + 1i64;
    }                                          double-free (5 frees, 1 buffer)

The local is declared OUTSIDE the loop and projected on each iteration, but the
retraction that would hand ownership to the literal is STATIC and fires once.
Note the blind spot this sits in: the guard's own doc prescribes a FOLLOWING
STATEMENT as the corrective for one-statement false negatives, and the stacked
form is clean here in both directions -- only a LOOP reaches it. Pinned as
`asan_discarded_branch_literal_field_over_a_loop_outer_local_declines`.

WHAT CLOSING IT ACTUALLY NEEDS -- not a wider gate at the discard site. The
`let`-BOUND spelling does not transfer ownership either:

    let t = mkp(9);
    let p = P { a: t.a, b: 1 };
    println(p.a.len());                                clean, 5 loop iters too

is clean precisely BECAUSE `p` never owns `p.a` -- `t` still frees it at scope
exit. So the field-move takeover B-2026-08-31-34 built for FRESH TEMPS
(`consume_freshtemp_field_move` -> `zero_struct_field_move_cap`, which zeroes
the field in the source's slot so the literal is the sole owner) has to be
extended to NAMED LOCALS on the general aggregate-literal path. Once the source
is zeroed, all three forms fall out: solo and loop-inner are freed once, and the
loop-outer cell reads NULL on iterations 2..n, so the double free above cannot
occur either. That is a change to the seven aggregate-literal consume sites, not
to the discard registration, which is why it is a separate row rather than a
widening of B-2026-08-31-44.

A MERGE-POINT ZERO IS THE WRONG SHORTCUT and is recorded so it is not retried:
the registration decision is made after the branch has merged, so zeroing the
source there fires even when the OTHER arm ran, which converts the `not_taken`
cell (source never consumed, currently clean) into a leak. The zero has to be
emitted INSIDE the arm, where the field is read -- i.e. on the general path.

SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-31-44's close rather than left inside it,
per the ledger rule that a closed investigation's live remainder gets its own
row. All measurements above are from that row's session.

RE-MEASURED 2026-09-01, AND THIS ROW'S OWN NUMBERS NEEDED CORRECTING. Measured
through `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s harness at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` with
`auto_par=false`, reading STDERR (the row's original figures came from a run
that read the wrong stream in places -- at the default `-O2` every cell here is
clean, the allocation being dead, so any measurement of this row MUST pin -O0).

    solo                     3 B / 1      (row: 38 B -- same defect, shorter string)
    stacked                  3 B / 1      (row says CLEAN -- WRONG, see below)
    loop, `t` inside        60 B / 20
    loop, `t` outside       17 B / 6
    nested field `n.inner.a` 3 B / 1
    let-bound projection     clean        (row: clean -- confirmed)
    bare binding arm         clean        (B-2026-08-31-44's admitted half)
    BOTH arms mint           clean

TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The STACKED form leaks; this row and B-2026-08-31-44 both
record it clean, which was a -O2 artifact. (2) More useful: the leak does NOT
require the projecting arm to RUN. `solo` above takes the ELSE arm -- the one
that mints `payload()` -- and still leaks, while the same program with both arms
minting is clean. So the mere PRESENCE of a projecting arm costs the sibling arm
its owner: the decline is per-construct, not per-path.

THE PRESCRIBED FIX WAS TRIED AND IS NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT. Extending
`consume_freshtemp_field_move` to NAMED LOCALS (a `consume_named_local_field_-
move` arm resolving the slot and struct name from the variable tables, so all
nine aggregate-literal consume sites get it at once) plus dropping
`field_init_aliases_a_temp`'s decline entirely takes 10 of 12 cells to clean --
including `loop, t outside`, which used to abort. It leaves two:

  * `no-else-proj` (`if c { P { a: t.a, b: 1 } };`) still leaks 2 B. That
    spelling reaches the ARM-LEVEL owner rather than the statement discard site,
    so it needs its own registration.

  * `then-taken-loop-outer` -- `t` declared OUTSIDE the loop, projected on each
    iteration, THEN arm taken -- becomes a DOUBLE FREE, which is worse than the
    leak it replaces, so the whole attempt was reverted rather than landed.

WHY THAT CELL RESISTS, which is the finding worth keeping.
`zero_struct_field_move_cap` clears the field's CAP, not its POINTER -- that is
enough to make the SOURCE's drop skip the buffer, and it is why the fresh-temp
version is safe (a fresh temp is minted anew each evaluation). A NAMED local is
not: on iteration 2 the literal reads `{ptr, len, cap}` and gets the SAME
non-null pointer with cap 0, so the literal's own drop frees it a second time.
Nulling the pointer instead would break the source's later reads.

SO THE REMAINING CELL IS PROBABLY NOT A CODEGEN BUG AT ALL. `P { a: t.a }`
evaluated repeatedly over a local declared outside the loop MOVES `t.a` out on
the first iteration; every later iteration is a USE AFTER MOVE. Ownership does
not reject it today. Closing this row likely needs that diagnostic -- at which
point the double-free cell becomes unreachable and the takeover above can land
unguarded -- rather than more codegen. Whoever picks this up should settle that
question FIRST; the codegen half is written and measured and is cheap to redo.

fix:
FIXED by b7674909, for the Vec-ROOTED chain at any depth. The remaining roots are
filed as a follow-up rather than half-built -- see the end.

`try_compile_ref_binding` had arms for an IDENTIFIER base and a FIELD base; an
INDEX base (`v[i]` as the object of another index) reached neither and hit the
decline. The interpreter always handled the shape -- `v[i]` evaluates to the
inner `Value::Array`, which its existing arm matches -- so this was a codegen
GAP against a working backend, not a divergence in either direction.

NO NEW ADDRESS ARITHMETIC WAS NEEDED, which is the part worth recording for
whoever extends it. The element pointer of `v[i]` IS the inner `Vec` header, and
`lower_indexed_elem_ptr_vec_at` (the by-pointer core split out for
B-2026-08-09-21) already indexes a header it is handed. So the outer hop reuses
the named lowering, the inner hop reuses the pointer one, and both inherit their
bounds checks -- a nested out-of-range index panics at whichever hop is out of
range, matching the flat spelling.

THE FIRST CUT WAS DEPTH-LIMITED AND LOOKED COMPLETE. It required the inner
object to be an `Identifier`, so `v[0][1]` -- the row's example -- worked while
`v[0][0][1]` still failed the build. Nothing in the row would have caught that;
probing triple nesting did. The resolver is now recursive, and double, triple
and quad are all pinned, with the aliasing contract (a write through the
container visible through the borrow) asserted at each depth so the binding is
demonstrably a pointer into the nested buffer rather than a copy.

MEASURED, remaining roots -- all correct under `--interp`, all `BUILD-FAIL`:

    let a: Array[Vec[i64], 1]  ->  ref a[0][1]
    let v: Vec[Array[i64, 2]]  ->  ref v[0][1]
    struct field               ->  ref h.grid[0][1]
    let s: Slice[Vec[i64]]     ->  ref s[0][1]

Each needs its own slot handling: an `Array`'s slot IS the storage rather than a
header, a `Slice` carries a start offset, and a field root needs
`lower_field_access_ptr`. Guessing a layout the helper has not checked is
exactly the defect class B-2026-08-30-21 turned out to be, so the resolver
returns `None` for all four and the caller emits the shared decline message.
Worth noting for whoever takes them: `nested_index_field_base_elem` already
lowers `h.grid[i][j]` for indexed READS, so the field root is the closest to
reach.

Twinned in both test files. Pre-fix the codegen half fails and the interpreter
half passes -- the honest shape for a gap row, where the interpreter is the
oracle rather than a regression witness.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH RECORDING: this fix invalidated an existing test's premise.
B-2026-08-31-37's `ref_binding_codegen_gap_explains_itself` asserts that the
decline message offers `--interp` for exactly the shapes the interpreter
handles, and it used nested `ref v[0][1]` as that case -- which now compiles, so
there is no diagnostic to assert. The suite caught it; the case moved to a
`Slice` root, which still declines. That one assertion has been revised twice by
neighbouring fixes in a single session (B-2026-08-31-36 for its `Map` wording,
this row for its nested case), which is an argument for working a family
consecutively rather than weeks apart: each correction was one line when caught
immediately.
title: CODEGEN DECLINES A NESTED `ref v[0][1]` WITH THE INTERNAL STRING `unreachable: Ref handled in compile_expr` WHILE THE INTERPRETER READS THE ELEMENT CORRECTLY -- the same arm as B-2026-08-31-37, reached by a spelling that has nothing to do with `Map`
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-31-36, and NOT that bug: this half is codegen's,
and the interpreter is the side that is right.

    fn main() {
        let v: Vec[Vec[i64]] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
        let g = ref v[0][1];
        println(g);
    }
      interp                 -> `2`   CORRECT
      jit / aot              -> error: codegen failed: unreachable: Ref handled in compile_expr

The interpreter gets this for free: `v[0]` evaluates to the inner
`Value::Array`, so the existing Array arm of `eval_ref_borrow` matches and
binds the element. Codegen's `try_compile_ref_binding` declines a non-trivial
base and falls to the `unreachable:` arm in `expr_ops.rs`.

WHY IT IS FILED SEPARATELY from B-2026-08-31-37, which reports the same string:
that row is about a `Map` BASE and frames the remedy as a diagnostic, on the
reasoning that a `ref` over a map element is genuinely unsupported. A NESTED
VEC index is not unsupported in the same sense -- one backend already
implements it, and the element has a perfectly good address -- so the right
outcome here is a LOWERING, not a better refusal. Merging the two would bury
that difference under a shared error message.

SCOPE NOTE: B-2026-08-31-37's proposed wording ("run with `--interp`") is
correct for THIS row and wrong for its own. B-2026-08-31-36 made the
interpreter decline a `Map` element `ref`, so `--interp` is no longer a
workaround there; it still is here, because the interpreter handles nested
indexing correctly.

NOT MEASURED: deeper nestings (`v[0][1][2]`), a nested index through a `Slice`
of `Vec`, and whether the same arm is reached by any other base shape.

title: A BARE `if` WITH NO `else` IN STATEMENT POSITION, WHOSE ARM LITERAL CONSUMES A LIVE LOCAL, RUNS THAT LOCAL'S `Drop` BODY TWICE UNDER `--interp` AND ONCE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- the compiled answer is the correct one, and this is the single cell of the B-2026-08-31-35 family where the backends disagree rather than agreeing on the doubled transcript
detail:
A BARE `if` WITH NO `else` IN STATEMENT POSITION, whose arm tail is a struct
literal consuming a live local, runs the local's `Drop` body ONCE on both
compiled backends and TWICE under `--interp`. Both compiled surfaces are
right; the interpreter is the odd one out.

    struct D { a: String, b: i64 }
    impl Drop for D { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dD{self.b}") } }
    struct W { r: D, b: i64 }

    fn main() {
        println("A");
        let t = mkd(7);
        if seed() == 0 { W { r: t, b: 1 } };
        println("B");
    }

                    --interp    A dD7 dD7 B      (two bodies, one object)
                    karac run   A dD7 B          correct
                    karac build A dD7 B          correct

WHY THE COMPILED SIDE IS THE CORRECT ONE. `t` is moved into a `W` that is
discarded at the statement, so the discard registration runs `W`'s field bodies
-- one `dD7` -- and `t` has handed its value over and must not run its own.
That is what both compiled backends do.

PRE-EXISTING, and measured as such rather than assumed: reproduced on a
pristine `main` build (91eca61) with no local changes applied, while
investigating B-2026-08-31-35. It is NOT a consequence of that row's fix --
which touches the ESCAPING-site hook that a discarded arm never reaches -- and
the same transcript appears with those changes reverted.

WHY IT HID. The two-tail spellings of the same discard (`if .. else`, `match`,
`let _ = if ..`) double on ALL THREE backends, so they are an agreed gap and no
A/B parity gate fires. Only the no-`else` spelling is a divergence, because
that one is the shape codegen owns INSIDE the arm
(`discarded_arm_owned_aggregate_tail`, B-2026-08-29-30) while the interpreter
still routes it through the same doubling path as its two-tail siblings.

WHERE TO START: the interpreter's discard dispatch for a bare `if` STATEMENT.
`discard_arm_tail_is_ownable` already declines a bare `Identifier` tail whose
name is still live, for exactly this reason -- firing there would double a live
local's body. The struct-literal tail needs the sibling treatment: the local
its field consumed has to be recorded moved-out, as
`record_conditional_move_tail` now does for the ESCAPING positions.

RELATED: B-2026-08-31-35 is the two-tail / bound-wrapper family this was found
inside. Its bound half is fixed; its discarded half is still open and is an
AGREED gap, not a divergence. This row is the one cell of the family where the
backends disagree.
fix:
FIXED by e49a85f -- which is B-2026-08-31-35's fix and was not aimed at this
cell. Measured before it was claimed, then verified by isolating that one
commit; this row's own regression cases are pinned by 0a32717.

WHAT THE FIX DID FOR THIS CELL. The row's "WHERE TO START" named the
interpreter's discard dispatch for a bare `if` statement, and that is exactly
where e49a85f landed. It added `disarm_discarded_tail_sources`, which peels
through `taken_discarded_tail` to the TAKEN arm's tail and records that tail's
aggregate-literal sources as moved-out. `taken_discarded_tail` handles an `If`
by walking `[then_block.final_expr, else_branch]` and flattening -- a no-`else`
`if` simply contributes one candidate instead of two, so the no-`else`
spelling was carried along with its two-tail siblings without a line aimed at
it. That is the sibling treatment the row asked for: the local whose value the
arm's field consumed is recorded moved-out, so it does not run its own body at
scope end.

MEASURED, PRE AND POST, ON THE ROW'S OWN SHAPE.

    fn go(n: i64) -> i64 { let t = R { id: 7 };
                           if n == 0 { S { r: t, k: 1 } };
                           return 7; }

    tree                          --interp        AOT
    e49a85f^ (bf63d1a)            dR7 dR7 v=7     dR7 v=7
    a3fe237 (main, post-fix)      dR7 v=7         dR7 v=7

The pre-fix column is not a recollection from the -35 session: it was
re-measured by reverse-applying e49a85f's `src` half -- and ONLY that half --
onto current `main` (`git diff e49a85f^ e49a85f -- src | git apply -R`, three
files, applies clean), rebuilding, and running the new cases. They go red with
exactly the row's transcript. `git checkout e49a85f^ -- src` was tried first
and rejected as evidence: it reverts ALL of `src` to that commit, which also
undoes other sessions' work landed since (`default_args.rs`, `float_math.rs`,
`typechecker/*`), so a red from it isolates nothing.

WHAT LANDED FOR THIS ROW. Two cases in
`e2e_an_arm_literal_consuming_a_local_runs_one_body`, both exercising the
no-`else` spelling across interpreter / JIT / AOT / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`:
the arm TAKEN (`go(0)`), which is the row's repro; and the arm NOT TAKEN
(`go(3)`), the control that pins the other half of the same predicate -- when
the branch does not run, nothing consumed `t`, so `t` must still run its own
body and the transcript is the same `dR7`. Without the second case a fix could
pass by unconditionally disarming the local and silently lose a body on the
not-taken path.

CORRECTION TO THE ROW'S OWN ATTRIBUTION. The row states this is "NOT a
consequence of that row's fix -- which touches the ESCAPING-site hook that a
discarded arm never reaches". The first half is right (it was pre-existing, and
the row's pristine-`main` measurement at 91eca61 stands). The second half
describes the fix as it was SCOPED when this row was written, not as it
shipped: e49a85f's interpreter half is not the escaping-site hook at all -- it
is a disarm at the three DISCARD sites, one of which is the bare-`if` statement
arm this row is about. So the codegen half of e49a85f left this cell alone and
the interpreter half closed it, which is why the divergence resolved in the
direction of the compiled backends rather than against them.

CLASSIFICATION NOTE. `class` stays `run-vs-build`: the defect as filed was a
backend disagreement, and it is the interpreter that moved to meet the compiled
answer. The two-tail siblings of the same family were an AGREED gap (all three
backends doubled) and were fixed under B-2026-08-31-35; the remainders of that
family that are still agreed gaps are tracked as B-2026-09-01-17 (projected
spelling) and B-2026-09-01-18 (block wrapper / bare literal statement).

GATES: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets`
clean on BOTH feature legs; `cargo test --features llvm --test codegen` green.

FIXED by 71bb567 (regression test in 722eb5f). Every `codegen failed:` now
carries a source position and a caret, the way every front-end diagnostic
already did.

    error: codegen failed: codegen: a `ref` binding over a `Map` element ...

    error: codegen failed: r2.kara:4:5: codegen: a `ref` binding over a `Map` ...
      |
    4 |     let r = ref m[1];
      |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

(1) THE ROW'S CENTRAL ESTIMATE WAS WRONG, IN A USEFUL DIRECTION, and this is
the part worth carrying forward. It proposed an INCREMENTAL fix -- add a span to
each of the ~248 messages "message by message rather than in one sweep",
wherever the emitting site happens to have one in scope -- and recorded as
unmeasured "how many of the ~135 sites actually have a span in scope (the value
is in the ones that do)".

NO PER-SITE WORK IS NEEDED, and none was done. `compile_expr` has stamped
`tracing.current_span` with the node it is about to compile since the Level 2
crash diagnostics landed, so that `emit_panic` can print
`panic at <file>:<line>:<col>`. A codegen bail is raised while compiling the
very node that stamped it. So the span is read ONCE, at the boundary, and all
248 messages gain a position together. The row's premise -- that a span is a
property of each message -- is what made this look like a 135-site job; it is a
property of the WALK, and the walk was already tracking it for another feature.

(2) THE FIRST DRAFT PUT THE CARET ON THE WRONG LINE, which is worse than the
bare sentence it replaced, and is the reason there are two cursors rather than
one. `let r = ref m[1];` is rejected in `compile_stmt`, BEFORE the right-hand
side is walked, so the expression cursor still held the PREVIOUS statement's
last sub-expression: measured, line 3 reported for an error on line 4, with a
confident caret under unrelated source.

Fixed with a dedicated `tracing.diag_span`, stamped by BOTH `compile_expr` and
`compile_stmt`, and restored on SUCCESS ONLY. The asymmetry is the mechanism:
leaving a successful node restores the parent, so the cursor always names the
innermost node still in progress; leaving a FAILED one does not, so the
innermost failing node is what propagates to the boundary.

It is deliberately NOT `tracing.current_span` itself. That field belongs to the
crash-diagnostics feature and is stamped by `compile_expr` alone; teaching it
about statements would move the position baked into runtime panic messages,
which is a tested user-visible behaviour and nothing to do with this row.

(3) THE CONVERSION WAS FAR CHEAPER THAN ITS FOOTPRINT SUGGESTS. `CodegenError
{ message, span }` replaces `String` on the 18 public entry points, against 776
`Err(...)` sites and 171 `Result<_, String>` signatures inside codegen and 310
call sites outside it. `Display` (rendering the message alone) keeps every
existing `{e}` formatting byte-identical, and `From<String>` keeps `?`
propagation from every internal site working untouched. Measured fallout: FOUR
edits in `src/`, plus ~15 mechanical `.message` additions in tests and two
examples. Nothing internal to codegen changed.

(4) THE DEFAULT CLIPPY LEG CAUGHT WHAT THE `--features llvm` LEG COULD NOT.
`render_codegen_error` named `crate::codegen::CodegenError` unconditionally, but
`pub mod codegen` is `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`, so the whole crate stopped
building WITHOUT the feature while the llvm leg stayed green -- exactly the trap
CLAUDE.md documents, and the leg CI runs. Now `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`.

VERIFICATION. The regression test is RED-verified by rebuilding the pre-change
binary against the same fixture: it prints the bare sentence, with no
`:13:5:`, no source line and no caret, so all three assertions fail. The
fixture puts two statements ahead of the failing one on purpose, and the test
asserts the LINE NUMBER -- a regression to the expression-only cursor would
still print a position and still print a caret, and still be wrong.

Span accuracy checked on both shapes: a STATEMENT-level bail (the `ref`-over-Map
binding) points at the statement, and an EXPRESSION-level one
(`fence(MemoryOrdering.Relaxed)` inside a multi-statement fn) points at the call
itself, `3:14`, with the caret under it. Full `--features llvm` suite 16,000
passed / 0 failed; re-verified after a rebase that brought in a codegen fix
touching `src/codegen/stmts.rs`, the same file this restructures: cli 734,
codegen 3,522, memory_sanitizer 1,354, all green. Both clippy legs clean.

NOT DONE, stated rather than implied.

  * The `error: codegen failed: ` prefix is unchanged, deliberately. It is what
    distinguishes a backend bail from a front-end rejection, and this suite
    asserts on the phrase in over a hundred places; the position and caret are
    added around it, not in place of it.
  * A span-LESS failure still renders as today's bare sentence. Module
    verification, target-machine setup and linker invocations have no source
    position, and inventing one is the (2) failure mode on purpose.
  * PROJECT-MODE `--output=json` keeps the bare message. `run_multi_file_codegen`
    passes no filename and no source text because a project has no single one,
    so a bare `line:col` would name no file -- the same reason
    `map_entry_lint` sits out project mode (B-2026-08-04-7). Single-file
    `--output=json` is likewise untouched: the row flagged the schema question
    as unmeasured and it stays open, since adding a position FIELD is a schema
    change its consumers should be surveyed for first.
title: CODEGEN'S ERROR CHANNEL CARRIES NO SPAN, SO EVERY `codegen failed: ...` DIAGNOSTIC IS SOURCE-LESS -- ~135 messages render as a bare sentence with no line, column or caret, and no single message can be fixed without reworking the channel
detail:
FILED BY B-2026-08-31-37, whose row asked for "a structured diagnostic with
the operand's span" and got only the MESSAGE half. The span half is not a
property of that one message -- it is the channel.

    codegen returns `Result<_, String>`; the CLI renders it as
        eprintln!("error: codegen failed: {e}")            (cli/build_cmds.rs)

so a codegen diagnostic has no span to render even when the emitting site knows
one. Measured on the row's own fixture:

    error: codegen failed: codegen: a `ref` binding over a `Map` element is
    not supported — ...

against what every FRONT-END diagnostic gives for the same file:

    error[typecheck]: /tmp/d.kara:4:17: 'Set[i64]' does not support indexing

WHY IT IS A CHANNEL PROBLEM AND NOT 135 MESSAGE PROBLEMS: `grep -c '"codegen: '`
over `src/codegen/*.rs` finds ~135 messages, and NONE of them carries a span,
including the ones whose emitting site has the expression in hand. The
`--interp` pointer that several of them end with exists precisely because the
user cannot otherwise tell WHERE the gap was hit.

WHERE TO START. The narrow version is a `CodegenError { msg: String, span:
Option<Span> }` with `From<String>` so the ~135 existing `Err("...".into())`
sites keep compiling unchanged, plus a helper for the sites that do know a span;
the CLI then renders `file:line:col` when present and falls back to today's
shape when absent. That keeps the change additive and lets spans be added
message by message rather than in one sweep.

NOT MEASURED: how many of the ~135 sites actually have a span in scope (the
value is in the ones that do), and whether `--output=json` consumers of
`build_cmds.rs`'s `message:` field would need a matching schema field.

title: A BRANCH MIXING AN F-STRING ARM WITH A STRING-LITERAL ARM LEAKS THE F-STRING -- `if c { f"i{n}" } else { "lit" }.contains("i")` strands the 2 B buffer that the all-f-string spelling now frees, because the fail-closed predicate requires EVERY tail to mint and a rodata literal mints nothing; admitting it is a runtime no-op at the one free site that was read, but weakens the quantifier that keeps an aliased-place arm out at seven
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the deliberate remainder of B-2026-08-30-3, split out rather than
folded into it. That row admitted an `InterpolatedStringLit` tail to
`branch_tail_mints_fresh_owned_temp_inner`, closing nine spellings. A branch
whose arms MIX an f-string with a string LITERAL still declines, because the
predicate is fail-closed on every tail and a `StringLit` tail is not admitted.

MEASURED (KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, valgrind, at B-2026-08-30-3's fix):

    let p9 = if c { f"i{n}" } else { "lit" }.contains("i");
                                                2 B / 1 object   LEAKS

    CONTROL -- both arms f-strings (the fixed population):    clean
    CONTROL -- both arms literals:                            clean
        let g = if c { "lit1" } else { "lit2" }.contains("lit");
        (rodata, cap == 0; there is nothing to free)

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE EXTENSION OF ITS PARENT. Admitting `StringLit` /
`MultiStringLit` to the same leaf looks free, and at the FREE SITE it is:
`free_str_vec_buffer_if_heap` branches on `cap > 0` and a rodata literal has
`cap == 0`, so the emitted free is a runtime no-op. That is an argument about
ONE of the seven gates this predicate feeds, and the others were not measured.
`discard_arm_tail_qualifies` already admits both literal kinds, which is a hint
-- but the discard frame is the only owner there, so it is not evidence, the
same caveat its parent row recorded.

THE REAL COST IS THE FAIL-CLOSED RULE, NOT THE NO-OP FREE. The predicate's
"EVERY tail must mint" quantifier is what keeps an ALIASED-PLACE arm out, and
that rule is load-bearing: a tail handing out a binding leaves it readable
afterwards, so a use-site free would DANGLE rather than leak -- strictly worse.
Admitting a shape that mints nothing weakens the quantifier's meaning from
"every tail mints" to "every tail mints or is harmless", and each future
candidate for "harmless" then has to be re-argued against seven gates. Worth a
row that measures it rather than a line that assumes it.

SEVERITY: one rendered f-string per evaluation, unbounded in a loop; no double
free and no wrong answer -- the same profile as the parent, and the same
reason for low rather than medium. Narrower than the parent too: it needs a
branch that mixes an interpolated arm with a literal arm, where the parent
covered every all-f-string spelling.

NOT MEASURED: whether the other six gates tolerate a cap-0 value (only the
`free_str_vec_buffer_if_heap` receiver site was read); whether a `Binary`
string-concat tail -- which `discard_arm_tail_qualifies` admits via
`string_typed_exprs` -- belongs in the same widening; and the `match` spelling
of the mixed shape, which should behave identically but was not run.

fix:
FIXED by fcb6696 (the two codegen leaks and the quarantine split) and
03fe517 / B-2026-09-01-14 (a THIRD red gate found while verifying this one:
the DEFAULT `cargo test` leg, red since 02:54Z the same day).

THE LEG IS GREEN AND ITS QUARANTINE HAS EXACTLY ONE OWNED LINE. Of the three
failures, TWO WERE REAL CODEGEN LEAKS and are fixed; the third is the
deliberately-declined shape B-2026-09-01-5 already owns, and it is the only
thing on the list.

The row's own framing turned out to be the right one: the finding was not any
one of the three but that NOTHING RUNS THIS LEG. All three predate the work
that found them, and one arrived green-on-arrival at -O2 the same day. Both
leaks below are invisible at the default -O2 for the same reason the file's
header states -- the stranded allocation is dead, so LLVM deletes the whole
chain along with the evidence.

LEG 1 -- `asan_wildcard_let_discard_owns_what_its_arm_hands_out`
(`payload-braced-arm`): A BLOCK-BODIED ARM OF A DISCARDED `match` STRANDED
WHATEVER ITS TAIL NAMED.

`compile_if` has told each arm whether the construct's value has a consumer
since B-2026-08-29-25 (`discard_stmt_owns_value` -> `branch_arm_value_discarded`).
`compile_match` NEVER ASKED: it set `arm_tail_owner_ctx` and nothing else, so a
braced arm compiled through `compile_block_with_frame` with the flag clear --
i.e. as though a consumer existed -- and ran `suppress_block_tail_cleanup`.
That call is a HANDOVER: it takes the tail's buffer away from whatever owns it
so the branch's consumer can own it instead. With no consumer the buffer is
stranded.

    let o: Option[R] = Some(mk(1));
    let _ = match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { mk(9) } };   38 B, per evaluation
    match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { mk(9) } };           38 B (bare statement too)
    let r = mk(41);
    let _ = match n { 9 => { r } _ => { mk(9) } };            38 B (an enclosing local)

THE BRACES ARE THE UNIT, not the match: `Some(r) => r,` on the identical value
is clean, because `compile_match`'s own arm-tail hook gates that same
suppression on `owns_result`. Only the braced spelling reaches the block
compiler, where the gate was missing. Fixed by giving `compile_match` the
`compile_if` signal, with a parts-form `discarded_match_arms_qualify` beside
the existing `discarded_if_parts_qualify` so the two spellings cannot answer
differently, and set only for a body that is DIRECTLY a block -- the same gate
the arm context uses, since that is the only shape reaching the block compiler
AS THIS ARM.

A SECOND, ADJACENT HALF found by the same probe matrix and fixed in the same
commit: the MINTED arm of a discarded match the statement site DECLINES (one
arm yields a place, so freeing the phi could double-free) had no owner at all
in the BARE spelling.

    let o: Option[R] = None;
    let _ = match o { Some(r) => r, None => mk(9) };          38 B on the taken path

That one is also a RUN-VS-BUILD divergence, not only a leak: the interpreter
fires `dR9`, both compiled backends were silent, and they agree now. The
braced spelling of the same program was already owned, which is what localises
it to the bare-arm path -- `compile_if_let` has had exactly this
`!owns_result && expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` registration since
B-2026-08-29-5 and `compile_match`'s bare-arm path never grew it.

LEG 2 -- `asan_structpat_iflet_destructure_no_double_free`: A BOXED STRUCT
PAYLOAD DESTRUCTURED BY `if let` / `while let` / `let .. else` WITH A
READ-ONLY BODY LOST EVERY BOUND FIELD.

    let o: Option[Holder] = Some(Holder { name: f"...47 bytes...", id: i });
    if let Some(Holder { name, id }) = o { println(name.len() + id); }
                                       141 B / 3 blocks over three iterations

All three constructs ran `suppress_boxed_payload_struct_destructure`
UNCONDITIONALLY, on a comment asserting it was "self-gated on
`boxed_enum_payload_vars` membership -- only a binding OWNED here is
registered, so borrow scrutinees no-op". That table is a property of the
SCRUTINEE VARIABLE, not of the binding mode, so it says nothing about whether
the arm took ownership. When the body only READS, `set_scrutinee_shape_flags`
classifies the scrutinee `pattern_binding_is_borrow` (via
`scrutinee_is_readonly_owned_enum_local`), `bind_pattern_values` registers no
`track_vec_var` for the leaf (gated on that same flag), and the fields ALIAS
the box -- so disarming the box left them with no owner anywhere.

The `match` spelling has gated this on `!pattern_binding_is_borrow` since it
was written (`if scrut_ref_ptr.is_none() && !pattern_binding_is_borrow`), and
is clean on the identical value: another B-2026-08-28-67 asymmetry, one more
suppressor the three `let`-family paths never inherited. Two controls fix the
axis: making the body MOVE a field (`slen(name)`) flips the bind to owned and
is clean before AND after -- the disarm must still fire there or the binding
and the box both free the buffer -- and a direct (non-Option) struct scrutinee
was clean throughout, so the boxed payload is what routes through the
suppressor at issue. Traced rather than inferred: an instrumented build prints
`bind leaf name=name bound_vec_elem=true is_borrow=true` plus `boxfld disarm
Holder.name` for the `if let` and the SAME bind line with NO disarm for the
`match`.

LEG 3 -- `asan_discarded_branch_literal_over_a_binding_frees_once`
(`discarded_branch_literal_field_over_a_loop_outer_local_declines`): NOT A
DEFECT AND NOT FIXABLE HERE. Its own doc comment says the projection strands
38 B by design and B-2026-09-01-5 states why it cannot be closed at the
discard site, so the fixture asserted ASAN-clean on a program documented as
leaking -- it could never pass at -O0, and passes at -O2 only because the
optimizer deletes the allocation. Split into its own `#[test]` (which is also
the name B-2026-09-01-5's prose already cited and that did not exist) and
quarantined against that row, so the other two cells of the original fixture
stay live on the leg instead of being silenced along with it.

VERIFIED: `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` green, matching the one-line quarantine
exactly. Both new fixtures FAIL at -O0 with `src/` stashed and pass with it
(141 B and 38 B, the pre-fix numbers). Every shape checked across all four
surfaces -- `--interp`, JIT, `karac build`, and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`
-- byte-identical, with `Drop` bodies included; the codegen E2E carries those
as assertions.

NOT CHANGED, deliberately: `match o { Some(r) => r, .. };` handing out a
heap-carrying `Option` payload is still silent on both compiled backends and
fires on the interpreter. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING against a pristine `main`
build rather than assumed, and it is B-2026-08-31-28's, whose population this
row's gates neither cause nor reach.
title: THE -O0 ASAN LEG IS RED ON `main` WITH THREE UNOWNED FAILURES AND AN EMPTY QUARANTINE LIST -- `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` reports 1339 passed / 3 failed, every one reproducing without the change that found them; one fixture landed GREEN on the default -O2 leg and red at -O0 the same day, so the two-way ratchet is only a ratchet when somebody runs it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by running scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh as a gate for
B-2026-08-30-3, and confirmed to PREDATE that work -- both fixtures fail with
that row's `src/` stashed away, i.e. at plain `main`.

MEASURED (scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh, x86_64 Linux, archives current, at 91eca61):

    test result: FAILED. 1339 passed; 3 failed; 9 ignored; finished in 203.34s

    memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_discarded_branch_literal_over_a_binding_frees_once
    memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_structpat_iflet_destructure_no_double_free
    memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_wildcard_let_discard_owns_what_its_arm_hands_out

EACH REPRODUCES ON PLAIN `main`, verified individually by checking `src/` out
at 91eca61 and re-running -- so none is fallout from the row that found them.
The third is the newest and the most telling: its fixture arrived the SAME DAY
in 1b5c026 (B-2026-08-31-44's fix), green on the default -O2 leg and red at -O0
from the moment it landed. A fixture can therefore be authored, reviewed and
merged without anyone learning it fails at -O0.

The first fails on its `payload-braced-arm` case:

    fn go() -> i64 { let o: Option[R] = Some(mk(1));
        let _ = match o { Some(r) => { r } None => { mk(9) } };
        1 }

    ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
    Direct leak of 38 byte(s) in 1 object(s)
        #1 payload

38 B is the `R.s` String, i.e. the payload of the value the arm hands out. The
arm body is a BLOCK whose tail names the bound payload `r`, under a
wildcard-`let` discard -- the shape whose ownership the owning row was written
to settle, in its braced spelling.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE TWO FIXTURES. The quarantine list
(tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt) is EMPTY, and its header states the
consequence plainly: "with nothing quarantined, ANY -O0 failure is a new
failure". So the leg is red on `main` with no row owning either failure, which
is the exact state the two-way ratchet exists to prevent. The list was last
measured 2026-08-06 at 225a4553; `main` has moved several hundred commits since,
and the leg is not part of the default or `--features llvm` legs, so nothing
runs it automatically. That is the real finding: the ratchet only ratchets when
somebody turns it.

NOT MEASURED: which commit introduced either failure (no bisect run); whether
`asan_structpat_iflet_destructure_no_double_free` is a leak or a genuine
double free -- only the wildcard-`let` one was read in detail; and whether
either reproduces at the default -O2, which would make them ordinary
memory-sanitizer failures rather than -O0-only ones. Bisecting is the obvious
next step and is cheap, since the leg names the fixtures.

DELIBERATELY NOT QUARANTINED. Adding both to
tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt would turn the leg green and is what its
header invites ("or add the fixture ... WITH the bug row that owns it") -- this
row is that owner, but quarantining before anyone has looked at the defect
trades a red gate for a permanent allowlist entry, which is the decay the list
documents itself against. Left red so the next run still reports it.

title: THE NON-CONSTRUCTOR ARMS OF A DISCARDED BRANCH STILL DISAGREE IN THREE SHAPES -- a CALL arm registers nothing on either compiled backend where the direct call spelling runs the own body, and a LIVE-LOCAL arm makes the interpreter drop that local at the branch (doubling the enum's own body in the `let _ =` spelling) where both compiled backends correctly leave it to its own scope end
detail:
THREE SHAPES OF THE B-2026-08-31-22 FAMILY WHOSE ARMS ARE NOT INLINE
CONSTRUCTORS still disagree between the backends. All are PRE-EXISTING:
measured byte-identical on a pristine `main` build (5e878b4) with that row's
changes reverted, so they are the remainder its all-arms gate deliberately
declines, not a consequence of it.

    struct R { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn mke(n: i64) -> E { return E.A(mk(n)); }

(1) A CALL ARM -- compiled registers NOTHING, interpreter runs the own body.

    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { mke(9) };
                          interp   dE          jit/aot   (nothing)

    The direct spelling `let _ = mke(8);` is `dE` on all three, so the
    interpreter is the correct one here and compiled loses even the own body.
    `discarded_match_value_tail` admits the construct (a call IS a fresh owned
    temp), so `tail` is the branch node, but no arm of the enum leg can name a
    type from it -- and B-2026-08-31-22's redirect deliberately declines it,
    because walking the payload would contradict the direct spelling.
    Registering the OWN body alone is what this shape wants, which is a
    different registrar from the one that row wired.

(2) A LIVE-LOCAL ARM, `let _ =` spelling -- the interpreter runs the enum's own
    body TWICE and drops the local early.

    let e = mke(3);
    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { e };
    println("mid");
                interp    dE dE dR3 mid          (two own bodies, `e` early)
                jit/aot   dE dR8 mid ... dE dR3  (correct)

(3) The same with the BARE-STATEMENT spelling -- one own body, but the local
    still dies at the branch rather than at its own scope end.

                interp    dE dR3 mid
                jit/aot   dE dR8 mid ... dE dR3  (correct)

    In both, the taken arm is the CTOR arm, so `e` is never consumed and must
    keep its own scope-exit body -- which is what compiled does. The
    interpreter instead treats the branch as having moved `e` out. (2) then
    additionally fires the discard walker on top, giving the doubled `dE`.

WHY THEY ARE ONE ROW: all three are the same question -- what a DISCARDED branch
owes when an arm is not an inline construction -- and the answer differs per arm
kind, so they want one matrix rather than three investigations. (1) is a
compiled gap; (2) and (3) are interpreter gaps; the compiled transcript is the
correct one in all three.

DO NOT fix (1) by widening B-2026-08-31-22's all-arms gate to admit calls. That
gate exists because the walk is value-driven: admitting a call arm would run the
payload walk over a call-produced enum, which the direct spelling does not,
turning an agreed answer into a divergence in the other direction. The own body
needs its own registration at that site.

SOURCE NOTE: found as the SAFETY controls in B-2026-08-31-22's 19-shape matrix,
written to check that its all-arms gate declines what it should. It does; these
are what remains behind the decline.
fix:
FIXED by ee15b92 (shape 1, codegen) and 33a1dc6 (shapes 2 and 3, interpreter).

SHAPE 1 was ARM ORDER, not constructor arms, and the row's diagnosis pointed at
the wrong gate. `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp` resolves a discarded
branch's type from its FIRST arm, through `discard_branch_tail_type_name`, and
that resolver understood a struct literal and a plain fn call but not an enum
CONSTRUCTION. A call in first position named the type; a constructor in first
position yielded `None`, and the whole discard battery then registered nothing.
The mirror-image spelling is the proof, and it was correct all along:

    let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { mke(9) };   interp dE, jit/aot NOTHING
    let _ = if c { mke(8) } else { E.A(mk(9)) };   dE on all three

Two arms on that resolver (`E.A(x)`, whose enum is the path's first segment, and
the `E.B` unit spelling) plus an all-ctor exclusion on the two branch arms that
call it: an all-constructor branch belongs to B-2026-08-31-22's
representative-tail redirect, which runs the payload walk too, so naming it here
as well would register a SECOND owner and double the own body. The row's
"DO NOT widen the all-arms gate" warning was right and is respected — that gate
is untouched.

Measured over a 36-cell matrix — {ctor-first, call-first, unit-first, all-ctor,
all-call, bare call} x {`let _`, bare statement} x {both branches taken} on
interp/jit/aot: 12 cells diverged before, 0 after, no agreeing cell moved.

SHAPES 2 AND 3 were one interpreter defect, and both of the row's readings of
them are wrong (corrected below). Both interpreter gates asked a STATIC all-arms
question — `discard_producer_runs_payload_walk` for the payload walk,
`hands_out_live_binding` / `owns` for ownership itself — and declined the whole
construct when ANY arm named a live local. The hazard they exist for is real,
but it belongs to the arm that RUNS: the interpreter has recorded which arm tail
produced the value since B-2026-08-29-31, so both gates now ask the taken tail,
which is how each compiled backend decides it, one arm's basic block at a time.

The payload-walk half is NARROWED to the live-local population deliberately,
and the narrowing is measured. Only that decline varies per run: a CALL arm's
decline is a statement about what `let _ = mke(9);` does — the own body alone,
on every backend — which does not vary. Re-asking it per run made shape 1's own
repro print `dE dR8` in the interpreter against `dE` on jit and aot, i.e. traded
this row's divergence for a fresh one; the guard cell that pins it is in the
regression test.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ROW AS FILED, both measured on its own repro:

(a) There is NO drop-PLACEMENT divergence. The row says the interpreter "drops
    that local at the branch ... where both compiled backends correctly leave it
    to its own scope end", and renders compiled as `dE dR8 mid ... dE dR3`. Run
    with a `println("mid")` between the branch and the scope end, ALL THREE
    backends print `dE dR8 dE dR3 mid` — the local dies before the marker, not
    after it. A control where the local is never mentioned in the branch prints
    `dE dR3 dE dR8 mid` on all three: it dies at its own `let`. That is NLL
    last-use placement, and the backends agree on it.

(b) `dE dE` is the right COUNT, not "the enum's own body TWICE". One `dE` comes
    from the discarded value and one from the local. What was missing is `dR8`,
    the discarded value's PAYLOAD walk; the bare-statement spelling lost the
    discarded value entirely rather than just its payload.

Regression tests: `e2e_a_discarded_branch_with_a_non_ctor_arm_runs_its_own_body`
(13 cases) and `e2e_a_discarded_branch_whose_sibling_arm_names_a_live_local`
(14 cases) in `tests/codegen.rs`, plus
`asan_a_discarded_branch_with_a_ctor_first_arm_is_owned_once` (11 cases) in
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`. Each is red without its half of the fix. The guard
cells carry the boundaries: an arm's own PATTERN BINDING is a different
population from an enclosing local, a no-`else` `if` records no arm tail when
its condition is false, and the all-ctor branch and the call arm must keep the
counts they already had.

REMAINDER, split out rather than folded in: the run where the TAKEN arm is
ITSELF the live local and that local carries a payload. Compiled runs the
payload's body there and the interpreter does not, and the `if` and `match`
spellings disagree with each other on BOTH backends in opposite directions. It
is pre-existing (identical before and after this fix) and is a different
question from this row's, which is about the run where the OTHER arm produced
the value. Filed as B-2026-09-01-39.

Fixed in 605208d9. The row's own program is now a type error, and so is every
sibling spelling: `let d: f32 = 0.1f64`, `-0.1f64`, `0.1f64 * 2.0`, `0.1f32`
into an `f16`, and the same literal at an argument, a struct field, a `Vec`
element, an array element, a return, and an `Option`/`Result` payload.

THE ROW'S PREMISE — that this needs a language decision between (a) suffix
wins, (b) slot wins and (c) reject — DOES NOT SURVIVE MEASUREMENT. The tree
already rules: design.md's implicit-widening table says any narrowing needs an
explicit `as`, and both halves are enforced for a variable — `let d: f32 = c`
with `c: f64` and `let d: i32 = c` with `c: i64` are hard errors naming the
cast. Integers already behave as (b) as well: `let d: i32 = 2147483647i64;
d + 1` overflows exactly as the unsuffixed control does, so the annotation
types the binding and the suffix is inert. Floats were the outlier, and the
question was never which of three policies to adopt but why one construct was
exempt from the policy the language already has. So (c) landed, as the row
recommended, but as the closing of a hole rather than as a choice.

TWO MEASUREMENTS THE ROW DID NOT HAVE, both of which change its shape.

FIRST, the worse case is not a run-vs-build split at all. `let d: f32 =
16777217.0f64` bound 16777217 on ALL FOUR surfaces — interp, JIT, AOT and
auto-par-0 agreeing on a value no `f32` can represent. The annotation was not
merely overridden, it was falsified, and because every backend agreed there was
nothing for an A/B fixture to catch. The row saw only the `Option` spelling,
where the two backends happen to disagree, and therefore classified the whole
thing as run-vs-build.

SECOND, the `Option` spelling needed a SECOND fix at a different site, so the
row's "one decision, one patch" framing understates it. A payload slot is
seeded from the expectation and is checked at the generic-call site rather than
by `check_expr`'s prologue — and that site had an INTEGER narrowing gate
(B-2026-08-08-9) and no float one, because its `seeded_arg_narrows` pre-filter
reasons in `int_signed_width`. Adding the float sibling there is what closes
the row's own program, and it also closes `Option.Some(c)` with `c: f64`, which
had no diagnostic on any route.

THE FIX, in one sentence each. `check_float_narrowing_coercion` used to run its
compile-time-constant exemption FIRST and unconditionally; the exemption's own
justification is that an unsuffixed literal is inferred AT the destination's
width and so never narrows, which is precisely what a suffix undoes, so it now
covers a constant only while none of its float leaves names a width of its own
(`0.1`, `-1.0` and `0.0 * (0.0 - 1.0)` stay exempt for the reason they were
exempted; `0.1f64` does not). And the seeded-argument site gains the float gate
it never had.

THE SECOND DEFECT, the misleading warning, is fixed by WITHDRAWAL rather than
rewording. `redundant_suffix` fires on a suffix naming the DEFAULT type and
never consults the destination, so it called `0.1f64` in an `f32` slot
"redundant" — a claim about the program that is false, since deleting the
suffix changes the literal's width and therefore its value. It is worse than
wording: the lint carries a machine-applicable fix that DELETES the suffix,
justified in its own comment by exactly the redundancy that does not hold here,
so `karac fix` would have applied it on a wrong premise. The deletion happens
to be the right edit now — it is what the new error recommends — so the fix
survives and only the false claim goes, matched by span CONTAINMENT so the
`-0.1f64` spelling (gate span = the unary expression, lint span = the literal)
is covered too.

WIDENING IS UNTOUCHED and deliberately so: `let w: f64 = 0.1f32` still holds
the f32 value widened, which `test_float_literal_width_respects_f64_slots_and_
suffixes` pins. A suffix NARROWER than its destination is the author choosing a
coarser constant, which loses nothing.

BLAST RADIUS, measured rather than hoped: the full `--features llvm` suite was
green at 15970 before the new fixtures, so the gate rejects nothing that
existed, and the entire `.kara` corpus contains one `f64` suffix — inside a
string literal in `runtime/stdlib/protobuf.kara`.

design.md § Numeric Semantics > Literal suffixes now states the rule, including
the integer half (governed by the range check instead) and the widening
carve-out.

Tests. `tests/typechecker.rs::a_literal_suffix_wider_than_its_destination_is_
rejected` enumerates the positions rather than sampling them, because they
reach the gate by two different routes and a fix to one says nothing about the
other; it also pins the four accepted shapes, each for its own reason.
`a_contradicting_suffix_withdraws_the_redundant_suffix_warning` covers the lint
half on both routes and asserts the genuinely-redundant cases keep it.
`tests/interpreter.rs::test_contradicting_suffix_repairs_agree_across_backends`
and its `tests/codegen.rs` twin pin that the two repairs the diagnostic offers
agree on every surface — the obligation
`test_float_narrowing_as_cast_rounds_to_the_target_width` states for the
earlier gate, that a fix-it must not trade a silent narrowing for a split.

REMAINDER, filed as B-2026-09-01-19 rather than folded in: the INTEGER sibling
this row lists as unmeasured. It splits, in three shapes, one of which changes
the SIGN — `Option[u8] = Option.Some(300i64)` is `Some(300)` interpreted and
`Some(44)` compiled, and `Option.Some(-1i64)` is `Some(-1)` against `Some(255)`
— with no diagnostic beyond the same false `redundant_suffix`. Its cause is
different: `check_int_widening_coercion` exempts suffixed literals on the
stated ground that they were "already range-checked against the contextual type
at the top of `check_expr`", which is true of the `check_expr` route and false
of the seeded one that never reaches it.
title: A SUFFIXED FLOAT LITERAL WHOSE SUFFIX CONTRADICTS THE DESTINATION WIDTH SPLITS THE BACKENDS -- `let d: Option[f32] = Option.Some(0.1f64)` is `Some(0.1)` under `--interp` and `Some(0.10000000149011612)` compiled, and the warning calls the suffix "redundant" when it is contradictory
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING B-2026-08-31-20, and MEASURED PRE-EXISTING: the same program
diverges identically on a build with that fix stashed, so it is neither caused
nor fixed by it.

    fn main() {
        let d: Option[f32] = Option.Some(0.1f64);
        println(f"{d}");
    }
      interp -> Some(0.1)
      jit / aot / aot-par0 -> Some(0.10000000149011612)

WHY B-2026-08-31-20 DOES NOT COVER IT. That fix records a narrow destination
width on an UNSUFFIXED literal only -- a suffix is the author naming the width,
and `record_narrow_float_literal` honours it by design. So the recursion reaches
this literal and correctly declines to re-record it. The interpreter then keeps
the f64 value the suffix asked for; codegen narrows to the SLOT's f32. Both are
defensible in isolation, which is why this needs a decision rather than a patch.

THE DECISION IS A LANGUAGE ONE, and design.md should say which:
  (a) the suffix wins and the value stays f64 -- then codegen is wrong, and an
      f64 value in an f32 slot is a representation the slot cannot hold;
  (b) the slot wins and the literal narrows -- then the interpreter is wrong,
      and the suffix is silently overridden;
  (c) it is a type ERROR to write a suffix that contradicts its destination --
      which is the only option under which nobody is silently overruled, and is
      what the existing `redundant_suffix` warning is groping toward.

(c) looks right and is the smallest surface: the two backends already disagree
only on programs the checker could reject outright.

SECOND, SMALLER DEFECT IN THE SAME PROGRAM. The warning reads:

    warning[redundant_suffix]: redundant `f64` suffix: f64 is the default type
    for this literal

In an `Option[f32]` slot f64 is NOT the default type for that literal -- the
destination is f32 -- so the suffix is CONTRADICTORY, not redundant, and the
message states a falsehood about the program. Whatever is decided above, this
wording is wrong for the conflicting case and should be split from the genuinely
redundant one (`let a: f64 = 0.1f64`).

NOT MEASURED: the `f32`-suffix-into-`f16`-slot direction, the widening direction
(`let d: Option[f64] = Option.Some(0.1f32)` -- which the existing over-reach
guard `test_float_literal_width_respects_f64_slots_and_suffixes` pins as
"suffix wins" at an annotated `let`, suggesting (a) is the current intent
there), and whether the same split exists for INTEGER suffixes.

fix:
Done in 43a0e728. The audit's deliverable is a list, and here it is: ELEVEN
surfaces probed differentially -- the same program written once with a free
function `f(..)` and once with `impl H { fn f }` called as `H.f(..)` -- and
compared on all four executors.

    surface                                          verdict
    ---------------------------------------------    ------------------------
    argument LABELS (infer_call's param_names)        GAP -- fixed in 43a0e728
    DEFAULT arguments (default_args.rs)               GAP -- filed as
                                                        B-2026-09-01-20
    effect inference + public-declaration check       both spellings
    par / module-binding write conflict               both spellings
    ref-return ownership                              both spellings
    call-site `mut` marker requirement                both spellings
    exclusive-borrow aliasing across arguments        both spellings
    arity checking                                    both spellings
    generic inference                                 both spellings
    `?` propagation                                   both spellings
    `deprecated` lint                                 both spellings

THE LABEL GAP IS THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE SHAPE THIS ROW NAMED, and it is the
worst of the four, because it did not fail -- it succeeded wrongly.
`infer_call` looks the LAST SEGMENT of a two-segment path up in
`env.functions`, where an associated fn does not live under `f` or under
`H.f`; the lookup returned `None`, so `param_names` was `None` and
`validate_labels` was never called. Labels were therefore not merely unchecked
but DISCARDED: `H.f(b: 3, a: 10)` bound positionally and computed `a - b` as
`3 - 10`, printing `-7` on interp, JIT, AOT and auto-par-0 alike, and
`H.f(zz: 3, qq: 10)` -- labels naming no parameter of anything in the program
-- was accepted in silence. The bare spelling and the INSTANCE-METHOD spelling
reject both, which is what identifies it as a spelling asymmetry rather than a
policy about labels.

The resolution it needed was twenty lines below it the whole time. The
`callee_where_clause` lookup in the same function consults the impl table FIRST
(`env.find_method`) and falls back to the bare-name table only on a miss, and
its comment explains both halves as load-bearing -- B-2026-08-22-10 for the
false negative that motivates the impl lookup, B-2026-08-22-11 for the false
positive that requires it to come first (keyed on the last segment alone,
`H.take(x)` finds an unrelated global `take`). The param-name arm now uses the
same shape, and the test carries that false-positive guard explicitly.

THE PATTERN THE ROW PREDICTED HELD, WITH A CORRECTION TO ITS SCOPE. It expected
each finding to be a qualified-vs-bare asymmetry. The labels one is exactly
that. The DEFAULTS one is not: instance methods reject the omitted argument
too, so the real boundary there is free-function versus every impl-block
spelling, and the sweep's own axis would have mislabelled it. Worth recording
because it is the failure mode of an audit organised around one axis -- a probe
along that axis found the defect, and the axis then described it wrongly.

The row's other suspicion is NOT CONFIRMED. It wondered whether the typechecker
and resolver share the asymmetry, and whether the three known instances being
in codegen and the interpreter was selection bias. Both gaps found here are in
the TYPECHECKER, so the asymmetry is not confined to the back half -- but the
ownership and effect phases, which the three fixed rows made the natural
suspects, came back clean on five separate probes.

WHAT REMAINS UNSWEPT, stated so the next reader does not take this list for
exhaustive. The probes cover surfaces a Kara program can OBSERVE. Sites whose
only effect is on performance were not probed: `inline_hints.rs`'s call census
(which does handle a one-segment `Path` and not a two-segment one) and the
RC-elision classification in `ownership/elision.rs`, whose five bare-name
callee matches are the largest remaining cluster. Neither can produce a wrong
answer, only a missed optimisation, so a differential run cannot see them and
they would need an IR-level or counter-level assertion instead. Trait methods
and trait default bodies were not probed at all.
title: THE QUALIFIED `Type.method` CALLEE SPELLING IS RESOLVED DIFFERENTLY FROM THE BARE ONE IN AT LEAST THREE PLACES, AND NOBODY HAS SWEPT FOR THE REST -- three rows filed separately turned out to be one root, each with a different symptom, so the remaining sites are unknown rather than known-absent
detail:
FILED AFTER FIXING B-2026-08-30-21, -20 and -22 CONSECUTIVELY, which is the only
reason the pattern was visible: each row was filed separately by whoever hit its
symptom, and no single row could show it.

    site                                    symptom of the SAME program shape
    ------------------------------------    ---------------------------------
    let-binding type hint (stmts.rs)        binding typed as the HOLDER, so a
                                            field read died on "cannot resolve
                                            field 'id' on this receiver"
    track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg        argument had NO OWNER: no `Drop`
      (call_dispatch.rs)                    body on any backend, 76 bytes lost
    run_fresh_temp_arg_drops' two guards    no suppression, so a passthrough
      (interpreter eval_call.rs)            temp's body ran TWICE

One program shape -- `H.f(...)` where `impl H { fn f(a: R) -> R }` -- and three
unrelated-looking failures. Each site had its own reason for missing: one took
`segments[0]` as the return type, one matched only `ExprKind::Identifier` on the
callee, one searched only `Item::Function` while `Value::Function` carries the
bare name.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN is how many more there are. Three were found by walking into
them one at a time; nothing has swept for the shape. The mechanical starting
points:

    grep -rn "ExprKind::Identifier" src/ --include=*.rs | grep -i callee
    grep -rn "Item::Function(f)" src/ --include=*.rs        # bare-name search
    grep -rn "fn_return_type_names.get" src/codegen/        # key construction

and for each hit ask the one question that separated the three above: does a
two-segment `Path` callee reach this, and does it get the same answer as the
bare spelling? A site that legitimately only applies to free functions should
say so; the three fixed rows all read as though the author had not considered
the qualified form at all.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN ROW rather than folded into any of the three: it is an AUDIT,
not a fix. It has no reproducer of its own, its deliverable is a list (each
entry either "handles both spellings" or a new bug id), and its value is
proportional to coverage rather than to any single finding. Folding it into a
fix row would have meant either doing it half-way or holding that fix behind it.

NOT MEASURED: whether the typechecker and resolver have the same asymmetry --
all three found so far are in codegen and the interpreter, which may be
selection bias from the ownership-heavy rows being worked, or may be real.

title: THE DEFAULT `cargo test` LEG WAS RED ON `main` FOR TWO HOURS BECAUSE A CODEGEN-DIAGNOSTIC ASSERTION IS NOT GATED ON THE llvm FEATURE -- `ref_binding_codegen_gap_explains_itself` shells out to `karac build` and asserts strings only codegen emits, so on the leg CI runs it read the `falling back to type check` note instead, and since `cargo test` stops at the first failing test BINARY every suite after `cli` silently did not run
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by running the DEFAULT `cargo test` leg as a pre-push gate
for B-2026-09-01-10, and confirmed to be someone else's commit rather than
fallout from that work -- it reproduces with this session's `src/` stashed,
i.e. at plain `main`.

MEASURED (x86_64 Linux, at fcb6696's parent, and identically with the working
tree stashed):

    cargo test
    ...
    test ref_binding_codegen_gap_explains_itself ... FAILED
    test result: FAILED. 642 passed; 1 failed; ...
    error: test failed, to rerun pass `--test cli`

    [map] the message does not mention the construct:
    note: karac build requires the llvm feature; falling back to type check
    All checks passed.

THE TEST IS CORRECT AND ITS LEG IS WRONG. It is B-2026-08-31-37's regression
test: it shells out to `karac build` and asserts the stderr names the `ref`
construct, the container class, and (for the nested shape) `--interp`. All
three strings are emitted by CODEGEN. On the default leg `karac` HAS no
codegen, so `karac build` type-checks, prints the fallback note and exits
zero -- the assertion can never hold there, for the same structural reason
`tests/codegen.rs` and `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` are `#[cfg(feature =
"llvm")]` modules outright.

`tests/cli.rs` already carries 98 `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]` gates for exactly
this population. This test simply missed one; nothing else about it needs to
change.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE TEST, and why it is filed rather than folded
silently into an unrelated commit: `cargo test` stops at the first failing test
BINARY, and `cli` sorts early. So from the moment `15f9133` landed
(2026-09-01 02:54Z), the default leg -- the one CI runs, and the one every
session runs before pushing -- has been failing, and every test binary after
`cli` has not been running at all. That is the same failure mode as
B-2026-09-01-10 one level up: a gate that reports on something its
configuration cannot produce, and a suite that stops being a suite.

The window was about two hours, which is short only because someone happened to
run the default leg. Nothing in `15f9133` itself is wrong -- the diagnostic it
adds is right and its `--features llvm` leg is green.
fix:
Added `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`, the gate the other 98 `karac build`-asserting tests in `tests/cli.rs` already carry, with a comment recording why the default leg cannot satisfy the assertion and what the missing gate cost. Nothing about the diagnostic or its `--features llvm` coverage changes -- the test still runs, and still fails without B-2026-08-31-37's fix, on the leg where `karac build` actually reaches codegen.

VERIFIED: default `cargo test --no-fail-fast` 10217 passed / 0 failed after, against `642 passed; 1 failed` plus an aborted run before; `--features llvm` 15952 passed / 0 failed across 126 test binaries, with `cli`, `codegen`, `memory_sanitizer` and `par_codegen` all confirmed to have run.

MEASURED WHILE VERIFYING, and worth recording because it is the same class one notch down: the default leg is INTERMITTENT independently of this. Over four runs of the same tree, one run failed 5 tests and three passed clean. All five are git/registry fixture tests (`git_fetch::tests::{clones_default_branch_and_resolves_head, checks_out_a_specific_rev, checks_out_a_tag}`, `registry_proxy::tests::{cache_miss_fetches_then_hit_serves_without_refetch, corrupted_cache_entry_is_refetched}`) and they fail in SETUP, not in an assertion -- `git ["commit", "--quiet", "-m", "init"] failed:` with EMPTY stderr, inside `make_upstream`. Their temp paths are already unique (pid + atomic counter) and git identity is configured, so path collision and missing identity are both ruled out; the cause is not established here. Not filed as its own row on this evidence -- one capture, no isolation -- but recorded so the next session that sees a red default leg checks whether it is these five before concluding a regression.

FIXED by 2143f047, all four roots — and a fifth the row had not measured,
`Array[Array[T, N], M]`, which fell out of the same dispatch.

THE ROW'S PREDICTED ORDER HELD EXACTLY, which is worth recording because the
ordering was the useful half of the filing:

  * FIELD root: four lines. `nested_index_field_base_elem` already computed the
    address for indexed READS -- including the `self.grid[i][j]` normalisation
    -- and returns the same (pointer, element `TypeExpr`) pair the nested
    resolver threads, so it only had to be routed in. This is the shape that
    motivated the row: a 2D grid on a struct, read from a method.
  * `Slice[Vec]` and `Array[Vec]` roots: widening the resolver's ROOT
