    classification to the same three-way dispatch the FLAT `ref c[i]` arm
    already performs, so the two indexed lowerings agree on what a container is
    -- the rule B-2026-08-31-29's comment sets out.
  * `Vec[Array]`: the one that needed a new piece, exactly as suspected. After
    the first hop the pointer aims at an `Array` INLINE in the outer
    container's buffer, and `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_array` required a `VarSlot`
    that nothing describes. Split out `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_array_at`,
    mirroring what B-2026-08-09-21 did to the `Vec` lowering for the identical
    reason: only the LLVM type and the storage pointer were ever slot-specific.

THE DECLINE WAS PROTECTING SOMETHING REAL. A `Vec` slot holds a
`{ptr, i64, i64}` header and an `Array` slot IS the storage; reading one as the
other is the B-2026-08-31-29 segfault (element 0 taken as the data pointer,
element 1 as the length, bounds check comparing against a payload word). The
resolver therefore dispatches on the recorded `TypeExpr` at every hop rather
than inferring from the pointer, which is what makes `Vec[Array]` and
`Array[Vec]` both correct instead of one of them reading a length as an address.

MEASURED, all six shapes agreeing across all four surfaces, with the aliasing
contract asserted at each root (a write through the container visible through
the borrow, so these are pointers into the nested buffer rather than copies).
Regression controls kept: the flat `Vec` and `Array` spellings, and the plain
and triple Vec nests from B-2026-09-01-6.

A SIXTH ROOT CAME FREE AND WAS NOT IN THE FILING: a `VecDeque` root nests too.
It shares the `Vec` header layout and the tail's class match already admitted
it, so it started building without a line aimed at it. Measured, not assumed.

STILL DECLINING, measured: a `Map`-VALUE root (`m[k][i]` over the ordinary
`Map[K, Vec[V]]` multimap) and a TUPLE base (`t.0[1]`), both correct under
`--interp`. `nested_index_field_base_elem` already lowers the map-value shape
for indexed READS, so it is the same "route it in" job the field root turned
out to be; the tuple base has no precedent. Neither was in the original filing.

SIDE EFFECT, and it is the SECOND time this family has done it:
B-2026-08-31-37's `ref_binding_codegen_gap_explains_itself` needs a shape
codegen declines while the interpreter handles it, and every fix in this family
removes one. Its case began as a nested `ref v[0][1]` (lowered by
B-2026-09-01-6), became a `Slice` root (lowered here), and is now the
`Map`-value root. The test comment now says so explicitly, along with how to
pick the next one -- verify `interp` correct and `build` declining rather than
assume -- because the assertion is the stable part and the program
demonstrating it is expected to keep changing.
title: A NESTED `ref c[i][j]` STILL DECLINES ON FOUR ROOTS THE Vec-ROOTED LOWERING DOES NOT MODEL -- `Array[Vec[T], N]`, `Vec[Array[T, N]]`, a struct FIELD and a `Slice`, each correct under `--interp` and a hard `karac build` failure
detail:
FILED BY B-2026-09-01-6, which lowered the Vec-ROOTED nested chain (`ref
v[i][j]`, any depth) and deliberately declined everything else rather than
guessing a slot layout it had not checked.

MEASURED, all four correct under `--interp` and all four `BUILD-FAIL`:

    let a: Array[Vec[i64], 1] = Array[[1, 2]];      ref a[0][1]   -> 2 / FAIL
    let v: Vec[Array[i64, 2]] = [Array[1, 2]];      ref v[0][1]   -> 2 / FAIL
    struct Hh { grid: Vec[Vec[i64]] }               ref h.grid[0][1] -> 2 / FAIL
    let s: Slice[Vec[i64]] = v.as_slice();          ref s[0][1]   -> 2 / FAIL

The Vec-rooted case now works at any depth (double, triple, quad pinned), so
these are specifically about the ROOT container, not about nesting.

WHY EACH NEEDS ITS OWN HANDLING, which is why B-2026-09-01-6 declined rather
than widened:

  * an `Array`'s slot IS the storage -- there is no `{ptr, i64, i64}` header to
    index, which is exactly what B-2026-08-31-29 fixed for the FLAT spelling
    (lowering an Array as though its slot were a Vec header read element 0 as
    the data pointer and SEGFAULTED);
  * a `Slice` carries a start offset, so the element index shifts by the
    window's start -- the same equivalence B-2026-08-31-36 used on the
    interpreter side;
  * a struct FIELD root needs `lower_field_access_ptr` to reach the container
    before any indexing happens.

THE FIELD ROOT IS THE SHORTEST REACH of the four: `nested_index_field_base_elem`
(`calls.rs`) already lowers `h.grid[i][j]` for indexed READS, including the
`self.grid[i][j]` normalisation, so the address computation exists and only has
to be routed into the `ref`-binding arm. The `Slice` root is next -- the offset
rule is already written down. The two `Array` shapes are the ones that most
deserve a fresh measurement, since B-2026-08-31-29's segfault is what the
current decline is protecting against.

NOT A REGRESSION AND NOT NEW: all four failed the same way before
B-2026-09-01-6, which only narrowed the declining set. The message they land on
is the structured one from B-2026-08-31-37, so a user gets the container class
and the `--interp` pointer rather than an internal invariant string.

NOT MEASURED: a `VecDeque` root, a `Map` VALUE root (`m[k][i]`, which
`nested_index_field_base_elem` mentions handling for reads), and whether the
`mut` spellings of any of these differ -- `let g = mut ref ...` is a parse error
on every base today (B-2026-08-31-36), so there is nothing to compare yet.

title: A STRUCT WHOSE FIELD IS PASSED BY VALUE FROM INSIDE AN INTERPOLATED-STRING ARGUMENT HAS ITS `Drop` DEFERRED TO SCOPE EXIT ON ALL THREE COMPILED SURFACES -- `println(f"field={readf(h.r)}")` is interp `field=43 drop 40 end` vs compiled `field=43 end drop 40`, against design.md line 866; hoisting the call to its own `let` makes all four agree, and the callee returns `i64`, which is B-2026-08-31-4's own passing CONTROL
detail:
ANOTHER TRIGGER of the class B-2026-08-31-4 opened, found while verifying
B-2026-08-29-63 and PRE-EXISTING to it: the divergence reproduces byte-identically
under `KARAC_MOVE_STRUCT_PARAMS=0`, which restores the exact pre-transfer
lowering, so that fix is not its cause.

That row quotes design.md line 866 -- "Destructors fire at each binding's
live-range end, not at lexical scope end ... a value whose last use is mid-scope
is dropped at that use and does not appear in the end-of-scope stack at all" --
and reports one trigger for the compiled backends deferring anyway: a local whose
last use is a `ref` ARGUMENT to a callee returning a HEAP value. This one is
neither, which is why it is filed rather than folded in.

    struct Res { id: i64, buf: Vec[i64] }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    struct Holder { r: Res }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> Res { ...8-element buf... }
    fn readf(r: Res) -> i64 { return r.buf[3]; }

    fn main() {
        let b = mk(20);
        let hb = hand(b);
        println(f"hand={hb.buf[1]}");
        let h = Holder { r: mk(40) };
        println(f"field={readf(h.r)}");   // last use of `h`
        println("end");
    }

        interp:            hand=21  drop 20  field=43  drop 40  end
        jit / build / np:  hand=21  drop 20  field=43  end  drop 40
                                                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^ deferred

`h`'s last use is the `readf(h.r)` call. The interpreter drops it there; all
three compiled surfaces defer it past `println("end")` to the enclosing scope's
exit. `karac run` (JIT) agrees with `karac build`, so the split is
interpreter-vs-compiled rather than JIT-vs-AOT.

`readf` RETURNS `i64`, which is what makes this distinct from B-2026-08-31-4:
`ret_i64` is that row's own CONTROL, the case where the compiled backends get it
right. So "callee returns a heap value" is not what selects the deferral here. A
by-value FIELD argument (`h.r`) does it with a scalar return.

HOISTING THE CALL OUT OF THE ARGUMENT MAKES IT AGREE, which narrows the trigger
further and is the tell worth keeping. The identical program with the call in its
own statement --

    let rf = readf(h.r);
    println(f"field={rf}");

-- prints `drop 40` before `field=43` on ALL FOUR surfaces. So the deferral needs
the call to sit inside the `println` argument; a `let`-bound result is early-fired
correctly. In the same program the plain shapes agree too: a param that dies
inside the callee (`eat(a)`) and a by-value passthrough result (`let hb =
hand(b)`) are identical on all four surfaces, both spellings. So the compiled
early-fire (`fire_due_user_drops`, B-2026-07-21-1) is reaching most bindings and
missing this one -- the defect is in WHICH bindings it admits, not in whether it
exists.

Bodies run EXACTLY ONCE on every backend and the program is valgrind-clean (0
errors). This is purely a SEQUENCE difference, which is why no leak or
double-free gate sees it.

WHICH SIDE IS RIGHT is settled and it is the interpreter: design.md line 866
specifies live-range end, so the compiled backends are the ones to move. Same
direction as B-2026-08-31-4, and the same consequence that row names -- the NLL
drop rule exists partly to close the lock-held-too-long footgun, so a `Drop`
releasing a lock or an fd is held past its live range here.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE SPEC. kara-katas' verification rule is `run` ==
`build`, byte for byte, and a `Drop` body that prints is exactly what that rule
polices. A kata wrapping RAII-style logging around a helper called inside an
interpolated string fails A/B today with nothing in its source that looks
order-dependent.

NOT ISOLATED, stated rather than implied: a LARGER fixture (the 10-shape probe
this came from) also showed the `hand(b)` passthrough result deferring, but the
reduction above does NOT reproduce that -- `hb` agrees on all four surfaces in
both spellings tried. So either a third ingredient in that fixture is required or
the original reading of its diff was wrong; it is recorded here as an open thread
rather than asserted as a second trigger.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by a 12-shape A/B probe built to prove B-2026-08-29-63's
by-value-struct transfer changed no observable behaviour. It did not --
transfer-on and transfer-off outputs are byte-identical on every probe, this one
included.

title: THE PROJECTED SPELLING OF B-2026-08-31-35 STILL RUNS THE LOCAL'S `Drop` BODY TWICE -- `let _ = if c { W { r: t.r, b: 1 } } else { .. };` over a local `W` doubles on all three backends because the aggregate-literal source walker resolves a bare NAME and not a field projection, so the disarm e49a85f wired up never names `t`
detail:
THE HALF OF B-2026-08-31-35 THAT e49a85f DOES NOT REACH. That row's fix
readmits a discarded branch as an escaping site when the discard owns the
value, and both backends then disarm the taken arm's consumed sources. The
sources come from `collect_aggregate_literal_sources`, which resolves a bare
identifier (and nested aggregates, tuples, array/Vec prefixes) but NOT a field
projection -- so `W { r: t.r, b: 1 }` yields no name and `t` stays armed.

MEASURED (all four surfaces byte-identical, so an AGREED GAP not a divergence):

    struct D { a: String, b: i64 }
    impl Drop for D { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dD{self.b}") } }
    struct W { r: D, b: i64 }
    let t = mkw(7);
    let _ = if n == 0 { W { r: t.r, b: 1 } } else { W { r: mkd(9), b: 2 } };
                                        dD7 dD7   (want dD7)

The WHOLE-VALUE spelling (`W { r: t, .. }`) is one body since e49a85f, and the
bare-statement and `match` spellings of the projection double identically, so
the projection is the axis rather than the statement kind.

ITS MEMORY IS BALANCED, and that corrects what B-2026-08-31-35 recorded. That
row's 2026-09-01 note calls this shape a DOUBLE FREE on JIT and AOT
(`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, glibc-detecting ~1 run in 5). Not
reproducible: 0 non-zero exits over 20 runs, valgrind-clean at the default -O2
AND at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, and clean over a 5-iteration loop (10 bodies, 0
errors). Also clean at `ebaacfc`, a tree predating both of 2026-09-01's
discarded-branch commits, so nothing landed since is masking it. The second
body runs over the moved-from husk rather than re-freeing.

WHERE TO START: widen `collect_aggregate_literal_sources` to resolve a field
projection to its place ROOT, on both backends together -- they share one
definition of "what this literal consumed" by construction and must keep it.
The hazard to measure first is a projection that is NOT a move: reading a
scalar field, or a field of a local that stays live and is read afterwards.
The enclosing-frame `UserDrop` guard codegen already applies is the natural
place for that test, and the interpreter's `drop_method_keys` check is its
twin.

PINNED at the doubled transcript on BOTH backends -- `codegen::e2e_discarded_
branch_of_body_less_heap_literals_keeps_one_owner` and its interpreter twin --
so a one-sided fix fails loudly, which is how e49a85f's own missing half was
caught.

title: A DISCARDED AGGREGATE LITERAL BEHIND A BLOCK WRAPPER, OR WRITTEN BARE IN STATEMENT POSITION, RUNS ITS CONSUMED LOCAL'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON THE INTERPRETER AND ONCE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `{ W { r: t, b: 1 } };`, `let _ = { W { r: t, b: 1 } };` and `W { r: t, b: 1 };` all diverge, while the `if` / `match` spellings agree
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-31-35, and confirmed PRE-EXISTING
rather than caused by it -- measured byte-identical with that row's `src/`
stashed, i.e. at plain `main`.

MEASURED (interpreter vs `karac build`; the JIT agrees with AOT):

    let t = mkd(7); { W { r: t, b: 1 } };          interp dD7 dD7   aot dD7
    let t = mkd(7); let _ = { W { r: t, b: 1 } };  interp dD7 dD7   aot dD7
    let t = mkd(7); W { r: t, b: 1 };              interp dD7 dD7   aot dD7

    control, and the one that agrees:
    let t = mkd(7); let _ = W { r: t, b: 1 };      interp dD7       aot dD7

So the compiled pair is correct in all four and the interpreter doubles in
three: the two BLOCK-wrapper spellings and the BARE-STATEMENT direct literal.
Only the wildcard-`let` direct literal agrees, because `stmts.rs` retracts its
sources statically there and the interpreter's let-rebind hook does the same.

WHY e49a85f LEFT IT. That row's disarm is keyed on the arm that RAN
(`taken_branch_tail` on the interpreter, an `i1` in the arm's own basic block
on codegen), and a plain block has no ARM to name -- `taken_arm_tail_of`
returns `None`, so the interpreter's `disarm_discarded_tail_sources` declines.
Codegen's seed WOULD reach the wrapper (`discarded_match_value_tail` recurses
through a block), so it was deliberately narrowed to a direct `if`/`match`:
seeding the wrapper there alone fixes the compiled pair and leaves the
interpreter doubling, trading an agreed gap for a run-vs-build divergence --
the trade this family is repeatedly held back to avoid. Measured in exactly
that shape before the narrowing.

WHAT CLOSING IT NEEDS: the interpreter half first. For a non-branch tail there
is exactly one path, so `taken_discarded_tail` can return the tail itself --
but NOT unconditionally, because the wildcard-`let` direct literal is already
correct at one body and would go to ZERO. The bare-statement direct literal
(third row above) is the same shape and is NOT correct, so the two spellings
need separating before either is touched. Once the interpreter agrees, drop
the `matches!(.., If | Match)` narrowing in codegen's
`note_escaping_stmt_sites` and the wrapper falls out.
fix:
FIXED by 0033588.

THE MECHANISM, which the row's "WHERE TO START" guessed at and got half right.
The row proposed making `taken_discarded_tail` return a non-branch tail so
`disarm_discarded_tail_sources` would reach it, and warned that doing so
unconditionally would take the wildcard-`let` DIRECT literal from one body to
ZERO. That warning rested on a wrong premise, and finding out why is what
located the real site.

The disarm set was never involved. Instrumenting all seven
`moved_out_user_drop_bindings.insert` sites showed NOT ONE of them fires for
ANY of the four spellings, including the correct one. What makes
`let _ = W { r: t, b: 1 };` correct is `suppress_let_rebind_user_drop`, which
RETRACTS `t`'s `CleanupAction::Drop` from the enclosing frame -- a different
channel entirely. It reaches that spelling because it matches the literal
SYNTACTICALLY at a `Let`'s RHS:

    let source_names = match &value.kind {
        ExprKind::Identifier(n)         => vec![n],
        ExprKind::StructLiteral { .. }  => <field identifier sources>,
        _ => return,                       // <-- everything else fell out here
    };

A block wrapper is not a `StructLiteral`, and a bare statement is not a `Let`
at all, so all three of the row's spellings hit that `_ => return`.

THE FIX, in two pieces sharing one rule.

1. `retract_user_drop_actions_for` -- the retraction body factored out of
   `suppress_let_rebind_user_drop`, so its new sibling applies the same rule
   rather than a second copy of it. (Drift across the `let _ =` /
   bare-statement pair is what B-2026-08-29-20 had to repair once already.)

2. `discarded_struct_literal_tail` peels `Block`/`Seq`/`Unsafe` wrappers to
   the struct literal underneath, and is used at two entry points: the `let`
   hook consults it so `let _ = { W { .. } };` answers as the direct spelling
   does, and a new `suppress_discarded_literal_source_user_drops` handles
   `StmtKind::Expr` so `W { .. };` and `{ W { .. } };` reach the rule at all.

The `Identifier` arm is deliberately NOT peeled -- a wrapped bare name reaches
its own hooks -- and the whole thing is restricted to STRUCT literals: tuple
and array literals take the whole-value channel in
`record_container_bodies_move_sources` and were measured correct in every
spelling of this family.

MEASURED, PRE AND POST, ALL FOUR SURFACES (`R { id }` with an `impl Drop`,
`S { r: R, k: i64 }`, `S2 { r: R, s: R, k: i64 }`; I = `--interp`,
J = `karac run`, A = `karac build`):

    spelling                            pre  I / J,A          post I / J,A
    S { r: t, k: 1 };                   dR7 dR7 / dR7         dR7 / dR7
    { S { r: t, k: 1 } };               dR7 dR7 / dR7         dR7 / dR7
    let _ = { S { r: t, k: 1 } };       dR7 dR7 / dR7         dR7 / dR7
    let _ = S { r: t, k: 1 };  control  dR7     / dR7         dR7 / dR7
    S2 { r: t, s: u, k: 1 };            dR8 dR7 dR8 dR7 / dR8 dR7   dR8 dR7 / dR8 dR7
    let w = S { r: t, k: 1 };  ORACLE   dR7     / dR7         dR7 / dR7

The TWO-SOURCE row is the generalization the row did not measure: pre-fix the
interpreter ran the whole pair twice, and it now runs each once. The BOUND
`let` is the oracle throughout -- correct on all four surfaces before and
after -- which is what fixes what "once" means here: the literal owns `t`'s
value, so `t` must not run its own body.

A MEASUREMENT CORRECTION worth recording, because it nearly became a filed
claim. An intermediate sweep appeared to show the compiled backends LOSING a
sibling field's body in the multi-field shapes (`S2 { r: t, s: mk(9) }`
printing only `dR7` on AOT). That was an artifact: `cargo test --no-fail-fast`
on the DEFAULT leg had rebuilt `target/debug/karac` without `--features llvm`,
so `karac build` type-checked and emitted nothing and the harness was reading
a stale binary from an earlier build. Rebuilt with `--features llvm`, the
two-source shapes agree on every surface. The tell was in the build output all
along -- `note: karac build requires the llvm feature; falling back to type
check` -- and CLAUDE.md's `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` warning is about
the adjacent version of the same trap.

TWO REMAINDERS, both measured PRE-EXISTING and filed rather than folded in:

  * B-2026-09-01-21 -- `S2 { r: t, s: R { id: 9 }, k: 1 };` (one live source,
    one MINTED sibling): the compiled pair runs only `dR7`, losing the minted
    sibling's body, while the interpreter runs `dR9 dR7`. Divergent before
    this fix and after it; codegen's `discarded_owned_literal_tail` declines
    the whole literal because one field is not fresh, so no owner registers.

  * B-2026-09-01-22 -- `{ { S { r: t, k: 1 } } };` (a DOUBLY nested wrapper):
    both compiled backends run `dR7` TWICE. Pre-fix the interpreter did too,
    so it was an AGREED gap; this fix makes the interpreter correct and leaves
    the compiled pair as it was, which turns it into a divergence. Recorded as
    such deliberately rather than restricting the peel to one wrapper level,
    which would be an arbitrary rule buying an agreed-wrong answer. The second
    compiled body runs over the moved-from husk (codegen nulls the source slot
    at the move) -- the same diagnosis e49a85f measured for its own case -- so
    it is a spurious body, not memory corruption.

GATES: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets`
clean on BOTH feature legs; `cargo test` 10230 passed / 0 failed;
`cargo test --features llvm --no-fail-fast` clean.

title: AN OUT-OF-RANGE INTEGER LITERAL WITH A WIDER SUFFIX REACHES A GENERIC PAYLOAD SLOT UNCHECKED, SO THE BACKENDS DISAGREE AND ONE SHAPE FLIPS SIGN -- `Option[u8] = Option.Some(300i64)` is `Some(300)` under `--interp` and `Some(44)` compiled, `Option.Some(-1i64)` is `Some(-1)` against `Some(255)`, and the only diagnostic is a `redundant_suffix` warning that is itself false
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-09-01-12, which lists this as its "NOT MEASURED"
remainder ("whether the same split exists for INTEGER suffixes"). It does, in
three shapes, and unlike the float case one of them changes the SIGN:

    fn main() {
        let a: Option[u8]  = Option.Some(300i64);        println(f"{a}");
        let b: Option[i32] = Option.Some(5000000000i64); println(f"{b}");
        let c: Option[u8]  = Option.Some(-1i64);         println(f"{c}");
    }
      interp                -> Some(300) / Some(5000000000) / Some(-1)
      jit / aot / aot-par0  -> Some(44)  / Some(705032704)  / Some(255)

The only diagnostic on the program is three copies of
`warning[redundant_suffix]`, which is itself false here (dropping the suffix
does not leave the value unchanged -- it makes the literal type-check against
`u8` and be REJECTED).

EVERY EQUIVALENT SPELLING IS ALREADY REJECTED, which is what makes this a hole
rather than a policy:

    let a: u8  = 300i64;        -> error: integer literal 300 out of range for 'u8'
    let a: u8  = 300;           -> error: same
    let a: u8  = 300u8;         -> error: same
    let c: u8  = -1i64;         -> error: negative integer literal -1 cannot
                                          initialize unsigned type 'u8'
    let d: Option[u8] = Option.Some(300);   -> error: out of range for 'u8'
    let d: Option[u8] = Option.Some(v);     -> error: implicit coercion from
                                          'i64' to 'u8' would narrow or change sign
                                          (with `v: i64`)

So the payload position DOES receive the destination type, and the range check
DOES reach it -- for an UNSUFFIXED literal and for a variable. Only the
i64-SUFFIXED literal walks through.

MECHANISM. `Option.Some(x)` is a generic associated call whose payload slot is
seeded from the expectation, so it is checked at the seeded-argument site in
`typechecker/exprs.rs` (`seeded_from_expectation && seeded_arg_narrows` ->
`check_int_widening_coercion`), not by `check_expr`'s prologue. And
`check_int_widening_coercion` EXEMPTS suffixed integer literals, on a
justification stated in its own doc comment:

    "integer *literals* (bare or suffixed) -- already range-checked against
     the contextual type at the top of `check_expr`"

That is true of the `check_expr` route and false of this one: `check_expr`'s
two `*_int_literal_value` blocks are exactly what the seeded path skips. The
exemption is therefore load-bearing on a precondition the caller does not
establish, which is why the bare and suffixed spellings of the same program
diverge from each other as well as between backends.

SUGGESTED FIX, smallest surface: at the seeded-argument site, run the
contextual literal range check (`check_int_literal_fits(value, target, ..)`)
for a SUFFIXED literal before falling into the exemption -- the same check
`check_expr` line ~453 runs, applied on the route that never reaches it.
Loosening the exemption inside `check_int_widening_coercion` itself is the
broader alternative and would cover every call site at once, but it risks a
duplicate diagnostic on the `check_expr` route, which already errors and
returns `Type::Error` for these values.

NOT MEASURED: the `Result.Ok`/`Result.Err` payloads (the same seeding path, so
expected to behave identically), user-defined generic fns (`fn id[T](x: T)`,
which B-2026-08-08-9 already covers for the non-literal case), and whether the
same hole exists for a `char`/bool-shaped narrowing.

Severity medium: silent, no diagnostic, both a wrong value and a wrong SIGN,
and the same program means two different things depending on the executor --
but it needs a suffixed out-of-range literal in a generic payload position,
which is not a shape ordinary code reaches by accident.
fix:
Fixed in f366e42e. All three shapes the row measured now error, plus two it
listed as unmeasured.

    Option[u8]  = Option.Some(300i64)        -> integer literal 300 out of range for 'u8'
    Option[i32] = Option.Some(5000000000i64) -> out of range for 'i32'
    Option[u8]  = Option.Some(-1i64)         -> negative integer literal -1 cannot
                                                initialize unsigned type 'u8'
    Result[u8, i64] = Result.Ok(300i64)      -> out of range for 'u8'
    let e: u8 = id(300i64)                   -> out of range for 'u8'
      (with `fn id[T](x: T) -> T`)

The suggested fix was the one taken, and the row's diagnosis held: the
seeded-argument site now runs the same contextual check `check_expr` runs. The
broader alternative the row also listed -- loosening the exemption inside
`check_int_widening_coercion` itself -- was not taken, for the reason recorded
there: the `check_expr` route already errors and returns `Type::Error` for these
values, so the duplicate-diagnostic risk is real and the narrower change buys
the same coverage.

IN-RANGE STAYS ACCEPTED, deliberately, and this is the half worth stating
because it is what makes the fix narrow rather than a policy change. Like the
`check_expr` arm it mirrors, the check emits ONLY when the value does not fit,
so `Option.Some(5i64)` into an `Option[u8]` is untouched -- the permissiveness
that keeps the `Box.new(5)` shapes seeding exists for working. The suffix
remains inert for an in-range value and the annotation types the binding, which
is the integer rule B-2026-09-01-12 measured (`let d: i32 = 2147483647i64;
d + 1` overflows exactly as the unsuffixed control does).

THE `redundant_suffix` WARNING IS LEFT ALONE HERE, unlike in B-2026-09-01-12
where the same lint was withdrawn. The difference is that on the integer side
the claim is TRUE: dropping the `i64` suffix leaves an unsuffixed literal that
is typed by the destination and rejected identically, so the suffix really is a
no-op and its deleting fix-it is sound. On the float side dropping the suffix
CHANGED THE VALUE of a program that compiled, which is what made the same
sentence a falsehood there. Two lints that look alike, one of which had to go
and one of which is correct -- worth the paragraph, because the temptation
is to treat them as one case.

NOT FIXED, and not caused here: `Option[Option[u8]] =
Option.Some(Option.Some(5i64))` is rejected as a plain type mismatch
("expected 'Option[u8]', found 'Option[i64]'") rather than a range error,
because the payload is not seeded through two levels. The UNSUFFIXED control
produces the identical message, which is what identifies it as pre-existing
rather than a false positive introduced by this change. It is a rejection, not
a silent split, so it is a diagnostic-quality remainder rather than a
correctness one; no row filed.

Tests. `tests/typechecker.rs::an_out_of_range_suffixed_literal_is_rejected_in_
a_seeded_slot` covers the five rejected shapes and the four accepted ones. The
NEGATIVE case is asserted separately from the out-of-range ones because it
takes the other arm of `check_int_literal_fits` -- a fix comparing only against
the maximum would pass three of the four rejection assertions and still admit
`Some(-1i64)` into a `u8`. Verified RED without the change (the test fails) and
GREEN with it. `tests/interpreter.rs::test_seeded_slot_range_check_boundary_
agrees_across_backends` and its `tests/codegen.rs` twin pin the boundary the
check draws rather than the rejections, which have no runtime left: an in-range
suffixed literal still compiles and means what it says, `255i64` sits on the
edge where an off-by-one would show, and the `300i64 as u8` an author writes to
mean the truncation gives the same 44 on all four surfaces instead of the
300/44 split the unchecked literal used to.

title: DEFAULT ARGUMENTS ARE FILLED FOR FREE FUNCTIONS ONLY -- `H.f(1)` and `h.g(1)` both fail with `expected 2 argument(s), found 1` for a parameter that has a default, while the identical free function accepts the omitted argument, and design.md scopes the feature to no function kind
detail:
FOUND by the B-2026-09-01-13 sweep, probing whether a default argument is
filled through the qualified `Type.assoc_fn(..)` spelling. It is not -- and the
boundary turned out not to be the one the sweep was looking for. Defaults work
for FREE FUNCTIONS ONLY; every impl-block spelling rejects the omitted
argument, associated fn and instance method alike.

    fn f(a: i64, b: i64 = 7) -> i64 { return a + b; }
    fn main() { println(f(1)); }                         -> 8

    struct H { x: i64 }
    impl H { fn f(a: i64, b: i64 = 7) -> i64 { return a + b; } }
    fn main() { println(H.f(1)); }
      -> error[typecheck]: expected 2 argument(s), found 1

    impl H { fn g(ref self, a: i64, b: i64 = 7) -> i64 { return self.x + a + b; } }
    fn main() { let h = H { x: 100 }; println(h.g(1)); }
      -> error[typecheck]: method 'g' expects 2 argument(s), found 1

Supplying the defaulted argument explicitly works in every spelling, so the
signature parses and the parameter is real -- only the FILLING is absent.

DESIGN.MD DOES NOT SCOPE THE FEATURE TO FREE FUNCTIONS. ss "Default parameter
values" opens "Parameters may have default values, allowing callers to omit
them", and its five rules (pure-constant defaults, evaluated per call, no
reference to an earlier parameter, trailing-only, label required to skip)
mention no restriction to any function kind. The stdlib already writes such a
signature on a METHOD -- `runtime/stdlib/column.kara:137`,
`fn fillna(ref self, value: T, treat_nan_as_null: bool = false)` -- so the
declaration form is in use on the surface where the call form does not work.

MECHANISM. `src/default_args.rs:326` fills defaults in a `walk_expr` arm that
matches only `ExprKind::Identifier` on the callee, and looks the name up in a
table (`self.table`) keyed by bare function name. A qualified call is
`ExprKind::Call { callee: Path { segments: ["H", "f"] } }` and never reaches
the arm; a method call is `ExprKind::MethodCall`, a different node entirely.
Whether the table even holds impl fns has NOT been checked -- if it does not,
the fix is two-part (populate it, then match the two extra callee shapes)
rather than one.

SUGGESTED FIX. Mirror what `typechecker/expr_call.rs` does for the where-clause
and (as of B-2026-09-01-13) for parameter-name lookup: resolve a two-segment
path through the impl table FIRST, falling back to the bare-name table only
when the impl lookup misses -- the ordering matters, because keying on the last
segment alone lets `H.take(x)` pick up an unrelated global `take` and fill ITS
defaults. The `MethodCall` arm needs the receiver's type to pick the impl,
which `default_args.rs` may not have at the point it runs; if it does not, this
may have to move or consult the typechecker's method table.

SEVERITY medium. It is a compile ERROR, not a silent miscompile, so nothing
runs wrong -- but a documented language feature is unavailable on two of the
three call forms, the stdlib already declares one such signature, and the
diagnostic ("expected 2 argument(s), found 1") does not hint that defaults
exist or that they are free-function-only, so a user hits a wall with no
pointer.

NOT MEASURED: whether `default_args`'s table holds impl fns at all; trait
methods and trait default bodies; whether the label-required-to-skip rule
(design.md's fifth) works for any impl-block spelling once filling does.


PARTIAL FIX in 2dba3851 -- the ASSOCIATED-FN half only. The row stays OPEN for
the instance-method half.

DONE. `H.f(1)` now fills exactly as the free function does, verified against the
free-function fixture's own four shapes and expected values on all four
surfaces: omit every default, omit the tail, skip one by label, and mix a
positional override with two labels. The associated half needs no inference at
all -- the path NAMES the type, so the key is exact and a miss simply leaves the
call alone.

Three guards, each a silent-wrong-program risk rather than a missing-feature
one, are pinned by
`tests/typechecker.rs::associated_default_fill_does_not_borrow_another_function_s_defaults`:
associated fns live in their own map so a free `take`'s defaults cannot reach
`H.take`; a `Type.method` claimed by both an inherent and a trait impl is
ambiguous here (the call names no trait) and is dropped rather than guessed;
and both sides keep their own defaults when both declare one.

NOT DONE, and blocked rather than deferred for effort. `h.g(1)` needs the
RECEIVER'S TYPE to pick the impl, and `fill_default_args_in_program` runs
pre-resolve, from `desugar_program`, where no type information exists. The
tempting shortcut -- fill by bare method name when exactly one method of that
name has defaults -- was considered and rejected: stdlib types are themselves
Kara source with defaulted method signatures (`Column.fillna`'s
`treat_nan_as_null: bool = false` is the row's own example), so a unique-name
match can land on a stdlib method the receiver does not have, and the rewrite
is silent. Closing this half means either giving the pass a type source or
moving method filling after typecheck; the second is the larger change and the
one that matches where the information actually is.

A test pins that `h.g(1)` is still an arity error, so the day it starts working
is a deliberate change carrying its own fixture rather than a side effect.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW AS FILED: it reads the gap as an oversight
("`default_args.rs:326` ... matches only `ExprKind::Identifier`"). The module
doc states the scope decision outright -- "Method / associated-function calls
and module-qualified `Path` callees are out of scope for this slice" -- so this
is an unfinished slice of B-2026-08-17-19, not a site that forgot a case. The
gap between design.md's unconditional wording and the implementation is real
either way, which is why the row stands.
fix:
FIXED by fc67e1f (tests in 10054c2), closing the half the partial fix left open. `h.g(1)` now fills
exactly as `f(1)` and `H.af(1)` do.

(1) THE BLOCKER WAS REAL, AND THE ROW'S OWN SUGGESTION WAS THE ANSWER. The row
recorded this half as blocked rather than deferred: `fill_default_args_in_program`
runs pre-resolve from `desugar_program`, so nothing there knows a receiver's
type, and it rejected the shortcut -- fill by bare method name when exactly one
method of that name has defaults -- because a stdlib method can then claim a
call on a type that does not have it, silently. That reasoning holds; I
re-derived it before looking for another way, and the refinement that first
looks sound (require the name to be unique across the WHOLE program, not just
among defaulted methods) fails for the same reason one level out: BUILTIN
methods are not Kara source, so the pass cannot count them, and a user calling
`s.find(c)` on a String would collect an unrelated user `find`'s default.

Its closing sentence names the fix: "either giving the pass a type source or
moving method filling after typecheck; the second is the larger change and the
one that matches where the information actually is." It does, and the place to
put it already existed.

(2) WHERE IT LANDED, AND WHY THERE. Two phases, because between them they hold
the two halves of the information:

  * `method_user_impl.rs` PLANS the fill. It is the first point at which the
    receiver has a type and `sig` names the resolved impl, so the table lookup
    is exact rather than a guess by method name -- which is precisely what makes
    this safe where the earlier pass could not be.
  * `lowering::lower_program` APPLIES it. That phase runs after typecheck and,
    per its own doc, "before effectcheck / ownership / interpret / codegen", so
    one splice serves all three backends. This is what preserves the property
    the `default_args` module doc is built around: every later phase sees "an
    ordinary full-arity call, which is what makes the three-surface parity rule
    hold by construction rather than by three hand-kept implementations."

The plan itself comes from the SAME `try_fill` the free-function and
associated-function spellings use, so labels, contiguity and the
no-name-destructuring rule cannot drift between the three.

Both halves are needed and the failure mode without the second is not subtle:
with only the typechecker change, `karac check` passes, the INTERPRETER answers
correctly, and codegen dies in the module verifier with `Incorrect number of
arguments passed to called function`. A run-vs-build divergence, arrived at by
fixing half a feature.

(3) ONE SITE, MEASURED RATHER THAN READ. Nine sites emit an arity diagnostic for
a call. Rather than guess which handles methods, each candidate was tagged and
the tree rebuilt: all four receiver shapes -- a local, a field (`w.h.g(1)`), a
call temporary (`mk().g(1)`) and an index (`v[0].g(1)`) -- report through
`method_user_impl.rs` alone. One chokepoint, so no site could be missed.

(4) THREE THINGS THE FIRST DRAFT GOT WRONG. Each was found by running the
compiler, and each is recorded because the wrong version is the plausible one:

  * THE FILL MUST PRECEDE `validate_labels`. Placed after it, `h.g(1, c: 9)` is
    rejected with "label 'c' does not match parameter 'b' at position 2" --
    which is the diagnostic doing its job on a list the author deliberately left
    incomplete. A fill exists precisely so a label may SKIP a defaulted
    parameter, so every check from the label validation onward has to see the
    completed list.
  * THE CHAIN KEY IS DISAMBIGUATED BY SPAN LENGTH, NOT BY THE METHOD NAME. The
    first comment claimed the latter, copying the shape of `method_impl_dispatch`'s
    rationale. Instrumented: `a.same().same()` records `(242, 15)` for the outer
    call and `(242, 8)` for the inner -- a `MethodCall` takes its receiver's
    OFFSET but its own extent, and `SpanKey` is `(offset, length)`. Checked
    deliberately on two same-named methods carrying DIFFERENT defaults
    (`A.same(k = 100)` returning a `B` whose `same` defaults `k = 200`), because
    that is the program a real collision would silently corrupt; it prints 300
    on every surface.
  * THE AMBIGUITY DROP IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT BELT-AND-BRACES. The first comment
    argued a wrong-signature fill was already impossible since the table is read
    only after the impl is resolved. It is not: the key is `Type.method`, which
    cannot separate an inherent `impl S` from an `impl T1 for S`, and the
    resolved `FunctionSig` carries no default EXPRESSIONS to key on instead.
    Without the drop, `s.m()` would take whichever impl was inserted last. The
    cost is stated rather than hidden -- a type with both gets no fill on
    either, and falls back to the arity error.

(5) CORRECTION TO THE ROW AS FILED. It offers `Column.fillna`
(`runtime/stdlib/column.kara:137`) as evidence that "the stdlib already writes
such a signature on a METHOD ... so the declaration form is in use on the
surface where the call form does not work." MEASURED against the pre-change
tree: `c.fillna(0)` already type-checked and ran. `fillna` is
`#[compiler_builtin]` and dispatches through the builtin surface, not through
the user-impl path this row's symptom lives on. It is also the ONLY defaulted
method signature in the whole of `runtime/stdlib` (swept), so the stdlib was
not in fact blocked by this. The row stands on its actual symptom -- a
user-declared method -- which did fail and now does not.

VERIFICATION. Eight call shapes on four surfaces (`--interp`, JIT, `build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`), byte-identical: full omission, partial omission,
label-skip, a fully-supplied call, and local / field / temporary / index
receivers. Plus generic impls (`impl[T] Box[T]`), trait impls, `mut ref self`,
same-named methods on two types, and the chain cases in (4). Negatives keep
their errors: too few arguments even for the defaults, too many, and a method
with no defaults at all; a defaulted method's expectation now reads as a RANGE
("expects 1 to 2 argument(s)"), matching the phrasing the free-function path
already used.

NOT DONE, stated rather than implied. The inherent-plus-trait ambiguity above is
declined, not resolved -- resolving it needs the default expressions keyed by
the RESOLVED impl rather than by `Type.method`. Trait DEFAULT BODIES were not
probed. And the label-required-to-skip rule is now exercised on methods, which
the row listed as unmeasured for every impl-block spelling.

title: A DISCARDED STRUCT LITERAL MIXING A LIVE LOCAL SOURCE WITH A MINTED SIBLING LOSES THE MINTED FIELD'S `Drop` BODY ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `S2 { r: t, s: R { id: 9 }, k: 1 };` runs `dR9 dR7` under `--interp` and only `dR7` on `karac run` / `karac build`, because one non-fresh field declines the WHOLE literal at `discarded_owned_literal_tail`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-09-01-18, and measured PRE-EXISTING
rather than caused by it -- the divergence is present with that row's `src`
stashed, i.e. at plain `main`, and is unchanged in direction by its fix.

MEASURED (I = `--interp`, J = `karac run`, A = `karac build`; `R { id: i64 }`
with an `impl Drop`, `S2 { r: R, s: R, k: i64 }`):

    let t = R { id: 7 };
    S2 { r: t, s: R { id: 9 }, k: 1 };

                 pre-B-2026-09-01-18   post
        I        dR9 dR7 dR7           dR9 dR7
        J, A     dR7                   dR7

The interpreter is right: the discarded literal owns both fields, so both
bodies run once. (Its pre-fix third `dR7` was -18's double, now gone.) The
compiled pair runs ONE body, and that one is `t`'s own scope-exit body -- not
the literal's field walk, which never registers at all. `R { id: 9 }`'s object
is never dropped.

CONTRAST that pins it. Every neighbouring shape agrees on all four surfaces:

    S2 { r: t, s: u, k: 1 };            dR8 dR7   TWO live sources -- agrees
    { S2 { r: R{id:7}, s: R{id:9} } };  dR9 dR7   ALL minted -- agrees
    let w = S2 { r: t, s: u, k: 1 };    dR8 dR7   the bound ORACLE -- agrees

So it is specifically the MIX -- at least one live-local source AND at least
one minted field -- that loses the minted half.

WHERE TO START: `discarded_owned_literal_tail` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`). Its
STRUCT arm requires `fields.iter().all(|f| discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr(..))`,
and an `Identifier` naming a live Drop-bearing local is not fresh, so ONE such
field declines the whole literal and no owner registers for any field. The
TUPLE arm beside it already has the escape hatch this needs: B-2026-08-01-8
admits an element that is a `tuple_elem_is_movable_drop_struct_place` and has
the two CALLER sites retract that source's UserDrop, so the temp's element walk
becomes the single owner. Giving the struct arm the same admission plus the
matching retraction is the shape of the fix; the interpreter half already
behaves this way, so this is a codegen-only change.

RELATED: B-2026-09-01-18 (the interpreter double this was found beside, fixed
in 0033588) and B-2026-09-01-22 (the doubly-nested-wrapper sibling).
fix:
FIXED by e3b9e67.

THE MECHANISM, exactly as the row's "WHERE TO START" predicted.
`discarded_owned_literal_tail`'s STRUCT arm required every field to satisfy
`discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr`, and an `Identifier` naming a live
Drop-bearing local does not. One such field therefore declined the WHOLE
literal, no owner registered for ANY field, and the minted sibling's object was
simply never dropped. The single body that did print was `t`'s own scope-exit
body, not the literal's field walk -- which is why the shape looked like "one
body" rather than "no owner".

THE FIX, and the reason it is not a widening of that predicate.

  * `discarded_movable_literal_tail` is a SEPARATE entry point that admits a
    struct field which is `tuple_elem_is_movable_drop_struct_place` -- the same
    shape the TUPLE arm has admitted unconditionally since B-2026-08-01-8.
    Both share one body, `discarded_literal_tail_inner`, parameterized by a
    flag, so the wrapper-peeling recursion cannot drift between them.

  * `discarded_owned_literal_tail` is UNCHANGED, because it also feeds
    `discarded_arm_owned_aggregate_tail`, whose own doc comment records why a
    field naming a live binding must stay declined THERE: an arm-level owner
    performs no caller-side retraction, so a second owner would double-free
    rather than supply a missing body. Only the two statement-discard sites --
    the wildcard `let` arm and the bare-statement arm -- use the new predicate,
    and both retract.

  * `discarded_literal_moved_place_sources` replaces the two hand-inlined
    `if let ExprKind::Tuple(elems) = ..` retraction blocks at those sites with
    one helper covering tuple ELEMENTS and struct FIELDS alike, so the
    admission and the retraction can no longer disagree about which sources
    the temp's walk has taken over.

MEASURED, PRE AND POST, ALL THREE BACKENDS (I = `--interp`, J = `karac run`,
A = `karac build`; `R { id: i64 }` with an `impl Drop`, `S2 { r: R, s: R,
k: i64 }`):

    let t = R { id: 7 };
    S2 { r: t, s: R { id: 9 }, k: 1 };

                          pre                     post
        I                 dR9 dR7                 dR9 dR7
        J, A              dR7                     dR9 dR7

The `let _ =` and block-wrapper spellings measure identically, and so does the
MINTED-FIRST ordering (`S2 { r: R { id: 9 }, s: t, k: 1 }` gives `dR7 dR9` on
all three, matching the literal's own field order reversed). The BOUND `let` is
the oracle and was `dR9 dR7` on every surface before and after.

NO REGRESSION on the neighbouring shapes the widening now also admits, each
measured on all three backends before and after and unchanged: TWO sources and
no mint (`dR8 dR7`), ONE source in a single-field literal (`dR7`), and the
ALL-MINTED literal (`dR9 dR7`). The two-source case matters most, because the
widening moves it from "two scope-exit bodies" to "one field walk with both
sources retracted" -- a different route to the same transcript, ORDER included.

ASAN, AND THE HALF THIS FIX DOES NOT REACH. The widening hands codegen
ownership of a moved-from source, which is the double-free / leak boundary, so
`asan_a_discarded_literal_mixing_a_source_and_a_mint_frees_once` runs the
DOUBLE-OWN GUARDS with a `String` field -- the bound `let` and the all-minted
literal, where a second owner would be a double free -- and is clean at -O2 and
at -O0 alike. No double free: the retraction is correctly paired.

The `-O0` leg then caught what -O2 hides. The six literal shapes run every
`Drop` BODY once but never FREE the field heap: 76 B / 2 allocations, the two
`String` payloads. Measured IDENTICAL on unmodified `main` with this fix's
`src` reverted, so it is pre-existing and this fix neither caused nor cured it
-- bodies-then-leak is strictly better than no-bodies-then-leak. And the TUPLE
leg's own `let _ = (t, 20);` -- B-2026-08-01-8's shape, a month old and
untouched here -- leaks 38 B / 1 the same way, which is what shows the memory
gap is shared by both legs rather than introduced by the struct admission.

Split out as `asan_a_mixed_discarded_literal_still_leaks_its_field_heap` and
QUARANTINED on the -O0 leg against B-2026-09-01-25, which carries the
measurement and the site (the registrar's memory leg is gated ALL-FRESH exactly
as its bodies leg was, and only the bodies leg ever got a mixed path). Split
rather than quarantining the whole function, so the double-own guards stay on
the leg asserting real cleanliness -- the decay the known-failures file
documents itself against. With that line added, the leg matches its quarantine
list exactly (2 known failures).

ONE ROW THAT WAS WRITTEN AS A CONTROL AND FAILED, now filed as
B-2026-09-01-24. `S2 { r: R{id:1}, s: R{id:9}, k: t.id };` -- an ALL-MINTED
literal whose only mention of the local is a SCALAR FIELD READ -- leaks both
minted objects on the compiled backends (76 B / 2 allocations under ASAN).
Measured identical on unmodified `main`, so it predates this fix. It is the
same "one non-fresh field declines the whole literal" mechanism with a
different field shape, but NOT the same fix: a scalar read is a copy that moves
nothing, so it needs an admission with no retraction --
`discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr`'s own fallback arm is already meant to admit
it and only reaches its slot-type test through an `Identifier` guard, so a
`FieldAccess` never gets there. Hoisting the identical read into its own `let`
makes the program correct on every surface, which is what isolates it to the
field position.

GATES: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets`
clean on BOTH feature legs; `cargo test` 10233 passed / 0 failed;
`cargo test --features llvm --no-fail-fast` 15994 passed / 0 failed;
`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` matches its quarantine list exactly.

ID NOTE: the two follow-ups above were filed as B-2026-09-01-23 and -24 and
RENUMBERED to -24 and -25 when the push landed. Another session had allocated
-23 for an unrelated row (the arm-owner slot) in the same window and pushed
first, which is exactly the allocation race CLAUDE.md warns about and does not
solve. Their row keeps -23; every cross-reference here, in
`tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt` and in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` names the
renumbered ids. The FIX COMMIT e3b9e67 predates the renumber and so cites
"B-2026-09-01-24" in its message where it means -25 -- recorded here rather
than rewritten, since it is already on `main`.

title: A DISCARDED STRUCT LITERAL BEHIND **TWO** BLOCK WRAPPERS RUNS ITS CONSUMED LOCAL'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `{ { S { r: t, k: 1 } } };` prints `dR7 dR7` on `karac run` / `karac build` against one body under `--interp`, while the ONE-wrapper spelling is correct everywhere
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-09-01-18 and EXPOSED by it rather than
caused by it. Pre-fix the interpreter doubled here too, so this was an AGREED
gap that no A/B parity gate could report; 0033588 makes the interpreter correct
and leaves the compiled pair exactly as it was, which turns the agreed gap into
a divergence. Recorded here deliberately rather than capping that row's wrapper
peel at one level -- an arbitrary rule whose only purpose would be to keep both
backends wrong together.

MEASURED (I = `--interp`, J = `karac run`, A = `karac build`; `R { id: i64 }`
with an `impl Drop`, `S { r: R, k: i64 }`):

    let t = R { id: 7 };
    { { S { r: t, k: 1 } } };        pre  I dR7 dR7   J,A dR7 dR7   (agreed)
                                     post I dR7       J,A dR7 dR7   (divergent)

    ONE wrapper, the control:
    { S { r: t, k: 1 } };            post I dR7       J,A dR7       (agrees)

So the extra `{ }` is the whole difference, and it flips the compiled side from
correct to doubling -- which also says the two nesting depths take different
paths in codegen.

WHAT THE SECOND BODY IS. It is `t`'s own scope-exit body running over the
MOVED-FROM husk: codegen nulls the source slot at the move, so the walk runs
against a zeroed struct. Same diagnosis e49a85f measured for its own case, and
the reason the transcript is a spurious `dR7` rather than memory corruption --
the object printed is not freed twice. Severity is medium on that ground; it
would be higher for a source whose body observes its own fields.

WHERE TO START -- and one dead end already excluded. It is NOT
`discarded_owned_literal_tail`: instrumenting it to log every call and verdict
shows it returns `None` for this program at every nesting depth, so the owner
that runs the field walk here comes from somewhere else. `try_track_discarded_
user_drop_temp` is also excluded -- it has `Match` / `If` / `Call` /
`MethodCall` arms and no struct-literal or block arm. The likely candidate is
the INNER block being compiled as a value-position block, whose tail temp is
registered by a path that never consults the field-freshness question the
statement-level gates ask. Whatever registers it must also retract `t`'s
UserDrop, exactly as the interpreter's `suppress_discarded_literal_source_user_
drops` now does.

RELATED: B-2026-09-01-18 (fixed in 0033588) and B-2026-09-01-21 (the
minted-sibling loss found in the same sweep).
fix:
FIXED by 1fcdb47. The guard that lets a value-position block stand
down when the enclosing STATEMENT already owns its tail had drifted out of
sync with the statement sites it speaks for.

`compile_block_with_frame` computes `stmt_owns_block_tail` by asking the
statement-discard batteries' admission predicates about the block's tail; when
one says yes, the block suppresses instead of registering an owner of its own.
It asked `discarded_owned_literal_tail`. B-2026-09-01-21 had widened both
statement-discard sites to `discarded_movable_literal_tail` -- which also
admits a struct literal whose field MOVES a live Drop-bearing local
(`S { r: t, k: 1 }`) -- and left this guard on the old predicate. The guard
then answered "the statement does not own this" about a value the statement
had just taken AND retracted the source's UserDrop for, so every enclosing
block armed the arm-discard leg over the same value.

The count tracked NESTING DEPTH exactly, which is what identified the site:

    let t = R { id: 7 };
    let _ = { { S { r: t, k: 1 } } };      I dR7    J,A dR7 dR7
    let _ = { { { S { r: t, k: 1 } } } };  I dR7    J,A dR7 dR7 dR7
    let _ = { S { r: t, k: 1 } };          I dR7    J,A dR7        (correct)

The ONE-wrapper spelling was correct BY COINCIDENCE, which is why the family's
earlier rows never surfaced this: its tail is the literal itself, and the
arm-discard leg (`discarded_arm_owned_aggregate_tail`) declines a bare literal
with a non-fresh field for the same freshness reason. Only a tail that is
ITSELF a block reaches the registration -- probed directly rather than read off
the registrar: with two wrappers the statement's literal battery fires exactly
once at the literal's span, and a probe at the block-level registration fires
once per ENCLOSING block (spans 220 then 218 at depth 3, never at the
innermost).

THE ROW'S "WHERE TO START" WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE PATH AND WRONG ABOUT THE
PREDICATE. It correctly named the inner value-position block as the registrar
and correctly excluded `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp`. Its one dead end
was recording `discarded_owned_literal_tail` as excluded because instrumenting
it showed `None` at every depth -- true, and the reason: that predicate is
exactly the one the guard was asking, and its `None` IS the bug. The measurement
was sound; the inference from it inverted cause and symptom.

THE FIX is one token: ask `discarded_movable_literal_tail`. Both predicates
peel block wrappers, so the guard now agrees with the statement site at every
depth. This is the only correct direction -- the statement site performs the
source retraction (`discarded_literal_moved_place_sources`) that makes its
single owner safe, and a block-level owner does not, the asymmetry
`discarded_movable_literal_tail`'s own doc records. Widening the ARM-discard
leg instead would double-free rather than dedupe.

IT IS A DOUBLE FREE, not the leak this family usually produces, so it
reproduces at every optimization level and needed no `-O0` quarantine. ASAN
reports `attempting double-free` on the moved source's `String` at depth 2 and
again at depth 3; clean after. The extra `Drop` body is the visible half of the
extra free, which is how the row was found.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run`, `karac build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`) at depths 1/2/3, across the struct-literal,
tuple, all-minted, call-tail and mixed-source/minted-sibling shapes, plus the
