title: THE BRANCH ARM-OWNER SLOT IS ONE PER CONSTRUCT AND RESET EACH PASS, so a branch inside a loop whose owner frame lives OUTSIDE the loop frees only the LAST pass's escaping value -- `while i < 3 { let k = if i > 0 { mkA(n) } else { t }.contains("aaa"); }` strands `iterations - 1` of them (42 B in 2 blocks at 3 iterations, 72 B in 4 at 5); the same branch with the sibling binding declared INSIDE the loop body is clean, which isolates the frame CHOICE rather than the slot as the cause
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the measured remainder of B-2026-08-30-11, split out rather than
left inside it. That row gave the MINTING arm of a mixed branch an owner by
borrowing the sibling binding arm's frame, which closed the straight-line
shapes (`if`, `match`, f-string interpolation) completely. This is what the
same fix leaves behind in a loop.

MEASURED (valgrind, KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and 2 identical; per-arm payload sizes
chosen so the leaked block identifies which arm produced it -- `mkA` 15 B,
`mkB` 27 B):

    let t = mkB(n);                       // handed out on pass 0
    while i < 3 { let k = if i > 0 { mkA(n) } else { t }.contains("aaa"); .. }
                                          pre B-2026-08-30-11:  57 B / 3 blk
                                          post:                 42 B / 2 blk
    the same at 5 iterations              post:                 72 B / 4 blk

    CONTROL -- sibling binding declared INSIDE the loop body:  clean.

The surviving blocks are `t` (27 B) plus every `mkA` temp except the last, so
the count is `iterations - 1` and grows without bound.

WHY. `own_escaping_tail_value` allocates ONE slot per construct and
`reset_vec_slot_at_block_end` zeroes it in the block that dominates the arms,
which makes the slot mean "THIS pass's escaping value, if any" -- correct, and
required: without the reset, a pass in which the arm does not run would leave
the previous pass's already-freed header in place for this pass's drain to free
again (B-2026-08-30-2 measured that as a double free). But the cleanup the slot
is registered under lives in the frame the value's owner was BORROWED from, and
when the sibling binding was declared outside the loop that frame drains ONCE,
after the loop. So each pass overwrites the header the previous pass stored,
and only the survivor is ever freed.

The control is what isolates the cause: move the sibling binding inside the loop
body and the borrowed frame becomes the body's, which drains every pass, and the
whole shape is clean. Nothing about the slot or the reset changed -- only which
frame holds its cleanup.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT OBVIOUSLY RIGHT. "Use the innermost live frame
instead" would free per pass here and is exactly what B-2026-08-30-11's row
records as WRONG for the wrapped case: when the branch is itself wrapped, the
innermost frame is the wrapper's, which drains BEFORE the value escapes, and a
draft that used it double-freed on `selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run` (the
unwrapped spelling was clean, which is why a single-level fixture misses it).
The two cases want opposite answers and the difference is whether the branch's
value is CONSUMED inside the enclosing frame or ESCAPES it -- which is a
property of the consumer, not of the arm, and is not available at the point the
owner is registered.

WHERE TO START, so the next session does not re-derive it. Two candidate
shapes, neither explored beyond reasoning:

  - ONE SLOT PER PASS rather than per construct -- the second route
    B-2026-08-30-11's row offered and this fix did not take. A slot allocated in
    the loop body's frame, with the OUTER frame's cleanup retained only for the
    value that survives the loop, would give each pass its own owner. The
    question is what registers the per-pass cleanup without reintroducing the
    double free the reset exists to prevent.
  - A CONSUMER-POSITION signal: register in the innermost frame when the
    branch's value is consumed within it, and in the borrowed frame when it
    escapes. `current_branch_expr_span` and the tail-position machinery may
    already carry enough to decide this; nothing has been measured.

SEVERITY low rather than medium: it is a leak only -- no double free, no
dangling read, no wrong answer at either optimization level -- and it needs a
loop AND a sibling binding declared outside it, which is a narrower shape than
the straight-line ones B-2026-08-30-11 closed. Unbounded in that loop, which is
why it is not `wontfix`.

Pinned at its current leaking value by
`asan_loop_arm_owner_slot_keeps_only_the_last_pass` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs)
under the leak-tolerant ASAN runner, with the clean CONTROL in the same
fixture, so a future fix that turns this into a memory error fails loudly
rather than trading one class for a worse one.

ID NOTE: filed as B-2026-09-01-23 after B-2026-09-01-21 -- the id this row's own fix commit (1c0b4d5f) and its test doc named -- was taken by a concurrent session during the test run. The id was computed before a ~25-minute suite and re-checked after, which is the window CLAUDE.md's "compute the next id as late as possible" rule is about; a rebase in between is not enough on its own. The test's references are corrected; the pushed commit message still says -21 and cannot be, so this note is the pointer.

fix:
FIXED by 7ef82d3.

THE MECHANISM, confirmed by instrumentation rather than inferred. The row named
`discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr`'s fallback arm and was right. Logging that
predicate's verdict and the type it resolves for every field of the repro:

    S2 { r: R { id: 1 }, s: R { id: 9 }, k: t.id };

    field            te resolved by `infer_arg_elem_te`   verdict
    R { id: 1 }      Path(["R"])                          true
    R { id: 9 }      Path(["R"])                          true
    t.id             Path([""])          <-- EMPTY        false

The fallback is meant to admit exactly this shape -- its own comment says "a
place / unknown shape: safe only when its type is a scalar primitive" -- but it
reaches its slot-type test only through `if let ExprKind::Identifier(n)`, and
none of `infer_arg_elem_te`'s three resolvers (`enum_name_of_expr`,
`type_name_of`, `scalar_type_name_of_expr`) handles a `FieldAccess`. So the name
came back EMPTY, `te_head_is_scalar_primitive` failed on it, and one non-fresh
field declined the whole literal at `discarded_owned_literal_tail`.

THE FIX. `place_projection_is_scalar` answers from the DECLARED field type --
`struct_field_names` + `struct_field_type_exprs`, the pair `expr_is_char`'s
`FieldAccess` arm already uses -- and recurses through the object via
`expr_user_struct_name`, so a nested projection resolves too.

Placed in the predicate ITSELF, not in a separate discard-site-only entry point
the way B-2026-09-01-21's admission had to be. The difference is move vs copy: a
scalar read creates no second owner of anything, so it needs no source
retraction and is safe for every consumer of the predicate, including
`discarded_arm_owned_aggregate_tail` where -21's admission would double-free.

MEASURED, PRE AND POST, ALL THREE BACKENDS (I = `--interp`, J = `karac run`,
A = `karac build`; `R { id }` with an `impl Drop`, `S2 { r: R, s: R, k: i64 }`,
`Outer { inner: Inner, m: i64 }`):

    shape                                       pre I / J,A          post
    S2 { r: mk1, s: mk9, k: t.id };             dR9 dR1 dR7 / dR7    all: dR9 dR1 dR7
    let _ = S2 { .. k: t.id };                  dR9 dR1 dR7 / dR7    all: dR9 dR1 dR7
    { S2 { .. k: t.id } };                      dR9 dR1 dR7 / dR7    all: dR9 dR1 dR7
    S2 { .. k: o.m };        DEPTH-1            dR9 dR1     / --     all: dR9 dR1
    S2 { .. k: o.inner.n };  NESTED             dR9 dR1     / --     all: dR9 dR1

The two projection rows are worse pre-fix than the row's own repro: the compiled
backends printed NOTHING at all, losing both minted objects with no body
anywhere, because `Outer` carries no `Drop` of its own to supply the incidental
one that made the `t.id` case print `dR7`.

THE ROW'S TWO "NOT YET MEASURED" SHAPES, now measured, and one of them refutes
the row's guess:

  * NESTED projection (`o.inner.n`) -- the row expected it to behave the same
    way, and it did: both objects lost on the compiled backends, fixed here.
  * INDEX of a scalar element (`v[0]`) -- the row expected the same and it is
    WRONG. That shape AGREED on all three backends before this fix and after it
    (`dR9 dR1`), so it was never affected. `type_name_of` has an `Index` arm
    that resolves the element type through `var_elem_type_exprs`, which is
    exactly the resolution a `FieldAccess` lacked. Kept as a control.

CONTROLS, unchanged before and after: the same read HOISTED into its own `let`
(`let n = t.id;` -- correct throughout, which is what isolates the defect to the
field POSITION rather than to the read); a literal that does not mention the
local; and B-2026-09-01-21's movable-place shape, to show the two admissions do
not interfere.

ASAN. `asan_a_scalar_projection_field_leaves_the_literal_owned` runs the five
fixed shapes plus three guards with a `String` field. Since the admission is a
COPY there is no retraction to get wrong and no double-free direction to guard;
what the guards pin is that admitting the projection did not disturb the shapes
that already had owners (the index, the hoisted read, and the bound `let`).
Clean at -O2 and at -O0, and the `-O0` leg matches its quarantine list exactly.

GATES: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets`
clean on BOTH feature legs; `cargo test` 10233 passed / 0 failed;
`cargo test --features llvm --no-fail-fast` clean; `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`
matches its quarantine list exactly.
title: A DISCARDED ALL-MINTED STRUCT LITERAL WITH ONE FIELD THAT IS A SCALAR FIELD READ OF A LIVE LOCAL LEAKS EVERY MINTED OBJECT ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- `S2 { r: R{id:1}, s: R{id:9}, k: t.id };` runs `dR9 dR1 dR7` under `--interp` and only `dR7` on `karac run` / `karac build`, dropping 76 B in 2 allocations under ASAN
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-09-01-21, as a row that was WRITTEN AS
A CONTROL in that fix's ASAN test and failed. Measured PRE-EXISTING: identical
76 B / 2 allocations on unmodified `main` with that fix's `src` stashed, so it
is not caused by it, and its fix is a different one (see below).

MEASURED (I = `--interp`, J = `karac run`, A = `karac build`; `R { id: i64 }`
with an `impl Drop`, `S2 { r: R, s: R, k: i64 }`):

    let t = R { id: 7 };
    S2 { r: R { id: 1 }, s: R { id: 9 }, k: t.id };

        I      dR9 dR1 dR7      correct -- both minted fields, then `t`
        J, A   dR7              the minted PAIR is never dropped

The single `dR7` is `t`'s own scope-exit body; the literal registers no owner
at all, so `R{id:1}` and `R{id:9}` are leaked outright. Under
`-fsanitize=address` that is `SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 76 byte(s) leaked in
2 allocation(s)` with the allocation site in `mk`. The `let _ =` spelling
measures identically.

THREE CONTROLS, all agreeing on every surface, which is what isolates it to
the field POSITION rather than to the read:

    let t = R{id:7}; println(f"{t.id}");                 7 dR7
    let t = R{id:7}; S2 { r: R{id:1}, s: R{id:9}, k: 5 }; dR7 dR9 dR1
    let t = R{id:7}; let n = t.id;
                     S2 { r: R{id:1}, s: R{id:9}, k: n }; dR7 dR9 dR1

So hoisting the very same read into its own `let` makes the program correct.
It is having the projection INSIDE the discarded literal that loses the owner.

WHERE TO START: `discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr` (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`).
Its fallback arm is meant to admit exactly this -- "a place / unknown shape:
safe only when its type is a scalar primitive" -- but it reaches the slot-type
test only through `if let ExprKind::Identifier(n) = &e.kind`, so a
`FieldAccess` never gets there and answers false. One non-fresh field then
declines the whole literal at `discarded_owned_literal_tail` and no owner
registers, which is the same mechanism as B-2026-09-01-21 with a different
field shape.

WHY IT IS NOT THE SAME FIX. B-2026-09-01-21's field is a MOVE (a live
Drop-bearing local handed into the literal), so its admission has to be paired
with retracting that source's UserDrop, and is deliberately confined to the
two statement-discard sites that do retract. A scalar field read is a COPY: it
moves nothing, creates no second owner, and needs no retraction -- so the
right change is to make `discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr` itself answer true
for a place expression whose resolved type is a scalar primitive, which is
what its own comment already claims it does. That also makes it safe for the
predicate's other consumer, `discarded_arm_owned_aggregate_tail`, where
B-2026-09-01-21's admission is not.

NOT YET MEASURED: whether an INDEX (`v[0]` of a scalar element) and a nested
projection (`t.inner.id`) behave the same way. Both go through the same
fallback arm, so both are likely, but neither was run.

RELATED: B-2026-09-01-21 (the move-shaped sibling, same predicate),
B-2026-09-01-18 and B-2026-09-01-22 (the wrapper/statement family this was
found inside).

fix:
FIXED by f909f9a.

THE MECHANISM, and this row's own prose was wrong TWICE before a probe found
it. Both wrong answers came from reading the registrar; the right one came from
measuring. That pattern is the row's most transferable content, so the two
corrections are left in the detail above rather than edited away.

  * The row as filed blamed the memory leg inside
    `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` for being gated all-fresh like its
    bodies leg. Wrong: an `eprintln!` on that registrar's struct arm is silent
    for the leaking program.
  * fd4ba33's correction blamed the `literal_tail` battery for never calling
    the registrar. Also wrong: it does call it, two lines below its shared leg.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, from three probes. The registrar is entered seven times
for the leaking program and NEVER with the `S2` type -- twice with `i64` and
five times with `{ ptr, i64, i64 }`, all other sites' String/Vec temporaries.
The `literal_tail` branch is never taken, because `literal_tail` is computed
only `if tail.is_none()` and none of the four predicates admits this shape at
all: probed directly, `owned=false unitvar=false matchval=false movlit=false`.

`movlit` is the one that should have been true, and the reason it is not is the
whole bug. `discarded_movable_literal_tail` admits a field that is
`tuple_elem_is_movable_drop_struct_place`, and that predicate required the
moved type to run a USER `Drop`:

    && self.type_runs_user_drop(tn.as_str(), &mut Vec::new())

The ASAN fixture's `R { id: i64, s: String }` declares no `impl Drop` -- it is a
pure MEMORY fixture -- so the field was declined, the literal was declined, no
owner registered, and both field buffers leaked. The predicate was answering
the BODIES question at a caller that needed the MEMORY one.

THE CONTRAST THAT LOCATED IT was already sitting in the passing half of the
same test file: `S2 { r: mk(7), s: mk(9), k: 1 };` -- all-minted, every field a
`Call`, so `discard_tuple_elem_is_fresh_expr` admits them and
`discarded_owned_literal_tail` registers the owner -- is memory-clean at -O0
and always was. The only difference from the leaking shape is the one live-local
field.

THE FIX. `tuple_elem_is_movable_drop_struct_place` now also admits a
non-shared struct that merely CARRIES heap (any field for which
`type_expr_has_drop_heap` holds), alongside the existing user-`Drop` test. One
predicate, four words of condition; the move is the same move either way.

Safe because the caller-side retraction that pairs with this admission was
already unconditional at both discard sites (B-2026-09-01-21's
`discarded_literal_moved_place_sources`), and for a no-user-`Drop` struct
`suppress_user_drop_for_var` is simply a no-op -- there is no body to retract,
only memory to transfer, which is exactly what was missing.

MEASURED at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, where the allocations survive to be counted:

    shape                                        pre        post
    S2 { r: t, s: mk(9), k: 1 };                 76 B / 2   clean
    let _ = S2 { r: t, s: mk(9), k: 1 };         76 B / 2   clean
    { S2 { r: t, s: mk(9), k: 1 } };             76 B / 2   clean
    S2 { r: mk(9), s: t, k: 1 };   minted first  76 B / 2   clean
    S2 { r: t, s: u, k: 1 };       two sources   76 B / 2   clean
    S { r: t, k: 1 };              single field  38 B / 1   clean
    let _ = (t, 20);               the TUPLE leg 38 B / 1   clean

The tuple row is the one the row flagged as "check rather than assume": it is
B-2026-08-01-8's own movable-place shape, a month old and untouched by
B-2026-09-01-21, and it shared the same cause after all -- the predicate is
shared, so one condition fixed both legs.

NO DOUBLE FREE. The widening hands codegen ownership of a moved-from source,
which is the other direction this could have gone, so the guards that were
split off for the quarantine went back in and are clean: the BOUND `let` (owned
by its binding, not the site), the ALL-MINTED literal (which already had an
owner), the hoisted read, and the scalar-index shape.

QUARANTINE LINE REMOVED, which is the completion signal the -O0 ratchet is
built to demand: it fails when a listed fixture starts PASSING, and this one
now does. `asan_a_mixed_discarded_literal_still_leaks_its_field_heap` is gone
and its rows are back in
`asan_a_discarded_literal_mixing_a_source_and_a_mint_frees_once`, where they
were split from -- so the whole family is on the leg again rather than half of
it. The list is back to its one pre-existing entry (B-2026-09-01-5's).

GATES: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets`
clean on BOTH feature legs; `cargo test` 10236 passed / 0 failed;
`cargo test --features llvm --no-fail-fast` 16001 passed / 0 failed;
`scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` matches its quarantine list exactly (1 known failure,
B-2026-09-01-5's, which predates this row).
title: THE MEMORY HALF OF B-2026-09-01-21: a DISCARDED aggregate whose fields/elements MIX a live-local source with anything else runs every `Drop` BODY once but never FREES the field heap -- `S2 { r: t, s: mk(9), k: 1 };` leaks 76 B / 2 allocations at -O0, and the TUPLE leg's own `let _ = (t, 20);` leaks 38 B / 1 identically, so the gap is shared by both legs
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by the `-O0` ASAN leg while landing B-2026-09-01-21, which
is exactly the direction that leg exists for -- at the default -O2 LLVM deletes
the provably-dead allocations and every one of these shapes passes.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT FIXED. B-2026-09-01-21 made a discarded struct literal whose
fields mix a live-local source with a minted sibling run EVERY field's `Drop`
body exactly once on all three backends (it previously ran none of them, the
whole literal having been declined). It did not make the field HEAP get freed.
So the state is bodies-correct / memory-leaking, where it was
bodies-missing / memory-leaking before -- strictly better, and the remaining
half is this row rather than a regression in that one.

MEASURED at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (`R { id: i64, s: String }` with an
`impl Drop`, `S2 { r: R, s: R, k: i64 }`):

    let t = mk(7); S2 { r: t, s: mk(9), k: 1 };     76 B / 2 allocations
                                                    (both `String` payloads)

Identical for the `let _ =` spelling, the block-wrapper spelling, the
MINTED-FIRST ordering, the TWO-SOURCE shape and the single-field `S { r: t }`.
And identical on unmodified `main` with B-2026-09-01-21's `src` reverted, which
is what establishes it as pre-existing.

THE TUPLE LEG LEAKS THE SAME WAY, which is the finding that says where to look:

    let t = mk(7); let _ = (t, 20);                 38 B / 1 allocation

That is B-2026-08-01-8's own shape -- the movable-place hatch on the TUPLE arm,
a month old and untouched by B-2026-09-01-21. So the gap is not something the
struct admission introduced; it is shared by both legs and predates both.

WHERE TO START: the discard sites' comment in `src/codegen/stmts.rs` states the
split plainly -- "the registrar's internal bodies leg is gated ALL-FRESH
(shared with the call-arg position, where a place element's body belongs to its
binding), so a MIXED tuple's bodies register here instead". The BODIES got a
mixed path (`track_discarded_tuple_elem_bodies`, and B-2026-09-01-21's struct
equivalent). The MEMORY leg inside
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` did not: it is gated on the same
all-fresh question and skips a mixed aggregate entirely, so nothing frees the
fields. The fix is a mixed-aggregate memory registration to sit beside the
mixed-aggregate bodies registration, for tuples and structs alike.

QUARANTINED, not silenced: `asan_a_mixed_discarded_literal_still_leaks_its_field_heap`
is on `tests/asan-o0-known-failures.txt` naming this row. It is its own
`#[test]`, split from
`asan_a_discarded_literal_mixing_a_source_and_a_mint_frees_once` so that test's
DOUBLE-OWN GUARDS (the bound `let`, the all-minted literal) stay on the `-O0`
leg asserting real cleanliness -- quarantining the whole function to cover this
is the decay that file documents itself against. When this row is fixed the
ratchet will fail in its listed-fixture-now-PASSES direction and the line comes
off.

RELATED: B-2026-09-01-21 (the body half, fixed), B-2026-08-01-8 (the tuple
leg's movable-place hatch, which has the same memory gap), and
B-2026-09-01-24 (a different field shape declining the same predicate).

DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED 2026-09-01, and the row's own "WHERE TO START" is WRONG.
It said the memory leg inside `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` is gated
on the same all-fresh question as the bodies leg and skips a mixed aggregate.
Measured by instrumentation, that is not what happens: THAT REGISTRAR IS NEVER
CALLED AT ALL for this shape.

An `eprintln!` on the registrar's struct arm -- the `else if let Some(name) =
self.owned_struct_temp_arg_name(arg)` branch, which `S2 { .. }` does satisfy
(`path.last()` names a struct) -- prints NOTHING while compiling

    let t = mkshort(7); S2 { r: t, s: mklong(9), k: 1 };

so no gate inside it is declining; control never arrives. The bare-statement
discard site in `src/codegen/stmts.rs` guards the registrar call with

    if let Some(tail) = tail { ... self.track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg(val, tail, false); }

on the `tail` binding (`discarded_owned_temp_tail` / `discarded_unit_variant_tail`
/ `discarded_match_value_tail`). The discarded-LITERAL path is the SEPARATE
`literal_tail` binding, computed only when `tail.is_none()`, and its battery
registers BODIES without ever reaching that call. That is why the bodies print
and the memory is never freed, and it is a structural miss rather than a gate.

BOTH allocations leak, not one: with the two `String` payloads made equal
length the report is 2 allocations / 76 B, so neither the moved-in source's
buffer nor the minted sibling's is freed. The whole aggregate is unowned on the
memory axis.

WHERE TO START, corrected: give the `literal_tail` battery the memory
registration the `tail` battery gets -- either by calling
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` on the literal tail too, or by factoring the
memory half out of that registrar so both batteries share it. The TUPLE leg's
`let _ = (t, 20);` (38 B / 1) should be checked against the same site rather
than assumed identical: its `literal_tail` battery does have a
`track_discarded_tuple_elem_bodies` call, so the two legs may miss the memory
registration in different places.

NOT ATTEMPTED. Establishing the above consumed the session's remaining budget
for this row; the fix is unwritten. Recorded here so the next session starts
from the corrected pointer instead of re-walking the registrar's gates, which
is where this one spent its time.

CORRECTION TO THE CORRECTION, same day. The paragraph above got the CONCLUSION
right (the aggregate registrar never sees this value) and the REASON wrong, and
the wrong reason is on `main` in fd4ba33 -- recorded here rather than edited
away, since a bad pointer that was pushed is worth showing as such.

It said the `literal_tail` battery "registers BODIES without ever reaching that
call". That is false: the battery at `stmts.rs` DOES call
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg(val, lt, false)`, two lines below its shared
leg. Three probes, each restored before the next:

  1. On the registrar's STRUCT arm -- silent, which is what prompted the wrong
     inference.
  2. On the registrar's ENTRY -- it is entered SEVEN times for this program and
     never once with the `S2` type: twice with `i64` (early-returns, not a
     StructType) and five times with `{ ptr, i64, i64 }` (early-returns as the
     vec-struct). All seven are other call sites' String/Vec temporaries.
  3. On the `literal_tail` branch itself -- SILENT. The branch is never taken.

So the real reason is one level up: `literal_tail` is computed only
`if tail.is_none()`, and for this program `tail` is already `Some`, so the
literal battery is bypassed entirely. The `tail` battery runs
`track_discarded_temp_cleanup(tail, val)` -- which is where the BODIES come
from -- and reaches `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` only inside an
`if let Some(en) = self.enum_name_of_expr(enum_probe)` guard, i.e. for ENUM
constructors. A struct literal answers `None` there, so it gets bodies and no
memory registration.

SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the regression fixture for B-2026-08-30-16.

leak that would make it fail for the wrong reason.

A `match` over a FRESH-TEMP enum whose arm MOVES a heap payload out leaks that
payload when the match sits in a NESTED EXPRESSION position instead of being
let-bound:

    enum Ve { A(String), B }
    impl Drop for Ve { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dVe") } }
    fn mkVe(n: i64) -> Ve { return Ve.A(f"payloadpayload{n}") }

    // CLEAN -- the let-bound spelling
    let out = match mkVe(9) { Ve.A(s) => { s } Ve.B => { "none".to_string() } };
    println(f"out[{out}]");

    // LEAKS 15 B -- the same match, interpolated
    println(f"out[{match mkVe(9) { Ve.A(s) => { s } Ve.B => { "none".to_string() } }}]");

Both print `dVe out[payloadpayload9]` on every surface, so the OUTPUT is right
and only the memory is wrong -- which is why nothing in the suite catches it.

THREE THINGS THAT NARROW IT, each measured rather than assumed:

  * NOT SHARED-SPECIFIC. Reproduces identically on a plain value enum and on a
    `shared enum`; the 15 B is the moved-out `String`, not the box.
  * THE PAYLOAD MUST BE HEAP. The same nested spelling with an `i64` payload
    (`Ve.A(n) => { n }`) is clean, so it is the moved-out buffer that has no
    owner, not the match temp itself.
  * IT IS THE POSITION, not the consumer. A call argument leaks it too
    (`sink(match mkVe(9) { .. })`, and a bare `println(match ..)`), so any
    nested expression position does it; only the `let` binding is clean.

LEAKS AT BOTH OPT LEVELS -- 15 bytes in 1 block at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` AND at
the default `-O2` (valgrind), unlike the -O0-only leak class, so a regression
fixture for it has real coverage on the default leg.

SEVERITY: one buffer per evaluation, unbounded in a loop; no double free and no
wrong answer, and the shape (a match interpolated into a log line) is an
ordinary one.

WHERE TO START: the let-bound spelling is clean, so the owner exists and the
nested position is not reaching it -- the same value-position-vs-statement-
position split B-2026-08-30-12 and B-2026-08-30-13 turned out to be, one
construct over. Compare what the `let` arm registers for the arm's moved-out
payload against what the expression path registers when the match's value flows
into an enclosing expression instead of a binding.

title: `if let` AND `while let` OVER AN `Option` WITH A STRUCT PAYLOAD LOSE THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY, where the `match` spelling of the identical program runs it -- a spelling-dependent split, and the third time this family has had one
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-31-32, and MEASURED AGAINST THE PRE-FIX TREE so the
attribution is not a guess: both spellings were already losing the body before
that row's change, which touched the `if let` site. This is neither fallout nor
a regression from it.

    struct R { s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR[{self.s}]") } }
    struct P { r: R, n: i64 }
    fn opt(t: String) -> Option[P] { return Option.Some(P { r: R { s: t }, n: 1 }); }

    fn main() {
        match opt("m1") { Some(p) => { println(p.n) } None => { println("x") } }
        if let Some(p) = opt("i1") { println(p.n) }

        --interp     : m 1 dR[m1] i 1            <- the `if let` body is lost
        jit / build  : m 1 dR[m1] i 1 dR[i1]     correct

The `while let` spelling loses it too, on a driver that yields two values:

    while let Some(p) = c.next() { println(p.n) }

        --interp     : 1 2                       <- BOTH bodies lost

odd one out is the interpreter's `let` forms.

Bodies only -- no leak or double-free on any surface, so no memory gate sees

title: AN `Option` WHOSE PAYLOAD OWNS HEAP LEAKS THAT HEAP WHENEVER THE VALUE IS PASSED AS A FUNCTION ARGUMENT -- under BOTH parameter modes, by value AND `ref`, generic AND non-generic; the `let`-bound spelling of the identical value is clean
detail:
An `Option` (or `Result`) whose payload owns heap LEAKS THAT HEAP whenever the
value is passed as a function ARGUMENT, and it leaks under BOTH parameter modes
-- by value, where the callee should free it, and `ref`, where the caller should.
The `let`-bound spelling of the identical value in `main` is clean, which is the
contrast that isolates it to the argument path.

Found while fixing B-2026-08-31-39, when the asan twin that row wanted could not
be made green. NOT that row's defect: the plain NON-GENERIC spelling leaks
identically, and every measurement below is byte-identical on pristine `main`
and with that row's fix applied.

MEASURED, `-fsanitize=address` + LeakSanitizer on Linux, each program a
3-iteration `while` loop so a leak reports as three independent blocks rather
than one ambiguous one:

    fn show(x: Option[Vec[String]])         333 B in 6 allocations
        (288 B direct in 3 objects -- one buffer per iteration --
         plus 45 B indirect in 3, the `String` inside each)
    fn show[T: Display](x: Option[T]), T = String    26 B in 2 allocations
    fn show[T: Display](x: ref Option[T]), T = Vec[String]    LEAKS
    let o: Option[Vec[String]] = Some(vs); println(f"{o}")    CLEAN

The generic and non-generic spellings leak the same way, so this is about the
argument, not about monomorphization. The `ref` row is the one that says the
defect is not simply "the callee forgets to free what it was given": under `ref`
the caller keeps ownership and its own scope exit should free, and does not.

WHY IT HAS STAYED HIDDEN. A leak needs a payload that owns heap AND a call that
takes the whole `Option`, and the two most common shapes miss it -- a scalar
payload owns nothing, and the overwhelmingly common `Option` use is
`match`/`if let` on a local rather than handing the whole thing to a function.
The `let`-bound control above is exactly the shape almost every fixture uses.

NOT MEASURED: whether `Result[T, E]` behaves the same (very likely -- it shares
the payload registration path); whether the leak survives when the callee
DESTRUCTURES the payload rather than displaying it; whether a user struct with a
heap field as the payload leaks the same way; and whether the interpreter leaks
too (it is GC-free and reference-counted, so probably not, but LSan does not
cover it).

BLOCKS: the aggregate-instantiation memory-balance fixture B-2026-08-31-39
wanted. Once this lands, that fixture becomes writable.

PARTIAL FIX, cc0ee45 (2026-09-01) -- the DOUBLE-FREE half. This row REMAINS OPEN
for the leak it was filed on, and the opening measurements below are CORRECTED.

WHAT THE OPENING ROW GOT WRONG. It says the leak happens "under BOTH parameter
modes, by value AND `ref`, generic AND non-generic". The by-value half is true
only for a FRESH TEMP argument. A named binding by value is CLEAN:

    let mut vs: Vec[String] = Vec.new(); vs.push(...);
    show(Some(vs));                 LEAKS 333 B / 6 allocations
    let o: Option[Vec[String]] = Some(vs); show(o);      CLEAN

The row generalised from two measurements taken on different spellings -- the
by-value probe used a fresh temp and the `ref` probe a named binding -- and
neither of those facts implies the other. The `ref` half stands and is
unexplained: `fn show(x: ref Option[Vec[String]])` leaks for a NAMED binding
too, where the caller keeps ownership and its own scope exit should free.

FULL MATRIX, LSan on Linux, 3-iteration loop, `karac build`:

    by value, fresh `Some(vs)`                   LEAK 333 B / 6
    by value, fresh `Some(vs.clone())`           LEAK 336 B / 6
    by value, fresh `Some(mkv())`                CLEAN
    by value, named `let o = Some(vs)`           CLEAN
    `ref` param, named binding                   LEAK 333 B / 6
    `ref` param, fresh temp                      LEAK 333 B / 6
    payload `String` / `Vec[i64]`                LEAK 39 B / 96 B
    payload a STRUCT with a String field         CLEAN
    payload scalar, or `None`                    CLEAN
    `Result` (`Ok(vs)` / `Err(vs)`)              LEAK, same shape
    method / assoc / generic spellings           LEAK, same shape
    bare `fn show(x: Vec[String])` (no Option)   CLEAN  <- control
    `let o = Some(vs); println(f"{o}")` in main  CLEAN  <- control

CAUSE OF THE LEAK, traced but NOT fixed here. `optres_arg_is_unowned_temp`
(call_dispatch.rs) decides whether the caller owns a fresh `Option`/`Result`
temp, and for an enum CONSTRUCTOR it recursed into the payload on the reasoning
that "`Ok(mkv())` manufactures its payload, `Ok(x)` wraps a buffer `x` still
owns". The second half is false at a call site: the constructor MOVES `x` in, so
the binding's cleanup is disarmed and the envelope is the only owner left. The
`.clone()` row above is what shows the predicate is asking the wrong QUESTION
rather than being incomplete -- a `.clone()` result is unambiguously a fresh temp
nothing else owns, and it is rejected for being spelled as a `MethodCall`.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS NOT LANDED, measured rather than argued. Widening that
arm to "an enum constructor at an argument position is always an unowned temp"
fixes every leaking row above and passes the whole 1357-case ASAN suite. It also
turns THREE shapes that are clean today into DOUBLE FREES, because the caller
then owns a buffer some other frame already owns:

    fn sink(acc: mut ref Vec[Option[String]], x: Option[String]) { acc.push(x) }
    fn wrap(x: Option[String]) -> Bag { let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(x);
                                        return Bag { xs: v } }

the STORE route (`sink`) and the RETURNED-AGGREGATE route (`wrap`), the latter in
free-fn, method and assoc spellings alike.

THE UNDERLYING ASYMMETRY, which is the real finding. The caller-side predicate
`callee_optres_param_entry_copied` answers from the param's TYPE alone, while the
callee emits the entry copy only for a param in `nonescaping_param_names`
(functions.rs). So for every callee that merely READS its `Option` param -- an
f-string hole is not a "scrutinee" use -- the caller believes a copy was made and
none was: the callee neither copies nor registers a cleanup, and the caller
declines to own the temp. Nobody frees. That is the leak, and it is one
`if`-condition apart from a double free in the other direction.

THE UNIFORM RULE WAS TRIED AND REVERTED. Making the callee entry-copy EVERY
admitted by-value `Option`/`Result` param (so the callee always owns its copy and
the caller always owns its temp) is the coherent fix: it makes 14 of the 15
probe shapes above green, including all three double-free routes, and needs no
escape analysis at all. It then breaks the PASSTHROUGH convention --
`fn idopt(o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o }` with a named-binding
argument leaks 51 B / 3, because `passthrough_owner_alias` forwards the consuming
arm's disarm to the SOURCE binding on the assumption that one buffer is moved
through, and under the uniform rule there are now two. That is a fourth coupled
mechanism, and rewriting the by-value `Option` ownership convention across all
four is a design change rather than a bug fix. Reverted rather than landed
half-understood; everything above is measured and nothing from that attempt is
on `main`.

WHAT DID LAND. The STORE route's double free, at all three call sites. A callee
that pushes the argument into a place outliving the call owns it, so the caller
must not; the gate is exact rather than conservative, because a callee cannot
both store the argument and entry-copy it (a stored param is escaping, and the
entry copy fires only for non-escaping params). Measured on an unmodified tree,
`sink(mut acc, Some(mks(i)))` aborts with `attempting double-free`; after the
fix it completes.

The fix converts that double free into a LEAK -- nobody frees, because the callee
did not copy -- which is strictly safer and strictly incomplete. The fixture
says so: `asan_stored_optres_temp_arg_has_one_owner` runs with LEAK DETECTION OFF
and asserts only that the memory error is gone, and carries the instruction to
move to `assert_clean_asan_run` when the leak half lands.

STILL OPEN: the leak this row was filed on (every row marked LEAK above); the
`ref`-parameter half, which is a different and unexplained mechanism; and the
RETURNED-AGGREGATE double-free route, which is a live memory-unsafety on `main`
today, reachable without any of this row's changes, and is filed as
B-2026-09-01-35. `Some(Some(s))` also leaks 45 B / 3 both before and after, and is
out of reach of all of the above: its payload exceeds the boxing-word limit, so
the param is never admitted in the first place.

SECOND PARTIAL FIX, b3dbcee (2026-09-01) -- the BY-VALUE LEAK half, landed
together with B-2026-09-01-35's gate. This row REMAINS OPEN for the `ref` half.

Every by-value row of the matrix above is now clean, on all four surfaces:

    show(Some(vs))                 333 B / 6   -> clean
    show(Some(vs.clone()))         336 B / 6   -> clean
    show(Some(w.f))                leaked      -> clean
    showr(Err(vs))                 leaked      -> clean
    h.show(Some(s))   method       leaked      -> clean
    show(Some(mkv(i)))             clean       -> clean   (control)
    let o = Some(vs); show(o)      clean       -> clean   (control)

THE PREVIOUS UPDATE SAID THIS WIDENING COULD NOT LAND, and that was true of the
widening alone. `optres_arg_is_unowned_temp`'s enum-constructor arm now answers
`true` unconditionally, which by itself turns three shapes into double frees --
a callee that stores the argument or returns it inside an aggregate already owns
it. What made it safe is B-2026-09-01-35: the caller's ownership gate now reads
the SAME escape analysis the callee's entry copy is emitted from, so ownership
is taken only where the callee provably copies. See that row for the analysis
and for the passthrough regression that showed the two questions must stay two
predicates.

The previous update also recorded a UNIFORM-RULE attempt (make the callee copy
every admitted by-value param) that got 14 of 15 probe shapes green and broke
the passthrough convention. That attempt is superseded, not revived: the landed
fix leaves the callee's copy gated on escape exactly as before and only widens
it by the one read-only position, so `passthrough_owner_alias`'s
one-buffer-moves-through assumption still holds.

STILL OPEN, and now the whole of this row:

  * The `ref`-PARAMETER half. `fn show(x: ref Option[Vec[String]])` leaks
    333 B / 6 for a NAMED binding and for a fresh temp alike, where the caller
    keeps ownership and its own scope exit should free. Untouched by this fix,
    which is entirely about by-value temp ownership, and still unexplained.
  * `Some(Some(s))`, 45 B / 3 before and after. Out of reach of all of the
    above: an `Option[Option[String]]` payload exceeds the boxing-word limit, so
    the param is never admitted and neither side of the copy convention applies.

title: A BARE-`T` BY-VALUE GENERIC PARAM'S OWNERSHIP CONVENTION DEPENDS ON THE COMPILER NOT KNOWING ITS ELEMENT TYPE, so a better-informed monomorph strands the caller's temporary (leak) and the obvious caller-side compensation double-frees a match-arm return
detail:
A BARE-`T` BY-VALUE GENERIC PARAM'S OWNERSHIP CONVENTION DEPENDS ON THE
COMPILER NOT KNOWING ITS ELEMENT TYPE, so any change that makes the monomorph
better-informed flips the param from move to deep-copy and strands the caller's
temporary -- and the obvious caller-side compensation double-frees a different
shape.

    fn echo[T](x: T) -> T { x }
    fn takeout[T](b: T) -> T { match b { v => { return v; } } }

The mono prologue enters a bare non-borrow param into `owned_vecstr_params`
only when it lands in `vec_elem_types`, which needs the ELEMENT. For an
argument the side-table resolvers cannot read -- anything but a plain
identifier: `x.clone()`, a collection literal, a call result -- the element is
invisible, so the param stays OUT of `owned_vecstr_params` and the body MOVES
the buffer through. The caller-side materialization gate
(`is_fresh_vec_temp_for_owned_param`, src/codegen/mono.rs) is calibrated
against precisely that: it EXCLUDES a bare-`T` param whose type param appears
in the declared return type, on the argument that a forwarding tail hands the
caller's own buffer back out.

So the two sides agree only by accident of ignorance. Measured, by feeding the
monomorph the type the call actually instantiated `T` at (B-2026-08-31-39's
exact-`TypeExpr` channel, gated OFF for this shape for exactly this reason):

  * `echo([r, r + 1, r + 2])` in a 3-iteration loop LEAKS 72 B in 3
    allocations. The body now deep-copies at the return, the caller's result
    binding frees the copy, and the array-literal temporary is orphaned.
    `asan_return_owned_generic_param_no_double_free` catches it.
  * Widening the materialization gate to admit a bare-`T` spelling -- i.e.
    dropping the return-type exclusion, which is what "the value the caller
    binds is always an independent buffer" would justify -- turns `takeout`
    into an ASAN DOUBLE-FREE.
    `asan_generic_unused_bare_type_param_temp_arg_no_leak` catches that.

THE REAL DEFECT IS THE NON-UNIFORMITY, and the `takeout` result is what shows
it: a `return v;` whose `v` came from a MATCH-ARM BINDING still moves, while a
bare `return x;` of an `owned_vecstr_params` param deep-copies. Two return
shapes in one convention, so no single caller-side rule can be right for both.
`generic_param_is_owned_container`'s doc already asserts the copy happens "at
every retaining consume site INCLUDING the return" -- true for the `Vec[T]`
spelling it describes, and NOT true for a match-arm return.

WHY IT HAS NOT BITTEN YET: the element is invisible for exactly the argument
forms that produce a fresh temporary, which is the only case where ownership of
the argument is in question. A named binding keeps its own let-drop either way.
So the accident is stable under today's resolvers, and only a change that
widens what the monomorph knows disturbs it -- which is how it was found.

FIX DIRECTION (not attempted): make the deep-copy uniform across return shapes,
so `owned_vecstr_params` means one thing, and then the caller-side rule can be
stated positively (materialize a fresh temp for any by-value param that is
caller-retains) rather than as a syntactic exclusion. Until then, any future
work that resolves a monomorph's type params more precisely must check these
two ASAN fixtures FIRST -- they are the tripwire, and they both fired.

NOT MEASURED: whether a `String` (rather than `Vec`) bare-`T` param has the
same split -- the String arm of the materialization gate is separate and fired
correctly throughout; and whether an `if let` return behaves like the `match`
one.
fix:
FIXED by e49ba40.

TWO OF THE ROW'S OWN CLAIMS ARE WRONG, and the first changes what this is.

"WHY IT HAS NOT BITTEN YET" -- it has. The non-uniformity is a REPRODUCIBLE
DOUBLE FREE on today's compiler with no change of any kind:

    fn takeout[T](b: T) -> T { match b { v => { return v; } } }
    fn main() {
        let c: Vec[String] = ["cccccccccccc", "dddddddddddd"];
        let r = takeout(c);
        println(r[0]);
    }

    free(): double free detected in tcache 2

Under valgrind: THREE invalid frees -- both element buffers and the outer one.
The caller's binding and the result binding each own the whole thing, because
the callee moved instead of copying and the caller never stood down.

So the class was `soundness` and it is `double-free`; the severity was `medium`
on the reasoning that nothing observable had happened yet, and that reasoning
does not hold.

THE ELEMENT TYPE IS WHY IT HID, and it is why the row's own probes missed it.
Every shape but one is clean, including the two a probe reaches for first:

    takeout + Vec[String]   DOUBLE FREE
    takeout + Vec[i64]      clean   -- no inner heap elements to double-free
    takeout + String        clean   -- one buffer, and the caller stands down
    echo    + anything      clean   -- the bare `return x;` spelling

Only a `Vec` whose ELEMENTS are heap exposes it: `Vec[i64]` has no inner
buffers, and a plain `String` has a single one that the existing stand-down
already covers. The row's measurements used `Vec[i64]` and fresh temporaries,
which is exactly the pair that says "fine".

The second wrong claim follows from the first: "only a change that widens what
the monomorph knows disturbs it". No -- a named `Vec[String]` argument disturbs
it today. What B-2026-08-31-39's channel would have done is widen the shapes it
reaches, not create it.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is the row's own diagnosis: `owned_vecstr_params` is what
makes a retaining consume site deep-copy rather than hand the buffer on, and it
holds PARAM NAMES. A match arm rebinds the value under a NEW name, so the
return-position copy (`maybe_defensive_copy_return_value` ->
`maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg`, which keys on `Identifier(n)` with
`n` in the set) asked about `v`, was told "not an owned param", and moved.

FIX: `propagate_owned_param_to_whole_arm_binding`
(src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs), called beside the `suppress_*` family that
already reconciles arm bindings against their scrutinee, and from the three
sibling binding sites in `control_flow.rs`. It carries the param's
membership -- and the `vec_elem_types` / `var_elem_type_exprs` entries the copy
helper reads the element type from, without which it silently no-ops -- onto the
arm's binding. That is the row's stated fix direction: make the convention mean
one thing, so `owned_vecstr_params` answers the same question at every return
shape.

DELIBERATELY NARROW. It fires only for a bare-identifier scrutinee naming such a
param, and only for a pattern that binds the WHOLE value. A destructure binds a
PART, whose ownership belongs to the payload/field machinery beside this call
and which has its own disarm rules; widening to sub-patterns is how this would
turn into the over-copy the row warns about.

BOTH TRIPWIRES HOLD -- the row names them as what must be checked FIRST, and
they are the two directions this could have gone wrong in:
`asan_return_owned_generic_param_no_double_free` (the leak direction, if the
copy over-fires) and `asan_generic_unused_bare_type_param_temp_arg_no_leak`
(the double-free direction, whose `takeout` line is this exact function). Both
pass.

MEASURED AFTER, under valgrind: 0 errors and 0 bytes in use at exit for every
shape in the matrix above, the FRESH-TEMP argument form included -- the case the
row flags as the one where ownership of the argument is actually in question.

FIXTURE: `asan_whole_arm_binding_of_owned_generic_param_no_double_free`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) carries all three element types so a future
narrowing cannot pass by covering the easy two, and keeps `echo` as the control
that must stay single-free. RED-verified against pristine `src`: 1 failed.

BOTH OF THE ROW'S REMAINING QUESTIONS ARE ANSWERED, and the second one widened
the fix.

A `String` bare-`T` param does NOT have the split -- measured clean above, one
buffer and the existing stand-down already covers it.

An `if let` return DOES behave like the `match` one, and so does `let ... else`:
three invalid frees each, identical to the `match` spelling, on a compiler that
already had the `match` fix. So the first version of this fix -- which wired
only the `match` arm the row happened to name -- would have shipped one
convention with two answers, which is the defect restated rather than repaired.
`propagate_owned_param_to_whole_arm_binding` is therefore called from all four
whole-value binding sites: the `match` arm, `compile_if_let`,
`compile_while_let` and `compile_let_else`.

NEARLY MISSED, and the near-miss is worth recording. The `if let` probe was
first run against a `target/debug/karac` that a RED-verification had just
rebuilt from STASHED (pristine) `src`, so it reported the pre-fix answer for
every shape -- including the `match` one the fix demonstrably repairs. The tell
was exactly that: a shape known to be fixed still showing three errors. Any
probe run right after a stash-based RED check is measuring the wrong compiler
unless the binary is rebuilt first.

FINAL MATRIX, all under valgrind, all `0 errors / 0 bytes in use at exit`:
`match`, `if let`, `let ... else`, a NESTED `match` rebind (which chains,
because the inner scrutinee is now itself an owned param), and the bare
`return b;` control.

Fixed in edaca15.

`discard_producer_runs_payload_walk` had an `ExprKind::Call` arm -- which is how
the tuple-variant constructor `Tv.A(r)` is spelled -- and NO `StructLiteral`
arm. An enum struct-variant construction is spelled as a struct literal, so the
predicate answered `false`, `inline_ctor` stayed false, the discard took the
own-`Drop`-enum branch (own body, no payload walk), and the payload's body never
ran.

TWO CONTROLS LOCALIZE IT, and the second sharpens the row past how it was filed.
The tuple-variant spelling was correct in every discard shape. And a
struct-variant whose ENUM declares no `Drop` of its own was ALSO correct --
`enum Nd { H { inner: R } }` with no `impl Drop` takes the
`run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` branch instead and always ran `dR`. So the
bug required BOTH an own-`Drop` enum AND a struct-shaped variant; the row's
title named only the second.

SAME BLIND SPOT AS B-2026-08-31-8, ONE PREDICATE OVER: that row's classifier
looked up `path.last()` for the same literal and got the VARIANT name. This
reuses that row's `qualified_struct_variant_enum_name` rather than re-deriving
the resolution, so the argument site and the discard site now answer the same
question about the same path.

THE ARM-LEVEL TEST DELIBERATELY ANSWERS DIFFERENTLY, and that asymmetry is
measured, not defensive. For a struct-variant literal the compiled backends run
the payload walk as a DIRECT producer, a BLOCK tail, and the single tail of a
no-`else` `if` -- but emit NO body at all, not even the enum's own, as an arm of
a TWO-TAIL `if` or a `match`. Since `discard_arm_yields_fresh_enum` delegates to
the producer test, a plain widening would have moved this backend from
disagreeing at one body to disagreeing at TWO on those shapes. It now excludes
the shape explicitly. That exclusion is load-bearing only while B-2026-09-01-34
(codegen's half) is open; when that closes, remove it and add the two shapes to
the twinned fixtures, which record the omission for this reason.

QUALIFIED only, as in B-2026-08-31-8: the unqualified `Hold { .. }` runs `dSv`
here and nothing at all on the compiled backends, so claiming it would deepen a
divergence rather than close one (B-2026-09-01-32).

Verified across `--interp` / JIT / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` on fifteen
probe shapes (five wrapper positions x struct/tuple variant, plus the
no-own-`Drop` enum and a heap-carrying payload). RED-verified: pre-fix the
fixture yields exactly `dSv\nd\n` against `dSv\ndR1\nd\n`. Gates: both clippy
legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `tests/interpreter.rs` 1899 passed
/ 0 failed and `tests/codegen.rs` green, in a per-target batched run (the
single-pass suite exhausts this container's disk allowance).
title: A DISCARDED enum STRUCT-VARIANT literal loses its PAYLOAD's `Drop` body under `--interp` -- `let _ = Sv.Hold { inner: R { .. } }` runs `dSv` against `dSv dR1` on all three compiled surfaces; the tuple-variant spelling of the identical program is correct everywhere
detail:
Measured on 95fbe26 (B-2026-08-31-8's fix), all four surfaces.

    struct R { id: i64 }         impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum Sv { Hold { inner: R }, Nil }
    impl Drop for Sv { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dSv") } }
    enum Tv { A(R), Nil }
    impl Drop for Tv { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dTv") } }

    fn a1() { let _ = Sv.Hold { inner: R { id: 1 } }; println("d") }
    fn a2() { let _ = Tv.A(R { id: 2 });              println("d") }

      a1   interp -> `dSv`        jit / build / np -> `dSv dR1`
      a2   interp -> `dTv dR2`    jit / build / np -> `dTv dR2`

Only the PAYLOAD's body is lost; the enum's OWN body fires. That is what
separates this from B-2026-08-31-8, whose classifier lost the type name
outright and so lost both -- here the discard walker plainly resolved the type,
since `dSv` runs, and it is the payload walk beneath it that does not.
`run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` handles `EnumData::Struct` correctly
(inspected), so the miss is upstream of it: the discard path does not reach that
walker for a struct-variant value.

THE TUPLE-VARIANT CONTROL IS THE WHOLE POINT, and it is a2 above: the same
discard of a tuple-variant literal runs both bodies on all four surfaces. So the
variable is the struct-variant spelling, not the discard.

NOT FIXED BY B-2026-08-31-8. That row's fix is in `fresh_temp_arg_type_name`,
the ARGUMENT classifier; a discard reaches a different site and was measured
still wrong after it landed.

Bodies only on the evidence to hand -- the payload owns no heap here, so a
heap-carrying one should be measured before assuming the memory side is
balanced.

SOURCE NOTE: found in B-2026-08-31-8's probe matrix while checking which other
sites lose an enum struct-variant's owner.

fix:
Fixed in d620c7d, both backends in one commit as the row required.

TWO HALVES, AND THE ROW WAS RIGHT THAT THEY HAD TO MOVE TOGETHER.

Interpreter: `fresh_temp_arg_type_name`'s struct-literal arm resolves a type
through `find_struct_def(path.last())` and then
`qualified_struct_variant_enum_name`, which wants at least two segments. Adds
`unqualified_struct_variant_enum_name`, the one-segment sibling, restricted to
STRUCT-shaped variants — a brace literal can only construct one, and answering
`Some` for a tuple or unit variant of the same name would hand callers an owner
for a value this spelling never builds.

Codegen: `enum_name_of_expr`'s struct-literal arm was guarded `path.len() >= 2`,
so it answered `None` for the one-segment spelling and every caller keying a
fresh owned temp's drop off it — the aggregate-argument tracker among them —
registered no owner at all.

THE CODEGEN HALF IS THE MORE INTERESTING FINDING, because the backend already
understood the spelling on the other side of itself: `compile_expr`'s
struct-literal arm routes `Hold { .. }` to `compile_enum_struct_variant_init`
on exactly the "not a struct, find the enum declaring the variant" condition,
mirroring the typechecker's `unqualified_enum_struct_variant`. So a correctly
typed `Sv` was being CONSTRUCTED and then DROPPED as if it were nothing. The
construction and ownership halves disagreed about what the expression is, which
is why the value existed, was passed, died, and left no trace.

The unqualified TUPLE twin `eat(A(r))` was correct on every surface throughout,
exactly as the row's control showed. The reason is now explicit rather than
incidental: it parses as an `ExprKind::Call` and already reached
`enum_name_for_variant_ctor`. The new brace arm calls that SAME helper, so the
two spellings answer through one lookup instead of two that happen to agree,
and it inherits the helper's user-enum-over-seeded-builtin preference for free.
That preference matters: a plain scan of `enum_layouts` picks an arbitrary
match on a name collision, since that map has no meaningful iteration order.

PRECEDENCE IS THE ONE WAY THIS FIX COULD HAVE BROKEN WORKING PROGRAMS, and it
is pinned. Both halves check for a real struct of the name BEFORE reading the
segment as a variant, mirroring what the two construction sites already do, so
an ordinary `R { .. }` literal keeps its own drop in a program that also
declares a variant called `R`. The fixture row `struct wins over a same-named
variant` exists for that alone — a fix that dropped the struct check would pass
every other row in the table.

VERIFICATION, and one correction to my own process worth recording.

Twinned output fixtures in `tests/interpreter.rs` and `tests/codegen.rs` (seven
rows: the unqualified literal, the qualified control, the unqualified tuple
control, a named local, the precedence row, a heap-carrying payload, and two
argument-order rows), plus an ASAN case in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`. Each
half was negative-controlled separately by reverting it alone; each fails only
its own backend, which is what says both were load-bearing rather than one
masking the other.

THE HEAP-CARRYING ROW EXISTS BECAUSE THE ROW'S REPRO COULD NOT HAVE FOUND THIS
CLASS. It was measured on a SCALAR payload, where the entire defect is a
missing line of output and the memory side says nothing at all — so a fix can
look complete against it while leaving a heap-carrying value unbalanced. A
`String` plus a 32-element `Vec` makes the frees observable: measured clean
under valgrind (0 errors, nothing lost) and under ASAN.

PROCESS NOTE. While adding that heap row I measured the unqualified spelling
still losing both bodies and concluded the codegen fix was incomplete — that it
had created the very run-vs-build divergence B-2026-08-31-8 avoided. That was
wrong, and the cause was mine: the measurement ran against the binary left over
from the NEGATIVE CONTROL, where the codegen arm had been removed. The source
was restored; the binary was not rebuilt before measuring. Rebuilding made the
same program correct on all four surfaces. This is the stale-artifact class
CLAUDE.md documents for the runtime archives, one level up and with the same
signature: nothing errors, the measurement is simply of a different compiler
than the one on disk. The rule that catches it is to rebuild after restoring a
control, not to reason about whether a restore "should" need one.

VERIFIED at d620c7d: all four surfaces byte-identical on every discriminator
(`run --interp`, `run`, `build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`); default suite 10257
passed / 0 failed; codegen 3547/0; memory_sanitizer 1367/0; par_codegen 276/0;
interpreter 1909/0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all
--all-targets -- -D warnings` clean on BOTH the default and `--features llvm`
legs.
title: The UNQUALIFIED enum struct-variant literal `Hold { .. }` loses BOTH `Drop` bodies on ALL FOUR surfaces, while the unqualified TUPLE-variant spelling `A(r)` is correct on all four
detail:
Measured on 95fbe26, all four surfaces. NOT a run-vs-build divergence -- every
backend agrees, and every backend is wrong, which is why no A/B parity gate can
see it.

    struct R { id: i64 }         impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum Sv { Hold { inner: R }, Nil }   impl Drop for Sv { println("dSv") }
    enum Tv { A(R), Nil }               impl Drop for Tv { println("dTv") }

    fn b1() { eatS(Hold { inner: R { id: 3 } }) }   // unqualified struct variant
    fn b2() { eatT(A(R { id: 4 })) }                // unqualified tuple variant

      b1   interp / jit / build / np -> `e`            (both bodies gone)
      b2   interp / jit / build / np -> `e dTv dR4`

The unqualified spelling is LEGAL and is a real construction, not a curiosity:
`interpreter.rs` builds a `Value::EnumVariant` for it at the
`path.len() == 1 && find_struct_def(name).is_none()` branch, mirroring the
typechecker's `unqualified_enum_struct_variant` routing (B-2026-06-13-12). So a
value is constructed, is used, dies -- and no `Drop` body runs for it anywhere.

THE TUPLE CONTROL LOCALIZES IT to the struct-variant half: b2 is the same
unqualified construction one spelling over and is correct on every surface.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-31-8. That row fixed the QUALIFIED spelling
(`Sv.Hold { .. }`) in the interpreter's argument classifier, and deliberately
stopped there: the unqualified spelling was wrong on BOTH backends, so claiming
it on the interpreter alone would have converted an agreed answer into a fresh
run-vs-build divergence -- the worse of the two, and the trade that row's fix
comment records. Closing this one therefore needs BOTH backends moved together,
which is why it is filed separately rather than folded in.

SOURCE NOTE: found in B-2026-08-31-8's probe matrix; it is the spelling that
row's fix declined to claim.

fix:
Fixed in a6e5b28.

`karac_drop_<E>` runs an enum's OWN body alone; the payload walk lives in the
separate `__karac_dropelems_enum_<E>`. A STRUCT differs -- its wrapper carries
the field bodies from inside -- and that asymmetry is what the fn-call producer
arm of `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst` got wrong: it registered the
`OwnWrapper` and the memory free and no walker, so the payload's body never ran.
The arm's own comment notes "an enum payload is a different walk" while
declining the struct-shaped MASK, but nothing then registered the unmasked
walker.

CONFIRMED BY INSTRUMENTING THE REGISTRATION POINT, which is also what caught a
wrong first patch. `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp` is a near-identical
chokepoint for the DISCARD position and is not on this path; patching it changed
nothing. A backtrace from `track_user_drop_var_with_fn` named the real arm in one
run:

    producer arg (broken)  OwnWrapper        karac_drop_Sv
    inline ctor (correct)  ContainerElemBodies __karac_dropelems_enum_Sv
                           OwnWrapper        karac_drop_Sv

NOT STRUCT-VARIANT SPECIFIC, which corrects this row's own framing. It was filed
out of B-2026-08-31-8's matrix, where the struct-variant spelling was the
variable; here the TUPLE spelling `eatT(mkT(6))` loses the payload identically.
The axis is the producer-call-into-argument shape for any own-`Drop` enum.

THREE CONTROLS LOCALIZE IT, all already correct and all now fixture rows: a
NAMED LOCAL (`let x = mk(5); eat(x)`) is registered by the `let` path; an INLINE
CONSTRUCTOR argument (`eat(E.A(R { .. }))`) by the ctor arm; and an ASSOCIATED
producer (`Mk.s(10)`, a 2-segment `Path` callee) reaches this same arm and was
correct for the wrapper half. Only the temp returned FROM A CALL had half the
pair.

THE MEMORY FREE HAD TO MOVE AHEAD OF THE BODIES, and this is the part of the fix
that could have gone wrong. The arm pushed the free AFTER the wrapper, so the
frame drained the free FIRST -- harmless for as long as no walker existed to
read through it. Registering the walker without moving the free would have
turned a missing body into a USE-AFTER-FREE: the payload body reads a `String`
and a `Vec`. The ctor arm already orders memory-before-bodies for exactly this
reason (B-2026-08-01-2); this arm now matches it, and the new
`memory_sanitizer.rs` case pins that direction with a heap-carrying payload
(`dR5:pay:3` proves the body reads live memory).

ASAN WOULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT THE ORIGINAL DEFECT, and the RED run says so in its
own words: pre-fix the sanitizer case fails with "ASAN passed, but output
mismatched", left `["e", "dSv", "e", "dTv"]`. A missing body is invisible to
every sanitizer; only the transcript sees it.

Verified across `--interp` / JIT / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` on six
shapes plus a heap-carrying payload. RED-verified: pre-fix the codegen fixture
yields exactly `e dSv` against `e dSv dR5`. Re-verified after rebasing onto
224a8b3, which CLOSED B-2026-09-01-38 and landed design.md's partial-move
rejection -- a breaking rule that could have made these probes stop compiling.
It does not touch them: these shapes move a whole enum into a call, not a field
out of a `Drop` struct. Gates: both clippy legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
clean; `tests/codegen.rs` 3539 passed / 0 failed, `tests/interpreter.rs` 1903 /
0, `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` 1363 / 0 (LSan), `tests/par_codegen.rs` 275 / 0.
title: A PRODUCER-FN argument loses the enum payload's `Drop` body on BOTH compiled backends -- `eat(mk(5))` runs `dSv` against the interpreter's `dSv dR5`, for the tuple-variant spelling equally; routing the same value through a NAMED LOCAL is correct everywhere
detail:
Measured on 95fbe26, all four surfaces. The interpreter is the CORRECT side here
-- the opposite direction to B-2026-08-31-8, which is why the two must not be
conflated.

    fn mkS(i: i64) -> Sv { return Sv.Hold { inner: R { id: i } }; }
    fn mkT(i: i64) -> Tv { return Tv.A(R { id: i }); }

    fn c1() { eatS(mkS(5)) }                      fn c2() { eatT(mkT(6)) }
    fn c3() { let x = mkS(7); eatS(x) }           fn c4() { let y = mkT(8); eatT(y) }

      c1   interp -> `e dSv dR5`   jit / build / np -> `e dSv`
      c2   interp -> `e dTv dR6`   jit / build / np -> `e dTv`
      c3   interp -> `e dSv dR7`   jit / build / np -> `e dSv dR7`
      c4   interp -> `e dTv dR8`   jit / build / np -> `e dTv dR8`

NOT STRUCT-VARIANT SPECIFIC, and that is the correction worth recording: c2
shows the TUPLE-variant spelling loses the payload identically. An earlier draft
of this row asserted the struct-variant spelling was the variable, on the
strength of a single-spelling probe; adding the tuple control refuted it. The
axis is the PRODUCER-FN-into-argument shape, for any Drop-bearing enum payload.

THE NAMED-LOCAL CONTROL (c3 / c4) is what puts the axis there rather than on the
callee or on the enum: routing the identical value through a `let` first is
correct on every surface, both spellings. So the value and its `Drop` glue are
fine; it is the call-argument temporary produced by a function call that loses
the payload half of its walk. The enum's OWN body still runs, so the temp is not
unowned -- only its payload walk is missing.

MEMORY, NOT JUST ORDERING. A lost payload body on the COMPILED backends is the
direction that leaks: unlike the interpreter, whose `Value` drop releases the
memory regardless, codegen's payload walk is what frees it. A heap-carrying
payload should be measured under LSan (the Linux CI `memory-sanitizer` job)
before sizing this -- it may well be a leak row rather than a bodies-only one.

SOURCE NOTE: found in B-2026-08-31-8's probe matrix, as the row that forced the
`producer-fn` case OUT of that row's twinned fixtures -- pinning it there would
have asserted one side of this live disagreement.

fix:
Fixed in b0b3401.

TWO DECLINES AT ONCE, which is why the value had NO owner rather than a wrong
one:

  * `branch_arms_all_inline_enum_ctors` had no `StructLiteral` arm, so it
    answered `false` for any branch containing a struct-variant literal and the
    representative-tail redirect (`enum_probe`) never took the value;
  * the battery that would otherwise own it resolves its type through
    `discard_branch_tail_type_name`, whose `StructLiteral` arm answers
    `path.last()` -- the VARIANT name for this spelling, a type that does not
    exist.

Neither half claimed it, so nothing ran -- not even the enum's own body.

FIXING ONLY THE GUARD CHANGES NOTHING, and that was measured rather than
assumed: with the guard admitting the spelling, `enum_probe` hands back the
struct-variant literal and the gate immediately after admits only
`ExprKind::Call | ExprKind::Path`, so the probe was dropped before
`enum_name_of_expr` -- which already resolves the shape through its
`path[len - 2]` arm -- ever saw it. Both gates are required; each was run on its
own.

THE `path.last()` ASSUMPTION IS NOW THREE SITES DEEP. B-2026-08-31-8 hit it in
the interpreter's fresh-temp ARGUMENT classifier, B-2026-09-01-31 in its DISCARD
producer predicate, and this row in codegen's discarded-branch type resolver.
All three read a struct literal's last path segment as its type name, which is
right for `P { .. }` and names the VARIANT for `E.V { .. }`. Worth treating as a
known shape rather than three coincidences.

THE TUPLE TWIN LOCALIZES IT: `E.A(r)` is a `Call` through a `Path`, matches the
guard's existing arm, takes the redirect, and was correct in both the two-tail
`if` and the `match` spelling. The axis is the struct-variant literal, not the
branch.

CLOSES THE LOOP LEFT OPEN BY B-2026-09-01-31. That fix had
`discard_arm_yields_fresh_enum` decline this shape DELIBERATELY -- firing the
payload while codegen ran nothing would have moved the interpreter from
disagreeing at one body to disagreeing at two -- and recorded, in the code
comment and in both twinned fixtures, that the exclusion was load-bearing only
while this row stayed open. Codegen now owns the value, so the exclusion is
removed and the fixtures gained the `two-tail-if` and `match` rows they said to
add, plus a tuple-variant control.

THIS ROW'S `leak` CLASS IS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT, and the row flagged the risk
itself. It was filed `leak` on STRUCTURAL grounds -- an aggregate that reaches
its death with no owner is how heap goes unreclaimed -- while stating plainly
that the heap half had not been measured and that the class rested on inference.
It has now been measured: pre-fix the new `memory_sanitizer.rs` case reports
"ASAN passed, but output mismatched" over a `String` + `Vec` payload, so the
memory WAS reclaimed and only the bodies were missing. Reclassed `run-vs-build`.
The lesson is narrow and worth keeping: "no owner registered" does not imply
"leaks" -- the memory-only registrations are a separate channel from the body
walk, and only one of them was absent here.

Verified across `--interp` / JIT / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` on five
shapes plus a heap-carrying payload. RED-verified: pre-fix the codegen fixture
yields exactly `d` -- no bodies at all -- against `dSv dR7 d`. Gates: both
clippy legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
title: A DISCARDED enum STRUCT-VARIANT literal in a TWO-TAIL `if` or a `match` arm emits NO `Drop` body at all on the compiled backends -- not even the enum's OWN -- while the same literal as a direct producer, a block tail, or a no-`else` `if` tail runs both; the tuple-variant spelling is uniform across all five
detail:
Measured on edaca15 (B-2026-09-01-31's fix), all four surfaces. Re-measured
after ee15b92 ("name a discarded branch's enum when its FIRST arm constructs
it"), which is adjacent but does NOT reach this spelling -- the numbers below
are post-ee15b92.

    struct R { id: i64 }         impl Drop for R { println(f"dR{self.id}") }
    enum Sv { Hold { inner: R }, Nil }
    impl Drop for Sv { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dSv") } }

    fn q3(c: bool) { let _ = if c { Sv.Hold { inner: R { id: 3 } } } else { Sv.Nil }; }
    fn q5(n: i64)  { let _ = match n { 1 => { Sv.Hold { inner: R { id: 5 } } } _ => { Sv.Nil } }; }

      q3   interp -> `dSv`   jit / build / np -> (NOTHING)
      q5   interp -> `dSv`   jit / build / np -> (NOTHING)

THE ENUM'S OWN BODY VANISHING IS THE SHARPER HALF. A missing payload walk is a
gap in one walker; a missing OWN body means the value reached its death with no
owner registered at all, which is why this is filed as a leak rather than a
bodies-only divergence.

THE SAME LITERAL IS CORRECT IN THREE NEIGHBOURING POSITIONS on these same
backends, which is what makes this an inconsistency rather than a blanket gap:

      direct    `let _ = Sv.Hold { .. }`        -> `dSv dR1`
      block     `let _ = { Sv.Hold { .. } }`    -> `dSv dR4`
      no-else   `let _ = if c { Sv.Hold { .. } }` -> `dSv dR5`

THE TUPLE-VARIANT TWIN IS UNIFORM ACROSS ALL FIVE (`dTv dRn` everywhere, both
backends), so the axis is the struct-variant literal, not the wrapper.

WHY B-2026-09-01-31 DID NOT CLOSE THIS. That row fixed the INTERPRETER's
discard payload walk for this literal, and deliberately excluded the two-tail
