title: A FRESH-TEMP `Option`/`Result` ARGUMENT IS DOUBLE-FREED when the callee pushes it into a LOCAL it then RETURNS INSIDE AN AGGREGATE -- neither escape guard sees that route, and it blocks B-2026-09-01-29's leak fix
detail:
A FRESH-TEMP `Option`/`Result` ARGUMENT IS DOUBLE-FREED when the callee pushes it
into a LOCAL that it then RETURNS INSIDE AN AGGREGATE. Live memory-unsafety on
`main`; no generics, no `Drop` impl, no unsafe.

    struct Bag { xs: Vec[Option[String]] }
    impl Bag {
        fn wrap(x: Option[String]) -> Bag {
            let mut v: Vec[Option[String]] = Vec.new();
            v.push(x);
            return Bag { xs: v };
        }
    }
    fn mks(n: i64) -> String { return f"payloadpayload{n}"; }

    fn main() {
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < 3 { let b = Bag.wrap(Some(mks(i))); println(f"{b.xs.len()}"); i = i + 1; }
    }

    karac build, -fsanitize=address:
        ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free ... ABORTING
    --interp: correct

Found while fixing B-2026-09-01-29; INDEPENDENT of it -- reproduced on an
unmodified tree with none of that row's changes applied.

CAUSE, same asymmetry as -29's and the third of its three escape routes.
`track_optres_arg_temp` (B-2026-08-12-1) gives the CALLER ownership of a fresh
`Option`/`Result` temp, on the reasoning that the callee entry-copies the param
and frees only its own copy. Two guards stand that ownership down when some
other frame takes the value over: `call_arg_flows_into_return` (the callee hands
it back) and `call_arg_moves_into_outliving_place` (the callee stores it through
a `mut ref` param, closed for all three call sites by -29's fix). Neither sees
a param pushed into a LOCAL that is returned inside an aggregate: the value
escapes through the return, but not as the return, and not through any
parameter.

So the caller frees the temp and the returned `Bag`'s element drop frees it
again.

REACH, measured. The ASSOC spelling above is the one reachable today, because
that is the site whose ownership registration has no
`call_arg_flows_into_return` guard at all (`assoc_call.rs`). The free-function
and METHOD spellings of the same program are clean today ONLY because the
payload spelling that reaches the ownership is narrow -- `Some(mks(i))`
manufactures its payload, while `Some(s)` for a named `s` is (wrongly) treated as
owned elsewhere. Widening that predicate, which is what -29's leak half needs,
makes all three spellings double-free, which is why that widening cannot land
until this row does.

WHAT A FIX NEEDS, and why it is not a one-line gate. The question is "does the
callee let this argument escape its frame", and the two existing predicates
answer only the two syntactic routes they were each written for.
`crate::result_escape` has the shape of the right analysis but the wrong
resolution: `nonescaping_param_names` counts a non-scrutinee USE as an escape,
so a callee that merely prints its param is already excluded, and
`unused_param_names` is stricter still. What is missing is a use-classifying walk
-- read positions (an f-string hole, a field read, a `ref` argument) do not
escape; a store into any place, and any path to a `return`, do.

NOT MEASURED: whether the same route double-frees a bare `Vec`/`String`
argument rather than an `Option`/`Result` one (the ownership site is
Option/Result-specific, so probably not, but the aggregate-return escape route
is not); and whether a closure capturing the param behaves like the store route
or like the return route.
fix:
FIXED by b3dbcee, and the fix is the analysis this row said was missing rather
than a third syntactic gate.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND ITS PRESCRIPTION WAS TOO BIG. It called for "a
use-classifying walk -- read positions do not escape; a store into any place,
and any path to a `return`, do". Only the READ half had to be written. The
escape side already existed: `crate::result_escape` classifies every
non-scrutinee use as an escape, which is conservative in the safe direction and
already covers all three routes -- returned bare, stored through a `mut ref`
param, and returned inside an aggregate -- because each of them is a use that is
not a `match` scrutinee. Nothing had to learn about aggregates or about `push`.

What was missing is that the two SIDES of the copy asked different questions.
`compile_function` emits the by-value `Option`/`Result` entry copy only for a
param the escape analysis clears; the caller's
`callee_optres_param_entry_copied` answered from the param's TYPE alone. So the
caller took ownership of a temp for callees that never copied it, and the
container or the returned aggregate owned it too.

THE FIX, in three parts:

  * `by_value_nonescaping_param_names` (src/result_escape.rs), the looser
    sibling of `nonescaping_param_names`, differing in one position: a
    bare-identifier interpolation hole (`f"{x}"`) is a READ, not an escape. It
    is intercepted exactly as the `Match` arm intercepts its scrutinee, and
    suppressed inside a closure for the same capture reason. The strict sibling
    is untouched, because its `Result[shared]` RC consumer needs the stricter
    rule -- see its doc for the `takeout` shape that fools anything looser.

  * `compile_function`'s entry-copy gate now reads that set.

  * `callee_optres_param_entry_copied_and_owned` reads the SAME set off the
    callee's AST, and only the caller's temp-ownership site uses it.

THE SPLIT IN THAT LAST POINT IS THE CORRECTION WORTH RECORDING. The obvious
move -- fold the escape check into the existing predicate -- is wrong, and
measured wrong: that predicate has a SECOND consumer,
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move`, which asks whether the caller's
BINDING should hand its buffer over. Narrowing the shared predicate fired that
suppressor on every PASSTHROUGH callee, so the caller's named binding lost its
cleanup while the callee still moved the buffer through, and two passthrough
fixtures went from clean to a 10 B leak. Two questions, two predicates.

B-2026-09-01-29's LEAK HALF LANDS WITH THIS, and neither is correct alone.
`optres_arg_is_unowned_temp`'s enum-constructor arm now answers `true` for any
constructor at an argument position instead of recursing into the payload: the
constructor MOVES its payload in, so a named binding's cleanup is disarmed and
the envelope is the only owner left. That widening ALONE turns the three escape
routes into double frees; this row's gate ALONE leaves the leak. Together they
are the single rule "the caller owns a fresh temp exactly when the callee
provably does not let it escape".

MEASURED, `-fsanitize=address` + LeakSanitizer, 3-iteration loops:

    Bag.wrap(Some(mks(i)))         assoc, returns it in an aggregate
    m.wrap(Some(mks(i)))           method, same
    wrapf(Some(mks(i)))            free fn, same
    pass(Some(vs))                 returned bare
        all four: DOUBLE-FREE ABORT before (assoc reachable on an unmodified
        tree; the other three once the leak-half widening is applied) -> clean

    show(Some(vs))                 333 B / 6 -> clean
    show(Some(vs.clone()))         336 B / 6 -> clean
    show(Some(mkv(i)))             clean -> clean       (control)
    show(Some(w.f))                leaked -> clean
    showr(Err(vs))                 leaked -> clean
    h.show(Some(s))                leaked -> clean
    let named = Some(e); show(named)   clean -> clean    (control)

Fixtures: `asan_optres_temp_arg_ownership_follows_callee_escape` (all three
escape routes plus the six leak shapes and both controls), RED pre-fix with the
double-free abort. `asan_stored_optres_temp_arg_has_one_owner` is UPGRADED from
its `detect_leaks=0` form to a full `assert_clean_asan_run`, which is exactly

ONE FIXTURE CASE WAS RETARGETED, and the reason is a separate defect: the

title: A REPL CELL BINDING WHOSE OWN TYPE IS `shared` CANNOT JOIN THE JIT SNAPSHOT TIER: admitted, `s.n` reads the POINTER'S OWN BITS instead of the field (two different garbage values from the same expression where `--interp` prints `3`), because `register_var_from_type_expr` -- the registrar the snapshot replay path defers to -- re-registers a shared name as an INLINE struct; the OWNERSHIP half is fine (retracting the queued `RcDec` HOLDS the reference), and `shared` as a COMPONENT (`struct W { s: S }`, `Vec[S]`) round-trips correctly
detail:
A REPL cell BINDING whose own type is `shared` cannot join the JIT snapshot
tier: admitted, it reads a POINTER'S OWN BITS instead of the field.

Split out of B-2026-08-30-7 (closed) rather than left in it, because the cause
is not the one that row's remaining-work list assumed. That list expected
`shared` to be hard for an OWNERSHIP reason -- "the one remaining case where a
shallow transfer is not merely a leak but a potential dangle, since a second
owner elsewhere in the session could drop the last reference while the global
still points at the object". That fear inverts the mechanism: capture RETRACTS
the queued `RcDec`, which HOLDS the reference rather than dropping it, so the
global owns one and nothing can free the object under it. The dangle would come
from copying the pointer WITHOUT retracting -- the opposite move. Ownership is
fine.

What is not fine is REPLAY. A direct `shared` binding's slot holds a pointer to
the RC object and its field reads go through the shared dispatch channel;
`register_var_from_type_expr` -- the registrar the snapshot replay path defers
to, precisely so a replayed binding is indistinguishable from a fresh one --
re-registers the name as an INLINE struct. `s.n` then GEPs the slot itself and
loads the pointer's own bits.

MEASURED (on a tree with `Type::Shared` admitted to `SlotTransfer`):

    shared struct S { n: i64 }
    let s: S = S { n: 3 };
    println(f"{s.n}");     JIT: 43825771313        --interp: 3
    println(f"{s.n}");     JIT: 94568180881400     --interp: 3

Two different garbage values from the same expression, which is the tell that
the read is of a live pointer rather than of a stale copy. With the mutating
spelling (`shared struct S { mut n: i64 }`, `s.n = 7`) the admitted version
printed `1` -- the initializer -- so the shape's failure mode varies.

WHY IT IS A ROW RATHER THAN A KNOWN LIMITATION: the shape is DECLINED today, so
the user-visible behaviour is the ordinary pass-through divergence (reads back
the initializer, wrong but plausible, and warned about where the note's
conditions apply). The row exists because admitting it is a one-line change to
`snapshot_kind_for_type` that looks obviously right and is not -- and because
the registration gap it exposes may not be snapshot-specific. NOT MEASURED,
stated rather than implied: whether any OTHER consumer of
`register_var_from_type_expr` mis-registers a `shared` type the same way; the
registrar is used by the ordinary `let` arm too, and if that arm reaches it for
a shared binding on some path, the same garbage read would be reachable outside
the REPL entirely.

NARROW: a `shared` type as a COMPONENT is fine and is measured so -- `struct W
{ s: S }` and `Vec[S]` both round-trip correctly through the tier
(`repl_jit_slot_transfer_admits_shared_as_a_component_not_as_a_binding` pins
both halves). Only a binding whose own type is `shared` is affected. `Rc[T]` /
`Arc[T]` are declined alongside it, but that is untested rather than known-bad:
neither is reachable as a REPL surface type today (`Rc.new(...)` resolves as an
undefined name).

WHAT THE FIX WOULD BE, so the next session does not re-derive it: give the
replay path the shared-binding registration a fresh `shared` let performs
(whatever `s.n` dispatches through -- `var_type_names` plus the shared-ness the
field-read site consults), the way B-2026-08-30-7's inline-envelope half had to
add `register_replayed_inline_envelope_payload` for the payload-var sets. Then
re-admit `Type::Shared` at the top of `snapshot_kind_for_type` and re-run the
measurement above.

REPRODUCTION: remove the `Type::Shared(_) | Type::Rc(_) | Type::Arc(_)` decline
in `snapshot_kind_for_type` (src/repl/util.rs), rebuild BOTH `karac` and
`karac_jit_runner`, and run the three cells above.

title: A STRUCT LITERAL USED AS A CALL ARGUMENT, ALONE IN A REPL CELL, SILENTLY PRODUCES NO OUTPUT on BOTH backends -- `println(f"{take(H { n: 1 })}")` prints nothing with no diagnostic, and the `v.push(H { .. });` spelling additionally poisons the session so the next cell reports `undefined name 'v'` for a binding accepted two cells earlier; the same code in a `.kara` file works on both backends, and the same statements in ONE cell work
detail:
A STRUCT LITERAL USED AS A CALL ARGUMENT, alone in a REPL cell, SILENTLY
PRODUCES NO OUTPUT on both backends -- and in the `v.push(H { .. });` spelling
it also poisons the session, so the next cell reports `undefined name 'v'` for a
binding that was declared and accepted two cells earlier.

Not a snapshot bug and not backend-specific: `karac repl` and `karac repl
--interp` behave identically, and the same code in a `.kara` file works on both.
Found while writing fixtures for B-2026-08-30-7, whose tests now route around it
through a helper function.

MEASURED, one statement per cell:

    cells                                              JIT     --interp   .kara file
    struct H { n: i64 } / println(f"{H { n: 1 }.n}")    (none)  (none)     1
    struct H { n: i64 } / fn take(h: H) -> i64 {...}
      / println(f"{take(H { n: 1 })}")                  (none)  (none)     1

    struct H { n: i64 }
    let mut v: Vec[H] = Vec.new();
    v.push(H { n: 1 });        -> resolve error: undefined name 'v'
    println(f"{v.len()}");     -> parse error: file contains both top-level
                                  statements and an explicit `fn main()`
                                  (defined at line 3) ...

"(none)" means the cell completes with NO output and NO diagnostic -- the
`println` simply does not happen. That is the worst shape of this failure: a
silent no-op is indistinguishable from a program that legitimately printed
nothing.

CONTROLS, which localize it to the cell boundary rather than to struct literals
or to calls:
  - the SAME statements in one cell work (`let mut v: Vec[H] = Vec.new();
    v.push(H { n: 1 }); println(f"{v.len()}");` prints `1`).
  - a struct literal bound by a `let`, alone in a cell, works
    (`let h: H = H { n: 1 };` then `println(f"{h.n}")` prints `1`).
  - the same program as a `.kara` file with an explicit `fn main()` prints
    correctly on both backends.

So the trigger is a struct literal appearing INSIDE A CALL ARGUMENT in a cell
whose whole content is that statement. The cascading `fn main()` parse error in
the third case points at the REPL's cell classifier / source-replay path
(`strip_main` and the statements-vs-items split) mis-reading the literal's
braces as a block or an item body, which would also explain the silent no-op:
the statement is classified as something the cell does not execute.

ALSO MEASURED, same silent no-op on both lanes, so the trigger is the literal's
braces rather than anything about structs or about arity:
  - an ENUM STRUCT-VARIANT literal as a call argument --
    `enum E { V { x: i64 } }` / `println(f"{take(E.V { x: 1 })}")` prints
    nothing.
  - a NESTED call around one -- `println(f"{take(id(H { n: 1 }))}")` prints
    nothing.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: whether the notebook and
browser-playground front ends, which share the cell classifier, show it too; and
whether the poisoning in the `v.push(...)` case is recoverable within the session
or persists past `:reset`.

title: design.md's "partial moves out of a struct field are rejected if the struct has a `Drop` impl" is UNIMPLEMENTED, and the consequence is that a user's `drop` body RUNS ON THE ZEROED FIELD -- `match h { H { r, .. } }` prints `dR[d:3] dH dR[:0]` on both compiled backends
detail:
Measured on ce7f602, all four surfaces.

design.md line 9240 (Part 8: `Drop`, "Interaction with move semantics") states
the rule outright:

    Partial moves out of a struct field are rejected if the struct has a `Drop`
    impl: the drop body assumes all fields are present, so the compiler cannot
    permit a half-moved struct to reach the destructor. A struct without a
    `Drop` impl may have individual fields moved out, because the compiler can
    track which fields remain and drop only those.

NOTHING ENFORCES THIS. There is no such check in `ownership.rs` and no
diagnostic anywhere in `src/` that mentions it (grepped). So the shape the rule
exists to forbid compiles, and reaches the destructor exactly as the rule
predicts it must not:

    struct R { s: String, xs: Vec[i64] }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR[{self.s}:{self.xs.len()}]") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }
    impl Drop for H { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dH") } }

    fn main() {
        let h = H { r: R { s: "d", xs: [1, 2, 3] }, n: 4 };
        match h { H { r, .. } => { println(r.s) } }
        println("end")
    }

      --interp                  ->  d  dH  dR[d:3]  end
      jit / build / build np    ->  d  dR[d:3]  dH  dR[:0]  end

THE SECOND `dR[:0]` IS THE FINDING. `R`'s `drop` body runs TWICE on the compiled
backends: once for the moved-out binding `r`, and again for the moved-FROM field
slot, which by then is zeroed -- an empty `String` and a zero-length `Vec`. That
is the drop body observing a cleared field, which is precisely the hazard the
design.md sentence gives as its rationale.

MEMORY-SAFE AS MEASURED, SEMANTICALLY NOT. The zeroed `Vec` frees nothing, so
this is not a double free; `xs.len()` printing 0 is the evidence the slot was
cleared rather than left dangling. But for the resource type the `Drop` trait
exists for it is a live hazard rather than a cosmetic one: `struct F { fd: i32 }`
with `host.close(self.fd)` runs `close(0)` on the residue, closing STDIN. A body
that decrements a refcount runs twice. Neither is caught by ASAN, which is why
the `memory-sanitizer` job is green on this.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-31-33. That row reports the `Option`-wrapped spelling
(`Some(H { r, .. })`), where the interpreter runs `dR[a]` alone against
compiled's `dH dR[a]`, and asks which backend is right -- noting the question
"design.md does not currently answer". IT DOES ANSWER, at the line quoted
above: neither, because the program should not compile. That row's resolution
therefore depends on this one, and the two should be settled together.

THREE SPELLINGS, ONE MISSING RULE. All three move a field out of a `Drop`-
implementing struct and all three should be rejected under the quoted rule:

      match h { H { r, .. } => .. }             -> compiled runs the body twice
      let m = h.r                               -> `dH c dR[c]`, all backends agree
      match o { Some(H { r, .. }) => .. }        -> B-2026-08-31-33's divergence

The middle one AGREES on every backend today, which is why it has never been
filed as a bug -- agreement is not correctness when the program is one the spec
forbids.

SCOPE NOTE FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS. Implementing the rule is a BREAKING change:
it turns currently-compiling programs into errors. A rough count of the test
corpus (`, .. }` in files that also contain `impl Drop`) is ~77 occurrences
across 7 test files, not all of which are this shape -- so the real fixture cost
needs measuring, not guessing. Whether the rule extends to ENUM struct-variant
payloads (`Sv.Hold { inner }` where `Sv` has its own `Drop`) is not stated by
design.md and is the first thing to settle, since a large part of the
drop-machinery corpus is written that way.

SOURCE NOTE: found while working B-2026-08-31-33, checking that row's claim that
design.md leaves the question open.

NEW MEASUREMENTS (2026-09-01, from B-2026-08-31-31's probe matrix). Two, and
both widen this row.

(A) THE COMPILED `Drop` BODY OBSERVABLY READS A CLEARED FIELD. Earlier rows in
this family compared body COUNTS. Making the wrapper's body print what it sees
shows the hazard directly:

    impl Drop for H { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dH[sees r.s={self.r.s} n={self.n}]") } }

      match h { H { r, .. } => .. }   interp -> dH[sees r.s=a n=4]   compiled -> dH[sees r.s= n=4]
      let m = h.r                      interp -> dH[sees r.s=b n=4]   compiled -> dH[sees r.s= n=4]

So on the compiled backends `H::drop` runs against a half-cleared `self` in BOTH
spellings -- exactly what design.md's rationale ("the drop body assumes all
fields are present") exists to prevent, now demonstrated as observable by user
code rather than argued from the spec. Note the SECOND line: B-2026-08-31-31
records `let m = h.r` as "CORRECT on both backends", and by body count it is;
its drop body simply never read the moved field. A resource type reading
`self.fd` there gets a cleared handle.

(B) A FULL DESTRUCTURE SHOWS THE SAME DEFECT, which bears on this rule's SCOPE.
`match h { H { r, n } => .. }` binds every field and so is not a "partial" move
by the letter of line 9240, yet it leaves the wrapper reading a husk and runs
each field's body a second time on cleared slots (two Drop-bearing fields ->
`dR[e] dR[d] dH2 dR[] dR[]`). The RATIONALE covers it -- after a full
destructure no field is present at all -- but the wording does not. So the rule
as drafted needs to say whether it reaches a full destructure, alongside the
enum-struct-variant question already noted above; if it does not, this defect
survives the rule and needs its own fix.

title: A LIVE LOCAL HANDED OUT OF A DISCARDED BRANCH LOSES ITS PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY, and the `if` and `match` spellings disagree in OPPOSITE directions on the two backends -- `let _ = if c { E.A(mk(8)) } else { e };` with the `e` arm taken is interp `dE` / compiled `dE dR5`, while the `match` spelling of the same thing is interp `dE dR5` / compiled `dE`

A `let`-BOUND SCALAR FIELD READ OFF A STRUCT WITH ITS OWN `impl Drop` RUNS A DROP-BEARING SIBLING FIELD'S BODY AN EXTRA TIME ON EVERY COMPILED SURFACE -- `let h = H { r: R { .. }, n: 4 }; let q = h.n;` is `dH dR3` under `--interp` and `dR3 dH dR3` on jit/build/no-auto-par, with the field fully LIVE in both bodies; the same read spelled INLINE (`println(f"{h.n}")`) agrees
detail:
A `let`-BOUND SCALAR FIELD READ OFF A STRUCT THAT HAS ITS OWN `impl Drop` RUNS A
DROP-BEARING SIBLING FIELD'S BODY AN EXTRA TIME ON EVERY COMPILED SURFACE.

Nothing is moved. The read is of a scalar (`i64`), the struct stays whole, and
the sibling field is never named -- yet its `Drop` body runs twice.

    struct R { s: String, xs: Vec[i64] }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.xs.len()}") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }
    impl Drop for H { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dH") } }

    fn main() {
        let h = H { r: R { s: "d", xs: [1, 2, 3] }, n: 4 };
        let q = h.n;
        println(f"{q}");
        println("end");
    }

      --interp                       ->        dH  dR3  4  end
      jit / build / build no-auto-par ->  dR3  dH  dR3  4  end

The LEADING `dR3` is the defect: it fires at the `let`, before `h` has died,
and `xs.len()` reads 3 in BOTH bodies -- so unlike B-2026-09-01-38's residue
case the field is fully LIVE each time, and a body that releases a resource
releases it twice over a live object.

ASAN IS GREEN ON IT (measured, `assert_clean_asan_run` with a heap `String`
payload: "ASAN passed, but output mismatched"). The heap is freed once; it is
the user body that runs twice. So this is a `Drop`-semantics defect, not a
double free, and no sanitizer job will ever catch it -- the same blind spot
B-2026-09-01-38 records for its own family.

FOUR DISCRIMINATORS, ALL MEASURED, WHICH TOGETHER NAME THE SHAPE:

  * `let h = H { .. }; println("mid");`     -- no field read at all -> AGREE
  * `println(f"{h.n}");`                    -- the SAME read, INLINE -> AGREE
  * `let q = h.n; let w = h.n;`             -- two reads -> still exactly ONE
                                               extra body, so it is keyed on
                                               the binding, not on the read
  * the identical program with `struct P` (no `impl Drop` on the WRAPPER)
                                            -> AGREE

So all three conditions are required: the read must be bound by a `let`, the
wrapper must declare its own `Drop`, and the sibling field's type must declare
one (with the `impl Drop for R` line removed the transcripts match).

NOT B-2026-08-28-21, which is fixed and whose shape is an ESCAPING field --
`fn take(w: W) -> R { let W { r, n } = w; r }`, a destructure that hands the
field out of a call. Here nothing escapes and nothing is destructured.

NOT B-2026-09-01-38 either, though it was found while reproducing it. That row
is about a PARTIAL MOVE out of a `Drop` struct, which design.md says should be
rejected outright; this program performs no move, so the spec rule that would
delete -38's shape leaves this one compiling and still wrong. If -38's rejection
lands first, this row stays live and its repro is unaffected.

SOURCE NOTE: found as the intended NEGATIVE CONTROL for B-2026-09-01-38 -- the
"same shape but only a scalar field is touched" cell, written to check that the
partial-move hazard needed an actual move. It did not agree.
fix:
Fixed in cf75c62.

`disarm_struct_field_bodies_at` REPLACES a per-binding `__karac_dropbodies_*`
walker after a field move-out: it retracts the existing registration through
`suppress_struct_field_bodies_for_var` and registers a masked one. That is right
for a struct with no `Drop` of its own.

A struct that HAS one has no per-binding walker at all -- it runs its field
bodies from inside `karac_drop_<T>`, the type-level wrapper, registered as a
separate `OwnWrapper` action. So the retraction found nothing and the
registration ADDED a second walk on top of the wrapper's, and every surviving
field's body ran twice.

LOCATED BY INSTRUMENTING THE REGISTRATION POINT rather than by reading, after
two wrong hypotheses. `disarm_user_drop_fields_for_moved_field` already gates on
`type_runs_user_drop(field_type)` and so returns early for a scalar field, and
the heap move-out suppressors are all gated on a tracked destination -- neither
is reachable here. A print in `track_user_drop_var_with_fn` settled it in one
run:

    broken   OwnWrapper        karac_drop_Hd
             StructFieldBodies __karac_dropbodies_Hd$keep0$s1   <- the extra
    control  OwnWrapper        karac_drop_Hd

THE FIX takes the whole-wrapper mask (`disarm_user_drop_field_bodies_masked`)
when the struct owns a body, which is the surgery that fits the shape and is
already what the param-view caller in `runtime.rs` selects for an own-`Drop`
struct before it ever reaches this helper. The invariant was stated in that
caller's comment ("no per-binding walker to mask -- only the whole-wrapper
swap") and enforced only there; it is now enforced in the helper, so a third
caller cannot forget it.

ALL FIVE OF THE ROW'S DISCRIMINATORS were already correct and stay so, and each
is a fixture row: no field read, the same read INLINE, a wrapper without its own
`Drop`, two reads producing exactly one set of bodies, and reading the
DROP-BEARING field -- that last one takes the whole-wrapper swap at the
`let`-path caller, which is why it never doubled.

A SIXTH DISCRIMINATOR found while probing, and it is the one that localizes the
branch: `let q = h.n + 1` AGREES. The RHS must be a BARE `FieldAccess` for
`disarm_struct_field_move_bodies` to match at all, so the same read inside any
larger expression never enters this path. Two further probes place the extra
fire precisely: with `h` still live after the `let` it lands at `h`'s death, not
at the `let`, so it is an extra ACTION IN THE FRAME rather than an NLL
placement; and a struct with TWO Drop-bearing fields doubles BOTH, in walk
order, which is what identified the extra as a whole field battery.

ASAN AND THE DIRECTION IT PINS. The row's measurement that ASAN was green
pre-fix is confirmed and is the point: the extra walk ran bodies and freed
nothing, so no sanitizer would ever have caught it. The new
`memory_sanitizer.rs` case therefore pins the OPPOSITE direction, which is this
fix's own risk -- removing a registration is how bodies and memory go missing --
and asserts the transcript alongside, so a "fix" that silenced the double by
losing the surviving field's body fails on output rather than passing quietly.
On Linux that case runs LeakSanitizer; the full suite is green there.

Verified across `--interp` / JIT / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build` on nine
shapes, scalar and heap-carrying, and re-verified after rebasing onto 71e534f.
RED-verified: pre-fix the codegen fixture yields exactly `dR3 dH dR3 4` against
`dH dR3 4`. Gates: both clippy legs and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean;
`tests/codegen.rs` 3537 passed / 0 failed, `tests/interpreter.rs` 1901 / 0,
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` 1362 / 0 (LSan), `tests/par_codegen.rs` 275 / 0.

NOTE ON ONE FIXTURE EXPECTATION: the "reading the Drop-bearing field" row was
first written as `z dR5 dH` and is `dR5 dH z` -- both drops precede the trailing
`println`, because NLL places them at the last use, not at scope end. The fix
was never in question; the expectation was written from intuition when the
measurement was already to hand.

title: A STRUCT'S `Vec` FIELD IS NEVER FREED when the struct is declared OUTSIDE a loop, the field is pushed to INSIDE it, and the loop body also makes a heap TEMPORARY -- all three needed, the element type is irrelevant, and the whole Vec leaks
detail:
A `Vec[Option[String]]` STRUCT FIELD never frees its elements, while the
identical `Vec` held as a LOCAL is clean. No generics, no `Drop` impl.

    struct Bag { xs: Vec[Option[String]] }
    impl Bag {
        fn sink(mut ref self, x: Option[String]) { self.xs.push(x); }
        fn size(ref self) -> i64 { return self.xs.len(); }
    }
    fn mks(n: i64) -> String { return f"payloadpayload{n}"; }

    fn main() {
        let mut b = Bag { xs: Vec.new() };
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < 3 { b.sink(Some(mks(i))); println(f"{b.size()}"); i = i + 1; }
    }

    karac build, -fsanitize=address + LeakSanitizer:
        SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 173 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocations

THE CONTRAST IS THE WHOLE FINDING, and it is what rules out the argument path.
The same program with the accumulator as a LOCAL passed by `mut ref` --

    fn sink(acc: mut ref Vec[Option[String]], x: Option[String]) { acc.push(x); }
    let mut acc: Vec[Option[String]] = Vec.new(); sink(mut acc, Some(mks(i)));

-- is CLEAN, in both the free-function and the method spelling. Same element
type, same pushes, same values; the only difference is where the `Vec` lives. So
the elements' `Option` payloads are reachable and freeable, and the struct's own
drop is not walking them.

Found while fixing B-2026-09-01-35, whose fixture wanted the struct-field
spelling. INDEPENDENT of it: measured IDENTICALLY (173 B / 4) on an unmodified
tree and with that fix applied, which is why the fixture was retargeted at the
local spelling and this filed instead.

NOT MEASURED, and each of these splits the search: whether a plain
`Vec[String]` field leaks the same way (if it does, this is about Vec fields in
general rather than about the `Option` element); whether a `Vec[Option[i64]]`
field -- elements with no heap -- is clean, which it should be if the gap is the
element walk rather than the buffer; whether the field's drop frees the OUTER
buffer and only misses the elements, which the 4-allocation count hints at but
does not settle; and whether the interpreter agrees (it is refcounted and very
likely clean, so this is probably codegen-only, but LSan does not cover it).

PREMISE CORRECTED (2026-09-01), no fix yet. The row's title is WRONG in three
separate ways, and each one points at a different file than the real defect, so
the corrections matter more than the leak's size.

  * NOT the elements. `Vec[Option[i64]]` -- elements with no heap at all --
    leaks 128 B in ONE allocation, which is the buffer. The `Option` and the
    `String` are incidental; a plain `Vec[String]` field leaks too (141 B / 4).
  * NOT "field vs local". A LOCAL `Vec` grown in the same loop is clean, but so
    is the same STRUCT created INSIDE the loop (71 allocations, clean). The
    contrast the row drew was real and its explanation was not.
  * NOT the method. `b.xs.push(...)` written directly at the call site leaks
    identically to `b.sink(x)`.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS, a CONJUNCTION of three conditions. Remove any one and the
program is clean:

  1. a struct local declared OUTSIDE a loop,
  2. whose `Vec` FIELD is pushed to INSIDE that loop, and
  3. a heap TEMPORARY also produced in the loop body (a `println` f-string is
     enough).

    struct Bag { xs: Vec[Option[String]] }
    fn main() {
        let mut b = Bag { xs: Vec.new() };          // (1) outside the loop
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < 3 {
            b.xs.push(Some(f"payloadpayload{i}"));  // (2) field push inside
            println(f"{i}");                        // (3) an unrelated temp
            i = i + 1;
        }
    }

    LSan: 173 byte(s) leaked in 4 allocations -- the field's whole Vec, buffer
    and every element.

THE THIRD CONDITION IS THE SURPRISING ONE and is what makes this look like a
one-slot clobber rather than a missing drop. `println(f"{i}")` touches nothing
the struct owns. Dropping just that line makes the identical program clean at
every iteration count measured (2, 3, 4). And the leak SCALES with the element
count -- 158 B / 3, 173 B / 4, 188 B / 5 for two, three and four iterations,
i.e. a constant 128 B buffer plus exactly one 15-byte element per iteration --
so the field's cleanup is not firing at all rather than firing at a stale
length. Compare B-2026-09-01-23, "the branch arm-owner slot is one per construct
and reset each pass", which is the same shape one construct over.

CONTROLS, all measured clean, each isolating one condition:

    push OUTSIDE the loop, temp inside               clean   (kills 2)
    LOCAL Vec pushed inside, temp inside             clean   (kills 1)
    struct STRING field assigned inside, temp inside clean   (needs the Vec)
    struct created INSIDE the loop, temp inside      clean   (kills 1)
    push inside, NO temp in the body                 clean   (kills 3)
    three pushes UNROLLED outside any loop           clean
    one-iteration loop                               clean

NOT VACUOUS, checked rather than assumed. Every "clean" row above was re-run
under `KARAC_ASAN_ALLOC_AUDIT=1` and allocates 11-17 times against the ASAN
runtime's own floor of 3, so none of them is the `-O2`-deleted-the-allocation
trap that `asan_generic_owned_vec_param_temp_arg_no_leak`'s doc warns about.

INDEPENDENT of B-2026-09-01-35, whose fix was landing when this was found:
measured identically (173 B / 4) before and after it.

NOT MEASURED: whether the interpreter leaks (LSan does not cover it); whether a
`for` loop behaves like the `while` loop used throughout; whether a second
heap-carrying FIELD on the same struct leaks together with the first or instead
of it, which would say whether the clobbered slot is per-struct or per-field;
and whether a nested loop leaks once or once per level.

title: A `while let` LOOP-EXIT MISS RUNS NO `Drop` BODY for the scrutinee temporary that ended the loop, on all four surfaces, where the IDENTICAL miss through `if let` runs it -- two temporaries created and one `dE` printed; design.md's fourth "Scrutinee temporary scope" bullet says "After the loop terminates (the pattern stopped matching), the final iteration's scrutinee temporaries are already dropped", and the missing body is a LOST SIDE EFFECT rather than a leak of memory, so no valgrind/LSan gate fires and the backends agreeing hides it from the A/B rule too
detail:
A `while let` LOOP-EXIT MISS RUNS NO `Drop` BODY for the scrutinee temporary
that ended the loop, on all four surfaces, where the IDENTICAL miss through
`if let` runs it.

Found while fixing B-2026-08-30-17 (the `if let` miss ORDERING row) — `while
let` was probed as the adjacent construct, its ORDER turned out to be correct,
and the count turned out to be wrong. Different defect from that row: this is a
MISSING body, not a misplaced one, so it is filed rather than folded in.

MEASURED. Two scrutinee temporaries are created and only one body runs:

    struct R { id: i64 }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> E { if n < 1 { return E.A(R { id: n }) } return E.B }

      let mut i: i64 = 0;
      while let E.A(r) = mk(i) { println(f"v{r.id}"); i = i + 1; }
      println("after")

        interp / jit / build:   v0 dE after
        expected:               v0 dE dE after

`mk(0)` yields `E.A` (matches, body runs at the end of that iteration — correct
per design.md's fourth bullet) and `mk(1)` yields `E.B`, whose temporary ends
the loop and is never dropped.

THE `if let` CONTROL, which is what makes this a defect rather than a design
choice: the same non-matching temporary through `if let E.A(r) = mkB() { … }`
prints `dE`. Two spellings of "evaluate a fresh temp, fail to match, discard
it" disagree — the spelling-dependent split this family keeps having to close
(B-2026-08-28-67).

WHAT design.md SAYS. § `if let` and `let...else` > "Scrutinee temporary scope",
fourth bullet: "In **`while let` iterations**: each iteration's scrutinee
temporaries drop at the end of that iteration's body before the next
iteration's scrutinee is evaluated. After the loop terminates (the pattern
stopped matching), the final iteration's scrutinee temporaries are already
dropped." The last sentence is the one this violates — the final temporary is
not dropped at all.

WHY IT SURVIVES EVERY GATE, same as B-2026-08-30-17: all four surfaces agree,
so the A/B parity rule reports green, and the missing body is a LEAK of an
observable side effect rather than of memory (the temp's storage is still
reclaimed), so no valgrind/LSan check fires either. Only an absolute
expected-output assertion catches it, and none existed.

MEDIUM rather than low: unlike the ordering row, a body that never runs is a
lost side effect, not a mis-timed one. The `Lease` example design.md uses
throughout this section would leak a pooled connection per loop exit — the
resource is never returned, for the lifetime of the process.

WHERE TO START. Codegen has `drop_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee_on_miss`
(control_flow_match.rs) and its slot is literally named
`__whilelet_miss_scrut`, so the intent exists; either it is not called on the
loop-exit edge or it is declining (it bails on `!force &&
!expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, on a non-`StructValue` scrutinee, on a shared
enum, and when `emit_enum_drop_switch` returns `None`). The interpreter agrees
with codegen here, so its `while let` site needs the same audit — and the two
must move together, since this row exists precisely because they already agree.

NOT MEASURED, stated rather than implied: whether a `while let` over an
`Option`/`Result` scrutinee (a different staging slot) behaves the same; whether
`break` out of the loop body leaves that iteration's temporary undropped too;
and whether the STRUCT-pattern flavour of the scrutinee shows it.
fix:
FIXED by f8e28a7, both backends in one commit.

THE INTENT EXISTED AND WAS NOT DECLINING -- it was emitting half the work,
which is why the row's "either it is not called on the loop-exit edge or it is
declining" found neither. `drop_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee_on_miss` IS called,
and its gates all pass; it emitted only `emit_enum_drop_switch`, which is the
MEMORY half. The enum's own user `Drop` body and its payload's bodies were
never run, so the loop-exit temporary was freed silently.

Exactly the memory/bodies split B-2026-06-10's enum arm fixed for a
call-argument enum temporary (`call_dispatch.rs`, the `fresh_enum_temp`
branch), whose comment states the rule reused here: for an enum, UserDrop and
EnumDrop are COMPLEMENTARY rather than mutually exclusive, because the
wrapper's field-cleanup half (`emit_struct_drop_synthesis`) is a no-op for an
enum type name. Three calls now, in that order.

THE EARLY RETURN MOVED rather than gaining a companion, and that is what
covers the row's own repro. The row lists "`emit_enum_drop_switch` returns
`None`" among the bail conditions without noting that this IS the row's own
program: that helper answers `None` for an enum with no heap-bearing variant,
and `enum E { A(R), B }` over `R { id: i64 }` is entirely scalar. So the repro
registered NOTHING AT ALL, not merely the memory half -- and the HEAP-carrying
spelling, which does reach the switch, was equally silent, which is what shows
the missing piece was never about heap. Bailing now requires all three actions
to be absent.

THE ORDER IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. A bound local of the very value that ends
the loop prints `dB dW7` on every surface -- the enum's own body, then the
payload's. The let-path produces that by draining its frame LIFO over
(memory, walker, own-body); the miss edge emits inline rather than through a
frame, so the sequence is written out directly. That oracle is asserted beside
the loop in the fixture, so the exit temporary cannot drift from what a plain
binding of the same value does.

BOTH BACKENDS MOVED TOGETHER, as this row required. The interpreter's
`while let` carried a comment calling the miss drop "a documented residual in
BOTH backends"; that is no longer true and the note is corrected in the same
commit. `run_user_drop_body_on_value` is the twin of the `karac_drop_<T>`
wrapper codegen emits and `run_enum_payload_user_drops_value` the twin of
`emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`, so the two produce the same
transcript by construction rather than by convention. Each half is
independently load-bearing: stashing the interpreter half fails the new
fixture on `interpreter`, stashing the codegen half on `run and build must
agree`.

TWO FIXTURES WERE PINNING THE RESIDUAL AS EXPECTED OUTPUT, which is the part
worth recording. `e2e_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee_while_let_runs_user_drop_per_iter`
and `test_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee_runs_user_drop` (B-2026-07-11-26) both call
`next(i)` FOUR times -- i = 0, 1, 2 yield, i = 3 stops -- so four temporaries
exist and four bodies are due, and both asserted THREE. So the residual was
not merely undocumented: it was asserted, on both backends, by the two
fixtures covering this construct, with the interpreter's source comment as the
prose half of the same claim. Both now assert four, each with a note saying
what the fourth one is. They failed the suite, which is how they were found --
the probe matrix this fix was developed against did not include them.

THE ROW'S THREE UNMEASURED SHAPES ARE ANSWERED:
  * enum STRUCT-variant scrutinee -- broken the same way, FIXED, and pinned.
  * `break` out of the loop body -- ALREADY CORRECT. It creates no further
    temporary (`v0 dE v1 dE after` before and after), so there was nothing to
    lose. Pinned as a control so the fix cannot start over-firing on it.
  * `Option`/`Result` scrutinee -- broken, and NOT fixed here. Those keep
    their own payload machinery (the same carve-out the call-argument
    precedent makes), so the fix deliberately excludes them.

AND THAT LAST ONE CORRECTS THE ROW'S ARGUMENT. The row leans on the `if let`
control to establish this is a defect rather than a design choice: "the same
non-matching temporary through `if let E.A(r) = mkB() { … }` prints `dE`".
True for a USER ENUM. For `Result[W, W]` whose `Err` arm carries a `Drop`
type, `if let Ok(w) = mkErr()` loses the body too -- so the `Result` miss is
a different site, not a `while let` one, and is filed separately rather than
folded in.

MEMORY WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM and is unchanged: 11 allocs / 11 frees, 0
valgrind errors at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, before the fix as well as after, on
the heap-carrying spelling and the payload-carrying one alike. The missing
body was a lost side effect, exactly as the row says -- which, with all four
surfaces agreeing, is why neither the A/B parity rule nor any LSan gate could
see it.

VERIFIED across all four surfaces on a ten-case matrix (all-scalar payload,
heap-carrying payload, struct-variant, payload-carrying enum, `break`, the
`if let` control, a loop that never matches, and the two `Option`/`Result`
shapes that stay carved out); the eight-row fixture
`e2e_while_let_loop_exit_drops_the_temporary_that_ended_it` carries it.

title: `partial_move_of_drop_struct` IS REGISTERED AT `Warn` WHERE design.md SAYS "rejected" -- eight `--features llvm` fixtures use the shape, and seven of them are the regression tests for bugs FIXED in it, so `Deny` today would delete that coverage; the corpus is otherwise clean (0 hits across 1171 `.kara` files, 10246/0 on the default suite at `Deny`)
detail:
`partial_move_of_drop_struct` LANDED AT `Warn` WHERE design.md SAYS "rejected".
The rule itself is implemented and correct (B-2026-09-01-38); what is deferred is
only its LEVEL, and the deferral is a measurement rather than a judgement call.

At `Deny`, eight `--features llvm` fixtures stop compiling, caught by the
check-gate in `tests/common/mod.rs` that asserts every codegen test program
passes `karac check`:

    codegen_tests::e2e_discarded_own_drop_parent_temp_orders_its_body_first
    codegen_tests::e2e_freshtemp_struct_scrutinee_runs_its_own_drop_body
    codegen_tests::e2e_own_drop_parent_runs_a_returned_fields_body_once
    codegen_tests::e2e_param_view_field_moved_back_out_runs_one_body
    codegen_tests::e2e_pool_acquire_reuse_at_cap_and_struct_element
    codegen_tests::test_e2e_fresh_temp_struct_scrutinee_arm_binding_runs_its_body
    memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_discarded_own_drop_parent_temp_order_is_memory_balanced
    memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_own_drop_parent_masking_a_returned_field_frees_it

Everything else is already clean: 0 hits across all 1171 `.kara` files in both
repos, and 10246 passed / 0 failed on the DEFAULT suite with the lint at `Deny`
(both measured).

WHY THIS IS NOT A ONE-LINE FLIP. Seven of the eight are REGRESSION TESTS FOR
BUGS FIXED IN THIS EXACT SHAPE — B-2026-08-28-21's `let W { r, n } = w` family,
the fresh-temp struct-scrutinee family, the param-view family. Rewriting them to
a legal spelling does not preserve what they test: their subject IS the drop
behaviour of a partially-moved `Drop` struct. So promoting the level means
deciding, per fixture, whether the fix it guards is still reachable by a legal
program — and where it is not, whether the coverage should be retired with the
shape or kept under an explicit `-A`.

The eighth, `e2e_pool_acquire_reuse_at_cap_and_struct_element`, is different and
should be fixed rather than grandfathered: it is an ordinary program, and its
`let cv: Conn = sc.val;` moves the payload out of a `PooledConnection` whose
`Drop` returns it to the pool. That is a true positive — the RAII-guard hazard
the rule exists for — so the FIXTURE is wrong, not the rule.

DO THIS WHEN: the eight are resolved. Flip `default_level` to `LintLevel::Deny`
in `src/lints.rs`, and update the two paragraphs that record the `Warn` choice —
the registry `description` and design.md § Part 8 `Drop` — since both state the
reason explicitly and would otherwise be left asserting something false.
