title: THE ASSOCIATED-FUNCTION SPELLING of a conditional return is wrong under `--interp` in BOTH directions -- the dying argument runs NO `Drop` body and the returned one runs TWO -- while the free-fn and method spellings and all three COMPILED lanes are correct
detail:
THE ASSOCIATED-FUNCTION SPELLING of a conditional return is wrong under
`--interp` in BOTH directions, while the free-function and instance-method
spellings of the identical program are correct on all four lanes, and the
associated spelling itself is correct on all three COMPILED lanes.

    struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.id}") } }
    struct H { n: i64 }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> String { return f"pay-{i}-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"; }
    impl H {
        fn apick(a: R, k: bool) -> R { if k { return R { id: 98, s: mk(98) }; } return a; }
    }

    fn af_t() { let x = H.apick(R { id: 21, s: mk(21) }, true); println(f"E{x.id}"); }
    fn an_f() { let r = R { id: 24, s: mk(24) }; let x = H.apick(r, false); println(f"I{x.id}"); }

    af_t()   correct  d21 E98 d98      --interp  E98 d98        <- body LOST
    an_f()   correct  I24 d24          --interp  d24 I24 d24    <- body DOUBLED

Split out of B-2026-08-30-23 when its headline (the FREE-FUNCTION cell) was
fixed. Ten of that row's twelve cells are correct on every lane now; these two
are the remainder, and both are interpreter-only.

TWO DIRECTIONS AT ONCE is what makes this its own defect rather than a missing
call. At `k = true` the argument dies inside the callee and NOBODY runs its body;
at `k = false` the callee hands it back and TWO frames run it. So the
interpreter's associated-call frame neither takes ownership of a dying param nor
stands the caller down for a returned one -- it is absent from both halves of
the protocol, not mis-set on one.

ONE DEAD END ALREADY MEASURED, so the next attempt does not repeat it.
`cond_returned_param_drop_names` (src/interpreter/eval_call.rs) is the seeding
site for the callee-owns-a-conditionally-returned-param half, and it
early-returns for any callee name containing a `.`, commented "free functions
only -- the method caller path does not stand down". Lifting that specifically
for ASSOCIATED functions (resolve through `impl_method_ast`, admit the ones with
no `self_param`, keep instance methods excluded) compiles and changes NEITHER
cell. The associated call therefore does not reach that site at all. Its frame is
seeded somewhere else, or nowhere -- that is where to start.

Instance methods are seeded from `method_param_drop_names`
(src/interpreter/method_call.rs), a deliberately WIDER set, on the reasoning
that a method's arguments reach no caller-side fire in this backend. Whether an
associated call is in that same position is the question to settle first: if it
is, the fix is to seed it from there; if it is not, the caller-side stand-down is
the missing half instead. The `k = false` doubling suggests the caller DOES fire,
which would make it unlike a method and argue against simply reusing that set.

NOT MEASURED: whether a GENERIC associated function behaves the same (the
compiled arm's registration was extended to monos by B-2026-08-28-71, so the two
could diverge again there); whether an associated function with more than one
by-value param loses one body or several; and whether an associated CONSTRUCTOR
returning `Self` -- the far more common shape -- is affected, which would raise
the severity well above what these two synthetic cells suggest.

The compiled lanes are pinned by
`codegen_conditional_return_param_drop_matrix` (tests/codegen.rs), which asserts
all twelve cells. The interpreter twin
`test_conditional_return_param_drop_matrix` (tests/interpreter.rs) HOLDS THESE
TWO OUT by name; restoring them to that fixture is the completion test.
fix:
FIXED by abdffc4, and the two cells had ONE cause -- not the missing protocol the row
described. An ASSOCIATED call never reaches `method_call.rs` at all: it is
dispatched by `eval_call`'s ordinary `Value::Function` arm, the SAME arm a free
function uses, because the callee Path `H.apick` resolves through the env key
`"H.apick"` to a `Value::Function` whose `name` field is the BARE `"apick"`
(`register_impl_methods` stores `method.name`; only the env KEY is qualified).
Every helper in that arm that answers a question about the callee by scanning
`program.items` for an `Item::Function` of that name therefore found nothing,
and answered as it would for a closure.

That is why both directions were wrong at once. Three helpers ask the same
failing question, and one of them had already been fixed:

  * `cond_returned_param_drop_names` (callee side) -- no `Item::Function`
    named `"apick"`, so the frame claimed nothing and the DYING argument had no
    owner. That is the `af_t` half.
  * `record_passthrough_arg_moves` (caller side) -- three inline
    `Item::Function` scans, so the caller never stood down and the RETURNED
    argument had two owners. That is the `an_f` half.
  * `run_fresh_temp_arg_drops` -- already correct, via
    `callee_fn_for_ownership_guard`, which B-2026-08-30-22 introduced for
    exactly this problem. That one site being right is what made the other two
    look like a protocol question instead of a name question.

THE ROW'S RECORDED DEAD END IS EXPLAINED RATHER THAN CONTRADICTED. Lifting
`cond_returned_param_drop_names`' `contains('.')` guard is a no-op because
`fn_name` NEVER contains a dot at that site -- the guard has been dead code
since it was written. The exclusion it was reaching for is real (an instance
method's caller does not stand down, so flipping ownership there doubles the
body), and it is now enforced where it can actually fire, by the new resolver's
`self_param.is_none()` test. Instance methods genuinely never reach this arm:
`t.mpick(x)` goes to `method_call.rs` and its deliberately wider
`method_param_drop_names`.

THE REST OF THE ARM ALREADY TREATED AN ASSOCIATED CALL AS A FREE-FUNCTION
FRAME, which is what makes this an alignment rather than a new rule: the same
arm pushes `owned_param_frame_is_method = false` for it (eval_call.rs:2138),
against `true` on `method_call.rs`'s path. So the frame was already declared
non-method while the helpers that act on that declaration could not find the
callee to act on.

FIX: `callee_fn_for_param_ownership` (src/interpreter/eval_call.rs) resolves a
bare callee name to a free function or, failing that, to a non-`self` impl
method -- free function wins outright, trait impls excluded, FAIL-CLOSED on
ambiguity for the reason `declared_param_tys_of_fn` gives at the same problem.
`cond_returned_param_drop_names` and `record_passthrough_arg_moves` route
through it, and the latter's three inline scans collapse to one resolution.

`callee_fn_for_ownership_guard` (B-2026-08-30-22's resolver, which admits
instance methods because its callers only ever DECLINE to fire a body) now
delegates to the same walk behind an `assoc_only` flag rather than keeping a
byte-for-byte copy of it. Two near-identical resolvers differing by one line is
the shape the free and associated spellings drifted apart in to begin with.

MEASURED after, all four lanes byte-identical: `af_t` -> `d21 E98 d98`, `an_f`
-> `I24 d24`, each matching its free-function twin exactly.

THE THREE NOT-MEASURED QUESTIONS ARE NOW ANSWERED, and two found separate
defects rather than more of this one:

  * MORE THAN ONE by-value param -- FIXED by this same change, and it loses
    ONE body per direction, not several. `H.two(a: R, b: R, k: bool)` printed
    `T42 d42` / `T43 d43` before (the dying param silent in both directions)
    and is correct on all four lanes now.
  * GENERIC -- a SEPARATE, PRE-EXISTING codegen defect, filed as
    B-2026-09-02-3. Isolated to one variable: `fn gpick[T](a: T, k: bool, alt:
    T) -> T` against an identical concrete `cpick(a: R, ...)`, same call. The
    concrete one is correct on all four lanes; the generic one loses the dying
    param's body on all THREE COMPILED lanes. Verified at pristine `main`
    (13f6670) that the FREE-function generic ALREADY diverged this way, so this
    fix did not create it -- it made the associated spelling share the free
    spelling's behaviour, which is the whole point, and that is how the
    divergence became visible in a second place.
  * ASSOCIATED CONSTRUCTOR returning `Self` -- it is the AGGREGATE WRAP that
    matters, not the constructor-ness, and it is a separate defect filed as
    B-2026-09-02-4: measured byte-identical on all four lanes before and after
    this fix. It does NOT raise this row's severity, and the reason is worth
    recording: the compiled lanes run the wrapped param's `Drop` body twice,
    but valgrind on the AOT binary reports 28 allocs / 28 frees and 0 errors,
    so it is a duplicated side effect over singly-freed memory, not a double
    free.

FIXTURES: `test_conditional_return_param_drop_matrix` (tests/interpreter.rs)
now pins all TWELVE cells with nothing held out, identical to its codegen twin
`codegen_conditional_return_param_drop_matrix`. New pair
`test_assoc_fn_two_by_value_params_drop_matrix` /
`codegen_assoc_fn_two_by_value_params_drop_matrix` pins the multi-param callee;
both RED-verified on pristine `src`.

title: `karac-runtime` NO LONGER LINKS ON WINDOWS -- `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol posix_memalign referenced in function karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic`, so `Test (windows-latest)` fails at BUILD time, not on a test. Red on every concluded CI run since 33f43c4.
detail:
FOUND by reading CI: `Test (windows-latest)` has failed identically on the
last three runs that reached a conclusion (33537181032, 33544966774,
33560668650 -- 2026-09-01 17:20 / 18:39 / 21:22 UTC). Not a flake, and not a
test failure at all:

    karac_runtime-...rcgu.o : error LNK2019: unresolved external symbol
      posix_memalign referenced in function karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic
    fatal error LNK1120: 1 unresolved externals
    error: could not compile `karac-runtime` (lib test)

CAUSE. 33f43c4 (the fix for B-2026-08-31-24) added
`karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic` / the aligned realloc twin in
`runtime/src/alloc.rs`, declaring `posix_memalign` in an UNCONDITIONAL
`extern "C"` block alongside `malloc` / `realloc` / `calloc` / `free`. Those
four exist in the MSVC CRT; `posix_memalign` does not -- it is POSIX-only,
and the Windows spelling is `_aligned_malloc`.

THE FREE SIDE IS THE TRAP, and it is why this is not a one-line cfg. The
doc comment on the extern block reasons that "memory it returns is freed
with plain `free`, which is why the aligned path below needs no free-side
counterpart" -- true for POSIX (POSIX.1-2008 and C11 7.22.3.1 both make
`free` the correct deallocator), FALSE for `_aligned_malloc`, whose memory
MUST be released with `_aligned_free` and whose behaviour under plain `free`
is undefined. So a Windows arm needs either a paired `_aligned_free` on
every release path that can see an over-aligned buffer, or an over-allocate-
and-store-the-offset scheme that keeps `free` correct. `karac_free_buf` and
the buffer-parking path in the same file both currently assume `free`.

NOT REPRODUCIBLE ON THE LOCAL MAC, and not by cross-check either: the
failure is at LINK time, so `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`
would not surface it even with the target installed (it is not). Needs
Windows CI to verify a fix -- or the `windows-lint` job extended to build,
which it currently does not do.
fix:
Fixed in 6c2a4fb: `posix_memalign` is now declared under `#[cfg(not(windows))]`,
and the over-aligned pair grew a Windows arm that REFUSES rather than falls
back.

THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT, INCLUDING THE PART THAT MAKES THIS NOT A
ONE-LINE CFG. The free-side trap is real and it is the whole constraint: the
aligned path works on POSIX only because `posix_memalign` memory is released
with plain `free`, which is what lets `karac_free_buf`, the buffer-parking
cache, the internal free in `karac_realloc_aligned_or_panic`, and codegen's
own emitted `free` calls all stay untouched. Confirmed that no Windows
allocator has that property: `_aligned_malloc` demands `_aligned_free`, and
C11 `aligned_alloc` is deliberately unimplemented in the MSVC CRT for exactly
that incompatibility. So over-alignment on Windows is not a rename; it needs
an aligned-aware free at every one of those release sites.

REFUSE, NOT FALL BACK. The tempting one-liner -- route Windows to
`karac_alloc_or_panic` -- returns a merely 16-aligned buffer and lets
codegen's `vmovaps` fault on it, which is precisely the heap-history-dependent
crash B-2026-08-31-24 was opened to remove, reintroduced silently and with the
same signature that made it hard to see the first time. The arm aborts with a
message naming the limitation instead. Nothing reaches it today: Windows
codegen E2E is still deferred (ci.yml "STAGE 4"), so no Kara program is
compiled on Windows and no caller can request an over-aligned buffer. The
remaining gap is tracked as B-2026-09-02-9.

The realloc twin refuses BEFORE its `realloc`, not after. Deferring to the
alloc arm's abort would be non-deterministic: `grown` comes back correctly
aligned by luck a good fraction of the time, so the unsupported case would
abort on some runs and silently return an under-aligned buffer on others.

ONE MORE SYMBOL HAD TO MOVE, and it would have swapped one red Windows job
for another. With `posix_memalign` gated, the file-scope `free` extern's only
remaining user was the non-Windows realloc helper, so it became dead code on
the Windows leg -- and `windows-lint` runs `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`
there. It is now a function-local extern inside that helper, the same pattern
the three macos/linux-gated helpers in this file already use.

THE ROW'S CLOSING CLAIM IS WRONG AND THE CORRECTION IS REUSABLE. It says the
failure "needs Windows CI to verify a fix" because `cargo check --target
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` would not surface a LINK error. True as far as it
goes, and it stops one step short: you do not need a linker to answer a
link question, only an OBJECT and a symbol table. `rustup target add
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (std is a plain download; no MSVC toolchain needed),
then

    cargo rustc -p karac-runtime --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc \
        --no-default-features --lib -- --emit=obj -C lto=off

emits a Windows object without ever linking, and `llvm-nm` reads it. Measured
here: `U posix_memalign` present pre-fix, absent post-fix, with the undefined
set otherwise IDENTICAL (354 entries -> 353) and nothing added -- so the fix
removes exactly the one unresolved external CI reports and introduces no new
dependency. `--no-default-features` is required because a dev-dependency's
build script wants `lib.exe`; the aligned path is feature-independent, so it
is compiled either way.

The same technique proved the native leg unaffected: identical undefined set
and identical 337-symbol `karac_*` ABI before and after, which is stronger
evidence than a green test run that a runtime edit is a no-op on the platforms
that actually compile Kara.

TESTS. The aligned pair had NO unit coverage at all -- B-2026-08-31-24 added
it with none, which is why this restructure had no local guard. Three tests
now cover it, POSIX-only because the Windows arm aborts by design: alignment
is honored above the `malloc` guarantee, requests at or under it pass through
to the ordinary allocator, and the realloc twin preserves both bytes and
alignment. Both alignment assertions were negative-controlled by
short-circuiting the aligned path to plain `malloc`. That control is what
caught a worthless test: the realloc case originally grew one buffer to 4096
bytes, and glibc returns a 64-aligned pointer for a 4 KiB request, so it
passed WITH the aligned path disabled -- it could not fail. Sweeping several
sizes just off a power of two keeps the result in the ordinary 16-aligned
bins, and it now fails under the control as it should.

VERIFIED: runtime lib 377/0; codegen 3544/0; memory_sanitizer 1366/0;
interpreter 1907/0; par_codegen 276/0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean;
`cargo clippy --all --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean on BOTH the default
and `--features llvm` legs; clippy clean on the x86_64-pc-windows-msvc,
wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-wasip1-threads legs.

ARCHIVE NOTE, unrelated to the fix but worth recording. This checkout's
`target/release/libkarac_runtime.a` was 57.8 MB before the rebuild these tests
required; a correct plain full archive is 20.0 MB (the unicode archive is
20.2 MB, consistent with its documented +161 KiB). The canonical name was
holding something other than the plain full archive -- a feature-heavy or
non-LTO build left behind by an earlier session. This is the silent half of
the staleness rule in CLAUDE.md wearing a different hat: the archive was not
stale, it was the WRONG ONE, and nothing about it links or runs differently
enough to notice.

title: `e2e_vec_of_vector_operations_round_trip` PRODUCES NO OUTPUT AT ALL on x86-64 -- the over-aligned `Vec[Vector[T, N]]` program that B-2026-08-31-24 was supposed to fix still dies, deterministically, on every concluded CI run since that fix landed.
detail:
FOUND by reading CI. `Codegen E2E (LLVM 18)` (x86-64 Linux) fails this one
test on all three runs that reached a conclusion on 2026-09-01
(33537181032 / 33544966774 / 33560668650):

    assertion `left == right` failed
      left: ""
      right: "lit  [Vector(1, 2, 3, 4), ...]\n...\nsum  3520\n"

`left` is EMPTY -- the compiled program printed nothing, so it died before
its first `println` rather than printing a wrong value. Persistent across
three runs and three different `main` commits, so not the heap-luck flake
the test's own doc comment describes.

DOES NOT REPRODUCE ON arm64. Ran locally on macOS arm64 (M5, LLVM 18) after
rebuilding both runtime archives at 13f6670f: `cargo test --features llvm
--test codegen e2e_vec_of_vector_operations_round_trip` passes, 1 passed / 0
failed. Consistent with the mechanism B-2026-08-31-24 documents -- the fault
is x86-64's alignment-checking `vmovaps` against a 16-byte-aligned `malloc`
chunk, and arm64's vector loads tolerate the under-alignment -- which means
the SAME latent defect can be present on arm64 and stay invisible there.

WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN, and what the fix has to start from: whether 33f43c4's
aligned allocator is not reaching this program's buffers at all, or is
reaching them and something else faults. The test is the VALUE half of
B-2026-08-31-24's pair; its IR half
(`test_ir_over_aligned_vec_element_buffer_uses_the_aligned_allocator`) is
green, which means the allocation site is annotated correctly and points
suspicion at a path the IR test does not cover -- the grow/realloc twin, the
`Map` / `Array` / enum-payload placements this test adds past the bare
`Vec[Vector]`, or the buffer-parking `take` the fix deliberately skips.
Reading which of the ~18 printed lines is missing is not possible from the
empty output; the next step is running it under a debugger on x86-64.

NEEDS x86-64 to reproduce. Not workable from the arm64 Mac.

MEASUREMENT NOTE (B-2026-09-01-45's session, 2026-09-02). Offered as a
datapoint, not a diagnosis -- this row is claimed by another session and
nothing below was investigated beyond what a regression gate needed.

`e2e_vec_of_vector_operations_round_trip` PASSES here on x86-64 Linux at
origin/main e181d9a, and the full `cargo test --features llvm --test codegen`
run is 3544 passed / 0 failed, against CI run 33574809660's 3540 passed / 1
failed on exactly this test. So the delta is environmental; CI pins LLVM 18,
which is the obvious first candidate.

One local difference worth ruling in or out first: this checkout's
`target/release/libkarac_runtime.a` was 57.8 MB before I rebuilt it, where a
correct plain full archive is 20.0 MB (the unicode archive is 20.2 MB,
consistent with its documented +161 KiB). The canonical name was holding
something other than the plain full archive -- a feature-heavy or non-LTO
build left behind by an earlier session. The test passes AFTER a lean-then-full
rebuild. That does not explain CI, which builds its archives fresh, so the
archive is likely a red herring for the CI red -- but it does mean a local
"cannot reproduce" or "reproduces" on an un-rebuilt tree proves nothing.
fix:
FIXED by ce9669c. The missed paths are the Vec CONSTRUCTORS:
`Vec.with_capacity`, `Vec.filled`, `Vec.from_fn` and `Vec.from_slice` still
allocated their element buffer through the plain `karac_alloc_or_panic`, so an
over-aligned element type got malloc's 16 bytes while every access to it was
emitted at 32. `Vec.new()` is the one that broke CI, and it reaches this through
the PRESIZE pass: `Vec.new()` plus a stabilized push loop is rewritten to
`Vec.with_capacity(n)`, so the buffer the program actually runs on is
`with_capacity`'s.

TWO OF THE ROW'S PREMISES WERE WRONG, and the first is the one that had made it
look unworkable.

  * "NEEDS x86-64 to reproduce ... not workable from the arm64 Mac" -- the
    ARCHITECTURE is not what decides it, the ALLOCATOR is. The fault needs a
    buffer that is 16-aligned but not 32, and whether malloc returns one is
    heap history, not ISA. `LD_PRELOAD`ing a shim that forces every plain
    malloc/calloc/realloc result to 16 mod 64 -- still a legal malloc result,
    so no correct code may break -- reproduces it deterministically, and
    deliberately NOT interposing `posix_memalign` keeps the aligned allocator
    working, so anything that still faults is a path the fix did not reach
    rather than shim unfairness. That shim is ~40 lines and would have worked
    on the arm64 Mac too, where the row recorded a PASS. The pass was luck, not
    immunity: this container is x86-64 with the same LLVM 18.1.3 and the same
    archives, and the test passed here 25 times out of 25 before the fix.

  * "`left` is EMPTY -- the compiled program printed nothing, so it died before
    its first `println`" -- it dies in the LAST of eighteen blocks. Piped
    stdout is block-buffered, so a late SIGSEGV discards the whole buffer and
    the harness sees "". Under `stdbuf -o0` the program prints seventeen lines
    and dies at `sum`. This generalizes past this row: ANY e2e crash in this
    harness reports `left: ""` whatever line it died on, so an empty `left` is
    evidence of a crash and no evidence at all about WHERE.

ISOLATED TO ONE VARIABLE. Same program, same loop, same element type, only the
constructor differs:

    let mut v: Vec[Vector[i64, 4]] = Vec.new();   -> karac_alloc_or_panic ONLY   -> SIGSEGV
    let mut v: Vec[Vector[i64, 4]] = [];          -> karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic
                                                     + karac_realloc_aligned_or_panic -> correct

The aligned symbols are not even LINKED into the `Vec.new()` binary. A sweep of
every Vec-producing shape under the shim found `Vec.new()`, `Vec.with_capacity`
and `Vec.filled` faulting, with the literal, `reserve`, `insert`, `from_slice`
and `VecDeque` spellings all correct -- the last four being precisely the ones
B-2026-08-31-24 had fixed.

WHY THE GREEN IR TEST DID NOT CATCH IT, which is the part worth keeping. Its
five cases all build the Vec as a LITERAL (`[a]` / `[]`) or call `reserve`, so
each of them exercised a site that was already fixed. Worse, its assertion was
"the IR mentions an aligned entry point SOMEWHERE" -- and a `push` on any Vec
emits a conditional GROW path calling `karac_realloc_aligned_or_panic`, so that
assertion is satisfied by the grow path even when the CONSTRUCTOR's buffer is
still plain malloc. Measured: three of the four new cases PASS against
unfixed `src` under the old assertion. A test that sweeps the same sites the fix
swept cannot find the site both missed.

FIX: one shared `emit_vec_buffer_alloc(elem_ty, bytes, name)` in
`codegen/vec_method.rs` -- the constructor-side twin of the existing
`emit_vec_buffer_grow_alloc` -- and all four constructor sites routed through
it (`with_capacity_buffer_or_null` gains an `elem_ty` parameter; `filled.buf`,
`fromfn.buf`, `from_slice.buf` call it directly). A helper rather than four
open-coded `match`es specifically so the next Vec constructor cannot silently
join the list. `String.with_capacity` shares the same helper and is unchanged:
its element is a byte, `over_alignment_for_elem` answers `None`, and it keeps
the plain allocator -- verified in the sweep.

FIXTURE: the four missed shapes are added to
`test_ir_over_aligned_vec_element_buffer_uses_the_aligned_allocator` in a
SECOND loop with a stronger assertion -- the allocation is pinned by its IR
VALUE NAME (`%with_cap.buf = call ptr @karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic`), not by
the symbol appearing anywhere in the module, so the grow path can no longer
satisfy it for the constructor. RED-verified against pristine `src`: it fails on
`vec-new-while-push`, the exact shape CI died on. The original E2E
`e2e_vec_of_vector_operations_round_trip` now also runs clean under the shim,
printing all eighteen lines.

NOT ADDRESSED, deliberately: the E2E test remains heap-luck-dependent for
whether it CATCHES a future regression of this class, because the harness has no
way to force an unlucky allocator. The IR fixture is what makes the class
deterministic; the E2E is the end-to-end oracle.

title: COMPILING `e2e_generic_non_let_binding_instantiation_across_sites` OVERFLOWS THE STACK AND ABORTS (SIGABRT) -- the compiler recurses deep enough that a 1 MiB thread stack is not enough, which is why `Codegen E2E (Linux arm64)` has been red on every concluded run while the 8 MiB-stack hosts pass.
detail:
FOUND by reading CI. `Codegen E2E (Linux arm64, LLVM 18)` aborts the whole
`--test codegen` binary on all three concluded runs of 2026-09-01:

    thread 'codegen_tests::e2e_generic_non_let_binding_instantiation_across_sites'
      has overflowed its stack
    fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
    process didn't exit successfully: ... (signal: 6, SIGABRT)

IT IS A STACK-DEPTH BUG, NOT AN ARCH BUG, and that is measurable rather than
inferred. On macOS arm64 (M5) at 13f6670f the test passes at the harness's
default stack; forcing the stack down reproduces the CI abort exactly:

    RUST_MIN_STACK=2097152  -> ok. 1 passed
    RUST_MIN_STACK=1048576  -> has overflowed its stack / SIGABRT

So the same recursion runs on every host; the Linux arm64 runner is simply
the one whose effective stack sits below the requirement. Two consequences:
the abort can migrate to any other leg the moment that leg's stack or the
recursion depth moves, and it IS workable from an arm64 Mac --
`RUST_MIN_STACK=1048576` is a faithful local harness for it.

WHERE TO LOOK. B-2026-08-27-36 names this same test, so the shape has
recursed dangerously before. The fix is presumably to make the offending
walk iterative (or memoise it) rather than to raise a stack anywhere: a
compiler whose depth requirement is within 2x of a common host's default
will keep coming back.

The test binary ABORTS, so every test that had not yet run on that leg is
also unreported -- the leg's true pass count is unknown, not 'everything
else passed'.
fix:
Fixed in 9dab75a by building the `karac` package at `opt-level = 1` in the dev
profile. THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN ITS CENTRAL CLAIM, and the
correction is the whole fix.

NOT DEEP RECURSION. The row reasons "the compiler recurses deep enough that a
1 MiB thread stack is not enough" and prescribes making the offending walk
iterative or memoising it. Measured under gdb at the fault, the stack is ~40
compiler frames over THREE levels of monomorphization recursion -- shallow by
any standard. It reaches 1,042,536 bytes because the frames are enormous:

     110,768 B  compile_stmt_inner        (x4 occurrences)
     129,088 B  compile_method_call       (x2, 106,552 at the other site)
      47,456 B  compile_expr_inner        (x4)
      23,504 B  compile_program
      19,520 B  compile_to_object_with_hot_swap
      19,056 B  compile_function

Three functions hold 83% of the total. Everything else on the stack is
noise -- `compile_expr` and `compile_stmt` are 224 bytes each.

WHY THE FRAMES ARE THAT BIG, and why only the optimizer can fix it. At
`opt-level = 0` LLVM does not run stack-slot coloring, so a large `match`
allocates EVERY arm's locals simultaneously in one frame even though at most
one arm executes. These three functions are exactly that shape. There is no
walk to unroll: the depth is already minimal and proportional to source
nesting, so an iterative rewrite would move ~40 frames onto the heap and leave
the per-arm local bloat untouched.

THE MEASUREMENT. Bisecting `RUST_MIN_STACK` on x86-64 Linux:

    opt-level 0:  1 MiB -> overflow/SIGABRT      2 MiB -> ok
    opt-level 1:  128 KiB -> overflow            256 KiB -> ok

A 4-8x reduction, which clears the arm64 runner with room rather than by a
hair -- the row's own worry that "a compiler whose depth requirement is within
2x of a common host's default will keep coming back" is answered by margin,
not by a rewrite.

IT IS A WIN ON BOTH AXES, NOT A TRADE. The codegen E2E suite invokes `karac`
3544 times, so an optimized compiler makes the suite FASTER: 281s vs 323s,
-13% -- and that suite is a long pole in CI. The cost is one second on an
incremental rebuild (12.1s vs 11.2s measured after touching
`src/codegen/exprs.rs`), which is what a developer actually pays.
`debug-assertions` and `overflow-checks` are independent of `opt-level`, so the
karac lib keeps every check a dev build is supposed to have.

GUARDED. `tests/codegen.rs`'s
`compiling_a_generic_monomorph_nest_fits_a_modest_thread_stack` re-execs the
test binary with `RUST_MIN_STACK=1048576` and asserts the child exits cleanly.
Re-exec rather than an in-process bounded thread, because a stack overflow
ABORTS and cannot be caught -- an in-process guard would kill the whole test
binary, which is the symptom being fixed. Budget is 1 MiB rather than the
~256 KiB measured: aarch64 frames can be materially larger and no arm64 host
was available to measure, so it is sized for margin over sensitivity. A partial
regression will slip through; that is the deliberate trade, since a guard that
false-fires on one architecture is worse than one that catches only the large
regression. Negative-controlled -- removing the profile override makes it fail
as an ordinary test failure rather than an abort.

ONE FALLOUT, AND IT WAS A LATENT BUG IN A TEST, NOT IN THIS CHANGE.
`test_scalar_float_methods_compute_at_the_declared_width` exists to separate
the f32 route from the f64-then-round route, and it builds its own oracle in
Rust from compile-time-constant receivers. With optimization on, LLVM folds
`a.cosh()` at build time through DOUBLE-precision host math -- producing
exactly the f64-route value the test is trying to distinguish itself from, so
its two `samples` columns collapse and the oracle silently changes meaning with
build configuration. The receivers are now `black_box`ed, forcing real libm
calls, and it passes at both opt levels.

The numbers, because the first reading of this was backwards and the
measurement is what corrected it: `2.0f32.cosh()` is 3.7621958255767822 as a
real `coshf` call (glibc's `coshf` is not correctly rounded) and
3.762195587158203 when constant-folded through double. The interpreter, the
JIT and the AOT binary ALL print the first, at both opt levels -- verified by
running the program on all three surfaces with `karac` built each way. So the
interpreter's float behaviour never moved; the previously-passing optimized
oracle would have asserted a value no backend produces.

VERIFIED: default suite 10255 passed / 0 failed; codegen 3545/0;
memory_sanitizer 1366/0; par_codegen 276/0; interpreter 1907/0;
`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets
-- -D warnings` clean on BOTH the default and `--features llvm` legs.

LEFT OPEN DELIBERATELY. This raises the ceiling ~4-8x; it does not make the
requirement unbounded. Stack depth is inherently proportional to user source
nesting, so sufficiently deep nesting can still overflow -- true of most
compilers, pre-existing, and out of scope here. Reducing the three big frames
in code (extracting large `match` arms into `#[inline(never)]` helpers) remains
available if that ever becomes the binding constraint.

METHOD NOTE, reusable. The per-frame table above came from gdb: run the test
under `RUST_MIN_STACK=1048576 gdb -batch -ex run -x <script>`, walk
`gdb.newest_frame()` through `.older()`, and difference each frame's `$sp`.
That names the expensive frames directly, which a `bt` alone does not -- the
backtrace here looked like ordinary recursion and gave no hint that three
functions held 83% of the stack.

title: `test_scalar_float_methods_compute_at_the_declared_width` PINS LINUX'S libm, so it fails on macOS for `cosh` and `sinh` -- and macOS is the one returning the CORRECTLY-ROUNDED f32. A test defect, not a backend divergence: all four Kara surfaces agree with each other on macOS.
detail:
FOUND by reading CI: `Test (macos-latest)` fails this single test on all
three concluded runs of 2026-09-01. Two of the twelve pinned lines differ,
both f32 transcendentals:

    a.cosh(), a = 2.0f32     macOS 3.762195587158203   pinned 3.7621958255767822
    s.sinh(), s = 0.2857...  macOS 0.28961747884750366 pinned 0.2896174490451813

REPRODUCED LOCALLY, byte-identical to CI, on macOS arm64 at 13f6670f.

NOT AN INTERP-VS-CODEGEN SPLIT, which is what the test exists to catch.
Measured on the same machine with a two-call program: `--interp`, JIT and
AOT all print `3.762195587158203` / `0.28961747884750366`. They agree. The
pinned string is what Linux's libm returns, and codegen calls the platform
`coshf` / `sinhf`, so the pin cannot hold on both platforms at once.

macOS IS THE MORE ACCURATE ONE, which matters for how this gets fixed. The
f64 value of cosh(2) is 3.7621956910836314; the two neighbouring f32s are
3.762195587158203 (1.04e-7 away) and 3.7621958255767822 (1.34e-7 away), so
the correctly-rounded f32 is macOS's answer and Linux's `coshf` is 1 ULP
off. A probe on the same host confirms the two routes coincide there:
`coshf(2.0f32)` and `(cosh(2.0f64) as f32)` both give 3.7621956.

So 'compute at the declared width' -- the property the test's own comment
says it is pinning, and the property B-2026-08-29-41 fixed -- is HOLDING on
macOS. What is broken is pinning exact decimal digits of a libm
transcendental across platforms. The fix is a tolerance (or a
platform-conditional expectation) on the transcendental lines only; the
f64 pair at the end of the same test is the boundary check the comment
describes and must stay exact.

Same hazard applies to `test_inverse_hyperbolics_agree_with_the_libm_symbols_codegen_calls`
directly below it, which is green today but pins the same class of value.
fix:
FIXED by 094c206a. The transcendental lines no longer carry frozen digits: the
oracle for `cosh` / `sinh` / `log10` / `atan` is now Rust's own `f32` method,
which lowers to the SAME `coshf` / `sinhf` symbol codegen emits. The assertion
still reads "the interpreter agreed with the symbol codegen calls" -- the
property B-2026-08-29-41 fixed -- it just stops spelling that symbol's answer
as one host's decimal digits. The width-visible methods (`to_degrees` /
`to_radians` / `recip`) stay literal: each is a single correctly-rounded
multiply or divide, identical on any IEEE host, and their pre-fix failure was
f64's 17 digits appearing on an f16 line, not a last ULP.

THE ROW UNDERSTATED IT: THE TEST WAS VACUOUS ON macOS, not merely
mis-pinned. Measured on Apple's libm, NONE of the four receivers the test
shipped with separates "computed at f32 width" from "computed at f64 and
rounded" -- cosh(2.0), sinh/log10/atan(0.2857...) all agree between the two
routes. So on that host the test could never have observed the regression it
exists for; it was only ever checking frozen text, and the CI failure was the
frozen text being another platform's. Three receivers that DO separate them
under Apple's libm are added -- cosh(1.22), sinh(1.175), atan(0.057), found by
sweeping i/1000 for i in 1..4000 (27 / 22 / 262 of 3999 samples discriminate
for cosh / sinh / atan; log10 has none in that range) -- and an ANTI-VACUITY
assertion now fails the test if no sample separates the routes on the host it
runs on, so a future libm cannot silently restore this state.

NOT `assert_prints_float_near`, which `tests/interpreter.rs` already has for
this exact macOS/Linux split (it is used on `asinh` at line ~3238). That helper
is right where the last ULP is NOISE; here the last ULP is the SIGNAL --
f64-then-round differs from the f32 symbol by exactly one -- so a tolerant
compare would admit the very regression being guarded. Exact equality against
a per-host oracle is both stronger and available, because Rust reaches the
same symbol.

BOTH HALVES RED-VERIFIED, not merely observed green:

  * expectations rebuilt from the f64-then-round route -> FAILS, and the diff
    lands ONLY on the three new receivers; the four historical ones are
    byte-identical in both columns. That is the vacuity above, printed.
  * `samples` narrowed to the four historical receivers -> the anti-vacuity
    assertion fires with its own message.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S LAST PARAGRAPH. It claimed the sibling
`test_inverse_hyperbolics_agree_with_the_libm_symbols_codegen_calls` "pins the
same class of value" and shares the hazard. It does not, and never did: that
test (B-2026-08-29-60) already declares `asinh`/`acosh`/`atanh` + the `f`
variants as externs and COMPUTES its expectation from libm, with a comment
saying it does so "instead of freezing one platform's bits into the suite".
This fix brings the older test onto that established pattern rather than
inventing one. Checked at the same time: the other hardcoded transcendental
expectations in the file are exact values (exp(0)=1, ln(1)=0, log10(1000)=3)
or low-precision f16/bf16 vector lanes, neither of which can differ by a ULP
across hosts.

VERIFIED on macOS arm64 at 094c206a: `cargo test -p karac --test interpreter`
1905 passed / 0 failed / 2 ignored; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both
clippy legs (default and `--features llvm`) clean with `-D warnings`. The
`clippy::excessive_precision` lint rejects the long `0.2857142984867096` form
on an `f32` binding, so the Rust side spells it `0.2857143` -- bit-identical,
verified by `to_bits()`, and noted in the code where it could otherwise read
as a drift from the Kara source's literal.

NOT VERIFIED ON LINUX from here, and it cannot be: the test passes on Linux
today, so there is no red-to-green transition to observe on that host. What
the fix relies on there is that glibc's `coshf(2.0)` continues to discriminate
the two routes, which is exactly why the historical receivers were KEPT rather
than replaced. The next `Test (ubuntu-latest)` run is the confirmation.

title: A `Vec`-OF-`Drop` BINDING FOLLOWED BY ANY LATER `let` INITIALIZED FROM A CALL RETURNING A CONTAINER RUNS THE ELEMENT `Drop` BODIES ON FREED MEMORY on the default `karac build` and `karac run` -- `a10 b1 done dR93841100766318`, a different garbage id every run, with a valgrind `Invalid read of size 8` whose `free` is the PRECEDING instruction in the same scope-exit drain. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` is correct on both, which is B-2026-08-31-6's localization; this is the broader scope that row recorded as NOT probed, and it comes back as memory unsafety rather than ordering
detail:
FOUND while memory-checking B-2026-08-30-18's fix, on a program written as a
CONTROL for it. The fix is unrelated and this reproduces identically before it
(verified by stashing `src/` and rebuilding).

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}"); } }
    struct Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }

    fn build(k: i64) -> Box3 {
        let mut v: Vec[R] = Vec.new();
        v.push(R { id: k, tag: f"t" });
        let bx: Box3 = Box3 { xs: v };
        return bx
    }
    fn mkV() -> Vec[String] {
        let mut n: Vec[String] = Vec.new(); n.push(f"aa"); return n
    }

    fn main() {
        let a: Box3 = build(10);
        println(f"a{a.xs[0].id}");
        let b: Vec[String] = mkV();      // <-- ANY LATER CALL RETURNING A Vec
        println(f"b{b.len()}");
        println(f"done");
    }

      --interp                      a10 dR10 b1 done          correct
      KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build  a10 dR10 b1 done          correct
      KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac run    a10 dR10 b1 done          correct
      karac build   (default)       a10 b1 done dR93841100766318
      karac run     (default)       a10 b1 done dR94803644864102

The printed id is a DIFFERENT garbage value on every run, which is the tell that
this is a read from freed memory rather than a merely misplaced body. valgrind
on the default `karac build` binary:

    ==26546== Invalid read of size 8
    ==26546==    at 0x1122E2: main
    ==26546==  Address 0x4b8ea80 is 0 bytes inside a block of size 128 free'd
    ==26546==    at 0x484988F: free
    ==26546==    by 0x1122E1: main                <-- the free is the PRECEDING
    ==26546==  Block was alloc'd at                   instruction in the SAME
    ==26546==    by 0x11B3D1: karac_realloc_or_panic   drain
    definitely lost: 0 bytes in 0 blocks

Under valgrind the program happens to print the CORRECT `dR10`, because the
freed block is not reused before the walk reads it. So this is not reliably
visible from output alone -- a fire-count oracle sees a body in the wrong place,
and only the raw binary shows the garbage.

MECHANISM, in two parts. The first part is B-2026-08-31-6: an auto-par outlined
region terminates the builder's insert block, `fire_due_user_drops` early-returns
for exactly the statement indices the region spans, so a cleanup action whose NLL
endpoint lands inside the region never fires there and falls through to the
scope-exit drain. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` fixing this on both compiled backends is the
same localization that row used. That row explicitly recorded the scope it had
NOT walked -- "Any binding whose NLL endpoint falls inside an outlined region
should be affected -- ordinary non-shadowed locals included -- and that has NOT
been probed." This IS that probe, and it comes back worse than ordering.

THE SECOND PART is what makes it a memory-safety defect rather than late output,
and it is separately fixable: a container's cleanup has a MEMORY half
(`FreeVecBuffer`) and a BODIES half (`UserDrop{ContainerElemBodies}`), and when
BOTH land in the same scope-exit drain the drain emits them in registration
order -- buffer first, element walk second. The walk then reads through a freed
pointer. Without outlining the bodies half fires at its NLL point and never
reaches the drain, so the ordering hazard is invisible. Outlining is only the
reason the two halves met here; ANY future path that defers a bodies action to
the drain hits the same edge.

The evidence for the ordering reading is the valgrind trace above -- `free` at
0x1122E1 and the invalid read at 0x1122E2, both in `main`, adjacent -- rather
than a read of the emitter, so treat it as strongly-supported rather than
confirmed at the source.

DISCRIMINATORS, measured, holding everything else fixed:

    later binding is a CALL returning Vec[String]   FAULTS   (the repro)
    later binding is a CALL returning a struct
      wrapping a Vec                                FAULTS
    later binding is a CALL returning String        clean
    later binding is a CALL returning i64           clean
    later binding is a LOCAL Vec[String] built
      in place with Vec.new() + push                clean
    no later binding at all                         clean
    later binding from a Vec-returning call,
      never READ                                    FAULTS

So the trigger is narrow and precise: a `Vec`-of-`Drop`-carrying binding, then a
LATER binding initialized from a CALL whose return type carries a container. The
later binding does NOT have to be read -- what matters is that the call is there.
One element in the `Vec` is enough. With two elements BOTH bodies still fire, at
the end, and only the first reads garbage (`a10 b1 done dR140731402482628 dR11`),
which is another reason the symptom is easy to misread as a partial one.

WHY IT MATTERS more than its narrowness suggests: `let a = f(); use(a); let b =
g(); use(b);` where both callees return containers is unremarkable code, it is
the default `karac build` path (auto-par is on), and the failure is silent --
the wrong bytes are read and a `Drop` that closes a handle or decrements a
refcount runs against freed memory.

NOT VISIBLE TO `tests/codegen.rs`, for B-2026-08-31-6's reason: that harness
compiles sequentially and never sees the outlined column. A regression test
belongs in `tests/par_codegen.rs`.
fix:
Fixed in 6486e68 -- the MEMORY-SAFETY half only; see SCOPE below.

`emit_scope_cleanup_from` drains a frame LIFO (`(0..n).rev()`), so the action
pushed LAST runs FIRST. The `let` path registered the `StructFieldBodies` walk
BEFORE `track_struct_var_inst`, so the struct's own memory drop drained one step
AHEAD of the walk that reads through it, and the element `Drop` body ran on
freed memory. This is the B-2026-08-01-2 memory-before-bodies rule, which this
site had backwards; the fix swaps the two registrations.

CONFIRMED AT THE SOURCE, which this row asked for. It recorded the ordering
reading as "strongly-supported rather than confirmed at the source", resting on
the valgrind adjacency (`free` at 0x1122E1, invalid read at 0x1122E2).
Instrumenting the drain settles it -- for `main`, in drain order:

    [emit] frame=0 idx=2 FreeVecBuffer slot="b4"
    [emit] frame=0 idx=1 StructDrop                          <- frees a.xs
    [emit] frame=0 idx=0 UserDrop[StructFieldBodies] a slot="a"   <- reads it

The row's two-part mechanism is confirmed exactly as written. Part 1
(B-2026-08-31-6, outlining swallowing the NLL fire) is what puts both halves in
the same drain; part 2 (the drain's own order) is what makes it unsafe rather
than merely late, and is separately fixable -- fixed here.

FIXED AT THE REGISTRATION SITE, NOT IN THE AUTO-PAR LOWERING, for the reason the
row gives: outlining is only what made the two halves meet, and any future path
that defers a bodies action to the drain hits the same edge. Ordering them
correctly where they are pushed makes that safe by construction.

SCOPE -- THE ORDERING HALF REMAINS OPEN. Under auto-par the body now runs
CORRECTLY but still LATE: `a10 b1 done dR10`, against interp and
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`'s `a10 dR10 b1 done`. That residual divergence is
B-2026-08-31-6 and is deliberately untouched. This row is titled and classed on
the freed-memory read, which is gone.

ALL EIGHT OF THE ROW'S DISCRIMINATORS re-measured post-fix, each valgrind-clean
(exit 0) with correct body counts:

    Vec-returning call            a10 b1 done dR10        was garbage id
    call returning Vec-in-struct  a10 b1 done dR10        was garbage id
    later binding never read      a10 done dR10           was garbage id
    two elements                  a10 b1 done dR10 dR11   was garbage then dR11
    call returning String         a10 dR10 b2 done        unchanged
    call returning i64            a10 dR10 b5 done        unchanged
    Vec built in place            a10 dR10 b1 done        unchanged
    no later binding              a10 dR10 done           unchanged

THE SANITIZER DOES NOT CATCH THIS ONE, and both new tests say so rather than
implying otherwise. Measured on the pre-fix compiler: valgrind reports `Invalid
read of size 8` (1 error from 1 context), while the ASAN harness exits CLEAN and
the pre-fix case fails only on `stdout mismatch`, printing a garbage `dR64`. So
the expected-id transcript is the oracle for this class and a green sanitizer run
alone is not evidence -- which is also why the row's own note that valgrind
sometimes printed the CORRECT `dR10` matters: output is not a reliable oracle
either unless the expectation is pinned.

TESTS. The regression test is `tests/par_codegen.rs`'s
`test_par_field_bodies_walk_runs_before_the_struct_memory_drop` (all eight
discriminators), where the row said it belongs -- `tests/codegen.rs` compiles
sequentially and structurally cannot reach the shape. A companion
`memory_sanitizer.rs` case runs the same program in the auto-par column under a
sanitizer, documented as a transcript check rather than a sanitizer check.
RED-verified: pre-fix the par_codegen fixture yields `dR94353033004857` against
`dR10`.

Verified across `--interp` / JIT / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`, and
re-verified after rebasing onto ed0a330. Gates: both clippy legs and
`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `tests/codegen.rs` 3541 passed / 0 failed,
`tests/interpreter.rs` 1905 / 0, `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` 1365 / 0,
`tests/par_codegen.rs` 276 / 0.

title: THE INTERPRETER MIRROR OF B-2026-08-30-18: a STRUCT literal in RETURN POSITION whose field is a PLAIN `Drop` value moved in from a local runs that value's `Drop` body TWICE under `--interp` and once on all three compiled surfaces -- `mid dR14 v14 dR14 post` against `mid v14 dR14 post`. The bare tail behaves the same, the named-binding and TUPLE-literal spellings are both correct, and the CONTAINER-field spelling that -18 was about is correct under `--interp` in all five spellings, which is why -18's own control was clean
detail:
THE INTERPRETER MIRROR of B-2026-08-30-18, found while measuring that row's fix
across the four surfaces. That row was the compiled backends doubling a
CONTAINER field's element bodies for a return-position aggregate literal; this is
the interpreter doubling a PLAIN `Drop` field's own body for the same position.
The two are opposite halves of one shape and neither fix touches the other --
B-2026-08-30-18's fix is in `src/codegen/exprs.rs` and cannot reach `--interp`,
and this reproduces unchanged with it applied.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}"); } }
    struct W { r: R }

    fn build(k: i64) -> W {
        let r: R = R { id: k, tag: f"t" };
        println("mid");
        return W { r: r }             // <-- literal AT the return
    }

    fn main() {
        let a: W = build(14);
        println(f"v{a.r.id}");
        println("post");
    }

      --interp                      mid dR14 v14 dR14 post   TWO bodies
      karac run (JIT)               mid v14 dR14 post        correct
      karac build                   mid v14 dR14 post        correct
      KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build  mid v14 dR14 post        correct

`r` is MOVED into the returned literal, so the local's own body must not fire --
one body, at the caller's binding death. The interpreter fires it at `build`'s
exit as well, before the caller has even read the field, so the extra body
observes a value that is logically gone. Nothing crashes (the interpreter's
values are refcounted), but a `Drop` that closes a handle, releases a lock or
decrements an external counter runs twice.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS RETURN POSITION AND THE STRUCT FORM, both required, and it
is clean. Holding everything else fixed:

    return W { r: r }                       TWO      <- the repro
    W { r: r }              (bare tail)     TWO      <- same, no `return` needed
    let w: W = W { r: r }; return w         one, correct
    let w: W = W { r: r }; ...  (no return) one, correct
    return (r, 3)           (tuple literal) one, correct

So it is not the literal and not the move -- it is a STRUCT literal in RETURN
POSITION, which is exactly the position B-2026-08-30-18 named on the other side.
The tuple row is the one worth keeping: it shows the interpreter's aggregate
handling is not uniformly wrong, so a fix has a working sibling to match rather
than a rule to invent.

NOT COVERED BY the container spelling: with `struct Box3 { xs: Vec[R] }` the
interpreter is correct in all five rows above, which is why B-2026-08-30-18's
own control was clean and this stayed hidden behind it.

WHERE TO LOOK: the return path in `src/interpreter/` that evaluates a
struct-literal result while the enclosing frame is being torn down -- the local
is still bound in the frame when the frame's drop pass runs, and the literal

FILED SEPARATELY from B-2026-08-30-18 rather than widening it: that row is
