title: A GENERIC function's conditionally-returned by-value param loses the DYING one's `Drop` body on ALL THREE COMPILED lanes while `--interp` runs it -- the byte-identical CONCRETE function is correct on all four
detail:
Isolated to ONE variable -- `[T]` versus a concrete `R` -- in one program, with
the same call and the same argument shapes on both sides:

    struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.id}") } }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> String { return f"pay-{i}-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"; }

    fn gpick[T](a: T, k: bool, alt: T) -> T { if k { return alt; } return a; }
    fn cpick(a: R,  k: bool, alt: R)  -> R  { if k { return alt; } return a; }

    concrete   let x = cpick(R{11}, true, R{12})    d11 C12 d12   on ALL FOUR lanes
    generic    let x = gpick(R{21}, true, R{22})    d21 G22 d22   --interp
                                                        G22 d22   JIT / AOT / AOT+auto-par

`a` dies inside the callee on the `k = true` path, so its body must run exactly
once; the three compiled lanes run nothing for it. The ASSOCIATED spelling
(`H.gpick(...)`) behaves identically to this free-function one, so the variable
is generics, not how the callee is spelled.

NOT A MEMORY BUG, and that is what makes it invisible to the existing gates.
Measured under valgrind on the AOT binary: 13 allocs, 13 frees, "All heap blocks
were freed -- no leaks are possible", 0 errors. The compiled backends free the
dying param's `String` correctly and skip only the user `Drop` BODY, so no
ASAN/LSan fixture in the tree can catch it -- the A/B parity rule is the only
thing that sees it.

PRE-EXISTING, verified rather than assumed. Measured at pristine `main`
(13f6670), before B-2026-09-01-44's fix, where the FREE-function generic already
diverged exactly this way. That fix touches only the interpreter's
associated-call name resolution; it did not create this, it made the associated
spelling share the free spelling's behaviour, which is how the divergence became
visible in a second place.

WHERE TO START. `cond_returned_param_drop_names` (src/interpreter/eval_call.rs)
claims generics "like any other shape since B-2026-08-28-71", and that row's
whole point was that `compile_mono_function` had gained the matching
registration -- so a mono registration exists and does not fire for this shape.
The question to settle first is which half: the mono's own parameter
registration, or the CALL-SITE stand-down (codegen's `call_arg_flows_into_return`
/ `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` pair) answering against the GENERIC AST
at a monomorphized callee. Instrumenting which of the two declines costs one
build and rules out half the search.

NOT MEASURED: a `[T: Display]`-BOUNDED generic; a generic with exactly ONE
conditionally-returned param (the probe above has two, `a` and `alt`); and
whether a generic METHOD -- as opposed to a free or associated fn -- makes a
third answer.

SIBLING: B-2026-09-02-4 is the other shape this same probe sweep turned up
(an aggregate that WRAPS the param), and it is a different defect -- that one
also involves the compiled lanes, but in the opposite direction.
fix:
FIXED by 56cb337, and it is one line of substance: the mono registration
read the parameter's DECLARED type off the GENERIC AST.

`compile_mono_function`'s conditionally-returned-param registration
(src/codegen/mono.rs) ends in a `drop_method_keys` lookup keyed by the first
path segment of `param.ty`. For a param declared `a: T` that segment is the
literal string "T", no such type exists, the lookup fails, and the registration
silently does not happen -- so the value that died inside the callee had no
owner on any compiled lane, while `--interp` (which resolves a generic by its
declared name) ran its body.

The row's "WHERE TO START" offered two halves to instrument -- the mono param
registration, or the call-site stand-down answering against the generic AST. It
is the FIRST, and the instrumentation says so exactly. At that site:

    [MONOCOND] fn=gpick param=a
        raw=Path(["T"])  substituted=Path(["R"])  names={"T": "R"}

The gate FIRES (`fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` is true); only the type
lookup underneath it fails. `subst_monomorph_type_params` -- the resolver that
already exists and is already live at that point -- answers `R`, so the fix is
to consult the resolved type rather than the declared one. No new channel, no
new plumbing.

WHY B-2026-08-28-71 LOOKED COMPLETE, which is the part worth keeping. Its
measurement was `genf(R { id: 1, name: f"i1" }, false, 7)`, and every generic
case it left behind in `e2e_conditionally_returned_param_user_drop_body_runs_once`
has the same shape: the conditionally-returned param is declared CONCRETELY
(`r: R`, `h: H`) and the type parameter `T` is used only for an extra scalar
argument. That hands the lookup a real struct name, so all of them passed. The
gap is exactly and only the param whose declared type IS the type parameter --
which no case in the family had.

THE BLAST RADIUS IS WIDER THAN THIS ROW'S PROBE SHOWED, and all three of its
NOT-MEASURED questions answer the same way. Measured on pristine `src`, every
one of these lost the dying param's body on ALL THREE compiled lanes and is
correct on all four now, from this single change:

    fn pick[T](a: T, k: bool, alt: T)              both branch directions
    fn pickd[T: Display](a: T, k: bool, alt: T)    BOUNDED type parameter
    impl H { fn agen[T](a: T, ...) }               ASSOCIATED function
    impl H { fn mgen[T](ref self, a: T, ...) }     instance METHOD

So a bound does not route the type differently, the free / associated / method
spellings do not differ, and which of the two params dies does not matter.

FIXTURES: three cases added to the existing pair,
`e2e_conditionally_returned_param_user_drop_body_runs_once` (tests/codegen.rs)
and `test_conditionally_returned_param_user_drop_body_runs_once`
(tests/interpreter.rs), kept verbatim in step as that pairing requires. The
codegen half RED-verifies on pristine `src` -- `left: "42\ndrop n42\n"` against
`right: "drop n41\n42\ndrop n42\n"`, the missing body. The interpreter half was
already correct and is pinned as the TARGET, which is what the existing generic
cases in that table are for too.

STILL TRUE FROM THE OPENING MEASUREMENT: this was never a memory bug. Valgrind
on the AOT binary reported 13 allocs / 13 frees and 0 errors -- the compiled
backends freed the dying param's `String` correctly and skipped only the user
`Drop` BODY. That is why no ASAN/LSan fixture could catch it and why the A/B
parity rule was the only thing that saw it.

title: AN ASSOCIATED fn returning an AGGREGATE THAT WRAPS a by-value param diverges in BOTH directions at once -- the compiled lanes run the wrapped param's `Drop` body TWICE and `--interp` loses it when the param dies -- while the FREE-function twin agrees on all four lanes and is wrong on one cell everywhere
detail:
struct R { id: i64, s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.id}") } }
    struct Box2 { r: R }
    impl Drop for Box2 { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"B{self.r.id}") } }
    struct H { n: i64 }
    fn mk(i: i64) -> String { return f"pay-{i}-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"; }

    fn fmake(r: R, k: bool) -> Box2 {
        if k { return Box2 { r: R { id: 77, s: mk(77) } }; } return Box2 { r: r };
    }
    impl H { fn amake(r: R, k: bool) -> Box2 { ...same body, fresh id 87... } }

Four cells, each `let x = <call>(R { id: N, .. }, k); println(f"C{x.r.id}")`:

    ft  free   k=true    all four lanes  C77 B77 d77       dN LOST on every lane
    ff  free   k=false   all four lanes  C53 B53 d53       correct
    at  assoc  k=true    --interp        C87 B87 d87       d55 LOST
                         3 compiled      d55 C87 B87 d87   correct
    af  assoc  k=false   --interp        C57 B57 d57       correct
                         3 compiled      d57 C57 B57 d57   d57 TWICE

TWO SPELLINGS OF ONE BODY DISAGREE IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, and neither backend
is right about both cells. `at` is the interpreter losing a body the compiled
lanes get right; `af` is the compiled lanes running one the interpreter gets
right.

`ft` IS A THIRD DEFECT AND IT IS THE REASON THIS IS NOT "MAKE INTERP MATCH
COMPILED": the FREE spelling at `k = true` loses the dying param's body on ALL
FOUR lanes -- a shared gap, so it produces no A/B divergence to notice -- which
means the compiled answer at `at` is not self-evidently the intended one either.
Settle what the free spelling should print before porting either backend to the
other.

NOT A MEMORY BUG in the `af` direction. Measured under valgrind on the AOT
binary: 28 allocs, 28 frees, "All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are
possible", 0 errors. The second `d57` is a duplicated user `Drop` BODY over
memory freed exactly once, not a double free -- so the cost is a wrong
observable side effect, and no ASAN fixture catches it.

WHY THIS IS NOT B-2026-09-01-44. Measured byte-identical on all four lanes
before and after that fix. The predicates that decide ownership here are the
AGGREGATE-return ones, and this shape falls between them:
`fn_always_returns_param` admits a returned aggregate (`Box2 { r: r }`) per its
own doc, while `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` declines it because the
hand-back is not bare -- so a param wrapped on one path and absent on the other
satisfies neither. That gap is what -44's name resolution newly exposes the
associated callee to, not something it introduced.

NOT MEASURED: the ENUM-VARIANT spelling of the same wrap (`Slot.Held(r)`), which
`record_ctor_arg_moves` handles through a different channel; a two-level wrap;
and whether an instance METHOD spelling produces a third answer.

SIBLING: B-2026-09-02-3 is the other shape this same probe sweep turned up (a
GENERIC conditionally-returned param), which loses a body on the compiled lanes
where this one duplicates one.

title: A PARAM-VIEW ASSIGNMENT `h2 = h` OVER A `Drop`-BEARING STRUCT LEAKS THE MOVED-IN VALUE'S `String` AT `-O0` -- one block per assignment that actually runs, and 0 errors at `-O2`, which is exactly the masking B-2026-08-04-19 recorded for the ENUM sibling of the same branch. The struct leg takes no `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg` call because a code comment asserts `h2 = h` is already clean; the `-O0` leg says otherwise
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-30-53's fix, which measured it and did not cause it: the
numbers are IDENTICAL before and after that fix (verified against a stashed
`src/`), and that fix reduces the total on a program that exercises both paths
only because it restores a body that frees on the other one.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

    fn f(h: R) -> i64 {
        let mut h2: R = R { id: 1, tag: f"a" };
        h2 = h;                                 // <-- param-view assignment
        return h2.id
    }
    fn main() { let v: i64 = f(R { id: 4, tag: f"b" }); println(f"v{v}") }

      KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 karac build -> valgrind: definitely lost: 1 bytes in 1 blocks
      KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=2 karac build -> valgrind: 0 errors, 0 bytes lost

The leaked block is the MOVED-IN value's `String` field -- 1 byte for `f"b"`, 2
for a two-character tag, so it tracks the payload exactly. Output is correct on
every surface (`dR1 dR4 v4` on all four); this is memory only.

DISCRIMINATORS, measured:

    `h2 = h` with `impl Drop for R`             LEAKS at -O0
    the same struct with NO `impl Drop`         clean
    `out = p` inside a fn, param moved in       LEAKS at -O0 (2 bytes)
    `out = r` where the arm is NOT taken        clean (no move happened)
    a FRESH value assigned (`out = R { .. }`)   clean
    every shape above at -O2                    clean

So the trigger is precisely the shape B-2026-08-01-16's `rhs_is_param_view`
branch handles, and only when the struct carries a user `Drop`. That branch
disarms the TARGET's bodies (now per-path, B-2026-08-30-53) and relies on the
memory half being "name-blind and survives the retraction". The -O0 measurement
says that claim does not hold for the SOURCE's heap here: the param's entry copy
is moved into the target and its buffer is freed by neither.

-O2 CLEANLINESS IS NOT EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE, and it is why this needs its own row
rather than a note: the same optimizer that hides it here has hidden the same
class before (B-2026-08-04-19 was "masked at -O2 by DSE"). The `-O0` leg is the
authoritative one for this class.

NOT the same as B-2026-08-04-19, which is the value-ENUM sibling of this branch
and already zeroes the source's payload caps via
`suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg`. The STRUCT leg takes no such call -- the
code comment says "the struct sibling is already disarmed upstream (`h2 = h` is
clean)", and that sentence is what this row contradicts at -O0.

WHERE TO START: the `if lhs_is_tracked_value_enum { self.suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg(value); }`
line in the Assign arm's param-view branch, and the question of why the struct
leg is exempt from it.

title: A `cond_move_drop_flags` PER-PATH DROP FLAG IS INITIALIZED IN THE ENTRY BLOCK, SO IT IS ARMED ONCE PER CALL AND NOT ONCE PER LOOP ITERATION -- an assignment that runs on SOME iterations leaves it `false` for all later ones and a later iteration's freshly-declared target loses its own `Drop` body. Identical output before and after B-2026-08-30-53 (that fix neither causes nor cures it), and the limitation has been in the mechanism since B-2026-08-28-51
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-30-53's fix. That fix replaced an all-paths retraction of
an assignment target's `Drop` body with a per-path bool flag
(B-2026-08-28-51's `cond_move_drop_flags`, applied to the TARGET). The flag is
allocated and initialized to `true` in the function's ENTRY block, which
dominates every path -- and is therefore executed ONCE per call, not once per
loop iteration. An assignment that runs on SOME iterations leaves the flag
`false` for all later ones, so a later iteration's freshly-declared target loses
its own body.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }

    fn dies(p: R) -> i64 {
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        while i < 2 {
            println(f"it{i}");
            let mut out: R = R { id: 90 + i, tag: f"t" };
            if i == 0 { out = p; }              // <-- runs on iteration 0 only
            acc = acc + out.id;
            i = i + 1;
        }
        return acc
    }
    fn main() { println(f"acc{dies(R { id: 5, tag: f"q" })}") }

      --interp     -> `it0 dR90 it1 dR91 dR5 acc96`   correct
      karac build  -> `it0 dR90 it1 dR5 acc96`        R{91}'s body LOST

IDENTICAL PRE- AND POST-B-2026-08-30-53, verified against a stashed `src/`, so
that fix neither causes nor cures this -- before it the all-paths retraction lost
the body, after it the stale flag does. It is filed against the flag because the
flag is the mechanism that owns the path now, and because the remedy is
different: the retraction had no per-path story at all, whereas this needs the
`true` re-armed at the binding's declaration rather than at the function's entry.

WHY THE OBVIOUS PLACEMENT IS NOT AVAILABLE, stated so the next attempt does not
re-derive it: the flag is created LAZILY at the assignment site, which codegen
reaches AFTER it has already compiled the enclosing `let`. There is no recorded
per-variable declaration position to go back and insert a `store true` into, and
the loop body is compiled once, so a re-arm emitted at the `let` on a later pass
does not exist. Either the flag creation moves earlier (an AST pre-scan at the
`let` for `<name> = <bare identifier>` anywhere in the function, conservative and
cheap) or the re-arm goes at the top of the innermost enclosing loop body,
restricted to bindings whose action lives in a frame opened inside that loop.

SCOPE. `cond_move_drop_flags` has carried this limitation since B-2026-08-28-51,
so every flag-owned binding is exposed to it, not only assignment targets. What
makes the target case reachable at all is that the RHS must be an owned param or
a view of one: matching a param in a loop consumes it, so the MATCH spelling of
B-2026-08-30-53 cannot reach this -- an `if`-guarded assignment can, which is
what the repro uses. The use-after-move that the repro's second iteration
implies is reported as a WARNING rather than an error today (B-2026-08-29-64),
which is why it compiles.

title: A `while let` ARM THAT BINDS ITS PAYLOAD RUNS THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE PER PASS UNDER `--interp` AND ONCE ON BOTH COMPILED BACKENDS -- the compiled column is the correct one (one value, one body), the surplus scales with the iteration count, and the same loop binding NOTHING is correct on all three, which isolates the trigger to the binding rather than to the loop
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-31-38, in the `while let` row of that fix's own
regression matrix. PRE-EXISTING and independent of it: the interpreter column is
byte-identical against the stashed pre-fix compiler, and that fix touches
`src/codegen/control_flow.rs` only -- the interpreter is not in its diff at all.
It became visible because -38's fix repaired the COMPILED column of the same
program from zero bodies to one, which is what turned an agreed-and-wrong cell
into a divergence.

    fn pad(t: i64) -> String { .. }              // a 44-byte String
    struct R { s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.s.len()}") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }

                                                     interp        build
    let mut q: Option[H] = Some(H { .. });
    while let Some(H { r, .. }) = q { ..; q = None } 44 dR44 dR44   44 dR44
    // whole-payload binding, payload IS the `Drop` type
    while let Some(r) = p { ..; p = None }          44 dR44 dR44   44 dR44
    // CONTROL -- binds nothing
    while let Some(_) = u { ..; u = None }          hit dR44       hit dR44
    // two passes, a fresh value stored each time
    while let Some(H { r, .. }) = z { ..; z = Some(..) or None }
                                     44 dR44 dR44 44 dR44 dR44     44 dR44 44 dR44

ONE `R` IS CONSTRUCTED PER PASS, so ONE body is due per pass, which makes the
COMPILED column correct here and the interpreter the surplus. The
wildcard-pattern control is what pins the cause: the same loop over the same
value, differing only in whether the arm BINDS the payload, is correct at one
body on every surface. So the trigger is the binding, not the loop and not the
`Option` envelope.

IT SCALES. The two-pass row runs four bodies against the two that are due, so
the surplus is one per iteration and unbounded in a longer loop -- which is why
this is medium and not low even though it is bodies-only.

THE `if let` TWIN IS CORRECT, which is what makes this specifically the
`while let` leg: the identical destructure under `if let` runs exactly one body
on all three surfaces after B-2026-08-31-38. Both spellings share
`compile_if_let`'s suppression battery on the codegen side, so the asymmetry is
on the interpreter's side of the loop.

BODIES ONLY -- no memory fault is implied. `valgrind --leak-check=full` at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` on the compiled binary is 12 allocs / 12 frees, 0 errors;
the interpreter's surplus is a second CALL of the body over the same live
value, not a second free. A payload whose body MUTATES `self` would observe the
difference twice, which is the user-visible harm.

WHERE TO START: the interpreter's `while let` desugaring and its
`pattern_consumes_user_drop_payload` twin -- the loop appears to both hand the
arm's binding a body AND leave the scrutinee's own walk armed for the same
pass, where `if let` picks one. Compare against
`eval_stmt.rs`'s `if let` leg, which is the shape that is right.

PINNED as the `while let` row of `e2e_a_let_family_destructure_runs_the_payload_
drop_body_once` (tests/codegen.rs), whose interp column deliberately records
`47 dR47 dR47 end` against the compiled `47 dR47 end`. Closing this row will
fail that fixture, which is the intent -- update the row's interp expectation in
the same commit.

NOT MEASURED: whether a `for` loop over a container of the same payload has the
same shape, and whether a `while let` over a `Result` differs from `Option`.

ID NOTE: filed as B-2026-09-02-3; renumbered to B-2026-09-02-7 before landing because a concurrent session had already published a different bug under that id. The ledger's id-allocation race, exactly as CLAUDE.md describes it -- both sessions computed the same next id from the same base.
fix:
FIXED by 51491e9. THE INTERPRETER'S `while let` NEVER CALLED THE DISARM ITS
`if let` TWIN CALLS. `if let` runs
`disarm_moved_out_enum_payload_one(value, &val, pattern, Some(then_block))`
before the match test: when the pattern MOVES a Drop-bearing payload out of an
identifier / `self` place, that place's own payload-body walk is retracted, so
the body comes from the arm's binding and from nothing else. `while let` had the
stash half (B-2026-07-30-11's `pending_arm_drop_bindings` push) and not the
retraction half, so on every matched pass the arm's binding ran the body AND the
source's still-armed walk ran it again. That is the whole surplus: the row's own
wildcard control was right because a pattern that binds nothing never pushes a
stash.

THE FIX IS THE PAIR, NOT THE CALL, and adding the call alone would have been a
regression. An arm that only READS THROUGH the payload moves nothing out, so
`takes_payload` declines and the source keeps its walk — an ungated stash then
doubles exactly as before. So `if let`'s `reads_through` gate moved across in
the same commit and `consuming_scrutinee` now carries `!reads_through`, which is
how the two spellings answer the same question the same way.

THE FRESH-TEMP CASE IS DELIBERATELY UNTOUCHED, and this is where the row's
"WHERE TO START" pointed at the right file for a reason that needed correcting.
B-2026-08-28-67 had declined to gate this leg, reasoning that "the scrutinee is
re-evaluated per iteration, so there is no stable binding whose walk could be
handed the payload back". That is true of a FRESH TEMP and only of one. An
IDENTIFIER scrutinee is re-READ per iteration but is the same binding
throughout, and it has exactly the walk `if let` hands the payload back to.
`place_walk_is_retractable` is the line between the two, so
`while let Some(r) = v.pop()` keeps its stash and is byte-identical before and
after (measured on both compilers). That comment has been rewritten in place
rather than deleted, since the half of it that is true is load-bearing.

THE OVERWRITE WAS NOT THE SECOND BODY'S SOURCE, which is worth recording
because `q = None` sits in every repro and looks like the obvious suspect. The
same loop with a bare `break` in place of the assignment doubled identically
(`47 dR47 dR47 end` interp, `47 dR47 end` compiled), which is what localizes the
surplus to the scope-exit walk of the source rather than to the assignment's
overwrite drop.

MEASURED, pre-fix / post-fix, interpreter (compiled columns unchanged and
correct throughout — the diff is `src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs` only):

    destructure binding, one pass    47 dR47 dR47   ->  47 dR47
    whole-payload binding            47 dR47 dR47   ->  47 dR47
    arm moves the payload out        47 dR47 dR47   ->  47 dR47
    two passes, fresh value each     47 dR47 dR47 47 dR47 dR47 -> 47 dR47 47 dR47
    binds nothing (control)          hit dR47       ->  hit dR47
    fresh temp `v.pop()` (control)   pop47 dR47 pop47 dR47  ->  unchanged

BOTH "NOT MEASURED" ITEMS ANSWERED. A `while let` over `Result` behaves exactly
as the `Option` one does and is fixed by the same change — the disarm keys on
the PLACE, not on the envelope — and so does a `while let` over a USER enum
(`W.C(H { r, .. })`). A `for` loop over a container of the same payload never
had the defect: all three surfaces agree there, deferring both bodies to the
loop's end.

THE TWO-PASS ROW IS ALSO AN AUTO-PAR PROBE, and reading it wrong nearly cost a
spurious filing. `karac build`'s DEFAULT leg prints `47 47 end dR47` for it —
both bodies deferred to scope exit and one of the two lost — against the correct
`47 dR47 47 dR47 end` from `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` and from the E2E
harness. That is not a new defect and not this row's: it is B-2026-08-31-6, an
outlined region swallowing the NLL drop points of the statements it spans,
reproduced here on a `while let` rather than on a shadowed binding. Measured
identically against the pre-fix compiler. Recorded rather than filed.

THE `while let` SPELLING OF B-2026-09-02-8 EXISTS TOO, and is untouched by this
fix (nothing binds the `Drop`-bearing field there, so neither the disarm nor the
stash is in play): `while let Some(H { n, .. }) = y` prints `4 end` under the
interpreter against `4 dR47 end` on both compiled backends, exactly as that
row's `if let` spelling does. Pinned as a control in the new fixture so the two
spellings close together.

TESTS. `e2e_while_let_binding_runs_the_payload_drop_body_once_per_pass`
(tests/codegen.rs) is the eleven-row cross-backend matrix — every shape above
plus the `Result`, user-enum, `for`-loop and B-2026-09-02-8 controls, each with
separate interpreter and compiled expectation columns.
`test_while_let_binding_runs_the_payload_drop_body_once_per_pass`
(tests/interpreter.rs) carries the same shapes on the DEFAULT leg, because the
fix is interpreter-only and the E2E matrix is gated on `--features llvm` — CI's
default leg would otherwise see none of it. The `while let` row of
`e2e_a_let_family_destructure_runs_the_payload_drop_body_once` pinned this
divergence deliberately (`47 dR47 dR47` interp against `47 dR47` compiled) and
is updated in the same commit, which is what that pin was for.

title: AN `Option`-ENVELOPED STRUCT PATTERN THAT BINDS ONLY THE NON-`Drop` FIELD LOSES THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY IN THE INTERPRETER on both the `if let` and `match` spellings -- and the `let ... else` spelling of the same pattern loses it on ALL FOUR SURFACES, which is agreed-and-wrong rather than a divergence; the same pattern WITHOUT the `Option` envelope, and the same envelope binding NOTHING, are correct everywhere
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-31-38, as a CONTROL row in that fix's matrix that
was expected to be uninteresting. PRE-EXISTING and independent of it: that fix
touches `src/codegen/control_flow.rs` only, and the `match` cell below -- whose
leg the fix demonstrably never reaches (traced: the retraction it gates does not
fire on the `match` leg for this program) -- shows the identical interpreter
answer.

    fn pad(t: i64) -> String { .. }              // a 44-byte String
    struct R { s: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.s.len()}") } }
    struct H { r: R, n: i64 }

                                                       interp     build
    A  if let Some(H { n, .. }) = a { .. }             A4         A4 dR44
    B  match b { Some(H { n, .. }) => .., None => {} } B4         B4 dR44
    C  if let H { n, .. } = c { .. }      // no envelope
                                                       C4 dR44    C4 dR44
    D  match d { H { n, .. } => .. }      // no envelope
                                                       D4 dR44    D4 dR44
    E  let Some(H { n, .. }) = e else { return };      E4         E4
    G  if let Some(H { .. }) = g { .. }   // binds nothing
                                                       G dR44     G dR44

ONE `R` IS CONSTRUCTED PER ROW, so ONE body is due in every one of them. The
bound field `n` is an `i64`; nothing the pattern names owns the `String`, and
`r` is never mentioned, so the envelope's own walk should run the body exactly
as it does when the pattern binds nothing (row G).

THE FOUR CONTROLS ARE THE DIAGNOSIS. Removing the `Option` envelope fixes it
(C, D). Binding nothing fixes it (G). Binding the `Drop` field itself is
correct on all three after B-2026-08-31-38. So the defect is the intersection:
an `Option`/`Result` envelope AND a struct sub-pattern that binds SOME field but
not the `Drop`-carrying one -- a partial destructure the envelope's
payload-bodies walk apparently treats as a full consume.

ROW E IS THE HALF THAT IS NOT A DIVERGENCE, and it is the more serious one:
`let ... else` loses the body on the interpreter AND both compiled backends, so
`karac run`, `karac build` and `--interp` agree on the wrong answer and the A/B
rule cannot catch it. It is kept in this row rather than split because it is the
same shape -- same envelope, same partial destructure -- and a fix that
understands the shape should settle all three spellings at once. If it turns out
they need separate mechanisms, split E out then.

BODIES ONLY as far as measured: the compiled column of A/B is correct, so no
memory question arises there; row E's memory side has NOT been measured and
should be, since a body that never runs on any backend may or may not mean the
buffer is also stranded. Run it under the Linux LSan leg before assuming this is
bodies-only.

PINNED as two deliberately-divergent rows of `e2e_a_let_family_destructure_runs_
the_payload_drop_body_once` (tests/codegen.rs) -- the `if let` and `match`
spellings of A/B, whose interp column records the missing body against the
correct compiled one. Closing this row will fail that fixture, which is the
intent. Row E is NOT pinned there and should be added when this is fixed.

NOT MEASURED: the `Result` envelope, an enum struct-variant payload in the same
position, and whether binding a SECOND non-`Drop` field alongside `n` changes
anything.

ID NOTE: filed as B-2026-09-02-4; renumbered to B-2026-09-02-8 before landing because a concurrent session had already published a different bug under that id. The ledger's id-allocation race, exactly as CLAUDE.md describes it -- both sessions computed the same next id from the same base.
fix:
FIXED by b86bef0. BOTH BACKENDS DECIDED THE `Option`/`Result` PAYLOAD
RETRACTION SHAPE-ONLY, and a partial destructure is the shape that breaks.
Retracting a source's payload-bodies walk is a HAND-OFF: the pattern moves the
`Drop`-bearing payload out and its new binding runs the body instead. The
Option/Result leg of that decision asked only whether the sub-pattern binds
ANYTHING -- `patterns.iter().any(pattern_claims_ownership)` in the interpreter's
`pattern_consumes_user_drop_payload`, `patterns.iter().any(pattern_consumes_
field)` in codegen's `suppress_optres_payload_bodies_for_match`. `Some(H { n, ..
})` binds `n: i64` and leaves the `Drop`-bearing `r: R` untouched, so it counted
as a consume: the walk was retracted and nothing took over. The interpreter's arm
stash is filtered by what the bindings actually own and came out empty; the
`let ... else` binding that escapes owns nothing either. The body ran nowhere.

BOTH SITES NOW CONSULT DECLARED FIELD TYPES for a struct sub-pattern --
`optres_sub_takes_drop_bearing`, added arm-for-arm to each backend and reading
the same two declaration sources (program then baked stdlib), resolving either a
struct name (`["H"]`) or an enum STRUCT VARIANT (`["V", "A"]`).

A BARE BINDING KEEPS THE SHAPE ANSWER, deliberately, and that is the part the
original comment got right. `Some(r)` names a payload whose declared type is a
generic parameter, invisible to both backends, and there the over-approximation
IS a no-op: an `Option[i64]` source registers no walk to retract. Only a
DESTRUCTURE has field types to consult, and only a destructure can name a
position the source's walk was covering for. An unknown type name falls back to
the shape answer rather than silently declining, which keeps every unrecognised
shape exactly where it was.

ONE PREDICATE SETTLES BOTH FAILURE MODES, which the row predicted and left
conditional ("If it turns out they need separate mechanisms, split E out then" --
they did not). Rows A and B were interpreter-only divergences; row E lost the
body on ALL FOUR surfaces, because there the compiled retraction is not gated
away by B-2026-08-31-38's `optres_bindings_owned` -- that flag is TRUE on the
`let ... else` leg, by design, since its binding escapes and owns. So the same
over-approximation showed up as a divergence on two spellings and as an
agreed-and-wrong answer on the third.

MEASURED, pre-fix -> post-fix, all four surfaces (`--interp`, `karac run`,
`karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build`); one `R` is constructed per row,
so one body is due:

    A  if let Some(H { n, .. }) = a       interp A4        -> A4 dR47
                                          compiled A4 dR47 -> unchanged
    B  match b { Some(H { n, .. }) => .. } interp B4       -> B4 dR47
                                          compiled B4 dR47 -> unchanged
    E  let Some(H { n, .. }) = e else { } ALL FOUR E4      -> dR47 E4
    F  binds the `Drop` field (control)   F47 dR47         -> unchanged
    W  bare whole payload (control)       W47 dR47         -> unchanged
    C  no envelope (control)              C4 dR47          -> unchanged
    G  binds nothing (control)            G dR47           -> unchanged

E's body lands BEFORE the `println` on every surface, which is where it belongs:
nothing bound out of the scrutinee survives the destructure, so the source dies
there.

ALL THREE "NOT MEASURED" SHAPES MEASURED, and all three were affected and are
fixed: the `Result` envelope (`Ok(H { n, .. })`), an enum STRUCT-VARIANT payload
(`Some(V.A { n, .. })` -- which is why the declaration lookup resolves a
two-segment path), and a second non-`Drop` field bound alongside the first
(`Some(H3 { n, m, .. })`). A fourth, mixed shape was added and is also correct:
binding the `Drop` field AND a scalar (`Some(H3 { r, n, .. })`) still hands over
and still runs exactly one body.

THE `while let` SPELLING WAS AFFECTED TOO and closes here with the rest. It was
pinned as a control by B-2026-09-02-7's fixture one commit earlier, on the
expectation that the two spellings would close together; they did.

BODIES ONLY, now measured rather than assumed -- the row asked for exactly this.
`valgrind --leak-check=full` at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` on row E's program: 13
allocs / 13 frees PRE-fix, 14/14 post (the extra pair is the restored body's own
f-string), 0 errors both times. The buffer was never stranded; only the
user-visible body was lost. Pinned as
`asan_optres_partial_destructure_body_reads_live_memory`, whose bodies read
`self.s.len()` through the payload's heap buffer in a reallocating loop -- the
shape that would turn a restored body into a use-after-free if the payload it
reads had already been reclaimed.

TESTS. `e2e_an_optres_partial_destructure_keeps_the_payload_body`
(tests/codegen.rs) is the twelve-row matrix above, one expectation column for
both backends since they now agree everywhere.
`test_optres_partial_destructure_keeps_the_payload_drop_body`
(tests/interpreter.rs) carries the same shapes on the DEFAULT leg, because half
the fix is the interpreter's and the E2E matrix is gated on `--features llvm`.
The three rows that PINNED this divergence -- two in
`e2e_a_let_family_destructure_runs_the_payload_drop_body_once` and one in
`e2e_while_let_binding_runs_the_payload_drop_body_once_per_pass` -- are updated
to agreement in the same commit, which is what those pins were for.

title: OVER-ALIGNED ALLOCATION IS UNSUPPORTED ON WINDOWS -- `karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic` aborts there rather than honoring an alignment above `malloc`'s 16-byte guarantee, because the MSVC CRT has no `free`-compatible aligned allocator and every release path assumes plain `free`.
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-09-01-45 so the Windows link fix is not mistaken for
Windows over-alignment SUPPORT. 6c2a4fb restored the link by refusing on
Windows; this row is the refusal.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE PORT. The aligned path works on POSIX because
`posix_memalign` memory is released with plain `free` (POSIX.1-2008; C11
7.22.3.1 says the same for `aligned_alloc`). That single property is what lets
FOUR release paths stay untouched: `karac_free_buf`, the buffer-parking cache
in the same file, the internal `free` in `karac_realloc_aligned_or_panic`, and
codegen's own emitted `free` calls (LLVM `free` declarations are added in at
least json.rs, vec_method.rs, assoc_call.rs, task_group.rs, once.rs and
coro.rs). No Windows allocator has the property: `_aligned_malloc` requires
`_aligned_free` and is undefined under plain `free`; C11 `aligned_alloc` is
deliberately unimplemented in the MSVC CRT for exactly that incompatibility.

THREE DESIGNS WERE CONSIDERED AND TWO ARE TRAPS.

(a) Fall back to the ordinary allocator. REJECTED, and it is the one that
looks cheapest. It returns a merely 16-aligned buffer, codegen emits element
accesses at the type's natural alignment, x86-64 selects `vmovaps`, and it
faults -- intermittently, according to heap history. That IS B-2026-08-31-24,
reintroduced with the same signature that made it hard to see the first time.

(b) Over-allocate and store the offset, as B-2026-09-01-45's own detail
suggests. This does NOT keep `free` correct, which was the stated reason for
preferring it: `free` requires the exact pointer the allocator returned, so an
interior pointer is undefined no matter what precedes it. Recovering the base
needs the free site to KNOW the buffer is padded, and a self-describing magic
header read at `ptr[-1]` is a heuristic in a deallocator -- not acceptable.
Making every buffer padded uniformly would corrupt the heap at codegen's
direct `free` sites listed above.

(c) Pair an aligned-aware free with the aligned alloc. The real fix, and
symmetric with what already exists: codegen calls `karac_alloc_aligned_or_panic`
exactly where `over_alignment_for_elem` answers `Some(a)`, and it knows the
same answer at the buffer's free sites (it already computes `cap * elem_size`
there for `karac_free_buf`'s `bytes_hint`). So a `karac_free_buf_aligned`
routed to `_aligned_free` on Windows costs nothing on the hot path and needs
no distinction at runtime. A Windows-only side registry of over-aligned base
pointers would also be correct but puts a lock on every free; prefer (c).

NOT REACHABLE TODAY, which is why this is low and not medium. Windows codegen
E2E is deferred (ci.yml "STAGE 4 ... deferred") and `Test (windows-latest)`
runs the non-LLVM workspace suite, so no Kara program is compiled on Windows
and nothing can request an over-aligned buffer. The abort exists to make the
gap loud the moment Windows codegen lands rather than to be hit now.

TRIGGER: Windows codegen E2E landing, or any native Windows `karac build`.
Until then the arm is unreachable and the refusal is the correct behaviour.

VERIFYING A FIX WITHOUT WINDOWS. B-2026-09-01-45's close records the method:
`rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (std is a plain download, no MSVC
toolchain), then `cargo rustc -p karac-runtime --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
--no-default-features --lib -- --emit=obj -C lto=off` emits a Windows object
without linking, and `llvm-nm` reads its undefined-symbol table. That answers
symbol-level questions locally; it does NOT answer whether `_aligned_free`
pairs correctly at runtime, which still needs a Windows runner.

title: B-2026-08-01-19's OVER-SUPPRESSION TRADE IS NOW A VISIBLE DIVERGENCE: a param view assigned into ONE field silences EVERY Drop-bearing field's body on the base, on all three compiled surfaces, while the interpreter is per-field since B-2026-08-30-54 -- a sibling that was never moved, never viewed and is read on the line before loses its body (`dR30 s dE dR8 v39` against `--interp`'s `dR30 s dR31 dE dR8 v39`). The flag is keyed by BINDING and the reason is per FIELD; only a struct with two or more Drop-bearing fields can show it
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-30-54's fix, which narrowed this and made what remains
VISIBLE as a divergence for the first time. B-2026-08-01-19 introduced the trade
and documented it in its own code comment -- "Over-suppression trade (documented
on the -19 row): the base's OTHER Drop-bearing fields' bodies go silent too" --
at a time when both backends were wrong here, so nothing observable pointed at
it.

    struct R { id: i64, tag: String }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    struct H2 { f: R, g: R }

    fn dies(b: E) -> i64 {
        let mut h: H2 = H2 { f: R { id: 30, tag: f"t30" }, g: R { id: 31, tag: f"t31" } };
        match b { E.A(r) => { h.f = r; } E.B => { } }   // <-- a view lands in `f`
        println("s");
        return h.f.id + h.g.id
    }
    fn main() { let v: i64 = dies(E.A(R { id: 8, tag: f"t8" })); println(f"v{v}") }

      --interp                      dR30 s dR31 dE dR8 v39   `g`'s body runs
      karac build / run             dR30 s dE dR8 v39        `dR31` LOST
      KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build  same as karac build

The sibling `g` was never moved, never viewed, and is still fully live -- `h.g.id`
is read on the line before. Its body is silenced only because a DIFFERENT field
of the same base received a param view.

THE SECOND SHAPE is the same loss one step later: assign the sibling a FRESH
value after the view and its body is still silenced.

    match b { E.A(r) => { h.f = r; } E.B => { } }
    h.g = R { id: 9, tag: f"t9" };

      --interp        dR30 dR31 s dR9 dE dR8 v17
      karac build     dR30 dR31 s dE dR8 v17        `dR9` LOST

Note the `dR31` in the compiled column: the DISPLACEMENT of `g`'s initializer is
correct (B-2026-08-30-54 fixed that half -- an earlier cut of its guard lost it,
which is what forced the guard to be per-field). What is missing is `g`'s body at
`h`'s death.

MECHANISM, and it is a granularity mismatch rather than a missing rule.
B-2026-08-30-54 replaced -19's all-paths retraction with a per-path
`cond_move_drop_flags` bool, but that flag is keyed by BINDING and guards the
base's whole `UserDrop{StructFieldBodies}` action, while the thing that disarms
it is one FIELD. The interpreter has no such coarseness -- it went through
`moved_out_struct_field_bodies`, a `(binding, field)` mask -- so the two backends
now disagree exactly where the granularities differ. That fix deliberately did
NOT widen its re-arm to cover this: re-arming the base while a sibling still
holds a view would resurrect the VIEW's body, trading a lost body for a doubled
one.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE: codegen already has the per-field machinery in
`struct_moved_field_bodies` + `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn_skipping`
(`disarm_struct_field_bodies_at`), which masks ONE field out of a re-emitted
walker. The missing piece is a walker whose masked field is decided at RUNTIME
rather than at emission -- a per-field flag word the walker reads, or two
emitted walkers selected by the existing per-binding flag. The first is the
honest shape; the second is cheaper and enough for one masked field.

SCOPE. Only a struct with TWO OR MORE Drop-bearing fields can show this, which
is why every shape in B-2026-08-30-54's own repro and regression test is clean:
they all use `struct H { f: R }`. Measured pre-B-2026-08-30-54 as well, where
the divergence was wider (the interpreter additionally doubled the view's own
body), so that fix strictly narrowed this rather than causing it.
fix:
Fixed in d3f7d4b, codegen only.

WHAT IT TOOK, against the row's own two candidate shapes. The row offered a
per-field flag word read by the walker ("the honest shape") or two emitted
walkers selected by the existing per-binding flag ("cheaper and enough for one
masked field"). The fix is neither exactly: ONE FLAG PER VIEWED FIELD, with the
base's death branching on those flags to a walker masked to the subset a view
actually landed in on that path.

THE CHEAP OPTION IS RULED OUT BY MEASUREMENT, not by taste, and this is the one
finding here the row did not already contain. Two fields taking views on
INDEPENDENT paths is a third shape:

    match b { E.A(r)  => { h.f = r;  } E.B => { } }
    match c { E.A(r2) => { h.g = r2; } E.B => { } }

with only the FIRST landing, measured pre-fix as `dR30 s dE dE dR18 w81`
against `--interp`'s `dR30 s dR32 dR31 dE dE dR18 w81` -- TWO bodies lost, not
one. A single bool cannot say "f holds a view AND g still owns its value",
whichever walker it selects, so the cheap option fixes the row's two shapes and
leaves this one wrong. It is pinned as its own fixture row in both twins
precisely so a future cut cannot regress to it and still pass.

The all-armed leaf calls the REGISTERED `drop_fn` verbatim rather than a
re-emitted equivalent, so the no-view path is byte-identical to before; every
other leaf ADDS its runtime subset to whatever emission-time mask that walker
already carries (`struct_moved_field_bodies`), which is what keeps it faithful
to a field masked by an earlier move-out instead of resurrecting it. Capped at
three viewed fields -- the tree has 2^n leaves -- past which it declines to the
old coarse guard, which is over-suppression rather than a double fire, so the
fallback stays on the safe side.

TWO SIMPLIFICATIONS FALL OUT, and both are the row's mechanism paragraph read
back. The re-arm loses its "only if this is the sole recorded field" condition,
which existed solely because one bool could not hold two answers. And a field
view no longer touches the base's `cond_move_drop_flags` entry at all: three
readers -- the two fire sites, `arg_producer_mints_fresh_owned_temp`, and
`disarm_flags_for_handed_over_bindings` -- take a key's mere PRESENCE there as
"this binding was handed over", and a field view never hands the base over, so
the shape comes off all three. That was a latent mis-classification the row did
not name.

`emit_cleanup_action` takes `&mut self` now, since selecting a masked walker
means emitting one; its three borrow-holding callers clone the action first
(`CleanupAction` gained `Clone`).

VERIFICATION, and the negative control is the part worth reading.

Twinned fixtures in `tests/codegen.rs` and `tests/interpreter.rs` (six rows:
the row's two shapes, the two-views-one-taken row above, the all-armed
boundary, a re-arm with a sibling still viewed, and a fresh-value-only control),
plus an ASAN case.

WITH `src/` REVERTED, THE CODEGEN AND ASAN FIXTURES FAIL AND THE INTERPRETER
TWIN PASSES. That last half is the load-bearing one: it says the interpreter
was already the oracle here -- its `(binding, field)` mask has always matched
the granularity of the reason -- so this is codegen-only by construction rather
than by my say-so. The pre-fix codegen output also lost `dR40`/`dR42`/`dR7` in
the re-arm row, more than the row predicted, because the old single-field
condition made the DISPLACEMENT decline as well.

THE ASAN ROW EXISTS BECAUSE THE ROW'S REPRO COULD NOT HAVE FOUND ITS CLASS.
Measured on a scalar-plus-short-tag payload, the entire defect is a missing line
of output and the memory side says nothing -- so a fix can look complete against
it while leaving a heap-owning sibling unbalanced. Restoring a silenced body is
also exactly the change most able to introduce a DOUBLE free, and re-arming the
wrong field would be a use-after-free on a husk. A `String` plus an 8-element
`Vec[String]`, looped three times, makes both visible; the body prints the Vec's
length from inside itself, so a body running on a moved-from object shows as a
wrong count rather than passing quietly. Clean under ASAN and under valgrind
(0 definitely lost, 0 indirectly lost).

TWO ENVIRONMENT NOTES recorded because each cost real time and neither is in
CLAUDE.md in this form.

The full runtime archive on this container was 57 MB where a correct one is
20 MB, and nothing had flagged it -- the lean archive also predated the last
`runtime/src` commit. Rebuilding lean-then-full gave 11.6 MB / 20 MB, with the
optional unicode sibling at exactly +161 KiB, which is the figure CLAUDE.md
documents and is what confirms the rebuild rather than the size alone.

And `cargo test --test interpreter` (no `--features llvm`) REPLACES
`target/debug/karac` with a non-llvm build, so a subsequent `karac build`
type-checks and silently emits nothing. That reads exactly like a run/build
divergence -- the "build" column is a shell error, not output -- and I briefly
recorded one before checking that the binary existed. The tell is
`note: karac build requires the llvm feature; falling back to type check`,
which does not appear unless you run the build directly.

VERIFIED at d3f7d4b (post-rebase, on a tree that also carries d1394db, f8e28a7
and e49ba40 -- three sibling fixes in this same Drop-ownership area, which is
why the suites were re-run after the rebase rather than before): all four
surfaces byte-identical on every discriminator (`run --interp`, `run`, `build`,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`); default suite 10259 passed / 0 failed; codegen
3549/0; memory_sanitizer 1369/0; par_codegen 276/0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
clean; `cargo clippy --all --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean on BOTH the
default and `--features llvm` legs.

title: A READ-ONLY `match v[i]` ARM STILL RUNS THE PAYLOAD'S `Drop` BODY TWICE ON ALL THREE COMPILED SURFACES -- `index got 4 dR3 dE dR3` against `--interp`'s `index got 4 dE dR3`. The arm consumes nothing, so B-2026-08-31-3's rule accepts it; the extra body is the DEFENSIVE COPY's payload, one level in from the enum wrapper B-2026-08-29-37 already withheld on the same clone. Valgrind-clean, so bodies-only
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-31-3's fix, and it is the half that fix does NOT cover.
That row rejected an arm that CONSUMES its binding out of a `v[i]` scrutinee; a
read-only arm consumes nothing, so the rule accepts it -- and the two backends
still answer differently.

    struct R { id: i64, v: Vec[i64] }
    impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dR{self.id}") } }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> E { let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(n); return E.A(R { id: n, v: v }) }

    fn main() {
        let mut v: Vec[E] = Vec.new();
        v.push(mk(3));
        println("index");
        match v[0] { E.A(r) => { println(f"got {r.id + r.v.len()}"); } E.B => { } }
        println("index end");
    }

      --interp                      index got 4      dE dR3 index end   ONE body
      karac run (JIT)               index got 4 dR3  dE dR3 index end   TWO
      karac build                   index got 4 dR3  dE dR3 index end   TWO
      KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build  index got 4 dR3  dE dR3 index end   TWO

The arm only READS `r` -- `r.id` and `r.v.len()`, both projections through the
binding -- so nothing is moved out of `v` and the element is destroyed exactly
once, at `v`'s death. One `dR3` is due. The compiled backends run an extra one
BEFORE the enum's own `dE`, which is the defensive copy's payload being
destroyed: `match v[0]` materializes a clone of the element (B-2026-06-14-12's
`heap_index` path), and that clone's payload body fires as well as the
original's.

VALGRIND-CLEAN at both opt levels, so this is a bodies-only divergence: the
clone's heap is correctly freed, and only the observable `Drop` body is doubled.
Which is the same asymmetry B-2026-08-30-18 turned on -- the memory and bodies
halves have separate owners -- and the same reason a fire-COUNT oracle is the
only thing that sees it.

WHY IT SURVIVED B-2026-08-29-37, which fixed a neighbouring shape: that row
stopped the ENUM's own `Drop` body (`dE`) from running on a defensive copy, and
the fix is verified by
`codegen::ir_defensive_scrutinee_copy_keeps_memory_cleanup_and_drops_the_user_body`
asserting `karac_drop_E` is absent from the clone's block. The PAYLOAD's body is

title: AN `Option`/`Result` SCRUTINEE WHOSE NON-MATCHING ARM CARRIES A `Drop` TYPE LOSES THAT PAYLOAD'S BODY ON ALL FOUR SURFACES -- and through `if let` as well as `while let`, so it is the OPTRES ENVELOPE rather than the loop; this is what B-2026-09-01-42 deliberately carved out, and it also refutes that row's `if let` control, which holds for a USER enum and not for `Result`
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-09-01-42 rather than folded into it, because it is a
DIFFERENT SITE. That row fixed the `while let` loop-exit miss for a user enum
by giving `drop_freshtemp_enum_scrutinee_on_miss` the enum's own `Drop` body
and its payload-bodies walk beside the memory switch it already emitted.
`Option`/`Result` are excluded there on purpose -- they keep their own payload
machinery, the same carve-out the call-argument precedent
(`call_dispatch.rs`'s `fresh_enum_temp` branch) makes -- so the fix does not
reach them and this is what is left.

MEASURED on the post-fix build, all four surfaces identical:

    struct W { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for W { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dW{self.id}") } }
    fn mkr(n: i64) -> Result[W, W] {
        if n < 1 { return Ok(W { id: n }) }
        return Err(W { id: 7 });
    }

    let mut i: i64 = 0;
    while let Ok(w) = mkr(i) { println(f"v{w.id}"); i = i + 1; }
                                        v0 dW0 after      <- `dW7` never runs

    fn mkErr() -> Result[W, W] { return Err(W { id: 7 }); }
    if let Ok(w) = mkErr() { println(f"v{w.id}") }
                                        (nothing)         <- same, through `if let`

Two `W` values are constructed in the loop shape and one body runs; one is
constructed in the `if let` shape and none runs.

THE `if let` CELL IS THE POINT, and it CORRECTS B-2026-09-01-42's own
argument. That row establishes its defect is a defect rather than a design
choice by appealing to the `if let` control: "the same non-matching temporary
through `if let E.A(r) = mkB() { .. }` prints `dE`". That is true for a USER
ENUM and false for a `Result` -- so the control does not generalize, and the
optres miss is not the `while let` leg's doing at all. Any fix here belongs on
the optres payload path, which both spellings share.

WHY IT SURVIVES EVERY GATE, inherited from its parent: all four surfaces agree
on the wrong answer, so the A/B parity rule reports green, and the missing
body is a lost SIDE EFFECT rather than a leak of memory -- the temporary's
storage is reclaimed. Only an absolute expected-output assertion catches it,
and none exists for this shape.

NOT MEASURED: the `Option` spelling with a `Drop`-carrying payload in the
`None` position is not expressible (a `None` carries nothing), so the shape
needs a `Result` or a user enum with payload in BOTH arms -- the latter is
covered and FIXED by the parent. Also unmeasured: whether `let ... else` over
the same `Result` loses it, and whether a BOXED optres payload (one whose
struct carries heap) behaves differently from the all-scalar one above.

title: A DISCARDED ENUM STATEMENT RUNS THE ENUM'S OWN `Drop` BODY BUT NOT ITS PAYLOAD'S, on all four surfaces -- `mk(1);` prints `dB` where the BOUND spelling `let x = mk(1);` of the identical value prints `dB dW7`, so the two differ only in whether the value is named
detail:
FOUND while building the drop-order ORACLE for B-2026-09-01-42. That row's fix
needed to know what transcript a loop-exit temporary owes, so a bound local
and a discarded statement of the very same value were measured side by side.
The bound local answered the question; the discarded statement turned out to
be missing a body.

MEASURED on the post-fix build, all four surfaces identical:

    struct W { id: i64 }
    impl Drop for W { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"dW{self.id}") } }
    enum Bx { Full(W), Empty(W) }
    impl Drop for Bx { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dB") } }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> Bx {
        if n < 1 { return Bx.Full(W { id: n }) }
        return Bx.Empty(W { id: 7 });
    }

    let x = mk(1);   println("mid");        dB dW7 mid      <- correct
    mk(1);                                  dB              <- `dW7` never runs

One `Bx` and one `W` are constructed in each; the enum's own body runs in both
and the payload's runs only when the value is BOUND. The two spellings differ
in nothing but whether the value gets a name, so the bound one is the oracle
and the discarded one is short a body.

IT IS THE PAYLOAD-BODIES WALK, not the own body. That is the same MEMORY /
BODIES split B-2026-09-01-42 fixed one site over, and the same one
B-2026-06-10's enum arm fixed for a call-argument temporary: for an enum,
the own-body wrapper and the payload-bodies walker are COMPLEMENTARY
registrations, and a site that registers one without the other loses exactly
this. The discard path evidently registers the wrapper (`dB` runs) and not
`emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn` / its interpreter twin
`run_enum_payload_user_drops_value`.

WHY IT SURVIVES EVERY GATE: all four surfaces agree, so the A/B parity rule is
green, and the missing body is a lost side effect rather than a leak -- the
storage is reclaimed either way. Only an absolute expected-output assertion
catches it.

WHERE TO START: the statement-discard registrar for a fresh enum temporary,
and its interpreter twin. B-2026-09-01-42's fix is the shape to copy -- it had
to emit the own-body wrapper AND the payload walker on the loop-exit edge, in
that order, because a bound local of the same value produces both.

NOT MEASURED: the `let _ = mk(1);` wildcard spelling as distinct from the bare
statement (the two have diverged before in this family); whether a
HEAP-carrying payload behaves the same as the all-scalar `W` above; and
whether the payload's own nested `Drop`-bearing fields are reached once the
walker is registered.

DEPTH NOTE (2026-09-02, a session that mapped this and did NOT land it). The
diagnosis in this row is right and INCOMPLETE in a way that matters: the fix is
not "add the payload walk at the discard sites", it is "RELAX A GATE that exists
only because codegen did not walk". Getting that backwards costs double bodies,
measured twice below.

CODEGEN. `try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp` (call_dispatch.rs) computes
`field_bodies_only = !has_user_drop`, and the enum payload walker
(`emit_enum_payload_user_drop_bodies_fn`) is reachable ONLY inside that
`field_bodies_only` arm. So an enum that declares its own `Drop` takes the
first arm, gets `bodies_fn = None`, and the tail registers
`track_user_drop_var` alone — the `karac_drop_<E>` wrapper, whose
field-cleanup half is a no-op for an enum name and therefore cannot reach a
variant payload. The wrapper and the walker are COMPLEMENTARY for an enum, the
rule the call-argument registrar in the same file already applies (its
`fresh_enum_temp` branch registers both). Registering the walker beside the
wrapper, pushed BEFORE it so the LIFO drain yields own-body-then-payload, makes
every compiled spelling match the bound-local oracle. That half was built and
measured working: `mk(1);`, `let _ = mk(1);` and the heap-carrying variants all
went to `dB dW7` on jit, build and auto-par-0.

THE INTERPRETER IS WHERE IT IS DELICATE, and the shape of the difficulty is
this: several discard sites ALREADY carry their own payload-walk companion,
each installed by a different row, and each GATED to match what codegen walked
at the time. The wildcard-`let` site's gate is `inline_ctor`
(`discard_taken_producer_runs_payload_walk`), and its comment states the reason
outright -- "compiled runs the payload body for a variant built AT the discard
but not for one that arrives from a call". That premise is exactly what the
codegen change above removes. So the interpreter change is to WIDEN those gates
to admit the call-shaped producer, NOT to add another walk beside them.

TWO DOUBLE-FIRES WERE MEASURED, both from adding rather than widening:

  * widening the shared walker `run_discarded_value_user_drops`'s own-Drop-enum
    arm --  `let (_, _) = (mk(1), 5);` went to `dB dW7 dW7`, because
    `run_wildcard_destructure_leaf_user_drops` calls that walker and then adds
    the payload walk itself (B-2026-08-28-40, whose comment gives precisely
    this hazard for the walker's ~31 callers).
  * adding a second walk at the wildcard-`let` site -- `let _ = Bx.Empty(W { id: 7 });`
    went to `dB dW7 dW7`, stacking on the `inline_ctor`-gated companion that
    site has carried since B-2026-08-28-39.

SITES THAT NEED THE WIDENING, from reading the dispatch: the wildcard-`let`
discard (the `inline_ctor` gate above) and the bare-statement discard's
free-function-call arm (eval_stmt.rs, the `Identifier` callee leg -- its
siblings, the `Path` ctor and bare-unqualified arms, already walk). NOT the
shared walker, and NOT the wildcard-destructure leaf.

ONE THING UNEXPLAINED, and it should be settled first: an edit to that
`Identifier`-callee enum arm had NO observable effect on `mk(1);`, so that
spelling appears not to reach the arm it looks like it should. Instrument the
dispatch before editing it -- that is the next step, not another patch.

THE WILDCARD SPELLING IS ALREADY ANSWERED (this row listed it as NOT
MEASURED): `let _ = mk(1);` behaves exactly like the bare statement, `dB` where
the bound local gives `dB dW7`, on all four surfaces. A HEAP-carrying payload
behaves the same as the all-scalar one. Two controls hold and should be kept in
any fixture: an enum with NO own `Drop` but a Drop-bearing payload is correct
(payload only), and an own-`Drop` enum with a payload that has no `Drop` is
correct (own body only).

NOTHING WAS LANDED. The codegen half alone cannot be: it moves the compiled
side ahead of the interpreter on the bare statement, converting an
agreed-and-wrong shape into a divergence. The two must land together.
